# Matthew

## 1:1 Introduction: On the Interpretation of Holy Scripture
4. For God has not only entrusted to us the most holy deposit of His Word, but has also instituted an Ecclesiastical Ministry among us, whose chief duty it is to interpret the Scriptures: This is the Ministry of the Spirit, 2. Cor. 3. v. 8. through which He desires to lead us into all truth, Iohan. 16. v. 13. Therefore we must not quench the Spirit, 1. Thess. 5. v. 19.

5. Thus Christ, conversing in the form of a traveler with those going to Emmaus, beginning from Moses and all the Prophets, He interpreted to them in all the scriptures the things concerning Himself Luc. 24. v. 27. The same Sitting at the right hand of the Father, not only gave of old Prophets, and Apostles, and Evangelists, but also today gives Pastors and Teachers Eph. 4. vers. 11. For the perfecting of the Saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ, v. 12.

6. Thus the History Matth. 11. & Luc. 7. concerning the sending of the disciples of John to Christ shows that, in difficult questions concerning religion, judgment is not to be taken from the opinions of men, but the mouth of Him of whom the Father said must be consulted, Hear Him, Deut. 18. vers. 18. He in turn sends us to the Scriptures Ioh. 5. vers. 39. and expresses His answer to the disciples of John with the words of Scripture in that same place. Nor, however, is the Ministry to be despised for that reason as idle and useless, but Christ, having set forth the sayings of the Prophets, sends the messengers back to John, so that they might use his labor in investigating the explanation of the meanings of Scripture.

7. But also these Church interpreters, whatever degree of dignity they may truly hold , ought not to bring in private senses of Scripture, but just as the sacred writings were written by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, so too must they be expounded according to his dictate; whence we pronounce the Holy Spirit to be the supreme and authentic Interpreter of Scripture.

8. This is gathered evidently from the passage of the Apostle 2. Pet. 1. vers. 20. πᾶσα προφητεία ἰδαφῆς, ἰδίας ἐπιλέσεως οὐ γίνεται, why? verse 21, because holy men of God spoke long ago not by their own and private will, but by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. The same one, therefore, who is the author of Scripture, he is also its supreme and authentic Interpreter. He who makes the law is the best and supreme interpreter of the law.

9. But about this it is asked, what is ἰδία ἐπίλυσις?, from where should the dictate of the Holy Spirit be sought in interpreting the Scriptures? From where can it be recognized whether those Church interpreters rightly attain the mind of the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scriptures?

10. The Papists determine that this must be attributed to the Church , namely that in her and through her we are taught clearly and infallibly which is the true and genuine meaning of the sacred letters: that Scripture in itself and by itself is a dead letter, which can be explained in various ways and bent like wax to any shape, but that the Holy Spirit teaches us through the Church which is the true and authentic interpretation of Scripture.

11. And because the hinge of the matter turns on this, therefore, that we may more fully perceive their opinion , we shall relate what Nicholas of Cusa the Cardinal disputes concerning this matter in his Letters against the Bohemians; for from those we shall be able to understand what they mean by the honorable name of Church, how great authority they attribute to it in interpreting the Scriptures, finally what kind of thing they determine the infallible interpretation of the Holy Scriptures to be.

12. Thus therefore Cusanus: Some say that obedience must be rendered first to the precept of Christ , then to the Church, and if the Church should command something other than Christ, obedience must be given not to the Church but to Christ: (he then adds ἐπίκρισιν) Certainly here is the beginning of all presumptions, when particular individuals judge their own sense in divine precepts to be more conformable to the divine will than that of the universal Church. But he remains in the Church who does not presumptuously raise his own sense above the dictate of the greater part of the Priests, to whom the word was entrusted, and who exercise the embassy of Christ: for in obeying that judgment which he sees the sounder part of the Church affirm, the Christian incurs no danger: The truth adheres to the chair, wherefore the members united to the chair and joined to the Pontiff make up the Church.

13. And afterwards. We see that various talents of men expound various senses in the understanding of the Scriptures, and that there exists a varied opinion concerning the authority of the Scriptures, and whether it would be possible for either an insuperable doubt about their authority or their understanding to suspend the minds of men—where will there be a sure refuge for those on pilgrimage? certainly in nothing else than in the use and approval of the militant Church, whether this concern the Scripture and its authority and understanding, or outside Scripture in custom received through the Church: for in these things is the firmness , as solid rock and pillar of truth—not so that by the authority of the Scriptures one might proceed toward the Church, and, if she does not accord with the Scripture, according to the understanding of the ancients or his own, be able scorn her with impunity in the practice of works and cling instead to the Scripture. This truly is the judgment of all who understand soundly, who found the authority or understanding of the Scriptures (as Augustine says of the Gospels) upon the approval of the Church, which receives the one and rejects the other, and do not conversely place the foundation of the Church in the authority of the Scriptures.

14. From this foundation [the author] responds to the argument of the Bohemians. You will perhaps say, the Church of today does not walk in the rite of communion as it did before these times, when most holy men maintained that the Sacrament of both kinds was necessary by the force of Christ’s precept, both in word and in deed. Could the Church have erred then? Certainly not. But if not, how is that not true today which was then affirmed by the opinion of all, when this Church is none other than that one? Certainly, let this not move you, that in different times one rite of Sacrifices and also of Sacraments after another is found while the truth remains, or that the Scriptures are adapted to the time and variously understood, so that at one time they were expounded according to the current Universal rite, and with the rite changed, the opinion was changed again, etc. Wherefore, even if today the interpretation of the same Evangelical precept by the Church is different than it once was, nevertheless this sense now current in use for the governance of the Church, as being congruent to the time and a way of salvation, ought to be accepted.

15. What kind of Church he understands by this, he explains afterwards. Wherefore the entire Catholic Church gathered together to Peter's chair will never depart from Christ, who is truth , since He promised that He would always remain with her. Finally he concludes. From what has been set forth above it is established that the entire Catholic Church cannot be bound to the letter of the Scriptures, though it can be bound to the spirit: for when the letter does not serve edification and the spirit, it receives that which more serves the spirit. Wherefore neither is it any wonder if at one time the practice of the Church interprets Scripture in one way, and at another time in another way: for understanding runs along with practice: for the understanding that concurs with practice is the life-giving Spirit. Therefore just as the Church receives Scripture, so also it interprets it: therefore the Scriptures follow the Church, which is prior, and on account of which there are the Scriptures, and not vice versa.

Thus far Cusanus. Briefly Hosius the Cardinal sets forth all these things concerning the express word of God. If anyone possesses the interpretation of the Roman Church, even if he neither knows nor understands whether and how it agrees with the words of Scripture, nevertheless he possesses the very word of God itself.

16. From these things it can be evident, what the Fathers of the Council of Trent mean, when in session 4., decree 2., they seriously prohibit lest anyone dare to interpret Sacred Scripture against that sense which mother the Church held and holds—whose office it is to judge about the true sense and interpretation of the holy Scriptures—or against the unanimous consent of the Fathers.

17. Let us see, how Bellarmine explains the mind of the Council . It is agreed between us and our adversaries, he says in book 3. de verbo Dei chapter 3., that the Scriptures ought to be understood by that Spirit by which they were made, i.e. the Holy Spirit. Therefore the whole question lies in this, where that Spirit is found. We (the Papists) think that although this Spirit is often granted to many private persons, yet it is certainly found in the Church, that is, in a Council of Bishops confirmed by the supreme Pastor of the whole Church, or in the supreme Pastor together with a Council of other Pastors: whence he concludes that the judge of the true sense of Scripture is the Church, that is, the Pope together with a Council.

18. We cannot yet dismiss Bellarmine. Since he joins the Council to the Pope together with , we ask whether the Holy Ghost then speaks through the Pope alone immediately, when along with the Council and in the Council he defines something with other Pastors, or indeed also then, when alone outside a Council he publishes his own opinion? Secondly we ask, whether greater authority in interpreting the Scriptures belongs to the Council or to the Pope: for it is well known that the Pope does not always agree with the Councils.

19. To the former question Bellarmine answers, Book 4 on the Roman Pontiff chapter 2: The very infallibility is not in the assembly of counselors nor in a Council of Bishops, but in the Pope alone. To the latter he answers, Book 2 on Councils, chapter 13: Catholics do not yet agree among themselves about this matter. Chapter 14 he sets forth three opinions of doctors (Popish ones): Some assert that a Council is above the Pope; some hold that indeed the Pope is above a Council, nor can he be judged by a Council against his will, but he can subject himself to a Council, and allow his cause to be judged by a Council, and if he has done so, then he must acquiesce in the Council's decision. Others however assert that the Pope is so far above a Council that he cannot even subject himself to its coercive judgment, which opinion he says is the common one, and follows the same.

20. From all these things we gather that the Papists establish that the true interpretation of Scripture is to be sought from the treasure-chest of the Popish breast alone; for at last by those long windings of disputations about the authority of the Church they lead us to this, which the more sensible and honest men among themselves will not deny , whence writes. Bellarmine, Book 4 on the Pontiff, chapter 2: All Catholics agree in this, that the Pope alone, or with his particular Council, determining something in a doubtful matter, whether he can err or not, is to be heard obediently by all the faithful.

21. But there are far more errors of this opinion.⟧ It is Πρῶτον Ψεῦδος of the whole structure, that they separate the sense of the Holy Spirit from the words of Scripture, which nevertheless ought not to be separated and torn apart, but joined together most tightly. The Holy Spirit speaks to us in the Scriptures and through the Scriptures; therefore in those very words of Scripture sounds the voice and meaning of the Holy Spirit, not to be brought into Scripture from elsewhere, but to be drawn from it and heard. To this belong all those declarations in which it is said that the mouth of the Lord spoke, and it is asserted that holy men of God spoke when moved by the Holy Spirit accordingly Scripture is θεόπνευςος: nay rather, the whole of Christianity rests upon this foundation, that the Holy Spirit marked down through the Prophets and Apostles those things which we read in the Scriptures.

22. Undoubtedly, the Papists propose to us such an Idea of Scripture, that it is as it were a certain skeleton and a mute and dead statue, which must first be animated by the Spirit in the Church and through the Church, that is, through the speaking Pontiff. But the word of God is living and effective Hebr. 4. v. 12. And let anyone consider how far this opinion of the Papists is from Schwenckfeldianism, which likewise says that the letter of Scripture is to be neglected as dead, and that the internal Spirit is to be followed.

23. The words of Scripture are the words of the Holy Spirit,⟧ therefore they set forth his mind to us. We must always come to the reading of the Scriptures with this disposition, as if we were hearing the Holy Spirit speaking in them and through them. Just as the Pope speaks to his people in the Decretals, so the Holy Spirit speaks to us in the oracles of Scripture. If anyone wishes to separate the sense of the Holy Spirit from the words of Scripture, he will also have to separate the Pope's sense from the words of the Decretals, and thus today no one would be able to know what the ancient Popes meant. Nay rather, the present-day Pope cannot express his own view otherwise than through words; therefore if anyone should wish to make the exception that these are indeed the Pope's words, but that inquiry must still be made about the sense of the words, and that the same must be sought from elsewhere, he will rightly be laughed at, because words are signs of thoughts of the mind. Therefore just as absurd are the Papists, when they disconnect and separate the words of Scripture and the meaning of the Holy Spirit, for from those words of Scripture the sense of the Holy Spirit must be drawn, not imported into it from elsewhere.

24. Let us clarify the matter with an example. When Bellarmine and other Papal writers attempt to show that we have made a secession from the doctrine of the Fathers, they are always accustomed to reiterate: Thus Jerome established, thus Augustine thinks, thus Ambrose speaks, etc. I ask, therefore, whence do they know that this was the opinion of Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, etc.? Certainly from their own words, for they have nothing else to answer. Likewise, we also say: Thus the Holy Spirit established, thus He thinks, thus He speaks. If they ask whence we know that this is the mind of the Holy Spirit—as if they wish to urge upon us that the opinion of the Holy Spirit must be drawn from the voice of the Church, the Church, the Church—what else can we answer than that the mind of the Holy Spirit must be learned from the words of Scripture.

25. Since therefore it is first granted that Scripture is θεόπνευς ον,, that the Prophets and Apostles were scribes of the Holy Spirit (which no Christian, as such, can deny ), it must straightway also be granted that the mind of the Holy Spirit is to be learned from that book and those very words, nor is there need that we at last draw from the breast of the Roman Pontiff what the mind and judgment of the Holy Spirit is: for could the artificer of mind and tongue not speak eloquently, says Lactantius, Divine Institutes 6, chapter 21? Nay rather, by supreme providence he willed that things divine lack coloring, so that all might understand what he himself was speaking to all.

26. That very thing which the Prophets and Apostles set before their hearers, the same, I say, and nothing else did they by will reduce into the Scriptures of God, Iren. lib. 3. adversus haer. c. 1. Therefore just as the will of God, which is the mind and judgment of the Holy Spirit, could be perceived by the hearers of the Prophets and Apostles from those men's own words, so also we readers of the Prophetic and Apostolic writings can perceive from those men's books what the will of God is, what the mind and judgment of the Holy Spirit is. Preaching and external writing are accidents, which do not change the essence of the thing, and as speech is ἀπεικόνισμα of the senses of the mind, so writing is ἀπεικόνισμα of words uttered by mouth, concerning which matter the Philosopher discourses περὶ ἑρμην. chapter 1. ἔςι μεν οὖν τὰ ἐν τῇ τ ωνῇ τῶν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ παθημάτων σύμβομα, και γραφόμένα των έν τη θωνῇ.

27. What of this, that the Pope, when about to publish his judgment, does not always use those Legates of his at his side who might expound it with living voice, but often sends only Diplomas, and, as they say in his Court, Briefs: he who hears these says that he hears the Pope's judgment: so the Holy Spirit not only formerly sent Prophets and Apostles, who expounded his mind with living voice, but even today hands over to the Church the Prophetic and Apostolic Writings, in which the Prophets and Apostles speak to us, and through them the Holy Spirit; therefore let him who reads or hears these judge that he knows the judgment of the Holy Spirit.

28. Let us approach more closely. The Papist says that one must learn who the true sense of Scripture is from the Church alone, that is, from the Pontiff. I ask, therefore, whence they prove this privilege of the Pontiff: they bring forward various texts of Scripture from the Old and New Testaments, particularly that saying of Christ, I will give to thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven, &c. Upon this rock I will build my Church: I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not, &c. (as may be seen in Bellarmine, *On the Word of God*, book 3, ch. 4 & 5), which are expounded by them in this sense: that the promise of an infallible authority for interpreting the Scriptures was given to the Roman chair and to the Pontiff sitting upon it, and that in them he will always attain the genuine meaning of the Holy Spirit. What if I doubt concerning that interpretation of the sayings of Scripture, whether they are to be accepted in this sense? Whither will the Papist lead me? Certainly to the cabinet of the Papal breast. A truly excellent confirmation! This privilege of not erring belongs to the Pope because he interprets the places of Scripture in such a way as to show that it belongs to him, and those places of Scripture are to be understood in that way because the Pope willed them to be so understood.

29. But you see that the Father whom he interprets the Scriptures thus: this explanation is true and genuine because the Roman Pope proposed it! And why do the Jesuits today wish to seem to dispute laboriously from the Scriptures, consulting the sources, comparing passages &c.? The whole matter could be finished briefly, if they were to say: these articles are to be believed, and the Scripture is to be expounded in this way, because the Pope has so defined. Surely the Pope is a procrastinator in his office; long ago he ought entirely to have made some authoritative interpretation of Scripture, whether of Lyra or of another ; otherwise how will it be able to be known which is properly the Interpretation of the Roman Pontiff?

30. The Roman Pontiff certainly attributes to himself, and allows to be attributed to him, a great privilege in interpreting the Scriptures; but let him show us the charters and seals of that privilege—I mean the divine oracles. Perhaps they might be found if the outer side of the parchment on which the Donation of Constantine is written were inspected more accurately, as was once advised to the Venetians in a similar case, as witnessed by Camerarius, part 1, historical meditations, chapter 61.

31. The passages which the Jesuits today produce from Scripture to confirm that privilege are sought far too widely, and always deal either with the High Priest of the Old Testament, or with the Church in general, or with Peter; but no testimony can be brought forward in which mention is expressly made of the Pope. But in the wording of privileges mention must clearly and explicitly be made of him to whom such things are granted, for so do the jurists teach. The special treatment of those passages which the Jesuits propose in this matter belongs to the article of faith of Rome concerning the Pope. τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ λαμβάνουσι.

32. Let us see further how he has used this great privilege (if any was ever granted to them), and how skillfully he has interpreted the Scriptures: for the jurists teach that benefits conferred by privilege are lost through abuse. The theme is sufficiently worn out in the Decrees of the Popes: Bishops and Priests are not to be accused or condemned by a Prince and secular judge. Clement proves this in his first Letter from the fact that Paul says, It should be a very small thing for us to be judged by such men or on a human day. Anacletus in Letters 1, 2, 3 proves it from the fact that Christ says, He who touches you touches the pupil of my eye: because Peter writes, God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble: because John warns, that we believe not every spirit: because Paul declares, each one will give account for himself: because the Lord did not cast the buying and selling Priests out of the temple by another, but with a whip himself: because it is said by the Royal Psalmist, God stands in the assembly of gods, and said, You are gods and sons of the Most High all of you: because Paul asks, Who are you, who judges another man's servant? Ielesphorus thence proves it, because the Lord denies that a disciple is above his Master.

33. Thus Siricius, Letter 4, and Innocent, Letter 3, wish to prove that the marriages of Priests are unlawful, because it has been written: Be ye holy, since I also am holy: Those who are in the flesh cannot please God: If a priest should be defiled by carnal concupiscence, with what shame will he sacrifice, or with what conscience, or indeed on what merit does he believe himself heard, when it is written, To the pure all things are pure, but to those who are defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure? See chapter Decernimus, distinction 28, chapter Proposuisti, distinction 82, chapter Tenere, distinction 31, etc., and volume 1 of the Councils, fol. 422.

34. That the Roman Church obtained from the Lord the primacy and eminence of power over all Churches and over the flock of the entire Christian people, Anacletus proves from this, because Christ said to Peter, Thou art Peter, and upon this rock, that is, the Roman see, I will build the universal Church: because Paul says, that without ceasing he makes mention of the Roman Church in his prayers: because there was granted to Peter by the Lord that he should take precedence before the other Apostles, and hold the position of Cephas, that is, head and beginning of the apostolate.

35. Thus chapter Solitae, Extra, concerning greater matters and obedience (which the Gloss says is much alleged) Innocent wishes to prove that Imperial authority must obey the Priesthood, because it was said to the Priest, Behold, I have set thee over nations and kingdoms, to root up and

scatter, to build and to plant: Likewise, because God made two great lights in the firmament of heaven, that is, instituted two dignities in the Church, which are pontifical authority and royal power: but as great as is the difference between the Sun and the Moon, so great is the difference between Pontiffs and Kings.

36. So in that famous chapter (as the Interpreters call it) 'One holy' likewise. Boniface VIII interprets the Scriptures thus. When the Apostles were saying, Behold, here are two swords, namely in the Church, the Lord did not answer, it is too much, but enough. Therefore there are two swords in the Church, namely the spiritual and the temporal. Likewise, Put your sword back, says the Lord to Peter, into its sheath. Therefore the temporal sword is in Peter's power.

Very many such things can be gathered from the Decretals of the Popes, in which they do not interpret the Scriptures, but plunder them; they do not expound them, but by means of them impose upon men, and so by that very fact show themselves to have most wickedly abused their privilege of interpreting authoritatively, and thereby through that abuse to have lost it, even supposing any such thing had been granted at all.

37. But what kind of ἀκυρολογία and monstrous license is this, that under the name of the Church they understand only the Pope! Is one man the Church? What proof of this matter will they be able to bring forward from the Scriptures? Let him be, by hypothesis, the Vicar of Christ, let him be the Successor of Peter, let him be the head of the Church; nevertheless he is not on that account alone to be understood by the name of the Church. And how pernicious are those frauds, to produce that Roman Ape dressed up in the honorable mantle of the Church, so that everything said in the Scriptures about the Church should be referred either to the Pope alone, or certainly κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν to himself alone! Why do they use those circumlocutions, so as to say 'the Church,' and yet understand only the Pope?

38. Nay indeed, if the Pope is the supreme and authentic Interpreter of the Scriptures, it will follow that the immediate and infallible assistance of the Holy Spirit must be assigned to him himself, and thus consequently his Decrees and interpretations will have to be equated with the Prophetic and Apostolic writings: for whatever is brought forth from the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit corresponds to the prophetic and apostolic utterances.

39. Why then should we not offer to the Pope such letters along with those forged ones of the envoys of Gabriel, Patriarch of Alexandria, in which this title is prefixed: Father of fathers, Prince of patriarchs, Thirteenth Apostle, Fifth Evangelist, Successor of St. Peter? Suscitab. part, 1. chap. 16. from Dousa. Why should we not acclaim him ourselves, as we read about Bernard today 2. de consid. ad Eug. col. 1023.: You are the prince of bishops, you the heir of the Apostles, you Abel in primacy, Noah in governance, Abraham in patriarchy, Melchizedech in order, Aaron in dignity, Moses in authority, Samuel in judgment, Peter in power, Christ in anointing. Why should we not conclude with Gratian, c. In Canonicis. dist. 19., that the decretal epistles of the Popes ought to be numbered among the canonical Scriptures , which opinion Gratian assigns to Augustine under the charge of forgery, as though he taught any such thing in 2. de doctr. Christc. 8., when it never entered Augustine's mind. Bellarmine, 2. de Conc. chap. 12., acknowledges Gratian's offense, yet meanwhile softens it so far as to say that he was deceived by a corrupted copy of Augustine. He finally grants that the decretals of the Popes can in their own manner be and be called sacred and canonical writings. Why should we not address the Pope with Angelo Poliziano, from the oration pro Senem: We congratulate you, Most Blessed Father, because having been carried aloft to the very pinnacle of human affairs, nay plainly elevated to divinity itself, you behold all things except God as lessers, inferiors beneath you, just as even the kings themselves likewise and

Princes shall adore thy footsteps submissively, and shall not disdain to lick the dust of thy feet, but shall desire it as a most excellent gift. 40.

40. It is customary for Pontifical writers to transfer to the Roman Pontiff those things which Scripture pronounces concerning the High Priest of the O. T. I no longer dispute by what right, since we know that in the O. T. a certain High Priest was constituted by God himself, to be a type of Christ, as the Epistle to the Hebrews teaches, but in the N. T. we acknowledge no other High Priest and ΑςΧιεςία besides Christ: about this matter, as I said, I no longer dispute, but this I ask, Whether authentic and absolute authority of judging and interpreting the Scriptures was given to that O. T. Priest? By no means truly, because the rule of judgment is constituted the divine law, Deut. 17. v. 11. nor is such authority claimed for him alone, but the Judge is called into partnership with him, v. 12. Therefore as the civil Judge ought not to depart from the norm of the forensic laws in rendering judgment in civil causes, so also the Priest ought not to go away from the norm of the moral and ceremonial laws in rendering judgment in ecclesiastical matters. Cajetan the Cardinal, at this place, as Interpreter, changed this passage, for in the Hebrew it is read 'or to the judge,' where the prudent reader should note that the definition of an ambiguous cause is described not by one, but by many Priests and the judge: to command the execution is attributed either to the Pontiff or to the Judge &c. Jerome, as Oleaster says, on this passage: 'It is not free for the Judges to judge as they will, but according to the laws: and they are to be obeyed when they have judged according to them.'

41. But where do we read, that the doctrine which the Prophets and Apostles preached, was examined by the pious hearers themselves according to the sentence of the supreme Sacordo-is, or that its examination was commanded? Esai-s chapter 56. v. 10. complains: His watchmen blind-

all, they have not known, all of them. Jeremiah cries out chapter 6. v. 13. From the Prophet even to the Priest all deal falsely. Ezekiel laments chapter 7. v. 26. The law shall perish from the Priest, and Counsel from the Elders. The book of the divine law was sometimes held in such price, that long lost it was at length found again under Josiah. 2. Reg. 23. v. 2. Malachi c. 2. v. 7. joins right and deed. The lips of the Priest keep knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth (this of right) but v. 8. But ye have departed from the way, ye have been a stumblingblock to many in the law, ye have corrupted the covenant of Levi, saith Jehovah of hosts- (this of deed) Eminent v. interpreters of prophetic preaching these would have been, if their people had carried their sentence through!

42. So in the time of Christ and of the Apostles the supreme priests and the whole Senate of the Porcine Ecclesiastical Elders condemned the doctrine of Christ and of the Apostles, as is evident from the records of the Gospel History; what sort of interpreters of Apostolic doctrine, then, would they have been, if the people had consulted them? Since, therefore, the Prophets and Apostles afterward reduced to the Scriptures the same things which they preached, from this we conclude: if to the supreme Pontiff of the Old Testament, raised by God himself to that degree of sublimity, there did not belong a certain authentic and absolute power of judging concerning the true sense of the Prophetic and Apostolic preaching, much less will such a power belong to the Roman Pope, by which he could render an absolutely authentic and simply infallible judgment concerning the true sense of the doctrine comprehended in the Prophetic and Apostolic Writings.

43. The Prophets appealed to the law and to the testimony Is. 8. v. 20. Christ invited his hearers to search the Scriptures Ioh. 5. v. 39. the Apostles urged that Moses and the Prophets be consulted, outside of whom they protested that they said nothing, Act. 26. v. 12. and the Bereans are commended by the Holy Spirit because they daily searched the Scriptures, inquiring whether the preaching of Paul and Silas agreed with them, Acts 17. v. 11.

44. Christ indeed says Matt. 23. v. 3. that all things must be kept and done which the Scribes and Pharisees sitting on Moses' seat shall say: but lest anyone should think that some absolute privilege of judging and interpreting the Scriptures is granted to them, therefore elsewhere Matt. 5. 6. 7. and even in this very 23rd chapter he sharply rebukes their doctrines, by which they shut up before men the doors of the kingdom of heaven, with great θαααησία, and in ch. 16. v. 6. he warns them to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees, that is, of their perverse doctrine, as is plainly expounded in v. 12. Therefore those words, The Scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses' seat; whatsoever they shall say unto you, keep and do, are to be taken reduplicatively, namely insofar as they sit on Moses' seat, that is, insofar as they teach those things which agree with the doctrine of Moses. But if they teach certain things from the chair of pestilence, and corrupt the purity of Mosaic doctrine with the leaven of private opinions , then to that extent they are not to be heard. Biel, 4. sent. dist. 1. q. 4. art. 3.: It is not permitted to despise the counsel of a Prelate when it is true, unless he has spoken against the divine law, because thus in commanding he does not sit upon Moses' seat, for such things proceed not from the chair, that is, from the doctrine of Moses, but from the chair of pestilence. Wesselus, who lived about the year 1455 : The precepts of Prelates must be observed so long as, sitting in Moses' seat, they teach according to Moses; and if they determine anything contrary to or beyond it, we are not bound, for we are servants of God, not of the Pope.

45. Shall we reduce to a summary what we establish concerning the true Interpretation of Scripture in the opinion of the Pontificers? 1. They separate the Holy Spirit's meaning from the words of Scripture, as though the Holy Spirit's meaning were to be sought from somewhere else than from the words of Scripture . 2. They make Scripture out to be a dead letter, needing to be animated by the spirit of the Church. 3. They establish a real distinction between that which the Prophets and Apostles preached and that which they afterwards reduced into the Scriptures, as though their preaching could be understood without their writings being interpreted by something drawn from elsewhere . 4. By the name of the Church they understand one Pontiff. 5. They attribute that authentic privilege of interpretation to the Pontiff άτερ-ραφης. 6. They are compelled to accept the most absurd interpretations and accommodations of Scripture, which we read in the Decrees of the Pontiffs. 7. They grant to their Pontiff a prerogative owed only to the Prophets and Apostles. 8. They grant to him something of such a kind that it did not belong even to the High Priest of the Old Testament, appointed by God Himself. 9. Finally, they are compelled to make the last resolution of their faith into the treasure-chest of the Papal breast: but how impure that sometimes is, the histories bear witness, in which the sayings and doings of the Pontiffs are recorded. Matth. 12. vers. 33. Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.

46. From what source then, you ask, can we be certain about the true Interpretation of Scripture? Is a private Spirit to be followed in interpreting the Scriptures? Or will you not be forced to confess that Scripture is obscure in some places and needs Interpretation? From where is that to be drawn? Is it not better to claim this authority of interpreting for the Church alone than to concede license to any private person whatever to follow his own spirit? Was it not said most truly by Jerome on Galatians 1, let us not think that the Gospel lies in the words of the Scriptures, but in the sense; not on the surface, but in the marrow; not in the leaves of words, but in the root of reason? From where therefore is that sense to be drawn? Scripture cannot say what its true sense is, says Bellarmine, Book 3 de verbo Dei chapter 9. Scripture cannot interpret itself, all heretics appeal to Scriptures, all boast of the Spirit: These and similar things the Papists repeat speciously and pompously, to whom we respond in this manner.

47. All knowledge operates between the thing to be known and the understanding of the knower, because intellection is the reception of a species, abstracted from the knowing object, into the intellect, upon which follows the action of the agent intellect, as Scaliger disputes on this matter in his Exercitations 307, section 21. Therefore there is required between the knowing intellect and the thing to be known an adequacy, just as in vision, which is as it were the shadow of intellection and ω-ά-μγμα.

48. Because therefore the mysteries of faith set forth in the Scriptures are divine, having proceeded from God's immediate revelation, our understandings, wretchedly corrupted by sin, exceed their sphere, so to speak; for the natural man perceiveth not the things of the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness unto him, neither can he know them, 1. Cor. 2. v. 14. hence besides the native powers and primeval resources, so to speak, of our understanding, there is required an irradiation of divine light; otherwise the mysteries set forth in the Scriptures will be a book closed and sealed.

49. Hence Dr. Luther says in the book On the Bondage of the Will, vol. 3, Jena edition, p. 167, that not even one iota in the Scriptures is clear without the light of the Holy Spirit, since all things in this way and in this respect are obscure to flesh and to human acuteness without the light of the Holy Spirit. Indeed a light has been left to our reason, whereby we can use it in knowing and investigating earthly matters, philosophical disciplines, and a certain part of the divine law accusing outward sins; but for knowing plainly the divine mysteries in the Scriptures it is quite blind, nay, even though they are proposed externally, yet it cannot attain a saving and solid knowledge of them without the internal illumination and light of the Holy Spirit, whence flowed forth the distinction between the knowledge of the letter and of the spirit.

50. That we may obtain this divine and supernatural light of the Holy Spirit prayers are necessary, for the Holy Spirit is given to those who ask, Luke 11. v. 3. The Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, reveals to us the mysteries of our salvation. John 1. v. 18. in turn No one comes to the Son unless the Father draws him. John 6. v. 44. The Father therefore must be prayed to, that he draw us to the Son: the Son must be prayed to, that he reveal the Father to us. The anointing is that which teaches concerning all things 1 John 2. v. 27. It is the Spirit who leads into all truth, John 16. v. 13. Therefore the Holy Spirit must be prayed to, so that he himself may write upon our hearts and seal there what is outwardly set forth in the word.

51. This illumination of the Holy Spirit is necessary for knowing and interpreting the whole Scripture and any part of it savingly. Hence, for obtaining that illumination of divine light, prayers are necessary—and indeed earnest ones—for whatever readers and interpreters of sacred letters whatsoever. Psalm 119. v. 10. Lord, do not allow me to err from thy commandments. v. 12. 26. 64. 68. 124. Teach me thy statutes. v. 18. Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wondrous things out of thy law. v. 73. 125. Give me understanding, that I may learn thy commandments &c. 52. The pious ancients knew this. Iren. lib. 4. c. 14. Without God GOD is not known, which the Christian poet expressed thus:

Cease wondering that no one sees the Divinity without the Deity; Who beholds the sun without the sun?

Origen. homily 17. on Exodus. We must supplicate the Lord, that he himself, receiving the sealed book, deign to open it; for he himself is who opens minds, that the Scriptures may be understood. Hieron. to To Pammachius he likewise says that Scripture is a sealed book, which no one can open nor unseal its mysteries, unless the lion of the tribe of Judah: therefore the Lord must be prayed to, and with Peter one must say: Declare to us this parable. Theophylactus on John 10. έθεί-θνένματι ά-ίωνοοαμρνσν και -ραφαι -ειχννομσιν ημίν τόν Χριόν, ειχότος θνρωρος τόν θνενμα ά-ιον.

53. We shall bring here Augustine's very brief prayer, which exists in Book 11 of the Confessions, chapter 2: "My Lord God, give heed to my prayer, and let your mercy hear my desire. Let your Scriptures be my chaste delights, and let me neither be deceived by them nor deceive others out of them. Lord, attend and have mercy on me. My Lord God, light of the blind and strength of the weak—and also light of those who see and strength of the strong—attend to my soul and hear it crying from the depths. For unless your ears are present even in the depths, whither shall we go? To whom shall we cry? Yours is the day and yours is the night: at your nod the moments fly past. Grant therefrom space for our meditations on the hidden things of your law, and do not close it against those knocking: for not in vain did you will so many pages' dark secrets to be written. See, Father, look and behold and approve, and may it please in the sight of your mercy that I find grace before you, so that the inner meanings of your words may be opened to me as I knock. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, through him I beseech—I beseech through him—who sits at your right hand and intercedes for us, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden: him I seek in your books; about him wrote Moses—that itself he said, that truth said."

Moreover, what we have said thus far concerning the necessary illumination of the Holy Spirit for understanding the Scriptures, we intend chiefly and principally regarding the understanding of the mysteries of faith set forth in Scripture. For although certain things in the Scriptures are arranged such that they do not exceed the grasp of human understanding—for example, the outer rind of histories—nevertheless, for knowing the mysteries of faith soundly and savingly, the human mind cannot rise by natural force of light without the irradiation of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, those not yet illumined by the Holy Spirit can have known doctrines of the Scriptures and hold historical faith through the external ministry of the word, but to have certain, solid, and saving knowledge of ωροηροφοριαν we cannot without the Holy Spirit inwardly enlightening our minds

55. The necessity of seeking this illumination by the Holy Ghost is required on account of the darkness of our understanding: but it does not prove that the Scriptures are obscure when setting forth the mysteries of faith: thus act Bellarmine and other Papist writers, who labor to prove their opinion about the obscurity of the Scriptures from this foundation: The eyes of the blind do not perceive even the most luminous objects, nor therefore the Sun itself; yet who would wish on that account to attribute darkness to the Sun? So our understanding is so darkened that it does not apprehend the mysteries of faith set forth in Scripture in ever so clear and plain words; yet who would wish on that account to attribute this darkness to Scripture itself? άθαι-έντως

56. Far be it from us indeed to allow that divine Scriptures should on that account be assigned darkness; rather we maintain that light ought to be attributed to them, and thus the power of enlightening our understanding, because the Holy Spirit through that very Scripture enlightens our mind. Which all those sayings confirm, in which the word of God proposed in the Scriptures is compared to a place whose proper property is to illuminate Ps. 19. v. 9. The commandment of the Lord is bright. Psalm. 119. vers. 105. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my paths. Prov. 6. v. 23. The commandment is a lamp, and the law is light. 2. Pet. 1. v. 19. Λόγος θροφητιχός is λνΧνος φ-ννων φί άνΧμηρω τόθω: As natural light drives away darkness; so through the light of Scripture the spiritual darknesses of our understanding are illuminated: whence also φωτισ μός is attributed to the word of God. 2. Cor. 4. vers. 4.

57. We say, therefore, that the light of the Holy Spirit is required for a saving understanding of the divine oracles, but we add that, through the diligent handling of the word, the Holy Spirit is willing to kindle that light within us. Therefore, it is not to be thought that an immediate illumination from on high is to be expected from the Holy Spirit before we approach the reading, meditating upon, and searching of the Scriptures: but that light of the Holy Spirit is to be sought and obtained in the Scriptures and through the Scriptures. Whence St. Peter said, That attention must be paid to the Prophetic word, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day (of divine recognition) dawns, and the Morning Star (Christ, that morning star Apoc. 22. v. 16. ) rises in our hearts.

58. Indeed, those things which are necessary for everyone to know for salvation are set forth in the Scripture in proper, clear, and perspicuous words, as we have shown in its place: for understanding and interpreting those things, therefore, no external light or far-fetched interpretation is required, but the Holy Spirit himself speaks clearly and perspicuously in them, and through them wishes to dispel the native darkness of our intellect.

59. Just as therefore the most splendid radiance of the Sun sets objects in clear light: so through this light of Scripture the native blindness of the mind is driven out. Besides that έμφντον χαι σόμφντον dimness of our mind there is also another blindness of certain persons -θίχτιτος, whereby they spurn that light of the Holy Spirit and voluntarily turn their eyes away from it, just as if anyone should voluntarily and knowingly shut his eyes while they are to be illumined -v- or are illumined by the light of the Sun. Concerning this blindness see Esai. 6. v. 10. Close the eyes of this people &c.

60. From this blinding and hardening of the wicked it must likewise not be concluded that the Scriptures are obscure in teaching the mysteries of faith and need an external light, just as it is not permissible to conclude: some men shut their own eyes so that the light of the Sun may not appear to them. Therefore another illumination besides is required for beholding the light of the Sun. 2. Cor. 4. v. 3. If our Gospel veiled, it is veiled among those who perish. v. 4. Among whom the God of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, lest the light of the Gospel of the glory of Christ should shine upon them.

61. From those perspicuous passages of Scripture there is gathered the rule of faith, which is a certain summary of heavenly doctrine, collected from the most open places of Scripture. Its parts are two: the former concerning faith, whose principal heads are expounded in the Apostles' Creed; the latter concerning charity, whose sum the Decalogue sets forth. 2. Tim. 1. v. 13. hold fast the form of sound words, which you heard from me, in faith and love in CHRIST JESUS. ὑωοτύπωσινέχε

62. Whatever things therefore are necessary are manifest in the sacred writings, says Chrysostom, homily 3 on 2 Thessalonians. If any things therein are more obscure, the knowledge of them is not equally necessary to all for salvation, and consequently even though we do not always attain their proper and genuine interpretation, yet it suffices that in interpreting them we bring forward nothing that opposes the rule of faith. Rom. 12. v. 6. Prophecy (to be instituted) χατ' άναλογιαν τς πι-εως.

63. Care must therefore be taken that in the interpretation of more obscure passages nothing be brought forward that conflicts with the settled and perpetual sense, which concerning each head of heavenly doctrine is contained in Scripture in plain words. For the whole Scripture is one body, hence all things in it are mutually consistent, nothing here contrary, nothing conflicting or at variance with itself. θεόπνευ-οσ, συναληθ,

64. Those more obscure passages of Scripture are such either taken by themselves and separately, or when compared with others. For many things, considered by themselves and apart, are quite clear, which nevertheless seem to conflict with other declarations of Scripture. For although no true contradiction exists in the Scriptures, yet the apparent contradiction of places brings upon them a certain obscurity: we will remove ένανηω σν from Scripture, εανηοφάνειαν we cannot deny of certain passages. Thus it is quite clear what the Lord says Ezech. 18. v. 20. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the Father: but a certain obscurity is brought upon it from the place Exodus 20. v. 5. I Jehovah, a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the sons unto the third and fourth generation. To this obscurity a remedy is brought by the harmonization of places, drawn from their circumstances, and conformed to the analogy of faith.

65. Things that are obscure when taken by themselves and separately are so either on account of the matters, or on account of the words. For there is a perpetual bond between matters and words as between things signified and signs, and therefore if the matters are obscure, obscurity accrues to speech or writing even though the words are clear: conversely, if the words are obscure, likewise obscurity accrues to speech or writing even though the matters are known and clear.

66. To the obscurity of matters the Holy Spirit's illumination brings a remedy, since without it the articles of faith remain obscure, and it is a book closed and sealed. And because the matters or mysteries of faith are set forth in Scripture in two ways, here catechetically, that is, briefly, simply and generally (which manner of teaching is called milk, 1. Cor. 3. v. 2. Hebr. 5. v. 12. 13.) elsewhere abundantly, clearly and specifically (which manner of teaching is called solid food); in the school of Aristotle the former treatment would be called acroamatic, the latter exoteric: therefore it contributes not a little toward removing this obscurity arising from the matters, to hold firmly in any article certain fixed axioms, to which we should always look as to the Cynosure, lest we bring forward anything against them in the interpretation of Scripture.

67. That obscurity which arises through the words of Scripture is twofold: for one kind is born from the words taken singly, another from those joined together. For just as for an utterance or some writing (which are equivalent in this respect) words taken separately do not suffice, but they must be joined and fitly connected so that they become enunciations; so also to understand an utterance or some writing there is required not only to understand the words taken separately, but the same words taken jointly must also be understood.

68. Obscurity arising from words taken separately is likewise twofold , for words are either proper or figurative. Grammar serves for understanding and interpreting proper words, namely the exposition of terms and the observation of emphases: here moreover any careful interpreters of Scripture will discover, if it be diligently observed, where the same word is used in other places of Scripture, that this comparison and observation has by far the greatest use. For whether that word is used in the same meaning or in another, always to observe this belongs to the concern of theological study and of a faithful interpreter of the Scriptures. Rhetoric serves for the exposition of tropes and figures.

69. Scripture uses metaphors and parables, which, since they are drawn from the innermost recesses of Nature, the knowledge of natural things is most highly useful for explaining them. For who will rightly interpret those parables of the Savior concerning leaven, tares, a grain of mustard seed, a vineyard, etc., unless he has had their natural properties exactly, or at the very least popularly, perceived?

70. If any obscurity of Scripture is brought about by connected words, it arises from the phrase, or from the whole manner of the discourse. For learning the phrases of Scripture, not only Grammar serves, but very especially a prudent and diligent comparison of the passages of Scripture. For rightly understanding the whole context, the observation of the order and of the circumstances serves. To the observation of order belongs the Dialectical observation of the scope and of the members in the discourse. The circumstances are various, which we can refer to these headings: Person, Occasion (cause, purpose), Time, Place, Manner, (Instrument.) All these can be further subdivided. For concerning the person, consideration must be given to Who speaks, to whom, about whom, before whom, &c. 71. Let us reduce to a summary what we determine concerning the true Interpretation of Scripture . 1. In knowing and interpreting the Scriptures our mind is blind without the light of the Holy Spirit. 2. Besides this natural blindness of us all, certain men are blinded by their own malice and obstinate insolence, whose eyes the Holy Spirit has either opened, or wished to open: but they themselves stubbornly resist him: yet neither blindness makes or proves the Scriptures to be obscure. 3. Because our mind is blind, therefore the light of the H. S. must be implored through pr-eces. 4. But that illumination of the mind the Holy Spirit confers not immediately, but through the light of the word hea-d and meditated. 5. Since indeed the dogmas necessary for anyone to know for salvation are set forth in Scripture in proper, clear and perspicuous words. 6. From these the remaining passages of Scripture derive light. 7. for from the ex-perspicuous passages of Scripture the rule of faith is gathered, to which the exposition of the rest must be conformed. 8. And even if we do not attain the most proper and genuine sense of all the passages, nevertheless it suffices to bring forward nothing against the faith άναλογίαν in interpreting them. 9. Nevertheless it is useful, even to interpret rightly and skillfully those more obscure passages of Scripture; which will come to pass, if we apply suitable remedies for removing the obscurities. 10. That we may find those remedies, the fountains of the obscurity must be sought. 11. Certain passages of Scripture are obscure in themselves and considered separately, others when compared with others, no wonder if they seem to conflict with other passages: the reconciliation of passages cures this obscurity. 12. Those that are obscure in themselves and separately are found to be such, either on account of the things, or on account of the words. Certain fixed ax-ioms in the individual articles of the faith bring a remedy for the obscurity of the things, which must be observed like a cynosure. 13. For the obscurity of the words serve the Grammatical unriddling of the words, the Rhetorical exposition of tropes and figures , the Dialectical observation of order and circumstances, finally the Physical knowledge of natural things; indeed also a prudent and diligent comparison of the passages of Scripture will afford the greatest help in all these, where either the same words and phrases, or different ones, are used to express the same or different things.

72. These things having been said in general concerning the means which we require for the legitimate interpretation of Scripture. We declare the supreme and authentic Interpreter of Scripture to be the Holy Spirit, who proposes the dogmas of faith necessary for salvation for anyone to know in true, proper, and perspicuous [terms] in Scripture; but for the correct interpretation of those things which, beyond these, are more obscure in the Scriptures, we require prayers; knowledge of the languages which the amanuenses of the Holy Spirit used; observation of the order and circumstances in any given passage; a prudent and diligent collation of passages; and above all, we say that the rule of faith must be diligently attended to, lest anything be brought forth against it in the interpretation of more obscure matters.

73. We shall treat of all these things specifically later on at greater length, when we shall first have set forth what means the Papists propose to us. For just as they establish their Pope in the place of the supreme authentic Interpreter, so also they substitute other means which we ought to use in the Interpretation of the Scriptures. Stapleton has treated this matter sufficiently at length in book 11 of the principles of faith, and in the sixth controversy of the rereading of the same, whom let us hear.

74. He proposes four means by which we can arrive at the true sense of Scripture. The First is the rule of faith: the Second the practice of the Church: the Third the consenting interpretation of the Fathers: the Fourth the prescriptions and decrees of Councils: he says these alone are certain and authentic means. Let us therefore look at these one by one, and afterwards weigh against the standard of truth whatever he brings forward against our own means.

75. Stapleton requires the rule of faith, and we require the same too, but in a plainly different sense: By the rule of faith we understand those clear passages of Scripture in which the articles of faith are set out in plain and explicit words: To this belong all those arguments by which we proved in its proper place that Scripture is perfect and perspicuous, and consequently the Canon of all Theological controversies. όμοια μ-ύ λαλούμ-υ, άνόμοια δεφπονούμ-υ.

76. Moreover, because the highest and chief heads of this Rule are set out in the Creed of the Apostles, therefore the Fathers call that the rule of faith. Irenaeus, book 1, Against Heresies, chapter 2, explaining the rule of faith refers himself to the Creed of the Apostles. Tertullian, On Veiling Virgins: There is indeed one altogether single rule, immovable and incapable of reform, namely of believing in one God Almighty, maker of the world, and His Son Jesus Christ, born of the virgin Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, raised again from the dead on the third day, received into the heavens, sitting at the right hand of the Father, coming to judge the living and the dead even through the resurrection of the flesh. Augustine, in Enchiridion ch. 56. Unless the Holy Spirit were God, He would not be placed before the Church in the rule of faith. Ambrose, sermon 38. To this end the Apostles were gathered together into one, that they might prescribe the rule of faith.

77. In these sayings the Apostles' Creed is called the rule of faith, but because all and each of its articles are set forth in Scripture in plain words, therefore elsewhere Scripture itself is by those men called the Rule of Faith. Irenaeus, book 4, ch. 69, calls the word of God the rule of truth. Clement, Epistle 5, says that the entire and firm rule of truth must be sought from the divine Scriptures. Augustine, On the Good of Widowhood, ch. 1, Sacred Scripture fixes the rule of our doctrine. Book 2 against the Donatists, ch. 6, he calls the sacred Scriptures the divine balance. Book 11 of the City of God, ch. 33, Although we could not search out the will of the author of this book, yet we have not strayed from the rule of faith, which through other sacred letters of the same authority is sufficiently known to the faithful. Chrysostom, homily 13 on 2 Corinthians, calls Scripture άπάιτων άχέβ ζυγόν καλ γνωμονα καλ ηάνονα. Gerson, On Communion under Both Kinds, Sacred Scripture is the rule of faith, against which, rightly understood, the authority of men is not to be admitted.

78. The Papists propose another rule of faith. They add traditions to Scripture, which they decree are to be embraced with an equal affection of piety. But this rule is very irregular, as we have demonstrated in its proper place. Scripture is the total and perfect canon, seeing that nothing is to be added to it nor taken away; therefore, if traditions agree with Scripture, we accept them: but if they dissent, we rightly repudiate them.

79. The second means was the practice of the Church. But at its proper place we shall show that the Church is subject to the Scriptures, but not the Scriptures to the Church : what the true Church is, what the true and saving practice of the Church is, all that must be learned from the Scriptures. Prescription, practice and custom divine, Christ said, Not custom but truth.

80. As, therefore, the Papists do not rest in the practice of the Church, but approve and follow only that practice of the Church which has been confirmed by the Pontiff (which an analysis of the Pontifical opinion shows), so we, with far greater right, do not rest in the bare practice of the Church, but approve and follow only that practice of the Church which has its foundation in Scripture. Briefly, what the Pontiff pronouncing *ex cathedra* is to them, that the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scriptures is to us.

81. The Papists say that hearers ought to follow their Pastors: that, in turn, Pastors ought to follow the Bishops, and the Bishops themselves ought to follow the instruction of the Pope: so we also say that hearers ought to follow their Pastors, but that the Pastors themselves ought to follow the instruction of the Holy Spirit, in the Scriptures which have proceeded from God.

82. The Papists say that, in interpreting the Scriptures, the rule of faith to be followed is the practice of the Church, the consenting interpretation of the Fathers, and the Decrees of Councils. We do not disapprove of these means; but just as they add that the rule of faith is what the Pope approves, the practice of the Church is what the Pope keeps, those interpretations of the Fathers are finally to be followed which the Pope has not rejected, the Decrees of those Councils are to be embraced which the Pope confirms—so let them allow us likewise to add that the true rule of faith is what Scripture sets forth, the true practice of the Church is what Scripture approves, the true interpretation of the Fathers is that which agrees with Scripture, and the true Decrees of Councils are those which accord with the Scriptures. Augustine, Book 11 against Faustus, chapter 5.

Canonical Scripture stands established on high, as it were upon a certain seat, to which every faithful and pious understanding must submit.

83. The third was the consenting Interpretation of the Fathers: The fourth, the Decrees of Councils. There will be its own place for speaking about Councils. We do not despise the Interpretations of the Fathers, but we highly esteem them: yet we neither equate nor prefer them to the declarations of Scripture, but we grant such honor to them as they themselves claim for themselves, indeed such as Truth itself attributes to them.

84. Thus therefore we proceed. First: the authority of the Fathers the Papists themselves deny to be always authentic. Baronius vol. 1. year 34. §. 213. However much it may be evident that those most holy Fathers, whom we rightly call Doctors of the Church on account of their lofty learning, are imbued above others with the grace of the Holy Spirit, still he is not followed in all things in the Interpretation of Scripture by the Catholic Church. Bellarmine 2. on Councils ch. 12. The writings of the Fathers are not rules, nor do they have the authority of binding. Pererius on Genesis bk. 3. ch. 2. q. 5. Irenaeus affirms that what he hands down concerning Paradise he received from the presbyters of Asia, disciples of the Apostles. But what then afterward? Ought whatever was handed down by those presbyters to be held as a certain and undoubted dogma of Christian doctrine? Is it not established that these very presbyters, while Irenaeus himself relates this, taught some things both false and contrary to the divine letters? Canus bk. 7. of Theological Loci ch. 3. testifies that the Fathers often erred. Cajetan in the preface upon the books of Moses asks that he not be blamed if at any time he disagrees with the stream of the Fathers. Stapleton in his Relections on the principles of faith controversy 6. q. 4. in explaining the article says: those things which the Fathers write occasionally in passing, while engaged in other matters, must be distinguished from those which they treat deliberately and principally, for these latter carry great weight, but the former very little. Again those things which they state once, versus those which they constantly and frequently repeat and reaffirm. But especially must be distinguished those things which they teach dogmatically and assertively in positive treatment, from those which they pronounce contentiousness and in disputation against an adversary even in matters of faith. From this latter kind of sayings no testimonies ought to be taken, because it easily happens in such cases to exceed due measure and to cross the line of truth. So far Stapleton, enclosing the Interpretations of the Fathers within fixed limits himself.

85. Secondly: That consensus of the Fathers is rather asserted in words than shown in fact. For it is established that they do not agree in all things, neither in doctrines nor in the interpretation of Scripture. And lest we seem to speak gratuitously, we will confirm this by one example and another: The Psalmist says Psalm 66. verse 12. We passed through water and fire, and thou broughtest us out into refreshment. Origen, Homily 25 on Numbers, applies this passage to his purgatory, which the Papists follow. But do the Fathers expound this passage unanimously in that manner? We shall run through some of them. Arnobius (or whoever is the author of those Commentaries) on Psalm 65. (for so the Latins number it) understands it of the fire of martyrdom and the water of baptism. Cyril, mystical Catechesis 5, understands it of passing through temptation. Augustine, on this place, explains fire of adverse circumstances, water of the abundance of -culum. Cardinal Hugh follows Augustine. Jerome, on this place, understands it of the torments of the martyrs. In the same sense Hilary also explains it. Euthymius understands by fire and water various calamities, which inflame and submerge the soul. So too Theodoret. Rufinus expounds it of temptations. Haymo of the martyrs, whose course could be hindered neither by fire nor by water. Beda of various tribulations. Bernard, sermon on the transfiguration, interprets fire of sorrows, water of softnesses: so also Cassiodorus on this passage. Lyra adapts it to the servitude of the Israelites in Egypt: 'We passed through fire,' that is, the labor of fire for cooking, 'and water' which they carried on their own shoulders to mix with earth, that bricks might be formed from it. Is this then a consenting interpretation of the Fathers?

86. That which the Apostle says Rom. 7. v. 14. I am carnal, sold under sin, Jerome, Athanasius, and Ambrose take thus, as if Paul there spoke not about himself but in the person of a man not yet regenerated: truly Aug. 2 against Julian ch. 2 confirms this must be understood concerning the Apostle himself. So when at Rom. 3. v. 28. it is said, We hold that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law, there Ambrose takes the word 'man' of the Gentiles alone, Chrysostom of all men. By 'works of the law' Jerome understands the Ceremonies, Augustine and Ambrose the whole law, etc. Very many more such things could be brought forth.

87. Thirdly: Hence the Papists themselves subject the interpretation of the Fathers to the Roman Pope. Thus Bellarmine, book 3 on the Word of God ch. 3, constitutes the Pontiff together with a Council as the supreme Interpreter of Scripture. Whence in book 2 on Councils ch. 12 he disputes that the Decrees of the Popes are rightly called sacred Scriptures, so that they may be distinguished from profane writings, and Canonical, so that they may be distinguished from the Sacred Writings of the Fathers, which are not rules nor do they have authority to bind. Stapleton, book 10 principle ch. 11, says the Interpretation of the Bishops and Doctors of the Church is to be received, provided these conditions are applied. 1. If only they remained in Catholic unity, that is, if they quietly and peacefully submitted themselves to the authority of the Pontiff. 2. If they agreed with their fellow-Bishops, etc. Pistorius, Hodgeg., p. 51, says the Interpretations of the Fathers avail only then when the Church approves them: that is, as the last analysis teaches, the Roman Pontiff. Therefore since the authority of the Fathers is subjected by the Romans to the Pontiff, how much greater right do we have to subject it to Scripture? Let those who are called Fathers be our fathers indeed: let us obey them as Parents whenever they prescribe something according to divine law and authority: if they prescribe anything contrary to the rule of heavenly doctrine, let us obey not them but God. Let them also be held as Luminaries, but not as Divinities.

88. Fourth: That which is so constituted that it has not always been a rule for interpreting Scripture, or which has not always possessed the authority of an authentic judgment, that very thing ought not to have the force of a rule or judgment even now: for a rule, in order that it may always be one, requires that it be certain, firm, and invariable. But the consenting interpretation of the Fathers was not always a rule for interpreting Scripture, because at one time there were no writings of the Fathers; few of them wrote before the four-hundredth year after Christ. Therefore, it will not be a rule of Scripture even now.

89. Fifth: To the unanimous consent of the Fathers, Stapleton requires that they should have consented with all their fellow-bishops, but whence can we know this? For there were many other bishops in their times, of whom no writings or monuments at all survive. Whence will it be certainly established that Augustine, Ambrose, and others consented with all their fellow-bishops?

90. Sixthly: But how great a labour would it be to go through all the writings of all the Fathers, so that we might at last be certain about their consenting interpretation of those who wrote? And what span of human life would suffice for this task? Now indeed the rule of judgment and truth in the Church ought to be prepared, so that any Christian whatsoever may betake himself to it, since upon all alike rests to test the spirits, 1. Iohan. 4. v. 1. and to beware of false prophets Matth. 7. v. 15. 91.

91. Seventhly: The Fathers themselves deny to themselves any such authoritative power of judging and of interpreting the Scriptures, which can be demonstrated in as many places as possible. How often does even a single Augustine distinguish the canonical excellence of the sacred Scriptures from the little works of posterity? see book 11. against Faustus ch. 5. book 2. against Cresconius chap. 32. book 2. against the Donatists chap. 3. Letter 19. to Jerome. Letter 48. to Vincentius. Letter 112. to Paulinus. The same thing Jerome repeats, on Psalm 86. on 2. Micah 19. Isaiah on 36. Ezekiel, &c. Basil, book On the Holy Spirit ch. 7. Origen on 2. Romans. Athanasius on the Synods. See also the chapters Noli, Neque, Ego Solis, Negare, distinction 9.

92. Eighthly: But neither are all the books of those Fathers who wrote extant, and those that are extant have often been corrupted, and many counterfeit writings are set forth under the venerable mantle of the Fathers, and many things also the Expurgatory Indexes sensed.

93. Ninthly: The Fathers sometimes speak unfittingly in the heat of disputation. (Basil, Letter 64. concerning Gregory of Neo-Caesarea: This thing which he said—that the Son and the Father ὑποςάσει are one—he did not say from decree, but it was said έριςικῶς. Erasmus gives the same judgment about Jerome when he writes against Vigilantius) They use stronger rhetoric in exhortation: Thus Jerome concerning himself; excusing certain things said unfittingly: We have made use of rhetoric and yielded something to declamations. Sixtus Senensis, book 6. of the Library, annotation 152. warns that the words of preachers are not always to be received with strictness, since they first arrive at the ears of their hearers, for they very often pronounce and press upon them many things by way of hyperbole, whether drawn by the occasion of places, persons, times, or hurried by the force of the emotions, or swept along by the flow of their discourse, and Theodore concludes in Dialogue 3. that this happens sometimes even to Chrysostom. I do not take as the rule of doctrines and decrees those things which are said in the Church panegyrically and declamatorily.) They spoke more securely before the contests had been stirred up, (So Augustine acknowledges in book 1 against Julian, chapter 2, deliberating that the ancients spoke more carelessly about Free Choice and Original Sin while the Pelagians were not yet disputing.) They indulged something to their own times. (So Augustine says in Epistle 119, that on account of avoiding scandals of certain persons, whether holy or troublesome, he did not disapprove some things rather freely. Canus, book 11 of Common Places, chapter 6: We cannot deny that men otherwise most weighty both scattered rumors concerning especially the miracles of the Saints and received them, and even handed them down in writings to posterity, in which matter they either indulged themselves too much, or certainly the common people of believers :) sometimes they speak recitatively and historically, not dogmatically) Otto of Freising, book 4, chapter 18: it must be considered according to what the authors speak, what by opining, what by asserting ) and thence later Fathers explain the sayings of earlier onesaccording to the analogy of faith: or plainly reject them, if they cannot be reconciled with it. So Augustine openly refutes that which exists in Justin, Irenaeus, Clement and Tertullian, that the nations were saved by the law of Nature: The same man explains according to the analogy of faith those things which were brought forward quite plausibly by the Pelagians from the sayings of the Fathers for establishing the integrity of Free Choice.

94. Tenth: The Fathers did not write to that end, that they might illuminate the Scriptures with some external and new light, but that they might serve the men and controversies of their own time; therefore they also profess that they have drawn their own [teachings] from the sacred letters, and they strive to prove everything from them.

95. Eleventhly: Many of the Fathers were deprived of knowledge of languages, whence they could not attain the proper sense of each passage. Let someone read Augustine's Expositions on the Psalms, and he will see how far he sometimes departs from the Hebrew truth. Most of them pursue a more copious manner of speaking, especially hunting homoioptoia and homoioteleuta, rather than scrupulous considerations of texts and grammatical elucidations of words: many touch the literal sense lightly, then immediately depart to allegories. Who therefore will simply acquiesce in the interpretation of the Fathers?

96. Twelfthly: Finally, that our Churches have made a secession from the unanimous confession, dogmas, or Interpretation of Scripture of the Fathers, has not yet been proven by the Papists. There is no dogma of our confession, no head of controversies, for the confirmation of which we cannot bring forward many and evident testimonies of the Fathers. In turn, a unanimous and consenting Interpretation of the Fathers cannot be brought forward by the adversaries, by which they might confirm Papal indulgences, the invocation of Saints, pilgrimages, the veneration of relics, works of supererogation and other contested dogmas.

97. These things, then, concerning the means of interpreting Scripture, which the Papists thrust upon us, let them have been said: which we do not simply repudiate, but say they are to be subordinated to the authority of the Scriptures. We contend that the rule of faith is set forth in Scripture: we do not repudiate the practice of the Church, the opinions of the Fathers, the Decrees of Councils, provided only they receive their strength from Scripture: for our Faith ought not to be resolved into the opinion either of the Fathers or of the Councils, but into the sacred Scripture. For we are built upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles,Eph. 2. v. 20. and we acknowledge Christ as the unique supreme and authentic Teacher of faith, Matt. 23. v. 8. whose voice sounds in the Scriptures. Let us see what they bring against our means.

98. The Papists dispute in this way. First they say that these means of ours are shared in common with all heretics, indeed even with the Jews, sometimes also with the pagans. For they likewise compare passages of Scripture, weigh antecedents and consequences, examine the sources, observe turns of phrase: yet nevertheless they are absent from the true understanding of the Scriptures by just as much as possible. Thus Stapleton disputes, thus the remaining writers.

99. Resp. If these means are said to be common to all, even to heretics and pagans, in the sense that all are able to use them, we concede what is assumed in the argument: for God speaks to all in the Scriptures, and He desires that they be read and known by all, and heard in them. But if those means are said to be common to all in the sense that they actually and legitimately use them, and prove their own heresies through them, then we say that this is most false. We concede it *de iure* [by right], we deny it *de facto* [in fact]. No one has ever erred in interpreting the Scriptures through the legitimate use of these means, and heretics, Jews, and pagans can be sufficiently refuted from the Scriptures through these means when legitimately applied, which the writings of our people clearly demonstrate. He who does not acquiesce in the judgment of Scripture—that is, of God speaking through the Scriptures—will acquiesce far less in the judgment of the Fathers, Councils, or the Pope!

100. Secondly they say that these means are acquired by study and human industry, and therefore are merely human, and probable only, or even at times fallacious, while theirs rest on divine authority.

101. Reply. Truly men are those who use those means, meanwhile the means themselves are and remain divine. For the clearer passages, from which the obscure ones are illuminated, are utterances of the Holy Spirit; the antecedents and consequences are declarations of the Holy Spirit; the Hebrew and Greek sources contain the words of the Holy Spirit; the style and turn of phrase is the speech of the Holy Spirit. Before the use of these means we set the Magisterium of the Holy Spirit to be implored by prayers, and the analogy of faith, that is, the voice of the Holy Spirit sounding in the clear passages. When therefore Bellarmine, book 3 on the word of God, chapters 3 and 9, disputes that we lead men away to the private spirit of each individual, observe most accurately: If some private person judges concerning a controversy of religion from the clear places of Scripture, this proceeds not from a private Spirit, but is the judgment of the public Holy Spirit speaking in the Scriptures; conversely, if even a person placed in a public office of the Church brings forth something in articles of faith beyond and outside Scripture, that has proceeded from a private Spirit, even though he himself should sit as Pope, or be some supreme Bishop.

102. From this foundation Panormitan declares, chapter Significasti, extra on election, that to a private man and believer who brings better reasons, credit ought rather to be given than to the whole Council and the Pope. Gerson, on the examination of doctrine, consideration 5: It would stand that someone simple and unauthorized might be so excellently learned in the sacred letters that more credit ought to be given, in a case of doctrine, to his assertion than to the Pope's declaration; for more is to be credited to the Gospel than to the Pope.
