Marsilius of Padua, in the Defense of Peace: In matters pertaining to the faith, the saying of even a single private layman is to be preferred to the saying of the Pope, if he is moved by better authorities of the Old and New Testament than the Pope. John Francis Pico of Mirandola, On the Faith and Order of Believing, theorem 16: Credit must rather be given to a simple rustic and infant and little old woman than to the Supreme Pontiff and a thousand Bishops, if the latter were to speak against the Gospel, the former for the Gospel.

103. But their means are truly human and merely probable: For the rule of faith, insofar as it embraces traditions, is uncertain and doubtful, and contains institutions of men. For most of those things which they sell off as divine traditions were instituted by Popes, as Platina and Polydore Vergil testify. The Church is an assembly of men. Councils are gatherings of men. The Fathers were men. The Pope is a man (unless perhaps we should wish to say with the Gloss on chapter 'cum inter nonnullos', Extra, On the significance of words, under the word 'we declare': 'The Pope our Lord God'; or with the gloss on the Prologue of the Clementines, under the word 'Papa', that he is a certain middle thing between God and men). The Church, Councils, Fathers, Pope can err, unless they be governed by the Holy Spirit as teacher. That teaching office of the Holy Spirit is either the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit, such as was in the Prophets and Apostles, or governance through the guidance of the Scriptures. The former cannot be said, otherwise the Decrees of the Church, Councils, Fathers and Pope would be equal to the Prophetic and Apostolic Writings; therefore the latter remains, and consequently sacred Scripture is the rule of the Church, Councils, Fathers and Pope.

104. Thirdly they say, that those means of ours are wholly subject to which they themselves propose, nor do they have any firmness except insofar as they agree with them. For unless some such sense be brought out by observing what precedes and follows, comparing passages, inspecting the sources &c., which agrees and accords with the rule of faith, the Decrees of Councils and the doctrine of the holy Fathers, let them judge them plainly fallacious and harmful.

105, Ans. 1. We confess, that those means are subject to the rule of faith, but indeed that rule of faith is set forth in the clear and perspicuous places of Scripture, whereas they want the rule of faith to extend more broadly than Scripture. 2. The practice of the Church, the decrees of Councils, the opinions of the Fathers must be measured against Scripture, but not conversely Scripture fitted to them as to a standard, for this would be to subject the voice of God to the pronouncements of men. 3. The practice of the Church is changeable, and often faulty. Neither do all Councils nor all the Fathers define every controversy, or interpret every passage of Scripture: nay rather, later Fathers often disagree with earlier ones, and likewise later Councils with earlier ones.

106. Therefore hence 4. the Pontificals themselves subject all those things to the Roman Pope, for they approve that practice of the Church, which the Pope observes; they approve the decrees of those Councils over which the Pope either presided, or at least confirmed them. They receive the opinions of those Fathers whom the Pope approved: We much more rightly subject all these things to Scripture. This will not be against the true Church, the true Councils, the true Fathers, for they always subjected all their own things to Scripture.

107. Therefore we say 5. that in the interpretation of Scripture one must not rashly depart from the practice of the Church, the Decrees of Councils, and the opinions of the Fathers: but if Scripture itself, that is, the voice of God sounding in the Scriptures, commands something different, who would not rather choose to hear God than men? So too, if inspection of the sources, observation of what precedes and follows, likewise comparison with the sayings of the N.T., shows that Augustine did not touch the genuine sense of the passage in the Psalms, who would not rather follow him who, with the aid of these means, brings forth the true and genuine exposition, than Augustine? Augustine himself commanded this, when he says in the Preface to Book 3 on the Trinity that he desires not only a pious reader, but also a free corrector.

108. Finally 6. because pious and diligent study of the Scriptures is subjected to the practice of the Church, the Councils and the Fathers, while however the Romanists further subject all these things to one Pope alone, someone might deservedly say with Erasmus in his annotations upon 1. Cor. 7. p. 373. If it is true what some assert, that the Roman Pontiff can never err through judicial error, what need is there of General Councils: what need to summon Jurists and learned Theologians into a Council, if the one pronouncing cannot slip? Why was room given for appeal either to a Synod, or to the same pontiff more rightly instructed, after the Pontiff has once pronounced on the case? To what purpose are so many Academies racked in treating questions of faith, when it is permitted to hear what is true from one single Pontiff? Nay rather, how does it happen that this Pontiff's Decrees fight with those other Decrees? Which he afterwards confirms with many examples.

109. They dispute thus in general against our means. In particular against the observation of antecedents and consequents, Stapleton urges this, that sometimes indeed it helps very much, yet the mean is uncertain and deceptive. 1. Because the context of sacred Scripture is not continuous discourse, nor methodical demonstration, but historical, mystical and tropological senses are mixed together in one and the same context. 2. The order of speaking in them is often interrupted, sometimes inverted, and this happens especially frequently in Paul, suddenly passing from one subject to another . 3. Because in one and the same statement some things are said properly, others improperly etc. 110. Answer. We do not propose this as the sole means, as if it were sufficient for explaining all passages of Scripture, but we say that in certain cases the inspection of the sources, in others the comparison of places, avails most greatly; matters go excellently well with us if, with all those means employed, we finally arrive at the true sense of Scripture, and even if we by no means attain the genuine meaning of each passage, nevertheless we would not stray from the rule of faith . Therefore it is not disapproved by us, which from Augustine's lib. 1. On Genesis according to the letter, last chapter, Stapleton brings forward: That above all should be chosen which the circumstance of Scripture does not hinder, and which agrees with sound faith. But if the rae circumstance of Scripture cannot be treated and discussed, at least let that alone be held which sound faith prescribes. Most truly indeed, but Augustine does not establish nor seek that rule of faith in the shrine of the Pope's breast, but in the Scriptures themselves, as we showed above.

111. The examples which Stapleton brings forward, by which he proves that this method is slippery and uncertain, can easily be explained when other methods are applied such as we propose; nay rather, this very method in those cases is not altogether without effect. Thus when Gen. 3. v. 7. it is said that the eyes of the first parents were opened after eating the forbidden fruit, what precedes shows that this must be taken figuratively, wherein it is said that Eve saw the fruit of the tree, beautiful to look upon.v. 6. So what is said in Psal. 22. v. 1., My God, why hast thou forsaken me? far from my salvation are the words of my sins: the comparison of passages explains, because Christ witnesses in Matth. 27. v. 46. that this was his voice and complaint. The latter words the inspection of the sources explains, for thus they ought to be rendered: far from my salvation art thou, from the words of my roaring. Likewise what is said in Ioh. 1. v. 10., the world was made through him, and the world knew him not: there, in the former part of this saying, the word World is to be taken properly, but in the latter metaphorically, as what goes before and follows show. Also the comparison of passages. All things were made through him, v. 3. God said &c.Gen. 1. v. 3.By the Word of God the heavens were established,Ps. 33. v. 6. therefore the world was made through the Son. Light came into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light.Ioh. 3. v. 19.The light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it, Ioh. 1. v. 5.He came unto his own and his own received him not, v. 11. Whatever is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and the pride of life. 1. Ioh. 2. v. 16.The devil is the Prince of the worldIoh. 14. v. 30.Therefore so the world knew not the Son. Likewise what is said in Ioh. 4. 35., Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are white already to harvest: what follows, v. 36., shows that this must be understood figuratively concerning the spiritual harvest. Whoever reaps receives wages and gathers fruit unto eternal life. verse 38. I sent you to reap that on which ye laboured not.

112. But indeed, if our means are not sufficient for the explanation of these passages, I ask what assistance will traditions, Councils, the practice of the Church, the opinion of the Pope, or the exposition of the Fathers provide us in their explanation? Commentaries of the Fathers perhaps will be able to provide something, although they sometimes entangle the matter more than they explain it. But from traditions and Councils, clearly no assistance is to be hoped for in this regard. And as for the Pope, how many have not even known the location of these passages, let alone their genuine sense?

113. From the observation of the phrase nothing certain can be established, thus Stapleton proves it. 1. because each of the Writers both of the Old and of the New Testament has his own manner of speaking; Isaiah, nurtured in the royal court, speaks otherwise than Amos the Shepherd; Paul otherwise than Peter, &c. Answer: nor do we say that this means, taken by itself and alone, is sufficient for explaining all the passages of Scripture: it is enough that we are sometimes helped by it. Plutarch relates, in the Apophthegms, concerning Scylurus, King of the Scythians, that when about to die, he proposed to his sons whom he was leaving behind him a bundle of eighty darts, ordering each of them to break it; and when each said he could not, he himself, drawing out the darts one by one, easily broke them all, admonishing them that thus they would be strong and powerful if they persevered together , but weak if they were separated and divided: In the same way Stapleton acts. Joined together, our arguments he cannot break; therefore he strives to break them separately. He fights by ambushes; he ought to attack our arguments as if they were military forces joined together, but he attacks them scattered.

114. What therefore is said about variety of speaking, we easily concede, but we add that by diligent study that variety can be detected and thoroughly learned. All the Prophets and Apostles spoke under the inspiration of one Holy Spirit: they had one Master of speaking, nor did Amos among the shepherds, or Isaiah in the court, learn those things which he uttered, but from the Holy Spirit. But surely is that dissimilarity explained in the Decretals of the Popes? Surely in the Decrees of Councils? The Fathers perhaps explain it, yet are not those very men most unlike themselves in style?

115. The second thing which Stapleton brings forward against the observation of phraseology, this is, because the variety of Interpreters, or even of originals, produces uncertainty concerning the same phrases and manner of speaking; for a phrase observed according to the translation from the Greeks will mean something other than according to the translation from the Hebrew. Answer: therefore to this means we add the inspection of the sources, which do not have such great variety. The New Testament contains many Hebraisms, which must be learned from the phraseology of the O.T. And although there is a variety of phrases in the very sources, it can far more rightly be known through the prudent comparison of passages diverted [from context], than from the impure comments of the Rabbins, or from Interpreters ignorant of the Hebrew tongue, which Forster confirms most clearly in the Preface to his Lexicon.

116. The third thing which Stapl. urges against the observation of phraseology consists in this, because in the very rules and observations of this kind nothing is certain and perpetual, but each rule and observation suffers many exceptions . Answer: Therefore because rules are not absolutely universal, shall they on that account have no use whatsoever? Those very rules, and the exceptions added to the rules, must be drawn from the Scriptures: here likewise the Popes can rarely help, who are rarely taught either in Greek or Hebrew. Thus Stapleton wishes to prove that a general rule cannot be established, that mercy is signified through the eyes of the Lord himself, wrath through his face, because countenance is also somewhere taken for clemency. But to what end does he bring forth this? namely that he may prove that the rules concerning modes of speaking are not absolutely universal: yet it suffices that some universality can exist in certain rules, and whenever any exception must be added to a rule, the Scripture itself will teach this. Thus then one means serves another: the comparison of passages helps the observation of phraseology: the comparison of passages is governed by the rule of faith &c.

117. That the comparison of passages is a very weak means is fallacious and uncertain, so Stapleton proves: First, because when Scriptures are compared, something seems to be said similarly or dissimilarly, not so much from the similarity or dissimilarity of the passages themselves, as from the disposition and preconceived opinion of those comparing them. Answer: We require such an Interpreter of Scripture, who approaches this matter without prejudice, neither infuses his own meaning or preconceived opinions into the Scriptures, but draws out truth from the Scriptures, nor forces what he assumed before reading should seem understood to be contained in the sayings, as Hilary speaks, Book 1 on the Trinity.

118. Moreover, whether the comparison of similar or dissimilar passages is legitimate and sound can be known otherwise than from the circumstances of each passage? What help can the Fathers bring here, who likewise deal less skillfully when they compare passages? What Councils, which do not use that comparison? What the Pope, who pronounces from the chair and by the fullness of power? He who will not consent to rightly and properly compared Scriptures will be far less moved by the Pontiff's judgment. Besides, we do not say that this mean is to be taken by itself and alone, but we join it with the others and subject it to the rule of faith. Stapleton produces, for example, the words of the Supper: This is my body: but he says that those things could not yet be brought together to be compared, but rather that they are wretchedly corrupted by comparison of various passages; the same thing Bellarmine also urges, Book 3 on the Word of God, chapter 9; but we shall deal with this most fully a little later here.

119. Next against the comparison of passages Stapleton brings forward this , that neither the same word nor the same phrase sounds and signifies the same everywhere. Answer: But can that be learned anywhere else than from the very inspection of each passage itself and its circumstances? Therefore it is useful to compare not only passages or phrases or matters that are similar among themselves, but also those which are dissimilar either in phrase or in matter τὰ γαρ παράλλνλα Φανεςωτερα. Those varied meanings of a single term could nowhere better be known and explained than from the comparison of passages.

120. The third is this, because certain passages are said only once in the Scriptures, such as to be buried with Christ, to be crucified with Christ, to live together, to reign together etc. Answer: Nor do we say that the use of this means exists in all passages. Things said only once as far as the words go are nevertheless repeated elsewhere as regards the very matter itself, and are either plain, or their knowledge is less necessary to salvation to know. What it is with the Apostle to be buried with Christ, to be crucified with Christ, to live together, to reign together etc., the very context of the apostolic discourse explains most clearly, and the same thing is expounded elsewhere in other words.

121. Fourth is, because all heretics, comparing the Scriptures

most diligently, nevertheless erred most shamefully. Answer: This is insulting to the divine tables, that careful and diligent comparison of the Scriptures should be the cause of error, since Christ will pronounce the contrary: That the ignorance of the Scriptures is the source of error for heretics. Matt. 22. v. 10. But how does Stapleton prove his assertion? The Arians, he says, compared that saying of Christ, I and the Father are one, with that other, John 17. v. 21. I pray, Father, that all may be one, as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee: and yet according to the rule of faith the Church believes that the Son is one with the Father by unity of essence.

122. But that rule of faith can be sought from nowhere else than from the clear passages of Scripture which prove the Divinity of the Son. Most truly Bellarmine, Book 2 on Councils, ch. 12: When the Council of Nicaea defined that Christ is όμοούσιον, of the Father, it drew the conclusion from the Scriptures. Let us weigh then the passage John 10. v. 30. and it will clearly appear that Christ speaks there about unity of essence. 1. Christ says: No man shall snatch my sheep out of my hand. v. 28. My Father who gave them to me is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of my Father's hand, v. 29. I and the Father are one v. 30. Therefore he demonstrates between himself and the Father unity of power. Now however power and essence in God are one. 2. He says that he gives eternal life to his sheep but this is proper to God alone, who is αύτοζωὴ. 3. The Jews immediately perceived that Christ had said of himself that he was όμοούσιον of the Father, and therefore wished to overwhelm him with stones as a blasphemer. Augustine, tractate 48 on John. Behold, the Jews understood what the Arians do not understand, for they were angry because they perceived that I and the Father are one cannot be said unless where there is equality of Father and Son. 4. Therefore, just as the unity of believers in John 17. v. 21. is rightly taken as unity of will and mind (for so it is expounded in Acts 4. v. 32. Rom. 12. v. 16.) so also the unity of Father and Son John 10. verse 30. likewise it is rightly understood concerning unity of will, but so that the unity of essence is included (because in God will and essence are one thing, which has no place among things human). Therefore the comparison must not be extended more broadly than the matter itself permits. Just as it is not permitted to infer, GOD commands, that we be holy, as he himself is holy,Leviticus 11. v. 14.that we be perfect, as he himself is perfect,Matthew 5. v. 48.that we be merciful, as he himself is merciful,Luke 6. verse 36. therefore holiness, perfection, and mercy are likewise accidents in God, as in us: so also it is not permitted to infer, believers are one just as the Father and Son are one: therefore there is in GOD only such a unity of affection. But by no means, because the reason for the dissimilarity is evident. Will and essence in GOD are one thing, and through the unity of essence the Father and Son will one thing, can do one thing, are one.

123. Stapleton brings forward another example, by which he might prove that the collation of passages is an uncertain and fallacious means: because the Pelagians explained that [passage] of the Apostle Romans 5. v. 2. in whom all have sinned, in such a way that that [phrase]: in whom: might signify because of whom, since that phrase is so accepted in Psalm 118. and Acts 7. and yet the Church believes, according to the rule of faith, that that [phrase]: in whom: they have sinned: signifies the sin itself, or certainly the person of the sinning Adam.

124. That very rule of faith is set forth in the Scriptures. If even at most that little word ἐΦ᾽ ᾧ is taken so as to signify a rendering of cause—for thus it is sometimes used, as Varinus, Budaeus, and Suidas prove by examples, an explanation which Dr. Luther also follows—nevertheless nothing whatsoever supports Pelagius' error. Death passed upon all men, because all have sinned. Therefore sin is propagated in all. Pelagius corrupted the text with a perverse interpretation, namely that eternal death reigns over those only who follow Adam with actual transgressions, whereas nevertheless in verse 14 the Apostle says expressly that death reigns also over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam. Aug. 6. against Julian ch. 12, that translation: on account of which: he rejects because of Pelagius' corrupt distortion, and follows another, which renders the text thus, in whom, namely in the first man, all sinned originally, and commonly, as in the union of the mass. But there he refutes Pelagius from those very passages of Scripture which he had brought forward for his own opinion, and shows from the circumstances of the passages that this comparison is corrupt, which strongly opposes Stapleton.

125. Finally, that the inspection of the sources/fountains is an uncertain and fragile means, Stapleton proves thus. 1. Because the sources themselves are not so pure and incorrupt as they once were. 2. Because the Latin version today is authoritative/authentic. Answer: we have demolished this in its place, and against these light-fleeers we maintain the integrity of the sacred Scriptures as the fountain-sources. We also showed that the Council of Trent neither ought nor could confer authentic authority upon the Vulgate translation. 3. Because there are various interpretations of one and the same source. Answer: it suffices if they are not contradictory, or conflict with the rule of faith; and whether what version should be most approved cannot and ought not be learned from the sources themselves? 4. Because heretics today falsely seize the name of the sources as a refuge of falsehood sometimes indeed, abandoning the Vulgate translation, they follow the Hebrew text, at other times they follow the Latin version while leaving the source. Answer: it goes badly for the Romanists, whose errors are to be refuted by the sources of truth, whereby out of the Latin translation they might produce some deception; hence Albertus Ingolstadiensis used to say that many mysteries of the (Papal) faith lie hidden in the old letter of the Vulgate edition; see examples of this matter with Dr. Chemnitius part 1, examination of the Council of Trent, chapter on the version of Scripture. And yet, who will forbid anyone to hasten to the pure water of the fountain if the streams flow muddy? When we press the Vulgate translation, we do so for this purpose, that we may more greatly confute the Papists, who are compelled to stand by its authority, seeing that it was made authoritative for them in the Council of Trent. Therefore With κατά πςᾶγμα and όλήθειαν we construct arguments, we follow the sources: if κατ᾽ ἄιθςωκον,, we press against the Pontificals the Vulgate translation.

126. The Pontificals try to set aside the use of our means by means of these are those machines, these rams. But those things remain unshaken. We conclude therefore, because Scripture is 1. perfect, that is, it contains everything which pertains to faith, morals, worship, and so much to the attainment of salvation, that there is no need for it to take on foreign doctrines. 2. it is perspicuous, that is, it uses proper, clear and perspicuous words in setting forth the dogmas of the faith, so that it needs no external light whatsoever, since indeed the other things derive their light from clearer ones. 3. finally, because the rule of faith, the comparison of passages, the observation of what precedes and follows, the inspection of the sources &c., are not something outside Scripture, therefore this is the legitimate interpretation of Scripture , which is made from itself and through itself.

127. Thus Esdras and his fellow-initiates Nehem. 8. v. 9. were reading the book of the divine law expounded מפורש Mephorasch, and while explaining they gave understanding through the Scripture, for thus out of the Hebrew of Tremellius וגביכו במשרא Vaiiabinù Bammikrà. And Peter in 2. Ep. 1. v. 20. shows that Scripture must be interpreted by the same Spirit by which it was long ago published. Now however the Holy Spirit speaks to us today only in the Scriptures and through the Scriptures . Therefore Scripture is to be interpreted by itself and from itself. That sense of Scripture is not its sense which is brought into it from elsewhere, nor should what appears found out by human judgment be accepted as the word of God.

128. Christ [Christus] Matth. 4. He suppresses the Devil, who perverts the Scriptures, by the authorities of the Scriptures, and teaches by his own example that adversaries who variously twist the Scriptures are to be refuted by the testimonies of the Scriptures themselves, when compared with one another and prudently and correctly applied. The ancient Rabbis said: In whatever place of Scripture you find an objection for heretics, you will immediately find the remedy at its side. For Scripture, where it speaks more obscurely, explains itself, sometimes immediately in the same place, sometimes most abundantly in other places. The Prophets illustrate the writings of Moses, and the Old Testament is opened in the New.

129. On which matter the Fathers speak thus. Irenaeus, book 2, against heresies, chapter 47: If we commit certain questions to God, and preserve our faith, all Scripture given to us by God will be found consistent with us, and the parables will accord with those things that are plainly spoken, and the plainly spoken passages will resolve the parables, and through many voices of expressions he will perceive in us one harmonious melody praising God with hymns, etc. Book 4, chapter 63: The lawful exposition of Scripture without danger is according to the Scriptures themselves. Tertullian, on the veiling of virgins: Let truth itself arise and interpret the sacred Scriptures, which custom does not know. Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 7: Let each thing that is demonstrated be confirmed again out of the Scriptures, from the Scriptures. Origen, homily 7 on Leviticus: It is good to grasp understanding from the divine Scriptures according to their own teaching. Homily 25 on Matthew: Just as all gold outside the temple is not sanctified, so every sense that is outside the Scripture, however admirable it may seem, is not holy, because it is not contained within the sense of the Scripture, which usually sanctifies that sense. Hilary, On the Trinity, book 1: That reader is best who expects the meaning of what is said from the words rather than importing it, and brings more than he brought, nor forces something to appear contained in the words which before reading he presumed should be understood. Therefore when there shall be discourse about the things of God, let us grant knowledge of himself to God, and serve his sayings with pious reverence: for he is a witness sufficient to himself, unless known through himself. Augustine, in the book On Christian Doctrine, often admonishes that the Scriptures must be interpreted from themselves. Jerome, in the Apology for the books against Jovinian: The office of the commentator is to expound not what he himself wishes, but what he whom he interprets thinks: otherwise, if he speaks contrary, he will be not so much an interpreter as an adversary of him whom he strives to explain. Chrysostom, Genesis, Homily 13: Let us reach toward the very scope of Scripture, which interprets itself. Sacred Scripture, whenever it wants to teach such a thing, explains itself, and does not allow the hearer to go astray. Vigilius, book 2, against Eutyches, at the beginning: Various indeed and diverse, yet emerging from one fountain of heretical depravity, has been the error, worst pivot and origin of evils, which gave birth from itself occasions of impiety for all men—this is it: while the force of heavenly sayings, corrupted by the fault of badly interpreting men, is weighed not according to the quality of its own sense, but is diverted onto other matters at the judgment and choice of the reader, otherwise than the rule of truth demands. Gerson, Which truths are to be believed, against the assertions of Master John Parvus, article 14. Scripture sets forth its rules by means of itself, according to various passages of Scripture, concerning communion under both kinds. Sacred Scripture is as it were one conjunctive speech, whose one part confirms, elucidates, and expounds the other.

130. Let these things be said thus in general concerning the means of legitimate Interpretation of the Scriptures; I judge it will be worth the labor to treat next of those matters in particular. First it was required, that the rule of faith which Scripture sets forth in its own and plain words should be observed; from which thesis I gather these corollaries. 1. That the interpretation of Scripture ought to be literal and proper. 2. That we must not depart from the letter, especially in articles of faith, unless Scripture itself shows and explains the improper sense . 3. That there is no dogma of faith which is not set forth somewhere in Scripture in its own and plain words. 4. That the rule of faith is to be accepted entire, nor are its parts to be opposed to one another. 5. If in more obscure passages we cannot attain the genuine sense, nevertheless we must not depart from the rule of faith.

131. That we may perceive these corollaries more rightly and deeply, we shall treat by way of hypothesis of the various senses of Scripture, on which matter Bellarmine disputes thus in book 3. de verbo Dei chapter 3. It is proper to divine Scripture, because it has God as author, that it often contains two senses, the literal or historical, and the spiritual or mystical. The literal is, which the words immediately bear before themselves. The spiritual is, which refers elsewhere than to what the words immediately signify; which division is gathered from the Apostle 1. Cor. 10. where he says, All these things happened to the Jews as a figure of us. The literal is twofold: one simple, which consists in the property of the words; the other figurative, whereby words are transferred from their natural signification to a foreign one: and of this there are as many kinds as there are kinds of figures. The spiritual sense is established by the more recent Theologians as threefold, Allegorical, Tropological, Anagogical. They call it Allegorical when the words of Scripture beyond the literal sense signify something in the N.T. pertaining to Christ or the Church. Thus Gal. 4. the Apostle shows that Abraham, who truly according to the letter had two wives, one free and one a handmaid, and two sons, Isaac and Ishmael, signifies God of the two Testaments, and father of two peoples. They call it tropological when words or deeds are referred to signifying something that pertains to morals. Deut. 25. You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain, which is understood literally of real oxen, signifies spiritually that preachers ought not to be forbidden to receive food from the people, as the Apostle explains 1. Cor. 9. They call it anagogical when words or deeds are referred to signifying eternal life, as in that Ps. 94. To whom I swore in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest: as far as the letter is concerned it is understood of the land of promise, but spiritually it is referred to eternal life, as the Apostle explains Hebr. 4.

132. Bellarmin proceeds and adds: From these senses the literal is found in every sentence of both the Old and the New Testament, nor is it improbable that sometimes several literal senses are found in the same sentence. But the spiritual indeed is found entirely in both Testaments. For concerning the Old Testament no one doubts that it has an allegorical, tropological and anagogical sense; concerning the New Testament very many think the same, and deservedly. But although these things are so, nevertheless a spiritual sense is not found in every sentence of Scripture, neither in the Old Testament nor in the new. For that, You shall love the Lord your God, and similar precepts, have only one sense, that is, the literal. These things being so established, it is agreed between us and our adversaries that efficacious arguments must be sought from the literal sense alone, for the sense which is gathered immediately from the words is certain to be the sense of the Holy Spirit. But mystical and spiritual senses are various, and although they edify, when they are not against the faith or good morals, yet it is not always established whether they are intended by the Holy Spirit. All this in the very words of Bellarmine.

133. On this matter we hold thus. There is one proper and genuine sense of each passage, which the Holy Spirit intends, and which is gathered from the very genuine signification of the words, and from this literal sense alone effective arguments are drawn. Allegories, tropologies, anagogies are not various senses, but various collections made from one sense, or various accommodations of that one sense and of the thing which the letter expresses. The same History can be applied in diverse ways, so that it is treated either allegorically, or tropologically, or anagogically (whether this division of the mystical sense is sufficiently convenient, and whether the terms by which those kinds of the mystical sense are expressed are sufficiently suitable, we do not now inquire: Τροπολογία it would rather be called moral exposition, because Τρόπος most commonly signifies morals: ἀναγωγῆς and ἀλληορίας confuse the appellation, Dionys. Eccles. Hier. c. 2. Aug. de vera relig. c. 50. Hieron. ad Hedib. super Esai. 1. and elsewhere frequently. And if on account of the subject-matter a difference between allegory and anagoge is sought, why is not likewise another kind established of that spiritual sense which deals with the Church militant, with Christ, with the Sacraments &c.) meanwhile there remains one proper and literal sense of the words by which the History is described.

134. Various allegories, sometimes very different ones, are drawn by the Fathers from some one History of Scripture; but far be it from us to say that there are so many senses of that one passage, because, as Bellarmine rightly says, it is not established whether they were intended by the Holy Spirit, but they are arbitrary accommodations of one literal sense. But when Scripture itself interprets something typically, there the whole and entire sense of the passage is not in the words properly taken, but part is in the sign, part in the thing signified; in either of these considered separately and by itself only part of the sense is contained, but from both joined together at once the full and perfect sense is completed. For then it stands confirmed by the interpretation of the Holy Spirit himself that this typical sense is contained in that History, concerning which in allegories devised by the Fathers we are not certain.

135. Moreover, what Bellarmine says, namely that this belongs to Scripture alone, because it has God as author, so that it often contains two senses—that writings such as the Mythology of Fulgentius, and Natale Comes, Palaephatus On Histories Not To Be Believed, Sabinus's Commentary on the Metamorphosis, and other works abound in plenty. And what connection is there here? Scripture has God as author. Therefore it is proper to it to contain two senses: nay rather, since the craftsman of mind and tongue speaks in Scripture, therefore he speaks clearly, and expresses in speech all that he embraces in his mind: for that speech is best which fully and clearly sets forth the meanings of the mind ἀπεικονίζει. If it must still be guessed what someone wants for himself in his own words, in what sense they are to be taken—if he says one thing and hides another—this is not approved among the wise.

136. We accept therefore that saying of Bellarmine, that firm and effective arguments can and ought to be drawn from the literal sense alone. If allegory, trope, and anagogy were genuine senses of Scripture, then certainly effective arguments would also be sought even from those, as things pronounced by the Holy Spirit—which when Bellarmine denies (and rightly), he really denies that allegories, tropes, and anagogies are various senses of Scripture. We approve that saying of Jerome on Matthew 13: From mystical senses the doctrines of faith cannot effectively be confirmed. Which he repeats on Zechariah 8, on Malachi 1, Augustine Book 2 On the Merits of Sin

last chapter, Book 2 On Christian Doctrine chapter 9, Letter 48 against Vincent. But this must be understood concerning mystical senses devised by interpreters: For if the Apostles interpret something allegorically, firm arguments are nevertheless drawn from those allegories.

137. But now let us speak more fully about allegories. Augustine, bk. 15, On the City of God, ch. 27, asserts that we must not agree with those who receive only the History without allegorical significance, nor with those who receive only the figures while rejecting the truth of history. Bk. 17, On the City of God, ch. 3: just as I think those greatly err who judge that no deeds recorded in this class of writings signify anything other than what was done in that way, so do those venture much who contend that everything there is entirely wrapped up in allegorical meanings. Jerome, on the Letter to Pammachius, most justly complains of Origen because he allegorizes in such a way as to take away the truth of history. The Fathers were quite generous with allegories; today certain men are quite hostile to them; therefore what should be determined concerning allegories?

138. Those who treat these matters carefully warn that there is a distinction between allegory and type. A type is, when some deed of the Old Testament is shown to have prefigured or foreshadowed something done or to be done in the New Testament. An allegory is, when something from the old or new Testament is expounded with a new sense and adapted to spiritual doctrine or instruction for life. The type consists in comparing things done; the allegory is occupied not so much with facts as with the discourses themselves, from which it draws forth useful and hidden doctrine. Types are gathered together under certain definite heads—concerning Christ, concerning the Church, etc.; but allegories lie open very widely and spread through whatever materials. Hence one and the same History can be expounded both typically and allegorically. If I say that the History of David with Goliath signifies the contest of Christ with the Devil, it will be exposition by type: if I say that the fight of flesh and spirit is meant, it will be an allegory. But indeed the Fathers do not always observe this distinction, and the Apostle Gal. 4. v. 24. he asserts that things are said per allegoriam, which however, strictly speaking, are typical; hence Chrysostom in his Commentary on that place rightly warns that the word allegoria is there used for type.

139. You ask, how far one should proceed in allegories? Ans. 1. The chief care must be for the literal sense, which is to be drawn from the words and from the context itself: for that sense which is gathered immediately from the words is the certain sense of the Holy Spirit: from that literal sense various doctrines, exhortations, consolations, and ἔλεγΧοι of adversaries can be drawn: Basil in Hexaëm. 2 commends this literal exposition of Scripture most highly. If the Holy Spirit himself interprets something in the Scriptures typically or allegorically, there we safely follow the allegory, for we can be certain that the Holy Spirit had regard to it. 2. In moral precepts, promises, threatenings, and treatments of dogmas, no allegories are to be sought. Hieron. on Gal. 4. An allegory is not to be sought in precepts that pertain to life, or in things that are clear and manifest. 3. Interpreters are therefore inept and perverse who seek allegories in every passage of Scripture. August. 8 de Gen. ad lit. c. 1. Those who believe that all things are said figuratively in the sacred writings are deceived. 4. The ceremonial laws of the O. T. may be treated allegorically, because they were shadows and types of good things to come. 5. Histories likewise can be treated allegorically, yet so that the historical truth is preserved unshaken. David conquered Goliath, so Christ conquered the Devil, so the pious affection of the flesh &c.; meanwhile let it remain that truly long ago a great Goliath was conquered by David. 6. Allegories in dogmas do not produce firm proofs (I except -emper those which Scripture itself sets forth), but they only adorn the faith. 7. The use of allegories therefore is more suitable for popular sermons to be delivered than for convincing the adversaries of the truth. When decently and moderately employed, they delight, stir up, remove tedium, and so are especially suited for exordiums. 8. But one must diligently labor that the allegories be apt, and above all that they be analogous to the faith.

140. But how are allegories to be conformed, so that they may be fitting and analogous to the faith? The scope of the whole Scripture is Christ, therefore his office, his benefits, his kingdom must above all be expounded in the allegories. Thus Christ applies the figure of the manna and of the brazen serpent, the history of Solomon and Jonah to himself, John 3. and 6. Matt. 12. Thus the Apostle applies the type of the paschal lamb, of the propitiatory, of water from the rock &c. to Christ 1. Cor. 5. Rom. 3. 1. Cor. 10. Therefore the articles of the faith must first be accurately perceived from the proper and clear statements of Scripture before anyone wishes to go over to the allegories, and care must be diligently taken lest anything against αναλογίαν the faith, i.e. the constant and perpetual judgment of Scripture concerning the doctrines of the faith, be brought forth in the allegories. Here there is a propensity to slip, and therefore judgment and carefully considered prudence are required.

141. An allegory gains the greatest grace if its sources can be shown from Scripture itself: for often a single little word is a key for opening the allegorical sense. Thus, most members of the precept concerning the paschal lamb can be accommodated to Christ and his faithful people, because Paul 1. Cor. 5. v. 7. says, Christ our Passover is sacrificed for us. Those are the most apt and most sweet allegories which can be elicited from the words of Scripture compared among themselves, and to which some support or at least illustration can be applied from the very voices of Scripture.

142. Care must be taken, however, lest the enemies of allegory hold sway too widely, for then they will be crude and harsh; nor should they conflict with the principal parts of the History, which we wish to treat allegorically. Nor ought one linger on them longer than is right, but so that favor may accrue to them, let them be touched upon briefly in only a few words, shrewdly and with a certain sweet sharpness, and let them not be overly intricate and confused. Briefly, it is not for just anyone to handle allegories aptly and decently; therefore let those less experienced act soberly and prudently here. Those who treat allegories unseasonably and without judgment can easily bring forth what the skilled despise, the malicious mock, and by which the weak are offended. Certainly Origen was reproached by the ancients on this account.

142. Hyperius teaches most correctly: sometimes necessity itself compels us to pursue allegories, sometimes indeed only utility counsels it. The necessity of expounding by allegory arises from three causes: First, when the Scriptures, unless you admit that a trope underlies them, carry falsehood before them. Thus Ps. 91 v. 13. You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, you shall trample the lion and the dragon: Christ is not read to have done this, therefore it must be explained concerning the Devil, the world, sin, and death overcome and subdued. Second, when the words of Scripture, taken in the grammatical sense, produce absurdity. Thus human affections are attributed to GOD, anger, fury, weariness; yet these are rather incongruous with the spiritual and immutable nature of God; therefore they must be explained concerning the effect, not the affection. Third, ⟦f3⟨when the grammatical sense conflicts with the rule of faith. Aug. 3. de doctr. Christ. c. 10. Whatever in divine discourse cannot properly be referred either to the honesty of morals or to the truth of faith is known to be figurative. c. 16. If a preceptive utterance seems to command a disgrace or crime, or to avoid usefulness and benevolence, it is figurative."}

143. Thus Christ commands to pluck out the eye, and to cut off the hand and foot, Matt. 18. v. 8. and 9. But taken in the literal sense this fights against the Lord's Precept: You shall not kill. Therefore, as Chrysostom warns, homily 17 on Matthew, the words are not spoken about destroying the structure of the members, but the evil of pleasure is reproved. We are commanded not to mortify the members of our body, but those of the old Adam, which are upon the earth, namely fornication, uncleanness, lust, wicked concupiscence, and covetousness, as it is expounded in Colossians 3. verse 5.

144. Utility urges that allegories be employed when the very words themselves taken grammatically seem to bring forth no useful doctrine or instruction, or even if something indeed appears, yet far richer fruit would come if an allegorical interpretation were joined. Thus we read that Jacob was deceived by Laban, Leah being substituted in place of Rachel: interpret that allegorically, that God deceives many men of this age through love of earthly things, so that they think it is Rachel, that is, most beautiful and lasting goods, but when they awake from sleep of wicked concupiscence, they recognize that it is Leah.

145. Augustine, On the Usefulness of Believing chapter 3, and elsewhere, distributes rather differently the method of interpreting Scripture, for he establishes it fourfold: first according to History, namely when it is taught what was written or what was done. The second κοτ᾽ αίτιολογίαν, when it is shown for what cause something was said or done. The third κατ᾽ ἀναλογίαν, whereby the agreement of both Testaments is demonstrated. The fourth κατ᾽ ἀλληγορίαν, when it is taught that the things written are not to be received literally, but understood figuratively. This he subdivide in the book On True Religion chapter 50 into the allegory of history, the allegory of deed, the allegory of speech, and the allegory of Sacrament.

146. We have said enough concerning the allegorical sense. That however manner of interpreting

reason κατ᾽ άίολογίαν is not a new sense besides the literal one, but ought to be referred entirely to it: for neither is departure made there from the grammatical sense, but only, when the cause of what was done or said has been set forth, the meaning becomes clearer, and in quite many places the true and genuine sense cannot be investigated without the aid of αἰτιολογίας, namely, so that attention be paid to who says something, to whom, with what counsel and end he brings it forward. Likewise Αναλογία introduces no new sense of Scripture, but compares sayings or deeds of the New Testament with the sayings or deeds of the Old Testament, and shows their agreement. Just as this is required in the whole scribal institution toward the kingdom of heaven, that he be like a father of a family, who brings forth out of his treasure things old and new, Matt. 13. v. 52.

147. These things having thus been expounded we return to our corollaries, drawn from that theorem, that the rule of faith is above all to be observed in the interpretation of Scripture. The first was, that the interpretation of Scripture ought to be literal and proper. The confirmation and true understanding of this corollary can appear from those things which we have just now spoken concerning the various senses of Scripture. Irenaeus book 2 chapter 46: That sound sense is safe and free from danger, which is placed openly and without ambiguity in the very words in the Scriptures.

148. The second was, that one should not depart from the letter, especially in articles of faith, unless Scripture itself show and explain the impropriety. This follows from the first. If the Holy Spirit had wished us to understand something else, He could easily also have spoken otherwise. Therefore that sense beyond doubt is the sense of the Holy Spirit which is gathered from the very words. If any impropriety in articles of faith is contained in Scripture, it is explained elsewhere in proper words. The Prophetic books and Apostolic ones are inscribed throughout the whole Church O. and N. Testamentum. Now indeed those most weighty admonitions of the -Ctorum are well known, whereby they forbid any departure from the words of the Testaments taken properly. Chrysost. upon Isaiah 5. Sometimes several passages of divine Scripture must be interpreted allegorically, wherever it beseems us to follow the mind of Scripture, and to employ the trope of allegory after that fashion. For it did not allow that the authority of applying its sayings to whatsoever things or persons hearers pleased should rest with the hearers, but Scripture itself, forestalling this, has interpreted Scripture.

149. The third was, that there is no dogma of faith which is not set forth somewhere in Scripture in proper and clear words. This follows from the second; for if the improper signification of words in the articles of faith must be demonstrated and expounded from Scripture itself, then assuredly all the dogmas of faith are set forth somewhere in Scripture in proper and clear words. It is confirmed by the same thing from the perfection and perspicuity of Scripture. For if among the articles of faith there were anything to report which is not proposed anywhere in Scripture in proper and clear words, its perfection and perspicuity would certainly perish. Things improperly spoken can be variously exposed; therefore those alone which are spoken properly and clearly furnish a fixed and unmoved opinion. Iren. lib. 2. cap. 46. Because parables can admit many resolutions, abandoning from themselves assertions regarding the inquiry of GOD—who, though professing love of truth, will not acknowledge that they are exceedingly precipitating themselves into peril and unreason? Aug. Epist. 48. Who does not strive most shamelessly to interpret something placed in allegory in his own favor, unless he has plain testimonies whereby the obscure are illustrated? Thom. part 1. q. 1. art. 1. Nothing contained under the spiritual sense is necessary to faith which Scripture does not somewhere plainly deliver according to the literal sense.

150. It was the fourth point that the rule of faith must be accepted entire, nor are its parts to be set against one another. The reason of this corollary is evident, because all things which belong to the rule of faith are utterances of the Holy Spirit, which cannot and ought not to be set against one another. Therefore wherever any article of faith is proposed, the literal sense must be retained, nor should it be opposed to the other articles of faith. E.g., the Arians deny the Deity of the Son, because there is one God, not attending to what follows from the rule of faith, namely that we must believe not only the unity of the divine essence but also the Trinity of persons. The Tritheists introduce three Gods, because there are three persons of the Deity, not attending to what follows from the rule of faith, namely that we must believe not only the Trinity of persons but also the unity of the divine essence.

151. It was the fifth point that, even if at most we do not attain the genuine sense in more obscure passages , nevertheless we must not depart from the rule of faith. We must indeed labor diligently so that we may attain the genuine sense of each passage, but if ever we cannot investigate it thoroughly, let us beware lest we bring forth anything contrary to the analogy of faith, concerning which matter we spoke above. Augustine, Book 11 of the City of God, chapter 33: "The obscurity of this treated saying has been discussed not without profit (that by the light the good Angel, and by the darkness the evil one, may be understood), because although we could not track down the will of the author of this book, yet we did not stray from the rule of faith, which through other sacred letters of the same authority is sufficiently known to the faithful." The same, Book 1 of On Genesis Literally Interpreted, chapter 21: "When we read the divine books, amid such a multitude of true understandings, which are drawn out from few words and fortified by the soundness of the Catholic faith, let us love especially that which appears certain, that he whom we read thought thus. But if this lies hidden, then certainly that which the circumstance of Scripture does not hinder, and which accords with sound faith. But if even the circumstance of Scripture cannot be examined and weighed, at least that which sound faith prescribes. For it is one thing not to discern what the Writer chiefly meant; another to stray from piety. If both are avoided, the fruit of reading stands perfectly well. But if neither can be avoided, even though the will of the Writer be uncertain, it is not useless to hold an opinion agreeable to sound faith."

152. The use of these observations and their consequences, which we have set forth, is very great in the interpretation of Scripture. Let me declare the matter by example. Bellarmine, Book 3 on the Word of God, chapter 9; Stapleton, in his Relections on the principal matters of faith, controversy 6, question 7; and other writers argue thus: Because already so many years, indeed centuries, there has been dispute about the words of the Supper, and yet the matter is still unsettled, therefore Scripture cannot say what its true sense is, therefore the interpretation of Scripture from Scripture itself is doubtful and uncertain. Therefore the means of interpretation proposed above are insufficient, consequently some infallible and authoritative judge and interpreter besides Scripture itself is required.

153. But let us follow the guidance of these rules. The interpretation of Scripture ought to be proper and literal, especially in articles of faith. Now truly in those passages which deal with the Lord's Supper, an article of faith is presented. Therefore the words must be retained in their proper and literal sense. Conversely, in articles of faith one must not depart from the letter unless Scripture itself explains the improper usage: now Scripture nowhere teaches that the words of the Supper are to be expounded thus: Bread is a sign of the body of Christ: Wine is a sign of the blood of Christ: nor have they even yet been able to produce any suitable example of their own (so-called) sacramental metonymy from the Scriptures. Therefore such tropological and figurative speech is not to be introduced into the words of the Supper. Further, there is no dogma of faith which is not somewhere set forth in Scripture in proper and clear words. Now truly Matt. 26. Mark 14. Luke 22. 1. Cor. 10. and 11. treat expressly of the doctrine concerning the Supper, and this is the proper seat of this teaching. Therefore those passages are to be taken in their proper and literal sense.

154. If they say, the rule of faith compels us to depart from the literal sense , namely because according to the rule of faith it must be asserted that the body of Christ is a true and natural body. Likewise that Christ has ascended into heaven with his body: the fourth observation comes to aid, that the rule of faith is to be accepted entire, nor are its parts to be set against one another. Scripture teaches both, that Christ's body is truly a human body, and yet that it is truly distributed in the Supper; therefore both are to be believed, neither is to be opposed to the other. For Christ's body is not only truly a human body, but also the proper body of the Son of God. Christ not only ascends into the heavens, but also sits at the right hand of GOD.

155. These therefore are not contradictory: Christ's body is a true body: and Christ's body is eaten in the holy Supper: because both the words of Scripture teach in their proper and literal sense. Scripture is not to be heard in one place only, that Christ has a true body, but also in the other, that that true body is present in the Supper. If they absolutely wish either one to be denied, whether the truth of the body or its eating in the Supper: let them explain to us the reason why they would rather deny the eating of Christ's body in the Supper on account of the truth of the body, than the truth of the body on account of its asserted eating in the Supper.

If they say, the truth of the body is an article of faith, we must ask whence they know this? They will answer surely, from Scripture, and indeed from the literal sense of Scripture: But, I say, Scripture likewise teaches, and indeed in the literal sense, that the body of Christ is present in the Supper and is eaten. Therefore even that presence and eating of Christ's body in the Supper is an article of faith.

156. Let someone say, like a Marcionite, that the body of Christ is not a true and natural body, because in the sacred Supper it is distributed to be eaten. Therefore those passages which state that the body of Christ is truly a human body must be understood figuratively, so that the article concerning his Supper may remain intact. Certainly this can be met in no other way than by saying that both things are to be asserted and believed: that the body of Christ is truly a human body, and yet that it is eaten in the Supper; nor are these articles of faith opposed to one another, but both are to be accepted by the obedience of simple faith. Unless that fixed and settled point is held, then with the same license by which departure is made from the literal sense of the words of the Supper, a Marcionite will also depart from the literal sense of those passages in which the truth of the human nature in Christ is asserted.

157. But Bellarmine concludes far too broadly. Book 3 on the Sacraments of the Eucharist, chapter 19: the words of the Supper, if taken properly, necessarily imply transubstantiation: The bread, he says, is changed either metaphorically or truly and really. We answer: nay rather, there is given a third option, the bread is changed sacramentally, that is, it becomes the medium, ὄΧημα and instrument, through which, in which, and with which the body of Christ is distributed. And the pronoun This: in the words of the Supper indeed denotes the bread, but not only (for what sort of construction would that be, αςτος τοῦ ζ? ), but the whole complex. For when two things are united in some manner, customary usage expresses the predicate that is worthier and less obvious to the senses, but does not express the other part, which is obvious to the senses.

158. But since we began to treat the controversy about the Interpretation of the words of the Supper by way of example, the very greatness of the matter requires us to discuss those things more broadly. Perkins disputes in his book on the unique manner of the Lord's Supper, p. 49, τὸ ῥητὸν that what is preserved in the words of the Supper fights against the Ascension of Christ and against the Nature of the Sacrament: but that new sense of theirs, namely that the bread is a symbol of the body of Christ being absent (for so he writes), agrees first with the analogy of faith. 1. Christ truly ascended into heaven, that is, was taken up from earth into heaven locally and visibly; therefore his body is not to be received by mouth in the Supper, but by faith in heaven. 2. He was born of the Virgin Mary. Therefore he had a true and natural body, long, wide, tall, situated somewhere and circumscribed by place; whence it is established that the bread in the Supper cannot properly be his very body, but only its symbol.

159. Answer. The essence of the bread literally is not the body of Christ, but sacramentally, so that when that mystical bread is eaten, at the same time the body of Christ is eaten—which does not fight against the analogy of faith, as we just showed; therefore no necessity compels us to depart from the literal sense of the words and seek a new sense. It is not asked whether Christ has truly ascended bodily into heaven, and whether he has a true body; but whether it fights against the article of the Ascension and against the truth of the body of Christ, that his body is present in the Supper , concerning which several things are set forth below.

160. Secondly it fights τὸ ῥητὸν (says Perkins) with the circumstances of the given passage. 1. He took, he broke: here it is not likely that Christ, sitting among the disciples, took and broke his own body with his hands: Therefore, the Bread is only a sign and seal. Answer. What God hath joined together, let not man separate. The Evangelists report that Christ not only took and broke the bread, but also blessed it, distributed that blessed bread, and clearly added what he distributes, while declaring this to be his body. Therefore it is neither true nor likely that Christ distributed mere bare bread to his disciples; otherwise he would have mocked them with deceitful words. 2. Delivered for us. Bread can by no means be said to be delivered for us, but the body of Christ. Therefore, bread according to τὸ ῥητὸν is not the body, but symbol. Answer: We turn it around: That thing which Christ distributed at the Supper was what was delivered for us unto death. But now bare bread has not been delivered for us unto death, but the body of Christ has been delivered for us unto death. Therefore He did not distribute bare bread, but His own body. 3. The cup is the New Testament not properly, but by metonymy. Therefore nothing prevents there likewise being metonymy in these words, This is my body. Answer: The cup is not simply called the New Testament, but something is added: in Christ's blood, that is, on account of Christ's blood, whose is κοινωνία. 1 Corinthians 10, verse 16. Matthew and Mark express it thus: This is my blood of the New Testament, which comparison τὸητον confirms. The cup does not signify the New Testament, but is the New Testament—how so? Not in itself, but in Christ's blood, which it presents to those who drink. 4. Christ Himself ate the bread, yet not His own body. Answer: Where indeed does Scripture assert this, that Christ partook of the mystical bread together with the disciples! 5. Do this in remembrance of me: Therefore Christ is present not bodily to the mouth, but spiritually to the faith of the heart. Answer: They confuse the substances of the Supper and its saving fruit. The Supper was instituted for the commemoration of Christ. Do this, He says, in remembrance of me. Is therefore Christ absent from the Supper? Nay rather, because the Supper was instituted in remembrance of Christ, therefore truly present there He distributes His very body. 6. Until he come; therefore Christ is absent in body. Answer: He departed, and here He is, He will return again, nor do we serve . In vain do we await His return from heaven, and nevertheless we believe His body is distributed in the Supper, for He commands us to believe both things in His word. 7. Christ did not say, under the species of bread or in the bread, but this, that is, this bread is my body. Answer: The hypothesis is false, since the particle This: denotes bread alone.

161. Thirdly, it is said to fight against τὸ ῥητὸν the nature of the Sacraments, in which an analogy must be placed between the sign and the thing signified, which can be none at all, if the bread is properly the body of Christ: Answer. Concerning any Sacrament we must judge from its description in its proper place, nor are general statements pronounced about the Sacraments of both Testaments to be fabricated ἄτες γραΦῆς. And what prevents placing an analogy between bread and the body of Christ, even though that is truly present on earth?

162. Fourthly, that new sense is said to agree with similar passages Gen. 17. verse 10. This is my covenant between me and you: You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, that it may be a sign of the covenant. Answer. It proceeds from the particular: there the covenant is put for the sign of the covenant. Therefore also in the words of the Supper the body for the sign of the body. Moreover when it is said, Circumcision is the covenant, circumcision is described by its form, and thus, Circumcision is the covenant, that is, a Sacrament and covenantal action, just as Baptism too is the covenant. When afterwards it is said, Circumcision is a sign of the covenant, the Sacrament of Circumcision is described by its end, just as in Rom. 4. it is said, Circumcision is a seal of the righteousness of faith, namely effectually sealing it, just as Augustine says in his confession concerning article 13 that the Sacraments are testimonies and signs of the divine will. 2. 1. Cor. 10. v. 4. They drank from the spiritual rock, and the rock was Christ. Answer. The Apostle speaks of the spiritual rock which accompanied the Israelites; but this did not signify Christ, but was Christ himself: from this spiritual rock all drank, yet with this distinction, that the wicked drank in the type only, but the devout in the type and faith together. 3. Rom. 4. v. 11. And he received the sign of circumcision, which sealed the righteousness of faith. Ans. The Apostle expressly explains the word 'sign' so that by it the sealing σΦραγὶς is understood. 4. Exod. 12. v. 11. It is the passing over, and immediately after, c. 13. v. 9. The lamb is a sign of the passing over. Ans. Neither proposition is found in Moses, much less does the exposition of the night-time watcher hold any place, even if it were granted most fully that circumcision signified the covenant on some definite ground, and the rock signified Christ: yet this could not be applied to the business of the Supper without destroying the distinction between the Sacraments of the Old and New Testament; those properly were σκιαῆ and figures, but in these there is place for εἰκῆν and the very substance of the thing formerly shadowed forth. 5. Act. 22. v. 16. Baptism is the washing away of sins. Ans. By the name of Baptism is understood the entire Sacrament, not merely the external washing, but also the Word added to the Element concerning regeneration, adoption, and eternal life: and in this sense Baptism does not signify the washing away of sins, but is most truly the laver of regeneration. But where does Scripture say that the washing of water in Baptism signifies the washing away of sins? elsewhere more fully on this matter. 6. Ioh. 6. v. 35. I am the bread of life. Ans. Christ is the bread of life, the term 'bread' being taken not metonymically but metaphorically. If in the words of Christ there is such a sacramental metonymy, what will their paraphrase be? surely this: Christ signifies the bread of life: nay rather, He does not signify it, but is most truly that bread of life which can satisfy our spiritual hunger. 7. 1. Cor. 10. v. 16. The cup of blessing, which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread, which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? that is, the sign of communion. Ans. But what license of twisting things is this , taking 'communion' for the sign of communion? Where then at last does Scripture speak expressly and clearly about the Supper? And what kind of paraphrase will this be? The bread is the communion of the body of Christ, i.e., the bread is the sign of the communion of the sign of the body. For thus they insist that in the words of the supper the term 'body' must be taken for the sign of the body, and so the bread will be a sign of a sign. Nay rather, from this passage of the Apostle the firmest argument can be drawn for our opinion, namely that the mystical bread is not a signification of the body of Christ absent, but rather a communion of Him present.

163. Fifthly, that new sense is said to agree with the precepts of Logic: for what is dissimilar is not spoken of the dissimilar except by way of Trope. Resp. The false hypothesis keeps returning, namely that the little word This: denotes bread alone; besides, whether by Trope in these propositions, God is man, Man is God? Not what suits the precepts of Logic, but what suits the words of Christ must be sought: τὰ ήμέτερα ύπὲρ λόγοι, says Justin. Finally, that new sense is said to agree with received custom of speech: Thus we use rods for empire, scepter for kingdom, gown for peace. Resp. But what Author ever speaks thus: The rods are the empire, the scepter is the kingdom, the gown is peace.

146. Let us return, after this digression, which this Writer wished to carry out within this very problem concerning the Interpretation of Scripture, ἐργασὸα, to our own undertaking. We have said that the rule of faith is to be accepted entire, and that its parts are not to be opposed to one another, seeing that the articles of faith, taken in their proper and literal sense, do not conflict with one another, but human reason fabricates contradictions for itself; and this is the fountain of all heresies. Tertul. against Praxeas chap. 18: Scripture runs no peril, such that you should come to its rescue with your argumentation , lest it seem contrary to itself. It has good reason, both when it establishes one God, and when it sets forth two, Father and Son, and it suffices for itself.

165. Surely judgment concerning true contradiction in articles of faith must not be permitted to human reason, otherwise it would be established as the Mistress of Scripture, since nevertheless it is neither a fit rule for discerning the will nor the power of God. Not of his will, because no man hath seen God at any time; the Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him,John 1. v. 18. Nor of this [power], because God ὑπὲρεκπεριου οδ can do more than we understand.Eph. 3. v. 20. Therefore every thought must be taken captive πᾶν νόημα into obedience to Christ.2 Cor. 10. v. 5. And care must be taken lest we suffer despoilation by Philosophy.Colossians 2. v. 8.

166. Here there is a proneness to fall, therefore it will not be absent from propriety if we speak somewhat more fully about the use of Philosophy in the Interpretation of Scripture. Its use can be threefold. Οργανικὸς, κατασκευα-ικὸς, κοὶ ὰναικευαςικὸς. The organic use is when our reason brings along with itself, drawn from the philosophical disciplines, Grammar for the proper signification of words, Dialectic for observing order, Rhetoric for expounding figures, and Physics for knowledge of natural things, so as to dig up the treasure of divine wisdom hidden in the Scriptures. We commend this use most highly, nay rather we say it is necessary: and those eulogies which are attributed to Philosophy, but especially indeed to Logic, by the ancients quite honorably, should be referred here. Aug. 1. against Cresconius c. 15. v. 20. 2. on Christian doctrine c. 31. 3. against the Academics c. 13. Basil on Isaiah 5. etc.

167. As far as the use κατασκευαςικὸν is concerned, it is thus to be held. There is a certain natural knowledge of God Rom. 1. v. 19. and 20. yet it ought to be subordinate to that which has been revealed divinely in the Word: wherever it dissents, let it yield to it; in what things it consents, it receives strength and certainty from it. Briefly, let Philosophy serve that Lady as her handmaid and minister, and rise reverently before her. Gerson, book 1, On the Consolation of Theology, prose 1: Philosophy is not cast off by Theology, but taken up by it into its service. To this also belongs Philo's allegory in the book On the Cherubim, who compares Philosophy to Hagar, but Theology to Sarah.

168. Scaliger disputes in his Exercises, 6, section 3, that the craftsman receives questions, statements, utterances, conclusions from another craftsman in two ways. One way is when the knowledge of the lower science depends entirely on the principles of the higher, which happens in subordinate sciences. The other way is when the craftsman admits those things laid down by another, which he could know even without him, but n--n as principles of his own, nor approved by that other as though he himself were unable to approve them, but so that he may examine and judge them. In this latter manner the Theologian receives certain things from the Philosopher. For the Theologian accepts that theorem, that God exists, from Philosophy, not as though apart from the principles of Philosophy he could not know it from Scripture as a principle of his science ὀικείῳ, but because in examination he observes its truth according to the standard of his own principle. Gerson, book 3, On the Consolation of Theology, prose 4: Theology approves the doctrines of Philosophy, if they are true, if right, if wholesome, using e-s by its own right and making them Catholic; if they are more obscure, it illumines them; if mixed with harmful errors, it separates the precious from the vile, retaining the former and expelling the latter.

168. Ανασκευαςικὸς or ἐλεγκμκὸς, that the use may be legitimate, it ought to be compared thus. Erroneous doctrines must first be refuted from the foundations of Sacred Scripture, as the unique and proper principle of Theology; afterwards philosophical reasons too may be added, so that it may be shown that that false dogma conflicts not only with the light of grace but also with the light of nature.

But where the truth of any dogma has been firmly demonstrated from the immovable foundations of Holy Scripture, let us not suffer ourselves to be led away from it by any philosophical reasons, however specious. Ανασκευαςικὸς [Refutatory].

170. The Sayings of Antiquity on this matter belong here. Justinian, question 117. It cannot happen that an assertion concerning things done above Nature by divine power be established by natural reason. Tertullian, On the Prescription: What has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What have the Academy and the Church? What have heretics and Christians? Our institution comes from the porch of Solomon. Chrysostom, homily 5 on 1 Corinthians: To wish to understand divine things through philosophy is to touch glowing iron not with tongs, but with fingers. The same, homily 21 on Genesis: It is great peril to commit matters of faith to human reasons. Ambrose on Psalm 118: Nothing have we to do with philosophy, lest it lead our faith astray through the elements of this world; but truly we know the Arians fell into unbelief while thinking the generation of Christ was to be gathered from the custom of the age; they left the Apostle and follow Aristotle. Book on Faith, chapter 5: Take away arguments where faith is sought. Bernard, Letter 190: What is more against faith than to refuse to believe what you cannot reach by reason? Mary is praised because she anticipated reason with faith, and Zechariah punished because he tested faith with reason. Junilius, book 2, questions, chapter 30: Those things which reason teaches, faith understands; and where reason fails, faith runs ahead. Anselm in his letter on faith to Pope Urban, chapter 2: If anyone can understand, let him give thanks to God; if he cannot, let him not raise horns to winnow, but bow down his head to venerate: whence concludes Altissiodorensis in the Preface of the Summa. With Aristotle an argument is a reason making faith about a doubtful thing, but with Christ faith makes the argument.

171. What indeed, since the very Philosophers themselves acknowledge this in such a manner ? Plato in the Timaeus says, that the Philosopher should be confirmed concerning divine things only so far as that very thing is confirmed by divine Oracles. In the Phaedrus he says, men are brought back from errors to knowledge by two vehicles of true reasons, of which one is through demonstration of known things, which mode of knowing he calls ἀπὸδειξιν:; the other truth descending to us from God, which he names θειον λὸγον, and there concludes that human wisdom accomplishes nothing compared with that which is had from the Oracles. He also said, as Theophrastus reports, Aeneas Gazaean p. 720. in the works of Philo, that one must believe up to the point when someone wiser than oneself arrives, yet none is wiser than GOD. Aristotle λὸγους καρτερικωτέρους (by whom some understand divine authority) somewhere excepts, and does not disapprove that assent be suspended on their account. In the Metaphysics he praises that worn-out saying of Simonides: Concerning divine things and those beyond Nature belief must be given to GOD alone. 1. an--. ch. 7. con. 59. requires that it become the συγγέιρια of terms without proof, nor let there be made μετα βασες είς ὰγγο γέιος: ὰοὰγκη εκ τοδ ὰυτοδ γειους τὰ ὰκρα καί τὰ μέσα είναι. Alphrabnus the Arab, book 1. protrep., wished divine things and those credible by pure faith to be of a higher order, whose comprehension weakens human reasonings, nor can they attain them, as Peter Gregory reports in his comment on the article of wonders ch. 1. p. 11. Beautifully Scaliger, exercise 77. sect. 2.: What was said above, the laws of Nature are not to be judged from the laws of Nature. Exercise 365. sect. 3.: So much the worse for certain ones of those Theologians who persuaded themselves that they could measure out the immense fields of our religion with the ten-foot rod of the ancients, sect. 9.: It belongs both to our piety and to the immensity of GOD to sense those things which we cannot sense—to sense indeed in Him Himself, through Him Himself, what we cannot sense through ourselves. Erasmus brings forward a most beautiful example in the Symbolic Catechesis 2. p. 43.: If any Idiot were to shout down such a Philosopher as Aristotle or Pythagoras was, or anyone more learned than either, discoursing about prime matter, about first principles of things, about the Infinite or the magnitude, motion, nature of the heavenly orbs, doubting all things which he could not attain—would he not seem arrogant and mad? But how much greater is the madness, therefore not to believe divine things because of Philosophy, seeing that many things are not attained by human understanding! Moreover between God and man however erudite the difference is infinitely many parts greater than between the wisest man and the most foolish rustic.

172. The force of truth has deserved their assent: which we complain they do not observe everywhere . Calvin, Book 3, Institutes, chapter 23, section 4.
