It is unworthy to reduce that law to the works of God, so that as soon as their reason has not been established before us, we dare disapprove it. Beza, in Epigrams, page 249. Those things which God has handed down to us by his own voice cannot be known by human reason. Sadeel, in the preface to his Theological Works, on method, Disputation of Theology. Since theology is above all sciences, to subject it to philosophical principles is not merely absurd but also most unjust and most unworthy. Aretius, part 1, problem 2. What insolence is this, to make divine mysteries subject to the common laws of Nature, which since they are inexplicable to all human reason ought rather to be adored than debated? Zanchius, volume 5, On the Nature of God, chapter 2, page 620. The Word of God and human prudence always fight against each other. Peter Martyr, class 2, Common Places, chapter 1, §. 25. First what we wish to be believed must be shown from the sacred letters; then if we cannot attain that, we rely upon faith and set aside reason. Mornay, preface to the book On True Religion. So far is human reason from being the measure of faith that it cannot even be the measure of Nature because of ignorance and depravity. The same author, preface to the book On the Eucharist, page 44. Thomas restricts his doctrine directly to Scripture—how unlike those who wish to dispute against it from the principles of Philosophy or other disciplines according to the rule of Logic μὴ μετα βαίνειν εἄς ὰλλο γένος, do not pass from one science to another, since according to the true use of Logic our reasoning ought to derive from the principles of one science the theorems, and from these the corollaries pertaining to that same science. This he says most rightly.

173. Is there then something true in Philosophy, you ask, which is false in Theology? Answer. We treated this matter in a certain Metaphysical Disputation on Truth, from which we shall copy out what pertains here. To be at the same time both true and false cannot occur, namely per se and ὡσὰντως. For no Being simultaneously is and is not. Yet some say that what is true philosophically is false theologically. It must be understood with a certain respect, namely by reason of a faulty application. 'A virgin gives birth,' 'a virgin does not give birth': these are not contradictory per se. For the latter is understood naturally according to the ordinary course of Nature—for Physics deals with things that happen naturally and ordinarily—therefore its axioms are to be received with this limitation. The former is understood to come about through God's supernatural and extraordinary power. If therefore anyone wishes to set the former against the latter, he abuses that axiom: ἀφιλὸσοφον for it is to take what is particular and relative as universal and absolute. Nothing natural is to be opposed to the supernatural. For nature is not opposed to its creator.

God is Lord of Nature, Nature is His minister, Whom it is right to follow reverently, obeying her Lord's commands. Nor does the use of a thing extend itself more widely than the thing itself; The philosophical principles moreover are natural ones.

174. They therefore act in an inverted and perverse order, who assail the literal sense in some article of faith on philosophical principles: For the literal sense must not be abandoned in articles of faith because of an absurdity of reason. Gryn. disp. Heidelb. de Coena thes. 25. & 26. Bucanus in locus 48. pag. 711. distinguish between corrupted reason and that which after regeneration has become spiritual: to the former they refer what is said in the Scriptures about taking captive the understanding under obedience to Christ, about guarding against Philosophy συλαγωγία &c.; but they say that faith ought not to be diminished when it comes to the latter, since it was made πνευμαηκὴ. after regeneration. What should be determined concerning this matter?

175. Answer. Human reason can and ought rightly to be considered in two ways. In one way in those resources which by its own native ability, using its own principles, such as common notions, senses, experience, induction, it possesses as acquired; in the other in those which it receives within itself from elsewhere, namely from divine revelation. Or in one way as left to itself and set free, in the other as enclosed and disciplined within the sphere of the divine word. Or in one way, as running without bridle, when it is carried along by its own reasoning wherever its feet lead; in the other as running under bridle, restrained through the word of GOD and restricted under obedience to Christ. Or, in one way, such as it is both in man and in the Philosopher, insofar as he is man and Philosopher; in the other such as it is in man or in the Christian Philosopher, not insofar as he is simply man or Philosopher, but insofar as he is a Christian man and a Christian Philosopher, just as Mr. Schröd. most skillfully proposes and explains this in de princ. fid. c. 1. sect. 2. §. 3.

176. Now therefore the question is, when a man already born again attacks the literal sense in articles of faith from principles of reason, is he to be said to do this according to regenerated reason? Answer. By no means indeed; for even though the reason of such a man has been reborn, nevertheless inasmuch as he wishes to dispute against the articles of faith from his own principles, to that extent it is no longer reborn, because reborn reason disputes from the principles of the word. Whoever disputes from principles of reason against the mysteries of faith does so not insofar as he is a Christian, but insofar as he is a man abusing Philosophy. Therefore, just as whoever is born of God does not commit sin 1 John 3. v. 9. namely insofar as he is such, and insofar as he retains the grace of regeneration; but if he should wish to follow the lusts of the flesh, he sins and becomes subject to death, Rom. 8. v. 13. thus rebirth does not oppose the articles of faith, namely insofar as he is such, and insofar as he follows the leading of the word; but if he should wish to attack the word of GOD out of his own principles, he errs and is no longer reborn.

177. Let us declare the matter by an example, which we also used above . It is asked, Is the body of Christ truly, really, and substantially present at the Supper? The churches of our side affirm it, because Christ says: Take, eat, this is my body. On the contrary the adversaries deny it on this principle, because a true and natural body cannot be simultaneously and at once in several places. They add that renewed reason cannot determine otherwise about the body, therefore its testimony must be heard. But, I say, renewed reason (insofar as it is such) determines about the articles of faith from the word of God, and does not go beyond its limits. Now indeed the word of GOD is, This is: take, eat, this is my body. If reason disputes against this word of CHRIST out of its own principles, it is no longer renewed, but follows its own leading, and just so must it not be heard, as the Philosopher ought not be heard when he disputes against the resurrection of bodies from that principle: No individual that has once perished can return again the same in number: or an anti-Trinitarian disputing against the mystery of the Trinity from this principle:

One thing cannot be three. Or an Arian disputing against the eternal generation of the Son from this principle: What is begotten is later than the one begetting.

178. But, someone says, reason arguing against the presence of the body of Christ in the Supper does not rely simply on its own principles, but on Scripture's declaration concerning the truth of Christ's body: Response. One ought to hear Scripture not only in one respect, namely that Christ has a true body, but also in the other, namely that Christ's true body be present in the Supper. The rule of faith must be accepted entire. It is not here asked whether Christ's body is a true body, but this is asked: whether, given the standing truth of the body, it follows rightly from there that God cannot make that true body present in the Supper. They say: the nature of a body does not admit it, for it is finite; I ask whence they know that this stands opposed to Christ's body being simultaneously present in several places? Certainly from the principles of reason. For Scripture says the contrary: therefore the final resolution of the argument returns to a conclusion drawn from a principle of reason, and it is viciously set against the words of Christ. Let that sophistical hiding-place therefore be removed which they wish to prepare for themselves in that distinction between regenerate reason, or, as they speak, spiritual, and unregenerate.

179. To this place belongs that observation which St. Basil proposes in a certain Epistle, that we should not rashly conclude from what is written what is not written. Indeed Gregory Nazianzen rightly says, Orations 5 on Theology, that those things which are gathered from the Holy Scriptures are to be regarded just as if they had been written in them; but great care is needed here. Stealthily human reason thrusts itself in, and by its own judgment accommodates Scripture to its inventions. Therefore let the rule be: whatever is gathered from Scripture that conflicts with other plain passages of Scripture must be judged to have been less legitimately collected.

180. And let these things be said concerning the rule of faith more fully indeed, but so did the matter itself require: we shall treat of the remaining matters more briefly. We said above that obscurity arises in certain passages of Scripture because they seem to conflict with other texts. For although there is nowhere any true contradiction in the Sacred Scriptures, according to the testimony of Chrysostom, homily 1 on Genesis, since πᾶσςα γραφὴ that sacred writing is θεόπνευςος:, nevertheless an apparent contrariety and ἐιανριοθανές of some kind very often presents itself. Augustine, Book 5 of De Genesi ad litteram, chapter 8: "We must strive to bring it about that no absurdity or inconsistency be thought to exist in the Sacred Scriptures, which might offend the reader's opinion." Origen, on Romans 3: The one who faithfully and wholly gathers together the sense of the sacred volumes ought to show that the things which appear contrary in Holy Scripture are not contrary.

181. To reconcile that apparent contrariety, this remedy must be applied: that we inquire into the true and genuine sense of each place from the words themselves and the circumstances. For, because a true contradiction has no place in the Scriptures, therefore, as soon as the genuine sense of each place is established, every contrariety that seemed to be present is removed. The ambiguity and repugnance which appears in the sacred letters must be removed from the consequences and adjuncts of the text itself. Aug. 3 de doctr. Christ. c. 2; lib. 1 de Gen. ad lit. c. ult.

182. Let this be the rule for reconciling των έναντιοθανων. If any contrariety seems to arise between certain passages compared with one another, let it be taught that the opposition is not of the same thing, but of the name only, or not according to the same respect, or not toward the same end, or not in the same manner, or not at the same time. Thus in Matthew 10 verse 10 Christ forbids the Apostles to take a wallet for their journey, nor two tunics, nor shoes, nor a staff: this seems contradicted by what is said in Mark 6 verse 8: And he commanded them that they should take nothing for the journey except a staff only, no wallet, no bread, no money in their belt, but that they should wear sandals. Reconciliation: With Matthew is meant a staff that arms for defense; with Mark, a rod that supports travelers. The shoes in Matthew are new ones, diligently procured for the journey; the sandals in Mark are not new, but those worn daily upon the feet. It can also be said that Christ's saying in Mark is to be understood comparatively. Even if they were equipped with neither staff nor footwear, which nonetheless seem especially necessary for a journey, still his purpose was that they should not be hindered.

183. To this general rule very many special ones can be added, which by reason of circumstances can be distributed into certain classes. Now these circumstances are: The Person (who speaks, to whom, about whom, before whom he speaks); the Occasion (the counsel, the end); Time, Place, Manner.

184. These rules pertain to the circumstance of the person. 1. Persons in the Scriptures are often bionymous. Jerome against Helvidius. Thus Gideon, Jerubbaal Judg. 6. verse 32. and Jerubbesheth. 2. Sam. 11. v. 21. Thus Abimelech. 1. Sam. 21. verse 3. And Abiathar. Mark 2. v. 26. Thus Solomon 1. Sam. 12. v. 24. And Jedediah v. 25. Thus Simon, Peter, and Cephas. 2. Distinct persons are often mononymous. Examples occur in the genealogy of Christ described by Matthew and Luke. 3. Sonship is either natural or legal; natural comes by generation, legal by adoption. Thus Luke, in describing the genealogy of Christ, follows the natural order, Matthew the legal. 4. Different things are said concerning the regenerate because they have, as it were, two men within themselves, the old and the new. Thus the regenerate are said to be sold under sin, Rom. 7. verse 14. namely on account of the old man; the regenerate do not commit sin. 1 John 3. verse 9. namely on account of the new man.

5. Concerning Christ some things are said according to his divine Nature, some according to his human nature, some according to both, etc.

185. To the Circumstance of Counsel, End and Occasion this rule pertains. The understanding of sayings must be taken from the causes of speaking. Hilary, Book 4 on the Trinity. Thus Christ Matt. 19. v. 21. to the young man instructed in the school of the Pharisees, and falsely glorying in his perfect fulfillment of the law, proposes this special pre-cept, that he sell everything and distribute to the poor, and in this way follow Christ; namely, Christ wished to convince the man that he had not first fulfilled the commandment about loving God above all things. Thus Christ proposes the Gospel to those who are terrified and crushed, but sends away the Scribe swollen with the opinion of his merits back to the Law. Luke 10. v. 26.

186. Many rules can be given concerning the circumstance of time , yet truly there is that old saying, Distinguish times and you will harmonize the Scriptures. 1. Some sayings deal with the time of the humiliation, some with the time of the exaltation of Christ. 2. Time is taken either completely or incompletely. 2. And its parts are taken either inclusively or exclusively. Thus Matt. 17. v. 1. Truly after six days Jesus takes Peter etc.; Luke 19. v. 28. But it came to pass after these words, as it were eight days etc. Matthew places exclusively only the intervening days, which flowed by in full: Luke counts even the outermost days inclusively. 4. In rounder numbers often what is lacking or exceeds is not reckoned. Augustine, question 47 on Exodus. Thus Judges 11. v. 26. it is said that Israel dwelt in Heshbon and Aroer three hundred years, although an exact computation offers more. So too the Seventy Greek Interpreters are commonly so called, although they are seventy-two. 5. Sometimes a finite number is put for an infinite. Seven times daily the just falls, seven times daily shall I sing praise to you etc. 6. In sacred computations, because of the wickedness of a Prince, his name or the number of years during which he governed badly is omitted. 1. Sam. 13. verse 1. Saul reigned over Israel two years — understand legally, or as Lyra says, by right. 7. If a king hindered either by foreign war or old age or disease while alive established his son as vice-king, then in computing the years of father and son reigning together, the years of reign are sometimes counted jointly, sometimes separately. Use was made of this rule in collecting the years of the kings of Israel. 8. Thus what is said at Mark 15. verse 25., It was the third hour when they crucified Jesus, and John 19. v. 13. It was about the sixth hour, then he says to the Jews: Behold your King: various persons reconcile in various ways. Some acknowledge a fault of the Greek writer, who painted γ. instead of ς.; some distinguish between the beginning and the completion of the act. Augustine [says] the Jews crucified Christ at the third hour with their tongue, the soldiers at the sixth hour with their hands. But the simplest reconciliation seems to be that the Easterners divided the artificial day variously, both into twelve ordinary planetary equal hours and also into quarters (just as night into four watches), which take their name from the immediately preceding hour.

187. These rules deal with the circumstance of place. 1. In Scripture often two names are assigned to one place . 2. Often one name is given to distinct places . Thus Jerusalem, Jebus and Salem denote one city. There were two Canas. Succoth is the name of three places: the first is in Egypt Exod. 12 v. 37., the second in the tribe of Gad Josh. 13. v. 37., the third in the tribe of Manasseh 1 Kings 7. v. 46. . 3. The sacred writers often designate a place by that appellation which was customary at the time in which they themselves lived and wrote. Thus Gen. 12. v. 5. afterwards setting out thence toward the east to the hill country, the district of Bethel. So the place was called in Moses' time, but in Abraham's time not Bethel but Luz, Gen. 28. v. 19. etc.

188. Likewise many rules can be handed down concerning the circumstance of Manner. 1. Thus some sayings are ἁπλῶς,, others κατὰ τὶ.. 2. Some simply, others comparatively. Parents are to be honored, and yet with a certain regard they are to be hated, Luke 14. v. 26. That is, their authority is to be set aside, namely if they command anything against the heavenly Father. 3. Sayings specially detract from general ones, just as the Jurists also say: in the whole body of law the genus is derogated by the species. 4. Moral precepts take precedence over ceremonial ones. 5. The second table of the Law yields to the first. 6. Some sayings speak about the Nature of a thing in itself, but others are understood as sayings per accidens. Thus Christ says he came not to send peace, but a sword, Luke 12. v. 15. Namely because Satan and the impious stir up persecutions against the doctrine of Christ. So far concerning the rules to be observed in reconciliation ἐναντιοφανῳν; a diligent and faithful Interpreter of Scripture will gather more of them; here it suffices for us to have pointed out the sources.

189. We still advise one further point on the reconciliation of passages, that the best method of reconciling is, if possible, that an arbiter be given from Scripture, namely some third passage of Scripture which harmonizes those conflicting places, or clearly confirms the reconciliation brought forward by us. Thus the regenerate are sold under sin, Rom. 7. v. 14. and the regenerate does not commit sin, 1 John 3. v. 9. how are these to be reconciled? The Apostle answers, Rom. 7. v. 22. I delight in the law of God according to the inward man. verse 23. But I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind, and leading me captive to the law of sin which is in my members. Thus the doctrines of the Law and Gospel seem contrary, but the Apostle constitutes himself arbiter. Rom. 3. v. 30. do we destroy the law through faith? Far be it, rather we establish the law. Gal. 3. verses 21.

does the law act against the promises of God? Far be it. Thus they appear to be contradictory. Circumcision is to be observed Gen. 17. v. 17. Circumcision is not to be observed, Act. 15. v. 24. Christ constituted himself arbiter, Matth. 11. vers. 13. The Law and the Prophets were until John.

190. If certain passages of Scripture taken by themselves and separately are obscure, such obscurity arises either from things or from words. To remove the obscurity arising from things, besides the illumination of the Holy Spirit, which must be obtained through prayers on feast days, it is useful to hold fast certain fixed axioms in any article whatever of Christian doctrine , which serve as a kind of guiding star and standard against which the treatment of all other passages must be measured. We can call such axioms Catechetical or Elementary; commonly they are called Theological rules. They can indeed be gathered by a diligent and faithful Interpreter of Scripture according to the series of Theological places. We shall go before with an example.

191. On the Article concerning God these axioms are to be observed. The works of the Trinity toward the outside are undivided, yet preserving order and distinction among the persons. Augustine, Letter 99; On the Trinity, Book 1, chapter 5; elsewhere frequently. Athanasius, Oration against Gregory, Sabellius etc. The essential attributes are common to the three Persons of the Godhead. There is nothing in God which is not God himself. Bernard, On Consideration, Book 5, to Eugene. That which operates is the single essence common to the three. Nazianzen, Oration 2 on Theology. Works which God performs outside every creature within himself are not common to the three persons, but belong to only one person. An exclusive predication used about one Person of the Godhead does not exclude another. Cyril: God is confusedly one and inseparably three. In divine matters we shall neither separate the substance nor confuse the persons. ού φθάνω τὸ ἐνιοησομ και τοις τροςι περολάμπομαι, ού φθάνω τά τροια ςιέλειν, και -ς ρὸ ἐν αναφέρομαι. Nazianzen, On Holy Baptism.

192. In the article concerning Christ these axioms are proposed. The properties of Nature become common to the Person. Vigil., book 2, against Eutyches. Theodoret, Dialogue 3. In Christ there is ἄγγοκαι αγγο, but not ἄγγος και αγγος.. Damascus, On the Orthodox Faith, book 3, chapter 5. In the works of the Mediator both Natures act with the participation of the other. Council of Chalcedon. Whatever things are said to be given to Christ in time are to be understood as given according to his humanity, Athanasius and the ancients everywhere.

193. In the place concerning the law these are the axioms. Whatever accuses and condemns sin belongs to the law, whether used in the Old Testament or in the New. Forensic and ceremonial laws are abolished in the New Testament. The moral law was not first set forth on Sinai, but engraved upon the hearts of men before the fall. Those who are reborn are not under the curse of the law, yet meanwhile they are not free from obedience. By the word 'law': when sins are named specifically, all sins of the same kind, their causes, occasions, entanglements, and opposite virtues are signified by those particular sins. The rule and measure of obedience in affirmative precepts is You shall love GOD with your whole heart; in negative ones, You shall not covet. God commands not only the hand and outward members, but the whole man. The promises and threats added to the law, together with the condition of obedience, are to be understood thus: the former with the condition of perfect obedience, the latter with the condition of repentance. The promises of this life given to the godly are to be understood with the exception of the cross.

194. In the locus concerning the Church these are the axioms. Because in the militant Church the good are mixed with the wicked, hence something is often pronounced about the whole Church because of its more noble part. Here dwells the Jebusite among the Jerusalemites; here in the garden of the father of the family salamander-herb and fir-tree, nettle and myrtle grow side by side; in Jacob's flock animals white and black, lambs and kids; in Peter's net fish good and bad; in the Lord's field lilies among thorns; on the Lord's threshing-floor grain along with chaff; in Christ's cellar wine with sour grapes, oil with dregs. Chrysostom. Sacred Scripture sometimes speaks in the person of the head of the Church, namely Christ, sometimes in the person of the body. Augustine, in Psalm 40. Outside the Church there is no salvation; he who has not the Church for mother on this earth has not God for father in heaven. Augustine, On the Creed [de Symbolo], book 4, chapter 10. These things are joined together and most intimately connected: God, the Word, Faith, the Church, Salvation and eternal life, etc. More axioms could be gathered from these very places and others of Christian doctrine. It suffices for us to have pointed a finger at the sources.

195. The obscurity of Scripture arising from the words can be remedied by grammatical exposition of the terms, attention to the idioms of the original language, and rhetorical explanation of tropes and figures.

Therefore the faithful interpreter must know the languages in which the Old and New Testament were written, concerning which we spoke in the Disputation on Scripture. It is profitable therefore to collect certain rules according to fixed classes, by which the idioms of the Hebrew tongue are explained. We shall again set forth examples beforehand.

196. It is known how Grammarians distribute the parts of speech; rules are to be collected according to their order. Concerning nouns there are these rules. Proper names are frequently taken in the Scriptures for patronymics and national designations, as Ishmael, Esau, Jacob, Israel, for the whole posterity.

The name of a highly proper accident is put for the thing itself, as dryness for land: desirable things for treasures. A noun is often put for an Adverb: Judge justifications, that is, justly. Death has been swallowed up into victory, that is, destroyed victoriously. Abstract nouns are often put for persons: thus foreskin for the Gentiles, Circumcision for the Jews, etc.

197. Concerning these there are also the following rules. Words of knowledge among the Hebrews often connote an effect of the heart. "The Lord knows the way of the righteous," that is, he approves and promotes it. The Hebrews use Neutral verbs in the third conjugation transitively. "God arises the sun," that is, makes the sun arise; "he triumphs us in Christ," makes us triumph. Simple words are often used for compounds, to call for to invoke. Verbs are often taken habitually. Thus to sin sometimes denotes not only the action but also the habit. Concerning participles these rules are handed down: Participles are often placed for nouns; thus πειράζων tempting for tempter. The present participle is used for the present indicative, "glorifying" for "we glory." Concerning adverbs these are the rules: Adverbs are often used for nouns, "the day tomorrow," that is, tomorrow's day. The adverb "until" denotes the duration or existence of some thing in such a way that meanwhile it by no means intimates that afterwards it ceased or that the contrary followed, etc. It is fitting to gather very many such rules, on which matter see Flaccius p. 2, Key, Treatise 3; Abdias Praetorius concerning the phrases of Scripture. Idiotisms must also be observed not only in the parts of speech considered absolutely, but also in their government. But let someone skilled in languages arise who might accomplish something absolute for us in this respect; here it suffices to have pointed out the sources.

199. Things said tropically and figuratively are to be explained according to the precepts of the rhetoricians. Now Scripture has certain peculiar figures, on which matter see Flaccius, part 2 of the Key, treatise 4. Thus anthropopathy is spoken of when members and human affections are attributed to GOD. Rules can be gathered according to certain classes by which the tropes and figures customary in Scripture are explained. The synecdoche of Holy Scripture is most usual, by which a general word signifies specially, and conversely: nothing for little, none for few, eternal for a long time. Augustine, Book 6 against Julian, chapter 12, where observe: restrictions in the articles of faith to be demonstrated from Scripture itself. So when it is said that Christ suffered for all, it does not suffice to say that the universal particle 'All' is taken for many. Therefore also here. By no means! but it must be shown that in this very matter it is taken restrictively. For it was stated above that in the articles of faith we must not depart from the proper sense of the words unless Scripture itself shows and explains the improper usage. An enallage of the past tense for the future is frequent in the oracles of the Prophets on account of the certainty of the thing foretold. Ellipsis signifies either brevity or swiftness of emotions. Pleonasm signifies either force and emphasis, or multitude, or distribution, or diversity and variety. Let someone arise here who would likewise perform something absolute for us here! It suffices here to point out the sources.

199. Concerning parables and similitudes (which are nothing else than continued Metaphors) it must be observed that the same thing can sometimes furnish similitudes in a good sense, sometimes in a bad one. Thus leaven is taken in a good sense, when Christ says: The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven: but on the contrary in a bad sense, when he says: Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees. Likewise in parables not all parts always, nor simply, can be fitted to the subject at hand, but it must be diligently observed what by analogy can fit or aim most directly at the present scope. Chrysostom on Matthew 20. In parables individual words and members are not to be pressed beyond and outside the purpose for which they are employed in Scripture, nor are other doctrines to be built upon them than those which Scripture demonstrates should be drawn from them. Moreover, knowledge of things makes figurative and parabolic expressions more vivid, when the Natures of animals or stones or herbs are clearly perceived. See Lemnius on Biblical Herbs, and ηριθςαφίαν Biblical.

201. For discerning the force of words and phrases, the comparison of passages contributes very greatly toward the true understanding of Scripture, by which passages are placed side by side as parallels, so that their meaning may shine forth more clearly. Acts 9. v. 22 Saul was growing ever stronger and was confounding the Jews who dwelt at Damascus, συμιάζων demonstrating by the testimonies brought together (as craftsmen intending to fit something together are accustomed to adjust the individual parts among themselves, so that some square with others according to the rule) that he [Jesus] is the Christ.

13. By comparing things comparable, having a certain similarity of speech declaring the same thing both in senses and in dogmas, so that in the mouth of two, three, or more witnesses cited from Scripture every word of God may be founded and confirmed. Homil. 24. in Num. What is sought in the Scriptures is found more easily if it is brought forth from several passages which are written concerning the same matter.

202. To this belongs that precept, that the more obscure be explained by the clearer, the fewer things by the many. Irenaeus, book 2, chapter 47: Let the parables accord with those things which are spoken plainly, and the things which are plain resolve the parables. Tertullian: The fewer things must be understood according to the many, lest a single word overthrow many others, but it will have to be taken according to all things rather than against all things. Basil, On the Ascetic Life, 267. τα άμφίολα έπιχεχαλυμμένως είρηομ δοχντα ν τισί τόποις της εοπνέυ ροφης ύπό των ν άλλοις τόποις όμολομένων σαφηνίζεται. Aug. 2. on the doctrine of Christ, chap. 9. For the illustration of more obscure modes of expression, examples are to be taken from clearer passages, and certain testimonies of settled teachings are to take away doubt concerning uncertain matters. 3. on the doctrine of Christ, chap. 26. Where meanings are set forth more plainly, there one is to learn how they are to be understood in obscure places. Jer. on Isa. 19. It is the manner of the Scriptures to connect the plain with the obscure, and to utter aloud what they had earlier spoken under enigmas.

203. The comparison of passages is twofold. The first is of a given passage with itself repeated elsewhere in Sacred Writ. Thus Isa. 6. verse 10. Make the heart of this people fat &c. this passage is repeated six times in the N.T. Matth. -3. v. 14. Marc. 4. v. 12.Luc. 8. v. 10.Iohan. 12. v. 40.Act. 28. v. 27.Rom. 11. v. 8. But repeated passages sometimes have certain variations, both έξησεως, and for the sake of brevity. Psal. 110. v. 1.Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies the footstool of thy feet -uorum.1. Cor. 15. v. 25.Christ must needs reign, un til he shall have put all his enemies under his feet. Thus Deut. 16. v. 13.Thou shalt fear Jehova thy God, and serve him.Matth. 4. v. 10.Thou shalt adore the Lord thy God, and him alone shalt thou serve. Thus Es. 29. v. 13.Their reverencing of me is a commandment taught by men.Matth. 15. v. 9.In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines, the commandments of men. For the comparison of such passages serve the Parallels of Franc. -unii. Observe here the rule which Dr. Chemnitius sets forth in book 2 of the Harmony, chap. 17: Whenever any saying from the Old Testament is alleged in the New Testament, not only those very words that are alleged are to be considered, but the whole passage is to be inspected, so that that portion may be considered the more diligently.

204. To this in a certain way pertains the comparison of the type with the antitype, and of predictions with their fulfillment. Jonah 1. v. 7. Jehovah had prepared a great fish, which might swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the bowels of that fish three days and three nights. Matth. 12 g. 39. An evil and adulterous nation seeks a sign, and there shall not be given to it, except the sign of the Prophet Jonah etc. Thus Psalm. 62. v. 29. They gave for my food bitterness, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. Ioh. 19. v. 28. That the Scripture might be fulfilled, he said, I thirst. v. 29. A vessel therefore was there placed full of vinegar. Thus Exod. 12. vers. 46. You shall not break a bone from it. Ioh. 19. v. 26. For these things were done, that the Scriptures might be fulfilled, you shall not break a bone of him. He who will rightly observe these things, will be a Scribe learned for the kingdom of heaven, able to bring forth from his treasure things old and new. Matth. 13. v. 52.

205. The second comparison is of a given passage with others either similar or dissimilar. Similar passages are, which agree either in phrase or in meaning, Gen. 3, 15. The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent: Rom. 16. v. 15. God shall crush Satan under your feet. For seeking out such passages, Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and German Concordances are useful; for they exist in all these languages.

206. As to meaning, very many passages agree, for one and the same thing, one and the same head of heavenly doctrine is more often repeated in the sacred writings της σαφένείας άσφαλείας. Deut. 6. v. 4. Hear O Israel, the Lord thy God is one. 1. Cor. 8. v. 6. Although there are those who are called Gods, yet to us there is one God. For seeking these out, the Thesaurus of Vogel, the Syntagma of Judex, the Pandecta of Brunfels etc. are useful. Someone will indeed arise, who may so treat all and singular the articles of faith, that all and singular the passages of Scripture, which treat of one and the same thing, may be referred under some one head, and may be explained by the very words and foundations of Scripture. ένανΤιοφανη

207. Dissimilar passages are those which do not agree either in phrase or in sense. For it is useful not only to compare those passages of Scripture in which the same word is used in the same meaning, but also such ones in which the same word and phrase is used differently. But if certain passages seem not to agree in sense, let a prudent reconciliation analogous to faith be applied. Yet anyone at all understanding must confess that that great Chemnitius was almost a master craftsman in the comparison of passages άμίμέτον.

208. Thus far concerning the obscurity which words or phrases of Scripture occasion: if any arises from the whole context and habit of speech, it will be removed by that observation of the scope, circumstances, connection of members, and manner of speaking customary to any writer: for this is άναχςίνειν τας ςαφας Acts 17. verse 11. attending to reading, 1. Tim. 4. v. 13. meditating in the law of the Lord, Ps. 1. v. 2. έρευνάν τάς αφας John 5. v. 39. etc. 209. Let us hear on this matter the precepts of the Fathers. Clement of Alexandria, 7th Stromata: It is proper to heretics Χρηα ραφαίς τελείας δ ως τό σωμα ά τό ύφ της προφέταίας ωαορέυει. Augustine, book 83 questions, q. 69: The circumstance of Scripture usually illuminates the sense, when the things surrounding the Scripture touching the present question are treated with careful discussion. The same, On the Words of the Lord, sermon 2: Let him read what is below and above, and he will find the sense which the perverse man wished badly to misinterpret. Hilary, 9 On the Trinity: The understanding of sayings should be sought from what precedes or from what follows. Cyril, book 8, Th., chapter 2: Before all else, when we wish rightly to understand a passage of Scripture, three things must diligently be considered, the time when what is written was written: the person who speaks or through whom he speaks, or about whom it is spoken: and the subject on account of which or about which it is written. Chrysostom, upon Psalm 2. As building without a foundation is weak, so unless the goal is found, Scripture is useless. Lactantius, Divine Institutes 4, chapter 5: He who strives to grasp the truth ought to apply his mind not only to understanding the words of the Prophets, but also to inquire most diligently into the times in which each of them lived.

210. The goal of the whole Scripture is Christ; that we may find Him in the Scriptures, this ought to be our chief care. The Apostle judged that he knew nothing else except Christ, and Him crucified1. Cor. 2. v. 2. All the Prophets give testimony to HimActor. 10. v. 43. In Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms things were written concerning Him.Luc. 24. v. 44. Εςευνάτ τάς ραφάς, the Savior says,Iohan. 5. v. 39. For you think that in them you have eternal life, and they are they which testify of me. Just as miners diligently search out the veins of gold or silver: so we ought to seek in the Scriptures that true vein of life, Christ έρευνάν. Aug. tract. 9. in Iohan. The Old Scripture does not taste, if Christ is not understood in it. On Psalm. 71. All things that are written in the Sacred Letters are referred to Christ. Nor will you unfittingly refer to the Prophetic and Apostolic writings what Prudentius says of the ancient Christians:

All things of Christ, through Christ all things speak.

211. The goal of each passage and chapter will be made plain by its careful examination. The Apostle says 1. Tim. 1, 7. of the seducers, that they do not attend to what they are speaking about, nor what they affirm or deny concerning it. He wills therefore that we hold and observe the Nature of the propositions, that is, whether it be subject or predicate, the definitions of each thing, and the whole matters and arguments of entire books, or even of individual parts.

212. To this place belongs that observation, that there is somewhere in Scripture a kind of certain and proper seat for each doctrine, while elsewhere it is merely touched upon. Now judgment must be made about any doctrine from its own seat, nor should those places be pressed in which only ⟦f1 casually and incidentally something is said about it, against the treatment set forth in its proper seat. Thus the doctrine of Justification is treated expressly and as it were in its proper seat in Rom. 3. and 4. Eph. 2. Gal. 2. and 3. Therefore all the other passages of Scripture that deal with Justification are to be brought to conformity with it. The Articles concerning the Supper have their proper seat in Matth. 26. Marc. 14. Luc. 22. 1. Cor. 10. and 11. therefore let the doctrine of the Supper be drawn from those passages, not from foreign ones. ως παδω

213. One could also discourse in this place in general about the style of the sacred writings, and likewise in particular about the Historical, Dogmatic, and Prophetic Books of the Old Testament, and about the Evangelical and Apostolic Books of the New Testament; what the diversity of style is in all these, and what is peculiar and proper in each of them: but we aspire at last to the end. Concerning this matter, one may consult Aug. lib. 4. de Doctr. Christ., Iunil. de Partib. sacr. literar., Pagninus in Isagoge ad Biblia, Flac. part. 2. Clavis tr. 5., and others passim.

214. And having spoken thus far about the means of Interpretation, let it suffice, which, in order that they may be effective, wholesome and fruitful, require these three things: Prayer, Meditation, and Temptation/Trial, all of which the Prophet David treats throughout Psalm. 119. About Prayer we spoke above. By the term Meditation we understand frequent and constant study of the Scriptures, to be undertaken with ardent fervor of spirit. Blessed is he who in the law of the Lord meditates day and night. Psalm. 1. vers. 3. where is the voice הוה which Reuchlin says, on the authority of Rabbi Joseph, is metaphorical, taken from birds that murmur/chatter, and so has a twofold meaning: first, diligently to meditate; secondly, continually to mutter over it. Timothy knew the sacred letters from infancy, 2. Tim. 3. v. 15. and yet he is commanded by the Apostle to give attention to reading. 1. Tim. 4. v. 13. For frequent reading of the divine Scriptures produces understanding of them. Theophylact on the Epistle to the Romans.

215. Therefore that precocious δοξοσοφία, is above all things to be fled, by which half-scholars, as soon as ever they have read some little thing in the Scriptures, and have at least touched those most limpid (though profound) springs of Israel (like the dog come from the Nile), too hastily promise themselves a perfect and absolutely complete knowledge of them; contrary to which δοξομανίαν Dr. Luther often thunders. In reading (he says) the Scriptures, you will never be too diligent; what you shall have read diligently, you will never have understood too accurately: what you shall have understood rightly, you will never have taught too faithfully : what you shall have taught faithfully, you will never have sedulously expressed in life as an example.

216. To the head of meditation belongs also this precept, that other Interpreters be consulted, especially that venerable hoary-headed band of the ancient doctors of the Church. For although their Interpretations are not authentic, nor to be set on a level with the Canonical Scriptures: nevertheless with grateful mind the pious labours of those men ought to be acknowledged and commended. 1. Thessal. 1. v. 19. Despise not the Spirit v 20. Do not reject prophecies. v. 21. Test all things; hold fast that which is good. Nor is God to be deemed to have preserved in vain the testimonies of a purer Antiquity, but rather that they might be a kind of support for investigating the sense of Scripture, and that, when the true opinion has been plainly discerned from the very Scriptures, their minds may be the more confirmed. For what could be more pleasant than to gaze upon that kinship of doctrine (as Tertullian says in his De praescriptione) which the Churches of us Christians have with that primitive race of the Fathers?

217. To this point pertains what Augustine writes against two Letters of the Pelagians, book 5, chapter 8: "Since the Church of Christ, both Western and Eastern, shuddered at the profane novelties of speech of the Pelagians, I judge it to pertain to our care, not only to bring forward the holy Canonical Scriptures as witnesses against them, which we have already done sufficiently, but also to produce some testimonies from the writings of the Saints who handled those matters before us with most celebrated fame and immense glory — not because any authority of a disputant is equalled by us to the canonical books, as though it were altogether impossible that something better or truer be felt by one Catholic than by another Catholic likewise, but so that those may be admonished who think that these men say something, how on these matters, before the new babblings of such men, the Catholic Bishops followed the divine utterances, and let them know that the right and anciently founded Catholic faith is defended by us against the presumption and mischief of the recent heretics the Pelagians." Let there be therefore in view the example of Jerome, who writes about himself in the Letter to Minervinus: "It is my judgment to read the ancients, to approve individual things, to hold fast what is good, and not to depart from the faith of the Church." Luther on Genesis chapter 2, p. 27: "The labors of the Fathers ought to be venerated; they were great men, yet nevertheless men, who could stumble, and did fall."

218. By the name of temptation we understand the practice, which Epiphanius, book 2, tome 1, heresy 61, p. 221 calls in Greek άησιν. πάντα (he says) τά α αηματα χ άλληορίας δται, άλλά ως έΧει; εωςίας δέ δείτα χαί άιησεως, είς τό δένα έχάης ωοέσεως την δύναμιν. But if άιησις be joined to Theory, it will attain that which Augustine writes On the Ladder of Paradise, chapter 2.

Reading inquires, Meditation finds, Prayer asks, Contemplation tastes; whence the Lord himself says: "Seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you." Seek by reading, and you will find by meditation: knock by praying, and it shall be opened unto you by contemplation. Reading sets before the mouth, as it were, solid food; meditation chews and breaks it; prayer acquires its flavor; contemplation is that very sweetness which delights and refreshes: Reading [deals] with the rind, Meditation with the fat. Prayer in the petition of desire, Contemplation in the delight of the sweetness attained. Bernard, On the manner of praying, column 1252. Reading is, as it were, the foundation; it comes first, and having given the material sends us on to Meditation. But Meditation more diligently inquires what ought to be desired, and, as it were digging up the treasure, finds and shows it; but since it cannot obtain it by itself, let it send us on to prayer; prayer, raising itself with all its strength toward the Lord, obtains the desirable treasure, the sweetness of contemplation; this in turn, coming upon us, rewards the labor of the aforementioned three, while it intoxicates the thirsty soul with the heavenly dew of sweetness.

219. That trial or temptation, whether action or άιηοιν or practice or contemplation, we establish for the sake of teaching as twofold. One kind lies in Exercises of penance, faith, prayer and piety, so that all these things may be serious and proceed from the inner man: another lies in the cross and calamities, both inward ones (which the Apostle calls fears, 2. Cor. 7. v. 5. commonly called spiritual temptations) and outward ones or calamities. Unless this twofold practice and inward taste of the Scriptures come along, their treatment will be barren and sterile.

220. "It is good for me, O Lord, that thou hast humbled me, that I might learn thy statutes," says the Psalmist Ps. 119. v. 71. "Affliction gives" "understanding," says Isaiah, chapter 28, verse 19. Therefore the best way to the knowledge of God is the school of the cross and calamity. "The school of the cross is the school of light."

221. It is not our intention to suspend the efficacy of the divine word from the dignity or quality of the minister (for we know that it matters little whether water for irrigating garden beds passes through a stone conduit or indeed through a silver one , ), meanwhile, so that the treatment of Scripture may be useful to the minister himself and more fruitful for the hearers, we most deservedly require that practice and interior taste of divine sweetness (as it speaks ).

222. If you wish me to weep, you must first feel grief yourself, says Horace in *De Arte Poetica*; thus also, if you wish to inflame me, you must first burn yourself. Wood capable of flame does not burn unless fire is applied, and he who wishes to stir pious affections in others must himself be piously affected first. Those things that ought to descend into the hearts of others must needs ascend from the heart, and those things which the inner man brings forth, those also strike the ears of the inner man. You will never enter into the sense of Paul, says Bernard in his sermon to the brothers on the mount, unless you have imbibed the Spirit of Paul.

223. If anyone considers diligently, says Savonarola book 3, on the division of sciences, p. 800, he will perceive that Scripture is learned rather by purity of heart, good works, contemplation, and the illumination of the Holy Spirit than by force of intellect. Rightly therefore Gerson concludes in prosa 4, De consolatione theologiae, lib. 4, that Theology (the bare knowledge of Theology), unmixed with faith, hope, and charity, inflates and harms. Therefore just as with Cicero the Orator is described as being a good man skilled in speaking, so we call a theologian a good man educated in sacred letters, indeed not by an education of the understanding alone, but much more of the affections, so that what he understands through Theology he may transfer through continual ruminating into the affection of the heart and the carrying out of the deed. For just as reason, the most excellent gift of men (these are still Gerson's words), turns to the ruin of themselves and others among the reprobate—so also wine makes those who do not use it toward soberness all the madder the better it is, not through fault of the wine but of the drinkers—the same must be said of Theology."

224. If any man will do the will of the Father, says Christ, Ioh. 5. v. 44. he shall know of my doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself. How can you believe, he says again Iohan. 5. v. 44. which receive honour one of another, and seek not the honour that cometh from God only? Wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body that is subject unto sin, it is said Sap. 1. v. 4. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, it is said in the Scriptures not once. Consider accurately what these sayings mean, and you will find that the affairs of the Christian religion would be in a far better state if we were to apply ourselves more to the cultivation of the inner man. Concerning which matter we have spoken in the preface to the *Sacred Meditations*, and perhaps we shall say more in its proper place.

225. Consider what that Martyr of Christ Ignatius wrote on this matter, Epistle 11 to the Ephesians, p. 63. άμεινόν έι σιωπάν έιναι, η λαλίν μη έιναι. χ ν λόω τ η Βασιλία ε, άλλ ν δυνάμει. Καλόν τό διδάσχειν, ό έάν λέων ποιη. ός άρ άν ωοιησει διδάξει, τ μέας ν τη Βασιλεία. ό χύςι ημάν ό ες Ιησς Ξςιός ό αός τ ε ωντ πρωτον έωοίησε χαί τότε έδίδαξε. Justin Martyr, in his Paraenesis: Not in words but in deeds do the matters of our religion consist. These are those lights of the ancient Church, when greater regard was still had for conscience than for knowledge; for the heart than for the mouth.

226. Out of gratitude of mind someone might refer here what the ancient philosophers hand down concerning the purification of souls , necessary for the knowledge of divine things.

Hermes Trismegistus, in sermon 1 of the Poimandres, when asked by what means anyone can ascend to life, answered: This can happen when man becomes aware of himself as sharing in Mind. For Mind is not present to all men, but only in those who are pious, good, pure, religious, holy, and who grant their body over to death, despising the enticements of the senses, judging the deadly allurements of the senses worthless, shutting off access to shameful flatteries, and extinguishing the kindling-sticks of lusts; whereas on the contrary it is absent from the ignorant, envious, wicked, slothful, unjust, murderers and impious, and dwells very far away from them. The same, in sermon 7 of the Poimandres: First of all you must strip off the garment which you carry about, the clothing of ignorance, the foundation of depravity, the bond of corruption, the dark covering, living death, the sentient corpse, the portable tomb, finally the household thief, who while flattering hates, and while hating envies. Such is the enemy-shade that you carry about. It drags you down upon yourself, lest perhaps seeing the beauty of truth and the nearest good, you hate this depravity of yours, nor ever perceive beforehand its snares, which it continually plots against you within. This dulls and blunts the keenness of your inner senses, smothers it with gross matter, makes it drunk with abominable and loathsome pleasure, so that you should never hear nor clearly see those things which ought rightly both to be heard and above all looked upon. The same, in the second part of the Poimandres, sermon 1: Unless you make yourself equal to God, you will never understand God. For like is always known by its own like. In the same place: The soul must be stripped from the body not through true separation, but through the mortification of sensible pleasures, so that one may be able to understand divine things, and so that the soul may be transformed into God, it must be made godlike, that is, rendered most similar to God. The same, in the same place: Extend yourself into boundless magnitude, emerge out of the body, surpass wholly time, become eternity: thus at last shall you know God.

227. The rest imitated this Philosophy of Trismegistus. Zoroaster, in the Oracles: Man contracts God into himself in a certain manner, when, retaining nothing mortal, he is wholly made drunk with divine draughts. Same place: Since there are two principal diseases of the mind, namely ignorance and wickedness or dishonesty, so too there were needed two expellers or Physicians who remain firm, namely doctrine and purity of life. He says likewise that a kind of vehicle must be ascended, so that the soul may return thither whence it came; but this vehicle is nothing else than the elevation of the mind to God. Pythagoras: Let no one dare speak about God without light. There exists the Letter of Lysis the Pythagorean to Hipparchus concerning purification necessary before Philosophy, by which he teaches that all vices must be expelled from souls, so that someone may acquire true knowledge of things human and divine. Plato, in the Sophist, says that this purification is nothing other than casting out what is crooked from the soul, while preserving the remainder. In the Theaetetus he taught that we must flee from the world up to heaven, so that one becomes most like unto God, and he says this flight is itself the likeness of God, as far as lies within us: but likeness consists in being holy and just together with prudence. Proclus says: those who strive to arrive at the highest good need not science and exercise of intellect, but firmness of soul, quiet and tranquility. Truly we ought not seek the highest good through any science or working of intellect, nor aspire to it, but rather offer ourselves and commend ourselves to the divine light, and, our senses closed off, rest in that unknown and hidden unity of Beings.

We have wished to adduce these things from the philosophy of the ancients, not as if we approve of everything, much less as if we desire to prove our own [theology] by them, but for the sake of the mind we wished to show that even those ancient philosophers (most of whom traveled as far as Egypt, so that they might be instructed in Mosaic institutions) sought a certain purgation of the soul, and an elevation and illumination of the mind toward God in the knowledge of sacred things.

229. And thus much has been said concerning the Interpretation of Scripture, more fully indeed, if you regard the sheet: but what concerns the excellence of this subject, and what our weakness, quite briefly. It was my intention to add more, especially certain things most carefully to be observed in composing sermons (which apply the Scripture legitimately expounded, and doctrines gathered from it, to the edification of others), but time admonishes me, thanks having been humbly rendered to GOD, άξιομν: μόνευτα

"Now to read the shore, and turn the prow toward land."

TO GOD ALONE BE GLORY.

My Blessed Father, in his Method of Theological Study, Chapter IV., gave counsel to the cultivators of Sacred Theology by no means to be despised, namely advising that when about to read the Sacred Scriptures accurately he take care to bind together four volumes of clean paper, two of which in folio should be assigned to the books of the Old Testament, two in quarto to those of the New, (into which he wishes referred whatever things occur either in the accurate reading of the Bible, or also in the reading of other Theological writers, and indeed 1. The sum and scope of any given chapter. 2. Its general division. 3. The particular emphases of words or phrases. 4. The various interpretations of the Doctors of the Church ancient or more recent. 5. The solutions of apparent contradictions. 6. Singular doctrines and observations, which certainly do not meet one at first glance, but breathe forth a certain hidden investigation. 7. The sinewy sayings of the Fathers. And he concludes: Whoever shall have noted, or shall have had noted down, these seven members in any chapter of the Bible, will procure for himself a splendid treasury of Theological learning, and will be furnished with aid far and away most useful for the exercise of sermons and disputations.) This very thing itself quite as diligently as ever was possible for him amid other connected business and labors, he followed too. Hence, besides those longer Commentaries which he adorned partly on some books of the Old, partly of the New Testament, are the present annotations. Which although some judged would answer nothing to the fame of my Blessed Father acquired through writings published thus far among the learned world: yet there were others who thought scarcely could I escape the charge of envy unless at last even these annotations, after all those things which while he lived had not yet beheld the light had been published by me, and those truly sent out before into public now again committed to the press by my diligence either in a more elegant form or enlarged, I communicated to students of Sacred Theology. I complied with their wish, and so already now with God's blessing I commit these posthumous annotations to the public light throughout the entire New Testament: chiefly therefore lest anyone might rightly accuse me as though I wished to fail even in the smallest matter toward the cultivators of sacred letters There was nevertheless another copy too, though a secondary one, for the purpose of making these annotations public. On account of which my Blessed Father, who belonged to those who pursued studies, endeavored by every kind of promptness to assist them, and shared out those Collectanea with not a few of his Auditors, so that they might transcribe them for the advantage of their own studies, hence it became a concern to me, lest those transcribed copies, which anyone anywhere may find, should someday fall into less trustworthy hands, and perhaps even be brought to light by a possessor of rather poor good faith (and indeed, as commonly happens, in very corrupted form): I did not see how I could better deliver myself from that fear, nor consult more fittingly for my father's reputation, than if I myself took care to set forth in type these Annotations, gathered together by my Blessed Father for private use, with such diligence and fidelity as could be achieved. But lest I appear altogether άύμΒολος here, it seemed good, for the sake of those whose slimmer means do not allow them to purchase lengthy commentaries, and also of those who wish to become more intimately acquainted with the sacred volume through the exercise of disputation, to insert occasionally a fuller exposition of those passages upon which either the Orthodox are wont to defend their position, or upon which the Heterodox most wickedly misuse toward screening and concealing their erroneous doctrines (which distinction the labor of the present B. F. will mark with the signs of asterisk and parenthesis); yet likewise drawn from other labors of the B. F. published long ago, or else surely from the writings of the orthodox Doctors of the Church. Neither shall I hide their names, nor from what passage each exposition was derived: for this I have always considered to belong to an upright heart. But lest I seem to have wholly cast off Oriental studies, once my delight, to which up till now it has been impossible for me to give leisure amid other small employments, it seemed good to summon into council also the versions of the N. T. which they call Oriental, that is, the Syrian, Arabic, and Ethiopic ones, above all in cases where either the genuine reading, when the reader stands at the fork of the road, is confirmed by the ballot of those witnesses called from the East, or where some illumination can be supplied to the text from the said versions, or lastly where certain peculiar emphases can be discovered in them. Such are L. A. C., which I deemed necessary, so that they may reach the knowledge of you who stand before the frontispiece.

Latin:

4. Etenim non tantùm Verbi sui depositum sanctissimum Deus nobis concredidit, sed etiam Ministerium Ecclesiasticum inter nos instituit, cuius officium est praecipuum Scripturas interpretari: Istud est Ministerium Spiritus,2. Cor. 3. v. 8.per quod in omnem veritatem nos ducere cupit,Iohan. 16. v. 13.Spiritum ergò non debemus extinguere,1. Thess. 5. v. 19.

5. Ita Christus in forma viatoris euntibus in Emaus eonversans, exorsus à Mose & omnibus Prophetis interpretabatur illis in omnibus scripturis, quae de se scriptaLuc. 24. v. 27. Idem Sedens ad dextram Patris non solùm dedit olim Prophetas, & Apostolos & Evangelistas, sed & hodiè dat Pastores & DoctoresEph. 4. vers. 11.Ad praeparationem Sanctorum, in opus ministerii, in aedificationem corporis Christi,v. 12.

6. Sic HistoriaMatth. 11. & Luc. 7. de ablegatione discipulorum Iohannis ad Christum ostendit, in arduis quaestionibus de religione non sumendum esse iudicium ex hominum opinionibus, sed consulendum os illius, de quo Pater dixit, Hunc audite,Deut. 18. vers. 18. is vicissim ad Scripturas nos ablegat Ioh. 5. vers. 39. & Scripturae verbis ibidem responsionem suam discipulis Iohannis exprimit. Neque tamen Ministerium ut otiosum & inutile ob id contemnendum, sed Christus propositis Prophetarum dictis Legaros rursus mittit ad Iohannem, ut eius operâ in investiganda sententiarum Scripturae explicatione utantur.

7. Sedetiam Interpretes isti Ecclesiastici, quocunque sanè dignitatis gradu consistant, non debent privatos aliquos sensus Scripturae inferre, sed ut ex Spiritus S. inspiratione conscriptae sunt sacrae tabulae, ita quoque secundùm eiusdem dictamen exponi debent, unde Spiritum S. esse supremum & authenticum Scripturae Interpretem pronunciamus.

8. Colligitur id evidenter ex loco Apostolico 2. Pet. 1. vers. 20.πᾶσα προφητεία ἰδαφῆς, ἰδίας ἐπιλέσεως οὐ γίνεται, quare? vers. 21. quia nec proprio & privato arbitrio olim locuti sunt sancti Dei homines, sed ex inspiratione Spiritus sancti. Idem ergò, qui Scripturae autor, is supremus & authenticus eiusdem est Interpres. Qui condit legem, optimus & supremus legis est Interpres.

9. De eo autem quaeritur, quae sit ἰδία ἐπίλυσις? unde petendum sit Spiritus sancti in Scripturis interpretandis dictamen? unde agnosci possit, Ecclesiasticos illos Interpretes mentem Spiritus Sancti in Scripturis loquentis rectè assequi?

10. Pontificii statuunt, Ecclesiae hoc tribuendum esse, quòd in ea & per eam evidenter atque infallibiliter doceamur, quae sit vera & genuina sacrarum literarum sententia: Scripturam in se & per se esse literam mortuam, quae explicari possit modis variis & instar, nasi cerei quovis inflecti, sed Spiritum Sanctum per Ecclesiam nos doccre, quae sit vera & authentica Scripturae interpretatio.

11. Et quia cardo rei in hoc vertitur, ideò ut ipsorum sententiam pleniùs percipiamus, referemus quae Nicol. Cusanus Cardinalis, hac de re disputat in suis contra Bohemos Epistolis; ex illis enim poterimus intelligere, quid honorabili Ecclesiae nomine intelligant, quamvè in Scripturis interpretandis autoritatem ei tribuant, denique quamnam esse infallibilem S. S. interpretationem statuant.

12. Sic ergò Cusanus: Dicunt aliqui, praecepto Christi oboediendum esse primo loco, deinde Ecclesiae, & si aliud praeceperit Ecclesia quàm Christus, non Ecclesiae, sed Christo oboediendum: (subiicit deinde ἐπίκρισιν) Certè in hoc est omnium praesumtionum initium, quando particulares iudicant suum sensum in divinis praeceptis voluntati divinae conformiorem, quàm universae Ecclesiae. Iste verò in Ecclesia manet, qui suum sensum praesumtuosè non elevat supra dictamen maioris partis Sacerdotum, quibus verbum creditum est, & qui Christi legatione funguntur: in oboediendo enim illi sententiae, quam saniorem Ecclesiae partem videt affirmare, nihil periculi incurrit Christianus: Veritas cathedrae adhaeret, quare membra cathedrae unita & Pontifici coniuncta Ecclesiam efficiunt.

13. Et postea. Videmus in Scripturarum intelligentia varia hominum ingenia varios sensus explicare, variam-ue autoritatis Scripturarum opinionem existere, possibile-ue fore, aut in autoritate earundem, aut in intellectu inextricabilem dubietatem hominum mentes suspendere, ubi erit solidum refugium peregrinantium? certè in alio nullo, quàm in militantis Ecclesiae usu atque approbatione, sive haec sit circa Scripturam & eius autoritatem atque intellectum, sive extra Scripturam in consvetudine accepta per Ecclesiam: in his enim firmitas est, ut solida petra & veritatis columna, non ut per Scripturarum autoritatem ad Ecclesiam pergat, & eam, si cum Scriptura non concordat, iuxta priscorum aut suum intellectum in operis exercitio impunè spernere possit & Scripturae in haerere. Haec est omnium sanè intelligentium sententia, qui Scripturarum autoritatem aut intellectum (ut Augustinus de Evangeliis dicit) in Ecclesiae approbatione fundant, quae unam accipit, & alteram abiicit, & non è converso Ecclesiae fundamentum in Scripturarum autoritate locant.

14. Ex hoc fundamento respondet ad argumentum Bohemorum. Dices fortassè, Ecclesia hodierna non ita ambulat in ritu communionis, sicut ante ista tempora, quando sanctissimi viri utriusque speciei Sacramentum necessarium esse, vi praecepti Christi & verbo & opere astruebant. Potuitnè tunc Ecclesia errare? certè non. Quod si non, quomodo id hodiè verum non est, quod tunc omnium opinione affirmabatur, cùm non sit alia Ecclesia ista quàm illa? Certè hoc tenon moveat, quod diversis temporibus alius atque alius ritus Sacrificiorum & etiam Sacramentorum stante veritate invenitur, Scripturas-ue esse ad tempus adaptatas & variè intellectas, ita ut uno tempore secundum currentem ritum Universalem exponerentur, mutato ritu, iterum sententia mutaretur &c. Quare etiamsi hodiè alia fuerit interpretatio Ecclesiae eiusdem praecepti Evangelici quàm aliquando, tamen hic sensus nunc in usu currens ad regimen Ecclesiae inspiratus, uti tempori cong-uus & salutis via debet acceptari.

15. Qualem autem Ecclesiam intelligat, postea explicat. Quare universa Catholica Ecclesia & ad Petri cathedram conglobata à Christo nunquam recedet, qui veritas est, cum qua Christus semper se mansurum pollicitus est. Tandem concludit. Ex praemissis constat, quod tota Catholica Ecclesia non potest ad literam Scripturarū obligari, licet ad spiritum: quando enim litera non servit aedificationi & spiritui, recipit id, quod magis servit spiritui. Quare nec mirum, si praxis Ecclesiae uno tempore Scripturam interpretatur uno modo, & alio tempore, alio modo: nam intellectus currit cum praxi: intellectus enim, qui cum praxi concurrit, est Spiritus vivificans. Ecclesia igitur sicut recipit Scripturam, ita & interpretatur: sequuntur igitur Scripturae Ecclesiam, quae prior est, & propter quam Scripturae, & non è converso.

Hactenus Cusanus. Breviter haec omnia effert Hosius Cardinalis de expresso Dei verbo. Si quis habet interpretationem Romanae Ecclesiae, etiamsi nec scit nec intelligit, an & quomodo cum Scripturae verbis conveniat, is tamen habet ipsissimum verbum Dei.

16. Ex his constare potest, quid sibi velint Patres Concilii Tridentini, quando sessione 4. decreto 2. seriò prohibent, ne quis sacram Scripturam interpretari audeat contra eum sensum, quem tenuit & tenet mater Ecclesia, cuius sit iudicare de vero sensu & interpretatione Scripturarum sanctarum, aut contra unanimem consensum Patrum.

17. Videamus, quomodo Bellarminus mentem Concilii explicet. Convenit inter nos & adversarios, ait 3. de verb. Dei c. 3. Scripturas intelligi debere eo Spiritu, quo factae sunt, i. e. Spiritu S. Tota igitur quaestio in eo posita est, ubi sit iste Spiritus. Nos (Pontificii) existimamus, hunc Spiritum etsi multis privatis hominibus saepè concedatur, tamen certò inveniri in Ecclesia, id est, in Concilio Episcoporum confirmato à summo Ecclesiae totius Pastore, sive in summo Pastore cum Concilio aliorum Pastorum: unde concludit, iudicem veri sensus Scripturae esse Ecclesiam, id est, Pontificem cum Concilio.

18. Nondum dimittere possumus Bellarminum. Cum enim Pontifici adiungat Concilium, quaerimus, an Spiritus S. tùm solùm immediatèper Pontificem loquatur, quando cum Concilio & in Concilio aliorum Pastorum aliquid definit, an verò etiam tùm, quando solus extra Concilium suam promulgat sententiam? quaerimus secundo loco, an Concilii, an Pontificis maior in Scripturis interpretandis autoritas: notum enim est, non semper convenire Pontifici cum Conciliis.

19. Ad prius respondet Bellarm. 4. de Pontifice Rom. c. 2. Ipsa infallibilitas non est in coetu Consiliariorum vel in Concilio Episcoporum, sed in solo Pontifice. Ad posterius respondet 2. de Concil. c. 13. nondum hae de re convenire inter Catholicos. c. 14. subiicit tres Doctorū (Papisticorum) sententias. Aliqui asserunt, Concilium esse supra Pontificem, aliqui volunt, Papam quidem esse supra Concilium, nec posse invitum à Concilio iudicari, at posse seipsum Concilio subiicere, & causam suam Concilio iudicandam permittere, ac si id fecerit, tùm ipsi in Concilii sententia esse acquiescendnm. Alii verò asserunt, Papam adeò esse supra Concilium, ut non possit etiam se subiicere eius sententiae coactivae, quam opinionem dicit esse communem, eandem-ue sequitur.

20. Ex his omnibus colligimus, Pontificios statuere, quòd vera Scripturae interpretatio ex solo Papalis pectoris scrinio sit petenda, eo enim tandem per longas istas ambages disputationum de Ecclesiae autoritate nos deducunt, quod cordatiores atque ingenui inter ipsos non negabuntunde scribit. Bellarm. 4. de Pont. c. 2. Omnes Catholici in hoc conveniunt, Pontificem solum vel cum suo particulari Concilio aliquid in re dubia statuentem sive errare possit, sive non, esse ab omnibus fidelibus oboedienter aud iendum.

21. Sunt autem huius opinionis errores longè plurimi. Πρῶτον Ψεῦδος totius structurae est, quod Spiritus S. sensum à verbis Scripturae separant, quae tamen non separanda & distrahenda, sed coniungenda sunt arctissimè. Spiritus sanctus in Scripturis & per Scripturas ad nos loquitur, ergò in illis ipsis Scripturae verbis sonat Spiritus S. vox & sententia, non aliunde inferenda in Scripturam, sed ex ea haurienda atque audienda. quò pertinent omnia illa pronunciata, in quibus os Domini locutum esse dicitur, & sanctos Dei homines à Spiritu S. actos locutos esse asseriturut proinde Scriptura sit θεόπνευςος: imò verò totus Christianismus nititur hoc fundamento, quòd Spiritus S. per Prophetas & Apostolos ea, quae in Scripturis legimus, annotârit.

22. Nimirum Pontificii proponunt nobis talem Scripturae Ideam, quòd sit quasi sceleton quoddam & statua muta atque mortua, quae sit priùs animanda per Spiritum in Ecclesia in Ecclesia & per Ecclesiam, id est, per Pontificem loquentem. At vivus sermo Dei & efficaxHebr. 4. v. 12. & cogitet quilibet, quantùm absit haec Pontificiorum sententia à Svencfeldianismo, qui itidem literam Scripturae ut mortuam negligendam esse dicit, & internum Spiritum sequendum.

23. Verba Scripturae sunt verba Spiritus S., eius ergò mentem nobis exponunt. Eo semper animo ad Scripturarum lectionem accedendum, ac si in illis & per illas loquentem Spiritum sanctum audiamus. U-enim Pontifex loquitur suis hominibus in Decretalibus, ita nobis Spiritus sanctus loquitur in Scripturae oraculis. Si quis velit sensum Spiritus sancti à verbis Scripturae separare, illum etiam oportebit sensum Pontificis separare à verbis Decretalium, & sic nemo hodiè nosse poterit, quid sibi voluerint prisci Pontifices. Quinimò hodiernus Pontifex non potest aliter exprimere suam sententiam, quàm per verba: si quis ergò velit excipere, esse quidem haec verba Pontificis, sed quaerendum adhuc de verborum sensu, eundem-ue aliunde petendum esse, is meritò ridebitur, quia verba sunt sensuum animi notae. Perinde igitur absurdi sunt Pontificii, quando verba Scripturae & sententiam Spiritus sancti disiungunt ac separant, nam ex illis Scripturae verbis sensus Spiritus sancti hauriendus, non aliunde in illa inferendus.

24. Declaremus rem exemplo. Quando Bellarminus & alii scriptores Pontificii conantur ostendere, nos à Patrum doctrina secessionem fecisse, semper solent ingeminare. Ita statuit Hieronymus, ita sentit Augustinus, ita loquitur Ambrosius &c. Quaero igitur, unde sciunt hanc fuisse sententiam Hieronymi, Augustini, Ambrosii &c? utique ex ipsorum verbis, aliud enim quod respondeant, non habent: perinde etiam nos dicimus: ita statuit, ita sentit, ita loquitur Spiritus sanctus; si quaerant, unde sciamus, hanc esse Spiritus sancti mentem, ut si urgere nos velint, ex Ecclesiae, Ecclesiae, Ecclesiae voce Spiritus S. sententiam hauriendam esse, quid aliud respondere possumus, quàm ex verbis Scripturae Spiritus sancti mentem discendam esse.

25. Quàm ergò primùm conceditur, Scripturam esse θεόπνευς ον, Prophetas & Apostolos fuisse Spiritus sancti amanuenses (quod nullus Christianus, quâ talis, negare potest) statim etiam concedi oportet, Spiritus S. mentem ex illo libro & illis verbis discendam esse, nec opus esse, ut ex Pontificis Romani pectore demùm hauriamus, quae sit Spiritus S. mens & sententia: num enim mentis & linguae artifex disertè loqui non posset, ait Lactanctius 6. div. Instit. c. 21? imò verò summâ providentiâ carere fuco voluit ea, quae divina sunt, ut omnes intelligerent, quae ipse omnibus loquebatur.

26. Idem illud, quod Prophetae & Apostoli suis auditorib. proposuerunt, idem, inquam, & nihil aliud in Scripturas Dei voluntate redegerunt, Iren. lib. 3. adversus haer. c. 1. Perinde igitur, ut ab auditoribus Prophetarum & Apostolorum percipi potuit, quaesit Dei voluntas, quae Spiritus sancti mens & sententia, ex ipsorum verbis: ita quoque nos lectores Scriptorum Propheticorum & Apostolicorum ex ipsorum libris percipere possumus, quae Dei sit voluntas, quae Spiritus sancti mens & sententia. Praedicatio & scriptio externa accidentia sunt, quae rei essentiam non mutant, & ut sensuum animi ἀπεικόνισμα est oratio, ita verborum ore prolatorum ἀπεικόνισμα est scriptio, quâ de re disserit Philosophus περὶ ἑρμην. cap. 1. ἔςι μεν οὖν τὰ ἐν τῇ τ ωνῇ τῶν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ παθημάτων σύμβομα, και γραφόμένα των έν τη θωνῇ.

27. Quid, quod Pontifex suam promulgaturus sententiam non semper utitur suis illis à latere Legatis, qui vivâ voce eam exponant, sed saepè mittit tantùm Diplomata, & ut in Curia eius loquuntur Brevia: qui haec audit, Pontificis sententiam se audire dicit: ita Spiritus sanctus non solùm misit olim Prophetas & Apostolos, qui vivâ voce mentem eius exposuerunt, sed etiam hodiè tradit Ecclesiae Scripta Prophetica & Apostolica, in quibus Prophetae & Apostoli nobis loquuntur, & per illos Spiritus sanctus, qui ergò haec legit vel audit, Spiritus sancti sententiam se cognoscere statuat.

28. Accedamus propiùs. Dicit Papista, ex sola Ecclesia, id est, Pontifice discendum, quis sit verus Scripturae sensus, quaero igitur, unde hoc Pontificis Privilegium probent: afferunt ibi varios Scripturae textus ex V. & N. Testamento, peculiariter illud Christi, Tibi dabo claves regni coelorum &c. Super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam: rogavi prote, ne deficiat fides tua &c. (ut videre est apud Bellarminum 3. de verbo Dei c. 4. & 5.) quae hoc sensu ab illis exponuntur, quòd cathedrae Romanae ac Pontifici super eam sedenti data sit promissio de infallibili Scripturas interpretandi autoritate, quòd in illis semper sit assecuturus Spiritus S. genuinam sententiam: Quid si de illa interpretatione dictorum Scripturae dubitem, an hoc sensu ea sint accipienda? quò me deducet Pontificius? utique ad scrinium Papalis pectoris. Egregia verò confirmatio! Papae competit hoc non errandi privilegium, quia Scripturae loca ita interpretatur, ut sibi illud competere ostendat, & loca illa Scripturae ita sunt intelligenda, quia Papa ita intelligi voluit.

29. Quem verò ex Patribus ita vides Scripturas interpretari: haec explicatio est vera & genuina, quia Papa Romanus eā proposuit! & cur Iesuitae hodiè videri volunt, quod operosè ex Scripturis disputent, consulendo fontes, conferendo loca &c? Compendio tota res finiri poterit, si dicant: hi articuli sunt credendi, & Scriptura hoc modo exponenda, quia Papa ita definivit. Nimirū Papa cunctator est in suo officio, dudum omninò debuisset interpretationem quandam Scripturae vel Lyrani vel alterius facere authenticam, aliàs quomodo sciri poterit, quae sit propriè Romani Pontificis Interpretatio?

30. Magnum certè in Scripturis interpretandis privilegium sibi tribuit ac tribui patitur Romanus Pontifex, sed ostendat nobis privilegii istius tabulas ac sigilla, divina inquam oracula: fortè reperiri poterunt, si membranae, in qua donatio Constantini perscripta, pars exterior accuratiùs inspiciatur, ut olim à Venetis in casu dissimili est monitus, teste Camer. parte 1. medit. histor. cap. 61.

31. Quae pro confirmando illo privilegio ex Scripturis hodiè producunt Iesuitae, nimis longè sunt petita, & semper τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ λαμβάνουσι. vel enim de summo Pontifice Veteris Testamenti, vel de Ecclesia in genere, velde Petro agunt, nullum autem proferri potest testimonium. in quo disertè fiat Pontificis mentio. At in tenore privilegiorū perspicuè & expressè fieri debet mentio illius, cui talia conceduntur, ita enim docent Icti. Specialis istorum locorum tractatio, quae in hoc argumento proponunt Iesuitae, pertinet ad articulum fidei Romanensis de Pontifice.

32. Vide amus in super, quomodo magno isto privilegio (si quod unquam ipsi concessum) Pontifex sit usus, & quàm dextrè Scripturas fuerit interpretatus: docent enim Icti, beneficia per privilegium concessa, abusu amitti. Thema est in Decretis Pontificum satis tritum: Episcopos & Sacerdotes non esse accusandos: aut damnandos à Principe & iudice seculari. id Clemens Epist. 1. probat ex eo, quia Paulus dicit, Pro minimo nobis esse debet, ut à talibus argumur vel ab humano die.
