Sacram lecturus, quatuor volumina ex charta pura, quorum duo in folio adsignentur libris V. T. duo in quarto N. T. libris, compingi curet, (in quae referri vult, quaecuna vel in accuratâ Bibliorum lectione, vel etiaem in aliorum scriptorum Theologicorum lectione occurrunt, & quidem 1. Summam & scopum cuiusq; Capitis. 2. Eiusdem generalem partitionem. 3. singulares vocum vel phrasium emphases. 4. Diversas veterum vel recentiorum Ecclesiae Dd. interpretationes. 5. Apparentium contradictionum solutiones. 6. Singulares doctrinas & observationes, quae scil. non occurrunt primostatim intuitu, sed reconditam quandam indagationem spirant. 7. Nervosa Patrum dicta. & concludit: Quisquis haec septem membra in quovis Bibliorum Capite annotaverit, vel annotata habuerit, is praeclarum eruditionis Theologicae Thesaurum sibi comparabit, & ad concionum ac Disputationum exercitium adminiculo instructus erit longè utilissimo.) hoc ipsum sanè quàm diligentissimè, quantum modò per alia concatenata negotia ac labores integrum ei fuit, secutus & ipse est. Natae hinc praeter Commentarios illos prolixiores, quos partim in V. partim in N. T. libr. quosd. adornavit, praesentes notae sunt. Quas ut ut nonnulli minimè B. Parentis famae, per edita hactenus scripta in orbe erudito acquisitae, responsuras existimarint: fuerunt tamē contrà, qui invidiae crimen vix me effugiturum putarunt, nisi vel tandem & has adnotationes, postquam omnia, quae ipso vivente nondum lucem adspexerant, â me publicata, quae verò antea in publicum emissa, denuò vel elegantiori forma vel auctiora studio meo destinata prelo, cum S. S. Theologiae Studiosis communicarem. Morem illis gessi, atadeo iam nunc bono cum Deo posthumas has annotationes in totum T. N. luci committo publicae: ideò maximè, ne quis accusare me iure possit, quasi vel in tantillo deesse sacrarum litterarum cultoribus voluerim Fuit tamen & alia, sed secundaria ea, publicandarum harum notarum causa. Ex quo B. Parens meus, quâ fuit eorum, qui studia sectantur, conatus omnibus modis iuvandi promtitudine, Collectanea isthaec cum Auditoribus suis non paucis, ut in studiorum suorum commodum describerent, communicavit, verendummihi hinc fuit, ne descripta ista exempla, quae passim reperire licet, in manùs aliquando incidant minus fideles, ac fortè etiam â possessore minùs bonae fidei in lucem proferantur (& quidem, uti fieri adsolet, corruptissimè:) non vidi, qui metu isto liberari meliùs possim, famaepaternae rectiùs consulere, quàm si ipse Annotationes has, in privatum usum â B. Parente collectas, eâ quâ fieri diligentia potest ac fidelitate, typis describendas curarem. P. labore distinguet) inserere: sed itidem eam ex aliis B. P. Lucubrationibus pridem luci datis, vel certè ex Orthodoxorum Eccles. Dd. monumentis desumtam. ## 1:1 Introduction: I. N. I. P. Address to the Reader B. C
Appellation. The sacred Canonical Books, written after the ascension of Christ the Savior into heaven by the Evangelists & Apostles, are called ά ης χαινης διαηχης, books of the N.T. It is probable that έπιςαφην was prefixed by John the Evangelist & Apostle himself, collector & arranger of the books of the N.T. The Syrian retained the Greek name * (thus the printed copies have it, but Code MS. IV. of the Four Evangelists at Altdorf רג, &, unless I am mistaken, more correctly)*. Appel. seems to be taken from Jer. 31. v. 31. Behold, days come, saith the Lord, διαηομαι ωόιχω Ισςαηλ ω όιχω Ιούδα διαηχην χαινην, whose parallel apostolic passage is 2. Cor. 3. v. 6. God hath made us able ministers χαινης διαηχης, against which on both sides is opposed η παλαιάδιαηχν, Jeremiah 31. v. 32. 2. Cor. 3. v. 14. Now Sacred Scripture is called Testament μεωνυμιχως by reason of its matter, because it contains διαχην the Testament of God. But Jerome notes in his Questions on Deuteronomy that the Hebrew ברית signifies both testament & covenant, and accordingly it is rendered by the Seventy interpreters sometimes through διαηχην, sometimes through μαςύςιον. Augustine on Psalm 62.: In the Scriptures a Testament is said to be not only that which has force only when the testators are dead, but every covenant & agreement is called a Testament. Most derive it from ברה, which means to choose, to select out, for it denotes a thing which two persons choose, & about which they agree together, a pact, a covenant. Therefore Scripture is called διαηχη Testament 1. because it sets forth GOD'S covenant with men, which consists in mutual promise & obligation. Since this covenant is twofold, O. & N., therefore also the Biblical books are distinguished into books of the O. & N.T. 2. because just as in a will the mind & writing of the testator is contained: so in the sacred & canonical books the will of God the Testator is expressed. 3. because it is that instrument whereby believers, as adopted sons of GOD, are called by grace to the paternal inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. Radulphus Ardens, Sunday 12. after Trinity. The Sacred Scripture is called a Testament on account of a triple cause: because it is as it were a charter testifying to the covenant made between God and man; because it attests to us the divine will, which we ought to do; because it is as it were the Testament of the inheritance promised to us by GOD. 4. Because just as among human affairs no pact or agreement is firmer than testamentary, Gal. 3. v. 15. so also Scripture is of unmoved truth, since it declares the testamentary promise of GOD, and therefore the unmoved firmness of the divine will Hebr. 6. v. 17. Isidorus of Pelusium lib. 2. Epist. 196. ην συνθηχην, ουέςι. ην έπαελίαν, διαηχην η εία χαλεί ςαφ διά ό ΒέΒαιον άπαςάΒαον. συνηχα μέν άς πολλάχις άναςέποναι, διαηχ-ι δέ νόμιμοι όυδαμως. 5. because all the requirements of a Testament are present: testator, goods bequeathed, witnesses, heirs. Moreover Augustine lib. 3. against two Epistles of the Pelagians c. 4. prefers to call them books of the O. and N. instrument, 1. because they instruct us unto salvation what we ought to believe, what to do, what to hope1. Tim. 3. v. 15. 2. because they are that wholesome instrument through which God converts, illumines, regenerates, renews, saves usIoh. 20. v. 31. 3. because they are as it were public and authentic Instruments, drawn up by most approved writers, namely divine Notaries, and sealed by witnesses most worthy of faith, hence suspected of no falsehood. But the name of Testament is more significant, because the old covenant of GOD was confirmed by the typical blood of animals Exod. 24. v. 8. the new by the Blood of his own Testator, the Son of GOD Hebr. 9. v. 15. whence the Church preferred to use the name Testament rather than Instrument. Tertullian lib. 4. cont. Marcion. cap. 1. says, that he divided two Gods, one belonging to one instrument, or, as it is more customary to say, of one Testament. Compare thereon Pamelius; likewise the same Tertullian lib. de pudic. C. 10. and the aforementioned lib. c. 3.

II. The principal efficient cause. As for the Canonical books of the O. T., so also for the books of the N. T. the principal efficient cause, or primary author, is the true God, one in essence, triune in Persons, from whom also the divine and Canonical authority of the books of the N. T. depends. This is proved 1. from the saying of the Apostle.2. Tim. 3. v. 16. πάσα ςαφη

Pet. 1. v. 21. so also by the impulse and inspiration of the same they wrote, and therefore were organs of GOD not only in preaching heavenly doctrine but even in writing, whence at the beginnings of their books they call themselves servants of GOD and Apostles of Christ.

2. from the command to write. In the last times God has spoken to us in his Son or through his Son Hebr. 1. v. 1. who declared to us the will and counsel of his heavenly Father concerning our salvation, Ioh. 1. v. 18. He commanded the Apostles, called immediately by himself, equipped with the gift of miracles and adorned with extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit, to teach all nations,Matth. 28. v. 19. not of that time only but also of the coming age, as appears from the promise added v. 20. therefore he also commanded them to embrace the doctrine in writing: for they could not teach all nations even of the coming age by living voice without writing, whence the office of the Apostles is established, namely to testify of Christ not only by preaching with living voice but also by writing Ioh. 21. v. 24.1. Therefore. Likewise. That Scripture which proceeded from immediate divine command and impulse, that is divine, authentic and Canonical. The Scripture of the N. T. proceeded from immediate divine command and impulse. Therefore. Iren. lib. 3. adv. haereses cap. 1. The Apostols, after first proclaiming these things, afterwards handed them down to us in scriptures by the will of GOD. Aug. lib. 1. de consens. Evang. cap. ult. When those (Evangelists and Apostles) wrote what he showed and said, it must be denied in no way that he himself did not write, since his members performed what they knew under the dictation of the head; but whatever he wished us to read of his sayings and deeds, this he commanded them to write as with his own hands, Theoph. praefat. in Matth.

As in the O. T. δέδωχεν ό φιλάνςωπος εός άς ςαφάς, so also in the N. T. έυδόχησε ςαπηναι ά υαέλια.

3. From the matter of the writing. The things contained in the books of the New Testament were not devised by human ingenuity, but are mysteries of the faith revealed by God. The Apostles learned what they wrote partly in the School of Christ the Son of GOD, in which they were instructed for more than three years, partly in the School of the Holy Spirit, poured out upon them extraordinarily and most abundantly on the day of Pentecost. Paul, caught up to the third heaven 2. Cor. 12. v. 2. heard άραηα αημαα, which it is not lawful for man to utter, v. 4. Peter testifies that he was άυόπην έπόπην ης μεαλειόηος Χςις 2. Epistle 1. v. 16. άχουςην φωνης of him: This is my beloved Son, v. 17. 18. John testifies that he writes from the revelation of Christ Apoc. 1. v. 1. and 10.

4. From συμφωνία of the books of the Old and New Testament. What in the Scripture of the Old Testament is foretold and prefigured as future and to be fulfilled in its own time, that the Scripture of the New Testament announces as completed, Act. 26. v. 22.Rom. 3. v. 21.chap. 16. v. 26. Therefore the author of the books of both Testaments is one and primary, and equal is the authority of the books of the Old and New Testament, namely divine, Canonical and authentic. We therefore reject what Socinus writes in his book On the Authority of Scripture, p. 18. It is certain that no one can by any means seriously receive the Christian religion unless at the same time he confess that in its revelation there was clearly recognized that the sense of the prophecies concerning Jesus Christ and the matters belonging on that account to the Christian religion was at least in some part other than that which according to the letter of the O. T. appears to be, and such that without that revelation no one could even suspect it.

5. From the divine efficacy of Scripture. As the Old so also the New Testament Scripture has divine efficacy in converting men, enlightening them, regenerating them, renewing them, and leading them to faith and salvation Ioh. 20. last verse 2. Tim. 3. v. 16. It affords the same effectual consolation in all adversities Rom. 15. v. 4. consequently it cannot fail to be divine, authentic, and derived from GOD himself as its primary Author.

6. From the testimony of the Church μαςυςία. The books which are found in the Biblical Code of the N. T. enjoy the consenting witness of the Christian Church through all successions of ages of ages. Augustine, book 11, against Faustus, chapter 5. "The excellence of Canonical authority of the Old and New Testament is distinct from later books, which was confirmed by the times of the Apostles through successions of Bishops and propagations of Churches, established on high as it were upon a certain seat, to which all faithful and pious understanding yields service." Conzenius, in the preliminary questions on the four Gospels, question 3, § 1, says, "our faith rests in the consensus and judgment of the firstborn Church, whose judgment can by no means be deceptive." Yet 1. the testimony of the Church, especially of the primitive Church near to the times of the Apostles, does not confer authority upon the writings of the Evangelists, but merely manifests it. 2. Nor is the divine and Canonical authority of these writings recognized from the testimony of the Church alone, but also from other κριτηρίοις. 3. There is added also the inner witnessing and sealing of the Holy Spirit, so that thus there are universally three classes of witnesses, through which both the authority of the whole Scripture and likewise that of the Evangelists becomes known to us. 4. Conzenius, ibid., from Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 11: "So great is the firmness concerning the Gospels that even the heretics themselves bear witness to it, and going out from them each one tries to confirm his own doctrine." The same Conzenius, in the defense § 5, attributes to us by slander that we "repudiate the testimony of the primitive Church and flee to the private Spirit alone." But the distinction between "Canonical books of the first and second order" must be noted, about which at its proper place.

III. The "ministerial cause of the books of the New Testament" are the Evangelists and Apostles, whom therefore we rightly call "the hands of Christ and Secretaries of the Holy Spirit." Tertullian, book 4 against Marcion: "We establish above all that the Gospel instrument has the Apostles as authors, upon whom this task of publishing the Gospel was imposed by the Lord himself." Although however only two of the Evangelists, namely Matthew and John, were Apostles, instituted in the School of Christ teaching here on earth and endowed with abundant pouring-out of the Holy Spirit, yet nothing is detracted from that by the authority of Mark and Luke, since they too wrote "moved and inspired by the Holy Spirit," being φερόμενοι. Each was from the number of the seventy disciples, Luke 10. v. 1.; the History of each received such divine testimony, indeed that of Mark from Peter, but that of Luke from Paul. The writing of each was confirmed by divine miracles performed by the Apostles. Ambrose, in the explanation of the preface of Luke, tome 5, p. 7. Matthew did not attempt, Mark did not attempt, John did not attempt, but by divine Spirit ministering abundance to all their sayings and matters, begun without any effort, they completed everything. Epiphanius against Αλόγους. Then the Holy Spirit impels Luke, so that he might bring forth from the deepest depth a statement refuting those who were deceived. Truly Gordonus Huntlaeus disputes in Controversies 2, chapter 15, p. 190, that St. Luke wrote from the disciples' report alone: But in this point he is abandoned by his own colleagues. Didacus Stella on Luke, folio 3: Although Luke heard from the blessed Virgin Mother of God and from the Apostles, nevertheless he wrote with the Holy Spirit dictating and moving him. Adamus Conzenius, volume 2, on Luke chapter 6: It is certain that the primary cause of writing the Gospel was not Pauline writing, but heavenly revelation and command.

IV. The Matter. The books of the New Testament comprise both historical, both doctrinal, both prophetic things, whence they are distinguished into Historical, Doctrinal, and Prophetic. Historical ones hand down History either of Christ, as the four Evangelists: or of the Apostles, as Acts. Doctrinal ones are the five letters of the Apostles, Paul, James, Peter, John and Jude. Some of Paul's epistles were written before captivity, which are seven in number. 1. the former to the Thessalonians. 2. the latter to the Thessalonians. 3. the former to Timothy. 4. the former to the Corinthians. 5. to Titus. 6. the latter to the Corinthians. 7. to the Romans. Some during captivity, to which class belong the remaining six, concerning which it is not established so certainly in what order they were written; some however assign this order: 1. to the Philippians. 2. to the Colossians. 3. to Philemon. 4. to the Ephesians. 5. to the Galatians. 6. the latter to Timothy. There is one prophetic book of the New Testament, namely the Apocalypse of John.

V. The Form of the books of the New Testament is either internal, or external. Internal form is the very divine authority and majesty of these books, which draws its origin from the immediate breathing-forth of the Holy Spirit, as the proper and adequate efficient cause, and from the sublimity of the matters which they expound, as the proper and adequate matter. External form is both the idiom of the Greek language, in which the books of the New Testament are transcribed, and the property of speech and style, indeed even singularity, having simplicity and

majesty joined together by a truly divine miracle. Compare Exegesis on Scripture, chapter 12, §. 305. and following. It is asked at this place. 1. Were all the books of the New Testament written by the Evangelists and Apostles in the Greek idiom? Some except the Gospel of Matthew and the Epistle to the Hebrews, which two [they say were written] in the Hebrew language; and the Gospel of Mark, which they judge was written in the Latin tongue. But it is more correctly said that all the books of the New Testament without exception were written in the Greek idiom by the very Evangelists and Apostles themselves, whence those who maintain the contrary are compelled to confess, that the Evangelists and Apostles had the Greek edition of the entire New Testament as authors, or at least as approvers. Bellarmine, book 2, De V. T., chapter 7.

Q. 2. Why did the Evangelists and Apostols wish to write not in their native tongue, namely Hebrew or Syrian, but in Greek? Answer. Just as before Christ was manifested heavenly doctrine was committed to writing in that idiom which was proper and ancestral to the Israelites, to whom it was entrusted τὰ λόγια τοῦ σθεοῦ, Rom. 3. v. 2. who were God's peculiar people and περιούσιος, Deut. 7. v. 7. etc.; so after Christ was manifested God willed the same to be written in the Greek language, that it might be propagated more easily toward gathering together the Church out of all nations. For the Greek language at that time was. 1. most widely spoken. For although the monarchy of the Romans then extended far and wide, nevertheless the Latin tongue was not yet so widespread, on the testimony of Cicero Pro Archia. 2. Among the languages of the nations outstanding above all others. 3. The books of the Old Testament were read by Jews and Gentiles according to the version of the Seventy Interpreters. 4. In this language the whole philosophy of the Gentiles was written down, God wished that language to be retained whereby the philosophy of the Gentiles was sealed, in order that he might refute it more readily.

It must be noted here. 1. Although the Evangelists and Apostles wrote in the Greek tongue, nevertheless many Hebrew idioms occur in their writings.

2. The Evangelists and Apostles retained many Latin words received in usage at that time, reduced however to Greek inflection, such as ἀσσάριος, δηνάριος κεντυρίων, κίνσος, κουςωδία, λεγεων, λεντίον, μάκελλον, λιβερτῖνος, μίλιον, μεμβράνα, μόδιος, ξέςης, σικάριος, σουδάριον, σπεκουλάτωρ, ταβόρνα, φοδον, τίτλος, φραγελλοῦν, φραγέλλων. 3. All the terms of the New Testament, if they are neither Greek nor Latin, are either Chaldaic in origin itself, or if they are Hebrew, they are nevertheless pronounced in Chaldaean form.

4. Sayings of the Old Testament are cited by the Evangelists and Apostles. 1 Either according to the sense alone, or according to both sense and words together. Concerning citation as regards the sense, Jerome writes thus in the book on the best kind of interpreting, vol. 2: The writers of the Gospels, when they bring forward the Prophets as witnesses of what Christ either said or did, sometimes take care to cite not so much the very words as their sense, that they may show that the kingdom of God consists not in speech but in power. If they cite the prophetic oracles according to both sense and words together, then they do this. 2. Either according to the version of the Seventy Interpreters, or according to the Hebrew text. Concerning the former manner of citation Jerome writes thus in the questions upon Genesis, ch. 46: This must be observed generally, that wherever the holy Apostles or apostolic men speak to the peoples, they make use mostly of those testimonies which had already been published among the nations, namely through the translation of the Seventy Interpreters. Concerning the latter the same man argues thus, Letter 151 to Algasia: Wherever the Evangelists and Apostols brought forth testimonies from the Old Instrument, it must be diligently observed that they did not follow the words but the sense, and wherever they differ from the Hebrew, they expressed the Hebrew sense in their own language. Book 2 against Rufinus: Apostolic men use the Hebrew Scriptures. That the very Apostles and Evangelists did this is evident. The Lord our Savior, wherever he mentions the old Scripture, sets examples from the Hebrew volumes, as is that saying: Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water. And on the cross itself, Eli Eli lama azabtani, which is interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me, not as it stands in the Septuagint, My God, look upon me, why hast thou forsaken me? And many things similar to these. Nor do we say this because we would condemn the Seventy, but because greater authority belongs to the Apostles and to Christ, and wherever the Seventy do not disagree with the Hebrew, there the Apostles took examples from their interpretation; but where they differ, they set down in Greek what they had learned from the Hebrews. (Similar examples, where the Evangelists and Apostles departed from the version of the Seventy Interpreters and followed the sources/fountains, occur everywhere. Matt. 2. v. 15. from Hosea 11. v. 1. Matt. 4. v. 15. from Isaiah 9. v. 1. Matt. 8. v. 17. from Isaiah 53. v. 4. Matt. 12. v. 18. from Isaiah 42. v. 2. etc.)

VI. The end of the Scripture of the New Testament is the same as that of the Scripture of the Old Testament, namely with regard to GOD, the saving knowledge and glorification of him; with regard to ⟦f1 us, the end is either an intermediate, or the last. The intermediate ends are explained by the Apostle Rom. 15. v. 4.2. Tim. 3. v. 16. namely that they are διδασκαλία, ἔλεγχος, έπανόρσθωσις, πα-δεία and παράκλησις. But the last and highest end of Scripture, with respect to us, is our salvation and eternal life. John 5. v. 39.ch. 20. v. 31.2. Tim. 3. v. 15. Compare Method. studii Theolog. part. 2. sect. 4. ch. 2. Exeges. de Script. ch. 17. §. 361. & seqq.

VII. Adjuncts. 1. Clarity. Augustine, in questions on Exodus, q. 73: In the Old Testament the new lies hidden, in the New the old lies open. Book 12, against Faustus, ch. 1: The N.T. is veiled in the Old, the Old revealed in the New. Book 15, against Faustus, ch. 14: The Old Testament is the prophecy of the new. Paulinus: In the old there is newness, in the newness antiquity. Luther was often accustomed to say: The N.T. seemed to himself to be the sun, by which the moon of the O.T. is illumined.

2. Dignity. Aug., book 20, On the City of GOD, ch. 4: The testimonies of the O.T. are earlier in time, but the new ones must be preferred before them in dignity, because those old things are the heralds of the new. Therefore the new must be placed first, since, that we may prove it more firmly, the old also are taken up. Among the old are held the Law and the Prophets, among the new the Gospel and the apostolic letters. And Christ himself, demonstrating that this order must be kept, says: every scribe instructed in the kingdom of God is like a father of a family bringing forth from his treasure new things and old. He did not say old things and new, which he would certainly have said unless he had rather chosen to preserve the order of merits than of times. Yet this must not be understood in a Photinian sense, as though there were some inequality in respect of authority—which everywhere is the same—but only in respect of clarity.

Theophilus Nicolaides, in defense of the treatise of the Socinians concerning the Church, ch. 4, p. 67, about to respond to a certain passage of Isaiah, writes thus: Certainly if any Apostle had testified concerning that matter, it would have been far weightier than when a prophet of the old covenant testifies concerning that matter. Ostorod, in the Institut., part 3, fol. 187, calls the O.T. imperfect, the new perfect, and accordingly concludes that the former yields to the latter—which, as regards shadows, figures, and ceremonies of the O.T., is most true, but as regards the moral law and the promise concerning Christ is false.

3. Integrity. That neither certain canonical books of the N.T. have perished, nor has the authentic Greek text been corrupted, is demonstrated elsewhere against Papists. Confession, Exeges. de Script. ch. 6. §. 108. & seqq.; ch. 16. §. 353. & seqq.

4. Necessity. Adam. Conzen. on the preliminary questions on the four Gospels, question 6, denies that the Scriptures are wholly and absolutely necessary, since the Church long lacked them. Yet neither do we establish absolute necessity, but that which is called εξ ὑποσθέσεως,, about which matter we treat in Exeg. de Script. § 20 & seqq.; whence Conzen. himself acknowledges that there is agreement in this question. But it matters little, lest Conzen., while commending the utility of Scripture in words, deny it in fact, when he adds § 3: Innumerable contentions over Scripture assail the world; many would rather have preferred not to have read than to have read adulterated Scriptures. And afterward: I give warning that the condition of those times was not so wretched, who lacked the Scriptures, as the heretics suppose.

5. Division into chapters and verses. Neither existed from the beginning of the N.T.; therefore, when the Doctors of the Church, who were nearest to the times of the Apostles, cite some testimony from the N.T., we see that mention is made not of any chapter but only of the whole book. Balaeus, Century 3, ch. 87, and from him the Centuriators of Magdeburg, cols. 687 and 1114, note that division into chapters was made around the year 1220. Some wish that it was introduced by Stephen Langton, Bishop in England, whom Pope Innocent III raised to the cardinalate in the Year of Christ 1207. The first author of dividing the chapters into verses seems to have been Robert Estienne.

I think I shall be doing something worthwhile if I append two things to these Prolegomena: I.

A catalogue of writers, ancient and modern, who have adorned the whole of Holy Scripture, or at least most of its books, with Commentaries, Paraphrases, notes, animadversions, etc.; omitting, however, those whose monuments have never seen the light, nor perhaps ever will see it: but as they have been kept until now in the cloisters of monks, so they are to be kept hereafter as well, and condemned to perpetual darkness.

T. librorum causa efficiens pri-cipalis sive autor primarius est verus Deus, in essentia unus, in Personis trinus, ex quo etiam divina & Canonica librorum N. T. autoritas dependet. Petr. 1. v. 21. ita quoq; eiusdem impulsu & inspiratu scripserunt, adeoq; non solùm in praedicatione doctrinae coelestis, sed etiam in scriptione fuerunt DEI organa, unde in ipsis librorum exordiis sese DEI servos & Christi Apostolos vocant.

2. ex scribendi mandato. In novissimis temporibus locutus est nobis Deus in Filio suo sive per Filium suum Hebr. 1. v. 1. qui voluntatem & consilium Patris sui coelestis de salute nostra nobis enarravit, Ioh. 1. v. 18. Is Apostolos immediatè â se vocatos, dono miraculorum instructos & extraordinariis Spiritus Sancti donis exornatos iussit docere omnes gentes,Matth. 28. v. 19. non illius solùm sed etiam secuturi temporis, ut constat ex promissione addita v. 20. ergo etiam iussit eos doctrinam scripto complecti: neq; enim omnes gentes etiam secuturi temporis vivâ voce absq; scripto docere poterant, unde Apostolorum officium statuitur, non solùm vivâ voce praedicando, sed etiam scribendo de Christo testificari Ioh. 21. v. 24.1. Ioh. 1. v. 3. v. 4.Apoc. 1. v. 2. v. 3. ac unus eorum, Iohannes scil. expressum & speciale scribendi mandatum divinitus accepit, Apoc. 1. v. 11.v. 19.cap. 2. v. 1.8.12.v. 18.cap. 3. v. 17.v. 14.cap. 14. v. 13.cap. 19. v. 9.cap. 21. v. 5. ex quo sic inferimus. Cuius iussu & mandato Evangelistae & Apostoli scripserunt, is est summus librorum N. T. autor. Atqui Dei iussu & mandato Evangelistae & Apostoli scripserunt. Ergo. Item. Quae Scriptura est ex immediato mandato & impulsu divino profecta, ea est divina, authentica & Canonica. Scriptura N. T. est ex immediato mandato & impulsu divino profecta. Ergo. Iren. lib. 3. adv. haereses cap. 1. Apostoli, quae primum praeconiaverunt, poste a per DEI voluntatem in scripturis nobis tradiderunt. Aug. lib. 1. de consens. Evang. cap. ult. Cum illi (Evangelistae & Apostoli) scripserunt, quae ille ostendit & dixit, nequaequam dicendum est, quòd ipse non scripserit, quandoquidem membra eius id operata sunt, quae dictante capite cognoverunt, Quic quid vero ille de suis dictis & factis nos legere voluit, hoc scribendum iis tanquam suis manibus imperavit, Theoph. praefat. in Matth.

3. Ex scriptionis materia. Quae in libris N. T. continentur, non sunt humano ingenio excogitata, sed mysteria fidei divinitùs revelata. Apostoli ea, quae scripserunt, partim in Schola Christi Filii DEI, in qua ultra triennium fuere instituti, partim in Schola Spiritus Sancti, extraordinariè & copiosissimè die Pentecostes in ipsos effusi, didicerunt. Epist. 1. v. 16. άχουςην φωνης illius: Hic est Filius meus dilectus v. 17. 18. Iohannes testatur, ex revelatione Christi sese scribere Apoc. 1. v. 1. & 10.

4. Ex συμφωνίαlibrorum V. ac N. T. Quod in scriptura V. T. futurum ac suo tempore implendum praenunciatur ac praefiguratur, illud Scriptura N. T. annunciat esse completum, Act. 26. v. 22.Rom. 3. v. 21.cap. 16. v. 26. Unus ergo librorum utriusq; Testamenti autor primarius, ac aequalis est librorum V. ac N. T. autoritas, divina scil. Canonica & authentica. Improbamus ergo, quae Socinus lib. de Autor. Script. p. 18. scribit. Certum est, non posse quenquam ulla ratione seriò recipere Christianam religionem, quin simul confiteatur, in eius patefactione clarè agnitum fuisse, vaticinationum de Iesu Christo & reb. ad ipsum, ob ida ad Christianam religionem pertinentibus, saltem aliqua ex parte aliam sententiam esse ab ea, quae iuxt a literam V. T. esse videtur, eama eiusmodi, ut sine patefactione ista de ea ne suspicari quidem quis quam posset.

5. Ex divina Scripturae efficacia. Ut V. ita quoq; N. T. Scriptura divinam habet efficaciam in hominibus convertendis, illuminandis, regenerandis, renovandis, adeoq; ad fidem & salutem perducendis Ioh. 20. v. ult. 2. Tim. 3. v. 16. Eadem efficax solatium praestat in omnibus adversis Rom. 15. v. 4. proinde non potest non esse divina, authentica & ab ipso DEO tanquam Autore primario profecta.

6. Ex Ecclesiaeμαςυςία. Libri, qui in Codice Biblico N. T. habentur, gaudent consentiente Ecclesiae Christianae per omnes seculorum culorum successiones testimonio. August. lib. 11. contra Faustum cap. 5. Distincta est à posteriorum libris excellentia Canonicae autoritatis V. & N. T. quae Apostolorum confirmata temporibus per successiones Episcoporum & propagationes Ecclesiarum tanquam in sede quadam sublimiter constituta, cui servit omnis fidelis & pius intellectus. Conzenius in quaestionib. prooemialibus in quatuor Evang. q. 3. §. 1. dicit, in consensu & iudicio Ecclesiae primogeniae, cuius iudicium nequaquam fallax esse possit, fidem nostram acquiescere. Atqui 1. testificatio Ecclesiae, praesertim primitivae Apostolorum temporibus vicinae, non confert Evangelistarum scriptis autoritatem, sed duntaxat eam manifestat. 2. nec ex sollus Ecclesiae testimonio, sed & ex aliis κριτηρίοις divina & Canonica horum scriptorum autoritas agnoscitur. 3. Accedit etiam interior Spiritus Sancti testificatio & obsignatio, ut sic in universium tres sint testimoniorum classes, per quae ut totius scripturae, ita quoq; Evangelistarum autoritas nobis innotescit. 4. Conzenius ibid. ex Iren. lib. 3. cap. 11. tanta est circa Evangelia firmitas, ut & ipsi haeretici testimonium ei reddant, & ex ipsis egrediens unus quisa eorum conetur suam confirmare doctrinam. Idem Conzenius del. §. 5. per calumniam nobis tribuit, quod testificationem Ecclesiae primitivae repudiemus, & ad solum privatum Spiritum confugiamus. Notandum tamen discrimen inter libros Canonicos primi & secundi ordinis, de quo suo loco.

III. Causa ministerialis librorum N. T. sunt Evangelistae & Apostoli, quos propterea Christi manus, & Spiritus Sancti Notarios meritò appellamus. Tertull. lib. 4. adv. Marcion. Constituimus inprimis Evangelicum instrumentum Apostolos autores habere, quibus boc munus Evangelii promulgandi ab ipso Domino sit impositum. Quamvis verò duo tantùm ex Evangelistis, videlicet Matthaeus & Iohannes, fuerint Apostoli, in Schola Christi in his terris docentis instituti & copiosâ Spiritus Sancti effusione donati, nihil tamen ex eo derogatur Marci & Lucae autoritati, cùm ipsi quoq; φερόμενοιimpulsi & inspirati à Spiritu Sancto scripserint. Uterq; fuit ex numero LXX. discipulorum, Luc. 10. v. 1. utriusq; Historia Evangelica divinum testimonium sort. ta est, Marci quidem â Petro, Lucae verò â Paulo. Utriusq; scriptura divinis miraculis per Apostolos editis fuit confirmata. Ambrosius in explic. prooem. Lucae tom. 5. p. 7. Non conatus est Matthaeus, non conatus est Marcus, non conatus est Iohannes, sed divino Spiritu ubertatem dictorum, reruma omnium ministrante sine ullo molimine caepta compleverunt. Epiphanius contra Αλόγους.Tunc Spiritus Sanctus impellit Luc. ut ab imo profundo proferret sententiam confutantem deceptos. Sanè Gordonus Huntlaeus Controv. 2. c. 15. p. 190. disputat, S. Lucam ex solae discipulorum relatione scripsisse: Sed deseritur hac in parte â propriis sociis. Didacus Stella in Luc. fol. 3. Lucas beatis simus quamvis audierit â Virgine Deipara & Apostolis, nihilominus Spiritu Sancto dictante & movente scripsit. Adamus Conzen. tom. 2. in Luc. c. 6. Certum est, primariam causam Evangelii scribendi non fuisse scriptionem Paulin, sed caelestem revelationem & imperium.

IV. Materia. Libri N. T. complectuntur tum Historica, tum dogmatica, tum Prophetica, unde distinguuntur in Historiales, Doctrinales, & Propheticum, Historiales tradunt Historiam vel Christi, ut quatuor Evangelistae: vel Apostolorum, ut Acta. Doctrinales sunt Epistolae quinq; Apostolorum, Pauli, Iacobi, Petri, Iohannis & Iudae. Epistolae Pauli quaedam scriptae sunt ante captivitatem, quae sunt numero septem. 1. prior ad Thessalonicenses. 2 posterior ad Thessalonicenses. 3. prior ad Timotheum. 4. prior ad Corinthios. 5. ad Titum 6. posterior ad Corinthios. 7. ad Romanos. quaedam in captivitate, ad quam classem pertinent sex reliquae, de quibus non usq; adeò certò constat, quo ordine scriptae fuerint, nonnulli tamen hunc assignant 1. ad Philippenses. 2. ad Colossenses. 3. ad Philemonem. 4. ad Ephesios. 5. ad Galatas. 6. posterior ad Timotheum. Propheticus N. T. liber unus est, videlicet Apocalypsis Iohannis.

V. Form a librorum N. T. est vel interna, vel externa. Interna est ipsa divina horum librorum autoritas ac maiestas, quae ex immediato Spiritus Sancti afflatu, utpote causa efficiente propria & adaequatâ, ac rerum, quas exponunt, sublimitate, utpote materiâ propriâ & adaequatâ, originem trahit. Forma externa est tum idioma linguae Graecae, quo libri N. T. sunt perscripti, tum sermonis ac styli proprietas, imo singularitas, simplicitatem &

maiestatem miraculo verè divino coniunctam habens. Confer Exeg. de Script. cap. 12. §. 305. & seqq. Quaeritur hoc loco. 1. An omnes N. T. libri Graeco idiomate ab Evangelistis & Apostolis perscripti? Quidam excipiunt Evangelium Matthaei & Epistolam ad Hebraeos, quae duo linguâ Hebraeâ; ac Evangelium Marci, quod linguâ Latinâ perscriptum censent. Sed rectiùs dicitur, omnes omninò N. T. libros Graeco idiomate ab ipsis Evangelistis & Apostolis esse scriptos, unde illi ipsi, qui contrarium statuunt, fateri coguntur, Graecam editionem N. T. universam Evangelistas & Apostolos autores vel certè approbatores habere. Bellarm. lib. 2. de V. T. cap. 7.

Q. 2. Quare Evangelistae & Apostoli non vernaculâ lingua, Hebraea scilicet vel Syrâ, sed Graecâ scribere voluerint. Resp. Quemadmodum ante Christum exhibitum doctrina caelestis eo idiomate fuit conscripta, quod erat proprium & patrium Israelitis, quibus concredita τὰ λόγια τοῦ σθεοῦ,Rom. 3. v. 2. qui erant populus DEI peculiaris & περιούσιος,Deut. 7. v. 7. &c. sic post Christum exhibitum voluit Deus eandem scribi Graecâ linguâ, ut ad Ecclesiam ex omnibus gentibus colligendam facilius propagaretur. Lingua enim Graeca tunc temporis fuit. 1. vulgatissima. Etsi enim Romanorum Monarchia tum longè lateq; patuerit, tamen lingua Latina nondumita diffusa erat, teste Cicerone pro Archia. 2. inter gentium linguas omnium praestantissima. 3. Libri V. T. ex LXX. Interpr. versione â Iudaeis & gentilibus legebantur. 4. Hâc linguâ tota gentilium Philosophia erat conscripta, illam ut Deus faciliùs redargueret, retineri voluit linguam eam, qua Philosophia gentilium erat consignata.

Notandum hoc loco. 1. Etsi Evangelistae & Apostoli Graecâ lingvâ scripserint, tamen multi in eorum scriptis occurrunt idiotismi Hebraici.

2. Evangelistae & Apostoli multas voces latinas usu tunc receptas retinuerunt, ad inflexionem tamen Graecam redactas, ut ἀσσάριος, δηνάριος κεντυρίων, κίνσος, κουςωδία, λεγεων, λεντίον, μάκελλον, λιβερτῖνος, μίλιον, μεμβράνα, μόδιος, ξέςης, σικάριος, σουδάριον, σπεκουλάτωρ, ταβόρνα, φοδον, τίτλος, φραγελλοῦν, φραγέλλων. 3. Omnia vocabula N. T. si non sunt Graeca aut Latina, ipsa origine Chaldaica sunt, aut si Hebraea sunt. Chaldaicâ tamen for-â enunciantur.

4. Dicta V. T. ab Evangelistis & Apostolis allegantur. 1 Vel iuxta sensum tantùm, vel ivata sensum & verba simul. De allegatione quo ad sensum, sic scribit Hieron. lib. de optimo genere interpr. tom. 2. Scriptores Evangeliorum dum Prophetas pro restimonio eorum, quae Christus vel dixit, vel fecit, afferunt, interdum non tam verba ipsa, quàm sensum illorum citare solent, ut ostendant, regnum Dei non esse in sermone, sed in vertute. Si iuxta sensum & verba simul Prophetica oracula allegant, tum id faciunt. 2. Vel iuxta LXX. Imerpp. versionem, vel iuxta textum Hebraeum. De priore allegationis modo sic scribit Hieronymus in quaest. super Genes. c. 46. Illud generaliter observandum, quod ubicuna S. Apostoli aut Apostolici viri loquantur ad populos, iis pleruna testimontis abutantur, quae iam fuerant in gentibus divulgata, videl. per LXX. Interpp. translationem. De posteriore idem sic disserit. Epist. 151 ad Algasiam. Ubicuna de Veteri instrumento Evangelistae & Apostoli testimonia protulerunt, diligentiùs observandum est, non eos verba secutos esse, sed sensum, & ubicuna ab Hebraeo discrepant, Hebraeum sensum suis expresisse sermonibus. lib. 2. contra Ruffin. Apostolici viri Scripturis utuntur Hebraicis. Ipsos Apostolos & Evangelistas hoc fecisse perspicuum est. Dominus atSalvator ubicuna veteris Scripturae meminit, de Hebraicis voluminibus ponit exempla, ut est illud: Qui credit in me, sicut Scripturadicit, de ventre eius fluent aquae vivae. Et in ipsa cruce Eli Eli lamma azabtani, quod interpretatur, Deus meus, Deus meus, quare me dereliquisti, non ut à LXX. positum est, Deus meus respice in me, quare me dereliquisti? Et multa his similia. Nec hoc dicimus, quod LXX. sugillemus, sed quod Apostolorum & Christi maior sit autoritas, & ubicuna LXX. ab Hebraeo non discordant, ibi Apostolos de interpretatione eorum exempla sumsisse; ubi verò discrepant, id posuisse in Graeco, quod apud Hebraeos didicerant. (Similia exempla, ubi Evangelistae & Apostoli discesserunt â versione LXX. Interpp. & fontes secuti sunt, passim occurrunt. Matth. 2. v. 15. ex Oseae. 11. v. 1. Matth. 4. v. 15. ex Esai. 9. v. 1.Matth. 8. v. 17. ex Esai. 53. v. 4.Matth. 12. v. 18. ex Esai. 42. v. 2. &c.

VI. Finis Scripturae N. T. idem qui Scripturae V. T. videl. respectu DEI, salutaris eiusdem agnitio & glorificatio; respectu nostri finis est vel intermedius, vel ultimus. Intermedii fines exponuntur ab Apostolo Rom. 15. v. 4.2. Tim. 3. v. 16. quod sint διδασκαλία, ἔλεγχος, έπανόρσθωσις, πα-δεία ac παράκλησις. Ultimus ac summus, respectu nostri, finis Scripturae est nostra salus ac vita aeterna. Ioh. 5. v. 39.cap. 20. v. 31.2. Tim. 3. v. 15. Confer Method. studii Theolog. part. 2. sect. 4. cap. 2. Exeges. de Script. cap. 17. §. 361. & seqq.

VII. Adiuncta. 1. Perspicuitas. August. in qq: super Exod. q. 73. In vetere Testamento novum latet, in novo vetus patet. lib. 12. contra Faustum cap. 1. Test. N. est in vetere velatum, vetus in novo revelatum. lib. 15. contra Faustum cap. 14. Vetus Testamentum est Prophetia novi. Paulinus: In veteri novitas est, in novitate vetustas. Lutherus crebrò fuit dicere solitus, N. T. sibi videri solem, à quo Luna T. V. illustretur.

2. Dignitas. Aug. lib. 20. de Civ. DEI cap. 4. Testimonia V. T. priorae sunt tempore, sed nova anteponēda sunt dignitate, quoniā illa vetera praeconia sunt novorum. Nova igitur ponenda sunt prius, quae ut firmius probemus, assumuntur & vetera. In veterib. habetur Lex & Prophetae, in novis Evangelium & Apostolicae literae. Hunc & ipse Christus ordinem servandum esse demonstrans, scriba inquit, eruditus in regno Dei similis est patrifamilias proferenti de The sauro suo nova & vetera. Non dixit vetera & nova, quod utiq; dixisset, nisi maluisset meritorum ordinem servare quàm temporum. Neq; tamen hoc accipiendum sensu Photiniano, quasi ratione autoritatis sit quaedam inaequalitas, quae utrobiq; eadem, sed tantum ratione claritatis.

Theophilus Nicolaides in defensione tract. Sociniani de Ecclesia cap. 4. p. 67. responsurus ad locum quendam Esaiae sic scribit. Certè si Apostolus aliquis eâ de re testatus fuisset, multò id magis valuisset, quā cùm Phropheta veteris federis eâ de re testatur. Ostorod. in Instit. part. 3. f. 187. V. T. vocat imperfectum, novum perfectum, adeoq; illud huic cedere concludit, quod quoad umbras, figuras, ac Ceremonias V. T. est verissimum, sed quoad legem moralem & promissionem de Christo falsum est.

3. Integritas. Nec libros quosdam N. T. Canonicos deperditos esse, nec Graecum textum authenticum corruptum, suo loco contra Pontificos demonstratur. Confes Exeges. de Script. cap. 6. §. 108. & seqq. cap. 16. §. 353. & seqq.

4. Necessitas. Adam. Conzen. in qq. prooemial. in quatuor Evang. q. 6. negat, Scriptur as esse prorsus & absolutè necessarias, cùm Ecclesia diu iisdem caruerit. Atqui absolutam necessitatem nec nos statuimus, sed eam, quae vocatur εξ ὑποσθέσεως, quâ de re egimus, in Exeg. de Script. § 20. & seq. inde Conzen. ipse agnoscit, esse in hac quaestione consensum. Parum verò a best, quin -onzen. Scripturae utilitatem verbis commendans, reipsâ eam neget, quando subiungit. §. 3. De scripturâ innumerae concertationes orbem conbellunt, multosa praestaret non legisse, quàm lectas adulter asse Scripturas. Et postea. Hoc moneo, non fuisse miserum adeò statum illorum temporum, quScripturis caruerunt, ut haeretici arbitrantur.

5. Distinctio per capita & versiculos. Neutra extitit ab initio N. T. ideò ab Ecclesiae Doctoribus, qui Apostolorum temporibus fuêre proximiores, allegantibus aliquod ex N. T. testimonium, nullam capitis, sed solùm totius libri mentionem fieri videmus. Balaeus Cent. 3. c. 87. ex eo Cent. Magd. col. 687. & 1114. annotant, distinctionem per capita factam circa annum 1220. Quidam volunt, eam introductam per Stephanum Langthonum Episcopum in Anglia, quem Pontifex. Innocentius III. Anno Christi 1207. ad Cardinalatum evexit. Distinctionis capitum in versiculos primus autor fuisse videtur Robertus Stephanus.

Operae pretium facturum me puto, si duo Prolegomenis his subiungam.

I. Catalogum Scriptorum, veterum ac recentiorum, qui in Ser. S. Universam, vel certè plerosq; illius libb. Comment aria, Paraphrases, notas, animadversiones &c. adornarunt; Omissis tamen illis, quorum Monumenta nunquam lucem viderunt, nec visura etiam fortè unquam sunt: sed in Monachorum claustris ut hactenus servata, ita deinceps quoq; servanda, perpetuisq; tenebris damna-da.

## 1:1 Introduction: Anecdotes to the Prologue Chapter I
II. What should be thought concerning those Eastern versions of the N.T., namely the Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic, which are believed to belong to such great antiquity, and how much learned men attribute to them.

Therefore, since what first concerns us is brought forth into light, the commentaries and notes on the entire Bible are almost these:

Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus in Syria, flourished in the year 430, edition Cologne 1573.

To this place can be referred the treatise entitled: Exposition of the Holy Fathers upon the Histories of both Testaments, printed at Naples 1636.

Isidore Junior, Bishop of Seville [Hispalensis]. He lived in the year 630, published at Paris 1580, in folio.

Haymo Bishop of Halberstadt, flourished in the year 830. Homilies on the Gospels, edited at Cologne 1532, Antwerp 1559. Commentary on Acts and on the Canonical Epistles, Cologne 1573; on the Epistles of Paul, Paris 1533; on the Apocalypse, Cologne 1529, Paris 1540.

Rabanus Maurus. Sixth Archbishop of Mainz, he lived in the year 840. From this man's works Strabus took his Gloss.

Strabus Monk of Fulda, pupil and scribe of Rabanus, lived in the year 880. To him is attributed the so-called ordinary Gloss over the entire Bible, edition Lyons in the year 1589, seven volumes in folio.

Anselm of Laon, Schoolman. He lived about 1077. His is the interlinear Gloss, which exists together with the ordinary Gloss and Lyra's Commentary, edited at Lyons in the year 1589.

Albert Bishop of Regensburg, by nationality a Swabian, of the Order of St. Dominic, teacher of Thomas of Aquino, on account of his outstanding learning surnamed the Great, is said to have written commentaries on nearly all of Sacred Scripture. Flourished about 1260, printed Cologne 1607.

Alexander of Hales, also called de Hales, by nationality an Englishman, teacher of Thomas Aquinas and of Bonaventure, of the Order of St. Francis, and the first of the Franciscans who attained the insignia of the Mastership, indeed the first Doctor, fountain and origin of all other scholastic Doctors, both in the order of Friars Minors and Preachers, and also in the assembly and college of all seculars, as Stephen Brulifer has concerning him, treatise on servile fear. He, I say, wrote also a Postilla over the whole Bible; he died in the year 1245.

Hugo de S. Caro, a Burgundian by nationality, Cardinal of St. Sabina of the Order of Preachers, lived circa 1240 A.D. His commentaries on the entire Holy Scripture, according to the quadruple sense, were published at Cologne in 1621 in eight folio volumes.

Nicholas of Lyra, converted from Judaism to Christianity and enrolled in the Order of Minors, lived in the year of Christ 1320. Some say he was by nationality an Englishman: but Drusius on the passages Gen. 15. and on the passage Exod. c. 33. writes that he was so named after a town of Brabant called Lira, because he originated from there. He wrote Commentaries, that is, Postils and Moralities, on the entire Bible, printed at Lyons 1590, also at Basel 1506. Concerning him this saying is commonly circulated: if Lyra had not played the lyre, Luther would not have dan-ced, whereby they wish to intimate that Blessed Luther owes much to Lyra: And indeed it can hardly be denied that Megalandrus judged Lyra's Commentary on the Old Testament most worthy of reading, concerning which matter see Blessed Pareus in his Patrologia, p. 627.

After blessed Luther himself and Philip Melanchthon, who everywhere illustrated the Holy Bible in their writings, among the Lutherans, likewise John Brenz (whose works exist printed in several volumes in folio at Tübingen in the year 1576 and following) and Luke Osiander (whose Commentaries came out again in three volumes in folio at Frankfurt in the year 1608, and in quarto at Tübingen 1591), all of whom flourished in the preceding century, others too published commentaries or notes on the entire Bible: Dr. John Quistorpius, (whose Annotations on all the books of the Bible appeared at Rostock in the year 1648,) Dr. Daniel Cramer on the summary of the Bible, Dr. Philip Henry Friedlieb, James Raupp (the third book of whose Portable Library presents Commentaries on the Bible, printed at Erfurt in the year 1654), and certain others. Above all, however, the Ernestine Bible deserves to be perused, which has thus far seen the light described several times by the Enderian presses, illuminated with continuous commentaries by various very learned and most illustrious men by the most gracious command of the Most Illustrious and Most High Prince and Lord, Lord ERNST, Duke of Saxony, Jülich, Cleves and Mountains &c., Most Glorious and Most Devout Prince, revised moreover by my late Father [Pareus], and examined anew by the late Dr. Glass, which Bible those will admit to be in the manner of many commentaries together who shall peruse it more diligently.

From the Calvinists they have published partly notes, partly homilies, and partly Commentaries on almost the entire Holy Scripture. Calvin himself, Conrad afterwards Pellican, likewise Rudolph Gwalther, Franciscus Junius, Paulus Tossanus, Johannes Piscator of Herborn, Ludovicus de Dieu, Hugo Grotius, Hugh Broughton, etc.

From the Papists there exist sufficiently thick volumes of very many, by which they have endeavored to explain the sacred codices.

From among the older writers are cited Basilius Zanchius Bergenas (whose annotations on all the books of Holy Scripture appeared at Rome 1553, Cologne 1602, in 8vo.), Peter Aureolus Archbishop of Aix (flourishing 1317; but his Compendious Commentary on the whole of Holy Scripture was published at Paris in the year 1565, in 8vo.), Denis the Carthusian of Rijkel (died in the year 1471; his Commentaries on the books of the Bible are found in vol. 7 and following of the edition printed at Cologne in the years 1535, 1538, and 1539), and others; from among those more recent, Franciscus Lucas Brugnensis (whose annotations on the sacred Bible, in which passages varying in divergent copies are examined, were published at Antwerp 1581, in 8vo.), Emanuel Sa the Portuguese of the Society of Jesus (whose annotations on Holy Scripture were edited at Antwerp 1596, Cologne in 4to., 1609), Cornelius Cornelii à Lapide of the Society of Jesus (whose Commentaries on the whole of Holy Scripture—except at least one or two books—published at various times at Antwerp make up eight volumes in folio), James Tirinus likewise a Jesuit (whose Commentaries on the Old and New Testament appeared at Antwerp in the year 1632), William Estius in his Golden Annotations on the more difficult passages of Scripture, published at Cologne in the year 1622, John Stephen Menochius a Jesuit, whose Commentaries were also printed at Cologne, Francis Lu-as, Gabriel à Costa, at Rome; Joh. Alba, Valencia 1615 in 4to.; Felicianus Capito, on disputed passages of the Old and New Testament, Venice.

To illustrate the New Testament, or the Evangelists—at any rate by commentaries, paraphrases, and notes—the Fathers enumerated above have labored abundantly, arranged in alphabetical order.

Augustine in the Questions on the Gospels, likewise On the Harmony of the Gospels, and also the Questions on the Old and New Testament, vol. 4 of his Works.

Anselm of Canterbury on various passages of the Gospels.

The Venerable Bede, vols. 5 and 8 of his Works.

Eusebius Pamphili in twenty books of expositions of the Gospel.

Gregory the Great in four books of Explanations of the Gospels.

Job Chrysostom, whose Homilies and Commentary appeared in Greek and Latin from the Commeline press in the year 1603.

Theophilus of Antioch's brief Comments and Allegories on the four sacred Gospels, in 4 books, are found in Vol. 1 of the Library of the Fathers.

Euthymius Zigabenus, Monk. Concerning him the Jesuit Tirinus writes that he gathered elegant commentaries on the Scriptures from the writings of Chrysostom and others of the ancients; he lived about A.D. 1118.

Theophylact, Bishop of the Bulgarians, wrote an epitome out of John Chrysostom. It has been published in Greek and Latin.

On the Pauline Epistles specifically Ambrose (though some doubt whether those commentaries attributed to vol. 5 are his), Aretas of Caesarea, Oecumenius, Andrew of Caesarea (these three exist in Greek and Latin), Theodoret, Primasius, Jerome &c.

Among our own writers there exist on the New Testament comments and notes by Lucas Lossius, Dr. Bugenhagen, Erasmus Sarcerius, Joachim Camerarius, Dr. Aegidius Hunnius, Matthias Flacius, Dr. Calixtus, &c.

Chemnitz–Lyser Harmony on the Four Evangelists, continued and completed by Blessed Parent, likewise the harmony of Dr. Althofer.

On the Pauline Epistles: Dr. Tilemann Heshusius, Dr. George Mylius, Dr. George Major, Dr. Nicholas Selnecker, Dr. David Runge, Dr. Friedrich Balduin, &c.

From among the Calvinians on the entire New Testament: Augustine Marlorate, Martin Bucer, Daniel Tossanus, Benedict Aretius, Theodore Beza, Balduin. Waleus, Henry Bullinger, Leo Judäus, Thomas Cartwright, James Cappellus, Louis Cappellus in the Spicilegium, Daniel Heinsius, and several others.

On the Evangelists separately: Ulrich Zwingli, Job Jacob Grynaeus, Louis de Dieu, John Cameron in the Myrothece, Bucer, Otto Brunfels, John Boys at London &c.

On the Pauline Epistles: Nicholas Hemming, Wolfgang Musculus Dušan, David Pareus, &c.

From among the Papists on the entire New Testament: Thomas Aquinas vols. 15 and 16, Alfonso Salmerón the Jesuit, Lorenzo Valla, Erasmus of Rotterdam, Johannes Benediktus, Johannes Gagnaeus, Frans Coster, Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, &c.

On the Evangelists: Cornelius Jansenius Bishop of Ghent, Johannes Maldonatus Jesuit, Adam Contzen Jesuit, Franciscus Lucas of Bruges, Sebastianus Barradius Jesuit, Diego de Estella, in folio, Lyons, Perez, Perpiñán, Pitseus, Sylveira, &c.

On the Epistles of Paul and the remaining Canonical ones: Marsilius Facinus, Benedictus Justinianus, Gulielmus Estius, Claudius Guilliaudus, Franc. Tilemannus. &c.

Very much will also help toward understanding the tables of either covenant to have diligently perused the Harmony of Holy Scripture of Mr. D. Walther and the Sacred Philology of B. D. Glassius, most fortunate interpreters of Scripture and theologians most deserving regarding the Church of Christ. To these there can be added by one especially devoted to philology, the Key to Scripture of Flacius, likewise writings of D. Franzius, Drusius, Caninius, Gataker, Amama, Corneille Bertram &c.

Those who wrote particular commentaries on this or that single book, whether of the Old or New Testament, shall be enumerated after the prolegomena of each book.

I proceed to the second member of the things to be said, intending to commemorate briefly of what authority and antiquity those more celebrated versions of the N.T. are: the Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic. This, however, not so much in my own words as in the words of our own theologians and other learned men.

So therefore concerning the authority and antiquity of the Syriac version Mr. D. Waltherus, Office of Libraries [Offic. Bibliothec.] p. 295 §. 345. and 346.: However we should relate the Syriac version to some one of the Evangelists or Apostles, or even to the very times of the Apostles themselves, and what immediately followed while their lives were still going on (which certain Syrians do, namely referring it to Mark the Evangelist, if faith is to be given to Gulielmus Postellus, which the same had reported shortly before out of Guido Fabricius: nay indeed B. D. W. Franzius in his treatise On the Interpretation of Scripture p. 56., and Immanuel Tremellius in the preface to the Paraphrases similarly warned us to reduce the Syriac version back to the Apostles and apostolic men) ought rightly to be religiously observed by us, partly because thus it would have divine authority, yet why we ourselves deny it to them will presently become plain, partly because absolutely no mention of it occurs among Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Eusebius, Athanasius, &c. and others from antiquity, who taught either in Syria or in Egypt , or about various they disagreed about the editions of the Scriptures: (the same reasoning, besides several others, B. Parens presses in his Method of Studying Theology, p. 64, likewise in the Exposition of the first Topic, §. 509.) Yet we by no means begrudge this version (the Syriac) every praise of antiquity, whoever made it & whenever—that God alone knows—but rather we abundantly confirm it, both because of the uncorrupted elegance of speech, and because of the absence of the latter Epistle of Peter, the second and third of John, likewise of Jude, of Revelation, and of the story of the adulteress, chapter 8. of John, which, even though they breathe the same Spirit as the remaining writings, yet among the very old ecclesiastical writers there was always debate about them, and those books were regarded as later than the rest—is not unclear. Rutgherus Spey Bopardianus testifies in the Preface to his Arabic Grammar that an Exemplar exists in the Heidelberg Library, copied by hand more than 800 Years ago. This Mr. D. Walther reports, loc. cit. The same man relates that the copy which Guido Fabricius collated with the Vienna one, was written in the Year 1500 of the Reign of Alexandria (that is, Anno Christi 1200.). Concerning the Syriac Codex of the Four Evangelists, which is kept in the Altdorf Library, brought out of Syria by Dr. Jacob Fetzero, I dealt with its antiquity in dissertation 2 on the Syriac N. T., twelve years before these times, when it was handled here, Q. 3. Furthermore, concerning the authority and also the usefulness of the said version, Mr. D. Walther writes thus, loc. cit. §. 347. The authority of the Syriac translation can only be human. 1. because it is merely a version. 2. because those entire books are wanting, just enumerated above, which however are found in all the Editions of the Greek fountain. 3. because in certain places it departs from the Greek Original. §. 348. Meanwhile its usefulness is very great, which Laurence Fabricius splendidly illustrates with a few examples in the Preface, which he prefixed to the Syriac Grammar and Lexicon of Crinesius. The same usefulness of this version is acknowledged also among our own countrymen by Dr. James Martin, when, in the Preface to the Syriac N. T. of Trostius, after he had illustrated certain passages of the N. T. by the benefit of the Syriac version, he concludes: From these and similar passages, with which the whole Codex of the N. T. abounds, the kindly disposed reader readily perceives the supreme usefulness of this Syriac version, nay its necessity, without which a pious and diligent interpreter of this New Testament can by no means do. And further: Wherefore those certain slander-mongers are by no means to be listened to, who do not blush to throw at us: that it is not so useful or necessary that such great expense and labor be expended on correcting and editing this Syriac Codex, seeing that in the Syriac tongue the N. T. was not written by the Evangelists and Apostles, and it cannot be denied that down to now many theologians most learned have flourished with the highest renown in the Church, who without the help of this version, and without any knowledge whatsoever of the Syriac tongue, have carried on their business most successfully in the version and interpretation of the Greek codex of the N. T. Truly admirable objections, and lamps smelling mightily of oil! For my part I freely grant both points, that the N. T. was not written originally in the Syriac idiom; and therefore that what is set forth in this Codex is only a version. Yet let those pestering and unfair critics know that the Syriac tongue is that in which either Christ himself conversed with his Apostles, or else which approaches closest to the mother-tongue of our Savior and of his compatriots, into which all the writings of the N. T. of the newly founded Church were transferred, and indeed at that very time when the Apostles, those divine teachers, trained by Christ himself, directly taught and informed by the Holy Ghost, were laying the earliest foundations of the Church of Christ among the nations. Prick up your ears, then, O Critic, whoever you are, whatever camp you belong to—you who carry your brains not in your heel but in your head; This is the Syrian version, but the first and most ancient of all: It is a version, I say, but to be preferred before all others as more reliable and fuller: it is a version, I still say; but either by some one of the Evangelists, or altogether by those who had the very Apostles present at Antioch, whom they were able to consult and hear about many obscure passages. Therefore to this alone, when some obscurity or difficulty occurs in the Greek sources, one safely approaches: this alone, when doubt arises concerning the interpretation and version of any passage, is safely consulted without error: through this alone is the Greek text truly illuminated and rightly understood. For the authority of this version alone comes nearest to the majesty of those very sources. And a little later: Our Germany lacked it, and therefore also the theologians in her, most learned men of their own century and time, [lacked] this first version, yet not without great loss. Since, however learned, eloquent, and ingenious those men may have been, nevertheless they could by no means attain the true meaning and sense of many places from the Latin version, nor even from the primitive Greek. B. D. Martini in his letter. With what praise—or greater—the Syriac version could be adorned, I indeed strongly doubt. But our Adversaries also hold said version in esteem. Let us hear at least one or another.

From among the Calvinians Daniel Chamier, Tom. 1. of Panstratiae lib. 12. c. 1. §. 14. concerning the Syr. version says thus: This work (the Syriac New Testament) he writes, is most ancient: but so much that Bonaventure Cornelius Bertram, a man exceedingly skilled above all in these languages, dares to attribute it to the nascent Church of Antioch, first called Christians in her, Preface to his Comparison of the Hebrew and Aramaic Grammar. (Alsted too does the same in lib. 2. praecognition. c. 113.) But even though this be uncertain, yet that it is most useful, no one will deny who has used it: Although there are some things which do not altogether please, I would easily grant to Bellarmine. John Cameron Praelections Tom. 1. p. 48. & 67. He calls the Syrian Interpreter both most ancient and most learned. From among the Papists Francis Lucas of Bruges, a most learned writer, in the Pref. upon the Comm. on the N. T. n. 6. says thus: This, he says, I hold undoubtingly, that the Syriac text of the N. T. must be held and revered as [from] the most ancient copy of the Greek, and indeed in its exact place. (Andrew Rivet concurs with Francis Lucas in the Isagoge p. 184.)

Moreover Various editions of the Syriac N. T. are available. For as soon as possible John Albert Widmanstad, Doctor of Laws and Chancellor of the provinces of Eastern Austria (by whose care and diligence, but at the expense of Emperor Ferdinand, the Syriac N. T., set forth by type, first saw public light at Vienna in the year of Christ 1555) broke the ice happily in this difficult undertaking; immediately many followed him, who partly transferred the Syriac text into Hebrew characters, partly furnished the version of the Syriac translation (which Tremellius attempted twelve years after the Viennese edition had come out, in the edition which saw light in the year 1568, and about the same time Guy Fabrice a Frenchman), striving to commend their diligence to the Church. The same Syriac translation also came out, but in Hebrew dress, at Antwerp in smaller form in the year of Christ 1575. It is also seen inserted in the Polyglot Bibles of Elias Hutter, then likewise in the Spanish, French and English Biblical work. But separately it was published in native letters and with a new version by Martin Trost of Cöthen in Anhalt in the year of Christ 1621.

But let this warning concerning the Syriac version suffice here. The Arabic version of the New Testament was indeed set forth in type many years after the Syriac version (and the Evangelists first at Rome by the Medicean Press together with the Latin version, in fol., in the year 1591, which edition sometimes αωμάίζειν, and much better paraphrases than it are found elsewhere, as Isaac Casaubon warns, Exercises 15, n. 12, p. 388; but the entire New Testament at Leiden, through the diligence, industry, and types of Thomas Erpenius, in the year 1616, in what is called quarto format. It is also contained in the French and English Biblical Work); thus it is judged to be of less authority or antiquity than that Syriac one. As concerns the author, Guilhelmus Fabricius attests in his Preface to the Syriac New Testament that there exists an Arabic paraphrase of both Testaments, whose author is Saadia Gaon (whose various writings among the Jews Buxtorf reviews in his Rabbinical Library). This very thing Erpenius confirms too with respect to the Old Testament in his Preface to the Arabic New Testament, who likewise gave hope of publishing that version of the Old Testament with translation and notes; but prevented by untimely death he could not stand by his promises, and the publication of the whole Arabic Old Testament was deferred until that French Biblical Work saw the light thirteen years ago. The English strove to surpass its magnificence by concise usefulness in their biblical work published this year.

Moreover, as regards the author of the Arabic translation of the New Testament, according to Erpenius on the place cited above, the Gospels seem to have been rendered (into the Arabic language) from the Greek by Nesielama son of Azalkelabi. But the said Author has some doubt about whether the remaining books of the New Testament have the same translator in their Arabic version, since they differ somewhat in phraseology from the Gospels, and seem closer to the Syriac text than to the Greek in most places. However that may be regarding the author, Erpenius held it placed beyond all risk of doubt that the New Testament had been turned into the tongue of the Arabs many centuries ago, and accordingly that the Arabic version would prove no less useful to all theologians, because of its antiquity equally with its fidelity, than that noble Syriac edition which came out at Vienna under the care of Widmanstadt. Moreover, that the ⟦f1 antiquity of the Arabic version of the New Testament can be gathered among other things also from this: that that manuscript codex which Erpenius used from the Library of the Academy of Leyden was written in the monastery of St John in the desert of Thebais in the year of the era of Diocletian 1059, that is, of Christ 1342; yet this very codex itself was copied from another exemplar, and that again from another, as appears from the colophon of the same. And whereas Erpenius declares concerning the Arabic version of the Epistles, namely that it seems closer to the Syriac than to the Greek text, he did not hesitate to pronounce the same thing concerning the Arabic version of the whole New Testament. Isaac Casaubon: indeed, he writes expressly the same thing, that the Arabic interpretation has been rendered mostly from the Syrian translation, Exercise 16. on the Annales Ecclesiastici of Baronius, Year 34. §. 73. p. 606. But whatever the truth of this matter may be, learned men nevertheless consider that version worthy to be diligently compared by lovers of the Sacred Letters with the Original Text, which Louis de Dieu did above all through all four Evangelists, likewise the Acts of the Apostles and the Epistle to the Romans; but before him the very Reverend Doctor Paul Tarnovius [did so] through John, who, being an eminent theologian, esteemed the Arabic version so highly that he did not hesitate to clothe his Arabic translation of the Gospel of John in Latin dress and illustrate it with notes.

Finally, as regards the Ethiopic version of the New Testament, Rome first saw light thereof in the year 1548, but not entire: for in that edition the Pauline Epistles are still wanting, at which you would not undeservedly wonder, since there can be seen therein besides the Johannine and Petrine Epistles, and also the Epistle of Jude and of James, likewise the Apocalypse and the Epistle to the Hebrews. Under whose auspices and care however that edition came forth into public, the closing formula of the book indicates, which is such as follows:

That is: This book was printed at Rome. In the time of Pope Paul Farnese, and of Gabriel Patriarch (of Alexandria) and of our King Claudius &c.

And this work was wrought by Tasfa Ziion Malchesinus, who set out to Jerusalem for the sake of the salvation of his soul and on account of piety. Therefore that first edition of the Evangelists, and the things appended to them, owed their birth to those Ethiopians who, pilgriming for the cause of religion from Ethiopia to Jerusalem, and from Jerusalem to Rome, arrived: for these very men erected Printing at Rome, and caused those sacred books brought with them from Ethiopia to be struck off. They were helped perchance by the generosity of wealthier men there, and among them especially of Nicholas the Deacon, Cardinal: whence he also wished his insignia to be displayed on the leaf adjoining the frontispiece of the book, with this subscription.

-- That is, Nicholas the Deacon, Cardinal. In the codex which I possess, these Ethiopian words, added in handwriting by I know not whom, are visible: -- Great pillar of the Church.

It is difficult to determine with certainty who is the author of the Ethiopian version of the New Testament, and of what antiquity this version is. And although now upwards of a hundred and ten years ago and indeed seven years before the Syriac, the version of the four Evangelists, of the Acts of the Apostles, of the Apocalypse, likewise of the Epistle to the Hebrews, of both Petrine ones, of Jude, of John and of James, came forth publicly in Ethiopian, printed with types in Europe, nevertheless that edition seems to have fallen into the hands of few Learned Men, either because the greatest part of the printed copies was sent into the kingdom of Abyssia, or because Europeans were quite convinced that the authority and usefulness of the said version was exceedingly slight. Hence also mention of this translation occurs very rarely among the Authors, who both back then and recently wrote concerning the various versions of the Bibles; much less was it ever compared with many, whether with the Greek text or with other versions, whereas on the contrary the Syriac version of the New Testament has been printed somewhat frequently; and is everywhere adduced by the Interpreters of Sacred Scripture. But what ought to be thought of the assertion of Cornel. à Lapide, who writes among other things: Grant that St. Matthew preached in hither Ethiopia, which lies nearer to Egypt, and is today called Sonnar, where the Ethiopians are darker/blacker, and that he is said to have died in the city of Luab, where temples still stand in honour of St. Matthew: nevertheless the remainder of Ethiopia, that is, Abyssia, received the Gospels, and the other Holy Scriptures, together with the faith of Christ, as it plainly reports, from a certain Ethiopian Monk, whose name was Aba Salama, that is, Father of peace, for the reason that he brought them true peace and salvation. Educated among the Eastern Arabs, he drank in from them the Christian faith and the Holy Scriptures, and thereafter communicated the same to the whole of Ethiopia; whence he is regarded as its Apostle. On which account the Ethiopian version of Holy Scripture agrees with the Arabic, as with its own mother. What, I say, ought to be thought of this, especially given that the Ethiopian version of the New Testament acknowledges the Arabic as its mother, or was translated from it, will appear from the comparison of the said versions, both among themselves and with others, which will occasionally be undertaken below. As also what should be judged concerning that judgment of Hugo Grotius, who gathers from the fact that the concluding clause of the Lord's Prayer stands both in the Syriac and in the Latin text, and in the Arabic, but is not read in the most ancient Greek copies, that not only the Arabic and Latin version, but also the Syriac was made, after the Churches λετουργία had received a settled form. But this too shall be dealt with at Chapter VI. of Matthew, verse 13. At any rate, let him who is curious about these matters weigh this point here: namely, that if the Arabic version is the mother of the Ethiopian, as I adduced Cornelius à Lapide asserting, how did it come about that in the Ethiopian version that clause is not read, whereas on the contrary it stands in the Arabic version of the Erpenian edition. But if the Arabic was for the most part rendered from the Syriac version, as Casaubonus holds, why is it wanting in the Arabic translation of the Roman edition, whereas on the contrary it is read in the Syriac? and indeed with all the witnesses concurring whom Learned Men have hitherto compared, the Syriac codices, from which even this most ancient manuscript codex of the Library of Altdorff does not stray.

Appeal. The name of evangelist is taken in two ways. 1. Generally for any teacher of the Church, because to all belongs -υαγγελίζεσθα-, Isa. 41. v. 27.2. Tim. 4. v. 5. 2. Specifically for a certain definite grade and order of Doctors in the primitive Church, Eph. 4. v. 11. concerning whom see the Locus on the Ministry of the Church §. 227. 3. Most specially, for those secretaries of the Holy Spirit, who, having embraced the evangelical History concerning Christ in letters, performed by divine impulse a service both useful and necessary toward gathering together the Church, not merely of their own times, but even unto the very end of the world. This word is taken in this latter signification when the four Evangelists are numbered.

Latin:

II. Quid sentiendum sit de versionibus illis N. T. Orientalibus, Syriacâ nempe, Arabica & Aethiopica, cuius illae credantur antiquitatis, & quantum viri eruditi eis tribuant.

Quod primum igitur concernit, in lucem quorum prodierunt Commentaria ac notae in Universa Biblia, ferè sunt isti:

Theodoretus, Cyri in Syriâ Episcopus flor. Anno 430. edit. Colon. 1573.

Referri huc potest tractatus, inscriptus: Expositio SS. Patrum in utriusq; Testamenti Historias, excusus Neapoli 1636.

Isidorus Iunior, Episcopus Hispalensis. vixit Anno. 630. editus Parisiis 1580. in fol.

Haymo Episcopus Halberstadiensis, floruit Ao. 830. Homiliae in Evang. editae Colon. 1532. Antuverp. 1559. Comment. in Acta & in Canonicas Epistolas, Colon. 1573. in Epist. Pauli, Parisiis. 1533. in Apocal. Colon. 1529. Parisiis 1540.

Rabanus Maurus. VI. Archi Episcopus Moguntinus vixit. Ao. 840. Ex huius operibus desumfit suam Glossum Strabus.

Strabus Monachus Fuldensis, Rabani auditor & scriba, vixit Ao. 880. Adscribitur huic Glossa, ordinaria quae dicitur, super Universa Biblia. edit. Lugduni Ao. 1589. septem Tomis in fol.

Anselmus Laudunensis, Scholasticus. vixit A. C. 1077. Huius est Glossa interlinearis, quae extat cum Glossa ordinaria & Lyrani Comment. edita Lugd. Ao. 1589.

Albertus Episcopus Ratisbonensis, natione Svevus, Ord. S. Dominici, praeceptor Thomae de Aquino, ob insignem Doctrinam cognominatus Magnus, in totam ferè S. S. Commentaria scripsisse dicitur. Flor. A. C. 1260. excus. Colon. 1607.

Alexander Halensis, de Hales aliis dictus, natione Anglus, Thomae Aquinatis ac Bonavent. praeceptor, Ordinis S. Francisci, primusq; Franciscanorum, qui Magisterii insignia adeptus est, imò primus Doctor, fons & origo omnium aliorum Doctorum quaestionariorum, tam in Ordine Minoritarum, quàm Praedicatorum, quàm etiam in Coetu & Collegio omnium secularium, ut habet de eo Stephanus Brulifer, tract. de timore servili. Is, inquam, scripsit quoq, Postillàm super tota Biblia, obiit v. A. 1245.

Hugo de S. Caro, natione Burgundus, Ordin. Praedic. Cardinalis S. Sabinae, vixit circa A. C. 1240. Comment. verò illius in Universam Scr. S. iuxta quadruplicem sensum edita Coloniae 1621. octo volum. in fol.

Nicolaus Liranus, ex Iudaismo ad Christianismum conversus & Ordini Minorum adscriptus vixit Ao. C. 1320. A nonnullis dicitur fuisse natione Anglus: sed Drusius ad loca Gen. 15. & ad loca Exod. c. 33. ita nominatum scribit â Brabantiae oppido, Lira dicto, quòd inde oriundus. Commentaria s. Postillam & Moralia scripsit in Universa Biblia, excusa Lugd. 1590. item Basil. 1506. De hoc circumfertur illud vulgatum: si Lyra non lirasset, Lutherus non sal-asset, quo innuere volunt, quòd multum B. Lutherus Lirano debeat: Et sanè negari haut potest, quòd Megalander Lyrae Comment. in V. T. lectione dignissima iudicarit, quâ de re videatur B. Parens in Patrol. p. 627.

E Lutheranis post ipsum B. Lutherum & Philippum Melanchthonem, qui passim in scriptis suis S. Biblia illustrarunt, Iohannem item Brentium (cuius opera aliquot Tomis in fol. Tubingae Ao. 1576. & seqq. excusa extant) ac Lucam Osiandrum (cuius Comment. iridem tribus voluminibus in fol. Francof. Ao. 1608. & in 4. Tubing. 1591. prodierunt) qui omnes superiori seculo floruerunt, in Universa Biblias. Commentaria sive notas ediderunt D. Iohannes Quistorpius, (cuius Annotationes in omnes libb. Bibl. prodierunt Rostochii Ao. 1648.) D. Daniel Cramerus in summ. Bibl. D. Philipp. Henric. Friedlib. Iacobus Rauppius (cuius liber tertius Biblioth. Portatilis Comment. in Biblia exhibet, excus. Erffurti Ao. 1654. ac alii nonnulli. Cumprimis tamen evolvi merentur Biblia Ernestina, quae aliquoties typis Enderianis descripta hactenus lucem viderunt, Illustrissimi Celsissimiq; Principis ac Domini, Domini ERNESTI, Saxoniae, Iuliae, Cliviae ac Montium &c. Principis Gloriosissimi atq; Pientissimi Mandato clementissimo â diversis Doctissimis Clarissimisq; Viris Commentariis perpetuis illustrata, revisa verò â B. Parente, ac denuò recognita â B. D. Glassio, quae Biblia multorum Commentariorum adinstar esse, fatebuntur, qui diligentiùs eadem evolverint.

E Calvinianis partim notas, partim homilias, partim Commentaria in Universam propè Scrip. S. ediderunt Calvinus ipse, Conradus postmodùm Pellicanus, Rudolphus item Gvalierus, Franciscus Iunius, Paulus Tossanus. Iob. Piscator Herbornensis, Lud. de Dieu, Hugo Grotius, Hugo Brougthonus, &c.

E Pontificiis plurimorum extant satis spissa volumina, quibus sacros codd, explanare sategerunt.

E veteribus recensentur Basilius Zanchius Bergenas (cuius notationes in omnes Sc. S. libb. prodierunt Romae 1553. Colon. 1602. in 8.) Petrus Aureolus Archi Episcopus Aquensis (flor. 1317. edita verò Compendiosa eius Com in Univers. Scr. S. sunt Parisiis Ao. 1565. in 8.) Dronysius â Rickel Carthusianus (obiit Ao. 1471. Comment. eius super libb. Bibl. habentur Tom. 7. & seqq edit.
