Coloniae Ao. 1535. 1538. & 1539.) & alii; Erecentioribus Franciscus Lucas Brugersis (cuius notationes in sacra Biblia, quibus variantia discrepantibus Exemplaribus loca discutiuntur, prodierunt Antuverp. 1581. in 8.) Emanuel Sa Lusitanus. S. I. (cuius notationes in Sc. S. editae Antuverpiae 1596. Colon. in 4. 1609.) Cornelius Cornelii â Lapide è S. I. (cuius Coment. diversis temporib. in Universam Scr S. excepto saltem uno atq; altero libro, Antuverp. edita octo volumina in fol. constituunt) Iacobus Tirinus itidem Iesuita (cuius Comment. in V. & N. T. Antuverp. prodierunt Ao. 1632.) Guilielmus Estius in Annotationibus aureis in difficiliora scripturae loca, editis Coloniae Anno 1622. Iohannes Stephanus Menochius Iesuita, cuius Comment. pariter impressa Coloniae, Francisus Lu-as, Gabriel à Costa, Romae; Ioh. Alba, Valentiae 1615 in 4. Felicianus Capito, in diff. loca V. & N. T. Venetiis.

Novum v. Testamentum vel Evangelistas saltem Commentariis, paraphrasibus notisq; illustrare praeter modò adductus sategeruntè Patribus. Ord. alphabetico locatis.

August--us in Qq. Evangel. item de Consensu Evang. nec non Qq. V. ac N. T. Tom 4. Op.

Ans-lmus Cantuariensis in varios Evangeliorum locos.

Beda Venerabilis t. 5. & 8. Oper.

Eusebius Pamphili in expositionum Evangel libris 20.

Gregorius Magnus libb. 4. explicationum Evangeliorum.

Iob. Chrysostomus, cuius homiliae & Comment. Graecè ac Latinè prodierunt ex officina Commelianâ Ao. 1603.

Theophili Antiocheni brevia Comment. f. allegoriarum in sacra IV. Evangelia libri 4. habentur Tom. 1. Biblioth. Patrum.

Euthymius Zigabenus Monachus. de hoc scribit Iesuita Tirinus, quòd è scriptis Chrysostomi aliorumq; veterum elegantes Commentarios collegerit in Script. vixit A. C. 1118.

Theophylactus, Bulgarorum Episcopus, scripsit Epitomen ex Ioh. Chrysostomo. Prodiit Graecè & Latinè.

In Epistolas Paulinas in specie Ambrosius (dubitant tamen nonnulli, an illius sint Comment. ipsi Tom. 5. adtributa) Aretas Coesariensis, Occumenius, Andreas Caesariensis (extant hi tres Graecè & Latinè) Theodoretus, Primasius, Hieronymus &c.

E nostratibus extant in N. T. Comment. ac notae Lucae Losii, D. Bugenbagii, Erasmi Sarcerii, Ioachimi Camerarii, D. Aegyd. Hunnii, Matthiae Flacii, D. Calixti, &c.

In IV. Evangelistas Harmonia Chemnitio-Lyseriana, continuata & absoluta â B. Parente, item Harmonia D. Althoferi.

In Epist. Paulinas D. Tilem. Heshusius, D. Georgius Mylius, D. Georgius Maior, D. Nicol. Selneccerus, D. David Rungius, D. Eriedericcus Balduinus, &c.

E Calvinianis in totum N. T. Augustinus Marloratus, Martinus Bucerus, Daniel Tossanus, Benedictus Aretius, Theodorus Beza, Balduinus. Walaeus, Henrious Bullingerus, Leo Iuda, Thomas Carduvightus, Iac. Capellus, Ludovicus Capellus in spicil. Daniel Heinsius, ac alii nonnulli.

In Evangelistas separatim Huldricus Zuvinglius, Iob. Iacobus Grynaeus, Ludovicus de Dieu, Iohan. Camero in Myroth. Bucerus, Otto Brunnfelsius, Ioh. Boisius Londini &c.

In Epistolas Paulinas Nicolaus Hemmingius, Wolffg. Musculus Dusanus, David Paraeus, &c.

E Pontificiis in totum N. T. Thomas de Aquino Tom. 15. & 16. Alphonsus Salmeron Iesuita, Laurentius Valla, Erasmus Roterodamus, Iohannes Benedictus, Iohannes Gagnaeus, Franc. Costerus, Iacobus Faber Stapulensis, &c.

In Evangelistas Cornelius Iansenius Episcopus Gandavensis, Iohannes Maldonatus Iesuita, Adamus Contzen Iesuita, Franciscus Lucas Brugensis, Sebastianus Barradius Iesuita, Didacus Stella, in fol. Lugduni, Perez, Perpinianus, Pitseus, Sylveira, &c.

In Epistolas Paulinas & reliquas Canonicas Marsilius Facinus, Bened. Iustinianus, Guilielmus Estius, Claudius Guilliaudus, Franc. Tilemannus. &c.

Plurimum v. etiam ad intelligendas utriusq; foederis tabulas iuvabit diligenter evolvisse Harmoniam Sc. S. Dn. D. Waltheri ac Philologiam Sacram B. D. Glassii, interpretum Scr. felicissimorum ac Theologorum de Ecclesia Christi meritissimorum. Quibus adiungi poterit â Philologiae cumprimis sectatore, Clavis Scr. Flacii, scripta item D. Franzii, Drusii, Canini, Gatakeri, Amamae Corn. B. Bertrami &c.

Qui singulares in unum atq; alterum tum V. tum N. T. librum scripserunt Commentarios, enumerabuntur post cuiusq; libri prolegomena.

Progredior ad alterum dicendorum membrum, breviter commemoraturus, cuiu tum autoritatis, tum antiquitatis sint versiones illae N. T. celebriores, Syriaca, Arabica, Aethiopica. Id verò nontam meis quàm Theologorum nostratium, aliorumq; Virorum Doctorum verbis.

Ita igitur de Syriacae versionis auctoritate & antiquitate Dn. D. Waltherus Offic. Bibl. p. 295 §. 345. & 346. Ut ut ad aliquem ex Evangelistis vel Apostolis, aut etiam ad ipsissim a Apostolorum tempora, & quae vitâ ipsis functis statim insecuta sunt, versionem Syriacam referre (id quod Syros quosdam facere, ad Marcum sc. Evangelistam eam referentes, si fides habenda Guilielmo Postellae est, idem paulo antè ex Gvidone Fabritio retulerat: quin etiam B. D. W. Frantzium in tract. de Interpret. Scr. p. 56. ac Imman. Tremellium in praefat. Paraphr. Syriacae versionem Syriacam ad Apostolos & Apostolicos viros reducere, pariter monuer at) meritò nobis debeat esse religio, partim quia sic auctoritatem haberet divinam, quam tamen cur ipsi denegemus, mox liquidum evadet, partim quia nulla prorsus illius fit mentio apud Clementem Alexandrinum, Originem, Eusebium, Athanasium, &c. & alios ex antiquitate, qui vel in Syriâ vel in Aegypto docuerunt, vel de variis scripturarum editionibus disserverunt: (eandem rationem praeter alias nonnullas urget B. Parens Methodo studii Theol. p. 64. item in Exegesi Loci primi §. 509.) antiquitatis tamen laudem omnem versioni huic (Syrae) nequaquam invidemus, quicuneam confecerit & quandocun-, quod Deus unus novit & solus: quin potiùs eam abunde confirmat cùm incorruptsermonis eleg-ntia, tum defectus Epistolae Petri posterioris, Iohannis secundae & tertiae, Iudae item, Apocalypseos, & accusationis adulterae cap. 8. Iohannis, quae tametsi eundem cum reliquis scriptis Spiritum redoleant, inter scriptores tamen Ecclesiasticos pervetustos de iis semper disceptatum, & illa coeteris habita fuisse posteriora, obscurum non est. Rutgherus Spey Bopardianus in Praefat. Gram. Arabicae tesfatur, Exemplar in Bibl. Heidelbergensi extare Syrum, ante 800. Annos manuscriptum. Haec Dn. D. Walth. l. c. Exemplum quod cum Viennensi Guido Fabritius contulit, Ao1500. Regni Alexandrini (hoc est Ao. C. 1200.) scriptum fuisse, idem prodit. De Codicis Syri IV. Evangelistarum, qui in Bibliothecâ Altdorffinâ habetur, è Syriâ â D. Iacobo Fetzero allatus, antiquitate egi in disp. 2. ad N. T. Syr. ante hos duodecim annos hic habita, Q. 3. De autoritate porrò atq; utilitate dictae versionis ita laudatus Dn. D. Waltherus l. c. §. 347. Autoritas translationis Syrae non nisi humana esse potest. 1. quia versio duntaxat est. 2. quia integri libri illi desunt, modò enumerati, qui tamen habentur in omnibus fontis Graeci Editionibus. 3. quia in quibusdam â Graeco Originali deflectit. §. 348. Utilitas interim eius est maxima, quam exemplis aliquot Laur. Eabricius pulchrè illustrat in Praef. quas praefixit Grammaticae & Lexico Syriacis Crinesii. Eandem versionis huius utilitatem ex nostratibus agnoscit quoq; B. D. Iacobus Martini, quando in Praefarad N. T. Syr. Trostii, postquam loca quaedam N. T. beneficio versionis Syriacae illustrasset, concludit: Ex his & similibus locis, quorum universus Codex N. T. plenis simus est, benevolus lector facilè intelligit summam Syrae huius versionis utilitatem imò necessitatem, quâ pius & industrius Novi huius Testamenti interpres-nullo modo carere potest. Et porrò: Quare audiendi nequaquam sunt nonnulli malèferiati, qui nobis obiicere non erubescunt: non adeò vel utile vel necessarium esse, uti tanti sumtus laboresq; Codici huic Syro emendando & edendo impendantur, cùm in lingvâ Syrâ N. T. Evangelistae & Apostoli non scripserint, & negari non possit, multos hactenus cum summa laude floruisse in Ecclesia eruditissimos Theologos, qui sine adminiculo huius versionis, sineq; omni lingvae Syrae cognitione in Graeci N. T. codicis versione ac interpretatione felicissimè fuerunt versati. Egregiae sanè obiectiones & lucernam valdè olentes! Equidem utrâq; largimur manu, N. T. originaliter Syro idiomate scriptum non esse; proindeq; quae hoc Codice exhibetur, tantùm versionem esse. Sciant nihilominus importuni & iniqui isti censores, Syram lingvam esse illam, in quâ vel Christus ipse cum suis Apostolis fuit loquutus, vel quae proximè ad vernaculam Servatoris nostri eiusq; sympatriotarum accedit, in quam novella Ecclesiae N. T. scripta omnia fuere transfusa, & quidem illo tempore, quo Apostoli, divini illi doctores, â Christo ipso instituti, â Sp. S. immediatè edocti & informati Ecclesiae Christi prima fundamenta apud gentes locarent. Arrige ergo aures, Censor, quisquis es, cuius es, qui cerebrum non in calcaneo, sed capite geris; Versio est haec Syra, sed omnium prima & antiquissima: Versio est, inquam, sed omnibus aliis ut probatior & plenior, praeferenda: versio est, adhuc dico; sed vel alicuius ex Evangelistis, vel omnino illorum, qui Antiochiae habuerunt ipsos Apostolos praesentes, quos de locis multis obscurioribus consulere & audire potuerunt. Ad hanc itaq; solam, quando in fontibus Graecis quaedam occurrit obscuritas vel difficultas, tutò acceditur: haec sola, quando de loci alicuius interpretatione versioneq; dubium movetur, tutò ac sine errore consulitur: per hanc solam Graecus textus verè illustratur, rectè intelligitur. Huius enim solius autoritas proximè ad ipsorum fontium maiestatem accedit. Et paulò pòst: Caruit Germania nostra, proindeq; Theologi in illâ, suo seculo ac tempore eruditissimi, primâ hac versione, sed non sine magnâ iacturâ. Quandoquidemq;, ut ut fuerint illi doctissimi, disertissimi, ingeniosissimi. multorum nihilominus locorum veram mentem ac sensum ex Latinâ versione, vel etiam ex Graecâ primigeniâ adsequi nequaquam potuerunt. Haec omnia B. D. Martini l. all. Quo elogio an maiori versio Syra exornari possit, vehementer equidem addubito. Sed Adversarii quoq; nostri in pretio dictam versionem habent. Audiamus unum saltem atq; alterum.

E Calvinianis Daniel Chamier, Tom. 1. Panstratiae lib. 12. c. 1. §. 14. de Syr. versione ita: Opus hoc (Novum Testamentum Syriacum) scribit, est antiquissimum: atadeò Bonaventurs Cornelius Bertramus, vir harum lingvarum in primis peritissimus, audet Ecclesiae Antiochenae nascenti, Christianissprimùm in eâ appellatis adscribere, Praefat. in suam Comparationem Grammaticae Ebraicae & Aramicae. (idem etiam Alstedius facit lib. 2. praecognit. c. 113.) Sed ut hoc incertum sit, esse certè utilissimum, nemo negaverit, qui eo sit usus: Etsi habere nonnulla, quae non omninò placeant, Bellarmino facilè concesserim. Ioh. Camero Praelect. Tom. 1. p. 48. & 67. Interpretem Syrum & antiquissimum & doctissimum vocat. Ex Pontificiis Franciscus Lucas Brugensis, Scriptor doctissimus in Praef. super N. T. Comment. n. 6. it a: hoc, inquit, teneo indubitanter, Syriacum N. T. textum vetustis simi exemplaris Graeci, & quidem exprimis loco habendum ac venerandum esse. (adstipulatur Fr. Lucae D. Andreas Rivetus in Isagog. p. 184.)

Coeterùm prostant Varia N. T. Syriaci editiones. Quamprimum enim in arduo hoc negotio feliciter glaciem fregit Ioh. Albertus Widmanstadius, Ictus & Provinciarum Austriae Orientalium Cancellarius (huius enim curâ atq; solicitudine, sed sumtibus Ferdinandi Imperatoris primùm Anno Chr. 1555. lucem adspexit publicam Viennae N. T. Syriacum typis descriptum) secuti mox plurimi sunt, qui partim in Characteres Ebraicos textum, Syriacum transfundentes, partim versionem translationis Syriacae adornantes, (id quod duodecennio pòst, quàm Viennensis editio prodiisset, tentavit Tremellius, in edit, quae lucem vidit Ao. 1568. & circa eadem tempora Guido Fabricius Gallus) suam Ecclesiae probare dillgentiam sategerunt. Eadem quoq; translatio Syriaca, sed veste Ebraeâ prodiit Antverpiae in forma minuscula Ao. Chr. 1575. Inserta etiam conspicitur Bibliis polyglottis Eliae Hutteri, tum quoq; operi Biblico Hispanico, Gallicano & Anglicano. Separatim verò nativis litteris ac nova versione Martini Trostii Cothenis Anhaltin. edita Ao. C. 1621.

Sed haec de Syriacâ versione monuisse hic sufficiant. Arabicaverò N. T. versio uti multis annis post Syriacam versionem typis descripta fuit (& Evangelistae quidem cum versione Latinâ primùm Romae è Typographiâ Mediceâ, in fol. Ao. 1591. quam editionem interdum αωμάίζειν, ac multò meliores paraphrases illâ alibi reperiri, Isaacus monet Casaubonus Exerc. 15. n. 12. p. 388. integrum verò N. T. Lugduni Batavorum, studio, industriâ atq; typis Thomae Erpenii Ao 1616. in quartâ, ceu dicitur, formâ. Idem quoq; habetur in Opere Biblico Gallicano & Anglicano) ita non tantae censetur, ac illa Syriaca, sive autoritatis, sive antiquìtatis. Autorem quod concernit, testatur Guido Fabricius Praefat. in N. T. Syriacum, extare utriusq; Testamenti Arabicam paraphrasin, autore Saadia Gaon. (Cuius Iudaei scripta diversa recenset Buxtorff. in Bibl. Rabb.) Quod ipsum ratione V. T. confirmat etiam Erpenius Praefat. N. T. Arabici, qui etiam spem fecit versionis illius V. T. cum interpretatione notisq; edendae; sed morte imatura praeventus promissis stare non potuit, dilataq; totius editio V. T. Arabica tantisper fuit dum Opus illud Biblicum Gallicanum tredecim abhinc annis lucem adspexit. Cuius Magnificentiam compendiosâ utilitate superare sategerunt Angli in opere Biblico, anno hoc publicato.

Coeterùm quod autorem translationis N. T. Arabicae spectat, CL Erpenio l. c. Evangelia è Graeco vertisse (in Arab. Lingvam) videtur Nesiulamam silius Azalkefati. De reliquorum verò N. T. libb. Arabica versione subdubitat dictus Autor, an eundem habeant interpretem, cùm & phrasi nonnihil ab Evangeliis discrepent, & Syro contextui, quàm Graeco plerisq; in locis videantur esse viciniores. Quicquid tamen de autore sit, id extra dubitationis aleam positum Erpenio est, multis abhinc seculis N. T. in Arabum sermonem conversum esse, adeoq; versionem Arabicam ob antiquitatem pariter & fidelitatem Theologis omnibus non minùs utilem futuram, quàm nobilem illam Syriacam editionem, quae Viennae Widmanstadii curâ prodiit. Antiquitatem verò versionis N. T. Arabicae inter alia colligere quoq; inde licet, quia codex ille manuscriptus, quo Erpenius è Bibliothecâ Acad. Leidensi usus, exaratus fuit in Monasterio S Ioannis in Thebaidos deserto anno aerae Diocletiani 1059. id est Christi 1342. qui ipse tamen Codex descriptus fuit ex alio exemplari, & hoc rursus ex alio, ceu ex clausulâ eiusdem patet. Quod autem de versione Epistol. Arabicâ pronunciat Erpenius, videri sc. eam Syro, quàm Graeco contextui viciniorem, idipsum de totius N. T. Arabicâ versione pronunciare non dubitavit Isaacus Casaubonus: imò expressè scribit idem, Arabicam interpretationem ut plurimum ex Syriaca translatione versam esse, Exerc. 16. ad Ann. Eccles. Baron. Ao. 34. §. 73. p. 606. Quicquid verò huius rei sit, dignam tamen censent Viri docti versionem istam, quam sacrarum litterarum cultores diligenter cum textu Originali conferant, id quod praeprimis fecit per omnes quatuor Evangelistas, Acta item Apostol. & Epistolam ad Romanos Lud. de Dieu, ante hunc verò B. D. Paulus Tarnovius per Iohannem, qui egregius Theologus tanti quoq; aestimavit versionem Arabicam, ut Evangelii Iohannis translationem Arabicam Latinitate donare, notisq; illustrare non dubitarit.

Aethiopicam tandem quod spectat N. T. versionem lucem ea primùm vidit Romae Ao. 1548. sed non integra: desiderantur enim adhuc in editione illâ Epistolae Paulinae, id quod non immeritò mireris, cum cernere ibi liceat praeter Iohanneas ac Petrinas Epistolas, nec non Epistolam Iudae ac Iacobi, Apocalypsin itemq; Epistolam ad Ebraeos. Cuius verò auspiciis curaq; editio illa prodierit in publicum, indicat libri clausula, quae talis:

Hoc est. Hic liber impressus est Romae. Tempore Papae Romani Pauli Farnesii, & Patriarchae (Alexandriae) Gabrielis, & Regis nostri Claudii &c.

Et elaboravit opus hoc Tasfa Ziion Malchesinus, qui propter salutem animae suae & pietatis causa Hierosolymam profectus est. Debet igitur prima illa Evangelistarum & quae his annexa sunt, editio natales suos Aethiopibus illis, qui religionis causâ ex Aethiopiâ Hierosolymam, & ex Hierofolymis Romam peregrinantes venerunt: hi ipsi enim Typographiam Romae erexerunt, ac libros istos sacros ex. Aethiopiâ secum allatos excudi fecerunt. Sublevati fortè ditiorum ibi liberalitate, ac inter eos cumprimis Nicolai Diaconi Cardinalis: unde etiam illius insignia in pagellâ frontispicio libri proximâ conspici editor voluit cum hâc subscriptione-.

-- Hoc est, Nicolaus Diaconus Cardinalis. In Codice; quem po-sideo, manu nescio cuius adscripta haec verba Aethiopica cernuntur: --Magnum fulerum Ecclesiae.

Quis verò versionis N. T. Aethiopicae autor, cuiusq; versio haec sit antiquitatis, difficile est certò definire. Et licet centum decemq; iamtum abhinc a--is, a deoq; septem annis priùs quàm Syriaca, in Europâ typis descripta versio quatuor Evangelistarum, Actuum Apostolicorum, Apocalypseos, Epistolae item ad Ebraeos, utriusq-Petrinae, Iudaeitem, Iohannis ac Iacobi Aethiopica prodierit in publicum, videtur tamen in paucorum editio ea devenisse Virorum Doctorum manus, vel quòd exemplaria excusa in Abysiae regnum maximam partem missa, vel quòd dictae versionis autoritatem utilitatemve admodùm exiguam esse Europaeis persvasum. Unde etiam admodùm rara eius apud Autores, qui tum olim, tum noviter---uoq; de variis Bibliorum versionibus scripserunt; translationis huius mentio fit, nedum utâ multis collata sive cum textu Graeco, sive cum aliis versionibus fuerit, cùm contrà Syriaca N. T. versio saepiusculè excusa sit; & passim â Scr. S. Interpp. adducatur. Quid verò de Cornel. à Lapide adserto habendum sit, scribentis inter alia: Esto, S. Matthaeus praedicarit in citeriori Aethiopia, quae vicinior est Aegypto, hodieSonnar nuncupatur, ubi nigriores sunt Aethiopes, ac mortuus dicatur in civitate Luab, ubi etiamnum templa in honorem S. Matthaei extant: tamen reliqua Aethiopia sive Abyssia Evangelia, ceterasSS. Scripturas, ae ac fidem Christi accepta refert evidam Monacho Aethiopi, cui nomen Aba Salama, id est Pater pacis, eò quòd veram pacem & salutem eis attulerit. Hic educatus apud Arabes Orientales, ab eis Christianam fidem & S. Scripturas hausit, ac deinde universae Aethiopiae easdem communicavit; Unde eius habetur Apostolus. Quocirca Aethiopica S. Scripturae versio cum Arabica, ceu matrice sua, consentit. Quid, inquam, de hoc habendum sit, cumprimis, quòd Aethiopica N. T. versio Arabicam matricem agnoscat, sive inde translata sit, ex dictarum versionum tum inter se, tum cum aliis collatione, quae infrà quandoq; instituetur, apparebit. Quemadmodum etiam, quid sentiendum sit de illâ Hugonis Grotii sententia, ex eo, quòd clausula Orationis Dominicae extet & in Syriaco & in Latino contextu, & in Arabico, in vetustissimis verò exemplaribus Graecis non legatur, colligentis, non Arabicam tantùm & Latinam versionem, sed & Syriacam factam, postquam Ecclesiarumλετουργίαformam certam acceperat. Sed de hoc etiam agetur ad Cap. VI. Matth. v. 13. Id saltem hoc loco consideret rerum harum curiosus, quod si Arabica versio Aethiopicae matrix, ceu Cornelium à Lapide affirmantem adduxi, quifactum, quòd in Aethiopica versione clausula illa non legatur, contrà verò in Arabicâ versione edit. Erpenianae extet. Si verò Arabica è Syriacâ versione utplurimum versa est, quod Casaubonus censet, cur in Arabica translatione edit. Romanae deest, contra verò in Syriacâ legitur? & quidem consentientibus omnibus, quos hactenus contulerunt Viri docti, Codd. Syriacis, â quibus etiam non abit hic Codex MS. antiquissimus Biblioth. Altdorffinae.

Appellatio. Evangelistarum nomen dupliciter accipitur. 1. Generaliter pro quovis Ecclesiae doctore, quia ad omnes pertinet -υαγγελίζεσθα-,Esa. 41. v. 27.2. Tim. 4. v. 5. 2. Specialiter pro certo quodam Doctorum in primitiva Ecclesia gradu atq; ordine, Eph. 4. v. 11. de quibus vide Loc. de Ministerio Eccles. §. 227. 3. Specialissimè, pro amanuensibus illis Spiritus Sancti, qui Evangelicam de Christo Historiam literis complexi Ecclesiae non illorum duntaxat temporum, sed etiam ad finem usq; mundi colligendae operam & utilem & necessariam divino impulsu praestiterunt. In hac postrema significatione haec vox accipitur, quando quatuor Evangelistae numerantur.

## 1:1 Introduction: Chapter II. On the Books of the Four Evangelists
But Gospel is taken 1. γενικως for the whole heavenly doctrine, by a designation drawn from the more excellent part. 2. έιδικως for that part of the heavenly doctrine which deals with the Person, office and benefits of the Messiah. In this signification it is again taken in two ways. 1. for the doctrine of the gratuitous remission of sins on account of Christ. 2. for the public proclamation of the Messiah exhibited. 3. for the Scripture narrating the History of the birth, life, death, resurrection and ascension of Christ exhibited.

2. The impulsive and final cause of writing. Thomas Aquinas, in the golden Catena, enumerates three reasons why the Evangelists set down the History concerning Christ. 1. that those whom they were unable to reach in person they might instruct through Scripture concerning the Gospel. 2. that those things which it behoves us to know about Christ's --ctis & facts might be preserved in everlasting memory. Hence Justinus, Apology 2. for Christianity, p. 58., speaks thus of the Evangelists, ως όι άπομνημονέυσαντες πάντα τά ωερί τού σωτήρος ήμων χριςού Ιηςού έδίδαξαν, όίς έπιςέυσαυεν. And in the Dialogue with Tryphon he calls the writings of the Evangelists άπ-μ--υονεύματα, so that you would say, matters entrusted to memory and recited, J. C. said ac----. 3. lest false history or doctrine concerning Christ sparg----ur by heretics.

3. The number of the Gospels. Irenaeus, book 3. against heresies, ch. 11. p. 186.: Nor can there be more in number than these, nor again fewer, Gospels. Since indeed there are four regions of the world in which we live, and four principal Spirits, and the Church has been dispersed over the whole earth, while the pillar and foundation of the Church is the Gospel and the Spirit of life, it follows that she has four pillars breathing out incorruption from everywhere and quickening men. The Cherubim are four-formed, and the images of their faces are the arrangement of the Son of God. For the first living creature, he says, resembling a lion, expresses his image and his principal and royal character. The second truly resembling a calf signifies the sacrificial and priestly ordering. The third truly having a face as of a man plainly describes his coming according to man: the fourth truly like an eagle soaring manifests the grace of the Spirit winging its flight into the Church. All which he pursues more fully in the same place. (Nicholas Gallasius, in his annotations on that passage of Irenaeus, assails this Speculation, as he calls it; yet in similitudes and allegories not everything needs to be carved to the quick, provided it agrees with the analogy of faith.) Jerome discusses this in the preface to his Gospel of Matthew. The first face, that of a man, signifies Matthew, because he takes his start almost from man: The book of the generation of Jesus Christ &c. The second, that of a lion, Mark, in whose case the voice of the lion roaring in the desert is heard, chapter 1. A voice of one crying in the wilderness. The third, that of a calf, Luke, because he took his beginning from Zechariah the Priest. The fourth, that of an eagle, John, because, taking the pinions of an eagle and hastening to loftier heights, he discourses of the Word of GOD. The same writer in the Epistle to Paulinus likewise calls the four Evangelists the four-horse team of the Lord shown to Ezekiel ch. 1. and to John Apoc. 4. For Matthew begins his Gospel History from the human generation of Christ, on which ground he is compared to a man; Mark begins from the preaching of John in the desert, and so is likened to a lion; Luke from the description of the legal sacrifices, and so is likened to a calf; John describes chiefly the divinity of Christ, on which ground he is likened to an eagle. The ancients among the godly adapt that prophetic vision to Christ in this fashion. Christ became for us a man by being born, a calf by dying, a lion by rising again, an eagle by ascending. Augustine, book 1. On the harmony of the Evangelists, ch. 7., says the Evangelists are that holy chariot of the Lord, borne upon which as in a triumphal course round about the circle of the lands he shed forth most richly the savour of knowledge and brought peoples under himself. book of the same ch. 16. likewise fits the forms of the four creatures to the Evangelists, but in the application he departs from Jerome, for he assigns the lion to Matthew (on the ground that he commended the royal Person of Christ above all others, for he records the Magi as having come from the East to seek and worship Christ the King; and Herod the king as having dreaded Christ while yet an infant. Now the lion is the symbol of royal power); he assigns the man to Mark (since neither the royal stock nor the priestly

or wished to relate either kinship or consecration, but dwells entirely on those things which Christ-man did in these lands) in Luke & John agree with Jerome. Primasius follows Augustine on chapter 4 of the Apocalypse, as also Bede in the preface of the Commentary on Luke. But Gregory follows Jerome, homily 4 on Ezekiel, as also Sedulius, book 1 of On the Paschal Works, applies to Christ:

This Matthew, acting as a man, fulfills universally, Mark roars like the high voice through the deserts of a Lion. The laws of the priesthood Luke keeps with the mouth of a young ox. After the manner of a soaring Eagle John seeks the stars by the Word. These four princes, feasting upon thee with one voice, are scattered like so many seasons rejoicingly through the round world.

Irenaeus, book 3, ch. 11, and several cited by Areta on chapter 4 of the Apocalypse, say that John is signified by the lion, Mark by the eagle. Lyranus at the end of the preface on Mark says, that that team of four of the Evangelists was shadowed forth by the four rivers going forth out of Paradise Gen. 2. v. 10. (which comparison Origen and Jerome also employ in the prefaces of their Commentaries on Matthew,) by the four chief Patriarchs, from whom Ciriat-harbe received its name, who were buried there together with their wives Ios. 15. v. 13.&54. by the four circles or rings, by which the ark of the covenant, guardian of the tablets of the law, was anciently carried about Exod. 25. v. 12. (Jerom. day 1.) by the four feet of the table of show-bread, chapter of the same v. 26. by the four horns of the altar of burnt-offering Exod. 27. v. 2. by the four rows of stones in the breastpiece Exod. 28. v. 17. by the four walkways of the house of Solomon 1. Reg. 7. v. 6. by the four winds quickening the dead Ezech. 37. v. 9. by the four least creatures of the earth, yet wiser than all others Prov. 30. v. 24. by the four men praising God in the furnace Dan. 3. v. 92. by the four smiths casting down the horns of heresies Zach. 1. v. 20. by the four chariots running through the world Zach. 6. v. 1. by the four living creatures full of eyes before and behind Apoc. 1. v. 6. Jerom. in the Epistle to Paulinus: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, throughout the whole body are full of eyes, sparks flash forth, lightnings dart about, they have feet straight and reaching upward, wings feathered and flying everywhere, they hold fast to one another, they are intertwined with one another and roll and go forward like a wheel within a wheel, whithersoever any breath of the Holy Spirit shall have borne them along.) Others add the four extremities of the ladder of Jacob Gen. 28. v. 12. four pillars of shittim wood overlaid with gold, from which the veil hung Exod. 26. v. 32. four golden rings, which were set at the four corners of the table of show-bread Exod. 25. v. 26. four cups, which were upon the shaft of the golden lampstand, chapter of the same v. 34. four beginnings of the linen cloth let down from heaven and beheld by Peter Actor. 10. v. 11. (Jerom. in the Epistle to Rusticus.) Aug. on Ps. 103. Wherefore, since the whole world (of which there are four quarters) was being summoned through the Gospel, four Gospels were written. book 1 de cons. Evang. ch. 2. For this reason perhaps there are four Evangelists, because there are four parts of the world, whose universality Christ's Church was declared to be extended by the very sacrament of their number. Compare Blasius de Viegas on chapter 4. Apocalypse p. 222. Schram, in the treatise Whether the Gospel of Matthew fits, Matthew ch. 4, p. 33. When the tribes of Israel were making their way through the desert of Arabia toward the promised land of Canaan, under four standards they arrayed themselves according to the stars Num. 2. v. 3. The Church, like well-disposed camps of soldiers Cant. 6. v. 9. pitches its camps under four standards of the Evangelists, making its way through the desert of the world toward the promised heavenly inheritance.

4. έΣυμθωνια. Socinus on the authority of Scripture, p. 15. That the Evangelists differ among themselves in matters of very little importance ought not only not to diminish their authority and faith, but even to increase it. And afterwards. It can happen that one has held the truth of such things better than another. p. 104. It can happen that all those things which History affirms concerning the Evangelists and Apostles were most true, and yet they themselves sometimes erred lightly in this respect. Erasmus writes almost in the same way in his annotations on chapter 2 and 27 of Matthew, that there should be no fear lest the authority of the whole Scripture collapse, if some slight error is detected in it, since it seems in no way able to be denied that the Evangelists have sometimes lapsed through memory. Chrysostom might seem somehow to favor them on Matthew, p. 3. If throughout everything they had agreed together, and with excessive diligence accuracy and toward all times and places so that individual words concurred equally everywhere, no enemy would ever have believed otherwise than that they had gathered together by a common plan of deceiving, and composed the Gospel as if out of a certain human conspiracy. But now what appears disagreement in small matters protects them from all suspicion, and sufficiently defends the reputation of men writing clearly.

But Augustine rightly admonishes in Epistle 8 to Jerome: If any falsehood were admitted into so great a height of authority, no particle of these books would remain which could not be called back into doubt, and accordingly he concludes in book 2 on the Consensus of the Gospels, chapter 12: all falsehood ought to be absent from the Evangelists, not only that which is uttered by lying, but also that which arises from forgetting. For if any error could have been committed by the author through ignorance, or forgetfulness, or any other human weakness whatsoever, then whenever any passage is brought forward from their writings, there can be a question about it whether the Evangelist did not nod while writing it. The same says on chapter 1 of Galatians: whether the Gospel is one or not one is judged not by the number of writers, but hence, whether the things written are the same or diverse. Whence it is plain that four Gospels are one Gospel. For since the four speak the same things, it is not one thing another because of the difference of persons, but one, because of the harmony of those who speak. Moreover, the general rules to be noted in the harmonization of the Evangelists, collected from Augustine's books On the Agreement of the Evangelists and from other Fathers, will be set forth in their place.

* (I think I shall do myself worthwhile service if here I insert what the Blessed Parent very usefully advised in his treatise De legitima SS. Scripturae interpretatione, thesis 1, LL. Th., ch. 12. He indeed speaks thus: Although nowhere at all is there any true contradiction in the Holy Scriptures, according to the testimony of Chrysostom, Tom. 1. on Genesis, since πασα λραφη is θεοπνευςος:, nevertheless an apparent contrariety and έναντιοθανές of a certain kind more frequently presents itself. Augustine, book 5 On Genesis According to the Letter, ch. 8.: We must strive to bring it about that no absurdity or repugnance should seem to be in the sacred Scriptures, which might offend the reader's opinion. Origen, on Romans 3: That things which appear contrary in H. Scr. are not contrary, must be shown by him who faithfully and wholly gathers together the consensus of the sacred volumes. §. 180.)

For reconciling that apparent contrariety, this remedy must be applied, namely that we inquire into the true and genuine sense of each passage from the very words and circumstances. For, since true contradiction has no place in Scripture, therefore as soon as the genuine sense of any passage is established, all the contrariety which seemed to lie hidden therein is removed. The ambiguity and discrepancy which seem to exist in the sacred writings must be removed by means of what follows upon and accompanies the text itself. Augustine, 3. On Christian Doctrine ch. 2; book 1, On Genesis According to the Letter, last chapter, §. 181.

Let this be the rule of concordance ρων έναντιοθανων. If any apparent contrariety seems to arise between certain passages compared together, let it be taught that the opposition concerns not the same thing but merely the name, or not according to the same aspect, or not toward the same end, or not in the same manner, or not at the same time. (This rule rests on those well-known requirements of true contradiction laid down by the Philosopher, book 1 of Sophistical Refutations, ch. 5, namely that something must be affirmed or denied of the same subject 1. ωσάυτως similarly, that is, so that the terms are taken in the same meaning. 2. ηαρ αυρό according to the same aspect, that is, concerning the same underlying subject, or according to the same part or nature. 3. πρός αυτό toward the same end, that is, so that regard is not had to different things outside the subject. 4. έν άυτω χρόνω at the same time) Thus Matt. 10. v. 10. Christ forbids the apostles to take a purse for their journey, nor two tunics, nor shoes, nor a staff: this seems contradicted by what is read in Mark 6. v. 8. Concordance. In Matthew is meant a staff that arms for defense; in Mark a rod that supports travelers, etc., §. 182.

182. To this general rule, very many special ones can be added, which by reason of circumstances can be distributed into certain classes. These circumstances are: Person (who speaks, to whom, of whom, before whom he speaks) Occasion (Counsel, End) Time, Place, Manner. §.

183. To the circumstance of Person pertain these rules. I. Persons in Scripture are often binominal. see Iud. 6. v. 32. & 2. Sam. 11. v. 21. Compare 1. Sam. 12. v. 24. 25. 2. Distinct persons are often uninominal. 3. Filiation is either natural or legal; natural is made by generation, legal by adoption. 4. Diverse things are pronounced concerning the Reborn, because they have, as it were, two men in themselves, the old and the new. Thus the reborn are said to be sold under sin, Rom. 7. v. 14. by reason of the old man: the reborn do not commit sin, 1. Ioh. 3. v. 9. namely, by reason of the new man. 5. Concerning Christ, some things are said according to the divine nature, some according to the human, some according to both. §. 184.

To the circumstance of the counsel, end and occasion belongs this rule. The understanding of sayings must be taken from the causes of speaking, Hilary, Book 4 on the Trinity. Thus Christ Matt. 19. v. 21. proposes to the young man instructed in the school of the Pharisees, who was falsely glorying in his perfect fulfillment of the law, this special precept, that he sell everything and distribute to the poor, and so follow Christ: namely, Christ wished to convince the man that he had first not fulfilled the precept concerning loving God above all things etc. §. 185.

Concerning the circumstance of time many rules can be given, for truly that old saying holds: distinguish the times and Scripture will agree. 1. Certain sayings deal with the time of Christ's humiliation, certain with the time of His exaltation. 2. Time is taken either completely or incompletely. 3. And its parts are taken either inclusively or exclusively, an example is found in Matt. 17. v. 1. compared with Luke 9. v. 28. 4. In the more perfect number often what is lacking or exceeds is not counted. Augustine, question 47 on Exodus 5. A finite number is sometimes put for an infinite one. Seven times a day the just man falls etc. 6. In sacred computations, because of the wickedness of a Prince, his name or the years during which he governed badly are omitted. 7. If a King hindered by foreign war, old age or disease while still alive appoints his son as vice-King, then in computing the years of father and son reigning together, the years of their reign are sometimes reckoned jointly, sometimes separately. Use is made of this rule in collecting the years of the kings of Israel. 8. So also it must be observed that the Easterners variously divided the artificial day, both into twelve equal hours, commonly called planetary: and also into quarters. From this the passages Mark 15. v. 25. and John 19. v. 14. can be reconciled. §. 80.

These rules treat of the circumstance of place. 1. Two names are often attributed to one place in Scripture, 2. One name is often attributed to distinct places. 3. Sacred writers often designate a place by that appellation which was customary at the time when they themselves lived and wrote. Compare Gen. 12. v. 5. with Gen. 28. v. 19. §. 187.

Likewise many rules can be given concerning the circumstance of manner. 1. Thus some things are said άπλως, some ηατα τι 2. Some simply, some comparatively. Thus fathers are to be honored, and yet with a certain regard they are to be hated, Luke 14. v. 26. that is, their authority must be set aside, namely if they command anything against our heavenly Father. 3. Particular statements specifically detract from general ones. 4. Moral precepts take precedence over ceremonial ones. 5. The second table of the law yields to the first. 6. Certain statements speak of the nature of a thing in itself, others however are understood as spoken accidentally. §. 188. This too can be observed, that the best method of reconciling is, if there can be given from Scr., so to speak as arbiter, namely a third, some passage of Scr. which may harmonize those contending passages, or may plainly approve the reconciliation brought forward by us . Compare Rom. 7. v. 14. and 1. Ioh. 3. v. 9. with Rom. 7. v. 12. §. 189. These and many other things B. Par. in the place cited p. 140. seqq. All which things the theologian most deserving regarding the Church of Christ Dn. D. Waltherus sets forth far more fully by rules both most common and common and special, declares excellently, and confirms with very many examples, in the golden and seven-times-published book of the Biblical Harmony, former part.) *

5. The brevity of the sacred writers. That not all the sayings or deeds of Christ were noted down by the Evangelists is evident from Ioh. 20. v. 30.cap. 21. v. 25. Justin Martyr, Apol. 2. for Christianity, pag. 47. ---. Yet this very thing detracts nothing whatsoever from the perfection of the Gospel history or of Sacred Scripture. Augustine, tractate 49 on John: The holy Evangelist testifies, that the Lord Christ both said and did many things which were not written, but those things were chosen to be written which seemed sufficient for the salvation of believers. Cyril, book 12 on John, last chapter: Not all the things which God did have been written down, but those which the writers thought sufficient , both for morals and for doctrines, that we might deserve to come to the kingdom of heaven shining with right faith and works.

6. Distinction. The Greeks formerly divided the several books of the Evangelists into τιτλούς,, the several ones into τιτλούς according to their ηεφάγαια; they called the larger parts τιτλούς, the smaller ηεφάγαια. In the Collections it is read according to Suidas, that in Matthew there are 68 titles, 355 chapters; in Mark 48 titles, 36 chapters. In Luke 348 chapters, 83 titles. In John 18 titles, 232 chapters. Which division Casaubon desires to be brought back into use in his notes on Matt. And the notes of those titles survive in certain editions of the Gospels published in Greek. Compare Camerarius in his annotations.

to the Gosp. p. 105. Where he recounts τιτλούς of Matthew, p. 141, where he enumerates τιτλούς of Mark, pag. 212, where he recites τιτλούς of Luke, p. 303, where he sets forth τιτλούς of John.

7. Contrary are the Apocryphal and rejected Gospel books, which were treated of in the Exegesis on Scripture, chapter 11, §. 301. and following. The Gospels of the Manichaeans were handed down by impostors, and they boasted falsely, as Augustine testifies, book 31 against Faustus, chapter 2. The Gospel according to the Hebrews is held to be threefold: 1. that of the Ebionites, which, although it was said to have been written by Matthew in Hebrew, was nevertheless truncated and corrupted by those heretics, as Irenaeus testifies, book 3, chapter 11, and Epiphanius, heresy 30. 2. that of the Encratites, by Tatian the Syrian, the author of that heresy, compiled from the four Evangelists, which he called σιαρέσσαρον,, in which he omitted the genealogies of Christ, Epiphanius, heresy 46, Theodoret, book 1, fab. haer-t 3. that of the Nazarenes, which is usually attributed to James, of which Origen makes mention, Tom. 2, tract. 8 on John, Clement, book 2 of the Stromata, Eusebius, book 1, chapter 25. Bede esteemed it so highly that he did not hesitate to write of it, that it is not to be numbered among the Apocrypha, but among the Ecclesiastical Histories. In the Preface on Luke. Moreover, the following Gospels are mentioned by others:

1. The Gospel according to the twelve Apostles, cited as Apocryphal by Origen, book 1 on Luke, and Jerome in the Preface on Matthew.

2. The Gospel of Peter the Apostle. Serapion, Bishop of Antioch, in the year of Christ 300, rejected it as false and Apocryphal. Eusebius, book 6 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapters 10 and 11.

3. The Proto-Gospel of James exists in the Orthodoxography of the Fathers, and is argued to be false by Antonius Possevinus, Tom. 2 of the Apparatus, p. 71.

4. The Gospel of Thaddaeus the Apostle is condemned by Gelasius, dist. 15, c. Sancta Romana.

5. The Gospel of Thomas, familiar to the Manichaeans, is condemned by Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis, p. 100 and p. 151.

6. The Gospel of Barnabas, of which mention is made in Clement the Roman, in the book of Recognitions, as Apocr-phum; Gelasius rejects it.

7. From the Apocryphal Gospel of Bartholomew Dionysius the Areopagite cites this saying, the Gospel is small and great.

8. Mention is made of the Gospel of Andrew in Eusebius, book 3, c. 25, Augustine against the adversaries of the law and the prophets, c. 20, and Jerome, Preface on Matthew; but it is reckoned among the Apocrypha by Gelasius.

9. The Gnostics made the greatest use of the Gospel of Philip. Epiphanius, heresy 26, p. 3, calls it fabricated.

10. Eusebius cites the Gospel of Matthew, but Clement of Alexandria teaches in Stromata books 2 and 7 that it served the errors of Marcion and Basilides.

11. Irenaeus, book 1, Against Heresies, chapter 35, p. 91, records that among heretics the Gospel of Judas the traitor was in use. Compare Epiphanius, Heresy 38.

12. The same, book 3, chapter [u], p. 188. Those who are sprung from Valentine, without all fear, bringing forth their own writings, glory that they possess many things which are themselves Gospels; indeed they have advanced to such boldness that they title what was lately written by them the Gospel of Truth, agreeing in nothing with the Gospels of the Apostles. Compare Tertullian, Against Heresies, p. 110.

13. The Gospel of Nicodemus exists in the Orthodoxography of the Fathers mo-um. But there are many signs of falsehood in it. Hence Sixtus Senensis rejected it, Library, book 2.

14. Jerome mentions the Gospel of Apelles in the Prologue on Matthew.

15. Jerome mentioned the Gospel of the Egyptians elsewhere; Clement of Alexandria, Stromata book 3, p. 200, which the Valentinians and Sabellians used; Clement elsewhere, p. 118; Epiphanius, Heresy 62, p. 168.

16. Ambrose mentions the Gospel of the Basilidians in the Preface on Luke, and Jerome in the Prologue on Matthew.

ΕΕιβραφη Ευαγγέλιον ηατά ΜατΘαιον According-to-Matthew, that is, of Matthew; for -- in Hebrew signifies not only according to, as -- according to our image Gen. 1. v. 26. but also sometimes must be rendered by the genitive, as -- A Psalm of David; the Syrian rendered the Gospel -- of Matthew. That this title was added by Matthew himself is proved by Schramus in the treatise How we know that the Gospel of Matthew is Matthew's.

2. Encomium of the Author. Matthew, by force of his name, means gift; for called from the toll-booth to apostleship he instructed the Church both by speech and writing, whence he must be judged a distinguished instrument of God and an outstanding gift given to the Church. Tertullian, On the Flesh of Christ, chapter 22, p. 37, calls him the most faithful expounder of the Gospel and companion of the Lord. Chrysostom, or whoever is the author of the imperfect work, says: that he preached the Gospel to sinners not only by his word but also by the amendment of his own life. To this praise of the Gospel belongs what Eusebius, book 5 of the History, chapter 10, and Jerome, On Illustrious Men / on ecclesiastical writers, in Pantaenus, chapter 36, testify: Bartholomew, setting out for India, took with him Matthew's Gospel written out, and left it there.

3. Numerus Evangeliorum. Irenaeus lib. 3. advers. haeres. cap. 11. p. 186. Nea plura numero, quàm haec sunt, nea rursus pauciora capit esse Evangelia. Quoniam enim quatuor regiones mundi sunt, in quo sumus, & quatuor principales Spiritus, & disseminata est Ecclesia super omnem terram, columna autem & firmamentum Ecclesiae est Evangelium & Spiritus vitae, consequens est, quatuor eam habere columnas undia flantes incorruptibilitatem & vivificantem homines. Cherubim quadriformia & formae ipsorum imagines sunt dispositionis Filii DEI. Primum enim animal, inquit, simile leoni effiabile eius & principale & regale significans. Secundum vero simile mile vitulo sacrificalem & sacerdotalem ordinationem significans. Tertium verò habens faciem quasi humanam, eum qui est secundùm hominem adventum eius manifestè describens: Quartum verò simile aquilae volitantis, Spiritus in Ecclesiam advolitantis gratiam manifestans. Quae omnia ibidem latiùs persequitur. (Nicolaus Gallasius in annotat. ad illum locum Irenaei hanc Speculationem, quam ita vocat, impugnat, sed in similitudinibus & allegoriis non sunt omnia ad vivum resecanda, modò fidei analogiae congruant.) Hieronymus in prooem. Evangel. Matthaei sui disserit. Prima hominis facies Matthaeum significat, quia quasi de homine exorsus est praescribere. Liber generationis Iesu Christi &c. Secunda leonis Marcum, in quo vox leonis in eremo rugientis auditur cap. 1. Vox clamantis in deserto. Tertia vituli Lucam, quia â Zacharia Sacerdote sumsit initium. Quarta aquilae Iohannem, quia sumtis pennis aquilae & ad altiora festinans de verbo DEI disputat. Idem in Epist. ad Paulinum itidem quatuor Evangelistas vocat quadrigam Domini ostensam Ezechieli cap. 1. & Iohanni Apoc. 4. Matthaeus enim Evangelicam suam Historiam orditur â generatione Christi humana, quâ ratione homini comparatur; Marcus orditur â praedicatione Iohannis in deserto, & sic confertur leoni; Lucas â descriptione Sacrificiorum legalium, & sic confertur vitulo; Iohannes praecipuè divinitatem Christi describit, quâ ratione confertur aquilae. Pii veteres visionem illam Propheticam ad Christum accommodant hoc modo. Christus nobis homo factus nascendo, vitulus moriendo, leo resurgendo, aquila ascendendo. Augustinus lib. 1. de cons. Evang. cap. 7. Evangelistas dicit esse sanctam illam Domini quadrigam, qua tanquam cursu triumphali per orbem terrarum vectus odorem cognitionis sparsit uberrimum ac populos sibi subegit. lib. eiusdem cap. 16. itidem formas quatuor animalium ad Evangelistas accommodat, sed in applicatione ab Hieronymo discedit, leonem enim tribuit Matthaeo (eô quòd rigiam Christi Personam maximè commendaverit, nam & Magos commemorat ad Christum Regem quaerendum & adorandum venisse ex Oriente; ipsumq; Herodem Regem Christum adhuc infantem formidasse. Leo autem est Symbolum regiae potestatis) hominem tribuit Marco (quia nec stirpem Regiam, neq; sacerdotalem

vel cognationem vel consecrationem narrare voluit, sed totus in eis verfatur, quae homo Christus gessit in his terris) in Luca & Iohanne consentit cum Hieronymo. 4. έΣυμθωνια. Socinus de autor. Script. p. 15. Quod Evangelissae in quibusdam rebus minimi momenti inter se differunt, hoc non solùm illis non minuere, sed etiam augere debet autoritatem & fidem. Et postea. Fieri potest, ut alius alio talium rerum veritatem meliùs tenuerit. pag. 104. Fieri potest, ut verissima ea omnia essent, quae de Evangelistis & Apostolis Historia affirmat, & tamen ipsi nonnunquam hac in parte leviter errassent. Erasmus eodem ferè modo in annotat. ad cap. 2. & 27. Matthaei scribit, non esse metuendum, ne totius Scripturae corruat autoritas, si levis aliquis error in ea deprehendatur, cùm nullo modo negari posse videatur, Evaengelistas interdum memoriâ fuisse lapsos. Favere illis quodammodo videri posset Chrysostomus in Matth. p. 3. Sex toto, inquè omnibus consonarent & cum nimia diligentia atcura & ad tempora ac loca omnia usad singula aequaliter verba concurrerent, nemo inimicus credidisset unquàm, quin illi communi ad decipiendum consilio congregari quasi ex humana quadam conspir atione Evangelium condidissent. Nunc verò quae videtur in rebus exiguis dissonantia ab omni illos suspicione tuetur, satisa clarè scribentium existimationem defendit.

Sed Augustinus Epist. 8. ad Hieron. rectè monet; Admisso in tantum autoritatis fastigium aliquo mendacio, nullam horum librorum particulam mansuram, quae non possit in dubium revocari, ac proinde lib. 2. de cons. Evang. cap. 12. concludit, omnem falsitatem ab Evangelistis abesse decere, non solùm eam, quae mentiendo promitur, sed ettam eam, quae obliviscendo. Quod si nama erratum aliquod ab Evangelistis sive imperitiâ, sive oblivione, sive alia quacuna humana imbecillitate ab autore committi potuit, quicuna locus ex eorum scriptis proferatur, de eo quaestio esse poterit, an in eo Evangelista scribendo non dormitaverit. Idem in cap. 1. Galat. ut unum sit Evangelium aut non unum, non aestimatur numero scribentium, sed hinc, eademne sint, an diversa, quae scribuntur. Unde dilucidum est, quatuor Evangelia esse unum Evangelium. Cùm enim quatuor eaedem loquuntur, non est aliud ataliud ob personarum differentiam, sed unum, ob eorum, qui loquuntur, consonantiam. Coeterum Gen. regulae in conciliatione Evangelistarum notandae ex Augustini libris de consensu Evangelistarum & ex aliis Patribus collectae suo loco proponuntur.

Generali huic regulae speciales addi possunt quamplurimae, quae ratione circumstantiarum in certas classes distribui possunt. sunt autem hae circumstantiae. Persona (quae loquitur, ad quam, de quâ, coram quâ loquitur) Occasio (Consilium, Finis) Tempus, Locus, modus. §. 183.

Ad circumstantiam Personae pertinent hae regulae. I. Personae in Scr. saepè sunt binomines. vid. Iud. 6. v. 32. & 2. Sam. 11. v. 21. Conf. 1. Sam. 12. v. 24. 25. 2. Distinctae personae saepè sunt uninomines. 3. Filiatio est vel naturalis, vel legalis, natur alis fit generatione, legalis adoptione. 4. De Renatis pronunciantur diversa, quia duos quasi in se habent homines, veterem aec novum. Sic renati dicuntur venundati sub peccatum,Rom. 7. v. 14. ratione veteris hominis: renati peccatum non faciant,1. Ioh. 3. v. 9. sc. ratione novi hominis. 5. de Christo quaedam dicuntur secundùm divinam naturam, quaedam secundùm humanam, quaedam secundùm utrama. §. 184.

Ad circumstantiam Consilii, finis & occasionis pertinet haec regula. Intelligentia dictorum sumenda ex causis dicendi, Hilar. 4. de Trin. Sic Christus Matth. 19. v. 21. iuveni in Schola Pharisaeorum instituto, & de perfectâ legis impletione falsò glorianti proponit hoc speciale praeceptum, ut omnia vendat ac pauperibus distribuat, atq; hoc modò Christum sequatur: nimirum voluit Christus hominem convincere, quòd primum praeceptum de Deo super omnia diligendo non impleverit &c. §. 185.

De circumstantiâ temporis multae tradi possunt regulae, verum enim illud vetus, distingue tempora & concordabit Scriptura. 1. Quaedam dicta agunt de tempore exinanitionis, quaedam de tempore exaltationis Christi. 2. Tempus sumitur vel completè vel incompletè. 3. Eiusq; partes sumuntur vel inclusivè vel exclusivè, exemplum habetur Matth. 17. v. 1. coll. cum Luc. 9. v. 28. 4. In numero perfectiori saepè quòd deest vel superest, non computatur. August. q. 47. in Exod. 5.Numerus finitus ponitualiquando pro infinito. Septies in die cadit iustus &c. 6. In supputationibus sacris propter impietatem Principis vel nomen eius vel numerus annorum, quibus malè administravit, omittuntur. 7. Rex vel externo bello vel senio vel morbo impeditus, si pro-Regem filium vivus constituit, tum in computationibus annorum patris & filii simul regnantium, anni regiminis aliquando coniunctim, aliquando separatins sumuntur. Huius regulae usus est in colligendis Regum Israeliticorum annis. 8. Sic observandum est, quòd Orientales variè distinxerint diem artificialem, tum in horas aequales duodecim, vulgo planetarias: tum etiam in quadrantes. Conciliari hinc possunt loca Marc. 15. v. 25. & Ioh. 19. v. 14. §. 80.

De circumstantiâ loci agunt hae regulae 1. Uni loco in Scr. saepè duo tribuuntur nomina, 2. Distinctis locis saepè unum tribuitur nomen. 3. Scriptores Sacrsaepè locum denominant eâ ap-ellatione, quae fuit usitata eo, quo ipsi vixerunt & scripserunt, tempore. Confer. Gen. 12. v. 5. cum Gen. 28. v. 19. §. 187.

Sic Patres sunt honorandi, & tamen certo respectu sunt odio habendi, Luc. 14. v. 26. id est, autoritas ipsorum est postponenda, videlicet si quid contra coelestem Patrem iubeant. 3. Dicta specialiter derogant generalibus. 4. Moralia praeferuntur ceremonialibus. 5. Secunda legis tabula cedit primae. 6. Quod ipsum tamen perfectioni Historiae Evangelicae vel Scripturae Sacra nihil quicquam derogat. Cyrillus lib. 12. in Ioh. cap. ult. Non omnia, quae Deus fecit, conscript a sunt, sed quae scr-bentes tam ad mores, quàm ad dogmata putarunt sufficere, ut recta fide & operibus rutilantes ad regnum coelorum pervenire mereamur.

Ebionitarum, quod tametsi à Matthaeo scriptum dicebatur Hebraicè, ab haereticis tamen illis truncatum ac vitiatum est, teste Iren. lib. 3. cap. 11. Epiph. haer. 30. 2. Encratitarum, â Tatiano Syro, haereseos istius autore ex quatuor Evangelistis conflatum, quod appellavit σιαρέσσαρον, in quo genealogias Christi omisit Epiph. haeres. 46. Theodor. lib. 1. fab. haer-t 3. Nasarenorum, quod Iacobo tribui solet, cuius meminerunt Orig. Tom. 2. tract. 8. in Ioh. Clem. lib. 2. strom. Euseb. lib. 1. cap. 25. Beda tanti illud fecit, ut de eo scribere non dubitaverit, non esse numerandum inter Apocryphas, sed Ecclesiasiicas Historias. In Praefat. sup. Lucam. Coeterùm ab aliis seqq. Evangelia commemorantur:

1. Evangelium secundùm duodecim Apostolos, ut Apocryph. citatur ab Orig. lib. 1. in Luc. Hieron. Praefat. in Matth.

2. Evangelium Petri Apostoli. Serapion Episc. Antiochenus Ao. Christi 300. ut falsum & Apocryphum reiecit. Euseb. lib. 6. Histor. Eccles. cap. 10. & 11.

3. Prot Evangelium Iacobi extat in Orthodoxog. Patrum, falsitatis ab Anton. Possevino Tom. 2. Appar. p. 71. arguitur.

4. Evangelium Thaddaei Apostoli reprobatur â Gelasio dist. 15. c. Sancta Romana.

5. Evangelium Thomae, Manichaeis familiare, reprobatur â Cyrillo Hieros. Catech. p. 100. & p. 151.

6. Evangellum Barnabae, cuius mentio sit apud Clementem Romanum in lib. Recog. ut Apocr-phum reiicit Gelasius.

7. Ex Evangelio Bartholomaei Apocrypho Dionysius Areopagita citat hanc sententiam, Evangelium esse parvum & magnum.

8. Evangelii Andreae mentio fit apud Euseb. lib. 3. c. 25. Aug. contra adv. legis & Proph. c. 20. Hieron. Praef. in Matth. sed inter Apocrypha â Gelasio recensetur.

9. Evangelio Philippi Gnostici maximè utebantur. Epiph. haeres. 26. p. 3. vocat confictum.

10. Evangelium Matthiae citat Euseb. d. l. sed Clemens Alex. lib. 2. & 7. strom. Marcionis & Basilidis errorib. inserviisse docet.

11. Iren. lib. 1. adv. haeres. cap. 35. p. 91. Cainis haereticis Evangelium proditoris Iudae in usu fuisse memorat. Conf. Epiph. haeres. 38.

12. Id. lib. 3. cap. u. p. 188. Hi qui sunt â Valentino existentes, extra omnem timorem, suas conscriptiones proferentes, plur a habere gloriantur, quae sint ipsa Evangelia, siquidem in tantum processerunt audaciae, ut quod ab his non olim conscriptum est, veritatis Evangelium titulent, in nihilo conveniens Apostolorum Evangeltis. Confer Tertull. advers. haeres. p. 110.

13. Evangelium Nicodemi extat in Orthodoxogr. Patrum mo-um. Sed multa in co falsitatis indicia. Inde repudiat illud Sixt. Sen. lib. 2. Biblioth.

14. Evangelii Apellis meminit Hieron in prolog. Matth.

15. Evangelii Aegyptiorum mominerunt Hieron. d. l. Clem. Alex. lib. 3. strom. p. 200. quo utebantur Valentin. & Sabelliani, Clem. d. lib. p. 118. Epiph. 62. haeres. p. 168.

16. Evangelii Basilidianorum meminit Ambros. Praefat. in Luc. & Hieron. prolog. Matth.

## 1:1 Introduction: Chapter III. On the Gospel of Matthew
3. The impulsive and final cause of writing. 1. Epiphanius, heresy 51, testifies that Matthew wrote his Gospel at the command of the Apostles. Matthew, he says, was the first to begin proclaiming the Gospel; for to him was committed and imposed the task of preaching the Gospel from the beginning. 2. Chrysostom, homily 1 on Matthew, and from him Baronius, Year 41, section 17, assert that Matthew undertook this work when the Jews who had believed demanded it. 3. Eusebius, book 3 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 24 (or 18): When Matthew had first preached to the Hebrews, and was about to pass over to others, he handed down his Gospel in his native tongue through letters, and filled up by means of letters what those whom he was leaving might lack after his presence was withdrawn. Nicephorus, book 2 of the History, chapter 45: departing, he compensated his absence with present writing. But these causes or occasions are subordinate to the divine impulse. Salmerón, tome 3, treatise 25: The principal cause which moved Matthew to write was the Holy Spirit. For he likewise engendered in the brethren who had received Christ by faith from among the circumcised so great a desire that they should obtain from Matthew the writing of the Gospel.

4. The time of writing. Irenaeus, book 3 against heresies, chapter 1, says Matthew wrote at that time when Peter and Paul were preaching the Gospel at Rome, whence some infer that Matthew wrote 21 years after Christ's Ascension. Theophylact, at the beginning of his Commentary on Matthew, says Matthew wrote the first of all the Gospels eight years after Christ's Assumption. But Nicephorus, book 2 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 45, holds that Matthew wrote fifteen years after Christ's Ascension. Eusebius in his Chronicle says that Matthew wrote his Gospel in the year of Christ 41, which coincides with Theophylact's reckoning. The same is held by Baronius, Annals, tome 1, year 41, n. 15, warning that Irenaeus's words must not be taken in such a sense as if Matthew did not write until after the arrival of Peter and then of Paul at Rome (for from that it would follow that Matthew did not write first among the Evangelists, since Paul came to Rome in the year of the Lord 59, at which time both Mark and Luke had already published their Gospel histories; Likewise that Matthew did not write his Gospel before the Apostols set out into the various provinces of the world) but in that sense, that almost at the very beginning of the foundation of the Roman Church the Gospel was written by Matthew, seeing that Peter indeed came to Rome and gathered the Church there to Christ by the preaching of the Gospel, which happened in the year of Christ 45.

5. Language. Many of the ancients assert that Matthew wrote his Gospel in Hebrew. Papias, in Eusebius, book 3, Hist., chap. 33. Epiphanius, heresy 29, concerning the Nazarenes. But they have Matthew's Gospel most perfectly in Hebrew: for among them this is plainly preserved, even as it was first written, still in Hebrew letters. Irenaeus, book 3, chap. 1. Matthew published among the Hebrews, in their own language, a writing of the Gospel. Athanasius, in the Synopsis: The Gospel according to Matthew was composed and published by him in the Hebrew dialect at Jerusalem. Gregory Nazianzen, in his verses:

Ματθαιος μέν έλραΨεν Εβραιοις θαυματα χριςού,Μαρηος σ Ιτάγιη, δούηας Αχαιασι,Πασι σέ τωάννης ηηρύξ μέλας αυρανοθοιτης .Matthew writes Christ's miracles to the Hebrews, Mark to Italy, Luke to Achaea. But mighty herald John writes to all.

Jerome, in the Catalogue, under the word Matthew. First, in Judaea, on behalf of those who had believed out of the circumcision, he composed the Gospel of Christ in Hebrew letters and words. In the same place he says, the Hebrew itself is kept even to this day in the Library of Caesarea, which Pamphilus the Martyr compiled with the utmost diligence. To me likewise, through the Nazarenes, who make use of this volume in Beroea, a city of Syria, there was granted the opportunity of copying it . Similar things occur in the Preface to the 4 Gospels addressed to Damasus, in chap. 12 of Matthew, in chap. 11 of Hosea, etc. (where he says, that Pantenus found Matthew's Hebrew Gospel in India, whither it had been carried by Bartholomew) in Augustine, book 1, De Consens. Evang., chap. 2, Eusebius, book 3, Hist. Eccles., chap. 24, book 5, chap. 8, Epiphanius, heresy 30, Nicephorus, book 4, chap. 32. * (beside the Fathers already cited, the Syrian interpreter confirms the same opinion in the closing colophon of Matthew's Gospel, which, because in the Altdorf MS. codex it differs somewhat -a from the printed codices, it pleased to set down entire, as it is given there, such being the reading:) The Syrians are followed by the Arabic, which likewise attests in its clausula that Matthew wrote his own Gospel , that is, in Hebrew)* whom follow Baronius ann. 34. num. 165. (where he writes most boldly: I say that, of what faith the Greek text is, nless it be compared with the Hebrew original, we can by no means affirm) Bellarmine lib. 2. de verb. Dei cap. 7. In the preceding century Sebastian Münster and Johannes Tilius [wrote upon] the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew in the publication of the edition of the Hebrew Gospel, first edited by Johannes Tilius at Paris in the Year 1551, at Martin the Younger's, παααηιαςιχως wrote: No one can doubt that this very thing is that Gospel which Matthew wrote in Hebrew.

But against this opinion arguments of no small weight do battle. I. Erasmus in the annotations on chapter 1 of Matt. so argues: By the authority of Jerome it was once settled that this Gospel was written by Matthew in Hebrew, which however Chrysostom dares not assert, but it is said, he says, that although it be settled, I nevertheless prefer it to exist rather than to be settled. 2. The same man, on chapter 8 of Matt. p. 34: It does not seem probable to me that Matthew wrote in Hebrew, seeing that no one testifies that he ever saw any trace of any volume in Hebrew; indeed, that which they call that of the Nazoraeans is testified by Jerome not to be written in Hebrew, but in Chaldee, merely with Hebrew formulae, and is reckoned among the Apocrypha; next, the style of Matthew plainly agrees with the style of Mark, and differs not greatly ssenti-ally from the diction of John. (We confess that the later argument about the agreement of style is not apodictic; therefore we shall not enumerate the objections of Conzenius to it, although in those he seeks a beginning, bringing forward that Mark wrote in Latin.) Against the former Conzenius objects: Papias saw the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew, on the testimony of Eusebius lib. 3. Hist. cap. 33. which afterward perished. Answer: 1. Concerning άυοψία Papias no word there simply records that Matthew wrote in the Hebrew tongue, which he could have had from the report of others. 2. Papias also suffered himself to be imposed upon in other matters, especially in the error of the Millennarians through traditions, since he was of weak judgment. 3. If the Hebrew text of Matthew had been authentic, divine providence would not have permitted it to perish. Conzenius retorts, those books perished, which are mentioned by Jerome, and out of various Greek versions now nothing survives except one alone. Answer to the former, those were not Canonical. To the latter, the case of the authentic text and of a version is different.) 3. Cajetan sternly warns, that Matthew's Gospel was not written in Hebrew, with an argument not absurd, drawn from the rendering of Hebrew words, as ch. 1. v. 23. Emmanuel, which is, if you interpret it, God with us. ch. 27. v. 46. Eli, Eli, lamma sabachthani, that is, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me. For the Hebrew edition could not thus interpret, nor ought any translator to do so, as appears from the example of other words. Maldonate & Conzenius q. 5. proœm. resp. 1. those interpretations are not the Author's, but the interpreter's, as at1. Kings 7. v. 12.where the Seventy interpret Eben-Ezer λίθον Βοη. But in this answer the principle is begged, for it presupposes that this Greek text of Matthew belongs to some interpreter, not to the Evangelist himself. 2. that what Isaiah said in Hebrew, Matthew, writing in Syriac, expounded in his own tongue. Answer. Again the principle is begged, namely that Matthew wrote in Syriac, since the ancients assert he wrote in Hebrew. Nor is there such diversity between the Hebrew and Syrian language, that the Hebrew word Emmanuel would need to be explained in Syriac. But, says Conzen, the Syrian turned a Syriac name into Syriac. Why then could not Matthew turn a Hebrew word into Syriac? Answer. The Syrian translated from the Greek, therefore it is no wonder that, following his thread, he wished a Syriac rendering of the Hebrew name added. 4. The remaining Apostles first wrote in the Greek tongue, not only indiscriminately to all Jews and Gentiles: but also specifically to the Jews. Why then should we wish to judge differently concerning Matthew? His very calling to the Apostolate required him to write in a well-known tongue. 5. Yet let that original edition be produced, whether Hebrew or Syriac. For they do not yet agree among themselves whether Matthew wrote in pure Hebrew, or rather in Syriac, which latter Albertus Widmanstadt affirms, in the Preface to the Syriac edition of the N. T., Guy Fabrice, Bellarmine book 2. de verbo DEI chapter 4. Conzen. q. 5.

proœm. (Luke of Bruges on ch. 1. of Matthew. Opinions differ as to whether Matthew wrote in the very language which the Prophets used, or in -o, which at that time was the vernacular tongue of the Hebrews.) 6. The edition which circulates today is not genuine. The Gospel in Hebrew which Münster published cannot be Matthew's own, for whoever its author was, he was not even taught in Hebrew. Concerning the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew edited by Til(i)us, Mercerus, Paris professor, warns in the Preface to his version that sometimes some Rabbinical matter is found mixed in it. In chapter 1 there is , a barbarism together with a solecism. Chapter 2: What is ? And what again is ? And what are forms always without a question mark? Chapter 5: and . And countless other things, which testify that this is a recent work, and that the author knew nothing more in Hebrew than what he could pick up from school usage, and thence turned himself to making a version. Bailius the Jesuit in the Catechism of Controversies, treatise 1, question 14: The true Hebrew text of Matthew does not exist. That one which Münster published, and the other which Johannes Til(i)us had printed, are judged spurious, and smell of the workshop of the Jews. 7. Whatever the case may be, those very authors who report that Matthew wrote in Hebrew confess that the Gospel which we possess in Greek was published in Greek within the times of the Apostles themselves and commended to the Church as authoritative, *(besides others see Cornelius à Lapide on the Four Gospels, p. 41. a.)* which suffices for us. ( Bellarmine, book 2 On the Word of God, chapter 7, acknowledges: the Greek edition of the New Testament has the Evangelists and Apostles as its authors. In ancient times, while the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew still existed, only the Nazarite and Ebionite heretics claimed the Hebrew text for themselves, with Jerome in the catalogue of writers and Epiphanius, Heresies, as witnesses. 29. From the beginning Catholics have always embraced the Greek.) Although they do not agree as to who rendered it from Hebrew into Greek: Athanasius in the Synopsis attributes this to James the brother of the Lord; Jerome in the Catalogue of Illustrious Men; Eusebius, book 3, chapters 34 and 39, book 5, chapter 10, to Mark; Theophylact to John; Anastasius in Genesis, Sermon 8, to Luke and Paul. Therefore we reject that most audacious pronouncement of Baronius, that it can only be affirmed upon comparison with the Hebrew original how much faith should be given to the Greek text, which Casaubon rightly attacks in Exercitation 15, chapter 12.

page 388. For if the authority of the Greek text of the Gospel according to Matthew depends on the Hebrew text, since the Hebrew copies long ago perished and do not extend down to this day, it follows necessarily that today that Gospel ought to have no weight, no authority whatsoever. Conzenius question 5, preface to the disputation: since the Gospel of Matthew was written in Hebrew, but that version does not exist today, therefore we must necessarily fall back upon the divine and infallible authority of the Church, by which being denied there would be no use of this Gospel, since the faith of the Interpreter is uncertain and his name unknown. Response. 1. As many as among the ancients determine that Matthew wrote in Hebrew add that it was immediately translated into the Greek language by another Apostle. 2. Whence Bellarmine in the said book confesses that the Greek edition of the entire New Testament has the Evangelists and Apostles as authors, which suffices for us. 3. Conzenius himself adds below. §. 4. What if Mark himself converted the Gospel of Matthew into the Greek language? §. 5. The interpreter of Matthew, if not an Apostle, certainly was an apostolic man, as Tertullian says. Compare on this question Gulielmus Whitaker against Reynolds, chapter 12, page 307; Capellus, book 2, Vindiciae for Casaubon, chapter 8, column 43; Chamier, Tome 1, Panstratia, book 11, chapter 8, §. 8; Flacius in the Preface to the New Testament. * (To these may be added Gomarus in the dissertation on the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew; Rivetus, Isagoge to the Holy Scriptures, ch. 8, §. 4; Johannes Crocius, Anti-Beza, page 27; Hottinger, Philological Treasury, book 2, p. 518; and several others.) * The objections of Conzenius against the arguments of Flacius need not be refuted. 1. because those arguments of Flacius are not all of equal strength. 2. Conzenius confesses that this question does not belong to faith. 3. We will fight with no one who determines that Matthew wrote in Hebrew, provided he grants that the Greek text has an Apostle or apostolic man as author, and consequently is authentic.

6. Contraries: Cerinthus, as Philastrius testifies, accepted only the Gospel of Matthew, having rejected the other three. Irenaeus lib. 1. cap. 26. p. 8. Those who are called Ebionites use only that which is according to Matthew, and reject the Apostle Paul. The same [author], lib. 3. cap. 2. Epiphanius in heresy 30. Eusebius lib. 3. Hist. Eccles. cap. 21. testify the same concerning the Ebionites, that they received only Matthew from among the Evangelists. But they received none other than a depraved and mutilated Gospel of Matthew, as the same Epiphanius reports in the said place.

7. Distribution. The older Latins divide this Gospel according to Hilary's arrangement into 33 canons; according to Christian Druthmar's division into 67 canons; but more recent ones into 8 chapters. Among the Greeks, according to Euthymius and Oecumenius, into 68 chapters; according to Suidas however into 68 titles, but 355 chapters. Likewise Ammonius and Eusebius [divide] into 355 chapters. In our Greek and Latin Codices it is divided into 28 chapters.

Matthew explains. 1. the Person. 2. The office of Christ. To the Person belongs the enumeration of his ancestors, the description of his birth and upbringing. To the office belong: 1. The solemn preparation for it. 2. Its public administration, namely 1. Of the Prophetic Office through the preaching of the Gospel and the working of miracles, completed in three years and a half of ministry. 2. Of the Priestly Office through the Passion and death. 3. Of the Royal Office through the Resurrection and Ascension.

In the order of Evangelical History Matthew beautifully describes the state of a true Christian. 1. We are born carnally. 2. We are regenerated spiritually through Baptism. 3. Temptation follows. 4. Afterward the Christian teaches not so much by words as by deeds and examples. 5. From then on he awaits death. 6. Knowing certainly that he will rise again with Christ and ascend into heaven. Ferus here.

I think it would be for the curiosity of holy readers of Sacred Scripture, if I should here append a brief list of some who, besides those mentioned above, furnished particular commentaries on Matthew, or otherwise attempted to illustrate this Evangelist either with notes or with homilies.

Therefore there may be referred here from among the Fathers and those who lived nearest after them: Jerome of Strido, Hilary of Poitiers, Claudius the Scot, Rupert of Tuiti.

from the Papists Thomas Aquinas -t. 14. of the Works, Tostatus of Avila (whose Commentaries on Matthew, printed at Venice in the year 1529, constitute three proper volumes in folio.) Claude Guillard of Bellay, John Hessels of Louvain, Laelius Bisciola the Jesuit, Isidoro Clario of Brescia, Johannes Ferus, John Major the Scot, João Soares Bishop of Coimbra, William of Auvergne, Matthias Bredenbach, Paulus de Palatio (especially commended by Tirinus) Stanisław Sokołowski Canon of Kraków, Nicolaus Buccasenus, Porreda, printed at Venice 1602. Matthaeus, inquit, primus caepit Evangelium annunciare, huic enim commissum erat ac impositum, ut Evangelium praedicaret aeb initio. 2. Chrysostomus homil. 1. in Matth & ex eo Baronius An. 41. sect. 17. asserunt, taentum opus aggressum fuisse Matthaeum Iudaeis, qui crediderunt exposcentibus. 3. Eusebius lib. 3. Hist. Eccles. cap. 24. Causa praecipuae, quae Matthaeum ad scribendum permovit, Spiritus S. fuit. Nam & ille propterea magnum desiderium in fratribus, qui ex circumcisione Christum fide receperant, ingeneravit, ut â Matthaeo conscriptionem Evangelii obtinerent.

4. Tempus scriptionis. Irenaeus lib. 3. advers. haeres. cap. 1. Matthaeum scripsisse dicit eo tempore, quo Petrus & Paulus Romae Evangelizabant, ex quo quidam colligunt, Matthaeum 21. post Christum ascensionem anno scripsisse. Theophyl. initio Coment. in Matth. dicit, Matthaeum omnium primum scripsisse Evangelium post octo â Christi assumtione annos. Sed Nicephorus lib. 2. Histor. Eccles. cap. 45. statuit. Matthaeum decimo quintpost Christi ascensionem anne scripsisse. Eusebius in Chronico dicit, Matthaeum anno Christi 41. Evangelium suum scripsisse, quod cum Theophyl. computationcoincidit. Idem statuit Baronius Annal. tom. 1. ann. 41. n. 15. monens, Irenaei verba non esse eo sensu accipienda, ac si non nisi post Petri ac demum Pauli Romam adventum Matthaeus scripserit (ex eo enim sequeretur, Matthaeum non scripsisse primum inter Evangelistas, cum Paulus Romam venerit anno Domini 59. quo tempore & Marcus & Lucas suam iamdum ediderant Evangelicam Historiam; Item Matthaeum non scripsisse Evangelium suum, antequā Apostoli in diversas orbis provincias proficiscerentur) sed sensu eo, quasi ipso initio fundationis Romanae Ecclesiae â Matthaeo Evangelium sit conscriptum, cùm sc. Petrus Romam accessit & Evangelii praedicatione Ecclesiam Christo ibi collegit, quod factum anno Christi 45.

5. Idioma. Matthaeum Evangelium suum Hebraicè scripsisse, multi ex veteribus asserunt. Papias apud Euseb. lib. 3. Hist. cap. 33. Epiph. haeres. 29. de Nazaraeis. Habent autem Matthaei Evangelium perfectissimum Hebraicè: apud ipsos enim hoc clarè, quem admodum ab initio scriptum est, Hebraicis literis adhuc servatur. Irenaeus lib. 3. cap. 1. Matthaeus in Hebraeis ipsorum lingva Scripturam edidit Evangelii. Athanasius in Synopsi: Evangelium secundùm Matthaeum ab ipso Hebraicâ dialecto conseriptum est, & editum Hierosolymis. Gregor.
