## 1:1
v. 1. Moses, describing man's primeval χίσιν πλάσιν, speaks thus Gen. 3. v. 1. This is the book of the generations of Adam. Matthew, describing the άνάχισιν άνάπλαιν, wrought for mankind through the second Adam, uses the very same phrase. Jacobus Faber Stapulensis on this passage: Just as Moses began the book of the old law from the Genesis of the world, so also Matthew begins the book of the new law, which is the eternal Gospel, from the Genesis of Christ, the maker of the world. Remigius: Since the Evangelist knew that the book of the generations of Adam had been written, therefore he began thus, setting book against book, and the new Adam over against the old Adam, through whom all things were restored that had been corrupted through him. This is what the Evangelist meant to say. Moses has described for you the generation of Adam, according to which we are all born children of wrath; I will describe a happier generation, not of a man corrupted by sin, but of Christ Jesus the Savior, who won back for us anew what we lost in Adam.

With the Hebrew phrase Βιβλος γενέσεως is called genealogy, for among the Hebrews is not only book, but any enumeration, from he enumerated, counted, Gen. 5. v. 1. II. Reg. 5. v. 5. 6. 7. chap. 22. v. 13. even a letter is called a book. Jeremiah 32. the book of purchase is called the deed of purchased possession, 2 Chron. 2. v. 17. The Evangelist speaks in the singular. Although indeed he enumerates several generations, still they are all referred to that one which belongs to the Messiah, as both the preface and the closing of this enumeration show. Some, such as Thomas, Lyra, Ferus etc., take that Book of the generation etc. to mean the same as a book beginning, taking its starting point from the generation of Christ; for books, following the custom of the Hebrews, commonly lay claim to their subject matter in their openings. Yet 1. the title of this book is not the generation of Christ, but the Gospel of Matthew, as the title itself declares. 2. Here book is used for catalogue or enumeration. The Syriac version has the word description, Writing. (And likewise the Arabic and Ethiopic, and the latter indeed: i.e. book of the generation. Though these words intimate nothing other than the genealogy, I nonetheless wonder, not without cause, why concerning the Ethiopian alone Cornelius à Lapide writes, that it has word-for-word, Genealogy; but the others, namely the Greek, Syrian, Arabic texts etc., word-for-word The book of the generation, since likewise the Ethiopian also expresses the genealogy with the phrase book of the generation)*.

TO THE FIRST CHAPTER OF MATTHEW.

Word-for-word ενςσεως some understand ων πςωοόνων of the ancestors, from whom Christ draws his origin. But there is no need here to introduce a certain ellipsis. For genesis is placed here for origin or rising. Now indeed it is evident that Matthew proposed to weave together the genealogy of Christ and describe his very rising from his ancestors, whence he notably adds βιβλος γενέσεως Ιησ Χςις, and even traces the line γενέσεως quite clearly down to Christ himself in verse 16: Jacob begot Joseph the husband of Mary, from whom ἐγεννήθη Christ was born.

The old interpreter confuses ένεσιν and έννησιν, but the former is from είνομαι,, the latter from εννάω.. Erasmus thinks έννεσιν should be rendered by birth; γένεσις can be rendered by offspring.

*( and they enlarge the borders of their garments.

It is asked, How does Matthew say that he is writing the book of the generation of Jesus Christ, when he does not trace his genealogy to Christ, but to Joseph, who was merely the supposed father of Christ? Matt. 3. v. 23. Answer: 1. Some think it sufficient that he shows, that Mathan, from whose common stock Jacob the father of Joseph and Eli the father of Mary descended, had his origin from David and Abraham. 2. But this evasion is unnecessary, since he traces the line of generation all the way to Christ, verse 16: Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom ἐγεννήθη Christ was born; verse 17: from the transmigration of Babylon unto Christ νεαί fourteen generations. Verse 18: the generation of Jesus Christ η έννησς was thus. 3. Although however Christ was not begotten of Joseph in the manner in which Joseph was of Jacob, that is, through carnal generation, nevertheless he was begotten of Mary the wife of Joseph, in a supernatural and unusual manner, which suffices so that he could be called son of Joseph.

Among the Hebrews under the name sons are understood also grandchildren and descendants; therefore it could be thought that Christ is called son of David and son of Abraham because he was born from their posterity. But the Evangelist without doubt by the appellation the sons looks to the form of the promises, which sound thus, as if immediately from those very ones that blessed seed was going to be born. Abraham stood out among the Patriarchs, David among the Kings and Prophets, and to each of the two the Messiah was promised in a special way Gen. 12. v. 3.chap. 22. v. 18.2. Sam. 7. v. 12. etc. To Abraham first of all it was said: In thy seed shall all nations be blessed. It was said to David: Of the fruit of thy belly I will set upon thy throne. Therefore also the Evangelist calls Christ the son of Abraham and of David, so as to show that Christ is King, insofar as he is from David, and father of many nations, insofar as he is from Abraham. The Messiah was promised with an oath to those alone. Indeed to Abraham Gen. 22. v. 16.Luke 1. v. 73. to David Psalm 132. v. 11.Psalm 89. v. 36.

v. 1. Moses describens primaevam hominis χίσιν πλάσιν sie loquitur Gen. 3. v. 1.Hic est liber generationis Adam. Matthaeus describens humani generis άνάχισιν άνάπλαιν, factam per secundum Adamum, eâdem phrasi utitur. Iacobus Faber Stapul. in hunc locum: Ut Moses â Genesi mundi librum veteris legis inchoavit, sic & Matthaeus librum novae legis, quod est Evangelium aeternum, â Genesi Christi conditoris mundi. Remigius: Quiae noverat Evangelista, scriptum esse librum generationis Adae, ideò sic exorsus est, ut opponeret librum libro, Adamum novum Adae veteri, per quem omnia restituta, quae per illum corrupta. Evangelista voluit hoc dicere. Moses descripsit vobis generationem Adae, iuxta quam omnes nascimur filii irae, ego feliciorem generationem describam, non hominis peccato corrupti, sed Christi Iesu Salvatoris, qui nobis iterum promeruit, quod in Adamo amisimus.

Βιβλος γενέσεως phrasi Hebraicâ dicitur genealogia, enim Hebraeis est non solùm liber, sed quaelibet recensio, â recensuit, numeravit,Gen. 5. v. 1.II. Liber generationis &c. intelligunt idem esse, quod liber incipiens, initiuma sumens â generatione Christi; Solent enim libri Hebraeorum more ab initiis nomina sibi vendicare. Atqui 1. nomen huius libri non est generatio Christi, sed Evangelium Matthaei, ut habet titulus. 2. liber hic ponitur pro catalogo sive recensione. Syrus habet nomen descriptio, Scriptura. *(Eodem quoque modo Arabs & Aethiops, & hic quidem: i. e. liber generationis. quae verba licet nihil aliud innuant, quàm genealogiam, miror tamen non immeritò, quare de solo Aethiope Corn. â Lapide scribat, quòd ad verbum habeat, Genealogia; Reliqui autem, textus nempe Graecus, Syriacus, Arabicus &c. ad verbum Liber generationis, cùm itidem, ac illi Aethiops genealogiam exprimat phrasi liber generationis)*.
