## 1:2
v. 2. From βςαμ έέννσε όν ισαα, It is asked, why Matthew begins the line of descent from Abraham, while Luke chapter 3, last verse, traces the same down to Adam? Chrysostom observes, that Matthew adapted the recounting of the genealogy to those to whom he wrote this Gospel, for he wrote chiefly to the Hebrews, to whom he also preached, and who he knew would be most grateful if they perceived that Christ was the son of Abraham and of David, to whom Christ was specially promised, and whose memory among themselves was most sacred. Luke, because he wrote the Gospel to the Gentiles, extends the series of the genealogy from Adam up to the Lord himself, so that they might understand that the grace of Christ pertains not only to the Jews but to all men. Irenaeus book 3 against heresies chap. 33 p. 221. Luke traces the genealogy of the Lord back to Adam, joining the end to the beginning, and signifying that he himself recapitulated in himself all the nations dispersed thence from Adam, and all tongues, and the generation of mankind together with Adam himself. Not from Ishmael, but from Isaac, more the son of promise than of flesh, Gen. 21. v. 12.Rom. 9. v. 9. does Christ take his origin, born less by the working of Nature than of the Holy Ghost. He willed to be born not from the son of a handmaid, but from the son of a free woman, Gal. 4. v. 22. because he was being born to deliver the human race, John 8. v. 36.

Ισααχ δέ ἐγέννησε όν Ιαχωβ. Not from Esau, hated by God, but from Jacob loved by God did he will to be born, Mal. 1. v. 3. Rom. 9. v. 13. because he was that ό άαπηος, in whom God took pleasure, Matt. 3. v. 17.chap. 12. v. 18.

It is asked, why mention is made of Judah's brothers, since in what precedes there was no mention made of Ishmael, who was Isaac's brother, nor of Esau, who was Jacob's brother? Some answer that the reason is this, because the promise concerning Christ belonged to Judah and his brothers, but not to Ishmael or Esau, seeing that they were separated from the holy family of Abraham and Isaac, in which at that time the Church was contained. But indeed the promise about the Messiah was restricted also to Judah, born of his own posterity, Gen. 49. v. 10.; nor were Ishmael and Esau absolutely excluded from the Church, which assertion favors an absolute decree of reprobation. It is more correctly said that mention is made of Judah's brothers because the twelve sons of Jacob were heads of the tribes of Israel, out of which the one people of the Hebrews consisted, from whom Christ was expected. Ιαχωβ δέ ἐγέννησε όν Ιδαν σ άδελφς άυ.

Latin:

v. 2. A βςαμ έέννσε όν ισαα, Quaeritur, cur Matthaeus lineam generationis inchoet ab Abrahamo. Lucas verò cap. 3. v. ult. eandem deducat usq; ad Adamum? Chrysostomus annotat, Matthaeum genealogiae recensionem accommodasse iis, quibus scripsit hoc Evangelium, scripsit enim potis simùm Hebraeis, quibus etiam praedic avit, quibus gratisimum fore sciebat, si perspexissent, Christum esse filium Abrahae ac Davidis, quibus peculiariter Christus erat promissus, & quorum memoria apud ipsos erat Sacrosancta. Lucas, quia gentibus Evangelium scripsit, ab Adamo ad ipsum usa Dominum porrigit genealogiae seriem, ut intelligerent, Christi gratiam non solum ad Iudaeos, sed ad omnes homines pertinere. Irenaeus lib. 3. adv. haeres. cap. 33. pag. 221. Lucas genealogiam Christi usa ad Adamum deducit, finem coniungens initio, & significans, quoniam ipse, qui omnes gentes exinde ab Adam dispersas & universas lingvas & generationem hominum cum ipso Adam in semetipso recapitulatus est. Non ex Ismaele, sed ex Isaaco, promissionis magis, quàm carnis filio, Gen. 21. v. 12.Rom. 9. v. 9. originem ducit Christus, non tam Naturae, quàm Spiritus S. operatione natus. Non ex filio ancillae, sed ex filio liberae nasci voluit, Gal. 4. v. 22. quia ad liberandum genus humanum nascebatur, Ioh. 8. v. 36.

Ισααχ δέ ἐγέννησε όν Ιαχωβ. Non ex Esavo, odio â Deo habito, sed ex Iacobo â Deo dilecto nasci voluit, Mal. 1. v. 3. Rom. 9. v. 13. quia erat ille ό άαπηος, in quo Deo complacuit, Matth. 3. v. 17.cap. 12. v. 18.

Ιαχωβ δέ ἐγέννησε όν Ιδαν σ άδελφς άυ. Quaeritur, cur mentio fiat fratrum Iudae, cùm in praecedentibus non fuerit mentio facta Ismaëlis, qui fuit frater Isaaci, nec Esavi, qui fuit frater Iacobi? Quidam respondent, causam esse eam, quòd promissio de Christo ad Iudam & fratres eius, non autem ad Ismaëlem & Esavum pertinuerit, quippe qui segregati erant â sancta familia Abrahae & Isaaci, in qua tunc inclusa erat Ecclesia. Atqui etiam ad Iudam astricta est promissio de Messia, ex ipsius posteritate nascituro, Gen. 49. v. 10. nec fuere Ismael & Esavus absolutè ab Ecclesia exclusi, quod asserere absoluto reprobationis decreto favet. Rectiùs dicitur, ideò mentionem fieri fratrum Iudae, quòd duodecim filii Iacobi fuerunt capita tribuum Israeliticarū, ex quibus unus populus Hebraeus, ex quo Christus expectabatur, constabat.

## 1:3
v. 3. Judas begot Phares and Zara. He expressed both, first because they were twins brought forth by one birth, then on account of the mystery, because they signify the Jewish and Gentile people. Of Thamar. Christ did not disdain to be born of sinful and Gentile women, because he became man precisely so that he might save sinners, and make Gentiles fellow-citizens of his kingdom and of the Israelite people. The Greek codices write this name through έσςωμ. *(so too the Ethiopian interpreter, who has )*, the Hebrew, Syrian and Latin through -n. *(& thus also the Arab)* Αςάμ. The Greek interpreters call him Aram, the Hebrew text Rom.

Latin:

v. 3. Iudas genuit Phares & Zara. Utrumq; expressit, tum quia fuere gemelli uno partu editi, tum propter mysterium, quia designant populum Iudaicum & gentilem. Ex Thamar. Non dedignatus est Christus ex mulieribus peccatricibus & gentilibus nasci, quia ideò homo natus est, ut peccatores salvos faceret, & gentiles regni sui, populiq; Israelitici confortes faceret. έσςωμ. Graeci Codd. hoc nomen scribunt perm. *(sic etiam interpres Aethiops, qui habet )* Hebraeus, Syrus & Latinus per-n. *(& ita quoq; Arabs)* Αςάμ. Graeci interpretes eum vocant Aram, Hebraeus textus Rom.

## 1:4
v. 4. Aminadab was Prince of the tribe of Judah at the going-out of Israel from Egypt, Lyranus reporting from the Hebrews. Naasson was chief of the tribe of Judah in the desert, Num. 1. v. 7., cap. 2. v. 3., cap. 7. v. 12. He willed himself to be born of the princes of the tribe of Judah, who is the lion of the tribe of Judah, Apoc. 5. v. 5.; for the lion is a figure of princely and royal dignity.

Latin:

v. 4. Aminadab fuit Princeps tribus Iuda in exitu Israel de Aegypto, referente ex Hebraeis Lyrano. Naasson fuit princeps tribus Iuda in deserto, Num. 1. v. 7.cap. 2. v. 3.cap. 7. v. 12. Ex principibus tribus Iuda nasci voluit, qui est leo de tribu Iuda,Apoc. 5. v. 5. leo enim figura est principalis & regiae dignitatis.

## 1:5
v. 5. Salmon begot Boaz of Rahab. Sanctes Pagninus in the new edition of the Scriptures struck out πςοσδιοςισμόν of Rahab, supported by no sound reasoning whatever and authority, when the Greek and Latin codices agree here *(indeed even the Eastern interpreters, the Syrian, Arab, Ethiopian)*. He says, this generation does not exist in the Sacred writings. Answer: 1. Why therefore do you reject in the following generation that word of Ruth, although nevertheless this generation is found in the sacred writings? 2. If that generation must be rejected for this reason, that it does not appear in the Scriptures, almost all those in the third fourteenth will have to be rejected. 3. Also the names Jannes and Jambres2. Tim. 3. v. 8. are to be deleted. Moreover, how Rahab bore the type of the Church gathered from the Gentiles, Chrysostom explains, Homily 5 on Repentance, Augustine on Psalm 86. Rahab was of Jericho, Ruth a Moabitess; He willed the Savior to be born from those women as a prelude of the calling of the Gentiles to participation in His kingdom. Yet Theophylact thinks that this Rahab is another woman besides Rahab of Jericho.

Latin:

v. 5. Salmon genuit Booz de Rahab. Sanctes Pagninus in nova editione Scripturarum πςοσδιοςισμόνde Rahab expunxit, nullâ planè ratione firmâ & autoritate subnixus, cùm Graeci & Latini Codd. *(quin & Interpp. Orient. Syrus, Arabs, Aethiops)* hic consentiant. Dicit, hanc generationem non extare in Sacris literis. Resp. 1. cur igitur reiicit in seq. generatione verbum illud ex Ruth, cùm tamen haec generatio inveniatur in sacris literis. 2. si generatio illa reiicienda propterea, quòd non extat in Scripturis, omnes fermè in tertia tesseradecde reiiciendae erunt. 3. etiam nomina Iannes & Mambres2. Tim. 3. v. 8. erunt expungenda. Coeterùm quomodo Rahab typum gesserit Ecclesiae ex gentilibus collectae, explicat Chrysost. hom. 5. de poenit. August. in Psal. 86.Rahab fuit Hierichuntina, Ruth Moabitis, ex illis nasci voluit Salvator in praeludium vocationis gen tium ad regni sui consortium. Theophyl. tamen putat, hanc Rahab esse aliam â Rahab Hierichuntina.

## 1:6
v. 6. David κατ άντονομασιαν έμφτιηην is twice called King, and indeed with the article. 1. because he first administered by God's command the kingdom of Israel. He is the first King from the tribe of Judah, through whom the order of descent runs down to Christ. Hugh on this passage: All the others were Kings in the second set of ten generations on account of David, because they descend from his royal stock. But He willed Him to be born of Kings, who was to be King of the whole world. Therefore by this title there is indicated a change of state among the people of God: for under David legitimate kingship began among the people of Israel. 2. because the Messiah had been promised specially to him, namely that he would restore his fallen kingdom and raise it up again, Is. 9. v. 7.Luc. 1. v. 32. 33. 3. because David was in a special way a type of Christ, whence the very name of David is given to the Messiah, Es. 55. v. 3.Ierem. 23. v. 5.Ezech 34. v. 23.chap. 37. v. 25. and the Messiah was commonly called by the most widespread title son of David,Matth. 22. v. 42.Ioh. 7. v. 42. etc. *(The epithet of King, which appears twice in the text, the Syrian omits in the latter place, with the Altdorf codex also agreeing: but the Arabic and Ethiopic acknowledge it together with the Greek text.)* It is asked at this point: How could it happen that between Salmon and David only three men should be counted, Boaz, Obed and Jesse, since it is established that between the entrance into the land of Canaan and the birth of David there intervened 366 years? Answer: it is not incredible that four men in that age, when life was longer-lived, equaled all that span. Furthermore it could come about that they received offspring not in youth or mature manhood, but already close to old age, which is clearly evident concerning Boaz from the History of Ruth. That the aged Boaz begot Obed is evident from Ruth. 3. v. 10. that Jesse was advanced in years when he begot David is evident from 1. Sam. 16. v. 11. nor is the genealogy always woven through firstborn sons, as is shown by the examples of -da, David, Solomon, etc.

Lyra and Bullinger hold that after Salmon there were three men of the same name Boaz, father, son and kinsman, who two former ones because of συνωνυμιαν were omitted, and only the third, who married Ruth, was named: but this harmonization is contradicted by what the Evangelist adds below, v. 17. πάσαι all or all the generations from Abraham until David are fourteen generations, which he does not repeat in the second decade-of-fourteen, in which three kings are omitted. Add that Ruth. 4. v. 18. 1. Paral. 2. v. 11. Luc. 3. v. 32. weave the genealogy in the same manner as here. Moreover, according to this hypothesis Boaz begot Obed not as father begets son, but as great-grandfather his great-great-grandson. But Lyra's opinion rests upon a false foundation, since he takes from Joseph, namely, that Boaz begot Obed from Ruth at the time of Eli the priest; whereas from the time of Joshua, in whose time Salmon took Rahab as wife, down to Eli intervened a period of almost three hundred years. But the hypothesis is false, that the History of Ruth occurred at the time of Eli the priest. The Hebrews more correctly hold that before the times of Eli Boaz begot Obed, and that he himself was one of the judges, called by another name Abesan.Ruth. 1. v. 1.

Ε'η της τού' Ον-ίον namely γεγονια her who had formerly been Uriah's, namely she who had formerly been his wife. It is a periphrasis for Bathsheba. *(Here there is a double ellipsis. 1. of the noun wife. 2. of the verb had been. The Syrian supplied the former, inserting his wife, Uriah's; the Arab the latter, adding 'was'.)* By this added λελονέιας, God's kindness is commended, in that on account of the adultery committed by David with Bathsheba, together with the murder joined to it, He did not merely withdraw the promise concerning the Messiah in any way, but even willed to continue through Solomon, born of Bathsheba, the line of descent of the promised Messiah. Justin Martyr in the questions and answers to the Orthodox, q. 78. f. 265.: God kindly honoring repentance placed the lineage of David in the offspring of Uriah's wife, and for the same reason made it so that Christ would take His origin from her. Some, such as Salmeron etc., add, that in this genealogy the Holy Spirit wished the name of Uriah expressed as a faithful and just servant of David, but suppressed in the case of Bathsheba on account of the mark of adultery. But it is more probable that Bathsheba was violated by force by the King; and above mention is made of Tamar, who enticed Judah her father-in-law into unlawful intercourse.

Latin:

v. 6. Davidκατ άντονομασιαν έμφτιηην bis vocatur Rex, & quidem cum articulo. 1. quia regnum Israeliticum primus Dei iussu administravit. Est primus Rex de tribu Iuda, per quem ordo generationis decurrit usq; ad Christum. Hugo in hunc locum: Reliqui omnes in secunda tesser adecade fuerunt Reges propter Davidem, quia ex regia eius stirpe descendunt. Ex Regibus autem nasci voluit, qui futurus erat Rex universi orbis. Indigitatur igitur hâc appellatione mutatio statûs publici in populo Dei: sub Davide enim caepit legitimum regnum in populo Israelitīco. 2. quia illi peculiariter promissus erat Messias, quòd sit collapsum eius regnum restituturus & iterum erecturus, Es. 9. v. 7.Luc. 1. v. 32. 33. 3. quia David fuit peculiari ratione Christi typus, unde ipsum Davidis nomen Messiae tribuitur, Es. 55. v. 3.Ierem. 23. v. 5.Ezech 34. v. 23.cap. 37. v. 25. ac Messias vulgatissima appellatione vocabatur filius David,Matth. 22. v. 42.Ioh. 7. v. 42. &c. *(Epitheton Regis, quod bisin textu legitur, posterioriloco omittit Syrus, consentiente quoq; Cod. Altdorffino: sed agnoscunt cum Graeco textu Arabs & Aethiops.)* Quaeritur hoc loco: Qui fieri possit, ut inter Salmonem & Davidem non nisi tres viri, Booz, Obed & Iesse numerentur, cùm constet, inter introitum in terram Canaan, & nativitatem Davidis annos 366. intercessisse? Resp. non est incredibile, quatuor homines illo aevo, quo vita erat diuturnior, totum illud spacium aequasse. Fieri insuper potuit, ut prolem non in iuventute vel virili aetate susceperint, sed senectuti iam proximi, quod de Booz ex Historia Ruth manifestè constat. Quod Booz senex generaverit Obed, constat ex Ruth. 3. v. 10. quod Isai grandaevus fuerit, quando genuit Davidem, constat ex 1. Sam. 16. v. 11. neq; genealogia semper texitur per primogenitos, ut constat exemplis -dae, Davidis, Salomonis, &c.

Lyranus & Bullingerus statuunt, post Salmonem tres Booz eius dem nominis fuisse, patrem, filium & -epotem, qui duo priores propterσυνωνυμιανfuerint omissi ac tertius tantum, qui Rutham duxerit, nominatus: sed huic conciliationi repugnat, quod v. 17. subdit Evangelista. πάσαιomnes sive universae generationes ab Abrahamo usad Davidem generationes 14. quod in secunda tesseradecade, in qua tres Reges omissi, non repetit. Adde, quod Ruth. 4. v. 18. 1. Paral. 2. v. 11. Luc. 3. v. 32. eodem modo, quo hoc loco texitur genealogia. Praeterea iuxta hanc hypothesin Booz genuisset Obed, non ut pater filium, sed ut proavus pronepotem. Sed Lyrani sententia nititur falso fundamento, quod accipit â Iosepho, videl. Booz genuisse Obed ex Ruth, tempore Heli Sacerdotis, â tempore autem Iosuae, cuius tempore Salmon Rahab duxit uxorem, usq; ad Heli intercessit tempus ferè trecentorum annorum. At falsa est hypothesis, tempore Heli sacerdotis Historiam Ruth contigisse. Hebraei rectiùs statuunt, ante tempora Heli Booz genuisse Obed, ac ipsum fuisse unum ex iudicibus, alio nomine dictum Abesan.Ruth. 1. v. 1.

Ε'η της τού' Ον-ίον sc. γεγονιαex ea, quae Uriae, sc. uxor olim-fuerat. Periphrasis est Bethsabeë. *(Duplex hîc ellipsis. 1. nominis uxor. 2. verbi fuerat. Priorem supplevit Syrus, inserendo uxore eius, Uriae; posteriorem Arabs, addendo fuit.)* Commendatur hoc λελονέιας, adiecto Dei benignitas, quod propter Davidis adulterium cum Bethsabeë commissum, eiq; coniunctum homicidium non solùm promissionem de Messia minimè revocaverit, sed etiam per Salomonem ex Bethsabea susceptum lineam nativitatis promissi Messiae continuare voluerit. Iustin. Martyr in qq. & resp. ad Orthod. q. 78. f. 265. Deus benignè poenitentiam honorans, in uxoris Uriae progeniem collocavit genus Davidis, eademde causa fecit, ut ex eâ Christus ortum duceret. Quidam uti Salmero &c. addunt, quòd Uriae ut fidelis & iusti sorvi Davidis nomē Spiritus S. in hac genealogia voluerit expressum, Bethsabeae verò ob adulte-ii notam suppressum. Sed verisimilius est Bethsabeam pervim â Rege fuisse raptam, ac superius mentio fit Thamaris, quae Iudam socerum ad illicitum concubitum pellexit.

## 1:8
v. 8. Joram is said to have begotten Uzziah. But it is established from 2. Reg. 14. v. 1. 8. v. 29. 2. 3. 11. 22. 11. 2. 25. 23.)

ch. 11. v. 2.Ch. 12. v. 27. 2. Paral. 3. v. 11. ch. 22. v. 11. Joram was not the father, but the great-great-grandfather of Uzziah, and Uzziah was not the son, but the great-great-grandson of Joram; therefore Joram begot Uzziah not immediately but through Ahaziah his son intervening, (also called Jehoahaz 2. Paral. 25. v. 23.) Joash grandson, Amaziah great-grandson.

It is asked therefore, why those three Kings Ochozias, Joash and Amaziah were omitted in the genealogy of Christ? 1. Some in Abulensis q. 17. Likewise Wolfgangus Musculus *(so also decides Gaspar Sanctius on the book 4. Reg. ch. 14. v. 18.)* think that this was done through the carelessness of copyists, who, having slipped immediately from reading the word Joram to Uzziah, either read Uzziah instead of Ochozias, and misled by the similarity of the names Ochozias and Ozias fell down from him to Jotham. But the tessaradecad would not be consistent for itself if those three were added *(And moreover let it be noted, that the Greek Codices unanimously so read, to which also testify the Syrian, Arabian, Ethiopian versions.)*

2. Some, as Hilary can. 1. in Matth. &c. Maldonatus, attribute the cause of this omission to the idolatrous marriage of Joram. For because Joram had mingled himself with the blood of Jezebel by taking her daughter Athaliah, God, by His just judgment, according to the tenor of His threat 1. Reg. 21. v. 21., had so avenged that crime unto the third and fourth generation, that the curse of the daughter of Ahab (Athaliah) was as great as the blessing of Jehu was on account of the destruction of the house of Ahab. 2. Reg. 10. v. 30. The mother of Ahaziah was Athaliah, the daughter of Ahab, 2 Reg. 8. v. 18. chap. 11. v. 1. hence it is said of him in 2. Paral. 22. v. 3. that he walked in the ways of the house of Ahab. Those ways were such that they were not only idolaters, but also shed the blood of the faithful.

3. Some, as Rupertus lib. 5. in Matth., maintain that because of impiety, especially because they did not allow the Prophets to propose their prophecies concerning the Messiah (for Joash killed Zechariah the son of Jehoiada 2. Paral. 24. v. 22. & chap. 25. v. 16. Amaziah, insulting the divine prophet, replied: Art thou made of the King's counsel? forbear, why shouldest thou be smitten?), these three Kings of the promised seed were excluded, and on the contrary, three sinful women of foreign birth, Tamar, Rahab, and Ruth, were inserted into the genealogy.

4. Some respond, that Matthew proposes not a genealogy of blood properly so called, but only a genealogy in succession with respect to inheritance and kingdom, which nevertheless he does not treat with an exact reckoning of generations, judging it sufficient that in a matter then manifest to all he should show by three tessaradecads that Christ descended from Abraham and David. Therefore, in order that this second tessaradecad might hold together for itself, those three Kings were omitted.

5. There is a twofold end of the Biblical genealogies, immediate or proximate, and mediate or ultimate. The proximate end was that the continuation of the Davidic kingdom might be set forth in the Church of GOD. For it had been foretold concerning the Messiah that he would be heir of the Davidic kingdom, its restorer and eternal preserver. The ultimate end was that it might be shown from this continuation of the Davidic kingdom that the succession of the kingdom finally came to Christ. The former end belongs to the genealogy described in 1 Chron. 3; the latter is especially intended by Matthew, who, because he hastened toward that goal and ultimate end, omitted those three Kings. Ezra, book 1, chapter 7, verse 1, recounting the catalogue of the high Priests, omits six who are enumerated in 1 Chron. 6, verse 3. Therefore it is not foreign to the custom of the Scriptures that some persons be omitted in genealogies.

Latin:

v. 8. Ioram dicitur genuisse Oziam. At constat ex2. Reg. 14. v. l. 8. v. 29.

cap. 11. v. 2.Cap. 12. v. 27. 2. Paral. 3. v. 11. cap. 22. v. 11. Ioramum non fuisse patrem, sed abavum Oziae, ac Oziam non fuisse filium, sed abnepotem Iorami, genuit ergo Ioram Oziam non immediatè sed mediante Ochozia filio, (etiam Iechoachazo dicto 2. Paral. 25. v. 23.) Ioa nepote, Amasia pronepote.

Quaeritur proinde, quare hi tres Reges Ochozias, Ioas & Amasias in genealogia Christi fuerint omissi? 1. Quidam apud Abulens. q. 17. It. Ivolffg. Musculus *(ita quoq; statuit Caspar Sanchez in lib. 4. Reg. c. 14. v. 18.)* existimant, librariorum incuriâ id esse factum, qui â lectione vocis Ioram statim ad Oziam delapsi, vel pro Ochozia legerint Oziam, ac ab illo ad Ioatham similitudine nominum Ochoziae & Oziae seducti prolapsi sint. Sed tesseradecas sibi non constaret, si tres illi adderentur *(Ac notandum insuper, quòd unanimi consensu Codd. Graeci ita legant, quibus etiam adstipulantur Syrus, Arabs, Aethiops.)*

2. Quidam. ut Hilarius can. 1. in Matth. &c. Maldon causam huius omissionis tribuunt idololatrico Iorami coniugio. Propterea enim quod Ioram sangvini Iezabel ducendo siliam eius Athaliam se admiscuerat, Deum iusto suo iudicio secundum tenorem comminationis suae 1. Reg. 21. v. 21. scelus illud in tertiam & quartam generationem ita fuisse ultum, ut tanta filiae Achabi (Athaliae) fuerit maledictio, quanta propter deletionem domus Achabi Iehu erat benedictio. 2. Reg. 10. v. 30. Mater Achasiae fuit Athalia Achabi filia, 2 Reg. 8. v. 18.cap. 11. v. 1. inde de ipso dicitur 2. Paral. 22. v. 3. quod ingressus fuerit per vias domûs Achab. Viae illae erantut non modo essent idololatrae, sed etiam sangvinem fidelium funderent.

3. Quidam ut Rupertus lib. 5. in Matth. propter impietaetem, cumprimis quod non concesserint Prophetis sua de Messia vaticinia proponere (Ioas enim occidit Zachariam filium Ioiadae 2. Paral. 24. v. 22. & cap. 25. v. 16. Amasias vati divino insultans respondit: Num Consiliarius Regis es? quiesce, ne interficiam te) tres Reges seminis promissi domesticos exclusos fuisse statuunt, ac contrà tres foeminas peccatrices alienigenas Thamar Rahab & Ruth genealogiae insertas.

4. Quidam respondent, Matthaeum non genealogiam sangvinis propriè sic dictam, sed tantùm genealogiam in successione quoad hereditatem & regnum proponere, quam tamen exactâ generationum supputatione non pertractet, satis esse iudicans, si in re tum omnibus manifesta per tres tesser adecadas ostenderet, Christum ex Abrahamo & Davide descendisse. Ut ergo secunda haec tesseradecas sibi constaret, tres ill-s Reges omissos esse.

5. Duplex est finis genealogiarum Biblicarum, immediatus sive proximus, & mediatus sive ultimus. Finis proximus fuit, ut regni Davidici continuatio proponeretur in Ecclesia DEI. De Messia enim praedictum erat, quod regni Davidici haeres, instaurator & conservator aeternus sit futurus. Ultimus, ut ostenderetur ex hac regni Davidici continuatione, successionem regni tandem ad Christum pervenisse. Prior finis competit genealogiae. 1. Paral. 3. descriptae; posterior â Matthaeo praecipue intenditur, qui quia ad scopum & finem illum ultimum properavit, tres illos Reges omisit. Esdras lib. 1. cap. 7. v. 1. catalogum summorum Sacerdotum recensens, sex omittit, qui 1. Paral. 6. v. 3. recensentur. Ergo â consvetudine Scripturarum alienum non est, quosdam in genealogiis omitti.

## 1:11
v. 11. Josiah begot Jeconiah. Jakim the son of Josiah, father of Jeconiah, is omitted, whom certain manuscripts count among them, reading thus: Jehoiakim begot Jakim, Jakim begot Jechoniah. Which reading Robert Estienne restored, bears witness. 1. the genealogy 1 Chron. 3, v. 17. 2. very ancient codices, whose authority Erasmus Rhenanus [Faber Stapulensis] and Bucer attest. 3. The second group of fourteen seems altogether to require the same reading, since it ends at Jakim, while the third begins from Jeconiah. 4. Jerome on chapter 1 of Matthew likewise holds that it should be read so. In the Gospel, he says, according to Matthew one generation appears to be lacking in the later place, because the second tetrad ends at Joakim the son of Josiah, and the third begins from Jachim the son of Joakim etc. Epiphanius also, book 1 against heresies, heresy 8, writes: Jakim the father of Jeconiah has been omitted through the fault of copyists, because the Greeks and Latins held Jeconiah or Jehoiachin (as he is called 2 Chron. 36, v. 9, and 2 Sam. 24, v. 6) together with his son, and Joakim the father, on account of the similarity of their names, as one person. Lest therefore the same name be repeated twice according to their opinion, the other must be supplied.

Against which Chrysostom, or whosoever; the Author of the imperfect work on Matthew, homily 1, and Augustine book 2 On the Consensus of the Gospels chapter 4 hold that the name of Joakim was purposely omitted by the Evangelist, just as in verse 8. the names of Ochozias, Joas and Amasias. 1. because Joakim or Jakim became king not by divine appointment, but by the power of the king of Egypt he was constituted. 2. because through the Babylonian migration a defection from him took place among foreign nations. And so that the fourteenfold division may stand consistent, they hold that one Jeconiah was numbered twice , once before the migration and once after: before it while he lived as King among kings, after it while he lived as a private person among private persons. But the first response is simpler and safer. (Yet I cannot dissemble that the Syrian also, and the Arabic and the Ethiopic, here lack Jakim.) Euthymius judges that by Jeconiah is meant in this passage Joachaz, son of Josias, who at 3. Esdras 1. v. 34. is called Jeconias. Yet 1. the Greek copy there, in place of Iechonia (which stands in the Latin codices), writes Ιωάχαε.; 2. nor did Joachaz beget Jeconiah, but Joakim. 2. Reg. 24. v. 5. 6. 1. Paral. 3. v. 16. 17. 3. Esdras 1. v. 43.

The question arises here. 1. How is Josias said to have begotten Jeconiah and his brothers, whereas Jeconiah lacked brothers, both those born of the same parents and those born of the same mother?

Ans. Some respond quite plainly, even though no mention is made of Jeconiah's brothers in the Scriptures, still it must not be doubted that he had brothers, since in historical questions we cannot draw negative conclusions from the Scriptures. Others say that this Jeconiah was Eliakim or Joakim, whose brothers were Joachaz 2. Reg. 23. v. 30. and Mathanias 2. Reg. 24. v. 17. renamed Zidkias by the king of Babylon, and because they themselves also reigned, Joachaz before Joakim, and Zidkias after Jeconiah the son of Joakim, therefore the Evangelist made mention of them. But Jeconias was not Joakim, but the son of Joakim. This therefore must be held. Josias begot four sons. 1. Joachaz or Johannas. 2. Eliakim or Joakim. 3. Mathanias or Zidkias. 4. Sallum. 1. Paral. 3. v. 15. Joachaz indeed was substituted in the place of his father Josias now deceased and was constituted King, but after three months he was carried off captive into Egypt by Pharaoh, and his own brother Eliakim or Joakim was placed over the kingdom in his stead 2. Reg. 23. v. 31. In turn, upon him likewise, as a notorious despiser of God, having been dragged into the Babylonian captivity and dying miserably, his son Jeconias or Joachin succeeded in the kingdom. 2 Kings 24. v. 8. But since this Jeconiah too, grandson of Josiah, son of Jehoiakim, was brought under the power of the Chaldeans on account of his impiety and was held captive more than 37 years, he left behind Zedekiah his uncle, king descended from Solomon, the last successor of the kingdom; who nevertheless, being captured by Nebuchadnezzar in the eleventh year of his rule, carried off into Babylonia, died there most wretchedly. Therefore Josiah begot his nephew Jeconiah through his father Jakim or Jehoiakim, because he begot Jakim, and Jakim begot Jeconiah. He also begot the paternal uncles of Jeconiah, Jakim's own brothers , namely Joahaz or Johanna, Shallum, and Mattaniah or Zedekiah, who was substituted in the kingdom in place of Jeconiah [-son of] Jakim. 2 Kings 24. v. 27. On account of which ground of succession Zedekiah, brother of Jakim, according to the usage of the Hebrews, is called his son, yet brother of Jeconiah, 2 Chron. 36. v. 10.; although he was his paternal uncle, or father's brother, 1 Chron. 3. v. 16. 17. For by the term brethren all kinsfolk connected by blood are wont to be called among the Hebrews by idiomatic usage, Gen. 13. v. 8. ch. 20. v. 21. ch. 22. v. 15. Certain copies read Ιωαηημ. for Ιεχονίω

Q. 2. In what way does Matthew say that Josiah begot his sons in the Babylonian captivity, seeing that he died eight years before the captivity of the son of Jehoiakim (mention of which is made Dan. 1. v. 1.) years before Jeconiah was taken 11. and years before the deportation moreover of Zedekiah 22. did he pass away? 2 Kings 23. Ans. Matthew makes mention of the captivity, not that Josiah begot his sons in it—for this conflicts with History—but that the posterity of Josiah was led away into it, so that by this means he might set before our eyes the adverse fortune of the best of parents in children and grandchildren, and intimate the change of the royal state. For the sake of reconciliation therefore. 1. Some reply that the preposition in is to be expounded as around, Gen. 2. v. 2. Exod. 12. v. 15. έπί της μετοικεσίας in the migration, i.e. about the time of the migration. Syr. under exile, just as is placed for or

2. Some hold that the sons of Josiah are said to have been born in the captivity because they were born with God foreseeing it and the captivity already imminent.

3. Some say that some word is here to be supplied in this manner: his brethren, who lived at the time of the Babylonish captivity. 4. It is answered most simply, that the words έπί της μετοικεσίας are not to be referred to the verb ἐγέννησε, but to the children of Josiah whom he begot, into whose times that deportation fell in successive turns. *(so that there is an ellipsis, and the expression is taken as standing for τούς έπί της etc.)* For it began under Jakim or Jehoiakim, grew under Jeconiah his son, 2 Kings 8. and was completed under Zedekiah. 2 Kings 25. v. 7. and following verses. Dan. 9. v. 2. Joseph. book 10. antiquities ch. 8. 9. & 11.

Μετοιηεστα is used for μετσιηισμός when otherwise μετοιηέιν signifies to be an inhabitant, which does not fit this passage; μετσιηισμός is the very transportation of the captives. But when the Evangelist calls the Babylonian captivity μετοικεσίαν or μετσιηισμόν a removal of dwelling, he then softens the harshness of the thing by the mildness of the word, for μετονηεσία also suits those who change their dwelling of their own accord. Salmerón rejects this, laying down that the Evangelist spoke rather thus, so as to show that the Hebrews were led away to Babylon not so much as exiles and captives, but as inhabitants and foreigners, whom the King of the Chaldeans had known to be warlike and intolerant of foreign rule, and on that account had transferred into his own land. And yet although Jeconiah went to Babylon voluntarily with the people, nevertheless Joakim was led away to Babylon bound with two chains, and Sedecias likewise was carried there captive. On account of the promised return, the term μετοικεσίας could more rightly be said to be borrowed.

Some however distinguish between μετοικεσίαν and captivity. Jeconiah surrendered himself and departed into Babylonia with several thousand Jews; they think that that migration of Jeconiah is properly called μετοιη-σίαν,; after eleven years had elapsed from that time followed the captivity of Zedekiah and the devastation of the whole city 2. Reg. 24. this they think is properly called άιχμαλωσίαν captivity.

But it is more probable that the Evangelist here comprehends at once all three of those deportations, which succeeded one another mutually and grew step by step.

Latin:

v. 11. Iosias genuit Iechoniam. Omittitur Iakim Iosiae filius, Iechoniae pater, quem nonnulli Codices annumerant, legentes hoc modo: Iostas genuit Iakim, Iakim genuit Iec boniam. Quam lectionem Robertus Stephanus restituit, --i fidem facit. 1. genealogia 1. Paral. 3. v. 17. 2. Codices vetustissimi, quorum fidem faciunt Stapulensis & Bucerus. 3. Eandem lectionem omninò requirere videtur tesseradecas secunda, quae in Iakimo finitur, cùm tertia incipiat â Iechonia. 4. Hieron. in cap. 1. Matth. & in cap. 1. Danielis itidem statuit sic legendum. In Evangelio, inquit, loco posteriore secundum Matthaeum videtur una deesse generatio, quia secunda -esseradecas in Ioakim definit filio losiae, & terriaincipit â l-achim filio Ioacim &c. Epiphanius quoq; lib. 1. contra haereses haeres. 8. scribit. Iakim Iechoniae patrem vitio librariorum esse omissum, propterea quòd Graeci & Latini Iechoniam seu Ioachim (ut vocatur 2. Paral. 36. v. 9. & 2. Reg. 24. v. 6.) filium & Ioakim patrem propter nominum convenientiam pruno habuerint. Ne ergo ex illorum sententia idem nomen bis repeteretur, alterum esse exp---um.

Contrà Chrysostomus vel quicun-; Autor oper. imperf. in Matth. homil. 1. & Augustinus lib. 2. de cons. Evang. cap. 4. statuunt, nomen Ioakim ab Evangelista studio esse omissum, perinde ut in v. 8. nomina Ochoziae, Ioae & Amasiae 1. quia Ioakim sive Iakim non ordinatione divinâ, sed potentia Regis Aegyptiaci Rex sue-it consti-utus. 2. quia per Babylonicam transmigrationem ab eo in extraneas gentes facta fuerit deflexio. Ut ergo tesseradecas sibi constet, statuunt, unum Iechoniam bis numeratum fu-sse, semel ante transmigrationem, & semel post: ante eam cùm Rex fuit inter Reges, post eam cum privatus inter privates vixit. Sed prior responsio est simplicior ac tutior. *(dissimulare tamen non possum, Syrum quoq; Arabem & Aethiopem Iakimum hic ignorare)* Euthymius existimat, per Iechoniam intelligi hoc loco Ioachaez, Iosiae filium, qui 3. Esdrae. 1. v. 34. vocatur Iechonias. Atqui 1. exemplar Graecum ibi pro Iechonia (qui est in Latinis Codd.) scribit Ιωάχαε. 2. nec Ioachaz, sed Ioiakim genuit Iechoniam. 2. Reg. 24. v. 5. 6. 1. Paral. 3. v. 16. 17. 3. Esdrae 1. v. 43.

Quaeritur hoc loco. 1. Quomodo Iosias dicatur genuisse Iechoniam & fratres eius, cùm Iechonias fratribus tum germanis, tum uterinis caruerit?

Resp. Quidam simpliciter respondent, quamvis fratrum Iechoniae non fiat in Scripturis mentio, tamen non dubit andum esse, ipsum habuisse fratres, cùm in quaestionibus Historicis non posimus negativè ex Scripturis concludere. Quidam Iechoniam hunc dicunt fuisse Esiakim sive Ioakim, cuius fratres fuere Ioachaz2. Reg. 23. v. 30. & Matthanias2. Reg. 24. v. 17. â Rege Babylonis Zidkias nominatus, qui quia & ipsi regnarunt, Ioachaz ante Ioiakim, Sedekias post filium Ioiakimi Iechoniam, idcircò eorum ab Evangelista factam esse mentionem. Sed Iechonias non fuit Ioiakim, verùm Ioiakimi filius. Sic ergo habendum. Iosias genuit quatuor filios. 1. Ioachaz sive Iohannam. 2. Eliakim seu Ioiakim. 3. Matthaniam seu Zidkiiam. 4. Sallum. 1. Paral. 3. v. 15. Ioachaz surrogatus quidem fuit in locum patris Iosiae defuncti & Rex constitutus, sed post tres menses â Pharaone in Aegyptum captivus fuit abductus, ac frater ipsius Elia kim sive Ioiakim in regno ei substitutus 2. Reg. 23. v. 31. illi itidem tanquā insigni Dei contemtori in Babylonicam captivitatem adducto & miserè mortuo successit in regno filius Iechonias seu Ioachen. 2. Reg. 24. v. 8. Cùm verò & hic Iechonias Iosiae nepos, Ioiakimi filius, in Chaldaeorum potestatem propter impietatem redigeretur ac ultra annos 37. captivus teneretur, Zidkiiam patruum suum Regem ê Salomone ultimum successorem regni reliquit, qui tamen anno regiminis undecimo â Nabuchodonosore captus, in Babyloniam translatus, ibiq; miserè mortuus est. Iosias igitur tanquam avus nepotem Iechoniam mediante patre eius Iakimo vel Ioiakimo genuit, quia genuit Iakimum, Iakimus verò Iechoniam. Genuit etiam patruos Iechoniae, Iakimi sefratres, videlicet Ioachaz sive Iohannam, Sallum & Matthaniam sive Zidkiiam, qui pro Iechonia Iakimo fuit suffectus in regno. 2. Reg. 24. v. 27. ob quam successionis rationem Zidkias frater Iakimi, ex Hebraeorum consvetudine eiusdem filius, Iechoniae verò frater dicitur, 2. Paral. 36. v. 10. cuius tamen erat patruus, sive parentis frater, 1. Paral. 3. v. 16. 17. Fratrum enim appellatione propinqui omnes & sangvine iuncti Hebraeorum idiotismo vocari solent Gen. 13. v. 8. cap. 20. v. 21. cap. 22. v. 15. Quidam Codices pro Ιεχονίω legunt Ιωαηημ.

Q. 2. Quomodo Matthaeus dicat, Iosiam filios suos in captivitate Babylonica genuisse, cùm octennio ante Ioiakimi filii captivitatem (cuius Dan. 1. v. 1. fit mentio) ante captum Iechoniam annis. 11. ante Zedekiae verò transportationem annis 22. interierit?2. Reg. 23. Resp. Matthaeus captivitatis mentionem facit, non quòd in ea Iosias filios suos genuerit, hoc enim repugnat Historiae, sed quòd posteritas Iosiae in eam fuerit abducta, ut hac ratione optimi parentis fortunam adversam in liberis & nepotibus ante oculos poneret & mutationem regii status insinuaret. Conciliationis igitur causâ. 1. quidam respondent, praepositionem in exponendam esse per ante,Gen. 2. v. 2.Exod. 12. v. 15.έπί της μετοικεσίαςin transmigratione i. e. circa tempus transmigrationis. Syr. sub exilium, ut positum sit pro sive

2. Quidam statuunt, Iosiae filios propterea dici in captivitate natos, quia praescio DEO & iam imminente captivitate nati sint.

3. Quidam dicunt, subintelligendum verbum aliquod hocmodo, fratres eius, qui fuerunt sub tempus Babylonicae captivitatis. 4. Simplicissimè respondetur, verba έπί της μετοικεσίας non esse referenda ad verbum ἐγέννησε, sed ad liberos Iosiae, quos genuit, in quorum tempora deportatio illa trib. vicibus incidit. *(ita ut sit ellipsis, dictumq; statuatur pro τούς έπί της &c.)* Coepta est enim sub Iakimo sive Ioiakimo, aucta sub Iechonia eius filio, 2. Reg. 8. & sub Zedekia consummata. 2. Reg. 25. v. 7. & seqq. Dan. 9. v. 2. Ioseph. lib. 10. antiq. cap. 8. 9. & 11.

Μετοιηεστα ponitur pro μετσιηισμός cùm alioqui μετοιηέιν significet incolam esse, quod huic loco non convenit, μετσιηισμός est ipsa captivorum transportatio. Quando autem Evangelista captivitatem Babylonicam vocat μετοικεσίαν sive μετσιηισμόν domicilii translationem, tum rei acerbitatem verbi lenitate temperat, μετονηεσία enim etiam illis convenit, qui suâ sponte domicilium mutant. Salmero hoc repudiat, statuens, Evangelistam potiùs sic locutum, ut ostenderet, Hebraeos non perinde ut exules & captivos in Babylonem abductos, sed ut incolas & peregrinos, quos ut bellicosos & imperii alieni impatientes Rex Chaldaeorum cognoverat, & idcircò in regionem suam transtulerat. Sed enim quamvis Iechonias cum populo spontè in Babylonem abierit, tamen Ioakim catenis duabus vinctus in Babylonem est abductus, Sedecias itidem captivus eo abductus est. Propter promissam reductionem posset rectiùs dici usurpatum μετοικεσίας vocabulum.

Quidam tamen inter μετοικεσίαν & captivitatem distinguunt. Iechonias deditione factâ cum aliquot millibus Iudaeorum in Babyloniam abiit, illam Iechoniae translationem existimant propriè vocari μετοιη-σίαν, post exactos inde annos undecim secuta est captivitas Zedekiae & totius urbis devastatio 2. Reg. 24. hanc propriè vocari putant άιχμαλωσίανcaptivitatem.

Sed verisimilius est, Evangelistam simul tres illas abductiones, quae mutuò se consecutae sunt, ac gradatim creverunt, hoc loco comprehendere.

## 1:12
v. 12. Μετά σέ την μετοικεσίαν. This must not be understood of the time following upon the release of the Babylonian captivity, because Jeconiah, abducted to Babylon in the nineteenth year of his age, begot Shealtiel during the very Babylonian exile itself. But it must be taken of the time following upon the Babylonian migration, so that the sense is: after they had been carried off into the Babylonian captivity.

Ιεχονίας ἐγέννησε τον ηαλασθιηλ. It is asked. 1. whether this Jeconiah is the same as him whose mention was made in the preceding verse? Ambrose on Luke, Jerome at the beginning of Daniel and Matthew deny it: for they think that this Jeconiah was not the son of Josiah but his grandson. And indeed they judge rightly that the Jeconiah mentioned in this verse is the grandson of King Josiah, but from this they less correctly infer that he is distinct from him whose mention is made in the preceding verse; for we showed above, in the preceding verse, according to the most approved codices, that it should be read Ιωσίας ἐγέννησε τόν Ιωαηείμ, Ιωαηείμ σέ ἐγέννησε τόν ίέχονίαν. 1. If the Jeconiah were the same everywhere, either the second or third tessardecad would not be completed. 2. The name of Jeconiah the prince is written at the end through , the name of Jeconiah the son through 2 Kings 24. which difference neither the Greek nor the Latin interpreter observed.

Q. 2. How is Jeconiah said to have begotten Shealtiel, when from Jeremiah ch. 22, verse 30, it might seem able to be gathered that Jeconiah died without children? Answer: certainly some concede that Jeconiah died without children. Therefore what is here said—that he begot Shealtiel—they explain thus: that he had him as successor to the kingdom. Indeed it is rightly said that Shealtiel is called the son of Jeconiah because he was his successor in the kingdom. But it is less correctly established that Jeconiah plainly departed άτεηνον childless; for he could have had sons, none of whom nevertheless succeeded in the kingdom. In Jeremiah it is not denied that there was seed or a son of Jeconiah, but a successor in the kingdom from among the sons is denied. Childlessness is altogether twofold: of offspring and of succession; the Prophet speaks of the latter, not of the former.

Q. 3. How is Jechonias said to have begotten Salathiel, when 1. Paral. 3. v. 16. it is said that the son of Jechonias was Asir, not Salathiel? Resp. Asir there is not a proper name, but an appellative, which signifies bound, so that the sense is: the sons of Jechonias, however, were bound or carried away captive into Babylon. 2. Reg. 24. v. 17. Salathiel is expressly called the son of Jechonias.

Q. 4. Whether one the same Shealtiel is understood in this place and in Luke 3, ver. 27

Answer: so some establish, presupposing that Shealtiel, or what is the same, Salathiel, who succeeded Jeconiah in the kingdom, was the natural son of Jeconiah, which they confirm from the Chronicle of the Jews, Seder Olam.

But we warned a little before that there are two kinds of childlessness, childlessness of offspring and of succession. Childlessness of offspring is, when someone entirely lacks children. Childlessness of succession, when someone indeed has sons, but none of whom succeeds his father in royal dignity. Judg. 9. v. 8. We grant that Jeconiah had natural sons, and therefore was not wholly bereft of offspring. But those sons of Jeconiah did not succeed in the kingdom, rather they lived as private men: we deny therefore that Jeconiah had any one of his sons as successor to the kingdom, and that one and the same Shealtiel is described by Matthew and Luke. God himself testifies Jerem. 22. v. 24.Ezek. 36. v. 30. that no one sprung from the blood of Jeconiah will ever possess the throne of David. It follows therefore that Shealtiel and Zerubbabel were not descended from the blood of Jeconiah, since it clearly stands established that Zerubbabel sat on the throne of David and reigned as prince in Judah.

Therefore when Matthew says, Jeconiah begot Shealtiel, either he does not understand the Shealtiel described by Luke, but a natural son of Jeconiah, if he had one, who led merely a private life, excluded from succession to the King's throne; or if he designates this man, from whom Zerubbabel the Prince was born, he constituted him a son of Jeconiah for no other reason than because he succeeded him in the kingdom, which succession seemed otherwise due to another natural son. For it is known from Luke that Shealtiel, the father of Zerubbabel, was the natural son not of Jeconiah, but of Neri, sprung from the stock of Nathan. Therefore Jeconiah is said to have begotten, that is, according to the phrase of Scripture, that he procured for himself an heir and successor of the kingdom Shealtiel.

Q 5. How can Shealtiel be said to have begotten Zorobabel, since, 1. Chron. 3. v. 19. Pedaiah is called the son of Shealtiel? For verse 18 reads thus. Melchiram, Phedaiah, Sheneazar and Jecamiah, Sama and Nadabiah, the Hebrews supply, were the sons of Shealtiel. Answer. Shealtiel begat Zerubbabel not immediately, but through Pedaiah intervening, for Pedaiah was the son of Shealtiel, and Zerubbabel the son of Pedaiah; therefore, since Shealtiel begat Pedaiah, from whom Zerubbabel was born, hence also Zerubbabel can be said to have been begotten by him. Zorobabel is also called in other places of Scripture son of Salathiel. 1 Esdr. ch. 3, v. 2 and 8; 2 Book of Esdras, chapter 7, v. 7; 3 Book of Esdras, chapter 5, v. 48, chapter 6, v. 2; Hag. 1, v. 1 and 12. Therefore just as Esdras and Aggaeus called Zorobabel the son of Salathiel, omitting Pedaiah, so Matthew used their example by the same right.

Question 6. Why did Matthew pass over Pedaiah in this genealogy? Answer. 1. So that the fourteenth group might be kept intact. 2. Because nothing noteworthy about him is recorded, except that mention of him is made in the place cited above. 3. In the times of the Evangelists the succession of the family of David was still known not only publicly but also had been committed to certain volumes already from the time of David onward. 4. The grandson of Zerobabel was perhaps brought up by his grandfather Sealthiel, and therefore was enrolled as a son under his grandfather. 5. Here the Evangelist follows Esdras, book 1, chapter 3, v. 2, 8, and Haggaeus, chapter 1, v. 1 and 12. In Zorobabel both lines agree, having previously descended through different sons of David. After Zorobabel the lines again diverge, but come together again in Matthan. Some, however, among whom is Andreas Osiander, posit two Zorobabels, as well as two Sealthiels.

Zerubabel is said to be named from , which means to alienate among the Hebrews and Chaldaeans, and because he alienated or led away the Judaeans from Babel. For since he was born of royal blood, namely great-grandson of Iechonias, he was appointed Leader of the Judaeans returning from the Babylonian exile into Judea, their fatherland, by the grant of Cyrus, although he was still quite young, 1 Esdr. ch. 2, v. 2. The same man after the death of Cyrus obtained from King Darius permission to finish the building of the temple begun under Cyrus but interrupted by the envy of the neighboring peoples, and to promote this undertaking he returned to his native land in the second year of Cyrus with many Jewish exiles and completed the construction of the sacred edifice, 1 Esdr. ch. 5, v. 1 and following; Josephus, book 11, Antiquities, chapter 4.

Latin:

v. 12. Μετά σέ την μετοικεσίαν. Hoc non intelligendum de tempore, solutionem captivitatis Babylonicae insecuto, quia Iechonias anno aetatis 19. in Babylonem abductus in ipso exilio Babylonico genuit Sealthiel. Sed accipiendum de tempore, transmigrationem Babylonicam insecuto, ut sit sensus, postquam abducti essent in Babylonicam captivitatem.

Ιεχονίας ἐγέννησε τον ηαλασθιηλ. Quaeritur. 1. an hic Iechonias idem sit cum eo, cuius in versic. praeced. facta fuit mentio? Ambrosius in Lucam, Hieronymus in initia Danielis & Matthaei negant: existimant enim, Iechoniam hunc non fuisse Iosiae filium, sed nepotem. Et sanè rectè statuunt, Iechoniam illum, cuius in hoc versiculo fit mentio, esse Iosiae Regis nepotem, sed ex eo minùs rectè inferunt, distinctum esse ab eo, cuius fit mentio in v. praeced. ostendimus enim superiùs in versie. praeced. iuxta Codd. probatissimos legendum esse Ιωσίας ἐγέννησε τόν Ιωαηείμ, Ιωαηείμ σέ ἐγέννησε τόν ίέχονίαν. 1. Si idem utrobiq; esset Iechonias, vel secunda vel tertia tesseradecas non absolveretur. 2. Iechoniae principis nomen in fine scribitur per Iechoniae filii nomen per 2. Reg. 24. quam differentiā Graecus ac Latinus interpres non observarunt.

Q. 2. Quomodo Iechonias dicatur genuisse Sealthielem, cùm ex Ierem. 22. v. 30. videatur colligi posse, Iechoniam esse mortuum absliberis? Resp. sanè quidam concedunt, Iechoniam absq; liberis fuisse mortuum. Quod ergo hoc loco dicitur genuisse Sealthielem, illud sic explicant, quòd habuerit eum regni successorem. Rectè quidem dicitur, quòd Sealthiel ideò dicatur Iechoniae filius, quia fuit eius in regno successor. Sed minùs rectè statuitur, Iechoniam planèάτεηνονdecessisse, potuit enim habere filios, quorum tamen nullus in regno successerit. Apud Ieremiam non negatur Iechoniae semen vel filius, sed successor in regno ex filiis negatur. Duplex omninò est orbitas, prolis, & successionis, de posteriore Propheta agit, non de priore.

Q. 3. Quomodo Iechonias dicatur genuisse Sealthielem, cùm. 1. Paral. 3. v. 16. filius Iechoniae dicatur fuisse Asir, non Sealthiel? Resp. Asir ibi non est nomen proprium, sed appellativum, quod significat vinctum, ut sit sensus, filii autem Iechoniae vincti seu captivi in Babyloniam deportati. 2. Reg. 24. v. 17. Sealthiel expresse vocatur Iechoniae filius.

Q. 4. An unus idemSealthiel intelligatur hoc loco &Luc. 3. v. 27.

Resp. ita quidam statuunt, praesupponentes Sealthielem, vel quod idem est, Salathielem Iechoniae in regno successorem fuisse Iechoniae filium naturalem, id quod confirmant ex Iudaeorum Chronico Sedar Olam.

Sed monuimus paulò antè, duplicem esse orbitatem, prolis & successionis. Orbitas prolis est, cùm quis planè caret liberis. Orbitas successionis, quando quis filios quidem habet, sed quorum nullus patri in dignitate regia succedit. Iud. 9. v. 8. Concedimus, Iechoniam filios habuisse naturales, ac proinde non fuisse omninò prolis orbum. Sed filii illi Iechoniae non successerunt in regno, verùm privati vixerunt: negamus ergo, quòd Iechonias unum ex filiis regni successorem habuerit, ac quod unus & idem Sealthiel apud Matthaeum & Lucam describatur. Deus ipse testatur Ierem. 22. v. 24.Ezech. 36. v. 30. neminem ex sangvine Iechoniae oriundum, qui modo mundano solium Davidis sit possessurus. Consequens ergo est, Sealthielem & Zorobabelem non fuisse ex sangvine Iechoniae prognatos, cùm manifestè constet, Zorobabelem in solio Davidis sedisse, & tanquam principem in Iuda regnasse.

Proinde quando Matthaeus dicit, Iechoniam genuisse Sealthielem, vel non intelligit Sealthielem apud Lucam descriptum, sed filium Iechoniae, si quem habuit, naturalem, qui privatam solummodo vitam egit â successione in solio Regis exclusus; vel si hunc, ex quo Zerubabel Princeps natus est, indigitat, nullam aliam ob causam eum constituit Iechoniae filium, quàm quod in regno ei successerit, quae successio filio naturali alioqui deberi videbatur. Notum enim ex Lucâ, Sealthielem Zerubabelis patrem non Iechoniae, sed Neri ex stemmate Nathanis oriundi naturalem filium fuisse. Dicitur ergo Iechonias genuisse, id est iuxta phrasin Scripturae, heredem & successorem regni sibi su--ogasse Sealthielem.

Q 5. Quomodo Sealthiel dicatur genu-sse Zorobabel, cùm, 1. paral. 3. v. 19. Pedaia dicatur Sealthielis filius? Ad vers. enim 18. qui sic habet. Melch-ram, Phadaia, Sennesar & I-camia, Sama & Nadabia, subaudiunt Hebraei, fuerunt filii Sealthiel--. Resp. Sealthiel genuit Zerobabel non immediatè, sed mediante Pedaia, filius enim Sealthielis fuit Pedaia, Pedaiae filius Zerubabel; quia ergo Sealthiel genuit Pedaiam, ex quo natuZerubabel, inde etiam Zerubabelem genuisse dici potest. Zorobabel etiam in aliis Scripturae locis vocatur filius Salathielis. 1. Esdr. 3. v. 2. & 8. 2. lib. Esdr. cap. 7. v. 7. lib. 3. Esdr. cap. 5. v. 48. cap. 6. v. 2. Agg. 1. v. 1. & 12. Ut ergo Esdras & Aggaeus Zorobabelem filium Salathielis dixerunt, omisso Pedaia, ita codem iure ipsorum exemplo Matthaeus fuit usus.

Q. 6. Quare Matthaeus Pedaiam in hac gene alogiâ praeterierit? Resp. 1. ut tesseradecas sibi constaret. 2. quia de eo nihil insigne commemoratur, nisi quod eius d. l. fiat mentio. 3. temporibus Evangelistarum succesio familiae Davidicae non solùm publicè adhuc nota erat, verùm etiam certis voluminibus iam inde â Davide comprehensa. 4. nepos Zerobabel ab avo Sealthiel forsitan fuit educatus, ideoq; avo ut filius adscriptus. 5. sequitur hac in parte Evangelista Esdram lib. 1. cap. 3. v. 2. 8. & Haggaeum cap. 1. v. 1. & 12. In Zorobabele convenit utraq; linea per diversos Davidis filios antea ducta. Post Zorobabelem iterum lineae discrepant, sed in Matan rursus conveniunt. Quidam tamen, inter quos Andreas Osiander, duos Zorobabeles, ut & Sealthieles statuunt.

Zerubabel dicitur â quod Hebraeos & Chaldaeis est alienare & quia alienavit seu abduxit Iudaeos â Babel. Cùm enim essot regio sangvine natus, pronepos sc. Iechoniae, inde Iudaeorum ex Babylonico exilio in Iudaeam patriam Cyri indultu revertentium Dux constitutus fuit, quamvis adhuc admodùm iuvenis esset, 1. Esdr. 2. v. 2. Idem post Cyri mortem â Rege Dario impetravit, ut caeptam sub Cyro templi aedificationem, at vicinarum gentium invidiâ interruptam, liceret perficere, ad quam promovendam secundo anno Cyri cum pluribus exulibus Iudaeis in terram patriam rediit & sacrae fabricae extructionem absolvit, 1. Esdr. 5. v. I. & seqq. Ioseph. lib. 11. antiq. cap. 4.

## 1:13
v. 13. ζοςαβάβελ ἐγέννησε τόν ἀβιούδ. Yet this Abiud is not listed among the sons of Zorobabel in 1 Paralipomenon ch. 3, v. 19–20, even though an accurate enumeration of them is given there. Some therefore wish Abiud to be the one who is counted second in the place cited above among the sons of Zorobabel, called Hananiah. The firstborn Mosollam succeeded his father in the princedom which he held in Babylonia, but not in that which he exercised in Judea , as the Hebrews hand down. Others hold that this Abiud was not the son of Zorobabel but his grandson.

Latin:

v. 13. ζοςαβάβελ ἐγέννησε τόν ἀβιούδ. Atqui hic Abiud inter Zorobabelis filios 1. Paral. 3. v. 19. 20. non recensetur, cùm tamen accurata eorum ibi fiat enumeratio. Quidam ergo volunt, Abiud esle eum, qui d. l. secundus numeratur inter Zorobabelis filios, Hananias dictus. Primogenitus Mosollam successit patri in principatu, quem in Babylonia gessit, non autem in eo, quem in Iudaea exer cuit, ut Hebraei tradunt. Alii statuunt, hunc Abiud non fuisse Zorobabelis filium, sed nepotem.

## 1:14
v. 14. The generations from Abiud down to James, the father of Joseph, which are enumerated in this passage, do not occur in the Sacred Scriptures, or certainly not under these names. Matthew therefore received them either from the written genealogies of the Hebrews (among whom he was most studious of such matters, especially in recording the family of David, namely from which the Messiah who was to be born was awaited), or from divine revelation. (See above all Mr. D. Walther, Centuria Miscellanearum Theologicarum, Qu. LXXVII, p. 549 sqqq.)

Latin:

v. 14. Generationes iliae, quae ab Abiud usq; ad Iacobum Iosephi parentem hoc loco recensentur, non extant in Sacris literis, vel certè sub his nominibus non extant. Matthaeus ergo eas accepit vel ex scriptis Hebraeorum genealogiis, (quarum illi maximè -rant studiosi, cumprimis in annotanda Davidis familia, utpotex qua Mesias nasciturus expectabatur) vel ex divina revelatione. *(Vid. omninò Dn. D. Walth. Centur. Miscell. Theol. Q. LXXVII. p. 549. seqq.)*

## 1:15
v. 15. Eusebius, Book 1 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 6, relates on the authority of Africanus that Mathan's wife was named Estha, and that from her he begot an only son, Jacob, the father of Joseph. This Mathan was Mary's grandfather on her father's side, that is, the father of Joachim, whose brother was James, the father of Joseph; so that Joseph and Mary were the children of two brothers, and that Mathan was the grandfather of Mary and Joseph, but the great-grandfather of Christ.

Latin:

v. 15. Eusebius lib. 1. Histor. Eccl. cap. 6. ex Aphricano memorat, uxorem Mathan dictam fuisse Estham, ex qua genuerit unicum filium Iacob, Iosephi parentem. Mathan iste fuit avus Mariae paternus, pater sc. Ioacim, cuius frater fuit Iacobus Iosephi parens, ita ut Ioseph & Maria fuerint duorum fratrum liberi, ac Mathan ille fuerit Mariae & Iosephi avus, Christi verò proavus.

## 1:16
v. 16. Ιακωβ δέ έγέννησε τόν Ιωσάφ. But how does Matthew make Joseph the son of Jacob, when Luke makes him the son of Heli? Answer: 1. Eusebius, Book 1 of the History, chapter 7, reports from a certain Letter of Julius Africanus that Joseph was called the son of Heli in Luke because he had been born after his death from his wife, whom James, the half-brother of Heli, had married in order to raise up seed to his brother, since he had had no children by her. With Africanus agree Ambrose, Book 3 on Luke, p. 37, and Augustine, Book 2 of the Retractations; for they judge that Jacob was the natural father of Joseph, but Heli his legal father. Theophylact likewise holds that Jacob was the natural father of Joseph, who, after the death of left without children, took as wife the woman left behind by Heli, so that Matthew looks to [the former], whereas Luke names Heli the father of Joseph νομικόν or legal. The Nazianzene holds the same in his poem.

And going to the deceased, he raised up offspring for him, since he left none; he visited the house, the bed of Jacob, though not born of the same father, and begat a noble son for his brother, Joseph; this one indeed was his own, but the register wrote him down as belonging to Joseph.

Justin, in the Questions and Answers to the Orthodox, question 66, p. 334, draws an observation of this kind from him. By the arrangement of His divine grace God anticipated the birth of Christ from the virgin, so that the virgin was betrothed to a husband although she had two fathers, one according to Nature through conjugal union, the other according to the Law without marital union, depicting beforehand the birth of Christ, who was indeed generated of the Holy Spirit the Son of GOD, yet generated of a woman the son of Joseph. If what was generated of the woman of Heli is the son of Heli, much more what was brought forth of the woman of Joseph is the son of Joseph without wedded intercourse, according to the good pleasure of GOD. Compare question 133, p. 374. (*Africanus,* indeed a very ancient author, but one who, by the judgment of Isaac Casaubon, Exercise 1 upon the Appendix to Baronius, p. 29, records many false things reported by others, embraces not only this opinion but also attempts to overthrow by several arguments the view that immediately follows, n. 3, Simon Episcopius, the Coryphaeus of the Arminians, in the Response to the Sixty-Four Questions, Question 1, vol. 2, p. 2, as anyone may see. Bonaventure Cornelius Bertram also treats this matter quite amply in his Labours, Frankfort, chapter 6; but since the design of this little work does not allow of weighing the arguments commonly brought forward on either side, and besides this material is treated expressly by my revered father-in-law Mr. Günther Henry Plathner, Doctor of Both Laws, in Book 1, κυριακων, άνεκδότων indeed, but which will presently come to light, κύριος σςελήση, it seems best to send the reader back to the aforementioned authors.*) Moreover, against this distinction between the natural and the legal father Osiander brings two objections. First, that it would be unheard-of among the Jews for that deceased man to be called the father of such a firstborn, and for his son to take his wife and raise up seed to his brother, since in the Hebrew it is not read that he takes her, but rather ויבמפ 'and shall perform the levirate toward her,' that is, shall have her by the right of the levir. Second, that no one can beget such a successor or legal son from the wife of the deceased unless he is the full brother of the deceased. Now James and Heli were not full brothers, because Matthew traces the genealogy of Christ from David through Solomon, but Luke through Nathan, neither of whom died childless.

2. Some say that Heli was not Joseph's father, but either Eliud or Eliezer, one of Joseph's grandfathers or ancestors, and they argue, -um Luke does not say 'Heli begot Joseph,' but he was τού of Heli, that is, through an intervening generation from Heli.

3. Augustine in book 2 of On the Harmony of the Gospels chapter 3, and in book 3 against Faustus chapter 3, thinks that Joseph had two fathers, one by whom he was born, another by whom he was adopted. The former is described by Matthew, the latter by Luke. *(nor is it unusual even for Scripture to reckon adopted sons in the place of sons, which it shows extends even so far as γεννάν, , proving this from the Rabbis, D. Hospinian to Lippomanus p. 424. Confirm also Mr. Walter's Harmony of the Bible p. 373.)* 3. Most simply it is answered that Heli, that is Joachim, was Mary's natural parent, but this man, according to the customary manner among the Hebrews (according to which Naomi calls Ruth her daughter-in-law daughter, Ruth 2. v. 22.), is called the father of Joseph because Joseph, who was the son of Jacob by nature, was the son-in-law of Heli. Luther vol. 8 Jena German fol. 125. 126. Andrew Osiander on the Harmony of the B. D. Chemnitz Harmony ch. 3. Otherwise it can be observed here that the Names Eli and Jehoiakim agree. For Jehoiakim signifies to be raised up, Eli exalted.

Τόν άνδρα Μαρίας. Joseph is said to be Mary's husband, not by reason of carnal mixing, but by reason of marital betrothal. Augustine book 23 against Faustus chapter 8. Not because he did not mix in bed-concubiting, therefore he is not husband.

When the Evangelist pointedly calls Joseph the husband of Mary, he intimates two things. 1. That Joseph belongs to this genealogy of Christ in no other way than insofar as he is the husband of Mary the mother of Christ, since he himself is not Christ's natural father. 2. That the family of Joseph and Mary is one and the same, and their ancestors the same. He had promised that he wished to weave together the genealogy of Jesus Christ, and had traced it from Abraham all the way to Joseph the husband of Mary, from whom Christ was born. Therefore he says in fact that Mary was so joined in marriage to Joseph that she was of one family, the same ancestors and the same household, from which Joseph came; otherwise the Evangelist would not have performed what he had promised.

(Since therefore Mary was betrothed to Joseph, Luke 1. v. 27. and in that regard Joseph is called her husband in this place, and conversely she his wife shortly after v. 20. ( for it is the custom of the Scriptures that those espoused are called husbands, and the brides wives, Jerome in the Commentary on Matthew 1. vol. 6 Opera p. 1., which saying is cited also in the Chapter Genuit. 27. q. 2.; likewise in the Chapter Qui desponsatam Cause 27. q. 2. a similar saying of Gregory is brought forward: It is the custom of the divine law to call brides spouses.) it is plain that it is a figment of the Papists when they assert that Mary made a vow of continence and looked toward it with these words: How shall this come about, since I do not know a man? But concerning the true sense of these words there will be discussion below Luke 1. v. 35 The passages make for confirming the opinion of Jerome and likewise of Gregory Genesis 29. v. 21.Deuteronomy 22, 24.

(The Arabic interpreter uses the name in both places which denotes wife, from yoke, whence the word joined, i.e., joined in marriage, took a wife. See Matt. 5. v. 32.ch. 22. v. 30.Luke 13.Matt. 1. v. 20. But the bride is called the spouse's wife, not because she actually is such, but because she shortly will be such, because she is the hoped-for, pledged and promised wife, though not yet delivered into the husband's power. And although perhaps apart from the present passage Matt. 1. v. 16. another place occurs nowhere in Holy Scripture where the spouse is called man or husband, nevertheless it is evident that the same reasoning holds here, and that on account of the same reason, namely on account of the betrothal made, Joseph is called Mary's husband, on account of which she is his wife. And to this the Arab interpreter of the New Testament looked, when he calls Joseph both here and in the following verse , that is, Mary's Bridegroom, just as also in v. 20 the same translator calls Mary , that is, Joseph's Bride. For the noun descends from the root , which means he betrothed, as is plain from this very chapter of Matthew, where the Arabic has in v. 18 , when she had been betrothed, likewise from Luke 1. v. 27. where he calls Mary , the virgin betrothed. The Ethiopian, imitating the Arab, likewise calls Joseph , her bridegroom of Mary (here incidentally must be noted the custom of this interpreter frequently using πλεονας ικως the pronoun. This is also quite customary in Syriac, as the same text at this place has , that man of that Mary.) He derives in v. his origins from the verb , betrothed, in which sense it occurs in v. 18, , and having been betrothed &c. So too Luke 1. v. 27. The same also calls Mary in v. 20. , Bride. Yet however many interpreters take the nouns husband and likewise wife in the manner now stated, including some of our own countrymen: nothing stands in the way, indeed it is more fitting, if it be said that Joseph is called by Matthew Mary's husband, and she his wife, not only because Mary was betrothed to Joseph and promised to him, but because truly she was given over to him, and led by the same into his house, and thus even a true marriage intervened between them:

which the Jesuit Cornelius à Lapide himself also confesses on ch. 1 of Matt. p. 52, likewise on ch. 1 of Luke p. 12. Nor however should it be inferred from this that therefore Mary was also known by Joseph: for carnal union did not... ούσίαν, but concerns only the use of marriage.*)

Εξ ής έγεννήθη Ιησούς. There is emphasis in προσδιορισμω έξ ής. The angel, v. 20. seq., said to Joseph in dreams, τό έν άυτή γεννηθε ν what was born of her. Therefore lest anyone think that the Son of GOD carried his flesh with him to heaven, and transmitted it through Mary as through a channel, on this account the Son of GOD is notably said to be born not only of Mary, but also from Mary, namely from her purified and sanctified womb. The Son of GOD assumed human nature not only in Mary, but also from Mary. Tertullian says: He denied conception from intercourse, he did not deny it from flesh: indeed, he confirmed it from flesh, because he did not thereby deny it from flesh, just as he denied it from intercourse. The Marcionites, as the same Tertullian reports in the book against Valentinus chapter 27, and the book On the Flesh of Christ chapter 20, corrupted this passage by substituting the particle through. But they accomplish nothing by this corruption. Paul removes all doubt in Rom. 1. v. 3. when he says that Christ was born of the seed of David according to the flesh.

Ἐγεννήθη and conceived and was born or was brought forth into the light. That is the internal birth, this the external; this word is employed in this History to signify both births, for the former below at v. 20., for the latter in chapter 2, v. 1. Now ἐγενν. is the passive form of the verb ἐγέννησε, which the Evangelist had used several times previously in this genealogy. Εγεννήθη therefore signifies both he was born and begotten, so that it may more secretly indicate that Christ had no begetter on earth, but only a bearer, namely that Virgin who alone is θεοτόκος. γεννάομαι It is used not only of the bringing forth of offspring into the light, Matth. 2. v. 1. but also of the fetus generated by conception in the maternal womb and formed from the substance of the mother, Iob. 3. v. 3.cap. 14. v. 1.cap. 15. v. 7.Ioh. 9. v. 34.Gal. 4. v. 29. And that Christ is said to be born of Mary not only in the former sense but also in the latter is evident from this, that in Luc. 1. v. 42. he is called the fruit of Mary's womb.

It should also rightly be noted that the Evangelist does not say, consistently with what precedes, 'And Joseph begot Jesus,' nor [does he speak] of by whom, namely Joseph, Jesus was begotten, but of whom, namely Mary the wife of Joseph, Jesus was begotten; whose mystery he will explain shortly after.

Latin:

v. 16. Ιακωβ δέ έγέννησε τόν Ιωσάφ.At quomodo Matthaeus Iosephum statuit filium Iacobi, cùm Lucas eum statuat filium Eli? Resp. 1. Eusebius lib. 1. Hist. cap. 7. ex Epistola quadam Iulii Aphricani refert, ideo apud Lucam Heli filium dictum fuisse Ioseph, quod natus esset post ipsius mortem ex eius uxore, quam duxerat Iacob, frater uterinus Eli ad suscitandum videlicet semen fratri, cùm is ex ea nullos suscepisset liberos. Cum Africano faciunt, Ambrosius lib. 3. in Luc. p. 37. & Augustin. lib. 2. retractat existimant enim, Iacobum fuisse Iosephi patrem naturalem, Eli verò eiusdem patrem legalem. Theophylactus itidem statuit, Iacobum fuisse patrem Iosephi naturalem, qui mortuo absliberis Eli relictam eius uxorem duxerit, ateò respicere Matthaeum: Lucam verò nominare Eli patrem Iosephiνομικόνseu legalem. Idem statuit Nazianz. in carm.

Φλεί δέ φθιμένοιο έκεί γόνον ούτιν έλειπενάίψα δόμον τς λέχος τ ίακωβ ούκ ων όμαπατρος, -έξατο κτέκεν ύιόν άδελφω έσθλόν ίωσήφ,ούτος τόυ μέν έην, τω δ έγραφε ύεσμός ἰωσὴφ.

Iustinus in qq. & respons. ad orth. q. 66. pag. 334 eiusmodi observationem ex eo deducit. Divina gratia dispositione suâ Christi ex virgine nativitatem praevenit, ut virgo duos habenti patres viro desponderetur, alterum secundum Naturam ex coitione coniugali, alterum secundum legem sine coniunctione maritali, in illius nativitate priùs depingens Christi nativitatem, qui genitus quidem est ex Spiritu S. filius DEI, genitus autem ex muliere Iosephi filius Iosephi. Si id quod muliere Eli genitum est, filius Eli est, mul-ò magis, quod ex muliere Iosephi editum est, filius Iosephi est sine connubiali concubitu secundum beneplacitum DEI. Confer q. 133. p. 374. *( Africani, scriptoris quidem admodùm antiqui, sed qui Isaaci Casauboni iudicio Exere. 1. ad App. Baronii p. 29. multa falsa ab aliis narrata commemorat, sententiam amplectitur non solùm, sed illam quoq;, quae mox sequitur n. 3. aliquot rationibus destruere conatur Simon Episcopius, Arminianorum Coryphaeus in Resp. ad LXIV. Qq. Q. 1. tom. 2. p. 2. qui potest videri. Agit quoq; de hâc re satis prolixè Bonavent. Corn. Bertramus Lucubr. Franktall. c. 6. sed cûm opusculi huius ratio non permittat, rationes, quae in partem utramq; afferri solent, excutere, & insuper materiam hanc ex professo pertractet B. Socer meus D. Günth. Henricus Plathnerus, Ictus, lib. 1. κυριακων, άνεκδότων quidem, sed quae propediem κύριος σςελήση, lucem videbunt, placet ad dictos autores lectorem remittere.)* Coeterùm distinctioni isti inter patrem naturalem & legalem Osiander duo opponit. Primò quòd inauditum sit apud Iudaeos, mortuum illum dici patrem huiusmodi primogeniti, ipsumfilium illius, cùm in Hebraeo non legatur, & suscitet semen fratri, sedויבמפ & leviritabit eam, id est, leviri iure eam habebit. Secundò quod talem successorem seu filium legalem nemo possit ex uxore defuncti procreare, nisi frater defuncti germanus. Iam verò Iacob & Eli non fuerunt fratres germani, quia Matthaeus genealogiam Christi deducit â Davide per Salomonem, Lucas autem per Nathanem, quorum neuter sine liberis decessit.

2. Quidam dicunt, Eli non fuisse Iosephi patrem, sed vel Eliud vel Eleeser, unum ex Iosephi maioribus vel atavis fuisse, contendunt, -ùm Lucas non dicat, Heli genuit Ioseph, sed fuit τού Heli, sc. per mediatam generationem ab Heli.

3. August. lib. 2. de consens. Evang. cap. 3. & lib. 3. contra Faustum cap. 3. existimat, Iosephum duos habuisse patres, unum â quo fuerit natus, alterum â quo fuerit adoptatus. Priorem describi â Matthaeo, posteriorem â Luca. *(nec insolens quoq; esse Scripturae adoptivos filiorum loco reputare, quin & γεννάν eo usq; extendere, ostendit ex Rabbinis D. Ha-ksp. ad Lippom. p. 424. Conf. etiam Dn. D. Walth. Harm. Bibl. p. 373.)* 3. Simplicissimè respondetur, Heli seu Ioiakim naturalem Mariae parentem fuisse, hunc verò apud Lucam usitato apud Hebraeos more, (secundum quem Naëmi Ruth nurum suam vocat siliam, Ruth. 2. v. 22.) vocari patrem Iosephi, quia Iosephus filius Iacobi naturalis, Heli gener fuit. Luth. tom. 8 Ien. Germ. f. 125. 126. Andr. Osiand. in Harm. B. D. Chemn. Harm. c. 3. Aliàs observari hic potest, quòd Nomina Eli & Iechoiakim conveniant. Iechoiakim enim significat erigendum, Eli sublimem.

Τόν άνδρα Μαρίας. Ioseph dicitur Mariae maritus, non ratione carnalis commixtionis, sed ratione maritalis desponsationis. Aug. lib. 23. contra Faustum cap. 8. Non quia non concubitu permixtus, ideò non maritus.

Quando Evangelista Iosephum notanter vocat virum Mariae, duo insinuat. 1. non aliter Iosephum ad hanc genealogiam Christi pertinere, quâm quatenus est maritus Mariae matris Christi, cùm ipse non sit Christi naturalis pater. 2. unum atq; idem genus Iosephi & Mariae esse, eosdemq; maiores. Promiserat, se velle genealogiam Iesu Christi texere, eam ab Abrahamo usq; ad Iosephum maritum Mariae, ex qua natus est Christus, deduxerat. Reipsa igitur dicit, Mariam sic fuisse Iosephi coniugem, ut ex uno genere, iisdem maioribus & familia eadem fuerit, ex qua Iosephus, alioqui Evangelista non praestitisset, quod erat pollicitus.

*(Quoniam igitur Maria desponsata fuit Iosepho, Luc. 1. v. 27. eoq; respectu Iosephus illius vir hoc loco, & vicissim illa huius uxor paullò post v. 20. vocatur ( consvetudinis enim est Scripturarum, quòd sponsi viri, & sponsae vocentur uxores, Hieronymus in Comment. Matth. 1. t. 6. Oper p. 1. quod dictum etiam citatur C. Genuit. 27. q. 2. sic C. Qui desponsatam Caus. 27. q. 2. adducitur dictum simile Gregorii: Divinae legis est mos, sponsas appellare coniuges.) patet, sigmentum esse Pontificiorum, quando adserunt, Mariam votum continentiae emisisse, & ad illud respicere verbis istis: Quomodo fiet istud, quoniam virum non cognosco. Sed de vero verborum horum sensu infrà agetur Luc. 1. v. 35 Faciunt pro confirmandâ Hieron. itemq; Gregorii sententiâ loca Gen. 29. v. 21.Deut. 22, 24.

(Arabs interpres dd. ll. adhibet nomen quod coniugem notat, â iugum, â quo verbum iugavit, it. matrimonio coniunxit, uxorem duxit Vid. Matth. 5. v. 32.c. 22. v. 30.Luc. 13.Matth. 1. v. 20. Dicitut autem sponsa uxor sponsi, non quòd actu talis sit, sed quòd propediem talis fit futura, quòd sit uxor sperata, pacta & promissa, nondum tamen in potestatem mariti tradita. Licet verò fortè praeter praesentem Matth. 1. v. 16. in Scr. S. non occurrat locus alius, ubi sponsus vir sive maritus dicatur, patet tamen, quòd par ratio hic sit, quòdq; propter eandem rationem, videl. propter factam desponsationem, Iosephus Mariae vir vocetur, propter quam illa huius uxor. Et huc respexit Arabs N. T. interpres, quando Iosephum tum hoc, tum seq. v. 19. nominat id est, Sponsum Mariae, quemadmodum etiam v. 20. idem Mariam vocat id est Sponsam Iosephi. Descendit enim nomen â radiec quòd desponsavit significat, ceu patet ex hoc ipso cap. Matth. ubi ita Arabs v. 18. cum desponsata esset, item ex Luc. 1. v. 27. ubi Mariam vocat virginem desponsatam. Arabem imitatus Aethiops Iosephum itidem nominat Sponsum eius Mariae (obiter hic notanda consvetudo interpretis huius saepè πλεονας ικως adhibentis pronomen. Id Syro quoq; admodùm solemne est, quemadmodum idem h. l. habet virum illius Mariae.) Arcessit v. natales suos â verbo desponsavit, quo sensu occurrit v. 18. & desponsata &c. Sic quoq; Luc. 1. v. 27. Idem quoq; Mariam v. 20. vocat Sponsam. Verùm ut ut plurimi Interpretes, ex nostratibus quoq;, nomen viri itemq; uxoris in praesens dicto modo sumant: nihil tamen obstat, imò magis conveniens est, si dicatur, Iosephum Mariae virum, illam huius uxorem vocari â Matthaeo, non solùm quia Maria Iosepho desponsata fuit, ac promissa, sed quia reverà illi tradita, ab eodemq; etiam in domum ducta, quôdq; adeoq; verum matrimonium inter eos intercesserit:

Εξ ής έγεννήθη Ιησούς. Emphasis est in προσδιορισμω έξ ής. Angelus v. 20. seq. dicebat Iosepho in somnis, τό έν άυτή γεννηθε νquod in eanatum. Ne quis igitur cogitaret, Filium DEI carnem suam coelo secum detulisse, ac per Mariam tanquam per canalem traduxisse, ideò Filius DEI notanter dicitur, non solùm in Maria, sed etiam ex Maria natus, videlicet ex purificatis & sanctificatis eius visceribus. Filius DEI nonsolùm in Maria, sed etiam ex Maria hum. Naturam assumsit. Tertull. d. l. Negavit ex concubitu, non negavit ex carne: Imò confirmavit ex carne, quia non proinde negavit ex carne, sicut negavit ex concubitu. Marcionitae, referente eodem Tertulliano lib. adv.
