Ἐγεννήθη& conceptus & natus est seu in lucem editus est. Illa est nativitas interna, haec externa, ad utramq; nativitatem significandam adhibetur istud verbum in hac Historia, ad priorem inferius v. 20. ad posteriorem cap. 2. v. 1. Est verò ἐγενν. passivum verbi ἐγέννησε, quo hactenus Evangelista aliquoties in hac genealogia fuerat usus. Εγεννήθη ergo significat & natus & genitus est, ut secretius indieetur, Christum in terris non habuisse genitorem, sed solam genitricem, eam sc. Virginem, quae sola est θεοτόκος. γεννάομαι non tantùm de editione partûs in lucem, Matth. 2. v. 1. verûm etiam de foetu per conceptionem in utero materno generato, & ex substantiâ matris formato usurpatur Iob. 3. v. 3.cap. 14. v. 1.cap. 15. v. 7.Ioh. 9. v. 34.Gal. 4. v. 29. Christum verò non tantùm in priore, sed etiam in posteriore significatione ex Maria dici natum, patet ex eo, quod Luc. 1. v. 42. vocatur fructus ventris Mariae.

Probè etiam notandum, quod Evangelista non dicat cum praecedentibus conformiter, Ioseph autem genuit Iesum, nec, de quo, se. Iosepho genitus est Iesus, sed de qua sc. Maria Iosephi coniuge genitus est Iesus, cuius mysterii rationem paulô post explicabit.

## 1:17
v. 17. Matthew established three tessaradecads. 1. so that he might confirm memory. 2. that he might point out the triple state and change of the people. What mystery these three tessaradecads contain, Prudentius explains in the Apotheosis against the Phantasiasts. Rupertus laid down such a mystery. The Christ promised to Abraham deferred his coming on account of the selling of Joseph. Promised to David, he deferred his coming on account of the adultery and murder of David. Promised through the Prophets under Hezekiah, he deferred his coming on account of the sin of Manasseh, who shed blood. Moreover the Evangelist traces the genealogy of Christ through three tessaradecads, which he distributed according to the three remarkable changes that befell the people of GOD. The first tessaradecad he traces from Abraham even unto David inclusive, for to him the promise about the Messiah was solemnly renewed, which he celebrates in his very last words as a favor of singular kind. The second tessaradecad he traces from Solomon the son of David even unto Jechonias at the time of the Babylonish captivity. The third tessaradecad he traces from Jechonias even unto Joseph the reputed father of Christ, again inclusive.

The first tessaradecad embraces those who lived in the land of Canaan without a kingdom. The second tessaradecad enumerates those who were Kings. The third tessaradecad includes those who, after the kingdom had been lost, were merely Leaders. It is thereby signified that the condition of the people, whether under Patriarchs and Judges, or under Kings, or under Leaders, looked forward to Christ, who alone is the true Judge, the true King, and the true Priest. In v. 8 the Evangelist passes over three kings Ochozias, Joas, Amasias, so that the tessaradecad might come out right for him.

But neither the second nor the third tessaradecad appears to come out right, since in either case only thirteen generations are found.

Ans. In the second tessaradecad by the fault of copyists Jakim or Jehoiakim was omitted in some manuscripts; when he is added to the count, that tessaradecad comes out right; for from Solomon down to Jakim inclusive there are set forth 14 generations; from Jeconiah the son of Jakim, who is the first among the persons of the tessaradecad, down to Christ inclusive there are likewise counted 14 generations. That Christ is here to be reckoned in is plain from v. 1. Others reply differently, but less fittingly. Ambrose, Epiphanius, and Maldonatus, who followed them, say: that in the third tessera-decade one generation has dropped out. Some wish that these tessera-decades are rather of persons than of generations, so that accordingly the first tessera-decade ends in David thus, that David should be the last Person of the first tessera-decade and the first Person of the second tessera-decade. In the same manner Josiah would be the last person of the second tessera-decade and the first of the third tessera-decade; by which reasoning they think that, although Christ is not counted among them, nevertheless the third tessera-decade stands complete. Theophylact records that some reckoned the time of the migration itself in place of the fourteenth generation.

Some say that both boundaries of the first and third tessera-decades ought to be understood inclusively, namely so that the first and the last are counted together in those tessera-decades, but that both boundaries of the second tessera-decade are to be understood exclusively, namely so that neither the first nor the last is counted together. But the former response is the simplest and most agreeable to the text.

The Evangelist subtracted the sum total, in order to show that nothing through forgetfulness was omitted by himself in this genealogy, and consequently that nothing is to be added or taken away by anyone. Christ closes these tessera-decades, who is the end of the law Rom. 10. v. 4. toward whom the constitution of the entire Jewish polity uniquely looked.

Hugh of Saint Cher in his comment on this passage, and Adam Reissner following him in the book which he entitles Messias, published at Frankfurt in 1566, expounds all those names which are enumerated in this genealogy both in Matthew and in Luke, and adapts them in a mystical sense to Christ.

Concerning this truly genealogy of Christ the Savior

Q. 1. How can what Paul says be reconciled with it, since 1. Tim. 1. v. 4.Tit. 3. v. 9. he seems to disapprove study of genealogies. Ans. 1. On account of those sayings of the Apostle Faustus the Manichean rejected the genealogy of Christ altogether, as Augustine testifies, book 23 against Faustus, chapter 6, and contended that it was written neither by a good man nor was any part of the Gospel. 2. but one must distinguish between the times of the O. and N. T. In the O. T. the Holy Spirit himself diligently recorded genealogies through his scribes, Gen. 5. v. 10. & 11. 1. Paralipomenon 3. v. 9. Book 1 of Ezra ch. 2. For at that time the recording of genealogies was not only useful but also necessary, then because of the distinction of tribes and inheritances, whose confusion God had forbidden Num. 36. v. 7. then on account of succession to the priestly office, to which none were admitted unless born of the tribe of Levi; then on account of the rights of firstborn sons, to whom a double portion of inheritance was owed; then especially because of the promise concerning the Messiah, who was to be born of the tribe of Judah and family of David Gen. 49. v. 10.2. Sam. 7. v. 16. But in the New Testament all these causes have been taken away, and so the study of genealogies is no longer necessary. 3. Meanwhile the genealogy of Christ noted at the beginning of the New Testament by the Evangelists has its own use, and indeed a very great one, which we shall recount shortly. 4. Paul does not condemn those genealogies marked out by the Holy Spirit, but ἀπεράντους or endless ones, which provide more question than edification—such as those which were brought forth outside Scripture from books δευτερωσεων either of Gentiles joined together with most trifling fables (see Chrysostom on 1. Tim. 1.) or of Jews boasting of their fleshly descent from Abraham and his free wife Sarah and despising the Gentiles on this account. Rupert of Deutz says, The Apostle condemns all other genealogies introduced after that of Christ, the end of all before it—which nevertheless ought not to redound to the discredit of the genealogies of Princes or others recorded for political reasons.

Q. 2. What is the use of this genealogy of Christ noted by the Evangelists? Ans. This genealogy proves. 1. the truth of Christ's human Nature—that He was born a true man from men. Thus Matthew and Luke prove Christ's humanity against the Valentinians, Manicheans, and Marcionites, just as John proves His deity against Ebion and Cerinthus. 2. the truth of the foundational article of the Christian faith—that Christ is that promised Messiah exhibited in the New Testament, since He is the son of Abraham and of David, from whose seed the true Messiah was to be born. Truly that genealogy does not directly and immediately prove that Christ is the true Messiah promised in the Old Testament and exhibited in the New; yet it supplies the property and condition which was necessarily required in the promised Messiah, namely, that He should be descended from the seed of David. On this ground they rejected Christ, because they thought Him not to be of the seed of David. Ioh. 7. v. 49. and 52. Osiander in his Harmony states, that genealogy of Matthew was placed chiefly on account of two kinds of men, of which one consisted of those who did not yet grasp that either Christ had to be born of a virgin or that Jesus was thus born. The other kind consisted of those who, although they would not deny that Mary sprang from the house of David, and that Jesus was born of her without the operation of a man, nevertheless asserted—if Joseph derived his origin from another tribe than Judah—that Mary along with her Son must be reckoned not to that tribe from which she was born, but to that in which she had been placed by marriage, for this reason, that spouses, even though they are still virgins, are one flesh. They believed that this latter kind of men, when they knew that Christ had to be born of the seed of David, would hold it a firm argument that Jesus could not be the true Christ, the Son of Mary, unless they recognized Joseph, Mary's husband, as David's descendant. The Evangelist wished to bring aid to the error of both, or to remedy their weakness.

3 The firmness of the divine promise. By means of most grievous scandals and most atrocious persecutions stirred up against the lineage of the Messiah, the Devil tried to hinder the fulfillment of the divine promise; but from this genealogy traced out from Abraham through David all the way to Christ we acknowledge that faith in the given promise concerning Christ was set free, born of the seed of Abraham and David.

4 The conformity of true and saving faith between the Patriarchs, Prophets and other believers of the O.T. on the one side, and those believing in the N.T. on the other. For He whom they awaited as about to come, these believe in as already manifested. Both alike believe they are saved by no other means than through the grace of Jesus Christ, Acts 15. v. 10.

5. Finally, this genealogy has attached to it a sweetness of consolation, since from it it shines forth, for the comfort of our weakness and lowliness, that among the ancestors of Christ there existed not only insignificant men, but also ones stained by most serious sins. Rupertus on this passage: Just as he deigned to die for sinners, so he deigned to be born of sinners. In this genealogy of Christ there are enumerated not only Kings and Dukes, but also commoners and obscure persons; not only men, but also women; not only Jews, but also Gentiles; not only the just, but also sinners, that we may understand Christ to have been born for the consolation and salvation of all. See Luther, vol. 4. Lat. fol. 292.

Jerome, book 1. Commentary on Matthew, chapter 1. It must be noted in the genealogy of the Savior that none of the holy women were taken, but rather those whom ⟦f1 Scripture reproaches, so that he who came because of sinners, being born of sinners, might blot out the sins of all. (The contrary is asserted by Jac. Faber, who excuses all those women. He says Rahab was an innkeeper, not a harlot, and Bathsheba was carried off by force by David, hence their mention occurs rather on account of their righteousness.) Lemnius, book 3. De occultis naturae mirabilibus, chapter 1. In recounting the generation of Christ there are listed those begotten outside the state of marriage, which itself Chrysostom interprets as done deliberately and by design, in his homily 3. on Matthew, lest anyone swell with pride at the dignity of his forebears, nor cast down his spirit if humble and lowly ancestors were allotted to him.

Q. 3. How is the apparent contradiction between the genealogy of Matthew and Luke to be reconciled?

1. Some hold that with Matthew and Luke there are merely different names, but the very same men, under which title Conzenius touches upon Melanchthon, who thought the same. But this opinion is rightly rejected.

2. Beza produces a codex of venerable antiquity, in which the genealogy of Christ both descending, as with Matthew, and ascending, as with Luke, leads down to Solomon, not to Nathan, while the others remain unchanged upward all the way to Adam, with only those added whom Matthew had passed over in establishing the four-decades. But all the remaining codices disagree. Setting aside therefore these and similar methods of reconciliation.

Ans. Concerning this reconciliation, let it be noted in general:

1. At that time when Matthew and Luke recorded these genealogies, the succession of the family of David was not only publicly still known to everyone, but also already contained in certain volumes ever since David. Eusebius, book 1, Ecclesiastical History, chapter 6, whence not even the Priests themselves, the Scribes and Pharisees, most bitter enemies of Christ in those times, were able to find any fault whatever in those genealogies. By the voice of the whole people, carrying palm branches, Christ was called son of David. Nor did his accusers raise before either the governor or the people any question about the family from which he was born—assuredly things they would not have omitted unless it had been firmly established that Christ was of the race of David.

2. The Jews kept two kinds of books of genealogies. With books of one kind they embraced properly so-called genealogies, in wherein it was set forth how by natural generation and propagation, born one from another, and one succeeded to the other according to generation in family, blood, and descending line. Books of the other kind contained genealogies of successions in inheritance and government, in which was reckoned the succession in inheritance and kingdom, in which often someone is called the son of his predecessor and assumed his name, who was truly not the son of the former. 1. Paral. 3. v. 16. Luc-e's purpose was to recount the natural lineage of Christ, so that he might show that Christ sprang from David according to the promise 2. Sam. 7 v. 12. because the lineage of Christ traces back from Adam, the first parent of humankind, and because he derives it from David through Nathan, from whom Christ must have sprung, since he did not spring from Solomon, whose lineage indeed became extinct in Jeconiah. But Matthew's purpose was to recount especially the legal lineage, so that he might show that Christ lawfully succeeded to the kingdom of David according to the second promise attached to the foregoing one. And so he descends through Solomon to Jeconiah, although Christ did not spring from Solomon, yet nevertheless he lawfully succeeded him in the kingdom, because he sprang from Nathan, to whose posterity the rule was lawfully transferred in Shealtiel, Jeconiah the Solomonic having become extinct without natural successors.

3. Eusebius on this passage, and Nicephorus lib. 1. Hist. Eccl. cap. 11., out of Julius Africanus's Letter to Aristides concerning the harmony of the Gospels, bring forward this: Among the nation of Israel the names of generations are now counted according to Nature, now also according to the order of the Law. Those successions belong to Nature which descend by truth of seed or blood; but those of the Law when someone is substituted in place of another begetter under the name of a brother deceased without children, &c. Therefore from each Evangelist there is recorded a succession of both kinds, that is, so that one of them set forth him whom he had begotten, while the other set forth him who seemed as though he had begotten him: and thus it comes about that neither Gospel lies, while one follows the order of Nature, and the other carries out the rule of the Law.

4. Just as daughters-in-law are called by a Hebrew idiom daughters, and sons-in-law are called sons, [illegible] reason of mutual relationship mothers-in-law are called mothers, and fathers-in-law are called fathers.

Hence Andreas Osiander, in his Harmony, states: Luke did not wish to compose the genealogy of Joseph, since at the very first threshold he admonishes that Jesus was not the son of Joseph, but only thought to be. Therefore what Joseph is said to be the son of Eli must be understood thus, that Joseph was the son of Jacob, but the son-in-law of Eli, whose [son]. Now Eli, who by his true name was called Jehoiakim, was the father of the Virgin Mary and the maternal grandfather of Christ according to the flesh; hence also the Evangelist speaks simply of Joseph as being of Eli, so that we might be free to understand under it 'son-in-law,' and not 'son.'

He adds: It would be absurd, if it were established that the genealogy of Joseph is set forth by both Evangelists, while the genealogy of the virgin is altogether neglected, although the crux of the matter depends on her herself.

5. Proper names of the Hebrews, when migrating to foreign languages, often deviate from their original source by the permutation of a single letter or syllable by writers.

6. Both Evangelists recorded the direct genealogy of Christ, but Matthew gives the κατιούσαν descending one, or downward; Luke the άνιούσαν ascending one, or upward. That descending manner is more suited to Nature, and therefore more customary.

Matthew does not record the genealogy properly so called, namely of lineage and blood, but the genealogy of succession, inheritance, and royal office, whence he also omits three Kings in the descending line, Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah. Luke, however, enumerates those who succeeded one another in the straight natural line through generation as fathers and natural sons. Justinian, in Questions and Answers to Orthodoxus, question 131, page 372: In the genealogy of Luke, Eli alone ηωτά τόν νόμον is the legitimate or rather legal father of Joseph; but from Eli down to Nathan, all who are enumerated in order are the natural sons of those joined to them, νποτεταλμένοι ηατά φνσιν, who indeed by that relationship which Eli holds toward Joseph belong to Joseph alone (legally), but of all the others they are held to be natural grandfathers. Others, however, state the contrary, that Eli was the natural father of Joseph, but Jacob the legal one.

7. Joseph and Mary descended not from the blood and family of Solomon, but from the blood and posterity of Nathan, who was Solomon's brother 2. Sam. 5. v. 14. 1. Paral. 3. v. 5., and consequently from the posterity of David: for David begot Solomon and Nathan by Bathsheba, upon whose descendants, when the throne of the Davids failed, the kingdom after the Babylonish captivity was transferred, because the line of Solomon had come to an end. Yet to this opinion—that the line of Solomon came to an end in Ahaziah dying without children, and that Joash from the posterity of Nathan succeeded him in the kingdom—some object. 1. that Joash was the natural son of Ahaziah 2 Kings 11 v. 2. Chronicles v. especially Chronicles v. Chronicles v. that the throne of the kingdom is promised to be established forever for Solomon just as for David 2 Sam. 7 v. 13. Psalm 89 v. 21. Compare 1 Kings 11 v. 11. & seqq. chap. v. Chronicles v. chap. v. that Solomon not only bore the type of Christ, but was also his parent according to the flesh. Psalm 72 throughout. Heb. 1 vers. 5. 8.

8. Zerubbabel begot both Abiud and Meshullam or Rhesa. Abiud begot Eliakim, he Azor, he Sadoc, he Achim, he Eliud, he Eleazar, he Matthan, he Jacob, he Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Christ was born. Meshullam or Rhesa begot Joanna, he Judah, he Joseph, he Simeon, he Mattathiah, he Maath, he Nagge, he Esli, he Naum, he Amos, he Mattathiah, he Joseph, he Janna, he Melchi, he Levi, he Matthat, he Heli, he Mary the wife of Joseph. Matthew follows the former line, Luke the latter. Consult Luther, vol. 5, Wittenberg, fol. 525 b. Cornelius Bertram, Lucubrations, Frankenthal, chapter 6.

9. Matthew traces Christ's genealogy through Solomon down to Joseph the husband of Mary; but Luke derives it through Nathan, another son of David, to Mary's parents. The cause of this diversity is this: that Matthew wished to describe the lineage of Joseph, Luke that of Mary, so that thus both Persons—Joseph, the supposed parent of Christ, and Mary his wife—might be shown to have descended from David. From Zerubbabel Matthew enumerates the ancestors of Joseph, to whom Mary was betrothed, but Luke those of Mary, so that from both genealogies it might be made evident that Christ was the Son of David, both by nature and by right of marriage. Osiander, Harmony: It came about by divine providence that Luke wrote the genealogy of the virgin just as Matthew wrote the genealogy of her spouse Joseph, so that whichever way you turn, whether you judge her to come from her parents or from her husband, yet always you will find her together with her son in the house and family of David.

Q. 4. Were Christ's forebears according to Matthew of the tribe of Judah; while those whom Luke lists were of the tribe of Levi? Baronius, Appendix, no. 30.

from Augustine, Hilary, Julian, Toledan &c., discusses this matter thus: Matthew, who undertakes to set forth and intimate the royal person in Christ, enumerates the natural generations of Christ from the Kings of the Jews. Luke, however, wishing to show the Priestly person in Christ, runs through the generations of the adoption of Christ. In support of this opinion it could be urged that Elisabeth, the daughter of Aaron, is said to be Mary's σνγγενης. Luc. 1. v. 5. & 36.

But Casaubon, exerc. 1. cap. 13. pag. 94. warns that the Fathers who thought thus were moved by reasons too little firm. They knew that Christ was to be no less a Priest than a true King: this moved them to believe that that origin was from the Priestly tribe (Levi) as well as from the Royal tribe (Judah); pag. 95. he adds: It is false that the persons mentioned by Luke belonged to any tribe other than Judah. The diversity of names is not a firm enough argument for us to judge that different tribes are described by them, since the Jews for the most part had the same names, and νιωσις adoption into sonship, the calling of a son, happened for various reasons, whether by gift or by Nature, or by the law of Moses concerning raising up seed to a dead brother; likewise by adoption or arrogation, and also on account of affinity. For the son-in-law was called the son of his father-in-law; add succession to the kingdom or to a private inheritance, for even those were counted their sons to whom they had succeeded.

Q. 5. How can it be proved from the genealogy described by Matthew and Luke that Christ is from the tribe of Judah and the posterity of David, when both terminate not in Christ or his mother, but in Joseph, who nevertheless was not the natural parent of Christ?

Resp. 1. Jerome, Chrysostom, Euthymius, Theophylact, h. l., Damascene lib. 4. Orth. fid. cap. 13. say that it is not the custom of the Scriptures to weave the order of women into the genealogies. Accordingly the Evangelist wished to draw the genealogy down to Joseph, the putative Father of Christ. But from 1. Paral. 2. v. 16. it appears that women are sometimes taken account of in genealogies.

2. Chrysost. homil. 3. in Matth. contends that the Evangelists tried to show the Jews that Christ was of the seed of David and of Abraham, yet they did not wish the mystery of that new admirable birth (of Christ born of the virgin Mary) to be manifest to the Jews while the time was still recent, and therefore they set out the genealogy of Joseph alone, who was of the tribe and family of David. But Luc. 3. 23 Joseph is expressly said to be the putative Father of Christ.

3. August. lib. 2. de cons. Evang. cap. 1. thinks it sufficient that Joseph was regarded as the Father of Christ: nay, that he was even Christ's father, because he was the husband of Mary the mother of Christ, not indeed with mingling of bodily sex, but with the affection of the mind preserved, not by the conjunction of bodies, but, which is dearer, by the conjunction of souls. This opinion of Augustine is not improbable. For if he who was born of the wife of him who had died leaving her without children was counted his, even though after his death he was born of another man, that is, of his brother, how much more must he be counted the son of someone who is born of his own wife while he himself is still living, and was begotten by no other man, even though he was not begotten by him either. Since Joseph was joined in lawful marriage to the virgin Mary, and Mary's body was therefore his body, nay, since he himself was one flesh with her, by right, though not in fact (for spouses are one flesh by right before they come together, but in fact afterwards), the offspring begotten of Mary's flesh is rightly counted as begotten of his flesh.

4. Some think, that the genealogy of Joseph was described for this reason, that the estimation of men, by which Christ was held to be the son of Joseph, might be satisfied. But the Holy Spirit did not wish to confirm men in a false opinion through the Evangelists; rather, He expressly refutes it. Luc. 3. v. 23.

5. Some therefore say that in the person of Joseph, according to the law Num. 36. v. 5. the lineage of Mary is comprehended, since among the twelve tribes of the Israelites it was not permitted in the holy land to marry outside one's tribe. Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, Epistle 7, and Andrew Osiander oppose to that opinion these arguments, that a wife had to be taken from the same tribe. 1. that testimony is not found in the Hebrew truth. 2. that Moses did not write it, since he himself did not observe it, for he took a wife from his own tribe. 3. that the eleven tribes were not pleading the law of GOD but their own oath, by which they were the less able to give their daughters in marriage to the Benjamites, Jud. 11. 4. that Josabeth, sister of King [Jeho]ram, of the tribe of Judah, was married to Joiada the High Priest, of the tribe of Levi. 2. Paral. 22. 5. that Elizabeth was of the tribe of Levi, and yet is said to be the kinswoman of Mary. But indeed although marriages could be contracted among the Hebrews between persons who were not of the same tribe, nevertheless this was not permitted when women were the sole heirs of their paternal goods; for then they were bound to marry a man who was not only of the same tribe, but also of the same family. Therefore, since the Blessed Virgin had no brothers, and as heir of the paternal goods married a man of her own family, the Evangelist, weaving the catalogue of the ancestors of Joseph, and showing that he drew his lineage from David, shows by the same token that the Blessed Virgin was of the same stock and family.

Eusebius Emissenus, in his homily on the nativity of Mary, proves it at length, That Mary, although she was an only-born daughter, or at least had no brothers, was sent out by her parents to a kinsman. Euthymius on chapter 19 of John, v. 25, holds that Mary was the only daughter of her own parents, who had not only no brothers, but not even any sisters.

6. We reply most simply: Luke describes the genealogy of Mary, Matthew that of Joseph, and thus both ways it has been shown that Christ descended from the family of David, as we noted above nn. 4 and 9. Tob. 6. v. 7. Raguel says that his only daughter ought to be joined in marriage to his kinship.

Q. 6. If therefore Mary was of the tribe of Judah, how is Elizabeth called her σνγγενης or kinswomanLuke 1. v. 36.since she was of the daughters of Aaron. v. 5.

Ans. Some think these two tribes were joined together. Exod. 6. 2 Paral. 22. It must be observed that the little word σνγγεννης is used 1. broadly for the whole Jewish people and all sprung from it. Rom. 9. v. 3.Mark 6. v. 4.Rom. 16. v. 7. 2. strictly, as it denotes relatives or those joined by blood, Luke 1. v. 58.chapter 4. v. 44.Acts 10. v. 24. If we embrace the broader meaning, the matter lies open to view. If anyone wishes to press the stricter meaning, it will have to be answered that some Levite—to whom by law it was permitted to marry into whatever tribe (because the Levites were not counted among the twelve tribes, nor had any proper lot of land, and therefore by marrying introduced no confusion of possessions)—had among his ancestors someone originating from the tribe of Judah; in this way Elizabeth could be both a kinswoman of Mary and a daughter of Aaron.

Latin:

v. 17. Matthaeus Tres constituit tesseradecades. 1. ut memoriae confuleret. 2. ut triplicem populi statum & mutationem indigitaret. Quid mysterii contineant hae tres tesseradecados, explicat Prudentius in Apotheosi contra phantasmaticos. Rupertus tale statuit mysterium. Christus promissus Abrahae distulit venire obsce--venditionis Iosephi. Promissus Davidi, distulit venire ob aedulterium & homicidium Davidis. Promissus per Prophetas sub Ezechia, distulit venire propter peccatum Manassae fundaentis sangvinem. Coeterùm genealogiam Christi Evangelista per tres tesseradecades deducit, quas iuxta tres insignes mutationes, quae in populo DEI contigerunt, distribuit. Primam tesseradecada deducit ab Abrahamo usq; ad Davidem inclusivè, illi enim promissio de Messia solenniter fuit repetita, id quod in novissimis suis verbis singularis beneficii loco celebrat. Secundam tesseradecada â Davidis filio Salomone deducit usq; ad Iechoniam in captivitate Babylonica. Tertiam tesseradecada deducit â Iechonia usq; ad Iosephum putativum Christi patrem iterum inclusivè.

Prima tesseradecas complectitur eos, qui in regione Cananaea absq; regno vixerunt. Secund- tessoradecas enumerat eos, qui fuerunt Reges. Tertia tesseradecas comprehendit eos, qui post amissum regnum fuerunt tantummodò Duces. Significatur, populi sive sub Patriarchis & Iudicibus, sive sub Regibus, sive sub Ducib. statum ad Christum spectare, qui solus verus est iudex, verus Rex, ac verus Sacerdos. In v. 8. omittit Evangelista tres Reg-Ochoziam Ioam, Am asiam, ut tesseradecas sibi constaret.

At nesecunda nec tertia tesseradecas sibi constare videntur, -ùm in utraa duntaxat tredecim generationes inveniantur.

Resp. in secunda tesseradecade vitio librariorum in quibusdam Codd. omissus fuit Iakim sive Ioiak m, quo annumerato tesseradecas illa sibi constat, â Salomone enim ad Iakim inclusivè constituuntur generationes 14. â Iakimi filio Iechonia, qui inter personas tesseradecadis primus est, usq; ad Christum inclusivè itidem numerantur generationes 14. Christum enim hic annumerandum patet ex v. 1. Alii aliter respondent, sed minùs commodè. Ambrosius Epiphanius, eosq; secutus Maldonatus dicunt, in tertia tess-radecade unam generationem excidisse. Quidam volunt, tesseradecades hasce ess potius personarum, quam generationum, proinde primam tesseradecada in Davide sic terminari, ut David sit ultima primae tesseradecadis & prima secundae tesseradecadis Persona. Eodemmodo Iosiam esse ultimam personam secundae tesseradecadis & primam tertiae tesseradecadis; quâ ratione putant, Christo non annumerato, nihilominus tertiam tesseradecada sibi constare. Theophylactus memorat, quosdam ipsum transmigrationis tempus numerasse loco decimae quartae generationis.

Quidam dicunt, primae & tertiae tesseradecadis utrumq; terminum intelligi debere inclusivè, ita sc. ut primus & ultimus in illa tesseradecade connumerentur, at secundae tesseradecadis utrumq; terminum intelligendum esse exclusivè, ita sc. ut nec primus, nec ultimus connumeretur. Sed prima responsio est simplicissima ac textui maximè congrua.

Subduxit summam Evangelista, ut ostenderet, nihil â se per oblivionem in hac genealogia omissum esse, ac proinde nihil â quoq; addendum vel subtrahendum. Christus tesseradecades hasce claudit, qui est finis legis Rom. 10. v. 4. ad quem totius politiae Iudaicae constitutio unicè respexit.

Hugo de S. Charo in comm. huius loci eumq; secutus Adamus Reisnerus in libro, quem inscribit Messias, edito Francofurti 1566. omnium illorum nomina, qui in hac genealogia tum apud Matthaeum, tum apud Lucam recensentur, explicat, & in sensu mystico ad Christum accommodat.

De hac verò genealogia Christi Salvatoris

Q. 1. Quomodo cum ea conciliari possit, quod Paulus1. Tim. 1. v. 4.Tit. 3. v. 9.genealogiarum studium improbare videtur. Resp. 1. propter dicta illa Apostolica Faustus Manichaeus genealogiam Christi in universum reiecit, teste Augustino lib. 23. contra Faust. cap. 6. eamq; nec â viro bono scriptam, nec Evangelii partem esse, contendit. 2. sed distinguendum est inter tempus V. ac. N. T. In V. T. ipse Spiritus S. genealogias per suos amanuenses diligenter co-signavit, Gen. 5. v. 10. & 11. 1. Paral. 3. v. 9. lib. 1. Esdr. 2. eo enim tempore annotatio genealogiarum non utilis solùm erat, sed etiam necessaria, tum ob distinctionem tribuum & haereditatum, quarum confusionem Deus interdixerat Num. 36. v. 7. tum ob successionem in officio Sacerdotali, ad quod non nisi oriundi ex tribu Levi adsciscebantur; tum ob iura primogenitorum, quibus dupla hereditatis portio debebatur; tum inprimis propter promissionem de Messia ex tribu Iuda & familia Davidis oriundo Gen. 49. v. 10.2. Sam. 7. v. 16. In N. autem T. hae causae omnes sunt sublatae, proinde genealogiarum studium non ampliùs est necessarium. 3. interim genealogia Christi in principio N. T. ab Evangelistis annotata suum habet usum, eumq; longè maximum, quem paulò post recensebimus. 4. Paulus non improbat genealogias â Spiritu S. annotatas, sed ἀπεράντους seu interminabiles, quae quaestionem magis praestant quàm aedificationem, quales erant, quae extra Scripturas ê libris δευτερωσεων afferabantur, vel gentilium cum fabulis nugacissimis coniunctarum (vid. Chrysost. in 1. Tim. 1.) vel Iudaeorum de carnali ex Abrahamo & libera eius coniuge Sara propagatione gloriantium & gentiles hoc nomine despicientium. Rupertus Tuitiensis dicit, Apostolum improbare omnes alias genealogias post illam Christi priorum omnium finem introductas, id quod tamen Principum vel aliorum genealogiis ob causam politicam annotatis fraudi esse non debet.

Q. 2. Quis sit usus huius genealogiae Christi ab Evangelistis annotatae? Resp. Probat haec genealogia. 1. veritatem humanae Christi Naturae, quod ex hominibus verus homo natus sit. Sic ergo Matth. & Luc. probant Christi humanitatem contra Valentin. Manich. Marcior. sicut Iohanes divinitatem contra Ebion Cerinth. 2. veritatem fundamentalis Christianae fidei articuli, quod Christus sit promissus ille Messias in N. T. exhibitus, cùm sit Abrahae ac Davidis filius, ex quorum semine verus Messias erat nasciturus. Sanè genealogia illa directè & immediate non probat, Christum esse verum Messiam in V. T. promissum, in N. exhibitum, proprietatem tamen & conditionem supplet, quae in promisso Messia necessariò requirebatur, videlicet prognatum esse ex semine Davidis. Hoc nomine Christum repudiabant, quod putarent, eum non esse ex semine Davidis. Ioh. 7. v. 49. & 52. Osiander in Harm. statuit, genealogiam istam Matthaei propter duo hominum genera praecipuè positam esse, quorum unum fuit corum, qui vel Christum ex virgine nasci debere, vel Iesum ita natum esse, nondum comprehendebant. Alterum eorum, qui licet Mariam de domo Davidis ortam, Iesumex ea sine opera virili natum esse non abnuerent, tamen si Iosephus ex alia, quàm tribu Iudae originem duxisset, asserturierant, Mariam cum filio suo non in eam tribum, ex qua nata, sed in qua fuisset matrimonio collocata, referri debere, propterea, quod coniuges, quamvis adhuc virgines sint una caro. Utrumhoc hominum genus, cùm Christum è semine Davidis nasci oportere scirent, nisi Iosephum Mariae coniugem Davidis nepotem agnovissent, firmum argumentum, quod Iesus Mariae filius verus Christus non esse posset, se habere credidissent. Utrorumvel errori succurrere, vel infirmitati mederi Evang. voluit.

3 Firmitatem divinae promissionis. Diabolus per gravissima scandala & atrocissimas persecutiones contra lineam Messiae excitatas complementum divinae promissionis impedire conatus fuit, sed ex hac genealogia ab Abrahamo per Davidem ad Christum usque deducta agnoscimus, liberatam esse fidem datae promissionis in Christo, ex semine Abrahae & Davidis nato.

4 Conformitatem verae & salvificae fidei in Patriarchis, Prophetis & aliis fidelib. V. T. ex parte una, & credentibus in N. T. ex parte altera. Quem enim illi expectarunt venturum, in illum hi credunt iam exhibitum. Utrique non alia ratione, quàm per gratiam Iesu Christi salvari credunt, Act. 15. v. 10.

5. Habet denique haec genealogia annexam consolationis suavitatem, quippe ex quâ elucet, in solatium nostrae infirmitatis & vilitatis, non viles solùm homines, sed etiam gravissimis peccatis inquinatos inter Christi maiores extitisse. Rupertus in hunc locum: Sicut mori dignatus est pro peccatoribus: ita nasci dignatus est de peccatoribus. In hac Christi genealogia recensentur non solùm Reges & Duces, sed etiam plebei & ignobiles; non solùm viri, sed etiam foeminae; non solùm Iudaei, sed etiam gentiles; non solùm iusti, sed etiam peccatores, ut in omnium consolationem ac salutem Christum natum esse intelligamus Conf. Luth. tom. 4. Latin. f. 292.

Hieron. lib. 1. Comment. in Matth. cap. 1. Not andum in genealogia Salvatoris nullam sanctarum assumi mulierum, sed eas, quas Scriptura reprehendit, ut qui propter peccatores venerat, de peccatoribus nascens omnium peccata deleret. (Contrarium statuit Iac. Faber, qui omnes illas mulieres excusat. Rahabem dicit fuisse hospitam, non meretricem, Bathsebe per vim à Davide raptam, proinde potiùs ob iustitiam earum fieri mentionem) Lemnius lib. 3. de occ. Nat. mirac. cap. 1. In enumeranda Christi generatione recensentur, qui extra coniugii statum prognati, quod ipsum studio ac datâ operâ factum interpretatur Chrysostomus bomil. 3. in Matth. ne quis intumescat progenitorum dignitate, nec aenimum abiiciat, si humiles abiectossortitus est.

Q. 3. Quomodo apparens contrarietas inter genealogiam Matthaei & Lucae concilianda?

1. Quidam statuunt, apud Matth. & Lucam esse tantùm nomina diversa, homines eosd. quo nomine Melanchthonem idem sentientem perstringit Conzenius, Sed haec sententia meritò repudiatur.

2. Beza producit Codicem venerandae vetustatis, in quo genealogia Christi sicut apud Matthaeum descendendo, sic apud Lucam ascendendo, iis tantum adiectis, quos Matthaeus in tesseradecadibus constituendis praeterierat, ad Salomonem non ad Nathanem caeteris sursum ad Adamum usque invariatis deducit. Sed reliqui Codd. omnes repugnant. Hisce ergo ac similibus conciliandi modis praetermissis.

Resp. De hac conciliatione in genere notandum.

1. Eo tempore, quo Matthaeus & Lucas hasce genealogias annotarunt, successio familiae Davidicae non solùm publicè omnibus adhuc nota erat, verùm etiam certis voluminibus iam inde â Davide comprehensa. Euseb. lib. 1. Hist. Eccl. cap. 6. unde ne ipsi quidem Pontifices, scribae ac Pharisaei hostes Christi acerrimi istis temporibus quidquàm in illis genealogiis reprehendere potuerunt. Christus voce totius populi, palmas praeferentis, vocabatur filius David. Nec eius accusatores vel apud praesidem, vel apud populum quaestionem de familia, ex qua natus fuit, ipsi moverunt, non praetermissuri utique, nisi liquidò constitisset, Christum esse ex genere Davidis.

2. Iudaei duplices habuerunt genealogiarum libros. Unius generis libris complectebantur genealogias propriè sic dictas, in, quibus recensebatur, quomodo per naturalem generationem & propagationem alter ex altero natus fuerit, atque alter alteri secundùm generationem in prosapia, sangvine & linea descendente successerit. Alterius generis libri continebant genealogias successionum in here ditate & regimine, in quibus recensebatur successio in hereditate & regno, in quo saepe quis dicitur filius prioris & nomen eius assumsit, qui verè filius prioris non fuit. 1. Paral 3. v. 16. Luc-e propositum fuit, recensere genus Christi naturale, ut ostenderet, Christum ortum ex Davide secundum promissionem 2. Sam. 7 v. 12. quia genus Christi ducit inde ab Adamo, primo humani generis parente, & quia illud deducit â Davide per Nathanum, ex quo Christum ortum esse oportet, cùm non sit ortus ex Salomone, quippe cuius genus in Iechonia fuit extinctum. Matthaeo verò propositum fuit, recensere genus praecipuè legale, ut ostenderet, Christum legitimè succesisse in regnum Davidis secundum alteram promisionem superiori annexam. Itaque per Salomonem descendit ad Iechoniam, cùm tamen ex Salomone Christus ortus non sit, sed tamen illi in regno legitimè successit, quia ortus est ex Nathane, ad cuius posteros in Sealthiele principatus legitimè translatus est, Iechonia Salomonita sine success. naturalibus extincto.

3. Eusebius d. l. & Nicephorus lib. 1. Hist. Eccl. cap. 11. ex Iulii Aphricani Epist. ad Aristidem de Evangelior. consonantia haec adducunt. Apud gentem Israël generationum nomina nunc secundùm Naturae, nunc etiam secandùm legis ordinem numerantur. Naturae quidem successiones habentur, quae ex seminis vel sangvinis veritate descendunt; legis autem, cùm quis filius alio generante substituitur sub nomine fraetris defunctisine liberis, &c. A singulis itaque Evangelistarum utriusque modi commemorata sucessio est, id est, ut alter eorum eum, quem genuisset, alter verò eum, qui quasi genuisse videretur, exponeret: & ita fit, ut neutrum Evangelium mentiatur, dum aliud Naturae ordinem, aliud verò legis exequitur regulam.

4. Sicut nurus idiotismo Hebraeo dicuntur siliae, & generi dicuntur filii, s-c ratione mutuae relationis socrus dicuntur matres, & soceri dicuntur patres.

Inde Andr. Osiand. in Harm. statuit, Lu-tam non voluisse contexere genealogiam Iosephi, cùm in primo limine admoneat, Iesum non fuisse filium Iosephi, sed tantùm putatum. Ergo quod Iosephus dicitur filius Eli, sic accipiendum esse, quod Iosephus fuerit filius Iacobi, gener verò Eli, illius s-. Eli, qui vero nomine dictus Iehotakim, fuit Pater virginis Mariae & avus Christi maternus secundùm carnem, inde etiam Evangelistam simpliciter de Iosepho dicere, qui fuit Eli, ut nobis liberum esset subintell-gere, gener, & non filius.

Addit, absurdum esse, si statuatur, genealogiam Iosephi ab utroque Evangel sta proponi, virginis autem genealogiam prorsus negligi, cùm tamen summa rei ab ipsa dependeat.

5. Propria Hebraeorum nomina ad linguas exteras migrantia saepè â scriptoribus unius literae aut Syllabae permutatione â primogenia origine deflectunt.

6. Genealogiam Christi directam uterque Evangelista recensuit, sed Matthaeus κατιούσανdeclivem, sive descendentem; Lucas άνιούσανacclivem sive ascendentem. Est autem illa declivis ratio magis Naturae accommoda, ideoque usitatior.

Matthaeus genealogiam propriè sic dictam, generis sc. & sanguinis non recenset, sed genealogiam successionis, hereditatis & officii regii, unde etiam tres Reges in linea descendente, Ochoziam, Ioas & Amasiam omittit. Lucas verò enumerat eos, qui in linea rectâ naturali per generationem tanquam patres & filii naturales sibi successerunt. Iustin. in qq. & resp. ad Orthod. q. 131. pag. 372. In genealogia Lucae solus Eliηωτά τόν νόμονlegitimus vel potiùs legalis est Iosephi pater, ab Eli autem ad Nathan usque, qui ordine recensentur omnes, naturales eorum, qui illis subiunguntur, sunt silii,νποτεταλμένοι ηατά φνσιν,qui quidem eâ, quam Eli obtinet ad Iosephum necessitudine, Iosephi solius (legalis) caeterorum verò omnium naturales habentur avi. Alii tamen contra statuunt, Eli fuisse naturalem Iosephi patrem, Iacobum verò legalem.

7. Iosephus & Maria non ex sangvine & prosapia Salomonis, sed ex Sangvine & posteritate Nathanis, qui Salomonis frater fuit 2. Sam. 5. v. 14. 1. Paral. 3. v. 5. & consequenter exposteritate Davidis descendebant: David enim ex Bathsabea Salomonem & Nathanem genuit, ad cuius posteros, deficiente solio Davidin linea Salomonis, regnum post captivitatem Babylonicam translatum est. Sententiae tamen huic, quôd linea Salomonis in Ochozia sine liberis moriente defecerit, eique in regno successerit Ioam ex posteritate Nathanis, â quibusdam opponitur. 1. quod Ioam fuerit naturalis Ochoziae filius2. Reg. 11. v. 2. 2. Paral. 22. v. 11. cumprimis 1. Paral. 3. v. 11. 2. Paral. 23. v. 3. 2. quod Salomoni aequè ac Davidi promittatur regni thronus stabiliendus in a-ternum2. Sam. 7. v. 13.Psal. 89. v. 21.Confer1. Reg. 11. v. 11.& seqq. cap. 15. v. 4. 1. Paral. 17. v. 12. cap. 22. v. 10. 3. quod Salomo non solùm typum Christi gesserit, sed etiam eius secundùm carnem parens fuerit.Psal. 72.per tot.Hebr. 1. vers. 5.

8. Zorobabel genuit tum Abiud, tum Mesullam sive Resam. Abiud genuit Eliakim, hic Azor, hic Sadoc, hic Achim, hic Eliud, hic Eleazar, hic Matthar, hic Iacob, hiIoseph virum Mariae, ex qua natus est Christus. Mesulla sive Resa genuit Iohannam, hic Iudam, hic Ioseph, hic Simei, hic Matathiam, hic Maath, hic Nangae, hic Esli, hic Naum, hic Amos, hic Mattathiam, hic Ioseph, hic Iannam, hic Melchi, hic Levi, hic Matthat, hic Heli, hic Mariam uxorem Iosephi. Priori lineae insistit Matthaeus, posteriori Lucas. Confer Lutherum tom. 5. Witteb. fol. 525. b. Cornel. Bertramum lucubrat. Franckenthal. cap. 6.

9. Matthaeus Christi genealogiam per Salomonem ad Iosephum maritum Mariae; Lucas verò per Nathanem alterum Davidis filium ad parentes Mariae deducit, cuius diversitatis causa haec est, quod Matthaeus Iosephi, Lucas Mariae genus describere voluit, ut sic utraque Persona Ioseph, putativus Christi parens, & Maria ipsius uxor ostenderetur â Davide descendisse. A Zorobabel enumerat Matthaeus maiores Iosephi, cui Maria erat desponsata, Lucas verô maiores Mariae, ut ex utraque genealogia manifestaretur, Christum esse Davidis filium, tùm Naturae, tum connubiorum iure. Osiand in Harm. Divinâ providentia factum est, quod Lucas scripserit genealogiam virginis, sicut Matthaeus scripsit genealogiam Iosephi sponsi ei, ut quoquo te vertas, sive Mariam exparentibus aestimes, sive ex marito, semper tamen eam cum filio suo in domo & familia Davi lis invenias.

Q. 4. An maiores Christi apud Matthaeum fuerint ex tribu Iuda; illi ver-, -uos Lucas recenset, ex tribu Levi? Baronius in Apparat. n 30.

ex Augustino, Hilario, Iulia no, Toletano &c. hac de re sic disserit: Matthaeus, qui regiam in Christo personam instituer at insinuare, naturales Christi ex Regibus Iudaeorum generationes enumerat. Lucas verò Sacerdotalem in Christo personam ostendere volens, generationes adoptionis Christi percurrit. Pro qua sententia urgeri posset, quòd Elisabetha filia Aaronis, dicatur Mariae σνγγενης.Luc. 1. v. 5. & 36.

Sed Casaubonus exerc. 1. cap. 13. pag. 94. monet, rationibus parùm firmis motos fuisse Patres, qui ita senserunt. Sciebant, Chrisium non minùs Sacerdotem esse futurum, quàm Regem verum: hoc ipsos permovit, ut ortum illum crederent, tam ex tribu Sacer dotali (Levi) quàm ex tribu Regia (Iuda) pag. 95. subiicit. Falsum est, personas â Luca memoratas ad aliam tribum pertinere, quàm Iudae. Nominum diversitas non satis firmum argumentum est, ut diversas tribus existimemus ab illis describi, eùm Iudaeorum pleriduo nomina habuerint, &νιωσιςassumtio in filium, filiia appellatio ex variis causis contingerēt, put a vel Naturâ, vel ex lege Mosis de semine fratri mortuo excitando Item adoptione vel arrogatione, nec non propter affinitatem. Nam gener socero filius dicebatur, adde successionem in regnum vel privatam hereditatem, nam etiam hi eorum filii censebantur, quibies successerant.

Q. 5. Quomodo ex genealogia, à Matthaeo & Luca descripta, probari possit, Christum ê tribu Iuda ac posteritate Davidis esse, cùm utranon in Christo aut ipsius matre, sed in Iosepho, qui tamen non fuit parens Christi naturalis, terminetur?

Resp. 1. Hieronymus, Chrysostomus, Euthymius, Theophylactush. l. Damascenus lib. 4. Orth. fid. cap. 13. dicunt, non esse consvetudinis Scripturarum, ut mulierum in generationibus ordo texatur. Proinde Evang. genealogiam voluisse deducere ad Iosephum, Patrem Christi putativum. Sed ex. 1. Paral. 2. v. 16. apparet, mulierum quandoque in genealogiis haberi rationem.

2. Chrysost. homil. 3. in Matth. contendit, Evangelistas conatos fuisse ostendere Iudaeis, Christ. esse de semine Davidis atAbrahae, noluisse tamen recenti adhuc tempore novi illius admirandipartus mysterium (de Christo ex Maria virgine nato) Iudaeis esse manifestum, ideoIosephisolùm, qui ex tribu & familia Davidis fuerit, genealogiam pe--exuisse. Sed Luc. 3. 23 Iosephus expressè dicitur putativus Christi Pater.

3. August. lib. 2. de cons. Evang. cap. 1. sufficere existimat, quod Iosephus habitus fuerit Christi Pater: quin & fuisse ipsum Christi patrem, quia fuerit Mariae matris Christi coniunx, non quidem permixto corporis sexu, sed custodito mentis affectu, non coniunctione corporum, sed, quod carius est, coniunctione animorum. Haec Augustini sententia non improbabilis. Quod si namq; is, qui nascebatur ex uxore illius, qui eâ sine liberis relictâ decesserat, eius censebatur, quamvis post mortem ipsius ex alio viro, id est, ex fratre eius nasceretur, quantò magis filius alicuius censendus est is, qui ex ipsius uxore, ipso adhuc vivente, nascitur, nec ab ullo alio viro generatus fuit, licet neque etiam ab ipso fuerit generatus. Cùm legitimo matrimonio iunctus esset Iosephus virgini Mariae, essetque proinde Mariae corpus, corpus illius, quin & ipse cum esset una caro, iure, etsi non re, (sunt enim coniuges una caro iure, priusquam convenerint, re autem pòst) proles ex Mariae carne genita ex eius carne genita meritò censetur.

4. Quidam censent, Iosephi genealogiam propterea descriptam, ut existimationi hominum, quâ Christus Iosephi filius habebatur, satis fieret. Sed noluit Spiritus Sanctus homines in falsâ opinione per Evangelistas confirmare, quinimò disertè eam refellit Luc. 3. v. 23.

5. Quidam ergo dicunt, in Iosephi persona secundùm legemNum. 36. v. 5.genus Mariae comprehendi, quoniam duodecim tribubus Israëlitarum in terra sancta non licuit extra tribum nubere. Isid. Pelus. lib. 1. Epist. 7. Andr. Osiand. sententiae illi, quòd ex eadem tribu uxor fuerit ducenda, haec opponit argumenta. 1. testimonium illud non inveniri in Hebraea veritate. 2. Mosen id non scripsisse, quod ipse non observavit, neenim uxorem duxit ê tribu sua. 3. Undecim tribus non legem DEI, sed iuramentum suum praetexere, quô minus filias suas Beniamitis elocare poterini Iud. 11. 4. Iosabeam sororem Regis lorami de tribu Iudae nupsisse I-iadae Pontifici de tribu Levi. 2. Paral. 22. 5. Elisabetham fuisse de tribu Levi, & tamen dici cognatam Mariae. Sed enim quamvis possent matrimonia apud Hebraeos copulari inter personas, quae non essent eiusd. trib. non tamen hoc licebat, cùm foeminae essent paternorum bonorum unicae heredes, tunc enim tenebantur viro nubere, qui non solùm esset exeadem tribu, sed etiam ex-dem familia. Cùm ergo B. Virgo nullos habuerit fratres ac paternorum bonorum heres viro familiae suae nupserit, texens Evangelista catalogum maiorum Iosephi, & illum â Davide genus duxisse ostendens, eadem, operá B. Virg. eiusd. stirpis & familiae fuisse ostendit.

Euseb. Emissenus homil de nat. Mariae latè probat, Mariam, cùm esset unigenita, aut saltem nullos haberet frartres, à parentibus elocatam fuisse contribuli. Euthymius in cap. 19. Ioh. v. 25. statuit, Mariam fuisse u-icam parentum suorum filiam, quae non tantùm nullos fratres, sed nec ullas habuerit sorores.

6. Simplicissimè respondemus, Lucam genealogiam Mariae, Matthaeum Iosephi describere, sicque utroque modo ostendi, Christum ex familia Davidis descendere, ut monuimus superius n. 4. & 9. Tob. 6. v. 7. dicit Raguel, filiam suam unicam debere coniungi cognationi suae.

Q. 6. Quod si ergo Maria fuit ex tribu Iuda, quomodo Elizabetha dicitur eiusσνγγενηςsive cognataLuc. 1. v. 36.cum illa fuerit de filiabus Aaron. v. 5.

Resp. Quidam existimant, has duas tribus fuisse coniunctas. Exod. 6. 2. Paral. 22. Observandum verò, voculam σνγγεννης sumi 1. latè pro tota gente Iudaica & omnibus ex illa ortis. Rom. 9. v. 3.Marc. 6. v. 4.Rom. 16. v. 7. 2. strictè, prout denotat propinquos sive sangvine iunctos, Luc. 1. v. 58.cap. 4. v. 44.Act. 10. v. 24. Si latiorem significationem amplectamur, res est in propatulo. Si quis strictam significationem urgere velit, respondendum erit, Levitam quendam, cui per legem in quamvis tribum abnubere licebat (eò quod Levitae inter duodecim tribus non numerarentur, ac sortem terrae propriam nullam haberent, ideoque nullam confusionem possessionum abnubendo inducerent) duxisse quandam ex maioribus Elifabethae è tribu Iuda oriundam, quo modo Elisabetha & cognata Mariae, & filia Aronis esse potuit.

## 1:18
v. 18. μνηςεν θείςης. Augustin, De nuptiis & concupiscentiâ cap. 11, lib. 23 Contra Faustum cap. 8, rightly holds that Mary was not only espoused and promised to Joseph, but also given over, because the Angel in v. 20 calls Mary Joseph's wife, Luke ch. 2. v. 5. μεμνηςενμένην λνναίηα. Moreover Ambrose adds in lib. 2 on Luke: It cannot be that Scripture frequently calls Mary Wife, for what is set forth is not the taking away of virginity, but the attesting of wedlock and the celebrating of the marriage. Finally, no one sends away whom he has not received, and therefore he who wished to send her away confessed that he had received her.Luke 2, 5. μεμνηςενμένη she is said to be already a wife. Theophylactus, Idyllion 18. μναςησας έλέναν όνεωτεσέος υἱὸς. Whom the younger son of Atreus, though only betrothed, had taken as his wife, Helen. The Syriac version here uses the word , which signifies not only espoused but given over, purchased, which suits a wife rather than a Spouse.

For the maiden's untarnished reputation to be kept safe, betrothal alone was not sufficient; there was need of true matrimony and of dwelling together in the same house. That only betrothals intervened is thought by Origen, Homily 1; Epiphanius, Heresy 78; Nazianzen, On the nature of the Savior; Cyril, Catechesis 10; Bernard.

Christ willed to be born from a betrothed woman. 1. That he might honor marriage, just as he had honored virginity by his birth from a virgin . 2. That the virginal birth might be hidden from the devil. Ignatius. 3. That the family from which Christ was born might become known through a man. 4. Lest suspicion arise that Christ had been conceived in fornication. 5. That Joseph might be witness and guardian of her virginal integrity, lest that temple of the Holy Spirit be defamed; for no one would have believed that she had conceived by the working of the Holy Spirit without male seed. 6. That Mary might have a companion and helper in life in the bringing up of the child, in the flight, and in any circumstance whatsoever, so much so that Joseph was father of care, though not of Nature. 7. That it might be signified that the spiritual generation of the sons of GOD likewise takes place from a virgin and Bride, which is the Church, mother of all the faithful. 8. That just as the origin of sin was once drawn from the disobedience of a married virgin, so the origin of righteousness might begin through a betrothed virgin. Compare Ambrose on Luke book 2, page 16; Jerome against Helvidius, vol. 3, p. 2; Damascus book 4, On the Orthodox Faith, chapter 15; Bernard homily 2 upon Missus est; Thomas in the Golden Treasury.

Πσίν η συνελθεῖν αὐτοὺς. -ννέσχεθαι denotes marital intercourse by means of ένχημισμόν, in which sense the Hebrews use the word ⟦f3 he knew, Gen. 4. v. 1. They also have a similar phrase when they say to go in unto a woman. Gen. 6. v. 4. chap. 16. v. 2. and 4. Theophylact expounds μιληναι.

They err therefore who refer this to domestic cohabitation, such being the meaning: Before they had come together into the same dwelling; for after the betrothal had taken place the Bride was immediately led away into the house of the Bridegroom, according to the testimony of Chrysostom, homily 4 on Matthew. Wherefore since the betrothal had already taken place, as appears from what precedes, there was no need of joining of dwellings or leading into the house, which today customarily happens finally on the very day of the wedding itself. *(The blessed Luther seems to have looked toward this in the German version. However, whether it were perpetual and universal that the Bride should pass over immediately from the day of the espousals into the Bridegroom's house, while nevertheless this did not happen presently, is rendered quite probable by those things which will soon be said: But to that which follows, μη φοβηθης παραλαβεῖν, & then, παθέλαβε την λννάιηα αὐτοῦ (by which also Hugo Grotius was moved, who takes τό συνελθεῖν here of dwelling-place, not truly of conjugal union; he is answered shortly after, in the notes on verse 20. Moreover the Arabic notably rendered before they knew each other. It is indeed established in what sense the word to know is used in Scripture concerning spouses: nay even in secular writers both Greek and Latin, as D. Fesselius showed, Adversaria Sacra p. 121. The Arabic itself uses this verb in this sense at v. 25 of this chapter.)

Unless the virgin had been joined to Joseph in such a way that she could be known by him without a mark of disgrace—which could not happen before the solemnity of the wedding—and unless she had been married to him for so long a time that -x she might be believed by all to be pregnant from the marital bed-chamber, sufficient provision would not have been made both for the reputation of the virgin and for the honor of the son about to be born.

Εν λαςθί ἔχουσα. This is a periphrasis of pregnancy, customary among the Greeks, in which the word of the embryo is understood. The Syrian has the term derived from the Hebrew belly/womb. Cyprian: He was not infused, but found in the womb without male seed.

The little word ένθέθη refers to the unexpected outcome, that beyond expectation she was observed to carry a womb [be pregnant].

Εη πνεύματος άλίούς. Syr. In this place the particle σημιονρλιηως, denotes not the material cause, but the efficient cause, in which meaning it is used at Rom. 11. v. 36. where all things are said to be from God: σπερματιηως. is taken, not . For Christ was not of the substance of the Holy Spirit, but of his power; nor was he conceived by generation, but by command and blessing, says Faustus Bishop, On the Rule of Faith ch. 4, from Augustine sermon 6 on the seasons. Athanasius in the Oration against Arius p. 51: She was found having in her womb from the Holy Spirit—not that the Father of our Savior should be called the Holy Spirit, so that two fathers would be believed, but because with the Father and the Son the same Holy Spirit is co-worker and of one power. Ambrose, book 2 On the Holy Spirit ch. 5: What is from someone is either from his substance or from his power. From his substance, as the Son, who says: Out of the mouth of the Most High I came forth; from his power, as that saying: one God, from whom are all things. How therefore did Mary have him in her womb? If as from the substance of the Holy Spirit, then the Spirit was turned into flesh and bones? Not so. But if the Virgin conceived as from his working and power, who will deny the Spirit to be creator? Augustine in the Enchiridion ch. 37: It must not be conceded that whatever is born from someone straightway is named his Son—otherwise those who are born of water and the Spirit would have to be called sons of water. The Schoolmen: When we say 'conceived of Mary,' it is of the material; when we say 'of the Holy Spirit,' it is of the potential. Hugh Etherianus On Heresies vol. 3, Bibliotheca Patrum p. 1144: The Holy Spirit is not the Father of Christ, because he is not from him as from a Father, but rather from him who prepared the fruitful womb for the consubstantial Word and created the flesh without the law of mingling, in a manner wholly divine and ineffable, so that he exists not as the son of the H.S., but according to Nature of the most holy Virgin. This must be opposed to those who, following Augustine's sermon on the season, determined that the Holy Spirit served as seed, whom there he rightly calls most criminal. For neither in the conception of Christ was any decision made out of the substance of the Holy Spirit—for he is immutable—or infusion of some matter, for thus Christ would be the son of him from whom that seed was drawn; but the conception took place through the immediate working of the Holy Spirit.

And let us look back at the purpose of this account. Joseph, who was ignorant of this mystery and of the divine working (concerning the immediate action of the Holy Spirit ένερλεία in the conception), is meanwhile not denied to have understood that Christ was conceived of Mary. *(for Scripture itself sufficiently hints at this very thing, when everywhere it asserts the truth of Christ's flesh, as Luc. 1. v. 42.Ebr. 2. v. 14.Rom. 1. v. 3.c. 9. v. 5.Gal. 4. v. 4.)* That phrase, of the Holy Ghost, comprises three things. 1. άμεσο ένέρλειαν, that he gave the Virgin the faculty of conceiving offspring without male seed, beyond the order of Nature. 2. θανμάσιον άλιασμόν, that he sanctified those drops of blood from which the body of the Son of GOD was formed, and cleansed from them the poison of sin. 3. άααητον ένωσιν, that he united the divine and human Nature into the one person of Christ. Compare Exeg. art. on the person of Christ §. 107.

Moreover προσσιορισμός is not to be referred to all that preceded, for neither did Joseph, who perceived his wife to be pregnant, understand her to be pregnant by the operation of the Holy Spirit , much less did others understand this mystery, but it must be referred to the nearest word, having him in her womb. Therefore indeed the Evangelist added this at once, lest anyone suspect that she had conceived by adultery.

Q. 1. Why should the conception of Christ have taken place not from male seed but from the Holy Spirit? Ans. 1. so that the flesh of Christ might be distinguished from nature in holiness. 2. so that he who was begotten true God from the Father alone without the mother before time would be born true man in time from the mother alone without the father. 3. so that the birth of him who is the fountain of all purity might be free from every stain of impurity.

Q. 2. Since the conception of Christ, being as it were a work ad extra, is common to the whole Trinity, why is it attributed particularly to the Holy Spirit

Ans. 1. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of sanctification, Rom. 3. v. 4. he wiped away the poison of sin from Mary's womb in the conception of Christ, and sanctified that mass out of which Christ was to be formed, Luc. 1. v. 35.

2. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of love, 2. Tim. 1. v. 7. and of grace Zach. 12. v. 10. but now the work of incarnation is singular --pus divine grace and love. As power is attributed to the Father, wisdom to the Son, so goodness is attributed to the Holy Spirit: but the incar-nation is a singular work of divine goodness.

3. The Holy Spirit is the ineffable communion of the Father and the Son Aug. 5. de Trinit. cap. 11. to him, therefore, it was also fitting to unite the divine and human Nature in Christ personally.

4. The Holy Spirit is the finger of GOD, Matth. 12. v. 17. Luc. 11. v. 20. therefore it befitted him to form the body of him who was about to fulfill for us the law written by the finger of GOD, and also to write it on our hearts.

5. The Holy Spirit in the first creation, by brooding over the waters, rendered them fruitful, Gen. 1. v. 2. to the same, therefore, it was fitting in the second creation to render the Blessed Virgin fruitful for conceiving the Savior.

6. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of cleanness and purity, therefore it befitted him to accomplish this work of conception, most foreign to all filth.

* (Moreover the Photinians think, as appears from Socinus in his lib. suas. p. 36. likewise contr. Wuiek. p. 217. Smalcius in exam. 157. err. p. 6. and others;

whose footsteps too they follow after their fashion} The Arminians, as may be seen from their Apol. p. 48, say that Christ among other causes was therefore called the Son of GOD, because he was to be born of a mother whom the power of the Most High was to overshadow, and who by the coming upon her of the Holy Spirit was to bear a child in her womb. Indeed the Remonstrants write, loc. cit., that nothing stands in the way of its being said that Christ, even by reason of this production, calls him his Father τόν ίδιον or his own proper Father, Ioh. 5. v. 18. But lest they themselves should seem to have been the first among the Reformed to have posited such a cause of the filiation, they bring forward similar passages from Rudolph Gualther on Luke ch. 1, and also from Jerome Zanchi, part 2, de tribus Elohim, lib. 2, c. 6. With whom his countryman Sociinus may see how he agrees, Marcus Friedrich Wendelin, when in his System. Christianae Theol. Mai. lib. 1, c. 14, p. 565, to the Question: Was the Holy Spirit, by whom Christ was conceived, truly and rightly called the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ? answers, and rightly too, negatively. But if the Holy Spirit, for this reason, because through him, while he gave the virgin, by his own άμέδως ένεργέια power, the faculty of conceiving a fetus without male seed, contrary to the order of nature, and likewise while he sanctified that mass from which the body of Christ was formed, that is, cleansed it from every poison of sin (Simon Episcopius, the chief defender of the Arminian sect, does not err lightly, when in his Respons. ad defens. Cameronis c. 13, or tom. 2, p. 291. a, he exclaims: Nay, because the human nature of Christ, produced by the Holy Spirit, is the same as ours, that is, endowed with free will, peccability must have had a place in it.), and finally, while he άααήτω ένωδει united the divine and human nature into the one person of Christ, as was shown above, is called the Father of Christ at his conception, then it follows that, for the same reason, Christ is not to be called the Son of GOD, but rather on account of the eternal generation. Moreover, against the aforesaid error of the Photinians and Arminians we set: 1. The appellation of Christ, for he is called άπάτωρ Ebr. 7. v. 3. according, namely, to his human nature. 2. The procession of the Holy Spirit from Christ. Ioh. 15. v. 26. 3. The proper operation of the Holy Spirit, by which, in the admirable conception of Christ, he had not himself γεννητικῶς, nor πατρικῶς, nor σπερματικῶς, but δημιουργικῶς. 4. The suitable exposition of the particle διό Luc. 1. v. 35., exposition, namely, since it is there not οοιτιολογιηή causal, but ουλλογις ιηή rational, that is, it contains the reasoning, conclusion and gathering from all the things premised in v. 31, 32 and 33. 5. of the Bishop's own first among the Armenians Confession: so truly here lib. 4. Instit. c. 9. p. 417. The preposition έκ cannot signify the material cause in this place ( Matt. 1. v. 18.20. ) they prove by these two arguments. 1. because thus Christ would properly have been the son of the Holy Spirit, which is not only foreign to the style of Scripture but also no less absurd than if anyone were to call us sons of the Holy Spirit, because we are said to be begotten of the Holy Spirit, that is, regenerated and born again. 2. because thus Christ would have been nothing but spirit. &c. Moreover against the error mentioned of the Photinians and Arminians see more in Mr. D. Calovius Socinianismi profligati pag. 205. seqq. B. D. Feurborn. in Anti-Osterodo Disp. 6. §. 47. B. Par. in Exeg. L. IV. §. 54.

Latin:

v. 18. μνηςεν θείςης. Aug. 1. de nupt. & concup cap. 11. lib. 23. contra Faustum cap. 8. rectè statuit, Mariam non tantùm desponsatam & promissam fuisse Iosepho, verùm etiam traditam, propterea quod Angelus v. 20. Mariam vocet Iosephi coniugem, Lucas cap. 2. v. 5. μεμνηςενμένην λνναίηα. Addit verò Ambros. lib. 2. in Luc. Non tmopeat, quod frequenter Mariam Scriptura Coniugem vocat, non enim virginit atis ereptio, sed coniugii testificatio & nuptiarum celebratio declaratur. Deniquam non accepit, nemo dimittit, & ideò qui volebat dimittere, fateb. acceptam.Luc. 2, 5.μεμνηςενμένη dicitur, quae iam uxor erat. Theoe. Idyll. 18. μναςησας έλέναν όνεωτεσέος υἱὸς.Qui despons. duxerat Helenam iunior filius Atrei. Syrus h. l. utitur voce quae non modo despons. sed traditam, emtam signif. quod in coniug.

potiùs, quàm Sponsam competit. Ut fama integra servaretur virgini, non satis erat desponsatio, opus erat vero matrimonio & cohabitatione in iisdem aedibus. Sola Sponsalia intercessisse, putat Origen homil. 1. Epiph. haeref. 78. Nazianz. de naturâ Salvat. Cyrill. Catech. 10. Bernhardus.

Voluit Christus ex desponsatâ nasci. 1. ut honoraret coniugium, sicut virginitatem honorav-rat suâ ex virgine nativitate. 2. ut partus virginalis lateret diabolum. Ignat. 3. ut familia, ex qua Christus natus, per virum innotesceret. 4. ne suspicio oriretur, Christum ex fornicatione susceptum. 5. ut Iosephus esset virginalis integritatis testis atq; custos, ne templum illud Spiritus S. infamaretur, nullus enim credidisset, eam ex Spiritus S. operatione sine virili semine concepisse. 6. ut Maria haberet vitae socium & adiutorem in pueri educatione, in fuga, & in quavis fortuna, adeoq; ut Iosephus esset pater curae, etsi non Naturae. 7. ut significaretur, Spiritualem filiorum DEI generationem itidem fieri ex virgine & Sponsâ, quae est Ecclesia, mater omnium fidelium. 8. ut sicut origo peccati ex coniugatae virginis inobedientia quondam tracta est, ita origo iustitiae per virginem inciperet desponsatam. Confer Ambros. in Lucam lib. 2. pag. 16. Hieron. contra Helvid. tom. 3. p. 2. Damase lib. 4. de Orth. fid. cap. 15. Bernhard. homil. 2. super Missus est. Thomam in cat. aurea.

Πσίν η συνελθεῖν αὐτοὺς. -ννέσχεθαι congressum maritalem per ένχημισμόν denotat, quo sensu Hebraei utuntur voce cognovit,Gen. 4. v. 1. Habent iidem phrasin affinem, quando dicunt ingredi ad mulierem.Gen. 6. v. 4.cap. 16. v. 2. & 4. Theophylactus exponit μιληναι.

Errant igitur, qui hoc referunt ad contubernium domesticum, ut fit sensus: Priusquam in easdemaedes convenissent; post factam enim desponsationem Sponsa statim in domum Sponsi deducebatur, teste Chrysostomo homil. 4. in Matth. Quare cùm, iamdum facta fuerit desponsatio, ut constat ex praecedentibus, non opus erat domicilii coniunctione vel deductione in domum, quae hodie ipso nupitarum demum die fieri consvevit. *(Ec huc respexisse B. Lutherus videtur in versione Germanicâ. Ut ut verò non satis constet, an perpetuum fuerit ac universale, ut Sponsa statim â sponsalium die in Sponsi domum transiret, quin tamen impraesentiarum factum id sit, admodùm probabile redditur ex iis, quae mox dicentur: Ad illud verò, quod sequitur, μη φοβηθης παραλαβεῖν, & deinde, παθέλαβε την λννάιηα αὐτοῦ (quibus & Hugo Grotius motus, τό συνελθεῖν de domicilii, non verò de tori coniunctione h. l. accipit paulò pòst respondetur, in notis adv. 20. Coeterùm Arabs notanter reddidit antequam sese cognoscerent. Constat verò, quo sensu cognoscendi verbum in Scr. de coniugibus adhibeatur: Imo etiam in profanis scriptoribus tum Graecis, tum Latinis, ceu ostendit D. Fesselius Adv. S. p. 121. Arabs ipse, hôc sensu, verbo isto utitur v. 25. huius capitis.)

Nisi ita coniuncta fuisset virgo Iosepho, ut absq; infamiae notâ ab eo cognosci potuisset, quod ante nuptiarum solennitatem fieri non poterat, ac nisi tanto tempore ei nupta fuisset, quanto -x connubiali thalamo gravida esse ab omnibus credi potuisset, non satis consultum fuisset tum virginis famae, tum nascituri filii honori.

Εν λαςθί ἔχουσα. Periphrasis est praegnantis, apud Graecos usitata, in qua subintelligitur vocabulum embryonis. Syrus habet nomen deductum ex Hebraeo venter. Cyprian Non infusus, sed inventus est in utero sine virili semine.

Vocula ένθέθη respicit eventum inopinatum, quod praeter expectationem observata sit uterum gerere.

Εη πνεύματος άλίούς. Syr. Vocula exnon denotat hoe loco causam materialem, sed efficientem, in qua significatione usurpatur Rom. 11. v. 36. ubi omnia dicuntur esse ex Deo: accipitur σημιονρλιηως, non σπερματιηως.Christus enim non de Spiritus S. substantiâ, sed de eius potentiâ; nec generatione, sed iussione & benedictione conceptus est, inquit Faustus Episc. de ratio. fidei cap. 4. ex August. serm. 6. de temp. Athanasius in Orat. contra Arium p. 51. Inventa est in utero habens de Spiritu Sancto, non quòd Salvatoris nostri pater dicendus Spiritus S. ut duo credantur patres, sed quòd cum Patre & Filio idem Spiritus S. cooperarius & unius potestatis est. Ambros. lib. 2. de Spiritu S. cap. 5. Quod ex aliquo aut ex eius substantiâ, aut ex potestate est. Ex substantiâ, sicut Filius, qui ait: Ex ore Altissimi prodii: ex potestate, sicut illud: unus Deus, ex quo omnia. Quomodo ergo in utero habuit Maria? siquasi ex substantiâ Spiritus S. ergo Spiritus in carnem & ossa conversus est? non utia. Si quasi ex operatione & potestate eius Virgo concepit, quis neget Spiritum creatorem. Aug. in Enchir. cap. 37. Non concedendum, ut quod ex aliquare nascitur, continuò eiusdem Filius nuncupetur, aliàs illi, qui ex aqua & Spiritu nascuntur, aquae filii dicendi erunt. Scholastici: Cùm dicimus de Maria, est de materiale; cùm dicimus de Spiritu Sancto, est de potentiale. Hugo Aethereanus de haeretibus tom. 3. Bibl. Patrum p. 1144. Non est Christi Pater Spiritus S. quia non ex eo est, tanquam ex Patre, sed ut ex eo, qui praeparavit uterum facundum consubstantiali Verbo, carnema condidit absa lege commixtionis, divino prorsus & ineff abili modo, quo fit, ut non S S. filius, sed sanctissimae Virginis secundùm Naturam existat. Opponendum hoc illis, qui referente Aug. serm. de tempore, statuerunt, Spiritum S. fuisse pro semine, quos ibid. meritò vocat sceleratissimos. Neq; enim in conceptione Christi facta est decisio aliqua ex substant. Spiritus S. est enim immutabilis, vel infusio alicuius materiae, sic enim Christus esset illius filius, â quo semen illud desumtum, sed immediatâ Spiritus S. operatione facta est conceptio.

Ac respiciendus huius descriptionis scopus. Informatur Ioseph, qui erat mysterii huius & operationis divinae (de immediatâ Spiritus Sancti ένερλεία in conceptione) ignarus, interim non negatur, Christum ex Maria esse conceptum. *(hoc ipsum enim Scriptura satis innuit, quando passim veritatem carnis Christi adserit, uti Luc. 1. v. 42.Ebr. 2. v. 14.Rom. 1. v. 3.c. 9. v. 5.Gal. 4. v. 4.)* Phrasis illa, ex Spiritu S. tria complectitur. 1. άμεσο ένέρλειαν, quod dederit Virgini facultatem sine virili semine praeter Naturae ordinem concipiendi foetum. 2. θανμάσιον άλιασμόν, quòd guttulas illas sangvinis, ex quibus corpus Filii DEI formatum, sanctificaverit, & venenum peccati ex illis terserit. 3. άααητον ένωσιν, quod divinam & humanam Naturam in unam Christi personam univerit. Confer Exeg. art. de persona Christi §. 107.

Porrò προσσιορισμός non est referendus ad totum illud, quod praecessit, neq; enim Iosephus, qui deprehendit, uxorem esse gravidam, Spiritus Sancti operatione gravidam esse intellexit, multò minus alii hoc mystetium intellexerunt, sed referendus est ad proximum verbum, in utero habens. Ideo verò Evangelista statim hoc adiecit, ne quis suspicaretur, eam ex adulterio concepisse.

Q. 1. Quare non ex virili semine, sed ex Spiritu S. conceptio Christi fieri debuerit? Resp. 1. ut in sanctitate caro Christi differret â natura. 2. ut ex sola matre sine patre nasceretur verus homo in tempore, qui ex solo patre sine ma te verus Deus erat natus sine tempore. 3. ut ab omni impuritatis labe immunis esset eius nativitas, qui est fons omnis puritatis.

Q. 2. Cùm conceptio Christi, ut pote opus ad extra sit toti Trinitati communis, quare peculiariter tribuatur Spiritui S.

Resp. 1. Spiritus S. est Spiritus sanctificationis,Rom. 3. v. 4. is in conceptione Christi venenum peccati ex Mariae viscerib. extersit, & massam illam, ex qua Christus formandus erat, sanctificavit, Luc. 1. v. 35.

2. Spiritus Sanctus est Spiritus dilectionis,2. Tim. 1. v. 7. & gratiae Zach. 12. v. 10. iam verò opus incarnationis est singular --pus divinae gratiae & dilectionis. Sicut Patri potentia, Filio sapientia, sic Spiritui S. bonitas tribuitur: est autem in -arnatio singulare opus divinae bonitatis.

3. Spiritus S. est ineffabilis Patris & Filii communio Aug. 5. de Trinit. cap. 11. illi ergo conveniebat etiam, divinam & humanam in Christo Naturam personaliter unire.

4. Spiritus S. est DEI digitus,Matth. 12. v. 17.Luc. 11. v. 20. illi ergo conveniebat formare corpus eius, qui legem digito DEI scriptam pro nobis impleturus, camq; cordibus nostris inscripturus erat.

5. Spiritus S. in prima creatione aquis incubando faecundas reddidit, Gen. 1. v. 2. eidem ergo conveniebat in secunda creatione Beatam virginem ad concipiendum Salvat. saecundam reddere.

6. Spiritus S. est Spiritus munditiei & puritatis, illi ergo conveniebat opus hoc conceptionis ab omni sorde alienissimum perficere.

*(Coeterùm existimant Photiniani, ceu ex Socino in lib. suas. p. 36. item contr. Wuiek. p. 217. Smalcio in exam. 157. err. p. 6. aliisq;
