## 1:19
v. 19. Ιωσήφ δέ ό άνήρ άυτής δίκαιος ων. The Hebrew just is taken also for merciful, just as is received for benefit and almsgiving, which proceeds from justice and kindness, and by which the just are known. Matt. 6. v. 1. έλεημοσύνην the Vulgate rendered justice. Psalm 24. v. 5. the Hebrew the LXX. rendered έλεημοσύνην. *( Dan. 16. to denote mercy, Lud. de Dieu also observes, Animadv. in V. T. p. 396. Let there be added also B. D. Franzius Oraculo LIX. p. 775.)* Therefore because Joseph was merciful and kind, he did not wish to use strict right against his Bride, nor publicly accuse her, so that she might be stoned according to the Mosaic law for breaking the conjugal bond. Deut. 22. v. 20. Peter Chrysologus sermon 146. Rightly just, because pious; and pious, because just, who while he pondered piety lacked cruelty, while he tempered the case kept judgment, while he deferred vengeance escaped the crime, while he shunned the accuser fled the sentence.

-ίκαιος among other things also signifies a moderate and kindly disposition, which έπιεικεία keeping τό άκριβοδίκαιον or thinks at all of pursuing strict right. *(So the prince of philosophers himself lib. 5. Ethicorum Nicom. c. 14. writes τό έπιιικές, , δικάιου τινός όν, βέλτιόν έςι δίκαιον, χαί ουχ ως άλλό τι γένος όν, βέλτιόν έςιτού δικάιου. Τό άυτο άρα δίκαιον χαί έπιεικές. And near the end of the said chapter: φανερόν δέ έκ τούτου χαί έπιεικής τίς ἐστιν. ό γάρ τοιούτων προυιρετικος. χαί πρακτικός. χαί ό μή άκριβοδίκαιος έπί τό χείρον. άγγ έλαττωτικός. &c. and concludes, χαί ήεξις άυτηέπιείκεια, δικαιοσύνη τις ούσα, χαί ούχ έτέρα τις έξις.. Chrysostom on Joseph on c. 1. Matt. hom. 4. p. 31. δίκαιος ούν ων, τούτ έςι χρης ός χαί έπιειμις. the same a little before: δικαιον έντάυθα, τόν ένάρετον έν άπαοι λέγει. )*

The word δίκαιος can also be taken properly for him who is just and acts justly, even as the Syrian renders it by from the Hebrew root which sounds in the Niphal, he was steadfast, upright, firm, so that this is the sense. Joseph did not wish to summon his Spouse at once to court, before the matter had been fully known and perceived. It was proof of rare and utterly unheard-of uprightness, when he saw his Spouse's swelling womb and unmistakable signs of conception, neither to remonstrate with his wife, nor to complain before her parents or relatives, nor to be tormented by jealousy, but merely to suppress his feelings within himself alone, thinking in his mind only about a secret divorce. John Ferus on this passage * (But it is asked: Whether, if Joseph had become firmly persuaded that his betrothed was guilty of adultery, he would himself have been bound by divine law to report the manifest adultery to the magistrates or judges to burden her by his testimony? This doubt is raised by Episcopius in Book 3 of his Institutes of Theology, Section 2, Chapter 7, and he answers negatively, both because GOD willed this to be done only in the crime of idolatry (namely, that all who were privy to it individually, even those not summoned to give testimony, should accuse the guilty) * and because Joseph would have been unworthy of that praise with which the Evangelist adorns him, whereas conversely he would without doubt have done it, if the reason of justice required it, namely to accuse her and burden her with his testimony. It seems that a distinction must be made between the strict rigor of the law, and between έπιείκειαν, with regard being had to circumstances; likewise between different acceptations of the word just. B. D. Chemnitius, Harmony, p. 84. The Law of Deuteronomy 22, verse 21, does not compel the husband to institute such an action: just as the LawNumbers 5, verse 11concerning Jealousies. And righteousness among the Hebrews often signifies gentleness, έπιείκειαν, one yielding something of his right.

Some understand under it the disjunctive particle, however, so that the sense is: Although he was just, yet he did not wish to expose her. Justice urged him to bring before the judges his Spouse, whom he saw to be pregnant, while he knew she had not been known by himself, and consequently suspected that the fault had been committed upon her by another, so that after examining the case they might set forth their judgment against her, by visiting capital punishment upon her. But since he saw her chaste manners, and therefore inclined more toward this opinion than before the espousals—when through human weakness, especially of her sex, she might have admitted a man whom she could still marry if she were freed from that engagement—he preferred rather to take this milder course. Yet we warned above that the exposing of Mary had already preceded by so long a time that others could believe her pregnant from the marriage bed of Joseph.

χαί μή θέλων άυτήν παραδειγματίσαι. Augustine, Letter 59, p. 7, interprets it as setting forth as an example, that is, to make an example upon her, to take care that she should be an example to all, as the Comician speaks, *(see especially Don Laurentius Ramirez de Prado πεντηκοντ. chapter 22).* This word carries the sense of severe censure and public chastening, or τιμωρίας.; Polybius, book 11 of his History, uses χαί μετά τιμωρίας παραδειγματιζόμενον.; Demosthenes κατ άνδρωτιωνος. Παραδειγμαποιήσαι τοίς άλλοις, ήν ωσι μειριω τεροι.; the LXX Num. 25. v. 4. employ it of the public and likewise most grievous punishment of fornicators. This word also finds place when the penalty is not inflicted by a judge, as at Plutarch's account Archilochus is recorded to have παραδειγματίσαι. himself over certain little verses he had published that were scarcely honorable. Fabricius Stapulensis explains this less fittingly: since he did not want to hold her under suspicion in any respect, since he did not want to think anything unfavorable about her. Yet the plan of a private dismissal shows that Joseph certainly thought something unfavorable about her. The Syrian translator has the word : he slandered her, defamed her, stripped her bare, made her public. It is read also Col. 2. v. 15. where in the Greek we find έδειγματισεν.. The Arabic rendered it simply as to expose her, even as the Ethiopic too: for that version employs the word , here

Some interpret it thus: he wished to dismiss her secretly, supposing that a bill of divorce was given. But an adulteress was not granted a bill of divorce; according to the law of Moses she was to be stoned. Therefore this must be understood of a secret withdrawal. Secret dismissal stands opposed to public accusation and judicial censure. έβουλύθη λάτρα άπολύσαι άυτήν.

The Evangelist indicates a twofold motion and affection in Joseph's mind, so to speak mutually counteracting. One, that he was righteous; the other, that he did not wish to disgrace her. By the former is designated hatred of adultery, by the latter love of his wife, whence arose an inclination toward the milder course, namely, toward a secret dismissal. She was his kinswoman, born of parents who were honorable and loving toward her, endowed with chaste manners; therefore he did not wish to decree anything harsher against her. The matter was still hidden, the girl still young, worthy of compassion on account of the virtues shining forth in her; therefore he did not wish to publicly defame her. It belongs to justice not to bring out into public a true crime that remains concealed and cannot be proven.

Question on this passage. Why did the Blessed Virgin not reveal to her Husband the mystery of her conception by the Holy Spirit? Answer: either because she despaired of being able to persuade him of this unheard-of miracle, whose example had never occurred since the very beginning of the world, or because she committed this whole matter to GOD, from whom she knew Elizabeth had learned of it, Luke 1. v. 43. whence she conceived the hope that it would also be revealed to Joseph by divine means. Mary dared not disclose the matter to her husband, lest she incur the mark of presumption, nor let Joseph fall into unbelief, as Zechariah did, nor seem to wish to defend and cover up the crime committed, as suspicion suggested, by some fiction. Ferus on this passage.

Potest etiam δίκαιος propriè accipi pro eo, qui iustus est & iustè agit, sicut & Syrus reddit per â rad. Ebr. quae in Niphal sonat, stabilis, rectus, firmus fuit, ut sit sensus. Rarae & prorsus inauditae probitatis erat argumentum, cùm Sponsae uterum tumentem & indubitata conceptionis signa videret, nec cum uxore expostulare, nec conqueri apud parentes vel affines, nec Zelo-ypia discruciari, sed suos aestus apud se duntaxat premere, tantùm in animo secum de secreto divortio cogitare. Ioh. Ferus h. l. *(Quaeritur verò: Num, si Iosephus desponsatam suam adulterii ream esse certò sibi habuisset persvasum, ipse vi legis divinae obstrictus fuisset, ad deferendam adulterii manifestam ad Magistratus sive Iudices ea-a testimonio suo gravare? Movet hoc dubium Episcopius lib. 3. Instit. Theol. sect. 2. c. 7. ac respondet negativè, tum quòd in crimine idololatriae solo id fieri DEUS voluerit (ut nempe omnes viritatis conscii, etiam non vocati ad testimonium ferendum, sontes accusarent)* tùm quòd elogio isto, quo ipsum Evangelista ornat, indignus Iosephus esset, ac contra ipse etiam facturus sine dubio, si iustitiae ratio postulabat, ut eam accusaret, & testimonio suo gravaret. videtur distingvendum inter strictum iuris rigorem, & inter έπιείκειαν, ratione circumstantiarum habitâ: it. inter diversam vocis iustus acceptionem. B. D. Chemn. Harm. p. 84. Lex Deut. 22. v. 21. non cogit Sponsum, talem instituere actionem: ficut LexNum. 5. v. 11.de Zelotypiâ. Et iustitia apud Ebraeos saepè significat mansvetudinem,έπιείκειαν,de iure suo aliquid remittentem.

Quidam subintelligunt particulam discretivam, tamen, ut sit sensus. Quamvis esset iustus, tamen noluit eam traducere. Iustitia cum impellebat, ut Sponsam, quam gravidam esse videbat, â se autem cognitam non esse noverat, ac proinde ab alio ei-vitium illatum esse suspicabatur, deferret ad iudices, ut illi causâ cognitâ exemplum in eam statuerent, capitis supplicio eam afficiendo: Sed cùm videret castos illius mores, ac proinde in hanc opinionem magis inclinaret, quàm ante Sponsalia secum contracta ex infirmitate humana, praesertim sexus, virum admisisset, cui adhuc nubere posset, si ab istà sponsione esset liberata, mitiorem hanc viam ingredi maluit. Verùm monuimus superius, traditionem Mariae iamdum tanto tempore praecessisse, quanto ex connubiali Iosephi thalamo gravida esse credi ab aliis potuerat.

Ramirez de Prado πεντηκοντ. cap. 22)* Verbum hoc habet significationem severae animadversionis & publicae castigationis sive τιμωρίας. Polyb. lib. 11. Hist. χαί μετά τιμωρίας παραδειγματιζόμενον. Demosth. κατ άνδρωτιωνος. Παραδειγμαποιήσαι τοίς άλλοις, ήν ωσι μειριω τεροι. LXX. Num. 25. v. 4. utuntur de publica, eademq; gravissima scortatorum poena. Verbum hoc etiam locum habet, cum non â iudice poena infligitur, ut apud Plutarchum Archilochus scribitur editis parum honestis verficulis sese παραδειγματίσαι. Fab. Stapulensis minùs commodè explicat, cùm nollet eam in aliquo suspectam habere, nollet de ea quidquam sinistrè cogitare. Atqui consilium dimissionis ocultae, ostendit, Iosephum omninò deea aliquid sinistri cogitasse. Syrus habet verbum traduxit, diffamavit, denudavit, publicum fecit. Legitur etiam Col. 2. v. 15. ubi in Graeco est έδειγματισεν. Arabs nudè reddidit manifestare eam, quemadmodùm etiam Aethiops: utitur enim ille verbo hic

έβουλύθη λάτρα άπολύσαι άυτήν. Quidam sic exponunt, voluit eam occultè dimittere, dato se. repudii libello. Atqui adulterae non dabatur libellus repudii, sed erat iuxta legem Mosaicam lapidanda. Ergo de occulto secessu hoc intelligendum. Occulta dimissio opponitur publicae accusationi & animadversioni.

Geminum in animo Iosephi motum & affectum quasi reciprocantem indicat Evangelista. Unum, quod iustus esset, alterum, quod nollet eam traducere. Priore designatur odium adulterii, posteriore amor coniugis, ex quo facta inclinatio in partem mitiorem, videlicet in occultam dimissionem. Erat consangvinea, erat honestis & sui amantibus parentibus orta, erat castis moribus praedita, ideò noluit durius quid in eam statuere. Res erat adhuc occulta, puella adhuc tenera, ob virtutum, quae in ea relucebant, studium commiseratione digna, ideò noluit cam publicè infamare. Iustitiae est, nec verum crimen, quod est occultum, & probari non potest, proferre in publicum.

Q. hoc loco. Quare B. Virgo Sponso mysterium conceptionis ex Spiritu S. non manifestarit? Resp. vel quod desperabat, se posse crinauditum hoc miraculum, cuius exemplum â primâ inde mundi origine non praecesserat, persvadere, vel quòd DEO totum hoc negotium commisit, â quo Elizabetae illud patefactum fuisse noverat, Luc. 1. v. 43. ex quo spem concepit, fore ut etiam Iosepho divinitus manifestetur. Non audebat Maria marito rem indicare, ne praesumtionis notam incurreret, neve Ioseph in incredulitatem incideret, ficut Zacharias, neve videretur commissum flagitium, ut suspicio ferebat, velle defendere & obumbrare aliquo figmento. Ferus in h. l.

## 1:20
v. 20. This Angel of the Lord was without doubt Gabriel, who had made known to Daniel the Prophet the time of the Messiah's coming, Dan. 9. v. 21. and 24., who shortly before had brought the announcement of the conception to the Blessed Virgin, Luke 1. v. 26. indeed he had even announced to Zechariah the birth of John the Baptist, the precursor of the Messiah. v. 19.

Abulensis q. 55. on Matthew and q. 2. on 1 Kings 9. enumerates four modes of appearances. 1. when the Angel of GOD came having taken the figure of a man, appears and speaks. Judges 6. v. 12. chap. 13. v. 3. 2. when he appears by voice alone, as when a certain voice is emitted to someone awake, with no image of the speaker, which manner GOD appeared to MosesExodus 20. v. 1.Numbers 7. v. 89.and to Samuel1 Samuel 3. v. 4.3. by transformation of the understanding, where God extraordinarily raises someone's understanding in deep mysteries to understand supernaturally, this in two ways, sometimes with έκςάςει or ecstasy2 Corinthians 12. v. 2.sometimes without έκςάςει 2 Kings 3.etc. 4. through impressions upon the imagination, or through dreams μαντικά containing sure divination.

But dreams are either bare όράματα or θεωρηματικά, such visions as represent secret things and future events expressly and explicitly apart from figures and enigmas Genesis 20. v. 3.ch. 31. v. 24. or αλληγορικά, those which are covered and wrapped up with certain figures, allegories and enigmas, so that they cannot be understood without interpretation Genesis 37. v. 6.ch. 41. v. 1.Daniel 2. v. 3. Hugh on this passage. He fittingly appeared to him in sleep, to show that he was lulled as it were by the slumber of ambiguity; for in a certain way the soul sleeps when it wavers in uncertainty.

Ιωσήφ ύιός -αβιδ. The Angel pointedly calls him son of David, as descended from the family of David, so that by the very name he might be reminded of the promise concerning the Messiah made to David. For neither was it unknown to Joseph that the Messiah was expected to be born from the family of David (from which he himself survived along with few others still remaining alive, most of those sprung from that royal stock having been removed by death under Herod's execution, Josephus, book 14, Antiquities, ch. 17, book 15, ch. 1 and 9, Galatinus, On Hidden Things, book 4, ch. 6.). And he knew this too from Isaiah's prophecy, ch. 7. v. 14., that the Messiah would be born of a virgin, so that by this reasoning he could more easily be persuaded by the Angel that Mary was pregnant by the working of the Holy Spirit.

Μή φοβηθής παραλαβεί Μαριάμ τήν γυναωκα σου. But he had already received her before, how then is he commanded to receive her? Resp. In the book on the altercation of the Synagogue and the Church it is reported, that it was not permitted for brides to enter the house of the bridegroom before the wedding. According to this hypothesis it should be established that Mary had only been betrothed to Joseph, but not yet led into the house or received, therefore Joseph was commanded to lead her into his house without any scruple. Bened. Arias Montan. on this passage. Casaub. on this passage παρά both in this place and below chapter 4. verse 5. it has the same force as in παρακαλείν, when it signifies to call to oneself. Therefore παραλαβείν is to take up, to join to oneself. But as we warned above, Chrysostom in homily 4 on Matthew more correctly established, that among the Hebrews it was formerly the custom that the bride was received into the house of the bridegroom immediately after the betrothal was made, of which custom the same book on the altercation of the Synagogue and the Church makes mention. If Mary had not yet been led into the house of Joseph before the conception, it would follow that she conceived not in marriage, but before marriage, and thus among the Jews she could not have escaped the stigma of fornication and the penalty of death established by law, because she did not yet have a husband. Therefore that which Joseph is commanded regarding Mary παραλαβείν, that. 1. is opposed to the plan of secret dismissal. Joseph was thinking of dismissing his bride secretly, therefore he is commanded by the Angel παραλαβειν that is, not to dismiss, nor to give her a bill of divorce: for affirmative words among the Hebrews are put for the contrary negative ones. As to hate for not to love, to receive for not to dismiss. Niceph. book 1 of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 8. Do not doubt to receive her, whom you, as far as in you lies, have repudiated and cast out. Chrysost. on this passage he had repudiated her in his mind, therefore he is commanded to receive her. 2. that is to be understood concerning reception into care, guardianship, and the protection of chastity.

That Mary is called Joseph's wife most take to be said on account of the betrothal, for denomination is often sought from a future event, and in Sacred Scripture things are described not as they now are, but as they shall be, Gen. 1. v. 1.Deut. 22. v. 24. whence a bride immediately after betrothal is called wife, namely promised, pledged, future. Gen. 29. v. 21. give me my wife, that is, my bride; and violation committed upon a bride counts as adultery Deut. 24. v. 1. where to take a wife and to marry her are distinguished. But because nothing required for perfect marriage was lacking in the union of Mary and Joseph, and bodily intercourse belongs not to -υσίαν but only to the use of marriage, therefore it is more correctly said that Mary was truly the wife of Joseph, not by reason of the joining of bodies, but by reason of the joining of souls. Aug., book 1, On Marriage and Concupiscence, ch. 11: Every good of marriage was fulfilled in those parents of Christ: offspring, faithfulness, sacrament. We recognize the offspring in the Lord Jesus himself; faithfulness, because there was no adultery; sacrament, because there was no divorce.

Ibid.: She is called spouse (Mary of Joseph) by the first fidelity of betrothal, which he neither knew by intercourse nor was going to know; nor did the designation of spouse perish or prove false, where there neither had been nor ever would be any mingling of flesh. For she was a virgin, and therefore pleased her husband more holily and more wondrously, when even fruitful without a man, unequal in offspring, equal in faith. Wherefore both deserved to be called faithful parents of Christ, and not she alone mother, but also he father of her, as spouse of his mother, both in spirit, not in flesh.

*(Moreover our men argue against the feigned vow of virginity issued by Mary from this passage thus. Whoever allows herself to be betrothed to another so as to become his wife (for in this regard Mary is called Joseph's wife) has not issued a vow of virginity, else she might seem to mock γάμον άγαμον in contracting it before God and men. Yet Mar. E. against the objections of Bellarmine 1: Mary, after the betrothal was made, issued a vow, Answer: Either she did this unknown to Joseph, or with him consenting. Not beforehand, as the Papists themselves grant, see Cornelius à Lapide on Luke p. 18. a.; and Bellarmine b. 2, On Monks, c. 22, § Here too, and it is evident likewise from 1. Cor. 7. v. 4. nor afterward, as may be gathered from Matth. 1. v. 18. & 19. and especially let it be noted that Joseph still hoped for the consummation of the marriage, and would even have consummated it had the divine conception not intervened, and the same was revealed by the Angel alike to Joseph and to Mary. 2. Mary never had an explicit intention of consummating the marriage, for otherwise she would not have been a virgin in soul, but only in flesh; yet she did not trifle with her husband, but truly gave absolute authority over her body to Joseph: moreover, taught by divine revelation, she knew that Joseph would never seek the consummation of the marriage, and therefore held an explicit will of remaining continent forever. Answer: Of this revelation no trace exists anywhere in Holy Scripture: if such a thing had been done for her, the Evangelists would not have passed it over. 3. She was handed over to Joseph for keeping, however, not betrothed in marriage. Answer: Nay rather, Mary is expressly called μεμνηςευμένη γυνή Luke 2. v. 5. Compare Matth. 1. v. 18. and Luke 2. v. 5. Add that they wished συνελθεῖν v. 18, which word is applied in Holy Scripture to brides and husbands, and denotes conjugal use. see 1. Cor. 7. v. 5. Concerning the saying of Luke 1. v. 34. from which above all the Papists labor to draw strength for their cause, treatment will be given in its place. Let many passages on this matter be compared in B. P. L., On Marriage, § 510; likewise Catholic Confession, book 2, Specimen, part 2, p. 334 sqq.; B. D. Chemnitz, Examination of the Council of Trent, part 3, c. 9, p. 481.)*

Τό γάρ έν άυτή γεννηθέν. Thus in her, just as also from her, Luke 1, verse 36. Gal. 4, verse 4. which Tertullian earnestly urges in his book On the Flesh of Christ. Euthymius observes, that this too is insinuated, that the body of Christ at the first moment of conception was completely formed but without a soul. Beautifully says Tertullian: We do not acknowledge him as Christ who bore nothing of our body, since he received nothing from Mary; for he did not come to us, if he was not seen in our substance.

Εκ πνέυματός ἐστιν άγίου. As not from you, so neither from another man, but from the Holy Spirit. The whole thing brought about is divine. The angel announced, the Father overshadowed, the Holy Spirit prepared the womb. The Son filled it. All things are new, because a new offspring shall be born. Augustine, Enchiridion, chapter 37: What you suspect to be from another man is from the Holy Spirit. The same, Letter 54: It is not a crime, but of the Deity. Jerome, in Exposition of the Catholic Faith: Not as certain criminals mockingly say, do we declare the Holy Spirit to serve as seed, but we say it was wrought by the power and might of the Creator ('Set forth instead of ύπό, Rom. 11. v. 33. has [it], says the Syrian; are Peter Chrysologus, sermon 145. It is not a human lapse, but a divine descent; not man's theft, but GOD'S treasure; not a cause of death, but of life. Athanasius in his Discourses against the Arians proves before an upright judge the divinity of the Holy Spirit from this work of conception. Of such great power or creation of the Holy Scriptures is it shown, he says, that by His cooperation the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, which was given to us in the Sacrament of faith, was formed in the womb of the virgin &c. v. 21. τέξεται δε υίόν Chrysostom observes that it is not said she shall bring forth son, as used to be said in the Scriptures concerning wives who conceived by their husbands, that they bore sons, but absolutely, she shall bring forth a son, just as also the Holy Spirit in Isa. 7. v. 14. and the Angel Luke 1. v. 31. speak, because namely Mary had not conceived this son from Joseph's seed, nor from any man, but she brought forth this son to God alone; although if we consider the fruit of this birth, this son is rightly said to be born both of Mary and to Joseph and to the whole world, in which sense it is said in Isa. 9. v. 6., unto us a child is born.

The name JESUS was not uncommon among the people of GOD, but it was bestowed on all the others only typically and with respect to bodily Salvation; to this little boy alone does it belong really and with respect to spiritual Salvation, just as the Angel immediately explains the reason of the name. After the name was attributed to the Son of GOD manifested in the flesh, all the rest thereafter abstained from it.

Σωζειν more than αύεν. Jesus saves His people from sins. 1. not only with respect to merit, but even with respect to efficacy; not only through the acquisition of this outstanding benefit, but even through its application; not only performing the work of redemption, but also preventing lest remaining sins of weakness still impede those reborn from the inheritance of Salvation. *(B.P. expounds these things at greater length in the Exposition of Topic 4. §. 6. and 7.)*

The Angel speaks in the plural, to show that we are saved through Christ not only from original, but also from actual sins. Isa. 53. v. 6. Tit. 2. v. 14.1. John 1. v. 7. *(let it be noted here too that there is employed in the text the plural their, with the agreement of the Syrian, Arabic and Ethiopian versions: for people is a collective noun, embracing all believers)* The Calvinists gather from this passage that Christ died only for the elect, since He is said to save His people from sins. Calvin on this passage, Piscator in Antithesis, Schafmann p. 43. Against the Remonstrants in the Hague Colloquy page 124. &c. Answer 1. No exclusive particle is added, that He would save only His people from sins, nor is it added that this people consists solely of the elect. 2. Christ Luke 2. v. 32. is called the Savior of Gentiles and Israelites. That is, the Savior of all men. 3. Scripture speaks differently about the acquisition of Christ's merit and differently about its application; the former is universal, the latter becomes particular through the fault of men. *(Compare Gen. 22. v. 18.1. Tim. 2. v. 6.ch. 4. v. 10.Tit. 2. v. 11.Luke 2. v. 10. and see B.P.'s Book on Election §. 118.)*

The Angel intimates three arguments for the divinity of Christ. 1. From being conceived by the Holy Spirit, he intimates the divine majesty of this child, because he has this in common with no man. 2. To save from sins, is a work purely divine. Isa. 43. v. 11. chap. 45. v. 17., since sin committed against infinite good becomes infinite evil. 3. To have a people peculiar and his own, likewise befits GOD alone. Proclus, sermon on faith to the Armenians p. 35. λαός όυκ άν έιη άνθρωπυ, άλλά θεού.

Cassianus lib. 5. de incarn. cap. 1. -sta two things, to free from sins and [to make] his own people, do not befit anyone except him who is by Nature GOD. The Syrian neglected the affinity of the words, for instead of he put he shall quicken, which has the same sense, for he made alive those who were dead in sin.

The emphasis is in this phrase, he shall save his people from their sins: for it is opposed to the Jewish dream concerning liberation from the power of the Romans, which they expected solely from the Messiah; concerning liberation from sin, the source of every evil, they were either not at all solicitous, or they were persuaded that they could acquire it by their own works.

From this passage Conzenius gathers that we are truly freed from sins. To be freed from disease, he says, they are said to be not those in whose bodies pain and wasting remain, but when health and strength are restored καχεξία and infirmity is taken away. Answer. 1. We confess that Christ has merited for us not only imputed but also inherent righteousness. 2. But the latter in this life exists only inchoately. 3. The benefits of Christ must be estimated not only with respect to this life but also the future life. 4. That infirmity remains in us cannot be denied. From the same passage, however, such an argument is rightly woven together against the merits of works. Jesus alone saves his people from their sins. For this exclusive statement is added Acts 4. v. 12. Yet our works are not Jesus. Therefore [they do not save]. The Papists object, that in the same way conclusions can be drawn concerning the Sacraments and faith. Answer: the reasoning is unequal. An exclusive particle added to some cause excludes all the remaining causes established within that kind of causing. Good works are held by the Papists to be a meritorious cause of salvation; therefore rightly are they removed from this kind of causing by the exclusion. But the Sacraments are an instrumental cause on God's side, faith on ours, against which an exclusion of a meritorious cause, when added, is not opposed. John Ferus on this passage: He himself will do it, not the law, not works. For if righteousness comes from the law, then Christ died in vain. He shall save his people from their sins. Moreover, to the argument we form from this place: Christ is Savior. Therefore not the saints—Aegidius Hunnius objects? No—Conradus Cozzius objects: If the preachers of the Gospel are Saviors, much more the saints, who pray for us. But earlier 1. Tim. 4. Answer: the reasoning is unequal. Preachers belong to the order of instrumental cause, but the Saints—to the order of meritorious cause, if we believe the Papists.

v. 20. Angelus hic Domini dubio procul fuit Gabriel, qui tempus adventûs Messiae Danieli Prophetae manifestaverat, Dan. 9. v. 21. & 24. quiq; paulô antè B. Virgini conceptionis nuncium attulerat, Luc. 1. v. 26. quin & Zachariae nativitatem Iohannis Baptistae, Messiae praecursoris, nunciaverat. v. 19.

Abulensis q. 55. in Matth. & q. 2. in 1. Reg. 9. quatuor apparitionum modos numerat. 1. cùm Angelus DEI sumtâ figurâ hominis venit, vide-ur ac loquitur. Iud. 6. v. 12. cap. 13. v. 3. 2. quando apparet solâ voce, ut cùm ad vigilantem aliquem hominem vox aliquae emittitur, nullâ loquentis effigie, quâratione DEUS apparuit MosiExod. 20. v. 1.Num. 7. v. 89.& Samueli1.
