Somnia verò funt vel nudaόράματα sive θεωρηματικά, eiusmodi visa, quae expressè & explicitè citra figuras, & aenigmata repraesentant res arcanas & futuros eventus Gen. 20. v. 3.cap. 31. v. 24. vel αλληγορικά, quae figuris, allegoriis & aenigmatibus quibusdam sunt tecta atq; involuta, ut citra inter pretationem intelligi nequeant Gen. 37. v. 6.cap. 41. v. 1.Dan. 2. v. 3. Hugo in hunc locum. Eleganter apparuit ei in somnis, ut ostenderet, eum sopitum quasi somno ambiguitatis, quodam enim modi dormit animus, cùm in ambiguo fluctuat.

Ιωσήφ ύιός -αβιδ. Angelus notanter cum vocat Davidis filium, ut pote ex familia Davidis oriundum, ut ipso nomine admoneretur promissionis de Messia Davidi factae. Neq; enim Iosepho ignotum erat, Messiam ex Davidis familia, (ex qua ipse cum paucis adhuc superstes erat, plerisq; ex regio illo stemmate oriundis per Herodem mortis supplicio sublatis, Ioseph. lib. 14. antiq. cap. 17. lib. 15. cap. 1. & 9. Galat. de arcanis lib. 4. cap. 6.) nasciturum expectari. Noverat & hoc ex vaticinio Esaiae cap. 7. v. 14. Messiam ex virgine nasciturum ut hac ratione faciliùs ab Angelo persvaderi potuerit, Mariam ex Spiritus Sancti operatione esse gravidam.

Μή φοβηθής παραλαβεί Μαριάμ τήν γυναωκα σου.At iam antè eam acceperat, quomodo ergo eam iubetur accipere? Resp. in lib. de altercat. Synagogae & Ecclesiae refertur, quod Sponsae ante nuptias non licuerit domum Sponsi intrare. Iuxta hanc hypothesin statuendum fuerit, Mariam tantùm fuisse Iosepho desponsatam, nondum autem in domum deductam vel receptam, iuberetur ergo Iosephus eam in domum suam sine ullo scrupulo deducere. Bened. Arias Montan. in hunc locum. Casaub. in h. l. παρά& hoc loco & infrà cap. 4. v. 5. eandem habet vim, quam inπαρακαλείν,quando significat ad se vocare. Ergoπαραλαβείνest assumere, sibiadiungere. Sed uti superiùs monuimus, Chrysostomus homil. 4. in Matth. rectiùs statuit, apud Hebraeos moris olim fuisse, ut Sponsa statim post factam desponsationem in aedes Sponsi reciperetur, cuius moris idem liber de altercat. Syngogae & Ecclesiae meminit. Si Maria nondum fuisset ante conceptionem in domum Iosephi deducta, sequeretur, quòd conceperit non in matrimonio, sed ante matrimonium, sicq; apud Iudaeos non potuisset effugere notam fornicationis & poenam mortis lege constitutam, quia virum nondum habebat. Quod ergo Iosephus iubetnr Mariam παραλαβείν, illud. 1. opponitur occultae dimissionis consilio. Iosephus cogitabat. Sponsam suam occultè dimittere, iubetur igitur ab Angelo eam παραλαβειν hoc est, non dimittere, nec libellum repudii ei dare: verba enim affirmata apud Hebraeos ponuntur pro contrariis negantibus. Ut odisse pro non amare, accipere pro non dimittere. Niceph. lib. 1. Hist. Eccles. cap. 8. Ne dubites eam recipere, quam tu, quantum in to est, repudiasti & extrusisti. Chrysost. in hunc locum mente eam repudiaverat, ideòiubetur eam accipere. 2. illud intelligendum de receptione in curam, tutelam & patrocinum castitatis.

Quod Maria dicitur Iosephi uxor, illud plerique accipiunt dictum ratione desponsationis, denominatio enim rei saepè â futuro eventu petitur, ac in Sacris litteris res describitur, non qualis nunc est, sed qualis futura est, Gen. 1. v. 1.Deut. 22. v. 24. unde Sponsa statim post Sponsalia dicitur uxor, sc. promissa, pacta, futura. Gen. 29. v. 21.da mihi uxorem meam, id est, Sponsam, ac stuprum Sponsae illatum pro adulterio habetur Deut. 24. v. 1. ubi uxorem accipere, & eam maritare distinguuntur. Sed quia nihil eorum, quae ad perfectum matrimonium requiruntur, in Mariae & Iosephi coniunctione defuit, ac copula carnalis non ad -υσίαν sed tantùm ad usum matrimonii pertinet, ideò rectiùs dicitur, Mariam verè fuisse uxorem Iosephi, non ratione coniunctionis corporum, sed ratione coniunctionis animorum. August. lib. 1. de nupt. & concup. cap. 11. Omne nuptiarum bonum impletum est in illis parentibus Christi, proles, fides, Sacramentum. Prolem cognoscimus ipsum Dominum Iesum; fidem, quia nullum adulterium: Sacramentum, quia nullum divortium,

Ibid. Coniux vocatur (Maria Iosephi) ex primâ fide desponsationis, quam concubitu nec cognoverat, nec fuer at cogniturus: nec perierat, nec mendax manserat coniugis appellatio, ubi nec fuerat nec futura er at ulla carnis commixtio. Erat quippe illa virgo, ideò & sanctiùs & mirabiliùs iucunda suo viro, quiae etiam foecunda sine viro, prole dispar, fide compar. Propter quod fidele coniugium parentos Christi vocari ambo meruerunt, & non solùm illa mater, verùm etiam ille pater eius, sicut coniux matris eius, utrumamente, non carne.

*(Coeterùm argumentantur nostrates contra fictum virginitatis votum â Maria emissum ex praesenti loco hoc modo. Quaecunq; alteri se patitur desponderi, ut fiat eius coniux, (hoc enim respectu Maria dicitur Iosephi uxor) ea non emisit votum virginitatis, aliàs enim γάμον άγαμον contrahendo Deo & hominibus illudere videri posset. Atqui Maria. E. Ad except. Bellar. 1. Mariam post factam desponsationem votum emisuse, Resp. Aut fecit hoc inscio Iosepho, aut ipso consentiente. Non prius, ceu ipsi Pontificii largiuntur, vide Corn. â Lapide in Luc. p. 18. a. ac ipsum Bellarm. l. 2. de Monachis c. 22. §. Hic etiam, & patet quoq; ex 1. Cor. 7. v. 4. nec posterius, ceu colligere licet ex Matth. 1. v. 18. & 19. ac cumprimis notandum, quòd Iosephus coniugii consummationem adhuc speraverit, ac consummasset etiam, nisi divina conceptio intervenisset, eademq; ab Angelo Iosepho pariter ac Mariae fuisset manifestata. 2. Mariam nunquam habuisse explicitum animum consummandmatrimonium, alio qui enim non esse virginem animo, sed solùm carne, nec tamen lusisse virum, sed reverà dedisse absolutam potest atem Iosepho in corpus suum: scivisse autem divinâ revelatione edoctam, nunquam Iosephum matrimonii consummationem expetiturum, & ideò habuisse explicitam voluntatem semper continendi. Resp. de revelatione hac nullum in Scr. S. extat vestigium: si talis illi sact a fuisset, Evangelistae non praetermisissent. 3. Traditam fuisse Iosepho in -ustodiam, non autem in matrimonium desponsatam. Resp. Imò verò disertè vocatur Maria μεμνηςευμένη γυνήLuc. 2. v. 5. Confer Matth. 1. v. 18. & Luc. 2. v. 5. Adde, quòd voluerint συνελθεῖν v. 18. quod verbum de sponsis ac coniugibus adhibetur in Scr. S. usumq; coniugalem notat. vid. 1. Cor. 7. v. 5. De dicto Lucae 1. v. 34. unde potissimum causae suae robur petere satagunt Pontificii, agetur suo loco. Conferantur plura in hanc rem apud B. P. L. de Coniug. § 510. item Confes. Cathol. lib. 2. Spec. par, 2. p. 334. seqq. B. D. Chem. Exam. Concil. Trident. part. 3. c. 9. p. 481.)*

Τό γάρ έν άυτή γεννηθέν. Sic in ea, ut etiam ex ea,Luc. 1. v. 36.Gal. 4. v. 4. quod gnaviter urget Tertull. lib. de carne Christi. Euthymius notat, infinuari etiam illud, quod corpus Christi in primo conceptionis momento integrè formatum atanimaetum fuerit. Pulchrè Tertull. Non eum agnoscimus Christum, qui nibit nostri corporis gessit, dum nihil ex Maria accepit, nobis enim non venit, si in nostra substantia visus non est.

Εκ πνέυματός ἐστιν άγίου. Ut non ex te, ita nec ex alio viro, sed ex Spiritu S. Totum divinum est, quod geritur. Angelus nunciavit, Pater obumbravit, Spiritus S. uterum praeparavit. Filius implevit. Nova sunt omnia, quia nova proles nascetur. August. in Ench. cap. 37. Quod tu esse de alio viro suspicaris, de Spiritu S. est. Idem Epist. 54. Non est criminis, sed Numinis. Hieron. in expos. fid. Cath. Non sicut quidam seeleratis, simi, Spiritum S. dicimus esse pro semine, sed potentia & virtute creatoris dicimus esse operatum ('Ex positum est pro ύπό,Rom. 11. v. 33. habet Syrus sunt Petrus Chrysologus serm. 145. Non est humanus lapsius, sed divinus illapsus; non hominis furtum, sed thesaurus DEI; non causae mortis, sed vitae. Athanas. in Dtsp. contra Arianos coram Probo iudice divinitatem Spiritus S. ex hoc conceptionis opere probat. Tantae, inquit, potestatis vel creationis S. S. ostenditur, ut ipso cooperante corpus Domini Iesu Christi, qui nobis in Sacramento fidei datus est, in utero virginis formaretur &c. v. 21. τέξεται δε υίόν Chrysostomus annotat, non esse dictum pariet t--i filium, quemadmodum de uxoribus, quae ex maritis conceperunt, dici in Scripturis consuevit, quod virsuis pepererint, sed absoluté, pariet filium, quo modo etiam Spiritus Sanctus Es. 7. v. 14. & Angelus Luc. 1. v. 31. loquuntur, quia sc. Maria hunc filium non conceperat ex Iosephi semine, nec ulli viro, sed soli DEO hunc filium pariebat, quam vis si fructum huius nativitatis respiciamus, hic filius & Mariae & Iosepho & toti mundo rectè dicatur natus, quo sensu Es. 9. v. 6. dicitur, parvulus natus est nobis.

Nomen IEsu non erat in populo DEI infrequens, sed reliquis omnibus tantùm typicè & ratione corporalis Salutis tribuebatur, huic soli puerulo reipsa & ratione spiritualis Salutis competit, sicut Angelus nominis rationem statim explicat. Postquàm Filio DEI in carne manifestato nomen huic attributum, reliqui omnes inposterum ab co abstinuerunt.

Σωζειν plus est, quàm αύεν. Iesus salvat populum suum â peccatis. 1. non solùm ratione meriti, sed etiam ratione efficaciae; non solùm per beneficii huius eximii acquisitionem, sed etiam per eiusdem applicationem; non solùm redemtionis opus perficiendo, sed etiam prohibendo, ne peccata infirmitatis in renatis adhuc reliqua ab hereditate Salutis eos impediant. *(pluribus haec exponit B. P. in Exegesi Loci 4. §. 6. & 7.)*

Loquitur Angelus in plurali, ut ostendat, non solùm ab originali, sed etiam ab actualibus peccatis per Christum nos salvari. Es. 53. v. 6. Tit. 2. v. 14.1. Ioh. 1. v. 7. *(notetur quoq; hoc loco quòd adhibeatur in textu pluralis eorum, consentientibus Syro, Arabe & Aethiope: est enim populus nomen collectivum, omnes credentes complectens)* Calviniani ex hoc loco colligunt, Christum pro electis tantum esse mortuum, cùm dicatur populum suum â peccatis salvare. Calv. in hunc locum, Pisc. in antith. Schaffm. p. 43. ContraRemonst. in Collat. Hagiensi pag. 124. &c. Resp. 1. non additur exclusiva, quòd tantùm populum suum sit â peccatis salvaturus, nec additur, hunc populum esse solos electos. 2. Christus Luc. 2. v. 32. dicitur Salvator gentium & Israëlitarum. E. est omnum hominum Salvator. 3. aliter loquitur Scriptura de acquisitione, aliter de applicatione meriti Christi, illa universalis est, haec vitio hominum fit particularis. *(Confer Gen. 22. v. 18.1. Tim. 2. v. 6.cap. 4. v. 10.Tit. 2. v. 11.Luc. 2. v. 10. ac adi B. P. L. de Elect. §. 118.)*

Tria divinitatis Christi argumenta insinuat Angelus. 1. Ex Spiritu Sancto concipi, divinam huius pueri maiestatem insinuat, quia cum nullo homine hoc commune habet. 2. Salvare â peccatis, est opus mere divinum. Es. 43. v. 11. cap. 45. v. 17. cum peccatum contra infinitum bonum commissum fit malum infinitum. 3. Habere populum peculiarem & proprium, itidem soli DEO convenit. Proclus serm. de fide ad Armenios p. 35. λαός όυκ άν έιη άνθρωπυ, άλλά θεού.

Cassianus lib. 5. de incarn. cap. 1. -sta duo, liberare â peccatis & populum suum, non conveniunt nisi ei, qui Natura DEUS est. Syrus vocum affinitatem neglexit, nam pro posuit vivificabit, quod eundem sensum habet, nam illos, qui mortui erant peccato, vivificavit.

Emphasis est in hac phrasi, salvabit populum suum â peccatis corum: opponitur enim Iudaico somnio de liberatione ex potestate Romanorum, quam â Messia unicè expectant, de liberatione â peccato omnis mali fonte vel planè non erant soliciti, vel suis operibus eam se acquirere posse, erant persvasi.

Conzenius ex hoc loco colligit, nos verè liberatos à peccatis. Liberari à morbo, inquit, dicuntur non illi, in quorum corporibus dolor & tabes permanet, sed cum sanitate, & viribus restitutisκαχεξίαinfirmitasque tollitur. Resp. 1. fatemur, Christum non solùm impu tatam, sed etiam inhaerentem iustitiam nobis promeruisse. 2. sed posterior in hae vita est tantùm in choata. 3. beneficia Christi non solum ratione huius, sed etiam futurae vitae aestimanda. 4. infirmitatem in nobis remanere, non potest negari. Ex eod, verò rectè contra operum merita tale argumentum nectitur. Solus Iesus salvat populum suum â peccatis. Haec enim exclusiva additur Act. 4. v. 12. Atqui opera nostra non sunt Iesus. Ergo. Excipiunt Pontificii, de Sacramentis & fide codem modo concludi posse. Resp. est dispar ratio. Exclusiva particula addita alicui causae excludit omnes causas reliquas in illo causandi genere constitutas. Bona opera statuuntur á Pontificiis causa salutis meritoria, rectè ergo censentur ab hoc causandi genere per exclusivam removeri. Sed Sacramenta sunt causa instrumentalis ex parte DEI, fides ex parte nostra, quibus exclusiva causae meritoriae addita non opponitur. Ioh. Ferus in hunc locum. Ipse faciet, non lex, non opera. Nam si ex lege est iustitia, Christus gratis mortuus est. I-se salvum faciet populum suum à peccatis eorum. Porrò ad argumentum, quodex hoc loco formamus. Christus est Salvator. E. non sancti, excipit Conzenius. Si praecones Evangelii sunt Salvatores, multò magisancti, qui pro nobis orant. At prius1. Tim. 4. Resp. est dispar ratio. Praecones sunt in ordine causae instrumentalis, Sancti in ordine causae meritoriae, si Pontificiis credimus.

## 1:22
v. 22. τού το σέ ολον. That is, what has been said thus far about Mary's betrothal, her conception by the Holy Spirit, the Angel's appearance, and the bestowal of the name Jesus. The Greek Fathers think these also are the words of the Angel, but it is more correctly said that they are the words of the Evangelist.

Cozzius here: first he tries to solve our countrymen's argument—that since the Evangelist cites the Scriptures, he proves that everything must be demonstrated out of the Scriptures in the articles of faith. But he objects, there are many narratives in the New Testament without citations from the Old Testament. Answer: our argument deals not so much with historical passages as with doctrinal ones, and it stands entire thus: Not only the Apostles but even Angels, indeed Christ himself proved doctrines of faith from the Scriptures. Therefore nothing should be asserted in matters of doctrine without the testimony of the Scriptures. Secondly, he labors to prove from this passage the obscurity of Scripture. Answer: we do not say that Scripture is everywhere plain, but we say that all the articles of faith are plainly set forth somewhere in Scripture.

Latin:

v. 22. τού το σέ ολον. Scil. quod hactenus dictum de Mariae desponsatione, de conceptione ex Spiritu Sancto, de Angeli apparitione, de nominis Iesu impositione. Graeci Patres existimant, etiam haec esse verba Angeli, sed rectiùs dicitur, esse verba Evangelistae.

Conzenius hîc. 1. solvere conatur argumentum nostratium, quòd Evangelista adducens Scripturas, omnia ex Scripturis in fidei articulis demonstranda esse probat. Excipit autem, multas esse in N. T. narrationes, sine V. T. citatione. Resp. non tam. de Historicis, quàm dogmaticis agit argumentum nostrum, quod integrum sic habet. Non solum Apostolis sed etiam Angeli, imò Christus ipse dogmata fidei probarunt ex Scripturis. Ergo sine testimonio Scripturarum in dogmatibus nihil asserendum. z. evincere ex hoc loco satagit obseuritatem Scripturae. Resp. non dicimus, Scripturam in omnibus locis esse perspicuam, sed omnes fidei articulos alicubi in Scriptura perspicuè propositos esse dicimus.

## 1:23
v. 23. η πάρθένος.. The article ἡ answers to the prefixed emphatic , because in the Prophet there is a certain virgin of surpassing excellence, chosen unto this by the eternal decree of God. *(The Syriac also uses the name in the emphatic form i.e. this Virgin. So also the Arabic, with the article )* The Hebrew does not signify any kind of maiden in general, but an young woman, still constituted in years of adolescence, Gen. 24. v. 43.Exod. 2. v. 8. from the root because she is hidden from man, that is, not yet known by a man. Jerome on this passage, and in book 1 against Jovinian chapter 18, and in his Commentary on Galatians states in book 7 on architecture [de arc.] chapter 15 that the demonstrative particle refers to the place Prov. 30. v. 19. Moreover the word occurs seven times in the Scriptures, and always denotes an unblemished virgin. Gen. 24. v. 43.Exod. 2. v. 3.Psal. 68. v. 26.Cant. 1. v. 3. and 6.Prov. 30. v. 19. *(This must be well observed against the Ebionites, Cerinthians, Carpocratians &c., who taught that Christ was born from conjugal intercourse, as Irenaeus records concerning them, l. 1. c. 24. and 25, lib. 3. c. 24. Epiphan. heresy 28, pag. 53, likewise heresy 30. Tertull. On Prescription c. 48. Aug. book On Heresies chapters 8 and 10. Philaster On Heresies p. 17. 18. The Photinians and Vorstius chatter that Christ was begotten from matter brought forth by God. Concerning whom, just as also concerning the errors of the Apellites, Eutychians, Swenckfelders &c., see Coll. Isagog. p. 340.)*

Εν γαςθι έξει.. Jerome to Pamphilus reads in the present tense. *(But the Greek codices consistently read in the future, and so too the Syrian, Arabic, Ethiopian have translated it.)* In the Hebrew there is pregnant, heavy with child, where either a verb of the present or of the future time can be understood. But since the virgin is predicted to become pregnant, it must be understood not in a divided sense (by which reasoning neither would it be a sign nor a miracle), but in a composite sense, namely that she will conceive and nevertheless remain a virgin, because she shall conceive and bring forth a son while her virginity remains intact. Hence it is called a miraculous sign, and the particle of attention Behold is added.

But how could what was going to follow after several centuries at last be a sign of that promise, that Rezin King of Syria and Pekah King of Israel should not prevail over the house of David? Answer: 1. It is frequent among the Prophets to pass from things of the O.T. to things of the N.T., from figures to the thing signified. 2. The preservation of the polity of Israel was owed to the promise about the Messiah, who was to be born from this people and indeed from the family of David. 3. Because this sign of GOD, who is truth itself, rested upon a promise, therefore it ought to be held no less certain than if it had been exhibited presently.

Certain signs are πρόσρομα and προηγούμενα,,, certain ones ύπόσρομα χαι έτόμενα.. The sense is: before this kingdom and the stock of David be destroyed, it shall certainly beforehand come to pass that, proceeding from this royal blood, the Virgin mother bring forth her son Emmanuel into the light, who shall destroy these kings together with their kingdoms. Galatinus, book 3, On the Arcana, chapter 8, and book 7, chapter 14, brings forward testimonies of the Rabbis, who expound that prophetic passage concerning the Messiah.

χαι χαγέσούσι το ονομα άυτού. Thus read the most ancient Greek codices, *(to which there can also be added here the very ancient Greek Extracts, Bibliotheca Norib., as well as the Ethiopian Interpreter. Coherence persuades us toward the same reading. For the words of the commanding angel ceased, and begin the words of the Evangelist himself drawn from Isa. 7, by which those things are confirmed which the angel had announced to Mary.)* as well as the Syriac and Latin Interpreters. Likewise Justin Martyr in his Dialogue with Tryphon, Epiphanius in the Anchoratus, Jerome on Isaiah chapter 7, so that the sense is: they will call, that is, they will invoke; by invocation they will testify that they acknowledge him as the true God. In Isa. 7:14 in the Hebrew it is ; the LXX has καλέσεις and you will call, O thou virgin, or thou house of David. Whence even Eusebius judges that it should be read καλέσεις.. Which, he says, when some were not paying attention, made out of καλέσει 'you will call,' 'they will call,' although the prophetic text did not have it thus. For the Hebrew word means 'you will call', and all the Interpreters, translating it consistently, rendered it thus . Compare Galatinus, book 3, On the Arcana, chapter 18. Beza likewise in his Animadversions at this place judges that instead of καλέσουςαι one should read καλέσεις.. Drusius, book 1, [says] it was passed over through a slip of the writer; he judges that καλέσεις should be read as καλέσουςαι. So it will be an apostrophe addressed to the virgin, of whom mention was already made above in verse 21. καλέσουςαι

Moreover, the Hebrew can also be rendered in the third person singular, and she will call, namely the house of David, or indeed the virgin mother herself. And this is gathered from what was cited above. Exod. 5:16 your people has sinned. Deut. 31:29 evil befall you. Isa. 60:18 salvation shall happen to your walls. The Targum of Jonathan likewise rendered it in the third person feminine and she will call, but not in the second person and you will call. Jerome, writing to Pammachius, likewise says The Hebrew codices point out the third person feminine. And shall call, namely she herself, the virgin. The same in chap. 7 of Isa.: Word which all have interpreted, and thou shalt call, can be understood as and she shall call, namely that she herself, the virgin, who shall conceive and bring forth, should thus call Christ by name. in the Prophet has the contracted form for Gen. 33. v. 11.Psal. 118. v. 23.Deut. 31. v. 29. (where and R. D. Kimchi says in the Book of Roots are permuted.) Es. 60. v. 18. Lev. 25. v. 21. Exod. 5. v. 16. (to which passage R. Aben Ezra in his exposition of the said Es. 7. v. 14 sends back the reader.) But even if we retain most especially the received reading καλέσουσι,, nothing falls away from the sense, nor is there any suspicion of corruption here. For it might be said that the Evangelist changed the singular number into the plural, that he might show that not only the mother Virgin, or the house of David, but absolutely all the faithful were going to call this Son of the Virgin Emmanuel. *(The Arabic renders and he shall be called.)*

έμμανοηλ. It is not signified that Christ must be called by those very syllables in His circumcision, but that He was to be such in reality, that this name could truly be predicated of Him. Chrysostom on this place: The manner of Scripture is to set events of things in the place of names. See Es. 1. v. 26. chap. c. v. 6. Jerem. 23. v. 6. Ezek. 48. v. 35. &c. Most beautifully indeed this word Emmanuel expresses the person, office, and benefits of Christ , namely that He is God and man in unity of person, sharing with us the same human nature and with GOD the Father the divine: that He is Mediator between God and men, that He makes it so that God is with us, that is, He reconciles God to us and us to GOD, that He dwells in us through grace, that He fights for us through power, that He is with us in all straits; for which reason this appellation agrees with the name Jesus, since it denotes the very person of the Messiah. For no one can save from sins unless he be God and man.

Latin:

v. 23. η πάρθένος.. Articulus ἡ respondet praefixo emphatico, quia apud Prophetam est eximia quaedam virgo, aeterno Dei decreto ad id electa. *(Syr. quoq; nomen in formâ emph. adhibet q. d. haec Virgo. Sic & Arabs cum articulo )* Hebraeum non significat in genere qualemcunq; virginem, sed adolescentulam, in annis adolescentiae adhuc constitutam, Gen. 24. v. 43.Exod. 2. v. 8. â rad. eò quod sit viro abs--ndita, id est, nondum â viro cognita. Hieron. hoc loco & lib, 1. contra Iovin. cap. 18. Galat. statuit lib. 7. de arc. cap. 15. demonstrativam particulam respicere locum Prov. 30. v. 19. Coeterùm septies vox in Scripturis invenitur, ac semper denotat virginem illibatam. Gen. 24. v. 43.Exod. 2. v. 3.Psal. 68. v. 26.Cant. 1. v. 3. & 6.Prov. 30. v. 19. *(Probè hoc observandum contra Ebionitas, Cerinthianos, Carpocrationos &c. qui Christum ex maritali congressu natum esse, docuerunt, ceu memorant de illis Irenaeus l. 1. c. 24. & 25. lib. 3. c. 24. Epiph. haeres. 28. pag. 53. item haeres. 30. Tertull. de praescript. c. 48. August. lib. de haeres. cap. 8. & 10. Philastrius de haeres. p. 17. 18. Photiniani & Vorstius Christum ex materiâ à Deo allata genitum esse garriunt. De quibus, sicuti etiam de Apellitarum, Eutych. Swencfeld. &c. erroribus Vid. Coll. Isag. p. 340.)*

Εν γαςθι έξει.. Hieronymus ad Pammach, legit in tempore praesenti. *(Codd. verò Graeci constanter legunt in fut. & ita quoq; transtulerunt Syrus, Arabs, Aethiops.)* In Hebraeo est praegnans, gravida, ubi subaudiri potest vel praesentis, vel futuri temporis verbum. Coeterùm quòd virgo praedicitur futura gravida, intelligendum est non in sensu diviso, (quâ ratione nec signum, nec miraculum esset.) sed in sensu composito, quòd conceptura sit ac nihilominus virgo mansura, quod illaesâ virginitate filium sit conceptura ac paritura. Inde vocatur signum miraculosum, & additur particula attentionis Ecco.

At quomodo illud, quod post aliquot demum secula secuturum, poterat esse signum promissionis illius, quod Rasin Rex Syriae & Phacee Rex Israël non sint praevalituri do mui Davidis? Resp. 1. frequens est apud Prophetas, â rebus V. T. transire ad res N. T. â figuris ad rem significatam. 2. conservatio politiae Israëliticae debebatur promissioni de Messia, qui ex hoc populo & quidem ex familia Davidis erat nasciturus. 3. Quia hoc signum DEI, qui est ipsa vecitas, promissione nitebatur, ideò non minùs certum haberi debebat, quàm si praesens exhibitum fuisset.

Quaedam signa sunt πρόσρομα & προηγούμενα,, quaedam ύπόσρομα χαι έτόμενα. Sensus est, antequàm regnum hoc & stirps Davidis exterminetur, certò priùs futurum esse, ut ex hoc regio sangvine Virgo mater prodiens filium suum Immanuelem in lucem edat, qui Reges hos unâ cum regnis suis sit exterminaturus. Galat. lib. 3. de arc. cap. 8. & lib. 7. cap. 14. adducit testimonia Rabinorum, qui locum illum Propheticum de Messia exponunt.

χαι χαγέσούσι το ονομα άυτού. Ita legunt antiquiss. Codd. Graeci, *(quibus addi quoque hic possunt Eclogae Graecae antiquiss. Bibl. Norib. nec non Interpres Aethiops. Cohaerentia eandem lectionem persvadet. Desiverunt enim Angeli praecipientis verba, & incipiunt verba ipsius Evangelistae ex Es. 7. depromta, quibus confirmatea, quae Angelus Mariae nunciaverat.)* nec non Syrus, & Latinus Interpretes. Item Iustinus Martyr in Dial. cum Tryphone, Epiph. in Ancorato, Hieronymus in cap. 7. Esai. ut sit sensus, vocabunt, id est, invocabunt, invocatione testabuntur, se ipsum agnoscere pro vero Deo. Es. 7, 14. in Hebraeo est LXX. καλέσεις & vocabis, tu virgo, aut tu domus David. Unde Eusebius etiam h. i. legendum censet καλέσεις.Quae, inquit, cùm aliqui non anim adverterent, in Evangelie Matthaei exκαλέσειvocabis feceruntκαλέσουςαιvocabunt, cùm ita non haberet Prophetica lectio. Nam vox Hebraica vocabis sonat, & omnes Interpretes congruenter eam transferentes ita eareddiderunt. Confer Galatin. lib. 3. de arcan. cap. 18. Beza in animadv, ad h. l. itidem pro καλέσουςαι legendum censet καλέσεις. Drusius lib. 1. praeteritur lapsu scriptoris pro καλέσεις legi καλέσουςαι censet. Sic erit apostrophe ad virginem, cuius & antea v. 21. facta mentio.

Coeterùm Hebraeum potest etiam reddi in tertia persona num. sing & vocabit, scil. domus David, vel etiam ipsa mater virgo. Idque colligitur ex dictis superius citatis. Exod. 5. v. 16.peccavit populus tuus.Deut. 31. v. 29.obveniat vobis malum. Es. 60. v. 18. eveniet salus muris tuis. Targum Ionathae itidem reddidit in tertia pers. foeminina & vocabit, non autem in secunda & vocabis. Hieron. ad Pammach. itidem dicit, Hebraeos Codices tertiam personam foemínini indigitare. Et vocabit, ipsa sc. virgo. Idem in cap. 7. Esai. Verbumquod omnes interpretati sunt, & vocabis, potest intelligi, & vocabit, quod ipsa sc. virgo, quae concipiet & pariet, hoc Christum appellatura sit nomine. apud Prophetam habet formam contractam pro Gen. 33. v. 11.Psal. 118. v. 23.Deut. 31. v. 29. (ubi & R. D. Kimchi in lib. Radic. dicit esse permutatas.) Es. 60. v. 18. Lev. 25. v. 21. Exod. 5. v. 16. (ad quem locum R. Aben Ezra in expositione dicti Es. 7. v. 14. lectorem remittit.) Ac si vel maximè retineamus vulgatam lectionem καλέσουσι, sensui nihil decedit, nec ulla hic corruptelae suspicio. Dici enim posset, Evangelistam mutasse numerum singularem in pluralem, ut ostenderet, non solùm matrem Virginem, aut domum Davidis, sed omnes omninò fideles hunc Virginis filium vocaturos Immanuelem. *(Arabs reddit. & vocabitur.)*

έμμανοηλ. Non significatur, quod iisdem syllabis Christus in circumcisione appellandus sit, sed quod talis reipsâ sit futurus, ut hoc nomen de eo verè praedicari possit. Chrysost. in h. l. Mos Scripturae, eventus rerum ponere loco nominum. Vide Es. 1. v. 26. cap. c. v. 6. Ierem. 23. v. 6. Ezech. 48. v. 35. &c. Pulcherrimè autem haec vox Immanuelis personam, officium, & beneficia Christi exprimitquod sit in personae unitate Deus & homo, eiusdem Naturae sc. humanae nobiscum & divinae cum DEO Patre consors: quod sit Mediator inter Deum & homines, quod faciat, ut Deus sit nobiscum, id est, reconciliet nobis Deum & nos DEO, quod habitet in nobis per gratiam, quod pugnet pro nobis per potentiam, quod sit nobiscum in omnibus angustiis, quâ ratione haec appellatio congruit cum nomine Iesu, quod ipsam connotat Messiae personam. Salvum enim facere â peccatis nemo potest, nisi sit Deus & homo.

## 1:24
v. 24. διεγερθεὶς having been awakened. Joseph was not disobedient to the heavenly oracle, but, giving credence to the angelic admonition, offered himself as obedient. Hugh on this place: He did not only what He had commanded, but also just as He had commanded, in which perfect obedience is marked.

Latin:

v. 24. διεγερθεὶςexpergefactus. Non fuit Ioseph inobediens coelesti oraculo, sed fidem ei adhibens Angelico monito sese obsequentem praebuit. Hugo in h. l. Fecitnon solùm, quod praeceperat, sed etiam ficut praeceperat, in quo notatur perfecta obaedientia.

## 1:25
v. 25. χαι τούη ἐγίνωσκεν (Certain copies read, οὐκ έλνω αυρην, έως ού έρεηεν, ) &c. Helvidius wished to infer, 1. from the particle έως τού.., 2. from the appellation first-born, that Mary after her childbearing having been known by Joseph bore other children. Those following Helvidius were the Antidicomarianites. But as regards the former point, this theological rule must be noted: the particle until so excludes what goes before that it does not straightway posit what follows.Psal. 110. v. 1.Matth. 28. v. 20.Gen. 28. v. 15.Deut. 34. v. 6.1. Sam. 15. v. 35.2. Sam. 6 v. 23.Psal. 123. v. 2.Esai. 22. v. 14. Jerome uses this example. Helvidius, before he had done penance, was anticipated by death, and nevertheless it does not follow that he did penance after death. Basil, sermon on the Nativity of the Lord: the particle until indeed seems in many places to signify some determination of time, but really indicates something undefined, as is that saying: Behold I am with you, &c.

Compare Isidore of Pelusiota, Book 1, Epistle 18, page 5. Certain men set forth this rule thus. The particle 'until' excludes without exception, expressing the thing as not done at a certain time, whereby it could --deri be done, leaving it to be understood that afterwards it was done far less.

As regards the latter point, the rule of Bede on this passage is to be noted: He is called firstborn before whom none was born, even though there are none born after him, that is, although he may not have brothers by the womb. Es. 12. v. 29. Exod. 13. v. 2.Num. 18. v. 16. &c. The name firstborn is taken either negatively and absolutely, that is, before whom no one was; or comparatively and affirmatively, that is, before whom indeed no one was, but after whom someone is. The aim of the Evangelist is to show that according to the prophetic oracle Mary --rgo conceived, and a virgin gave birth. First he showed in v. 18 that before they came together she was found to have what was in her womb from the Holy Spirit; secondly in this verse, he did not know her until she bore, &c., so that the sense is: He had not known her when she was found pregnant; nor had he known her when she bore. There is no doubt that it was brought about by divine providence that Mary's husband was named Joseph, so that from this it might be understood that he followed both the name and likewise also the continence of the patriarch Joseph.

Joseph, led by religion, did not touch her whom he knew to be pregnant from the Holy Spirit with the mother of the Messiah θεανθραπού, nor is there any doubt that through Mary he learned more fully the mystery of this deed. Jerome reasons thus: If Joseph, from the mere report of the Angel in dreams, was moved with such reverence as not to know Mary until she brought forth, how would he have been moved afterwards, when he heard the shepherds, Simeon, Anna, the Magi proclaiming things so divine concerning that boy,

τον ύιον αύτης τον πρωτότοκον,, There is an emphasis in the article repeated twice . She brought forth her son, whom she had conceived by the singular operation of the Holy Ghost, this firstborn, whose types were all the firstborn of the Old Testament, and who was that firstborn especially beloved by GOD. He is called firstborn for our consolation, so that it may be shown that we are spiritual brothers of Christ.

χαι έηάγεοσε. The Syriac has the feminine verb she called, namely Mary, her son Jesus, so that it is intimated that Christ was born of Mary, but not begotten of Joseph, and therefore that this name was not imposed on him by Joseph, just as elsewhere fathers were accustomed to give names to children born of themselves. And indeed even in the Greek text the word έηάγεοσε can be referred most closely to the immediately preceding word αυτης.

But since in verse 21. -νομαθεσια is attributed by the Angel to Joseph, therefore it is more conveniently referred to Joseph, *(which was also done by the Arabic version, which has and he called. Likewise by the Ethiopic, in which and he called.)* nor can any special mystery be sought in the fact that Mary, not Joseph, gave this name. For this name was delivered from heaven, and made known by the Angel before birth to both of them.

Summary of the chapter. The consequences of the birth of Christ. 1. On the occasion of the coming of the Magi , first to Jerusalem, secondly to Bethlehem. 2. The flight of Christ into Egypt, which was followed by the Infanticide committed at Bethlehem. 3. The return of Christ and His parents out of Egypt to Nazareth. Connection. After the Evangelist had treated of the genealogy and of the History of the conception and birth of Christ, he goes on to recount those things which befell Christ while still in childhood

Latin:

v. 25. χαι τούη ἐγίνωσκεν (Quaedam exemplaria legunt, οὐκ έλνω αυρην, έως ού έρεηεν,) &c. Helvidius. 1. ex particula έως τού.. 2. ex appellatione primogeniti inferre voluit, Mariam post partum virgincum â Iosepho cognitam alios peperisse liberos. Helvidium secuti sunt Antidicomaritae. Sed quod ad prius attinet, notanda est regula Theologica: particula donec ita excludit praecedens, ut non statim ponat soquens.Psal. 110. v. 1.Matth. 28. v. 20.Gen. 28. v. 15.Deut. 34. v. 6.1. Sam. 15. v. 35.2. Sam. 6 v. 23.Psal. 123. v. 2.Esai. 22. v. 14. Hieronymus utitur hoc exemple. Helvidius antequàm p---itentiam egit, morte praeventus est, nec tamen sequitur, quod post mortem egerit poenitentiam. Bas-l. concion. de nat. Dom. particulae donec in multis quidem locis quandam temporis determinationem significare videtur, revera autem indefinitum indicat, quale est illud: Ecce ego vobis cum, &c.

Confer Isidorum Pelusiotam lib. 1. Epist. 18. pag. 5. Quidam hanc regulam sic efferunt. Particula donec absa exceptione excludit, rem nunquàm factam certo tempore exprimens non factam, quo --deri facta poterat, intelligendum relinquens, postea multò minùs esse factam.

Quod ad posterius attinet, notanda est regula Bedae in h. l. Primogenitus dicitur, ante quem nullus, licet post eum nulli, id est, licet non habeat uterinos fratres Es. 12. v. 29. Exod. 13. v. 2.Num. 18. v. 16. &c. Primogeniti nomen accipiturvel negative & absolutè, id est, ante quem nemo fuit; vel comparatè & affirmativè, id est, ante quem quidem nemo, sed post quem aliquis est. Scopus Evangelistae est, ostendere, quòd iuxta vaticinium Propheticum Maria & --rgo conceperit, & virgo pepererit. Prius ostendit v. 18. antequam convenirent, inventa est in utero habens ex Spiritu Sancto: postorius hoc versiculo, non cognovit eam, donec peperit, &c. ut sit sensus: Non cognoverat eam, quando inventa est gravida: nec cognoverat eam, quando peperit. Dubium non est, divinâ providentrâ factum, quòd Mariae maritus Ioseph fuerit dictus, ut ex co intelligeretur, illum ut nomen, ita quoq; continentiam Patriarchae Iosephi assecutum esse.

Iosephus religione ductus illam non attigit, quam ex Spiritu sancto gravidam Messiae θεανθραπού matrem esse cognoverat, nec dubium, quin ex Maria pleniùs cognoverit huius facti mysterium. Hieron. sic ratiocinatur. Si Ioseph ex sola relatione Angeli in somnis tali reverentiâ motus est, ut non cognosceret Mariam, donec pareret, quidui motus fuisset postea, cùm audiret pastores, Simeonem, Hannam, Magos, tam divina de puero illo praedicantes,

τον ύιον αύτης τον πρωτότοκον,, Emphasis est in articulo bis repe-ito. Peperit filium suum, quem ex singulari Spiritus Sancti operatione conceperat, illum primogenitum, cuius typi fuerunt omnes primogeniti V. T. quique fuit primogenitus ille peculiariter DEO dilectus. Dicitur primogenitus ad consolationem nostam, ut ostendatur, nos esse Christi fratres spirituales.

χαι έηάγεοσε. Syrus habet verbum foemini vocavit illa, scil. Maria filium suum Iesum, ut innuatur, Christum ex Maria natum, non autem ex Iosepho genitum, ac proinde non esse ei nomen impositum à Iosepho, sicut aliàs patres liberis ex se natis nomina imponere consueverunt. Et sanè etiam in textu Graeco verbum έηάγεοσε ad verbum proximè praecedens αυτης referri potest.

Sed cùm in v. 21. -νομαθεσια illa Iosepho ab Angelo tribuatur, ideò commodiùs ad Iosephum refertur, *(id quod etiam factum ab Arabe, qui habet & vocavit ille. Similiter ab Aethiope, apud quem & vocavit ille.)* nec potest singulare mysterium in eo quaeri, quod Maria, non Iosephus hoc nomen imposuerit. Erat hoc nomen caelitus delatum, & utriq; ab Angelo ante partum manifestatum.

Summa capitis. Consequentia nativitatis Christi. 1. Magorum adventu, sprimò in Hierosolymam, secundò in Bethlehemam. 2. Christi in Aegyptum fuga, quam insecutum fuit Infanticidum Bethleemiticum. 3. Reditus Christi & parentum ex Aegypto in Nazareth. Connexio. Post quàm Evangelista de genealogia ac conceptionis & nativitatis Christi Historia egerat, porrò commemorat ea, quae in aetate infantili Christo obtige-unt.

## 2:1
v. 1. τού σέ Ιησού γεννηθέντος. The particle σέ in this passage is connective or copulative of the sentence, whence the Vulgate rendered it not unaptly therefore.

The Author of the unfinished work on Matthew [reads] Immediately when he was born, namely on the thirteenth day from the birth, which is the commonly held opinion; what is to be determined concerning it will be explained a little later. Casaub., Annals 1, n. 19, proves that it ought to be rendered, when Christ had been born a short time before, since such is the force of the aorist participle. Compare Heb. 11, v. 23.

έν Βηθλεὲμ της Ἰουδαίας. It is so called to distinguish it from the other Bethlehem, which was in Galilee, in the allotment of the tribe of Zebulun, Josh. 19. v. 14. Here Judaea is understood not for the whole land of the twelve tribes, but for the allotment of the tribe of Judah, beneath which the allotment of the tribe of Benjamin is comprised, Matt. 2. v. 22. chap. 3. v. 1. and 5. John 7. v. 1. 2. and it is distinguished from Samaria, Peraea, Trachonitis, and both Galilees. Josh. 19. v. 18. it is called Bethlehem Juda, that is, of the tribe of Judah, in which manner also the Vulgate rendered it here. Conzenius maintains that Juda should be read, not Judaeae, because this reading possesses the weightier witnesses of antiquity. And yet the Greek text reads Ἰουδαίας,, which is the most ancient of all. *(Together with the printed copies, which read thus according to the very oldest Greek manuscripts, the Greek Excerpts of the Nuremberg Library also agree.)* Jerome notes that through a fault of the copyists Judaeae was written for Juda. For Bethlehem exists nowhere except in Judaea; even that which is in Galilee is nevertheless of Judaea, namely Galilee too is a part of Judaea itself. But it is stated more correctly that the name Judaeae is here taken specifically. Bethlehem signifies the house pa-is. This can be fitted mystically to Christ. John 6. v. 51.

L--i makes mention of the nativity, in order to show that the Prophecy of Micah was fulfilled in Christ. Having proved from the genealogy that Jesus Christ is the promised Messiah, the same man now proves it from the place of the nativity.

CHAPTER II.

εν ημέραις Ἡρῴδου βασιλέως.. Namely in the 33rd year of that kingdom, as Epiphanius notes, into which year of the kingdom fell the first registration of the world Luc. 2. v. 1. under which Christ was born. Baronius held that Christ was born in the 29th year of the reign of Herod, counted from its beginning.

Some look for an emphasis in the word days, so that the brevity and transience of earthly kingdoms may be noted, which, although they last a long time, must nevertheless be reckoned as of few d--axat days, if they are compared with eternity. But the word days is put, in Hebrew phrase, for time in general and for years in particular. The sense therefore is: in the days of Herod, that is, in the time of Herod, when Herod held the rule.

This Herodes was an Idumaean by nation, a proselyte by profession of religion, of plebeian stock. Subject to the Roman Emperor. He was otherwise called the Ascalonite, from his homeland Ascalon in the region of Edom. Also Herod the elder, the first, the great. His parent was Antipater the Idumaean. Josephus, book 14 of the Antiquities, chapter 26, records of him that he was made King by the Roman Senate. From the series of the History it can be gathered that in that very year in which Christ was born, the Jews — otherwise most impatient of foreign rule — of their own accord granted to him himself the full right of kingship for himself and his heirs. The Hebrews relate in the book Baba bathra that Herod was a foreigner, and from the slaves of the house of the Asmonaeans or Maccabaeans. In Josephus, book 14 of the Antiquities, chapter 26, Antigonus reproaches Silo and the army of the Romans because they acted unjustly, in giving the kingdom to Herod, a private man and an Idumaean. This Herod had utterly taken away the kingdom from Judah and Israel, so that he removed out of the way almost all those sprung from the royal stock, on which the right of kingship that he coveted depended; Galat. book 4, de arcan. cap. 6. To this belongs what Josephus records of the death inflicted by Herod, first upon forty-five leading men of the faction of Antigonus and upon Antigonus himself, book 15 of the Antiquities, cap. 1; then upon all the judges of the great Synedrion, except one, Samea, book 14, cap. 17, book 15, cap. 1; and lastly upon Hyrcanus, the last survivor of the Jewish royal race, book 15, cap. 9.

This therefore is the third argument by which the Evangelist proves that Jesus is the promised Messiah. For as he had hitherto proved it from the family and the place of birth, so now he proves the same thing from the condition of the time. For it had been foretold that the Messiah would be born at that time when the scepter and the right of making laws had been taken away from Judah, Gen. 49. v. 10. That this was fulfilled at the time when Jesus was born is evident from the fact that Herod was a foreign-born man, subject to the empire of the Romans. By what means Herod came to the kingdom, and how he succeeded Hircanus, the last king of the Jews of the race of the Asmonaeans or Maccabees, Josephus explains.

This Herod, called the Ascalonite, son of Antipater, was King of all the land of the twelve tribes of Israel; hence the Gospel calls him absolutely King. At his command the Bethlehemite massacre of infants was carried out. His son, bearing the same name, Herod, called Antipas, was tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea Luc. 3. v. 1.; by the order of John the Baptist he was taken out of the way.

Herodes Agrippa, grandson of the Ascalonite Herod through his son Aristobulus, having the same name as his grandfather, was King of Trachonitis, Ituraea and Galilee. Act. 12. v. 1. and following: at his command James, brother of the Apostle John, was killed, and Peter cast into prison.

Ἰδοὺ Μάλος άπό ἀνατολῶν παρολένοντο ετς Ἱεροσόλυμα. Concerning these Magi it is asked, 1. Who and what sort were they? 1. In the Syriac paraphrase they are called , which word in the Thalmudic books is shameful, and denotes those devoted to magical or diabolical arts. Hence Justin, in the Dialogue with Tryphon, p. 87., Jerome on chapter 19 of Isaiah, roman 2, fol. 168., Theophylactus on Matthew chapter 2, fol. 7., state that even these Magi, who are said to have been led to the manger of Christ by the rising of a new star, were poisoners and enchanters. Theodoret writes on this place, that Christ summoned these prophets of the Devil before others to adore himself, and fetched the first-fruits of the nations from their very innermost recesses of hell. But such jugglers and evil-doers are rather called γοητες among the Greeks than Μάγοι.. 2. Yet in the New Testament Syriac, just as also among the Persians, the name of Magus is an honorable term, and signifies men distinguished for wisdom and religion. *(The Arabic interpreter of the New Testament likewise retains the very word Magi both in this verse and in verses 6 and 16 following; for expressly he has but elsewhere, where likewise το μαγος occurs in the Greek text, namely Acts ch. XIII. v. 6. and 8., he describes either by a man sa juggler, sorcerer, as v. 6., or even rendered it absolutely by , as v. 8.; which the Syrian too observed, who in Act. 13. v. 6. has a certain juggler , and v. 8. nu—ly . But the Ethiopian Interpreter did not approve at all, whether to remove all ambiguity, or because the name Magi sounds not well enough among his own Gentiles, to retain the said name in Matth. 11. v. 1.7.16. Nay rather, in its place he substituted another thing: he interprets namely v. 1. and 7. , that is, excellent ones, which word is known also to the Rabbins, since they denote a wise man by , teaching Buxtorff in the Talmudic-Rabbinic Lexicon); v. 16. however by , that is, men most excellent, and likewise by . On the contrary, Acts 13. v. 6. by , that is, an enchanter. It descends from , from the root he enchanted, Ps. 57. v. 6. (according to the Hebrew text Ps. 58. v. 6.). Cornelius à Lapide notes that the Ethiopian in Matth. 2. v. 1. renders Magi by adores, because these Magi came to adore Christ: truly , and thence arising , denotes not one who adores, but an excellent one. He seems to have read instead of Cornelius, or whoever gave aid to Cornelius; which if it be in use, perhaps denotes those who adore, from the root he prayed, dered, which occurs several times both in the Ethiopic Psalter and in the Ethiopic version of the New Testament, as is sufficiently plain from Ps. 5. v. 8.Ps. 21. v. 30.Matth. 4. v. 9. 10.Luc. 24. v. 52. and other places, where the verb προσηυνειν stands in the Greek text. But that astrologers themselves, or even wise men, should be called Magi by the Ethiopians cannot be proved satisfactorily; nor do even Pliny and Tertullian, whom Cornelius alleges as witnesses, disclose that very thing. And yet I wonder that so many learned men have until now been deceived by the error which crept into Pliny b. 25. c. 2., and imposed upon Cornelius à Lapide, Hugo Grotius and others, so that they thought that students of nature, who formerly dwelt in Arabia and Ethiopia, are called Magi by Pliny. Indeed rather preferable to the common and far beyond doubt corrupt reading is the correction of B. D. Calixtus, who substitutes in place of magis another word, namely fields or regions, and such an emendation certainly the construction itself appears to require.)*

Herodotus, Book 1 of the Histories, chapter 26. The Magi were wise men of the Persians. Jerome on chapter 2 of Daniel calls them the philosophers of their nation. *(The words of Jerome, tome 4, p. 497, are: The Magi are those who philosophize about single things, nor are they sorcerers, but philosophers of the Chaldaean race, and through the knowledge of this art the kings and princes of that same people do all things. Whence also the Magi at the Savior's nativity were the first to understand his arising, and coming to holy Bethlehem adored the child. Compare also concerning honorable magic Philo, in the book On the Special Laws)* Apollonius in the Letter Μάγνς ό-ομάον Τύς -όυς όι Πός-ι. Μάγες όύ κ-Τ φύ-ινσθ-ό-, ι σθ-ρ-πιυΤκς Των. Among the Platonic texts in the Alcibiades it is said, The Magi of the Persians were interpreters of divine and human law, and professors of universal Philosophy. Pliny, book 10 of Natural History, writes, Magic embraces three arts, Physics, Metaphysics and Astrology. Strabo, book 15: That region, Persis, is inhabited by the Achaimenids and Magi who pursue a certain honorable manner of living Id., book 16: There were Magi among the Persians, among the Indians the Gymnosophists, among the Babylonians the Chaldaeans, among the Hebrews Moses, who handed over divine precepts and teachings to his own people. Caelius Rhodiginus, book 9, chapter 23: And scarcely anyone else among the Persians is a Magus than an Interpreter and worshipper of divine things. Suidas writes thus of them: The Magi among the Persians are φιλόσ---ι and φιλ--, who received the name after Zoroaster. The same: Magic is Astrology, which had its beginning from the Maguseans 3. From this D. Chemnitius in his Harmony rightly gathers, because Matthew calls them Magi from the East, that these were not such Magi as existed in Egypt, namely enchanters and poisoners, whose profession was punishable by death. That they were Gentiles is certain, whence Bernard, sermon 3 on Epiphany, calls them the first-fruits of the nations.

Q. 2 Whether they were Kings? The common opinion is that they were Kings. Thus Tertullian in the book against the Jews, page 1-0, and others of the Fathers. For proving this opinion they apply that Psal. 72. v. 10. Kings coming forth out of Arabia and Saba shall offer gifts to him (that is, the Messiah). See Maldonatus on this passage, column 43. *(They likewise maintain this, Baronius and Barradius, to whom Cornelius à Lapide also gives his assent in the Commentary on Matthew, page 60, and likewise Tirinus; though these do not fully agree with themselves, seeing that they explain the word of Kings as meaning lesser rulers or princes. Jerome again Xavier, a famous Jesuit, considering this point settled beyond the risk of controversy, expressly declares in the History of Christ written in Persian -onscription, that this is, three kings came to Jerusalem. But to the objection that they are not so called by the Evangelist and other ancients, he answers thus:

that is, the Interpreter Louis de Dieu: Although those three men were kings, yet they were most often called wise men: since at that time people arrived at royal dignity through the intervention of wisdom, therefore they preferred rather to be called wise than to be themselves called kings.)*

But indeed. 1. The Evangelist nowhere calls them Kings, which he would not have passed over if they had been Kings, because from that no small accumulation of honors would have accrued to the birth of Christ.

2. Among Cyprian, Chrysostom, Gregory of Nyssa, Theodoret, and Cyril, where they treat this History, no mention, not even the slightest, is made of royal majesty.

3. It is not likely that Herod would have wished to receive in the metropolis of the kingdom foreign Kings with their troop and companions, especially since he exercised hostilities with the Persian Kings, the Arsacids situated in the region of Persia.

4. Nor would it have been easy for them to approach the cradle of Christ and flee back again so secretly that they would not be betrayed, if indeed they had proceeded in royal fashion, surrounded by crowds.

5. Nor would they have left Christ and his mother laboring in such slender fortune, that she could offer only a pair of turtledoves in the days of her purification, Luc. 2. v. 24. which was the offering of those whose means and fortunes were most slender. Lev. 12. v. 8.

6. Jansen, on the Harmony of the Gospels, chapter 9, fol. 56, refutes that opinion, that these Magi were Kings, and shows there that the passage Ps. 72. must not be understood concerning these Magi. Baronius, on the year of Christ n. 24., denies it. Bellarmine, tome 6, lecture 14, column 152, likewise speaks doubtfully. Those Magi, he says, were perhaps Kings. The matter itself shows that that prophecy is general about any Kings whatsoever converted to Christ, nor can it be applied specifically to these Magi, who are said to have come άπό άναΤολων. But now Arabia and Saba are situated not to the East, but to the south with respect to Judea Matt. 12. v. 42.

7. It is indeed established that this class of men at some time enjoyed the greatest honors among the kings of the East, and so at times held the reins of kingdoms, as Cicero, Strabo, Pliny testify; yet neither was that perpetual, nor was it customary at that time when Christ was born; therefore Strabo, when he treats of the honors formerly bestowed upon the Magi , adds: that came about έν Τόις πςό ημων before his memory. Now Strabo lived in those very times in which Christ was born.

8. That opinion, therefore, concerning the Magi being Kings, arose without doubt from the fact that among the Persians, Kings were once elected from the number of the Magi, and that Kings were previously instructed in their School. For Cicero, in book 1 of *De Divinatione*, testifies: That the Magi were the counselors of the Persian Kings, and that no one was raised to the helm of the empire who had not first been instructed in their School. Pliny says: that magic commands Kings in the East. Caelius Rhodiginus, in book 3, *Lectiones Antiquae*, chapter 42, defines Magic: that it is the knowledge of divine things and worship, with which the Kings of the Persians were imbued, or that it was a higher, holier philosophy.

9. The Fathers who call those Magi Kings use the word of Kings in a broader sense for great, honored, outstanding and illustrious men—such as these Magi were—as the circumstances of the History show, especially however the gifts. Augustine, book 3, On the Marvels of Scripture, chapter 4, calls them Kings, but 1. it is not a genuine offspring of Augustine, which Thomas also acknowledged, part 3, q. 45, art. 3, ad 2. 2. the passage is corrupted. The words read thus: The Magi came to Jerusalem; thence, having found the oracles of the Israelite prophets concerning the child to be born, and being told by a deceitful message where the place of his birth would be, the Kings go eagerly. In place of the Kings one should read of the King, as the context shows.

Q. 3. From what were the Magi named? Most hold that they took their name from the Hebrew , which means to meditate, examine, inquire.Psalm 1. v. 2. *(D. Reinesius embraces this opinion too, in ιςοςουμ. of the Punic Language)* Reuchlin says it on the authority of R. Joseph.

which Something should be taken from the birds that chirp/murmur, so that one both diligently meditates and continually discourses. For these men were Magi, philosophers of the Gentiles, searchers out of natural things, devoted to the studies of Astronomy, and instructors of the Persian kings.

Q. 4. Concerning the number and proper names of these Magi 1. Leo the Great in his Sermons on Epiphany gathers from the three gifts that there were three Magi who came to the manger of Christ, but this argument is weak, nor is it approved by Lyra, who laid down that the individuals offered three gifts. Chrysostom, homily 2 on Matthew, maintained that there were fourteen. The Ordinary Gloss on this passage likewise decided that there were more than three. The Evangelist did not state the number.

2. By the same reasoning he did not express their names either; whence various fabrications concerning them. 1. Zacharias Chrysopolitanus says these were their Hebrew names: Apellius (others read Appolius), Amerus (others relius), and Damascus. But those are the Greek ones: Magalath (others Malgalatb), Galgalath (others Galath.), and Saracin (others Sar him.). These same names are found in Peter Comestor in the Historia Scholastica, who himself also set forth those latter ones as genuinely Greek. 2. Casaubon in his notes, p. 184, records that these are contained in a fairly ancient Greek codex of the Library at Heidelberg. Τά -νόμαΤΤων έν Βκσθλείμ π-ιμίνων Μι-λ, ΑΧε-λ, Κυςι-κός και ΣΤ-φανος. Τ Μ-λων όνόμ-Τα Των πςο--νΤων Τόν Κ-ςιον, ΑΤως, ΣάΤως, ΠεςαΤωςάς.

3. Bede brings forward these Latin names of theirs: Melebior, Gaspar and Balthasar. Caspar Hedio part 4. of the Chronicles relates, that in the Year certain Monks came from India to Strasbourg, intending to visit Rome and Cologne, who reported that seven Monks indeed had undertaken this journey, but that two of them had died along the way, and that they consumed a full two years on that journey. That the Magi, of whom mention is made in the History of the Gospel, were three Kings, and came from India; the name of the first was Melchior, King in Nubia; the name of the second Balthasar, King in the Islands Codali and Saba; the name of the third Gaspar, King of Tharsis; and that Thomas the Apostle bade them acknowledge at the Tomb in a certain Island of theirs, Grosvilla, the Archbishop and Supreme Magistrate, Presbyter John.

But all these things are doubtful and uncertain, whence it is a wonder that the authors of the Douay edition of the Bible were not forbidden to defile the margins with the names of the Magi and other fables of that kind.

(Moreover, whether Xavier counts at least three Magi along with the other Papists, who came to Jerusalem to adore the newly born King of the Jews: yet they themselves, in order to increase the religion of the simple folk—or rather their own purses—are wont to display bodies showing a propensity toward six Magi, namely three at Cologne; but another three at Milan at Saint Eustorgius’s. Unless someone wish to say with Corn. à Lapide that those sacred bodies were first preserved at Milan and transferred to Cologne: entirely against the will of the Milanese, yet nonetheless by a pious and praiseworthy theft—for that things of this kind are bestowed upon λειψανολωτροιαν for the augmentation of matters among the Papists, the Epigram of Dionysius the Areopagite in the church of St. Emmeram at Regensburg sufficiently makes manifest, which Aventinus presents in book 4 of the Annals of the Bavarians, p. 277. Yet it should be known that today it is read there somewhat otherwise (if it even still stands there, as I described it eighteen years ago άυτόπτης) than it is set forth by Aventinus, epithets having plainly been added to the word theft: for it seemed not sufficiently fitting that those relics had been carried off by theft from the Parisians, unless Pontifical piety had added that this deed was a pious and praiseworthy theft.)

Q. 5. From what region did these Magi come? For the Evangelist speaks in general terms, saying that they came από ανατολων from the Easts, that is, from the Eastern parts.

Ans. 1. Justin in the Dialogue with Trypho, p. 237, holds that they came from Arabia, whence he also calls the Magi Arabian. The same is the opinion of Epiphanius near the end of the Panarion and of others. But Arabia with respect to Judaea is not positioned toward the East, but toward the south. Matt. 12. v. 42. Lucas Burgensis here says, that they came from Chaldaea, or—which, because of its closer position, is more probable—from deepest Arabia. For it is agreed that the Chaldaeans, both by origin and by kingdom, were devoted to the pursuit of Magic before the Persians ---s, and that the Arabs, neighbors of the Chaldaeans, were devoted to the same science, whence Pliny lib. 25. chap. 2. among the celebrated Magi, after Pythagoras and Democritus, before they wrote concerning the na-tures of herbs, traveled through among-others-the-Magi of Arabia He adds, that Job also and his friends were Magi; moreover that Job was great among all the Easterners, a neighbor of the Sab-aeans, hence accordingly an Arab.Job. 1. v. 3. & 15. To that objection, that Arabia was not eastern relative to Judaea, he responds, that Arabia, bordering Judaea beyond-Jor-dan on the side of the Ea-st, stretching farther from there eastward toward Chaldaea u advanc-ing, is distinguished by a threefold name. One is called Arabia Deserta, which inclines toward the North and has Bosra as its metropolis. Another is Arabia Petraea, a certain part of which, such as Idumaea, lies south of Judaea, whose metropolis is Petra. The third is Arabia Felix, situated wholly to the East of Judaea, midway between the Desert on the north and the Petraean on the south, whose metropolis is Saba (not that of Ethiopia, which lies south of Judaea,Matt. 12. v. 42.) but another one of the Arabs—to which point belongs the fact that the Author, discoursing on the chief works of Christ, names the Magi Arabs and inhabitants of Saba. *(They embrace the same opinion, namely that these Magi were Arabs, Corn. à Lapide also, and likewise Tirinus, who nevertheless, taking too little account of that distinction of Franc. Lucas between the Saba of Ethiopia and the other of the Arabs, write that these Magi came from the same Saba, whence the Queen who paid visit to Solomon, 3. Kings 10. v. 1. Nor do they pause over the fact that she is called the Queen of the South, that is, from the South, Matt. 12. v. 42. whereas these are recorded to have come from the East.

But if those Magi also came from that same Arabia whence the Queen of the South came to Solomon—that is, Sheba, which lies at a distance of 606 French leagues from Jerusalem (according to Adrichomius in his Description of the Holy Land, whom Cornelius à Lapide cites on Matt., ch. 12, v. 42, p. 270)—I do not see how this same Cornelius could by any argument oppose the distance of place against the opinion of those who hold that the Magi came from Persia, though he especially tries to do just that: for after he had recorded, following Baronius, that Clement of Alexandria, Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria, and St. Leo are of the view that they came (the Magi, the firstfruits of the Gentiles) from Persia, since this lies eastward with respect to Judaea, he adds: but their excessive distance stands in the way. For Persia is three hundred leagues distant from Judaea, which journey the Magi could scarcely have completed in thirteen days. It is true that with dromedary-riders, who daily cover forty leagues, this journey could absolutely have been accomplished in all those days by runners: but kings, accustomed to the comforts of their carriages, are not runners, nor are they wont—indeed, nor can they—to travel thus without pause. But that hypothesis too is false, namely that the Magi came to Jerusalem immediately on the thirteenth day after Christ was born. Moreover, Hugo Grotius, whose judgment it is that these Magi came from Arabia—a view that pleases him greatly—attempted, as usual, to bring aid to the Papists, and that partly because the Jews commonly called Arabia by this very name as lying adjacent toward the sunrise, witness Gen. 10. v. 30.25. v. 6.18.Ios. 1. v. 3.Iud. 6. v. 3.1. Reg. 4. v. 30.Es. 11. v. 14.Ier. 49, 28.

partly because the gifts which they brought were Arabian, not Persian, and finally because not only the sages of the Persians, using the Greek tongue among the Hebrews They are called Magi, but also others. For anciently Arabia too had its wise men, both students of all Nature and especially of the stars. Indeed even the very word έλύμας, which Luke renders μάλος, Acts 13. v. 8. comes from Arabia, and Pliny mentions the Magians of Arabia &c. But whether these arguments prove that the Magi of whom we treat here came from Arabia, not indeed from Persia, we shall see in the actual course of the disputation, lest these gleanings grow too long. This at least it pleases me to indicate for the present, that it is not so certain that the word έλύμας Acts 13. v. 8. comes from Arabia. For although quite a few learned men such as Beza, Fuller, Drusius, Cornelius à Lapide, yea our own B. himself Glassius, likewise Louis de Dieu embrace that opinion; yet others, equally most skilled in the Arabic language, hesitate here: whence the esteemed Louis de Dieu too, a man than whom none more excellent in ανατολιηοπολύλγωττολνωσει, changed his opinion in his Annotations on Acts 13. v. 8. But perhaps occasion will be given To Your Honor elsewhere to say more about this matter. If however it be granted above all that the name of Elymas perhaps came from Arabia, still it does not follow that the wise men of other peoples were also distinguished by the name of Magi: nay rather among others or concerning others it is mostly taken for a sorcerer, as that very passage from Acts confirms.)

But even though that circumstance, that they came from the East, could best fit the Magi of the Arabs, nevertheless it is not yet proven from that that these Magi came from Arabia, since almost nearly all writers place the Magi in Persia.

2. Abulensis on chapter 2 of Matthew attempts to prove that they came from Mesopotamia.

3. It is more probable that they came from Persia, and indeed from the capital of the kingdom, namely from the city Susa, where there was the Academy of the Magi. Basil the Great, homily on the Nativity of Christ: έθνος Περσιηον Μάλθι. Chrysostom, homilies 5 and 6 on Matthew always calls them Persians. Strabo, Cicero, Plato place the Magi in Persia. Daniel makes mention of the Magi in Chaldea, chapter 2, and Abraham, who came from the land of the Chaldeans, is said to be called from the East, Isa. 41. v. 2. I rather agree with Chrysostom, says Casaubon in his note p. 182, who without any doubt interprets the words of the Evangelist of the Persian Magi, rather than Justin, Epiphanius and some others, who derive those ones from Arabia into Judaea.

Q. 6. Why did GOD wish to call the firstfruits of the Gentiles from the East to the manger and kingdom of Christ?

Ans. 1. Paradise, in which sin had been perpetrated, was situated toward the East. Since, therefore, Christ had come to make satisfaction for the sin which was perpetrated in the Eastern Paradise and on account of which Paradise was closed to our first parents and all their posterity, for that reason He wished to gather the firstfruits of His kingdom from the East.

2. In the East the human race had been cursed on account of sin. Since, therefore, Christ had come to take away that curse, for that reason He began to gather a holy and blessed seed from the East.

3. In the East the tower of Babylon had once been begun to be built out of human and vain presumption. Gen. 11. v. 2. Aug. 16 de Civ. DEI cap. 4. which is called by Jerome Epist. 17. the tower of pride. Christ, therefore, who had come to expiate our pride by His humility, called the Magi from the East to His manger.

4. In the East the beginning of all idolatry was made around the idol Bel, which was the most ancient idol. Berosus lib. 1. Polyd. Virg. lib. 1. de rer. invent. cap. 5. Christ, therefore, who had come to destroy all idolatry, summoned the firstfruits of His kingdom from the East.

5. Christ is the Sun of righteousness,Mal. 4. v. 2. the Orient from on highLuc. 1. v. 18. therefore rightly do the first-fruits of the Gentiles come from the East. Bernard, sermon 3. on Epiphany: Rightly did they come from the East, who announce to us the new rising of the Sun of righteousness, and illumine the whole world with joyful tidings. Chrysostom, or whoever else be the Author of the incomplete works upon Matthew, homily 2.: From the East they came, whence the day is born; thence went before the beginning of the faith, because faith is the light of souls.

Q. 7. At what time did they come to Jerusalem? 1. The common opinion is that they came on the thirteenth day after the birth of Christ, and adored Him. This opinion leans upon no other foundation than that uncertain tradition concerning the three miracles wrought on the sixth of January . Nicephorus, book 1. of Ecclesiastical History, chap. 13., relates, Some, in order that they may be able to uphold this opinion, invent that the star of the Magi appeared two years -nte Christi na--nitatem, on account of which they themselves, leaving their fatherland, set out upon the road. But the Magi say expressly, they saw in the East the star of the King of the Jews, not about to be born, but born. v. 2. Others therefore invent marvelous dromedaries, which the Magi made use of, so that within so narrow a span of time they were able to cover so long a journey.

2. Eusebius in Chronicon, Epiphanius lib. 1. tom. 2. & lib. 1. tom. 2. against the Ebionites hold that the Magi came to Jerusalem in the year after Christ's nativity second, nearly two years being fully spent, which conjecture Epiphanius proves from this, that Herod commanded the little ones of two years old to be slain. Nicephorus writes thus. When two years had elapsed after that voluntary seed-less conception, she brought forth her womb-birth, while the virgin mother was in the dwelling-place of Bethleëm, they came. Tatian's Harmony too places the coming of the Magi after the History of the Purification. This opinion leans upon a certain other tradition, which the Author of the unattributed work recounts from a certain apocryphal book, that the Magi dwelt in the farthest parts of the East up to the very Ocean, possessing a Writing under the name Seah concerning the appearing of such a star, and that the star, which appeared at Christ's birth, went before the Magi setting out throughout two years while meanwhile their provision for the journey did not fail on the way.

3. Osiander in the Harmony likewise holds that the Magi came a long while after the purification. First, because the days of purification for a male child newly born are only 33. Lev. 12. v. 4. whereas within so brief a time the Magi could not have accomplished so long a journey. Secondly, Herod slew the boys from two years old and beneath. There had therefore flowed away from the nativity of Christ the whole two years or rather less. Thirdly, after the purification the parents of Jesus had returned again into Bethlehem. *(With Osiander chiefly agrees D. Erhardus Leichnerus in his analytical Commentary on the Time of the Magi, wherein he labors at length to defend this judgment, that it is of altogether as great moment surely to know, believe, affirm that the journey of the Magi befell quite a long while after the completed days and the offerings of purification, thence to know, believe, assert, as (in the almost-most points just now recounted) that history itself is, which altogether he can well seem to do.)*

4. Yet more rightly it is established that the Magi came within the days of purification , and indeed not long before the end of those -rerum. First, because what the History says, γεννηθέντος' Ιησου refers to the child recently born, as we showed above. And the Magi do not ask about a King born two years before, but who was lately born, verse 2. Secondly, when the Magi inquire about the newly born King of the Jews, all Jerusalem is troubled, as over a new matter, concerning which nothing had been heard until now. Verse 3. But after the History of the Purification, that solemn attestation made by the distinguished persons Simeon and Anna in the celebrated place of the temple, Luke 2. v. 25. and following verses, could not be entirely hidden and unknown in the city. Thirdly Luke says, the parents after the purification removed not to Bethlehem, but to Nazareth. Chapter 2, verse 39. Fourthly, Chrysostom gathers from the adverb ἰδοὺ Behold, that the Magi came not long after the birth. Augustine likewise plainly determined that the Magi arrived within the days of the purification, whom Gerson follows in the Monotessaron.

The terminus of the journey of the Magi is set at Jerusalem, the metropolis of Judaea. This city was first called Royal Sedec, whence its kings were named Melchisedec, Adonisedec, Gen. 14. v. 18. Jos. 10. v. 1. King of righteousness, Lord of righteousness. Afterwards it was called Salem, peace. Gen. 14. v. 18. Finally Jerusalem, from the word he saw, joined with the name Salem, so that it might be distinguished from another Salem, of which Gen. 33. v. 18. because this one lies situated on higher ground among mountains, it would seem visible from afar. Josephus, book 3 of the War, chapter 2: surpassing the other cities of Judaea, eminent among all its inhabitants like a head upon a body. Some derive the reason of the appellation from the History Gen. 22. v. 14. where the name of that place is given by Abraham The Lord will see or will provide.

But the Magi hasten directly to Jerusalem for this reason: because it was the metropolis of the whole kingdom. They hoped, therefore, that either that new King of the Jews was born there, or that it could be inquired of there from the Scribes and Doctors of the Law where he was born.

Observation. Christ is the very wisdom of the Father, therefore wise men are led first of all out of the Gentiles to his manger.

Casaub. ann. 1. n. 19. probat, reddendum esse, Christo paulò antè nato, cùm haec sit vis participii aorisii. Confer Hebr. 11. v. 23.

Iudaea h. l. non pro universa ducdecim tribuum terra, sed pro sorte tribus Iudae, sub qua sors tribus Beniamin comprehenditur, accipitur, Matth. 2. v. 22.cap. 3. v. 1. & 5. Ioh. 7. v. 1. 2. distinguiturque â Samaria, Perae:, Trachonitide & utraquae Galilaea. Ios. 19. v. 18. vocatur Bethlehem Iuda, id est, in tribu Iuda, quo modo etiam Vulg. hic reddid it. Norib.)* Hieron. notat, librarii vitio pro Iudae scriptum fuisse Iudaeae. CAPUT II.

εν ημέραις Ἡρῴδου βασιλέως.. Anno scil. regni illius 33. ut notat Epiphanius, in quem regni annum incidit prima descriptio orbis Luc. 2. v. 1. sub quam Christus natus est. Baronius statuit, Christum natum Anno regni Herodis 29. inchoato.

Quidam emphasin quaerunt in voce dierum, ut notetur brevitas & fi-acitas regnorum terrenorum, quae licet diu durent, tamen paucorum d--axat dierum sint censenda, si cum aeternitate conferantur. Sed nomen dierum phrasi Hebraica pro tempore in genere & pro annis in specie ponitur. Sensus igitur est, in diebus Herodis, hoc est, tempore Herodis, cùm Herodes imperium teneret.

-uit hic Herodes Idumaeus natione, proselytus religionis professione, genere plebeius. Romano Imperatori subiectus. Dictus aliàs fuit Ascalonita, â patria Ascalon in regione Edom. Item Herodes senior, primus, magnus. Parens eius fuit Antipater Idumaeus. Iosephus lib. 14. antiq. cap. 26. de ipso commemorat, quòd creatus fuerit Rex â Senatu Romano. Ex serie Historiae colligi potest, quòd illo ipso anno, quo Christus natus est, Iudaei alieni Imperii alioqui impatientissimi sponte suâ ipsi concesserint plenum ius regni pro se & heredibus. Hebraei in libro Baba bathra tradunt, Herodem fuisse alienigenam, & ex servis domus Assamonaeorum sive Maccabaeorum. Apud Ioseph. lib. 14. Antiq. cap. 26. Antigonus improperat Siloni & exercitui Romanorum, quod praeter iustitiam egerint, dum Herodi privato & Idumaeo regnum dederunt. Herodes iste â Iuda & Israële regnum prorsus abstulerat, adeò ut plerosque omnes è stirpe Regia oriundos, ad quod ius regni, quod ille affectabat, spectabat, ê medio sustulerit, Galat. lib. 4. de arcan. cap. 6. quò pertinet, quod Iosephus memorat de morte ab Herode illatâ inprimis quadraginta quinque primatibus factionis Antigoni & Antigono quoq; ipsi, lib. 15. Antiq. cap. 1. deinde iudicib. omnibus Synedrii magni, excepto uno Samea, lib. 14. cap. 17. lib. 15. cap. 1. deniq; Hircano postumo ê Iudaica gente Regi, lib. 15. cap. 9.

Tertium ergo hoc est argumentum, quo probat Evangelista, Iesum esse promissum Messiam. Ut enim ex familia & nativitatis loco hactenus id probaverat, ita idipsum iam probat ex conditione temporis. Praedictum enim erat, Messiam tunc nasciturum, quando sceptrum & ius legum condendarum â Iuda esset ablatum, Gen. 49. v. 10. id quod tempore nati Iesu impletum fuisse, patet ex eo, quod Herodes fuerit alienigena, Imperio Romanorum subiectus. Quâ ratione Herodes ad regnum pervenerit, sicq; Hircano ultimo Iudaeorum ex Assamonaeorum sive Maccabaeorum genere Regi successerit, exponit Iosephus.

Hic Herodes Antipatri filius, Ascalonita dictus, fuit Rex universae duodecim tribuum Israëlis terrae, inde Evang. absolutè eum vocat Regem. Eius iussu infanticidium Bethleëmiticum fuit peractum. Filius ei homonymus Herodes, Antipas dictus, fuit tetrarcha Galilaeae & Peraeae Luc. 3. v. 1. iussu Ioh. Baptista ê medio fuit sublatus.

Herodis Ascalonitae ex filio Aristobulo nepos, avo homonymus, Herodes Agrippa cognominatus, Rex Traconitidis, Ituraeae & Galilaeae fuit. Act. 12. v. 1. & seqq. eius iussu Iacobus Ioh. Apostoli frater occisus ac Petrus in vincula coniectus.

Nam Cicero lib. 1. de divinatione testatur, Magos fuisse Regum Persicorum Consiliarios, ac neminem ad imperii gubernacula fuisse evectum, qui non priùs in ipsorum Scholâ institutus fuerit. Patres, qui Magos illos vocant Reges, nomine Regum in significatione latiore utuntur pro viris magnis, honoratis, praestantibus & illustribus, quales hosce Magos fuisse, circumstantiae Historiae, praesertim verò munera ostendunt. August. lib. 3. de mirab. Script. cap. 4. vocat Reges, sed 1. non est genuinus Augustini foetus, quod etiam agnovit Thomas part. 3. q. 45. art. 3. ad 2. 2. locus est corruptus. Verba sic habent: Magi Hierosolymam venerunt, inde inventis Israēlitarum oraculis vatum de eodem nato, ubi nascendi locum acciperet, monente subdolo sermone Reges alacres eunt. Pro Reges legendum Regis, ut ostendit contextus.
