But more correctly it is called a Hebraism. 2. μελάδην. 3. ἀφσόσλα. *(The Syrian also and the Arabic express the same emphasis, but the Ethiopic omitted the word σφόδρα.)* They had begun to fear that they had consumed so long spaces of journey in vain, when such deep silence was kept about the newly born King whom they sought even in Jerusalem, the metropolis of the kingdom; but since they obtain that star, which they had possessed as the indicator of his birth, as guide of their way, on that account they are affected with very great joy.

*(To be noted here is the ellipse of certain words to be repeated from verse preceding, namely "the star standing above the house," after the word star, [that] the star was standing above the house in which the infant Jesus was. Glass. Gr. S. pag. 669.)*

Latin:

v. 10. Triplex emphasis gaudium Magorum exaggerat. 1. ἐχάρησαν χάραν, in quo quidam statuunt esse Atticam elegantiam, sicut Ιλιασ. β. dicitur πολεμὸν πολεμίζειν. Ιλ. κ. βουλὶς βουλένειν. Sed rectiùs dicitur, esse Hebraismum. 2. μελάδην. 3. ἀφσόσλα. *(Exprimunt eandem emphasin Syrus quoque & Arabs, sed Aethiops vocem σφόδρα praetermisit.)* Subvereri caeperant, se frustra tam longa itineris spacia consumsisse, cûm de recens nato Rege, quem quaerebant, tam altum sit Hierosolymis in metropoli regni silentium, sed quia stellam illam, quam habuerant nativitatis indicem, viae suae sortiuntur ducem, inde maximo afficiuntur gaudio.

*(Notanda hic ellipsis vocum quarundam è vers. praecedrepetendarum, post vocem stellae, stellam nempe stantem supra domum, in qua erat infans Iesus. Glass. Gr. S. pag. 669.)*

## 2:11
v. 11. ἀλσθόντες ἀις τὴν όιὀίαν. But Christ was born in a stable and laid in a manger? Those who want Christ to have been worshipped by the Magi in the same place where he was born reply that among the Hebrews every dwelling, even of beasts, is called a house. But it is more probable that the parents of Jesus together with the boy were received into lodgings by a citizen of Bethlehem whose stable that was, after the angelic appearance had become known both to themselves through the shepherds of Bethlehem and to the other fellow-citizens, and the gathering of strangers had been dissolved. It shows therefore that the term ὀικίας, indicates another time of the coming of the Magi than that of the birth of Jesus made in the stable.

εἶδον. The Vulgate rendered they found, because certain Greek copies read ἑῦρον. But the better manuscripts read εἶδον viderunt. *(And this reading is also confirmed by the very ancient Greek manuscript Excerpts of the Nuremberg Library; the Syrian follows the same, (here agreeing with the Altdorf manuscripts along with the printed editions), likewise the Ethiopian and the Arabic, at least as edited by Erpenius. For in the said edition there is expressly written & viderunt, but in the Roman edition of the Medici Press we find , that is, & invenerunt. From which example it may also be gathered that what was written by Casaubon was not without reason, the edition sometimes ῥωμαάζειν. Yet besides the Vulgate even Erasmus of Rotterdam embraces the former reading, so too Theodore Beza, indeed even the blessed Luther himself in his German version.)* Joseph is mentioned here nowhere, not because he was absent, but because he is understood to have contributed nothing to the birth of the Lord.

Some derive Προσεκύνησ-ν ἀυντῷ. Προσκυνεῖν from κυνεῖν to kiss, some from κύνες dogs. For it signifies a gesture of humble and lowly reverence, when someone throws himself down at another's feet.

Although however this word is taken indiscriminately in the Scriptures as an outward sign of civil or religious adoration of reverence; (whence certain ones, such as Drusius in book 1, Praeter., page 3, and several others maintain, that according to their ancestral custom, about which Seneca says in Letter 17, The kings of the Parthians cannot be greeted by anyone without a gift, and with this προσκυνήσει and offering of gifts alone they showed Christ some civil honor) nevertheless the circumstances of the text in this place show that the Magi worshipped Christ with religious adoration, and declared inward worship by the outward gesture of humility. *(Which other godly men also did in the New Testament, see Matt. 8. v. 2.5.ch. 9. v. 27.John 9. v. 38.Acts 7. v. 59.Rev. 22. v. 20.)* They adore therefore God in flesh, wisdom in infancy, power in weakness, majesty in lowliness.

Franciscus Lucas Brugensis annotates on this passage thus: The Magi followed after the boy with that honor which befits a king, nay rather which befits God. And they awaited no divine command, which Luther demands, whereby they might be brought to the greatest adoration of the Eucharist: but it sufficed them to have known the boy's majesty, from the tradition of their forebears, from the declaration of the star, finally from that light which had shone forth upon their minds from GOD as a kind of second star. Response 1. No one among us denies that Christ present in the Eucharist is to be adored, even though some special precept concerning the adoring of Christ in the Eucharist should not exist. 1. We deny, however, that the sacrament itself of the Eucharist, or all that which has been instituted by the Lord to be received, must be adored with the worship of latreia. For since the Eucharist consists of two things, earthly (bread and wine) and heavenly (the body and blood of Christ), therefore we say that adoration ought to be directed not toward the earthly thing or the earthly elements of bread and wine, lest together with the Creator we also adore the creature, but toward Christ σθεάνσ θρωπον, who in that action truly and substantially present distributes to us his Body and his Blood. 3. But we especially disapprove of the adoration of the bread carried about outside the use instituted by Christ, through which idolatry is committed. 4. We therefore invert the argument. The Magi adored Christ, but not the manger in which Christ lay (according to the hypothesis of those who hold that the Magi adored Christ in the stable), nor the lap of the mother, in which he was then reclining according to Luke the Burgundian: so we adore Christ present at the supper, but not the bread, in which and with which the body of Christ is sacramentally exhibited to us. 5. Nor can it be said that the Magi honored both Christ and his mother with one religious adoration, because on the hypothesis of the Papists latria is due to Christ, hyperdulia alone to Mary ἀρτολατρεία λατρεία, ὑπερδουλεία.

Ἀνοίξαντες τοὺς θησαυροὺς. From this the Papists conclude, that these Magi were Kings, since they brought treasures, hidden riches, with them. Answer: κθησαυρὰς properly signifies anything whatever in which something is stored up, whether it be baggage, or a case, or a sack. Ps. 125. v. 8. Who brings out the winds ἐκ τῶν θησαςρῶν ἀυτού. Cicero has memory of a treasure, that is, ταμεῖον of all things. Hence in the Arabic version the Magi are said to have opened their vessels. For it is not likely that they exported all their treasures from home into Palestine, and the treasure of the Persians would not have been valued as gold, frankincense, and myrrh only.

Προσήνεγκαν αὐτῷ δῶρα. As the adoration, so also some attribute the offering of gifts merely to the custom of the Eastern peoples, who offer gifts to their King when they worship him. But the Fathers teach with great consensus, and the very gifts show, that a deeper mystery lies here, concerning which the pious ancients discourse most sweetly.

Irenaeus book 3. chapter 10. page 180. By means of the gifts they offered, they showed what sort of person he was who was being worshipped. Myrrh indeed, because he himself was the one who would die and be buried for mortal humankind. Gold however because he was a King, whose kingdom had no end. Frankincense however because God, who was made known even in Judaea and manifest to those who did not seek him.

Hilary, canon 2 on Matthew. By confessing the King in the gold, God in the frankincense, and man in the myrrh. And thus, through the veneration of these, the knowledge of the whole Sacrament is consummated: in the man, that of death; in GOD, that of the resurrection; in the King, that of judgment.

Ambrose on chapter 2 of Luke. What are these gifts of true faith? Gold for the King, frankincense for GOD, myrrh for the deceased. For one thing is the insignia of a King, another is the Sacrifice of divine power, another is the honor of burial, which does not corrupt the body of the dead, but preserves it.

Jerome on chapter 2 of Matthew, from Juvencus. Gold, frankincense, myrrh, they bring as gifts to the King, to God, and to man.

Prudentius. The treasure and the fragrant odor of the Sabaean incense announce the King and God, but the myrrh-dust foretells the sepulcher.

Augustine, sermon 36 de tempore. They present gold, frankincense, and myrrh, offering more in mysteries than in their own consciousness. In the gift of gold, royal dignity is demonstrated; in the vapor of frankincense, divine majesty; in the appearance of myrrh, the humanity to be buried.

Gregory of Nyssa, sermon on the holy nativity of Christ, page 73. They offer frankincense as to GOD, and they honor royal dignity with gold, and they receive and designate and signify by myrrh that arrangement and administration which was disposed by a certain reason concerning the passion, through a certain Prophetic grace.

Chrysostom says, they certainly offer gifts to GOD, than which none more unworthy,

The same show how mystically gold, frankincense and myrrh can and ought also be offered by us to Christ. But in this accommodation there occurs a certain diversity. 1. Aug. sermon on Ephiphany, vol. 10. He receives gold from us, if we give alms; frankincense, if we pour out prayers; myrrh, if we die for him.

Bernard, sermon 3 on Epiphany. We offer gold to Christ, if we despise all earthly substance for our love toward him. We offer myrrh, if we mortify our members which are upon earth, and deny ourselves for his sake. Frankincense, if we hold our heart upward toward the Lord, and desire, savour, seek those things that are above.

2. Some establish that by gold faith is signified, by frankincense prayers, by myrrh the patient taking up of the cross and the mortification of the flesh, in which sense Gregory generally says, that by the gold of the Magi it was signified that the nations ought to offer to Christ true acknowledgment and faith, by frankincense burning prayer, by myrrh the mortification of the flesh.

3. Leo, sermon 6 on the Epiphany, chapter 1, proceeds thus. If we wish to look with a solicitous intellect at how that triple species of gift is offered by all who come to Christ with the step of faith, is not the same offering celebrated in the hearts of those who rightly believe? For he brings forth gold from the treasury of his soul who acknowledges Christ as King of the universe; he offers myrrh, who believes that the only-begotten of GOD has united the true nature of man to himself: and he venerates him with a certain incense, who confesses him in nothing unequal to the paternal majesty.

4. Bonaventure applies it thus. Let us offer gold, that is love, on account of the good things bestowed; incense, that is devotion, on account of the joys prepared; myrrh penitence, on account of the evils committed.

Latin:

v. 11. ἀλσθόντες ἀις τὴν όιὀίαν.At Christus natus erat in stabulo ac repositus in praesepio? Qui volunt, Christum eodem loco â Magis adoratum, in quo erat natus, respondent, apud Hebraeos omnem mansionem etiam bestiarum, domum vocari. Sed verisimilius est, parentes Iesu cum puero in aedes â Bethlemitico cive, cuius stabulum illud erat proprium, esse receptos, postquam per Pastores Bethleemiticos apparitio Angelica ipsi & reliquis cóncivibus innotuerat, ac conventus peregrinorum erat solutus. Ostendit igitur nomen ὀικίας, indicari aliud tempus adventûs Magorum, quàm nativitatis Iesu in stabulo factae.

εἶδον. Vulg. reddidit invenerunt, quia quaedam exemplaria Graeca habent, ἑῦρον. Sed probatiores Codd legunt εἶδον viderunt. *(Et hanc lectionem confirmant quoque Eclogae Graecae MSS. vetustissimae Bibl. Noriberg. sequuntur eandem Syrus, (consentiente hic MSS. Altodorff. cum Codd. excusis) Aethiops ac Arabs, prout quidem ab Erpenio editus est. Expressè enim in dictâ edit. legitur & viderunt, sed in Romanâ editione Mediceae Typographiae habetur id est, & invenerunt. E quo exemplo colligere quoque licet, non frustra â Casaubono scriptum, editionem haninterdumῥωμαάζειν. Amplectuntur tamen priorem etiam lectionem praeter Vulgatum Erasmus quoq; Roterodamus, Theod. Beza, quin ipse B. Lutherus in vers. Germanicâ.)* Iosephi nulla hic sit mentio, non quòd abfuerit, sed quod â Magis intellectum, ipsum nihil ad nativitatem Domini contulisse.

Προσεκύνησ-ν ἀυντῷ. Προσκυνεῖν quidam deducunt ex κυνεῖνosculari, quidam â κύνεςcanes. Significatur enim humilis & abiectae venerationis gestus, cùm aliquis ad pedes alterius sese abiicit.

Quamvis verò hoc verbum in Scripturis sumatur promiscuè pro externo reverentiae civilis vel religiosae adorationis indicio; (unde quidam, uti Drusius lib. 1. Praeter. pag. 3. & alii nonnulli statuunt, ipsos more patrio, de quo Seneca Epist. 17. Reges Parthos non potest quisquam salutare sine munere, & hac προσκυνήσει & munerum oblatione duntaxat civilem aliquem cultum Christo exhibuisse) circumstantiae tamen textus h. l. ostendunt, Magos religiosa adoratione Christum coluisse, acinteriorem cultum exteriore humilitatis gessu declarasse. *(Id quod alii quoque pii fecerunt in N. T. vid. Matth. 8. v. 2.5.cap. 9. v. 27.Ioh. 9. v. 38.Act. 7. v. 59.Apoc. 22. v. 20.)* Adorant ergo Deum in carne, in infantia sapientiam, in infirmitate virtutem, in vilitate maiestatem.

Franc. Lucas Brug. ad h. l. sic annotat. Prosecuti sunt Magi puerum honore eo qui Regem, imò qui Deum decet. Nec expectarunt divinum praeceptum, id quod Luther. exposcit, utadter maximae Euchastiae adorationem adducatur: sed satis eis fuit, pueri cognovisse maiestatem, ex maiorum suorum traditione, ex stellae declaratione, denique ex ea luce, quae illorum mentibus quasi alterum quoddam sidus â DEO effulserat. Resp. 1. Christum in Eucharistia praesentem nemo nostrûm adorandum negat, etiamsi speciale aliquod praeceptum de Christo in Eucharistia adorando non extet 1. Ipsum verò Eucharistiae Sacramentum seu totum illud, quod â Domino, ut sumatur, institutum est, cultu latriae adorandum esse, negamus. Cûm enim Eucharistia constet duabus rebus, terrena (pane & vino) ac coelesti (corpore & sangvine Christi) ideò adorationem dirigendam esse dicimus non ad terrenam rem sive terrena Elementa panis & vini, ne cum creatore etiam creaturam adoremus, sed ad Christum σθεάνσ θρωπον, qui in illa actione verè ac substantialiter praesens suum corpus & suum Sangvinem nobis distribuit. 3. cumprimis verò improbamus adorationem panis, extra usum â Christo institutum circumgestati, per quam ἀρτολατρεία committitur. 4. Invertimus igitur argumentum. Magi adoraverunt Christum, non autem praesepe, in quo Christus iacebat (iuxta eorum hypothesin, qui in stabulo Magos adorasse Christum statuunt) nec gremium matris, in quo iuxta Lucam Brugensem tunc recumbebat: sic adoramus Christum in coena praesentem, non autem panem, in quo & cum quo Christi corpus Sacramentaliter praesens nobis exhibetur. 5. Nec dici potest, Magos & Christum & matrem eius una religiosa adoratione honorasse, quia ex hypothesi Pontificiorum Christo debetur λατρεία, Mariae tantùm ὑπερδουλεία.

Ἀνοίξαντες τοὺς θησαυροὺς. Ex eo colligunt Pontificii, Magos hosce fuisse Reges, quippe qui thesauros, opes reconditas, secum attulerint. Resp. κθησαυρὰς propriè significat quidvis, in quo aliquid repositum est, sive sit sarcina, sive theca, sive saccus. Ps. 125. v. 8.Qui educit ventosἐκ τῶν θησαςρῶν ἀυτού. Ciceroni memoria est thesaurus, id est, ταμεῖονrerum omnium. Inde in Arab. vers. Magi dicuntur aperuisse vasa sua. Neque enim verisimile est, illos omnes thesauros suos secum domo in Palaestinam exportasse, ac Persarum thesauri non auro, thure & myrrhâ tantùm fuere aestimati.

Προσήνεγκαν αὐτῷ δῶρα. Ut adorationem, ita quoque munerum oblationem quidam tantùm tribuunt mori Orientalium, qui Regi suo, quando eum adorant, munera offerunt. Sed Patres magno consensu docent, & munera ipsa ostendunt, altius hic latere mysterium, de quo pii veteres suavissimè philosophantur.

Irenaeus lib. 3. cap. 10. pag. 180. Per ea, quae obtulerunt munera, ostenderunt, quiderat, qui adorabatur. Myrrha quidem, quod ipse erat, qui pro mortali humano genere moreretur & sepeliretur. Aurum verò quoniam Rex, cuius regni non erat finis. Thus verò quoniam Deus, qui & notus in Iudaa factus & manifesta-us eis, qui non quaerebant cum.

Hilarius can. 2. in Matth. In auro Regem, in thure Deum, in myrrha hominem confitendo. Atque ita per venerationem corum Sacramenti omnis est consummata cognitio, in homine mortis, in DEO resurrectionis, in Rege iudicii.

Ambrosius in cap. 2. Luc. Quae sunt ista verae fidei munera? aurum Regi, thus DEO, myrrha defuncto. Aliud enim Regis insigne, aliud divinae potestatis Sacrificium, aliud honor est sepulturae, quae non corrumpat corpus mortui, sed reservet.

Hieron. in cap. 2. Matth. ex Iuvenco. Aurum, thus, myrrham, Regique, Deoque, hominia Dona ferunt.

Prudentius. Regem, Deuma annunciant Thesaurus & flagrans odor Thuris Sabaei, at myrrheus pul-is sepulchrum praedocet.

Augustinus serm. 36. de tempore. Exhibent aurumthus & myrrham, plus in mysteriis, quam in conscientiis offerentes. In auri munere regia dignitas, in thuris vapore divina maiestas, in myrrhae specie sepelienda demonstratur humanitas.

Gregor. Nyssen. serm. de sanct. Christi nativ. pag. 73. Illi tanquam DEO offerunt thus, ac regiam dignitatem auro colunt, atexcipiunt, eama quae circa passionem certa ratione disposita est ordinationem atadministrationem Propheticâ quadam gratiâ per myrtham designant atsignificant.

Chrysostomus dicit, munera offerunt DEO certè, quàm homindigniora.

Iidem ostendunt, quomodo mysticè etiam â nobis Christo aurum, thus & myrrha offerri possit atque debeat. Sed in accommodatione occurrit quaedam diversitas. 1. Aug. serm. in Epiph. tom. 10. A nobis aurum accipit, si eleemosynas faciamus: thus, siorationes fundamus; myrrham, si pro illo moriamur.

Bernhard. serm. 3. Epiph. Aurum Christo offerimus, siterrenam omnem substantiam pro nostro erga eum amore spernamus. Myrrham st nostra, quae super terram, membra mortificemus, nosque ipsi abnegemus. Thus, si cor sursum habeamus ad Dominum, quae sursum sunt, animo desideremus, sapiamus, quaeramus.

2. Quidam statuunt, per aurum significari fidem, per thus preces, per myrrham patientem crucis susceptionem & carnis mortificationem, quo ferè sensu Gregorius dicit, per aurum Magorum significatum fuisse, quòd gentes debeant Christo offerre veram agnitionem & fidem, per thus ardentem orationem, per myrrham carnis mortificationem.

3. Leo serm. 6. Epiphan. cap. 1. sic progreditur. Si solicito intellectu velimus aspicere, quomodo triplex illa species muneris ab omnibus, qui ad Christum gressu fidei veniunt, offeratur, nonne in cordibus rectè credentium eadem celebratur oblatio? Aurum enim de thesauro animi sui promit, qui Christum Regem universitatis agnoscit; myrrham offert, qui unigenitum DEI credit veram sibi hominis unisse Naturam: & quodam eum thure veneratur, qui in nullo ipsum paternae maiestati imparem confitetur.

4. Bonaventura sic applicat. Offeramus aurum dilectionis propter bona collata; thus devotionis propter gaudia praeparata; myrtham poenitentipropter mala perpetrata.

## 2:12
v. 12. They are said to be καὶ χρηματισθέντες. χρηματίζεσθαι warned, not only by those asking when God gives answers, but also those whom He deigns to address with His speech, even if they ask or expect nothing of such a kind. Hence the Syrian translates simply, it was revealed to them, or they were admonished by divine inspiration. *(So too the Arabic)* Justin, in his Dialogue with Tryphon, interprets κατ ᾽ποἀάλκιν ύψελευσθέντες as the secret declaration of righteousness. It can also be said that regard is had to the desire of the Magi, for without doubt they were anxious whether they should return to Herod, since, deprived of the guidance of the star, they desired a manifestation of the divine will.

Κατ ᾽ ὀναρ. Jerome states that this oracle was given to the Magi immediately by GOD, and asserts that χρησμὸν is so called whenever God responds by Himself. The Greeks think that just as Joseph, the supposed father of Christ, God addressed through an Angel in dreams Matt. 1. v. 20. and shortly afterward was going to address him again chapt. 2. v. 13. and 19., so likewise this divine response was made known to the Magi through an Angel.

Without doubt Herodes, enraged by that mud stained with blood , would have laid hands upon the very Magi themselves, unless, admonished by a divine oracle, they had returned to their own land by another way than that which led to Jerusalem. Iren. lib. 3. chapt. 18. pag. 204. Δὀ ἄλλης ὁδοῦ. 4 They departed by another way, returning no longer through the land of the Assyrians. Observation of Jacobus Faber Stapulensis on this passage: The Magi, who prefigured the Gentiles, therefore after worshipping the Lord returned to their own country by another way in mystery, and indeed by divine oracle, because our first way is that of the flesh, of sin and of the world; when Christ has been sought, known, and worshipped by that way, we must walk in it no more, but by another utterly contrary to it, which is that of the Spirit, of grace, and of GOD. But what is our country, except that to which we were created? And this is the heavenly dwelling.

Latin:

v. 12. καὶ χρηματισθέντες. χρηματίζεσθαι dicuntur, non solùm quib. interrogantibus Deus responsa reddit, sed etiam quos alloquio suo dignatur, etiamsi nihil tale quid quaerant vel expectent. Inde Syrus simpliciter vertit, revelatum est eis, vel divinitus admoniti sunt. *(Sic quoque Arabs)* Iustin in Dial. cum Tryphone interpretatur κατ ᾽ποἀάλκιν ύψελευσθέντεςarcanâ declaratione iusti. Potest etiam dici, quod respectus habeatur ad defiderium Magorum, procul dubio enim soliciti fuerunt, an ad Herodem debeant redire, ne-ne, proinde stellae ductu destituti divinae voluntatis manifestationem desiderarunt.

Κατ ᾽ ὀναρ. Hieronymus statuit, hoc oraculum fuisse immediatè â DEO Magis datum ac χρησμὸν dici asserit, quoties Deus per se respondet. Graeci existimant, ut Iosephum Christi putatum patrem Deus per Angelum in somnis allocutus erat Matth. 1. v. 20. & paulò post denuô allocuturus erat cap. 2. v. 13. & 19. ita quoque Magis per Angelum hoc responsum divinum fuisse patefactum.

Δὀ ἄλλης ὁδοῦ. 4 Procul dubio Herodes lutum illud sangvine maceratum, ipsis Magis iniecisset manus, nisi divino oraculo admoniti per aliam viam, quàm quae Hierosolymam ducebat, in patriam terram reversi fuissent. Iren. lib. 3. cap. 18. pag. 204. Per alteram abierunt viam, non iam per Assyriorum revertentes terram. Observ. Iac. Faber Stap. in h. l. Magi, qui figurabant gentes, adorato Domino ideò per aliam viam in regionem suam in mysterio regressi sunt, idque divino oraculo, quod prima via nostra sit carnis, peccati & mundi, quâ quaesito, cognito, adoratoa Christo non amplius nobis incedendum est, sed alia illi prorsus contraria, quae est Spiritus, gratiae atque DEI. Regio autem nostra quaenam est, nisi ad quam creati sumus, haec autem est coelestis mansio.

## 2:13
v. 13. Between the departure of the Magi and this flight of Christ into Egypt, there intervenes the history of the offering of Christ in the temple and the purification of Mary, which Luke recounts in chapter 2, v. 22 and following. Therefore, the rule of Augustine in *De consensu Evangelistarum*, book 2, chapter 5, is to be noted in this place. Each Evangelist so weaves his narrative that the series appears to be arranged as if he were omitting nothing. For by keeping silent about what he does not wish to tell, he so joins those things which he does wish to tell to those which he was telling, that they appear to follow immediately. Ἐγερθεὶς. [

From the following verse it appears that the sense of the oracle is that he should rise from bed without delay, and having shaken sleep from his eyes immediately flee into Egypt with the boy and his mother at that very moment of night. From this the greatness of the present danger is understood, and consequently also the fact that these things did not happen while Joseph was still staying in Jerusalem on the day of the purification and presentation, but, as some maintain, had already returned to Bethlehem or Nazareth; for Luke expressly says that he went straightway from Jerusalem to Nazareth. Luke 2. v. 39. Ἐγερθεὶς.

Observe how cautiously the Angel speaks: He does not say, rise and take thy son, but take the child and his mother, because this child was not begotten of Joseph. Nor does he say, take thy wife and her son, but take the child and his mother, because this child was so much his mother's son that he was even her Lord, whence in the order of speech he is set before her.

Egypt, the workshop of idolatry, offers lodging to the newborn Christ, which was just as much a prelude of the calling of the Gentiles to the kingdom of Christ as was the coming of the Magi.

Moses flees from Egypt into Judea, Christ from Judea into Egypt, because in the O.T. the Church was enclosed within the narrow borders of Judea, to which the faithful gathered themselves, but in the N.T. Christ converted Egypt and other idolatrous regions of the Gentiles into Judea through the preaching of the Gospel and the illumination of the Holy Spirit. ἕως ἂν εἴπω σοι (until I tell you).

From these words of the Angels Joseph could gather that he was not to remain forever in Egyptian exile, but would at some time be recalled from it. Μέλλει γὰρ Ἠρωδης, &c. Some copies read ζητεῖν τὸ παιδίον,, others indeed ἀποκτεῖναι. But the former reading better suits the text, for there follows καὶ ἀπολέσαι. ἕως ἂν εἴπω σοι.

Latin:

v. 13. Inter Magorum discessum & hanc Christi in Aegyptum fugam intercedit Historia oblationis Christi in templo & purificationis Mariae, quam recenset Lucas cap. 2. v. 22. & seqq. Notanda ergo hoc loco regula Augustini lib. 2. de cons. Evang. cap. 5. Unusquisa Evangelista sic contexit narrationem suam, ut tanquam nihil praetermittentis series digesta videatur. Tacitis enim quae non vult dicere, sic ea, quae vult dicere, illis, quae dicebat, adiungit, ut ipsa continuò sequi videantur.

Ἐγερθεὶς. Ex versic. seq. apparet, sensum oraculi esse eum, quod sine mora debeat lecto surgere, & excusso statim oculis somno illo ipso noctis momento cum puero & matre eius in Aegyptum fugere. Ex quo periculi praesentis magnitudo intelligitur, ac proinde etiam illud, quòd haec non contigerint, Iosepho Hierosolymis in purificationis & oblationis die adhuc commorante, sed, ut quidam volunt, Bethlehemam vel Nazaretham reverso, disertè enim dicit Lucas, quod Hierosolymâ Nazaretham immediatè se contulerit. Luc. 2. v. 39.

Observa, quàm circumspectè loquatur Angelus: Non dicit, surge & accipe filium tuum, sed accipe puerum & matrem eius, quia puer hic non erat ex Iosepho genitus. Nec dicit, accipe coniugem & filium eius, sed accipe puerum & matrem eius, quia hic puer sic erat matris filius, ut etiam eius esset Dominus, unde in ordine sermonis ei praefertur.

Aegyptus idololatriae officina Christo nato praebet hospitium, quod fuit aequè ac Magorum adventus, vocationis gentium ad regnum Christi praeludium.

Moses ex Aegypto in Iudaeam fugit, Christus ex Iudaea in Aegyptum, quia in V. T. Ecclesia angustis Iudaeae limitibus inclusa erat, cui fideles sese aggregabant, sed in N. T. Christus Aegyptum & alias gentilium regiones idololatricas convertit in Iudaeam per Evangelii praedicationem, & Spiritus S. illuminationem.

ἕως ἂν εἴπω σοι. Ex his Angeli verbis Iosephus colligere potuit, sibi non esse perpetuò in Aegyptiaco exilio haerendum, sed ex eo aliquando revocatum iri. Μέλλει γὰρ Ἠρωδης, &c. Quaedam exemplaria legunt ζητεῖν τὸ παιδίον, quaedam verò ἀποκτεῖναι. Sed prior lectio magis congruit textui, sequitur enim καὶ ἀπολέσαι.

## 2:14
v. 14. On that very night on which he had received the divine oracle, he fled, lest anyone should observe him fleeing and report to Herod by what route he had set out in flight.

Peter Martyr, writer of the Ocean Decades, writes in the third book of his Babylonian embassy that this place, to which Christ as a boy was withdrawn by flight from the cruel infanticide of King Herod, is called Matarea by the Egyptian inhabitants, and is beyond Cairo, but on this side of the place where Memphis, once celebrated for the miracle of the pyramids, was situated, and that it is distant from great Cairo by almost ten thousand paces, and that he himself visited that place for the sake of religion in the year 1502. The Moors also, in that place where it is said the Virgin's dwelling was, keep a lamp perpetually burning in memory of the boy Jesus kept there.

Observ. Fulgentius, sermon 5. He flees, not out of human fear, but by divine dispensation; not out of necessity, but by power.

God could hinder Herod's bloody designs even by His mere nod, nay rather remove him from the midst; moreover Christ, since He was God όμοουσιος endowed with divine power communicated personally to Himself according to His human Nature, could have done this, but it was the time of emptying Phil. 2. v. 7. and Christ wished to teach by His own example that flight is sometimes lawful.

The Greeks call death τελευτὴν metonymically, because, as Demosthenes says, it is πέρας τοΕ βίου ἑκάςῳ:; for it signifies ΤελευΤη, the end of each thing. Some think τελευτὴν is said as it were τελετὴν initiation, so that τελευτᾶν means as it were ΤελευΤαν to initiate or Τελεισθ,, because the pious through death are initiated into angelic life. But this etymology does not fit the death of Herod. ἕως τῆς λευτης

Latin:

v. 14. Ipsâ illâ nocte, quâ divinum oraculum acceperat, fugit, ne quis fugientem observarer, &, cui viae in fuga institisset, Herodi nunciaret.

Petrus Martyr, Decadum Oceanicarum scriptor, tertio legationis suae Babylonicae libro scribit, hunc locum, quò Christus puer â crudeli Regis Herodis infanticidio fuga subductus est, ab incolis Aegyptiis Mataraeam nuncupari, & ultra Cairum esse, sed citra locum, ubi olim miraculo pyramidum decantata Memphis sita erat, distareque â magna Cairo fermè passuum decem millibus, se autem eum locum religionis causa invisisse Anno 1502. Mauros quoque eo in loco, ubi fertur Virginis habitatio fuisse, perpetuò ardentem lampadem in pueri Iesu illic asservati memoriam conservare.

Observ. Fulgentius serm. 5. Eugit, non formidine humana, sed dispensatione divina; non necessitate, sed potestate.

Potaisset Deus vel solo nutu Herodis cruenta consilia impedire, imo ipsum ê medio tollere; quin & Chr-stus utpote Patri όμοουσιος divinâ potestate personaliter secundùm humanam Naturam sibi communicata hoc praestare potuisset, sed fuit tempus exinanitionis Phil. 2. v. 7. ac suo exemplo Christus docere voluit, fugam quandoque esse licitam.

ἕως τῆς λευτης Graecim ortem vocant τελευτὴν metonymicè, quod ut Demosthenes inquit, sit πέρας τοΕ βίου ἑκάςῳ: significat enim ΤελευΤη extremum cuiusque rei. Quidam putant τελευτὴν dici quasi τελετὴνinitiationem, ita ut τελευτᾶν sit quasi ΤελευΤανinitiare vel Τελεισθ, quia pii per mortem vitae Angelicae initiantur. Sed haec etymologia non congruit morti Herodis.

## 2:15
v. 15. Out of Egypt I called my son. This prophecy has been taken from Hosea 11, v. 1, and indeed from the Hebrew text. For the LXX rendered it in the plural: Out of Egypt I called his children, namely Israel's. For ינפל they read ונבל or ויבל.

But because it is manifest from the series of the Prophetic text that in the literal sense it treats there of the Israelite people, who are the firstborn, but the adoptive Son of GOD, Exod. 4. v. 22. thence arises the question, by what reasoning does the Evangelist apply this to Christ, who is the essential and natural Son of GOD?

1. Jerome states that this was done with regard to what happened τυπικῶς What τυπικὶς, he says, preceded in that people is referred according to truth and fulfillment to Christ. Opposing himself to him, Andreas Osiander, book 1 of the Harmony, chapter 11, collects many points of dissimilarity between the sojournings of Christ and of the Israelites in Egypt, in order to prove that this saying τυπικῶς cannot be accommodated to Christ; therefore he states that in the literal sense this saying concerns Christ, and accordingly translates it thus: Surely, by destroying, destroyed shall the king of Israel be, because Israel is foolish, yet I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son. But the sequence of the text clearly shows that directly and properly the Prophet speaks about the Israelite people. Nor can it be inferred from the fact that there are certain dissimilarities between the sojourning of Christ and of the Israelites in Egypt, that this was not a type of him; for it suffices that certain similarities could exist. Each was GOD'S people, beloved above others—the former above other peoples, the latter above all sharers in human Nature. Each was born in Judah or Canaan—for there Israel was formed into a people. Each was carried as an infant into Egypt—the former fleeing death which famine threatened , the latter fleeing death which loomed through treachery. As a child each lived as a stranger in Egypt. When grown, each was called out of Egypt by GOD after the slaying of the infant-killing kings—the former in the fourth generation Gen. 15. v. 16., which is the fourth year of the age of the people, the latter in the fourth year of age, or, as some wish, twice-fourth, that is, eighth. The comparison can also be made between the ends of the calling out of Egypt. Therefore Jerome's opinion should not be entirely rejected, according to which the Evangelist rightly could say that in the flight of Christ into Egypt, which preceded the recall out of Egypt, the prophetic oracle was fulfilled: Out of Egypt I called my son. For those sayings which set forth types, or the completion of prophecies, embrace both—namely both the type and the thing shadowed by the type—with respect to full and entire interpretation: prediction and completion.

2. Some, among whom is the blessed Luther, think that this fulfillment is said to have been made on account of the similarity. For since Christ was sent away into Egypt and recalled from it, something similar to this event preceded in the people of Israel.

3. It is answered simply, that Christ together with the faithful constitutes one mystical body, of which He Himself is the head, and that believers are received as sons by GOD on account of Christ. Therefore what is said by the Prophet concerning the members, that the Evangelist applies to the head. What is said by the Prophet concerning the adopted son, namely Israel, that is here applied to the natural and only-begotten Son of God, on whose account alone adoption as sons of GOD comes to believers. *(This especially supports the observation of the blessed Dr. Chemnitz, in Harm. Evang. chap. 12. p. 131., which the blessed Dr. Meisner also repeats, Comment. in Hoseam pag. 929., namely that prophetic prophecies are fulfilled in four ways

1. When that happens which is understood precisely and simply in the prophecy, as Matth. 1. v. 22. 23. and some think this can be called univocal fulfillment. Compare Mich. 5, 2. with Matth. 2, 6.

2. When something similar happens, which has kinship with the past event, as Matth. 2. v. 17. chap. 13. v. 35. and they think this can be called fulfillment analogi-am.

3. When the prophecy is general, and can be adapted to any other examples whatever, as Matth. 15. v. 7. cap. 13. v. 14. Ioh. 12. v. 40. Act. 28. v. 25 26. Rom. 11. v. 8. And they judge this can be called specific.

4. When the prophecy is fulfilled in the members and the head, in the type and antitype, as in the present passage Matth. 2. v. 15. Some again distinguish this mode, so that besides those there is another fulfillment, one being typical, and another mystical. According to this last mode they are rightly said to be fulfilled when they are adapted either to the members or to the head.)*

4. This agrees with the response mentioned above, that God loves the people of Israel only in Christ and on account of Christ His beloved Son, and bestowed upon it various benefits, among which also is the leading out of Egypt; accordingly what preceded in the people of Israel there is here applied to Christ.

Even the ancient Hebrews knew that the Messiah was to set out into Egypt and be called back from there by GOD, whence they expounded the passage of Psalm 80, v. 9, you brought up a vine out of Egypt, concerning the Messiah, since he is there called a vine. In the book Berachoth, chapter Haroah makom, and in Moses Hadarsan on Genesis ch. 40, v. 9.

Observation. Christ endured this pilgrimage so that he might establish the sons of Adam—exiles and wanderers, made strangers to the citizens of heaven and pilgrims from the sons of the heavenly Jerusalem—in the stability of the heavenly mansions, through this restless mutability of his own dwellings on earth.

Latin:

v. 15. Ex Aegypto voc avi filium meum. Defumtum est hoc vaticinium ex Oseae 11. v. 1. & quidem ex textu Hebraeo. LXX. enim reddiderunt in plurali. Ex Aegypto voc avi filios eius, scil. Israēlis. Proינפל legerunt ונבל vel ויבל.

Quia verò manifestum est ex serie textûs Prophetici, in sensu literali ibi agi de populo, Israëlitico, qui est primogenitus, sed adoptivus DEI filius,Exod. 4. v. 22. inde oritur quaestio, quāratione Evang. hoc applicet ad Christum, qui est essentialis & naturalis DEI Filius?

1. Hieronymus statuit, illud fieriτυπικῶς Quod τυπικὶς, inquit, praecessit in illo populo iuxta veritatem & adimpletionem refertur ad Christum. Illi opponens sese Andreas Osiander lib. 1. Harm. cap. 11. multas dissimilitudines colligit commorationis Christi & Israëlitarum in Aegypto, ut probet, non posse dictum hoc τυπικῶς ad Christum accomodari; statuit igitur, in sensu literali hoe dictum agere de Christo, ideò illud sic vertit. Manè extirpando extirpatus est Rex Israëlis, quia insipiens Israël, & tamen dilexi eum, & ex Aegypto vocavi filium meum. Sed series textus manifestè ostendit, directè & propriè apud Prophetam agi de populo Israëlitico. Neque ex eo, quod sint quaedam dissimilitudines commorationis Christi & Israëlitarum in Aegypto, inferri potest, hanc non fuisse illius typum, sufficit enim, posse quasdam similitudines dari. Uterque fuit DEI populus, prae caeteris dilectus, ille prae caeteris populis, hic prae omnibus humanae Naturae consortibus. Uterque in Iudaea sive Cananaea fuit natus, illic enim Israël in populum efformatus. Uterque infans in Aegyptum delatus est, ille mortem fugiens, quam c--minabatur fames, hic mortem fugiens, quae per insidias immine bat. Puer in Aegypto uterque peregrinus egit. Adultus ex Aegypto infanticidis Regibus sublatis â DEO uterque vocatus est, ille quartâ generatione Gen. 15. v. 16. qui quartus est annus aetatis populi, hic anno aetatis quarto, vel ut aliqui volunt bis quarto sive octavo. Potest etiam collatio inter finem vocationis ex Aegypto institui. Hieronymi ergo sententia non est penitus reiicienda, iuxta quam Evangelista rectè potuit dicere. In fuga Christi in Aegyptum, quae revocationem ex Aegypto praecessit, impletum fuisse oraculum Propheticum: Ex Aegypto vocavi filium meum. Dicta enim, quae typos proponunt, vel complementum vaticiniorum, respectu plenae & integrae interpretationis complectuntur utrumq;, videlicet & typum & rem typo adumbratam, praedictionem & complementum.

2. Quidam, inter quos B. Lutherus, putant, hanc impletionem dici factam propter similitudinem. Quod enim Christus in Aegyptum ablegatus, & ex ea revocatus, eius rei simile quid in populo Israëlitico praecessit.

3. Simpliciter respondetur, Christum cum fidelibus constituere unum corpus mysticum, cuius ipse est caput, ac propter Christum credentes in filios â DEO recipi. Quod ergo apud Prophetam dicitur de membris, illud ab Evangelista applicatur ad caput. Quod apud Prophetam dicitur de filio adoptivo, scil. Israële, illud hic applicatur ad naturalem & unigenitum DEI filium, propter quem solum credentibus adoptio in filios DEI contingit. *(Facit huc cumprimis B. D. Chemnitii observatio, in Harm. Evang. cap. 12. p. 131. quam repetit etiam B. D. Meisnerus Comment. in Hoseam pag. 929. videlicet vaticinia Prophetica quatuor impleri modis

1. Quum illud fit, quod praecisè & simpliciter in vaticinio intelligitur, ut Matth. 1. v. 22. 23. atque hanc existimant nonnulli, vocari posse impletionem univocam. Conf. Mich. 5, 2. cum Matth. 2, 6.

2. Quum simile aliquid fit, quod cognationem habet cum re praeterita, ut Matth. 2. v. 17.cap. 13. v. 35. & hanc putant dici posse analogi-am.

3. Quum vaticinium generale est, & ad quaevis exempla alia accommodari potest, ut Matth. 15. v. 7.cap. 13. v. 14.Ioh. 12. v. 40.Act. 28. v. 25 26.Rom. 11. v. 8. Et hanc adppellari posse censent specificam.

4. Quum vaticinium in membris & capite, in typo & antitypo impletur, ut praesenti loco Matth. 2. v. 15. Nonnulli distinguunt iterum hunc modum, ita ut ipsis. 5. alia impletio sit typica, ac alia mystica. Iuxta hunc postremum modum rectè dicuntur impleri, quando accommodantur sive ad membra, sive ad caput.)*

4. Cum memorata responsione congruit ista, quòd Deus non nisi in Christo & propter Christum dilectum suum Filium diligat populum Israēliticum, & varia beneficia, inter quae etiam est eductio ex Aegypto, ei contulerit, proinde quod in populo Israëlitico ibi praecessit, illud hic ad Christum accommodatur.

Etiam prisci Hebraei sciverunt, Messiam debuisse in Aegyptum proficisci & inde â DEO evocari, unde locum Psalmi 80. v. 9. transferes vitem ex Aegypto, de Messia exposuerunt, quippe qui vitis ibi appelletur. In libro Berachoth. cap. Haroah makom & apud Mosen Hadarsan in cap. 40. Gen. v. 9.

Observ. Christus hanc peregrinationem perpessus est, ut filios Adae exules & vagos, extraneos â coeli civibus factos & peregrinos â filiis coelestis Hierusalem, hac sua in terris mansionum irrequietâ mutabilitate, in coelestium mansionum stabilitate firmaret.

## 2:16
v. 16. ἐνεπαίχθη. But how did the Magi mock Herod, when warned by divine oracle they did not return to him? Answer: these things are said κασθ' υπόληψιν of Herod, seeing that he interpreted their secret departure into their homeland by another way as mockery. The word is Syrian.

is peculiar to the Syriac language, from the Hebrew הןב he has been mocked, from which it departs not far, except that it changes the third letter of the root ה into ח, being of the same organ and pronunciation. But wherever the Syrian uses it, it is always ח in place of ה.

From those things which had happened on the day of purification, a public rumor had grown strong that the boy Jesus had been proclaimed the Messiah in the temple by Simeon and Anna. From this he understood that the Magi had not kept the promise given to him.

The Scribes, as can be gathered from Josephus, book 17, chapter 3, occasioned by the prophetic prophecy Mic. 5. showed Herod that it had been decreed by GOD that upon the birth of the Messiah the sceptre of the kingdom would pass over to him, and all Kings worship him. This Herod, drunk with Pharisaic opinions, understood carnally of an earthly kingdom of the Messiah, and therefore feared for his own kingdom. Herod first persuaded himself that the Magi had been deceived because of φαινομένου ἀστέρος and consequently were ashamed to return, where they would hear no further report about the newly born King of the Jews. But when on the day of purification and offering a new rumor spread about the King Messiah having been born, and what had been prophesied of him by Simeon and Anna grew widespread at Jerusalem, then he felt that he had been mocked by the Magi.

(* ἰδὼν videns, that is understanding. See Gen. 8. v. 8. Matth. 9. v. 3. Iacob. 2. v. 24. Augustine on Exodus, question 73. Seeing is put for general of body and soul, as when we say; let there be seen concerning the which I have said. Thus Gen. 42. v. 1. Jacob saw &c. For also to see pre-understand, which is the seeing of the mind.)*

On the infanticide of Herod Macrobius thus discourses, book 2, chapter 4: When he had heard (Caesar Augustus) that among those boys whom King Herod ordered within two years of age to be killed in Syria, his own son too was slain, he said: better to be Herod's pig than his son. *(namely because out of feigned religion Herod was not accustomed to slaughter pigs.)* The same thing Philo relates. Josephus. Scaliger, Animadversions on Eusebius, page 162. The infan-ticide, which is remarkable, passed over silently by Josephus, occurred at almost the same time at which An-tipater was strangled by order of his father and the Doctors of the Law burned, shortly before the death of Herod himself, so that after passing through life amid so many slaughters he did not leave behind life without bloodshed. That the massacre of the boys happened not long before the fate of Antipater is established both from the Gospel, since this took place in the second year after Christ's birth, and παῖδας τοὺς κατὰ διετῶν from their having been slain being clearly declared there, then also from Macrob-us, who reports that infants were ordered by Herod to be slain, and that among them even Herod's own son paid the penalty. Herod deferred the bloody execution of his plan until another year, either by means of that accusation whereby he accused his sons Alexander and Aristobulus before Augustus at Rome of treachery and attempted kingship, im-p—ted, or because he saw that he could not carry it out immediately without uproar and sedition, since the report about the newly born King had stirred all men's minds toward hope of liberty, while the judgment of the Sanhedrin still retained some authority. Some think that Herod doubted whether that star signified the nativity or the conception of the King of the Jews, and accordingly designated such an age for the massacring of the infants that among them he would comprehend the already-born Messiah, whether the star signified his conception or his nativity. But if it be said that, out of precaution, and with respect to the time sought out by the Magi and the place pointed out by the Scribes, Herod added a certain breadth, so that he slew not only in the city Bethlehem but also throughout all the borders of Bethlehem, not only children of two months and three months, but also little ones of two years—it can be granted that he perpetrated that child-murder immediately upon the departure of the Magi.

Because among the killed boys there was also Herod’s son, whom his wife from the tribe of Judah had borne to him, who without a doubt was educated in the King’s palace, it can be thought that by a public edict of the King all the little ones under the age of two from the house and family of David, wherever they were being educated, were summoned under some pretext within the borders of Bethlehem; for not all who were of the house of David lived within the borders of Bethlehem during that confusion of the tribes. Nicephorus, book 1, *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 14, mentions, John, together with his mother Elizabeth, was kept safe in a certain cave in the hill country.

These infants of Bethlehem, received into the covenant of GOD by circumcision, and shedding their blood on account of Christ, are rightly held to be Martyrs. Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 18, page 204: He himself, when he was an infant, making the infants of men Martyrs, sent them before him into his kingdom. Chrysostom: O blessed little ones, newly born; never tempted, not yet weaned, and already crowned. Augustine: Christ sent these first-fruits to the Father. An infant came, and infants come. The infant to us, the infants to heaven. The same: they are called the flowers of the Martyrs, whom, sprung up in the cold of unbelief, a certain frost of persecution scorched, like the first gems bursting forth of the Church.

Prudentius. Hail, flowers of the Martyrs, and first victims of Christ, tender flock of the slaughtered, before the altar of Christ, simple ones, you play with palm and crowns.

The same: Hail, flowers of the Martyrs, whom the persecutor, at the very threshold of the light, snatched away, as a whirlwind snatches roses as they are born. Sebastianus Hornoldus, Ictus, on the Infanticide.

A bitter thing, a bitter-sweet passion, in the wanton little city of Bethlehem. So to perish and pass away under this rather harsh lot of Martyrs, these little flowers. By the fury of an impious king, little boys, lovely, blessed, prattling, and little boys whole and dainty, little boys most tender, to the number of forty-four thousand. To whom add twice fifty thousand. As is believed among the acts of the Christians. A new fury, not known anywhere before — O horror of the night! O the dim beginnings of day! O the order of times turned upside down! O how great an aqueous force of tears flowed on every side, &c.

The Missa Aethiopum defines the slain infants as fourteen thousand in number. Stapulensis applies to these infants the passage Apoc. 14., by which reckoning one hundred and forty-four thousand would have been slain at the command of Herod. The Church sings of these little infants: Not speaking, but by dying they bore witness.

ἀποστείλας. ἀποςέλλειν to send after command given. 1 Kings 21.John 7. The cruelty of Herod extended both 1. the place, for out of abundant precaution he even embraced the borders of Bethlehem, so that there the newly born King might be destroyed together with others beyond doubt; and 2. the time, because those two years old were killed, and also those below that age, lest perhaps there should escape him whom alone he desired extinguished.

Euthymius teaches that those words, according to the time which he had diligently inquired from the Magi, must be referred only to the little word below. For when he ordered children of two years to be slain, he did not do this according to the time of the star's rising perceived by the Magi, but according to his own cruelty. He falsely claimed that minors under two—not all down to an infant of one day—were to be slain according to that time of the star's rising; therefore he spared those who were still within six weeks. Although it is not likely that the executioners had an exact reckoning of that time.

In the History of the Lord's Nativity the Angels announced that peace was brought to the world through the birth of this child; but lest this be understood concerning external and civil peace, the History of the infanticide follows. They announced that there was good pleasure toward men in God: but lest this be taken in such sense as if he wished to distribute to them bodily goods of every kind in this life, therefore the sermon on the cross follows. They announced that this child was King and Lord, but lest anyone think he was a worldly King, therefore the History about the exile and infanticide is added.

Latin:

v. 16. ἐνεπαίχθη.At quomodo Magi illuserunt Herodi, cùm divino oraculo moniti non redierint ad ips-m? Resp. haec dicuntur κασθ' υπόληψιν Herodis, quippe qui occultam ipsorum per aliam viam in patriam profectionem interpretabatur illusionem. Verbum Syr.

peculiare est lingvae Syrae, ab Hebraeo הןבillusus est, â quo non longè discedit, nisi quod tertiam literam thematis ה in ח mutat eiusdem organi & prolationis. At ubicunq; Syrus eo utitur, semper est ח loco ה.

Ex illis, quae die purificationis acciderant, increbuerat publicus rumor, puerum Iesum â Simeone & Hanna Messiam in templo renunciatum esse. Ex eo intellexit, Magos fidem sibi datam non servasse.

Scribae. ut colligi potest ex Ios. lib. 17. cap. 3. occasione vaticinii Prophetici Mich. 5. Herodi ostenderant, DEI decretum esse, ut nato Messia sceptrum regni ad illum transferretur, ac omnes Reges ipsum a dorarent. Hoc Herodes, Pharisaicis opinionibus ebrius, de terreno Messiae regno carnaliter intellexit ac proinde suo regno timuit. Herodes priùs sibi persuadebat, Magos exortu φαινομένου ἀστέρος fuisse delusos ac proinde erubuisse reverti, ubi nullum de recens nato Iudaeorum Rege rumorem ampliùs audiret. Cùm verò in die purificationis & oblationis novus de Rege Messia nato rumor spargeretur, ac quae â Simone & Hanna de eo prophetata, Hierosolymis increbescerent, tunc se â Magis delusum fuisse, sensit.

(* ἰδὼν videns id est intelligens. vid. Gen. 8. v. 8.Matth. 9. v. 3.Iacob. 2. v. 24. August. in Exod. quaest. 73. Ponitur visus progenerali sen--corporis & animi, ut cùm dicimus; videatur de -is, quae dixi. sic Gen. 42. v. 1.Vidit Iacob &c. nam & videre printelligere, quod est visus mentis.)*

De infanticidio Herodis sic disserit Macrobius lib. 2. cap. 4. Cùm audisset (Augustus Caesar) inter pueros, quos in Syria Rex Herodes intra bimatum iussit interfici, filium quoque eius occisum, ait, melius est Herodis porcum esse, quàm filium. *(quia videlicet Herodes fimulata religione porcos non solitus fuit mactare.)* Idem refert Philo. Ioseph. Scaliger animadv. in Euseb. pag. 162. Infanti-idium, quod mirum est, tacitum à Iosepho, contigit eodem ferè tempore, quo Antipat-r iussu patris strangulatus & Doctores legis combusti sunt, paulò ante mortem ipsius Herodis, ut qui inter tot caedes vitam transmisisset, vitam sine caede non relinqueret. Quod puerorum caedes non multò praecesserit Antipatri casum, tum ex Evangelio constat, cùm anno secundo à Christo nato id contigisse, &παῖδας τοὺς κατὰ διετῶνinterfectos fuisse perspicuè ibi declaratum fit, tum etiam ex Macrob-o, qui infantes ab Herode caedi iussos & inter illos filium quoque ipsius Herodis poenas dedisse refert. Distulit Herodes sangvinariam sui consilii executionem in alterum usque annum, vel actione illâ, quâ filios suos Alexandrum & Aristobulum Romae coram Augusto insidiarum & affectati regni accusavit, imp-ditus, vel quia vidit, se non posse sine tumultu & seditione illud statim exequi, cùm fama de recens nato Rege omnium animos in spem libertatis excitasset, ac iudicii Sanhedrin adhuc aliqua autoritas esset. Quidam existimant, Herodem dubitasse, an stella illa nativitatem, an conceptionem Regis Iudaeorum significaverit, ac proinde talem aetatem trucidandorum infantum designasse, ut inter illos iam natum Messiam comprehenderet, sive stella conceptionem sive nativitatem eius significasset. Si verò dicatur, quòd cautionis gratiâ & tempori â Magis exquisito, & loco a Scribis monstrato Herodes latitudinem quandam addiderit, ita ut occiderit non tantùm in urbe Bethlehema, sed etiam in omnibus finibus Bethleemiticis non solùm bimestres ac trimestres, sed etiam bimulos, concedi potest, quòd statim post Magorum discessum puericidium illud perpetrarit.

petrârit. Quia inter, occisos pueros fuit etiam Herodis filius, quem ipsi coniux de tribu Iuda pepererat, qui dubio proculin au-a Regis fuit educatus, cogitari potest, publico Regis edicto omnes parvulos infra bimatum de domo & familia Davidis, ubicunq; educarentur, praetextu quodam intra fines Bethleemiticos convocatos fuisse, neq; enim omnes, qui erant de domo Davidis, in illa tribuum confusione habitabant intra fines Bethleemiticos. Nicephorus lib. 1. Hist. Eccl. cap. 14. memorat, Iohannem unà cum matre Elisabethâ in spelunca quadam ad regionem montanam salvum fuisse conservatum.

Infantes hi Bethleēmitici per circumcisionem in foedus DEI recepti, ac propter Christum sangvinem suum fundentes meritò pro Martyribus habentur. Iren. lib. 3. cap. 18. pag. 204. Ipse infans cùm esset, infantes hominum Martyres parans praemisit eos in suum regnum. Chrysostomus. O parvuli beati, mod-nati; nunquàm tentati, nondum ablactati & iam coronati. Augustinus. Has primitias Christus misit Patri. Venit infans, & veniunt infantes. Infans adnos, infantes ad coelum. Idem: dicuntur flores Martyrum, quos in frigore infidelitatis exortos velut primas erumpentes Ecclesiae gemmas quaedam persecutionis pruina decoxit.

Prudentius. Salvete flores Martyrum, & prima Christi victima, Grex immolatorum tener, Ante aram Christi simplices, palmâ & coronis luditis.

Idem: Salvete flores Martyrum. Quos lucis ipso in limine Christi insecutor sustulit, ceu turbo nascentes rosas. Sebastianus Hornoldus Ictus in Infanticidio.

Acerba res, amarulent a passio, Bethlemis in procace civitatulâ.Sub hacce crudiore sorte Martyrum perire sic & interire flosculos.Furore Regis impii puellulos Amabiles, beatulos, loquaculos,Et integellulos & elegantulos Puellulos ubia delicatulos,Ad usa quadragint a mille quatuor. Quib. bis adde quinquagint a millia.Ut inter acta Christiana creditur. Novus furor, nec antè notus ullibi,O noctis horror! ô adorta fuscula dies! ô anteversus ordo temporum,O quanta fluxit undiquaa fletuum Aquosa vis, &c.

Missa Aethiopum interfectos infantes numero quatuordecim millium definit. Stapulensis applicat ad hos infantes locum Apoc. 14. quâ ratione centum quadraginta quatuor millia fuissent Herodis iussu occisa. Ecclesia de hisce infantulis canit. Non loquendo, sed moriendo testati sunt.

ἀποστείλας. ἀποςέλλειν est dato mandato mittere. 1. Reg. 21.Ioh. 7. Crudelitas Herodis dilatavit 1. locum, pro abundantiâ enim cautionis etiam fines complexa fuit Bethleëmiticos, ut eò certiûs recens ille natus Rex unà cum aliis perderetur 2. tempus, quia interfecti sunt bimuli, & qui infra illam aetatem, ne fortè elaberetur, quem unicè cupiebat extinctum.

Euthymius docet, verba illa, secundùm tempus, quod exactâ perquisiverat â Magis, referenda esse tantùm ad voculam infra. Quod enim bimos interfici iussit, illud non fecit secundùm tempus exortae stellae â Magis perceptum, sed secuncùm suam crudelitatem. Bimis minores non omnes usque ad infantem unius diei, sed secundum illud tempus ortus stellae occidi mendavit, pepercit ergo illis, qui erant adhuc infra sex hebdomadas. Quanquàm non est verisimile, satellites exactam illius temporis rationem habuisse.

In Historia nativitatis Dominicae Angeli nunciaverant, pacem per pueri huius nativitatem mundo allatam, ne verò de externa & civili. pace hoc intelligeretur, sequitur Historia infanticidii. Nunciaverant, DEO beneplacitum esse in hominibus: ne verò hoc eo sensu acciperetur, ac si omnis generis bona corporalia in hac vita ipsis distribuere velit, ideò sequitur conció de cruce. Nunciaverunt, hunc puerum esse Regem & Dominum, ne quis verò cogitaret, esse mundanum Regem, ideò subiungitur Historia de exilio & infanticidio.

## 2:17
v. 17. τοΤε έπληρ ώθη τὸ ῥηθὲν ὑπὸ Ιερεμίοτου Προφητου λέγοντος. Some copies read τὸ ῥηθὲν ὑπό Κυρίου διὰ Ιερεμίου, etc.; how Matthew usually speaks, what precedes shows. There would be great emphasis in this phrase—that not the prophets themselves spoke, but the mouth of the Lord speaking through the prophets Luke 1. v. 70. *(But the former reading is followed by the Eastern interpreters, the Syrian, Arabic, Ethiopian, likewise the Greek Eclogues, the manuscripts of the Library at Nuremberg. The Syrian, in his manner, rendered ύπὸ by , that is, by the hand, which phrase indeed usually indicates the instrumental cause, yet it must be noted that he uses it also for the principal cause, as appears from John 1, 3. and 17,Rom. 11, 36. nor otherwise too in the Hebrew text רים

sometimes received. See Is. 50. v. 11. The Arabic New Testament, where the Syriac uses such a phrase, simply employs the prefix BE, just as also the Ethiopic Ba; however, the interpreter of the Arabic Psalter, having followed the Hebrew text, retains the same phrase . See Ps. 77. which among the Arabs is 76. v. 21. Compare altogether Mr. Dilherr on the Syriac Ecclesiastes.) Moreover, since the Prophet was about to describe the immense misery and disaster of the people of Israel through προσωποποϊίαν, he introduces Rachel buried in that place, as if she were bewailing the disaster of her descendants: so likewise here the Evangelist says that the misery of the inhabitants of Bethlehem at the time of that massacre of the children was so great that even Rachel, dead and buried there, would bewail it.

Latin:

v. 17. τοΤε έπληρ ώθη τὸ ῥηθὲν ὑπὸ Ιερεμίοτου Προφητου λέγοντος. Quaedam exemplaria legunt τὸ ῥηθὲν ὑπό Κυρίου διὰ Ιερεμίου, &c. quomodo Matthaeum loqui solere, superiora ostendunt. In hac phrasi esset magna emphasis, non ipsos sc Prophetas, sed os Domini per Prophetas loqui Luc. 1. v. 70. *(Sed priorem lectionem sequuntur Interpp. Orient. Syrus. Arabs, Aethiops, item Ecl. Graecae MSS. Biblioth. Norib. Syrus more suo ύπὸ vertit per id est, per manum, quâ phrasi licet plerumque causam instrumentalem indigitare soleat, s-iendum tamen, quòd eandem quoq; de causa principali adhibeat, -eu patet ex Ioh. 1, 3. & 17,Rom. 11, 36. nec aliter quoq; in textu Ebr. רים

aliquando accipitur. Vid. Es. 50. v. 11. Arabs N. T. ubi Syrus tali phrasi utitur, simpliciter adhibet praefixum BE, quemadmodum & Aethiops Ba; Psalterii tamen Arabici interpres Ebraeum textum sequutus eandem phrasin retinet. Vid. Ps. 77. qui ap. Arab-m est 76. v. 21. Conf omnino Dn. Dilherr. in Ecl. Syr.)* Coeterùm Propheta ingentem miseriam & cladem populi Israëlitici descripturus per προσωποποϊίαν introducit Rachelem eo loco sepultam, quasi defleat cladem posterorum suorum: ita Evangelista h l. dicit, tantam fuisse Bethlehemitarum miseriam tempore illius puericidii, ut vel mortua Rachel ibidemque sepulta hoc defleret.

## 2:18
v. 18. φωνὴ έν Ῥαμὰ ἰκούθη. Ramah was a city in the tribe of Benjamin, situated not far from Bethlehem. Jos. 18. v. 25.Judg. 19. v. 13. There was also another certain city of this name in the tribe of Benjamin. *( σθρῖνος, καὶ κλαυθμὸς και ὶδυρμὸς πολὺς. The Arabic expresses everything: But the Syriac and Ethiopic omit the single word indicating mourning.)*

Ραχὴλ κλαίουσα. Jerome warns that the name of Rachel is placed not for the woman but for the place, because Rachel was buried there near Bethlehem. Likewise, that the word Ramah is not the name of a place, but signifies among the Hebrews high, so that you understand a loud and elevated voice of one weeping. A voice heard on high, that is, a lofty voice was heard, which has been spread far and wide. Those who take the word Ramah as the proper name of a place say that by ἄυξησιν there is set forth the voice of mothers lamenting their children cruelly slain, heard from Bethlehem in Ramah, twelve miles distant from it, that is, from the tribe of Judah into Benjamin, so that it might be signified that the mourning was common to those two tribes.

The prophecy exists at Jer. 31. v. 15 which, when it speaks of the ten tribes of Israel led away into captivity, whose calamity Rachel, mother of Benjamin and Joseph, father of Ephraim and Manasseh, is said to have bewailed by way of a certain προσωποποΐίαν, the question arises, by what reasoning is that applied by the Evangelist to the infanticide at Bethlehem? Answer. It is said that at the time of the infanticide that oracle was fulfilled, either by way of a similarity, because in that infanticide a misfortune equally great, if not greater, oppressed the inhabitants of Bethlehem and their neighbors than [oppressed] the tribes of Israel at the time of being carried off into captivity, or perfectly with regard to the intention of the Holy Spirit, because when the Holy Spirit proposed this oracle through Jeremiah, he looked not only to the carrying off of the ten tribes, but also to this infanticide at Bethlehem. Therefore it is introduced by means of a certain pathetical Πλάσιν Rachel, buried some centuries ago near Bethlehem, to bewail her children slain at one time by the Assyrians and Babylonians, at another by King Herod. But by Rachel are understood the mothers of Bethlehem descended from her, and dwelling near Rachel's tomb. For although there were more both of the boys killed and of the mourning mothers from the tribe of Judah than from the tribe of Benjamin, yet Rachel is reckoned the mother of all, both by right of marriage and by right of living together.

ὅτι ὸυκ εἰσί. The Evangelist follows the interpretation of the LXX. In the Hebrew it is, because he himself is not, that is, because none of them survives. It is a Hebrew phrase whereby sudden death is almost described, or an unexpected removal, Gen. 5. v. 24.Ps. 37. v. 36.Ps. 39. v. 14.Jeremiah 49. v. 10. Therefore the sense is, that they are not, that is, that they have been destroyed, that they have ceased to be among men. *(The Eastern interpreters here imitated this manner of speaking: for the Syrian translates similarly so also the Arab that they themselves, namely, are not. The Ethiopian: because the sons are not. But the Photinians, quite absurdly gathering from this phrase, which expresses dying, through Τό not being, that in death the body of man is reduced to nothing. (See Smalcald Examination, Century of errors, chapter on the saints, page 33, where among other things: We firmly believe that the departed saints do not exist. When the -body has been dissolved from the soul, and the body reduced to nothing, the Saints are no longer, but only their souls. However, since shortly after he limits it thus: therefore namely the saints can be said in no way to exist with respect to their entire substance: Yet it is plain that he adds this limitation at least for that reason, because Smiglecius the Jesuit had charged him with asserting that the Saints in no way exist as regards their whole substance: meanwhile about the body he willingly grants, nor is the judgment concerning its annihilation attributed to him and his associate unjustly, and he labors to establish even this error among others from the said phrase in On the Divinity of Jesus Christ, treatise, ch. 13. Resurrection, he writes, or rising again is nothing else than out of not existing to exist again. Hence of the dead it is said, that they are not, namely, when the nature of the thing is looked at. In the margin this very passage from Matthew is cited.) we oppose. 1. the description of death handed down in Holy Scripture. For death is described now by ἀνάλυσιν, Phil. 1. v. 23.2. Tim. 4. v. 6. whereby it comes about that indeed the natural union is dissolved, yet no part of nature is reduced to nothing, since the soul, i.e., spirit returns to God, but the dust to the earth, Ecclesiastes 12. v. 7. now by τοῦ σκηνόματος ἀπόσθεσιν, as 2 Peter 1. v. 14. now by ἐπιγείου κμἡν οἰκίας τοῦ σκήους κατάλυσιν, 2 Corinthians 5. v. 1. 2. 2. the divine threatening. Whereby it comes about that indeed the body returns to dust, Genesis 3. v. 19.Eccl. 12. v. 7. and sees corruption, Psalm 16. v. 10.1 Corinthians 15. v. 42. but is by no means reduced to nothing. 3. the divine promise made to the godly. By which they can be certain that all their bones shall be kept, lest any of them perish, Psalm 34. v. 21. 4. the comparison instituted in Scripture between death and seed and sleep. Our bodies are said to be sown in death, John 12. v. 24.1 Cor. 15. v. 43. Now however seed committed to the ground indeed rots, yet is not annihilated, but germinates in due season; the same must likewise be hoped of our bodies, Isaiah 26. v. 14. Thus death is expressed throughout Holy Scripture by sleep and falling asleep. Now however bodies oppressed by sleep rest, they are not annihilated; the same must be said of the bodies of the deceased. See Isaiah 26. v. 20. 21.Daniel 12. v. 2.John 5. v. 28. 29. 5. the consequence of the inconvenience flowing from that error. For if to die is to be reduced to nothing, it follows that none of those who were raised up by Christ and by the holy men of GOD, both in the O.T. and in the N.T., truly died, since the body of none of them was reduced to nothing, but the soul was merely recalled back to the dwelling-place of the body, whence it had gone forth a little before; nay, neither would Christ Himself have truly died, since it is expressly denied that His body saw corruption, Psalm 16. v. 10.Acts 2. v. 27. much less that it was reduced to nothing. 6. A convenient explanation of the phrase objected. For what is said of the dead, that they themselves are not, must be taken not ἁπλῶς, but κατ ά τι i.e. συγκριπκῶς, that is, in this sense, that they are no longer upon the land of the living, whether so as to praise GOD in the Church militant, or to be able to assist their own people with consolation or help. That this phrase must necessarily be taken in this way is evident from Genesis 5. v. 24. where of Enoch thus:

And Enoch walked with GOD, and he was not, because God took him: Add also that this phrase is applied to the whole composite being; therefore, if annihilation were indicated by it, it would follow that both parts—that is, not only the body but also the soul—are annihilated after death, which if the Photinians wished to assert, I fear they would be beaten even by the somewhat wiser Gentiles. But let these things suffice for the present. Concerning the other foundations of the Photinians there will be discussion in its own place. Let there also be compared among our own theologians Mr. D. Feurb. in AntiOster. pages 590 sqqq.; B. D. Meisn. Theol. Phot. cons. page 325 sqqq.; B. D. Stegmann, Photinianismi page 905 sqqq.; Mr. D. Calov. Socinismi Profl. p. 1017 sqqq.; B. P. L. on death.) *

A twofold consolation indeed is set forth in the said Prophecy. 1. with respect to those mourning who were left behind. 2. with respect to the children slain. As regards those mourning who were left behind. 1. divine hearing. The Lord has heard your tears. 2. divine address and speech. Cease from weeping. As regards the children slain. 1. most awaited return. 2. most abundant fruit.

Obs. 1. When Pharaoh ordered the infants of the Israelites to be cast into the flowing river, one out of their number was preserved safe, who became the people's deliverer: So in this slaughter of the innocents the boy Jesus, marvelously preserved, became the Savior of the world. 2. The death of these infants is a punishment for the ingratitude of the parents. When Christ had been born in Bethlehem, little care was given him by the Bethlehemites, his parents were despised, the shepherds were simple men, therefore no faith was placed in their testimony.

Latin:

v. 18. φωνὴ έν Ῥαμὰ ἰκούθη. Rama fuit urbs in tribu Beniamin, non procul â Bethlehem sita. Ios. 18. v. 25.Iudic, 19. v. 13. Fuit & alia quaedam eius nominis urbs in tribu Beniamin. *( σθρῖνος, καὶ κλαυθμὸς και ὶδυρμὸς πολὺς. Arabs omnia exprimit: Sed Syrus & Aethiops unam vocem luctus indicem omittunt.)*

Ραχὴλ κλαίουσα. Hieronymus monet, Rachelis nomen positum non pro muliere, sed pro loco, quia Rachel ibi iuxta Bethlehem fuit sepulta. Item vocem Rama non esse vocabulum loci, sed Hebraeis significare excelsum, ut claram & elatam plorantis vocem intelligas. Vox in excelso audita, id est, vox alta audita est, quae longè lateque sit sparsa. Qui vocem Rama accipiunt ut propriam loci, dicunt per ἄυξησιν statui, vocem matrum deplorantium liberos suos crudeliter interfectos, ê Bethlehem in Rama, duodecim milliaribus ab ea dissitam, hoc est, ex tribu Iuda in Beniamin auditam, ut significetur, luctum his duabus tribubus fuisse communem.

Va-cinium extat Ierem. 31. v. 15 quod cùm loquatur de decem tribubus Israël in captivitatem abductis, quarum calamitatem Rachel mater Beniamini & Iosephi, patris Ephraimi & Manasse, per quandam προσωποποΐίαν deplorasse dicitur, quaeritur, quà ratione illud ad Bethleemiticum infanticidium ab Evangel-sta accommodetur? Resp. Dicitur tempore infanticidii oraculum illud impletum, vel per quandam similitudinem, quia in illo infanticidio aequè magna, si non maior calamitas Bethleemitas & eorum vicinos oppressit, quàm Israëliticas tribus tempore abductionis in captivitatem, vel perfectè respectu ad intentionem Spiritus S. habito, quia cùm Spiritus S. hoc oraculum per Ieremiam proponeret, respexit non solùm ad abductionem decem tribuum, sed etiam ad hoc infanticidium Bethleemiticum. Introducitur igitur per patheticam quandam Πλάσιν Rachel, ante aliquot secula in vicinia Bethlehemae sepulta, liberos suos tum ab Assyriis & Babyloniis, tum ab Herode Rege interemtos deplorare. Per Rachelem autem intelliguntur matres Bethleemiticae ex ea descendentes, & in vicinia sepulchri Rachelis habitantes. Quamvis enim plures cùm puerorum interfectorum, tum matrum lugentium essent ex tribu Iuda, quàm ex tribu Beniamin, omnium tamen mater censetur Rachel, tum iure coniugii, tum iure cohabitationis.

ὅτι ὸυκ εἰσί. Sequitur Evangelista interpret. LXX. In Hebraeo est, quia non ipse, id est, quia nemo eorum superest. Phrasis est Hebraea, quâ subitanea ferè mors describitur, vel inopinata translatio, Gen. 5. v. 24.Ps. 37. v. 36.Ps. 39. v. 14.Ierem. 49. v. 10. Sensus igitur est, quòd non fint, id est, quod peremti sint, quòd desierint esse inter homines. *(Interpretes Orientales eundem loquendi modum imitati hic sunt: Syrus enim similiter vertit sic Arabs quoque quòd non ipsi, sc. sint. Aethiops: quoniam non sunt filii. Photinianis verò, perquam ineptè è phrasi hâc, quâ mori exprimitur, per Τόnon esse, colligentibus, in morte corpus hominis in nihilum redigi. (Vid. Smalc. Exam. Cent. err. C. de sanct. pag. 33. ubi inter alia: Sanctos vitâ functos non existere, firmiter credimus. Dissoluto -nim corpore ab anima, & corpore in nihilum redacto, Sancti non sunt ampliùs, sed tantùm animae ipsorum. Ut ut verò paulò post limitet: ideo scil. dici posse, sanctos nullo modo existere, quod ad totam sui substantiam: Patet tamen quòd eo saltem fine limitationem hanc addat, quoniam Smiglecius Iesuita ipsi imputaverat, quasi adserat, Sanctos quoad totam substantiam nullo modo existere: interea de corpore lubens concedit, non iniuriâ ipsi ac sociennis sententiam de eius annihilatione attribui, & hunc quoque errorem inter alia è dictâ phrasi stabilire satagit in de divinit. Iesu Christi tr. c. 13. Resurrectio, scribit, vel resurgere nihil aliud est, quàm ex non existente iterum existere. Hinc de mortuis dicitur, quòd non sint, naturâ sc. rei inspectâ. In marg. allegatur hic ipse locus ex Matthaeo.) opponimus. 1. mortis in Scr. S. traditam descriptionem. Describitur enim mors modò per ἀνάλυσιν,Phil. 1. v. 23.2. Tim. 4. v. 6. per quam fit, ut unio quidem naturalis solvatur, netura tamen pars in nihilum redigatur, cùm anima s. Spiritus ad Deum, pulvis verò in terram revertatur, Eccles. 12. v. 7. modò per τοῦ σκηνόματος ἀπόσθεσιν, uti. 2. Petr. 1. v. 14. modò per ἐπιγείου κμἡν οἰκίας τοῦ σκήους κατάλυσιν,2. Cor. 5. v. 1. 2.divinam comminationem. Quâ fit, ut corpus quidem in pulverem revertatur, Gen. 3. v. 19.Eccl. 12. v. 7. ac corruptionem videat, Ps. 16. v. 10.1. Cor. 15. v. 42. minimè verò in nihilum redigatur. 3. divinam piis factam promissionem. Ut quâ certi esse possunt, omnia ipsorum ossa custodienda, ne ullum eorum pereat, Ps. 34. v. 21. 4. mortis cum semente ac somno institutam in Scr. comparationem. Dicuntur corpora nostra seminari in morte,Ioh. 12. v. 24.1. Cor. 15. v. 43. iam. verò semen terrae concreditum computrescit quidem, non tamen annihilatur, sed suo tempore progerminat, idem & de corporibus nostris sperandum, Es. 26. v. 14. Sic mors per somnum & obdormitionem exprimitur in Scr. S. passim. iam verò corpora somno oppressa quiescunt, non annihilantur, idem de corporibus defunctorum dicendum. Vid. Es. 26. v. 20. 21.Dan. 12. v. 2.Ioh. 5. v. 28. 29. 5. incommodi, quod ex errore isto fluit, consecutionem. Si enim mori est in nihilum redigi, sequitur, neminem eorum, qui â Christo ac Sanctis DEI hominibus tum in V. tum in N. T. resuscitati sunt, verè fuisse mortuum, cùm nullius eorum corpus in nihilum fuerat redactum, sed anima ad corporis domicilium, è quo paullò antè egressa erat, duntaxat revocata fuit, quin nec ipse Christus verè fuisset mortuus, cùm disertè negetur, ipsius corpus corruptionem vidisse, Ps. 16. v. 10.Act. 2. v. 27. nedum ut in nihilum fuerit redactum. 6. Commodam phraseos obiectae explicationem. Quod enim de defunctis dicitur, quòd non sunt ipsi, accipiendum non ἁπλῶς, sed κατ ά τι s. συγκριπκῶς, hoc est eo sensu, quòd non sint ampliùs in terrâ viventium, sive ita, ut DEUM in Eccl. militante laudent, suisque solatio vel auxilio adesse possint. Phrasin verò hanc eo modo necessariò sumendam esse, patet ex Gen. 5. v. 24. ubi de Enocho ita:

Et ambulavit Henoch cum DEO,& non ipse, quia tulit eum Deus: Accedit, quòd de toto composito phrasis illa adhibeatur, sequeretur igitur, si per eam annihilatio indicatur, utramque partem, hoc est non solùm corpus, sed animam quoque post mortem annihilari, quod si adserere Photiniani velint, vereor, ne ab ipsis paullò sapientioribus Gentilibus vapulent. Sed haec impraesentiarum sufficiant. De reliquis Photinianorum fundamentis suo agetur loco. Conferantur etiam è nostratibus Theologis Dn. D. Feurb. in AntiOster. pag. 590. seqq. B. D. Meisn. Theol. Phot. cons. pag. 325. seqq. B. D. Stegmann, Photinianismi pag. 905. seqq. Dn. D. Calov. Socinismi Profl. p. 1017. seqq. B. P. L. de morte.)*

Duplex verò consolatio in dicto Prophetico proponitur. 1. respectu lugentium relictorum. 2. respectu liberorum interemtorum. Quoad lugentes relictos. 1. divinus auditus. Dominus audit lachrymas tuas. 2. divinum alloquium & affatus. Cessa â lachrymis. Quoad liberos interemtos. 1. expectatissimus reditus. 2. abundantissimus fructus.

Observ. 1. Cùm Pharao infantes Israëlitarum in profluentem fluvium proiici iuberet, unus ex illorum numero incolumis servabatur, qui factus est populi liberator: Sic in hoc puericidio puer Iesus mirabiliter servatus, factus est mundi Salvator. 2. Mors horum infantum est poena ingratitudinis parentum. Cùm Christus in Bethlehem natus esset, parum curabatur â Bethlehemitis, parentes erant contemti, pastores simplices, ideò testimonio ipsorum non habent fidem.

## 2:19
v. 19. τελέυτησαντος σέ τουΗπωσου, understand την ξωην. For so Herodotus, book 1. of History τελουταν τόν αιωνα. Meanwhile τελευταν is also used absolutely for to die. *(Examples are found in Xenophon, whence also the Syrian rightly renders after he died, just as likewise the Arab and also the Ethiopian.)*

On the death of Herod see Josephus, book 17. of Antiquities chapter 8. and book 1. On the Jewish War chapter 21. how, besides other diseases, being afflicted with rottenness of his private parts, breeding of worms and trembling of limbs, several times on account of the violence of pain he attempted to lay violent hands upon himself.

Between the death of Herod and the return of Christ from Egypt there intervenes an interval of several months. For Herod died about the time of Passover, but Joseph returned with the boy to the land of Israel while Archelaus was reigning, v. 22, and therefore when that Archelaus had come back from Rome, whither he had set out after his father's death.

Latin:

v. 19. τελέυτησαντος σέ τουΗπωσου, subaudi την ξωην. Sic enim Herodot. lib. 1. Hist. τελουταν τόν αιωνα. Interim τελευταν etiam absolutè pro mori ponitur. *(Exempla apud Xenoph. habentur, unde etiam Syrus rectè exprimit postquam mortuus, quemadmodum & Arabs itemque Aethiops.)*

De morte Herodis vide Ioseph. lib. 17. antiquit. cap. 8. & lib. 1. de Bell. Iudaic. cap. 21. quomodo praeter alios morbos etiam verendorum putredine, vermium generatione & membrorum tremore divexatus, aliquoties sibi ipsi violentas manus ob doloris vehementiam inferre conatus fuerit.

Inter Herodis mortem & reditum Christi ex Aegypto intercedit aliquot mensium intervallum. Herodes enim mortuus est circa tempus Paschatos, Iosephus autem cum puero rediit in terram Israëlis, Archelao regnante v. 22. ac proinde Archelao illo Româ reverso, quò post mortem patris sui profectus fuerat.

## 2:20
