v. 20. Now this manner of speaking is used a second time by the Angel and the Evangelist: Take the child and his mother, lest anyone think this way of speaking lacks the mystery indicated above.

Observed. The Lord of all angels had been born, therefore the appearances of angels are so frequent.

τεθνήκασι. Of one Herod he speaks in the plural, because 1. it could be referred to the multitude of Herod's ministers, who were ready to carry out the King's commands. While Herod lived, many flatterers attended him who were plotting this very thing, as appears from Josephus.

2. Or to those manifold deaths which Herod experienced through various diseases by the just judgment of GOD.

3. But most simply it is said to be familiar among the Hebrews that a plural is placed for a singular and vice versa. Nah. 2. v. 6. *(So Gen. 34. v. 27. compared with v. 5. and 13. likewise Ezech. 46. v. 10.)*

4. Meanwhile it is thought not without reason that regard is had to the type Exod. 4. v. 19. where nearly the same words occur.

To seek the soul. is an ambiguous phrase, for it is taken both in a good sense Prov. 29. v. 10. and in a bad Ps. 39. v. 13. In this passage it is evident that it is taken in a bad sense, for it means to seek someone's life, namely in order to destroy it, Ps. 40. v. 15.

Latin:

v. 20. Iam alterâ vice haec loquendi forma usurpatur ab Angelo & Evangelista: Accipe puerum & matrem eius, ne quis putet, hanc loquendi formam carere mysterio, quod superiùs indicatum.

Observ. Natus erat Angelorum omnium Dominus, ideò tam frequentes sunt Angelorum apparitiones.

τεθνήκασι. De uno Herode in plurali loquitur, quod 1. referri posset ad copiam ministrorum Herodis, qui parati erant ad exequenda Regis mandata. Herodi, dum viveret, multi adfuerunt assentatores, qui hoc idem moliebantur, ut constat ex Iosepho.

2. Vel ad multiplices illas mortes, quas in variis morbis Herodes iusto DEI iudicio expertus erat.

3. Sed simplicissimè dicitur, familiare esse Hebraeis, plurale poni pro singulari & vice versa. Nah. 2. v. 6. *(Sic Gen. 34. v. 27. coll. cum v. 5. & 13. item Ezech. 46. v. 10.)*

4. Interim haud absurdè cogitatur, respectum haberi ad typum Exod. 4. v. 19. ubi eadem fermè habentur verba.

Quaerere animam. est phrasis ambigua, nam & in bonam partem sumitur Prov. 29. v. 10. & in malam Ps. 39. v. 13. hoc loco manifestum est, in malam partem accipi, significat enim vitam alicuius petere, videlicet ad perdendum eam, Ps. 40. v. 15.

## 2:21
v. 21. Some hold that Christ was brought back from Egypt in the fourth year of age, others indeed in the tenth year of age.

Observed. It came about by divine providence that upon the death of a foreign-born king the proper and native King of the Jews should return, and that after Herod no other King of the Jews should be appointed by the Romans.

Latin:

v. 21. Quidam statuunt, Christum anno aetatis quarto ex Aegypto reductum, quidam verò anno aetatis decimo.

Observ. Divinâ providentiâ factum, ut mortuo Rege alienigenâ rediret proprius & patrius Iudaeorum Rex, atque ut post Herodem nullus â Romanis Iudaeorum Rex designaretur.

## 2:22
v. 22. Here Archelaus, son of great Herod, conceived by Martha the Samaritan, had been left by his father as successor to the kingdom; he took as wife Glaphyra, daughter of Archelaus King of the Cappadocians, the widow left behind by Alexander his brother. He was an impious tyrant, having abused for some time the title of King, since he had been constituted by Emperor Augustus ethnarch of Judaea, and only half of the dominion which his father had held had been granted to him on account of his tyranny he was driven into exile by the same emperor and betook himself to Vienna in Gaul. Jos. book 17. antiquities ch. 1. 10. 11. 13. 15.

Here it is most manifest, Iudaea [Judea] is taken in a special signification for the lot of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, so that it may be distinguished both from the land of Israel and from Galilee. Archelaus presided over this; Herod, surnamed Antipas, brother of Archelaus, was tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea.

Into Galilee, namely he withdrew into the parts of lower Galilee. For there are two Galilees, upper and lower. Josephus, book 3, On the Jewish War, chapter 2.

Latin:

v. 22. Hic Archelaus Herodis magni filius, ex Marthaca Samaritana susceptus regni successor â patre relictus erat, Glafiram Archelai Cappadocum Regis filiam, Alexandri fratris sui relictam viduam in uxorem duxit. Fuit impius Tyrannus, abusus aliquandiu nomine Regis, cùm ab Imp. Augusto Ethnarcha Iudaeae constitutus, ac dimidia tantum pars ditionis, quam pater obtinuerat, ei concessa fuisset, propter Tyrannidem ab eodem in exilium pulsus Viennam Galliae sese contulit. Ioseph. lib. 17. antiq. cap. 1. 10. 11. 13. 15.

Hic manifestissimum est, Iudaeam accipi in significatione speciali pro sorte tribuum Iudae ac Baniamin, ut distinguatur tum â terra Israël, tum â Galilaea. Huic praeerat Archelaus, frater Archelai, Herodes cognomine, Antipas erat tetrarcha Galilaeae & Peraeae.

In Galilaeae, scil. inferioris partes secessit. Est enim duplex Galilaea, superior & inferior. Ioseph. lib. 3. de bello Iud. cap. 2.

## 2:23
verse 23. Κατῴκησεν he dwelt, chose out a home for himself, in which he would not sojourn for a time, as in Egypt, but dwell together with his family.

For among the Greeks ηατοιηειν and ταροιηειν, differ, just as among the Latins to inhabit and to sojourn; hence Peter calls our life ταροιηειν., First Epistle, chapter 1, verse 18.

Nazareth was a city of Lower Galilee, the homeland of Joseph and Mary, situated in the tribe of Zebulun, distant from Mount Tabor by about two hours' journey, toward the West, built on a mountain Luke 4. v. 29.

Observation. Nazareth was an obscure and lowly little town John 1. v. 46. therefore because Christ willed to be conceived and brought up in Nazareth, it is thereby signified that He wishes to choose those things that are cast down and despised in this world, 1. Cor. 1. v. 28.

Question. Where does this Prophecy concerning Christ exist?

1. Chrysostom, Homily 9 on Matthew, thinks that this oracle was drawn from some volumes which have perished either through the negligence or impiety of the Jews, or through the injuries of times and wars. *(Osterodian the Photinian asserts the same thing also in the Institutes, chapter 27, and indeed for this purpose, that he may prove that certain words formerly existed written in the law, i.e., in the canonical books of the Old Testament, although today they are not found in it.)* But Chemnitz rightly warns that this solution is dangerous, since it presupposes that the Church does not still hold safe and intact all the books of Scripture which existed at the time of Christ and the Apostles. *(But against Osterod B. D. Feurbach rightly objects in the Examination, chapter 27, page 391, that Scripture is said to be fulfilled then too when what happened in the type occurs in the antitype, or when something else similar happens, as Jer. 31. v. 15. Matt. 2. v. 16. 17. And he also warns that this passage of Matthew pertains in this manner. For since at Isa. 11. v. 1. He is called a twig or sprout, therefore He was named after the place of His upbringing, from Nazareth, as it were the city of twigs.)*

2. Andr. Osiander judges that it is not written in the Prophets, because the words of the Evangelist sound thus. 'It was spoken by the Prophets.' He judges therefore that it is a tradition which the sons of the Prophets drew down from some following Scriptures. Close to this is what Stapleton contends, that by 'the Prophets' in this place are understood not those famous Prophets received into the canon, but certain more obscure and hidden authors. But at Matt. 21. v. 4. the same phrase occurs, where nevertheless some prophecy taken from Zechariah is cited. Moreover it is dangerous, to entrust to uncertain titles of traditions those things which pertain to the confirmation of faith.

3. Some hold that regard is had to the Nazirites of the Old Testament, who were types of Christ, (Gen. 49. v. 26.) Tertullian, book 4, against Marcion: Christ the Creator's was destined to be called a Nazarene according to Prophecy, whence even by that very name we Jews call us Nazarenes through Him. For we too are such as are written of: Nazarenes are whiter than snow, namely those who behind their backs are yellowed with the stains of wrongdoing, and blackened with the darknesses of ignorance. But the appellation Nazarene would come to belong to Christ on account of the hiding-places of His infancy, to which He went down near Nazareth so as to avoid Archelaus the son of Herod. In the Letter of Lentulus the Proconsul the appearance and form of Christ are described, namely that He was such as the Nazirites were. (But this Letter is spurious, fabricated by some unlearned man.)

Although however Christ did not perform that vow which the Nazirites used to perform, Num. 6. v. 2. yet He was a true Nazarene, namely holy, innocent, undefiled, and separated from sinners, Heb. 7. v. 26. therefore it came about by the wonderful arrangement of GOD that He dwelt for a while in Nazareth, and thus obtained that surname, owed to Himself for another reason. *(This opinion Hugo Grotius especially embraces in his Annotations on this passage, who also, to the question concerning the spelling, namely that it is not Ναζωραῖος, but Ναζωραῖος and Ναζαρηνός (which comes into use in most

of the Gentile appellations of the Eastern peoples, as Stephanus teaches,) answers why Christ should be so called in the New Testament, namely: there being a diversity of pronunciation, not of sound. He also rightly warns that the letters ῖ and ῦ are sometimes interchanged among the Oriental peoples: and hence it is that the Syrian expresses the name Ναζωραῖος in this place by , just as the Arabian by , but the Ethiopian by , who moreover adds out of himself the name of the Son, for he expressly has , that is, my Son shall be called a Nazarene.)*

4. To this opinion there closely approaches what certain persons determine, (as Calvin and others,) namely that respect is had to the type of Samson, of whom Iud. 13. v. 5. it is said, he shall be a Nazarite from the womb. For it is agreed that Samson bore the type of Christ in many respects. Junius and Piscator deny that the Evangelist looked to the Nazarites of the Old Testament. Stapleton also denies this very thing. Their opinion can be proved from this, because it is not written Ναζωραῖος or Ναζωραῖος (by which name those were called who in the Old Testament were by vow bound to the divine worship) but Ναζωραιος, and Marc. 1. v. 24. Luc. 4. v. 34. Ναζαρηνός.

5. Erasmus writes thus in his annotations. Nasir () means among the Hebrews holy or consecrated; now truly in the Old Testament not in one place, but everywhere, holy is said, and in Daniel [he is called] holy of holies.

6. Very many judge that respect is had to the prophecies Esa. 4. v. 2. cap. 11. v. 1. cap. 60. v. 21. Ierem. 23. v. 5. cap. 33. v. 15. Zach. 3. v. 8. cap. 6. v. 12. where Christ is called and , a sprout, partly because it is said in the plural, that what was spoken through the Prophets has been fulfilled, partly because in the Syriac paraphrase it is written not by ῖ but by ῦ. Jerome on chapter 11 of Isaiah: That which in the Gospel of Matthew all ecclesiastical writers seek, and do not find, where it is written, Because he shall be called a Nazarene, the learned among the Hebrews think is taken from this passage. Pagninus proves from the title of the Lord's cross preserved at Rome, and from the commentaries of the ancient Hebrews, that the appellation of the city Nazareth and of Christ derived from it ought to be written by , not by . Compare Francis Junius in the Parallels. Stapleton: It is the custom of the Hebrews, when they cite something, saying of the Prophets, through the Prophets, in the Prophets, or in some other similar manner of citation, without any particular named Prophet brought forward, generally to understand that what is cited is drawn from the Book of the 12 Prophets, which are also called the Lesser Prophets. Since therefore the Evangelist cites after this fashion, it is consistent that this saying be found in the Book of the 12 Prophets. Now it is contained Zach. 6. which Jonathan explains in the Chaldee translation, interpreting it of the Messiah. *(Isaiah chapter 11 verse 1, and Zechariah, hinted at this very thing about which Matthew treats here, as Constantine L' Empereur likewise determined in his Annotations to Moses Kimchi οσοιπορ pages 94 and 152. And the same man admonishes that, whereas the Jews jeer at our manner of drawing conclusions, it must be set against them that their most ancient Doctors long ago already approved this mode of teaching by their own example.)*

The Author of the imperfect work on Operation, in this place: If he had set forth an example fixed from the Scriptures, he would never say 'what was said through the Prophets.' But simply, 'what was said through the Prophet.' Now however, citing the Prophets in the plural, he shows that he gave not the words of one Scripture but the sense of many.

7. Less probable is what some maintain, that Nazarene should be interpreted as guardian, preserver from the root he guarded, he preserved, whence the shoot, which is wont to be carefully preserved lest it perish. And indeed in the prophetic books the name of guardian and keeper is frequently given to Christ.

Connection. From those things which happened to Christ in childhood, the Evangelist passes over to those things done by him in adult age, beginning with those which were set before his public ministry of teaching. The parts of the chapter are two. 1. Of John, the precursor of Christ ηηρυγμα. 2. Of Christ the Savior βάπτισμα. παροσηευης

Latin:

v. 23. Κατῴκησενhabitavit, domicilium sibi delegit, in quo non commoraretur ad tempus, sicut in Aegypto, sed cum familia habitaret.

Nam apud Graecos differunt ηατοιηειν & ταροιηειν, sicut apud Latinos habitare & commorari, inde Petrus vitam nostram vocat ταροιηειν. 1. Epist. 1. v. 18.

Nazareth erat civitas Galilaeae inferioris, Iosephi & Mariae patria, sita in tribu Zabulon, distans â monte Thabor duarum horarum itinere circiter, Occidentem versus, aedificata in monte Luc. 4. v. 29.

Observ. Erat Nazareth oppidulum obscurum & humile Ioh. 1. v. 46. quod ergo Christus in Nazareth & concipi & educari voluit, eo ipso significatur, quod ea, quae sunt in hoc mundo abiecta & contemta, eligere velit, 1. Cor. 1. v. 28.

Q. Ubi extet haec de Christo Prophetia?

1. Chrysostomus homil. 9. in Matth. existimat, hoc oraculum adductum esse ex aliquo voluminum, quae vel negligentiâ vel impietate Iudaeorum, vel temporum ac bellorum iniuriâ perierint. *(Idem hoc adserit quoque Osterodus Photinianus in Instit. cap. 27. & quidem eo fine, ut evincat, verba quaedam olim in lege scriptâ s. libb. V. T. authenticis extitisse, tametsi hodie in illâ non reperiantur.)* Sed Chemnitius rectè monet, hanc solutionem esse periculosam, quae praesupponit, Ecclesiam non omnes Scripturae libros, qui Christi & Apostolorum tempore extiterunt, hodie adhuc salvos & incolumes habere. *(Osterodo verò rectê opponit B. D. Feurb. in Exam. cap. 27. pag. 391. quòd tunc quoque Scr. S. impleri dicatur, quando in antitypo obtingit, quod factum est in typo, vel quando simile quid aliud evenit, uti Ier. 31. v. 15.Matth. 2. v. 16. 17. Et ad hunc modum pertinere quoque monet locum hunc Matthaei. Cùm enim Es. 11. v. 1. dicuntur surculus seu germen, ideò â loco educationis, â Nazareth, quasi civitate surculorum, denominatus fuit.)*

2. Andr. Osiander censet, non esse scriptum in Prophetis, quia verba Evangelistae sic sonant. Dictum est per Prophetas. Censet igitur, esse traditionem, quam filii Prophetarum bonâ consequentiex Scripturis deduxerint. Huic affine est, quod Stapletonus contendit, per Prophetas h. l. non celebres illos & in caenonem receptos Prophetas, sed obscuriores aliquos & secretos autores intelligi. Sed Matth. 21. v. 4. ponitur eadem phrasis, ubi tamen ex Zacharia scriptum aliquod vaticinium allegatur. Periculosum insuper est, incer-is traditionum titulis committere ea, quae ad fidei confirmationem pertinent.

3. Quidam statuunt, ad Nazaraeos V. T. qui fuerunt typi Christi, ( Gen. 49. v. 26.)respectum haberi. Tertull. lib. 4. adv. Marc. Nazaraeus vocari habebat secundùm Prophetiam Christus creatoris, unde & ipso nomine nos Iudaei Nazaraeos appellant per eum. Nam & sumus, de quibus scriptum est, Nazarei exalbati sunt super nivem, qui scilicet retrò luridati delinquentiae maculis, & nigrati ignorantiae tenebris. Christo autem Nazaraei appellatio competitura erat ex infantiae latebris, ad quas apud Nazareth descendit vitando Archelaum filium Herodis. In Epistola Lentuli Proconsulis Christi habitus & forma describitur, quod talis fuerit, qualis erat Nazaraeorum. (Sed haec Epistola est commentitia, â quodam indocto conficta.)

Quamvis verò Christus non praestiterit votum illud, quod Nazaraei praestare solebant, Num. 6. v. 2. fuit tamen, verus Nazarenus, videl. sanctus, innocens, immaculatus & â peccatoribus separatus,Hebr. 7. v. 26. factum ergo mirabili DEI dispositione, ut aliquandiu habitarit in Nazareth, & sic cognomen illud, aliâ ex causa fibi debitum, sortiretur. *(Sententiam hanc praecipuè amplectitur Hugo Grotius Annot. ad h. l. qui etiam ad dubium de scriptione, quòd nempe non Ναζωραῖος, sed Ναζωραῖος & Ναζαρηνός (quod in plerisq;

appellationibus gentilitiis Orientalium populorum usu venire, Stephanus docet.) Christus In N. T. dicatur, respondet, videlicet: pronunciationis esse, non vocis diversitatem. Idem quoque rectè monet, litteras. ῖ & ῦ aliquando inter se apud Orientales permutari: atque hinc est, quòd Syrus nomen Ναζωραῖος hoc loco exprimat per quemadmodum & Arabs per Aethiops verò per qui etiam addit de suo nomen Filii, expressè enim habet id est, ut Nazaraeus vocetur Filius meus.)*

4. Ad hanc sententiam proximè accedit, quod quidam, (uti Calv. & alii) statuunt, in specie respectum haberi ad typum Simsonis, de quoIud. 13. v. 5.dicitur, erit Nazaraeus ab utéro. Constat enim, Simsonem in multis typum gessisse Christi. Iunius & Piscator negant, Evangelistam respexisse ad Nazaraeos V. T. Negat etiam id ipsum Stapletonus. Illorum sententia probari potest ex eo, quòd non scribitur Ναζωραῖος aut Ναζωραῖος (quo nomine appellabantur, qui ex voto in V. T. erant divino cultui obstricti.) sed Ναζωραιος & Marc. 1. v. 24.Luc. 4. v. 34.Ναζαρηνός.

5. Erasmus in annot. sic scribit. Nasir ( ) Hebraeis sanctus sive consecratus dicitur, iam verò in V. T. non uno loco, sed passim dicitur sanctus, & apud Daniel-m sanctus sanctorum.

6. Plerique censent, respectum haberi ad vaticinia Esa. 4. v. 2.cap. 11. v. 1.cap. 60. v. 21.Ierem. 23. v. 5.cap. 33. v. 15.Zach. 3. v. 8.cap. 6. v. 12. ubi Christus dicitur & surculus, tum quia in plurali dicitur, impletum esse, quod dictum est per Prophetas, tum quia in Syriaca paraphrasi non per ῖ sed per ῦ scribitur. Hieron. in cap. 11. Es. Illud, quod in Evangelio Matthaet omnes quaerunt Ecclesiastici, & non inven-unt, ubi scriptum sit, Quoniam Nazaraeus vocabitur, eruditi Hebraeorum de hoc loco a-su nium putant. Pagninus ex titulo Dominicae crucis Romae asservato, & ex veterum Hebraeorum commentariis probat, civitatis Nazareth & Christi appellationem ex ea deductam per non per scribendam esse. Confer Franc. Iunium in parall. Stapul. Mos Hebraeorum est, cùm quippiam allegant, dicendo apud Prophetas, per Prophetas, in Prophetis, aut alio simili allegationis modo, nequaquam certo sub nomine adducto Propheta, ut plurimum intelligere, quod allegatur, id desumtum esse ex libro 12. Prophetarum, qui & minores Prophetae appellantur. Cùm ergo hunc in modum citet Evangelista, consentaneum est, hoc dictum in libro 12. Prophetarum reperiri. Habetur autemZach. 6.quod dictum Ionatha in transl. Chald. de Messia exponit. *(Esaiam cap. 11. v. 1. & Zachariam hoc ipsum, de quo Matthaeus hic agit, innuisse, statuit quoque Const. L' Emper. in Annot. ad Mosis Kimchi οσοιπορ pag. 94. & 152. Iudaeis verò concludendi rationem sugillantibus opponendum monet idem, quòd ipsorum Dd. antiquissimi hunc docendi modum suo exemplo iam olim approbarint.)*

Autor oper. imperf. in h. l. Si fixum de Scripturis posuisset exempium, nunquam diceret, quod dictum est per Prophetas. Sed simpliciter, quod dictum est per Prophetam. Nunc autem pluraliter Prophetas citans, ostendit, se non verba unius Scripturae, sed multarum sensum dedisse.

7. Minus probabile est, quod aliqui statuunt, Nazarenum interpretandum esse custodem, praeservatorem â rad. custodivit, praeservavit, unde germen, quod solicitâ cura praeservari solet, ne pereat. Iam vero in libris Propheticis Christo frequenter tribui nomen custodis ac conservatoris.

Conn. Ab illis, quae in pueritia Christo obtigerunt, transit Evangelista ad ea, quae in aetate virili ab ipso gesta, initium faciens ab iis, quae παροσηευης causâ publico docendi ministerio praemissa. Partes capitis sunt duae. 1. Iohannis praecursoris Christi ηηρυγμα. 2. Christi Salvatoris βάπτισμα.

## 3:1
v. 1. These things did not immediately follow upon Christ's return from Egypt, but at least twenty years intervened. Therefore the sense is: At that time, when Jesus was still dwelling in Nazareth, in the fifteenth year of Tiberius. Luke 3. v. 1. And even from this passage it is evident that among the Hebrews times are meant by the word days.

παραγίνεται comes, arrives. λινεσΘια is taken for ειναι. It signifies: 1. something unexpected being described. 2. That John the Baptist had until now been silent. 3. But that at this time he came forth into public with ready and eager spirit.

Κηρύττειν means to preach with a clear and resounding voice, to proclaim something publicly to many, just as Κηρυκες heralds are accustomed to do, whence John afterwards says: I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, from Isaiah 40, 3.

έν τη έρημω της Ἰουδαίας. By the wilderness of Judaea is understood the region around Jordan, not far from Jericho, inhabited by few settlers, which in 2. Sam. 17. v. 16. and 22. are called the plains of the wilderness. Whence John is said to have come into all the region round about Jordan. Luke 3. v. 3.

Zacharias, priest, parent of John the Baptist, dwelt in a certain city of Juda, as is gathered from Luke 1. v. 39. 40. Now six cities situated in the wilderness were assigned by lot to the tribes, and they also had their villages Joshua 15. v. 61. Therefore John did not hide himself in the innermost parts of the neighboring wilderness called great, but kept himself near the entrance of the wilderness.

Therefore it is noted under the name wilderness not indeed a place entirely remote from human sight and habitation, but a wooded region and therefore less cultivated, in which Zacharias lived, where also was the house of Joab. 2. Sam. 2. v. 34. Nor did John always remain in the wilderness, but taught also in the court of Herod. Wilderness in the Scriptures denotes not only places wholly uncultivated and frequented only by wild beasts, but also those which are indeed cultivated by men, yet less so, as mountainous regions usually are, in which, it is evident, the house of Zacharias father of the Baptist was located, Luke 1. v. 39. This meaning of the word της έρημου very many sayings of Scripture confirm. Gen. 14. v. 6.Josh. 15. v. 61. 1. Paralipomenon 7. v. 78. 2. Paralipomenon 8. v. 4. &c.; thence also an uninhabited desert,Gen. 11. v. 20.Jeremiah 9. v. 26.

CHAPTER III.

As for those Papists who, from the fact that John is said in this place to have preached in the desert, strive to approve of the eremitic life, we oppose them both with the fact that the word "desert" in Holy Scripture is often taken even for such a place where men dwell, as was shown a little before, and truly with the words of Maldonatus on chapter 3 of Matthew, where he argues that John the Baptist dwelt in a completely solitary desert (which hypothesis, however, is entirely false) because it was written of him: The voice of one crying in the desert, because it was fitting that the law, once promulgated in the desert, should die in the desert. But these causes are proper and peculiar to John. How, therefore, can it be said that John wished to inaugurate the eremitic life and invite others to such a life by his own example? It is truly ridiculous that Corn. à Lap. writes in his Commentary on Matthew, chapter 3, that John, from the fact that he lived angelically with the Angels in the desert, was esteemed an Angel, nay, is called an Angel by Malachi, chapter 3, and by Christ in Matthew 11, v. 10, on account of his monastic life: as if, forsooth, other Ministers of the Church, even those living in wedlock, are not sometimes called Angels—which is the same as messenger—by God in Holy Scripture? For it is a name of office, not of nature. That, indeed, is so clear that not even the Papists themselves can deny it. See, among many, Ludov. ab Alcasar on chapter 2 of the Apocalypse, pages 214, 215, and Libertus Fromondus Haccurianus, who came into the public eye just last year, in his Commentary on the Apocalypse, page 28.)*

It is called the desert of Judea, namely, specifically so called, Matth. 2. v. 1 and 22, because there was no greater one in Judea, which, extending from the village of Anathoth, situated midway between Jerusalem and Jericho, bends above Gilgal as far as the desert of Tekoa and Engedi near the Dead Sea, Matth. 4. v. 1, whose plains John traversed and preached to the inhabitants of that place.

Observation. John was like the dawn and the morning star, going before the rising of the sun ; like a herald, announcing the coming of the King; like the friend of the bridegroom, preparing access for the spouse.

John was a herald of repentance; therefore, he wished to make the beginning of his preaching in the desert.

When John began to preach in the wilderness of Judaea, it was thereby signified that the whole of Judaea was a kind of spiritual wilderness, destitute of the worship and fear of the true God and of true piety.

## 3:2
v. 2. ΜετανοειΤε. Μετανοεινε means to grow wise after the deed, to grieve over the error committed and amend it, to change the judgment of the mind, to put on another mind, to be drawn along by repentance for one's former life and disposition.

Compare the Treatise on Penitence, § 7.

Tertull., book 2 against Marcion, ch. 24: In the Greek sound the name of penitence is compounded from a change of mind. The Syrian has the word of turning (See , and how the Arabic uses the same verb here: But Acts 3, 19. τό έπιςρέΦεσΘαι expresses by ; yet the verb signifies, whence Syr. and Arab. properly he turned back: for when we sin, we turn ourselves away from God and depart from him, Is. 59, 2. whereas when we perform penitence, we return again to GOD, see Deut. 30, 2. 1 Kings 8, 35. Rightly indeed it must be noted that what Matthew here calls indefinitely μετανοειτε, i.e. perform penitence, Mark expresses distinctly in ch. 1, 15: Μετανοειτεχαι πιςέυετεέν τω έυαμμελιω. From this it is evident that the verb μετανοειν,, as well as the noun μετανοιας:, can be understood in two ways, viz. sometimes broadly for the whole conversion of man, as here and vv. 8. 11., likewise Luke 3, 8. ch. 5. 7. ch. 13, 3. &c.; sometimes however strictly, for only one part of conversion, namely for contrition alone, as Mark 1, 15. Acts 20, 21. Luke 24, 47. Whereby it can nevertheless be recognized where ολιηως, and where μεριηως is being taken, is shown in the Collectanea Isagogica, p. 757. Finally, against the Pelagians, Synergists and other patrons of free will, who infer from the fact that in Holy Scripture conversion is demanded of man, as here and frequently elsewhere, συνέρλιαν of the human will in conversion, it must be observed that these admonitions are efficacious instruments of the Holy Spirit, by which He wishes to rouse men out of the sleep of sins and to convert them themselves, so that what they cannot do of themselves (see John 15, 5. Col. 2, 13. Eph. 2, 1. &c.) they may be able to do by His grace and gift. Just as when in the Gospel history Christ says: Maid, arise, Lazarus, come forth, no one infers from those words that they could raise themselves up from corporeal death by their own powers, or cooperate towards their own raising, but this whole work is ascribed to Christ and His quickening word as brought to pass: so too the matter stands here. Compare further matters in the Collectanea Isagogica, p. 615.) just as Peter also joins Acts 3, v. 19. μετανοειν και έπιςρέΦεσθαι together.

From this word Lucas Brugensis gathers proper satisfactions. The word μετανοιας,, he says, signifies something more by the usage of the authors of sacred Scripture than a change of mind for the better, namely also what usually accompanies it and is a sure indication of repentance and a better mind: to be anxious about what you destroy and in a certain way weigh out by means of pious duties, so that you avenge upon yourself your offenses.2 Cor. 7, 9, 10. & 11.Matt. 11, 21. For true ηαταχρηαιηως, desires three things: sorrow, new life, and care or zeal for avenging upon oneself one's own offenses, and thus for appeasing God when angry.

Reply. 1. If by zeal for avenging offenses external signs of true and serious contrition are understood, we admit that penitence includes them, since contrition is part of it. 2. But we deny that by that vengeance of sins satisfaction is made to GOD or God is appeased, for this belongs to Christ alone and his most holy merit. 3. Hence George Cassander in Consult., art. 12, p. 947, argues thus. There will not be such great ground for complaint concerning satisfaction, if according to the judgment of the Church it is taught in this manner: that the passion and death alone of the only-begotten Son of God is the satisfaction and propitiation for our sins, whether those which we contracted from origin, or those which before or after regeneration we committed through the weakness of the flesh; which satisfaction is offered and applied to us by the Ministry of the Gospel, i.e. the word of GOD and the Sacraments, but is received by faith, which itself too is a gift of God. And although by the power of this satisfaction of Christ both guilt and eternal punishment due to sin are wiped away, yet it is certain that God requires from penitents, especially on account of graver offenses, tears, fastings, prayers, alms and the other indications of a truly penitent soul, and finally the changing and amending of the whole life for the better; and when we do this, we are said to satisfy GOD for sins, (not in the proper meaning of the word, but καταχρησιῦς,, for there follows:) not because we offer a price worthy and sufficient for washing away sins, but because we perform those duties which God requires of the sinner to whom He wishes to impart the satisfaction of His Son. 4. From this it is also evident that the parts of penitence are enumerated insufficiently, for faith is omitted, which lays hold of the satisfaction of Christ offered to it in the word of the Gospel. *(Not to be passed over here, that Hugo Grotius also rightly denies that Mark 1, 4. that the word μετανοειτε is here taken more strictly, a view which he also admirably approves in the same place.)*

Ἤγγικε The Vulgate rendered it in the past tense, has drawn near, yet it can also be turned into the present: for it is one of those verbs which in their past form carry the sense of the present. Erasmus translated, is at hand. But John in this place, and Christ too, who uses the same word in chap. 4. v. 17., by no means intend this, that the kingdom of heaven is not far away, but that the hearers have already come to that time of the kingdom.

Η βαοιλεια ιων ουρανων, the heavenly kingdom promised so often by the Prophets in the O. T. For the Baptist looks back to the prophetic predictions concerning the Messiah and his kingdom. Is. 56, 1. *(Why the name ῶρανων is used in the Greek text, whereas otherwise the Greeks everywhere make use of the singular number, Grotius shows on this passage, as it appears: the same writer also rightly remarks there that the kingdom of the heavens is nothing else here than the kingdom of GOD, since indeed that highest heaven is, as it were, the citadel and royal seat of GOD, therefore it is wont to be put for GOD. This very point was moreover admirably proved by B. D. Glassius, Rhet. S. p. 42., from Ps. 73, 9.Dan. 4, 23. Thus the word 'of-the-heavens,' namely for GOD, is wont to be taken Luke 15, 18.21.ch. 20, 4. The Rabbins imitate this everywhere, several of whose formulae Glassius noted in the place cited. There may be added, from Pirke Abhoth ch. 4., this saying: כל בנםיה i. e. Every congregation that comes into being on account of hea- םופה לחתקים ven, that is, on account of the glory of GOD, its end is that it remain firm: but that which does not come into being on account of God does not remain firm. In the Midrash Koheleth ch. 5. v. 6. these words are read: He who visits the sick says: חשמים i. e. May the heavens, i. e. God, have mercy upon you. To this also pertains the Abbrev. Rabb. בםר, whereby is signified רשמיא בםעתא i. e. by the help of the heavens, i. e. OF GOD. The Eastern interpreters of the N. T. imitate the same manner of speaking. For they use it not in the present only in this place, but also below ch. 2-, 25.; likewise Luke 15, 18.21.ch. 20, 4. Whence what the Heb. Rabbins employ in place of a wish, בשש or in Chaldee בםר, can be expressed in Syriac in Arabic in Ethiopic although, according to the usage of the Ethiopians, you would say more correctly i. e. In the name of the Father, and Son and Spirit Holy, of the ONE GOD. But according to the custom of the Arabs that is, In the name of God, merciful, compassionate This prayer-formula is so worn out among the Turks that it seems to be prefixed almost to every individual Surah of the Alcoran. Indeed the Persians are accustomed to shape the figure of a bird from that symbol, as Mr. Olearius shows in his Persian Itinerary. But this ως έν παροσω )

Jerome on this passage: John the Baptist first preaches the kingdom of heaven, that he might be honored by the precursor of the Lord with this privilege. The same, Letter 129, to Dardanus: And heavenly kingdoms are promised also to me in the Gospel, which the old instrument does not mention. Chrysostom on this passage: Then blessed John begins for the first time to preach with a most clear voice those things which the Jews had heard neither from the Prophets nor from any others whatsoever. These sayings of the Fathers Lucas Brugensis brings forward in his explanation of this passage: but those things, 1., must not be taken in such sense as if in the Old Testament spiritual, heavenly and eternal goods were not promised to believers. 2. Nor in such sense as if Christ according to His divine Nature had possessed no kingdom either of power or of grace in the Old Testament. 3. But because, since the Son of God was now exhibited in the flesh, the heavenly kingdom without any wrappings of figures and earthly goods is offered to all in the word of the Gospel. For by kingdom of heaven is understood that time of grace in which Christ had come in the flesh, and of manifestation through the preaching of the Gospel. Therefore what Francis Lucas adds needs a very convenient interpretation: Before Christ nevertheless there existed men endowed with generous spirit in whom God reigned excellently, and upon whom heavenly blessedness remained among the foremost, among others Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; yet because they were few and rare, and not equally manifest, the institution of that kingdom under which they lived was earthly, bodily and servile, nor did heavenly blessedness lie open beyond death; therefore the kingdom of heaven began not before Christ. And afterwards on verse 7: The clear, public doctrine of such eternal matters (concerning the immortality of the soul, concerning the resurrection of the dead, concerning the eternal rewards of good men and punishments of evil ones) appears to have been reserved for the Messiah. For the ancient fathers say that John, the precursor of the Messiah, announced first, ⟦f1 the kingdom of heaven and eternal punishment. Yet 1., although with regard to the New Testament there were few in the Old in whom God reigned through grace, still considered in themselves they were far more numerous. 2. Nor was the kingdom merely earthly, bodily and servile under which the godly lived during the time of the Old Testament, but they had also the promise about the Messiah and His benefits, which both could and ought to apply to themselves by true faith, and in this way became partakers of the spiritual and heavenly kingdom. There were not lacking, says Conzenius in the Preface, 1., to the Gospels, in the Old Testament many righteous men acceptable to God, but by the benefit of the New Testament, which lay veiled and hidden in the Old Testament. Which agrees with the saying of Augustine, Letter 20, to Honoratus. Those saints administered the old Testament fittingly for their times, but belonged to the New Testament. For even when they enjoyed temporal happiness, they understood eternal, true and preferable [happiness], and ministered the latter in mystery, that they might attain it hereafter. 3. That the souls of the departed before Christ were not made partakers of heavenly blessedness is a false hypothesis, as is shown in its proper place. *(Compare further matters on this subject against the Photinians, Arminians and Anabaptists, who hold that only earthly goods were promised in the Old Testament, in Blessed Pareus, Vol. V. Systematic Theology on the Church §. 19. likewise vol. IX. §. 30. Academic Dissertations p. 623. B. D. Meisner, Theological Considerations on Photinus p. 745. sqq. B. D. Feurbach? Against Ostervald? p. 326. sqq. Mr. D. Calovius, Refutation of Socinianism p. 317. sqq. likewise in Consideration of Arminianism p. 333 sqq. Mr. Hackspang, Inaugural Oration on Hinckelman. On the Anabaptists, Dissertation 1, error 4. B. D. Hutters, Systematic Theology p. 499. B. D. Wilhelm Lyser, in dissertation on the religion of the Adamites. B. D. Himmler?, dissertation on the mode of justification in the Old and New Testament, etc.)*

Lucas Brugensis ex hoc verbo colligit satisfactiones proprias. Voxμετανοιας, inquit, ex autorum sacrae scripturae usu plus aliquid signat, quàm animi in melius mutationem, nimirum etiam id, quod comitari solet, certumque resipiscentiae ac melioris mentis indicium, solicitum esse, quod piis officiis deleas & quodammodo penses, atin teipso ulciscaris delicta.2. Cor. 7, 9, 10. & 11.Matth. 11, 21.Tria enim desiderat veraηαταχρηαιηως,dolorem, novam vitam, & curam sive studium ulciscendi in seipso delicta, itaque placandi iratum Deum.

Resp. 1. si per studium ulciscendi delicta intelligantur externa signa verae & seriae contritionis, admittimus poenitentiam, utpote cuius pars est contritio, eadem includere. 2. negamus verò, per illam delictorum ultionem DEO satisfieri vel Deum placari, soli enim Christo & eius sanctissimo merito hoc competit. 3. Inde Georg. Cassander in Consult. art. 12. p. 947. sic disserit. De satis factione non tantus erit conquerendi locus, si ex Ecclesiae sententia hunc in modum doceatur, quòd solapassio & mors unigeniti Filii Dei sit satisfactio & propitiatio pro peccatis nostris sive eo, quod ex origine contraximus, sive iis, quae ante velpost regenerationem ex carnis infirmitate commisimus, quae satisfactio offertur & applicatur nobis Ministerio Evangelii i. e. verbi DEI & Sacramentorum, accipitur autem fide, quae & ipsa Dei donum est. Quamvis autem virtute huius satisfactionis Christi & culpa & poena aeternapeccato debita deleatur, certum tamen est, Deum à poenitentibus ob graviora praesertim delicta lachrymas, ieiunia, preces, ele-mosynas & reliqua verè paenitentis animi indicia, ac denique totius vitae in melius immutationem ac emendationem exigere, quod cum facimus, DEO satisfacere pro pecca-o dicimur, (non proprio verbi significatu, sed καταχρησιῦς, sequitur enim) non quôd precium dignum & sufficiens diluendis peccatis offeramus, sed quod officia ista praestemus, quae Deus à peccatore, cui Filii sui satisfactionem impartiri velit, requirit. 4. Ex quo etiam constat, partes paenitentiae insufficienter enumerari, praetermittitur enim fides, quae satisfactionem Christi in verbo Evangelii sibi oblatam apprehendit. *(Non praetermittendum hîc, Hugonem quoque Grotium rectè negare ad Marc. 1, 4. vocem μετανοειτε strictiùs hîc accipi, quam sententiam quoque egregiè ibidem probat.)*

Quin & avis formam ex symbolo illo figurare Persae solent, quemadmodum ostendit Dn. Olearius Itiner. Pers. Sed haec ως έν παροσω)*

Hieronymus in h. l. Primus Baptista Iohannes regnum coelorum praedicat, ut praecursor Domini hoc privilegio honoretur. Idem Epist. 129. ad Dardanum: Et mihi in Evangelio promittuntur regna coelorum, quae instrumentum vetus non nominat. Chrysostomus in h. l. Tunc primùm incipit B. Iohannes ea, quae Iudaei nunquam vel à Prophetis, vel à quibus cuna aliis audierant, voce clarissima praedicare. Haec Patrum dicta in explic. h. l. adducit Lucas Brugensis: sed ista 1. non sunt eo sensu accipienda, ac si in V. T. spiritualia, coelestia & aeterna bona non fuerint fidelibus promissa. 2. nec eo, ac si Christus secundùm divinam suam Naturam nullum habuerit regnum vel potentiae vel gratiae in V. T. 3. Sed quòd Filio DEI in carne iam exhibito regnum coeleste sine ullis figurarum & terrenorum bonorum involucris in verbo Evangelii omnibus offeratur. Per regnum enim coelorum intelligitur tempus illud gratiae, quo Christus in carnem venerat, & manifestationis per Evangelii praedicationem. Perquàm igitur commodâ interpretatione indiget, quod Franc. Lucas subiicit: Ante Christum tame-si erant, in quibus liberali animo praeditis Deus excellenter regnaret, quosque inter primos coelestis beatitudo maneret, inter alios Abraham, Isaac & Iacob, tamen quia pauci & rarierant, nec perinde manifesti, institutuma eius regni, sub quo degebant terrenum, corporeum & servile erat, nec patebat à morte coelestis beatitudo, ideo non ante Christum regnum coelorum caepit. Et postea ad v. 7. Videtur clara, publicaa huius modi rerum aeternarum doctrina (de immortalitate animae, de resurrectione mortuorum, de aeternis bonerum praemiis & malorum suppliciis) Messiae reservata fuisse. Nam veteres patres Iohannem Messiae praecursorem primum dicunt annunciasse, regnum coelorum & supplicium aeternum. Atqui 1. quamvis respectu N. T. in V. pauci fuerint, in quibus per gratiam Deus regnaret, tamen in se considerati fuêre longè plurimi. 2. nec fuit duntaxat terrenum, corporeum & servile regnum, sub quo pii tempore V. T. degebant, sed habuerunt etiā promissionem de Messia & eius beneficiis, quae verâ fide sibi applicare & potuerunt & debuerunt, atque hac ratione regni spiritualis & coelestis participes facti sunt. Non defuerunt, inquit Conzenius q. prooem. 1. in Evangel. in V. T. viri iusti, Deoa accepti, fuêre plurimi, sed beneficio N. T. quod erat in V. T. velatum & absconditum. quò accommodat dictum August. Epist. 20. ad Honoratum. Dispensabant illi sancti pro congruentia temporis Testamentum vetus, pertinebant verò ad Test. Novum. Nam & quando temporalem felicitatem agebant, aeternam, veram & praeferendam intelligebant, & istam ministrabant in mysterio, ut illam consequerentur in pro oemio. 3. quòd animae ante Christum defunctorum non fuerint coelestis beatitudinis factae participes, falsa est hypothesis, ut suo loco ostenditur. *(Confer plura in hanc rem contra Photinianos, Arminianos & Anabaptistas, statuentes, terrena duntaxat bona in V. T. fuisse promissa, apud B. Par. Tomo V. L. L. Theol. de Eccl. §. 19. it. tom IX. §. 30. Dispp. Acad. p. 623. B. D. Meisn. Consid. Theol. Photin. p. 745. seqq. B. D. Fewrb. Anti Ost. p. 326. seqq. Dn. D. Calovius Socinism. profl. p. 317. seqq. it. in Consid. Arminianismi p. 333 seqq. Dn. Hackspan. in Orat Auspic. Hinckelm. De Anabapt. Disp. 1. err. 4. B. D. Hutt. L. L. Theol. p. 499. B. D. Wilh. Lyser. in disp. de relig. Adamit. B. D. Himmel. disp. de modo iustif. in V. ac N. T. &c.)*

## 3:3
v. 3. θωνη βοωντος namely there will be, or will be heard. The Hebrew קול קורא can be rendered both as a voice crying and as the voice of one crying. The Seventy Interpreters rendered it in the latter way, whom the Evangelist follows here. But there is no contradiction here. For the voice of one crying in Hebrew idiom means a crying voice, just as πτωχοι των άγιων the poor of the saints are the holy poor, Rom. 15. v. 26. and the mystery of piety is the pious mystery, 1. Tim. 3. v. 16.

Concerning the little word βοωντος some understand GOD under it. From this they seek a mystery in the fact that John is called η Φωνη the VOICE OF GOD, but Christ λογος the WORD OF GOD. Epiphanius, heresy 69: A voice is that which prepares men's hearing; for those who cry out usually first produce an unformed sounding voice, calling from afar those who ought to hear something from them: and when those persons have heard only the voice and turned their mind toward listening, and prepared their ears, then he who emitted the sounding voice thereafter articulates the speech which he wishes to speak. So also John was a voice, preparing the ears of men; for he himself was not the Word, but after him came the Word, on account of which he was a preparatory voice.

But since we warned earlier that the voice of one crying is by Hebrew idiom the same as 'a voice crying', therefore with Euthymius the little word βοωντος is more rightly referred to John himself, the herald of Christ. This is evident from John 1. v. 15. where the Evangelist speaks thus about him: John bears witness concerning him and cries out, saying.

By the word βοάν the same thing is intimated as in v. 1., namely ηηρύττέιν, that is, that John discharged the office of preaching publicly, freely, and diligently, just as heralds are accustomed to announce the coming of the King with a public and free voice.

Εν τη ερημω This ωροσσιορισμόν the LXX. and the Evangelist following them join with what precedes, so that the sense is that John preached in the wilderness of Judaea. v. 1. But in the Hebrew text this προσσιορισμος seems to be joined with what follows according to Francis Lucas: Prepare ye in the desert the way of the Lord, to which corresponds what έξηγητιηως is added immediately after in the prophet: Make straight the paths of our GOD in the solitude. Yet the pointing allows that במרבר also be referred to what precedes קיל שירא: for there is on both sides an accent, constituting a disjunctive mark. And the matter itself demands that in the desert be joined with what precedes according to the LXX. and the Gospel, because John was in the desert when he preached.

Ετοιμάσατε In Heb. it is פנו from the root פנה, which some render level ye; others purge ye; the LXX. and the Evangelist following them, prepare ye, because by purging and leveling the road is made prepared and expedited.

Prepare ye the way of the Lord, whereby, namely, he is about to come to you. The Hebrew can also be rendered: Prepare ye the way for the Lord, namely, who will come to you through grace, now that he has already come through the incarnation.

Ευ θέιος ποιέιτε make level, straight, and smooth his paths. The Prophet and the Evangelist persist in the metaphor drawn from the solemn entrance of some king. When citizens wish to receive their king honorably, then they remove all filth, all hindrances and inconveniences, moreover they level the road, and make it pleasant by strewing leaves or grass: So they are commanded to prepare the way for Christ coming through true repentance, first by removing the filth of sins adverse to the purest eyes of this King, and the obstacles of transgressions, which prohibit his spiritual entrance; then by adorning the same path through serious amendment of life and pursuit of virtues. For that preparation must take place through acknowledgment and abhorrence of sins, through serious humiliation, through desire for grace and a saving conversion to God.

The uprightness of paths is set forth against. 1. pride lifting up the heart. 2. hypocrisy having joined together the disparity of heart and mouth.

In the Hebrew it is singular, and to the name OF GOD there is added a relative pronoun thus: Make straight in the wilderness a path for OUR GOD or for our God. But the sense remains the same in both.

Latin:

v. 3. θωνη βοωντος sc. erit, vel audietur. Hebr. קול קורא verti potest & vox clamans, & vox clamantis. Posteriore modo reddiderunt LXX. Interpretes, quos Evangelista hîc sequitur. Sed nulla hîc contrarietas. Dicitur enim vox clamantis phrasi Hebraicâ vox clamans, sicut πτωχοι των άγιωνpauperes sanctorum sunt pauperes sancti, Rom. 15. v. 26.mysterium pietatis est pium mysterium, 1. Tim. 3. v. 16.

Circa voculam βοωντος quidam subintelligunt DEI. Inde mysterium quaerunt in eo, quòd Iohannes dicitur η Φωνηvox DEI, Christus autem λογοςverbum DEI. Epiph. haeres. 69. Vox est praeparatìva auditus hominum, primum enim inarticulatam vocem sonantem reddere solent clamantes, è longinquo vocantes eos, qui ab ipsis aliquid audire debent: & ubi illi vocem solam audierint, & mentem ad audiendum converterint, aures que praepar averint, tunc is, qui sonantem vocem emisit, de caetero distingvit sermonem, quem dicere volunt. Sic & Iohannes vox fuit, aures hominum praeparans, non enim erat ipse verbum, sed post ipsum venit verbum, propter quod praeparativa fuit vox.

Sed quia iam antè monuimus, vocem clamantis phrasi Hebraeâ esse idem, quod vocem clamantem, ideo cum Euthymio vocula βοωντος rectiùs ad ipsum Iohannem Christi preconē refertur. Manifestum hoc est ex Ioh. 1. v. 15. ubi Evangelista de eo sic loquitur: Iohannes testimonium perhibet de ipso & clamat, dicens.

Per verbum βοάν idem insinuatur, quod v. 1. ηηρύττέιν videlicet quod Iohannes publicè, liberè ac sedulò praedicandi munere perfunctus fuerit, sicut praecones solent publicâ & liberâ voce adventum Regis denunciare.

Εν τη ερημω Hunc ωροσσιορισμόν LXX. & eos secutus Evangelista connectunt cum praecedentibus, ut sit sensus, quòd Iohannes in deserto Iudaeae praedicaverit. v. 1. In Hebraeo autem textu Franc. Lucae coniungi videtur hic προσσιορισμος cum seqq. In deferto parate viam Domini, cui respondet, quod έξηγητιηως statim apud prophetam additur: Rectas facite in solitudine semitas DEI nostri. Punctatio tamen admittit, ut illud במרבר etiam ad praecedens קיל שירא referatur: utrobique enim habetur accentus, incisum manus constituens. Ac res ipsa postulat, ut illud in deserto coniungatur cum praecedentibus iuxta LXX. & Evang. quia Iohannes in deserto erat, cùm praedicabat.

Ετοιμάσατε In Hebr. est פנו à rad. פנה quod quidam verrunt, complanate; alii expurgate; LXX. & eos secutus Evangelista, parate, quia expurgando & complanando via parata atque expedita redditur.

Parate viam Domini, quâ sc. ad vos venturus est. Hebraea etiam reddi possunt: Parate viam Domino, sc. qui ad vos venturus est per gratiam, cùm iam venerit per incarnationem.

Ευ θέιος ποιέιτεplanas, rectas & aquabiles facite semitas eius. Persistit Propheta & Evangelista in metaphorâ, à solenni alicuius Regis ingressu ducta. Quando cives Regem suum honorificè excipere cupiunt, tum removent omnes sordes, omnia impedimenta atque incommoda, viam insuper complanant, & sparsis frondibus vel gramine amoenam reddunt: Sic Christo venienti per veram poenitentiam iubentur viam praeparare, tum removendo peccatorum sordes purissimis huius Regis oculis adversas, & delictorum obstacula, quae spiritualem eius ingressum prohibent; tum exornando eandem per seriā vitae emendationem ac studium virtutum. Praeparatio enim illa fieri debet per peccatorum agnitionem & detestationem, per seriam humiliationem, per desiderium gratiae & salutarem ad Deum conversionem.

Rectitudo semitarum opponitur. 1. fastui cor elevanti. 2. hypocrisi disparitatem cordis & oris coniunctam habenti.

In Hebr. est singulare & nomini DEI additur pronomen relativum hoc modo. Rect am facite in solitudine semitam DEI nostri seu DEO nostro. Sed sensus utrobique manet idem.

## 3:4
v. 4. John is described. 1. by his clothing or garment. 2. by his food. His clothing is said to have been αποτριχων καμήλου. Something similar is reported of Elijah 2 Kings 1., 8. He was בעל שער a hairy man, either because he nourished hair on his body Gen. 25. v. 25. or because he wore a hairy garment. Zech. 13. v. 4. it says concerning false prophets: And has not worn אדרת שער garment or mantle of hair, so that they might lie. Such deceivers were clothed out of ηαηοζηλια sackcloth and garments פרזשים so that men would believe their lies, appearing to be true prophets on account of the roughness and suitability of their dress.

Because John was to precede Christ in the spirit and power of Elijah, Luke 1. v. 17. and was that true Elijah who was to come, Malachi 4. v. 5. Matt. 11. v. 13. therefore he also wished to fashion himself after the clothing of Elijah the Tishbite. The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews chap. 11. v. 37. calls such a lowly garment of the prophets μηλωτας χαι αιγεια σερματα sheepskins and goatskins, for they were so poor and needy that they were compelled to clothe themselves with skins not yet prepared. However some think that this garment of John was shaggy, made from camel skin still bearing its hairs, but not woven from fabric out of camel hides, because a garment of this latter kind belongs to the class of soft and splendid clothes, which type of clothing Christ expressly denies to John. Matt. 11. v. 8. But it seems more probable that garments hard to wear were formerly also made from the hairs of camels. And thus Francis Lucas of Bruges takes this passage: He wore not camel skin, but a garment woven from camel hair, which clothing was easy to make, cheap, rough and shaggy, suitable for subjecting the body. For since John was to be the herald of penance, he therefore wished also to use a harsher and cheaper dress, so that thus he might give an example of penance not only by his preaching but also by his habit and manner of life. His clothing was therefore humble, rustic, hard, yet not woven from raw scraps of skins, as Denis the Carthusian holds, but woven from hair; nor was it peculiar or monstrous, as Maldonatus seems to think, but customary among country folk and men of poorer fortune; nor was it a hairshirt from camel bristles pricking the skin, as the same Maldonatus says *(whom Cornelius à Lapide also follows)*, deliberately chosen, because the hairshirt was not in ordinary use, but in extraordinary mournings, and camels do not have bristles but soft wool. *(Moreover the Syriac Interpreter translates: The garment wasof the hairs of Camels, the Arabic i.e. from the hairs of Camels, the Ethiopian; And the garment of John, with which he was clothed, was of the hair of a Camel.)*

Ζωνην σηερματινην περι την οσφύν αυτού. Something similar is also recounted of Elijah the prophet. 2. Kings 1 v. 8. He was girt with a leather belt about his loins. Therefore John was girded not with some precious belt marked with gold or silver studs, but with a leathern and consequently cheap belt, expressing in himself the likeness of Elijah even in this respect.

The Eastern peoples used long robes, and therefore when about to undertake some task they girded up their loins, so as to be unimpeded for that task. To this Scripture looks, when it commands that we be with our loins girt,Luke 12. v. 35.Eph. 6. v. 14.1. Pet. 1. v. 13. both because it behoves us to be occupied in mortifying the vicious affections of the flesh, and because it behoves us to be ready for every good work.

Η σέτροθηάυτου ην ἀκρίδες. Now what these ἀκρίδες? are, Epiphanius against the Ebionites, which is heresy 30., notes, certain Jews corruptly read for ἀκρίδες έγηρτσες, which word signifies sweetmeats made with honey, as appears from Athenaeus book 3. ch. 27. and b. 14. ch. 14. Others take it of a kind of fish called by the Greeks ηαρις, by the Latins locusta. Moreover 1. Nicholas Perottus takes άηρσας of a certain shrub, just as also the Interpreter of Justin Martyr in the dialogue with Tryphon p. 247. renders άηρσας the topmost shoots of little trees. The same Isidore of Pelusium establishes in book 1. Epistle 132. p. 33. saying Αηρσες, those things on which John fed are not animals, as some ignorantly suppose, resembling beetles. Far be it, rather άηρέμονες βορανων η Φυτων. i.e. the tops of herbs or plants. Euthymius likewise thinks it truer that they are sprigs of herbs, or a herb whose name is locusts. Paulinus held the same view in the poem on John the Baptist. Theophylact on this place reports that some hand down άηρσας to have been herbs called by another name μέλαγρα, some interpret άηρσας άηρσρυα that is, buds and fruits of trees, wild pears. Nicephorus book 1. Ecclesiastical History chap. 14. John lived on άηροις σρυων the summits of trees, which the Evangelists call άηρσας. Willich wrote a Dialogue concerning locusts, in which likewise he maintains άηρσας to be the tips of herbs, which as such ευποριςοις John used in the desert. Baronius dares not condemn this opinion, but judges that a revelation must await ed. *(Yet here the boldness of Jerome Montui, Lord of Mirabel and physician of the Most Christian King, Order b. On Preserving Health ch. 3., may be noted, who writes άηρόμονες, άηρσας by a slippery slip, I believe, has been supposed inMatthew 3. as the food of Saint John. But against this rashness there should be opposed not only the constant reading of the Greek Codices, both printed and manuscripts, with which here the manuscript readings of the Ecclesiastical Histories of the Nuremberg Library also agree, but also the ancient Interpreters, both Oriental and Western.)*

2. But Casaubon in his notes on this passage, and in exercise 13, chapter 7, rightly admonishes, following Baronius, that by locusts certain definite kinds of animals are meant, which were thus named from the fact that they graze down the outermost parts of plants (So too the extremities of animals, namely heads, snouts, ears, feet, hoofs, are denoted by the Greeks with αηρα, άηρωα and αηρωτηρια, as Mr. D. Reinesius observes, Variae Lectiones, book 3, chap., p. 515.) παράτό τάς αηρς των Φυτων νέμεσθαι. For the Syrian rendered it by קמצא locusts, from gathering, so called because locusts are wont to be gathered in Syria by persons of the meaner sort and to be hardened by smoke for use as humble food. The Vulgate likewise rendered it locusts. *(Thus also the Arab, who has; the Ethiopic similarly renders; but that this word signifies locusts is plain from Ps. 77, 47. where for the Hebrew ארבה the Ethiopic Interpreter of the Psalms employs this name. Therefore Cornelius à Lapide, a most famous Jesuit, was again deceived by his Teacher when he writes in his Commentary on this passage: Fourthly others interpret άηρσας as herbs, or the tops of branches and leaves. Whence the Ethiopic translates: His food were anuota, i.e. extremities of herbs with wild honey, dipped in honey. He was deceived, as I said, and Cornelius deceives the reader, asserting this about the Ethiopian. For nowhere in any place of Scripture does he prove that signifies the extremities of herbs: nay rather, the Ethiopic Interpreter of the Psalter expresses by this very word the Hebrew word ארבה, i.e. locust, Ps. 77, 47. likewise Ps. 104, 34. Ps. 109, 23. Nor does the Ethiopic read: with wild honey, as though John had dipped that food in honey, but just as the Syrian and the Arab translate: i.e. And his food was locusts and wild honey, or honey of the desert.)* 2. That men were accustomed in Syria, and among certain peoples of the Ethiopians, to feed upon locusts hardened by smoke, is established from Pliny, book 11, chapter 29, and book 6, chapter 30, from Strabo and other writers.

Jerome, book 2 against Jovinian, chapter 6: The Eastern peoples and those of Libya, because clouds of locusts are found throughout the desert and the hot waste of the wilderness, are accustomed to feed on locusts; that this is true John the Baptist also proves. Compel a Phrygian or a Pontic man to eat locusts, and he will think it wickedness. Moses de Kotzi, in the great Book of Precepts, 139, 4: A man eats locusts both alive and slaughtered. Pliny, Natural History, book 6, chapter 30, reports that certain peoples of Ethiopia live on no other food than locusts, which they harden for this use with smoke and salt. In book 11, chapter 29, he mentions that among the Parthians they are held in delight. Nicholas Clenardus, book 1, Letter 9, to Latomus: A few days ago at Fez (that is a city of Africa) you would have seen the sky covered with columns of locusts, which here not merely leap, but fly after the manner of birds; the peasants wage vigorous war against them. For they bring wagons full of locusts into Fez, for commonly here they destroy these enemies. In Letter 15, to Streyterius, he repeats the same thing. Johannes Leo, in the Description of Africa, book 9: The peoples of the Arabian and Libyan deserts regard the arrival of locusts as a happy omen, for either boiled or dried in the sun they pound them into flour and eat them. Eustathius, in οσυω Φ, relates that there were once peoples who, because they fed on locusts, were called without άηρισοΦάγοι, whom Strabo too remembers, book 16, and Diodorus, Library, book 3, chapters 11 and 2. Jerome Mercurialis, Italian physician, On the Diseases of Children, book 1, chapter 3: Agatharchides relates in the book On the Red Sea, άηρισοΦάγού, that is, that those who feed on locusts have bodies extremely wasted and lean. *(You may read the same from Agatharchides also in Photius' Bibliotheca, excerpt Αγαθαρχισου περι άηρισοΦάγων, p. 736, edition of Hoeschel, where he also shows the method of preparing such little creatures. Compare also concerning the use of άηρισων as food Aristophanes in the Acharnians, and Plutarch in the Symposium.)* Scaliger, against Cardano, exercise 639: Among the Syrians those locusts are received as food which lack wings, which Dioscorides calls Asraci, and Pliny attelabi.

And this opinion, that John’s food was locusts, a certain genus of animals, is embraced by the ancients Origen, Hilary, Ambrose, Chrysostom, Augustine, Jerome, and among the more recent, by most interpreters. Such is the view of Corn. à Lapide, Hugo Grotius, Lud. Capellus, Piscator, Beza, Aretius, and among our own, the blessed Luther, the blessed D. Chemnitius, the blessed Osiander, etc. See Lucas Brug. on this passage; Julius Caesar Scaliger in book 5 of Aristotle’s History of Animals, ch. 28; Daniel Chamier, book 20 of Panstratia, ch. 22, p. 400; and very many others.)*

Now John wished to feed on locusts. 1. because it was a cheap food of little value, whence Clenardus in the Epistle to Latomus says, that he would rather have one partridge than twenty locusts. For the preacher of penitence a cheap garment, and likewise cheap food, was fitting. 2. it was food easily obtainable in the desert. 3. Some add, that it was a food prohibited in the Levitical law, and that therefore by eating it John wished to make manifest that the Levitical distinction of foods, and so the whole Levitical worship, was about to cease in the N. T. Hist. Magd. Cent. 1. lib. 1. cap. 6. col. 250. Those locusts were a species of land crabs, representing some species of locusts, inasmuch as they lack claws, yet they have certain spines in their shell & longer horns than the other crabs. John perhaps used these, because the Jewish fishermen cast them away as prohibited fish, but John, on account of Evangelical liberty, ate them.

But Pisc. Tossan. Brugens. and others deny this third point, who hold that those locusts were little four-footed birds, because Moses calls a kind of flying creatures חגב clean for eatingLev. 1. v. 21. & 22. *(Moreover Chamier attributes these words to Brugensis in place of Luke: His food was not bread, not seeds, not vegetables, much less the flesh of cattle, birds, or fish, but locusts: But I confess I have nowhere been able to find those words in Brugensis.)*

Μέλι αγριαν Palestine, on account of its fertility, is said everywhere by Moses to have flowed with milk and honey, on account of the abundance of both in it, by which, synecdochically, the abundance of all things necessary for the sustenance of life is described. That wild honey, made by wild bees, often flowed out of the hollows of rocks and the splits of trees, Jud. 14. v. 8.1. Sam. 14. v. 26.Ps. 81. v. 17. Theophylact. το άπο άγριαν μέλισσων γεωργουμενον, έν σένσροις έυρισηόμενον χαι πςτραις. Pliny, book 11 of his History, chapter 6: A third kind of honey, by no means approved, is the wild kind, which they call ericaeum. It is gathered after the first rains of autumn, when the heath alone blooms in the woods, and for this reason it resembles sand. Isidore Pelusiota, book 1, Epistle 132: Wild honey is not a certain herb, but mountain honey, which is made by rustic bees, it is of the highest quality and bitter in taste. But this bitterness is to be taken only comparatively, because it is less sweet than domestic honey.

By this food and clothing John 1. he wished to intimate that he came in the power and Spirit of Elijah. 2. he wished to win for himself the authority necessary in the new proclamation. Luc. 3. v. 15. Therefore his testimony was the weightier and of greater authority, the more he himself was alien not only from every crime, but also from all pursuit of earthly things. Nicephorus, book 1 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 18. That man indeed as seen at first sight, but in his very mind and soul altogether divine, most magnificent, and as qu-sp-am the Angel might say, having assumed a body. 3. he wished to commend by the roughness of his food and clothing that penitence which he taught in words. James Faber Stapulensis on this passage: His vile and despised clothing showed contempt of the world contempt of himself and the d-spl--entiam of a life past; its roughness, flight from delights; the p-llicea girdle about the loins, a strict guard of continence; his easy and neglected food, a bridle for the gullet; his drink of water, every manner of sobr-etatem.

But how does it agree with this description of the food of John, what Christ says below, chapter 11, verse 18, that he neither ate nor drank. Answer: 1. some judge that by ἄυξησιν this saying is meant that he used food so sparing, cheap, and alien from the common food of the Jews, that he could be said to have lived among the Jews without food. 2. the true sense is gathered from the opposition. John came neither eating, sc. common foods, nor drinking, sc. strong drink and wine, Luc. 1. v. 15. The Son of man came eating and drinking, sc. in the common manner, and indeed even feasting with sinners and not hesitating to be present at feasts. Thence Luc. 7. v. 33. the determination is added: John the Baptist came neither eating bread nor drinking wine. Where, however, no force is to be laid on the word bread, as Stapleton, Brugensis, and Baronius will, as if John had wholly abstained from its use, but it is signified that he abstained from delicate and customary foods. Lyranus on Matth. 11.: not eating, nor drinking, i.e. living in the greatest abstinence; for he who eats little is said not to eat according to the common manner of speaking, just as he who sees hardly at all is said not to see. Dionysius Carthusianus on chapter 7 of Luke: By this l-o bread and wine the customary and delicate dishes of men, pocul- are signified. Toletus on the same: Abstaining from common foods and drinks. This agrees with the Hebrew idiom, according to which under the name bread every kind of edibles comes.

Bellarmin. On Monks ch. 39. Stapleton Antidotum Evangelicum on Matthew ch. 3. Maldonatus there Salmer ----. 4. treatise 4. Baronius year 31. nn. 11. 12. 13 decree, that John was in this his garb and diet the author of the Monastic life. Answer. 1. Nowhere is it read that John prescribed this manner of living to his disciples. 2. For he himself alone was that Elijah whose coming was promised in the Old Testament, he alone came in the spirit and power of Elijah. Concerning him alone was it foretold by the Angel that he would drink neither wine nor strong drink,Luke 1. v. 15. concerning him alone does Christ recall it as something special and singular, that he ate no bread and drank no wine.Luke 7. v. 33. Therefore κακοζηλία it is, if anyone wishes to imitate him in this respect. 3. Only in the third age was the Eremitical and Monastic life introduced by Paul the Theban and Antony. Therefore John the Bap[tist] is not its author. Polydore Vergil book 7. de rer. invent. cap. 1. Some assign the beginning of this matter to Antony, others to a certain Paul the Theban. But the beginning of this matter can most rightfully be referred to Antony, who, although he was not the first before all, was nonetheless the first who instituted the rule of the Monks. 4. There Polydore adds: Certain ones thinking more deeply about Elijah and John the Baptist make them the authors of this thing. But as he ought to be deemed more than a prophet, so he ought to be deemed more than a Monk. 5. Among the various orders of Monks none is given that has any food besides locusts and wild honey; no clothing unless made of camels' hair. How then could John be able to be the author of the Monastic life? 6. Maldonatus discusses on Matthew ch. 3, that John therefore wore a singular and monstrous garment and dwelt altogether in a quite solitary desert, because concerning him it was written: The voice of one crying in the wilderness, because the law formerly promulgated in the desert had to end in the desert, because it behoved the Messiah to be seen. But these causes are proper and peculiar to John. Therefore the Monks imitate his example out of κακοζηλία. 7. In the Rules of the Society of Jesus neatness and fineness of garments and of diet is prescribed. See the Summary Rule of the Society S. 46. 47. 48. Common Rules §. 19. Rules of the Superior of the House of Professed. c. 6. of the Sub-Procurator General, Procurator of the House of Professed, Procurator of the College through the whole Rules of the steward §. 5. Rules of the Prefect of the Refectory §. 1. 2. of the Cook. And in general such an order of bodily refinement is laid down that it can hardly admit of greater splendour. Wherefore Loyola too, the Institutor of the Order, willed this to be among the Rules of the Society. We allow ourselves to be surpassed rather more easily by other religious Orders in fastings, watchings and the austerity of the rest of our mode of life. By true and perfect obedience, by the surrender of their own will and judgment, I desire above all, most beloved brethren, that those be conspicuous whosoever serve God our Lord in this society, and that they be distinguished as the legitimate offspring of the society by this sort of badge. In the Letter to the companions on the virtue of obed[ience]. §. 3. (Therefore either John the Baptist was not a Monk, or the Jesuits will not be Monks.)

v. 4. Describitur Iohannis. 1. vestitus sive amictus. 2. victus. Vestimentum eius dicitur fuisse αποτριχων καμήλου. Tale quid refertur de Elia 2. Reg. 1., 8.Eratבעל שערpilosus, vel quòd pilos in corpore nutriret Gen. 25. v. 25. vel quòd vestem pilosam gestaret. Zach. 13. v. 4. dicitur de falsis prophetis: Et non indueritאדרת שערvestem sive chlamydem pili, propterea ut mentiantur. Induebantur eiusmodi seductores ex ηαηοζηλια saccis & vestibus פרזשים ut homines ipsorum mendaciis crederent, pro veris prophetis ob vestitus asperitatem & convenientiam eos habentes.

Quia Iohannes in Spiritu & virtute Eliae Christum praecedere debebat, Luc. 1. v. 17. ac erat verus iste Elias, qui venturus erat, Malach. 4. v. 5.Matth. 11. v. 13. ideò etiam in vestitu Eliae Thesbitae sese conformare voluit. Autor Epistolae ad Hebraeos cap. 11. v. 37. vilem eiusmodi prophetarum vestitum vocat μηλωτας χαι αιγεια σερματαpelles ovillas & caprinas, erant enim tam pauperes & egeni, ut pellibus nondum praeparatis amiciri & indui cogerentur. Putant e. nonnulli, vestem. illam Iohannaeam fuisse villosam, ex pelle cameli, habente adhuc suos pilos, non autem ex telâ contexta ê pelis camelorum, quia posterioris huius generis vestis est ex genere mollium & splendidarum, quod genus vestium Christus disertè Iohanni derogat Matth. 11. v. 8. Sed probabilius videtur, etiam ex pilis Camelorum vestes olim duras paratas fuisse. Et ita accipit hunc locum Franc. Lucas Brug. Non pellem camelinam, sed vestimentum ex pilis cameli contextum gest avit, qui vestit us suit facilis paratu, vilis, asper & horridus, corpori subiug ando congruus. Quia enim Iohannes debebat esse praeco poenitentiae, ideò etiam vestitu uti voluit austeriore ac viliore, ut sic non solùm praedicationis loco, sed etiam habitu ac victus genere exemplum poenitentiae daret. Fuit igitur vestitus humilis, rusticus, durus, non tamen ex crudis pellium minutiis contextus, ut vult Dion. Carth. sed ex pilis contextus: nec singularis aut monstrosus, uti Maldonato videtur sed agrestibus & tenuioris fortunae hominibus usitatus: nec fuit cilicium ex setis camelorum pungentibus cutem, ut ait idem Maldon *(quem sequitur etiam Corn. à Lapide)* a cule atum, quia cilicium non fuit in usu ordinario, sed in luctibus extraordinariis, nec cameli setas habent, sed lanam mollem. *(Caeterùm Interpres Syrus vertit: Vestimentum fuitpilorū Camelorū, Arabs i. e. è pi-is Camelorum, Aethiops; Et fuit Iohannis vestimentum, quo induebatur, pilorum Cameli.)*

Ζωνην σηερματινην περι την οσφύν αυτού. Tale quid etiam de Elia propheta commemoratur. 2. Reg. 1 v. 8. Cingulo pelliceo accinctus erat circa renes suos. Voluit autem Iohannes ideò locustis vesci. 1. quia erat cibus vilis & precii exigui, unde Clenardus in Epistolam ad Latomum dicit, se malle unam perdicem, quàm locust as viginti. Praeconi poenitentiae ut vestitus, ita quoque cibus vilis erat conveniens. 2. erat cibus in deserto parabilis. 3. Quidam addunt, quod fuerit cibus in lege Levitica prohibitus, cuius proinde comestione Iohannes manifestum facere voluerit, Leviticum ciborum discrimen, adeoa totum cultum Leviticum in N. T. esse desiturum. Hist. Magd. Cent. 1. lib. 1. cap. 6. col. 250. Fuerunt illae locustae species cancrorum terrestrium, locustarum aliquam speciem repraesentantes, siquidem chelis carent, habent tamen spinas quasdam in crusta & cornulongior a, quàm caeteri cancri. His fortè usus est Iohannes, quia piscatores Iudaici eos abiecerunt tanquàm prohibitos pisces, Iohannes verò pro libertate Evangelica eos comedit.

Sed tertium hoc negant Pisc. Tossan.
