v. 6. έξομολογούμενοι τὰς ἁμαρτία ςἀυτῶν. Differunt ἀξομολόγησις peccatorum, & eorundem έξαγόρευσις.Lev. 16. v. 21. summus Pontifex totius populi peccata iubetur confiteri, quam fuisse generalem & publicam confessionem, constat ex circumstantiis.

*(Bell. lib. 3. de poenit. c. 2. ex h. l. stabilire satagit specialem peccatorum confessionem. Qui ad Iohannis, inquit, Baptismum accesserunt, in specie peccata sua confessi sunt,Matth. 3.Marc. 1. Resp. 1. Corn. à Lap. in h. l. negat, Confessionem Iohanni Bapt. factam fuisse Sacramentum, & peccata condonasse, uti fit in confessione à Christo instituta. Enon valida est consequentia à confessione illa ad hanc, cum haec ex Pontificiorum quidem mente Sacramentum sit, & peccata condonet, illa non, quid quod Pontificii ferè cōmuniter doceant, demum Ioh. 20. h. e. post Christi resurrectionem Sacramentum poenitentiae fuisse institutum & special. pecs. enumerationem requisitam: 2. Nullibi dicitur, quòd in specie singula peccata enumerarint. 3. Pontificii plerique statuunt, in Confessione ante Baptismum non esse necessariam specialem peccatorum enumerationem. Iam verò Iohannis auditores ante susceptum Baptismum confessi fuere. id quod Syrus quoque Interpres innuisse h. l. videtur, dum vertit: Et baptizabantur ab eo in Iordanis fluvio postquam confiterentur sive confessi essent peccata sua. 4. Evangelistae memorant, quod Hierosolyma omnisque Iudaea & omnis regio circa Iordanem ad Iohannem exiverit. Si omnes ad Bapt. Iohannis accedentes omnia & singula peccata confessi fuissent, toto ministerii tempore Iohannes nihil agere potusset, quàm confessiones singulorum audire. 5. Non est quaestio, an confessio specialis & auricularis coram Ministro Ecclesiae sit licita, utilis ac salutaris, sed in Pontificiis reprehenditur, quòd 1. in Confessione auriculari requirant omnium & singulorum peccatorum mortalium, quotquod post diligentē praemeditationem & districtum conscientiae examen in memoriam venerunt, ab omnibus, qui ad annos discretionis venerunt, quotannis certo tempore in aures Sacerdotis denarrationem. 2. Quòd non solùm peccata mortalia, sed etiam circumstantias, quae peccati speciem mutant, vel illud aggravant, in confessione recensendas esse statuant. 3. quod specialem illam peccatorum enumerationem iure divino statuant esse necessariam. 4. quòd eandem statuant esse meritoriam, quâ peccatum deleri &c. existimant. Conf. plura apud B. P. Conf. Cath. l. 2 spec. part 3. p. 38. seqq. item tom. 3 LL. Th. de poen. §. 102. seqq. Dn D. Hulf. in Manuali A. C. p. 321. 331. 534. seqq. ac alios nostrates Theologos.)*

Franc. Luc. Brug. in h. l. Non praestabat Baptismus Ioh. peccatorum remissionem, sed per poenitentiam, quam testabatur, praeparabat. Iudaeorum animos, quò capaces essent illius beneficii. Contrà Luc. 3. v. 3. Iohannes erat in deserto baptizans & praedicans Baptismum poenitentiaein remissionem peccatorum, quae loquendi formula de Baptismo Apostolorum usurpatur Act. 2. v. 38.cap. 22. v. 16. Ac testatur ipse Baptista, Pharisaeos potuisse effugere iram venturam, si in vera poenitentia & fide suscepissent Baptismum à se administratum h. c. v. 7. Luc. 3. v. 7. quem quia spreverunt, ideò dicūtur consilium DEI, utiq; de salute suâ sprevisse,Luc. 7. v. 30.

## 3:7
On the sects of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and also of the Essenes, Joseph treats at length, Antiquities book 13, ch. 9, book 18, ch. 2, Jewish War book 2, ch. 7; Epiphanius, book 1 of the Panarion; Andrew Osiander in his annotations on the Harmony, book 1, ch. 13, cites such a passage out of the Talmudic book which is called ch. 2. The seven kinds of Pharisees are these. The Pharisee of Shechem. The stumbling Pharisee. The blood-shedding Pharisee. The mortar Pharisee. The Pharisee who says 'what ought I to do' and does it. The Pharisee out of love, and the Pharisee out of fear. They call him the Pharisee of Shechem because he took up his religion for the sake of some fleshly advantage, just as the Shechemites long ago sought circumcision in order to obtain marriage with Dinah, Jacob's daughter; the Stumbling One, because he kept striking his feet against stones; the Blood-Shedder, because he often dashed his head against walls or pillars until he dripped with much blood; the Mortar One, because his head was covered by a hood or cap, out of which he looked forth as out of the depths of a mortar; they call him the Pharisee who says 'What ought I to do?' and does it, because he would repeatedly utter these words out of empty glory; they call him the Pharisee out of love, because he pursued his religion out of love of reward; the Pharisee out of fear, because he had fallen into his superstition through fear of God. From this he gathers that the Pharisees were not called in Hebrew but and then in the vernacular tongue of Jerusalem from the verb which means to separate, namely because they separated themselves from other men, whose food and clothing seemed unclean to them and their life contaminated by sins, lest they be contaminated by those things which they themselves... Luke 18, v. 11.

Epiphanius, vol. 1, book 1, ch. 16. They were called Pharisees because they were separated from others on account of the voluntary superfluous religion received among them. For Phares in the Hebrew language signifies separation. Benjamin in the Itinerary. Rabbi Asher שורפה the Pharisee שרפנש who has been separated from worldly affairs, and has devoted himself day and night to books, and fasted, nor eaten meat. Whether one writes scribes with צ ןיצרפ from the verb ץרפ as Jerome does in Gen. 38, 29. or with ש ןԉשיךפ from the verb שרפ as the Hebrews do and the Syriac Testament, both verbs mean to separate and divide.

Some wish that the Pharisees were so called because they were םישרפה הרותה תא Interpreters of the Law. On this reasoning they should not have been named with the passive participle form םישורפ but with the present participle active form And the interpreters and teachers of the Law were called םישרופ. Scribes. But the Pharisees observed the law and its interpretation handed down by the Fathers through successive hands. םירפום

(Moreover, concerning the Pharisees, Essenes, and other sects of the Jews besides Josephus [Antiquities] book 18, ch. 2; Wars book 13, ch. 23 and 24; book 17, ch. 31; Bell. Jud. book 1, ch. 4; book 2, ch. 7 and 12; Sigonius On the Hebrew Republic book 5, ch. 10 and 11; Paul Tarnov on John p. 247; Calixtus in Harmony p. 94 sq.; Spanheim part 3, Doubts Concerning Gospel Matters doubt 28; Drusius On the Sects of the Jews; Scaliger in the Refutation of Nicholas Serarius' Threefold Heresy; Fuller in Miscellaneous Works book 1, ch. 3; book 2, ch. 3; book 4, ch. 3; Schindler's Lexicon p. 618, root ׳דםח; Cameron in Myrothece of the Gospels Matt. 3, 7.; Casaubon Exercises 1 against Baronius n. 8; Bertramus On Jewish Polity ch. 18; Drusius The First Commentary on New Testament Words p. 131—whom Mr. D. Quistorpius cites in Biblical Annotations on the N.T., p. 3, where he also presents the doctrines of the Pharisees briefly—they can likewise be consulted: Buxtorf, Rabbinical-Talmudic Lexicon pp. 1851 and 1852; Mr. Dilherr in the Syrian Eclogues on Matthew; Martin's Etymological Lexicon under the word Pharisee. Concerning the Sadducees specifically, Mr. Hackspan's Inaugural Oration; Matthias Martin's Etymological Lexicon under the word Sadducee; concerning the Scribes, Mr. Daniel Fessel's Sacred Disputations book 1, ch. 1, p. 16 sqq. Finally, the Syrians likewise call the Pharisees , from ; the Arabians and Ethiopians, translators of the New Testament, retained the Hebrew name; this one translates it here , that one , whence little help is to be hoped here from those said translators.)

The Sadducees were named after their teacher קורצ Antigonus of Socho, who received from Simon (who had lived at the beginning of the second temple, called ורע the Just, whom Josephus, Antiquities book 12, chapter 8, calls Jaddua) the law transmitted orally. He had two disciples, קורצ Zadok and םותיב Boethus. When they had learned from their teacher Antigonus: God is not to be served slavishly for reward (for Antigonus had handed down to them these words: Be not like servants who serve the Lord on the condition of receiving a reward, but be like servants who serve the Lord without any condition of receiving a reward, and let the fear of heaven—that is, of GOD—be upon you)—from this they drew the perverse inference that there is no resurrection of the dead, nor reward of the righteous in another life (for they said: If our fathers had known that there would be a resurrection of the dead and a giving or payment of the reward of the righteous in the world to come, they would not have taught thus.) Their disciples were called םיקורצ Sadducees and םיםותיב Boethusians. Acts 23, v. 8. The Sadducees say there is no resurrection, neither angel, nor spirit. But the Pharisees confess both. Josephus, Antiquities book 13, chapter 18: The Pharisees delivered to the people many constitutions accepted from their forefathers by tradition, which are not written among the laws of Moses, and therefore the Sadducees annul their authority, saying that only those things should be kept which are contained in writing; hence arose a great controversy between the two parties, while the wealthier side stands with the Sadducees, and the Pharisees rely on the favors of the remaining multitude. Compare the Harmony, chapter 155.

Γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν. John looks 1. to the poison of sin and wickedness in the Pharisees and Sadducees. Just as a pregnant viper is full of venom, so those men were pregnant with malice and with desire to harm. The viper is an exceedingly poisonous animal, inflicting death by a light touch. Acts 28. v. 4. 2. To their malicity handed down to them by hereditary right. They were κακοκ ῦόρακος κακὸν ὦον. In their perversity they fully requited the malice of their forefathers, hypocrites born of hypocrites, Matt. 23. v. 31. the offspring of vipers or of the serpent John 8. v. 44. 1 John 3. v. 8. But Isidore of Pelusium, Book 1, Letter 105: John called the Jews an offspring of vipers, as the broods of wicked parents being more wicked than they. You are not the offspring of the Patriarchs or Prophets, but of vipers. This he sets against their boasting about holy and distinguished ancestors. 3. To their apostasy from God their creator and father. Pliny, Book 10, chapter 62, relates that vipers are born by gnawing through their mother's womb, whence also the viper gets its name, because she brings forth violently. Hence Isidore of Pelusiot[a], Book 1, Letter 105, applies this thus to the Pharisees: They say that when this beast comes out into the light, it gnaws away its mother's womb. Since therefore they abandoned God who begot them, and extinguished all grace granted to themselves (that is, reduced to nothing) they are deservedly compared to venomous creatures, which blot out—or rather devour—the benefits received, by ingratitude. 4. To their hypocrisy. Pliny, Book 11, Natural History, chapter 37: The teeth of vipers are hidden within the gums. When this same creature is pregnant, upon striking with its teeth it pours venom into its bites. Just as vipers seem harmless, and unprepared to bite, while their teeth lie hidden within their gums, so the Pharisees seemed innocent, because their malice was stored up and concealed under hypocrisy. 5. To their slander. Just as vipers poured venom into their bites upon striking with their teeth, so those men poured out the venom of slander on others, especially on faithful teachers. 6. To their cruelty. Alonso de Castro, Book 2, Against Heresies, under the word Soul, heresy 6. They are called a brood of vipers, for the reason that just as those [vipers] are born by devouring their mothers, similarly they, after they had killed the Fathers, that is, the teachers and prophets, then by doing penance are spiritually born. Matt. 23. v. 29.

Observ. The herald of repentance does not palm off flattery on anyone, nor does he depart from the prescription of his office on account of the honors which were offered to him by the Pharisees and Sadducees. John 1. v. 19. *( Ἐναντιοφ. [Apparent contradiction]

( Ἐναντιοφ. 1. Matthew at this place writes that John the Baptist said to the Pharisees and Sadducees: Brood of vipers &c. But Luke ch. 3, 7. records that these things were said to the crowds. Ans. Some think these words were spoken on different occasions, at one time to the crowd, at another to the Pharisees and Sadducees; others say that since they were addressed to the Pharisees and Sadducees when mixed in with the crowd, because of them Luke records these words as having been said to the whole crowd. And such synecdochical modes of speech are not unusual in Holy Scripture. 2. John calls the Pharisees and Sadducees offspring of vipers. But Christ declares him liable to judgment who speaks abuse against his neighbor. Ans. This was not abuse, which is forbidden to private persons, but was an office, which befits ministers of the word, whose task it is publicly to rebuke the sins of the people. Mr. D. Walth. Harm. Bibl. p. 844.)

Τὶς ὑπέδειξεν ὐμ-ν θύγεῖν, understand underneath ὑδὸν, by what way you may flee τὴν ὐργὴν from the wrath to come, by which ματωνυμικῶς eternal punishment of hell is understood, to be inflicted out of the just anger of GOD upon those who do not repent. Ὑπὸ is placed for πρὸ who has forewarned. The compound is used for the simple ἔδειξεν. Acts 9. 16. *(The Vulgate seems to have read ἀπέδειξεν, for it rendered showed, but the former reading rests on the greater consensus of the Greek Codices, the Eastern interpreters also agreeing, the Syrian, Arabic, Ethiopian, among whom this one uses the verb -ille iste , all of which carry the meaning of showing sc. pointing out. Hence even the Latin translator of the Arabic version, which came forth at Rome from the Medicean press, seems here rather to have followed the Vulgate than to have attended to the genuine signification of the Arabic word, while he translates: showed.)*

Why do you come to Baptism, as if you too desired to become partakers of divine grace and of divine benefits, when yet you Pharisees are most wicked hypocrites, and you, Sadducees, rather Epicureans and impious men? I cannot persuade myself that you, led by true repentance, come to Baptism, since your malice and hypocrisy are innate and long-rooted in you. I cannot bring my mind to believe that it is seriously your care and concern to escape the future wrath of GOD, since all that is yours, so also this outward show of repentance, is hypocritical. Who could have persuaded you this, that you should come to receive Baptism from me, and by this means strive to escape the coming wrath, seeing you are most evil vipers, that is, dishonest men and detestable hypocrites. *(John therefore used those harsh words, not because he himself was unwilling that the Pharisees should repent, but that he might cast down their hypocrisy and pride.)*

Latin:

v. 7. De sectis Pharisaeorum & Sadducaeorum, uti etiam Essaeorum prolixè agit Iosephus lib. 13. antiq. cap. 9. lib. 18. cap. 2. lib. 2. de bell. Iud. cap. 7. Epiphanius lib. 1. Panarii. Andreas Osiander in annot. Harmon. lib. 1. cap. 13. ex libri Thalmudici, qui inscribitur cap. 2. huiusmodi citat locum. Septem sectae Pharisaeorum sunt hae. Pharisaeus Sichemitae. Pharisaeus impingens. Phaerisaeus sangvinem effundens. Pharisaeus mortariarius. Pharisaeus, quid debeo facere & faciam illud. Pharisaeus ex amore, & Pharisaeus ex timore. Pharisaeū Sichemitam vocant, quod religionem suam carnalis alicuius commodi causâ susceper āt, sicut Sichemitae olim Circumcisionem ob nuptias Dinae Iacobi filiae impetrandas; Imp-ngentem, quod pedib. subindè in lapides impingeret: sanguinem fundentem, quod caput crebrè parietibus aut columnis illideret, donec multò sanguine manaret; Mortariarium, quod capitio seu calyptrâ caput opertus esset, ex qua velut ex profundo mortario prospiceret; Pharisaeum, quid debeo facere, & faciam illud, vocant, quod haec verba inanis gloriae causâ subinde eiacularentur; Pharisaeum ex amore vocant, quod amore praemii suam religionem sectaretur; Pharisaeum ex timore, quod metuirae DEI in suam superstitionem incidisset. Ex quibus colligit, Pharisaeos Hebraice nonseddeinde vernacula Hierosolymorum linguaà verbo quod segregare significat, dictos esse, eò quod seipsos à caeteris hominibus, quorū victum & amictum immundum & vitam peccatis contaminatam videri, volebant, segrag assent, ne ab illis quoa ipsi contamiarentur.Luc. 18. v. 11.

Epiphanius tom. 1. lib. 1. cap. 16. Dicebantur Pharisaei eò quod separati essent ab aliis propter spontaneam supersluam religionem apud ipsos receptam. Phares enim Hebraicá linguá separationem significat. Beniamin in Itinerario. R. AserשורפהPharisaeusשרפנשqui fuerit separatus à negotiis mundi, & incubuerit libris diu noctu-, & ieiunaverit, nec comederit carnem. Sive scribas per צ ןיצרפ à verbo ץרפ uti facit Hieronymus in Gen. 38, 29. sive per ש ןԉשיךפ â verbo שרפ uti faciunt Hebraei & Syriacum Testam. utrumque verbum significat separare & dividere.

Quidam volunt, Pharisaeos sic dictos esse, quod fuerint,םישרפה הרותה תאInterpretes Legis. Hac ratione non םישורפ forma participii passivi vocandi fuissent, sed forma participii praesentis activi םישרופ. Sed Legis interpretes & doctores dicebantur םירפוםSerihae. Pharifaei autem observabant legem & eius expositionem à Patribus per manus traditam.

*(Caeterùm de Pharisaeis, Essaeis, aliisque Iudaeorum sectis praeter Iosephum lib. 18. A. I. c. 2. l. 13. c. 23. & 24. l. 17. c. 31. de B. I. I. 1. c. 4. l. 2. c. 7. & 12. Sigonium de Rep. Ebr. l. 5. c. 10. & 11. Paulum Tarnov. in Ioh. p. 247. Calixt. in Harm. p. 94. seq. Spanh. part. 3. Dubiorum Evangelicorum dub. 28. Drusium de sectis Iudaeorum, Scaligerum in Elench. Trihaeresii Nic. Serrarii, Fullerum in Miscell. lib. 1. c. 3. l. 2. c. 3. l. 4, c. 3. Schindl. Lex. p. 618. rad. ׳דםח Cameronem in Myroth. Ev. Matth. 3, 7. Casaub. Exerc. 1. contr. Baron. n. 8. Bertramum de Polit. Iudaic. c. 18. Drus. Comm. priore ad voces N. T. p. 131 quos B. D. Quistorpius in Annot. Bibl. in N. T. p. 3. adducit, ubi etiam dogmata Pharisaeorum compendiosè exhibet, consuli quoque possunt Buxtorff. Lex. Talmud. Rabb. p. 1851. & 1852. Dn. Dilherr. in Eclog. Syr. Matth. Martinius Lex. Etymolog. voce Pharisaeus. De Sadducaeis in specie, Dn. Hackspan. Orat. auspic. Matt. Martinius Lex. Etym. voce Sadd. de Scribis, Dn. Dan. Fesselius Advers. Sacr. l. 1. c. 1. p. 16. seqq. Syris tandem Pharisaei itidem dicuntur à Arabs & Aethiops Nov. T. Interpp. nomen Ebr. retinuerunt, vertit n. hic ille unde parum hîc à dictis Interpp. sperandum subsidii.)*

Sadducaei dicti fuerunt à praeceptore suo קורצ Antigonus Sochaeus ex Simeone (qui sub initium secundi templi vixerat, nominatus ורעiustus, quem Ioseph. lib. 12. antiq. cap. 8. vocat Iaddum) legem oretenus traditam accepit. Is duos habuit discipulos קורצ Zaddocum & םותיב Baiiethosum. Illi cùm ex praeceptore suo Antigono didicissent: Deum non esse colendum serviliter mercedis causâ (tradiderat enim illis Antigonus haec verba. Non sitis similes servis, qui serviunt Domino eâ conditione, ut accipiant mercedem: sed sit is similes servis, qui serviunt Domino sine conditione, ut mercedem accipiant, & sit timor coeli sive DEI super vos) ex eo perversè inferebant, non esse resurrectionem mortuorum, nec praemium iustorum in altera vita (dicebant enim: Si scivissent patres nostri, quod futura sit resurrectio mortuorum & donatio seu persolutio mercedis iustorum in futuro mundo, non it a docuissent.) Horum discipuli dicti fuerunt םיקורצ Sadducaei & םיםותיב Baiieth osaei. Act. 23. v. 8.Sadducaei dicuntnon esse resurrectionem, neque Angelum, neque Spiritum. Pharisaei verò utraa confitentur. Ioseph. lib. 13. antiq. cap. 18. Multas constitutiones à maiorib. permanum acceptas Pharisaei tradiderunt populo, quae non sunt scriptae inter leges Mosaicas, & ideò Sadducaei his autoritatem abrogant dicētes, oportere eas tantum servari, quae scripto continentur; ata hinc magna inter utrosa exorta controversia, dum ditiores stant à Sadduc aeorum partibus, Pharisaei caeterae multitudinis nituntur favoribus. Confer Harmon. cap. 155.

Γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν. Respicit Baptista 1. ad venenum peccati & malitiae in Pharisaeis & Sadducaeis. Sicut vipera praegnans est veneno, sic isti praegnantes erant malitiâ & nocendi cupiditate. Vipera est animal maximè venenosum, mortem levi attactu inferens. Act. 28. v. 4. 2. ad malitiam hereditario iure in eos traductam. Erant illi κακοκ ῦόρακος κακὸν ὦον. Perversitate sua maiorum malitiam ex asse referebant, hypocrytae de hypocrytis nati Matth. 23. v. 31.filii viperae seu serpentis Ioh. 8. v. 44.1. Ioh. 3. v. 8. Sed Pelus. lib. 1. Epist. 105. Viper arum progeniem Iohannes Iudaeos appellaevit, ut improborum parentum improbiores faetus. Non estis progenies Patriarcharum vel Prophetarum, sed viper arum. Hoc opponit vaena ipsorum de sanctis & illustribus maioribus gloriationi. 3. ad apostasiam â Deo creatore & patre suo. Plinius lib. 10. cap. 62. memorat, viperas nasci eroso matris ventre, unde etiam vipera dicitur, eô quod vi pariat. IlluIsidorus Pelusiota lib. 1. Epist. 105. sic applicat ad Pharisaeos. Aiunt hanc feram maternum ventrem, cùm in lucem editur, arrodere. Quoniam igitur Deum, qui eos genuit, dereliquiverunt, ata omnem sibi con-essam gratiam extinxerunt (eâ videl. in irritum redactâ) meritò proinde venenatis animantibus eos confert, per ingratitudinem accepta beneficia obliter antibus, ne dicam corrodentibus. 4. ad illorum hypocrisin. Plinius lib. 11. N. H. cap. 37. Viperae dentes gingivis conduntur. Haec eadem praegnans veneno impresso dentium repulsu virus fundit in morsus. Sicut viperae vid-ntur innoxiae, nec ad mordendum paratae, cùm dentes earum gingivis conduntur. sic Pharisaei videbantur innocentes, quia malitia eorum condebatur atque occultabatur hypocrisi. 5. ad maledicentiam. Sicut viperae impresso dentium repulsu virus fundebant in morsus: sic isti virus maledicentiae in alios, praesertim fideles doctores, fundebant. 6. ad crudelitatem. Alph. de Castro lib. 2. adv. haereses in verbo Anima haeres. 6. Progenies viperarum vocantur, eò quod sicut illae devorantes matres suas nascuntur, similiter illi, postquam Patres h. e. magistros & prophetas occiderant, tunc poenitentiam agentes spiritualiter nascuntur.Matth. 23. v. 29.

Observ. Praeco poenitentiae nemini obtrudit palpum, nec discedit ab officii praescripto, propter honores, qui ipsi à Pharisaeis & Sadducaeis offerebantur. Ioh. 1. v. 19.

*( Ἐναντιοφ. 1. Scribit Matthaeus h. l. Iohannem Baptistam ad Pharisaeos ac Sadducaeos dixisse: Progenies viper arum &c. Sed Lucas c. 3, 7. commemorat, ad turbam fuisse dicta. Resp. Quidam existimant, diversis vicibus haec verba fuisse dicta, alio tempore ad turbam, alio ad Pharisaeos & Sadducaeos; alii dicunt, quòd ad Pharisaeos ac Sadducaeos, qui cùm turbae fuerint immixti, propter hos ad totam turbam haec dicta cōmemorari à Luca. suntque huiusmodi Synecdochicae locutiones in Scr. S. non inusitatae. 2. Iohannes Pharisaeos ac Sadd. appellat genimina viperarum. At Christus eum pronunciat iudicio obnoxium, qui convitium dicit in proximum. Resp. Non erat hoc convitium, quod interdicitur privatis, sed erat officium, quod decet verbi ministros, quorum est, peccata populi publicè reprehendere. Dn. D. Walth. Harm. Bibl. p. 844.)*

Τὶς ὑπέδειξεν ὐμ-ν θύγεῖν, subintellige ὑδὸν,quâ viâ effugere possitisτὴν ὐργὴνiram venturam, per quam ματωνυμικῶς intelligitur aeternum inferni supplicium, ex iusta DEI ira impoenitentibus immittendum. Ὑπὸ ponitur pro πρὸquis praemonstravit. Compositum ponitur pro simplici ἔδειξεν.Act. 9. 16. *(Vulg. legisse videtur ἀπέδειξεν, reddidit enim demonstravit, sed prior lectio nititur maiori Codd. Graecorum consensu, adstipulantibus quoque Interpp. Orientalibus, Syro, Arabe, Aethiope, quorum hic utitur verbo -ille iste , quae omnia ostendendi s. monstrandi significationem. habent: unde etiam Interpres Latinus versionis Arabicae, quae Romae è typographiâ Medicaâ prodiit, potiùs Vulgatum sequutus hîc videtur, quàm genuinam vocis Arabicae significationem attendisse, dum vertit: demonstravit.)*

Cur acceditis ad Baptismum, ac si & ipsi desideratis participes fieri divinae gratiae ac divinorum beneficiorum, cùm tamen vos Pharisaei sitis hypocritae pessimi, vos autem, Sadducaei, Epicuraei atqui impii? Non possum mihi persuadere, vos poenitentiâ verâ ductos ad Baptismum venire, cùm vestra malitia & hypocrysis sit vobis innata atque inveterata. Non possum animum inducere, ut credā, vobis seriò curae cordi que esse, ut futuram DEI iram effugiatis, cùm ut omnia vestra, ita quoque haec poenitentiae significatio sit hypocritica. Quis potuit vobis hoc persuadere, ut ad suscipiendum à me Baptismum veniretis, & hac ratione iram futuram effugere studeretis, cùm sitis viperae pessimae h. e. homines improbi & hypocritae detestandi. *(Usus igitur Iohannes asperis istis verbis est, non quasi resipiscentiam Pharisaeorum ipse noluerit, sed ut hypocrisin eorum & fastum deprimeret.)*

## 3:8
v. 8. Ποιήσατε οὖν καρπὸν &c. ἄξιος παρὰ τὸ ἄγειν, is properly said of that which is equal in weight and moment, the metaphor being taken from the reasoning about weighing. The Syrian translates with the word from Heb. הוש, which signifies to be equal. *(The Ethiopian renders it thus: Make good fruit which becomes you penitents. But since the said Interpreter uses the singular number, just as the Arabic also does, while the Syrian employs the plural, make fruits worthy, it appears in some way that the Arabic and Ethiopic versions were not translated from the Syriac Paraphrase, nay rather that the Interpreters did not use even agreeing copies.)* Fruits worthy of repentance are works (see Act. 26, 20.) which become truly penitent ones converted to God, whom the Apostle calls fruit of the Spirit, Gal. 5. v. 22. Eph. 5. v. 9. fruit of righteousness, Phil. 1. v. 11.

The Papists labor to prove from these words their satisfactions. Answer: the Baptist requires amendment of life and newness, as appears from v. 10. sqq., The axe is laid at the root of the tree, and from Luc. 3. v. 11. where he prescribes specifically to each order what fruits they ought to produce. Those fruits are called worthy of repentance after that manner of speaking whereby the regenerate are commanded to live worthily of the Gospel Eph. 4. v. 1. worthily of the calling, Col. 1. v. 0. worthily of God, 1. Thess. 2. v. 12. that is, as becomes those who have been converted to God through the preaching of the Gospel. Chrys. on this passage: If you truly repent, as you profess before others, so live that it may appear that you have repented and hold repentance from your former life from the heart. The same: How shall we be able to make fruits worthy of repentance? Thus, if we do things contrary to our sins. Have you stolen another's goods? Begin now to give away your own. Have you committed fornication for a long time? Suspend yourself from lawful use of marriage. Have you cut anyone with injury either by deed or speech? Return words of blessing for revilings, and seek to appease him who strikes you, now with services, now with kindnesses. To this exposition of Chrysostom Erasmus appeals in his annotations, as also Franc. Luc. Brug., who comments on this passage thus: Fruits worthy of repentance are said to be those which befit repentance, or penitents, such is the sense. Bring forth fruits which it is fitting for repentance to produce, because by deeds they declare that you are truly moved by repentance for the sins you have committed. Fruits of this kind are corrected manners and all those works which proceed from a truly penitent soul.

Latin:

v. 8. Ποιήσατε οὖν καρπὸν &c. ἄξιος παρὰ τὸ ἄγειν, propriè de eo dicitur, quod aequalis est ponderis ac momenti, translatione à ratione ponderandi desumta. Syrus vertit voce ab Hebr. הוש quod significat aequale esse. *(Aethiops circumscribit h. m. Facite fructum bonumqui decet vos poenitentes. Cùm verò dictus Interpres singulari numero utatur, quemadmodum & Arabs, Syrus verò pluralē adhibeat, facite fructus dignos, patet, quodammodo, quod Arabica & Aethiopica versiones non sint translatae è Syriacâ Paraphrasi, imò quòd Interpp. ne Codd. quidem consentientib. fuerint usi.)* Fructus poenitentiâ digni funt opera (vid. Act. 26, 20.) quae decent verè poenitentes & ad Deum conversos, quos Apostolus vocat fructus Spiritus,Gal. 5. v. 22.Eph. 5. v. 9.fructus iustitiae,Phil. 1. v. 11.

Pontificii ex his verbis satisfactiones suas probare satagunt. Resp. exigit Baptista vitae emendationem ac novitatem, ut apparet ex v. 10. seq. Securis ad radicem arboris posita est, & ex Luc. 3. v. 11. ubi singulis ordinibus in specie praescribit, quos fuctus facere debeant. Fructus illi vocantur digni poenitentia eo loquendi modo, quo renati iubentur vivere Evangelio dignèEph. 4. v. 1.vocatione dignè,Col. 1. v. 0.Deo dignè,1. Thess. 2. v. 12. h. e. prout decet eos, qui ad Deum per Evangelii praedicationem sunt conversi. Chrys. in h. l. Si verè vos poen-tet, ut prae vobis fertis, sic vivite, ut appareat, vos resipuisse & ex animo pristinae vitae poenitentiae teneri. Idem: Quomodo poterimus fructus paenitentiâ dignos facere? utia si peccatis adversa faciamus. Aliena rapuisti? incipe iam donare propria. Longo es tempore fornicatus? à legitimo quoa usu suspendere coniugii. Iniuriam vel opere vel sermone cuiquā secisti? Refer benedictionis verba conviciis & percutientes te nunc officiis, nunc beneficiis placare contende. Ad hanc Chrysostomi explicationem Erasm. in annot. provocat, uti etiam Franc. Luc. Brug. qui ad h. l. sic commentatur: Fructus poenitentiâ digni dicūcur, qui deceant poenitentiam, sive poenitentes, ut sit sensus. Edite fructus, quos dignuns est poenitentiam producere, quia factis declarent, verè vos admissorum peccatorum poenitentia duci. Eiusmodi fructus sunt mores correcti ca opera omnia, quae ab animo verè poenitenti proficiscuntur.

## 3:9
v. 9. Κοα μί δόξητελέγεν. -οκείν means to persuade oneself through arrogance and haughtiness of spirit, to take pleasure in something concerning oneself, Mark 10. v. 42.Phil. 3. v. 4. Therefore the sense is: Do not please yourselves in this thought, nor impose the same upon yourselves. *(The Arabic rightly expresses the force of the word, rendering , and do not glory.)*

Πατέρα έχομεν τόν Αβραάμ. Μιμητικως records the boastful words of theirs about their descent from holy forefathers, which afterwards we read they used, John 8. v. 33. and 39. He therefore refers to that commonly circulated saying, frequent on their lips, ארהם Our father Abraham.

They appealed to the promise made by God to Abraham and to the covenant of grace entered into with him Gen. 2 v. 217. and following, chap. 26. v. 5. and persuaded themselves that by virtue of those promises the posterity of Abraham could not be rejected by God, whatever they might finally do.

-ύναται ό θεός έκ των λίρωντούτων έγείραι τέκνατω Αβραάμ. -εικτικόν τούτων is emphatic: out of those stones which here you see placed before you. *(Indeed some think, such as Jerome and Bede, that John speaks here of the Gentiles having hearts harder than stone, not of those stones which they saw on the bank of the Jordan; and there favors their opinion that in a certain old manuscript copy and in the edition of Theophylact printed at Rome it reads έκ των λιθων: But indeed the former reading is confirmed by most Greek codices, whom also the Syrian, Arabic, and Ethiopic follow. Yet we do not altogether deny that the Baptist looked even toward the conversion of the nations. Whether however John baptized and preached in that place where the Israelites under Joshua crossed the Jordan dry-footed, marvelously divided and dried up by GOD, whence in memory of so great a miracle Joshua erected twelve stones in the same place in the middle of the bed of the Jordan; and whether those stones were here designated and pointed out by John, as Remigius and Anselm judge, whom Pineda follows—let others consider. That John baptized in Bethabara, that is, in the house of crossing, namely where the Sons of Israel crossed the Jordan dry-footed, seems to favor their opinion, as indeed Cornelius à Lapide holds both here and in his Commentary on) John 1, 28.)*

The sense here is this. Although you were born according to the flesh from Abraham, nevertheless you are not sons of that Abraham to whom belongs the promise of eternal salvation, because this belongs at last to those who are spiritual sons of Abraham, who follow in the footsteps of his faith, Rom. 4. v. 12.chap. 9. v. 7. & following. Hilary on this passage: For succession of flesh is not sought, but inheritance of faith; the dignity of origin consists in examples of works, and the glory of descent is retained by imitation of faith. Nor should you think that God would be vain and false in His promise unless He fulfilled it upon you descending from Abraham through bodily succession of lineage, since there are no other sons of Abraham. For God would rather create sons for Abraham out of those stones than fail to fulfill His promise. But out of stones in this passage means the same thing as from whence it could least be hoped, because between rational man and stones there is so great a distance that not only can men not be raised up from stones by human power, but also what can be conceived by human reason cannot comprehend that sons of Abraham might be raised up from stones. Yet God, to whom nothing is άδύνατον or difficult, is able to accomplish this.

There seems to be regard had to the prophetic place Isaiah 51. v. 1. Look to the rock from which you were hewn, and to the hole of the pit from which you were dug, where Abraham and Sarah are spoken of metaphorically as rock and hole of the pit, as appears from verse 2 following, both because through Nature, barren in old age, they finally begot by divine virtue their son Isaac, and because just as very many stones arise from a quarry, so all the Israelites were propagated from those parents. The sense therefore is: That same God, who cut you down as it were from the rock when He caused Isaac, the father of your race, to be born from barren and exhausted parents, even today can raise up or awaken sons of Abraham from stones by that same power. God is able, after all of you have been destroyed, to restore the posterity of Abraham, and Himself to raise up sons from stones, just as He formed Adam from earth, Isaac from parents dead in barrenness and old age unto generation, like stones.

Yet at the same time regard is had to the calling of the Gentiles, from whom God built up for Himself a holy temple through the preaching of the Gospel and their reception into His kingdom, since they were as hard and unhewn stones; for by this calling even the nations became sons of Abraham Rom. 4. v. 11.

Clement of Alexandria, in the Exhortation to the Nations. From stones, that is, from the Gentiles, who worshipped stones and wood, and were foolish like stones.

Latin:

v. 9. Κοα μί δόξητελέγεν. -οκείν est aliquid sibi per arrogantiam, & animi elationem persua vel sibidere, de aliquo placere, Marc. 10. v. 42.Phil. 3. v. 4. Sensus igitur est. Nolite vobis in hac cogitatione placere, ac eadem vobis ipsis imponere. *(Arabs vim vocis rectè exprimit, reddens & ne gloriemini.)*

Πατέρα έχομεν τόν Αβραάμ. Μιμητικως recitat Baptista gloriabunda ipsorum de propagatione ex sanctis maioribus verba, quibus postea leguntur usi Ioh. 8. v. 33. & 39. Respicit ergo ad vulgatum illud, quod frequens in ipsorum ore ארהםAbraeham pater noster.

Provocabātad promissionem Abrahae divinitus factam & ad foedus gratiae cum ipso initum Gen. 2 v. 217. & seqq. cap. 26. v. 5. sibique persuadebant, vi illarum promissionum non posse à Deo Ahrahae posteros repudiari, quicquid tandem agant.

-ύναται ό θεός έκ των λίρωντούτων έγείραι τέκνατω Αβραάμ. -εικτικόν τούτων est emphaticum, ex illis lapidibus, quos hîc coram vobis positos cernitis. *(Existimant quidem nonnulli, ut Heronymus ac Beda, Iohannem hîc loqui de gentilibus, corda laepide duriora habentibus, non de istis, quos videbant in Iordanis ripâ, lapidibus: favetque illorum sentētiae, quòd in vetusto quodam exemplari & apud Theophylactū Romae excusum habetur έκ των λιθων: Verùm priorem lectionem confirmant Codd. Graeci plerique, quos etiam sequuntur Syrus, Arabs, Aethiops. Neque tamen penitus inficias imus, respexisse Baptistam etiam ad gentium conversionem. An verò eo loco Iohannes baptizarit & praedicarit, ubi Israelitae duce Iosua sicco pede Iordanem, miraculosè à DEO divisum & siccatum transierunt, unde in memoriam tanti miraculi Iosua eodem loco duodecim lapides erexit in medio Iordanis alveo; atque illos lapides hîc Iohannes designarit ac demonstrarit, uti Remigius & Anselmus, quos Pineda sequitur, censent, alii dispiciant. Favere illorū sententiae videtur, quòd Iohannes in Bethabara, i. e. in domo traiectus, ubi sc. Filii Israel sicco pede Iordanem transierunt, baptizarit, uti quidem statuit Corn. à Lapide tum hîc, tùm Comm. ad Ioh. 1, 28.)*

Sensus hic est. Quamvis secundum carnem orti sitis ab Abrahamo, tamen non estis illi Abrahae filii, ad quos pertinet promissio salutis aeternae, quia haec ad illos demum pertinet, qui sunt spirituales Abrahae filii, qui insistunt vestigiis fidei ipsius, Rom. 4. v. 12.cap. 9. v. 7. & seqq. Hilarius in h. l. Non enim successio carnis quaeritur, sed fidei hereditas, dignitasa originis in operum consistit exemplis & prosapiae gloria fidei imitatione retinetur. Nec est, quòd existimetis, Deum in promissione suâ fore vanum ac falsum, nisi eam in vobis carnali generis successione ex Abrahamo descendentibus impleat, cùm nulli alii sint Abrahae filii. Nam Deus potiùs ex lapidibus illis crearet Abrahamo filios, quàm ut promissionem suam non impleret. Ex lapidibus autem h. l. idem est, quod inde, unde minimê sperari poterat, quia inter hominem rationalem & lapides est tanta distantia, ut non solùm virtute humanâ non possint ex lapidibus homines excitari, sed etiam humanâ ratione comprehendi nequeat, quod ex lapidibus Abrahae filii excitari possint. Deus autem, cui nihil est άδύνατον vel difficile, hoc praestare potest.

Respectus haberi videtur ad locum propheticum Esai 51. v. 1.Respicite ad petraem, unde excisi estis, & ad cavernam putei, de qua praecisi estis, ubi Abraham & Sara metaphoricè dicuntur petra & caverna putei, ut ex v. seqq. 2. apparet, tùm, quia per Naturam steriles in senectute demum divinâ virtute filium Isaacum genuerunt, tam quia ut ex latomia lapides plurimi oriuntur, sic Israelitae omnes ab illis parentibus sunt propagati. Sensus igitur est. Idem Deus, qui ex petra quasi vos praecidit, quando ex sterilibus & effaetis parentibus Isaacum generis vestri parentem nasci fecit, adhuc hodie potest eadem virtute filios Abrahae ex lapidibus suscitare vel excitare. Potensest Deus vobis omnibus deletis posteritatem Abrahae instaurare, ipsique filios excitare ex lapidibus, quemadmodum Adamum formavit ex terra, Isaacum ex parentibus, sterilitate & senio ad generandum instar lapidum emortuis.

Simul tamen respectus habetur ad vocationem gentilium, ex quibus Deus per praedicationem Evangelii & receptionem in suum regnum templum sanctum sibi extruxit, cùm essent velut duri & impoliti lapides, per hancenim vocationem etiam gentes facti sunt Abrahae filii Rom. 4. v. 11.

Clemens Alexandrin. in exhortat. ad gentes. Ex lapidibus h. e. ex gentilibus, qui lapides & ligna adorabant, & instar lapidum insipientes erant.

## 3:10
v. 10. The conjunction Φδη δέ χαί ή άξικη πρός τήν ρίζαντων δένδρων κείται. is emphatic. After John the Baptist had removed one hindrance to repentance, namely boasting about descent from holy forebears, he now further removes another hindrance, namely the empty persuasion of deferring the punishment of wickedness to a distant time. In the Hebrew book entitled χαί there is found something similar: Just as they cut down a dry tree, which bears no fruit, useful for nothing else but fire, so is he who today learns what he learned two days ago and remains forever in one lesson. ראשת

Man is compared to a tree. 1. on account of motion. 2. on account of ornament. 3. on account of use in constructing buildings. 4. on account of fruit. 5. on account of standing. 6. on account of outcome.

Luke Bruges draws from this comparison of man with a tree free will in man in spiritual matters. Man, he says, is frequently compared to a tree: the just to a fertile one, the impious to a barren one, yet such as it has been placed in those very trees, whether fruitful of good fruits by its own goodness, or barren by its own evil, although for the latter she suffices of herself, while for the former she needs the help of grace. Answer. 1. That comparison rather proves the opposite: a tree barren by Nature cannot make itself fruitful. Now all men are barren trees by Nature. 2. That help of grace which is required gives a man spiritual powers, by which he begins to be a fruitful tree, but it finds no spiritual powers in him, since man by nature is dead to every good work.

The axe laid to the root signifies 1. the nearness of destruction and uprooting. 2. The totality of that destruction. Just as trees that have often disappointed the gardener are at last cut down root and branch when the axe is applied: so John the Baptist warns the Jewish people πανολεθρίαν that on account of their unrepentance and contempt for the Gospel there hangs over them something very imminent, Luke 13, v. 7.

In the preceding verse 8 he had compared them to trees, requiring that they bear fruits worthy of repentance; now he returns to that metaphor, teaching that those who do not bear such fruits, like barren trees, must be cut down by the axe of divine wrath and cast into the fire.

There is an emphasis in the word κείται: for it is signified that the axe of divine judgment was not merely about to be applied, but has already been applied, and indeed not to the branches, nor to the trunk, but to the very root itself, which being cut away leaves no hope of rebirth or reflowering in the tree.

Πάν ούν δένδρον. He infers this from what precedes. Because the axe is laid to the root of the trees, therefore every fruitless tree will be cut down. There is an emphasis in the particle πάν, a mark of universality. For it stands opposed to boasting of descent from holy ancestors and to the vain persuasion that either riches, or noble birth, or hypocritical holiness can preserve anyone from the impending destruction awaiting the unrepentant and unbelieving.

Μή ποιούν. He does not say, which did not make, but in the present tense, which does not make; for it is not enough to have once been a good and fruitful tree, but continuation and perseverance in good works is required. Nor does he say in the future, which shall not make, but in the present, which does not make. For neither should conversion and amendment of life toward better things be deferred, but because the axe is even now laid to the root, therefore repentance must be practiced immediately, in the present time.

Καρπόν καλόν. He does not say, which makes evil fruit, but which does not make good fruit. For certainly it is not enough to cease from doing evil: one must also do good. To do nothing good is itself to do evil.

Observation. If such great danger threatens the fruitless tree, since the axe is already laid to its root, what will become of the tree evil, which bears not merely no fruits, but even vicious ones?

The verbs of the present tense are emphatic, by which both the certainty and the nearness of the divine judgment are intimated, and therefore the wrath of GOD, i.e. the punishment to be inflicted out of just wrath and judgment, is shown not as something far off in the future, but set before our eyes as already present. Εκκόπτεται χαί είς πύρ βάλλεται.

In verse 12 he calls this fire unquenchable; therefore the fire of hell is understood. Cutting down takes place through death, casting out into the fire through being thrust down into Gehenna. For since the impenitent are barren and unfruitful trees, their only use is that, like barren trees, they should be cut down by the axe of the divine wrath and cast into the infernal fire. But the godly, as fruitful trees, are transplanted through death into the heavenly Paradise.

Juvencus, book 1, verse 337, rendered this passage thus:

Now now close upon the roots of the oak stands the sightBefore all men's eyes: axes lifted up,the barren woods shall be felled, fires will burn them.

*(Compare more sayings of the Fathers making this point in B. Par. L. de Extremo Iudic. §. 18, likewise in the Practical Aphorisms, title on the end of the world and the Last Judgment.)

Latin:

v. 10. Φδη δέ χαί ή άξικη πρός τήν ρίζαντων δένδρων κείται. Coniunctio χαί est emphatica. Postquam Baptista removerat unum poenitentiae impedimentum, videl. gloriationē de propagatione ex sanctis maioribus, iam porrò removet alterum impedimentum, videl. inanem persuasionem de differenda in longum tempus impietatis poena. In libro Hebraico, cui titulus ראשתprincipium breve sapientiae, habetur hoc simile. Sicut arborem aridam, quae non fert fructum, excindunt, ad nullam aliam rem utilem quàm ad ignem, talis est qui hodie discit, quod nudius tertius didicit & semper manet in lectione una.

Homo comparatur arbori. 1. ratione motus. 2. ratione ornatus. 3. ratione usus in extruendis aedificiis. 4. ratione fructus. 5. ratione status. 6. ratione eventus.

Luc. Brug. ex hac comparatione hominis cum arbore colligit liberum hominis arbitrium in spiritualibus. Homo, inquit, frequenter comparatur arbori: iustus fertili, impius sterili, sed in quae ipsa situm sit, sive foecundam esse bonorum fructuum suo bono, sive sterilem suo malo, quanquam ad hoc per se ipsa sufficiat, ad illud opus habeat gratiae auxilio. Resp. 1. comparatio illa contrarium potiùs probat: arbor per Naturam sterilis non potest seipsam reddere frugiferam. Iam verò per Naturam omnes homines sunt steriles arbores. 2. auxilium illud gratiae, quod requiritur, confert homini vires spirituais, per quas incipit esse arbor frugifera, nullas autem in homine invenit vires spirituales, cùm homo per naturam ad omne opus bonum sit emortuus.

Securis ad radicem posita notat 1. excidii & eradicationis propinquitatem. 2. eiusdem excidii totalitatem. Sicut arbores hortulani spem saepiùs frustratae tandem securi admotâ radicitus excinduntur: sic monet Ioh. Baptista, Iudaicae genti πανολεθρίαν propter impoenitentiam & contemtum Evangelii proximè imminere, Luc. 13. v. 7.

In v. praeced. 8. arboribus eos comparaverat, requirens, ut ferrent fructus poenitentiâ dignos, iam redit ad illam metaphoram, docens eos, qui non ferunt eius modi fructus, instar arborum infrugiferarum securi irae divinae esse exindēdos & in ignem abiiciēdos.

In verbo κείται est emphasis: significatur enim, securim divini iudicii non esse demum admovendam, sed iamdum admotam, & quidem non ramis, non trunco, sed ipsi radici, quâ excisâ nulla spes renascentiae ac reflorescentiae in arbore.

Πάν ούν δένδρον. Infert hoc ex prioribus. Quia securis ad radicem arborum posita, ideò omnis arbor infrugifera excidetur. Emphasis est in particula πάν universalitatis nota. Opponitur enim gloriationi de nativitate ex sanctis maioribus & inani persuasione, quòd vel divitiae, vel generis nobilitas vel hypocritica sanctitas, ab imminente impoenitentibus & incredulis excidio praeservare aliquem possint.

Μή ποιούν. Non dicit, quae non fecit, sed in praesenti, quae non facit, neque enim sufficit olim fuisse arborem bonam & frugiferam, sed requiritur continuatio & perseverantia operis boni. Nec dicit in futuro, quae non facie, sed in praesente, quae non facit. Neque enim conversio & vitae in melius emendatio differenda, sed quia securis iamdum ad radicem posita, ideò in praesenti statim tempore poenitentia agenda.

Καρπόν καλόν. Non dicit, quae facit fructum malum, sed quae non facit fructum bonum. Neque emin sufficit cessare à malo: sed oportet etiam facere bonum. Nihil boni facere hoc ipsum est male facere.

Observ. Si tantum periculum imminet arbori infrugiferae, quod securis iamdum ad eius radicem posita, quid fiet de arbore mala, quae non solùm nullos, sed etiam vitiosos fert fructus.

Εκκόπτεται χαί είς πύρ βάλλεται. Verba praesentis temporis sunt emphatica, quibus & certitudo & propinquitas divini iudicii insinuatur, adeoque DEI ira i. e. poena ex iusta ira & iudicio irroganda non tanquam procul futura demonstratur, sed veluti iam praesens oculis subiicitur.

Ignem hunc v 12. vocat inextinguibilem, intelligitur ergo inferni ignis. Excisio fit per mortem, abiectio in ignem per detrusionem in gehennam. Cùm enim impoenitentes sint arbores steriles & infrugiferae, ideò nullus eorum est usus alius, quàm ut instar arborum sterilium securi divinae irae abscindantur & in ignem infernalem abiiciantur. Pii verò ut arbores frugiferae per mortem in Paradisum coelestem transplantantur.

Iuvencus lib. 1. v. 337. locum hunc sic reddidit.

Proxima roboreis iamiam radicibus instatCunct orum ante oculos acies sublata securisCaedentur sylvae steriles, ignema fovebunt.

*(Conf. plures Patrum sententias hâc facientes apud B. Par. L. de Extremo Iudic. §. 18. it. in Aphorismis Pract. tit. finis mundi, & supremum Iudicium.)

## 3:11
verse 11. Εω μέν βαπτιζω ύμάς ή ύδατνεις μετάνοιαν. From Luke chapter 3 verse 15 it is established that John uttered these words on this occasion, because everyone had begun to think that he himself was the Christ; and with these very words he removes that false opinion conceived about him, and teaches that he is not the Christ himself, but the forerunner of Christ.

Luke, Bruges edition, thus παροφρόζει. I baptize you with water alone, naked water, which has no efficacy for renewing souls. Compare Bellarmine, book On Baptism, chapter 23. *(Cornelius à Lapide also decides the same in his Commentary on this passage, p. 88, where he explains the words unto repentance thus: so that stir you up to doing penance by your washing of body, prepare yourselves for receiving the cleansing of the soul in the baptism of Christ. Therefore the baptism of John was a profession of repentance. Hence those baptized in it were made aware of their own sins, but there was not forgiveness of guilt. Many other Papists explain similarly, such as Tirinus on this passage, Lorinus on chapters 1 and 5 of Acts, Barradius vol. 2, Commentaries on the Councils, Evangelical part, p. 20.) *But 1 the exclusive particle is not added here. 2 Nor can it be gathered from the contrast, as is shown shortly afterwards. 3 John expressly adds, I baptize unto repentance. Therefore certainly the baptism of John was not devoid of all spiritual efficacy. For where true repentance is, there faith also is; where faith is, there is remission of sins, whence Luke 3. v. 3. this is expressly added. John was in the desert baptizing and preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. Brugensis objects, -n repentance to be nothing else than unto the confession of sins and the profession of repentance. But more things are comprehended by this phrase, as the passage just cited Luke 3. v. 3. shows, together with a comparison with the parallel passages Acts 2. v. 38. chapt. 22. v. 16. where the Holy Spirit uses the same phrase concerning the Baptism of the Apostles. It is established from the preceding v. 7. that the Pharisees could escape through John's Baptism, received in true repentance and faith, the coming wrath of GOD; therefore truly penitents baptized by Joh., having believed in Christ, received the remission of sins and the other heavenly goods promised in the Gospel. Brugensis himself, in his annotations on v. 15. sqq., reports among the causes of the Baptism undergone by Christ also this one, that he might invite all men to the Baptism which he had determined to institute, itself in form nothing unlike [the Baptism] of Joh. Yet if the Baptism of Christ was in form nothing unlike the Baptism of Joh., surely also in respect of efficacy it was not wholly different in kind.

Ο δέ ὀπίσω μου έρχόμενος. He speaks of a present thing, nor does he mark one about to come, but him who already is on the way, and hence near; whence he also says όπίσω μου, not μετ έμέ after me, so as to signify that Christ was now imminent behind [my back]. The Greek participle έρχόμεν ος is of the voice of the present tense, but of meaning ambiguous between present and future. To this place the present time suits better: for it is signified that Christ is on the way, and thus near.

Ἰσχυρότερός μουέςιν, as in time and order of preaching I am later, so in power he is prior by infinite degrees.

ού ούκ έιμί ίκανός τά ύποδήματα βαστάσαι ικανός properly means sufficient, the Vulgate rendered rightly according to sense, worthy.

ά ύποδήματα the Vulgate rendered shoes/calceamenta, but it properly signifies sandals/soleas, so called because bound under the soles of the feet. Matt. 10. v. 10. Mark 6. v. 9. To carry sandals is a proverbial manner of speaking, used Psalm 60, v. 10. whereby the most lowly ministry is signified, arising, as some will have it, from the custom of the Jews, who when about to enter some holier place were accustomed to take off their shoes and hand them over to be carried by a servant, and to wash the feet of arriving guests.

*(See Sanctius on chapt. 13 Acts p. 267, likewise on chapt. 1 Song p. 74, where he also proves the custom of the Romans, by which those about to recline at table were accustomed to remove their sandals, out of Horace and Martial. Thomas Gataker also treats of the same custom at length in Cinn. p. 378. 379. & 380.) *The sense therefore is, I judge myself unworthy even to claim for myself the lowest and filthiest part of his ministry. No part of the ministry is lower than to clean someone's shoes, to unfasten and carry the same, should the Lord wish either to change them or lay them aside on account of a holy place.

Αυτός ίμάς βαπτισειη πνέυματι άγίω χαί πυρί. Βαπτισει. He will pour out upon you abundantly and copiously the Holy Spirit. Chrysost. The very metaphor of addition expresses the largeness of grace. Furthermore, Erasmus m--et, that the word fire is not found in the Greek exemplars: *(The same is also noted by Beza, namely that it is missing in some ancient codices. Thus also the most ancient Greek manuscript Eclogae, which are held in the Nuremberg Library, do not acknowledge it. Hugo Grotius suspects that the little word πυρί in this place gave the cause to bolder scribes to teach that most ancient custom, by which some used burning alongside Baptism. That custom, namely of marking the newly baptized with a cautery, is still observed among the Ethiopians, authors note everywhere, and an example also was provided to me seven years ago by a certain nobleman, an Abyssinian Priest, who had traveled for the sake of religion to Jerusalem, and from there to Rome, but led by the fame of the most pious Prince, Lord Ernest, Duke of Saxony &c. had gone to Gotha, with whom also by the most clement command of the praised Prince I conversed familiarly for several weeks in the Gotha court: in him, however, that sign impressed on the face with a glowing iron could still be seen. Moreover, against the error of Seleucus and Hermias, who because of these words of the Evangelist taught that Baptism ought to be performed in fire, Felicianus Capitonus, Archbishop of Avignon, argues at length in Expl. Cath. part. Sec.)* Meanwhile, not only from the Latins Hilary and Jerome, but also from the Greeks Chrysostom in this place and Cyril in his book on the true faith read it, and parallel passages* (especially Luke 3:16, where Beza testifies that it is read by the highest consensus of all codices. The already cited manuscript Eclogae agree)* testify that it is entirely to be read. *(And they also confirm this reading -nterpret. Oriental. Syrian, Arabic, Ethiopian. But which Ethiopian Interpreters Cornelius à Lapide understands, when he writes about them, that they receive the Holy Spirit through fire in this place, I confess that I do not grasp. If he understands the Ethiopian Interpreter of the N.T., it can no more be asserted of him than of the Syrian or Arab, since he translates in this place i.e. & he himself will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.)*

What is to be understood by the name fire varies among the opinions of the Interpreters. 1. Hilary, canon 3 on Matthew, expounds it of the fire of the last judgment, by which those who are already baptized with the Holy Spirit shall at some time be consumed.

2. Chrysostom, homily 3 of the imperfect work, understands the fire of tribulation.

3. The Papists * (as Suarez alleges, Cornelius in this place)* άτερ γροφής understand it of the fire of purgatory. But Bellarmine himself, book On Baptism, chapter 2, does not press this exposition, but speaks alternatively. By fire, he says, either the fiery tongues are meant, in which the Holy Spirit appeared over the Apostles on the day of Pentecost, or the fire of purgatory, or the fire of divine judgment, or the fire of tribulation. *(Cornelius à Lapide abandons this exposition no less than the others already mentioned, and says that properly with the Holy Spirit and fire is here expounded as fiery and igniting Spirit. With the Holy Spirit, who is fire, that is, who is like fire and almost fire, burns and kindles. And so also other Papist Interpreters feel quite commonly. That however this passage is taken neither by the Fathers nor by the sounder Papists themselves of purgatory, B. Par., t. 8, LL. Th., §. 275, shows.)*

4. Some, taking the name fire effectively and μεταφορικως, understand the fiery power of the Holy Spirit and effectual, so that the sense is: he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire, that is, with the Holy Spirit, enlightening and inflaming the hearts of men, and therefore making them fiery. Beza in this place: The name fire seems to be opposed to water, so that they may know that a certain fiery and spiritual power for our illumination and purification through the water of Baptism—the element, namely, most fit for washing away filth—is represented most effectually. Tossanus in this place: by fire is understood the virtue of the Holy Spirit, illumining, kindling, and purifying the heart. To this they accommodate the rule: When two nouns are joined, one takes the place of an adjective, which figure they call hendiadys. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire, that is,

with kindling spirit, acting effectually in the manner of fire and inflaming the hearts.

5. It is established most simply that in this other member of the antithesis there is to be described not, as in the former, the baptism of water, but the baptism of fire, i.e., the visible outpouring of the Holy Spirit made in the form of tongues of fire on the day of Pentecost, so that the sense is: He will baptize some of you with the Holy Ghost inwardly, and with fire by his external symbol outwardly.Act. 2. v. 3.

For α the word of the future tense is used βαπτίσει. If John the Baptist were speaking about the common gifts of the Holy Spirit, which they call sanctifying, he ought to have spoken in the present tense, he himself baptizes you with the Holy Spirit. And even if those of the Papacy wish very much to raise doubt concerning the baptism of John, whether through him the sanctifying gifts of the Holy Spirit were bestowed, yet they cannot deny that John and the disciples of Christ baptized at the same time Ioh. 4. v. 1. therefore at least through the baptism of the apostles those common and sanctifying gifts of the Holy Spirit were bestowed, with respect to which John certainly ought to have said, he himself baptizes you with the Holy Spirit. *(Indeed the Syriac Interpreter reads thus, translating i.e., baptizing: But more correctly the Arabic and Ethiopic versions, following older and better Greek codices (whose reading is also confirmed by the Greek MS Excerpts in the Nuremberg Library), render it in the future tense. For the Ethiopic expressly has i.e., he shall baptize you. Similarly also the Arabic )*

β. One must not depart from the property of the letter without urgent cause. Now the word fire, taken properly, refers us to the external symbol of fire, in which the Holy Spirit was visibly and miraculously poured out upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost.

γ. Christ himself clearly confirms this explanation. For when he was just about to ascend into heaven and commanded the disciples not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the promise of the Father,Act. 1. v. 14. he adds άιτιολογικως, because John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit, not many days after this. v. 5.

δ. Peter Act. 11. v. 16. applies those words expressly to the visible and miraculous outpouring of the Holy Spirit, that is, to the baptism of fire.

The Lyon Greek exemplar in the Concordance refers us to the margin for the comparison of these passages. Mark 1. v. 8.Luke 3. v. 16.John 1. v. 26.Acts 1. v. 5.ch. 11. v. 16. * (So also the Jesuit Tirinus did. And likewise Beza in the margin, which however you would rightly wonder at, since here he writes the same thing in his notes: this passage is badly applied to tongues of fire, which settled upon the Apostles on the day of Pentecost, whereas this place concerns inner baptism, common to all the elect, not about particular grace joined with the apostolic office. But also Cornelius à Lapide, Commentary on Acts ch. 1 v. 5, treating of the visible outpouring of the Holy Spirit, writes: This is what St John the Baptist himself answered to the Jews when they asked him about his baptism: I indeed etc.Matt. 3, 11. Johannes Lorinus too, fellow-member of Cornelius's society [the Jesuits], writes clearly that ChristActs 1, 5.alludes to John, who said that Christ's baptism would be in the Holy Spirit and in fire, understanding both the Sacrament of Christ's baptism and the giving of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost under the external form of fire. And he brings forward for this matter the above-named Jesuit's authorities Cyril of Alexandria, Damascus, Chrysostom, Euthymius, Lyra, and also Jerome and Bede. That Jerome, Theophylactus, and Euthymius explain the Holy Spirit descending fiery from heaven upon the disciples on the day of Pentecost was noted by Barradius as well. Since these things are so, it is astonishing that the Jesuit Hager, who elsewhere otherwise claims to yield very much to the Fathers, seems willing to write without blushing that some dream that the saying here (Matt. 3, 11.) concerns the sending of the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost. p. 172. Comparison of the Augustana Confession and the Council of Trent with the word of GOD. Joh. Cameron in Myroth. Evang., arguing for this opinion—that John looks toward the outpouring of the Holy Spirit made on the day of Pentecost—presses this point: that John did not say πυρί χαί πνέυματι, how he ought to have spoken if he had wished this, Christ will baptize you with the Spirit, which is as it were a certain spiritual fire; just asJohn 3, 5.it is said ύδατος χαί πνέυμωτος: But πνέυματιχαί πυρί. Which can be observed against Beza. Let there also be added Lud. Capell. in Spicilegio, p. 9, and Grotius on this place.) ε.

Jerome on this place likewise understands it concerning tongues of fire seen upon the Apostles on the day of Pentecost. ζ.

Franc. Lucas Brugensis on this place: This promise of the Baptist looks first to the visible pouring forth of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles and those who were with them on the very day of Pentecost, then afterward upon many more believers; for the Savior himself, while promising this, alluding to these very words of John saysActs 1. v. 5.John indeed baptized you with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not after many days hence.

Brugensis indeed subjoins, that this promise also secondly looks to the invisible bestowal of the Holy Spirit, since therefore at times Christ gave the Holy Spirit visibly so that he might make men certain concerning the invisible bestowal through the Sacraments. But reply. 1. Although we judge that the words of John should be taken properly and most fittingly of the visible outpouring of the Holy Spirit, nevertheless we do not simply reject it if anyone judges that John wished to distinguish between the external ministry, which he attributes to himself, and the inner efficacy of Baptism, which he transfers to Christ. John 1. v. 23. 1. Cor. 3. v. 6. 2. Nor does he speak only about the future, he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire, but says even in the present tense, John 1. v. 33. This is he who baptizes with the Holy Ghost. 3. From this it cannot be inferred that the baptism of John was devoid of all spiritual efficacy, because it is one thing for the external ministry of John to be distinguished from the inner efficacy of Baptism, another for that efficacy to be utterly separated from the ministry of John.

Latin:

v. 11. Εω μέν βαπτιζω ύμάς ή ύδατνεις μετάνοιαν. Ex Luca constat cap. 3. v. 15. haec verba eâ occasione â Iohanne esse prolata, quòd omnes cogitare coeperant, ipsum esse Christum, quam falsam de se conceptam opinionem verbis hisce à se removet, ac se non ipsum Christum, sed Christi praecursorem esse docet.

Luc. Brug. sic παροφρόζει.Baptizo vos solâ, nudâa aquâ, quae adrenovandos animos nullius est efficacitatis. Conf. Bellarm. libro de Bapt. cap. 23. *(Idem quoque statuit Corn. à Lap. in Comm. ad h. l. p. 88. ubi verba in poenitentiam ita exponit, ut s-il. excitem vos ad agendam poenitentiam vosa abluendo corpore, praeparem ad ablutionem animae recipiendam in Baptismo Christi. Bapt. ergò Iohannis erat professio oenitentiae. Unde baptizandiin eo conficebantur sua pecc-ta, non autem erat condonatio culpae. Similiter explicant Pontificii alii plurimi, uti Tirinus in h. l. Lorinus in c. 1, 5. Actorum, Barrad. t 2. Com. in Conc. Ev. p. 20.) *Atqui 1 exclusiva non additur. 2. nec potest colligi ex oppositione, ut paulò pòst ostenditur. 3. Iohannes disertè addit, se baptizare ad poenitentiam. Utique ergo Baptismus Iohannis non fuit omni efficacia spirituali destitutus. Ubi enim vera poenitentia, ibi etiam fides; ubi fides, ibi remissio peccatorum, unde Luc. 3. v. 3. disertè ea additur. Iohannes erat in deserto baptizans & praedicans Baptismum poenitentiae in remissionem peccatorum. Excipit Brugensis, -n poenitentiam nihil aliud esse, quam in peccatorum confessionem & poenitentiae professionem. Sed plura hac phrasi comprehendi, ostendit locus modò adductus Luc. 3. v. 3. ac collatio cum locis parallelis Act. 2. v. 38.cap. 22. v. 16. ubi Spir. S. de Apostolorum Baptismo eâdem phrasi utitur. Constat ex praeced. v. 7. Pharisaeos potuisse per Baptismum Iohannis, in verâ poenitentiâ & fide susceptum, effugere venturam DEI iram, utique ergo verè poenitentes à Ioh. baptizati fide in Christum acceperunt remissionem peccatorum & reliqua bona coelestia, in Evangelio promissa. Ipse Brugensis in annot. ad v. 15. seq. inter causas suscepti à Christo Baptismi etiam hanc refert, ut ad Baptismum, quem ipse à Ioh. Baptismo formâ nihil dissimilem, instituere decrever at, omnes invitaret. ## 3:12
v. 12. ού τό πτύον έν τή χειρί άυτού. Thus far John had invited his hearers by kindly promises to receive Christ; now he frightens them with the threat of judgment. Πτύον here means not fan among the Greeks λίκνος. but shovel, just as they too rendered this place: Tertullian, book On Flight, Cyprian, Letter 51, Augustine on Psalm 92. It is called πτύον from πτύειν, because it spits out, as it were, what things are useless.

By this πτύον are understood those means by which Christ separates believers and the godly from hypocrites and the impious, which are threefold: the preaching of the Gospel, the cross, the last judgment. But chiefly treated here is the final and universal winnowing and separation of chaff from wheat, which will follow on the day of judgment, as is evident from what follows. Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, Letter 65 understands by the word threshing floor the Church spread over the whole world, into which he gathers the entire harvest of human nature. And by the term fan he calls the righteous judgment, which, distinguishing and defining the rank of him who is fit for it, consigns to flames certainly the chaffy, so to speak, and unstable men, who are tossed hither and thither by every wind of sin; while those who abounded in purity of works and fruits of repentance the righteous judge says are gathered into the barn, that is, a dwelling suited to the pious deserving laborers, like farmers. *(Observation: The Church is compared here to a threshing floor, in which both wheat and chaff are stored up: but in the last judgment the floor will be thoroughly cleansed, the wheat being gathered into the heavenly barn, but the chaff burned with unquenchable fire. Augustine, tractate 6 on John: We confess that there are both good and evil in the Catholic Church, but as chaff and grains. This is to be noted against the Audians, Novatians, Donatists, and Anabaptists, concerning whom see Blessed Paul, Book on the Church, §. 49.)*

ού τό πτόον έν τή χειρί άυτού. This is a Hebraism, whereby the relative pronoun is placed twice. (The Syrian and Ethiopian imitate the Hebrew in this, but the Arabic translates simply: 'and in his hand [there shall be] a winnowing fork.') The sense is: the winnowing fork [shall be] in whose hand. The nearness of judgment is signified; for when the farmer has taken up the fork openly in his hand, the separation of chaff from wheat is at hand.

ακαθαρέι he will thoroughly purge, that is, he will cleanse wholly, fully, and perfectly; for such is the force of the preposition διά. So also κατακάυσει will burn up, will consume entirely to nothing. By floor μετωνομικως is understood what lies on the floor.

The godly are compared to wheat 1. because they are small in humility. 2. white in sincerity of soul. 3. fruitful in virtues. 4. firm in piety. 5. weighty in constancy and perseverance. The ungodly are compared to chaff. 1. on account of their lightness and inconstancy. 2. on account of barrenness in good works. 3. because finally they will be fuel for eternal fire. They are easily carried off by winds of evil desires, they are empty of virtues, they possess a bare appearance of piety, they spring from the same root from which the wheat springs, they lie upon the same threshing-floor of the Church.

Ασβεςος is that fire which not only is not extinguished—since it needs no fuels for preserving itself—but even never extinguishes those whom it burns. Therefore άσβεςος is both in itself and in those whom it torments. (Parallel passages concerning the eternal punishments of the wicked and demons against the Socinian Photinus, who attempts on p. 414 to weaken the emphasis of this word against Dr. Franzius, writing: 'unquenchable' can mean perishable, just as also the fire by which Sodom was burned down is called eternal, although today there is none of it, since indeed it brought everlasting destruction upon that city.) In what follows these may be observed: Is. 66, 24.Matt. 25, 46.Luke 9, 44. 45. 46.Rev. c. 9, 6.14, 11.c. 20, 10. Moreover Cornelius warns

à Lapide on this passage. To condemn here the error of Origen, who thought that the punishments of hell would not be everlasting, but would come to an end after Plato's great year. But besides the fact that several persons wish Origen to be immune from this error, bringing forward not a few testimonies taken from Origen himself against it — see Jacobus Merlinus in his Apology for Origen, and Sixtus Senensis, book 5 of the Bibliotheca, p. 377 — let the Jesuit take heed lest the Roman Pontiff himself too be dragged along into partnership in the error. For it is handed down not only by Damascenus, but also in Bridget's Revelations (which, by the testimony of Possevinus himself in Apparatus, tome 1, letter S., Johannes de Turrecremata Cardinal and other learned men before him, more than two hundred years ago, approved and spread abroad with public authority, after a diligent examination had first been made; and the Jesuit Tirinus seconds this, writing expressly that those revelations written down by Card. de Turrecremata are of great authority among the learned), concerning Gregory, Pope of Rome, that by his prayers he delivered the Emperor Trajan, a heathen who had died nearly five hundred years before his own time, from the punishments of hell. Yet however much Cornelius himself may write in his Commentary on chapter 17 of Luke, p. 203, that that story is thought fabulous by Baronius, Bellarmine, and others, still it is well known that Alphonsus Ciaconus, a Dominican monk, with the leave and authority of the Pope, published an Apology in defense of that history. To this is added the fact that neither the jests of Damascenus nor of Bridget were ever entered in the Pontifical Indexes of Expurgated Books.)*

But ponder and shudder at this fire, which no floods, no tears, no prayers, no powers either of men or of devils can extinguish.
