## 3:13
v. 13. Mark Christ's humility. He did not send for John to come to Him, as a Lord sends for His minister, but He Himself went to him.

Various causes are enumerated as to why Christ should have willed to receive Baptism, seeing that He had need neither of penitence nor of remission of sins. He sets forth the chief cause Himself, when in v. 15 He says to John: Thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness; to this righteousness belongs also the sanctification of the Sacraments, inasmuch as they are the means through which righteousness, won by Christ's Passion and death, is applied to us. The chief cause therefore of the Baptism received by Christ is the consecration of the waters unto saving Baptism and the sanctifying of our Baptism. Chrysostom on chap. 3 of Matthew: He deigned to be baptized, that He alone might sanctify the waters of Baptism, for the washing away of the sins of believers. Never for how could the waters of Baptism have cleansed the sins of believers, unless they had been sanctified by the touch of the Lord's body? The Author of the Sermon on the Baptism of Christ found among Cyprian's writings: Christ came to Baptism, not because He needed the washing, wherein there was no sin, but that by the Sacrament everlasting authority might be bestowed upon it.

The second principal cause is the washing away of our sins. The Son of GOD, bearing the person of all of us as Mediator, came to Baptism as a lamb laden with the sins of the whole world John 1, 29. about to cast all our sins laid upon him into the Jordan, indeed into the depth of the sea, Micah 7 19. Justin in his Dialogue with Trypho, p. 246. We hold it certain that he did not come to the river because he needed either the washing of Baptism or the coming of the Spirit in the form of a dove, just as he endured being born and circumcised and crucified not out of any need of such functions, but for the sake of the human race, which through Adam had fallen into death and the deceit of the serpent's seduction—to say nothing meanwhile of his own fault toward himself acting wickedly of anyone. Ambrose on chapter 3 of Luke: He was baptized so that, though needing no purification, by purifying himself for us he might in one moment in one body abolish the deceit of the ancient error, pour forth the grace of the heavenly kingdom, and, sinking down alone, wash all. Sedulius, book 2, On Christ:

In himself he washes all the contaminations of our life; Having nothing himself that could be lost, holy, By his body he cleansed the flowing waters, blessed The streams of the deep, and healed the rivers with his own limbs.

Damascene, book 4 of the Orthodoxy of Faith, chapter 10: Christ was immersed so that he might crush the heads of Dragons in the water, bury sin, and entomb the entire old man Adam in the water. * (Nazianzen, Oration on the Holy Lights: John baptizes and Jesus comes forward, sanctifying even the one who baptizes, yet chiefly so that he might also bury the old Adam in the waters. And shortly after: Jesus ascends from the water, in a way drawing up and raising with him the world sunk below. *) Several secondary causes can be listed. 1. the prefiguration of our renewal and deliverance from the calamities of the waters. 2. the demonstration of his union with the Church. 3. the commendation of humility and of the use of the Sacraments. Augustine, Letter 57: He was baptized so that by his humility he might more highly commend the Sacrament of our regeneration. Pantaleon, sermon on the Holy Lights, tome 1, Orthodoxographa, p. 396: He submits himself to the use of Baptism, since he himself is the Baptism of the one baptizing. Arator, book 2.

—— He gives form to all, so that they run to him from the pious fountain; let mortal kind not forsake the sacred wave any further than the Lord had deemed worthy with his pure body.

4. initiation into the most holy Ministry. John 1. v. 31. 5. the fulfillment of types gone before in the supreme Priest of the O. T. Compare article on Baptism §. 178. & following.

Latin:

v. 13. Observa Christi humilitatem. Non accersit ad se Iohannem, tanquam Dominus ministrum, sed ipse ad eum venit.

Causae, ob quas Christus Baptismum suscipere voluerit, cùm tamen nec poenitentiâ, nec remissione peccatorum opus haberet, variae recensentur. Principalem exponit ipse Christus, quando v. 15. ad Iohannem dicit. Sic nos decet implere omnem iustitiam, ad hanc iustitiam pertinet etiam Sacramentorum sanctificatio, quippe quae sunt media, per quae iustitia, Christi passione & morte parta, nobis applicatur: Principalis ergo suscepti à Christo Baptismi causa est aquarum in salutarem Baptismum consecratio & nostri Baptismi sanctificatio. Chrysost. incap. 3. Matth. Baptizari dignatus est, ut aqu-s Baptismi solus sanctificaret, ad diluenda peccata credentium. Nunquam quam enim aquae Baptismi eredentium peccata purgare potuissent, nisi tactu Dominici corporis fuissent sanctificatae. Autor sermonis de Bapt. Christi apud Cyprianum. Veniebat Christus ad Baptismum, non egens lavacro, in quo peccatum non erat, sedut Sacramento perennis daretur autoritas.

Altera principalis causa est peccatorum nostrorum ablutio. Filius DEI nostrum omnium personam ut Mediator sustinens, ut agnus onustum totius mundi peccatis venit ad Baptismum Ioh. 1, 29. proiecturus omnia nostra peccata sibi imposita in Iordanem, imò in profundum maris, Mich. 7 19. Iustinus in Dial. cum Tryphone. p. 246. Ad amnem eum non ideò venisse pro comperto habemus, quòd vel Baptismi lavatione, vel Spiritus, in specie columbae, adventu opus ei fuerit, sicut nec nasci & circumcidi & crucifigi propter functionis huiusmodi indigentiam sustinuit, sed humani generis causâ, quod per Adam in mortem & fraudem seductionema serpentis conciderat, ut interim propriam pro se malignè agentis cuiusa culpam taceam. Ambrosius in cap. 3 Luc. Baptizatus est, ut purificans se pro nobis, qui purificatione non egebat, uno momento in uno corpore fraudem vetusti erroris aboleret, gratiam regni coelestis effunderet, unusa mersus lavaret omnes. Sedulius lib. 2. de Christo.

In se cuncta lavat nostrae contagia vitae;Ipse nihil, quod perdat, habens, sanctoliquentesCorpore mundavit latices, lymphasbeavitGurgitis & propriis sanavit flumina membris.

Damasc. lib. 4. orth. fid. cap. 10. Tinctus est Christus, ut capita Draconum in aqua contereret, ut peccatum obrueret, ac totum veterem hominem Adamum in aqua sepeliret. *(Nazianz Orat. in sanct. lumin. Iohannes baptizat & accedit Iesus, sanctificans quidem & ipsum, qui baptizat, praecipuè tamen, ut & veterem Adam sepeliat in aquis. & paulo post: Adscendit Iesus de aqua, secum quodammodò demersumeducens & elevans mundum. *) Secundariae causae plures recenseri possunt. 1. renovationis nostrae & liberationis ex aquis calamitatum praefiguratio. 2. sua cum Ecclesia coniunctionis demonstratio. 3. humilitatis & usus Sacramentorum commendatio. August. Epist. 57. Baptizatus est, ut nostrae regenerationis Sacramentum suâ humilitate altius commendaret. Pantaleon serm. de sanct. lumin. tom. 1. Orthodoxogr. p. 396. Baptismi se usui submittit, cùm ipse sit baptizantis Baptisma. Arator lib. 2.

—— Formam facit omnibus ad seCurrere fonte pio, sacram ne deserat undamUlterius mortale genus, quam corpore mundoEt Dominus dignatus erat.

4. adsacrosanctum Ministerium initiatio.Ioh. 1. v. 31. 5. typi in summo V. T. Sacerdote antegressi adimpletio. Confer. artic. de Bapt. §. 178. & seqq.

## 3:14
v. 14. Ο δέ Ιωάννης διεκωλυεν άυτόν. -ιακωλύειν means obstinately to forbid, to persist in the undertaking of forbidding. But it is gathered from this prohibition that John even then began to recognize Christ. Therefore what is called John 1. v. 33. the sign given to him of the descending Holy Spirit, by which he might recognize Christ, must not be understood of the first degree of recognition, but of the confirmation of knowledge. *(The same reconciliation by the distinction between the beginning of cognition and its confirmation Mr. D. Walther also approves in Harm. Bibl. page 732, where he also lists several others.)

έγω χςείαν έχω ύπό σου βαπτισθῆναι. He acknowledges that he needs Christ's Baptism, i.e., that it is necessary for himself, that he be cleansed from sins by the blood and Spirit of Christ. Indeed, in the womb he was filled with the Holy Spirit; meanwhile, however, because of the inherent weaknesses of sin, he acknowledges that he still has need of daily cleansing through Christ.

* (Cornelius à Lapide annotates thus on this passage: It is unbecoming for Christ to be baptized with his own baptism, since he himself, as it were a Hierarch, instituted Baptism, as a remedy for sin and the mark and character of himself and his Church, and adds that Thomas, Suárez and others everywhere hold this view. Bellarmine too writes that hardly can Christ's Baptism be attributed to him without injury to him, since it is the laver of regeneration etc. But it is answered. 1. Christ underwent circumcision, which nevertheless according to those very Papists was not a few times a Sacrament of regeneration. Therefore he could also undergo his own baptism.

Observe therefore 2. that he was not baptized for his own sake, but for ours: for the reception of Baptism took place vicariously in our stead etc. Beautifully Lactantius, Book 4, Divine Institutes, about the middle, p. 220. When he first began to grow up (Christ) was baptized by John the prophet in the river Jordan, so that by a spiritual washing he might abolish sins not his own, which had no ways, but those of the flesh which he bore (that is, ours, which he had taken upon himself to be cleansed in himself): so that just as he saved the Jews by receiving their circumcision, so also he might save the nations by baptism, i.e., by being purified through a pouring of water. They have this twofold testimony from St. Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, on Matthew, Canon 2, and Theophylact on this passage.*

Και σύ έρχηπρός με. In the pronouns σύ and μέ there is great emphasis, which Nazianzen explains thus in the sermon on the Epiphany. ό λύχνος τω ήλίω φησίν, ή φωνή τω λόγω, ό φίλος τω νυμφίω, ό έν ηεννητοίς γυναιων ύπέρ άπαντας τω πρωτοτόκω πάσης φύσεος, ό προοκιρτήσας άπό γαςρός τω έν γαςρί προσκυνηθέντι, ό δρομων χαι προδρομούμενος τω φανέντι χαι φανησομένω, έγω χρέιαν έχω ύπό σου βαπτιροήναι, πρόροες χαι ύπέρ σου, ήδει γάρ τω μαρτυρίω βαπτιροησόμενος, χαι σύ έρχηπρός έμέ. Pantaleon on the said place: Thou comest to me: gold to mire, the Sun to the lamp, the torch to the spark, the fountain to the thirsty, to the him who was born of the Virgin. It can be added: the son to the servant, the Lord to the precursor, the just one to the sinner, the creator to the creature. The author of the book On the Works of the Cardinals, Christ's sermon on Baptism among the works of Cyprian: To loose the strap of the shoe he professed himself unworthy, nor does the sacred head of Christ suffer what slopes downward to itself. Therefore trembling, he denies consent to the one requesting the ministry with humble supplication, not because he subtracts obedience, but because he judges it rash for a man to lay hands upon God, and thinks it superfluous to wash him in whom there is no sin.

Latin:

v. 14. Ο δέ Ιωάννης διεκωλυεν άυτόν. -ιακωλύειν est obnixè prohibere, in prohibendi instituto persistere. Colligitur autem ex hac prohibitione, Iohannem iam tum coepisse Christum agnoscere. Quod ergò Ioh. 1. v. 33.datum illi dicitur symbolum descendentis Spir. S. ex quo Christum agnosceret, id non est intelligendum de primo agnitionis gradu, sed de notitiae confirmatione. *(Eandem conciliationem per dist. inter cognitionis inchoationem, & confirmationem, approbat quoque Dn. D. Waltherus in Harm. Bibl. pag. 732. ubi plures etiam alias recenset.)*

έγω χςείαν έχω ύπό σου βαπτισθῆναι. Agnoscit, se Christi Baptismo indigere. i. e. sibi necessarium esse, ut sanguine & Spiritu Christi à peccatis mundetur. In utero quidem repletus erat Spiritu Sancto, interim tamen ob adhaerentes peccati infirmitates agnoscit, se quotidiana adhuc mundatione per Christum indigere.

* (Corn. à Lapide in h. l. sic annotat: Christum non decult suo baptismo baptizari, quia ipse, quasi Hierarcha, Baptismum instituit, quasi peccati remedium ac sui suaea Ecclesiae notam & characterem, & addit; ita statuere Thomam, Suarezium aliosque passim. Bellarminus quoque scribit, vix posse sine iniuria eius Christi Baptismum ipsi tribui, cùm sit lavacrum regenerationis &c. Verùm respondetur. 1. Christus suscepit circumcisionem, quae tamen iuxta ipsos Pontificios non paucos fuit Sacramentum regenerationis. Ergo & baptismum suum potuit suscipere.

Obs. igitur 2. quòd non sui causâ fuerit baptizatus, sed nostri causâ: fuit enim vicaria nostri loco Baptismi susceptio &c. Pulcrè Lactantius l. 4. divin. Instit. circa medium, p. 220. Cùm primùm coepit adolescere (Christus) tinctus est à Iohanne propheta in Iordane flumine, ut lavacro spirituali peccata non sua, quae utia non habebat, sed carnis, quam gerebat (h. e. nostra, quae in se expianda susceperat) aboleret: ut quemadmodum Iudaeos susceptâ circumcisione, sic etiam gen-es baptismo i. e. purificatiroris perfusione salvaret. Gemella his habent D. Hilarius Pictav Episcop. in Matth. Canone 2. & Theophyl. in h. l.)*

Και σύ έρχηπρός με. In pronominibus σύ & μέ est magna emphasis, quam Nazianz. in conc. de Epiph. sic explicat. ό λύχνος τω ήλίω φησίν, ή φωνή τω λόγω, ό φίλος τω νυμφίω, ό έν ηεννητοίς γυναιων ύπέρ άπαντας τω πρωτοτόκω πάσης φύσεος, ό προοκιρτήσας άπό γαςρός τω έν γαςρί προσκυνηθέντι, ό δρομων χαι προδρομούμενος τω φανέντι χαι φανησομένω, έγω χρέιαν έχω ύπό σου βαπτιροήναι, πρόροες χαι ύπέρ σου, ήδει γάρ τω μαρτυρίω βαπτιροησόμενος, χαι σύ έρχηπρός έμέ. Pantaleon d. l. Tu ad me venis, ad lutum aurum, ad lychnum Sol, ad scintillam fax, fons ad sitientem, ad na-um ex semine, qui ex Virgine natus. Addi potest, ad servum filius, ad praecursorem Dominus, ad peccatorem iustus, ad creaturam creator. Autor libr. de operib. Cardin. Christi serm. de Bapt. apud Cyprianum. Adsolvendam calceamenti corrigiam se profess-indignum, acclive sibi esse sacrum Christi caput non patitur. Ideoa tremebundus humili satisfactione postulanti ministerium negat assensum, non quod obadientiam detrabat, sed quia Deo hominem manus imponere iudicat temerarium, & lavare eum, in quo peccatum non est, arbitratur superstuum.

## 3:15
v. 15. Απουριροείς δέ From this word it is gathered that John made an attempt both by speech and by hand to hinder the purpose of Christ.

Αφες άρτι. He does not refute the Baptist's reasoning, but grants it, as fitting the dispensation of temporal self-emptying. For the little word άρτι shows that Christ admonished that he was already dwelling in the state of self-emptying, and requires the economy of redemption, namely that he receive Baptism from him.

ούτω γάρ πρέπον ἐστιν ήμίν πληρωται πάσαν δικαιοσύνυν. These things are explained variously by interpreters.

1. Some interpret to fulfil all righteousness as performing every duty commanded by GOD to each, as the little word Let all be taken distributively, and let the sense be: It behoves You to fulfil Your righteousness, and me indeed mine, i.e. the parts of the office entrusted to carry out.

2. Beza explains it thus: Because the law of Baptism has now been established by the decree and institution of GOD, it is therefore just that I should submit myself to it for the sake of the human race. Franc. Luc. Brug. on this passage: This cause brought it about that Christ wished to be baptized by John, so that He might humbly undergo the reception of the Baptism preached by John, which He knew to be pleasing to GOD. *(In the same way, Camero also explains it in Myroth. on this passage.)*

3. Socinus in Epist. ad Siemichoviam p. 372 applies it thus: It becomes us in this manner to fulfill all righteousness, i.e., to do all things which are generally commanded by God to the whole people.

4. But all these things are so compared together that they do not attain the emphasis of Christ's words, which embrace several things altogether. Hence Dr. Chem. Harm. ch. 17. p. 12. discusses thus. When the fulfilment of all righteousness is attributed to Christ the Mediator, the meaning here is that the Father sent the Son, that He might become righteousness for us.1. Cor. 1. v. 30.that, made under the law, He might become for us a victim and condemn sin because of sin, that so righteousness might be fulfilled in us,Rom. 8. v. 8.or that He might give the ministry of reconciliation, that so we might be made the righteousness of GOD in Christ.2. Cor. 5. v. 21.Therefore it was the office of the Mediator of Christ to fulfil all those things which pertain to attaining that righteousness by which we are justified before GOD unto eternal life, that so He Himself might entirely be our righteousness. Now He fulfilled this righteousness. 1. when, having been made a victim for us, He took away our sins and satisfied the law for us with most perfect obedience. 2. In order that that righteousness may become ours and be applied to us, means or organs are required, through which that righteousness, acquired by the obedience and blood of Christ, may be distributed to us and effectively applied to us by the Ho. Sp. Christ therefore willed to sanctify even those means or organs, which themselves also belong to the righteousness of faith, that we might know that God wishes to be effectual through it,Rom. 1. v. 16.So therefore, in order that all righteousness might be fulfilled by Him, these means of salvation, and consequently Baptism also, had to be sanctified by Him. *(Yet neither is the Ministry of John to be excluded here, as Mr. Doctor Walth. observed quite rightly in the Harm. Bibl. p. 733, where he expounds this passage most beautifully, noting among other things that the Lord makes John a partaker of the fulfilment of righteousness, not meritoriously with regard to acquisition,Esa. 63, 3. but organically, with regard to of application, 1. Cor. 3, 9. 2. Cor. 5, 19. Whence also B. D. Fewrb. writes that this full and genuine sense of the present saying is: we must fulfill all righteousness, namely I indeed, that by the will and decree of GOD I might merit for the whole world the righteousness of faith, whereby believers are justified before the divine tribunal, and be organs, through which this righteousness is offered and conferred upon men, and thus even sanctify the baptism of water received from me: but you so as to be a minister administering. And this is πρέπον, what here does not denote outward comeliness, as it is taken 1. Cor. 11, 13. but that which ought to be done by the good pleasure and command of GOD, just as it is accepted Heb. 2, 10. ch. 7, 26. So God had commanded the baptism of water. Nor was Christ baptized on his own account, but on ours, namely not that he might acquire cleanliness for himself, but that he might cleanse the streams for us, Aug. vol. 10. serm. 36. de tempore. Thus B. D. Feurb. Anti-Osterwaldian, p. 574. Also compare entirely the following passages Luke 3, 3. and Acts 19, 4. together with Heb. 7, 26. Isa. 53, 6. 2 Corinthians 5, 21.)*

Αφίησιν forgives, comes, the present tense is placed for the past. *(A similar enallage occurs immediately in the next chapter, verse 11, and elsewhere frequently. The Syrian therefore, the Ethiopian, and the Arabian rightly render it by the past tense. Whence on the word habeat Schindler, and whatever version of the New Testament in Arabic he used, while writing in his Lexicon of the Pentateuch, p. 1990., that the Arabian renders the former words: only permit, I confess I have not yet been able to discover how he translates אתרך certainly the Roman and Leiden editions have )* omitted forbidding him, he no longer refused to admit him to Baptism.

Observation. That is true humility which does not resist obedience, for one virtue does not exclude another.

Latin:

v. 15. Απουριροείς δέ Ex hoc verbo colligitur, Iohannem conatum fuisse; & oratione & manu Christi propositum impedire.

Αφες άρτι. Non refellit Baptistae rationem, sed remittit cum ad tempori exinanitionis congruam dispensationem. Vocula enim άρτι ostendit, quòd Christus monuerit, se iam versari in statu exinanitionis, & oeconomiam redemtionis requirere, ut Baptismum ab ipso suscipiat.

ούτω γάρ πρέπον ἐστιν ήμίν πληρωται πάσαν δικαιοσύνυν. Variè haec ab interpp. explicantur.

1. Quidam implere iustitiam exponunt perficere omne officium, utrique à DEO mandatum, ut vocula omnis accipiatur distributivè, ac sit sensus. Te decet tuam, me verò meam iustitiam i. e. partes officii demandati explere.

2. Beza sic exponit. Quia lex Baptismiex DEI decreto & inflituto iam posita, ideò iustum est, ut me ei propter humanum genus subiiciam. Franc. Luc. Brug. in h. l. Haec causa fecit, cur à Ioh. Christus baptizari voluerit, ut quam noverat DEO gratam esse Baptismatis à Iohanne praedicati susceptionem, humiliter subirei. *(Eodem modo explicat quoque Camero in Myroth. ad h. l.)*

3. Socinus in Epist. ad Siemichoviam p. 372. sic applicat, Decet nos hac ratione omnem iustificationem implere i. e. omnia facere, quae generatim toti populo divinitus praecipiuntur.

4. Sed haec omnia ita comparata sunt, ut non assequantur emphasin verborum Christi, quae plura omninò complectuntur. Inde D. Chem. Harm. cap. 17. p. 12. Sic disserit. Quando Christo Mediatori tribuitur impletio omnis iustitiae, sensus hic est, quòd Pater miserit Filium, ut fieret nobis iustitia.1. Cor. 1. v. 30.ut factus sub lege fieret pronobis victima & de peccato damnaret peccatum, ut ita iustitia in nobis impleretur,Rom. 8. v. 8.uta daret ministerium reconciliationis, ut it a nos efficeremur iustitia DEI in Christo.2. Cor. 5. v. 21.Fuit ergo officium M-diatoris Christi, omnia illa, quae ad consequendam illam iustitiam, quâ coram DEO, ad vit. aeter. iustificamur, pertinent implere, ut ita ipse in solidum esset iustitia nostra. Implevit autem hanc iustitiam. 1. quando victima pro nobis factus, peccata nostra sustulit & perfectissimâ obaedientia legi pro nobis satisfecit. 2. ut iustitia illa fiat nostra & nobis applicetur, opus est mediis sive organis, per quae iustitia illa oboedientiâ & sanguine Christi acquisita, nobis distribuatur & efficacia Spi-. S. nobis applicetur. Christus igitur illa etiam media sive organvoluit sanctificare, quae & ipsa pertinent ad iustitiam fidei, ut sciremus, Deum per illam velle efficacem esse,Rom. 1. v. 16.Sic ergo, ut omnis iustitia ab ipso impleretur, haec salutis media & proinde etiam Baptismus ab ipso fuit sanctificandus. *(Neque tamen Iohannis quoque Ministerium excludendum hîc est, ceu probè observavit Dn. Doct. Walth. in Harm. Bibl. p. 733. ubi pulcerrimê hunc locum explicat, notans inter alia, quòd Dominus Iohannem impletionis iustitiae faciat participem, non meritoriè ratione acquisitionis,Esa. 63, 3. sed organicè, ratione applicationis,1. Cor. 3, 9.2. Cor. 5, 19. Unde & B. D. Fewrb. hunc plenum & genuinum praesentis dicti sensum esse scribit: omnem iustitiam oportet nos implere, me quidem, ut ego ex DEI voluntate & decreto iustitiam fidei, quâ credentes coram tribunali divino iustificantur, toti mundo promeream, & organa, per quae haec iustitia hominibus offertur & confertur, & sic etiam baptismum aquae, à me susceptum, sanctificem: te porrò uti ministrum dispensantem. Et hoc estπρέπον,quod hîc non notat externum decorum, sicut sumitur1. Cor. 11, 13.sed id, quod ex DEI beneplacito & iussu fieri debet, ceu accipitur Ebr. 2, 10. c. 7, 26. E. Deus baptismum aquae mandaverat. Nec Christus propter seipsum baptizatus est, sed propter nos, nimirum non ut sibi munditiem acquireret, sed ut nobis fluenta mundaret, Aug. t. 10. serm. 36. de temp. Haec B. D. Feurb. AntiOster. p. 574. Conf. etiam omninò loca seqq. Luc. 3, 3. & Act. 19, 4. cum Ebr. 7, 26.Esa. 53, 6.2. Corinth. 5, 21.)*

Αφίησιν dimittit, venit, praesens ponitur pro praeterito. *(Similis enall. occurrit statim c. seqq. v. 11. & alibi passim. Syrus igitur, Aethiops atque Arabs rectè per praeteritum vertunt. Unde v. habeat Schinderus & quâ N. T. versione Arabicâ usus fuerit, dum in Lex. Pent. p. 1990. scribit, Arabem priora verba: sine modò, ita transferre אתרך fateor me indagare nondum potuisse, certè Romana ac Leydensis edit. habent )* omisit illum prohibere, non ampliùs renuit eum ad Baptismum admittere.

Obs. Ea est vera humilitas, quae non repugnat obaedientiae, una enim virtus non excludit alteram.

## 3:16
v. 16. βαπτιροείς ό Ιησούς ά έβη έυθύς άπό τού ύδατος. Francis Lucas holds that the adverb έιθύς is not referred to that thing to which it is added, namely that Christ ascended straightway out of the water, but to what follows, that straightway the heavens were opened, the Holy Spirit descended, so that the sense should be: *(or rather, he had scarcely ascended or when he ascended, suddenly there came about what follows. Just as Grotius explains it, who also brings forward in support of this interpretation that Mark uses nearly the same manner of expression έυθέως in ch. 1, 29. and ch. 11, 2.; and he notes that there is a similar kind of speech in Aeschylus' Prometheus likewise and in Aristotle, Book 3 of Politics, ch. 13.)*

But anyone sees that this is forced; more correctly then it is said that Christ ascended straightway because he had no need of such admonitions, exhortations and instructions, such as John the Baptist was accustomed to join with his Baptism. *(Moreover none of the Eastern interpreters approves such a transposition in their reckoning here. But as concerns the passages brought forward by Grotius, we acknowledge Mark 11, 2. τό έυθέως must be referred to what follows further on, just as also B. Luther clearly indicated this in the German version, and likewise the Syrian Interpreter: But to anyone inspecting the text carefully it easily appears that the reason is not the same in both places. The same judgment applies to ch. 1, 29. Yet we should not conceal that the parallel passage Mark 1, 10. seems especially to favor Grotius' opinion)*

Ανεωχ θησαν άυτω όι ούρονοί Some refer the pronoun άυτω to John the Baptist, for there follows, and saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him, in which way this phrase is understood Acts 7. v. 55. and 56. I see the heavens opened. But it is more correctly referred to Christ, for it precedes, Jesus immediately went up from the water, by which reasoning the pronoun άυτω is to be explained in the manner in which it is taken Acts 2. v. 3. ωφθησαν άυτοίς αί γλωαςαι were seen by them, that is, tongues above them. With this explanation what follows does not conflict, saw the Holy Spirit descending and coming έπ άυτόν, for this can be rendered reflexively upon himself, for that relative often takes the place of the reciprocal.

By this opening of the heavens it was signified. 1. that this teacher was heavenly or sent from heaven.

2. That Christ by his passion and death would merit for us the opening of heaven Ephes. 1. v. 10.

3. That in Baptism and through Baptism heaven is opened to us, because Baptism saves us 1. Pet. 3. v. 20.

The ministry and baptism of John were likewise confirmed by this opening of the heavens.

But what sort of heavens are those which the Evangelist says were opened? Francis Lucas of Bruges understands the neighboring region of air or fire closest to the heavens, which frequently receive the name of heaven. For it is not necessary, he says, to understand the very highest heavens themselves, which, since they are not subject to corruption, are not believed capable of being torn apart against the Nature God implanted in them, whereas the tearing open of the element of air or fire would suffice for understanding that the appearance of the dove which was seen and the voice which was heard proceeded from the heavens, for this indeed was why it was done. Thus in the supreme region of air or rather of fire a deep rift was formed, flashing with wondrous light, visible to the eyes of Jesus and John. *(Corn. à Lapide holds nearly the same view about this opening in his comment on this passage)* But it is said more correctly that the ethereal heavens themselves were opened. Nor indeed was this opening φαινόμνον some physical thing, but an extraordinary and divine miracle, by which the mysteries enumerated shortly before ought to be confirmed. Nor does the solidity of the heavens stand in the way of its having been able to happen. For He who could make a way passable through the solid heavens for Christ ascending could also tear open the heavens for Christ baptized.

But not the whole heaven, nor over all the earth, but only that part of heaven where Christ was praying on the bank of the Jordan, was opened above him himself; this is gathered from the pronoun άυτω. For the heaven was opened in such a way that it was seen not above John, nor above the others who were present, but above Christ alone, which could be understood more clearly from the shining light and the descent of the Holy Spirit.

Jerome held that that opening of the heavens was made not by the unsealing of the Elements, but was offered to spiritual eyes as a vision, which Jesus alone saw, as happened in some manner to Ezekiel and Stephen. Some prove this from the phrase of Scripture. For when any more splendid manifestation of the divine majesty is described, then heaven, because it is the hidden seat of the glory of GOD, is said to be open Ezek. 1. v. 1.Acts 7. v. 56.chap. 10 v. 11. *(In the same way also, namely that the opening of heaven κατάφάσιν should rather be taken than actually done, Hugo Grotius holds at this place.)* But since not only Jesus, but also John and the other spectators saw the heaven open, and since the vision of the dove was not imaginary, but corporeal, and the hearing of the paternal voice was sensible, therefore we rightly insist upon the letter, and say that the heavens were truly open. Chemn.

Καί είδέ τό πνεύμα τού θεού καταβαίνον. Some refer this to John, seeing that Christ was to be manifested to him. John 1. v. 32. I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven. v. 33. He who sent me to baptize in water, he said to me, upon whom you shall see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he it is who baptizes in the Holy Spirit. But it is referred more correctly to Christ himself, as the sequence of words shows. For although John and the other spectators saw this Holy Spirit descended upon Christ in the form of a dove, as is established from the other Evangelists. *(but this, that John and the other spectators are said That they saw the Holy Spirit descending upon Christ must not be understood in such a sense that they immediately beheld the very essence of the Holy Spirit, but as it is explained in Luke 3, 22. The Holy Spirit was descending in bodily form, as a dove. Therefore they saw that dove, and because the Holy Spirit was specially manifesting himself in that form of a dove, they are rightly said to have seen the Holy Spirit itself. B. P., Commonplaces on the Holy Spirit, § 31. The blessed Dr. Meisner also urges this same example against the Photinians and concludes: that if it could truly be said by John that he had seen the Holy Spirit descending, although at least in the form of a dove temporarily assumed he was seen, not according to his essence: so too can it truly be said that the only-begotten Son of GOD died, although not according to his Divinity or according to his divine being, but he died in the flesh which he had assumed. Photin. Consid. p. 503.) yet Matthew here properly treats of Christ, namely that he himself saw the Spirit descending upon him, whereby he was confirmed concerning that divine office to which he was being initiated by this solemn σθεοφανείᾳ in his Baptism. For it is gathered from the arrangement of this History together with other divine revelations, in which heaven was opened, that the heaven above Christ praying on the bank of the Jordan was split into two parts, and out of that cleft there gleamed forth heavenly light through rays extending from heaven down to Christ, and likewise out of that cleft of heaven and in that heavenly light the Holy Spirit settled in the bodily form of a dove, until that form of a dove rested upon Christ, so that by this means all might see that this and no other person was designated by that voice of the heavenly Father.

The Gloss, interlinear, applies [this] simultaneously to Christ and John.

Question 1. Whether besides Christ being baptized and John baptizing others also, spectators, saw the opening of heaven and the descent of the Holy Spirit? Carthusianus and Cajetan deny it.

1. That seems to be attributed to John as some peculiar benefit. Ioh. 1. v. 32. I saw the Spirit descending.

2. If others besides him had also seen it, he would have spoken not in the singular I saw, but in the plural we saw, and this testimony would have been far more illustrious if he could have brought forward other witnesses of this vision.

3. If any others had seen it, this must be said especially of the disciples of John, since they were his inseparable companions. But if those men had seen it, John would not have needed to strive so greatly to remove their false opinion, that he was not the Messiah.

4. About to draw them away from himself to Christ, he does not press upon them this vision, but his steadfast testimony Ioh. 3. v. 28.

5. God has not been accustomed from the very beginning to open at once and completely to the promiscuous crowd those supreme mysteries, such as above all that of the Most Holy Trinity. Christ did not even transfigure himself before all his disciples, but only before three, Matth. 17. v. 1. also adding the prohibition that they should not reveal it to anyone before the resurrection.

6. Ioh. 5. v. 37. Christ says. The Father who sent me, he himself has borne witness concerning me. And ye have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape.

Chemnitius lays down, that besides John others also saw this. He offered, he says, a most brilliant spectacle to many, that astonishing revelation with beholding admirers, which opinion can be confirmed by these arguments. 1. The end of this divine manifestation was, that there might be public testimony of the doctrine & person of Christ. 2. Luke says ch. 3. v. 21. that this disclosure occurred not when John & Christ were alone, but when all the people were being baptized. *(From the fact that John, having seen the dove in which the H. Sp. was descending, could truly say, he saw the Holy Spirit, on account of that special revelation of the H. Sp. in the species of a dove, yet without any transubstantiation, B. P. L. gathers in On the Sacred Supper §. 136. pag. 117., with consecrated bread exhibited & eaten, it is rightly said, the body of Christ is exhibited & eaten, on account of the special union of the body of Christ with that symbol & sign of bread, yet without any transubstantiation.)*

Q. 2. Wherefore did the Holy Spirit descend upon Christ? Ans. Not because Christ had formerly been destitute of the Holy Spirit, but that by this external symbol the inward indwelling of the Holy Spirit in Christ might be confirmed, and from this public testimony it might become manifest that Christ is he who baptizes with the Spirit, Ioh. 1. v. 33. Augustine book 2. On the Trinity chap. 5. He descended in the species of a dove, that hearts stirred by outward sights might be converted from the temporal manifestation of him coming to the hidden eternity of him ever present. *(The same in book 15. On the Trinity c. 26. Nor then was Christ anointed with the Holy Spirit, when over him baptized there descended as it were a dove. For then his body i.e. his Church he deemed worthy to prefigure, in which above all the baptized receive the Holy Spirit. But by that mystical & invisible unction he is to be understood as anointed, when the Word of GOD was made flesh, i.e. when human nature, without any preceding merits of good works, was united to the Word of God in the womb of the Virgin, so that with him it became one person. Cyril of Alexandria On John book XI. c. 25. p. 562. Because the flesh of Christ, not holy by nature, was sanctified in Christ by the Word of GOD which dwelt in it, which at that time through his spirit sanctified it & led it over to the sanctification of his nature, therefore the Holy Spirit descended from heaven upon him in the species of a dove, as John perceived: that we may learn that upon Christ first the spirit descended as upon a man susceptible of sanctification, for the renewal of our nature. Nor do we say that Christ was then sanctified according to the flesh, when the Baptist saw the Spirit descending in the species of a dove. For he was holy in his mother's womb &c. but this was given as a sign to the Baptist*)

Therefore the Holy Ghost descended upon Christ visibly 1. on account of the fulfillment of the prophetic oracle, Isa. 61. v. 1. Psalm 45. v. 8. to which Christ himself recalls his hearers Luke 4. v. 18. 2. because of the solemn inauguration of Christ to his office. 3. on account of the confirmation of the Baptism administered by John. 4. for the promise of gracious indwelling in believers. Believers are members of Christ. Therefore they also receive the Holy Ghost from Christ. Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 19, p. 207. The Holy Spirit descended upon the Son of GOD made the Son of man, becoming accustomed with him to dwell in the human race and to rest in men, and to dwell in the molded form of GOD, working the will of the Father in them and renewing them from oldness into the newness of Christ. The Holy Spirit is called the finger of GOD Matt. 12. v. 28. therefore he descended upon Christ, so that by this as it were finger it might be shown to whom the voice of the Father sounding from heaven is to be referred.

Q. 3. Why did he descend in the species of a dove? Ans. Nicephorus, book 1, History, chapter 18. This was done both on account of the purity of that bird itself, and because long ago it foretold the end of the flood with joyful message. We are sent back then by this appearance

1. to the type Gen. 8. v. 12. Christ is the heavenly Noah, our true comforter. The ark is the Church. The dove is the Holy Ghost. The olive leaf is the Gospel, healing the wounds of our heart. The Author of the life of Jesus recounts seven properties of the dove and applies them here. 1. It has a groaning instead of song. 2. It lacks gall. 3. It harms nothing with its beak. 4. With its claws it snatches nothing. 5. It feeds its young diligently. 6. It rests above the waters. 7. It feeds on pure grains.

2. On the properties of this bird. First, the dove is a gentle animal, familiar to man; secondly, loving purity. You see how the dove comes to the white dwellings. Let the filthy tower receive no birds. Thirdly, rejoicing in good odors, for it is driven away by stenches. Fourthly, fruitful. All these things can be applied to the Holy Spirit.

*(Baldwin of Paris, Commonplaces on the Holy Spirit, §. 31., discusses this matter thus: Therefore the Holy Spirit manifested himself in the form of a dove because he brings this about in the hearts of the elect, that they groan over their sins in true contrition like a dove, Isa. 38, 14. and ch. 59, 11. that in true faith they hide themselves like doves in the holes of the rock, Song 2, 14. 1. Cor. 10, 4. that they are simple like doves, Matt. 10, 16. etc.)*

Certain properties of the dove can also be applied to Christ, upon whom the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove. In the dove there is commended simplicity Matt. 10. v. 16. gentleness, love toward its young, purity; all these can be applied to Christ. Compare Isa. 42, 1. 2. 3. Matt. 10, 16. Dr. Chemnitius at this place: Scripture shows that the dove is a figure of the ministry of the Gospel and of the Church, which is gathered through this ministry, Isa. 60. v. 8. Psalm 68. v. 14. Song 2. v. 10. Since therefore the Holy Spirit, about to anoint Christ for preaching the Gospel, descended in the form of a dove, without doubt under that external form he prefigured what kind of thing the ministry of Christ would be, and what effects it produces in the Church.

Q. 4. Whether this form was a true dove, or only a likeness of a dove?

Later most of the Papists assert [these things]. 1. Because such appearances signifying only the likeness of a thing were customary in visions. Just as in Acts 2. v. 3. not true fire but only a likeness of fire is expressed by the particle ὡσεὶ: so here likewise by the same not a true dove but a likeness of a dove is expressed.

2. Because the particle ὡσεὶ. is added.

3. Luke calls it εἶδος. The Syrian rendered it there by תומר

4. Thus they seem to be supported by Chrysostom, homily 11. on Matthew, Augustine.

Letter 102. Book 2. On the Trinity, chapter 5. Ambrose, Book 1. On the Sacraments, chapter 5. In the preface of Book 3. On the Holy Spirit, the book concerning those who are initiated, chapter 4.

First, others among the ancients assert. Tertullian, On the Flesh of Christ chapter 3, states, as truly was the dove, so truly was the Spirit. The Author of the book De Agone Christiano (among Augustine's works) chapter 22 writes: The Spirit did not deceitfully appear to the eyes of men and delude the spectators with an imaginary phantom, but was a true creature, newly created without the ministry of other doves, which immediately after performing that office ceased to be. Thomas p. 3 q. 39 art. 7 ad 1: The Spirit is said to have descended in the species or likeness of a dove, not to exclude the truth of the dove, but to show that he himself did not appear in the species of his own essence. Reasons can be formed:

1. Luke expressly says that in the bodily species of a dove the Holy Spirit descended.

2. In the sacrament of truth nothing ought to be false.

3. Just as it was a true voice, in which and through which the Father manifested himself: so also it was a true dove, in which the Holy Spirit manifested himself.

D. Chemnitz seems to leave the question open. No article of faith is involved, he says, provided only the presence and anointing of the Holy Spirit be retained in this History, which was indicated and sealed by the external and visible species of a dove.

It would seem to be replied that it was not some natural dove, i.e. begotten in a natural manner from other doves. 2. Yet that it was not merely some external species of a dove, without a subject body: but the Holy Spirit, by his divine power, suddenly formed out of elemental matter a body resembling the body of a dove, which having performed, upon completion of the office for which and because of which it had been formed—that is, once the special signification of his presence had been carried out—it returned and ceased to exist back into those elements from which it had been formed. *(Hugo Grotius on this passage Quite certainly -redo, columbaesi e---m appeared, perhaps fiery, just as fiery tongues were seen s-nt s-p-r the Apostles: Φάσμα ὄρνισθος said Origen. And Justin plainly reports that fire appeared at that time in the Jordan, Colloq. with T----, from handed-down report not doub-tedly. But if that species of the dove had been fiery, the Evangelist here—or certainly Luke, who wrote out the same history—would undoubtedly have added it, as he did Act. 2, 3.

And indeed, if the species had been fiery, it could accurately have been recognized that it was the species of a dove—which nevertheless all the Evangelists relate. But what Justin hands down, That a fire was then seen in the Jordan, if that is true, it can be understood as flashes of lightning. For some report that when the heaven was then split open, a certain more majestic and divine light erupted from that fissure of heaven, such as Luc. 1, 9. and from there the voice of the Father erupted like thunder, and that this was done for this purpose, that the people might be stirred by the brilliance of the light to hear the voice of the Father. Chrysostom also notes that the Holy Spirit descended upon Christ in the form of a dove for this reason, because Christ came into the flesh and the world as meek as a dove to remit sins and to absolve sinners. But on the day of judgment he is to come as a severe judge and to punish the impious by fire.

(Furthermore, to the objection of Bellarmine, who tries to confirm the dogma of Papal transubstantiation by this apparition, in that the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove because of the analogy between the dove and the Holy Spirit, and yet, he says, there was no need for that dove to be a true dove as to substance, but it was sufficient that it had the outward form of a dove: I respond: Whatever may be the case regarding that dove, whether it was a true natural dove or only a likeness of a dove, it is sufficient that that form of a dove was not without some subject body, which Barradius acknowledges in vol. 2 of the Evangelical Concordances. The Blessed Father L. brings forward the passage in his work on the Holy Supper §. 127. It is also pleasing to transcribe the testimony of Corn. à Lapide, the most famous Jesuit. Thus, indeed, he comments on this passage: You will insist: was this therefore a phantom and a phantastic dove? It is answered, by no means: for it was a true solid body, having the form of a dove, as St. Augustine teaches in On Christian Doctrine, ch. 21. The Blessed Father also urges this in the same place, that in the Eucharist there is not proposed some vision or apparition, such as was the Holy Spirit in the form of a descending dove, but the most holy Sacrament, for which is required the truth not only of the heavenly thing, but also of the earthly, so that the sacramental union may have a place. But someone might say: the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove, or even in some body having the likeness of a dove, and yet it was not a true dove, nor is he to be called a dove on that account, it follows that Christ also only appeared in the form of a man, and it is not necessary to establish that he assumed a true human nature, and thus that he was a true natural man. As once

Saturninus, Basilides, the Cerdonians, the Marcionites, the Manichaeans, and Heterus, and in the previous century the Anabaptists and Schwenckfeld taught. But I respond 1. one must distinguish here between different modes of union. For there is one unto -ποςαΤικὴ, that is, personal, such as is [the union] of two natures in Christ; another συμβολικὴ, such as there was between the Holy Spirit and the appearance of a dove. Of the former it follows that the Son of God is called man, just as the son of Mary is said to be Son of ----ssimi; but of this latter union nothing at all so great follows. 2. It must be noted that the Son of God assumed human nature in such a way that he was born of a woman,Gal. 4, 4.of the fathers according to the flesh.Rom. 9, 5. Hence just as children are partakers of flesh and blood, καὶ ἀυτὸς παραπλησίως μετέοχε τῶν ἐυτῶν. But of the Holy Spirit nothing of this sort can be asserted at all, namely that he thus assumed the dove: whence neither anywhere on account of such a symbolic assumption of the dove is the dove itself so called, just as Christ everywhere is called man. 3. The ends of the assumption must be distinguished. The Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove in order that in that form he might descend upon Christ and make known to John that this very man was the Son of God and Messiah, John 1, 31. 32. 33. by no means however in any wise that he might save doves: but the Son of God willed to become a partaker of our human nature for this end, and to assume the same -ν ύπόςασιν as his own, that through and in it he might satisfy divine justice in our place and accomplish the work of our Redemption, as is clearly evident from Heb. 2, 14. sqq., Gal. 4, 4. 5. and other oracles of Sacred Scripture.)*

v. 16. βαπτιροείς ό Ιησούς ά έβη έυθύς άπό τού ύδατος. Franc. Luc. statuit, adverbium έιθύς non referendum ad illud, cui additur, videlicet quòd Christus à Baptismo statim ex aqua ascenderit, sed ad subsequentia, quod statim coeli aperti, Spiritus S. descenderit, ut sit sensus: *(sive, vix adscenderat s. ut adscenderat, subito factum est, quod sequitur. Quemadmodum Grotius explicat, qui etiam pro hâc expositione adfert, quod simili ferè modò Marcus έυθέως utatur c. 1, 29. & cap. 11, 2. simileque dicendi genus apud Aeschylum Prometheo itemq; apud Aristot. 3. Pol. 13. esse, annotat.)*

Sed quilibet videt, hoc esse coactum, rectiùs ergò dicitur, Christum ideò statim ascendisse, quia non opus habebat talibus admonitionibus, exhortationibus & informationibus, quales Ioh. Baptista cum Baptismo suo coniungere solebat. *(Caeterùm nullus Interpp. Orientalium talem traiectionem hîc calculo suo adprobat. quod verò concernit loca à Grotio adducta, fatemur Marc. 11, 2.τό έυθέως referendum esse ad consequēs remotius, quemadmodum etiam clarè hoc indicavit B. Luth. in versione Germanicâ, tum quoque Interpres Syrus: Verùm textum accuratè inspicienti facilè apparet, quòd non sit eadem utrobique ratio. Idem iudicium est de c. 1, 29. Favere tamen, ne & hoc dissimulemus, Grotii sententiae cumprimis videtur locus parallelus Marc. 1, 10.)*

Ανεωχ θησαν άυτω όι ούρονοί Quidam referunt pronomen άυτω ad Iohannem Baptistam, sequitur enim, & vidit Spiritum Dei descendentem sicut columbam & venientem super ipsum, quo modo haec phrasis accipitur Act. 7. v. 55. & 56. Video coelos apertos. Sed rectius ad Christum refertur, praecedit enim, Iesus confestim ascēdit ab aqua, qua ratione pronomen άυτω explicandum eo modo, quo accipitur Act. 2. v. 3.ωφθησαν άυτοίς αί γλωαςαιvisae sunt eis h. e. supra eos linguae. Cum hac explicatione non pugnat, quod sequitur, vidit Spiritum S. descendentem & venientemέπ άυτόν, potest enim hoc verti reciprocè super se, relativum enim illud saepè sustinet vicem reciproci.

Per hanc coelorum apertionem significatum fuit. 1. hunc doctorem esse coelestem sive coelitus missum.

2. Christum suâ passione & morte coeli apertionem nobis promeriturum esse Ephes. 1. v. 10.

3. In Baptismo & per Baptismum coelum nobis aperiri, quia Baptisma nos salvat 1. Petr. 3. v. 20.

Ministerium & Baptismus Iohannis fuit itidem hac coelorum apertione confirmatus.

Quales verò hi coeli, quos Evangelista dicit fuisse apertos? Franc. Lucas Brug. intelligit coelis proximam aeris aut ignis regionem, quae coeli nomen frequenter accipiunt. nea enim, inquit, necesse est, ipsos summos coelos intelligere, quos, cùm corruptioni haud subiaceant, credibile non est, Deum contrà eam, quam illis indidit Naturam, diffidisse, cùm Elementi aeris aut ignis diffissio ad hoc sufficeret, ut intelligeretur, ê coelis proficisci cam, quae videbatur, columbae speciem & quae audiebatur, vocem, idcirco enim hoc factum fuit. Formatus itaa in suprema aëris ignis ve regione profundus hiatus fuit, prodigiosâ luce coruscus, Iesu & Iohannis oculis conspicuus. *(Eodem ferè modo de hac apertione sentit Corn. à Lapide in h. l.)* At coelos ipsos aethereos fuisse apertos, rectius dicitur. Neque enim haec apertio fuit φαινόμνον aliquod physicum, sed extraordinarium & divinum miraculum, per quod mysteria paulò ante enumerata confirmari debuerunt. Neque obstat coelorum soliditas, quò minùs illud fieri potuerit. Qui enim per solidos coelos potuit ascendenti Christo viam patefacere, ille etiam potuit Christo baptizato, coelos diffindere.

Non autem universum coelum, nec super totam terram, sed illam tantùm coeli partem, ubi Christus in ripa Iordanis orabat, super ipsum apertum fuisse, colligitur ex pronomine άυτω. Eo enim modo fuit apertum coelum, ut non super Iohannem, nec super reliquos, qui aderant, sed super solum Christum visum fuerit, id quod ex lucis emicantis & Spiritus S descensu clariùs intelligi potuit.

Hieronymus statuit, apertionem illam coelorum fuisse factam non reseratione Elementorum, sed oculis spiritualibus oblatam vistonem, quam solus Iesus viderit, quale quid Ezechieli ac Stephano contigerit. Id quidam probant ex phrasi Scripturae. Quando enim illustrior aliqua divinae maiestatis apparitio describitur, tunc coelum, quia est arcana sedes gloriae DEI, dicitur apertum Ezech. 1. v. 1.Act. 7. v. 56.cap. 10 v. 11. *(Eodem quoque modo, quòd nempe coeli apertio κατάφάσιν potiùs, quàm reipsâ facta fuerit, accipit Hugo Grotius ad h l.)* Sed quia non solùm Iesus, sed etiam Iohannes & reliqui spectatores coelum viderunt apertum, & quia visio columbae non fuit imaginaria, sed corporalis & auditio vocis paternae fuit sensibilis, ideò meritòliterae insistimus, & coelos reverâ apertos fuisse, dicimus. Chemn.

Καί είδέ τό πνεύμα τού θεού καταβαίνον. Quidam hoc referunt ad Iohannem, quippe cui manifestandus fuerit Christus. Ioh. 1. v. 32.Vidi Spiritum descendentem quasi columbam de coelo.v. 33.Qui misit me baptizare in aqua, ille mihi dixit, super quem vi-eris Spiritum descendentem & manentem super cum, best qui baptizat in Spiritu Sancto. Sed rectius refertur ad ipsum Christum, ut series verborum ostendit. Quamvis enim Iohannes & reliqui spectatores viderint hunc Spiritus S. super Christum in specie columbae descensum, ut constat ex reliquis Evangelistis. *(hoc verò, quod Iohannes & reliqui spectatores dicuntur vidisse Spir. S. super Christum descendentem, non eo accipiendum sensu est, quòd ipsam Sp. Sancti essentiam immediatè viderint, sed ut exponitur Luc. 3, 22.Descendebat Sp. S. corporali specie, sicut columba. Illam igitur columbam viderunt, & quia Sp. S. peculiariter in illa specie columbae sese manifestabat, ipsum Sp. S. vidisse rectè dicuntur. B. P. Loc. de Spir. S. §. 31. Idem hoc exemplum urget quoque B. D. Meisnerus contra Photinianos & concludit: quòd si verè potuit dici à Iohanne, quòd Spiritum Sanctum descendentem viderit, licet saltem in specie columbae ad tempus adsumtae fuerit visus, non secundùm essentiam: ita quoa verè dici, unigenitum Filium DEI mortuum, licet non secundùm Deitatem vel secundùm esse divinum, sed in adsumta carne fuerit mortuus. Photin. Cōsid. p. 503.)* tamen Matthaeus hoc loco propriè agit de Christo, quòd ipse viderit Spiritum super se descendentem, quâ ratione confirmatus fuit de divino illo munere, ad quod solenni isthac σθεοφανείᾳ in suo Baptismo initiabatur. Colligitur enim ex collocatione huius Historiae cum aliis divinis patefactionibus, in quibus coelum apertum fuit, quòd coelum supra Christum in ripa Iordanis orantem fuerit in duas partes scissum, & ex illa scissura micuerit & per radios è coelo usque ad Christum se porrexerit lux coelestis, quôdq; exilla scissura coeli & in coelesti illa luce Spiritus S. corporali specie columbae se domiserit, donec species illa columbae Christo insideret, ut hac ratione omnes viderint, hanc & non aliam personam voce illa Patris coelestis designari.

Gloss. interlin. ad Christum & Iohannem simul applicat.

Q. 1. An praeter Christum baptizatum & Iohannem baptizantem etiam alii spectatores viderint coeli apertionem ac Spiritus S. descensionem? Carthusianus & Caietanus negant.

1. Iohanni tanquam peculiare aliquod beneficium illud tributi videtur. Ioh. 1. v. 32.Vidi Spiritum descendentem.

2. Si praeter ipsum etiam alii vidissent, dixisset non in singulari vidi, sed in plurali vidimus, ac fuisset hoc testimonium longè illustrius, si alios huius visionis testes adducere potuisset.

3. Si qui alii vidissent, maximè hoc dicendum de discipulis Iohannis, utpote qui erant individui eius comites. At si illi vidissent, non fuisset Iohanni tantoperè laborandum, ut illis falsam opinionem eximeret, se non esse Messiam.

4. Abducturus eos à se ad Christum non inculcat eis hanc visionem, sed constans suum testimonium Ioh. 3. v. 28.

5. Deus summa illa mysteria, quale est inprimis SS. Trini-atis, non consuevit ab ipso mox initio semel atque integrè promisevo vulgo aperire. Christus ne quidem coram omnib. discipulis suis sese transfiguravit, sed tantùm coram tribus, Matth. 17. v. 1. addi-a etiam prohibitione, ne cui illud ante resurr. revelarent.

6. Ioh. 5. v. 37. dicit Christus. Qui misit me Pater, ipse testimonium perhibuit de me. Nevocem eius unquam audistis, nea speciem eius vidistis.

Chemnitius statuit, praeter Iohannem etiam alios hoc vidisse. praebuit, inquit, valdè illustre spectaculum multis, stupendam illam revelationē cum admiratione spect antibus, quae sententia confirmari potest hisce rationibus. 1. finis huius divinae manifestationis fuit, ut esset publicum testimonium doctrinae & personae Christi. 2. Lucas dicit cap. 3. v. 21. hanc patefactionem factam esse, non cùm soli essent Iohannes & Christus, sed cùm baptizaretur omnis populus. *(Ex eo, quòd Iohannes visâ columbâ, in quâ descendebat Sp. S. verê dicere potuit, se vidisse Sp. Sanctum, propter peculiarem illam revelationem Sp. S. in specie columbae, sine ullâ tamen transubstantiatione, colligit B. P. L. de Sacr. v. 17. Καὶδοἰ φωνὺ ὴκ τῶν οὐρανῶν λέγουσα. Concerning the peculiar mode of divine revelation which flourished especially under the second temple, called by the Rabbins לוק תב or daughter of the voice, see Drusius book 1. praeter. ch. 6. Tremellius in the notes on the Syriac paraphrase Acts 12. v. 22. likewise *(Schindler. Lexicon Pentaglotton under the word לוק, Buxtorf. Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum p. 320. & 321. B. D. Glassius Rhetica Sacra p. 251. The Syrian here rendered nakedly just as also ch. 17, 5. likewise Luke 3, 22.Mark 1, 11.John 12, 28. But Acts 12, 22. defines similarly Heb. 3, 15. & Galatians 4, 20. by that is, daughter of the voice. Yet the Arabic and Ethiopic versions express it nakedly in these places too. Which manuscript the Ethiopian followed when Acts 12, 22. renders:

with the negative particle omitted, I confess escapes me.)* But The voice of the Father, which was heard in this place, was most distinct from that manner of revelation, inasmuch as it was articulate, magnificent, majestic, carried down from the opened heavens in the flashing of light upon the descending Christ.

Victor of Antioch says, that this voice did not come forth as proper to the Father, but was formed in the person of the Father through the ministry of the Angels. *(The same thing concerning the dove Cornelius à Lapide teaches above, namely that, to wit, the appearance of the dove was fashioned, stirred up and moved by an Angel, so that it descended upon Christ.)* But it is more correctly said that it was formed by the immediate heavenly power of the Father, since by it the Father made himself manifest.

Q. Why was this voice brought down from heaven?

1. Neither would the dove without the voice, nor the voice without the dove, have surely demonstrated Christ. If the dove had descended, with the voice of the Father not being heard, it could by no means have been understood what that descent of the dove signified. If the voice of the Father had been heard, with the dove not descending, it might have seemed uncertain whom that voice of the Father designated. 2 Just as the Holy Spirit had manifested himself in the appearance of a descending dove: so the Father manifested himself in the sound of a voice delivered from heaven, so that σθεοφάνεια might be full. The Son, the second Person, stood beside the banks of the Jordan and was beheld in the assumed flesh; therefore accordingly the Father manifested himself by Voice, the Begotten by the river, the Breath by the bird. The Word is, as it were, the offspring of the voice; fitly therefore does he make himself manifest in the voice who was the ὑποςατικοῦ Begetter of the Word.

*(But let someone say here: If the forming of that voice delivered from heaven, of that flesh in which the Son appeared in the Jordan, and of the dove which descended upon Christ, is the work of the whole Most Holy Trinity—a point which must certainly be held to be affirmed, since, according to the common rule of the theologians (of which Augustine himself makes mention vol. 3, book 4, On the Trinity, chapter 21, likewise vol. 10, sermon 63): the outward works of GOD are undivided, it follows that that voice cannot be attributed to the Father, the flesh to the Son, the appearance of the dove to the Holy Spirit, and hence further that the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity cannot be proved from such an appearing. But the reply: Certainly it can. Whence also the ancients attributed so much to this appearing that they believed it could safely be opposed to all τςιαδ-μάΧοις σθεοφαι -αν, saying: If you do not yet believe the Trinity, go with John to the Jordan, and you shall see. Nor ought the rule of antiquity to be denied, that the outward works of GOD are undivided. Yet at least this must be added to it, which the ancients themselves added:* The distinction of persons being preserved. Therefore a distinction must be made between the formation of the voice, the flesh, and the dove, and between their appropriation, assumption, or manifestation through them. And just as the very work of the incarnation can be considered in two ways, inchoatively i.e. effectively, or with respect to the act, which is common to the whole Holy Trinity, and terminatively or with respect to the terminus of the flesh assumed, which is τοῦ λόγου ὑπόςασις:, so too in a certain way that voice and the dove can be considered in two ways, namely with respect to the act i.e. effectively, which are the work of the whole Trinity; and with respect to the terminus, which is the appropriation of such symbols, and in them and through them the manifestation, which is that the voice is of the Father alone, the flesh of the Son alone, the dove of the Holy Spirit alone. See B. Par. Coll. Isagog. Loc. 3. de SS. Trin. c. 6. §. 4. and Loc. 6. de pers. & Off. Christi c. 7. §. 30. But what further things are to be observed, both concerning the arguments for the mystery of the Holy Trinity drawn from this σθεοφανείᾳ, and indeed concerning the objections of the Photinians, can likewise be seen in the aforesaid earlier locus §. 5. Contra Valentin. Smalcii in refut. thes. Schop. p. 14. the exception in particular, of one who says: how can Christ be reckoned a person equally divine as the person of the Father? since it can only be said blasphemously that anything but a man is baptized, and that into God, moreover, the Spirit of GOD descends and remains in him. Observation 1. that the two natures in Christ must not be confused, nor set in opposition to one another. 2. that it detracts nothing from the Deity of any person that it descends and dwells in us, since the Savior expressly affirms this not of the Father any less than of himself and the Holy Spirit Ioh. 14, 23. nor is it foreign to the Deity of a person that it inhabit the hearts of men; see Iohan. 15, 5. 6. likewise Ephes 3, 17. 3. that it is by no means blasphemy to say, that one person of the Deity remains in another. For this our Savior teaches quite clearly, saying: Iohan. 10, 37. Believe the works: that you may know and believe that the Father is in me and I in him, on account of όμοουσίαν namely. But such a union, writes B. D. Chemn. in the said l. Harm. Evang. c. 105. p. 256. cannot be found in all creatures, that two should be found of which one is so in the other that they are one and the same in nature and number. But of GOD the Father and GOD the Son the nature and essence is thus one and the same, that the essence of the Father is wholly in the Son, and the essence of the Son in turn is wholly in the Father, so that thus the whole Father is in the Son, and the Son subsists in the whole Father. See also Ioh. 14, 9.)*

The voice was indeed, as much as the dove, an effect of the whole Trinity; meanwhile the dove κατ᾽ ἰδιοποιίαν signified the Holy Spirit alone by appropriation, and the voice the Father alone.

Q. 2. Whether those formal words are described by Matthew. This is so; or whether by Mark & Luke: Thou art?

1. Certain men *(such as Franc. Lucas, Jansenius, Maldonatus, Corn. à Lapide, and several other Papists)* judge that the formal words were those which Mark & Luke recite: You are my son; [and that] Matthew therefore changed the second person into the third, so as to signify that God the Father wished John to be made certain of that matter.

2. Osiander, in *Harmon.* lib. 1. cap. 15, judges that the voice of the Father heard from heaven, although it was one, nevertheless generated different sounds in different ears, so that Christ heard: You are my beloved son, in you I am well pleased, as Mark & Luke commemorate, but the others [heard]: This is my beloved son, in whom I am well pleased, as Matthew commemorates; just as also the Apostles, when they had received the Holy Spirit and were preaching the magnificent works of GOD, were heard in one and the same speech to speak in different sounds and different languages.

3. D. Chemnitius decided more correctly, that utterance of the Father was repeated twice: first, just as Luke writes, addressed to Christ himself, 'Thou art my Son'; secondly, because this Prophet was being proclaimed here as One who must be heard by the whole human race, that utterance was directed to John and to the spectators, just as Matthew writes: This is my beloved Son.

This is that Son of mine. Taken from Psalm 2. v. 6. 7. ὁ ἀγαπητὸς. The article is again emphatically repeated, that beloved one. It looks back to the figures of Isaac Gen. 22. v. 2. and Solomon 2 Kings 12. v. 25.

Hilary, book 3 on the Trinity, p. 26; book 12, p. 255. Many are our sons, but such a Son as this there is not. For He is the true and proper and only-begotten Son; by origin, not by adoption; by truth, not by naming; by birth, not by creation. Leo, sermon on the Transfiguration: This Son is not adopted, but proper; not created from elsewhere, but begotten of Me; nor made comparable to Me out of another Nature, but born equal to Me out of My essence. This is My Son, whom the Godhead does not separate from Me, power does not divide, eternity does not distinguish. The name Son is placed before the name beloved. For He, because He is the Son, therefore is beloved; we, however, because we are loved, therefore are sons.

In this Son we also are adopted as children of GOD; in this beloved One we are regarded by GOD as objects of His love. Eph. 1. v. 6.

Ἐν ω έυσόησα. This word has the meaning of excellent reputation and of what greatly pleases.

Δοηειν means to think and to judge, thence έυςοηέιν to approve. But because we also favor those things which we approve, thence it also signifies to be well disposed toward someone. Again, since this inclination of mind arises from the fact that some thing has fully satisfied us—for in ordered delight judgment must precede the mind's consent—therefore έυςοηέιν likewise means the same as to acquiesce or to rest in some thing, which the Greeks call έναναπαυέσΘαι,,, by which sense it is also taken here. Christ is the only-begotten and proper Son of GOD, that unique Mediator, whom when the Father looks upon, and us in him, he lays aside all the indignation conceived against us. Compare the type Exod. 28. v. 36. and the prophecy Isa. 42. v. 1. The Syriac has the word צבא, to please, to be pleasant.

The Seventy Interpreters are accustomed to render the word רצה constructed with a preposition by the word έυςοηέιν,, by which they wished to express an inclined mind and a certain special affection toward someone. Ps. 146. v. 10. 11. Ps. 149. v. 4. It is therefore signified that this Son alone and uniquely pleases the heavenly Father, so that not only does nothing in him displease the Father, but others also please the Father in him and are loved in this beloved One.

Anselm says on this passage, the wilderness in which Christ was tempted was between Jerusalem and Jericho, where very many robbers dwelt. It was near that wilderness in which John the Baptist was brought up. Christians afterwards called this wilderness the Wilderness of Quarantana from this history. Εις ρην έρημον.

Q. Why did Christ withdraw into this wilderness? Ans. That he might fulfill the type of Moses and the prophet Elijah. 2. That by this withdrawal he might win authority for himself. 3. That, removed from the sight and company of men, he might commend his entire ministry to the heavenly Father through more fervent prayers. 4. That he might present himself to the tempting Devil like a valiant soldier with undaunted spirit.

François Lucas of Bruges says on this passage, Solitude is suited to the fellowship of those who agree together, and the hermitage to witnesses, for those who, having rejected the desires of the world, ponder a new and heavenly life, so that they may easily avoid the polluting association of men, so that by abstinence they may tame the flesh, so that they may give constant attention to prayer and the contemplation of divine things. Ans. 1. To go into the wilderness without a calling is, according to ηαχοζηλια, to tempt God. 2. This withdrawal of Christ into the wilderness, just like the forty days' fast, is not set before us for imitation. 3. There is a certain temporary solitude and a perpetual one; we commend the former, we disapprove the latter. 4. Separation from the world takes place not so much by place as by affection.

That this Spirit, by which Christ was driven into the wilderness, was not an evil spirit or the Devil but God, Basil teaches in the book On the Holy Spirit ch. 16, Chrysostom homily 13 on Matthew, Hilary canon on Matthew, Cyprian sermon On Fasting p. 306, Jerome on chapter 4 of Matthew, Gregory homily 16 on the Gospels. For 1. from Luke ch. 4. v. 1. this is evident. Ιποτούπνέέυματος.

## 4:1
CHAPTER IV.

Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit into the desert.

2. The article του here, just as also in Luke there is αναΦοριηός: was being led by him by the Spirit, namely by that Spirit who had descended upon Him in bodily form of a dove in His Baptism. *(The Arabic likewise uses the emphatic article here, rendering )*

3. John expressly says, that the Spirit remained upon Christ, chap. 1. v. 32.

4. The Syrian rendered it, *(with the agreement also of the printed Altdorf MS. Codex, [Syriac text])* by the Holy Spirit. But the Arab and the Ethiopian translate it nakedly here, just as the Greek text has it.)* *(

*(Just as this Holy Spirit brought forth and impelled Christ to the contest: so likewise He impelled the same One to another temptation or contest with Satan before the last Passover, as is evident from Heb. 9, 14. It is indeed objected against this exposition that πνέύμα stands here absolutely or without the article, whereas now the rule of Didymus of Alexandria holds that only when the article has been placed before the name πνέυματος does it signify the person of the Holy Spirit: but that rule is not universally true.)*

Q. By what means was Christ led into the wilderness by the Holy Spirit? The author of the unfinished work on Matthew, homily 5, writes, Jesus was led by the Holy Spirit into the wilderness, not as though the lesser were commanded by the greater, but as though the greater were encouraged by the lesser. But these things introduce inequality among the persons in divine matters, and therefore smack of Arianism.

This leading therefore, 1. is not opposed to the equality of the persons in divine matters, 2. nor is it opposed to the free and spontaneous will of Christ. 3. Rather it signifies the most holy and most perfect obedience of Christ, because the human spirit of Christ offered itself obediently to the impulse of the Holy Spirit, whose divine essence is numerically the same as that of Christ and of the Father, the divine essence. Therefore since the Holy Spirit is credited here with this lead ing and instigation, neither the Father nor the Son is excluded thereby, but through a certain ιςιοποριαν that, which pertains to the work of sanctification, is appropriated to the Holy Spirit in the familiar phrase of Scripture. Rom. 8. v. 14. Those who are led by the Spirit of GOD are sons of GOD.

Observation. Those who through baptism have been made sons of GOD ought to follow the prompting of the Holy Spirit.

Christ is not said to have sought out temptations, but to have been led by the Holy Spirit into the place of temptation, as into a theater and arena, lest anyone rashly expose himself to temptations.

ΠέιροσΦηναι -ποτου διαβόλου. God tests, the Devil tests. The former for good, the latter indeed for evil. God tests, so that he may bring forth man's faith and constancy into the light, the Devil tests, so that he may cast man down from faith and constancy: for this is what the Devil aims at in his temptation, that he may plunge man headlong into sins and destruction.

Q. Why did Christ both will and deserve to be tempted by the Devil? Ans. 1. that he might conquer our temptations by his own temptations, just as he came to overcome our death by his death, says Anselm on chapter 2 of Hebrews. Our nature, still intact when it met with this tempter succumbed, but now human Nature in that seed of the woman again won victory back from Satan, says Gregory, homily 16 on the Gospel.

To this may also be referred other sayings of the ancients worthy of piety. Jerome on Psalm 44. The Lord's victory is the triumph of His servants. Ambrose on chapter 4 of Luke. Unless He had contended, that one would not have conquered me. Damascus, book 3 of Orthodoxy of Faith, ch. 20. He was tested and conquered, that he might win victory for us, and give to Nature the power to conquer the adversary.

2. So that He might show the truth of Human Nature in Himself. Gregory, in the same place. And it is man who is tempted by the Devil, and it is God who is ministered to by the Angels.

3. So that He might be able to sympathize with our infirmities. Heb. 2. v. 18. For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted. Ch. 4. v. 15. We have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.

4. So that He might provide a trial of His battle against Satan. Christ had come into this world to storm the Tyranny of Satan and to destroy his kingdom; therefore, by this single combat, He wished to gird Himself for invading Satan and his kingdom, and as it were to prepare the way for Himself.

5. That He might show that Theology must be learned not only from Θεωρια, but also from πράξει.

6. To teach that no one, however holy and pleasing to GOD, ought to be secure, as if he were not exposed to the temptations of Satan in this life. For if the Devil dared to attack the Head himself, how will he spare the members? Hilary, can. 3 on Matthew. Christ by his own temptation indicates that the temptations of the Devil rage most of all against us who are sanctified, because victory over the saints is more desired by him.

7. That He might offer us an example of fighting against Satan. Augustine, book 4, On the Trinity, chapter 13. He who by the Spirit living raised up his own dead flesh, the true Mediator of life, cast out by the Spirit that mediator of death and death himself, dead, from the spirits of those believing in him, so that he would not reign within, but attack from without; yet he did not storm him, since he offered even himself to be tempted by him, that he might be a Mediator for overcoming even his temptations, not only through help but also through example. Treatise 2 on the First Epistle of John. He repelled the temptation and taught the soldier how to fight. Gregory Nazianzen, Oration on Holy Baptism, skillfully refers these temptations to three heads, which concern us too for resolving contests against the same enemy, namely want, elation of mind, and greed.

Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, Letter 75. Take heart at Christ's victory lawfully won. For vain glory has been trampled underfoot, pride extinguished, greed crushed, the adversary covered with shame—he who could not pierce his very breast with any of his arrows. Therefore, if in the same way you, striving, display the greatness of soul that is fitting, having overcome the swords by which the soul is wounded, and commit yourself to tranquility of mind, Angels will minister to you after the victory.

In this battle against Satan we take the weapons of our warfare, namely the word, from the hand of the supreme Emperor, as Anselm says in the Commentary Eph. 6. with this two-edged sword we cut off the Dragon's head, as Chrysostom says, Sermon 24 on Ephesians.

Observation. Christ, tempted immediately after receiving Baptism, taught that Satan attacks us especially then, when, enrolling ourselves under the banner of Christ, we declare hostility against the Devil. Cor., Ecclesiasticus 11, 1.

ύπο τουσιαβόλου. Syrian: by spreading slander, which Junius-Tremellius explains in the notes on this passage. Διαβάλλέιν means to pierce through, whence the word has been transferred to accusations, especially unjust ones, by which men are pierced as if by most poisonous darts.

That wicked spirit is called the Devil 1. because he slandered God before Adam most shamelessly, as though He envied man. 2. because he entices men to sin, and when they have fallen headlong into sin slanders them before God, Rev. 12. v. 10.

By the Devil without doubt ηατ αντοναμασιαν is understood the chief of the Devils, Matt. 25, 41. Rev. 12. v. 9. who overcame our first parents in Paradise by his temptations, so that thus he might be overcome by the second Adam, whereas he had been the victor over the first; and when the Prince of Demons was conquered, all the rest were likewise to be overcome for the use of the faithful by Christ.
