Q. Quâ ratione à Spiritu S. Christus fuerit in desertum ductus? Autor imperfecti operis in Matth. homil. 5. scribit, Iesum ductum esse à Spiritu Sancto in desertum, non quasi minorem maioris praecepto, sed quasi maiorem minoris hortatu. Sed haec in aequalitatem personarum in divinis introducunt, ac proinde Arianismum sapiunt.

Hic ergo ductus. 1. non opponitur personarum in divinis aequalitati 2. nec opponitur liberae & spontaneae Christi voluntati. 3. Sed potiùs significatur sanctissima & perfectissima Christi oboedientia, quòd se. Spiritus Christi humanus sese obsequentem praebuerit Spiritus Sancti impulsui, cuius Spiritus Sancti divina essentia est numero eadem, quae Christi & atris essentia divina. Proinde quandSpiritui Sancto hic duct -s atque instinctus tribuitur, non excluditur ab eo vel Pater vel Filius, sed per quandam ιςιοποριαν illud, quod ad opus sanctificationis pertinet, familiari Scripturae phrasi Spiritui Sancto appropriatur. Rom. 8. v. 14.Qui Spiritu DEI aguntur, sunt Filu DEI.

Obs. Qui per baptismum filii DEI facti, illi debent instinctum Spiritus S. sequi.

Christus non dicitur expetiisse tentationes, sed à Spiritu S. in tentationis locum velut in theatrum & agonis locum ductus, ne quis temerè seipsum tentationibus obiiciat.

ΠέιροσΦηναι -ποτου διαβόλου. Tentat Deus, tentat Diabolus. Ille ad bonum, hic verò ad malum. Deus tent at, ut hominis fidem & constantiam in lucem producat, Diabolus tentat, ut hominem à fide & constantia deiiciat: hoc enim in tentatione sua Diabolus agit, ut hominem in peccata & exitium praecipitet.

Q. Quare Christus à Diabolo tentari & voluerit & debuerit? Resp. 1. ut tentationes nostras suis tentationibus vinceret, sicut nostram mortem suâ morte super aturus vener at, inquit Anshelmus in cap. 2. ad Hebr. Nostra natura adhuc integra cum hoc tentatore congressa succub-it, sed nunc Natura humana in semine illo mulieris rursus victoriam ex Satana retulit, inquit Gregorius homil. 16. in Evang.

Hûc referri possunt etiam alia piorum veterum dicta. Hieronymus in Psal. 44.Victoria Domini servorum est triumphus. Ambrosius in cap. 4. Lucae. Nisi ille certasset, non mihi iste vicisset. Damasc. lib. 3. orth. fid. c. 20. Tentatus est & vicit, ut nobis victoriam pararet, & daret Naturae virtutem vincendi adversarium.

2. Ut ostenderet Naturae humanae in se veritatem. Gregor. d. l. Et homo est, qui tentatur à Diabolo, & Deus est, cui ab Angelis ministratur.

3. Ut posset compati nostris infirmitatibus. Hebr. 2. v. 18. In eo, in quo passus est ipse & tentatus, potens est & eis, qui tentantur, auxiliari. Cap. 4. v. 15.Non habemus Pontificem, qui non possit compati nostris infirmitatibus, tentatum autem per omnia secundùm similitudinem absa peccato.

4. Ut suae adversus Satanam pugnae tyrocinium ederet. Venerat Christus in hunc mundum ad Tyrannidem Satanae expugnandam & regnum eius destruendum, ideò hac monomachia ad Satanam eiusque regnum invadendum sese accingere, sibiq; viam quasi parare voluit.

5. Ut ostenderet, non solùm ex Θεωρια, sed etiam ex πράξει Theologiam esse discendam.

6. Ut doceret, quòd nemo, quantumvis sanctus & DEO placens, securus esse debeat, quasi in hac vita non sit expositus Satanae tentationibus. Si enim Diabolus ipsum caput aggredi est ausus, quomodo membris parcet? Hilarius can. 3. in Matth. Christus tentatione suâ indicat, in nobis sanctific atis maximè Diaboli tentamenta grassari, quia victoria est ei magis expotata de sanctis.

7. Ut exemplum pugnandi contra Satanam nobis praeberet. August. lib. 4. de Trinit. cap. 13. Ille, qui Spiritu vivus carnem suam mortuam resuscit avit verus vitae Mediator, illum Spiritu mortuum & mortis Mediatorem à Spiritibus in se credentium foras misit, ut non regnaret intrinsecus, sed forinsecus oppugnaret; nec tamen expugnaret, cui se ipse quoque tentandum praebuit, ut ad super andas etiam tentationes eius Mediator esset, non solùm per adiutorium, sed etiam per exemplum. tract. 2. in primam Iohannis. Repulit tentationem & docuit pugnare militem. Gregor. Nazianz. orat. in S. Baptism. scitè istas tentationes ad tria refert capita, quae spectent etiam nos ad solvenda adversus eundem hostem certamina, penuriam scilicet, animi elationem ac avaritiam.

Isid. Pelusiota lib. 1. Epist. 75. Ad Christi victoriam legitimè partam animum adiice. Inanis enim gloria calcata est, extincta superbia, oppressa avaritia, pudorea suffusus adversarius, ut qui nulla sagittarum suarum ipsius pectus traiicerepotuisset. Ad eundem igitur modum si tu quoa eam, quam par est, animi magnitudinem praestiteris, gladiisa, quibus anima convulneratur, superatis, te in animi tranquillitatem asserveris, Angeli tibi post victoriam ministr abunt.

In hac contra Satanam pugna arma militiae nostrae, verbum sc. accipimus de manu Imperatoris summi, ut loquitur Anshelmus in Comm. Eph. 6.hoca gladio ancipiti caput Draconis amputamus, ut Chrysost. serm. 24. ad Eph. loquitur.

Observ. Christus statim post perceptum Baptismum tentatus docuit, tunc maximè Satanam nos oppugnare, quando sub vexillum Christi nos conferentes Diabolo hostilitatem indicimus. Co-r, Ecclesiastici 11, 1.

ύπο τουσιαβόλου. Syrus: à pervulgante obtrectationem, quam sin Tremel. in notis h. l. explicat. Διαβάλλέιν est traiicere, inde vox translata ad criminationes, praesertim iniustas, quibus veluti venenatissimis -eliboni transfiguntur.

Dicitur autem malignus ille Spiritus Diabolus. 1. quia Deum apud Adamum impudentissimè fuit calumniatus, quasi homini invideret. 2. quia homines ad peccatum solicitat, & in peccatum praecipitatos apud Deum calumniatur, Apoc. 12. v. 10.

Per Diabolum dubio procul ηατ αντοναμασιαν intelligitur princeps Diabolorum, Matth. 25, 41. Apocal. 12. v. 9. qui primos parentes in Paradiso tentationibus suis superavit, ut sic vinceretur à secundo Adamo, qui primi extiterat victor, ac in Principe Doemonum superato reliqui omnes in usum fidelium â Christo superarentur.

## 4:2
v. 2. The mention of nights is added after Και νηστεύσας ημέρας τεσσαράκοντα και τεσσαράκοντα νύκτας., lest anyone think this fasting was such as that of the Jews, who were commanded to fast during the day but took food in the evening.

Q. Why did Christ fast so many days and nights? Ans. 1. That by the harshness of fasting he might conquer the Devil, who had deceived and overcome the first men by the sweetness of forbidden food. Iren. lib. 5. cap. 18. p. 343. Christ fasted, that the adversary might have ground on which to engage him. For since at the beginning he seduced unsated man by food to transgress the commandment of GOD, at the end he could not persuade sated man to refuse the food that came from GOD. Therefore what was in Paradise the fullness of man through a double tasting was dissolved through want in this world.

So that just as Moses and Elijah had given authority to their teaching by a fast of 40 days Exod. 24. v. 18. and chap. 34. v. 28. Deut. 9. v. 9. 1 Kings 19. v. 8., so also by this fast of 40 days and nights he would give the same authority to his own teaching. And by this reasoning he showed that his Gospel agreed with the Law and the Prophets.

3. That He might demonstrate the truth of human Nature in Himself. Iren. d. l. Christ fasted for forty days similarly to Moses, likewise Elijah; afterwards He hungered, that we might understand Him to be a true and solid man, for it is proper for a fasting man to hunger.

4. That by his example he might commend to us temperance, abstinence, and fasting according to the reason of persons, places &c. Are prayers joined with fasting a firm bulwark against the temptations of the Devil ? *(Compare the examples of ancient Christians Acts 13. 3.c. 14, 22.)*

There is therefore a great difference between the fast of Moses and Elijah on the one hand, and that of Christ on the other. 1 The fast of Moses and Elijah is not meritorious and satisfactory, as is the fast of Christ. For they were Ψιχοιαν θρωποι subject to the weaknesses of the flesh, but Christ truly is Θεάνρωπος free from every stain of sin.

2. Moses was enabled to endure the fast of 40 days by the presence and address of GOD, Exod. 34. v. 28. Elijah by the strength of food brought by an Angel 1. Kings 19 v. 8. but Christ sustained the human Nature he had assumed by his own power of his Divinity, lest he should faint under the weight of so long a fast.

The Papists, not satisfied with these limits, add that Christ instituted the forty-days' fast by his example, whence they sing in their temples during Lent: Lawgiver of the forty-day abstinence, Jesus. Who for the salvation of souls sanctioned this fast. Lucas Brugensis on this passage: The number forty serves penance and affliction; that the Savior wished, by observing fasts according to our measure, to be commended to us by his example, the Apostles understood, on the authority of Jerome, Epistle 54. to Marcella. Alphonsus de Castro book 8 against heretics, under the word fast, heresy 2, writes that many men not of low rank but of very great authority, authors not recent but most ancient, affirm that the fast of Lent was instituted by Christ. *(But Barradius brings forward for this matter, tom. 2, Commentary on the Harmony of the Four Gospels, book 2, p. 61, certain passages from Jerome on Matthew chapter 4, likewise book 2 against Jovinian chapter 11, St. Maximus homily 3 On the Forty Days' Fast, Chrysologus sermon 11, Ambrose sermon 34, Augustine epistle 119 chapter 15.)* Stapleton in his Promptuary Catholic, Dominica in Quadragesima §. 1., asserts that Christ commended Lent to us by his example. The Anglican Remigians on this passage bring forward from Jerome the saying that Christ fasted 40 days so that by his example he might leave us those solemn days of fasting.

Answer. 1. They do not agree among themselves about the institution of Lent. For some attribute it not to Christ, but to the Apostles. Nauclerus part 2, generation 2. Bellarmine book 2 on good works, chapter 14. Pererius disputation 31 on John chapter 14, p. 414. Alphonsus de Castro in the place cited. Baius in his Catechism, controversy treatise 2, question 10. *(Barradius tries to reconcile this diversity in the place cited, warning, that the example of the Lenten fast is indeed the Lord’s; but that its institution and tradition are the Apostles’.]

Some indeed assert that the quadragesimal fast was instituted by the Church. For this institution is attributed to Telesphorus, canon Statuimus dist. 4; among Platina in the Life of Telesphorus fol. 19; Polydore Vergil, book 6 On the Invention of Things, chapter 3. They attribute it to the Church: Hosius in the Confession of Petrikau chapter 4; Cornelius Jansenius in the Harmony of the Gospels chapter 15. *(Yet since very many of the ancients went down into that opinion, judging that the Lord dedicated the Quadragesima by his own fast: Whence furthermore it must be pointed out that fasts instituted on fixed days are by no means simply disapproved, condemned, or rejected. See somewhat above observation 4. However)* 2. We disapprove of the quadragesimal fast, as it is observed today in the Papacy, on account of the corruptions clinging to it. First, on account of the form. For they do not define fasting by abstinence from food and bodily pleasures, but constitute it solely in the selection of kinds of food. Second, on account of the end. They fast, or rather feign themselves to fast, so that they may make satisfaction for their sins and merit eternal life. Third, on account of the attendant circumstance. They thrust this fast upon the Church under an opinion of necessity, so that whoever does not fast on those days is judged to sin mortally, even if he fasts at some other time; out of fasting they make divine worship; out of dispensations from fastings they make sheer markets of money. 3. Therefore we oppose this opinion. First, the absence of a divine mandate: for neither Christ nor the Apostles are anywhere found in the Scriptures to have instituted the Quadragesima. Second, the true doctrine concerning fasting, namely that fasting is not in itself and for its own sake worship of GOD, but then becomes pleasing to God when it is joined to penitence and prayer, that is, if it is directed toward this end, that the flesh be curbed. Romans 14. verse 17. 18. 1 Corinthians 8. verse 8. 1 Timothy 4. verse 8. Hebrews 13. verse 9. Third, Christian liberty. Fourth, the diversity of fasting customary in the primitive Church. *(Chrysostom speaks well, homily 47 on Matthew: He did not say that his fast is to be imitated, but: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart. Compare further matters bearing on this in B. Par. Of the Catholic Consension, part 3, specially pp. 983 sqq.)*

῞Γςερονέτεινασε. The fast of forty days proves in Christ the truth of divinity; Hunger after that fast proves the truth of humanity. But he hungered not simply by necessity of Nature, since He is Lord of Nature, but by free will. Hence Augustine writes, that it was more wonderful in Christ, that when 40. days had been completed, he hungered, than that while they were slipping away he ate nothing.

After the fortieth day, when the divinity of Christ withdrew His humanity to its own weakness, the human nature began to be assailed by natural hunger and to seek food.

Latin:

v. 2. Και νηστεύσας ημέρας τεσσαράκοντα και τεσσαράκοντα νύκτας.Noctium mentio additur, ne quis existimet, fuisse tale ieiunium, quale Iudaeorum, qui interdiu ieiunare iussi, vesperi cibum assumebant.

Q. Quare Christus tot dies & noctes ieiunaverit? Resp. 1. ut asperitate ieiunii Diabolum vinceret, qui primos homines vetiti cibi suavitate deceperat ac superaverat. Iren. lib. 5. cap. 18. p. 343. Ieiunavit Christus, ut haberet adversarius, ubi congrederetur. Quoniam enim in principio per escam non esuerientem hominem seduxit transgredi praeceptum DEI, in fine esuerientem non potuit dissuadere eam, quae à DEO esset, sustinere escam. Quae ergo fuit in Paradiso repletio hominis per duplicem gustationem, dissoluta est per eam, quae fuit in hoc mundo, indigentiam.

Ut quam Moses & Elias doctrinae fuae conciliaverat 40. dicrum ieiunio autoritatem Exod. 24. v. 18. & cap. 34. v. 28.Deut. 9. v. 9.1. Reg. 19. v. 8. eandem etiam hoc 40. dicrum & noctium ieiunio suae doctrinae conciliaret. Atque hac ratione Evangelium suum legi & Prophetis monstraret esse consentaneum.

3. Ut humanae Naturae in se veritatem demonstraret. Iren. d. l. Ieiunavit Christus diebus quadragint a similiter ut Moses, item Elias postea esuriit, ut hominem eum verum & firmum intelligamus, proprium enim est hominis ieiunantis esurire.

4. Ut suo exemplo temperantiam, abstinentiam ac pro ratione personarum, locorum &c. ieiunium nobis commendaret. Preces cum ieiunio coniunctae sunt firmum adversus Diaboli tentationes munimentum? *(Confer exempla veterum Christianorum Act. 13. 3.c. 14, 22.)*

Magnum ergo discrimen inter ieiunium Mosis & Eliae ex parte una, & Christi, ex parte altera. 1 Ieiunium Mosis & Eliae non est meritorium & satisfactorium, sicut Christi ieiunium. Illi enim fuere Ψιχοιαν θρωποι infirmitatibus carnis obnoxii, Christus verò est Θεάνρωπος ab omni peccati labe immunis.

2. Moses ad tolerandum 40. dierum ieiunium consortabatur praesentiâ & alloquio DEI, Exod. 34. v. 28. Elias fortitudine cibi ab Angelo allati 1. Reg. 19 v. 8. Christus propriâ divinitatis suae virtute assumtam humanam Naturam sustentavit, ne sub huius in ediae pondere fatisceret.

Pontisicii non contenti hisce finibus addunt, Christum suo exemple quadr agesimale ieiunium instituisse, unde canunt in suis templis tempore quadragesimae: Iesu quadr agenariae Dicator abstinentiae. Qui ob salutem mentium, Hoc sanxer as ieiunium. Lueas Brug. in h. l. Quadragenarius numerus poenitentiae servit & afflictioni, quem in ieiuniorum pro modulo nostro observantiâ voluisse Salvatorem exemplo suo nobis esse commendatum, Apostoli intellexerunt, autore Hieron. Epist. 54. ad Marcellam. Alph. de Castro lib. 8. adv. haeres. verbo ieiunium, haeres. 2. scribit, multos non insimae sortis, sed maximae autoritatis viros, eosa non recentes, sed vetustissimos autores affirmare, reiunium quadrage fimae à Christo institutum esse. *(Adducit verò in hanc rem Barradius t. 2. Comm. in Conc. Quat. Evang. l. 2. p. 61. loca quaedam ex Hieron. in c. 4. Matth. it. l. z. contra Iovinianum c. 11. D. Maxim. hom. 3. de Ieiun. Quadr. Chrysologo serm. 11. Ambros. serm. 34. August. epist. 119. c. 15.)* Staplet. in promt. Cathol. Dom. quadrag §. 1. Christum suo exemplo quadragesimam nobis commendasse, asserit. Anglo Remens. in h. l. ex Hieronymo afferunt dictum, Christum ieiun asse dies 40. ut suo exemplo nobis relinqueret solennes illos ieiuniorum dies.

Resp. 1. de institutione quadragesimae Pontificii non consentiunt. Quidam enim non Christo, sed Apostolis eam tribuunt. Nauclerus part. 2. generat. 2. Bellarmin. 2. de bon operib. cap. 14. Pererius disp. 31. in cap. 14. Ioh p. 414. Aphonsus de Castro d. l. Bailius in Catech. controv. tract. 2. q. 10. *(Diversitatem hanc Barradius d. l. conciliare conatur, monendo, Domini quidem esse exemplum quadragesimalis ieiunii; Apostolorum autem esse institutionem & traditionem.)*

Quidam verò ab Ecclesia quadragesimale ieiunium institutum esse, asserunt. Telesphoro enim eius institutio tribuitur c. statuimus dist. 4. apud Platinam in vita Telesphorif. 19. Polydor. Virgil. lib. 6. de rer. invent. cap. 3. Ecclesiae eam tribuunt Hosius in Confess. Petricov. cap. 4. Cornel. Iansenius in Harm. Evang. cap. 15. *(Cùm tamen plurimi veterum in eam descenderint sententiam, ut existimarint, Dominum ieiunio hoc suo quadragesimam dedicasse: Unde monendum porrò, quòd ieiunia certis diebus instituta minimè simpliciter improbentur, damnentur, vel reiiciantur. Vide paulò ante obs. 4. Attamen)* 2. ieiunium quadragesimale, prout in Papatu hodie servatur, improbamus propter corruptelas eidem adhaerentes. Primò ratione formae. Non enim definiunt ieiunium per abstinentiam à cibo & delitiis corporis, sed in solo cibo-um delectu illud constituunt. Secundo ratione finis. Ieiunant vel potiùs ieiunare se fingunt, ut pro peccatis satisfaciant & vitam aeternam mereantur. Tertiò ratione accidentis. Obtrudunt hoc ieiunium Ecclesiae sub opinione necessitatis, ut mortaliter peccare iudicetur, qui illis diebus non ieiunat, etiamsi alio tempore ieiunet; ex ieiunio faciunt cultum divinum; ex dispensationibus ieiuniorum faciunt meras pecuniarum nundinationes. 3. Opponimus ergo huic opinioni. Primò defectum mandati divini: nam nec Christus, nec Apostoli uspiam in Scripturis leguntur instituisse quadragesimam. Secundò veram de ieiunio doctrinam. quòd ieiunium per se & propter se non sit cultus DEI, sed tunc Deo probetur, quando coniungitur poenitentiae & orationi, h. e. si refertur ad hunc finem, ut caro coerceatur. Rom. 14. v. 17. 18.1. Cor. 8. v. 8.1. Tim. 4. v. 8.Hebr. 13. v. 9. Tertio libertatem Christianam. Quartò div-rsit atem ieiunandi in primitiva Ecclesia usitatam. *(Benè Chrysostomus homil. 47. in Matth. Non dixit ieiunium suum imitandum ised: discite à me, quia mitis sum, & humilis corde. Confer plura huc facientia apud B. Par. Consessionis Cathol. part. 3. speciali p. 983. seqq.)*

῞Γςερονέτεινασε. Ieiunium quadraginta dierum probat in Christo veritatem divinitatis; Esuries post illud ieiunium veritatem humanitatis. Esuriit autem non simpliciter Naturae necessitate, cum Naturae sit Dominus, sed libera voluntate. inde August. scribit, mirabilius in Christo fuisse, quod exactis 40. di-bus esuriit, quàm quod labentibus illis nil comedit.

Post diem quadragesimum, divinitate Christi assumtam humanitatem suae ipsius infirmitati relinquente, caepit humana Natura fame naturali corripi & cibum expetere.

## 4:3
v. 3. Και προσελΘων άυτω. Seizing the opportunity of tempting from the hunger of Christ, the Devil appears in visible form, because approaching belongs to bodily motion. Without doubt he had tried him variously throughout all the preceding 40. days, which Luke seems to intimate, ch. 4, 1.; but when he had accomplished nothing, and at last noticed that he was suffering from hunger, having assumed an external form, he attacked him. *(Let this passage be consulted entirely in B. D. Frantzius on the Interpreters of Scripture, p. 1062.)*

Ο πειραξων he who tempts. The participle has the force of a noun. By that word Satan is indicated, according to a usage not unusual in Holy Scripture. See 1. Thess. 3, 5. Now πειραξειν here means to explore treacherously, to entice maliciously. *(See 1. Chron. 21, 1., although it is also sometimes used in a good sense. However, the observation of Hugo Grotius is not unworthy of notice, that נחש among other things also signifies to tempt, and therefore from there descends the name נחש serpent, which furnished figure and name to the Devil, Gen. 3, 1. Rev. 12, 9. ch. 20. 2.; we are referred by this very name tempter, given to the Devil, to the Mosaic History described in Gen. 3. )*

Ει ύός εΙ του θεου, ειπέ. The imperative ειπέ is placed in this passage for ηέλσθε.; for among the Hebrews אמר is both to say and to command, Job 9, 7. because whenever God says something, He commands. *(Yet it pleases Hugo Grotius better that ειπέ τω θεω. be understood, Since indeed the ancient Writers do not deny, nor without weighty arguments, that the Devil recognized something greater than man in Christ at this time. Although however no Greek Codex so reads it, nor is that reading added either by the Syrian or by the Arabic or Ethiopic version: nevertheless it might seem, according to Grotius' opinion, to favor it, that, when even absolutely it is asked: Did the Devil know that Jesus was the Son of GOD? our countrymen commonly respond, that the Devil knew Jesus to be the son of GOD, not by certainty of knowledge, but by conjecture of firm opinion, and should be judged rather to suspect than to know. Compare B. Par. Coll. Isagog. Book 7. treatise latter, ch.) προσσιοροσμός

6. §. 18. If yet, though ever so much, the Devil conjecturally at least opined that Jesus was the Son of God—which is the view of many—nevertheless all the more by these very words that he wanted to test him can be said in this way: if by mere command or word he had turned stones into bread, it will be certain that he was the Son of GOD; therefore he did not say pray, but speak. As B. D. Chemnitius observes, Harm. Evang. cap. 19. p. 188. But more probably it is established that the Devil wished rather to cast Christ into distrust than that he himself feared being tested, as the B. Author warns shortly afterward in his discussion on Luke. Our countrymen's opinions are supported also because τό έιπέ comman- has this meaning here, see Camero in Myrotheco and Gatak. in Cinnus p. 333, likewise in the dissertation de Stilo N.T. p. 226, where he also disputes whether the Evangelist took such usage of this word from the Hebrews rather than from the Greeks.

Some call this temptation a temptation of gluttony. (For they write that this first temptation was the lust of the flesh, the second pride of life, the third lust of the eyes, 1. Ioh. 2. v. 16. But far loftier and subtler were those temptations with which Satan assailed Christ.) But it is said more correctly that it is a ptation of distrust: for with this venomous sarcasm the Devil solicits Christ toward distrust concerning the voice brought down from heaven. If you were the Son of GOD, God would not allow you, as His beloved Son, to be pressed by hunger. Therefore there was illusion and φάντασμα that voice brought down from heaven.

Franc. Lucas Brugensis: He explores thus, whether he is the Son of GOD, so that at the same time he may attempt to draw in other sins, and indeed to gluttony as the root of the others. For he solicits one afflicted by hunger to impatience of hunger, by which, distrusting that he is a care to GOD, he might himself prepare sustenance for himself by illicit means, complying with the Devil’s counsel and exerting his power untimely, so that he might satisfy the necessity of his belly, he might transmute the natures of things by a miracle, if he could, and, famished, might devour the received bread more greedily than is fitting. From which he attempts to evince against Calvin, that the first temptation was of gluttony.

Resp. 1. Brugiensis himself writes somewhat earlier: you may say, the Devil makes sport of that voice which formerly had been heard and understood by him from heaven: You are my beloved Son, which is what Chrysostom says together with his school. Certainly then the Devil solicits Christ not toward gluttony but toward distrust, so that since he sees himself pressed by hunger, he might throw away confidence and conclude neither that he is cared for by GOD nor that he is the son of GOD. 2. With the same temptation he attacked our first parents, attempting to draw them away from the word, so that he might plunge them headlong into the sin of unbelief. What therefore Brugiensis says, from there Satan began (his temptations against Christ) whence he had already conquered (the first parents;) this rather confirms our opinion. 3. Brugensis presupposes, that by this temptation the Devil wished to explore whether He were truly the Son of GOD. When by hunger, he says after Beda on Luke, he saw Him worn out and enduring mortal things of His humanity, everything which he had thought concerning His divinity came into doubt through his own pride of . In this way then, what he fears, he explores, whether Jesus be Christ the Son of GOD. But yet it was not unknown to the Devil, by the voice of the Father brought down from heaven, that Christ had been publicly proclaimed the Son of God; therefore he did not doubt about Him, but strove to cast Christ into doubt and distrust, as the very form of the words shows. 4. Thence Brugensis himself explains it thus παραφράζει. After you see that you are deserted by GOD the Father, necessity compels you to provide food for yourself; but in this place you are far removed from all supply of provisions, where nothing supports itself except stones. Therefore succor your necessity, if you can. Therefore indeed Satan wished to persuade Christ, by the argument of the hunger which He endured, that He was deserted by God, and consequently could not be the Son of GOD. 5. If Christ had done anything contrary to His calling out of impatience of hunger, He would have sinned through distrust. For He ought to have determined certainly to submit Himself to the divine will, and that He was under the care of God the Father, which also He did, in entirely vain attempt toward the distrust, to be conceived from the feeling of hunger, solicited by the Devil. 6. From Christ's answer it is evident that it was a temptation of distrust. Brugensis himself states it thus παραφράζει. By sacred doctrine we have truly received from promise, that those who obey believing in God ought not to doubt or be anxious in any difficulties of affairs, whatever present themselves in the exercise of obedience by faith, but to believe that the providence of GOD is most certain. And afterward. Since I have come here by the guidance of the Holy Ghost, I ought not, distrusting GOD, to wish to provide food for myself. Certainly, to whichever temptation faith is opposed, by that the Devil wished to assault trust.

Latin:

v. 3. Και προσελΘων άυτω. Ex esurie Christi tentandi occasionem captans Diabolus visibili formâ apparet, quia accedere pertinet ad motum corporalem. Procul dubio totis superioribus 40. diebus variè tētaverat, idq; innuere videtur Lucas c. 4, 1. sed cùm nihil profecisset, ac tandem esurie ipsum laborare animadvertisset, assumta formâ externâ eum aggressus est. *(Videatur omninò hîc B. D. Frantzius de Interpp. Scr. p. 1062.)*

Ο πειραξωνille qui tent at. Participium habet vim nominis. Indicatur voce illâ Satan, more Scr. S. non inusitato. Vid. 1. Thes. 3, 5. Est autem πειραξειν h. l. infidiosè explorare, admalum solicitare. *(Vid. 1. Paral. 21, 1. quamvis etiam aliquando in bonam partem adhibeatur. Notatu verò non indigna est observatio Hug. Grotii, quod נחש inter alia etiam tentare significet, cùm itaque inde descendat nomen נחשserpens, qui Diabolo figuram & nomen praebuit, Gen. 3, 1.Apoc. 12, 9. c. 20. 2. remittimur hoc ipso tentatoris nomine, Diabolo tributo, ad Historiam Mosaicam Gen. 3. descriptam.)*

Ει ύός εΙ του θεου, ειπέ. Imperativus ειπέ ponitur hoc loco pro ηέλσθε. Hebraeis enim אמר est dicere & iubere,Iob. 9, 7. quia quando Deus aliquid dicit, imperat. *(Hugoni tamen Grotio magis arridet, ut intelligatur ειπέ τω θεω.Siquidem constanter, nec sine magnis argumentis negent antiqui Scriptores, Diabolum maius aliquid homine in Christo hoc tempore agnovisse. Licet verò nullus Codex Graecus ita compleat, nec addatur quoq; iste προσσιοροσμός s. à Syro s. ab Arabe vel Aethiope: videri tamen posset, pro Grotii sententiâ facere, quòd, quando etiam absolutè quaeritur: An Diabolus cognoverit, Iesum esse Filium DEI? respondeant nostrates communiter, quòd noverit Diabolus, Iesum esse DEI filium, non per certitudinem scientiae, sed per coniecturam opinionis firmae, ac magis suspicari, quàm nosse censendus sit. Conf. B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. 7. tr. poster. c.

6. §. 18. Si tamen vel maximè Diabolus coniecturaliter saltem, quae multorum sententia est, opinatus est, Iesum esse Filium Dei, nihilominùs eo magis his ipsis verbis explorare eum voluisse, dici potest, an Iesus verè esset Filius DEI, hác ratione: si-solo iussu seu verbo lapides in panes converterit, certum erit, ipsum esse Filium DEI; ideò non inquit, ora, sed dic. Uti observat B. D. Chemn. Harm, Evang. cap. 19. p. 188. Sed probabiliùs statuitur, quòd Diabolus Christum potiùs in diffidentiam coniicere voluerit, quàm quod ipse timuerit, explorare, ut paulò pòst B. Autor circa Franc. Lucae discursum monet. Adstipulantur verò sententiae nostratiū, quòd τό έιπέiuben-- significationem hoc loco habeat, Camero in Myroth. ac Gatak. in Cinno p. 333. item in dissert. de Stylo N T. p. 226. ubi etiam disputat, an ab Ebraeis potiùs, quàm à Graecis talem usum istius verbi sumseriEvangelista.

Hanc tentationem quidam dicunt esse tentationem gulae. (Scribunt enim, primam hanc tentationem fuisse concupiscentiam carnis, alteram superbiam vitae, tertiam concupiscentiam ocusorum,1. Ioh. 2. v. 16. Sed longè sublimiores ac subtiliores fuerunt hae tentationes, quibus Satan Christum aggressus est.) Sed rectiùs dicitur, quòd sit -entatio diffidentiae: hoc enim virulento sarcalmo Diabolus Christum solicitat ad diffidentiam de voce caelitus prolatâ. Si esses Filius DEI, Deus non permitteret, te, ut pote dilectum suum Filium, fame premi. Ergo fuit illusio acφάντασμαvox illa caelitus delata.

Franc. Lucas Brugensis: Ita explorat, ansit Filius DEI, ut simul avaria peccata conetur per-rahere & quidem ad gulam ut caeterorum raditem. Nam fame afflictum ad famis impatientiam solicitat, quâ diffisus se DEO curae esse, ipse sibi illicitis modis victum paret, Diaboli confilio morem gerens & potentiam intempestivè exsertans, rerum Naturas, ut ventris necessitati satisfaciat, miraculo transmutet, si possit, & acceptum panem avidiùs quàm par sit, famelicus voret. Ex quo contra Calvinum evincere eonatur, primam tentationem fuisse gulae.

Resp. 1. Brugensis ipse paulò ante scribit: dicas, Diabolum alludere ad vocem eam, quae pridem caelitus ipsi audita fuerit & intellecta: Tues Filius meudilectus, id quòd dicit cum sua schola Chrysostomus. Utiq; ergo Diabolus Christum non ad gulam, sed ad diffidentiam, solicitat, ut quia se fame premi videt, fiduciam abiiciat, ac statuat, nec se DEO curae esse, nec se DEI filium esse. 2. Eâdem tentatione primos parentes aggressus est, à verbo eos abducere conatus, ut in peccatum incredulitatis ageret praecipites. Quod ergo Brugensis dicit, inde coepit Satanas (suas adversus Christum tentationes) unde iam vicerat (primos parentes,) illud nostram potiùs confirmat sententiam. 3. Brugensis praesupponit, Diabolum hac tentatione voluisse explorare, an verè sit DEI Filius. Cùm fame, inquit ex Beda in Lucam, ipsum confectum cerneret & mortalia perpeti humanitatis videret, omne quod de eius divinitate opinatus fuerat, ipsi fastu suae superbiin dubium venit. Hoc itaa, quod timet, explorat, an Iesus sit Christus Filius DEI. Atqui Diabolo non erat ignotum per vocem Patris coelitus delatam, Christum publicè renunciatum esse DEI Filium, de eo ergo non dubitabat, sed Christum in dubitationem ac diffidentiam coniicere satagebat, ut ipsa verborum forma ostendit. 4. Inde Brugensis ipse ea sic παραφράζει.Postquam vides, te à DEO Patre deseri, necessitas cogit, ut tibi ipse de victu prospicias, hoc autem loco procules ab omni commeatus copia, ubi nihil praeter lapides suppetit. Succurre igitur necessitatituae, si potes. Utique ergo Satanas Christo persuadere voluit, argumento famis, quam sustinebat, quòd sit à Deo desertus, ac proinde non possit esse DEI Filius. 5. Si Christus ex impatientia famis quidquam contra suam vocationem egisset, diffidentiâ peccasset. Divinae enim voluntati se submittere, seque Deo Patri curae esse certò statuere debuit, quod etiam fecit, frustraneo planè conatu ad diffidentiam, ex sensu famis concipiendam, â Diabolo sollicitatus. 6. Ex Christi responso manifestum, quòd fuerit tentatio diffidentiae. Brugensis ipse illud sic παραφράζει.Sacrâ doctrinâ illud verè accepimus promissi, eos qui Deo credentes oboediunt, non oportere dubitare aut solicitos esse in ullis rerum difficult atibus, quaecuna in oboedientiae fideia exercitatione se offerant, sed credere, certissimam esse DEI providentiam. Et postea. Cùm Spiritus S. ductu huc venerim, non debeo DEO diffisus mihi ipse velle de cibprovidere. Certè cui tentationi fides opponitur, per illa voluit Diabolus fiduciam expugnare.

## 4:4
v. 4. The Devil had acted with human reasons, Christ fights with the arms of Sacred Scripture.

Man lives not by bread alone. To live by the word of GOD, Maldon. &

Franc. Lucas Brug. explain by metonymy of cause for effect, namely for In whatsoever matter God shall have commanded. Man's life can please GOD in whatsoever matter and after whatsoever manner. Salmerón takes it metaphorically concerning the food of the soul.

The Hebrews say. The Law is the food of the soul, and the food of the soul is the word of the law. (How these words, Not by bread alone &c., which Christ brings forward from Deut. 8, 3., are to be understood, is expounded at length in Comment. in Deut. p. 516. seqq., where among other things he says that this is the proper and genuine sense of the said saying: The Israelites in the desert laboured under want of bread, but because, following the calling of GOD and the word that had gone forth from his mouth, they had betaken themselves into the desert, therefore God did not allow them to die of famine, but gave them manna from heaven, that from the miraculous feeding they might understand that God is not bound to second causes, but is able even without food to sustain man, just as he sustained Moses on mount Sinai, and Elijah and Christ in the desert for 40 days without food; and is able also to sustain men through some other means than through usual and common bread, just as he fed the Israelites for 40 years with manna rained down from heaven in the desert.)

Ζήσεζαι. By the usage of the Hebrews the future is put for the present, as also the Syrian version has, for it renders It is an enallage of force, to signify something more, as if he is wont to live, or can live, whether the future is to be taken for the potential mood.

But by every word, that proceedeth out of the mouth of GOD. Heb. by every outgoing of the mouth of GOD. i.e., by everything which shall have gone forth from the mouth of GOD, or which God has constituted and decreed.

Observ. The Devil had said, If thou art the Son of GOD. Christ answers: Not by bread alone does man live. Bread or other food is not absolutely necessary for man in order that he may live, much less for the Son of GOD.

They are the words of Moses to the Israelites, whom God had sustained for forty years in the desert with manna rained down from heaven.

Latin:

v. 4. Diabolus egerat rationibus humanis, Christus pugnat Sacrae Scripturae armis.

Non solo pane vivit homo. Vivere ex verbo DEI, Maldon. &

Franc. Lucas Brug. exponunt per metonymiam causae pro effectu, videlicet pro quacuna re, quam iusserit Deus. Ali potest hominis vita quacunque re & quocunque modo DEO placuerit. Salmero metaphoricè accipit de cibo animae.

Hebraei dicunt. Lex est cibus animae, & cibus animae est ver legem. *(Quomodo verba haec: Non solo pane &c. quae Christus ex Deut. 8, 3. adducit, intelligēda sint, prolixè exponit B. Par. Coment. in Deut. p. 516. seqq. ubi inter alia dicit, hunc esse proprium & genuinum dicti sensum. Israelitae in deserto laborabant penuriâ panis, sed quia vocationem DEI & verbum, quod ex ore eius egressum erat, secuti in desertum concesserant, ideò Deus non permisit illos fame mori, sed manna è coelo ipsis dedit, ut ex miraculosâ cibatione intelligerent, Deum non esse alligatum causis secundis, sed posse etiam sine cibo hominem sustentare, sicut Mosen in monte Sinai, & Eliam ac Christum in deserto per 40. dies sine cibo sustentavit; ac posse etiam per aliud quoddam medium, quàm per panem usualem & communem homines sustentare, sicut Israelitas per 40. annos mannâ coelitus depluto in deserto cibavit)*

Ζήσεζαι. More Hebraeorum futurum ponitur pro praesente. quomodo etiam Syrus habet, reddit enim Vis enallages est, ut significet aliquid amplius, q. d. Vivere solet, vel potest, ufuturum accipiatur pro modo potentiali.

Sed in omni verbo, quòd procedit de ore DEI. Hebr. de omni exitu oris DEI. h. e. omni eo, quod egressum fuerit ex ore DEI, sive quod Deus constituerit & decreverit.

Observ. Diabolus dixerat, si Filius DEI es. Christus respondet: N-n in solo pane vivit homo. Non est homini, ut vivat, absolutè necessarius panis vel alius cibus, multò minùs Filio DEI.

Sunt verba Mosis ad Israēlitas, quos Deus per quadraginta annos in deserto manna coelitus depluto sustentaverat.

## 4:5
v. 5. παραλαμβάνει leads away with him, carries over thence what was received. (See on this idiom B. Glass. Gramm. S. p. 229 seqq. Mr. Dilherr. Disp. Acad. tom. 1. p. 475.) In the order of the temptations Matthew and Luke seem to differ. But because Matthew employs particles of order, it must be said that a sure order was marked by himself, (but not by Luke: Jacobus Faber Stapulensis indeed delivers -s, Codices with certain ancients hold the same order of temptations in Luke as Matthew holds, so that the change of order, which exists in Luke, might seem to have arisen from the fault of the writers But since the most approved Greek Codices confirm the received reading, with the assent likewise added both of Latin Codices and of the Eastern versions, the Syrian, the Arabic, the Ethiopian, it is perilous σφάγμα λραφιηον to decide thus against so many Codices. It is therefore better to say that Luke mentioned the temptations in the order in which they presented themselves, while Matthew did so in the order in which they took place. Nor does anything thereby fall away from the authority of the Evangelists. For Augustine rightly warns in Book 2 De consensu Evangelistarum ch. 16., that nothing touches the substance of the matter, nor does anything perish from the truth, because one Evangelist sets forth the same teachings in different words and sometimes in a different order than another, provided it be plain that all those things which are written actually happened. See further material with Mr. D. Walther in his Harmony of the Bible. Yet the Jesuit Cornelius à Lapide makes the convenient observation that here the order of the temptations corresponds to the natural course of temptations, namely that a passage be made from gluttony to vain glory. Thus, he says, even today novices are wont first to be tempted in respect of faith and religion by gluttony and the stings of the flesh; when these are overcome, the temptation of vainglory follows next. For carnal men are prone to gluttony, whereas lofty and spiritual men are prone to pride. Against the boast of the Papists, that monastic life is a state of perfection, this confession ought to be set in opposition; on which topic B. Par. treats at length in the Confessio Catholica tom. 3. p. 227. sqq.)* Theophylact on Mark ch. 4. fol. 16. ed. Gr. infers from the word Παραγαμβάνειν that this was done αιοθητως, in such wise that the Devil brought Christ down through the air. Chrysostom: Concerning Christ being taken up and borne about, do not reflect on the power of the devil, but on the patience of the Son of GOD, who humbled Himself for our sake.

Gregory. It is not a wonder if Christ permitted himself to be transported by the Devil, who permitted himself to be lifted onto the cross by the members of the Devil.

Certain ones *(such as Euthymius, Anselm, Maldonatus and several others)* maintain, that Christ was taken up by the Devil in that manner in which Matth. 7. v. 1. the Apostles are said to be taken up by Christ, i.e. led, using which word to lead Luke speaks in the description of this temptation. But if the Devil led Christ out of the desert near Jericho to Jerusalem, and from there onto some exceedingly high mountain, this journey would not have been of a single day only. And what shall we reply to the point that the Devil himself stationed Jesus upon the pinnacle of the temple. *(More correctly concur those who say, That Christ was snatched out of the desert through the airs onto the pinnacle of the temple. And thus expound Jerome, Gregory, the Author of the Opus Imperfectum, the Glossa, Thomas 3. p. q. 41 a. 4. ad 7. Cornelius à Lapide, Tirinus, others. But farther off from the truth still go those who hold that there was at least an imaginary translation, i.e. one wrought either by an alteration of the fancy, or by a representation, whereby an outward appearance was set before the outer senses and the gaze, so that, as it appeared, the Savior himself seemed to stand upon the top of the temple and upon the crest of the mountain, beneath which lay spread the image of the splendor of the temporal kingdoms. Yet surely, if a leading forth done even by mere fancy is granted, anyone may grant the same of the fasting and the conference, yea of the whole temptation. Which is perilous, if not reckless. And how could there have been laid upon Christ the command that he cast himself down κάτω v. 6. if he had not beforehand truly been set ανω;? It is unbecoming moreover to believe that the devil so falsely mocked the fancy of Christ, especially since over the inner man of Christ the devil possessed no power, as Cornelius à Lapide rightly observes. He too cautions that such imaginary translations oftentimes belong to witches, while they seem to themselves to be carried away by the Devil, whereas in very deed they are not carried away, but the Devil makes sport of their imagination, so that they only imagine this and dream it. Markedly, however, Cornelius says oftentimes such are of witches translations—for neither does it seem deniable that at times witches are truly conveyed from place to place by the Devil. And this is proven 1. from the condition of the properties. For the devil is a sturdy spirit, the Prince of the air, Eph. 2, 2. Compare Iob. 1, 7. 2. from the contrary working of the good Angels, as the example of Habakkuk teaches, Supplement Dan. 14, 35. and Philip Act. 8, 39. 3. from the attestation of the present example. Where nevertheless it must be marked that in Christ taken up and borne about, not ought to be assigned to the power of the devil, but to the patience of the Son of GOD, who for our sake humbled himself, that for our sake he might overcome our adversary. See B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. de Ang. Mal. c. 6. §. 7. B. D. Bald. Cas. Cons. p. 735. seqq. Comm. in 2. Cor. c. u. p. 720. B. D. -ònig Append. Caf. Cons. cas. 2. p. 39. seqq. That however witches are at times truly carried through the airs, sundry examples plainly confirm beyond the aforementioned authors, Martin Delrio, Jesuit and likewise Professor of Theology in the University of Salamanca, book 5. Disquis. Magic. sect. 3. pag. 708. seqq.

To these let there further be added Camerar. Cent. 1. Horar. subcis. c. 72. Bodinus in De Magorum Daemonomania praefat. p. 28. likewise l. 2. c. 5. Don Franciscus Torreblanca Villalpandus l. 2. Daemonol. c. 36. Thom. de Aquino 2. 2. q. 92. & 93. l. 3. contra Gent. c. 104. & 105. Franc. Victoria in his relection on Magic q. 7. Annan. l. 4. on the nature of daemons. Guil. Paris. in the Summa de Univers. near the end c. 23. Cardin. Turrecremata c. Episc. h. 26. q. 5. Simanca on Catholic instruction t. 37. Mart. Alpizqueta, called Navarrus, in the Manuale c. 11. n 38. Damhauder. in the Praxis chapter 61. Nic. Remig. l. 1. Daemonol. c. 14. 29. 29. 74. Franc. Peña in the Directory of Inquisitors part. 2. com. 68. Ronsaeus on sicknesses from poisonings l. 2. c. 8. l. 3. c. 8. Caesalpinus his book on investigating daemons c 20. Grillandus, on Sorcery q. 4. n. 26. Pet. Binsfeld. in the Confessions of malefactors m. 1. Concl. 12. Spina on witches c. 17. seqq. Tanner. Scholastic Theology t. 3. p. 994. and others.) *

Christ did not use the Devil's craft to travel, but permitted himself to be carried by the free choice of the Devil who was tempting him of his own accord.

From Luke it is established that Jerusalem must be understood. It is called the holy city 1. on account of the holy worship of GOD, for which it was destined. 2. on account of the holy seed or certain holy remnants, whom God kept for himself in this city. έις την άγιαν πόλιν.

Jerome on chapter 27 of Matthew & in Letter 150 to Hedibia question 8. We ought to take the holy city Jerusalem by way of distinguishing all cities, which then served idols, for in this one alone was there the temple & the worship of one GOD & true religion. *(See also B. D. Glassius, Sacred Grammar, p. 9. Now this title is common, by which Jerusalem is designated also in Isaiah ch. 48, 2. cf. I Chronicles 9, 17. below ch. 27, 53. Dan. 9, 6.Apoc 11, 2. There are also extant coins marked with Hebrew letters, such as I myself possess one and another, which display on one side these words surrounding a censer; on the other however these i.e. Holy Jerusalem, surrounding the rod of Aaron. Indeed older ones than these are found, as Waser reports l. de num. Ebr. p. 72. with an inscription indeed on one side this: but on the other . But Philo too in Against Flaccus calls it by the same word ιέροπολιν ηαθ ισρυζαι ότού ύφιςού θεού νεως αγιος. Moreover concerning the very city of Jerusalem somewhat more may be seen in Villalpandus on Ezekiel, Adrichomius in the Description of the Holy Land, Heidmannus on Palestine ch. 2.)*

Το πτερύγιον ρού ιερού is the wing of the temple, that is, that parapet with which the flat roof of the temple was surrounded, lest anyone fall off. Deut. 22. v. 8. Beza. *(So also Grotius decides on this passage, likewise D. -ònig App. Cas. Cons. p. 43.)*

Some understand it of the very highest pinnacle of the temple, or on the crest of the tower of the temple. It was, says Franc. Lucas Brug., on the front face of the inner temple, embracing the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies, which by itself bore the appearance of the form of a house covered over, namely a vestibule, built in the shape of a tower, one hundred and twenty cubits high. Upon the crest of this vestibule the Devil set Jesus, so that if Jesus had slipped and fallen, he would have dropped into the court of the Priests, between the temple and the altar,Matt. 23. v. 35.that is, between the vestibule and the altar,Joel 2. v. 17.while the Priests and all the peoples looked on who had come together for the divine worship. *(Others too may be seen on this matter, both Corn. à Lapide and Adamus Conzenius, Comm. on this passage, p. 63, where he also furiously inveighs against our doctrine of justification by faith alone, and likewise of the certainty of salvation and election; and he compares it with that confidence or rather recklessness to which the devil here solicited Christ. Now this is the common complaint of the Papists, that it is vain and an unrighteous accusation has long ago been shown by our own writers. Let him consult at least B. Par. Dispp. Academ. p. 429. 430. 451. 460. 472. 687. 735. 954. and elsewhere. Furthermore, nothing avails for pilgrimages to the places of the saints, that Jerusalem is here called the holy city, as is shown elsewhere. See B. Par. L. de Morte §. 137. Comm. in Post. Epist. Petri p. 127.)*

Latin:

v. 5. παραλαμβάνειsecum abducit, inde acceptum transfert. *(Vid. de hoc idiotismo B. Glass. Gramm S p 229 seqq. Dn. Dilherr. Disp. Acad. t. 1. p. 475.)* In ordine tentationum videntur Matthaeus & Lucas discrepare. Sed quia Matthaeus particulas ordinis adhibet, ideò dicendum, quòd ab ipso certus ordo fuerit annotatus, *(à Luca verò non: Tradit quidem Iac. Faber Stapulen. -s, antiquos quosdam Codd. in Lucâ eundem habere ordinem tentationum, quem habet Matthaeus, ut ordinìs mutatio, quae in Lucâ est, videri possit accidisse ex Scriptorum viti-. At enim cùm Codd. Graeci probatissimi receptam lectionem confirment, accedente quoque tum Codd. Latinorum, tum Interpp. Orientalium Syri, Arabis, AEthiopis applausu, periculosum estσφάγμα λραφιηονin tot Codd. statuere. Satius igitur est, dicere, quôd Lucas eo ordine tentationes commemoraverit, quô occurrerent, Matthaeus verò eo, quo acciderunt. Nec per hoc quicquam autoritati Evangelistarum decedit. Rectè enim August. l. 2. de consens. Evang. c. 16. monet, ad summam rei nihil interesse, nec aliquid deperire veritati, quòd unus Evangelista easdem sententias aliis verbis & alio interdum ordine, quàm alter explicat, dum manifestum sit, omnia illa, quae scribuntur, esse facta. Vid. plura apud Dn. D. Walth. in Harm. Bibl. Commodè verò observat Iesuita Corn. à Lapide, quòd hic tentationum ordo naturae tentationum sit congruus, ut à gulâ sc. fiat transitus ad vanam gloriam. Sic, inquit, etiamnum Novitii & fide & religione primò tentari solent gulâ & carnis stimulis, quibus super atis succedit tentatio vanae gloriae. gulae enim obnoxii sunt homines carnales, superbiae verò excelsi & spirituales. Opponenda confessio haec gloriationi Pontificiorum, quòd Monachatus sit status perfectionis. de quo themate agit prolixè B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. 3. p. 227. seqq.)* Theoph. in c. 4. Marc. f. 16. ed. Gr. ex voce Παραγαμβάνειν colligit, hoc factum esse αιοθητως, ita ut Diabolus in aëre Christum deduxerit. Chrysostomus: In assumto & circumducto Christo non cogites diaboli potentiam, sed filii DEI patientiam, qui propter nos se humiliavit.

Gregorius. Non est mirum, si Christus permisit, se transportari à Diabolo, qui permisit, se in crucem levari à membria Diaboli.

Quidam *(uti Euthymius, Anselmus, Maldonatus & nonnulli alii)* statuunt, -hristum à Diabolo fuisse assumtum eo modo, quo Matth. 7. v. 1. Apostoli dicuntur â Christo assumti i. e. ducti, quo ducendi verbo Lucas in descriptione huius tentationis utitur. Sed si Christum Diabolus ex deserto Hierichunti vicino Hierosolymam, & inde in montem aliquem altissimum duxit, nō fuit hoc iter unius duntaxat diei. Et quid dicemus ad id, quod Diabolus ipse Iesum statuerit super pinnaculum templi. *(Rectiùs ergsentiunt, qui dicunt, quòd Christus ex deserto raptus fuerit per aëra in pinnaculum templi. & ita exponunt Hieronymus, Gregorius, Autor Op. Imperf. Glossa, Thomas 3. p. q. 41 a. 4. ad 7. Corn. à Lapide, Tirinus, alii. Longiùs verò adhuc à vero abeunt, qui statuunt imaginariam saltem translationem, h. e. quae vel per immutationē phantasiae facta, vel per repraesentationem, quâ sensibus exterioribus & obtutui externa species obiecta, ut apparuerit, qs. consisteret ipse Salvator in fastigio templi & in vertice montis, cui subiecta imago magnificentiae regnorum temporalium. At enim, si ductio per phantasian saltem facta statuitur, potest aliquis idem de ieiunio & colloquio, imò de totâ tentatione statuere. Id quod periculosum, si non temerarium. Et quomodo iniungi potuisset Christo, ut se deiiceret κάτω v. 6. si non priùs verè fuisset collocatus ανω; Indignum insuper est, credere, diabolum tam falsò illusisle phantasiae Christi, praesertim cùm in interiora Christi diabolus nullam habuerit potestatem, uti rectè notat Corn. à Lapide. qui etiam monet, tales imaginarias translationes saepè esse sagarum, dum videntur sibi transferri à Diabolo, cùm reverà non transferantur, sed Diabolus imaginationi illarum illudat, ut tantùm id imaginentur & somnient. Notanter autem Cornelius dicit, sepè tales esse sagarum translationesneque enim negandum videtur, quandoque verè de loco in locum à Diabolo Sagas transportari. Idque probatur 1. ex proprietatum conditione. est enim diabolus spiritus robustus, Princeps aëris, Eph. 2, 2. Conf. Iob. 1, 7. 2. ex opposità Angelorum bonorum operatione, ceu exemplum Habacuci, Suppl. Dan. 14, 35. & Philippi Act. 8, 39. docent. 3. ex praesentis exempli testificatione. Ubi tamen notandum, quòd in adsumto & circumducto Christo non cogi-anda sit diaboli potentia, sed Filii DEI patientia, qui propter nos sese humiliavit, ut propter nos adversarium nostrum vinceret. Vid. B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. de Ang. Mal. c. 6. §. 7. B. D. Bald. Cas. Cons. p. 735. seqq. Comm. in 2. Cor. c. u. p. 720. B. D. -ònig Append. Caf. Cons. cas. 2. p. 39. seqq. Quòd verò Sagae quandoque reverà per aēra transportentur, aliquot exemplis luculenter praeter dictos autores confirmat Martinus Delrio, Iesuita idemque in Acad. Salmant. Theol. Profess. lib. 5. Disquis. Magic. sect. 3. pag. 708. seqq.

Addantur quoque Camerar. Cent. 1. Horar. subcis. c. 72. Bodinus in de Magorum Daemonomania praefat. p. 28. it. l. 2. c. 5. Don Franciscus Torreblanca Villalpandus l. 2. Daemonol. c. 36. Thom. de Aquino 2. 2. q. 92. & 93. l. 3. contra Gent. c. 104. & 105. Franc. Victoria in relect. de Magia q. 7. Annan. l. 4. de nat. daemon. Guil. Paris. in summa de Univers. p. fin. c. 23. Cardin. Turrecr. c. Episc. h. 26. q. 5. Simanca de Cathol. instit. t. 37. Mart. Alpizqueta, dictus Navarrus in Manuali c. 11. n 38. Damhauder. in Praxi cap. 61. Nic. Remig. l. 1. Daemonol. c. 14. 29. 29. 74.
