Binsfeld. in Confess. malefic. m. 1. Concl. 12. Spina de strig. c. 17. seqq. Tanner. Theol. Schol. t. 3. p. 994. & alii.)*

Non utebatur Christus operâ Diaboli, ut veheretur, sed Diaboli ultrò id tentantis se permisit arbitrio.

έις την άγιαν πόλιν. Ex Luca constat, intelligendam esse Hierosolymam. Dicitur illa civitas sancta 1. propter sanctum DEI cultum, cui erat destinata. 2. propter semen sanctum sive sanctas quasdam reliquas, quas Deus in hac urbe sibi servabat.

Hieron. in cap. 27. Matth. & in Epist. 150. ad Hedibiam q. 8. Sanctam civitatem Hierosolymam debemus accipere ad distinctionem omnium civitatum, quae tunc idolis serviebant, in hac enim sola fuit templum & unius DEI cultus & vera religio. *(Vide etiam B. D. Glassium Gram. Sacr. p. 9. Est autem titulus iste communis, quo & apud Esaiam c. 48, 2. designatur Ierusalem. add. I, Paral. 9, 17. infrâ c. 27, 53. Dan. 9, 6.Apoc 11, 2. Extant quoque numismata, litteris Ebraeis insignita, cuiusmodi & ipse unum atque alterum possideo, quae in uno latere sistunt has voces thuribulum ambientes; in altero verô istas i. e. Ierusalem Sancta, virgam Aaronis cingentes. Quin antiquiores his inven-ri, Waserus proditl. de num. Ebr. p. 72. cum inscriptione ab altero quidem latere istâ: ab altero autem . Sed & Philo in Flaccum eandem vocat ιέροπολιν ηαθ ισρυζαι ότού ύφιςού θεού νεως αγιος. Caeterùm de ipsa Hierosol. urbe pluscula videantur apud Villalpandum in Ezech. Adrichom, in deser. terr. Sanctae, Heidman. in Palaest. c. 2.)*

Το πτερύγιον ρού ιερού est ala templi h. e. ambitus ille, quo planum templi tectum cingebatur, ne quis decideret. Deut. 22. v. 8. Beza. *(Ita etiā statuit Grotius in h. l. it. D. -ònig App. Cas. Cons. p. 43.)*

Quidam accipiunt de summo templi fastigio, five in cacumine turris templi. Erat, inquit Franc. Lucas Brug. in anteriori facie templi interioris, complectentis sanctum & sanctum sanctorum, quod solum --ctopertum domûs formam referebat,vestibulum, in turris formam aedificatum centum viginti cubitis altum. In huius vestibuli cacumine statuit Diabolus Iesum, unde si defiliisset Iesus, delapsus fuisset in atrium Sacerdotum, inter templum & altare,Matth. 23. v. 35.scu-nter vestibulum & altare,Ioël. 2. v. 17.cernentibus Sacerdotibus & populis universis, qui ad rem divinam convenerant. *(Pluribus etiam hâc de re videri potest tum Corn. à Lapide, tum Adamus Conzenius Comm. h. l. p. 63. ubi etiam vehementer invehitur in doctrinam nostram de fide solâ iustificante, itemque de salutis & electionis certitudine. comparatque eam cum eâ confidentia vel temeritate, ad quam diabolus Christum hîc solicitavit. Est autem communis haec Pontificiorum querela, quam tamē vanam esse, & iniquam accusationem, dudum à nostratibus ostensum. Videatur saltem B. Par. Dispp. Academ. p. 429. 430. 451. 460. 472. 687. 735. 954. & alibi. Nihil porrò facit pro peregrinationibus ad loca sanctorum, quod Ierusalem hîc civitas sancta vocatur, uti alibi ostenditur. Vid. B. Par. L. de Morte §. 137. Comm. in Post. Epist. Petri p. 127.)*

## 4:6
v. 6. Βάλε ςεαυτον, cast thyself down. This temptation was of vain confidence. If thou art the Son of GOD and that promised Messiah, hurl thyself headlong from the height, so that men, seeing this miracle, may believe thee to be the Messiah, and by this means thou wilt be able to win for thyself a great name. Since indeed thou hangest upon the providence of GOD in such wise that even amid utter want of all things thou dost not doubt that thou canst be sustained by him even without bread, cast thyself downward, that thou mayest show still more that thou dependest upon his providence.

Observation 1. The Devil can persuade one to leap down headlong, but he cannot throw one down unless willing. *(This observation is confirmed by the example of Jerome in Cassian, Collations 2, chapter 4.)* *(Observation 2. Because the Devil fell down out of heaven into hell, he strives also to drag others down to the same depths; but lift up your hearts, where Christ is. Compare John 8, 23.Phil. 3, 20.)*

He was conquered by Christ with the weapons of Scripture. Therefore he wishes to seem to use those very same against Christ. Ιέλραπτολ γαρ.

Vincent of Lérins: What will wretched little men do here, since the Lord himself assailed him with testimonies of the Scriptures?

David speaks not in the singular but in the plural: he commanded his Angels, because a godly man has many Angels appointed for his guardianship Ps. 34.1. Reg. 6. v. 17. *(The question belongs here too, Whether some certain Angel be destined as guardian for each godly man: on which see B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. de Angel. c. 8. §. 8. Some things will also be noted at Act. 12, 15)

Προσσιοροσμόν The Devil omits in all thy ways. Because it was contrary to his own purpose. *(Bernard on the Psalms, sermon 14 on Who dwelleth: What did he command? namely what follows in the Psalm: To guard thee in all thy ways. Surely not in precipitous places? could anyone send down such paths from the pinnacle of the temple? This is not a way, but a fall. Compare the same on Ps. 90. sermon 12; and concerning the guarding of Angels let there be seen many excellent sayings of the Fathers in the Practical Aphorisms under the title 'the custody of Angels'. Rightly moreover Cornelius à Lapide on this passage, Ignatius Der Kennis Jesuit, tr. de Angelis Disp. 6. c. 3. §. 1. p. 520, other Papists together with the Schoolmen (See Thomas p. 1. q. 113. a. 4. Alensis 2. sent. dist. 11.), indeed even the Fathers Chrysostom, Jerome and Hilary on this passage, deny that Christ had guardian Angels in the days of his flesh. The reasons of the Schoolmen are briefly recounted by B. Par. Coll. Isag. L de Angel. c. 8. §. 6. Accordingly the gloss of the Socinians must be rejected, who hold that Christ, though he had no need of the help of Angels for his salvation, nevertheless needed, or at least might have needed them for his defense, namely so that they might drive away the wild beasts which Satan had gathered together to terrify Christ. See Valentinus Smalcius Ref. monstr. p. 92, likewise ref. l. 2. de Err. Arian. p. 216. Crellius Comm. on this passage p. 250. But truly he who without the aid of Angels could repel the hellish lion and conquer him, much more could protect himself from wild beasts without any working of Angels. Isidore of Pelusium book 4. epistle 164. to John the Deacon, on that text 'Thou shalt not tempt': To one brought into danger, but not tempting, God promised that he would bring help; to one placed in necessity, but not making a show of himself and pursuing empty glory. For I do not yet say that the writer of the Psalms uttered that saying not about myself, του καὶ ἄγγελοι χρηζουσιν, by whose operation and help the very Angels themselves have need, so far am I from needing them (thus emphatically and correctly transfers it I C. έγγηνιηωζτος, Conradus Rittershusius) but about a just man. Moreover Chrysostom, Jerome, Hilary on this passage confirm the aforementioned exposition of Isidore, likewise Origen, homily 24 on Luke, and Nazianzen Oration on Baptism, teaching that the devil falsely cites Holy Scripture here: for in that place it speaks of pure men, not of Christ θενθρωπω. Since he had no guardian Angel as other men have, because the Guardian of his humanity was his very Divinity itself. Meanwhile we by no means deny that the devil gathered together wild animals of every kind, lest Christ could be torn apart by them. For Mark clearly hints at this when mentioning this temptation ch. 1, 12. If you please, see B. D. Franzius, Scholae Sacrif. Disp. 13. §. 71. seqq. p. 377.)

-πι χοιρων αρουσι σε they shall bear thee up in their hands. It is a metaphor of careful guardianship, taken from those who lift some burden onto their shoulders to carry it.

Latin:

v. 6. Βάλε ςεαυτον,proiice teipsum. Tentatio hac erat vanae confidentiae. Si es filius DEI & promissus ille Messias, è sublimi te praecipitem mitte, ut homines miraculum hoc videntes credant, te esse Messiam, hac ratione magnum nomen tibi comparare poteris. Quando quidem ita pendes à DEI providentia, ut ne in summa quidem omnium rerum penuriâ dubites, te ab illo etiam sine pane sustentari posse, deorsum te praecipita, ut magis etiam ostendas, te ab eius providentia pendere.

Observ. 1. Suadere praecipitium Diabolus potest, praecipitare nisi volentem non potest. *(Confirmat hanc observ. exemplum Hieronis apud Cassianum Collat. 2. c. 4.)* *(Obs. 2. Quia Diabolus è coelo deorsum cecidit in tartara, alios quoque deorsum ad eadem trahere molitur, Sed sursum corda, ubi Christus est. Conf. Ioh. 8, 23.Phil. 3, 20.)*

Ιέλραπτολ γαρ. Victus erat à Christo Scripturae armis. Videri igitur vult, iisdem contra Christum uti.

Vincent. Lyrin. Quid hic faciet misellis hominibus, qui ipsum Dominum maiestatis Scripturarum testimoniis appetivit?

Non in singulari, sed in plurali dicit David: mandavit Angelis suis, quia pius homo multos habet ad sui custodiam deputatos Angelos Ps. 34.1. Reg. 6. v. 17. *(Pertinet huc quaestio, An cuique pio homini certus Angelus destinatus sit custos: de quâ vid. B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. de Angel. c. 8. §. 8. Monebuntur quoque nonnulla ad Act. 12, 15)*

Προσσιοροσμόνin viis tuis, omittit Diabolus. Quia erat contrarius ipsius proposito. *(Bernh. in Psalm. Qui habitat serm. 14. Quid mandavit? nempe quod in Psalmo sequitur: Ut custodiant te in omnibus viis tuis. Numquid in praecipitus? qualivia haec de pinnaculo templi mitterese deorsum? Non est via haec, sed ruina. Conf. idem in Ps. 90. serm. 12. ac de Angelorum custodia videantur multae egregiae Patrum sententiae in Aphorismis Practicis tit. Angelorum custodia. Rectè porrò Corn. à Lapide in h. l., Ignatius Der Kennis Iesuita, tr. de Angelis Disp. 6. c. 3. §. 1. p. 520. aliiq; Pontificii cum Scholasticis (Vid. Thom. p. 1. q. 113. a. 4. Alens. 2. sent. dist. 11.) quin & Patribus Chrys. Hieron. & Hilario in h. l. negant, Christum in diebus carnis suae habuisse Angelos custodes. rationes Scholasticorum breviter commemorat B. Par. Coll. Isag. L de Angel. c. 8. §. 6. Reiicienda proinde glossa est Socinianorum, statuentium, Christum, licet ad salutem suam non egeret operâ Angelorum, eguisse tamen vel saltem egere potuisse ad sui defensionem, nempe ut feras, quas Satanas ad Christum terrendum coëgerat, abigerent. Videantur Valent. Smalcius Ref. monstr. p. 92. it. ref. l. 2. de Err. Arian. p. 216. Crellius Comm. in h. l. p. 250. Imò verò qui absque Angelorum auxilio repellere infernalem leonem poterat, eundemque vincere, multò magis à feris se absque ulla Angelorum operâ tueri poterat. Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 4. ep. 164. ad Ioh. Diac. in illud non tentabis: In periculum adducto, non autem tentanti Deus auxilium se laturum promisit; In necessitate constituto, non autem se ostentanti & vanam gloriam consectanti. Nondum enim dico, psalmorum scriptorem illud dictum non de me,του καὶ ἄγγελοι χρηζουσιν,cuius ope & auxilio ipsi quoa Angeli indigent, tantum abest, ut ego ipsorum indigus sim (ita emphaticè recteq; transfert I C. έγγηνιηωζτος, Conradus Rittershusius) sed de viro iusto protulisse. Confirmant autem praedictam Isidori expositionem Chrysostomus, Hieronymus, Hilarius in h. l. Orig. it. hom. 24. in Luc. ac Nazianz. Orat. in Bapt. docentes, diabolum falsò hîc citare S. Scripturam: Psaltem enim eo loco loqui de hominibus meris, non de Christo θενθρωπω. Cùm hic non habuerit Angelum custodem, ut habent caeteri homines, quia humanitatis suae custos fuerit ipsa eius divinitas. Interea minimè negamus, quòd diabolus omnis generis feras s. bestias coëgerit, num ab istis dilaniari Christus posset. Id enim non obscurè insinuat Marcus, tentationis huius mentionem faciens c. 1, 12. Vide si placet, B. D. Franzium Scholae Sacrif. Disp. 13. §. 71. seqq. p. 377.)*

-πι χοιρων αρουσι σεmanibus te gestabunt. Metaphora est diligentis custodiae, ducta ab illis, qui onus aliquod gestaturi attollunt Illud in humeros.

## 4:7
v. 7. Πάλιν γέγραπται Christ does not set these two passages of Scripture against each other as conflicting, but so compares them with one another that he refutes by comparison with the other passage the false interpretation of the passage which the Devil had brought forward.

We are taught by what method we must meet the false distortions of Scripture which heretics bring forth, namely by a pious and prudent comparison of Scripture. *(Irenaeus book 4, Against Heresies, chapter 63. The legitimate exposition of Scripture, without danger, is according to the Scriptures themselves. Compare more similar sayings of the Fathers in B. Par., On the Interpretation of Holy Scripture, §. 129.)*

εηπειροσεις Κύροιον τον θεόν σου. The Hebrews express the prohibitions by the future tense, which stands in place of the imperative. The preposition added to the verb is άυξητιηη You shall not test the Lord. Since above at verse 1 the simple verb πειροαζειν is used for to provoke to evil, here the compound έηπειροάζειν is placed for to try, prove, explore, which is the proper signification of the verb πειροαζειν.

The passage exists at Deut. 6. v. 16. Where in the Hebrew there is plural, since speech is made concerning the whole people. But the plural includes the singular. The LXX rendered it by the singular.

He tempts God who wishes himself to take trial of the power of GOD, his wisdom, goodness, or faithfulness in keeping promises, where it is not necessary, subjecting his promises to unjust examination; whether he acts this out of presumptuous confidence, expecting from God that which can be obtained by human reason, or seeking that which is beyond all necessity; or out of unbelief or distrust not leaving to God the provision of necessities, as has been wisely ordered. Franc. Lucas Brugensis on this passage. Jansenius Harmony chapter 15.

Of the latter kind was that temptation by which the Israelites, laboring under a scarcity of water and food in the desert, tempted God Exod. 17. v. 7., which Moses added for the sake of example in the aforementioned place of Deuteronomy. But it would have been of the former kind if Christ had rashly cast himself headlong from the pinnacle, where a descent by stairs was open from it. *(In how many ways God may be tempted will be advised in the notes to Deut. 6, 16. See meanwhile B. Par. Comm. on the said place.)*

*(Corn. à Lap. raises a question here: Whether in necessity it is lawful, for the sake of avoiding a greater precipice, to cast oneself into a lesser one, if no other way of escaping is available. He himself defends the affirmative. He further adds: Thus many holy virgins, that they might escape the hands of persecutors attempting to violate their virginity, when they could not do so by another way, cast themselves into rivers, preferring to die as martyrs than to have their virginity violated; for the precipice of virginity is greater than that of life; for the honor and dishonor of the former is greater than that of the latter. Adelhelmus, Abbot of Malmesbury, is also of the same opinion. But it is more correctly denied that such virgins have a sufficient αύραχειροιας cause. Let Augustine be seen, book 1 of the City of God, chapter 17, discussing this matter professedly. Jerome also notes in his epistle to Marcella concerning the death of Blesilla under the person of GOD: I do not receive such souls that have departed from the body without my will. Martin Bonacina of Milan, Doctor of Sacred Theology and Canon and Civil Law, also embraces the negative opinion, vol. 2 of his Works on Moral Theology on Restitution in part, Disp. 2, last question, section 1, point 5, p. 550, Venetian edition. B. D. Bald. also discusses this argument gravely in his book on Cases of Conscience, book 3, chapter 4, p. 708. Let B. D. -ònig, Cases of Conscience, p. 46, also be added.)*

Latin:

v. 7. Πάλιν γέγραπται Christus non opponit haec duo Scripturae loca, ut pugnantia, sed sic inter se confert, ut falsam illius loci, quem Diabolus adduxerat, interpretationem ex alterius collatione evincat.

Docemur, quâ ratione falsis Scripturae detorsionibus, quas haeretici proferunt, occurrendum sit, videlicet pia & prudenti Scripturam collatione. *(Irenaeus l. 4. adv. haeres. c. 63. Legitima & sine periculo est expositio Scripturae secundùm ipsas Scripturas. Conf. plura similia Patrum dicta apud B. Par. L. de Interpr. Sc. S. §. 129.)*

εηπειροσεις Κύροιον τον θεόν σου. Hebraei prohibitiones efferunt per futurum, quod loco imperativi ponitur. Praepositio addita verbo est άυξητιηηNon pertentabis Dominum. Cùm superiùs v. 1. simplex verbum πειροαζειν usurpetur pro eo, quod est ad malum solicitare, hîc compositum έηπειροάζειν ponitur pro experiri, probare, explorare, quae est propria verbi πειροαζειν significatio.

Locus extat Deut. 6. v. 16. Ubi in Hebraeo est plurale, cùm ad totum populum fiat sermo. Sed plurale includit singulare. LXX. reddiderunt per singulare.

Tentat Deum, qui experimentum ipse vult sumere potentiae DEI, sapientiae, bonitatis aut fidelitatis in servandis promissis, ubi necesse non est, promissiones eius subiiciens iniusto examini; sive id ex praesumtuosâ agat cōfidentiâ, à Deo expectans id, quod humana ratione potest assequi, aut expetens id, quod praeter omnem est necessitatē; sive ex incredulitate vel diffidentia Deo nō relinquens necessariorum, uti consultum fuerit, providentiam. Franc Luc. Brug. in h. l. Iansenius Harm. c. 15.

Posterioris generis fuit ea tentatio, quâ Israëlitae, aquae cibiq; penuriâ in deserto laborantes, Deum tentaverunt, Exod. 17. v. 7. quā Moses addidit exempli gratia superiori Deuteronomii loco. Prioris autem generis fuisset, si Christus è pinnaculo se temerè praecipitem dedisset, ubi descensus per scalas ex eo patebat. *(Quot modis Deus tentetur, monebitur in notis ad Deut. 6, 16. Vid. interea B. Par. Comm. ad d. l.)*

*(Movet hîc Corn. à Lap. quaestionem: An in necessitate liceat, maioris praecipitii vitandi causâ in minus se coniicere, si alia via evadendi non suppetat. Cuius affirmativam ipse defendit. addit porrò: Sic multae sanctae virgines, ut manus persecutorum, -llarum virginitatem violare conantium effugerent, cùm aliâ viâ id facere non possent, in flumina se praecipitarunt, malentes mori martyres, quàm violari virgines; maius enim est praecipitium virginitatis, quàm vitae; illius enim prae hâc maius est decus aea ac dedecus. In eadem sententia est quoque Adelhelmus Abbas Malmosburiensis. Verùm rectiùs negatur, tales virgines sufficiētem habere αύραχειροιας causam. Videatur August. l 1. de C. D. c. 17. ex professo hâc de re disserens. Notanter quoque Hieronymus in ep. ad Marc. de obitu Blesillae sub personâ DEI: Non recipio tales animas, quae me nolente exierunt è corpore. Negativam quoque sententiam amplectitur Martinus Bonacina Mediolan. SS. Th. & I. U. D. t. 2. Oper. de Mor. Theol. -r. de Restit. in part. Disp. 2. q. ult. sect 1. punct. 5. p. 550. edit. Venetae. Graviter quoque de argum: hoc disserit B. D. Bald. in de Cas. Consc. l. 3. c. 4. p. 708. addatur quoque B. D. -ònig Cas. Consc. p. 46.)*

## 4:8
v. 8. Εις ορος ύψηλον λιαν. Some wish it to have been the highest mountain of the whole world, to which the Devil transported Christ with him through the air. Some establish that it was a mountain of that very desert in which Christ was tempted, which for that reason they call the Devil's mountain. *(so Adrich., Brocardus, and Bredenbach establish in the description

of the Holy Land. Add also Saligniacus, book 9, chapter 7; Heidmanus in Palestine, chapter 7, n. 92, 93; Bunting, Itinerary of the Holy Land, part 2, p. 10.)*

Q. How could the Devil have shown Christ all the kingdoms of the world from a mountain, especially in a moment of time, which Luke adds?

1. The height of no mountain can be so great that all the kingdoms of the world could be seen from it, and even if some mountain were exceedingly high, nevertheless the human eye could not reach to the sight of all things, especially in a moment of time. 2. From this various opinions of interpreters arise. For first, certain men restrict the mark [of universality], he showed him almost all the kingdoms, namely all those which could be seen from that mountain.

Secondly, Chrysostom held that the Devil, as it were extending his finger, merely pointed out in what part of the globe the chief kingdoms of the world then lay, and that he explained by telling in words whose power each was. But this seems not sufficiently to agree with what Luke says, that this showing was made ἐν ςιγμῇχρόνον *Moreover, this explanation is also embraced by Euthymius, as well as Thomas Aquinas, part 3, question 41, article 4, and several others. Jansenius and Cornelius à Lapide likewise favor the same opinion, who however think it must be added that the Devil not only showed Christ the location of each kingdom, but also, in the manner of a painter, represented in a new way and, as it were, painted in the air—which he had variously condensed—images of all the kingdoms through various refractions of the light of the sun, as happens in the rainbow, and did so that through them all the things that were glorious and splendid in the kingdoms might appear and be set before the eyes of Christ—and that in a moment.*

Thirdly, therefore, certain men judge that that ἐν ςιγμῇχρόνου should be referred to the preceding member—that the Devil lifted up the Lord to a lofty mountain in a moment of time—since it would seem impossible that all the kingdoms of the earth were shown to Him in an instant of time. Since those kingdoms are situated here and there, and it cannot happen that anyone at once sees what lies before and behind, as well as what lies on either side, and since it is probable that some delay intervened in that showing, so that when the vastness of the kingdoms of the world had been considered He might be seized with desire of possessing them.

Fourthly, Ambrose runs off into allegory, book 1, On Cain and

Abel, vol. 1, fol. 228. Well said concerning the moment, because they cannot last long, wait but a little while, they quickly pass away. On chapter 4 of Luke, vol. 2, fol. 229. In a moment of time earthly and worldly things are well shown forth, for not so much is swiftness of sight indicated, as the frailty of transitory power is expressed. For all those things pass by in a moment, and often the honor of the world departs before it has come. For what can be lasting of the world, when even the ages themselves are not lasting?

Fifthly, some hold that this was done by fascination, that is, that the Devil so bewitched the eyes of Christ, as if he saw all kingdoms. Nor should this seem absurd, both because Christ ought to be tempted in all things as we are, and also because it is greater, which he brought upon himself in leading him onto the pinnacle of the temple. To nearly this view goes Theophylact, holding that the Devil presented to Christ external and sensible appearances of all the kingdoms. Bruges: This could have been done partly by the force of perspective or optical art, by which art spectacles are made by men, which subject most exactly to the eyes things very far distant, partly by casting a spell over the eyes of Christ.

Sixthly, Dr. Chemnitius holds, ch. 19 of his Harmony, that all kingdoms were shown to Christ by the Devil in such a way, that is, he might say: By this reason just as now you act, you will not subject all kingdoms to yourself, although it was promised of the Messiah, do you see them occupied by those who obey me. *(Seventhly, Dr. ---nig Append. Cas. Cons. p. 43. judges it safest to say either that πάσας βασιλείας here is taken distributively, not collectively, in this sense, that there were shown to Christ all the kingdoms which indeed could be subjected to the eyes, meanwhile without excluding those which lay farther off yet were of the same kind; or that the greater part of the Kingdoms is meant, since πᾶν or all in Holy Scripture being accepted for the greater part too is not altogether unusual. Matt 9, 26.ch. 27, 45.)*

καὶ τὴνδοξαν ἀυτῶν He caused the glory of the kingdoms of the world to appear before the eyes, namely how one kingdom was illustrious for wealth, another for strength, a third for the multitude of peoples. And likewise whatever in the kingdoms of this world is glorious and magnificent, such as riches, honors, servitude, palaces, military forces, attendances, triumphs, embassies.

Latin:

v. 8. Εις ορος ύψηλον λιαν. Quidam volunt, fuisse montem totius orbis altissimum, ad quem Diabolus Christum per aërem secum transportarit. Quidam statuunt, fuisse montem illius ipsius deserti in quo Christus tentatus, quem ob id Diaboli montem vocant. *(ita statuunt Adrich. Brocardus & Bredenbach. in descript.

terrae Sanctae. Add. quoque Saligniacus t. 9. c. 7. Heidmanus in Palaest. c. 7. n. 92. 93. Bunting. Itiner. S. p. 2. p. 10.)*

Q. Quomodo Diabolus ex monte potuerit omnia mundi regna Christo demonstrare, praesertim in momento temporis, quod Lucas addit?

1. Nullius montis altitudo potest esse tanta, ut omnia mundi regna inde conspici possint, & si vel maximè mons aliquis tam excelsus esset, tamen oculus humanus non posset ad inspectionem omnium, praesertim in temporis momento, pertingere. 2. Inde variae oriuntur Interpretum sententiae. Nam primò quidam notam Universalem limitant, ostendit illi pleraregna, videlicet omnia, quae ex illo monte videri poterant.

Secundò Chrysostomus statuit, quòd Diabolus quasi digitum intendens tantùm monstraverit, in quâ orbis parte sita tunc fuerint potissima mundi regna, & quod verbis narrando exposuerit, quae sit cuiuspotentia. Sed hoc non satis congruere videtur illi, quod Lucas dicit, monstrationem hanc factam ἐν ςιγμῇχρόνον *(Caeterùm expositionem istam amplectitur quoque Euthymius, nec non Thomas de Aquino 3. p. q. 41. art. 4. ac alii nonnulli. Eadem arridet etiam Iansenio ac Corn. à Lapide, qui tamen addendum putant, quòd Diabolus non solùm cuiusque regni situm Christo ostenderit, verum etiam instar pictoris omnium regnorum imagines in aëre à se variè condensato, per varias fulguris solis refractiones, uti in iride fit, novo quodam modo repraesentasse & quasi pinxisse, fecisseque, ut per eas omnia, quae in regnis erant gloriosa & splendida, apparerent, & obiicerentur oculis Christi. idque in momento.)*

Tertiò quidam ergo existimant, illud ἐν ςιγμῇχρόνου ad praecedens membrum esse referendum, quôd Diabolus Dominum in momento temporis in montem sublimem subduxerit, cùm videatur fieri non potuisse, ut in puncto temporis ei ostensa sunt omnia regna terrae. Cùm regna illa circumquaquam sita sint, fieri autem nequeat, ut quis simul cernat, quae ante & post, nec non quae ad latera, ac probabile sit in illa ostensione intercessisse aliquam moram, ut amplitudine regnorum mundi consideratâ caperetur illorum possidendorum desiderio.

Quartò Ambrosius decurrit ad allegoriam. lib. 1. de Caino &

Abele tom. 1. fol. 228. Benè momento, quia diutura esse nequeunt, paululùm expecta, citòtranseunt. In cap. 4. Luc. tom. 2. f. 229. Bene in momento temporis secularia & terrena demonstratur, non enim tam conspectus celeritas indicatur, quàm caducae fragilitas potestatis exprimitur. In momento enim cuncta illa praetereunt, & saepe honor seculi abit, antequam venerit. Quid enim seculi potest esse diuturnum, cum ipsa diuturna non sint secula?

Quintò quidam statuunt, hoc factum fuisseper fascinum, h. e. Diabolum ita fascinasse oculos Christi, ac si omnia regna videret. Neque hoc debere videri absurdum, tum quia Christus in omnib debuit tentari ut nos; tum quia maius est, quod Christum secum duxerit in pinnaculum templi. Eô ferè abit Theophyl. statuens, quòd Diabolus externas & sensibiles omnium regnorum phantasias Christo repraesentaverit. Brug. Potuit hoc fieri partim prospectivae seu opticae artis vi, qua arte ab hominibus conficiuntur inspicilla, quae longissimè distantes res oculis exactissimè subiieiunt, partim praestigio perstringens oculos Christì.

Sextò D. Chemnitius statuit, cap. 19. Harm. Christo ita omnia regna esse à Diabolo ostensa. qs. dixerit. Ea ratione sicut nunc agis, non subiicies tibi omnia regna, quod tamen de Messia praedictum, vides illa occupari ab iis, qui mihi obsequuntur. *(Septimò D. ---nig Append. Cas. Cons. p. 43. existimat, tutissimum esse, si dicatur, aut πάσας βασιλείας hîc sumi distributivè, non collectivè, hoc sensu, Christo ostensa fuisse omnia regna, quae quidem oculis subiici potuerint, non exclusis interim illis, quae longiùs dissita, eiusdem tamen generis fuerint; aut maiorem Regnorum partem intelligi, cùm πᾶν sive omne in Sc. S. pro maiore etiam parte accipi, insolens omninò non sit. Matth 9, 26.c. 27, 45.)*

καὶ τὴνδοξαν ἀυτῶν Fecit ante oculos apparere regnorum mundi gloriam, quomodo sc. unum opibus clarum, alterum viribus, tertium populorum frequentiâ. Itemque quic quid in regnis huius mundi gloriosum & magnificum, qualia sunt opes honores, famulitia, palatia, copiae militares, obsequia, triumphi, legationes.

## 4:9
v. 9. Ταῦτα πάντα σοι δώσω Satan had learned by real experience that nothing so wicked and criminal existed which men would not dare for the sake of ruling. Therefore Satan attempts, by this showing of the kingdoms of the world and by adding a magnificent promise, to excite desire for them in the mind of Christ, and by this means to drive him into most shameful apostasy.

He demands that divine honor be shown to him, and for this reason, although he was cast down from heaven on account of pride, he nevertheless remains like himself, because long ago he wished to be like GOD. Therefore, what he could not obtain from the Angels in heaven, he hopes he can attain from men on earth. *(

But from the fact that the Devil tempted Christ here to worship him, the Jews and Photinians ineptly conclude that Christ is not true God. For if he were such, says Crellius, he would not have been tempted by the Devil to worship. 1. Because this is unworthy of GOD. 2. It would have had no end. 3. Nor would the Devil have dared it, since he trembles at the sight of the divine Majesty, etc. But these and other sophistries of the Photinians can easily be refuted if it is observed: 1. That Christ was tempted not according to his divine, but according to his human nature. 2. That he was then in a state of humiliation, and did not always display the rays of his majesty, but only as often as it pleased him in full light. 3. Whence also the divine majesty of Christ was not always sufficiently perceived by the devil. But concerning these things, see more in Mr. Dr. Calovius in the Examination of the books of Crellius §. 434. B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. de Mal. Ang. c. 4. §. 18. Mr. Dr. Mull. Iud. p. 961.)*

But Satan lies in many ways. 1. because all kingdoms are GOD'S. Job 41. v. 11. God says, everything under heaven is mine. Seneca acknowledged this from the book of Nature, whence he writes in book 7 of Benefits, chapter 3, folio 64: This is the voice of GOD, all things are mine. 2. because no Monarch ever gave his entire kingdom to another. 3. because what Satan promised he was unable to perform. 4. because even if Christ had worshipped Satan at most by way of an impossible hypothesis, still he would not have kept his promises.

Latin:

v. 9. Ταῦτα πάντα σοι δώσω Reipsâ expertus erat Satanas, nihil tam impium ac nefarium esse, quod regnandi causâ homines non auderent. Conatur igitur Satanas hac regnorum mundi ostensione & additâ magnificâ pollicitatione desiderium eorum in animo Christi excitare, atque hac ratione ad turpissimam apostasian eundem impellere.

Divinum honorem sibi postulat exhiberi, atque hac ratione quamvis ob superbiam coelo deiectus sit, tamen sui similis manet, quia iam olim DEO similis esse voluit. Quod ergo in coelo ab Angelis obtinere non potuit, id in terris ab hominibus se consequi posse sperat.

*(Ex eo verô quòd Christum Diabolus hic solicitavit ad sui adorationem, ineptè colligunt Iudaei ac Photiniani, quòd Christus non sit verus Deus. Talis enimsi esset, dicit Crellius, non fuisset à Diabolo ad adorandum solicitatus. 1. quia hoc indignum DEO. 2. nullum finem habuisset. 3. nec Diabolus id ausus fuisset, cùm contremiscat ad divinae Maiestatis conspectum &c. Verùm his aliisque Photinianorum sophisticationibus facilè fieri satis potest, si observetur. 1. quod Christus fuerit tentatus non secundùm divinam, sed secundùm hum. naturam. 2. quòd fuerit tum in statu exinanitionis ac maiestatis suae radios nō semper, sed quoties ei placuit plenâ luce exeruerit. 3. Unde etiam non satis diabolo fuit semper perspecta divina Christi maiestas. Ast de his plura videantur apud Dn. D. Calov. in Exam. libb. Crellii §. 434. B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. de Mal. Ang. c. 4. §. 18. Dn. D. Mull. Iud. p. 961.)*

Multis verò modis Satanas mentitur. 1. quia omnia regna sunt DEI. Iob. 41. v. 11. inquit Deus, omne, quod sub coelo, meum est. Agnovit hoc Seneca ex libro Naturae, unde lib. 7. de benef. cap. 3. f. 64. scribit: Haec vox DEI est, omnia mea sunt. 2. quia nullus Monarcha unquam totum suum regnum alteri dedit. 3. quia quod promittebat Satanas, praestare non poterat. 4. quia si vel maximè per hypothesin impossibilem Christus Satanam adorasset, non tamen promissis suis stetisset.

## 4:10
v. 10. λ παγέ, away with your deceitful and lying promises. Origen observes that the Devil is addressed simply with ὕπαγε, but Peter with ὕπαγε οπισωμου, because here [Peter] is invited to follow along, while the other is repelled. But this is more subtle than solid. Indeed in certain copies there is added at this place *(to which also agree the Ectypes, MSS., of the Bibliotheca Noribergensis, as well as the Ethiopian, who translates just as namely Matt. 16, 23. that is, )* also at this place this: ὀπίσω μου. But it is not genuine. *(just as neither the Syrian nor the Arabic acknowledges this addition. In the Leiden edition after there is inserted but the Roman has nothing of the kind.)*

Satan. The Devil wished to be held as God, but Christ shows what he really is, namely the adversary OF GOD AND MEN. To the Hebrews שטן, Syr. Satana. To the Greeks Σατανᾶς. *(The Arabs and Ethiopians also retain the same name.)* And rightly at this point Christ addresses him by the name Satan, because he was openly conducting himself as an adversary of GOD and of divine things.

Christ brings forward all the Scriptures which he cites from Deuteronomy, according to the custom of the Jews, who were especially occupied with it, as it is an epitome of the whole law. *(

*(Moreover Christ's example teaches us with what weapons we can fight against Satan and overcome him. Namely, when Satan labors to tempt us, let us put on the spiritual armor and fortify ourselves against his assaults, just as the Apostle also exhorts us Eph. 6, 12. sqq. But we can and ought to resist Satan 1. with the sword of the word,Eph. 6, 17.Heb. 4, 12. Christ used this means in the present contest. 2. With the shield of faith, embracing the word, 1 Pet. 5, 9.Eph. 6, 16. Let us accustom ourselves through faith to believe from the word of the Gospel that we have Christ as Victor over Satan, our Leader and champion, who as he crushed the head of the Serpent in his own person Gen. 3, 15. so also will overcome him in us, Rom. 16, 20. Beautifully Bernard, in Meditations devout, ch. 14, col. 1201: Whenever we resist, we conquer the Devil, rejoice the Angels, glorify God. For he himself urges us to fight; he helps us to win. In battle he watches those fighting, lifts up those failing, crowns those conquering. 3. By faithful prayer,Matt. 17, 21.ch. 26, 41.Eph. 6, 13. For prayer is David's harp, which drives away the infernal spirit; it is Gideon's sword, Samson's jawbone, David's scrip. 4. By spiritual watchfulness,Matt. 26, 41.1 Pet. 5, 8. to which belong sobriety Matt. 17, 21. and constancy. Bern., Ep. 1, col. 757: The enemy pursues you fleeing more willingly than he endures your resisting, and presses upon you from behind more boldly than he withstands you face to face. Compare further passages in B. Par., Coll. Isag., Book On evil angels, ch. 10, §. 2.)*

προσκυνήσεις. In the Hebrew and Greek at Deuter. 6. v. 13.chap. 10. v. 20. there stands you shall fear, which Christ changed into you shall worship, in accommodation to his aim. Fear is a general term, embracing the entire divine service, of which religious adoration is by no means the least part. *(See Pineda Comm. on ch. 1. Job, p. 27. Lorinus vol. 1. on Ps., p. 312, likewise on Acts, p. 349. But compare with the present passage Camero in Myroth. Evang. on this place and following places Ruth 2, 10.2. Sam. 14, 4.Job. 1, 20. Yet let it be noted that in the two former passages civil respect is treated of, here however religious adoration, for such was what the Devil sought.)

The exclusive particle (alone) is not added in Deuteronomy, but it is included in the pronoun him, which must be taken emphatically together with exclusion of any other object whatsoever. Maldonatus himself explains it thus in his comment: You shall adore the Lord your God alone, and him alone shall you serve.

François Lucas of Brussels: You shall adore the Lord Father, Son and Holy Spirit, not anyone else whoever he may be, nor anything else whatever it may be. *(This divine oracle concerning worshipping GOD alone does not oppose our doctrine about the adoration of Christ as man, as has been shown elsewhere. See Coll. Isag. page 372. Rightly indeed do our countrymen construct against the invocation of Saints an argument from this place, whose firmness is then also set forth at length according to the state of the controversy in the said place, p. 1792 sqqq. Moreover, both because Christ in this place added the exclusive word, which indeed is not read expressly at Deut. 6, 13., to which passage the Savior looks, and which even the Syrian, Arabic and Ethiopian versions retained here, and because interpreters, including also the Vulgate, did so in somewhat more places where it is not found in the Hebrew text—as those places are listed by the learned Dr. Helvicus, Vind. LL. Sc. S. V. Test. p. 182—it is easy to conclude that besides his merits blessed Luther too should be accused so greatly by the Papists as a corrupter of the text when he added the particle alone in the German version of Rom. 3, 24., since the matter itself required it then. But this will be discussed further in the said place. Finally, vain here are the Papists who try to blunt the force of the argument drawn from this place against the invocation of Saints by a distinction between δουλείαν and λατρείαν,. See Bellarmine book 1. On the Beatitude of Saints, ch. 14. Paludanus in Vind. Theol. on this place, p. 212. Cornelius à Lapide, Tirinus and several others on this place. For indeed the verb ףבד which is read at Deut. 6, 13. the Seventy sometimes render by λατρΕύιειν, as in the aforementioned place, just as also at chap. 10, 12, sometimes by δουλεύειν.

use 1. Sam. 7, 3. c. 12, 20. Nor can it be denied that this distinction is by no means observed by Christ and the Apostles. Whence the Jesuit Conzen himself also in this place acknowledges that that distinction between λατρείαν and δουλείαν is not so accurately observed in Scripture, that λατρεύειν is not also said of creatures, and δουλεύελν of God, but that it is at least a custom of the Church. Paludanus in the book cited above denies that Catholics render to the Saints that office which pertains to God alone, namely to place all hope in them, to offer sacrifice, and other things of that kind. But it is not only forbidden to place all hope in the deceased Saints, but even any confidence at all. Which, however, the Papists do, as B. Par. shows in L. de Morte §. 365. But do not the Papists also offer sacrifices to the saints, and other things of that kind, when they pour out prayers to them, by which they seek from them the relief of the fallen, the consolation of the afflicted, the illumination of minds, the mortification of the lascivious flesh, etc.? All of which have long since been shown by our people from Holy Scripture to be the benefits of God and Christ alone. Furthermore, it is not permitted to treat this argument more prolixly. Let B. D. Chemn. part. 3. Exam. Concil Trid., B. D. Hopfnerus Evangelic. Saxon. p. 206. seqq., B. D. Himmelius in a special treatise on Invocation, opposed to the Papists and Photinians, B. Par. L. de Morte §. 370. seqq., Confess. Cathol. t. 3. p. 549. seqq., B. D. Bald. Cas. Consc. l. 2. c. 5. cas. 5. and also c. 7. cas. 2. be seen. It is indeed strange that the Photinians, although they themselves confess, see Volck l. 4. de Ver. Relig. c. 8. p. 206., Crellius in comm. ad h. l. p. 249., nay Socinus himself Resp. ad c. 10. Wuiek. p. 423. (Ostorodus however dissents, frivolously distinguishing between τὸ to serve, and to adore) that God alone is to be adored, and that in the commandment Deut. 6, 13. it is insinuated that He can by no means bear a rival, and although in the Hebrew the little word Only is not added, that the force of the words is such that other Gods are excluded from this worship etc., nevertheless, lest they be forced to confess that Christ is the true God because religious adoration is attributed to Him in Holy Scripture, they assert that Angels were religiously adored in the Old Testament. Concerning which Photinian error it will be spoken of at Apoc. 19, 10. But rather the most firm argument for the true Deity of Christ is sought from the cult of adoration, by which He is to be affected by the command of the Holy Scriptures. And the distinction which the Socinians and Arminians invent here between the supreme God and another subordinate one is of no moment. Nor, finally, does our hypothesis concerning the adoration of Christ the man infringe the force of that argument , as has been shown elsewhere.)

v. 10. λ παγέ, apage cum fallacibus & mendacibus tuis promissis. Origenes observat, Diabolo simpliciter dici ὕπαγε, Petro autem ὕπαγε οπισωμου, quia hic ad sequelam invitatur, ille repellitur. Sed hoc subtilius, quàm firmius. Additur quidem in quibusdam exemplaribus *(quibus adstipulantur quoque Eclog. MS. Graecae Bibl. Noriberg. nec non Aethiops, qui eodem modo, quo Matth. 16, 23. vertit. nempe ) *etiam h. l. illud: ὀπίσω μου. Sed non est genuinum. *(quemadm. nec Syrus nec Arabs additionem hanc agnoscunt. In edit. Leidensi post inseritur sed Romana nil tale habet.)*

Satana. Diabolus volebat haberi Deus, sed Christus ostendit, quisnam sit, videl. DEI & hominum adversarius. Hebraeis שטן Syr. Satana. Graecis Σατανᾶς. *(Retinent quoq; idem nomen. Arabs & Aethiops.)* Meritò autem hoc loco Christus eum Satanae nomine compellat, quia apertum DEI, divinarumq; partium adversarium sese gerebat.

Scripturas omnes, quas citat, affert Christus ex Deuteronomino, pro Iudaeorum more, qui in eo, utpote totius legis epitome, praecipuè versabantur.

*(Caeterùm admonet nos Christi exemplum, quibus armis pugnare contra Satanam, eumque vincere possimus. Quando videl. Satanas tantare nos satagit, spiritualem armaturam induamus ac contra eius insultus nos muniamus, ceu etiam Apostolus nos adhortatur Eph. 6, 12. seqq. Resistere verò possumus ac debemus Satanae 1. gladio verbi,Eph. 6, 17.Ebr. 4, 12. medio hoc usus est Christus in praesenti certamine. 2. Scuto fidei, verbum amplectentis, 1. Petr. 5, 9.Eph. 6, 16. Solemur nos fide ex verbo Evangelii, quòd Christum Satanae victorem Ducem & promachum habeamus, qui ut in persona propriâ contrivit caput Serpentis Gen. 3, 15. ita quoq; in nobis eum superabit, Rom. 16, 20. Pulcrè Bernhardus in medit. devot. c. 14. col. 1201. Quoties resistimus, Diabolum superamus, Angelos laetificamus, Deum honorificamus. Ipse enim nos hortatur, ut pugnemus; adiuvat ut vincamus. Certantes in bello spectat, deficientes sublevat, vincentes coronat. 3. oratione fideli,Matth. 17, 21.c. 26, 41.Eph. 6, 13. Oratio enim est Davidis Cythara, quae infernalem spiritum propellit. est gladius Gideonis, maxilla Samsonis, pera Davidis. 4. Vigilantiá spirituali,Matth. 26, 41.1. Petr. 5, 8. ad quam pertinent sobrietas Matth. 17, 21. & constantia. Bernh. ep. 1. col. 757. Libentiùs te insequitur adversarius fugientem, quàm sustinet repugnantem, & audaciùs insistit à tergo, quàm resistat in faciem. Confer plura apud B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. de Angelis malis c. 10. §. 2.)*

προσκυνήσεις. In Hebraeo & Graeco Deuter. 6. v. 13.cap. 10. v. 20. est timebis, quod Christus mutavit in adorabis, in accommodatione ad suum scopum. Timoris nomen generale est, complectens totum divinum cultum, cuius pars non minima est religiosa adoratio. *(Videatur Pineda Com. in c. 1. Iob. p. 27. Lorin. t. 1. in Ps. p. 312. c. it. in Acta p. 349. Confert autem cum praesenti loco Camero in Myroth. Evang. ad h. l. seqq. loca Ruth 2, 10.2. Sam. 14, 4.Iob. 1, 20. Sed notandum, quòd in duobus prioribus locis agatur de cultu civili, hîc verò de adoratione religiosâ, talem enim Diabolus expetebat.)*

Exclusiva ( soli) non additur in Deuteronomio, includitur autem in pronomine illi, quod emphaticè cum exclusione cuiuscunque alterius obiecti accipiendum. Maldonatus ipse in cōm. sic explicat, Dominum Deum tuum solum adorabis & illi soli servies.

Franc. Luc. Brug. Adorabis Dominum Patrem, Filium & Spiritum S. non alium quicuna ille sit, nec aliud quicquid illud sit. *(Non obstat oraculum hoc divinum de solo DEO adorando doctrinae nostrae de adoratione Christi hominis, ceu alibi ostensum. Vid. Coll. Isag. pag. 372. Rectè autem contra invocationem Sanctorum argumentum ex h. l. nostrates extruunt. cuius firmitas tum quoq; controversiae status prolixè ostenditur d. l. p. 1792. seqq. Porrò ex eo, tum quòd Christus h. l. exclusivam vocem, quae quidem Deut. 6, 13. ad quem locum Salvator respicit, expressè non legitur, addidit, quam etiam Syrus, Arabs & Aethiops hîc retinuerunt, tum Interpr. etiā Vulgatus locis plusculis, ubi in textu Ebraeo non habetur, ceu loca ista sistit B. D. Helvicus Vind. LL. Sc. S. V. Test. p. 182. colligere pronum est, praeter meritum B. Lutherum tanquam falsatorem textus tantopere à Pontificiis accusari, quando particulam sola in vers. Germ. Rom. 3, 24. addidit, cùm res ipsa tum requisiverit. Sed hàc de re d. l. pluribus agetur. Denique frustra hîc sunt Pontificii, qui argumenti, quod ex h. l. contra invocationem Sanct. depromitur, vim elidere conantur distinctione inter δουλείαν ac λατρείαν, Vid. Bell. l. 1. de beatit. Sanct. c. 14. Paludanus in Vind. Theol. ad h. l. p. 212. Corn. à Lapide, Tirinus ac alii nonnulli in h. l. Etenim verbum ףבד quod Deut. 6, 13. legitur, LXX. modò per λατρΕύιειν reddunt, ut d. modò loco, sicuti etiam c. 10, 12. modò per δουλεύειν

uti 1. Sam. 7, 3. c. 12, 20. nec negari potest, à Christo & Apostolis differentiam istam minimè attendi. Unde ipse quoque Iesuita Conzen in h. l. agnoscit, discrimen iliud interλατρείαν ac δουλείανin Scr. non ita accuratè observari, ut non &λατρεύεινde creaturis dicatur, & δουλεύελνDeo, sed eam saltem Ecclesiae esse consuetudinem. Paludanus l. suprà cit. negat, Catholicos Sanctis illud deferre officium, quod ad solum Deum pertinet, videlicet omnem spem in illos ponere, sacrificium offerre, & eius generis alia. Sed non solùm prohibitum, omnem spem in Sanctos defunctos ponere, verùm etiam aliquam saltem fiduciam. Id quod tamen Pontificii faciunt, ceu ostendit B. Par. L. de Morte §. 365. Annon verò & sacrificia sanctis offerunt Pontificii, & eius generis alia, quando preces ad illos fundunt, quibus lapsorum allevationem, afflictorum consolationem, mentium illuminationem, carnis lascivientis mortificationem &c. ab iisdem expetunt. Quae omnia solius DEI & Christi beneficia esse, pridem à nostratibus ex Scr. S. ostensum. Caeterùm de hoc argum. non licetiam agere prolixiùs. Videantur B. D. Chemn. part. 3. Exam. Concil Trid. B. D Hopfnerus Evangelic. Saxon. p. 206. seqq. B. D. Himmelius in pecul. tract. de Invocatione, Pontif. & Photin. opposito, B. Par. L. de Morte §. 370. seqq. Confess. Cathol. t. 3. p. 549. seqq. B. D. Bald. Cas. Consc. l. 2. c. 5. cas. 5. it. c. 7. cas. 2. Mirum verò, quòd Photiniani, cùm ipsi tamen fateantur, videatur Volck l. 4. de Ver. Relig. c. 8. p. 206. Crellius in comm. ad h. l p. 249. imò Socinus ipse Resp. ad c. 10. Wuiek. p. 423. (dissentit tamen Ostorodus, frivolè distinguens inter τὸservire, & adorare) Deum solum esse adorandum, adeoin mandatoDeut. 6, 13.hoc insinuare, quòd rivalē pati ferreipse minimè possit, ac licet in Ebraeo vocula Soli non sit addita, eam tamen verborum vim esse, ut excludantur ab hoc cultu alii Dii &c. nihilo tamen minùs, saltem ne fateri cogantur, Christum verum esse Deum eò, quôd adoratio religiosa ei in Sc. S. tribuitur, adserant, Angelos in V. T. religiosè adoratos fuisse. de quo Photin. errore dicetur ad Apoc. 19, 10. Quin potiùs firmissimum pro verâ Christi Deitate argumentum à cultu adorationis, quo Scr. Sacrae mandato ipse adficiendus, petitur. Nulliusque momenti distinctio est, quam Sociani atque Arminiani hîc fingunt inter Deum summum, ac alium subordinatum. Nec infringit denique argumenti illius vim hypothesis nostra de adoratione Christi hominis, ut alibi ostensum.)*

## 4:11
v. 11. Not one, but several Angels came, in visible form, as is judged probable, since the Devil tempted Christ in visible form. The same is gathered from the word προσῆλθον.

The ministry of the Angels was this: that they brought food to him when hungry, as once to Elijah, 1. Reg. 19. that they congratulated him on his victory, that they led him down from the summit of the mountain onto level ground &c.

In Christ the head an example is set forth. 1. of divine kindness, how, namely, God takes care of those who entrust themselves wholly to the divine will, and do nothing contrary to their calling or the word of God. 2. of divine truthfulness, because he adds Angels as companions to those who walk in the ways of their calling. Hilary, canon 3, on Matthew: When he has been conquered by us, when the head of the Devil has been trampled underfoot, neither the ministries of Angels nor the offices of heavenly virtues shall fail us. 3. the weakness of the Devil, because the Devil cannot prevail by all his powers and deceits against those who fortify themselves with spiritual arms against him. Jas. 4. v. 7. Resist the Devil.

Latin:

v. 11. Non unus, sed plures Angeli accedunt, in visibili, uti verisimile censetur, specie, cùm Diabolus in visibili forma Christum tentaverit. Idem colligitur ex verbo προσῆλθον.

Ministerium Angelorum hoc fuit, quòd esurienti cibum attulerunt, sicut olim Eliae, 1. Reg. 19. quòd de victoriâ ipsi fuerint gratulati, quod ex cacumine montis in planiciem deduxerint &c.

Proponitur in Christo capite exemplum. 1. divinae benignitatis. quomodo sc. Deus illorum curam suscipiat, qui se totos divinae voluntati credunt, neque quidquam contra suam vocationem vel verbum Dei agunt. 2. divinae veracitatis, quod Angelos illis addat comites, qui in viis vocationis suae ambulant. Hilarius can. 3. in Matth. Victo à nobis, calcatoDiaboli capite, & Angelorum ministeria & virtutum in nos coelestium officia non sunt defutura. 3. Diabolicae infirmitatis, quod Diabolus omnibus suis viribus & fraudibus non possit praevalere illis, qui spiritualibus armis adversus ipsum sese muniunt. Iac. 4. v. 7.Resistite Diabolo.

## 4:12
v. 12. Here must be inserted what John describes in chapters 1, 2, 3 and 4. For after the fast and temptations Christ returned to John, by whom, adorned with remarkable testimonies, he gathered some disciples, and setting out with them into Galilee he changed water into wine. Shortly afterward he went back from Galilee into Judaea for the feast of Passover, where he drove out the buyers and sellers from the temple, instructed Nicodemus by night, and having stayed in Judaea for some months baptized through the ministry of his disciples, until he heard that John had been given over into captivity; then he returned into Galilee.

ὀτι Ιωάννηςπαρεδόθη, namely he was denounced to Herod by the Scribes and Pharisees, but cast into prison by Herod himself. Judaea was subject to a Roman garrison. Therefore, because John was baptizing in Judaea, he could not have been seized by Herod the tetrarch of Galilee unless the consent and cooperation of the Scribes and Pharisees, whose authority in the Judaean Republic was great, had intervened. Compare Matt 17. v 12.

Ἀνεχώρησεν i.e. ἐπανῆλθεν ανὰ here means the same as πάλιν Matt. 2. v 12 Some translate widrew. But if Jesus wanted to withdraw in order to avoid the tyranny of Herod, why would he go into Galilee, which was under the dominion of Herod Antipas, and not rather remain in Judaea, which had now been reduced to a province? Christ therefore did not withdraw into Galilee out of fear of persecution—for from there he had come into Judaea, that he might be baptized by John—but rather straightway betook himself again to the Galileans, and there began to gather disciples, fearing nothing the rage of Herod, until he heard that John had been put to death, and that Herod also threatened him; for only then is it said that he withdrew. εἰς τὴν ἐρήμου τόπον, Matt. 14. v. 13. Beza. That maritime city Capernaum was far more celebrated than Nazareth. Therefore he did not withdraw.

Franc. Luc. on this passage He withdrew from Judea because of the malice of the Scribes and Pharisees, who were plotting his captivity and slaughter no less than John's. He had offended them by casting out those buying and selling from the temple; added to this was the fact that he was gathering more disciples through Baptism than had ever been done by John, since his fame and authority daily took greater increase.

How did he withdraw into Galilee because of John's arrest, when Herod, who had cast John into prison, was tetrarch of Galilee? Answer: he fled not from Herod but from the Scribes and Pharisees, for whom it had not been convenient to make use of Herod's help in seizing Jesus, just as [they seized] John, since Jesus had not offended Herod, as John had.

This return of Christ into Galilee was the second, as appears from John 1. v. 43. and chap. 4. v. 3. where both returns are described. The other Evangelists make mention only of this second return. For after the first return Christ did not remain long in Galilee; nor do the other Evangelists describe Christ's yearly departures into Judea for the solemn feasts, which John alone does: they make mention only of the last return into Judea, as of this one alone into Galilee, after which he remained a long time in Galilee.

Latin:

v. 12. Hîc inserenda sunt ea, quae Iohannes describit in cap. 1. 2. 3. & 4. Post ieiunium enim & tentationes rediit Christus ad Iohannem, à quo insignibus testimoniis ornatus discipulos aliquot collegit, cum quibus profectus in Galilaeam aquam mutavit in vinum. Paulò pòst reversus fuit ex Galilaea in Iudaeam ad festivitatem paschalem, ubi eiecit ementes ac vendentes in templo, Nicodemum nocte instruxit ac mensibus aliquot in Iudaea commoratus discipulorum suorum ministerio baptizavit, donec audiret Iohannem in captivitatem esse traditum, tunc rediit in Galilaeam.

ὀτι Ιωάννηςπαρεδόθη, sc Herodi à Scribis & Pharisaeis, ab Herode autem in carcerem coniectus. Iudae erat Romano praesidi subiecta. Quia ergo Iohannes baptizabat in Iudaea non potuisset ab Herode tetrarcha Galilaeae comprehendi, nisi Scribarum & Pharisaeorum, quorum in Republ. -udaica erat magna autoritas, consensus & cooperatio accessisset. Confer Matth 17. v 12.

Ἀνεχώρησεν i. e. ἐπανῆλθεν ανὰ idem hîc valet, quod πάλινMatth. 2. v 12 Quidam vertunt s ---ssit. Sed si secedere volebat Iesus, ut Herodis Tyrannidem vitaret, cur iret in Galilaeam, quae erat in ditione Herodis Antipae, ac non potiùs maneret in Iudaea, quae iam redacta erat in provinciam? Christus ergo persecutionis metu non secessit in Galilaeam, ex quâ in Iudaeam venerat, ut à Iohanne baptizaretur, sed potiùs ad Galilaeos statim recurrit, & ibi discipulos colligere caepit, nihil veritus Herodis rabiem, doneaudiret, Iohannem interemtum, & Herodem sibi quoque minitari, nam tum demum dicitur secessisse εἰς τὴν ἐρήμου τόπον,Matth. 14. v. 13. Beza. Urbs illa maritima Capernaum multò celebrior fuit, quàm Nazareth. Ergo non secessit.

Franc. Luc. in h. l. Secessit ex Iudaea ob Scribarum & Phariseorum malitiam, qui ipsius non minùs, quàm Iohannis captivitatem ac caedem moliebantur. Offenderat illos eiectione ementium ac vendentium è templo, accedebat, quod plures discipulos per Baptismum colligebat, quàm unquam à Iohanne factum, quodipsius fama & autoritas quotidiè maiora capiebat incrementa.

Quomodo secessit in Galilaeam ob Iohannis traditionem, cum Herodes, qui Iohannem in carcerem coniecerat, fuerit Galilaeae tetrarcha? Resp. non fugit Herodem, sed Scribas & Pharisaeos, quibus non fuerat oportunum uti operâ Herodis ad capiendum Iesum, quemadmodum Iohannem, cùm Iesus Herodem non offendisset, quemadmodum Iohannes.

Fuit hic Christi in Galilaeam reditus secundus, ut constat ex Ioh. 1. v. 43. & cap. 4. v. 3. ubi uterque reditus describitur. Reliqui Evangelistarum solius huius secundi reditus mentionem faciunt. Nam post primum reditum Christus non diu mansit in Galilaea; nec describunt reliqui Evangelistae anniversarias Christi in Iudaeam ad solennia festa profectiones, quod facit solus Iohannes: solius postremi reditus in Iudaeam mentionem faciunt, ut huius solius in Galilaeam, post quem diu mansit in Galilaea.

## 4:13
v. 13. Why Jesus transferred his dwelling to Capernaum, he himself explains the reason in John 4. v. 44. namely because a Prophet is not acceptable in his own country.

Κατῴκησε. Not that he fixed continuous residences there, but that he dwelt more frequently and lodged there in a hired house than elsewhere.

Capernaum is called παραθαλα-διὰ maritime, namely πίλις. On account of this, because of the sea or lake of Gennesaret (which others the sea of Tiberias is said to lie nearby), for Nazareth was closer to the great sea than Capernaum. It was a most flourishing city of Galilee and an emporium of most illustrious name, which therefore Christ chose for his dwelling, so that his preaching might become known to more people, both to Israelites and to the Gentiles, who flowed there on account of trade. For besides being near the lake of Gennesaret toward the south, and the Jordan toward the east, through it there was passage across those regions to the great sea. *(Moreover, concerning the city of Capernaum, and its situation, splendor, size, and miracles performed by Christ in it, see more in Adrichomius in Descriptio Terrae Sanctae, B. D. Chemnitius in Harmonia Evangelica everywhere. Bünting in Itinerarium Sacrae Scripturae part 2. p. 12. 13. Heidmannus Palaestra c. 9. §. 60. seqq. Cornelius à Lapide in this place. But concerning the etymology of the name, besides the authors mentioned, Georgius Pasor can also be consulted, Appendix to the Lexicon of the New Testament. The Syrian expresses it by Cepharnachum, the Arab likewise in the same way, rendering but the Ethiopic has it with K., for it has Kaphrenacham.)*

Within the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, because near it met the boundaries of the lots of northern Zebulun and southern Naphtali, whence some assign it to the lot of Zebulun, others to the lot of Naphtali.

Capernaum was situated within the borders of both Galilees, as it were midway between the two, and hence convenient for the dwelling of Christ, since it had been proposed to him, by decree of the heavenly Father, to sow the seed of the Gospel in Galilee.

Latin:

v. 13. Quare Iesus habitationem transtulerit in Capernaum, eius rei causam exponit ipse Ioh. 4. v. 44. quia sc. Propheta non sit acceptus in patriaia.

Κατῴκησε. Non quòd sedes continuas illic fixerit, sed quòd domo illic conductâ frequentiùs egerit & diversatus sit ibi, quàm alibi.

Capernaum vocatur παραθαλα-διὰmaritina, sc. πίλις. Propterea, quod mari sive lacui Genezareth (qui aliis mare Tiberiadis dicitur) adiaceret, nam magno mari vicinior erat Nazareth, quàm Capernaum. Florentissima fuit Galilaeae civitas & praeclarissimi nominis emporium, quam proinde Christus habitationi suae elegit, ut pluribus notior fieret ipsius praedicatio tum Israëlitis tum gentibus, negotiationis gratia eò confluentibus. Praeterquam enim quod proxima esset mari Genezareth versus meridiem, & Iordani versus Orientem, erat per eam regionib. transamnanis transitus ad mare magnum. *(Caeterùm de urbe Capernaum, eiusq; situ, splendore, amplitudine, ac miraculis à Christo in illa editis videantur plura apud Adrich. in descript. terr. Sanctae, B. D. Chemn. in Harm. Evang. passim. Bü nting in Itin. S. part. 2. p. 12. 13. Heidm. Palaest. c. 9. §. 60. seqq. Corn. à Lap. in h. l. De nominis verò etymologia praeter dictos autores consuli quoque potest Georg. Pasor Append. Lex. N. Test. Syrus exprimit per Cepharnachum, eod. quoque modo Arabs, reddens sed Aethiop. per K. habet enim Kaphrenacham.)*

Infinibus Zabulon & Naphthali, quia prope eam concurrebant termini sortium Aquilonaris Zabulon & Australis Naphthali, unde quidam eam ad sortem Zabulon, quidam ad sortem Naphthali referunt.

Sita erat Capernaum in finibus utriusque Galilaeae, quasi media inter utramque, ac proinde habitationi Christi commoda, quippe cui ex decreto Patris coelestis propositum erat, in Galilaea semen Evangelii spargere.

## 4:14
*(v. 14. ἵνα πληρωθῇ etc. From the fact that in Holy Scripture of the New Testament, when remission is made to the Old Testament, the phrases are exchanged—it is said, and it is written, and accordingly are held as equivalent—it is rightly concluded by our own men against the Papists, that between the word of GOD and Scripture taken materially there is no real distinction. Thus it says that what was spoken might be fulfilled, Matthew 1, 22. chapter 4. 15. 23. here, likewise chapter 12, 17. elsewhere, what was written i.e. Scripture, Mark 15, 28. John 19, 36. Matthew 26, 54. But on this matter let further things be seen in B. Pareus, Colloquia Isagogica, Book on Scripture, chapter 1. §. 4. Therefore absurd are the pronouncements of certain Papists, namely that the written word is not the word of GOD, if we wish to speak truly and properly, as Melchior Canus holds, Book 3 of Locorum Theologicorum, chapter 3, foundation 4; likewise, that the nature of the Word of the Gospel shrinks back from writing, as Lindanus writes, Book 1 of Panoplia, chapter 23; likewise that Christ willed neither that his Church hang upon paper writings, nor that he commit his mysteries to membranes . How much more correctly Andradius, Book 2 of Defensio Fidei Tridentinae, folio 100: No one denies that knowledge of divine mysteries must chiefly be sought from the divine letters. Cornelius à Lapide, Preface to the Gospel, truly and weightily: Holy Scripture, he writes, is the word of GOD, is the very speech and voice of GOD, whereby God announces his wisdom to us, shows the way to virtue, salvation, and eternal happiness. Compare on this matter more things in the cited book in Cornelius.)*

Latin:

*(v. 14. ἵνα πληρωθῇ &c. Ex eo, quòd in Script. S. N. Test. quando remissio fit ad V. Test. permutantur phrases dictum est, ac scriptum est, adeoq; tanq. aequipollentes habentur, rectè colligunt nostrates contra Pontificios, inter verbum DEI, & Scripturam S. materialiter acceptam, non esse reale aliquod discrimen. Sic dicitur impleri, quod dictum,Matth. 1, 22.c. 4. 15.23. hîc, item c. 12, 17. alibi, quod scriptum s. Scriptura,Marc. 15, 28.Ioh. 19, 36.Matth. 26, 54. Sed de hâc re plura videatur apud B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. de Script. c. 1. §. 4. Absurda igitur sunt pronunciata nonnullorum Pontificiorum, quòd verbum scriptum non sit verbum DEI, si verè & propriè loqui velimus, ut habet Melch. Canus l. 3. L. T. c. 3. fund. 4. item, quod verbi Evangeliei natura adhorreat à scripto, ut Lindanus scribit l. 1. Panopl. c. 23. item quòd Christus nec Ecclesiam suam à chartacis scriptis pendere, nec membranis mysteria sua commi-tere voluerit. Quantò rectiùAndradius l. 2. Defens. fidei Trid. f. 100. Nemo inficiatur, divinorum mysteriorum cognitionem ex divinis litteris potissimùm petendam esse. Corn. à Lapide Prooem. in Evang. verè ac graviter: S. Scriptura, scribit, est verbum DEI, est ipsa DEI loquela & vox, quà s--l. Deus suam sapientiam nobis enunciat, viamad virtutem, salutem & felicitatem aeternam demonstrat. Conf. in hanc rem plura d. l. apud Cornelium.)*

## 4:15
v. 15. By the land of Zebulun is understood the region which fell by lot to the tribe of Zebulun. In the same sense it is called the land of Naphtali.

ὁδὸνθαλάοσης One must understand under it κατα or παρὰ Theophylact on this passage. γῆ κααθ᾽ ὁδὸνθαδάοσες It signifies ἡ παραλία that is, that portion of Galilee which lies at the lake of Gennesaret or the sea of Tiberias, in which were situated Capernaum, Bethsaida and Chorazin. Some wish it to be called the way of the sea, because it stretched toward Tyre, to the sea. Likewise in Hebrew one must understand under it ל by or near the sea.

Πέραν του Ιορδάνου. πέρον here does not mean beyond, since, when Judea is taken into account, both Galilees are on this side of the Jordan, but it corresponds to the Latin word alongside. *(See Buxtorf, Lexicon Talmudicum Rabbinicum, under the word ירדן But that the word πέραν is sometimes so taken, namely for alongside i.e. near or by, appears both from verse LXX., Num. 32, 19. and from John 1, 28. So also some Interpreters take it in Matt. 19, 1. such as Maldonatus, and thus Pasor also takes it in his Lexicon: Cornelius à Lapide however dissents, who nevertheless rightly warns out of Maldonatus that Galilee was so named from the first crossing of it, whereby the Israelites, setting out from Egypt, crossed over the Jordan and came into Judaea and Galilee. Which the Syrian too perhaps looking to this renders: that is, the tranfitus of the Jordan.)*

Some understand it with respect to those who dwelt beyond the river, then neighbors (the Gerasenes, the Bataneans, among whom were the allotments of the tribes of Gad, Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh), then distant peoples, Arabs, Chaldeans, others dwelling toward the East.

Γαλιλαία τῶν ἐθνῶν גליל Galilee has its name from גלל or to roll, because it lay along the seashore, on account of the winding recesses, namely, of the shores, or because the waves are driven back there by those winds or by the tide, and play rolling round, or finally on account of the heaps of sand piled up there. *(Cornelius à Lapide applies this mystically. For he writes: In Galilee Christ revolved and turned the lost morals of men, he circled them as it were, so that like a sphere they might touch the earth and earthly things only at a point; but being wrapped and rounded in their whole mass, they might look toward the rounded heavens turned. Some, such as Beza, Tossan, Brugensis, etc. (so also the blessed D. Quistorp understands it in this place) understand here Upper Galilee (which recedes to the North, toward Caesarea Philippi and Mount Lebanon, having Lower Galilee to the south, the Jordan to the east, and the maritime cities, Sidon, Tyre, and Ptolemais to the west) which is called Galilee of the Gentiles, both because it was bordering on the Tyrians and Sidonians, and because it comprised those twenty cities which Solomon gave to the King of Tyre 1. Reg. 9. v. 11. complecteretur. Others, such as Casaubon, understand it of Lower Galilee (which has Upper Galilee to the north, Samaria to the south, the Sea of Tiberias to the east, and the Great Sea to the west. Josephus, book 3 of the war, chapter 2. It extends along the Jordan, and lies adjacent to the Sea of Tiberias or the Lake of Gennesaret.) which is called Galilee of the Gentiles, because it is a most populous and fertile region, Deut. 33. v. 23. for in the Scriptures it often denotes the same thing, which עם. Whence the Syrian in this place rendered it, Galilee . Josephus, book 3 of the Jewish War, chapter 2. The cities in Galilee are frequent, and where the multitude of villages is populous on account of its opulence, so that the smallest has over fifteen thousand inhabitants. This Galilee, being the outermost part of Palestine, had nations on its borders: the Tyrians and Sidonians to the west, the Trachonites to the east, and the Syrians to the north. Josephus, in the same place. (Upper Galilee was in the tribe of Asher and Naphtali, and in this was Capernaum; Lower Galilee was in the tribe of Issachar and Zebulun, and in this was situated Nazareth. See Buxtorff, Lex. Chald. Talm. Rabb. p. 436. 4-7. Heidm. Palaest. c. 9. §. 10. 32. 59. 60. seqq.)

The same regions are understood by the way of the sea beyond the Jordan and Galilee of the Gentiles, which is through the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali. The prophet calls the land of Zebulun the way of the sea beyond the Jordan: the land of Naphtali Galilee of the Gentiles. For it is the custom of the prophets to repeat one and the same thing with different words . He calls the land of Zebulun the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, because, extended from the Jordan as far as the Great Sea, it provided a straight path to it, not only for its own inhabitants and neighbors, but also for all peoples living far beyond the Jordan to the East, Arabs, Chaldeans, and others. He calls the land of Naphtali Galilee of the nations, because it comprised the greater part of Galilee of the nations, or upper Galilee.

Zebulun and Naphtali are not to be taken so strictly as not to include neighboring tribes—Naphtali Asher, and Zebulun Issachar—or even nearer places: therefore just as in other passages of Scripture, so also here denomination is made from the more important.

Latin:

v. 15. Per terram Zabulon intelligitur regio, quae sorte obtigit tribui Zabulon. Eodem sensu dicitur terra Naphthali.

ὁδὸνθαλάοσης Subaudiendum κατα vel παρὰ Theophyl. ad h. l. γῆ κααθ᾽ ὁδὸνθαδάοσες Significatur ἡ παραλία h. e. ea portio. Galilaeae, quae est ad lacum Genezareth sive mare Tiberiadis, in qua fitae sunt Capernaum, Bethsaida & Corazin. Quidam volunt vocari viam maris, quòd ea tenderet Tyrum versus ad mare. In Hebraeo itidem subintelligendum לad vel iuxta mare.

Πέραν του Ιορδάνου. πέρον h. l. non significat trans, quia habitâ ratione Iudaeae Galilaea utraque est cis Iordanem, sed respondet Latinae voci secus. *(Vid. Buxt. Lex. Talm. Rabb. voce ירדן Quod verò dictio πέραν ita aliquando sumatur, nempe pro secus s. iuxta vel ad, patet tum ex vers. LXX. Num. 32, 19. tum ex Ioh. 1, 28. Sic accipiunt quoque Matth. 19, 1. nonnulli Interpr. uti Maldonatus, & ita etiam sumit Pasor in Lexico: dissentit verò Corn. à Lapide, qui tamen ex Maldonato rectè monet, Galilaeam ita dictam fuisse à primò eius traiectu, quo Israelitae profecti ex Aegypto transierunt Iordanem inque Iudaeam, ac Galilaeam venerunt. quo & Syrus h. l. fortè respiciens reddit: i. e. tranfitus Iordanis.)*

Quidam intelligunt respectu eorum, qui habitabant trans amnem, tùm vicinorum (Gerasenorum, Batanaeorum, inter quos erant sortes tribuum Gad, Ruben & dimidiae tribus Manasse) tùm longinquorum, Arabum, Chaldaeorum, aliorum ad Orientem habitantium.

Γαλιλαία τῶν ἐθνῶνגליל Galilaea nomenhabet à גלל vol vere, quod maris littori adiaceat, propter sinuosos sc. littorum recessus, vel quia fluctus illis ventis aut aestu reciprocantur, volutatimq; ludunt, vel denique propter congestos illic arenarum tumulos. *(Corn. à Lapide accommodat hoc mysticè. scribit enim: In Galiaea Christus revolvit & tornavit perditos hominum mores, eosquasi circinavit, ut instar globiterram & terrena tantùm in puncto tangerent; totâ verò reliquâ mole convoluti & rotundi coelos rotundos tornatosrespicerent.)* Quidam, uti Beza, Tossan, Brugensis &c. *(ita quoque accipit B. D. Quistorp. h. l.)* intelligunt hîc Galilaeam superiorem (quae in Septentrionem recedit, Caesaream Philippi & Libanum montem versus, àmeridie habens inferiorem, ab ortu Iordanem, ab occasu maritimas urbes, Sidonem, Tyrum & Ptolomaida) quae dicitur Galiaea gentium, tum quod Tyriiis & Sidonis esset finitima, tum quod viginti illas urbes, quas Tyriorum Regi dedit Salomo1. Reg. 9. v. 11.complecteretur. Alii, uti Casaubonus, accipiunt de Galilaea inferiore (quae à septentrione habet superiorem, à meridie Samariam, ab ortu mare Tiberiadis, ab occasu mare magnū. Ioseph. lib. 3. de bello cap. 2. Protenditur secundum Iordanem, & ad mare Tiberiades sive lacum Genezareth adiacet.) quae dicitur Galilaea gentium, quia est populofissima & fenacissima regio,Deut. 33. v. 23. enim in Scripturis saepiùs idem notat, quod עם. Unde Syrus h. l. reddidit, Galilaeam . Iosephus lib. 3. de bell. Iudaic. cap. 2. Civitates in Galilaea crebrae sunt, & ubimultitudo vicorum propter opulentiam populosa, ut qui sit minimus, supra quindecim millia colonorum habeat. Galilaea haec, utpote extima Palaestinae, in confiniis habuit gentes, ab occidente Tyrios & Sidonios, ab Ortu Trachonitas, ab Aquilone Syros. Ioseph. d. l. *(Galilaea superior erat intribu Aser & Naphthali, & in hâc erat Capernaum; inferior in tribu Isaschar & Zabulon, & in hac sita erat Nazareth. Vid. Buxtorff. Lex. Chald. Talm. Rabb. p. 436. 4-7. Heidm. Palaest. c. 9. §. 10. 32. 59. 60. seqq.)*

Eaedem regiones intelliguntur per viam maris trans Iordanem & Galilaeam gentium, quae per terram Zabulon & terram Naphthali. Terram Zabulon propheta vocat viam maris trans Iordanem: terram Naphthali Galilaeam gentium. Prophetis enim in more positum, unam eandemque rem diversis vocabulis r-petere. Terram Zabulon vocat viam maris trans Iordanem, quia à Iordane ad mare usque magnum protensa rectum iter praebebat ad illud, non solùm in colis suis & vicinis, verùm etiam populis omnibus, ongè ultrâ Iordanem ad Orientem habitantibus, Arabibus, Chaldaeis & aliis. Terram Naphthali vocat Galilaeam gentium, eò quod maiorem partem Galilaeae gentium sive superioris complectebantur.

Zabulon & Naphthali non tam strictè accipienda, ut non comprehendant vicinas tribus, Naphthali Ase-, & Zabulon Isaschar, aut viciniora etiam loca: ut ergo in aliis Scripturae locis, ita & hic à potiore fit denominetio.

## 4:16
v. 16. Ὁ λαὸς. The people of those regions, namely, of the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, or by the way of the sea beyond Jordan, and of Galilee of the nations, that is, the peoples of Upper and Lower Galilee.

Ὁ καθήμενος. Casaubon on this passage ηαθήμενα Places situated in valleys and low-lying are called by the Greeks. Thus most elegantly the people ἐυσκότει καθήμενος. are said to sit who he wished to be understood as being in darkness.

Isaiah has the word walking, Matthew uses the word sitting, looking to the long duration of those calamities, in respect of which the Israelites could be seen to have settled and become fixed deep within them. To walk however and to sit is used for to act and to dwell.

By this sitting in darkness some think there is regard had to the calamities of that people, because they were led away into captivity by Salmonassar king of the Assyrians 1 Kings 17 v. 6 But spiritual darkness of ignorance, sin, and death are rather rightly understood.

For the land of the shadow of death Matthew says the region and shadow of death by the figure διὰ δὰο in the same sense. The shadow of death is a deadly and lethal shadow: therefore it denotes that we are subject not only to the darkness of ignorance and sin but also to temporal and eternal death. Others expound it thus: the shadow of death צל־ מות is a shady or darksome death. But the matter comes back to the same thing.

In the region which the shadow of death occupies, that is, the densest darkness. צלמות properly means that color which imminent death draws over the eyes and face of a man, which is as it were the shadow of approaching and drawing-near death. Hence the densest darkness, out of which one cannot emerge, and extreme dangers which threaten present death, are metaphorically called shadow of death in Holy Scripture.

But why are these peoples said specifically to sit in darkness, in the gross ignorance of errors? Answer. 1. They were far removed from the temple of Jerusalem, which was the workshop of divine θεογνωσίας and worship. 2. They were mixed among the nations, namely the most impious Tyrians and Sidonians. *(But what is here said about certain peoples in particular—that, deprived of the light of the saving knowledge of Christ, they sat in darkness—can be affirmed generally of all unregenerate men, the Holy Scriptures teaching so. See John 1, 5.Acts 26, 18.Luke 1, 79.Rom. 1, 21.Eph. 4, 18.ch. 5, 8.1. Tim. 6, 5. add 1. Cor. 2, 14.ch. 3, 5.1. Pet. 2, 9. which oracles must be noted against the Papists, heralds after the fall.)*

For the word of shining, which Isaiah uses, Matthew employs the word of rising, having regard to the circumstance of that time, when the splendor of the Gospel had recently arisen. Chrysostom: not that this people came to the light, but that the light came to them.

This prophecy was fulfilled when Christ chose for himself a dwelling in the city of Capernaum, situated on the borders of both Galilees, midway between each of those regions. For by this means it came about that in both Galilees the preaching and miracles of Christ shone forth like a new light. v. 13 and 23.

The people of Galilee saw this light not alone, but first, because with such brightness it did not shine upon another people before, v. 17. But from there it spread throughout the whole world.

The light of evangelical preaching in the New Testament is called great. 1. with respect to the preaching in the Old Testament, which compared to this light, v. 17, must be reckoned almost a mere spark. 2. with respect to its spreading, because it poured itself out through the whole world.

*(Here the Jews accuse the Evangelist, both because he cited the Prophet's words incompletely, and because he applied them to Christ, whereas the Prophet treats of the deliverance accomplished in the time of Sennacherib, when an angel was sent who, after slaying their enemies, stirred up immense joy in the Israelite people. But Mr. D. Müller has fully satisfied this objection in his Iudaismus, p. 1336 sqq. Briefly we note at this place that anxiety existed in the land of Israel not only in the time of Sennacherib, but also shortly before the coming of Christ, when above all the corruption of true doctrine aroused great sadness in the hearts of the godly—which shadows of sadness were driven away by the arising Sun of Righteousness, Christ. That however is treated of in this prophetic oracle is evident from what precedes and follows. See ch. 7, 14. ch. 8, 14. likewise from the comparison of parallel passages. See ch. 60, 2. ch. 49, 9.) Zech. 9, 9. Moreover, to Hugo Grotius too the prophet's words plainly seem to deal directly with some deliverance which occurred nearer those times. On which matter elsewhere. Let B. D. Chemnitius's Harmonia Evangelica ch. 35 be consulted.

Latin:

v. 16. Ὁ λαὸς. Populus istarum regionum, sc. terrae Zubulon & terrae Naphthali, sive viae maris trans Iordanem, & Galilaeae gentium h. e. Galilaeae superioris & inferioris populi.

Ὁ καθήμενος. Casaub. ad h. l. ηαθήμεναGraecis dicuntur loca in convallibus posita & depressa. Itaa pereleganter populusἐυσκότει καθήμενος.vocatur, quem in tenebris esse, voluit intelligi.

Esaias habet verbum ambulandi, Matthaeus utitur verbo confidendi, respiciens ad calamitatum illarum diuturnitatem, cuius respectu videri poterant Israëlitae in illis penitus consedisse & defixi esse. Ambulare autem & sedere usurpatur pro agere & versari.

Per hanc sessionem in tenebris quidam putant respectum haberi ad calamitates illius populi, quia à Rege Assyrio Salmanasser erant in captivitatem abducti1. Reg. 17. v. 6. Sed rectiùs intelliguntur spirituales tenebrae ignorantiae, peccati & mortis.

Pro terraumbrae mortis dicit Matthaeus regionem & umbram mortis per figuram διὰ δὰο eodem sensu.
