Umbramortis est umbra mortifera & lethalis: denotatur igitur, nos non solùm esse tenebris ignorantiae & peccati, sed etiam temporalis & aeternae mortis obnoxios. Alii exponunt hoc modo. Umbramortisצל־ מותest umbrosa seu tenebricosa mors. Sed res eodem redit.

In regione, quam occupat umbra mortis i. e. densissimae tenebrae. צלמות propriè est color ille, quem mors proximè instans oculis ac faciei hominis obducit, qui quasi umbra est adventantis appropinquantisque mortis. Unde tenebrae densissimae, è quibus nequeas emergere, & extrema pericula, quae praesentem intentant mortem, umbra mortis metaphoricè in sacris literis dicuntur.

Quare verò peculiariter hi populi dicuntur in tenebris errorum ata ignorantiae sedere? Resp. 1. longè aberant à templo Hierosolymitano, quod erat divinae θεογνωσίας & cultus officina. 2. erant permixti gentibus, videl. Tyriis & Sidoniis impiissimis. *(Quod verò hîc de quibusdam populis in specie dicitur, quôd luce salutiferae Christi cognitionis destituti consederint in tenebris, in genere de omnibus hominibus irregenitis affirmari potest, docente Sc. S. Vid. Ioh. 1, 5.Actor. 26, 18.Luc. 1, 79.Rom. 1, 21.Eph. 4, 18.c. 5, 8.1. Tim. 6, 5. add. 1. Cor. 2, 14.c. 3, 5.1. Pet. 2, 9. quae oracula contra Pontific. L. A. post lapsum praecones notanda sunt.)*

Pro verbo splendendi, quod est apud Esaiam, Matthaeus utitur verbo exoriendi, respiciens ad circumstantiam illius temporis, quo splendor Evangelii recens fuerat exortus. Chrysost non quod populus hic ad lucem, sed quod lux ad eos venerit.

Impletum est hoc vaticinium, quando Christus habitationem sibi delegit in civitate Capernaum, sita in finibus utriusque Galilaeae, inter utramque harum regionum media. Hac enim ratione factum, ut in utraque Galilaea praedicatio & miracula Christi instar novae lucis splenduerint. v. 13 & 23.

Lucem hanc vidit Galilaeae populus non solus, sed primus, quia non ea claritate alii populo priùs illuxit v. 17. Sed ex eo in universum terrarum orbem propagata est.

Lux praedicationis Evangelicae in N. T. dicitur magna. 1. respectu praedicationis in V. T. quae collata ad hanc lucem v. 17. scintilla quasi quaedam aestimanda. 2. respectu propagationis, quia per totum terrarum orbem se effudit.

*(Iudaei accusant hîc Evangelistam, tum quòd verba Prophetae non integra citaverit, tum quòd ad Christum applicaverit, cùm tamen Propheta agat de liberatione tempore Sanherib facta, quando missus fuerit Angelus, qui interfectis hostibus populi Israëlitici ingens gaudium excitavit. Sed huic obiectioni ex asse satisfecit Dn. D. Müllerus in Iudaismo p. 1336. seqq. Breviter h. l. notamus, quòd non solùm tempore Sanherib anxietas in terrâ Isr. fuerit, verùm etiam paullō ante Christi adventum, ubi cumprimis verae doctrinae corruptio in cordibus piorum magnam tristitiam excitavit, quae tristitiae tenebrae pulsae fuerunt exorto Iustitiae sole Christo. Quôd autem de hoc in vaticinio prophetico agatur, patet ex antec. & conseq. Vid. c. 7, 14. c. 8, 14. it. ex locorum parall. collatione. Vid. c. 60, 2. c. 49, 9. Zach. 9, 9. Caeterùm Hugoni quoque Grotio prophetae verba planè videntur directè agere de liberatione aliqua, quae propiùs illa tempora contigerit. Quâ de re alibi. Consulatur B. D. Chemn. Harm. Evang. c. 35.

## 4:17
v. 17. ἀπο τὸτε. From that time, namely from when John had been handed over he came into Galilee, and transferred his dwelling to Capernaum.

He began to preach. * (Cornelius à Lapide writes on v. 12 of this chapter that Matthew here marks the beginning of Christ's preaching from the imprisonment of John the Baptist. And he continues: For before his incarceration Christ committed to him the office of preaching, so that he might prepare the way for himself. But truly *) Christ also preached beforehand in Judaea, for neither did he perform those miracles about which John 2. v. 23. and ch. 4. v. 45. without teaching, but more sparingly while John the precursor was still fulfilling his own function; then indeed in Galilee and afterwards in Judaea he began, for the sake of publicly, continually, diligently preaching and publishing the Gospel, to go through all places. Luke 23. v. 5. * (Whence Cornelius also adds there: When John was imprisoned Christ succeeded him in preaching, just as the sun succeeds its morning star, and then began to proclaim the gospel publicly and solemnly. *)

Μεεῖανοεῖτε. The sum of Christ's sermons is briefly comprehended by the word μετανοεῖε, repent ye, because the practice of the whole of Christianity is repentance, and all the sermons of the Doctors of the Church of the faithful ought to be directed to this end, that repentance be done.

Christ begins his ministry in the same manner, namely by the preaching of repentance. 1. That he might show that he brings the same doctrine which John had brought, and that between himself and John there is the highest agreement. 2. That he might confirm John's ministry and the testimonies which he bore concerning him. 3. That by the very fact he might demonstrate that he is the one whose precursor John was. * (Conradus Clingius quite absurdly attempts to prove from this passage, Book 4, LL., ch. 31, the institution of the Sacrament of Penance, since however not only had John the Baptist already previously preached repentance, whence also Cornelius à Lapide writes on this passage, The same thing, which Christ preaches here, John had preached as it were Christ's forerunner and outrunner: but even in the Old Testament commands are given for doing penance, as is abundantly evident from several passages. And Cotonus freely grants it, p. 616, Institutiones Catholicae. Moreover, if therefore penance is a sacrament because Christ commanded the same, it follows that almsdeeds also, nay rather also prayer, vigilance, love etc. should be sacraments. Add that the Council of Trent, session 14, ch. 1, decrees, That Christ instituted the Sacrament of repentance especially at that time when, raised from the dead, He breathed on the disciples, saying: Receive &c. (But the Margrave of Brandenburg objects in the Apology of the Mirror of Truth, Cologne edition, A. 1653, p. 140, following Bellarmine, book 1, On Repentance, chapter 9, that Philip Melanchthon in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, under the title On the Number and Use of the Sacraments, right at the beginning, counts repentance among the true Sacraments, nay, Bellarmine labors to make us guilty of perjury, since we thus make our secession from the Augsburg Confession. Answer: The word Sacrament is taken in two ways. 1. Broadly, for that which in respect of its end, which is the confirmation of our faith concerning the remission of sins, agrees with the divine command along with the other Sacraments properly so called; 2. Strictly and most properly for that which agrees, both in respect of its end and in respect of its matter and form, with the other Sacraments most properly so called, that is, to which all the requirements of a Sacrament most properly so called belong. When now the Apology of the Augsburg Confession attributes the name of Sacrament to repentance, it takes the word Sacrament broadly, for it is expressly said there: If we call Sacraments those rites which have the command of GOD and to which the promise of grace has been added, it is easy to judge which are properly Sacraments. For rites instituted by men will not be Sacraments properly so called in this manner. For it is not of human authority to promise grace. Truly, therefore, Baptism, the Supper of the Lord, and Absolution, which is the Sacrament of repentance, are Sacraments. For these rites have the command of GOD and the promise of grace, which is proper to the New Testament. But by no means is the word Sacrament, taken most properly, attributed to absolution by the Apology, nor can it be attributed, which can easily be shown, if only a comparison be instituted between absolution and the substantial requirements of the Sacraments most properly so called, which by the consensus of all are Baptism and the Supper of the Lord. But those requirements are enumerated by the learned D. Chemnitz, part 2, Examination of the Council of Trent, p. 14, 15, likewise by the learned D. Hutter in the Loci Majores, p. 591 b, 624 a. Nor does it stand in the way that the Apology says Absolution is a truly and properly a Sacrament, for it uses those words both to declare that there is some analogy between Absolution and the Sacraments most properly so called, namely in respect of the divine command and the end, such as cannot be shown in rites instituted by men, and in opposition to those said rites. Therefore the Apology uses those particles not ἁπλῶς, but συγκριτικῶς and κατὰ τί. Let many things be compared on this matter in B. Par. t. 3. L. C. de Poenit. §. 24. likewise Confess. Cathol. t. 4. p 176. B D. Cundis. not. ad Compend. Hutt. p. 1038. Especially in B. D. Chemn. Part. 2. Exam. Concil. Trid. p. 15.)*

Ἤγγικε. Erasmus translated, presses hard upon. Yet Christ by no means wished the kingdom of heaven to be far off, but already to have come to them: therefore it is more correctly rendered, has drawn near, Is. 56. v. 1. By the kingdom of heaven is understood that time of grace in which Christ came in the flesh, and of manifestation through the preaching of the Gospel. Compare chapter 3. v. 2. *(Why the Church, especially that of the New Testament, is called the kingdom of heaven, B. Par. shows at length in L. de Eccl. §. 19.)*

Latin:

v. 17. ἀπο τὸτε. Ex eo tempore, sc. quo Iohanne tradito venerat in Galilaeam, & habitationem transtulerat Capernaum.

Coepit praedicare. *(Scribit Corn. à Lap. ad v. 12. huius cap. Matthaeum hîc or diripraedicaetionem Christi à carcere Iohannis Baptistae. ac pergit: Ante enim eius incarcerationem Christus eidem munus praedicandi commisit, ut ipse sibi viam sterneret. Verùm)* Praedicaverat quoque Christus anteà in Iudaea, neque enim miracula illa, de quibus Ioh. 2. v. 33. & cap. 4. v. 45. absque doctrina ediderat, sed parciùs quamdiu Iohannes praecursor suo adhuc fungebatur, tunc verò in Galilaea & postea in Iudaea coepit publicè, continuè, assiduè praedicandi divulgandiq; Evangelii causâ per loca omnia discurrere. Luc. 23. v. 5. *(Unde etiam Corn. d. l. addit: Iohanne incarcerato Christus ei in praedicatione successit, qs. sol lucifero suo, tunca publicè & solenniter evangelizare coepit.)*

Μεεῖανοεῖτε. Summa concionum Christi breviter comprehenditur voce μετανοεῖε, quia praxis totius Christianismi est poenitentia, atque omnes fidelium Ecclesiae Dd. conciones eò directae esse debent, ut agatur poenitentia.

Christus eodem modo, videlicet praedicatione poenitentiae suum exorditur ministerium. 1. ut ostenderet, se eandem afferre doctrinam, quam Iohannes attulerat, ac summum esse inter se & Iohannem consensum. 2. ut confirmaret Iohannis ministerium ac testimonia, quae de ipso tulerat. 3. ut ipso facto demonstraret, se esse eum, cuius Iohannis fuerat praecursor. *(Satis ineptè ex h. l. Conradus Clingius l. 4. LL. c. 31. institutionem Sacramenti Poenitentiae probare conatur, cûm tamen non solùm iam antè Iohannes Baptista poenitentiam praedicarit, unde etiam Corn. à Lap. in h. l. scribit, Idem, quod Christus hîc praedicat, Iohannem quoBaptistā quasi Christi prodromum & percursorem praedicasse: verùm etiam in V. T. poenitentiae agendae praecepta habeantur, ceu ex pluribus locis abunde patet. Et ultro concedit Cotonus p. 616. Inst. Cathol. Praeterea si propterea poenitentia Sacramentum est, quia Christus eandem praecepit, sequitur, quòd eleemosynae quoque, imò & oratio, vigilantia, dilectio &c. Sacramentum sint. Accedit, quòd Concil. Trident. sess. 4. c. 1. decernit, Christum tum praecipuè poenitentiae Sacramentum instituisse, cùm à mortuis excitatus insufflavit discipulos dicens: Accipite &c. *(Sed obiicit Marchio Brandenburg. in Apol. Speculi veritatis edit. Colon. A. 1653. p. 140. sequutus Bellarminus l. 1. de Poen. c. 9. quòd Philippus Melanch. in Apolog. A. C. sub titulo de num. & usu Sacr. statim initiô. Poenitentiam veris Sacramentis accenseat, quin Bellarminus periurii nos reos facere satagit, cùm ab A. C. secessionem ita faciamus. Resp. Sacramenti vox sumitur dupliciter. 1 latè pro eo, quod ratione finis, qui est fidei nostrae de peccatorum remissione confirmatio, ac mandati divini cum reliquis Sacramentis propriè dictis cōvenit; 2. strictè ac propriissimè pro eo, quod tum ratione finis, tum ratione materiae ac formae cum reliquis Sacr., propriissimè dictis convenit, h. e. cui omnia competunt requisita Sacramenti, propriissimè sic dicti. Quando iam Apol. A. C. poenitentiae Sacramenti nomen attribuit, tum Sacramenti vocem latè accipit, expressè enim ibi dicitur: Si Sacramenta vocamus ritus, qui habent mandatum DEI & quibus addita est promissio gratiae, facilè est iudicare, quae sint propriè Sacramenta. Nam ritus ab hominibus instituti non erunt h. m. propriè dicta Sacramenta. Non est enim avioritatis humaenae, promittere gratiam. Verè igitur sunt Sacramenta Baptismus, Coena Domini & Absolutio, quae est Sacram. poenitentiae. Nam hi ritus habent mandatum DEI, & promissionem gratiae, quae est propria Novi Testamenti. Minimè verò vox Sacramenti propriissimè accepta absolutioni ab Apologia tribuitur, vel tribui quoq; potest, id quod ostēdi facilè potest, si modò collatio instituatur inter absolutionem & inter requisita substantialia Sacramentorum propriissimè dictorum, qualia omnium confensu sunt Baptismus & Coena Domini. recensent verò ista requisita B. D. Chemnitius part. 2. Exam. Concilii Trid. p. 14. 15. it. B. D. Hutterus in LL. Mai. p. 591. b. 624. a. Nec obstat, quod Apologia dicit, Absolutionē esse verè & propriè Sacramentum, utitur enim istis vocalibus tum ut declaret, analogiam aliquam esse inter Absolutionem ac Sacramenta propriissimè dicta, nempe ratione mandati divini ac finis, qualis in ritibus ab hominibus institutis ostendi haut potest, tum in oppositione dictorum rituum. Utitur igitur istis particulis Apol. non ἁπλῶς, sed συγκριτικῶς ac κατὰ τί. Conferantur plura in hanc rem apud B. Par. t. 3. L. C. de Poenit. §. 24. it. Confess. Cathol. t. 4. p 176. B D. Cundis. not. ad Compend. Hutt. p. 1038. Cumprimis apud B. D. Chemn. Part. 2. Exam. Concil. Trid. p. 15.)*

Ἤγγικε. Erasmus vertit, instat. Atqui Christus nequaquam hoc voluit, regnum coelorum nō procul abesse, sed iam ad eos pervenisse: rectiùs igitur vertitur, appropinquavit,Es. 56. v. 1. Per regnum coelorum intelligitur tempus illud gratiae, quo Christus venit in carnem, & manifestationis per praedicationem Evangelii. Confer cap. 3. v. 2. *(Cur Ecclesia, N. T. praesertim, regnum coelorum vocetur, prolixè ostendit B. Par. L. de Eccl. §. 19.)*

## 4:18
v. 18. Περιπατῶν. He did not walk idly who, while walking, caught the very fishermen themselves fishing in the sea.

παρὰ τὴν θάλαασαντῆς Γαλιλαίας. Understood is the lake or pond of Genezareth, as Luke calls it, chapter 5. The Hebrews call all larger bodies of waters, whether salty or sweet and drinkable—congregations that extend over a great space in length and breadth and are stirred by frequent motions of waves—seas. *(See Gen. 1, 10.2. Kings [Reg.] 16, 17. In the same way Virgil also used it, noted by Drusius, book 9. Observ. ch. 20.)* But the History of the calling of the Apostles which Luke there records is the same as that which Matthew here recounts. *(There seems indeed to be some discrepancy among the Evangelists concerning certain circumstances. Yet it must be known that it was not the purpose of the Evangelists to describe the sayings and deeds of Christ in a fixed and distinct series of times, but rather summarily at least to mark out the principal heads, as Dn D. Walther well observed. Harm. Bibl. p. 736. That however the history of the calling of the Apostles here is the same as that which Luke also hands down, Cornelius à Lapide also determined, followed therein by Tirinus, abandoning not only Lyra but also their own fellow-Jesuits, Francis Toledo and John Maldonate. But Chrysostom too, Theophylact, Euthymius, Franc. Lucas, Jansenius and others hold that it is the same history which Matthew here and Luke chapter 5 hand down.)*

This lake is called Gennesaret, the sea of Galilee, from the region beside which it lies, whose eastern boundary separates it from the region of the Gerasenes and Gaulanitis. Josephus, book 3 of The Jewish War, chapter 18, describes this lake thus: that it has a length of one hundred stadia, a breadth of forty, ending in shores and sands, and is cut through its middle by the river Jordan. *(See more in the notes on Luke 5, 1.)*

Christ calls brothers to the apostolate, so that he may commend fraternal harmony to the Ministers of the Church.

Simon or Simeon, having his name from שמע, that is, from hearing, received the name Peter when he was chosen by Christ for the apostolate Mark 3. v. 16. The Ministers of the Church ought to be Simons, hearing the word of Christ, and strengthened in the faith of Peter. *(Cornelius à Lapide comments on this passage, that Peter was called by Christ Cephas, i.e., Rock or Peter.John 1, 42.because, he says, he was going to build his Church upon him,Matt. 16, 18. From this, moreover, the Papists conclude, that the Roman Pontiff cannot in any way define anything heretical to be believed by the whole Church, as Bellarmine holds, book 4 On the Roman Pontiff, ch. 2, and he says this is the most common opinion of almost all Catholics. But [the Church was built] not upon Peter, but upon the confession of Peter, as the Fathers of the Council of Soissons hold, or as Haymo Bishop of Halberstadt expounds, upon this faith, i.e., upon Christ, whom Peter confessed, the Church was built. Denis à Ryckel, Carthusian, also agrees, for at the words: upon this rock,Matt. 16, 18. he adds: h. e. the firmness and foundation of this faith. Or, upon this rock which he confessed, h. e. upon myself, the corner stone and highest mountain, of which the Apostle speaks1. Cor. 3. Another foundation etc. Beautifully Augustine, book On Faith and Works, ch. 16: It was said openly: For another foundation no one can lay besides what has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. But if Christ, then without doubt the faith of Christ, since indeed through faith Christ dwells in our hearts. Also notably Nicholas of Lyra on Matt. 16, 18: The Church does not consist in men by reason of ecclesiastical or secular power or dignity, because many Princes and supreme Pontiffs (N.B.) and others have been found to have apostatized from the faith, on account of which the Church consists in those persons in whom there is knowledge and true confession of faith and truth. But more will be dealt with concerning this matter in the notes on Matt. 16, 18. Meanwhile see B.P., vol. 1, Conf. Cath. p. 290 sqqq.)*

Andrew is said to be from strength: for ἀνδρεῖος among the Greeks means manly and strong. The ministers of the Church ought to be endowed with a manly and strong spirit.

Ἀμφίςβλησρον is a kind of net, named from ἀμφὶ and βάλλειν,, because when it is cast it expands from narrow into wide, and, curved into the shape of half an egg into a circle, it embraces a vast expanse of water. *(The Interpreters rightly warn in this place that Christ is to be supplied here from Luke 5, 1. seqq., when the numerous crowds, who had gathered with ardent desire to hear the word of GOD, pressed upon him and all but pushed him from the shore into the lake, so that he ascended into Peter's boat (as he had already begun to use by custom more than a year before, John 1, 42.) and taught the people, and soon commanded Peter to cast the net into the sea, who immediately drew in an immense quantity of fish. And so by the miracle he wished to confirm his doctrine, lest the hearers doubt that he had come as a teacher sent by God. But that this was truly a miracle, B. D. Chemn. in Harm. Evang. c. 36 shows most beautifully from the circumstances of time, place, the diligence previously employed &c. noted by Luke, and he moreover warns that Ps. 8. 8. is to be noted here)*

Those who were called by Christ to discipleship were followers of a harmless art; they sought a meager livelihood from the public lake. The very fishing reminded them of a new and spiritual fishing.

Latin:

v. 18. Περιπατῶν. Non otiosè ambulavit, qui inter ambulandum ipsosè mari piscatus est piscatores.

παρὰ τὴν θάλαασαντῆς Γαλιλαίας. Intelligitur lacus sive stagnum Genezareth, ut vocat Lucas cap. 5. Hebraei omnes maiores aquarum, sive salsae sint, sive dulces & potabiles, congregationes, quae magno spacio porriguntur in longum & latum, ac crebris undarum motibus agitantur, maria vocant. *(Vid. Gen. 1, 10.2. Reg. 16, 17. Eod. modo & Virgilius adhibuit, notante Drusio l. 9. Observ. c. 20.)* Eadem verò est Historia vocationis Apostolorum, quam Lucas ibi commemorat, cum ea, quam hic Matthaeus recenset. *(Videtur autem quod circumstantias nonnullas esse inter Evangelistas discrepantia. Verùm sciendum, quòd Evangelistis non fuerit propositum, certâ & distinctâ temporum serie dicta & facta Christi describere, sed summatim saltem praecipua notare capita, uti benè notavit Dn D. Walther. Harm. Bibl. p. 736. Quòd verò eadem hîc historia sit vocationis Apostolorum cum ca, quam Lucas quoque tradit, statuit quoque Corn. à Lapide, cumque secutus Tirinus, deserentes non solùm Lyranum, sed & proprios suos sociennos, Franciscum Toletum ac Ioh. Maldonatum Iesuitas. Sed & Chrysostomus, Theoph. Euthymius, Franc. Luas, Iansenius aliique statuunt, candem esse hist., quam hîc Matth., & Lucas cap. 5. tradunt.)*

Lacus iste Genezareth vocatur mare Galilaeae, à regione iuxta quam situs est, cuius est terminus Orientalis, separans eam à regione Gerasenorum & Galaaditide. Ioseph. lib. 3. de bello Iudaico cap. 18. hunc lacum sic describit, quòd habeat longitudinem centum stadiorum, latitudinem quadr aginta, undiin littora & arenas desinens, mediusfluvio Iordane secatur. *(Conf. plura in notis ad Luc. 5, 1.)*

Fratres Christus ad Apostolatum vocat, ut Ministris Ecclesiae fraternam concordiam commendet.

Simon vel Simeon à שמע ab audiendo nomen habens, Petri nomen accepit, quando à Christo ad Apostolatum electus est Marc. 3. v. 16. Ministri Ecclesiae debent esse Simones, verbū Christi audientes & Petri in fide roborati. *(Commentatur ad h. l. Corn. à Lapide, quòd Petrus à Christo dictus fuerit Cephas i. e. Petra vel Petrus.Ioh. 1, 42.quia, inquit, super eum aedificaturus erat Ecclesiam suam,Matth. 16, 18. Ex quo porrò colligunt Pontificii, Pontificem Rom. non posse ullo modo definire aliquid haereticum à totâ Ecclesia credendum, ut habet Bell. l. 4. de P. R. c. 2. & hanc dicit esse communissimam opinionem ferè omnium Catholicorum. Ast non super Petrum, sed super confessionem Petri, ut habent Patres Concilii Suessionesis, vel ut Haymo Episc. Halberst. exponit, super hanc fidem i. e. super Christum, quem Petrus confessus est, aedific ata est Ecclesia. Adstipulatur quoque Dionys. à Rickel Carthusianus, ad verba enim: super hanc Petram,Matth. 16, 18. addit: h. e. fidei huius firmitatem & fundamentum. Vel, super hanc petram, quam confessus est h. e. super me ipsum lapidem angularem & montem altissimum, de quo aeit Apostolus1. Cor. 3. Fundamentum aliud &c. Pulcrè Augustinus l. de fide & operibus c. 16. Apertè dictum est: Fundamentum enim aliud nemo ponere potest, praeter id quod positum est, quod est Christus Iesus. Si autem Christus, procul dubio fides Christi, per fidem quippe habitat Christus in cordibus nostris. Notanter quoque Nicolaus de Lyra in c. 16, 18. Matthaei: Ecclesia non consistit in hominibus ratione potestatis vel dignitatis Ecclesiasticae velsecularis, quia multi Principes & summi Pontifices (NB.) & alii inventi sunt apostatasse à fide, propter quod Ecclesiae consistit in illis personis, in quibus est notitia & verae confessio fidei & veritatis. Sed de hâc re pluribus agetur in not. ad Matth. 16, 18. Videatur interim B. P. t. 1. Conf. Cath. p. 290. seqq.)*

Andreas à sortitudine dictus: ἀνδρεῖος enim Graecis virilis ac fortis dicitur. Ministri Ecclesiae debent virili & forti animo esse praediti.

Ἀμφίςβλησρον est genus retis, dictum ab ἀμφὶ & βάλλειν, quod cùm iacitur, ex angusto in latum expandatur, & incurvatum in formam dimidiati ovi in orbem, complectatur ingens aquae spacium. *(Rectè monent Interpp. in h. l. supplendum hîc esse ex Luc. 5, 1. seqq. Christum, cùm frequentes turbae, quae ardenti desiderio audiendi verbum DEI convenerant, ipsum urgerent, ac tantum non è littore in stagnum, propellerent, adscendisse in naviculam Petri, (ut cuius consuetudine ante annum & ampliùs iamtum uti coeperat, Ioh. 1, 42.) atque populum docuisse, mox iussisse Petro, ut mitteret rete in mare, qui illicò attraxit ingentem piscium copiam. atque ita miraculo voluit confirmare doctrinam suam, ne dubitarent auditores, ipsum venisse doctorem à Deo missum. Quòd autem hoc verum fuerit miraculum, B. D. Chemn. in Harm. Evang. c. 36. ex circumstantiis temporis, loci, diligentiae antè adhibitae &c. à Lucâ annotatis pulcerrimè ostendit, ac notandum insuper hîc esse monet locum Ps. 8. 8.)*

Erant illi, qui à Christo ad discipulatum vocabantur, artis innoxiae sectatores, è publico lacu tenuem victum quaerebant. Piscatio ipsa novae ac spiritualis piscationis eos admonebat.

## 4:19
v. 19. Δεῦτε ὀπήσω μου. Hebraism. Follow me. Long ago Peter and Andrew, moved by the preaching of John the Baptist, had believed in Christ and had followed him, John 1, 35.37.39. 40. 41. 42. and had been frequently present with Jesus teaching, and perhaps also performing miracles, both then in Cana of Galilee and in Judea, John 2. v. 2.11.23. and when he returned from there into Galilee John 4. v. 846. Whence Peter Acts 1 v. 21. 22. testifies, that he and the other Apostles had companied with Jesus from the baptism of John unto the day on which he was taken up. But they had not yet wholly devoted themselves to Christ, nor did they so inseparably cleave to him that they did not meanwhile return to fishing, as to the art which they professed, from which they procured for themselves the means of life. Christ therefore, calling them away from this manner of life and occupation, invites them to an inseparable following, and wills that, having left the craft of fishing, they give themselves wholly to his discipleship , by which they may be taught a higher manner of fishing.

They are not called to faith in Christ, since they had long ago embraced it; nor are they called so that they might become disciples of Jesus, which they already were, but so that at their own time they might be Apostles or in hope of apostleship. For indeed the Apostolic office is not yet laid upon them; meanwhile they are enrolled into the peculiar fellowship and family of Christ, that they may be formed for the Apostolic office.

I will make you fishers of men. Regard is had to the prophetic oracle, Jer. 16. v. 16. Behold, I will send many fishers, saith the Lord *(That Christ suggested this prophecy's meaning by this saying to the Apostles, Tertullian writes, l. 4. adv. Marc. c. 9. Compare also the type Ezek. 47, 10. Deep is the lowly sea, out of whose mud the works of the ministers of the Church are to be drawn toward the light of the heavenly dwelling-place, Hilary canon 3. on Matthew. Moreover Marcus Antonius de Dominis Archbishop of Spalatro presses this saying among others against that fabricated monarchy of the Roman See, l. 1. de Rep. Eccl. c. 2., namely because from it it follows that Christ entrusted the same office equally to all the Apostles, while that [of Peter] is merely ministerial. Furthermore there would here be ample occasion for speaking about the avarice and simony of the Roman Pontiffs together with their clergy, on account of which they deserve rather to be called disturbers of Churches than successors of Peter and the Apostles; rather fishers of money than of men; rather ministers and priests of the treasury than of Christ. There is nothing, writes Aeneas Sylvius, afterwards called Pope Pius II of Rome, letter 66, which the Roman court does not obtain for itself by silver. For even the very laying on of hands and the gifts of the Holy Ghost are sold. Nor is remission of sins bestowed except for coined money. Truly Peter did not know how to handle his fishing net thus, unlike those feigned successors of his, the Roman Pontiffs, whence he was compelled to profess Acts 3, 6. Silver and gold have I none. Lest they should be forced to repeat this complaint again and again, the Popes of Rome bent all the sinews of their genius to spreading their nets more effectively for capture. Nor was their fishing barren either. Which Rome, Latium, Aemilia, Flaminia and the kingdom of Naples—for whose redemption out of the Roman fisherman's net the King of Spain is bound to pay yearly seven thousand ducats along with a noble horse—abundantly attests. Yet not content with that catch, the Popes of Rome led further out into the deep, and having spread the nets of Jubilees and Indulgences , it can scarcely be said how vast a haul of money they made from the entire world properly so called. Let him read at least Onuphrius Panvinius of Verona, Friar Eremitic Augustinian, both everywhere elsewhere and especially in the life of Sixtus IV, p. 363, likewise in the life of Alexander VI, p. 373 & following pages, edition Cologne A. 1593. Thus however the said author, l. c. p. 376, concerning Alexander VI. These things which they gathered then partly from the college of 80 writers of Briefs, whose several posts went for 750 golden pieces, partly from the tax-revenues, partly from the selling of Cardinalitial hats, since their enormous expenditures did not suffice, when want was pressing hard, fierce with a savage genius against whom he had as priest in his court, and among these certain Cardinals richer than the rest he resolved to remove by poison, so that, having reduced their resources into his treasury and gained possession of them, he might give away most lavishly, satisfy the insatiable greed of his son (the son, namely, of Caesar Borgia) &c. Behold the fair successors of Peter! behold fishers well skilled in their own craft! whom unless the Catholic Writers betrayed them, even today likewise the liberality of the present Supreme Pontiff Alexander VII, which his grandsons and granddaughters (or, if anyone prefers, sons and daughters) daily sufficiently experience, would set forth before us alive again; certainly no one would know it so well. Far better indeed would the Most Reverend Fathers act if they called themselves rather the successors of Simon than of Peter, since thereby they would offer greater sacrifice to the truth. For truly Francis Petrarcha, noble Tuscan poet, who lived about A.D. 1339, writes in the Dialogue on avoiding the Roman Curia, that Simon Magus together with his wife Simony came back to life at Rome.)*

The nets are changed into doctrine, the desire of gain into love of the salvation of souls, the sea becomes land; the ship the Church, good and bad men fishes wandering upon the earth, as fishes in the confused sea. By this metaphor is commended the diligent and unwearied study of winning as many as possible for GOD. *(By this designation it is indicated that the office of the Ministers of the Church is 1. laborious, Luc. 5, 5. 2. perilous, 2. Cor. 11, 23. 3. fruitful, Act. 2, 41. Chrysostom speaks elegantly in the sermon on St. Andrew: The Apostles were fishermen, but their instruments were new and awkward. For instead of a rod they make use of preaching; instead of a line, memory; instead of a hook, power; instead of bait, miracles; for a boat they have other gear: instead of fishes they catch even kings themselves: instead of a dragnet they spread out the Gospel: instead of skill they apply divine grace: instead of the sea they treat with human life: instead of net, the cross, just as they are accustomed to use a kind of dragnet. Who ever saw living men caught as fish by dead fishermen? O great power of the Crucified One! O pre-eminence of divine dignity! O supreme benefits of the Apostles! Furthermore, why and how men are compared with fishes is shown by Master John Binnichius, Mellificium Theologicum, part 2, p. 206. 207.; more at length, however, by Cornelius à Lapide, Commentary on the Prophet Habakkuk, ch. 1, 14, p. 51. seqq. Let there also be read without fail concerning spiritual fishing B. D. Glassius in the Appendix joined to the Exegesis of the texts of the Gospels and Epistles, p. 9. 10.)*

Latin:

v. 19. Δεῦτε ὀπήσω μου. Hebraismus. Sequimini-me. Iamdudum Petrus & Andreas, praedicatione Iohannis Bapt. moti, in Christum crediderant, eumque secuti fuerant, Ioh. 1, 35.37.39. 40. 41. 42. & adfuerant frequenter docenti Iesu, fortassis etiam miracula edenti tum in Cana Galilaeae, tum in Iudaea, Ioh. 2. v. 2.11.23. indeque in Galilaeam revertenti Ioh 4. v. 846. Unde Petrus Actor. 1 v. 21. 22. testatur, se caeterosApostolos cum Iesu fuisse conversatos à Baptismate Iohannis usin diem, qua assumtus est. Sed nondum se prorsus Christo addixerant, nec ita indivulsè ei adhaerebant, quin redirent interea ad piscationem, tanquam ad artem eam, quam profitebantur, ex quâ vitae subsidia sibi comparabant. Ab hoc igitur vitae genere atque instituto Christus ipsos avocans invitat ad individuam sequelam, vultque ut relicto piscandi artificio se totos in disciplinam ipsius dedant, quâ doceantur sublimiorem piscand rationē.

Non vocantur ad fidem Christi, quippe quam dudum fuerant amplexi; nec vocantur, ut fint discipuli Iesu, quod iam erant, sed ut sint suo tempore Apostoli sive in spem Apostolatus. Nondum quidem ipsis iniungitur Apostolicum munus, interim in peculiare consortium & familiam Christi cooptantur, ut ad munus Apostolicum formentur.

Faciam vos piscatores hominem. Respectus habetur ad vaticinium Propheticum, Ierem. 16. v. 16.Ecce ego mittam piscatores multos, dicit Dominus *(Cuius Prophetiae intellectum dicto hoc Apostolis Christum suggessisse, scribit Tertull. l. 4. adv. Marc. c. 9. Conf. etiam typum Ezech. 47, 10.Profundum est hu---li mare, ex cuius limo opera ministrorum Ecclesiae trahendi sun -ominein lumen coelestis habitaculi, Hilarius can. 3. in Matth. Marcus porrò Antonius de Dominis Archi Ep. Spalat. l. 1. de Rep. Eccl. c. 2. contra fictam istam P. R. Monarchiam inter alia & hoc dictum urget, utpote è quo constet, quòd idem munus omnibus Apostolis aequaliter Christus demandarit, illud verò ministeriale tantùm sit. Caeterùm prolixus hic dicendi locus esset de avaritiâ ac Simoniâ Pontif. Rom. cum suo clero, ob quam rectiùs Ecclesiae turbatores, quàm Petri & Apostolorum successores; rectiùs nummorum, quàm hominum piscatores; rectiùs fisci quàm Christi ministri ac Sacerdotes appellari merentur. Nihil est, scribit, Aeneas Sylvius, posteà Pontifex Rom. Pius V. dictus, epist. 66. quod absa argento Romanae curia dedat. Nam etsi ipsae manus impositiones & Spiritus S. dona venduntur. Nec peccatorum venia nisi numatis impenditur. Sanè non ita rete piscatorium tractare noverat Petrus, ceu fictitii eius successores Pontifices Romani, unde profiteri cogebatur Act. 3, 6.Aurum & argentum non est mihi. Hanc ne PP. RR. ingeminare querelam cogerentur, in id omnes ingenii sui nervos intenderunt quò meliùs retia sua in capturam laxarent. Nec sterilis etiam piscatura eorum fuit. Id quod Roma, Latium, Aemilia, Flaminia ac regnum Neapolitanū, pro cuius redemtione ex nassâ piscatoris Romani Hispaniarum Rex quotannis septem ducatorum millia cum equo generoso solvere tenetur, abunde testatur. Nec tamen contenti istâ piscatura PP. RR. magis in altum duxerunt, laxatisq; Iubilaeorum ac Indulgentiarum retibus, dici vix potest, quàm amplam pecuniae ex universo propriè orbe fecerint capturam. Legatur saltem Onuphrius Panvinius Venonensis, Fr. Eremtia Augustinianus cum alibi passim, tum praecipuè in vitâ Sixti IV. p. 363. itemque in vitâ Alexandri VI. p. 373. & seqq. edit. Colon. A. 1593. Ita verò dictus auctor l. c. p. 376. de Alexandro VI. Haec, quae tùm ex 80. scriptorum Brevium collegio, quorum loca singula 750. aureis veniere, tum ex vectigalibus, tum ex venditis pileis Cardinalitiis colligebant, cùm ingentibus sumtibus non sufficerent, inopiae meturapax atimmani ingenio saevus, opulentissimum quemin aulâ sacerdotem, & in his aliquot Cardinales coeteris ditiores veneno tollendos constituit, ut eorum opibus in fiscum redactis potitus, profusissimè largiretur, inexplebilemfilii (no. thi, nempe Caesaris Borgiae) cupiditatem expleret. &c. En puleros Petri successores! en piscatores artis suae probè gnaros! quos Scriptores Catholici nisi proderent, nec hodierni quoque P. M. Alexandri VII. liberalitas, quam nepotes neptesq; eius (vel, si quis malit, filii filiaeque) cottidie satis experiuntur, redivivos sisteret, nemo certè tam benè nosset. Satiùs profectò agerent PP. RR. si Simonis se successores potiùs dicerent, quàm Petri, sic quippe magis veritati litarent. Verè enim Franciscus Petrarcha, nobilis Poëta Hetruscus, qui circa A. 1339. vixit, Dial. de Rom. Curiâ vitandâ scribit, Romae Simonem Magum cum coniuge suâ Simoniâ revixisse.)*

Mutantur retia in doctrinam, lucri cupiditas in amorem salutis animarum, fit mare terra; navis Ecclesia, pisces boni maliq; homines in terra vagi, ut pisces in confuso mari. Commendatur hac metaphora diligens & indefessum studium, quàm plurimos DEO lucrandi. *(Indicatur hâc appellatione, quòd officium Ministr. Eccl. sit 1. laboriosum, Luc. 5, 5. 2. periculosum. 2. Cor. 11, 23. 3. fructuosum, Act. 2, 41. Eleganter Chrysostomus serm. de S. Andrea: Apostoli piscatores fuerunt, sed illorum instrumenta nova & inufit at a fuerunt. Nam pro arundine praedicatione utuntur; pro funiculo memoria; pro hamo potentiâ, pro esca miraculis; pro scapha habent ali are: pro piscibus reges etiam ipsos capiunt: pro sagenâ Evangelium expandunt: pro arte divinam gratiam adhibent: promari vitam humanam tractant: pro reti-us cruce, ve ut sagenâ quadam uti solent. Quis unquam vidit à mortuis piscatoribus viventes homines tanquam pisces capi? O magnam crucifixi potentiam! ô divinae dignitatis praestantiam! ô Apostolorum summa beneficia! Caeterùm, cur & quomodo homines cum piscibus conferantur, ostendit M. Ioh. Binnichius Mellificii Theol. part. 2. p. 206. 207. prolixiùs verò Corn. à Lapide Com in Proph. Habac. c. 1, 14. p. 51. seqq. Legatur quoque omninô de piscaturâ spirituali B. D. Glassius in Appendice, Exegesi Evangel. & Epist. textuum annexâ p. 9. 10.)*

## 4:20
v. 20. Α'Φέντες θα δίκτυα. Beza gathers from the word ἀΦέντες that the Apostles so abandoned their ships, viz. that they never afterward returned to fishing. But the contrary is gathered from John 21. v. 3. where Peter and other Apostles return to fishing. David was going forth to fight with Goliath αΦηχε θαωροβαθα Φύλαηι. 1. Sam. 17. v. 20. yet he later returned to those things.

Under 'nets' are also to be understood the other gifts pertaining to fishermen, and indeed the very craft of fishing, likewise hired men, partners, friends, household servants, Matt. 19. v. 27.

Because the Evangelist had made express mention beforehand only of nets, and by themselves the nets would thus be left so as soon to become prey for anyone whatever—for the ship was not taken away quite so quickly, since shortly after they could determine to whom they wished it given—but the fish were not so much theirs as Christ's, whose miracle they had received through him; therefore he says nothing else than 'leaving their nets': but he understands all things being left, and pointedly that manner of life to which all their property served. For if at some time thereafter they are read to have fished, this was not exercising the trade of fishermen, but fleeing idleness or relieving a sorrowful mind. Fran. Lucas, Burgensis.

And yet Matthew likewise is said to have followed Christ having left everything, who nevertheless prepares a banquet for Christ Matt. 9, 9. and 10. John likewise is said to have left everything, and yet receives the mother of Jesus -ις θαισια, John 19. v. 29. Therefore they did leave their former occupation of life, meanwhile they did not immediately renounce ownership of all their goods.

Latin:

v. 20. Α'Φέντες θα δίκτυα. Beza ex verbo ἀΦέντες colligit, Apostolosita dim-sisse naves, qs. nunquam adpiscationem postea redierint. Sed contrarium colligitur ex Ioh. 21. v. 3. ubi Petrus & alii Apostoli ad piscationem revertuntur. David pugnaturus cum Goliatho αΦηχε θαωροβαθα Φύλαηι.1. Sam. 17. v. 20. ad quae tamen postea reversus est.

Sub retibus caetera intelligenda veniunt muneris piscatorii, adeoq; ipsum opificium piscatorium, mercenarii quoque, socii, amici, domestici, Matth. 19. v. 27.

Quia Evangelista non nisi retium antè expressam mentionem fecerat, ac sola retia sic relinquebantur, ut mox quorumvis essent praeda, navis enim non ita mox aufertur, quin paulò pòst definire potuerint, cui vellent illam datam, pisces autem non tam ipsorum erant, quàm Christi, cuius miraculo illos acceperant, ideò non aliud quidem dieit, quàm relictis retibus: sed intelligit relictis omnibus & signanter illo vitae genere, cui res omnis ipsorum serviebat. Quod si aliquando postea piscati legantur, non hoc fuit piscatoriam exercentium, sed otium fugientium aut moestum animum relaxantium. Franc. Luc. Brugensis.

Atqui Matthaeus itidem dicitur relictis omnibus Christum secutus, qui tamen Christo instruit convivium Matth. 9, 9. & 10. Iohannes itidem dicitur omnia reliquisse, & tamen matrem Iesu recipit -ις θαισια,Ioh. 19. v. 29. Ergo pristinum vitae opificium quidem reliquerunt, interim non omni statim rerum proprietate sese abdicarunt.

## 4:21
v. 21. James τόν του θεβεσαιου that son of Zebedee, namely, for another too bearing the name James was called among the disciples of Christ. *(But even so do the Syrian, Arabic, and Ethiopian fill out the ellipsis. Moreover Lud. Capellus judges in his Spicileg. p. 10. that Rabbi Jacob, son of Zebedee, mentioned in Bereshith Rabba, perhaps is that James Zebedee here treated of, and warns It was worth the effort to observe such things as these, since they serve for faith or for the confirmation of the truth of Gospel history, as so many testimonies for the truth in the mouth of their own enemies. He derives the foundation of the said opinion from Acts 15. & 21, 20.)*

Zebedee signifies liberal and munificent, from ןבר to give, endow. Munificent certainly was he who gave both his sons, the staffs of his old age, to Christ.

*(But however Christ here called fishermen, i.e., unlettered men, to preach the Gospel (of which cause Jerome shows besides others, writing on this passage: Fishermen and unlettered men are sent to preach, lest the faith of believers should be thought to come about by eloquence and teaching rather than by the power of GOD. Compare 1. Cor. 1, 17.c. 2, 4.13. Beautifully Augustine, On the Words of the Lord in the Gospel according to John, sermon 59: The words of fishermen are now read, and the necks of orators bow to them. See also sermon 28, On the Words of the Apostle, p. 384, vol. 10, and Book 2, de Civ. Dei, c. 5; Basil of Seleucia, Oration 30.), nevertheless by that example the Anabaptists will hardly be able to defend themselves, while out of the lowest benches of craftsmen they admit to the ecclesiastical ministry those instructed with no learning, no skill in Sacred literature. For one must distinguish between an immediate calling, such as that of the Apostles was, and a mediate one, of what sort is today in use. Those whom Christ called immediately, he also illuminated immediately and miraculously and equipped with special gifts of the Holy Spirit, which when the Ministers of the Anabaptists cannot show, it is plain that neither can they glory in such a calling. Add 1. Cor. 14, 40.Tit. 1, 9.)*

Καθαρτιζονθας. Christ calls those intent upon the work, for he does not wish teachers of the Church to be idle.

Latin:

v. 21. Iacobum τόν του θεβεσαιου illum Zebedaei, sc. filium, nam & alius Iacobi nomine inter Christi discipulos vocabatur. *(Atqui ita etiam ellipsin supplent Syrus, Arabs, Aethiops. Coeterùm existimat Lud. Capellus in Spicil. p. 10. quòd Rabbi Iacob, F. Zebedaei, cuius mentio fit in Bereschith rabba, fortè sit iste Iacobus Zebedaei, de quo hîc agitur, monetq; operae pretium esse, haec talia observare, cùm faciant ad fidem seu confirmationem veritatis historiae Evangelicae, tanquam totidem testimonia pro veritate in ore hostium suorum. Fundamentū dictae opinionis desumit ex Act. 15. & 21, 20.)*

Zebedaeus fignificat liberalem & munificum à ןברdonare, dotare. Munificus certè fuit, qui utrumque filium suum, baculos senectutis suae, Christo donavit.

*(Ut ut verò Christus piscatores h. e. homines illiteratos ad Evangelium praedicandum hîc vocarit, (cuius causam praeter alios ostendit Hieronymus in h. l. scribens: Piscatores & illiterati mittuntur ad praedicandum, ne fides credentium non virtute DEI, se eloquentiâ & doctrinâ fieri put aretur. Conf. 1. Cor. 1, 17.c. 2, 4.13. Pulcrè August. de verbis Domini in Evang. secundùm Ioh. serm. 59. Leguntur modò verba piscatorum, & colla subduntur oratorum. Videatur idem serm. 28. de verb. Apost. p. 384. t. 10. ac l. 2. de C. D. c. 5 Basil. Seleuc. Orat. 30.) minimè tamen exemplo isto Anabaptistae tueri sese poterunt, dum ex infimis opificum subselliis nullâ eruditione, nulla Sacr. litt. peritiâ instructos ad ministerium Eccesiasticum admittunt. Distingnendum enim inter vocationem immediatam, qualis Apostolorum fuit, ac mediatam, cuiusmodi hodiè in usu est. Quos immediatè Christus vocavit, hos etiam immediatè ac mirabiliter illuminavit ac peculiaribus Sp. S. donis instruxit, quae cùm Anabaptist. Ministri ostendere nequeant, patet quod nec de tali vocationegloriari possint. add. 1. Cor. 14, 40.Tit. 1, 9.)*

Καθαρτιζονθας. Christus operi intentos vocat, non enim ignavos vult esse Ecclesiae doctores.

## 4:22
v. 22. ΑΦέντες τό πλοιον, Having left the boat. *(And thus too the Syrian, Arabic, Ethiopian.)* The Vulgate, following the preceding verse 20, renders, having left the nets.

*(But rightly it is here to be noted, that the Apostles, while they deserted everything, and indeed James and John even their Father, did that because of a special calling. Whoever do not have it, yet are impelled by no necessity to abandon their family, ought by no means to follow their example. See 1. Tim. 3, 5. Whence we also read that those who offered themselves to follow Christ without being called were forbidden by him. See Luke 8, 38. & 9, 59. But concerning that case speaks Christ Matt. 10, 37. ch. 19, 29. and the Apostle Hebr. 10, 34. This must be opposed to the Mendicant Monks and to the doctrine of the Papists concerning the vow of poverty. See B. D. Chemnitz, part 2, LL. CC. title on Poverty, ch. 1 and 2, p. 235 sqq.; B. Pareus' Catechetical Confession, vol. 3, p. 302 sqq.)

The Quadriga of the Apostles is here called so. Simon teaches us to obey Jesus when he calls; Andrew, to act manfully; James, to overthrow the enemy; John, to diligently implore GOD'S grace for performing these things.

Latin:

## 4:23
v. 23. Περοηγεν ογηύ την γαλιλαιαν. He went about twice through all Galilee. Thus among the Greeks έλλειΨις. Παραιηγεν έαυτον ηαθ ολην την γαλιλαίαν, means to withdraw oneself, to depart; and έωαγειν is taken for to go. αλειν

Christ did not remain in one place, as John the Baptist, but as supreme Shepherd sought the straying sheep; as true Physician, sought the sick; as Savior, sought what was lost.

Our Evangelist describes the deeds and sayings of Christ in Galilee and neighboring places in continuous series from this point up to chapter 19.

έν θαιςσυναγωγαις. The Temple, i.e. the place of sacrifice, was by God's command unique for the Jews, Deut. 12. v. 13. and ultimately in Jerusalem: but synagogues were more numerous in Christ's time throughout individual cities and villages, indeed often several in one city, Acts 6. v. 9. In Jerusalem, whither people flowed together from all provinces and regions, there are said to have been daily four hundred and eighty, in which people gathered especially on Sabbaths not for sacrifice, but for the circumcision of infants, for the reading and exposition of the law and prophets, for sacred preaching, and finally for prayer. Acts 15. v. 21.

Franciscus Lucas Brugensis infers from the fact that the Evangelicals do not offer a sacrifice that they have synagogues, not temples. Answer: 1. There was a relation between the temple of the O.T. and sacrifice, because sacrifices could not lawfully be offered outside the temple of Jerusalem. 2. But between the temples of the N.T., ευιητηραα formerly called oratories by the ancients, and external sacrifices there is no such relation, since in the N.T. external sacrifices of this kind are given no longer, except the one sacrifice of Christ, offered upon the altar of the cross. 3. Shortly before, Brugensis says: The word synagogue derives from the Seventy Interpreters, who wherever mention is made of the assembly of the children of Israel in the books of Moses almost always rendered it thus in translating. Exod. 12. v. 3. 19. 42. Num. 16. v. 2. συναγωγηυ

that the word is derived to drive together, to gather together; what would suit the Jews, driven together by the terror of the law into one Commonwealth; used in two ways in usage for the word Synagogue. In one way for the assembly or gathering of Israelites professing worship of GOD according to the prescription of the Mosaic law: in the other for the place whither they were accustomed to come together for sacred things. But neither meaning, nor any of all those things, suits our temples or congregations. 4. Bellarmine disputes in book 3 on the Church ch. 1.: the people of the O.T. are properly called Synagogue, i.e., congregation; the people of the New Testament are nowhere called Synagogue, but always Church, i.e., calling out, since to be gathered is common to man with beasts, but to be called out is proper to men. Yet we are neither beasts nor the people of the O.T. Therefore according to Bellarmine's hypothesis we do not have Synagogues. *(Moreover, when the Apostles preferred to give the people of the N.T. the name Church rather than Synagogue—because this name is assigned almost only to the congregation of the Jews in the N.T.—B. Part. brings forward some reasons for that matter in his treatise On the Church §. "who"; who also warns in §. 5. d.l. that the Papists assert quite immodestly in the Roman Catechism p. 111, that the people of the Old Testament are called Synagogue because they looked upon only earthly and perishable goods. The Papists clearly look back at that saying of Bellarmine, that being gathered συνάγειν is common to man with beasts. Truly concerning that error of the Papists there has been discussion elsewhere. Here let these passages be noted at least: Acts 10, 43.ch. 26, 22.Rom. 1, 2.Gal. 3, 8. That finally the Church of the N.T. is sometimes even called Synagogue (contrary to what Bell. writes b. 3 on the Church ch. 1.) is sufficiently evident from Jas. 2, 2. likewise Heb. 10, 25. Cornelius à Lapide himself expounds the former passage about preaching, the Liturgy of Holy Communion, as that which took place in the synagogue, i.e., meeting and church, as he himself says. Now indeed it is established that Holy Communion is a sacrament of the N.T. That the latter passage likewise speaks of the Church of the N.T. can scarcely be denied. Therefore William Estius warns in his Commentary on said epistle: the Apostle writing to the Hebrews perhaps wished to use this Greek word, otherwise rare, lest he should seem to depart too far from the term synagogue, which was in a certain way proper to the assembly of the Hebrews.)* συνάγειν

Christ did not teach in a corner or in secret, but in the public synagogues. 1. lest his doctrine suffer slander. John 18 verse 20. 2. so that opportunity to hear might be given to all. 3. so that he might show his doctrine to be consistent with the Law and the Prophets. For in the synagogues Moses and the Prophets were read aloud Act. 15. v. 21. (And at the same time it was explained, that which duty was deferred by the Rulers of the Synagogues to grave and learned men, as is evident from Act. 13, 15. Compare Tertull. book 4. Hugo Grotius well observes on this passage that this custom remained for some time in the Christian Church, so that by the permission of the Bishops the scriptures were interpreted, not only by presbyters or Deacons, but also by οι της χειραθονιας ουσέπω τετυχηχότες. The same man cites Eusebius, whom he mentions as proving by the example of Origen and others, λαιηους ομιγειν οὐκ άνειθςον but τηρουΠαραεςωτος -πιτροπη. Compare also 1. Cor. 14, 29. This is to be noted among other things against the Papists, who depress the laity to such an extent that they scarcely grant them to read the Holy Scriptures in the vulgar tongue. But the blessed Doctor Heilb. treats of the argument at length in Papatûs Acathol. art. 20. and the blessed Doctor Zeaem. in Apol. dict. art. B. Par. Exeg. L. de Sc. S. §. 480. seqq. Compare Cathol. vol. 1. p. 184. 134. 329. Dispp. Acad. p. 28. 318. Compare also the blessed Doctor Gerlach. vol. 2. disp. p. 8. It is also worth the effort to know how much study of the Holy Scriptures was once required in the King of the People of Israel, as Schickardus learnedly declares and shows from the monuments of the Rabbis in Iure Reg. Ebr. chapter 2. Theor. 5. and 6.)

Το ευαγγέλιοντηςβασιλεις, a message concerning the kingdom of the Messiah, Gospel, in which the heavenly kingdom is offered: for it is taught in the Gospel, how we miserable men, corrupted by sin, can become participants of the heavenly kingdom. Castalio translates it not very aptly: royal Gospel. John the Baptist Matth. 3. v. 2. and Christ himself Matth. 4. v. 17. explain the genuine reason for the appellation Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.

(Corn. à Lapide rightly writes on this passage Admire, here in Christ the tireless zeal for preaching and the Evangelical, nay, Angelic labors, and imitate them. These things must be opposed 1. to the clamors of the Papists, who call the ministers of our Church preachers in contempt, thinking that they do us a great injury with that name, when nevertheless the office of preaching is very honorable, since the name of preachers and the office of a preacher is attributed not only to the Prophets, Ier. 7, 2.c. 19, 2. Jonah 1, 2. John the Baptist, Matth. 3, 1. and the Apostles, Matth. 10, 7.Marc. 16, 15. but also to Christ himself, both here, and Esa. 61, 2.Luc. 4, 44. etc. Compare more things pertaining to this in the blessed Doctor Heilbr. in Papat. Acath. p. 606. 616. It is also according to Thomas Aquinas himself part. 3. q. 67. art. 1.) To preach is the principal and proper act of a Bishop, and more dignified than to baptize. 2. The pride and supine negligence of the Roman Pontiff and of his flatterers, the Papal Cardinals and Bishops, so that you may see them doing nothing less than preaching the Gospel. And yet that one, the universal Pastor and Bishop, and these successors of the Apostles, are eager to be heard. Well said John Gerson, a man of immense learning and piety, with which just encomium the Jesuit Possevinus adorns him in the Apparatus, part 2, sermon at the Council of Rem[?], Dominica 2 after Easter: The office of preaching is annexed of necessity to the pastoral dignity. A hard saying for some, but most true. Altenstaig cites it in the Theological Lexicon printed at Cologne, under the word praedicare. On this negligence of the duty owed among the Papists, see B. D. Bald. instit. Minist. Eccl. c. 4. B. Par. t. 3. Confess. Cathol. p. 162 seqq. L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 130. Dn. D. Hülsem. in Anti Hag. pag. 754. seqq. others.)*

Christ is said first to have taught, and afterwards to have healed, because the medicine of the soul, in the word, is more excellent than that of the body, and because Christ had not come chiefly for this end, that He might be a Physician of bodies, but that He might heal souls. He employed the miracle of healing to confirm His doctrine.

Franc. Luc. Brug. says, the Greek of Matthew, the Interpreter, and also the Evangelists themselves, when speaking of the healings performed by Christ, were misusing the word Φεροπευιειν, which properly signifies to cure with drugs, whereas Christ healed the sick not with drugs or by medical art, but by the word with His command alone. And yet the word Φεροπευιειν signifies not only to apply remedies to the sick, but is also used of one who is at hand for the sick man, attending to his care and performing for him the necessary services. Wisd. 16. v. 12. Not herb, not poultice έΦεροπευισεν αιυτους.

How does μαλαηια differ from νοσέ; the LXX. word μαλαηια, although they denote weakness and sickness, Gen. 42. v. 4.Deut. 7. v. 15. 2 Paral. 16. v. 12. And just as the Evangelist couples πασμν μαλακίαν καὶ πασυν νοσον, so in Moses Deut. 28 v. 61. πασα μαλαηια and πασα πγηγηλη are joined. Luther rendered asser- -euch und -ranctheit.

Some distinguish μαλαηια from νοσω thus, that νοσον they render a long-lasting alteration of the condition of the body, but μαλακίαν languor; But in 2 Paral. 21. v. 15. and 19. mention is made μαλαηιασ πονηρας. Euthymius: νοσος it is a long-lasting distortion of the condition of the body; μαλαηια it is a weariness of the body, the forewarning of a disease.

Πασαν νοσον from every disease, of whatever kind the disease might be, however incurable by medical art; for he did not heal from every single disease.

## 4:24
v. 24. η ἀκοὴ report i. e. fame of him was spread in this way into all Syria. *(As regards the phrase by which report i. e. fame or rumor is said to go out, Gataker warns, On the Style of the N. T. p. 143, that it is a Hebraism, with which he also compares the passage Esther 9, 4. The Syriac translated: and his fame was heard. The Arabic and it became known i. e. his fame spread abroad. The Ethiopic rendered word for word and his report went out.)* Into all the regions far and wide round about, Idumaea, Palaestina, Syrophaenicia, Syria of Damascus, Syria of Antioch, Coelesyria, Arabia: not only into the neighboring ones, Judaea, Peraea, Batanaea, Galilee, Decapolis. Samaria. For all these regions and certain others adjacent to them are comprehended under the name of Syria, whose boundaries are described: on the north Cilicia, on the south Egypt, on the west the great sea, which on that account is also called the Syrian sea, on the east the river Euphrates.

Κακῶς ηχονΦας Syr. who were badly badly afflicted, where the doubling of the noun makes a superlative out of the positive.

Ποικίλαις νόσοις. Euthymius connects it with the preceding words, all who were ill with various diseases; but it is more correctly joined with what follows, those seized with various diseases and torments.

Βάσανος properly means the touchstone by which gold is tested; afterwards it is transferred to questions of any kind, even those of tortures. In this place are denoted the agonies and torments of diseases, all cruel diseases which torture the sick with the sharpest pains, as it were those laid upon the rack and the torture-engine. Bez. Brug.

Συνεχομενους. Erasmus translates constrained, as if it were συνοεσεμενούςτθ έχεσθαι; here it means the same as to be seized, held and possessed, as it were, by the disease; for those whom a more serious disease occupies, it fixes them as its chosen ones and holds them as it were captives. Euthym. drawn together, compressed.

Δαιμονιζόμενσι are ένεργούμενοι, those bodily possessed by the Devil, driven by demons,

When Christ healed them, He demonstrated a heavenly efficacy within Himself, contrary to the kingdom of the Devil, 1. Ioh. 3. v. 8. Σεληνιαζόμενοι [Lunatics].

Σεληνιαζόμενοι. This word is formed from σηληνη,, which means the Moon. Therefore the σεληνιαζόμενοι, are those who are affected by the Moon, or act after the manner of the Moon, or suffer from lunar periods, i.e., those who fare badly at certain times of the Moon, in whom the force of the disease increases or grows according to the variation of the moon. Most take this of Epileptics, that is, persons subject to the falling sickness. *(That epileptics should be understood here, Peter Kirstenius labors to prove at length on Matt. ch. 4, as well as Adrien Turnèbe, Book 11, Adv. c. 5. To the same view also leans B.D. Chemnitz in his Harmony of the Evangelists, ch. 41, p. 327; yet he himself understands not mere epileptics, but partly also σαιμονιζομηνους., just as Grotius, Cornelius à Lapide, and other interpreters likewise hold at this place.)* Basil, on Psalm 15. οι -πιληΨιας ποιούντες ςαιμονες ηαβα βας Παραιοςούς της σεληνης ςθπιτεθέμενοι τοις πτωχοις. says: Demons, who stir up epilepsy, torment wretched men according to the motion of the Moon. *(And B.D. Chemnitius thinks there is this difference between ςαιμονιζομηύούς, and σεληνιαζομενους in his Harmony of the Evangelists, p. 327: that those demonic possession never forsakes, whereas from these the evil spirit sometimes withdraws and again attacks them at a fixed time, namely when, according to the motion of the moon, lunatics are seized by the falling sickness; for then they are at the same time harassed by the evil spirit and driven into frenzies. Yet this cannot be said of all epileptics.) But since men are afflicted with this disease chiefly because of the motion of the Moon, hence it is that Aretaeus, in the book On Causes and Signs of Chronic Diseases, ch. 4, writes concerning epilepsy: ςοηει τοισιές ττιύ σεληέη αλιτροισι αΦιηνεισθαι ηνούσος. Moreover, how harmful the rays of the moon are to sleeping men and to those exposed to them, physicians report everywhere. Among these, Zacutus Lusitanus, Admirable Medical Practice, Book 1, p. 35, relates about the keeper of a vineyard that, having slept overnight under the open sky in the vineyard after leaving his hut, he was found in the morning stupefied, and afterwards, since he could never recover with any remedies whatever, on the twelfth day gave up his soul. Nor is it strange, he says: for the lunar rays strike the nerves with their moist and subtle quality; therefore to sleep beneath its light is bad, for paleness and heaviness of the head follow, as Galen warns, Book 2, On Critical Days, 2. And Plutarch confirms this opinion, Problems, Book 3, problem 10, expressly asserting that the rays of the moon strike those asleep and make them stupid and torpid in their senses. Let there be consulted too, on the effects of the Moon upon things below, Macrobius, Book 7 of the Saturnalia, last chapter; Apuleius, Book 11 of the Metamorphoses, right at the beginning; and Beroaldus on that book; Langius, Medical Letters, Book 1, p. 64; Hannibal Rossellus of Calabria, on the Pymander of Mercury Trismegistus, part 4, comment 5, question 1, chapter 1, pp. 35 sqq.; Guido Bonatus of Forlì, in his Astronomy, throughout various places; Jerome Cardan, On Subtlety, Book 5, right at the beginning. Yet neither must the influences of the Sun, the Moon, and the other stars be extended too far upon these lower things, a matter treated at length by B. Par. Coll. Isag. de Creat. c. 5. sect. 4. §. 7.)*

1. The comitial or falling sickness is called σεληνιαηός Lunar, chiefly because it is nearly always the disease of those who were born at the new moon. *(Hence also among other non-natural causes of epilepsy the learned Mr. D. Rolfincius, today easily the prince of physicians, lists being brought forth into the light at the new moon. Epit. method. cognoscendi & curandi partic. corp. aff. l. 1. part. 1. c. 15. p. 53. Indeed several report that conception performed while the moon is silent or during a lunar eclipse causes epilepsies, supporting this by the authority of Ptolemy next. And perhaps this is why among the Greeks women in childbirth invoked Diana, and among the Romans Juno Lucina (whom Varro teaches to be the same as the Moon), as noted besides Rosinus, Ant. Rom., pag. 250, and Aelius Donatus on Terence's Adelphoe? [Andria], Act. 3. sc. 1, and others; see Vincentius Chartarius of Reggio in his Italian treatise On the Images of the Gods, rendered into Latin by Antonius Verderius, Lord of Val di Privata, pap. 73. And this is sufficiently evident even from Terence, at least in the Andria, Act. 3. sc. 1. But whether the Jews, having fallen into idolatry, worshipped the Moon on account of the same cause—which according to Lucan's opinion came to them under the name of Astarte—is not entirely clear. That they themselves worshipped the Moon is certain. Thomas Dempster of Muresk, Parallels to Rosinus, p. 541: The Ebrei, he says, that is, the Jews, venerated the Moon in place of the supreme God. And to this point tend those remarkable epithets by which they marked out the same goddess, calling her indeed השמם queen of heaven, Jer. 7, 8. c. 44, 17. From the impiety of their ancestors—to which modern Jews seem most unlike—in the walls of the lying-in chamber they take care to write these words, yet not without a mark of superstition: ארם, that is, Adam, Eve, begone Lilith. As Schindler reports in his Lexicon Pentaglotton, pag. 935, where the noble jurist Johannes Selden rightly judges in his Treatise on the Syrian Gods , p. 250, that the same spectre is meant, or the same Goddess of the Gentiles, whom elsewhere the Greeks... έληθοια,, which is formed from ליל by a slight change, seems to be so named. But the very name לילית Johannes Buxtorf, in his Synagoga Judaica, p. 70, believes comes from the Hebrew word ליל signifying night. The same Buxtorf demonstrates the origin of the Jewish superstition both on this passage and in his Lexicon Talmudicum Rabbinicum, p. 1140. 1141. But that I may return to the moon: concerning its influence upon these lower things there is sufficient testimony of Gentile idolatry. For among other causes why the Gentiles in the most ancient times worshipped the Sun, the Moon and the rest of the host of heaven, this indeed is thought not the least, that they learned by experience itself the influx of the stars into these lower things. See B. Par. Comm. on Deuteronomy, p 1010. More about the worship of the Moon will perhaps be given opportunity to say at Jer. 7, 18 In the meantime let them consult Corn. à Lap. on this passage; Selden, l. c., Syntagma 2, ch. 2.), also because he rebukes them under the defect of the Moon.

2. Those commonly called lunatics do not have the symptoms which σεληνιαζομένοις Matthew assigns in chapter 17, verse 15. But epileptics have them. For they often fall into fire, often into water, tear themselves, foam, gnash their teeth, Luke 9 v. 39.Mark 9. v. 17.

3. With Trallianus, book 1, chapter 15, σεληνιαηός, is said of him who labours under epilepsy.

4. The Arab renders σεληνιαζομένους in this passage *( )* driven (namely by pains) in the beginnings of the moons. *(And likewise below ch. 17, 15 the father of the lunatic says: is afflicted, or is distressed or tortured greatly in the beginnings of the moonings, that is, of the new moons, for which in Greek there is σεληνιαζετολ ος ηαηως παχει.) )*

The Syrian rendered , which Tremellius expounds as and son of the fields or wild, who shrinks from the custom of the rest, as is read of Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel. But Füllerus refutes this interpretation of Tremellius in book 2 of Miscellaneous sacred matters, chapter 17, and brings forward another. בר, he says, among the Syrians is έξω that is, outside but everywhere σωμαβα signifies roofs. *(See Matt. 10, 27.ch. 24, 17.Luke 12, 3.Mark 2, 4.ch. 13, 15.Acts 10, 9.)* It must therefore be understood so that the sense is, those who are outside the roofs, namely dwellers, that is, who willingly inhabit vast and desert places, not inhabited by any men. *(The Ethiopian translates:

but what is denoted by the name itself will be pointed out below at ch. 17, 15.)*

They are joined δαιμονιζόμενοι καὶ σεληνιαζόμενοι, because the Devil is accustomed to mix himself into the Comitial disease for the most part, as experience testifies; but this disease also is sometimes procured by the Devil , Matth. 17. v. 15.18. *(Theophylact gives the reason why the devil especially mixes himself with that disease: The Demon, he says, wishing to persuade men that the stars are malevolent, observes the moon when it is full, (but it was noted above from the opinion of the Arab Interpreter and others that this happens at the new moon) and then lies in wait, so that the Moon may be seen as the cause of the passion and disease, and the workmanship of GOD be defamed: just as the Manichaeans err.)*

Παραλυτλκοὶ, suffering from paralysis. Now paralysis is a dissolution of the limbs, *(Celsus παράλυσιν translates a resolution of the nerves: for the principal subject of paralysis is the nerve in the muscle)* whence also in the Syrian Interpreter they are called παραλυτικοὶ, the name being derived from dissolution. *(The Arab renders it by which is from the Arab root which in the 4th Conjugation denotes dislocated, dissolved. So also the Gr. παράλυσις is said from παρὰ which particle has the force of diminishing here, and λύεσθαι to be loosened. In distinction to τῶν λυομένων or apoplectics, who are perfectly loosened. Furthermore H. Grotius παραλυτικοὺς translates here 'sideratos' (struck by the stars), following Plautus, who likewise says of a paralytic: he is struck by the stars, he cannot be moved. And he adds, that the translation is drawn from trees, which, touched by the canicular star, wither away.)*

These species of diseases are so constituted that they almost surpass the medical art, so that divine power may be shown in their healing. Ἐθεράπευσεν.

Ἐθεράπεύσεν. Some Codices read ἐθεράπευσεν ἀυτοὺς,, but others καί πάντυς ἐθεράπευσε. *(The latter reading is embraced by most Gr. Codices & with these the Gr. Eclogues of the MSS. Bibl. Norib. also the Syrian, Arab, Ethiopian.)*

Samariam. Σεληνιαζόμενοι. Vox haec formata à σηληνη, quod Lunam significat. Sunt ergo σεληνιαζόμενοι, qui à Luna, vel in morem Lunae aguntur, aut lunationibus afficiuntur i. e. qui certis Lunae temporibus malè habent, quibus augescit vel crescit vis morbi pro lunae variatione. Plerique accipiunt de Epilepticis five morbo Comitiali obnoxiis. *( Epilepticos h. l. intelligi, prolixè probare satagunt Petrus Kirstenius in cap. 4. Matth. nec non Adrianus Turnebus L. 11. Adv. c. 5. Eodem quoque inclinat B. D. Chemn. in Harm. Evang. c. 41. p. 327. neque tamen meros Epilepticos ipse intelligit, sed ex parte quoque σαιμονιζομηνους. quomodo etiam sentiunt Grotius, Cornelius à Lapide, aliique Interpp. in h. l.)* Basilius in Psal. 15.οι -πιληΨιας ποιούντες ςαιμονες ηαβα βας Παραιοςούς της σεληνης ςθπιτεθέμενοι τοις πτωχοις.Do-mones, qui Epilepsiam concitant, iuxta Lunae motum miseros excruciant. *(Atque hanc differentiam inter ςαιμονιζομηύούς, ac σεληνιαζομενους esse putat B. D. Chemnitius in Harm. Evang. pag 327. quòd illos obsessio Diaboli nunquam deserat: ab his verò malus ille spiritus aliquando recedat, & certo tempore rursus illos invadat, nempe cùm iuxta lunae motum lunatici morbo comitiali corripiuntur, tunc enim simul à malo spiritu exagitantur & in furias aguntur. Id quod tamen non de omnibus Epilepticis dici potest. Cùm verò praecipuè pro Lunae motu homines isto morbo affligantur, inde est, quod Aretaeus lib. de caus. & sign. diuturn. c. 4. de Epilepsia scribit: ςοηει τοισιές ττιύ σεληέη αλιτροισι αΦιηνεισθαι ηνούσος. Caeterùm quàm noxii lunae radii hominibus dormientibus, iisque expositis sint, passim produnt Medici. inter hos Zacutus Lusitanus, prax. Med. admir. lib. 1. p. 35. de vinearum custode refert, quòd cum relicto turgurio in vineâ per noctem obdormisset sub dio, manè stupidus inventus fuerit, postea verò cùm nullis unquam auxiliis convalescere potuerit, d. 12. animam egerit. Nec mirum, inquit: nam radii lunares qualitate humidâ ac tenui, nervos feriunt: quare sub eius lumine dormire, malum, nam pallor & capitis gravitas subseq vuntur, monente Galeno lib. 2. de diebus decret. 2. Cuius sentētiam & Plutarchus confirmat l. 3. probl. 10. disertè affirmans, quòd lunae rad-i dormientes feriant, stupidos & sensibus obtorpentes reddant. Conferantur quoque de Lunae effect. in inferiora Macrob. l. 7. Saturn. c. ult. Apuleius l. XI. Metamorph. statim initio & Beroaldus in d l. Langius epist. Medic. lib. 1. p. 64. Hannibal Rosselus Calaber ad Pymandrum Mercur. Trismegisti t. 4. com. 5. q. 1. c. 1. p. 35. seqq. Guido Bonatus Foroliviensis in de Astron. tract. passim, Hieron. Cardanus de subtilit. lib. 5. statim initio. Neque tamen Solis, Lunae aliorumque astrorum influentiae in haec inferiora nimis extendendae, quâ de re prolixè agit B. Par. Coll. Isag. de Creat. c. 5. sect. 4. §. 7.)*

1. Morbus Comitialis vel caducus dicitur σεληνιαηόςLunaris, tum quod eorum ferè sit morbus, qui in interlunio nati sunt. *(Unde etiam inter alias Epilepsiae causas non naturales Dn. D. Rolfincius, Medicorum hodie facilè princeps, refert, Ortum in lucem in interlunio. Epit. method. cognoscendi & curandi partic. corp. aff. l. 1. part. 1. c. 15. p. 53. Quin & conceptionem, silente lunâ aut in eclipsi lunari factam, epilepsias causam esse, nonnulli produnt, seq; Ptolomaei autoritate muniunt. Atque haec causa fortè est, cur apud Graecos Dianam, apud Romanos Iunonem Lucinam (quam eandem cum Luna esse, Varro docet) parientes invocarint, notante praeter Rosinum Ant. Rom. pag. 250. Ael. Donatum ad Terent. Andr. Act. 3. sc. 1. aliosque, Vincentio Chartario Rhegiensi in de Imag Deorum tract. Italico, ab Antonio verò Verderio, Vallisprivatae Domino Latinitate donato pap. 73. Ac patet hoc satis vel ex Terent. saltem in Andr. Act. 3. sc. 1. An verò propter eandem causam Iudaei in idololatriam prolapsi Lunam, quae iuxta Luciani opinionem, Astartes eis veniebat nomine, coluerint, non satis liquet. Quòd Lunam ipsi coluerint, certum est. Th. Demsterus à Muresk Paral. ad Rosinum p. 541. Ebraei, inquit, s. Iudaei pro summo Deo Lunam vener abantur. Atque huc spectant egregia illa epit heta, quibus eandem insigniebant, nominantes quippe השמםreginam coeli,Ier. 7, 8.c. 44, 17. Aqua maiorum suorum impietate quô maximè alieni hodierni videantur Iudaei, in parietibus cubiculi puerperae isthaec exarari verba curant, nec tamen sine superstitionis nota: ארם i. e. Adam, Eva, foràs Lilith. ceu refert Schindlerus in Lex. Pentagl. pag. 935. Ubi per Lilith rectè censet Nobil. IC. Ioannes Seldenus in de Diis Syris Synt. p. 250. idem denotari spectrum, vel eandem gentilium Deam, quae aliàs Graecis έληθοια, quod levi mutatione ex ליל formatur, videtur dicta. Ipsum autem nomen לילית Iohan. Buxtorffius in Synagn. Iudaicâ p. 70. ortum putat à voce Ebraea לילnoctem significante. Superstitionis Iudaicae originem idem Buxt. ostendit tum d. l. tum Lex. Talm. Rabb. p. 1140. 1141. Vid. B. Par. Comm. in Deut. p 1010. Plura de Lunae cultu dicendi dabitur fortè occasio ad Ier. 7, 18 Videantur interim Corn. à Lap. ad d. l. Seldenus l. c. Synt. 2. c. 2.)* tum quod illos sub defectum Lunae corripit.

2. Lunatici, vulgò sic dicti, non habent symptomata, quae σεληνιαζομένοις Matthaeus cap. 17. v. 15. tribuit. Epileptici autem habent. Hi enim saepiùs in ignem cadunt, saepiùs in aquam, lacerant se, spumant, strident dentibus, Luc. 9 v. 39.Marc. 9. v. 17.

Coniunguntur δαιμονιζόμενοι καὶ σεληνιαζόμενοι, quia Diabolus Comitiali morbo plerunque se admiscere solet, experientiâ teste; sed & hic morbus à Diabolo nonnunquam procurari sole-, Matth. 17. v. 15.18. *(Rationem, quare diabolus morbo isti cumprimis se admisceat, reddit Theophylactus: Doemon, ait, volens hominibus pers-adere, quòd stellae mateficae sint, observat lunam, quum integra est, (sed suprà ex Arabis Interpr. aliorumque sententiâ notatum, quòd in novilunio id fiat) & tunc insidiatur, ut videatur Lunae p-ssionis & morbi causa, & infametur opificium DEI: quemadmodun& M-nithaei erraent.)*

Species hae morborum ita comparatae sunt, ut Medicam artem fermè superent, ut divina virtus in eorum curatione ostendatur.

## 4:25
v. 25. *( Ἐθεράπευσεν, he healed. Chrysostom is grave on this passage: When we have some passion of the body, we do everything, we purchase everything, so that we may be freed from the remaining sickness: but when the soul is ill-affected, we dissemble, we always defer. Therefore we are not even freed from the languors of the body, since we deem those things which are most necessary to be superfluous. Τὴν πηγὴν τῶν κακῶν ἀφύντες, τοὺς ῥυακας` ἐκκαθέρειν ἐθέλομεν. ὁτιγδ` τῶν ἐν τῷ σώματι κακῶν ἡ πονηρία τῆςπσυχῆς αἰτία. Ἀνάωμεν τόινον τῶν κακῶν τὴνπη γ-ὺ, καὶ κάντα ςήσεται τῶν νοσημάτων τὰῥεύματα. οὐγδ` τὸ παραλελύσθαι μόνον νόσημα, αλλὰ καὶ τὸ ἁμαρτάν. καὶ τοῦτο μᾶλλον ἢ ἐκεἆνο, ὅσῳ καὶ πσυχὴ σώματος ἀμείνων. &c. I cannot but also refer here the excellent sentiment which is ascribed to Epiphanius in his life. Paralysis had invaded the Emperor Theodosius: he therefore sent to Epiphanius, then famous for the glory of miracles, so that by prayers poured out for him to the supreme Deity he might free him from the disease. Which when Epiphanius had done: and Theodosius rising from his bed had said to Epiphanius, who had previously admonished him toward piety and the right faith: Father, always command me, and I will execute your commands: Epiphanius replied: Have the words of GOD in your mind, and you will have no need of Epiphanius. In the Greek text it sounds equally well: ἔχε τοὺ τοὺς τοῦ θεοῦ λόγους κατὰ πσυχήν σου, καὶχρείαν μὴ ἕξεις Ἐπιφανίου. έξ-ς έπιφανίου. The life of Epiphanius was written by Polybius, Bishop of the Rhinocurura.)*

Decapolis was a region partly on this side, partly beyond the Jordan and the sea of Galilee, so called because it comprised ten cities, in whose enumeration authors do not agree; yet by universal consent one of them, and indeed the greatest, was Bethsan, otherwise called Scythopolis, situated on this side of the Jordan, at the point where it flows out into the sea of Galilee. Pliny, Book 5 of Natural History, chapter 18. Josephus, Book 3 On the War, chapter 16.

Πέραν τοῦ Ιορδάνου. It must be repeated from what precedes ἀπὸ, from the regions situated beyond the Jordan. Of these, adjoining to the Jordan were Peraea and Batanaea, formerly the kingdoms of Sehon King of the Amorites and Og King of Bashan. Farther off lay triple Arabia.

(Summary. The present chapter contains 1. the description of true blessedness , from verse 1 to 13. 2. an admonition to faithfulness in preaching the word and study for B. O., from verse 13 to 17. 3. the end of the law and the explanation of certain commandments, especially those of the second, fifth and sixth [commandment], from verse 17 to the end.)

Proptereae ne corporis quidem languoribus liberamur, quoniam quae maximè necessariae sunt, superfluum esse ducimus.Τὴν πηγὴν τῶν κακῶν ἀφύντες, τοὺς ῥυακας` ἐκκαθέρειν ἐθέλομεν. ὁτιγδ` τῶν ἐν τῷ σώματι κακῶν ἡ πονηρία τῆςπσυχῆς αἰτία. Decapolis erat regio partim citra, partim ultra Iordanem & mare Galilaeae, ex eo sic dicta, quod decem complectebatur civitates, in quarum enumeratione autores non conveniunt, omnium tamen consensu earum una, eaque maxima erat Bethsan, aliàs Scythopolis dicta, citra Iordanem sita, ad egressum illius in mare Galilaeae. Plin. lib. 5. N. H. cap. 18. Ioseph. lib. 3. de bello cap. 16.

Πέραν τοῦ Ιορδάνου. Repetendum ex praecedentibus ἀπὸ,ex regionibus ultra Iordanem sitis. Ex iis Iordani adiacebant Peraea & Batanaea, olim regna Sehon Regis Amarhaeorum & Og Regis Basan. Ulteriùs sita fuit triplex Arabia.

*(Summa. Sistit praesens caput 1. verae beatitudinis descriptionem, à v. 1. ad 13. 2. fidelem ad verbi praedicationem ac B. O. studium admonitionem, à v. 13. ad 17. 3. legis finem ac quorūdam praeceptorū, cumprimis secundi, quinti ac sexti, explicationem. à v. 17. ad finem.)*

## 5:1
