Verse 1. This discourse of Christ was not given immediately upon Christ's first entrance into Galilee, but after several histories which are described in what follows, among which is also the history of the calling of Matthew.

(Cornelius à Lapide confirms this at length in his Commentary on this passage.)

Some think that Christ here speaks with the Apostles alone, and that Christ therefore said he had withdrawn to the mountain so that he might draw away his disciples from the crowd, when it had been removed he could converse with them alone. They judge that the other discourses described in the following chapters were not delivered at one time, but at separate times and places. Others, by contrast, hold that this discourse of Christ was delivered while a great multitude of men was present, and furnished him the occasion Luke 6. v. 17. 18.20.

The mountain onto which Christ ascended and on which he gave this discourse lies near the sea of Galilee. Mark 3. and verse 13. By the very height of the place and of the seat he wished to intimate that he would hand down nothing vulgar or lowly, but everything lofty and heavenly. (Isidore of Pelusium infers from the fact that Christ gave a discourse about blessedness on a mountain that no one is judged blessed by God unless he has drawn himself off from things below: By the things, he writes, which he did, he showed that it cannot happen that one who has in no way drawn himself off from earthly matters, yet has risen to the summit of virtue, should be judged blessed by GOD or attain the highest goods. ὁ γὰρ τὰ άνω φρονῦν, εκεῖ κατοικεῖ, οὗ χριςὸς ἐστιν, ἐν δεξιᾄ σθεοῦ κασθεζόμενος. book 1, letter 77.)

(How through this mountain, on which Christ explained the moral law at the beginning of his ministry, the Church is signified allegorically, the Blessed Parisiensis explains at length in his Book on the Church, §. 32.)

(But how can Matthew here be reconciled with Luke, since the latter writes that Christ, descending with them, said in a level place: Blessed &c., Chapter 6, 17, whereas Matthew relates that this discourse was given on a mountain? Some think that the Evangelists do not report the same discourse, although they agree in the doctrine itself regarding most of the things Christ is said to have spoken. Thus Osiander decides, whom Jacobus Tadaeus follows in the Biblical Concordance, p. 167. But Blessed Doctor Chemnitius refutes this opinion in his Harmony, and Mr. Dr. Walther supports it in the Biblical Harmony, p. 737; and the same view is held even among the Papists by Jansenius, Franciscus Lucas and Cornelius à Lapide, maintaining that the election of the Apostles was made by Christ on the top of the mountain; but that this discourse was given during the descent of the mountain, i.e. in a level place. Therefore the Evangelists would thus be reconciled, namely that Christ ascended the mountain and there chose disciples, but afterwards descended again and delivered this discourse both to the Apostles and to the crowds. Hence it must be said that Matthew omitted both the election of the Apostles and the descent here .)

CHAPTER V.

Latin:

v. 1. Hic sermo Christi non fuit statim in primo Christi in Galilaeam ingressu habitus, sed post plures Historias, quae in seqq. describuntur, inter quas etiam est Historia vocationis Matthaei.

*(Prolixè hoc confirmat Corn. à Lapide Com. in h. l.)*

Quidam existimant, Christum hîc loqui cum solis Apostolis, ac Christum ideò dici secessisse in montem, ut abstraheret suos discipulos à turba, eâdemremotà cum illis solis posset colloqui. Reliquas conciones in sequentibus capitibus descriptas staetuunt non uno tempore fuisse habitas, sed distinctis temporibus aclocis. Alii contrà statuunt, praesente magnâ hominum multitudine hunc sermonem Christi fuisse habitum, eandemaoccasionem Christo exhibuisse,Luc. 6. v. 17. 18.20.

Mons, in quem Christus ascendit & in eo sermonem huncce habuit, vicinus est mari Galilaeae. Marc. 3. & 7. v. 13. Ipsâ loci ac cathedrae celsitudine insinuare voluit, nihil plebeium aut humile se traditurum, sed ardua & coelestia omnia. (*Isidorus Pelusiota ex eo, quòd Christus in monte sermonem de be atitudine habuerit, colligit, ncminem beatum censeri à Deo, nisi ab inferis se abstraxerit: Per ea, scribit, quae faciebat, illud ostendebat, fieri non posse, ut qui ab inferis rebus minimè se abstraxisset, atad virtutis fastigium adscendisset, beatus à DEO censeretur, aut summa bona consequeretur.ὁ γὰρ τὰ άνω φρονῦν, εκεῖ κατοικεῖ, οὗ χριςὸς ἐστιν, ἐν δεξιᾄ σθεοῦ κασθεζόμενος. lib. 1. ep. 77.)*

*(Quomodo per montem hunc, in quo Christus legem moralem in principio ministerii sui explicavit, allegoricè significetur Ecclesia, exponit prolixè B. Par. L. de Eccl. §. 32.)*

*(Quomodo verò conciliari hîc Matthaeus potest cum Luca, dum hic scribit, quòd Christus descendens cum illis in loco campestri dixerit: Beati &c. Cap. 6, 17. Matthaeus verò tradit, quòd concio haec habita fuerit in monte? Nonnulli existimant, quòd Evangelistae non referant eandem concionem, licet in doctrinâ ipsâ quoad plurima illa quae Christus loquutus dicitur, conveniant. Ita statuit Osiander quem sequitur Iac. Thaddaeus in Concil. Biblico p. 167. Opinionem verò hanc refutat B. D. Chemn. in Harm adstipulaturque Dn. D. Walth. Harm. Bibl. p. 737. idemq; etiam sentiunt è Pontificiis Iansenius, Franc. Lucas ac Corn. à Lapide, staruentes, Apostolorum electionem à Christo factam esse in cacumine montis; sermonem verò hunc habitum esse in descensu montis s. in loco campestri. Ita igitur conciliandi essent Evangelistae, quòd Christus adscenderit in montem, ibidemque elegerit discipulos, postea verò descenderit iterum, actum ad Apostolos tum ad turbam habuerit hunc sermonē. Dicendum proinde, quòd Matthaeus tum Apostolorum electionē, tum descensum hîc praetermise-it.)*

CAPUT V.

## 5:2
v. 2. Ἀνοίξας τὸ στόμα ἁυτοῦ. This is a periphrasis for the speech of one beginning, met frequently throughout the Hebrew text of the Old Testament. But it signifies not just any -ening of the mouth, but that which is joined with gladness and meditation & intensity of voice. (Bernard, sermon 1. on the feast of All Saints: Truly open is his mouth, in which all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are stored up.)

It is suggested that what Christ brought forth in this discourse was serious, weighty and lengthy. For those who wish to handle such things do not rashly burst out into words, but after careful prior meditation at last loosen the reins upon their mouths.

Latin:

v. 2. Ἀνοίξας τὸ στόμα ἁυτοῦ. Periphrasis haec est dicere exordientis, in Hebraeo textu V. T. passim obvia. Significatur autem non quaevis -pertio oris, sed cum alacritate ac meditatione & vocis intentione coniuncta. *(Bernh. serm. 1. in festo omnium sanctorum: Verè apertum est os eius, in quo omnes thesauri saepienti& scientiae sunt reconditi.)*

Insinuatur, ea, quae Christus in hoc sermone protulit, fuisse seria, grandia ac prolixa. Talia namque qui tractare volunt, non temerè in verba prorumpunt, sed praeviâ accuratâ meditatione tandem ori frena laxant.

## 5:3
v. 3. Μακάριοι όι πτωχοὶ τί πνέυματι. (Christ begins His sermon with blessedness, just as David did the book of Psalms: since all seek blessedness, but few find it.) By blessedness here we understand not eternal life itself, but good things pleasing to God, as Luther elsewhere rightly rendered it: Bohl dem. Thus well is it with the poor in Spirit, because although outwardly they are afflicted and pressed down by poverty, inwardly nevertheless they enjoy a tranquil conscience and hope of future glory, and therefore amid their miseries they can rejoice and exult. Syr. the Beatitudes, namely, belong to the poor. Blessed are they. 1. by the beginning of blessedness. 2. by infallible expectation Rom. 8. v. 24. (Whence Cornelius à Lapide explains it not inconveniently thus: Blessed in hope, but not yet in act; blessed with the blessedness of the journey, not of the homeland; blessed in the beg-inni-ng of virtue & peace, not in the consummation of the crown & glory.)

By the poor in Spirit. 1. Some understand those who are prompt and ready to sustain poverty, if the confession of the Gospel demands it. For Spirit is more often taken for the internal affection, which proceeds from a sincere mind and whole heart, Rom. 1, v. 9.cap. 2. v. 29.1. Cor. 5. v. 3.Rom. 12. v. 11. just as it is said afterwards, Blessed are they who suffer insults for my sake, i.e., they are ready to bear insults and persecutions. Akin to this exposition is that by which, by poor in Spirit, are understood those who, as though they did not have the riches they possess, do not set their heart upon them, do not trust in them, do not love them, do not greedily hoard them, but distribute them. For those who are endowed with this spirit are also so disposed in mind that, where the reason of piety demands it, they would not in the least refuse to make a loss of all their wealth.

2. Some understand those who acknowledge their spiritual poverty, because they are destitute of the righteousness by which they might stand before GOD Matth. 11. v. 5. For they are πτωχοὶ πνέυματι extremely poor in Spirit, since πτωχὸς is derived from πτωοσειν, which signifies to tremble in fear, that which is accustomed to happen to the extremely poor; thus, therefore, πτω-χοί πνὶυματι will be those who find no help and support for salvation in themselves. *(The notable passage of Athanasius Q. to Antioch. q. 91 to the Questions pertains to this. If anyone has grown old in sins, is unable to moderate his life by fasts or alms or a similar way, how can such a one be saved? he answers: ὅιω πρόπῳ ἐσὰσθη ὁ τελωνης. & according to the Prophet saying: I was humbled and the Lord saved me. & after having brought forward the present passage another from Psal. 51, 19, he concludes: τάυτην οὖν τὴν ὁδὸν τἶς σωτηρίας πένης καὶ ἀσθενὴς καὶ γέρων καὶ ἰδιὰτης ὁδεῦσαι δύναται )*

3. Some understand those who are poor in Spirit, i.e., in mind, by patiently bearing the imposed burden of poverty, who in tolerating poverty render due obedience to GOD. Who bear the poverty in which they live, God willing, with equanimity, and out of love toward God prefer it to riches, not seeking to become rich. *(And Grotius also embraces this exposition, by which are understood by the poor those who are such regarding the meagerness of their means, and that both because Luke writes simply: μακάριοι οί πτωχοὶ c. 6, 20, and opposes the rich to them, without the word of spirit added: and because πτωχοὶ for those who are spiritually such or humble, are scarcely found.)*

He says, therefore, that Christ pronounces the poor blessed in the same sense in which he follows with the mourning, because rich and prosperous things are the fuel of vices)* The world pronounces the rich to be blessed, but the poor to be most miserable Ps. 144. v. 25. Christ preaches blessed the poor.

4. Some call those who, subdued by poverty or other calamities, or voluntarily touched by a sense of their own sins, submit themselves humbly to GOD. Leo, Sermon on that which is written: Seeing the crowds. When he says poor in spirit, he shows that the kingdom of heaven belongs to those whom humility of souls commends more than lack of resources.Prov. 16. v. 19.Esai. 57. v. 15. Also שפלי־רוח humbled in spirit and meek, who are opposed to the proud and fierce. Chrysostom, Homily 15 on Matthew ὁι ταπρνοὶ καὶ συντετριμμένοι, τὴν διάνοιαν, er Ps. 34. v. 19.Ps. 51. v. 19. But although none of these interpretations conflicts either with the analogy of faith or with the rest, nevertheless from verse 6 of this chapter and from chapter 11. v. 5. it appears that the discourse here is chiefly about spiritual poverty, opposed to confidence in one's own righteousness, John Ferus on this passage. ענԉԉם

*(Related to this explanation is that which Cornelius à Lapide relates he heard from a certain man, himself beyond doubt a Roman Catholic. Blessed are the poor in spirit, i.e., blessed are those who do before God what beggars do before the rich, who confess their poverty with such humility of spirit, and seek grace before God with such earnestness, as beggars press alms from the rich)*

Julian the Apostate, Letter 43 p. 308, sophistically twists this to mean that Christians' possessions ought to be taken away, so that they might enter the kingdom of heaven more easily. ἵν᾽ εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν ἐυοδώτερον πορευσθῶσλ, that they might come into the kingdom of heaven more easily.

The Papists apply it to the vow of poverty. Francis Lucas of Bruges on this passage: First and especially there are pronounced blessed here those who obeyed the Savior's counselMatt. 19. v. 21. If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have. who not only possess no riches nor desire any, but also spontaneously abandoned all those things which they had possessed and could have possessed. Bellarmine, Book on Monks ch. 20. Maldonatus on ch. 5 of Matthew *(Cornelius à Lapide on this passage: The poor are properly understood here, for they are set against the rich,Luke 6, 24. and shortly after: Therefore the poor are called blessed here who, by a praiseworthy will inspired by the Holy Ghost, are poor, as happens with religious men, who profess and vow it.)*

Ans. 1. Those poor, of whom Christ treats, are poor in spirit. Yet not all who vow poverty are poor in spirit, for sometimes they vow poverty neither freely nor with due intention. 2. Of those poor, of whom Christ treats, is the kingdom of heaven. But not of all those who vow poverty is the kingdom of heaven. John Ferus on this passage: There are others who willingly renounce riches, and yet even this does not suffice for obtaining this blessedness, otherwise Socrates too and other philosophers would be blessed. It is not a great thing, to abandon, but it is laborious to abandon oneself, whence he says 'poor in Spirit.' 3. A vow of poverty taken up without necessity lacks the commandment and example of Christ and of the Apostles. 4. To those poor, of whom Christ here speaks, there are opposed in Luke certain kinds of rich men, to whom Christ pronounces a woe. And yet Christ does not imprecate that woe upon the rich properly so called, otherwise it would be lawful for no Christian to hold riches. *(Toletus indeed argues in his Commentary on Luke, that -ios the poor are described in Luke, -lios here in Matthew, but Cornelius à Lapide plainly compares the discourse in Luke ch. 6, 24. with the present passage, and points out, that Luke ch. 6, 24. sets over against each beatitude its own misery, threatening against them a woe, i.e. eternal damnation and Gehenna.)* 5. The Apostles had a command to forsake all things for Christ and for the preaching of the Gospel, which the Monks lack. Therefore their poverty is not apostolic, and consequently it was not commended by Christ in this place either. 6. Maldonatus in this passage admits that by poor in spi-rit the greater part of the Fathers understands the humble, and for this exposition he cites Hilary, Chrysostom, the Author of the unfinished work, Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory of Nyssa, Epiphanius, Leo, Gregory. But if this exposition has the authority of the greater part of the Fathers, then by the hypothesis of the Papists it deservedly ought to be received. 7. Toletus on chapter 6 of Luke: They are poor in spirit who affec-tion do not hav-e in these earthly riches and in honors, they desir-e none of those things, they seek the will of GOD and set it above all things, themselv-es rejoi-ce in what po-vr-ty can be in ri-che-s. *(Likewise let those things be compared wholly to this point which are contained in vol. 3. Catholic Confession of B.P. p. 308. & the following pages. But to the sayings of the Fathers, which the Papists press here in support of their opinion, Daniel Chamier responds sufficiently at length in vol. 3. Panstrat. book 20. chap. 9. which may be consulted.)*

Ambrose, lib. 2. offic. cap. 4., from the fact that Christ pronounces the poor in spirit blessed, gathers that riches provide no aid toward a blessed life.

The kingdom of heaven is life happily eternal, and eternally happy, which is described hereafter by various names, according to the suitability of each kind of good man to whom it is promised. Not content to promise riches instead of poverty, he also promises the kingdom.

Nor yet does it follow from this and other promises of Christ that it was permitted to do good works out of regard for eternal reward, as Bellarmine tries to prove from the fact that Christ and John began their preaching from the promise of reward Matt. 3. 4. and 5. For it must be known that both invite to repentance with the added reason that the Messiah has drawn near with his heavenly kingdom and come to save—not those who are puffed up by the Pharisaic conceit of their own righteousness, or hardened persist in sins in Epicurean security—but those who practice true and serious repentance, acknowledge their sins, look upon the Lamb of God with true faith, and bring forth fruits worthy of repentance. Therefore poverty of spirit here is by no means set forth as some kind of merit of the kingdom of heaven, but it is shown who are capable of the Gospel doctrine concerning the kingdom of heaven, namely those who, humbled by the acknowledgment of their sins and by a sense of divine wrath on account of their powers, virtues, and works—that is, despairing of their own righteousness—find nothing in themselves which they could oppose to the judgment of GOD. At the same time consolation is also offered to those who in this life lack necessary things, that the spiritual goods of the kingdom of heaven already belong to them, and by faith they are already heirs of eternal life. We therefore invert Bellarmine's argument: Where poverty of spirit is commended, there the opinion about merits is overthrown, since those alone are truly poor in spirit who recognize themselves to be devoid of merits before GOD. But Christ here commends poverty of spirit. Therefore he overthrows the opinion about merits. Likewise, those whose the kingdom of heaven already is need not at last acquire it by their own merits. But the kingdom of heaven belongs to those who are poor in spirit. Therefore they need not at last acquire it by their own merits. As is well gathered by B. Par., L. de B. O., §. 127. Moreover, bodily poverty, however not self-invited but sent by God, is understood in this passage by B. D. Chemnitius

and Philip Melanchthon; but spiritual poverty by B. D. Hunnius and B. D. Quistorp, on this passage, likewise by D. Winckelman, Festival of All Saints. Furthermore the Papists maintain that Christ acts here as a new lawgiver. But just as the remaining matters, of which below elsewhere in the Old Testament, are read as having been proposed long ago, so too what the Savior delivers here had place in the Old Testament, as appears from Ps. 68, 11.c. 72, 2.4.13.Ps. 107, 4.Ps. 113, 7.Psal. 140, 13.Prov. 19, 17.Es. 14, 30. &c., it is evident. But if it be asked to which precept of the Decalogue this doctrine should be referred, Blessed Luther answers in the Postil on the Gospel for the Feast of All Saints, that it belongs to the first commandment. Finally, by no means can it be proved from this passage that poverty of spirit, even if taken chiefly of spiritual poverty, is a meritorious cause of eternal life. Nor does the particle ὅτι. suggest this; for αἰτιολιγικὴ here is not present, declaring the cause of eternal salvation, and that a meritorious one, but shows at least the subject, namely those to whom the kingdom of heaven falls, not on account of what.)*

It is called the kingdom of heaven. 1. because it is heavenly, which is not seen in these earthly things. 2. because it is eternal. 3. because it is given to those whose πολίτευμα is in heaven, whose soul is heaven, that is, the seat of GOD. *(Yet it pleases Hugo Grotius more on this passage, if by the kingdom of heaven are understood the heavenly riches, that is, spiritual ones in this world, namely knowledge of the truth, forgiveness of sins, the gift of the Spirit, and whatever else comes under the name of that kingdom.)*

Latin:

v. 3. Μακάριοι όι πτωχοὶ τί πνέυματι. *(Christus à beatitudine exorditur concionem, sicut David librum Psalmorum: cùm omnes beatitudinem quaerant, pauci verò inveniant.)* Per beatitudinem h. l. non ipsa vita aeterna, sed res bona ac Deo placens intelligitur, sicut Lutherus alibi roctè reddidit: Bohl dem. Sic benè est pauperibus Spiritu, quia quamvis foris affligantur & pauperie premantur, intus tamen tranquillâ conscientiâ & spe futurae gloriae fruuntur, ideoque in mediis miseriis possunt gaudere & exultare. Syr. Beatitudines, sc. sunt pauperibus. Beati sunt. 1. beatitudinis inchoatione. 2. expectatione infallibili Rom. 8. v. 24. *(Unde Corn. à Lap. explicat non incommodè ita: Beati in spe, sed nondum in re; beati beatitudine viae, non patriae; beati in in-hoati-n- virtutis & pacis, non in consummatione coronae & gloriae.)*

Per pauperes Spiritu. 1. quidam intelligunt eos, qui promti ac parati sunt ad sustinendam paupertatem, si exigat confessio Evangelii. Spiritus enim saepiùs accipitur pro interno affectu, qui ex animo sincero & toto corde proficiscitur, Rom. 1, v. 9.cap. 2. v. 29.1. Cor. 5. v. 3.Rom. 12. v. 11. sicut postea dicitur, Beati, qui patiuntur convitia propter me i. e. parati sunt ad ferenda convitia & persecutiones. Huic expositioni affinis est ea, qua per pauperes Spiritu intelliguntur, qui quas habent divitias, tanquam non habētes sunt, non illis cor apponunt, non confidunt, non amant, non avarè adservant, sed erogant. Qui enim hoc animo praediti sunt, illi etiam animo sic comparati sunt, ut ubi pietatis ratio id exigat, incunctanter opum omnium iacturam facere, minimè recusent.

2. Quidam eos, qui agnoscunt spiritualem suam paupertatem, quod destituti sint iustitiâ, quâ coram DEO consistere possint Matth. 11. v. 5. Sunt enim πτωχοὶ πνέυματι extremè pauperes Spiritu, cùm πτωχὸς deducatur à πτωοσειν, quod significat in metu trepidare, id quod solet extremè pauperibus accidere; sic ergo πτω-χοί πνὶυματι erunt, qui nihil auxilii & subsidii ad salutem in seipsis inveniunt. *(Facit huc insignis locus Athanasii Q. ad Antioch. q. 91. ad Quaes. enim. Si quis in peccatis consenuerit, neieiuniis vel eleemosynis vel simili modo vitae suae vale at moderari, quomodo talis servari possit? respondet: ὅιω πρόπῳ ἐσὰσθη ὁ τελωνης.& secundum Prophetam dicentem: Humiliatus sum & servavit me Dominus. & post adductum locum praesentem aliumexPsal. 51, 19,concludit:τάυτην οὖν τὴν ὁδὸν τἶς σωτηρίας πένης καὶ ἀσθενὴς καὶ γέρων καὶ ἰδιὰτης ὁδεῦσαι δύναται)*

3. Quidam intelligunt eos, qui Spiritu i. e. animo pauperes sunt, patienter ferendo impositum paupertatis onus, qui in tolerandâ paupertate debitam DEO oboedientiam praestant. Qui eam, in qua Deo volente degunt, paupertatē, ae quanimiter ferunt, & prae amore erga Deum divitiis praeponunt, non quaerentes fieri divites. *(Et hanc expositionem, quâ per pauperes intelliguntur ii, qui quoad facultatum tenuitatem tales sunt, amplectitur quoq; Grotius, idque tum quòd Lucas simpliciter scribat: μακάριοι οί πτωχοὶ c. 6, 20. eisque opponat divites, non addita spiritûs voce: tum, quòd πτωχοὶ pro iis, qui spiritualiter tales sive humiles, vix reperiantur.

Dicit igitur, Christum pauperes eodē sensu beatos pronunciare, quo versu seq lugentes, quia res opimae & secundae fomenta sint vitiorum)* Mundus divites beatos esse pronunciat, miserrimos autē pauperes Ps. 144. v. 25. Christus pauperes beatos praedicat.

4. Quidam eos, qui paupertate aliisve calamitatibus domiti sive ultrò sensu suorum peccatorum tacti DEO sese humiliter subiiciunt. Leo serm de eo, quod scriptum est: Videns turbas. Cùm dicit pauperes Spiritu, ostendit eis regnum coelorum, quos humilitas commendat animorū magis, quàm indigentia facultatum.Prov. 16. v. 19.Esai. 57. v. 15. vocantur. שפלי־רוח Item ענԉԉםhumiliati Spiritu & mansueti, qui opponuntur superbis & ferocibus. Chrysost. homil. 15. in Matth. ὁι ταπρνοὶ καὶ συντετριμμένοι, τὴν διάνοιαν, er Ps. 34. v. 19.Ps. 51. v. 19. Quamvis verò nulla harum interpretationum vel cum fidei analogia vel cum reliquis pugnet, tamen ex huius cap. v. 6. & ex cap. 11. v. 5. apparet, de spiritualt paupertate, fiducie propriae iustitiae oppositâ, praecipuè hîc sermonē esse: Ioh. Ferus in h. l.

*(Adfinis huic explicationi est ea, quam Corn. à Lapide à quodam, procul ambiguo Catholico-Romano & ipso, se audivisse memorat. Beati pauperes spiritu i. e. beati qui faciunt apud Deum, quod faciunt mendici apud divites, qui sc. tant â humilitate spiritûs confitentur suam paupertatem, tantoa effectumenditant gratiam apud Deum, quanto stipitem à divitibus f--gitant mendici.)*

Iulianus Apostata Epist. 43 p. 308. sophisticè id eò torquet, quòd Christianis possessiones propriae adimendae sint. ἵν᾽ εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν ἐυοδώτερον πορευσθῶσλ,quò faciliùs in regnum coelorum venirent.

Pontificii accommodant ad votum paupertatis. Franc. Luc. Brugensis in h. l. Primùm ac praecipuè hîc beati praedicantur, qui obsecuti fuerint Salvatoris consilloMatth. 19. v. 21. Si vis perfectus esse, vade, vende quae habes. qui non solùm nullas habent aut appetunt divitias, verùm etiam ea omnia, quae habuerant & habere poterant, sponte dereliquerunt. Bellarm: lib de Monachis cap. 20. Maldonatus in cap. 5. Matt. *(Corn à Lapide in h. l. Pauperes propriè hîc accipiuntur, opponuntur enim divitibus,Luc. 6, 24. & paulò pòst: Beati ergo hîc dicuntur pauperes, qui laudabili voluntate à Sp. S. inspiratâ sunt pauperes, uti fit à religiosis, qui cam profitentur & vovent.)*

Resp. 1. Illi pauperes, de quibus Christus agit, sunt paeuperes spiritu. Atqui non omnes, qui vovent paupertatem, sunt pauperes spiritu, quandoq; enim nec liberè, nec debitâ intentione paupertatem vovent. 2. Illorum pauperum, de quibus Christus agit, est regnum coelorum. At non omnium eorum, qui paupertatem vovent, est regnum coelorum. Ioh. Ferus in h. l. Sunt alii, qui divitiis voluntariè aebrenunciant, nec tamen hoc sufficit ad hanc beatitudinem consequendā, alioqui & Socrates, aliia philosophi beati essent. Non magnum est, relinquere, sed laboriosum est, seipsum relinquere, unde dicit pauperes Spiritu. 3. Votum paupretatis sine necessitate susceptum destituitur mandato, exemplo Christi & Apostolorum. 4. Pauperibus illis, de quibus Christus hîc loquitur, apud Lucam opponuntur eius modi divites, quibus Christus vae pronunciat. Atqui divitibus propriè sic dictis Christus non imprecatur illud vae, aliàs nulli Christiano liceret habere divitias. *(Disputat quidem Toletus Comm. in Lucam, a-ios pauperes describi aepud Lucam, aelios hîc apud Matthaeum, verùm Corn. à Lapide disertè concionem apud Luc. c. 6, 24. confert cum praesenti loco, monetq;, quòd Lucas c. 6, 24. singulis beatitu dinibus opponat singulas infelicitates, comminans illis vae i. e. aeternam damnationem & gehennam.)* 5. Apostoli habuerunt mandatum, omnia propter Christum & praedicationem Evangelii deserendi, quo Monachi destituuntur. Ergo illorum paupertas non est Apostolica, proinde etiam à Christo non est h. l. commendata. 6. Maldonatus in h l. fatetur, per pauperes spiri-u à maiore Patrum parte intelligi humiles, pro qua expositione adducit Hilarium, Chrysostomum, Autorem imperfecti operis, Ambrosium Augustinum, Gregor. Nyssenum, Epiphanium, Leonem, Gregorium. At si haec expositio maiorum Patrum partem habet autorem, ex hypothesi Pontificiorum meritò est acceptanda. 7. Toletus in cap. 6. Lucae. Pauperes spiritu sunt, qui affect-m non hab-nt in his terrenis divitiis & in honoribus, nihila eorum d-si-erant, DEI voluntatem quaerunt ac eam praeponunt omnibus, i-sama s qu-ntur, quae pauper-as in diviti-esse potest. *(Conferantur omninò hûc quoque ea quae habentur tom. 3. Confess Cathol. B P. p. 308. & seqq Ad dicta verò Patrum, quae pro sua sententiâ hîc urgent. Pontificii, satis prolixè respondet Dan. Chamier t. 3. Panstr. lib. 20. c. 9. qui potest videri.)*

Ambrosius lib. 2. offic. cap. 4. ex eo, quod Christus pauperes spiritu beatos pronunciat, colligit, divitias nullum praestare adminiculum ad vitam beatam.

Regnum coelorum est vita feliciter aeterna, inque aeternum felix, quae variis dehinc nominibus describitur, pro congruentiâ cuius cunque generis bonorum hominum, cui promittitur. Non contentus divitias pro paupertate promittere, etiā regnum promittit.

*(Neque tamen ex hâc aliisque Christi promissionibus sequitur, quòd intuit is mercedis aeternae licitum sit bona opera operari, ceu Bell. ex eo, quòd Christus & Iohannes à promissione mercedis praedicationem suam exorsi sintMatth. 3. 4. & 5. evincere conatur. Sciendum enim, utrumque invitare ad poenitentiam, additâ ratione, quòd Messias cum coelesti suo regno appropinquarit ac salvare venerit, non eos qi Pharisaicâ iustitiae propriae opinione turgidi, vel Epicuraeâ securitate in peccatis perseverent praefracti; sed eos, qui veram & seriam agunt poenitentiam, peccata agnoscunt, Agnum DEI verâ fide respiciunt & fructûs poenitentiâ dignos faciunt. Paupertas igitur spiritus h. l. nequa quam ponitur tanquam meritum quoddam regni coelorum, sed ostenditur, qui sint capaces doctrinae Evangelicae de regno coelorum, videl. illi qui agnitione peccatorum suorum & sensu irae divinae humiliati de suis viribus, virtutibus & operibus h. e. de propriâ iustitiâ desperant, ac nihil quod iudicio DEI opponere possint, in se inveniunt. Proponitur etiam simul consolatio illis, qui in hâc vitâ rebus necessariis destituti sunt, quòd bona spiritualia regni coelorum iam sint ipsorum & fide iam sint heredes vitae aeternae. Invertimus igitur Bell. argumentum: Ubi commendatur paupertas spiritûs, ibi evertitur opinio de meritis, siquidem illi demum verè sunt spiritu pauperes, qui sese meritorum coram DEO inopes esse agnoscunt. At Christus h. l. paupertatem spiritus commendat. E. evertit meritorum opinionem. It. Quorum iam est regnum coelorum, illi non necesse habent, suis meritis demum illud acquirere. Sed eorum, qui sunt spiritu pauperes, est regnum coelorum. E. non necesse habent suis meritis id demum acquirere. Uti benè colligit B. Par. L. de B. O. §. 127. Caeterùm de corporali paupertate, non tamen sponte accersitâ, sed à Deo immissâ, locum hunc accipiunt B. D. Chemn.

ac Phil. Melanchthon; de spirituali verò B. D. Hunnius ac B. D. Quistorp. in h. l. it. D. Winckelm. Fest. omnium Sanctor. Statuunt porrò Pontificii, Christum novum hîc agere legislatorem. Verùm sicuti reli qua, de quibus infrà, alibi in Vet. T. iamtum proposita leguntur, ita etiam, quae hîc Salvator tradit, in V. T. locum habuerunt, ceu ex Ps. 68, 11.c. 72, 2.4.13.Ps. 107, 4.Ps. 113, 7.Psal. 140, 13.Prov. 19, 17.Es. 14, 30. &c. liquet. Si verò quaeratur, ad quod Decalogi praeceptum doctrina haec referenda sit, illi respondet B. Luth. in Post. ad Evang. in Festo omnium Sanct. quòd ad praeceptum primum. Minimè tandem ex h. l. probari potest, paupertatem spiritûs, si vel maximè etiam de spirituali accipiatur, esse causam meritoriam vitae aeternae. nec innuit hoc particula ὅτι. neq; enim αἰτιολιγικὴ illae hîc est, declarans causam aeternae salutis, eamque meritoriam, sed ostendit saltem subiectum sive eos, quibus obtingat regnum coelorum, non propter quid.)*

Regnum coelorum dicitur. 1. quia est coeleste, quod in his teri is non videtur. 2. quia est aeternum. 3. quia illis datur, quorum πολίτευμα in coelis, quorum anima est coelum h. e. sedes DEI. *(Hugoni tamen Grotio in h. l. magis arridet, si per regnum coelorum intelligantur divitiae coelestes s. spirituales in hoc mundo, cognitio nempe veritatis, remissio peccatorum, donum spiritûs & quae alia regni istius nomine veniant.)*

## 5:4
v. 4. By τοὺς πενσθούντας. 1. some understand those to whom all adverse things happen in this world, even though they fear God. John 16. v. 20.Acts 14. v. 22. 2. others indeed those who mourn over their sins and lack of righteousness, for to them the consolation of the Gospel is owed, Matt. 11. v. 5. Compare Isaiah 57. v. 18.2. Cor. 7. v. 10.

In the Greek codices πενθοῦντες stands second, πρᾳεῖς third; but among the Latins the meek stands second, those who mourn third. The Greek codices are followed by Chrysostom, the author of the unfinished work Theophylact, Titus, Euthymius, as also the Syrian Interpreter. *(just as also the Arabic and Ethiopic versions; nor does any one of the Greek codices, which the Parisians and Robert Stephanus diligently collated, observe another order.)* The Latin codices are followed by Jerome, Augustine, and authors later in age.

The world judges blessed those who are free from sorrow and grief, with all things succeeding according to the heart's desire, lead a joyful and pleasant life, enjoying the agreeable pleasures of the world. Christ, on the contrary, proclaims blessed those who live a life sad in the judgment of men, far removed from the pleasures of the age and from fleshly lusts, who set before their eyes those things which produce mourning, their own and others' sins, the flesh rebellious against the spirit, who are pressed down by adverse circumstances and bear them with equanimity.

But how does Christ here declare those who mourn to be blessed, when shortly after in v. 12 he commands the faithful to rejoice and exult? Cf. also Phil. 4, 4. Resp. Both can have a place in the faithful at the same time, joy and mourning. Mourning, indeed, 1. on account of the omission of good and the commission of evil, concerning which sorrow it is treated in 2. Cor. 7, 11. 2. on account of the imposition of the cross and the affliction of the world, Ps. 44, 24. Matth. 10, 30. Luc. 9, 29. Rom. 8, 36. Ioh. 16, 33. 1. Cor. 15, 31. 3. on account of the infestation and temptation of Satan, Matt. 6, 13. c. 26, 41. Luc. 22, 32. 1. Petr. 5, 8. The pious, however, ought to and can rejoice 1. on account of divine consolation, Es. 57. v. 18. Ioh. 16, 20. 2. Cor. 7, 10. 6, 10. & here. 2. on account of certain liberation from all evils, the changing of pain into joy, eternal glorification, and the most bountiful reward promised by GOD, Luc. 16, 25. Ioh. 16, 32. 1. Thess. 2, 16. Cf. more on this matter in Mr. Dr. Walth. Harm. Bibl. p. 738. Παρακλησθήσοντοι |

Παρακλησθήσοντοι they shall receive eternal consolation,2. Thess. 2. v. 16.their sorrow shall be turned into joy,Esa. 35. v. 10.cap. 51. v. 11. (* Luc. 16, 26.Ioh. 16, 20.Iac. 1, 12.Apoc. 7, 17.)* But also in this life they shall be lifted up by the consolation of the Spirit. 2. Cor. 6. v. 10.Always rejoicing. *(Compare 1. Cor. 10, 13.2. Cor. 1, 3.)*

Πρᾳεῖς. Theophylact on this passage The meek are those who do not altogether fail to become angry, but who possess the power of anger, yet restrain it, and grow angry when it is fitting.

Chromatius on this passage The meek are the gentle, humble, modest, simple in faith and patient toward every injury, who, instructed by the precepts of the Gospel, imitate the example of the Lord's gentleness.

Those are called meek who do not murmur against GOD either because of the prosperity of the wicked or because of their own adversity; who are not eager for vengeance when they suffer injury; who strive to win over the hearts of all men by the sweetness of their character.

*(But Christ went before us by His example. See below ch. 11, 29, likewise 1. Petr. 2, 23.)*

Κληρονομήσουσι τὴν γῦν. This is taken from Ps. 37. v. 11. κληρονομεῖν more than κτᾶσθαι, For to possess by right of inheritance means to possess without labor and trouble, as one possesses an inheritance that falls to him from his parents. Therefore a pleasant and tranquil possession is denoted. Likewise also a stable and eternal possession (if it be understood of the new earth).

1. Chrysostom, homily 15 on Matthew, Augustine On the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount, Euthymius and Theophylact on this passage take it of the earth which we inhabit in this life, so that the sense is, they will enjoy this life peacefully together with their goods, and will hand them on to their posterity. God will bless even in this life and distribute bodily goods.

2. Origen, homily 26 on Numbers, Basil on Ps. 33. Cyril on chapter 58 of Isaiah, Nyssen On Beatitudes, Jerome on this passage, Damascus book 2 On the Orthodox Faith chapter 1, take it of the new earth in the future life. Apoc. 21. v. 2. Esa. 66. v. 22. Petr. 3. v. 13.

Both explanations can be joined together, since godliness holds promise of the present life and of that which is to come, 1. Tim. 4. v. 8. *(The learned Dr. Glassius also confirms both interpretations, Rhet. S. p. 269.)* No one makes use of what is his own more quietly and with less difficulty than a meek spirit, which obtains more from GOD and from men through gentle forbearance than the harsh man does who tries to wrest things away by violence. *(Meanwhile, if under the name of earth there is meant that earth which we inhabit, this promise, no less than the others concerning bodily happiness, is to be received with the exception of the cross. Otherwise, with Hugo Grotius, Christ τ--ὺγῆν seems to declare them blessed who hold firm and steadfast friendships, which on earth is by far the best possession. But those who are of a mild and peaceful disposition can most easily win these for themselves.)*

The world preaches as blessed those who are powerful and fierce, because they almost always enjoy possession of lands, seeing that no one dares set himself against them. But Christ declares blessed the meek, who, exposed to the injuries of the mighty, are driven out from their possessions.

Latin:

v. 4. Per τοὺς πενσθούντας. 1. quidam intelligunt eos, quibus omnia adversa in hoc mundo accidunt, etiamsi Deum timeāt. Ioh. 16. v. 20.Act. 14. v. 22. 2. quidam verò eos, qui lugent ob peccata & iustitiae defectum, illis enim consolatio Evangelii debetur, Matth. 11. v. 5. Confer Esai. 57. v. 18.2. Cor. 7. v. 10.

In Codicibus Graecis πενθοῦντες secundo, πρᾳεῖς tertio loco ponuntur; sed apud Latinos mites secundo, lugentes tertio loco ponuntur. Graecos Codices sequuntur Chrysostomus, Autor imperfecti operis Theophy lactus, Titus, Euthy mius, ut & Syrus Interpres. *(quemadmodum etiam Arabs ac Aethiops. nec ullus quoque Codd. Graecorum, quos Parisienses ac Rob. Stephanns diligenter contulerunt, alium ordinem observat.)* Latinos Codices sequuntur Hieronymus. Augustinus & aetate inferiores.

Mundus illos arbitratur beatos, qui à moerore ac luctu alieni, rebus omnibus ex animi voto succedentibus, vitam laetam & amoenam ducunt, iucundis mundi voluptatibus perfruuntur. Christus contrà beatos praedicat eos, qui vitam degunt iudicio hominum tristem, à voluptatibus seculi & carnalibus concupiscentiis alienam, qui ea sibi ob oculos ponunt, quae luctum gignunt, sua & aliena peccata, carnem spiritui rebellem, qui rebus premuntur adversis, easque aequanimiter ferunt.

*( Quomodo verò Christus lugentes beatos hîc praedicat, cùm mox v. 12. fideles gaudere iubeat & exultare? Conf. etiamPhil. 4, 4. Resp. Utrumque in fidelibus simul potest habere locum, gaudium & luctus. Luctus quidem 1. ob boni omissionem ac mali commissionem, de quâ tristitiâ agitur 2. Cor. 7, 11. 2. ob crucis impositionem ata mundi afflictionem,Ps. 44, 24.Matth. 10, 30.Luc. 9, 29.Rom. 8, 36.Ioh. 16, 33.1. Cor. 15, 31. 3. ob Satanae infestationem, ac tentationem,Matt. 6, 13.c. 26, 41.Luc. 22, 32.1. Petr. 5, 8.Gaudere verò debent ac possunt pii 1. ob divinam consolaetionem,Es. 57. v. 18.Ioh. 16, 20.2. Cor. 7, 10.6, 10. & hîc. 2. ob certam ab omnibus malis liberationem, doloris in gaudium mutationem, aeternam glorificationem ac largissimam à DEO promissam renumerationem,Luc. 16, 25.Ioh. 16, 32.1. Thess. 2, 16. Conf. plura in hanc rem apud Dn. D. Walth. Harm. Bibl. p. 738.)*

Παρακλησθήσοντοιconsolationem aeternam accipient,2. Thess. 2. v. 16.dolor eorum vertetur ingaudium,Esa. 35. v. 10.cap. 51. v. 11. (* Luc. 16, 26.Ioh. 16, 20.Iac. 1, 12.Apoc. 7, 17.)* Sed & in hac vita consolatione Spiritus erigentur. 2. Cor. 6. v. 10.Semper gaudentes. *(Conf. 1. Cor. 10, 13.2. Cor. 1, 3.)*

Πρᾳεῖς. Theophyl. in h. l. Mites sunt, non qui prorsus non irascuntur, sed qui irae vim habent, continent autem, & quando oportet, ir ascuntur.

Chromatius in h. l. Mites sunt mansueti, humiles, modesti, in fide simplices & ad omnem iniuriam patientes, qui praeceptis Evangelicis instituti Dominicae mansuetudinis imitantur exemplum.

Mites dicuntur, qui DEO non obmurmurant vel ob impiorum prosperitatem, vel ob suam adversitatem; qui non sunt cupidi vindictae, quando iniuriâ afficuntur; qui morum suavitate omnium animos sibi conciliare nituntur.

*(Exemplo verò praeivit Christus. Vide infrà c. 11, 29. it. 1. Petr. 2, 23.)*

Κληρονομήσουσι τὴν γῦν. Desumtum hoc ex Ps. 37. v. 11.κληρονομεῖν plus est, quàm κτᾶσθαι, est enim hereditario iure possidere h. e. sine labore ac molestia, ut hereditatem, quae à parentibus obtingit, possidere. Denotatur igitur iucunda ac tranquilla possessio. It. stabilis & aeterna possessio (si de terra nova accipiatur.)

1. Chrysost. hom. 15. in Marth. August. de serm. Dom. in monte, Euthymius & Theophyl. in h. l. accipiunt de terra, quam incolimus in hac vita, ut sit sensus, paeificè hac vita & bonis suis fruentur, eaa ad posteros suos transferent. Deus etiam in hac vitae ipsis benedicet & bona corporalia distribuet.

2. Origines homil. 26. in Num. Basilius in Ps. 33. Cyrillus in cap. 58 Esa. Nyssenus de beatitud. Hieronymus in h. l. Damasc. lib. 2. de orth. fid. cap. 1. accipiunt de terra nova in futura vita.Apoc. 21. v. 2.Esa. 66. v. 22. Petr. 3. v. 13.

Potest utraque explicatio coniungi, cùm pietas habeat promissionem praesentis & futurae vitae,1. Tim. 4. v. 8. *(Utramque etiam expositionem confirmat B. D. Glassius Rhet. S. p. 269.)* Nemo quietiùs & minore cum difficultate suis utitur, quàm mitis animus, qui plus à DEO & hominibus impetrat mansuetâ tolerantiâ, quàm immitis, extorquere conantium violentia. *(Interea si terrae nomine intelligatur ea terra, quam incolimus, promissio haec non minùs ac aliae felicitatis corporalis, accipienda cum exceptione crucis. Coeterùm Hugoni Grotio Christus τ--ὺγῆν dicere videtur firm as atconstantes amicitias, quae in terris longè optima sit possessio. Has verò comparare sibi facillimè posse, qui miti ac placido sunt animo.)*

Mundus beatos praedicat potentes ac feroces, quòd ii ferè fruantur terrae possessione, eò quod nemo illis sese opponere audeat. Sed Christus mites pronunciat beatos, qui potentum iniuriis expositi à possessionibus suis deturbantur.

## 5:6
v. 6. Μακάριοι ὁι πεινῶντες καὶ διψῶντες τόν δικαιοσύνην. Those are meant who anxiously hunger for the righteousness of Christ; for the proud hypocrites do not hunger, but belch forth righteousness, says Augustine. *(Moreover, that τὸ to hunger and to thirst are used in Holy Scripture mostly for a vehement and burning desire, chiefly of spiritual goods, is evident from Ps. 42, 3. Ps. 63. 2. Es. 41, 17. c. 55, 1. Amos. 8, 11 Matth. 5, 6. Luc. 6, 21. Ioh. 7, 37.

&c. Indeed, that the same expression is found among secular authors in this same signification, Gataker shows, On the Style of the New Testament, p. 195. sqq.)*

The world judges those unhappy who are forced to suffer hunger and thirst, but Christ declares them blessed, provided that this hunger for food arises from a hunger for righteousness or has it conjoined. For Luke speaks of corporal hunger in chapter 6, verses 21 and 25, and Matthew of spiritual hunger, and one brings light to the other. *(Gataker, in 'On the Style of the New Testament', chapter 20, thinks that both Evangelists can be most conveniently reconciled in this way, if it is said, that whatever the Savior said, Blessed are you, who while oppressed here, are forced to hunger for justice to be done to you against those who oppress you, you hunger and thirst in vain: for it will come to pass that you shall be satisfied, and you shall obtain your right, which you now seek so anxiously but in vain, to the fullest satisfaction. But the Evangelical righteousness, concerning which the Savior primarily treats in this place, must not be passed over. Just as also the renowned Rivetus, volume 2 of his Works, page 69, in his Commentary, namely on Ps. 16., rightly explains this place thus: By hunger, he writes, and thirst is expressed a vehement constant desire for divine righteousness, i.e., justification, sanctification in Christ; and sorrow mourning from the sense of sins and one's own injustice, because sorrow and desire accompany the hunger and thirst of the body. Conversely, by the promise of being satisfied, the abundance of the benign grace and mercy of GOD, to be exhibited in its own time, is denoted.)*

By righteousness, Franc. Lucas Brug. says is understood in this place that general virtue which embraces in itself all virtues, and thus everything that is consonant with virtue and equity and pleasing to God, so that those are said to hunger and thirst for righteousness, who hold all iniquity in themselves and others as hateful, and desire everything that is pleasing to GOD to be performed by themselves and by all. And yet Brugensis himself admits that it is Evangelical righteousness that is properly treated in this place, which does not consist in our works, but is the righteousness of faith. Ioh. 6. v. 35. He who comes to me shall not hunger: and he who believes in me shall never thirst.

Ξορζασθήσονζαι They shall be satisfied. 1. from the study of the divine word, as the Author of the imperfect work explains in homily 9.

2. With the goods of perfect satiety in heaven. They shall be filled, says Hilary, canon 4, in Matthew.

Psal. 16. v. 15. I shall be satisfied, when it has appeared. Matth. 8. v. 11. they shall recline with Abraham in the kingdom of heaven.

They shall be filled 1. with righteousness, which they hungered for. They shall be filled with perfect and complete righteousness. 2. With goods of every kind and with eternal felicity. Ps. 36. v. 9. 3. With GOD himself, the fountain of all goods, who alone refreshes and never fails. Therefore they shall be filled fully, so that no hunger shall ever return. *(Well known is the manner of Holy Scripture, by which almost all the benefits of GOD are set forth under the name of food and drink. See Is. 55, 2. 3.ch. 65, 13Luc. 14, 15.Ioh. 6, 27.50. &c.)*

Latin:

v. 6. Μακάριοι ὁι πεινῶντες καὶ διψῶντες τόν δικαιοσύνην. Intelliguntur illi, qui iustitiam Christi anxiè desiderant, superbi enim hypocritae non esuriunt, sed eructant iustitiam, inquit Augustinus. *(Caeterùm quòd τὸesurire ac sitire in Sc. S. pro vehementi atq; ardenti desiderio, spiritualium utplurimum bonorum, adhibeatur, patet ex Ps. 42, 3.Ps. 63. 2.Es. 41, 17.c. 55, 1.Amos. 8, 11Matth. 5, 6.Luc. 6, 21.Ioh. 7, 37.

&c. Quin & apud profanos autores eadem hoc significatu inveniri, ostendit Gatak. de styl. N. T. p. 195. seqq:)*

Mundus eos infelices iudicat, qui famem ac sitim pati coguntur, sed Christus, eos beatos praedicat, dummodò ea cibi fames ex iustitiae fame oriatur aut coniunctam illam habeat. Nam de corporali fame Lucas cap. 6. v. 21. 25. de spirituali Matthaeus locutus est, alterque alteri lucem affertt *(Utrum que Evangelistam ita cōmodissimè conciliari posse, existimat Gatakerus in de stylo N. T. c. 20. si dicatur, quòd utrumdixerit Sa-vator, Bea-i estis, qui dum istic oppressi, esurire cogimini iustitiam vobis fieri adversus eos, qui vos opprimunt, frustra esuritis & sititis: futurum est enim, ut sattemini & ius vestrum, quod tam anxiè, sed in cassum nunc quaeritis, ad satisfactionem plenissimam obtineatis. Sed non praetereunda iustitia Evangelica, de qua cumprimish. l. Salvator agit. Quemadmodum etiam Cl. Rivetus t: 2. Op. p. 69. Comment. nempe in Ps. 16. rectè h. l. ita explicat: Fame, scribit, & siti exprimitur vehemens constantdivinae iustitiae i. e. iustificationis, sanctificationisin Christo desiderium; & dolor luctusex sensu peccatorum & iniustitiae propriaequia famem & sitim corporis dolor & desiderium comitatur. Contr àsaturandi promissione benigna gratiae & misericordiae DEI copia, suo tempore exhibenda, denotatur.)*

Per iustitiam Franc. Lucas Brug. dicit intelligi h. l. generalem illam virtutem, quae in se omnes virtutes complectitur, adeoomne id, quod virtuti & aequitati consonum ac Deogratum, ut sie esurire ac sitire dic antur iustitiam, qui iniquitatem omnem in se & aliis exosam habent, desider antidomne, quod DEO gratum, à se & ab omnibus praestari. Atqui fatetur ipse Brugensis de iustitia Evangelica hoc loco propriè agi, quae non consistit in operibus nostris, sed est iustitia fidei. Ioh. 6. v. 35.Qui venit ad me, non esuriet: & qui credit in me, non fitieunquam.

ΞορζασθήσονζαιSaturabuntur. 1. ex verbi divinistudio, ut explicat Autor operis imperf. homil. 9.

2. Bonis perfectae in coelo satietatis. explebuntur, ai Hilarius can. 4. in Matth.

Psal. 16. v. 15.Satiabor, cum apparuerit.Matth. 8. v. 11.recumbent cum Abrahamo in regno coelorum.

Satur abuntur 1. iustitiâ, quam esurierunt. donal untur perfectâ & absolutá iustitiâ. 2. Omnis generis bonis & aeternâ felicitate. Ps. 36. v. 9. 3. DEO ipso, bonorum omnium fonte, qui solus reficit, nec deficit. proinde saturabuntur plenè, ut nulla fames unquam sit recursura. *(Notus est mos Scr. S. quo omnia ferè DEI benefica cibi ac potûs nomine proponuntur. Vid. Es. 55, 2. 3.c. 65, 13Luc. 14, 15.Ioh. 6, 27.50. &c.)*

## 5:7
v. 7. ὁι ἐλεήμονες. From the righteousness of faith arises love, which exercises itself in compassion toward one's neighbor. For mercy consists in this, that we do not grow hardened at the evils and miseries of our neighbors, and that we strive according to our ability to relieve them. *(The merciful are understood -ffectu and affectu. For in the school of Christ that saying of the Stoics has no force, who taught that to help is the part of the wise man, but to pity is not. For they thought mercy to be a vice of the soul, and that it does not befit a wise man. Let us therefore exercise not only mercy, but also put on --λάγχνα ὀικτιρμῶν Col. 3, 12. But this matter will be treated more at length below.)*

The world judges that it is more blessed to receive than to give, but Christ teaches that it is more blessed to give, than to receive.Act. 20. v. 35.

Ἐλεηθήσονται. They shall obtain mercy, not only from men, but also from GOD himself. The Syriac, there shall be mercies toward them. *(Beautifully Nazianzen, Oration on the care of the poor: Be a god to the unfortunate, so that in turn God may be a God to you in your misfortune.)*

They shall obtain that mercy by which, delivered from all miseries, they are made partakers of eternal life. But also in this life the merciful obtain from GOD mercy, namely the remission of sins, and of infinite goods, which are given to them by GOD the Father of mercies: indeed they also obtain mercy from men, who were previously merciful toward others. *(On the contrary, against the unmerciful κρίσις ἀνίλεως judgment shall be exercised, Iac. 2, 13.)*

Iac. 2, 13.)* *(Furthermore, against the merits of good works, the Blessed Pareus argues thus from this place, L. de B. O. §. 89. That which is given out of mercy does not come to pass from merits. But the rewards of good works are given out of grace and mercy. Therefore. The exception of Bellarmine is answered there at length. Compare also Coll. Isag. p. 927.)*

Latin:

v. 7. ὁι ἐλεήμονες. Ex iustitia fidei oritur dilectio, quae se exerit per compassionem erga proximum. Misericordia enim in eo sita est, ut proximorum malis ac miseriis non insolescamus, iis que sublevandis pro virili studeamus. *(Intelliguntur misericordes -ffectu & affectu. neque enim in Scholâ Christi valet illud Stoicorum, qui docebant, succurrere sapientis esse, misererinon item. Putabant enim, misericordiam esse vitium animi, nec cadere eam in virum sapientem. Exerceamus igitur non solùm misericordiam, sed & induamus --λάγχνα ὀικτιρμῶνCol. 3, 12. Sed hâc de re d. l. agetur prolixiùs.)*

Mundus iudicat, beatius esse accipere, quàm dare, sed Christus beatius esse docet dare, quàm accipere.Act. 20. v. 35.

Ἐλεηθήσονται.Misericordiam consequentur, non solùm ab hominibus, sed etiam ab ipso DEO. Syrus, erga illos erunt miser ationes. *(Pulcrè Nazianz. Orat. de curâ paup. Esto calamitoso Deus, ut vicissim Deus in tuâ calamitate sic tibi Deus.)*

Consequentur eam misericordiam, quâ à miseriis omnibus liberati vitae aeternae participes reddantur. Sed & in hac vitâ misericordes à DEO consequuntur misericordiam videl remissionis peccatorum, & infinitorum bonorum, quae à DEO Patre misericordiarum ipsis donantur: quin & ab hominibus misericordiam consequuntur, qui priores in alios misericordes fuêre. *(Contrà adversus immisericordes κρίσις ἀνίλεως exercebitur Iac. 2, 13.)*

*(Porrò contra merita bonorum operum ita ex h. l. argumentatur B. Par. L. de B O. §. 89. Quod ex misericordiâ datur, illud non contingit ex meritis. At praemia bonorum operum dantur ex gratiâ & misericordiâ. E. Ad except. Bell. prolixè ibi respondetur. Confer, etiam Coll. Isag. p. 927.)*

## 5:8
v. 8. ὁι καθαροὶ τῇ ξαρδίᾳ Cleanliness of heart is taken either specifically for chastity, which is called ἁγιασμὸσ Hebr. 12. v. 14. or generally for the right disposition of the mind by which he is free both from false opinions about GOD and from wicked affections, Ps. 24. v. 4. Augustine renders clean of heart.

Those whose hearts are purified through faith,Act. 15, v. 9. who, hating everything that displeases GOD, cultivate most simple purity, who are of a heart that is simple, upright, ἀνυποκρίτῳ who strive to keep their heart clean from the filth of vices, evil desires, and perverse intentions, as far as can be done within the weakness of this life. Prov. 4. v. 23. With all keeping guard your heart. *(Christ speaks of purity in justification by imputation, and likewise of that begun through the grace of the Holy Spirit. But Solomon Prov. 20, 9. speaks of natural and perfect purity.)*

σθ. It does not suffice to observe works of holiness outwardly, unless the heart be intact from perverse intention and vicious affections.

Τὸν σθεὸν ὄψονται. Just as in a thoroughly cleansed mirror the shining image is clearly seen: so in a pure heart the face of GOD shines forth and appears.

Chromatius. The soul with a clean heart shall see God with the mind, and without any dimness of malice it shall behold without hindrance the inaccessible brightness of GOD.

Aug. book 1. On the Trinity ch. 2. That highest good is discerned only by minds most purified, since the weak keenness of the human mind is not fixed in such excellent light unless it be strengthened, nourished through the justice of faith, or as the Lombard, book 1. Sentences distinction 2. n. z., be cleansed.

Just as, apart from the air being illuminated as medium, the eye of the body does not see bodily things; so, apart from the heart being thoroughly cleansed as medium, the mind, the eye of the soul, does not see God. What darkness or clouds in the intervening air do to the eye with respect to seeing things, that the filth and darkness of sins in the heart do to the mind with respect to seeing GOD.

Some refer this to the reward of chastity. The customary punishment of lusts is blindness. Gen. 19. v. 11.Rom. 1. v. 24. Ephesians [Epli.] 4. v. 18. Gregory of Nyssa, oration 6. on the Beatitudes folio 815, expounds thus, They shall have God in themselves, because God is not set before them ὡς ἀμτιπρόσωπόν τι σθέαμα. But the same thing is intimated which is said elsewhere more openly. The kingdom of GOD is within you.

Most take this concerning the beatific vision of GOD in eternal life: They shall see God, i.e., they shall dwell with God in eternal life, and being made perfect they shall acknowledge him, 1. Cor. 13. v. 12.1. Ioh. 3. v. 2.Hebr. 12. v. 14. *(Not, however, inconveniently is also at the same time understood thereby the gracious vision of GOD in the Word. Concerning which Rivetus discusses elegantly, Isagog. ad Sc. S. c. 18. §. 2. seqq. But concerning the beatific vision of GOD there will be a lengthy treatment at 1. Cor. 13, 12.)*

Latin:

v. 8. ὁι καθαροὶ τῇ ξαρδίᾳMundicies cordis vel accipitur specialiter pro castitate, quae vocatur ἁγιασμὸσHebr. 12. v. 14. vel generaliter pro recta animi constitutione quâ ille vacuus est tum à falsis opinionibus de DEO, tum à pravis affectibus, Ps. 24. v. 4. August. reddit mundicordes.

Quorum corda sunt per fidem purificata,Act. 15, v. 9. qui omne quod DEO displicet, odio habentes, simplicissimam puritatem colunt, qui corde sunt simplici, integro, ἀνυποκρίτῳ qui à sordibus vitiorum, pravis desideriis, perversis intentionibus cor mundum servare student, quantum in huius vitae infirmitate fieri potest. Prov. 4. v. 23.Omni custodiâserva cor tuum. *(Agit Christus de puritate in iustificatione imputatà, itemq; de inchoatâ per Sp. S gratiam. Salomon verò Prov. 20, 9. agit de naturali ac perfectâ puritate.)*

σθ. Non sufficit opera sanctitatis observasse exteriùs, nisi cor sit à perversa intentione & vitiosis affectibus integrum.

Τὸν σθεὸν ὄψονται. Sicut in speculo perpurgato fulgens imago liquidò conspicitur: Sic in corde puro relucet & qs. apparet facies DEI.

Chromatius. Anima corde munda Deum mente cernet & sine aliqua malitiae lippitudine inaccessibilem DEI claritatem sine impedimento conspiciet.

August. lib. 1. de Trinit. cap. 2. Illud summum bonum non nisi purgaissimis mentibus cernitur, quta humana mentis acies invalidain tam excellenti luce non figitur, nisi per iustitiam fidei nutrita vegetetur, vel ut Lombardus lib. 1. sent. dist. 2. n. z. emundetur.

Quemadmodum nisi medio aëre illuminato non videt oculus corporis corporea; ita nisi medio corde perpurgato non videt mens, oculus animae, Deum. Quod officiunt oculo tenebrae vel nebulae in medio aëre, quoad visionem rerum: id officiunt menti sordes & tenebrae peccatorum in corde, quoad visionem DEI.

Quidam referunt ad praemium castitatis. Usitata poena libidinum est caecitas. Gen. 19. v. 11.Rom. 1. v. 24. Epli. 4. v. 18. Gregor. Nyssen orat. 6. de beatit f. 815. sic exponit, Deum in seipsis habebunt, quia non proponitur Deus ὡς ἀμτιπρόσωπόν τι σθέαμα. Sed idem innuitur, quod alibi apertiùs dicitur. Regnum DEI intra vos est.

Plerique accipiunt de visione DEI beatifica in v. aet. Videbunt Deum i. e. habitabunt cum Deo in v. aet & perfecti eum agnoscent, 1. Cor. 13. v. 12.1. Ioh. 3. v. 2.Hebr. 12. v. 14. *(Non in commodè tamen etiam fimul intelligitur visio DEI gratiosa in verbo. Quâ de pulerè disserit Rivetus Isagog. ad Sc. S. c. 18. §. 2. seqq. De visione autem DEI beatificá prolixè agetur ad 1. Cor. 13, 12.)*

## 5:9
v. 9. Ἐιρηνοποιοὶ. They are συμβιβαςικοὶ authors of peace, concord, agreement. The Syrian rendered עבךי שלמא working peace. Chrysost.: It does not suffice Christians themselves to be at peace, unless there is added the zeal of making peace among others.

Chromatius: The peacemakers are those who reconcile to themselves those by whom they themselves were offended; those who disagree among themselves to one another mutually; finally those who do not agree with God, they endeavor to reconcile to God.

*(But by no means may one infer from the said words that it is not lawful for a Christian to wage wars. For that a war lawfully undertaken may be waged lawfully is shown elsewhere by the oracles and examples of Sacred Scripture. See Isagog. p. 1512. seqq. Likewise neither can syncretism in religion with Papists, Calvinians, and other heterodox persons be confirmed from this passage. See Zach 8, 19.)*

ὁι ἀυτὸι οὶ σθεοῦ κληθήσονται. They shall be called i.e. they shall be; the word signifies among the Hebrews also something so called that by this name it is celebrated by all.

Peacemakers are called children of GOD, because they imitate God, who is the God of peace, Rom. 15. v. 33.cap. 16. v. 201. Cor. 14. v. 33.Phil. 4. v. 9.1. Thess. 5. v. 23 but such as anyone is called by GOD, such he is: they imitate the only-begotten Son of GOD, who through the blood of the cross made peace both of things on earth and of things in heaven Col. 1 v. 20Eph. 2. v. 14.

They shall be called, they shall be acknowledged by all, namely in the retribution of the just. He did not say, they shall be, because even now they are children of GOD, but it does not yet appear what they shall be,1. Ioh 3. v. 2.

*(Concerning the said meaning of the word to be called there was also discussion in the notes on Matthew p. 87. 88.)*

Latin:

v. 9. Ἐιρηνοποιοὶ. Sunt συμβιβαςικοὶ pacis, concordiae, compositionis autores. Syrus reddidt עבךי שלמאoperantes pacem. Chrysost. Non sufficit Christianos ipsos esse pacatos, nisi accesserit pacu inter alios conciliandae studium.

Chromatius. Pacifici sunt, qui eos, à quibus ipsi offensi sunt, sibi; cos, qui inter se dissident, sibi mutuò; denia cos, quibus cum Deo non convenit, Deo reconc-liare conantur.

*(Minimè verò colligere ex dictis verbis licet, Christiano non licitū esse bella gerere. Quòd enim bellum legitimè susceptum licitè geratur, Sc S. oraculis & exemplis alibi ostenditur. Vid. Ifag. p. 1512. seqq. Pariter nec syncretismus in religione cum Pontificiis Calvinianis, aliisque heterodoxis ex h. l. confirmari potest. Vid. Zach 8, 19.)*

ὁι ἀυτὸι οὶ σθεοῦ κληθήσονται.Vocabuntur i. e. erunt; verbum Hebraeis significatetiam aliquid ita vocari, ut hoc nomine ab omnibus celebretur.

Pacifici vocantur filii DEI, quia imitantur Deum, qui est Deus pacis,Rom. 15. v. 33.cap. 16. v. 201. Cor. 14. v. 33.Phil. 4. v. 9.1. Thess. 5. v. 23 qualis autem quisque à DEO vocatur, talis est: imitantur unigenitum DEI Filium, qui per fanguinem crucis, sive quae in terris, sive quae in coelis pacisicavit Col. 1 v. 20Eph. 2. v. 14.

Vocabuntur, ab omnibus agnoscentur, videl. in retributione iustorum. Non dixit, erunt, quia iamnunc sunt filii DEI, sed nondum appara-t, quid futuri sint,1. Ioh 3. v. 2.

*(De dictâ significatione verbi vocari actum quoque in notis ad Matth. p. 87. 88.)*

## 5:10
v. 10. Μα άριοι οι δεδιωγμένοι ἕνεκεν δικαιοσύνης, ὅτι ἀυτῶν ἐστιν ἡ -ασιλ-ία τῶν οὐρανῶν. Clement of Alexandria, book 4 of the Stromata, chapter 3, mentions another reading. μα άριοι ὁι δεδιωγμένσι ὑπο τῆς δικαιοσύνης for righteousness' sake or on account of righteousness, ὅτι ἀυτοὶ ἔσονται τέλςιοι; καὶ μακάριοι

ὁι δεδιωγμένοι ἕνεκα ἐμοῦ, ὅτι ἕξουσι τόπον, ὅπου ὀν διω θ---ται. But Clement uses the Vulgate reading.

can be referred to the final cause and to the efficient cause.

Apollinaris. Where there is not the truth of Christ, there is not the truth of martyrdom.

Persecution happens to the saints even by words; it is defined thus, that it is persistent reviling aimed at destroying. It is not necessary that you suffer persecution on account of justice, so that you become blessed; but rather this is necessary, that you be of such a mind that, when persecution against you has been stirred up, you do not turn aside from righteousness. *(Nor is the particle in the present passage , but Whence also it is said here, that theirs already now is the kingdom of heaven, not because on account of persecutions endured, as though on account of merit, it falls to their lot.)*

*(Moreover, that flight in persecutions was not always unlawful, Athanasius beautifully teaches in his Apology concerning his own flight, vol. 1, p. 555, and he shows this by examples of Paul and Peter, whom he writes withdrew themselves not through cowardice and softness of soul, but rather that they might exercise themselves with greater force and intensity, and he adds: Ἀλλ᾽ο οὐδὲ ἀνωφελὴς ἀυτοῖς ὁ τοιοῦτος ἐγίνετο κάματος. ὡς γὰρ χρυσὸν ἐν χωνευτηρίῳ δοκιμασθέντας έύρισκεν ἀυτοὺς ὁ σθεὸς ἀξίους ἑαυτοῦ. καὶ ἀυτοὶ τότε μᾶ λλον ὡς οσσινσθῆρες ἀνέλαμπον. The same man also admonishes that Jacob the Patriarch while fleeing was deemed worthy of several visions, and those divine ones, and that the more deserted and forsaken he was, the more he had the Lord for himself. But it is not permitted me to bring all things here which that vigorous defender of the orthodox faith discusses excellently there about the excellence and usefulness of flight.)*

Augustine thinks that by this, that it returns to the head ( for theirs is the kingdom -of-heaven ), namely the prize of the first degree is signified, that to those who are of this order are owed and all the other prizes enumerated in order, —to the most perfected the most perfect degree of beatitude.

Latin:

v. 10. Μα άριοι οι δεδιωγμένοι ἕνεκεν δικαιοσύνης, ὅτι ἀυτῶν ἐστιν ἡ -ασιλ-ία τῶν οὐρανῶν. Clemens Alexandrinus lib. 4. stromat. cap. 3. meminit alterius lectionis. μα άριοι ὁι δεδιωγμένσι ὑπο τῆς δικαιοσύνηςpraeiustitia vel propter iustitiam,ὅτι ἀυτοὶ ἔσονται τέλςιοι; καὶ μακάριοι

ὁι δεδιωγμένοι ἕνεκα ἐμοῦ, ὅτι ἕξουσι τόπον, ὅπου ὀν διω θ---ται. Utitur autem Clemens vulgatâ lectione.

& ad finalē & ad efficientē causam referri potest.

Apollinaris. Ubi non est veritas Christi, ibi non est veritas Martyrii.

Persecutio fit sactis vel verbis; definitur, quòd sit pertinax ad perdendum insectatio. Non necesse est, ut persecutionem iustitiae causâ patiaris, ut beatus fias; caeterùm id necesse est, eo sis animo, ut motâ adversum te persecutione à iustitia non deflectas. *(Neque particula in praesenti loco est , sed Unde etiam dicitur hîc, quòd iamtum sit illorum regnum coelorum, non quòd propter persecutiones perpessas, tanquam propter meritum illis obtingat.)*

*(Caeterùm sugam in persecutionibus non illicitam semper esse, pulcrè docet Athanasius Apol. de fuga sua t. 1. p. 555. idq; ostendit exemplis Pauli & Petri, quos non per ignaviam mollitiemque animi sese subduxisse scribit, sed potius, ut se maiori vi intentioneq; exercerent, & subdit: Ἀλλ᾽ο οὐδὲ ἀνωφελὴς ἀυτοῖς ὁ τοιοῦτος ἐγίνετο κάματος. ὡς γὰρ χρυσὸν ἐν χωνευτηρίῳ δοκιμασθέντας έύρισκεν ἀυτοὺς ὁ σθεὸς ἀξίους ἑαυτοῦ. καὶ ἀυτοὶ τότε μᾶ λλον ὡς οσσινσθῆρες ἀνέλαμπον. Monet quoq; idem, quòd Iacobus Patriarcha inter fugiendum pluribus visionibus iisque divinis dignus fuerit habitus, & quò magis desertus destitutusq; fuerit, eò magis Dominum pro se habuerit. Sed non licet omnia huc afferre, quae egregiè ibi de fugae praestantiâ & utilitate disputat fidei orthodoxae defensor strenuus.)*

Augustinus per hoc, quod ad caput reditur ( quia ipsorum est regnum -oe-orum) nempe ad primi gradus brabeum significari existimat, iis, qui huius sunt or dinis, deberi & caetera omnia ordine recensita brabea, --quam perfectissimis perfectissimum beatitudinis gradum.

## 5:11
v. 11. He turns his speech to the Apostles, and applies to them specifically the preceding saying, since they were to be fortified against grave and various persecutions soon to arise against them on account of the new preaching of the name of Christ.

Ὀνειδίσωσιν that is, κακολογήσωσιν. Tertullian in the Scorpion's Sting translates, they shall have disgraced. ὀνειδι ζειν pertains to the insults of private persons; διώκειν to public injury, which is armed with the authority of the Magistrate; ἔιπειλ ῥῆμα πονηρὸν to the injustice of witnesses and judges.

Ψευδόμενοι. The Syrian, in falsitate i.e. falsely, in the Hebrew phrase. For the substantive noun with the prefix ב often obtains the meaning of an adverb.

Latin:

v. 11. Convertit sermonem ad Apostolos, iisque applicat in specie superiorem sententiam, quia ipsi muniendi erant adversus orituras aliquando contra se persecutiones graves & varias ob novam nominis Christi praedicationem.

Ὀνειδίσωσιν h. e. κακολογήσωσιν. Tertull. in Scorpiaco vertit, dedecoraverint.ὀνειδι ζειν pertinet ad convicia privatorum; διώκειν ad publicam iniuriam, quae autoritate Magistratus armatur; ἔιπειλ ῥῆμα πονηρὸν ad testium & iudicum iniquitatem.

Ψευδόμενοι. Syrus, in falsitate i. e. falsò, phrasi Hebraicâ. Substantivum enim nomen profixo ב saepe adverbii significationem obtinet.

## 5:12
v. 12. Καίρετε. The Syrian adds, then, while, to wit, you are occupied in the midst of these evils. Not only should you not be broken in spirit, or even be affected by grief, but rather you should be filled with the highest joy of soul.

Ἀγαλλιᾶσθε you should attest to joy by the movement of the body. ἀγαλλιάω is more than simply joy- for it signifies showing joy by external gestures and dances. *(Conf. B. Par. Comm. in pr. ep. Petr. p. 67.)*

Luc Brug. in this place gathers merits from the word reward. Reward, he says, is rendered to those who have conducted themselves strenuously: it is therefore the merit of those who conduct themselves strenuously. It is an argument according to the Dialecticians from correlates, against the haters of the merits of virtues. *(The same is also urged by Corn. à Lapide in this place. Note, he writes, here against modern heretics the name reward: for from thence we gather the merits of good works. For merit is the reward of merit, and reward is the merit of merit. Bell. also draws from here an argument for the merits of works, book 5 de Iustif. c. 3.)* Resp. 1. there is reward of debt, and reward of grace: In reward is considered either merit, or consequence. 2. it is one question to whom the reward is given, to wit, to those who have conducted themselves strenuously; another, on account of what it is given, to wit, not because of any merit, but out of grace on account of a gratuitous promise. 3. Haters of merits are not immediately haters of virtues. 4. Brugensis adds, we do not bind God, so that He owes us something, but God binds Himself, willing to owe us the things He promised. But a gratuitous promise does not introduce merit, but dignity inherent in the work. *(The word reward is taken in two ways, namely, properly for reward of merit, and improperly for reward of grace sgratuitous -promise. Concerning the former, not the latter, is the controversy between us and the Pontificians, as is evident from Bell. l. 5. de Iustif. c. 1. That indeed the name reward is sometimes taken for the reward of gratuitous promise, or otherwise also for that which does not pre-require or presuppose merit, is evident from Gen c. 15, 1. c. 30, 18. Ps. 127, 4. Especially, however, does that same thing teach Paul Rom. 4, 45. c. 11. 6. To this pertain di- -atrum: Ambros. ep. 1. Another is the reward of liberality and grace, another the stipend of virtue, another the remuneration of labor. That indeed in this place the word reward is taken improperly, not properly, we prove, 1. from the appellation of eternal life. For it is called χάρισμα, Rom. 6, 23. If therefore even if eternal life itself were called a reward, (which however is denied) the Pontificians would not yet obtain what they want. For it is necessary that the word reward be taken improperly then, when Paul Rom. 6, 23. calls it the gratuitous gift of GOD in Christ Jesus. Eternal life comes to us as to children an inheritance. Now indeed children do not merit an inheritance. Conf. Matth. 25, 34. 2. From the Apostle's distinction. He expressly Rom. 4, 4. distinguishes between imputation according to grace, and according to debt. Conf. Es. 40, 23. κάρις Rom. 11, 35. 3. From the collation of a parallel place. For what is called here μισθὶς, Luc. 6, 32, 33. is called χάρις 4. from the testimony of the Fathers. Beautifully Aug. preface in Enarr. Ps. 31. It consists freely. You have done nothing good, and the remission of sins is given to you. Your works are attended to, and all are found evil. If God were to render what is owed to those works, he would condemn: for the stipend of sin is death. The same l. 2. de pecc. Orig c. 24. Grace is not grace in any way, unless it be gratuitous in every way. in Ps. 144. Where you hear grace, understand it as free. If therefore it is free, you have brought nothing, you have merited nothing, for if something is rendered to merits, it is a reward, not grace. Theodor. in c. 6. Rom. When he speaks of eternal life, which is rendered to justice, he did not say that it is a reward, but grace: for eternal life is the gift of GOD. Anselmus Bishop of Canterbury t. 2. p. 52. If anyone were to suffer all the bitterness of punishments, which can be suffered in the time of the present life, all those passions would not be a worthy merit for the attainment of future glory. Id. lib. de mens. crucis: If a man were to serve God for a thousand years, even if most fervently, he would not merit from condignity to be for half a day in the kingdom of heaven. Oecum. Comm. in ep. ad Rom. c. 6. ult. p. 283. οὐ εῖπεν ὁ μισθὸς τῶν κατορσθωμάτων, ἀλλὰ χάρισμα, δεικνὸς ὅτι οὐκ ἐκ καμάτων, ἀλλὰ κατὰ χάριν ἀπηλλάγησαν τῶν ἀμαρτιῶν. 5. from the confession of some of the Adversaries themselves. It would suffice indeed even that of one Ioh. Ferus, Preacher of the highest church among the people of Mainz, and by the witness of Sixtus Senensis, a man nobly learned in divine letters, who, by the same saying, wrote his lucubrations according to Catholic doctrine. He indeed in Comm. in c. 20. Matth. v. 8. thus: But if you sometimes hear a reward promised, know that it is not owed for any other reason than from the divine promise,

He promised freely, He repays freely. I shall also add the words of Thomas Stapleton in his Antidote on this place, p. 45. Indeed, he writes, the promise of GOD is free; but once the promise has been made, His repayment is not free but owed—not because God owes us something, but because He has become debtor to what He promised gratuitously, and cannot deny Himself. Cardinal Cajetanus on chapter 6 of the Epistle to the Romans: He does not say that eternal life is due to wages, but that eternal life is the gift of GOD, so that we may understand that we attain eternal life not by the merits of works, but by the gratuitous gift of GOD.

Πολὺς many things, great things, ample, immense, and incomprehensible to the human heart.

(But against Bellarmine, who by comparing this verse with v. 10 concludes that the reward of our works is heaven, i.e., eternal life, it must be observed, 1. that here expressly a distinction is made between heaven itself i.e. eternal life, and the reward in heaven. Compare Luke 6, 23.1. Tim. 4, 8. For the Apostle speaks here of degrees of glory in eternal life, not of eternal life itself. 2. that what is indicated here is not the cause or merit of eternal life, but at least the subject to whom eternal life is given. But it is one thing to ask to whom eternal life is given; another on account of what. 3. that there ought to be a proportion between the reward properly so called and the merit (especially when it is ex condigno). Now however between our sufferings and eternal life there is no proportion, Rom. 8, 18.1. Cor. 4, 17. Which St. Chrysostom also beautifully teaches, writing homily 15 on the Epistle to the Romans, p. 139: The retribution indeed seems equal, yet it is far more excellent than virtue itself &c. But human compassion is not equal to divine: and just as much as the measure of goodness differs from wickedness, so far is the latter distinguished from the former.)

Τοὺς πρὸ ὑμῶν. He animates them by the example of the prophets, 1. that he may show that it is not new or unusual for heralds of truth to be subject to the persecutions of the impious. 2. that he may set before them the constancy of the prophets to be imitated. The prophets, despite such persecutions, did not cease to announce the word of GOD. 3. that he may console them, because through persecutions patiently endured they are admitted into the holy fellowship of the prophets, and shall become partakers --nt of the same future happiness and glory with them.

Latin:

v. 12. Καίρετε. Syrus addit, tunc, dum videl. in mediis his malis versamini. Non solùm non frangamini animo, aut etiam moerore afficiamini, quin potiùs summo animi gaudio perfundamini.

Ἀγαλλιᾶσθε motu corporis laetitiam contestemini. ἀγαλλιάω plus est, quàm simpliciter gaud-o- significat enim externis gestibus ac tripudiis gaudium ostendere. *(Conf. B. Par. Comm. in pr. ep. Petr. p. 67.)*

Luc Brug. in h. l. ex voce mercedis colligit merita. Merces, inquit, redditur iis, qui strenuè sese gesserint: est igitur meritum eorum qui strenuè se gerunt. Argumentum est iuxta Dialecticos à correlatis, adversus meritorum virtutuma osores. *(Idem quoque urget Corn. à Lapide in h. l. Nota, scribit, hîc contra modernos haereticos nomen merces: inde enim colligimus merita bonorum operum. Meritum enim est mercedis meritum, & merces est meritimerces. Depromit etiam hinc Bell. arg. pro operum meritis lib. 5. de Iustif. c. 3.)* Resp. 1. est merces debiti, & merces gratiae: In mercede spectatur vel meritum, vel sequela. 2. alia quaestio est, quibus detur merces, videl. iis, qui strenuè sese gesserint; alia, propter quid detur, videl. non ob meritum aliquod, sed ex gratia propter gratuitam promissionem. 3. Osores meritorum non statim sunt osores virtutum. 4. Brugensis subiicit, non nos obstringimus Deum, it a ut nobis aliquid debeat, sed se ipse obstringit Deus, vulia nobis ipse debere suae promissa. Atqui promissio gratuita non introducit meritum, sed dignitas operi inhaerens. *(Sumitur nempe mercedis vocabulum dupliciter, sc. propriè pro mercede meriti, & impropriè pro mercedè gratiae sgratuit -prom ssionis. De illâ, non de hâc inter nos & Pontificios controversia est, ceu ex Bell. l. 5. de Iustif. c. 1. patet. Quod verò mercedis nomen aliquando pro mercede gratuitae promissionis accipiatur, vel aliàs etiam pro eo, quod non praerequirit vel praesupponit meritum, patet ex Gen c. 15, 1. c. 30, 18. Ps. 127, 4. Cumprimis verò docet quoque id ipsum PaulRom. 4, 45.c. 11. 6. Faciunt huc di- -atrum: Ambros. ep. 1. Alia est merces liberalitatis & gratiae, aliud virtutis stipendium, alia laboris remuneratio. Quòd verò h. l. impropriè mercedis vocabulum accipiatur, non propriè, probamus, 1. ex vitae aeternae adpellatione. Vocatur enim χάρισμα,Rom. 6, 23. Si igitur vel maximè ipsa vita aet. appellaretur merces, (quod tamen negatur) non tamen obtinerent Pontificii, quod volunt. necesse enim est, tunc accipi vocem mercedis impropriè, cum Paulus Rom. 6, 23. vocet gratuitum DEI donum in Christo Iesu. Obtingit nobis vita aeterna, ut filiis haereditas. Iam verò filii non merentur haereditatem. Conf. Matth. 25, 34. 2. Ex Apostoli distinctione. expressè Rom. 4, 4. distinguit inter imputationem secundùm gratiam, & secundùm debitum. Conf. Es. 40, 23.κάριςRom. 11, 35. 3. Ex loci paralleli collatione. Quod enim hîc vocatur μισθὶς,Luc. 6, 32, 33. vocatur χάρις 4. à Patrum testificatione. Pulcrè Aug. praefat. in Enarr. Ps. 31.Gratis constat. Nihil boni fecisti, & datur tibi remissio peccatorum. Attenduntur operatua, & inveniuntur omnia mala. Si quod debetur illis operibus, Deus redderet, utidamnaret: stipendium enim peccati mors est. Idem l. 2. de pecc. Orig c. 24. Gratia non est gratia ullo modo, nisi sit gratuita omni modo. in Ps. 144.Ubi audis gratiam, gratis intellige. Si ergo gratis, tu nihil attulisti, nihil meruisti, nam si meritis aliquid redditum est, merces est, non gratia. Theodor. in c. 6. Rom. Cùm loquitur de vitâ aeternâ, quae redditur iustitiae, non dixit, eam esse mercedem, sed gratiam: est enim donum DEI vita aeterna. Anselmus Episcopus Cantuariensis t. 2. p. 52. Si quis pateretur omnes poenarum acerbitates, quae in tempore praesentis vitae sufferri possunt, non essent omnes illae passiones dignum meritum ad consequutionem futurae gloriae. Id. lib. de mens. crucis: Si homo mille annis Deo serviret, etiamsi fe-v-ntissimè, non mereretur ex condigno, dimidium diem esse in regno coelorum. Oecum. Comm. in ep. ad Rom. c. 6. ult. p. 283. οὐ εῖπεν ὁ μισθὸς τῶν κατορσθωμάτων, ἀλλὰ χάρισμα, δεικνὸς ὅτι οὐκ ἐκ καμάτων, ἀλλὰ κατὰ χάριν ἀπηλλάγησαν τῶν ἀμαρτιῶν. 5. ab ipsorum Adversariorum nonnullorum confessione. Sufficere verò posset vel unius Ioh. Feri, summae apud Moguntinos aedis Concionatoris, ac teste Sixto Senensi, viri in divinis literis nobiliter docti, qui-, eodem dicente, lucubrationes suas iuxt a Catholicam doctrinam scripsit.
