Is verò Comm. in c. 20. Matth. v. 8. ita: Quod si aliquando mercedem audis polliceri, scias, non ob aliud esse debitum, quàm ex promissione divinâ,

gratis promisit, gratis reddit. Addamustamen & verba Thomae Stapletonis in Antidot. h. l. p. 45. Est quidem, scribit, promissio DEI gratuita, promissione autem semel factâ, retributis non est gratuita sed debitoria, non quia Deus nobis aliquid debet, sed quia eius, quod gratuito promisit, debitor factus est, & seipsum negare non potest. Cardin. Caietanuc in c. 6. ep. ad Rom. Non dicit propter stipendia iustitia vita aeterna, sed donum DEI vita aeterna, ut intelligamus, non ex operum meritis, sed ex gratuito DEI dono assequi nos profine vitam aeternam.

Πολὺςmulta, magna, ampla, immensa, humanoque cordi incomprehensibilis.

*(Contra Bellarm. verò, qui ex collatione huius vers. cum v. 10. colligit, mercedem nostrorum operum esse coelum s. vitam aeternam, observandum, 1. expressè h. l. distingui inter coelum ipsum s. vitam aeternam, & inter mercedemin coelo. Conf. Luc. 6, 23.1. Tim. 4, 8. Loquitur nempe Apostolus hîc de gradibus gloriae in vitâ aeternâ, non de ipsâ vitâ aeternâ. 2. non indicari h. l. causam s. meritum vitae aeternae, sed describi saltem subiectum, cui detur vitâ aeternā. aliud verò est quaerere, cui detur vita aeterna; aliud propter quid. 3. inter mercedem propriè dictam ac meritum (cumprimis quod est ex condigno) debere esse proportionem. Iam verò inter nostras passiones ac vitam aeternam nulla est proportio, Rom. 8, 18.1. Cor. 4, 17. Id quod etiam pulcrè docet S. Chrysostomus scribens hom. 15. in Ep. ad Rom. p. 139. Videtur aequalis quidem esse retributio, sed est tamen longè ipsâ virtute praestantior &c. Par autem non est humana miseratio ata divina: Sed quantum benevolentiae malitiaea descrimen est, tantum ab illa ista discernitur.)*

Τοὺς πρὸ ὑμῶν. Animat eos Prophetarum exemplo 1. ut ostendat, non esse novum aut insolens, praecones veritatis impiorum persecutionibus esse obnoxios. 2. ut constantiam prophetarum ad imitandum ipsis proponat. Prophetae ob eiusmodi persecutiones non omiserunt annunciare verbum DEI. 3. ut soletur eos, quod persecutionibus patienter toleratis in sanctam Prophetarum societatem asciscantur, & eiusdem cum ipsis felicitatis & gloriae futuri --nt participes.

## 5:13
v. 13. In the preceding verses he had set before them the example of the prophets, hinting that they succeed to the office and place of the prophets. Now he adds that they themselves were called to the higher office of apostleship, since the prophets served only the people of Israel.

Τὸ ἅλαςτῆς γῆς. You are chosen and called by me, so that you may be the salt of the earth; he leaves this to be understood subintelligibly. Therefore there is need that you abound in all abundance of virtues, and be leaders of the others. 1. Salt makes food otherwise dull and tasteless pleasing to the palate through its sharpness: So the Apostles were bound to season the whole human race, ungrateful and tasteless toward GOD, indeed even abominable, through the doctrine of the Gospel, and make it grateful to GOD, and therefore also they ought to adorn and, as it were, season their teaching by the example of their life, that it may be more acceptable. 2. Salt wipes away and consumes vicious humors; thus by the voice of the law accusing the whole world, they ought to wipe away sins. 3. Salt preserves from rottenness, thus the Apostles, by the sprinkling of evangelical doctrine, ought to preserve men from destruction. Theophylact on chapter 9 of Mark. Just as salt restrains flesh and does not allow worms to arise from it: so too the word of the teacher, if it be fresh and biting, restraining carnal men, does not permit the restless worm to breed in them. *(Hilary on this passage The Apostles are, as it were, salters of eternity: rightly named the salt of the earth, because through the power of their teaching they preserve bodies, as it were leaping, unto eternity.)*

Ἐὰν δὲ ἅλας μωρανθῇ. If the salt has become corrupt, having been made once vain and ineffective, with its flavor and sharpness lost. If the salt itself should be unsavory, how much more the other things, which lack the nature of salt, whence it comes about that nothing among the other things exists whereby the salt itself could be seasoned.

Ῥιζαὶ μωραὶ they are said by Dioscorides to be unsavory. Martial, book 13, epigram 13, calls unsavory beets foolish. And τὸ μωραίνεσθαι has kinship with the word μαράινεσθαι. to wither and to languish, hence foolish is placed for unsavory, since it has lost all sharpness.

Preachers become unsavory salt 1. When, abandoning faith and divine wisdom, they rush headlong into heresy. An example is Ecebolius in Socrates, book 3, Church History, chapter 13. Trample upon me, unsavory salt. 2. when they do not sprinkle their sermons with Mosaic salt, i.e., do not rebuke sins. 3. when they themselves play the fool and stumble over grievous stones. Mark 9. v. 50.

εἰς οὐδὲν ἰοχύει, ἔτι εἰ μὴ βληθῆναι ἔξω. Hosea 4. v. 6. Because you rejected knowledge, I will reject you.

If you fall away from the truth of doctrine or integrity of life, you will be useless and cast down from your station, you shall come to utter contempt, and indeed you will also be thrown into outer darkness.

Latin:

v. 13. Proposuerat ipsis in praeced. exemplum prophetarum, innuens, ipsos in Prophetarum functionem & locum succedere. iam subiicit ad sublimius officium Apostolatûs ipsos vocatos esse, cùm Prophetae soli Israélitico populo servierint.

Τὸ ἅλαςτῆς γῆς. Delecti & vocati à me estis, ut siris sal terrae; Subintelligendum relinquit. Ergo opus est, ut polleatis omni virtutum copia, ac sitis coeterorum duces. 1. Sal cibum alioqui fatuum & insipidum acrimonia suâ reddit palato gratum: Sic Apostoli per doctrinam Evangelii universum genus humanum DEO ingratum & insipidum, imò abominabile, condire ac DEO gratum reddere debebant, proinde etiam exemplo vitae doctrinam ornare & quasicondire debent, ut sit gratior. 2. Sal abstergit & absumit vitiosos humores; sic voce legis, totum mundum accusantis, peccata abstergere debebant. 3. Sal praeservat à putredine, sic Apostoli doctrinae Evangelicae aspersione de-ent homines ab exitio praeservare. Theoph. in cap. 9 Marci. Quemadmodum sal carnes cohibet, nec vermes inde creari sinit: it a & sermo doctoris si recens & mordax sit, carnales homines constringens, non sinit in ipsis generari vermē irrequietum. *(Hilarius in h. l. Apostoli sunt aeternitatis quasi salitores: meritò sal terrae nuncupati, quia per virtutem doctrinae quasi salientes aeternitati corpora servant.)*

Ἐὰν δὲ ἅλας μωρανθῇ. Si sal computruerit, evanidum & inefficax semel factum fuerit, sapore & acrimoniâ deperditâ. Si ipsum sal fuerit insulsum, quantò magis res caeterae, Naturâ salis expertes, quo fit, ut nihil caeterarum rerum sit, quo ipsum sal possit condiri.

Ῥιζαὶ μωραὶ dicuntur Dioscoridi insipidae. Martiales lib. 13. epigr. 13. betas insipidas vocat fatuas. Ac τὸ μωραίνεσθαι cognationem habet cum verbo μαράινεσθαι.marcescere & elanguescere, Sal ego fatuum ponitur pro insipido, quod omnem acrimoniam amisit.

Concionatores fiunt sal insipidum 1. Cùm relictâ fide & sapientia divinâ, in haeresin ruunt. Exemplum Ecebolii apud Socrat. lib. 3. Hist. Eccles. cap. 13. Conculcate me sal insipidum. 2 quando conciones suas non conspergunt sale Mosaico i. e. non arguunt peccata. 3. quando ipsi desipiunt & lapidibus atrocibus implicantur. Marc. 9. v. 5.

εἰς οὐδὲν ἰοχύει, ἔτι εἰ μὴ βληθῆναι ἔξω. Oseae. 4. v. 6. Quia scientiarepulisti & ego repellam te.

Si à doctrinae veritate aut vitae integritate defeceritis, eritis inutiles ac deturbati à gradu vestro, in extremum venietis contemtum, quin & in tenebras externas proiiciemini.

## 5:14
v. 14. -- The Rabbis call wise men generally by the term -- in the Book of Selected Gems, on the chapter concerning Wisdom: The wise are upon earth what lamps are in heaven. For they illuminate the world and drive out the shadows of errors. Compare the Author of the unfinished work on this passage.

In the book Juchasin: Many are called the light of the world who nevertheless are the darkness of the world. Christ is the light of the world John 1, 49.8. v. 12.ch. 9. 5. as regards merit, the fountain and efficacy of doctrine. *(and in this sense the Apostles are not light, John 1, 8.)* The Apostles are called the light of the world with respect to ministry, propagation and testimony.

Hilary on this passage. Augustine, sermon on the saints 43: You are the light of the world, so that you bring into the world, beset with the shadows of errors, the light of the Gospel. Christ utters these things for the admonition of the Apostles, that they may know what their duty is.

*(Compare here the passage of B. P. On the Ministers of the Church §. 35. p. 18. a.)* Francis Lucas of Bruges: Here Christ calls himself the light of the world, John 8. v. 12. which serves against heretics, showing that what is proper to Christ is granted after his own manner to the saints, 1. Corinthians 3. v. 11. Revelation 21. v. 14. Answer: certain things belong to Christ so properly that none of them is shared with the saints, such as the honor of merit, of satisfaction, the work of redemption, the glory of being invoked, the duality of Natures in the unity of Person; but certain things are attributed both to Christ and to the saints, yet in different ways—to Christ as the principal and meritorious cause, to the saints as the ministerial cause. Thus Christ is the fountain of light shining forth to the world. The Apostles are light kindled, light shining with a light received from Christ, as Bruges himself adds below. Hence he compares Christ to the sun, the Apostles to the moon, which illumines the world with borrowed light from the sun. *(St. Athanasius explains from this saying the passage Ps. 77, 19. The voice of thy thunder in a wheel: the lightnings shone forth over all the earth. The earth saw and trembled: What else, he writes, does he call thunder than Baptism? But the lightnings the holy Apostles, who made known the voice of thunder to the circle of the lands? For these are they who heard: You are that light of the world. But the earth was moved at this thunder unto cultivation, and the Nations were transferred by the illumination of the stars from ignorance unto the knowledge of God. Dialogue 3. On the Holy Trinity, vol. 2. p. 202. Moreover, however much Christ enlightened the nations through the Apostles, still they did not therefore become light in that way in which Christ is said to be the Light John 1, 49. For we must observe here what the celebrated Athanasius warns us of in similar cases, in the cited book, Dialogue 5, writing: Even if those of whom it is said that they are the light of the world had performed true righteousness, they are nevertheless not -υτο-ι-αιοσύνη. God the Word, ό θεός γολος, αυτοσιηαιοσύνη ων righteousness itself, having taken the form of a servant made unto us righteousness, sanctification and redemption. He Himself, I say, who is righteousness, became—if regard be had to human nature—righteousness, that He might justify us who were not righteous, by His grace. In the same way Christ, who dwells in unapproachable light and is eternal light, 1. John 1, 5.1. Timothy 6, 16. was made light unto us, that we might be light in the Lord, Eph. 5, 8. that is, He illuminated us (the Apostles) unto the saving knowledge of Himself, that thereafter we should draw others to Christ by doctrine and conduct. In sum, Christ is the Light κατὰ Φύσιν i.e. ο--ιον that is, ουιωσως ένεργητιηως, έξοχιηως; the Apostles, Doctors of the Church and any believers whatsoever are light κατὰ χάειν. So too believers are called children of light, Luke 16, 8.Eph. 5, 8.1. Thess. 5, 5. Christ is light essentially, substantially, originally, eminently and independently; the Apostles and Doctors of the Church instrumentally, dependently, etc., and doctrinally, because by doctrine and example they shine before others unto eternal life.)*

(Moreover, from the fact that the Apostles are called the light of the world, not only by reason of their life but also of their doctrine, and of that doctrine handed down not only by living voice but also reduced to writing, our countrymen rightly conclude that Holy Scripture is clear and perspicuous with respect to those things which are necessary to be known and believed for salvation. Above all let this notable passage be compared: 2. Cor. 4, 3. The objections of the Papists can easily be sufficiently answered, namely at point 1. that therefore the writings of the Apostles are compared with light, not because they are easily understood, but because when understood they illuminate, and show the way to Christ. Resp. Thus the writings of the Evangelists and Apostles would be perspicuous not per se but only per accidens, namely by reason of an interpretation to be supplied by the Church. But the Apostles themselves in this place are said to be light by reason of their doctrine, both delivered in writing and by living voice. Their writings possess that light in themselves. Nor do we exclude interpretation, but we say it must be drawn from Holy Scripture itself. Moreover, if the writings of the Apostles are not clear per se, and

the light leading men to the saving knowledge of GOD, it follows either that the Apostles could not show the way of salvation equally clearly in their writings as they did by living preaching; or that they were unwilling. But neither can be said. Not the latter, for they would then have acted against the command of the Savior; add also Rom. 15, 4.2. Tim. 3, 15. Nor that argument either. For if today S-r. S. interpreters are able to set forth the articles of faith from the Holy Writings quite plainly, why could the Apostles not perform the same thing in their writings, being especially illumined by the H. Ghost. 2. That Christ speaks of the light of examples, uprightness and morals. Answer: subordinate matters must not be opposed to one another. Thus Christ is called light of the world in both ways too Ioh. 8, 12. Next let it be noted that Christ speaks chiefly concerning the office of the Apostles, as appears from the preceding verse. Hence also the words which follow soon after: They do not light a lamp &c. Marc. 4, 21. and Luc. 8, 16. are repeated and expressly referred to the preaching of the Word. Rightly therefore Marcus Antonius de Dominis Archbishop of Spalato, l. 1. de Rep. Eccl. c. 2. p. 21., explains this passage, writing: These men (the Apostols) are the light of the world, because through them the Lord handed over to this world the light of faith and true knowledge; and delivered nations and peoples out of the darkness of errors and sins. Nay, even Cornelius à Lapide himself on this place p. 132.: Lamps, he says, and torches here, just as elsewhere in Scripture, signify holy men, especially apostolic ones, who shine before and gleam upon others with the light of doctrine and holiness. The Jesuit Adam Contzen likewise is compelled to admit the same explanation, namely of the light of doctrine, while he writes on this place: If the Apostles are light, they cannot scatter darkness, therefore teach nothing contrary to the WORD OF GOD. Above all let the parallel passages be marked here too, Ps. 19, 9.Ps. 119, 105.Prov. 6, 23.Act. 13, 46. 47.c. 26, 18.2. Petr. 1, 19. whose emphasis our countrymen showed long ago, and whose clarity they defended against the mists which the Papists attempted to cast over them. See B. Par. Exeg. L. de Scr. S. §. 414. seqq. Comm. in post. Ep. Petri. p. 154. seqq. Confess. Cath. t. 2. p. 211. seqq. B. D. Graverus Prol. in A. C. p. 55. seqq Dn. D. Walt. Off Bibl. Arc. 4, p. 80. seqq. others. Beautifully Lactant. l. 6. Ins-tidivin. c. 2. Can God, the craftsman of mind and tongue, not speak eloquently (clearly)?*

*(The Calvini-sts, among other arguments to prove the hypothesis that the word world is taken for the elect alone, bring forward also this passage among others. But we deny that here under the name to be understood by the world. For the Apostles were sent into the whole circle of the earth, so that they might illuminate it with the light of preaching and heavenly doctrine.)*

--- This can be referred both to the ministry of the word and the doctrine of the Church, which Christ does not wish to be secret but public, and to the life of the Ministers, which is observed more diligently. It can also be applied to this, that Ministers ought not hide their talent.

Just as previously to salt and light, so here he compares the Apostles to a city set upon a mountain. You who are distinguished with the honor of apostleship I have placed on a higher spot, so that all eyes should be cast upon you: Beware therefore lest you fail in your duty, lest you seek hiding places out of fear of persecutions, and because of the dangers joined together shun the preaching of the Gospel. Franc. Luc. Brug.

Bellarm., book 3, On the Church, chapter 12, tries to prove from this passage that the Church is not invisible, but visible. Response: 1. We do not deny the visibility of the Church, but we say that it is visible and invisible in different respects. 2. According to Maldonatus, Jansenius, Barradius, Brugensis *(with whom Cornelius à Lapide also agrees)*, Christ's saying properly concerns the Apostles, as the context also proves, since in what precedes he had compared them to salt and light. *(Meanwhile it is not denied that the Church itself may also fittingly be compared to a mountain, see Is. 2, 2.Mic. ch. 4, 1. and indeed 1. by reason of visibility, i.e. 2. by reason of the legal promulgation and explanation of the moral law made here by Christ. Especially however Joel 3, 16. 3. by reason of the most firm foundation, Matt. 16, 18.Is 14, 32. etc. But how the Church is held invisible by us is explained in the Confession of the Orthodox Faith [Confess. Cath. B.P.] vol. 2, p. 1088, likewise LL. Theol. vol. 5, Book on the Church §. 69 sqq., and briefly in Coll. Isag. p. 1227.)*

Latin:

v. 14. -- Rabbini in genere viros sapientes vocant -- in lib. selectar. gemm. in cap. de Sapientia. Sapientes in terra sunt, quod luminarta in coelo. Nam illuminant mundum & pellunt tenebras errorum. Confer Autorem imperfecti operis in h. l.

In libro Iuchasin. Multi dicuntur lux mundi, qui tamen sunt tenebrae mundi. Christus est lux mundi Ioh. 1, 49.8. v. 12.c. 9. 5. quod attinet meritum, doctrinae fontem & efficaciam. *(& hoc sensu Apostoli non sunt lux, Ioh. 1, 8.)* Apostoli vocantur lux mundi, quoad ministerium, propagationem & testimonium.

Hilarius in h. l. August. serm. de sanctis 43. Vos estis lux mundi, ut in mundum, errorum tenebris obsitum, Evangelii lucem inferatis. Christus haec profert ad Apostolorum commonitionem, ut sciant, quae sui sint officii.

*(Confer hîc locum B. P. de Minist. Eccles. §. 35. p. 18. a.)* Franc. Luc. Brugens. Christus hîc Apostolos,Ioh. 8. v. 12.se lucem mundi vocat, quod adversus haereticos servit, monstrans, id quod Christo est proprium, suo modo sanctis tribui,1. Corinth. 3. v. 11.Apoc. 21. v. 14. Resp. quaedam Christo ita sunt propria, ut nihil eorum communicet sanctis, qualia sunt honor meriti, satisfactionis, opus redemtionis, gloria invocationis, dualitas Naturarum in personae unitate; quaedam verò Christo & sanctis tribuuntur, sed diversimodè, Christo ut causae principali & meritoriae, sanctis ut causae ministeriali. Sic Christus est fons luminis, mundo lucentis. Apostoli sunt lux accensa, lux lucens lumine, à Christo accepto, ut ipse Brugensis subiicit. Inde Christum confert soli, Apostolos Lunae, quae lumine à sole mutuato mundum illustrat. *(S. Athanasius ex hoc dicto explicat locum Ps. 77, 19. Vox tui tonitru in rota: emicuerunt fulguratua universae terrae. Vidit terra & commota est: Quid, scribit, aliud vocat tonitru, quàm Baptismum? Fulgura verò sanctos Apostolos, qui vocem tonitru orbi terrarum patefecerunt? Hi sunt enim, qui audierunt: Vos estis lux illa mundi. Commota est autem ab hoc conitru terra ad culturam, & Gentes collustratione siderum ab ignorantia ad Dei cognitionem traductae. Dial. 3. de S. S. Trin. t. 2. p. 202. Coeterùm ut ut Christus per Apostolos gentes illustrarit, ipsi tamen propterea non eo modo fuere lux, quo Christus lux dicitur Ioh. 1, 49. Observandum enim hîc, quod in simili casu monet laudatus Athan. l. c. Dial. 5. scribens: Etiamsi isti, de quibus dicitur, quòd sint lux mundi, veram iustitiam praestiterint, non sunt tamen-υτο-ι-αιοσύνη.Deus autem sermo,ό θεός γολος, αυτοσιηαιοσύνη ωνipsamet iustitia est, acceptâ servi formâ factus nobis iustitia, sanctificatio & redemtio. Ipse, inquam, qui iustitia est, factus est, si humanam naturam respicias, iu stitia, ut nos qui iustitia non er amus, suâ gratiâ iustificaret. Eodem modo Christus, qui habitat lucem inaccessibilem & lux est aeterna, 1. Iohan. 1, 5.1. Timoth. 6, 16. factus est nobis lux, ut essemus lux in Domino,Eph. 5, 8. h. e. illuminavit nos (Apostolos) ad salutarem sui cognitionem, ut deinde alios ad Christum doctrinâ & moribus pertrahamus. Summa, Christus est luxκατὰ Φύσιν s. ο--ιον h. e. ουιωσως ένεργητιηως, έξοχιηως; Apostoli, Dd. Ecclesiae ac quivis fideles sunt luxκατὰ χάειν. Sic credentes dicuntur quoque filii lucis,Luc. 16, 8.Eph. 5, 8.1. Thess. 5, 5. Christus est lux essentialiter, substantialiter, originaliter, eminenter ac independenter; Apostoli & Dd. Ecclesiae instrument aliter, dependenter, &c. ac doctrinaliter, quia doctrinâ & exemplo aliis praelucent ad vitam aeternam.)*

*(Porrò ex eo, quòd Apostoli dicuntur lux mundi, non solùm ratione vitae, verùm etiam doctrinae, eiusdemque non solùm vivâ voce traditae, sed etiam in literas redactae, rectè colligunt nostrates, Scripturam S. esse claram & perspicuam quoad illa, quae ad salutem scitu ac creditu necessaria sunt. Conferatur cumprimis insignis locus. 2. Cor. 4, 3. Exceptionibus Pontificiorum facilè fieri satis potest, & quidem ad 1. quòd ideò cum luce cōferantur scripta Apostolorum, non quod facilè intelligantur, sed quia intellectae illuminent, & iter ostendant ad Christum. Resp. Sic scripta Evang. & Apostolorum non per se, sed per accidens tantùm essent perspicua, ratione nempe interpretationis ab Ecclesia inferendae. Ast ipsi Apostoli h. l. dicuntur lux ratione suae doctrinae, tum scripto tum vivâ voce traditae. E. in se habent scripta eorum illam lucem. neque tamen interpretationem excludimus, sed ex ipsâ Scr. S. eam desumendam dicimus. Si porrò scripta Apostolorum non per se clara sunt, &

lux ad salutarem DEI cognitionem homines ducens, sequitur aut non potuisse Apostolos aequè clarè viam salutis in scriptis suis ostendere, ac vivâ praedicatione fecerunt; aut non voluisse. At neutrum dici potest. non hoc, egissent enim contra Salvatoris mandatum, adde etiam Rom. 15, 4.2. Tim. 3, 15. nec illud. Si enim hodiè S-r. S. interpretes articulos fidei ex S. literis satis perspicuè proponere possunt, quî non idem in scriptis praestare Apostoli potuissent, peculiariter, à Sp. S. illuminati. 2. Quòd Christus loquatur de luce exemplorum, probitatis ac morum. Resp. subordinata non sunt sibi invicem opponenda. Sic Christus utroque etiam modo dicitur lux mundiIoh. 8, 12. Deinde notandum, Christum praecipuè loqui de officio Apostolorum, ceu patet ex versu praeced. Unde etiam verba quae mox sequuntur: Non accendunt lucernam &c. Marc. 4, 21. ac Luc. 8, 16. repetuntur ac disertè ad praedicationem verbi referuntur. Rectè proindè Marcus Antonius de Dominis Archi Epise. Spalat. l. 1. de Rep. Eccl. c. 2. p. 21. locum hunc explioat, scribens. Isti (Apostoli) sunt lux mundi, quia per ipsos lumen fidei & verae scientiae Dominus huic mundo tradidit; & ab errorum ac pe-catorum tenebris gentes ac populos eruit. Imò ipse Corn. à Lapide in h. l. p. 132. Lucernae, inquit, & faces hîc, uti & alibi in Scriptura, significant viros sanctos, praesertim Apostolicos, qui aliis luce doctrinae & sanctitatis praelucent & praefulgent. Eandem explicationem, de luce sc. doctrinae, Iesuita quoque Adamus Contzen admittere cogitur, dum in h. l. scribit: Si lux sunt Apostoli, tenebras spargere non possunt, ideò nihil verbo DEI contrarium docere. Cumprimis etiam hîc notentur loca parallela, Ps. 19, 9.Ps. 119, 105.Prov. 6, 23.Act. 13, 46. 47.c. 26, 18.2. Petr. 1, 19. quorum emphasin pridem ostenderunt, eorumque claritatem à nebulis, quas offundere illis Pontificii conati sunt, nostrates vindicarunt. Vid. B. Par. Exeg. L. de Scr. S. §. 414. seqq. Comm. in post. Ep. Petri. p. 154. seqq. Confess. Cath. t. 2. p. 211. seqq. B. D. Graverus Prol. in A. C. p. 55. seqq Dn. D. Walt. Off Bibl. Arc. 4, p. 80. seqq. alii. Pulere Lactant. l. 6. Ins-tidivin. c. 2. Num Deus & mentis & linguae artifex disertè (clarè) loqui non possi-?)*

*( Calvinia-i inter alia ad probandam hypothesin, vocem mundi sumi pro solis electis, adducunt inter alia & hunc locum. Sed negamus, solos electos hîc nomine mundi intelligi. Apostoli enim missi sunt in totum terrarum orbem, ut praedicationis ac doctrinae coelestis lumine eum illustrarent.)*

--- Referri hoc potest tum ad ministerium verbi & doctrinam Ecclesiae, quam Christus non vult esse clanculariam, sed publicam, tum ad vitam Ministrorum, quae diligentiùs observatur. Potest etiam eò accommodari, quod Ministri non debeant suum talentum abscondere.

Sicut prius sali & luci, ita hîc civitati supra montem positae Apostolos comparat. Vos Apostolatus honore insignitos in editiore loco collocavi, ut omnium oculi in vos sint coniiciendi: Cavete igitur, ne vestro desitis officio, ne persecutionum metu latebras quaeratis, & ob coniuncta pericula Evangelii praedicationem subterfugiatis. Franc. Luc. Brug.

Bellarm. lib. 3. de Eccles. cap. 12. ex hoc loco probare conatur, Ecclesiam non esse invisibilem, sed visibilem. Resp. 1. visibilitatem Ecclesiae non negamus, sed diverso respectu eam visibilem & invisibilem esse, dicimus. 2. Iuxta Maldonatum, Iansenium, Barradium, Brugensem *(quibus etiā adstipulatur Corn. à Lapide)* dictum Christi propriè agit de Apostolis, uti etiam probat contextus, quia in praecedd. eos sali & luci comparaverat. *(Interea non negatur, quòd etiam Ecclesia ipsa cum monte non incomodè conferatur, vid. Es. 2, 2.Mich. c. 4, 1. & quidem 1. ratione visionis, h. l. 2. ratione legalis promulgationis & legis moralis explicationis, à Christo hîc factae. Cumprimis verò Ioel. 3, 16. 3. ratione firmissima fundationis,Matth. 16, 18.Es 14, 32. &c. Quomodo verò Ecclesia à nobis invisibilis statuatur, exponitnr in Confess. Cath. B. P. t. 2. p. 1088. it. LL. Theol. t. 5. L. de Eccl. §. 69. seqq. ac breviter in Coll. Isag. pag. 1227.)*

## 5:15
v. 15. οὐδὲ καίουσι λύχνον. The verb of the third person is used impersonally through a Hebraism, they kindle namely those kindling. ηαιουα properly means they burn, wherefore Luke said απρουσι, but it has here the Hebrew signification of the conjugation called Hiphil, so that it means to make burning or to kindle.

By λύχνον is understood either the very instrument, suppose a lamp, onto which oil or something else is placed to be lit, or the very thing that burns, suppose a torch or candle.

Augustine, Letter 120, chapter 3; Book 2 against the Letter of Parmenianus, chapter 14, concertation 23; on Ps. 118. treatise 54; on John he remarks concerning the saints that they are called lamps, so that they may be distinguished by their light from -ernal light.John 1. v. 8.chap. 5. v. 35. For a lamp receives light also from elsewhere, and can lose what it has received.

λ τό τον μοςιοβν. Synecdoche, whereby a certain kind of vessel is put for the uncertain. Luke chapter 8 verse 16 has in general terms under a vessel. The Syriac has hidden. Hilary on this passage: What fruit would there be of hidden expense, containing light?

The Author of the unfinished work, homily 10: The lamp is the divine word, which must be preached, that it may shine, that is, that it may appear and illuminate those who are in the house of GOD, which is the Church bearing the word of life. The candlestick is an ecclesiastical man carrying the word of GOD in his mouth.

Isidore of Pelusium, Book 1, Letter 32, page 8: God lights the lamp, that is, the Priest, and places him upon the candlestick, that is, της έαυτού Φωτοφόρού ηθέσρος upon the chair that bears His light, so that it may bring to the Church, like a flash of lightning, the splendor of doctrines and actions freed from all darkness; whence indeed the people, beholding the rays of quickening radiance, direct themselves toward them, proclaiming the glory of the Father of lights .

Latin:

v. 15. οὐδὲ καίουσι λύχνον. Impersonaliter ponitur verbum tertiae personae per Hebraismum, accendunt sc. accendentes. ηαιουα propriè est urunt, quare Lucas dixit απρουσι, sed habet hîc signisicationem Hebraicam coniugationis, quae vocatur Hiphil, ita ut sit urerefacere sive accendere.

Per λύχνον intelligitur vel instrumentum ipsum, puta lampas, cui oleum aut aliud quippiam imponitur, quod accendatur, vel idipsum quod ardet, puta fax aut candela.

Aug. Epist. 120. cap. 3. lib. 2. contra Epist. Parmeniani cap. 14. conc. 23. in Ps. 118. tract. 54. in Ioh. sanctos notat vocari lucernas, ut ab --erna luce distinguantur.Ioh. 1. v. 8.cap. 5. v. 35. Lucerna enim & aliunde lumen accipit, & acceptum potest amittere.

λ τό τον μοςιοβν. Synecdoche, quâ certum vafis genus pro incerto ponitur. Lucas cap. 8. v. 16. in genere habet sub vase. Syrus habet satum. Hilarius in h. l. Quis fructus sit clausi impensam luminis contincre?

Autor operis imperf. homil. 10. Lucerna est verbum divinum, hoc est praedicandum, ut luceat h. e. ut appareat & illuminet, qui sunt in domo DEI, quae est Ecclesia baiulans verbum vitae. Candelabrum est vir Ecclesiasticus in ore portans DEI verbum.

Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 1. Epist. 32. pag. 8. Deus lucernam h. e. Sacerdotem accendit accandelabre imponit h. e. της έαυτού Φωτοφόρού ηθέσροςsuae lucem ferenti cathedrae, ut & dogmatum & actionum ab omnt caligine liberarum splendorem Ecclesiae fulgetri instar afferat, quò nimirum plebs, vivifici fulgoris radios spectans, ad eos sese dirigat, Patrisluminum gloriam praedi-et.

## 5:16
verse 16. ούτω λαμΨάτω το Φως ύμων. By light he understands evangelical doctrine, to be preached throughout the whole world by the Apostles. *(Compare altogether B D. Glassius, Philologia Sacra, p. 624. The truth of this explanation appears hence, because the preaching of heavenly doctrine is the chief fruit of the Apostle, just as false doctrine was that of the False Prophets, Mark 7, 20.)*

Τα καλὰ ἔργα. That seeing your good works, conformed to that doctrine of yours, they may glorify your Father, whose heralds they see you to be not only, but also obedient worshippers and servants, and let them turn to Him.

*(From the fact that in this place the works of believers are called good, Bellarmine gathers against Luther, all the works of the righteous are not mortal sins. But it should be known that M. Luther does not say absolutely, M. W. that the works of the regenerate are mortal sins, but with regard to a certain aspect, namely in the strict judgment of GOD and with divine mercy set aside, whereby it comes about that the imperfection and uncleanness adhering to our works is covered by the merit of Christ, and thus the obedience of the regenerated, although imperfect and contaminated by sins, is approved before the heavenly Parent. As is shown more fully by M. Par., Book on M. W., §. 39. Markedly Augustine, Book 9 of the Confessions, last chapter: Even the praiseworthy life of men is wretched, if you examine it with mercy removed.)*

(Chamier relates this, vol. 1, Panstr. bk. 3, ch. 12, among other arguments by which the Papists labor to prove the powers of free will, namely this, that good works are called ours, which also happens Rom. 2, 6. Apoc. 2, 2. But he presses, following Calvin, the following passages instead of instances: Matt. 6, 11. ch. 9, 2. 22. Rom. 1. 12. Yet since Bellarmine and Pighius do not press this argument, perhaps detecting its weakness, there is no reason why anyone should dwell long on it.)

Δοξάζ-ιν to glorify is a Hebrew phrase meaning to proclaim gloriously the majesty and praises of GOD. See especially Origen, homily 8 on Ezekiel.

Observation. It does not suffice to shine before the world in word and doctrine, but it is required that we shine forth also in deed and life.

Christ does not say, that they may see your good works, and praise [you], but that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father. For all glory must be referred to God, as the One who gives the power of doing good.

Franciscus Lucas Brugensis: God is the Author of those very good works which we perform; therefore the glory that springs from them is owed to Him Himself, although because of free will they are called ours. Therefore, if God is the author of the good works which we perform; if all the glory that comes from them is uniquely owed to Him, how can our works be established as meritorious? We must glory in nothing, because nothing is ours, said Cyprian, which Augustine often repeats from him. *(Nor can it be proved from this, that they are called ours, since that must be understood χα-τι not Φύσει. Thus heavenly doctrine at this place is also called ours. Compare also Rom. 2, 16. likewise faith, Heb. 2, 4. Rom. 1, 17.)*

Latin:

v. 16. ούτω λαμΨάτω το Φως ύμων. Per lucem intelligit doctrinam Evangelicam, in toto mundo ab Apostolis praedicandam. *(Conf. omninò B D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 624. Patet huius explicationis veritas exinde, quia praedicatio doctrinae coelestis est praecipuus fructus Apostoli, sicut Pseudoprophetarum doctrma falsa, Marc. 7, 20.)*

Τα καλὰ ἔργα.Ut videntes opera bona, doctrinae illi vestrae conformia, laudent Patrem vestrum, cuius vos non solùm praecones, sed etiam obedientes cultores & servos esse vident, & ad eum convertantur.

*(Ex eo, quòd h. l. fidelium opera dicuntur bona, colligit Bell. contra Lutherum, opera iustorum omnia non esse peccata mortalia. Verùm sciendum, quòd B Luth. non absolutè dicat, B. O. renatorum esse mortalia peccata, sed certo respectu, nempe in rigido DEI iudicie & remotà misericordiâ divinâ, quâ fit, ut imperfectio & immundicies, quae operibus nostris adhaeret, merito Christi tegatur, sicque obedientia renatorum, etsi imperfecta & peccatis contaminata, coelesti parenti probetur. Ceu pluribus ostendit B. Par. L. de B. O. §. 39. Notanter August. l. 9. Confess. c. ult. Vae etiam laudabili hominum vitae, si remotâ misericordiâ discutias eam.)*

*(Refert Chamier t. 1. Panstr. l. 3. c. 12. in alia argumenta, quibus Pontificii liberi arbitrii vires probare satagunt, & hoc, quòd bona oper a dicantur h. l. nostra, quod etiam fitRom. 2, 6.Apoc. 2, 2. Instantiae autem loco urget cum Calvino seqq. loca Matth. 6, 11.c. 9, 2.22.Rom. 1. 12. Sed cùm Bell & Pighius argumentum hoc, fortè imbecillitatem eius deprehendentes, non urgeant, non est, cur diu illi quis inhaereat.)*

Δοξάζ-ινglorificare, phrasi Hebraicâ est DEI maiestatem & laudes gloriosè praedicare. Vide omninò Originem homil. 8. in Ezechiel.

Obs. Non sufficit, mundo praelucere verbo & doctrinâ, sed requiritur, ut praeluceamus etiam opere & vita.

Non dicit Christus, ut videant bona opera vestra, & laudent, sed ut videntes bona opera vestra Patrem vestrum glorificent. Ad Deum enim, utpote qui dat bonum operandi virtutem, omnis gloria referenda.

Franc. Luc. Brug. Auctor est Deus ipsorum bonorum operum, quae facimus, idcircò ipsi ea, quae ab illis prosilit gloria, debetur, quanquam propter liberum arbitrium nostra vocentur. Atqui si Deus autor bonorum operum, quae facimus; si omnis quae ab illis provenit gloria, ipsi unicè debetur, quomodo opera nostra poterunt statui meritoria? In nullo gloriandum, quia nihil nostrum, dicebat Cyprianus, quod ex eo saepè repetit Augustinus. *(Nec probari hoc inde potest, quòd nostra vocentur, siquidem id intelligendum χα-τι non Φύσει. Sic doctrina coelestis h. l. dicitur etiam nostra. Conf. etiam Rom. 2, 16. item fides, Ebr. 2, 4.Rom. 1, 17.)*

## 5:17
v. 17. Μηνομισητε, οτι ηλθον ηαταλύσαιτον νομον. He sets forth this occupation and safeguard beforehand, lest his doctrine, opposed to the corruptions of the Pharisaical law, might seem to be set against the Mosaic law.

Καταλύσαι is more than to violate. To dissolve the law means to abolish and destroy it, Gal. 2. v. 18. Christ was troubled by this suspicion, whether He wished to annul the law. *(See Capellus' Spicilegium, p. 11.)

Καταλύσαι An elegant metaphor, because men are bound by laws as by chains . Through By the dissolution of the law is understood its destruction, rejection, abrogation, or even transgression, as some hold. But καταλῦσαι does not signify the private violation of the law, which occurs through transgression; but corruption, which comes about by interpreting falsely, or the erasure or abrogation of the law altogether. *(See John 10, 35.)*

ούηρηλθον ηαζαλύσαι, αλλα πληρωσαι. Christ fulfilled the law in four ways. 1. By rendering to it perfect obedience, absolute in all degrees and parts. 2. By fulfilling the figures of the Ceremonial laws. 3. By interpreting it sincerely and removing the Pharisaical corruptions. 4. By giving the Holy Spirit, through whom we begin to render obedience to the law. *(Therefore Christ freed us from the obligation of the law—not evangelical, but legal—and from its curse.)*

But how did he not come ηαζαλύσαι, to destroy, when the ceremonial and forensic laws were abolished in the New Testament? Answer: 1. The precepts of morals he by no means abolished. Therefore neither the moral law. 2. The forensic and ceremonial laws are only appendages of the moral law. 3. He abolished the ceremonial laws by fulfilling them, but did not reject them as though they had not proceeded from God. The law itself had predicted the future, namely that at the coming of the Messiah the ceremonial laws would be done away, since the body being present, prefigured by the shadow of those laws, as the Epistle to the Hebrews teaches.

Πληρωσολ is not to fulfill in the manner in which a vessel is filled, as Socinus wants, but to bring to completion, Rom 8. v. 4. chap. 13. v. 8. Gal. 5. v. 14. *(Nor yet should this fulfillment be so understood, as if Christ added certain new commandments, as the Photinians want (see Osterode, Institutes German, ch. 22, 23; Catechism of Rakow, larger German edition, p. 162 sqqq.; John Volkel, On the truth of religion; and others), or evangelical counsels, as the Papists teach—errors long ago destroyed by our own writers. See B. D. Fecht, Against the Socinians, Disputation 22; B. D. Stegmann, on Photinianism, Disputations 18 and 19; B. Parr, Academic disputations, pp. 479, 1190 sqqq., likewise L. on the Gospel, § 64 sqqq.; B. D. Meisner, against Photinus, p. 529 sqqq.; Mr. D. Calovius, Overthrow of Socinianism, p. 296 sqqq.; and others.) Rather, by the fulfillment of the law this is indicated: that Christ himself perfectly and fully observed the divine law for us, that is, in our stead and place, and by that perfect obedience made satisfaction for our disobedience, just as then also, conversely, indicates the loosing of the law, whereby the transgression and abrogation etc. of the law is signified.* Ioh. 5, 18.c. 7, 23. then by the comparison of parallel passages, see Matth. 18, 11.Rom. c. 5, 18.c. 10, 3.Gal. 4, 4. 5. &c., it can be solidly demonstrated against the Photinians. But against the Antinomians, who hold that the moral law also was so fulfilled by Christ that its preaching ought now to be wholly banished from the Church, and that new obedience does not pertain to the kingdom of Christ, but to the world &c., it is to be observed that Christ even in the N. T. urges and expounds the law, as is sufficiently clear even from the present passage; likewise, that the law is not destroyed through faith, but rather established, Rom. 3, 20. But on this many may seem to be consulted: B. Par. L. de Evang. §. 19. likewise L. de lege §. 204. seqq. B. D. Schlüsselb. Catal Haeret, lib. 4. B. D. Hutter. in Explic F. C. others.)*

Franc Luc. Brug. refers this fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets to the fact that Christ, having expounded the precepts of conduct, fulfilled them, in that he added those Evangelical counsels most useful for the most perfect observance of the law, where those things were lacking or were thought to be lacking for perfection. Yet 1. the law of the Lord is perfect, requiring perfect love of GOD and neighbor; nothing could, nor ought, to be added to this perfection. 2. Thence Brugensis speaks alternately, which were lacking or were thought to be lacking. 3. Those things that are hawked about as Evangelical counsels either pertain to the moral law, which binds all men absolutely, or are prescribed to certain persons according to the reason of the circumstances, in whose observance they do not perform certain undue works of supererogation, but serve GOD and the Church according to the reason of their own office and their own gifts. *(But Christ fulfilled the law not only by passive obedience but also by active. Which is to be noted against Piscator. See B. P. L. de Iustif. §. 309. B. D. Fewrb. Synt. Sec. p. 152. 262. &c.)*

Latin:

v. 17. Μηνομισητε, οτι ηλθον ηαταλύσαιτον νομον. Hanc occupationem ac praemunitionem praemittit, ne videatur doctrinam suam, corruptelis legis Pharisaicis oppositam, legi Mosaicae opponere.

Καταλύσαι plus est, quàm violare. Dissolvere enim legem est abolere ac destruere, Gal. 2. v. 18. Gravabatur Christus hac suspicione, qs. legem vellet antiquare. *(Vid. Capelli spicil. p. 11.)

Καταλύσαι Elegans metaphora, quia homines legibus qs. vinculis constringuntur. Per dissolutionem legis intelligitur eius destructio, reprobatio, abrogatio, vel etiam transgessio, ut quidam volunt. At καταλῦσαι non significat privatam violationem legis, quae fi per transgressionem; sed depravationem, quae fit interpretando, aut deletionem seu abrogationem legis in universum. *(Vid. Ioh. 10, 35.)*

ούηρηλθον ηαζαλύσαι, αλλα πληρωσαι.Christus quatuor modis legem implevit. 1. perfectam & omnibus gradibus ac partibus absolutam oboedientiam ei praestando. 2. figuras legum Ceremonialium implendo. 3. sincerè interpretando ac corruptelas Pharifaicas removendo. 4. Spiritum S. donando, per quem legi oboedientiam praestare incipiamus. *(Liberavit igitur nos Christus ab ab obligatione legis non Evangelicâ, sed legali eiusque maledictione.)*

At quomodo non venitηαζαλύσαι,cùm ll. Ceremoniales & forenses abrogav-rit in N. T.? Resp. 1 praecepta morum minimè abrogavit. Ergo nec legem moralem. 2. forenses & Ceremoniales ll. sunc tantùm appendices legis moralis. 3. Ceremoniales leges abrogavit implendo, non autem reprobavit, tanquam non à Deo profectas. Lex ipsa futurum praedixerat, ut in adventu Messiae leges Ceremoniales abolerentur, praesente sc. corpore, per legum istarum umbram prae figurato, ut docet Epistola ad Hebr.

Πληρωσολ non est implere co modo ut vas impletur, quod vult Socinus, sed perficere,Rom 8. v. 4.cap. 13. v. 8.Gal. 5. v. 14. *(Neq: tamen haec perfectio ita intelligenda, quasi Christus nova quadam praecepta, quod Photiniani volunt (vide Osterodum Instit. Germ. c. 22. 23. Catech. Racov. Germ. mai. p 162. seqq. Ioh. Volck. de verit. relig. & alios) vel consilia Evangelica, ceu Pontificii docent, praeceptis moralibus addiderit, quos errores dudum destruxerunt nostrates. Vid. B. D. Fewrb. Anti Ost. Disp. 22. B. D. Stegm. Photinianismi Disp. 18. & 19. B. Par. Dispp. Acad. p. 479. 1190. seqq. it. L. de Evang. §. 64. seqq. B. D. Meisn. Photin. p. 529. seqq. Dn. D. Calov. Socinismi Proflig. p. 296. seqq. & alii. Sed per legis impletionem hoc indicatur, quòd ipse Christus legem divinam pro nobis i. e. vice & loco nostro perfectè & plenè observaverit, & istâ perfectâ oboedientiâ nostram obedientiam expiarit, ceu tum ex oppositâ legis solutione, per quam legis transgressio, abrogatio &c. indicatur, conf. Ioh. 5, 18.c. 7, 23. tum ex locorum parallelorum collatione, vide Matth. 18, 11.Rom. c. 5, 18.c. 10, 3.Gal. 4, 4. 5. &c. adversus Photinianos solidè ostendi potest. Contra Antinomos verò, qui legē moralem etiam, ita impletam à Christo fuisse statuunt, ut planè exulare iam eius praedicatio ab Ecclesia debeat, quòdque nova oboedientia non pertineat ad regnum Christi, sed ad mundum &c. observandum, quòd Christus etiam in N. T. urgeat & explicet legem, ceu vel ex praesenti loco satis patet, item, quòd lex per fidem non destruatur, sed potiùs stabiliatur, Rom. 3, 20. Sed de hácre multis videri possunt B. Par. L. de Evang. §. 19. it. L. de lege §. 204. seqq. B. D. Schlüsselb. Catal Haeret, lib. 4. B. D. Hutter. in Explic F. C. alii.)*

Franc Luc. Brug. ad hanc impletionem legis & Prophetarum refert, quòd Christus praecepta morum, iis quae ad perfectionem deerant aut deesse put abantur, expositis, perfecerit, quoda consilia Evangelicae utilissima illa ad perfectissmam legis observationem addiderit. Atqui 1. lex Domini perfecta est, dilectionem DEI & proximi perfectam exigens, huic perfectioni nihil potuit, nec debuit addi. 2. inde Brugensis alternativè loquitur, quae deerant aut deesse put abantur. 3. Quae pro consiliis Evangelicis venditantur, illa vel ad legem moralem, omnes omninò obligantem, pertinent, vel certis personis pro ratione circumstantiarum praescribuntur, quorum observatione non praestant indebita quaedam supererogationis opera, sed pro ratione sui officii, suorumque donorum DEO & Ecclesiae serviunt. *(Implevit verò Christus legem, non solùm obedientiâ passivâ sed & activâ. Id quod contra Piscatorem notandum. Vid. B. P. L. de Iustif. §. 309. B. D. Fewrb. Synt. Sec. p. 152. 262. &c.)*

## 5:18
v. 18. The little word Αμην the Evangelist and the Apostle retained unchanged in writing in Greek. August. lib. 2. de doctr. Christ. cap. 11. On account of its more sacred authority, antiquity has been preserved. Beda in cap. 21. Luc. He commends greatly the fact that Christ pronounced it thus .

It is used then for the confirmation of things that are affirmed, and then it is to be rendered verily: then of things that are desired, and then it is to be rendered let it be done. *(Conf. Dn. Dilh. Eclog. Syr. p 3. B. Par. Harm. Evang. p. 276. 6. 8. 1129. 1550. 1567. 1997, where it is taught that it occurs 102 times in the writings of the Evangelists , and that Christ used this word seventy-five times.)*

Εως αν παρέλθη ο ούροανος καὶ η λη, Until shall have passed away, shall have ceased to be. Franc. Lucas Brug. limits it thus, according to the present state, in which heaven and earth serve generation and corruption. But the emphases of the words, by which the Holy Spirit describes this passing away, favor rather a substantial abolition. *(Until here denotes eternity, although it is added to transitory creatures, for the law of GOD is eternal. Compare similar expressions Gen. 49, 26.Ps. 72, 7.)*

Iod is the divine letter, by which the ancient Hebrews indicate the sacred name of GOD, while they write with marks, since it is the first of the name ανέηΦωνητού -- it indicates, therefore, that those commandments, which the Pharisees hold as the least, are divine.

The Greek ωζα corresponds to the Hebrew Iod, which is the smallest of all letters. *(Since Iod is brought forward in this place as the smallest letter, and indeed the same is quite large in the Samaritan language, from this the famous Schikardus in -- p. 83, thinks it can be proven, as if by a principal argument, that the Samaritan script is not genuine and truly Hebrew, namely the ancient one, in whose place some think that the Chaldean script was adopted by Ezra out of hatred for the Samaritans. But however easily we may grant that opinion about the substitution of Chaldean letters in the place of the ancient Hebrew ones (which, after Jerome in the preface to the books of Kings, very many and not low-ranking philologists, such as Scaliger, Calvisius, Drusius, Waserus, Capellus, Casaubon, Gerh. Ioh. Vossius, Ioh. Selden, Hugo Grotius, Hieron. Pradus, Biacensis, Ioh. Bapt. Villalpandus, and others have embraced and even undertaken to defend) does not stand on such a firm footing, as was shown long ago by the Blessed Par. Coll. Isag. Disp. 1. c. 5. q. 4. Exeg. L. de Scr. S. §. 115. (Let those things also be compared which the famous Buxtorf published concerning this controversy.) it seems, however, that that opinion can in no way be weakened by a reason drawn from this place, since most defenders think the change was already made by Ezra. If it is so, already at the time of Christ the Samaritan script had ceased to be, in whose place the Chaldean characters were substituted, in which indeed the letter Iod is the smallest, and thus nothing is lost to their opinion by this. Unless someone wishes to say that the truth of that oracle of Christ, i.e., the eternal and divine immutability of the law, is not sufficiently established, unless the Iota is always established as the smallest of legal things. To which also contribute those things which the Blessed Hacksp. brings forward from the Rabbis, tr. de Script. Iudaic. in Theol. usu. p. 425. seqq.)*

By ηεραιαν some understand the highest part of a letter, others a tiny little dot, from which a letter is composed. *(some vocal points.)*

ού μη παρέλθη. It is the same word which is at the beginning of the sentence. He therefore opposes to heaven and earth, which shall pass away, a law that shall never pass away.

It signifies that not even the least thing, which might seem to be a commandment in the law, is fleeting and dissolvable, but that all things are firm and solid. For since the law is divine and issued from the eternal and unchangeable truth, therefore it is altogether indissolvable

Latin:

v. 18. Voculam Αμην Evangelistae & Apostoli Graecè scribentes retinuerunt invariatam. August. lib. 2. de doctr. Christ. cap. 11. Ob sanctiorem autoritatem servata est antiquitas. Beda in cap. 21. Luc. Multùm commendat, quod Christus it a pronuncia-.

Adhibetur tum ad confirmationem eorum, quae adfirmantur, & tunc reddenda est verè: tum eorum, quae optantur & tunc reddenda est, fiat. *(Conf. Dn. Dilh. Eclog. Syr. p 3. B. Par. Harm. Evang. p. 276. 6. 8. 1129. 1550. 1567. 1997, ubi docetur, quòd in Evangelistarum scriptis 102. occurrat, & quod Christus quin quagies hàc voce usus.)*

Εως αν παρέλθη ο ούροανος καὶ η λη,Donec transierit defeceri-, -sse desierit. Franc. Lucas Brug. id sic limitat, iuxt a praesentem statum, quo serviunt coelum & terra generationi & corruptioni. Sed emphases verborum, quibus Spiritus S. hanc praeteritionem describit, potiùs favent substantiali abolitioni. *(Donec hîc notat aeternitatem, licet creaturis addatur transitoriis, lex enim DEI aeterna est. Conf. similes locutiones Gen. 49, 26.Ps. 72, 7.)*

Iod est litera divina, qua sacrum DEI nomen veteres Hebraei, dum notis scribunt, indicant, quippe prima nominis ανέηΦωνητού-- indicat ergo, mandata illa, quae Pharisaei pro minimis habent, esse divina.

Graecorum ωζα respondet Hebraeorum Iod, quae est omnium literarum minima. *(Cùm Iod h. l. adducatur tanquam littera minima, & verò eadem in lingua Samaritana sat magna sit, inde Cl. Schikardus in -- p. 83. evinci posse, tanquam palmario argumento, censet, scriptur am Samaritanam non esse genuinam ac verè Ebraeam, veterem nempe, in cuius locum ab Esdra Chaldaeorum scripturam odio Samaritanorum adscitaem fuisse, nonnulli existimant. Sed ut ut facilè largiamur, sententiam. illam de substitutione literarum Chaldaicarum in locum veterum Ebraearum (quam post Hieronymum in praefat. super libb. Regum, plurimi iidemq; non infimi subsellii Philologi, uti Scaliger, Calvisius, Drusius, Waserus, Capellus, Casaubonus, Gerh. Ioh. Vossius, Ioh. Seldenus, Hugo Grotius, Hieron. Pradus, Biacensis, Ioh. Bapt. Villalpandus, alii amplexi sunt ac defendendam etiam susceperunt) non adeò firmo stare talo, ceu pridem à B. Par. Coll. Isag. Disp. 1. c. 5. q. 4. Exeg. L. de Scr. S. §. 115. ostensum (Conferantur etiam, quae Cl. Buxtorff. de hâc controversiâ edidit.) videtur tamen, sentētiam illam minimè ratione ex h. l. depromtâ infirmari posse, siquidem plerique defensores mutationem iamtum ab Esdrâ factam esse putant. Quod sit ita est, iamtum tempore Christi Samaritana scriptura esse desiit, in que eius locum Chaldaeorum characteres substituti, in quâ utique Iod litteta minima, atque adeò per hoc illorum sententiae nihil decedit. Nisi quis dicere velit, non satis constare isti Christi oraculo suam veritatem, h. e. aeternam & divinam legis immutabilitatem labefactari, nisi Iota semper minima legalium statuatur. Quò faciunt etiam, quae ex Rabbinis adducit B. Hacksp. tr. de Script. Iudaic. in Theol. usu. p. 425. seqq.)*

Per ηεραιαν quidam intelligunt summum literae fastigium, quidam punctulum minutulum, ex quo litera componatur. *(quidam puncta vocalia.)*

ού μη παρέλθη. Eadem est vox, quae in initio sententiae. Opponit igitur coelo & terrae transituris legem nunquam transituram.

Significat, ne minimum quidem, quod in lege esse videri possit praeceptum, esse fluxum & solubile, sed omnia firma & solida. Cùm enim lex sit divina & ab aeterna atque incommutabili veritate edita, ideô prorsus est insolubilis

## 5:19
v. 19. οςέοιν τού λύση μιαν των έντολων τούτων ἐλαχίστων. He said above ηαζαλύσαι v. 17. Augustine book 20 de Civ. Dei cap. 9. This is to loose, not to keep, not to do.

From these least of commandments i.e. which the Pharisees hold as least. For the Pharisees introduced such a distinction between great and small commandments . Franc. Lucas explains most absurdly of the commandments of Christ added to the law: For thus ΠαραΦροζει. Whoever shall transgress one of these commandments, which I am soon about to bring forth, that I may fulfill, for which reason I came, the law and the Prophets. Yet Christ opposed this doctrine not to the Mosaic law, but to the Pharisaic corruptions.

καὶ διδάξῃ ούρως, who, as far as in him lies, has attempted ηαξαλύσαι to abrogate, reject, destroy.

Beza: Whoever by the example of an evil life has corrupted his hearers. Unless we prefer καὶ for ηαν to take and interpret in this sense, has taught men, i.e. who, as far as life is concerned, indeed violates the precepts, yet teaches what the law commands, so that ούτως it not be referred to λύση, but to the law itself. For those who neither do nor say what is right must not only be considered of least account in the Church; but even to be fled. *(Vid. B. Par. Loc. de Minist. Eccl. §. 275. where more things bearing on this are brought forward. Beautifully Ignatius ep. 3. ad Magnesianos: πρέπον σοι μη μόνον ηαλέιθαιχριςιανούς, αλλάηαι -ναι; ού γάρ τό λέγεσθ-, αλλα τό -ναι μαηαρον ποιει. Conf. Luc. 6, 46.Ioh. 15. 14.Iac. 1, 22.Rom. 2, 13.)*

ἐλάχιος κληθήσεται ὐτῇ βασιλείᾳ τῶν οὐρανῶν. He shall be called least, i.e., he shall be last, he shall be held in no place, he shall be unworthy to be admitted, nay, worthy to be cast out, as being an adversary of the divine law, which God established as eternal. *(For in heaven there is nothing but what is great, as Augustine speaks. Least in this place in the kingdom of heaven is said of him who is excluded from it, and great, of him who enters it. By almost the same manner of speaking, by which Matth. 19. v. last, Luc. 13. 30. first are called those who shall be rendered participants of heavenly blessedness, last s. s-ul-imi, those who shall fall from it.)*

Beza rejects this exposition as forced, by kingdom ---oeorum he understands the Church, so that regard is had to the restoration, which was soon to follow, with Pharisaism about to fall.

If he shall be held least who has despised these least things, then certainly in truth they are not least. *(Chamier also urges this place r. 3. Panstr. l 6 c. 12. § 20. against the Papists, teaching that certain sins are by their own nature venial. To the exceptions of Bellarmine he responds in the same book § 21. & following. Which thing also B. Par. L. de Pecc. Act. § 94 did.)*

Ως δὲ αἰ ποιήσῃ καὶ διδάξῃ August. All deeds are judged, when whatever is not done, is forgiven.

He placed action before doctrine, for one must teach first by deeds, then by words, by the example of Christ Act 1. v. 1. which Chrysostom urges homil 72. to the people of Antioch. *(See hom 16 in Matth. hom. 5. in 2. Thess. St. Jerome Comm to Tit. 2. Lactant. l 3. c. 16. lib. 5 c. 2. Isid. Pelusiota l. 2. ep 235 l. 3 ep. 120. & 362 which places and several others making for this, C. Rittershufius learnedly collected in Sacr. Lectionum lib. V. c. 13. who is altogether to be seen.)*

Μέγας κληθήσεται he shall be called great i.e., he shall be in the kingdom of heaven. For thus the Hebrews use the word to be called. Amos 6. v. 1. who are called the beginning of the nations.

If he shall be great who has done those least things and has taught that they are to be done, again those in truth are not least.

Latin:

v. 19. οςέοιν τού λύση μιαν των έντολων τούτων ἐλαχίστων. Supra dixit ηαζαλύσαι v. 17. August. lib. 20. de Civ. Dei. cap. 9. Hoc est solvere, non servare, non facere.

Ex mandatis his-e minimis i. e. quae Pharisaei pro minimis habent. Pharisaei enim tale discrimen inter mandata magna & parva introdux-ant. Franc. Luc. absurdissimè exponit de mandatis Christi legi super additis: Sic enim ΠαραΦροζει.Qui transgressus fuerit --num mandutorum istorum, quae ego mox ad adimplendum, propter quod veni, legem & Prophet as productur us sum. Atqui Christus hanc doctrinam non legi Mosaicae, sed corruptelis Pharisaicis opposuit.

καὶ διδάξῃ ούρως, qui quantum in se est, conatus fuerit ea ηαξαλύσαιabrogare, reprobare, destruere.

Beza: Qui malae vitae exemple auditores corruperit. Nisi malimusκαὶproηανac-ipere & interpretari hoc sensu, liceit a docuerit homines h. e. qui quod ad vitam attinet, -raecepta quidem violat, docet tamē, quod lex praecipit, it a utούτωςnon referatur adλύση,sed adipsam legem. Qui enim nea faciunt, nea dicunt, quod rectum est, non modè minimi habendi sunt in Ecclesia; sed etiam fugiend-. *(Vid. B. Par. Loc. de Minist. Eccl. §. 275. ubi plura huc facientia adducuntur. Pulcrè Ignatius ep. 3. ad Magnesianos: πρέπον σοι μη μόνον ηαλέιθαιχριςιανούς, αλλάηαι -ναι; ού γάρ τό λέγεσθ-, αλλα τό -ναι μαηαρον ποιει. Conf. Luc. 6, 46.Ioh. 15. 14.Iac. 1, 22.Rom. 2, 13.)*

ἐλάχιος κληθήσεται ὐτῇ βασιλείᾳ τῶν οὐρανῶν.Minimus vocabitur i. e. ultimus erit, nullo loco habebitur, indignus erit, qui admittatur, imò dignus, qui eiiciatur, utpote legis divinae, quam Deus aeternam statuit, adversarius. *( In coelo enim non nisi magnum est, ut loquitur Augustinus. Minimus hoc loco in regno coelorum dicitur, qui eo excluditur, & maximus, qui illud ingreditur. eodem ferè loquendi genere, quo Matth. 19. v. ult. Act. §. 94.)*

Ως δὲ αἰ ποιήσῃ καὶ διδάξῃ August. Censentur facta omnia, quando quicquid non fii, ignoscitur.

Actionem doctrinae praeposuit, priùs enim factis, deinde verbis docendum, exemplo Christi Act 1. v. 1. quod urget Chrysostomus homil 72. ad pop. Antioch. *(Confidem hom 16 in Matth. hom. 5. in 2. Lectionum lib. V. c. 13. qui omninò videndus.)*

Si magnus eriqui minima illa fecerit & facienda esse docuerit, iterum --illa --verà non esse minima.

## 5:20
v. 20. Εα--η ρισθσυσῃ δικαιοσύνη ὑμῶν. Greater, richer, fuller, more absolute righteousness, than that which was of the Scribes and ----. He names Scribes here, because they were the teachers of the law and of righteousness, and Pharisees, because they wished to appear before others as observers of the law even to the most minute things also.

Piscator, from the word ὑμῶν,, from comparison with the righteousness of the Pharisees, and from the following exposition of the precepts of the Decalogue, concludes that the discourse in this place is not about imputed righteousness, but about inherent righteousness, which consists in good works. But the analogy of faith teaches that both the righteousness of faith and of works are to be joined together as cause and effect. For the righteousness of the godly is more excellent than that of the Pharisees: 1. through faith in Christ. 2. through the inward renewal of the heart, so that not only outward works are performed, but purity of heart also is present and cheerfulness of spirit toward what is good. Hence Tossanus, who otherwise closely follows in Piscator's footsteps, decided more correctly that the righteousness of faith is opposed to the external righteousness of the Pharisees. *(For neither by inherent righteousness, but by the imputed righteousness of Christ can we become heirs of eternal life. Which thing, against the Papists, who labor to establish the merits of Good Works from this passage, should rightly be noted, and it holds both from Rom. 6, 23. and because eternal life is called an inheritance everywhere in Holy Scripture. Nor does it follow that, because Christ suspended entrance into the kingdom of heaven upon the condition of the righteousness of faith and works, as upon cause and effect... The promises of the Gospel are conditional. For one must distinguish between conditions considered in any manner whatever, namely with respect to the apprehension of the means ordained by GOD, likewise with respect to the very merit of Christ; and between a condition requiring our own works, those same works being required not as a consequence of saving faith, but as the meritorious cause of salvation and of eternal life. In the former way, that is, insofar as the use of the means of salvation is required, and also insofar as Good Works are required as fruits and signs of true faith, it is granted that the promises of the Gospel are conditional; but in the latter way, that is, insofar as they are required by the Papists as the meritorious cause of salvation and of eternal life, it is denied. See many things bearing on this in B. Par., De Evang., §. 22.)*

Spiritual righteousness excels Pharisaical discipline. 1. by repentance. 2. by faith. 3. by newness of Spirit. 4. by true invocation. 5. by successes in one's calling. 6. by victory against the Devil.

Beza in his annotations understands that to the righteousness of the Pharisees is opposed sincerity both of doctrine and of life: and indeed he gathers chiefly that the matter here concerns doctrine, from the following rebuke of false interpretations. Whence he expounds entrance into the kingdom of heaven concerning the office of teaching in the Church. But the little word of righteousness shows that the matter here concerns not only doctrine, but also li corresponding to the doctrine, and there- That the kingdom of heaven must be understood chiefly as the blessed kingdom in eternal life.

Ὀυ μὴ εἰσέλθητε. Some take it in the potential mode. You cannot enter. But the future can be retained, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven. He explains what he had said, he will be least in the kingdom of heaven.

Christ looks to the type of the O.T. Num. 14. v. 30. You shall not enter into the land, Ps. 95. v. 11. They shall not enter into my rest. Those who had been persistent transgressors of the divine law could not enter into the promised land.

Christ teaches 1. that there is a kingdom of heaven besides worldly kingdoms. 2. that we are not born into it, but that we must enter into it. 3. that righteousness is required for entrance into it. 4. and indeed one more excellent than the kind of righteousness which was that of the Scribes and Pharisees, since it was imperfect, hypocritical, and joined with confidence in their own merit.

Latin:

v. 20. Εα--η ρισθσυσῃ δικαιοσύνη ὑμῶν. Maiorem locupletiorem, pleniorem, absolutiorem verequi-iustitiam, quàm quae erat Scribatum & ----. Scribas hîc nominat, quia illi erant doctores legis & iustitiae Pharisaeos verò, quia prae caeteris videri voluerunt legis observantes usque ad mi-utissima quoque.

Piscator ex voce ὑμῶν, ex collatione cum iustitia Pharisaeorum & ex sequente declaratione praeceptorum Decalogi colligit, sermonem hoc loco esse non de iustitia imputata, sed de iustitia inhaerente, quae consistit in operibus bonis. Sed fidei analogia docet, utramq; iustitiam fidei & operum velut causam & effectum coniungendam esse. Praestantior enim est piorum iustitia, quàm Pharisaeorum. 1. per fidem in Christum. 2. per interiorem cordis renovationem, ut non externa solum opera praestentur, sed cordis etiam puritas adsit & Spiritus ad bonum alacritas. Inde Tossanus, qui aliàs Piscatoris vestigiis arctè insistit, rectiùs statuit, fidei iustitiam externae Pharisaeorum iustitiae opponi. *(Neque enim per inhaerentem iustitiam, sed per imputatam Christi iustitiam possumus fieri heredes vitae aeternae. Id quod contra Pontificios, ex h. l. merita B. O. stabilire satagentes, probè notandum, & constatidem tum ex Rom. 6, 23. tum quod vita aeterna hereditas dicatur in Sc. S. passim. Nec sequitur, si Christus ingressum in regnum coelorum suspendit à conditione iustitiae fidei & operum, veluti à causâ & effectu. E. promissiones Evangelicae sunt conditionales. Distinguendum enim inter conditiones, quocunq; modo consideratas, nempe respectu apprehensionis mediotum à DEO ordinatorum, item respectu ipsius Christi meriti; ac inter conditionem, nostra opera requirentem, eademq; non ut consequens fidei salvificae, sed ut causam meritoriam salutis ac vitae aeternae. Priori modo h. e. quatenus requiritur mediorum salutis usus, it. quat. B. O. requiruntur ut fructus & signa verae fides; conceditur, promissiones Evangelicas esse conditionatas; sed posteriori modo, h. e. quat. requiruntur à Pontificiis ut causa meritoria salutis ac vitae aeternae, negatur. Conf. plura huc facientia apud B. Par. L. de Evang. §. 22.)*

Iustitia Spiritualis praecellit disciplinae Pharisaicae. 1. poenitentia. 2. fide. 3. novitate Spiritus 4. verâ invocatione. 5. successibus in vocatione. 6. victoria adversus Diabolum.

Beza in annot. intelligit Pharisaeorum iustittae opponi sinceram tum doctrinam tum vitam: & quidem potissimùm de doctrina hîc agi, colligit ex sequenti reprehensione falsarum interpretationum. Unde ingressum in regnum coelorum exponit de munere docendi in Ecclesia. Sed vocula iustitiae ostendit, non solùm de doctrina, sed etiam vit doctrinae respondente, hîc agi, ac per regnum coelorum potissimùm intelligendum esse beatum in vita aeterna regnum.

Ὀυ μὴ εἰσέλθητε. Quidam accipiunt in modo potentiali. Non possitis intrare. Sed potest futurum retineri, non intrabitis in regnum coelorum. Exponit quod dixerat, minimus erit in regno coelorum.

Respicit Christus ad typum V. T. Num. 14. v. 30.Non intrabitis in terram,Ps. 95. v. 11.Non introibunt in requiem meam. Qui fuerant legis divinae pervicaces transgressores, non poterant intrare in terram promissam.

Docet Christus 1. esse regnum coelorum praeter regna mundana. 2. nos in eo non nasci, sed in illud nobis ingrediendum esse. 3. requiri ad ingressum eius, iustitiam. 4. & quidem praestantiorem, quàm qualis erat Scribarum & Pharisaeorum iustitia, quippe quae erat imperfecta, hypocritica & cum fiducia propriae dignitatis coniuncta.

## 5:21
v. 21. Ἠκούσατε, ὅτι ἐρρέθη τοῖ ἀρχαίοις. This can be explained two ways, either ρὸςτοὺς ἀρχαίους to the ancients, or ὑῶὸτῶν ἀρχαίων by the ancients. *(Christ does not say, you have read that it was said or written by Moses or the Prophets, but said by the ancients (examples of such construction are found in Luc. 24, 34. 1. Cor. 15, 16.) namely by your forefathers, not indeed those who lived in the time of Moses, but the Pharisees, who corrupted and debased the law with their false comments. Therefore the Savior opposes the corruptions of the law, not the Mosaic doctrine or that delivered and published by GOD through Moses and the Prophets in the O.T., to the genuine interpretation and sense of the law, which must rightly be noted against the Photinians and Anabaptists, and long ago also observed by those who disputed against them, concerning whom elsewhere. Therefore the Papists will by no means be able to prove from this passage either that Christ is a new lawgiver, i.e. that he prescribed certain works more perfect than those commanded in the moral law; or that the Gospel properly so called is a doctrine of works. But on this see more fully B. P. L. de Evang. §. 19.)* But Christ soon sets himself up as Teacher over against those ancients. The Doctors of the Synagogue were accustomed to preface the names of the elders or ancients with their false interpretations.

Ὁςδ αὓφονευσῃ, namely with the hand, for the Pharisees taught out of ancient traditions that only external homicide was prohibited in the divine law.

From the first negative commandment of the second table, the Savior begins to show how the righteousness of those who desire to enter the kingdom of heaven ought to be more abundant than that of the Pharisees. The Pharisees taught that only external homicide was prohibited therein, but Christ shows that anger is also prohibited therein. Ἔνοχος ἔσται τῇ κρίσει. | He shall be liable to the judgment, his case shall be cognizable by the political court, subject to the examination of the judges, so that, unless he killed by accident or imprudently, he himself shall soon be killed according to the sentence of the law.

He shall be liable to judgment, and his case shall be tried before a civil court, subjected to the examination of judges, so that, unless he has killed by chance or unwittingly, he himself shall soon be put to death according to the sentence of the law. Ἔνοχος ἔσται τἧ κρίσει.

When the Scribes handed down the law about not killing in these words (which, however, are nowhere set forth in the law), they had regard to the judgment which was among them in each city, of twenty-three men, before which capital cases were tried. *(See Deut. 16, 18. and 21, 2.)*

There were formerly among the Jews three classes of judges. One was called the house of judgment of three men, to which lesser cases were referred, such as theft, injuries to private persons, and monetary judgments.

The second was called the house of judgment of twenty-three, or the lesser Sanhedrin, before which capital cases, that is, judgments of souls, were tried.

The third and chief was called the house of judgment of seventy-two, or the great Sanhedrin, and by a corrupted word Sanhedrin, from the Greek συωέδριον., which was the College of seventy-two Doctors in the law of GOD and judges, in imitation of the seventy-two Elders whom Moses had chosen out of all the tribes to be his helpers, Num. 11. v. 24.; before them the weightiest cases, pertaining to the whole Commonwealth, were accustomed to be treated. Josephus, book 14, Antiquities, chapter 17. The Syriac in this place rendered Synedrium as congregation, namely, of Judges. This great Sanhedrin was at Jerusalem, but the other lesser Sanhedrins of twenty-three and of three men in each city were established by this great Sanhedrin. To these classes the Scribes looked in their exposition of the law about not killing, as also the Savior himself in this place. *(Moreover, if anyone desires to know more about these judgments of the Hebrews, he may peruse Paulus Fagius on chapter 16 of Deuteronomy; Buxtorf, Lex. Chald. Talm. Rabb. p. 513. 514. 1513, likewise in the Abbrev.

Pentagl. root. רון Matth. Martin. Lex. Etym. under the word Synedrium. Schiek. מהמ p. 56. seqq. Drusius L. 1. Praeter. p. 10. Ioh. Cocceius on the Sanhedrin, Constant. It is not my purpose to treat such things at length in these Analects.)*
