## 5:22
v. 22. Ἐγὼ δὲ The point is that God wills to punish any transgression of the law according to the merit and magnitude of the offense. I am a doctor sent to you from heaven and commended by the voice of the heavenly Father Matth. 3. v. ult. A prophet like Moses raised up for you by God, Deut. 18 v. 18. Franc. Lucas Brugensis on this passage rightly notes: Christ does not set himself against Moses or the law, much less against the author of the law, but against the expositors of the law, the Scribes; for he had not merely said it was said to those of old, but you have heard, because it was said: in which sense D. Thomas book 2. q. 107. art. 2. says that those precepts, You shall not kill, and You shall not m--haberis, the other [precepts], the Savior fulfilled, expressing the true meaning of the law, which the Scribes and Pharisees had not attained. This must be opposed to the Scholastics and certain more recent Pontificals, who wished to prove from this passage *(as Corn. à Lapide also does here)* that Christ delivered in the N. T. precepts more perfect than those which had been set forth by Moses in the V. T. *(Above all, however, the Photinians abuse the present passage to palliate their error, that Christ was a new lawgiver, concerning whom see above.)*

Our exposition, however, is conformable to the doctrine of Augustine, who in book 19 against Faustus, chapter 23, writes thus: Because they did not understand homicide except as the destruction of a human body, by which life would be deprived, the Lord revealed that every iniquitous movement to harm a brother is to be reckoned in the category of homicide. And because they thought that only illicit bodily commixtion with a woman was called adultery, the Master demonstrated that such concupiscence is also nothing else. c. 38. Therefore, either all or almost all things which He advised or commanded, where He added: But I say to you, are found also in those ancient books. There, against anger, it is said: My eye is troubled by anger Ps. 6:8; and: Better is he who conquers anger than he who takes a city Prov. 16:32.

Furthermore, Justin Martyr in Apolog. p. 49, Commel. edition, renders this first member of v. 22 thus, ὃς αὒ But whoever shall be angry, is liable to the fire of judgment. There is a double variation. 1. He omits the little word εἰκῇ, which does not exist in all the Codices. 2. For ἔνοχο *(The same Justin, however, elsewhere, namely in the epistle to Zenas and Serenus, acknowledges the little word εἰκῆ in the sentence of the Savior. Bellarmine indeed doubts in de Script. Eccles. book one, page 48, whether the said epistle is by Justin, yet he confesses, that it is worthy of Justin as author. Irenaeus also acknowledges the same word, whom Epiphanius in heresy 42 τῶν Ἀποςόλων διάδοχον,. Lindanus, however, in book 4, Panopl. c. 22, 46, 82, designates him as a most ancient defender of the Apostolic faith and a most serious man. The places of Irenaeus, moreover, are book 2, advers. Haeres. c. 56, and book 4, c. 31, indeed also Clement of Rome, book 2, Apost. c. 6. But it is especially to be noted that in all the Greek manuscript Codices, of which indeed very many were consulted both by the Parisians and by Franciscus Lucas, with the Greek and Syriac interpreters supporting, that little word is read today, as Franciscus Lucas confesses, with the exception of a single Greek Codex of the Vatican Library. Finally, Isidore of Pelusium also reads the word εἰκῆ in book 4, epistle 111.

Erasmus maintains that this word εἰκῆ was added by a bold person. *(The Jesuit Conzenius agrees, writing on this passage: it could easily have crept from a marginal gloss into the text. Franc. Lucas thinks that it should by no means be added to the Latin.)* The Vulgate version and Luther likewise do not read the particle εἰκῆ.. Jerome on this passage and in Dialog. 2 against the Pelagians denies that it is found in ancient copies of proven reliability. Augustine, book 1 of Retractations, chapter 19, says the Greek codices do not have without cause, just as it is placed here. On the contrary, Chrysostom, homily 16 on Matthew, and Laurentius Valla judge that the little word εἰκῆ should by all means be added. In the Lives of the Fathers, the prefect of the Scythian Monastery, being asked what that saying of the Gospel was: He who is angry with his brother without cause, defined the only just cause of anger as separation from God, and that he who is angry at any other injuries, however great they may be, is angry without cause. With which agrees the point that one should be angry at the vice of a brother, not at the brother.

The Syrian paraphrast has the word *(The Altdorf manuscript codex has just as the remaining codices Phil. 2, 16. read, in which place it is used for the Greek εἰς κενὸν )* formed from the word εἰκῆ and adapted to his own language.

*(Hugo Grotius thinks that this was done by the Syrian on account of the force of the word εἰκῆ, which, he says, he considered so proper and significant in this place, that he preferred to retain it rather than translate it. But however much neither the Arab of the Roman edition (for in the Leiden edition it is expressly read i.e. in vain, rashly) nor the Ethiopian interpreters acknowledge this particle, I would by no means say with Contzen that it should immediately be considered as written for those who today insert it into their versions. The Jesuit indeed urges, that neither older nor better exemplars have it than Jerome and Augustine: But however much perhaps nothing certain can be pronounced about the Greek codices which the Parisians and Robertus Stephanus collated, whether or not some of them reach or even exceed the age of Augustine and Jerome; Justin and Irenaeus can certainly be rightly opposed to the Jesuit, Fathers both Greek and much older than Jerome and likewise Augustine, who in any case acknowledge the word εἰκῆ in this place. Indeed, even Clement, whom the Papists otherwise esteem highly. Therefore, however much Jerome and Augustine omit this little word, the same or a similar one is nevertheless understood, as the associate of Contzen, Cornel. à Lapide, admits in this place. I pass over now the Syrian interpreter, whom the Syrians from ancestral tradition affirm to be Mark the Evangelist himself, if indeed faith is to be placed in Guilielmus Postellus, who signified that very thing, which he had heard from the Syrians, to Guido Fabricius by letter. Indeed, Franc. Lucas himself, a Papist writer sufficiently versed in such matters, He holds without doubt that the Syriac text of the New Testament is to be regarded and revered as that of a very ancient Greek copy. Moreover, it is said to happen εἰκῇ, what occurs without divine ordinance and good pleasure, likewise without a just and sufficient cause, as appears by comparison of Rom. 13, 4. But such anger, which is without a just—that is, a cause founded in the Word of GOD—or which private desire for vengeance and frivolity excites, not the glory of GOD, honesty, necessity and equity, was also prohibited in the O.T., just as the slandering of a brother, as can be seen from Gen. 4, 6.Lev. 19, 16.Ps. 4, 5.Ps. 37, 7.Prov. 15, 18.c. 18, 8.c. 24, 20.c. 29, 22. etc. But someone will say, if unrighteous anger and reviling were ever so much forbidden in the O.T., nevertheless they were not forbidden under such a threat—namely eternal damnation—as here by Christ. Answer: certainly indeed. For whatever was forbidden in the divine law, the transgression of it brings eternal death unless forgiveness be obtained from God, Deut. 27, 27. Which ought properly to be noted against the Photinians. Furthermore, whether and how it is lawful to be angry with one's neighbor, B.D. teaches at length and learnedly, Bald. Cas. Conscient. l. 4. cap. 17. cas. 6. Next, concerning the restraining of anger, besides the most learned books of Seneca On Anger, Justin Martyr above all may be read, or whoever even is that author of the letter alleged above and attributed to Justin, since it has been inserted among his writings; likewise Basil and Chrysostom in their homilies on anger, Gregory M. on Job c. 30. Very many sayings of Greeks and Latins bearing upon this matter have been collected by Zwingl. in the Theatre, Magirus in Polymnia, Langius in the Florilegium. To these the adages of the Arabs can quite aptly be added, such as: A fool is known by six properties. That he becomes angry without reason. That he speaks useless things. That he trusts anyone, etc. likewise:

i.e. The beginning of anger is rage, the end repentance. likewise Count not yourself among men while anger prevails over you. But the divine oracles are deservedly to be preferred before the admonitions of all wise men, especially Ps. 4, 5.Prov. 22, 5.Eccles. 7, 10.Gal. 5, 20.Eph. 4, 26.Col. 3, 7.Iac. 1, 19. 20.1. Ioh. 3, 15. etc. Also see the Practical Aphorisms of B. Par. under the title on anger. Now that some anger is lawful is attested both by the examples of the godly in Holy Scripture and by very famous sayings. See Gen. 30, 2.Exod. 11, 8.ch. 16, 20.ch. 32, 19.Numbers 13, 14.ch. 16, 15.ch. 25, 7.2. Kings [2. Reg.] 13, 9.Matt. 3. 7.Luke 24, 25.Gal. 3, 1.Ps. 101, 3.Ps. 119, 104.113.Ps. 139, 20. just as this and other testimonies of Holy Scripture are brought forward by Blessed Paraeus, School of Piety, book IV, chapter 12, §. 4. Gregory the Great knows well, ch. 30, Moralia on Job [Iob], ch. 5: It must be wisely known that there is one anger which impatience stirs up, another which zeal for justice forms. That one is generated from vice, this one from virtue. For if no anger arose from virtue, Phinehas would not have appeased the rush of divine chastening with his sword. Because Eli did not possess this anger, he stirred up against himself inexorably the movement of heavenly vengeance. For in proportion as he grew lukewarm toward the sins of his subjects, so far did the severity of the eternal Ruler blaze forth against him. Of this it is said through the Psalmist: Be angry, and sin not. If we are commanded to love our neighbors as ourselves, it remains that we should be angry at their errors as at our own faults etc. Let Chrysostom also be compared on Ps. 4. urging the example of Paul Acts 13, 8. and Peter Acts 5, 9. where among other things he writes: He is the one who rashly becomes angry, who avenges himself; but he who corrects others' wrongs is the most gentle of all.)*

By the name Ὃς αὒ here, as is understood also in the first member, in the genitive proximi, meaning 'neighbor,' namely he who by right of Nature is our brother. ἀδελφῆ

The Hebrew word, or rather Syrian signifies empty or vain, and is understood by synecdoche as empty-brained or void of judgment. The Syrians use it in Rom. 1. v. 21. for μάταιος. Therefore, by a term customary in those places, it denotes a lighter and milder taunt directed at acquaintances. (*add Glaucus [Glassius], Sacred Philology, book 1, p. 235. The Arabic translator retained the name Raka, but the Ethiopic has Yet it seems to be a typographical error, and likewise should be read or But whether the origins of the word ῥακά derive from the Syrian root , which among the Syrians means no less than among the Hebrews רקק i.e. ורק he spat, he spit out, and occurs more than once in the New Testament Syrian text, let them be derived, as Theophylact thought, whose exposition Blessed Crinesius considers the most correct of all in his Syrian Lexicon, namely that ῥακὰ denotes a man κατάπτυςον to be spat upon. This same etymology pleases Blessed Dr. Chemnitz above the rest in his Harmony; but whether it comes from the verb הרוק, i.e. he emptied, drained, just as in 2. Sam 6, 20. and likewise 2. Kings [Reg.] 4, 3. men vain רקים are said [so called], because it pleases Buxtorf, Hugo Grotius, Angelus Caninius and others, and long ago also it seemed so to Hesychius, Hilary, Jerome l. 2 contra Pelagianos, and the Author of the unfinished work on Matthew, namely that ῥακὰ signifies a man empty-brained, devoid of judgment, just as the Germans also say du thummer Hund / the case is still under judgment. B. D. Franzius, De Interpretatione Sacrarum Scripturarum oraculorum 129, joins both meanings and adapts them to this place. Moreover, Cornelius à Lapide recites several opinions on this passage, yet there he betrays his own ignorance of the Arabic tongue, having been persuaded—I know not by whom—that the Arab renders raca as ragged, torn, beggar-like, one clad in patchwork or in a garment stitched together out of a hundred pieces. It is rather certain that the Arab served his own translation with the very word that is read in the text. As even the interpretation of the Latin version of the Arabic Gospels might have taught the Jesuit, brought forth at Rome in the Year 1591. And the same, moreover, seems to be maintained concerning the Ethiopian Interpreter (whom Cornelius reports to render in this place thus: Whosoever shall say to his brother that he is poor through contempt and in rags, shall be liable to the Council). For although here he has in this place: i.e. and whosoever shall say to his brothershall be liable to the Council. Nevertheless, since among the Ethiopians the root scarcely occurs, just as neither among the Hebrews, Chaldaeans, Syrians, nor Arabs can any such thing be found, it is exceedingly probable that, by a typographical error (of which sort the Ethiopian New Testament printed at Rome teems, as Ludolph de Dieu long ago also observed, Annotationes on the Acts of the Apostles p. 26.), ought to be read there instead of or . But perhaps Cornelius's exposition can be sustained, if likewise a typographical error be posited in the said Ethiopian edition, yet it would then have to be corrected , since an easy slip passes from to ; whereas from that root descends the noun corresponding to the Hebrew ןויבא Ps. 12, 6. But since nearly all the interpreters retain the word Raka here, and the Ethiopian Interpreter of the New Testament likewise employs, for the Greek πτωχῷ, not the said name but either as Matth. 19, 21. or, what is more usual, the name as Matt. 26, 9. Marc. 10, 21. Luc. 16, 20. and everywhere else repeatedly, the typographical error will more likely, I take it, be corrected according to the mind of the Ethiopian Translator, by him who substitutes than by him who . But on this point let the Masoreths of the Ethiopians look to it. If, however, altogether denotes a badly-clothed man, the Ethiopian version appears to lean upon this ground, that it lay within the custom of the Greeks to call a good-for-nothing man ῥάκος, from a worn-out garment, which is so called by the Greeks, the insult being taken, as Augustine notes on this passage. Furthermore, Corn. à Lapide writes that Beza ineptly judges here that Christ said Raca for רשע i.e., impiously. But I confess that I could find nothing of the sort in Beza, at least in the fourth edition, which, having been diligently revised by him, saw the light in the year 1588. If Beza thinks so in earlier editions, he himself corrected his opinion. Moreover, Beza writes that some think the name Raca seems to be able to be derived from the Syrian theme רה (Rach.) which declares to spit. But just as Beza noted a little before, that racha is read wrongly in the Latin Vulgate edition, so he himself must be corrected here entirely: for it is not רה tach for the Syrians, but רה Rak that signifies to spit: nor does Drusius, whom Beza praises for himself, write thus. But Cornelius's slip must be corrected again, when he soon adds that the Hebrews called their council from the Greek συνεδρίῳ sanedr-m. But the Hebrews do not say םנהרוים, but םנהרוין, which slip, however slight it may be, it pleased me to note in the supercilious Jesuit, since not once, but several times, both here and in his Commentary on Deut. 17, 9., Cornelius writes it, and the same error is also made by Cornelius's epitomizer, the Jesuit Tirinus. But it is customary for Jesuits not to care much about such things, whence it is not unusual for the same Tirinus, when citing the Targum, to say in the Thargo; thus the Jesuits Salmeron and Conzen say that in the Syrian there is -ka, when nevertheless the Syrian expressly has iki, just as the Old MS Codex also reads with vowel points added. But I pass over these things, as being foreign to this passage.

Basil in μωρὲ Jerome, book 2 against the Pelagians & in Matthew ῥακὰ it is said κενὸς, that is, empty and void, whom we can call ---insulting without a brain. Hesychius ῥακὰ κενὸς Hilary in Matthew Raca is a reproach of emptiness . The author of the imperfect work on Matthew Raca indeed ---in Hebrew is empty, although as far as the sense of the word is concerned, it is one, --fool, and raca. For he who is a fool, he is empty, and he who is empty, he is a fool, and of both

the word seems to be one insult. And afterwards Raca was a common word among the Jews, which they said variously, not out of anger, nor out of hatred, but from some impulse, more for the sake of familiarity than of anger.

Chrysostom, Homily 16 on Matthew, teaches that raca is not a word of heavier or more savage insult, but proceeds from impatience of a chafing spirit [stomachoq; loquen tis], just as we say to servants speaking peevishly: Be off with you. He brings forward the testimony of the Syrian tongue, in which racha is placed for what means you. Theophylact says that ῥακὰ is a Syriac word, and signifies a man καταπτυςὸν of nothing, worthless and to be spat upon, by which reasoning it would be derived from the verb רקק, which means to spit. The Syriac Raka likewise seems to some to be derived from רקק, a defective verb in the second [conjugation? letter?], which it has in common with the Hebrew and Chaldee, whence among the Hebrews there is from this root the noun רק, and among the Chaldeans רוקא, which means spittle. Therefore Raca would signify a man to be spat upon, unworthy, whose name should not honorably be uttered, at whose title or even mention of his name one should spit. But on this account ῥακὰ would be a graver insult than μωρὲ,, which does not fit Christ's purpose.

Erasmus in his Annotations thinks that raca is the voice of one indignant, as it were an interjection, since otherwise no difference remains between raca and fool, which he drew from Augustine, who adds that he received this from a certain Jew. Angelus Caninius in his Investigations of the Passages of the New Testament: In Massecheth Berachot one often reads רוקה. It is moreover an insult not harsh, but familiar, as when a superior rebukes an inferior familiarly out of authority. This lightness of indignation cannot be expressed in a Greek word, therefore the word Raca was retained.

Some nevertheless judge it to be neither a Hebrew nor a Syrian, but a Greek word. For the Greeks call a man of nothing ῥάκος, from worn-out clothing cast-off refuse, as Augustine indicates on this passage.

Franciscus Lucas Brugensis establishes this distinction between ῥακὰ and μωρὲ: that by the word ῥακὰ some fault either of nature or of fortune is reproached to the brother; while by the word μωρὲ the brother's wickedness and impiety are marked.

πὀρ

Μωρὸς properly signifies insipid. Thus the fool is so called by metaphor, because he is as it were insipid, i.e., least sweet and pleasing to a wise man. The Syrians rendered it by , which is formed from the Hebrew . אליל, is therefore denoted as a graver insult than is ῥακὰ.

Because in the Holy Scriptures, especially in the Proverbs of Solomon , impious men are called fools, lacking the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom, therefore some judge that this sentence of Christ is directed against him who speaks an insult of deadly crime to his brother; whose anger proceeds so far that he marks his brother with some wickedness or impiety. (And thus it is the same as if he were to name ἄθεον, in German a devil's beast. So decides Mr. Dilherrus, Elect. lib. 2, cap. 20, p. 299. That it is not unusual for Holy Scripture to designate idolatry by the name of folly, Pineda shows in t. 1, in Iob, p. 159, from Deut. 32, 6.Rom. 10, 19.Psal. 73, 18.Iob. 1, 10.. Casp. Barth. also thinks the same, lib. 5, Adv. cap. 14)*

*(D. Frantz, de Interp. Sc. S. Orac. 129, and D. Glassius, Rhet. S. p. 452, observe that by that phrase, to say to his brother Raca, and to call him a fool, συιεκδοχικῶς, all kinds of indications of a malevolent and angry mind and calumnies are understood. Thus also by the name of anger the Savior comprehends all interior motions in the mind, will, and heart, not conforming to the norm of the fifth commandment.)*

*(But it must be well observed here that the insult is prohibited here which proceeds from hatred of a person and is a sign of an angry mind, but not certain severe rebukes of the Doctors of the Church, which proceed from true zeal. It is one thing to speak a contumelious word for infamy and confusion; it is another to use harsher words, out of zeal for religion and faith, for correction. For an insult is one thing; the office of a faithful Doctor is another. To the latter are to be referred the sayings Luc. 24, 25.Gal. 3, 1., but the former is what is prohibited here. And the matter is also clear. For if it is granted to parents and the Magistrate to strike for a just cause, and it can be done without any sin, indeed the sword is divinely handed to the Magistrate so that he may sharpen it against the guilty: how much more is it granted, and can be done without any sin, for one whose office requires it to use harsh words against the guilty. Thus we read that not only Christ, but also the Apostles, just as John the Baptist, used very harsh words (and, outside of a certain case, i.e., if they are brought forth rashly, prohibited ones) at times, as is evident from Luc. 24, 25.Matt. 23, 17.33.c. 3, 7.Act. 13, 10. etc., yet without any sin. Nor is it permitted to doubt that even today the Doctors and Ministers of the Church are granted the same, if indeed they have just causes of indignation, i.e.

if the glory of GOD demands it. For the Doctors of the primitive Church did the same, although otherwise distinguished by the praise of gentleness. It certainly befits a faithful servant of GOD as much as possible, that when it is a matter of the honor of GOD or when the reason of heavenly truth demands it, he should show himself more powerful than a lion against the impious and heretics, but on the contrary, in sustaining private evils and adversities, he should be milder than a lamb, and, as the prophet says of our Savior, be silent before the shearer. And just as not only do those not sin who are angry with cause, but on the contrary unless they have been angry, they sin, with Chrysostom warning in homily 11 on Matthew, so also the Ministers of the Church not only do not sin when they mark heretics and schismatics, yes even obstinate transgressors of the divine commandments, with titles suited to them, provided private hatred be absent, but on the contrary unless they call a spade a spade, they sin.

Or συνεδρ must be understood supplied, or the phrase has been changed by means of the letter ל,, which now stands for the article of the dative case, now for the preposition εἰς. τῆ κρίσει τοὐ θεοῦ, ὁ μωνυμίᾳ

(Concerning the word ἔνοχος let it be noted that wherever something is added to it in construction, that addition either expresses the kind of punishment, as here at Conf. Deut. 19, 6.Mark. 3, 29.ch. 14, 64., or that thing whose violation brings obligation upon penalty, as Exod. 22, 2.Num. 30, 5.Deut. 21, 1.ch. 19, 10.Jas. 2, 10. The use of this rule is against the Calvinians concerning the explanation of the passage 1. Cor. 11, 27.)

At Jos. 15. v. 8.Isaiah 30. v. 33.Jeremiah 7. v. 31. mention is made of the valley of Ben Hinnom or of the sons of Hinnom, about which Luther in the marginal notes on Jeremiah 7. writes thus: Ge Ben Hinnom, according to Jerome, is a most abominable valley, near the city of Jerusalem. Lyra in his commentary. Luke 23. relates that in this valley the Israelites sacrificed their children to the idol Moloch (which was a bronze image, hollow within so that it could be filled with burning coals), into whose arms they laid the wretched children to be horribly burned; meanwhile the priests had trumpets and drums sounded, lest they hear the cries and wailings of their own children. From this detestable fire of the idol Moloch the word Gehenna began to be used for the place in which the impious are tormented by the eternal flames of hell. But the name of the said place was transferred to designate hell, both on account of the dire savagery with which the worshippers of Moloch were accustomed there to burn up their children as burnt offerings , Jeremiah 7. v. 31. then because of the foul and abominable filthiness of the place which had formerly been most pleasant and delightful. For lest anyone should any longer sacrifice his son or his daughter there by fire, God indeed contaminated the place with the corpses of a great multitude of those slain there, Jeremiah 7. v. 32 and chap. 19. v 6. but Josiah, the pious King, made it filthy and abominable with the bones of dead men, the carcasses of beasts, dung and filth, which he ordered to be brought thither from the neighboring city Jerusalem. 2 Kings 23 v 10.

In the books of the Hebrews we find the fire of its gehenna It is therefore said, as it were by hypallage, gehēna of fire for fire of gehenna, by the idiom of the language. *(The Arab expresses this clearly) * just as greenness of the Hebrew for Hebrew of greenness. *(See similar examples in the Scriptures, Ps. 145, 5.Matt. 24, 15.Ephesians 1, 18.Colossians 1, 27.2 Thess. 1, 8. Moreover, concerning the word Gehenna and the valley of Hinnom one may consult B. D. Glassius, Sacred Philology, p. 878. B. D. Chemnitzius on the Harmony of the Evangelists p. 442. 667. 1001. 1002 Mr. Dilherr, Eclogues, Syriac, p. 126. 127. B. D. Quistorpius on 2 Kings 23, 23. B. D. Calixtus, Harmony of the Evangelists, p 131. B Par., Book on hell § 8. p. 184 Harmony of the Ev. p. 596. 1998. Drusius on the Hebrew Words of the New Testament. Cornelius à Lapide, Salmerón, Jansenius, Francis Lucas, Hugo Grotius and others, Commentaries on this passage. Cornelius à Lapide on Jer. 7, 31. Selden, Syntagma 1, On the Syrian Gods, ch. 6. Hornbeck, book 8, In Refutation of the Jews, ch. 7. p. 570. Buxtorf, Chaldean, Talmudic, Rabbinical Lexicon p. 395. -96. likewise in the Hebrew Lexicon under the word ניא. Pasor, Lexicon of the New Testament p. 163 Schindler, Lexicon of the Polyglot, root נוא p. 286. Matthew, Etymological Lexicon. Samuel Petit, book 1, Various Readings, ch. 5. p. 25 26. The Eastern interpreters retain the word Gehenna, for the Syriac translates the Arabic the Ethiopic )*

Beza warns in his annotations, three degrees are here established by Christ among those who, contrary to human opinion, are held to be murderers before God. One degree belongs to those who are moved against their neighbor inwardly only, whom Tertullian in the book On Patience calls the anger of a restrained mind; another belongs to those who boil up so far as to vomit forth some angry utterance. Finally, the third belongs to those who break out into open reviling. But from the word raca added to the second degree, and from the noticeably added verb whoever shall say it is gathered that Christ is marking not an unformed sound, but articulate speech: and from the diversity of punishment attached it is evident that Christ advances from lighter wrath to heavier.

But although Christ alludes to the civil judgments of the Jews, which were three, nevertheless he does not accommodate three kinds of sins to three distinct species of Jewish judgments and punishments—assigning the desire of harming to the punishment of the least judgment, light reviling to the punishment of the small one, and atrocious reviling to the punishment of the great judgment—but applies the first sin to the second judgment, the second sin to the third judgment, and the third sin to eternal damnation. For 1. the word judgment in verse 21 is not taken for the triumviral court, but for the lesser Sanhedrin or small court. For homicide was altogether a capital offense, yet concerning capital matters judgment was not rendered in the triumviral court. *(See Samuel Petitus, l. 1. Var. Lect. c. 5. p. 23.)* 2. The aim of Christ is to exaggerate the severity of divine judgment against those desiring to harm and against revilers. For if he who says to his brother in anger Raca is liable to the fire of Gehenna, that is, fiery hell, how much more he who has cursed him and struck him without killing him? *(Whence also Blessed D. Glassius rightly admonishes, Rhet. S. p. 495: that Christ alludes to the form of civil courts among the Jews and to the punishments customarily inflicted by them on the guilty; but understands eternal punishments, and distinct degrees of these according to different degrees in sins. But that there will be degrees of infernal torments, will be shown below in the notes on Matt. 10, 15.)*

*(However, even though the Savior here threatens the fire of Gehenna, and therefore eternal punishments, to transgressors of the divine law, it still does not follow from this that threats and terrors are contained in the Gospel properly so called, or that consequently the definition of the Gospel must be corrected, while it is defined that it is the joyful and consoling word: just as indeed Bellarmine decides in book 4, De Justificatione, chapter 2, writing: It is better to correct that definition—that the Gospel is the joyful and consoling word—than to say that the greatest part of the Sermon is not the words of Christ but of Moses, and that Christ preaches nothing in the Gospel but threats. Answer: 1. Since the Gospel nourishes carnal security without the Law, just as the Law makes either hypocrites or despairers without the Gospel—and medicine is greatly sought only when the disease is known—for this reason Christ placed the doctrine of the Law before the doctrine of the Gospel, and then also so that he might free himself from that unproven accusation, namely that he would entirely annul and abolish the moral Law. Above all, however, the Savior delivered the doctrine of the Law whenever he had to deal either with the secure or with those bewitched by persuasion of their own righteousness, showing the imperfection of our righteousness and declaring the wrath of GOD against transgressors of the Law. But where hearts had been softened by the hammer of the Law, then at last he applied the sweet liquor of the Gospel. Therefore in no way should the doctrine of the Law and of the Gospel properly so called be confused, nor the definition of the Gospel changed, because Christ proposed both. But it is false that} The greatest part of the sermons of Christ are words of the law, it is said, that Christ in the Gospel preached nothing less than the Gospel. *(But the Papists furthermore deny that in all those threats there is a regard to eternal damnation, but rather that in this very saying of Christ is founded the distinction, that some sins are mortal, but some are by their nature venial, not a few think. Petrus Cotonus the Jesuit, Confessor to the King of the Gauls, Instit. Cathol. book 3, chapter 6, page 472, rhetorizes thus: That every fault is indeed mortal by itself, but is considered venial solely by the mercy of GOD, the masters of the new doctrine, the architects of the new Church, claim, and with a specious covering, as it seems to them, they suppress the truth. And a little later: But could it happen that he who is our Advocate and at the same time judge, Father and at the same time brother, Leader and Master, actor and at the same time witness, would have passed over in silence this distinction (between mortal sin and that which is venial by nature) in which the glory of the supreme divinity is at stake? By no means, it would have been fitting to state it explicitly, if it is true that punishment and fault refer mutually to one another: for chapter 5 of St. Matthew we read that a movement of anger sometimes makes a man liable to judgment, sometimes to the council, (or council) at other times even, to speak with the scripture, to hell: where it shines clearer than the sun that not the same punishment is established by divine judgment for every crime. Agreeing with Cotonus are his associates Becanus, part 2, Theol. Scholast. treatise 2, chapter 2, question 1, page 136, and Adamus Conzen in this place, question 1, page 88. The same teaches from Corn. à Lapide in this place, page 135, and brings into this matter also Caietanus in the summary under the word Ira and Toletus, Instruct. Sacerd. book 7, chapter 57. Add also Bellarm. volume 4, book 1, Amiss. grat. chapters 9, 12, 13.

Resp. 1. The Lutherans, whom Cotonus reviles, do not abolish the distinction between mortal and venial sins. 2. Nor do our churches teach that all sins are equal, which Edmund Campianus, in his 8th reason, attributes to us through calumny , and thus compares us with Jovinian , from which crime, however, Bellarmine himself absolves us in book 3 de Iustific. chapter 16, § 1. 3. Nor does this follow from the fact that we say all sins are by their nature mortal: for one sin, even a mortal one, can be graver than another, and thus also be punished more gravely and more bitterly than another, which Azorius also long ago noted in volume 1, book 4, Instit. chapter 9, article 5. 4. And hence also against the Photinians we establish that there are degrees in the very infernal punishments, following Holy Scripture, see. Matt. 10, 15. ch. 11, 21. Luke 12, 47. 48. Rom. 2, 9. &c., and to these degrees also of infernal torments the Savior looks here; but he teaches this not, that certain sins by their own nature are sixfold venial. But the degrees of infernal torments can, just as the inequality of sinners, very well coexist with our hypothesis, that all sins committed against the law of GOD are mortal sins of themselves, i.e. that through them man becomes guilty of eternal damnation, unless forgiveness comes about through Christ. 5. Nor is this argument firm: Christ adjudges to hell the punishment of Gehenna, i.e. of the underworld, for the third sin, while exempting the first and second from it, or teaching that they do not deserve it, although as regards diversity of degrees it is not so severe as the third. For it must be noted that Gehenna of fire signifies here not simply infernal punishment, but joined with greater and more atrocious torment: just as the Council likewise decreed capital punishments, but the Sanhedrin graver ones, namely burning. Hence the Ordinary Gloss rightly on this passage: By these three, judgment, council, Gehenna, the universal mansions in eternal damnation are significantly expressed according to the measure of the sin. Hugh of St. Cher the Cardinal assents; for thus says he: Note that judgment, council, Gehenna signify infernal punishment. But because the quality of the punishment varies according to the quality of the fault, God wished by variety of names to signify variety of punishment. Nor do Francis Suarez and Sebastian Barradius dissent, both Jesuits. 6. That however even sins of the former kind merit eternal punishment, and therefore are mortal sins of themselves, is plain, because anger is reckoned by the Apostle among the works of the flesh, Gal. 5, 19. 20. and John expressly testifies concerning the angry man that he has not life remaining in him, for the reason that he is a murderer; now every murderer has not eternal life remaining in him, 1. Epistle 3, 14, 15. Indeed Cornelius à Lapide distinguishes here between anger, if one wish serious evil to his neighbor, and that which desires slight evil against his neighbor; he grants that the former is a mortal sin, but denies it of the latter. Yet Christ acknowledges here no distinction as regards unlawful i.e. rash anger, such that one should be a mortal sin by its nature and another not, nor indeed do the Apostles make the said distinction. Wherefore since the law makes no distinction, neither is it ours to invent one. 7. Therefore the Jesuit Tirinus rightly on this passage He uses, he says, will go, Christ, to declare the gravity of wrath and punishment, employs a threefold kind of penalty by means of a metaphor familiar and known to the Jews, punishments customarily inflicted upon offenders among them. And after recounting those kinds he adds: But hellish torments exceed all measure of human punishments. If he who wrongs his neighbor merely with insulting words shall be compelled to undergo them, what punishments await the murderer, who out of anger or hatred sheds blood in act?

Moreover, from the same false hypothesis—that Christ does not here adjudge eternal punishment to the first and second sin, but at least a temporal penalty—there has also flowed another perversion of the present dictum by the Papists, while indeed some, such as Bellarmine (t. 1. Controv. l. 1. de Purg. c. 8. col. 733 & 734), Maldonatus (t. 2. de Sacr. p. 144), and Schoppius (in Apolog. c. 58. f. 82. b. [It is to be observed, however, that very many Papists, striving to establish purgatory *ex professo* and otherwise bringing forward other passages of Holy Scripture, omit this place, as can be seen from Petrus Cotonus, Julius Caesar Coturius, Pistorius, Becanus, and others, since they perhaps themselves detected the nullity of the consequence]) maintain: While Christ threatens judgment and the Council for the first and second sin, and these [terms] can judge of nothing but a temporal penalty, it follows that after this life there are also temporal punishments, namely purgatory, in which he who dies suddenly or while sleeping is compelled to sustain those punishments defined and imposed by the judgment and the council, so that he has no space for repentance.

Truly Answer 1. Before all things it must be known that Christ expresses or declares the gravity of divine judgment against sins by a metaphor drawn from the judgments of the Hebrews, which the Jesuit Tirinus himself grants. 2. Therefore by those words judgment, council and Gehenna are signified not human or temporal but divine and eternal punishments, which Christ here indicates await all transgressors of the fifth commandment, unless forgiveness has been made. And this very thing Cardinal Hugh of St. Cher and the Jesuit Barradius freely grant, indeed even

the Jesuit Francis Suarez, vol. 4 on Thomas, disputation 45, p. 557, confesses, that this passage does not pertain to the controversy concerning Purgatory, since it is highly probable that all those members, of judgment, of the council, of hell, signify eternal damnation and greater and lesser punishment according to the quality of the offenses. Alphonsus Salmeron also, one of the first of the Jesuit order, vol. 5, tract 35, p. 201, writes thus on this passage: When it is said of him, he writes, who is angry with his brother, He shall be in danger of the judgment, the word judgment is taken metaphorically for eternal punishment, by a certain proportion owed to the anger of the mind. This exposition is confirmed by Salmeron himself by the authority of Irenaeus, book 2, chapter 57, saying: Not only he who kills shall be guilty of killing unto damnation, but also he who is angry with his brother without cause. Indeed, other Fathers can be added to Irenaeus. Zacharias Chrysopolitanus: Different mansions in eternal damnation are expressed according to the measure of the sin. Isidore, book 4, epistle 204: He wishes us to be pure not only from slaughter, but also from anger, etc. And to those who do not obey, he has threatened πὀρ ἄσβεςον an unquenchable fire. 3. For that he who is angry or hates his brother incurs divine judgment and eternal punishment was shown a little before from Gal. 5, 19. 20. and 1. Ioh. 3, 14. 15. 4. Christ himself, verse 25, 26, teaches what he wishes to be understood in this passage by the name of judgment. Cf. Luc. 12, 28. 5. And this is also sufficiently manifest from the general clause annexed to the Decalogue Deut. 27, 26. add. Gal. 3, 10. 6. What is more, if by the name of judgment only human punishment were understood, it would follow that even a murderer would not deserve eternal punishment, or if he did, at most not unless he performs penance. The reason for the consequence shines forth from verse 21. Bellarmine indeed says: The old law threatens murderers with no other death than temporal, that this is evident, he writes, from Exod. 21. But does that curse pressing upon everyone, even in the O.T., who does not continue in the words of the law, unless, namely, remission has been made, comprehend and threaten at least temporal punishments, but not at the same time eternal death? Nay rather, especially eternal death, as is clear from the opposite blessing, which primarily includes eternal salvation. Although some Photinians and Papists bitterly deny this, it has nevertheless been sufficiently proven by our own people. See, if you please, Mr. D. Calov, Prostration of Socinianism, p. 274. Mr. D. Feuerborn, Anti-Oster, p. 326. Mr. Pareus, L. on eternal life, §. 30. item, Commentary on Deut. p. 528. Academic Disputations p. 626. 1137. Mr. D. Chemnitz, part 2, Loci Theologici, p. 24. Mr. D. Gerlach, Disputation 13, §. 16. seqq. But this is especially clearly evident from the comparison. Levit. 19, 18. with Luc. 10, 25. seqq. Nor does the passage Exod. 21. prove anything else. For it distinguishes between civil punishment and divine malediction. Of the latter it treats in Deut. 27, 27., of the former in Exod 21, 1415.; nor is the statement of the one the exclusion of the other. Nor does it follow that he who is absolved from capital civil punishment is also absolved from the malediction of the law; as is evident from the comparison of the present passage with Exod 21, 19.21., and is well noted by B. D. Rungius, Comm. in Exod. p. 829. Moreover, for more arguments against the error of the Papists, that certain sins are by their nature venial in themselves, consult B. D. R-nig Vindic. Sacr. L. 23. §. 5. seqq.; B. D. Hutterus, LL. Th. p. 352. seqq.; B. Par. L. de it. in Vindic. t. 2. p. 615. Pecc. § 93. seqq.; others. Add from Calvin, Crocius, in Anti Bec. t. 2. p. 671. 672.; Chamier, t. 3. Panstr. l. 6. c. 9. seqq. But against those who labor to elicit purgatory's fire now from the present passage, now from other places of Scripture, let there be brought out B. D. Balduinus, Disp. 7. ad Artic. Smale.; B. D. Mentzer, Anti Pist. L. 12.; B. D. R-nig l. c.; B. Par. L. de Morte §. 270. seqq.; Confess. Cath. t. 3.; B. D. Meisner, Disp. 9. Ἀνθρωπολ. Sacrae q. 2. th. 12. seqq.; Opuse. 2. Indulg. Pap. oppos. p. 327. seqq.; B. D. Gerlach, t. 2. Disp. D. ult.; Dn. D. Hüls. Man. A. C. Especially B. D. Chemnitz, Part. 3. & 4. Exam. Concilii Trident. To the Calvinians may be added Daniel Chamier, t. 3. Panstr. 26. c. 6.)*.

Latin:

v. 22. Ἐγὼ δὲ Scopus est, quod Deus quam libet legis transgressionem iuxta meritum & magnitudinem delicti velit punire. Ego doctor vobis coelitus missus & voce Patris coelestis commendatus Matth. 3. v. ult. Propheta similis Mosi vobis à Deo suscitatus, Deut. 18 v. 18. Franc. Luc. Brug. ad h. l. rectè annotat. Non Mosi aut legi Christus se opponit, multò minùs legis autori, sed legis explanatoribus Scribis, non enim solùm dixerat dictum est antiquis, sed audistis, quia dictum est: in quam sententiam D. Thomas l. 2. q. 107. art. 2. dicit, quod praecepta ista. Non occides, & Non m--haberis, aliaSalvator impleverit, exprimendo verum legis intellectum, quem Scribae & Pharisaei non fuerint assecuti. Opponendum hoc Scholasticis & quibusdam recentioribus Pontificiis, qui ex h. l. evincere voluerunt, *(id quod etiam Corn. à Lapide hîc facit)* Christum perfectiora in N. T. tradidisse praecepta, quàm à Mose in V. T. fuerint proposita. *(Cumprimis autem Photiniani praesenti loco pro errore suo, quòd Christus novus legislator fuerit, palliando abutuntur, de quibus suprà.)*

Conformis autem nostra expositio est doctrinae Augustini, qui lib 19. contra Faustum cap. 23. sic scribit. Quia non intelligebant homicidium nisi peremtionē corporis humani, per quam vita privaretur, aperuit Dominus, omnem iniquum motum ad nocendum fratri in homicidugenere putari. Et quoniam putabant, tantummodò corporalem cum foemina illicitam commixtionem vocari moechiam, demonstravit Magister, etiam talem concupiscentiam nihil esse aliud. c. 38. Itaq; vel omnia vel penè omnia, quae monuit seu praecepit, ubi adiungebat: Ego autem dico vobis, inveniuntur & in illis veteribus libria. Ibi contra iram dictum est: Turbatus est praeira oculus meus; &: Melior est, qui vincit iram, quàm qui capit civitatem.

Porrò primum hoc v. 22. membrum Iustinus Martyr in Apolog. p. 49. edit. Commel. sic effert, ὃς αὒQui verò excanduerit, ad ignem condemnationi est obnoxius. Duplex variatio. 1. omittit voculam εἰκῇ, quae non extat in omnibus Codicibus 2. pro ἔνοχο *(Idem tamen Iustinus alibi, nempe epistolâ ad Zenam & Screnum, voculum εἰκῆ in Salvatotis sententia agnoscit. Dubitat quidem Bell. in de Script. Eccles. lib. uno pag. 48. num dicta epistola sit Iustini, fatetur tamen, Iustino autore eam esse dignam. Agnoscit eandem vocem & Irenaeus, quem Epiphanius haeres 42. τῶν Ἀποςόλων διάδοχον, Lindanus verò l. 4. Panopl. c. 22. 46. 82. antiquissimum Apostolicae fidei propugnatorem ac virum gravissimum insignit. Loca autem Irenaei sunt lib. 2. advers. Haeres. c. 56. it l. 4. c. 31. imò & Clemens Romanus l. 2. Apost. c 6. Cumprimis verò notandum quòd in Graecis Codd. MSS omnibus quorum sanè plurimos tum Patisienses, tum Franc. Lucas consuluerunt, suffragantibus tractatoribus Graecis & Syricis exemplaribus, vocula illa hodiè legatur, fatente Fr Lucâ excepto unico Codice Graeco Bibliothecae Vaticanae. Legit denique vocem εἰκῆ Isidorus quoque Pelusiora l 4 epist. 111.

Erasmus ab audaculo hanc vocemεἰκῆadiectam statuit. *(Adstipulatur Iesuita Conzenius, in h. l. scribens: facilè ex marginali glossa in textum irrepere potuisse. Franc. Lucas existimat, nullo modo Latmis addendam esse.)* Vulg, versio & Lutherus itidem non legunt particulam εἰκῆ. Hieronymus in h. l. & Dialog. 2. adversus Pelag. negat -n vetustis & probatae fidei exemplaribus eam reperiri. Aug. l. 1. retractat. cap. 19. Codices Graeci non habent sine causa, sicut hîc p-situm est. Contrà Chrysostomus homil. 16. in Matth. & L-urentius Valla voculam εἰκῆ omninò addendam censent. In Vitis Patrū praefectus Monasterii Scythi rogatus, quid esset illud Evangelii: Qui irascitur fratri sine causa, solam iustam inae causam d--nivit separationē à Deo, caeteris quamlibet magnis iniuriis acceptis, qui irascitur, eum sine causis irasci. Cum quo congruit illud, quòd vitio fratris, non fratri irascendum sit.

Syrus paraphrastes habet vocem *(Codex MS. Altd. habet quomodo etiam reliqui Codd. Phil. 2, 16. legunt, quo loco adhibetur pro Gr. εἰς κενὸν)* formatam ex voce εἰκῆ & ad linguam suam accommodatam.

*(Existimat Hugo Grotius, id factum esse à Syro propter vim vocisεἰκῆ,quam inquit, tam propriam atq; significantam hoc loco existimavit, ut retinere eam maluerit, quàm vertere. Ut ut verò nec Arabs editionis Romanae (nam in Leidensi editione expressè legitur i. e. frustrà, temere) nec Aethiops Interpp. particulam hanc agnoscant, minimè tamen cum Conizenio dicam statim scribendam existimaverim illis, qui hodiè versionibus suis inserunt. Urget quidem Iesuita, quòd nevetustiora, neq; meliora illi exemplaria habeant, quàm Hieronymus & Augustinus: Verùm ut ut fortè nihil pronunciari certi possit de Codd. Gr., quos Parisienses ac Robertus Stephanus contulerunt, annon quidam eorum Augustini ao Hieronymi aetatem attingant, vel etiam superent; iure sanè opponi Iesuitae Iustinus ac Irenaeus potest, Patres & Graeci & Hieronymo itemque Augustino multò antiquiores, qui utique vocem εἰκῆ h. l. agnoscunt. quin & Clemens, quem magni aliàs Pontificii aestimant. Ut ut igitur Hier. & Augustinus voculam hanc omittant, subintelligitur tamen eadē aut similis, fatente Contzenii socienno, Cornel. à Lapide in h. l. Taceo iam Interpretem Syrum, quem ipsum Marcum Evangelistam esse, Syri ex avitâ traditione affirmant, si fides quidem habenda Guilielmo Postello est, qui idipsum, quôd ex Syris audiverit, Guidoni Eabritio per litteras significavit. Ipse fanè Franc. Lucas, Scriptor Pontificius in his talibus satis versatus, indubitanter tenet, Syriacum N. T. textum vetustissimi exemplaris Graeci & quidem ex primis habendum ac venerandum esse. Caeterùm dicitur fieri εἰκῇ, quod fit sine divinâ ordinatione ac beneplacito, it. sine iustâ ac sufficienti causâ, ceu ex collatione Rom. 13, 4. patet. Talis verô ira, quae est absque iustâ h. e. in verbo DEI fundatâ causâ, sive quam non DEI gloria, honestas, necessitas & aequitas, sed privatae vindictae cupiditas ac levitas excitat, etiam in V. T. prohibita fuit, quemadmodum & fratris criminatio, prout ex Gen. 4, 6.Lev. 19, 16.Ps. 4, 5.Ps. 37, 7.Prov. 15, 18.c. 18, 8.c. 24, 20.c. 29, 22. &c. videre licet. Sed dicat aliquis, si vel maximè ira iniqua ac vituperatio in V. T. prohibita fuerūt, non tamen sub tali cōminatione, aeternae nempe damnationis, ut à Christo hîc prohibita illa fuerunt. Resp. utique. Quicquid enim in lege divinâ prohibitum fuit, illius transgressio, nisi remissio à Deo obtineatur, aeternam affert mortem, Deut. 27, 27. Id quod contra Photinianos probè notandum est. Caeterùm an & quomodo fas sii proximo irasci, prolixè atque eruditè docet B. D. Bald. Cas. Conscient. l. 4. cap. 17. cas. 6. Porrò de irâ moderandâ praeter doctissimos libb. Senecae de Ira, cumprimis legi Iustinus Martyr potest, vel quisquis etiam autor ille fit epistolae suprà allegatae ac Iustino adscriptae, ceu etiam scriptis eius inserta est. it. Basilius ac Chrysostomus homiliis de irâ, Greg. M. in Iobum c. 30. Plurimas verò Graecorum ac Latinorum sententias huc spectantes collegerunt Zwing in Theatro, Magirus in Polymn. Langius in Florilegio. Quibus Arabum adiungi adagia non inscita possunt, cuiusmodi sunt: Sex proprietatibus cognoscitur stullus. Quod absre irascatur Quod loquatur inutilia. Quod fidat cuilibet &c. item:

i. e. Initium iraefuror est, finis v. poenitentia. it. Ne te hominibus annumeres, quamdivirate superat. Sed omnium sapientum monitis meritò praeferenda divina oracula sunt, cumprimis Ps. 4, 5.Prov. 22, 5.Eccles. 7, 10.Gal. 5, 20.Eph. 4, 26.Col. 3, 7.Iac. 1, 19. 20.1. Ioh. 3, 15. &c. Add. quoque Aphor. Pract. B. Par. tit. de irâ. Quòd autem quaedam ira licita sit, testantur tum piorum in Sc. S. exempla, tum dicta clarissima. Vide Gen. 30, 2.Exod. 11, 8.c. 16, 20.c. 32, 19.Numer. 13, 14.c. 16, 15.c. 25, 7.2. Reg. 13, 9.Matth 3. 7.Luc. 24, 25.Gal. 3, 1.Ps. 101, 3.Ps. 119, 104.113.Ps. 139, 20. ceu haec & alia Sc. S. testimonia adducit B. Par. Scholae Pietatis lib. IV. c. 12. §. 4. Scitè Gregorius M. c. 30. Expos. Moral. in c. 5. Iol. Solerter sciendum est, quòd alia est ira, quam impatientia excitat, alia quam zelus iustitiae format. Illa ex vitio, haec ex virtute generatur. Si enim nulla ira ex virtute surgeret, divinae animadversionis impetum Phinees per gladium non placasset. Hanc iram quia Heli non habuit, motum contra se implacabiliter supernae ultionis excitavit. Nam quo contra subditorum vitia tepuit, eo contra illum districtio aeterni Rectoris exarsit. De hâc per Psalmistam dicitur: Irascimini, & nolite peccare. Si proximos ut nos amare praecipimur, restat, ut sic eorum erroribus, sicut nostris vitiis irascamur &c. Conferatur quoq; Chrysostomus in Ps. 4. urgens exemplum Pauli Act. 13, 8. & Petri Act. 5, 9. ubi inter alia: Ille est, scribit, qui temerè irascitur, qui seipsum ulciscitur: qui autem aliena corrigit, is est omnium mansuetissimus.)*

Ὃς αὒ Nomine ἀδελφῆ in hoc, ut & primo membro intelligitur in gene re proximus, qui iure Naturae noster frater est.

Vox Hebraea vel potiùs Syriaca significat vacuum seu inanem, & intelligitur per Synecdochen, vacuus cerebro seu iudicio. Syrus Rom. 1. v. 21. usurpat pro μάταιος. Reg. 4, 3. homines vani רקים dicuntur, quod Buxtorffio, Hug Grotio, Angelo Caninio aliisque arridet, & iam olim quoque ita Hesychio, Hilario, Hieronymo l. 2. contr. Pelagianos, & Auctori operis imperfecti in Matthaeū visum fuit, quòd scil. ῥακὰ significet hominem cerebro vacuum, iudicio carentem, sicut Germani etiam dicunt du thummer Hund/adhuc sub iudice lis est. Caeterùm plures opiniones recenset Cornelius à Lapide in h. l. ubi tamen suam in Arabicâ linguâ ignorantiam prodit, persuaderin. sibi à nescio quo, passus est, Arabem raca vertere pannosum, lacerum, mendicum, qui vestitus centone sive veste ex centum plagulis consarcinatâ. Certum potiùs est, Arabem ipsam vocem, quae in textu legitur, suae translationi inservisse. Quod vel Latina versionis Evangelistarum Arabicae interpretatio, quae Romae Anno 1591. prodiit, docere Iesuitam potuisset. Idem verò & de Aethiopico Interprete (quem h. l. ita vertere, Cornelius prodit: Qui dixerit fratri suo, quòd pauper sit per contemtum & laceris vestibus, reus erit Concilio) adserendum videtur. Licet enim hic ita hoc loco habeat: i. e. & qui dixerit fratri suoreus est Concilio. attamen cùm apud Aethiopes radix vix occurrat, quemadmodum nec apud Ebraeos, Chaldaeos, Syros ac Arabes talem invenire licet, perquam verisimile est, errato typographico (cuiusmodi Aethiopicum N. T. Romae excusum scater, ceu pridem etiam Lud. de Dieu Anim. ad Act. Apost. p. 26. notavit,) legi ibi pro vel At palliari fortè Cornelii expositio potest, si pariter erratum typographicum in dicta editione Aethiopicâ statuatur, sed ita emendandum cùm facilis lapsus à ad descendit verò à radice isthac nomen respondens Ebr. ןויבאPs. 12, 6. Sed cùm omnes penè interpp. vocem Raka hîc retineant, & Aethiops quoque N T. Si tamen omninò hominem malè vestitum notat, videtur Aethiopis versio niti eo fundamento, quòd Graecis in more positum, hominem nihili vocare ῥάκος, à veste detrita, quae Graecis ita dicitur, sumto convicio, notante Augustino super h. l Scribit porrò Corn. à Lapide, ineptè Bezam hic censere, Christum pro Raca dixisseרשעi. e. impie. Sed fateor, me nihil tale apud Bezam, in edit. quidē quartâ, quae diligenter ab eo recognita An. 1588. lucem adspexit, invenire potuisse. Si in prioribus editionibus Beza ita sentit, ipse opinionem suam correxit. Scribit autem Beza onnullos putare, Nomen Raca deductum videri posse à themate Syroרה(Rach.) quod spuere declarat. Caeterùm sicuti Beza paullò ante notavit, perperam in Vulg. editione Lat. legi racha, ita omninò hîc ipse corrigendus est: neque enim Syris רה tach, sed רה Rak spuere significat: nec Drusius quoque, quem pro se Beza laudat ita scribit. Sed iterùm corrigendus lapsus Corneli, quando mox subdit, à Graeco συνεδρίῳ Ebraeos suum concilium vocasse sanedr-m Verùm Ebraei non םנהרוים dicunt, sed םנהרוין qui lapsus ut ut leviculus sit, notare tamen in supercilioso Iesuita illum placuit, cùm non semel, sed aliquoties tum hîc, tum Comm. ad Deut. 17, 9. Cornelius d. m. scribat, eundemque errorem erret quoque Cornelii epitomator Iesuita Tirinus. Sed solenne Iesuitis est, ist haec talia non multum curare, unde eidem Tirino non insolens est Targhum alleganti dicere in Thargo; sic Iesuitae Salmeron ac Conzen dicunt, apud Syrum esse -ka, cùm tamen expressè Syrus habeat iki quomodo etiam adiectis punctis vocalibus legit Cod. MS. Alt. Sed missa haec facio, utpote ab h. l aliena.)*

Basilius in μωρὲ Hieronymus lib. 2. advers. Pelag. & in Matth. ῥακὰ dicitur κενὸς,id est inanis & vacuus, quem nos ---iniurí absq; cerebro dicere possumus. Hesychius ῥακὰ κενὸς Hilarius in Matth. Raca vacuitatis oppro-rium est. Autor operis impers. in Matth Raca quidem ---Hebraicè vacuus, quamvis quantum ad sensum verbi unum est, --fatue, & raca. Nam qui fatuus est, ille vacuus est, & qui vacuus, ille est fatuus, & utriusq;

verbi una videtur esse iniuria. Et postea Raca vulgare verbum erat apud Iudaeos, quod non ex ira, neq; ex odio, sed aliquo motu variè dicebant, magis fiduciae causâ, quàm iracundiae.

Chrysostomus homil. 16. in Matth. tradit, raca non esse vocem gravioris aut atrocioris convitii, sed ab impatientia stom achoq; loquē tis proficisci, quomodo servis stomachosiùs loquentes dicimus. Abi tu. Adducit testimonium linguae Syriacae, in quâ racha ponitur pro eo, quod est tu. Theophylactus dicit, ῥακὰesse vocabulum Syriacum, & significare hominemκαταπτυςὸνnihili, futilem ac conspuendum, (quâ ratione deduceretur à verbo רקק quod spuere significat. Syriacum Raka itidem nonnullis deduci videtur à רקק deficiente verbo in secunda, quod cum Hebraeo & Chaldaeo commune habet, unde Hebraeis ab hac radice est nomen רק & Chaldaeis רוקא quod sputum significat. Raca igitur significaret hominem conspuendum, qui indignus sit, cuiusenomen honestè exprimatur, ad cuius tiam vel nominis mentionem expuatur. Sed hac ratione ῥακὰ foret gravius convitium, quàm μωρὲ, quod non congruit Christi scopo.

Erasmus in annot. existimat, raca esse vocem indignantis velut interiectionem, cùm alioqui nulla relinquatur differentia inter raca & fatuum, id quod hausit ex Augustino, qui addit, se à Iudaeo quodam id accepisse. Angelus Caninius in disq. locor. N. T. In Massecheth Berachot saepius legiturרוקהEst autem convictum non acre, sed familiare, ut cùm maior minorem pro autoritate familiariter obiurgat. Indignationis levitas non potest Graeca voce exprimi, ideò vox Raca retenta est.

Quidam tamen non Hebraeam, nec Syram, sed Graecam vocem esse statuunt. Graeci enim hominem nihili vocantῥάκος,à veste detrita reiiculasumto convitio, ut indicat Augustinus super h. l.

Franc. Lucas Brug. inter ῥακὰ & μωρὲ hocce statuit discrimen, quod per vocem ῥακὰexprobretur fratri vitium aliquod aut Naturae aut fortunae; per vocemμωρὲfratris scelus ac impietas notetur.

πὀρ

Μωρὸς proprie significat insipidum. Sic appellatur stultus per metaphoram, quòd sit quasi insipidus h. e. minimè suavis & gratus homini sapienti. Syrus reddidir per quod formatum ab Hebr. אליל, denotatur ergò gravius convitium quàm est ῥακὰ.

Quia in Scripturis Sacris, praesertim in Proverbiis Salomonis stulti vocantur homines impii, carentes Dei timore, qui est initium sapientiae, ideô quidam censent, hanc Christi sententiam adversus eum feri, qui sratri suo contumeliam dicit criminis mortiferi; cuius ira eò usque progreditur, ut fratrem suum alicuius sceleris aut impietatis notet. (Adeoque perinde sit, ac si nominet ἄθεον, Germanicè ein Ieuffels. Rind. ita statuit Dn. Dilherrus Elect. l. 2. c. 20. p. 299. Quòd verò Scripturae S. non insolens sit, idololatriam stultitiae nomine insignire, ex Deut. 32, 6.Rom. 10, 19.Psal. 73, 18.Iob. 1, 10. ostendit Pineda t. 1. in Iob. p. 159. Idem etiam sentit Casp. Barth. l. 5. Adv. c. 14)*

*(Observant D. Frantz. de Interp. Sc. S. Orac. 129. ac D. Glassius Rhet. S. p. 452. phrasi illâ, dicere fratri suo Raca, & stultum eum vocare,συιεκδοχικῶς omnis generis indicia malevoli ac irati animi & calumnias intelligi. Sic quoque irae nomine comprehendit Salvator omnes interiores motus in mente, voluntate & corde, non congruentes cum normâ quinti praecepti.)*

*(Probè autem hîc observandum, prohiberi hîc convitium, quod ex odio personae profectum & animi irati signum est, non verò severas quasdam Dd. Ecclesiae increpationes, ex verò zelo profectas. Aliud est dicere verbum contumeliosum ad infamiam & confusionem; aliud durioribus verbis uti, zelo religionis & fidei ad correctionem. Aliud enim est convitium; aliud fidelis Doctoris officium. ad hoc referenda dicta Luc. 24, 25.Gal. 3, 1. illud verò hîc prohibitum. Et res quoque clara est. Si enim caedere iustâ de causâ parentibus & Magistratui concessum est, & absque ullo peccato fieri potest, imò Magistratui divinitùs gladius traditus, ut acuat contra sonres: quantò magis concessum est & abs ullo peccato fieri potest, ut duris verbis adversus nocentes utatur, cuius officium id requirit. Sic legimus, non solùm Christum, sed & Apostolos, quemadmodum & Ioh. Bapt. duris admodùm verbis (& extra certum casum s. si temerè proferantur, prohibitis) usos quandoque fuisse, ceu ex Luc. 24, 25.Matt. 23. 17.33.c. 3, 7.Act. 13. 10. &c patet, absque ullo tamen peccato. Nec dubitare licet, quin adhuc hodie Dd. & Mini---is Ecclesiae idem concessum sit, si nempe iustas indignationis h. e.

exigente id glorià DEI, habuerint causas. Idem namque & primitivae Ecclesiae Doctores, licet alioquin mansuetudinis laude insignes, fecerunt, Decet sanè fidelem DEI servum quàm maximè, ut cùm de DEI honore agitur vel quando veritatis coelestis ratio exigit, ut adversus impios ac haeretieos valentiorem sese praebeat leone, contrà verò in privatis malis & adversitatibus sustinendis mitior agno sit, ac, quod de Salvatore nostro propheta dicit, coram tondente obmutescat. Quemadmodum itaque non solùm non peccant, qui cum causâ irascuntur, sed è contrà nisi irati fuerint, peccant, monente Chrysostomo hom. 11. in Matth. sic non solûm non peccant Ecclesiae Ministri, qui haereticos ac schismaticos, quin & pertinaces divinorum mandatorum transgressores titulis, illis convenientibus insigniunt, modò privatum absit odiū, sed ècontra nisi scapsam vocent, peccant.

*(De voce ἔνοχος notandum, quòd ubi illi aliquid in constructione additur, illud vel genus supplicii exprimat, ut h. l. Conf. Deut. 19, 6.Marc. 3, 29.c. 14, 64. vel rem illam, cuius violatione obligatio ad poenam contrahatur, uti Exod. 22, 2.Num. 30, 5.Deut. 21, 1.c. 19, 10.Iac. 2, 10. Cuius reg. usus est contra Calvinianos circa explicationem loci 1. Cor. 11, 27.)*

Ios. 15. v. 8.Esai. 30. v. 33.Ierem. 7. v. 31. mentio fit vallis Ben Hinnom sive filiorum Hinnom, de quo Luth. in not. marginalib. Ierem. 7. sic scribit: Ge Ben Hinnom, referente Hieronymo, fisit amanissima vallis, urbi Hierosolymae propinqua. Lyranus in comm.Luc. 23.refert, quòd in hac valle Israelitae liberos suos immolârint idolo Moloch (quod erat imago aenea, intus vacuut prunis ardentibus impleri posset) in cuius brachia deposuerunt liberos miseros miserè comburendes; interim Sacerdotes buccinas & tympana sonare facieban, ne paerentes clamores & eiulatus liberorum suorum audirent. Ab hoc execrando igne idoli Moloch vocabulum gehennae usurpati caepit pro loco, in quo impii aeternis inferorum flammis cruciantur. Translatum verò nomen dicti loci ad infernum designandum, tum ob diram immanitatem, quâ cultores Moloch illic liberos suos in holocausta adolere solebant, Ierem. 7. v. 31. tum ob foedidam atabominabilem loci spurcitiem qui aliquando amoenissimus ac deliciosissimus suerat. Ne quis enim ampliùs filium suum aut filiam suam per ignem ibi sacrificaret, Deus quidem occisorum illic magnâ multitudine cadaveribus locum contaminavit, Ierem. 7. v. 32 & cap. 19. v 6. Iosias verò pius Rex mortuorum hominum ossibus, iumētorum cadavenbus, excrementis & sordibus, quas è vicina Hieros urbe eò deferri iussit, spurcum & abominandum reddidit. 2. Reg 23 v 10.

Lucas, Hugo Grotius ac alii Comment. ad h. l. Corn. à Lapide Ier. 7, 31. Seldenus Synt. 1. de Diis Syr. c. 6. Hornbeck l. 8. pro Convinc. Ivaeis c. 7. p. 570. Buxtorff. Lex. Chald. Talm Rabb p. 395. -96. it. in. Lex. Ebr. voce ניא. Pasor Lex. N. T. p. 163 Schindl. Lex. Pentagl rad. נוא p. 286. Matth. Lexico Etymol. Samuel Petitus l. 1 Var. Lect. c. 5. p. 25 26. Orientales Interpp. vocem Gehennae retinent, Syrus enim vertit Arabe Aethiops )*

Beza in annot. monet, tres hîc à Christo constitui gradus eorum, qui contra hominum opinionem pro homicidis apud Deum habentur. Unum graedum esse eorum, qui intus duntaxat aedversus proximum commoventur, quam Tertull. lib. de paetient. vocat iram restricti animi, A'terum eorum, qui eò usq; effervescunt, ut iracundum aliquod evomant. Tertium deniq; eorum, qui in apertum aliquod convitium erumpunt. Sed ex voce raca addita secundo gradui, & ex verbo dixeric notanter addito colligitur, Christum non notare vocem inconditam, sed articulatam: & ex annexa poenae diversitate constat, Christum ab ira leviori ad graviorem progredi.

Quamvis verò Christus alludat ad iudicia civilia Iudaeorum, quae tria erant, non tamen tria peccatorum genera tribus distinctis iudiciorum & poenarum Iudaicarum speciebus accommodat, affectum nocendi poenae iudicii minimi, leve convitium poenae parvi, atrocique convitium poenae iudicii magni, sed peccatum primum iudicio secundo, peccatum secundum iudicio tertio, tertium peccatum aeternae damnationi applicat. Nam 1 vox iudicii v. 21. non sumitur pro iudicio triumvirali, sed pro Synedrio minori sive iudicio parvo. Hommicidium enim omninò delictum erat capitale, de capitalibus verò in triumvirali iudicio nō cognoscebatur. *(Vid. Samuel. Petitum. l. 1. Var. Lect. c. 5. p. 23.)* 2. Scopus Christi est exaggerare severitatem iudicii divini adversus cupiditatè nocendi & convitiatores. Quod si enim reus est gehennae ignis sive igneae, qui iratus fratri dixerit satue, quantò magis is, qui ei malè precatus fuerit ac citra caedem eum percusserit? *(Unde etiam benè monet B. D. Glassius Rhet. S. p. 495. Christum alludere ad formam civilium Iudiciorum apud Iudaeos & ad poenas sontibus irrogari ab iis solitas; intelligere autem poenas aeternas, & distinctos horum gradus ratione diversorum in peccatis graduum. Quòd verò gradus supplieiorum infernalium futuri sint, infrá in notis ad Matth. 10, 15. ostendetur)*

*(Ut ut verò Salvator ignem gehennae, adeoque aeternas peenas legis divinae transgressoribus h. l. comminetur, non tamen sequitur inde, quòd in Evangelio propriè dicto contineantur comminationes ac terrores, vel quòd proptereà corrigenda sit definitio Evangelii, dum definitur, quòd sit verbum laetum & consolatorium: ut quidem Bellarminus lib. 4. de Iustif. c. 2. statuit, scribens, satiùs esse corrigere definitionem illam, quòd Evangelium sit verbum laetum & consolatorium, quàm dicere, maximam partem sermonem Christi non esse verba Christi, sed Mosis, & Christum in Evangelio nihil minàs quàm Evangeliū praedicare. Resp. 1. Cùm Evangelium sine lege securiatem alat carnalem, quemadmodum lex sine Evangelium vel hypocritas vel desperabūdos facit,) nec nisi morbo cognito Medicina magnopere quaeratur, inde Christus doctrinae Evangelii praemisit legis doctinnam, tum etiam, quò sese liberaret ab intentato isto crimine, quasi legem moralem totam annihilaret ac tolleret. Cumprimis verò legis doctrinam Salvator tradidit, iustitiae nostrae imperfectionem ostendit, iramque DEI adversus legis transgressores declaravit, quoties vel cum securis vel cū illis, qui iustitiae propriae persuasione fascinati erant, negotium ipsi fuit. Ubi verô pectora malleo legis fuerunt emollita, tunc utique gratum Evangelii liquorem assudit. Nequaquam igitur doctrina legis & Evangelii propriè sic dicti confundenda, vel definitio Evangelii mutanda, eò quòd Christus utrumque proposuit. Falsum verô est, quòd maxima pars sermonum Christi sint verba legis, it, quòd Christus in Evangelio nil minùs quàm Evangeliū praedicarit.)* *(Sed negant porrò Pontificii, in omnib. istis comminationibus respici ad aeternam damnationem, quin potiùs in hoc ipso Christi dicto fundari distinctionem, quòd quaedam pecca: a sint mortalia, quaedam verò naturâs. ex se venialia, non pauci existimant. Petrus Cotonus Iesuita, Galliarum Regi à Confessionibus, Instit. Cathol. l. 3. c. 6. p. 472. sic rhetoricatur: Omnem culpam ex se quidem esse mortalem, solâ verò DEI misericordiâ venialem censeri, musteinovae doctrinae Magistri, novae Ecclesiae architecti ferunt, & specioso, ut illis quidem videtur, involucro veritatem opprimunt. ac paullô pòst: Sed fierine posset, ut qui noster Advocatus simul est & iudex, Genitor unà frater-, Dux & Magister, actor unà testis-, hanc distinctionem (inter peccatum mortale & naturâ veniale) silentio praetermisisset, in quâ de gloria supremi numinis ageretur? minimè verò, decuit id disertè, si verum est, poenam & culpam mutuo ad sese referri: nam c. 5. D. Matihaei legimus, iracundiae motum efficere nonnunquam hominem reum iudicii, aliquando consilii, (l. concilii) alias etiam, ut cum scripturâ loquar, gehennae: ubi sole clarius lucet, non omni sceleri candem esse poenam divino iudicio constitutam. Adstipulantur Catoni socienni Becanus part. 2. Theol. Scholast. tr. 2. c. 2. q. 1. p. 136. & Adamus Conzen in h. l. q. 1 p. 88. Idem è Corn. à Lapide in h. l. p. 135. docet, adducitque in hanc rem Caietanum quoque in summula verbo Ira ac Toletum Instruct. Sacerd. l. 7. c. 57. Add. quoque Bellarm. t. 4. l. 1. Amiss. grat. c. 9. 12. 13.

Resp. 1. Distinctionem inter peccata mortalia ac unialia Lutherani, quos Cotonus sugillat, non tollunt. 2. nec omnia etiam peccata paria esse, Ecclesiae nostrae docent, quod per calumniam Edmundus Campianus rat, 8. attribuit, adeoq cum Ioviniano nos confert, à quô tamen crimine ipse Bell. nos absolvit l. 3. de Iustific. c. 16. §. 1. 3. nec sequitur etiam hoc ex eo, quòd omnia peccata naturâ suâ mortalia esse dicimus: potest enim unum peccatum, etiam mortale, gravius esse altero, adeoque & graviùs acerbiùsque, quàm alterum puniri, quod pridem etiam Azorius t 1. lib. 4. Instit. c. 9. art. 5. notavit. 4. Atque hinc etiam contra Photinianos in ipsis infernalibus suppliciis gradus esse, statuimus, praeviâ Sc. Sacrâ, Vid. Matth. 10, 15.c 11, 21.Luc. 12, 47. 48.Rom. 2, 9. &c. & ad istos quoque gradus suppliciorum infernalium respicit hîc Salvator: non verò hoc docet, quòd quaedam peccata naturâ suâ sex se sint venialia. Possunt verò suppliciorum insernalium gradus, sicuti & poccatorum inaequalitas, optimè consistere cum hypothesi nostrâ quôd omnia peccata contra legem DEI commissa ex se sint mortalia peccata h. e. quòd per ea homo reus fiat aeternae damnationis, nisi per Christum fiat remissio. 5. Nec haec equela firma est: Christus tertio peccato adiudicat gehennae s. inferni supplicium E. primum & secundu ab isto eximit, vel non mereri illud, licet quoad graduum diversitatem non tam grave ac tertium, docet. Notandum enim, Gehenuam ignis non notare hîc poenam infernalem simpliciter, sed cum maiore & atrociore cruciatu coniunctam: sicuti Concilium itidem capitales poenas decernebat, at Synedrion graviores, nempe combustionem. Unde Glossa Ordin rectè in h. l. His tribus, iudicio, Concilio, Gehenna universae mansiones in aeterná daemnatione pro modo poeccati signanter exprimuntur. Adstipulatur Hugo de S. Charo Cardinalis: ita enim ille: Nota, quòd iudicium, Concilium, gehenna poenam significant infernalem. Sed quia secundùm qualitatem culpae variatur qualitas poenae, voluit Deus nominum varietate varietatem poenae significare. Nec dissentiunt Franc. Suarez ac Seb. Barradius, uterque Iesuita. 6. Quòd verò & prioris generis peccata aeternum supplicium mereantur, adeoque ex se mortalia peccata sint, patet, quia ira ab Apostolo Gal. 5, 19. 20.inter opera carnis refertur, & de irato expressè testatur Iohannes, quòd non habeat vitam inse manentem, eo quòd homicida est, omnis verò homic. non habet vitam aeternam in se manentem, 1. Epist. 3, 14, 15. Distinguit quidem hîc Corn. à Lapide inter iram, si optet grave malum proximo, & inter illam, quae leve malum proximo appetat; illam mortale peccatumesse, concedit, de hâc verò negat. Verùm nullam hîc Christus quoad iram illicitam s. temerariam agnoscit distinctionem, quod nempe alia naturâ suâ mortale peccatum sit, alia verò non, nec Apostoli etiam d. ll. distinctionem faciunt. Ubi igitur lex non distingvit, nec nostrum est, distinctionem fingere. 7. Rectè igitur Iesuita Tirinus ad h. l. Utitur, sci ibit, Christus ad gravitatem irae & supplicii declarandum metaphora Iudaeis familiari & nota triplicis generis suppicii, sontibus apud illos infligi soliti. & post recensita ista genera subiicit: Sed omnem mensuram poenarum humanarum excedunt infernalia tormenta. Quae si subire cogatur, qui solis contumeliosis verbis in proximum suum iniurius est; quanta supplicia manebunt homicidam, qui exira, velodio sanguinem actu profundit?

Ex eadem autem hypothesi falsâ, quòd Christus peccato primo &s secundo non adiudicet hîc aeternum supplicium, sed saltem temporalem poenam, profluxit quoque alia Pontificiorum praesentis dicti perversio, dum nempe nonnulli, uti Bellarm. t. 1. Controv. l. 1. de Purg c. 8. col. 733. & 734. Maldon. t. 2. de Sacr. p. 144. Schoppius in Apolog. c. 58. f. 82. b. (Observandum tamen, plurimos Pontificios ex professo purgatorium stabilire satagentes, ac alia Sc. S. dicta alioquin afferentes, locum hunc omittere, ceu ex Petr. Cotono, Iulio Caesare Coturio, Pistorio, Becano aliisque, dum nullitatē consequentiae fortè ipsi deprehenderunt, videre est) statuunt. dum Christus peccato primo ac secundo minatur iudicium ac Concilium, haec verò non nisi de temporali poena iudicare possint, sequi, post hanc vitam daeri quoq; poenas temporales, nempe purgatorium, in quo poenas illas à Iudicio ac concilio definitas atq; impositas sustimnere cogatur, qui moritur repente vel dormiens, ita ut nullum habeat spatium poenitentiae.

Verùm Resp. 1. Sciendum ante omnia est, Christum metaphorà à Iudiciis Ebraeorum desumtà exprimere vel declarare gravitatem iudicii divini adversùs peccata, quod ipse Iesuita Tirinus largitur. 2. Significantur igitur per ista vocabula Iudicii, Concilii & Gebennae supplicia non humana vel temporalia, sed divina atque aeterna, quae omnes transgressores quinti praecepti manere, Christus h. l. indicat, si non facta fuerit remissio. Et hoc ipsum Cardinalis Hugo de S. Charo ac Barradius Iesuita ultro largiuntur, quin &

Iosuita Franc. Suarez t. 4. in Thom. disp. 45 p. 557. fatetur, hunc locum non spectare ad controversiam de Purgatorio, cùm valdè probabile sit, omnia illa membra, iudicii, concilii, gehēnae, significare aeternam damnationem & poenam maiorem & minorem pro qualitate delictorum. Alphonsus quoque Salmoron, unus è primis Iesuitutis t. 5. tr. 35. p. 201. ita in h. l. Cùm de eo, scribit, qui irascitur fratri suo, dicitur, Reus erit iudicio, metaephoricè vox iudicii, accipitur pro poenâ aeternâ, proportione quadam debitâ irae mentis. Confirmatur haec expositio ab ipso Salmerone auctoritate Irenaei, l. 2. c. 57. dicentis: Non solùm, qui occidit, reus erit occisionis ad damnationem, scd & qui irascitur sine causae fratri suo. Adiungi verò Irenaeo & alii Patres possunt. Zacharias Chrysopolitanus: Exprimuntur pro modo peccati diversae mansiones in aeterna damnatione. Isidorus lib. 4. epist. 204. Non solùm à caede puros nos esse vult, verùm etiam abira &c. Et non obedientibus ignem inextinguibilemπὀρ ἄσβεςονcomminatus est. 3. quod enim iudicium divinum ac poenam aeternam incurrat, qui irascitur vel odit fratrem suum, paullò ante ex Gal. 5, 19. 20. ac 1. Ioh. 3, 14. 15. ostensum 4. Christus ipse v. 25. 26. docet, quid nomine iudicii h. l. intellectum velit. Conf. Luc. 12, 28. 5. acsatis etiam hoc manifestum est ex clausulâ generali, Decalogo annexa Deut. 27, 26. add. Gal. 3, 10. 6. quid quòd si nomine iudicii intelligeretur tantùm poena humana, consequens esset, nec homicidam mereri aeternum supplicium, vel si maximè non agat poenitentiam. ratio consequentiae elucescit ex v. 21. Dicit quidem Bellarm. Veterem legem aliam mortem, quàm temporalem non comminari homicidis, idpatere, scribit, ex Exod. 21. Sed num maledictio illa premens omnem, etiam in V. T. qui non permanet in sermonibus legis, nisi scil. facta remissio fuerit, temporales saltem poenas comprehendit ac minatur, non verò aeternam simul mortem? Imò verò aeternam potissimùm mortem, ceu ex oppositâ benedictione, quae cumprimis aeternam salutē includit, liquet. Quod licet Photiniani ac Pontificii nonnulli acriter negent, satis tamen id ipsum à nostratibus evictum est. Vid. si placet Dn. D. Calov. Socinianismi Prost. p. 274. B. D. Fewrb. Anti-Oster. p. 326. B. Par. L. de vit. aet. §. 30. it. Comment. in Deut. p. 528. Disp. Acad p. 626. 1137. B. D. Chemn. part. 2. LL. Th. p. 24. B. D. Gerlach. Disp. 13. §. 16. seqq. Cumprimis autem luculenter hoc patet ex collat. Levit. 19, 18. cum Luc. 10, 25. seqq. Nec locus Exod. 21. aliud evincit. Disting. enim inter poenam civilem, ac maledictionem divinam. De hâc agitur Deut. 27, 27. de illâ Exod 21, 1415. nec unius positio alterius exclusio est. Nec sequitur etiamqui à civili poenâ capitali absolvitur, eum etiam à maledictione legis absolvi, ceu ex collatione praesentis loci cum Exod 21, 19.21. patet, & benè notatum à B. D. Rungio Comm. in Exod. p. 829. Coeterùm pluribus contra Pontificiorum errorem, quòd peccata quaedam naturâ suâs. in sese sint venialia, confer. B. D. R-nig Vindic. Sacr. L. 23. §. 5. seqq. B. D. Hutterus LL. Th. p. 352. seqq. B. Par. L. de it. in Vindic. t. 2. p. 615. Pecc. § 93. seqq. alios. Add. ex Calvin. Croc. in Anti Bec. t. 2. p. 671. 672. Chamier. t. 3. Panstr. l. 6. c. 9. seqq. Contra illos verò, qui purgatorium elicere ignem tum è praesenti, tum aliis Scr. locis satagunt, evolvantur B. D. Bald. Disp. 7. ad Artic. Smale. B. D. Mentz. Anti Pist. L. 12. B. D. R-nig l c. B.
