## 5:23
v. 23. Ἀνθρ.

The particle οὖν shows that this is inferred from what precedes. But the connection seems rather obscure. For in what precedes Christ spoke of the anger and hatred of our neighbor toward us; here, however, He commands that we resist anger and hatred. How are these to be reconciled?

Answer. 1. Christ has regard to our nature, which is such that when we recall that our neighbor is angry with us, or that we are held in hatred by him, anger in turn immediately exerts itself within us.

2. The Scribes and Pharisees held that if anything had been committed against the law of not killing, it could easily be expiated by the external ceremonies of sacrifices, even if they were offered without faith in the Messiah, nor did reconciliation with the offended neighbor need to precede, although both ought to proceed entirely from love, as love from faith. This Pharisaic error Christ further refutes.

3. Therefore, just as in what precedes He had taught what is forbidden in the law by not killing, which the Pharisees did not understand: so He further teaches what is commanded in the law, which they did not understand, namely, that concord and reconciliation with one's neighbor are so necessary that without them no sacrifices, no worship, can please God.

4. Because it is evident from the explanation of the fifth commandment delivered by Christ, that in the infirmity of this life the transgression of it is very prone, He shows the remedy, namely, that we should seek forgiveness for the transgression from God and quickly return to agreement with our neighbor.

*( Ἐὰν ροσφέρης, if you offer, i. e. if you wish or you have it in mind to offer. See Gen. 24, 58.Exod. 12, 48.2. Sam 21, 9Matth. 13, 13c. 23. 8.)*

Πρὸς τὸθυσιαςήριον. alludes to the legal form of divine worship prescribed in the O. T., and in a prophetic manner speaks of the worship of the N. T. with words accustomed to be used concerning the worship of the O. T.

Ἔχειτὶ κατὰ σοῶ, if he has anything against you. Apoc. 2. v. 14. namely if you have harmed him, or have afflicted him with some injury.

*(Just as the most full satisfaction of Christ, rendered to the divine law, removes our own satisfactions before GOD both for sins and for the punishments of the same; (As the Blessed P. L. shows at length in De Poenit. §. 118. 119. 120. 121. 122. seqq.) so satisfaction before men can well consist with the satisfaction of Christ. And it is not only lawful, but also necessary, as is evident also from the present passage. Beautifully Isidore of Pelusium l. 4. epist. 111. Great run τῷ θεῷ λόγῳ i. e. Christ's reconciliations of men among themselves. For that same one, who restored the grace of heavenly things with earthly, dissolves the hatreds of men, permitting not &c. for he says: Do not wish to be angry with your brother rashly. But because he has well known human infirmity, which is impelled to a fall in a light moment, he even dissolves the roots of enmities, and so bears with an even mind the imperfect duty of the neighbor until we return to concord among ourselves. & a little later: You seek, he says, humanity kindness from me; but he who has been afflicted with injury by you, demands vengeance. You indeed call me merciful: but he calls me just. & again: You do not sell the right of another's vengeance with a gift: you do not corrupt my judgment with a bribe. Compare more ibid. Things twin to these are read also in Chrysostom hom. 16. in Matth. at this place. For thus among other things the Father mχρρυσοῤῥων

O admirable, he exclaims, kindness and ineffable love of GOD toward men. He despises his own honor, while he requires charity in the neighbor. For what could be milder than these words? what gentler? let my worship be interrupted, he says, so that your charity may be made whole. The reconciliation of brothers is a sacrifice to me. & a little later to the words: Go first &c. Let those hear, who, having certainly been initiated into the sacred mysteries, approach the communion of the altar with enmities. Thus if you offer prayer even with such a will, it is better to leave the prayer, and run to the reconciliation of the brother. & afterwards: He did not indeed say, when you have been greatly harmed, then be reconciled: but even if he has had something light against you. He does not add, whether justly or unjustly, but simply, if he has had anything against you. For even if you are angry justly, it is not fitting, however, to cherish and extend hatred for too long. But especially the oracles of Holy Scripture are to be weighed here, Levit. 19, 17.Sir. 28, 1. seqq. Matth. 6, 14. 15.c. 18, 35.Marc. 11, 25.Luc. 17, 3Eph. 4, 32.Col. 3, 13.1. Tim. 2, 8. &c. concerning which at length B. Par. Scholae Piet. l. 4. c. 21. But how he ought to conduct himself, who litigates with another in the forum and wishes to approach the Holy Supper, the Blessed D. Bald. teaches in Cas. Cons. l. 2. c. 12. Cas. 4. Furthermore, by what reason reconciliation was instituted among the Jews, Drusius reports from the book Musar l. 1. Praeter. p. 13. which can be seen. Add the same Drusius to Loc. diffic. Numer. c. 16. p. 359. But Capellus notes a similar admonition and reconciliation left by R. Iona in Spicil. p. 114.)*

Latin:

v. 23. Ἀνθρ.

Particula οὖν ostendit, hoc ex praecedentibus inferri. Sed connexio videtur obscurior. Nam Christus in praecedentibus egit de ira & odio proximi erga nos: hîc verò praecipit, ut nos resistamus irae & edio. quomodo -aec concilianda?

Resp. 1. respicit Christus ad ingenium nostrum, quod tale est, ut cùm recordamur, nobis irasci proximum, aut nos odio ab illo haberi, mox sese in nobis vicissim ira exerat.

2. Scribae & Pharisaei statuebant, si quid contra legem de non occidendo commissum, id externis sacrificiorum Ceremoniis facilè expiari posse, etiamsi sine fide in Messiam offerrentur, nec praecederet reconciliatio cum proximo offenso, quae tamen ex dilectione, sicut dilectio ex fide proficisci omninò debebant. Hunc errorem Pharisaicum Christus porrò refellit.

3. Sicut ergo in praecedentibus docuerat, quid in lege de non occidendo prohibitum, quod non intelligebant Pharisaei: ita porrò docet, quid in lege mandatum, quod illi non intelligebant, videl. concordiam & reconciliationem cum proximô tam necessariam esse, ut absque ea nulla sacrificia, nullus cultus Deo placere possit.

4. Quia ex tradita à Christo explicatione quinti praecepti constat, in huius vitae infirmitate transgressionem illius esse admodùm proclivem, monstrat remedium, videl. ut à Deo transgressionis veniam petamus & cum proximo citò in gravam redeamus.

*( Ἐὰν ροσφέρης,si obtuleris, i. e. si vis vel in animo habes offerre. Vid. Gen. 24, 58.Exod. 12, 48.2. Sam 21, 9Matth. 13, 13c. 23. 8.)*

Πρὸς τὸθυσιαςήριον. alludit ad legalem cultus divini formam in V. T. praescriptam, ac more prophetico de cultu N. T. loquitur verbis de V. T. cultu usurpari solitis.

Ἔχειτὶ κατὰ σοῶ, si habet quod de te queratur. Apoc. 2. v. 14. nimirum si tu eum laeseris, aut iniuriâ aliquâ affeceris.

*(Quemadmodum plenissima Christi satisfactio, legi divinae praestita, proprias nostras tum pro peccatis tum pro eorundem poenis satisfactiones coram DEO tollit; (Ceu prolixè ostendit B. P. L. de Poenit. §. 118. 119. 120. 121. 122. seqq.) ita benè satisfactio coram hominibus cum Christi satisfactione consistere potest. Estque ea non licita solùm, sed etiam necessaria, ceu ex praesenti quoque loco patet. Pulcrè Isidorus Pelusiota l. 4. epist. 111. Maxima cursuntτῷ θεῷ λόγῳ h. e. Christo hominum inter se reconciliationes. Nam idem ille, qui c-lestium cum terrestribus gratiam redint egravit, odia quohominum dissolvit, neenasctea permitrens &c. ait enim: Nolis irasci fratri tuo temerè. Quia verò probè cognitam habet humanam infirmitatem, quae levi momento ad lapsum impellitur, etiam exeris inimicitiis dissolvit earum radices, adeoproriam munus imperfectuu mantre aequo animo fert quo adusg; inter nos in concordiam redeamus. & paullò pòst: Tu qu--em,, inquit, humantiatem benignitatemapud me quaeris; at is qui abste iniuria affectus est, ultionem poscit. Tu quidem misericordem me vocas: at ille iustum. & iterum: Non vends munere ius alienae ultionis: non adultero incorruptum iudicium meum. Conf. plura ibid. Gemella his & apud Chrysostomum hom. 16. in Matth. ad h. l. leguntur. Ita enim inter alia Pater mχρρυσοῤῥων

ó admirabilem, exclamat, benignitatem atineffabilem erga homines amorem DEI. Honorem suum despicit, dum in proximo charitatem requirit. Quid enim his verbis mitius esse posset? quid lenius? interrumpatur, inquit, cultus meus, ut tua charitas integretur. Sacrificium mihi est fratrum reconciliatio. & paullò pòst ad verba: Vade priùs &c. Audiant hi, qui sacris certè mysteriis initiati, cum inimicitiis ad communionem altaris accedunt. Itasi orationem etiam cum tali offeras voluntate, meliùs est orationem relinquere, & ad reconciliationem fratris excurrere. & posteà: Non verò dixit, quum magnopere laesus fueris, tum reconciliare: sed etiam si leve aliquid habuerit contrate. Neaddit, sive iure sive iniuria, sed simpliciter, si babuerit aliquid adversus te. Nam etiamsi iure succenseas, non tamen convenit odium diutiùs sovere & extendere. Cumprimis autem perpendenda hîc Seripturae Sacrae oracula sunt, Levit. 19, 17.Sir. 28, 1. seqq. Matth. 6, 14. 15.c. 18, 35.Marc. 11, 25.Luc. 17, 3Eph. 4, 32.Col. 3, 13.1. Tim. 2, 8. &c. de quibus prolixè B. Par. Scholae Piet. l. 4. c. 21. Quomodo verò sese gerere debeat, qui in foro cum altero litigat & S. coenam accedere vult, docet B. D. Bald. Cas. Cons. l. 2. c. 12. Cas. 4. Caeterùm quâ ratione apud iudaeos reconciliatio fuerit instituta, è libero Musar refert Drusius l. 1. Praeter. p. 13. qui potest videri. Add. eund. Drusium ad Loc. diffie. Numer. c. 16. p. 359. Similem autem admonitionem ac reconciliationem à R. Iona relictam annotat Capellus in Spicil. p. 114.)*

## 5:24
v. 24.

The scope is, 1. that the business of reconciliation ought not to be deferred for a long time, nor should the offering of the sacrifice be sent ahead to him first, but without any delay one must return to favor with one's neighbor, so that afterward even the gift left before the altar can be offered to GOD and forgiveness of admitted sins obtained. 2. That a gift pleasing to God cannot be offered unless one first returns to favor with his neighbor; as long as we remain in offense against any of our brothers, so long also does God remain offended with us. 3. That without true and serious repentance, whose primary part is faith, exercising itself through love and brotherly reconciliation, outward worship and outward Ceremonies by no means please God.

Observe therefore the order of worship or of good works. 1. Let faith shine in the heart. 2. Let moral obedience be rendered. 3. Let the legitimate use of ceremonies be added. For ceremonies without a foundation, that is, without faith and without moral obedience, do not please God in the least.

Latin:

v. 24.

Scopus est, 1. reconciliationis negotium non debere in longum differri, nec oblationem sacrificii eidem praemittendam, sed sine omni mora cum proximo in gratiam esse redundum, ut postea etiam munus coram altari relictum DEO offerri & peccatorum admissiorum venia impetrari possit. 2. quod munus Deo gratum non possit offerri, nisi cum proximo quis priùs in gratiam redeat, quamdiu nos in alicuius fratrum manemus offensâ, tamdiu etiam nobis Deus manet offensus. 3. quod absque verâ & seriâ poenitentiâ, cuius pars primaria est fides, per dilectionem & fraternam reconciliationem sese exerens, externus, cultus & externae Ceremoniae Deo minimè placeant.

Observa igitur ordinem cultuum seu bonorum operum. 1. In corde luceat fides. 2. moralis oboedientia praestetur. 3. accedat usus legitimus Ceremoniarum. Nam Ceremoniae sine fundamento h. e. sine fide & sine morali obaedientia Deo minimè placent.

## 5:25
v. 25.

Some think that Christ is still dealing with him who has harmed his neighbor. The Savior warned us, says Franc Lucas, in the previous sentence, to take care that we return immediately to favor with those whom we have offended, if we wish to please God, that our works may be pleasing to Him. He warns of this same thing again, terrifying us with the severity of divine judgment, if we do not do so.

But it is more correctly said that, after the Savior in the preceding verse had dealt with him who offended his neighbor, and had exhorted him to seek reconciliation: He is now further dealing with the offended party, warning him to show himself easy and benevolent to the neighbor who is entreating him, and not to deal with him by the highest law.

Ἐυνοῶν benevolent. Some, with Augustine as witness, have rendered it concordant. Luth. Gen willf--rig.

Ἀντίδικος is adversary, creditor, who moves a lawsuit in the name of a debt. The Syrian, Lord of your lawsuit. Here, however, it is used generally of anyone by whom one has been harmed.

ὐν τῇ ὁδῷ. This present life is nothing other than a way by which we proceed to death and from death to the tribunal of GOD.

εἰς φιλακὴν. Gregory, homily 39 on the Gospel. The exactor is sent into prison, because he is shut up in hell by the evil Spirit.

*(Since in this place Christ urges that we be reconciled to our neighbor, lest he accuse us before the Judge and we be thrown into prison, it is evident that civil judgments in the N. T. are not abolished. Otherwise Christ would have condemned the accuser and the judge, who throws the guilty into prison, rather than having given counsel to the accused on how he ought to free himself from the accuser. This is to be observed against the Photinians, as noted by B. P. L. on Civil Magistrates §. 272. compare also D. Calov. Socia. proflig. page 1009.

Latin:

v. 25.

Quidam existimant, Christum adhuc agere de eo, qui proximum laesit. Monuit nos Salvator, inquit Franc Lucas, superiori sententia, curare, ut mox redeamus cum: is, quos offendimus, in gratiam, si Deo placere, illiopera nostra grata esse velimus. Hoo idem rursus monet, terrens iudicii divini severitate, nî fecerimus.

Sed rectiùs dicitur, postquam Salvator in vers. praeced. egerat de eo, quia proximum offendit, eumque exhortatus fuerat, ut quaerat reconciliationem: ipsum iam porrò agere de offenso, eummonere, ut proximo deprecanti se facilem & benevolum praebeat, nec summo iure cum ipso agat.

Ἐυνοῶνbenevolus. Quidam, Augustino tes-e, reddiderunt, concors. Luth. Gen willf--rig.

Ἀντίδικος est adversarius, creditor, qui litem debiti nomine movet. Syrus, Dominus litis tuae. Hîc verò generaliter usurpatur de quovis, à quo quis laesus est.

ὐν τῇ ὁδῷ. Praesens haec vita nihil aliud est quàm via, quâ ad ad mortem & à morte ad DEI tribunal pergimus.

εἰς φιλακὴν. Gregorius homil. 39. in Evang. Exactor in carcerem mittitur, quia per malignum Spiritum in inferno recluditur.

*(Cùm h. l. Christus suadeat, ut reconciliemur proximo, ne apud Iudicem nos accuset ac coniiciamur in carcerem, patet, quòd iudicia civilia in N. T. non sint sublata. Aliàs enim Christus damnasset potiùs accusantem ac iudicem, qui sontem in carcerem coniicit, quàm ut consilium accusato dedisset, quomodo ab accusatore sese liberare debeat. Id quod contra Photin. observandum, notante B. P. L. de Mag. Polit. §. 272. conf. etiam D. Calov. Socia. proflig. pag. 1009.

## 5:26
v. 26. φιλακὴ.

Κοδράντης is a Latin word bent into Greek form. *(Not a few words of this kind, which were transferred into Greece along with the Roman Empire, and so are found even in the Greek text of the New Testament, were long ago collected by learned men: but at a single glance B. D. Glassius presents them in his Philologia Sacra, book 1, page 238; Thomas Gataker in On the Style of the New Testament, p. 53; and somewhat more fully the same words were expounded by Bartholomaeus Mayer, Philologia Sacra, part 1, p. 251 sqqq., and Georgius Pasor in the Appendix to the New Testament Lexicon.)* In place of it Luke, devoted to purer Greek idiom, has set down the mite, signifying the fourth part of an assarium, which others otherwise call a teruncius or triuncius. From Mark 12. v. 42. it is gathered that it signifies a coin of least value, comprising two mites. The Syrian rendered it , which means an eighth, that is, the eighth part of an As, which was the smallest piece and could not be divided further. Tremellius in his notes. Plutarchus, in his Life of Cicero: They called the smallest bronze coin a quadrans. *(Compare Buxtorf, Lexicon Talmudicum Rabbinicum, p. 2125, under the word קררינפם..)*

*(This passage is almost the palm-tree here, from which the Papists strive to shore up their Purgatory—just as this very passage is brought forward in confirmation of Purgatory by Cardinal Bellarmine, book 2, De Purgatorio, chapter 7; Johann von Eck in the Enchiridion, p. 217; Conrad Kling, book 4 of the Laws and Constitutions, chapter 49; Franz Fevardentius, book 12 of the Theomachia Calvini, chapter 1, n. 7 sqqq.; Martin Eisengrein, Pro Cancione, Academic Press at Ingolstadt, Funeral Oration 2 and 4; the Jesuits Peter Canisius, Catechism, chapter on penance, question 9, p. 309; Martin Becanus in the Manuale, book 1, chapter 8, p. 151; Franz Costerus, Enchiridion Controversiarum, chapter 24, fifth proposition, p. 682; Salmerón, tome 5, tract 37, p. 212; Tirinus, Conzen, Cornelius à Lapide, likewise Franz Lucas on this passage; the apostate Schoppe in the Apology, chapter 55, page 78, likewise Commentary on Indulgences, chapter 46, fol. 35; Johannes Pistorius, Wegweiser der Deutschen, chapter 12, pp. 539, 575 sqqq.; among others. But thus Cardinal Bellarmine draws conclusions about the present saying—the remaining Papists of lesser rank commonly follow him as their leader like ordinary soldiers; yet some others, who perhaps examine the emphasis of the sayings more carefully, abandon him, such also as the Jesuit Coturius, since although he labors to establish Purgatory with many authorities of the Fathers, indeed even with certain sayings of Scripture, in the Enchiridion Controversiarum, p. 430 sqqq., nevertheless he passes over this passage deliberately in silence—which Gregory of Valencia also did. Others, however, such as Jansenius and Stapleton, openly deny that this passage treats of Purgatory, whose words will be cited below.)* Since by the Adversary God is understood, whom the sinner offends, by the judge Christ, by the prison Purgatory: by the last farthing the most minute sins, therefore the sense is: As long as you are in this life, make satisfaction to God for your sins, while there is a place for mercy: because otherwise after this life the entire debt, even of the smallest sins, will be most strictly exacted from you in Purgatory. Thus Bellarmine very briefly repeats the sentiment, as Becanus does in his Manual, p. 151. He indeed cites chapter 4, but it is chapter 7, just as also in the same place a comma has been inserted between Eusebius and Emessenus (perhaps so that the number of the Fathers might be increased), although he is one author, and moreover the passage taken from him was brought forward by Bellarmine from a spurious writing, which both Bellarmine and Becanus ought to have learned from Baronius, at A.D. 441.

Moreover, we shall send away for the present the seven testimonies of the Fathers brought forward by Bellarmine, by which, even if those men should prove the Popish Purgatory ever so much from this passage, other Fathers can be opposed to them, concerning whom see below. But that they do this least of all was shown long ago by our own writers. Let them at least consult B. D. Meisner, Opuscula, second treatise on Purgatory, p. 360, and B. Pareus, Book on Death, §. 269. To these, if it pleases, there may be added from among the Calvinists Daniel Chamier, Panstratia, t. 3, l. 26, c. 7; Philippe du Mornay, Lord of Plessis-Marly, l. 3, On the Holy Eucharist, c. 8; Johannes Crocius in his Anti-Becanus, t. 2, Controversy 8, p. 178 sqqq. Nor do six or even seven twisted sayings of the Fathers constitute an article of faith, such as the Papists think the doctrine of Purgatory to be. It suffices us that Francis Suarez (the common Master of all in Spain, an acute Theologian and Philosopher, according to the eulogy of Drexelius in Aurifodina, part 1, c. 7, or, if anyone prefers to rise up with the judgment of the Jesuit Tanner, a great Theologian and at this time almost a certain leader and standard-bearer of theologians, preface to t. 1 of Scholastic Theology) voluntarily grants to us that Ambrose, Jerome, and Athanasius are cited here in vain, since they say almost nothing else than that even the smallest sins are punished by God, and that no one departs thence until he pays. Whether however anyone pays after this life, they do not declare. Yet let the same judgment be made concerning certain other Fathers brought forward by Bellarmine, whose authority he himself rejects elsewhere; some writings are attributed to them spuriously. Therefore those who deny that Purgatory is treated in this passage do not wage war against the Fathers, though the Jesuit Cosensus strives hard indeed to persuade the reader of this.

That, however, in this place there is no dealing with Purgatory, nor can it be firmly proven from there, we prove 1. by an examination of the Pontifical doctrine concerning Purgatory according to the standard of faith, or by a comparison of the same with the analogy of faith. The Papistic Purgatory is not only ἄγραφον, but also ἀντίγραφον.. For the doctrine of the Pontificians concerning Purgatory is repugnant in many ways to Holy Scripture, and indeed 1. while it distributes men into three classes, when Scripture distributes them into no more than two classes, namely into believers and unbelievers, sheep and goats, etc. Matth. 7, 13. seqq. c. 8, 11. 12. c. 25, 31. 33. 41. Rom. 2, 6. 7. 8.Gal. 6, 8. 2. while it introduces a time of repenting after this life, when nevertheless Scripture teaches that the time of this life alone is the time of laboring, running, etc., that is, of repenting, believing, and consequently of obtaining the remission of sins, etc. Matth. 25, 10Ioh. 9, 4.1. Cor. 7, 29.Gal. 6, 8.10.2. Tim. 4, 7. &c. 3. while besides the Levitical or external, and the spiritual or internal purgation, both of which have a place only in this life, it promises some third one after this life, of which, however, there is no mention anywhere in Scripture. 4. while it threatens the faithful and believers with some torments to be sustained after this life, and such indeed as differ from the fire of hell only in duration: when on the contrary Scripture teaches that all who truly believe in Christ are happy and blessed immediately from death, and their souls, as soon as they are loosed from the bond of the body, are transferred immediately in the very moment of dissolution without interval into Paradise. As then the examples of Enoch, Gen. 5, 24. Elijah, Lazarus, Stephen, Act. 7, 59. the Thief, Luc. 23, 43. and all the pious, Sap. 3, 1.3.c. 4, 1.Es. 57, 2.Ioh 3, 18.36.c. 12, 26Phil. 1, 13.Ebr. 4, 3.Apoc. 14, 13. &c. clearly testify. 5. while it introduces some third receptacle of souls separated from the body, when nevertheless Holy Scripture presents no more than two of this kind, and is ignorant of a third. See Matth. 3, 12.c. 7, 13.c. 8, 11.c. 25, 46Marc 16, 16.Luc. 16, 22.Ioh 3, 16. 6. while it asserts that the dead can be helped by the suffrages of the living after this life, which however Holy Scripture denies. See Psal. 49, 8. 9. & 10.Eccl. 9, 4.Matth. 5, 26.c. 25, 8. 9.Marc. 3, 31. Furthermore, Purgatory undermines the article concerning the mercy of GOD, which remits guilt and punishment. Matth. 8, 27. concerning His justice, which, with the guilt remitted, remits also the punishment. the efficacy of the merit of Christ, as He who provided to God the most full satisfaction not only for original but also for our actual sins, for punishments both temporal and eternal owed to us on account of sins, Ex. 53, 4. 5. 6.John 1, 29.Gal. 3, 131. Peter 2, 24. concerning saving repentance, whose fruit is the plenary remission of sins, Ps. 32, 5.Luke 24, 47.Acts 3, 19. concerning the total and gratuitous remission of sins, Ps. 25, 7.Ps. 32, 1.Jer. 31, 31.Mic. 7, 19. concerning our peaceful and plenary justification. Rom. 5, 1. 2.c. 8, 1.24.33, 34.c. 12, 12.John 3, 36. etc. concerning the last day. For if, regarding those who die before the final day, there is need of Purgatory, there will also be need of the same regarding those whom the last day will find alive. For no reason for a difference can be given. But this conflicts with the doctrine concerning the final day. But the blessed Par. deduces this at greater length in Confess. Cath. vol. 3, p. 423, et seqq. add. L. de Morte §. 182, et seqq. Dispp. Acad. p. 440. Compare also the blessed D. Gerlach, Vol. 2, Dispp. Theol. Disp. 28, p. 4037.

Furthermore, that the Popish Purgatory is not being treated here is proven 2. from the circumstances, as well as the consideration of the preceding and following context. It is treated in the preceding verses 23, 24 concerning fraternal reconciliation. Therefore, through the Adversary in this verse also, our neighbor is most conveniently understood. Thus Peltanus, Salmeron, Iansenius, Franc. Lucas, and others in this place. Others, through the Adversary, writes the Jesuit Maldonatus in this place, p. 121, understand him of whom he had spoken a little before, go first, be reconciled to your brother. Thus Hil. can. 4. Ambr. b. 7. in Luke c. 12. Auct. Op. Imp. hom. 11. Hier. in Comm. And this is the true sense. Our adversary, therefore, is he whom we have injured, whom we have called raca or fool, who has a lawsuit against us before God. In the same way, Ioh. Ferus also explains in his Comm. on this place. In external, he says, matters, it is sometimes better to settle with an adversary even on unfair terms than to pursue lawsuits and contentions. Bellarminus, on the contrary, understands God by Adversary, the Jesuit Conzen the Devil, with whom how we ought to settle even on unfair terms, or even how we ought to have goodwill toward the Devil, I for one do not see. S. Aug. teaches something different when in his book de decem chordis, c. 3. Who is this Adversary? This adversary is not the Devil. For Scripture would never exhort you to be in concord with the Devil. Whence S. Basil in reg. brevior. interr. 222. Who is the adversary of one of us, or how shall we be in agreement with him? Resp. precisely in this place the Lord calls that person an adversary who tries to take away from us something of those things which pertain to our right. Furthermore, we are in agreement with them if we keep that precept of the Lord: Whoever wishes to contend with you in judgment, and take your tunic, let him have your cloak etc. Tertullian does not dissent in his book de anima c. 35. How Card. Bell. and the Jesuit Conzen wish to accommodate these things either to God or to the Devil, let them see to it themselves. Furthermore, by prison Bell., Conzen, and the patrons of Purgatory understand purgatory, by farthing the most minute sins, whence Conzen is also very occupied here to teach how minute a type of coin a farthing is. But whatever may be the case regarding this matter, how the smallest sins can be paid back to God, let the Card. and the Jesuit consider. It is certain that the expression is metaphorical and the speech is accommodated to forensic custom, as the Jesuit Maldonatus warns. But now Bellarminus himself, book 3 de V. D. c. 3, teaches that effective arguments ought to be sought from the literal sense alone, just as Ludov. ab Alcasar also writes in c. 11. Apoc., that symbolic Theology is not argumentative. Other Papists agree, such as Alphonsus de Castro b. 1 adv. haeres c. 3. b. 4, under the word Council, Salmeron Proleg. 19, p. 340, etc. Therefore, from this place, Purgatory, even if it could be distorted to the Papist Purgatory in the highest degree, cannot be solidly proven. But it is better to understand prison as hell itself, just as the Holy Fathers, Hieronymus, Augustinus, Theophylactus, and others also take it, nor does Ambrosius seem to have understood it otherwise, while he holds it as the same with outer darkness, Matt. 22, 13. and with the furnace of fire, Matt. 13, 42. In the same way also the Glossa Interlin., Dion. Carthus., Alphonsus Tostatus, Maldonatus in this place, Franc. Toletus, Didacus Stella in c. 12. Lucae, and others take it.

Indeed the overseers of Purgatory object that this exposition is hindered by the particle until, by which it is signified that those to whom Christ here threatens prison shall at some time come out of it, whereas now no redemption is given from hell. I answer that here it is not necessary to establish a liberation from prison. For although that particle sometimes determines a past time and excludes the future, yet it is often taken indefinitely, so that it includes all the following time, so that it should never be so expounded. Examples of this kind, a few in number, occur in Holy Scripture, and have been noted by the Jesuits themselves. The Jesuit Tirinus confirms this acceptation from 2. Reg. 6, 23. Matth. 1, 23. Other Jesuits teach the same, as is clear from Gasp. Sanctio, Comm. in libb. Reg. p. 628. Corn. à Lapide likewise, Comm. in libb Reg. t. 2. p. 25. and also Comm. in Matth, p. 58. Similarly they observe that the particle until in Cantic. 3. v. 4. must be so understood, Mich. Ghislerius Romanus, of the clerics regular of S. Silvester &c., Comm. in Cant. p. 410. a. Let also Felicianus Capitonus Narniensis be consulted, Explic. Cath. p. 375. Guilielmus Estius, Professor of Theology at Douai, Comm. in Epist. Pauli t. 1. pag. 487. a Bernh. Paxillus de Brzezek, of the Order of Preachers of S. Dominic, in Monomach. pro Def. fidei SS. Trinit. p. 623. & 828. Iodocus Coccius, to the same effect, adduces passages from Theophylact and Ambrose, lib. 3. Thes. Cath. p. 278. 280. Moreover the most laborious Jesuit Ioh. Lorinus confirms this very thing with a few more examples, Comm. in Ps. t. 3. p. 263, where, for that signification, that until does not determine always a certain time, he brings forward Exod. 15, 16.Deut. 7, 24.2. Reg. 6, 23.Ps. 109, 1.Ps. 111, 8.Ps. 122, 2.Matth. 1, 25.c. 10, 23. c, last v. 20. 1. Tim. 4, 13. But that also here the particle until must be taken in such a signification, the most ancient Fathers teach. The Jesuit Joh. de la Haye himself supplies us with a passage on this matter sufficiently clear from Jerome on chapter 1 of Lamentations of Jeremiah, in the Triumph of Truth, p. 293. What Augustine's opinion is, the Jesuit Maldonatus teaches. But when he says, he writes in his Commentary on this place, p. 121, that we shall not come out thence until we pay the last farthing, he does not mean, as Augustine says, that they will come out afterwards; but that they will never come out, because those who are in hell, since they always pay the punishments owed—for they owe infinite punishments for any mortal sin—never finish paying. See also Theophylact on Luke ch. 12. To bring forward more opinions of the Fathers is scarcely necessary. Perhaps it will rather suit our taste to hear the fellow-members and fathers of Conzæus, seeing indeed that he wishes salvation to the Society of Jesus. Thus therefore Cornelius à Lapide on Matthew ch. 1, p. 58, Matth. 5, 26. You shall not come out thence, until you pay &c., that is, you shall never leave the prison of hell. Yet the same man, forgetful of himself, writes on this place: Come quickly so that you may be reconciled to your brother, before you are handed over to God the judge as a defendant, who by just vengeance may consign you to prison, until you pay all the debt, either lethal and eternal in hell, or venial and temporal in purgatory: for the little word 'until' inclines toward purgatory, which signifies a punishment to be ended, for this ends in Purgatory, whereas in hell it will never end, eternal abode: More consistent is the Jesuit Maldonatus on this place. In the same sense, he writes, must the word 'until' there be understood, as above on chapter 1, 25. He excepts.

but truly the Sophist Bellarmine says, and The proof that Purgatory is treated here, because of that: until you pay the last farthing, does not seem to be able to be said correctly, unless there is going to be an end to the payment at some time. He continues: the examples of Augustine do not suffice; for when it is said: He did not know her, until she gave birth, it is not indeed permitted to infer, therefore he knew her afterwards, but it is permitted to infer, therefore she was going to give birth at some time; similarly when it is said, sit at my right hand, until I place etc. it is correctly inferred, therefore all the enemies of Christ will at some time be placed under his feet: so therefore when it is said: Non o-ies until you pay the last farthing, we infer correctly, therefore he will at some time pay the last farthing, and consequently will go out from there. The Jesuit Adam Conzen also inculcates these very things as his own to the reader in his Comm. on this place. But I respond 1. if it were even granted in the highest degree that it is hinted by this very thing that it will happen at some time that he pays the last farthing, it does not follow that he must therefore go out from that prison, and that consequently that prison is purgatory, and not rather hell. Since the damned always pay the debts of punishment, because for any sin whatsoever they owe infinite punishments, they nevertheless never pay them off, writes Augustine. In the same way Jerome in c. 1. Thr. Ierem. He signifies that he will never go out, because he always pays the last farthing, while he pays the eternal punishments of earthly sins. 2. Nicolaus de Lyra on this place denies that in hell a repayment is ever possible, and thus teaches that until in this place is to be explained as never. 3. This is evident, that those who depart with mortal sin (of which there is speech in this place, namely of hatred and implacability, conf. Matth. 18, 17.Gal. 5, 20.1. Ioh. 3, 5.Apoc. 21, 8.) cannot satisfy or pay the last farthing, also from the fact that the Papists themselves teach that such are not sent into Purgatory, but into hell. See Corn. à Lap. on Matth. p. 359. b. and the same is evident from the alleged places. 4. But Bellarmine and Conzen insist, nevertheless from similar expressionsPs. 110.andMatth. 1, 25.it is manifest, when the particle until is placed, two things are always added, of which it is necessary that one or the other happens. I respond. We give the instance Matth. 18, 24.34. where it is similarly said that the Lord delivered him, who owed ten thousand talents, nor was he yet able to pay, to the torturers, ἕως οὗ until he should pay all that he owed. To this very place Conzen himself annotates thus: What is the punishment of the servant? That he should pay all, which when he could not, he owed eternally, therefore he remained in prison. Otherwise if it were a smaller sum, he could have paid it. God demands all things to the extreme, when someone begins to be cruel to his neighbors. In the same way Arias Montanus also proposes, as well as Corn. à Lapide on this place, where for the same explanation he also brings forward Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius. We grant therefore 5. that the last farthing is to be paid in that prison, i.e., that for sin, even if it seems the least, unless a man has obtained remission before death, which cannot happen unless he has laid aside hatred against his neighbor, the damned in hell must pay the deserved punishments, and are to be tortured for so long until they pay, they pay off, yet the consequence of this is not that they are also able to pay off, and thus are about to go out from that prison. We distinguish therefore with Jerome between payment or the rigid exaction of payment, and full payment or discharge. We concede that the former are required from the damned, but it does not follow from that that they go out from prison; but we deny that the latter can ever be performed by the damned, because the punishment of those who depart hence with anger, hatred, and a desire for vengeance, i.e., with mortal sin, is infinite and eternal. And Augustine looked to this, when he said: Whence, he says, is that debt paid, where there is no longer a place for repentance or correction. Let the Jesuits hear their fellow, Cardinal Bellarmine and Conzen, Didacus de Baeza, in the work on Christ figured, about which Franciscus de Sorio, Censor of the Office of the Inquisition, judges thus, that it is composed more for admiration than it needs censure. He, however, by no means twists this place to the fire of purgatory, but takes it entirely concerning eternal flames Clearly, he writes, in the reprobate not only huge crimes, but also the least ones kindle eternal flames. For not only for the sake of great debts are the reprobate detained in the prison of hell, but for the debt of the least farthing. Looking to which the LordMatth. 5.says to the impenitent sinner: Let the judge deliver etc. By the last farthing D. Hieron. and D. Aug understand the most minute sins, which are to be punished in the prison of hell, which will always remain whole there, they will never give enough punishments, so that the reprobate can see the end of them. Thus far the cited Jesuit p. 83.

We prove [this] by argument 3. from the scope and intention of Christ. For it is certain that Christ wished to urge his own people, by holding before them the danger of eternal punishment, so that quickly, while still on the way, they might seek reconciliation, lest they fall into punishments which they will not be able to escape forever. But this serious and necessary exhortation is wickedly weakened if the opinion of Purgatory stands against it: Even if you are cast into prison, you can get out of there, once the penalty of Purgatory has been fully paid either by yourself or through the intercessions of others. Therefore you will not need to be so anxious about reconciliation while you are on the way. So the great Chemnitz in his Harmony of the Gospels, ch. 51, p. 445.

We confirm our fourth point, that this passage does not treat of Purgatory, by the testimony of the Fathers. That Jerome on chapter 1 of the Lamentations of Jeremiah favors our exposition, the Jesuit de la Haye concedes; that Augustine here is ours, Tostatus Abulensis teaches, and the Jesuit Didacus de Baeza, on Christ figuratively, p. 83, and Maldonatus on this passage. The Cardinals Bellarmine and the Jesuit Cosmas also concede it. That this saying of Christ is expounded quite otherwise than of Purgatory by Chrysostom, homily 24 on Matthew, and by the Greek Fathers, Francis Suarez, Jesuit, expressly attests—first Professor of Theology at the Academy of Alcalá, afterwards at Salamanca, then at Rome and finally at Coimbra in Portugal. That our Venerable Bede too is ours, Thomas Aquinas teaches in the Catena on Luke, as well as Francis Lucas on this passage. And hence it can easily be judged how much credit the apostate Pistorius deserves when he appeals to the Fathers: for he writes in his Hodegoricus, p. 578: All the Fathers equally (gleichmössig) expound this passage of Purgatory. Yet even the Papists themselves, being pressed, freely admit that Jerome, Augustine, Chrysostom, Venerable Bede and the Greek Fathers do not interpret this passage of Purgatory but of eternal punishments. But let it also be considered what must be decided about him, on whom nevertheless Pistorius' hypothesis rests almost solely—that this passage cannot be understood except of Purgatory—when he writes: those who departed hence with wrathful and implacable mind had (namely at the time when they departed) true and living faith. p. 578. Let this assertion be compared with 1 Tim. 1, 19. John 4, 8. James 2, 17.

Finally we add fifthly, the confession of certain of the Adversaries themselves, even of Cardinals and Jesuits. For although not a few follow Bellarmine here with blind impulse, yet there have never been lacking some prudent men who, though elsewhere they thought the fire of Purgatory ought diligently to be kept alive—for knowing full well that unless that fire burns, their kitchens grow cold—and indeed having rendered services elsewhere not useless to the Roman Curia, yet passing over Placentia made straight for Verona. Which appears from this, while Others dealing with Purgatory expressly omit this statement, such as the Jesuits, Coturius and Greg. de Valentia; others assert that it is being dealt with here concerning hell, and not concerning Purgatory, such as the Jesuits Maldonatus in this place and Seb. Barradius vol. 2, Conc. Evang. book 7, ch. 17; others freely grant that Purgatory cannot be certainly proven from this place, such as the Jesuits Iacobus Reihing in the Manuale Cath. art. 10 and Iansenius in this place. Whence also Thomas Stapletonus, Royal Professor in the Academy of Louvain, in his Antidotum on this place, bids one note Calvin, that there are very few today who expound this passage in that way (concerning Purgatory); others finally concede that this passage can be expounded otherwise than concerning Purgatory. Thus Stapletonus himself, just cited. And those also can be referred here who expound τὸ until in this place as never, such as Maldonatus in this place, Corn. à Lap. on ch. 1 of Matthew, Franc. Toletus (a Cardinal and likewise a Jesuit excelling in great praises of talent, solid learning, and perspicuity, by the commendation of Possevinus in his Appar.) on ch. 12 of Luke—all these Jesuits, likewise Alphonsus Tostatus in this place and Didacus Stella the Lusitanian, a Bishop of the Order of Minors, on ch. 12 of Luke, Didacus de Baeza comm. all. p 83. b., and others. But we bid Bellarmine and his followers finally to be strong with their purgatorial fire, not undeservedly fearing lest, where they have once approached the fire after this life, they may never be freed from it, even if a thousand Masses be celebrated for them, but that it will come to pass that they will grow hot there more than enough, and in reality experience that τὸ until in this place signifies the same as never.

Latin:

v. 26. φιλακὴ.

Κοδράντης vox est Latina Graecè flexa. *(Huiusmodi non paucae, quae cum Romano Imperio in Graeciam translatae, adeoque in Graeco etiam N. T cōtextu reperiuntur, pridem à viris doctis collectae sunt: uno verò intuitu sistunt illas B. D. Glassius Philol. S. lib. 1. pag. 238. Thomas Gatak. de stylo N. T. p. 53. paulloque prolixiùs easdem exposuerunt Barcholomaeus Mayerus, Philol. S. part. 1. p. 251. seqq. Georgius Pasor in App. Lex. N. T.)* pro qua Lucas purioris Graecismi studiosus posuit minutum, significans quartam partē assis, quam aliàs teruncium vel triuncium vocant. Ex Marc. 12. v. 42. colligitur, quòd significet minimi precii nummulum, duo minuta complectentem. Syrus reddidit quod significat octavum i. e. octavam partem Assis, quae fuit minima, nec potuit ulteriùs dividi. Tremell in notis. Plutarchus in Cicerone: Minimum ex aere numisma quadrantem appellarunt. *(Conf. Buxt. Lex. Talm. Rabb. p. 2125. voce קררינפם.)*

*(Palmarius ferè hic locus est, è quo Pontificii Purgatorium suum statuminare nituntur. quemadmodum hic ipse pro Purgatorii confirmatione adducitur à Cardinali Bell. l. 2. de Purg. c. 7. Ioh. ab Eck in Enchir. p. 217. Conrado Klingio lib. 4. LL. CC. cap. 49. Franc. Fevandentio l. 12. Theomach. Calvin. c. 1. n. 7. seqq. Mart. Eisengrentio Pro Canc. Acad. Ingolst. Conc. fun. 2. & 4. Iesuitis Petro Canisio Catech. c. de poenit. q. 9. p. 309 Martino Becano in Manuali l. 1. c. 8. p. 151. Franc. Costero Euchirid. Controv. cap. 24. prop. quinta p. 682. Salmerone tom. 5. tr. 37. p. 212. Tirino, Conzen. Corn. à Lapide, it. Franc. Lucâ in h. l. Apostatis Schoppio in Apolog. c. 55pag. 78. it. Comm. de Indulg. c. 46. f. 35. Ioh. Pistorio Hodeg. Germ. c. 12. p 539. 575. seqq. aliis. Ita verò de praesenti dicto colligit Card. Bellarminus, (quem reliqui minorum gentium Pontificii ceu milites gregarii suum ducem sequi ferè communiter solent; alii tamen, qui accuratiùs fortè dictorum emphasin examinant, eundem deserunt, ceu etiam Iesuita Coturius, utpote qui licet plurimis Patrum autoritatibus, quin & nonnullis Scripturae dictis stabilire Purgatorium satagat in Enchir. Controvers. p. 430. seqq. locum tamen hunc studiò silentio praeterit, quod etiam fecit Greg. de Valentia. Alii verò, uti Iansenius ac Stapletonus apertè negant, locum hunc de Purgatorio agere, quorum verba infra adducentur.) Cùm per Adversarium intelligatur Deus, quem peccator offendit, per iudicem Christus, per carcerem Purgatorium: per ult--um quadrantem minutissima peccata, sensus ergo est: Quamdiu es in hâc vitâ, satisfacias Deo pro peccatis tuis, dum locus est misericordiae: quia aliàs post hanc vitam totum debitum, etiam minimorum peccatorum rigidissimè à te exigetur in Purgatorio. Ita Bell. sententiam brevissimè repetit Becanus in Manuali p. 151. allegat quidem cap. 4. ed est c. 7. quemadmodum etiam impertinenter ibidem inter Eusebium & Emyssenum comma insertum est (fortè ut numerus Patrum augeretur) cum tamen sit unus autor, & locus insuper ex eo à Bell. adductus, depromtus è supposititio scripto, quod vel à Barnonio Ad A. 441. discere tum Bellarminus, tum Becanus debuissent.

Coeterùm mittemus impraesentiarum adducta à Bell. septem testimonia Patrum, quibus, si vel maximè illi purgatorium Papisticum ex h. l. probarent, alii opponi Patres possunt, de quibus infra. Sed minimè eos hoc facere, pridem à nostratibus ostensum fuit. Videantur saltē B. D. Meisnerus Opusc. sec. de Purg. p. 360. ac B. Par. L. de Morte §. 269. Quibus, si placet, adiungi è Calvin. possunt Daniel Chamier Panstrat. t. 3. l. 26. c. 7. Philippus Mornayus, Plessiaci Marliani Dominus l. 3. de S. Euchar. c. 8. Ioh. Crocius in AntiBecano t. 2. Controv. 8. p. 178. seqq. Nec sex insuper septemve Patrum dicta contorta articulum fidei efficiunt, qualem esse putant Pontificii de Purgatorio. Nobis sufficit, quôd Franc. Suarez, ( communis omnium in Hispaniâ Magister, Theologus & Philosophus acutus, Drexelii in Aurifod. part. 1. c. 7. elogio, vel si quis malit Iesuitae Tanneri iudicio adsurgere, Theologus magnus & hoc tempore quidam quasi Theologorū Coryphaeus & antesignanus, praef. ad t. 1. Theol. Scholast.) ultrò nobis largiatur, frustrà hîc citari Ambrosium, Hieronymum & Athanasium, cùm ferè nihil aliud dicant, quàm minimae etiam peccata puniri à Deo, & nemi-em inde exire, donec solvat. an verò aliquis solvat post hanc vitam, non declarent. Idem verò esto iudicium de aliis quibusdam à Bellarm. adductis Patribus quorundam autoritatem alibi reiicit ipse; quibusdam scripta supposititia tribuuntur. Non igitur contra Patres actionem instituunt, qui h. l. de Purgatorio agi negant, ceu Iesuita Conzen persuadere quidem lectori satagit.

Quòd autem h. l. non agatur de Purgatorio, nec firmiter inde probari illud possint, probamus 1. doctrinae Pontificiae de Purgatorio ad fidei amussim examine, sive eiusdem cum fidei analogiâ collatione. Est Purgatorium Papisticum non solùm ἄγραφον, sed etiam ἀντίγραφον. Repugnat enim doctrina Pontificiorum de Purg. multis modis S. Scripturae, & quidem 1. dum homines in tres classes distribuit, cùm Scrnon nisi in duas classes distribuat, nempe in credentes & incredulos, oves & haedos &c. Matth. 7, 13. seqq. c. 8, 11. 12. c. 25, 31. 33. 41. Rom. 2, 6. 7. 8.Gal. 6, 8. 2. dum tempus a a-quod resipiscendi post hanc vitam introducit, cùm tamē Scriptura doceat, solum huius vitae tempus esse tempus laborandi, currendi &c. hoc est resipiscendi, credendi & per consequens peccatorum remissionem obtinendi &c Matth. 25, 10Ioh. 9, 4.1. Cor. 7, 29.Gal. 6, 8.10.2. Tim. 4, 7. &c. 3. dum praeter Leviticam s. externam, & spritualem s. internam purgationem, quarum utraque in hâc tantùm vita locum habet, teritam aliquam post hanc vitam promittit, cuius tamen nuspiam in Scr fit mentio. 4. dum fidelibus ac credentibus cruciatus aliquos post hanc vitam fustinendos & tales quidem, qui sola duratione ab inferni igne differant, minatur: cûm contrà Scriptura doceat, omnes verè in Christum credentes statim à morte felices ac beatos esse, ac animas eorum quamprimùm corporis nexu solvuntur, immediatè in ipso solutionis momento sine intervallo in Paradisum transferri. Ceu tum exempla Henochi, Gen. 5, 24. Eliae, Lazari, Stephani, Act. 7, 59. Latronis, Luc. 23, 43. & omnium piorum, Sap. 3, 1.3.c. 4, 1.Es. 57, 2.Ioh 3, 18.36.c. 12, 26Phil. 1, 13.Ebr. 4, 3.Apoc. 14, 13. &c. luculenter testantur. 5. dum tertium aliquod animarum à corpore separatarum receptaculum ordinarium introducit, cùm tamen Scr. S. non nisi duo huius modi sistat, tertium ignoret. Vid. Matth. 3, 12.c. 7, 13.c. 8, 11.c. 25, 46Marc 16, 16.Luc. 16, 22.Ioh 3, 16. 6. dum suffragiis vivorum mortuos invari post hanc vitam posse, adserit, quod tamen Scr. S. negat. Vid. Psal. 49, 8. 9. & 10.Eccl. 9, 4.Matth. 5, 26.c. 25, 8. 9.Marc. 3, 31.Labefactat insuper Purgatorium articulum de DEI misericordia, quae culpam & poenam remittit. Matth. 8, 27.de eiusdem iustitia, quae remissâ culpâ etiam poenam remittit. -e meriti Christi efficacia, ut qui non tantùm pro orig sed etiam pro actualibus nostris peccatis, pro poenis tum temporalibus tum aeternis propter peccata nobis debitis plenissimam satisfactionem Deo praestitit, Es. 53, 4. 5. 6.Ioh 1, 29.Gal. 3, 131. Petr. 2, 24.de salutari poenitentia, cuius fructus plenaria peccatorum remissio, Ps. 32, 5.Luc. 24, 47.Act. 3, 19.de remissione peccatorum totali ac gratuita,Ps. 25, 7.Ps. 32, 1.Ier. 31, 31.Mich. 7, 19. de iustificatione nostri pacifica & plenariâ. Rom. 5, 1. 2.c. 8, 1.24.33, 34.c. 12, 12.Ioh. 3 36. &c. de die novissimâ. Si enim quoad illos, qui ante diem extremum moriuntur, opus est Purgatorio, eodem quoque opus erit quoad hos, quos dies novissimus vivos deprehendet. neque enim dari potest diversitatis ratio. At hoc pugnat cum doctrina de die extremo. Sed haec pluribus deducit B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. 3. p. 423. seqq add. L. de Morte §. 182. seqq. Dispp. Acad. p. 440. Conf. etiam B. D. Gerlach. Tom. 2. Dispp. Theol. Disp. 28. p. 4037.

Porrò de Purgatorio Papistico h. l. non agi, probatur 2. à circumstantiarum, tum quoantec. & conseqq. consideratione. Agitur in v. praeced. 23. 24. de reconciliatione fraternâ. Igitur per Adversarium etiam in hoc versiculo commodissimè intelligitur proximus noster. Ita Peltanus, Salmeron, Iansenius, Franc. Lucas & alii in h. l Alii per Adversarium, scribit Iesuita Maldonatus in h. l. p. 121. intelligunt eum, de quo paullò ante dixerat, vade priùs, reconciliare fratri tuo. Ita Hil. can. 4. Ambr. l. 7. inLuc. c. 12.Auct. Op. Imp. hom. 11. Hier. in Comm. Atque hic verus est sensus. Adversarius igitur noster est ilie, quem lasimus, quem raca aut stultum appellavimus, qui actionem apud Deum contra nos habet. Eod. modo explicat etiam Ioh. Ferus in Com. h. l. In externis, inquit, rebus, nonnunquam satiùs est, etiam iniquis conditionibus cum adversario componere, quam lites & contentiones sequi. Bellarminus contrà per Advers. intelligit Deum, Iesuita Conzen Diabolum, cum quibus quomodo etiam iniquis conditionibus componere debeamus, vel etiam quomodo benevolentiam cum Diabolo habere debeamus, equidem non video. Diversum etiam docet S. Aug quando lib. de decem chortis. c. 3. Quis est iste Advesarius? Adversarius iste non est Diabolus. Nam nunquam te hortaretur Scriptura, ut cum Diabolo concordares. Unde S. Basil. in reg. brevior. interr. 222. Quis est adversarius unius cuiusnostrum, quomodove cum eo consentientes erimus? Resp. praecisè h. in l. Dominus adversarium illum appellat, qui aliquid nobis conatur adimere eorum, quae ad nostrum ius pertinent. Porrò illi consencientes sumus, si praeceptum Domini illud servamus: Qui vult tecum iudicio contendere, & tunicam tuam tollere, dimitte ei pallium &c. Non dissentit Tertullian. l. de anima c. 35. Haec quomodo Card. Bell. ac Iesuita Conzen s. ad Deum s. ad Diabolum accommodare velint, ipsi viderint. Porrò per carcerem Bell Conzen. ac Purg. Patroni intelligunt purgatorium, per quadrantem minutissima peccata, unde etiam Conzen admodùm occupatus hîc, est ut doceat, quàm minutum numismatis genus sit quadrans. Quicquid verò de hâc re sit, quî minima peccata Deo reddi possint, Card. ac Iesuita dispiciant. certum est, locutionem esse metaphoricam & sermonem ad forensem consuetudinem accommodatum, monente Iesuitâ Maldonato. Iam autem Bellarminus ipse l. 3. de V. D. c. 3. docet, ex solo sensu litterali peti debere argumenta efficacia. quemadmodum etiam Ludov. ab Alcasar in c. 11. Apoc. scribit, quòd Theologia symbolica non sit argumentativa. Adstipulantur Pontificii alii, uti Alphonsus de Castro l. r. adv. haeres c. 3. l. 4. verbo Concilium, Salmeron Proleg. 19. p, 340. &c. E. ex h. l. Purgatorium, si vel maximè detorqueri is ad Purg. Pontif. posset, solidè probari nequit. Satiùs verò est, per carcerem intelligere ipsum infernum, prout etiam accipiunt Sancti Patres, Hieronymus, Augustinus, Theophylactus, alii, nec aliter quoque intellexisse Ambrosius videtur, dum pro eodem habet cum tenebris exterioribus,Matth. 22, 13. it. cum camino ignis,Matth. 13, 42. Eodem quoque modo sumunt Glossa Interlin. Dion. Carthus. Alphonsus Tostatus, Maldonatus, in h. l. Franc. Toletus, Didacus Stella, in c. 12. Lucae. alii.

Regerunt quidem Purgatorii aediles, obstare huic expositioni particulam donec, quâ significetur, illos, quibus Christus hîc carcerem minatur, aliquando inde exituros esse, iam verò ex inferno nullam dari redemtionem. Respond. nec hîc necesse esse, liberationem è carcere statuere. licet enim particula illa aliquando tempus praeteritum determinet, & futurum excludat; saepè tn. indeterminatè accipitur, ita ut sequens tempus omne includatur, adeoper nunquam exponenda sit. Cuiusmodi pluscula exempla in S. litt. occurrunt. & ab ipsis Iesuitis notata sunt. Iesuita Tirinus confirmat hanc acceptionem ex 2. Reg. 6, 23.Matth. 1, 23. Idem docent Iesuitae alii, ceu patetex Gasp. Sanctio Comm. in libb. Reg. p. 628. Corn. à Lapide itidem Comm. in libb Reg. t. 2. p. 25. it. Comm. in Matth, p. 58. Similiter particulam donec Cantic. 3. v. 4. accipiendam esse, observant Mich. Ghislerius Romanus, ex clericis regul. S. Silvestri &c. Comm. in Cant. p. 410. a. Evolvantur etiam Felicianus Capitonus Narniensis Explic. Cath. p. 375. Guilielmus Estius, Prof Theol. Duacenus Comm. in Epist. Pauli t. 1. pag. 487. a Bernh. Paxillus de Brzezek, Ord. Praed. S. Domin. in Monomach. pro Def. fidei SS. Trinit. p. 623. & 828. Iodocus Coccius in eand. sententiam loca ex Theophylacto & Ambrosio adducit, lib. 3. Thes. Cath. p. 278. 280. Plusculis autem exemplis confirmat hoc ipsum Iesuita laboriosissimus Ioh. Lorinus Comm. in Ps. t. 3. p. 263. ubi pro signif. illâ, quòd donec non certum semper tempus determinet, affert Exod. 15, 16.Deut. 7, 24.2. Reg. 6, 23.Ps. 109, 1.Ps. 111, 8.Ps. 122, 2.Matth. 1, 25.c. 10, 23. c, ult. v. 20. 1. Tim. 4, 13. Quod verò & h. l. particula doneo in tali significatione accipienda sit, docent Patres antiquissimi. Locum in hanc rem ex Hieron. in c. 1. Lament. Ierem. ipse Iesuita Ioh. de la Haye nobis suppeditat satis clarum, in Triumpho verit. p. 293. Quae Augustini sententia sit, docet Iesuita Maldonatus. Quod autem, scribit Comm. in h. l. p. 121. dicit, nos inde non exituros, donec ultimum quadrantem persolvamus, non significat, ut ait Augustinus, exituros postea; sed nunquam exituros, quia qui in inferno sunt, cùm semper debitas poenas solvant, quia pro quolibet mortali peccato infinitas poenas debent, nunquam persolvunt. Conf. etiam Theoph. super c. 12. Lucae. Plures Patrum sententias adducere, vix opus est. Fortè magis ad placitum erit, audire Conzenii sociennos ac patres, ut quidem salutari volunt, societatis Iesu. Ita igitur Corn. à Lapide ad c. 1. Matth. p. 58. Matth. 5, 26.Non exies inde, donec reddas &c. hoc est, nunquam exibis de carcere inferni. Idem tamen sui oblitus ad h. l. scribit: Age citò ut reconcilieris fratri tuo, antequam Deo iudici quasi reus tradaris, qui iustâ vindicta te mancipet carceri, donec omne debitum solvas, vel lethale & aeternum in inferno, vel veniale & temporale in purgatorio: ad purgatorium enim inclinat vocula donec, quae finiendam significat ponam, haec enim finitur in Purgatorio, cùm in inferno nunquam terminetur, sitaeterna: Constantior Iesuita Maldonatus in h. l. Eodem scribit, sensu h. l. dictio illa, donec, accipienda est, quo supra c. 1, 25. Excipit.

verò Sophista Bellarminus, dicitque, probari de Purg. hic agi inde, quia illud: donec solvas ultimum quadrantem, non videtur rectè posse dici, nisi aliquando sit faturus finis solutionis. pergit: neexempla Augustini satis faciunt; nam cùm dicitur: Non cognoscebat eam, donec parere, non licet quidem inferre, ergo postea cognovit eam, sed inferre licet, ergo illa aliquando paritura erat; similiter cùm dicitur, sede à dextris meis, donec ponam &c. rectè infertur, ergò aliquando ponentur omnes inimici Christi sub pedibus eius: ita orgo cùm dicitur: Non o-ies donec solvas ultimum quadrantem, inferimus rectè, ergò aliquando solvet ultimum quadrantē, & consequeuter exibit inde. Haec ipsa tanquam sua lectori inculcat quoque Iesuita Adamus Conzen Comm. in h. l. Verùm resp. 1. si vel maximè concedatur, innui hoc ipso, futurum aliquando ut solvat ultimum quadrantem, non tamen sequitur, quòd propterea exire debeat ex illo carcere, quòdq; adeo carcer ille sit purgatorium, non verò infernus. Quum semper debitas poenas solvant damnati, quia pro quolibet peccato infinitas poenas debent, nunquam tamen persolvunt, scribit Augustinus. Eod. modo Hieronymus in c. 1. Thr. Ierem. Significat, semper non exiturum esse, quia semper solvit novissimum quadrantem, dum sempiternas poenas terrenorum peccatorum luit 2. Nicolaus de Lyra in h. l. negat, in inferno unquam esse possibilem redditionem, adeoque donec h. l. per nunquam exponendum esse, docet. 3. patet hoc, quòd illi, qui cum, peccato mortali, (de quo h. l. sermo est, nempe de odio & implacabilitate, conf. Matth. 18, 17.Gal. 5, 20.1. Ioh. 3, 5.Apoc. 21, 8.) decedunt, non possint satisfacere vel solvere ultimum quadrantem, etiam inde, quia ipsi Pontificii docent, quòd tales non in Purgatorium, sed in infernum mittantur. Vid. Corn. à Lap. ad Matth. p. 359. b. & patet idem ex all. locis. 4. Sed instant Bell. ac Conzen, nihilominus ex similibus locutionibusPs. 110.acMatth. 1, 25.manifestum, cùm particula donec ponitur, duo semper addi, quorum alterutrum fieri necesse est. Resp. Damus instantiam Matth. 18, 24.34. ubi similiter dicitur, quòd Dominus tradiderit eum, qui debebat decem millia talentorum, nec erat tamen solvendo, tortoribus,ἕως οὗdonec redderet totum, quod debebat. Ad h. v. locum ipse Conzen sic annotat: Quae poena servi? Ut omnia redderet, quae cùm non posset, aeternum debuit, ideoin carcere permansit. Alioqui si minor summa, persolvere potuisset. Deus quotum omnia ad extremum exigit, cum in proximos crudelis quispiam esse coepit. Eod. modo proponunt quoque Arias Montanus, nec non Corn. à Lapide in h. l. ubi pro eadem explicatione adducit quoque Chrysostomum, Theoph., Euthymium. Largimur igitur 5. quòd ultimus quadrans in carcere illo sit solvendus h. e. quôd pro peccato, si vel minimum etiam videatur, nisi ante obitum homo remissionem impetraverit, quod fieri non potest, nisi odium adversus proximum deposuerit, in inferno damnati promeritas poenas persolvere debeant, & torquendi sint tantisper, dum solvants. exsolvant, huius tamen consequens non est, quòd etiam persolvere possint, adeoque exituri è carcere illo sint. Distingvimus igitur cum Hieronymo inter solutionem sive rigidam solutionis exactionem, & persolutionem sive exolutionem. Illae à damnatis requiri, concedimus, sed exinde non sequitur, quôd exeant è carcere; hanc verò negamus praestari à damnatis unquam posse, quia poena eorum, qui cum ira, odio & vindictae cupido animo h. e. cum peccato mortali hinc discedunt, infinita ac aeterna est. Et huc respexit Augustinus, quando: Unde, inquit, solvitur illud de bitum, ubi iam non datur poenitendi aut correctionis locus. Audiant Iesuitae, Cardinalis Bell. ac Conzen sociennum suum, Didacum de Baeza, in de Christo figurato opere, de quo Franciscus de Sorio Officii Inquisitionis Censor ita iudicat, quòd magis admirationi compactum sit, quàm censurâ egeat. Ille verò neutiquam ad purgatorium ignem locum hunc torquet, sed omninò de aeternis flammis accipiPlanè, scribit, in reprobis non solùm ingentia scelera, sed & minima eternas flammas accendunt. Non enim ob sola magnae debita detinebuatur reprobi in inferni carcere, sed ob minimi quadrantis debitum. Quo respiciens DominusMatth. 5.ait peccatori impoenitenti: Iudex tradat &c. In novissimo quadrante intelligunt D. Hieron. & D. Aug m-nutissima quaepeccata, quae in carcere inferni punienda sunt, quae qu ibi semper integra manebunt, nunquam satis poenarum dabunt, ut possint reprobi illorum videre finem. Hactenus Iesuita allegatus p. 83.

Probamus 3. ex Christi scopo & intentione. Certum enim est, voluisse Christum proposito periculo aeterni supplicii suos impellere, ut citò, dum in viâ sunt, quaerant reconciliationem, ne incidant in poenas, quas in aeternum evadere non poterunt. Sed haec seria ac necessaria exhortatio blasphemè enervatur, si purgatorii opinio contradicat: Etiam si mitraris in carcerem, poteris inde exire, persolutâ vel per te, vel per aliorum suffragia purgatorii poenâ. non igitur adeo opus erit, ut tam solicitus sis de reconciliatione, dum in viâ es, Ita Magnus Chemnitius in Harm. Evang. c. 51. p. 445.

Confirmamus 4. nostram sententiam, quôd h. l. non agat de Purgatorio, Patrum testificatione. Hieronymum in c. 1. Thren. Ierem. favere nostrae expositioni, concedit Iesuita de la Haye; Augustinum, nostrum hîc esse, docent Tostatus Abulensis, Iesuita Didacus de, Baeza, de Christo fig. p. 83. & Maldonatus in h. l Largiuntur quoq; Cardinalis Bellarminus & Iesuita Conzen; Dictum hoc Christi à Chrysostomo hom. 24. in Matth. & Graecis Patribus longè aliter, quàm de Purgatorio exponi, expressè testatur Iesuita Franciscus Suarez, primò in Acad. Complutensi, postea in Salmanticensi, deinceps Romae ac denique Conimbricae in Lusitania Theologiae Professor primarius; Bedam quoque Venerabilem nostrum esse, docet Thomas Aquinas in Catenâ in Lucam, nec non Franc Lucas in h. l. Atqs hinc iudicari facilè potest, quam fidem mereatur Apostata Pistorius, quando ad Patres provocat: scribit enim is in Hodeg. p. 578. Omnes Patres aqualiter (gleichmossig) locum hunc de Purgatorio exponere. Cùm tamen Pontificii ipsi modò adducti ultrò fateantur, Hieronymum, Augustinum, Chrysostomum, Bedam Venerabilem ac Patres Graecos non de purgatorio, sed de suppliciis aeternis locū hunc interpretari. Cogitetur verò etiā, quid statendum de eo sit, cui tamen fermè unicè nititur Pistorii hypothesis, quòd non possit hic locus aliter nisi de purgatorio accipi, quando scribit: illos, qui iracundo & implacabiti animo hinc discesservnt, habuisse (eo nempe tempore, quo discesservnt) veram ac vivificam fidem. p. 578. Quod assertum conferatur cum 1. Tim. 1, 19.Ioh. 4, 8.Iac. 2, 17.

Addimus denique 5. ipsorum quorundam Adversariorum, Cardin. etiam ac iesuitarum, confessionem. Ut ut enim non pauci coeco impetu Bellarminum hîc sequantur, nunquam tamen defuerunt cordati quidam viri, qui licet purgatorium ignem diligenter aliàs fovendum putarint, probè scientes, quòd nisi ignis ille ferveat, culinae ipsorum frigeant, quin & Curiae Romanae aliàs non inutilia servitia praestiterint, hîc tamen Placentiam praetervecti rectà Veronam contenderunt. Id quod inde patet, dum alii de Purgatorio ex professo agentes dictum hoc praetermittunt, uti Iesuitae, Coturius ac Greg. de Valentia; alii de inferno hîc agi, non v. de Purgatorio, adservnt, uti Iesuitae Maldonatus in h l. ac Seb. Barradius t. 2. Conc. Evang. l. 7. c. 17. alii, non posse ex h. l. Purgatorium certò probari, ultrò largiuntur, uti Iesuitae Iacobus Reihing in Manuali Cath. art. 10. ac Iansenius in h. l. Unde etiam Thomas Stapletonus, Profess. regius in Acad. Lovaniensi in Antidoto h. l. Calvinum advertere iubet, paucissimos hodie esse, qui hunc locum eo modo (de Purgatorio) exponant; alii denique concedunt, posse locum hunc aliter, quàm de Purgatorio exponi. ita ipse Stapletonus modò citatus. Et referri quoque huc possunt, qui τὸdonec h. l. exponunt per nunquam, uti Maldonatus, in h. l. Corn. à Lap. in c. 1. Matth. Franc. Toletus, (Cardinalis idemque Iesuita magnis ingenii laudibus, solidâ doctrinâ, & perspicuitate praestans, praeconio Possevini in Appar.) in c. 12. Lucaeomnes hi Iesuitae, item Alphonsus Tostatus in h. l. ac Didacus Stella Lusitanus, ex ordine Minorum Episcopus in c. 12. Lucae, Didacus de Baeza comm. all. p 83. b. alii. Sed valere tandem iubemus Bellarminum ac sequaces cum igne suo purgatorio, non immeritô veriti, ne, ubi semel accesserint ignem post hanc vitam, unquam ab eo liberentur, si vel mille etiam Missae pro illis celebrentur, sed fore ut incalescant ibi plus satis, & reapse experiantur, τὸdonec h. l. idem significare, quod nunquam.)*

## 5:27
v. 27. Ἠκοὸσατε,

Connection. From the explanation of the fifth commandment, Christ passes to the exposition of the sixth commandment and its vindication from Pharisaic corruptions.

It must be understood, however, that the Pharisees and Scribes taught that by the law concerning not committing adultery, only the act of illegitimate intercourse is prohibited, but not the inner desire and the depraved concupiscence of the same, especially the involuntary one. And that he who does not commit adultery outwardly fulfills this commandment sufficiently.

Ioseph. book 12, antiq. ch. 13. For to have willed, and not also to have performed a sacrilege, does not seem a thing worthy of punishment. R. D. Kimchi in Comm. Ps. 66. Even if I had seen iniquity in my heart, which I was even prepared to bring into act, even though it be before God, even if I had uttered it with my lips, yet the Lord will not hear it. i.e., He will not count it as a crime for me. *(It is truly wonderful how the Jews disagree among themselves here. For even in the Talmud itself a sentiment is read not unlike this oracle of Christ. And thus it stands באשה בכוונה כאילו בא עליה ׃ כל המםתכל i.e., Whoever looks at a woman with intention, it is as if he had had relations with her. Buxt. lists more in Lex. Talm. Rabb. page 1475, also B. Hacksp. tr. de, Script. Iudaic. in Theol. usu. But the Jews in the said place speak not of every look, but of an illicit one, namely of such a woman whom one has neither joined to himself in marriage, nor can join, nor wishes to. And that the Savior's words are also to be accepted in this way, B. D. Franz teaches in de Interpr. Sc. S. Orac. 67.)*

But rightly must it be observed here, that although Cornelius à Lapide on verse 21 states, that Christ sets himself against not only the Scribes and Pharisees and their interpretations of the law, but also against the law of Moses itself, and to supply the imperfections and defects of both, yet here he must acknowledge, just as also at verse 34, that Christ sets himself against the corruptions of the Pharisees, not against the law itself. Which thing other more learned Papists also confess to be done at verses 21 and 22. Maldonatus (a Jesuit otherwise sharp-witted, and otherwise so stubbornly clinging to the errors of the Papists, that even though he sometimes detects another interpretation of others to be most probable and supported by the consensus of the Fathers, he nevertheless refuses to follow it, because it is not Papist, but chooses another less probable one, provided only that it conflicts more with the sense of the Calvinists, for he holds that this is a great argument of probability for him, as can be seen from his Commentary on John chapter 6, verse 62, p. 652) here takes our side, i.e., lays down that in vv. 21 seqq. Christ deals only against the perverse interpretations of the law of the Pharisees, therefore he here sets himself not against the law and Moses, but only against the Scribes and Pharisees and their interpretations of the law, which Cornelius freely grants. But still another witness contradicting the Jesuit Cornelius to his face must also be heard. That man indeed is Franciscus Lucas, Theologian and Dean of the Cathedral Church of Saint-Omer, whose Commentary on the Gospels came forth with this encomium of the Bishop of Saint-Omer and the Theologians of Douai, that they contain nothing contrary to the orthodox faith, but are moreover composed with great zeal and trusty diligence.

Here however, on Matthew 5:22: He does not oppose himself to Moses or the law, to the author of the law; but to the interpreters of the law, the Scribes. But Capellus in Spicil. p. 13 thinks indeed & -udov. from this verse 27, that it is clear that by the name τῶν ἀρχαίων v. 21, it cannot be understood to be those, who lived either in the time of Christ, or a little before the times of Christ, but that τὸ ἐῤῥέθη τοῖς ἀρχαίοις signifies, it was said by Moses to your ancestors, since the teachers of the Jews, who lived in the time of Christ, are not the authors of that law οὐ μοιχεύσεις. But I answer, even if those Doctors were not the authors of the said law, they nevertheless restricted the sixth commandment to the external act of illicit intercourse only. Which Capellus could have learned sufficiently even from his Master John Calvin, for he rightly notes in Comm. in Harmon. Evang. p. 49, although Christ refers to the words of the law, he nevertheless reproves the gross adulterous sense, which sinister Interpreters had introduced, namely that one must beware of nothing but external adultery, or illicit intercourse, from that.

Latin:

v. 27. Ἠκοὸσατε,

Connexio. A praecepti quinti explicatione transit Christus ad sexti praecepti expositionem & à corruptelis Pharisaicis vindionem.

Subintelligendum verò, quòd Pharisaei & Scribae docuerint, lege de non moechando tantùm prohiberi illegitimi concubitus actum, non autem interius desiderium & concupiscentiam eiusdem pravam, maximè involuntariam. Quòdq; sufficienter hoc praeceptum impleat, qui exteriùs non moechetur.

Ioseph. lib. 12. antiq. cap. 13. Voluisse enim tantùm, ac non etiam perfecisse sacrilegium, non videtur res supplicio digna. R. D. Kimchi in Comm. Ps. 66.Etiamsi viderim iniquitatem in cerde meo, quam vel paratus essem in actum perducere, ut ut illa sit coram Deo, atsi eam labiis protulissem, tamen non audiet eam Dominus. q. d non ducet eam mihi sceleri. *(Mirum verò, quomodo Iudaei inter se hîc discrepent. Nam & in ipso Talmud sententia legitur non dissimilis huic Christi oraculo. Ita verò ea sese habet באשה בכוונה כאילו בא עליה ׃ כל המםתכל i. e. Quicunadspicit mulierem cum intentione, perinde est, ac si rem habuisset cum ea. Plures recenset Buxt. Lex. Talm. Rabb. pag. 1475. it. B. Hacksp. tr. de, Script. Iudaic. in Theol. usu. Loquuntur verò Iudaei d. l. non de omni, sed de illicito s. talis mulieris, quam quis matrimonio sibi nec coniunxit, nec iungere etiam potest, aut vult, adspectu. & ita quoque accipienda Salvatoris verba esse, docet B. D. Franz. de Interpr. Sc. S. Orac. 67.)*

Probè verò hîc observandum, quòd licet Cornelius à Lapide ad versum 21. statuat, Christum non tantùm Scribis & Phariseis eorumque legis interpretationibus sese opponere, sed ipsi etiam legi Mosis, & utrorumimperfectiones & defectus supplere, hîc tamen, quemadmodum etiam vers. 34. agnoscere, Christum Pharisaeorum, eorruptelis sese opponere, non ipsi legi. Id quodetiam alii doctiores Pontificii vers. 21. & 22. fieri, fatentur. Maldonatum, (Iesuitam aliàs acutum, ac tam pertinaciter alioquin Pontificiorum erroribus adhaerentem, ut licet aliotum interpretationem probabilissimam ac Patrum consensu suffultam aliquando deprehendat, nolit tamen eam sequi, quia non Pontificii est, sed aliam minùs probabilem, modò magis cum Calvinistarum sensu pugnet, id enim magnum sibi probabilitatis argumentum esse. ceu ex Comm. eius in, c. 6. Ioh. v. 62. p. 652. videre licet,) nobiscum hic facere, h. e. statuere, Christum v. 21. seqq. tantùm agere contra perversas Pharisaeorum legis interpretationes, ideoipsum hîc non se opponere legi & Moysi, sed tantùm Scribis & Pharisaeis corumlegis interpretationibus, ultrò Cornelius largitur. Audiendus verò & alter adhuc testis est, in os contradicens Iesuitae Cornelio. Ille verò Franciscus Lucas est, Ecclesiae Cathedralis Audomaropolitanae Theologus & Decanus, cuius Comm. in Evang. cum hoc elogio Episcopi Audom. & Theologorum Duacensium prodierunt, quòd nihil contineant orthodoxae fidei contrarium, sed magno insuper studio ac fidâ diligentiâ compositi sint.

Hic verò ad v. 22. Matthaei: Non Mosi aut legi se opponit, mumtnùs legis auctori; sed legis explanatoribus S-ribis. Putat verò & -udov. Capellus in Spicil. p. 13. è vers. hoc 27. liquere, nomine τῶν ἀρχαίων v. 21. non intelligi posse eos, qui vel Christi tempore, vel paulo ante Christi tempora vixerunt, sed τὸ ἐῤῥέθη τοῖς ἀρχαίοις significare, dictum est à Mose maioribus vestris, cum Iudaeorum docteres, qui Christi tempore vivebant, non sint autores legis illiusοὐ μοιχεύσεις. Verùm resp. etsi Doctores illi non fuerunt dictae legis autores, restrin-erunt tamen sextum praeceptum ad externum tantùm illiciti concubitûs actum. Quod vel à Magistro suo Ioh. Calvino satis discere poterat Capellus, rectè n. ille Comm. in Harmon. Evang. p. 49. monet, quamvis Christus referat verba legis, crassum tamen atadulterinum sensum, quem sinistri Interpp. induxerant, quod nempe nonnisi ab externo adulterio, sive illicito concubitu, cavendum sit, ab eo reprebendi.

## 5:28
v. 28. Ἐγὼ

ὁ βλέπων. * ( לינא ועינא תרי םרםורי רחטאה נינהו is read in En Israel p. 47. col. 1. i. e. The heart & the eyes are two procurers of sin.)* The Hebrews say. The eyes & the heart are procurers of love.* (Compare here B. Par. Comm in Post. epistle of Peter p. 281. Marcell. Donatus Dilucid. on Suetonius Tiber. c. 7. Thes. Crit. t. 6. p. 566. Corn. à Lap. Rittershus on Salvianus p. 96. seqq. [in h. l p. 141. a.] also Grotius on h. l. B. D. Chemn. t. 2. LL. p. 76. Furthermore, that the very will to sin was held as a sin even by the Gentiles, Capell. shows in Spicil page 14.)*

*(With the Papists teaching that Christ, not content with the old law, handed down through Moses, had guarded against the vision of the eyes, as Didacus de Baeza speaks in Christo fig. p. 35. we set forth for consideration the places Exod. 20, 17.Iob. 24, 15.c. 31, 1.Prov. 6, 24.c. 23, 33.Ier. 5, 8.Ezech. 6, 9.c. 23, 16. Which are also to be opposed to the Photinians, since they conspire here with the Papists. see B. P. L. de Ev. §. 78.)*

Γυναῖκα. he does not say, the wife of his brother, but simply, a woman, so that he may also teach that an unchaste look at a woman, loose from marriage, is prohibited by divine law. *St. Chrysostom in the homily inscribed: That it is dangerous to attend spectacles, gravely concludes from the present place, and discourses at length, that spectacles in which women acting and dancing are present are to be avoided by young men. The same is also done by Basil the Great in the sermon on drunkenness & luxury. Let those things also be compared which D. Rittersh. collected on this matter in Comm. on Salvianus p. 191. & 194.)*

The Papist tries to prove from the little word Πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι ἀυτῆς. that here only wicked voluntary, contrived and sought-out lust is condemned, by which, namely, a man attempts to stir up within himself, casting his eyes upon a woman for this purpose, so that he may feed himself with that lust already kindled inwardly in his mind. But this proceeds from ignorance of the Greek phrase. Πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι ἀυτῆς is the same as ὥςε ἐπιθυμῆσαι ἀυτῆς, so as to lust after her: for what is signified is not the end of looking, but an accompanying circumstance whereby the manner or outcome of the looking—which arises from the sight—is declared, even apart from the intention of the one who looks. *(Cornelius à Lapide acknowledges this very thing himself, writing on this passage: Note that it signifies not only the end, but also the attainment or consequence: not only is he an adulterer who sees and gazes at a woman with this end, that he might delight himself with her appearance and lust, but also he who gazes at her out of curiosity etc. Meanwhile, however, the same Cornelius errs, asserting shortly before that under this law first and involuntary motions of lust are neither forbidden nor condemned, since these are not within man's choice and power. But this is an old error of the Papists, long ago noted and refuted by our own writers. See Dr. Chemnitius, vol. 2, Theological Lectures, p. 89, 90; Pastor of Heidelberg, Catholic Confession, vol. 4, p. 434 sqqq.; likewise On Sin, § 36 sqqq.; Dr. Mylius on the Augsburg Confession, art. 34 sqqq.; Dr. Gerhard, part 1, on the Augsburg Confession, p. 291 sqqq., others.)* A similar phrase occurs Job 31:1⟧ 1 John 5:16⟧ ρὸς

*(Since he seems to himself to have obtained here most ample field for inveighing against the female sex, Cornelius à Lapide, a most famous Jesuit—whence, after citing some opinions of others recently reviewed—he adds also this maxim of his own: Woman is a basilisk in sight, a siren in voice; she enchants with her voice, destroys with her sight; she ruins and kills both ways. And indeed the same fellow-soldier runs over the same field along with Cornelius, Diego de Baeza of Ponferrada, of the Province of Castile, Allegorical and Moral Commentary on Christ figured in the Old Testament—from which, should anyone happen to need material for invectives against the female sex, he can obtain it abundantly, especially pp. 80, 81, 270, 414, 432, 219, 233.)*

Ἐμοίχευσενἀυτὴν, committed adultery with her. The species is put for the genus συνεκδοχικῶς, violated her.

Salvian. lib 3. de provid. From this we can clearly understand how -st the Savior commanded us to be, who even cut off the license of vision. For knowing that the windows of our minds are in a way the of our eyes, and that all wicked desires enter into the heart through the eyes, as if through natural tunnels, He wished to extinguish them completely on the outside, lest they should arise within and perhaps grow strong in the soul with lethally growing fibers, if they had sprouted in the sight. *(Conf. also Justin Martyr. Apolog 2. pro Christ. p. 48)*
