v. 28. Ἐγὼ

ὁ βλέπων. * ( לינא ועינא תרי םרםורי רחטאה נינהו legitur in En Israel p. 47. col. 1. i. e. Cor & oculi duo proxenetae peccati sunt.)* Hebraei dicunt. Oculi & corproxenetae amoris.* (Conset hîc B. Par. Comm in Post. epist. Petri p. 281. Marcell. Donatum Dilucid. ad Suetonii Tiber. c. 7. Thes. Crit. t. 6. p. 566. Corn. à Lap. Rittershus ad Salvianum p. 96. seqq. [in h. l p. 141. a.] it. Grotiū ad h. l. B. D. Chemn. t. 2. LL. p. 76. Caeterùm ipsam peccandi voluntatem ab Ethnicis quoque pro peccato suisse habitam, ostendit Capell. in Spicil pag 14.)*

*(Pontificiis docentibus quòd Christus non contentus veteri legi, per Mosen traditae, oculorum quovisionem caverit, ut loquitur Didacus de Baeza in Christo fig. p. 35. consideranda sistimus loca Exod. 20, 17.Iob. 24, 15.c. 31, 1.Prov. 6, 24.c. 23, 33.Ier. 5, 8.Ezech. 6, 9.c. 23, 16. Quae ipsa etiam Photinianis opponenda, cum Pontificiis hîc conspirantibus. vid. B. P. L. de Ev. §. 78.)*

Γυναῖκα. non dicit, mulierem fratris sui, sed simpliciter, mulierem, ut etiam impudicum solute à matrimonio foeminae aspectum lege divinâ prohibitum esse, doceat. *S. Chrysostomus homil inscriptâ: Periculosum esse adire spectacula, è praesenti loco graviter concludit, ac prolixè disserit, vitanda esse à iuvenibus spectacula, quibus mulieres agentes ac saltantes intersunt. Idem quoque facit Basilius Magnus serm. de ebriet. & luxu. Conferantur quoq; quae in hanc rem collegit D. Rittersh. Cōm. ad Salvianum p. 191. & 194.)*

Πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι ἀυτῆς. Pontificii ex vocula ρὸς evincere conātur, hîc tantûm voluntariam, procuratam & expetitam concupiscentiam pravam damnari, quā sc. homo in se excitare conatur, oculos eo fine in mulierem coniiciendo, ut eoncupiscentia in animo intus iam accensâ sese pascat. Sed hoc procedit ex ignorantiâ Graecae phraseos. Πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι ἀυτῆς idem est, quod ὥςε ἐπιθυμῆσαι ἀυτῆς,ita ut eam concupiscat: non enim significatur finis aspectus, sed adiunctum, quo declaratur aspiciendi modus vel eventus, qui ex aspectu existit, etiam praeter intentionem aspicientis. *(Agnoseit hoc ipse Corn. à Lapide, scribens ad h. l. Adverte, Iò ad non tantùm significare finem, sed & consequutionem sive sequelam: non tantùm moechus est, qui videt & intuetur mulierem hoc fine, ut eius adspectu & concupiscentiâse oblectet, sed & is, qui eam intuetur ex curiositate &c. Interea tamen errat idem Cornelius, adserens paullo ante, hâc lege nō vetari, nec damnari primos & involuntarios concupiscentiae motus, cùm hi in hominis arbitrio ac potestate non sint. Sed antiquus hîc Pontificiorum error est, pridem à nostratibus notatus ac refutatus. Vid. B. D. Chemn. t. 2. LL. Th. pag. 89. 90 B. Par. Conf. Cath. t. 4 pag. 434. seqq. item L. de Pecc. §. 36. seqq B. D. Mylius in A. C. 34. seqq. B. D. Graverus part. 1. in A. C. p. 291. seqq. alii.)* Similis phrasis extat Iob. 31. v. 1.1. Ioh 5. v. 16.

*(Amplissimum nactus sibi videtur hîc campum invehendi in sexum mulierem, Cornelius à Lapide, Iesuita famosissimus unde post recensitas aliquot aliorum sententias de suo quoque addit hanc gnomam: Foemina visu est Basiliscus, voce Siren; voce incantat, visu demontat; utroperdit & necat. Eundem verò cum Cornelio decurrit campum eiusdem sociennus, Didacus de Baeza Ponferradiensis è Provinc. Castellana, Comment. alleg. & moral. de Christo fig. in V. T. è quo si quis invectivis in sexum mulierem opus fortè habuerit, petere abunde potest, cum primis pag. 80. 81. 270. 414. 432. 219. 233.)*

Ἐμοίχευσενἀυτὴν,adulterium cum ea commisit. Species pro genere συνεκδοχικῶς ponitur, constupravit eam.

Salvian. lib 3. de provid. Hinc intelligere planè possumus, quàm -stos nos esse Salvator iusserit, qui etiam licentiam visionis abscidit. Sciens enim, fenestras quodammodo esse nostrarum mentium, lum-n aculorum, & omnes improbas cupiditates in cor per oculos, quasi per natur ales cuniculos introire, extinguereeas penitus foris voluit, ne intus orirentur & letaliter crescentibus fibris convalescerent fortassè in animo, si germinassent in visu. *(Conf. etiam Iustin Martyr. Apolog 2. pro Christ. p. 48)*

v. 29. τῶν

v. 29. τῶν

## 5:30
v. 30. Καὶ εἰ ἥ δεξία σου &c.

Connection. On the occasion of what He had said. Whoever looks at a woman &c. He commands to pluck out the eye that causes scandal. The same precept is repeated below in chapter 18. v. 9.

By the right hand, they say a friend is signified; by the eye, a counselor: *(And the interpretation of Salvian can be referred to here, who understands it concerning those of the household, lib. 3 de Gubern DEI p. 88. Furthermore, whether it is the literal sense, if these words are taken concerning the mortifying of members, or concerning separation from a neighbor if he is a scandal to us, or whether it is spiritual, which Lyra wants, Rivetus discusses in Isag. ad Scr. S. c. 14)* But this precept of Christ is more correctly understood concerning the wicked concupiscence in those members being mortified, namely that we ought to restrain and mortify wicked concupiscence, in whatever members of the body it may manifest itself, through the Spirit, even if this is not accomplished without pain and difficulty, just as neither can an eye be plucked out nor a hand cut off without pain. *(From the fact, however, that this precept of Christ concerning plucking out the eye and cutting off the foot is not to be understood literally, it is clear how ineptly some bring an argument from this place for ἀυτοχειρία concluding: If it is expedient, as Christ says, to cut off these members of the body for the sake of avoiding scandal, it will not be whereby it is illicit to kill oneself, if some necessity demands it. But concerning this matter, one can see above all B. D. Ronte in Cas. Consc. p. 48 where he learnedly answers to the sayings and examples of Scripture which are accustomed to be brought forward for ἀυτοχειρία. Conf. also B. Par L. de Lege Dei §. 155.)*

A parallel passage exists Col. 3. v. 5. Mortify your members, which are upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness, softness, evil concupiscence, and avarice. *(Conf. also Rom 6, 6. Some warn that the present words of Christ can also be taken as spoken by hyperbole, i.e., if scandal cannot be avoided otherwise, one must proceed to the digging out of the eye: understand, however, if it were licit, and you could not otherwise avoid the scandal: But you can do this, and that is illicit. See B. D. Calixt. in Harm. B. D. Glass. Rhet. S. p. 475. B. D. Ro^enig Cas. Conscient. p. 50.)*

Of the right eye and of the right hand mention is made as of the principal members, for the parts on the right are superior and more ready for action, and therefore also dearer.

Ἔξελεἀυτὸν, withdraw yourself by sight from that thing which allures you to sin: act thus, as if your eyes had been plucked out. *(See very similar sayings of the Rabbis in Buxtorff, Lex. Talm. Rabb., under the word אמה, page 114.)*

Bernard, sermon 2, on the feast of Michael. Who would not be moved by what follows in the Gospel: If thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out. For are we admonished to pluck out this bodily eye, or one of those hands; likewise also to cut off one foot? Far be such a fleshly and altogether too ridiculous thought from us. But after the divine discourse has deterred us from outward scandals, rather harshly enough, as you have heard, it gives counsel as to what should be done about the scandal which we suffer inwardly, finding a contrary law in our members. Surely so diligently and steadfastly must scandals be resisted, that it is fitting rather to pluck out eyes and cut off hands than to cherish scandals and depart from the commandments of God. *(Lactantius also ought certainly to be seen, book 6, Institut. divin., chapter 23. In general, however, those who treat of scandals can especially be consulted, whom B. D. Fewrb. supplies, Fascic. 5, Diss. Theol.; B. D. Frantzius, de Interpret. Sc. S., p. 279; B. D. Hutt., LL. Mai., p. 912 sqq.; B. D. Chemn., Harm. Evang., chapters 70, 79, 92; B. Par., Harm. Ev., p. 1482, 1483; B. D. Cundis., notes on Hutt., p. 1167 sqq.)*

Latin:

v. 30. Καὶ εἰ ἥ δεξία σου &c.

Connexio. Occasione eius, quod dixerat. Qui aspicit mulierē &c. praecipit oculum standalizantem eruere. Idem praeceptum repetitur infrà cap. 18. v. 9.

Per dextram, amicum; per oculum Consiliarium significari dicunt: *(Et huc referri potest Salviani interpretatio, qui de demesticis accipit, lib. 3 de Gubern DEI p. 88. Caeterùm an sit sensus litteralis, si verba haec accipiantur de mortificandis membris, velde separatione à proximo, si scandalo nobis est, an verò spiritualis, quod Lyra vult, discutit Rivetus in Isag. ad Scr. S. c. 14)* Sed rectius de prava concupiscentiâ in illis membris mortificandâ hoc Christi praeceptum accipitur, quod videl. concupiscentiam pravam, in quibuscunque tandem corporis membris sese exerat, per Spiritum refrenare & mortificare debeamus, etiamsi hoc non sine dolore & difficultate peragatur, sicutnec oculus sine dolore erui nec manus abscindi potest. *(Ex eo autem, quòd praeceptum hoc Christi de eruendo oculo & abscindendo pede, non propriè intelligendum, patet, quàm ineptè nonnulli argumentum ex h. l. pro ἀυτοχειρία ducant concludentes: Si expedit, dicente Christo, haec atilla corporis membra abseindere scandali vitandi causâ, non erit quoillicitum, seipsum interficere, necessitate aliquâid exigente. Sed de materiâ hâc cumprmis videri B. D. Ronte potest in Cas. Consc. p. 48 ubi ad Scripturae dicta & exempla. quae pro ἀυτοχειρία proferri solent, eruditè -espondit. Conf etiam B. Par L. de Lege Dei §. 155.)*

Locus parallelus extat Col. 3. v. 5.Mórtificate membra vestra, quae super terram, stuprum, immunditiem, mollitiem, concupiseentiam, malam & avaritiam. *(Conf. etiam Rom 6, 6. Monent nonnulli, presentia Christi verba per hyperbolen quoq; dicta accipi posse h. e. si scandalū evitari aliter non queat, procedendum esse ad effossionē oculi: intellige tamen, si licita foret, neq; scandalo occurrere aliter nō possis: Sed & hoc potes, & illicita illa est. Vide B. D. Calixt. in Harm. B. D. Glass. Rhet. S. p. 475. B. D. Ro^enig Cas. Conscient. p. 50.)*

Dextri oculi & dextrae manus tanquam praecipuorum membrorum fit mentio, dextrae enim partes potiores sunt & ad opus expeditiores, ac proinde etiam cariores.

Ἔξελεἀυτὸν, abstrahe te ab illius rei, quae ad peccatum te allicit, aspectu: sic age, ac si oculi tibi essent eruti. *(Videantur similes ferè sententiae Rabb. apud Buxtorff. Lex. Talm. Rabb. voce אמה pag. 114.)*

Bernhard. serm. 2. de festo Michaēlis. I am quem non moveat, quod sequitur in Evangelio: Si oculus tuus dexter te scandalizaverit, erue illum. Nunquid enim corporalem hunc oculum monemur eruert, aut unam ex manibus istis; similiter & unum abscindere, pedem? absit à nobis omninò eiusmodi carnalis & nimis ridicula cogitatio. Sed postquam ab exterioribus scandalis nos deterruit sermo divinus, asperè satis, sicut audistis, consilium dat, quid de eo agendum sit scandalo, quod interius patimur, contrariam invenientes legem in, membris nostris. Tàm sedulò nimirum & constanter resistendum esse, scandalis, ut oculos potiùs eruere & manus abscindere conveniat, quàm ut scandaia foveamus, & à mandatis Dei discedamus. *(Videatur omninò Lactantius lib. 6. Instit. divin. c. 23. De scandalis autem in universum legi cumprimis possunt, quae suppeditant B. D. Fewrb. Fascic. 5. Diss. Theol. B. D. Frantzius de Interpret. Sc. S. p. 279. B. D. Hutt. LL. Mai. p. 912. seqq. B. D. Chemn Harm. Evang. c. 70. 79. 92. B. Par. Harm. Ev. p. 1482. 1483. B. D. Cundis. not. ad Hutt. p. 1167. seqq.)*

## 5:31
ver. 31. Πρὸς

From the fact that he does not add, it was said to them of old time, some conclude that this doctrine of Christ concerning not putting away a wife is opposed no longer to the corruptions of the Pharisaical law but to the law itself Deut. 24. ver. 1. . *(So also thinks Hugo Grotius on this passage.)* But it is said more correctly that even this doctrine of Christ is opposed to the corruptions of the Pharisees, who rashly approved of repudiation, and therefore ἀπὸ κοινοῦ must be repeated from the preceding τοῖς ἀρχαίοις.. For the Pharisees taught that what Moses had conceded on account of σκληροκαρδίαν to avoid a greater evil, as a political judge, was simply lawful and pleasing to God, and that therefore repudiations, made for any cause whatsoever, were free from all blame.

Ἀποστάσιον is used for βιβλίῳ ἀποστάσιον,, as is the Hebrew םמר כריתות. The LXX rendered it a book of cutting off, of abscission, Deut. 24. v. 1. & 3.. The Syrian calls it (i.e., a book of repudiation: the Arab a book of dismissal: thus the Jubilee year Lev. 25, 13. in the Arabic Pentateuch is called i.e., the year of dismissal. The AE likewise renders it nakedly i.e., dismissal. Furthermore, in what form the little book of repudiation was conceived, and also for what causes it was given, will be shown below at c. 19, 7.) It was, however, a schedule subscribed by the hand of the man, by which he testified that this woman had been repudiated by him, and he ceded his right over her, so that it would henceforth be entirely lawful for her to marry another, whom she might wish.

Latin:

v. 31. Πρὸς

Ex eo, quod non addat, dictum est antiquis, quidam colligunt, hanc Christi doctrinam de non dimittenda uxore non ampliùs corruptelis legis Pharisaicis, sed ipsi legiDeut. 24. v. 1.esse oppositam. *(Ita quoque sentit Hugo Grotius ad h. l.)* Sed rectiùs dicitur, etiam hanc Christi doctrinam corruptelis Pharisaeorum, temeraria repudia approbantium, esse oppositam, ideoque ἀπὸ κοινοῦ ex praeced. repetendum τοῖς ἀρχαίοις. Quod enim Moses propter σκληροκαρδίαν vitandi maioris mali ut politicus iudex concesserat, illud simpliciter licitum & Deo gratum esse, adeoque repudia, quavis ex causâ facta, omni culpâ carere, Pharisaei docebant.

Ἀποστάσιον usurpatur pro βιβλίῳ ἀποστάσιον, uti Hebraeum, םמר כריתותliber succisionis, abscissionis, LXX. red diderunt Deut. 24. v. 1. & 3. Syrus vocat *(i. e. librum repudii: Arabs librum dimissionis: sic annus Iubilaeus Lev. 25, 13. in Pentat. Arab. vocatur i. e. annus dimissionis. AE. itidem nudè reddit i. e. dimissionem. Caeterùm quâ formâ libellus repudii conceptus fuerit, quibus item de causis datus, infrà ad c. 19, 7. ostendetur.)* Erat autem schedula viri manu subscripta, quâ testabatur, foeminam hanc à se repudiatam esse, ac suo in eam iuri cedebat, ut porrò integrum ei esset alteri, cui vellet, nubere.

## 5:32
v. 32. Γυναῖ

Separation is granted on account of adultery because it fights directly against the matrimonial faith, by which a woman has handed over the power of her body to her husband, and vice versa 1. Cor. 7. v. 4.

Ποιεῖ μοιχᾶσθαι. For whether she marries another, or remains unmarried and commits fornication, she commits adultery, since the bond of the former marriage still remains. *(The reason for that woman who has been dismissed on account of fornication or adultery is different. For as concerns such a one, theologians indeed warn that it would be better if she were affected by a just and deserved punishment, namely capital punishment: meanwhile, since today, because of the preposterous indulgence of the Magistrate, life is granted to certain adulterers, certainly out of ἀπιεικεία, regard for conscience and dangers, it is granted to them (but nevertheless under certain conditions, about which B. D. Tarnov. tr. de Coni. p. 920) that they may enter into marriage again. But the Papists object: If to such adulterous wives, i.e., those who have been dismissed on account of fornication, the power of a new marriage can be given, but to others, who have not been dismissed with the intervention of adultery, such power is not given, it follows that the condition of the innocent is worse than that of those. Resp. by denying the consequence. B. Par. t. 4. Conf. Cath. p. 264. gives an instance from infidels, to whom the Papists themselves permit marriage after divorce, but not to the faithful; and yet they will hardly concede that they are in a better place before God than the faithful. But that through fornication or adultery, a consummated marriage is dissolved even as to the bond, so that the power of entering into another marriage must be given to the innocent party, our people have hitherto firmly proven against the Papists from this passage. But so that the foundations of our opinion may be more correctly perceived, observe 1. that the particles παρεκτὸς, and εἲ μὴ Matth. 19, 9. are exclusive, as is evident from 2. Sam 20, 39.c. 21, 9.1. Reg. 3, 18.c. 12, 20.Act. 26, 29.Matth. 11, 26.c. 12,c. 17, 8.c. 21, 9. 2. that the exception concerning πορνείᾳ is to be repeated also in the following member. 3. That the force of that exception is such that if a wife is dismissed for the cause of fornication, i.e., if a divorce is instituted, the husband cannot be said to commit adultery if he marries another. 4. That the foundation of this explanation, by which the cause of adultery is excepted from the general prohibition of divorce, can be demonstrated from the very nature of adultery. 5. That the passage Marc. 10, 11.Luc. 16, 18. is to be supplemented from Matthew. To the exceptions of the Papists, especially of Felicianus Capito and other more recent ones, answer will be made below in the notes to Matth. 19, 9.. Meanwhile, let B. D. Tarnov. l. 3. de Coni. c. 10. Dn. D. Carpzov. Iurisprud. Ecclesiast. l. 2. t. 11. dist. 189. n. 10. 11. 12. B. Par. Conf. Cathol. t. 4. pag. 246. seqq. L. de Coniug. §. 564. seqq. be seen, add Collegium Isagog. pag. 1671. seqq. B. Hacksp. Disp. 3. de Locutionibus Sacris §. 29. seqq. Conf. from the Calvinists D. Rivetus Comment. ad cap. 2. Hos. v. 2. quaest. 2. p. 526. & 527. Dan. Chamier t. 3. Panstr. lib. 16. c. 16.)*

Latin:

v. 32. Γυναῖ

Propter adulterium ideò conceditur separatio, quia directè pugnat cum fide matrimoniali, quâ mulier viro potestatem corporis sui tradidit, & vice versâ 1. Cor. 7. v. 4.

Ποιεῖ μοιχᾶσθαι. Sive enim alteri nubat, sive innupta fornicetur, adulterium comittit, cum prioris matrimonii vinculumadhuc maneat. * (Alia est ratio illius, quae propter fornicationem s. adulterium dimissa est. Quod talem enim concernit, monēt quidem Theologi, satiùs esse, si iustâ ac promeritâ adficererur poenâ, eapitali nempe supplicio: interea cùm hodie ex praeposterâ Magistratûs indulgentiâ quibusdam adulteris vita donetur, sanè ex ἀπιεικεία, ratione conscientiae & periculorum habitâ, illis (sed certis tamen conditionibus, de quibus B. D. Tarnov. tr. de Coni. p. 920) conceditur, ut iterum matrimonium ineant. Sed instant Pontificii: Si buiusmodi adulteris uxoribus b. e. quae propter fornicationem dimisse sunt, potestas novi matrimonii fieri potest, aliis autem, quae non intercedente adulterio dimissae sunt, talis potestas non fit, sequitur, deteriorem, innocentium esse conditionem, quàm illarum. Resp. negando consequentiam. B. Par. t. 4. Conf. Cath. p. 264. dat instantiam ab infidelibus, quibus ipsi Pontificii permittunt post divortium nubere, fidelibus verò non; & tamen vix concedent, meliori illos apud Deum loco esse, quàm fideles. Quòd verô per fornicationem s. adulterium, matrimonium consummatum etiam quoad vinculum solvatur, ita ut parti innocenti potestas facienda sit aliud ineundi matrimonium, firmiter ex hoc loco nostrates adversus Pontificios hactenus evicerunt. Quò verò nostrae sententiae fundamenta rectiùs percipiantur, observ. 1. particulas παρεκτὸς, it. εἲ μὴMatth. 19, 9. esse exclusivas, uti constat ex 2. Sam 20, 39.c. 21, 9.1. Reg. 3, 18.c. 12, 20.Act. 26, 29.Matth. 11, 26.c. 12,c. 17, 8.c. 21, 9. 2. exceptionem de πορνείᾳ in sequenti etiam membro repetendam esse. 3. Exceptionis istius vim esse eam, ut si causâ fornicarionis uxor dimittatur h. e. divortium instituatur, non possit dici maritus moechari, si aliam duxerit. 4. Fundamentum huius explicationis, quâ excipitur causa adulterii à generali divortii prohibitione, ex ipsâ adulterii naturâ demonstrari posse. 5. locum Marc. 10, 11.Luc. 16, 18. supplendum esse ex Matthaeo. Ad Pontificiorum, cumprimis Feliciani Capitonis ac aliorum recentiorum, exceptiones infrà in notis ad Matth. 19, 9. respondebitur. Videantur interea B. D. Tarnov. l. 3. de Coni. c. 10. Dn. D. Carpzov. Iurisprud. Ecclesiast. l. 2. t. 11. dist. 189. n. 10. 11. 12. B. Par. Conf. Cathol. t. 4. pag. 246. seqq. L. de Coniug. §. 564. seqq. add. Collegium Isagog. pag. 1671. seqq. B. Hacksp. Disp. 3. de Locutionibus Sacris §. 29. seqq. Conf. è Calvinianis D. Rivetus Comment. ad cap. 2. Hos. v. 2. quaest. 2. p. 526. & 527. Dan. Chamier t. 3. Panstr. lib. 16. c. 16.)*

## 5:33
v. 33. ὃρκο

Lev. 19. v. 12. You shall not swear falsely or untruthfully. The Pharisees interpreted this law of GOD concerning oaths in such a way that only perjuries, but not rash oaths, were prohibited by it, little mindful of the command set forth in the Decalogue: You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, Exod. 20. v. 7. Deut. 5. v. 11. by which very commandment they taught that only perjuries, but not rash oaths, are prohibited, . *(Lud. Cappellus thinks that this latter part of the verse was taken from Deut. 23, 23. how ὃρκος might be the same as a vow confirmed by an oath. The opinion of Hugo Grotius on this passage seems to be almost the same. But whether all oaths, even those extorted by force, are to be kept, or which of them are, is taught everywhere by theologians, especially by moralists. See, besides our own theologians, D. Bald. D. R-nig / B. Par. L. de Leg. and others; among the Calvinists, Perkins, Anatomy of Conscience. Hugo Grotius on this passage; among the Papists, Martin Bonacina, vol. 2, Works on Moral Theology, Disp. 4, q. 1, point 3, and following. Antoninus, part 2, tit. 10, c. 4. Thomas Aquinas 2. 2. q. 89. a. 1. Sot-sl. 8. q. 1. art. 7. & q. 2. a. 3. Navarrus c. 12. n. 10. Azorius c. 5. q. 3. Fr. Toletus, Instruction for Confessors, book 4, c. 21, p. 383, and following. Gabriel 3. dist. 39. q. 2. Th. Cajetanus in the Summa, Gr. de Valentia, question 7, point 2. Leonh. Lessius n. 23. Fumus under the word Perjury, Tabiena and Sa under the word Oath. Molina vol. 1, Disp. 149, vol. 2, Disp. 271. Ioh. Altensteig under the words Oath & Perjury. Adamus Tannerus of the Society of Jesus, Scholastic Theology, vol. 3, Disp. 5, q. 5, dub. 1, n. 10, and following. Iohannes de Rada Aragonius, Bishop of Pactia, Controversies between Thomas and Scotus, part 3, Controversy 17, art. 2, p. 466, and following. Furthermore, concerning other matters which must be observed regarding the administration and taking of oaths, the Lord Doctor Carpzov treats at length in Ecclesiastical Jurisprudence, book 3, tit. 1, and following.

Latin:

v. 33. ὃρκο

Lev. 19. v. 12.Non iurabis falsò sive mendaciter. Hanc legem DEI de iuramentis Pharisaei sic interpretabantur, quòd periuria tantùm, non autem temeraria iuramenta eâdem sint prohibita, parùm memores praecepti in Decalogo propositi: Non assumes nomen Dom ni EI tui in vanum,Exod. 20. v. 7.Deut. 5. v. 11. quo ipso praecepto tantùm periuria, non autem temeraria iuramenta prohiberi, docuerunt. *(Posterius vers. huius membrum Lud. Cappellus in Spicil. p. 14. desumtum putat ex Deut. 23, 23. quomodo ὃρκος idem esset, ac votum iureiurando confirmatum. Eadem fermè videtur esse sententia Hug. Grotii ad h. l. Caeterùm an omnia iuramenta, etiam vi extorta, servanda sint, vel quae ex illis, passim docetur à Theologis, cum primis à Moralistis. Vid. praeter nostrates Theologos, D. Bald. D. R-nig / B. Par. L. de Leg. aliosque, è Calvinianis Perkinsus Anatom. Conscientiae. Hug. Grotius in h. l. è Pontificiis Martinus Bonacina t. 2. Oper. de Morali Theolog. Disp. 4. q. 1. punct. 3. seqq. Antoninus part. 2. tit. 10. c. 4. Thomas de Aquino 2. 2. q. 89. a. 1. Sot-sl. 8. q. 1. art. 7. & q. 2. a. 3. Navarrus c. 12. n. 10. Azorius c. 5. q. 3. Fr. Toletus Instruct. Sacred. lib. 4. c. 21. p. 383. seqq. Gabriel 3. dist. 39. q. 2. Th. Cajetanus in summa, Gr. de Valentia quaest. 7. punct. 2. Leonh. Lessius n. 23. Fumus voce Periurium, Tabiena ac Sa voce Iuramentum. Molina t. 1. Disp. 149. t. 2. Disp. 271. Ioh. Altensteig voc. Iuram. & Periur. Adamus Tannerus è S. I. Theolog. Schol. t. 3. Disp. 5. q. 5. dub. 1. n. 10. seqq. Iohannes de Rada Aragonius, Episcopus Pactensis Controv. inter Thomam & Scotum part. 3. Controv. 17. art. 2. p. 466. seqq. Caeterùm de aliis, quae circa Iuramentorum delationem & praestationem observanda sunt, prolixè agit Dn. D. Carpzov. Iurispr. Eccles. lib. 3. tit. 1. seqq.)*

## 5:34
v. 34. 'Εγω The infinitive, according to the customary Hebraism, is put for the imperative. Do not swear at all. The Syriac has i.e., do not swear at all. *(So also the Arabic: i.e., do not swear at all. and likewise the Ethiopian. Furthermore, the blessed Doctor Quistorpius wishes to note in his notes on this passage that the word at all is not correctly separated by punctuation (:) from what follows, but that it should be read in this passage without punctuation. But since not only do the Greek codices almost consistently use a colon here, but the Syriac interpreter also distinguishes here, it will perhaps be better, with the distinction lost here, to explain the discourse of Christ in such a way that he indeed prohibits rash oaths entirely, whether one swears by the name of GOD or by creatures. Furthermore, since it is lawful to swear only by God, as is evident both from this passage and from Es. 65, 16., it is asked: what is to be thought about the passages Deut. 4, 26. Genes. 42, 15.

1. Sam. 20, 32. I answer briefly. They are grave obtestations and vehement asseverations, but not oaths properly so called and direct. Compare more in B. Par. L. on the Law of GOD §. 119, also Commentary on Genesis p. 736, Commentary on Deuteronomy p. 206, Rung. on Genesis p. 1206, Gesner on Genesis p. 780, Lord Doctor Walt. Biblical Harmony p. 172 & 745, and following. Whether finally the expression אמן & the word which corresponds to this in the German language, truly, is an oath properly so called, and if not, whether it is correctly used in common speech? also why Christ used the asseveration by this little word so often, the blessed Doctor Keslerus elucidates at length in Theology of Conscience, p. 279, and following.

Christ opposes the true explanation of the law to the corruptions of the Pharisees, namely that not only perjuries, but also any vain and unnecessary oaths are prohibited in it, so that one must not swear lightly and rashly not only by the name of God, but not even by creatures. For that the particle ὅλως is to be accepted with a certain restriction concerning light oaths and rash ones in a trivial matter, is understood both from the antithesis and from the formulas themselves, which Christ disapproves. Therefore, the rule is to be repeated in this place: certain things seem to be prohibited simply, when nevertheless they are not prohibited except in a certain respect. Ex. 20. v. 10. no work is to be done on the Sabbath, namely profane work. Luc. 7. v. 28. there has not arisen a greater than the Baptist, namely among those who were born in the ordinary way. *(Add 1. Cor. 9, 22. c. 10, 23. Phil. 4, 13.)*

Augustine, Epist. 154. This indeed seems to me to have been said for this reason, not because it is a sin to swear truly, but because to perjure oneself is a huge sin. Book on Lying, chapter 15. It is to be understood that which is placed as 'at all,' is placed for this purpose, that as much as is in you, you should not desire, you should not love, you should not, as it were, seek an oath for a good thing with any delight. R. Maimon in the tract on Oaths, chapter 12. It is best for a man not to swear at all.

Some accept that ὅλως in this way, you ought not to swear either by the name of GOD, or by creatures, but it must necessarily be understood, rashly, in a trivial matter, without an urgent cause. For an oath is not prohibited absolutely and simply. *(This is to be observed not only against certain ancient heretics, called Apostolics, about whom Bernh. serm. 66. in Cantic and Wiclef can. 43, but also against the modern Anabaptists and Photinians of this time, about whom we are going to treat in the notes to James 5, 12. Let B. D. Chemn. part. 2. LL. Th. p. 46. seqq., B. D. Lobech. in A. C. p. 430. seqq., Theologi Marpp. T. 1. p. 249. seqq., B. D. Schlüsselb. Haereseol. l. 12., B. D. Fewrb. in Anti Ostor, and other theologians against the Phot. B. D. be seen in the meantime.)* R-entg/Append. Cas. Consc. p. 101. B. D. Bald. Cas. Consc. p. 17. 327. seqq. B. Par. L de Lege §. 116. 117. it L. de Evang. §. 74.) *But it is the worship of GOD, if it has three companions, truth, justice & judgment. *(These three companions, besides very many of our own, the Master of Sentences also recounts l. 3. dist. 39. add also Aquin. 2. 2. q. 89. art. 3. This observation is indeed taken from Jer. 4, 2. See Jerome t. 4. p. 239.)* Some interpret that ὅλως as frequently and sub--e, just as διὰ παντὸς Sir. 23. v. 21. See by all means Lyranus in the commentary. But the best interpretation is gathered from the antithesis.

Latin:

v. 34. 'Εγω Infinitivus iuxta usitatum Hebraismum ponitur pro Imperativo. Ne iures omninò. Syrus habet. i. e. neiuretis omninò. *(Sic & Arabs: i. e. non iuretis omninò. ac pariter Aethiops. Notari porrô vult B. D. Quistorpius in notis ad h. l. vocem omninò non rectè interpunctione (:) à sequentibus separari, sed sine interpunctione esse h. l. legendum. Verùm cùm non solùm Codd. Graeci consentienter ferè colon hîc adhibeant, sed & Syrus Interpres hîc distinguat, satiùs fortè erit, distinctione hîc amissâ sermonem Christi ita exponere, quòd nempe prohibeat iuramenta temeraria omninò, sive iuretur per nomen DEI, sive per creaturas. Caeterùm cùm per solum Deum licitum sit iurare, ceu tum ex h. 1. tum ex Es. 65, 16. patet, quaeritur: quid sentiendum sit de locisDeut. 4, 26.Genes. 42, 15.

1. Sam. 20, 32. Resp. breviter. sunt graves obtestationes ac vehementes adseverationes, non verò iuramenta propriè ita dicta & directa. Conf. plura apud B. Par. L. de Lege DEI §. 119. it. Comm. in Gen. p. 736. Comm. in Deut. p. 206. Rung. in Ggen. p. 1206. Gesner. in Gen. P. 780. Dn. D. Walt. Harm. Bibl. p. 172 & 745. seqq. An tandem dictioאמן & quae huic in Germ. ling respondet vox warlich/ sit iuramentum propriè dictum, & si non, an in vulgari sermone rectè adhibeatur? it cur Christus toties adseveratione per hanc voculamusus fuerit, pro lixè dilucidat B. D. Keslerus in Theol. Cas. Consc p. 279. seqq.)*

Pharisaeorum corruptelis opponit Christus veram legis explicationem, videl. quôd non solùm periuria, sed etiam quaevis vana ac non necessaria iuramenta in ea prohibeantur, ita ut non modò non per nomen Dei, sed ne quidem per creaturas leviter & temerè sit iurandum. Quod enim particula ὅλως cum quadam restrictione de iuramentis levibus ac temerariis in re levicula sit accipienda, intelligitur tum ex arstithesi, tum ex subiectis formulis, quas Christus improbat. Repetendà ergo h. l. regula: quaedam videntur. simpliciter prohiberi, cùm tamen non nisi secundùm quid prohibeantur.Ex. 20. v. 10. nullum opus faciendum in Sabbato, sc prophanum. Luc. 7. v. 28.non surrexit maior Baptista, sc. inter eos, qui vulgari modo nati sunt. *(Adde 1. Cor. 9, 22. c. 10, 23. Phil. 4, 13.)*

Augustinus Epist. 154. Hoc quidem propterea mihi dictum videtur, non quia verùm iurare peccatum est, sed quia peier are immane est peccatum. lib. de mendacio cap. 15. Intelligendum est illud-, quod positum est omnino, ad hoc positum, ut quantum in te est, non affectes, non ames, non qs. pro bono cum aliqua delectatione appetas, iusiurandum. R. Maimon in tract. de Iuram. cap. 12. Est optimum homini, ut non iuret omninò.

Quidam illud ὅλως sic accipiunt, nec per nomen DEI, nec per creaturas iur are debetis, sed necessariò subintelligendum, temerè, in re levicula, sine urgente causâ. iuramentum enim non absolutè & simpliciter prohibetur. *(Id quod observandum non solùm contra veteres quosdam haereticos, Apostolicos dictos, de quibus Bernh. serm. 66. in Cantic & Wiclefum can. 43. verùm etiam huius hodiernos Anabaptistas ac Photinianos, de quibus acturi sumus in notis ad Iacob. 5, 12. Videantur interim B. D. Chemn. part. 2. LL. Th. p. 46. seqq. B. D. Lobech. in A. C. p. 430. seqq. Theologi Marpp. T. 1. p. 249. seqq. B. D. Schlüsselb. Haereseol. l. 12. B. D. Fewrb. in Anti Ostor, & alii Theologi contra Phot. B. D. R-entg/Append. Cas. Consc. p. 101. B. D. Bald. Cas. Consc. p. 17. 327. seqq. B. Par. L de Lege §. 116. 117. it L. de Evang. §. 74.) *Sed est cultus DEI, si comites tres habeat, veritatem, iustitiam & iudicium. *(Tres hos Comites praeter plurimos nostratium recenset quoque Magister Sentent. l. 3. dist. 39. add. quoque Aquin. 2. 2. q. 89. art. 3. Desumta verò observatio haec ex Ierem. 4, 2. Vid. Hieronym. t. 4. p. 239.)* Quidam illud ὅλως interpretantur frequenter ac subi--e, sicut διὰ παντὸςSir. 23. v. 21. Vide omninò Lyranum in comm. Sed optima interpretatio colligitur ex antithesi.

## 5:35
v. 35. πορνε

From Matt. 23. v. 16.18.22. it is gathered that the Pharisees made little of oaths by creatures, so much so that they denied that they were binding if they had been made by certain creatures. But Christ in this place teaches that one must not swear rashly, not only not by the name of God, but not even by creatures. *(That rash oaths by creatures were lawful among the Jews, D. Hoornbeck shows lib. 7. contr. Iudaeos c. 4.)*

To swear by heaven was a custom formerly used by the Hebrews, *(Concerning this and other oaths of the Hebrews, likewise what the Hebrew Masters determine concerning Oaths, one may see Sam. Petitus Var. Lect. lib. 1. c. 16. p. 59. seqq. Ludov. Capellus in Spicil. p. 14. Buxtorff. Lex. Talm. Rabb. p. 2441. Hugo Grotius in h. 1. Dn. Dilherr. Disp. Acad. t. 1. p. 187. but especially B. D. Iohan. Tob. Maior. in a special Dissertation on Oriental Oaths.)* which flowed from a perverse understanding of certain places of Scripture, of which kind is Amos 4. v. 2. The Lord has sworn by his holiness i. e. by himself. But R. D. Kimchi & R. Aben Ezra explain it concerning heaven. He swore by his holiness i. e. by heaven: for those swearing used to lift their hand to heaven. (From where, however, will they be able to prove that God ever swore by a created thing?) Thus, what they swore by Jerusalem, they strove to confirm by the passage Amos 8. v. 10. The Lord has sworn by the excellency of Jacob, by which they desire to prove that Jerusalem is understood, from Ps. 47. v. 9.The excellence of Jacob, which he loved. (But by the excellence of Jacob in the prophetic saying, God himself is understood.)

No trace of the formulas of swearing by the earth and by the head is found in the Scriptures; therefore, without a doubt, the Jews are said to have borrowed these formulas of oaths from neighboring nations. Thus, in the Poet: I swear by this head.

Heaven is GOD'S throne, the earth is his footstool. This is taken from Esa. 66. v. 1. By this form of speaking, GOD'S majesty, infinity, immensity, and omnipresence are signified, because being present in heaven and earth he rules all things, and yet is not contained by heaven and earth. Some argue subtly that heaven is therefore called GOD'S throne, because God in heaven offers his face to be seen by the Angels and blessed men; but that the earth is called his footstool, because on earth he exhibits himself to be known through works and effects. *(Moreover, Bell. attempts from this, that in this place oaths by heaven are prohibited, and that for the reason that it is the throne of GOD, to prove that images of the saints are to be worshipped, namely on account of the relation to God. But B. shows the weakness of the consequence in Confess Cath. vol. 3. p. 734. In this place, at least this can be noted, that Bell.'s argument can rather be inverted. If it is not permitted to swear by creatures, even insofar as they otherwise have a relation to God, therefore it is not permitted to religiously invoke creatures, even insofar as they have a relation to God, since the reason for an oath and for religious adoration is the same. If furthermore it could be proven from this place that creatures are to be religiously worshipped on account of some relation to God, it would also follow that the city of Jerusalem is to be religiously worshipped. But the Pontiffs themselves deny the latter. E.)*

Jerusalem is called the city of the great King. This is taken from Ps. 41. v. 3.Ps. 48. v. 2. but by the name great King God himself is understood. Mal. 1. v. 4. *(The holiness and preeminence of the city of Jerusalem will be treated in the notes to Matth. c. 27. 53.)*

The sense is this. Rash oaths, even if they are not made by the name of GOD, but by creatures, nevertheless result in no less dishonor to GOD, because all creatures are subject to God, and in all of which the glory of GOD shines forth.

Latin:

v. 35. πορνε

Ex Matth. 23. v. 16.18.22. colligitur, Pharisaeos iuramenta per creaturas parvi fecisse, adeò ut neg-rint, ea, si per certas quasdā creaturas fuerint facta, esse obligatoria. Christus verò hoc loco docet, non solùm non per Dei nomen, sed nec per creaturas esse temerè iurandum. *(Quòd apud Iudaeos iuramenta temeraria per creaturas licita, fuerint, ostendit D. Hoornbeck. lib. 7. contr. Iudaeos c. 4.)*

Per coelum iurare erat mos Hebraeis olim usitatus, *(De hoc aliioque iuramentis Ebraeorum, item quid Ebr. Magistri de Iuram. statuant, videri possunt Sam. Petitus Var. Lect. lib. 1. c. 16. p. 59. seqq. Ludov. Capellus in Spicil. p. 14. Buxtorff. Lex. Talm. Rabb. p. 2441. Hugo Grotius in h. 1. Dn. Dilherr. Disp. Acad. t. 1. p. 187. cumprimis verò B. D. Iohan. Tob. Maior. in pecul. Dissert. de Iuram. Orient.)* qui manavit ex pravo intellectu quorundam locorum Scripturae, cuiusmodi est Amos 4. v. 2. Iuravit Dominus per sanctitatem suam i. e. perseipsum. Sed R. D. Kimchi & R. Aben Ezra exponunt de coelo. Iuravit per sanctitatem suam i. e. per coelum: nam iurantes manum ad coelum elevabant. (Unde verò probare poterunt, Deum unquam per rem creatam iurasse?) Sic quod per Hierosolymam iurabant, illud confirmare nitebantur per locum Amos 8. v. 10. Iuravit Dominus per excellentiam Iacobi, per quam intelligi Hierosolymam, probare cupiunt ex Ps. 47. v. 9.Excellentiam Iacobi, quam dilexit. (At per excellentiam Iacobi in dicto prophetico Deus ipse intelligitur.)

Formulae iurandi per terram & per caput nullum in Scripturis invenitur vestigium, procul dubio igitur Iudaei à vicinis gentibus has iuramentorum formulas dicuntur mutuasse. Sic apud Poëtam: per caput hoc iuro.

Coelum DEI thronus, terra scabellum pedum eius. Desumtum hoc ex Esa. 66. v. 1. Significatur hac loquendi formâ DEI maiestas, infinitas, immensitas, omnipraesentia, quod in coelo ac terra praesens omnia regat, nec tamen coelo & terrâ concludatur. Quidam subtiliter disputant, coelum ideò vocari DEI chronum, quia Deus in coelo Angelis & beatis hominibus faciem suam conspiciendam praebet; terraem verò dici scabellum pedum eius, quia in terra per opera & effecta sese cognoscendum exhibet. *(Caeterùm conatur Bell. ex eo, quô h. 1. iuramenta per coelum prohibita, idque ideò quôd thronus DEI est, probare, imagines sanctorum esse colendas, propter relationem nempe ad Deum. Sed consequentiae infirmitatem ostendit B. Par Confess Cath. t. 3. p. 734. Hoc loco id saltem notari potest, quòd inverti potiùs Bell. argumentum possit. Si per creaturas, etiam quatenus aliàs ad Deum relationem habent, non licet iurare. E. nec creaturas, etiam quat. ad Deum relationem habent, religiosè invocare licet, cùm ead. sit iuramenti ac religiosae adorationis ratio. Si porrò ex h. l. posset probari, creaturas propter relationem aliquam ad Deum religiosè esse colendas, sequeretur etiam, Hierosolymorum urbem religiosè esse colendam. Sed posterius ipsi Pontif. negant. E.)*

Hierosolyma dicitur civitas magni Regis. Desumtum hoc ex Ps. 41. v. 3.Ps. 48. v. 2. nomine autem magni Regis intelligitur ipse Deus. Mal. 1. v. 4. *(De Hierosol. urbis sanctitate & praecellentiâ agetur in notis ad Matth. c. 27. 53.)*

Sensus hic est. Temeraria iuramenta, etiamsi non per DEI nomen, sed per creaturas fiant, nihilo tamen minùs cedere in DEI ignominiam, quia omnes creaturae Deo sunt subiectae, ac in quibus omnibus DEI gloria relucet.

## 5:36
v. 36. Εγω

That one cannot make one hair white or black, some take this concerning the production of hairs, in the sense that one cannot by one's own power produce even the smallest white or black hair. But Chrysostom rightly warns that this is more correctly understood concerning the change of color in hairs, namely that no one can make a white hair from a black one, and vice versa, and that is far less than producing a hair according to its substance. *(Franc. Lucas Brugensis warns in his notes on the Greek text that a certain Parisian codex, with the distinction removed, has ἣ, λευκὴν ποιῆσαι μέλαινον, so that the sense is plain: to render one white hair black, or the contrary: But he rightly adds: Not only in Greek, but also in Latin and Syriac, a disjunctive is read. Similarly, the Arab also expressly has it, או )*

To this verse two things can be objected.

1. That Joseph swears by the life of Pharaoh Gen. 4. v. 15. Resp. That oath was not religious and properly so called, but a certain political attestation or asseveration. Aben Ezra in his commentary Exod. 6. v. 8. reports, that the Egyptians swore by the head of the King, and he who violated that oath was punished by death, nor could he redeem himself with any money. Schultetus answers otherwise, namely that this is to be attributed to Egyptian superstition, that Joseph swore by the life of Pharaoh. But without urgent necessity, the deeds of the holy Patriarchs are not to be argued as superstition or sin. *(Indeed, Calvin and Grynaeus incline to the same view as Schultetus in this place, p. 337. Ioh. Piscator argues that either impiety, or rashness, or adulation is to be attributed to Joseph on this account. Concerning which opinion, as well as other interpretations of the said passage, see more in B. Par. Comm. in Gen. p. 42. Furthermore, that Joseph did not swear in the proper sense of the word, B. D. Rungius also notes in Gen. p. 1206. Dn. D. Waltherus in Harm. Bibl. p. 172, who also notes in the said place p. 747 that oaths by creatures are found in Holy Scripture, but that they are indirectly so, and he rightly warns, that it is not of evident force to use these indirect oaths. See altogether the praised Dn. D. Waltherus treating these things quite prolixly. Furthermore, concerning the sufficiently difficult question: Ah, is it permitted, either to extort an oath from him, or even to admit one who offers himself to an oath of his own accord, whom you know will perjure himself? see B. D. R-nig in Cas. Consc. Append. Case 5. Furthermore, Augustine argues in sermon 11 on the Beheading of John.

which is found in T. 10. Op., that to provoke to an oath him whom you know will swear falsely is a crime more grave than homicide. Because the murderer, he says, kills only the body, but he who swears falsely kills the soul. He also records that a certain man named Tutilimenus, because he had demanded such an oath, was severely whipped at night before God. That is also notable which Clinias, a friend and intimate of Pythagoras, preferred to pay three talents rather than to swear, even rightly and lawfully. Basil the Great reports this in his Address to Young Men on how utility may be taken from Greek books.)*

2. That hair can be covered with a dyed color. Resp. Christ speaks of a true and natural color, which a man cannot induce upon his hair at will.

Latin:

v. 36. Εγω

Quòd non possit quis capillum unum album vel nigrum facere, id quidam de productione capilorum accipiūt, sensu eo, quòd ne minimum quidem capillum album vel nigrum suapte virtute producere possit. Sed Chrysostomus rectè monet, de mutatione coloris in capillis rectiùs hoc accipi, quòd sc. nemo possit ex capillo nigro album facere, & vice versâ, idque longè minus est quàm capillum secundùm substantiā producere. *(Monet Franc. Lucas Brugens. in notis ad textum Graecum, Codicem quendam Parisiensium sublatâ distinctione ἣ, habere λευκὴν ποιῆσαι μέλαινον, ita ut planus sit sensus, unum album capillum reddere nigrum, aut ècontrà: Sed rectè addit: Non Graecè tantùm, sed & Lat. ac Syriacè disiunctivam legi. Similiter & Arabs, expressè eum habet, או)*

Huic versiculo duo possunt obiici.

1. Quod Iosephus iuret per vitam PharaonisGen. 4. v. 15. Resp. non fuit illud iuramentum religiosum ac propriè sic dictum, sed politica quaedam attestatio sive asseveratio. AbenEsra in coment. Exod. 6. v. 8. refert, Aegyptios iurasse per caput Regis, quod iusiurandum qui violabat, capite plectebatur, nec ullâ pecuniâ se redimere poterat. Schultetus aliter respondet, videlicet superstitioni Aegyptiaca hoc tribuendum, quòd Iosephus per vitam Pharaonis iuraverit. sed sine urgente necessitate sanctorum Patriarcharum facta non sunt superstitionis vel peccati arguenda-. *(Ecdem verò, quo Scultetus, inclinant quoque Calvinus, ac Grynaeus in h l. p. 337. Ioh. Piscator vel impietatem, vel temeritatem vel adulationem hoc nomine Iosepho tribuendam esse, disputat. De qua sententia, sicuti & de aliis interpretationibus dicti loci pluribus videatur B. Par. Comm. in Gen. p. 42. Caeterùm quòd Iosephus propriè loquendo non iuraverit, notant quoq; B. D. Rungius in Gen. p. 1206. Dn. D. Waltherus in Harm. Bibl. p. 172. qui etiam annotat d. l. p. 747. inveniri iuramenta in Scr. S. per creaturas, sed & ea indirect esse, ac probè monet, nō evius vis esse, indirectis hisce iuramentis uti. Videatur omninò laudatus Dn D. Waltherus satis prolixè haec pertractàns. Caeterùm de quaestione satis difficili: Ah liceat, vel iuramentum ab eo extorquere, vel etiam sp-nte sese adiuramentum offerentem, admittere, quem scis peieraturum? videatur B. D. R-nig in Cas. Consc. Append. Casu 5. Porrò disputat August. serm. 11. de Decoll. Ioh.

qui habetur T. 10. Op. provocare ad iuramentum eum, quem scis iuraturum falsum scelus esse gravius homicidio. Quia homicida inquit, tantùm corpus, ille autem peierantis animam occidit. Idem quoque memorat, quòd quidā Tutilimenus nomine eò quòd tale iuramentum exegerit, noctu coram Deo graviter fuerit flagellatus. Illud etiam notabile est quòd Clinias, amicus & familiaris Pythagorae, maluerit tria talenta solvere, quàm iurare, etsi rectè & licitè. refert Basilius M. ad Adolescentes, quomodo ex Graec. libb. capienda utilitas sit.)*

2. Quòd fucato colore capilli possint obduci. Resp. Christus loquitur de eolore vero ac nativo, quem non potest homo pro arbitrio capillis suis inducere.

## 5:37
v. 37. λευκ From these words of Christ is taken that passage of James ch. 5. v. 12. But let your speech be, yes, yes, no, no.

Mercerus in ch. 30 of Gen. says, that the Jews have a proverb of this kind: The yes of the just is yes, and their no is no; where they say, yes, is as certain as if they had sworn a hundred times, from which he thinks that saying of Christ is taken. *(Capellus in his Spicilegium p. 15 reports the formula of the Jews similar to this of Christ from Maimonides.)*

However, the words of Christ can be accepted in a double sense. 1. That by those repeated particles of affirming and denying it is signified that in every single speech at all, and with a bare affirmation or negation as the truth of things holds, we ought to be content, in which sense most interpreters accept the words of Christ. 2. That our yes ought to be yes, and our no ought to be no, which sense agrees more with the parallel passage of James, which is as follows: Ἤτω ὑμῶν τὸ ναὶ, ναὶ, καὶ τὸ ὀυ, ὀυ.

But that which is more than these, is from the evil one. 1 Chromatius comments on this place thus. By that which is more than these, a lie ought to be understood; for that is more than yes, yes, no, no, that is, than truth. And that is from the evil one, i.e., from the Demon, who is the father of lies, John 8. v. 44. Obs. here, that by Τὸν πονηρὸν Chromatius, just as some others, understands the Devil, that evil and malignant Spirit. But it is more correctly accepted in the neuter gender. *(Pasor in his Lexicon of the New Testament p. 565, Maldonatus, Piscator, and some others accept it in the masculine gender in this place, and among the ancients also Theophylact; against this in the neuter gender are Franciscus Lucas, Corn. à Lapide, Tirinus, Hugo Grotius, etc., in this place, whom among the ancients Augustine favors, book 1 of the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount. The Syriac renders it by the Arabic by the Ethiopic by which expressions can all be explained both by the masculine and by the neuter, provided they are used adjectivally or substantively, although more often in that way.)*

2. Augustine, Sermon 1 on the words of the Lord on the mount. It is not evil with respect to the one swearing if something is added to a simple assertion, but with respect to the incredulity of the one to whom the oath is made; for that incredulity is evil.

3. A simpler exposition is gathered from the context. That which exceeds these (to wit, is, and is not), which is added to a simple affirmation and negation, but understands an oath, that is from evil, proceeds from malice.

Some refer this to the object, as we just saw from Augustine, that is to say, that men do not believe one who simply affirms something; but it is more correctly referred to the subject, that the custom of swearing rashly and without an urgent cause is evil and to be disapproved. Compare D. Bald.

Latin:

v. 37. λευκ Ex his Christi verbis desumtum illud Iacobi cap. 5. v. 12. Sit autem sermo vester, est, est, non, non.

Mercerus in cap. 30. Gen. dicit, Iudaeos eiusmodi proverbium habere: Iustorum etiam est etiam, & non illorum est non; ubi dicunt, etiam, tam certum est, quàm si centies iurassent, ex quo desumtum censet illud Christi. *(Form. Iudaeorum huic Christi similem ex Maimon. refert Capellus in spicil. p. 15.)*

Duplici autem sensu possunt verba Christi accipi. 1. quòd repetitis illis adfirmandi & negandi particulis significetur, in omni omninò sermone simplici, ac nudâ aut affirmatione, aut negatione prout sererū veritas habet, nos debere esse cōtentos, quo sensu pleriq; Interpp. verba Christi accipiunt. 2. quòd nostrum etiam debeat esse etiā, & nostrū non debeat esse non, qui sensus magis cōgruit loco parallelo Iacobi, qui sic habet: Ἤτω ὑμῶν τὸ ναὶ, ναὶ, καὶ τὸ ὀυ, ὀυ.

Quod autem his abundantius est, à malo est. 1 Chromatius in h. l. sic commentatur. Per illud, quod autem abundantius his est, intelligi debet mendacium; illud enim abundatius est, quā est, est, non, non, h. e. quàm veritas. & illud est à malo i. e. à Daemone, qui est pater mendacii,Ioh. 8. v. 44. Obs. hîc, per Τὸν πονηρὸν Chromat. sicut & quosdam alios, intelligere Diabolum, malum & malignum illum Spiritum. Sed rectiùs accipitur in genere neutro. *(In genere Masculino accipiunt Pasor in Lex. N. T. p. 565. Maldonatus, Piscator ac alii nonnulli in h. l, ex veteribus etiam Theophylactus; contra in genere neutro Franciscus Lucas, Corn. à Lapide, Tirinus, Hugo Grotius &c. in h. l. quibus ex veteribus favet August, l. 1. de serm. Dom. in monte. Syrus reddit per Arabs Aethiops per quae dictiones omnes tum per masc. tum per neutrum exponi possunt, dum modò adiectivè substantivè adhibentur, quamvis eo modo saepius.)*

2. Augustinus serm. 1. de verb. Domini in monte. Non respectu iurantis malum est, si quid simplici asseverationi addatur, sed respectu incredulitatis eius, cui iur atur, ea enim incredulitas mala est.

3. Simplicior expositio colligitur ex contextu. Quod ultra haec (sc. est, & non) accedit, quod simplici affirmationi & negatreni adiicitur, intelligit autem iuramentum, illud est ex malo, proficiscitur ex malitia.

Quidam hoc referunt ad obiectum, ut ex Augustino modò vidimus, quòd sc. simpliciter aliquid affirmanti homines non credant; sed rectiùs refertur ad subiectum, quod mos, temerè & sine urgente causâ iurandi sit malus & improbandus. Confer. D. Bald.

## 5:38
v. 38. ὅλως

The law of retaliation for an eye being plucked out for one plucked out, and being knocked out for one knocked out, is held to have been given divinely Exod. 21. v. 23. 24. 25.Levit. 24. v. 19. 20.. The Pharisees were corrupting that in such a way that even a private person, out of a desire for vengeance, could return like for like to another without transgression of the law concerning loving one's neighbor. What had been said in the law concerning the office of the Magistrate, the Pharisees understood in such a way that it was permitted even to private persons to avenge themselves. But God had prohibited that private vengeance by an express law. Lev. 19. v. 18. Thou shalt not seek revenge, nor be mindful of the injury of thy citizens. Therefore, Christ did not oppose this doctrine of His to the divine law, but to the corruptions of the Pharisees.

Latin:

v. 38. ὅλως

Lex talionis de eruendo oculo pro eruto, & excu-iendo de dente pro excusso divinitus lata habetur Exod. 21. v. 23. 24. 25.Levit. 24. v. 19. 20. illam Pharisaei sic depravabant, quod etiam privatus ex vindictae cupiditate par pari alteri referre sine transgressione legis de diligendo proximo possit. Quod in lege de officio Magistratus dictum erat, id Pharisaei sic intelligebant, quòd privatis etiam con-essum sit, seipsos vindicare. At privatam illam vidictam Deus expressâ lege prohibuerat. Lev. 19. v. 18.Non quaeras ultionem, nec memor eris iniuriae civium tuorum. Ergo & hanc suam doctrinam Christus non opposuit lege divinae, sed corruptel is Pharisaicis.

## 5:39
v. 39. Εγω

Ἀντιςναι. The infinitive is placed for the imperative by a customary Hebraism.

To resist evil, is to repel an inflicted injury with another injury; to avenge oneself. Chromatius on this passage: It is not fitting for a Christian to return the turn of an injury, lest he be judged similar to him to whom he returns the turn. For if it is evil to do an injury, he is not alien from guilt who repays an evil turn; and by this he cannot be held to be good who imitates evil.

This commandment: 1. is not given to the Magistrate, but to private individuals. 2. It is not forbidden to avoid injury. 3. Nor is it forbidden to defend oneself with the moderation of blameless self-defense. 4. Nor is it forbidden to seek the Magistrate's help, and to commit vengeance to him. But this is opposed solely to the desire for private vengeance. *(As for whether it is even lawful under the New Testament to seek vengeance legitimately from the Magistrate, or whether this is forbidden by Christ here, the Photinians contend otherwise, urging that Christ's words are set in opposition to the Law of the Old Testament, by which private vengeance was likewise forbidden, but public vengeance was at least permitted. See Osterodius in Instit. Germ. c. 26, Valentin Smalcius in Refut. Thes. D. Frantzii, and indeed Disp. 7, de B. O., p. 237ff. The Arminians do not differ much from these, whose standard-bearer Simon Episcopius, Resp. ad Q. 27, t. 2, p. 25, writes that by the indulgence of the Mosaic Law it was permitted to the injured party to demand or claim back an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth. By what right? The right of retaliation. To what end? Of revenge and vengeance, with no good for the one demanding it, and only with the harm and loss of him who had first done injury, that is, who had knocked out the eye or the tooth. Opposed to this is Christ's prohibition. Compare the same author in Tract. de Mag. Polit., c. 4, p. 75. But to that opinion—that Christ sets his own words in opposition to the divine Law itself, which the Arminians hold along with the Photinians, and that even public vengeance, carried out through the Magistrate, is unlawful under the New Testament, as the Photinians dream—we oppose, first, a consideration of what precedes and what follows, from which it is clear that Christ sets his words in opposition not to the divine Law itself, but to "the ancients," that is, to the corrupted understanding of the Pharisees. And although in verse 38 the word "ancients" is not repeated, it must nevertheless be understood, as even Hugo Grotius—who otherwise is not much averse to the Arminian sect—freely grants in this passage. Indeed, Socinus himself too, in his book against Palaeologus, p. 157, admits that Christ's words here are not opposed to the words of the Law, but to the corrupted Pharisaic understanding of the Law. For it must be known that, since GOD, by a just and most wise 323 judgment (for Smalcius is insane, not to say something more severe, not hesitating to write, nothing of reason to be in it, so that he who offends me may be punished in such a way that no advantage returns to me. Nay, rather it suffices that divine justice is satisfied through public punishment, which is as similar as possible to the punishment of retaliation, and that in such a way crimes are punished and furthermore the desire of harming one's neighbor is restrained) the law of retaliation was not only permitted to be exercised by the magistrate, but also commanded Exod. 21, 24.Lev. 24, 20. The Pharisees and their predecessors corrupted the divine law with their own corruptions and twisted it into another sense; namely, that it is also permitted for private individuals, having received an injury, to avenge themselves and render evil for evil, provided the measure of retaliation is not exceeded. Which corruption of the law was also prohibited in the O. T., as can be seen from Lev. 19, 18.Prov. 24, 29. We therefore oppose the Photinians. 2. of the divine law, by which the power of bearing the sword was given to the magistrate, the repetition and repeated confirmation in the N. T., See Rom. 13, 4.1. Petr. 2, 14. Whence it is manifest that Christ does not bind the hands of the Judge against the wicked, nor does He snatch the sword from the magistrate, but at least restrains private individuals and curbs the desire for vengeance, to be exercised privately at one's own discretion. 3. the consequence of an absurdity. If Christ had wished by these words simply to have all vengeance or legitimate self-defense abolished, then He Himself would have acted against His own words afterwards, and would have weakened the force of His own law by His own example. The consequence is proved from Ioh. 18, 23. It would also follow that the Apostles contradict both the example, see Act. 23, 3. and the doctrine of the precepts of their Master. It is therefore evident that these words of Christ are not to be taken ἁπλῶς, but συγκριτικῶς. 4. The contrary assertion of Christ Himself. for He expressly says in the preceding verse 17, that He did not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it. We add 5. the proper explanation of the divine law. for neither is that law, as even the Jews themselves warn today, to be taken so rigidly, as if precisely an eye must be gouged out again or a hand amputated from him who did such a thing: but in a proverbial sense, that namely the damage ought to be estimated by the Judges, how much should be given for an eye or a tooth knocked out. See B. Par. Comm. in Deut. p. 1175. We add 6. of this divine law (that a just punishment ought to be inflicted upon the guilty party, even if the injured person receives nothing in the way of specific advantage or any compensation for his own person, provided that such an exercise of public vengeance and the infliction of just punishment

for the reparation of injured justice, and for the correction of the guilty party who did the injury, and then also for the warning of others, so that they may not be so inclined to inflict damage upon their neighbor) with the conformity and agreement of the law of nature and of nations. Concerning which matter, let some things be seen in B. Par. L. de Mag. Pol. §. 259. Comment. in Deut. p. 1180. Tannerus, Theolog. Scholast. T. 3. Disp 4. q. 2. D. 4. n. 66. et seqq. Hugo Grotius both in this place and in the treatise de I. B. & P. But against the Photinians and Anabaptists, besides B. P. l. c., there can be read here especially B. D. Chemnitius Part. 2. LL. Th. p. 116. B. D. Meisnerus tr. de Leg. p. 223. et seqq. item in Consid. Theol. Phot. p. 190. et seqq. B. D. Fewrbornius Antiost. p. 369. et seqq. B. D. Iacobus Martini Photin. c. 13. p. 354. et seqq. B. D. Huttus LL. Mai. p. 998. Dn. D. Calovius Socin. Proflig. p. 1005. et seqq. B. D. R-nig Cas. Consc. pag. 680.)*

*(Furthermore, how the moderation of blameless defense does not conflict with this precept of Christ, is likewise clear. For Christ does not speak here of such an injury by which one is endangered either regarding his own life or the life of his own, nor can he otherwise escape the danger, but he speaks at least of a light injury, which he advises should be borne with a calm mind rather than that one should strike back at his neighbor, or out of a desire for private vengeance, call him to law. Moreover, how that moderation ought to be constituted, theologians and jurists teach in various places. Let there be seen from their number B. D. Chemnitius part. 2. LL. Th. p. 130. et seqq. B. D. Baldus Cas. Consc. l. 4. c. 1. Cas. 13. B. Par. L. de Lege Dei §. 158. B. D. Meisnerus in Theol. Phot. Consid p. 203. et seqq. from these Christoph. Besoldus part. 2. Delib. Iuris ex lib. 48. Pandect q. 25. p. 153. & consil. 89. n. 1. et seqq. Vol. 2. fol. 379. Obrechtus in tr. de necess. defens. c. 1. n. 13. et seqq. Gail. L. 1. de pace publ. c. 16. n. 7. et seqq. but especially the Magnif. Dn. D. Carpzovius Pract. Crimin. part. 1. q. 28. et seqq. Briefly: it is required for the moderation of blameless defense, that it be done immediately. 2. with the intention of defending oneself and repelling extreme force, not with the purpose of taking revenge. 3. no other way is given for escaping, or avoiding the danger or the supreme injury. 4. the weapons be equal. Moreover, that moderation or the necessary defense of one's own body rests 1. on divine law, Exod. 22, 2. 3. 2. on the law of charity arg Prov. 24, 11. Gen 14, 14. 3. on the law of nature.)*

ὅστις σε ῥαπίσει ῥαπίζειν properly is to strike with the palm or with an open hand. Suidas ῥαπίσαι says it is Χιτὼν

In a certain old Glossary, ῥαπίζω to strike with the palm, to slap. Nonnus in his work on John τὸ ῥαπίζειν expresses it thus in chapter 18, verse 22: Χιτὼν: and again in chapter 19, verse 4: Χιτὼν. Furthermore, what are called by the Greek jurists ῥαπίσματα of slaves being manumitted, Latin authors call slaps, and Sedulius the Christian poet ῥαπίζειν translates as to strike with the palms. *(Compare more on the meaning of the word ῥαπίζειν in Mr. Dilherr, Academic Disputations, vol. 2, p. 19 ff. How indeed slaves were formerly manumitted by the intervention of a slap, C. Ritterhusius teaches, book 3, Sacred Readings, ch. 10. The same author also observes in the said place that in the sacrament of confirmation, as the Papists call it, they formerly inflicted a slap, as Guil. Durand confirms in Rationale of Divine Offices, p. 225.)*

Comparatively this is to be understood. Rather than returning a slap, you should even offer the other cheek to be struck.

Latin:

v. 39. Εγω

Ἀντιςναι. Infinitivus usitato Hebraismo ponitur pro Imperativo.

Malo resistere, est iniuriam illatam aliâ iniuriâ propulsare; seipsum vindicare. Chromatius in h. l. Non convenit Christiano vicem iniuriae reddere, ne similis ei, cui vicem restituit, iudicetur. Si enim malum est, iniuriam facere, non est alienus à culpa, qui vicem malam rependit; ac per hoc non potest bonus haberi, qui malum imitatur.

Praeceptum hoc 1. non est datum Magistratui, sed privatis. 2. Non prohibetur, iniuriam declinare. 3. nec seipsum cum modetamine inculpatae tutelae defendere. 4 nec auxilium Magistratus implorare, eiq; vindictam committere. Sed privatae vindictae cupiditati unicè hoc est oppositum. *(Caeterùm nec à Magistratu ut vindicta legitimè petatur, licitum in N. Test. esse, sed à Christo hîc prohiberi, Photiniani contendunt, urgentes, quòd Christi verba opponantur legi V. Test. quâ vindicta privata itidem prohibita, sed publica saltim concessa erat. Vid. Osterod. in Instit. Germ. c. 26. Val. Smalcius in Refut. Thes. D. Frantzii, & quidem Disp. 7. de B. O. pag. 237. seqq. Non multum ab his abludunt Arminiani, quorum antesignanus Simon Episcopius Resp. ad Q. 27. t. 2. p. 25. Indultu, scribit, legis Mosaicae permittebatur laeso, oculum pro oculo, dentem pro dente postulare aut reposcere. Quo iure? talionis. Quo fine? ultionis & vindictae, nullo bono postulantis & solo tantùm malo ac damno eius, qui prior laeser at i. e. oculum aut dentem excusser at. Huic oppositum est Christi inter dictum. Conferatur idem in Tract. de Mag. Polit, c. 4. p. 75. Verùm sententiae illi, quòd Christus ipsi legi divinae verba sua oppotiat, quod cum Photinianis Arminiani statuunt, quòdque etiam publica, per Magistratum quae fit, vindicta illicita in Nov. Test. sit, ceu Photiniani somniant, opponimus 1. antecedentium & consequentium considerationem, utpote è quibus liquet, quòd Christus verba sua non ipsi legi divinae, sed antiquis h. e. depravato Pharisaeorum sensui opponat. Et licet vers. 38. non repetatur vox antiquis, debet tamen subintelligi, quemadmodum etiam Hugo Grotius, qui aliàs non admodùm ab Arminianorum sectâ abhorret, ultrò in h. l. illud largitur. Imò ipse quoq; Socinus l. cont. Palaeol. pag. 157. fatetur, verba Christi h. l. non opponi verbis legis, sed sensui legis depravato Pharisaico. Sciendum enim est, quòd cùm DEUS iusto ac sapientissimo iudicio (insanus enim, ne quid gravius dicam, Smalcius est, scribere non veritus, nihil in eo inesse rationis, sics, qui me offendit, ita puniatur, ut nihil in me redeat commodi. Imò potiùs sufficit, quòd iustitiae divinae per publicam poenam, quae talionis poenae quàm similima est, fiat satis, quòdque tali modo delicta puniantur ac praeterea -aedendi proximum libido coērceatur) ius talionis per magistratum exerceri non solùm permisisset, Sed & praecepisset Exod. 21, 24.Lev. 24, 20. Pharisaei horumq; praecessores corruptelis suis legem divinam depravarint, & in alium detorserint sensum; nempe, licere quoque privatis acceptâ iniuriâ sese ulcisci ac malum pro malo reddere, modò non excedatur modus talionis. quae legis corruptio etiam in V. T. prohibita fuit, ceu ex Lev. 19, 18.Prov. 24, 29. videre est. Opponimus igitur Photinianis. 2. legis divinae, quâ magistratui gladii gerendi potestas facta, in N. T. repetitionem ac iteratam confirmationem, Vid. Rom. 13, 4.1. Petr. 2, 14. Unde manifestum est, quòd Christus non liget Iudici manus in sceleratos, nec eripiat magistratui gladium, sed privatos saltem coërceat & vindictae libidinem, privatim pro arbitrio exercendae, compescat. 3. absurdi consequntionem. Si Christus verbis hisce simpliciter omnem vindictā sive legitimam sui defensionem voluisset sublatam, tunc ipse contra verba sua postmodum egisset, ac legis suae vim proprio suo exemplo enervasset. Conseqq. prob. ex Ioh. 18, 23. Sequeretur etiam, Apostolos contrariari tum exemplo, vid. Act. 23, 3. tum doctrinâ Magistri sui praeceptis. Patet igitur, quòd haec Christi verba non accipienda sint ἁπλῶς, sed συγκριτικῶς. 4. Contrariam ipsius Christi adseverationem. expressè enim dicit vers. praeced. 17. quòd non venerit solvere legem, sed implere. Addimus 5. commodam legis divinae explicationem. neque enim lex illa, ipsis etiam Iudaeis hodiè monentibus, ita rigidè accipienda est, quasi praecisè oculus iterum exculpendus vel manus amputanda illi sit, qui tale quid fecit: sed sensu proverbiali, quòd nempe damnum aestimari à Iudicibus debeat, quantum pro oculo vel dente excusso sit dandum. Vid B. Par. Comm. in Deut. p. 1175. Adiicimus 6. legis huius divinae (quòd sonti iusta infligi poena debeat, si vel maximè laesus quoad suam personam nihil in specie commodi vel compensationem aliquam inde accipiat, modò faciat tale publicae vindictae exercitiū ac iustae poenaeir.

irrogatio ad laesae iustitiae reparationem, ac rei, qui laesit, correstionem, tum quoq; ad aliorum, ne ita proclives sint ad damnum proximo inferendum, praemonitionem) cum iure naturae & ac gentium conformitatem ac consensionem. Quâ de re videantur nonnulla apud B. Par. L. de Mag. Pol. §. 259. Comment. in Deut. p. 1180. Tannerum, Theolog. Scholast. T. 3. Disp 4. q. 2. D. 4. n. 66. seqq. Hug. Calov. Socin. Proflig. p. 1005. seqq. B. D. R-nig Cas. Consc. pag. 680.)*

Neque enim Christus loquitur hîc de tali iniuriâ, quâ qui vel de suâ vel suorum vitâ periclitatur, nec periculum evadere aliter potest, sed loquitur saltem de iniuriâ levi, quam aequo potiùs animo ferendam suadet, quàm ut quis proximum repercutiat, vel ex privatae vindictae cupiditate, in ius vocet. ὅστις σε ῥαπίσει ῥαπίζειν propriè est palmâ seu manu apertâ percutere. Suidas ῥαπίσαι dicit esse Χιτὼν

Comparatè hoc intelligendum. Potiùs, quàm alapam regeras, etiam alteram maxillam percutiendam offeras.

## 5:40
v. 40. Χιτὼν.

Χιτὼν is a tunic or inner garment of lesser value, ἱμάτιον is an outer garment of greater value. This distinction, however, is not perpetual.

Euthymius on this passage: Sometimes every garment is now ἱμάτιον, now χιτὼν, sometimes called a cloak, sometimes a tunic: more often also ὁ χιτὼν τὸ ἱμάτων is said, and conversely, that is, tunic, cloak; and cloak, tunic. Luke places the cloak first, therefore it is understood most simply thus: if anyone wishes to snatch one garment from you, permit him rather to take away the other also, than that you should return injury out of a desire for private vengeance.

*(That Anabaptists and some Photinians less correctly gather from this passage that it is repugnant to the doctrine of Christ for Christians to exercise civil judgments, is shown at length, besides our own people in various places, also by Simon Episcopius the Arminian, who often otherwise photinianizes, in his Treatise on the Political Magistrate, ch. 4.)*

Latin:

v. 40. Χιτὼν.

Χιτὼν est tunica sive vestis interior ac minoris precii, ἱμάτιον est exterior & maioris precii vestis. Haec tamen differentia non est perpetua.

Euthymius in h. l. Inter dum omnis vestis nuncἱμάτιον,nuncχιτὼν,modò pallium, modò tunica appellatur: Saepiùs etiamὁ χιτὼν τὸ ἱμάτωνdicitur & è contrario, id est tunica, pallium; & pallium, tunica. Lucas praeponit pallium, simplicissimè ergo sic accipitur, si quis tibi vult eripere vestem unam, permitte potiùs ut auferat etiam alteram, quàm ex privatae vind-ctae cupiditate iniuriam referas.

*(Quod ex h. l. minùs rectè Anabaptistae ac Photiniani nonnulli colligant, repugnare doctrinae Christi, ut Christiani iudicia civilia exerceant, prolixè praeter nostrates passim, ostendit quoque Simon Episcoius Arminianus, saepè alias photinianizans, Tr. de, Mag. Pol. c. 4.)*

## 5:41
v. 41. Χιτὼν Couriers were called the runners of the Persian Kings. Suidas: Χιτὼν it is therefore a word of Persian origin. Gloss. Suidae. Χιτὼν It was permitted to the couriers of the Persians, just as it is today for the Turks, to seize the horses or ships of anyone, or even the men themselves for the journey, whence it happened that ἀγγαρεύειν. angaria may be taken as to compel to run, or to carry something. What ἀγγάρειον, was, Herodotus describes in book 8. *(Suidas citing Phavorinus under the word Χιτὼν Cf. more in Phavor. in Lex. p. 13.)*

ἀγγαρεύειν [To impress/compel into service]. ἀγγάρειον, [A station for couriers/an impressment], Χιτὼν [Tunic] Agathias lib. 2. The Persians divided their journeys into parasangs, and therefore the couriers and porters, as soon as they had reached the parasang, would rest, and would entrust their burdens to others going further to be transferred by turns.

R. Isaac Satizan in the book in which he illustrates the affirmative precepts. The reason for angaria is when someone takes away a donkey, with its master following him, and he takes away every donkey he meets, and restores the former to the one to whom it belongs, but the second follows his own donkey until he has met another. As the author of this explanation he praises Solomon Jarchi. Therefore, by this word a kind of servitude is declared that is clearly intolerable, as one may gather from the examples which Drusius recounts from the Talmudic books in book 1 of his Praeterita on this passage. Compare Josephus, book 13 of the Jewish Antiquities, chapter 3, in the Epistle of Demetrius to Jonathan and the Jewish people, where the interpreter is Ruffinus. Nor after this sanction, let the beasts of burden of the Jews be subject to the violence of angariae.

What is ἀγγαρειον to the Greeks is to perform angaria to the Rabbis, as Drusius proves with examples taken from the Talmud in book 1 of his Animadversiones, chapter 38. Ἄγγαροι are called רצים by the Hebrews Esth. 3. v. 15.

The word angariae was used by Ulpian in the Code, title on Angariae and Parangariae, and by P. Nigidius in A. Gellius, book 19, Noctes Atticae, chapter 14. *(Let there be seen here also, besides the lexicographers, Don La-r. Ramirez de Prado in Pentecont. p. 146. seqq. Brodaeus of Tours, book 6, Miscellanea, chapter 6, T. 2, Thes. Crit. p. 553 & 554. Mr. Dilherr, Disp. T. 1. p. 137, 138. The Syrian expresses the word ἀγγαρεύειν both here and in Matt. 27, 32. by by which very word the Arab also uses everywhere: but שחר denotes to both the Syrians and the Arabs compelled, drove. The Ethiopian likewise uses one and the same word in both places, namely in the same sense. Furthermore, the same word שחר, which the Syrian and Arab used in this passage, Onkelos or the Chaldean Paraphrast also used Num. 16. 15. for the Hebrew נשא. at which passage Raschi says שחריה)*

i. e. It is of the Aramaic or Syro-Chaldaic language, it is so called the King's Angaria שחוור, ἄγγαρος or a prefect, compelling to angariae. Dn. D. Reinesius also suspects, in book 2, Var. 14, p. 240, & in Epil. p. 684, that the name Angariani was also once in use, and that by the same, according to the Glossary of Isidore, he is designated who rents a field, so that he may receive angaria.)*

All these things are said by Christ comparatively and by hypothesis, because anything is rather to be endured, not only by private individuals, but even in judgments, than that anything should be committed out of private vengeance; because we are prepared to endure repeated injuries rather than to avenge ourselves for one; with which agrees almost what Augustine teaches in Epistle 5 to Marcellinus, book on lying ch. 15, book 22 against Faustus ch. 76, These precepts pertain more to the preparation of the heart, which is within, than to the work, which is done in the open.

Latin:

v. 41. ΧιτὼνAngari Regum Persicorū cursores dicebantur. Suidas: Χιτὼν est ergo vocabulum origine Persicum. Gloss. Suidae. Χιτὼν Persarum cursoribus, sicut & hodiè Turcarum fas erat cuiusvis equos vel naves, aut ipsos etiam homines rapere ad cursum, unde factum, ut ἀγγαρεύειν. angar iare accipiatur pro cogere ad currendum, vel ad ferendum aliquid. Quid fuerit ἀγγάρειον, describit Herodotus lib. 8. *(Suidas allegante Phavorino voce Χιτὼν Conf. plura apud Phavor. in Lex. p. 13.)*

Agatias lib. 2. Dividebant Persaeitinera sua in parasangas, & ideò tabelliones & baiuli, ut quosparasanga attigisent, quiescebant, & onera sua aliis ulteriùs euntibus per vices transferenda cōmittebant.

R. Isaac Satizan in libro, quo praecepta affirmantia illustrat. Ratio angaria est, cùm aliquis aufert asinum, huius Domino sequente illum & omnem asinum urimum occurrentem aufert, & restituit priorem ei, cuius est, secundus autem sequitur asinum suum, donec obviam factus fuerit alius. Cuius explic-tionis autorem laudat Salomonem Iarium. Declaratur igitur hac voce servitutis genus planè intolerabile, ut colligere licet ex exemplis quae ex libris Thalmudicis recenset Drusius lib. 1. praeterit. ad h. l. Confer Iosephum lib. 13. antiquit. Iudaic. cap. 3. in Epistolam Demetrii ad Ionathan & populum Iudaeum, ubi Ruffinus Interpres. Nec post hanc sanctionem, Iudaeorum iumeuta violentiis angariarum subiaceant.

Quod Graecis est ἀγγαρειον id Rabinis est facere angariam, ut exemplis è Thalmud petitis probat Drusius lib. 1. animadv. cap. 38. Ἄγγαροι Hebraeis dicuntur רציםEsth. 3. v. 15.

Vocabulo angariae usi fuêre Ulpianus in C. tit. de Angar. & parang. P. Nigidius apud A. Gellium lib. 19. N. A. cap. 14. *(Videantur quoque hîc praeter Lexicographos, Don La-r. Ra-irez de Prado in Pentecont. p. 146. seqq. Brodaeus Turonensis l. 6. Miscell. cap. 6. T. 2. Thes. Crit. p. 553 & 554. Dn. Dilherr. Disp. T. 1. p. 137, 138. Syrus verbum ἀγγαρεύειν tum hic, tum Matt. 27, 32. exprimit per quo ipso etiam verbo utitur quoque Arabs urobique: notat verò שחר tum Syris, tum Arabibus c-ëgit,adegit. Aethiops patiter utroq; loco unum & idem verbum adhibet, nempe eodem sensu. Caeterùm eodem verbo שחר, quo Syrus & Arabs h. l. usi sunt, usus quoque est Onkelos s. Paraphrastes Chaldaeus Num. 16. 15. pro Ebr. נשא. ad quem locum Raschi ita שחריה

i. e. Linguae Aramaeae s. Syro-Chaldaicae est, sic vocatur Angaria Regisשחוור,ἄγγαρος sive praesectus, ad angarias cogens. Suspicatur quoque Dn. D. Reinesius l. 2. Var. 14. p. 240. & in Epil. p. 684. Angariani quoque nomen olim in usu fuisse, eodemque iuxta Gloss. Isidori designatum eum, qui agrum locat, ut angariam accipiat.)*

Haec omnia à Christo comparatè & ex hypothesi dicuntur, quod quidvis potiùs olerandum non solùm à privatis, sed etiam in iudiciis, quàm ex privatâ vindicta quidquam cōmittendum; quod parati simus iniurias iteratas potiùs tolerare, quàm de una, aliquâ nos vindicare: cum quo ferè congruit, quod Augustinus Epist. 5. ad Marcellinum, lib, de mendacio c. 15. lib. 22. contra Faustum cap. 76. docet, Praecepta ista magis ad praeparationem cordis, quae in-est, quàm adopus, quod in aperto fit, pertinere.

## 5:42
v. 42. τῷ αιτοῦντί σε, δίδου etc. He says simply and absolutely, to him who asks of you. Luc. 6. v. 30. the universal give to everyone who asks, is added, so that it may signify, whoever he may be, who implores our help of any kind, whether he be a friend or an enemy; whether he can return the favor, or less, we ought to do good and gratify him. In whatever ways we can, whether by gift or by loan, we are bound to succor the indigence of our neighbor.

Latin:

v. 42. τῷ αιτοῦντί σε, δίδου &c. Simpliciter & absolutè dicit, petenti à te.Luc. 6. v. 30. additur universalis da omni petenti, ut significet, quisquis ille sit, qui nostram opem quamcunq; imploret, sive sit amicus sive inimicus; sive referregratiam possit, sive minùs, illi nos debere benefacere & gratificari. Quibuseanq; possumus modis sive dono, sive mutuo, indigentiae proximi fuccurre redebemus.

## 5:43
v. 43. Χιτὼν

That appendix concerning hating the enemy nowhere exists in the law, but was a figment of the Pharisees, who from the law concerning the love of the neighbor inferred that an enemy could lawfully be hated, because by the name of neighbor they wrongly understood only a friend. The contrary is rather commanded in the law. Lev. 19. v. 17. 18. Exod. 23. v. 4. 5 1. Sam. 24. 1. 5. cap. 26. v. 9. 2 Reg 6. v. 21. Iob. 31. v. 29 Prov. 25. v. 21. From this verse, therefore, it shines forth more clearly than the sun that this doctrine of Christ is opposed not to the divine law, but to the Pharisaical corruptions of the law. * (It is to be wondered at, therefore, that not only Photinians, so that they might establish their hypothesis about Christ as a new legislator, maintain that in the old law it was lawful to hate an enemy: But also that the Jesuit Maldonatus should here act as a reinforcement to the Photinians, and when the Photinians have been reduced to the point that they are forced to concede that it no longer exists in the Mosaic Law, it could have happened that those words: And you shall hate etc.
