-where in the written law they existed: even if today they are not found in it, as Ostorodus tries to defend himself with such an evasion, Instit. Germ. p. 171, not blushing to drag into this matter the passage Deut. 25, 19. The same is also maintained by Alphonsus Salmeron in the explanation of the passage Ioh. 13, 24. But Corn. à Lapide rightly departs here from these Socinians of his, and warns, the old law commanded that not only friends, but also enemies be loved, that this is evident from Exod. 23. 3. and Lev. 19, 18. it is said: You shall love your neighbor, they inferred: therefore you shall hate your enemy. But by neighbor they understood a neighbor by name and race, as if only Jews were to be loved by Jews; but other nations were to be hated. Which is a manifest error. Thus far the Jesuit Corn. à Lapide, correcting the Jesuit Maldonatus. Cornelius is followed by his follower, the same Jesuit Tirinus. But long before Cornelius, the same thing was taught quite prolixly by Tostatus Abulensis Comm. in Matth. quest. 345. Rightly the Jesuit Gaspar Sanctius Comm. in Zach. p. 170. Christ took the former part of this verse from Leviticus: the latter he reproves and condemns, because the Jews had taken that not from the text, but from their own head. The same is also maintained by Alphonsus Mendoza, Th. D. and in the Academy of Salamanca, head of the Scotist Chair, Controv. Theolog. page 377, and also Felicianus Capitonus Archbishop of Avignon, Explic. Cathol. part. 2. p. 425, and even Bellarmine himself l. 4. de Iustif. c. 3. 4. But B. D. Fewrb. in Anti Ost. disp. 25. page 390 seqq. shows the futility of the exception of Ostorodus. But B. Hackspan. Tract. de script. Iud. usu p. 296, conveniently urges against Smalcius the Photinian, who errs the same as Ostorodus and asserts that the book in which the command concerning the hatred of enemies existed had been lost, that it is not said by Christ, you remember that it is written, you shall hate etc., but you have heard that it was said , also that Christ had said a little before, not even an iota will perish from the law; so far, therefore, is it from the case that an entire book of Canonical Scripture has perished. But we ought to love our enemies, not as they are impious and haters of GOD, for thus we ought to pursue their vices with hatred, Ps. 139, 21. but as they are men. Briefly, we ought to love our enemies, as God loves them, namely not by approving their vices, but so that they may be amended by doing good to them.

Latin:

v. 43. Χιτὼν

Appendix illa de odio inimici nuspiam in lege extat, sed erat figmentum Pharisaeorum, qui ex lege de dilectione proximi infere. bant, inimicum posse licitè odio haberi, quia proximi nomine perperam intelligebant solum amicum. Contrarium potiùs in lege praecipitur. Lev. 19. v. 17. 18.Exod. 23. v. 4. 51. Sam. 24. 1.5.cap. 26. v. 9.2 Reg 6. v. 21.Iob. 31. v. 29Prov. 25. v. 21. Ex hoc ergo vers. Sole clariùs elucescit, hanc Christi doctrinam non legi divinae, sed Pharisaicis legis corruptelis oppositam esse. * (Mirandum ergò, non Photinianos solùm, quò hypothesin suāa de Christo novo legislatore stabilire possint, statuere, in veteri lege licitum fuisse, inimicum odisse: Verùm etiam Iesuitam Maldonatū Photinianis hîc succenturiaree, & cùm Photimiani eò redacti sint, ut concedere cogantur, non extare ampliùs in Lege Mosaicâ, fieri potuisse, ut ea verba: Et odio habebis &c.

-spiam in lege scripta extiterint: tamet si hodie in illa non reperiantur, ceu Ostorodus tali effugio tueri se conatur, Instit. Germ. p. 171. non erubescere, in rem hanc trahere locum Deut. 25, 19. Idem etiam statuit Alphonsus Salmeron in expl. loci Ioh. 13, 24. Sed rectè à Sociennis istis suis discedit hîc Corn. à Lapide, monetque, legem veterem praecepisse, non solùm amicos, sed & inimicos diligi, idpatere exExod. 23. 3.&Lev. 19, 18.dicitur: Diliges proximum tuum, inferebant: ergo odihabebis inimicum tuum. Per proximum verò intelligebant proximum cognomine & gente, quasi Iudaeis soli Iudaei essent diligendi; Coeterae verò gentes odio habendae. qui manifestus est error. Hactenus Iesuita Corn. à Lapide, Iesuitam Maldonatum corrigens. Cornelium sequitur adsecla eiusdem Iesuita Tirinus. Dudum verò ante Cornelium idem hoc satis prolixè docuit Tonstatus Abulensis Comm. in Matth. quaest. 345. Rectè Iesuita Gaspar Sanctius Comm. in Zach. p. 170. Priorem partem huius vers. sumsit Christus ex Levitico: posteriorem reprehendit & damnat, quiae illam non è textu, sed è suo capite sumerant Iudaei. Idem quoq; statuunt Alph onsus Mendoza, Th. D. & in Acad. Salmant. Scoti Cathedrae praefectus, Controv. Theolog. pag. 377. nec non non Felicianus Capitonus Archi Episc. Avinion. Explic. Cathol. part. 2. p. 425 quin ipse Bellarm. l. 4. de Iustif. c. 3. 4. Futilitatem autem exceptio--s Ostorodi ostendit B D Fewrb. in Anti Ost. disp. 25. pag. 390 seqq. Commodè verò B. Hackspan. Tract. de script. Iud. usu p. 296. adversus Smalcium Photinianum, eundem cum Ostorodo errantem errorem, adserentemque, quòd liber, in quo extiterit mandatum, de inimicorū odio, amissus fuerit, urget, quòd à Christo non dicatur, meministis, scriptum esse, odio habebis &c. sed audistis dictum ---ss--e, item quòd Christus paullò antè dixerit, ne Iota quidem de lege periturum; tantum igitur abest, integrum librum Scripturae Canonicae periisse. Diligere verò debemus inimicos nostros, non quat. sunt impii ac DEI osores, sic enim odio prosequie enorum vitia debemus, Ps. 139, 21. sed quat. sunt homines. Breviter, debemus diligere inimicos nostros, ut Deus eos diligit nempe non vitia eorum, approbando sed ut emendentur, iis benefaciendo.

## 5:44
v. 44. Χιτὼν &c. Χιτὼν are joined. The first regards the mind and the affection of the heart. The second regards the tongue, because we ought to pray well for enemies. The third regards the works themselves, external. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, and the proof of love is the exhibition of the work. The Vulgate version omitted the second member, εὐλογεῖτετοὺς καταρωμένους ὑμας. Chrysostom also does not read it, whence some suspect that it was transferred here from Luke 6. verse 28.. But the Greek codices* (to which the Greek manuscript Eclogae of the Nuremberg Library also attest)* constantly read that member not only in Luke, but also in this place in Matthew. Indeed, Chrysostom himself interprets it. For he discourses thus in homily 18 on Matthew: He commands to ascend to a higher degree, who determines that one must not stop at love alone, but also proceed to works, because after he said: Love your enemies, he added, Do good to them. *(The Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopian also read this second member and acknowledge it as a genuine part of the text. Of these, the latter expressly has , the former , that one: It is to be observed, however, that in the Roman Arabic edition this member was omitted. This was perhaps done intentionally by the Pontifical editor, so that, namely, the Vulgate version might be believed to have the patronage or applause of the Arabic . But even the Jesuit Corn. à Lapide himself expounds this member as a genuine part of the present passage.)*

*(From the fact, however, that Christ here commands to love enemies, the Photinians and Anabaptists ineptly conclude: 1. that wars in general are illicit for Christians today. 2. that it is not permitted for a Christian Magistrate to inflict capital punishments upon the guilty. 3. nor is it lawful to contend with a neighbor in court. Furthermore, those errors of the Photinians and Anabaptists are dealt with elsewhere. The nature of our undertaking does not permit that the arguments for our orthodox opinion be brought forward here, or that the arguments of the adversaries be examined in order. See, if you please, B. D. Chemn. LL. Th. part 2. p. 67. 20. B. Par. L. de Magistr. Polit. passim. in particular, however, concerning the present passage §. 281. 305. 381. Dn. D. Calov. Socin. Proflig. p. 979. seqq. B. D.

Fewrb. AntiOst. p. 410. B. D. Meisn. Consid. Theol. Photin. p. 225. seqq. B. D. Stegm. Disp. 54. Photin. p. 865. seqq. Distinguish above all between the desire for private vengeance, and the public office of the magistrate, divinely committed to him. Distinct virtues are not to be opposed to one another. Charity and Justice are such virtues.

Augustine rightly warns in tract. 5 on the 1st Epistle of John: not any kind of beneficence toward an enemy is commanded to us, but that which proceeds from charity, which is higher than love itself. Speaking absolutely, it is indeed easier to do good to an enemy than to love him, as Gregory proves in homily 17 on Ezekiel; therefore Christ does not demand just any beneficence, but that which proceeds from love; this is something higher than love itself.

Ἐυλογεῖται (The examples not only of the prophets and other pious men seem to be contrary to this precept of the Savior. See Gen. 9, 25.2. Sam. 15, 31.Ps. 6, 11.Ps. 35, 1.Ps. 96, 29.Ps. 94. 2.Ps. 109. etc. 1. Cor. 16, 22.Gal. 5, 12.2. Thess. 3, 2.Apoc. 6. 10. but also of Christ himself Matth. 11, 21. following. But one must distinguish between imprecations that have proceeded from vice or affection, and those uttered from pious zeal and a prophetic spirit. Blessed Augustine, book 16 against Faustus the Manichaean, ch. 27: Curses, when they are spoken from prophecy, are not from an evil wish, but from the foreknowing spirit of the one denouncing. The imprecations of Christ and the Prophets against wicked men were not made by the wish of those desiring, but by the spirit of those foreseeing; not from a desire for private vengeance, but from a pious zeal for promoting justice. It is one thing to curse from the judgment of justice, another from the malice of vengeance. The former is permitted, the latter is prohibited. Let the Blessed D. Balduinus, Cases of Conscience, book 3, chapter 7, case 8, be compared entirely.)

He also commands us to pray for enemies. 1. So that we do not think that vengeance against enemies is to be sought from God. 2. So that, even if we ourselves are unable to do good to our neighbor, we may nevertheless pray to God that He may do good to them. 3. So that by the example of the heavenly Father we may demonstrate in reality that we seriously seek the salvation of all men.

Some wish the word ἐπηρεάζειν to be a military word derived from ἀπὶ and ἄρης which signifies Mars, whence ἐπήρια as if ὲπάρεια a martial and hostile assault. Others wish it to be a forensic word, and its meaning to be to calumniate, as Casaubon shows in his notes. Budaeus writes in his earlier annotations on the Pandects that Pliny, Celsus, Tranquillus, and others have said to be infested through ἐπηρεάζειν

Latin:

v. 44. Χιτὼν &c. Coniunguntur Χιτὼν Primum spectat ad animum & cordis affectum. Alterum ad linguam, quòd benè precari debeamus inimicis. Tertium ad ipsa opera, externa. Ex abundantia enim cordis os loquitur & probatio dilectionis est exhibitio operis. Vulg. versio secundum membrum, εὐλογεῖτετοὺς καταρωμένους ὑμας omisit. Chrysostomus quoq; illud non legit, unde quidam suspicantur, exLuc. 6. vers. 28.esse húc translatum. Sed Codd. Graeci* (quibus etiam adstipulantur Eclogae MSS. Graecae Bibl. Norib.)* constanter illud membrum non solùm apud Lucam, sed etiam hoc loco apud Matthaeum legunt. Quin & Chrysostomus ipse illud interpretatur. Sic enim disserit homil. 18. in Matth. Altiorem gradum conscendere iubet, qui non in sola dilectione sistendum, sed & ad opera progrediendum statuit, quia post quam dixit: Diligite inimicos, addidit, Benefacite eis. *(Legunt quoque secundum hoc membrum, & tanquam genuinam textus partem agnoscunt Syrus, Arabs, Aethiops. quorum, hic expressè habet ille isle: Observandum tamen, quòd in edit. Arabica Romana membrum hoc omissumsit. id quod fortè studio ab editore Pontificio factum est, quò scil. Vulgata versio patrocinium vel applausum Arabis -abere credatur. Sed & ipse Iesuita Corn. à Lapide membrum hoc tanquam genuinam loci praesentis partem exponit.)*

*(Ex eo autem quòd Christus h. l. inimicos diligere iubet, ineptè Photiniani atque Anabaptistae c---igunt, 1. bella in universum esse hodie Christianis illicita. 2. non permissum esse Magistratui Christiano, ut sontibus supplicia capitalia irroget. 3. nec licitum esse, in iudicio contendere cum proximo. Caeterùm de istis Photimanorum atque Anab. erroribus alibi agitur. Instituti nostri ratio non permittit, ut orthodoxae nostrae sententiae argumenta hîc in medium proferantur, Adversariorum verò argumenta ordine examinentur. Videantur, si placet, B. D. Chemn. LL. Th. part. 2. p. 67. 20. B. Par. L. de Magistr. Polit. passim. in specie verò de praesenti loco §. 281. 305. 381. Dn. D. Calov. Socin. Proflig. p. 979. seqq. B. D.

Fewrb. AntiOst. p. 410. B. D. Meisn. Consid. Theol. Photin. p. 225. seqq. B. D. Stegm. Disp. 54. Photin. p. 865. seqq. Dist. ante omnia inter privat am vindicte cupiditatem, & inter poublicum magistratûs efficium, divinitus illi commissum. Virtutes distinctae nonn sunt sibi invicem opponendae. Caritas & Iustitia sunt tales virtutes E.)*

Rectè antem monet Augustinus tract. 5. in 1. Epist. Ioh. non qnamcunbeneficentiam adinimicum nobis praecipi, sed illam, quae ex caritate procedit, quae ipsâ dilectione altior est. Absolutè quidem loquēdo facilius est benefacere inimico, quàm illum diligere, ut probat Gregorius homil. 17. in Ezech. ideò Christus non quam cunq; beneficentiam exposcit, sed eam, quae procedit ex dilectione, haec est altius quid ipsâ dilectione.

Ἐυλογεῖται *(Videntur huic Salvatoris praecepto contrariari exempla non solùm prophetarum aliorumq; piorum hominum. Vid Gen. 9, 25.2. Sam. 15, 31.Ps. 6, 11.Ps. 35, 1.Ps. 96, 29.Ps. 94. 2.Ps. 109. &c. 1. Cor. 16, 22.Gal. 5, 12.2. Thess. 3, 2.Apoc. 6. 10. verùm etiam ipsius Christi Matth. 11, 21. seqq. At disting. inter imprecationes, ex vitio so affectu profectas, & à pio zelo ac spiritu prophetico prolatas. B. Aug lib. 16. contra Faustum Manich. c. 27. Maledicta cùm; ex Prophetià dicuntur, non sunt de malo voto, sed de praescio spiritu denunciantis. Imprecationes Christi & Prophetarum adversus homines pravos non sunt factae voto optantium, sed spiritu providentium; non, privatae vindictae desiderio, sed pio iustitiae promovendae zelo. Aliud est maledictum ex iudicio iustitiae, aliud ex livore vindictae. illud concessum, hoc prohibitum. Conferatur omninò B. D. Balduinus Cas. Consc. lib. 3. cap. 7. cas. 8.)*

Orare etiam iubet pro inimicis. 1. ne existimemus, vindictam adversùs hostes esse à Deo petendam. 2. ut, si vel maximè nos non possimus proximo benefacere, Deum tamen oremus, ut ipsis benefaciat. 3. ut exemplo Patris coelestis omnium hominem salutem nos seriò expetere, reipsa demonstremus.

Verbum ἐπηρεάζειν quidam volunt esse verbum militare ab ἀπὶ & ἄρης quod Martem significat, deductum, unde ἐπήρια quasi ὲπάρεια Martius & hostilis insultus. Alii volunt esse verbum forense, & significationem eius esse calumniari, ut Casaubonus in notis, ostēdit. Budaeus inannot prioribus in Pandectas scribit, Plinium, Celsum, Tranquillum & alios dixisse infestari perἐπηρεάζειν

## 5:45
v. 45. ὅπως γένησθε υἱοὶ τοὐ πατρὸ ὑμῶν &c. ὅπως γένησθε Since no one performs what is required here unless impelled and moved by the Spirit of the heavenly Father, and no one receives that Spirit unless he has been adopted by God the Father into the Son, therefore the rule has a place here: many things are said to be done when they are declared to have been done. (For the confirmation of this rule, the following passages are also usually cited John 8:31 c. 15:8 Rom. 3:4 2 Tim. 2:21. The meaning, therefore, in this place is that you may be declared or be acknowledged as sons of GOD. For charity does not make sons of GOD, but shows them, John 13:35 1 John 3:14. But faith alone makes us sons of GOD, while it grafts us into Christ, John 1:12 James 2:18 Gal. 3:27. See B. Par. Harm. Evang. p. 1199. B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 279. Rightly, therefore, Corn. à Lapide on this place: That you may be i.e. by the force of show, that you are sons of GOD, or rather that you may be in reality through imitation i.e. imitators of GOD, who already are sons of GOD through grace and adoption. But not that you may be, just as Conzenius explains in this place. The same exposition is also held in the commentary of Ferus, but castrated, whence perhaps it was forced upon him . Ferus does, however, cite the passage John 13:35 which is entirely relevant here.

God the Father is the highest good, kind and beneficent toward all in the highest degree; therefore, there is no more genuine mark from which His sons are recognized than charity and kindness toward one's neighbor.

Augustine observes an emphasis in the pronoun ἁυτοὐ His sun i.e. which He Himself created, which is His own proper creature. So that from this we may be admonished, he says, with how much liberality we ought to provide for our enemies according to His precept, things which we did not create, but have received as His gift. Observe also that Christ proposes such an example of divine beneficence, which is the source and fountain of all temporal benefits which we can provide to a neighbor. For by the heat of the sun and the irrigation of rain, the earth is made fertile, so that it may bring forth crops and all things necessary for the sustenance of life.

Ἀνατέλλει is not placed here neutrally, but transitively, in which way it is also used by Homer in the Iliad, and βασιλεύειν signifies among the LXX to appoint a King. Thus among the Hebrews, verbs in the Qal are sometimes used in the meaning of verbs in the Hiphil, in which conjugation the Syrian expressed that verb in this place. Meanwhile without emphasis the Greek ἀνατέλλει is used here, so that the action of GOD with creatures and through creatures may be expressed. *(Seneca has twin sentiments to this one of the Savior in book 1 de benef. c. 1. and book 4 de Benef. cap. 15, which B. D. Quistorpius cites in this place. A similar sentiment is also read in Pirke Abhoth and is ascribed to Antigonus. Mr. Dilh. reports this in Elect. l. 1. c. 22. p. 133. Compare also on the present passage Greg. Nazianz. t. 1. pag. 457.)*

Latin:

v. 45. ὅπως γένησθε υἱοὶ τοὐ πατρὸ ὑμῶν &c. ὅπως γένησθε Cùm nemo nisi impulsus & actus Spiritu Patris coelestis praestet, quod hîc exigitur, ac nemo Spiritum illum accipiat, nisi qui in filium à Deo patre adoptatus est, ideò hiîc loeum habet regula: multa tunc fieri dicuntur, quando sacta esse declarantur.* (Pro confirmar dà hâc reg. adduci solent etiam loca Ioh. 8, 31.c. 15, 8.Rom. 3, 4.2. Tim. 2, 21. Sensus igitur h. l. est ut declaremini sive agnoscamini filii DEI. Charitas enim non facit filios DEI, sed ostendit, Ioh. 13, 35.1. Ioh. 3, 14. Sola autem fides nos DEI filios facit, dum Christo inserit, Ioh. 1, 12.Iac. 2, 18.Gal. 3, 27. Vid. B. Par. Harm. Evang. p. 1199. B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 279. Rectè igitur Corn. à Lapide ad h. l. Ut sitis i. e. vi osten-atis, vos esse filios DEI, aut potiùs ut sitis reipsâ per imitationem i. e. imitatores DEI, qui iam estis filii DEI per gratiam & adoptionem. Non autem ut siatis, sicuti Conzenius hoc loco exponit. Eadem expositio habetur, quoq; in com. Feri, sed castratis, unde fortè illi invi obtrusa. Adducit tn. Ferus locum Ioh. 13, 35. qui omninò huc facit.

Deus Pater est summum bonum, erga omnes in summo gradu benignus ac beneficus, nulla ergo germanior nota, ex qua filii ipsius agnoscuntur, quàm caritas & benignitas erga proximum.

Augustinus emphasin observat inn pronomine ἁυτοὐsuum Solem i. e. quem ipse creavit, qui est propria ipsius creatura. Ut hinc admoneamur, inquit, quantâ liberalitate inimicis nostris ex praecepto eius praestare debeamus, quae nos non creavimus, sed ex munere eius accepimus. Observa etiam tale divinae beneficentiae exemplum Christum proponere, quod omnium temporalium beneficiorum, quae proximo praestare possumus, fons est & scaturigo. Solis enim calore ac pluviae irrigatione terra faecundatur, ut fruges & omnia ad vitae sustentationem necessaria proferat.

Ἀνατέλλει non ponitur hîc neutraliter, sed transitivè, quo modo etiam usurpatur ab Homero Iliad. e. ac βασιλεύειν significat apud LXX. Regem constituere. Sic apud Hebraeos verba in Cal quandoq; usurpantu in significatione verborum in Hiphil, quâ coniugatione Syrus illud verbum hoc loco expressit. Interim nosine emphasi Graecum ἀνατέλλει hic usurpatur, ut actio DEI cum -reaturis & per -eaturas exprimatur. *(Gemellas sententias huic Salvatoris habet Seneca l. 1 de benef. c. 1. l. 4. de Benef. cap. 15. quas adducit B. D. Quistorpius in h. l. Similis quoque sententia in. Pirke Abhoth legitur & Antigono adscribitur. refert Dn. Dilh. Elect. l. 1. c. 22. p. 133. Conf. etiam de praes. loco Greg. Nazianz. t. 1. pag. 457.)*

## 5:46
v. 46. Χιτὼν &c.

Just as the former argument was drawn from relatives, so this latter is deduced from comparatives. How honorable it is, by beneficence and the love of enemies, to imitate the heavenly Father as His genuine sons: so shameful and detestable it is to be surpassed by publicans in beneficence and love, or certainly to be merely equal to those whom you ought to have preceded by many parasangs in the stadium and pursuit of virtues.

Τοὺς ὰγαπῶντας ὑμας The exclusive particle μόνον is to be understood, which is added in the verse immediately following. *( Μισθὸν See notes on Luc. 6, 32.)*

Τελῶναι are so called from τέλος tax, because they collected taxes or other revenues of the Roman people bought at a fixed price. They were in the highest hatred among the Jews. 1. because the rule of foreigners, namely the Romans, was very adverse to the Jews; they wished to be a free people, therefore they paid taxes to the Romans most unwillingly, and consequently also hated the exactors of taxes. 2. because the publicans, out of avarice, increased the taxes bought at a fixed price, extorting more than was permitted by the Magistrates. 3. because, since most were Jews, having regard more for profit than for religion, they associated familiarly with the Romans and hired out their services to them. *(More will be treated concerning Publicans at Marc. 2, 16. but concerning that which the Gentiles also love their friends, see the note on Luc. 6, 32.)*

Latin:

v. 46. Χιτὼν &c.

Sicut prius argumentum ductum erat à relatis, ita hoc posterius deducitur à comparatis. Quàm honorificum est, beneficentià & dilectione inimicorum vos Patrem coelestem tanquam genuinos ipsius filios imitari: tam propudiosum ac detestandum est, à publicanis in beneficentia & dilectione superari, vel certè iis duntaxat vos esse pares, quos in stadio ac studio virtutum multis parasangis antecedere oportebat.

Τοὺς ὰγαπῶντας ὑμας Subintelligenda particula exclusiva μόνον quae additur in versu proximè sequente. *( Μισθὸν Vide notas ad Luc. 6, 32.)*

Τελῶναι dicti sunt à τέλος vectigal, quia vectigalia aliosve, populi Rom. reditus certo precio redemtos colligebant. Erant illi in summo apud Iudaeos odio. 1. quia Iudaeis alienigenarum, videlicet Romanorum imperium valdè adversum fuit, voluerunt esse liber populus, aegerrimè igitur vectigalia Romanis solvebant, ac proinde etiam vectigalium exactores oderant. 2. quia publicani vectigalia certo precio emta ex avaritiâ augebant, plus extorquentes, quàm à Magistratibus permissum erat. 3. quia cùm pleriq; essent Iudaei, maiori lucri quàm religionis ratione habitâ Romanis familiariter conversabantur ac operam suam illis locabant. *(De Publicanis pluribus agetur ad Marc. 2, 16. de eo verò, quod Ethnici quoque diligant amicos suos, vid. not. ad Luc. 6, 32.)*

## 5:47
v. 47 Χιτὼν

Ἀῶάζεσθαι signifies to embrace lovingly, to greet with a kiss and embrace, which was the custom of those nations. Homer. Iliad. Χιτὼν But these rejoiced and with the right hand lovingly received, with sweet words. This custom was received not only among the Jews, but also among the Greeks and Romans. *(So also among Christians in the primitive Church, and even now among some peoples, as will be shown more fully below at 2. Cor. 13, 12.)*

Then it is used for salvation. The Syrian rendered it: If you inquire about the peace of your brothers, i. e. if you greet them humanely and dutifully.

Moreover, by the one duty of greeting, according to the custom used among the Hebrews συνεκδοχικῶς, all other things are also included. * ( τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς Thus also the Syrian, Arab, and Ethiopian read. But some Greek codices have φίλους, just as it is also read in the Eclog. MSS. Bibl. Norib.)*

ὁι τελῶναι Thus the Royal codices have it, along with most others. * (to which also the Greek Eclogae MSS. of the Nuremberg Library agree.)* But certain Greek books, with Chrysostom agreeing in his commentary, read ὁι ἐθηκοὶ, in which way the Latin Interpreter also translates. * (And thus, also the Ethiopian reads, who has here the word similarly. The Arab according to the Roman edition: for it is read in the said edition but in the Leiden one the word is held, denoting publican. The Syrian likewise reads in this manner, for he renders )*

Latin:

v. 47 Χιτὼν

Ἀῶάζεσθαι significat amanter complecti, salutare osculo & complexu, qui mos isarum erat gentium. Homer. Iliad. ΧιτὼνHi verò gavisi dextrâ amicè excipiebant, verbisisuavibus. Erat hic mos non solùm apud Iudaeos, sed etiam Graecos & Romanos receptus. *(Sic etiam apud Christianos in primitivâ Ecclesiâ, & etiamnum apud nonnullos populos, uti infrà ad 2. Cor. 13, 12. pluribus ostendetur.)*

Deinde usurpatur pro salutare. Syrus reddidit: Si interrogetis de pace fratrum vestrorum i. e. si humaniter & officiosè eos salutetis.

Caeterùm uno salutandi officio more apud Hebraeos usitato συνεκδοχικῶς etiam caetera comprehenduntur. * ( τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς Ita quoq; legunt Syrus, Arabs, Aethiops. Codd. verò nonnulli Graeci habent φίλους quomodo etiá legitur in Eclog. MSS. Bibl. Norib.)*

ὁι τελῶναι Ita habent Codd. Regii cum plerisq; aliis. * (quibus etiam adstipulantur Eclogae MSS. Graecae Bibl. Norib.)* Quidam verò Graeci libri, astipulante Chrysostomo in commentario, legunt ὁι ἐθηκοὶ quo modo etiam Latinus Interpres vertit. * (Etita, quoq; legit Aethiops, qui habet hîc vocem similitee. Arabs secundùm editionem Romanam: legitur enim in dictâ editione in Leidensi verô habetur vox publicanum notans. Syrus itidem h. m. legit, reddit enim )*

## 5:48
v. 48. Χιτὼν

Be perfect, i. e. emulate the perfection in the example of the heavenly Father proposed to you thus far, so that you may perform not only external, but also internal obedience to the law, and not only love friends, but also enemies. * (Against the Papists, who strive to prove from this place that regenerate men can perfectly fulfill the law, it must be observed that a distinction is made between absolute perfection or of degrees; and conditional, respective, or of parts. More will be advised below at Matth. 19, 21. See also Camero in Myroth. p. 12. & 300.)*

In the little word ὑμεῖς there is emphasis. You, who ought to be much more excellent and more perfect than publicans, who have been set apart into the people of GOD, nay, have been adopted into the sons of GOD.

Ὤῶερ ὁ πατὤρ a likeness is insinuated, not an equality: for we shall never be able to attain the perfection of GOD in the imperfection of this life. *(The comparison is not ἰσότητος but ὁμοιότητος not of equality, but of likeness.)*

There are two parts of the chapter. The former διδακτικὴ, in which is handed down the manner 1. of giving alms. 2. of praying. 3. of fasting. The latter ἀποτρεπτικὴ, in which Christ dissuades us. 1. from avarice. 2. from preposterous care for sustenance.

Latin:

v. 48. Χιτὼν

Sitis perfecti i. e. aemulemini perfectionem in exemplo Patris coelestis vobis hactenus propositam, ut non externam duntaxat, sed etiam internam obaedientiam legi praestetis, nec solùm amicos, sed etiam inimicos diligatis. * (Contra Pontificios, qui ex h. l. probare satagunt, posse homines renatos perfectè legem implere, observandum, quòd dist. sit inter perfectionem absolutams. graduum; & conditionatam, respectivam sive partium. Plura monebuntur infrà ad Matth. 19, 21. Co-etiam Camero in Myroth. p. 12. & 300.)*

In vocula ὑμεῖς est emphasis. Vos, qui publicanis multd praestantiores, & perfectiores esse debetis, qui in populum DEI segregati, imò in filios DEI adoptati estis.

Ὤῶερ ὁ πατὤρ similitudo insinuatur, non aequalitas: perfectionem enim DEI in huius vitae imperfectione assequi nunquam poterimus. *(Comparatio non est ἰσότητος sed ὁμοιότητος non aqualitatis, sed similitudinis.)*

Partes capitis duae sunt. Prior διδακτικὴ, in qua traditur modus 1. eleemosynas dandi. 2. orandi. 3. ieiunandi. Posterior ἀποτρεπτικὴ, in qua Christus nos dehortatur. 1. ab avaritiâ. 2. à praeposterae victûs cura.

## 6:1
v. 1. ἀπόδοσ

Connection. After He had purged the divine law from Pharisaical corruptions, He now further shows in what manner or with what spirit the good works prescribed in the divine law are to be done. Just as the doctrine of the Pharisees has been brought forward thus far, so those things which are handed down in the former part of this chapter are opposed to the life of the Pharisees, because the Pharisees did all their works with this spirit, that they might be seen by men. Matth. 23. v. 5.

(The blessed Luther expounded this whole chapter excellently in vol. 5 of the German Jena edition, pages 106 et seqq.)

Προσὲετε. The word ροσέχειν properly signifies to apply, therefore it seems that the noun τοὐ νοὸς. is to be understood, Apply your mind, attend diligently. August. rendered it Beware. *(Beautifully Chrysost. hom. 19. on Matth. declares the emphasis of the word ροσέχετε: Consider, he exclaims, whence our Savior began, who spoke as if about some most insidious serpent, most powerful for deceiving him who had not watched with his whole mind. Attend, he says, lest you do your alms before men. So also Paul Phil. (cap. 3, 2.) warns: Beware, he says, of dogs, beware of evil workers. For the beast enters secretly, all things well-growing inside with the greatest quiet and without any sense of the one losing, it carries off. And a little later: Since thus Christ when he had exhorted his hearers to liberality, he consequently uproots all things which strive to kill this most beautiful and most fruitful olive tree. Consistently with these, Aug. writes in book on the perfection of righteousness, ch. 17, that this chief vain glory, growing upon these external works of virtue, easily destroys them, not otherwise than the most beautiful ivy of Jonah. worm.Jon. 4, 7. Compare also Jerome on chap. 5. of the epistle to the Galatians. Let Gregory the Great also be added entirely in Morals p. 226.)*

CHAPTER VI.

Ἐλεημοσύνην. Some codices read τήν δικαιοσύνην. Hence Augustine in sermon 59 on the seasons cites this passage thus: Attend, -e that you may live justly with this intention, so that men may see you. And afterwards. He named justice generally, then he executes it particularly, for a work which is done through alms is some part of justice. Beza likewise contends that it must be read δικαιοσύνην. * (John Lorinus the Jesuit also, in his Commentary on the Post. Epistle of Peter c. 1, 1, among other places from which he thinks it can be confirmed that the word justice is taken for mercy, refers to this passage also, and thinks the word justice is taken similarly Ps. 30, 2.Is. 6, 1.2. Cor. 9. 10. Likewise 2. Pet. 1, 1. Eman. à Sa in the said place thinks the name justice is put for mercy. So also where in the Hebrew text there is צרקה the LXXII sometimes have the word ἐλεημοσύνης. See Deut. 6, 25.Ps. 103, 6.Is. 1, 27. &c.)*

But 1. the more approved and more numerous codices read τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην. *(Thus the Complutensian and Royal codices have it, according to Corn. à Lap. in this place. In the same way also all the Paris MSS. codices read, of which there were sixteen themselves; except at least one, according to Franc. Lucas. Similarly also the Greek MSS. Eclogues of the Nuremberg Library have it. Nor could Fr. Lucas, who nevertheless diligently compared the Greek MSS. codices, name any that has it otherwise, except that second Parisian one, which however Fr. Lucas himself, in his notes on the Greek Matthew, more than once reveals to have been corrected according to the Vulgate version. And this perhaps was one of those two which Beza names, and with them strives to confirm the reading by δικαιοσύνην, which he himself follows. Erasmus however, who likewise compared MSS. codices, mentions none that reads otherwise than ἐλεημ. in this place.)* 2. By the names of alms, prayer, and fasting συνεκδοχικῶς are understood duties of every kind owed to the neighbor, to God, and to ourselves, so that we may live δικαιως, σεβῶς σωφρόνως Tit. 2, 12. Compare Augustine in the book on the reason of perfect justice c. 17. 3. The first two verses of this chapter are completed in one period, of which ρότασις v. 1 is negative, ἀπόδοσις v. 2 is affirmative. Since therefore this has the word ἐλεημοσύνης, that one also must necessarily have the same. 4. The added little word ὑμῶν hints that it must be read τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην. 5. The little word δικαιοσύνηο seems to have crept into certain Greek codices from the Latin version . Furthermore, to the Hebrews צרקה and Chald. צרקא that is, righteousness, sometimes signifies alms, by which very thing it is insinuated that munificence toward the needy is not the least part of righteousness, owed to them by the very law of Nature. *(Strigelius notes in this place that the Emperor Tiberius II, when he was reproached because he was exhausting the treasury with alms, replied that money would never be lacking to the royal fisc as long as the poor were to receive alms.)* Hieron. lib. 2. ad v. Pelag. cap. 4. Take heed that you do not do your righteousness, i.e., your alms, before men. 6. Chrysostom & other Greek Fathers read ἐλεημοσύνην. 7. The Savior elsewhere never placed δικαιοσύνην for ἐλεημοσὺνη. *(Finally, the Ethiopian likewise reads ἐλεημοσύνην, for he translates he uses the noun otherwise for ἐλεημοσύνην, as it is permitted to see from the following verses 2. 3. 4. also Acts 3, 2.5c. 9, 36. &c.)*

*(As far as the Syriac interpreter is concerned, he has in this place with which word he himself uses elsewhere throughout for ἐλεημοσύνην, as of this chap. v. 2. 3. 4. also Luke 11, 41.c. 12.Acts 3, 2. 310.c. 9, 35.c. 10, 24.31.c. 24, 17. But where δικαιοσύνη is had in the Greek text, he himself does not use this word, but the noun or as in this very chapter vers 33.John 16, 8.10.Rom. 4, 6. and in many other places, or even the noun as Matt. 5, 6.10.c. 21, 32.Rom. 1, 17. &c. Although indeed both names, namely & descend from the same Root i.e., he was righteous, the Syrian nevertheless accurately distinguishes between the two, so that he uses this at least for δικαιοσύνῆ, not for ἐλεημοσύνῆ;, that for ἐλεημοσύνῆ,, but not for δικαιοσύνῆ,, a thing which Lexicographers have not observed accurately enough, as can be seen both from the Syr. Lexicon of Crinesius, and from the Syro-Chald. Dictionary of Guido Fabricius, which is inserted into the Apparatus of the Royal Spanish Work (for it is expressly read in it: זרוקותא Alms, righteousness, equity.) and from others. Which very difference also not weighing sufficiently, Corn. à Lapide without hesitation affirms, that the Syrian δικαιοσύνη reads: nay rather ἐλεημοσύνην, since elsewhere also he expresses this, and not that word, with the diction . And what you might wonder at, Hugo Grotius himself also annotates in this place thus:

Since it appears that the Syrian & Arab read thus ( τὴν δικαιοσύνην ὑμῶν ) nor is the authority of books lacking, I judge that it happened here entirely, as often elsewhere in these books, that the other reading was born from an interpretation of a gloss. Because δικαιοσύνη in the sense of ἐλεημοσύνης was a gloss, that is, a word less used, & better known to the Hellenists than to the Greeks, therefore the other word of more frequent use was added. But from where does it appear that the Syrian read thus? Nay rather he reads ἐλεημοσύνην, for he uses such a word, by which he otherwise expresses the Gr. ἐλεημοσύνην, as was shown a little before. As concerns the Arab, it can certainly be said by no appearance of probability at least, that he read δικαιοσύνην here: for he has according to the Roman and Leid. edition לא הצנעוא מראהמצם i.e., do not do your alms. Concerning the remaining conjectures elsewhere. Franc. Lucas, a man sufficiently knowledgeable in these matters, writes to this place: In Syriac it is Zedketho, which is ambiguous toward alms and righteousness. The just-mentioned author continues: for also in the Hebrew, Chaldaic and Arabic language the same word צרקה sedaka, which signifies righteousness in general, is also used properly for beneficence, which the Greeks ἐλεημοσύνην call. That in the Heb. & Chald. language the name צרקה, Chald. צרקא and צרקתא and by their imitation the Gr. word δικαιοσύνη is used now for righteousness, now for alms, is most well known, and learned men besides the Lexicographers confirm this same thing at length throughout with their own vote. See B. D. Quistorp. Annot. Bibl. p. 319. B. D. Frantz de Interpr. Sc. S. p. 788. B. D. Tarnov. in Mich. p. 134 Dn. Dilherr. Dispp. Acad. p. 1. p. 88. Thomas Gatak. de stylo N. T. pag. 248. Grotius ad c. 1. Matth. p. 15. But whether the Arabic is used equally for righteousness, and beneficence or alms, someone might doubt. The Arab N. T. Interpreter certainly uses for δικαιοσύνῃ throughout the name and from he was righteous, ce-, it is evident from Matt. 6, 34.John 16, 8.10Rom. 3, 5c. 4, 5.9.1. 12. &c, but for ἐλεημοσύνῃ he uses the name as pres. chap. v. 2. & 4 for it was done through a lapse of memory, when Schindler in Lex. Pentag. pag 1521. writes that the Arab Matt. 6 has: Do not do צרקהכם your alms, when the Arab has in both the Rom. and Leid. edit. Nor yet do I deny that the Arab N. T. Interpreter sometimes uses the name for ἐλεημοσύνη: it is certain

for this from v. 4 of this chapter, likewise from Acts 3, 2. 3.10.ch. 9, 36.ch. 10, 2. etc. But do others perhaps also look into justice?

Πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι θεᾶσθαι is more than ὁρᾶσθαι,, just as among the Latins to be looked at is more than to be seen.

The preposition ρὸς here denotes the end, not the event or the consequence; it is τελικὴ, not ὐκβατικὴ.. It does not forbid things rightly done from being seen. Matt. 5. v. 16. Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, but it forbids good works from being done with that intention and for that end, that we may be looked at, i.e., that we may seek praise and admiration among men. *(A twin sentiment is held in Chagiga. For thus it is read there f. 5. 2. It is read concerning R. Iannaeus, that when he had seen someone giving alms to a poor man במרהםיא i.e., publicly, he said to him, מוטב רלא יהבת ליה׃ i.e., it would have been better if you had given him nothing. Otherwise, the Jews perform alms greatly. Whence that common saying of the Rabbis מלח ממון צרקה i.e., Salt (by which, namely, they can be preserved from corruption) of riches is alms. Thus also this gnome is theirs: נרולה צרקה שמקרבת דלואד i.e., So great is alms, that it brings near redemption. Conforming to this is that proverb of the Arabs: The liberal man is a neighbor of GOD, a neighbor of men, a neighbor of paradise, remote from the fire of hell. See Prov. Arab. Scalig. Cent. 1. p. 55. Furthermore, it is to be noted that in that sentence of Christ, by alms, all duties to be shown to a neighbor out of charity συνεκδοχικῶς are understood.)*

Μισθὸν -κ ἔχετέ Franciscus Lucas Brug infers the merits of works from the word reward. Reward, he says, looks to merit, by merit a reward is rendered. Therefore, according to the doctrine of our Savior, of good works, namely those rightly instituted, there is a reward, and so also a merit. But the reward of debt and of grace are confused. Between the reward of debt and merit there is a relation, but not between the reward of grace and merit. Franciscus retorts, where a reward is promised, unless it is gratuitous in origin, it is not, but it is a debt to him who performed the work. I reply, it is one thing to have the debt of a promise, but another to have the debt of justice: the former consists with the reward of grace, for what God promised out of grace, He renders out of truth and justice. The latter debt consists in the quality of the works themselves, which fights with the reward of grace. The same Franciscus in his commentary on v. 4. It does not fight, that the same thing is from a promise a reward, and from its origin mercy, which he proves from Matt. 5. v. 7. *(Compare what was noted above at ch. 5, 12.)*

Latin:

v. 1. ἀπόδοσ

Connexio. Postquam legem divinam à Pharisaicis corruptelis repurgasset, iam porrò ostendit, quo modo quove animo bona opera in lege divina praescripta sint facienda. Ut autem hactenus prolata Pharisaeorum doctrinae, ita quae in priore huius capitis parte traduntur, Pharisaeorum vitae sunt opposita, quia Pharirisaei omnia sua opera eo animo eo animo faciebant, ut ab hominibus viderentur. Matth. 23. v. 5.

(Totum hoc caput egregiè exposuit B. Luth. t. 5. Germ. Ienens. pag. 106. seqq.)*

Προσὲετε. Verbum ροσέχειν propriè significat adhibere, videtur igitur subaudiendum nomē τοὐ νοὸς.Animum adhibete, diligenter attendite. August. reddidit Cavete. *(Pulcrè Chrysost. hom. 19. in Matth. emphasin verbi ροσέχετε declarat: Considera, exclamat, unde Salvator noster fuerit exorsus, qui quasi de insidiosissima aliquo serpente loqueretur, potentissimoad fraudandum eum, qui non totâ prorsus mente vigilasset. Attendite, inquit, ne eleemosynam vestram faciatis coram hominibus. Sic etiam Paulus Phil. (cap. 3, 2.) monet: Videte, inquit, canes, videte malos operarios. Clam quippe ingreditur bestia, cunctabenè orientiae intus maximâ cum quiete & absullo sensu perdentis exportat. Et paullô pòst: Cùm itaChristus undiauditores ad liberalitatem esset cohortatus, consequenter cuncta, quae pulcherrimam & feracissemam hanc oleam necare nituntur, evellit. Consentaneè his scribit Aug. l. de perfect. iustit. ratioc. 17. quòd praecipua isthaec externorum virtutis operum, annascens inanis gloria, facilè interimat, non aliter, quàm pulcherrimam Ionae hederam, vermis.Ion. 4, 7. Conf. etiam Hieron. in cap. 5. epist. ad Gal. Addatur quoque omninò Gregor. Magn. in Moral. p. 226.)*

CAPUT VI.

Ἐλεημοσύνην. Quidam Codd. legunt τήν δικαιοσύνην. Inde Augustinus serm. 59. de temp. locum hunc sic citat: Attendite, -e hoc animo iustè vivatis, ut videant vos homines. Et posteà. Iustitiam generaliter nominavit, deinde particulariter exequitur, est enim pars aliqua iustitiae opus, quod per eleemosynnam fit. Beza itidem contendit, legendum esseδικαιοσύνην. * (Iohannes quoque Lorinus Iesuita Comment. in Post. Epist. Petri c. 1, 1. inter alia loca, ex quibus iustitiae vocem pro misericordia accipi, confirmari posse cenfet, hunc quoque locum refert, ac similiter iustitiae vocabulum sumi putat Ps. 30, 2.Es. 6, 1.2. Cor. 9. 10. Pariter 2. Petr. 1, 1.iustitiae nomen pro misericordiâ poni, existimat Eman. à Sa in d. l. Sic quoque ubi in textu Ebraeo est צרקה LXXII. aliquando habent vocabulum ἐλεημοσύνης. Vid. Deut. 6, 25.Ps. 103, 6.Es. 1, 27. &c.)*

Atqui 1. probatiores ac plures Codd. legunt τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην. *(Ita habent Codd. Complut. ac Regii, teste Corn. à Lap. in h. l. Eodem quoque modo legunt omnes Codd. MSS. Paris. quorum ipsi sedecim fuerunt; excepto saltem uno, teste Franc. Luca. Similiter quoque habent Eclog. MSS. Graecae Bibl. Norib. Nec potuit Fr. Lucas, qui tamen diligenter Codd. MSS. Graecos contulit, ullum, qui aliter habeat, nominare, praeter illum secundum Parisiensem, quem tamen ad Vulg. vers. correctum fuisse, haut semel ipse Fr. Lucas, in notis ad Matth. Graecum prodit. Et hic fortè unus fuit ex illis duobus, quos Beza nominat, iisq; lectionem per δικαιοσύνην, quam ipse sequitur, confirmare nititur. Erasmuss tamen, qui itidem Codd. MSS. contulit, nullum memorat, qui aliter, quàm ἐλεημ. h. l. legat.)* 2. Eleemosynae, orationis & ieiunii nominibus συνεκδοχικῶς intelliguntur omnis generis officia proximo. Deo & nobis ipsis debita, ut vivamus δικαιως, σεβῶς σωφρόνωςTit. 2, 12. Confer August lib. de perfect. iustitiae ratio c. 17. 3. Duo primi huius capitis versiculi unâ absolvuntur periodo, cuius ρότασις v. 1. negans est, ἀπόδοσις v. 2. affirmans. Cùm ergo haec habeat vocem ἐλεημοσύνης, illa quoque eandem habeat necesse est. 4. Adiecta vocula ὑμῶν innuit, legendum esse τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην. 5. Vocula δικαιοσύνηο ex versione Latinâ in Graecos quosdam Codd. irrepsisso videtur. Caeterùm Hebraeis צרקה ac Chald. צרקא id est, iastitia, quandoque signifcat eleemosynam, quo ipso insinuatur, munificentiam erga inopes esse iustitiae partem non postremam, ipso Naturae iure eisdem debitam. *(Notat Strigelius in h. l. quòd Imper. Tiberius II. cùm reprehenderetur, quòd aerarium eleemosynis exhauriret, responderit, nunquam defuturam esse pecuniā fisco regio, quamdiu pauperes eleemosynas accepturi essent.)* Hieron. lib. 2. ad v. Pelag. cap. 4. Cavete ne iustitiam h. e. eleemosynam vestram faciatis coram hominibus. 6. Chrysostomus & alii Patres Graeci legunt ἐλεημοσύνην. 7. Salvator alibi nuspiam pofuit δικαιοσύνην pro ἐλεημοσὺνη. *(Aethiops denique itidem legit ἐλεημοσύνην, vertit enim utitur v. nomine aliàs pro ἐλεημοσύνην, ceu videre licet ex vers. seqq. 2. 3. 4. it. Act. 3, 2.5c. 9, 36. &c.)*

*(Quod Syrum interpretem attinet, habet ille h. l. quâ voce ipse alibi passim pro ἐλεημοσύνην utitur, ut huius cap. v. 2. 3. 4. it. Luc. 11, 41.c. 12.Act 3, 2. 310.c. 9, 35.c. 10, 24.31.c. 24, 17. Ubi verò δικαιοσύνη in textu Graeco habetur, non hâc ipse voce utitur, sed nomine vel ceu hoc ipso cap. vers 33.Ioh. 16, 8.10.Rom. 4, 6. aliisque plurimis locis, vel etiam nomine uti Matth. 5, 6.10.c. 21, 32.Rom. 1, 17. &c. Licet verò utrumque nomen, nempe & ab eadem Radice i. e. iustus fuit descendat, Syrus tamen accuratè inter utrum que distinguit, ita ut hoc saltem pro δικαιοσύνῆ utatur, non pro ἐλεημοσύνῆ; illo pro ἐλεημοσύνῆ, non verò pro δικαιοσύνῆ, id quod Lexicographi non satis accuratè observarunt, ceu tùm ex Lex Syr. Crinesii, tum ex Dictionario Syro-Chald. Guidonis Fabricii, quod Apparatui Oper. Regii Hisp. insertum est (expressè n. in eo legitur: זרוקותאEleemosyna, iustitia, aequitas.) tùm ex aliis videre est. Quam ipsam etiam differentiam non satis perpendens Corn. à Lapide absque haesitatione affirmat, quod Syrusδικαιοσύνηlegat: imò potiùs ἐλεημοσύνην, quandoquidem alibi quoq; hanc, non verò illam vocem dictione exprimit. Et quod mireris, ipse quoque Hugo Grotius in hoc loco ita annotat:

Cùm ita ( τὴν δικαιοσύνην ὑμῶν) legisse Syrum & Arabem appareat, nec desit librorum autoritas, omninò hîc accidisse arbitror, quod alibi saepè in his libris, ut alter a lectio ex interpretamento glossematis nata sit. Quia enimδικαιοσύνηin sensuἐλεημοσύνηςerat glossema, id est vox minùs usitata, & Iudas Hellinistis quàm Graecis notior, Ideò adscripta est vox altera usus frequentioris. At unde apparet, Syrum ita legisse? imò potiùs legit ἐλεημοσύνην, utitur quippe tali voce, quâ alias Gr. ἐλεημοσύνην exprimit, ut ostensum paullo antè. Quod Arabem concernit, nullâ sanè probabilitatis saltem specie dici potest, quòd δικαιοσύνην hîc legerit: habet enim iuxta Romanā ac Leid. editionē לא הצנעוא מראהמצם i. e. ne faciatis eleemosynas vestras. De reliquis coniecturis alibi. Franc. Lucas, vir harum rerum satis gnarus, ad h. l. scribit: Syriacè est Zedketho, id quod ad eleemosynam & iustitiam ambiguum est. Pergit dictus modo auctor: nam & Ebraico, Chaldaico atArabico sermone idem verbumצרקהsedaka, quod iustitiam in genere significat, usurpatur etiam propriè pro beneficentia, quam Graeciἐλεημοσύνηνdicunt. Quòd in Ebr. & Chald. sermone nomen צרקה, Chald. צרקא ac צרקתא horumq; imitatione Gr. vox δικαιοσύνη modò pro iustitia, modò pro eleemosyna adhibeatur, notissimum est, confirmantque praeter Lexicographos idem hoc prolixè passim calculo suo viri docti. Vid. B. D. Quistorp. Annot. Bibl. p. 319. B. D. Frantz de Interpr. Sc. S. p. 788. B. D. Tarnov. in Mich. p. 134 Dn. Dilherr. Dispp. Acad. p. 1. p. 88. Thomas Gatak. de stylo N. T. pag. 248. Grotius ad c. 1. Matth. p. 15. An verò Arabicum aequè pro iustitiâ, ac beneficentia vel eleemosyna usurpetur, dubitare aliquis posset. Arabs sanè N. T. Interpres pro δικαιοσύνῃ passim adhibet nomen ac à iustus fuit, ce-, patet ex Matth. 6, 34.Ioh. 16 8.10Rom. 3, 5c. 4, 5.9.1. 12. &c, pro pro ἐλεημοσύνῃ verò utitur nomine ceu praes. cap. v. 2. & 4 factum enim per memoriae lapsum, quando Schindlerus in Lex. Pentag. pag 1521. scribit, quòd ArabsMatth. 6 habeat: Ne faciatisצרקהכםeleemosynam vestram, cùm Arabs tum in Rom. tum Leid. edit. habeat Neque tamen inficias eo, Arabem N. T. Interpr. aliquando nomine pro ἐλεημοσύνη uti: constat

enim hoc ex v. 4 huius capitis, item ex Actor. 3, 2. 3.10.c. 9, 36.c. 10, 2. &c. Num vero etiam pro iusttiâ? alii dispiciant.)*

Πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι θεᾶσθαι plus est, quàm ὁρᾶσθαι, sicut apud Latinos spectari plus est quàm videri.

Praepositio ρὸς hic finem denotat, non eventum vel sequelam; τελικὴ est, non ὐκβατικὴ. Non prohibet conspici rectè facta. Matth. 5. v. 16.Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant bona opera vestra, sed prohibet eo animo ac eo fine bona opera fieri, ut spectemur, i. e. ut laudem & admirationē apud homines quaeramus. *(Gemella sententia in Chagiga habetur. ita enim ibi f. 5. 2. Legitur de R. Iannaeo, quòd cùm vidisset quendam eleemosynam dantem pauperiבמרהםיא i. e. publicè, dixerit ei,מוטב רלא יהבת ליה׃ i. e. si-us fuisset ut nihil ei dedisses. Magni caeteroquin eleemosynas Iudaei faciunt. Unde tritum illud Rabb. מלח ממון צרקה i. e. Sal (quo conservari scil. possint à corruptione) divitiarum est eleemosyna. Sic eorundem est & haec gnoma: נרולה צרקה שמקרבת דלואד i. e. Tam magna est eleemosyna, ut appropinquet redemtionem. Huic conforme illud Arabum proverb. Liberalis vicinus est DEI, vicinus hominum, vicinus paradisi, remotus ab igne inferni. Vid. Prov Arab. Scalig. Cent. 1. p. 55. Coeterùm notandum, quòd in, illâ Christi sententia per eleemosynam omnia officia proximo ex charitate exhibenda συνεκδοχικῶς intelligantur.)*

Μισθὸν -κ ἔχετέ Franciscus Lucas Brug ex voce mercedis operum merita infert. Merces, inquit, mer-urespicit, merito n redditur merces. Est ergo ex Salvatoris nostri doctrina operum bonorum, videl. rectè institutorum ut merces, ita & meritum. Atqui confunditur merces debiti, & gratiae. Inter mercedem d-b-ti & meritum est relatio, non autem inter mercedem grat ae & meritum. Regerit Franciscus, ubi pramium promissum est, nisi origine gratuitum non est, sed debitum ei, qui opus praestitit. Resp. aliud est d-bi-um promissionis, aliud verò debitum iusti-iae: illud consistit cum mercede gratiae, quod enim Deus ex gratia promisit, ex veritate & iustitia reddit. Posterius debitum in ipsa operum qualitate consistit, quod cum mercede gratiae pugnat. Idem Franciscus in comm. ad v. 4. Non pugnat, idem ex pro---sso esse merced-m, & ex origine misericordiam, quod probat exMatth. 5. v. 7.*(Confer quae suprà notata ad c. 5, 12.)*

## 6:2
v. 2. Ἐλεημ . *( Ποιῇς. Cameron's observation from the present passage is beautiful, when in Myrothec. Evang. p. 76, from the fact that since in the preceding verse the Savior had addressed his Apostles in the plural number, but here he slips into the singular number, he gathers, that the commandment proposed here does not concern the Disciples as Apostles, or insofar as they are Apostles, but insofar as they are Christians. It is certainly true that those things which Christ commanded his Apostles are in a double, or even triple difference; for some concern them as Apostles, and these do not extend beyond their person, in the way they are commonly understood Matth. 20, 8.c. 26, 13.Luc. c. 22, 28. some were said and promised under their person to all ministers of the Church, indeed to their successors in the office of teaching, of which kind are read Ioh. 20, 21.23.Matth. 28, 19.Marc. 16, 15.Luc 24, 47.1. Cor. 5, 20. Where, however, one must accurately distinguish the office of teaching and baptizing itself from that special determination added, that they ought to teach among all nations: just as also a divine calling must be distinguished from the immediate and extraordinary mode of calling, etc. The office of teaching and preaching concerns all ministers of the Church, but the determination concerning preaching the Gospel among all nations pertains to the Apostles alone, and so in other extraordinary things. Finally, some things said and commanded under their person are to be understood as for all the faithful, and these concern the Apostles not as Apostles, nor as Ministers of the Church, but as Christians. Thus are to be understood those things commanded to the Apostles in this place, and many others. And concerning precepts of this kind, that saying of Christ must finally be understood Marc. 13. last, What I say to you, I say to all, watch. Compare more on this matter in Mr. D. Musaeus, disp. post. de comm. sub utraque specie §. 16. seqq. B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 222. Furthermore, Camero notes in the place cited the rule by which those precepts which Christ gives to his Apostles that are common to all Christians can be distinguished from those precepts which are peculiar to the disciples as they are Apostles, that it depends either on the locutions of Christ, or on the nature and condition of the thing of which Christ speaks. For while, he says, he addresses the Disciples, while he gives them precepts, as often as it is a matter of those things which pertain properly to their Apostolic office, he addresses them all, he does not use the singular number, but the plural. Again, when it is a matter of those things which are appropriate for the Disciples, not insofar as they are Apostles, but insofar as they are Christians, he indeed uses the plural number , but he immediately slips into the singular. Let this be for an example Matth. 18. v. 10.15. But Came. 10 adds: but this is the most certain rule, that we should look at the things themselves, about which it is a matter, whether they are of such a kind that they are appropriate for a certain order of men, or indeed, whether they belong to all men in general etc. The Papists themselves also acknowledge the difference between those things which were commanded to the Apostles by Christ, (See Franc. Suarez T. 3. q. 8 D. 71. sect. 2. Becanus Theol. Scholast. de Sacram. in specie c. 24. p. 11. obi. 2.) nevertheless, they none the less ineptly transfer to themselves and attempt to imitate many of those things which were said and commanded to the Apostles as Apostles; and some things also which were commanded to the Apostles as Christians or believers, but not specifically as Apostles or Ministers of the Church, they arrogate to Priests and Clerics alone. Concerning which matter elsewhere.)*

Μὴ σαλπίσῃς do not sound a trumpet, or taking the word Kal for Hiphil, do not cause to be sounded. (concerning this form of speaking see B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 320.) Syr. Do not cry out with a horn, or as others render it: Do not cry a cry. It is a Hebraism. Do not proclaim and divulge that. (Arab i. e. do not sound a trumpet before you. Similarly also the Ethiopian.)

The Pharisees, about to distribute alms in the principal places of the city, caused a trumpet to be sounded, indeed under the pretext that the poor might be called together from everywhere to receive alms, but in reality so that they might obtain the praise of beneficence among all.

(Chrysostom, and his follower Theophylact, accept this metaphorically, whose opinion is embraced by H. Grotius, and also the Jesuit Maldonatus, tacitly refuted by his fellow Jesuit Conzenius. And indeed there does not seem to be sufficient cause why anyone should depart here from the literal meaning, or establish a proverb, since nothing prevents it from being said that the Pharisees themselves in reality caused the poor to be called together by trumpet to receive alms, both because that manner of calling the people was sufficiently frequent in those times, and because in such a great city the poor could scarcely have been called together without a sign.)

341 And thus, namely in its proper sense, do St. Jerome on this passage, Strabus, Lyranus, and others understand this expression. See also among more recent writers especially B. D. Chemn. on H. E. p 466. The passages that testify to the manner and custom of calling the people together by trumpet blast are marked )* Judg. 3, 27.c. 6, 34.2. Sam. 2, 28.Ps. 81, 4.Num. 10, 7.

ὑποκριταὶ. Which for the Greeks is ὑῶοκριτὴς,, for the Latins is properly an actor, who sustains some person in a play, and the usage of this word agrees with that which he had said a little before ρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι,, namely as if in a theater, which was named from this very word, and which likewise used to resound with flute players. Most beautifully also this kind of men, of whom Christ speaks, is compared with actors even by that name, because just as actors are accustomed to surpass in outward action those who sustain such parts from the heart or from duty, and exhibit themselves as more spectacular than those who act from the heart, so also men of feigned holiness are of greater admiration to men than the truly pious.

In Syriac they are called נםבי באפא, those who take faces, that is, they put on masks, so that they may transform themselves, so that they may appear other than they are, which itself also agrees with actors. Actors in those composed actions seek nothing other than praise among men: thus those, of whom Christ speaks, uniquely pursue glory among men.

ὐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς, either because they distributed alms in the areas before sacred houses after the poor had been summoned by the sound of a trumpet, or because they summoned them into the Synagogues themselves, and after divine worship was finished, bestowed alms upon them, which argues for greater hypocrisy.

ὐν ταῖς ῥύμαις is said from ῥύω to flow, to flow into, to rush into; it signifies therefore that place in a city into which all flow in rivalry.

ὅπως δοξασθῶσιν, δόξα signifies both opinion and glory. Both significations agree with this place. That they may win for themselves an opinion of beneficence and singular holiness, and that they may be praised by men.

Ἀπέχουσι τὸν μισθόνσου. Ἀπέχειν. here is the same as ἀπολαμβάνειν. Because they did good to the poor for the sake of obtaining glory, therefore after they have obtained that glory, they have received their reward. Thus in Plutarch, he who has relations with a woman for the sake of pleasure is said to have received his reward, namely pleasure, απέχειν

Latin:

v. 2. Ἐλεημ. *(Ποιῇς. Pulcra est Cameronos observatio ex praesenti loco, quando in Myrothec. Evang. p. 76. ex eo, quôd cùm versu praecedente Salvator Apostolos suos alloquutus fuisset in plurali numero, hîc verò dilabatur ad numerum singularem, colligit, quòd mandatum hîc propositum non concernat Discipulos, ut Apostolos, sive, quatenus Apostoli, sed quatenus Christiani sunt. Certum sanè est, quòd eae, quae Christus Apostolis suis mandavit in duplici, imò triplici sint differentiâ, quaedam enim concernunt eos ut Apostolos, & haec ultra eorum personam sese non extendunt, quomodo communiter accipi solent Matth. 20, 8.c. 26, 13.Luc. c. 22, 28. quaedam sub eorum persona omnibus Ecclesiae ministris, quippe eorum in docendi munere successoribus, dicta ac promissa sunt, cuiusmodi leguntur Ioh. 20, 21.23.Matth. 28, 19.Marc. 16, 15.Luc 24, 47.1. Cor. 5, 20. Ubi tamen accuratè distinguendum ipsum docendi ac baptizandi officium ab illa speciali determinatione additâ, quòd docere debeant inter omnes gentes: sicut etiam vocato divina à vocationis modo immediato & extra ordinario &c. distingui debet. Officium docendi & praedicandi concernit omnes Ecclesiae ministros, sed determinatio de praedicando Evang. inter omnes gentes ad solos Apostolos pertinet, & sic in aliis extraordinariis. Quaedam denique sub eorum personâ omnibus fidelibus dicta ac mandata intelligenda sunt, & haec concernunt Apostolos non ut Apostolos, nec ut Ecclesiae Ministros, sed ut Christianos. Ita accipienda sunt quae h. l. Apostolis mandata, & alia plurima. Ac de huiusmodi demum praeceptis intelligi debet illud Christi Marc. 13. ult. Quae vobis, dico, omnibus dico, vigilate. Conf. plura in hanc rem apud Dn. D. Musaeum disp. post. de comm. sub utraque specie §. 16. seqq. B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 222. Caeterùm notat Camero l. c. regulam, quâ distingui possint illa, quae Christus dat Apostolis suis praecepta cum omnibus Christianis communia, ab iis praeceptis, quae discipulis, quâ sunt Apostoli, peculiaria sunt, pendere vel à locutionibus Christi, vel à rei, de quâ loquitur Christus, natura & conditione. Nam dum, inquit, Discipulos alloquitur, dum iis dat praecepta, quoties agitur iis de rebus, quae ad eorum munus Apostolicum spectant propriè, compellat eos universos, no utitur singulari numero, sed plurali. Rursus quum agitur iis de rebus, quae Discipulis conveniunt, non quatenus Apostolis, sed quatenus Christiani sunt, plurali quidem utitur numero quando-, sed ad singulurem statim delabitur. Exempli loco esto Matth. 18. v. 10.15. Subiicit verò Came. 10: sed certissima norma haec est, ut res ipsas, de quibus agitur, intueamur, sintne eiusmodi, quae certo cuidam hominum ordini conveniant, an verò, quae omnibus hominibus in universum competant &c. Agnoscunt quoque differentiam inter ea, quae Apostolis à Christo mandata, & ipsi Pontificii, (Vid. Franc. Suarez T. 3. q. 8 D. 71. sect. 2. Becanus Theol. Scholast. de Sacram. in specie c. 24. p. 11. obi. 2.) nihilo tamen minùs multa eorum, quae Apostolis ut Apostolis dicta ac praecepta, ineptè ad se transferunt ac imitari conantur; nonnulla quoque quae Apostolis ut Christianis vel fidelibus, non verò specialiter ut Apostolis vel Ecclesiae Ministris mandata, solis Sacerdotibus ac Clericis arrogant. quâ de realibi.)*

Μὴ σαλπίσῃςne buccinaveris, vel accepto verbo Kal pro Hiphil, ne cur averis buccinandum. *(de hâc loquendi formâ vid. B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 320.)* Syr. Ne clamaveris cornu, vel ut alii reddunt: Ne clames clamorem. Hebraismus est. Ne illud praedices ac divulges. *(Arabs i. e. ne canas ante te tubâ. Similiter & Aethiops.)*

Pharisaei eleemosynas distributuri in praecipuis civitatis locis buccinâ cani curabant, eo quidem praetextu, ut pauperes undiquaque ad eleemosynas accipiendas convocarentur, sed reverâ sine eo, ut laudem beneficentiae apud omnes consequerentur.

*(Chrysostomus, huiusque Sectator Theophy lactus metaphoricè hoc accipiunt, quorum sententiam amplectitur H. Grotius, nec non Iesuita Maldonatus, tacitè refutatus à socienno Iesuita Conzenio. Et sanè non satis causae videtur, cur hîc à propriâ significatione discedere quis debeat, vel paroemian statuere, cùm nihil repugnet, quò mivùs dici possit, Pharisaeos ipsos reverà pauperes ad eleemosynam accipiendam buccinâ convocari curasse, tum quòd modus iste populum convocandi illis temporibus satis esset frequēs, -m quòd in tātâ urbe absq; signo pauperes cōvocari vix potuerint.

Et ita, propriè nempe, locutionem hanc accipiunt S. Hieron. in h. l. Strabus, Lyranus, alii. Vid. quoq; è recentioribus cumprimis B. D. Chemn. in H. E. p 466. De modo v. ac cōsuetudine populū buccinâ convocandi testantur loca Iudic. 3, 27.c. 6, 34.2. Sam. 2 28.Psal. 81, 4.Num. 10, 7.)*

ὑποκριταὶ. Qui Graecis ὑῶοκριτὴς, Latinis propriè est histrio, qui personam aliquam in fabula sustinet, ac convenit usus huius vocabuli cum eo, quod paulò ante dixerat ρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι, videlicet tanquam in theatro, quod ab hoc ipso verbo fuit appellatum, ac quod itidem tibicinibus perstrepebat. Pucherrimè etiam huiusmodi hominum genus, de quo Christusagit, cum histrionibus vel eo nomine comparatur, quòd quemadmodum histriones exteriori actione vincere eos solent, qui ex animo aut officio eiusmodi partes tuentur, ac magis spectabile se exhibent, quam ii qui ex animo agunt, ita quoque simulatae sanctitatis homines maiori admirationi sint hominibus, quàm vere pii.

Syris dicuntur נםבי באפא,qui facies sumunt h. e. larvas induunt, ut se transforment, quò alii, quàm sint, appareāt, quod ipsū quoque histrionibus congruit. Histriones in compositis istis actionibus nihil aliud, quàm laudem apud homines quaerunt: sic illi, de quibus Christus agit, gloriam apud homines unicè sectantur.

ὐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς, vel quôd in areis ante aedes sacras pauperibus tubae cantu convocatis eleemosynas distribuerint, vel quòd in ipsas Synagogas eos convocârint, ac finito divino cultu eleemosynas in ipsos contulerint, quod maiorem hypocrisin arguit.

ὐν ταῖς ῥύμαις dicitur à ῥύωfluo, influo, irruo; significat ergo eum in urbe locum, in quem certatim omnes influunt.

ὅπως δοξασθῶσιν, δόξα significat & opinionem & gloriam. Utraque significatio huic loco congruit. Ut opinionem beneficentiae ac singularis sanctitatis sibi concilient, & ut ab hominibus laudentur.

Ἀπέχουσι τὸν μισθόνσου. Ἀπέχειν. hîc idem est, quod ἀπολαμβάνειν. Quia gloriae consequendae causâ pauperibus benefecerunt, ideò postquam gloriam illam consecuti sunt, mercedem suam receperunt. Sic apud Plutarehum qui voluptatis causâ cum muliere rem habet, mercedem suam, sc. voluptatem, dicitur απέχειν

## 6:3
v. 3. Σοῦ &c Iuvencus the Christian Poet book 1. v. 590. expressed it thus: Do not let your left hand know what your right hand does. Most correctly, for do not let know in this place is the same as do not permit that it knows.

Augustine in sermon 60. on the seasons determines that by the right hand must be understood the love of GOD; but by the left hand, from which we must guard ourselves, vanity and the desire of the world. *(Theophylactus thinks that by the left hand is understood vain glory, and by the right hand almsgiving, so that the sense may be: let not vain glory know of the almsgiving. Bellarmine book 3. on Good Works in Part. chapter 13. § 1. likewise attributes to Augustine, that in tractate 6. on the epistle of John (which is held in volume 9. of the Works of Augustine) he understands in this place by the right hand the intention of working for the sake of eternal life: and by the left hand he understands the intention of working for the sake of temporal honor: so that the sentence of the Lord may be this, when you do alms, beware lest the intention of human favor mix itself with the intention of eternal life. For what purpose this sentence is attributed to Augustine by Bellarmine cannot be unknown to one who knows that the opinion that it is lawful to perform Good Works with a view to an eternal reward is defended by the same Bellarmine. book 5. on Justification chapter 8. But it must be known that Augustine in the said place by no means speaks in such a way that we ought to do alms, or do good works, for the sake of eternal life. He says indeed that we ought to desire our salvation, not the vain glory of the world: but from that it does not follow that we ought to do good works for the sake of eternal life, that is, with a view to an eternal reward, which is the opinion of the Papists, refuted at length by B. Par. Catholic Confession vol. 4. p. 920. following.)*

Chromatius in Orthodox Monuments p. 2. f. 1212. understands by the right hand the just, by the left hand sinners, and concludes, that the impious ought to be ignorant of what the pious are doing.

Franc. Luc. Brug. on this place ( It is a figurative expression, by which he commands that our almsgiving be most secret, entirely devoid of ostentation, for it is as if the hand which is applied to the distribution is the one conscious of the alms, wherefore if it suffices for the right hand to be made conscious, let not the left also be applied. But this is a certain kind of ostentation, to be offered with both hands, which can be exhibited by one alone.)

Concerning these and other expositions of this kind Maldonatus judges thus. While the Interpreters seek a metaphor, they have produced an incredible variety of interpretations. Chrysostom and Theophylactus seem to me to have hit the mark with a needle that the expression is not metaphorical but hyperbolic, so that the sense is, that beneficence toward the poor is to be hidden with such great zeal, that if it were possible, even the left hand itself, which is nevertheless most closely joined to us, and cooperates with the right in distributing alms, should be ignorant of it.

(B. D. Glassius, Rhet. S. page 190, refers such a locution to prosopopoeia, which can be seen. Corn. à Lapide, having followed Theophylact, determines it to be a parabolic hyperbole, and says that this is the sense in this place: So flee the ostentation of your alms and virtue, that if by impossibility your left hand had eyes, it could nevertheless not see what good your right hand is doing.)

It is gathered, therefore, from this passage, that in the pursuit of beneficence we ought not to seek glory among men, that the giver ought not to inquire solicitously, and as the Poet speaks, to compute with anxious fingers, what, how much, and to whom he has given, that he ought not to capture profit from alms, so as to hold those whom he has bound to himself by benefits in the place of slaves, indeed that he ought not even to flatter himself by a calculation of benefits, and seek some reward of merit in them, but to forget them.

Isidorus Pelusiota, book 1, Epist. 84, p. 23. Since vain glory and ostentation are accustomed to be in upright actions, therefore let no good be done by you with a vicious affection of the mind, nor let a wicked and preposterous thought accompany a noble deed joined with virtue. (Beautifully S. Jerome in the Epitaph of Fabiola: Hidden virtue rejoices in GOD as judge . These things of the gentiles also contribute to this: Persius, Sat. 1. Do not seek yourself outside. Pliny the Younger, book 1, ep. 8. The fruit of honesty is stored with a greater spirit in conscience than in fame.)

Latin:

v. 3. Σοῦ &c Iuvencus Poëta Christianus lib. 1. v. 590. sic expressit: Tu quod dextra facit, facias nescire sinistrā. Rectissimè, nam ne sciat h. l. idem est, quod ne permittas, ut sciat.

Augustinus serm. 60. de temp. per dextram accipienndum statuit amorem DEI; per sinistram verò, à qua nobis cavendum, vanitatem & cupiditatem seculi. *(Theophylactus per sinistram putat intelligi vanam gloriam, per dextram eleemosynam, ut sensus sit: nesciat eleemosynam inanis gloria. Bellarm. lib. 3. de B. O. in Part. cap. 13. § 1. itidem Augustino tribuit, quòd tr. 6. in epist. Ioh. (qui habeturt. 9. Op. Augustini) h. l. per dexteram intelligat intetionem operandi propter vitam aeternam: & intentionem operandi propter honorem temporalem, per sinistraem intelligat: ut sententia Domini sit haec, cùm facis eleemosynam, cave ne intentio favoris humani se admisceat intentioni vitae aeternae. Quo fine haec sententia Augustino tribuatur à Bellarmino, ignotum esse non potest, qui noverit, defendi ab eod. Bell. sententiam, quòd licitum sit, operari B. O. intuitu mercedis aeternae. l. 5. de Iustif. c. 8. Verùm sciendum est, quòd Augustinus d. l. minimè ita loquatur, quòd propter vitam aeternam eleemosynas facere, vel benè operari debeamus. Dicit quidem, quod salutem nostram appetere debeamus, non vanam mundi gloriam: sed ex eo non sequitur, quòd propter vit. aet. benè operari debeamus h. e. intuitu mercedis aeternae, quae Pontificiorum sententia est, prolixè refutata à B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. 4. p. 920. seqq.)*

Chromatius in Monum. Orthodox. p. 2. f. 1212. per dextram intelligit iustos, per sinistram peccatores, & concludit, impios ignorare debere, quid pii operentur.

Franc. Luc. Brug. ad. h. l. ( Figurata locutio est, quâ iubet, secretissima ut sit eleemosyna nostra, prorsusostentationis expers, sit enim qs. conscia cleemosynae manus, quae ad erogationem adhibetur, quare si dextram consciam fieri sufficiat, non adhibeatur etiam sinistra. At haec ostentationis quoddam genus est, utraq; manu porrigi, quod alter â solâ exhiberi potest.)

De his & aliis eiusmodi expositionibus Maldonatus sic iudicat. Dum metaphoram Interpp. quaerunt, incredibilem interpretatioonum varietatem pepererunt. Rem mihi Chrysostomus & Theophylactus acu tetigisse videntur, non met aphoricam sed hyperbolicam esse locutionem, ut sit sensus, tanto studio occultandamesse in pauperes beneficentiam, ut si fieri posset, ipsa etiam sinistra, quae tamen nobis coniunctissima est, & in distribuendis eleemosynis dextrae cooperatur, eam ignoret.

*(B. D. Glassius Rhet. S. pag. 190. talem locutionem refert ad prosopopoeiam, qui potest videri. Corn. à Lapide sequutus Theophylactum statuit, esse hyperbolem parabolicam, dicitque hunc esse h. l. sensum: Adeo fuge eleemosynae & virtutis tuae ostentationem, ut si per impossibile sinistra tua oculos haberet, videre tamen non posset, quid dextra tua faciat boni.)*

Colligitur ergo ex hoc loco, quòd in studio beneficentiae non debeamus gloriam apud homines quaerere, quòd dator non debeat solicitè inquirere, & ut Poëta loquitur, solicitis articulis computare, quid, quantum & quibus dederit, quòd non debeat ex eleemosyna lucrum captare, ut mancipiorum loco eos habeat, quos beneficiis sibi devincivit, imò quòd nec sibiipsi supputatione beneficiorum debeat blandiri, ac meriti aliquam mercedem in illis quaerere, sed eorum oblivisci.

Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 1. Epist. 84. p. 23. Quoniam probarum actionum inanis gloria & ostentatio esse solet, idcircò nullum bonum abs te cum vitiosa animi affectione fiat, nec improba & praepostera cogitatio praeclarum & cum virtute coniunctum facinus comitetur. *(Pulcrè S. Hieronymus in Epitaphio Fabiolae: Celata virtus DEO iudic -gaudet. Faciunt huc & illa gentilium: Persius Sat. 1. Ne te quaestiveris extra. Plinius Iunior. l. 1. ep. 8. Maiore animo honestatis fructus in conscientia, quàm in fama reponitur.)*

## 6:4
v. 4. Ὅπως ᾖ σου

ὐν τῷ κρυπτῷ. Alms is called by the Hebrews a gift in secret, whence they are accustomed to superscribe this sentence of Solomon on treasuries: מתן בםתר יכפה אף A gift in secret turns away anger. (In the Talmud, Massechet Baba Bathra, chapter 1, a sentence is read, very akin to this precept of Christ: בםתר יותר ממשה רבינו׃ נרול העושה צרקה i. e. He who distributes alms in secret is greater than Moses our teacher. Compare more in praise of Alms according to the opinion of the Jews in Hackspan. Trde usu libb.

Rabb. Lipmanno annexed p. 439. seqq. Nevertheless, others can be added to these. Thus in Pirke Aboth c. 1, this sentence is ascribed to R. Iose F. Iochanan: יהי ביתך פתוח לרוחה ויהיו ענים בני ביתך i. e. Let your house be open towards the street, let the poor be the children of your house. Furthermore, there exist very many divine admonitions concerning the giving of alms, regarding which see Jas. 2, 13.

Christ looks in this command not so much to the thing, as to the intention of the agent. For if either the glory of GOD or the necessity of a neighbor requires that the alms be done in public, he who distributes alms in the sight of others does not sin; nay rather, by that very act he promotes the glory of GOD and the edification of the neighbor, Matt. 5. v. 16. provided that the desire of hunting for human praise is avoided. (In almost the same way ἐναιτιοφ. is reconciled by Lord Dr. Walth. in Harm. Bibl. at this place.)

O βλέπων ἐ τῷ κρυπτῷ. To whose eyes, brighter than the sun, all things are naked and open, Sir. 23. v. 28. Heb. 4. v. 13. He admonishes that we should strive to approve our actions to God. Cyprian, sermon on the Lord's prayer: Let us know that God is present everywhere, hears and sees all, and by the fullness of his majesty penetrates into hidden and secret things, which he proves from Jer. 23. v. 23. & 24. Prov. 15. v. 3.

ἐ τῷ φανερῷ. The Latin version omits this ῶροσδιορισμὸν, but it is held in the Greek and Syriac Codices. (The Arab and Ethiopian also read it, and indeed Augustine, as witnessed by Corn. à Lapide at this place. On the contrary, Franc. Lucas writes, that St. Augustine, around the beginning of book 2 of the Lord's sermon on the mount, testifies that it had been omitted by the Greek copies which he consulted, ἐ τῷ φανερῷ: to which, Fr. Lucas adds, today the Greek Codex of the Vatican Library agrees, and, without doubt by the correction of Jerome, the Vulgate edition. The other Greek books which we have seen, with the Greek and Syriac copies as commentators supporting them, all read it: (and thus also the MS. Greek Eclogues of the Nuremberg Library) nor is it easily to be taken away from them. He continues, however: so that not to be added to the Latins. Namely, so that the Greek Codices might not prejudice the Latins in any way. But the context requires this ῶροσδιρισμὸν: for an opposition is instituted between secret alms and the manifest remuneration of God.) Luke 14. v. 14. is explained: in the resurrection of the just.

Therefore, reward of grace, is understood, to be rendered to pious benefactors on the day of judgment, in which God will reveal the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest, the counsels also of the hearts, 1 Cor. 4. v. 5. He who in this life has done his alms in secret, then in public will have God as the herald and rewarder of his beneficence.

Latin:

v. 4. Ὅπως ᾖ σου

ὐν τῷ κρυπτῷ. Eleemosyna Hebraeis dicitur donum in occulto, unde Gazophylaciis solent hanc sententiam Salomonis superscribere: מתן בםתר יכפה אףDonum in occulto flectit iram. *(In Talmud, Massechet Baba Bathra cap. 1. sententia legitur, admodùm huic Christi praecepto affinis: בםתר יותר ממשה רבינו׃ נרול העושה צרקה i. e. Qui eleemosynas erogat in occulto, maior est Mose doctore nostro. Confer plura in laudem Eleemosynarum ex Iudaeorum sententiâ apud Hackspan. Trde usu libb.

Rabb. Lipmanno annexo p. 439. seqq. Possunt tamen istis & alia addi. Sic in Pirke Aboth c. 1. R. Iose F. Iochanan haec sententia adscribitur: יהי ביתך פתוח לרוחה ויהיו ענים בני ביתך i. e. Esto domus tua aperta versus plateam, sintpauperes filii domûs tua. Caeterùm de eleemosynis faciendis plurimae extant divinae admonitiones, de quibus ad Iac. 2, 13.)*

Respicit Christus hoc mandato non tam ad rem, quam ad agentis intentionem. Nam si vel DEI gloria vel proximi necessit-s requirat, ut eleemosyna in publico fiat, non peccat, qui eleemosynam in aliorum conspectu distribuit, quin potiùs eo ipso DEI gloriam & proximi aedificationem promovet, Matth. 5. v. 16. modò humanae laudis aucupandae studium caveatur. *(Eod. ferè modo ἐναιτιοφ. hanc conciliat Dn. D. Walth. in Harm. Bibl. ad h. l.)*

O βλέπων ἐ τῷ κρυπτῷ. Cuius oculis Sole lucidioribus omnia sunt nuda & aperta, Sirac. 23. v, 28.Heb. 4. v. 13. Admonet, ut Deo actiones nostras probare satagamus. Cyprian. serm. de orat. Domin. Sciamus, Deum ubiesse praesentem, audire omnes & videre, & maiestatis suae plenitudine in abdita quo& occulta penetrare, quod probat ex Ierem. 23. v. 23. & 24.Prov. 15. v. 3.

ἐ τῷ φανερῷ. Versio Latina hunc ῶροσδιορισμὸν omittit, sed habetur in Graecis & Syriacis Codicibus. *(Legunt quoque Arabs & Aethiops, quin & Augustinus, teste Corn. à Lapide in h. l. ontrà Franc. Lucas scribit, D. Augustinum circa initium libri. 2. de serm. Domini in monte, testari, ab iis, quae consuluit, Graecis exemplaribus omissum fuisseἐ τῷ φανερῷ:quibus, subiicit Fr. Lucas, hodie, onsonat Codex Graecui Bibl. Vaticanae, & ex Hieronym haut dubium correctione, Vulgata editio. Coeteri Graeci libri, quos vidimus, suffragantibus tractatoribus Graecis & Syricis exemplaribus, omnes illud legunt: (& sic quoque Eclogae MSS. Gr. Bibl. Norib.) nec facilè est illis auferendum. pergit tamen: ut neLatinis addendum. Ne, scil. Graeci Codd. Latinis quicquam praeiudicent.
