Requirit verò ῶροσδιρισμὸν hunc contextus: instituitur enim oppositio inter eìcemosynam occultam, & inter remunerationem Dei manifestam) * Luc. 14. v. 14. exponitur: in resurrectione iustorum.

Intelligitur igitur m-rces gratiae, reddenda piis benefactoribus in die iudicii, in qua Deus r-v-labit abscondita tenebrarum, & manifefesta, sesta eruntetiam occulta cordium,1. Cor. 4. v. 5. Qui in hac vita eleemosynam suam fecerit in occulto, tunc in publico Deum praeconem & remuneratorem beneficentiae suae habebit.

## 6:5
v. 5. ῶροευχη

--Ταν ῶροευχη. The Vulgate rendered it in the plural, when you pray, do not be. But all Greek codices have the singular. *(So also the Syriac: but the Arabic and Ethiopic have the plural number.)*

ἐ ταἶς συναγωγαῖς ῶροσευυχεσθαι. But how does it agree with this prohibition of Christ, that Paul commands to pray in every place, 1. Tim 2, vers. 8.

Response. Just as in the preceding, so also in this place Christ does not look to the thing itself, but to the intention of the agent. He does not forbid praying in a public place, in synagogues, in temples, since he testifies that the publican praying in the temple went down to his house justified, Luc. 18. v. 13. and Peter and John are said to have gone up into the temple at the hour of prayer, namely the ninth, Act. 3. v. 1. but he condemns the preposterous zeal of those who pray in public for this reason, that they may hunt for praise among men. He does not condemn public prayers, but the hypocrisy of those who pray in public for this reason, that they may be seen by men.

*(In the same way Theophylact responds. Thus, he says, in this place: What then, shall I not pray in the Church? By all means, but with an upright mind and without ostentation. ταἶς συναγωγαῖς ῶρ. For the place does not harm, but the manner and the intention. For many, even praying in secret, do this so that they may please men.)*

ἐ ταῖς γωνίαις τίν πλατειῶνν. In the corners or turnings of the streets there are accustomed to be two-way, three-way, and four-way intersections, and thus from different ways a gathering of many men. Prov. 7. v. 12.

Ἑστῶτες. Among the Israelite people it was a received custom that they should pray standing, whence the name stations, in which they read in the work of Beresith and prayed. Rabbi Manahem explains that place Gen. 19. v. 27. where Abraham had stood before the Lord, thus: Where he had prayed.

Tertullian also records concerning the Christians, that they had stations, in which they prayed standing.

Latin:

v. 5. ῶροευχη

--Ταν ῶροευχη. Vulg. reddidit in plurali, cùm oratis, non e-itis. Sed Graeci Codd omnes habent singulare. *(Sic quoque Syrus: sed Arabs & Aethiops habent pluralem numerum.)*

ἐ ταἶς συναγωγαῖς ῶροσευυχεσθαι.At quomodo cum hac -rohibitione Christi convenit, quod Paulus iubet in omni loco orare,1. Tim 2, vers. 8.

Resp. Sicut in praecedentibus, ita etiam hoc loco Christus non adrem ipsam, sed ad intentionem agentis respicit. Non prohibet in loco publico, in Synagogis, in templis orare, cùm publicanum in templo orantem iustificatum in domum suam descendisse, testetur, Luc. 18. v. 13. ac Petrus & Iohannes horâ orationis, nonâ sc. in templum dicantur adscendisse, Act. 3. v. 1. sed praeposterum eorum studium damnat, qui ideò in publico orant, ut apud homines laudem aucupentur. Non damnat preces publicas, sed hypocrifin eorum; qui ideò in publicò erant, ut ab hominibus videantur.

*(Eodem modo respondet Theophylactus. Ita n. h. l. Quid igitur, in Ecclesiâ non orabe? Omninò, sed recto animo & citra ostentationem.ταἶς συναγωγαῖς ῶρ.Locus enim non nocet, sed modus & intentio. Multi enim etiam in abscondito orantes, hoc, ut hominibus placeant, faciunt.)*

ἐ ταῖς γωνίαις τίν πλατειῶνν.In terminis -ive diverticulis platearum solent esse bivia, trivia, quadrivia, adeoque ex diversis viis multorum hominum concursus. Prov. 7. v. 12.

Ἑστῶτες. In populo Israëlitico more receptum erat, ut stantes orarent, unde nomen stati-num, in quibus legebant in opere Beresith & precabantur. R Manahem locum illum Gen. 19. v. 27. Ubi Abraham steterat ante Dominum, sic exponit: Ubi oraverat.

Tertullianus etiam de Christianis memorat, quòd habuerint --as stationes, in quibus stantes oraverint.

## 6:6
v. 6. ταἶς συναγωγαῖ.

Ταμιεῖον signifies some more secret place, in which it is accustomed to store something, here it is placed for a bedchamber or a more secret room. But if one must pray in a closed bedchamber, how is one to pray in every place, 1. Tim. 2, 8. Resp. 1. Some reconcile it thus, that Christ here speaks specifically of prayers which are made privately, but not of those which are made in public assemblies of the Church. 2. The ancients by bedchamber μεταφορικῶς καὶ ἀλληγορικῶς understand the secret of the heart. Ambrose lib. 6. de Sacram. c. 3. tom. 4. p 445. You can pray everywhere, and always pray in your bedchamber. You have your bedchamber. Even if you are placed among the Gentiles, among the Jews, you still have your secret. Your bedchamber is your mind. Although placed among the people, you nevertheless preserve your secret in the inner man. Augustine lib. 2. de serm. Domini in monte tom. 2. col. 1242. The bedchamber is the secret of the heart. in enarr. Ps. 33. conc. 3. When you enter into your heart, you enter into your bedchamber. *(Gregory Nazianzen in his sentences: Let this study be perpetual for you, that you build your mind as a temple for God: for thus you will have him as a spiritual statue in your inmost heart) * 3. It is answered most simply, that Christ speaks comparatively. It is so far from the case that you should wish to pray in public to hunt for the glory of men, in the manner of the hypocritical Pharisees, that you ought rather to close the bedchamber, when you are about to offer your prayers to God. Chrysostom rightly warns, it can happen that someone hides himself for that reason, so that he may be understood to be about to pray secretly. Therefore here one must look not to the thing itself, but to the manner of the thing and the intention of the agent. *(Christ himself uttered the prayers, which he appended to his farewell discourse Ioh. 17. with a loud voice. For however much Isaac Casaubon Exer. 16. Annal. c. 62. p. 589. may hesitate here and leave it to great Theologians to think about, that the ancients observe that Christ, as often as he wished to pray to the Father with greater intensity, was accustomed to withdraw from the disciples and pray κατὰ μόνας, whether he kept that custom also in those prayers, described by John in the said place, when he conceived that admirable prayer: yet others judge more correctly, that in the same place in which the farewell discourse was held, namely in the upper room, and thus with the disciples present and listening, the prayers were recited by the Savior. Augustine tr. 104. in Ioh. approves this opinion. Since, however, the action of Christ is our instruction, just as also Nicholas of Lyra writes in c. 17. Ioh.: Christ did not only pray to obtain something, but also to give us an example of praying. Hence, prayers which are made in a public place are by no means to be disapproved. And men are to be admonished not to neglect the public worship of GOD in temples, of which not the least part is devout prayers . There is added the fact that the presence of many devout men kindles devotion in those who are praying, etc. Looking to which, Tertullian also says in Apolog. ch. 39: We come together, he says, into a meeting and gathering, so that we may surround God with our prayers as if with a formed band; this force is pleasing to God. All of which things are rightly to be opposed to the enthusiasts and the destroyers of Temples (concerning which matter some things will be advised at 1. Cor. 3, 16.. Let the passages Matth. 18, 19.Luc. 18, 10.20.Act. 3, 24.c. 6, 6. be seen in the meantime). Nor, however, are they to be extended so far, as if God were more present and heard prayer more easily in a temple, which Bellarmine, book 3 on the worship of Saints, ch. 4, strives to prove (Compare also Thomas Stapleton, Prompt. Cath. Sunday 9 after Pentecost, § 1; Cosmas Magalianus of Braga, book 1 of Hierarchical Works, p. 292; Beierlinck, Select Sermons 40, p. 745). For the present passage can rightly be opposed to this opinion, as well as the sayings Ioh. 4, 21. and 1. Tim. 2, 8.. Compare also the examples of Christ, Matth. 26, 39., and of the Apostles, Act. 1, 24.24.c. 4, 24.c. 16, 25. Rightly, therefore, Origen, book 7 against Celsus: Let even the unlearned Christian have it most firmly persuaded that any place in the world is a part of the universe, and that the whole world is a temple of GOD, and let him pray in any place with sensible eyes closed, but with the eyes of the soul raised up, and thus he ascends above the whole world. Basil agrees in his exhortation to Baptism, vol. 1: Not the place, but the beginning of the purpose is required. For Jeremiah was in the mud, and he drew God to himself. Daniel in the lions' den appeased God. The three boys in the furnace merited God. The thief was not prevented by the cross from attaining Paradise. Job in the dung (as also Peter and Paul in prison) provoked God to mercy. Therefore wherever you are, pray, or if before a Judge, pray. Compare also Prosper, book of sentences from Augustine, sentence 333, and Chrysostom, vol. 5, homily 79, and other Fathers, both on this and on the passages just mentioned. The sum: The place does not sanctify the prayers, but the prayers sanctify the place.

Τῶ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ. The Vulgate version refers to the word πρόσευξαι

*(The same which the Arab does)* but the article added in the Greek shows this ῶροσδιορισμὸν is to be referred to the noun immediately preceding, namely to the heavenly Father. *(The Syrian confirms this reading, who expressly has which is in secret. The Ethiopian likewise follows this reading.)* But the heavenly Father is said to be in secret, either because He is in heavenly glory, which is not conspicuous and obvious to the eyes of men, or because He sees in secret, which explanation is handed down in v. 4 preceding. In vain, therefore, Lucas Brugensis prefers the Vulgate version here to the Greek text. And to the thing itself, he says, and to the preceding, that your alms may be in secret, it seems to fit more aptly that which reads and translates the old Interpreter, omitting τῷ or which is, before the preposition in, in which way there are also those who note that it is in certain Greek books today. But it is well that Franc. Lucas himself immediately adds through ἐπίληξιν. Although afterwards, v. 18, where it is treated concerning fasting, the old Interpreter reads in a similar manner with the Greek and Syrian books: That you may not appear to men fasting, but to your Father, who is in secret. Why therefore can it not be read so in this place also?

ἐποδώσει σοι. But prayer is a testimony of grace, says August. Epist. 105. By prayer we testify to our indigence, and we seek necessary things from God, how therefore is a reward rendered by prayer? Resp. This descends from the liberal and gratuitous promise of GOD, that as with other good works, so also He wills that prayer be remunerated out of grace. By that very thing, therefore, which Christ asserts is repaid to our prayers, He declares quite clearly that whatever reward is promised throughout Scripture to good works is not paid as a reward of merit owed, but is a gratuitous gift.

Franc. Lucas Brug. retorts that Chrysostom writes thus on this place. If therefore you pray thus, you will surely receive a very great reward. He does not say, He will give to you, but He will render, he says, for He has indeed constituted Himself a debtor to you. Resp. Chrysostom does not speak of a debt of justice, to be rendered to our good works out of merit, but of a debt of promise, which does not fight against the reward of grace. *(That our Savior speaks of a debt of promise in sayings of this kind, the Jesuit Conzen voluntarily grants. For after he had instituted a question around v. 1 of this Chapter: Whether by the words of Christ: You shall not have a reward: merit and reward are proven? he concludes with these words: We quo-

in reward call grace and the reward itself gratuitous: but nevertheless out of debt, not by the force of a good work, but by the will of GOD promising. He above, promising every merit by spontaneous gratuitous mercy, constituted a reward, so that it was owed by covenant, by doing that He also made a merit; which without a promise was none.)*

Kings and Princes of this age judge it a great kindness if they lend their ears to the prayers of suppliants. But God is so good and beneficent that He wishes not only to hear those praying, but also to reward the prayer itself out of grace.

Latin:

v. 6. ταἶς συναγωγαῖ.

Ταμιεῖον significat locum aliquem secretiorem, in quo recon--i aliquid solet, hîc ponitur pro cubiculo seu conclavi secretiori. At --lauso cubiculo orandum, quomodo in omni loco orandum,1. Tim. 2, 8. Resp. 1. quidam sic conciliant, quòd Christus hîc in specie loquatur de precibus quae privatim fiunt non autem de illis, quae fiunt, in publicis Ecclesiae conventibus. 2. Veteres per cubiculumμεταφορικῶς καὶ ἀλληγορικῶς intelligunt cordis secretum. Ambrosius lib. 6. de Sacram. c. 3. tom. 4. p 445. Potes ubiorare, & in cubiculo tuo semper orare. Habes ubicubiculum tuum. Etsi inter gentes, inter Iudaeos positus sis, habes tamen tuum ubisecretum. Cubiculum tuum mens tua est. In populo licet positus, tamen in interiore homine arcanum secretumtuum conservas. Augustinus lib. 2. de serm. Domini in monte tom. 2. col. 1242. Cubiculum est cordis secretum. in enarr. Ps. 33. conc. 3. Cùm intras in cor tuum, intras in oubieulum tuum. *(Gregorius Nazianz. in sententiis: Perpetuum sit tibi hoc studium, ut mentem tuam templum Deo exstruas: sic enim eum pro spirituali --tatua in intimo corde habebis) * 3. Simplicissimè respondetur, hristum loqui comparatè. Tantum abest, ut in publico ad aucupandam hominum gloriam orare velis, Pharisaeorum hypocritarum more, ut cubiculum potiùs claudere debeas, preces tuas Deo oblaturus. Chrysostomus rectè monet, fieri posse, ut idcircò se aliquis abdat, quò secretè oraturus intelligatur. Ergo hîc non ad rem, ipsam, sed ad rei modum & agentis intentionem respiciendum. *(Christus ipse preces, quas valedictoriae concioni subiunxit Ioh. 17. sonorâ voce protulit. Ut ut enim Isaacus Casaubonus Exer. 16. Annal. c. 62. p. 589. hîc haereat ac magnis Theologis cogitandum relinquat, tùm veteres observent, Christum, quoties maiori contentione orare Patrem voluit, solitum à discipulis secedere & orareκατὰ μόνας,an eum morem & in istis precibus, à Iohanne d. l. descripris tenuerit, cùm illam admirabilem orationem concepit: rectius tamen alii censent, quòd in eodem loco, in quo valedictorius sermo fuit habitus, nempe in oenaculo, adeoque praesentibus ac audientibus discipulis preces --ae fuerint à Salvatore recitatae. Approbat hanc sententiam Austinus tr. 104. in Ioh. Cùm autem Christi actio sit nostra institutio, sicuti etiam Nicol. de Lyra in c. 17. Ioh. scribit: Non tantùm oravit hristus ad aliquid impetrandum, sed etiam ad dandum nobis orandi exemplum. Inde minimè improbandae preces sunt, quae in publico loco fiunt. admonendique homines sunt, ne negligant publicum DEI in templis cultum, cuius pars non minima devotae preces suAccedit, quòd praesentia plurium devotorum hominum devotionem in orantibus accendit &c. Quo & Tertull. respiciens Apolog. cap. 39. Coimus, inquit, in coetum & aggregationem, ut Deum quasi manu facta precationibus ambiamus orantes, haec vis Deo grata est. Quae omnia rectè enthusiastis ac Templorum eversoribus opponenda, (quâ de re ad 1. Cor. 3, 16. quaedam monebuntur. Videantur interim loca Matth. 18, 19.Luc. 18, 10.20.Act. 3, 24.c. 6, 6.) Neque tamen eousextendenda sunt, ac si Deus magis praesens sit & faciliùs orationem exaudiat in templo, id quod Bell. l. 3. de cult. Sanctorū c. 4. evincere satagit (Conf. etiam Th. Stapletonus Prompt. Cath. Domin. 9. post Pentec. §. 1. Cosmas Magalianus Bracarensis, l. 1. Oper. Hierarch. p. 292. Beierlinck. Concion. select. 40. p. 745.) Huic enim sententiae rectè opponi praesens locus potest, tum quoque dicta Ioh. 4, 21. it. 1. Tim. 2, 8. Confer. etiam exempla Christi, Matth. 26, 39. & Apostolorum, Act. 1, 24.24.c. 4, 24.c. 16, 25. Rectè proinde Origenes l. 7. contra Celsum: Christianus etiam idiota persuasissimum habeat, quemvis mundi locum partem esse universi, & mundum universum esse templum DEI, & in quovis loco precatur clausis sensibilibus oculis, erectis autem animae luminibus, atita super totum mundum ascendit. Adstipulatur Basilius exhort. ad Bapt. t. 1. Non locus, sed propositi initium requiritur. Hieremias enim in luto erat, & DEum attraxit. Daniel in leonum lacu Deum placavit. Tres pueriin camino Deum promeruere. Latro non cruce prohibitus, quin Paradisum adsecutus fuerit. Iob in stercore (ut & Petrus atPaulus in carcere) Deum admisericordiam provocavit. Igitur ubicunfueris ora, velsi ante Iudicem, ora. Conf. etiam Prosper libro sent. ex Aug. sent. 333. it Chrysost. t. 5. h. 79. & alii Patres tum in hunc, tum ad all. modò locos. Summa: Locus non sanctificat preces, sed preces locum.)*

Τῶ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ. Vulg. vers. refert ad verbum πρόσευξαι

*(Idem quofacit Arabs)* sed articulus in Graeco additus ostendit, hunc ῶροσδιορισμὸν referendum esse ad nomē proximè praecedens, videl. ad Patrem coelestem, *(Confirmat hanc lectionem, Syrus, qui expressè habet qui in occulto. sc. est. Aethiops itidem lectionem hanc sequitur.)* Dicitur verò Pater coelestis esse in occulto, vel quòd sit in gloria coelesti, quae non est oculis hominum conspicua & obvia, vel quod videat in occulto, quae explicatio traditur in v. 4. praeced. Frustrà igitur Lucas Brugensis vers. Vulg. hîc praefert textui Graeco. Et rei ipsi, inquit, & superioribus, ut fit elemosyna tua in abscondito, aptius quadrare videtur id quod l-git ac vertit vetus Interpres, omissoτῷsive qui est, ante praepositionem in, quo modo etiam hodie esse in quibus dam libris Graecis, sunt, qui notent. Sed bene habet, quòd ipsemet Franc. Lucas statim per ἐπίληξιν subiungat. Quanquam pòst, v. 18. ubi de ieiunio tractatur, ad similem modum legat cum Graecis & Syricis libris & vetus Interpres: Ne videaris hominibus ieiunans, sed Patri tuo, qui est in abscondito. Cur ergo etiam hoc loco non ita legi possit?

ἐποδώσει σοι. At oratio est gratiae testificatio, inquit August. Epist. 105. Oratione nostram testamur indigentiam, & necessaria à Deo petimus, quomodo igitur oratione merces redditur? Resp. descendit hoc ex liberali & gratuita DEI promissione, quòd ut reliqua bona opera, ita quoque orationem ex gratia remunerari velit. Illo ipso igitur, quod Christus precibus nostris rependi asserit, satis perspicuè declarat, quicquid mercedis bonis operibus in Scriptura passim promittitur, non tanquam debitam mercedem meriti solvi, sed esse gratuitum donum.

Regerit Franc. Lucas Brug. Chrysostomum in h. l. sic scribere. Si ergo sic oras, plurimam accipies profecto mercedem. Non ait, donabit sibi, sed reddet, inquit, debitorem tibi se quippe constituit. Resp. Chrysostomus non loquitur de debito iustitiae, bonis operibus nostris ex merito reddendo, sed de debito promissionis, quod non pugnat cum mercede gratiae. *(Quòd verò Salvator noster de, debito promissionis in huiusmodi dictis loquatur, ultrò largitur, Iesuita Conzen. Postquam enim ís circa vers. 1. huius Capitis quaestionem instituisset: An verbis Christi: Mercedem non habebitis: meritum & merces probetur? concludit his verbis: Nos quo-

in mercede gratiam & ipsam mercedem gratuitam dicimus: sed tamen ex debito, non vi operis boni, sed voluntate DEI pollicentis. Is supra, omne meritum sponte gratuita misericordia promittens, mercedem constituit, ut ex pacto esset debita, idfaciendo etiam meritum fecit; quod sine promissione nullum erat.)*

Reges & Principes huius seculi magnum iudicant beneficiam, si precibus supplicantium aures accommodant. Sed Deus tam bonus ac beneficus est, ut non solùm orantes audire, sed etiam orationem ipsam ex gratia remunerari velit.

## 6:7
v. 7. Μὴβα.

Conn. He corrects another vice in prayer. *(A parallel passage exists in Syr. 7, 15.)*

Μὴβατολογήσητε. βαττολογίαν he explains immediately by πολυλογίαν,, whence the Syrian rendered it, do not be a babbler, the Arab: Do not multiply words. Vulg. Do not speak much. Battus was a certain inept and verbose Poet, who wrote hymns in which he inculcated the same things over and over. Ovid alluded to this in Metamorphoses 2, v. 730, when he makes Battus an informer repeating the same things. In those mountains, he says, they were, and they were in those mountains. Mercury, having imitated his battology: And you betray me to myself, treacherous one, you betray me to myself, he says. Thence Suidas says, βαττολογεῖνν is derived from βαμυ:, with which it by no means conflicts that some prefer the word to be derived from the fable of Battus, because Ovid alluded to the poet Battus.

Others think that Battus was some stammerer and hesitating in speech, of an impeded tongue, to which kind of men it is peculiar to repeat the same words, again and again. Erasm. in ann. He was the founder of Cyrene, Βάττος, whom Herodotus in book 4 narrates to be τραυλὸν καὶ ἰχνόφωιονν lisping and stumbling, of which Battus Pindar also makes mention in ode 4 of the Pythians.

Nicolaus Fullerus in book 4 of the Sacred Miscellanies, chapter 16, reads βααπτολογήσητε, for βαττολογήσητε and interprets the Syriac paraphrase of that place thus: Do not be gushing: that is, redundant and overflowing in speech. Compare Casaubon, exerc. 14 to Baronius.

Conformable to this doctrine of Christ is the saying of Joseph Albo , a Spanish Jew, in the Book of the Articles of Faith, sermon 4, chapter 23. In prayer, which is pleasing to GOD, three things are required: brevity, the agreement of the mouth with the heart, and humility or dejection. *(To this point also looks the opinion of R. Jonah in the book of Fear: Do not be more prolix than is fitting while praying in the Synagogue, lest by chance that be attributed to vainglory or mockery itself.)*

But how does it agree with this doctrine of Christ, that the saints are said to have recited long prayers? Nay, Christ himself is read to have prayed through the whole night. Luc. 6, 12. ὴν διανυκτερευων ἐ τῇ ῶροσἐξῆ τουθεοῦ *(Thus Christ Luc. 18, 1 says: It is necessary always to pray and not to faint. Conf. Eph. 6, 18. 1. Thess. 5, 17. item the example of Moses Deut. 9, 25.)* Resp. 1. Christ immediately adds an explanation: The heathens think that it will come to pass that in their πολυλογία i. e. because of their much speaking they will be heard. This, therefore, he disapproves, if anyone attributes some singular merit to πολυλογία in prayers, and determines that he is heard on account of that. 2. What therefore Christ teaches here does not pertain to the prolixity of prayers, but to those who superstitiously repeat the same little prayers without end, and place the confidence of being heard in the prolixity of prayers. 3. It is one thing to extend prayers, another to pursue much speaking in prayers. Augustine Epist. 121. cap. 10. Let much speaking be absent from prayer, but let not much prayer be absent, if fervent intention persists. *(Gravely Cyprian: What sloth is it, to be alienated and captured by inept and profane thoughts, when you pray to the Lord, as if there were anything else that you ought to think about more than what you are speaking with GOD? How do you demand to be heard by GOD, when you do not hear yourself? You wish GOD to be mindful of you, when you ask, when you yourself are not mindful of yourself.)*

*(Furthermore, concerning βαττολογίᾳ and πολυλογίᾳ of the heathens, and of the Papists who strenuously imitate them in their sacred rites, a sufficiently ample field of speaking is opened here. But I do not wish to do what has already been done: for long since, learned men have most diligently collected all things that exist concerning this matter both among Christians and gentile authors, from whom above all are to be seen B. D. Chemnitius part. 3. Exam. Concilii Trid. pag. 837. B. D. Hunnius tr. de Apostasiâ Eccl. Rom. B. D. Bald. Cas. Consc. l. 2. cap. 7. Cas. 7. B. D. Hōpfn. Sax. Ev. p. 366, 367. B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. 4. p. 940. seq. it p. 1006. David Maierus in Transennâ Hist. Theol de Papatu Romanēsi per Ethnicismum impraegnato, Casaubonus Exerc. 14. ad Baron. c. 8. p. 324. seqq. Seld, in proleg. de Diis Syr. p. 52. Abr. Scultetus Observ. in Matth. c. 17. Philipp. Caroli prodr. nov. lect. f. 9. Dn. Ioh. Conr. Dieterich in Disput. Philolog. de usu lectionis scriptorum secularium & antiq. in alt. litteraturâ, quae inserta T. 1. Disp. Acad. Dn. Dilherri, who also himself may be seen lib. 2. Elect. c. 5. Moreover, there can be unrolled Erasmus tr. de modo orandi, and likewise Nic. Fullerus l. 2. Miscell. c. 16. Ioh. de Pineda Com. in Iob. t. 1. p. 507. a. attempts to borrow light for the present saying both from Apuleius lib. 8. who writes that the worshippers of the Syrian Goddess were accustomed to blather many things fanatically, and from.)* 3. Reg. 18, 27. where it is commemorated that Baal was accustomed to be invoked with much clamor. But Grotius also shows at this place that this custom was censured by the Gentile poets themselves. For our theologians rightly advise (See B. D. Glassius lib. IV. Gr. S. p. 728. also Rher. S. p. 574.), although pleonasms are given in the Holy Scriptures, nevertheless βαττοογία or ταυτολογία vain things are by no means to be established in it. Also, that here those prayers are not censured by Christ in which both little words and even entire sentences are sometimes repeated (for such are read even in the sacred letters themselves. See Syrac. 23. and 36. also Ps. 136.), but at least the custom of those is taxed who, so that they may be held as devout by men, are prolix in prayers: Or who are of that vain persuasion, as if God measures prayers from prolixity and external labor rather than from the inner affection of the mind. At the same time, however, we are admonished that we bring due attention, lest we be forced to repeat prayers recited without intention later with attention because of shame. See B. D. Frantz de Interpret. Sc. S. Orac. 140. p. 1325. Let it be considered whether πολυλογία is not manifestly approved in the Pontifical Church, while it is imposed upon some that they sometimes murmur or chant the Pater noster a hundred times a day. Thus Abrah. Bzovius at the year 1204, n. 11, concerning Innocent III, reveals that by the authors of the murder of Conrad, Bishop of Würzburg, among other parts of penance, he also enjoined this, that they should chant the Lord's Prayer 100 times between day and night. It is also imposed upon a regular soldier that he say the Pater noster 150 times every day, as can be seen from the Pontifical fol. 85. fac. z. To this polylogy of the Pontificians can deservedly be opposed the history or fable which Fr. Pelbardus de Themeswar noted in sermon 2 for the 11th Sunday after Trinity, in these very words: An example is narrated in the book which is called Spec. Exempt. di exe-p110. that a certain religious virgin was offering to the Blessed Virgin Mary 150 salutations, and because of the multiplicity, less devoutly. To whom the Blessed Virgin appeared saying: To God and to me, any small service with devotion is more acceptable than much, exhibited negligently and without devotion.

Latin:

v. 7. Μὴβα.

Conn. Alterum in oratione vitium corrigit. *(Locus parallelus extat Syr. 7, 15.)*

Μὴβατολογήσητε. βαττολογίαν statim explicat per πολυλογίαν, inde Syrus reddidit, ne sit is multilo qui, Arabs: Non multiplicate verba. Vulg. Nolite multum loqui. Battus fuit quidam ineptus & verbosus Poëta, qui conscripsit hymnos, in quibus eadem subinde inculcavit. Allusit eò Ovidius 2. Metam. v. 730. quando Battum facit indicem eadem iterantem. In illis montibus inquit, erant & erant in montibus illis. Cuius battalogiam imitatus Mercurius: Et me mihi perfide prodis, Me mihi prodis ait. Inde Suid-s dicit, βαττολογεῖνν deduci βαμυ: um quo minimè pugnat, quod quidam ex fabula Batti vocem deductam malunt, quia Ovidius ad Battum Poëtam allusit.

Alii existimant, Battum fuisse quempiam balbum & haesi--ntem ore, impeditaesinguae, cui hominum generi peculiare est, voces easdem, interum atinterum repetere. Erasm. in ann. Fuit conditor CyrenesΒάττος,quem Herodotus lib. 4. narratτραυλὸν καὶ ἰχνόφωιοννblaesum & titubantem, cuius Batti etiam Pindarus mentionem fatit odâ 4. Pythiorum.

Nicol. Fullerus lib. 4. miscell. sacror. cap. 16. pro βαττολογήσητε legit βααπτολογήσητε, ac Syriacam paraphrasin illius loci sic interpretatur Nesi-ts scaturientes: h. e. sermone redundantes ac superfluentes. Confer Casaub. exerc. 14 ad Borou.

Conforme huic Christi doctrinae est dictum Iosephi Albonis Iudaei Hispani in Libr. de artic. fid. serm. 4. c. 23. In precatione, quae DEO placeat, tria requiruntur, brevitas, consensus oris cum corde, & humilitas sive deiectio. *(Huc spectat & sententia R. Ionae in, lib. Timoris: Ne inter orandum in Synagoga plus aequo sis prolixus, ne sortè id deputetur ipsi inanini gloriae vel derisioni.)*

At quomodo cum hac Christi doctrina congruit, quòd sancti quandoprolixas preces recitasse dicūtur? Quinimò ipse Christus per totam noctem orasse legitur. Luc. 6, 12.ὴν διανυκτερευων ἐ τῇ ῶροσἐξῆ τουθεοῦ *(Sic Christus Luc. 18, 1 inquit: Oportet semper orare & non deficere. Conf. Eph. 6, 18.1. Thess. 5, 17. item exemplum, Mosis Deut. 9, 25.)* Resp. 1. Christus explicationem statim subiungit: Ethnici putant, fore ut in suaπολυλογία i. e. ob multiloquium suum exaudiantur. Hoc ergo improbat, si quis πολυλογία in precibus singulare aliquod meritum tribuat, & propter illam se exaudiri statuat 2. Quod ergô Christus hîc docet, non pertinet ad precum prolixitatem, sed ad illos, qui superstitiosè easdem preculas sine fine iterant, ac fiduciam exauditionis in precum prolixitate collocant. 3. Aliud est preces protendere, aliud in precibus multiloquium sectari. Augustinus Epist. 121. cap. 10. Absit ab oratione multa locutio, sed non desit multa precatio, se fervens perseveret intentio. *(Graviter Cyprianus: Quae segnitia est, alienari & capi ineptis cogitationibus & profanis, cùm Dominum deprecaris. quasi sit aliud, quod magis debeas cogitare, quàm quod cum DEO loqueris? Quomodo audiri te à DEO postulas, cùm te ipse non audias? Vis esse Deum memorem tui, ùm rogas, quando tu ipse memor tui non fis.)*

*(Caeterùm de βαττολογίᾳ ac πολυλογίᾳ Ethnicorum, ac qui hos in sacris suis strenuè imitantur, Pontificiorum sat amplus hîc dicendi campus aperitur. Sed nolo actum agere: iampridem n. diligentissimè omnia, quae de materia hâc tum apud Christianos, tum gentiles autores extant, viri docti collegerunt, è quibus cumprimis videndi B. D. Chemnitius part. 3. Exam. Concilii Trid. pag. 837. B. D. Hunnius tr. de Apostasiâ Eccl. Rom. B. D. Bald. Cas. Consc. l. 2. cap. 7. Cas. 7. B. D. Hōpfn. Sax. Ev. p. 366, 367. B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. 4. p. 940. seq. it p. 1006. David Maierus in Transennâ Hist. Theol de Papatu Romanēsi per Ethnicismum impraegnato, Casaubonus Exerc. 14. ad Baron. c. 8. p. 324. seqq. Seld, in proleg. de Diis Syr. p. 52. Abr. Scultetus Observ. in Matth. c. 17. Philipp. Caroli prodr. nov. lect. f. 9. Dn. Ioh. Conr. Dieterich in Disput. Philolog. de usu lectionis scriptorum secularium & antiq. in alt. litteraturâ, quae inserta T. 1. Disp. Acad. Dn. Dilherri, qui & ipse videatur lib. 2. Elect. c. 5. Evolvi praeterea possunt Erasmus tr. de modo orandi, itemque Nic. Fullerus l. 2. Miscell. c. 16. Ioh. de Pineda Com. in Iob. t. 1. p. 507. a. praesenti dicto lucem foenerari conatur tum ex Apuleio lib. 8. qui Deae Syriae cultores multa phanatice effutire solitos scribit, tum ex. 3. Reg. 18, 27. ubi commemoratur, invocari solitum Baal multo clamore. Sed & ab ipsis Poetis Gentilibus morem hunc reprehensum fuisse, ostendit Grotius ad h. l. Coetenìm benè monent nostrates Theologi, (Vid. B. D. Glassius lib. IV. Gr. S. p. 728. it. Rher. S. p. 574.) licet in Sc. S. pleonasmi dentur, minimè tamen sive βαττοογία s. ταυτολογία vana in illâ statuenda sit. item, quòd hîc à Christo non reprehēdantur illae preces, in quibus & voculae & integrae quoque sententiae aliquando repetantur (tales n. & in ipsis sacris litteris leguntur. Vid. Syrac. 23. & 36. it. Ps. 136.) sed saltem taxari illorum morem, qui ut ab hominibus devoti habeantur, prolixi in precibus sunt: Vel qui vanâ istâ persuasione sunt, quasi Deus preces ex prolixitate potiùs & labore externo, quàm intimo animi affectu metiatur. simul tamen admonemur, ut debitam attentionem afferamus, ne preces sine intentione recitatas prae podore postea cum attentione repetere cogamur. Vid. B. D. Frantz de Interpret. Sc. S. Orac. 140. p. 1325. Cogitetur, annon manifeste πολυλογία in Pontificia Ecclesiâ approbetur, dum quibusdam imponitur, ut centies aliquando de die Pater noster demurmurent vel decantent. Sic Abrah. Bzovius ad A. 1204. n. 11. de Innocentio III. prodit, quòd autoribus coedis Conradi Episcopi Herbipolenus inter alias poenitentiae partes & hoc iniunxerit, ut orationem Dominicam 100. inter diem & noctem decantarent. Militi quoque regulari imponitur, ut singulis diebus 150. dicat Pater noster, prout videre est è Pontificali fol. 85. fac. z. Huic Pontificiorum polylogiae meritô opponi potest Historia vel fabula, quam Fr. Pelbardus de Themeswar serm. 2. Domini. XI. Trin. annot vit, his quidem verbis: Exemplum narratur in libro, qui dicitur Spec Exempt. di exe-p110. quòd quaedam virgo religiosa offerebat B. Virgim Mariae cocditit CL. salutationes, & propter multiplicitatem minùs devotè. Cui apparuit B. Virgo dicens: Deo & mihi acceptius est quantumlibet parvum servitium cum devotione, quàm multum, negligenter & fine devotione exhibitum.)*

## 6:8
v. 8. Οἰδ.

Οἰδεγδ`. If it is not undeservedly turned into a fault for someone to wish to teach a knowing man with many words, how much more before God, to whom all things present, past, and future are most exactly known, ought we not to be talkative.

The word πατρὸς is emphatic, occurring to a silent objection. For lest anyone should think that, although He knows my necessity well, He must nevertheless be swayed with many words to pity and to bring aid: Christ answers, He is of a fatherly mind toward you, therefore πολυλογία is not required by man.

Latin:

v. 8. Οἰδ.

Οἰδεγδ`. Si vitio alicui haud immeritò vertitur, multis verbis hominem scientem docere velle quantò magis coram Deo, cui omnia praesentia, praeterita & futura sunt exactissimè cognita, non debemus esse multiloqui. *(Confer infrà not. ad v. 32.)*

Vox πατρὸς est emphatica, occurrens tacitae obiectioni. Ne quis enim cogitaret, quamvis necessitatem meam probè habeat Cognitam, tamen multis verbis ad commiserationem & auxilium ferendum flectendus est: respondet Christus, paterno erga te est animo, ergo nec ab homine πολυλογία requiritur.

## 6:9
v. 19.

Matthew seems to signify here that Christ did not deliver this prayer because he was asked, but of his own accord. But Luke chapter XI, 1. 2. indicates that the Lord delivered this prayer because he was asked by an Apostle. Rupertus thinks that Christ taught the same form of praying twice on a different occasion. The contrary seems more probable to Maldonatus: For to what end, he says, would he have taught the same disciples the same prayer twice. But Rupertus does not say that he taught this prayer twice to the disciples alone. Christ could therefore have first proposed to the disciples separately, and indeed a certain form of prayer when a certain disciple was asking for a manner of praying, and Luke looked to this; but nothing stands in the way of his having proposed the same form of praying again to the crowd, as those who had not yet heard it. And that this was done by Christ, Matthew hints here. If, however, one should wish to establish entirely that the Lord's Prayer was delivered by the Savior only once, then it could perhaps be said that Matthew, out of a desire for brevity, or rather so that he might propose a synopsis of the whole Christian doctrine at once in one view as it were, joined those things which Christ delivered at different times, namely the sermon on the mount, held in the first year of his ministry, and the form of praying, delivered only in the third year of his ministry, and thus he wishes to be understood, that which was noted by Luke, namely that he himself, induced by the prayers of a certain disciple, taught this form of praying to his disciples. Thus it seems to Corn à Lapide and Jansenius. But nothing stands in the way of asserting that the Lord's Prayer was delivered by Christ twice. These, writes B. D. Calixtus Concord p. 136, which are said in this chapter in Matthew & Luke Chapters 11, 12, & 16, were not said once, but many times, it was not the care of the Evangelists to enumerate the individual words of the Savior, & to recount all things in the order in which they were said &c.)*

The pronoun ὑμεῖς placed after the verb is emphatic, so that it may distinguish us more clearly from the Gentiles.

ὅυτως προσεύχεσθε does not restrict our prayers absolutely to this form, so that we ought to use this one and no other ever, but it hands down a form of praying, to which all others may be recalled.

The Lord's Prayer excels other forms of praying. 1. by authority, 2. by brevity, 3. by perfection, 4. by order, 5. by efficacy, 6. by necessity. Bellarmine proves the individual members in book 1 de bon operib. cap. 4.

Tertullian, book de orat. cap. 9, calls it the discipline of praying & cap. the breviary of the whole Gospel.

Augustine, Epist. 121. cap. 12. If you run through the words of holy prayers in every way , you will find nothing which this Lord's prayer does not contain & conclude. Ib. However many other words we may say, we say nothing else than what is placed in this Lord's prayer, if we pray rightly & congruently. Chrysostom, homil. 14. in Matthew. He who does not pray as Christ taught, is not a disciple of Christ, because the Father does not willingly hear a prayer which the Son did not dictate. For the Father knows the senses & words of His Son, nor does He receive what human usurpation has devised, but what the wisdom of Christ has set forth. *(Pelbartus de Themeswar in de tempore, summer part, serm. 29, from Richard in l. 4. sent. dist. 15. q. 4. a. 8. teaches that the Lord's prayer is more worthy than all other prayers & commendable and more efficacious on account of three things: 1. on account of the sublimity of the author. 2. on account of the brevity of the senses (of the words). 3. on account of the utility of the petition. Firstly, on account of the sublimity or holiness of the author, since Christ, the supreme Lord of all, made it immediately with His own mouth and taught it to the disciples. But other prayers were given by other saints. Whence Augustine says: Greatest reverence is to be shown by all the faithful to the Lord's prayer itself, since it was made by the supreme Teacher of all himself. And therefore notwithstanding that someone might sometimes feel greater sweetness in another prayer: nevertheless this one is more worthy by reason of what was said and more to be revered. For if someone could give you a gem or such a precious stone that had stood in the mouth of Christ or in the middle of His heart, would you not hold it with the greatest reverence: so it is in the matter of the Lord's prayer, which was turned over in the mouth of Christ, nor is there doubt that the heavenly Father hears it more quickly when it is offered to Him. Because we see among men that a carnal Father hears more the requests made by a beloved son in letters written by his own hands. The same Pelbartus in the said place, from Isidore de sum. bon. l. 1. c. 22, writes that the efficacy of the Lord's prayer is so great that the symbol of faith, and that the Lord's Prayer, suffices for the whole law of the little Church to attain the kingdoms of heaven.)*

See entirely Cyprian, sermon 6, in the explanation of the Lord's Prayer. *(Beautifully here the said author among other things: Let the Father recognize the words of His Son, when we make prayer; he who dwells within in the breast, let him be also in the voice. And since we have him as an advocate before the Father for our sins, when we sinners ask for our offenses, let us put forth the words of our advocate. For since he says, that whatever you shall ask from the Father in my name, he will give to you, how much more effectively do we obtain what we ask in the name of Christ, if we ask by his own prayer.)*

Moreover, we ought to consider in this formula of the Lord's Prayer. 1. artful brevity. 2. wonderful richness of things. It embraces everything that can be prayed for rightly and conveniently. 3. elegant harmony of order. We ask in this prayer. 1. the end of our life, then the principal one, which is the glory of GOD, it asks. 1. then the subordinate one, which is our salvation, it asks. 2. 2. those things which lead to both that end, namely first the acquisition of the means, then of the principal, which is piety, it asks. 3. then of the secondary, which is the sustenance of life, it asks. 4. Secondly the removal of impediments, namely of sins, then of past ones, it asks. 5. then of future ones, it asks. 6. Thirdly, deliverance from all adversities, it asks. 7. Compare Thomas 2. 2. q. 183. art 9.

In the first four petitions we pray for goods, in the three remaining we pray against evils. In the three first petitions we ask for: eternal things, in the four remaining temporal things. The three first petitions look directly to the glory of GOD, the other four are composed for our necessities in this life.

Cornelius Iansenius proceeds thus. We ask first for the bestowing of good things. Secondly, for the removal of evil things. Among good things: 1. the good of GOD, petition 1. 2. our highest good, petition 2. 3. our intermediate good, namely the grace of fulfilling the commandments, petition 3. 4. our lowest good, petition 4. Among evil things: 1. the removal of past evil, petition 5. 2. of future evil, petition 6. 3. of present evil, petition 7. *(Pelbartus, following Richard and others, proceeds thus. Since every man ought to ask 1. to obtain good things. 2. for evil things to be removed, and indeed: the highest good is God himself, whom we ought to love and worship above all, thence the first petition is placed. The second good is to possess the kingdom of GOD, which is asked for in the 2nd petition. The third good is the way, by which we may arrive at the kingdom of God, namely conformity to the will of GOD, concerning which is the 3rd petition. The fourth good is the aid, by which we can be helped to arrive, and this is necessary sustenance, for the body indeed for daily life, but for the soul for perpetual life, concerning which is the 4th petition. Finally, we ask for evil things to be removed, among which the worst is the evil of fault, and concerning this is the 5th petition. The second evil is the fall of temptation, which inclines to fault, concerning which is the 6th petition. The third evil is of punishment, especially perpetual, concerning which is the 7th petition. *)

We divide the six postulates into two orders, so that the three former pertain directly or immediately to God; the three remaining to us; but these partly in bodily things, at3 to these is assigned the fourth petition, partly in religious things, which are comprehended by the remaining two. Chamierus tom. 4 lib. 9. cap. 11. §. 26. But these proceed from that hypothesis, which is of Calv. lib. 3. Instit. cap. 20. §. 35. I. Piscator in Expos. Orat. Domin, Ursinus in Explic. Catech, page 887. *(Danaeus expl. Orat. Domin p. 101. & 103. Grynaeus in h. l. Matthaei, Polanus Synt, page 614. Wendelinus Christianae Theol. System, mai, 1. 2. c. 5. p. 1602. and of other Calvinists.)* whom also the Photinians follow here. See Catech Racov. p. 169. just as also the Arminians, as is evident from Confess. c. 14.) that those words, and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil, contain only one petition. But they are more correctly said to contain two distinct petitions, since preservation in temptations is one benefit, and deliverance from all evil is another. Aug. Enchir. Cap. 115. counts seven petitions. lib. 2. de serm. Domini in monte. cap. 16. The last and seventh petition is, but deliver us from evil.

It is not likely that the Lord, who a little before had said: When you pray, do not use many words, would prescribe such a form of praying in which one and the same thing is signified by different words, that is, sentences. Furthermore, if they are exactly the same: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil, we shall not be asking to be delivered from past evil, but only from future; nor from the evil of punishment, but from the evil of fault. For temptation, into which we ask not to be led, is not a past evil, but a future one; nor is it an evil of punishment, but of fault.

*(Let the same Augustine be compared in his Epistle to Proba. Indeed, they follow the division of Augustine. Thomas Aquinas p. 2. q. 83. a. 9, Nicholas of Lyra, Ordinary Gloss on this passage, and others.)*

Traces of this form of praying exist in the book Musar. 49. 1. Our God, who art one in heaven, may Thy name be established forever; may Thy kingdom reign over us for ever and ever; but may Thy name be sanctified through our works. *(Mr. Dilherr in Eclog. Syr. p. 46 and Louis Cappel in Spic. p. 16 report it a little differently.)* Ibid. 9. 12. Do not lead us into the hands of sin, but deliver us from evil encounter.

*(And this petition is read formed a little differently in Cappel, loc. cit. There is also in my possession a sufficiently ancient Jewish ritual book, which was transferred to me from the library of John Schröter, M.D. and Count Palatine of the Empire and first Rector in this Academy of Halle, inscribed הבית יוטם צורת בעל, in which, among others, a prayer is also read which begins: etc. יהי רצון מלפניך ײ אלהי אלהי אבותי i. e. May Thy will be done before Thee, O Lord, my God, God of my fathers etc.)*

Πάτερ ἡμῶν, ὁ ἐν Τοῖς Ούρανοῖς. In this preface we proclaim the kindness of GOD, in the words, Our Father; and His immense power, in the words, who art in heaven. These are the two supports of our confidence, by which we can be confirmed concerning being heard. Aug. lib. 2. de serm. Domini in monte, c. 1. Cyprian, serm. de orat. Dom. None of us would dare to touch this name (Father) in prayer, unless the abundance of His condescension and goodness had permitted it. Bernard, serm. de Natali B. Mariae: These words remind us of divine adoption, while we say, Our Father: and of earthly pilgrimage, while we add, who art in heaven, so that we may understand that we need help, because we are pilgrims, and we conceive, because we are children of GOD. Those words excite in us the fear and love of GOD: they insinuate the reason why God ought to and can hear us. *( And this is the designation of piety and power: Tert. book, on prayer.)*

Damasc. book 1. of the orthodox faith, chapter 15. Κυριώτερον ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν -ςὶν πατὴρ, ὁἐκ μὴ ὄνΤων εἶναι Παραγαγὼν ἢ ὁι γεννὴσαντες ὁιἰξ αὐτοὑ καὶ Τὸ εἶναι καὶ Τὸ γενναῦ εἰληΦότες.

Pater noster [Our Father] is: 1. in respect of creation and formation in the womb. 2. in respect of spiritual regeneration and adoption. 3. in respect of fatherly love. 4. in respect of conservation and nutrition. 5. in respect of defense. 6. in respect of introduction into the heavenly inheritance. *(Pelbartus, in the cited book: How is God the Father of men? Resp. 1. By creation. 2. By the impression of the image, and thus He is the Father of all men. 3. By adoption, and thus He is the Father of Christians. 4. By the heavenly inheritance, which He promised to the elect, Rom. 8.)*

Whatever benefits an earthly father provides to his children, the same, nay more and greater, the heavenly Father confers upon us, because His love toward us exceeds in infinite ways the love which earthly parents bear toward their children. Eph. 3. v. 15.

*(Augustine: By the name of Father, charity is stirred up ( for what is dearer to sons than a father?) and a suppliant affection, and a certain presumption of obtaining: for what will He not give to sons, who gave that they should be sons. But there is a huge difference when Christ calls His heavenly Father His Father, and when we call God our Father. Epiph. heresy 69. p. 253. He said, he writes, My God and your God, and My Father and your Father: ( Ioh. 20, 17.) My Father indeed according to nature in the Godhead: and your Father by grace, through Me in adoption: but My God, because I have assumed your flesh; and your God, according to nature and truth. Which things are to be noted against Photinus.)*

Let this appellation, however, exhort us to reciprocal love toward God, and to the rendering of filial obedience to Him. Cyprian, in the same place: We ought to remember and know that when we call God Father, we ought to act as children of GOD, so that just as we please ourselves in GOD the Father, so He may also please Himself in us His children.

It is asked here 1. whether the name of Father is taken here οὐσιωδῶς, or ὑΠο ςμΤικῶς concerning the first person of the Trinity? Resp. that it is taken οὐσιωδῶς, the worship of invocation which is owed to all and each of the persons of the Trinity shows. ( α )* (And in this way, namely that οὐσιωδῶς, the word Father is to be taken in this place, the Jesuits themselves, Maldonatus, Barradius, and Corn. à Lapide, advise. This is to be noted against those Papists who, to the argument of our countrymen, which they oppose to the invocation of saints from this passage, since only God is named who is to be invoked by us, object that the Lord's Prayer is referred to the Father alone, and yet it is permitted to invoke the Son and the Holy Spirit. Otherwise, therefore, the Jesuit Conzen objects, and abandoning both that and Bellarmine's response: for thus he says in this place The argument of the Magdeburg Centuriators is Cent. 1, book 1, ch. 4. When Christ teaches his own the manner of praying, he teaches them to invoke God, not the saints; therefore they are not to be invoked. Conzen adds: Bellarminus once responded that Christ in this place shows what things are to be sought: he does not deal with those from whom they are to be sought. And indeed he is entirely occupied with the subject matter of prayer. Another solution can also be given, and indeed a clear one. That the Lord was asked about the manner of praying to God, about religious worship, about the subject matter of prayer, but not about that which is deferred to the saints. For from the saints nothing is sought except intercession. The subject matter of prayers is the same in both cases. For God did not wish to bind us entirely to these words. For other prayers of Christians have been heard, conceived in other words, asAct. 4, 24.ch. 7.the penultimate verse.ch. 8, 15. 16. 17.He only wished to show what things it was necessary to seek. No creature is to be invoked by religious prayer, but one can be asked in another way, whether he lives in this age, or is joined with God in heaven, and through Him recognizes our necessities. Resp. 1. We concede that by that prayer of Christ it is not enjoined upon Christians that they should not seek from the true God those things of which they have need, and also celebrate the name of God and pay thanks to Him for benefits received, in any words other than those of which the Lord's Prayer consists. 2. But it does not follow from that, that just as we can propose in other words those things which we seek from the true and supreme God, so also we can direct our prayers to another besides the true, that is, the omnipotent and omniscient God, and hope for help from him as from the giver of salvation. That the former is indifferent is clear from Holy Scripture, just as we do not at all deny that the passages brought forward by Conzen prove this very thing: but that this is indifferent, that is, that it is equally free for me whether I wish to direct religious prayers to the true God, the creator of heaven and earth, or indeed to a mere creature, is simply denied.

nor will it ever be able to be proven from the Holy Scriptures. Certainly, if this could be proven from the H. S. just as well as that other point, Gonzen would have brought forward at least one single passage, just as he proved that other point, about which, however, there is no controversy, with three sayings of H. S. 3. That which the Jesuit brings forward concerning the addressing of the living has little to do with the matter: it is indeed known that this consequence, by which the Papists commonly infer the religious invocation of the dead from the addressing of the living, (See Cotonus, Instit. Cath. p. 92; Coturius, Epit. Controv. p. 459; Costerus, Enchir. controv. p. 659; Becanus, Man. Controv. l. 1, c. 7, §. 7.) The Catholic Achilles is greeted by Eck in the Enchiridion, p. 149, nor does the boasting of Bellarmine, book 1 on the blessedness of the saints, chapter 19, escape us, that it will never happen that this argument can be solved by us. But that these are vain persuasions, with which the Papists flatter themselves, is sufficiently shown by very many writings of our countrymen, by which the weakness of the said consequence is demonstrated to the eye, and that Achilles has been utterly prostrated. For, to pass over other things now, how great, I ask, is the difference between the addressing of the living and the invocation of the dead. To the former I can expose my calamities, and I am so certain that they then know them; but concerning these dead ones, I am always forced to doubt whether they hear my vows and prayers, or whether it ever comes to their knowledge what I hope for and pray for from them. Whence even the Papists themselves cherish widely differing opinions, whence and how the dead saints learn of the calamities of the living, just as also the prayers poured out to them. Whether, indeed, from the report of the angels, or through the dead who migrate from here into heaven, or from the revelation of God, or finally while they themselves are everywhere by a certain wondrous speed of nature. (Just as the blessed Pareus reviews and refutes these modes in his book on Death, § 321 and following.) Then, it is especially to be noted that there is a huge distinction between the mode of addressing, since that honor which is exhibited to the living, while they, being conscious of our calamity, are asked that they might wish to join their prayers to ours, is merely human; but that which is exhibited to the dead saints in their invocation is more than human, since invocation and religious adoration are defined by the Papists (See Bellarmine, book 1 on the blessedness of the saints, chapter 14; Suarez, volume 2, Commentary on Thomas, question 27, Disputation 22, section 1). Whence also the addressing of the living pertains to the second table of the Decalogue and is a work of charity, and both its precepts and examples exist approved in divine things (See 1. Tim. 2, 1.Iac. 5, 16.1. Sam. 7, 8.Iob. 42, 8.Rom. 15, 30. &c.) but the invocation of the departed pertains to the first table of the Decalogue and is a cult of religion, which is owed to God alone. Therefore, it is so far from the case that a command for it exists in Holy Scripture (a thing which the Papists themselves also concede, see Eccius in Enchir. page 156, Bell. book 1 on the saints of the blessed, chapter 20, Becanus book loc. cit. § 26, Cotonus loc. cit.) or even an approved example, that it is rather most severely prohibited, and indeed in all those places where religious adoration is claimed for God alone. But as for what Conzen distinguishes between religious prayer and mere invocation, by which we seek help from the living as well, as Julius Caesar Coturius writes in Epit. page 466, and wishes to persuade us that the departed saints are perhaps affected by the latter by the Papists, but not by the former: in this, both the doctrine and the practice most well-known in the Papal Church contradict his own attempt. The Jesuit Cotonus indeed urges in the aforementioned place, as one well knowing how little this distinction is heeded by his own, that it is good, rather useful, and indeed even necessary, to warn all Christians to teach more often that they should not make gods out of the Saints, or make them equal and equivalent to the one Divinity to be worshipped alone, but I fear that he beats the air, unless he simultaneously persuades the Pope or the Fathers of the holy inquisition to abolish the Psalter of Mary, printed at Venice in the year 1476 by Ioh. de Hallis, and again committed to the press by the Jesuits in Bavaria, by means of the Expurgatory Index; and that those same men should also note and remove by the Expurgatory Index those ill-fated dogmas, that the saints are to be adored with adoration properly so called, that the Lord's Prayer is to be recited in honor of the saints, that I ought to ask of them those things which it is the prerogative of God alone to bestow, that trust is to be placed in them, which are inculcated everywhere by the Jesuits. But more on these things elsewhere. Let those things which have been written at length concerning the invocation of saints by our own people be compared, especially D. Chemn. part 3 of the Examination of the Council of Trent, D. Ioh. Himmelio and D. Ioh. Iac. Bernhardo in their special books published on the Invocation of Saints, D. Mentzer in Disp. VI of the Antipistor, B. Part 8 of the Theological Commonplaces, likewise the Catholic Confession, vol. 3: Academic Disputations, page 4 and following, page 320, &c., D. Lobech. on the A. C. Disp. 23, D. Mylio, D. Gravero, and others on Article 22 of the A. C.

( β ) Thus Cyprian, Chrysostom, Rupert, and several others accept it. By no means, however, in that sense, as if Christ wished to teach by this very thing, that the Father principally is God, as Hieronymus Zanchius Tom. 1. part. 2. de Trib. Eloh. 1. 1. c. 3. §. 1. p. 486. thinks. Nor also as if divine benefits principally proceed from the Father, as it seems to Ioh. Piscator of Herborn, Vol. 1, Thes. Theol. L. 11, th. 32, page 139. (Twin opinions to which are found also among other Calvinists, as the blessed Par. shows in Dispp. Acad. p. 1124. Wendelin can also be added to them, who in lib. 1, Synt. Christ. Theol. c. 2, p. 224, ὑΠεροχ-ὐ or the prerogative of the Father over the Son, considered outside of the flesh and the mediatorial office, by reason of operation, established in clear words, and he also teaches in the same place that the name of GOD in the H. S. is often καΤ ἐξοχ-ὐ attributed to the Father.) For such a prerogative is not given among the persons of the Deity, (See Ioh. 5. 19.) and it provides a handle of this kind ἀκυρολογἰα, to the Photinians and Arminians to chatter more boldly about the subordination among the persons of the H. Trinity, and as far as they are concerned, finally to deny completely the true Deity of Christ, as is sufficiently evident from Catech. Racov. p. 176, Socin. in Antiwui. p. 28, Sim. Episcopius Lib. IV, Instit. Theol. sect. 2, c. 32, p. 333 & 334, add also c. 33. Whence also the Remonstrants are rightly noted here by the Contra-Remonstrants in Censur. p. 216, because they separate the Son from that one true God in the sanctification of the divine name as if.)* concerning the Father of our Savior Christ Jesus, whom he is accustomed to call both his and our Father, and to refer everything to him as to the first origin and source, yet the Son and the Holy Spirit are not on that account excluded from the object of adoration. For since there is one Deity of these three persons, namely the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and equal glory and an undivided essence, therefore also when one person is named, the other is named; when one person is invoked, the other is invoked.

*(Q. 2. Whether this prayer was also in use among the faithful in the O. T. The Photinians deny it, and from there they further conclude that Christ increased the first table of the Decalogue by adding to it the Lord's Prayer. See Catech. Racov. p. 164, Smalc. de divin. Christi. c. 5. Response: one must distinguish above all between the matter, i.e., the things which are requested in the prayer, and the external form, i.e., the connection and order of the words observed in the present prayer. As far as the form concerns, we willingly grant that such a prayer is nowhere read in the O. T., namely if one wishes to count the words and letters, and to that extent we concede that this prayer is proper to the N. T. But as far as the matter, further concerns, namely the things which we ask of GOD in the Lord's Prayer, it can certainly hardly be denied with any appearance of probability that the same things were both promised by GOD to the pious in the O. T. and also requested by the faithful. This is so clear that not even Smalcius himself could entirely deny it. For thus he writes in Disp. 7, contr. Frantz.: It is not asked whether or not in their own way they could also have prayed the same things (namely by the power of the divine promise made concerning being heard) and whether certain holy men under the Old Testament prayed for those things which are prescribed to us in the Lord's Prayer: but whether this manner of praying was prescribed to all in general; and whether all prayed or ought to have prayed in this way: this is in question. But if the Photinians have conceded in this way, that the pious could both pray for and also did pray for the same things which we ask for in the Lord's Prayer, their dogma will easily collapse, that Christ increased the first table, and thus is a new legislator. For to this end it is not sufficient that those things which the pious in the Old Testament prayed for are proposed at least by a new method, but that other things also be asked for, indeed be commanded to be asked for, and that better promises also exist. But let someone say: Nevertheless it was not commanded to all in the Old Testament that they themselves also should ask from God those things which we ask for in the Lord's Prayer, and, indeed, precisely by this formula of prayer prescribed by Christ. I respond: I deny that there is here a certain prescribed law, or that the formal words must be kept so precisely that, while the subject matter is preserved, no one can pour out their prayers to God in other words. Whence the Photinians themselves also in the Racovian Catechism, p. 169, note, that it is free even in the New Testament to invoke God in another manner and form than that prescribed in the Lord's Prayer: since neither here nor elsewhere is it prohibited. At least let it be guarded against that what we ask does not conflict with the divine will. But this form of praying was commanded by Christ to this end, that we might know what we ought always and necessarily to ask from God. But that it was by no means enjoined upon the Jews in the Old Testament through the Decalogue (to omit now the notable passage Ps. 50, 15. as well as the frequent admonitions of the prophets to perform repentance) that they should expect the sanctification of the divine name, the coming of the Kingdom of God, etc., I hope even the Jews of today will hardly grant to the Socinians. Moreover, that the faithful asked for such things as these is abundantly clear from the Davidic psalms alone. It is added that almost the same words, of which the Lord's Prayer consists, are even now found in the writings of the Jews: whence indeed it is easy to conclude that their ancestors asked from God the same things which we in the New Testament ask from God. It behooves us, writes Grotius in this place, p. 142, that those things which are cited by others from the books of the Hebrews, not so much this formula conceived by Christ in His own words, as that whatever was praiseworthy in the prayers of the Hebrews was gathered into it: Just as in His admonitions He uses proverbs known in that age throughout. Let Act. 4, 12.c. 15, 11.Matth. 1, 21. be compared entirely.

Πάτερἡμῶν. Just as the name Father reminds us of the love of GOD: so the pronoun our admonishes us of the love of neighbor. For because we have a common Father in the heavens, therefore we ought to embrace one another with brotherly love. Gregory of Nyssa, oration 2 on the Lord's Prayer, warns that those who are not children of God, nor wish to be, inasmuch as they voluntarily persist in mortal sin, say mendaciously; Our Father who art in the heavens. For when they invoke the Father, they do not invoke God, but the Devil, because they are from the father the Devil, but the Devil is not in the heavens, but in the underworld.

The author of the imperfect work on Matthew, He said, not, my. God gladly hears when a Christian prays not only for himself, but for another. For to pray for oneself is of nature, for another of grace: to pray for oneself, the necessity of the thing compels, but for another, the charity of brotherhood exhorts. But the prayer is sweeter before God, not which the necessity of the thing transmits, but which the charity of brotherhood commends.

Ambrose, book 1 on Cain and Abel, chapter 9. You are taught to pray especially for the people, that is, for the whole body, for all the members of your mother, in which is the sign of mutual charity. For if you pray for yourself, you will pray only for yourself, but now because individuals pray for all, all also pray for individuals.

Ο ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς. Cyril, Ambrose, and Augustine understand by heavens the minds of the Saints, in which GOD dwells through grace, Gregory of Nyssa, Chrysostom, Cassian, Bernard, the corporeal and properly so-called heavens, which better agrees with the phrase of Scripture. *(But when God is said to be in those heavens, then it is not to be accepted as if God were included in them, or filled heaven locally, for such filling is not to be understood Ier. 23, 24. for neither do the heavens of heavens contain Him,1. Reg. 8, 27. inasmuch as He is an immense essence. Therefore God is said to be in the heavens not by reason of inclusion, but by reason of Φανερώσεως i. e. manifestation, because He exerts His majesty more excellently in that , and by reason of συγκαταβάσεως of our information, because heaven is more sublime than all earthly creatures. To which point Albertus Magnus 1. 8 Phys. tr. 4. c. 6. makes this: All nations agree in this, that God is in heaven, not that He is there as in a place, who properly speaking has no place, but because the greater effects appear there. These things are consistent with those which are read in the Philosopher 1. de coel. text. comm. 22. God is in heaven, not as a body is in a place by circumscription: nor as water in a vessel by equality, but rather by the most manifest signs of His operation. For there the power of His divinity and goodness shines forth more. Conf. More concerning the omnipresence and immensity of GOD in B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. de Deo c. 5. § 15. Fr. Suarez Dispp. Metaph. t. 2. D. 30. s. 4. p. 5. seqq. Hannibal. Rossellus to the Pymander of Mercury Trismegistus lib. 3. pag. 135. seqq. and elsewhere passim, Petr. Fonseca the Lusitanian in lib. 5. Metaph. Aristot. p. 890. seqq. and others, the Scholastics especially to lib. 1. sent. dist. 37.)* God is not said to be in heaven for this reason, that He may be understood to be included in heaven, but that it may be insinuated that He presides over all created things, rules all, and contains all in His hand. Ps. 113. v. 11. Our God is in heaven, He has done whatsoever He willed. God is therefore said to be in heaven, not because He is not everywhere, but because in heaven He most manifests the glory of His presence. For both the blessed in heaven see God face to face; and we from the contemplation of heaven most understand the wisdom and power of God. *(Beautifully Augustine ep. 57. to Dardanus It must be confessed, that God is everywhere by the presence of His divinity, but not everywhere by the grace of His habitation. For because of this habitation, where without doubt the grace of His love is recognized, we do not say, Our Father, who art everywhere, although this also be true: but, Our Father, who art in heaven, so that we may rather commemorate His temple in prayer, which we ourselves ought to be, and in as much as we are, to that extent we pertain to His society and family of adoption. For if the people of GOD not yet made equal to the Angels is still called His temple in this pilgrimage: how much more is His temple in the heavens, where the people of the Angels are, to whom we are to be gathered and made equal, when the pilgrimage is finished, which is what was promised, we shall be. Therefore the modes of divine presence are to be distinguished: concerning which matter elsewhere. As regards the phrase itself: Our Father who art in heaven, Barth. Mayerus l. 2. Philol. sacrae p. 99. warns that it is Targumic (for what Deut. 33. 6. is read הלוא אביך that the Jerusalem Targum expresses הלא הוא אבןכזן דבשמיא and from there he further concludes, that our Savior, just as the Apostles sometimes used phrases from the Targumim or Targumic writings, so that the Jews might more easily ἐν διασω ερᾶ (as those to whom Targumic writings were very familiar, and who were accustomed to that speech) coalesce with the Greeks, and come together into one body of the Church. Lud. Capellus also mentions in Spic. p. 16. that in the Machazor f. 76. it is read: Accepted are the prayers and supplications of all Israel קרם אבוהוןךבשםיא before their father who is in heaven. The same is also testified, in the books of the Tephilloth of the Jews. The Lusitanians address God in this way: פשע םימשבש וניבא עםנו חסף. )*

Raymundus observes that it is said in the Lord’s Prayer, "who art in heaven," but not "who art on earth." 1. So that it may be shown that when we pray, we ought not to think of earthly things but heavenly. Col. 3. 1, 2. 2. So that we may know that through prayer there come to us not earthly goods, which are base, but heavenly, which are supreme and eternal.)* Αγιασθήτω τὸ ὄνομά σου. |

Αγιασθήτω τὸ ὄνομά σου. This first petition makes a beginning from the end of things to be sought. The name of God is hallowed, not in an absolute sense, as if God in Himself and by reason of Himself were to be hallowed by us, but in a relative sense, because God, existing as holy, is acknowledged as such by us. That happens in three ways. 1. δοθητικῶς by sound doctrine. 2. ἐνεργητικῶς by a holy life. 3. πα θητικῶς by sufferings, endured for the confession of the Gospel. In prayer we ought not to be solicitous first of all about ourselves, but about the glory of GOD, to which, as to the ultimate end, all things ought to be referred.

The name of G O D is God Himself, as He is named among men, i.e., acknowledged and celebrated. This name of GOD is hallowed, i.e., is held and preached as holy.

1. Through the conversion of infidels and heretics. 2. Through the holy conversation of the faithful. 3. Through the glorification of the divine name. Isa. 8. v. 13.Matt. 5. v. 16.1. Pet. 2. v. 12.chap. 3. v. 15.

*(Corn. à Lapide writes in this place, that St. Augustine, Chrysostom, and others explain this petition thus, saying: Grant, O Lord, not that the name of idols or demons, or of Mahomet, or of Arius, Luther, Calvin etc. but thy name may be held holy by men. Resp. What commerce has Luther with idols or demons? What with Mahomet etc.? Those calumnies, with which some Papists have bespattered the Blessed Luther, as if he had hated the mystery of the Holy Trinity with Arius, and had not sincerely acknowledged the Deity of the Son, our people have long since wiped away. What did Luther ever teach in common with the fables of Mohammed? Nay rather, that there is no small agreement between the institutions, dogmas, figments, etc., of the Papists and of Mohammed, one might not rashly affirm. Are not the pilgrimages of the Papists to places which they call holy sufficiently akin to the customs and laws of the Turks, by which individuals are bound to visit the sepulcher of Mohammed annually, deceived, however, by those splendid promises that they might thus obtain the remission of their sins? And who, I ask, does not know that the Papist purgatory is an Ethnic, Jewish, and Turkish figment? Whence also Cardinal Bellarmine, among other reasons and foundations by which he labors to prop up the ruinous edifice of Purgatory, urges this also in the third place, that the Mohammedans also confess Purgatory. Concerning the Mohammedans, he says, it is clear from the Alcoran, (but it is treated in this concerning Purgatory in Surah 10 and 29) where they expressly confess purgatory. A friendly conspiracy between the doctrine and customs of the Papists and the Mohammedans could indeed be shown in many more things, if we were now about that. Let the Papists unfold the treatise on Turco-Papism, opposed to the calumnies of William Giffort in Calvino-Turcismo, and published long ago, namely in the year 1604 at London, and it will sufficiently appear whether the Roman Pontiffs may be joined with Mahomet with greater right than our Blessed Luther. Who profanes the name of GOD more than the Papists? No one ever so placed Luther in the number of the Saints as to affirm that he was ἀ ναμἀρτητον, or hoped for help from him while he is already triumphing among the celestials, and invoked him to this end. That this, however, is a custom among the Papists with their saints, experience itself abundantly testifies. Who, I ask, does not know that the deceased saints are believed by the Papists to be the givers of celestial benefits and the guardians of human affairs? What kingdom is there, what region, which does not have its own God or tutelary Goddess from among those saints (of whom, however, it is uncertain whether many ever existed in the nature of things, or whether they even have beatitude

Many also were heretics or otherwise infamous, as B. Par. L. de Morte §. 480. it. Confess. Cath. t. 3. pag. 547. 548. 587. Dn. D. Hülsem. AntiHag. p. 898. seqq. B. D. Lobech. in A. C. p. 536. show.) number? Scarcely can a disease be imagined for which a patron and helper is not feigned from that assembly of saints. (as B. D. Chemn. part. 3. Exam. Con. Trid. p. 234. 235. B. D. Heilbrun. Papat. Acathol. p. 207. B. Par. Loc. de Morte § 353. exhibit a specimen of this idolatry.) Let the Papists themselves consider whether by that idolatry the most holy name of GOD is profaned, and GOD, to whom alone we ought to flee in tribulations, is affected with ignominy. What, I ask, is the canonization of deceased men which the Roman Pontiff arrogates to himself, and from which he makes no light gain, other than an express ἀποθεώσως an image of the Gentiles? Must it not be judged that the name of GOD is profaned, and Christ is affected with ignominy, but on the contrary, the name of the deceased, whom they call saints, is sanctified by the Papists, while it is persuaded to the simpler folk in the Papacy that the Saints are more propitious, clement, and merciful, nay, more prompt to hear and help than Christ himself, as those who have themselves experienced the same calamities in the flesh? The Jesuit Corn. à Lapide would have done better, therefore, if he had not stirred this Camarina, and by imputing to us, who are called Lutherans for the sake of distinction, without any appearance of probability, as if we sanctify the name of Luther, i.e., affect him with such honor, which, as it is not right to exhibit to a man who has deserved very well of the Church while the first petition remains intact, he would have thus provided an opportunity for touching those little ulcers of the Pontifical Church a little more harshly.)

Latin:

v. 19.

*( Matthaeus significare hîc videtur, Christum non rogatum, sed sponte orationem hanc tradidisse. At Lutas cap. XI, 1. 2. indicat, Dominum ab Apostolo rogatum orationem hanc tradidisse. Rupertus existimat, Christum eandem orandi formam bis diversâ occasione docuisse. Contrarium Maldonato videtur probabilius: Quorsum, enim, inquit, eos dem discipulos bis eandem oreationem docuisset. At Rupertus non dicit, quòd solos discipulos bis docuerit hanc orationem. Potuit igitur Christus primò seorsim discipulis, & quidem ertam orationis formam discipulo quodam petente, orandi modum proponere, & huc Lucas respexit; nihil verò obstat, quò minùs iterum eandem orandi formam turbae proposuerit, ut quae nondum illam audierat. Et hoc à Christo factum esse, Matthaeus hîc innuit. Si tamen omninò quis statuere velit, quòd semel duntaxat oratio Dominica tradita à Salvatore fuerit, tum dici fortè poterit, quòd Matthaeus illa, quae Christus diversis temporibus tradidit, nempe sermonem in monte, primo ministerii anno habitum, ac orādi formam, tertio demum ministerii anno traditam, brevitatisstudio, vel potiùs ut synopsin totius doctrinae Christianae simul uno quasi intuitu proponeret, coniunxerit, adeoque subintellectum velit illud, quod à Lucâ annotatum, scilicet quòd ipse, Discipuli cuiusdam precibus adductus hanc orandi formam, Discipulos suos docuerit. Ita Corn à Lapide ac Iansenio videtur. Sed nihil obstat, quò minùs adseratur, bis à Christo Orationem. Dominicam fuisse traditam. Haec, scribit B. D. Calixtus Concord p. 136. quae hoc cap. apud Matth. & Lucam Cap. 11. 12. & 16. dicuntur, non semel, sed pluries dicta sunt, necurae fuit Evangelistis, adnumerare singula verba Servatoris, & omnia quo ordine dicta sunt, recēsere &c.)*

Pronomen ὑμεῖς postpositum verbo est emphaticum, ut manifestius ab Ethnicis nos distingvat.

ὅυτως προσεύχεσθε non restringit preces nostras absolutè ad hanc formam, qs eâ solâ non aliâ unquam uti debeamus, sed tradit orandi formam, ad quam reliquae omnes revocari possint.

Oratio Dominica praestat aliis orandi formis. 1. autoritate, 2. brevitate. 3. perfectione. 4. ordine. 5. efficacitate. 6. necessitate, Singula membra probat Bellarm. lib. 1. de bon operib. cap. 4.

Tertull. lib. de orat. cap. 9. vocat orandi disciplinam & cap. breviarium totius Evangelii.

Augustinus Epist. 121. cap. 12. Si per omnia pre-ationum sanctarum verba discurras, nihil invenies, quod non ista Dominica, contine & concludat oratio. Ib. Quamlibet alia verba dicamus, nihil aliud dicimus, quàm in ista Dominica oratione positum est, si rectè & congruente oramus. Chrysost. homil. 14. in Matth. Qui non sic orat, quemadmodum docuit Christus, non est Christi discipulus, quia nec Pater libenter exaudit orationem, quam filius non dictavit. Cog--scit enim, Pater Filii sui sensus & verba, nec suscipit, quae usurpatio humana excegitavit, sed quae sapientia Christi exposuit. *(Pelbartus de Themeswar in de tempore, part. aestivali serm. 29. ex Richardo in l. 4. sent. dist. 15. q. 4. a. 8. docet, quòd oratio Dominica aliis orationi-us omnib sit dignissima & commendabilis ac efficacior propter tria, 1. propter auctoris sublimitatem. 2. propter sensus (verborum) brevitatem. 3. propter petitionis utilitatem. Primô propter autoris sublimitatem vel sanctitatem, quoniam summus omnium Dominus Christus ore suo immediatè illam fecit & discipulos docuit. aliae a. orationes sunt -ditae ab aliis sanctis. Unde August. dicit: Maxima reverentia ab omnibus fidelibus exhibenda est ipsi orationi Dominicae, quoniam ab ipso summo omnium Doctore facta.
