Secundo &c, ac alii nonnulli adserunt. 2. nec ita in hac vita peccata, etiam dum perfectè remittuntur à Deo, deleri, ut nullae eorum in carne superstites maneant reliquiae. 3. nec B. Virginem Deiparam sine peccato originali cōceptam esse, id quod ipse Iesuita Conzen, quod probè observandum est, contra communem sociennorum suorum sententiam (Vid. Bell. l. 4. de amiss grat. c. 15. Suarez in Thom. pag. 3. q. 27. art. 1. Coster. in Christ. Instit. l. 5. Perer. qui Disp. 6. in cap. 3. ad Rom. scribere non veretur, certum esse in Ecclesia Catholicâ, B. Virginem omnis peccati, etiam levissimi ac minimi per omnem vitam fuisse expertem. adde Corn. à Lap. in Lucam p. 25. l. c. Gravinam c. 16. Curr, Triumph. p. 108. alios.) haut dubiè cōcedit, quippe ad quaestionem: An sit homo aliquis, qui nunquam ullum habuer it peccatum, ita in h. l. p. 121 b. respondens cum Augustino, nullum fuisse, esse, futurum, excepto solo CHRISTO, cùm in peccato nati sint omnes. Neque tamen 3. ex eo, quòd peccatorum remissionem quotidie petere iubemur, sequitur, quòd solùm pro culpa s. peccatis, non verò pro omnibus eorumdem poenis Christus satisfecerit, id quod Pontif. docent, ceu videre est apud Bell. l. 4. de poenit. c. 2. § 4. Greg. de Valent. t. 2. in Thom. Disp. 6. q 17. punct. 5. alios. At enim & culpae & poenae relaxationem petimus. Etiam iustus, scribit Conzen in h. l. p. 142. a. semper dicit: dimitte nobis debita nostra, peccatum scil. & paenam peccati, neque tamen hinc sequitur, quòd Christus pro iis non plenariè satisfecerit: disting enim inter acquisitionem, & applicationem: nec subordinata sibi invicem opponenda. At dicat aliquis: Si in Ovat. Domin. petimus, ut Deus peccata nobis nostra remittat, sicuti nos remittimus debitoribus nostris, sequitur, quòd non gratu, propter Christi seil. satisfactionem, nobis remittantur peccata nostra a, sed quod nostra condonatione illam mereamur. Resp. negando consequentiam, Rectè Card. Toletus in c. 11. Luc. p. 653. Cùm debita dimitti petimus, peccata deleri & auferri à nobis rogamus, gratis quidem &sine pretio respectu nostri, non tamen respectu Christi, qui pretium pro nobis solvit peccatorum. Sed instet aliquis, signisicari tamen particular sicut, quod etiam ex parte nostra adsit aliqua causa impulsiva vel meritoria, quá effician us vel mere amur, ut Deus nobis peccata remittat. Resp. Particula ὅτι h. l non est τροπογικὴ, ostendens modum ac regulam, quam Deus in dimittendis peccatis sequatur: multò plura enim debemus & â DEO remitti nobis petimus, quâm alii nobis debent, ceu benè monet Corn. à Lap. in h. l. Nec est αἰτιολογικὴcausalis. Cùm gratis iustificemur, absque ullo operum, nostrorum merito, ceu passim testatur Sc. S. (unde etiam Iesuita Tirinus non malè ad h. l. notat: deprecemini mala, quae vos à tantis bonis consequendis remorari possunt. Primum peccata, ut meritis Christi vobis condonentur. Simeritis Christi condonantur peccata, non, meremur eorum remissionem nostris operibus.) Sed est συμπλεκτικὴ connectensmembrum sequens cum antecedente, ac simul conditionem includens, quam Deus observatam à nobis vult. Adiunxit planè, scribit Cyprianus serm 6. de Oratione Domin. p. 239. & addidit legem, certa nos condittione & sponsione constringens, ut sic nobis dimitti debita postuiemus, secundùm quod & ipsi debitoribus nostris dimittimus. Idem etiam insinuat Salvator noster alibi, uti Matth. 7, 2.Matth. cap. 18, 32. seqq. Marc. 11, 25. 26. Sed iterum aliquis urgeat: ergò promissiones Evangel caesunt conditionales, id quod passim docent Pontificti, nostrates verò negant. Resp. Controversia inter nos ac Pontisicios est de conditione causali ac meritori-, quae praecedat misericordiam divinam Deumque moveat, vel mereatur etiam, ut nobis remittat peccata, nostra. Hîc verò agitur de tali conditione, quâ homines obstringuntur, ne postquam gratis per ac propter Christi meritum idque, solum, Deus ingens illud peccatorum debitum illis remisit, ipsi tanto beneficio abutantur, tanquam privilegio turpitudinis & licentiae. Ideò Christus adiecta hâc clausulâ orantium propositum tanquam publicâ & solenni conditione ac sponsione obstringit, quòd velint inposterum peccata cavere, vitam emendare ac proximo delicta sua remittere ceu exemplum à Christo Matth. 18. propotum luculenter hoc declarat. Cons. omninò hîc B. D. Chenin. in H. E. c. 51 p. 458. Summa, aliud est quaerere de conditione, quâ apud Deum promereamur peccatorum remissionem vel à qua Deus peccatorum remissionem ac gratium suam suspendat; aliud de ea, quae Deum incitet, ur beneficium remissionis gratis factae ipse retrahat & retractet. Sermo igitur non est de causâ meritoria remissionis, sed tum de remissionis coram Deo notâ, tum de qualitate obiecti, tum denique de remotione impedimenti obtainedae remissonis, Vid. B. Par. Co-. in Prior. ep. etri p. 640.)*

*( Μὴ εἰσενέγκης εἰς πειρασόν.ne inducas. i. e. ne permittas nos induci. Tentatio enim hîc intelligitur Diaboli, Matth. 4, 3.1. Thess. 3, 5. & corruptae carnis seu concupiscentiae malae, Iac. 1, 14. ab hâc tentatione nos liberari petimus. Cons. 1. Cor. 10, 13 Quod verò verba activa in Sc. S. de permissione intelligenda quandoque fint docet B. D. Glassius Gr. S. l. 3. p. 256. & 257. exempli loco inter, inter alia affert seqq. dicta, Iob. 1, 21.Ps. 119, 31.Es. 63, 17.Ier. 15, 15.Ioh. 6, 39.1 Cor. 6, 7.)*

*( Μὴ εἰσενέγκης εἰς πειρασόν. Similem ferè Iudaeorum petitionem exillorum Seder Tephilloth refert Lud. Capellus in Spic. ad h. l. Ne porrò quis ex h. l. colligat, quasi Deus causa peccati sit, cùm precemur hîc, ne nos inducat in tentationem, conferendus omninò locus Iacob 1, 14. Explicandum igitur hîc verbum actiyum permissivè. Quomodo etiam alibi adhibetur. Confer Rom. 1, 24. cum Act. 14, 16. it. Deut. 28, 28. cum Hos. 4, 16. 17. Quomodo igitur concurrat Deus ad tentationem, docent haec dicta Ps. 81, 13.1. Cor. 10, 13. Pilcrè S. Augustinus tr. 43. in Ioh. Duae sunt tentationes, Una quae decipit, altera, quae probat. Secundùm eam, quae decipit, Deus neminem tentat. Secundùm eam, quae probat, tentat vos Dominus Deus vester, ut sciat si diligitis eum. Conseratur idem ep. 146. De priori tentatione agit Iacobus cap. 1, 13. & ita quoque tentandi verbum accipitur pro solicitatione ad malum, Matth. 4, 1. Posteriori modo accipitur Gen. 22, 1.Deut. 8, 2.Deut. c. 13, 3. Deus nos tentat ad bonum, est que haec tentatio probationis. Contrà Diabolus, mundus ac caro nostra tentant nos ad malum, est que haec tentatio deceptionis, perditionis ac seductionis. Precamur igitur in praesenti petitione, ne Pater coelestis permittat nos potestati & libidini Satanae, neque sinat, ut ille humani generis hostis suâ tentatione vel in peccatum vel in desperationē nos cōiiciat; quin potiùs potenti suâ dextra nos protegat. Cons. plura apud B. Par. Co-. in Deut. p. 800. it. in Aphor. Pract. tit. Tentationes, nec non B. D. Ronig Cas. Consc. Casu 8.)*

Aug. in Psal. 6. Non nobis expedit esse sine tent ationibus, nec rogaemus Deum, ut non tentemur, sed ut non inducamur in tentationem.

## 6:13
v. 13. ἀπὸ τοὑ πονηροῦ can be referred to the thing, that is to say, from malice. Chrysost. in this place warns, that because of the added article it should rather be referred to the Devil: for it is his to tempt, and he is opposed to the Father, from whom the prayer began. Beza in his annotations expressed the article, translating from that evil. He adds: not so much for the sake of emphasis as to show the false exposition of those who think that here is requested the aversion of evils, that is, of inconveniences and calamities. (Others of the Calvinists agree with Beza. See Piscator in this place, Alstedius in Theol. Catech. p. 838, Abr. Scultetus observ in Matth. cap. 20. p. 27.) Tossanus determines the same, citing Matth. 5. v. 13 Matth. cap. 13. v. 9. Luther's explanation in the Greater Catechism 1. Ioh. 2. v. 13. Eph. 6. v. 16. (It must be known, however, that B. Luther in the Greater Catechism does not exclusively understand by the noun τοὑ πονηροῦ in this place the Devil, but expressly adds: Nevertheless, however, those things also are included together, whatsoever evils can happen to us under the kingdom of the Devil, of which kind are poverty, disgrace, death, and in short, the tragedy of all calamities and miseries, which is manifold and immense on earth. See F. C. p. 532. Not only our own people agree with B. Luther, let B. D. C. Chemnitius Harm. Evangel. Cap. 51. p. 488 and B. D. Meisn. Colleg. Adiaph. Disp. 4. §. 54 be compared, but even Calvin himself and also Bullinger in this place. Furthermore, B. D. Ronig Cas. Cons. Cas. 9 treats more prolixly of the present passage. For us at present it suffices both that πονηρὸν even with the article sometimes denotes an evil thing rather than a person, as is evident from Rom. 12, 9. and Matth. 5, 37. and that Calvin himself and Bullinger favor the exposition of B. Luther. The Syriac rendered it ambiguously, for it has which can be of the feminine gender, and masculine in the emphatic form. Whence it is used sometimes for an evil thing, as Matt. 5, 11. Matt. c. 6, 23. etc., sometimes personally, as Matth. 18, 32. and indeed for the Devil in particular, as Matth. c. 13, 19. 38. 1. Ioh. 2, 13, 14 and elsewhere. The Arab, however, uses the masculine gender The Ethiopian, on the contrary, translates concerning an evil thing, namely, adversities, for he translates that is, from every evil.)

This liberation from every evil, which we ask of God in the 7th petition, will finally be done fully and perfectly on the last day. Looking to which, Blessed Luther, vol. 3, Jena, German, f. 507, writes: There cannot be a true Christian, nor can he recite the Lord's Prayer, who does not desire this day with his whole heart.

That conclusion, For thine is the kingdom etc. is added in all the Greek exemplars, and Theophylact interprets it. It is not held in Latin exemplars, nor is it expounded by Jerome or by any ancient interpreter, perhaps, except for Chrysostom and his abbreviator Theophylact, and also the author of the Imperfect work on Matthew. From this the Papists conclude, that it is not a genuine part of the Gospel. Thus Benedictus Arias Montanus determines, that this clause, although it is held in Greek exemplars, nevertheless is not of the text, but was inserted into the text by some, he attempts to prove this from the fact, that the Greeks even at this day say, that it is permitted only to the Priest to utter those words. For so he is accustomed to respond in the Mass, when the choir has said: but deliver us from evil. Item; that no Latin interpreter makes mention of it, Bellarmine, book 2, on the Word of God, chapter 7, section 9, denies these words are of the text, but that they were added by the Greeks 1. because Tertullian, Cyprian, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine make no mention of these words. 2. The Greeks recite those words in their Liturgy, but they do not contain them with the Lord's Prayer. Maldonatus thinks, that this happened from the custom of the Greeks, to whom it was customary to end prayers with some δοξολογία and praise. I respond 1. Robertus Stephanus found it in a very ancient Greek codex, which was the most ancient outside of one. 2. The Syriac has it. 3. Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius interpret it. 4. Paul 2 Tim. 4, v. 18, rendering the final petition concerning liberation from every evil, adds that clause, to whom be glory for ever. 5. They are words consonant with Scripture, and especially with the thanksgiving of David 1 Chron. 29, v. 11. 6. Because it was long omitted among the Latins, it was not useful for the Church to be moved over that matter, which is utterly offended by novelties.

*(That this δοξολογία is read in all Greek codices, Erasmus testifies in this place, Dietenberger in the glosses, indeed even Cardinal Bellarmine himself, book 2, on the Word of God, chapter 2, last section. The same also concerning all Parisian codices, (except at least one, which however he himself strongly suspects to have been corrected according to Latin exemplars. That this also happened to the Vatican codex, to which Cornelius à Lapide appeals, one can hardly doubt, to whom the custom of the Papists, of correcting all good books according to the mind of the Roman Church, is not entirely unknown.) Franciscus Lucas Brugensis reveals in his notes on the Greek Gospel of Matthew. Robertus Stephanus found this conclusion in a very ancient codex, which he writes was the most ancient outside of one. The same words are also read in the Greek manuscript Eclogues, venerable for their antiquity, in the Nuremberg Library. The Syriac Paraphrase also has this clause, which Fr. Lucas holds undoubtedly to be a most ancient Greek exemplar, and indeed to be held and venerated in the first place. The Arabs and Ethiopians also acknowledge it. Of whom the latter expressly has: the former I omit now the Persian version of the four Evangelists, in which this conclusion is likewise read. Just as also in the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew edited by Münster. Meanwhile, it must not be concealed that this clause is missing in the Arabic version of the four Gospels, which appeared at Rome. But it must be noted that this edition, as was also observed long ago by Casaubon, ρ῾ωμαΐζειν, which also seems to be asserted entirely concerning the Institutions of the Christian religion, which appeared at Paris in the Armenian language, by the study of Petrus Paulus, an Armenian priest. For it is evident from those things which are read in Alphonsus à Castro against heresies, Cassander, Guido in his summary on the heresies of the Bohemians, on the customs of the gentiles, Burchard in his description of the Holy Land, Vitriacus in his History of the Orient, Adam Olearius in his Persian Travels, and others concerning the Armenians and their religion, that they depart in not a few things from the Roman Church, but on the contrary depart closer to the Greeks, who acknowledge this particle. But among the ancients, Chrysostom (which, however much Beza denies it, Erasmus nevertheless confesses, and many Papists confess, such as Franc. Lucas, Maldonatus, Cornelius à Lapide, etc.), Theophylact, Euthymius, and the author of the imperfect work on Matthew expounded this conclusion, as testified by Franc. Lucas in his notes on the Greek Matthew, and also by Maldonatus and Cornelius à Lapide. So that Erasmus is deceived and deceives, quite boldly denying, that it was expounded by any of the ancient interpreters at all, except for Chrysostom and his abbreviator Theophylact. Thomas Aquinas also in his Cat. Aurea reports a beautiful explanation of this place from Chrysostom. It is added that this clause is conformable to Holy Scripture, especially to the thanksgiving of David, 1 Chron. 29, 11. And it is well to be noted that the Apostle 2 Tim. 4, 18, repeating the final petition, adds the conclusion: to whom be glory for ever. Add also Apoc. 5, 13c. 7, 121 Pet. 4, 11

c. 5, 11. The Jesuit Gretser indeed takes exception to this, and says, if on account of the Holy Scripture ought to be considered new, because it was translated from the book of Chronicles, then Hunnius, against whom Gretser disputes there, could by his own cleverness increase the Gospels daily by many parts. But it is one thing to add something to the Gospels from the Old Testament anew against the faith of the Greek Codices; it is another to prove that what the Greek Codices consistently have is in conformity with Scripture. But that it was not expounded by the Latin Fathers, that happened because they discovered it omitted in the Latin Codices: they did not wish, therefore, for the Church to be disturbed over that matter. The account of the Greek Fathers, therefore, must be held as more important here, as those who followed the authentic Greek text, and had the most ancient Codices at hand. Rightly, therefore, let this crown be acknowledged as a genuine part of Canonical Scripture, and indeed here also, and let the Latin Codices be amended by the addition of the same, since as Laurentius Valla well advises in his exposition of the Lord's Prayer, nothing has been added to Canonical Scripture here, but has been taken away by the Latins. Finally, it will not be useless to note here that in the Roman Catechism, which was first published by the decree of the Council of Trent and by the order of Pope Pius V, and afterwards appeared elucidated by the industry of Andreas Fabritius of Liège, Councilor to the Counts Palatine of the Rhine and the Dukes of both Bavarias, part 4, chapter D, page 443, it is expressly said, that divine formula, which Christ the Lord wished to be known to the Apostles and through them to their successors, and to all who would subsequently embrace the Christian religion, contains all the necessary elements of prayer. But in chapter 3, question 1, it is added, there are two principal parts of prayer; petition, and thanksgiving. If now the Lord's Prayer contains all the elements of necessary prayer or supplication, it is certainly required that thanksgiving also be present; but this cannot be shown if that crown is separated from the Lord's Prayer, and cast away as a superfluous part, which is what the Papists otherwise desire. What has been brought forward thus far must be observed against the Papists, some of whom, more modest than the rest, write, that these words seem to have been added by the Greeks, out of pious and solemn custom, just as the same people add to the Angelic salutation: Because you have brought forth our Savior. and to the Psalms: Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit. Thus Cornelius à Lapide in this place. Franciscus Lucas can also be referred to the same, to whom indeed from that, that the particle

let it be omitted in the Latin Bibles, let it not be expounded by Latin commentators, and finally let it not be recited in the Liturgy of the Latin Church, and indeed, as he himself believes, it is likely that this conclusion was added by the Greeks to the text of the Gospel from the Liturgy or some solemn custom, just as the same people annex ὁΤι σωτῆρα &c. to the Angelic salutation. Others, however, assert this as if it were indubitable. Thus Bellarmine, book 1, on the Blessed Eucharist, chapter 6. Cornelius Jansenius in his Commentary on the Harmony of the Gospels, p. 303. Conzen, Maldonatus, Franciscus Haraeus on this passage. Gretser in his defense of Bellarmine, and several others. Among the Reformed, unless you prefer to count him among the Arminians, Hugo Grotius agrees with them, as he likewise presupposes this as certain, and writes that it exhibits the same argument, from which we may learn that not only the Arabic and Latin versions, but also the Syriac was made after the Churches λειτουργία had received a certain form. But if Hugo has no surer argument against the antiquity of the Syriac version than that which he draws from that conjecture and false hypothesis of the Papists, the antiquity of the said version will not be much endangered. But how, I ask, will Grotius also prove the novelty of the Latin version by this argument, when in the Latin Codices, for instance the Vulgate version, and it is of this that we are speaking at present, this clause is not read? Which, however, he himself asserts, against the will of the Papists and the protest of the most ancient Latin Codices. The Arminians also, in their Confession, chapter 14, judge concerning this Epilogue, that it does not necessarily pertain to the substance of the matter in itself. Since the Leiden Censors pass over these words in silence, there is hardly any doubt that they are of the same opinion here as the Arminians. And why not? Since Heinrich Bullinger of Zurich, a Theologian of great authority among the Reformed, in Decade 5, sermon 5, on the Lord's Prayer, writes expressly, that the rashness of those who have not feared to sew their own trifles onto such a divine prayer is to be censured (he is speaking indeed of δοξολγία this) to sew. Let Abraham Scultetus, Observations on Matthew ch. 22 p. 27, also be compared. But Wendelin rightly departs from his associates here, when in his System of Theology, p. 1620, he says thus: To Bellarmine, he says, the clause: For thine is the kingdom &c. seems to be surreptitious. But since all the Greek and Syriac copies have it, and weighty reasons are brought forward in it for obtaining a hearing, we judge that it should not be omitted. But neither should Daniel Chamier be passed over in silence here, who most beautifully [defends] the trustworthiness of the Greek Codices

defends against the Papists regarding this part also, T. 1. Panstr. lib. 12. c. 13. §. 28. et seqq. But we shall return to the Papists, some of whom proceed to such a degree of audacity, that these words trifles, as is the piety of Erasmus, they call them, and indeed they accuse the Greek N. T. of corruption, among other things also on this account, that δοξολογία this is read in Greek Codices, but not in Latin ones. So says Cardinal Bellarmine l. 2. de V. D. c. 7. and the Jesuit Gordon Huntlaeus Epit. controv. 1. c. 12. §. 3. p. 43. Nay, rather the Latin Codices are to be accused of imperfection, and to be amended according to the original Greek text, and the most ancient Codices of this, and these approved by the most ancient Interpreters. Nor is the suspicion of the Papists and Hugo Grotius of great moment, that since this clause is read in the Liturgy of the Greeks, (nay, rather the Liturgies of the Greeks extant today, which are sufficiently ancient, testify to the contrary, as the Blessed Par. shows Confess. Cath. t. 2. p. 118.) it crept from that into the Biblical Codex. For even if it could have happened in one or another Codex, that it should happen in all is not even credible at least. And if they crept into the Greek Codices from some Liturgy, how did it happen that the clause added to the Angelic salutation in the Liturgy by the Greeks did not creep into even a single Codex? Away therefore with that vain conjecture, relying on which H. Grotius wishes even the word Amen, which nevertheless is read in some Latin Codices no less than in almost all Greek ones, and is even expounded by Jerome and Euthymius, to be expunged from the authentic Codex. But also that must be observed against Hug. Grotius, that in the Seder Tephilloth of the Portuguese Jews δοξολογία, something, in some way similar to this, is found: just as Lud. Capell. reports it in Spic. p. 16. Now indeed Grotius himself wishes to note in his notes to Matth. 6, 9. that this formula or the Lord's prayer was not so much conceived by Christ in his own words, as that whatever was praiseworthy in the Hebrew prayers was gathered into it. If therefore this δοξολογία. is also held in Hebrew prayers, it is certainly established more probably according to the stated hypothesis of Grotius himself, that the Savior transferred it from there, than that this crown crept from the Liturgy of the Greeks into the Greek text, and indeed, not into one or another, but into almost all, and those the most ancient Codices. But neither should this be ignored, that the first this fable (so Erasmus himself designates his Annotations in the N. T. in the preface) namely that δοξολογία in the Lord's Prayer from the Liturgy of the Greeks has crept into the authentic text, Erasmus of Rotterdam undertook to argue, whom, although at other times the Papists today do not value highly, sometimes calling him a semi-Christian, sometimes a precursor of heretics, sometimes comparing him to Lucian, sometimes proclaiming him a man of no great faith, (as such judgments of the Papists concerning Erasmus may be read in B. Par. Cons. Cath. vol. 1, p. 19), here however they attribute very much to him, certainly to such an extent that the Jesuit Conzen did not hesitate to transcribe whatever Erasmus patched together on this matter into his Commentary, at least so that they might not be forced to admit that it was omitted in the Liturgy of the Latin Church and the Vulgate version without cause. And from this it also happened that the Latins, Tertullian, Cyprian, Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine omitted the same. Unless we would rather say that the same ones took the Lord's Prayer from Luke, where δοξολογίαν we freely grant that this is not read even in Greek codices, and therefore it was also rightly omitted by the Vulgate there. But someone could urge that since the same Luke Ch. 11, 4. was omitted, from that it is manifest that it is not a genuine part of the sacred Code. I respond: Many other things were omitted or proposed rather briefly by Luke, which are handed down more prolixly in the remaining Evangelists. Therefore, are those also to be expunged in the remaining Evangelists, or called adulterated, because they are not repeated by Luke in the same number of words? By no means! We know that Matthew sometimes proposed the sayings and deeds of Christ more broadly than the remaining Evangelists, whose writings, however, are by no means to be argued of imperfection on account of this, nor is it to be asserted of the Gospel of Matthew that something was added to it by others. I pass over that the third and last petitions themselves were also omitted by Luke according to the opinion of the Papists. Without, however, the suspicion that they crept into Matthew from elsewhere. For although the Greek codices, just as also the Syriac and Ethiopic, and indeed the Arabic of the Roman and Leiden editions, read them, it does not, however, seem likely to Francisco Luca that those petitions belong to this Gospel. And others of the Papists feel the same, as Franc. Toletus on Luke p. 656. a., Corn. à Lap. on Luke, and others.

Thus, indeed, the Papists fight for the integrity of their Vulgate version, so that, provided that this Helen is preserved, they care little whatever may be determined about the sources. But let it suffice for the present to have brought these things forward for the sincerity of the Greek text. Let there also be compared B. D. Glassius Philol. S. p. 149, Dn. D. Walth. H. B. p. 751, B. Par. Exeg. LL, Th. de Scr. S. §. 360, Confess. Cathol. vol. 2, p. 117 seqq., B. D. Helvicus Vindic. LL. Sc. S. p. 33, B. D. R-nig Cas. Consc. p. 192 seqq.

(But from this clause of the Lord's Prayer, an excellent argument can be formed against the Photinians for the true Deity of Christ. To whom the kingdom, power, and glory belong forever, he can be religiously invoked, and consequently is the true and eternal God. But the kingdom, etc., belongs to Christ. Therefore. The major premise is clear, and is evident from the present passage. Socinus, in his Disputation with Franc. David, p. 93, likewise concedes that the minor proposition is sufficiently firm from 2 Pet. 3:13. Apoc. 5:12, 13. Apoc. c. 17:14. c. 19:16. And with Socinus himself admitting it, the Apostle calls the kingdom of G O D also the kingdom of Christ, Eph. 5:5. and consequently the same kingdom belongs to both, the same glory and power, and furthermore the same religious invocation belongs to both. Socinus, however, objects to the major premise, that Christ taught the Apostles what they ought to pray for, not whom they ought to pray to, and that this is evident from the petition Luke 11:1. Resp. Nay, rather the contrary is evident from the parallel passage mentioned. For the disciple was asking the Lord absolutely that he might be willing to teach him and the remaining disciples to pray. Now, however, no one correctly teaches to pray who teaches only what things are to be sought, but not at the same time from whom one ought to seek something, or to whom one ought to direct his prayers, so that he may be certain of being heard. Nor does it pertain more to a prayer pleasing to God that it be observed what it is permitted to seek, than from whom and how. Unless, therefore, Christ had taught this also, he would not have sufficiently shown the legitimate form of praying to the disciple who was asking, a thing which is by no means to be asserted. We perceive, however, here how well the Photinians agree with the Papists. For we saw above that Bellarmine, whom some other Papists also follow, uses the same exception.)

Matth. 5, 37. tum quòd Calvinus ipse ac Bülling. expositioni B. Lutheri faveant. Syr. Porrô ambiguè reddidit, habet enim quod & foemin. generis esse potest, & Masc. in form. Emph Unde etiam modò pro re malâ, uti Matt. 5, 11.Matt. c. 6, 23. &c. modò personaliter, uti, Matth. 18, 32. & quidem pro Diabolo in specie, uti Matth. c. 13, 19.38.1. Ioh. 2, 13, 14 & alibi adhibetur. Arabs tamen Masculinum genus adhibet Aethiops contra de re mala, scil. adversitatibus, vertit enim i. e. ab omni malo.)*

*(Liberatio haec ab omni malo, quam in 7. petitione à Deo petimus, plenè & perfectè demum fiet in die novissimo. Quo respiciens B. Lutherus t. 3. Ienens. Germ. f. 507. scribit: Non potest esse verus Cbristianus, nec recitare or ationem Dominicam, qui non toto corde bunc diem desider at.)

Coronis illa, quia tuum est regnum &c in omnibus Graecorum exemplaribus est adiecta, & interpretatur eam Theophylactus. In Latinorū exemplaribusnō habetur, nec exponitur ab Hieronymo aut ullo fortè interprete antiquo, praeterquam à Chrysost. & eius abbreviatore Theophylacto, nec non auctore operis Imperfecti in Matthaeum. Colligunt hinc Pontificii, non esse eam genuinam Evangelii partem. Sic Bened. Ar. Mont. statuit, banc clausulam, licet in Graecis exemplaribus babeatur, tamen non esse de textu, sed à nonnullis textui insertam, id probare conatur ex co, quòd Graecietiam bodierna die dicunt, Sacerdoti duntaxat licere illa verba proferre. Ita enim respondere solet in Missa, quando chorus dixit: sed libera nos à malo. Item; quod nullus Latinorum Interpretum eius mentionem faciat, Bel. larm. 1. 2. de verbo DEI c. 7. §. 9. verba haec negat esse de textu, sed à Graecis esse addita I. quia Tertull. Cyprian. Ambros. Hieron, August borum verborum nullam faciunt mentionem. 2. Graci in sua Liturgia recitant illa verba, sed cum oratione Dominica non continant. Mal. donatus putat, ex more Gracoram boc accidisse, quibus usitatum preces terminare aliquâδοξολογία& laudatione. Resp. I. Rob. Stephanus in vetuftissimo Cod. Graeco reperit, qui extra unum fuit antiquisfimus. 2. Syrus habet. 3. Chrysostomus, Theophyl. Euthymius interpretantur. 4. Paulus 2. Tim. 4. v, 18. reddens ultimam petitionem de liberatione ab omni malo, clausulam illam addit, cuigloria in secula. 5. sunt verba consona Scripturae, & cumprimis gratiarum aconi Davidis 1. Paral. 29. v. 11. 6. quia apud Latinos diu omissa, non erat utile, Ecelesiam super ea re commoveri, quae novitatibus oppidò offendtur.

*(Quod in omnibus Codd. Grae δοξολογία haec lagatur, testantur Erasmus in h. l. Dietenbergerus in glossis, quin ipse Card. Bellarminus 1. 2. de V. D. c. 2. § ult, Idem quoque de omnibus Codd Parisiensibus, (excepto faltem uno, quem tamen ad Lartna exempla castigatum esse, vebmenter ipse fuspicatur. Id quod etiam Codici Vaticano, ad quem Corn, à Lapide provocat, contigisse, dubitare vix protest, cui mos Pontificiorum, bonos quosque libros ad mentem Eecl. R. castigandi, non penitus ignotus est.) prodit Franciscus Lucas Brug. in notis ad Ev. Matth. Graecum. Robertus Stephanus in vetusti----Codice coronidem hanc reperit, quem extra unum fuisse antiquissimum, scribit. Eadem quoque verba leguntur in Eclogis MSS. Gr. antiquitate venerandis, Bibl. Noribergensis. Habet quoque hanc clausulam Pataphrasis Syriaca, quam Fr. Lucas indubitanter tenet, vetustissimi exemplaris Graeci, & quidem ex primis loco habendum ac vener andum esse. Agnoscunt quoq; Arabs ac Aethiop. Quorū hic expresè habet: ille Omitto iam versionē quatuor Evangelistarum Persicam, in quâ similiter coronis haec leguitur. Quemadm. etaim in Evangelio Matthaei Ebraico à Münstero edito. Interra nec dissimulandum, quòd desideretur haec clausula in Arabica quatuor Evang. versione, quae Romae prodiit. Ast notandum, editionem hanc, ceu pridem etiam à Casaubono observatum est, ρ῾ωμαΐζειν, id quod etiam de Institutionibus Christianae religionis, quae Parisiis Lingu â Armenâ, ftudio Petri Pauli Sacerdotis Armeni prodierunt, omninò adserendum videtur. Constat enim ex iis, quae apud Alphonsum à Castro contra haeres. Cassandrum, Guidonem in sum de haeres. Boëm. de moribus gent. Burchardum in descript. terrae sanctae, Vitriacum Hist. Orient. Adamum Olearium in Itin. Pers. aliisque de Armeniis horumque religione leguntur, quòd non in paucis à Romanâ Ecclesiâ ipsi discedant, contrà verò propiùs à Graecis, qui particulam hanc agnoscunt, abeant. Exposuserunt verò è veteribus coronidem hanc Chrysostomus, (quod ut ut Beza neget, fatetetur tamen Erasmus, fatentur & plurimi Pontificii, uti Franc. Lucas, Maldon. Corn. à Lapide &c.) Theophylactus, Euthymius ac autor operis in Matthaeum imperfecti, tefte Franc. Lucâ in not. ad Matth. Graec. it. Maldonato ac Corn. à Lapide. Ut adeo fallat ac fallatur Erasmus, satis audacter negans, ab ullo prorsus veterum Interpretum, praeterquam à Chrysost. & huius abbreviatore Theophylacto, illam fuisse expositam. Thomas quoque de Aquino in Cat. Aureâ pulcram huius loci explicationem è Chrysostomo refert. Accedit quòd clausula ista Scripturae S. conformis, cum primis gratiarum actioni Davidis, 1. Paral. 29, 11. Ac probè notandum, quòd Apostolus 2. Tim. 4, 18. ultimam petitionem repetens, coronidem addat: c-igloria in secula. Adde etiam Apoc. 5, 13.c. 7, 12.1. Petr. 4, 11.

c. 5, 11. Excipit quidem ad hoc Iesuita Gretserus, dicitque, si propter-apars Scriptura S. novae existimari debet, quia ex libro Paral. hus translatum, tum Hunnius, quem contra disputat ibi Gretserus, pro sua solertia quotidie Evangelia multis partibus augere peterit. Verùm aliud est ex Veteri Testamento aliquid de nove contra Codd. Graecorum fidem Evangeliis addere; aliud, quod Codd. Graeci constanter habent, ut Scripturae conforme probare. Quòd verò à Patribus Latinis eadem non exposita fuit, inde factum, quia in Codd. Latinis omissam deprehenderunt: noluerunt ergo, Ecclesiam super eâ re commoveri. Graecorum igitur Patrum potior habenda hîc ratio, ut qui Graecum authenticum sequuti textum sunt, & antiquissimos Codd. ad manus habuerūt. Rectè proinde genuina pars Scripturae Canonicae, & quidem etiam hîc, coronis haec agnoscitor, ac Latini Codd. eiusdem additione emendantur, cùm ut benè monet Laurentius Valla in expos. Orationis Dominicae, nihil hîc à-r-cis Scripturae Canonicae additum, sed à Latinis detractum. Denique nec illud inutile fuerit hîc notare, quòd in Catechismo Romano, qui ex decreto Concilii Tridentini & Pii V. Pontif. Max. iussu primùm editus, ac postmodum industriâ Andreae Fabritii Leodii, Comitum Palat. Rheni ac utriusque Bavariae Ducum Consiliarii elucidatus prodiit part. 4. c. D. p. 443. expressè dicatur, omnes necessariae precationis numeros continere divinam illam formulam, quam Christus Dominus Apostolis & per illos eorumk 3 suocessores, omnibus deinceps, qui Cbristianam religionem susciperent, notam esse voluit. cap. verò 3. q. 1. subiiciatur, duas esse praecipuas partes orationis; postulationem, & gratiarum actionem. Si iam Oratio Dominica omnes numeros orationis s. precationis necessariae continet, requinitur sanè, ut adsit quoque gratiarum actio; haec verò non poterit ostendi, si ab Orat. Dom. coronis illa sequestretur, & tanquam superflua pars, id quod Pontificii aliàs volunt, abiiciatur. Quae hactenus allata observanda sunt contra Pontificios, quorum aliqui, reliquis modestiores, scribunt, videri baec verba à Graecis fuisse additâ, ex pià & solenni consuetudine, sicut iidem salutationi Angelica addant: Quia tu peperisti Salvatorem nostrum. & Psalmis: Gloria Patri & Filio & Spiritui Sancto. Ita Corn. à Lapide in h. l. Eodem referri Franciscus quoq; Lucas potest, cui quippe ex eo, quòd particula

hac in Latinis Bibliis omittatur, à tractatoribus Latinis non exponatur, in Liturgiâ deni3 Ecclesiae Latinae non recitetur, & quidem, ut ipse credit, iam inde ab Apostolorum temporibus, verisimile sit, coronidem hanc à Graecis ad Evangelii textum fuisse adscriptam ex Liturgiâ aut solenni aliquâ consuetudine, ceu salutationi Angelicae annectunt iidem,ὁΤι σωτῆρα &c. Alii autem, tanquam indubium hoc sit, adservnt. Ita Bellarm. l. 1. de B. O. c. 6. Corn. Iansenius in Cimment. Conc. Evang p. 303. Conzen, Maldonatus, Franc. Haraeus in h. l. Gretserus def. Bell. & alii nonnulli. Quibus ex Reformatis, nisi eurn accensere Arminianis malis, adstipulatur Hugo Grotius, ut qui itidem hoc tanquam certum praesupponit, idemhoc exhibere argumentum scribit, unde discamus, non Arabicam tantùm & Latinam versionem, sed & Syriacam factam esse, post quam Ecclesiarūλειτουργίαformam certam acceperat. At si nullum certius Hugoni suppetit contra versionis Syriacae antiquitatem argumentum, quâm quod ex coniectura istà ac falsa Pontificiorum hypothesi depromit, non multum dictae versionis periclitabitur antiquitas. Sed quomodo, quaeso, Latinae quoque versionis novitatem argumento hoc probabit Grotius, cùm in Codd. Latinis, puta versionis vulgatae & de haec impraesentiarum sermo est, clausula haec non legatur? quod tamen invitis Pontificiis ac reclamantibus Codd. Lat. antiquissimis ipse adserit. Arminiani quoque in Confess. suâ c. 14. de hoc Epilogo iudicant, quòd ad substantiam rei per se haut necessariò pertineat. Quae verba cùm Censores Leidenses silentio praetermittant, vix dubium, quin in eadem cum Arminianis hîc sententiâ sint. Et quî non? cùm Henricus Bullingerus Tigurinus, magnae apud Reform. auctoritatis Theologus, Decad. 5. serm. 5. in Orat. Domin scribat expressè, taxandam; esse illorum temeritatem, qui non veriti sunt tam divinae precationi suas nugas (loquitur verò de δοξολγία hâc) adsuere. Conferatur quoque Abr. Scultetus Obs. in Matth. c. 22. p. 27. Rectè verò à sociennis suis discedit hîc Wendelinus, quando system. Theol. p. 1620. ita: Bellarmino, in quit, clausula: Quia tuum est regnū &c. irreptitia videtur esse. Cùm verò omnia exemplaria Graeca & Syriaca eam habeant, & ponderosae. in ea causae pro impetranda exauditione adducantur, non omittendam eam esse iudicamus. Sed nec tacendus hîc Daniel Chamier est, qui pulcerrimè Codd. Graecorum fidem

contra Pontificios quoad hanc etiam partem defendit T. 1. Panstr. lib. 12. c. 13. §. 28. seqq. At revertemur ad Pontificios, quorum aliqui eò audaciae procedunt, ut verba haec nugas, quae Erasmi pietas est, vocent, quin & N. T. Graecum corruptionis arguant, inter alia & hoc nominee, quòd δοξολογία ist haec &c. in Codd. Graecis legatur, in Latinis verò non. Ita dictus Card, Bellarminus l. 2. de V. D. c. 7. ac Iesuita Gordonus Huntlaeus Epit. controv. 1. c. 12. §. 3. p. 43. Imò potiùs Latini Codd. imperfectionis arguendi, ac iuxta textum Graecum originalem, huiusque Codd. antiquissimos, & hos ab antiquissimis Interpp. approbatos, emendanbi. Nec magni etiam momenti est suspicio Pontificiorum ac Hugonis Grotii, quòd cùm, in Liturgiae Graecorum clausula haec legatur, (imò verò contrarium testantur Liturgiae Graecorum hodie extantes satis antiquae, ceu ostendit B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. 2. p. 118.) ex illâ in Codicem Biblicum irrepserit. Etenim si vel maximè in uno atque altero id potuisset Codice contingere, ut tamen in omnibus id fieret, minimè vel credibile saltem est. Et si ex Liturgiâ quadam in Codd. Graecos irrepserunt, quî factum, quòd clausula salutationi Angelicae in Liturgiâ à Graecis adiecta, ne in unicum quidem Codicem irrepserit? Apage igitur cùm vanâ illâconiecturâ, qua fretus H. Grotius & ipsam vocem Amen, quae tamen in Latinis non minùs quibusdam, quàm omnibus penè Graecis Codd. legitur, quin & ab Hieronymo atque Euthyomio exponitur, è Cod. authentico expungi vult. Verùm & illud contra Hug. Grotium observandum, quòd in Seder Tephilloth Iudaeorum Lusit. δοξολογία, aliqua, huic aliquo modo similis reperiatur: quemadmodum illam refert Lud. Capell. in Spic. p. 16. Iam verò notary vult ipsemet Grotius in notis ad Matth. 6, 9.Formulam hanc s. orationem Dominicam non tam suis verbis à Christo conceptam esse, quàm in eam congestum esse, quicquid in Ebrasrum precibus er at laudabile. Si igitur & haec δοξολογία. in Ebr. precibus habetur, magis sanè iuxta dictam ipsius Grotti hypothesin probabiliter statuitur, quòd inde Salvator transtulerit, quàm quòd è Graecorum Liturgia coronis haec in textum Graecum, & quidem, non unum saltem atque alterum, sed propè in omnes, eosque antiquissimos Codd. irrepserit. Sed nec hoc ignorandum, quòd primus sabulam hanc (ita ipse Erasmus Annotationes suas in N. T. indigitat in praefat.) quòd nempe δοξολογία in Orat. Dominica è Liturgiâ Graecorum in textum authenticum irrepserit, agendam susceperit Erasmus Roterodamus, quem ut ut aliàs Pontificci hodie non magni aestiment, modò Semi Cbristianum, modò baereticorum praecursorem appellantes, modò Luciano cum comparantes, modò virum non magnae fidei proclamantes, (ceu talia Pontificiotum de Erasmo iudicia legenda sit B. Par. Cons. Cath. t. 1. p. 19.) hîc tamen plurimum ei tribuunt, in tantum certè, ut Iesuita Conzen quicquid Erasmus hâc de re consarcinavit, in Comment. suum transcribere non dubitaverit, saltem ne fateri cogantur, quòd in Liturgiá Ecclesiae Latinae ac Vulgatâ versione praeter causam omissa ea sit. Atque hinc etiam factum, quôd Latini, Tertullianus, Cyprianus, Ambrosius, Hieronymus & Augustinus eandem omiserint. Nisi potiùs dicere velimus, quòd iidem ex Lucâ orationem Dom. desumserint, ubi δοξολογίαν hanc nec in Gr. Codd. legi, ultrò largimur, adeoque etiam rectè à Vulg. ibi omissam. Sed posset aliquis urgere, quòd cùm eadem inLuca Cap. 11, 4.omissa fuerit, exinde manifeftum esse, quod non sit genuina Codicis sacri pars. Resp. Multa alia omisla vel breviusculè proposita sunt à Luca, quae in reliquis Evangeliftis prolixiùs traduntur. Ergone & illa in reliquis Evangelistis expungenda, vel adulterina dicenda, quia à Luca non totidem verbis repetuntur? Minimè! Novimus, quòd Matthaeus Christi dicta & facta aliaquando latius proposuerit, quàm reliqui Evangelistae, quorum tamen scripta propter hoc minimè imperfectionis arguenda, nec de Matthaei Evangelio adserendum, quòd aliquid ab aliis illi adiectum. Taceo, quòd à Luca ipsae quoque tertia & ultime petitiones ex sententià Pontificiorum omissae sint. Absque tamen suspicione, quod aliunde eae in Matthaeum irrepserint. Ut ut enim Codd. Graeci, quemadmodum etiam Syrus ac Aethiops, quin & Arabs Romanae ac Leidensis editionis eas legant, non tamen fit verisimile Francisco Lucae, petitiones illas huius esse Evangelii. Idemq; sentiunt & alii pontificii, uti Franc. Toletus in Lucam p. 656. a. Corn. à Lap. in Lucam, alii.

Ita nempe pro Vulgatae suae versionis integritate Pontificii pugnant, ut, modò Helena ista servetur, parùm curent, quicquid etiam de fontibus statuartur. Sed haec pro textûs Graeci sinceritate attulifse in praesens sufficiat. Conferantur quoque B. D. Glassius Philol. S. p. 149. Dn. D. Walth. H. B. p. 751. B Par. Exeg. LL, Th. de Scr. S. §. 360. Confess. Cathol. t. 2. p. 117. seqq. B D. Helvicus Vindic. LL. Sc. S. p. 33. B. D. R-nig Cas. Consc. p. 192. seqq.

*(Potest verò ex hâc clausulá Orat. Domin. egregium formariarg. contra photin. pro verâ Christi Deitateh. m. Cui competit regnum, potentia & gloria in seoula, ille religiosè invocari potest, & per consequens est verus & aeternus Deus. Atqui Christo competit regnum &c. E. Maior clara est, & patet ex praesentiloco. Minorem propos. Socinus in Disp. cum Franc. David. p. 93. itidem concedit satis firmam esse ex 2. Petr. 3, 13. Apoc. 5, 12. 13.Apoc. c. 17, 14.c. 19, 16. eodemque Socino fatente, Apostolus regnum D E I etiam Christi regnum vocat, Eph. 5, 5. & per consequens utriusque idem regnum est, eadem gloria & potentia, ac porrò eadem utrique religiosa invocatio competit. Excipit verò Socinus ad maiorem, Christum docuisse Apostolos, quid orare, non quem orare debeant, idg 3 patere ex petitioneLuc. 11, 1. Resp. Imò verò contrarium patet ex dicto loco parallelo. Nam absolutè rogabat Dominum discipulus, ut docere ipsum ac reliquos Discipulos velti precari, Iam verò nemo rectè docet orare, qui petenda saltem docet, non vero sumul, à quo quis aliquid petere, vel ad quem preces suas dirigere debeat, utde exauditione certus esse queat. Nec magis ad Orationem Deo gratam pertinet, ut observetur, quae petere liceat, quàm à quo & quomodo. Nisi igitur Christus & hoc docuisset, minimè sufficienter legitimam orandi formam petenti discipulo ostendisset. id quòd minimè adserendum. Deprehendimus verò hîc, quàm benè conveniat Photinianis cum Pontificiis. Vidimus enim suprà, quòd Bellariminus, quem alii quoque Pontificii nonnulli sequuntur, eadem exceptione utatur.)*

## 6:14
v. 14. Τὰ παραπΤώμα-α, are lapses, i.e., sins and injuries by which our neighbors have harmed us, having lapsed from the straight course of life from παραπίπΤω.

Amen. 1. It is the seal of the Father promising. 2. The testimony of Christ subscribing. 3. The suffrage of the Church consenting. 4. The desire of the one praying.

Latin:

v. 14. Τὰ παραπΤώμα-α, sunt lapsus i. e. peccata & iniuriae, quibus nos laeserunt proximi, lapsi in recto vitae cursu â παραπίπΤω.

Amen. 1. est Patris promittendis sigillum. 2. Christi subscribentis testimonium 3 Ecclesiae consentientis suffragium. 4. Orantis desiderium.

## 6:16
v. 16. ὅταν νηστεύητε &c.) Concerning the right institution of fasting, and also concerning the custom of fasting once received, see the singular dissertations of the blessed D. Höpfner and D. Calixtus. Add against the pontiffs the blessed Pareus, Conf. Cath. vol. 4 p. 950. seqq. with the blessed D. Chemnitz, Exam. Concil. Trid. part 4. the blessed D. Gerlach, vol. 2. Disp. 26. In this place it is at least pleasing to note the ingenuous confession of the Jesuit Salmeron, vol. 8. tr. 10. p. 81, writing: Fasting of itself does not have goodness, but in order that it may become honest and praiseworthy, it has need of being adorned by some just and praiseworthy cause. But what is a just cause for fasting is shown elsewhere. Notably the blessed D. Quistorpius in this place: To fast, so that the body may obey the mind for the duties of piety, is a holy work; to fast, so that you may be held as holy, is hypocrisy; to fast, so that you may increase your wealth, is avarice; to fast, so that you may be healthier in body, is medicine. Cyprian in the sermon on fasting: To the sweats of fasts, praise importunately inserts itself, and penetrating the soul with most subtle stings, while it softens, it exalts; while it anoints, it pricks; it turns virtue into hypocrisy, it perverts things well begun. But concerning fasting, one may also consult the blessed Pareus, Aphor. Pract. title fasting. The blessed D. Baldus, Cas. Consc. book 2. c. 14. also the Lord D. Quenstedt, my singularly beloved kinsman in inaugural public lecture, where the curious reader will find many things not unworthy of note. Here one must strive for brevity.)

Μὴ γίνεσθε ὥασερ ὑωοκρ. σχυτρωπόι. Syr. do not be atr ati, clothed in black garments. Hence idolatrous priests are called כמורים: for in mourning they are accustomed to put on black garments. *(That through frequent fasts a man also becomes dark according to the opinion of the Jews, Buxtorf shows, Lex Talm. p. 234. It seems, however, by the judgment of the Syrian that our Savior is not only looking at the dark countenance of the Pharisees, but also criticizing their dark clothing. It is known, indeed, that not only in the present time among certain peoples is the dark color and dark clothing held as foul and sad (as Schickard reports concerning the Turks in Tarich. p. 14.) But already long ago also they used black garments almost only in mourning. This is evident concerning the Greeks from Artemid. book 2. c. 3, concerning the Romans from Paulus the Jurist book 2. R. S. cap. 21. add. Dempster, Paral. to book 4. Antiq. Rom. Rosin. c. 4. Whence also those in black were once removed from banquets, as perhaps something will be advised concerning this matter at Matth. 22, 12. Furthermore, if we look here at the text, the Savior especially taxes this in the Pharisees, that, so that they may testify to all their more frequent fasts and their austere life, they obscure their faces, with their natural brightness and color as if exterminated and extinguished, but on the contrary having summoned a certain squalor and sordid horror of countenance, which might testify to their fasts, as likewise the Jesuit John de Pineda explains the present place, Com. in c. y. Iob. p. 364. Furthermore, that something similar to this command of Christ is found in the books of the Jews, Capellus teaches, Spicil. p. 16.)*

Σκυθρωπὴς is said, as if ὁ σκυθρὸς τοὺςὦπας i.e. bearing an angry or sad countenance, σκύθεσθαι is to be angry.

ἈΦανίζουσιν they disfigure their faces i.e. the brightness of their faces. For thus it is used a little later in v. 19 & 20. Hom οδ. Τ. uses the word ἐ αρεσθζ in this way. μηκἑΤι νδν Χρόα καλὸν ἐναίρεο. The Scholiast explains it as ἀΦάνιζε, which is a most suitable word. Casaub in notes.

Christ speaks here of fasting, undertaken as a private devotion, but not of a public fast.

Isocrates to Demonicus Ἔθιζε σεαυΤὸν εἰναι μἡ σκύθρωπον ἀλλὰ σύννουν, δἰ ἐκεῖνο μεὴ γδ ἀυθάδης Διὰ Τ῭ Τοῦ-ο Φρόνιμ´ος εἶναι δόζεις. Accustom yourself not to a sternness of countenance, but to gravity. For the former carries with it stubbornness, but the latter indeed prudence.

Xenophon ἰλαραὶ Τ῭ ἄνΤι σκυθρωπῶν ἦσυι. With a sad countenance placed, they were joyful. Luc. 24. v. 17. the disciples going to Emmaus were σκυθρωπὸι certainly not with a sullen countenance, but a sad one. Gen. 40 v. 7. Τὶ ὅΤι -ὰ πξόσωπα ἡμῶν σκυθρωπὠ. Dan. 1. v. 10. εἴδη -ὰ Πρόσωτῑα ὑμῶν σκυθρωπά.

Latin:

v. 16. ὅταν νηστεύητε &c.) De Ieiunio rectè instituendo, tum quoque de more ieiunandi quondam recepto Vid. Dessert. singulares Bb. D. Höpfneri ac D. Calixti. add. contra pontif. B. Par. Conf. Cath. t. 4 p. 950. seqq. cumpr. B. D. Chemn. Exam. Concil. Trid. part. 4. B. D. Gerlach. T. 2. Disp. 26. Hocloco saltem placet annotare Confessionem ingenuam Iesuitae Salmeronis, t. 8. tr. 10. p. 81. scribentis: Ieiunium per se bonitatem non habet, sed ut fiat honeslum & laudabile, opus habet, aliqua iustâ & laudabili causâ cohonestaric Quae verò iusta causa sit ieiunii, alibi ostenditur. Notanter B. D. Quistorpius in h. l. Ieiunare, ut corpus animo ad pietatis munia obtemperet, sanctum opus est; ieiunare, ut sanctus habearis, hypocrisies est; ieiunare, ut rem augeas, avaritia est; ieiunare, ut corpore rectiùs valeas, medicina est. Cypr. in serm. de Ieiun. Ieiuniorum sudoribus laus importuna se ingerit & subtilissimis aculeis animam penetrans dum emollit, extollit; dum ungit, pungit; virtutem in hypocrisin vertit, beneg 3 inchoatapervertit. Inaug. lect. publ. ubi satis multa Lector curiosus inveniet, notatu non indigna. Hîc brevitati studendum.)*

Inde Sacerdotes idololatrici dicuntur כמורים: in luctu enim solent nigrae vestes indui. *(Per ieiunia quoque frequentia hominem Iudaeorum sententiâ atrum fieri, ostendit Buxtorff. Lex Talm. p. 234. Iob. p 364. Porrò simile quid huic Christi mandato in Iudaeorum libris inveniri, docet Capellus Spicil. p. 16.)*

## 6:17
v. 17. Anoint your head i.e. flee hypocrisy and the external boasting of fasting, for Christ speaks of the custom of that time, in which they were accustomed to use anointings in joy. Psal. 23. v. 5. Judith, about to set out to Holofernes, anointed her face. See Hieron. in this place.

*(The following places of Holy Scripture contribute to this Iudith c. 10, 3.Iudith c. 16, 10.Ruth. 3, 3.Ps. 23, 5.Ps 2, 11Eccles. 9, 8.Amos 6, 6.Luc. 7, 46.2 Sam. 12, 20. Sam c. 11, 2. and add concerning Anointing and anointments B. Par. Harm Evang p. 47. 48. ic 8, Dn. Dilh. t. I. Disp. Acad also Abs Scultetum obs in Matth c. 20. Ioh. Brodaeum 1. 4. Mise. c 5. Marc Donatum Dilucid ad Sueton, c. 27. Thom, Gatak, advers Miscell p. 349. Bochius and Lorinus in Psol 23. Sanctius in Cant Cant. p. 42. In particular concerning the Chrism given by the Pontiff, as they say, Claud Esponcaeus, Theolog. Paris. Adpend Comm. ad Timoth. Therefore our Savior looks in these words: Anoint your head, to a rite especially customary in Palestine, where on feast days they are accustomed to anoint the head. He commands so much, that when we fast, we should show ourselves cheerful and festive, as Jerome teaches in this place, and here we should conceal our fasting, rather with joy, than that we should make it publicly known with a sad countenance and seek its praise among men. For just as a manifest treasure is quickly spent; so also any virtue whatsoever, when it has become known or has been published, will be destroyed. For just as wax is melted from the face of the fire, so also the soul is emptied by praises, and loses the rigor of virtues, Saint Syncletica said not unwisely, as is reported in the lives of the Fathers, book 5, booklet 8, n. 19.

*(But we can gather from the present passage that some thing, which is indifferent in itself, can become damnable when abuse is added, that is, if either a spiritual and divine operation is attributed to it, or it is employed at an inconvenient time. Thus fasting is in itself lawful and indifferent: indeed it also merits praise, Daniel 10, 3 not lacking its utilities, provided it is undertaken in a due manner and for a due end, if however anyone should wish to fast with this intention, that he may be glorified by men; as the Pharisees once fasted for this end, and the Papists today, or should persuade himself that his fasting contributes to the expiation of faults and satisfaction for sins, that which the Papists, see Petrus à Soto in ads. sid. Cathol. p. 49. Thomas Aquinas 2. 2. q. 147. art. 1. Azor. t. 1. Instit. Mor. l. 7. c. 14. q. 3. Bell. l. 2. de B. O. c 11. and others teach, it becomes damnable. Thus to anoint the head and also the remaining members of the body with oil for the strengthening of the powers (for the brain, cold by nature, is refreshed by the fragrant odor and heat of ointments, as Plutarch notes in Isis) and thus to be of a cheerful mind, to anoint is a thing in itself indifferent, and therefore not illicit, whence also Christ commanded it here, and he himself admitted the anointing Matth. 26, 7. if however such anointing is employed out of luxury, or if anyone at that time wishes to be cheerful and to anoint himself with oil or ointments to declare joy, when common misery requires commiseration, he is deservedly reproved. To which the passage Amos 6, 6. pertains. In sum: Use has praise, abuse has crime.)*

Latin:

v. 17. Unge caput tuum i. e. fuge hypoerisin & externam ieiunii iactantiam, loquitur enim Christus de more illius temporis, quo soliti fuere uti unctionibus in laetitia. Psal. 23. v. 5. Iudith ad Holofernem profectura unxit faciem suam. Vid. Hieron. h. l.

*(Faciunt huc seqq. loca Sc. S. Iudith c. 10, 3.Iudith c. 16, 10.Ruth. 3, 3.Ps. 23, 5.Ps 2, 11Eccles. 9, 8.Amos 6, 6.Luc. 7, 46.2 Sam. 12, 20. Sam c. 11, 2. ac adde de Ung. & uncti. B. Par. Harm Evang p. 47. 48. ic 8, Dn. Dilh. t. I. Disp. Acad it. Abs Scultetum obs in Matth c. 20. Ioh. Brodaeum 1. 4. Mise. c 5. Marc Donatum Dilucid ad Sueton, c. 27. Thom, Gatak, advers Miscell p. 349. Bochius ac Lorinus in Psol 23. Sanctius in Cant Cant. p. 42. In specie de Chrismate Pentif dacto, ùt loquuntur, Claud Esponcaeus, Theolog. Paris. Adpend Comm. ad Timoth. Respicit igitur Salvator noster verbis istis: Vegecaput tuum, ad ritum in Palestinà cumprimis usitarum, ubi diebus sestis solent ungere caput. Pracipitg 3 adeò, ut quando ieiunamus, lae & festivos nos monftremus, docente Hieron. in h. l, atque hic ieiunium nostrum dissimulemus, potiùs laetitia, quàm ut tristi vultu illud publicè notum faciamus atque eius laudem apud homines quaeramus. Sicut enim thesaurus manifeftus citò expenditur; ita & virtus quaelibet cùm innotuerit vel publicata fuerit, exterminabitur Scut enim cera solvitur à facie ignis, ita & anima laudibus exinamitur, & amittit virtutum rigorem, non inscitè dixit S. Syncletica, quemadmodum proditur in vit. Pacrum l. 5. libello 8 n. 19.)*

*(Colligere verò ex praesenti loco possumus, quòd res aliqua, quae per se adiaphora est, possit fieri damnabilis, cùm abusus accedit, h. e si vel spiritualis ac divina operatio illi tribuatur, vel tempore incommodo adhibeatur. Ita ieiunium per se licitum & adiaphorum est: imò & laudem meretur, Daniel 10, 3 non carens quippe suis utilitatibus, modò debito modo & fine suscipiatur, si quis tamen hâc intentione ieiunare velit, ut ab hominibus glorificetur; ceu Pharisaei hoc fine olim ieiunabant, ac hodie Pontificii, vel sibi persuadeat quòd ieiunium suum faciat ad culparum expiationem & satisfactionem pro peccatis, id quod Pontificii, vid Petrus à Soto in ads. sid. Cathol. p. 49. Thomas de Aquino 2. 2. q. 147. art. 1. Azor. t. 1. Instit. Mor. l. 7. c. 14. q. 3. Bell. l. 2. de B. O. c 11. & alii docent, damnabile fit. Sic oleo caput ac reliqua etìam corporis membra ad virium confortationem (cerebrum enim naturâ frigidum fragranti unguētis odore ac calore recreatur, notante Plut. in Iside) atque adeò laeto esse animo, ungere est res per se adiaphora, adeoq; non illicita unde etiem Christus hîc mandavit, ipseque unctionem admisit Matth. 26, 7. si tamen ex luxuriâ adhibeatur talis unctio, vel si quis illo tempore laetari & ad laetitiam declarandam oleo sive unguentis se inungere velit, quo communis miseria commiserationem requirit, is meritò reprehenditur. Quo facit locus Amos. 6, 6. Summa: Usus habet laudem, crimem abusus habet.)*

## 6:18
v. 18. Reward in this place is not reward of merit but gratuitous compensation arising from the liberal promise of GOD, by which he wishes to remunerate true repentance, which reveals itself through fasting and other signs. Compare Matth. 6. v. 46. with Luke v. 32. by the words he has received his reward v. 16. nothing else is understood, than that the Pharisees fast in vain.

Therefore by the force of the opposites through the words, The Father will reward you, it is indicated, that the pious do not fast in vain.

*( Ἐν τῶ φανερῶ Beza testifies that these words are not read in all the ancient codices. His opinion is confirmed both by the fact that Franc. Lucas reveals that the same are missing in all the Parisian codices, of which there were sixteen; and by the fact that neither the Syriac, whose version was nevertheless adorned from a most ancient codex, reads them; and finally by the fact that neither the Greek Eclogues of the MSS. Bibl. Norib. have them. Thus, neither does the Vulgate Interpreter read them. Yet many printed Greek codices show the same today, just as Erasmus also found them in Greek MSS. codices. What of the fact that Origen also and Chrysostom had already read the same in their own time in Greek codices, when they explain them here, unless one wishes to say that they repeat them from the preceding. Thus the Arabic Interpreter of both editions, i.e., the Roman and the Leiden, renders the words said here (for it is expressly read i.e., manifestly, openly.) likewise the Ethiopian, which similarly as in v. 4 and 6 has i.e., manifestly. Similarly, other interpreters read this particle in the present place, such as the French, Spanish, Italian, English, B. Luther, Erasmus. Indeed, not even Beza himself thought it should be moved in this place, since they respond excellently to the antithesis. Nor is t-. to be inferred from this as a corruption of the authentic text, which some Papists wish, but at least a varying reading, which we willingly grant is given in the Bibles: but it does not follow at all from there that the text is also corrupted. Concerning which matter see B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. 2. p. 104. B. D. Glassius Philol. S. page 139.)*

Latin:

v. 18. Merces h. l. non est merces meriti sed gratuita compen satio ex liberali DEI promissione orta, quâ veram poenitentiam, quae per ieiunium & alia signa sese prodit, remunerari velit. Confer Matth. 6. v. 46. cum Luc. v. 32. per verba receperit mercedem suam v. 16. nihil aliud intelligitor, quàm frustra Pharisaeos ieiunare.

Ergò vi oppofitorum per verba, Pater reddet tibi, indicatur, pios non frustra ieiunare.

*( Ἐν τῶ φανερῶ Verba haec in omnibas vetustis Codd. non legi, testatur Beza. Cuius sententiam etiam confirmat tum quòd Franc. Lucas prodit, eadem in omnibus Parisiensium Codd. quorū sedecim fuerunt, desiderari; tum quòd nec Syrus, cnius tamen versio ex antiquissimo Codice adornated fuit, legit; tum deniq; quòd nec Eclog. Graecae MSS. Bibl. Norib. illa habēt. Sic nec Vulggatus Interpres legit. Exhibent tamen eadem hodie multi Codd. Graeci excusi, sicuti etiam Erasmus in Codd. MSS. Graecis illa invenit. Quid quod Origenes quoq; & Chrysostomus eadē iamtum fuo tempore in Gr. Codd. lagerint, cùm hîc explicent, nisi quis dicere velit, quòd ex superioribus repetant. Sic reddunt hîc dicta verba Interpres Arabs utriusq; editionis h. e. Romanae ac Leidensis (expressè enim legitur i. e. manifestè, palam.) item Aethiops, qui pariter ut v. 4. ac. 6. habet i. e. manifestè. Similiter particulam hanc praesenti loco legunt Interpp. alii, uti Gallus, Hispanus, Italus, Angl. B. Lutherus, Erasmus. Quin nec ipse Beza hoc loco eam movēdam hîc putavit, cùm egregiè antithesi respondeant. Neq; t-. hinc textus authentici corruptio colligenda, quod Pontisicii nonnulli volunt, sed saltem varians lectio, quam in Bibliis dari, libenter largimur: minimè v. inde sequitur, quòd textus quoque corruptus sit. Quâ de re Vid. B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. 2. p. 104. B. D. Glassius Philol. S. pag 139.)*

## 6:19
v. 19. Θησαυροὶ ἐ᾽πὶ τῆς γῆς are earthly treasures, which are accustomed to be collected from earthly things and stored in earthly places. Θησαυρὸς from ἄυριον tomorrow time and --Θημι I place, hence Θησαυρὸς laid up for tomorrow.

Σῆς Βρῶσις It seems to be ἓν δ-ὰ δυοῖν for it is nothing else than σῆς Βρώσκουσα, whence garments σηΤόΒρω-α Iob. 13, 28. iac. 3. z. thus Casaubon. In the Talmudic treatise which is called Baba Bathra chapter 1. King Mombaz (called Monabazus by Josephus) was squandering his treasures and those of his fathers. Having been warned about this matter by friends, he replied: My fathers stored up treasures below, i.e., in the earth. I above, i.e., in heaven. They stored up in a place where the hand dominates, I store up in a place where the hand does not dominate. They stored up treasures of money, I of the soul. They stored up that which brings forth no fruit, I that which brings forth fruit. They for others, I for myself. *(B. Hacksp. presents the Hebrew words from the Talmud in the treatise on the utility of reading Rabbinic Scripture, annexed to Lipmann c. 3. p. 439. Moreover, that Mombaz (or rather Monbas) was King, son of Helena from the lineage of the Hasmonean Priests, as is held in the book Caphtor. 1. 119. Conformably, however, to the said King, Chrysostom: What, he exclaims, Is it not folly to leave behind there that from which you are about to depart, and not to send ahead there, to which you are about to go? Treasure up where you have a fatherland. Cyprian also beautifully says in his sermon on Works and Alms: The inheritance is placed in safety, which is kept with God as its guardian. Manna reserved in private houses rotted, but when stored in the Lord's threshing floor it remained unharmed; thus, things which men collect only for private uses perish, but those which are contributed for divine worship and the sustenance of the poor, their fruit remains forever. See B. Par Harm. Ev. p. 635. a.)*

The Syrian calls the treasure from the root which signifies to blind, to make blind, whence blind, because the treasures of this world blind the eyes of men.

The warning of Christ concerning not gathering treasures on earth must be understood not ἁπλῶς i.e., absolutely, as if that affection and that study were also prohibited by which one moderately and lawfully seeks wealth, so that he may then honestly sustain himself and his own with them, and also be able to succor a needy neighbor at some time—for such a prohibition would be contrary to the doctrine of the Apostle 2. Cor. 12, 14.—but the mandate of the Savior must be accepted συγκριτικῶς i.e., comparatively. Namely, that earthly treasures are not to be sought first or primarily, but heavenly ones. Compare v. 33. And if there is perhaps a fear that while you seek these, you might make a loss of those, rather these, the earthly ones, are to be neglected and avoided. And hence the preposterous piety of the Photinians is by no means to be approved, which, while displaying it, they simply establish that every, and thus also the most moderate study of riches themselves is avarice, and that hence it is in no way permitted for a Christian to seek riches, as the minister of that sect of the Church, Christoph. Osterodus, explains the mind of the Photinians to us in Instit. Germ. c. 31. p. 229. where he defines avarice, prohibited in the holy letters, especially in the tables of the new covenant, as being a desire which requires more than the necessity of our life demands. He urges especially the following places Luc. 12, 15.1. Tim. 6, 9. 10.Matth. 6, 23. but something will be advised concerning each in its own place. For the love of brevity, we remit the reader to B. D. Fewrb. both in Anti Ostor. Disp. 29. and in the second Syntagma of Sacr. Disquis. p. 242. seqq. B. D. Stegmann. Photinianismi Disp. 55. quaest. 6. Dn. D. Calov. Socin. Proflig. p. 307. seqq. Meanwhile, may it be far from us that we should ever wish to undertake the patronage of avarice properly so called, but rather we consider it to be fled worse than a dog and a snake, as persuaded not only by our Savior with the holy choir of the Apostles and other Doctors of the Church, but even by the Heathens themselves, as below at 1. Tim. 6, 10. Some very grave warnings about avoiding avarice will be brought forward. This alone is to be noted for the present, that those little beasts, which bring great damage to riches and things, are small not only in bulk, but also in name (for the moth, which destroys garments, is called in Greek σὴς; that which destroys wood, δῆξ,; that which destroys horn, ἴψ;; that which destroys the vine, ἴξ;; that which destroys fruits, πρῶξ;; that which destroys the fig, ψὼν): let us therefore consider it shameful and beneath our dignity to cling to those things which not only powerful enemies seek with fire and sword, but which even the most contemptible little beasts can devour and snatch away from us. Furthermore, even long ago, a place seemed to favor the vow of poverty to certain heretics, as Augustine reveals, ep. 89 to Hilary. But against the aforementioned heretics, and their followers today, the mendicant monks, must be opposed, besides the Pauline saying brought forward above, both the utterances and warnings of Holy Scripture, Prov. 6, 6.Sirac. 25, 5.1. Tim. 5, 8. and approved examples Gen. 41, 48. 49.Ioh. 6, 12.c. 12, 6.Act. 11 29. In what sense, however, Christ forbids storing up in this place, Cardinal Toletus explains not badly, when in his Commentary on chapter 12 of Luke, p. 746, he says thus: What this storing up is, is explained by Paul in 1 Tim. 6. They who wish, he says, to become rich, fall into the snare of the Devil, but those are they who intend nothing else than to acquire and accumulate riches, proposing this to themselves as an end, whom David expressed in Ps. If riches abound &c. and a little later: therefore riches are not condemned, nor are the rich bound to cast away riches, but not to set their heart upon them, nor to propose them to themselves as a principal end, by serving them, and again: he therefore who gathers riches for the uses of his own and his family and children provides and preserves, so that he may distribute them in their times for the necessity of those emerging and for an honest reason, does not store up in such a way that he cannot be rich according to God.

Furthermore, from the fact that in this place it is commanded to us not to lay up treasures on earth, the Papists ineptly infer Free Will (namely in spiritual matters). No one, writes the Jesuit Maldonatus on this passage, is so insane as to say that God commands us to do things which we cannot do. They urge, above all, both Maldonatus and also Conzen, that in this place in certain codices it is read μὴ θέλητε Do not. Christ would not command, says Conzen, unless to will and not to will were in the power of those who are able, that is, the free. But, even if this reading μὴ θέλητε were to be admitted in the highest degree, which is nevertheless destitute of the authority of Greek codices—of which they themselves collated sixteen Parisian ones, to omit those which Erasmus and Beza consulted—which neither the Syrian nor the Arab nor the Ethiopian, indeed not even the Greek interpreters approve, there is nevertheless no consequence which the Jesuits construct from this: God commands that we will, therefore by our own and natural powers we are able to will spiritual goods. Indeed, rather, that statement of Augustine from De Gratia et Libero Arbitrio, chapter 16, is to be approved: It is certain, he writes, that we will when we will, but He makes it so that we will the good, of which it is said, It is God who works in us both to will and to perform. But how God rightly demands from us what we are not able to perform by natural powers is shown in the Coll. Isag. p. 603.)*

Latin:

v. 19. Θησαυροὶ ἐ᾽πὶ τῆς γῆς sunt thesauri terreni, qui ex terrenis rebus colligi & in terrenis locis recondi solent. Θησαυρὸς ab ἄυριονcrastinum tempus &--Θημιpono, hinc Θησαυρὸςin cnastinum repositam.

Σῆς Βρῶσις Videtur esse ἓν δ-ὰ δυοῖν nihil n. aliud est, quam σῆς Βρώσκουσα, unde vestimenta σηΤόΒρω-αIob. 13, 28. iac. 3. z. ita Cafaubonus. In tractatu Thalmudieo, qui Baba Bathra vocatur cap. 1. Mombaz Rex (Iosepho dictus Monabazus) prodigebat thesauros suos & patrum suorum. Monitus bac de re amicis respondit: Patres mei recondiderunt thesauros infra i. e. in terra. ego supra i. e. in caelo. Illirecondiderunt in loco ubimanus dominatur, ego recondo in loco ubí non dominatur manus. Illi recondiderunt thesauros pecuniae, ego anima. Illi recondiderunt quod nullum fructum profert, ego quod fructum profert. Ilti aliis, ego mihi. *(Verba Ebraea ex Talmud sistit B. Hacksp. tr. de util. lect. Script. Rabb, Lipmanno adnexo c. 3. p. 439. Fuit autem Mombaz ille (vel Monbas potiùs,) Rex filius Helenae ex genere, Hasmonaeorum Sacerdotum, ut habetur in lib. Caphtor. 1. 119. Conformiter autem dicto Regi Chrysostomus: Quae, exclamat, stultitia, illic relinquere unde exiturus es, & non illic praemittere, quo iturus es? Thesauriza, ubi patriam habes. Pulcrè quoq; Cyprianus serm. de Op. & cleemos. In tuto haereditas ponitur, quae Deo custode servatur. Manna in privatis aedibus reservata computruit, sed in aream Dominicam reposita illaesa mansit, sic quae homines ad privatos tantùm usus colligunt, pereunt; quae verò ad cultum divinum & pauperum alimoniam conferuntur, eorum fructus in aeternum manet. Vid. B. Par Harm. Ev. p. 635. a.)*

Thesaurum Syrus vocat à rad. quod significat exoculare, excaecare, unde coecus, quia thesauri huius mundi excae canthominum oculos.

*(Intelligendum autem Christi monitum, de Thesauris in terrà non colligendis, nonἁπλῶς s. absolutè, quasi etiam ille affactus Illudq; studium sit prohibitum, quo quis moderate, ac legitimè querit opes, ut tum se suosq; honestè sustentare iis, tum quoq; proximo egenti succurrere aliquando possit, talis n. prohibitio contraria esset doctrinae Apostoli 2. Cor. 12, 14. sed accipiendum Salvatoris mandatum est συγκριτικῶς s. comparatè. Quòd nempe non primò vel potissimùm sint quaerendi thesauri terreni, sed coelestes. Conf. v. 33. Et si metus fortè sit, ne dum hos quaeris, illorum iacturam facias, potiùs hos, terrenos, esse negligendos ac vitandos. Atq; hinc minimè approbanda praepostera Photinianorum pietas est, quàm ostentantes simpliciter statuunt, quòd omne, & sic etiam modemtissimipsarum opum studium sit avaritia, quòdg 3 hinc nullo modo liceat Christiano opes quarere, ceu Photinianorum mentem ita nobis exponit Ecclesiae illius secte minister Christoph. Osterodus Instit. Germ. c. 31. p. 229. ubi avaritiā in sactis litteris, praesertim in novi foederis tabulis prohibitā, desinit, quòd sit cupíditas, quae plus requirat, quàm necessitas vita nostrae postulat. Urget cumprimis seqq. loca Luc. 12, 15.1. Tim. 6, 9. 10.Matth. 6, 23. sed de singulis suo loco aliquid monebitur. Brevitatis amore remittimus lectorem ad B. D. Fewrb. tum in Anti Ostor. Disp. 29. tum in Syntagmate secundo Sacr. Disquis. p. 242. seqq. B. D. Stegmann. Photinianismi Disp. 55. quaest. 6. Dn. D. Calov. Socin. Proflig. p. 307. seqq. Interea absit, ut avaritiae propriè dictae, patrocinium suscipere unquam velimus, quin potiùs cane peius atque angue fugiendam eam ducimus, suadente non solùm Salvatore nostro cum sancto Apostolorum aliorumq; Ecc1esiae Dd. choro, verùm etiam ipsis Ethnicis, uti infrà ad 1. Tim. 6, 10. gravissima nonnulla monita de avaritiâ vitandâ adducentur. Hoc solùm in praesens notandum, quòd bestialae illae, quae divitiis rebusq; magnum damnum in ferunt, non mole solùm, sed & nomine (tinea enim, quae vestes demolitur, Graecis σὴς dicitur; quae ligna, δῆξ, quae cornu, ἴψ; quae vitem ἴξ; quae poma, πρῶξ; quae ficum, ψὼν) parvae sint: turpe igitur & infrà dignitatem nostram ducamus, illis bus adhaerescere, quas non solùm f1amma ac serro hostes potentes petunt, sed quas contemtissimae quoque bestialae devorare atque eripere nobis possunt. Caeterum & iam olim haereticis quibusdam locus sic paupertatis favere voto visus est, ceu prodit August, ep. 89. ad Hilarium Ast opponenda memoratis haereticis, eorumque hodie sectatoribus Monachis mendicantibus praeter dictum Paulinum suprà adductum, tum Sc. S. effata ac monita, Prov. 6, 6.Sirac. 25, 5.1. Tim. 5, 8. tum approbata exempla Gen. 41, 48. 49.Ioh. 6, 12.c. 12, 6.Act. 11 29. Quo sensu autem Christus h. l. thesaurizare prohibeat, non malè explicat Cardinalis Toletus, quando Com in cap. 12. Lucae p. 746. ita: Quid sit hoc thesaurizare, explicatur à Paulo 1. Tim. 6. Lui volunt, inquit, divites fieri, incidunt in laqueum Diaboli, ii autem sunt, qui non aliud intendunt, quàm divitias acquirere & accumulare, id sibi tanquam sinem proponents, quos David expressit Ps. Divitiae si assuant &c. & paullò post: non igitur damnantur divitiae, nec tenentur divites divitias abiicere, sed non apponert cor in eis, nec sibie as tanquam sinem proponere praecipuum, eis serviendo, & iterum: qui igitur congregat divitias in usus suorum ac familia & filiorum provide3 conservat, ut temporibus suis distribuat proemergentium necessitate & ratione honesta, non sic thesaurizat, ut dives sicundùm Deum esse non possic.

*(Ex eo porrò, quòd hoc loco nobis praecipitur, ne thesauriztmus in terra, ineptè Pontificii Lib. Arb. (in rebus nempe spiritualibus) colligunt. Nemo, scribit Iesuita Maldonatus in h. l. tam est insanus, ut Deum nobis praecipere dicat, quae sacere non possumos. Urgent cumprimis tum Maldonatus, tum etiam Conzen, quòd h. l. in quibusdam Codd. legatur μὴ θέλητεNolite. non praeciperet, inquit Conzen, Christus, nisi velle & non velle valentibus h. e. liberis. Verùm, si vel maximè lectio haec μὴ θέλητε admittatur, quae tamen Codd. Gr., quorum ipsos sedecim Parisienses contulerunt, ut omittam illos, quos Erasmus ac Beza consuluerunt, destituitur autoritate, quam etiam nec Syrus nec Arabs nec Aethiops, imò nec Interpp. Graeci adprobant, nulla tamen est consequentia, quam hinc Iesuitae exstruunt: Deus praecipit, ut velimus, ergò propriis ac natur alibus viribus pussumus velle bona spiritualia. Imò potiùs approbandum illud Augustini de G. & L. A. c. 16. Certum est, scribit, nos velle ùm volumus, sed ille facit, ut velimus bonum, de quo dictum est, Deus -st, qui o-eratur in nobis velle & perficere. Quomodo verò Deus iure exigat à nobis, quae natural bus viribus praestare non possumns, o enditur in Coll. Isag. p. 603.)*

## 6:20
*(v. 20. But treasure up for yourselves treasures in heaven. We will be able to perform this when we have apprehended the merit and righteousness of Christ with a firm and constant faith: (for He Himself was made poor for our sake, that we might be enriched by His poverty, 2. Cor 8, 9. namely in spiritual riches, the remission of sins, the grace of GOD, the hope of eternal life, etc. Compare Apoc. 3, 17. 18.) and have declared that faith by good works, especially by mercy toward the poor. For whatever we have done to one of the least of Christ's brothers, Christ will consider it done to Himself, Matth. 25, 40. and in this sense the son of Sirach in chapter 40, 19 says: alms remain forever; and the Christian poet says of the same:

The wealth you have given to others, you alone will possess.

Nor, however, can the Papists construct any merit of good works from this, since eternal life is χἀρισμα τοὑ θεοῦ Rom. 6, last. add Rom. 4, 4.Gal. 4, 11. 12.Eph. 2, 8. 9. 10. and one must accurately distinguish here between faith considered formally, and as regards its effects.)*

Latin:

*(v. 20. T---aurizate autem vobis thesauros in coelis. Praestare hoc poterimus, ubi Christi meritum ac iustitiam firma ac constante side apprehenderimus: (ipse enim factus est pauper propter nos, ut nos paupertate illius due sceremus,2. Cor 8, 9. in divitiis nempe spiritualibus, remissione peccatorum, gratiâ DEI, spe vitae aeternae &c. Conf Apoc. 3, 17. 18.) illam que fidem bonis operibus, misericordiae cumprimis erga paperes declataverimus. Quicquid enim uni ex minimis Christi f-atribus fecerimus, sibiipsi Christus cenesebit factum, Matth. 25, 40. atque hoc sensu Siracides c. 40, 19 dicit: elecmo--na in aternum permanet; ac poeta Christianus de iisdem:

Quas aliis dederis, solus habebis opes.

Neque tamen hinc ullum B O. meritum Pontificii exstruere possunt, cùm vita aeterna sit χἀρισμα τοὑ θεοῦ Rom. 6, ult. adde Rom. 4, 4.Gal. 4, 11. 12.Eph. 2, 8. 9. 10. & accurate hîc dist. inter fidem formaliter consideratam, ac quoad effectus suos.)*

## 6:21
v. 21. Where your treasure is, there also is your heart. It is signified that the highest good is by no means to be established in riches, which claim for themselves the whole heart of man and all his affections, which ought rather to be occupied with heavenly treasures. He calls heart the intention and gaze of the mind. The sense therefore is: If your mind gazes upon heavenly things, your treasure is in heavenly things. If upon earthly things, it is in earthly things. This intention he later understands by the eye. *(Thus καρδίαν Justin Martyr also in this place accepts Apol. 2, namely, so that through it νοῦς. may be understood. But blessed Zehnerus explains this Adage in Proverb. Sc. S. page 422. Grotius, however, discourses philosophically concerning this principle in this place. Since, therefore, it is so arranged that we direct all our thoughts and all our zeal toward that which we love, our Savior warns in the present sentence, lest we pursue riches and those things which the world esteems highly with inordinate love, lest perhaps, carried away by too much zeal for obtaining them, we direct all our thoughts solely or at least primarily toward earthly things, but that we may solely pant after better goods, namely, heavenly treasures acquired for us by Christ, and if by chance earthly riches are added to us, we use them in such a way as if not having or possessing them. Conf. 1. Cor. 7, 29. seqq., and so with a ready mind we distribute our resources to the poor, or even if the honor of GOD demands it, we abandon them entirely, -ὰ ἄνω Φρονοῦντες καὶ ζηΤοῦντες, ὁ τοῦ χριςός δςη μὴ -ὰ -πὶ τῆς γῆς just as the Apostle also exhorts, Col. 3, 1. 2, add. Phil. 3, last. For the schema of this world passes away, 1. Cor. 7, 31. but in heaven we shall be with Christ, always 1. Thess. 4, 17.
