Conf. also Cant. 8, 14. with Psal. 121, 1. since Christ is the sole treasure of our soul, to whom He also compares Himself, Matth. 13 p 44. He Himself ascends into heaven Col. 3, 1. Let us also ascend with Christ in heart, until we follow in body, warns Aug. serm. 176. de tempore.

Latin:

v. 21. Ubi est thesaurus tuus, ibi & cor tuum. Significatur summum bonum nequaquam statuendum in divitiis, quod totum bominis coratque omnes eius affectus sibi vendicent, qui potiùs circa thesaurus coetestes occupati esse debeant. Cor appellat animi intentionem & intuitum. Sensus ergò est. Si animus vester intuetur in coelestia, in coelestibus est thesaurus vester. Si in terrestria, in terrestribus. Hanc intentionem postea intelligit per oculum. *(Sic καρδίαν Iustinus quoque Martyr h. l. accipit Apol. 2. nempe, ut perillam intelligature νοῦς. Explieat verò Adagium hoc B. Zehnerus in Proverb. Sc. S. pag 422. Philosophicè autom de principio hoc disserit Grotius in h. l. Cùm igitur ita comparatu sit, ut in illud quod diligimus, omnes nostras congitationes nostras omneque studium dirigamus, monet Salvator noster praesenti sententiâ, ne divitias ac ea, quae mundus, magni aestimat, inordinate amore prosequamur, ne nimio fortè illorum consequendorum studio abrepti omnes cogitationes unicè vel certè primariò ad terrena dirigamus, sed meliora bona, coelestes nempe thesaurus, à Christo nobis acquisitos, unicè anhelemus, ac si fortè divitiae nobis adii-iantur terrenae ita illis utamur, quasi non habenets aut possidentes. Conf. 1. Cor. 7, 29. seqq. adeoque promto animo in pauperes facultates nostras distribuamus, vel etiam si honor D E I efflagitaverit, prorsus deseramus, -ὰ ἄνω Φρονοῦντες καὶ ζηΤοῦντες, ὁ τοῦ χριςός δςη μὴ -ὰ -πὶ τῆς γῆς ceu Apostolus quoque hortatur, Col. 3, 1. 2, add. Phil. 3, ult. Praeterit enim huius mundi schema, 1. Cor. 7, 31. in coele autem erimus cum Christo, semper 1. Thess. 4, 17. Conf quoque Cant. 8, 14. cum Psal. 121, 1. Christus sit unicus animae nostrae thesaurus, cui etiam sese comparat, Matth. 13 p 44. Ipse adscendit in coelum Col. 3, 1.Adscendamus & nos cum Christo corde, donec sequamur corpore, monet Aug. serm. 176. detempore.)*

## 6:22
v. 22. If your eye shall be simple i. e. if you shall look upon the goods of your neighbor with a simple and fair mind, so that you do not envy him, for thus ἁπλότης is used Rom. 12. v. 8. 2. Cor. 8. v. 2. 2. Cor. cap. 9. v. 11. then your whole body shall be bright i. e. cheerful, you shall be entirely filled with cheerfulness. Πονηρὸς is used for envious Matth. 20. v. 15. just as also Prov. 23. v. 6. Prov. cap. 28 v. 22. an envious person is called an evil eye. He commands that the heart be kindled by the divine light of true doctrine with zeal for GOD, of true piety and heavenly things, not obscured by errors, ignorance of God, and distrust, otherwise all actions will be depraved. Bell. 4. de Iustif. cap. 15. Christ wishes to teach by metaphorical speech that men often stumble, because they do not act by the preceding light of the divine word, but then act rightly, when they follow the light of the divine word and the lamp of faith shining before them. (John Ferus has similar things in this place. But these testimonies are to be observed against ἐθελοθρπ σκίαν the Papists, concerning which let some things be seen in B. P. Confess.

Cath. c. 4. p. 788. item against the same, Sc. S. contempt, while they sometimes deny that it is the rule and judge of controversies of faith, sometimes argue for its imperfection and obscurity, concerning which matter the B. P. C. C. t. 1. p 74. seqq. is also to be seen, it. p. 86. seqq. t. 2. p. 210. &c.)

As the eye is the light of the body, and directs it: so the mind is the light of man and rules all his actions. If the eye is dark, the body is poorly ruled: so if the mind is occupied by depraved desires, avarice, or care for sustenance, destruction hangs over man.

Beza in annot. Since the eyes are the principal indicators of the mind, therefore among the Hebrews the eye is put for the whole disposition of man, and so the judgment of the mind itself is signified here, to which we ought to apply ourselves by comparing rather than by accumulating wealth: so that just as the body is governed by the eyes, so also our whole life might be governed by right reason, that is, by the Spirit of God. Therefore he understands simple as pure and integral, to which is opposed evil, that is, defiled by some vice. Some, having followed the series of the text, explain it in this way, that the desire for temporal goods extinguishes the light of the mind. Chrysost. understands it concerning the mind, if that shall be pure, also all the operations of man will be pure, he applies it thus to the text, if the mind shall be fixed upon the desire of earthly things, all operations will be more involved in darkness.

See the Epistle of Nazianzen in Basil, p. 525. Furthermore, that this similitude, which Christ uses here, by comparing judgment to the eyes, is also customary among the Philosophers, Hugo Grotius shows at length here, who can be consulted. That excellent statement of Maimonides also seems to be referred here, while he writes: יש להם עינים ראיוםמהשאין רואיםהפחאים׃ לבת החבמים i. e. the hearts of the wise have eyes, with which they see what the simple do not see.

Moreover, Cardinal Bellarmine argues from this passage for the perfection of good works, in book 4 of Justification, chapter 15, section 'Third'. In this manner: If your eye is simple, that is, if the intention is upright, the whole body will be luminous, that is, the works themselves also will be good, and they will not have any part of darkness, Luc 11, 36. But the eye of a regenerated man is simple, that is, his intention is upright. Therefore, his works also will be good, and indeed perfectly such, and in no way mortal sins, which the Lutherans teach. Becanus also urges this same present statement in his Manual, book 1, chapter 13, question 1, section 6.

But Luther's words, that the good works of the reborn also, when considered in the rigor of divine justice, are sins, are also censured by Corn. à Lap. in chapter 64 of Isaiah. Resp. 1. Symbolical theology is not argumentative, which is a common axiom of theologians, taken from Dionysius, writes Lud. ab Alcasar, notes X. prooem. n. 5. in Apoc. And yet in this place a pambola, is proposed, as Conzenius, Corn. à Lapide, Tirinus, Barradius, and other Jesuits say, Comm. in h. loc., or a similitude, taken from the eye of the body, as the Jesuit Maldon speaks, in h. l. p. 150. 2. In which sense the G. W. of the reborn are called sins by B. Luther, and indeed mortal ones, he himself explains in art. 32 where he expressly writes, that they are such only then if they are considered in the rigid judgment of God. Nor does St. Augustine think otherwise, for he says expressly in l. 9. Confess. c. 13. v-, even of the praiseworthy life of men, if it be discussed with mercy removed. Therefore the G. W. of the reborn are called sins not ἀπ λώς and formally or by their own nature, but κα-Τὶ according to something and in the stated respect. 3. And the reason is also manifest. Since the G. W. are contaminated by the remnants of sin still clinging in the flesh of the reborn, they cannot indeed sustain the rigor of divine justice, which requires perfect obedience: meanwhile, however, that clinging imperfection is covered by the merit of Christ apprehended by faith. Therefore, the G. W. of the reborn are by no means judged by GOD as sins, but are rather pleasing and acceptable to Him. 4. Nor does it follow, the intellect of a reborn man is illuminated by the word, and the mind is purged of vicious affections by the grace of the H. S., therefore the works which the reborn performs are so perfectly good that they can sustain the rigor of divine justice. Nay rather, since the renewal and purging in this life is at least begun, Gal. 5, 17.Rom. 8, 23. Conf. Coll. Isag. p. 694. seqq., and thus the spiritual eye of the reborn man is only incipiently purged, and some vicious humors of clinging sin remain surviving as long as man lives in this mortal body, thence it happens that the operation also cannot be perfect in all its numbers. Which imperfection of one's own actions, however, is not imputed to the reborn man who apprehends the perfect righteousness of Christ with true confidence. Nor yet is it to be established from this that the G. W., viewed in themselves, are perfect and pure from every stain of clinging imperfection, if they are considered in the rigid judgment of GOD. Since therefore Christ speaks hypothetically, if the eye be simple etc., therefore even if the intention could be proven by the eye, the Jesuits must prove that that spiritual eye or intention of the reborn man is so perfectly pure that no harmful humor of sin clings to it. The contrary of which Holy Scripture testifies everywhere. Indeed, some Papists themselves also agree with our opinion concerning the clinging imperfection of the G. W. of the reborn. Ioh. Ferus in his Comm. already castrated by the Fathers of the holy inquisition upon Matth. c. 12. p. 265. Nay, he writes, also; in our good works something of evil concurs. All our righteousnesses are as filthy rags. Whence does this proceed if not from the remnants of Adam himself? When Christ by His grace stimulates to a good work, Adam himself, that is, our perversity, adds something either of his own complacency, or of his own advantage, etc., whereby it happens that the work itself is NEVER PERFECT, although by the mercy of God it IS NOT IMPUTED. But if the Jesuits should perhaps reject the authority of this man, we oppose the words of Gregory the Great, Pope of Rome, book 5 of Morals, ch. 8. Our very, he says here, righteousness, when brought to the examination of divine justice, is unrighteousness: and that which shines in the estimation of the doer, is filthy in the strictness of the judge. The same man confesses in book 35 of Morals, ch. 16, after the middle. What of the fact that the Jesuit Coton himself writes in his Catholic Institutions: There is always something of man in our actions, that is, something of imperfection and misery admixed.

Latin:

v. 22. Si oculus tuus fuerit simplex i. e. si proximi bona animo simplici & aequo aspexeris, ut ipsi non invideas, ita enim usurpatur ἁπλότηςRom. 12. v. 8.2. Cor. 8. v. 2.2. Cor. cap. 9. v. 11.tunc totum corpus eru lucidum i. e. hilare, totus eris hilaritate repletus. Πονηρὸς pro invide usurpatur Matth. 20. v. 15. sicut & Prov. 23. v. 6.Prov. cap. 28 v. 22. invidus vocatur malus ocule. Praecipit, ut cor sit divino lumine verae doctrinae a accensum studio DEI, verae pietatis ac rerum coelestium, nó erroribus, ignorantia Dei ac diffidentia obscuratum, alioqui omnes actiones fore pravas. Bell. 4. de Iustif. cap. 15. Christus metaphorico sermone decere vult, hominies sape impingere, quia non agunt previa lace verbi divini, tunc verò rectè agere, quando lumen verbi divini & sidei lampadam praelucentem sequuntur. *(Similia habet Ioh. Ferus in h. l Observandam autem testimonia haec sunt contra ἐθελοθρπ σκίαν Pontificiorum, quâ de videantur nonnulla apud B. P. Confess.

Cath. c. 4. p. 788. i em contra corund, Sc. S. contemtum, dum modò regulam ac iudicem controversiarum fidei cam esse negant, modò imperfectionis ac obscuritatis arguunt, quâ de re itid videndus B. P. C. C. t. 1. p 74. seqq. it. p. 86. seqq. t. 2. p. 210. &c.)*

Ut oculus est lumen corporis, illudque dirigit: sic animus est lumen hominis & regit omnes actiones. Si oculus est tenebricosus, malè regitur corpus: sic si animus occupatus est pravis cupiditatibus, avaritia, curâ victus, imminet homini exitium.

Beza in annot. Quoniam oculi sunt praecipui mentis indices, ideò pro toto hominis ingenio apud Hebraeos oculus ponitur, itag 3 mentis ipsiq iudicium hîc significatur, cui comparando potiùs, quàm accumulandu opibus incumbere nos oportuit: ut sicut oculis corpus, ita etiam rectâ ratione i. e. Spiritu Dei illustrasta tota vita nostra regeretur. Simplicem ergo intelligit purum & integrum, cui opponitur malus i. e. aliquo vitio inquinatus. Quidam seriem textus secuti exponunt hoc modo, quòd cupiditas bonorum temporaliū lumen mentis praestinguat. Chrysost. intelligit de mente, si illa fuerit para, etiam omnes hominis operationes erunt purae, id sic applicat ad textum, si mens cupiditati rerum terrenarum erit affixa, omnes operationes tenebris magis erunt in volutae.

Vide Epistolam Nazianz. apud Basilium p. 525. *(Porrò, quôd similitudo haec, quâ Christus hîc utitur, conferendo nempe iudicium oculis, apud Philosophos quoque usitata sit, prolixè hîc ostendit Hugo Grotius, qui potest evolvi. Referendum huc quoq; egregium illud Maimonidis videtur, dum scribit: יש להם עינים ראיוםמהשאין רואיםהפחאים׃ לבת החבמים i. e. corda sapientum habent oculos, quibus vident, quod non vident simplices.)*

*(Caeterùm argumentatur ex hoc loco pro B. O. perfectione Card. Bell. l. 4. de iustif. c. 15. §. Tertium. h. m. Si oculus tuus fuerit simplex, i. e. sirecta fuerit intentio, totum corpus erit lucidum h. e. opera ipsa quog 3 erunt bona, nec ullam quog 3 habebunt tenebrarum partem,Luc 11, 36.Atqui hominis regeniti oculus est simplex h. e. illius intentio rect. test. E. ipsius quog 3 opera erunt bona, & quidem persectè talia, nec ullo modo peccata mortalia, quod Luther ani docent. Idem hoc praesens dictum urget quoque Becanus in Manual, lib. 1. c. 13. q. 1. §. 6.

Lutheri verò verba, quòd renatorum quoque B. O. in rigore iiftitidivinae considerata peccata sint, sugillat quoque Corn. à Lap. in c. 64. Esaiae. Resp. 1. Theologia symbolica non est argumentativa, quod commune Theologorū axioma esse, ex Dionysio desumiū, scribit Lud. ab Alcasar notat. X. prooem. n. 5. in Apoc. Atqui hoc loco proponitur pambola, dicente Conzenio, Corn. à Lapide, Tirino, Barradio, allisque Iesuitis, Comm. in h. loc. vel similitudo, ab oculo corporis desumta, ceu loquitur Iesuita Maldon, in h. l. p. 150. 2. quo sensu à B. Luthero renatorum B. O. vocentur peccata, & quidem mortalia, ipse explicat art. 32 ubi expressè scribit, quòd tum demum talia sint si in rigido Deiiudicio considerentur. Nec aliter quoque sentit S Augustinus, disertè enim l. 9. Confess. c. 13. v-, inquit, etiam laudabili vitae hominum, si remot â misericordiâ discutiatur. discuntur itaq; B. O. renatorum peccata nonἀπ λώςac formaliter vel sua naturâ, sed κα-Τὶsecundùm quid ac dicto respectu. 3. Et ratio quoq; manifesta est. Cùm n. reliquiis peccati in carne renatorum etiam adhuc haerentibus B. O. contaminentur, non possunt sanè rigorem iustitiae divinae, quae perfectam requirit obedientiam, fustinere: interea tamen legitur illa adhaerens imperfectio merito Christi fide apprechenso. Itaq ita B. renatorum O. minimè censentur à DEO peccata, sed ipsi potiùs grata & accepta sunt. 4. nec sequitur, hominis regeniti intellectus per verbum illuminatur, animus que per gratiam Sp. S. à vitiosis affectibus repurgatur, E. opera, quae renatus praestat, ita perfectè bona sunt, ut rigorem iustitiae divinae sustinere possint. Imò potiùs cùm renovatio ac repurgatio in hàc vita sit saltem inchoata, Gal. 5, 17.Rom. 8, 23. Conf. Coll. Isag. p. 694. seqq. adeoque oculus hominis renati spiritualis tantùm inchoatè sit repurgatus, ac vitiosi aliqui adhaerentis peccati humores superstires maneant, quamdiu homo in mortali hoc corpore degit, inde fit, ut nec opetatio quoq; omnibus numeris perfecta esse possit. quae tamen propriarum actionum impersectio homini renato, perfactum Christi iustitiam verâ fiduciâ apprehendenti non imputatur. neque tamen hinc statuendum, quòd B. O. in se spectata, perfecta sint & ab omni adhaerentis imperfectionis labe, si in rigido DEI iudicio considerentur, pura Cùm igitur Christus hypotheticè loquatur, si oculus simplex fuerit &c. proindesi vel maximè per oculūintelligi intètio possit probare Iesuitae debent, quòd oculus ille spiritualis sive intentio hominis renati ita perfectè pura sit, ut nullius peccati noxius humor illi adhaereat. Cuius contrarium passim testatur Sc. Sacra. Adstipulantur verò nostrae sententiae de adhaerente imperfectione renatorum B. O. ipsi quoque pontificii nonnulli. Ioh. Ferus in Comm. iamtum à Patrisbus sanctae inquisitionis castrato super Matth. c. 12. p. 265. imò, scribit, etiam; in bonis operibus nostris nonnibil mali concurrit. Omnes iustitiae nostrae tanquam pannus menstruaetae. Unde boc provenit nisi ex reliquiis ipsius Adam? Cùm Cbristus gratiâ sua ad B. O. exstimulat, ipse Adam b. e. perversantura, adiicit aliquid vel propriae complacentiae, vel proprii commodi &c. quo sit, ut opus ipsum N U NQUAM sit PERFEOTUM, quamvis ex misericordia Dei NON I MPUTETUR. Sed si huius reiecient fortè Iesuitae autoritatem, opponimus verba Gregorii M. P. R. lib. 5. Moral. c. 8. Ipsa, inquit hîc, iustitia nostm ad examem divinae iustitae deducta, iniustitia est: & sordet in districtione iudicis, quod in aestimatione fulget operantis. Confetatur idem 1. 35. mor. c. 16. post med. Quid quod ipse iesuita Cotonus in Instit. Cathol. scribat: Semper aeliquid bominis est in actionibus nostris, b. e. aliquid imperfectionis & miseriae admixium.)*

## 6:23
(v. 23. If the light that is in you is darkness &c. But if it is permitted to argue from parabolic expressions, which is customary for the Papists, we can firmly argue from this place against the same, that an unregenerate man, inasmuch as he is not illuminated by the light of the divine word, and whose intellect is therefore mere darkness, to such an extent that he does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of GOD &c 1. Cor. 2, 14.Eph. 4, 17.Eph. 18. 19.Eph. c. 5, 8. &c. does not have the powers of Free Will to perform works that are morally good, that is, which are good before God and in the divine judgment, which Bellarmine nevertheless wishes in book 5 of Grace and Free Will, chapter 9. But concerning this matter, let more be seen in volume 2 of the Theological Commonplaces of B. P. concerning Free Will, § 67. Catholic Confession, volume 4, page 523 and following. Moreover, Thomas Aquinas favors our opinion, both in the Catena on John 15, at verse 4, and in book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 41, question 1, article 1, §. Response, and also Lombard at the same place.)

Latin:

*(v. 23. Si lumen quod in te est tenebrae sunt &c. Quod si ex patabolicis locutionisbus argumentari licet, id quod Pontificiis solenne est. firmiter ex h. l. argumentari contra eosdem possumus, quòd homo irregenitus, quippe luce verbi divini non illuminatus, ac cuius proinde intellectus merae tenebrae sunt, in tantum ut non percipiat, quae sunt Spiritus DEI &c 1. Cor. 2, 14.Eph. 4, 17.Eph. 18. 19.Eph. c. 5, 8. &c. non habeat vires L. A. faciendi opera moraliter bona h. e. quae coram Deo & in iudicio divino bona, quod Bell. tamen vult 1. 5. de G. & L. A. c. 9. Sed hâc de re plura videanturt. 2. LL. Theol. B. P. de L. B. § 67. Confess. Cath. t. 4. pag. 523. seqq. Favet autem nostrae sententiae cumprimis Thomas de Aquino tum in Caten. Ioh. I5. ad v. 4. tum in 1. 2. sent. dist. 41. q. 1. a. 1. §. Resp. nec non Lomb. d. l.)*

## 6:24
(v. 24. No one can serve two masters. It is a proverbial sentence, and it was without doubt customary among the Jews in the time of Christ. Zehnerus in Adag: facris pages 424, 425, shows at length the use of the saying, and at the same time also that similar admonitions concerning philosophy and political faculties occur among Gentile writers. Let H. Grot. also be compared on this passage). He calls them two masters ἀνομίαν ἔχοντες καρδιων, who are endowed with dissimilar temperaments or hostile minds, as Athanasius speaks in Dial. de Trin., or as Theophylact notes in this place, τοὺς -ὰ ἐνανΤὶα -πι-ὰτον-ας.

ἀνθέξεται he will cleave to one. The Old Interpreter rendered it he will sustain, Augustine he will suffer, as if it were from αν᾽τέχειν. But αν᾽τέχεσθαι signifies to cleave tenaciously and to be addicted. The Syriac translates, he will hold in price and honor. The one is to be referred to the affection of the mind itself, but the other to the actions which follow those affections. Casaubon, in his notes: He teaches the Lord, how it can happen that one serves two masters. Because, he says, either he will hate one, loving the other: or even, although he may love both, it will be able to happen that, while you are more intent upon executing the will of one, you may conduct yourself more negligently toward the other, so that it is distinguished in ἀγαπᾶν and ἀντέχεσθαι. *(The Syrian uses the word which in Conjugation 1 denotes he was heavy, he was burdened. But in Pael it means he held someone as heavy or precious, he honored, for the Greek Τμᾶν as it occurs thus Matth. 15. 4.Matth. c. 19, 19. The Arabic has which is from likewise he honored, he glorified, signifying.)*

The blindness of the human heart is noted, because it thinks it can persuade God of this, which it cannot persuade men in the polity and economy by servants who adhere to and listen to the adversary of their Master. Chrys. homil. 6. in Ep. Philipp. Christ says, spare the poor; Mammon says, snatch from the poor what they have; Christ says, communicate liberally what you have. Mammon says, seize what you do not have.

Mammon. Luc. 16. v. 13. It is written with a single m, because it is a Syriac word Drasius derives that word from אםן he was firm, for indeed in riches, signified by the Syriac name, men are accustomed to place the strength of their mind. Hamon המון in Hebrew signifies an abundance of any thing, and is used for riches. The Syriac language made Mamon from Hamon, with the addition moreover at the end of א. Jerome in chapter 6 of Matthew and question 6 to Algasia says that riches are called in the language of the Syrians unjust Mammon, for the reason that they are collected from iniquity.

Some establish that it is a Syriac and Punic word, which signifies gain or riches, as Jerome and Augustine note: but here the Lord attributes a person to it by prosopopoeia, so that He may accommodate Himself to the temperament and customs of the avaricious, who make those riches a God for themselves, while they place their hope and trust in them. Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 8, p. 178: Mammon is according to the Jewish speech, which the Samaritans also use, covetous and wishing to have more than is fitting. But according to the Hebrew it is said adjunctively Mam or it signifies a glutton, i.e., one who cannot restrain himself from gluttony. What is to be determined concerning this interpretation, Gallas teaches in his notes. Compare Jerome, Epistle 22 to Euthymius and Epistle 151 to Algasia. Lombard, book 2, distinction 6: Mammon is a Demon, who presides over riches, but it is refuted from Luke 16.

Haymo, Bishop of Halberstadt, around the year 840, comments on this passage thus: Christ does not say, you cannot serve GOD and have riches, but he says thus, you cannot serve GOD and riches. For he who serves riches is a slave of riches, because he does not distribute them as a Lord, but guards them as a slave, to whom the Lord says elsewhere: Woe to you rich, because you have your consolation. (Also relevant here is that of Bernard, sermon 21 on the Canticles: The avaricious man hungers for earthly things, like a beggar; the faithful man despises them, like a Lord. The former begs by possessing; the latter saves by despising. Well also Gregory the Great, book 10 of the Morals, chapter 28: Wealth is not a crime, but the affection is. Likewise Saint Jerome, epistle to Salvianus: Neither do riches hinder the rich man, if he uses them well, nor does poverty make the poor man more commendable. Notably Augustine in Ps. 131. God does not attend to the means, but to the desire. Conformably also to these are some Papal commentators. Cornelius à Lapide on this passage writes: Note, he does not say: You cannot have riches and God: for Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David, Solomon and many Saints had both, who did not affix their heart to riches, because they used them for pious works: but you cannot serve GOD and Mammon: for he who serves Mammon is a slave of riches, wherefore he does not rule them as a Lord, but is ruled by them as a chattel. John Lorinus the Jesuit Commentary on Ps. 61. v. 11 It is an error that riches are in themselves evil and illicit: which the Council of Gangra condemned in Eustathius, in Nicholas, book 9, chapter 16. These things must be opposed to the Cardinal and the same Jesuit Bellarmine, who in volume 4 of his Works, book 3, on the Good Life, chapter 7, §. Fourthly thus: the question is about superfluous riches by reason of superfluity i.e. whether the rich are bound to distribute what is superfluous, because they are superfluous, whatever may be the case regarding the extreme or grave necessity of the needy. And although there are not lacking grave Theologians who think the contrary, we nevertheless judge that opinion to be safer and truer, which teaches that superfluous riches cannot be retained without sin. Which opinion Saint Thomas follows in 2. 2. question 66 article 7. and question 87. article 1. to 2. and Quodlibet 6. article 12. and besides Albert, Richard, Paludanus and others in 4. Sentences distinction 15. In which place Saint Thomas question 2. article 1. question. 4. he writes that this is the common opinion of the Theologians. But Bellarmine attempts to prove this opinion from the present passage, where among other things he writes: he who gathers, and keeps idle money, or garments or other things of that kind, without doubt serves Mammon. But let Bellarmine take care, lest he migrate into the camps of either the Manichaeans or the Pelagians, who taught their disciples, that the rich of this world cannot be saved, unless after Baptism they bestowed their riches upon the poor. Compare Augustine, epistle 19 to Hilary, q. 4, or of the modern Photinians, about whom above. But more on this matter will perhaps be brought forward below at Matth. 19, 24.

To serve Mammon. What it is here to serve riches, is evident from equivalent phrases Iob. 31, 24. Psalm. 62, 11. Prov. 11, 29. Syrac. 31, 7. Marc. 10, 24. 1. Tim. 6, 17. He who thus serves Mammon is not a friend of GOD. Whence also such service is seriously prohibited in the sacred writings, with a most severe threat added. See the places just cited, and add Iob. 27, 10. Prov. 15, 27. c. 11, 27. Amos 9, 1. 1. Cor. 6, 10. Eph. 5, 5. Col. 3, 5. 1. Tim. 6, 9. Compare altogether more on this matter in B. Par. Schol. Pier. l. 5. c. 11. likewise in Aphor. pract. tit. Avarice.)*

Elias. Gain or profit and substance and riches are signified in Chaldean by Mammon and Mammona. It has a relationship with the Hebrew לוס i.e. reproach, because immoderate and illicit gain is worthy of reproach. In the History of Joseph. What profit is it to us, what gain will come, if we kill him. In Hebrew it is Mammon. Suidas. Μαμωνᾶς, πλοῦτος γηΐνος χ ξυσὸς οὐχὶ ὁ ἐκ τοὑ Σα-ανἄ, ἀλλ ὁ ΠριπΤὸς χαὶ ὑΠὲρ τὴν Χξείαν Those riches which are not from Satan, but which are present beyond substance and necessary use. There is one who explains it thus: ממונא is a Heemanthic noun, formed from the נונא, verb known to the Syrians and Chaldeans, which the hand that came out from the wall wrote in Daniel. נונא the family is numbered. Mammon therefore signifies both money and things numbered, in which riches are situated. (More could be brought forward here both concerning the writing and the meaning of the word Mammona from Chemnitius, Drusius, Waserus, Glassius, Scultetus, H. Grotius, Buxtorfius, and others, but it pleases to refer those to Luc. 16, 9.)

Just as our Savior firmly concludes from that axiom, That no one can serve two masters, that no one can adhere to God with firm trust who places his trust in riches and serves them: (Compare the following, namely the passages 1 Sam. 2, 3.1 Kings 18, 21.Matt. 13, 22.Luke 1, 74. 75.Rom. 6, 19.ch. 7, 6.) so we conclude no less firmly from the same 1. against the Papists, that the Saints cannot be religiously invoked and worshipped, saving the worship due to the one true eternal GOD alone, which worship, however, is nothing more frequent among the Papists. 2. against the Photinians, that if Christ were not the true eternal God, which they themselves stubbornly deny, he could likewise not be religiously invoked by us, which, however, the Photinians, with us, namely by the Holy Scriptures, establish, or certainly wish to appear to teach as such. The figment of subordination does not help them here, since subordination has no place among the persons of the Most Holy Trinity, nor can truly religious worship be attributed to anyone unless he is the supreme and eternal God. 3. against the Calvinists, that the reborn or rather even the elect can lose the grace of GOD, the Holy Spirit, and justifying faith for a time, and indeed do lose them, namely when they serve sins, as David committing adultery and murder, since indeed saving faith and the gracious indwelling of the Holy Spirit can no more coexist with sins committed against conscience than someone can serve two masters. Compare John 8, 35.Rom. 6, 20. Wendelin objects in Exerc. 42. § 18. two things: 1 he says, Christ is speaking of a service that is clearly voluntary, to be rendered to two contrary masters at the same time, which, he says, ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων is. But to adhere to God with firm trust, and to crucify the flesh, which the Apostle requires of the reborn Gal. 5, 16. add. v. 24. and on the contrary to leave room for the suggestions of the Devil and the flesh and to perform the works of the flesh, are in this state. Therefore, that he who commits adultery and murder, which David, being reborn and without doubt also elect, did, performs the works of the flesh and casts off the grace of God, I think is sufficiently clear from the same Apostle in the place cited v. 19. 20. 21.

Nor do I doubt that Wendelin will concede that God and the Devil are contrary masters, and that those who perform the works of the flesh do not merely slip out of weakness, but do not serve GOD in the Spirit, but the Devil. 2. Wendelin thinks it should be observed that it is said ambiguously, to be a slave of sin. Since not only is he said to be a slave to sin, who commits sin reigning, i.e., which is perpetrated with the full consent of the will, and to whom the sinner does not resist through the grace of the Holy Spirit, but also he is said to be a slave to sin, who is held bound by the shackles of sin, and is dragged into sins while the Spirit struggles against it, and in this way Paul says that he serves the law of sin with the flesh, Rom. 7, 25. But unless Wendelinus has proven that David sinned at least in the latter way, our opinion will persist, that the regenerate and therefore also the elect sometimes totally lose the grace of GOD, namely by serving sin in such a way that full consent of the will is added. But who would doubt that David committed adultery with the full consent of the will? But more on this matter elsewhere. 4. Against hypocrites, that they do not sin lightly, while they attend the sacred rites of heretics either for the sake of at least a small gain or out of fear, simulating consent with them by external gestures, or at least not indicating dissent. But B. D. Bald. Cas Consc. page 197 deals with this business at greater length.)*

Latin:

*(v. 24. Nemo potest duobus Dominis servire. Est sententia proverbialis, fuitque procul ambiguo & inter Iudaeos tempore Christi ea usitata. Usum verò dicti proverbii, simul etiam, quòd apud Gentiles scriptores similes ferè admonitiones de Philosophia & facultatibus politicis occurrant, prolixè ostendit Zehnerus in Adag: facris pag. 424. 425. Conferatur quoque H. Grot. in h. l.). Duos vocat Dominos ἀνομίαν ἔχοντες καρδιων, qui dissimilibus ingeniis aut animis hostilibus sunt praediti, ut loquitur Athanas. Dial. nde. Trin. vel ut Theoph. h. l. annotat, τοὺς -ὰ ἐνανΤὶα -πι-ὰτον-ας.

ἀνθέξεταιuni adhaerebit. Vetus interpres reddidit sustinebit, Augustinus patietur, quasi esset ab αν᾽τέχειν. Sed αν᾽τέχεσθαι significat tenaciter adhaerere & addictum esse. Syr. vertit, in precio & honore habebit. Alterum referendum est ad ipsum mentis affectum, alterum verò ad actiones, quae affectus illos consequuatur. Casaub, in notis. Docet Domino, qui fierine queat, ur duobo Dominis idem serviat. Quia, inquit, velunum odio habebit alierum amans: autetiam, licet amet utrumg 3 fieri poterit, ut dum in alterius voluntate exequenda eris intentior, erga alterum se ger at negligentius, ut sic distinguatur inἀγαπᾶν & ἀντέχεσθαι. *(Utitur Syrus verbo quod in Coni. 1. notat gravis, gravatus fuit. in Pael vero gravem vel preciosum habuit aliquem, honoravit, pro Gr. Τμᾶν ceu ita occurrit Matth. 15. 4.Matth. c. 19, 19. Arabs habet quod est à pariter honoravit, glorificavit, significante.)*

Notatur cordis humani caecitas, quod cogitat se hoc posse Deo persuadere, quod hominibus in politia & oeconomiâ à servis, qui adversario Domini sui adhaerent & auscultant, persuaderine quit. Chrys. homil. 6. in Ep. Philipp. Christus dicit, parce pauperibus, Mammonas dicit, eripe pauperibus, quod habent; Christus dicit communica liberaliter, quae habes. Mammon inquit, rape quae non habes.

Mammona. Luc. 16. v. 13. scribitur per m simplex, quia vox Syra est Drasius illam vocem deducit ab אםןfirmus fuit, etenim in divitiis, nomine Syriaco significatis, robur animi hominess collocare solent. Hamon המון Hebraicè significant cuiuslibet rei copiam, ac usurpatur pro divitiis. Syriaca lingua ex Hamon fecit Mamon, addito insuper in fine א. Hieron in cap. 6. Matth. & q. 6. ad Algasiam divitias linguâ Syrorum dicit vocari iniustum Mammona, eò quòd de iniquitate collectae sunt.

Quidam statuunt esse vocem Syriacam & Punicam, quod significet lucrum vel divitias, ut Hieron. & August. annotant: hî auté Dominus per prosopopaeian personam illi tribuit, ut avarorū ingenio & moribus sese accommodet, qui illas divitias sibi Deum faclunt, dum in illis spem & fiduciam collocant. Iren. lib. 3. cap. 8. p. 178. Mammonas est secundùm Iudaicam loquelam, quâ & Samaritae utuntur, cupidus & plusquam oportet habere volens. Secundùm autem Hebraicam adiunctivè dicitur Mam vel significat gulosum i. e. qui non possit se à gula continere. Quid de hac interpretatione statuendum sit, docet Gallas in not. Confer Hieron. Epist. 22. ad Euthym & Epist 151. ad Algas. Lomb. lib. 2. dist. 6. Mammona esse Daemonem, qui praesidet divitit-, sed-refollitur ex Euc. 16.

Haymo Episc. Halberst. circa ann. 840. in h. l. sic commentatur. Non dicit Christus, non potestis DEO servire, & divitias habere sed sic ait, non potestis DEO & divitiis servire. Qui enim devitiis servit, servus est divitiarum, quia non distribuit eas ut Dominus, sed cuslodit, ut servus, quibus Dominus alibi ait: Vae vobis divitibus, quia habetis consolationem vestram, *(Facit quoq; hue illud Bernhardi serm. 21. in Cantic. Avarus terrena esurit, ut mendicus; sidelis contemnit, ut Dominus. Ille possidendo mindic at; iste contemnendo servat. Benè quoque Greg. M. 1. 10. Mor. c. 28. Non est census in crimine, sed affectus. Pariter S. Hieronymus, epist. ad Salvianum: Nec opes obsunt diviti, si illis benè utatur, nec egest as facit pauperem commendabiliorem. Notanter August. in Ps. 131.Non attendit Deus facultatem, sed cupiditatem. Conformiter quoque his Commentatores nonnulli Pontificii. Corn. à Lapide in h. l. Nota, scribit, Non dicit: Non potestis opes habere & Deum: utrumg 3 enim habuit Abraham, Isacc, Iacob, David, Salomon multig 3 Sancti, qui divitiis non affixere cor, quia eis usi sunt ad pia opera: sed non potestis DEO servire & Mammonae: qui enim servit Mammonae, opum est servus, quare eas non regit ut Dominus, sed ab eis regitur quasi mancipium. Ioh Lorinus Iesuita Co-. in Ps. 61. v. 11Error est, per se malas & illicitas esse divitias: quam damnavit in Eustathio Concilium Gangrenense, apud Nic. 1. 9. c. 16. Opponenda haec sunt Cardinali eldem que Iesuitae Bellarmino, qui t. 4. Oper. l. 3. de B. O. c. 7. §. Quartò ita: quaestio est de super fluis opibus ratione superfluitatis i. e. an divites teneantur super flua erogare, quia superfsua sunt, quicquid sit de necessirate extrema vel gravi egenorum. Et quamvis non desint graves Theologi, qui contrà sentient, nos tamen tutiorem & veriorem eam sententiam arbitr amur, quae docet, superfluas opes sine peccato retineri non posse. Quam sentenciam sequitur S. Thomas in 2. 2. quaeft. 66 art. 7. & quaest. 87. art. 1. ad 2. & Quodlib. 6. art. 12. & praeterea Albertus, Richardus, Paludanus & alii in 4. Sent. dist. 15. Quo loco S. Thomas q. 2. art. 1. q. 4. scribit, bane esse communem Theologorum sententiam. Probare verò hanc sententiam contaur Bell. ex praesenti loco, ubi inter alia: qui congregat, scribit, & custodit otiosas pecunias, aut voftes aut alia id genus, sine dubie Mammonae servit. Dispiciat verò Bellarminus, ne migret in castra vel Manichaeorum ac Pelagianorum, qui docuerunt discipulos suos, divites huius seculi non posse salvari, nisi post Baptismum divitias pauperibus elargirentur. Conf. August. epist. 19. ad Hilarium, q. 4. vel hodiernorum Photinianorum, de quibus suprà. Ast plura hâc de re afferentur fortè infrà ad Matth. 19, 24.)*

*( Servire Mammonae. Quid hîc sit servire divitiis, pater ex phrasibus aequipollentibus Iob. 31, 24.Psalm. 62, 11.Prov. 11, 29.Syrac. 31, 7.Marc. 10, 24.1. Tim. 6, 17. Qui ita Mommonae servit, non est amicus DEI. Unde etiam seriò talis servitus prohibetur in sacris literis, additâ comminatione severissimâ. Vid. loca modò citata, & adde Iob. 27, 10.Prov. 15, 27.c. 11, 27.Amos 9, 1.1. Cor. 6, 10.Eph. 5, 5.Col. 3, 5.1. Tim. 6, 9. Confer. omninò plura in hanc rem apud B. Par. Schol. Pier. l. 5. c. 11. it. in Aphor. pract. tit. Avaritio.)*

Elias. Lucrum sive quaestus & substantia & divitiae Chaldaicè significantur per Mammon & Mammona. Cognationem habet cum Hebraicoלוסi. e. vituperium, quia quaestus immodicus & illicitus vituperatione dignus est. In Historia Iosephi. Quae nobis utilitas, quod lucrum accedet, si interficiamus eum. In Hebr. est Mammon. Suidas. Μαμωνᾶς, πλοῦτος γηΐνος χ ξυσὸς οὐχὶ ὁ ἐκ τοὑ Σα-ανἄ, ἀλλ ὁ ΠριπΤὸς χαὶ ὑΠὲρ τὴν ΧξείανDivitiae illae quae non sint ex Satana, sed quae praeter substantiam & usum necessarium adsint. Est qui ita explicat: ממונאest nomen Heemanthicum, àנונא,verbo Syris & Chaldaeis noto formatum, quod manus è pariete apud Danielem egressa scripsit.נונאnumerata est familia. Mammon igitur & pecunias & res numeratas, in quibus divitiae sitae sunt, significat. *(Possent hîc tum de scriptione, tum de significatione vocis Mammonae pluscula ex Chemnitio, Drusio, Wasero, Glassio, Sculteto, H Grotio, Buxtorffio aliisque afferri, sed reiicere illa placet ad Luc. 16, 9.)*

*(Quemadmodum autem Salvator noster axiomate illo, Quod nemo possit duobus Dominis servire, firmiter colligit, quôd nemo queat firmâ fiduciâ Deo adhaerere, qui fiduciam collocat in divitiis, iisque servit: (Confer. seqq. Sc. loca 1. Sam. 2, 3.1. Reg. 18, 21.Matth. 13, 22.Luc. 1, 74. 75.Rom. 6, 19.c. 7, 6.) ita non minùs firmiter ex eodem colligimus 1. contra Pontificios, quôd non possint, salvo cultu soli vero aeterno DEO debito, Sancti religiosè invocari & coli, quo cultu tamen nihil apud Pontificios frequentius est. 2. contra Photinianos, quôd si Christus non esset verus ataeternus Deus, id quod ipsi illi pertinaciter negant, itidem non possit religiosè à nobis invocari, quod tamen nobiscum Photiniani praeviâ Sc. Sacrâ statuunt, certè quôd ita doceant, videri volunt. Nil iuvat hîc eos subordinationis figmentum, cùm inter personas SS. Trinitatis subordinatio locum non habeat, nec cultus verè religiosus tribui alicui possit, nisi fit Deus summus & aeternus. 3. contra Calvinianos, quôd renati quo-, imò & electi gratiam DEI, Sp. Sanctum ac fidem iustificantem ad tempus amittere possint, ac etiam amittant, quando nempe peccatis serviunt, uti David adulterium & homicidiū committens, siquidem fides salvifica ac Sp. Sancti gratiosa inhabitatio, cum peccatis contra conscientiam commissis haut magis simul cōsistere queunt, quàm aliquis duobus servire Dominis potest. Conf. Ioh. 8, 35.Rom. 6, 20. Excipit Wendelinus Exerc. 42. § 18. duo 1 dicit, Christum loqui de servitute planè voluntariâ, duobus contrariis Dominis simul praestandâ, quae, inquit, ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτωνest. Atqui Deo firmâ fiduciâ adhaerere, & carnem crucifigere, quod à renatis requirit Apostolus Gal. 5, 16. add. v. 24. ac contrà Diaboli ac carnis suggestionibus locum relinquere & opera carnis perficere, ita sese habent. E. Quôd verò ille, qui adulterium ac homicidium committit, id quod David renatus, ac procul dubio etiā electus, fecit, opera carnis perficiat & gratiam Dei excutiat, satis puto liquet ex eod. Apost. l. c. v. 19. 10. 21.

Nec dubito quoque, Wendelinum concessurum, Deum ac Diabolum esse Dominos contrarios, eosque, qui opera carnis perficiunt, non ex imbecillitate saltem labuntur, Spiritu haut servire DEO, sed Diabolo. 2. observandum putat Wendelinus, quôd ambiguè dicatur, servum esse peccati. Siquidem non solùm is dicatur peccato servire, qui peccatum regnans h. e. quod pleno voluntatis consensu perpetreatur, & cui peccator per Sp. S. gratiam non resistit, committit, verùm etiam ille dicatur servire peccato, qui peccati implicatus tenetur nexibus, & obluctante Spiritu ad peccata rapitur, & hoc modo Paulum dicere, se carne servire legi peccati,Rom. 7, 25. At nisi Wendelinus evicerit, quôd David posteriori saltem modo peccaverit, persistet nostra sententia, quôd renati adeoque etiam electi totaliter gratiam DEI aliqn. amittant, ita nempe peccato servientes, ut plenus voluntatis consensus accedat. Quis verò ambigat, Davidem pleno voluntatis consensu adulterium commisisse? Sed hâc dere alibi prolixiùs. 4. Contra hypocritas, quôd non leviter peccent, dum vel lucelli saltem gratiâ vel ex metu sacris haereti corum intersunt, externis gestibus consensum cum illis simulantes, vel saltem dissensum non indicantes. Sed de hoc negotio pluribus agit B. D. Bald. Cas Consc. pag. 197.)*

## 6:25
v. 25. Μεριμνᾶν is to be solicitous and to be anxious, which they derive from μερίζειν, so that εειμνᾶν is as it were ερίεδιν τὸν νοῦν, because solicitude pulls the soul into various parts. The true and genuine meaning of this passage depends on the proper explanation of this word. But τῶ μεριννᾶν is akin to μερμερίζειν. Hom. πολλὰ φρέσι μερμηρίζων, Virgil renders it.

But now he divides the swift soul hither, now thither, and drags it into various parts, and turns it through everything:

The heart indeed thinks something about the promises in its solicitudes, but it does not rest upon them with true faith, but a trembling and anxious solicitude distracts the soul. *(Similar sentiments of Christ are also found among the ancient Jews, just as Buxtorffius noted them in Lex. Talm. Rabb. under the word קטן p. 2017.)*

*(The Photinians abuse the present passage, while they strive to prove by this very thing that every pursuit of becoming rich is prohibited in the N. T. For if, they say, food and clothing which are nevertheless necessary for human life are prohibited by Christ, how much more must the care and pursuit of riches, as things which we can do without in human life, be considered prohibited. See Osterod Instit. Germ. c. 31. p. 234. seqq. Resp. Just as Christ did not simply forbid the care of food and clothing here, but at least insofar as it calls us away from the pursuit of seeking the kingdom of God, as Osterodus himself admits d. l. p. 135. or also insofar as it is joined with diffidence or excessive anxiety: so also the pursuit of riches must not be considered simply prohibited, but at least insofar as it is joined with either excessive anxiety of mind, or fraud and evil arts, or diffidence, or neglect of the kingdom of God, and is not undertaken with the intention of helping the needy and supporting oneself and one's own honestly, i.e., as the status and condition of each requires, and especially of promoting divine glory. We therefore oppose to the Photinians both the sayings 1. Cor 12, 14.1. Tim. 5, 8. and the examples of those who even in the N. T. were rich, i.e., possessed more than was necessary for the sustenance of life, physically considered, whose piety, however, riches did not harm. Compare more on this matter in B. D. Fewrb in AntiOst. Disp. 29. §. 21. seqq. it. B. D. Stegm. Disp. AntiPhot. LV. q. 6. 2. Bellarminus, while he tries to show from it that by daily bread in the Lord's Prayer one cannot understand either primarily or solely bodily bread. It is not credible, he writes l. 1. de B. O. in part. c. 6. p. 1364. that the Lord wished bodily bread to be asked for so solicitously either solely or primarily, when in the same sermon he commanded that solicitude for bodily things should be avoided, saying: Do not be solicitous etc. And a little later: If they were to say that these goods ought to be asked of God as additions, incidentally, implicitly, rarely: their response would not be to be despised: but that they themselves want these to be asked in the middle of the Lord's Prayer, which we ought to pour out daily with the greatest attention, and with the greatest zeal, does not rightly excuse the vice of excessive solicitude and anxiety. For how shall we not be too solicitous about the food of the body, if we beg for it so frequently and with such great attention? Perhaps someone might not badly have applied here to Cardinal Bellarminus what a learned man pronounced about Seneca, the encomiast of poverty, who nevertheless Tacitus reveals possessed three thousand times a hundred thousand sesterces: namely, that it was easy for this philosopher to praise poverty, who abounded in riches. Thus while Cardinal Bell. with the rest of the sycophants of the Roman curia with riches and delights

may abound, and may luxuriate from those goods which were once destined by pious Emperors and Kings for the promotion of divine worship, one might easily believe that they could so far cast off the care of temporal things, and even prayers for daily bread, that is, for those things which are necessary for food and clothing, that they might even reckon it among vain anxieties to think about such things, or to ask God that He might bestow them upon them out of His kindness. But, these things being omitted, we oppose to Bellarmine his associates Maldonatus and other Jesuits brought forward above, who assert that it is entirely a matter of bread alone in the fourth petition. But finally, it is so far from the case that prayers for those things which we need to sustain our life must be referred to the anxieties prohibited by Christ, that these things rather conflict with each other as much as possible, since Christ prohibits care joined with anxiety and diffidence, but he who hopes for, asks for, and expects from almighty God all things which he needs does not have such care. And who does not see that divine providence, prayers, and the labor of procuring what is necessary for life for oneself and one's own are subordinate, not opposed, (just as also in Holy Scripture labor and decent concern for sustenance is commanded. See. Eph. 4, 28.1. Tim. 5, 19.Genes. 3, 19.Prov. 6, 6.Eph. 4, 28. etc. and much more also prayers for the divine blessing of our labors.)* Hieron. in cap. 6. Matth. Labor must be exercised, solicitude must be cultivated.

*( Is not the soul etc. The blessed D. Glassius rightly notes in Gr. S. p. 659 that this is an elliptical expression here, and it must be understood: And yet God granted the soul life & body. Why therefore will He not also give food, as that which is less.)*

Chry-. hom. 16. oper. imperf. Because God created it in such a way that it is preserved by food, it is necessary that He give it food, as long as He wishes it to be what He made.

*(There is a notable passage here concerning divine providence, with which parallel passages can also be compared Deut. 8, 3.Psal. 104, 21.Ps. 136, 25.Psal. 145, 15.Matth. 10, 29. 30.Act. 17, 25. etc.)*

*( Do not be anxious for your soul. There are those who think that by soul here life is denoted, by metonymy, namely of the cause for the effect, Cf. Matth. 10, 19.cap. 16, 25. in which way the word נפש is also accepted Iob. 2, 6. thus after Augustine, Franc. Lucas in h. l. Polanus Synt. Theol. Gross. Theatr. Theol. p. 847. Erasmus Beza. To others it is more pleasing that by the name ψυχῆς belly and appetite for food should be understood, and they refer to this the passages Ezech. 7, 19.Ps. 107. 9. thus the blessed D. Quistorpius in h. l. who also in the notes to Luc. 12, 19. shows that among profane Greek authors those things are attributed to the soul which otherwise belong to the body )*

* (The Vulgate omits what they shall drink. That which, when it acted against the faith of all the Greek Codices which the Parisians and Beza compared, and indeed the Syrian Interpreter as well (I pass over the fact that both below v. 32. and in Luke c. 12, 29. the same things are read), so that he might not be thought to have done it alone, the Roman censors took care that in the Arabic edition of the N. T. also, which appeared at Rome, the same words should be omitted: yet the Leiden edition of the N. T. Arabic shows the fraud. Furthermore, the same words are also omitted in the Ethiopic N. Test., which saw the light at Rome in the year 1548.)*

Latin:

v. 25. Μεριμνᾶν est solicitum & anxium esse, quod derivant à μερίζειν, ut ita εειμνᾶν sit quas. ερίεδιν τὸν νοῦν, quia solicitudo animam in partes rapit varias. Ex propria huius verbi explicatione pendet verus & genuinus huius loci sensus. Est verò τῶ μεριννᾶν affine μερμερίζειν. Hom. πολλὰ φρέσι μερμηρίζων, id Virgil. reddit.

Atanimam celerem nunc huc, nunc dividit illuc,In partesrapit varias, peromnia versat:

Cogitat quidem in solicitudinibus cor aliquid de promissionibus, sed in eas non incumbit verâ fide, sed trepida & anxiâ solicitudo distrahit animum. *(Similes huic Christi sententiae & apud veteres Iudaeos reperiuntur, quemadmodum Buxtorffius eas annotavit in Lex. Talm. Rabb. voce קטן p. 2017.)*

*(Abutuntur praesenti loco 1. Photiniani, dum eo ipso omne ditescendi studium in N. T. prohibitum esse, evincere satagunt. Si enim, inquiunt, victûs & amictûs quae tamen ad vitam humanam necessaria sunt, cum à Christo prohibita est, quoantò magis cura ac studium divitiarum, utpote quibus in vitâ hum. carere possumus, prohibitum censendum est. Vid Osterod Instit. Germ. c. 31. p. 234. seqq. Resp. Quemadmodum Christus non simpliciter victûs & amictûs curam hîc vetuit, sed eatenus saltem, quatenus à studio quaerendi regni Dei nos avocat, ceu ipse fatetur Osterodus d. l. p. 135. vel etiam quatenus cum diffidentiâ vel nimiâ anxietate est coniuncta: ita quoq: divitiarum studium non simpliciter prohibitum censendum est, sed eatenus saltem, quat. vel cum nimiâ animi anxietate, vel fraude malisque artibus, vel diffidentiâ, vel regni Dei neglectu coniunctū est, nec intentione egenos iuvandi ac se suoshonestè h. e. prout cuius que status & conditio exigit, sustentandi, cumprimis verò divinam gloriam promovendi suscipitur. Opponimus igitur Photinianis tum dicta 1. Cor 12, 14.1. Tim. 5, 8. tum exempla eorum, qui etiam in N. T. d-vites fuerunt h. e. plura possiderunt, quàm ad sustentationem vitae, physicè spectatae, fuerunt necessaria, quorum tamen pietati divitiae nihil nocuerunt. Confer. plura in hanc rem apud B. D. Fewrb in AntiOst. Disp. 29. §. 21. seqq. it. B. D. Stegm. Disp. AntiPhot. LV. q. 6. 2. Bellarminus, dum ex eo ostendere conatur, quôd per panem quotidianum in Orat. Domin. non intelligi possit vel praecipuè vel solus panis corporalis. Non est credibile, scribit l. 1. de B. O. in part. c. 6. p. 1364. Dominum voluisse tam solicitè peti panem corporalem aut solum aut praecipuè, cum in eodem sermone praeceperit, cavendam esse sollicitudinem rerum corporaliū, dicens: Nolite solliciti esse &c. Et paulò post: Si dicerent, haec bona peti à Deo debere, ut additamenta, obiter, implicitè, rarò: non adspernanda esset eorum responsio: quod autem ipsi volunt, haec peti in media Omtione Dominica, quam debemus quotidie summâ attentione, summostudio fundere, non rectè vitium nimiae sollicitudinis & anxietatis excusat. Quomodo enim non erimus de cibo corporis nimium solliciti, fi eum tam crebro & tantâ cum attentione flagitemus? Fortè non malè quis hîc accommodaverit ad Cardinalem Bellarminum, quod de Seneca, paupertatis encomiaste, quem ter millies tamen sestertium possedisse Tacitus prodit, vir doctus pronunciavit: facilè nempe Philosophu huic fuisse, paupertatem laudare, qui divitiis affuebat. Sic dum Cardinalis Bell. cum reliquis curiae Romanae gnathonibus divitiis delitiis

affluant, ac de bonis illis, quae à piis quondam Imperatoribus ac Regibus cultui divino promovendo destinata sunt, luxurientur, facilè aliquis crediderit, eos intantum temporalium curam, adeoetiam preces pro pane quotidiano h. e. illis quae ad victum & amictum necessaria sunt, abiicere posse, ut inter vanas quoque sollicitudines reputent, de his talibus cogitare, vel Deum ut ex suâ benignitate ipsis largiatur, rogare. Caeterùm omissis his opponimus Bellarmino sociennos suos Maldonatum aliosque Iesuitas suprà adductos, qui omninò de solo pane in quartâ petitione agi, adserunt. Tantum verò denique abest, ut preces pro iis, quibus ad vitam nostram sustentandam opus habemus, impetrandis ad Deum fuse inter sollicitudines à Christo prohibitas referri debeāt, ut potiùs quàm maximè isthaec invicem pugnent, cùm Christus prohibeat curam cum anxietate & diffidentia coniunctam, talem vero non habet, qui à Deo omnipotente omnia sperat, petir, expectat, quibus opus habet. Et quis non videt, quôd providentia divina, preces, ac labor procurandi sibi suisque necessaria ad vitam, fint subordinata, non opposita, (sicuti etiam in Sc. S. labor ac decens victûs solicitudo mandatur. Vid. Eph. 4, 28.1. Tim. 5, 19.Genes. 3, 19.Prov. 6, 6.Eph. 4, 28. &c. acmulto magis etiam preces pro benedictione divinâ nostrorum laborum.)* Hieron. in cap. 6. Matth. Labor exercendus, solicitudo collenda.

*( Nonne anima &c. Rectè notat B. D. Glassius. Gr. S. p. 659. esse hîc ellipticam locutionem, ac subintelligendum: Et tamen Deus animam s-vitam & corpus concessit. quidni igitur & alimenta dabit, ut quod minus est.)*

Chry-. hom. 16. oper. imperf. Quod Deus sic creavit, ut per escam servetur, necesse est, ut det ei escam, quamdin vult esse, quod fecit.

*(Est insignis hîc locus de providentia divinâ, cum quo etiam conferri possunt loca parallela Deut. 8, 3.Psal. 104, 21.Ps. 136, 25.Psal. 145, 15.Matth. 10, 29. 30.Act. 17, 25. &c.)*

*( Ne sit is soliciti anima vestrae. Sunt qui per animam hîc vitam denotari putant, per metonym. sc. causae pro effectu, Conf. Matth. 10, 19.cap. 16, 25. quomodo etiam accipitur vox נפשIob. 2, 6. ita post Augustinum Franc. Lucas in h. l. Polanus Synt. Theol. Gross. Theatr. Theol. p. 847. Erasmus Beza. Aliis magis placet, ut nomine ψυχῆς intelligatur venter ac cibi appetitus, atque huc referunt loca Ezech. 7, 19.Ps. 107. 9. sic B. D. Quistorpius in h. l. qui etiam in notis ad Luc. 12, 19. ostendit, quôd apud prophanos autores Graecos anima tribuantur ea, quae aliàs corpori competunt-)*

* (Vulg. omittit quid bibituri. id quod cùm contra omnium Codd. Graecorum, quos Parisienses ac Beza contulerunt, quin Syri quoque Interpretis fidem (taceo, quod tum infrà v. 32. tum apud Lucam c. 12, 29. eadem legantur,) fecerit, ne solus fecisse existimetur, curarunt Romani censores, ut in edit. quoque N. T. Arabica, quae Romae prodiit, eadem verba omitterentur: ostendit tamen fraudē editio N. T. Arab. Leidensis. Caeterùm omissa quoque eadem verba in N. Test. Aethiopico, quod Romae A. 1548. lucem adspexit.)*

## 6:26
v. 26. Let it be a shame not to derive customs from small animals, says Seneca, book 1, On Providence. The Lord could have brought forward examples of men whom God provided for by special grace, such as Ishmael and Hagar, Gen. 21. Moses, Exod. 24. Elijah 1. Kings 19. but He studiously omits these examples and brings forward the birds, and not those which are studiously kept by men for their song, but the birds of the air, which fly in the free air, and indeed in Luke mention is made specifically of sparrows and ravens, of which the former are annoying to them with their noisy song, while the latter are hated by all because of their black color. *( Your Father feeds them. See the remarkable passage pertaining to this, both from Kiddushin in the Mishnah and from the Gemara of the Jerusalem Talmud, in Buxtorf, Lex. Talm. Rabb. p. 2028.)* *(Are you not of much more value? It seems Τὸ μᾶλλον here πλεονάζειν, but he adds a singular emphasis to the word, as the blessed D. Glass well advises, Gr. S. page 517.)*

Latin:

v. 26. Pudeat ab exiguis animalibus non trahere mores, ait Seneca lib. 1. de provid. Poterat Dominus exempla hominum proferre, quibus Deus ex peculiari gratia prospexit, ut Ismaelis & Agaris, Gen. 21. Mosis, Exod. 24. Eliae 1. Reg. 19. sed haec exempla studiosè omittit & produeit volucres, nec illas, quae studiosè ob cantum ab hominibus aluntur, sed volucres coeli, quae in libero aëre volitant, & quidem apud Lucam mentio fit in specie passerum & corvorum, ex quibus illis strepero suo cantu sunt molesti, hi verò propter colorem atrum omnibus invisi. *( Pater vester alit eas. Vide insignem locum tum ex Kidduschin in Mischna, tum ex Gemara Talmud Hierosolymitani huc facientem apud Buxtorff. Lex. Talm. Rabb p. 2028.)* *(Non vos multum praestatis? Videtur Τὸ μᾶλλον hîc πλεονάζειν, sed singularem emphasin verbo addit, uti benè monet B. D. Glass. Gr. S. pag. 517.)*

## 6:27
v. 27. Why does He mention a cubit? Not as if we could add a palm or a finger, but not a cubit, but because, as Euthymius noted, the measure of a man's stature corresponds to the quadruple proportion of his cubit, which is the interval from the bend of the arm to the top part of the middle finger.

Latin:

v. 27. Quare meminit cubiti? non qs. nos vel palmum vel digitum, non autem cubitum addere possimus, sed quia, ut Euthym. annotavit, mensura staturae hominis respondet quadruplae proportioni cubiti eius, qui est intervallum à slexu brachii ad supremam partem medii digiti.

## 6:28
v. 28. Old Lexicon. κατααανθάνω I consider. Sir. 9. v. 5. πααρθένον αὴκαταμάνθανε do not contemplate.

I saw in the morning the rose born with the light of the Sun, And I saw it again, as the Sun was setting, die.

*(The Savior intends, namely, that from the lilies of the field, which nevertheless so quickly perish and are as it were reduced to nothing, we should nonetheless take an argument for divine providence, since they are adorned so very beautifully by God.)*

Latin:

v. 28. Lexicon vetus.κατααανθάνωconsidero.Sir. 9. v. 5.πααρθένον αὴκαταμάνθανεne contemplare.

Vidi ego mane rosam nasci cum lumine SolisEt vidi rursum, Sole cadente, mori.

*(Vult nempe Salvator, ut ex liliis agri, quae tamen adeô citò pereunt & in nihilum qs. rediguntur, nihilominùs tamen admodum pulcrè à Deo ornantur, providentiae divinae argumentum sumamus.)*

## 6:29
(v. 29. Not even Solomon in all his glory.) Camero notes in Myroth. Ev. p. 12. δόξων is taken here for splendor, and he compares it with this passage Acts 22:11 also 1 Cor. 15:40. Thus בבוך is accepted for a splendid garment Ps. 45:15 Esth. 15:4 Is. 10:16 as observed by Drusius in the second part of Annotations on the New Testament p. 13. Compare here the excellent sentiment of Solon in Diogenes Laërtius in his life p. m. 34. and add Macarius hom. 32. p. 415. 417.)

Latin:

*(v. 29. Ne Salomonem quidem in omni gloria suâ.) Notat Camero Myroth. Ev. p. 12. δόξων hîc sumi pro splendore, ac confert cum hoc loco Act. 22, 11. it. 1. Cor. 15: 40. Sic בבוך accipitur pro amictu splendido Ps. 45, 15.Esth. 15, 4.Es. 10, 16. observ. Drusio parte alt. Annot. in N. T. p. 13. Conf. hîc egregia sententia Solonis apud Diog. Laërtiū in eius vita p. m. 34. ac adde Macariū hom. 32. p. 415. 417.)*

## 6:30
(v. 30. If God so clothes the grass of the field. The clothing here with flowers, as Macarius notes in the said place, is internal, which, just as similar passages Ps. 104:2 Job 10:11, is to be opposed to Bellarmine asserting in his book on the grace of the first man ch. 6 that a garment is something external, and furthermore from the fact that original justice Eccl. 17:1 3 is compared with a garment, striving to prove that it was at least an external gift to the first man.)

( Which exists today &c. Let Gataker be seen entirely here in his work on the style of the New Testament p. 169. 170. and compare Ps. 90:5, 6)

( Tomorrow is cast into the oven. See B. D. Glass. Exeg. on the Gospel for the 15th Sunday after Trinity p. 477. H. Grot. on this passage.)

( Will He not much more clothe you. These words are not to be taken as if Christ were calling us away from the due labors of our office, and promising that, just as God clothes the lilies of the field, although they neither toil nor spin, are accustomed to weave, so also for us the same is to be expected without any labor of our own. No. For καθάπερ As Chrysostom well warns in hom. 22 on Matthew. Which is to be observed both against the Euchites, against whom Augustine is to be seen in his book on the Work of Monks, add also Theod. b. 4. Hist. ch. 11. and against the modern Monks who are candidates for sloth, about whom Cassian writes in b. 2. on the Nocturnal Canons. But more on these at 2 Thess. 3:8. Furthermore, the genuine sense of the present admonition of Christ, besides B. D. Chem. in the Harmony of the Gospels and other commentators, is shown excellently and sufficiently at length by B. D. Frantzius on the Interpretation of the Oracles of Holy Scripture p. 130. But the present passage is also treated quite copiously by the Expositors of the Sunday Gospels. One must see especially B. D. Glassius in the Exegesis of the Sunday Gospels for the XV after Trinity. To which can be added from the Papists Henr. Lancelotz of Mechelen in the Anatomy of the Deformed Christian p. 139. seqq. who also distinguishing solicitude into) illicit and condemned, concerning which Christ is in this place, and licit. concerning which he writes that the Apostle Jude treats in his Epistle v 3. he ineptly calls this meritorious. He omits moreover also another, likewise licit solicitude, concerning which Gen. 41Prov. 6.Eph. 4, 28.2. Thes. 3, 12.

( Ὀλιγόπιστοι. The passage Iac. 1, 5. seems to stand in the way. But distinguish between heathen doubt, and between the infirmity of the flesh, concerning the former it is treated v. 31. 32. and Iac. 1, 5. concerning the latter in the present verse.)

Latin:

*(v. 30. Si herbam agri Deus ita vestit. Vestitus hîc floribus, uti Macarius d. l. notat, intrinsecus est, id quod, sicuti & similia loca Psal. 104, 2.Iob. 10, 11. opponendum Bellarmino adserenti l. de gr. pr. hom. c. 6. quôd indumentum sit aliquid extrinsecum, atporrò inde, quôd iustitia originalis Eccl. 17, 1.3. conferatur cum veste, evincere satagenti, fuisse eam saltem donum extrinsecum primo homini.)*

*( Quae hodiè extat &c. Videatur omninò hîc Gatakerus in de stylo N. Test. p. 169. 170. ac conf. Ps. 90, 5. 6.)*

*( Cras in clibanum mittitur. Vid. B. D. Glass. Exeg. Dom. 15. post Trin. p. 477. H. Grot. in h. l.)*

*( Nonne vos multò magis. Verba haec non ita accipienda sunt, quasi Christus à debitis officii laboribus nos avocet, promittatque, sicuti Deus lilia agri vestit, licet neque fatigentur s. laborent, nenere soleant, ita & nobis absullo nostro labore idem esse expectandum. Non. Etenim καθάπερ Uti benè monet Chrysost. hom. 22. in Matth. Id quod observandum tum contra Euchitas, quos contra videndus August. lib. de Opere Monachorum, add. quoque Theod. l. 4. Hist. c. 11. tum contra hodiernos Monachos desidiae candidatos, de quibus Cassian. l. 2. de Can. Noct. At de his plura ad 2. Thess. 3, 8. Caeterùm genuinum praesentis admonitionis Christi sensum, praeter B. D. Chem. in Harm. Evang. aliosque commentatores, egregiè ac satis prolixè ostendit B. D. Frantzius de Interpret. Sr. S. Orac. 130. Sed & ab Expositoribus Evangeliorum Dominicalium praesens locus satis copiosè tractatur. Videndus cumprimis B. D. Glassius Exeg. Evang. Domin. XV post Trinit. Cui adiungi ex Pontificiis potest Henr. Lancelotz Mechliniensis in Anatom. Christiani deformati p. 139. seqq. qui etiam solicitudinē distinguens in illicitam ac damnatam, de qua Christus h. l. & licitam. de quâ Apostolum Iudam agere scribit in Epist. suâ v 3. hanc ineptè meritoriam vocat. Omittit insuper & aliam, itidem licitam sollicitudinem, de quâ Gen. 41Prov. 6.Eph. 4, 28.2. Thes. 3, 12.)*

*( Ὀλιγόπιστοι. Videtur obstare locus Iac. 1, 5. Verùm disting. inter dubitationem E hnicam, & inter carnis infirmitatem, de illa agitur v. 31. 32. it Iac. 1, 5. de hâc praes. vers.)*

## 6:31
(v. 31. Therefore do not be anxious etc. Compare Phil. 4, 5.Psal. 55, 22. August. sermon 33. on Luke: The love of earthly things (so also excessive solicitude) is the birdlime of spiritual wings, the heart is dragged down and as it were glued to earthly things, so that it cannot be raised by serious study to heavenly and celestial things. Conf. 1. Tim. 6, 9. With what we shall be clothed. Still more to be reprehended is the solicitude concerning that clothing with which some are proud. Concerning which matter see B. D. Bald. Cas Consc. p. 866. following.)

Latin:

*(v. 31. Ne igitur estote soliciti &c. Confer Phil. 4, 5.Psal. 55, 22. August. serm 33. in Lucam: Amor rerum terrenarum (sic quoque sollicit. nimia) est viscus spiritualium pennarum, detrabitur cor & quasi agglutinatur ad terrena, ut serio studio ad superna & coelestia elevari nequeat. Conf. 1. Tim. 6, 9.Quo amiciemur. Magis adhuc reprehendenda sollicitudo de eo vestitu, quo nonnulli superbiunt. Quâ de re vid. B. D. Bald. Cas Consc. p. 866. seqq.)*

## 6:32
v. 32. Ἔθνη ἐπιζητεῖ ταδτα, they anxiously seek those things and with every effort of the mind are intent upon them, Christians ought not to do that, but let earthly things be for them in use, heavenly things in desire.

( Your Father knows that you need all these things. What need is there therefore for prayers? Resp. This is opposed not to pious prayer, as being commanded in the Holy Scripture Ps. 50, 15.Matth. 7, 7. nor to moderate care, of which there exist in the Holy Scripture both precepts Prov. 6, 6.Eph. 4, 28.1. Tim. 5, 8.2. Thes. 3, 10. 11. 12, and examples Gen. 41, 33.Ioh. 6, 12. 13.Act. 11, 28. 29., but to immoderate solicitude, as is evident from the context. See v. 30.33. Interlinear Gloss to v. 34. Labor and providence (much less prayers) are not condemned, but solicitude, suffocating the mind. Theophylact also has similar things in this place. Nor do we pour out prayers to GOD for this end, that our necessities might become known to Him, or do we labor for this reason, as if God could not sustain us without the labor of our hands: But because He Himself has so ordained and commanded. In whose most wise ordination it is entirely our duty to acquiesce, and to obey His most wholesome commands. But how temporal things are to be sought, B. D. K-nig Cas. Consc. page 175 teaches excellently.)

Latin:

v. 32. Ἔθνη ἐπιζητεῖ ταδτα, anxiè ea quaerunt & omni animi conatu sunt illis intenti, id Christiani non debent facere, sed terrena illis sint in usu, coelestia in desiderio.

*( Novit Pater vester vos indigere his omnibus. Quid opus igitur precibus? Resp. Oppositum hoc non orationi piae, utpote in Sc. S. mandatae Ps. 50, 15.Matth. 7, 7.nec moderatae curae, cuius in Sc. S. & praecepta Prov. 6, 6.Eph. 4, 28.1. Tim. 5, 8.2. Thes. 3, 10. 11. 12, & exempla Gen. 41, 33.Ioh. 6, 12. 13.Act. 11, 28. 29. extant, sed sollicitudini immoderatae, ceu ex contextu patet. Vid. v. 30.33. Glossa Interlin. ad v. 34.Non labor & providentia (multò minùs preces) damnantur, sed sollicitudo, mentem suffocans. Similia & Theophylactus habet in h. l. Quomodo verò temporalia petenda sint, egregiè docet B. D. K-nig Cas. Consc. pag. 175.)*

v. 33. August. book 2. on the sermon of the Lord on the mount col 2158. What difference there is between the good, which is to be sought, and the necessary, which is to be taken, this sentence has declared. For when He says that first, He signified, that this latter is to be sought, not in time but in dignity, that as our good, this as our necessary, but necessary on account of that good.

## 6:34
v. 34. Some establish an ellipsis in the phrase. Be not anxious for the morrow, i.e. ἀποβλέποντες looking toward. Prov. 27. v. 1. boast not of the morrow i.e. of future time. Exod. 13. v 14. If your son asks you tomorrow; where R. Solomon says: Tomorrow is taken properly also for future time, as here and in that place. When your sons shall say tomorrow. *(add. Deut. 6, 20.Ioh. 4, 6.21.)* Furthermore μεριμνᾶν εις τὴ ἄυριον, is a phrase of the Hebrews, but it is also of the Greeks: For in Athenaeus book 7 there is φροιτίζειν εἰς ἄυριον.

Reservation for the morrow is not simply prohibited, but anxiety, so that, namely, they should not be so anxious that anxiety itself separates us from God, whom we ought to serve. For He did not say: keeping nothing for the morrow, but do not be anxious for the morrow. Theophyl. It is enough for you that you are overwhelmed by today's affliction; but if you are also anxious for the morrow, when will you have leisure for God, always torturing yourself for temporal things?

Believe me, daily cares return with the Sun, believe me, daily meals return with the Sun.

*(v. 35. Do not be anxious. But Solomon seems to imply the contrary Prov 6, 6. The Jesuit Becanus, lib. 1. Manual. Controv. c. 1. §. 7. ἐνατιφ. refers to this among those apparent contradictions, which create great difficulty for the reader. But if anyone just looks at the present text a little more diligently, he will easily discover that our Savior does not prohibit the labor of duty or moderate care about the future, to which Solomon urges the sluggard, but at least wishes us to be free from too anxious and immoderate solicitude, and that which is joined with diffidence and neglect of those things which pertain to the salvation of the soul. As I judge to be sufficiently clear from what was said before. Beautifully Chrysost. in c. 6. Matth. Let not the care of a further day crush you: for since you do not know the span of the day you will see, for what reason are you tormented by the solicitude of that one? Furthermore, since by prosopopoeia the care is ascribed here to the day itself, Chrysostom judges that it was done not without emphasis: βουλόθυος, he writes hom. 22. Matth. ἐμφατικ And again a little later: ἵναμειζ. The Blessed D. Quistorpius exhibits the dissuasions of Gentile writers from frivolous solicitude about the future in this place. Drusius, however, presents those of the Jews, lib. 1. Praeter. p. 22. Let Zehnerus also be added, Cent. 1. Adag. 8. & 9. p. 428.)*

*( The malice of the day is sufficient. In Greek it is κακία, which word for κακώοει or affliction (just as among the Hebrews רעה See 1. Sam 6, 9. Esa. 45, 7. Amos 3, 6. which passages Chrysost. also cites here, to which add Deut. 32, 23. Jonah 3, 10. and others, it is accepted,) it is the common opinion of interpreters that it is placed here. Thus St. August. Jerome, Chrysostom, Euthymius, Theophylact. Whence our Blessed Luther not badly translated it Plage/

affliction, just as Beza and Erasmus also rendered it. The Syrian, however, and the Arab use such words here which likewise almost together κακίαν i.e., denote the evil of fault.)*

Jerome in Epistle 147 to Amandus. You ask what that means in the Gospel according to Matthew: Do not be anxious about tomorrow, for the day's own evil is sufficient for it. Tomorrow in the Holy Scriptures signifies future time, just as Jacob also speaks in Genesis: My righteousness will answer for me tomorrow. He therefore who forbade us to think about future things, granted it concerning present things on account of the fragility of human life. But what he adds, the day's own evil is sufficient for it, understand it in this way, it is sufficient for us to think about the present straits of this age. What necessity is there to extend the sense to uncertain or future things, which we either cannot attain or, once found, quickly lose. κακία for, which the Latin translates as evil, signifies two things among the Greeks, both evil and affliction, which κάκωσιν the Greeks call, and here affliction ought rather to have been translated instead of evil. But if anyone is led by contention, unwilling κακίαν to sound as affliction and straits, but as evil, it must be explained in that sense in which the world is placed in the wicked one, that is, in evil, and in the Lord's Prayer we say, deliver us from evil, so that it may be sufficient for us to have the present struggle against the evil of this age.

*A brief disposition and summary of this chapter. In this chapter nine most wholesome admonitions are proposed, namely concerning two things to be avoided and seven to be done. To be avoided and shunned are --rash judgment of one's neighbor, or condemnation, v. 1. 5. 2. profanation of heavenly doctrine, v. 6. The number of things to be done constitutes 1. ardent prayer, v. 7. 11. 2. relief of one's neighbor, v. 12. 3. walking in the narrow way, v. 23. v. 14. 4. diligent caution against False Prophets, v. 15. 20. 5. declaration of faith by Good Works. v. 21. 6. conformation of life to the norm of the heard word, v. 24. 27. 7. estimation and pious admiration of the sermons of Christ, vers. 28.) *

Sam 6, 9.Esa. 45, 7.Amos 3, 6. quae loca & Chrysost. hîc adducit, quibus adde Deut. 32, 23. Ionae 3, 10. & alia, accipitur,) hîc poni, communis Interpp. sententia est. Ita S. August. Hieron. in Epist. 147. ad Amandum. Interrogas, quid significet illud in Evangelio iuxta Matthaeum: Nolite soliciti esse de crastino, sufficit enim diei malitia sua. Crastinum in Scripturis sanctis futurum tempus significat, sicut & Iacob in Genesi loquitur: Exaudiet me cras iustitia mea. Qui ergo de futuris nos cogitare prohibuit, concessit de praesentibus propter humanae vitae fragilitatem. Quod autem adiicit, sufficit diei malitia sua, hoc modò intellige, sufficit nobis de praesentibus huius seculi angustiis cogitare. Quid necesse est, sensum ad incerta aut futura extendere, quae aut consequi non possumus aut citò inventa perdamus.κακίαenim, quam Latinus vertit malitiam, duo significat apud Graecos & malitiam, & afflictionem, quamκάκωσινGraeci dicunt, & hîc magis pro malitia transferri debuit afflictio. Quod fi contentione quis ducitur, nolensκακίανafflictionem sonare & angustias, sed malitiam, illo sensu explicandum est, quo mundus in maligno h. e. malo positus sit, & in Dominica oratione dicimus, libera nos à malo, ut sufficiat nobis contra malitiam huius seculi praesens habere certamen.
