O. declaratio. v. 21. 6. vitae ad normam verbi auditi conformatio, v. 24. 27. 7. sermonum Christi aestimatio ac pia admiratio, vers. 28.) *

## 7:1
* (v. 1. Do not judge. By these words the Savior prohibits private judgment, and that not every kind, but unjust, rash, supercilious, arising from mere suspicions, and proceeding from contempt of one's neighbor and φιλαυτίᾳ having no regard for human infirmity, as Interpreters note with unanimous consent. Jerome in this place: If He prohibits judging, by what consequence does Paul in Corinth judge the fornicator, and Peter convict Ananias and Sapphira of lying? But from the consequences He shows what He prohibited, saying: For with what judgment you judge, so shall it be judged of you. Here He did not prohibit judging, but taught. Chrysostom in this place likewise teaches at length that judgment is not only permitted, but sometimes even necessary. He concludes therefore: Let us weigh more diligently what this is, therefore, that has been said, And to the prudent indeed from these things which follow, He shows most clearly the virtue of this law, by saying: Why do you see the mote &c. But if to the many of the slow this seems obscure, we will -tempt to elucidate that same thing more fully. ( Compare more in the cited Father, as also Augustine, sermon 202. de Temp. Therefore the rule holds here, to be noted concerning the interpretation of Holy Scripture: Certain things are set forth or prohibited in Holy Scripture ἁπλῶς, which nevertheless κατὰ τὶ are to be understood as prohibited. Thus, in this place, judging others is prohibited, which, however, is to be accepted not concerning every judgment, but concerning private, and therefore rash, judgment. Therefore, Christ by no means prohibits or abolishes 1. the public judgment of the Political Magistrate, since it is sufficiently founded in the Holy Scriptures. See Deut. 1, 16. 17. (which saying the Savior also alleges Ioh. 7, 24.) 2. Paral. 19, 6. Ps 58, 2.Rom. 13, 1. etc. and that the contrary cannot be gathered from this place, some judge to be evident from the fact that Christ was preaching here not to the Political Magistrate, but to the promiscuous crowd. Nor 2. the judgment of the Ministers of the Church concerning both doctrine and the correct interpretation of Scripture, 1. Cor. 14, 29. and concerning the life of the hearers. For such judgment is so far from being taken away from the Ministers of the Church that it is rather required of them in the highest degree, See Tit. 1, 9. Conf. Esa. 5, 20. nor 3. is the judgment of a neighbor proceeding from love, looking toward his amendment, prohibited. For such fraternal correction is likewise sufficiently founded in Holy Scripture. See Lev. 19. 17.Prov. 22, 15. etc. Matth. 18, 15. (which place Chrysostom also adduces) nor 4. is the judgment of hearers concerning preached doctrine taken away. See Matth. 7, 15.1 Cor. 10, 15.c. 11, 13.1. Thess. 5, 21.1. Ioh. 4, 1. as all these things are shown more prolixly in their own place. Which things are to be well noted partly against the Anabaptists, who strive to take away the power of judging from the Magistrate, and partly against the Papists, who command that hearers should simply acquiesce in the doctrine of Pastors, and institute no scrutiny from Holy Scripture, and others. Furthermore, some Latin codices add to this member: Do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned. Which reading the Jesuit Maldonatus strives to defend at length. But since the most corrected and most ancient Greek codices do not recognize those words, and hence neither does the most ancient Syrian Interpreter, just as also neither the Arab, the Ethiopian, and the author of the Gospel of Matthew, edited in Hebrew by Münster, to say nothing now of the Fathers, Greek and Latin alike, such as Chrysostom, the author of the Opus Imperfectum, Euthymius, Theophylact on this place, from the Latins Tertullian

CHAPTER VII.

in his book on patience, Ambrose in his book on the sermon of the Lord, Jerome, Hilary, Bede, Strabo, Rupert on this place, and others, we consider it rash, with so many witnesses from the East and West denying their suffrage, nay, reclaiming, to desert the received Greek reading. Which matter also moved the very associates of Maldonatus, Corn. à Lapide, Tirinus, Barrhadius, and others, to acknowledge that those words are not a genuine part of this place, but were transferred from Luke into certain Latin codices of Matthew. Corn. à Lapide explicitly: Suppose, he says, that it be heldLuc. 6, 37. and yet this is the principal reason of Maldonatus. Furthermore, it agrees with the Savior's warning, the maxim of R. Joshua ben Perachiah, which is expressed in Pirke Avoth in these words: הוי רן את צל הארם לצף זצות judge every man to the scale of innocence.

You shall not be judged, i.e., you shall not be punished by God for the reason that you have so hatefully exaggerated another's splinter, not perceiving the beam in your own eyes; or God will not permit that another in turn -estra so spitefully perverts, lacerates, and carps. The Hebrews say: He who hates his brother always judges him by the scale of sin (that is, of condemnation) but he who loves him, judges by the scale of equity.

Latin:

* (v. 1. Nolite iudicare. Prohibet his verbis Salvator iudicium privatum idque non omne, sed iniquum, stemerarium, superciliosum, ex meris suspicionibus ortum, è proximi contemtu acφιλαυτίᾳprofectum, nullamque infirmitatis humanae rationem habens, ceu unanimi consensu notant Interpretes. Hieronymus in h. l. Si iudicare prohibet, quâ consequentiâ Paulus in Corintho iudicat fornicantem, & Petrus Ananiam & Sapphiram mendacii coarguit? Sed ex consequentibus quid prohibuerit, ostendit, dicens: Quomodo enim iudicaveritis, sic iudicabitur de vobis. Hic non prohibuit iudicare, sed docuit. Chrysostomus in h. l. itidem prolixè docet, quòd omninò iudicium non solùm concessum, sed etiam necessarium aliquando sit. Concludit igitur: Quidnam hoc sit ergo, quod dictum est, diligentius ponderemus,Et prudentibus quidem ex his quae sequuntur, lucidissimè virtutem istius legis ostendit, dicendo: Quid vides festucam &c. Si verò plurimis tardorum istud videatur obscurum, plenius idipsum elucidare -entabimus. ( Conf. plura apud laudatum Patrem tum quoque August. serm. 202. de Temp. Valet ergò hîc regula, circa Sc. S. interpretationem notanda: Quaedam in Sc. S. efferuntur vel prohibenturἁπλῶς, quae tamen κατὰ τὶprohibita sunt intelligenda. Sic h. l. iudicare de aliis prohibetur, quod tamen accipiendum non de omni iudicio, sed de iudicio privato, eoque temerario. Minimè igitur Christus prohibet vel abolet 1. Iudicium publicum Magistratus Politici, quippe quod satis in sacris literis fundatum. Vid. Deut. 1, 16. 17. (quod dictum etiam allegat Salv. Ioh. 7, 24.) 2. Paral. 19, 6. Ps 58, 2.Rom. 13, 1. &c. nec contrarium ex h. l. colligi posse, nonnulli exinde patere censent, quòd Christus non Magistratui Politico, sed promiscuae plebi hic concionatus fuerit. nec 2. Iudicium Ministrorum Ecclesiae tum de doctrinâ ac rectâ Scripturae Interpretatione, 1. Cor. 14, 29. tum de vitâ auditorum. Tale enim iudicium tantum abest, ut ademtum Ministris Ecclesiae sit, ut potiùs quammaximè ab illis requiratur, Vid. Tit. 1, 9. Conf. Esa. 5, 20. nec 3. prohibetur iudicium proximi ex amore profectum, eius dememendationem respiciens. Talis enim correctio fraterna itidem in Sc. S. satis fundata. Vid. Lev. 19. 17.Prov. 22, 15. &c. Matth. 18, 15. (quem locum etiam Chrysostomus adducit) nec 4. ademtum auditoribus iudicium de doctrina praedicatâ. Vid. Matth. 7, 15.1 Cor. 10, 15.c. 11, 13.1. Thess. 5, 21.1. Ioh. 4, 1. uti suo loco haec omnia prolixiùs ostenduntur. Quae partim contra Anabaptistas, iudicandi potestatem Magistratui adimere satagentibus, partim contra Pontificios, iubentes ut auditores in doctrinâ Pastorum simpliciter acquiescant, nullumque ex Sc. lib. de patientiâ, Ambros. libro de serm. Non iudicabimini i. e. non puniemini à Deo proptera quod alienam festucam adeò odiosè exaggeraveritis, non cernentes in oculis vestris trabem; vel non permittet Deus, ut alius vicissim -estra ita lividè pervertat, laceret, carpat. Hebraei dicunt. Qui odit fratrem suum, semper iudicat illum lance peccati (id est condemnationis) Qui verò amat eum, iudicat lance aequitatis.

## 7:2
v. 2. In Sanhedrin tractate on Judges, chapter במרה שארם מורר בה מוררים לו ׃ חלק That measure, with which a man measures, they shall measure to him. (Buxtorf in Lex. Talm. p. 1171, from Sotah c. 1, in Mishna Shab. f. 100. 1, alleges this sentence thus: במרה שמורר ארם מוררין לו ׃ The blessed D. Glassius also notes in Rhet. S. p. 500, that in the Targum Hieros. Gen. 38 these things are read: With what measure a man measures, with the same shall others measure to him, as regards a good measure and as regards a bad measure. Let the same l. c. p. 406 be compared also entirely, to the aforementioned, also the note to Mark 4, 24. The blessed D. Tarnovius mentions in l. 3, de Coni. p. 957, that some abuse this sentence, and from it try to prove that husbands ought to receive back adulterous wives, since God also forgives spiritual adulteries to the husbands themselves when they repent. But the praised Theologian responds, distinguishing between the forgiveness of guilt, and reception into the marital covenant, and notes that this saying speaks of the former, not of the latter.)

*( Cast out first the beam. See Zehnerus, illustrating this adage in many ways in Adag. sacr. p. 423, seqq. A similar sentence also from the book Erachin f. 16. 2, Buxtorf: in Lex. Chald Talm. pag. but from Elijah Levita in Tisbi root. נטל Lud. Capell. brings forward in spic. p. 18. This proverb is also explained in vol. 2. Dispp. Dn. Di-herri p. 329. and also by B. D. Glassius Rhen. S. p. 291. But the Savior depicts in this allegorical expression the character of slanderers, namely that they are too curious and more sharp-sighted than Argus in examining and criticizing the infirmities of others, even light ones; but in recognizing their own, even if they are grave, they are blinder than a mole. Therefore, he who is about to reprehend others ought first to examine and shake out his own life severely, and then perhaps he will pronounce more kindly concerning the d-lictis of his neighbor: Confer the excellent sentiment. Greg. M. part. 2. Curae Pastor. c. 10.)*

Druf. in Prov. Rabini. decur. 7. prov. 5. brings forward from the Rabbis. מרה צננר מרה Measure for measure. *(Conf. more on this matter Capellus in spicil. p. 17. where he brings forward a similar sentiment of the Jews from the Misna.)*

Latin:

v. 2. In Sanhedrin tract. de Iudicibus capite במרה שארם מורר בה מוררים לו ׃ חלקMensura illa, qua homo metitur, eidem metientur illi.* (Buxtorf. in Lex. Talm. p. 1171. ex Sotah c. 1. in Mischna Schab. f. 100. 1. sententiam hanc ita allegat: במרה שמורר ארם מוררין לו ׃ Notat quoque B. D. Glass. Rhet. S. p. 500. in Targhum Hieros. Gen. 38 haec legi: Quâ mensurâ homo metitur, eadem metientur ei alii, quoad mensuram bonam & quoad mensuram malam. Conferatur quoque omninò idem l. c. p. 406. ad d. quoq; not. ad Marc. 4, 24. Memorat B. D. Tarnov. l. 3. de Coni. p. 957. quosdam hâc sententiâ abuti, & exinde probare conari, quòd viri uxores adulteras recipere debeant, cùm Deus quoque ipsis viris poenitent ibus spiritualia adulteria remittat. Respondet verò laudatus Theologus, dist. inter condonationem culpae, & receptionem in foedus coniugale, notatque de priori loqui hoc dictum, non de posteriori.)*

*( Eiice priùs trabem. Vide multis adagium hoc illustrantem tem Zehnerum in Adag. sacr. p. 423. seqq. Similem quoque sententiam ex libro Erachin f. 16. 2. Buxtorf: in Lex. Chald Talm. pag. ex Eliâ verò Levita in Tisbi rad. נטל adfert Lud. Capell. in spic. p. 18. Exponitur quoque proverbium hoc. t. 2. Dispp. Dn. Di-herri p. 329. nec non à B. D. Glassio Rhen. S. p. 291. Depingit verò Salvator allegoricâ hâc locutione calumniatorum ingenium, quòd nempe in aliorum infirmitatibus, levibus etiam, examinandis & suggillandis nimiùm curiosi ac Argo oculatiores sint; in propriis verò, licet gravibus, agnoscendis talpâ coeciores Alios igitur reprehensurus propriam priùs severè examinare atque excutere vitam debet, & tum fortè benigniùs de proximi d-lictis pronunciabit: Confer egregiam sententiam. Greg. M. part. 2. Curae Pastor. c. 10.)*

Druf. in Prov. Rabini. decur. 7. prov. 5. ex Rabinis adducit. מרה צננר מרהMensura pro mensura. *(Conf. pluribus in hanc rem capellus in spicil. p. 17. ubi similem Iudaeorum sententiam ex Misna adducit.)*

## 7:3
v. 3. Why do you see the speck. August. serm. 202. de temp. Let us see what the speck, what the beam signify. For sudden anger is a speck, anger kept for a long time in the heart is a beam. Therefore, let not inveterate anger be turned into a beam. With what forehead does he, who keeps hatred in his heart, presume to judge him, in whose eye he recognizes there is not a beam, but a speck, for a speck disturbs the eye of the heart, a beam blinds it. *(H. Grotius has gathered more twins to this sentence of Christ from the Greek and Latin Poets in h. l. Becanus lib. 1. Manual. c. 14. p. 225. from the fact that Christ compares a certain (mortal namely, as the Jesuit explains) sin with a beam, and a certain (venial, according to the same) with a speck, of which the latter does not extinguish the eye, but lightly injures it; but the former does extinguish the eye, concludes, that there are certain sins, venial by their own nature. But Becanus took this in his own way from Cardinal Bellarm. l. 1. de amiss. gr. & stat. pecc. c. 9. (Dion. Carthus. is also delighted by the same similitude in c. 6. Lucae.) whom the Jesuit Coturius also follows Epit. Controv p. 407. where he also urges this, that Scripture never indicates that it calls this or that sin small, because God is about to pardon it: but another great, because he is not about to pardon it -gitur, he concludes, it must be judged, -um to speak of sin as it is according to itself and its own nature es-- The same place is also opposed to us by ----Coronus lib. 3. Ins-it. Cathoc. 6. p. 475. and so also Pont--- -l-rimi re-p. 1 We willingly grant, that Christ disti-guishes in this place between greater sins and lesser, and teaches, that there are degrees among sins. For such degrees of sins are so far from being denied that they are rather supported by many sayings of Holy Scripture ad--uant. And who, I ask, will be so absurd, as to persuade himself, that homicide, -heft, adultery etc. are not greater sins than hatred, simple concupiscence of another etc. nor yet is it permitted from thence immediately to infer. E-that certain sins are venial by their own nature. Parricide is a graver sin than mere homicide, sacrilege than simple -heft, incest, ad----um than fornication. Therefore, on account of this homi-cide, -imple theft and s-ornication are not to be called mortal sins? Far from it! Briefly: it is one thing to compare sins among themselves, in which way one is even by its own nature greater or less than another: another with the -ivine law, in respect to which all sins are by their own nature mortal, since the law also forbids even venial sins under male--&, see Deut. 27, 26.Galat. 3, 10.Iac. 2, 10. that the name and definition of sin etc. also apply to such, ceprelixè shows B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. 4 p. 390. 2. it is known that parabolic Theology is not argumentative, even the more prudent -ontificials conceding it. It does not follow therefore that the speck (with which a lesser sin is compared -aivatore, -otius, which comparatively at least speaking with respect to the greater is judged as such, as Fr. Lucas also notes, thus writing in h. l.: lesser and lighter sins are signified, either truly of such a kind, or by comparison of those sins to which he is liable, who takes upon himself the role of judge) does not extinguish the eye, therefore neither does a lesser pe-ccat sin extinguish the life of grace. Impotiùs rather just as it is possible, that even a small speck may extinguish the eye, unless it is removed, so also a lesser sin can at-tract eternal death to a man, nay it truly does attract it, unless by faith in Christ he obtains liberation from it.

But neither is it necessary that similar things should agree in all respects; it is sufficient that they agree in one third. 3. regarding the reasoning of Coturius, by conceding that Holy Scripture does not therefore always call it sin small, because God is going to forgive it, nor great, because He is not going to forgive it: for we know that God forgives even the most grievous sins to those who are seriously penitent and believing in Christ; on the contrary, He does not forgive even those things which, speaking comparatively, are small, to the Gentiles. From that, however, it likewise does not follow that certain sins are venial by their own nature, that is, not worthy of eternal death, if they are considered in the strict judgment of GOD.)*

Latin:

v. 3. Quid vides festucam. August. serm. 202. de temp. Quid festuca, quid trabes significent, videamus. Subita enim iracundia festuca est, iracundia diu in corde servata trabes est. Ergo ira inveterata non vertatur in trabem. Qufronte ille, qui odium servat in corde, illum iudicare praesumit, in cuius oculo non trabem, sed festucam esse cognoscit, nam cordis oculum festuca turbat, trabes excaecat. *(Plures gemellas huic Christi sententiae è Poëtis Graecis & Latinis congessit H. Grotius in h. l. Becanus lib. 1. Manual. c. 14. p. 225. ex eo quòd Christus quoddam ( mortale nempe, uti Iesuita explicat) peccatum comparat cum trabe, quoddam ( veniale, iuxta eundem) cum festuca, quorum haec oculum non extinguat, sed leviter laedat; illa verò oculum extinguat, colligit, dari quaedam peccata, ex naturâ suâ venialia. Desumsit verò hoc Becanus more suo è Cardinali Bellarm. l. 1. de amiss. gr. & stat. pecc. c. 9. (eâdem tamen similitudine & Dion. Carthus. delectatur in c. 6. Lucae.) quem sequitur etiam Iesuita Coturius Epit. Controv p. 407. ubi & hoc urget, quòd Scriptura nunquam indicet, se ideò hoc vel illud peccatum dicere parvum, quia Deus illud condonaturus est: aliud verò magnum, quia non condonaturus est -gitur, concludit, censendum est, -um loqui de peccato prout secundum se & natura sua es-- Eundem locum opponit quoque nobis ----Coronus lib. 3. Ins-it. Cathoc. 6. p. 475. & ita quoque Pont--- -l-rimi re-p. 1 Ultrò largimur, quòd Christus disti-guat hoc loco inter peccata maiora ac minora, doceatque, esse inter peccata gradus. Tales enim peccatorum gradus adeò non negant ut potiùs multis Scripturae S. dictis ad--uant. Et quis quaeso adeò absurdus erit, ut sibi persuade at, non maioresse peccata homicidium, -urtum, adulterium &c. quàm odium, alienae simplex concupiscentia &c. nec tamen exinde licet statim in ferre. E-quaedam peccata naturâ suâ venialia sunt. Parricidium gravius est peccatum nudo homicidio, sacrilegium simplici -urto, incestus, ad----um scortatione. Ergone propterea homi-cidium, -implex furtum ac s-ortatio non dicenda peccata mortalia sunt? Absit! Breviter: aliud est conferre peccata inter se, quomodo unum altero etiam ex naturà suà maius vel minus est: aliud cum lege -ivinà, cuius respectu ex naturâ suâ omnia peccata sunt mortalia, cùm lex eti-m vemalia peccata sub male--& prohibeat, vid. Deut. 27, 26.Galat. 3, 10.Iac. 2, 10. talibus etiam nomen ac cefinitio peccati &c. competat, ceprelixè ostendit B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. 4 p. 390. 2. notum est quòd Theologia parabolica non sit argumentativa, ipsis prudentioribus -ontificiis concedentibus. Non sequitur igiturfestuca (cum quo peccatum minus confertur -aivatore, -otius, quod comparativè saltem loquendo respectu maioris tale cense-ur, ceu etiam Fr. Lucas notat, ita in h. l. scribens: significantur peccata minora levioraq-, aut revera eiusmodi, aut eorum peccatorum comparatione quibus obnoxius is est, qui sibi sumit partes iudicis) non extinguit oculum, ergò nec minus pe-catum vitam gratiae extinguit. Impotiùs quemadmodum potest, ut etiam festuca exigua oculum extinguat, nisi eximatur, ita quoque peccatum minus homini aeternam mortem at-rahere potest, imò revera attrahit, nisi fide in Christum liberationem ab eo impetret.

Sed nec opus, ut similia in omnibus conveniant, sufficit, quòd in uno tertio. 3. in speciead Coturii ratiocinationē, concedendo, quòd Sc. S. non ideò semper peccatum vocet parvum, quòd Deus illud sit condonaturus, nec magnum, quòd non condonaturus: scimus enim, quòd Deus etiam gravissima peccata seriò poenitentibus & in Christum credentibus remittat; contrà gentilibus etiam ea, quae comparativè loquendo parva sunt, non condonet. Ex eo tamen itidem non sequitur, quòd peccata quaedam suâ naturâ venialia sint, h. e. non digna morte aeternà, si in rigido DEI iudicio considerentur.)*

## 7:6
v. 6. Chrysost. homil. 16. in Genes. Let those hear who speak simply to everyone without discrimination. For Christ did not give a command there about swine, but He denotes men with swinish habits, who like those brutes are wallowed in the mire of sin, teaching us that we should inquire into the diversity of persons and the ways of life, when it is necessary to expound any of the divine utterances, lest we harm both them and ourselves. The same, homil. 24. in Matth. f. 235. See Isid. Pelus. lib. 4. Epist. 181. Oecum. in Canon. Ioh. p. 233. Iobium de verbo incarn. 7. cap. 33. apud Phot. Biblioth. fol. 325. The Word and the Sacraments are not to be communicated to the secure, the contumacious, and the impenitent. The author of the book which is entitled Selection of gems teaches that this is a proverb, for thus we read there. Do not cast gems before swine. And in the Scholium: It is an adage, which he explains immediately. Do not hand over wisdom to him who does not know its dignity, for it is more precious than gems, and he who does not seek it is worse than a pig, which defiles and wallows itself in the dung-heap; thus he who does not know the dignity of wisdom profanes its glory. from cap. 1. Sap.

Swine, Theoph. h. l. are οἱ βορβορώδη βίον ἔχοντες who lead an impure life. We are warned not to communicate the doctrine of the Gospel and the Sacraments to blasphemous persecutors or Epicurean swine with the profanation of the divine name. Clem. Alex. lib. 2. ςρωμ. f. 156. We are forbidden to give holy things to dogs as long as they remain beasts. For it is not fitting that the divine and pure stream of living water should be poured out upon those who, as far as their morals are concerned, are envious, disturbed, and still unbelieving and shameless to the point of barking against the question proposed. Dogs are shameless men, contemners of the divine word. Swine are the impious and Epicureans, who like pigs wallow themselves in the mire of sins. Swine are Epicureans, dogs are hypocrites, by whom the gifts of the Gospel are torn with a cruel bite. Euthymius in h. l. He named dogs and swine, who are held by immedicable impiety, dogs indeed, as barking at Christ, but swine, as if wrapped in the mire of disturbances.

*( Do not give what is holy to dogs etc. Some think that by holy and pearls one and the same thing is denoted in this place. But if anyone should think that different things are signified, he may, with Chrysostom, understand by holy the Holy Baptism and the Eucharist; but by pearls the mysteries of truth included in divine words in the depth of the sea, i.e., the height of Holy Scripture. By dogs, however, the Savior signifies here men living in immedicable impiety and having no hope of conversion for the better; by swine, however, those continually dwelling in the mud of unbridled luxury, as has just been shown from Chrysostom, homily 24 on Matthew. Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, epistle 43, explains it in almost the same way. By dogs, he writes, he understands the Jews, who have often received the divine word, and return again to their vomit; or heretics, who betake themselves to true doctrine, and return again to the former perversity of their opinion. By swine, however, he understands those who wallow in vicious deeds and follow a swinish manner of life. Theophylact in this place explains it in almost the same way, as does Origen, homily 1 on Ps. 37. Jerome also notes in this place, by dogs, by some, those are understood who after the faith of Christ return to the vomit of their sins. But by swine, those who have not yet believed the Gospel and wallow in the mud of unbelief and vices. And this interpretation, namely that by dogs and swine only those are to be understood here who, like swine, wallow in the mud of various crimes without repentance, or who, like rabid dogs, gnaw at, bark at, and blaspheme orthodox doctrine, as those Jews of whom Acts 13:45 speaks, is also acknowledged by the Papist interpreters, as is evident from Maldonatus, Contzen, and others on this place. Vet-t, writes Corn. à Lapide on this passage Christ, lest anyone should wish to teach those who are obstinate in their crimes and incorrigible, like dogs and swine, and So that from this it may be manifest to anyone how inept, proud, and indeed even unjust some Papists are toward Christian laymen, whom they call (he cites on this matter B. P. t. 2. Confess. Cat-. p. 185. b. Alphonsus de Ca-tro l. 1. adv. haeres. c. 13. Bunderius in Compend. rerum Theolog. t. 32. art. 1. Sixtus Senensis lib. 6. Biblioth. annot. 152. Alphonsus Virvesius in Philipp. 2. Censura Colon. p. 13.) who, with Card. Hosius on the express word of GOD t. 1. page 664, do not fear to write, that to permit the reading of the -triptu-res to the laity, is to cast holy things to dogs and pearls to swine . As if it were not certain that in the Papistic Church the ears of the learners are for the most part purer than the lips of the teachers, and that hardly among any others are more crimes discovered than among the Supreme Pontiffs themselves, the Purpurat-s Fathers, and the mass-priests. Let the Political Magistrate learn from this, however, how much he is valued by those supercilious men, namely that he is held by those holy fathers in the place of swine and dogs without distinction. Furthermore, since in the sacred writings by dogs are sometimes indicated infidels outside the Church, as Apoc. 22, 15. sometimes heretics, persistently and manifestly persevering in fundamental error, Phil. 3, 2. sometimes also notorious sinners, who persevere in public crimes against conscience, and offer no sign of true repentance, Prov. 26, 11. 2. Peter 2, 20. 22. our people rightly conclude from this that such a kind of men are not to be admitted to the Holy Supper, as being that in which the most holy body and blood of Christ is distributed to the communicants, until they have bid farewell to an evil life and heresy and have performed serious repentance. But why the Savior handed over the body and blood to Judas the traitor is shown elsewhere. See what is noted on Luke 22. 20. It is the common opinion that a distinction must be made between sinners, whose sins are hidden (i.e., known only to God) and whose sins are notorious. They advise that these, but not those, in whose number Judas also was, are to be barred from the use of the Holy Supper. See among our own B. D. Hunnius t. 3. Oper. on c. 13. John page 916. B. Par. L. de S. Coenâ §. 223. B D. Bald. Cas. Consc. p. 1080. B. D.

--nig C C. p. 472. 473. let there also be added Mr. D. Carpz. Iurispr. Consist. I. 2. t. 18. d. 184. from the Papists Maldonatus on this passage, Cardin. Ft. Toletus summ. de Instruct. Sacerd. l. c. 17. and others. Finally to the question, How the present admonition of the Savior is to be reconciled with His own commandMatt. 28, 19.Mark 16, 15.& the practice of the Apostles, will be shown in the Annotations on the said day. The Blessed D. Quistorpius on this passage: In this place Christ intends this, that the most abstruse mysteries should not be prodigally poured out even to the unfaithful, but should be instilled step by step, lest they be deterred by the sublimity of the mysteries. Distinguish, therefore, between the preaching itself, and the manner or order of proposing the dogmas and mysteries of the faith. But how the Savior confirmed by His own example the warning given here to the Apostles, while He answered nothing to Herod, whom cruelty had made a dog and the pleasures of the flesh a pig, the Blessed Par. shows in Harm. Evang. c. 192. p. 1880. b.)

*( Lest perhaps. Alphonsus Mendoza notes in Controv. Theol. p. 532. As when sometimes Holy Scripture uses the adverb perhaps, where nevertheless there is no doubt, and which therefore then means the same as certainly or indeed, & consequently all doubt is removed from the divine knowledge. And he refers the present passage to this as well. The same was also observed long ago by St. Jerome, when he writes in his Comm. on Jer. 6, 26.: An ambiguous word, perhaps, cannot befit the Majesty of the Lord, but He speaks according to our affect, so that the free will of man may be preserved, lest from His foreknowledge he be compelled as if by necessity either to do something or not to do it. Compare also Theoph. on c. 10 of Luke, Ambrose l. 2. de poenit. c. 5. Remigius, Tostatus, and Thomas on c. 11 of Matthew. Among our own, the same observation is inculcated by Dn. D. Walther. Harm. Bibl. p. 31. B. D. Glassius Gramm. S. p. 494. seqq. B. Par. Exeg. Loc. 2-. 254. But the said observation is to be opposed both to the Photinians, attempting to prove their error from such places, that God does not foreknow the future sins of men (see Socin. Prael. Theol. c. 8. 9. 10. 11.) and to the Calvinists, asserting that all things, and therefore even sins, happen necessarily, because the foreknowledge of GOD is infallible: Resp. Nay rather God speaks these things (if perhaps they themselves might hear) with the affect of one who is doubting, so that He may show the free will of man: nor does the foreknowledge of future evil and good make immutable what God has known will be future. For it is not because He knows things that are to come, that it is necessary to do what He has foreknown, but what we are going to do by our own will, He knows will be future as God, as the praised Jerome rightly warns in c. 2 of Ezekiel. But as for what concerns the present passage, it is held in the Greek text μήποτε, which properly signifies lest at any time, and therefore indicates no doubt, even though the Vulgate has rendered it doubtfully lest perhaps. The Syrian translates here by which word is also used by the same Matt. 25, 9. where likewise in the Gr. it is μήποτε, it. Acts 8, 20. where in the Gr. text it is εἰ ἄρα. But the Blessed D. Glass. Gram. S. p. 496. notes that the Vulgate there wrongly rendered it by if perhaps, when rather ἄρα adds force, τῷ εἰ so that joined together it is the same as ὅπως δὴ, that indeed.)*

Latin:

v. 6. Chrysost. homil. 16. in Genes. Audiant, qui sine discrimine simpliciter omnibus colloquuntur. Neque enim ibi Christus de porcis praecepit, sed homines porcinis moribus denotat, qui sicut bruta illa in peccati luto involvuntur, docens nos, ut personarum diversitatē & vitae rationes inquiramus, quando aliquid divinorum eloquiorum exponere opus fuerit, ne & illos & nosmetipsos laedamus. Idem homil. 24. in Matth. f. 235. Vide Isid. Pelus. lib. 4. Epist. 181. Oecum. in Canon. Ioh. p. 233. Iobium de verbo incarn. 7. cap. 33. apud Phot. Biblioth. fol. 325. Verbum & Sacramenta securis, contumacibus & impoenitentibus non sunt communicanda. Autor libri, qui inscribitur Electio gemmarum proverbium id esse docet, sic enim ibi legimus. Ne proiicite gemmas coram porcis. Et in Scholio: Adagium est, quod mox explicat. Ne tradite sapientiam ei, qui non novit dignitatem eius, nam est preciosior gemmis, & qui non quaerit eam, peior est porco, qui foedat & volutat se in sterquilinio, sic qui non novit dignitatem sapientiae, prophanat eius gloriam. ex cap. 1. Sap.

Porci Theoph. h. l. sunt οἱ βορβορώδη βίον ἔχοντεςqui vitam impuram agunt. Monemur, ne doctrinam Evangelii & Sacramenta blasphemis persecutoribus aut porcis Epicuraeis cum profanatione nominis divini communicemus. Clem. Alex. lib. 2. ςρωμ. f. 156. Sancta canibus impe-tiri vetamur, quamdiu bestiae manserint. Neque enim convenit, ut iis qui quantum ad mores sunt invidi, perturbati, et iamnum infideles & impudentes ad latratum adversus quaestionem propositam, divinum & purum fluentum aquae vivae infundatur. Canes sunt homines impudentes, contemtores verbi divini. Porci sunt impii & Epicuraei, qui porcorum instar se volutant in coeno peccatorum. Porci sunt Epicuraei, canes hypocritae, à quibus Dd. Evangelii crudeli morsu lacerantur. Euthymius in h. l. Canes & porcos nominavit, qui immedicabili tenentur impietate, canes quidem, tanquam Christo oblatrantes, porcos verò, qs. perturbationum luto obvolutos.

*( Ne date, quod sanctum est, canibus &c. Per sanctum & margaritas unum idemque h. l. denotari, nonnulli existimant. Si quis verò diversa significari putaverit, poterit per sanctum cum Chrysostomo intelligere S. Baptismum & Eucharistiam; per margaritas verò mysteria veritatis inclusa divinis verbis in maris profunditate i. e. Sc. Sacrae altitudine. Per canes autem significat hîc Salvator homines in impietate viventes immedicabili spemq; omnem conversionis in melius non habentes; per porcos verò, in luto infrenis luxuriae iugiter commorantes, ceu ex Chrysostomo hom. 24. in Matth. modò ostensum. Similiter ferê etiam exponit Isidorus Pelus. l. 1. ep. 43. Per canes scribit, intelligit Iudaeos, qui divinum sermonem per saepè acceperunt, ac rursus ad vomitum suum revertuntur; aut haereticos, qui ad veram doctrinam sese conferunt, ac rursum adpriorem sententiae perverfitatem redeunt. Per porcos verò intelligit, qui in vitiosis effectibus volutantur, ac porcinum vitae genus sequuntur. Eod. prope modo Theophylactus in h. l. nec non Orig. hom. 1. in Ps. 37. Hierony mus quoque in h. l. notat, per canes à quibusdam eos intelligi qui post fidem Christi revertuntur ad vomitum peccatorum suorum. Porcos autem eos, qui nec dum Evangelio crediderunt, & in luto incredulitatis vitiisq; versantur. Atque hanc interpretationem, quòd nempe per canes & porcos non nisi illi intelligendi hic sint, qui instar porcorum variorumque scelerum luto abque poenitentià volutantur, vel qui rabiosorum instar canum orthodoxam doctrinam arrodunt, oblatrant ac blasphemant, ceu Iudaei illi, de quibus Act. 13, 45. ipsi quoque agnoscunt Interpretes Pontificii, prout ex Maldonato, Contzenio aliisque in h. l. patet. Vet-t, scribit Corn. à Lapide super h. l. Christus, ne quis eos, qui in sceleribus, suis obstinati sunt, & incorrigibiles, ut canes & porci, docere velit & Ut hinc cuilibet manifestum sit, quàm inepti, superbi, atque adeò etiam in Christianos laicos, quos ivocant, iniqui sint Pontificii nonnulii, (allegat in hanc rem B. P. t. 2. Confess. Cat-. p. 185. b. Alphonsum de Ca-tro l. 1. adv. haeres. c. 13. Bunderium in Compend. rerum Theolog. t. 32. art. 1. Sixtum Senensem lib. 6. Biblioth. annot. 152. Alphonsum Virvesium in Philipp. 2. Censuram Colon. p. 13.) qui cum Card. Hosio de expresso DEI verbo t. 1. pag. 664. scribere non verentur, quòd laicis lectionem -triptu-arum pe-mitter-, sit sanctum canibus & margaritas porcis pro--ce--. Quasi verò non constet, quòd in Ecclesiâ Papisticâ aures discentium plerumque puriores sint labiis docentium, ac quòd vix apud ullos plura deprehendantur scelera. quàm apud ipsos Pontificcs Maximos, Patres Purpurat-s ac sacrificulos. Discat verò hinc Magistratus Positicus, quanti aestimetur a super ciliosis illis hominibus, nempe quòd sine discrimine porcorum & canum loco à sanctis illis patribus habeatur. Caeterùm cùm in sacris per canes modò indicentur infideles extra Ecclesiam, uti Apoc. 22, 15. modô haeretici, in errore fundamentali pertinaciter ac manifestò perseverantes, Phil. 3, 2. modò etiam peccatores notorii, qui in publicis sceleribus contra conscientiam perseverant, nec ullum verae poenitentiae significationem edunt, Prov. 26, 11.2. Petri 2, 20.22. rectè hinc colligunt nostrates, quòd id genus homines non priùs ad S. Coenam, utpote in quâ sacrosanctum Christi corpus & sangvicommunicantibus distribuitur, admittendi sint, quàm improbae vitae ac haeresi valedixerint & seriam egerint poenitentiam. Cur verò Salvator Iudae proditori corpus & sanguinem tradiderit, alibi ostenditur. Vid. quae notata ad Luc. 22. 20. Communis sententia est, quòd dist. sit inter peccatores, quorum peccata occulta sunt (h. e. soli Deo nota) & quorum peccata notoria. Hos, non verò illos, in quorum numero & Iudas fuit, ab usu S. Coenae arcendos esse monent. Vid. è nostratibus B. D. Hunnius t. 3. Oper. super c. 13. Ioh. pag. 916. B. Par. L. de S. Coenâ §. 223. B D. Bald. Cas. Consc. p. 1080. B. D.

Disting, igitur inter praedicationem ipsam, ac modum s. ordinem fidei dogmata ac mysteria proponendi. Quomodo verò suo exemplo Salvator monitum Apostolis hîc datum confirmarit, dum Herodi, uti quem crudelitas canem & carnis voluptates porcum fecerant, nihil respondit, ostendit B. Par. Harm. Evang. c. 192. p. 1880. b.)*

Sacram adverbio fortè, ubi tamen nulla dubitatio est, quodq; adeò tum illud idem valeat atq; certè vel utique, & ex consequenti omnis dubitatio à divinâ conitione removeatur. Et huc refert quoque praesentem locum. Idem etiam pridem observavit S. Hieronymus, quando Comm. super Ierem. 6, 26. scribit: Verbum ambiguum, forsitan, Maiestati Domini non potest convenire, sed nostro loquitur affectu, ut liberum hominis servetur arbitrium, ne ex praescientia eius quasi ex necessitate vel facere quid vel non facere cogatur. Conf. quoque Theoph. in c. 10. Lucae, Ambrosius l. 2. de poenit. c. 5. Remigius, Tostatus ac Thomas ad c. 11. Matthaei. E nostratibus eandem observationem inculcant Dn. D. Walther. Harm. Bibl. p. 31. B. D. Glassius Gramm. S. p. 494. seqq. B. Par. Exeg. Loc. 2-. 254. Opponenda verò dicta observatio tum Photinianis, ex huiusmodi locis probare conantibus errorem suum, quòd Deus futura hominum peccata nō praesciat (vid. Socin. Prael. Theol. c. 8. 9. 10. 11.) tum Calvinianis, adserentibus quòd omnia, adeoque etiam peccata necessariò fiant, quia DEI praescientia sit infallibilis: Resp. Imò verò loquitur Deus haec (si fortè vel ipsi audiant) ambigentis affectu, ut liberum hominis monstret arbitrium: npraescientia futurorum mali & boni immut abile faciat, quod Deus futurum noverit. Non enim quia ille ventura cognoscit, necesse est no f-cere, quod ille praescivit, sed quod nos propria voluntate s--facturi, ille novit futurum quasi Deus, ceu laudatus rectè monet Hieronymus in c. 2. Ezech. Quod verò praesentem locum concernit, habetur in textu Graec. μήποτε, quod propriè ne aliquand-, significat, adeoque nullam dubitationem indicat, ut ut Vulga-us dubitativè reddiderit ne fortè. Syrus vertit hîc per quae vox ab eodem quoque adhi--ur Matth. 25, 9. ubi itidem in Gr. est μήποτε, it. Act. 8, 20. u--in textu Gr. est εἰ ἄρα. Notat verò B. D. Glass. Gram. S. p. 496. & ibi Vulgatum malè per sifertè reddidisse, cùm potiùsἄραvimτῷ εἰaddat, ut coniunctim sit idem acὅπως δὴ,ut sanè.)*

## 7:6 Addition
This precept is to be understood thus: 1. that all things, even the highest mysteries, should not be prodigally poured out to the unfaithful, but should be instilled step by step, with an order accommodated for teaching, and as time or persons shall seem to demand. 2. that we should not immediately and at first glance deny our effort even to the unworthy, or even deem them unworthy to hear saving doctrine, but only then at last, when desperate wickedness has betrayed itself, of those hardening themselves against manifest truth: for then we wash the brick in vain. August. book 2 on the Lord's Sermon on the Mount, ch. 31. Care must be taken, lest anything be opened to him who does not grasp it, for he seeks better that which is closed than that which is open, or he attacks through hatred like a dog, or neglects through contempt like a swine.

* (I cannot but also add here what is noted in the margin of the most ancient Syriac MS. codex of the four Evangelists, which is preserved in the Altdorf Academy Library, at verse 6, although by a more recent hand, yet a Syrian one: namely these

Disposition. This chapter comprises four principal members. I. The healing of certain sick persons, namely 1. The leper v. 2. 4. 2. The centurion's servant v. 5. -13. 3. Peter's mother-in-law v. 14. 15. add in general v. 16. 17. II. The instruction of a scribe and a disciple concerning the right following of Christ v. 19. -22. III. The calming of the tempest on the sea v. 23. -27. IV. The deliverance of two possessed by demons. v. 18. to the end.

Latin:

Praeceptum hoc sic accipiendum. 1. ut ne prodigè effundantur infidelibus omnia etiam altissima mysteria, sed pedetentim instillentur, accommodato ad docendum ordine, ac prout vel tempus vel personae postulare videbuntur. 2. ut ne statim & primo intuitu etiam indignis operam nostram denegemus, aut etiam indignos existimemus, qui salutarem doctrinam audiant, sed tum demum, cùm se prodiderit desperata nequitia, obfirmantium se contra manifestam veritatem: tum enim frustrà laterem lavamus. August. l. 2. de serm. Domini in monte c. 31. Cavendum est, ne quid aperiatur ei, qui non capit, meliùs enim quaerit ia, quod clausum est, quàm id quod apertum est, aut infestat per odium ut canis, aut negligit per contemtum ut porcus.

Dispositio. Complectitur hoc caput quatuor praecipua membra. I. Quorundam aegrotorum sanationem, nempe 1. Leprosi v. 2. 4. 2. Centurionis famuli v. 5. -13. 3. Socrûs Petri v. 14. 15. adde in genere v. 16. 17. II. Scribae ac Discipuli de rectâ Christi sequelâ informationem v. 19. -22. III. Tempestatis in mari sedationem v 23. -27. IV. Duorum à Daemonibus obsessorum liberationem. v. 18. ad finem.

## 7:7
v. 7. Prayer rises. Ask, seek, knock, that we may be stirred up to perseverance in prayers, which is said Luc. 18. vers. 1. πάντοτε ροσεύχεσθαι καὶ μὴ ὐκκακεῖν. August, in Psal. 34. God would not urge us to knock if He did not wish to open to those who knock. (The same, serm. 226. de tempore: The prayer of the righteous is the key of heaven; prayer ascends, liberation descends. Confer more excellent sentiments concerning the utility, necessity, etc., of prayer, collected by B Par. in Aphorismis Theol. Pract. tit. Prayer p. 527. & seqq. of the newest edition. In this place I note at least this, that if we desire to be heard, we ought to pray 1. confidently, i.e., that our prayer may be supported by a firm faith in Christ; nor should we doubt concerning a benign hearing. See Ioh. 14, 13. c 15, 7. c. 16, 23. Rom. 10, 14. Ebr. 11, 6. Gal. 3. 27. c. 6, 6. &c. Whence τὸ everyone v. 8. is not to be understood absolutely, but is to be restricted d. m., as the Savior Himself teaches Matth. 21, 22. and also James c. 1, 6. 7. 2. decently, i.e., that we do not ask wrongly, -acob. 4, 3. also that we ask for those things which God has promised in His word to give, which is to ask according to the will of GOD. But for this it is required that we submit our will to the will of our heavenly Father, as Christ Himself went before us in this matter, as can be seen Luc. 22, 42. Thus we ought not to ask for and expect temporal goods except with a condition, namely, if they do not hinder our eternal salvation. Which when we have done, we shall discover that Bernard truly said in medit. devot. cap. 6. col. 1196. Before prayer goes out from our mouth, God commands it to be written in His book, and we can indubitably hope for one of two things: either He will give that which we ask, or that which is more useful. For what GOD takes away from the will, He bestows upon salvation. Therefore, consider here that of Prosper: He grants much, who denies what would be harmful. To this also looks the sentiment of Augustine tr. 73. in Ioh. Sometimes God is said to hear our prayers while He denies and refuses to do what we ask, which happens when we ask for those things which we think will be useful to us, and in reality they are not, but rather harmful. 3. fervently and constantly, lest we be rendered weary if God sometimes delays help. And to this the present admonition especially looks. If therefore it is not enough τὸ, to ask, let τὸ to seek be added; if this is not enough, let τὸ to knock be added. Beautifully Anselm in Medit. God delays to give, that He may teach how to ask: He pretends not to hear the petitioner, that He may make him a desirer. 4. penitently. For God does not hear those who persist in hatred with their neighbor and in other crimes against their conscience without true and serious repentance. See Ioh. 9, 31. and Conf. Sir. 28, 2. 1. Tim. 2, 8. Isidore: Just as no medicine profits a wound if the iron is still in it: so the prayer of him who keeps hatred and malice in his breast profits nothing. Bernard serm. 49. de med. viv. Prayer is hindered in two ways from obtaining what it asks: if a man still commits evils, or if he does not forgive from his whole heart one who sins against him. What further foundations are to be opposed to temptation and doubt concerning the hearing of prayers, B. D. Bald. shows in Cas. Cons. l. 2. c 7. cas. 7)*

*( If he shall ask of him bread &c. Savanarola in Ps. 51. Let us ask for the bread of the charity of Christ, by which he communicates himself to all as bread, he will not give a stone i.e. the hardness of the heart, Luc. 11, 11. Compare more in the Notes to chapter II of Luke v. 11. 12.)*

Latin:

v. 7. Oratio assurgit. Petite, quaerite, pulsate, ut ad perseverantiam in precibur excitemus quod Luc. 18. vers. 1. dicitur πάντοτε ροσεύχεσθαι καὶ μὴ ὐκκακεῖν. August, in Psal. 34.Non hortaretur nos Deus ut pulsaremus si nollet ap-rire pulsantibus. *(Idem serm. 226. de tempore: Oratio iusti est clavis coeli, adscendit precatio, descendit liberatio. Confer plures egregias de Orationis utilitate, necessitate &c. sententias, à B Par. collectas in Aphorismis Theol. Pract. tit. Oratio p. 527. & seqq. edit. noviss. Hoc loco illud saltem noto, quòd, si exaudin cupimus, orare debeamus 1. fidente h. e. ut firmâ in Christi fide oratio nostra fit suffulta; nec de benignâ exauditione dubitemus. Vid. Ioh. 14, 13. c 15, 7. c. 16, 23. Rom. 10, 14.Ebr. 11, 6.Gal. 3. 27.c. 6, 6. &c. Unde τὸquis quisv. 8. non absolutè intelligenda, sed d. m. restringenda est, ceu ipse Salvator docet Matth. 21, 22. nec non Iacobus c. 1, 6. 7. 2. decenter. h. e. ne malè petamus, -acob. 4, 3. it. ut ea petamus, quae Deus in verbo dare promisit, quod est secundùm DEI voluntatem petere. Ad hoc verò requiritur, ut voluntatem nostram submittamus voluntati Pa-nostri coelestis, ceu hac in re praeivit nobis Christus ipse, sicuti videre est Luc. 22, 42. Sic temporalia bona non nisi cum conditione petere & expectare debemus, nempe si aeternae nostrae saluti non obsint. Quod ubi fecerimus, deprehendemus verè dixisse Bernhardum in medit. devot. cap. 6. col. 1196.Priusquam ex ore nostro egrediatur oratio, scribi Deus eam iubet in libro suo, & unum indubit anter è duobus sperare possumus, aut dabit id, quod petimus, aut illud, quod ut ilius. Quod enim DEUS adimit voluntati, tribuit saluti. Cogites igitur hîc illud Prosperi: Multum concedit, quod nocitura negat. Huc spectat etiam Augustini sententia tr. 73. in Ioh. Aliquando Deus exaudire preces nostras dicitur, dum negat, & renuit facere, quod petimus, quod tunc fit, quando petimus ea, quae put amus utilia nobis futura, & reverà non sunt sed potiùs noxia. 3. ferventer ac constanter, ne lassi reddamur, si Deus differt aliquando auxilium. Atq: huc cumprimis spectat praesens admonitio. Si igitur non sufficit τὸ, petere accedat, τὸquaerere; si hoc non sufficit, accedat τὸpulsare. Pulcrè Anshelmus in Medit. Differt Deus dare, ut doceat, petore: Dissimulat audire petentem, ut faciat desiderantem. 4. poenitenter. Neque enim Deus eos, qui in odio cum proximo persistunt aliisque in sceleribus contra conscientiam absq; verà ac seriâ poenitentiâ perseverant, exaudit. Vid. Ioh. 9, 31. ac Conf. Sir. 28, 2.1. Tim. 2, 8. Isidorus: Sicut nullum proficit in vulnere medicamentum, si adhuc sit in eo ferrum: sic nihil proficit oratio illius, qui odium & livorem servat in pectore. Bernhardus serm. 49. de med. viv. Duobus modis oratio impeditur, ne impetret, quod postulat, si adhuc homo mala committit, aut si peccanti in se ex toto corde non dimittit. Quae porrò tentationi ac dubitationi de exauditione precum fundamenta opponenda sint, monstrat B. D. Bald. Cas. Cons. l. 2. c 7. cas. 7)*

*( Si petierit ab eo panem &c. Savanarola in Ps. 51.Petamus panem caritatis Christi, quâ se sicut panis omnibus communicat, non dabit lapidem i. e. cordis duritiem,Luc. 11, 11. Conf. plura in Not. ad cap. II. Lucae v. 11. 12.)*

## 7:8
*(v. 8. For everyone that asketh, receiveth. That this promise is not to be taken ἁπλῶς, but with a certain restriction, namely that the prayer be founded on firm faith, proceed from a pure & sincere heart, and that we ask according to the will of God, has already been said regarding the preceding verse. If anyone asks otherwise, he does not pray rightly, but rather tempts the supreme Deity, as if someone should wish to abstain entirely from drink and food, when they are nevertheless present, and nonetheless weary God with prayers that he might wish to protect him against hunger and consequently death. Thus is also the vain evasion of the Papists, when, since their forced celibacy, which is joined with great injury to the conscience, is objected to by our people, that well-worn saying of the Apostle 1. Cor. 7, 9.It is better to marry than to burn, then the oracle of the Savior Matth. 19, 11.not all receive this word, &c. likewise when they forbid the innocent party a repeated marriage, even if such celibacy is joined with the greatest injury to conscience, they appeal to this promise of the Savior, urging that in such a case one can obtain the gift of continence from GOD by prayers. See Concil. Trid. sess. 8. can. o. Bell. de Monach. c. 31. Cotur. Epit. controv. p. 363. although there exists nowhere a divine promise that this gift will be granted to those for whom another means against burnings is available, shown in the true GOD, by which they might preserve an unblemished conscience. Whence also the Apostle does not say, if younger widows cannot contain, let them seek the gift of continence from GOD, but let them marry.1. Tim. 5. 14. Conf. 1. Cor. 7, 9. But more will be said about this in the Annotations on 1. Ioh. 5, 14. Meanwhile, let those things be seen which our people have long since set against that common refuge of the Papists, especially B. D. Tarn. l. 1. de Coni c. 11. l. 3. c. 12. B. Par. L. de Coniug. §. 527. it. Conf. Cath. t. 3. p. 341.)

Latin:

*(v. 8. Quis quis enim petit, accipit. Quòd haec promissio non ἁπλῶς accipienda sit, sed certâ quadam cum restrictione, nempe ut oratio fundatur firmâ fide, è corde puro & sincero procedat, utq; secundùm voluntatem Dei petamus, iamtum ad vers. praeced. dictum. Si quis aliter petit, non rectè orat, sed supremum potiùs Numen tentat, Ut si quis penitus abstinere à potu ac cibo velit, cùm tamē adsint, ac nihilominus precibus Deum fatigare, ut contra famem & consequenter mortem tueri ipsum velit. Sic vanum quoque effugium Pontificiorum est, quando cùm coacto illorum ac magnâ cum conscientiae laesione coniuncto coelibatui obiicitur à nostratibus tritum illud Apostoli 1. Cor. 7, 9.Melius est nubere, quàm uri, tum Salvatoris oraculum Matth. 19, 11.non omnes capiunt verbū hoc, &c. item quando parti innocenti itetato matrimonio interdicunt, si vel maximè cu conscientiae laesione talis coelibatus coniunctus sit, ad hoc Salvatoris promissum provocant, urgentes, quòd tali in casu continentiae quis donum impetrare à DEO precibus possit. Vid. Concil. Trid. sess. 8. can. o. Bell. de Monach. c. 31. Cotur. Epit. controv. p. 363. cùm tamen nullibi extet promisso divina de dono hoc illis concedendo, quibus aliud suppetit contra ustiones medium, in vero DEI ostensum, quo conscientiam illibatam conservare possint. Unde etiam Apostolus non dicit, si iuniores viduae non possunt continere, continentiae donum à DEO petant, sed nubant,1. Tim. 5. 14. Conf. 1. Cor. 7, 9. Sed de hâc plura dicentur in Annot ad 1. Ioh. 5, 14. Videantur interea quae communi illi Pontificiorum effugio pridem reposuerunt nostrates, cum primis B. D. Tarn. l. 1. de Coni c. 11. l. 3. c. 12. B. Par. L. de Coniug. §. 527. it. Conf. Cath. t. 3. p. 341.)*

## 7:9
*(v. 9. Or who is there among you. Concerning the singular use of the particle; in argumentation See B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 604. The Syrian similarly uses a disjunctive particle, for it renders or. And so also the Arab, according to the Roman edition, but in the Leyden edition nothing exists here which corresponds to the particle ἢ, thus neither in the Ethiopian.)*

*( Ὁ υἱος αὐτοῶ &c. From the fact that the article ὁ is placed before the noun υἱὸς here, although it is not signified that some singular or unique son, but any son, provided he is the one whose father is he from whom he asks, Socin. resp. ad Wuiek. p. 260. holds it as persuaded to himself that it is sufficiently evident, that neither in the placeIoh. 20, 28.is the true and singular, i.e., eternal God indicated, but at least this, that Thomas acknowledged Christ not as the God of just anyone else, or of certain others, or simply God, but as his own God. Resp. 1. it is not the rule of our people, but of the Photinians, that the word θεὸς placed with the article is proper to the only true God, but placed without the article is common to others. Whence also Franciscus Davidis & Eniedinus pervert the aforementioned place in such a way that they say, the exclamation of Thomas was not directed to Christ, but to God the Father. But since this distortion has long since been condemned in the V. Synod of Constantinople Act. 3. can. 11. & the vanity of it also appears to anyone, Socinus, departing from his associates, grants that that exclamation was entirely directed to Christ. 2 Let Socinus know that our people do not urge the aforementioned article so much, (although the ancients also observed this against the Arians in this place, as can be seen from Cyril and Theoph., and it can also be urged, at least κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον, especially when other circumstances confirm the same) as they urge the added fiduciary pronoun: then also that no one is addressed so absolutely, unless he is the true and eternal God, as is shown elsewhere.)*

(Ἐπιδώσει. Junius thinks that τὸ ἑ-πὶ in this place is not redundant, but sounds just as if it were said, concerning his petition. The Syriac likewise translates it emphatically that is to say, to give with an outstretched hand. Compare Ioh. 20, 25.27.)

Latin:

*(v. 9. Aut quis est ex vobis. De singulari usu particulae; in argumentatione Vid. B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 604. Syrus similiter disiunctivâ particulâ utitur, reddit enim aut. Et ita quoque Arabs, iuxta edit. Roman sed in Leydensi editione nihil hîc extat, quod particulae ἢ respondeat, sic nec apud Aethiopem.)*

*( Ὁ υἱος αὐτοῶ &c. Ex eo, quòd art. ὁ nomini υἱὸς hîc praesigatur, cùm tamen non significetur singularis aliquis seu unicus filius, sed quilibet filius, modo ille, cuius pater sit is, à quo petit, persuasū sibi habet Socin. resp. ad Wuiek. p. 260. satis patere, quòd nec in locoIoh. 20, 28.verus ac singularis h. e. aeternus indicetur Deus sed saltemhoc, quòd Thomas agno verit Christum non cuiuspiam modò alterius, seu quorundam aliorum Deum, aut simpliciter Deum, sed suum ipsius Deum. Resp. 1. neque nostratium, sed Photinianorum regula est, quòd voxθεὸςcum articulo posita solius veri Dei propria sit, sed posita sine articulo sit aliis communis. Unde etiam Franciscus Davidis & Eniedinus ita d. l. pervertunt, ut dicant, Thomae exclamationem non ad Christum, sed ad Deum Patrem fuisse directam. sed cùm detorsio haec iamdudum damnata sit in Synodo V. Constantinopol. Act. 3. can. 11. & illius etiam vanitas cuilibet appareat, largitur Socinus, à sociennis suis discedens, quòd omninò ad Christum exclamatio illa fuerit directa. 2 Sciat Socinus, quòd nostrates non tam praemissum artiulum, (quamvis & hoc veteres contra Arianos h. l. observarint, ceu ex Cyrillo ac Theoph. videre est, &urgeri quoque possit, minimum κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον, cumprimis, quando aliae circumstantiae idem confirmant) quàm additum pronomen fiduciale urgeant: tum quoque quòd nemo ita absolutè compellatur, nisi sit verus aeternus que Deus, ceu alibi ostenditur.)*

*( Ἐπιδώσει. Iunius existimat, τὸ ἑ-πὶ h. l. non redundare, sed perinde sonare ac si dicatur, super petitione eius. Syrus itidem emphatice vertit q. d. extensa manu dare. Conf. Ioh. 20, 25.27.)*

## 7:10
v. 10. Or if a fish. Franc. Lucas notes that there is a beautiful opposition between the fish and the serpent, etc.; for although the figures are mutually very similar, they are diametrically opposed regarding their use for man. )* *(

Latin:

*(v. 10. Aut si piscem. Notat Franc. Lucas, pulcram esse oppositionem piscis & serpentis &c. figura enim mutuò cùm persimilia sint, ad hominis usumè diametro distant.)*

## 7:11
(v. 11. Since you are evil. Cornelius à Lapide restricts these words to the common people. For the Apostles, he writes, were good; but among the common people, many were evil, and ensnared by vices. Franciscus Lucas, Theologian and Dean of the Cathedral Church of Saint-Omer in Artois, dissents, who writes thus on this place: He calls all men evil, even the just: for those whom he calls evil, he immediately names sons of God, when he adds: Your Father who is in heaven, a thing which Blessed Augustine noted in ch. 3 book 3. against the two epistles of the Pelagians. But he calls them evil, not from nature itself, but from the corruption of nature, by which it happens that all are prone to every evil, and by no means live without frequent sins. Augustine has the former reason from Hilary treating Psalm 118, the letter samech, in the second book against Julian; the latter, from the first book against the adversary of the law and the prophets, chapter 22. These things must be opposed 1. to the common doctrine of the Papists, that the good works of the reborn in this life are perfect and pure from every stain of adhering sin. 2. in particular to the opinion of the Jesuits concerning the immaculate conception of the Virgin Mary, concerning which matter it has been treated more prolixly elsewhere.)

*( Your Father, namely he who is devoid of all evil, and alone good, Matth. 19, 17. & from whom πᾶσα πατριὰ Eph. 3, 15. Moreover, the word Father is taken in this place οὐσιωδῶς, so that it denotes all three persons of the SS. Trinity, as Schevichavius well observed in book 3 de sanct. Trin. c. 1. & it is also accepted in this way Deut. 32, 6. Mal. 2, 10. Es. 63, 15. Matth. 5, 16, 48. c. 6, 14. c. 10, 29. 30. c. 13. 43. 2. Cor. 6, 18. Augustine uses & indeed the H. S. uses this name, & attributes it to God, so that it may excite in us confidence, affection, reverence, imitation, etc., toward God, as appears from the stated places. God is called our Father 1. on account of paternal love, Es. 63, 16. Sap. 11, 25. 2. on account of creation, Es. 64, 8. Mal. 2, 10. 3. on account of sustenance, conservation etc. Deut. 32, 6. 4. on account of the offering of eternal inheritance, also adoption etc. as the Blessed Par. teaches at greater length in Harm. Evang. c. 151. p. 31.)*

Latin:

*(v. 11. Cùm sitis mali. Restringit Corn. à Lapide haec verba ad plebem. Apostoli enim, scribit, boni erant; in plebe autem, multi erant mali, & vitiis irretiti. Dissentit Franciscus Lucas, Ecclesiae Cathedr. Audomaropolitanae in Arthesiâ Theologus & Decanus, qui ita in h. l. Malos vocat homines omnes, etiam iustos: nam quos malos, eosdem mox filios Dei nominat, cùm addit: Pater vester qui in coelis est, id quod B. Augustinus not avit c. 3 l. 3. contra duas epist. Pelagianorum. Malos autem vocat, non ex naturâ ipsa, sed ex naturae corruptione, quippe quâ fiat, ut proclives ad malum omne omnes sint, & sine frequentibus delictis nequaquam vivant. Priorem rationem Augustinus ex Hilario tractante Psalmi 118. litteram samech habet libro in Iulianum secundo; posteriorem, libri primi contra adversarium legis & prophetarum cap. 22. Opponenda haec sunt 1. communi Pontificiorum doctrinae, quòd bona opera renatorum in hâc vita perfecta sint & ab omni peccati adhaerentis labe pura. 2. in specie sententiae Iesuitarum de immaculatâ Mariae Virginis conceptione, quâ de re alibi prolixiùs actum fuit.)*

*( Pater vester, nempe qui omnis mali expers est, ac solus bonus,Matth. 19, 17. & à quo πᾶσα πατριὰEph. 3, 15. Coeterùm sumitur vocabulum Patris hoc loco οὐσιωδῶς, ita ut notet omnes tresSS. Trinitatis personas, ut benè observavit Schevichavius l. 3. de sanct. Trin. c. 1. & ita quoque accipitur Deut. 32, 6.Mal. 2, 10.Es. 63, 15.Matth. 5, 16,48.c. 6, 14.c. 10, 29. 30.c. 13. 43.2. Cor. 6, 18. Utitur august. & verò Sc. S hoc nomine, Deoq; illud tribuit, ut in nobis siduciā, affectum, reverentiam, imitationem &c. erga Deum exciter, ceu è dictis locis apparet. Dicitur Deus noster Pater 1. propter paternam dilectionem,Es. 63, 16.Sap. 11, 25. 2. propter creationem,Es. 64, 8.Mal. 2, 10. 3. propter sustentationem, conservationem &c. Deut. 32, 6. 4. propter haereditatis aeternae oblationem, it. adoptionem &c. ceu pluribus docet B. Par. Harm. Evang. c. 151. p. 31.)*

## 7:12
v. 12. Prosper book 3 de vit. contempl. c. 15. This is the whole love of one's neighbor, that you should wish for the good that you wish to be conferred upon yourself, also for your neighbor; and the evil, which you would not wish to happen to yourself, you should not wish for your neighbor either. That saying, What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another: Alexander Severus not only willingly used, but also ordered to be proclaimed by heralds and to be inscribed in public and celebrated places. Nazianz. expressed it thus. οἶαπρὸς ἄλλον μὴ. Such things as you do not at all wish to suffer from another. Such things you also do not do to another lt. τὶχρνςότντος

*( ὀυν. is redundant here, or is a particle of order, as לכן Hos. 2, 14. noting D. Tarnov. Comment. in the way of the alleged place, page 69. and likewise D. Glassius in Gramm. S. p. 629. Moreover, the Syrian omits this particle, but the Arab connects it by a prefix. & translates, the Ethiopian by a suffix therefore.)*

*( Therefore whatever you wish that men should do to you, do also to them. Parallel places are Luc. 6, 31. Roman. 13, 8. 10. Gal. 5, 14. Tob. 4, 16. A similar saying is also drawn from the writings of the Jews by Buxtorff. Lex. Talm. Rabb. p. 1508. sounding thus: פירושה i. e. What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor.

This is the whole Law: the rest are nothing but its explanation. It is read in Schab. f. 31. 1. & is ascribed to Hillel. Concerning Alexander Severus see Aelius Lampridius. Conf. also Aug. contr. Faustum c. 7. l. 3. de D. C. c. 14. l. 2. de ord. c. 8. Hier. ep. 14. ad Celantiam. Isid. Pelus. l. 4. ep. 53. & 54. Camer. horar. subc. Cent. 1. c. 98. whom B. D. Quistorpius alleges on this matter in Annot ad h. l.)

This is the law & the Prophets. These words are not only to be referred to the immediately preceding rule, because the law & the Prophets do not only speak of the second table, but of the whole doctrine which he has handed down thus far. *( For this is the law & the Prophets. (Parallel passages Rom. 13, 8.Gal. 5, 14.) i. e. whatever the law & the Prophets prescribe concerning justice & right in civil society, all that can most conveniently be referred to this canon. thus B. Par. L de Mag. Polit. §. 234. (nor yet is the love of GOD excluded, but rather included, as it notes in Harm. Evang. c. 156. p. 507. and likewise Dn. D. Walth. H. B. p. 757.) Where he also from this passage at length and firmly asserts, that from the wealthy, i. e. those who seek money from us, not because of any urgent necessity, but so that they may trade with our money, make profit, buy estates &c. it is permitted to enter into such a contract, that they pay four or five for the use of a hundred florins annually, while the recovery of the principal remains intact. Since natural equity and gratitude established by Christ approves such a contract. But the case of the needy is far different, who, compelled by extreme poverty, seek something in loan at least so that they may sustain themselves. That usury can be exacted from these is so far from being approved by this passage and natural equity, that it rather suggests the contrary, as B. D. Bald. Cas. Consc. l. 4. c. 3. cas. 4. also brings forward this very passage along with other reasons and foundations against unjust usury of this kind.)*

Latin:

v. 12. Prosper lib. 3. de vit. contempl. c. 15. Haec est proximi tota dilectio, ut bonum quod tibi conferri vis, velis & proximo; & malum, quod tibi accidere nolis, nolis & proximo. Dictum illud, Quod tibi non vis fieri, alterine feceris: Alexander Severus non solum libenter usurpabat, sed etiam proclamari à praeconib mandabat ac publicis celebribus que in locis inscribi. Nazianz. sic expressit. οἶαπρὸς ἄλλον μὴ.Qualia ab altero omnino non vis pati. Talia & tu alterine feceris lt. τὶχρνςότντος

*( ὀυν. redundat hîc, vel est particula ordinis, uti לכןHos. 2, 14. notante D. Tarnov. Comment. in modò alleg. locum, pag. 69. itemque D. Glassio Gramm. S. p. 629. Coeterùm Syrus omittit hanc particulam, Arabs verò per praefixum copulat. & vertit, Aethiops per suff. igitur.)*

*( Quaecunigitur vultis, ut faciant vobis homines, ita & vosfacite. Loca parall. sunt Luc. 6, 31.Roman. 13, 8.10.Gal. 5, 14.Tob. 4, 16. Simile quoque dictum è Iudaeorum scriptis depromit Buxtorff. Lex. Talm. Rabb. p. 1508. ita sonans: פירושה i. e. Quod odiosum est tibi, proximo tuo ne feceris.

Haec est Lex tota: coetera nil sunt nisi eius explicatio. Legitur in Schab. f. 31. 1. & adseribitur Hilleli. De Alexandro Severo vide-tur Aelius Lampridius. Conf. etiam Aug. contr. Faustum c. 7. l. 3. de D. C. c. 14. l. 2. de ord. c. 8. Hier. ep. 14. ad Celantiam. Isid. Pelus. l. 4. ep. 53. & 54. Camer. horar. subc. Cent. 1. c. 98. quos in rem hanc allegat B D. Quistorpius Annot ad h. l.)*

Haec est lex & Prophetae. Haec verba non tantùm referenda sunt ad proximè praecedentem regulam, quia lex & Prophetae non tantùm loquuntur de secunda tabula, sed de tota doctrina, quam hactenus tradidit. *( Ist a enim lex & Prophetae. (Loca parall. Rom. 13, 8.Gal. 5, 14.) h. e. quicquid lex & Prophetae de iustitiâ & iure in societate civili praescribunt, illud omne ad hunc canonem referri commodissimè potest. ita B. Par. L de Mag. Polit. §. 234. (neque tamen excluditur, sed potiùs includitur amor DEI, ceu id m notat Harm. Evang. c. 156. p. 507. itemque Dn. D. Walth. H. B. p. 757.) Ubi etiam ex hoc loco prolixè ac firmiter adstruit, quòd ab opulentis, h. e. qui pecuniam à nobis expetunt, non ob urgentem aliquam necessitatem, sed ut nostrâ pecumâ negotientur, lucrentur, fundos emant &c. talem inire contractum liceat, ut quotannis pro centum florenorum usu quatuor vel quinque persolvant, salvâ interim sortis repetitione. Cùm naturalis aequitas ac gratitudo h-là Christo stabilita talem contractum comprobet. Longè verò diversa est ratio egenorum, qui summâ egestate compulsi, saltem ut sese sustentent, aliquid mutuò petunt. Ab his enim usuram exigi posse, tantùm abest, ut hic locus ac naturalis aequitas probet, ut potiùs contrarium suadeat, ceu hunc ipsum quoq; locum iuxta cum aliis rationibus ac fundamentis cōtra iniustam huiusmodi usuram adducit B. D. Bald. Cas. Consc. l. 4. c. 3. cas. 4.)*

## 7:13
v. 13. Basil. in enarr. Ps. 1. tom. 1. p. 218. There are two ways contrary to each other, one indeed broad and wide, the other narrow and strait. Just as many leaders also lead, of whom each one tries to snatch the traveler to himself: for that easy and broad way has the evil Demon as a leader deceiving from here, who through pleasure drags those following to perdition; but the good Angel possesses the rough and arduous one, who through labors and virtue leads to a blessed end. Lactant. lib. 6. cap. 3. There are two ways, through which it is necessary for human life to proceed is, one which carries to heaven, the other which depresses to the underworld, which both Poets have introduced in their songs and Philosophers in their disputations. Prosper Aquitanicus in sent, August, epigr. 191,

Narrow is the way that leads to the halls of true life, nor does the journey of the mind receive the joys of the flesh. Earthly pleasure walks in wide spaces, virtue seeks the heights in a narrow boundary.

That breadth of the way, leading to destruction, consists in the inclination of the flesh, the ease of erring, the variety of those who seduce, and the plurality of those who accompany. To the narrowness of the opposite way is referred the slipperiness of those going, the multiplicity of those failing, the rarity of those persisting, and the difficulty of the journey. August. in h. l. Few find this way, because there is no diligence in seeking, because in those who seek there is blindness of reason, perversity of the concupiscible, subtlety of the deceiving Devil, in us a proneness to falling, difficulty in rising, weakness in resisting, and a multiplicity of those drawing us away from the way.

*( Enter. In the parallel place Luc. 13, 24. there is held the emphatic word ἀγωνίζεσθε i. e. contend in the struggle, exert all your strength like those struggling or fighting, as if striving strenuously for life and eternal salvation. Gravely August. t. 9. lib. de Tripl. Habit. c. 4. One must strongly resist the pleasure of the flesh, one must strongly fight against the deceitful blandishments of this world, one must watch against the multiform suggestions of Satan. With all zeal the wide way of the age is to be avoided, which leads to death: but truly with all the desire of the heart the narrow way is the way of abstinence and chastity, of humility and all religion, which way Christ trod before us, by which way he migrated to his kingdom. Let us also follow his footsteps, until after him we arrive by the same way at the royal city, in which he himself reigns &c. Conf. The same t. cit. tr. de 4. virtur. char. in f. most beautifully discussing this way. it. serm. uno de temp. Barbar. c. 8. Where he most elegantly explains the narrow gate from the side of Christ, through which the thief having entered was changed, the penitent Jew, every pagan converted. What, he exclaims, is narrower than that hole, which one of the soldiers opened by striking the side of the crucified, and yet through these narrow straits almost now the whole world has entered. Observe, this against the Jesuit Conzenius, who inveighs against Chytraeus, for the reason that he accepts the narrow gate also concerning faith. But what the Jesuit adds as if he were going to do us a disservice, that while we urge faith in Christ, we neglect good works and wallow through every mire of crimes, in that if he he slanders us, as we who expressly teach that although faith alone justifies, yet it is never alone i. e. separated from good works.)*

*( Narrow is the way &c. Beautifully Ambrose in Ps. 1. There are two ways: one of the just, the other of sinners. Here is the liberty of desires, there the injury of servitude; here a banquet, there a fast; here the intemperance of joys, there the perseverance of tears; here dancing, there prayer; here sweet songs, there heavy groans. This way is narrow and hard, because through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of heaven, Act. 14, 22. The way leading to life is therefore narrow because of the cross, which deters very many from it, l. c. 2. because of the Devil, who blinds the travelers of the pleasures of this age, unless they diligently follow the shining light of the word. 3. because of the weakness of the flesh, which succumbs to the wiles of Satan, unless the traveler is strengthened by divine aid &c. God, however, has promised to succor infirmity with the staff of His word, and in truth also succors all, and even raises up the fallen, provided they themselves do not reject and maliciously despise the offered grace of GOD. But the way is by no means narrow by reason of any absolute divine decree, excluding the reprobate from salvation, as the Calvinists maintain. For the solemn adjuration of the grave supreme Deity, Ezech. 33, 11. the most sweet invitation of Christ, calling all those pressed by the burden of sins Matth. 11, 28. &c. nay, the shedding of most precious tears for the impenitence of men, &c. testify to something far different. Yet, setting all these aside, Marcus Fried. Wendelinus, Exerc. XLIII. §. 2., does not blush to pronounce that the orthodox opinion, which holds that God has not out of mere εὐδοκίᾳ i.e. a certain absolute hatred devoted the greatest part of men to eternal damnation, is to set one's mouth against heaven, and expressly to contradict the spirit of GOD. But in order to prove this, he compares the present passage with Matth. 20, 16. How frivolous, however, this proof of so grave an accusation is, will be shown at length at the said place. Here we note at least briefly that W. confuses things which are most distinct.

For it is something entirely different, That God has reprobated the greatest part of men, and that by a just judgment, punishing the final impenitence and unbelief of very many men, who stubbornly reject the offered means of salvation and pursue with hatred God, who seriously desires the salvation of all, which indeed He Himself foresaw from eternity; But another thing, that God out of mere εὐδο κίᾳ and absolute hatred, without any regard for the own malice of the reprobate, has reprobated the greatest part of men, nay, that reprobation is the cause that they persevere in their malice. The former we grant, and we teach, because the Holy Scriptures affirm it; but the latter we deny, because Holy Scripture protests as often as it testifies clearly and emphatically concerning the universal mercy of GOD, the universal merit of Christ, and the universal calling, and casts the cause of damnation upon the men themselves. Which it does everywhere.)*

*( Wide is the way &c. Namely, on account of the fragility and weakness of the flesh, the craftiness of Satan and the world, the sweetness of the pleasures of this age, the blindness of the intellect in spiritual matters, the ease of erring, the proclivity of corrupt nature toward evil, and the multitude of those who seduce and accompany. Hieron. s. Paulinus in Hieron. t. 1. ep. 14. If we are possessed by hatred and envy, if we yield to cupidity and avarice, if we prefer present advantages to future ones: we walk along the spacious way &c. Let us desert the wide way and the multitude of those who seduce. Let us follow Paul Phil. 3, 17. nay, Christ Matth. 11, 28. He Himself is the way, and the truth, and the life Ioh. 14, Conf. 1. Petr. 2, 21. 1. Ioh. 2, 6. Furthermore, what Christ teaches in this place with words; elsewhere, namely Luc. 16, 19. seqq., He declares by a notable example, as in it is proposed 1. the joyful entry of the wide way. 2. the sad outcome of the same. 3. the manner of declining this way, as the Blessed Pareus shows at length in Homil. Acad. part. 2. p. 314. 315.)*

Latin:

v. 13. Basil. in enarr. Ps. 1. tom. 1. p. 218. Duae sunt interse contrariae viae, una quidem lata & ampla, altera angusta & arcta. Totidem etiam ducunt duces, quorum uterque ad se rapere viatorem conatur: via namque illa facilis & lata ducem hinc decipientem Daemonem malum habet, qui per voluptatem sequentes ad perditionem trahit; asperam verò & arduam Angelus possidet bonus, qui per labores & virtutem ad finem beatum ducit. Lactant. lib. 6. cap. 3. Duae sunt viae, per quas humanam vitam progredi necesse est, una quae in coelum ferat, alterae quae ad inferos deprimat, quas & Poëtae in carminibus & Philosophi in disput ationibus suis induxerunt. Prosper Aquitanicus in sent, August, epigr. 191,

Arcta via est, verae quae ducit ad atria vitae,Nec recipit carnis gaudia mentis iter.Amplis incedit spaciis terrena voluptas,Angusto virtus limite celsa petit.

Consistit illa latitudo viae, ad perditionē ducentis, in carnis proclivitate, errandi facilitate, seducentium varietate, comitantium pluralitate. Ad angustiam viae contrariae refertur lubricitas euntium, deficientium multiplicitas, persistentium raritas, itineris difficultas. August. in h. l. Pauci inveniunt hanc viam, quia non est in quaerendo sedulit as, quia in quaerentibus est rationis caecitas, concupiscibilis perversit as, Diaboli fallentis subtilitas, in nobis eadendi pronit as, resurgendi difficult as, resistendi debilitas, retrahentium à via multiplicitas.

*( Intrate. In loco parall. Luc. 13, 24. habetur emphaticum verbum ἀγωνίζεσθε i. e. in agone contendite, omnes vires instar agonizantium sive pugnantium exerite, quasi pro vità & aet. salute strenuè certate. Graviter August. t. 9. lib. de Tripl. Habit. c. 4. Fortiter carnali resistendum est volupt ati, fortiter contra fallaces huius mundi blandicias pugnandum est, contramultimodas Satanae suggestiones vigilandum. Omni studio lata seculi via vitanda est, quae ducit ad mortem: at vero omni cordis desiderio via angusta, est via abstinentiae & castitatis, humilitatis & omnis religionis, quam viam ante nos Christus attrivit, quâ viâ ad suum regnum migravit. Cuius vestigia & nos sequamur, donec post cum eadem viâ ad urbem regiam perveniamus, in quâ ipse regnat &c. Conf. Idem t. cit. tr. de 4. virtur. char. in f. pulcherrimè de hâc viâ disserens. it. serm. uno de temp. Barbar. c. 8. Ubi elegantissimè portam angustam de latere Christi exponit, per quam ingressus latro mutatus, poenitens Iudaeus, paganus omnis conversus. Quid, exclamat, angustius illo for amine, quod unus è militibus percutiende latus crucifixi aperuit, & tamen per has angustias penè iam totus mundus intravit. Observ, hoc cōtra Iesuitam Conzeniū, qui dI in Chytraeum invehitur, eò quod angustam portam etiam de fide accipit. Quae verò Iesuita quasi aegrè nobis facturus subiungit, quòd dum fidem in Christum urgemus, bona opera negligamus ac per omne flagitiorom coenum volutemur, in eo si nos intolligicalumniatur, ut qui disertè docemus, quòd licet fides sola iustificet, tamen nunquam sit sola s. à B. O. separata.)*

*( Arcta est via &c. Pulcrè Ambros. in Ps. 1.Duae sunt viae: una iustorum, altera peccatorum. Hie libertas cupidit atum, illic servitutis iniuria; hic convivium, illie ieiunium; hìc intemperantia gandiorum, illic perseverantia lacrymarum; hîc saltatio, illie oratio; hîc cantus dulces, illic gemitus graves. Arcta est haec via & dura. quia per multas tribulationes oportet nos ingredi in regnum caelorum,Act. 14, 22. Arcta est igitur via ad vitam ducens propter crucem plurimos ab ea deterrentem l. c. 2. propter Diabolum, voluptatibus huius seculi viatores, nisi praelucentem verbi lucem diligenter sequantur, exeoeantem. 3. propter carnis imbecillitatem, nisi divino auxilio viator confirmetur, Satanae astutiis succumbentem &c. Deus tamen infirmitati baculo verbi sui succurrere promisit, ac reverà etiā omnibus succurrit, atq; lapsos etiam erigit, modò ipsi oblatam DEI gratiam non respuant ac malitiosè contemnant. Minimè autem arcta est via ratione absoluti alicuius decreti divini, reprobos à salute excludentis, ceu Calviniani statuunt. Longè diversum enim gravis supremi Numinis obtestatio, Ezech. 33, 11. suavissima Christi, omnes peccatorum onere pressos vocantis, invitatio Matth. 11, 28. &c. imò pretiosissimarum lacrymarum ob hominum impoenitentiam profusio, &c. testantur. Quibus tamen omnibus posthabitis Marcus Fried. Wendelinus Exerc.
