XLIII. §. 2. pronunciare non erubescit, sententiam orthodoxam, quae tenet, quòd Deus non ex merâ εὐδοκίᾳ s. absoluto quodam odio maximam hominum partem aeternae damnationi devoverit, os in caelum ponere, & expressè spirituz DEI contradicere. Id verò ut probet, confert praesentem locum cum Matth. 20, 16. Quàm frivola verò tam gravis accusationis probatio haec sit, prolixè ad d. l. ostendetur. Hîc illud saltem breviter notamus, quòd W. confundat, quae distinctissima sunt.

Aliud enim omninò est, Deum maximam hominum partem reprobasse, idque iusto iudicio, finalem plurimorum hominum, pertinaciter oblata salutis media reiicientium ac Deum, salutem torum seriò cupientem odioprose quentium, impoenitentiam & incredulitatem, quam sanè ab aeterno ipse praevidit, puniēte; Alliud verò, Deum exmerâεὐδο κίᾳ& absoluto odio absque propriae reprobo rum malitiae intuitu maximam hominum partem reprobasse, imo reprobationem in causa esse, ut illi in suâ malitiâ perseverent. Prius largimur, ac docemus, quia sacrae litterae affirmant; posterius verò negamus, quia Script. S. toties reclamat, quoties de universali DEI misericordiâ, universali Christi merito, universali vocatione luculenter & emphaticè testatur, inque ipsos homines damnationis causam reiicit. id quod passim facit.)*

*( Lata est via &c. Nempe propter carnis fragilitatem ac imbecillitatem, Satanae ac mundi calliditatem, voluptatum huius seculi suavitatem, intellectûs in spiritual. coeeitatem, errandi facilitatem, corruptae naturae ad malum proclivitatem, seducentium ac comitantium pluralitatem. Hieron. s. Paulinus apud Hieron. t. 1. ep. 14. Si odio atque invidiâ possidemur si cupiditati & avaritiae cedimus, sipraesentia commoda futuris praeferimus: per spatiosam viam incedimus &c. Deseramus viam latam ac seducentium multitudinem. Sequamur verò Paulum Phil. 3, 17. imò Christum Matth. 11, 28. ipse est via, & veritas & vitaIoh. 14, Conf. 1. Petr. 2, 21.1. Ioh. 2, 6. Coeterùm quod Christus h. l. verbis docet; alibi, nempe Luc. 16, 19. seqq. insigni exemplo declarāt, utpote in quo proponitur 1. laetus viae latae ingressus. 2. tristis eiusdem exitus. 3. viae huius declinandae modus, ceu prolixè monstrat B. Par. Homil. Acad. part. 2. p. 314. 315.)*

## 7:14
v. 14. The ancients read τι στενὴ in the form of one wondering, how narrow is the gate and the way pressed. Syr. םא קטין How small is the gate.

*( Few there are &c. That the number of the damned will be greater than that of the blessed, is easily evident, because there are many who enter through the wide way in such a manner that they never do penance, and do not allow themselves to be led back into the right way by that good Spirit of God.

The same also then from other sayings of Holy Scripture, as Luc. 13, 24. lib. 4. Esdrae c. 9, 15. 22. then by types Gen. 19. 24.Luc. 17, 29.1. Petr. 3, 20. it is evident. Meanwhile, although speaking comparatively the number of the damned will be greater, and so in respect to them few are to be saved, yet speaking absolutely the number of those to be saved will also be great, as we are explicitly taught Apoc. 7, 9. Whence without contradiction sometimes many are said to be saved, as Matth. 8, 11.Ebr. 2, 10. sometimes few, as in this place G-essius in Theatro Bibl p 1840. for the confirmation of the former member brings forward also Matth. 26, 28. and Rom. 5, 19. But the word many is taken there for all. For it is not treated there specifically of the elect alone, but in general of all men, as is shown elsewhere. But this same argument, that the number of the predestined is small in comparison to the reprobate, at length also treats Alphonsus Mendoza, in a certain Salmant. Acad. S--ti Cathedrae praefectus Controv. Theol. q. 1. propos. 3. p. 86. seqq. where among other things p. 88. he notably writes, that the salvation of the elect is called in Holy Scripture a lot, since just as lots sometimes fall and happen to a poor little man, a slave, and a noble &c. are accustomed to be frustrated of their hope, so of merits, (NB.) dignities, and human virtues there is absolutely no account taken by God the Best and Greatest for predestining anyone. Which words are not only to be opposed to some Scholastics (especially Occam and Biel) who explicitly profess, that God therefore predestined some, because He foresaw in them a good use of Free Will and merits: but also to the common opinion of the Papists, that God justifies and saves men on account of their own merits. If, however, in time God justifies and saves men on account of their own merits, it follows that He also predestined them on account of foreseen merits. Whatever subterfuges the Jesuits may seek here.)*

Latin:

v. 14. Veteres legunt τι στενὴ in forma admirantis, quàm angusta est porta & via pressa. Syr. םא קטיןQuàm exigua est porta.

*( Pauci sunt &c. Quòd maior futurus sit numerus damnatorum, quàm beatorum, facilè patet, quia multi sunt, qui ita per latam viam ingrediuntur, ut nunquam agant poenitentiam, seque in viam rectam à Spiritu illo Dei bono reduci patiantur.

Idipsum etiam tum ex aliis Scr. S. dictis, uti Luc. 13, 24. lib. 4. Esdrae c. 9, 15. 22. tum typis Gen. 19. 24.Luc. 17, 29.1. Petr. 3, 20. patet Interea licet comparativè loquendo maior futurus sit damnatorū numerus, adeoq; eorum respectu pauci sint salvandi, absolutè tamenloquendo salvandorum quoq; magnus erit numerus, ceu disertè docemur Apoc. 7, 9. Unde sine contradictione modò multi dicuntur salvandi, uti Matth. 8, 11.Ebr. 2, 10. modò pauci, uti h. l. G-essius in Theatro Bibl p 1840. ad prioris membri confirmationem adducit quoque Matth. 26, 28. ac Rom. 5, 19. At sumituribi vox multorum pro omnibus. Neque enim agitur ibi in specie de solis electis, sed in genere de omnibus hominibus, ut alibi ostenditur. Idem verò hoc argumentum, quòd exiguus praedestinatorum numerus sit in reproborum comparatione, proli-e quoque pertractat Alphonsus Mendoza, quodam in Salmant. Acad. S--ti Cathedrae praefectus Controv. Theol. q. 1. propos. 3. p. 86. seqq. ubi inter alia p. 88. notanter scribit, quod electorum salus in Sc. S. dicatur sors, cùm sicut sortes interdum cadunt & contingunt homini pauperculo, mancipio, & nobilies &c. suâ spe frusirari solent, ita meritorum, (NB.) dignitatum, virtutumq; humanarum nulla prorsus habeatur ratio à Deo Opt. Max. ad aliquem praedestinandum. Quae verba non solùm opponenda Scholasticis nonnullis (Occamo cumprimis ac Bieli) disertè profitentibus, Deum ideò aliquos praedestinasse, quia praeviderit in eis bonum usum Liberi Arbitrii & merita: verùm etiam communi Pontificiorum sententiae, quòd Deus propter merita propria homines iustificet & salvet. Si verò in tempore Deus homines propter ipso-um merita iustificat & salvat, sequitur quòd etiam propter praevisa mer-ta eos praedestinarit. Quaecunque etiam hî subterfugia Iesuitae quaerant.)*

## 7:15
v. 15. There are two γνωρίσματα of false Prophets. 1. illegitimate calling. They come not sent, Ier. 23. v. 21. 2. simulation of piety. Iren. lib. 3. adv. haer. cap. 18. p. 205. outwardly indeed sheep, through the speech which they have extrinsically they appear similar to us, speaking the same things with us, but inwardly wolves, for their opinion --mic--alis.. The prophets among the people of GOD for the most part were accustomed to wear μηγωτὰς or sheepskins, Hebr. 11. v. 37. the false prophets imitated the same habit , so that they might the more easily impose upon the simpler ones, which Zechariah c. 13. v. 4. said: to wear a garment of hair or a shaggy one for the sake of deceiving. Christ therefore retains this comparison, so that he may show that from external appearance, there are many things in common between false prophets and true prophets, such as the title of vocation, learning, eloquence, the gift of miracles, and the appearance of holiness in external conduct. Sheep's skins are: 1. specious titles, they boast that they are true and Catholic teachers. 2. flattering words, with which they adorn their doctrine. 3. the appearance of holy conduct: Athanas. orat. 2. against the Arians. They disguise their appearance, and are clothed with the voices of sacred letters as if with an honorable garment. Vincent. against heretics, ch. 36. What is the clothing of sheep, if not the utterances of the Prophets and Apostles, which the same men, with a certain sheep-like sincerity, have woven as if with a certain fleece for that immaculate lamb, who takes away the sin of the world? Who are the ravenous wolves? If not the wild and rabid senses of heretics, who always infest the sheepfolds of the Church and tear apart the flock of Christ wherever they can. A false prophet is one who corrupts the law or the Gospel, or confuses these kinds of doctrine, or urges the law while concealing the Gospel, or vice versa. Ignat. Epist. to the Philadelphians, f. 32. πολλοὶ λύκοι. Many wolves, having assumed a fleece, pretend to be sheep, and with their depraved enticements intercept them from the course of God. See also Epist. 10. f. 46. Tertull. on prescription against heretics, ch. 4. f. 202. What are these sheep's skins, if not the outward surface of the Christian name? What are the ravenous wolves, if not the senses and the deceitful spirit lurking within to infest the flock of Christ? Who are the false prophets, if not false preachers? Who are the false Apostles, if not adulterous evangelizers? Theoph. on Matth. 7. f. 29. καρηςολοο See Epiph. book 1. vol. 3. on the heretic Tatian, f. 171. The author of the imperfect work on Matthew, vol. 3. f. 578. August. book 2. on the Lord's sermon on the mount, vol. 4. f. 1171. Hieron. on ch. 7. Matth. vol. 9. f. 11. Clemens book 2. Constit. ch. 19. Let not a Layman say, I am a sheep, and not a shepherd, and I have had no account of myself.

the shepherd will see to it, he himself alone will pay the penalties for me. For just as when a sheep does not follow a good shepherd, it is exposed to wolves to perish: so again when a sheep follows a bad shepherd, the destruction of the sheep by the bad shepherd, who will devour it, is certain. Wherefore murderous shepherds are to be fled. They are 1. λύκοι lying in wait for the Lord's flock. The wolf devours the earth, so that it may be rendered heavier for seizing and retaining prey, thus heretics hunt for earthly favors. 2. they are, ἅρπαγες, they tear apart Scripture, the person of Christ, and all good ordinances. 3. they are stinging thorns. They affect dominion in the Church, just as is prefigured in the parable of the bramble, Judg. 9..

* ( Beware of false prophets. How caution may be fittingly exercised is clear from the following passages John 10:5 Rom. 16:7 2 Thess. 3:2 Tit. 3:10 2 John v. 10. Corn. à Lapide on this passage: False teachers teach that the way to heaven is not narrow, but broad, and therefore they send their followers not to heaven, but to the underworld. For they teach that one must not fast, must not confess, that virginity must not be kept, nor religious vows, and they indulge every freedom to the flesh, and take away from the Blessed O. every power of meriting. With these words the Jesuit tries to sting our people. But it must be known that this is a grave calumny. For our people do not forbid fasting itself, but at least they deny that the Papal fast is a true fast, since a true fast does not consist in the distinction of foods, as the Papists wish, but in the plenary abstinence from food and drink. Likewise, they disapprove of the prohibition of the eating of meats under the opinion of necessity, worship, and merit, which the Papists likewise urge. Thus our people do not abolish private confession, but they deny at least this, that in confession before a Priest the enumeration of all sins is necessary. So also in the rest, as has been shown elsewhere. Let the Jesuit rather learn from this passage that since it is commanded by Christ to all indiscriminately, both here and elsewhere, that they should beware of false prophets, hear the voice of Christ John 10:27, but not follow a stranger v. 5, test the spirits 1 John 4:1, Cf. Acts 17:11 Rom. 16:17 1 Cor. 10:5 1 Thess. 5:21, this can be done more conveniently than if the life and doctrine of false teachers be examined according to the norm of the divine word, contained in Holy Scripture Isa. 8:26 Gal. 6:16 2 Pet. 1:19, not only that laymen are not to be kept away from the reading of Holy Scripture but rather are to be invited to it. Contrary to what the common practice of the Papists teaches, which fights diametrically against Holy Scripture and the example of the pious in the primitive Church, as has been shown at length by our people long ago. If furthermore laymen ought to read Holy Scripture, and examine the dogmas of false teachers by it, it is also necessary that Bibles be translated into vernacular languages, which likewise is opposed to the decrees of the Papists. What is to be answered to the exceptions of the Papists will easily appear if those things are noted which B. Par. provides in Exeg. L. on Holy Scripture 454. Furthermore, from the fact that particular Churches are here commanded to beware of false teachers (Cf. also below c. 24, 13. 14. 25. Act. 20, 28. 29. 30. 31.2. Cor. 11, 2.) Our own people, among others, firmly conclude that they are not immune from the danger of error Against the Papists. Similarly, from this passage it can also be proven against the same that laymen are not to be excluded simply from the vocation of the ministers of the Church, nor from a decisive vote in Councils, since caution against false teachers and erroneous dogmas has been commanded to all Christians. Finally, from this same admonition, the blessed Doctor Balduinus, C. C. p. 463, proves among other things that an orthodox person cannot with a good conscience receive the Holy Supper from the Calvinists.)*

*( In sheep's clothing. What is indicated here by sheep's clothing, the blessed Doctor Glassius teaches at length in Rhetor. Sacr. p. 412. 413. namely, such clothing is the vain boasting of a true vocation, knowledge of languages, manifold erudition, the feigned production of miracles, etc. See Ierem. 23, 25.30.1. Reg. 13. 13.Matth. 7, 22.Rom. 16, 18.1. Cor. 13. 1. 2.2. Thess. 2, 9.1. Tim. 4, 1. 2. 3.2. Tim. 3, 5, 6.)*

*( Inwardly they are ravenous wolves. Therefore, heretics are to be cut off by the sword. Thus Bellarmine subsumes in l. de Laic. c. 21. and Ribaden. l. 1. de Princ. c. 26, p. 172. Compare also Coster in Enchir. p. c. 8. and Becanus in Manuali Controv. p. 484. See what is noted at Act. 20, 29. and let B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. t. p. 84. also be unrolled, and L. de Mag. Pol. § 356. At this place it can at least be noted, 1. that Symbolic Theology is not argumentative. 2. that Christ's scope here is not to compare heretics with wolves with respect to punishment, but both with respect to nature and disposition, and with respect to harm, and with respect to flight)*

*( Who come. τὸ to come is opposed here to divine mission and vocation, which is altogether necessary for the Ministers of the Church. Compare Ier. 23, 21. c. 27, 9. 14. 15. Rom. 10, 15. The exceptions of the Photinians have long since been satisfied by our own people, just as also the calumny of the Papists (which the Jesuits Conzen and Corn. à Lap. also repeat at this place), that the Ministers of our Church are not true ministers, for the reason that they are not sent by Bishops, i.e., Papists. See here against the Papists B. D. Mentzerus T. 2. Dispp. Marpurg. disp. 22. B. D. Hunnius T. 1. Oper. p. 1. seqq. B. P. Confess Cath t. 3. pag. 190. and Loc. de Minist. Eccles. p. 79. seqq. Dn. D. Haberkornius in Decad. Disput. Theol. de Ministerii Eccles. quod in Eccl. Protestantium orthodoxis est, solida veritate & efficacia, A. 1656. editis etc. in particular concerning the vocation of B. Luther D. Balduinus contra, Patzm. c. v. 13. but against the Photinians and Anabaptists Dn. D. Calovius Socin. Proflig. p. 95. seqq. B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccles. §. 55. seqq. B. D. Chemn. part. 3. LL. p. 119. seqq. B. D. Stegmann. Disp. 53. Photin. and others.)*

Latin:

v. 15. Duo γνωρίσματα sunt falsorum Prophetarum. 1. illegitima vocatio. Veniunt non missi, Ier. 23. v. 21. 2. pietatis simulatio. Iren. l b. 3. adv. haer. cap. 18. p. 205. à foris quidem oves, per camn. quam habent extrisecus loquelam similes nobis apparent, eadem obiscum loquentes, intrinsecus verò lupi sententia enim eorum --mic--alis.. Prophetae in populo DEI utplurimum μηγωτὰς sive ovillas gestare solebant, Hebr. 11. v. 37. eundem habitum imitabantur pseudo prophetae, ut simplicioribus tanto facilius imponerent, quod Zacharias c. 13. v. 4. dixit: vestem pili aut villosam induere fallendi gratia. Christus igitur hanc similitudinem retinet, ut ostendat exhabitu externo, pseudoprophetis cum veris prophetis multa esse communia, utpote titulum vocationis, eruditionem, eloquentiam, donum miraculorum, speciem sanctitatis in conversatione externa. Pelles ovium sunt. 1. speciosi tituli, gloriantur se esse veros & Catholicos doctores. 2. blanda verba, quibus doctrinam suam ornant. 3. species conversationis sanctae: Athanas. orat. 2. contra Arian. Speciem suam dissimulant, & literarum sacrarum vocibus quasi honesto culta induuntur. Vincent. contra haer. c. 36. Quid est vostitus ovium, nisi Prophetarum & Apostolorum proloquia, quae iidem ovili quadam sinceritate agno illi immaculato, qui tollit peccatum mundi, tanquam vellere quodam texuerunt? qui sunt lupi rapaces? nisi sensus haereticorum feri & rabidi, qui caulas Ecclesiae semper infestant & gregem Christi quaqua possunt dilacerant. Pseudopropheta est, qui legem aut Evangelium corrumpit, aut haec genera doctrinae confundit aut legem urget dissimulato Evangelio, vel contrà. Ignat. Epist. ad Philad. f. 32. πολλοὶ λύκοι.Multi lupi vellere assumto oves simulant, & pravis suis illecebris eas ex cursu Dei intercipiunt. Vide etiam Epist. 10. f. 46. Tertull. de praescript. adv. haer. cap. 4. f. 202. Quaenam sunt istae pelles ovium, nisi nominis Christiani extrinsecus superficies? Qui lupi rapaces, nisi sensus & Spiritus subdoli ad infestandum gregem Christi intrinsecus delite scentes? Qui Pseudoprophetae sunt, nisi falsi praedicatores? Qui Pseudo Apostoli, nisi adulteri evangelizato. res? Theoph. in Matth. 7. f. 29. καρηςολοο Vide Epi h lib. 1. tom. 3. de Tatiano haeret. f. 171. Autorem operis imperf. in Matth. tom. 3. f. 578. August. lib. 2. de serm. Dom. in monte tom. 4. f. 1171. Hieron. in c. 7. Matth. tom. 9. f. 11. Clemens lib 2. Constit. cap. 19. Ne Laicus dicat, Ego ovis sum, & non pastor, & nullam mei rationem habui.

pastor viderit, ipse solus pro me poenas dabit. Ut enim cùm ovis non sequitur bonum pastorem, lupis exposita est ad intereundum: sic rursus cùm ovis malum pastorem sequitur, certus est ovis interitus à malo pastore, qui eam devorabit. Quare fugiendi sunt pastores interfectores. Sunt 1. λύκοι insidiantes gregi Dominico. Lupus terram vorat, ut ponderosior reddatur ad praedam capiendam & retinendam, sic haeretici terrenos favores aucupantur. 2. sunt, ἅρπαγες, dilacerant Scripturam, personam Christi & omnes bonas ordinationes. 3. sunt spinae pungentes. Affectant dominium in Ecclesia, sicut in parabola de rhamno, Iud. 9. praefiguratur.

* ( Attendite à falsis prophetis. Quomodo cautela fieri decenter possit, patet ex locis seqq. Ioh. 10, 5.Rom. 16, 7.2. Thess. 3, 2.Tit. 3, 10. 2. Ioh. v. 10. Corn. à Lapide in h. l. Falsi doctores docent, viam in coelum non esse arctam, sed laxam, ideoq; suos sequaces non ad coelum, sed ad tartara transmittunt. Docent enim, non esse, ieiunandum, non confitendum, non esse servandam virginitatem, nec vota religionis, omnemque carni libertatem indulgent, ac B. O. omnem merendi vim adimunt. His verbis nostrates Iesuita pungere conatur. Sciendum verò, quòd gravis calumnia haec sit,. Neque enim I nostrates ipsum ieiunium prohibent, sed saltem, negant, Pontificium ieiunium esse verum ieiunium, cùm verum ieiun. non consistat in ciborum discrimine, ceu Pontificii volunt, sed in plenaria cibi potusque abstinentiâ. it. improbant prohibitionem esus carnium sub opinione necessitatis, cultùs ac meriti, quam itidem Pontificii urgent. Sic non abolent nostrates confessionem privatam, sed hoc saltem negant, in confessione, coram Sacerdote necessariam esse omnium peccatorum enumerationem. Sic etiam in reliquis, ut alibi ostensum. Discat potius ex h. l. Iesuita, quòd cùm indiscriminatim omnibus à Christo tum hic, tum alibi mandetur, ut à falsis prophetis attēdant, Christi vocem audiant Ioh. 10, 27. alienum autem non sequantur v. 5. Spiritus probent, 1. Ioh. 4, 1. Conf. Act. 17, 11.Rom. 16, 17.1. Cor. 10, 5.1. Thess. 5, 21. hoc verò commodiùs fieri non possit, quàm si vita ac doctrina falsorum doctorum ad normam verbi divini, in Scripturâ S. comprehensi, examinetur, Es. 8, 26.Galat. 6, 16.2. Pet. 1, 19. non solùm non arcendos à Script. Sacr. lectione esse laicos, sed potiùs ad eam invitandos. Contra ac communis Pontificiorum praxis docet, è diametro cum Sc. S. ac piorum in primitivà Ecclesiâ exemplo pugnans, ceu pridē prolixè à nostratibus ostensum. Si porrò laici Sc. S debent legere, ad eandemque falsorum Doctorum dogmata examinare, necesse quoque est, ut Biblia in Linguas vernaculas transferantur, quod itidem Pontificiorum Decretis adversatur. Quid ad exceptiones Pontificiorum respondendum sit, facilè apparebit, si notentur, quae suppeditat B. Par. Exeg. L. de Sc. S. 454. Porrò ex eo, quòd particulares Ecclesiae hîc iubentur, cavere Pseudodoctores (Conf. etiam inf. c. 24, 13. 14. 25. Act. 20, 28. 29. 30. 31.2. Cor. 11, 2.) firmiter colligunt, inter alia nostrates, eas ab erroris periculo non esse immunes Cōtra Pontificios. Similiter ex hoc loco contra eosdem evinci quoque potest, quòd laici non simpliciter à ministrorum Ecclesiae vocatione, item que à decisivâ sententiâ in Conciliis excludendi sint, cùm cautela à falsis Doctoribus atque erroneis dogmatibus omnibus Christianis mandata sit. Tandem ex ead. hâc admonitione inter alia probat B. D Balduinus C. C. p. 463. quòd orthodoxus nòn possit bonâ conscientiâ S. coenam à Calvin. accipere.)*

*( In vestimentis ovium. Quid per vestimenta ovium hîc indicetur, prolixè docet B. D. Glass. Rhetor. Sacr. p. 412. 413. nem--e sunt talia vestimenta verae vocationis vana gloriatio, lingua-um cognitio, multiplex eruditio, miraculorum conficta productio &c. Vid. Ierem. 23, 25.30.1. Reg. 13. 13.Matth. 7, 22.Rom. 16, 18.1. Cor. 13. 1. 2.2. Thess. 2, 9.1. Tim. 4, 1. 2. 3.2. Tim. 3, 5, 6.)*

*( Intus sunt lupi rapaces. E. forro exscindendi sunt haeretici. ita subsumunt Bellarminus l. de Laic. c. 21. ac Ribaden. l. 1. de Princ. c. 26, p. 172. Conf. quoque (oster. in Enchir. p. c. 8. ac Becanus in Manuali Controv. p. 484. Vid. quae notata ad Act. 20, 29. ac evolvatur quoque B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. t. p. 84. it L. de Mag. Pol. § 356. Hoc loco notari saltim potest, 1. quòd Theclogia Symbolica non sit argumentativa. 2. quòd Christi scopus hîc non sit, comparare haereticos cum lupis respectu poenae, sed tum respectu naturae & indolis, tum respectu damni, tum respectu fugae)*

*( Qui veniunt. Opponitur τὸvenire hîc missioni & vocationi divinae, quae Ecclesiae Ministris omninò necessaria est. Confer Ier. 23, 21. c. 27, 9. 14. 15. Rom. 10, 15. Photinianorum exceptionibus pridem satifactum à nostratibus, quemadmodum etiam, Pontificiorum calumniae, (quam etiam ad h. l. repetunt Iesuitae Conzen ac Corn. à Lap.) quòd Ecclesiae nostrae Ministri non sint veri ministri, eo quod non sint missi ab Episcopis, sc. Pontificiis. Videātur hîc contra Pontificios B. D. Mentzerus T. 2. Dispp. Marpurg. disp. 22. B. D. Hunnius T. 1. Oper. p. 1. seqq. B. P. Confess Cath t. 3. pag. 190. it Loc. de Minist. Eccles. p. 79. seqq. Dn. D. Haberkornius in Decad. Disput. Theol. de Ministerii Eccles. quod in Eccl. Protestantium orthodoxis est, solida veritate & efficacia, A. 1656. editis &c. in specie de vocatione B. Lutheri D. Balduinus contra, Patzm. c. v. 13. contra Photinianos autem atque Anabaptistas Dn. D. Calovius Socin. Proflig. p. 95. seqq. B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccles. §. 55. seqq. B. D. Chemn. part. 3. LL. p. 119. seqq. B. D. Stegmann. Disp. 53. Photin. alii.)*

## 7:16
v. 16. Τρίβολος εξ whence βόλος & βολὴ are said to be from a triple point, because, to wit, the pointed thing strikes in a threefold way, or from a triangular seed. Diosc. lib. 4. c. 15. Theoph. lib. 4. c. 11.

* ( By their fruits &c. The Ethiopian and the Arab prefix the copula and. The former, moreover, just as the Persian, has the singular fruit for the plural fruits. But our people rightly gather from this passage against the Papists that the pure preaching of the word is a mark of the true Church. And indeed, just as a sincere Doctor of the Church is distinguished from a False Prophet by incorrupt and pure doctrine, and is known from it, so also the purity of the doctrine sounding in the Church of GOD is its true and certain mark. Where it is also well to be noted that not a few Papists, and those not of the lowest rank, willingly grant that by fruits one must here understand doctrine, as Bellarmine expressly teaches, 5. de Gr. & L. A. c. 10. & so also Barradius, t. 2. Conc. Ev. l. 7. c. 30. p. 500. Corn. à Lapide, Tirinus, Conzenius in h. l. Nay, Thomas Stapleton, formerly royal Professor in the Acad. of Louvain, l. 10 de Princ. fid. doct. c. 1. confesses that most of the Fathers explain this passage in such a way that we ought to make a judgment about them from the doctrine which the False Prophets propose. The words of Barradius also are most clear: Evil fruits, he writes, from which the Savior indicates that False Prophets are to be recognized Matt. 7, 16. are not so much evil morals, since these can also fall to true Doctors, as false doctrine and evil consequences which flow from their own dogmas, [and] hinder the worship of GOD and true piety. But the Jesuit Maldonatus opposes himself to this exposition, who comments thus on this passage: Here it is a matter of faith, i.e., of recognizing the very doctrine of false prophets: but it is absurd to say that doctrine is proved by doctrine. All the ancient authors, therefore, (NB. that this is most false is evident from Jerome and Theophyl. in this passage, also the Author of the Op. Imperf. in Matth. hom. 19, Theodor. l. 3. haeret. fabul. in the beginning, Vinc. Lirin. advers. haer. c. 36. and others, and Stapleton also confesses it l. c.) understand by fruits the works which follow doctrine, evil works from a naturally evil doctrine, good works from a good one. Let the Jesuits see, however, how they reconcile their associates here. Among us it is certain that by fruits one must here primarily understand doctrine, and so also the parallel passage teaches Luke 6, 45. to which the Jesuit Tirinus himself also refers the reader. But someone might ask, how can false Doctors be recognized from doctrine? I answer: if it is brought to the Holy Scripture and examined. For the Apostle prescribed that as the norm Gal. 1, 8.; in it sounds the voice of Christ, which we ought to hear. But the ancient Fathers, custom, laws, or human traditions are by no means the rule of faith, which rule the Jesuit Conzenius prescribes here. But the Papists flee from that norm, to wit, the Holy Scripture, knowing well that most of their dogmas cannot sustain an examination by it. Corn. à Lapide warns that there is a double fruit: the first of false and impious doctrine: the second of evil morals and crimes following from it. What the same Jesuit further adds: Examples, he says, of this century were given by Luther and Calvin; for Luther teaches that vows do not bind a religious person, that man does not have free will, that he acts by fate, that he sins necessarily, that faith alone justifies, and that works merit nothing before GOD. These are partly denied to be evil fruits, since Scripture itself teaches us so, as was proved elsewhere concerning the last two assertions; [and] they are partly so constituted that, if anyone considers them in the sense which the Papists attach to the words of Luther, they are mere calumny. Just as the Jesuits have long striven to besmirch the blessed ghost of the great man with this, so the blessed Pareus has long since wiped away that stain. See Conf. Cath. c. 1. p. 930. t. 2. p. 368. t. 3. p. 587. &c.)*

*( They gather, i. e. they will be able to gather. See Glass. Gr. S. p. 246. But also the active verb can perhaps be taken here passively in the Hebrew manner, namely for they are gathered, or they can be gathered. Examples of such a Hebraism are given elsewhere in the N. T., as Luke 12, 20.John 15, 6.Rev. 16, 15. The Oriental interpreters, however, all express it by an active verb.)*

Latin:

v. 16. Τρίβολος εξ unde βόλος & βολὴ dicta à triplici cuspide, quod sc. cuspidatus trifariam feriat, vel à semine triangulari. Diosc. lib. 4. c. 15. Theoph. lib. 4. c. 11.

* ( Afructibus eorum &c. Aethiops & Arabs praemittunt, cop. et. ille insuper, sicuti & Persa pro plur. fructibus habent sing. fructu. Rectè verò ex hoc loco colligunt nostrates contra Pontificios, quòd pura verbi praedicatio sit nota verae Ecclesiae. Et enim quemadmodum sincerus Ecclesiae Doctor à Pseudopropheta per incorruptam ac puram doctrinam distinguitur, & ex eâ cognoscitur, ita quoque doctrinae in Ecclesia DEI sonantis puritas illius vera ac certa nota est. Ubi quoque probè notandum, quòd ipsi Pontificii non pauci, nec infimi subsellii ultrò largiantur, per fructus intelligendam hîc doctrinam, ceu disertè docet Bellarmil. 5. de Gr. & L. A. c. 10. & ita quoque Barradius, t. 2. Conc. Ev. l. 7. c. 30. p. 500. Corn. à Lapide, Tirinus, Conzenius in h. l. Imò Thomos Stapletonus, regius quondam in Acad. Lov. Professor l. 10 de Princ. sid. doct. c. 1. fatetur, plerosq; ex Patribus locum hunc ita exponere, quòd nempe ex doctrinâ, quam Pseudoprophetae proponunt, de iis facere iudicium debeamus. Barradii quoque verba, clarissima sunt: Fructus mali, scribit, ex quibus Pseudoprophet as agnoscendos esse Salvator innuitMatth. 7, 16.non tam sunt pravi mores, quippe qui etiam cadere possunt in veros Doctores, quàm falsa doctrina & prava consectaria, quae ex ipsorum dogmatibus stuunt, Deicultum & veram pietatem impediunt. Sed huic expositioni opponit sese Iesuita Maldonatus, qui ita in h. l. commentatur: Hic de fide i. e. de ipsa falsorum prophetarum doctrina cognoscendâ agitur: ab surdum verò dictu est, doctrinam ex doctrina probari. Omnes igitur veteres antores (NB. falsissimum hoc esse, ex Hieronymo ac Theophyl. in h. l. Autore item Oper. Imperf. in Matth. hom. 19. Theodor. l. 3. haeret. fabul. in princ. Vinc. Lirin. advers. haer. c. 36. aliisque patet, ac fatetur etiam Stapletonus l. c.) per fructus opera intelligunt, quae doctrinam naturâ malam mala, bonam bona consequuntur. Dispiciāt verò Iesuitae, quomodo suos hîc sociennos concilient. Apud nos certum est, per fructus praecipuè hîc intelligi doctrinam, & ita quoque docet locus parallelus Luc. 6, 45. ad quem ipse etiam Iesuita Tirinus lectorem remittit. Sed quaerat aliquis, quomodo ex doctrinâ falsi Doctores cognosci possint? Respond. si ad Scripturam Sacram, ea exigatur & examinetur. Illam enim normam Apostolus praescripsit Gal. 1, 8. in illa sonat vox Christi, quam audire debemus. Minimè verò fidei regula sunt Patres antiqui, consuetudo, leges s. traditiones humanae, quam regulam Iesuita Conzenius hîc praescribit. Illam verò normam, Scripturam sc. Sacram, Pontificii refugiunt, probè scientes, quòd plurima eorum dogmataexamen ad illam sustinere haut possint. Corn â Lapide duplicem fructum esse monet: primum falsae & impiae doctrinae: secundum pravorum morū ac scelerum ex eâ consequentium Quae v. idem Iesuita porrò subiungit: Exempla, inquiens, huius seculi dedere Lutherus & Calvinus, Lutherus n. docet, vota non obligare religiosum, hominem non habere liberum arbitrium, agi fate, necessariò peccare, fidem solam iustificare, O. B. nil apud DEUM mereri. Ea partim negatur esse malos fructus, eùm ipsa Scriprura nos ita doceat, ceu de duobus postremis adsertis alibi probatum; partim ita comparata sunt, ut si quis eo sensu, quem Pontificii dictis Lutheri affingunt, consideret, mera calumnia sint. quâ sicut pridem beatos megalandri manes conspurcare Iesuitae sategerunt, ita maculam istam dudum etiam abstersit B. Patens. Vid. Conf. Cath. c. 1. p. 930. t. 2. p. 368. t. 3. p. 587. &c.)*

*( Colligunt i. e. colligere poterunt. Vid. Glass. Gr. S. p. 246. Sed & passivè fortè more Ebraeo verbum activum accipi hîc potest, nempe pro colliguntur, vel colligi possunt. Qualis Ebraismi etiam alibi in N. T. exempla dantur, uti Luc. 12, 20.Ioh. 15, 6.Apoc. 16, 15. Interpp. tamen Orientales omnes per activum verbum exprimunt.)*

## 7:17
*(v. 17. Every good tree &c. Since all men after the fall are by nature evil trees, Conf. Eph. 2, 2. (just as, Augustine noted, when he writes in sermon 12 on the words of the Lord, Who, was found good by the Lord, when Christ died for the ungodly? He found all trees therefore to be evil: but He gave the power to become children of God to those believing in His name.) our people rightly assert, and among other things gather also from the present saying, that a man not yet reborn or an infidel cannot do a work that is truly or spiritually good, and therefore the whole life of infidels is sin. For just as thorns cannot bring forth grapes, so neither can the will of an unregenerate man will anything spiritually good, and therefore neither perform it. Costerus objects in Enchir. page 276, writing thus: The works of infidels do not arise from infidelity, but from elsewhere, as from natural instinct and the judgment of right reason, and no one would say these are sins. Resp. Nay, indeed, Christ Himself here calls them evil fruits, namely when considered spiritually, and consequently sins. Furthermore, from the fact that certain works of infidels proceed from the judgment of right reason, nothing else is proved than that an unregenerate man can sometimes fulfill civil righteousness in such a way that the works in themselves and in the kind of act are not sins: this we indeed willingly grant. But the question is about fruits that are spiritually good, that is, pleasing to God. Such an infidel cannot bring forth, since he is destitute of faith, which alone makes our works to be spiritually good and to please God. See Heb. 11, 6. And this the Jesuit Tirinus himself acknowledges, when he says from the Council of Orange that the good fruits in this place are those which are profitable for life and eternal salvation. Other Papists object, at least this is what the Savior means by the present saying, that an unregenerate man cannot always, nor in great numbers, bear spiritually good fruits. But I will believe this to be the scope of Christ only when the Jesuits have shown that even sometimes, or at least only a few grapes are accustomed to be gathered from thorns, and figs from thistles. To a Papist, indeed, that will perhaps not seem absurd, who has put faith in Bellarmine, who teaches that it can happen, that accidents nourish, yet in such a way that they are taken in great abundance. I fear, however, unless other revenues and fruits were available to the Jesuits, than such as these, that they might be forced to celebrate fast days frequently. But let someone say: Just as a regenerate person, since he is a good tree, can sometimes bring forth bad fruits, as the examples of David, Peter, etc., testify, so in turn a bad tree, namely an unregenerate man, can sometimes bring forth truly good fruits, that is, spiritually such pleasing to God. Resp. The consequence is denied. The reason for the diversity is that a regenerate man, as long as he is in this life, is as it were a double tree, good, in so far as he follows the leading of the Holy Spirit; bad, in so far as he grants dominion to the flesh. But an unregenerate man is nothing but a bad tree, with respect to producing spiritually good fruits. But however much a regenerate man may finally be a good tree, because the fuel and root of sin remains even in the flesh of the regenerate, as long as they are in this life, whence our people also rightly defend against the Papists, that even the good works of the regenerate, considered legally or in the strict judgment of GOD, are not perfect and pure from every stain of adhering sin. Whence, nor are they meritorious of eternal life. Orthodoxly Dionysius the Carthusian, a Carthusian monk and not unfamous for many published most learned commentaries on the Holy Scriptures: Our bad works, he says, are purely bad and are ours: but our good works are neither purely good, nor are they ours. in c. 18. Eccles. Nor yet for this reason are good works to be omitted, but one must work well, because this is the serious will of GOD, and we also know that not only that tree which brings forth bad fruits, but also that which brings forth no fruits, is cut down, Matth. 3, 10. Although, therefore, our good works are not the cause of reigning, they are nevertheless the way of the kingdom, as Bernard speaks, tr. de gr. & L. A. col. 1069. And we also have the divine promise that our heavenly Father wills to have our works pleasing for the sake of Christ, and to reward the same generously with temporal and eternal rewards.

Latin:

*(v. 17. Omnis arbor bona &c. Cùm omnes homines post lapsum naturâ malae arbores sint, Conf. Eph. 2, 2. (prout etiam, August. notavit, cùm de verbis Domini serm. 12. Quis, seribit, à Domino bonus inventus est, cùm Christus pro impiis mortuus sit? Omnes ergo malas arborer invenit: sed dedit potestatem, filios Dei fieri, credentibus in nomine eius.) rectè adserunt, & inter alia ex praesenti quoque dicto colligunt nostrates, quòd homo nondum renatus sive infidelis non possit opus verè sive spiritualiter bonum facere, adeoque omnis infidelium vita sit peccatum. Perinde enim atque spinae nequeunt uvas proferre, ita nec hominis irregeniti voluntas aliquid spiritualiter bonum potest velle, adeoque necoperari. Excipit Costerus in Enchir. pag. 276. sic scribens: Infidelium opera non ex infidelitate oriuntur, sed aliunde, velut ex naturali instinctu & rectae rationis iudicio, & haec nemo dixerit esse peccata. Resp. Imò verò Christus ipse hîc vocat, fructus malos, nēpe spiritualiter considerata, & per consequens peccata. Caeterùm ex eo, quòd ex iudicio rectae rationis quaedam infidelium opera proficiscuntur, nil aliud probatur, quàm hominē renatum civilem iustitiam ita aliquo modo interdum implere posse, ut opera ex se & in genere actûs non sint peccata: hoc vero nos libenter, largimur. Quaestio vero est de fructibus spiritualiter bonis h. e. Deo placentibus. Tales infidelis proferre non potest, cùm destituatur fide, quae, sola facit, ut opera nostra spiritualiter bona, sint, Deoque placeant. Vid. Ebr. 11, 6. Atque hoc ipse agnoscit Iesuita Tirinus, quando ex Concilio Arausicano fructus bonos h. l. dicit esse eos, qui prosint ad vitam & salutem aeternam. Alii Pontificii excipiunt, saltem hoc velle Salvatorem praesenti dicto, quòd homo irregenitus non semper, nec plurimos possit ferre fructus spiritualiter bonos. Sed scopum hunc Christi esse tum demum credam, ubi Iesuitae ostenderint, vel aliquando etiam saltem, vel paucas modò uvas è spinis colligi solere, & ficus è tribulis. Pontificio quidem id fortè non absurdum videbitur, qui Bellarmino fidem adhibuerit, docenti, fieri posse, ut accidentia nutriant, ita tamen ut in magnâ copia sumantur. Vereor autem, nisi alii Iesuitis reditus ac fructus suppeterent, quàm tales, ne esuriales celebrare ferias subinde cogantur. Sed dicat aliquis: Sicuti renatus, eùm sit bona arbor, potest aliquando malos fructus proferre, eta exempla Davidis, Petri &c. testantur, ita vicissim mala arbor, nempe homo irregenitus, potest interdum verè bonos fructus h. c. spiritualiter tales Deoplacentes proferre. Resp. Negatur consequentia. Ratio diversitatis est, quia homo renatus, quamdiu in hac vita est, est duplex quasi arbor, bona, quat. ductum Sp. Sancti sequitur; mala, quat. carni dominium concedit. Sed homo irregenitus non nisi mala arbor est, respectu fructuum spiritualiter bonorum producendorum. Ut ut verò denique homo regenitus sit bona arbor, quia tamen fomes & radix peccati etiam in carne renatorum manet, quam diu ipsi in hâc vita sunt, unde rectè quoque nostrates contra Pontificios defendunt, quòd etiam renatorum bona opera legaliter sive in rigido DEI iudicio considerata non sint perfecta & ab omni peccati adhaerentis labe pura. Unde, nec vitae aet. meritoria. Orthodoxè Dionys. à Rickel, Monachus Carthusianus multisque editis doctissimis in Sc. S. Commentariis non incelebris: Mala nostra, inquit, purè mala sunt & nostra sunt: bona autem opera nostra nec purè bona sunt, nec nostra sunt. in c. 18. Eccles. Neque tamen ob hoc omittenda B. O. sunt, sed benè operandum, quia seria haec DEI voluntas est, & novimus quoque, quòd non solùm illa arbor, quae malos, sed etiam, quae nullos fructus profert, exscindatur, Matth. 3, 10. Licet igitur, B. O. nostra non sint causa regnandi, sunt tamen via regni, ut loquitur Bernh. tr. de gr. & L. A. col. 1069. Et habemus quoque, promissionem divinam, quôd Pater noster coelestis opera nostra, propter Christum velit grata habere, eadem que temporalibus aeternisque praemiis largiter remunerari.)*

## 7:18
(v. 18. A good tree cannot bring forth bad fruits. Since in all men by nature there are bad fruits, this is an indication to us that all men by nature are bad trees, and thus that human nature is corrupted through sin, or which is the same thing, that original sin is given, which elsewhere the Holy Scripture also expressly testifies, especially Ps. 51, 7.Rom. 5, 12. But here, in turn, the Papists oppose us on the merit of B. O. (see Becan. l. 1. Man. Cōtrov. c. 18. p. 303.), that the regenerate or the just are good trees,Ps. 91, 13. Therefore they cannot produce bad fruits. I respond by distinguishing between good trees, in an inchoative sense, and perfectly so called. In the former way, we concede that the regenerate or the just are good trees, but in that sense it is denied that they cannot produce bad fruits. For although such persons do not produce bad fruits insofar as they are regenerate, they do produce them, however, insofar as the root of sin still clings in their flesh. See Rom. 7, 21. In the latter way, however, it is denied that the regenerate are good trees in this life. For Holy Scripture testifies to the contrary. See 1. Cor. 13, 10.2. Cor. 5, 16. Compare Prov. 20, 9.Iob. 10, 14. c. 14, 4. c. 15, 14. 15. 16. Matth. 15. 19. 20.Marc. 10. 14.Phil. 3, 12. and the Papists themselves are also forced to admit this, unless they wish to say that the just or regenerate person never sins, which I do not think they would affirm. Finally, Wendelinus also, Exerc. 30. §. 21., touches upon the present passage as well, and from it, when compared with certain other sayings of Holy Scripture, he strives to prove the immutability of human actions, especially the evil ones. But I respond by distinguishing between those things with which the will of man is concerned: some of these look to the upper hemisphere, some to the lower. The latter comprises natural, moral, and external sacred things; the former, merely spiritual and internal things. Now, although the will of man has been so corrupted by the fall that an unregenerate man no longer has any powers of himself to convert himself savingly to God, to believe in Chr---um, to live according to the Spirit, and thus cannot --si produce bad fruits (in opposition to the fruit of those spiritually good): yet as far as things that pertain to the lower hemisphere are concerned, it is denied that an unregenerate man can only produce bad fruits: For he still has some liberty in those matters. And since external sacred actions also pertain to the lower hemisphere, it is manifest that when a man maliciously and pertinaciously despises the offered means of grace, reprobation does not proceed from some absolute hatred of GOD. For it is in the power of man, even one not regenerate, in external or pedagogical sacred actions, which are ordinarily required in the regeneration and conversion of adults, either to conduct himself decently; or to contumaciously repel from himself the means of conversion divinely ordained through affected malice.)*

Latin:

*(v. 18. Non potest arbor bona fructus malos ferre. E Cùm in omnibus hominibus per naturam sint mali fructus, indicio hoc nobis est, omnes homines naturâ esse malas arbores, adeoque naturam humanam per peccatum esse corruptam, sive quod idem est, e. datur peccatum originis, quod alibi etiam disertè Sc. S testatur, cumprimis Ps. 51, 7.Rom. 5, 12. Sed hîc vicissim nobis pro merito B. O. opponunt Pontificii, (vid. Becan. l. 1. Man. Cōtrov. c. 18. p. 303.) Renatos sive iustos esse arbores bonas,Ps. 91, 13. Ergo non posse facere malos fructus. Resp. dist. inter bonas arbores, inchoativè, & perfectè ita dictas. Priori modo concedimus, renatos s. iustos esse bonas arbores, sed sic negatur, quòd non possint facere fructus malos. Licet enim tales non faciant malos fructus, quatenus renati sunt, faciunt tamen, quat. in ipsorum carne adhuc peccati radix haeret. Vid. Rom. 7, 21. Posteriori verò modò negatur, quòd renati in hâc vita bonae arbores sint. Contrarium enim Sc. S. testatur. vid. 1. Cor. 13, 10.2. Cor. 5, 16. Conf. Prov. 20, 9.Iob. 10, 14. c. 14, 4. c. 15, 14. 15. 16. Matth. 15. 19. 20.Marc. 10. 14.Phil. 3, 12. & ipsi quoque Pontificii fateri hoc coguntur, nisi dicere velint, quòd iustus s. renatus nunquam peccet, quod ipsos affirmaturos non existimo. Tandem & Wendelinus Exerc. 30. §. 21. praesentem quoque locum tangit, ex eodemque, collato cum aliis quibusdam Sc. S. dictis, immutabilitatem actionum humanarum, cumprimis malarum probare satagit. Verùm respond. disting. inter ea, circa quae voluntas hominis versatur: horum quaedam spectant ad hemisphaerium superius, quaedam ad inferius. Hoc complectitur res naturales, morales & sacras externas; illud res mere spirituales & internas. Iam licet hominis voluntas ita, per lapsum corupta sit, ut homo irregenitus nullas ampliù habeat vires ex se ad Deum salutariter sese convertendi, in Chr---um credendi, secundùm Spiritum vivendi, adeoque non possit --si malosfructus (in oppos fructum spiritualiter bonorum) facere: tamen quòd res ad hemilphaerium inferius specta-res attinet, negatur, quòd homo irregenitus non possit nisi malofructus facere: Habet enim in istis aliquam adhuc libertatem. cùmque ad hemisphaerium inferius spectent quoque actiones sacrae externae, manifestum est, quòd quando homo oblata gratiae media malitiosè ac pertinaciter contemnit, quòd reprobatio non ex absoluto quodam DEI odio proveniat. Penes hominem enim est, etiam non renatum, in actionibus sacris externis sive paedagogicis, quae ordinariè in adultorum regeneratione ac conversione requiruntur, vel decenter sese gerere; vel conversionis media divinitus ordinata per affectatam malitiam contumaciter à se repellere.)*

## 7:19
(v. 19. Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down &c. By the altogether just judgment of GOD. Now truly, if by the immutable decree of GOD, which the Calvinists desire, the reprobate were compelled to bear evil fruits, they certainly could not be sent into the fire by the just judgment of GOD. For no one can justly be the avenger of that thing of which he is the author. Although an unregenerate man cannot from his own powers make himself a good tree out of a bad tree, yet God wills to make a good tree out of him, provided he does not maliciously resist. See the book of Augustine against Adimantus the Manichaean. t. 6. of his Works. John the Baptist also used the same sentence, by which Christ exhorts to the bringing forth of good fruits, as our Evangelist commemorates above c. 3, 10. Furthermore, Chrysostom shows here at length and most emphatically that, although one and the same thing seems to be denoted by τὸ to be cut down and to be cast into the fire, a double punishment is nevertheless found, if one weighs the words diligently, namely, combustion in hell, and the loss of the kingdom of heaven, and that this latter punishment will be greater than that torture of flames.)

( He is cast into the fire. From this Bellarmine attempts to prove that there are also threats in the Gospel. Resp. I deny that these threats pertain to the Gospel. For it must be known that Christ and the Apostles proposed both legal and evangelical sermons. Compare more on this matter in B. P. L. on the Gospel §. 20.)

Latin:

*(v. 19. Quaecunarbor non fert fructum bonum excidtur &c. Iusto omninò DEI iudicio. Iam vero si per immutabile DEI decretum, quod Calviniani volunt, reprobi malos fructus ferre cogerentur, sanè non possent iusto DEI iudicio in ignē mitti. Nemo enim iure illius rei potest esse ultor, cuius est autor. Licet verò homo irregenitus ex malâ arbore non possit sese facere arborem bonam ex viribus propriis, Deus tamen ex ipso arborem bonam vult efficere, modò non malitiosè repugnet. Vid. librum Augustini contra Adimantum Manichaeum. t. 6. Oper. Eadem a. sententiâ, quâ Christus ad bonos proferēdos fructus hortatur, usus quoque est Iohannes Baptista, ceu noster Evang. commemorat suprà c. 3, 10. Porrò prolixè hîc atque perquàm emphaticè ostendit Chrysostomus, quòd licet unum idemque per τὸexcidi & in ignem coniici denotari videatur, duplex tamen, si quis verba diligenter expendat, inveniatur supplicium, nempe in ge hennâ combustio, ac regni coelorum amissio, quòdque haec posterior poena maior futura sit, quàm cruciatus ille flammarum.)*

*( In ignem coniicitur. Conatur hinc Bell. probare dari quoque in Ev. comminationes. Resp. Neg. comminationes has ad Ev. pertinere. Sciendum enim, quòd Christus & Apostoli tàm legales, quàm Evangelicas conciones proposuerint. Conf. plura in hanc rem apud B. P. L. de Ev. §. 20.)*

## 7:20
(v. 20. Therefore by their fruits &c. Chrysostom renders the cause of why the Savior repeats these words, already brought forth then in v. 16, saying: Lest he should seem to introduce the threat as if by design and as the principal thing, but rather that which might fulfill the role of counsel and admonition, he shook their minds with this intimidation from examination.)

Latin:

* (v. 20. Ex fructibus igitur &c. Cur Salvator verba haec, iam tum v. 16. prolata, repetat, illius rei causam reddit Chrysostomus, inquiens: Ne comminationem tanquam ex proposito & praecipuam videretur inducere, sed eam, quae consilii vicem atque admonitionis impleret, hâc eorum animos interminatione atexaminatione concussit.)*

## 7:21
v. 21. Syr. He who says to me, מרי מרי My Lord, my Lord. Furthermore, a negative particle placed before a universal affirmative sign constitutes a universal negative in the Hebrew phrase. Therefore all hypocrites are condemned, who on account of profession alone arrogate to themselves the title of the Church and of the children of GOD. (B. D. Glassius, however, thinks, Gr. S. p. 480, that this is a particular negation in this place, and that the sense in this place is: someone will enter, and someone will not enter, and he compares Num. 23, 17.*

* ( Lord, Lord &c. The opinion of the Apostle 1. Cor. 12, 3. seems to be contrary to this assertion. But it must be noted that it is one thing to call Christ Lord with external lips, Es. 29, 13. Matth. 15, 8. and with a hypocritical boasting of faith; and another thing with internal sighs and with a true inflammation of faith. The Apostle speaks of the former saying in the aforementioned place, and the Savior speaks of the latter in the present oracle. Moreover, since that true, soul-saving faith, from which internal sighs proceed, cannot be known by men except from its fruits, nor can a living faith be distinguished from a dead one: it is from this that Holy Scripture itself also describes true faith by its effects or fruits and proposes it to us for consideration, as is evident both from Matth. 25. Iac. 2. and other places, and also from the present saying. To which Chrysostom, Jerome, &c. also refer when they note that Christ in this place means that faith is of no value unless life or Good Works are present. And thus also the saying of Basil which Contzen cites in his Commentary on this place, p. 148, must be understood entirely. And the Blessed Doctor Chemnitz also refers to this when, in his Harmony of the Gospels, ch. 51, p. 52 a., he writes: The will of GOD is 1. that the sinner be converted, as Ezekiel says, ch. 33, 11. 2. Ioh. 6, 40. This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. 3. This is the will of God, our sanctification, that you abstain &c. 1. Thess. 4. 3. The Blessed Doctor Hunnius likewise compares here the following places 1. Tim. 1, 5. 2. Cor. 6, 6. Rom. 12, 9. 10. 1. Ioh. 3. Nor, however, is it to be thought that these things are contrary to the doctrine of our Churches, by which we profess that we are justified and saved before God by faith alone. For in this part we follow the Apostle, who Rom. 3. and 4. likewise Ephes. 2., according to the opinion of Moses and David, that is, of the Law and all the Prophets, expressly testifies that we are justified and saved freely, by faith without works; that the blessedness is of that man to whom God imputes righteousness without works; that we are saved by grace without works. In short: it is one thing to ask: Are Good Works necessary for those to be saved by reason of efficiency; it is another, whether by reason of presence: the former the Apostle denies, and we with him. The latter the Savior affirms, and we with him. And the Blessed Doctor Chemnitz also referred to this when, in the aforementioned place at the end of the chapter, he notably writes: The kingdom will be given, not to those doing nothing, not to those doing evil, not to those doing something, but to those hearing the word and doing it. It is not, however, given on account of doing, but on account of Christ apprehended by faith. Thus Chemn. Whence this three-pronged lightning bolt of the Savior does not in the least terrify or strike us, as indeed the Jesuit Conzen persuades himself, writing thus in this place: It is a wonder that, after this three-pronged lightning bolt, the solifidians still remain in their obstinacy. For we teach the same thing that our Savior teaches here, namely that true and saving faith is never alone nor idle, (For we also make our own that statement of Justin in Paroen. p. 25. Our religious matters consist not in words, but in deeds. Add. Luke 6:46.John 13:17.) Nor yet does it follow from this that Good Works are the cause of salvation, whether efficient or meritorious. And this is what we deny, being taught by the Holy Scriptures that all our Good Works are already owed to GOD beforehand, Luke 17:10. are imperfect, and are contaminated by many infirmities and the remnants of sin still clinging in the flesh. Isa. 64:6.Rom. 7:21. How then could those be called meritorious of eternal life? Let the Papists look rather to it, lest this lightning bolt strike them, while they strive bitterly to defend that faith (true faith, certainly, for it is of this that the question is) can exist without Good Works. We, however, deny that true faith is alone, i.e., separated from Good Works. And it is false what Conzen says, that those believe (we are speaking indeed of justifying faith) who, although they call Christ Lord, do not however do his will, nor demonstrate by works (at least internal ones) that they are true servants of GOD. For that such do not truly believe, or do not have true Christian faith, of whom Christ treats in this place, is evident enough from the fact that he himself explicitly John 6:47. says: Amen, Amen I say to you: he who believes in me has eternal life. But to those hypocrites and false prophets who simulate faith, he will one day answer: I never knew you v. 23. Furthermore, that true faith is not separated from Good Works is shown at greater length in Isag. LL. Theol. p. 885. also Confess. Cath. t. 4. Let the parallel sayings be compared with the present passage, Matt. 28:19, 20.John 13:17. c. 15, 14.)

* ( Did we not in your name δυνάμεις πολλὰς do many miracles ? That by δυνάμεις in this place miracles ought to be understood, is evident both from the comparison with c. 11, 20. c. 13, 58. etc., and from the confession of the Adversaries themselves, namely the Papists: See Cardinal Toletus Comm. in Luke p. 621. and others soon to be cited. Since therefore the Savior asserts in this place concerning false prophets that they are going to do many miracles, it is manifest that the glory of miracles cannot be established as a mark of the Church, which Bell does in l. 4 de Eccl. c. 14. For whatever does not belong to the true Church alone, that cannot be its certain and infallible mark. But miracles do not. Therefore. The major is certain, because marks ought to be proper, not common, as Bell himself teaches l. c. c. 2. §. Ac primum. The minor is evident from this place, and with it can also be compared below c. 24, 24. likewise the saying of the Apostle 2 Thess. 2:9. Miracles, writes the Jesuit Costerus in Enchir. Controv. de Eccl. c. 2. p. 99, are done for two reasons; the other is for the testimony of doctrine, so that they may be signs of the truth and holiness of the doctrine, in which way even the Scriptures confess that miracles can be produced by the impious. The Jesuit adds, however, as a place of proof the present saying, and then also 1 Cor. 13:2. The conclusion therefore stands. But the Jesuit Cardinal Julius Caesar Coturius comes to the rescue, distinguishing between true miracles, (concerning which he professes to speak, and trifles that God exhibits such only in the Roman Church, Epit. Controv. c. 4. § 2. p. 36.) and between prodigies and wonders, which can be performed even by false prophets through the art of the demon. And in this way the Jesuit thinks the cause of the Papists is sufficiently provided for, and he all but expects a triumph or at least an Ovation to be decreed to him by the Roman Veiovis with the applause of the people: Caesar has restored the state to us. But his fellow Jesuit Fr. Costerus renders the palm doubtful for the Jesuit, asserting in the place just alleged that miracles can be produced by the impious, so that they are signs of the truth and holiness of the doctrine. But that the Devil produces miracles through his organs for the confirmation of the truth is hardly credible. Nay rather more clearly that the Savior is speaking here of true miracles, and thus those done by GOD working, testifies Maldonatus, likewise a fellow Jesuit of Coturius, and he proves this same thing from the Fathers also: Thus indeed he comments in this place: Chrysostom, Jerome, Euthymius, Theophylact prove with examples that TRUE miracles are done even by others than Catholics; and from this very place, Many will say etc., it is easily gathered,

that those false Prophets, of whom he speaks, performed TRUE miracles &c. The Jesuit also renders a reason for the assertions, for he continues: Nor indeed does Christ answer that they are lying, but that He, although they did those things, does not know them, and the sentence demands that Christ signifies that they would perform TRUE miracles &c. The Jesuit Tirinus, while he explains τὸ in thy name in this place by τὸ by thy authority and delegation, seems to establish the very same thing, namely that the Savior is speaking of true miracles. But Gisbertus Schevichavius, likewise a Doctor of the Society of Jesus, agrees with Maldonatus, and thus also contradicts Coturius, expressly asserting that those gratuitous gifts (among them also the working of greater miracles) are common to the just with the impious, and he proves this from this place, lib. 5. de Trinit. c. 36. pag. 510. But also that most famous Jesuit Corn. à Lapide refutes Caesar Coturius, when in his Comment. on this place, A. 1649. edit. p. 182, he says thus on this place: He calls virtues miracles, and those true and sincere. Coturius therefore sees that true miracles are performed even by false Doctors. But just as from the fact that Pseudo-prophets can also produce miracles, as the Papists themselves teach from this place, it can be proven against Bellarmine that the glory of miracles is not a mark of the Church: so against the same it can likewise be shown from the present passage that the light of prophecy is not a genuine and infallible mark of the Church, since even Pseudo-prophets glory in the gift of prophecy (i.e., of predicting future things, as the Jesuits Tirinus, Schevichavius and others explain in the said place), and indeed not lying, as Maldonatus teaches in this place. Nay, Thomas Aquinas, (in whose words, however, the Jesuits are otherwise as it were forced to swear, as has been shown elsewhere from Gravina,) 2. 2. q. 172. art. 6. proves that even false Prophets sometimes predict true things, sometimes from the revelation of the Devil, sometimes from divine action.

* ( In your name. Conf. Acts 16:17 ch. 19:13: The Syriac and the remaining Oriental interpreters employ the prefix ב which sounds sometimes in, sometimes by. From the fact, indeed, that the false prophets were at some point to say that they performed miracles in the name of Christ, or by the name of Christ, as Erasmus translates, Costerus attempts to prove on p. 172 of the Enchiridion Controversiarum that faith exists even in sinners. This we deny, namely concerning sinners persevering in their malice without repentance: whom we say, through sins committed against knowledge and conscience , cast off faith and the gracious indwelling of the Holy Spirit. But the Jesuit confuses faith Salvific (which consists not in the bare knowledge of things to be believed, which indeed can have a place even in the most wicked men; but in the fiducial apprehension of the merit of Christ) with faith of miracles, (which has a place also in those who acquiesce in the sole and bare knowledge of Christ, Conf. 1 Cor. 13:2). We deny that the former, not the latter, can consist with sins committed against conscience: and the reason is, because justifying and salvific faith has the gift of renewal joined to it, Gal. 5:24 2 Cor. 5:17 1 John 2:3, 4. But that which is called of miracles, and that which we call salvific, is not one and the same faith, as is shown elsewhere. Conf. B. Par. L. de Iustif. §. 189. Nor is there any reason for anyone to say that they, while they performed miracles in the name of Christ, confessed Christ, and therefore truly believed, as Tirinus maintains, who explains it thus in this place: not everyone who believes in me, invokes me, acknowledges me as his Lord. Resp. I distinguish between the bare profession of faith and its vain boasting, and between the firm apprehension of Christ, or trust. That not the latter, but only the former was in the False Prophets, is evident -x coll. of this place with Matt. 10:32 and Rom. 10:10.

Latin:

v. 21. Syr. Qui dicit mihi,מרי מריDomine mi, Domine mi. Porrò particula negativa praeposita signo Universali affirmativo phrasi Hebraica constituit Universalem negativam. Damnan tu igitur omnes hypocritae, qui propter solam professionem titulum Ecclesiae & filiorum DEI sibi arrogant. *(Existimat tamen B. D. Glassius, Gr. S. p. 480. quòd hoc loco particularis negatio sit, ac sensum h. l. esse: aliquis intrabit, & aliquis non intrabit, ac confert Num. 23, 17.)*

* ( Domine, Domine &c. Videtur contrariari adsertioni huic sententia Apostoli 1. Cor. 12, 3. Verùm notandum, quòd aliud sit, Christum Dominum dicere externis labiis,Es. 29, 13.Matth. 15, 8.ac hypocriticâ fidei gloriatione; aliud internis suspiriis ac verâ fidei inflammatione. De hoc dicere loquitur Apostolus d. l. de illo Salvator in praesenti oraculo. Caeterùm cùm vera illa salvivifica fides, unde interna suspiria proveniunt, cognosci ab hominibus, nisi ex fructibus, nequeat, nec viva fides à mortua distingui: inde est, quòd ipsa quoque Script. S. fidem veram ab effectis sive, fructibus describit ac considerandum nobis proponit, ceu patet, tum ex Matth. 25.Iac. 2. aliisque locis, tum è praesenti quoq; dicto. quo etiam Chrysostomus, Hieronymus &c. respiciunt, quando notant, Christum h. l. id velle, quòd fides nihil valeat, nisi adsistat vita sive B. O. Et ita quoque omninò intelligēdum dictum Basilii quod Contzen adducit Comm. in h. l. p. 148. Atque huc etiam respicit B. D. Chemnitius, quando in Harm. Evang. c. 51. p. 52 a. scribit: Voluntas DEI est 1. ut peccator convertatur, sicut inquit Ezechiel c. 33, 11. 2. Ioh. 6, 40.Haec est volunt as ei--, qui misit me, ut omnis, qui videt Filium, & credit in ipsum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. 3. Haec est voluntas Dei sanctificatio nostra, ut abstineatis &c.1. Thess. 4. 3. B. D. Hunnius itid. confert hîc seqq. loca 1. Tim. 1, 5.2. Cor. 6, 6.Rom. 12, 9. 10.1. Ioh. 3. Neque, tamen existimandum est, quòd haec adversentur doctrinae Ecclesiarum nostrarum, quâ profitemur, solâ fide nos coram Deo iustificari ac salvari. Sequimur enim hâc in parte Apostolum, qui Rom. 3. & 4. item Ephes. 2. ex sententiâ Mosis ac Davidis h. e. legis omniumque Prophetarum disertè testatur, nos iustificari & salvari gratis, fide sine operibus; beatitudinem esse illius hominis, cui Deus acceptam fert iustitiam sine operibus; gratiâ nos salvari sine operibus. Breviter: aliud est quaerere: An salvandis B. O. sint necessaria ratione efficientiae; aliud, an ratione praesentiae: prius negat Apostolus, & nos cum ipso. Posterius affirmat Salvator, & nos cum ipso. Atque huc respexit quoque B. D. Chemnitius, quando l. c. in fine cap. notanter scribit: Regnum dabitur, non, nihil agen--bus, non malè agentibus, non aliquid agentibus, sed audientibus verbum & facientibus illud. Non autem datur propter facere, sed propter Christum fide apprehensum. ita Chemn. Unde minimè nos terret vel ferit trisulcum hoc fulmen Salvatoris, uti quidē Iesuita Conzen sibi persuadet, ita in h. l. scribens: Mirum est, post trisulcum hoc fulmen adhuc manere in pervicacia solifideanos. Etenim idem nos docemus, quòd Salvator noster hîc docet, nempe veram ac salvificā fidem nunquā esse solam nec otiosam, (Nostrum enim etiam facimus illud Iustini in Paroen. p. 25. Non in verbis, sed in factis res nostrae religionis consistunt. Add. Luc. 6, 46.Ioh. 13, 17.) Neque tamen hinc sequitur, B. O. esse salutis causam vel efficientem vel meritoriam. & hoc est quod nos negamus, è Sc. S. edocti, quòd omnia nostra B. O. iam antè DEO sint debita, Luc. 17, 10. sint imperfecta, multisque infirmitatibus ac peccati adhuc in carne haerentibus reliquiis contaminata. Es. 64, 6.Rom. 7, 21. quomodo igitur vitae aet. meritoria illa dici possint? Dispiciant potiùs Pontificii, ne ipsos feriat hoc fulmen, dum acriter, defendere satagunt, fidem (veram utique, nam de hâc est quaestio) esse posse sine B. O. Nos vero negamus, veram fidem esse solam, h. e. à B. O. separatam. Falsumque est, quod Conzen dicit, illos credere (loquimur vero de fide iustificante) qui licet Christum, Dominum vocent, non tamen eius voluntatem faciunt, nec ut veros DEI fervos se esse, operibus (saltim internis) demonstrant. Quòd enim tales non verè credant, sive veram Christianam sidem non habeant, de quibus Christus h. l. agit, vel inde satis patet, quia ipse disertè Ioh. 6, 47. ait: Amen, Amen dico vobis: qui credit in me, habet vitam aeternam. Illis vero hypocritis ac Pseudoprophetis, qui simulant fidem, respondebit ali quando: nunquam novi vos v. 23. Coeterùm quòd fides vera à B. O. non sit separata, pluribus ostenditur in Isag. LL. Theol. p. 885. it. Confess. Cath. t. 4. Conferantur autem cum praesenti loco seqq. dicta parallela, Matth. 28, 19. 20.Ioh. 13, 17. c. 15, 14.)*

* ( Nonne per nomen tuumδυνάμεις πολλὰςmiracula multa fecimus. Quòd per δυνάμεις h. l. miracula intelligi debeant, patet tum ex coll, cum c. 11, 20. c. 13, 58. &c. tum ex ipsorum Adversariorum, Pontificiorum nempe, confessione: Vid. Cardin. Toletus Comm. in Lucam p. 621. aliique mox adducendi. Cùm igitur de Pseudoprophetis hoc loco adserat Salvator, quòd multa miracula facturisint, manifestum est, quòd gloria miraculorum, non possit constitui nota Ecclesiae, id quod Bell facit l. 4 de Eccl. c. 14. Quicquid enim non competit soli verae Ecclesiae, illud non potest certa & infallibilis eius esse nota. Atqui miracula. E. Maior est certa, quia notae debent esse propriae, non communes, docente ipso Bell. l. c. c. 2. §. Ac primum. Minor patet ex h. l. cum avo etiam conferri potest infrà c. 24, 24. item dictum Apostoli 2. Thes. 2, 9.Miracula scribit Iesuita Costerus in Enchir. Controv. de Eccl. c. 2. p. 99 duabus ex causis fiunt, alter a est ad doctrinae testimonium, ut indicia sint veritatis & sanctitatis doctrinae, quo modo etiam ab impiis miraculaposse edi, fatentur Scripturae. Subiungit vero Iesuita probationis loco praesens dictum, tum quoq; 1. Cor. 13, 2. Stat ergo conclusio. Ast succurrit Cardinali Iesuita Iulius Caefar Coturius, distinguens inter miracula vera, (de quibus se loqui profitetur, ac talia in solâ Ecclesia Romana Deum exhibere nugatur Epit. Controv. c. 4. § 2. p. 36.) & inter ostenta & miranda, quae etiam per Pseudoprophetas arte daemonis patrari possint. Atque hoc modo satis causae Pontificiorum prospectum putat Iesuita, ac tantum non expectat, triumphum vel saltem Ovationem ipsi decerni à Veiove Romano cum populi applausu: Caesar nobis restituit rem. Ast palmam dubiam reddit Iesuitae sociennus eiusdem Fr. Costerus, adserens loco modò allegato, miracula ab impiis edi posse, ut sint indicia veritat is & sanctit at is doctrinae. Diabolum verò per sua organa miracula ad veritatis confirmationem edere, vix credibile est. Imô magis ad-uc clarè de veris miraculis, adeoque DEO operante factis, Salvatorem hîc loqui, testatur Maldonatus, itidem Coturii sociennus, probatque idem hoc ex Patribus etiam: Ita vero in h. l. commentatur: Chrysostomus, Hieronymus, Euthymius, Theophylactus probant exemplis, etiam per alios, quàm Catholicos VERA miracula fieri; & ex hoc ipso loco, Multi dicent &c. facilè colligitur,

falsos illos Prophetas, de quibus loquitur, VERA miracula fecisse &c. Reddit quoque Iesuita adserta rationem, pergit enim: Nec n. respondet Christus, mentiri eos, sed se eos, quamvis ista fecerint, nō nosse, & sententia postulat, ut Christus significet, eos VERA miraculafacturos &c. Iesuita Tirinus, dum τὸin nomine tuo h. l. expoint per τὸex autoritate & delegatione tuâ, idem omniò statuere videtur, quòd nempe de veris miraculis Salvator loquatur. Adstipulatur verò Maldonato, adeoque & Coturio contradicit Gisbertus quoque Schevichavius, itidem Doctor soc. Iesu, disertè adserens, gratuita illa dona (inter ea quoque operatio maiorum miraculorum) iustis communia esse cum impiis, idque ex h. l. probatl. 5. de Trinit. c. 36. pag. 510. Sed & Iesuita ille famosissimus Corn. à Lapide Caesarem Coturium redarguit, quando Comment. in h. l. A. 1649. edit. p. 182. ita ad h. l. Virtutes vocat miracula, eaque vera & sincera. Videt igitur Coturius, quod etiam à falsis Dd. vera fiant miracula. Sicuti autem ex eo, quòd Pseudoprophetae quoque possunt miracula edere, prout ex h. l. ipsi Pontificii docent, contra Bell. evinci potest, gloriam miraculorum non esse notam Ecclesiae: ita contra eundem pariter è praesenti loco ostendi potest, quòd lumen prophetiae non sit genuina & infallibilis Ecclesiae nota, quippe cùm etiam Pseudoprophetae de prophetiae (h. e. futur a praedicendi, ut explicant Iesuitae Tirinus, Schevichavius aliiq; d. l.) dono glorientur, & quidem non mentienres, cen Maldonatus in h. l. docet. Imò Thomas de Aquino, (in cuius tamē Magistri verba iurare quasi Iesuitae aliàs coguntur, ut alibi ex Gravina ostensum,) 2. 2. q. 172. art. 6. probat, etiam falsos Prophet as interdum vera praedicere, aliquando ex Diaboli revelatione, aliquando ex divinâ atione.)*

* ( Nomine tuo. Conf. Act. 16, 17. c. 19, 13: Syr. & reliqui Interpp. Orientales adhibent. praef. ב quod modò in, modò per sonat. Ex eo vero, quòd Pseudoprophetae aliquando dicturi, quòd in Christi nomine vel per Christinomen, ut vertit Erasmus, miracula fecerint, evincere conatur Costerus p. 172. Enchir. Controv. esse fidere etiam inpeccatoribus. Id quod nos negamus, nempe de peccatoribus in suâ malitiâ absque poenitentia perseverantibus: quos dicimus per peccata, contra scientiam ac conscientiam commissa, excutere fidem ac gratiosam Sp. S. inhabitationem. Verùm confundit Iesuita fidem salvificam (quae non in nudâ rerum credendarum notitiâ, quae utiq; etiam in sceleratissimis hominibus locum habere potest; sed in fiduciali apprehensione meriti Christi consistit) cum fids mir aculorum, (quae in iis quoque, qui in solâ ac nudâ Christi cognitione acquiescunt, locum habet, Conf. 1. Cor. 13, 2. Illam, non hanc, cum peccatis contra cōscientiam commissis consistere posse negamus: & ratio est, quia fides iustificans ac salvifica donum renovationis coniunctum habet, Gal. 5, 24.2. Cor. 5, 17.1. Ioh. 2, 3. 4. Non vero una eademque fides est ea, quae miraculorum dicitur, ac quam salvificam vocamus, ut alibi ostenditur. Conf. B. Par. L. de Iustif. §. 189. Nec est, quòd aliquis dicat, eos, dum miracula in Christi nomine ediderunt, Christum confessos esse, adeoque verè credidisse, ceu Tirinus statuit, qui ita h. l. explicat: non omnis, qui in me credit, me invocat, me Dominum suum agnoscit. Resp. dist. inter nudam fidei professionem vanamq; eius iactantiam, & inter firmam Christi apprehensionem, sive fiduciam. Quòd non haec, sed illa saltim in Pseudoprophetis fuerit, patet -x coll. huius loci cum Matth. 10, 32 ac Rom. 10, 10.)*

## 7:22
v. 22. Iust. in Dial. cum Tryph page 240. Among us usProphetic gifts exist, whence you also ought to understand that those which were once in your nation have been transferred to us. And just as among you in the time of the holy Prophets there were also False Prophets: so also among us there are very many false teachers, whom our Lord warned us to beware of: so that we require nothing, saying that he was foreknowing of all things which were to happen to us after his resurrection from the dead and ascension into heaven. The same in quaest. & respp. ad orth quaest. 5. p. 309. If the representation, proof, and indication of virtues and miracles were of the true religion, the Lord would by no means have rejected them and pronounced them unworthy of his familiarity, who had said: Lord, did we not etc. The same Apol. 2. pro Christ. p. 49. rightly gathers from this place, that those who are not found to live as Christ taught are not Christians, although they profess the doctrine of Christ with their tongue, since he teaches that not those who merely profess, but those confirming the profession with works at the same time τοὺς τὰ ἔργα πράττοντας will be saved. Ibid. he reads. Did we not eat and drink in your name and perform virtues. In the same way he reads in Dial. cum Tryph. p. 235. Why God grants the power of working miracles to the impious, he explains -sid. Pelus. lib. 1. Epist. 145. *(add. B. D. Bald. Cas. Conse. page 591. where he also shows why, if they are true miracles which the impious perform, the Apostle calls them prodigies 2 Thess. 2:9)*

Latin:

v. 22. Iust. in Dial. cum Tryph pag. 240. Apud nos huc usProphetica extant dona, unde & vos intelligere debetis, quae olim in genare vestro fuerunt, ea in nos esse translata. Ac quemadmodum apud vos sanctorum Prophetarum tempore etiam Pseudoprophet ae erant: it a & apud nos permulti sunt falsi doctores, quos cavendos esse, Dominus noster praemonuit: it a ut nihil requiramus, praescium eum fuisse dicentes rerum omnium, quae nobis post resurrectionem eius à mortuis & ascensionem in coelum eventura erant. idem in quaest. & respp. ad orth quaest. 5. p. 309. Virtutum ac miraculorum repraesentatio, siprobatio & indicium esset verae religionis, minimè Dominus eos reprobasset & indignos familiaritate suâ pronunciasset, qui dixerant: Domine, nonne &c. Idem Apol. 2. pro Christ. p. 49. ex hoc loco rectè colligit, quòd illi, qui non ita vivere comperiantur, sicut Christus docuit, non sint Christiani, quamvis doctrinam Christi linguâ profiteantur, cùm non profitentes tantum, sed operibus simul professionem confirmantes τοὺς τὰ ἔργα πράττοντας salvatum iri doceat. Ibid. legit. Nonne in nomine tuo edimus & bibimus & virtutes praestitimus. Eodem modo legit in Dial. cum Tryph. p. 235. Cur Deus virtutem operandi miracula concedat impiis, exponit -sid. Pelus. lib. 1. Epist. 145. *(add. B. D. Bald. Cas. Conse. pag. 591. ubi etiam ostendit, cur, si vera miracula sunt, quae impii faciunt, Apostolus appellet prodigia 2. Thes. 2, 9.)*

## 7:23
v. 23. οὐδέποτε, I never knew you. Syr. at no time I knew you. from no time or I never knew you. Theophyl. in h. l. τὸ δὲ That, I never knew you, is for, not indeed, when you were performing miracles, did I love you. For knowledge is called love in this place. Maldonatus in h. l. All the ancient authors have observed, and especially Origen, that the verb to know in this place and in other similar ones, signifies not knowledge, but affection, approval. You who work iniquity. Jerome in h. l. He did not say, you who have worked iniquity, lest he might seem to take away repentance, but you who work, that is, you who until the present hour, when the time of judgment has arrived, although you do not have the power of sinning, yet you have the affection.

*(Therefore τὸ to know must be understood both in this place and in the parallel place Matt. 25, 13, not of knowledge of simple vision or theoretical knowledge, for that it is different is evident from Ioh. 2, 25, c. 6, 64. c. 16, 30. c. 21, 17. Col. 2, 3. 4. And to this pertain all the sayings of Holy Scripture which speak of divine omniscience: But it is a question in this place of knowledge of affection or benevolent approval, or practical Ioh. 10, 14. Gal. 4, 9. 1. Cor. 8, 3. 2. Tim. 2, 19. so also among the Hebrews the verb ירע occurs Gen. 22, 12. Exod. 38. Ps. 1, last Ps. 37, 8. Ps. 31, 8. There is a notable passage on this matter in Hilary lib. IX. de Trinit. p. 129. where among other things: In the Gospels we find the Lord knowing many things not to know. Workers of iniquity &c, Even with an oath he does not know them, whom nevertheless he does not not know to be workers of iniquity. He does not know, therefore, not for that reason because he might not know, but because they are unworthy of his knowledge through the iniquity of their operation: confirming the same by the religion of an oath, and having in the virtue of nature that he might not not know, and retaining in the Sacrament of the will, that he might not know. The same a little later: The Lord Jesus Christ is not therefore who searches the hearts and reins is God, in that infirmity of nature, lest (read: that) he might not know: since he understands this very thing from the nature of knowledge, to be, what he might not know. But if any perhaps shall attribute ignorance to him, let them fear to be told by him, who knows their thoughts: Why do you think evil in your hearts. Conf. similar things in Greg. Magn. homil. 12. in Evang. and in August. quaest. l. 3. quaest. 152. and in Ps. 1. t. 8. The same serm. 23. on the words of the Lord: Does he not know them (the foolish virgins,) who knows all things? what is it therefore, I do not know you? I disapprove of you, I reject you. S. Paterius l. 2. on the Ev. Matth. c. 42. To know of God is sometimes said to be to recognize, sometimes to approve: and he knows the wicked, because by recognizing he judges: for he would not judge any wicked person, if he did not know him at all; and yet he does not know the wicked, since he does not approve of his deeds. And he knows, therefore, because he detects; and he does not know, since he does not recognize him in the appearance of his wisdom.
