It is also possible to distinguish here between general knowledge, which extends itself to all things and the causes of things, and special, which pertains at least to the elect, Rom. 8, 29. 1. Petr. 1, 2. It does not therefore follow: Christ never knew the Pseudoprophets by special knowledge, or as elect, because they never were such. Therefore by the Sacrament of initiation they were never (and thus not even in infancy) regenerated, as indeed Wendelinus Exerc. XLIII. §. 13. attempts to prove from this place. As if indeed, by denying special knowledge, by which Christ did not know the Pseudoprophets as elect, one must also immediately deny general knowledge, by which he knows them, as indeed regenerated, but ροσκαίρους. And from this it is also clear, how weak is the consequence of the same Wendelinus, when Exerc. LXIII. §. 9. from the fact that Christ is said not to have known the Pseudoprophets as being workers of iniquity, namely by special knowledge, by which he is said to know the sheep most specially so called, i.e., the elect Ioh. 10, 14. 27. he attempts to prove that the reprobate belong neither by reason of redemption nor of vocation to the fold of Christ, nor can they be called sheep. (He follows indeed in this matter his predecessors, as Scharpius Curs. Theol. p. 403. attempts to prove from this place, that Christ did not even die for them.) The same man nevertheless Exerc. 71. §. 9. confesses, and from this very place also gathers, not only the elect, whom mercy and love alone touch, in species and singularly so called, but also the reprobate through the preaching of the word, with the addition of

By the operation of the Holy Spirit, to be illuminated, and to progress somewhat. But why do those who are called and illuminated by the Holy Spirit not progress further? Is it because God has reprobated them by an absolute decree? By no means: but because they work iniquity, that is, because they resist the further operation of the Holy Spirit by their own and affected malice. Conf. Prov. 1, 24,Matth. 23, 37.Luc. 7, 30.Act. 7, 51. But Wendehnus is vehemently pleased with himself in that he says here that the Savior says that He NEVER knew the False Prophets, namely with the knowledge of love and benevolence, with which He knows His own, that is, those who have been adopted as sons of GOD. See the same in the same chapter, item Exerc. 118. §. 9. Response. There is an ambiguity in the word to know. For it is taken 1. for general knowledge, by which Christ knows all things, Ioh. 21, 17, 2. for special knowledge, which can also be called that of love and benevolence; by which He knows all men, since He gave Himself as a ransom for all, 1. Timoth. 2, 6. and indeed with this intention, that all might believe, and through faith become partakers of this fruit. And by this knowledge He knows even the reprobate, since He died even for those who perish, Rom. 14, 15. 3. for most special knowledge, by which He knows, nay, even from eternity foreknew the elect, that is, those who would finally believe in Him. In such a most strict and most special acceptance, the Greek γινώσκω, occurs Ioh. 10, 14.27. προέγνω Rom. 8, 29. πρόγνωσις, 1. Petr. 1, 2. and also here. Now, although Christ never knew the False Prophets in such a way as to acknowledge them as His own, that is, as the elect, who are to be at some time actual partakers of the acquired υιἱοθεσίας and of the heavenly inheritance: just as Daniel Chamier, vol. 2, Panstr. c. 11. §. 15, rightly explains here expressly concerning knowledge most specially so called, namely concerning predestination, from this, however, it does not follow that He did not acknowledge them with special knowledge, or love them in such a way that they could have become υιἱοθεσίας partakers, if only they themselves had willed it. Distinguish, therefore, between υιἱοθεσίας acquisition, and the saving fruit of the acquired benefit. It does not follow, the False Prophets do not apply to themselves the benefits acquired by Christ, therefore those things were not acquired for them by Christ. Christ gave the power to become sons of God, but NB. as many as receive Him and believe in His name, Ioh. 1, 12. And for this end also God sent His Son made under the law, that He might redeem those who were subject to the law, that we might receive υιἱοθεσίαν. Gal. 4, 5. Now, however, not only the elect were under the law, not only the elect υιἱοθεσίαν in

the first-formed had lost, but also the reprobate. E. But that the reprobate do not become children of God, to whom the inheritance of eternal life might eventually come to pass in act, the Holy Scripture teaches that the cause of that is not an absolute decree of reprobation, or that God absolutely willed that they themselves should not repent and be saved: but because they themselves They resist the Holy SpiritActs 7, 51.they are unwilling to come,Matt. 23, 37. or as our Savior speaks in this place, because they are workers of iniquity, from which they ought to depart, 2 Tim. 2, 19. It happens indeed that even the reprobate sometimes believe, nay, are truly regenerated, but because they are πρόσκαιροι, they are therefore deservedly repelled from the possession of eternal life. Conf. Matt. 24, 13.Apoc. 2, 10. It is furthermore evident from this place that reprobation was made from eternity. For if Christ never knew the reprobate, namely with a knowledge joined with eternal election, it follows that He reprobated them from eternity. Conf. Apoc. 13, 8.c. 17, 8. Finally, just as there is no consequence: Christ reprobated the false prophets from eternity, therefore He does this by an absolute decree. So likewise it is not sufficiently firmly subsumed thus: Christ reprobated the false prophets on account of evil works, or because they themselves are workers of iniquity, therefore He chose the elect to eternal life on account of good works. The reason is, because evil works are perfectly evil, but good works, even of the elect, are imperfectly such, already owed to God beforehand, etc., therefore they can in no way be meritorious of eternal life.

Latin:

v. 23. οὐδέποτε,nunquamnovi vos. Syr. aliquando noni. e. à nullo tempore sive nunquam novi vos. Theophyl. in h. l. τὸ δὲIllud, nunquam novi vos, est pro netum quidem, cùm miracula patrabatis, amabam vos. Cognitio enim amor dicitur hoc loco. Maldonatus in h. l. Omnes veteres autores observarunt, inprimisq; Origenes, cognoscendi verbum hoc loco aliisq; similibus, non cognitionem, sed affectum, approbationemsignificare. Qui operamini iniquitatem. Hieronymus in h. l. Non dixit, qui operati estis iniquitatem, ne videretur -ollere poenitentiam, sed qui operamini, hoc est, qui usin praesentem horam, cùm iudicii tempus advenerit, licet non habeatis facultatem peccandi, tamen habet is affectum.

*(Accipiendum igitur τὸnosse tum h. l. tum in loco paral Matt. 25, 13, non de notiti â simplicis visionis sive theoretica notitià, diversum n. patet ex Ioh. 2, 25,c. 6, 64.c. 16, 30.c. 21, 17.Col. 2, 3. 4. Atque huc pertinent omnia Sc. S. dicta, quae de omniscientia divinâ loquuntur: Sed agitur h. l. de notitiâ affectionis sive benevolae adprobationis, sive practica Ioh. 10, 14.Gal. 4, 9.1. Cor. 8, 3.2. Tim. 2, 19. ita quoque apud Ebr. verbum ירע occurrit Gen. 22, 12.Exod. 38.Ps. 1, ult. Ps. 37, 8.Ps. 31, 8. Est in hanc rem insignis locus apud Hilarium lib. IX. de Trinit. p. 129. ubi inter alia: In Evangeliis Dominum multa scientem nescire invenimus. Operarios iniquitatis &c, Etiam cum iureiurando eos non novit, quos taminiquit at is operarios esse nonnescit. Nescit ergo non idcirco quia nesciat, sed quia cognitione eius per iniquit atem operationis indigni sint: sidem dicti iurisiur andi religione confirmans, & habens in naturae virtute ne nesciat, & retinens in Sacramento volunt at is, ut nesciat. Idem paullò post: Non est igitur Dominus I. C. qui serut ans corda & renes D Eus est, in eā naturae infirmit ate, ne (leg. ut) nesciat: cum hoc ipsum ex naturae scientiae intelligat, esse, quod nesciat. Quòd si qui fortè ignorationem ei deputabunt ab eo, qui sciat cogitationes eorum, dici sibi metuant: Quid cogitatis malae in cordibus vestris. Conf. similia apud Greg. Magn. homil. 12. in Evang. it, apud August. quaest. l. 3. quaest. 152. it. in Ps. 1. t. 8. Idem serm. 23. de verbis Domini: Non novit illas (virgines fatuas,) qui novit omnia? quid est ergo, non novi vos? improbo vos, reprobo vos. S. Paterius l. 2. super Ev. Matth. c. 42.Scire Dei aliquando dicitur cognoscere, aliquando àpprobare: & scit iniovum, quia cognoscendo iudicat: neque enim iniquum quempiam iudicaret, si nequaquam cognosceret; & tamen iniquum nescit, quoniam facta non approbat. Et novit ergo, quia deprehendit; & non novit, quoniam hunc in suae sapientiae specie non recognoscit. Potest etiam distingui hîc inter notitiam generalem, quae ad omnes res & rerum causas sese extendit, ac specialem, quae ad electos saltem pertinet, Rom. 8, 29.1. Petr. 1, 2. Non igitur sequitur: Christus nunquam novit Pseudoprophetas notitiâ speciali, sive ut electos, quia nunquam tales fuerunt. E. per Sacramentū initiationis nunquam (atque adeò etiam ne quidē in infantia) fuerunt regeniti, uti quidem Wendelinus Exerc. XLIII. §. 13. ex h. l. evincere conatur. Quasi verò negatâ notitiâ speciali, qua Christus Pseudoprophetas non novit ut electos, neganda quoque statim etiam sit notitia generalis, quâ novit, ut regenitos quidem, sed ροσκαίρους. Atque hinc etiam liquet, quàm infirma sit consequentia eiusdem Wendelini, quando Exerc. LXIII. §. 9. ex eo, quòd Christus Pseudoprophetas utpote operarios iniquitatis non novisse dicitur, notitiâ nempe speciali, quâ oves specialissimè sic dictas h. e. electos nosse dicitur Ioh. 10, 14.27. evincere conatur, quòd reprobi nec ratione redemtionis nec vocationis ad Christi ovile pertineant, aut oves dici possint. (Sequitur vero hac in reantecessores suos, ceu Scharpius Curs. Theol. p. 403. ex h. l. probare conatur, Christum ne mortuum quidem pro his esse.) Idem tamen Exerc. 71. §. 9. fatetur, & ex hoc ipso quoque loco colligit, non tantum electos, quos solos attingat misericordia & dilectio, in specie & sutgulariter sic dicta, sed & reprobos per verbi pradicationem, accedente

Sp. Sancti operatione, illuminari, & aliquousprogredi. Cur vero non longiùs progrediuntur vocati & Sp. S. illuminati? An quia Deus ex absoluto eos decreto reprobavit? Minimè: sed quia operantur iniquit atem h. e. quia ulteriori operationi Sp. S. resistunt propriâ & affectata malitiâ. Conf. Prov. 1, 24,Matth. 23, 37.Luc. 7, 30.Act. 7, 51. At vehementer sibi placet Wendehnus in eo, quòd hîc dicat Salvator, se NUNQUAM novisse Pseudoprophet as, not itiâ nempe amoris & benevolentiae, quâ suos h e. est illos, qui in filios DEI adopt ati sunt, novit. Vid. ipsel. c. item Exerc. 118. §. 9. Resp. Ambiguitas est in verbo nosse. Accipitur enim 1. pro notitia generali, quâ Christus omnia novit, Ioh, 21, 17, 2. pro notitia speciali, quae amoris quoque & benevolentiae dici potest; quâ novit omnes homines, quippe qui sese dedit pretium redemtionis pro omnibus,1. Timoth. 2, 6. & quidem hâc intentione, ut omnes credant, & fructûs huius per fidem fiant participes. & hâc notitiâ novit etiam reprobos, cùm pro pereuntibus etiam fuerit mortuus, Rom. 14, 15. 3. pro notitia specialissimâ, quâ novit, imò ab aeterno etiam praescivit electos h. e. finaliter in ipsum credituros. In tali strictissimâ ac specialissima acceptione Graecorum γινώσκω, occurrit Ioh. 10, 14.27.προέγνωRom. 8, 29.πρόγνωσις,1. Petr. 1, 2. atque etiam h. l. Iam, licet Christus Pseudoprophetas nun quam ita cognoverit, ut agnoverit pro suis h. e. pro electis, qui acquisitae υιἱοθεσίας ac haereditatis coelestis actu participes aliquando futuri: quemadmodum etiam h. l. disertè de notitiâ specialissimè sic dictâ, nempe de praedestinatione, rectè exponit Dan. Chamier t. 2. Panstr. c. 11. §. 15. hinc tamen non sequitur, quòd nec speciali eos notitiâ agnoverit, sive ita dilexerit, ut potuerint υιἱοθεσίας fieri participes, si modò ipsi voluissent. Disting. igitur inter υιἱοθεσίας acquisitionem, ac salutarem ac quisiti beneficii fructum. Non sequitur, Pseudoprophetae non applicant fibi beneficia à Christo acquisita, E. non fuerunt eis à Christo illa acquisita. Dedit Christus potestatem filios Dei fieri, sed NB. quotquot ipsum recipiunt & credunt in nomen ipsius, Ioh. 1, 12. Et hoc fine quoque Deus misit filium suum factum sub lege, ut eos, qui legi erant obnoxii, redimeret, ut υιἱοθεσίαν acciperemus. Gal. 4, 5. Iam vero non electi saltem sub lege erant, non electi saltem υιἱοθεσίαν in

protoplastis amiserant, sed etiā reprobi. E. Quò verò reprobi nō fiant filii Dei, quibus vitae aet. haéditas, actu obtiget aliquando, illius causam S. S. esse docet non absolutum reprobationis decretum, vel quòd Deus absolutè noluerit, ut & ipsi illi poenitentiam agerent & salvi fierent: sed quia ipsi resistunt Sp. SAct. 7, 51.venire nolunt,Matth. 23, 37. sive ut h. l. Salvator noster loquitur, quia sunt operarit iniquit at is, à quâ discedere debebant, 2. Tim. 2, 19. Contingit quidem, ut & reprobi aliquando credant, imò verè regenerentur, sed quia sunt πρόσκαιροι, ideò meritò repelluntur à possessione vitae aeternae. Conf. Matth. 24, 13.Apoc. 2, 10. Patet porrò ex h. l. quòd reprobatio ab aeterno fuerit facta. Si enim Christus reprobos nunquam novit, notitiâ nempe cum aet. electione coniunctâ, sequitur quòd ab aeterno reprobaverit. Conf. Apoc. 13, 8.c. 17, 8. Denique sicuti nulla consequentia est: Christus Pseudoprophetas ab aeterno reprobavit, ergo ex absoluto decreto hoc facit. Ita pariter non satis firmiter ita subsumitur: Caristus Pseudoprophetas propter mala opera, sive quia ipsi operarii iniquitatis, reprobavit. e. electos propter bona opera ad vitam aet. elegit. Ratio est, quia mala opera sunt perfectè mala, bona vero, etiam electorum, opera sunt imperfectè talia, iam antè Deo debita &c. e. minimè vitae aet. possunt esse meritoria.)*

## 7:24
v. 24. Everyone therefore who hears, etc. Aug. in Ps. 103.Build on the rock, and not on the sand. To hear and not to do, is to build on the sand. To hear and to do, is to build on the rock. Neither to do, nor to hear, is to build nothing. Therefore one must build on the rock, so that temptation may not overturn it. (But since Christ is the most firm rock, Matt. 16, 18.c. 21, 24.Ps. 118, 22.Isa. 28, 1.1 Cor. 10, 4. he builds upon the rock, who adheres to Christ with firm and immovable trust, and places all the hope of his salvation solely in the most precious λύτρω provided by Him, see 1 Pet. 2, 6. 7. Although indeed saving faith is never separated from good works, whence it is also required of true believers that they be not only hearers of the word, but also doers,Jas. 1, 22. following, add 1 John 2, 4 yet the power of apprehending Christ or attaining eternal life is by no means to be attributed to one's own works. For those who seek to be justified (and saved) not by faith but by the works of the law, seek another foundation besides this one and true which is laid, 1. Cor. 3, 11. and so they stumble at this stone,Rom. 9, 32. but those who believe in him will not be put to shame. l. c. v. 33. the Savior will not say to them: I never knew you. But he will acknowledge them before the heavenly Father,Matth. 10, 32. Compare more on this matter in B. Par. Comm. on the 1st ep. of Peter p. 177. & add the notable passage from the author of the Imperfect work on Matt. hom. 20. in B. D. Quistorp. on this passage.)*

*( Everyone therefore who hears and does &c. The parallel passage Luc. 8, 15. pertains here. Corn. à Lapide writes on this passage: Note, against the Innovators, that faith without G. W. [Good Works], which faith prescribes and dictates must be done, does not suffice for salvation. For Christ here calls the sandy foundation s-founded on sand, faith alone, conceived from the hearing of preaching, which like sand is dry, useless, and flowing away, but he calls the rock faith, solidified by G. W. Tirinus has similar things on this passage. Resp. 1. I distinguish between the vain boasting of faith, and saving faith or trust. When it is taught in our Churches that men are justified and saved by faith alone, the discourse is about the latter, not the former: for it is known that our people freely profess that true faith is never alone, i.e., separated from G. W., although it alone saves, nor does Christ say in this passage that those who at least hear his sermons believe in him or have faith. For from hearing, both true faith can be conceived, and also at least a bare historical knowledge. 2. It is to be noted that it is one question whether G. W., which faith prescribes, are to be done by the justified, namely by reason of the divine command and duty: to which we answer entirely in the affirmative; but another question: Whether G. W. are meritorious of eternal life or whether one must strive for G. W. so that through and because of them we may obtain eternal life, and indeed as a due reward. Which the Papists affirm, but we deny. Nor can it be proved in any way, either from this passage or from other sayings of Holy Scripture. 3. The Savior does not say that faith is solidified by G. W. (for true faith rests solely on the most sufficient λύτρῶ, of Christ and is solidified by the same: for what solidity is to be sought in our imperfect and unclean works, when they cannot subsist in the rigorous judgment of God?) but this is indicated, that by G. W. it is declared or manifested to men, who those are who have been built by true faith upon the one rock, which is Christ. But Hugo Grotius seems to bring help here to Bell., noting thus on this passage among other things. These, (which have been prescribed by Christ) having been perceived and meditated upon, the will is bent to obedience of the understood truth. Whence arises in the mind love, which performs the role of root and foundationEph. 3, 17. This is what, against the blandishments of pleasures, the fear of pain, of poverty &c. retains that former assent and its profession unshaken. But it was long ago observed by B. D. Balduinus that the passage in the Ep. to the Ephesians does not treat of the love with which we love God, but with which God has embraced us in the Son, v. 18. Cf. Rom. 8, 32.1. Ioh. 4, 10. for our love toward him is far too weak to be able to root our faith and certify our salvation, as the praised Theologian well warns. But on this matter more in the cited place. I add at least this, that Cornelius himself a little later, namely in the notes to v. 26, writes: The root and fuel of all temptations is the inconstancy of the mind and diffidence in God! Therefore, on the contrary, the root and fuel of perseverance is faith, resting in the love of God and the merit of Christ. Furthermore, not man himself is called the rock, but the one building upon the rock. But Christ is the rock of salvation, in him all the promises of GOD are certain. He who believes in the Son has eternal life; he who does not believe, will not see life.Ioh. 6, 36. add. 2. Tim. 2, 13.1. Ioh. 5, 10.)*

Latin:

v. 24. Omnis igitur, qui audit &c. Aug. in Ps. 103.In petra adifica, & non in arena. Audire & non facere, in arenam aedificare est. Audire & facere, in petra aedificare est. Nec facere, nec audire, nihil aedificare est. Ergo in petra aedificandum, ut tentatio non evertat. *(Christus verò cùm petra sit firmissima, Matth. 16, 18.c. 21, 24.Ps. 118, 22.Esa. 28, 1.1. Cor. 10, 4. ille super petram. aedificat, qui firma & immota fiduciâ Christo adhaeret, omnemq; salutis suae spem in pretiosissimo λύτρω ab eo praestito unicè collocat, vid. 1. Petr. 2, 6. 7. Licet vero fides salvifica nunquam sit à B. O. separata, unde etiam requiritur à verè fidelibus, ut non solum auditores sermonis, sed etiam factores sint,Iac. 1, 22. seqq. add. 1. Iohan. 2, 4 minimè tamen vis apprehendendi Christum vel adsequendi vitam aeternam propriis operibus tribuenda est. Qui enim non ex fide sed ex operibus legis iustificari (ac salvari) quaeiunt, aliud quaerunt fundamentum praeter hoc unicum & verum, quod positum est, 1. Cor. 3, 11. adeoque impingunt in hunc lapidem,Rom. 9, 32. qui verò credunt in eum, non pudefientl. c. v. 33. non dicet ad eos Salvator: nunquam novi vos. Sed confitebitur eos coram Patre coelesti,Matth. 10, 32. Confer plura in hane rem apud B. Par. Comm. in Pr. ep. Petri p. 177. & adde insignem locum ex aut. operis Imperf. in Matt. hom. 20. apud B. D. Quistorp. in h. l.)*

*( Omnis ergo qui audit & facit &c. Pertinet huc locus paral. Luc. 8, 15. Corn. à Lapide in h. l. Nota, scribit, contra Novatores, fidem sine B. O. quae fides facienda praescribit & dictat, non sufficeread salutem. Christus enim hîc fundamentum arenarium s-in arena fundatum vocat solam fidem, ex auditu praedicationis conceptam, qua instar arenae arida est, inutilis & diffluens, petram vero vocat fidem, B. O. solidatana. Similia habet Tirinus in h. l. Resp. 1. dist, inter vanam fidei iactantiam, & inter fidem salvificam s. fiduciam. Quando docetur in nostris Ecclesiis, solâ fide homines iustificari & salvari, de hâc, non de illa, sermo est: notum enim, quòd ultrò profiteantur nostrates, veram fidem nunquam esse solam h. e. à B. O. separatem, licet sola salvificet, nec dicit Christus h. l. illos qui saltem audiunt eius sermones, in ipsum credere vel habere fidem. Potest enim ex auditu tum vera fides concipi, tum nuda saltem notitia historica, 2. Notandum est, quòd alia sit quaestio, an B. O. quae fides praescribit, à iustificatis sint facienda, nempe ratione mandati divini ac debiti: ad quam omninò aff. respondemus; alia verò: An B. O. sint meritoria vitae aet. vel an propterea B. O. studendum, ut per ac propter ea vitā aet. consequamur, & quidem ut mercedem debitam. Quod Pontificii affirmant, nos verò negamus. Nec ullo modò s. ex h. l. sive ex aliis Sc. S. dictis id probari potest. 3. Non dicit Salvator, quòd per B. O. fides solidetur (innititurenim vera fides unicè sufficientissimo Christi λύτρῶ, eodemque solidatur: quae enim in imperfectis & immundis nostris operibus quaerenda soliditas est, cùm in rigoroso Dei iudicio subsistere nequeant?) sed hoc indicatur, quòd per B. O. declaretur sive hominibus manifestetur, quinam sint illi, qui verâ fide super unicâ petra, quae Christus, aedificati sunt. Ast suppetias hîc ferre Bell. videtur Hugo Grotius, ita in h. l. annotans inter alia. His, (quae à Christo praescripta sunt) percept is atmedit at is, flectitur voluntas inobedientiam intellectae verit at is. unde insurgit in animo dilectio, quae radicis & fundamenti vicem praestatEph. 3, 17.Haec est, quae adversus blanditias voluptatum, formidinem doloris, paupert at is &c. assensionem illam priorem eiusprofessionem ineoncussam retinet. Verùm pridem observatum à B. D. Balduino est, agi dicto loco in Ep. ad Ephes. non de dilectione, quâ nos Deum diligimus, sed quâ Deus nos complexus est in Filio, v. 18. Conf. Rom. 8, 32.1. Ioh. 4, 10. nostra enim erga ipsum dilectio longè infirmior est, quàm ut fidem nostram radicare & salutem certificare possit, ut benè monet laudatus Theologus. Sed de hâc re pluribus d l. Hoc saltem addo, quòd ipse Cornelius paulò pòst, nempe in notis ad v. 26. scribit: Radix & fomes omnium tent at ionum est mentis inconstantia & diffidentia in Deum! E. econtrario radix & fomes perseverantiae est fides, in Dei dilectione ac Christi merito requiescens. Praetereà non ipse homo petra dicitur, sed aedificans supra petram. Christus verò est salutis petra, in eo omnes DEI promissiones sunt certae. Qui credit in Filium habet vitam aet. qui vero non. credit, non videbit vitam.Ioh. 6, 36. add. 2. Tim. 2, 13.1. Ioh. 5, 10.)*

## 7:25
(v. 25. The rain descended &c. That by water, torrent or rivers in Holy Scripture sometimes adversities, calamities, temptations &c. are signified, is taught at length by B. D. Glassius in Rhet. S. p. 257. 258. also B. Par. in Postill. Salom. part. 2. p. 486. 541. 548. and it is also sufficiently evident from 2. Sam. 22, 17. Ps. 18, 17. Ps. 32, 6. Ps. 66, 12. Ps. 69, 2. Ps. 124, 5. Ps. 110, 7. Thus also that by winds, especially strong and vehement ones, temptations & tribulations are sometimes designated, is observed by Hieronymus Lauretus Cervariensis in Sylva Allegoriarum page 73. D. Botasaccus also compares heresies with wind in Promt. Alleg. p. 776.)

( It did not fall; for it was founded upon the rock But when the reborn are founded upon the rock, i.e., believe in Christ, Ludov. Crocius in de Persev. Sanct. and other Calvinists gather from this, that they cannot entirely lose their faith and righteousness, and fall from the grace of GOD. Resp. if they themselves understand by the reborn only the elect, as it entirely seems, we distinguish between total, if I may so speak, and final fall. We concede that the elect cannot fall in such a way that they never rise again. (For thus they could not be called elect:) but from this it does not follow that they cannot fall even for a time, namely when they allow themselves to be moved from that rock of salvation by mortal sins as if by the impetuous waves of Satan. For since the elect contend no less than the reprobate through a rough and slippery path to the heavenly fatherland, it can certainly easily happen that they fall, and indeed in such a way that they shake off the grace of the Holy Spirit and lose their faith, as the examples of David, Peter, and others sufficiently teach. But nevertheless, the elect fall in such a way that they rise again through true repentance. Which is true Regarding those reborn in general, it is certain that these can be so tossed by the storms of sins and crimes, if indeed they knowingly and willingly follow the leading of Satan and the world, that they may be utterly dislodged from the rock of salvation, upon which they had previously been built. Nor do these words stand in the way, since they are to be understood with a reduplication, (like those of the Savior John 4:14 ch. 10:29 for the promises of GOD are not absolute, but conditional) namely in this sense: that the reborn, as long as they are and remain such, i.e., as long as they hear and do the words of Christ, can be subverted neither by the wind of persecutions nor by the waves of tempests: yet it is not permitted to infer from this that they cannot be absolutely subverted, if they even most greatly turn themselves away from Christ of their own accord through mortal sins, and freely loosen the reins to the desires of the flesh. Hence the Apostle commands that we work out our salvation with trembling. Compare more on this matter in B. P. L. de B. O. §. 144. also B. D. Tarnovius in the inaugural Disputation which is on the Perseverance of the Saints, B. D. Mentzer against Apelius chapter 10, Durfeld against Croc on the perseverance of the Saints, especially in the Theologians of Marburg, in the Deduct. Fund p. 269. following.)

Latin:

*(v. 25. Descendit pluvia &c. Quòd per aquam, torrentem vel flumina. in Sc. S. quandoque adversitates, calamitates, tentationes &c. significentur, prolixè docent B. D. Glassius Rhet. S. p. 257. 258. it. B. Par. Postill. Salom. part. 2. p. 486. 541. 548. ac satis etiam patet ex 2. Sam. 27, 17.Ps. 18, 17.Ps. 32, 6.Ps. 66, 12.Ps. 69, 2.Ps. 124, 5.Ps. 110, 7. Sic etiam per ventos, cumprimis validos ac vehementes, tent at iones & tribulationes designari aliquando, observat Hieronymus Lauretus Cervariensis in Sylva Allegoriarum pag. 73. haereses quoque cum vento confert D. Botasaccus in. Promt. Alleg. p. 776.)*

*( Non cecidit; fundat a enim erat super petram Cùm verò renati fundati sint super petram h. e. in Christum credant, colligunt hinc Ludov. Crocius in de Persev. Sanct. aliique Calviniani, eos non posse prorsus, fidem ac iustitiam suam amittere, & gratiâ DEI excidere. Resp. si per renatos intelligunt ipsi solos electos, uti omninò videtur, disting. inter casum, ut ita loquar, tot alem, ac finalem. Concedimus, electos non ita posse labi, ut nunquam resurgant. (Sic enim non possent dici electi:) ex hoc verò non sequitur, quôd ne quidem ad tempus, quando nempe per peccata mortalia tanquam per impetuosos Satanae fluctus à petra illa salutis dimoveri se patiuntur, possint cadere. Cùm enim electi non minùs, quàm reprobi per salebrosam & lubricam viam ad coelestem patriam contendant, facilè sanè contingere potest, ut labantur, & quidem ita ut Sp. Sancti gratiam excutiant fidemque amittant, ceu exempla Davidis, Petri aliorumque satis docent. Sed tamen electi ita cadunt, ut iterum per veram poenitentiam resurgant. Quod verâ renatos in genere concernit, certum est, quòd hi ita peccatorum ac scelerum procellis iactitari possint, si nempe scientes ac volentes Satanae ac mundi ductum sequantur, ut penitus à salutis petra, cui antè superaedificati erant, deturbentur. Nec obstant haec verba, quippe quae cum reduplicatione intelligenda, (uti illa Salvatoris Ioh. 4, 14.c. 10, 29. neque enim promissiones DEI absolutae sunt, sed conditionatae) nempe hoc sensu: quod renati, quamdiu tales sunt ac manent, h. e. quamdiu Christi verba audiunt & faciunt, nec persecutionum vento nec tempestatum fluctibus subverti possint: inde tamen inferre non, licet, quòd absolutè subverti nequeant, si vel maximè etiam à Christo per peccata mortalia sponte sese avertant, ac carnis desideriis liberè frena laxent. Iubet hinc Apostolus, ut cum tremore salutem operemur. Conf. plura in hanc rem apud B. P. L. de B. O. §. 144. item B. D. Tarnovium in Disp. inaug. quae est de Persev. Sanct. B. D. Mentzerum contra Apelium cap. 10. Durfeld. contra Croc de pers. Sanct. cumprimis apud Dnn. Theol. Marpurg, in Deduct. Fund p. 269. seqq.)*

## 7:27
v. 27. The rain descending, viz. temptations, which are from the Demons, existing in the air and blowing the winds of ambition and vain glory, which are sent by the world, and the rivers of concupiscences coming upon it, which burst forth from the flesh, and rushing into that house, it did not fall, but stood, because the house was founded upon the rock i.e. Christ, or firm faith in Christ. Weidn in loc, fid. praec. tract. 2. p. 383. Jerome in chapter 64 of Isaiah. Wind in the Scriptures is mystically placed in two ways, either in the magnitude of temptations, as in this place, or concerning the perversity of doctrine, as Eph. 4. That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine.

Latin:

v. 27. Descendente pluvia, sc. tentationibus, quae sunt à Doemonibus, existentibus in aëre & flantibus ventis ambitionis & inanis gloriae, qui mittuntur à mundo, & supervenientibus fluminibus concupiscentiarum, quae erumpunt à carne, & irruentibus in illam domum, non cecidit, sed stetit, quia fundata erat domus super petram i. e. Christum, seu firmam fidem in Christum. Weidn in loc, fid. praec. tract. 2. p. 383. Hieron. in cap. 64. Esai. Ventus in Scripturis mysticè dupliciter ponitur, aut in tentationum magnitudine, ut h. l. aut de perversit ate doctrinae, utEph. 4.Non, circumferamur omni vento doctrinae.

## 7:29
(v. 29. Teaching as one having ἐξουσίαι &c. Cf. John 6, 63. Justin Martyr Apol. 2. for the Christians p. 47. concerning Christ: Βραφεῖς i. e. His sermons were brief and concise. For he was not a Sophist and caviller: but the power of GOD was his word. To this also pertain the sayings Ps. 45, 3.8.Isa. 50, 4.c. 61, 1. And this was that long-expected great and true prophet 1. Maccab. 14, 41. Luke 7, 16. προήτης Luke 24, 19. add. Luke 4, 36.Matt. 5. throughout. But Bell. is vain, when in t. 4. lib. 4. de Iustif. c. 2. §. Tertio, he attempts to prove from this place, that laws properly so called are contained in the Gospel, strictly so called. For that by τὸ ἐζουσίαν is indicated here, he says, that Christ taught as a legislator, who interprets, or changes, or adds laws by authority, not as a lawyer, who only explains the law from knowledge. Barradius has similar things in t. 2. Concord. Evang. l. 5. page 297. They follow in this part the Council of Trent, which in sess. 6. ca. 21. promulgated such a decree: If anyone shall say, that Christ was given by God to men, as a redeemer, in whom they should trust, not also as a legislator, whom they should obey, let him be anathema. Resp. 1. We concede that the Son of God can be called and is a true, nay, the supreme legislator, as one who together with the Father & Holy Spirit not only inscribed the divine law on the hearts of the first-formed, but also solemnly promulgated the same on Mount Sinai, and caused it to be delivered to the Israelite people through Moses. 2. Nor do we deny this, that Christ in the days of his flesh, performing the ministry of preaching, i. e. in his prophetic office, joined the law & the Gospel, and taught the true sense of the law: But the question is not about this, but it is disputed between us and the Papists concerning this; Whether Christ in his Mediatorial office is a new legislator, & consequently, whether the Gospel, properly, strictly & specifically so called, is a doctrine of works? To which question we answer negatively; but the Papists, as appears among other things from that Tridentine decree, affirmatively. But our opinion is proved both from the opposition John 1, 17. and from the perfection of the Mosaic law, and from the description of a legislator, Rom. 7, 7. 8.11. and finally from the end of Christ's advent, Gal. 3, 13.c. 4. 5. as the blessed Par. shows at length.

Conf. Cath. t. 4. p. 783. But by the word ἐξουσίας, which Bellarmine urges most strongly here, is not indicated at present, that Christ promulgated new laws, or increased the Mosaic law: but that He proposed solid doctrine, with the highest majesty and perspicuity, with great simplicity and gravity of words, and finally with such authority and efficacy of spirit to move, that He seemed not only to speak or to win faith, but most efficiently to imprint His sayings in the breasts of men, striking love into some, terror into others. For He taught intrepidly, He did not speak to please, He flattered no one, but constantly rebuked vices without respect of persons. Furthermore, the integrity of His singular life, consistent with His doctrine, commended it. Finally, what He taught, He confirmed with stupendous signs and miracles; as Franciscus Lucas rightly explains in his commentary on this passage. Who also well warns that the dissimilarity between Christ and the Scribes was in this, that Christ taught in that manner, as has already been said, whereas the doctrine of the Scribes was torpid, weak, cold, diluted, painted. Since they themselves [used to discourse] about the most minute and for the most part superfluous things, (See below c. 23, 23. Mark 7, 3. 4.) about scrupulous and foolish questions and genealogies and inextricable, useless, fabulous, and vain arguments, which provided questions rather than edification (1 Tim. 1, 4. Tit. 1, 14. c. 3, 9.) then, having neglected the internal and chief worship of GOD, they were accustomed to discourse about the external only (see above v. 5. and 6.) and that in a very jejune and cold manner. If anyone compares with this description of the doctrine of the Scribes and Pharisees the just complaints by which most serious men have quite clearly indicated the corruption of heavenly doctrine in the Roman Church before the reformation undertaken by the Blessed Luther (of which kind the Blessed Par. exhibits many to be read in lib. 1 of the General Catholic Confession, part 1, c. 4), he will truly discover a great agreement between the Jewish Synagogue (such as it was constituted in the time of Christ) and the Roman Church, as it was to be seen indeed in the time of Luther and a little before; so that, just as the Israelite Church had such great need of a severe reformation, so also the Roman Papist [Church] equally and vehemently stood in need of a reformer, whom God also raised up, while He instructed the Blessed Luther and his fellow-ministers likewise with a singular ἐξουσίᾳ and a truly heroic spirit , so that they might undertake that stupendous work of reformation. Moreover, I cannot but [mention] what Cornelius Mussus of Piacenza, Bishop of Bitonto, a man, in the judgment of the Jesuit Possevin in Appar. p. 389, endowed with an almost incomparable felicity of genius, continence, and piety, [wrote] in Chapter 6 of the epistle to Rom. 279. Concerning these times he spoke gravely no less than truly, and having passed by Placentia entirely, heading straight for Verona, he left behind writings, which I shall add here. Thus indeed he said: Divine Scripture was once (he speaks indeed of the times which immediately preceded the reformation of B. Luther) alas! with what great loss to all was it neglected! There flourished a thorny and troublesome Theology, I know not what, concerning instants, relations, quiddities, and formalities. And likewise all these things were treated by syllogisms twisted with art and merely human subtleties, which without doubt, by the same authority they are received, can also be refuted. Almost an entire age of men was worn away by decrees, which, always fighting among themselves and never to be reconciled, nourish a perpetual strife through the centuries. He was considered a sublime Theologian who knew how to assign greater portents for his own little traditions, and a part of the value was the empty vainglory of not being understood in those grand words, which they weighed with a high brow among women philosophizing about sacred letters. All the leaders of the divine word had sworn by the words of the Masters; hence six hundred sects; Thomists, Scotists, Occamists, Baconists, Albertists, Aegidians, Alexandrians. O crime! The Gospels and Epistles were postponed; Christian philosophy lay hidden, it was treated by very few, but coldly, for I will not say insincerely. Most truly also another Cornelius (namely Agrippa) spoke of those Roman Pharisees, 1. de van. scient c. 97. p. 485. Instead of the Gospels, instead of the word of GOD, they rattle off mere trifles and human words.

*( Not as the Scribes. The Vulgate adds: and the Pharisees. The Syriac likewise adds i. e. and the Pharisees, and also attaches the suffix of them to the preceding noun. The Altdorf MS. Code also agrees with the printed Codes and the Parisian MS. Furthermore, the Greek Codes (agreeing with both the printed Codes and very many MSS. which learned men have compared, the Code, MS. Eclog. Graec. Biblioth. Norib.) constantly omit those words, except that in one or another MS. Code, which the Marquis Velesius Petrus Fraxardus the Spaniard used, it is added ἀυτῶν καὶ φαρισαῖοι. The Persian interpreter likewise adds the name of the Pharisees, but omits the pronoun. On the contrary, the Arab and the Ethiopian omit & the Pharisees, but add the pronoun, for the former reads here and the latter indeed that is, as their Scribes. We are speaking, however, of the Arabic version, which Erpenius previously brought to light, and most recently Mr. Walton in the London Polyglot Bibles : for in the Roman edition, which came forth in the previous century from the Medicean press it is read thus: i. e. As the Scribes & Pharisees.

Latin:

*(v. 29. Docens tanquam habensἐξουσίαι &c. Conf. Ioh. 6, 63. Iustinus Martyr Apol. 2. pro Christ. p. 47. de Christo: Βραφεῖς i. e. Breves & compendiosieius suerunt sermones. non enim Sophista & cavillator exstit: sed virtus DEI verbum eius erat. Huc etiam faciunt dicta Psal. 45, 3.8.Esa. 50, 4.c. 61, 1. Atque hic erat ille pridem expectatus magnus verusque propheta 1. Maccab. 14, 41. Luc. 7, 16.προήτηςLuc. 24, 19. add. Luc 4, 36.Matth. 5. pe-totum. Vanus autem Bell. est, quando t. 4. lib. 4. de Iustif. c. 2. §. Tertio, ex h. l. probare conatur, contineri in Evangelio, strictè ita dicto, leges propriè sic dictas. Id enim per τὸ ἐζουσίανhîc indicari, ait, quòd Christus docuerit sicut legislator, qui ex autoritate leges interpretatur, vel mutat, vel addit, non sicut legis peritus, qui solùm ex scientiâ legem explicat. Similia habet Barra dius t. 2. Concord. Evang. l. 5. pag. 297. Sequuntur hac in parte Concilium Tridentinum, quod sess. 6. ca. 21. tale decretum promulgavit: Si quis dixerit, Christum à Deo hominibus datum esse, ut redemtorem, cui sidant, non etiam ut legislatorem, cui obediant, anathema sit. Resp. 1. Concedimus, Filium Dei dici posse ac esse verum imò summum legislatorem, ut qui unà cum Patre & Sp. S. non solùm legem divinam cordibus protoplastorum insculpsit, etiam solenniter eandem in monte Sinai promulgavit, ac per Mosen populo Israelitico tradi fecit. 2. nec hoc negamus, quòd Christus in diebus carnis, praedicationis ministerio fungens s. in officio prophetico, legem & Evangelium coniunxerit, verumque legis sensum docuerit: At de hoc non est quaestio, sed de eo nos inter ac Pontificios cōtrovertitur; An Christus in officio suo Mediatorio sit novus legislator, & per consequens, an Evangelium, propriè, strictè & specificè sic dictum, sit doctrina operum? Ad quam quaestionem nos negativè respondemus; Pontificii verò, ceu inter alia ex decreto illo Tridentio apparet, affirmativè. Probatur verò nostra sententia tum ex oppositione Ioh. 1, 17. tum ex legis Mosaicae perfectione, tum ex legislatoris descriptioné, Rom. 7, 7. 8.11. tum deniq; ex adventus Christi fine, Gal. 3, 13.c. 4. 5. ceu prolixè ostendit B. Par.

Conf. Cath. t. 4. p. 783. Voce autem ἐξουσίας, quam potissimùm hîc urget Bellarminus, impraesentiarum non hoc indicatur, quòd Christus novas leges promulgaverit, sive legem Mosaicam auxerit: sed quòd solidam doctrinam proposuerit, summa dicendi maiestate & perspicuitate, magna verborum simplicitate & gravitate, tanta denique ad movendum autoritate & spiritûs efficacitate, ut non dicere tantùm aut fidem concilare, sed imprimere dicta in hominum pectoribus videretur efficientissimè, aliis amorem, aliis terrorem incutiens. Docebat enim intrepidè, non loque batur ad gratiam, neulli adulabatur, sed constanter vitia reprehendebat abspersonarum acceptione. Commendabat praeterea doctrinam singularis vitae integritas, doctrinae consentanea, Postremò quod docebat, stupendis signis & miraculis confirmabat; uti rectè exponit Franciscus Lucas Comm. in h. l. Qui etiam benè monet, dissimilitudinem inter Christum & Scribas in eo fuisse, quòd Christus eo modo docuerit, ceu iam dictum, Scribarum vero doctrina fuerit torpida, elumbis, frigida, diluta, fucata-. Cum ipsi illi de rebus minutissimis ac plerumq; supervacaneis, (Vid. infrà c. 23, 23. Marc. 7, 3. 4.) de quaestionibus scrupulosis & stultis & genealogiis atargumentis inextricabilibus, inutilibus, fabulosis & vanis, quae quaestiones magis praestarent, quàm aedificationem ( 1. Tim. 1, 4.Tit. 1, 14.c. 3, 9.) Dènineglecto interno eopraecipuo DEI cultu, de solo externo (vid. suprà v. 5. & 6.) idque admodum ieiunè & frigidè disserere solerent. Cùm hâc doctrinae Scribarum ac Pharisaeorum descriptione si quis contulerit iustas querelas, quibus doctrinae coelestis, ante B. Lutheri susceptam reformationem, in Romanâ Ecclesiâ, corruptionem gravissimi viri satis clarè indicarunt (cuiusmodi magno numero legendas exhibet B. Par. lib. 1. generali Confess. Cathol. part. 1. c. 4.) nae summam inter. Synagogam Iudaicam (qualis tempore Christi comparata erat) & Ecclesiam Romanam, uti quidem tempore Lutheri & paullò antè conspicienda erat, deprehendet convenientiam; ut adeò, sicuti Ecclesia Israelitica reformatione serverâ tam maximè opus habebat, ita & Romano Papistica pariter & vehementer indiguerit reformatore Qùem Deus etiam excitavit, dum B. Lutherum ac Symmystas itidem singulari ἐξουσίᾳ ac spiritu prorsus heroico instruxit, ut stupendum illud reformationis opus aggrederentur. Coeterùm non possum, quin quae Cornelius Mussus Placentinus, Episcopus Bitunitinus, Vir, Iesuitae Possevini in Appar. p. 389 iudicio, incomparabili penè ingenii felicitate, continentiâ ac praetate praeditus, in Cap. 6. ep. ad Rom. 279. de istis temporibus graviter non minùs quàm verè dixit, prorsusque Placentiam praetervectus rectà Veronam tendens scripta reliquit, huc adiiciam. Ita verò illo: Divinae Scripturae olim (loquitur verò de temporibus quae priximè B. Lutheri reformationem praecesserunt) proh dolor! quanto omnium damno negligebantur! vigebat spinosa & molesta, nescio quae, Theologia, de instantibus, relationibus, de quidditatibus, de formalitatibus. Itemq; haec omnia syllogismis arte contortis & humanis duntaxat argutiis, quae procul dubio, quâ autoritate recipiuntur, eâ & refelli possunt, pertractabantur. Tota penè aetas hominum decretis, quae inter se pugnantia semper, nullo tempore concilianda, alunt perpetuam per secula litem, conterebatur. Is sublimis Theologus habebatur, qui maiora portenta pro suis tradit iunculis assingere sciret, pretiiq; pars erat gloriola inanis, non intelligi grandia illa verba, quae alto supercilio inter muliercu--s de sacris litteris philosophantes trutinabant. Iuraverant universi divini verbi duces in Magistrorum verba; hinc sexcentae sectae; Thomistae, Scotistae, Occamistae. Bacconistae, Albertistae, Aegidiant, Alexandrei. O scelus! posthabebantur Evangelia, Epistolae; Christiana philosophia delitescebat, à paucissimis tractabatur, sed frigidè, non enim dicam insincerè. Verissimè quoque de Pharisaeis illis Romanis Cornelius alter (nempe Agrippa) 1. de van. scient c. 97. p. 485. Pro Evangeliis, pro verbo DEI meras nugas & humana verba crepant.)*

*( Nonsicuti Scribae. Vulgatus addit: eorum & Pharisaei. Syrus pariter addit i. e. & Pharisaei, ac praecedenti etiam nomini annectit suffixum illorum. Consentiente quoque MS. Cod. Altdorffino cum Codd. excusis ac MS. Parisiensi. Coeterùm Codd. Graeci (consentiente cum Codd. tam excusis, quàm plurimis MSS. quos Viri docti contulerunt, Codice, MS. Eclog. Graec. Biblioth. Norib.) constanter illa verba omittunt, nisi quòd in uno vel altero Codice MSS., quibus usus fuit Marchio Velesius Petrus Fraxardus Hispanus, additur ἀυτῶν καὶ φαρισαῖοι. Interpres Persa itidem addit nomen Pharisaeorum, sed omittit pronomen. Contrà Arabs & Aethiops omittunt & Pharisaei, sed addunt pronomen, ita enim hic legit ille verò h. e. sicut Scribae eorum Loquimur verò de versione Arabicâ, quam luci deditantehac Erpenius ac novis simè D. Walthonius in Bibliis Polyglottis Lo-dinensibus: in editione enim Romana, quae superiori seculo è typographia Medicea prodiit-ita legitur: i. e. Sicut Scribae & Pharisaei.)*

## 8:1
v. 1. When he had come down from the mountain. That mountain was Tabor, on which Christ often prayed and taught. Great multitudes followed him etc. Syr. Many crowds surrounded him.

Latin:

v. 1. Cùm descendisset de monte. Mons ille fuit Thabor, in quo Christus saepiùs oravit & docuit. Sequuta est eum &c. Syr. Cinxerunt eum turbae multae.

## 8:2
v. 2. Molinaeus thinks, because of the diversity of circumstances which the Evangelists Matt. ch. 8. Mark ch. 1. v. 40. and Luke ch. 5. v. 12. note, that not one leper is noted by them, as Flacius reports in his annotations on this place, but because Mark and Luke recorded the healing of their leper in almost the same words as Matthew, and since the latter expresses the order, occasion, and place, therefore the account of Mark and Luke must be conformed to the history of Matthew. Salm. vol. 6. tract. 21. Chemn. in Harm. *(But how the conformation ought to be made will be shown in the notes to Luke 5, 12.)* Λέπραἐπὸ του λέπειν which is to peel, λέπος and λεπὶς bark, λεπυρὸς peeled and by syncope, with τῷ υλεπρὸς. elided, Avicenna calls that disease exfoliating impetigo. In Hebrew it is said to be from penetrating, in Syriac from devastating. They also call this disease satyriasis, on account of the redness of the cheeks and an insatiable and shameless lust for coitus. Q. whether this leper was present at the sermon held on the mountain? He stood at some distance and heard Christ's sermon, from which he conceived faith in Christ.

*(Hugo Grotius indeed doubts in his Annotations on this place whether this vitiligo-sufferer believed that this Jesus was the promised Messiah, since Jesus himself had not yet openly professed it, nor had that rumor spread among the common people. But the Blessed D. Chemnitius in H. E. ch. 52. rightly notes that this leper, whom he sees with bodily eyes to be a man, recognized him with the eyes of faith to be God, because he heard him preaching with power. He adds the reason:) For unless he had held him to be the true God, he would never have listened to him, nor would he have appealed to him2. Reg. 5, 7.concerning the driving away of leprosy, a disease otherwise incurable. And since the leper asks this of Christ, he does so entirely with that exterior veneration which is shown through the inclination and prostration of the body, but at the same time with that interior λατρείᾳ, which is owed to one and only God. Conf. Deut. 4, 19.Psal. 99, 51. The same praised Theologian also rightly gathers from this place that in Christ not only the divine nature, but τὸ συναμφότερον is to be adored, and he teaches this also from the Fathers. But as for the reason for doubting which Grotius brings forward, it is denied, both because it had not yet been manifested by Christ that he himself is the Messiah, see at least the preceding chapter v. 21. following. And because, if the rumor about Christ's deity had not yet spread among the common people, the leper could not have believed that Jesus was the promised Messiah. For however much the leper may not have been taught about Christ's true deity from the rumor of the common people, he could nevertheless be taught about it, just as he was in fact taught, from the stupendous teaching of Christ (for he himself had been present at that most divine sermon held by Christ up to that point) and from the miracles which he himself was performing by an entirely divine power, and indeed in confirmation that he himself is the Messiah,Ioh. 4, 48.53. c. 20, 31. with Grotius himself admitting this at Luc. 7, 14. and that this δύναμιν is the mark τῆς ἐξουσίας, about which at the end of the preceding Chapter, Grotius himself also teaches at v. 29. of the said chapter. There is added what the same man immediately subjoins here, to the words of the leper: ἐὰν θέληςδύννασ αἰ με etc. that the persuasion concerning the power of GOD is accustomed to be the beginning of piety, and that it testifies to them what he believes Christ can do. Now, if he knows Christ to be endowed with divine power, so that he can use it at will, if only he wishes, it is certainly necessary that he recognized the same as the true God.)*

CHAPTER VIII.

*( He worshipped him. From the fact that Christ allowed himself to be worshipped here by the leper, and elsewhere by the Magi, Matth. 1. and also by the Centurion, below v. 6. the Jesuit Costerus in Enchir. p. 160 very ridiculously tries to prove that the Roman Church does not institute a life contrary to Christ, which is what our people object to the Romanists, and indeed for the reason that Christ (understand worldly, for the question between us and the Papists is about these, as Costerus himself acknowledges in the objection, not about divine ones, for these Christ not only admitted, but also taught, that the Father has given judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father,John 5:23) he may have fled, but the Roman Pontiff admits and seeks it. Costerus objects: the honor of adoration has never been offered to any Roman Pontiff, nor does the Roman Pontiff claim it for himself: but he refers it to Christ, whose place he holds on earth. And yet, if for that reason the Roman Pontiff admits worldly honors, because he holds the place of Christ on earth, and because he refers it to Christ, it will not be foreign to him also to admit the honor of adoration, which is absurd, nay, impious. But where did Christ command that the ministers of the divine word should receive worldly honors, and seek them with such ambition, as the Roman Pontiff does? Nay, he rather commanded the contrary. See Matt. 11:29Phil. 2:3 seqq. To say nothing now of the luxury and pride of the Roman Pontiff, of which Christ certainly provided no example at all. Whether the Roman Pontiff permits divine honors to be shown to him, nay, sometimes even commands them, such is his intolerable pride, let the judgment be with others. Let the kind reader only unroll the Epitome of the Catholic Confession, book 2, special part 1, p. 581 and following, and hear the Papal witnesses themselves, who are produced there in great number regarding this matter. But on this matter elsewhere.)

* ( If you wish. That God does not always hear in matters pertaining to this life according to our will, but according to our utility, the heathens also knew from the light of nature, proves the blessed D. Quistorp in this place from Juvenal, Satire 10. Compare the blessed Pareus, Practical Theological Aphorisms, title Prayer. See above p. 424 and below in the notes to 1 John 5:14. Let us learn, however, to submit our will to the divine, of which thing we have a notable example in the Savior himself Mark 14:36. Whence Chrysostom, homily 84 on Matthew, well warns, καὶ τῆς φύσεως αὺθελκούσης ἕπεσθαι τῷ θεῷ. This is the mortification of carnal desires, this is the denial of oneself, Matt. 16:24, this is that most pleasing sacrifice to GOD, through which we offer to Him not external victims, but our own will. To this also pertains that of Cyprian, treatise on Mortality: We ought to remember that we must do not our own will, but the will of GOD, according to what the Lord has commanded us to pray daily. ( Matt. 6:10) Compare 1 Sam. 3:18Acts 21:14 1 Maccabees 3:60.)*

* ( And with hand extended. Because Christ in, with, and through the flesh worked divine miracles, and indeed mθαυατουργία is a work truly divine. Thence the orthodox rightly conclude that omnipotence, or truly divine power, was communicated to the human nature of Christ, personally indeed, not essentially, yet really. Compare more on this matter in the notes to Ioh. 6, 51.

*( I will, be thou cleansed. From the fact that Christ by free will when and where He willed, and also for His own honor, performed miracles (such as the healing of the leper here, accomplished by a mere command. Conf. 2 Kings 5, 7.), as is evident from this place and also from John 2, 11. c. 5, 21, our people rightly prove the true Deity of Christ against the Photinians among other things. Conf. Ps. 72, 18.Ps. 136, 4.Acts 3, 12. And the bishops of the primitive Church did this also long ago. Beautifully Ambrose, book 5 on Luke, p. 59, vol. 5: He says 'I will' on account of Photinus (others write Photinum), He commands on account of Arius, He touches on account of Manichaeus. The Photinians object that God performed miracles through Christ. Acts 2, 22. Resp. 1. The name GOD is taken, as shown in d. 1, either essentially or personally. If in the former way, the consequence is denied. And it is so far from being the case that from the fact that the divine nature performed miracles through the assumed human nature it can be gathered that Christ is not God, that rather the true Deity of Christ is most firmly established therefrom; but if in the latter way, it is granted that Christ is not God, namely God the Father. For He is a distinct person from the person of the Father. 2. It is to be noted that τὸ through does not always denote an instrumental cause, as has been shown elsewhere, but often also a principal cause.)*

( Purgatory. Coster in Enchiridion of Controversies, p. 258. As, he writes, the leper was cleansed at this word of Christ, 'be cleansed' Matt. 8:3, so the word of Christ in the Sacrament effectively takes away sins, infuses justice and grace, and renders the sinner just and a son of God, not because it is heard or understood, but because it is pronounced by Christ through the ministry of the Priest. With the controversy now set aside concerning the infusion of justice, and likewise that sins are taken away through the Sacraments so that they do not exist at all, which the Papists desire (concerning which errors Theologians may be consulted throughout), we think it must be warned at least that the Jesuit wrongly opposes things which are nevertheless subordinate, and therefore falsely persuades himself that from the fact that Christ remits sins to us through the Sacraments, as means divinely ordained, it can be proven that it is done through the work worked, that is, without the faith of the user. For just as here the faith of the leper is not excluded, but rather presupposed, for he believed that Christ could heal him: so the divine operation through the Sacraments by no means takes away or excludes faith, but rather presupposes it. And indeed Bellarmine himself, in book 1 on Justification, chapter 8, section 'but let us add', concedes, That in this leper there was faith in omnipotence and Divinity. But he incorrectly asserts that certainty concerning special mercy was lacking in him. This is what the Cardinal strives to prove from the fact that unless the leper had doubted concerning special mercy, he would not have said: if you will, you can. Resp. 1. by denying that faith in omnipotence alone suffices for obtaining the desired good. For in this way even hypocrites, indeed the very Devils themselves, would be graciously heard, as they do not doubt concerning the omnipotence of God, otherwise they would not tremble, James 2, 19. 2. observe that the little words if you will are by no means words of one doubting concerning the special mercy of Christ: but rather of a man truly believing, and therefore, regarding the petition for a bodily benefit, humbly submitting himself to the will of Christ. Examples of this kind occur elsewhere in Holy Scripture, see 2 Sam. 15, 25. 26. Dan. 3, 17. 18. 1 Macc. 3, last. And Franc. Lucas also observed this, while he writes thus on this passage: A brief prayer, an index of great faith and remarkable modesty. For he did not say if you will because he doubted the kindness of the Lord; but because he submitted the matter to His will, acknowledging himself worthy of the plague which he was bearing. 3. distinguish between bodily benefits, and those same special ones, and between spiritual benefits. Just as we can ask for these without any condition, so our faith does not doubt at all that God wills to bestow them upon us. But as far as bodily benefits are concerned, they can and ought to be asked for with a condition. Nor does anything depart from the certainty concerning the special mercy of Christ through this, both because it does not regard bodily, but spiritual benefits, of which kind are the remission of sins, the grace of GOD, and eternal life; and because that is finally true confidence which is conformable to the word of GOD. This, however, teaches that God gives many things, if not according to our will, yet according to our utility. And if the restriction of our petition to the divine will were to take away certainty, it would follow that not even Christ would have been certain concerning the benevolent affection of His Father, since He prayed similarly: Father, if you will, remove this cup from me, Luke 22, 42. But to say that is absurd. Therefore. What the Jesuit Conzen. writes on this passage: They are ridiculous, he says, who construct confidence from this. We whisper the same to Cardinal Bellarmine and other Papists with greater right, when they attempt to elicit doubt concerning the gracious remission of sins from this passage. Conzenius himself, however, seems to approve there the explanation of Melanchthon, who among other things: Just as a boy who asks something from a dear Father, DOES NOT DOUBT that he is going to obtain it, and yet leaves everything to the judgment of the Father, if what he asks is fitting.)*

*(Subdubitat quidem Hugo Grotius Annot. in h. l. an vitilitiginosus hic crediderit, Iesum hunc esse promissum Messiam, cùm ipse Iesus nondum palam esset professus, neq; is rumor in vulgus manasset. Quod vero concernit rationem dubitandi, quam Grotius affert, negatur, tum quòd nondum à Christo fuerit manifestatum, quòd, ipse sit Messias, vid. saltem cap. praeced. v. 21. seqq. *( Adoravit eum. Ex eo quòd Christus adorari se passus hîc fuit à leproso, & alibi à Magis, Matth. 1. nec non à Centurione, infrà v. 6. ridiculè admodùm Iesuita Costerus in Enchir. p. 160. conatur probare, quòd P. R. non contrariam Christo vitam instituat, id quod nostrates Romanensibus obiiciunt, & quidem ideo quòd Christus honores (intellige mundanos, nam de his quaestio nos inter & Pontificios est, ceu ipse Costerus in obiectione agnoscit, non de divinis, hos enim Christus non solùm admisit, sed etiam docuit, propterea Patrem Filio dedisse iudicium, ut omnes honorent Filium sicut Patrem honorant,Ioh. 5, 23.) fugerit, Pontifex vero Romanus admittat & quaerat. R. mundanos honores admittit, quia Christi in terris vices gerit, & quia in Christum refert, non alienum quoque ab eo erit, adorationis honorem admittere, quod absurdum, imò impium. Ubi vero Christus mandavit, ut verbi divini ministri honores mundanos suscipiant, tantoque ambitu, ceu P. R. quaerant? Imò potiùs contrarium mandavit. Vid. Matth. 11, 29.Phil. 23. seqq Ut taceam iam luxum & fastum P. R. cuius sanè profectò exemplum minimè Christus praebuit. Annon vero P. R. honores sibi divinos exhiberi, permittat, imò aliquando etiam, qui intolerabilis eius fastus est, iubeat, penes alios esto iudicium. Evolvat modò B. L. Epitomes Confess. Cathol. lib. 2. spec. part. 1. p. 581. & seqq. audiatque ipsos testes Pontificios, qui ibi magno numero in rem hanc producuntur. Ast hac de re alibi.)*

* ( Si velis. Quòd Deus in rebus ad hanc vitam pertinentibus non semper ad voluntatem, sed ad utilitatem exaudiat, etiam ex lumine naturae cognovisse Ethnicos, probat B. D. Quistorp. in h. l. ex Iuvenali Satyr. 10. Conf. B. Par. Aphor. Theol. Pract. tit. Oratio. it suprà p. 424. & infrà in notis ad 1. Ioh. 5, 14. Reg. 5, 7.) fecit, ceu ex h. l. itemque ex Ioh. 2, 11. c. 5, 21. patet, rectè nostrates contra Photinianos inter alia veram Christi Deitatem probant. Conf. Ps. 72, 18.Ps. 136, 4.Act. 3, 12. Volo dicit propter Fotinum (alii Photinum,) imperat propter Arium, tangit propter Manichaeum. Excipiunt Photiniani, quòd Deus per Christum miracula fecerit.Act. 2, 22. Resp. 1. Est enim distincta persona à persona Patris. 2. Notandum, quòd τὸper non notet semper causam instrumentalem, ut alibi ostensum, sed saepè etiam causam principalem.)*

*( Purgator. Cost. in Enchir. Controv. p. 258. Sicut, scribit. mundatus est leprosus ad hoc Christi verbum, mundare ( Matth. 8, 3.) it a verbum Christi in Sacramēto efficaciter peccata tollit, infundit iustitiam & gratiam, atq; ex peccatore reddit iustum & filium Dei, non quia auditur vel intelligitur, sed quia à Christo per Sacerdotis ministerium pronunciatur. Missâ iam nunc controversiâ de iustitiae infusione, itemque quòd peccata per Sta tollantur, ita ut prorsus non sint, quòd Pontificii volunt (de quibus erroribus videri possunt Theologi passim) hoc saltem monendum ducimus, quòd Iesuita malè opponat, quae tamen sunt subordinata, adeoque ex eo, quòd Christus per Sacramenta, tanquam media divinitus ordinata, peccata nobis remittit, evinci posse, falsò sibi persuadeat, fieri illud per opus operatum h. e. absque fide utentis. Etenim quemadmodum hîc fides leprosi non excluditur, sed potiùs praesupponitur, credidit enim, quòd Christus ipsum sanare possit: ita operatio divina per Sacramenta fidem minimè tollit, vel excludit, sed potiùs praesupponit. Et sanè Bell. ipse lib. 1. de Iustif. c. 8. §. sed addamus, concedit, in leproso hoc fuisse fidem omnipotentiae & Divinitatis. Perperam verò adfferit, defuisse eidem certitudinem de misericordiâ speciali. id quod exinde probare Cardinalis satagit, quia leprosus nisi de misericordiâ speciali dubit asset, non dixisset: si vis potes. Resp. 1. negando, quòd solius omnipotentiae fides sufficiat ad bonum desidenatum impetrandum. h. m. enim & hypocritae, imò ipsi Diaboli gratiosè exaudirentur, ut qui de De omnipotentià nō dubitant, alioquin enim nō contremiscerent, Iac. 2, 19. 2. obs. quòd voculae si vis minimè sint verba de speciali Christi misericordia dubitantis: sed hominis potiùs verè credentis, adeoq; quoad corporalis beneficii petitionē voluntati Christi humiliter sese submittentis. Cuius modi exempla & alibi in Sc. S. occurrunt vid. 2. Sam. 15, 25. 26.Dan. 3, 17. 18.1. Macch. 3, ult. Atque hoc etiam Franc. Lucas observavit, dum ita in h. l. Brevis oratio magnae fidei insignisq; modestiae index. Non enim, quòd de benignit ate Domini dubit aret, dixit si vis; sed quòd eius voluntati negotium submitteret, se dignum agnoscens plagâ, quam serebat. 3. dist. inter beneficia corporalia, eademque specialia, & inter beneficia spiritualia. Haec uti absq; omni conditione petere possumus, ita fides nostra planè non dubitat, quin Deus illa nobis velit largiri. Quod verò corporalia beneficia concernit, ea cum conditione peti possunt ac debent. Nec per hoc quicquam certitudini de speciali Christi misericord â decedit, tum quia illa non corporalia, sed spiritualia beneficia, cuiusmodi sunt peccatorum remissio, gratia DEI ac vita aeterna, respicit; tum quia illa demum vera fiducia est, quae conformis est verbo DEI. Hoc verò docet, quòd Deus multa det, si non ad nostram voluntatem, tamen ad utilitatem. Et si restrictio nostrae petitionis ad divinam voluntatem, tolleret certitudinem, sequeretur, quôd nec Christus de Patris sui affectu benevolo fuisset certus, quippe similiter orans: Pater si vis, transfer poculum hoc à me,Luc. 22, 42. At illud dicere, absonum est. E. Quod igitur Iesuita Conzen. in h. l. scribit: Ridiculi, inquiens, sunt, qui hinc fiduciam fabricantur. Idem nos Card. Bellarmino alliqui Pontificiis maioni iure insusurramus, quando dubitationem de gratiosâ peccatorum remissione elicere ex h. l. conantur. Ipse verò Conzenius approbare ibid. Melanchthonis explicationem, videtur, qui inter alia: Perinde ac puer qui à Patre charo aliquid petit, NON DUBITAT, quin sit impetraturus, & tamen omnia Patris relinquit iudicio, si convenit, quod petit.)*

## 8:4
v. 4. That Christ forbids the divulging of the miracle, some explain this from the added antithesis, that it is to be accepted not simply, but in a certain respect, namely, that he should not divulge it before he showed himself to the Priest: for there was a danger, lest if the Priest had received by report that this man was cleansed by Jesus, he might pronounce a false judgment concerning his cleansing out of hatred for Jesus. *(This opinion pleases Gotius on this passage, and also the Bishop, q. XI.)* But because Christ also elsewhere forbids the divulging of miracles, Matth. 9. v. 30.cap. 12. v. 16, therefore three causes of this prohibition can be given. 1. He did not want men to stick to miracles, but that they should primarily regard the doctrine. 2. He wished to show by the very fact that he did not seek his own glory. Iohan. 8. v. 50. and to stifle the vice of άλαζονίας in us. 3. He was still in the state of emptying, nor had the time yet arrived in which miracles ought to be divulged. Tosf. Hilary says, that Christ by that prohibition wished to take care that other lepers and infirm might not come to him, not as if he did not wish to impart health to them also, but because he desired their conversion more than the healing of their bodies. Q. Therefore. Why did Christ forbid miracles to be divulged? Resp. 1. That he might teach that he was a stranger to the breeze of human glory and the pomp of boasting, and by his own example make us contemners of glory and boasting, as Chrysostom teaches hom. 26. in Matth. 2. lest miracles and doctrine be wrongly torn apart. For he knew that those whom he had cured had not made such progress in the doctrine of the Gospel, nor had been so learned, that they could have joined the doctrine with the publication of the miracles, wherefore he did not wish to entrust the preaching of either to them. 3. Since he knew best, what was in man,Ioh. 2. v. 25.

he did not want to have them as heralds of his works, through whom the course of the Gospel would have been hindered rather than promoted. 4. Since for every thing there is its own time Eccl. 3. v. 1. He who disposes all things by measure, number, and order Wisd. 11, 21. willed to defer the proclamation of his miracles until the appointed time; when this arrived, he set it forth to us through his Apostles as designated witnesses Acts 10, 41.. Some (as Tostatus q. 17.) think that Christ feigned, and willed the opposite, namely, the divulging of the miracle. But the words stand in the way. 1. Of Matthew: ὅρα. 2. Of Luke, who has the word ραγγέλματος,, the use of which in describing the edicts of Magistrates Acts 5, v. 28. 3. Of Mark, who uses the word ἐμβριμοῦσθαι. *(See more on this matter in the notes to Mark 7, 36. and also in Mr. Dr. Walther in Harm. Bibl. p 758. 759. as well as Sim. Episcop. in Resp. ad LXIV. Q9. Q. XI.)*

*(Tell no one. Beautifully Ambrose vol. 5. book 5. on Luke p 59. Lest leprosy be able to pass to the physician, let each one avoid boasting by the example of the Lord's humility. For why is it commanded to tell no one, unless to teach that our benefits are not to be made public, but to be suppressed, so that we may abstain not only from the reward of money, but also of praise? Perhaps also that is the reason why silence was commanded, because he thought those better who had believed by a more spontaneous faith than those who had hoped for benefits.)*

*( Show yourself to the Priest. Thus, in the singular indeed, the Greek Codices consistently have it. The Arab also and the Ethiopian, as well as the Latin Vulgate: the Syrian however (with the remaining Codices, both MSS. and the most ancient printed Codices of the Altdorf Academy, agreeing) has in the plural number led perhaps because the plural follows, as a testimony to them. The Persian follows the Syrian according to his custom. Furthermore, the Papists thus generally infer the necessity of auricular confession from this passage. If it was the office of the Priests in the O.T. to judge concerning leprosy. But sins are spiritual leprosy, it follows that the Priests of the N.T. ought to judge concerning sins. Now, however, they cannot judge except concerning things known. Therefore, if they ought to judge concerning sins and absolve a man from them, it is necessary that a special enumeration of sins precede. See Cornel. à Lapide on this passage. Bell. book 3 on penance ch. 2. Costerus Enchir. Controv. page 484. Stapletonus in promt. Cath. Sun. 3. after Epiph. Tirinus Ind controv. s-day controv. XXIII. n. 7. and others. Resp. 1. I deny the consequence. We grant indeed that there is some similarity between leprosy and sins (just as our own people also show in various places. See B. D. Glassius Exeg. Sun. 14. Trin. B. Par. Hom. Acad. part. 2. p. 640. 6 6. seqq. B. D. Botsaccus Promt. Alleg. p. 162. and p. 158. M. Binchius part. 2 Mellif. p. 284. but especially B. Mr. Chemn in Harm. Ev. on this passage) but it is denied that the reason is the same in respect to all things: for it would follow that just as houses and garments were also infected by leprosy, so the same are stained by sins, and must needs be cleansed from these by the Ministers of the Church, as those were among the Israelites: it would also follow that just as leprosy made only the body unclean, not the soul, so neither does sin [make] this [unclean]. Then, neither is the reason the same in all respects for the Priests of the O.T. and the Ministers of the Church of the N.T. for it would follow that just as the Priests in the O.T. were married, so also in the N.T. the Ministers of the Church could enter into matrimony, which however the Papists most fiercely deny. It would also follow that just as the Priests in the O.T. did not [lepers]* they made the worlds, but at least pronounced the worlds clean, so also in the N. T. let the Ministers of the Church at least pronounce sinners clean, but not truly make them such. This, however, the Papists deny. Hence Corn. à Lap. in h. l. Chrysostom l. 3. de Sacerd. teaches that the office of Christian Priests is far more effective and excellent than that of the Aaronic ones was of old, in that it was granted to these not to cure leprosy, but only to show it cured; but to those, not to show sins uncured, but truly to cure and forgive them. If therefore the more excellent reason of the Priests of the N. T. over the Priests of the O. T. is in this, that they can also forgive sins, why does it not also go, that a difference is conceded between these and those, that although it was necessary for those, the Priests of the O. T., to see the leper first, and thus to know the leprosy accurately before they pronounced concerning him: as regards these Priests of the N. T. no such thing is necessary, especially since neither did Christ ever require such an enumeration of sins before the remission of sins, see Matth. 9, 2.Luc. 7, 48.c. 15, 18.c. 19, 8. nor in the primitive Church, near to the Apostolic, was such a thing required. -. we deny that the Ministers of the Church of the N. T. are properly and specially Priests, nay rather all the Priesthoods of the O. T. are transferred to Christ alone and finished in him. item that if it pertains to them to judge concerning sins, it also pertains to the same to excarnificate the consciences of men by requiring the confession of all sins. 3. we urge that of Bell. l. 3. de V. D. c. 3. §. sed quanquam, that firm arguments must be sought from the literal sense alone. And also that statement of Ludovicus ab Alcasar from Dionysius, that symbolic (and typical) theology is not argumentative. Now indeed this collection proceeds at least from a type. Whence also the Jesuit Conzenius in this place inveighs heavily against Calvin and Bullinger, attributing to the Papists that they prove auricular confession from this place. We indeed, he writes, by no means prove auricular confession from that judgment; but many of the Catholics explain the use of confession by that comparison. And a little later: It is an explanation from a likeness, not a proof against the stubborn. The Jesuit Alphonsus à Castro has similar things also in book 4 against heresies under the word Confession. It suffices for us at present to have shown that the absolute necessity of auricular confession (that is, that all sins be revealed one by one to priests, according to the explanation of Bellarmine, book 3 on Penance, chapter 9, section 'Habemus') cannot be solidly proven from this place. Compare more on this matter in B. D. Helvicus, Vindication of the Holy Scriptures of the Old Testament, pages 150 and 151; B. P. Conf. Cath. volume 4, page 62.)

Augustine, book 2 of Gospel Questions, chapter 3. It was not fitting for the signifying sacrifices to be taken away before that which was signified had been confirmed by the testimony of the Apostles preaching and the peoples believing by faith. Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, Epistle 146. For that reason the leper was ordered to offer the gift prescribed by the law, so that the harmony of both Testaments might be demonstrated, and that he who now has driven away the disease is the same one who also imposed the law.

*( Concerning that Mosaic sanction, to which the Lord alludes here, see Lev. 14, 2.4.10. Since, however, a double gift had to be offered by the cleansed leper, first indeed two little birds with cedar, scarlet, and hyssop, then two lambs, or if he were poorer, one lamb with a pair of turtledoves or pigeons, with fine flour and oil added, some, among whom is also H. Grotius, think that the former gift is to be understood here, as that which was given on the very day of cleansing, Lev. 14, 17. Furthermore, the Lord sends lepers to the priest elsewhere also. See Luke 17, 14.)*

As a testimony to them, that is, so that they may be convinced. 1. That I am the true Son of GOD and the Messiah, performing such miracles. 2. That I am not an adversary of the Law. See more in Mark, chapter 1, verse 44. *(The same was also noted by the blessed D. Quistorpius from Jerome. And compare below, ch. 10, 8; ch. 24, 14.)*

v. 4. Quod Christus prohibet divulgare miraculum, id quidam ex addita antithesi sic exponunt, quòd accipiendum sit non simpliciter, sed secundum quid, ne sc. divulget antequam se ostēderet Sacerdoti: periculum enim erat, ne si, Sacerdos famâ accepisset, hunc esse à Iesu purgatum, falfum iudicium de ipsius purgatione ex odio Iesu pronunciaret. *(Arridet haec sententia G-otio in h. l. nec non Episcop. q. XI.)* Sed quia Christus etiam alibi prohibet miraculorum divūlgationem, Matth. 9. v. 30.cap. 12. v. 16, ideò tres causae huius prohibitionis dari possunt. 1. noluit, homines in miraculis haerere, sed doctrinam cumprimis respicere debere. 2. ostendere voluit ipso facto, se non quaerere suam gloriam. Iohan. 8. v. 50. ac vitium a άλαζονίας in nobis suffocare. 3. erat adhuc in statu exinanitionis nec dum advenerat tempus, quo miracula debebāt divulgari. Tosf. Hilarius dicit, Christū prohibitione illâ cavere voluisse, ne alii leprosi & infirmi adse venirent, non qs. nollet & illis sanit atem impert iri, sed quod magis conversionillorum exoptaret, quàm corporum sanationem. Q. igitur. Quart Christus miracula prohibuerit divulgare? Resp. 1. ut doceret, quòd esset alienus ab aurâ humanae gloriae ac pompâ iactantiae, suoque exemplo gloriae & iactantiae contemtores nos efficeret, ut Chrysost. docet hom. 26. in Matth. 2. ne miracula & doctrina, perperam divellerentur. Sciebatenim illos quos cura verat, rantos in doctrina Evangelii progressus non fecisse, nec ita eruditos fuisse, ut potuissent cum miraculorum publicatione doctrinam coniungere, quare neutrius praedicationem ipsis committere volebat. 3. cùm sciret optimè, quid esset in homine,Ioh. 2. v. 25.

noluit eos operum suorum habere praecones, per quos Evangelii cursus magis fuisset impeditus, quàm promotus. 4. cùm cuique reī suum sit tempus Eccl. 3. v. 1. voluit is, qui omnia mensurâ, numero & ordine disponit. Sapient. 11, 21. miraculorum suorum praedicationem in tempus destinatum differre; hoc ubi advenit, per Apostolos suos tanquam testes designatos Act. 10, 41. illa nobis exposuit. Quidam (uti Tostatus q. 17.) putant, Christum simulasse, & contrarium, divulgationem sc. marculi, voluisse. At obstant verba. 1. Matthaei: ὅρα. 2.
