Furthermore, that power θαυματουργικὴ, was given to Christ as man is taught at length against the Papists by B. Par. in the Catholic Confession, book 2, special part 1, art. 2, ch. 1, §. 3.)

Latin:

*(v. 16. Et multos malè habentes curavit. Corn. à Lapide in h. l. supplet ex Luc. 4, 40.manuum impositione. additque: Scilicet non dedignatus est Christus manibus suis purissimis & divinis tangere ulcerosos &c. ut contactus sui divini vim & efficaciam astenderet, illico omnes sanando. Idem etiam ad Matth. 28, 18. annotat, verba Christi: data est mihi omnis potestas, à Cyrillo, Nysseno, Athanasio, aliispropriè de hum. Christi natura intelligi, sed quà homo est. Eodem etiam modo d. l. explicat Iohan. Tirinus. Rectè omninò, contrà ac sociennus ipsius Greg. de Valentia, qui t. 4. Disp. 1. q. 13. punct. 1. p. 319. Dico, scribit, omnipotentiam (atqui absque hàc non potest divinus contactus Christo tribui) simpliciter necommunicatam esse, nec cōmunicari potuisse humanitati Christi, sic ut Christus etiam secundum hum. nat. sit omnipetens. Caeterùm quòd Christo homini data sit potestas θαυματουργικὴ, prolixè contra Pontificios docet B. Par. Confess. Cath. l. 2. spec. part. 1. art. 2. c. 1. §. 3.)*

## 8:17
v. 17. Matthew adapts the testimony of Isaiah to bodily healing, whereas in the Prophet it is used concerning the passion of Christ and the removal of the sins of men, and thus concerning spiritual healing, because 1. this healing had a type of that, which reason Chrysostom gives in homily 28. 2. Diseases are the effects and punishments of sins: therefore, by taking away diseases, Christ signified that he would take away our sins. 1 Peter 2, v. 24. Some add that the word חלון in Isaiah signifies not only diseases of the soul, but also diseases of the body.

(Indeed, it cannot be denied that Isaiah in his prophecy ch. 54, 4, which the Evangelist says is fulfilled here, deals primarily with healing from spiritual diseases, in which sense not only the most ancient interpreters of the Old Testament accept it (for the LXXII explicitly translate ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν φέρει.; Jonathan in the Targum: הוא יבע על חובנא i.e., he himself will pray for our sins. The Arab i.e., he himself bears our sins) but also the ὑπὸ θεοῦ φερόμευος Apostle Peter himself in 1 ep. 2, 24, alleges the prophetic passage in this way, concerning which one may also entirely see B. Par. in his Commentary on the Epistle of Peter. It must be known, therefore, as was also noted long ago by Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius, Hilary, and others among the ancients, Isaiah πρώτως to speak of the infirmities and diseases of the soul, that is, sins, and of their liberation through Christ: (A thing which can be demonstrated so clearly from the context that not even those sworn enemies of the satisfaction rendered by Christ, the Photinians, can deny it, as can be seen from Socinus in his explanation of the Loc. Sc. S. 73, Crellius against Hugo Grotius page 96, Osterod in his Institutions page 216.) Δευτέρως nevertheless, also to treat of the punishments of sins, and those not only eternal, but also temporal. For Christ has merited for us that we might be freed from every evil which follows upon sins: writes the Jesuit Tirinus on this passage. Entirely correctly. For his own followers err, asserting, both that Christ satisfied only for original, but not for actual sins, and also that Christ did not satisfy for all punishments of sins, both temporal and eternal, and consequently that after the remission of the guilt, the liability of temporal punishment often remains. These errors are refuted at length by the Blessed Father in the Confess. Cathol. book 2, Spec. part 3, art. 10, ch. 5, § 1 and 2, and in the LL. Theol. art. on Penance. But that fictitious purgatorial fire, which the Blessed Doctor Meisner extinguished in his learned work opposed to the Indulgences of the Roman Pope, was raised up from these hypotheses. Furthermore, the Blessed Doctor Chemnitius rightly warns that the passage of Isaiah is said to be fulfilled in Matthew ἀνναγωγικῶς. For because Christ was beginning to perform many miracles here, it could easily have happened that the common people might have thought that Christ was only some excellent surgeon: but to guard against this, Matthew wished to elevate the minds of men through ἀναγωγὴν and for them to hope for something higher concerning Christ, namely that such miracles were done for this reason, that that which Isaiah had predicted might be fulfilled, namely that the Messiah would be one who would bear the diseases of the soul, and would free men from them. And the Blessed Doctor deduces and confirms this opinion at greater length in his Vind. Sacr. Loc. XXCIII. The same explanation also smiles upon the Blessed Doctor Quistorpius on this passage. Simon Episcopius the Arminian also inclines toward the same in book 3 of his Instit. Theol. sect. 4, ch. 26, p. 109 and 191, and Rivetus in vol. 2 of his Works in his Explanation of ch. 53 of Isaiah, p. 822, where he also expressly refutes Socinus, who ineptly concludes that just as the prophecy of Isaiah was fulfilled while Christ took away the diseases of all the sick; so also he is to be said to have done the same when he took away all sins from us, especially their punishments, insofar as he showed the way of escaping the divine wrath, that is, the punishment established for sins and confirmed it, and also forgave sins to whomever he wished. Namely, lest he be forced to concede that Christ, by suffering and dying, satisfied for our sins. The same Socinus and his followers were also excellently refuted by the Lord Doctor Weller in his Explanation of ch. 53 of Isaiah, published in Wittenberg in the year 1634. The Blessed Doctor Grawerus in his Polem. Sacr. p. 710 and following. Let Constantijn l'Empereur van Oppyck be compared, Annotations to ὁδοιπορ. Moses Kimchi p. 185, where he rightly observes that Is. 53, 4. is the word םבל, which is always to carry, to bear, to take upon oneself, but never simply at least to remove. (Lord Dr. Weller proved this by the induction of many examples in the said place.) Pineda also adds this in c. 7. Job v. 21. n. 2. But Constantine himself thinks that Matthew means this: that Jesus Christ, by healing, removing, and carrying away bodily diseases, declared and made manifest that He had taken upon Himself the guilt of our spiritual diseases, which is the cause of them, and had borne the pains that were due: for Matthew uses to fulfill for to manifest, just as Paul also does Col. 1, 25.) just as a comparison teaches that the antecedent is understood from the consequent, and vice versa Ps. 68, 19. with Eph. 4, 8. But how did Christ bear our bodily diseases? Answer: not that He took them upon Himself, but because by satisfying for our sins He freed us from all the punishments of sins. See Blessed Dr. Glass, Rhet. S. p. 582. Some add that He also bore them through compassion. Just as the Apostle also says: Bear one another's burdens, Gal. 6.)*

Latin:

v. 17. Matthaeus Esaiae testimonium accommodat ad sanationem corporalem, cùm apud Prophetam de Christi passione, & sublatis hominum peccatis, adeoque de spirituali sanatione usurpetur, quia 1. haec sanatio illius typum habebat, quam rationem reddit Chrysost. hom. 28. 2. Morbi sunt effectus & poenae peccatorum: Christus igitur tollendo morbos, significavit, se peccata nostra sublaturum. 1. Petri. 2. v. 24. Quidam addunt quod vox חלון apud Esaiam non tantùm morbos animi, sed etiam corporis morbos significet.

*(Sanè negari non potest, quòd Esaias in prophetiâ suâ c. 54, 4. quam hîc impletam esse, Evangelista dicit, cumprimis agat de sanatione à morbis spiritualibus, quo sensu non solùm antiquissimi V. T. Interpr. accipiunt (LXXII. enim disertè vertunt ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν φέρει. Ionathan in Targhum: הוא יבע על חובנא i. e. pro peccatis nostris ipse deprecabitur. Arabs i. e. ipse portat peccata nostra) verùm etiam ipse ὑπὸ θεοῦ φερόμευος Apostolus Petrus 1. ep. 2, 24. locum propheticum ita allegat, de quo omninò etiam videri potest B. Par. Com. in ep. Petri. Sciendum igitur, uti, etiam pridem notatum Chrysostomo, Theophylacto, Euthymio, Hilario aliisque è veteribus, Esaiam πρώτως loqui de infirmitatibus ac morbis animae h. e. peccatis, eorumque per Christum liberatione: (Id quod adeò luculenter ex contextu demonstrari potest, ut nec iurati illi satisfactionis à Christo praestitae hostes Photiniani ire inficias possint, ceu ex Socino in explic Loc. Sc. S. 73. Crellio contra Hug. Grot. pag. 96. Osterodo Instit. p. 216. videre est.) Δευτέρως tamen etiam agere de peccatorum poenis, iisque non aeternis modò, sed & temporalibus. Nam Christus promeritus nobis est, ut omni malo, quod peccata consequitur, liberemur: scribit Iesuita Tirinus in h. l. Rectè omninò. Errant enim ipsius socienni, statuentes, tum quòd Christus solùm pro originali, non verò actualibus peccatis satisfecerit, it. quòd Christus non pro omnibus tam temporalibus, quàm aeternis peccatorum poenis satisfecerit ac proinde post remissam culpam soepè remanere reatum poenae temporalis. Quos errores prolixè refutat B. P. Confess. Cathol. l. 2. Spec. part. 3. art. 10. c. 5. §. 1. & 2. it in LL. Theol. art. de Poenit. Suscitatus verò ex istis hypothesibus fictus ille purgatorius ignis, quem extinxit B. D. Meisnerus erud. opusc. Indulgentiis Rom. Papae oppos. Porrò rectè monet B. D. Chemnitius, locum Esaiae apud Matthaeum dici adimpleri ἀνναγωγικῶς. Quia enim Christus multa hîc miracula edere incipiebat, facilè fieri potuisset, ut vulgus existimasset, Christum tantùm esse excellentem quendam chirurgum: ad hoc autem praecavendum Matthaeus hominum mentes per ἀναγωγὴν elevare & de Christo altius quid sperari voluit, nempe talia miracula ideò esse facta, ut impleretur illud, quòd Esaias praedirerat, Messiam sc. fore, qui morbos animi portaturus, & ab istis homines liberaturus esset. Atque hanc sententiam pluribus deducit & confirmat B. D. Vind. Sacr. Loc. XXCIII. Eadem explicatio erridet quoque B. D. Quistorpio in h. l. Eodem etiam inclinat Simon Episcopius Arminianus lib. 3. Instit. Theol. sect. 4. c. 26 p. 109. & 191. it. Rivetus t. 2. Oper. in Explic. c. 53. Es. p. 822. ubi etiam ex professo refutat Socinum, ineptè colligentem, quòd sicuti Prophetia Esaiae impleta fuit, dum Christus omnium aegrotorum morbos abstulit; ita etiam idem fecisse dicendus sit, cùm à nobis peccata omnia, potissimùm eorum poenas abstulit, quat. sc. viam irae divinae h. e. supplicii peccatis constituti effugiendi ostendit ac confirmavit, & peccata etiam cuicunque voluit, dimisit. Scil. ne concedere cogatur, Christum patiendo ac moriendo pro peccatis nostris satisfecisse. Eundem Socinum eiusque sequaces egregiè quoq; refutarunt Dn. D. Wellerus in Expl. c. 53 Esaiae, An. 1634. Witteb. luci datâ. B. D. Grawerus Polem. Sacr. p. 710. seqq. Conferatur Const. l Empereur ab Oppyck, Annot. ad ὁδοιπορ. Mosis Kimchi p. 185. ubi probè observat, quòd Es. 53, 4. sit verbum םבל, quod semper sit portare, gestare, in se suscipere, nunquam verò simpliciter saltem removere. (Multorum exemplorum inductione probatum hoc dedit Dn. D. Wellerus d. l.) add. quoque Pineda in c. 7. Iob. v. 21. n. 2. Ipse vero Constantinus existimat, hoc velle Matthaeum, I. Christum corporales morbos sanando, auferendo & asportando, declarasse & manifestum secisse, se spiritualium nostrorum morborum reatum qui illorum cansa est, suscepisse, doloresdebitos portasse:) nam implere pro manifestare usurpare Matthaeum, sicuti & Paulum Col. 1, 25.) quemadmodum ex consequente antecedens intelligi, & contra, doceat collatioPs. 68, 19.cumEph. 4, 8. Sed quomodo Christus morbos nostros corporales portavit? Resp. non quòd eos susceperit, sed quia pro peccatis nostris satisfaciendo ab omnibus peccatorum poenis nos liberavit. Vid. B. D. Glass. Rhet. S. p. 582. Addunt nonnulli, quôd portarit etiam per compassionem. Quomodo Apost. etiam dicat: Alter alterius onera portet, Gal. 6.)*

## 8:18
*(v. 18. Εκέλευσιν. Grotius observes an ellipsis here, which he supplies in this way: ἐκέλευσιν πάντα ἑτοιμᾶσαι εἰς τὸ ἀπελθεῖν. )*

Latin:

*(v. 18. Εκέλευσιν. Observat hîc Grotius ellipsin, quam hoc modo supplet: ἐκέλευσιν πάντα ἑτοιμᾶσαι εἰς τὸ ἀπελθεῖν.)*

## 8:19
*(v. 19. And when a scribe had approached etc. Christ here seems to refuse to receive the scribe, when nevertheless John 6, 37. He professes: him who comes to me, I will not cast out. Answer: Christ rejects the scribe, who did not desire to follow Him with the intention of learning the way of salvation (in which sense the passage John 6. is understood) but with a wicked ardor for gathering riches through the working of miracles, which he desired to learn from Christ, such as the mind of Simon Magus was, Acts 8, 19. He was not seeking a Master, but gain from the Master. Chrysologus, sermon 18: Christ did not repel the scribe who was willing, but exposed the one who was feigning and shuddered at the one who was presuming: or why would Christ, why would the author of piety, the bestower of salvation, prohibit that one who was coming willingly, who soon held back another disciple desiring to go, lest he depart? But that this scribe wished to follow Christ with such an intention, the Savior's answer hints clearly enough, and Chrysostom, Euthymius, Theophylact, Bede, Jerome, Lyra, and the Ordinary Gloss also approve with their calculation, as noted by Lord Dr. Walther in Harm. Bibl. p. 761. Grotius inclines to the same in this place.)*

Latin:

*(v. 19. Et quum accessisset &c. Christus hîc scribam recipere quasi recusat, cùm tamen Ioh. 6, 37. profiteatur: qui venit ad me, non eiiciam eum foras. Resp. Christus reiicit Scribam, qui non cupiebat eum sequi animo viam salutis discendi (quo sensu intell. locus Ioh. 6.) sed pravo ardore, divitias per operationem miraculorum, quae à Christo discere cupiebat, colligendi, qualisanimus & Simoni Mago erat, Act. 8, 19. Non Magistrum quaerebat, sed ex Magistro lucrum. Chrysologus serm. 18. Scribam Christus non repulit volentem, sed fingentem prodidit & horruit praesumentem: aut quare Christus, quare pietatis autor, largitor salutis istum venirvolentem prohiberet, qui mox alium discipulum ire cupientem ret---uit, ne abiret? Quòd verò tali intentione Scriba iste Christum voluerit sequi, satis clarè innuit Salvatorie responsio, ac calculo etiam suo approbant Chrysostomus, Euthymius, Theophylactus, Beda, Hieronymus, Lyra, Glossa ord. notante Dn D. Walthero in Harm. Bibl. p. 761. Eod. inclinat Grotius in h. l.)*

## 8:20
v. 20. The birds of the air have κατασκηνώσεις, places for the setting up of tabernacles, in which they may be shaded from the Sun & defended against the cold. Syr. מטללא shady places, from the root טלל & Heb. עלל thus are bird nests called, because they are accustomed to nest in shady thickets or trees. *(See also concerning this word Grot. in this place, likewise Gataker in Cinno p. 352. following.)*

φωλεὸς in the Glosses is a lair. Among Arist. lib. 9. Histor. animal. bears are said φωλεοῦ ἐξελσθεῖν to go out from a lair or bed. Aug. des. virgin. cap. 51. A certain proud and deceitful man had said this to him, Lord I will follow you, wherever you go, to whom he responds. Foxes have holes. He was arguing by the name of foxes a crafty deceitfulness, and by the name of birds a windy elation, in which he was finding no pious humility where he might rest.

*( Son of man. A Hebraism, for by the appellation ננר אךם men of a more base condition are accustomed to be designated in the Hebrew language, to whom are opposed בני איש as formerly observed by B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 147. B. D. Chemn. Harm. Evang. pag 925. B. Par. H. E. p. 750. likewise Exeg. L. de pres. & off. Christi §. 80. add. Grot. and Franc. Lucas in this place. Christ therefore while in this place & elsewhere, see below c. 11, 19. c. 12, 27. 32. 40. c. 17. 22. c. 18, 11. c. 16, 13. c. 20. 28. c. 26, 2. 24. Luc. 11, 30.Ioh. 3, 14.c. 8, 29. &c. attributes that name to himself, or caused it to be attributed to himself by others, See Ps. 8, 2.Dan. 7, 13.c. 10, 6.Ebr 2, 6. he wished to teach his emptying. Compare Ps. 22, 7.Phil. 2, 6. 7. At the same time, however, also his love. See Gisbertus Schevichavius lib. 4. de Trinit. c. 26. And hence also it is clear what must be answered to the objection of the ancient heretics, who maintained that Christ was conceived from the seed of Joseph, for the reason that he is not only said to be his Son, but is also expressly called ιὶὸς τοὑ ἀνθρώπου. For he is said himself to be the son of man both because he was born from the posterity of Adam, and on account of his humility. But the remaining interpreters imitate that Hebraism.

both Oriental and Occidental. For the Syrian translates the Arab (in the English Polyglot Bibles from the beginning τοῶ omitted without cause is detected here) The Ethiopian Regarding the Western interpreters, the matter is well known. Furthermore, the argumentation of R. Isaac is ridiculous, concluding from this passage as follows: If Christ is the son of man, he is not God. But Apella shamefully opposes things that are subordinate. For he is also called the Son of God, Matth. 3, 17.c. 16, 16.c. 27, 24. and God blessed forever. But Mr. D. M-llerus shows the vanity of the impostor at greater length in Judaism p. 966. Thus the so-called Rabbi argues equally ineptly, If Christ were true God, he would certainly have where to lay his head, because the earth is the Lord's Ps. 24, 1. But the leader of the blind hallucinates just as gravely, while he not only shamefully opposes the divine and human nature of Christ, but also does not attend to the distinction between the state of Christ's humiliation and exaltation.)

*( He has not where to lay his head. The Papists, and the Jesuits especially, (of whom someone said not ineptly, what he said of Seneca, namely that it was for that philosopher to praise poverty, who abounded in riches, yet Seneca possessed, if credit is to be given to Tacitus, three hundred million sesterces, i.e., seven million five hundred thousand Philippeans) are very curious here in commending the vow of poverty. See especially the Jesuits Corn. à Lapide, Adamus Conzen, on this passage, Seb. Barrad. vol. 2, p. 412. Indeed, Clichtovaeus, Roffensis, Bunderius, and others urge the example of Christ in this passage for establishing Monastic poverty. But note 1. that the reason for Christ's poverty, or why he himself willed to be poor, was far different, which the Apostle explains 2. Cor. 8. 9. but this has no place in others. 2. if the action of Christ is also our instruction regarding the present business, it follows that the Roman Pontiff, as one who very vainly boasts himself to be the vicar of Christ, ought especially to be an imitator of the poverty of Christ. The Jesuit Conzen indeed objects, and says, that the Roman Pontiff is the successor of Peter, As if he ought to express Peter his predecessor more than Christ his Master, whose vicar he names himself? And who ever detected in Peter such majesty as the Roman Pontiff arrogates to himself over all Kings and Princes, and even the Emperor himself? Who ever saw Peter walking with such pomp as the Roman Prelate shows himself to be seen? Indeed, Peter expressly confesses, That he left all things for the sake of Christ, this is what they wish to be accepted concerning the total abdication of the Papacy. 3. Since, therefore, the flatterers of the Pope easily perceive that the pride of the Roman Pontiff can in no way be reconciled with the humility of Christ, nor riches with poverty, they strive to settle the matter with a distinction. They say, namely, that Christ did this and counseled poverty as something more perfect, but did not command it as necessary for salvation. Thus Corn. à Lap. in this place. But if the poverty of Christ is proposed to us for imitation, whether as something necessary for our salvation, or even at least as a state of perfection, it is certainly fitting that the Roman Pontiff, the feigned vicar of Christ or at least his ape, should express such a state as much as possible by his own example and commend it to others. But how clearly he does not do this same thing is manifest. The Jesuit Corn. à Lapide reports in this place the opinion of Jerome in epistle 1 to Heliodorus: The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head, and do you measure out ample porticoes and vast spaces of roofs? Expecting the inheritance of the world, you cannot be a co-heir of Christ. A maxim truly worthy to be inscribed in golden letters on the Lateran of the Pope. Furthermore, lest the example of Christ be cast in his face, John XXII (by others XXIII) the Roman Pontiff took good care, and thus in the Extravag. Ioh. XXII de verb. signif. he defined, that Christ neither kept for himself the expropriation of all right in the property of any thing and in its use, (Alfonso Mendoza teaches the contrary in Relect. Theol. p. 668, 675, Platina in the life of Ioh. 23., and other Papists commonly) nor did he impose it upon the Apostles, nor was it received by them under a vow (NB. and the question is especially about that). Moreover, he pronounces the doctrine of those who assert the contrary to be pestiferous, erroneous, and condemned. And it is especially to be noted that in the rejection of that doctrine he did not even spare the Roman Pontiff Nicholas himself. As B. Par. shows at greater length in Confess. Cath. t. 3. p. 313. 4. Meanwhile, it is conceded that in a time of persecution all goods should rather be abandoned than that one should send word to heavenly truth. But the question between us and the Papists is about the spontaneous choice of poverty. But the Jesuits themselves prefer to be preachers of the poverty of Christ rather than imitators, just as from their rules Mr. D. H-lsem. teaches in Anti Hag. p. 552. If finally the Church is the mystical body of Christ, which the Papists themselves cannot deny, let them consider how well temporal happiness is established by them. the mark of the true Church, as if indeed, since Christ the head of the Church was pressed by many passions and calamities and lived in extreme poverty, the Church ought not also to be conformed to him, Rom. 8. 29. but always flourish with external happiness and splendor. Conf. Matth. 10, 24.Luc. 6, 46.

Latin:

v. 20. Volucres coeli habentκατασκηνώσεις, tabernaculorum collocationes, in quibus à Sole obumbrentur & contra frigus defendantur. Syr. מטללאumbracula, à rad טלל & Hebr. עלל sic vocantur avium nidi, quia in umbrosis dumis vel arboribuc solent nidificare. *(Vide etiam de hâc voce Grot. in h. l. it. Gatakerum in Cinno p. 352. seqq.)*

φωλεὸς in Glossis est cubile. Apud Arist. lib. 9. Histor. animal. ursi dicuntur φωλεοῦ ἐξελσθεῖνlatibulo exire vel cubili. Aug. des. virgin. cap. 51. Quidam superbus & dolosus hoc ei dixerat, Domine sequarte, quecunieris, cui respondet. Vulpes foveas habent. Arguebat nomine vulpium astutam dolositatatem, & nomine volucrum ventosam elationem, in quo ubire quiesceret, piam non inveniebat humilitatem.

*( Filius hominis. Ebraismus appellatione enim ננר אךם insigniri solent in lingvà Ebreâ homines vilioris conditionis, quibus opponuntur בני איש ut pridem observatum à B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 147. B. D. Chemn. Harm. Evang. pag 925. B. Par. H. E. p. 750. it. Exeg. L. de pres. & off. Christi §. 80. add. Grot. ac Franc. Lucas in h. l. Christus igitur dum h. l. & alibi, vid. infrà c. 11, 19. c. 12, 27. 32. 40. c. 17. 22. c. 18, 11. c. 16, 13. c. 20. 28. c. 26, 2. 24. Luc. 11, 30.Ioh. 3, 14.c. 8, 29. &c. id nominis sibi tribuit, aut aliis sibi tribui fecit, Vid. Ps. 8, 2.Dan. 7, 13.c. 10, 6.Ebr 2, 6. exinanitionem suam docere voluit. Confer Ps. 22, 7.Phil. 2, 6. 7. Simul tamen etiam amoram. Vid. Gisbertus Schevichavius lib. 4. de Trinit. c. 26. Atq; hinc etiam patet, quid respondendum sit ad obiectionem haereticorum veterum, qui statuebant, Christum conceptum esse ex semine Ioseph, eo quòd non solum illius dicatur Filius, verùm etiam disertè vocetur ιὶὸς τοὑ ἀνθρώπου. Dicitur nempe ipse filius hominis tum quia natus ex posteritate Adami, tum propter humilitatem. Imitantur verò Ebraismum illum etiam reliqui Interpp.

tum Orientales, tum Occidentales. Syrus enim vertit Arabs (in Bibliis Polygl. Anglic. ab initio τοῶ absque causâ omissum hîc deprehenditur) Aethiops De Occidentalibus Interpp. res nota est. Ridicula porrò est argumentatio R. Isaaci, ita ex h. l. colligentis: Si Christus est filius hominis, non est Deus. At turpiter opponit Apella, quae sunt subordinata. Etenim & Filius Dei dicitur, Matth. 3, 17.c. 16, 16.c. 27, 24. it. Deus benedictus in secula. Sed pluribus vanitatem impostoris ostendit Dn. D. M-llerus in Iudaismo p. 966. Sic dictus Rabbi pariter ineptè argumentatur, Si Christus esset verus Deus, haberet utiq;, ubi caput reclinaret, quia Domini est terra Ps. 24, 1. Sed itidem graviter hallucinatur coecorum dux, dum non solùm divinam & hum. Christi naturam turpiter opponit, verùm etiam non attendit discrimen inter statum Christi exinanitionis, & exaltationis.)*

*( Non habet, ubi caput reclinet. Pontificii, ac Iesuitae eumprimis, (de quibus non ineptê aliquis, quod ille de Seneca, farcu-- nempe Philosopho illi fuisse, paupert atem laudare, qui divitiis effluebat, possedit verò Seneca, si fides habenda Tacito est, ter millies sestertiûm i. e. septuagies quinquies centena millia Philippeorum) admodùm curiosi hîc sunt in commendando voto paupertatis. Vid. cumprimis Iesuitae Corn. à Lapide, Adamus Conzen, in h. l. Seb. Barrad. t. 2. p. 412. Imò exemplum Christi h. l. pro stabilienda Monasticâ paupertate urgent Clichtovaeus, Roffensis, Bunderius, alii. Verùm not. 1. quòd longè alia ratio fuerit paupertatis Christi, sive cur ipse pauper esse voluerit, quam exponit Apostolus 2. Cor. 8. 9. haec verò in aliis locum non habet. 2. si Christi actio etiam quoad praesens negotium est nostra institutio, sequitur, quòd cumprimis paupertatis Christi imitator esse debeat Pontifex Romanus, ut qui se Christi vicarium perquàm vanè gloriatur. Excipit quidem Iesuita Conzen, dicitque, quòd P. R. sit Petri successor, Quasi verò magis exprimere ille Petrum antecessorem debeat, quàm Christum Magistrum, cuius se nominat vicarium? & quis unquam in Petro talem maiestatem deprehendit, qualem P. R. in omnes Reges & Principes, ipsum que adeo Imperatorem sibi arrogat? quis unquam Petrum tali pompa vidit incedentem, quali conspiciendum se praebet Praesul Romanus? Imô Petrus disertè fatetur, quòd omnia propter Christum reliquerit, id quod de totali abdicatione Pontificii acceptari volunt. 3. Cùm igitur Pontificis adsentatores facilè deprehendant, nullatenus P. R. fastum cum Christi humilitate, divitias cum paupertate conciliari posse, distinctione expedire rem satagunt. Dicunt nempe, quod Christus hoc fecerit ac consuluerit paupertatem, ut perfectius quid, non autem praeceperit, ut necessarium ad salutem. Ita Corn. à Lap. in h. l. Ast si Christi paupertas proposita nobis ad imitationem sive ut aliquid ad salutem nobis necessarium, sive etiam saltem ut status perfectionis, convenit sanè ut quàm maximè talem exemplo suo exprimat aliisque commendet Pontifex Romanus, fictus Christi vicarius vel simia saltem. At quàm planè non idipsum ille faciat, palam est. Refert h. l. Iesuita Corn. à Lapide sententiam Hieronymi ep. 1. ad Heliodorum: Filius hominis non habet, ubi caput reclinet, & tu amplas porticus & ingentiatectorum spatia metiris? Hereditatem expectans seculi, Christi cohaeres esse non poteris. Digna profectò gnome, quae aureis literis Laterano Pontificis inscribatur. Caeterùm ne Christi exemplum sibi obiiceretur, benè cavit Iohannes XXII. (aliis XXIII.) P. R. adeoque in Extravag. Ioh. XXII. de verb. signif. definivit, Christum neque expropriationem omnis iuris in cuius cunrei proprietate & in eius usu in se servasse, (contrarium docet Alphonsus Mendoza Relect. Theol. p. 668. 675. Platina in vitâ Ioh. 23. alii Pontificii communiter) nec eam imposuisse Apostolis, nesub voto (NB. atque de eo cumprimis quaestio est) ab ipsis fuisse receptam. Eorum autem doctrinam, qui contrarium adservnt, pronunciat esse pestiferam, erroneam & damnatam. Ac cumprimis notandum, quôd in doctrinae illius reiectione ne ipsi quidem Pontifici R. Nicolao pepercerit. Ceu pluribus ostendit B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. 3. p. 313. 4. Interim conceditur, quòd tempore persecutionis bona potiùs omnia deserenda sint, quàm veritati coelesti nuncium mittendum. At quaestio inter nos ac Pontificios est de spontaneâ paupertatis electione. Sed Iesuitae ipsi paupertatis Christi esse malunt depraedicatores, quàm imitatores, quemadmodum exillorum regulis docet Dn D. H-lsem. in Anti Hag. p. 552. Si denique Ecclesia est mysticum Christi corpus, quod ipsi Pontificii inficias ire non possunt, cogitent, quàm benè ab eis felicitas temporalis statuatur nota verae Ecclesiae, quasi nempe, cùm Christus Ecclesiae caput multis passionibus & calamitatibus fuerit pressus & in summa paupertate vixerit, Ecclesia non debeat quoque illi conformari, Rom. 8. 29. sed externâ felicitate & splendore semper florere. Conf. Matth. 10, 24.Luc. 6, 46.)*

## 8:21
v. 21. Permit me to serve my father who is now old, to remain with him until he is dead, afterwards I will follow you. Toss. (so Theophylact in c. 9. of Luke, and from him Francisc. Lucas: but others more correctly with Ambrose, Chrysostom etc. maintain that the parent of that disciple was already dead at that time.) Syr. אפם לי permit me, borrowed from the Greeks ἄφες. Clem. Alex. lib. 3. strom f. 187. maintains that this disciple was Philip the Apostle, whom Christ wished to draw away from the care of his father's funeral. Tertull. de idolol. cap. 12. Even to bury a father, was slow for faith.

Parents more often asked Christ that he might obtain salvation for their children, but rare are the examples of children who prayed that they might prolong the life of their parents: it is read of only one who asked of Christ that space be given to him to bury his father: but he does not ask that Christ raise him from the dead.

Latin:

v. 21. Permitte, ut patrimeo iam seni inserviam, apud ipsum maneam, donec mortuus sit, postea te sequar. Toss. *(ita Theophylactus in c. 9. Lucae, & ex eo Francisc. Lucas: sed rectiùs alii cum Ambrosio, Chrysostomo &c. statuunt, quòd parens illius discipuli iam tum fuerit mortous.)* Syr. אפם ליdimitte mihi, mutuatum à Graecis ἄφες. Clem. Alex. lib. 3. strom f. 187. stâtuit, hunc discipulum fuisse Philippum Apostolum, quem Christus à cura paterni funeris retrahere voluerit. Tertull. de idolol. cap. 12. Etiam sepelire patrem, tardum fuit fidei.

Parentes saepiùs rogarunt Christum, ut liberis suis salutem impetrarent, sed rara sunt exempla filiorum, qui ut parentibus vitam prolongarent, precati sunt: de uno tantùm legitur, qui petiit à Christo, sibi dari spacium sepeliendi patrem: non autem petit, ut Christus à mortuis ipsum resusciter.

## 8:22
v. 22. August. repeats more often. As the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul. Iust. in qq. & resp. ad orth. q. 28. p. 319. Just as through the divorce of the soul from the body, the body is dead, foul, and unclean: so if the fear of GOD should withdraw from the soul, the soul is bloodless and ill-smelling and impure. Saying of the Hebrews The wicked while they live, or in their life; are called dead. It is held in comm. super Aboth cap. 3. (Therefore, by the common opinion of the Interpreters, those who are spiritually dead are denoted by the dead in the subject of the proposition, who are elsewhere called dead in sins. See Eph. 2, 1. for such are separated from that true life of the soul, which is in God, Eph. 4, 18. In a similar way also the verb to die and the noun dead occurs Luc. 15, 24.Ioh. 5, 25.1. Tim. 5, 6.Eph. 2, 5.c. 5. 14.Col. 2, 13. Chrysostom, Hilary, Jerome in h. l. and Ambrose in Ps. 48. specifically understand infidels by the dead here: but August. l. 4.

de Trin. c. 6. & quaest. 6. in Matth. in general He thinks that whatever sinners are indicated here by that name. The same author, book 20 of the City of God, chapter 6: Let the dead bury the dead in body. Compare, however, concerning spiritual death, B. Par. L. on Death §. 16. Homil. Acad t. 1. p. 636. Grotius notes in this place that also among other writers, those who are alien to true discipline, as that which is the life of the soul, are called dead. To this point serves that sentence of the Arabs: The wicked man is dead, even if he be in the mansions of the living: but the upright man is alive, though he has migrated into the mansions of the dead. Erpenius presents it in Arabic, Adage 96. In the predicate, however, by the phrase to bury the dead, one can also understand an excessive and preposterous care for secular things, which, namely, completely abstracts the soul from GOD and the care of eternal salvation. Cornelius à Lapide mentions in this place: Basil in the Monastic Constitutions shows from this place how much damage affection toward parents brings to spiritual and religious men, when familiarity with them. But note that those Constitutions are an adulterated and supposititious writing, falsely attributed to Basil. For besides the fact that the style is different from the remaining writings of Basil, it cannot be denied that Gregory Nazianzen in the life of Basil, where he nevertheless studiously reviews the remaining writings of Basil, makes no mention of the said Constitutions: Finally, how from the fact that sinful men indulging in sins are called dead, our countrymen rightly prove that no free will remains to man, so that he might be able by his own powers to rise again to spiritual life and convert himself, has been shown in the Annotations on Colossians, p. 89 and following.

Christ does not disapprove of the duties of charity and piety toward parents, but teaches that the divine vocation must be obeyed immediately and promptly, lest we suffer a delay to be cast upon us by the men of this age, but rather let us rejoice that we have been liberated from the vain conversation of paternal tradition 1 Peter 1 v. 18. Christ therefore does not simply prohibit the rendering of the highest honor and duty to parents, but teaches that the obedience owed to the second table of the decalogue must be postponed to the obedience owed to the first table, when indeed both cannot have a place at the same time. Well Ambrose, book 7 on Luke c. 9. The burial of a paternal funeral is prohibited, so that you may understand that human things must be postponed to divine things. A good pursuit, but a greater impediment. For he who divides his pursuit, diverts his affection: he who divides his care, delays his progress.

This passage is also accustomed to be taken by some in such a way that Christ does not forbid in general the duty of honestly burying deceased parents, but that he speaks specifically of those who are dead in their sins, whom he forbids to be adorned with an honest burial, even if they were placed in the position of parents and nearest kin. And the present saying is also brought forward in support of this opinion by B. Par. *L. de Morte* §. 91.)*

Latin:

v. 22. August. saepiùs repetit. Ut vita corporis est anima, ita vita animae Deus est. Iust. in qq. & resp. ad orth. q. 28. p. 319. Quemadmodum per divortium animae à corpore, mortuum, foetidum & immundum est corpus: ita siab anima secedat DEI timor, exanguis est & maltolens & impur a anima. Dictum Hebraeorum Improbi dum vivunt, sive in vita sua; mortui vocantur. Habetur in comm. super Aboth cap. 3. *(Denotantur igitur, communi Interrp. sententia, per mortuos in propositionis subiecto spiritualiter mortui, qui alibi dicuntur mortui in peccatis. Vid Eph. 2, 1. sunt enim tales à verâ illâ animae vitâ, quae in Deo est, separati, Eph. 4, 18. Simili etiam modo verbum mori & nomen mortu-s occurrit Luc. 15, 24.Ioh. 5, 25.1. Tim. 5, 6.Eph. 2, 5.c. 5. 14.Col. 2, 13. Chrysostomus Hilarius, Hieronymus in h. l. & Ambrosius in Ps. 48. in specie per mortuos hîc intelligunt infideles: sed August. l. 4.

de Trin. c. 6. & quaest. 6. in Matth. in genere quos libet peccatores hîc indicari isto nomine, censet. Idem l. 20. de C. D. c. 6. Animâ mortui sepeliant mortuos corpore. Conf. autem de morte spirituali B. Par. L. de Morte §. 16. Homil. Acad t. 1. p. 636. Notat Grotius in h. l. etiam apud alios Scriptores, eos, qui à vera disciplina, ut quae animi vita, alieni sunt, vocari mortuos. Huc facit illa Arabum sententia: Improbus mortuus est, etiamsi sit in mansionibus vivorum: at probus vivus est, licet migraverit in mansiones mortuorum. Arabicè exhibet Erpen. Adag. 96. In praedicato verò phrasi sepelire mortuos potest quoque intelligi nimia ac praepostera cura rerum secularium, quae videl. animum à DEO ac salutis aet. curâ penitus abstrahit. Memorat Corn. à Lap. in h. l. Basilium in Constit. Monast. ex h. l. ostendere, quantum damni viris spiritualibus & religiosis afferat affectus erga parentes, cum eisfamiliaritas. Sed not. quòd Constit. illae sint scriptum adulterinum & suppositititum, falsò Basilio tributum. Praeterquam enim, quòd stylus à reliquis Basilii scriptis diversus, negari haut potest, quòd Greg. Nazianzenus in vitâ Basilii, ubi tamen reliqua Basilii scripta studiosè recenset, nullam dictarum Constit. mentionem faciat: Quomodo denique ex eo, quòd homines peccatores peccatis indulgentes, mortui dicuntur, nostrates rectè probēt, nullum superesse homini liberum arbitrium, ut propriis viribus ud spiritualem vitam resurgere ac sese convertere possit, ostensum in Annot. ad Coloss. p 89 seqq.)*

Christus non improbat officia caritatis & pietatis erga parentes, sed docet, vocationi divinae statim ac promtè parendum esse, ne patiamur nobis remora-iniici ab hominibus huius seculi, sed laetemur potiùs, non liberatos esse à conversatione vana paternae traditionis 1. Petri 1. v. 18. *(Christus igitur non simpliciter prohibet supremum parentibus honorem & officium praestare, sed docet obedientiam secundae decal. tabulae debitam postponendam esse obed. primae tabulae debitae, quando nempe utraque simul locum habere nequit. Benè Ambros. l. 7. in Luc. c. 9.Pa-erni funeris sepultura prohibetur, ut intelligas, humana postponenda divinis. Bonum studium, sed maius impedimentum. Nam qui partitur studium, derivat affectum: qui dividit curam, differt profectum.

Solet hic locus ita à nonnullis etiam accipi, quòd Christus non prohibeat in genere officium honestè sepoliendi parentes defunctos, sed quòd in specie loquatur de illis, qui in peccatis suis mortui sunt, quos honestâ sepulturâ condecorare prohibeat, etiamsi parentum ac proximorum cognatorum loco fuerint constituti. Atque in hanc sententiam adducitur quoque praesens dictum à B. Par. L. de Morte §. 91.)*

## 8:23
v. 23. Join Ps. 107. which is a gloss of this whole context. See also Aug. in Ps. 93. The same, tract. 49 in John. The winds enter your heart, just as when you are sailing, when you are crossing this life like a stormy and dangerous sea, the winds enter, they move the waves, they disturb the ship. Who are the winds? You have heard an insult, you become angry: the insult is the wind, the anger is the wave. You are in danger, you prepare to answer, you prepare to return curse for curse, already the ship approaches shipwreck. Awaken the sleeping Christ, for you fluctuate and prepare to return evil for evil because Christ is sleeping in the ship. For in your heart the sleep of Christ is the forgetfulness of faith. *(The ancients also teach that the Church is beautifully depicted by this ship, which is attacked by storms. Among them, Chrysostom in Matthew The Church sails, equipped with the rudder of faith, on a happy course over the sea of this age, having God as its helmsman (Cf. Ps. 46, 4.Ps. 121, 4.) with angels as rowers, carrying the choirs of all the saints, with the salutary tree of the cross erected in its midst, on which the sails of evangelical faith are hung, and by the blowing of the Holy Spirit it is led to the port of paradise and the security of eternal rest. The storms of persecutions infest this ship Iob. 41, 22.Es. 57, 20. But Christ is carried in the ship, who indeed seems to some to be sleeping, but his heart is awake, Cant. 5, 2. and he must be awakened so that he may answer us from Ier. 31, 26. Since, therefore, the Church is signified by the little ship which is tossed by the waves, as is declared by Origen on Matth. c. 14., Hilary on Matthew can. 7. 13., Ambrose on Solomon 4 and on virgins 3, Jerome on Ezech. 26. and on Marc. 4., Hieronymus Lauretus Cervariensis in Sylv. Allegor. p. 712, it is manifest that temporal happiness is less correctly established by Bellarmine and other Papists as a mark of the Church. Christ indeed saves this ship from shipwreck, meanwhile he permits it to suffer the attacks and waves of temptations and persecutions in the sea of this age. Which are the very words of the said Lauretus, Abbot of the Monastery of S. Felix Gvixolensis.)*

Latin:

v. 23. Coniunge Ps. 107. qui est glossa totius huius contextûs. Vide etiam Aug. in Ps. 93. Idem tract. 49. in Ioh. Intrant venti cor tuum, utiubi navigas, ubi hanc vitam tanquam procellosum & periculosum pelagus transis, intrant venti, movent fluctus, turbant navim. Qui sunt venti? audisti convicium, irasceris: convicium ventus est, iracundia fluctus est. Periclit aris, disponis respondere, disponis maledictum maledicto reddere, iam navis prepinquat naufragio. Excita Christum dormientem, ideò enim fluctuas & mala pro malis reddere praeparas, quia Christus dormit in navi. In corde enim tuo somnus Christi oblivio est fidei. *(Pulcrè etiam per navem hanc, quae procellis oppugnatur, Ecclesiam depingi, antiqui docent. Ex illis Chrysostomus in Matth. Navigat Ecclesia instructa fidei gubernaculo felici cur super huius seculi mare, habens Deum gubernatorem (Conf. Ps. 46, 4.Ps. 121, 4.) Angelos remiges, portans choros omnium sanctorum, erectâ in medio ipsâ salut ari arbore crucis, in qua Evangelica fidei vela suspensa flante Spiritu Sancto ad portum paradisi & securitatem qucetis -ternae deducitur. Infestant hanc navem procellae persecutionum Iob. 41, 22.Es. 57, 20. Sed Christus vehitur in navi, qui videtur quidem aliquantis per dormire, sed cor ipsius vigilat, Cant. 5, 2. excitandus etiam est, ut respondeat nobis ex Ier. 31, 26. Cùm igitur Ecclesia significetur per naviculam, quae fluctibus iactatur, ceu ex Orig. super Matth. c. 14. Hilario super Matth. can. 7. 13. Ambros. de Salom. 4. & de virg. 3. Hieronymo super Ezech. 26. & super Marc. 4. declarat Hier. Lauretus Cervariensis Sylv. Allegor. p. 712 manifestum est, quòd à Bell. aliisque Pontificiis felicitas temporalis minùs rectè Ecclesiae statuatur nota. Anaufragio quidem navem hanc Christus servat, interea permittit, ut in seculi huius mars tentationum & persecutionem impetus & fluctus patiatur. Quae ipsissima sunt verba dicti Laureti, Abbatis Monasterii S. Felicis Gvixolensis.)*

## 8:24
(v. 24. He was sleeping. Jonah was a type, who likewise was sleeping, while the others in the ship were in danger. See what has been noted at Matt. 12, 39. Moreover, the security of power is expressed here, so that the greater authority might be shown.)

Latin:

*(v. 24. Dormiebat. Typus fuit Ionas, qui itidem dormiebat, coeteris in navi periclitantibus. Vide quae notata ad Matth. 12, 39. Exprimitur autem hîc potestatis securitas, quò maior ostenderetur autoritas.)*

## 8:25
(v. 25. Lord, save us. Conf. Ps. III, 8. From this invocation of Christ, it can indeed be proven both that his divinity is true, and that divine worship is owed even to him as a man. Conf. similar examples Matth. 2, 11.c. 15, 22.c. 20, 3.c. 28. 17.Luc. 17, 14.c. 23. 43. &c.)

Latin:

*(v. 25. Domine serva nos. Conf. Ps. III, 8. Potest verò ex hàc Christi invocatione tum vera eius deitas probari, tum quòd cultus divinus etiam ut homini ipsi debeatur. Conf. similia exempla Matth. 2, 11.c. 15, 22.c. 20, 3.c. 28. 17.Luc. 17, 14.c. 23. 43. &c.)*

## 8:26
v. 26. He commanded. That commanding and threatening was an external sign of the divine power of Christ, to whom all creatures are subject. Ps. 104. v 7Ps. 106. v. 9. (And this is a certain argument of the true Deity of Christ, since He performed miracles 1. most freely,Matt. 8, 5. 2. most powerfully, i.e., such as no man can perform, Ioh. 9, 32.c. 2, 19.c. 10, 18. in this place it is to be noted that God demonstrates His majesty in the production or excitation and calming of the winds. See Amos 4, 13.Ps. 17, 9.Ps. 65, 8.Ps. 89, 10.Ps. 107, 25Ps. 134, 7.Ier. 10, 13.Iob. 38, 10 11. 3. divinely, i.e., ὁμοίως in the same way in which the Father performs miracles. Ioh. 5, 17.19, 20. 4. gloriously, i.e., for the glory of Himself Ioh. 2, 11.c. 5, 23. Compare more on this matter in B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. on the eternal Son of GOD c. 3. §. 22. But it is usually asked here, how did Christ rebuke the winds and the sea? (for thus Maldonatus thinks it should rather be read, than he commanded, since in the Greek it is έπετίμησε. Indeed, also the Oriental Interpreters, the Syrian, the Arab, the Ethiopian, express it with such words as have the meaning of chiding or rebuking.) Maldonatus answers that Christ speaks to the winds, the tempest, and other similar things (see Marc. 4, 39.Luc. 4, 39.c. 8, 24.) just as He otherwise speaks to evil spirits (see below c. 17, 18. Marc. 1, 25.c. 9, 25.Luc. 4, 35. &c.) for the reason that diseases and tempests are often sent in by evil Spirits,Ps. 77, 49.Iob. 1, 19. Others, however, as Card. Toletus in Luc. p. 308, think that because the word of Christ was not only significative, but also virtuous and powerful, for that reason He could expel a fever and change insensible things with words: they add that Christ did not use this command so that the fever or insensible things might perceive the meaning, but so that those seeing the virtue of the word might be stirred up and recognize the power and dominion of the One uttering such words: These words therefore signified to men, but they worked in insensible things. By these words is indicated (writes B. D. Chem. in Harm. p. 699.) the virtue of the words of Christ, which is so great, that it penetrates even his command into the mute elements of the world: & a little later, Creatures are the lictors of GOD, who by his permission attack man, & punish him for sins. But if they should wish to exceed the measure, when he rebukes them: it is no otherwise, than if a Father had handed over a son to a tutor to be chastised, but this one could not keep the measure, then he would be called out & reprimanded by the father. Conf. Ps. 148, 8. How we ought to approach Christ with this confidence, that he himself can remove adversities of every kind with one word, B. Par. teaches at length in Hom. Acad part. 1. p. 407.)

Γαλήνη properly is the tranquility of the sea just as νηνεμία, is of the air. Eustathius derives it from γάλα when the air is milky or white. HenSteph. wishes it to be called γαλήνην as if γελαήνην namely παρὰ τὸ γελᾶνὲ laughing, because the air, when it is tranquil & serene, as if with a serene countenance laughs.

And there was a great calm. Aug. hom. 3. inter 17. quae extant t. 10. Imitate the winds and the sea: obey the creator under the command of Christ: the sea hears, and are you deaf? the sea hears and the wind ceases, and do you blow? What? I say, I do, I fashion: what is this other than to blow, and under the word of Christ to be unwilling to cease? Let not the wave overcome you in the perturbation of your heart. Conf. prolixè hoc arg. tractantem B. D. Chemn. in Harm. h. l.)* *(

Latin:

v. 26. Imperavit. Illud imperare ac interminari fuit externum signum divinae Christi potentiae, cui omnes creaturae sunt subiectae. Ps. 104. v 7Ps. 106. v. 9. *(Estque lioc certum argumentum verae Deitatis Christi, cùm miracula fecerit 1. liberrimè,Matt. 8, 5. 2. potentissimè h. e. talia quae nullus hominum facere potest, Ioh. 9, 32.c. 2, 19.c. 10, 18. h. l. illud notandum, quòd Deus in ventorum productione vel excitatione & sedatione maiestatem suam demonstret. Vid. Amos 4, 13.Ps. 17, 9.Ps. 65, 8.Ps. 89, 10.Ps. 107, 25Ps. 134, 7.Ier. 10, 13.Iob. 38, 10 11. 3. divinè i. e. ὁμοίως eodem modo, quô Pater miracula facit. Ioh. 5, 17.19, 20. 4. gloriosè h. e. in suipsius gloriam Ioh. 2, 11.c. 5, 23. Conf. plura in hanc rem apud B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. de aet. DEI Filio c. 3. §. 22. Quaeri verò hîc solet, quomodo Christus ventos & mare increparit? (ita enim potius legendum putat Maldonatus, quiam imperavit, cùm in Graeco sit έπετίμησε. Sanè & Orientales Interpp. Syrus, Arabs, Aethiops istiusmodi vocibus exprimunt, quae obiurgandi s. increpandi significationem habent.) Respondet Maldonatus, quòd Christus ventis, tempestati aliisque rebus similibus (vid. Marc. 4, 39.Luc. 4, 39.c. 8, 24.) ita loquatur, quemadmodum aliàs malis spiritibus loquitur (vid infrà c. 17, 18. Marc. 1, 25.c. 9, 25.Luc. 4, 35. &c.) ideò quia morbi & tempestates saepè per malos Spiritus immittuntur,Ps. 77, 49.Iob. 1, 19. Alii v. uti Card. Toletus in Luc. p. 308. existimant quòd quia verbum Christi non tantùm significativum, sed etiam virtuosum ac potens erat, idcirco potuerit verbis febrim expellere & insensibilia mutare: addunt, Christū non usum hoc imperio, ut febris aut insensibilia perciperent significationem, sed ut eam verbi virtutem videntes excitarentur & noscerent potestatem & dominium talia verba proferentis: significabant ergò verba haec hominibus, operabantur verò in rebus insensibilibus. Indicatur his verbis (scribit B. D. Chem. in Harm. p. 699.) virturs verborum Christi, quae tanta est, ut penetret etiam ipsius imperium in mutae lementa mundi: & paulò post, Sunt creaturae DEI lictores, qui eius permissione hominem adoriuntur, & ob peccata puniunt. Quòd si verò velint modum excedere, cum eas increpat: non aliter, quàm si Pater silium paedagogo tradidisset castigandum, hic verò modum servare non posset, tum à patre inclamaretur & reprehenderetur. Conf. Ps. 148, 8. Quomodo fiduciâ istâ, quòd omnis generis adversa uno verbo amovere ipse possit, Christum accedere debeamus, prolixè docet B. Par. Hom. Acad part. 1. p. 407.)*

Γαλήνη propriè est maris tranquillitas sicut νηνεμία, aeris. Eustathius deducit à γάλα cùm aër est lacteus vel albus. HenSteph. vult dictam γαλήνην quasi γελαήνην videl. παρὰ τὸ γελᾶνὲridendo, quod aër, cùm tranquillus & serenus est, quasi vultu sereno cideat.

*( Et facta est tranquillitas magna. Aug. hom. 3. inter 17. quae extant t. 10. Imitare ventos & mare: obtempera creatori sub imsione Christi: mare audit, & tu surdus es? mare audit & vent-cessat, & tu sufflas? Quid? dico, facio, fingo: quid est aliud, nisi sufflare, & sub verbo Christi nolle cessare? Non vos vincat fluctus in perturbatione cordis vestri. Conf. prolixè hoc arg. tractantem B. D. Chemn. in Harm. h. l.)*

## 8:27
*(v. 27. But the men wondered. By men in this place Jerome, Bede, Druthmar and others wish sailors to be understood. Jansenius and Maldonatus those who were following Christ in other little boats. But the same Maldonatus, with whom Corn. à Lapide followed Origen and the interlinear Gloss, deny that the Apostles can also be understood by men here, since the power of Christ in performing miracles was sufficiently known to them, and furthermore nowhere are they absolutely called men: But from Marc. 4, 41. and likewise from Luc. 8, 25. it seems to be sufficiently evident, that the Apostles also were amazed. Whence also B. D. Chemn. in Harmon. p. 699. (which the Jesuit Barradius also does, departing from his fellow member of the society) more correctly maintains, that Matthew thaeus Of men by name he also included the Apostles. And in this way also Jerome, Dionysius the Carthusian, and Cajetan establish it. Note indeed that the Apostles had the power of Christ, but they themselves were still of very little faith, on account of which they are even rebuked by Christ. But to that point that the Apostles are called men here, Jerome responds that they are so called, because they had not yet (sufficiently) known the power of the Savior.

Latin:

*(v. 27. Homines verò mirati sunt. Per homines h. l. Hieronymus, Beda, Druthmarus ac alii intellectos volunt nautas. Iansenius ac Maldonatus eos, qui in aliis naviculis Christum sequebantur. Idem verò Maldonatus, cum que eo Corn. à Lapide sequutus Originem & Glossam interlinearem, negant, Apostolos per homines hîc intelligi etiam posse, cùm satis illis Christi in patrandis miraculis potentia nota fuerit, & insuper nullibi absolutè homines vocentur: Verùm ex Marc. 4, 41. itemque ex Luc. 8, 25. satis patere videtur, quòd Apostoli etiam fuerint admirati. Unde etiam B. D. Chemn. in Harmon. p. 699. (quod etiam facit Iesuita Barradius à socienno suo discedens) rectius staiut, quòd Matthaeus thaeus hominum nomine etiam Apostolos complexus fuerit. Atq; h. m. statuunt quoque Hieronymus, Dion. Carthusianus, Caietanus. Nota quidem Apostolis Christi potentia erat, sed admodùm modicae adhuc ipsi erant fidei, ob quod etiam à Christo obiurgantur. Ad illud verò quòd Apostoli vocentur hîc homines, respondet Hieronymus, eos ita appellari, quia nondum (satis) noverant potentiam Salvatoris.)*

## 8:28
v. 28. Into the region of the Gergesenes. Epiphanius against the Manichaeans έλθὼν εἰος. Casaubon in his notes on Gerasa and Genasara, from which the lake is called Genesaretic, that they are the names of two cities, not one, no one will doubt who has consulted Ptolemy. Gadara because it has nothing in common with Genesaris. Eusebius on places. Gerasa is a distinguished city of Arabia. Some, however, think it is Gadara. But the Gospel also mentions the Gerasenes. The same on Gadara. It is a city across the Jordan, opposite Scythopolis and Tiberias on the eastern side. Situated on a mountain, at the roots of which hot waters burst forth, with baths built above. See also Suidas. And Osiander in his Harmony considers them different histories, and denies that it can be demonstrated that Gadara and Gergesa denote one and the same region. He attempts to prove the contrary from Jos. 12. and 13. where Gadara is placed in the borders of the Amorites, from whom the Gergesenes were different. Theophylact notes that in Mark chap. 5. v. 1. it is read in books of better quality Γεργεσηνῶν, as it is in Matthew. Strigelius in ὑῶομν. The names of this same town are Gerasa, Gadara, and Gergesa. About the lake of this town Strabo writes. There is in the Gadarene territory pestiferous water, by which when tasted, cattle lose their hair, hooves, and horns.

Gadara, according to the witness of Josephus book 17. chap. 13. was of Greek institution, therefore it ought not to be a wonder that there was a herd of swine there, the flesh of which was forbidden to the Jews. Matthew in this place has τῶν Γεργεσηνῶν of the Gergesenes, nor do any copies vary. Mark 5, 1. and Luke 8. v. 26. have Γαδαρηνῶν i.e. of the Gadarenes. The Syriac in this place רנרריא Gadara, from which Gadarenes, and Gergessa or Gerassa, from which Gergesenes, were different towns, both however situated near to the lake of Gennesaret, and their borders were mixed, so that when Christ is read to have come into the region of the latter, he is to be understood to have come into the region of the former as well. Tremellius and from him Casaubon, Tossanus. Both towns were situated on the other side of the lake of Gennesaret. ἀντιπεραν τῆς Γαλιλαίας, as Luke says. And Pliny and Ptolemy commemorate Gadara in this region. *(The Syrian in this place, from Mark 5, 1, reads of the Gadarenes, agreeing with the rest of the codices, both printed and manuscript, which learned men have compared, including the Altdorf one. A certain Greek manuscript codex of Gonville and Caius College in the Academy of Cambridge also reads in this place γαδαρηνῶν.. The Persian interpreter also did the same, who likewise has i.e. of the Gadarenes. But Mark 5, 1, and Luke 8, 26. The Ethiopian, however, and the Arab, having followed the received reading of the Greek text, not only in this place but also in the parallel places Mark 5, 1. and Luke 8, 26. read of the Gergesenes: the former has everywhere but the latter which word in the London Bibles Matthew 8, 28. is found punctuated thus but of Mark 5, 1, and Luke 8, 26. h. m As regards the Greek codices Mark 5, 1. there is the greatest variety there regarding the reading of this word. For although the common printed codices present Γαδαρηνῶν,, yet both the Cambridge codex and Stephen's 2 read Γαρασηνῶν, -mo March. Veles. and Steph. 8. and 9. codices Γεργεσηνῶν. But that this reading is of the more approved books, Victor of Antioch, Theophylact, and he whose scholia are mixed with the scholia of Euthymius note: for according to Matthew ch. 8, 28. the Greek books constantly read thus. Thus Franciscus Lucas in the notes to the Greek Gospel of Mark. But since the Greek codices Luke 8, 26. likewise constantly have Γαδαρηνῶν (unless some perhaps corrected to the Latin), nothing prevents the received reading from being retained also in Mark: not indeed as if Gadara, and Gergesa or Gerasa were the names of the same town, as Strigelius indeed thinks (Ptolemy however distinguishes them as two cities), but because the towns were very close. Both looked toward the region of Decapolis, as Cluverius mentions in Introduction book 5, chapter 22, both adjacent to the lake of Tiberias, both situated across the Jordan. So that when Christ came into the region of the Gadarenes, it is rightly said that he also came into that of the Gergesenes. Thus Tremellius in the notes to the New Testament, whose opinion the Blessed Doctor Glassius approves in Philologia Sacra page 829. And the Blessed Doctor Chemnitz in Harmony pages 693 and 707, and the Blessed Doctor Calixtus in Concordance page 144, establish the same. But if anyone desires to know more about the said towns, let him approach, besides the Blessed Doctor Chemnitz in the cited place, Christophorus Heidmann's Palestine chapter 9, § 76 following.)*

* ( Two demoniacs. Mark ch. 5, 2. & Luke ch. 8. v. 27. make mention of at least one demoniac, either because that one was more noble & famous, as it pleases August. b. 2 on the Harmony of the Gospels ch. 24, Strabo and Bede in their Commentaries, or because, as Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius & others wish, because one was more ferocious, being possessed by a legion of demons. And Chemnitz, Calixtus, and other commentators on this passage also embrace this explanation, or even because at least one wished to follow Christ, and when he was forbidden by Christ, by his command he proclaimed the benefit granted to him everywhere. As it pleases Dr. Calixtus. Furthermore, similar examples of this kind of synecdoche occur Matt. 20, 30. collated with Mark 10, 46. and Luke 18, 35. likewise Matt. 27, 44. & Mark 15, 32. collated with Luke 23, 39. and following. See more in B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 96.)*

* ( Coming out of the tombs. Just as these demoniacs were bodily possessed by devils and lived in the tombs, so even now the malignant spirit delights to dwell in those who are dead in sins, whose throat is like an open sepulcher Ps. 5, 11. Ps. 14, 3. Rom. 3, 13. from which the most foul stench of sins exhales, etc. See B. P. Homil. Acad. part 2. p. 210. Compare also at length on this matter Chrysost. homil. 29 on Matt. p. 286. Moreover, those demoniacs lived in the tombs because no one dared to receive them into their house as they were savage. What Maldonatus adds about the custom of placing crosses in tombs and sprinkling water consecrated by exorcisms, so that devils might not mock the bodies of the dead, are vain and reek of Papist superstition. Conzenius indeed struggles to bring aid to Maldonatus, but we oppose to both the oracle of Christ Matt. 17, 21. which Corn. à Lap. in vain restricts to devils of at least a higher kind. Contrary to what Chrysostom & Euthymius teach. It is truly a wonder that the Apostle, Eph. 6. while occupied in showing πανοπλίᾳ against evil spirits, either was ignorant of those weapons which the Jesuits recommend, or out of envy hid them from Christians.)*

Latin:

v. 28. In regionem Gergesenorum. Epiphan. contra Manich. έλθὼν εἰος.Casaub. in not. Gerasa & Genasara, unde lacus dictus est Genesareticus, duarum esse urbium nomina, non unius, nemo dubitabit, qui Ptolomaeum consuluerit. Gadara quonihil commune habet cum Genesaris. Euseb. de locis. Gerasa urbs insignis Arabiae. Quidam autem ipsam esse Gada-am existimant. Sed & Evangelium meminit Gerasenorum. Idem de Gadara. Urbs est trans Iordanem, contra Scythopolin & Tiberiadem ad Orientalem plagam. Sita in monte, ad cuius radices aquae calidae erumpunt, balneis desuper aedificatis. Vide etiam Suidam. And Osiand. in Harm. pro diversis Historiis habet, ac negat, demonstrari posse, quod Gadara & Gergesa, unam eandemque regionem denotent. Contrarium evincere conatur ex Ios. 12. & 13. ubi Gadara collocatur in finib. Amorrhaeorum, à quibus diversi fuerunt Gergeseni. Theoph. annotat, apud Marcum cap. 5. v. 1. legi in melioris notae libris Γεργεσηνῶν, ut apud Matthaeum. Strigelius in ὑῶομν.Eiusdem oppidi nomina sunt Gerasa, Gadara & Gergesa. De huius oppidi lacu scribit Strabo. Est in Gadaride aqua pestifera, quâ gustat â pecudes amittunt pilos, ungulas & cornua.

Gadara, teste Iosephlib. 17. cap. 13. erat Graecanici instituti, ergo mirum esse non debet, illic fuisse gregem porcorum, quorum carnes Iudaeis erant prohibitae. Matthaeus h. l. habet τῶν ΓεργεσηνῶνGergesenorum, nec ulla exemplaria variant. Marc. 5, 1. & Luc. 8. v. 26. habent Γαδαρηνῶν i. e. Gadarenorum. Syrus h. l. רנרריאGadara, à quo Gadareni, & Gergessa sive Gerassa, à quo Gergeseni, erant diversa oppida, ambo tamen vicina ad lacum Genezareth sita, & eorum fines erant commixti, ut cùm in horum regionem Christus venisse legitur, in illorum quoque regionem venisse intelligendus sit. Tremell. & ex eo Casaub. Tossan. Utrumque oppidum situm fuit in altero latere lacus Genesaretici ἀντιπεραν τῆς Γαλιλαίας, ut Lucas ait. Et Gadara in hoc tractu commemorant Plinius ac Ptolemaeus. *(Syrus h. l. ex Marc. 5, 1. legit Godaraeorum, consentiente cum reliquis Codd. tum excusis, tum MSS. quos viri docti contulerunt, etiam Altdorssino. Codex etiam quidam M. S. Graecus Collegii Gonvilli & Caii in Acad. Cantabr. legit h. l. γαδαρηνῶν. Idem quoque fecit Interpres Persa, qui itidem habet i. e. Gadarenorum. Marc. verò 5, 1. ac Luc. 8, 26. Aethio-tamen & Arabs receptam Graeci textus lectionem sequuti non solùm h. l. sed etiam in locis parallelis Marc. 5. 1. & Luc 8, 26.Gerge. seorum legunt: habet ille ubique hic verò quod vocabulum in Bibliis Londinensibus Matth. 8, 28. ita punctatum deprehenditur Marci verò 5, 1. ac Luc. 8, 26. h. m Quod attinet CoddGraecos Marc. 5, 1. maxima ibi quoad lectionē vocis huius est varietas. utut n. cōmuniter Codd. excusi sistant Γαδαρηνῶν, legit tamē tum Cod. Cantabr. tum Stephani 2. Γαρασηνῶν, -mò March. Veles. acSteph. 8. & 9. Codd. Γεργεσηνῶν.At-hanc lectionem esse probatiorum librorum, annotant Victor Antiochenus, Theophylactus, & is, cuius scholia Euthymii scholiis admista sunt: nam secundùm Matchaeum c. 8, 28. Graeci libri constanter ita legunt. Ita Franc. Lucas in not. ad Ev. Marc. Graecum. Sed cùm Codd. Graeci Luc. 8, 26. itidem constanter habeant Γαδαρηνῶν (nisi qui fortè ad Latinos correcti) nihil obstat, quò minus & apud Marc. recepta lectio retineatur: non quidem quasi eiusdem oppidi nomina Gadara, & Gergesa sive Gerasa fuerit, uti quidem Strigelius putat, (Ptolomaeus verò ut duas urbes distinguit) sed quia oppida maximè fuere vicina. Utraque spectavit ad Decapolis regionem, memorante Cluverio in Introd. l. 5. c. 22. utraque contermina lacui Tiberiadis, utraque sita trans Iordanem. Ut adeò cùm in Gadarenorum regionem venit Christus, etiam in Gergesenorum venisse, rectè dicatur. Ita Tremellius in notis ad N. T. cuius sententiam approbat B. D. Glassius Gr. S. pag 829. Idemque statuunt B. D. Chemn in Harm. p. 693. & 707. ac B. D. Calixtus in Conc. p. 144. Si quis verò de dictis oppidis plura cognoscere avet, adeat praeter B. D. Chemn. l. c. Christ. Heidmani Palaestinam c. 9. §. 76. seqq.)*

* ( Duo daemoniaci.Marcus c. 5, 2. & Lucas c. 8. v. 27. unius saltem daemoniaci mentionē faciunt, vel quia unus ille nobilior & famosior erat, uti August. l. 2. de Cons. Evang. c. 24. Strabo ac Bedae in Comm. placet, vel quod Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Euthymius & alii volunt, quia unus erat truculentior, quippe à legione daemonum obsessus. Et hanc explicationem amplectuntur quoque Chemnitius, Calixtus, aliique Comm. in h. l. vel etiam quia unus saltem Christum sequi voluit, & cùm à Christo prohiberetur, eiusdem iussu beneficium sibi praestitum passim depraedicavit. Ut D. Calixto arridet. Coeterùm similia huiusmodi synecdoches exempla occurrunt Matth. 20, 30. coll. cum Marc. 10, 46. ac Luc. 18, 35. it. Matth. 27, 44. & Marc. 15, 32. coll. cum Luc. 23, 39. seqq. Vid. plura apud B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 96.)*

* ( Emonuentis egressi. Sicuti daemoniaci hi s. corporaliter à Diabolis obsessi in sepulcris habitarunt, ita etiamnum malignus spiritus gaudet habitare in illis, qui sunt in peccatis mortui, quorum guttur est instar patentis sepulcri Ps. 5, 11.Ps. 14, 3.Rom. 3, 13. ex quo teterrimus peccatorum foetor exhalat &c. Vid. B. P. Homil. Acad. part. 2. p. 210. Conf. etiam prolixè in hanc rem Chrysost. homil. 29 in Matth. p. 286. Habitabant autem isti daemoniaci in sepulcris, quia nemo eos tanquam saevos domo excipere audebat. Quae Maldonatus addit de consuetudine, in sepulcris ponendi cruces & sacratam exorcismis aquam adspergendi, ne diaboli mortuorum corporibus illudant, vana sunt ac superstitionem redolent Papisticam. Suppetias quidem ferre Maldonato satagit Conzenius, sed opponimus utrique oraculum Christi Matth. 17, 21. quod Corn. à Lap. frustrà ad altioris saltem generis diabolos restringit. Contrà ac Chrysost. & Euthymius docent. Mirum verò, Apostolum, Eph. 6. dum in ostendenda πανοπλίᾳ adversùs malos Sp. S. occupatus est, arma illa, quae Iesuitae co-endāt, vel ignorasse, vel ex invidiâ Christianos celasse.)*

## 8:29
*( v. 29.What have we to do with thee? See examples of this in the Hebrews Jos. 22, 24.2. Sam. 16, 10.2. Chron. 35, 21. The Greeks otherwise insert πρᾶγμα, as Beza shows from Demosthenes and Herodotus in this place.)*

Jesus Son of GOD. Hilary, book 6 of the Trinity, near the end: Truth elicited a confession from the unwilling, and pain testified to the power of nature. They are conquered by virtue, when they abandon bodies long possessed, they render honor, while they confess the nature of God; that He is the Son of God among these things, Christ testifies both by work and by name. Jerome: That confession is not of the will, which the reward of the confessor follows, but an extortion of necessity, which drives the unwilling. Irenaeus, book 4 against heresies, ch. 14, p. 242. Christ received testimony from all, that He is truly man, and that He is truly God, from the Father, from the Spirit, and from the Angels, from creation itself, from men and from apostate spirits, and from the erroneous, and from the enemy, and lastly from death itself. But since the Devil is the Father of lies John 8, 44. the Lord Dr. Walther in his Harmony thinks he calls Christ the Son of God to this end, that if men hear this, they might conclude that this testimony is given to Christ by the Spirit of lies, rather than that He is the Son of GOD. It is also usually asked here: Whether the Demons knew that Jesus was the Son of GOD? The negative seems to be able to be proven from Matt. 4, 3. & 6. & 1. Cor. 2, 8. The affirmative [is proven] both from their own confession in this place, Luke 4, 41. Mark 1, 24. and from Mark 1, 34. ch. 3, 12. and the assertion of Luke in the said place. The blessed Pareus discusses this question in his book on evil Angels, ch. 6, § 19, and finally concludes that the demons knew Jesus was the Son of God, not through certainty of knowledge, but through conjecture of firm opinion, and that they are to be considered as suspecting rather than knowing. Furthermore, it is by no means credible that the Demons knew the mystery of the death of Christ, that is, that through it the human race was to be liberated from their tyranny: for if they had known this, they would never have incited Judas to betrayal, or the Jews to the crucifixion of Christ, demanded with so many outcries. Compare more in the notes to Mark 1, 34. )* *(

*( To torment us before the time. Distinguish here between the beginnings of torment, and the increases. For as in damned men, so also in devils, the torments will receive their greatest increases on the day of the final judgment, as much intensively as extensively. Therefore, in respect of consummated torments, evil spirits are said to be tormented less, while they still move about in the air, and are not yet shut up in the infernal prison. See Eph. 2, 2.c. 6, 12.)*

*( Before the time, that is, before the day of the final judgment. Thus August. book 8 de C. D. ch. 23. Chrysost. hom. 44. on John. Euthymius on this passage. See also 2. Peter 2, 4. Jude v. 6. Apoc. 20, 14. The Photinian Smalcius errs entirely, when, disputing against D. Frantz, he denies that Christ is speaking here of any affliction that will be at the end of the world. p. 414. Compare Luc. 8, 31.)*

Latin:

*( v. 29.Quid nobis tecum. Vid. Ebr. huius exempla Ios. 22, 24.2. Sam. 16, 10.2. Par. 35, 21. Graeci aliàs inserunt πρᾶγμα, ceu ex Demosth. & Herodoto ostendit Beza in h. l.)*

*( Iesu Fili DEI. Hilarius l. 6. de Trin. circa finem: Invitisveritas elicuit confessionem, & naturae potestatem testabatur dolor obediendi. Virtute vincuntur, cùm possessa diu corpora deserunt, honorem reddunt, dum naturam confitentur Dei se inter haec Filium, Christus & opere testatur & nomine. Hieronymus: Non voluntatis ista confessio est, quam praemium sequitur confitentis, sed necessitatis extorsio, quae agit invitos. Irenaeus lib. 4. adv. haer. c. 14. p. 242. Christus ab omnibus accepit testimonium, quoniam verè homo, & quoniam verè Deus, à Patre, à Spiritu, & ab Angelis, ab ipsa conditione, ab hominibus & ab apostaticis spiritibus, & ab erroneis, & ab inimico & novissimè ab ipsâ morte. Cùm verò Diabolus Pater mendacii sit, Ioh. 8, 44. existimat Dn. D. Walth. in Harm. eum hoc fine Christum Dei Filium vocare, ut si homines audiant, hoc testimonium Christo dari à Spiritu mendacii, potiùs colligant, ipsum non esse Filium DEI. Quaeri hîc etiam solet: An Daemones cognoverint, Iesum esse Filium DEI? negativa videtur probari posse ex Matth. 4, 3. & 6. & 1. Cor. 2, 8. Affirmativa tum ex ipsorum confessione h. l. Luc. 4, 41.Marc. 1, 24. tum ex Marc. 1, 34.c. 3, 12. ac Lucae d. l. adsertione. Ventilat quaestionem hanc B. Par. L. de Angelis malis c. 6. §. 19. ac tandem concludit, quòd noverint daemones, Iesum esse Filium Dei, non per certitudinem scientiae, sed per coniecturam opinionis firmae, quodq; magis suspicari, quàm nosse censendi sint. Praeterea minimè credibile est, Doemones scivisse mysterium mortis Christi, h. e quòd per eam genus humanum ex ipsorum tyrannide esset liberandum: etenim si hoc cognovissent, nunquam Iudam ad proditionem, aut Iudaeos ad crucifixionem Christi tot clamoribus impetratam incitassent. Conf. plura in not. ad Marc. 1, 34.)*

*( Ad cruciandum nos ante tempus. Dist. hîc inter cruciaetuum initia, & incrementa. Uti enim in hominibus damnatis, ita etiam in Diabolis cruciatus maxima in die iudiciis extremi capient in crementa, tam intensivè, quàm extensivè. Consummatorum igitur cruciatuum respectu dicuntur mali spiritus minùs torqueri, dum adhuc in aëre versantur, nec infernali carceri inclusi sunt. Vid. Eph. 2, 2.c. 6, 12.)*

*( Ante tempus, h. e. ante extremi iudicii diem. Ita August. l. 8. de C. D. c. 23. Chrysost. hom. 44. in Ioh. Euthymius in h. l. Vid. etiam 2. Petr. 2, 4. Iudae v. 6. Apoc. 20, 14. Errat omninò Smalcius Photinianus, dum contra D. Frantzium disputans negat, Christum loqui hîc de afflictione aliquâ, futurâ in mundi fine. p. 414. Conf. Luc. 8, 31.)*

## 8:30
v. 30. Gordonus Huntlaeus tries to prove from this passage that the Greek text is corrupt. For it is held in the Greek, A herd of swine was far from them. But in Latin more correctly. Not far. And I do not doubt, says Maldonatus, that the Latin reading is more uncorrupted. Because Mark & Luke teach, But there were there, that is, in that place. And Luke; ὐν τῷ ὄρει on the mountain. Mark, πρὸς τὰ ὄρη, near the mountains, which it is certain were near the lake. And because for that reason Christ granted that they might rush into the swine, so that those who were present might know from the destruction of the swine how many and how savage the demons were, which they would not have known if they had not seen the swine: nor would they have seen them if they had been far away. But Chamier replies in vol. 1 of his Panstr. book 12. ch. 13. §. 40. 1. It is read thus in Latin, against the testimony of all Greek copies, which testimony we ought not to disturb rashly. 2. The Greek reading has no inconvenience. They would not have seen, says Maldonatus, those who were present with Christ! But it is false that those things which are said to be μακρὰν absent are to be defined by such a distance that they cannot be perceived by the eyes. Luc. 15. v. 20.Matth. 27. v. 55. 3. The Greek reading is truer, so that the same μακρὰν is with Matthew, which is ὐν τῷ ὄρει with Luke and ρὸς τὰ ὄρη with Mark. For it is not likely that the swine were mixed with the men, that is, that they were in the same place with Christ and the others, but removed by some distance, namely grazing not on the shore itself, or if you prefer near the tombs, but at the roots of the mountain. *(Other Papists also criticize the same reading, such as Conzen, Franc. Lucas &c. Indeed, even the Calvinists Beza and Piscator. (to whom the Jesuit Conzen also appeals: but Chamier rightly departs from them in the cited book.) But beyond necessity, as has already been shown, and as the blessed D. Glassius also excellently taught in book 1 of Philol. S. section 2. p. 181. To whose observations I add at least this, that not only the most ancient MS Codex of Greek Eclogues which is held in the Nuremberg Library and the Fathers, Greek as well as Latin, such as Chrysostom, Theophylact, Hilary, Jerome &c. but also the Oriental Interpreters, namely the Syrian and the Ethiopian, confirm the received reading. The Arab, however, agrees with the Vulgate, for it has according to the Roman edition, i. e. & non erat longè &c. but according to the London and Leiden i. e. & erat ibi. Just as Luc. 8, 32. Nay, even the Persian, who explicitly: & erat prope eos. So constant is the reading of the Greek Codices here, that not even a single Codex out of those sixteen with which the Parisians compared the Greek edition of the N. T. approves the Latin Vulgate. Add that not one of those other sixteen, from which the Marquis Velesius Petrus Fraxardus of Spain collected various readings, (those eight indeed were taken from the Library of the King of Spain,) stands for the Latin reading. Nay, not even any of the MS. Codices which the English, in the preparation of the Polyglot Bible , gathered from almost the whole world, reads otherwise here than the printed ones. Therefore, it would be of great rashness to establish that so many Greek Codices are corrupted here.)*

Latin:

v. 30. Gordonus Huntlaeus ex h. l. evincere conatur, textum Graecum esse corruptum. In Graeco enim habetur, Longè ab illis erat grex porcorum. At Latinè rectiùs. Non longè. Nec dubito; inquit Maldonatus, Latinam lectionem incorruptiorem esse. Quia Marcus & Lucas docent, Erant autem ibi, id est, in eo loco. Et Lucas;ὐν τῷ ὄρει in monte. Marcus,πρὸς τὰ ὄρη, iu-ta montes, quos prope lacum fuisse certum est. Et quia propterea Christus concessit, ut in porcos irruerent, ut qui aderant, ex porcorum interitu cognoscerent, quàm multi & quàm saevi Doemones essent, quodnecognovissent, si porcos non vidissent: nec vidissent, si procul fuissent. Ast resp. Chamier t. l. Panstr. l. 12. c. 13. §. 40. 1. Latinè ita legitur, reclamante fide omniū Graecorum exemplarium, quā fidē non temerè solicitare debemus. 2. Graeca lectio nihil habet incommodi. Non vidissent, inquit Maldonatus, qui Christo aderant! At falsum est, ea quae μακρὰν abesse dicuntur, tanto spacio de finienda, ut non possint ea oculis usurpari. Luc. 15. v. 20.Matth. 27. v. 55. 3. Verior lectio Graeca, ut sit idem μακρὰν apud Matthaeum. quod ὐν τῷ ὄρει apud Lucam & ρὸς τὰ ὄρη apud Marcum. Neque enim verisimile est, permixtos fuisse porcos viris, id est, in eodem ipso loco fuisse cum Christo & reliquis, sed aliquanto remotos spacio, nempe pascentes non in ipso littore, sive mavis iuxta monumenta, sed in montis radicibus. *(Eandem lectionem suggillant etiam alii Pontificii, uti Conzen, Franc. Lucas &c. Imò & Calviniani Beza ac Piscator. (ad quos quidem Iesuita quoque Conzen provocat: sed meritò ab illis discedit Chamier l. c.) Verùm praeter necessitatem, uti iam ostensum est, & egregiè quoque docuit B. D. Glassius l. 1. Philol. S. tr. 2. p. 181. Cuius observationibus hoc saltem addo, quòd non solùm antiquissimus Codex MS. Eclogarum Graec. qui habetur in Bibl. Norib. ac Patres, Graeci pariter & Latini, uti Chrysostomus, Theophylactus. Hilarius, Hieronymus &c. sed etiam Orientales Interpp., Syrus nempe & Aethiops lectionem receptam confirment. Arabs tamen Vulgato adstipulatur, habet enim iuxta edit. Romanam, i. e. & non erat longè &c. iuxta Londinensem verò ac Leidensem i. e. & erat ibi. Prorsus uti Luc. 8, 32. Imò & Persa, qui disertè: & erat prope eos. Adeò verò constans Graecorum Codd. lectio hîc est, ut ne unicus quidem Codex è sedecim illis, cum quibus Parisienses Graecam N. T. editionem contulerunt, Vulgatam Latinam adprobet. Adde quòd nec unus è sedecim illis aliis, è quibus Marchio Velesius Petrus Fraxardus Hisp. varias lectiones collegit, (illorum verò octo è Bibliothecâ Regis Hispaniarum erant depromti,) pro lectione Latinâ stet. Imò ne ullus deniq; Codd. MS. quos Angli in adornatione Bibliorum Polyglott-è toto propè terrarum orbe conquisiverunt, aliter hîc, atque excusi, legit. Magnae itaque temeritatis esset statuere, tot Codd. Graecos hîc corruptos esse.)*

## 8:31
v. 31. Permitte nobis. Tertull. de fuga in persec. cap. 2. p. 582. The legion of the Devil did not have power over the herd of swine, unless it had obtained it from GOD, so far is it from having it over the sheep of GOD. I can say that the bristles of the swine were then numbered by God, much less the hairs of the Saints. *(That the devils can harm no one even in the smallest part, however much they may wish, unless divine permission is granted, besides the present example, is also shown by the passages Exod. 8, 18. Iob. 1, 7. 12. c. 2, 6. Whence rightly August. l. 2. de Civ. DEI c. 23. Demons can do only as much as they are permitted by the secret command of the Almighty. The same he repeats l. 7. c. 35. and l. 11. de Gen. ad litt. c. 22. Therefore, his admonition in the Comm. on Psal. 36. is to be observed: Whatever happens to the just man, let him attribute it to the divine will, not to the power of the enemy; he can rage, he can strike, if He does not will it, he cannot. Let more things pertaining to this be compared in Aphor. Pract. B. Par. tit. Diabolus.)*

*( Et ait: Abite. The imperative is to be explained permissively in this place, for the demons asked Christ, ἵνα ἐπετρέψη, Luc. 8, 32. Compare this verse with the preceding one, and there is added in Luke καὶ έπέτρεψεν ἀυτοῖς i.e. & he permitted them. Thus also elsewhere in the Holy Scripture, the imperative does not always indicate a command, but also συγχώρησιν, as is evident from 1. Reg. 22, 22.2. Reg. 2, 17. & it sometimes has the force of dissuading, as Ioh. 13, 17.Iud. 10, 14.Es. 21, 5.Ezech. 20, 39.Matth. 26, 45.Apoc. 22, 11.
