Question: Did Christ do an injury to the Gergesenes by permitting the devils to drown their swine? Answer: by denying. For the Lord himself is the supreme owner of all things, and just as all things which we have are from him and he gave all things from his own hand, which the wisest of mortals Solomon 1. Par. 29, 14.16. and Job ch. 1, 21. well acknowledged, so in taking away the same he rightly uses the right of recovery without any injury to us. Furthermore, it is one thing to do evil, another to permit it. But why Christ permitted that loss to be inflicted upon the Gergesenes will be advised at Marc. 5, 13.

Latin:

v. 31.Pormitte nobis. Tertull. de fuga in persec. cap. 2. p. 582. Ne in porcorum gregem Diaboli legio habuit potestatem, nisi eam de DEO impetrasset, tantum abest, ut in oves DEI habeat. Possum dicere, porcorum set as tunc numeratasapud Deum fuisse, nedum capillos Sanctorum. *(Quod diaboli nulli vel minimâ etiam ex parte nocere possint, ut ut quàm maximè velint, nisi divina accedat permissio, praeter exemplum praesens, ostendunt quoq; loca Exod. 8, 18.Iob. 1, 7.12.c. 2, 6. Unde rectè August. l. 2. de Civ. DEI c. 23. Daemones tantum possunt, quantum secreto omnipotentis imperio permittuntur. Idem repetit l. 7. c. 35. ac l. 11. de Gen. ad litt. c. 22. Observandum igitur eiusdem monitum Comm. in Psal. 36.Quicquid acciderit iusto, voluntati divinae deputet, non potestati inimici, saevire ille potest, ferire, si ille noluerit, non potest. Conferantur plura huc facientia in Aphor. Pract. B. Par. tit. Diabolus.)*

*( Et ait: Abite. Imperativus permissivè h. l. exponendus, togarunt enim Christum daemones, ἵνα ἐπετρέψη,Luc. 8, 32. Conf. hic vers. praeced. additurque apud Lucam καὶ έπέτρεψεν ἀυτοῖς i. e. & permisit eis. Sic & alibi in Sc. S. Imp. non semper praeceptum, sed etiam συγχώρησιν Indicat, ceu patet ex 1. Reg. 22, 22.2. Reg. 2, 17. & dehortandi quandoque vim habet, uti Ioh. 13, 17.Iud. 10, 14.Es. 21, 5.Ezech. 20, 39.Matth. 26, 45.Apoc. 22, 11. Q. a. Annon Christus iniuriâ affecerit Gergesenos, permittendo diabolis, ut porcos illorum submergerent? Resp. negando. Est enim ipse Dominus rerum omnium supremus, adeoque sicuti omnia, quae habemus, ab ipso sunt & de manu suâ dedit omnia, quod mortalium sapientissimi Salomon 1. Par. 29, 14.16. ac Iobus c. 1, 21. benè agnoverunt, ita in iisdem auferendis repetundarum iure rectè nec ullâ nostrâ iniuriâ utitur. Praeterea aliud est facere, aliud permittere malum. Cur verò Christus permiserit, damnum illud Gergesenis inferri, monebitur ad Marc. 5, 13.)*

## 8:32
v. 32. Syr. the whole herd directed itself upon the rock, and fell from there i.e. they cast themselves into the sea (Ethiopian: i.e. & behold the whole herd running in fear, came into the sea etc. Persian: the swine seized by horror went into the high precipice, and cast themselves into the sea. With the omission of what is in the Greek and others: & they died.

By the sea, into which the swine were cast, some understand a lake water, which was held in some part of the Gadarene field, not even drinkable by cattle without the danger of present harm. Strabo book 7. αδαρην In the Gadarene field, however, there is a certain water from a lake, very bad, by the tasting of which cattle lose their hair, hooves, and horns. And Ziegler suspects that this lake was not long after obstructed by the neighbors with earth, fearing, namely, that a plague might arise from the stench of the carcasses, and abominating the lake even more because of the presence of the more horrible demons, which was the cause why historians who lived after Strabo did not mention this lake. There was to the East of Gadara or Gadaris a lake, from thence called Gadarene, of most pestilential waters, indeed such that when tasted they stripped cattle of their hair, hooves, and horns. Into this the swine were cast, but not into the thermal springs, which the Gadarenes likewise had near their city, nor into the lake of Gennesaret, washing the city from the West. Thus Ziegler. But Casaubon refutes this opinion in his notes on this place and prefers the opinion of Jerome, who lived in those places, that the lake of Gennesaret is to be understood: for thus he writes in the book on Hebrew places. Today, above the mountain, a small village is shown near the lake of Gennesaret, into which the swine were cast down.

But why did they keep swine, when the Jews abhor swine's flesh? Resp. The Jews abhorred it, not the Greeks, such as Isaac Casaubon demonstrates the Gadarenes to have been in Exercitation 13 on the Annals of Baronius 1, from Josephus, who in book 17, chapter 13, in explaining the affairs of Pompey, writes that he took away from the Jews ἑλληνάδας πόλεις the Greek cities which were in Coele Syria, and among these he names Gadara. Then from Strabo, who writes κὶ ἀυτὴν ἐχιδιάσαντο Ιουδαῖοι, that the Jews also made Gadara their own, by force indeed, when it was a Greek city. 3. From the abundance of philosophers, philologists, and orators born in Gadara. (*B. D. Calixt. Concord. p. 144 thinks it likely, since those regions were near Arabia, that foreigners lived among the Jews, whose the swine were. Let also Mr. Dilherr, vol. 1, Disputations p. 195, and Wilh. Schick. מהמ page 148 be compared. Some add, among whom is also B. Chemn. H. E. p. 714, that those Jews did not indeed eat, but yet kept swine, namely for other uses, e.g., that they might sell them to the Gentiles, etc. See Lapide on Luke 8.*)

Latin:

v. 32. Syr. totus grex direxit se super rupem, & deciderunt inde i. e. praecipitarunt se in mare (Aethiops: i. e. & ecce currens totus grex praetimore, in mare venerunt &c. Persa: porci horrore correpti in praecipitium abierunt altū, & in mare se deiecerunt. Omisso quod in Gr. & aliis est: & mortui sunt.)*

Per mare, in quod porci praecipitati, quidam intelligunt aquam lacustam, quae in aliqua parte agri Gadaretani habebatur, ne pecoribus quidem sine periculo praesentis noxae potabilis. Strabo lib. 7. αδαρην In agro autem Gadareno est aqua quaedam ex lacu pessima, quâ degustatâ pecora pilos, ungues & cornua amittunt. Ac suspicatur Zieglerus, lacum istum non multò pòst à vicinis terrâ fuisse obstructum, timentibus scilicet, ne ex faetore cadaverum pestis oriretur, & lacum ob praesentiā horridiorū daemonum magis etiam abominantibus quae causa fuerit, cur Historici qui post Strabonem vixerunt, huius lacus non meminerint. Fuit Gadarae vel Gadaris ad Orientem lacus, exinde Gadarenus nuncupatus, aquarum pestilentissimarum, quippe quae gustatae pilis, unguibus; cornibus pecora exuerent. In hunc porci praecipitati sunt, non autem in thermas, quas itidem ad suam urbem habuere Gadareni, nec in lacum Genezarethicum, urbem ab Occidente alluentem. Ita Zieglerus. Sed hanc sententiam refellit Casaub. in notis h. l. ac praefert sententiam Hieronymi, qui in illis locis versatus est, quod intelligendus sit lacus Genesareticus: Sic enim scribit in lib. de loc. Hebraic. Hodie supra montem viculus monstratur iuxta stagnum Genezareth, in quod porci praecipitati sunt.

At cur aluerunt porcos, cùm Iudaei à carneporcina abhorreant? Resp. Iudaei abhorruerunt, non Graecanici, quales Gadarenos fuisse demonstrat Isaacus Casaubonus exerc. 13. ad annal. Baron. 1. ex Iosepho, qui l. 17. c. 13. in rebus Pompeii exponendis scribit, ademisse illum Iudaeis ἑλληνάδας πόλεις urbes Graecanicas, quae erant in Coele Syria, atque inter has nominat Gadaram. Deindè ex Strabone, qui scribit κὶ ἀυτὴν ἐχιδιάσαντο Ιουδαῖοι, Gadaram quoque Iudaei suam fecerunt, per vim nempe, cùm esset urbe Graecanica. 3. ex copia Philosophorum, Philologorum & Oratorum Gadaris ortorum. (*B. D. Calixt. Concord. p. 144. veresimile putat, cùm regiones illae vicinae essent Arabiae, inter Iudaeos habitasse alienigenas, quorum porci fuerint. Conferantur etiam Dn. Dilherr. t. 1. Dispp. p. 195. Wilh. Schick. מהמ pag. 148. Addunt nonnulli, quos inter & B Chemn. H. E. p. 714. quòd Iudaei illi non quidem comederint, sed tamen aluerint porcos, nempe ad alios usus, v. g. ut gentilibus venderent &c. Vid. Lapide ad Luc 8.)*

## 8:34
v. 34 The Gergesenes are more χοιροφίλοι, than χριςοφίλοι. Greeks, commentary on this place μακρὰν. *(Augustine in Epistle of John, tract 6, For the sake of a certain mystery and by a certain dispensation the Lord allowed the demons to go into the swine: that He might show that the devil rules in those who lead the life of swine.)*

*( And behold the whole city. The metonymy of the container for the contained is noted, city namely is put for inhabitants, of which metonymy it is permitted to find examples elsewhere also here and there. See Josh. 8, 7 Jer. 4, 29 Matt. 3, 5 c. 10, 15 c. 11, 20 c. 12, 25 Mark 1, 33 c. 6, 11 Luke 4, 43 Acts 8, 25. The Syrian and the Ethiopian retain the metonymical expression here.

The Arab, however, and the Persian render it literally.)*

* (Summa. In the present chapter, it is treated I. of the healing of certain sick persons, such as the paralyticv. 2., the woman with an issue of bloodv. 20. 21. 22., the two blind men,v. 28. 29. 30., the demon-possessed man,v. 32. 33. II. of the calling of Matthew v. 9. III. of the question of the disciples of John and Christ's response to it, v. 14. 1-. IV. of the resuscitation of the daughter of Jairus, v. 18. 19.23. 24. 25. V. of Christ's preaching and the performance of miracles v. 35. and following.)*

Latin:

v. 34 Gergeseni magis sunt χοιροφίλοι, quàm χριςοφίλοι. Graeci comment. h. l. μακρὰν. *(August. in ep. Ioh. tr. 6. Certi mysterii gratiâ & certâ dispensatione dimisit Dominus daemones ire in porcos: ut ostendat, diabolum in eis dominari, qui vitam porcorum gerunt.)*

*( Et ecce tota civitas. Nota est metonymia continentis pro contento, civit as nempe ponitur pro incolis, cuius metonymiae & alibi quoque passim reperire exempla licet. Vid. Ios. 8, 7.Ier. 4. 29.Matth 3, 5.c. 10, 15.c. 11, 20.c. 12, 25.Marc. 1, 33.c. 6, 11.Luc. 4, 43.Act. 8, 25. Syrus & Aethiops metonymicam locutionē hîc retinent.

Arabs verò & Persa propriè reddunt.)*

* (Summa. Agitur in praesenti capite I. de quorundam aegrotorum sanatione, uti paralyticiv. 2.haemorr housaev. 20. 21. 22.duorum coecorum,v. 28. 29. 30.Daemoniaci,v. 32. 33. II. de Matthaei vocatione v. 9. III. de Iohannis Discipulorum quaestione ac Christi ad eam responsione, v. 14. 1-. IV. de filiae Iairi resuscitatione, v. 18. 19.23. 24. 25. V. de Christi praedicatione ac miraculorum operatione v. 35. seqq.)*

## 9:1
v. 1. Ἐις τὴνἰδίαν πὸλιν. Some understand Capernaum. Theophylact from Chrysostom: Bethlehem brought forth Christ, Nazareth reared him, Capernaum had him as an inhabitant. Jerome understands Nazareth, which is called the city of Christ, because he was reared in it, just asLuke 2. 3. ἴδια πόλις of whom it is said, from whom is Jerome is followed by Benedictus Arias Montanus. But Augustine, in book 2 of the Harmony of the Gospels, chapter 25, more correctly determines, and gathers from Mark chapter 2, that it is Capernaum, where all the people were expecting him. *(And this opinion, after Theophylact and Euthymius, is embraced by almost all recent interpreters. Among the Lutherans: B. D. Chemnitz, H. E. p. 5. 96. & 719., D. Quistorpius, the Nuremberg Biblical Glossators, D. Calixtus, H. E. p. 145., Heidmann in Palestine, c. 9. §. 63., Bünting in Itinerary, p. 12; from the Pontificians: Tirinus, Maldonatus, Jansenius, Conzen, Corn. à Lapide, etc.)* This is called the city of Christ, 1. because immediately after he had begun his ministry, he transferred his dwelling there, John 2. v. 12.Luke 4, v. 31. 2. because he had a rented house there, for which he paid the tax Matthew 17. v. 24. 3. because he held more frequent sermons there and performed more miracles Matthew 11. v. 23. Chrysostom, homily 30 on Matthew, posits this reason, because Christ dwelt there for the most part. Briefly: Capernaum is called the city of Christ, 1. on account of his civil inhabitation. 2. on account of the more abundant exhibition of doctrine and miracles. 3. on account of the spiritual interpretation of the name. Capernaum in our language is beautiful village, it is denoted that Christ wishes to dwell in a heart adorned with virtues. *(Furthermore, concerning the location and pleasantness of the city of Capernaum, see Heidmann in Palestine, c. 9. §. 60. and following; Adrichomius in the description of the Holy Land; Bünting in Itinerary, p. 11 and following; B. D. Chemnitz in H. E. p. 224. 295.)*

CHAPTER IX.

If cities offer hospitality to the Gospel, and admit Christ with the ministry of the Word and Sacraments, they will become the own cities of Christ.

Latin:

v. 1. Ἐις τὴνἰδίαν πὸλιν. Quidam intelligunt Capernaum. Theoph. ex Chrysost. Bethleh-peperit Christuni, Nazareth educavit, Capernaum habuit-ncolam. Hieronym. intelligit Nazaretham, quae dicatur vitas Christi, propterea quòd in ea fuerit educatus, sicutLuc. 2. 3.ἴδια πόλιςcuiusdicitur, ex qua est oru-n--- Hieron. sequitur Bened. Ar. Mont. Sed rectiùs statuit Aug. lib. 2. de cons. Evang. cap. 25. & ex Marco cap. 2. colligit, esse Capernaum, ubi omnis populus eum expectabat. *(Et hanc sententiam post Theophylactum & Euthymium recentiores Interpp. amplectuntur ferè omnes. Ex Lutheranis B. D. Chemn. H. E. p. 5. 96. & 719. D. Quistorpius, Glossatores Bibl. Noriberg. D. Calixtus H. E. p. 145. Heidm. in Palaest. c. 9. §. 63. Būnt. in Itin. p. 12 ex Pontif. Tirinus, Maldonatus, Iansenius, Conzen, Corn. à Lapide &c.)* Dicitur haec Christi civitas 1. quia statim, postquàm ministerium suum exorsus fuerat, habitationem suam eò transtulit, Ioh. 2. v. 12.Luc. 4, v. 31. 2. quia ibi habuit domum conductitiam, pro qua numeravit censum Matth. 17. v. 24. 3. quia frequentiores ibi habuit conciones & plura miracula edidit Matth. 11. v. 23. Chrysost. hom. 30. in Matth. hanc ponit rationem, quia Christus plurimùm ibidem degit. Breviter: Dicitur Capernaum Christi civitas 1. propter civilem inhabitationem. 2. propter doctrinae & miraculorum uberiorem exhibitionem. 3. propter spiritualem nominis interpretationem. Capernaum in nostra lingua est Sch-ndorff/ denotatur, quòd Christus in corde virtutibus exornato habitare velit. *(Porrò de urbis Capernaum situ & amoenitate vid. Heidm. in Palaest. c. 9. §. 60. seqq. Adrich. in descr. terr. Sanctae. B-ntingus. in Itin. p. 11. seqq. B. D. Chemn. in H. E. p. 224. 295.)*

CAPUT IX.

Si civitates Evangelio praebent hospitium, & Christum cum ministerio verbi & Sacramentorum admittunt, fient propriae civitates Christi.

## 9:2
*(v. 2. Their faith. Namely, both of the bearers and of the paralytic himself as well. For that the paralytic had faith is clear 1. from the lowering down. 2. from Christ's address. Conf. John 1, 12. Gal. 26. 3. from the remission of sin, see Rom. 4, 5. 4. from the information of Holy Scripture, Hab. 2, 4.)*

Chrysost. Homil. 3. on Matt. Unless this paralytic had had faith, he would not have suffered himself to be lowered through the roof. *(The Jesuits Barradius, Salmeron, and Tirinus, and also the Bishop of Ghent, Corn. Jansenius, in this place, embrace Chrysostom's exposition, that the relative their ought to be referred not only to those carrying, but also to the paralytic himself. Corn. à Lapide likewise concedes that not only Chrysostom, but also Theophylact and Euthymius understand it of the faith of the paralytic himself, yet nonetheless he himself maintains that Christ speaks more of the faith of those offering, than of the sick man and paralytic himself.) Thom. de Trugillo in thesaur. concion. vol. 1. page 589. col. 2. edit. Lyon. Jesus called the paralytic son, in which it is shown that he was saved also by his own faith, for by this name Christ calls believers, to whom He gave the power to become children of GOD. Lyran. in this place. They do not seem to speak well, who say that their refers only to those offering, so that you were healed only through the faith of those offering. The same is said by Alb. Magnus and Dion. Carthus. in this place. In vain, therefore, does Staplet. promt. Cathol. part. 1. p. 267, deny from Hieron. and Ambrose that this paralytic had faith, because for receiving the remission of sins one's own faith is required. *(Corn. à Lapide also willingly grants this same thing: for intending to prove that Christ in this place does not speak of justifying faith, but of the faith of miracles and health, he urges this, that Christ speaks more of the faith of those offering, which could not justify the sick man, than of the sick man himself. The Jesuit Conzen also explicitly in this place Foreign faith never effects justification in another, it sometimes obtains certain temporal benefits. See notes on Acts 27, 24.)*

But if foreign faith does not effect justification in another, or does not impart the remission of sins to another, (which our own people also assert, and from this principle prove against the Papists that baptized infants have true faith, and are justified and saved by their own, not foreign faith) why is this reason brought forward, that Christ for this reason remitted sins to the paralytic, because He saw their, i.e., both the paralytic's and those offering's, faith? Resp. Two benefits were exhibited to the paralytic, bodily healing, and spiritual: the moving cause of the latter, not the former, was the regard for the faith of those offering. Yet the faith of the pious can obtain for a man still existing as impious conversion and his own faith, by which he may subsequently be justified. See D. Hann. in this place.)*

Petrus Cluniac. referring to Cent. Magd. 12. col. 835. The faith of the bearers obtains health for the paralytic. Therefore, the faith of another also saves an infant. *(The Jesuit Maldonatus is also quite bold in this place, writing: What madness it is, to prove that we are justified by faith alone to produce testimonies in which it is not a matter of one's own, but of another's faith. And yet, today, in the judgment of many, and especially in his own, they alone are wise. Although the Jesuit Contzen is forced to admit that the paralytic had faith, he nevertheless writes: The Evangelist speaks only of the faith of the bearers.)* Resp. The paralytic was not destitute of faith. Coster. part. 1. Conc. p. 524. Note that Christ did not attend only to the faith of the bearers, but to that of the sick man himself who had permitted himself to be carried and to be lowered with such great danger. *(The same also asserts the aforementioned Jesuit in Euchir. p. 254. where he says expressly: The paralytic underwent the danger of entering the house through the roof with great faith and hope, yet afterwards he heard, 'Take heart, son, your sins are forgiven' . As if he were saying, be of good courage, now I forgive you your sins, also about to cure the disease of the body. Similarly, the Jesuit Maldonatus also says expressly in this place: that the others (i.e., those who were healed in body by Christ, with the exception of Malchus alone), who were cured by faith, we believe were healed in soul not by faith alone, but nevertheless by the same faith by which they were healed in body. These confessions must be opposed, both to Iohannes Paludanus, Doctor of Theology and Professor in the Academy of Louvain, writing quite rashly in his Vindiciae on this place, p. 219: In no way can the words of Christ: 'Take heart, son, your sins are forgiven,' be understood of that act, by which one believes that his sins are certainly forgiven him through the death of Christ: But at least of that act by which those who were healed by Christ believed that he had the power of healing, and that they could be helped by him: and to Corn. à Lap. in this place, asserting: It is a matter here of the faith of miracles and of health, which is distinguished by us from justifying faith. Contzenius also agrees with Corn. à Lapide in this place. Moreover, from the fact that the remission of sins is ascribed here to faith alone, the Orthodox rightly infer that faith alone justifies. Bell. excepts in l. 1. de Iustif. c. 13. §. Hanc igitur, that it is hinted here that hope is a disposition to justification and the remission of sins. Henricus Lancelotz also uses almost the same exception in Anat. hom. Christ. p. 73.)* But if by hope they understand trust, i.e., the fiducial apprehension of the merit of Christ, they do not oppose us, as we who expressly constitute trust as a part of true faith; and through this also the paralytic was already made a participant in the remission of sins. But if by hope they understand something else, distinct from faith, it must be proved from the context. Nor does it follow that, because hope, humility, etc., were joined to the true faith in the paralytic, therefore he obtained the remission of sins through them.)*

Confine. Syr. אתלבב take heart, be of good courage, from לבב heart. He meets the threefold temptation in the heart of the paralytic: 1. timidity. 2. unworthiness. 3. lack of goods. You will obtain more than you ask, because you ask for the health of the body, but you will obtain the health of the soul.

Son. Hieron. O wondrous humility! He calls him son, whom the priests did not deign to touch, though he was despised and weak and dissolved in all the joints of his limbs. He is truly the son of GOD, to whom sins are forgiven. Conf. Ps. 103, 13. Es. 49, 15. )*

They are forgiven. R. Dav. Kimchi Ps. 41, 5 at the place. Heal my soul. He does not say, heal my body, because the cause of his disease was iniquity, but heal my soul. For when God heals the soul from its disease, which happens by the expiation of iniquities, the body is also healed. (Twin to this Kimchian thought is that of Zalmoxis in Plato: ὅπὣ The cause of the diseases of the body, if not always, at least very often ( John 9, 3.)

are diseases of the soul, that is, sins. See. Ioh. 5, 14.1. Cor. 11, 30.Eccles. 38, 15.Deut. 28, 58. 59. Whence Hieron. in h. l. Intelligence is given to us, that bodily weaknesses happen for the most part because of sins. Chrysostom beautifully: Therefore God scourges the body because of the sin of the soul, so that by the punishment of the inferior part, the superior may be turned to seeking a remedy.

*( Your sins are forgiven you, Thus, namely in the past, it is more correctly rendered, than in the future: they will be forgiven, or optatively: may they be forgiven. Compare Luc. 7, 47.1. Ioh. 2, 12. & the context also requires such an acceptance, just as B. Luth. also correctly rendered it. The Syrian has the particle, Peil which, since it is customarily explained by the past, Trostius & the Londoners had no reason why they should render it here by the present: they are forgiven. The same Londoners, however, translate the participle : are forgiven. It can also be rendered have been pardoned. This same word occurs above cap. 6, 12. it. Luc. 7, 47. 48.Iohan. 20, 23. The Ethiopian translates: i. e. your sin is forgiven you, but not: your sins are forgiven you, as Ludov. de Dieu in the Appendix to the Gospel of Matthew p. 522. (just as also the Londoners Marc. 2, 9.) translates. Who himself, that most learned man, also correctly notes a typographical error in the Roman edition, while the remaining words: Or to say: arise & walk, are omitted there. Edmundus Castellus in the Annotations on the Ethiopian N. T. version thinks the lacuna should be supplied thus just as it is also had in that same Ethiopian version in the parallel placeLuc. 5, 23.& thus almost in the other which parallel placeMarc. 2, 9.From the fact, however, that Christ here in the exercise of his Prophetic office did not absolve the paralytic in order before he had been absolved from sins in the divine judgment, and yet he truly & validly absolved: our people correctly conclude that nothing at all is lacking to the validity of the absolution, but that it certifies & confirms it, although the Priests or Ministers of the Church do not absolve in order before, see, than in their judgment the one confessing is absolved in divine judgment. Dn. D. H-ls in A. C. Man. p. 343. Furthermore, since Christ without the imposition of satisfaction remitted sins to the paralytic -uic (just as also elsewhere, as Luc. 7.to the sinful woman,cap. 18.to the publican, c. 23. to the thief,Ioh. 8.to the adulteress &c.) it is manifest that even today satisfactions ought not to be required by the absolving Minister. The Papists except, that Christ indeed could remit guilt & punishment at his own discretion, but that the reason for absolution, which is announced by his legates and ministers, is different. Resp. Nay rather, the Ministers act in such a case in the place of GOD. Whence also the hinge of the question turns on this, whether God remits the guilt, so that, however, not all the punishment. Which the Papists deny, but we assert, & among other things we prove from this also, because Christ, in remitting guilt, nowhere either required proper satisfactions, or threatened punishments to those to whom he remitted sins. But that it is false, cries Costerus, that the paralytic was absolved without any satisfaction: for the satisfaction of that man is seen in the prayers of both himself & his bearers, and in the grave danger of a fall, when he was carried up to the roof, & was let down through the roof by four ropes before the Lord on a bed, finally, being cured, he publicly carried his pallet, (& indeed at the command of Christ v. 6. which Peltanus urges) not fearing the calumnies of the Pharisees. In Enchir. p. 489. But how could the paralytic satisfy by the danger of a fall, when according to the opinion of the Papists no one can satisfy who is not yet in grace, and yet sins had not yet been remitted to the paralytic then. e. nor was he himself in grace, and so he could not satisfy before the remission. But as regards the carrying of the pallet, from which both Costerus and Peltanus in the book on satisfaction attempt to construct the satisfaction of the paralytic, it must be known that Card. Toletus in c. 5. of Luke, Corn. à Lapide in h. l. and other Papists, whom B. Par. Conf. Cathol. t. 4. p. 106. cites, bring forward this as the cause of that command, that the carrying of the bed might be a sign of most perfect health. And Beda also looks to this in h. l. Take up, he says, your bed, so that what was a testimony of infirmity, may be a proof of health.)*

Latin:

*(v. 2. Fidem illorum. Nempe & baiulorum & ipsius quoque paralytici. Quòd enim Paralyticus fidem habuerit, patet 1. ex demissione. 2. ex Christi alloquutione. Conf. Ioh. 1, 12. Gal. 26. 3. ex peccati --missione, vid. Rom. 4, 5. 4. ex Sc. S. informatione, Habac. 2, 4.)*

Chrysost. Homil. 3. in Matth. Nisi hic paralyticus fiaem habuisset, non suisset passus se ê te-demitti. *(Chrysostomi expositionem, quòd nempe relativum illorum non tantùm ad portantes, sed ad ipsum quoque paralyticu-referri debeat, amplectuntur etiam Iesuitae Barradius, Salme-, ac Tirinus, nec non Episcopus Gandav. Corn. Iansenius in h. l. Corn à Lapide itidem concedit, non Chrysostomum solùm, sed & Theophylactum atq; Euthymium de ipsius etiam Paralytici fide accipere, nihilo tamē minùs ipse statuit, Christum magis loqui de fide offerentium, quàm ipsius aegri & paralytici.)* Thom. de Trugillo in thesaur. concion. tom. 1. pag. 589. col. 2. edit. Lugd. Filium vocavit Iesus Paralyticum, in quo ostenditur, propriâ etiam fide illum fuisse salvum, hoc quippe nomine Christus credentes appellat, quibus dedit potestatem filios DEI fieri. Lyran. h. l. Non videntur benè dicere, qui dicunt, quòd illorum refertur tantùm ad offerentes, ita quod per fidem offerentium tantùm sis sanatus. Idem dicit Alb. Magnus ac Dion. Carthus. in h. l. Frustra igitur ex Hieron. & Ambrosto -egat Staplet. promt. Cathol. part. 1. p. 267. hunc paralyticum habuisse fidem, quia ad accipiendam peccatorum rrmissionem --ique propriâ opus est fide. *(Id ipsum quoque ultrò largitur Corn. à Lapide: probaturus enim, Christum h. l. non loqui de fide iustificante, sed de fide miraculorum & sanitatis, urget hoc, quod Christus magis loquatur de fide offerentium, quae aegruiustificare non poterat, quàm ipsius aegri. Disertè quoque Iesuita Conzen in h. l. Fides aliena iustificationem nunquam efficit in alio, quadam beneficia temporalia aliquando impetrat. Vid. notata ad Act. 27, 24.

Sed si fides aliena non efficit iustificationem in alio, vel non impertat alteri remissionem peccatorum, (quod etiam nostrates adserunt, & exprincipio hoc cōtra Pontificios probant, infantes baptizatos habere veram fidem, & suâ, nō alienâ fide iustificari ac salvari) cur ratio haec affertur, quòd Christus propteres remiserit paralytico peccata, quia vidit eorum h. e. tum paralytici, tum offerentium fidem? Resp. duo beneficia exhibita fuerunt paralytico, sanatio corporalis, & spiritualis: non huius, sed illius causa movens fuit intuitus fidei offerentium. Potest tamefides piorum homini adhuc impio existenti impetrare conve-ionem ac fidem propriam, qua deinceps iustificetur. Vid. D. Hann. in h. l.)*

Petrus Clnniac. referent. Cent. Magd. 12. col. 835. Portatorum fides paralytico impetrat sanitatem. E. aliena fices etiam salvat infantem. *(Satis etiam audacter Iesuita Malconatus in h. l. Quae, scribit, amentia est, ad probandum, nos solâ fide --stificari-. producere testimonia, in quibus non de propriâ, sed -lienâ fide agitur. Et tamen soli hodiè multorum iudicio, maximè verò suo, istasini sapiunt. Iesuita Contzen ut ut fateri cogatur, Paralyticum fidem habuisse, scribit tamen, Evangelistam de fide portantium duntaxat loqui.)* Resp. non fuit paralyticus fide destitutus. Coster. part. 1. Conc. p. 524. Nota, Christum non aettendisse solam portantium fidem, sed ipsius infirmi quo-, qui portari se permiserat & cum tanto periculo demitti. *(Idem --oque adserit memoratus Iesuita in Euchir. p. 254. ubi disertè: Paralyticus magna fide & she periculum subiit, in domum ingrediendi per tectum, postea tamen audivit, confide fili, remittuntur tibi peccata -us. Quasi diceret, bono anime esto, nunc tibi peccata remitto, -im etiam corporis morbum curaturus. Similiter etiam Iesuita Maldonatus in h. l. disertè: coeteros (h. e. qui à Christo corpore sanati fuerunt, excepto solo Malcho,) qui fide curati sunt, non sola sed eadem tamen fide, quâ corpore sanati sunt, animô credimus esse sanatos. Quae confessiones opponendae sunt, tum Iohanni Paludano Th. D. & in Acad. Lovan. Profess. satis temerè in Vindiciis ad h. l. p. 219. scribenti, nullo modo verba Christi: Confide fili, remittuntur tibi peccata tua, accipi posse de illo actu, quo quis credit, certò sibi peccata remissa, per Christi mortem: Sed de illo saltem actu, quo qui à Christo sanati sunt, credebant, cum habere sanandi potestatem, & se posse ab eo iuvari: tum Corn. à Lap. in h. l. adserenti, agi hîc de fide miraculorum & sanitatis, quae --xta nos à fide iustificante distingvatur. Cum Corn. à Lapide facit quoque Contzenius in h. l. Coeterùm ex eo, quòd foli fidei remissio peccatorum hîc adscribitur, rectè inferunt Orthodoxi, solam fidem iustificare. Excipit Bell. l 1. de Iustif. c. 13. §. Hanc igitur, innui hîc spem esse dispositionem adiustitiam & remissionem pecc-torum. Eâd. ferè except. utitur quoque Henricus Lancelotz in Anat. hom. Christ. p. 73. Verùm si per spem intelligunt fiduciai. e. fiducialem meri-i Christi apprehensionem, nobis nó a-versan-ur, ut qui disertè verae fidei partem constituimus fiduciam; & per-anc quoq; paralyticus remissionis peccatorum iamtum pa-tice-s fuit factus. Sin verò per spem intelligunt aliud quid, à fi--cidistinctem, è contextu probandum est. Nec sequitur etiam, paralytico verae fidei fuerunt coniuncta, spes, humilitas &c. E. perilla pecc. remissionem ipse obtinuit.)*

Confine. Syr. אתלבבrecipe cor, bono sis animo, à לבבcor. Triplici occurrit tentationi in corde paralytici 1. timiditati. 2. indignitati. 3. bonorumegestati. Plus impetrabis quàm petis, quia corporis sanitatem petis, sed animae sanitatem impetrabis.

*( Fili. Hieron. O mira humilitas! despectum & debilem totis membrorum compag--dissolutum, filium vocat, quem Sacerdotes non dignabantur attingere.Is verè filius DEI est, cui dimittuntur peccata. Ostendit quoque calvator compellatione hac promtum animi sui affectum ad sublevandum miserum. Conf. Ps. 103, 13.Es. 49, 15.)*

Remissa sunt. R. Dav. Kimchi Ps. 41, 5 ad locum. Sana ammam meam. Non dicit, sana corpus meum, quia causa morbi eius fuit iniquitas, sed sana animam meam. Nam cùm sanat Deus animam à morbo suo, quod fit expiatione iniquitatum, sanatur etiā corpus. *(Gemella huic Kimchianae est illa Zamolxis apud Platonem: ὅπὣ Causa morborum corporis si vel maximè non semper ( Ioh. 9, 3.)

saepè tamen morbi sunt animi h. e. peccata. Vid. Ioh. 5, 14.1. Cor. 11, 30.Eccles. 38, 15.Deut. 28, 58. 59. Unde Hieron. in h. l. Datur nobis intelligentia, propter peccata pleras que evenire corporum debilitates. Pulcrè Chrysostomus: Ideò Deus ob animi peccatum corpus flagellat, ut deterioris partis supplicio melior ad quaerendum remedium convertatur.)*

*( Remissa sunt tibi peccata tua, Ita, nempe in praeterito, rectiùs redd-tur, quàm in futuro: remittentur, vel optativè: remittantur. Confer Luc. 7, 47.1. Ioh. 2, 12. & talem quoq; acceptionem contextus requirit, quemadmodum etiam B. Luth. rectè reddidit. Syrus habet partic, Peil quod cùm usifatè per praeteritum exponatur, causam Trostius & Londinenses nullam habuerunt, cur hîc per praesens redderent: remit tuntur. lidem tamen Lond. participiū vertunt: remissa sunt. Potest etiam reddi condonata sunt. Occurrit idem hoc verbum suprà cap. 6, 12. it. Luc. 7, 47. 48.Iohan. 20, 23. Aethiops vertit: i. e. remittitur tibi peccatum tuum, non verò: remittuntur tibi peccata tua, prout Ludov. de Dieu in Append. ad Evang. Matth. p. 522. (quemadmodum etiam Londinenses Marc. 2, 9.) vertit. Qui ipse etiam doctissimus vir rectè notat mendum typographicum in edit. Romanâ, dum reliqua verba: An dicere: surge & ambula, ibi omissa sunt. Edmundus Castellus in Annotat. in Aethiopicam N. T. versionem lacunam ita supplendā censet quomodo etiam habetur in eâd. versione Aethiopicâ in loco paralleloLuc. 5, 23.& sic ferè in altero quoloco paralleloMarc. 2, 9.Ex eo verò, quòd Christus hîc in ratione officii sui Prophetici paralyticum non absolvit ordine priûs, quàm in iudicio divino à peccatis absolutus esset, & tamen verè & validè absolvit: rectè colligunt nostrates, quòd etiam validitati absolutionis nil quicquam decedat, sed eam certificet & confirmet, licet Sacerdotes sive Ministri Ecclesiae non absolva-ordine priùs, Vid. quàm ipsorum iudicio confitens in iud--o divino absolutus est. Dn. D. H-ls in A. C. Man. p. 343. Porrò cùm Christus sine impositione satisfactionis paralytico -uic (quemadmodum & alibi, uti Luc. 7.mulieri peccatrici,cap. 18.publicano, c. 23. Latroni,Ioh. 8.adulterae &c.) peccata remiserit, manifestū est, quòd nec hodiè à Ministro absolvente satisfactiones requiri debeant. Excipiunt Pontificii, quòd Christus quidem pro arbitrio culpam & poenam potuerit remittere, sed aliam esse rationem absolutionis, quae ab eius legatis ac ministris annunciatur. Resp. Imò verò Ministri agunt in tali casu loco DEI. Unde etiam quaestionis cardo in eo vertitur, an Deus culpam remittat, ut tamen non omnem poenam. Quod Pontificii negant, nos verò adserimus, & inter alia hinc quoque probamus, quia Christus remittendo culpam, nullibi vet satisfactiones proprias requisivit, vel poenas illis, quibus peccata remisit, comminatus fuit. Sed falsum esse, clamat Costerus, paralyticum sine omni satisfactione absolutum esse: conspici enim illius satisfactionem in precibus tam suis, quàm baiulorum, atq; in gravi periculo lapsûs, cùm super tectum deferretur, & per tectum quatuor funibus ante Dominum in lecto domitteretur, denicùm curatus publicè grabbatum gestaret, (& quidem iubente Christo v. 6. id quod Peltanus urget) non veritus calumnias Pharisaeorum. In Enchir. p. 489. Ast quî paralyticus periculo lapsûs satisfacere poterat, cùm ex Pontificiorum sententiâ nemo possit satisfacere, qui nondum in gratiâ atqui paralytico tum nondum peccata erant remissa. e. nec in gratia ipse erat, adeoq: nec ante remissionē satis facere poterat. Quod attinet verò gestationem grabbati, ex quâ tum Costerus, tum Peltanus lib. de satisf. adstruere paralytici satisfactionem conantur, sciendum est, quòd Card. Toletus in c. 5. Lucae, Corn. à Lapide in h. l. aliique Pontificii, quos adducit B. Par. Conf. Cathol. t. 4. p. 106. causam praecepti illius hanc afferant, ut lectuli portatio signum esset perfectissimae santiatis. Et huc etiam respicit Beda in h. l. Tolle, ait, lectum tuum, ut quodfuit testimonium infirmitatis, sit probatio santitatis.)*

## 9:3
( v. 3.This man blasphemes. Βλασφηεῖν is said here not of one who curses GOD, but of one who arrogates to himself what is GOD'S, as is evident from Mark 2:7. In the same way that word is taken in Matt. 26:65.)

Latin:

*( v. 3.Iste blasphemat.Βλασφηεῖν hîc dicitur non qui DEO maledicit, sed qui quod DEI est, sibi arrogat, uti patet ex Marc. 2, 7. Eodem -odo accipitur illud verbum Matth. 26, 65.)*

## 9:4
(v. 4. When Jesus had seen their thoughts. Rightly from this, as also from other parallel places, John 2:25.c. 21:17.Col. 2:3. the orthodox gather that Christ, according to his human nature, is omniscient.)

Latin:

*(v. 4. Quum vidisset Iesus cogitationes eorum. Rectè hinc tum ex aliis quoque locis pa--llelis, Iohan. 2, 25.c. 21, 17.Col. 2, 3. colligunt orthodoxi, quòd Christus, secundùm hum. naturam sit omniscius.)*

## 9:5
v. 5. Whether it is easier to say &c. For both are above human virtue and belong to divine power. See Exod. 34, 7. Es. 43, 25. Iob. 14, 4. Hoseae 14, 2. Ps. 115, 3. Ps. 135, 6. )

Latin:

*(v. 5. Utrum est facilius dicere &c. Utrumque enim supra humanam virtutem divinae potestatis est. Vid. Exod. 34, 7.Es. 43, 25.Iob. 14, 4. Hoseae 14, 2. Ps. 115, 3.Ps. 135, 6.)*

## 9:6
v. 6. But that you may know. There is ἀνανταπόδοτον, to be understood, for this follows, attend to what I am about to do.

Christ proves His divinity by a triple argument: 1. He forgives sins ἀυτοκρατορικῶς. 2. He looks into the faith of the friends and the thoughts of the enemies. 3. By a word He heals the paralysis.

*( The Son of man has power &c. From the fact that Christ had the power of forgiving sins, and indeed ἀυθεντικῶς καὶ ἀυτοκρατορικῶς, Marc. 2, 5.7. our people rightly conclude against Photinus that He is the true God. The things which they except will be discussed in the notes to Marc. 2, 7., especially the passage to be noted here Ioh. 5, 19.. But if Christ Himself had the power of forgiving sins, why does He pray to the Father on the altar of the cross, Luc. 23, 35., that He might forgive sins? Resp. Subordinate things are not to be opposed. The Father forgives sins as the granting cause, the Son as the meriting cause, the Holy Spirit as the sealing cause. Thus Mr. Dr. Walth. in H. B. p. 762. It can be added that Christ prayed to the Father for the remission of the sins committed by those crucifying Him as man, and indeed in the lowest state of humiliation, just as He also poured out prayers to the Father for deliverance from death. Ebr. 5, 7. Just as, however, notwithstanding this, He was able to raise Himself; Ioh. 2, 19.c. 10, 18. so neither do those prayers Luc. 23, 35. prevent Him from also ἀυθεντικῶς forgiving sins. By the same argument of proof, namely from miracles performed, Christ also proves His deity Ioh. 10, 25.38.c. 14, 1. likewise that He is the promised Messiah, Matth. 11, 5.)*

That addition on earth, Theophylact well weighs in c. 5. of Luke. As long as we are upon the earth, it is permitted to blot out our sins. But after we have migrated from the earth, there no longer remains for us hope of pardon, nor of repentance and confession any more. *(Augustine has a similar sentiment in Qq, ex utroq; Testam. q. 102. Let the patrons of Purgatory note this.)*

*( Arise &c. Bede skillfully in c. 5. v. 14. of John on the words: Behold you are made whole: He who healed from infirmity on the outside, He also saved from wickedness on the inside.)*

Latin:

v. 6. Ut autem sciatis. Est ἀνανταπόδοτον, subaudiendum enim hoc consequens, attendite, quod sum facturus.

Christus triplici argumento probat suam divinitatem 1. remittit peccata ἀυτοκρατορικῶς. 2. introspicit fidem amicorum & cogitationes nostium. 3. verbo sanat paralysin.

*( Filium hominis habere potestatem &c. Ex eo quòd Christus habuit potestatem remittendi peccata, & quidem ἀυθεντικῶς καὶ ἀυτοκρατορικῶς,Marc. 2, 5.7. rectè colligunt nostrates contra Photin. ipsum esse verum Deum. Quae illi excipiunt, discutientur in notis ad Marc. 2, 7. cumprimis h. l. notandus locus Ioh. 5, 19. Ast si Christus ipse habuit potestatem remittendi peccata, cur Patrem in ara crucis orat, Luc. 23, 35. ut ille dimittat peccata? Resp. subordinata non sunt opponenda. Pater remittit peccata ut causa largiens, Filius ut promerens, Sp. S. ut obsignans. Ita Dn. D. Walth. in H. B. p. 762. Addi potest, quòd Christus pro remissione peccatorum, à crucifigentibus ipsum commissorum, Patrem oraverit ut homo, & quidem in infimo exinanitionis statu, quomodo etiam pro liberatione à morte preces ad Patrem fudit. Ebr. 5, 7. Sicuti tamen hôc non obstante potuit seipsum resuscirare; Ioh. 2, 19.c. 10, 18. ita nec illae preces Luc. 23, 35. obstant, quò minùs ipse quoque ἀυθεντικῶς peccata remittat. Eodem verò probationis argumento, nempe à miraculis perito, suam deitatem probat quoque Christus Ioh. 10, 25.38.c. 14, 1. it. quòd promissus Messias sit, Matth. 11, 5.)*

Additionem illam in terris, probè expendit Theoph. in c. 5. Luc. Quamdiu super terra sumus, delere licet peccata nostra. At postquam è terra migraverimus, non ultrà nobis superest spes veniae, nepoenitentiae & confessionis ampliùs. *(Similem sententiam habet August. in Qq, ex utroq; Testam. q. 102. Notent hoc Burgatorii Patroni.)*

*( Surge &c. Scitè Beda in c. 5. v. 14. Iohannis ad verba: Ecce sanus factus es: Qui foris ab infirmitate, ipse etiam intus salvavit à scelere.)*

## 9:7
(v. 7. He went away to his house. Tropological. Bede in this place: Spiritually healthy is he who was languid, he carries his bed home, when the soul, having received the remission of sins, returns with the body itself to its own internal custody, lest after pardon it admits anything from which it may again be justly struck.)

Latin:

*(v. 7. Abiitdomum suam. Tropol. Beda in h. l. Spiritualiter sanus qui languidus erat, domum reportat lectum, cùm anima, peccatorum remissione accepta ad internam sui custodiam cum ipso se corpore refert, ne quid post veniam, unde iterum iustè feriatur, admitt at.)*

## 9:8
(v. 8. They marveled. The Greek codices commonly have ἐδόξασαν.. The Arab also reads it thus, translating they marveled. Similarly also Luther. In the same way Chrysostom and Theophylact. Beza notes, however, that some exemplar, which he himself used, has ἐφοβη-σαν they feared, and the Vulgate Latin interpreter followed this reading. Indeed, even the most ancient Syrian interpreter reads it thus, for he renders i.e., they feared. And in the same way the Ethiopian and the Persian read. But however much neither reading is contrary to the context, the former nevertheless seems to be preferred to the latter, as it is approved by the almost unanimous consent of the Greek codices, which the Greek manuscript selections that are held in the Nuremberg Library beautifully support here. (For as concerns the exemplar which Beza makes mention of, perhaps the same thing can be said of it that Franciscus Lucas suspects of the second Greek codex from those which the Parisians compared, namely that it was changed or corrected from the Latin. (However, two manuscript codices which are preserved in the Cambridge Academy also approve the same reading, according to the testimony of Mr. Brian Walton.) Some add that it is also most conformable to the context: since admiration, not fear, ought to have followed that work of Christ. Erasmus suspects that in certain codices ἐδάβησαν, was written for ἐδαὺμσαν, of which words there is a great affinity.)

Who had given such power to men.

Christ had said, The Son of man has power to remit sins: the people rightly adapt this to the ordination of the Ministry and the whole Church, and celebrate God, because He had given such power to men. (There are, however, some who think that the plural number in this place is placed by enallage for the singular. And that the sense is that the common people marveled that such right had been given to any of men. Thus thinks Dr. Friedlieb in this place. And the glossators of the Ernestine Bibles aim at this, bringing forward this place for the present sense: they praised God, because He had sent such a Prophet, who could remit sins and take away diseases incurable by nature. In the same way also Dr. Chemnitz in H. E. c. 43. For thus he explains this place: to men i.e., to human nature in Christ. He continues: They had not yet truly and sufficiently recognized the person of Christ, namely that He was God manifested in the flesh, and that to Him, the Messiah and Mediator, the power and authority of remitting sins had been given. Nevertheless, it was the beginning of faith and a step toward fuller recognition, etc. Compare entirely also Chrysostom, homily 30 on Matthew. All the Oriental interpreters, the Syrian, Arab, Ethiopian, and Persian, rendered it in the plural according to the Greek text.)

Latin:

*(v. 8. Mirata est. Graeci Codd. communiter habent ἐδόξασαν. Etita quoque legit Arabs, vertens admirati sunt. Similiter etiam Lutherus. Eod. modo Chrysost. & Theophyl. Notat tamen Beza, exemplar aliquod, quo usus ipse est, habere ἐφοβη-σανtimuerunt, & hanc sequutus lectionem est Interpres Lat. Vulgatus. Imò etiam antiquissimus Interpres Syrus sic legit, reddit enim i. e. timuerunt. Eodemque modo legerunt Aethiops ac Persa. Ut ut verò neutra lectio contextui adversetur prior tamē posteriori videtur praeferenda, utpote quam unanimi ferè cōsensu Codd. Graeci, quibus pulcrè hîc adstipulantur Ecclogae Graecae MSS quae habētur in Biblioth. Norib. approbāt. (Quod enim concernit exemplar, cuius Beza mentionem facit, idem fortè de eo potest dici, quod Franc. Lucas de secundo Cod. Graeco ex illis, quos Parisienses contulerunt suspicatur, eum nempe ex Latino mutatum s. correctum. (approbant tamen eandem lectionem, & duo Codd. MSS. qui in Acad. Cantabrig. adservantur, teste D. Briano Walthono.) Addunt, nonnulli, quòd etiam contextui maximè conformis sit: cùm opus illud Christi admiratio consequi, non metus debuerit. Erasmus suspicatur, in quibusdam Codd. pro ἐδαὺμσαν scriptum fuisse ἐδάβησαν, quarum vocum magna affinitas.)*

Qui dedisset talem potestatem hominibus.

Dixerat Christus, Filius hominis habet potestatem remittenpeccta: id populus rectè ad ordinationem Ministerii & totam Ecclesiam accommodat, Deumque celebrat, quòd dederit talem potestatem hominibus. *(Sunt tamen nonnulli, qui existimant, numerum plur. h. l. per Enal. positum pro singulari. Et sensum esse, quòd plebs admirata fuerit ulli hominum tātum iuris esse datum. Ita sentit D. Friedlieb. in h. l. Et huc collimant Glossatores Bibl. Ernestinorum, hunc proferentes locum praesentis sensum: laudabant Deum, quòd talem misisset Prophetam, qui peccata remittere ac morbos per naturam incurabiles tollere posset. Eôd. modô etiam B D. Chemn. in H. E. c. 43. Ita enim h. l. exponit: hominibus i. e. humanae naturae in Christo. Pergit: Nondum sanè rectè & satis personam Christi tunc agnoverunt, quòd sc. esset Deus manifestatus in carne, quòdque ipsi Messiae & Mediator potestas & autoritas remittendi peccata data esset. Initium tamen fidei & gradus ad pleniorem agnitionem fuit &c. Conf. omninò & Chrysostomus hom. 30. in Matthaeum. Interpretes Orientales omnes Syrus, Arabs, Aethiops, Persa in plur. iuxta textum Graecum reddiderunt.)*

## 9:9
v. 9. Τελώνης called ὑπὸ τοὑ τέλος ὠνεῖσθαι. Because the Publicans redeemed some public tax for a certain sum of money, and whatever they could exact beyond that sum by frauds, extortions, and rapine, that accrued to them as profit. Ulpian. Of what audacity of what rashness the factions of the publicans are, there is no one who does not know. Suidas describes a toll-booth, thus, that it is πεπυ *(Chrys. hom. 31. in Matth. concerning the office of the publicans: Τοτ Conf. noted at Matth. 5, 46.)* Chrysost. hom. 13. in Matth. Who can dissolve the bonds of sins, what is the wonder, if He made sinners Apostles? *(The same hom. 31. in Matthew: Why He said he sat in the toll-booth. He wishes to show the virtue of the caller, who, not yet having imposed an end to the depraved conversation of the publicans, drew him out from the middle of the sea of evils, just as He transformed the Blessed Paul who was raging and burning with every madness and bringing fire upon the Church.)*

And rising he followed him. Ambros. in cap. 5. Luc. p. 61. He abandons his own things, who used to seize the things of others, and leaving behind that vile seat, he proceeds with the whole trace of his mind after the Lord. *(

*( Who was called Matthew. It is a beautiful observation of the Fathers, that the other Evangelists, as Mark c. 2, 14. & Luke c. 5, 27. making mention of this history, do not call the Evangelist by his common name, namely Matthew, for the sake of modesty: but he himself does this. Jerome in this place. The other Evangelists, out of modesty and honor for Matthew, did not wish to call him by his common name, but said Levi. For he had a double name. But Matthew himself (according to that which is said by Solomon: Prov. 18. The just man is the first accuser of himself. And in another place, Is. 43. Tell your sins that you may be justified) names himself Matthew and a publican: so that he might show to those reading that no one ought to despair of salvation, if he has turned to better things: since he himself was suddenly changed from a publican into an Apostle. Chrysostom hom. 31. Ἄξιον To this also can be referred the example of Paul, 1. Cor. 15, 9. 1. Tim. 1, 16. Furthermore, to the objection of Faustus, that in this place it cannot be understood as the Evangelist Matthew himself, since otherwise it should have been said: He saw me and called me, and I followed him, Augustine responds quite lengthily in book 17 against Faustus the Manichaean, ch. 4, where among other things he observes, that writers of historical events are accustomed, when they come to their own person, to weave the narrative as if they were telling of another what they are telling about themselves. And he proves this with the example of Moses, and John in the last chapter, indeed of Christ himself Luc. 18, 7. Matth. 11, 18. Ioh. 5, 15.

( αὐτοἀνακειμένου: So also read the Vulgate, the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew of Münster, the Arab, B. Luther, and the more approved Greek codices: the Syrian, however, the Ethiopian, and the Persian read in the plural.)

( ἐν τῆ οἰκίἰα. Understand of Matthew, as is sufficiently manifest from Luc. 5, 20. whence also Erasmus rightly supplied it, by adding his. Moreover, the Arab according to the London edition explicitly: in the house of Matthew. According to the Roman edition, however, in that house. The Ethiopian, Syrian, and Persian likewise render it absolutely, not expressing in whose house they reclined. Beyond doubt, however, it is erroneous when the Arab according to the Leiden edition has in the house of Simon.)

Latin:

v. 9. Τελώνης dictus ὑπὸ τοὑ τέλος ὠνεῖσθαι. Quia Publicani certâ pecuniae summâ publicum aliquod vectigal redimebant, & quicquid ultra illam summam fraudibus, exactionibus & rapinis exigere poterant, id in lucrum illis cedebat. Ulpianus. Quantae audaciae quantaetemeritatis sint publicanorum factiones, nemo est qui nesciat. Suidas ita describit telonium, quod sit πεπυ *(Chrys. hom. 31. in Matth. de publicanorum officio: Τοτ Conf. notata ad Matth. 5, 46.)* Chrysost. hom. 13. in Matth. Qui potest peccatorum dissolvere vincula, quid mirum, si peccatores Apostolos fecit? *(Idem hom. 31. in Matthaeum: Cur dixit in telonio sedisse. Virtutem vocentis vol--t ostendere, qui non imposito adhuc sine pravae publicanorum conversationi, è medio malorum pelago ipsum abstraxit, sicut B. Paulum quofurentem ac omni ratis ardentem & ignem Ecclesiae inferentem transmutavit.)*

Atsurgens secutus est eum. Ambros. in cap. 5. Luc. p. 61. Propria derelinquit, qui rapiebat aliena, ac vile illud sedile destituens toto post Dominum vestigio mentis incedit.

*( Qui Matthaeus dicebatur. Pulera est observatio Patrum, quòd Evangelistae coeteri, uti Marcus c. 2, 14. & Lucas c. 5, 27. historiae huius mentionem facientes, Evangelistam verecundiae causa vulgato nomine, Matthaei nempe, non appellent: ipse verò hoc faciat. Hieronymus in h. l. Coeteri Evangelistae propter verecundiam & honorem Matthaei noluerunt eum nomine appellare vulgato, sed dixerunt Levi. Duplici quippe vocabulo fuit. Ipse autem Matthaeus (secundùm illud, quod dicitur à Salomone:Prov. 18.Iùstus accusator est sui in principio sermonis. Et in alio loco,Es. 43.Dic tu peccata tua ut iustificeris) Matthaeum se & publicanum nominat: ut ostendat legentibus, nullum debere salutem desperare, si admeliora conversus sit: cum ipse de publicano in Apostolum sit repentè mutatus. Chrysostomus hom. 31. Ἄξιον Huc quoque referri potest exemplum Pauli, 1. Cor. 15, 9.1. Tim. 1, 16. Porrò ad obiectionem Fausti, quòd h. l. non possit intelligi ipse Evangelista Matthaeus, cum aliàs dicendum fuisset. Vidit me & vocavit me, & secutia sum eum. satis prolixè respondet Augustinus lib. 17. contra Faust. Manichaeum e. 4. ubi inter alia observat, solere Scriptores rerum gestarum, cùm in suampersonam venerint, ita se contexere, tanquam de alio narrent; quod de se narrant. Probatque hoc exemplo Mosis, ac Iohannis c. ult, imò ipsius Christi Luc. 18, 7.Matth. 11, 18.Ioh. 5, 15.)*

*( αὐτοἀνακειμένου: Ita quoque legunt Vulgatus, Evang. Matth. Ebralcum M-nsteri, Arabs, B. Lutherus ac Codd. Graeci probatiores: Syrus tamen, Aethiops & Persa legerunt in plurali.)*

*( ἐν τῆ οἰκίἰα. Subintellige Matthaei, ceu satis manfestum ex Luc. 5, 20. unde etiam Erasmus rectè supplevit, addendo illius. Quin & Arabs secundùm editionem Londinensem disertè: in domo Matthaei. Secundùm editionem verò Romanam, in domo illā. Aethiops, Syrus, Perfi itidem absolutè reddunt, non exprimentes in cuius domo accubuerint. Procul ambiguo autem erroneum est, quando Arabs iuxta edit. Leydensem habet in domo Sim--onis.)*

## 9:10
v. 10. Matthew had left all things in such a way that he was nevertheless able to prepare a banquet for Christ. He had left behind all that business of his, and had dedicated himself entirely to Christ, so that he might do what He commanded: meanwhile, however, he did not cast away his resources, but used them insofar as his new calling permitted. *(And hence it is clear how that passage at Luc. 5, 28. is to be understood; namely, that Matthew bade farewell to the toll-booth, but retained his other goods, and used them in such a way that they in no way distracted his mind from the true worship of GOD. The objections which Contzen and other Papists raise will be discussed in the analysis on Luc. 5, 28.)*

Ambros. on chapter 5 of Luke. Matthew displays the preparation of a great banquet. For he who receives Christ into his internal dwelling is fed with the greatest delights of overflowing pleasures. Therefore, the Lord willingly enters and reclines in the affection of him who has believed. *(

*(11. Why with publicans &c. The Jewish Doctors in Berachot f. 43. 2. enumerate six things less becoming to a disciple of a Wise man. Among them the fifth is, if he reclines (to eat) with common men. Hence Buxtorf in Lex. Rabb. Talm. page 1146, and from him D. Quistorpius in Annot. ad h. l., thinks that Christ reproved the Pharisees. But association with evil men and heretics does not seem safe enough. Whence it is also forbidden by the Apostle Tit. 3, 10. But we must distinguish between association with sinners or even infidels or heretics, whence some spiritual advantage can return either to ourselves or to them, such as was the association of Christ with the Publicans; and between association, through which either scandal is offered to others, or danger to honest morals or to the faith is to be feared. The latter is to be disapproved; not the former. Therefore, just as Christ, to whom as the eternal wisdom of GOD no danger was to be feared from Publicans and sinners, rightly associated with them: so nothing prevents one who is well-founded in religion and piety from associating with heretics and sinners, since it may happen that in this way he may win them for Christ. Just as it is not only permitted to physicians, but is also required of them, that they be present with the sick, even if these labor under a most contagious disease they approach them; but on the contrary if others wish to do the same rashly , it is not undeservedly turned to their fault: so if learned, pious men, and those skilled in the Holy Scripture, associate with heretics and sinners so that they may restore spiritual health to them, it is so far from being the case that they ought to be reproved, that this zeal rather deserves praise. But it must be judged otherwise concerning those if any who are not sufficiently constant or founded in the sacred letters have dared to approach heretics more often and to associate familiarly with them.)*

*( Your Master. See what is noted at John 13, 13.)*

Latin:

v. 10. Matthaeus ita reliquerat omnia, ut tamen posset Christo convivium instruere. Reliquerat omnem illam negotiationem suam, seque in totum Christo addixerat, ut faceret, quod ille iuboret: interim tamen facultates suas non abiecit, sed iis usus est, quatenus per novam vocationem licuit. *(Atq; hinc patet, quomodo illud Luc. 5, 28. intelligendum sit; nempe quod Matthaeus telonio valedixerit, caetera verò bona sua retinuerit, atque ita illos usus fuerit, ut tamen animum ipsius à vero DEI cultu ea minimè abstraxerint. quae Contzenius aliiq; Pontificii excipiunt, discutientur in anal. ad Luc. 5, 28.)*

Ambros. in cap. 5. Luc. Matthaeus convivii magni exhibet apparatum. Qui enim domicilio Christum recipit interno, maximis delectationibus exuberantium pascitur voluptatum. Itaq; Dominus libenter ingreditur & in eius, qui crediderit, recumbit affectu.

*(11. Quare cum publicanis &c. Iudaeorum Dd. in Berachot f. 43. 2. enumerant sex res minùs convenientes Sapientis discipulo. inter illas quinta est, si accumbat (ad comedendum) cum hominibus plebeiis. Hinc Christum reprehendisse Pharisaeos putat Buxtorffius in Lex. Rabb. Talm. pag. 1146. & ex eo D. Quistorpius in Annot. ad h. l. Sed nec satis tuta videtur conversatio cum hominibus malis ac haereticis. Unde & ab Apostolo prohibita Tit. 3, 10. Verùm dist. inter conversationem cum peccatoribus vel etiam infidelibus aut haereticis, unde commodum aliquod spirituale sive adnos ipsos, sive ad illos redire potest, qualis fuit conversatio Christi cum Publicanis; & inter conversationem, per quam vel aliis scandalum praebetur, vel moribus honestis aut fidei periculum metuendum. Haec improbanda; non illa. Quemadmodum igitur Christus, cui uti aeternae DEI sapientiae nil metuendum periculi à Publicanis & peccatoribus fuit, rectè conversatus cum illis est: ita nil impedit, quo minùs is, qui in religione ac pietate benè fundatus est, conversetur cum haereticis & peccatoribus, cùm fieri possit, ut isto modo Christo eos lucrifaciat. Sicuti Medicis non solùm concessum est, sed ab illis etiam requiritur, ut aegrotis, si vel maximè contagioso morbo hi laborent, adsint eos-; accedant; contrà verò si alii idem temerè facere voluerint, nō immeritò vitio iis vertitur: sic si viri docti, pii, & Sacae Scripturae periti cum haereticis ac peccatoribus conversentur, ut eis spiritualem sanitatem restituant, tantum abest, ut reprehendi debeant, ut potiùs studium hoc laudem mereatur. Secus verò iudicandum de iis, si qui non satis constantes aut in sacris literis fundati haereticos saepius culè accedere & familiter cum eis conversari ausi fuerint.)*

*( Magister vester. Vid. quae notata ad Ioh. 13, 13.)*

## 9:12
v. 12. Those who are well have no need of a physician &c. Opt. Milevit book 1 against Parmen. p. 11. Health does not demand medicine. Clem. Alex. 1 paedag. chap. 1. f. 35. τοῖς νοσοῦσιτὸσῶμαἰατροῦ χρήζει. Hilar. can. 9 in Matt. For those who consider themselves healthy, no treatment is necessary. August. book 3 on the merit and remission of sins chap. 4. Jesus is not necessary for those who do not have sin, but for those who are to be released from sin.

The strong are well by themselves, they seek no Machaon,

The doubtful sick man flees to medical aid. Ovid. book 2 of Pontus. *(More will be discussed concerning this sentiment in the notes at Luke 5, 31. In this place, this at least can be observed, that the sense of the present saying is: that to those who do not acknowledge their sins as a spiritual disease of the soul, the Evangelical promises are of no benefit, since the oil of divine mercy is not poured except into a contrite heart, that is, into such a heart that acknowledges its own spiritual infirmity and the defect of its own righteousness, and seeks salvation in the satisfaction of Christ, who was made for us by GOD righteousness, wisdom &c. Christ does not enter into the hearts of men through the grace of the Gospel, unless John first prepares the way for Him through repentance. Furthermore, from the present utterance of the Savior, our people also rightly gather against certain Papists and Calvinists, that if man had not sinned, Christ would not have come in the flesh. Indeed, the Jesuit Maldonatus supports our opinion in his Comm. on this place, rightly warning, that the contrary opinion, while it imagines an uncertain benefit of Christ, diminishes that certain one, than which there could not be a greater, of our redemption. But concerning this matter, see more in B. Par. L. on Sin p. 125. b. also Colleg. Isagog. L. on the Person and Office of Christ c. 7. §. 42.)*

Latin:

v. 12. Qui valent, non egent medico &c. Opt. Milevit lib. 1. contra Parmen. p. 11. Sanitas non efflagitat Medicinam. Clem. Alex. 1. paedag. cap. 1. f. 35. τοῖς νοσοῦσιτὸσῶμαἰατροῦ χρήζει. Hilar. can. 9. in Matth. Eis qui se sanos existimant, necessaria curatio nulla est. August. lib. 3. de peccat. merit. & remiss. cap. 4. Non est necessarius Iesus eis, qui non habent peccatum, sed eis qui solvendi sunt à peccato.

Firma valent per se, nullumMachaona quaerunt,

Ad Medicam dubius confugit aeger opem. Ovid. lib. 2. de Ponto. *(Pluribus de hac sententiâ agetur in not. ad Luc. 5, 31. Hoc loco illud saltem observari potest, quòd sensus praesentis dicti sit: istis, qui non agnoscunt peccata sua, tanquam spiritualem animi morbum, non prodesse promissiones Evangelicas, quippe cùm oleum misericordiae divinae nō in fundatur nisi in cor contritum h. e. in tale cor, quod spiritualem suam infirmitatem ac propriae iustitiae defectum agnoscit, & in satisfactione Christi, qui factus nobis à DEO iustitia, sapientia &c. salutem quaerit. Christus non intrat in corda hominum per Evangelii gratiam, nisi lohannes ipsi viam priùs paret per poenitentiam. Coeterùm è praesenti Salvatoris effato rectè contra quosdam Pontificios & Calvin. colligunt quoque nostrates, quòd si homo non peccasset, nec Christus in carnem venisset. Adstipulatur verò nostrae sententiae Iesuita Maldonatus Comm. in h. l. rectè monens, sententiam contrariam dum incertum Christi beneficium fingit, certum illud, quo maius esse non potuit, redemtionis nostrae extenalare. Sed hâc de re pluribus vid. B. Par. L. de Peccato p. 125. b. it. Colleg. Isagog. L. de Pers. & off. Christi c. 7. §. 42.)*

## 9:13
v. 13. Ἔλεονθέλω. Hos. 6. v. 6. *(The same sentiment is repeated below. c. 12, 7. where certain things will be warned concerning it.)* Theoph. on this place. God shows greater mercy to sinners than sacrifice. Hieron. in cap. 6 Ose True and God-pleasing sacrifices are the salvation of believers and the conversion of sinners. Ambros. lib. 1. de poenit. cap. 11. tom 1. p. 160. Through sacrifice the righteous is commended, through mercy the sinner is redeemed. In the Law is sacrifice, in the Gospel is mercy.

And not is used among the Hebrews to signify rather than. Rend your heart, and not your garments, i.e., rather than your garments. Prover. 17. v. 12. Let a bear robbed of her whelps meet a man, and not a fool in his folly, i.e., rather let a bear than a fool meet him.

*(That indeed here a negative adverb is used for a comparative particle, is evident both from an inspection of the Prophetic text, from which the Savior alleged this sentence: for it is expressly added, and the knowledge of God (i.e., I am delighted with the knowledge of GOD) מעלות rather than burnt offerings; and from the fact that God by no means rejected sacrifices offered from a faithful heart, as they were things which He Himself had commanded. And there are also many similar examples in the Holy Scriptures. Such as Gen. 45, 8.Exod. 16, 8.Ps. 34, 11.Prov 8, 10.Ier. 7, 22.Ioel. 2, 13.Luc. 14, 12.Ioh. 5, 45.c. 6, 27.1. Cor. 1, 17. add Matth. 10, 20.Act. 5, 4.Eph. 6, 12.2. Thess. 4, 8. Maldonatus refers Ioh. 7, 16.c. 10, 20. to this. There are, however, those who judge that a negative signification has a place here: they warn, however, that Christ is speaking of sacrifices offered without faith out of hypocrisy, which God certainly does not want. See Es. 1, 11.Prov. 15, 8.c. 21, 27Es. 66, 3.Ierem 7, 9. 10. thus the Blessed D. Glass. explains in Gramm. S. p. 485. In which way also Chrysostom understood it in this place, as is evident from homil. 31. in Matth. But others take it as said elliptically and understand sacrifices offered from true faith. And the interpretation of the Blessed D. Tarnovius also aims at this, who in his Comm. on the said place thinks Hosea spoke elliptically, in this sense: I am delighted with piety and not only with sacrifice, by sub-understanding, namely, לבך, in which way also the particle μόνον in the N. T. is sometimes missing in the other member of the opposition. That this kind of ellipsis is most frequent in Holy Scripture in that which is not instituted simply, but in a certain respect, or with a certain determination, the praised Dn. Tarn. proves in his Comm. on Ioel. c. 2, 13. and the following cited passages Genes. 32, 28.1. Sam. 8, 7. ἀντιθέσει,

Ies. 31, 34.Hos. 6, 7.Matth. 9, 13.c. 10, 20.c. 18, 22.Marc. 9, 37.Ioh. 5, 30.c. 14, 24.c. 16, 26.c. 11, 44.2. Cor. 3, 6.2. Cor. 1, 17. But it is better to take it comparatively. In which way also the Blessed P. t. 3. LL. Th. pag. 23. also Comm. in Gen. p. 140. and also part. 2. Hom. 11. Acad. p. 441. take it. The Blessed D. Calixtus in Harm. on this place, D. Quistorp. on this place, the Blessed D. Meisnerus and the Blessed D. Himmelius on the said place of Hosea. From the Calvinists, D. Rivetus on the same place, from the Pontificals, Maldonatus, Cornelius à Lapide and others on this place. Conf. the mentioned Maldon. also on Luc. 11, 28. Iacob. Bonfrerius Praeloq. in Sc. S. can. 15. Moreover, that rule of the Theologians can be confirmed by that prophetic oracle, approved by the Savior, that ceremonial precepts yield to moral ones, even in the second table. Sacrifices, however, pertain to ceremonial ones, as is known. Furthermore, it makes for a comparative signification that August. l. 20. contra Faust. 16. & l. 2. de consensu Ev. c. 27. reads I desire mercy, rather than sacrifice. Ambrosius lib. de poenit. c. 2. I prefer mercy, rather than sacrifice. Thus also August. l. 10. de Civ. Dei c. 5. and Caesarius homil. 36. expressly have it.)*

And not the just. By the just can be understood either those who are plainly and habitually just, such as the first-formed were before the fall. And then Christ did not come for the sake of the just, because such just persons do not exist after the fall; or the just by their own persuasion and opinion, Luke 16, 15. c. 18. v. 9. Rom. 10. v. 3. for whom Christ did not come, not by intention and the absolute decree of GOD, *(for the contrary is evident from those classic sayings, Matt. 18, 11. Luke 28, 19. Luke 19, 10. 1 Cor. 5, 14. 1 Tim. 2, 6. 1 John 2, 2.)* but by accident, which is the proud and stubborn persuasion of such just persons, by which they wickedly reject Christ the Physician. The just, therefore, are called so here, not those who are truly such, so that they stand in need of no repentance, but those who establish themselves as such and wish to be held as such by others. Chrysost. hom. 31. in Matt. Theoph. in this place. *(In the same way Jerome accepts it in this place. Concerning the prophet, he writes, bringing forth testimony, he rebukes the Scribes and Pharisees: who, esteeming themselves just, avoided the company of sinners and of publicans. Among more recent Theologians, in this sense, namely for those who are just at least in their own opinion, but not in truth, Luke 18, 9. they accept the word of the just in this place. B. D.

Chemn. in H. E. in this place. B. D. Meisnerus Part. 2. Ανσθρωπ. Disp. 15. q. 6. c. 24. B. D. Glassius Exeg. Ev. Dom. XI. post Trin. page 142 & in Exeg. Ev Festo Matth. p. 190. B. D. Tarnov. in Amos page 123. from the Calvinists Gross. in Theat. Bibl. p. 856. Explicitly Chrysost. hom. 31. ad h. l. Ηπίβλη &c. But this explanation relies among other things on that canon, that Holy Scripture sometimes speaks κατὰ τὸ ἔνδοξον i.e., so that it says that such things or men are, not such as they really are, but such as they seem to be. Thus Matth. 8, 12 sons of the kingdom are called those who ought to have been such or seemed so to themselves. Conf. 1. Cor 8, 5. 6. Gal. 4. 4. B. D. Tarn. l. c. notes that the passages Gen. 18, 1. 19. c. 32. 24. 1. Sam 28, 13. Exod 20, 4. 18. Ps. 69, 29. Matt. 3, 5. Luc. 15, 7. 1. Cor. 1, 21. also look to this, but we are forced to admit that hardly one or another approves or confirms the present canon. Furthermore, Corn à Lap. and other Papists in h. l. think the word of the righteous is used here for those who are righteous in reality, since Christ also called Nathanael, likewise the Blessed Virgin, John and Elizabeth, who nevertheless were holy. They say therefore the Savior, not simply denying that He came to call the righteous, but κατὰ namely to repentance, which although it is not read here in the Lat. vers., (just as neither the Syrian nor the Ethiopian, nor the Persian have it in h. l.) is nevertheless held in Luke, and also in h. l. in the Greek Codices, and likewise in the Arabic. Resp. 1. We concede that Christ speaks of the calling to repentance: thus the genuine reading has it; we add however 2. not only famous sinners, but also those whom Holy Scripture sometimes calls righteous and holy, namely on account of the imputed righteousness of Christ (just as Cornelius himself admits here, that the holiness of those and all others flowed from the foreseen merits of Christ) have need of daily repentance, for the whole life of a Christian man is perpetual repentance, since the pious also stand in need of daily remission of sins. Matth. 6, 12. And this not even Corn. himself can deny, since he indeed brings forward the saying of the Apostle Rom. 3, 2. All have sinned. &c. Thus Ioh. de la Haye in Triumpho Verit. p. 35. compares with the present passage Luc. 19, 18. and 1. Tim. 1, 15. Christ therefore speaks of those who Superbly, but falsely they esteem themselves righteous and were boasting, when in reality they are sinners. And Cornelius himself confesses that Hilary, Jerome, Bede, Theophylact, and Euthymius understand the present passage in this manner.

(But sinners. Compare parallel passages Rom. 5, 21.Act. 10, 43.1. Tim. 1, 15.Matth 11, 4.27. Let someone here object with Piscator in the book on grace against Henning, p. 21: If Christ came to call to repentance only sinners, namely those who acknowledge their sins and grieve over them, such as the publicans in this place, it follows that the calling is not universal. Response: Nay, rather He came to call all men to repentance because all men are sinners, Rom. 5, 12.1. Ioh. 1, 8. 9. 10. Distinguish, however, between the calling considered according to the divine intention, and the calling hindered by the malice of men, that is, by the contempt of the means and the persuasion of their own righteousness. In the former way all are called, and in this way God is the Savior of all, 1. Tim. 4, 10. and in that way all are called because all are sinners. In the latter way He is the Savior of believers, ibid., and thus the righteous, that is, those who are swollen with the opinion of their own righteousness, are not called. Compare B. D. Fewrb. Synt. diss. Theol. 1. p. 51. & 318.)

(To repentance. Matth. c. 11, 28. He says that He calls sinners to refreshment. Compare below c. 20, 28. Ioh. 10, 11. add. Es. 61, 1.Luc. 10, 34. Repentance, however, includes the detestation of sin and the trustful apprehension of Christ, the consequence of which is the amendment of life. But Holy Scripture knows nothing of an imposed satisfaction which is necessary for obtaining or meriting justification and salvation. Bell. t. 1. Controv. l. 2. d. V. D. c. 14, where he defends the Vulgate version, where these words to repentance are missing, he babbles that those are superfluous. But not only do the Greek codices have them, but even the Vulgate interpreter himself Luc. 5, 32.)

Latin:

v. 13. Ἔλεονθέλω. Os. 6. v. 6. *(Eadem sententia repetitus infra. c. 12, 7. ubi quaedam de eâ monebuntur.)* Theoph. h. l. Deus maiorē facit misericordiam in peccatores, quàm sacrificium. Hieron. in cap. 6 Ose Vera ac Deo grata sacrificia sunt salus credentium & conversio peccatorum. Ambros. lib. 1. de poenit. cap. 11. tom 1. p. 160. Per sacrificium iustus commendatur, per misericordiam peccator redimitur. In lege sacrificium, in Evangelio misericordia.

Et non apud Hebraeos usurpatur ut significet potiùs quàm. Scindite cor vestrum, & non vestes vestras i. e. potiùs quàm vestes vestras. Prover. 17. v. 12. Occurrat ursus orbus in virum, & non stultus in stultitia sua i. e. potiùs ursus quam stultus occurrat.

*(Quod verò hîc negativum Adverbium pro comparativâ particulâ adhibeatur, patet tum ex inspectione textûs Prophetici, unde Salvator sententiam hanc allegavit: expressè enim subiicitur, & cognoscere Deum (s. cognitione DEI, delector) מעלותprae holocaustis; tum ex eo, quòd Deus sacrificia, ex fideli corde oblata minimè respuerit, utpote quae ipse mandaverat. Et suppetunt quoque plura similia in sacris literis exempla. Uti Gen. 45, 8.Exod. 16, 8.Ps. 34, 11.Prov 8, 10.Ier. 7, 22.Ioel. 2, 13.Luc. 14, 12.Ioh. 5, 45.c. 6, 27.1. Cor. 1, 17. add Matth. 10, 20.Act. 5, 4.Eph. 6, 12.2. Thess. 4, 8. Maldonatus huc refert Ioh. 7, 16.c. 10, 20. Sunt tamen qui negativam significationem hîc locum habere, omninò censent: monent verò, quòd Christus loquatur de sacrificiis sine fide ex hypocrisi oblatis, quae utiq; Deus non velit. Vid. Es. 1, 11.Prov. 15, 8.c. 21, 27Es. 66, 3.Ierem 7, 9. 10. ita exponit B. D. Glass. Gramm. S. p. 485. Quo modo & Chrysotomus h. l. intellexit, ceu patet ex homil. 31. in Matth. Sed alii ellipticè dictum accipiunt intelliguntque sacrificia ex verâ fide oblata. Atque huc etiam collimat B. D. Tarnovii interpretatio, qui in Comm. ad d l. ellipticè loquutum putat Hoseam, hoc sensu. Pietate delector & non solùm sacrificio, subintelligendo sc. לבך, quo modo etiam particula μόνον in N. T. aliquoties desit in altero oppositionis membro. Quòd verò hoc genus ellipseos in Sc. S. frequentissimum sit in ἀντιθέσει, ea, quae non simpliciter, sed secundum quid, seu certam determinationē in stituitur, probat laudatus Dn. Tarn. Comm. in Ioel. c. 2, 13. seqq. dictis Genes. 32, 28.1. Sam. 8, 7.

Ies. 31, 34.Hos. 6, 7.Matth. 9, 13.c. 10, 20.c. 18, 22.Marc. 9, 37.Ioh. 5, 30.c. 14, 24.c. 16, 26.c. 11, 44.2. Cor. 3, 6.2. Cor. 1, 17. Sed praestat comparativè accipere. Quomodo etiam accipiunt B. P. t. 3. LL. Th. pag. 23. it. Comm. in Gen. p. 140. nec non part. 2. Hom. 11. Acad. p. 441. B. D. Calixtus in Harm. h. l. D. Quistorp. in h. l B. D. Meisnerus ac B. D. Himmelius in d l. Hoseae. ex Calvinianis, D Rivetus in eund locum, ex Pontif. Maldonatus, Cornelius à Lapide & alii in h. l. Conf. memoratus Maldon. etiam ad Luc. 11, 28. Iacob. Bonfrerius Praeloq. in Sc. S. can. 15. Confirmari autem oraculo isto prophetico, à Salvatore approbato regula illa Theologorum potest, quòd ceremonialia praecepta cedant moralibus, etiam in secundâ tabulâ. Sacrificia verò pertinent ad ceremonialis, uti notum est. Facit porrò pro comparativâ significatine, quòd August. l. 20. contra Faust. 16. & l. 2. de consensu Ev. c. 27. legit misericordiam volo, quàm sacrificium. Ambrosius lib. de poenit. c. 2. misericordiam malo, quàm sacrificium. Ita quoq; disertè habent August. l. 10. de Civ. Dei c. 5. ac Caesarius homil. 36.)*

Et non iustos. Per iustos intelligi possunt vel planè & habitualiter iusti, quales fuêre protoplasti ante lapsum. Et tum Christus propter iustos non venit, quia tales iusti post lapsum non sunt; vel iusti ex propria persuasione & opinione,Luc. 16, 15.c. 18. v. 9.Rom. 10. v. 3. propter quos Christus non venit, non ex intentione & absoluto DEI decreto, *(contrarium enim patet ex classicis illis dictis, Matth. 18, 11.Luc. 28, 19.Luc. 19, 10.1. Corinth. 5, 14.1. Timoth. 2, 6.1. Iohan. 2, 2.)* sed ex accidente, quod est talium iustorum superba & praefracta persuasio, quâ Christum Medieum nequiter reiiciunt Iusti igitur hîc dicuntur, non qui revera tales sunt, ut nullâ poenitentiâ indigeant, sed qui se tales esse statuunt & ab aliis haberi volunt. Chrysost. hom. 31. in Matth. Theoph. h. l. *(Eodem modo accipit Hieronymus in h. l. De propheta, scribit, proferens testimonium, sugillat Scribas & Pharisaeos: qui iustos se aestimantes, peccatorum & publicanorum consortia declinabant. Ex recentioribus Theologis hoc sensu, nempe pro illis, qui suâ saltem opinione, non verò revera iusti sunt, Luc. 18, 9. accipiunt vocem iustorum h. l. B. D.

Chemn. in H. E. h. l. B. D. Meisnerus Part. 2. Ανσθρωπ. Disp. 15. q. 6. c. 24. B. D. Glassius Exeg. Ev. Dom. XI. post Trin. pag. 142 & in Exeg. Ev Festo Matth. p. 190. B. D. Tarnov. in Amos pag. 123. ex Calvinianis Gross. in Theat. Bibl. p. 856. Disertè Chrysost. hom. 31. ad h. l. Ηπίβλη &c. Nititur verò haec explicatio inter alia canone illo, quòd Sc. S. aliquando loquaturκατὰ τὸ ἔνδοξονh. e. ut tales res vel homines esse dicat, non quales reverasunt, sed quales esse videntur. Sic Matth. 8, 12silii regni dicuntur, qui tales esse debebant vel sibi videbantur. Conf. 1. Cor 8, 5. 6.Gal. 4. 4. B. D. Tarn. l. c. huc quoque spectare notat loca Gen. 18, 1.19.c. 32. 24.1. Sam 28, 13.Exod 20, 4.18.Ps. 69, 29.Matt. 3, 5.Luc. 15, 7.1. Cor. 1, 21. sedifateri cogimur, quòd vix unus atq; alter praesentē canonē approbet vel confirmet. Coeterùm Corn à Lap. aliiq; Pontificii in h. l. vocem iustorū pro iis hîc adhiberi putant, qui rever à iusti sunt, eùm & Nathaneelem, itē B. Virginem, Iohannem & Elisabetham, qui tamen sancti fuerint, Christus vocârit. dicunt proinde Salvatorē; nō simpliciter negare se venisse vocare iustos, sedκατὰnempe ad poenitentiam, quod licet in Lat. vers. hîc non legatur, (quemadmodum nec Syrus nec Aethiops, nec Persa h. l. habent) haberi tamen apud Lucam, nec non h. l. in Codd. Graecis, itemq; apud Arabem. Resp. 1. Concedimus, Christū loqui de vocatione ad poenitentiam: itan. habet genuina lectio addimus tamen 2. non solùm famosos peccatores, sed eos quoque, quos Script. S. aliquando iustos & sanctos vocat, nempe propter imputatam iustitiam Christi (quemadmodum ipse etiam Cornelius hîc fatetur, quòd istorum omniumaliorum sanctitas manaverit ex praevisis Christi meritis) opus habere cottidianâ poenitētiâ, tota quippe hominis (hristiani vita perpetua est poenitētia, cùm pii etiam cottidianâ peccatorum remissione indigeant.
