Matth. 6, 12. Atque hoc nec ipse Corn. abnuere potest, adducens quippe dictum Apostoli Rom. 3, 2. Omnes peccaverunt. &c. Sic Ioh. de la Haye in Triumpho Verit. p. 35. confert cum praesenti loco Luc. 19, 18. ac 1. Tim. 1, 15. Loquitur igitur Christus de iis, qui superbè, sed falsò se iustos aestimant & iactitabant, cùm revera sint peccatores. Atque h. m. praesentem locum intelligere Hilarium, Hieronymum, Bedam, Theophylactum & Euthymium, ipsemet Cornelius fatetur)*

*(Sed peccatores. Conf. loca parall. Rom. 5, 21.Act. 10, 43.1. Tim. 1, 15.Matth 11, 4.27. Opponat hîc aliquis cum Piscat. in lib. de grat. contra Henning. p. 21. Si Christus tantùm peccatores, nempe qui peccata sua agnoscunt & de iis dolent, quales h. l. Publicani, venit vocare adpoenitentiam, sequitur, quòd vocatio non sit universalis Resp. Imò potiùs venit vocare omnes homines ad poenit. quia omnes homines sunt peccatores, Rom. 5, 12.1. Ioh. 1, 8. 9. 10. Distingv. tamen inter vocationem ex intentione divinâ consideratam, & hominum malitiâ h. e. mediorum contemtu ac propriae iustitiae persuasione impeditam. Priori modo omnes vocati sunt, & hoc modò Deus est Salvator omnium1. Tim. 4, 10. atque eô modô omnes vocati sunt, quia omnes peccatores. Posteriori est Salvator credentium, ibid. & ita iusti h. e. qui propriae iustitiae opinione turgidi, non sunt vocati. Conf. B. D. Fewrb. Synt. diss. Theol. 1. p. 51. & 318.)*

*( Ad poenitentiam.Matth. c. 11, 28. dicit, se peccatores vocare ad refectionem. Conf. infrà c. 20, 28. Ioh. 10, 11. add. Es. 61, 1.Luc. 10, 34. Poenitentia verò complectitur peccati detestationem ac fiducialē Christi apprehēsionem, cuius consequens vitae emedatio est. Nihil verò Sc. S. novit de imposita satisfactione, quae ad iustificationem & salutem consequendam vel promerendam necessari sit. Bell. t. 1. Controv. l. 2. d. V. D. c. 14. quò defendatversionem Vulgatam, ubi haec verba ad poenitentiam, desunt, grarrit, illa esse superflua. Atqui non solùm Codd. Graeci habent, verùm etiam ipse Vulgatus Interpres Luc. 5, 32.)*

## 9:14
(V. 14. The disciples of John. But at Luc. 5, 33. the Pharisees themselves are said to have proposed this question. See the reconciliation in the Annotations on the said place of Luke.)

(Your disciples do not fast. Christ by no means disapproved of or prohibited ἁπλῶς fasts, but at least κατὰ τί,, namely if merit is attributed to them, or if they are observed too superstitiously, which is what the Pharisees were doing and κακοζηλίᾳ then the disciples of John, and today the Papists. Against whose rigorous precepts, by which they demand fasts on certain days most superstitiously, and assign to them I know not what merit of eternal life, while our people dispute, they certainly do not disapprove of fasts undertaken for that end, that we may be more fit for prayers. So that the Papists do us an injury when they shout that blessed Luther, by abolishing fasts, gave free rein to men for the lusts of the flesh, and that we are enemies of fasts. Which injuries, however, were long ago repelled by B. P. Confess. Cath. t. 4. pag. 996. Furthermore, concerning fasting, some things were noted above at) Matth. 4, 2.c. 6, 16. Compare furthermore the Blessed D. Chemn. in this place. Blessed Par. Hom. Acad. part. 1. Dom. Invoc. hom. 4. Cameron in Myrothec. Ev. p. 53, 54.)*

Latin:

*(V. 14. Discipuli Iohannis. At Luc. 5, 33. ipsi Pharisaei dicuntur quastionem hanc proposuisse. Conciliationem vid. in Annot. ad d l. Lucae.)*

*( Discipuli tui non ieiunant. Christus minimè ἁπλῶς iunia improbavit, aut prohibuit, sed saltem κατὰ τί, nempe si meritum illis tribuatur, vel nimis superstitiosè ea observentur, id quod faciebant Pharisaei & κακοζηλίᾳ tum discipuli Iohannis, hodie verò Pontificii. Contra quorum rigorosa praecepta, quibus perquàm superstitiosè certis diebus ieiunia exigunt, iisque nescio quod vitae aet. meritum adsignant, dum nostrates disputant, minimè sanè ieiunia eo fine suscepta, ut ad preces aptiores simus, improbant. Ut adeò iniuriâ nos afficiant Pontificii, dum clamitant, quòd B. Lutherus abrogatis ieiuniis ad carnis libidines hominibus srena laxarit. quòd que hostes simus ieiuniorum. quas tamen iniurias pridem depulit B. P. Confess. Cath. t. 4. pag. 996. Coeterùm de ieiunio suprà quaedā monita ad Matth. 4, 2.c. 6, 16. Confer praetereà B. D. Chemn. in h. l. B. Par. Hom. Acad. part. 1. Dom. Invoc. hom. 4. Cameronem. in Myrothec. Ev. p. 53, 54.)*

## 9:15
v. 15. ιἱσὶ του νυμφῶνος. Conf. Iudic. 14. Νυμφὼν the bridegroom's house or bridal chamber, just as ἀνδρὼν of the men. It is therefore a metonymy customary to the Hebrews. Those dwelling in the bridegroom's chamber. The Syriac has sons of the bridal chamber, i. e. friends of the bridegroom, whom he admits even into his own chamber. *(In Greek they are otherwise called παρα-όμφιοι., in Hebrew שושבינים (see Iudic. 14, 20.) It is indeed a sufficiently known Hebraism, of which see examples in our Evangelist c. 8, 12. cap. 23, 15. From the Hebrew text the Blessed D. Glass. Phil. S. l. 3. tr. 1. can. 36 provides several examples. Add. Gatak de Stylo N. T. p. 163. & 164. The Persian has here sons of the bridal chamber, the Ethiopian i. e. sons of the Bridegroom. The Arabic however sons of the wedding.)*

*( Νύμφιος. The Savior recalls, by comparing himself with the Bridegroom, to the disciples of John the saying of their Master, attributing the name νυμφίου to Christ, Ioh. 3, 29. Conf. Matth. 22, 2.c. 25, 5.6. 10.Apoc. 19, 7,9.c. 21, 2.9.c. 22, 17. and parallel places Marc. 2, 19. 20.Luc. 5, 34.)*

But the days will come. Jerome: When the weddings have passed, and the time of passion and resurrection has arrived. Theophylact: There will be a time, when after my passion and ascension they will fast, being hungry and thirsty, having suffered persecution. Rupert: they will clearly fast in those days that are about to come, when the Bridegroom shall have been taken away from them, when he shall have suffered, died, and been buried and risen again, and ascended into heaven, now no longer conversing with them bodily in this world. * (The Savior speaks therefore of absence or departure regarding visible presence: for he did not ascend into heaven in such a way that he has completely abandoned his Bride, Matth 28, 20. But the opinion of Christ is this, as the Blessed D. Chemn. warns in Harm. in this place, that Christians ought to accommodate themselves to the condition of the time, which and what kind God sends. Namely that they ought to rejoice when God grants weddings, i. e. joyful times; but on the contrary when adversities are presented, they should be patient, pray, call upon God, and so that prayers may be more apt, add fasts. For the cross and the gravity of affairs provide the occasion and show the times for fasting. Looking to which Jerome also comments thus in this place: According to tropology it must be known that as long as the Bridegroom is with us, and we are in joy, we can neither fast nor mourn. But when he has departed from us on account of sins, then a fast is to be proclaimed, then mourning is to be received.)*

*( Then they shall fast. Bell. vol. 4. book 2. ch. 16. §. The third as &c. establishes that the ancients brought forward the reason for the instituted Lent among others also this one, that this prophecy of Christ might be fulfilled. But the contrary will be shown in the Anal. on Mark 2, 20.)* *(Then they shall fast. Conf. Acts 13, 2. 3.ch. 14, 23.2. Corinthians 6, 5.)*

Latin:

v. 15. ιἱσὶ του νυμφῶνος. Conf. Iudic. 14.Νυμφὼνsponsi aedes seu conclave, sicut ἀνδρὼνvirorum. Est ergo usitata Hebraeis metonymia. Versantes in sponnsi conclavi. Syr. habet filii thalami i. e. amici sponsi, quos in suum usque thalamum admittit. *(Graecè aliàs dicuntur παρα-όμφιοι. Ebr. שושבינים (vid. Iudic. 14, 20.) Est verò Ebraismus satis notus, evius exempla vid. apud nostrum Evang. c. 8, 12. cap. 23, 15. Ex textu Ebr. pluscula exempla suppeditat B. D. Glass. Phil. S. l. 3. tr. 1. can. 36. Add. Gatak de Stylo N. T. p. 163. & 164. Persa habet hîc filii thalami, Aethiops i. e. filii Sponsi. Arabs verò filii sponsaliorum.)*

*( Νύμφιος. Revocat Salvator, comparando se cum Sponso, discipulis Iohannis in memoriam dictum Magistri eorum, Christo νυμφίου nomen tribuentis, Ioh. 3, 29. Conf. Matth. 22, 2.c. 25, 5.6. 10.Apoc. 19, 7,9.c. 21, 2.9.c. 22, 17. ac loca parall. Marc. 2, 19. 20.Luc. 5, 34.)*

Aderunt autem dies. Hieron. Quando transierunt nuptiae, & passionis ac resurrectionis tempus advenerit. Theophyl. Tempiis erit, cùm post passionem meam & ascensionem ieiunaturi sint infame & siti, persecutionem passit. Rupertus: planè ieiunabunt in illis proximè venturis diebus, cùm ablatus fuerit ab eis Sponsus, cum passus, mortuus & sepuitus resurrexerit, & in coelum ascenderit, iam non ultra cum eis in hoc mundo corporaliter conversatus. * (Loquitur igitur Salvator de absentia vel discessu quoad praesentiam visibilem: neque enimita ipse adfcendit in coelum ut Sponsam suam penitus deserverit, Matth 28, 20. Sententia autem Christi haec est, monente B. D. Chemn. in Harm. h. l. quòd Christiani temporis conditioni, quam & qualem Deus immittit, sese accommodare debeant. Nempe quòd laetari debeant, quando Deus concedit nuptias h. e. laeta tempora; contrà verò quando obiiciuntura adversitaes, sint patientes, orent, Deum invocent, & ut preces sint aptiores, ieiunia adiungant. Crux enim & negotiorum gravitas praebent occasionem & monstrant tempora ieiunandi. Quo respiciens & Hieronymus; ita in h. l. commentatur: Iuxta tropologiam sciendum, quòd quamdiu Sponsu nobiscum est, & in laetitiâ sumus, nec ieiunare possumus, nec lugere. Cùm autem ille propter peccata à nobis recesserit, tunc indicendum ieiunium est, tum luctus recipiendus.)*

*( Tunc ieiunabunt. Bell. t. 4. l. 2. c. 16. §. Tertia ut &c. statuit quòd veteres rationem institutae, Quadragesimae attulerint interalias etiam hanc, ut hoc Christi vaticinium impleretur. Verùm contrarium ostendetur in Anal. ad Marc. 2, 20.)* *(Tunc ieiunabunt. Conf. Act. 13, 2. 3.c. 14, 23.2. Corinth. 6, 5.)*

## 9:16
v. 16. Επίβλημα ῥάκους ἀγνάφου, a raw and new cloth, which has not yet been polished and shorn by the fuller ὑὸ τουγναφέος. Luke calls it ἱμάτιον καινὸν. In Martial book 11. smooth garments and worn out ones are opposed. γνὰπτω is by plucking or by pulling off, hence γναφευς a fuller, hence ἄγναφος raw, new, not yet having experienced the fuller's art. It is opposed to the Pharisees, who labored with untimely zeal in saving the traditions of the ancients, and determined that they should be joined at least with the new doctrine of the Gospel. Toss. The old garment and the old wineskins signify the infirmity of the disciples; the new cloth not fitting the old garment and the new wine, which is by no means to be stored in old wineskins; signifies fasting and other more severe exercises. The sense therefore is, that the disciples on account of their infirmity and tender condition cannot bear the more severe discipline of fasting.

*(Concerning the word ἀγνάφου see Anal. on Mark 9, 3.)*

Πλήρωμα. Syr. םליותה its fullness, τὸ supplement, i. e. that piece of cloth which was applied to fill the hole. Fullness for the thing which fills. A Hebraism.

Latin:

v. 16. Επίβλημα ῥάκους ἀγνάφου, pannum rudem ac recentem, qui nondum à fullone ὑὸ τουγναφέος sit politus ac rasus. Lucas vocat ἱμάτιον καινὸν. Apud Martialem lib. 11. opponuntur vestes pexatae & tritae.γνὰπτω est carpendo aut vellicando expolio, inde γναφευςfullo, hinc ἄγναφοςrudis, recens, fulloniam nondum expertus. Opponitur Pharifaeis, qui intempestivo zelo in salvandis veterum traditionibus laborabant, easqueut minimum cum novâ Evangelii doctrina coniungendas statuebant. Toss. Vestimentum vetus & uteres veteres significant discipulorum infirmitatem; pannus recens non conveniens veteri vestimento & vinum novum, quod in ut res veteres haudquaquam recondendum; significat ieiuntum & alia severior axercitia. Sensus igitur est, quod discipuli propter infirmit atemat teneram conditionem non possint ferre severiorem ieiunii disciplinam.

*(De voce ἀγνάφου vid. Anal. ad Marc. 9, 3.)*

Πλήρωμα. Syr. םליותהplenitudo eius,τὸsupplementum i. e. frustum illud panni. quod ad implendum foramen adhibebatur. Plenitudo pro re, quae implet. Hebraismus.

## 9:17
v. 17. Old wineskins. Who are to be understood by old wineskins, see Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, Epistle 57. The ancients by no means stored wine in jars, but in wineskins made of leather, Josh. 9, v. 13. and smeared with pitch, Judith 10, v. 5. It was not permitted to commit must in its first fermentation to aged wineskins, because there was a danger that, if they were burst, the must would be uselessly poured out. By this proverb Christ teaches that the superstitious traditions of the ancients are not to be confounded with the doctrine of the Gospel. μόνον the most mild and holy (as they are named by Epiphanius, book 1, tom. 3, f. 135) presbyters and teachers of the holy Church of GOD, who lived at Rome around the year of Christ 150, interpreted it a little differently. For when Marcion had proposed the adage to them in the place of a riddle, they answered meekly. κατὰ *(But the former explanation agrees more with the purpose of Christ. For Christ intends by both similitudes that, just as a new patch is less correctly sewn onto an old garment, nor is new wine committed to old wineskins: so neither are the traditions of fasts, which have been introduced either from legal discipline or from the constitutions of ancestors, and are therefore near to destruction on account of their antiquity, Heb. 8, last, to be sewn onto the novelty of the Evangelical doctrine, nor are those who are too addicted to these traditions capable of the Evangelical doctrine. As the blessed D. Chemnitius rightly explains in Harm. c. 66. With those, however, who compare the sewing of a piece of raw cloth into an old garment, the modern justiciaries (Papists) can be compared, while they strive to intrude their works into the article of justification, and to sew the same onto the merit of Christ. Lest therefore they be convicted of folly and malice from this text, they explain the present saying in another and entirely contrary way, as is evident especially from Bell. t. 4. Contr. l. 2. de B. O. in part. c. 8. Franc. Lucas and Cornelius à Lapide on this passage: namely, by old wineskins they understand the Apostles, upon whom, as being not very robust, Christ considers it less advisable to impose new, robust, and heavy burdens of rigid discipline, fasts, extraordinary prayers, and the like. But how clearly this explanation does not suit the purpose of Christ will be shown in the Anal. to Mark 2:21.)*

Luther in the margin Carnal hearts cannot grasp the doctrine of the righteousness of faith, but by hearing it they become worse. Origen, book 1, Peri Archon, chapter 3, He wants new wineskins to be made, that is, men to walk in the newness of life, so that they might receive the new wine, that is, the newness of the grace of the Holy Spirit.

*( Wineskins. By wineskins are understood metaphorically the minds of man, the reason for which metaphor Camero elegantly explains in Myrothecium Evangelicum on Heb. 2:1.)*

Latin:

v. 17. Utres vetres. Quinam intelligantur per utres veteres, vide Isidor. Pelus. lib. 1. Epist. 57. Veteres vinum nequaquam in dolia condebant, sed in utres ê corio factos, Ios. 9. v. 13. & pice illitos, Iudith. 10. v. 5. Mustum in primo fervore utribus inveteratis committere non licebat, quòd periculum esset, ne illis diruptis mustum inutiliter profunderetur. Christus hac paroemia docet, superstitiosas veterum traditiones cum doctrina Evangelii non esse confundendas. μόνονmites & sanctissimi (ut ab Epiphan. nominantur lib. 1. tom. 3. f. 135.) sanctae DEI Ecclesiae Presbyteri ac doctores, qui circa annum Christi 150. Romae vixerunt, paulò aliter interpretati sunt. Cùm enim Marcion ipsis adagium aenigmatis loco proposuisset, mansuetè responderunt. κατὰ *(Sed prior explicatio magis congruit Christi scopo. Hoc enim vult Christus utraq; similitudine, quòd quemadmodum panniculum novum minùs rectè adsuitur vestimento veteri, nec vinum novum committitur utribus veteribus: ita nec traditiones ieiuniorum, quae introductae sint vel ex legali disciplina, vel ex constitutionibus maiorum, ac proinde ob antiquitatem interitui vicinae sint, Ebr. 8, ult. adsuendae novitati doctrinae Evangelicae, neque illi, qui ististraditionibus nimiùm addicti sunt, doctrinae Evangelicae sint capaces. Ceu rectè explicat B. D. Chemnitius in Harm c. 66. Cum istis verò qui commissuram panni rudis immitum in vestimentum vetus conferri hodierni iustitiarii (Pontificii) possunt, dum opera sua articulo iustificationis intrudere, eademq; Christi meritò adsuere satagunt. Ne itaque stultitiae ac malitiae ex hoc textu convincantur, alio eodemque prorsus contrario modo praesens dictum ipsi exponunt, ceu eumprimis ex Bell. t. 4. Contr. l. 2. de B. O. in part. c. 8. Franc. Luca ac Cornelio à Lapide in h. l. patet: nempe per utres veteres intelligunt Apostolos, quibus utpote parùm robustis nova, robusta ac gravia rigidae diseiplinae, ieiuniorum, extra ordinariarum precum ac similium onera imponere, minùs consultum Christus ducat. At quàm planè non explicatio haec Christi se opo conveniat, ostendetur in Anal. ad Marc. 2, 21.)*

Lutherus in Marg. Corda carnalia doctrinam de iustitia fidei capere non possunt, sed eius auditu fiunt deteriora. Orig. lib. 1. periarchon cap. 3. Vult utres fieri novos i. e. homines in vitae novitate ambulare, ut vinum novum i. e. Spiritus S. gratiae susciperent novitatem.

*( Utres. Intelliguntur per utres metaphoricè animi hominis, cuius metaphorae rationem eleganter exponit Camero in Myroth. Evang. ad Ebr. 2. 1.)*

## 9:18
v. 18. Αρχων, namely τῆς σοναγωγῆς who by Mark c. 5:22 is called by a compound word ἀρχισοννάγωγος. *(Cf. Luke 8:41. c. 14:1. c. 18:18. etc. Concerning their office and dignity see B. D. Chemn. H. Ev. c. 67. p. 738. B. P H. E. p. 229. 290 Grotius on this passage.)*

Αρτι ἐτελευτησεν. Luke chapter 8, v. 42 has ἀπέθνησκεν. Mark chapter 5, v. 13 ἐχάτως ἔχει. how are these to be reconciled? It must be considered that when that ruler was departing to implore the help of Jesus, his daughter was already at that time in her death throes, whence he himself, when he had already arrived at Jesus, thought that in the meantime she had died, or certainly was about to die at any moment. *(Thus it is also explained in the Gloss of the Ernesti Bibles.)* Matthew metonymically puts death for the death throes, just as we commonly pronounce that it is all over for him who has been reduced to the last extremity. Jairus had known that his daughter was just then in her last moments; he had conjectured that she was already dead. The daughter was in her last moments and was dying, when Jairus left his house, but she was dead when he was beseeching the Lord in his house. *(This latter explanation is also embraced by Mr. D. Walther, Harm. B. bl. p. 762. Maldonatus thinks that the ruler of the synagogue did not say at the same time what Matthew narrates at the same time, namely, my daughter has just died, but come etc. But that he said these words: come, lay your hand upon her, before he knew that she was dead. But having heard of the death, he asked Christ, or thought to ask, that He should not come, since she was already dead, and because Mark and Luke narrate it so and

because upon receiving the news of the death Christ said to him, do not fear, only believe, and she was saved, as if he had already begun to fear that Christ, who could heal the dying, could not raise the dead, and because it does not seem credible that a Jewish man and a ruler of the synagogue had such great faith that he could believe that Christ could raise a girl already dead by the touch of His hand. Furthermore, more will be discussed on this matter at Luc. 8, 42. Andreas Osiander, in book 1 of his annotations on the Harmony, cap. 43., maintains that this history is different from that which Mark cap. 5. and Luke cap. 8. describe. Because Matthew says that this ruler came when Christ was still reclining at the banquet which he had prepared for Him in his house. In Mark and Luke, the ruler of the synagogue is said to have come to Christ when He was still around the sea which He had crossed. The time is different, because Mark and Luke agree with Matthew concerning the time of His calling, and yet they say that Jairus came to Christ a long time afterwards, whereas Matthew said he was present at the very time of the banquet. The persons are different; Matthew deals with a ruler, whom he calls ὄορχοντα i.e., a political magistrate. Luke and Mark deal with a ruler of the synagogue. (But the blessed Doctor Chemnitz has solidly discussed these reasons of Osiander in the Harmony at this place, the foundations of which will also be brought forward at Marc. c. 5, 22.)

*( ᾽δπίθες σὴν χεῖρά σου. Concerning χειροθεσίᾳ see Analecta on Marc. 6, 5.)*

Latin:

v. 18. Αρχων, sc. τῆς σοναγωγῆς qui à Marco c. 5, 22. voce compositâ vocatur ἀρχισοννάγωγος. *(Conf. Luc. 8, 41.c. 14, 1.c. 18, 18. &c. Dehorum officio & dignitate vid. B. D. Chemn. H. Ev. c. 67. p. 738. B. P H. E. p. 229. 290 Grotius ad h. l.)*

Αρτι ἐτελευτησεν. Lucas cap. 8. v. 42. habet ἀπέθνησκεν. Marcus cap. 5. v. 13.ἐχάτως ἔχει.quomodo haec concilianda? Cogitantandum, praefecto illo abeunte ad implorandam Iesu opem filiam eius iam tum fuisse in agone, unde ipse cùm iam ad Iesum pervenisset, putabat, interim esse defunctam, aut certè iamiam morituram. *(ita etiam exponitur in Glossa Bibliorum Ernestionorum.)* Matthaeus metonomicè mortem ponit pro mortus agone, sicut vulgò de eo iam actum esse pronunciamus, qui ad extrema redactus est. Filiam in extremis modò egisse, Iaitus sciverat, mortuam iam esse coniectavertat. Filia in extremis erat & morieb--ur, cùm domo sua Iairus exiret, mortua autem erat, cùm Domino in domo supplicaret. *(Postremam hanc explicationem amplectitur quoque Dn. D. Waltherus Harm. B. bl. p. 762. Maldonatus existimat, principem Synagogae non simul dixisse, quae Matthaeus simul narrat, nempe filia modô defuncta est, sed veni &c. Sed haec verba: veni, impone manum tuam super eam, dixisse, antequam mortuam esse sciret. Morte autem auditâ rogasse Christum, aut rogare cogitasse, ne veniret, cùm mortua iam esset, & quia Marcus ac Lucas ita narrant &

quia accepto nuncio de morte Christus illi dixit, noli timere, crede tantùm & salva erat, quasi iam timere coepisset, ne Christus, qui moribundam sanare poterat, mortuam suscitare non posset, & quia hominem Iudaeum eum que Synagogae principem credibile non videtur tantam habuisse fidem, ut credere posset, Christum mortuam iam puellam tactu manûs suscitare posse. Coeterùm pluribus hâc de re agetur ad Luc. 8, 42.)* Andr. Osiand. lib. 1. annot. in Harm, cap. 43. statuit, diversam esse hànc Historiam ab ea, quam Marcuscap. 5.& Lucascap. 8.describunt. Quia Matthaeus dicit, hunc primatem venisse, cum Christus in convivio, quod ei in domo suaparaverat, adhuc discumberet. Apud Marcum & Lucam ad Christum dicitur archisynagogus venisse, cum adhuc esset circamare, quod traiecerat. Diversum est tempus, quia Marcus & Lucas cum Matthaeo de tempore vocationis ipsius consentiunt, & tamen Iairum longo pòst tempore ad Christum venisse dicunt, cum Matthaeus sub ipsum convivit tempus adfuisse diceret. Diversae sunt personae, Matthaeus agit de primate, quem vocatὄορχοντα i. e. Magistratum politicum. Luc. & Marc. de archisynagogo. *(Sed has Osiandri rationes solidè discussit B. D. Chemn. in Harm. h. l. cuius etiam fundamenta adducentur ad Marc. c. 5, 22.)*

*( ᾽δπίθες σὴν χεῖρά σου. De χειροθεσίᾳ vid. Analecta ad Marc. 6, 5.)*

## 9:19
(v. 19. And Jesus rising &c. From the fact that Christ, at the prayers of Jairus, not reproaching him with the hostile spirit of the Pharisees and Scribes, immediately arose (Conf. John 4:34ch. 6:37), both the ancient and more recent interpreters rightly gather his supreme gentleness and readiness to help. The facility of Christ, writes Franc. Lucas on this passage, offering himself voluntarily to the requests of all who believe in him, with a zeal for doing good. Since the Savior has not yet put off this benevolent affection toward those who believe in him and call upon him (see Heb. 4:15), the Papists are truly unjust toward him (whom the blessed D. Chemn. also censures on this account in Harm. on this passage), when they imagine him to be so harsh, difficult, and inexorable to themselves, that they think they can obtain nothing from him unless he is entreated through the inhabitants of heaven. Conf. entirely B. D. Himmel. on the nature of religious invocation, p. 296. seqq.)

Latin:

*(v. 19. Et surgens Iesus &c. Ex eo, quòd Christus ad preces Iairi, non exprobrans ei hostiles Pharisaeorum ac Scribarum animo-, statim surrexit (Conf. Ioh. 4, 34.c. 6, 37.) rectè colligunt tum veteres Interpp tum recentiores, summam eius mansuetudinem ac iuvandi promititudinem. Facilitas Christi, scribit Franc. Lucas in h. l. omnibus in ipsum credentibus ultrò ad postulata offerentis, benefaciendi studio. Hunc igitur benevolum erga credentes ipsumque invocantes affectum cùm nondum exuerit Salvator (vid Ebr. 4, 15.) iniqui profectò in ipsum sunt Pontificii, (quos etiam hoc nomine perstringit B. D. Chemn. in. Harm. h. l.) quando ita durum, difficilem & inexorabilem sibi eum fingunt, ut nisi per coelites exoretur, nihil se ab eo impetrare posse putent. Conf. omninò B. D. Himmel. de naturâ relig invoc. p. 296. seqq.)*

## 9:20
v. 20. She touched the hem &c. Bernh. in soliloq. As if a thief carrying away health. Why does she touch the hem of the garment? Because she had heard that power went out from Christ, which healed everyone. She was placing her hope not in the hem, but in the invisible power of Him whose hem it was. Athan. tom. 2. p. 254.

Chrysost. homil. 51. in Matth. applies this to the Supper of the Lord. Let us touch (he says) the hem of his garment, or rather, the whole of him. For if we wish, not only his garment, but his body itself is set before us, so that we may not only touch, but eat and be satisfied. Let us therefore approach Christ, each of us sick, with great faith. For if those who then touched the hem of his garment were all rightly made whole, how much more shall we be strengthened if we have the whole of him within us.

Euseb. lib. 7. Hist. Eccles. cap. 18. αἱμοῤῥοοῦσαν makes this woman a citizen of Caesarea Philippi, whose house was shown even then around the year of Christ 312, having once had joined to its doors a bronze statue of a woman, kneeling, and stretching out her hands clasped together to the right hand of another extended figure, decently dressed in a double garment or cloak, representing the likeness of our Savior, in whose place, after it was lifted up and broken by the pagans, Julian the Apostate placed his own image, which, however, a heavenly lightning bolt shattered, while the Christians collected the fragments of the image of Christ and kept them in the Church, as is in the Tripartita lib. 6. cap. 41. Theoph c. 9. Matth. It is added that from the stone base of the statue an unknown species of herb grew, which, after it had reached the extremity of the Savior's garment in its growth, became a panacea, the grass of which, when taken in a small portion, removed any diseases, having no strength if it had been plucked on this side of that. Baron. ann. Christi 362. n. 158. Item anno Christi 57. n. 11. *(Maldonatus in h. l. notes that besides Eusebius and Theophylact, the aforementioned authors Sozomen also, lib. 5. c. 21., makes mention of the same statue, and Corn. à Lap. to Marc. 5, 25., as do Adamus, Conzen, and Iac. Ticinus in h. l. It is indeed alleged in Cornelius c. 121. from Sozomen, just as in Tirinus and Maldonatus c. 28, and from Cornelius c. 14. from Eusebius: But that is an error of the typesetters. But without doubt the whole history concerning that statue is of doubtful faith. The authority of Nicephorus, who likewise mentions this history l. 6. cap. 15., has long been rejected by the Pontificians. But it is established that Sozomen often lied in his testimony, from the very Bell. lib. 3. de Poenit. c. 14. and lib. 1. de Cler. c. 20. and Greg. de Valentia l. de Coelib. p. 869.) Melchior Canus, Professor of Theology at Salamanca, judges almost the same concerning Eusebius, LL. Th. p. 338. Whence it is clear how weak the proof of Cardinal Baronius is, when at A. C. 57. n. 11. he strives to evince, among other things, from the aforementioned statue also, that images were religiously worshipped.)* And yet 1. if she spent her entire substance on physicians, whence had she a house so sturdy that it could last up to Julian for 400 years? Whence had she the expenses for two bronze images? 2. When the Caesareans were slaughtering 20,000 Jews during the time of the Jewish war, they do not seem to have retained a statue placed in public, if the Jews knew it to be such, much less would the Jews themselves, the most hostile enemies of Christ and haters of statues, have left it unharmed for so long. 3. Euseb. cannot certainly say whether those figures are those of the woman with the issue of blood and Christ. They handed down, he says, a statue formed to the likeness of the face of Jesus. But what is not handed down today concerning sacred places? In the Greek Eusebius nothing is brought forward except hearsay. 4. It was more likely that that miraculous power of healing resided in a statue than in an herb. 5. The pagans would not have broken it in the time of Julian. 6. Earlier writers would have reported it to Eusebius.

(Moreover, from the fact that the woman with the issue of blood touched the hem of Christ and was healed, the Papists (see Bell. l. 2. de Imag. c. 3. Corn-à Lap. on Marc. 5. 28. Iansenius in Concord. Ev. p. 219. Stapleton. Promt. Cathol. p. 292. Cotonus Instit. Christ. relig. p. 120. Coturius Epit. Controv. p. 479. Maldonatus in h. l. and others) gather the use and worship of relics. But 1. a distinction must be made between the touching of relics and the religious worship of the same. The woman with the issue of blood is read to have touched the hem of Christ, not to have worshipped it religiously. 2. It is one thing to touch the garment of Christ living, another to touch the relics of the dead. 3. Not the contact of the hem, but faith in Christ restored health to the woman. See Marc. 5, 31. Nor does the woman with the issue of blood attribute the power of healing to the clothes, but to GOD, through the merits of the most holy Prophet Jesus, as Franc. Lucas has in this place. 4. Distinguish between an extraordinary example and a universal rule. 5. It is to be noted that the power and efficacy of healing did not go out from the hem, (as indeed

Corn. à Lapide wishes) but from Christ,Mark 5, 30.Luke 6, 19.c. 8, 46. Whence Theologians note, that the power of the Lord healed ἐερ γητικῶς, the faith of the woman ὀργανικῶς, Matthew 9, 22.Mark 5, 34.Luke 8, 48. the fringe or the contact of the fringe συμβολικῶς. 6. But if that, through which as through some symbol a miracle is performed, is not immediately to be pursued with religious worship, it is evident, because otherwise the rod of Moses would also have had to be treated with such worship, likewise the mantle of Elijah, the shadow of Peter etc. Thus also the bronze serpent would have had to be religiously adored. Which, however, the pious King Hezekiah broke and abolished, when the Israelites exhibited such worship to it, 2 Kings 18, 4. Thus in the time of the Apostles many were miraculously cured by oil, and today perhaps there are still certain miraculous cures through springs. But who is ever read to have exhibited religious worship to oil on that account? Or who is so absurd as to wish, because of a miraculous cure, to religiously worship or adore such springs? Recognizing therefore the weakness of the argument, which Papists are accustomed to weave from this place for the worship of relics, some themselves studiously abstain from it, to whom the Jesuit Conzenius in Comm. on the 4 Gospels, Costerus in Enchir. Controv., and others pass over this example in silence. See more in B. P. Confess. Cathol. vol. 3. Book on Death §. 113. p. 678. B. D. R-nig Vindic. Sacr. Book 39. B. D. Himmel. on Inov. Relig. p. 907. seqq.)*

*( The fringe of his garment. See notes on Mark 5, 28.)*

*( If I shall touch only. It is evident from this how remarkable the faith of this woman was, believing indeed that Christ could heal even inveterate diseases, incurable by other men, and indeed that He could perform these things not only by power obtained from GOD through prayers, but by His own proper power. See B. D. Chem. in H. F. c. 67. Chrysostom beautifully: You see a woman far superior to the Ruler of the Synagogue. She did not seize, she did not detain anything, she touched only with the tips of her fingers, and therefore although she had come later, she departed earlier cured Ει γδ τῷ πάσθει ἦνσυνδεδεμθύη, ἀλλὰ τῆ πίςει ἦν ἐπτερωμένη. i. e. although she was delayed by sickness, yet by faith she was flying.)*

Latin:

v. 20. Tetigit fimbriam &c. Bernh. in soliloq. Quasi furargestiens sanitatem. Quare tangit fimbriam vestimenti? quia audiverat, à Christo exire virtutem, quae sanabat universos. Non infimbria, sed in eius cuius erat fimbria, invisibili potentia spem suam collocabat. Athan. tom. 2. p. 254.

Chrysost. homil. 51. in Matth. hoc ad coenam Domini accommodat. Tangamus (inquit) simbriam vestimenti eius, imò verò totum ipsum. Si enim volumus, non vestis solùm, sed corpus ipsius propositum est nobis, ut non tangamus solummodò, sed ut comedamus & saturemur. Adeam us ergo Christum singuli aegrtantes magna cum fide. Nam si qui fimbriam vestimenti eius tunc tetigerunt, rectè omnes valuerunt, quantò magis corroborabimur, si totum in nobis habebimus.

Euseb. lib. 7. Hist. Eccles. cap. 18. αἱμοῤῥοοῦσαν istam facit civem Caesareae Philippi, cuius domus etiam tunc circa annum Christi 312, fuerit ostensa, olim habens coniunctam foribus statuam ex aere muliebrem, geniculantem, manusque complicatas porrigentem dextrae protensae alterius signi, decenter diploide amicti seu rogati, referentis speciem Salvatoris nostri, in cuius sublati fracti que mox à paganis locum Iulianus Apostata suam posuit effigiem, quam tamen fulmen coeleste disiecit, Christianis fragmenta imaginis Christi colligentibus & in Ecclesia servantibus, ut est in Tripartita lib. 6. cap. 41. Theoph c. 9. Matth. Additur, ex basi lapidea statuae incognitam speciem herbae enatam, postquam crescendo attigisset extremitatem indumenti Salvatoris, panaceam evasisse, cuius gramen exiguâ portione haustum quoslibet morbos sustulerit, nihil virium habens, si citrà fuisset decerptum. Baron. ann. Christi 362. n. 158. Item anno Christi 57. n. 11. *(Eiusdem statuae praeter Eusebium & Theophylactum dd. ll. Sozomenum quoque lib. 5. c. 21. mentionem facere, notat Maldonatus in h. l. & eo Corn. à Lap. ad Marc. 5, 25. Adamus it. Conzen ac Iac. Ticinus in h. l. Allegatur quidem in Cornelio c. 121. ex Sozomeno, sicut in Tirino ac Maldonato c. 28, à Cornelio c. 14. ex Eusebio: Verùm typothetarum iste error est. Sed procul ambiguo tota de statua illa historia sublestae fidei est. Nicephori, qui itidem huius historiae meminit l. 6. cap. 15. autoritas pridem à Pontificiis reiecta est. Sozomenum verò ex ipsius Bell. lib. 3. de Poenit. c. 14. ac lib. 1. de Cler. c. 20. ac Greg. de Valentia l. de Coelib. p. 869.) testimonio saepè mentitum esse, constat. De Eusebio idem ferè iudicat Melchior Canus Professor Salmanticēsis LL. Th. p. 338. Unde patet, quàm infirma sit probatio Cardinalis Baronii, quando ad A. C. 57. n. 11. inter alia ex praedicta quoq; statua, imagines religiosè fuisse cultas, evincere satagit.)* Atqui 1. si universam substantiam in Medicos impendit, unde illi domus tam valida, ut potuerit usq; ad Iulianum per annos 400. durare? unde illi sumtus in aereas imagines duas? 2. Cum tempore belli Iudaici Caesarienses 20000. Iudaeorum trucidarent, non videntur retinuisse in publico locatam statuam, si sciverunt Iudaei esse, multò minùs Iudaei ipsi, infestissimi Christi hostes & statuarum osores eam tamdiu incolumen reliquissent. 3. Euseb. certò dicere nequit, sintne illa signa haemorrhousae & Christi. Tradebant, in quit, statuam formatam ad similitudinem vultûs Iesu. Sed quid hodiè non traditur de locis sacris? In Eusebio Graeco nihil praeter auditum affertur. 4. Verisimiliùs, in statua, quàm in herba miraculosam illam vim sanandi fuisse. 5. pagani tempore Iuliani non confregissent. 6. Priores Eusebio scriptoreo retulissent.

*(Coeterùm ex eo quòd mulier haemorrhousa fimbriam Christi tetigit, ac sanata est, colligunt Pontificii (vid. Bell. l. 2. de Imag. c. 3. Corn-à Lap. ad Marc. 5. 28. Iansenius in Concord. Ev. p. 219. Stapleton. Promt. Cathol. p. 292. Cotonus Instit. Christ. relig. p. 120. Coturius Epit. Controv. p. 479. Maldonatus in h. l. ac alii.) usum & cultum reliquiarum. Verùm I. disting. est inter reliquiarum tactum, & inter religiosum earundem cultum. Tetigisse legitur haemorhousa Christi fimbriam, non religiosè coluisse. 2. aliud est tangere vestem Christi vivi, aliud reliquias defunctorum. 3. non fimbriae contactus, sed fides in Christum mulieri sanitatem restituit. Vid. Marc. 5, 31. Nec vestibus virtute sanandi tribuit haemorrhousa, sed DEO, per Iesu sanctissimi Prophetae merita, ut habet Franc. Lucas in h. l. 4. Dist. inter exemplum extraordinarium, & regulam universalem. 5. notandum, quòd virtus & efficacia sanandi non exierit ex fimbria, (uti quidē

Corn. à Lapide vult) sed ex Christo,Marc. 5, 30.Luc. 6, 19.c. 8, 46. Unde notant Theologi, quòd virtus Domini sanaverit ἐερ γητικῶς, fides mulieris ὀργανικῶς,Matth. 9, 22.Marc. 5, 34.Luc. 8, 48. fimbria s. contactus fimbriae συμβολικῶς. 6. Si verò illud, per quod tanquam per symbolum aliquod miraculum editurnon statim sit cultu religiosó prosequendum, patet, quia aliàs etiam virga Mosis tali cultu fuisset afficienda, item pallium Eliae, umbra Petri &c. Sic & serpens aeneus fuisset religiosè adorandus. Quem tamen pius Rex Hiskias confregit & abolevit, quando talem cultum Israelitae illi exhibuerunt, 2. Reg. 18, 4. Sic tempore Apostolorum multi oleo mira culosè fuerunt curati, ac hodie fortè dantur adhuc miraculosae quaedam curationes per fontes. quis verò unquam legitur propterea religiosum oleo exhibuisse cultum? vel quis adeo absurdus, ut velit propter miraculosam curationem tales fontes religiosè colere, vel adorare? Infirmitatem igitur argumenti, quod ex h. l. pro reliquiarum cultu Pontificii nectere solent, agnoscentes ipsimet nonnulli, studiò ab eo abstinent, cui Iesuita Conzenius in Comm. ad 4. Evang. Costerus Enchir. Controv. aliiq; exemplum hoc silentio praetereunt. Vid. pluribus B. P. Confess. Cathol. t. 3. L. de Morte §. 113. p. 678. B. D. R-nig Vindic. Sacr. L. 39. B. D. Himmel. de Inov. Relig. p. 907. seqq.)*

*( Fimbria vestimenti eius. Vid. notata ad Marc. 5, 28.)*

*( Si solùmtetigero. Patet hinc, quàm insignis fuerit mulieris huius fides, credens quippe quòd Christus etiam inveteratos morbos, aliis hominibus incurabiles, sanare possit, & quidem quòd haec praestare possit non tantùm precibus à DEO impetratâ virtute, sed proprià suâ virtute. Vid. B. D. Chem. in H. F. c. 67. Pulcrè Chrysostomus: Vides mulierem longè praestanti. orem Archisynagogo. non apprehendit, non quicquam detinuit, summis solùm digitis tetigit, & ideò cùm posterior venisset, prior cura tarecessitΕι γδ τῷ πάσθει ἦνσυνδεδεμθύη, ἀλλὰ τῆ πίςει ἦν ἐπτερωμένη. i. e. etsi aegritudine tardabatur, fide tamen volabat.)*

## 9:22
*(v. 22. But Jesus turning and looking at her etc. It is asked why Christ, who at other times sometimes forbade that the rumor of miracles performed by Him be spread among the common people, here did not allow the woman to remain hidden. Chrysostom answers that this was done 1. to free the woman from all fear, lest she be agitated by grief by the stings of conscience, as if she had stolen the healing. 2. to correct her faith, who thought she could have remained hidden. 3. to make her faith manifest, so that others could imitate it. Namely, by believing in Christ, not by touching the fringe, (for nowhere in Holy Scripture is it read that anyone else touched the garments of Christ or was healed by their contact.) 4. to confirm the ruler of the Synagogue, lest he corrupt everything with unbelief: for they had come who said: do not be troublesome to the Master, the girl is already dead.

*( Your faith. And that alone. see v. preceding 21. conf. Matt. 15. 18. including trust. See Rom. 4, 18. following. Conf. B. P. L. on Justif. §. 71. also Cathol. Confess. t. 4. p. 919.)*

*(Has made you safe. Against Alphonsus de Castro, who from this passage attempts to prove the merits of works, since Christ wills that the woman ought to trust in the faith which she had conceived concerning Christ, the explanation of Jerome is to be noted, who says thus in this place: He did not say: your faith is going to make you safe: but has made you safe: In that you have believed, you have already been made safe. Conf. also B. P. Cath. Confess. t. 4. p. 919.)*

Latin:

*(v. 22. Iesus verò conversus & intuitus eam &c. Quaeritur, quare Christus, qui alias prohibuit aliquando, ne miraculorum, ab ipso editorum rumor in vulgus spargeretur, hîc non passus fuerit. mulierem latere. Respondet Chrysostomus, id factum esse 1. ut ab omni formidine foeminam liberaret, ne conscientiae stimulis, quasi furata sanitatem, moerore exagitaretur. 2. ut fidem ipsius corrigeret, quae se putavit latere potuisse. 3. ut fidem eius manifestam faceret, ut alii possent eam imitari. Nempe in Christum credendo, non fimbriam tangendo, (nullibi enim in Sc. S. legitur, quòd ullus ampliùs vestimenta Christi tetigit aut illorum contactu fuerit sanatus.) 4. ut principem Synagogae confirmaret, ne incredulitate omnia corrumperet: venerant enim, qui dicerent: noli molestus esse Magistro, mortua iam puella est.

*( Fides tua. Eaque sola. vid. v. praeced. 21. conf. Matth. 15. 18. includens fiduciam. Vid. Rom. 4, 18. seqq. Conf. B. P. L. de Iustif. §. 71. it. Confess. Cathol. t. 4. p. 919.)*

*(Salvam te fecit. Contra Alphonsum de Castro, qui ex hocloco evincere conatur merita operum, cùm Christus velit, quòd mulier cōfidere debeat infide, quam de Christo conceperat, notanda explicatio Hieronymi, qui ita in h. l. Non dixit: fides tua te salvam factura est: sed salvam te fecit: In eo quod credidisti, iam salva facta es. Conf. etiam B. P. Confess. Cath. t. 4. p. 919.)*

## 9:23
v. 23. In mourning they were accustomed to employ flute players, which was μοναυλία a sad concert of one flute. Joseph. lib. 3. on the Jewish War With the death of Joseph announced πλείςουςμισθοῦσθαιτοὺς ἀυλητας, οἱ σθρήνων ἐξῆρχον ἀυτοῖς. Homer, when the corpse of Hector was brought, says that there were present ἀοιδοὺς σθρήννων ἐξάρχους, which the interpreters say were flute players. In the laws of the XII tables mention is also made of flute players. See Hotom. in the commentary on those laws p. 38. As they used the flute in mourning, so they used the lyre in joyful matters.

Lactantius. Religion commands that the trumpet be played for the deaths of elders, the flute for the younger. At the funeral of boys and girls they used the flute, which is an instrument of thin and narrow voice Ovid. 6. Fasti. The flute sings at sad funerals. The Syriac here employs זמרא *(So indeed read Tremellius, Boderianus, Trostius: but the Londoners more correctly have which reading the most ancient manuscript Codex of the Altdorff Library approves. Confer also Lud. de Dieu in Observations on the IV Gospels on this place.)* from זמר flute he played. The custom was very ancient among the Jews, to employ flute players for the mourning of the dead, whom the Talmudists call חייליז aulaedi. See Talmud Hierosolymit. tract. on blessings cap. 3. in tract. on Sabbath cap. 23. in Baba Mezia cap. 6. R. Salom. Comm. on Ezech. 25. writes. There are things which are accustomed to be employed for mourning and joy, but there is not the same reason in them, of which kind are the aulaedi for a bride and for the dead. Among the ancients ἀυλὸς was σθρητητικὸς ὄργα νον, for they lamented the dead πρὸς ἀυλὸν, as Lucian teaches in the book ῶεὶ πὲνθους. But they used the lyre only in joyful matters. Theophylact brings forward another reason why they were lamented, but an irrelevant one. Ἐπειδὴ *(Moreover, whether flute players were in use among the ancient Jews, that is, before the customs of the Roman Victor people passed to them, learned men hesitate. There are those who think that it is evident from 2. Chron. 25, 15.Jerem. 9, 17. and Grotius embraces the affirmative on this place, indeed Chytraeus in on death and eternal life p. 99 thinks that this custom was derived from the Jews to the gentiles. Yet it is the almost common opinion that that custom, of employing flute players for the mourning of the dead, flowed from the gentiles to the Jews. So thinks B. D. Chemnitius part. 3. Exam. of the Council of Trent p. 185. W. Schickard in on the Royal Law of the Hebrews, c 6. p. 162. D. Quistorpius on this place. B. D. Calixtus, H. E. p. 148. Mayer in Prodromus of the Sacred Chaldean p. 226. others Maldonatus on this place (who also writes that Ambrose, lib. 8. on Luke teaches, that this custom flowed from the gentiles to the Jews. But although Ambrose lib. V. on Luke c. 8. hands down that by ancient custom flute players were employed to kindle to excite mourning, he has nothing, however, about the origin of that custom in that place, much less in book VIII. on Luke.) Moreover, it is not of this place to settle that dispute, or to inquire more deeply into the origin of this rite. Many besides the authors already now adduced treat of it B. P. L. on Death 84. Kirchmann lib. 2. on Funerals c. 5. Dn. Dilherrus lib. 2. Elect. c. 21. and Academic Disputations t. 1. p. 197. following. Abrah. Scultetus Observ. on Matt. c. 29. p. 36. 37. Let there be conferred also Rosinus lib. VIII. Antiq. Rom. c. 6. p. 1251. on the professional mourners Pineda t. 1. on Job p. 198. That at least we add here, that the Ethiopian and the Persian either did not attain the meaning of the Greek word, or could not persuade themselves,

how flute players were employed in mourning (namely Music in mourning) for they translate the Greek ἀυλετὰς that indeed i. e. mourning women, (from he wept, whence weeping. But besides the mourning woman, flute players were also employed among the Jews, as he reports from their Masters. Buxtorff. Lex. Talm. p. 766. Conf. the same in the same place, page 152. 41525.) but here i. e. the people, but the rest thus παραφράζει, & the crowd, making much noise and wailing.)*

Latin:

v. 23. In luctu tibicines olim adhibere solebant, quae erat μοναυλία unius tibiae tristis concentus. Ioseph. lib. 3. de bello Iud. Nunciatâ morte Iosepiπλείςουςμισθοῦσθαιτοὺς ἀυλητας, οἱ σθρήνων ἐξῆρχον ἀυτοῖς. Homerus cadavere Hectoris allato dicit, adfuisse ἀοιδοὺς σθρήννων ἐξάρχους, quos Interpp. dicunt, fuisse tibicines. In ll. XII. tabb. fit etiam mentio tibicinum. Vide Hotom. in comment. illarum ll p. 38. Ut tibiâ in luctu, ita lyrâ in reb. laetis utebantur.

Lactantius. Iubet religio ut maioribus mortuis tuba, minoribus, tibiâ caneretur. In funere puerorum ac puellarum utebantur tibiâ, quae est instrumentum exilis & angustae vocis Ovid. 6. Fastor. Cant ab at moestis tibia funeribus. Syr. hîc adhibet זמרא *(Ita quidem legunt Tremellius, Boderianus, Trostius: verùm rectiùs Londinenses habent quam lectionem approbat Codex MSS. antiquissimus Biblioth Altdorff. Confer. etiam Lud. de Dieu in Animadv. ad IV. Evang. ad h. l.)* à זמרtibiâ cecinit. Mos fuit valdè antiquus apud Iudaeos, tibieines adhibere ad luctum mortuorum, quos Thalmudistae vocant חייליזaulaedos. Vide Thalmud. Hierosolymit. tract. de benedict. cap. 3. in tract. de Sabb. cap. 23. in Baba Mezia cap. 6. R. Salom. Comm. in Ezech. 25. scribit. Sunt quae adhiberi consueverunt ad luctum & laetitiam, sed non est in eis par ratio, cuiusmodi sunt aulaedi pro sponsa & pro mortuo. Apud veteres ἀυλὸς fuit σθρητητικὸς ὄργα νον, mortuos enim deflebant πρὸς ἀυλὸν, ut docet Lucianus in libr. ῶεὶ πὲνθους. Lyrâ autem non nisi in rebus latis utebantur. Theoph. aliam rationem affert, cur defleretur, sed alienam. Ἐπειδὴ *(Caeterùm an tibicines apud veteres Iudaeos, h. e. prius quam mores Populi Romani Victoris ad illos transirent, in usu fuerint, haerent viri docti. Sunt qui illud patere existimant ex 2. Chron. 25, 15.Ierem. 9, 17. amplectiturque affirmativam Grotius ad h. l. imò à Iudaeis ad gentiles morem hunc derivatum esse, existimat Chytraeus in de morte ac vita aet. p. 99. Est tamen communis propè opinio quòd consuetudo illa, tibicines ad luctum mortuorum adhibendi, à gentilibus ad Iudaeos manârit. Ita sentit B. D. Chemnitius part. 3. Exam. Concilii Trid. p. 185. W. Schickardus in de Iure Regio Ebraeorum, c 6. p. 162. D. Quistorpius in h. l. B. D. Calixtus, H. E. p. 148. Mayerus Prodromo Chald. Sacri p. 226. alii Maldonatus in h. l. (qui etiam scribit, Ambrosium, lib. 8. in Lucam docere, consuetudinem hanc à gentilibus ad Iudaeos promanasse. Sed utut Ambrosius lib. V. in Lucam c. 8. tradat, more veteri tibicines adincendendos excitandoslactus adhibitos dici, nihil tamen de orig, istius consuetudinis d. l. habet, multò minus libro IIX. in Lucam.) Coeterùm non est huius loci, litem istam dirimere, vel in ritûs huius originem altiûs in quirere. Multis de eo praeter autores iam nunc adductos agunt B. P. L. de Morte 84. Kirchmannus lib. 2. de Funer. c. 5. Dn. Dilherrus lib. 2. Elect. c. 21. ac Disp. Acad. t. 1. p. 197. seqq. Abrah. Scultetus Observ. in Matth. c. 29. p. 36. 37. Conferatur etiam Rosinus lib. VIII. Antiq. Rom. c. 6. p. 1251. de praeficis Pineda t. l. in Iobum p. 198. Illud saltem hîc addimus, Aethiopem ac Persam vel non adsecutos esse Graecae vocis significationem, vel sibi persvadere non potuisse,

quomodo tibicines in luctu adhibiti (nempe Musica in luctu) vertunt enim Graecum ἀυλετὰς ille quidem i. e. lamentatrices, (à flevit, unde fletus. Sed praeter lamentatricem etiam tibicines adhibiti apud Iudaeos, ceu ex eorum Magistris refert. Buxtorff. Lex. Talm. p. 766. Conf. idem d. l. pag. 152. 41525.) hic verò i. e. populum, reliqua verò ita παραφράζει,& turbam, multùm ftentes & planctum facientes.)*

## 9:24
*(v. 24. Ἀναχωρεῖτε. See Matth. 7, 23.)*

The damsel is not dead; but sleepeth.

She was truly dead, but Christ demonstrated in reality that she had indeed slept for him, because he raised her as if she were sleeping by a mere calling out. Tertull. de resurr. carn. p. 70. She was not raised to glory nor incorruptibility, but to another death.* (But however much the H. S. may pronounce in general concerning the dead that they sleep, Dan. 12, 2. especially concerning the pious, see Deut. 31, 16. 2. Sam. 7, 12. Es. 26, 20. Act. 7, 60. 1. Cor. 11, 30. c. 15, 20. &c. yet for a peculiar reason those who are soon to be recalled to this life by Christ, as here, Conf. Marc. 5, 39. Luc. 8, 52. are denied to be dead. Concerning which matter it is treated at greater length in the Analects to Act. 20, 10. & Ioh. 11, 11. where it is also shown how profane writers also designate death by the name of sleep.)*

*( And they laughed him to scorn. See 1. Cor. 2, 14. c. 1, 23.)*

Latin:

*(v. 24. Ἀναχωρεῖτε. Vid. Matth. 7, 23.)*

Non mortua est adolescentula; sed dormit.

Verè erat mortua, sed Christus reipsa demonstravit, illam quidem sibi dormivisse, quia eam tanquam dormientem sola inclamatione suscitavit. Tertull. de resurr. carn. p. 70. Non in gloriam nec incorruptibilitatem, sed in mortem aliam suscitabatur.* (Ut ut verò in genere de mortuis pronunciet Sc. S. quòd dormiant,Dan. 12, 2. cumprimis de piis, vide Deut. 31, 16.2. Sam. 7, 12.Es. 26, 20.Act. 7, 60.1. Cor. 11, 30.c. 15, 20. &c. tamen peculiari ratione illi, qui mox à Christo, ut hîc, Conf. Marc. 5, 39.Luc. 8, 52. in hanc vitam revocandi, negantur mortui. Quâ de re pluribus agitur in Analectis ad Act. 20, 10. & Ioh. 11, 11. ubi etiam ostenditur, quomodo profani quoque Scriptores mortem somni nomine indigitent.)*

*( Et deridebant eum. Vid. 1. Cor. 2, 14.c. 1, 23.)*

## 9:25
*(v. 25. And when the crowd was put forth. Beautifully regarding the tropological sense, Gregory l. 18. Moral. c. 28. The multitude of secular cares must be cast out from the heart, so that the dead soul may rise again. Gloss: With the mockers rejected, Christ entered into the minds of the elect.)*

*( He went in, not alone, but then having taken with him the parents of the girl, and then from the disciples Peter, James and John (as those whom it pleased him to employ as witnesses in more serious and secret matters as friends of intimate admission, just as he also did afterwards in the transfiguration Matth. 17, 1. likewise in that spiritual struggle, Matth. 26, 37.) Luc. 8, 51.)*

*( He took her by the hand. See what was noted above at c. 8, 15.)*

*( And she arose. Mark c. 5, 22. following and Luke c. 8, 41. following relate this history with more circumstances added. This girl arose not to immortal life, but mortal: See B. D. Hunn. in this place, for it is not to be doubted that she was again dead. But this is an example, just as also of those whom Christ in the days of his flesh, as well as the Prophets and Apostles, raised up,) Extraordinary: therefore the passage Heb. 9, 27 is not contradicted, since it speaks of the ordinary rule. However much the souls of those raised by Christ and the Apostles were entirely released from the body, and it cannot be certainly affirmed that they were made participants of heavenly happiness, yet it can by no means be said that they were in hell, and therefore an extraordinary receptacle must be assigned to them, yet by no means on that account is a purgatory (or Limbo) to be established. For just as from the peculiar and extraordinary resuscitation of those men to this mortal life it cannot be inferred that other men are also to be recalled to this mortal life after death: so from the peculiar and extraordinary receptacle of those souls it cannot be concluded that the souls of other men are also gathered into some intermediate place (for instance, Purgatory or Limbo) after death. See B. Par. L. on Death §. 68. D. R-nig Vindic. Sacr. L. 48. and those whom they cite. In this place it is to be noted that the Jesuit Corn. à Lapide himself establishes here such an extraordinary dwelling, which is neither hell, nor heaven, nor purgatory.)

Latin:

*(v. 25. Et eiectâ turbâ. Pulcrè quoad sensum tropolog. Gregorius l. 18. Moral. c. 28. Eiicienda est de corde secularium curarum mult itudo, ut anima mortua resurgat. Glossa: Reprobatis irrisoribus intravit Christus in electorum mentes.)*

*( Ingressiss, non solus, sed tum adsumtis puellae parentibus, tùm è discipulis Petro, Iacobo ac Iohanne (ut quos tanquam intimae admissionis amicos in gravioribus ac secretioribus negotiis ut testes adhibere ipsi placuit, uti & postea fecit in transfigurat Matth. 17, 1. item in luctá illâ spirituali, Matth. 26, 37.) Luc. 8, 51.)*

*( Prehendit manum eius. Vid. quae notata suprà ad c. 8, 15.)*

*( Et resurrexit. Marcus c. 5, 22. seqq. ac Lucas c. 8, 41. seqq. plusculis circumstantiis additis Historiam hanc referunt. Surrexit puella haec non ad vitam immortalem, sed mortalem: Vid. B. D. Hunn. in h. l. neque enim dubitandum, quin iterum fuerit mortua. Est verò exemplum hoc, sicuti & eorum, quos tum Christus in diebus carnis, tum Prophetae & Apostoli resuseitarunt, extraor dinarium: non contrariatur igitur locus Ebr. 9, 27. quippe qui loquitur de regulâ ordinariâ. Utut verò animae horum, à Christo & Apostolis resuscitatorum, omninò à corpore fuerint solutae, nec certò affirmari possit, quòd coelestis felicitatis factae sint participes, minimè autem dici possit, quòd in inferno fuerint, ac proinde extraordinarium receptaculum illis adsignandum, hautquaquam tamen propterea purgatorium (vel Limbus) statuendum. Sicuti enim ex peculiari & extraordinariâ illorum hominum ad vitam hanc mortalem resuscitatione inferri non potest, quòd etiam alii homines post mortem ad hanc mortalem vitam revocandi sint: ita ex peculiari & extraordinario illarum receptaculo concludi nequit, aliorum etiam hominum animas in locum quēdam intermediū (puta Purgatoriu vel limbum) post mortem colligi. Vid. B. Par. L. de Morte §. 68. D. R-nig Vindic. Sacr. L. 48. & quos illi allegant. Hoc loco notandum, quòd ipse Iesuita Corn. à Lapide tale extraord. habitaculum, quod neque gehenna sit, nec coelum, nec purgatorium, hîc statuat.)*

## 9:26
*(v. 26. And this fame went abroad etc. notwithstanding that Christ forbade the manifesting of this miracle, Mark 5, 43 Luke 8, 56. Thus indeed glory pursues those who flee it. But as to why Christ wished to hide this miracle, the reason for it is assigned by most interpreters as a zeal for humility and for avoiding the envy of the Pharisees. That Christ forbade the divulging of this miracle to avoid the envy of the Pharisees and Scribes, Maldonatus writes expressly on this passage. Maldonatus's fellow Jesuit Conzenius rejects both reasons: he himself, however, maintains that Christ did this to avoid suspicions of sedition: since, if the miracle had been made manifest while he was still in the city, it could have happened that the people would come and seize him, to make him king. Others think it better to embrace τὸ ἐπέχειν here, since the Holy Spirit has kept silent the reasons for the prohibition. Furthermore, concerning the reasons why the Savior sometimes forbade his miracles to be divulged, one may also consult B. D. Chemn. H. E. c. 42. p. 332. seqq. Dn. D. Walth. Harm. Bibl on this 30th chapter. Sim. Episc Qq & Resp. Q. 11. Compare also these very annotations on v. 30)*

Latin:

*(v. 26. Et exiit fama haec &c. non obstante, quòd Christus manifestare miraculum hoc prohibuerit, Marc. 5, 43.Luc. 8, 56. Ita nempe gloria fugientes persequitur. Cur verò Christus occultare miraculum hoc voluerit, illius causa adsignatur à plerisque Interpp. humilitatis ac declinandae Pharisaeorum invidiae studium. Ad vitandam Pharisaeorum ac Scribarum invidiam Christum divulgationem huius miraculi prohibuisse, disertè scribit Maldonatus in h. l. Reiicit utramq; causam Maldonati sociennus Conzenius: ipse verò statuit, fecisse hoc Christum, ad vitandas de seditione suspiciones: cùm, si miraculum fuisset manifesta cum dum adhuc in urbe erat, fieri potuisset, ut populus veniret, eumq; raperet, quò regem sacerent. Alii satiùs ducunt, τὸ ἐπέχειν hîc amplecti, cùm Sp. S. prohibitiōis causas tacuerit. Coeterùm de causis, cur Salvator mira cula sua divulgari, aliquando prohibuerit, evolvi quoque possunt B. D. Chemn. H. E. c. 42. p. 332. seqq. Dn. D. Walth. Harm. Bibl ad b. 30. praes. cap. Sim. Episc Qq & Resp. Q. 11. Conf. etiam has ipsas annot. ad v. 30.)*

## 9:27
v. 27. Christ healing two blind men shows himself to be the light of the world. (See Is. 61, 1.Luke 2, 32.John 1, 9.c. 3, 19.c. 8, 12.c. 9, 5.c. 12, 35. 36.46. &c. indeed even the promised Messiah. See Is. 35, 5. But he had beautifully supplied for the defect of sight through the eyes of the body. God in these blind men with a saving sharpness of mind. So that one could almost address them in the same way in which St. Anthony addressed Didymus, who was sad because of his blindness. Thus indeed he: Let nothing offend you, O Didymus, that you have been deprived of carnal eyes. For those eyes are missing which mice and flies and lizards have; but rejoice, because you have eyes which the Angels have, by which God is seen, through which a great light of knowledge is kindled for you. Rufinus reports this in H. E. book 2, ch. 7, in which he also mentions how Didymus, although he was deprived of his sight at a young age, nevertheless progressed excellently in the study of letters. Compare concerning the threefold opening of the eyes B. D. Quistorp, Annotations to 2 Kings 6, 26.)

Latin:

v. 27. Christus sanans duos coecos, ostendit se esse lucem mundi. *(Vid. Es. 61, 1.Luc. 2, 32.Ioh. 1, 9.c. 3, 19.c. 8, 12.c. 9, 5.c. 12, 35. 36.46. &c quin etiam promissus Messias. Vid. Es. 35, 5. Pulcrè verò de fectum visûs per oculos corporis suppleverat. Deus in coecis hisce salutari acumine mentis. Ut adeò eodem propè illos quis modo alloqui potuerit, quo S. Antonius Didymum ob coecitatem moestum. Ita verò ille: Nihil te offendat, ô Didyme, quòd carnalibus oculis fueris orbatus. Desunt enim oculi illi, quos mures & muscae & lacertae habent; sed laetare, quia habes oculos, quos Angeli habent, è quibus Deus videtur, per quos magnum tibi scientiae lumen accenditur. Refert Ruffinus l. 2. H. E. c. 7. in quo etiam memorat, quomodo Didymus, licet in parvâ aetate luminibus fuerit orbatus, egregiè tamen in literarum studiis profecerit. Confer de triplici oculorum apertione B. D. Quistorp. Annot. ad 2. Reg. 6, 26.)*

## 9:28
(v. 28. Do you believe that I can do this? Christ questions the blind men here, not because he himself was ignorant of what their faith was, (for the contrary is evident from this very chapter v. 4, add John 21, 17.) but so that he might manifest their faith to those standing around. Compare entirely what is noted at Luke 8, 45. At this place at least observe that God himself sometimes asks. See Gen. 3, 9. Furthermore, Bellarmine, book 1 on Justification, ch. 8, attempts to prove from this question that the object of justifying faith is not the special mercy of God, in that Christ here asked about faith in omnipotence, and when they professed that they had such, he was satisfied. The Jesuit Conzen aims at the same thing in this place. But I respond 1. the positing of one thing is not the exclusion of another: for it does not follow, Christ explored whether these blind men had faith in his omnipotence. Therefore, the object of faith is not special mercy. 2. It is denied that they believed at least in the power of Christ, but did not at the same time trust in his mercy. For their cry teaches this very thing sufficiently: have mercy on us, in the preceding verse. 3. If it could not be shown from the context even in the greatest degree that these blind men had faith in special mercy, which is necessary for justification; nevertheless, it should by no means be gathered from this that such faith is not necessary for justification, since elsewhere in its proper place the Holy Scripture teaches this in sufficiently clear words, as B. P. shows in many places in the Confessio Catholica, vol. 4, p. 613.)

Latin:

*(v. 28. Credit is, me hoc posse facere. Interrogat hîc Christus coecos, non quòd ipse, quae eorum fides sit, ignoraret, (contrarium enim ex hoc ipso cap. v. 4. adde Ioh. 21, 17. patet) sed ut circumstantibus illorum fidem manifestet. Conf omninò, quae notata ad Luc. 8, 45. Hoc loco saltem obs. quòd Deus ipse aliquando quaerat. Vid. Gen. 3, 9. Conatur porrò ex hâc quaestione Bell. l. 1. de Iustif. c. 8. evincere, fidei iustific antis obiectum non esse specialem Dei miseri cordiam, eò quòd hîc quaesiverit Christus de fide omnipotentiae, & cùm talem se habere profiterentur, acqui. everit. Eodem collimat Iesuita Conzen in h. l. Verùm Resp. 1. unius positio non est alterius exclusio: neque enim sequitur, Christus exploravit, num habeant hi coeci fidem omnipotentiae. E. fidei obiectum non est specialis misercordia. 2. negatur, quòd saltem potentiam Christi crediderint, non verò simul misericordiae eius fuerint confisi. Hocipsum enim satis docet illorum clamor: miserere nostri, v. praeced. 3. si vel maximè non posset è contextu ostendi, coecos hos habuisse fidem misericordiae specialis, ad iustificationem necessariae; minimè tamen hinc debet colligi, quòd talis fides non sit ad iustificationem necessaria, cùm alibi in propriâ sede de iustificatione Sc. S. sat claris verbis hoc doceat, uti multis ostendit B. P. Confess. Cathol. t. 4. p. 613.)*

## 9:29
*(v. 29. According to your faith be it done to you. Note 1. that mention is made here of faith alone, with other works or dispositions passed over, just as also a little before v. 22. it, Luc. 7. 50.c. 8, 50.Ioh. 1, 12.c. 3, 36.Rom. 5, 1. 2. Maldonatus on v. 22.Cap. 9. Matth. concedes, that all others, except Malchus, who were healed by Christ, were healed in soul by the same faith by which they were healed in body. 3. understand those who were healed in body by Christ to be those who implored his help, and were also healed in soul. Whence also Corn. à Lapide on v. 2. cap. 9. Matth. notes, that Christ, by saying to the paralytic: your sins are forgiven you, forgives sins first, then heals the paralytic, because the cause must be removed first, so that with it removed the effect may be taken away, namely paralysis and disease. And he mentions that it was sanctioned by canon law that physicians should provide for the health of the soul of the sick person before that of the body, and that this is strictly observed at Rome.)*

Latin:

*(v. 29. Secundùm fidem vestram vobis fiat. Nota 1. solius fidei fieri hîc mentionem, praetermissis coeteris operibus vel dispositionibus, quemadmodum etiam paullò ante v. 22. it, Luc. 7. 50.c. 8, 50.Ioh. 1, 12.c. 3, 36.Rom. 5, 1. 2. Maldonatum ad v. 22.Cap. 9. Matth. concedere, coeteros omnes, excepto Malcho, qui à Christo curati sunt, eâdem fide, quâ compore sanati sunt, animo esse sanates. 3. illos, q corpore sanati à Christo sunt, intellige, qui auxilium eius implorarunt, etiam animo fuisse sanatos. Unde etiam Corn. à Lapide ad v. 2. cap. 9. Matth. annotat, Christum, dicendo ad paralyticum: remitiuntur tibi peccata tua, priùs peccata dimittere, deinde curare paralycicum, quia priùs auserenda causa, ut eâ sublarâ tollatur effectus, puta paralysis & morbus. Atque hinc iniure canonico sancitum esse, memorat, ut Medici priùs animae, quàm corporis aegroti salutem procurent, idq; Romae strictè servari.)*

## 9:30
v. 30. ἐνεβριμήσατο ἀυτοῖς he sternly threatened, he was rebuking them sharply and as if angrily with austerity. βρεμοῦσθαι is simple from the verb βρέμειν to snort. Suidas, μετὰ ἀυςηρότητος ἐπετίμησε. The word ἐμβριμοῦμαι contains the meaning of anger and vehement threatening, with which we either threaten someone in such a way that he can and ought to be struck in spirit, the one whom we threaten, or by which even without threats someone is disturbed of his own accord because of the vehemence of the speech and the movement of the soul, which it indicates. It is signified that Christ forbade them with a vehement and snorting threat, so that it cannot be doubted that he seriously willed this. But why did he forbid his deeds to be divulged? Resp. That the prophetic predictions concerning Christ had to be fulfilled, which cause the Evangelist Matthew also alleges, citing Isaiah cap. 42, prophesying that Christ would not boastfully proclaim his benefits, but would rather suppress them with modest silence.

Latin:

v. 30. ἐνεβριμήσατο ἀυτοῖς graviter interminatus est, acriter ac velut iracundè comminabatur eis cum austeritate. Simplex est βρεμοῦσθαι à verbo βρέμεινfremere. Suidas, μετὰ ἀυςηρότητος ἐπετίμησε. Verbo ἐμβριμοῦμαι inest significatio iracundiae & vehementis comminationis, cum qua vel minamur alicui ita, ut animo percelli is possit & debeat, cui minamur, vel quâ sine minis etiam aliquis suâ sponte perturbatur propter orationis vehementiam & animi motum, quem indicat. Significatur cum vehemente & fremente comminatione interdixisse eis Christum, quô minùs dubitari possit, seriò eum hoc velle. Quare verò prohibuit facta sua divulgari? Resp. Proheticas praedictiones de Christo fuisse complendas, quam causam & Evangelista Matthaeus allegat, cita ns Esaiam cap. 42. varicinantem Christum beneficia sua non gloriocè iactaturum, sed modestô potiùs silentiò pressurum.

## 9:31
*(v. 31. But they going out spread his fame? Q Whether they acted rightly, by publishing the miracle against Christ's prohibition? Maldonatus answers in this place that all the ancient authors seem deservedly to excuse them, in that they did this not so much to disobey, as to be grateful. And they allege for this matter Chrysostom, Hieron. B-am, Theophylact, he adds: It is also likely that they believed that Christ did not seriously, but for the sake of his own modesty, wish them not to say it, -etuisse. Corn. à Lapide inclines to the same. There are also some of our own who think that deed of the blind men is worthy not only of excuse, but also of praise. See Lossius in this place. Others, although they think those blind men cannot be entirely excused, yet think that something must be granted to their joy, and that they sinned more lightly and humanely, because this matter served to amplify the glory of Christ. Thus B. D. Hunnius. But B. D. Chemnitius warns in this place that this deed admits of no excuse, since that grave threat of Christ should not have been so rashly neglected by them. Conf. more on this matter in the same place.)*

Latin:

*(v. 31. At illi egressi sparserunt eius famam? Q An rectè fecerint, contra Christi prohibitionim miraculum public ando Respondet Maldonatus in li. l. omnes veteres autores meritò videri eos excusare, eò quòd non cam ut non obedirent, quàm ut grati essent, id fecerint. Allegantquè in hanc rem Chrysostomum, Hieron. B-am, Theophylactum, addit: Est etiam verosimile, credidisse cos, Christum non feriò, sed modestiae suae causâ, ne id dicerent, -etuisse. Eodem inclinat Corn. à Lapide. Sunt etiam ex nostratibus, quifactum illud coecorum non excusatione solùm, sed & laude dignum putant. Vid. Lossius in h. l. Alii licet non omninò excusari coecos illos posse existiment: putant tamen, dandum aliquid illorum laetitiae, & eò leviùs peccasse atque humaniùs, quòd res haec subserviret amplificandae Christi gloriae. Ita B. D. Hunnius. Verùm monet B. D. Chemnitius in h. l. factum hoc nullo modo excusationem admittere, cùm gravis illa Christi interminationon ita temerè ab ipsis fuerit negligenda. Conf. plura in hanc rem apud eund. d. l.)*

## 9:32
(v. 32. They brought to him a mute man possessed by a demon. The devil, by whom he was corporally obsessed, had bound his tongue, so that he could not use it for intelligible speech. Chrysostom notes in homily 33 on Matthew that the soul of this man also had been bound by the force of the demon. Whence Christ did not demand faith from him, but immediately cured him as he was suffering. Furthermore, regarding those obsessed by a demon, those who discuss it at length can be consulted: B. D. Chemn. H. E. cap. 69. B. Par. Coll. Isagog. L. de malis Angel. c. 8. §. 20. seqq. B. D. Bald. in Cas. Consc. from the Pontifical Del Rio disquisit. Mag. lib. 3. p. 415. Iansenius Comment. in Conc. Ev. p. 187. & 188. and others. Moreover, although the word κωφὸς perhaps denotes deaf more than mute elsewhere, it is nevertheless more correctly rendered here by mute, since it is immediately added that, once the demon was cast out, the mute spoke. The Ethiopian, however, following the authority of I know not which Greek or Latin codex, refers it to hearing. For it translates he heard with deaf ears. The Londoners less correctly: the mute heard. for it more properly signifies deaf, and has an agreement with the Arabic he was deaf. I am more surprised why the same Londoners Matth. 15, 31. translate the words of the Ethiopian as the mute speak, when it should be rendered entirely as: the deaf hear. Just as they themselves rendered the same phrase Matth. 11, 5. and likewise Marc. 7, 37. Cardinal Caietanus τὸ refers mute less correctly to the demon; more correctly Corn. à Lapide, Franc. Lucas, Conzen and other interpreters refer it to the man. Just as the Syrian also rendered it clearly enough: they brought to him a mute, in quo erat daemonium similarly the Arab in quo daemonium. So also the Persian. The Ethiopian in the same place: adduxerunt surdum, cui daemonium. Finally, that this history of the healed demoniac is similar to that which our Evangelist relates below in c. 12, 22, yet it is not the same, as indeed the Jesuit Maldonatus thinks, but distinct, as besides our own people, see B. D. Chemnitius in H. E. c. 59, and even the associate of Maldonatus himself, Corn. à Lapide, and others, to whom may be added Iansenius in Conc. Evang. p. 224, establish and it is also evident to one accurately comparing both histories. But whether this history is the same as that which Luke c. 11, 14. describes, we shall see in the Analecta to the said place of Luke.)*

*( Loquutus est mutus, i. e. who had been mute. The H. S. is accustomed to speak thus everywhere. See below c. 11, 5. c. 12, 22. Mark 7, 37. And hence a canon was formed: Solent in H. S. denominativa & epitheta quandode to be predicated of their subjects, even if the reason for the denomination has ceased. Jerome in c. 26 of Matthew expresses it thus. Aliquando in S. mutatâ re, pristinum nomen manet. See B. D. Glassius Gramm. S. page 8. Dn. D. Waltherus Harm. Bibl. book 1. Chapter 3. §. 30. Why indeed the Devil is accustomed to bind the tongue of some men, whom he possesses corporally, B. D. Chemn. H. E. c. 69 explains.)*

Latin:

*(v. 32. Obtulerunt ei hominum mutum daemoniacum. Diabolus, à quo corporaliter obsessus erat, linguam eius alligaverat, quô minùs uti eâ ad loquelam intelligibilem poterac. Notat Chrysost hom. 33. in Matth. etiam animam huius hominis vi daemonis fuisse ligatam. Hnde nec fidem ab eo Christus efflagit averit, sed illico luborantem curaverit. De obsessis porrò à Daemone prolixè disserentes consuli possunt B. D. Chemn. H. E. cap. 69. B. Par. Coll. Isagog. L. de malis Angel. c. 8. §. 20. seqq. B. D. Bald. in Cas. Consc. è Pontif. Del Rio disquisit. Mag. lib. 3. p. 415. Iansenius Comment. in Conc. Ev. p. 187. & 188. ac alii Coeterùm ut ut vox κωφὸς magis fortè surdum quàm mutum aliàs noter, rectiùs tamen hîc per mutum redditur, cùm statim subiiciatur, quòd eiecto daemonio loquutus fuerit mutus. Aethiops tamē nescio evius Codicis Graeci vel Latini sequutus fidem ad auditum refert. Vertit enim audivit surdis. Londinenses minùs rectè: audivit mutus. enim magis propriè surdum significat, habetque convenientiam cum Arab. surdus fuit. Magis miror, cur iidem Londinenses Matth. 15, 31. verba Aethiop. transferant muti loquuntur, cùm omninò sit reddendum: surdi audiunt. Quomodo etiam ipsimet eandem phrasin reddiderunt Matth. 11, 5. ac pariter Marc. 7, 37. Card. Caietanus τὸmutum minùs rectè ad daemonium refert; rectiùs Corn. à Eapide, Franc. Lucas, Conzen ac alii Interpp. ad hominem referunt. Quemadmodum etiam Syrus satis clarè reddidit: obtu erunt ei mutum, in quo erat daemonium similiter Arabs in quo daemonium. Sic quoque Persa. AEthiops ibidem: adduxeruntsurdum, cui daemonium. Tandem ututhistoriae huic de sanato daemoniaco similis sit ea, quam Evangelista noster infrà c XII, 22. refert, non tamen est eadem uti quidem Iesuita Maldonatus censet, sed distincta, ceu praeter nostrates, vid. B. D. Chemnitius in H. E. c. 59. ipsius etiam Maldonati socienni, Corn. à Lapide, ac alii, quibus addatur Iansenius in Conc. Evang. p. 224. statuunt & patet etiam utramque historiam accuratè conferenti. Num verò eadem haec historia sit cum illa, quam Lucas c. 11, 14. describit, in Analect. ad d. l. Lucae videbimus.)*

*( Loquutus est mutus, h. e. qui fuerat mutus. Solet Sc. S. passim ita loqui. Vid infrà c. 11, 5. c. 12, 22. Marc. 7, 37. Atq; hinc formatus canon: Solent in Sc. S. denominativa & epithet a quandode subiectis suis praedicari, etiamsi denominationis ratio desierit. Hier. in c. 26. Matthaei ita effert. Aliquando in S. mutatâ re, pristinum nomen manet. Vid. B. D. Glassius Gramm. S. pag. 8. Dn. D. Waltherus Harm. Bibl. lib. pr. Cap. 3. §. 30. Cur verò Diabolus linguam hominibus nonnullis, quos corporaliter obsidet, ligare soleat, exponit B. D. Chemn. H. E. c. 69.)*

## 9:33
*(v. 33. Per principem daemoniorum. The same Pharisees vomited a similar horrible blasphemy elsewhere against the Savior, as is evident from Matthew 12, 24. where the Apology of Christ is also read. Furthermore, in the Greek it is ἐ, which is placed in the manner of a prefix (which the Syrian, Arab, and Ethiopian also have here) see Ps. 18, 30. Ps. 6, 14. for διὰ, just as it is also done elsewhere. See Mark 9, 29. Luke 21, 19. Acts 17, 31. etc. and the Pharisees wished to imply nothing else than that Christ casts out demons by the aid of the prince of the Devils.)*

Latin:

*(v. 33. Per principem daemoniorum. Similem horrendam blasphemiam iidem Pharisaei & alibi contra Salvatorem evomurunt, ceu patet ex Matth. 12, 24. ubi & Apologia Christi legitur. Coeterùm in Graeco est ἐ, quod positum est more praefixi (quod etiam Syrus, Arabs & Aethiops hîc habent) vid. Ps. 18, 30.Ps. 6, 14. pro διὰ, quemadmodum etiam alibi factum. Vid. Marc. 9, 29.Luc. 21, 19.Act. 17, 31. &c. ac nihil aliud innuere Pharisaei voluerunt, quàm quòd Christus auxiliô principis Diabolorum daemones eiiciat.)*

## 9:36
v. 36. He had compassion. * (Compare below c. 14, 14. c. 15, 32. Luke 7, 13. &c.) * In Greek it is ῶλαγχνίζεσθαι from the noun τὰ ῶλάγχνα bowels, that is, heart, liver &c. which are accustomed to be moved in some grave emotion. The Hebrews have the verb ךחם

Ἐκλελυμένοι to be restored ἐσκυλμένοι. For Beza admits that he found this in six ancient Codices. Erasmus also observed that Chrysostom, Jerome, Hilary, and Theophylact read it thus, and it fits this passage most excellently. σκύλλω properly signifies I vex, I weary, and not in just any way, but by the length and difficulty of a journey. They are therefore ἐσκυλμένοι troubled by troublesome journeys, while they followed Christ here and there.

As sheep. Parallel passages are Num. 27, 17. 1 Kings 22, 17. Ezek. 13, 14. c. 34, 6. Mark 6, 34. )*

Ἐκλελυμένοι reponendum ἐσκυλμένοι. Hoc enim Beza fatetur se reperisse in sex Cod. vetustis. The Arab uses here the word which it likewise employs in the places just cited.)* ὐκβάλλειν however is sometimes simply -placed for that which is to command that you go out.Mark 5, 10.40.Acts 9, 40.

*(or even for ἐχάγειν, as John 10, 4. Elsewhere it is expressed by ἀποςέλλειν, as Rom. 10, 15.)*

This Chapter consists of three parts. In I. is proposed the of the Apostles, instructed by the grace of miracles v. 1. and expressly named v. 2. 3. and 4. the sending forth to preach the Gospel. II. The instruction of the same. 1. regarding the object or to whom they ought to preach the Gospel, v. 5. 6. 2. regarding the matter or what is to be preached, v. 7. 3. regarding the adjuncts, that they ought to confirm the doctrine with miracles and that freely v. 8. but to commit the care of food and clothing to GOD v. 9. 10. 4. regarding the diversity of the hearers v. 11. 15. III. The prediction of future calamity and the annexed consolation. from v. 16. to the end.

Arabs utitur hîc verbo quod itid. allegaus modò locis adhibet.)* ὐκβάλλειν tamen quandoque simpliciter -onitur pro eo, quod est iubere, ut exeas.Marc. 5, 10.40.Act. 9, 40.
