Constat hoc Caput tribus membris. In I. proponitur Apostolorum, gratiâ miraculorum instructorum v. 1. & nomin-expressorum v. 2. 3. ac 4. ad praedicandum Evangelium ablegatio. II. Eorundem instructio. 1. quoad obiectum sive quibus Evangelium praedicare debe--t, v. 5. 6. 2. quoad materiam s. quid praedicandum sit, v. 7. 3. quoad adiuncta, quòd doctrinam confirmare miraculis idque gratis debeant v. 8. solicitudinem autem victûs & amictûs DEO committere v. 9. 10. 4. quoad auditorum diversitatem v. 11. 15. III. Futurae calamitatis praedictio & annexa consolatio. à v. 16. ad finem.)*

## 10:1
* (v. 1. And having summoned the twelve. Cur. 12. Why the Savior chose the Apostles, will be explained in the Anal. on Mark 3, 14. where also the name Apostle will be treated.)*

* ( He gave them power &c. A solid argument for the true Deity of Christ can be drawn from this against the Photinians. Concerning which see B. Par. Coll. Isag. p. 252. B. D. Fewrb Anti Ostor. Disp. 13. §. 14. From that, therefore, that Christ gave to the Apostles θεάνθρωπος ἐξουσίαν the power of performing miracles, it is evident that that power was communicated to and belongs to Christ as man in a far different manner than it was given to the Apostles. To these, indeed, by temporal assistance (Conf. Act. 3, 12.c. 4, 10.c. 9. 34.), but to the human nature of Christ by personal communication. Whence also he performed miracles where, when, and as often as he willed, Luc. 5, 17.Matth. 9, 6. &c. See B. D. Chemn. de duabus nat. in Christo c. 21.)*

* ( Ἐξουσίαν πνευμάτων i. e. εἰς or ὐπὶτὰ πνσύματα, as Luke has cap. 9, 1. and likewise the Orientals in this place & the Syrian indeed the Ethiopian power over spirits. the Arab emphatically power over or in all spirits. the Persian: power to cast out unclean spirits. Conf. which note on Luke 9, -. Furthermore, an example of a similar ellipsis is had Gal. 3, 22. add B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 108.)*

NOTAE AD CAP. X. MATTHAEI. SUMMA AC DISPOSITIO.

## 10:2
* (v. 2. The names of the twelve Apostles The Wechelian Bible, edited under the care of Junius, less correctly has of the Disciples. For not only the Greek Codices, which learned men have compared, but also the Oriental Interpreters, by the highest consensus, have of the Apostles. Indeed, the very context itself seems to require the word Apostles. For already at that time Christ had chosen twelve from all the disciples, and had instituted them as Apostles. Lud. de D-eu writes in this place that the Vulgate in this place has of the Disciples instead of of the Apostles: but it must be known that very few Latin Codices, and those same ones rejected by the Pontificians themselves, use the word Disciples here.)*

Πρῶτος Σίμων. The first is called so by reason of order, because he was the first to be called to the Apostleship with his brother Andrew. *(See Matth. 4, 18.Marc. 1, 6. Theophyl in this place He places before (the Evangelist) Peter and Andrew, since they were also called first. Then placing the sons of Zebedee, he places James before John: not because of dignity but because it had so happened: Alphonsus also Tostatus, Bishop of Avila, of the highest authority among the Pontificians, Comm. on chap. 10 of Matthew, q. 29, expressly asserts that because of time Peter is placed first: for he himself, he continues, was the first, who is read to have been called by Christ, above ch. 4. &Marc. 1. To that, indeed, that Andrew seems to have been called first, as one who was one of those two disciples who were with John the Baptist &c Ioh. 1, 37. the same responds, that the time of discipleship is not computed from then: that although they then went with Christ from Judea into Galilee: yet they left him returning to the office of fishing, so that it was necessary that Christ should call them anew again at the sea of Galilee, abovecap. 4.&Marc. 1.therefore from then the time of discipleship is computed, that they adhered firmly to remain with him: & then Peter is placed first, because perhaps he was older than Andrew when both were called at the same hour. Others think the order is arbitrary. Chrysostom homl. 33 in Matth: Mark indeed κατ ἀξίαν arranged them in order: for after the two who held the apex of the Apostleship ( μετὰ τοὺς δὺο κορυφαίους ) he placed Andrew: but this one not so. The same a little later: You see οὐκατὰ γῆν ἀξίαν τίθησῖν, that they are not numbered according to dignity. Chrysostom indeed speaks of the order observed here in the placement of James and John: but the same can also be said of Peter, namely that he is named first, not as if he were prior to the remaining Apostles in dignity, that is, in monarchical authority, but because he was with Andrew πρωτόκλητος )* And lest anyone should carve out a primacy of power from this appellation, for that reason Gal. 2, 9. James is placed before him. *(thus 1. Cor. 3, 22. he is placed after Paul, c. 9, 5. after all the remaining Apostles. There is therefore no need at all from this, as Beza suspects here, that the word πρῶτος was added by someone who wished to establish the primacy of Peter: since nothing follows that coheres. For not only do the Greek Codices (to which it is fitting to add the Greek MS Eclogues, which are preserved in the Nuremberg Library) constantly have that little word both here and in Mark, but also the most ancient Syriac interpreter, and furthermore the Fathers, Chrysostom, Jerome, and others acknowledge the same. Whence even Beza himself, as if correcting himself, adds: we find it, however, written thus in all the copies and in Theophylact the Roman. Nor yet, as we have mentioned, is the Monarchical, such as the Papists dream of, and among other things strive to construct from this as well, (See Bell. l. 1. de P. R. c. 18. Becan. lib. 1. Manual. c. 4. §. 45. Costerus Enchir. Controv. c 3 pag 113. Tirinus, Corn. à Lapide; Conzen and other Papist Commentators on this passage) Primacy of Peter (or rather of the Roman Pontiff, for it is for this one alone that it is sown here by the Papists, for this one alone it deserves to be supported can. For firstly, it is false that he is always numbered in the first place. The contrary is evident from Gal. 2, 9. Secondly, it is known from the Philosopher in the book of Categories, c. 12, that what is prior and therefore also first is said in various ways, namely 1. κατὰ χρόιον 2. κατὰ τὴβν τάξιν. 3. κατ᾽ ἀξίαν, or that πρότερον is called, which is βέλτιον καὶ τιμιώτερον. But it does not follow that Peter is called first and indeed such a one, which includes a Monarchical Dominion over the remaining Apostles. Certainly no more than if someone wished to subsume: Mary the mother of the Lord Act. 1, 14. is named in the last place of all women, therefore among all she was also κατ᾽ ἀξίαν the last. Thirdly, that dominion fights both with the sayings of Holy Scripture. See Luc. 22, 26. 2. Cor. 11, 5. Ε κατ᾽ ἀξίαν,

1. Petr. 5, 3. then with the testimonies of the Fathers. Cyprian: The other Apostles were that which Peter was, endowed with an equal partnership of honor and power. Finally, if we were to concede in the highest degree that Peter had some primacy among the Apostles, it does not in the least follow that such a thing pertains also to his fictitious successor, the Roman Pontiff. For they do not have the inheritance of Peter, who do not have the faith of Peter. According to Augustine. More will be discussed on this matter in the Analysis on Marc. 3, 16.

*( James &c. Ludov. de Dieu notes in this place that the Vulgate Interpreter places Philip and Bartholomew before James and John here. The same is also reported by Beza. But as many editions of the Vulgate version as we have consulted here, they place James and John in the first position.)*

* (v. 2. Nomina duo decim Apostolorum Biblia Wecheliana, curâ Iunii edita minùs rectè habent Discipulòrum. Etenim non solùm Codd Graeci, quos viri docti contulerunt, sed & Orientales Interpp. summo conser. su habent Apostolorum. Quin ipse quoque contextus vocem Apostolorum requirere videtur. Latini, iidemque ab ipsis Pontificiis reiecti, Discipulorum vocem hîc adhibeant.)*

Πρῶτος Σίμων.Primus vocatur ratione ordinis, quia primus cum fratre Andrea ad Apostolatum est vocatus. *(Vid. Matth. 4, 18.Marc. 1, 6. Theophyl in h. l. Praeponit (Evangelista) Paetrum & Andream, quoniam & primùm erant vocati. Deinde ponens fi ios Zebedaei praeponit Iacobum Iohanni: non propter di gnitatem sed quia ita acciderat: Alphonsus etiam Tostatus, Abulensis Episcopus, summae apud Pontificios autoritatis, Comm. in cap. 10. Matth. q. 29. disertè adserit, quòd propter tempus prior ponatur Petrus: ipse enim, pergit, fuit pri--us, qui vocatus legitur à Christo, fuprà c. 4. &Marc. 1. Ad illud verò, quòd Andreat videtur priùs vocatus, ut qui fuit unus de duobus illis discipulis, qui cum Ioh. Bapt erant &c Ioh. 1, 37. respondet idem, quòd non computetur tempus discipulatûs ex tunc: quòd licet tunc ivermt cum Christo de Iudaeâ in Galilaeam: tamen reliquerint eum redeuntes ad officum piscationis, ita ut oporteret, quòd Christus at novo iterum vocaret eos ad mare Gal--aeae, supràcap. 4.&Marc. 1.ideò ex tunc computari tempus discipulatûs, quod adhaeserunt firmiter manere cum eo: & tunc Petrum priorem poni, quia fortè fuerit maior aetate, quàm Andreas cùm ambo eâdem hora fuerint v-cāti. Alii putant, ordinem esse arbitrarium Chrysostomus homl. 33. in Matth: Marcus quidemκατ ἀξίανipsos ordine collocavit: post duos enim, qui apicem Apostolatus tenuerunt ( μετὰ τοὺς δὺο κορυφαίους) Andream posuit: hic verò haut ita. Idem paullò pòst: Videsοὐκατὰ γῆν ἀξίαν τίθησῖν,non ex dignitate ipsos numerari. Loquitur quidem Chrysostomus de ordine in collocatione Iacobi & Iohannis hîc observato: sed idem dici quoque potest de Petro, quòd nempe primus nominetur, non quasi dignitate h. e. autoritate monarchicâ reliquis Apostolis prior fuerit, sed quia cum Andrea fuit πρωτόκλητος)* Neve quis primatum potestatis ex hâc appellatione exsculpat, ideò Gal. 2, 9. praeponitur Iacobus. *(sic 1. Cor. 3, 22. postponitur Paulo, c. 9, 5. reliquis Apostolis omnibus. Minimè igitur hinc opus est, ut cum Beza hîc quis suspicetur, vocabulumπρῶτοςab aliquo additum esse, qui Petri primatum vellet stabilire: cum nihil sequatur, quod cohaereat. Etenim non solùm Codd. Graeci (quibus non immeritò accensere placet Eclogas MSS. Graecas, quae adservantur in Biblioth. Norib.) constanter voculam illam tum hîc, tum apud Marcum habent, verùm etiam antiquissimus interpres Syrus, ac praeterea Patres, Chysostomus, Hieronymus aliique eandem agnoscunt. Unde etiam ipse Bezi, seipsum qs. corrigens addit: reperimus tamen ita scriptum in omnibus exemplaribus & Theophylacto Romano. Neque tamen, ut commemoravimus, Monarchicus, qualem Pontificii somniant, & inter alia hinc quoque extruere satagunt, (Vid. Bell. l. 1. de P. R. c. 18. Becan. lib. 1. Manual. c. 4. §. 45. Costerus Enchir. Controv. c 3 pag 113. Tirinus, Corn. à Lapide; Conzen aliique Comment. Pontif. in h. l.) Primatus Petri (vel Pontificis proiùs Romani, nam huic uni hîc seritur à Papaeis, huic uni meritur fulciri potestEtenim primò sallum est, etrum semper primô loco numerari. Contrarium patet ex Gal. 2, 0.Secundo notum est ex Philosopho lib categ. c. 12. quòd prius adeoq; & primus variis modis dicatur, nempe 1. κατὰ χρόιον 2. κατὰ τὴβν τάξιν. 3. κατ᾽ ἀξίαν, seu qua-. illud πρότερον dicitur, quod est βέλτιον καὶ τιμιώτερον. Non autem sequitur, Petrus primus vo-atur, Ε κατ᾽ ἀξίαν, & quidem talem, quae Monarchicum Dominatum in reliquos Apostolos includit. Sanè haut magis, quàm si quis vellet subsumere. Maria mater Domini Act. 1, 14. omnium mulierum nominatur loco postremo, E. inter omnes etiam κατ᾽ ἀξίαν suit postrema. Tertio pugnat ille dominatus tum cum dictis Script. S. Vid. Luc. 22, 26.2. Cor. 11, 5.

1. Petr. 5, 3. tùm cum testimoniis Patrum. Cyprianus: Coeteri Apostoli erant id quod Petrus, pari consortio praediti honoris & potestatis. ## 10:3
v. 3. Matthew that Publican. And yet Matthew was no longer a publican, but at least he had once been such. Therefore, the rule of Jerome in this place is to be noted: Matt. 26. at the beginning. Sometimes in Scripture, the former name remains even when the thing has changed. *(B. Glassius confirms the rule of Jerome with many examples from Holy Scripture, especially Gen. 2, 23; Exod. 7, 12; Isa. 11, 6; Matt. 11, 5; ch. 26, 6; ch. 27, 53; John 9, 17; &c. in Philologia Sacra, pp. 8 & 9. Furthermore, the same Jerome observes in this place that the other Evangelists do not ascribe the name of publican, lest by recalling his former manner of life they might seem to disparage the Evangelist. But he himself (namely Matthew) calls himself a publican: so that where iniquity abounded, grace might superabound, Rom. 5, 20.)*

Lebbaeus surnamed Thaddaeus. *(The Vulgate omitted the words Λεββαῖος ὁ ἐπικληθεὶς against the faith of the Greek Codices, with the exception at least of the Cantuarensis. The Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic, Persian, and likewise Chrysostom, Theophylact, & other Fathers acknowledge the same.)* It seems that μετάθεσις must be established here, so that Thaddaeus is the Syriac, which is the same as the Hebrew Judas, the genuine name; but Lebbaeus is to be established as the surname given to him on account of his wisdom. *(Franc. Junius thinks so, from whom, however, Caninius departs, and Drusius, Scultetus, and others who follow him. Lud. de Dieu teaches that Thaddaeus in the Syriac language denotes a spring herb; and Lebbaeus a little heart. Concerning which matter in the Preface to the Epistle of Jude. B. Luther in the Gloss: This is the pious Judas Luc. 6, 16. is without doubt a fault in the Ethiopic version, while for Lebbaeus there is Lebdaeus. But not L-bdaeus, as Lud. de Dieu expresses in the Appendix p. 523. Yet the Londoners followed the reading through , nor was this fault observed by Castell in the notes.)*

Latin:

v. 3. Matthaeus ille Publicanus. Atqui Matthaeus non ampliùs erat publicanus, sed olim saltem talis fuerat. Notanda igitur h. l. regula Hieronymi in Matth. 26. sub init. Aliquando in Scriptura mutatâ re pristinum nomen manet. *(Regulam Hieronymi multis exemplis Sc. S. cumprimis Genes. 2, 23.Exod. 7, 12.Es. 11, 6.Matth. 11, 5.c. 26, 6.c. 27, 53.Ioh. 9, 17. &c. confirmat B. Glassius Gr. S. p. 8 & 9. Observat porrò idem Hieronymus in h. l. quòd coeteri Evangelistae publicani nomen non adscribant, ne antiquae conversationis recordantes sugillare Evangelistam viderentur. Iste verò (nempe Matthaeus) publicanum se appellet: ut ubi abundavit iniquitas, super abundet & gratia,Rom. 5, 20.)*

Lebbaeus cognominatus Thaddaeus. *(Vulgatus verba Λεββαῖος ὁ ἐπικληθεὶς contra fidem Graecorum Codicum, excepto saltem Cantuarensi, omisit. Agnoscunt eadē Syrus, Arabs, Aethiops, Persa, Chrysostomus item, Theoph. & alii Patres.)* Videtur hîc μετάθεσις statuenda, ita ut Thaddai Syrum, quod est idem cum Ebr. Iuda, nomen genuinum; Lebbaeus verò cognomen ob sapientiam ipsi inditum statuatur. *(Ita sentit Franc. Iunius, à quo verò discedit Caninius, & qui eum sequuntur Drusius, Scultetus, alii Lud. de Dieu docet, quòd Thaddaeus in Ling. Syr. notet herbam vernam; & Lebbaeus corculum. Quâ de re in Praeloq ad Ep. Iudae. B. Lutherus in Glossa: Disz ist ber fromme IudasLuc. 6, 16. procul ambiguo vitium est in Aethiopicâ versione, dum pro Lebbaeo habetur Lebdaeus. Non verò L-bdaeus, prout Lud. de Dieu in Append. p. 523. exprimit. Secuti tamē lectionem per sunt Londinenses, nec observatum quoq; hoc vitium à Castello in notis.)*

## 10:4
v. 4. Simon ὁ Κανανίτης. Luther, of Cana. Toussain criticizes this, and says that the reason for the name must be sought not from the city of Cana, but from the Hebrew קנאה, which signifies zeal, because in Luke 6:15 he is called the Zealot. But it could have happened that Simon, being born in Cana, was called the Zealot by a certain allusion. *(Compare more on this matter in the Analysis on Luke 6:15)* Nor, however, from the fact that Simon was born in Cana, can it be firmly concluded that he was that very bridegroom who celebrated the wedding at Cana, of which John 2 speaks, as Nicephorus, and from him Baronius, maintain.

καὶ Ιούδας ὁ Ισκαριώτης, τὸ Ισκαριώτης The Syrian expresses it by *(Franciscus Lucas and the Jesuit Conzenius less correctly present it through O)* which they derive from םכר wages and נטא he failed, he declined, so that יוטא might be the passive future of the third conjugation, thus; the whole surname, he will be led to defection by wages. *(Especially this method of naming is approved after Maldonatus and Adrichomius by Conzenius, to whom, however, it is not probable that this name was imposed either by Christ or by his parents.)* That he received this surname from Christ, as Peter and the sons of Zebedee did, declares that the deed of Judas was perfectly known to Christ; but if it was given to him by others, divine providence is commended, without which he would not have received that name, which so clearly would foreshadow his betrayal. Beza and Toussain, following Caninius in his Hebrew ch. 13, report that it is a compound Hebrew word, as if it were in Hebrew איש קרייות Man of Kerioth i.e. Keriothite, from a town of the tribe of Judah, John 15:25.

*(To that manner, namely, by which E-drae 2:23 and Gen. 24:13 the name אנשים is used. This etymology pleases Mr. D. Friedlib in his observations on the H. E. page 80, Grotius in this place, Pasor in his Etymologies of proper names p. 35, B. O. Glassius in his Sacred Grammar p. 125, and it is favored by the fact that in the -odex most ancient, which Beza used, for ἰσκαριώτης is read ἀπὸ τοὑ Κυριώτου.. Cornelius à Lapide likewise grants that Judas obtained that surname from his fatherland, not however from the city Cari--h of the tribe of Judah: but because he was born from the village Iscarioth in the tribe of Ephraim, not far from Samaria, and he brings forward for this opinion Jerome, both here and in Isa. 28:1. It is to be noted, however, that Jerome in this place speaks disjunctively, he adds namely: or he took the word from the tribe of Issachar.

Moreover, that opinion of old, that the name was derived from the fatherland of Judas the traitor, also pleased Chrysostom, who clearly in hom. 33 in Matth. ἀναγκα He also brings forward in this matter that certain famous men are named from their city, Ioh. Drusius lib. 1 Praeter. p. 25, a passage from Iuchasin, where it is thus: Those men who are called by the names of their land were distinguished and known in that place, as the man of Sereda, the man of Jerusalem, the man of Caphar Hanna. Similarly, I, by way of example, was in the kingdom of Spain and the remaining kingdoms of the Christians, when my books on Astrology had gone out: they said R. Abraham Sachuth, the man of Salamanca, i.e., Salamanticensis. Thus Antigonus, the man of Socho, i.e., S-chaeus. This custom certainly flowed down even to our ancestors, to whom it was very familiar to attribute a name to men famous for erudition from their fatherland. Thus the distinguished Mathematician Johannes Regiomontanus was so called from that, because he was born in Regiomons in Franconia. Thus Desiderius Erasmus obtained the surname Roderodamus from a famous city of Holland. Nicolaus Lyranus was also called from his fatherland. Similarly, Ioh. Hussus, Henricus Glareanus, Valentinus Trocedorfflius, Iohannes Gerson, Angelus Politianus, Ioh. Sleidanus, and very many other learned men obtained a surname from their native soil. Those who think that he was called Iscariot do not differ far from the said opinion, writing that he was of the tribe of Issachar, to whom such a name from the very deed fits best: for he sold Christ for a reward; for Issachar, from c. 30, 18 Gen. is called from שכר which signifies reward. The Londoners in Interp. Nominum Ebr. Chald. & Graec. note that Iscariotes is interpreted in Hebrew as man of killing, or man of extermination or of death. Franc. Iunius hands down that םכריות is called purse, so that Sechariuta may be ὁ ἔχωντὸ γλωσθόκομον, which is said of Judas, Ioh. 12. 6. Others think that he is so called by anticipation, as if to say strangled: for Sedar is to strangle among the Syrians, and Mascera is strangulation. Lud de Dieu in Comm. ad Matth. p. 36 seems to disapprove of both these opinions, since Mascera is found in no Lexicons. He teaches, however, that is the same for the Syrians as םכר he closed, he obstructed, so that thus according to him Judas obtained this name from there, not as if he strangled himself, but because he was divinely seized by some disease, by which the mouth of the fistula which is in the neck is accustomed to be obstructed, and was thus suffocated. Concerning which matter more will be treated in Anal. ad Matth. 27, 5. (The Arabs and Persians express this name by ח in the middle, for it has here and there . It is called otherwise (See Ioh. 6, 71.12, 4.c. 13, 2.) Judas of Simon, namely son, for the distinction of another Judas, who is called Judas of James, viz. brother, Ioh. 14, 22.)

( ὁ καὶ ραδοὺςἀυτόν. Similarly and elsewhere Judas Iscariot is described, as Matth. 26, 2538.Marc. 3, 19.c. 14, 42.44.Ioh. 6, 71.c. 13, 11.c. 18, 2. From the fact, however, that our Lord co-opted Judas into the number of the Apostles, whom nevertheless He did not ignore would be a traitor, it is not to be gathered that it is permitted to us also to assume evil men, or those whom we foreknow in their own way will be evil, to sacred functions in any way. As Franc. Lucas well warns in this place, who also notably adds that the Savior signified that in His Church and in all its orders there would always be evil men mixed with the good, until the threshing floor is cleansed (above c. 3, 12.) and that the administration of the Sacraments is by no means weakened or rendered empty on account of the unworthiness of the ministers. Which ingenuous confession is to be opposed to the common doctrine of the Papists, that the intention of the Minister is required for the integrity of the Sacrament. But the reason for intention and unworthiness is the same. And if it is true concerning the genus, viz. concerning the unworthiness and wickedness of the minister, that it does not weaken or render empty the administration of the Sacraments, i.e. their integrity, the same will be able to be asserted also concerning the species, i.e. concerning non-intention.) Finally, Chemnitz discusses the reason for the appellations widely in his Harmony. (Some things will also be warned concerning the same in the Analysis to Marc. 3, 17.)

Latin:

v. 4. Simonὁ Κανανίτης. Lutherus, von Cana. Tossanus hoc taxat, ac rationem appellationis petendam esse dicit non ex urbe Cana, sed ab Ebraeo קנאה, quod significat zelum, quia Luc. 6, 15. dicatur Zelotes. At fieri potuit, ut Simon Canâ oriundus, per allusionem quandam diceretur Zelotes. *(Conf. plura in hanc rem in Anal. ad Luc. 6, 15)* Neque tamen ex eo, quod Simon Canâ oriundus, firmiter colligi potest, quòd fuerit ipse sponsus ille, qui nuptias Canae celebravit, de quibus Ioh. 2. ceu Nicephorus, & ex eo Baronius statuunt.

καὶ Ιούδας ὁ Ισκαριώτης, τὸ Ισκαριώτης Syrus exprimit per *(Franc. Lucas ac Iesuita Conzen. minûs rectè per O exhibent)* quod deducunt à םכרmerces & נטאdefecit, declinavit, ut יוטא sit futurum passivum coniug tertiae, sic-; totum cognomen, mercede inducetur ad defectionem. *(Cum primis demoninandi ratio haec post Mald. & Adrich. ad probatur Conzenlo, cui tamen non est probabile, nomen hoc s. à Christo, sive à parentibus ei fuisse impositum.)* Hoc cognomensi à Christo accepit, ut Petrus & filii Zebedaei, declarat, factum Iudae Christo optimè fuisse cognitum; si verò ab aliis ei in ditum est, divina providentia commendatur, sine quâ illud nomen non accepit, quod adeo clarè proditionem eius praemonstraret. Beza & Tossanus ex Caninio in nomin. Ebr. c. 13. tradunt, esse vocem compositam Ebraeam, quasi sit Ebraicè איש קרייותVir Keriiotharum i. e. Keriiothensis, ab oppido tribus Iudae, Ioh. 15, 25.

*(Ad eum nempe modum, quo E-drae 2, 23. ac Gen. 24, 13. nomen אנשים adhibetur. Placet haec etymologia Dn. D. Friedlib. in observ. in H. E. pag. 80. Grotio in h. l. Pasori in Etymis nom. propr. p. 35. B. O. Glasfio Gramm. S. p. 125. favetque eidem, quòd in -odice vetustissimo, quô Beza usus fuit, pro ἰσκαριώτης legatur ἀπὸ τοὑ Κυριώτου. Corn. à Lapide itidem Iudam à patria cognomen illud adeptum esse largitur, non tamen ab urbe Cari--h tribus Iuda: sed quia oriundus ex vico Iscarioth in tribu Ephraim, nō longè à Samaria, & adducit pro hâc sententia Hieron. tùm hîc, tùm in Es. 28, 1. Notandùm tamē, quòd Hieron in h. l. disiunctivè loquatur, addit n.: vel ex tribu Isachar vocabulū sumsit.

Pridem autem sententia illa, quòd à patria Iudae proditori nomen illud cesserit, arrisit quoque Chrysostomo, qui disertê hom. 33. in Matth. ἀναγκα Adducit quoque in hanc rem, quòd viri quidam celebres in suâ urbe, ab ea denominentur Ioh. Drusius lib. 1 Praeter. p. 25. locum ex Iuchasin, ubi ita: Viri illi, qui vocantur de nominibus terrae suae insignes & noti erant in illo loco, ut vir Sereda, vir Ierusalem. vir Caphar Hanna. Similiter ego in modum exempli eram in regno Hispaniae & reliquis regnis Christianorum, quum exivissent libri mei de Astrologia: dicebant R. Abraham Sachuth vir Salamanca i. e. Salamanticensis. Sic Antigonus vir Socho i. e. S-chaeus. Mos sanè hic etiam ad maiores manavit nostros, quibus admodùm familiare erat, viris eruditione claris à patria nomen tribuere. Sic insignis Mathematicus Iohannes Regiomontanus exinde sic appellatus, quòd Regiomonte in Franconia oriundus. Ita Desiderius Erasmus à celebri Hollandiae urbe, Roderodamo cognomen sortitus. Nicolaus quoque Lyranus à patria dictus. Similiter Ioh. Hussus, Henricus Glareanus, Valentinus Trocedorfflius, Iohannes Gerson, Angelus Politianus, Ioh. Sleidanus aliique viri docti plurimi à patrio solo cognomen obtinuerunt. Haut procul à dictâ sententia abludunt, qui Ischariotem dictum existimant, perch scribentes, quòd de tribu Issaschar esset, cui tals nomen ex ipso quofacinore optimè conveniat: nam, mercede vendidit Christum; Issascharsiquidem ex c. 30, 18. Gen. àשכרquod mercedem significat, dictus est. Londinenses in Interp. Nominum Ebr. Chald. & Graec. notant, quòd Iscariotes Ebraicè interpretetur vir occisionis, vel vir exterminationis vel mortis.)* Franc. Iunius tradit םכריות appellari marsupium, ut Sechariuta sit ὁ ἔχωντὸ γλωσθόκομον, quod dicitur de Iuda, Ioh. 12. 6. Alii existimant, sic appellari per anticipationem q. d. strangulatum:: esse enim Sedar apud Syros strangulare, & Mascera strangulationem. *(Lud de Dieu in Comm. ad Matth. p. 36. utramque hanc sententia improbare videtur, siquidem Mascera in nullis Lexicis reperiatur. Docet tamen, Syris idem esse, quod םכרclausit, obstruxit, ut ita iuxta ipsum Iu das inde hoc nomen obtinuerit, non quasi seipsum strangularit, sed quia morbo aliquo, quo os fistnlae quae in collo est obturari solet, divinitus i-isso correptus fuerit & ita suffocatus. Quâ de re pluribus agetur in Anal. ad Matth. 27, 5.)* *(Arabs & Persa per ח in medio nomen hoc exprimunt, habet enim hic ille Vocatur aliàs (Vid Ioh. 6, 71.12, 4.c. 13, 2.) Iudas Simonis, nempe filius, ad differentiam alterius Iudae, qui Iudas Iacobi, sc. frater, dicitur Ioh. 14, 22.)*

*( ὁ καὶ ραδοὺςἀυτόν. Similiter & alibi Iudas Iscariotes describitur, uti Matth. 26, 2538.Marc. 3, 19.c. 14, 42.44.Ioh. 6, 71.c. 13, 11.c. 18, 2. Ex eo verò, quòd Dominus noster Iudam, quem tamen non ignoravit proditorem fore, in numerum Apostolorum cooptavit, non colligendum, quòd nobis etiam liceat malos, aut eos, quos malos fore suo modo praescimus, ad functiones sacras ullo modo adsumere. Uti benè monet Franc. Lucas in h. l. qui etiam notanter addit significasse Salvatorem, in Ecclesia sua & in omnibus illius ordinibus semper fore malos permixtos bonis, donec permundetur area (supra c. 3, 12.) & nequaquam enervari aut inanem reddi Sacramentorum administrationem propter ministrorum indignitatem. Quae ingenua confesssio opponenda doctrinae communi Pontificiorum, quòd intentio Ministri requiratur ad integritatem Sacramenti. Eadem verò ratio est non intentionis & indignitatis. Et si de genere, videl. de indignitate & improbitate ministri verum est, quòd non enervet, vel inanem reddat Sacramentorum administrationem s. integritatem, etiam. de specie, s. de-non-intentione adseri idem poterit)* Denique de ratione appellationum latè disserit Chemnic. in Harmoniâ. *(Monebuntur quoque nonnulla de iisdem in Anal. ad Marc. 3, 17.)*

## 10:5
(v. 5. Do not go into the way of the Gentiles. i. e. to the Gentiles. A similar construction is had Ier. 2, 18. But lest anyone from this and other similar places, as below c. 15, 24.Act. 16, 6. etc., perversely gather, as if God did not wish, nor does He wish, all men to be called, it is to be observed that a distinction must be made here between the grace of the calling being denied, and being delayed. This, not that, is indicated in these sayings; since they mean this, that first the Gospel ought to be preached to the Jews, afterward, however, to the Gentiles. From thence, however, it follows not at all, Therefore, to these it was not to be preached at all. Certainly no more than if anyone from delayed divine help on the cross should wish to gather, as if God does not wish at all to free us from calamities. Ambrose observed this well, who notably:) Grace was not denied to those peoples, but as far as it appeared, delayed. That the grace of vocation with respect to these peoples was at least delayed, is evident 1. from the general mercy of the heavenly Father, Ezech. 18 32.c. 33, 11.Ioh. 2. 16.Rom. 11, 32.1. Tim. 2, 4. 2. Petr. 3, 9. 2. from the universal satisfaction of Christ, Rom. 5, 18. 19.c. 8, 32.1. Cor. 5, 14.1. Tim. 2, 6.Ebr. 2, 9.Tit. 2, 10.Ioh. 1, 29.1. Ioh. 2, 2. 3. from the explicit information and attestation of the Holy Scripture, see especially Psal. 19, 5.Matth. 11, 28.Marc. 16, 15.Act. 17, 30.Col 1, 25. 4. from the rejection of the cause of damnation onto the men themselves, Prov. 1, 24.Matth 23, 37. Finally 5. from the consideration of the History of the Gospel. For Scripture testifies that the Samaritans also had the grace of vocation, thus Ioh. 4. through Christ's conversation with the Samaritan woman many were converted. Add Act. 1, 8c. 8, 1.5, 14.c. 9, 31.c. 15, 3. The same for the Asians is manifest from 1. Petr 1, 1.Apoc. 1 & 2. That, however, some are called more slowly, various causes of that can be assigned. This happens sometimes because of the fault of ancestors, who rejected the preached word; or because of a foreseen greater benefit. Thus the Gospel was to be preached to every nation, Matth 28, 19. But because it could not be done at once, therefore it was to be announced successively to one nation after another, and indeed to that nation first, from which more benefit would follow. There is added especially the divine promise and ordination, according to which Christ was constituted minister of the circumcision,Rom. 16, 8. For the promise had been made peculiarly to the Jews. And in this respect also Paul and Barnabas say Act. 13, 46. ἀναγκαῖον that it was necessary for the Gospel to be preached first to the Jews: Indeed, if the Gospel concerning Christ had not been preached first to the Jews, he could not have been believed to be the Messiah, since he was promised to the Jews especially in the O. T. Because therefore Christ had to preach first to the Jews, whence it was fitting, his disciples also, as those who ought to adhere to the Master, not elsewhere, except in Judea, were to preach initially in an ordinary way Actor. 13, 46.Roman 1, 16.Luc. 24, 47. -nor yet did the Samaritans and other Gentiles lack all vocation in the meantime: for they too were called by the voice of nature, of their own conscience, and of the fame of the miracles performed in the Church. Compare at greater length the Blessed Pareus, Book on Election, §. 141. Blessed D. Meisner. Ἀνθρωπ. Disp. 13. q. 2. §. 18. We add at least this, that Crocius himself in Volume 1 of AntiBec. page 108, reconciles the present passage with Mark 16:15 in the same manner, namely that this mandate pertains to a singular mission, made before the passion of Christ, with the wall between the Gentiles and the Jews not yet torn down, but not to a future time. And he proves it from John 10:16Matt. 8:11Luke 13:28Acts 13:46c. 17:30, 31. John Camero in Myroth. Evang. on Matt. 16:20 p. 43, establishes that Christ at that time and in the present did not omit his disciples for preaching the Gospel properly so-called, since he reserved this for himself; for now it was not for the disciples to teach while the Master was living and seeing. But at least he sent them out, so that they might prepare hearers and disciples for him. If this opinion is true, about which we shall not now dispute, it can by no means be gathered from the fact that he here forbade the disciples to enter into a city (i.e., into one of the cities) of Samaria, that God completely deprived the Samaritans of the grace of calling, and indeed out of a certain absolute reprobation.

*( Into a city of the Samaritans do not enter. Because the Samaritans observed some things from the law, 2 Kings 17, and from this the Apostles could think that they were not included under the name of the Gentiles, for that reason the Savior makes special mention of them.)*

Latin:

*(v. 5. In viam gentium ne abieritis. i. e. adgentes. Similis constructio habetur Ier. 2, 18. Ne verò aliquis ex hoc aliisq; similibus locis, uti infrà c. 15, 24.Act. 16, 6. &c. perversè colligat, qs. Deus non voluerit, neq; velit, omnes homines vocari, observandum, quòd distingvendum hîc sit inter gratiam vocationis negatam, ac retardatam. Haec non illa in his dictis indicatur; quippe quae hoc volunt, quòd prius Iudaeis Evangelium praedicari debeat, postmodum verò gentilibus. Exinde tamen mini mè se quitur, E. his prorsus non fuit praedi candum. Sanè haut magis, ac si quis ex dilato auxilio divino in cruce colligere velit, ac si Deus prorsus non velit nos liberare è calamitatibus. Probè hoc observavit Ambrosius, qui not-nter: Non fuit negata illis populis gratia, sed quantum apparuit, dilata. Quòd verò vocationis gratia respectu horum populorum fuerit saltem dilata, patet l. ex generali Patris coelestis miserarione, Ezech. 18 32.c. 33, 11.Ioh. 2. 16.Rom. 11, 32.1. Tim. 2, 4. 2. Petr. 3, 9. 2. ex universall Christi satisfactione, Rom. 5, 18. 19.c. 8, 32.1. Cor. 5, 14.1. Tim. 2, 6.Ebr. 2, 9.Tit. 2, 10.Ioh. 1, 29.1. Ioh. 2, 2. 3. ex disertâ Sc. S. informatione & attestatione, vid. cumprimis Psal. 19, 5.Matth. 11, 28.Marc. 16, 15.Act. 17, 30.Col 1, 25. 4. ex damnationis causa in ipsos homines reiectione, Prov. 1, 24.Matth 23, 37. Denique 5. ex Historiae Evang, consideratione. Testatur enim Scriptura, quòd Samaritani quoque habuerint vocationis gratiam sic Ioh. 4. per Christi colloquium cum Samaritanâ muliere multi fuerunt conversi. Adde Act. 1, 8c. 8, 1.5, 14.c. 9, 31.c. 15, 3. Idem dAsianis manifestum ex 1. Petr 1, 1.Apoc. 1 & 2. Quòd autem quidam tardiùs vocentur, illius variae adsignari possunt causae. Contingit hoc aliquando propter culpam maiorum, qui verbum praedicatum reiecerunt; vel propter praevisum maius emolumentum. Sic omni genti erat praedicandum Evangelium, Matth 28, 19. Sed quia simul fieri non poterat, ideò succesivè uni nationi post alteram erat annuciandum, & illi quidem genti priùs, unde plus conse quuturum emolumenti. Accedit cumprimis promissio ac ordinatio divina, iuxta quam Christus constitutus minister circumcisionis,Rom. 16, 8. Iudaeis enim peculiariter facta erat promissio Atque hoc respectu etiam dicunt Paulus & Barnabas Act. 13, 46.ἀναγκαῖονfuisse, primùm Iudaeis praedicari Evangelium: Sanè nisi Iudaeis primùm praedicatum fuisset Evangelium de Christo, non potuisset ipse credi Messias, quippe qui Iudaeis praecipuè erat in V. T. promissus. Quia igitut Christus in primis praedicare debebat Iudaeis, unde conveniens erat, dis-ipulos quoque eius, ut qui Magistro debebant adhaerere, non alibi, nisi in Iudeâ ordinariè initiò pradicare Actor. 13, 46.Roman 1, 16.Luc. 24, 47. -eque tamen Samaritani aliique gentiles interea temporis omni vocatione caruerunt: vocati enim & ipsi per vocem tum naturae, tum propriae conscientiae, tum famâ miraculorum, in Ecclesiâ factorum. Conf. pluribus B. Par. L. de Elect. §. 141. B. D. Meisn. Ἀνθρωπ. Disp. 13. q. 2. §. 18. Hoc saltem addimus, quòd Crocius ipse Tomo 1. AntiBec. pag. 108. praesentem locum cum Marc. 16, 15. d. m. conciliet, nempe quòd mandatum hoc pertineat ad missionem singularem, factam ante Christi passionem, maceriâ inter Gentes & Iudaeos nòndum dirutâ, non autem ad tempus futurum. Probatq; ex Ioh. 10, 16.Matth. 8, 11.Luc. 13, 28.Act. 13, 46.c. 17, 30. 31. Ioh. Camero in Myroth. Evang. ad Matth. 16, 20. p. 43. statuit, quòd Christus tum temporis & in praesenti Discipulos suos non omiserit ad praedicandum Evangelium propriè diclum, cum ipse sibi hoc reservarit; iam verò Discipuli non esse, vivente & vidente Magistro docere. Sed saltem emisisse, ut auditores & discipulos sibi pararent. Quae sententia si vera est, de quo iam non disputabimus, minimè ex eo, quòd hîc Discipulis prohibuit, ne in urbem (h. e. in unam ex urbibus) Samariae ingrediantur, colligi potest, quòd Deus Samaritanos vocationis gratiâ penitus privarit, & quidem ex absolutâ quadam reprobatione.)*

*( In urbem Samarit anorum ne intraveritis. Quia Samaritani nonnulla ex lege servabant, 2. Reg. 17. atque hinc Apostoli existimare poterant, illos nomine gentium non comprehendi, inde specialiter Illorum mentionem Salvator facit.)*

## 10:6
*(v. 6. Rather. It seems τὸμᾶλλον here to be redundant, as it is elsewhere also. See John 3:19, just as also ἢ Luke 18:14)*

*( Lost sheep. An expression taken from Isa. 53:6Jer. 50:6Ezek. 34:5. In the same way he also speaks below in c. 15:24. Ludov. Capellus writes in Spic. on this passage that this perdition, of which Christ speaks, is to be understood not of reprobation. For, he adds, Christ was not sent to the reprobate, but to the elect. But if Christ is the propitiation not only for our sins, but also for the sins of the whole world, 1 John 2:2, if he died for him, who -di can, Rom. 14:15, who can perish, 1 Cor. 8:11, it follows that he was also given for the reprobate, and sent to the reprobate. Meanwhile, we easily grant that Christ, by reason of a special office, or Prophetic one, to be performed in his own person, which consists in the preaching of the word and miracles, was sent to the Jews. Among these, however, there were many reprobates: who indeed were called they were unwilling to come,Matt. 23, 37. they neglected the calling, c. 22, 5. &c. meanwhile by reason of the general office, which consists in satisfaction for sins, likewise in the calling made through the Prophets & Apostles, he was sent to all men, as was shown a little before.)*

Latin:

*(v. 6. Poriùs. Videtur τὸμᾶλλον hîc redundare, ut alibi etiam. Vid. Ioh. 3, 19. sicuti etiam ἢLuc. 18 14.)*

*( Adoves perditas. Locutio desumta ex Es. 53, 6.Ierem. 50, 8.Ezech. 34, 5. Eodem modo loquitur etiam infrà c. 15, 24. Scribit Ludov. Capellus in Spic. ad h. l. quòd perditio haec, de qua Christus loquitur, intelligenda sit non de reprobatione. Nam, addit, adreprobos Christus non est missus, sed ad electos. Atqui si Christus est propitiatio non solùm pro nostris, sed etiam pro totius mundi peccat is,1. Ioh. 2, 2.si mortuus est pro eo, qui -di potest,Rom. 14, 15.qui potest perire,1. Cor. 8, 11. sequitur, quòd etiam pro reprobis sit datus, & ad reprobos missus. Interea facilè largimur, quòd Christus ratione officii specialis, sive Prophetici, in propriâ personâ peragendi, quod consistit in praedicatione verbi & miraculis, missus sit ad Iudaeos. Inter hos tamen & ipsos multi erant reprobi: qui nempe vocati venire noliserunt,Matth. 23, 37. vocationem neglexerunt, c. 22, 5. &c. interea ratione officis generalis, quod versatur in satis sactione pro peccatis, item in vocatione per Prophetas & Apostolos factâ, missus est ad omnes homines, ut paullò antè ostensum.)*

## 10:7
*(v. 7. But go, preach, saying: The kingdom of heaven is at hand. What ought to be understood by kingdom of heaven in this and similar sayings, was shown above at c. 3. v. 2. p. 145. seqq. The blessed D. Hunnius well advises in this place, page 218, that Christ does not wish that they should say or add nothing besides, or utter only these words: but that it seemed good to the Lord to summarize the argument of the sermon, the meaning of which is that men, having performed repentance for sins, ought to believe the Gospel, inasmuch as the kingdom of heaven has arrived. By the kingdom of heaven, however, according to the same, the Savior understands that kingdom of the Messiah desired and expected for many centuries, which God promised through the mouth of His holy Prophets from the very beginning of the world. Corn. à Lapide explains the preaching about the kingdom of heaven thus, as if to say Christ: I shall shortly by my death open heaven to men, closed for so many thousands of years on account of the sin of Adam. If by these words the Jesuit intends that the souls of the saints, deceased in the O. T., were not received into heaven before the death & resurrection of Christ, but were detained in limbo, (which is otherwise the common opinion of the Papists, and indeed of Cornelius himself, Comm. in ep. ad Eph. c. 4, 9.) he errs, since that Papist limbo is a mere figment, as has long since been shown by our people. See B. Pan Confess. Cathol. t. 2. p. 420. seqq. L. de Morte §. 166. seqq. B. D. Bald. in Epist. ad Eph. c. 4, 9. 3. Let at least these passages be noted here 1. Sam. 25, 29. Wis. 3, 1. Luke 16, 22.c. 23, 43.Heb. 11, 10,16.Eccles. 12, 7.)*

Latin:

*(v. 7. Profecti autem praedicate, dicentes: Appropinquat regnum coelorum. Quid per regnum coelorum in hoc similibusq; dictis intelligi debeat, ostensum suprà ad c. 3. v. 2. p. 145. seqq. Benè monet B. D. Hunnius in h. l. pag. 218. non velle Christum, ut nihil praetereà dicerent aut adderent, vel haec duntaxat verba proferrent: sed visum esse Domino, argumentum concionis summatim: perstringere, cuius sententia est, debere homines, actâ de peccatis poenitentia, credere Evangelio, siquidem regnum coelorum advenerit. Per regnum verò coelorum, iuxta eundem, intelligit Salvator optatum illud multisque seculis expectatum regnum Messiae, quod Deus per os sanctorum Prophetarum suorum iam inde à inundo exordio est pollicitus. Corn. à Lapide ita praedicationem de regno coelorum explicat, q. d. Christus: Ego brevi morte meâ patefaciam hominibus coelum, tot millibus annorum ob peccatum Adae clausum. Quibus verbis si hoc intendit Iesuita, quòd animae sanctorum; in V. T. defunctorum, ante Christi mortem & resurrectionem non receptae fuerint in coelum, sed in limbo detentae, (quae communis aliàs Pontificiorum sententia est, ipsiusque adeò etiam Cornelii, Comm. in ep. ad Eph. c. 4, 9.) errat, cum limbus ille Pontificius merum sit figmentum, cen pridem à nostratibus ostensum. Vid. B. Pan Confess. Cathol. t. 2. p. 420. seqq. L. de Morte §. 166. seqq. B. D. Bald. in Epist. ad Eph. c. 4, 9. 3. Notentur hîc saltem loca 1. Sam. 25, 29. Sap. 3, 1. Luc. 16, 22.c. 23, 43.Ebr. 11, 10,16.Eccles. 12, 7.)*

## 10:8
*(v. 8. Νεκροὺςεγείρετε. Beza notes that these words are missing in the Old Interpreter and Theophylact. Ludovicus de Dieu corrects Beza in this place. They are not missing, he writes, in the Old Interpreter, but are transposed: for it has it thus, Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers. But those words are entirely missing in some Latin Codices, and were without doubt lacking in that edition which Beza used. Indeed, Jerome himself does not acknowledge them. But however much the Sixtine Correctors may have left that particle, Franc. Lucas nevertheless does not hesitate to write in the notes to the Var. Lect of the Latin edition, those words added with no semblance of truth. But he pronounces the same thing concerning the Greek text also, that in it the words νεκροὺς ὲγείρετε might perhaps deservedly be omitted. He relies, however, chiefly upon these reasons: 1. that nine Parisian copies pass them over. With the commentators Euthymius and Theophylact also concurring: whence they are marked with an obelisk even in the Royal Bibles themselves. 2. that they are missing in the Syriac version, according to the Vienna edition. In the Commentary he adds 3. that in v. 1. such power given to the Apostles is not expressed. 4. that Christ himself used this power sparingly. Hugo Grotius urges against the authority of the said words, that no dead person is read to have been restored to life by the Apostles before the resurrection of Christ. I reply first to the reason of Grotius, that in Holy Scripture it is not permitted to argue negatively in histories. Then I reply to the reasons of Franc. Lucas, and indeed regarding 1. that although those words are missing in some Parisian codices, just as they are missing in some manuscript codices which the Londoners used, they are nevertheless held in other most ancient codices which both the Parisians and the Londoners compared. 2. that other Syriac editions have them, with the most ancient Altdorf manuscript also agreeing. And furthermore, the Arab and the Ethiopian acknowledge those words, even according to the Roman editions. 3. that although at the beginning of the chapter it is not so distinctly expressed with how many gifts the Apostles were instructed, it suffices nevertheless that they are indicated afterwards. 4. that Christ, Ioh. 14, 12. promised to him who believes in him, that μείζονα he shall do those things which Christ did.

Freely you have received, freely give. Christ does not forbid receiving necessary sustenance of life, as is evident from the verse immediately following, 10. and 1. Cor. 9, 14. but to make gain from the preaching of the Gospel and miracles, and to seek one's own advantage. *(The Anabaptists therefore err, ineptly gathering from this, that it is not lawful for ministers of the Church to receive a stipend. We grant indeed, that δώρεαν is sometimes opposed otherwise to payment of a price, and that Paul δωρεὰν he preached, 2. Cor. 11, 7. But it must be noted 1. that Christ here speaks principally of miraculous healings, which he himself forbids to be set out for sale. 2. It is by no means permitted to infer, therefore neither for the labors, by which the ministers of the Church are exhausted, is a stipend to be paid to them, or to accept such is illicit for them. For the contrary is evident from Luc. 10, 7.Rom. 5, 27.1. Cor. 9, 13.Gal. 6, 61.Philipp. 4, 15. Nor is that stipend, which is paid to the Ministers of the Church laboring in the word, properly a wage for spiritual gifts, but it is a sign of a grateful mind in the hearers toward them. Briefly: Distinguish between the sale of spiritual benefits, and the testimony of a grateful mind and the remuneration of labors. The former is prohibited, 1. Tim. 3, 3. and it also turned out badly for Gehazi, 1. Reg. 5, 27. and likewise for Simon Magus, Act. 8, 20. the latter is certainly not only permitted, but also worthy of praise. 3. Indeed Christ himself received τὰ ὑῶάρχοντα from women Luc. 8, 3. and had γλωσθόκομον, which was entrusted to Judas, Ioh. 12, 6.c. 13, 29. 4. The deed of Paul in the said place proves nothing. For although he preached the Gospel freely to the Corinthians, he nevertheless received a stipend from other Churches, as is immediately added in the said place v. 8. Finally, even if Christ had most strictly forbidden that the Apostles should receive a stipend even for the preaching of the Gospel, one ought not, however, to infer from that, that it should not be done in our times either. For the Savior's precept was temporary. And thus the rule of Augustine regarding the words of the Lord in sermon 26 is valid here: distinguish the times, and the Scriptures will agree. This, however, is certain, that the Savior wishes Simony to be avoided with the greatest zeal at all times. Which very thing Corn. à Lapide rightly strives to inculcate here with many examples and opinions. And he seals the discussion with the words of Francis, who, as Bonaventure testifies in his life: Money, he said, for the servants of GOD is nothing other than the Devil and a poisonous snake. Let this Jesuit inculcate this to the servant of servants, that is, the Roman Pontiff, as he for whom hardly anything is of more concern than to scrape together money from everywhere, and to enrich his own nephews and nieces with the same, and to raise them even to the highest dignities.

Latin:

*(v. 8. Νεκροὺςεγείρετε. Notat Beza, verba haec deesse apud Veterem Interpretem & Theophylactum. Corrigit Bezam Ludovicus de Dieu in h. l. Non desunt, scribit, apud Veterem Interpretem, sed transponuntur: sic enim habet, Infirmos curate, mortuos suscitate, leprosos mundate. At omninò verba illa desunt in nonnullis Codd. Latinis, ac procul ambiguo desiderata fuere in illâ editione, quâ Beza usus fuit. Sanè ipse Hieronymus ea non agnoscit. Ut ut verò Correctores Sixtidi particulam illam reliquerint, scribere tamen non dubitat Franc. Lucas in not. ad Var. Lect edit. Latinae, addita illa verba nullâ similitudine veri. Quin de Graeco quoque textu idem pronunciat, quòd in eo verba νεκροὺς ὲγείρετε meritò fortassis possent omitti. Rationibus verò nititur potissimùm ille hisce 1. quòd novem Parisiensium exempla praetereant. Suffragantibus quoq; Enarratoribus Euthymio & Theophylacto: unde & in ipsis Bibliis Regiis obelisco sint not ata. 2. quòd desint in versione Syriacâ, iuxta edit. Viennensem. In Comm. addit 3. quòd v. 1. talis potestas Apostolis data non exprimatur. 4. quòd ipse Christus parcè potestatè hâc usus fuerit. Hugo Grotius urget contra dictorum verborum autoritatē, quòd nullus mortuus ab Apostolis vitae redditus legatur ante Christi resurrectionē. Resp. primò ad rationem Grotii, quòd in Sc. S. non liceat in Historiis argumentari negativê. Deindè ad rationes Franc Lucae resp. & quidém quoad 1. quòd licet in Codd. nonnullis Parisiensibus verba illa desiderentur, quemadmodum desunt in nonnullis Codd. MSS. quibus Lond. usi fuere, habeantur tamen in aliis vetustissimis Codd. quos tum Parisienses tum Londinenses contulerunt. 2. quòd aliae editiones Syriacae habeant, consentiente quoque antiquissimo MS. Altdorffino. Et agnoscunt praeterèa verba illa Arabs & Aethiops, etiam secundùm Romanas editiones. 3. quòd licet initiò capitis non ita distinctè exprimatur, quot donis fuerint Apostoli instructi, sufficiat tamen, quòd postea illa indicentur. 4. quòd Christus, Ioh. 14, 12. credenti in ipsum promiserit, quòd μείζονα iis, quae Christus fecit, facturus sit.)*

Gratis accepistis, gratis date. Non prohibet Christus, necessariam vitaesustentationem accipere, ceu patet ex vers. statim seq. 10. ac. 1. Cor. 9, 14. sed ex Evangelii praedicatione & miraculis quaestum facere, & proprium commodum quaerere. *(Errant proinde Anabaptistae, ineptè hinc colligentes, quòd ministris Ecclesiae non sit licitum, stipendium accipere. Concedimus sanè, quòd δώρεαν aliquando opponatur aliàs solutioni pretii, quòdque Paulus δωρεὰν praedicarit, 2. Cor. 11, 7. Sed notandum 1. quòd Christus hîc praecipuè loquatur de miraculosis sanationibus, quas venales ex poni, ipse prohibet. 2. minimè verò licet inferre, ergò nec pro laboribus, quibus ministri Ecclesiae defatigantur, persolvendum illis stipeudium est, vel accipere tale, illicitum iis est. Contrarium enim patet ex Luc. 10, 7.Rom. 5, 27.1. Cor. 9, 13.Gal. 6, 61.Philipp. 4, 15. Nec stipendium etiam illud, quod Ministris Ecclesiae in verbo laborantibus persolvitur, propriè est merces pro donis spiritualibus, sed est grati animi in auditoribus erga, illos signum. Breviter: Dist. inter beneficiorum spiritualium venditionem, & intergrati animi testificationem ac laborum remunerationem. Illa prohibita est, 1. Tim. 3, 3. ac malè esse etiam cessit Gehasi, 1. Reg. 5, 27. nec non Simoni Mago, Act. 8, 20. haec utique non solùm concessa, sed etiam laude digna est. 3. Sanè ipse Christus à mulieribus τὰ ὑῶάρχοντα accepit Luc. 8, 3. ac γλωσθόκομον habuit, quod Iudae fuit concreditum, Ioh. 12, 6.c. 13, 29. 4. Factum Pauli d. l. nihil probat. Licet enim Corinthiis Evangelium gratis praedicarit, ab aliis tamen Ecclesiis stipendium accepit, uti d. l. v. 8. statim subiicitur. Denique si vel maximè Christus prohibuisset, ne etiam pro Evangelii praedicatione stipendium tum Apostoli acciperent, non tamen inde inferre debet, quòd nec nostris temporibus illud fieri debeat. Fuit enim Salvatoris praeceptum temporarium. Ac valet adeò hîc regula Augustini de verbis Domini serm. 26. distingue tempora, & concordabunt Scripturae. Id tamen certum est, quòd Salvator omni tempore Simoniam summo studio vitari velit. Quod ipsum etiam multis hîc exemplis & sententiis inculcare rectè Corn. à Lapidé satagit. Obsignatque discuisum verbis Francisci, qui teste Bonaventurâ in eius vitâ: Pecunia, dixit, servis DEI nihil aliud est, quàm Diabolus & coluber venenosus. Inculcer haec Iesuita servo servorum h. e. Pontifici Romano, ut cui vix quidquam magis curae est, quàm pecunias undique corradere, iisdemque nepotes suos neptesq; ditare, & ad summas adeò dignitates evehere.

## 10:9
*(v. 9. Do not acquire gold etc. It is not simply forbidden to the Apostles and their successors, that is, the Ministers of the Church, that they should not possess gold: for Christ himself had γλωσόκομον, of which Judas had the care, John 12:6 and money perhaps taken from there, for which food was bought, ch. 4:8. But this precept is special and temporal, concerning at least the journey of the Apostles. And so that nothing might delay it, the Savior wills that the Apostles undertake it without any burdens: indeed even without travel money, so that by this example of divine providence they might be the more confirmed for their future Apostolic function. Therefore the Papists are ridiculous, Alphonsus de Castro l. 12 adv. haer. under the word Poverty, Roffensis, Clichtovaeus, Bellarmine lib. 4 de P. R. c. 14 and l. b. 2 de Monach. c. 45, and others, when they strive to extract from the present saying the first Monastic vow, which they call that of poverty. Although they themselves, (besides the fact that this precept concerns only the Apostles as such, and at that time and was given to them, as Cardinal John de Turrecremata shows at length in Qq. Ev. fer. 2 Palm. q. 2, and also in this place, and John Arboreus, Doctor of Paris, agrees in l. 1 Theosophiae c. 31, the Jesuits Earradius, Tirinus, and others in this place; Conzenius, likewise a Jesuit, explicitly: quest. 1 in this place This regarding gold, sandals pertained to this single and temporary mission: for afterwards when they were scattered into all the earth, they carried with them the necessities received from the faithful. etc. Especially also the Jesuit Corn. à Lapide embraces the same opinion and proves it with many arguments in this place, although he does not deny that his associate Maldonatus maintains that those were perpetual precepts, so that the Apostles were obligated throughout their whole life, in which they preached to the nations, to this species of poverty. Let Paludanus Vind, Theol. p. 221 and Tirinus at Matt. 10:10 also be compared) maintain that vows ought to be of counsel, and thus arbitrary, not precepts. But that a precept is held here, Alphonsus à Castro l. c., Franc. Lucas, Tirinus, in this place, and others teach, and the father also the same thing from the very words of the Savior: μὴ κῖησησθε do not possess. That these words indeed have the force of commanding is evident both from similar places Matt. 15:17 c. 6:7 16:19 and from the context, especially v. 5.)

-ςτας ζώνας ὑμῶν Because in belts or in purses, made in the belt or attached to the belt, they were accustomed to store coins. *(Pater de Romanis from Suetonius in Vitellio c. 16, Lampridius in Alex.

Apuleius l. Miles. 7, Aulus Gellius l. 15 c. 12, Spartianus in the Life of Pescennius Niger; concerning the Jews from a certain Talmudic gloss, brought forward by Buxtorf in Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 1754.)* The sense is: Do not be solicitous about travel money, for I shall provide for you, lest anything necessary be lacking. Conf. Luke 22. 35.

Latin:

*(v. 9. Ne comparate aurum &c. Non simpliciter Apostolis horum que successoribus i. e. Ministris Ecclesiae interdicitur, quo minùs aurum possideant: habuit enim Christus ipse γλωσόκομον, cuius curam gerebat Iudas, Ioh. 12, 6. atque inde desumta fortè pecunia, pro quâ comparati cibi, c. 4, 8. sed praeceptum hoc speciale est ac temporale, concernens saltem Apostolorum peregrinationem. Quam ne quid remoretur, vult Salvator, ut Apostoli sine ullis sarcinis eam suscipiant: imò etiam absque viatico, quò hoc divinae providentiae exemplo ad futuram functionem Apostolicam eò magis confirmentur. Ridiculi proindè sunt Pontificii, Alphonsus de Castro l. 12. adv. haer. verbo Paupertas, Roffensis, Clichtovaeus, Bellarminus lib. 4. do P. R. c. 14. ac l. b. 2. de Monach. c. 45. ac alii, quando è praesenti dicto primum votum Monasticum, quod paupertatis vocant, eruere satagunt. Cùm tamen ipsi, (praeter quam quòd praeceptum hoc solos Apostolos ut tales, & isto quidem tempore -ncernat, illisc, datum sit, ceu prolixè ostendit Cardin. Ioh. de Turrecremata in Qq. Ev. fer. 2. Palm. q. 2. nec non in h. l. ac consentiunt Ioh. Arboreus Doctor Parisiensis l. 1. Theosophiae c. 31. Iesuitae Earradius, Tirinus aliique in h. l. Conze nius, itidem Iesuità, disertè: quaest. 1. in h. l. Hoc de auro, soleis alusad hanc unicam & temporariam missionem pertinebant: nam posteà cùm in omnem terram spargerentur, secum necessaria à fidelibus accepta deferebant. &c. Cumprimis etiam eandem sententiam amplectitur, multisq; probat Iesuita Corn. à Lapide in h. l. licet non diffiteatur, sociennum suum Maldonatum statuere, fuisse praecepta ea perpetua, ita ut Apostoli per omnem vitam, quâ praedicarunt gentibus, obligati suerint hac specie paupertatis. Conferatur & Paludanus Vind, T. eol. p. 221. ac Tirinus ad Matth. 10, 10.) statuant, vota debere esse consilii, adeoque arbitraria, non praecepta. Hîc verò praeceptum haberi, docent Alphi à Castro l. c. Franc. Lucas, Tirinus, in h. l. alii, & pater etiam id. ipsum ex ipsis verbis Salvatoris: μὴ κῖησησθεnolite possidere. quod verò haec verba imperandivim habecant. patet tum ex locis similibus Matth. 15, 17.c. 6, 7.16. 19. tum ex contexta, cumprimis v. 5.)*

-ςτας ζώνας ὑμῶν Quia in Zonis sive in crumenis, in Zona factis -el Zonae attextis, solebant nummos recondere. *(Pater de Romanis ex Suetonio in Vitellioci 16. Lamprid. in Alex.

Apuleio l. Miles. 7. Agellio l. 15. c. 12. Spartiano in Vitâ Pescennii Nigri; de Iudaeis ex glossâ quadam Talmud., adductâ à Buxtorffio Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 1754.)* Sensus est: Nolite esse deviatico soliciti, prospiciam enim vobis, ne quid necessariorum desit. Conf. Luc. 22. 35.

## 10:10
*(v. 10. Μὴ πήραν. But the Apostles at the time of the passion of Christ had wallets, Luke 22. 36. Resp. The times must be distinguished)*

*( Nor two tunics. But Paul left a cloak in Troas. 1. Tim. 4, 13. therefore he had abundant clothing. Resp. Christ prohibited the anxiety of superfluous clothing, but not the possession of necessary clothing. It is permitted therefore that the Apostle perhaps could have lacked that cloak at some time, yet at another time he had need of it. Toletus on c. 19. John p. 459. The Lord did not prohibit more garments, but changes of clothing. Furthermore, this command given to the Apostles in this place was temporary, as was shown a little before.)*

Μηδὲ ὑποδήματα. But Mark 6, 9. it is granted, that they may be ὑῶοδεδεμένοι σανδάλια. Resp. Christ did not wish the penury of those things which are required first and foremost for making a journey, a staff and shoes, to stand in the way of their journey for preaching. Do not possess shoes, i.e., others, besides those with which you are already clothed. Osiander b. 2. Annotations on the Harmony c. 19. Christ, when he had selected the twelve Apostles from the number of the remaining disciples, and had destined them for the office of preaching, prohibits in many words, not that they should not take with them on the way what they had: but that they should not anxiously seek out and hesitantly procure what they did not have, on account of that departure. But in Mark and Luke, when he was about to send them out to preach, he does not act on this, what they ought to procure or what they ought not to procure, since his urgent command left no leisure for those businesses, but he acts rather on this, that they should not take with them on the journey any of those little things which they had possessed, except sandals and a staff.

*(B. P. follows the explanation of Osiander, Harm. Evang. c. 175. p. 1222. likewise Hugo Grotius on this passage.)* Some respond that δύο, two pairs of soles must be repeated from the preceding, i.e., one pair which they put on when they are about to depart, the other which they carry with them for changing. *(The latter opinion is embraced by our own B. D. Hunnius on this passage, B. D. Chemn. Harm. Ev. c. 72, from the Papists Thomas Aquinas, Cajetan, etc., and is hinted at by August. b. 2. on the Harmony of the Gospels c. 20. Corn. à Lapide on this passage distinguishes between Sandals or soles, which protect only the sole of the foot, lest it strike against rocks: and between shoes, which cover the whole foot. He writes that the former are permitted by Christ, because Judea is a rough and rocky region: but the latter are forbidden, since they bind the foot and as it were imprison it, so that it is less free and ready for the journey. That the Apostles wore sandals after Christ's ascension, the same author proves from Acts 12, 8. Moreover, Cornelius reveals that Jerome, Euthymius, Jansenius, Toletus, Maldonatus, and even Augustine himself in book 2 of De consensu Evang. chapter 30, also explain the present passage in the stated way. To these can be added many others, such as Franciscus Lucas, Alphonsus Tostatus, Sebastian Barradius, volume 2 in Conc. Ev. l. c. c. 11, and Tirinus in this place. But it seems to stand against this opinion that ὑποδήματα by the force of the word are nothing other than soles or under-bindings, which, while they protect the soles of the feet, leave the upper part of the feet bare. Franciscus Lucas answers that the Evangelist took this name in the present instance generally, for that kind of footwear, namely, which covers and protects not only the soles, but also the whole foot on all sides.

nor a staff. In this place and Luke 9, 3. the use of a staff is forbidden to the Apostles, whereas in Mark c. 6, 8 it is permitted; how are these to be reconciled? I answer: The Lord did not grant such staves as they might use in place of weapons, or to inflict force upon others, or to repel force brought from elsewhere. But He granted them lighter staves or rods, with which they might steady their step while walking. The former rod is called שנט, but the latter כקל. and כשעב (Distinguish therefore between ρα--ον, ά ραβδον that is, between a defensive, punitive, or offensive rod, which ῥάβδος, is called ἀπὸ τού ῥαπίζειν, Matt. 5, 59. c. 20, c. 7. Mark 14, 65. John 18, 22. c. 19, 3. of which kind of rod or staff there is mention in Ps. 2, 9. Is. 14, 5. Exod. 21, 20. 1 Cor. 4, 21. and between a supporting or sustaining rod, Exod. 21, 19. c. 4, 2. Gen. 32, 10. in which way ῥαβὸος is called ἀπὸ τοὐ ῥαδίως βαδιζειν. This Christ granted to the Apostles, as Mark testifies in c. 6, 8; the former He forbade, as Matthew teaches here and Luke in c. 9, 3. This opinion is favored by the Lutherans B. D. Chemnitius in Harm. Evang. c. 72, p. 783, B. D. Hunnius in this place, Dn. D. Waltherus H. B., B. D. Glassius in Philol. S. l. 1, p. 181, and others; among the Papists by Caietanus, Jansenius, Franciscus Lucas, Cornelius à Lapide, etc. Among the Calvinists by Beza in this place, Gualterus in hom. 38 in Matt., Crocius in Anti Bec. p. 98. I would say that the Syrian also hinted at this difference, while he uses the word in this place, if he did not use the same expression for the same thing. Mark 6:8. Daniel Heinsius in Exerc. ὐνεοντιοφάνει-, intending to reconcile this, explains the particle εἰ in Mark as if indeed or nay, so that the sense may be: Nay, not the staff alone. But this reconciliation does not seem sufficiently safe, as Simon Episcopius also observed in Resp. ad LXIV. Qq. Q. 26. Episcopius himself, however, seems to incline toward the opinion of Euthymius, concerning which more later. He thinks, namely, that Matthew reports that which Christ had said generally at the beginning, as is wont to happen, but Mark reports that which Christ, perhaps upon his disciples asking whether they might at least take a staff and sandals with them, as a matter of small moment and not contrary to his purpose, allowed and conceded. And many hold this opinion: the Arminian went to prove it there, who can be consulted.)* Andreas Osiander, book 2, Annot. in Harm. c. 19, maintains that this passage in Luke is corrupt, and that instead of εἰ μὴ, μὴτε was written by a yawning or even bold scribe, which was easy for him, since the same particle μήτε, is repeated there four times. Some codices read ῥάβδους,, by which reasoning every apparent contradiction is removed. For it is not contradictory to permit one staff and to forbid more. *(There are indeed some codices, such as Steph. 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, and 12, which the Royal Bible itself follows, that read in the plural: but the received reading, which Beza and Camerarius record that they found in all ancient codices in their old book, has it in the singular. How also the Greek expositors read, as well as the Oriental interpreters, the Syrian, Arab, Ethiopian, and Persian. Euthymius answers that Christ indeed at the beginning forbade them to carry a staff or rod, but later, yielding to their weakness, he conceded it.)*

*( For the laborer is worthy of his food. Conf. Lev. 19:13.

Deut. 24:14.Sir. 34:27.Luke 10:7.1 Tim. 5:18.Tob. 4:15.Jas. 5:4.)*

Latin:

*(v. 10. Μὴ πήραν. Atqui Apostoli tempore passionis Christi habuerunt peras, Luc. 22. 36. Resp. distinguenda sunt tempora)*

*( Neduas tunicas. Atqui Paulus penulam in Troade reliquit. 1. Tim. 4, 13. habuit ergò vestes abundantes. Resp. prohibuit Christus superflui amictûs solicitudinem, non verò necessarii possessionem. Licet igitur Apostolus fortè aliquando carere penulâ illâ potuerit, alio tamen tempore eâ opus habuit. Toletus in c. 19. Ioh. p. 459. Non prohibuit Dominus plura vestimenta, sed vestes mutatorias. Praeterea mandatum hoc loco Apostolis datum fuit temporarium, ut paullò antè ostensum.)*

Μηδὲ ὑποδήματα. Atqui Marc. 6, 9. conceditur, ut sint ὑῶοδεδεμένοι σανδάλια. Resp. Christus ne eorum quidam penuriam obstare voluit itineri ad praeconium, quae ad faciendum iter inprimis requiruntur, bacillum & calceamenta. Nolite possidere calceamenta, sc. alia, praeter ea, quibus iam induti estis. Osiander l. 2. Annotat. in Harmon. c. 19. Christus apud Matthaeum cùm duodecim Apostolos ex reliquorum discipulorum numero selegisset, & ad munus praedicandi destinasset, prohiber multis verbis, non ut quae haberent, in viam secum non auferrent: sed ut quae non haberent, propter istam profectionem non anxiè conquirerent & cunctabundi compararent. Apud Marcum verò & Lucam cùm eos iamiam ad praedicandum emissurus esset, non hoc agit, quid comparare aut quid non comparare deberent, quippe cùm urgens eius mandatum nihil otii ad ea negotia relinqueret, sed hoc potiùs agit, neiis reculis, quas possederant, ad iter quicquam secum auferrent praeter sandalia & virgam.

*(Osiandri explicationem sequitur B. P. Harm. Evang. c. 175. p. 1222. it. Hugo Grotius in h. l.)* Quidam respondent, ex praecedentibus repetendū δύο, binas soleas, unas sc. quasinduant abituri, alteras, quas secum gestent ad permutandum. *(Posteriorem hanc sententiam ex nostratibus amplectuntur B. D. Hunnius in h. l. B. D. Chemn. Harm. Ev. c. 72. ex Pontificiis Thomas de Aquino, Caietanus &c. & innui August. l. 2. de Consensu Evang. c. 20. Corn. à Lapide in h. l. distinguit inter sandalia sive soleas. quae plantam pedis duntaxat muniant, ne in saxa impingatur: & inter calceos, qui pedem totum tegunt. Illas concedi à Christo, scribit, eò quòd Iudaea sit adspera & saxosa regio: hos verò prohiberi. cùm pedem stringant & quasi incarcerent, ut minùs sit liber & expeditus ad iter. Quòd verò Apostoli sandalia post Christi ascensionem gestarint, probat idem ex Act. 12, 8. Caeterùm dicto modo praesentem locum exponere quoque Hieronymum. Euthymium, Iansenium, Toletum, Maldonatum, ipsum que etiam Augustinum l. 2. de consensu Evang. cap. 30. Cornelius prodit. Quibus accenseri possunt alii plures, uti Franciscus Lucas, Alph. Tostatus, Sehast. Barrad. t. 2. in Conc. Ev. l. c. c. 11. Tirinus in h. l. Sed obstare huic sententiae videtur, quòd ὑποδήματα ex vi vocio nihil aliud sint, quàm soleae sive subligacula, quae cùm plantas pedum muniant, superiorem pedum partem relinquant nudam. Respondet Franc. Lucas, Evangelistam accepisse hoc nomen in praesenti generaliter, pro eo nempe calceamentorum genere, quod non plantas tantùm, verùm etiam totum obtegit ac munit undique pedem.)*

Nevirgam. Hoc loco ac Luc. 9, 3. virgae usus Apostolic interdicitur, apud Marcum c. 6, 8. conceditur, quomodo haec concilianda? Resp. Dominus non concessit eiusmodi baculos, quibus armorum vice uterentur, vel vim inferrent aliis, vel illatam aliunde propulsarent. Concessit autem illis baculos sive virgas leviores, quibus in eundo gressum firmarent. Illa virga dicitur שנט, haec verò כקל. & כשעב (Disting igitur inter ρα--ον, ά ραβδον h. e. inter virgam defensoriam, punitoriam aut offensoriam, quat. ῥάβδος, dicitur ἀπὸ τού ῥαπίζειν,Matth. 5, 59.c. 20,c. 7.Marc. 14, 65.Ioh. 18, 22.c. 19, 3. de quali virga s. baculo sermo est Psal. 2, 9.Es. 14, 5.Exod. 21. 20.1. Cor. 4, 21. & inter virgam fu-citoriam s. sustentatoriam,Exod. 21, 19.c. 4, 2.Gen. 32, 10. quo modo ῥαβὸος dicitur ἀπὸ τοὐ ῥαδίως βαδιζειν. Hanc Christus Apostolis concessit, teste Marco c. 6, 8. illam prohibuit, docente Matthaeo hîc ac Lucâ c. 9, 3. Arridet verò sententia haec ex Lutheranis B. D. Chemnitio Harm Evang. c. 72. p. 783. B. D. Hunnio in h. l. Dn. D. Walthero H. B. B. D. Glassio Philol. S. l. 1. p. 181. & aliis; ex Pontificiis Caietano, Iansenio, Franc. Lucae, Corn, à Lapide &c. Ex Calvinianis Bezae in h. l. Gualtero hom. 38. in Matth. Crocio in Anti Bec. p. 98. Dicerem, etiam Syrum differentiam hanc innuisse, dum h. l. adhibet vocem nisi eadem dictione idem uteretur Marc. 6, 8. Dan. Heinsius in Exerc. ὐνεοντιοφάνει- hanc conciliaturus, partic. εἰ apud Marcum exponit pro siquidem vel imò, ut sensus sit. Imò non virgam solam. At haut satis tuta videtur isthaec conciliatio, uti etiam observavit Simon Episcopius in Resp. ad LXIV. Qq. Q. 26. Ipse verò Episcopius in Euthymii sententiam, de quâ postea, inclinare videtur. Putat nempe, Matthaeum referre id, quod Christus principio, ut fieri solet, generaliter dixerat, Marcum verò id, quod Christus forts quaerentibus discipulis suis, Annon saltem virgam & sandalia secum sumere possent, tanquam rem parvi momenti & scopo suo non contrariam, indu sit ac concessit. Et hanc sententiam multi: probatum ibi ivit Arminianus, qui potest evolvi.)* Andrea: Osiander l. 2. Annot. in Harm. c. 19. statuit, hunc locum apud Lucam esse corruptum, & pro εἰ μὴ ab oscitante vel etiam audacl librario μὴτε fuisse scriptum, quod ipsi proclive fuerit, cùm eadem particula μήτε, quater ibi repetatur. Quidam Codd. legunt ῥάβδους, quâ ratione omnis apparens contrarietas tollitur. Neque enim pugnant, baculum unum permittere, & pluribus interdicere. *(Sunt sanè Codd. nonnulli, ut Steph. 2. 3. 4. 5. 7. 8. 9. 11. ac 12. quos ipsa etiam Biblia Regia sequuntur, qui in plurali legunt: verùm recepta lectio, quam Beza in omnibus vetustis Codd. ac Camerarius in suo veteri libro reperisse se memorant, habet in singulari. Quomodo etiam legerunt Expositores Graeci, nec non Interpretes Orientales, Syrus, Arabs, Aethiops, Persa. Euthymius respondet, quòd Christus quidem initiò prohibuerit, ne virgam s. baculum ferrent, postea tamen ad imbecillitatem eorum sese demittens concesserit.)*

## 10:11
v. 11. See whether any one in the city is worthy i. e. fit and suitable, with whom your labor may not be in vain, who is desirous of receiving the Gospel, v. 13. Act. 13. 46.

Latin:

v. 11. Videte an aliquis in civitate sit dignus i. e. aptus & idoneus, apud quem labor vester non sit frustraneus, qui cupidus sit, Evangelium recipiendi, v. 13. Act. 13. 46.

## 10:12
*(v. 12. Salute it Some Greek Codices, among which are to be referred primarily those five ancient ones which Beza used, add λέγονπς εἰρήνη τῷ οἴκῳ τέτῳ. And the Latin Vulgate Interpreter follows this reading, and Matthew the Hebrew Minister also presents it. But all the Oriental Interpreters omit the aforementioned words. Namely the Syrian, the Arab, the Ethiopian, and the Persian. And the context itself teaches that they are also superfluous, since the very force of the word εἰρήνης is sufficiently comprehended in the word ασπάζεται, as H. Grotius rightly observed.)*

Latin:

*(v. 12. Salutate eam Nonnulli Codd. Graeci, ad quos cumprimis referendi quinque illi vetusti, quibus Beza usus est, addunt, λέγονπς εἰρήνη τῷ οἴκῳ τέτῳ. Atque hanc lectionem sequitur Vulg. Interpres Latinus, ac sistit etiam Matthaeus Ebraeus Ministeri. Omittunt vero^e praedicta verba Orientales Interpp. omnes. Syrus nempe, Arabs, Aethiops ac Persa. Et superflua quoque esse, ipse contextus docet, cùm ipsa vis vocis εἰρήνης in verbo ασπάζεται satis comprehendatur, ut rectè observavit H. Grotius.)*

## 10:13
*(v. 13. And if indeed that house i. e. family. It occurs thus also Ioh. 4, 53.1. Cor. 16, 15. except that in the said place the family is distinguished from the head, but here it embraces both.)*

*( Ἐλθέτω let it come. The Syrian will come, just as the Hebrew Gospel of Münster also has יבוא and likewise the Latin Vulgate. And also the Ethiopian, rendering )*

*( Your peace, because indeed the Apostles were announcing it: otherwise it is properly the peace of GOD and of CHRIST,Ioh. 14, 27.Phil. 4, 7.)*

But if it is not worthy, your peace shall return to you. i. e. the fruit of the salutation will not return to the unworthy, but as if it had not been made, it will return to you. Es. 55, 11. See the fulfillment of this precept Act. 13, 51.c. 18. 6. *(A type is held Ps. 34, 12. 13. They repay me evil for good &c. and my prayer was returning upon my bosom. On which passage Hesychius: Into the bosom, he says, of Christ i. e. the Church of the Gentiles, the prayer of Christ reflected from the Jews fell back. Compare Es. 9. 8. Gregory 2. Moral. c. 30. Christ, whom the Jewish people rejected when He came to them, the Gentile people suddenly found Him. Furthermore, the Jesuit Becanus seeks support for prayers for the dead from the present passage. For intending to prove that prayers for the dead are not made in vain, he brings forward the passage Psal. 34, 13. to which he says our saying is similar. Not in vain, he writes l. 1. Manual.

c. 8. §. 15. (someone prays for the dead) For even if it obtains nothing for him for whom it prays (which often happens), the prayer is not on that account empty and fruitless. For it profits the one praying himself, according to that Ps. 34, 13. Peace shall return upon you Matt. 10, 13. Resp. The reason for the prayer of the Apostles and the prayer for the dead is different. The former has an express command and promise; the latter does not.

Complementum huius praecepti vide Act. 13, 51.c. 18. 6. *(Typus habetur Ps. 34, 12. 13.Reddent mihi malum pro bono &c. & oratio mea super sinum meum revertebatur.
