## 10:14
v. 14. Shake off the dust. That Christ commands to shake off the dust signifies the innocence of the Apostles, who would not take even a speck of dust from the impious. August. q. 7. in Matthew. Secondly, the magnitude of the punishment, which would be so great that the pious would not want to have even a communion of dust with the impious. Thirdly, it is a testimony of despised grace, how execrable they would be who rejected the offered salvation. It was also a prelude that He would shake off or pour out His wrath upon them.

It was customary among the Jews to add external symbols to words to strike more deeply. Not unlike this is what is read in Nehemiah 5, 13, that Nehemiah shook out the fold of his garment in testimony against those who had violated the faith given. (Compare also Acts 13, 57. c. 18, 6. It is gathered, however, among other things from this precept of Christ, that one must sometimes yield to the will of enemies or even of those who refuse to hear the word, by the example of Elijah, 1 Kings 19, 3. 4. and other holy men of God in the Old Testament, Heb. 11, 38. likewise of the Apostle Paul, Acts 9, 25. 2 Cor. 11, 32. 33. nay, of the Savior Himself, Matt. 9, 8. Compare Luke 9, 55. 56.)

Latin:

v. 14. Excutite pulverem. Quòd Christus iuber excutete pulverem, significationnocentiam Apostolorum, ne pulvisculum quidem ab impiis auferentium. August. q. 7. in Matthaeum. Deinde poenae magnitudinem, quae tanta futura, ut ne quidem pulveris communionem pii cum impiis habere velint. Tertiò est restimonium contemtae gratiae, quàm essent execrandi, qui oblatam salutem respuerent. Fuit quoque praeludium, quod iram suam in illos excussurus seu effusurus sit.

Usitatum erat apud Iudaeos verbis adiungere externa symbola ad magis percellendum. Non absimile est, quod Nehemiae 5, 13. legitur, Nehemiam excusisse oram vestimenti sui in testimonium contra eos, qui fidem datam violarant. *(Conf. etiam Actor. 13, 57.c. 18, 6. Colligitur autem inter alia ex hoc Christi praecepto, quod surori hostium vel etiam eorum, qui verbum audire renuunt, voluntati cedendum aliquando sit, exemplo Eliae, q. Reg. 19, 3. 4. aliorum que sanctorum Dei hominum in V. Test, Ebr. 11, 38. it. Apostoli Pauli, Actor. 9, 25.2. Cor. 11, 32. 33. quin ipsius Salvatoris, Matth. 9, 8. Conf. Luc. 9, 55. 56.)*

## 10:15
(v. 15. It will be more tolerable etc. It is clear from this that there will be degrees in punishments or infernal torments. This is also insinuated by our Evangelist c. 11, 21. 23. 14, 15. and Paul Rom. 2, 9. likewise Luke c. 10, 12. c. 12, 47. 48. Compare also the sayings of the Fathers in B. P. L. on Hell §. 75. St. Jerome in this place: If it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom etc., therefore there are also different punishments among sinners.)

( The land of Sodom etc. The Sodomites, who are commonly set forth as an example, as those who were destroyed by God in a singular kind of ruin. Compare 2 Pet. 2, 6. Jude v. 7.

( Than for that city. The Sodomites indeed also had a preacher of righteousness, Lot, who would call them back from wickedness: but he did not shine with such authority, nor was he conspicuous with as many miracles, as the Apostles sent by Christ. Compare Matt. XI, 23. Sins, therefore, are to be estimated not precisely only from their own nature, but also from other circumstances of things and persons, as H. Grotius notes in this place. Meanwhile, it is certain that even the sin of those who despised the preached Gospel was in itself and precisely by far the greatest and most grievous of all sins, drawing after it temporal and eternal punishments, Es. 60, 12. Just as B. Luther also rightly maintained, that unbelief alone is the adequate cause of damnation.

Latin:

*(v. 15. Tolerabilius erit &c. Patet hinc, gradus fore in suppliciis sive poenis insernalibus. Id quod etiam insinua noster Evangelista c. 11, 21. 23. 14, 15. & Paulus Rom. 2, 9. item Luc. c. 10, 12.c. 12, 47.48. Confer etiam dicta Patrum apud B. P. L. de Inferno §. 75. S. Hieronymus in h l. Si tolerabilius erit terrae Sodomorum &c. ergo & inter peccatores diversa supplicia sunt.)*

*( Terrae Sodomorum &c. Sodomitis, qui communiter in exemplum sistuntur, ut qui singulari exitii genere divinitûs sue de deleti. Conf. 2. Petr. 2, 6. Iudae v. 7.*

*( Quàm illucivitati. Habuerunt quidem & Sodomitae praeconem iustitiae Loth, qui revocaret eos à scelere: ast non taniâ â fulsit ille autoritate, nec tot miraculis fuit conspicuus, quot Apostoli à Christo missi. Conf. Matth. XI, 23. Peccata itaque non praecisè tantùm ex suapte natura, verùm etiam ex aliis circumstantiis rerum & personarum aestimanda sunt, notante H. Grotio in h. l. Interea certum est, quòd etiam peccatum illorum, qui Evangelium praedicatum contemserunt, in se ac praecisè omnium peccatorum fuerit longè maximum & gravissimumum, trahens post se temporales & aet. poenas, Es. 60, 12. Quemadmodum etiam B. Lutherus rectè adservit, quòd sola incredulitas adaequata damnationis causa sit.)*

## 10:16
v. 16. In the midst of wolves. A certain one of the ancients, as Herodotus reports in Melpomene, imposed upon his son the name οἰόλυκος, because he said that he would leave him in the greatest dangers. Christ says this same thing in this place concerning his own. Theophylact on this passage: Just as it cannot happen that sheep suffer nothing in the midst of wolves, so also you -ter the Jews. Euthymius on this passage: I, who can do all things, send you so that you may be bitten and torn to pieces, do not offer your hands or resist the furnace. Jerome: He calls the Scribes and Pharisees wolves, who are the clergy of the Jews. *(But Ioh. 14, 27. he promises peace. Resp. he speaks of internal peace, as is evident from c. 16, 33.)*

Be therefore prudent as serpents &c. Let there be a serpentine eye in a dove-like heart. Remigius in the Catena near Thomas: He beautifully advises the prudence of the serpent, because the first man was deceived by the serpent, as if he were saying, because the enemy was cunning in deceiving, you be prudent in liberating. He praised the wood, you praise the virtue of the cross, i. e. love tribulations, glory in persecutions, and thus you will overcome them and strike down the enemies. In the History of Prochorus concerning John the Theologian and Evangelist, vol. 1 of the Orthodox, p. 85, the speech of Peter to the remaining Apostles is reported: If anyone wishes to kill a serpent, it offers its whole body, so that it may hide its head: And we therefore, O dearest ones, will undergo death, nor will we refuse to be afflicted, just as doves are deprived of their young, and yet do not renounce the Lord. Ambrose, book 6, Ep. 42: In this let us follow the cunning of the serpent, that we do not cast our head into dangers, but keep it whole above all others. Moreover, our head is Christ; let this remain unharmed, so that the poisons of the serpent cannot harm us.

(Jerome has similar things in this place. Augustine, book of questions from Matth. c. 8., also book 2 of De D. C. c. 16. Caesarius Dialogue 4. A not dissimilar notable passage in Epiphanius, book 1 against heresies 37, against the Ophites, also pertains to this. There is no, writes Epiphanius in the book mentioned, from the version of Conrarius, prudence in the serpent, except for these two. The first, that while it suffers persecution, knowing that its whole life exists in its head, etc., where it wraps its whole body around its head, it indeed hides its skull, but offers the rest of its body through excellent cunning. Thus that only-begotten God who proceeded from the Father wishes us, in the time of persecution and in the time of temptation, to surrender all our things to the sword and fire: but to guard our own head, that is, not to deny Christ. For Christ is the head of every man, etc. The serpent has another prudence again, as those learned in the nature of things report about this animal. For when, pressed by thirst, it proceeds from its lair to water to drink, it does not take its poison with it at the same time, but leaves it in the lair, and thus having proceeded, it takes a drink of water. Therefore let us also imitate this, that when we come to the holy Church of GOD or to prayers or to the mysteries, we do not bring with us malice or pleasure, or enmity or anything else in our thoughts. Otherwise, how shall we be able to imitate the dove, not being removed from malice? B. D. Glassius draws the same doctrine from this similitude in Exeg. Domin. 22. after Trinity p. 997, which must be read entirely.) Isidorus Pelusiota book 1, Ep. 126, p. 23. The Lord commands us to be prudent as serpents. Namely, so that we may preserve our head, that is, faith in Christ, in every temptation. (The Pelusiota seems to have taken these from Chrysostom, Hom. 34 in Matth., where he has twin things.) For indeed in whatever adverse events and blows the serpent is attacked, it keeps its head safe and unharmed. And again, by art and cunning it sheds its old age, squeezing itself in a certain narrow and tight crevice and laying aside its old age. He wishes, therefore, that we through the narrow way and affliction should shed the old man, and in his place put on the new, who is renewed according to His image. (Similar things are read in Augustine, book of questions from Matth. c. 8., also Ambrose, book 3 of De fide c. 7. Caesar. Dial. 4. Eusebius, book 3 of Praepar. Evang. p. 68. πνευματικώτατον τὸ ζῶον ἔςι καὶ τἠν ἀσθὲένειαν τοῦ σώματονς ἐποδύεται. δοκει καὶ ἐατρικώτατον εἶναι)

τῆς γδ οξυδερκίας εὗρε τὸ φάρνακον καὶ μυσθεύετανι τῆς ἀναβιώσεως εἰδεναι τινὰ βοτἀνην. The serpent is a most prudent animal, and it sheds the infirmity of its body. It also seems to excel in the knowledge of medicine. For it has shown a remedy for the eyes, and it is told that it knows a certain herb by which it can recall itself, as it were, from death to life. (Basil in the shorter rules, interrog. 245, thinks that this precept is looked to for information, namely, that just as in paradise the serpent approached our first parents cunningly with a more flattering appearance, and by the probability of its words turned them away from God: so we ought to have regard for the person and the place and the time suitable for acting, and in all ways arrange our words so that we may turn men away from sin and lead them back to God. Remigius applies it in almost the same way. Bede in this place is a little different, following Augustine in Ps. 57, 5. The prudence of the serpent, he says, is that it presses one ear against a rock, and closes the other with its tail, so that it may not hear those charming it. Thus let the disciple of Christ close his ears against the suggestions of the devil and the wicked with his tail and the earth, i.e., with the meditation of the end, namely, of death and the sepulcher, and say to himself: Remember that you are dust.)

And simple as doves. In Greek it is ἀκέραιοι sincere, to whom there is nothing of evil deceit mixed in, from α and κεράω I mix. The Syrian whole. The dove is an innocuous animal, for whom the whole protection of safety is situated in the swiftness of its wings. Gregor. Nazianz. Orat. on his father. Τὸ γδ τοῦὄφεως φρόνιμον παρὰ τὸ κακὸν τῷ τῆς παριςερᾶς ἀκεραίῳ παρὰ τὸ καλὸν ἀναυίξας, οὄτε τὸ φρόνιμον εἴασε κακοῦργον γενέσθαι, οὄτε τὸἁπλῶν ἀνόντον, ἄλλ᾽ ἒν ἐρεπῆς εἶδονς, ὡς μάλιςα ἑνῆν ἐξ ἀμφοῖν ἀπηκριβώσατο. By mixing the serpent's prudence for evil with the dove's sincerity for good, lest he allowed prudence to be malicious, lest he allowed simplicity to become foolish, but he exquisitely constituted one form of virtue as much as was permitted from both. (Chrysostom has similar things in homily 34 on Matthew. Gregory book 4, ep. 31 to Maurice: Let the serpent's cunning sharpen the dove's simplicity, and let the dove's simplicity temper the serpent's cunning. Jerome vol. 1, ep. 13 to Paulinus: Have the simplicity of the dove, so that you may not plot deceits against anyone, and the cunning of the serpent, so that you may not be tripped up by the snares of the wicked. The same in chapter 10.

Matth. Serpentine prudence befits Christians, but at the same time dove-like simplicity is required, without which prudence is malice, just as simplicity without reason is folly. Hilary, book on the Synods, q. 309. Let the simplicity of the dove temper serpentine prudence, and let the prudence of the serpent instruct the simplicity of the dove, so that there may be both simple wisdom and wise simplicity. *(Compare the twin [saying] in Jerome on c. 7 of Hosea. Gregory, book 1 of Morals, c. 2; also part 3 of Pastoral Care, admonition 12; and also homily 30 on the Gospel.)* Erasmus in a letter to the brothers in lower Germany: Be simple as doves, so that you may not harm or circumvent anyone, but at the same time be wise, so that Satan, instructed in a thousand wiles, may not circumvent you. *(Bernard also alludes to the present admonition, ep. 334 to Cardinal Rolland. Thus, therefore, our Savior sets before us terrestrial animals as teachers, so that we may learn from them how we ought to conduct ourselves: from quadrupeds, indeed, the sheep, from which [we learn] obedience and simplicity; from reptiles, the serpent, from which [we learn] prudence and cunning; (Compare Eph 5, 15. 16. 17. Isaiah 52, 13. c. 50, 4. Rom. 16, 19.) from winged creatures, the dove, from which we ought to learn sincerity and integrity. Thus Blessed D. Glassius, Exegesis for the 23rd Sunday after Trinity, page 1031, where he also teaches at length how a Christian ought to imitate the dove: 1. by moaning for sins, Is. 38, 15. 2. by hiding oneself in the holes of the rock, Cant. 2, 15. 3. by pursuing peace and quiet. Compare the same, Exegesis for the Feast of the Purification, p. 20. Don Laur. Ramierez de Prado πεντηκ. c. 1, p. 31 et seqq., has also collected more things pertinent to this. However, the Montanists were less solidly striving to prove monogamy from the present passage and to destroy repeated marriages, as is evident from Tertullian, On Monogamy, chapter 8. For, to say nothing now of the fact that a comparison is not to be extended beyond the point for which it is applied (namely, the Savior wishes that Christians ought to be like doves regarding simplicity), it is still most uncertain of all whether among doves one male knows only one female, once the former has been killed. Indeed, rather, Epiphanius, heresy. 27. expressly: The genus of the dove is not praised in many things: for the genus of doves is petulant, and not alien to manifold mixing lascivious and given to pleasure at all times. It is therefore added: Therefore on account of innocence and long-suffering and the forgetting of evils in the animal, and furthermore because the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove: the divine word wishes us to imitate the will of the Holy Spirit and the innocence of the innocent dove, so that we may indeed be prudent toward good, but simple toward evil.)*

Latin:

v. 16. In medio luporum. Veterum quidam, referente Herodoto in Melpone, imposuit filio suo nomen οἰόλυκος, quòd diceret, eum se relicturum in maximis periculis. Idem hoc loco Christus de suis dicit. Theophylactus in h. l. Quemadmodum fieri non potest, ut nihil patiantur oves in medio luporum, sic & vos -ter Iudaeos. Euthymus in h. l. Ego, qui omnia possum, mitto vos ut mordeamini ac dilaniemini, neulcis camini aut manus repugnantes obiiciatis. Hieronymus: Lupos, Scribas & Pharisaeos vocat, qui sunt clerici Iudaeorum. *(Ast Ioh. 14, 27. promittit pacem. Resp. loquitur de pace interna, ceu patet ex c. 16, 33.)*

Estote ergò prudentes sicut serpentes &c. Sit serpentinus oculus in columbino corde. Remigius in Catenâ apud Thomam. Pulcrè serpentis prudentiam monet, quia primus homo per serpentem deceptus est, ac si diceret, quia hostis callidus fuit ad decipiendum, vos prudentes sitis ad liberandum. Ille laudavit lignum, vos laudate crucis virtutem, i. e. amate tribulationes, gloriamini in persecutionibus, & ita superabitis illast & consternetis hostes. In Historiâ Prochori de Iohanne Theol. & Evang. t. 1. Orthodox. p. 85. refertur sermo Petri ad reliquos Apostolos. Serpens si quis eum vult interficere, totum corpus praebet, quò caput abscondat: Et nos igitur, ô carissimi, mortem subibimus, nec affligi recusabimus, quemadmodum & columhae natis suis privantur, nec tamen Domino renunciant. Ambrosius l. 6. Ep. 42. In eo astutiam serpentis sequamur, ut caput nostrum non proiiciamus in pericula, sed praecoeteris integrum custodiamus. Caput autem nostrum Christus est, hoc maneat incolume, ut serpentis venena nobis non possint nocere.

*(Similia habent Hieronymus in h. l. August. lib. quaest. ex Matth. c. 8. it. l. 2. de D. C. c. 16. Caesarius Dialogo4. Facit huc quoque non dissimilis insignis locus apud Epiphanium l. 1. contra haeres. 37. contra Ophitas. Nulla, scribit Epiphanius l. d. ex vers. Conrarii, in serpente prudentia est, praeter duas has. Prima, quòd dum persecutionem patitur, cognoscens, quod in capite ipsius tota vita eius existit &c. ubi tottum corpus involvit in caput suum, occultat quidem cranium suum, tradit autem reliquum corpous per excellentem callidit atem. Sic vult nos unigenitus ille Deus ex Patre progressus, in tempore persecutionis & in tempore tentationis, omnia nostra atradere gladio & igni: custodire autem nostrum ipsorum caput, h. e. Christum non negare. Nam caput omnis viri Christus &c. Alteram rursus prudentiam habet serpens, velut naturae rerum docti de hoc animali tradunt. Quando enim siti pressus à latibulo procedit ad aquam ut bibat, non simul accipit secum venenum, sed in latibulo relinquit, & sic progressus potum aquarum sumit. Proinde & hoc imitemur, ut quando ad sanctam DEI Ecclesiam aut ad preces aut admysteria venerimus, malitiam aut vtuptatem, aut inimicitiam aut aliud quid in cognitionibus nostis nobiscum neferamus. Alioqui quomodo poterimus columbam imitari, non à malitia remoti. Eandem doctrinam ex similitudine hâc depromit B. D. Glassius Exeg. Domin. 22. post Trinit. p. 997. qui omninò evolvendus.)* Isidorus Pelusiota l. 1. Ep. 126. p. 23. Dominus nos prudentes, ut serpentes esse iubet. Sic nempe ut caput nostrum, hoc est fidem in Christum in omni tentatione conservemus. *(Desumsisse haec Pelusiota ex Chrysostomo videtur Hom. 34. in Matth. ubi gemella habet.)* Etenim quibuscunadversis casibus ac plagis serpens petatur, incolume atillaesum caput servat. Ac rursum arte ac versutia vetustatem exuit in arcta quadam & angustâ rimâ sese -omprimens ac senium deponens. Vult igitur, nos quoper arctam viam & afflictionem veterem hominem exuere, ac pro eo novum induene, qui ad eius imaginem renovatur. *(Similia leguntur apud August. lib. quaest. ex Matth. c. 8. it. Ambros. l. 3 de fide c. 7. Caesar. Dial. 4. Eusebius l. 3. de Praepar. Evang. p. 68. πνευματικώτατον τὸ ζῶον ἔςι καὶ τἠν ἀσθὲένειαν τοῦ σώματονς ἐποδύεται. δοκει καὶ ἐατρικώτατον εἶναι

τῆς γδ οξυδερκίας εὗρε τὸ φάρνακον καὶ μυσθεύετανι τῆς ἀναβιώσεως εἰδεναι τινὰ βοτἀνην.Prudentissimum animal est serpens, & infirmitatem corporis sui exuit. Videtur etiam medicinae scientiâ excellere. Nam & remedium oculorum monstravit, & narratur herbquandam nosse, quâ sese, velut ex morte in vitam revocare possit. *(Basilius in regulis brevior. interrog. 245. ad informationem praecepto hoc respici existimat, videl. quòd sicuti in paradiso serpens & blandiore adspectu callidè ad primos parentes accessit, & verborum probabilitate eos à Deo avertit: ita nos & personae & loci & idonei ad agendum temporis rationem habere debere & omnibus modis s-rmones disponere, ut à peccato homines avertamus & ad Deum reducamus. Eodem ferè modô applicat Rmigius. Paulò aliter Beda in h. l. sequutus August. in Ps. 57, 5.Prudentia serpentis, inquit, est, quòd unam aurem petrae opponit, alteram caudâ claudit, ne audiat incantantes. Ita Christi discipulus contra diaboli & impiorum suggestiones claudat aures caudà & terrâ i. e. meditatione finis, puta mortis & sepulcri, sibique dicat: Memento, quôd pulvis.)*

Et simplices sicut columbae. In Graeco est ἀκέραιοιsinceri, quibus nihil dolimali sit ad mixtum, ab α & κεράωmisceo. Syrus integri. Columba est animal innoxium, cui totum salutis praesidium in alarum pernicitate situm. Gregor. Nazianz. Orat. de suo patre. Τὸ γδ τοῦὄφεως φρόνιμον παρὰ τὸ κακὸν τῷ τῆς παριςερᾶς ἀκεραίῳ παρὰ τὸ καλὸν ἀναυίξας, οὄτε τὸ φρόνιμον εἴασε κακοῦργον γενέσθαι, οὄτε τὸἁπλῶν ἀνόντον, ἄλλ᾽ ἒν ἐρεπῆς εἶδονς, ὡς μάλιςα ἑνῆν ἐξ ἀμφοῖν ἀπηκριβώσατο.Serpentis prudentia ad malum columbae sinceritati ad bonum admiscendo, neprudentiam sivit malitiosam, nesimplicitatem fieri amentem, sedunam virtutis formam quam maximè licuit, ex ambo-us exquisitè constituit. *(Similia habet Chrysostomus homil. 34. in Matth. Gregorius l. 4. ep. 31. ad Maurit. Serpentis astutia columbae simplicitatem acuat, & columbae simplicitas serpentis astutiam temperet. Hieronymus t. 1. ep. 13. ad Paulinum: Habeto simplicitatem columbae, ne cuiquam machineris dolos, & serpeentis astutiam, ne à malorum supplanteris insidiis. Idem in c. 10.

Matth. Christianos decet serpentina prudentia, sed requiritur ipsa simul simplicitas columbina, sine quâ prudentia est malitia, ut simplicitas sine ratione est stultitia. Hilarius lib. de Synod. q. 309. Serpentinam prudentiam columbae simplicitas temperet, & simplicitatem columbae prudentia serpentis instruat, fiat& simplex sapientia, & sapiens simplicitas. *(Conf. gemella apud Hieron. in c. 7. Hos. Gregor. l. 1. Moral. c. 2. it. part. 3. Pastor. curae admonit. 12. nec non hom. 30. in Evang.)* Erasmus in ep. ad fratres in infer. German. Estotes simplices sicut columbae, ne quem laedatis aut circumveniatis, sed iidem estote sapientes, ne vos Satanas mille instructus astibus circum veniat. *(Alludit quoque ad praesentem admonitionem Bernhardus, ep334. ad Rollandum Cardinalem. Ita igitur Salvator noster animalia terrestria praeceptores nobis sistit, ut ab iis discamus, quomodo gerere nos debeamus, è quadrupedibus quidem ovem, à qua obedientiam & simplicitatem; ex reptilibus serpentem, à quo prudentiam & calliditatem; (Conf. Eph 5, 15. 16. 17. Esaiae 52, 13. c. 50, 4.Rom. 16, 19.) ex volatilibus columbam, à quâ sinceritatem & integritatem discere debemus. Ita B. D. Glassius Exeg. Dom. 23. post Trinit. pag. 1031. ubi etiam pluribus docet, quomodo Christianus imitari columbam debeat 1. ob peccata gemendo,Es. 38, 15. 2. in foraminibus peterae sese abscondendo,Cant. 2, 15. 3. pacem & qui-tem sectando. Conf. Idem Exeg. Fest. Purif. p. 20. Plura quoque huc facientia comportavit Don Laur. Ramierez de Prado πεντηκ. c. 1. p. 31. seqq. Minùs autem solidè Montanistae è praesenti loco monogamiam probare, iteratasque nuptias destruere satagebant, ceu patet ex Tertull. de Monog. cap 8. Etenim ut iam taceamus, quòd comparatio non sit extendenda ultra tertium, ad quod adhibetur, (vult nempe Salvator, Christianos columbis similes esse debere quoad simplicitatem,) maximè omninò adhuc incertum est, an inter columbas foemellam unam unus tantùm masculus noverit, priori occiso. Imò potius Epiphanius haeres. 27. disertè: Columbae genus in maltis rebus non laudatur: potulans est enim columbarum genus, & à multiplici mixtione non alienum làsscivum& per omne tempus voluptati deditum. subiungiigitur: Proinde propter innocentiam & longanimitatem & malorum in animali oblivionem, insuper & propterea, quòd in clumbae specie apparuit Spiritus Sanctus: imitarinos vult divinus sermo sancti Spiritus voluntatem & innocentis columbae innocentiam, ut simus quidem prudentes ad bonum, simplices verò ad malum.)*

## 10:17
(v. 17. Beware, however. Since the ministers of the word do not know among whom the word of faith may bear fruit, and to whom indeed it is the odor of death unto death 2 Cor. 2:16, therefore let them always act cautiously, and -um with modesty also correct those who resist the truth, etc. 2 Tim. 2:25. Being careful meanwhile, lest they trust too much in them and be circumvented by them. To which the example of Christ contributes John 2:24 thus B. D. Chemnitius in H. E. c. 72.)

( Of men. Namely, the sons of this age, who indeed have the eyes of a man ( Dan. 7:20) but within are ravenous wolves. Beware of men who are traitors, plotters, and persecutors. Yet in such a way that you do not deny Christ.)

For they will deliver you up to the councils etc. By councils are understood the assemblies of judges, which were held in the city of Jerusalem. By synagogues, the judgments which were exercised in the other cities of Judea. Others say that the synagogues of the Jews are the councils of the Gentiles. P. Gabinius, proconsul of Syria, according to Josephus, having added four councils to the Jerusalem one, distributed the nation into five parts, of which one acted in Jerusalem, the second in Gadara, the third in Amathus, the fourth in Jericho, the fifth in Sepphoris of Galilee. Since therefore there were five councils, some think Christ spoke in the plural. By councils can also be understood the assemblies of judges, by synagogues ecclesiastical meetings. Or perhaps he calls the judges themselves councils Sanhedrin, and the conjunction in this place is taken for the relative who, so that the sense may be: They will deliver you to the judges, who in their assemblies will scourge you. Thus Drus. l. 2. Animadv. c. 37. & l. 1. Praeteritp. 25. Finally, by synagogues can also be understood houses destined for ecclesiastical meetings, so that it may be signified that the fury of the enemies of the Gospel will be so great that when the Apostles have preached it in the synagogues, the prefects of those places will immediately scourge them, and not bring them to civil judges. (This last opinion pleases B. D. Chemn. in H. E. c. 72. p. 789. B. D. Glassius Philol. S. l. 1. tr. 2. p. 154. also l. 3. tr. 2. p. 201. Concerning the event of the prediction of this word, the history of the Apostles testifies. See.) Act. 5. 40. add 2 Cor. 11, 24.But how is this to be reconciled with this prediction of Christ, when the SaviorIoh. 16, 2.a little before his passion, similarly indicating to the Apostles that it would come to pass that they would be excluded from the Synagogues by the Jews and killed, expressly adds: That he had not told them these things from the beginning? Maldonato Comm. in Ioh. p. 929. and Iansenio Comment. in Concoro. Ev angc. 135. pag. 962. the opinion of those is especially approved: who think that those things which are reported here by Matthew were not said then by Christ to the disciples, when he first sent them out, but when the passion was imminent, just as these things are in John, or after the resurrection, when he was sending them not now among the Jews, but into the whole world to preach the Gospel: So that Matthew, on the occasion of that solemn mission described by him, might have gathered into one body, as it were, those things which Christ had pre-signified separately and at different times and places to the Apostles concerning their future lot. But this opinion, as not being sufficiently convenient, is deservedly disapproved by Toletus, Ribera, and others of their associates. B. Parenti in H. E. c. 179. p. 1496. Lyranus's exposition laughs at this, because Christ indeed had predicted persecutions even before, but not in this way, as in John, namely that he had added the consolation concerning the coming of the Holy Spirit. (And concerning this, namely, that he would console the Apostles in the cross and adversities, Augustine, Beda, Rupertus, Dionys. Carthus., Tirinus in Ioh. accept it.) Also because he had not predicted such things to them so harshly and bitterly, nor so clearly and perspicuously. Namely, that they were to be excluded from the Synagogues, and that they were to be killed with the opinion of singular worship. This exposition is indeed also that of Chrysostom hom. 77. in Ioh. and also of Euthymius. Among our own, the Glossators of the Bibl. Vinar. embrace the same, B. D. Calixtus H. E. l. 6. c. 6. Dn. D. Friedlieb Theol. Exeg. t. 2. p. 194. among the Papists Ribera, Toletus, Corn. à Lapide. Hugo Grotius in Ioh. also follows the same:

Latin:

*(v. 17. Cavete autem. Cùm verbi ministri ignorent, apud quos verbum fidei fructificare queat, quibus verò sit odor mortis ad mortem 2. Cor. 2, 16. ideò cautè semper agant, & -um modestiâ etiam corripiant eos, qui resistunt veritati &c. 2 Tim. 2, 25. Caventes interim, ne nimium ipsis fidant & ab ipsis circumveniantur. Quò facit exemplum Christi Ioh. 2, 24. itaB. D. Chemnitius in H. E. c. 72.)*

*( Ab hominibus. Filiis nempe huius seculi, qui oculos quidem habent hominis ( Dan. 7, 20.) sed intus sunt lupi rapaces. Cavete ab hominibus proditoribus, insidiatoribus ac perse cutoribus. Ita tamen, ne Christum negetis.)*

Tradent enim vos in Synedria &c. Per Synedria intelliguntur consessus Iudicum, qui celebrabantur in urbe Hierosolyma. Per Synagogas iudicia, quae exercebantur in coeteris Iudaeae urbibus. Alii dicunt, Synagogas Iudaeorum esse Synedria gentium. P. Gabinius Syriae proconsul, teste Iosepho, quatuor Conciliis Hierosolymitano additis gentem in quinque partes distribuit, quarum una Hierosolymis egit, altera Gadaris, tertia Amathunte, quarta Hierichunte, quinta Sephoris Galilaeae. Cùm ergo quinque Concilia essent, Christum in pl. loquutum nonnulli putant. Possunt quoque per Synedria intelligi consessus iudicum, per Synagogas conventus Ecclesiastici. Aut fortè Synedria dicit ipsos Iudices Sanhedria, & copula hoc in loco pro relativo qui sumitur, ut sit sensus. Tradent vosiudicibus, qui in conventibus suis flagellabunt vos. Ita Drus. l. 2. Animadv. c. 37. & l. 1. Praeteritp. 25. Possunt denique etiam per Synagogas intelligi domus destinatae conventibus Ecclesiasticis, ut significetur, tantum fore furorem hostium Evangelii, ut cùm Apostoli illud praedicarint in Synagogis, praefecti illarum eos statim sint flagellaturi, nec delaturi ad iudices civiles. *(Postrema haec sententia arridet B. D. Chemn. in H. E. c. 72. p. 789. B. D. Glassio Philol. S. l. 1. tr. 2. p. 154. it. l. 3. tr. 2. p. 201. De Eventû verò praedidictionis dictionis huius testatur historia Apost. Vid. Act. 5. 40. add 2 Cor. 11, 24.Quomodo verò cum hâc Christi praedictione conciliandum, quando SalvatorIoh. 16, 2.paullò ante passionem similiter indicans Apostolis, fore ut à Synagogis excludantur à Iudaei & interficiantur, disertè addit: Se isthac illis ab initio non dixisse? Maldonato Comm. in Ioh. p. 929. ac Iansenio Comment. in Concoro. Ev angc. 135. pag. 962. cum primis approbatur illorum sententia: qui existimant, ea, quae h. l. à Matthaeo referuntur, non fuisse tunc à Christo discipulis dicta, cùm primùm eos emitteret, sed instante passione, sicut haec apud Iohannem, aut post resurrectionem, cùm eos non iam inter Iudaeos, sed in totum terrarum orbead praedicandum mitteret Evangelium: Ut ita Matthaeus occasione solennis illius à se descriptae legationis in unum qs. corpus redegeritea, quae Christus seorsim & diversis temporibus & locia Apostolis de futurâ ipsorum sorte praesignificavit. Verùm sententiam hanc, ut potenon satis commodam, meritò improbant Toletus, Ribera aliique eorum socienni. B. Parenti in H. E. c. 179. p. 1496. Lyrani atridet expositio, quòd Christus quidem persecutiones praedixerit etiam antè, sed non hoc modo, ut apud Iohannem, nempe ut addiderit, consolationem de adventu Spiritus Sancti. (Et de hoc, nempe, quòd consolaturus sit Apostolos in cruce ac adversis, accipiunt Augustinus, Beda, Rupsertus, Dionys. Carthus., Tirinus in Ioh.) Item quòd non tam dura & acerba, nec tam clarè & perspicuè eis talia praedixerit. Videl. quòd à Synagogis sint excludendi, ac quòd cum opinione singularis clutûs sint interficiendi. Est verò expositio haec etiam Chrysostomi hom. 77. in Ioh. nec non Euthymii. Amplectuntur eandem è nostratibus Glossatores Bibl. Vinar. B. D. Calixtus H. E l. 6. c. 6. Dn. D. Friedlieb Theol. Exeg. t. 2. p. 194. ex Pontificiis Ribera, Toletus, Corn. à Lapide. sequitur eandem & Hugo Grotius in Ioh:

## 10:18
*(v. 18. Moreover you will be led to princes and kings &c. See the fulfillment of this prediction Act. 12, 23.c. 13. 45.c. 23, 24.)*

*( For my sake. See Act. 5, 41.)*

For a testimony against them i. e. so that seeing your παῤῥησίαι and constancy, they may be convinced of the truth of the Gospel, and may not be able to bring forward anything in the final judgment by which they might excuse themselves, Conf. Ioh. 15, 22.

Latin:

*(v. 18. Quin & ad principes ac reges ducemini &c. Vide praedictionis huius impletionem Act. 12, 23.c. 13. 45.c. 23, 24.)*

*( Propterme. Vid. Act. 5, 41.)*

In testimonium contra ipsos i. e. ut videntes vestram παῤῥησίαι & constantiam, de veritate Evangelii convincantur, nec possint in extremo iudicio quicquam afferre, quo se excusent, Conf. Ioh. 15, 22.

## 10:19
(v. 19. Do not think. In Greek it is μὴ μεριμνήσητε, which Erasmus hl. rightly rendered, do not be anxious. For not every meditation is excluded, Ps. 1, 2.1. Tim 4, 13. but that which is laborious and joined with excessive solicitude and anxiety of mind and distrust of divine help. In the same way, excessive care for food is prohibited above c. 6, 25.)

( It will be given to you in that hour what you should speak. This promise looks especially to the Apostles, but indeed also to those whom God otherwise calls immediately. For such men have certain singular gifts, concerning which also Luc. 12, 11. 12.c. 21, 15.Act. 6, 10.1. Cor. 2, 4. Whence since the Anabaptists are destitute of these such things, it is clear that they boast in vain of an immediate calling.)

Latin:

*(v. 19. Nolite cogitare. In Graeco est μὴ μεριμνήσητε, quod rectè Erasmus hl. reddidit, ne siti-soliciti. Neque enim omnis meditatio, Ps. 1, 2.1. Tim 4, 13. sed laboriosa ac cum nimiâ sollicitudine animique anxietate & diffidentiâ auxilii divini coniuncta excluditur. Eodem modo nimia victûs cura prohibetur suprà c. 6, 25.)*

*( Dabitur vobis in illâ horâ, quid loquamini. Haec promissio spectat cumprimis Apostolos, tum verò quos aliàs Deus immediatè vocat. Habent enim tales singularia quaedam dona, de quibus etiam Luc. 12, 11. 12.c. 21, 15.Act. 6, 10.1. Cor. 2, 4. Unde cùm his talibus Anabaptistae destituantur, patet, quòd vanè de immediata vocatione ipsi glorientur.)*

## 10:20
(v. 20. For it is not you who speak. i. e. it is not so much you, as the Spirit of your Father. So that the negation does not so much deny, as exaggerate. Compare similar examples Act. 5, 4.Eph. 6, 12.2. Thess. 4, 8. There can also be referred to here 1. Sam. 8, 7.Ier. 31, 34.Marc 9, 37.Ioh. 5, 30.Ioh 12, 44. Thus indeed the interpreters commonly accept the present passage. To whom can be added B. D. Glassius Gr. S. p. 490. Toletus Card. on Luke p. 621. Maldonatus on c. 11. of Luke p. -11. &c. Rightly indeed those things, whatever the Ministers of the Church do healthfully in their office, are attributed to the Holy Spirit, because he is the author and preserver of the Ministry. See B. Par. L. on the Ministry of the Church §. 50. Nevertheless, the Ministers of the Church remain the healthful and efficacious organs of Christ, through whom he himself works the conversion of men. Which our people rightly urge against the Schwenckfeldians. See B. Par. L. on the Ministry of the Church §. 249seqq. Furthermore, the promise of Christ, such as is also read Luc. 21, 15. was excellently fulfilled in Stephen the protomartyr, as Luke testifies Act. 6, 10. To this also pertain the passages Exod. 4, 11. 12.Ps. 8, 3. Sap. 10, 20. 21. Act. 2, 4.1. Cor. 2, 13.c. 12, 8.)

( He speaks in you, i. e. through you. Thus the prefix ב, to which τὸ ἐν corresponds, is often used in the Holy Scripture. See Hos. 1, 2.Ps 63, 12. And in this manner also in the present passage τὸ ἐν Rivetus accepts t. 2. Oper. p. 501. It is clear indeed from these words, how ineptly Eniedinus the Photinian p. 43. tries to prove from this passage, that it sometimes happens, that not the legate, who is present, but the one sending, who is absent, is said to do that which through the legate he does. As if the Holy Spirit were absent from the preaching Apostles: rather the Savior here affirms the contrary, teaching in express words, that the Holy Spirit speaks in or through the Apostles. Present indeed, not only by presence of power, which is otherwise accustomed to be called universal and general, Act. 17, 27. 28. but also of grace, which is accustomed to be called special, insofar as namely they were not only temples of the Holy Spirit, which benefit the Apostles had in common with other believers, 1. Cor. 6, 16. but also insofar as he taught them and suggested all things, which were said by Christ, Ioh. 14, 26. Compare c. 16, 13.

*( But of the Spirit of your Father &c. Lest anyone should gather from this, as if the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, it is to be noted that elsewhere the Holy Spirit is also called the Spirit of Christ, Rom. 8, 9. the Spirit of the Son, Gal. 4, 6. Conf. Act. 16, 7. the Spirit of truth, Ioh. 14, 17. c 15, 26. Christ however is the truth, Ioh. 14, 6. See Cyril of Alexandria, book 10 on John, last chapter.)*

Latin:

*(v. 20. Non enim vos estis, qui loquimini. i. e. non tam vos estis, quàm Spiritus Patris vestri. Ut ita negatio non tam neget, quàm exaggeret. Conf. similia exempla Act. 5, 4.Eph. 6, 12.2. Thess. 4, 8. Possunt etiam huc referri 1. Sam. 8, 7.Ier. 31, 34.Marc 9, 37.Ioh. 5, 30.Ioh 12, 44. Ita verò praesentem locum accipiunt Interpp. communiter. Quibus addi possunt B. D. Glassius Gr. S. p. 490. Toletus Card. in Lucam p. 621. Maldonatus in c. 11. Lucae p. -11. &c. Rectè verò ea, quaecunque Ministri Ecclesiae salutariter in officio suo agunt, Spiritui Sancto tribuuntur, quia ipse Ministerii autor & conservator. Vid. B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 50. Manent tamen Ministri Eccl. salutaria atque efficacia Christi organa, per quae ipse conversionem hominum operatur. Quod contra Schwenck seldianos meritò nostrates urgent. Vid. B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 249seqq. Porrò egregiè promissio Christi, qualis etiam legitur Luc. 21, 15. impleta fuit in Stephano protomartyre, teste Lucâ Act. 6, 10. Huc faciunt quoque loca Exod. 4, 11. 12.Ps. 8, 3. Sap. 10, 20. 21. Act. 2, 4.1. Cor. 2, 13.c. 12, 8.)*

*( Loquitur in vobis, i. e. per vos. Ita praefixum ב, cui τὸ ἐν respondet, saepè in Sc. S. adhibetur. Vid. Hos. 1, 2.Ps 63, 12. Atque h. m. etiam praesenti loco τὸ ἐν accipit Rivetus t. 2. Oper. p. 501. Patet verò ex his verbis, quàm ineptè Eniedinus Photinianus p. 43. ex h. l. probare conetur, quòd aliquando fiat, ut non legatus, qui adest, sed legans, qui abe-t, facere id dicatur, quod per legatum facit. Quasi v. Spiritus Sanctus absit ab Apostolis praedicantibus: impotiùs contrarium hîc Salvator ad-irmat, expressis verbis docens, quòd Sp. S. in vel per Apostolos loquatur. Praesens utique, non solûm praesentiâ potentiae, quae aliàs universalis ac generalis dici consuevit, Act. 17, 27. 28. sed etiam gratiae, quae specialis vocari solet, quat. nempe ipsi non solùm fuerunt templa Spiritûs Sancti, quod beneficium cum aliis fidelibus habuerunt Apostoli commune, 1. Cor. 6, 16. sed etiam quatenus ille docuit eos & suggessit omnia, quae à Christo dicta, Ioh. 14, 26. Conf. c. 16, 13.

*( Sed Spiritûs Patris vestri &c. Ne quis hinc colligat, quasi Sp. S. à solo Patre procedat, notandum, quòd alibi etiam Sp. S. dicatur Spiritus Christi,Rom. 8, 9.Spiritus Filii,Gal. 4, 6. Conf. Act. 16, 7.Spiritus veritatis,Ioh. 14, 17.c 15, 26. Christus autem veritas est,Ioh. 14, 6. Vid. Cyrill Alexand. l. 10. in Ioh c. ult.)*

## 10:21
*(v. 21. But brother shall deliver up brother to death &c. Examples of the fulfillment of this prediction in the primitive Church were collected by Corn. à Lapide in this place. For not without a copious shedding of blood was the doctrine of the Gospel, which is as it were a stake in the eyes of the Devil, introduced. Its author Jesus was most cruelly put to death, the Apostles and faithful followers and Confessors of the Christian faith were tortured with horrendous torments &c. And all this according to the prediction of Christ.)*

Latin:

*(v. 21. Tradet autem frater fratrem &c. Exempla impletae liuius praedictionis in primitivâ Ecclesiâ, collegit Corn. à Lapide in h. l. Neque enim sine copiosâ sangvinis effusione Evangelii doctrina, quae Diabolo qs. sudes in oculis, introducta est. Eius autor Iesus crudelissimè interfectus, Apostoli ac fideles Christianae fidei sectatores atque Confessores horrendis cruciatibus excarnisicati &c. Et hoc omne iuxta Christi praedictionem.)*

## 10:22
v. 22. Ο δὲ ὐπομείνας εἐς τέλος, οὗτος σωθήσεται. Τὸ ὑπομείνας Beza translates he who shall have endured. The Vulgate, he who shall have persevered, which Casaubon in his notes judges should be retained. For ὑπομὲνειν seem to be called those things which subsist, and do not lose τὸ εἶναι. Thus by the Philosopher they are called parts τοῦ χρόνου οὐχου ὐπ ένειν. *(The parallel passage is Apoc. 2, 10. Furthermore, although it is sufficiently manifest from this place that the elect cannot fall from the grace of GOD and lose faith finally: yet it is by no means to be inferred from this that they cannot lose faith totally, if indeed they rush into sins against conscience, But it is not the place here to treat of this matter at length. See D. Hutter in F. C. art. 11 p. 1134. seqq. also LL. Th. Mai. page 816. a. 6. The Lords Theologians of Marburg in fundam. deduct. p. 269. seqq. D. Mentzer in a special treatise on the question, Whether faith can be lost through sins, against Apelius. D. Tarnovius likewise in a single Disputation held under D. Affelmann. D. Wias---lm in a Disputation, Whether and how far the Justified can fall from the grace of GOD. also on the question, Whether those once justified can lose the Holy Spirit. vol. 2. Disp. Gies. p. 126. seqq. D. Hunnius vol. 1. Disp. Marp. p. 154. M.)* D-rfeld. tr. on the perseverance of the saints, against Crocius. Nor yet from this, that the perseverance of faith is required from those to be saved, ought it to be gathered that a man (a believer) cannot be certain of his own salvation, which Costerus p. 184 of the Enchiridion and other Papists strive to evince from this. Finally, from the present passage D. Meisnerus rightly forms an argument against Purgatory in his fruitful Opuscula, against the Indulgences of the Roman Pope, p. 272, which can be unfolded.)*

Latin:

v. 22. Ο δὲ ὐπομείνας εἐς τέλος, οὗτος σωθήσεται. Τὸ ὑπομείνας Beza vertit qui sustinuerit. Vulgatus, qui perseveraverit, quod Casaubonus in notis retinendum censet. Videntur enim ὑπομὲνειν dici ea, quae subsistunt, nec amittunt τὸ εἶναι. Sic à Philosophô dicuntur partes τοῦ χρόνου οὐχου ὐπ ένειν. *(Locus parall: est Apoc. 2, 10. Coeterùm licet ex h. l. satis manifestum sit, electos non posse excidere gratiâ DEI ac fidem amittere finaliter: minimè tamen hinc inferendum, quòd nec totaliter amittere fidem possint, si nempe in peccata contra conscientiam ruant, Sed hâc de re non est huius loci agere prolixè. Vid. D Hutter. in F. C. art. 11 p. 1134. seqq it. LL. Th. Mai. pag. 816. a. 6. Dnn. Theologi Marp. in fundam. deduct. p. 269. seqq. D. Mentzerus in pecul tr. de quaest. An fides per peccata amitti possit, contra Apelium. D. Tarnovius itid. in Disp. sing sub D. Affelmanno habitâ. D. Wias---lm in Disp. An & quat. Iustificati possint excidere gratia, DEI. it. de quaest. An semel iustificati Sp. S. amittere possint. t. 2. Disp. Gies. p. 126. seqq. D. Hunnius t. 1. Disp. Marp. p. 154. M. D-rfeld. tr. de perseverentiâ sanctorum, contra Crocium. Neque tamen ex eo, quòd fidei perseverentia à salvandis requiritur, colligi debet, quòd homo (fidelis) non possit esse de salute suâ certus, quod Costerus p. 184. Enchiridii aliique Pontisicii evincere hinc satagunt. Denique è praesenti loco rectè argumentum contra Purgatorium format D Meisnerus Opusc. fecundo, Indulgentiis Rom Papae opp. p. 272. qui potest evolvi.)*

## 10:23
*(v. 23. Flee into another Even today it is granted to the ministers of the Church that in time of persecution they may consult for themselves by flight. But yet in certain cases at least, concerning which our theologians can be consulted, especially B. D. Hutt. Append. Consil. Th. Dedekenni p. 187. On. D. Tarnov Consil. Theol. Dedek. part. 1. pag. 772. seqq. B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 177. & 291. B. D. Bald. Co-. in post. ep ad Corinth. c. 11. q. 3. p. 729.]*

You shall by no means finish the cities of Israel &c. τελεῖνταπόλεις can be conveniently explained by τὸ to finish by performing the duty, to execute which the Apostles were sent into them, as 1. Sam. 16, 12. *(So also B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 403 takes it.)* Until the Son of man comes viz. through the universal preaching of the Gospel to all nations & the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Tossanus. Christ here promises to the Apostles his presence in the function of teaching: for he himself was also about to teach publicly in Judea and Galilee and to make the embassy of the Apostles credible by stupendous miracles. *(So also Ioh. Camero Myroth. Evang. p. 43 explains it almost.)* Others take it concerning the gracious presence, by which Christ was effective through the word of the Apostles for the conversion of many. *(H. Grotius inclines toward this in this place and brings forward Ioh 14, 18.Act. 2, 33. to strengthen his opinion)*

Latin:

*(v. 23. Fugite in aliam Etiam adhuc hodiè ministris Ecclesiae concessum est, ut tempore persecutionis fugâ sibi consulant. Sed tamen in certis saltem casibus, de quobis consuli possunt nostratos Theologi, cumprimis B. D. Hutt. Append. Consil. Th. Dedekenni p. 187. On. D. Tarnov Consil. Theol. Dedek. part. 1. pag. 772. seqq. B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 177. & 291. B. D. Bald. Co-. in post. ep ad Corinth. c. 11. q. 3. p. 729.]*

Nequaquam obieritis urbos Israelis &c. τελεῖνταπόλεις commodè explicari potest per τὸperficere munus obeundo, ad quod exequendum in eas missi erant Apostoli, ut 1. Sam. 16, 12. *(Ita accipit quoq; B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 403.)* Donec veniat Filius hominus sc. per universalem Evangelii praedicationem in omnes gentes & Sp. S. effusionem. Tossanus. Promittit Christus hîc Apostolis suam in docendi functione praesentiam: nam & ipse publicè in Iudaeâ & Galilaeâ docturus & stupendis miraculis Apostolorum legationi fidem facturus erat. *(Ita ferè exponit etiam Ioh. Camero Myroth. Evang. p. 43.)* Alii accipiunt de praesentiâ gratiosâ, quâ Christus per verbum Apostolorum ad multorum conversionem fuit efficax. *(Inclinat huc H. Grotius in h. l. ad ducitq; sententiae suae firmandae Ioh 14, 18.Act. 2, 33.)*

## 10:24
v. 24. The disciple is not above the Master. And yet in an old Iambic poem it is said: πολλοὶ μαθνταὶ κρείττολες διδασκάλων. Resp. times must be distinguished. Theoph in this place ἕως ἂν ὦσι μαθνταὶ ἐλάττους εἐσὶ τῶν διδασκάλων. ἐὰν κρείττους γένωνται, σὀκ ἔτι λοιπὸν εἰσὶ μαθηταί. Furthermore, Christ does not look so much to the progress as to the fortune of the disciples, because that disciple is impudent and ungrateful who wishes more honor and reverence to be paid to himself than to his Master.

(This exposition is confirmed by the comparison John 15:20 with this place. For the Savior himself explains there how he wishes the proverbial expression to be understood. This admonition also occurs already Luke 6:40 John 13:16 and the Blessed Pareus explains it at length in Harm. Evang. ch. 178, p. 1452 & p. 1061.) In the Talmud a similar sentiment is read in the tractate on Blessings ch. 9 דיו לעבדs להיות כרבו׃ i.e. It is enough for the servant that he be as his Master. (Midrash also has the same sentiment in Ps. 10) Nonnus John 15 v. 82 δοῦλος ἀνὴς σἔκ ἐστιν ἑου βασιλῆοςἐρείων.

Latin:

v. 24. Non est discipulus supra Magistrum. Atqui in veteri Carmine Iambico dicitur: πολλοὶ μαθνταὶ κρείττολες διδασκάλων. Resp. distinguenda sunt tempora. Theoph in h. l. ἕως ἂν ὦσι μαθνταὶ ἐλάττους εἐσὶ τῶν διδασκάλων. ἐὰν κρείττους γένωνται, σὀκ ἔτι λοιπὸν εἰσὶ μαθηταί. Praeterea non tam ad progressus, quàm ad fortunā discipulorū Christus respicit, quòd impudens & ingratus sit distipulus, qui plus sibi honoris ac reverentiae, quàm Magistro suo, impendi velit.

*(Confirmat expositionem hanc collatio Ioh. 15, 20. cum h. l. Ipse enim Salvator ibi exponit, quomodo proverbialem locutionem intellectam velit. Occurrit verò admonitio haecet. iam Luc. 6, 40.Ioh. 13, 16. eamque prolixè exponit B. Par. Harm. Evang. c. 178. p. 1452. & p. 1061.)* In Talmud similis sententia legitur tract de Bened c. 9. דיו לעבדs להיות כרבו׃ i. e. Sufficit servo, ut sit sicut Dominus suus. *(Eandem sententiā habet quoque Midrasch in Ps. 10.)* Nonnus Ioh 15. v. 82.δοῦλος ἀνὴς σἔκ ἐστιν ἑου βασιλῆοςἐρείων.

## 10:25
v. 25. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub &c. Drusius book 1, Praeter. page 16, on this place. Beelzebub is not a name corrupted by Greek scribes, but the Jews changed it in that way as a reproach to the idol. See the book Misvoth Gadol f. 98, col. 3. Furthermore, the Latin and the Syrian have Beelzebub, and that it ought to be written so is evident from 2 Kings 1. Nazianzen against Julian is a witness that that god had the figure of a fly, either because he was believed to drive away flies, or because he gave oracles in the form of a fly. See also Selden, Synt. 2, on the Syrian Gods, ch. 6. (Selden notes on the said place 1. that entirely interprets Beelzebub as the Lord or God of the fly, and praises in this the words of Josephus discussing the fall of Ahaziah, 2 Kings 1, and calling Beelzebub Ἀκκάρων θεὸν Μ-αν i.e. a fly. The same also observes that both the 70 Elders and Gregory Nazianzen in Steliteutic Oration 2, and if any others followed the version of the 70, use that name. 2. That Procopius of Gaza takes this Divinity for the image of a Fly, but also doubts whether it was the name of a Demon, or of an old woman related among the Gods. 3. That it is disputed whether this name was invented by the Accaronites, or by the Jews as a reproach to the idol. Selden himself, however, embraces the former, which he also proves at length. (However, H. Grotius on this place, Buxt. Lex Rabb. Talm. under the word בעל זבוב, and others dissent.) 4. That mention of this idol is made in Matthew, Mark, and Luke, in which, however, for Beelzebub most Greek copies have the same; the best have Beelzebub. How in the most ancient Arabic version edited by Erpenius it is also read. But Beelzebub sounds like Jupiter, Bel, or Lord of Dung or Dung-like. 5. That Chrysostom, Origen, Athanasius, Cyril, and most of the ancients follow this reading with λ at the end, and even Prudentius. 6. That it is not poorly said that the word was invented as an insult to idolaters, as Drusius also thinks. To confirm which opinion, besides other things, he brings forward a passage from Abraham Benkatrun, where he explains verse 33 of chapter 23 of Exodus in this manner:) You shall not allow those who worship foreign Gods to dwell with you, or Dung-gods. But why the name Beelzebub or Beelzebub is used below in c. 12, 24 to denote the Prince of Demons, will be advised in the Analecta to Marc. 3, 22. where also more things will be brought forward concerning this very idol, and at the same time the coin marked with the image of a fly will be explained, which I keep in my antiquary.)*

Latin:

v. 25. Si ipsum patrem familiâs Beelzebub &c. Drusius lib. 1. Praeter. pag. 16. ad h l. Beelzebub non est nomen corruptum â Graecis librariis, sed ita immutarunt illud Iudaei in opprobrium idoli. Vide librum Misvoth Gadol f. 98. col. 3. Coeterùm Latinus ac Syrus habent Beelzebub, atque ita scribendum esse, patet ex 2. Reg. 1. Nazianzenus contra Iulianum, muscae figuram Deum illum habuisse, testis est, vel quòd muscas pellere crederetur, vel quòd forma muscae oracula dabat. Videatur etiam Seldenus Synt. 2. de Diis Syris c. 6. *(Notat d. l. Seldenus 1. quòd omninBeelzebub Dominum s. Deum muscae interpretetur, laudatque in hanc verba Iosephi de Ahaziae casu, 2. Reg. 1. descripto, disserentis, ac Beelzebub Ἀκκάρων θεὸν Μ-αν i. e. muscam appellantis. Observat quoque idem, & LXX. Seniores & Gregorium Nazianzenum Orat. Steliteur. 2. & si qui alii versionem LXX. sequuti, eo nomine uti. 2. pro Muscae imagine Numen hoc sumere Procopium Gazaeum, sed dubitare etiam, an Daemonis nomen fuerut, au vetulae in Divos relatae. 3. Controverti, utrum ab Accaronitis inventum fuerit hoc nomen, an à Iudaeis in idoli opprobrium. Ipse verò Seldenus prius amplectitur, quod probat etiam prolixè. (Dissentiunt tamen H. Grotius in h l. Buxt. Lex Rabb. Talm. voce בעל זבוב, alii) 4. Mentionem huius idoli fieri apud Matthaeum, Marcum & Lucam, in guibus tamen pro Beelzebub pleraq; Graecorum exempla eadem-; optima habeant Beelzebub. Quomodo in vetust-ssima versione Arabica ab Erpenio editâ etiam legatur Sonare verò Beelzebub Iovem, Belum s. Dominum Stercoris aut Stercoreum 5. sequi hanc lectionem per λ in fine D. Chrysostomum, Originem, Athanasium, Cyrillum ac veterum plerosque, quin & Prudentium. 6. non malè dici, in contumeliam idololatrarum vocabulum inventum, uti & Drusius sentiat. Cui sententiae confirmandae praeter alia adducit locum ex Abrahamo Benkatrun, ubi vers. 33. c. 23. Exodi ad hunc modum explicat: Non sines apud te habitare, qui colunt Deos peregrinos vel Stercoreos. Cur verò ad Principem Daemoniorum denotandum nomen Beelzebub aut Beelzebub infrà c. 12, 24. usurpetur, monebitur in Analect. ad Marc. 3, 22. ubi etîam de ipso idolo hoc plura afferentur, ac simul explicabitur Numisma muscae imagine insignitum, quod in antiquario meo adservo.)*

## 10:26
v. 26. There is nothing hidden i. e. although the truth of the Gospel -er through the malice of men is for a time suppressed & obscured, so that it may not be publicly announced, nevertheless it will at length break forth into clear light. * (This explanation pleases the Blessed D. Quistorpius more than the exposition of Jerome and Hilary, since indeed Christ wishes this: Do not fear the cruelty of persecutors and the rage of blasphemers, because the day of judgment will come, in which your virtue and their wickedness will be demonstrated. But the context proves the former explanation, as is evident from v. 27. 28.)*

Latin:

v. 26. Nihil est occultum i. e. quamvis veritas Evangelii -er hominum malitiam ad tempus prematur & obscuretur, ne publicè annuncietur, tamen in claram lucem tandem erumpet. * (Arridet haec explicatio B. D. Quistorpio prae Hieronymi ac Hilarii expositione, qs. nempe Christus hoc velit: Nolite timere persecutorum saevitiam & blasphemantium rabiem, quia veniet dies iudicii, in quo vestra virtus & eorum nequitia demonstrabitur. Probat verò priorem explicationem contextus, ceu patet ex v. 27. 28.)*

## 10:27
v. 27. What I say to you in darkness, speak in the light. Theophylactus in h. l. ὅπερ μόνοις & he adds, because dangers follow this παῤῥεγαλοφώνως, therefore it is subjoined: Do not fear those who kill the body. Author of the Imperfect Work. What you hear in secret alone, preach before all, hiding the word from no one, as one who stands upon the roofs and cries out. Jerome. What you hear in mystery, preach more openly. What you learn secretly, speak: what I have taught you in a small place of Judea, say boldly in all cities and in the whole world. Chrysostom ad h. l. He was speaking to them alone and in a small corner of Palestine, therefore as if for the future where by comparing these things he spoke thus. For he shows that you will preach not to one or two or three cities, but to the whole world, crossing seas, lands, inhabited and uninhabited places. Nor does he announce that you will say these things only to the poor or the unlearned, but to Kings, the wealthy, the powerful, the most acute Philosophers, the most eloquent Orators, openly and with bare head, freely and confidently. * (Our people rightly gather from h. l. that the assertion of the Papists is inept, That the Apostles were accustomed to preach some things to all, and some things only to Prelates, Bishops, and presbyters. The Papists, however, refer to the latter class not only those things which concern the government of the Church, but also those which look to the genuine sense of Holy Scripture and other matters, as is to be seen from Bellarmine, book 4, on the Word of God, chapters 4 and 11. But how coldly the Papists except against these and similar passages, the Blessed Pareus shows in his Exegesis of the Book on Holy Scripture, § 398. And for the dispelling of those mists, even a mere comparison of the sayings John 18:20Acts 20:271 John 1:1, 2 suffices. Irenaeus, a most ancient writer, and one who would have been least unaware if the Apostles had left behind any true traditions besides Holy Scripture, notes significantly in book 4, chapter 36: No other traditions, which are boasted of under the title or name of the Apostles, are to be received than those which are contained in Scripture and are agreeable to it. Tertullian also, easily the Prince of the Latin Fathers, in his De Praescriptione chapter 26: The Lord proclaimed openly, without any indication of any secret sacrament; He Himself had commanded that if they had heard anything in darkness and in secret, they should preach it in the light and on the housetops. He Himself had prefigured by a similitude that they should not keep one mina, that is, one word of His, without fruit in a hidden place. Furthermore, the passage John 18:20 seems to stand against this present assertion of Christ. Augustine suggests a reconciliation in tractate 113 on John, whose words, as well as the reconciliations of others, will be brought forward in the Analysis on John 18:20.

Κηρύξατε ὐπὶ τῶνδωμάτων Beza: Preach above the houses. Erasmus: on the housetops. He touches upon the custom of the ancients regarding both buildings and proclamations. For in order that the criers might be heard far and wide, they would ascend the flat roofs, Deuteronomy 22:8Isaiah 15:3. Jerome, epistle 135 to Sunnia and Fretela: A house in the Oriental provinces is called that very thing which with us is a roof. Compare 2 Samuel 11:3Jeremiah 32:28 *(Furthermore, concerning the form of the upper part of buildings among the Orientals as well as other peoples, one may see more in the Blessed Pareus, Commentary on Deuteronomy, p. 1315; Simon the Bishop, Theological Institutions, p. 12; Don Laur. Ramirez, chapter 27, Pentecont., p. 219 seqq.; Ribera on the Temple, book 1, chapter 12, pages 33, 34.)*

Latin:

v. 27. Quod dico vobis intenebris, dicite in luce. Theophylactus in h. l. ὅπερ μόνοις & addit, quia hanc παῤῥεγαλοφώνως pericula sequuntur, ideo subiungi: Ne timete eos, qui occidunt corpus. Autor Operis imperf. Qùod auditis in secreto soli, praedicate coram omnibus, nulli abscondentes verbum, qs qui stet supra tecta & clamet. Hieronymus. Quod auditis in mysterio, apertiùs praedicate. quod discitis absonditè, loquimini: quod vos erudivi in parvo Iudaeae loco, in universis urbibus & in toto mundo audacter dicite. Chrysostomus ad h. l Solis ipsis & in parvo angulPalaestinae dicebat, idcirco quasi ad futurum ubiingentem Evangelii sonitum haec conferendo ita dixit. Non enim uni aut duabus aut tribus civitatibus, sed toti terrarum orbi praedicabitis, matia, terras, loca habitata & inhabitata transituros ostendit. Nec pauperibus solum aut rudibus, sed Regibus, opulentis, potentibus, acutissimis Philosophis, facundissimis Oratoribus apertè ac nudo capite liberè ac fidenter haec dicturos praenunciat. * (Rectè ex h. l. colligunt nostrates, ineptam esse Pontificiorum adsertio nem, quòd Apostoli consueverint, quaedam omnibuspraedicare, quaedam solis Praelatis, Episcopis & presbyteris. Referunt autem Pontificii ad classem posteriorem non solùm ea, quae Ecclesiae gubernationem concernunt, sed etiam quae spectant genuinum Sc. S. sensum & alia, ceu videre est ex Bellarmino l. 4. de V. D. C. 4. & 11. Quàm frigidè verò ad haec & similia loca Pontificii excipiant, ostendit B. Par. Exeg. L. de Sc. S. §. 398. Sufficitque ad nebulas illas discutiendas vel sola collatio dictorum Ioh. 18, 20.Act. 20, 27.1. Ioh. 1, 1. 2. Notanter Irenaeus, Scriptor antiquissimus, & quem adeò minimè latuisset, si quas veras traditiones praeter Sc. S. Apostoli reliquissent, l. 4, c. 36. Nullae aliae traditiones, quae sub Apostolorum titulo vel nomine iactantur, recipiendae sunt, quàm quae Scripturâ comprehensae, & illi sunt consentaneae. Tertullianus quoque Patrum Latinorum facilè Princeps, de Praescript. cap. 26.Dominus palam edixit, sine ulla significatione alicuius taciti Sacramenti, ipse praeceperat, si quid in tenebris & in abscondito audissent, in luce & in tectis praedicaret. Ipse per similitudinem praefiguraverat, ne unam manam i. e. unum verbum eius sine fructu in, abdito reservarent. Caeterùm obstare praesenti Christi adserto videtur locus Ioh. 18, 20. Conciliationem suggerit Augustinus t. 113. in Ioh. cuius verba, sicuti & aliorum conciliationes adducentur in Anal. ad Ioh. 18, 20.)*

## 10:28
* (v. 28. They cannot kill the soul. Therefore, the soul of man is immortal. But it seems to stand against this: 1. that it is immediately added:

fear Him who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell. Resp. The Savior in the latter words deals with the second death, which does not happen by slaughtering and annihilating, but by tormenting with infernal punishments. Whence it is rightly to be noted that Christ does not say God ἀποκτείναι, but ἀπολέσαι ψυχὴν κὶσῶμα which ἀπόλεια may be tormented eternally. For it does not always denote the destruction of substance, but often a defect of goodness, as is evident from this very chapter Matthew v. 615:24c. 28:1114Mark 2:22, so the Blessed D. Bald in 2 Thessalonians 1 n. 6, p. 1201. Compare more in the Blessed Pareus, Book on Death, § 141. 2. Genesis 37:21 let us not strike him with the soul, that is, let us not kill him. Compare Matthew 2:20. Resp. Here the soul is taken for life, the effect indeed of the indwelling soul, a phrase used in Holy Scripture. See Drusius, book 1, Praet., p. 26; the Blessed Pareus Co-. on Genesis, p. 188; the Blessed D. Glass, Sacred Rhetoric, p. 7, 8.)*

He who can destroy both soul and body in hell. Since soul and body concur in sinning, the mind indeed as the author of the fault, but the flesh as the minister, according to Ambrose in his De Officiis, why should neither also be exempt from infernal punishments? Whence Cyprian, book 1, epistle 4: Those who are joined in fault are not separated in punishment. Furthermore, why hell or infernal punishments come under the appellation of gehenna has been said above at c. 5. v. 22., and more perhaps will be brought to this matter at Marc. 9, 43.. Since, however, reprobate men will finally be subjected to infernal punishments after this life, as far as the body is concerned, it is evident that the impious also are to be resurrected at some time. This is to be opposed to the Photinians, who speak very ambiguously about the resurrection of the impious, as B. Par. L. shows in his De Resurr. mortuorum §. 101. If the soul is also to be destroyed in hell, that is, if it is to be subjected to infernal punishments, which will be eternal, and to be tormented by them, it is manifest how gravely they err who have either expressly denied or called into doubt the immortality of the soul. Into whose number are to be referred 1. The Epicureans, whose voices Holy Scripture Es. 12, 13. 1. Cor. 15, 32. Sap. 2, 2. &c. reports. 2. The Sadducees, about whom Act. 23, 8.. 3. Certain Arabs, as witnessed by Eusebius, book 6, H. E. cap. 36. 4. certain heretics among Damascene, book on heresies, p. 585. 5. Many of the Gentile philosophers, such as Aratus, Zeno, among Augustine, book on Spirit and Soul, c. 43. &c. 6. The Photinians. And 7. Certain Roman Pontiffs, such as Iohannes 23. and Paul III, as B. Par. L. teaches at length in his De Morte §. 149. H. Grotius reviews the differing opinions of the Jews in this place.

Latin:

* (v. 28. Animam occidere non possunt. E. anima hominis est immortalis. Sed obstare videtur 1. quòd statim subiicitur:

timete eum qui potest animam & corpus perdere in gehenna. Resp. agit Salvator in post. verbis de morte secunda, quae non fit trucidando & annihilando, sed poenis infernalibus cruciando. Unde probè notandum, quòd Christus non dicat, Deum ἀποκτείναι, sed ἀπολέσαι ψυχὴν κὶσῶμα quae ἀπόλεια crucitatius sit sempiternis. Neque enim semper destructionem substantiae notat, sed saepè bonitatis defectum, ceu patet ex hoc ipso cap. Matth. v. 6.15. 24.c. 28, 11.14.Marc. 2, 22. ita B. D. Bald in 2. Thess. 1. n. 6. p. 1201. Conf. plura apud B. Par. L. de Morte §. 141. 2. Gen. 37, 21.ne percutiamus cum animâ i. e. ne interficiamus. Conf. Matth. 2, 20. Resp. Sumirtur h. l. anima pro vita, effecto nempe animae inhabitantis, phrasi in Sc. S. usitata. Vid. Drusius lib. 1. Praet. p. 26. B. Par. Co-. in Gen. p. 188. B. D. Glass. Rhet. S. p. 7. 8.)*

Qui animam & corpus perdere potest in gehenna. Cùm anima & corpus in peccando concurrant, animus quidem ut autor culpae, carò vero ut ministra, iuxta Ambros. de Officiis, quare neutrum quoq; à poenis infernalibus erit exemtum. Unde Cyprianus l. 1. ep. 4. Qui iunguntur in culpâ, in poenâ non separantur. Porrò cur infernus vel poenae infernales gehennae appellatione, veniant, dictum suprà ad c. 5. v. 22. ac plura fortè in rem hanc adducentur ad Marc. 9, 43. Cùm verò homines reprobi demum post hanc vitam, quantum ad corpus, poenis infernalibus subiicientur, patet quòd impii quoque aliquando sint resuscitandi. Quod opponendum Photinianis, de impiorum resurrectione, admodùm ambiguè loquentibus, uti ostendit B. Par. L. de Resurr. mortuorum §. 101. Si anima quoque perdenda in gehenna, h. e. si poenis infernalibus, quae aeternae erunt, subiicienda, iisque crucianda, manifestum est, quàm graviter errent, qui animae immorralitatem vel expresse negarunt, vel in dubium vocarunt. Quorum in numerum refere-di 1. Epicuraei, quorum voces Sc. S. Es. 12, 13.1. Cor. 15, 32. Sap. 2, 2. &c. refert. 2. Sadducaei, de quibus Act. 23, 8. 3. Arabes quidam, teste Euseb. l. 6. H. E. cap. 36. 4. haere--ci quidam apud Damasc. lib de haeres. p. 585. 5 Multi ex gentilibus Philosophis, uti Aratus, Zeno apud Aug. l. de Sp. & Anima c. 43. &c. 6. Photiniani. ac 7. Pontifices quidam Romani, uti Iohannes 23. ac Paulus III. ceu prolixè docet B. Par. L. de Morte §. 149. Iudaeorum discrepantes sententias recenset H. Grotius in h. l.)*

## 10:29
v. 29. Οὐχὶδύοςρουθία &c. Moschopulus. ςρουίαδὶ It is better, therefore, that little birds are understood, rather than little sparrows, since both the Greek and the Syriac word denote birds in general. *(B. D. Chemnitius, however, is more pleased if little sparrows are understood, since they are a most contemptible bird, if indeed according to Pliny, book 10, chapter 36, they are the least of life, and according to others also, they more often incur leprosy and the falling sickness.)*

*(Twin to this sentence of the Savior is that saying which, in Bereschith Rabba section 79, is fabulously attributed to a little bird: ירעלמ i. e. Without heaven's (i. e. divine nod) not even one is caught by fowling, how much less so many souls of the sons of men. Lud. Capellus relates the whole fable in Spicil. p. 20. Not dissimilar also is the maxim of Maimonides in More Nevochim part 3, chapter 48, If God takes care of beasts and birds, that they may not be affected by pain, כל שכן בבני ארם how much more will He have regard for men. Buxtorf mentions this in Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 176. Where he also has some other things pertaining to this: 1. Christ argues indeed from the lesser to the greater. And this testimony is also a sufficiently clear argument concerning general divine providence. Nor does the saying 1. Cor. 9, 9. stand in the way, for that this is to be accepted not ἁπλῶς, but κατὰ τὶ is evident both from the context and from other Holy Scripture sayings, as Wisdom 8, 1. c. 12, 13. Heb. 1, 3.Ps. 36, 6.Ps. 47, 1,9.Ps. 104, 27. 28.Job 38, 41.c. 39, 1. 2.Matt. 6, 26.Luke 12, 6 Especially, however, divine providence is concerned with men. See Wisdom 6, 8. Ps. 36, 6.Acts 17, 28. & elsewhere throughout.)*

Two sparrows. But in Luc. 12, 6 it is expressed thus: are not five sparrows sold for two farthings? Dr. D. Walther answers in H. B. p. 765 that Christ said this either at different times and thus used both expressions, or uttered both at one time in this manner: are not two sparrows sold for one farthing? nay, are not five sold for two farthings?)* *(

*( They are sold for an assarion. An assarion is the smallest kind of coin, since its weight is at least four grains of barley, as Maimon teaches from the opinion of the Rabbis, cited by Buxtorf, Lex. Rabb. Talm. under the word אנםר According to the blessed D. Chemn. H. E. p. 799, it denotes a half-coin or an obol. Furthermore, regarding the coins of the Hebrews, Greeks, and Romans, one may consult B. Mathesius in Sarepta, Schickardus in Tarich, p. 34, 5. and Bechin Happeruschim, p. 82. as well as in מהמ p. 39. 84. Waserus in the special treatise on Hebrew coins, Franc. Lucas Comm. in Matth. p. 446. Camero t. 2. Praelect. Alcasar Append. in Apocalypsin, Ioh. Bapt. Villalpandus in Ezechielem, Budaeus de Asse, the Londoners in the Apparatus, in the promised treatise 2 of the Polyglot Bibles. Renerus Rudelius Ruremundanus, Scaliger, Schnellius, -oachimus Camerarius, Iacobus Capellus, Marq. Freherus, Iacobus Bornitius, Pontus Heuterus, Constantinus Landus Count of Complani, Goltzius, Fulvius -rsinus, Abrahamus Gor aeus, Matthaeus Hostius, Fr. Hottomannus, Henricus Uranius, Alexander Sardus Aeneas Vicus & very many others. Furthermore, Hilary explains the present saying symbolically, writing: The two sparrows are the body and the soul, which are born as sparrows, so that they may fly to heaven with spiritual wings; but the sinner sells them to the Devil for an as, i. e., for a small pleasure, so that they may descend into the underworld.

* ( Without your Father i. e. without the will of GOD. Ineptly, certain Cal vini-ni from this try to prove that if a little sparrow does not fall without the will of God, neither did the first parents fall into sin without His will, namely of complacency and impulse (for this is the question). Since there is an absolute distinction between physical fall, and moral, i. e. without sin, and joined with sin, or a sinful and malicious fall. Meanwhile, we by no means deny that the protoplasts fell by the permission of GOD. Nor do we assert that God was at least an idle spectator, as Wendelinus falsely attributes to us in Exerc. 33. §. 15.)

v. 29. Οὐχὶδύοςρουθία &c. Moschopulus. ςρουίαδὶ Melius ergo aviculae, quàm passerculi intelliguntur, cùm & Graecum & Syriacum vocabulum aves in genere notet. *(B. D. Chemnitio tamen magis arridet, si passerculi intelligantur, cùm sint contemtissima avis, si quidem iuxta Plinium. l. 10. c. 36. sint minimum vitae iuxta alios quoque, lepram & morbum caducum saepiùs incurrant.)*

Sine coelis (i. e. divino nutu) ne una quidē capta est aucupio, quanto minùs tot & tot animae filiorū hominis. Totam fabulam refert Lud. Capellus Spicil. p. 20. Non dissimilis quoque est gnome Maiemonidis in More Nevochim part. 3. c. 48. Si Deus bestiarum & avium curam gerit, ne dolore afficiantur,כל שכן בבני ארםquanto magis rationem habebit hominum. Memorat Buxtorffius Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 176. Ubi & alia nonnulla habet huc facientia: 1. Argumentatur verò Christus à minori ad maius. Estque testimonium hoc satis etiam clarum de providentiâ divinâ generali argumentum. Nec obstat dictum 1. Cor. 9, 9. quod enim accipiendum hoc sit non ἁπλῶς, sed κατὰ τὶ patet tum ex contextu, tum ex aliis Sc. S. dictis, uti Sap. 8, 1. c. 12, 13. Ps. 36, 6.Act. 17, 28. & alibi passim.)*

Christum hoc dixisse aur diversis temporibus atque sic utramque locutionem adhibuisse, aut uno utrum que protulisse hunc in modum: nonne duo passeres asse vend untur unico? imò nunquid quinque veniunt dipondio.)*

Talm. voce אנםר Iuxta B. D. Chemn H. E. p. 799. notat dimidiatum nummū vel obolum. Porrò de numismatibus Ebraeorum, Graecorum, Romanorum consuli possunt B. Camero t. 2. Praelect. Alcasar Append. in Apocalypsin, Ioh. Bapt. Villalpandus in Ezechielem, Budaeus de Asse, Londinenses in Apparatu, Bibliis Polygl. promisso tr. 2. Renerus Rudelius Ruremundanus, Scaliger, Schnellius, -oachimus Camerarius, Iacobus Capellus, Marq. Freherus, Iacobus Bornitius, Pontus Heuterus, Constantinus Landus Complani Comes, Goltzius, Fulvius -rsinus, Abrahamus Gor aeus, Matthaeus Hostius, Fr. Hottomannus, Henricus Uranius, Alexander Sardus Aeneas Vicus & alii plurimi. * ( Sine Patre vestro i. e. absque DEI voluntate. Ineptè hinc quidam Cal vini-ni evincere conantur, quòd si absq; volunluntate Dei non cadit passerculus, nec primi parentes absque votate, nempe complacentiae & impulsu (nam, de hoc est quaestio) in peccatum fuerint prolapsi. Cùm omninò dist. sit inter lapsum physicum, & moralem. h. e. absque peccato, & cum peccato coniunctum, seu lapsum peccaminosum ac malitiosum. Interea minimè refragamur, quòd DEI permissione protoplasti lapsi sint. Nec adserimus, quòd otiosus saltem Deus fuerit spectator, ceu Wendelinus nobis affingit Exerc. 33. §. 15.)*

## 10:30
v. 30. But your hairs &c. Phesichta f. 18. col. 4. Do I not number all the hairs of every creature? A phrase taken from 1 Sam. 14, 45. *(Ineptly, certain Papists draw an argument from the present saying for the cult of relics. Chamier responds to that in t. 2. Panstr. lib. 20. cap. 9. that this place deals with the living, and not only with the saints. But we concede that the hairs of those who died piously in Christ, no less than their bones, are a care to God. Yet by no means can be inferred from this. Therefore, the relics of holy men are to be adored or pursued with religious cult. The hairs of the living are also numbered, which, however, no one pursues with religious cult for that reason. We by no means deny, however, that the relics of the saints are to be honored with an honest burial. Otherwise, from the present saying, the ancient Doctors of the Church gathered the resurrection of the dead, whose opinions were adduced by the blessed P. L. de Resurr. mort. §. 15. and in Harm. Evang. c. 106. p. 691. August. in Ps. 109.They are terrified in death concerning their souls. He gave them security even concerning their hairs. Does the soul truly perish, whose hair does not perish? Moreover, this care and protection is insinuated elsewhere in Holy Scripture, as is evident 2 Sam. 14, 11. 1 Kings 1, 52. Acts 27, 34.

Latin:

v. 30. Vestri autem capilli &c. Phesichta f. 18. col. 4. Nonne omnes capillos omnis creaturae ego numero? Phrasis desumta ex 1. Sam. 14, 45. *(Ineptè è praesenti dicto Pontificii quidam argumētum arcessunt pro cultu reliquiarum. Respondet ad illud Chamier. t. 2. Panstr. lib. 20. cap. 9. agi h. l. de viventibus, nec de solis sanctis. Verùm concedimus, etiam piè in Christo defunctorum capillos non minùs ac ossa Deo curae esse. Minimè tamen hinc inferri potest. E. Sanctorum hominum reliquiae sunt adorandae vel religioso cultu prosequendae. Etiam vivorum capilli numerati, quos tamen nemo cultu religioso propterea prosequitut. Honorandas tamen sanctorum reliquias honestâ sepulturâ esse, minimè negamus? Coeterùm è praesenti dicto Veteres Ecclesiae Dd. mortuorum resurrectionem collegerunt, quorum sententiae adductae à B. P. L. de Resurr. mort. §. 15. it. Harm. Evang. c. 106. p. 691. August. in Ps. 109.Illi in morte de animabus suis pertime scant. Ille ipsis securitatem etiam de capillis dabat. It ane vero anima perit, cuius capillus non perit? Insinuatur autem & alibi in Sc. S. phrasi hâc cura ac tutela, ceu patet ex. 2. Sam. 14, 11. 1. Reg. 1, 52.Act. 27. 34.)*

## 10:31
v. 31. You are of more value than many sparrows. For you are not only men, that is, rational creatures created by GOD, redeemed by Christ, and sanctified by the Holy Spirit, but also witnesses of divine truth and heralds of the Gospel, whom God, as His servants, takes under His protection.) *

Latin:

* (v. 31. Multis praestatis passerculis. Estis enim non solùm homines h. e. creaturae rationales à DEO creati, à Christo redemti & à Sp. S. sanctificati, verùm etiam divinae veritatis testes & Evangelii praecones, quos Deus ut servos suos in patrocinium suum fascipit.) *

## 10:32
v. 32. Whoever will confess ὐν ἐμοὶ i.e. in my name. It is a peculiar expression. Ἐξομολογεῖν has the meaning of celebrated preaching and free confession. ὐν ἐμοὶ i.e. ρὶ ἐμοῦ A Hebraism. Ps. 87, 3. glorious things are spoken of t-.

I will also confess him. Ambrose, 1 de poenit. c. 2. t. 1. p. 114. Where he confesses, he confesses for all, he embraces all. Where he denies, he does not deny all. For just as it is held above, everyone who will have confessed me, I will also confess him, i.e. everyone, it was consequent that he should say below as follows: But everyone who will have denied me. But lest he should seem to deny all, he thus added: But whoever will have denied me before men, I will also deny him. He promises grace to all, he does not threaten injury to all. That which is of mercy, he exaggerates; that which is of u-tion, he diminishes.

Before men. By men he understands especially those who persecute the pious, and against whom he warns v. 17. to be on guard. For thus Mark 8, 38. he himself interprets. Whoever will have confessed me in this adulterous generation. Chrysostom, hom. 25. in Matth. Alet Christians say, if the necessity of persecution arrives, before men I will deny with my mouth, but in my heart I hold the truth, therefore not, Christ says: whoever will have confessed me in his heart, but before men. For he who does not confess before men, it is of no profit that he believes in Christ with his heart, because he who denies with his mouth, it cannot happen that he believes in his heart. The root of confession is the faith of the heart, but confession is the fruit of faith. Therefore, just as long as the root is alive, it is necessary that it produce branches or leaves: if it has not produced them, without doubt you understand that its root has dried up in the earth: thus as long as the faith of the heart is whole, it always germinates confession in the mouth, etc. If confession of the heart were sufficient for you, God would have created only a heart for you, but now he has also created a mouth. (Moreover, the sermon in this place is about confession proceeding from true faith, and joined with final constancy. Conf. Rom. 10, 9. 10. and thus the effect of faith is put here for faith itself, according to Dr. Hutter in F. C. p. 366. 369. and Dr. Hafenreff. LL. Th. p. 684.) I will confess him, namely as a faithful servant and heir of the heavenly kingdom. (The parallel passages are Luke 12, 8. Rev. 2, 17.)

Latin:

v. 32. Qui confitibiturὐν ἐμοὶ i. e. in meo nomine. Est peculiaris locutio. Ἐξομολογεῖν significationem habet celebris praedicationis & liberae confessionis. ὐν ἐμοὶ i. e. ρὶ ἐμοῦ Hebraismus. Ps. 87. 3.mirabilia dicantur in t-.

Consit ebor & ego. Ambrosius 1. de poenit. c. 2. t. 1. p. 114. Ub confitetur, pro omnibus confitetur, omnes complectitur. Ubi negat, non omnes negat. Sicut enim suprà habetur, omnis qui me confessus fuerit, confitebor & ego eum i. e. omnem, consequens erat, ut infra quosic diceret: Omnis autem qui negaverit me. Sed ne omnes negare videretur, ita subiecit: Qui autem negaverit me coram nominibus, negabo & ego eum. Gratiam promittit omnibus non omnibus minatur iniuriam. Quod est miserationis, exaggerat; quod est u-tionis, extenuat.

Coram hominibus. Per homines intelligit potissimùm eos, qui pios persequuntur, & à quibus cavendum, v. 17. monnit. Sic enim Marc. 8, 18. ipse interpretatur. Qui me confessus fuerit in generatione istâ adiltera. Chrysostomus hom. 25. in Matth.
