Adicant Christiani, si necessit as persecutionis advenerit, cor--minibus ore denegabo, in corde autem veritatem teneo, ideo non, dicit Christus: qui me confessus fuerit in corde, sed coram hominibus. Qui enim coram hominibus non confitetur, non prodest, quòd corde in Christum credit, quia qui ore denegat, non potest fieri, ut in corde credat. Radix confessionis fides est cordis, confessio autem fructus fidei. Sicut ergo quamdiu radix est viva, necesse est, ramos producat aut folia: si non produxerit, sine dubio intelligis, quòd radix eius in terra siccata est: sic quamdiu cordis fides integra est, semper germinat confessionem in, ore &c. Si tibi sufficeret confessio cordis, cor tantùm Deus tibi creasset, nunc autem & os creavit. * (Sermo autem h. l. est de confessione ex verâ fide profectâ, & cum finali constantiâ coniuncta Conf. Rom. 10, 9. 10. pontiurque adeò hîc effectus fidei, pro ipsa fide, iuxta D. Hutterum in F. C. p 366. 369. ac D. Hafenreff. LL. Th. p. 684.)* Consitebor eum, sc pro fideli servo & regni coelestis haerede. *(Loca parallela sunt Luc. 12, 8.Apoc. 2, 17.)*

## 10:33
(v. 33. Whoever however shall deny me &c. Parallel passages are Mark 8, 38.Luke 9, 26.chap. 12, 9.2 Tim. 2, 12. Understand however nor shall have done penance. For the example of Peter teaches that the words of the Savior are to be understood in this way. Whence it is also established that the Novatians erred, denying pardon to those who in the time of persecution had denied the heavenly truth, but were seriously grieving over that committed sin, or at least leaving them doubtful whether they were about to obtain from GOD the remission of the denial. Nor is there any reason why the Novatians should object, that pardon can indeed be obtained from God, but that the Church sometimes (namely in the case of denial) cannot give it. For to whom God has given the hope of pardon, why should man deny it to him? Nor did God give the power of loosening and binding sins here on earth to the Church in such a way that He granted it to her only in some sins, and not in all, as the blessed D. Horneius well advises in Comp. Theolog. b. 2. c. 4. §. 39. Let also the blessed Par. L. on Penance §. 14, 15. and the blessed D. Dorscheus in his singular dissertation on the heresy of the Novatians be seen.)

( I will deny him also &c. It seems to stand in the way John 5, 45. Resp. Euthymius, by explaining the passage of John thus: Although it was fitting to do so, I will by no means do it, because I am merciful. Bede: I do not accuse for this reason, because I did not come to condemn, but to save. Distinguish between the first advent of Christ and the second. The latter is of justice, the former of mercy.)

From the fact, however, that Christ is about to deny again, that is, to condemn, those who have denied Him before men, it is manifest that the Elcesaites erred gravely, who, as Eusebius reports from Origen b. 6. H. E. c. 31. taught, that the denial of the faith is a certain indifferent thing. Which error others also held afterwards, as will be warned more fully in the Anal. on Luke 12:9.)*

Latin:

*(v. 33. Quisquis autem negaverit me &c. Loca parall. sunt Marc. 8, 38.Luc. 9, 26.cap. 12, 9.2. Tim. 2, 12. Subintellige verò nec poenitentiam egerit. Ita enim verba Salvatoris intelligenda esse, docet exemplum Petri. Unde etiam constat, errasse Novatianos, iis qui tempore persecutionis coelestem veritatem abnegaverant, sed ob commissum illud peccatum seriò dolebant, veniam denegantes, vel certè num abnegationis remissionem à DEO consecuturi, dubios relinquentes. Nec est, quod excipiant Novatiani, impetrari quidem apud Deum veniam posse, sed Ecclesiam interdum (nempe in abnegationis casu) dare non posse. Etenim cui Deus spem veniae fecit, cur illi eam homo neget? Nec ita Deus potestatem solvendi & ligandi peccata hîc in terris Ecclesiae dedit, ut eam illi in aliqua tantùm peccata, & non in omnia concederet, uti benè monet B. D. Horneius Comp. Theolog. l. 2. c. 4. §. 39. Videantur quoque B. Par. L. de Poenit. §. 14, 15. ac B. D. Dorscheus in dissertatione singulari de haeresi Novatianorū.) *

* ( Negabo eum & ega &c. Videtur obstare Ioh. 5, 45. Resp. Euthymius, locum Iohannis ita exponendo: Etsime id facere oportebat, minimè tamen faciam, quia clemens sum. Beda: ideò non accuso, quia non veni damnare, sed salvare. Dist. inter adventum Christi primum & secundum. Hic iustitiae, ille misericordiae.

Ex eo autem quòd Christus eos, qui ipsum coram hominibus negaverint, iterum abnegaturus h. e. condemnaturus, manifestum, est, graviter errasse Helcesaitas, qui uti ex Orig. refert Eusebius l. 6. H. E. c. 31. docuerunt, fidei negationem indifferens quiddam esse. Quem errorem & alii postmodum tenuerunt, ceu pluribus monebitur in Anal. ad Luc. 12, 9.)*

## 10:34
v. 34. Do not think that I came to send peace i.e., to bring such a doctrine as all might promptly receive and live in peace together. *(Rightly does B. D. Glassius, Gram. S. p. 298, warn that the proper action and final cause of Christ and the Gospel are not designated here (for the contrary is otherwise evident from Zech. 9:10.Rom. 5:1.c. 12:18.Eph. 2:17.Matt. 5:44.Luke 10:2538. Conflicts arise not from the nature of the Gospel, but from the malice of men resisting the truth), but only those things which were to follow κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς the coming of Christ and the preaching of the Gospel, etc. Therefore, it must be held firmly and fixed in the mind that the benefits of Christ pertain primarily to the future life. And it must be known that the peace of Christ is spiritual, not worldly. Whence the prophecies of Isa. 2:4.c. 11:6.Zech. 9:10. do not contradict the present assertion; for the Savior speaks here of earthly, worldly peace, the Prophets of spiritual peace, of which Christ also speaks John 14:27. and the Apostle Phil. 4:7.Rom. 14:17. Furthermore, Mr. D. Müller in Judaism p. 1049 and Simon Episcopus l. 3. Instit. Theol. c. 21 have responded at greater length to the argument of the Jews, which they draw from this passage to prove that the Messiah has not yet come, because his advent does not agree with the prediction of Isaiah c. 2 and 11. Places parallel to this of ours are Ps. 2:1, 2, 3.Ps. 4:7.Luke 12:51, 52.Acts 4:27.)*

* ( But a sword. Ostorodus, c. 18. Instit., thinks that the words of Christ cannot be understood as a dissension which is carried out by the sword, but that by sword are figuratively understood at least dissensions or quarrels. And from this he further attempts to prove that even in Rom. 13:4. the word sword ought to be taken figuratively, and that the Magistrate ought not and cannot inflict capital punishments. But although we do not deny that the word sword is sometimes used figuratively in Holy Scripture, nor do we deny that in the verses immediately following, domestic dissensions, which are stirred up and composed even without the shedding of blood, are submitted by Christ as examples , yet the testimonies in the primitive Church speak sufficiently that the proper [meaning] of the word The meaning of sword may likewise have a place here also. There are, however, those who do not understand sword here as persecutions, but as the sword of the divine word. Just as Blas. Viegas writes in ch. 9 of the Apocalypse, p. 398, the sword divides those things which are united and joined, so the sword of the divine word and of the counsels of Christ ought to divide those things which are most closely joined, i.e., to dissect the carnal affections of parents and blood relatives, and every conjunction of the flesh, in order to follow Christ more freely. Similarly, Cardinal Toletus also explains this in this place in Luke, p. 770. This sense seems to be confirmed by v. 37. and the following, but v. 35. and 36. favor the former exposition more.

Latin:

v. 34. Nolite putare, me venisse, ut pacem mitterem i. e. talem afferre doctrinam, quam omnes promtè recipiant & in pace simul vivant. *(Renè monet B. D. Glassius. Gram. S. p. 298. non designari hîc propriam Christi & Evangelii actionem & causam finalem, (contrarium enim aliàs patet ex Zach. 9, 10.Rom. 5, 1.c. 12, 18.Eph. 2, 17.Matth. 5, 44.Luc. 10, 2538. Pugnae oriuntur non ex Evangelii naturâ, sed hominum veritati resistentium malitiâ) sed duntaxat, quae Christi adventum & Evangelii praedicationem κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς erant secutura &c. Probè igitur firmiterque tenendum ac animo infigendum, quòd Christi beneficia potissimùm ad futuram spectent vitam. Sciendumq;, quòd pax ChriChristi sit spiritualis, non mundana. Unde nec contrariantur praesenti adserto vaticinia Es. 2, 4.c. 11, 6.Zach. 9, 10. loquitur enim Salvator hîc de pace terrenâs. mundanâ, Prophetae de spirituali, de qua etiam loquitur Christus Ioh. 14, 27. & Apostolus Phil. 4. 7.Rom. 14, 17. Coeterùm prolixiùs ad argumentum Iudaeorum, quòd ex hoc loco depromunt, ad evincendum, quòd Messias nōdum venerit, eò quòd adventus eius non conveniat cum praedictione Esaiae. c. 2. & 11. responderunt Dn. D. Müllerus in Iudaismo p. 1049. Simon Episcopus l. 3. Instit. Theol. c. 21. Loca buic nostra parall sunt Ps. 2, 1. 2. 3.Ps. 4, 7.Luc. 12, 51. 52.Act. 4, 27.)*

* ( Sed gladium. Existimat Ostoro dus, c. 18. Instit non; posse verba Christi intelligi de dissidio, quod gladio peragitur, sed per gladium figuratè intelligi dissidia saltem s. rixas Atque hinc porrò evincere conatur, quôd etiam Rom. 13. 4. Vox gladii figuratè accipi debeat, quòd que Maggistratus non debeat nec possit capitalia supplicia irrogare. Verùm licet non negemus, vocabulum gladii aliquando figuratè in Sc. S. adhiberi, nec eamus infi cias, in versiculis mox seqq. domesticorum dissidia, quae absque sangvinis effusione moventur ac componuntur etiam, exempli loca à Christo subiici, satis tamen martyria in primitiva Ecclesia loquūtur, quòd propria vocis gladii significatio pariter hîc quoq; locū habeat. Sunt tamen qui nomine gladii non intelligunt hîc persectiones, sed gladium verbi divini. Sicut, scribit Blas. Viegas in c. 9. Apoc. p. 398. gladius ea, quae sunt unita & coniuncta dividit, ita gladius verbi divini & consiliorum Christi debet ea, quae sunt maximè coniuncta, dividere. i. e. carnales parentum & consangvineorum affectus, omnemque carnis coniunctionem ad liberiùs Christum sequendum dissecare. Similiter etiam explicat h. l. Card. Toletus in Luc. p. 770. Videtur sensus hic confirmari v. 37. seqq. sed priori expositioni magis favet v. 35. & 36.)*

## 10:35
v. 35. ἠλθον διχὰσαι ἄνθρωπον. The word ἀνθρώπου or man is put for son. *(And thus Beza also translates, as well as the Persian, if indeed the Latin interpreter is to be trusted here. The Arab and the Ethiopian, however, imitate the Hebraism; the Syrian renders it by man. Luther likewise explains it as man, which was also done by the Vulgate and Erasmus.)* A similar phrase is in Prov. 21, 20. Sirac. 3, 13. The sense is that the sons of this age will persecute the confessors of the Gospel without any regard for kinship.

Latin:

v. 35. ἠλθον διχὰσαι ἄνθρωπον. Vox ἀνθρώπου sive hominis ponitur pro filio. *(Et ita quoque vertit Beza, nec non Persa, si quidem interpreti Latino habenda hîc fides est. Arabs tamen & Aethiops Ebraismum imitantur, Syrus reddit per virum. Lutherus itidem hominem exponit, quod etiam à Vulgato & Erasmo factum.)* Similis phrasis Prov. 21, 20.Sirac. 3, 13. Sensus est, quòd filii huius seculi confessores Evangelii sint persecuturi absque ullo cognationis respectu.

## 10:36
v. 30. A man's enemies are those of his own household. Taken from Mich. 7, 6. Seneca, ep. 141: As many servants, so many enemies. Impious persecutors, having broken the bonds of nature, rise up hostiley even against those of their own household and those most closely joined by blood.

Latin:

v. 30. Inimici hominis domestici eius. Desumtum ex Mich. 7, 6. Seneca ep. 141. Qùot servi, tot hostes. Impil persecutores ruptis naturae vinculis etiam contra domesticos & sanguine con-iunctissimos hostiliter insurgunt.

## 10:37
* (v. 37. He who loves father or mother more than me etc. Against some Papists, who teach that children can enter monasteries even against the will of their parents, and who strive to prove this from the present saying, see Bell. l. 2. de Monach. c. 26, it is to be noted that Christ desires such a love of GOD that if father, mother, etc., persuade one to act against God, one should flee them, as the Jesuit Conzen himself explains on Matthew, p. 211, who also warns that the perfection of leaving all things (to which they are accustomed to refer the Monastic state) is not being counseled here, but that it is a commandment to prefer nothing to GOD. See more on this in B. D. Bald. in 1 Tim. c. 5. quest. 3, p. 1346 and following; B. Par. L de Coniug. §. 522; Confess. Cathol. t. 3, p. 346 and following.)*

Latin:

* (v. 37. Qui amat patrem aut matrem supra me &c. Contra Pontificios nonnullos, docentes, quòd etiam invitis Parentibus liberi possint intrare Mònasteria, idque è praesenti dicto probare satagunt, vid Bell. l. 2. de Monach. c. 26. notandum, quòd Christus talem DEI amorem velit, ut si Pater, mater &c. contra Deum agere suadeant, eos fugiat, ceu ipse Iesuita Conzen Matth. p. 211. explicat, qui etiam monet, quòd hîc non consulatur perfectio omnia relinquendi (quo referre solent statum Monasticum) sed praeceptum sit, nihil DEO anteponendi. Plura in hanc vid. apud B. D. Bald. in 1 Tim. c. 5. quaest. 3. p 1346. seqq. B. Par. L de Coniug. §. 522. Confess. Cathol. t. 3. p. 346. seqq.)*

## 10:38
v. 38. Follows me from behind. The afflictions of Christians ought to have Christ as their leader and standard-bearer. *(Whence it appears what is to be thought of the flagellations and hairshirts of the Monks, concerning which see more in B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. 4, p. 114 and following.)*

Latin:

v. 38. Sequitur me à tergo. Afflictiones Christianorum debent habere ducem & antesignanum Christum. *(Unde paret, quid de flagellationibus & ciliciis Monachorum habendum sit, de quibus pluribus Vid. B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. 4. p. 114. seqq.)*

## 10:39
v. 39. He who finds his soul. Soul according to the manner of the Hebrews is accepted for life. He who finds his soul, i. e. he who thinks * (according to the rule which the blessed D. Glassius delivers in Gr. S. p. 282. &c.)* that he has found by the abnegation of the Gospel a means by which he can protect his life and obtain good days in this life, loses it, because, to wit, he falls into eternal death. Christ speaks according to the common usage, of those who think they have found life, when they have snatched it from the grave danger of death.

Latin:

v. 39. Qui invenerit animam suam. Anima more Hebraeorum accipitur pro vita. Qui invenit animam suam, i. e. qui putat * (iuxta reg. quam tradit B D. Glassius Gr. S. p. 282. &c.)* se per abnegationē Evangelii invenisse medium, quo vitam suam tueri ac dies bonos in hâc vitâ obtinere possit, amittit eā, quia sc. in aeternam mortem incidit. Cum vulgo Christus loquitur, qui putantse vitam invenisse, cùm ex gravi mortis periculo eam eripuerint.

## 10:40
* (v. 40. He who receives you, i. e. he who holds you for my Legates, 1. Cor. 4, 1.2. Cor. 5, 20. hears your word as mine, 1. Thess. 2, 13. &c. Compare Luc. 10, 16.1. Cor. 2, 1.1. Tim. 5, 17.Ebr. 13, 17. does good to you, Matth. 10, 14.c. 25, 40.Gal. 4, 14,c. 6, 6. receives me, as being my ministers. Compare more on the sense of the present passage in the blessed Par. H. E. c. 170. p. 1071. The observation of Barth. Mayer, Philol S. Part. 2. p. 170. seqq. also makes for this, noting that קבל received sometimes signifies the same as שמע hearkened, was obedient to the word, as Gen. 3, 17.c. 21, 12.c. 28, 7.Deut. 18, 15.Exod. 19, 5. & so in this place Gr δέχομαι is also to be taken. The same is maintained by Dn. D. Calov. Crit S. p. 454.)

Latin:

* (v. 40. Qui vos recipit, i. e. qui vos pro meis Legatis habet, 1. Cor. 4, 1.2. Cor. 5, 20. verbum vestrum, ut meum audit, 1. Thess. 2, 13. &c. Conf. Luc. 10, 16.1. Cor. 2, 1.1. Tim. 5, 17.Ebr. 13, 17. vobis benefacit, Matth. 10, 14.c. 25, 40.Gal. 4, 14,c. 6, 6.me excipit, quippe meos ministros. Conf. plura de praesentis loci sensu apud B. Par. H. E. c. 170. p. 1071 Huc facit etiam observatio Barth. Mayeri, Philol S. Part. 2. p. 170. seqq. notantis, quòd קבלaccepit aliquando idem significet quod שמעaudivit, dicto obediens fuit, uti Gen. 3, 17.c. 21, 12.c. 28, 7.Deut. 18, 15.Exod. 19, 5. & ita h. l. Gr δέχομαι etiam sumi. Idem statuit Dn. D. Calov. Crit S. p. 454.)

## 10:41
v. 41. In the name of a Prophet i. e. to the glory of GOD, because he is such a minister of God, sent by Him. By Prophet συννεκδοχικῶς is understood any sincere preacher of the Gospel.

He shall receive a Prophet's reward. i. e. a far most ample one, such as God promised to the Prophets.

* ( Reward. The word reward in this place is accepted not for merce- properly so called, as Hagerus Coll. A. C. p. 85 87. Coster. Enchir. p. 274. Bell. t. 4. &c. & from the present saying among other things attempt to prove: but for the reward of grace. This was noted long ago by August. in c. 4. ad Rom. That of his also makes for this, brought forward by the Jesuit Hagerus himself in Coll. A. C. p. 83: O great goodness of God! to whom when we ought to render obedience according to our condition, as being servants to the Lord; He promises back to us the rewards of friends, so that He may extort from us the due services of servitude. Compare what is noted at c. 5, 12. & 6, 1.)*

He who receives a just man in the name of a just man i. e. not because he is a kinsman, a friend, rich, honored, from whom a compensation is to be expected, but solely because he is such a one, whom he receives, is pious and fears God.

Latin:

v. 41. In nomine Prophetae i. e. ad DEI gloriam, propterea quòd talis est minister Dei, ab ipso missus. Per Prophetamσυννεκδοχικῶς intelligitur quivis sincerus Evangelii praedicator.

Accipiet Prophetae mercedem. i. e. longè amplissimam, qualem Deus promisit Prophetis.

* ( Mercedem. Vocabulum mercedis h. l. accipitur non pro merce- propriè dictâ, uri Hagerus Coll. A. C. p. 85 87. Coster. Enchir. p. 274. Bell. t. 4. &c. & ex praesenti dicto inter alia evincere conantur: sed pro mercede gratiae. Pridem hoc notatum ab August. in c. 4. ad Rom. Huc facit & illud eiusdem, ab ipso Iesuita Hagero in Coll. A. C. p. 83. adductūc Omagna bonitas Dei! cui cùm pro conditione reddere debeamus obsequi-, utpote ser-i Domino; amicorum nobis praemia repromittit, ut à nobis obsequia debitae servitutis extorqueat. Conf. quae not. ad c. 5, 12. & 6, 1.)*

Qui recipii iustum in nomine iusti i. e. non quòd sit cognatus, amicus, dives, honoratus, à quo compensatio sit expectanda, sed unicè proptereà, quin talis, quem recipit, est pius ac Deum timens.

## 10:42
v. 42. Ποτήριον ψυχροῦ, is to be understood δατος.. Surus hints at this with the plural word רקוירא of cold, which looks to the substantive מיא.. The Vulgate completed the ellipsis in the Greek, & explains a cup of cold water. *(The same also done by the Arab & Aethiop. e)* Compare Ps. 73, 10.2. Sam. 21, 16.

ού μὴ. A double negation denies more strongly.

(THE things which are treated in the present chapter can be recalled to five members: For there is proposed 1. The preaching of Christ. 2. The sending away of the disciples of John to him, and their instruction. 3. The testimony of Christ concerning John, and his notable commendation. 4. The complaint of Christ concerning the ingratitude of the Jews and his grave threatening. 5. And the thanksgiving of the same to the heavenly Father for the revelation and spreading of the Gospel, and his friendly invitation of sinners.)

Latin:

v. 42. Ποτήριον ψυχροῦ, subintell. δατος. Innuit hoc Surus plurali vooe רקויראfrigidarum, quae respicit substantivum מיא. Vulgatus ellipsin in Graeco complevit, & calicem aquae frigidae exponit. *(Idem quoq; factum ab Arabè ac Aethiop. e)* Confer Ps. 73, 10.2. Sam. 21, 16.

ού μὴ. Duplex negatio fortiùs negat.

*(QUAE in praesenti capite tractantur, ad quinq; revocari membra possunt: Proponitur enim 1. Christi praedicatio. 2. Discipulorum Iohannis ad eum ablega tio, eorundemq; informatio. 3. Christi de Iohanne testificatio, eiusque insignis commendatio. 4. Christi de Iudaeorum ingratitudine querela ac gravis comminatio. 5. Eiusdemque ad patrē coelestem pro Evangelii revelatione ac dilatatione gratiarum actio, & amica peccatorum invitatio.)*

## 11:1
(v. 1. διατάσσων to ordain. This τάξις embraces the instruction and information of the Apostles. And it is hinted that the ministers of the Church ought not to run rashly, but to await a legitimate calling and mission, Jer. 23, 21. since in the Church all things ought to be done κατὰ τάξιν καὶ εὐχημόνως, 1. Cor. 14, 40. Against the Anabaptists and Photinians, concerning whom can be consulted B. P. L. on the Ministers of the Church §. 64. seqq. Dn. D. Walth. Cent. Miscell. Q. 46. Dn. D. Calovius Socin. Proflig. p. 951. seqq. But what things are required for a legitimate calling, and also, whether anyone can desert an Ecclesiastical function and seek a new one, then also what things ought to be observed concerning the removal of Ministers of the Church, are prolixly expounded by the praised Dn. D. Walth. 1. c. Q. 1. B. D. Gerlachius t. 2. Dispp. Theol. p. 4002. seqq. B. D. Tarnovius in a special disputation on the abdication of the Ministers of the word &c. held at Rostock in the year 1620, and printed in the same place. B. D. Bald Disp. 17. on the Art. Smalk especially Dedekennus Consil. Theol. Vol. 1. part. 3. B. D. Hutter. LL. Th. p. 1032. seqq.)

( He departed. Namely, he followed the Apostles. Conf. Luke 20, 1. For he performed the office of both preacher and Visitor, as did Paul and Barnabas, Acts 14, 20. c. 15, 36.)

( καὶ κηρύσσειν & to preach. So also the Vulgate itself, and it translates correctly. Since therefore the Savior himself performed the office of preaching, it is a wonder how the Papists persuade themselves that they do us a great favor, when) They call us Preachers out of contempt, although this is the highest dignity, to preach the word of GOD purely, and to perform the same office which John the Baptist and the Apostles performed, indeed which Christ himself deigned to perform, as is evident from the present passage, and likewise from Matth. 3, 1.cap. 4, 17.c. 9. 35.c. 10, 7. & 27. etc. Furthermore, the Blessed D. Chemn. observes in Harm. Ev. page 806, from Theophylact, that the Lord studiously abstained from performing miracles as long as the Apostles were preaching and had been sent to perform miracles, so that their authority might be so much the greater. He adds: Miracles are not always and perpetually seals following sincere doctrine, in order to confirm it. But when the doctrine is already confirmed, there is no longer need for miracles. For just as the gift of tongues, so also the remaining miracles are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers. 1. Cor. 14, 22. Conf. B. D. Hōpsn, Sax. Evang. p. 64. 67. And from this it is also manifest that nothing is lacking to the ministry of the Blessed Luther, even if in the work of reformation he perhaps did not confirm with new miracles the heavenly doctrine which he himself preached. Nor, however, do we concede that Luther's Ministry lacked every miracle. For if anyone considers that singular gift of interpreting the Scriptures, and of purging the same from the Pontifical leaven, the revelation of the Anti-Christ, which was brought about by Luther's ministry, his intrepid spirit and the wonderful progress of the reformation, he will be forced to confess entirely that what that author has in the life of Ludov. Granatensis is not inappropriately applied to the Blessed Luther, while he says thus: The reader will perhaps ask me whether our Ludovicus performed any miracles, to whom I will answer the same thing which, as John Gerson, Chancellor of Paris, testifies, the supreme Pontiff John XXII once answered in the college of Cardinals, when enrolling the great Doctor of the Church, St. Thomas Aquinas, in the catalogue of Saints, namely, that although St. Thomas had never performed any miracle which would persuade one that he should be referred to the number of the Saints, he considered each and every article which he wrote to be like a miracle. And indeed, the said author continues, not undeservedly; for if we consider the method of his books, the series of writing, etc., no one at all will be found who would not immediately judge all this order of writing to be more sublime than that it should proceed from human ingenuity, etc. The same thing can and ought indeed to be said far more rightly concerning very many of the actions of the Blessed Luther.

TO CHAPTER XI. SUMMARY AND DISPOSITION.

In their cities. i.e. of the Apostles, that is, in the cities of Galilee, which were the fatherland of the Apostles, or which they had traversed while preaching. *(That it may thus be understood of the cities of the Israelites, to which the Apostles had been sent, so that they might preach the Gospel therein. See the preceding chapter v. 6. and this latter view pleases the Blessed D. Chemnitius in H. E. Let it be noted here indeed the Hebraism, by which the antecedent of the relative pronoun is not expressed, but is left to be understood from the circumstances, as if already known to the reader. For examples see Ps. 99, 8. 1. Reg. 5, 3. 2. Reg. 17, 24. below c. 12, 9.)*

Latin:

*(v. 1. διατάσσωνordinandi. Complectitur haec τάξις Apostolorum instructionem ac informationem. Innuiturq;, quòd ministri Ecclesiae non temerè currere debeant, sed expectare legitimam vocationem ac missionem, Ier. 23, 21. cùm in Eccleclesia omnia fieri debeant κατὰ τάξιν καὶ εὐχημόνως,1. Cor. 14, 40. Contra Anabapt. ac Photinianos. de quibus consuli possunt B. P. L. de Ministr. Eccles. §. 64. seqq. Dn. D. Walth. Cent. Miscell. Q. 46. Dn. D. Calovius Socin. Proflig. p. 951. seqq. Quae verò ad vocationem legitimam requirantur, itemque, num quis functionem Ecclesiasticam deserere ac novam appetere possit, tum quoq; quae circa Ministrorum Ecclesiae remotionem observanda sint, prolixè exponunt laudatus Dn. D. Walth. 1. c. Q. 1. B. D. Gerlachius t. 2. Dispp. Theol. p. 4002. seqq. B. D. Tarnovius in pecul. disput. de Ministr. verbi abdicatione &c. Rostochii Ao. 1620. habitâ, ibidemque impressâ. B. D. Bald Disp. 17. ad Art. Smalk cumprimis Dedekennus Consil. Theol. Vol. 1. part. 3. B. D. Hutter. LL. Th. p. 1032. seqq.)*

*( Digressus est. Sequutus nempe est Apostolos. Conf. Luc. 20, 1. Functus enim est officio tum praedicatoris, tum Visitatoris, ceu Paulas ac Barnabas, Act. 14, 20.c. 15, 36.)*

*( καὶ κηρύσσειν& praedicaret. Ita ipse quoque Vulgatus, & rectè vertit. Cùm igitur ipse Salvator praedicandi officio functus fuerit, mirum est, quomodo Pontisicii sibi persuadeant, admodùm aegrè sese nobis facere, ubi Praedicantes nos per contemtum vocant, cùm tamen summa haec dignitas sit, verbum DEI purè praedicare, eodem que munere fungi, quô Ioh. Baptista & Apostoli functi sunt, imò ipse Christus fungi dignatus est, ceu è praesenti loco, itemque ex Matth. 3, 1.cap. 4, 17.c. 9. 35.c. 10, 7. & 27. &c, patet. Observat porrò B. D. Chemn. in Harm. Ev. pag. 806. ex Theophylacto, Dominum studiosè à faciendis miraculis abstinuisse, quamdiu Apostoli praedicabant & ad edenda miracula missi fuerant, ut tantò maior illorum esset aucoritas. Addit: Neonim semper & perpetuò miracula sunt sigilla, sinceram doctrinam consequentia, ut illam confirment. Sed quando doctrina iam est confirmata, nō ampliùs opus est miraculis. Ut enim donum linguarū, ita etiam reliqua miracula, signū sunt non sidelibus sed infidelibo.1. Cor. 14, 22. Conf. B. D. Hōpsn, Sax. Evang. p. 64. 67. Atque hinc etiam manifestum est, nihil decedere B. Lutheri ministerio, ut ut in reformationis opere doctrinam coelestem, quam praedicavit ipse, novis miraculis fortè haut confirmarit. Neque tamen concedimus, quòd Lutheri Ministerium omni miraculo caruerit. Etenim si quis singulare illud Scripturas interpretandi, easdemq; à fermento. Pontificio repurgandi donum, Anti Christi revelationem, Lutheri ministerio factam, intrepidum eius animum ac mirandum reformationis progressum consideret, fateri omninò cogetur, quòd non incommodè ad B. Lutherum trahatur, quod in vitâ Ludov. Granatensis illius autor habet, dum ita: Petet forst. tan à me Lector, an ulla Ludovicus noster miracula ediderit, cui respondebo idipsum; quod teste Iohanne Gersone Cancellario Parisi. ensi, olim summus Pontifex Ioh XXII. magnum Ecclesiae Doctorem D. Thomam Aquinatem Catalago Sanctorum adscribens, in costegio Cardinalium respondit, scilicet, quamvis D. Thomas nullum unquam miraculum, quod eum in Sanctorum numerum referendum suaderet, fecisset, omnes & singulos, quos scripsit articulos, instar miraculi sese existimare. Et sanè, pergit dictus autor, non immerito; si enim methodum librorum eius scriptionisseriem &c. consideremus, nullus omninò reperietur, quin statim omnem hunc s-r-ptionis ordinem sublimiorem esse iudicet, quàm ut ab humane ingenio proficiscatur &c. Idem sanè longè rectiùs de plurimis B. Lutheri actionibus dici potest debetq;.)*

AD CAP. XI. SUMMA AC DISPOSITIO.

In civitatibus ipsorum. scil. Apostolorum i. e. in civitatibus Galilaeae, quae erant Apostolorum patria, vel quas praedicando peragrârant. *(Ut ita accipiatur de civitatibus Israelitarum, ad quas Apostoli erant missi, ut in illic Evangelium praedicarent. Vid. c. praeced. v. 6. placetque hoc posterius B. D. Chemnitio in H. E. Notetur verò hîc Ebraismus, quo pronominis relativi antecedens non exprimitur, sed ex circumstantiis, quasi iamtum lectori notum, intelligendum relinquitur. Exempla Vid. Ps. 99, 8.1. Reg. 5, 3.2. Reg. 17, 24. infrà c. 12, 9.)*

## 11:2
v. 2. ἐν δεσμωτηρίῶ. The Syrian, in the house of the bound. A prison is called δεσμωτήριον, because captives are accustomed to be held bound in prison. *(Corn. à Lap. establishes here in this place a hysterology, so that those things which Matthew narrates here concerning John from v. 2 to 20 happened before the mission of the Apostles, concerning which in the preceding Chapter 10. The same also seemed right to the Blessed Chemnitius, as one who likewise placed the history concerning the embassy of John to Christ before the sending away of the Apostles and the preaching of Christ after their sending away in H. Ev. in several chapters, for he treats of this in H. E. c. 72 & 73, of that in c. 55.)*

*( τὰ ἔργα, namely, the agreement with those things which were predicted concerning the Messiah in the O. T. Moreover, the Baptist wished his disciples to be eyewitnesses of these things, so that he might perform his office even in this also, above c. 3, 3. Marc. 1, 2. 3. Furthermore, just as runners in a race, having run the course, hand the torch to others, so John, having finished his preaching, resigned it to Christ. Compare Ioh. 3, 30.)*

He sent two of his disciples. The Syrian, by the hand of his disciples, in a Hebrew phrase. *(See Dn. Dilh. Eclog. Syr. p. 617. following, and Lud. de Dieu. Comm. to Ioh. 1, 17. also the Blessed D. Ioh. Tob. Maior in Philol. add above the note to c. 2, 17. The Syrian indeed omits the number of the sent disciples, which the Persian also does; however, the Arab and the Ethiopian, having followed the Greek text, expressly mention that John sent two of his disciples.)* Clement of Alexandria reports their names, that they were Silas and Carpus.

Latin:

v. 2. ἐν δεσμωτηρίῶ.Syrus, in domo vinctorum. Carcer dicitur δεσμωτήριον, quia in carcere vincti detineri solent captivi. *(Statuit hîc Corn. à Lap. in h. l. hysterologiam, ita, ut quae hîc de Iohanne narrat Matthaeus à v. 2. ad 20. contigerint ante missionem Apostolorum, de quà Cap. 10. praecedente. Idem quoque B. Chemnitio visum, ut qui historiam de legatione Iohannis ad Christum ablegationi Apostolorum ac Christi post horum ablegationem praedicationi itidem in H. Ev. aliquot capitibus praemisit, agit namque de hâc in H. E. c. 72. & 73. de illâ c. 55.)*

*( τὰ ἔργα, congruentia nempe cum iis, quae de Messia in V. T. praedicta. Voluit autem Baptista istorum oculatos testes esse discipulos suos, quò vel in hoc quoq; suo fungeretur officio, suprà c. 3, 3. Marc. 1, 2. 3. Praetereà quemadmodum cursores in stadio decursâ meta alteri lampada tradunt, sic Iohannes praedicatione suâ defunctus Christo eam resignavit. Conf. Ioh. 3, 30.)*

Misit duos discipulorum suorum. Syrus, per manum discipulorum suorum, phrasi Ebraicâ. *(Vid. Dn. Dilh. Eclog. Syr. p. 617. seqq. ac Lud. de Dieu. Comm. ad Ioh. 1, 17. it. B. D. Ioh. Tob. Maior in Philol. adde suprà not. ad c. 2, 17. Omittit verò Syrus numerum ablegatorum discipulorum, quod Persa quoque facit, Arabs tamen & Aethiops secuti textum Graecum disertè memorant, quòd duos è discipulis suis Iohannes miserit.)* Clemene Alexandrinus refert illorum nomina, quòd fuerint Silas & Carpus.

## 11:3
v. 3. He said to them: Art thou he that is to come &c. The parallel passage is Luc. 7, 20. John was not ignorant that Jesus was the Christ, because he had made that testified by his leaping in the womb, and he had seen the Holy Spirit descending and

remaining upon Christ, he had also heard the voice of the heavenly Father: This is my beloved Son, etc. Theophylact in this place: John did not send his disciples as if he himself were ignorant of who Jesus was, but πληροφορή--ν τοὺς μαθητάς. Hilary in Canon II on Matthew, Chrysostom in Homily 37 of the Imperfect Work, and Nicephorus in Book 1, Ecclesiastical History, Chapter 19, establish the same: He sends his disciples to Jesus, intending to abolish the opinion they had of him, for they thought John was much greater than Christ. From John 3 v. 26 and Matthew 9, 15 it appears how the disciples of John were affected toward Christ; therefore John sends them away to Christ, so that they might have a plenary knowledge of the Messiah, so that by seeking for himself, he might teach them. (Thus the Savior himself sometimes asked questions, not as if he were ignorant of those things, but so that he might instruct others. See John 6, 5 Matthew 22, 20). The same exposition, namely that John did not ask for his own sake, that is, as if he himself doubted whether Christ were the true promised Messiah, but that he might provide for his hesitating disciples, and that the supreme Physician might heal their blindness, while they held John with many others to be the Messiah Luke 3, 15 John 3, 26, is embraced by the ancients, including Cyril of Alexandria in Book 2, Thes. c. 4, Euthymius, Haymo, and others; and by most of the more recent ones. See, besides the Orthodox, Dionysius the Carthusian in this place, Thomas Stapleton in the Moral Promptuary, 2nd Sunday of Advent, p. 18, John Ferus in this place; indeed, even the Jesuits themselves, Alphonsus de Castro in Book 8 against heresies, title John the Baptist, likewise Maldonatus, Barradius, Corn. à Lapide, Tirinus, Conzen, and others in this place embrace this very one, and they deservedly prefer it to that which claims that John asked for himself, or that he asked whether Christ was about to descend into Limbo and liberate the Fathers from it, which is how Costerus twists the question of John, 3rd Sunday of Advent, p. 40 and 69, and before him Dionysius the Carthusian in this place. But especially the Jesuit Maldonatus writes explicitly concerning the latter exposition, that because a better one has not yet been found, the greatest part (which, however, will be shown elsewhere to be false) of the ancient authors has conceded to it. And his associate Adam Contzen in this place says: Those who have thought that he doubted concerning the death of Christ and his descent into hell, think less correctly. But Gregory the Great, Roman Pontiff, thought so too, and while the Jesuit refutes him so openly, I wonder how he does not fear the Papal thunderbolt.

What of the fact that Simon Episcopius the Arminian, in Book 3 of his Theological Institutions, Chapter 35, labors to obtain the words, σὺ εἶ ὁ ρχόμενος i. e. ὁ ἐλευσόμευος, not uttered, ἐρωτηματικῶς, but absolutely without questioning. Yet whether its foundations are sufficiently firm, let learned men examine.)* Jerome to Algasia q. 1. thinks, that John asked so that he might know whether he ought to preach about his coming among the dead. *(Cornelius à Lapide also mentions this exposition of Jerome, yet he adds, that that assertion of Jerome seems less appropriate and probable. It is indeed strange why Franciscus à Messana, Doctor of the Hieronymite order at Madrid, in his Treatise on the difficult places of St. Jerome, where he strives to establish most of the dogmas of the Papists from Jerome, under the title Hell, in which place he attempts to show that several recesses of hell exist according to the opinion of Jerome, passed over this passage in silence.)* But this opinion rests upon a false hypothesis concerning the limbo of the fathers, and is disapproved by Theophylact. Jerome himself also in ch. 11. M-th proves our opinion: for he writes, John asked so s--that the disciples might learn for themselves while the Master was asking. *(Nor is there any reason for anyone -icat. even if John himself did not doubt, and Christ -sset was about to die and descend to the dead, so that he might indeed free the fathers from limbo, yet his disciples -los perhaps doubted about that, and for that reason, so that they might be informed about that descent, John had sent them to Christ. For the context stands in the way. For those miracles, to the consideration of which Christ sends them back, do not prove that descent of Christ. Whence the Jesuit Maldonatus rightly judges concerning this exposition, that it is not fitting. He adds: For in what way could they have known from the miracles whether Christ was about to die &c.)* Gregory homily 6. on the Gospel says: John indeed knew that Jesus is the Messiah, yet in the meantime he himself doubted whether Christ was about to suffer and through death redeem the human race. But how could he doubt about the death of Christ, when he named him the lamb of God, John 1, 19. from Isa. 53. by which word the passion and innocence of Christ is denoted: Thomas 2. 2. q. 2. art. 7. It is not to be believed that John was ignorant that Christ was about to come to the passion, for he himself had said: Behold the lamb of GOD, foretelling his future immolation. Ambrose in ch. 7. of Luke says: John doubted not by faith, but by piety, for it seemed wonderful to him that such a man should wish to die. *(Justin Martyr also, or whoever is the author of the Questions and Answers to the Orthodox ascribed to Justin, (for that book is not the genuine offspring of Justin, B. D. Chemnitz, Whitaker, Rivet, Cocus, Perkins, Sylburg establish, led by B. Par. of Patrology p. 86.) quest. 38. p. 322. and also Tertullian book on Baptism ch. 1. 10. and likewise book 4. against Marcion ch. 18. establish, that John asked for himself, and that he himself was ignorant that Christ was that promised Messiah. But the sayings Matt. 3, 17. John 1, 32. persuade the contrary. For how could John be ignorant or doubt about Christ, who had been taught by such an illustrious revelation and sign from heaven, and had so often testified about Christ. Nor is it to be thought that he was broken by the calamity of prison or rendered doubtful: the encomium given to him by Christ in this very place v. 7. persuades otherwise.)* Burgensis in his additions says, John asked because he had known the person and office of Christ only from revelation, but not through experience. But the revelation of GOD is more certain than any experience. Furthermore John 1. he had known Christ from experience itself.

*( ὁ ἐρχόμενος. according to John Cameron in Myroth. p. 4. & 48. for ὁ ἔμελλε ἔρχεσθαι, as below c. 17, 11. ἔρχεται for ἔμελλε ἔρχε σθαι he who was to come. It is an epithet of the Messiah. See Gen. 49, 10.Deut. 18, 15.Ps. 40, 8.Es. 35, 4.Hag. 2, 8.Mal. 3, 1.Ioh. 3, 31.c. 6, 14.c. 11, 27.2. Ioh. v. 7. Why the Messiah is distinguished by this name, the blessed D. Chemnitius treats at length in H. E. c. 55. Indeed, regard was had by this name, while the Messiah was still expected, to the Prophetic oracles, by which the Messiah was promised to come in the flesh s-into this world. But this name is also accommodated to the Messiah already present, by allusion to Exod. 3, 14. add. Apoc. 1, 8.)* Προσδοκῶμεν, the present is put for the future, which is frequent in the N. T. *(See below c. 24, 40. c. 26, 29. above c. 2, 4. c. 5, 46. add. Luc. 13. 32.Ioh. 7, 27. &c.)*

Latin:

v. 3. Dixit iis: Tune is es &c. Locus parall. est Luc. 7, 20. Iohannes non ignorabat, Iesum esse Christum, quia exultatione suà in utero id testatum fecerat, ac Spiritum S. descendentem &

manentem super Christum viderat, vocem etiam Patris coelestis audierat: Hic est Filius meus dilectus &c. Theophylactus h. l. Non mittebat Iobannes discipulos quasi ipse ignoraret, quis esset Iesus, sedπληροφορή--ν τοὺς μαθητάς. Idem statuunt Hilarius Canone II. in Matth. Chrysostomus homil. 37. Oper. imperf. Niceph. l. 1. H. E. c. 19. Mittit discipulos ad Iesum, opinionem corum, quam de se habebant, aboliturus, maiorem enim multò Christo Iohannem esse, putabant. ExIoh. 3. v. 26.&Matth. 9, 15. apparet, quomodo affecti fuerint discipuli Iohannis erga Christum, ideò Iohannes ad Christum eos ablegat, ut plenariam de Messia haberent cognitionem, ut sibi quaerens, illis disceret. *(Sic ipse Salvator aliquando interrogavit, non quasi ipse ea ignoraret, sed ut alios instrueret Vid. Ioh. 6, 5.Matth. 22, 20. Eandem expositionē, quòd nempe ohannes non pro se quaesiverit, h. e. quasi ipse dubitarit, an Christus sit verus promissus Messias, sed ut discipulis suis haesitantibus consuleret, utque coecitati eorum, dum Iohannē cum multis aliis pro Messia habebant Luc. 3, 15.Ioh. 3, 26. mederetur summus Medicus, amplectuntur è veteribus etiam Cyrillut Alexandrinus l. 2. Thes. c. 4. Euthymius, Haymo, alii; è recentioribus verò plerique. Vid. praeten Orthodoxos, Dionysius (arthusianus in h. l. Thomas Stapletonus in Promt. Morali. Dom. 2. Adv. p. 18. Ioh. Ferus in h. l. quin ipsi etiam Iesuitae, Alphonsus de Castro l. 8. adv. haeres. tit. Ioh. Baptista. item Maldonatus, Barradius, Corn. à Lapide, Tir nus, Conzen & alii in h. l. hanc ipsam amplectuntur, eamque tùm illi, quòd Iohannes pro se quaesiverit, tum qs quaesiverit, an Christus in limbum descensurus sit & Patres ex eo liberaturus, quomodo quaestionem Iohannis detorquet Costerus Domin. 3. Advent p. 40. & 69. & ante hunc Dionysius Carthusianus in h. l. meritò praeferunt. Cumprimis verò Iesuta Maldonatus de posteriori expositione disertè scribit, quod meliore nondum invent â maxima pars (quod tamen falsum esse, alibi ostendetur) veterum autorum in eam concesserit. Huiusq; sociennus Adamus Contzen in h. l. Qui, inquit, de morte Christi & ad inferos descensu eum dubit asse arbitrati sunt, minùs rectè sentiunt. Ita verò sensit & Gregorius Magnus, P. R quem dum adeò apertè redarguit Iesuita, miror, quî non metuat fulmen Papale.

Quid quod Simon Episcopius Arminianus l. 3. Instit. Theol. c. 35. obtinere laborat, verba, σὺ εἶ ὁ ρχόμενος i. e. ὁ ἐλευσόμευος,non prolata,ἐρωτηματικῶς,sed absolutè sine interrogotione. Cuius tamen fundamenta an satis firma sint, viri docti dispiciant.)* Hieronymus ad Algasiam q. 1. existimar, Iohannem ideò quaesivisse, ut sciret, an apud inferos de eius adventu debeat concionari. *(Meminit quoque expositionis huius Hieronymianae Corn. à Lapide, adiicit tamen, quòd adsertum illud Hieronymi minùs appositum ac probabile videatur. Mirum verò, cur Franciscus à Messana, Hieronym. ordinis Madriti Doctor, Tr. ad diffic. S. Hieron loca, ubi pleraque Pontificiorum dogmata ex Hieronymo stabilire satagit, tit. Infernus, quo loco plures inferni sinus ex Hieron. sententia dori, ostendere conatur, locum hunc silentio praeterierit.)* Sed haec sententia nititur falsâ hypothesi de limbo patrum, & improbatur à Theophyiacto. Ipse etiam Hieroymus in c. 11. M-th probat nostram sententiam: scribit enim, Iohannem ideò quasiv s--ut M-gistro interogante sibi discerent discipuli. *(Nec est, ut al quis -icat. si vel maximè ipse Iohannes non dubitavit, ac Christus, -sset moriturus & ad inferos defcensurus, ut nempe ex limboliberaret patres, tamen discip -los eius fortè de co dubitasse, ac propterea, ut de isto discensu informarentur, Iohannens ad Christum eos ablegasse. Obstat enim contextus. Neque enim miracula illa, ad quorum considerationem Christus eos remittit, descensum illum Christi probant. Unde rectè Iesuita Maldonatus de istâ expositione iudicat, quòd non congruac. Addit: Quo enim modò ex miraculis, utrum Christus moriturus &c. cegnoscere potuissent.)* Gregorius homil. 6. in Evang dicit: Iohannem quidem scivisse, quòd Iesus sit Messias, interim tamen ipsum dubitasse, an Christus sit passurus ac per mortem genus humanum redemturus. At quomodo de morte Christi dubitare potuit, cùm ipsum nominarit agnum Dei,Ioh. 1, 19. ex Es. 53. quâ voce notatur passio & innocentia Christi: Thomas 2. 2. q. 2. art. 7. Non est credendum, quòd Iohannes ignoraverit, Christum ad passionem venturum, ipse enim dixerat: Ecce agnus DEI, praenuncians eius immolationem futuram. Ambrosius in c. 7. Luca dicit: Iohannem non fide, sed pietate dubitâsse, mirum enim ipsi visum fuisse quòd tantus vir mori velit. *(Iustinus quoque Martyr, vel quicunque autor Qq. ac Resp. ad orthodoxos Iustino adscriptarum, (Iustini enim genuinum foetum librum illum nō esse, B. D. Chemnitus, Whitakerus, Rivetus, Cocus, Perkins. Sylburgius statuunt, adducti à B. Par. Patrologiae p. 86.) quaest. 38. p. 322. nec non Tertullianus lib. de Bapt. c. 1. 10. itemque l. 4. contra Marc. c. 18. statuunt, Iohannem prose quaesivisse, ac quòd ipse ignoraverit, Christum esse promissum illum Messiam. Sed diversum suadent dicta Matth. 3, 17.Ioh. 1, 32. Quî enim ignorare vel dubitare Ioh. de Christo poterat, qui tam illustri revelatione & signo coelitus edoctus erat, ac tam saepè de Christo fuerat testatus. Nec cogitandum, quòd carceris calamitate sractus fuerit vel dubius redditus: aliud suadet encomium, hoc ipso loco v. 7. à Christo ei datum.)* Burgensis in additionibus dicit, Iohannem ideò quaesivisse, quòd Christi personam & officium cognovisset tantùm ex revelatione, non autem per experientiam. Atqui DEI revelatio certior omni experientiâ. Praetereà Ioh. 1. ex ipsâ experientiâ Christum cognoverat.

*( ὁ ἐρχόμενος. iuxta Ioh. Cameronē in Myroth. p. 4. & 48. pro ὁ ἔμελλε ἔρχεσθαι, sicuti infrà c. 17, 11. ἔρχεται pro ἔμελλε ἔρχε σθαιquem oportuerat venire. Est Epitheton Messiae. Vid. Gen. 49, 10.Deut. 18, 15.Ps. 40, 8.Es. 35, 4.Hag. 2, 8.Mal. 3, 1.Ioh. 3, 31.c. 6, 14.c. 11, 27.2. Ioh. v. 7. Cur v. Messias isto nomine insigniatur, prolixè pertractat B. D. Chemnitius H. E. c. 55. Respectus nempe isto nomine habebatur, dùm adhuc Messias expectabatur, ad vaticinia Prophetica, quibus promissus erat Messias venturus in carnem s-in hunc mundum. Accommodatur verò hoc nomen etiam ad Messiam iam praesentem, per allusionem ad Exod. 3, 14. add. Apoc. 1, 8.)* Προσδοκῶμεν, praesens pro futuro ponitur, quod frequens in N. T. *(Vid. infrà c. 24, 40. c. 26, 29. suprà c, 2, 4. c. 5, 46. add. Luc. 13. 32.Ioh. 7, 27. &c.)*

## 11:4
*(v. 4. ἀπαγγείλατε Ἰωάννη. Well here H. Grotius παραφράζει That he himself, in whom you place faith, may tell you what the Prophets said about him who is to do these things. Thus the proposition is most certain, resting on divine authority, the assumption which is undoubted, since it consists of eyewitness faith. Whence by necessity of consequence follows the inference, settling the question.)*

*( Which you hear and see. For at that very time Christ was healing many from diseases, etc. Luc. 7, 21. Whence also the Vulgate does not render it sufficiently conveniently in the Praet.)*

Latin:

*(v. 4. ἀπαγγείλατε Ἰωάννη. Benè h. l. H. Grotius παραφράζειUt ipse, cui vos fidem adhibetis, dicat vobis, quid de eo, qui ista sit facturus Prophetae dixerint. Ita propositio certissima, nixa divinâ autoritate, adsumtio quoindubitata, quippe cōstans oculata fide. Unde consequutionis necessitate sequetur illatio, quaestionem desiniens.)*

*( Quae auditis & videtis. Etenim eo ipso tempore Christus multos sanabat à morbis &c. Luc. 7, 21. Unde quoque Vulgatus non satis commodè in Praet. reddit.)*

## 11:5
v. 5. The blind see i. e. those who were blind, now see. According to the rule: D-nominated and epithets when they are predicated of their subjects, even if the foundation of them and the reason for the denomination has ceased. See Genes. 2, 23.Exod. 7, 12.2. Sam. 24, 23.Matth. 10, 3. *( Rom. 4, 5.Iac. 2, 25.)* Unless you wish to accept by metalepsis to see for being gifted with sight; to walk for being restored to health and gifted with the power of walking; to hear for being gifted with the power of hearing in the sermon of Christ, so that the sense may be: Those who are blind, they are gifted with sight by me. *(The blessed D. Glassius follows this interpretation Gra-. S. p. 8. 9. and confirms the same with several examples. Furthermore, how it was signified through bodily healing that Christ, having turned to the nations, who did not know God, would illuminate the hearts of the foolish, and would cause by the light of wisdom that those lacking truth would both hear and understand the divine voices of GOD, etc., Lactantius teaches at length in book 4 of the Divin. Instit. chap. 26, and Dionys. Carthus. in h. l. Moreover, the prophetic predictions are held in Es. 29, 18.c. 35, 5.c. 61, 3.2.c. 53. 4. coll. with Matth. 8, 17. From that fact, however, that Christ applies to himself that Prophetic prophecy Es. 35, 4. where he who is about to perform such miracles is called absolutely God, a distinguished argument for the true Deity of Christ is drawn against the Photinians. Which the blessed D. Tarnov. also defends excellently against the said heretics in his book on the SS. Trinit. p. 267. seqq.)*

Νεκροὶ ἐγείρονται. H. Grotius thinks that prophecies of the resurrection of the dead do not exist in the O. T., because they were to be expected from Christ. But it must be known that the Prophets, when they describe the office and advent of the Messiah, speak of the resurrection of the dead in such a way that they simultaneously embrace the universal resurrection, as in Es. 26, 19.Hos. 13, 14.)*

*( To the poor, namely spiritually such, i. e. those who are tormented by the sense of their sins, and acknowledge themselves to be destitute, and unable to bring anything by which they might merit the grace of GOD, as D. Quist. most conveniently explains in h. l. The Papists on the contrary, so that they may establish Monastic vows, among which is also the choice of voluntary poverty, understand or at least or especially corporally poor: these for since they are needy on earth, they hope they seek heavenly riches, which the Gospel promises. Corn à Lapide, in this place. Indeed the same Jesuit in in the parallel place Is. 61, 1., having rejected that opinion, that namely by the poor in Isaiah in the said place are understood men, especially Gentiles, who because of sins were impoverished, that is, destitute of grace and salvation; especially those who acknowledge themselves to be such. Which exposition he says is that of St. Ambrose, Origen, and Theophylact in Luke 4.; and likewise of Jerome, Tertullian in book 4 against Marc. c. 14., Eusebius in book 3 of the Demonstration 1, who accept poor in spirit, Matt. 5, 3.. These, I say, having rejected these expositions, he says that it is most plain, by which through the poor are understood properly such, that is, the needy and those who are of slender fortune, and that Christ also spoke of such in Matt. 11. So that namely an opposition may be established between the preaching of Christ and the Apostles, and between the preaching of the Pharisees, since the former preached to the needy crowd, the latter on the contrary, as greedy, neglected the poor, occupied about the rich and riches. Indeed the rich themselves cared little for the Gospel. Similarly almost Tirinus, Contzen, Barradius. But however much we do not deny that temporal calamities, among which is poverty, are accustomed to accompany the preaching of the Gospel, and it is known that the rich, unless they are at the same time poor in spirit, do not greatly care for the Gospel; nor do we deny that also in this place is described the external miserable lot and condition of believers in this world: it is certain, however, that the preaching of the Gospel is salutary primarily, indeed solely, to those who acknowledge their spiritual poverty, that is, the lack of their own righteousness Is. 57, 15. and seek true righteousness, and that which stands before God, in the most precious merit of Christ alone. Otherwise bodily poverty profits no one, nor are the Monks so absurd, persuading themselves that by the choice of voluntary poverty they can merit eternal life. For such, when they judge themselves rich, Apoc. 3, 17., that is, swell with the opinion of their own righteousness, they by no means seek true righteousness with ardent desire in the merit of Christ alone, and therefore the Gospel profits them nothing. Compare above c. 9, 12. also below v. 27. Mark 2, 17. Luke 5, 31. Which very thing acknowledging, perhaps the slightly more prudent Papists, [interpret] this passage concerning the poor, who are poor in spirit (that is, who acknowledge their spiritual indigence, Is. 57, 15.c. 61, 1. and thus they flee to Christ, seeking righteousness in Him alone) they explain. So Franc. Lucas, Dionysius à Rickel the Carthusian, and others.)*

διατάσ is taken passively by most, meanwhile an active meaning does not seem to be able to be entirely rejected, if πτωχὸς is taken for thin and impotent.

*(Indeed εὐαγγελίζονται is also taken actively elsewhere. See Luke 2, 10.c. 3, 18.c. 8, 1.c. 9, 6.c. 20, 1. etc. nor does it seem to be able to be understood ineptly through πτωχοὺς by the Apostles, as those who are called νήπιοι elsewhere, Matt. 11, 25. and hence also Theophylact and Euthymius take it actively in this place: Nevertheless, the blessed D. Glassius, Gr. S. p. 343, prefers the former interpretation to this latter one, as it is confirmed both by Isaiah c. 61, 1. add. Luke 4, 18. and by the context. Inasmuch as it is clear from v. 4. that it concerns the Evangelical preaching of Christ Himself. The Jesuit Maldonatus p. 236 opposes the opinion by which the word εὐαγγ. is taken actively in this place, because it is numbered among the miracles that the poor are evangelized; but it is not, he says, a miracle that the poor should announce the Gospel. For men of the lowest sort are often accustomed to be messengers of great things: but that the Gospel should be preached to the poor, i.e., that the kingdom of heaven should be promised, was very wonderful. But his fellow member Conzen p. 215. a. retorts, That the poor, chosen by God, should bring the message about the kingdom being given, indeed that they should have the power of inaugurating into the kingdom, that was something new and contrary to the custom of Kings, who send illustrious Legates in the greatest affairs of the kingdom. Indeed, the blessed D. Frantzius, de interpret. Sc. S. Orac. 115. p. 1033. seqq., excellently shows that it is perhaps an even greater miracle that the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom were revealed to the world through the Apostles, who in a moment were made Doctors from being, as it were, unrefined men and fishermen, than that the Gospel was preached to the poor, and at the same time he not a little strengthens that opinion that the word εὐαγγ. can also be taken most conveniently in an active sense in this place. Where he brings forward quite a few things for consideration, which are altogether most pleasant and useful to read.)*

Latin:

v. 5. Coeci vident i. e. qui fuerunt coeci, iam vident. Iuxta regulam: D-nominata & epitheta quandode subiectis suis praedicantur, etiamsi fundamentum ipsorum & denominationis ratio defierit. Vide Genes. 2, 23.Exod. 7, 12.2. Sam. 24, 23.Matth. 10, 3. *( Rom. 4, 5.Iac. 2, 25.)* Nisi per metalepsin videre pro visu donari; ambulare pro sanitati restitui & ambulandi potentiâ donari; audire pro audiendi potentiâ donari in sermone Christi velis accipere, ut sit sensus: Qui coeci sunt, illi visu à me donantur. *(Sequitur hanc interpretationem B. D. Glassius Gra-. S. p. 8. 9. eandemque plusculis exemplis etiam confirmat. Porrò quomodo per corporalem sanationem significatum fuerit, fore ut Christus cōversus ad gentes; quae Deum nesciebant, insipientium pectora illuminaret, luce sapientiae efficeret itē, ut veritatis expertes & audirent & intelligerent divinas DEI voces &c. prolixè docet Lactantius lib. 4. Divin. Instit. cap. 26. ac Dionys. Carthus. in h. l. Praedictiones autem prohetica habentur Es. 29, 18.c. 35, 5.c. 61, 3.2.c. 53. 4. coll. cum Matth. 8, 17. Ex eo autem, quòd Christus vaticinium illud Propheticum Es. 35, 4. ubi is, qui talia miracula editurus, vocatur absolutè Deus, ad se applicat, infigne argumentum pro verâ Christi Deitate contra Photinianos depromitur. Quod praeclarò etiam contra dictòs haereticos defendit B. D. Tarnov. lib. de SS. Trinit. p. 267. seqq.)*

Νεκροὶ ἐγείρονται. Existimat H. Grotius, de mortuorum resuscitatione non extare vaticinia V. T. quòd nempe à Christo expectanda. Verùm sciendum quòd Prophetae, ubi Messiae officium & adventum describunt, ita de mortuorum resuscitatione loquantur, ut simul complectantur universalem resuscitationem, uti Es. 26, 19.Hos. 13, 14.)*

*( Pauperibus, nempe spiritualiter talibus h. e. qui peccatorum suorum sensu torquentur, seque inopes, & nihil, quo gratiam DEI promereri possint adferre valentes, agnoscunt, uti D. Quist. in h. l. commodissimè exponit. Pontificii contrà, quò Monastivota, inter quae & paupertatis spontaneae electio, stabiliant, intelligunt vel saltem vel praecipuè corporaliter pauperes: hi enim cùm sint inopes in terrâ, sperant ambiuntopes coelestes, quas Evangelium promittit. Corn à Lapide, in h. l. Imò idem Iesuita in Coad locum parall. Es. 61, 1. reiectâ illâ sententià, quòd nempe per parperes apud Es. d. l. intelligantur homines, praesertim gentiles, qui ob peccata depauperati, id est, gratia & salute destituti erant; praesertim qui se tales esse agnoscunt. Quam expositionem S. Ambrosii, Origenis, & Theophylacti in Luc. 4. esse dicit; itemque Hieronymi, Tertulliani lib. 4. cont. Marc. c. 14. Eusebii l. 3. Demonstr. 1. qui accipiunt pauperes spiritu,Matth. 5, 3. His, inquam, expositionibus reiectis, planissimam esse, dicit, quâ per pauperes intelligantur propriè tales s. inopes & ii, qui tenui sunt fortunâ, ac de talibus etiā Christum Matt. 11. loquutum dicit. Ut nempe instituatur oppositio inter praedicationem Christi & Apostolorum, & inter praedic. Pharisaeorum, cùm illi turbae inopi praedicarent, hi contrà, ut avari, pauperes negligerent, circa divites & divitias occupati. Imô divites ipsi parùm Evangelium curarent. Similiter ferè Tirinus, Contzen, Barradius. Verùm utut non eamus inficias, quod calamitates temporales, quas inter & paupertas, Evangelii praedicationem comitari soleant, ac notum, quòd divites, nisi spiritu simul pauperes sint, Evangelium haut magnopere curent; nec negemus, quòd etiam h. l. describatur externa misera sors & conditio credentium in hoc mundo: certum tamen est, quòd Evangelii praedicatio illis cum primis, imò solis, salutaris sit, qui spiritualem suam paupertatem h. e. propriae iustitiae de. fectum agnoscunt Esa. 57, 15. veramq; ac coram Deo consistentem iustitiam in solius Christi pretiosissimo quaerunt merito. Aliàs corporalis paupertas nemini prodest, absurdi-ue adeò Monachi sunt, persuadentes sibi, quòd spontaneae paupertatis electione vitam promereri aeternam possint. Tales enim cùm se divites iudicent,Apoc. 3, 17. h. e. propriae iustitiae opinione turgeant, veram iustitiam minimè ardenti desiderio in solius Christi merito quaerunt, adeò-ue nec Evangelium iis quicquam prodest. Conf. suprà c. 9, 12. it. infrà v. 27.Marc. 2, 17.Luc. 5, 31. Quod ipsum agnoscentes fortè paullò prudentiores Pontificii, locum hunc de pauperibus, qui spiritus pauperes sunt (h. e. qui spiritualem suam indigentiam agnoscunt, Es. 57, 15.c. 61, 1. adeoque ad Christum confugiunt, in ipso solo iustitiam quaerentes) exponunt. Ita Franc. Lucas, Dionysius à Rickel Carthusianus, alii.)*

διατάσ à plerisque' passivè accipitur, interim activa significatio non omninò repudiari posse videtur, si πτωχὸς pro tenui & impotenti accipiatur.

*(Sanè εὐαγγελίζονται & alibi activè accipitur. Vid. Luc. 2, 10.c. 3, 18.c. 8, 1.c. 9, 6.c. 20, 1. &c. nec ineptè per πτωχοὺς Apostoli intelligi posse videtur, ut qui alibi νήπιοι dicuntur, Matth. 11, 25. atque hinc etiam activè h. l. accipiunt Theophyl. & Euthymius: Priorem tamen interpretationem huic posteriori praefert B. D. Glassius, Gr. S. p. 343. quippe quam tum Esaias c. 61, 1. add. Luc. 4, 18. tum contextus confirmet. Siquidem de Evangelica ipsius Christi praedicatione agi, pateat ex v. 4. Opponit sententiae, quâ activè verbum εὐαγγ. h. l. accipitur, Iesuita Maldonatus p. 236. quòd inter miracula numeretur, quòd pauperes evangelizentur; non autem inquit, miraculum, ut pauperes Evangelium annunciarent. Solent enim homines abiectissimi magnarum saepè rerum esse nuncii: ut autem pauperibus Evangelium praedicetur h. e. regnum coelorum promittatur, valdè mirum erat. Ast regerit eiusdem sociennus Conzen p. 215. a. A Deo electos pauperculos, qui de regno dando nuncium deferrent, imò quibus potest as esset inaugurandi in regnum, id quonovum & praeter Regum consuetudinem, qui maximis regni in negotiis illustres Legatos mittunt. Imò maius fortè adhuc miraculum esse, quòd mysteria regni coelestis per Apostolos, qui in momento quasi ex hominibus rudibus & piscatoribus facti Doctores, fuerunt orbi patefacta, quàm quòd pauperibus Evangelium praedicatum, egregiè ostendit, simulque sententiam illam, quòd verbum εὐαγγ. h. l. activè commodissimè etiam accipi possit, haut parum firmat B. D. Frantzius de interpret. Sc. S. Orac. 115. p. 1033. seqq Ubi pluscula in medium adducit, lectu omninò iucundissima & utilissima.)*

## 11:6
v. 6. Blessed is he who shall not be offended in me. i. e. he who is not offended by the absurdity of the doctrine which I profess, *( 1. Cor. 1, 23.)* or by the humble and abject appearance of my person, *(See Is. 52, 14.c. 53, 2. below c. 26, 31. Just as Gregory writes in homily 6 on the Gospel, the infidels were scandalized in Christ, when after so many miracles they saw Him dying on the cross. Hence the Apostles are not undeservedly proclaimed blessed, who were not scandalized in this vile appearance of Christ. It is also reported of the blessed D. Luther, that he was accustomed to say that he gave thanks to GOD for this reason, that he did not see Christ in that humble and despised appearance, for there was a danger that he might be scandalized by it. But however much many are scandalized by this humble appearance of Christ, it is nevertheless by no means to be gathered from this that GOD is the cause of their fall and sin, since there is a distinction between scandal given, and accepted. Concerning this division of scandal, just as also concerning the matter of scandal in general, the blessed D. Fewrborn discourses at length and learnedly in a special dissertation on Scandal, which is held in Fascicle 5 of his Theological Dissertations, Disp. 4. and 5.)* Or by the cross and the mass of troubles, which certainly accompanies the profession of the Gospel. *(See Matt. 16, 24.Acts 14, 23.Rom. 8, 17.29.1. Cor. 4, 9.2. Tim. 2, 3.c. 3, 12. etc. It must be known, however, that Christ is dealing primarily with the scandal that men take from the humble appearance of His person and His death.)*

What went you out into the desert to see, &c. Stapleton, in his Promptuarium Catholicum for the 2nd Sunday of Advent, ineptly attempts to prove pilgrimages to the places of the saints from the deed of the Jews, who went out into the desert to John. But who does not see the huge difference between that pilgrimage of the Jews and that of the Papists? For the latter institute a journey to the relics of the dead with the opinion of worship and merit; but the former went out to John while he was alive, not to exhibit religious worship to him, or to merit salvation by that pilgrimage, but to hear him teaching, and from hearing to conceive faith, and to be baptized by him for the remission of sins. That the worship of relics has any such fruit is nowhere read in the Holy Scriptures.)*

Latin:

v. 6. Qui non offensus fuerit in me. i. e. qui non offenditur doctrinae, quam profiteor, absurditate, *( 1. Cor. 1, 23.)* vel meae personae humili & abiectâ specie, *(Vid. Es. 52, 14.c. 53, 2. infrà c. 26, 31. Quemadmodum Gregorius homil. 6. in Ev. scribit, infideles scandalizatos fuisse in Christo, cùm post tot miracula morientem in cruce viderunt. Hinc non immeritò beati praedicantur Apostoli, qui non fuerunt in hâc vili specie Christi scandalizati Refertur quoque de B. D. Luthero, quod dicere fuerit solitus, se hoc nomine gratias DEO agere, quòd Christum non videret in illa humili & contemtâ specie, periculum enim subesse, ne eâ scandalizetur. Ut ut verò plurimi humili istâ Christi specie scandalizetur, minimè tamen colligendum hinc, quòd DEUS lapsûs ac peccati eorum causa sit, cùm dist. sit inter scandalum datum, & acceptum. De qua scandali divisione, sicuti etiam de materiâ scandali in genere, prolixè atque eruditè disserit B. D. Fewrborn. in pecul. diss. de Scandalo, quae habetur Fascic. 5. Dissert. eius Theol. Disp. 4. & 5.)* Vel cruce & mole aerumnarum, quae certò comitatur professionem Evangelii. *(Vid. Matth. 16, 24.Act. 14, 23.Rom. 8, 17.29.1. Cor. 4, 9.2. Tim. 2, 3.c. 3, 12. &c. Sciendum verò Christum cumprimis agere de scandalo, quòd ex humili personae eius specie ac morte homines capiunt.)*

*( Quid existis in desertum videre &c. Ineptè ex facto Iudáeorum, qui egressi sunt in desertum ad Iohannem Stapletonus Promt. Cath. Domin. 2. Adventus peregrinationes ad loca sanctorum probare conatur. Sed quis non videt ingens discrimen inter peregrinationem illam Iudaeorum, ac Pontificiorum. Hi enim ad reliquias defunctorum opinione cultus ac meriti iter instituunt: illi verò egressi sunt ad Iohannem vivum, nec ut cultum religiosum ei exhiberent, vel ut peregrinatione eâ salutem promererentur, sed ut docentem audirent, & ex auditu conciperent fidem, ab eoque baptizarentur in remissionem peccatorum. Cuius modi fructum cultum reliquiarum habere, nullibi in Sc. S. legitur.)**

## 11:7
v. 7. A reed, which is shaken by the winds. John is not a reed, but a pillar. Euseb. Emissenus serm. 3. advent. By the reed and the cane Scripture denotes the levity and inconstancy of the mind, 1. Reg. 14, 15.Es. 36, 6. *(Hugo Grotius thinks that the reed properly so-called is a sermon of Christ, so that the sense is: you had, I think, some reason, for which you ran with such zeal into those desert places. For it is not credible that you went out, so that you might see reeds shaken by the wind. This is because, outside of John, there was almost nothing else to see in those places. But the scope of Christ suggests otherwise, and sufficiently implies that the Savior wished to vindicate the praise of constancy for the Baptist with those words. Whence also rightly Chrysostom homil. 38. in Matth. pag. 358. observes that Christ wished to lead the multitude to better things with these words. Since the crowd could not know with what mind John was inquiring, and so think: Did not John bear many testimonies concerning that one? How therefore is he now changed and doubting, whether that one, or another is to come? Are there perhaps dissensions between him and Jesus, or has he perhaps become more timid by the affliction of prison. Therefore Christ shows that he is not changed from that his former opinion. μετεμ &c. Christ proceeds, from the fact that the Jews hastened with such zeal into the desert to John, to convince them that they would have done this least of all, unless they had thought him μέγαν τινὰ καὶ θαυμαςὸνκαὶτέτρας ςεῤῥότερον. On the contrary, they are similar to a reed, as the same Chrysostom warns, who never say the same thing, but driven hither and thither, are anxious to assert now these things, now those. Let us indeed imitate the constancy of John, let there be for us strength and triple brass around the breast, so that we may be moved neither by prosperous nor by adverse things from the solidity of faith: let not prosperous things lift us up, let not adverse things disturb us, as Greg. speaks hom. 6. in Ev. Conf. Ambros. l. 5. in c. 7. Lucae v. 24.)*

Latin:

v. 7. Arundinem, quae agitetur à ventis. Iohannes non est arundo, sed columna. Euseb. Emissenus serm. 3. advent. Per arundinem eius que calamum Scriptura levitatem & inconstantiam animi notat, 1. Reg. 14, 15.Es. 36, 6. *(Hugo Grotius de arundine propriè dicta Christo serm-m esse putat, ut sit sensus: habuistis puto causam aliquam, ob quam tanto studio in leca illa deserta cucurristis. Neenim credibile est, vos exivisse, ut arundines vento agitatas videretis. Hoc ideò, quia extra Iohannem nihil fermè aliud istis in locis erat spectare. Sed scopus Christi diversum svadet, satisque innuit, quòd Salvator verbis illis constantiae laudem Baptistae vindicare voluerit. Unde etiam rectè Chrysostomuhomil. 38. in Matth. pag. 358. observat, quòd Christus his verbis multitudinem ad meliora reducere voluerit. Quippe --m turbae nescire potuerint, quâ mente Iohannes interrogaret, adeo-ue cogitare: Nonne Iohannes multa de isto testimonia perhibuit? Quomodo igitur nunc mutatus ambigit, uttum iste, an alius venturus sit? Num dissidia forsan inter ipsum & Iesum sunt, an fortasse afflictione carceris timidior factus est. Ostendit igitur Christus, nō esse ipsum mutatum ab illa priori suâ opinione. μετεμ &c. Pergit Christus, ex eo, quòd tanto studio Iudaei in desertum ad Iohannem properaverint, ipsos convincere, quòd id minimè fecissent, nisi μέγαν τινὰ καὶ θαυμαςὸνκαὶτέτρας ςεῤῥότερον eum putassent. Arundini contrà sunt similes, eod. Chrysostomo monente, qui nunquam idem dicunt, sed huc atque illac pulsi, modò haec, modò illa soliciti sunt asserere. Imitemur verò Iohannis constantiam, sit nobis robur & aes triplex circa pectus, ita ut nec prosperis nec adversis à fidei soliditate moveamur: non elevent nos prospera, nō perturbent adversa, ut loquitur Greg. hom. 6. in Ev. Conf. Ambros. l. 5. in c. 7. Lucae v. 24.)*

## 11:8
(v. 8. Οἱ τὰμὰλακα φοροῦντες. It must be repeated from the preceding member of this verse ἱμάτια. For examples of this ellipsis see above c. 10, 42. Luc. 12, 47.c. 14, 18.Act. 19, 35. The Arab repeats the substantive. The Ethiopian translates: -who are clothed in cotton. It is noted indeed that also for the Arabs which agrees with the Ethiopian cotton, whether the Italians have their coton and the Spaniards their Algodon i.e. cotton from them, so that the name along with the thing migrated to them from the Arabs and Ethiopians (since among whom the shrub called cotton is born, witness Pliny book 19. Nat. Hist. c. 1.), is not for this place to investigate at length. By that very thing indeed, when Christ in this place says that those clothed in soft garments are in the houses of kings i.e. in courts , Schickard thinks in מה. p. 67. He indicates that the Savior implies that elegance of form is most especially becoming to kings or courtiers, a thing which he shows from Maimonides that Kings I--. also observed. But while Christ denies that John is to be numbered among those who are clothed in soft garments, he removes from him the pursuit of adulation. And Ministers of the Church are taught by the example of John not to be too soft in correcting the vices of their hearers. Conf. Es. 56, 10.Gal. 1, 10. Let hearers also learn not to be too delicate in receiving their admonitions. Conf. Prov. 27, 5. 6.Eccles. 7, 6. But how John reproved sinners without any respect of persons is sufficiently evident from Matth. 14, 4.c. 3, 7.c. 21, 32.Luc. 3, 10. 11, 12. having imitated in this Elijah, 1. Reg. 18, 18.

Latin:

*(v. 8. Οἱ τὰμὰλακα φοροῦντες. Repetendum è membro versiculi huius praecedente ἱμάτια. Cuius ellipseos exempla vid. supra c. 10, 42. Luc. 12, 47.c. 14, 18.Act. 19, 35. Arabs substantivum repetit. Aethiops vertit: -qui gossipio vestiuntur. Notat verò & Arabibus quod cùm Aethiop. convenit, gossipium, à quibus num Itali habeant suum coton ac Hispani suum Algodon i. e. gossipium, ut ita nomen cum re ab Arabibus atque, Aethiopibus (quippe apud quos frutex gossipium dictus gignitur, teste Plinio lib. 19. Nat. Hist. c. 1.) ad eos migrarit, non est huius loci prolixè indagare. Eo ipso verò, quando Christus h. l. dicit, mollibus vestimentis amictos in regum domibus s. aulis esse, putat Schickardus in מה. p. 67. Salvatorem innuere, quòd regios s. aulicos vel maximè deceat formae elegantia, id quod etiam Reges I--. observasse, ex Maimonide ostendit. Dùm verò Christus negat, Iohannem numerandum esse inter eos, qui vestiuntur mollibus, removet ab eo adulationis studium. Docenturq, Ministri Ecclesiae Iohan. exemplo, ne sint in corrigendis auditorum vitiis nimis molles. Conf. Es. 56, 10.Gal. 1, 10. Discant quoq; auditores, ne in excipiendis admonitionibus illorum nimis sint delicatuli. Conf. Prov. 27, 5. 6.Eccles. 7, 6. Quomodo verò Iohannes sine ullô personarum respectu peccatores redarguerit, satis patet ex Matth. 14, 4.c. 3, 7.c. 21, 32.Luc. 3, 10. 11, 12. imitatus in, hoc Eliam, 1. Reg. 18, 18.)*

## 11:9
v. 9. Περισσότερον προφήτου. John is greater than the remaining Prophets, because he is the precursor of the Lord, he begins a universal ministry in the Church, he institutes by divine revelation a new rite, of Baptism, and he points out the present Messiah with his finger, which happened to none of the Prophets. Irenaeus lib. 3. c. 11. pag. 185. The remaining Prophets all announced the coming of the father of light, but they desired to be worthy to see him whom they preached. John, however, announced beforehand similarly as the others, and demonstrated, and persuaded many to believe in him, so that he held the place of both Prophet and Apostle. Chrysostomus: why is John greater than the Prophets; κατα τὸ ἐγγὺς εἶναι του παραγθυομθύου, sc. χριστοῦ. and he continues. For just as those who ride closest to the royal vehicle are of greater dignity, so also John, preceding his very coming most closely, shone with greater grace: Therefore, the 1st assertion concerning Moses in Deut. last v. 10. does not conflict at all with the present passage. For it is denied at least that any of the Prophets was like Moses by reason of familiar discourse with GOD and power in performing many miracles. 2. nor this, that the Baptist Ioh. 1, 21. denies that he is a Prophet. For in what sense he himself denies that he is a Prophet is evident from the question proposed there. For the Legates of Jerusalem were asking whether he is a Prophet, i.e., one of those ancient Prophets, long since dead, and recalled to life by a certain μετεμψύχωσιν Pythagorean transmigration. As the blessed Pareus shows at greater length, L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 20. add. Dn. D. Walth. in H. B.

Latin:

v. 9. Περισσότερον προφήτου. Iohannes maior est reliquis Prophetis, quia est praecursor Domini, inchoat ministerium in Ecclesiâ universale, instituit divinâ revelatione novum ritum, Baptismi, & monstrat praesentem Messiam digito, quod nulli Prophetarum accidit. Irenaeus lib. 3. c. 11. pag. 185. Reliqui omnes Prophetae annunciaverunt adventum paterm luminis, concupiverunt autem digni esse videre eum, quem praedicabant. Iohannes autem praenunciavit similiter sicut alii, & demonstravit, & credere in eum suasit multis, ita ut ipse & Prophetae & Apostoli locum habuerit. *(Chrysostomus: cur maior Prophetis Iohannes;κατα τὸ ἐγγὺς εἶναι του παραγθυομθύου, sc. χριστοῦ. & pergit. Nam quemadmodum maiore dignitate hi sunt, qui proximè regium vehiculum equitant, sic & Iohannes proximè ipsius adventum praecedens maiore gratiâ fulsit: Minimè igitur pugnat cum praesenti loco 1. adsertio de Mose Deut. ult. v. 10. Negatur enim saltim ullus Prophetarum Mosi similis ratione familiaris cum DEO alloquii ac potentiae in plurimis edendis miraculis. 2. nec hoc, quòd Baptista Ioh. 1, 21. negat, se esse Prophetam. Quo sensu enim sese Prophetam esse, ipse negat, patet ex propositâ ibi quaestione. Interrogabant nempe Hierosolym. Legati, an sit Propheta h. e. unus ex antiquis illis Prophetis, iam olim demortuis, & per μετεμψύχωσιν quandam Pythagoricam in vitam revocatis. Uti pluribus ostendit, B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 20. add. Dn. D. Walth. in H. B.)*

## 11:10
(v. 10. I send my Angel. In how many ways the name Angel is accepted, and where this name is attributed to Ministers of the Church in the H. S., the blessed Pareus teaches in many places, L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 23. Coll. Isagog. de Angel. c. 1. §. 1. seqq. Add. Lud. Molin. in 1. part. Thom. t. 1. q. 50. Altensteig. Lex. Theol. under the word Angel)

Before thy face.Faustus Socinus ineptly gathers from the fact that Christ here, referring to the prophecy of Malachi and indicating that it is fulfilled in himself, does not say before my face, that John the Baptist did not prepare the way for Christ alone. For it is certain that Christ in the state of humiliation, as the Legate of the Father, Luc. 10, 16. refers all things to the Father. By which, however, he by no means excludes himself, See Ioh. 10, 10. c. 14, 10. c. 17, 10. as the blessed D. Tarnovius well advises in *De Trin.*, page 237, where he also beautifully shows how a solid argument for the true deity of Christ is drawn from this passage against the Photinians, since he to whom John ought to prepare the way is called Lord by Malachi, and he is indeed Christ himself, as is evident from this place.)

Latin:

*(v. 10. Mitto Angelum meum. Quot modis Angeli nomen accipiatur, & ubi hoc nomen Ministris Ecclesiae in Sc. S. tribuatur, multis docet B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 23. Coll. Isagog. de Angel. c. 1. §. 1. seqq. Add. Lud. Molin. in 1. part. Thom. t. 1. q. 50. Altensteig. Lex. Theol. voce Angelus)*

*( Ante faciem tuam. Ineptè ex eo, quòd hîc Christus, Malachiae Prophetiam referens & in se completam esse indicans, non dicat ante faciem meam, colligit Faustus Socinus, Ioh. Baptistam nō soli Christo praeparasse viam. Etenim constat, quòd Christus in statu exinanitionis, tanquam Legatus Patris, Luc. 10, 16. omnia ad Patrem referat. Per quod tamen se minimè excludit, Vid. Ioh. 10, 10.c. 14, 10.c. 17, 10. uti benè monet B. D. Tarnov. de Trin. pag. 237. ubi etiam pulcrè ostendit, quomodo solidum ex hoc loco pro verâ Christi deitate arg. contra Photinianos depromatur, cùm ille, cui viam praeparare Ioh. debeat, à Malach. dicatur Dominus, is verò ipse Christus est, ceu ex h. l. patet.)*

## 11:11
v. 11. Among those born of women i. e. among those who were born of women according to the common course of nature. John is compared here with those who lived before him, not those who followed him. He is placed before them with these words: he is placed after them in the following clause.

There is not a greater i. e. who has performed a more excellent office, who has proposed a doctrine so illustrious and full of consolation.
