Argumentamur verò contra absolutum illud Calvinianorum decretum h. m. Si Deus ex absolutà quadam voluntate s. beneplacito mysteria coelestia coram sapientibus illis abscondidit, sequitur, quòd non credendominimè illi peccarint. At consequens est absurdum, quia ἀπιςίσ est condemnationis causa, adeoque gravissimum peccatum. Vid. Marc. 16, 16.Iohan. 3, 18. Connexio probatur, quia sapientes isti non credendo implevissent DEI beneplacitum. Ne-ue credere illi potuerunt absque mysteriorum fidei notitiâ. Quam cùm DEUS iis, iuxta illam Calvinianorū hypothesin, ex absoluto quodam beneplacito subtraxerit, minime sanè imputari iisdem debet, quòd non crediderint.)*

## 11:27
*(v. 27. All things. Irenaeus b. 4. c. 37. In all things nothing is subtracted, and for this reason the same is the judge of the living and the dead.)* Tossanus notes that Christ speaks properly of those things which pertain to the office of Mediator, such as are to preach the Gospel, to gather the Church, to redeem it, to sanctify, to govern, to save. *(The Jesuit Tirinus in this place explains it concerning the communication of the divine essence, made through eternal generation. Becanus joins both expositions in Manual of Controversies b. 2. c. 1. § 31, following Bellarmine b. 3. on the Incarnation c. 16, writing that the words of Christ can be understood in two ways. 1. that all things were delivered to him through eternal generation. 2. that all things were delivered to him through the hypostatic union: not however in the humanity itself, but in the person of the Word, which subsists in the humanity. (The Jesuit perhaps wishes to say, in which the humanity subsists: for neither is ὑόςασις ιουλόγου in the assumed humanity, but this subsists in ὑοςάσει του λόγου) Although we by no means deny that all things were delivered to Christ as the only-begotten Son of GOD from eternity through eternal generation: for the clearest oracles of Holy Scripture testify to that very thing. Furthermore, unless οὐ omnipotence according to the divine nature itself belonged to him in this manner, it could not have been communicated to the assumed human nature in time.

σιωδῶς belonged to him, it could not have been communicated ὑοςατικῶς to the assumed human nature in time. Whence also some of the ancients explain it concerning both natures. See Cyril b. XI on John c. 15. some accept it concerning the giving according to the divine nature, as Hilary, Theophylact, Euthymius, and others: yet it must by no means be denied that in this place regard is had to the hypostatic communication, or that by which the human nature assumed through the assumption into the hypostasis τοῦ λόγου was made a partaker of divine glory and majesty. Thus St. Augustine explains a similar passage, namely John 17, 2., in tract 105 on John: That, he writes, power is given to Christ over all flesh, is to be understood according to man. For according to God all things were made through him, and all things were created in him: in heaven and on earth. Similarly Dionysius the Carthusian. Who himself also explains the present passage concerning the giving made according to the human nature. And the truth of this explanation is evident from the rule of antiquity, according to which those things which Christ is said to have received in time, he received not according to the divine nature, inasmuch as according to it he possesses all things from eternity, but according to the human nature. Compare Ps. 8, 7.John 3, 35.c. 10, 20.c. 17, 8.1. Cor. 15, 27. Although Christ in the state of exinanition abdicated the fuller use of majesty, so that he might suffer and die, and thus perform the work of redemption, the form of a servant being assumed, Phil. 2., yet he could rightly say even in that state that all things were given to him by the Father, by reason namely of κτήσεως, even if not χρήσεως Which things Wendelin, together with the Jesuits Conzenius, Bellarmine, and others, are objected to and excepted against here, will be discussed in the Analysis on John 3, 35.)*

*( No one knows the Son, except the Father. The Holy Spirit is not excluded. See 1 Cor. -, 11. c. 12, 3. nor the Son, Apoc. 29, 12. Just as Nicolaus de Lyra also rightly noted this, writing in this place: an exclusive diction added to one person in divine matters with respect to an essential term does not exclude another, but rather includes it: Because although the person of the Father is one, the person of the Son another, the person of the Holy Spirit another: yet these three persons are one God. So that neither in divinity, nor in essential things do they have any at--n. But an exclusive diction only ex--des, what imports alienation. But knowledge taken absolutely is taken essentially, and therefore is common to the three. More prolixly concerning the use of exclusive particles will be treated in the Analects on Ioh. 17, 3. Meanwhile, one may see Dn. D. Calovius de Theol Natur. & Revel. §. 18. B Par. Coll. Isag. Contin. L. de aet. Flii Deitate §. 18. in Exeg. L. 2. de Nat. & Attr. div. §. 100. B. D. Chemn. part. 1. LL. Th. p. 39. Furthermore, the last words of this verse also look to this: & to whom the Son wills to reveal him. For the knowledge of the Son is not derogated from the faithful, inasmuch as they ought to believe in him as Redeemer, and thus know him. Ioh. 17, 3. But this at least is indicated, that no man knows the Son of himself and without divine revelation. But God the Father reveals the Son to us not immediately, but by means of the word of the Gospel, inasmuch as it is a saving organ, through which the Holy Spirit illuminates our hearts, for knowing both the essence of God and his will concerning our salvation. Against the Enthusiasts. Furthermore, rightly from the fact that no one can naturally know the Son, except he to whom it is divinely revealed, an argument is drawn for the true deity of Christ. For by that it is indicated that the Son of GOD is invisible in such a way as God the Father is invisible, Conf. Coloss. 1, 15.1. Tim. 1, 17.c. 6, 16.Apoc. 19, 12. B. D. Tarnov. has abundantly satisfied the exceptions of the Photinians in de Sac. Trinit. p. 769. seqq. From the same place also, rightly against Scotus, although he was the Prefect of the same Chair in the Academy of Salamanca, Alphonsus Mendoza, Contr. Theol. Q. 3. p. 2 8 concludes, that God regarding the Trinity of persons cannot be known through a natural principle.)* And no one knows the Father, sc. of himself and without revelation, because God revealed to us through the Holy Spirit *(See Ioh 16, 13.1. Ioh. 2, 17.2. Cor. 3, 18.Eph. 1, 17.18.)* -renaeus lib. 4. c. 14. God taught that no one can know God, unless GOD teaches, that is, without God, God is not known. *(Simon Episcopius Arminianus lib. 4. Instit. Theol. c. 4. τὸ to see God,Ioh. 1, 18. (which passage is parallel to this one of ours,) rightly explains concerning the knowledge of GOD. from which, however, he less rightly excludes the knowledge of the divine essence, understanding it only concerning the knowledge of the divine will. For although we willingly grant that the discourse is primarily concerning the knowledge of the divine will, both here and in Ioh. 1., indeed we even concede this, that the divine essence is not perfectly known by us in this infirmity

power, yet by no means is the knowledge of the divine essence, in so far as it has been revealed to us in the Holy Scriptures, namely that God is one in essence, three in persons, and also that He is an infinite, eternal, spiritual essence, etc., to be separated from the saving knowledge of God. But since the assertion of Episcopius flows from the common error of the Arminians, namely that not all those things which pertain to the divine essence and all modes of operating are necessarily to be held; and since the Lord Doctor Calovius has solidly refuted him in the Consideration of Arminianism, p. 60 et seqq., I do not wish to do what has already been done.

Except the Son. The remaining persons of the Godhead are by no means excluded, but everything that is not God is. Compare 1. Cor. 2, 11. c. 12, 3. The parallel passages are Ioh. 1, 18. c. 3, 13. Indeed, this is a notable argument for the deity of Christ. Add 2. Cor. 4, 6. 1. Thess. 5, 23. Iacob. 1, 18.

*( To whom the Son will reveal Him. See Ioh. 1, 18. For just as we cannot behold this visible Sun and the stars without their own help and light, so neither can we behold God the Father, unless the Son illuminates us, who is ἀπάυγασμα τῆς δόξης αὐτου, Ebr. 1, 3. Compare Ioh. 1, 4. 5,8. 9.c. 14, 6.9. Schevichavius has collected several things pertaining to this in his books on the Most Holy Trinity, p. 16. & 157. Moreover, the Son wishes to reveal Him to all who come and hear Him. Irenaeus, book 4 against heresies, ch. 14, p. 242. It was not said that He shall reveal only in the future, as if the Word would then begin to manifest the Father when He was born of Mary, but it is placed generally throughout all time. For from the beginning the Son, standing by His creation, reveals the Father to all, etc. The following passages pertain to this: Exod. 19, 19. compared with Act. 7, 38. Exod. 23, 23. c. 33, 2. Es. 63, 9. Proverb. 9, 3. compared with Luc. 11, 49. From the fact, however, that no one can know the Father, except to whom the Son shall have revealed Him, namely through the reading or hearing of the revealed word, 1. Cor. 1, 12. Roman. 10, 17. Ioh. 17, 20. it is manifest that the work of conversion is to be ascribed entirely to God. To which the following sayings also pertain, Ioh. 15, 5. 1. Cor. 4, 7. c. 11, 3. 2. Cor. 3, 5. Against the Synergists.

See the Blessed D. Hutter treating of this matter at greater length in the Formula of Concord, p. 158. 159.)*

Latin:

*(v. 27. Omnia. Irenaeus l. 4. c. 37. In omnibus nihil subtractum est, & propter hoc idem iudex viventium & mortuorum.)* Tossanus annotat, Christum loqui propriè de iis, quae ad officium Mediatoris pertinent, qualia sunt, praedicare Evangelium, colligere Ecclesiam, eam redimere, sanctificare, gubernate, salvare. *(Iesuita Tirinus in h. l. explicat de communicatione divinae essentiae, per aeternam generationem factâ. Utramque expositionem coniungit Becanus in Manuali Controv. l. 2. c. 1. § 31. sequutus Bellarminum l. 3. de Incarn. c. 16. scribens, posse verba Christi dupliciter intelligi. 1. quòd omnia sint illi tradita per aeternam generationem. 2. quòd omnia sint illi tradita per unionem hypostaticam: non tamen in ipsâ humanitate, sed in personâ verbi, quae subsistit in humanitate. (Vult fortè Iesuita dicere, in quâ subsistit humanitas: neq; n. ὑόςασις ιουλόγου in adsumtâ humanitate, sed haec in ὑοςάσει του λόγου subsistit) Nos licet minimè eamus inficas, quòd Christo uti unigenito DEI Filio per aeternam generationem universa ab aeterno fuerint tradita: testantur enim id ipsum clarissima Sc. Sacrae oracula. Praeterea nisi ipsi h. m. sive secundùm divinam naturam omnipotentia. οὐ

σιωδῶς competeret, non potuisset eadem ὑοςατικῶς adsumtae humanae naturae in tempore communicari. Unde etiam veterum nonnulli de utranatura exponunt. Vid. Cyrillus l. XI. in Ioh. c. 15. nonnulli de datione secundùm divinam naturam accipiunt, ceu Hilarius, The ophylactus, Euthymius, alii: negandum tamen haut quaquam est, respectum h. l. haberi ad communicationem hypostaticam, sive eam, quâ humana natura adsumta per adsumtionem in hypostasin τοῦ λόγου particeps facta gloriae ac maiestatis divinae. Ita similem locum, nempe Ioh. 17, 2. exponit S. Augustinus tr. 105. in Iohannem: Quod, scribit potestas est Christo omnis carnis data, secundùm hominem intelligendum. Nam secundùm Deum omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & in ipso conditasunt omnia: in coelo ac in terrâ. Similiter Dionysius à Rickel Carthusianus. Qui ipse praesentem quoqu locum de datione secundùm hum: naturam factâ exponit. Patetque explicationis huius veritas ex regula antiquitatis, iuxta quam ea, quae Christus in tempore accepisse dicitur, non secundùm divinam naturam, utpote secundùm quam omnia ab aeterno possidet, sed secundùm hum. naturam accepit. Conf. Ps. 8, 7.Ioh. 3, 35.c. 10, 20.c. 17, 8.1. Cor. 15, 27. Licet verò Christus in statu exinanitionis plenorio maiestatis usu, quò pati & mori, adeoque opus redemtionis perficere posset, sese abdicarit, servi formâ adsumtâ,Phil. 2. rectè tamen etiam in illo statu dicere potuit, quòd omnia sibi data sint à Patre, ratione nempe κτήσεως, utut non χρήσεως Quae Wendel nus iuxta cum Iesuitis Conzenio, Bellarmino alilique hîc obiici, & excipi, discutientur in Arial. ad Iohan. 3, 35.)*

*( Nemo novit Filium, nisi Pater. Non excluditur Sp. Sanctus. Vid. 1. Cor. -, 11. c. 12, 3. nec Filius, Apoc. 29, 12. Sicuti etiam rectè id notavir Nicolaus de Lyra, in h. l. sra scribens: dictio exclusiva addita uni personae in divinis respectu termini essenvalis non excludit aliam, sed potiùs includit: Quia licet alia sit persona Patris, alia Filii, alia Sp. Sancti: tamen istae tres personae sum unus Deus. Ita quod nec in divinitate, nec in essentialibus habent alien at--n aliquam. Dictio autem exclusiva solùm ex--dit, quod alienitatem importat. Notitia autem absolutè sunita essentialiter accipitur, & ideò communis est tribus. Prolixiùs de usu particularum exclusivarum agetur in Analectis ad Ioh. 17, 3. Videri interea possunt Dn. D. Calovius de Theol Natur. & Revel. §. 18. B Par. Coll. Isag. Contin. L. de aet. Flii Deitate §. 18. in Exeg. L. 2. de Nat. & Attr. div. §. 100. B. D. Chemn. part. 1. LL. Th. p. 39. Spectant porrò etiam huc verba ultima huius versiculi: & cui voluerit Filius revelare. Neque enim fidelibus derogatur notitia Filii, utpote in quem ceu Redemtorem credere, adeoque eum nosse debent. Ioh. 17, 3. Sed hoc saltim indicatur, quòd nemo hominum es se & absque divinâ revelatione norit Filium. Revelat autem nobis Deus Pater Filium non immediatè, sed mediante verbo Evangelii, utpote quod est salutare organon, per quod Sp. S. corda nostra illuminat, ad cognoscendam Dei tum essentiam, tum voluntatem de nostra salute. Contra Enthusiastas. Rectè porrò ex eo, quòd nemo naturaliter possit cognoscere Filium, nisi cui id divinitus reveletur, depromitur argumentum pro verâ Christi deitate. Per illud enim indicatur quòd Filius DEI ita sit invisibilis, quemadmodum Deus Pater invisibilis est, Conf. Coloss. 1, 15.1. Tim. 1, 17.c. 6, 16.Apoc. 19, 12. Exceptionibus Photinianorum abunde satis fecit B. D. Tarnov. de Sac. Trinit. p. 769. seqq. Ex eodem quoque hoc loco rectè contra Scotum, eiusdem licer Cathedrae in Acad. Salmaticenti Praefectus, Alphonsus Mendoza, Contr. Theol. Q. 3. p. 2 8 concludit, Deum quoad personarum Trinitatem per principium naturale cognoscs haut posse.)* Ac nemo novit Patrem, sc. ex se & absque revelatione, quia nobis revelavit Deus per Sp. Sanctum *(Vid Ioh 16, 13.1. Ioh. 2, 17.2. Cor. 3, 18.Eph. 1, 17.18.)* -renaeus lib. 4. c. 14. Edocuit Deus quòd Deum scire nemo possit, nisi DEO docente, hoc est, sine Deo non cognosci Deum. *(Simon Episcopius Arminianus lib. 4. Instit. Theol. c. 4. τὸvidere Deum,Ioh. 1, 18. (qui locus huic nostro parallelus est,) rectè exponit de cognitione DEI. à quà tamen minùs rectè divinae essentiae cognitionem excludit, tantùm de voluntatis divinae cognitione illum intelligens. Etenim licet ultrò largiamur, cumprimis de voluntatis divinae cognitione, tum hic tum Ioh. 1. sermonem esse, quin & hoc concedamus, essentiam divinam in hâc infirmitate perfectè à nobis cognosci have

posse, haut quaquam tamen cognitio divinae essentiae, in quātum ea in saci is literis revelata nobis est, nempe quòd DEus sit unus in essentiâ, trinus in personis, item quòd sit essentia infinita, aeterna, spiritualis &c. à salutari DEI notitiâ sequestranda est. Sed cùm Episcopii adsertio è communi Arminianorum errore, nempe quòd non sint necessariò tenenda ea omnia, quae ad divinam essentiam & omnes operandi modos pertinent, profluat; illum verò solidè refutarit Dn. D. Calovius in Arminianismi consideratione p. 60. seqq. nolo actum agere.)*

*( Nisi Filius. Neutiquam excluduntur reliquae Deitatis personae, sed omne illud, quod non est Deus. Conf. 1. Cor. 2, 11.c. 12, 3. Loca parallela sunt Ioh. 1, 18.c. 3, 13. Est verò hoc insigne pro Christi deitate argumentum. Add. 2. Cor. 4, 6.1. Thess. 5, 23.Iacob. 1, 18.)*

*( Cui voluerit Filius revelare. Vid. Ioh. 1, 18. Etenim sicuti Solem hunc visibilem ac stellas sine ipsarum ope ac luce adspicere non possumus, ita nec Deum Patrem, nisi illuminet nos Filius, qui est ἀπάυγασμα τῆς δόξης αὐτου,Ebr. 1, 3. Conf. Ioh. 1, 4. 5,8. 9.c. 14, 6.9. Pluscula huc facientia collegit Schevichavius libb. de SS. Trinit. p. 16. & 157. Vult autem Filius revelare omnibus venientibus ac ipsum audientibus. Irenaeus lib. 4. adv. haeres. c. 14. p. 242. Revelaverit non solùm in futurum dictum est, quasi tunc inciperet Verbum manifestare Patrem, cùm de Maria natus est, sed communiter per totum tempus positum est. Ab initio enim adsistens Filius suo plasmati, revelat omnibus Patrem &c. Huc faciunt locaExod. 19, 19.coll. cumAct. 7, 38.Exod. 23, 23.c. 33, 2.Es. 63, 9.Proverb. 9, 3. coll. cumLuc. 11, 49.Ex eo autem, quòd nemo potest cognoscere Patrem, nisi cui Filius revelarit, nempe per verbi revelati lectionem vel auditum,1. Cor. 1, 12.Roman. 10, 17.Ioh. 17, 20.manifestum est, quòd conversionis opus in solidum Deo sit adscribendum. Quò faciunt etiam seqq. dicta,Ioh. 15, 5.1. Cor. 4, 7.c. 11, 3.2. Cor. 3, 5.Contra Synergistas.

Vid. pluribus hâc de re agentem B. D. Hutterum ad F. C. p. 158. 159.)*

## 11:28
v. 28. Come to me all, etc. August. bk. to Bonif. ch. 3. To come to Christ is to believe in Christ. in Ps. 45. If you believe, you come. *(Episcopius in Resp. ad Q. LXIV. Q. 12. raises a doubt from this place, how it is forbidden by John 1. ep. 5, 16. to pray for those who sin unto death, when yet pardon is here promised by Christ to all sinners. Furthermore, how ἐαντιοφ this is to be solved will be advised at the Johannine passage. Moreover, a parallel passage to this place John 6, 37. add. Matt. 8, 7. From the fact, however, that Christ invites those burdened with sins and admonishes them to come to him, it is not to be gathered or established with the Pelagians, as if man could convert himself to God by his own powers. Or with the Papists, see Bell. bk. 2. de G. & L. A. ch. 3. that man can cooperate with prevenient grace. The contrary is evident from Eph. 2, 1. add. August. bk. 1. against two epistles of the Pelagians ch. 19. and no one comes to Christ, unless the Father has drawn him. John 6, 44. Christ therefore does not indicate this as if man could come to him by the proper powers of nature, i.e., could salutarily convert himself through his own powers, but he hints at this, that man ought not to place an obstacle, harden himself, nor maliciously and stubbornly resist the divine calling. If he has done this, the Father will draw him, that he may come to Christ.)*

*( All who are burdened. By the burden of sins, namely, as Theophylact rightly explains. But all men after the fall are burdened by sin and all but oppressed by that burden, Rom. 2, 9. c. 5, 12. seqq. c. 7, 23. c. 11, 32. Therefore the calling is universal, extending itself even to the evil, or those who refuse to come. See Matt. 18, 11. c. 22. 3. c. 23, 37. Acts 13, 46. c. 17, 30. therefore no one is excluded from salutary rest or eternal salvation by some absolute hatred of GOD. Against the Calvinists, whose exceptions, that that divine calling is not serious as regards the reprobate, have been satisfied elsewhere.)*

Ὁι κοπιῶντες, who labor even to the point of exhaustion:

for thus κοπιᾶν differs from πονεῖν Terrified by the sense of divine wrath against sin. August. serm. 12. on the words of the Apostle. You who labor under the burdens of sins and the yoke of the evil Mistress of iniquity. *(Rightly the Jesuit Tirinus on this passage Learn that I am gentle, from the remission not only of the faults of sins, but also of the punishments. But if Christ remits the faults and punishments of sins to those coming to him, that is, to believers, what need is there further for personal satisfactions? What need for purgatorial fire?)*

Πεφοτισμθύοι who feel the burden of sins. Ambrose ep. 18. No pain is greater than that which wounds the conscience with the dagger of sin, nor is any burden heavier than the load of sins and the weight of crimes. *(Yet Christ does not call to himself only those who feel the burden of sins, groan under it, and come to him, as indeed D. Ioh. Georgius Grossius in Theatr. Bibl. p. 865 and other Calvinists maintain, but he calls absolutely all who are burdened by sin, and most humanely invites them and seriously urges them to come. For he speaks in this place not so much of the act of refreshment, as of the prompt and beneficent will to refresh, as the blessed Par. Coll. Isag. L. de Praedest. c. 6. §. 10 well advises. He calls not only those who come, but also those who refuse to come to they do not want to, Prov. 1, 24. Es. 65, 2. Ierem. 7. 14. Ezech. 33, 11. Matth. 23, 37. Act. 7, 51. c. 13, 46. Not only those who seek righteousness in the Gospel, but also those who pant under the law and were striving to obtain salvation and righteousness from the works of the law, as Ioan. Camero himself advises in Myroth. Evang. p. 16. Meanwhile, as far as concerns the salutary fruit of the calling, we readily grant that those at least are actually made partakers of the goods promised in the Gospel and expressed here by the name of refreshment, who come to Christ, that is, who believe in him. For just as serious contrition is the forerunner of true faith, so the blessed O. are its handmaidens. It is necessary, therefore, to feel the burden of sins and to grieve seriously over sins, who desire to obtain rest from Christ. Christ does not enter into the dwelling of our heart by grace, unless the herald of repentance, John, has first prepared the way through repentance. But it is by no means permitted to conclude: Those at least actually find rest with Christ who come to him and acknowledge the burden of sins. Therefore, Christ also wanted only those to come. Nay, rather, he wants all to come and acknowledge their sins. Conf.) 1. Tim. 2, 4. 2. Petr. 3, 9. Whence he also complains, that they are unwilling to come. Proverb. 1, 24. 25. Luc. 13, 34.

*( Ἀναπάυσω ὑμας Augustin. in Ps. 140.Christ in this life restores us, in the fatherland he will satisfy us. For now we are restored so that we may endure. For it is necessary that we hunger, until we are satisfied. *(Compare Es. 55, 1.c. 12, 3.Zach. 13, 1.Ioh. 4, 14. This passage is also accustomed to be urged here against the invocation of deceased saints: For the Savior does not send us here to deceased saints, but he alone promises rest, and commands that we come to him. Paludanus objects in Vindiciae on this passage p. 222. Just as nothing departs from the sufficiency of the Redeemer, because the faithful ask the living to pray for one another, so neither through the invocation of saints. But elsewhere (see Analecta on Col. 4, 3.) it has already been shown that there is an altogether huge difference between the invocation of the living, and the invocation of the deceased, whom they call saints. See also B. Par. L. de Morte §. 256.)*

Latin:

v. 28. Venite ad me omnes &c. August. l. ad Bonif. c. 3. Venire ad Christum, est credere in Christum. in Ps. 45.Si credis, venis. *(Movet ex h. l. Episcopius in Resp. ad Q. LXIV. Q. 12. dubium, quomodo àIoh. 1.ep. 5, 16. interdictum sit, precandi pro iis, qui peccant ad mortem, cùm tamen venia hîc promissa à Christo omnibus peccantibus sit. Coeterùm quomodo, ἐαντιοφ haec solvenda sit, ad locum Iohanneum monebitur. Locus porrò parallelus h. l. Ioh. 6, 37. add. Matth. 8, 7. Ex eo autem, quòd Christus invitat peccatis oneratos monetque, ut ad ipsum veniant, non colligendum aut statuendum cum Pelagianis, ac si homo propriis viribus ad Deum sese convertere possit. Vel cum Pontificiis, vid. Bell. l. 2. de G. & L. A. c. 3. quòd homo gratiae praevenienti cooperari possit. Contrarium patet ex Eph. 2, 1. add. August. l. 1. contra duas epist. Pelagii c. 19. ac nemo venit ad Christum, nisi Pater traxerit eum.Ioh. 6, 44. Christus igitur non hoc indicat, quasi propriis naturae viribus homo venire ad eum possit, h. e. salutariter sese per proprias vires convertere, sed hoc innuit, quòd homo non debeat obicem ponere, obdurare, nec malitiosè ac morosè vocationi divinae repugnare. Hoc si fecerit, Pater, ad Christum ut veniat, trahet.)*

*( Omnes qui onerati estis. Onere nempe peccatorum, uti rectè exponit Theophy lactus. At omnes homines post lapsum peccato onerati ac tantum non onere isto oppressi, Rom. 2, 9.c. 5, 12. seqq. c. 7, 23. c. 11, 32. E. vocatio est universalis, extendens sese ad malos etiam, sive qui venire recusant. Vid. Matth. 18, 11.c. 22. 3.c. 23, 37.Act. 13, 46.c. 17, 30. nullus igitur absoluto quodam DEI odio à salutari quiete sive salute aeternâ exclusus est. Contra Calvinianos, quorum exceptionibus, quòd vocatio illa divina, quantum ad reprobos non sit seria, alibi satisfactum.)*

Ὁι κοπιῶντες,qui laboratis ad defatigationem usque:

ita enim κοπιᾶν differt à πονεῖν Perterrefacti sensu irae divinae adversus peccatum. August. serm. 12. de verb. Apost. Qui laboratis sub sarcinis peccatorum & subiugo malae Dominae miquitatis. *(Rectè Iesuita Tirinus in h. l. Discite, me esse svavem, ex remissis peccatorum non modò culpis, sed & poenis. At si Christus peccatorum culpas & poenas venientibns aceum h. e. credentibus remittit, quid opus ampliùs propriis satisfactionibus? quid igne purgatorio?)*

Πεφοτισμθύοιqui sentitis onus peccatorum. Ambrosius ep. 18. Nullus maior est dolor, quàm is, qui peocati mucrone vulner at conscientiam, neque ullo gravius est onus, quàm peccatorum sarcina & pondus flagitiorum. *(Neque tamen Christus illos solùm ad se vocat, qui peccatorum onus sentiunt, sub eo ingemiscunt, & ad ipsum veniunt, uti quidem D. Ioh. Georgius Grossius in Theatr. Bibl. p. 865. aliique Calviniani volunt, sed vocat omninò omnes, qui peccato onerati sunt, eosque humanissimè in vitat ac seriò hortatur, ut veniant. Loquitur enim h. l. non tam de refocillationis actu, quàm de promtâ & beneficâ refocillandi voluntate, uti benè monet B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. de Praedest. c. 6. §. 10. Vocat non solùm qui veniunt, sed etiam qui venire recusant ad nolunt,Prov. 1, 24.Es. 65, 2.Ierem. 7. 14.Ezech. 33, 11.Matth. 23, 37.Act. 7, 51.c. 13, 46. Non solùm, qui in Evangelio iustitiam quaerunt, sed etiam, qui sub lege anhelant & ex legis operibus salutem & iustitiam conse qui satagebant, ceu ipse monet Ioan. Camero Myroth. Evang. p. 16. Intereà quod salutarem vocationis fructum concernit, facilè largimur, illos saltem bonorum in Evangelio promissorum & hîc refocillationis nomine expressorum actu reddi participes, qui veniunt ad Christum h. e. qui in eum credunt. Quemadmodum enim verae fidei pedisse qua sunt B. O. ita anteambuio est seria contritio. Oporter igitur onus peccatorum sentire ac seriò de peccatis dolere, quire quiem impetrare à Christo concupiscunt. Non intrat Christus in cordis nostri domicilium per gratiam, nisi poenitentiae praeco Iohannes viam priùs paraverit per poenitentiam. Minimè verò colligere licet: Illi saltem actu inveniunt apud Christum quietem, qui ad eum veniunt & peccatorum onus agnoscunt. E. etiam Christus illos saltem venire voluit. Imò potiùs vult, ut omnes veniant & peccata sua agnoscant. Conf. 1. Tim. 2, 4. 2. Petr. 3, 9. Unde etiam conqueritur, quòd venire nolint. Proverb. 1, 24. 25. Luc. 13, 34.)*

*( Ἀναπάυσω ὑμας Augustin. in Ps. 140.Christus in vit â reficit nos, in patriâ satur abit nos. Modò enim ut duremus, reficimur. Nam necesse est, esuriamus, quoad usque. satiemur. *(Confer. Es. 55, 1.c. 12, 3.Zach. 13, 1.Ioh. 4, 14. Urgeri etiam hic locus solet contra in vocationem sanctorum defimetorum: Etenim Salvator hîc non ad Sanctos defunctos. nos remittit, sed ipse solus requiem pollicetur, iubetque, ut ad ipsum veniamus. Excipit Paludanus in Vindiciis ad h. l. p. 222. Sicuti nihil dècedit Redemtoris sufficientiae, quòd à viventibus fideles petunt, ut pro invicem orent, it a nec per sanctorum invocationem. Verùm alibi (vid. Analecta ad Col. 4, 3.) iamtum Ostensum, quòd ingens omninò sit discrimen inter viventium -ompellationem, & sanctorum, quos vocant, defunctorum invocationem. Vid. etiam B. Par. L. de Morte §. 256.)*

## 11:29
v. 29. Take my yoke upon you. Both doctrine, as well as the chastisements which depend upon it, are called a yoke in the O. T., from which this metaphor is taken, Thren. 3, 9. It is also most customary to the Rabbis, as in פרקי אבות c. 3. *(See also Lud. Capellus in Spicil. p. 21. Hackspanius tr: de Util. Script. Rabb. p. 461. But Christ speaks in this place not of the yoke of the law,Gal. 5, 1.Matt. 23, 4. which is unbearable,Act. 15, 10. but of the cross. Which, although it is altogether a sufficiently heavy burden for the flesh, is nevertheless rendered a light and sweet burden to those believing in Christ. 1. On account of Christ helping and going before,Matth. 16, 24.Rom. 8, 17.2. Corinth. 12, 9. 2. On account of God, moderating the burden of the cross,1. Corinth. 10, 13.

*( and they enlarge the borders of their garments. Because of the same rewarder. See Mark 8:34.Luke 9:13.Rom. 8:18.2 Cor. 4:17.Apoc. 7:14. Whence also the pious boastRom. 5:3. of this yoke and rejoiceCol. 1:24. under the same. St. Augustine treats this theme at length in sermon 48 de tempore, from which I cannot, because I shall translate some of these things. But thus it is there: It seems wonderful to some, dearest brothers, when they hear the Lord saying: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take up my yoke etc. And they consider those who have submitted to that yoke with an intrepid neck, and have taken up that burden with most gentle shoulders, to be so agitated and exercised by the difficulties of this age, that they seem to be called not from labors to rest, but from rest to labor, when the Apostle says: All who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.2 Tim. 3. Someone therefore says, how is his yoke sweet etc. And having brought forward the passages 2 Cor. 6:4, 5.c. 11:23. and following, he concludes: Therefore all those works which the Apostle commemorated, he sustained more frequently and more abundantly, but surely the Holy Spirit was present to him, who would renew the inner man from day to day in the corruption of the outer man, and having tasted spiritual rest in the abundance of the delights of God, in the hope of future beatitude he would soften all present things, and lighten all harsh and heavy things. Behold how sweet the yoke. And with some things interspersed, by which he shows that men often sustain the hardest things for the sake of following temporal advantages, he seals it with excellent sentiments: Love makes all cruel and monstrous things entirely easy and almost nothing. How much more certainly and easily, therefore, does charity do for true beatitude what greed did as much as it could for misery? How easily is any temporal adversity tolerated, so that eternal punishment may be avoided, and eternal rest may be acquired? And again: Nothing is so easy to a good will as itself, and this suffices for God. The same author has similar things in sermon 9 on the words of the Lord and sermon 12 on the words of the Apostle: Let us hear etc. Compare also, especially concerning humility, Gregory the Great, book 4 of the Morals, ch. 39, book 20 of the Morals, ch. 16. Elias of Crete, Oration 4 of Nazianzen. Chrysostom, homily 9 on Genesis. With whose sweetest sermons John de la Haye adorned the chariot, which he inscribes in this way, in chapter 105, note 6. Furthermore, from the fact that the yoke of Christ is called Sweet, the Papists strive to prove, see Bell. vol. 4. Controv. book 4. on Justification ch. 11. Coturius Epit. Controv. Demonstr. 12. p. 259. Iacobus Bayus Instit. C. R. book 3. ch. 17. Council of Trent Sess. 6. ch. 11. Costerus Enchir. Controv. page 235.) that the law of GOD is a light yoke, and therefore can be perfectly fulfilled by the reborn, nay, that the same can do more than God has commanded them. But we respond 1. by repeating the previously cited distinction between the yoke of the law, and of the cross. That the Savior is speaking here of the latter, not the former, is evident both from the parallel passage, Matth. 16, 24. and from Act. 15, 10. 2. by noting that the very doctrine of Christ is in a certain way called a light burden, namely in comparison with the law of Moses or the moral law, as that which demands perfect obedience under the penalty of eternal curse Deut. 27, 26. 3. by observing that the law of Christ is called a yoke or light burden both imputatively, because believers know that Christ has freed them from the curse of the law, so that although they themselves cannot render perfect obedience to it, they must by no means despair, since the curse does not strike them. For the perfect obedience of Christ, by which He satisfied the divine law in our place, is imputed to believers through faith Act. 10, 43.Rom. 3. 24.c. 4, 5.2. Cor. 5, 12.Philipp. 4, 13. and inchoatively, because believers are renewed by the Holy Spirit, who causes them to imitate Christ, 1. Petr. 2, 21.Phil. 2, 5. and to render obedience to the law with a spontaneous spirit, Rom. 7, 22.Tit. 2, 14. which, although it is by no means obedience perfect in all respects, and therefore if it is considered legally, it cannot stand in the rigorous judgment of GOD: yet the same considered evangelically, i.e., insofar as God, on account of the most perfect obedience of Christ, covers the adhering stains and imperfections of sins, 1. Iohan. 2, 1.Roman. 4, 7. is accepted by Him with a fatherly mind. But from this it can neither be collected, nor ought it to be, that we can render perfect obedience to the divine law legally, and therefore by that fulfillment of the law merit eternal salvation: for we know that all our good works, if they are considered in the rigorous judgment of GOD, are impure, Isa. 64, 6. item; that eternal life is a gratuitous gift of GOD in Christ, Rom. 6, last.)*

Learn from me, for I am meek &c. This is explained in two ways: 1. so that the sense may be that we ought to learn this very thing from Christ, that he is humble, or the virtue of humility. Thus Athanasius, sermon 4 against the Arians; Jerome to Paula and Eustochium on the assumption of Mary; Chrysostom, homily 29 on Matthew *(also Augustine, book on Holy Virginity; Bernard, sermon 4 on the Advent of the Lord, and sermon 5 on the Vigil of the Nativity, &c.)* 2. so that the particle for may be causal, and a reason be rendered why we ought to learn everything from him, because, namely, he is most humble. Gregory, book 20 of Morals on chapter 30 of Job. *(Blessed Pareus embraces the former explanation, part 1, Academic Homilies, p. 509, and warns that merely hearing Christ does not make one a Christian, but it is also required that the word of Christ be fulfilled in deed as well. Nor do those hear Christ unto salvation who, although they hear this admonition to humility, nevertheless persevere in their pride. Blasius Viega accepts it in the latter way, especially in Apocalypse, p. 50, where he also shows with many sayings of Holy Scripture as well as opinions of the Fathers that meekness and humility in a Master most greatly invite one to listen and obey. The elegant maxim of the Arabs also contributes to this: He who is ashamed says nothing, nor does an irascible man teach. There is, however, hardly any doubt that the former exposition agrees more with the scope of Christ in this place. There are those who think that the Savior implies by those words that the doctrine of the Gospel is not leavened by the ferment of pride and harshness, since he immediately adds: ὁ γδ ζυγός μου &c. Which words he opposes to the yoke of the law, which was unbearable, especially with the new burden of human traditions added, concerning which Matt. 23, 4. and James Acts 15, 10. This exposition pleases my blessed father-in-law, Mr. Plathner, formerly Jurisconsult and Councilor of Saxe-Weimar, in his unpublished Ephemerides Autoschediasmaticae on the New Testament.)*

*( Humble in heart i. e. in mind. A Hebraism, as noted by Gataker on the style of the New Testament, p. 258. Blessed Pareus presents many excellent opinions on humility collected from the ancient Doctors of the Church in his Practical Theological Aphorisms, title. humility, which I do not wish to transcribe here.)*

Latin:

v. 29. Tollite iugum meum. Tam doctrina, quàm castigationes, quae ab eâ dependent, in V. T. vocantur iugum, unde sumta est haec metaphora, Thren. 3, 9. Rabbinis etiam usitatissima, ut in פרקי אבות c. 3. *(Vid. quoq; Lud. Capellus in Spicil. p. 21. Hackspanius tr: de Util. Script. Rabb. p. 461. Loquitur verò hoc loco Christus non de iugo legis,Gal. 5, 1.Matt. 23, 4. quod importabile,Act. 15, 10. sed crucis. Quae licet omninò carni satis grave onus sit, redditur tamen credentibus in Christum onus leve ac suave. 1. Propter Christum auxiliantem ac praecedentem,Matth. 16, 24.Rom. 8, 17.2. Corinth. 12, 9. 2. Propter Deum, crucis onus moderantem,1. Corinth. 10, 13.

3. Propter eundem lai giter remuner antem. Vid. Marc. 8, 34.Luc. 9, 13.Rom. 8, 18.2. Cor. 4, 17.Apoc. 7, 14. Unde etiam pii de iugo isto glorianturRoman. 5, 3. sub eodemque gaudent,Col. 1, 24. Prolixè hoc thema pertractat S. August. serm. 48. de tempore, è quo non possum, quia nonnulla haec transferam. Ita verò ibi: Mirum quibusdam videtur, fratres charissimi, cum audiunt Dominum dicentem. Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego reficiam vos. Tollite iugum meum &c. & considerant eos, qui iugum ipsum intrepidâ cervice subierunt, & illam sarcinam mansuetissimis humeris acceperunt, tantis agitari & exerceri difficultatibus huius seculi, ut non à laboribus ad quietem, sed à quiete ad laborem vocati videantur, cum Apostolus dicat: Omnes qui volunt piè vivere in Christo Iesu, persecutionem patientur.2. Tim. 3.Ait ergo aliquis, quomodo iugumeius suave est &c. Allatisque locis 2. Cor. 6, 4. 5.c. 11, 23. seqq. concludit: Omnia ergo (Apostolus) illa, quae commemoravit opera, & gravia, frequentiùs & abundantiùs sustinebat, sed profecto aderat ei Sp. S. qui in exterioris hominis corruptione interiorem renovaret de die in diem, & gustatâ requie spirituali in affluentiâ delitiarum Dei, in spe futurae beatitudinis omnia praesentia deliniret, aspera & gravia omnia relevaret. Ecce quám suave iugum. Et interiectis nōnullis, quibus ostendit, quòd ad temporaha commoda conse quentia homines saepè durissima sustineant, obsignat egregiis sententiis: Omnia saeva & immania prorsus facilia & prope nulla efficit amor. Quantò ergo certius ac facilius ad veram beati itudinem charitas facit, quod ad miseriam quantum potuit cupiditas fecit? Quam facilè toler atur quaelibet adversitas temporalis, ut aeterna poena vitetur, aeterna quies comparetur? & iterum: Nihil tam facile est bonae voluntati, quàm ipsasibi, & haec sufficit Deo. Similia habet idem serm. 9. de verbis Domini ac serm. 12. de verbis Apostoli: Audiamus &c. Conf. etiam, cumprimis de humilitate Gregor. M. lib. 4. Moral. c. 39. l. 20. Mor. cap. 16. Elias Cretensis Orat. 4. Naz. Chrysost. hom. 9. in Gen. Quorum dulcissimis sermonibus currum, quem ita inscribit, veritatis exornavit Ioannes de la Haye c. 105. not. 6. Ex eo porrò, quòd Christi iugum dicitur suave, evincere satagunt Pontificii, vid. Bell. t. 4. Controv. lib. 4. de Iustif. c. 11. Coturius Epit. Controv. Demonstr. 12. p. 259. Iacobus Bayus Instit. C. R. l. 3. c. 17. Concilium Trid. Sess. 6. c. 11. Costerus Enchir. Controv. pag. 235.) legem DEI esse iugum leve, adeoque à renatis perfectè posse impleri, quin posse eosdem plus facere, quàm Deus illis praecepit. Verùm resp. 1. repetendo antè allatam distinctionem inter iugum legis, & crucis. Quòd verò Salvator de hâc, non de illâ hîc loquatur, patet tum ex loco parallelo, Matth. 16, 24. tum ex Act. 15, 10. 2. notando, quòd ipsa etiam doctrina Christi certo modo onus leve dicatur, nempe in collatione, cum lege Mosis s. morali, ut quae sub maledictionis aeternae poenâ perfectam obedientiam exigit Deut. 27, 26. 3. observando, quòd lex Christi dicatur iugum s. onus leve tum imputativè, quia credentes sciunt, quòd Christus eos libera verit à maledictone legis, ut licet ipsi perfectam obedientiam praestare illi nequeunt, desperare tamen minimè debeant, cùm maledictio eos non feriat. Perfecta enim Christi obedientia, quâ legi divinae nostri loco satisfecit, per fidem credentibus imputatur Act. 10, 43.Rom. 3. 24.c. 4, 5.2. Cor. 5, 12.Philipp. 4, 13. tum inchoativè, quia credentes renovantur per Sp. Sanctum, qui efficit, ut Christum imitentur, 1. Petr. 2, 21.Phil. 2, 5. ac spiritu spontaneo obedientiam legi praestent, Rom. 7, 22.Tit. 2, 14. quae licet obedientia omnibus numeris perfecta haut quaquam sit, adeoque si legaliter consideretur, in rigeroso DEI iudicio consistere nequeat: eadem tamen Evangelicè considerata, h. e. quat. Deus, propter perfectissimam obedientiam Christi, adhaerentes peccatorum maculas & imperfectiones tegit, 1. Iohan. 2, 1.Roman. 4, 7. paterno ab codem animo acceptantur. Sed exinde colligi nec potest, nec debet, quòd legi divinae perfectam praestare obedientiam legaliter possimus, adeoque per istam legis impletionem salutem promereri aeternam: novimus enim, quòd omnia nostra B. O. si in rigeroso DEI iudicio considerentur, sint impura, Esa. 64, 6. item; quòd vit aeterna sit donum DEI gratuitum in Christo, Rom. 6, ult.)*

Diseite à me, quia mitis sum &c. Duobus modis hoc exponitur 1. ut sit sensus, nos hoc ipsum à Christo discere debere, quòd sit humilis, seu virtutem humilitatis. Ita Athanasius serm. 4. contr. Arianos, Hieron ad Paulum & Eusto chium de adsumt. Mar. Chrysostomus homil. 29. in Matthaeum *(it. August. lib. de S. Virgin. Bernahardus serm. 4. de Adventu Domini, ac serm. 5. in Vigil. nativ. &c.)* 2. ut particula quia sit causalis, & reddatur ratio, cur ab ipso omnes discere debeamus, quia scil est maximè humilis. Greg. lib. 20. Moral in c. 30. Iobi. *(Priorem explicationem amplectitur B. Par. part. 1. Homil Acad. p. 509. monetque, quòd audire solummodo Christum non Christianum faciat, sed requiratur etiam, ut opere quoque verbum Christi impleatur. Neque salutariter Christum audiunt, qui lieet hanc admonitionem ad humil. audiant, tamen in fastu suo perseverant. Posteriori modo accipit cumprimis Blafius Viega in Apoc. p. 50. ubi etiam multis tum Sc. S. dictis, tum Patrum sententiis ostendit, quòd mansuetudo ac humilitas in Magistro maximè inviter ad audiendum & parendum. Facit quoq; eò elegans Arabum gnome: Qui erube seit, nil dicit, nec iracundus docet. Vix autem dubium, quin prior expositio Christi scopo h. l. magis conveniat. Sunt, qui existimant, Salvatorem verbis illis hoc innuere, quòd doctrina Evangelii non sit superbiae ac diritatis fermento subacta, cùm statim subiiciat: ὁ γδ ζυγός μου &c. Quae verba opponit iugo legis, quod erat incolerabile, praesertim novo onere traditionum humanarum accedente, de quibus Matth. 23, 4. & Iacobus Act. 15, 10. Arridet expositio haec B. Socero, Dn. Plathnero, Icto ac Consil. quondam Saro-Vinariensi in Ephem. Autosch. in N. T. ineditis.)*

*( Humilis corde i. e. animus. Ebraismus, notante Gatakero de stylo N. T. p. 258. De humilitate multas egregias sententias ex antiquis Ecclesiae Dd. collectas sistit B. Par. in Aphorismis Theol. Pract. tit. humilitas, quae huc transcribere nolo.)*

## 11:30
v. 30. My yoke is easy. Aug. in the book on the usefulness of believing. Precepts are heavy to those who are unwilling, light and sweet to those who are willing, *(A most beautiful sentiment of the same Aug. in Ps. 59. vol. 8. col. 607. brought forward by B. Glassius, Sacred Rhetoric, p. 407. The doctrine of the Gospel is called a yoke, because it is the word of the cross, 1 Cor. 1:18. It embraces, however, true faith in Christ, and a pious life adorned with meekness, humility, and patience. For there are two supports, as it were, of our Christianity, faith and patience, Phil. 1:19. Heb. 6:12. Faith nourishes patience, patience proves faith, as B. D. Bald. well advises, C. C. p. 694. Beautifully B. D. Hunnius on this passage: Just as Christ takes away from them (the sinners coming to him) that intolerable burden of sins and casts it upon his own shoulders: so by a most desirable exchange he imposes another yoke and burden, which is convenient and light. Furthermore, in the Greek of this passage is ξρηςὸν which has a kinship with the name Christ, just as also some of the ancients, such as Justin Martyr, Apol. 2 for the Christians, p. 42, and Lactantius, book 4 of the Institutes, ch. 7, p. 202, record, derived the name Christ from the word χράομαι. The yoke of the cross is therefore 1. the yoke of Christ, because it is imposed upon us by his brotherly hand. It is 2. useful, because it ensures that we do not stray from the straight path to the heavenly fatherland. It is 3. sweet, because the sweetness of divine consolation refreshes us under that yoke, 2 Cor. 1:4, 5.)*

In the present chapter is proposed: I. A dispute of Christ with the Pharisees concerning the right celebration of the Sabbath. v. 1.—8. II. The healing of the man whose hand was withered. v. 9.—13. III. The withdrawal of Christ from Judea to the Gentiles on account of the evil counsels of the Pharisees. v. 14.—21. IV. The healing of the demoniac who was blind and mute, and the blasphemous disparagement of that miracle by the Pharisees, and the Lord's apology and defense against them. v. 22.—35. V. The explanation of the sign of Jonah. v. 38.—41. VI. A sweet instruction as to who are the mother and brothers of Christ. v. 47. to the end.

Latin:

v. 30. Iugum meum est facile. Aug. in lib. de sault. docum. Praecepta gravia sunt nolentibus, levia & suavia volentibus, *(Cons. eiusd. Aug. pulcerrima sententia in Psal. 59. t. 8. col. 607. adducta à B. Glassio Rhet. S. p. 407. Dicitur doctrina Evangelii iugum, quia est verbum crucis, 1. Corinth. 1, 18. Complectitur autem ea fidem in Christum veram, vitam piam ac mansuetudine, humilitate & patientiâ exornatam. Duo enim sunt qs. fulcra Christianismi nostri, fides & patientia, Phil. 1, 19.Ebr. 6, 12. fides potientiam alit, patientia fidem probat, uti benè monet B. D. Bald. C. C. p. 694. Pulcrè B. D. Hunnius in h. l. Quemadmodum Christus ab illis (peccatoribus venientibus) intolerabilem illam sarcinam peccatorum aufert & in suos humeros reiicit: ita exoptatissima permutatione iugum & onus aliud, quod commodum & leve sit, imponit. Coeterùm in Graeco h. l. est ξρηςὸν quod cognationem habet cum nomine Christi, quemadmodum etiam veterum nonnulli, ceu Iustinus Martyr. Apol. 2. pro Christ. p. 42. & Lactant. l. 4. Instit. c. 7. p. 202. memorant, à verbo χράομαι nomen Christi deduxerunt. Est igitur iugum crucis 1. iugum Christi, quia à fraternâ eius manu nobis imponitur. Est. 2. utile, quia efficit, ne à rectâ ad coelestem patriam semitâ aberremus. Est 3. suave, quia consolationis divinae suavitas sub iugo illo nos recreat, 2. Cor. 1, 4. 5.)*

Proponitur in praes. capite I. Christi de rectâ Sabbathi celebratione, cum Pharisaeis Disputatio. v. 1.—8. II. Hominis, cui manus arida, sanatio. v. 9.—13. III. Christi ob mala Pharisaeorum consilia è Iudaeâ ad gentes secessio. v. 14.—21. IV. Daemoniaci coeci & muti curatio, ac Pharisaeorum blasphema illius miraculi extenuatio, Dominique adversus illos Apologia & defensio. v. 22.—35. V. Typi Ionae explicatio. v. 38.—41. VI. Suavis, qui Christi mater ac fratres sint, informatio. v. 47. ad finem.

## 12:1
v. 1. Τοῖς σάββασι. On the Sabbath. The plural is certainly put for the singular, as Zech. 9. 9. Matt. 20, 1. (B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 94. refers hither v. 5. 10. 11. 12. Luke 4, 16. Acts 13, 14. The Oriental interpreters expressed it by the singular. But the Evangelist seems to follow the LXX, as those who Lev. 23, 32. translate the noun שבת of the singular number as σάββατα. Unless we would rather say that that is the genuine reading which has ἐνσαββάτω; yet the Greek MS. Eclogae of the Nuremberg Library also acknowledge the former reading. Luke 6, 1. where the same history is described, there is σάββατον δευτερόπρωτον, concerning which it will be treated more at length there.)

They began to pluck. Syr. They began plucking. The participle is put for the infinitive, after the manner of the Hebrews. That is to say, they had scarcely begun to pluck the ears of corn, when the Pharisees rebuked them on that account. Such plucking was permitted in the law. Deut. 23, 25.

Latin:

v. 1. Τοῖς σάββασι.Sabbatho. Pluralis pro singulari certo ponitur, ut Zach. 9. 9.Matth. 20, 1. *(B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 94. huc refert v. 5.10. 11. 12.Luc. 4, 16.Act. 13, 14. Orientales Interpp. expresserunt per singularem. Videtur autem Evangelista sequi LXX. ut qui Levit. 23, 32. nomen שבת sing. numeri vertunt σάββατα. Nisi potiùs dicere velimus, illam genuimam esse lectionem, quae habet ἐνσαββάτω; priorem tamen lectionem agnoscunt etiam Eclogae MSS. Graecae Bibl. Norib. Luc. 6, 1. ubi ead. hist. describitur, habetur σάββατον δευτερόπρωτον, de quo ibi prolixiùs agetur.)*

Coeperunt vellere. Syr. Coeperunt vellentes. Participium ponitur pro infinitivo, more Hebraeorum. q. d. vix dum coeperant vellere spicas, cùm Pharisaei eo nomine ipsos increparent. Talis evulsio concessa erat in lege. Deut. 23, 25.

## 12:2
(v. 2. Which it is not lawful to do on the Sabbath. Vulg. less correctly on the Sabbaths. But Francis Ribera of Villacastín gathers from these words, l. 5. de Templo c. 1. that the present history happened not on any feast day, but on the Sabbath properly so called, inasmuch as on it food could not be prepared, whereas on other feast days it was lawful, Exod. 12, 16. Otherwise it was by no means prohibited by divine law that anyone should pluck ears of corn to eat, even on the Sabbath properly so called, as if in passing, it is evident from Deut. 23, 25. but at least by παραδόσεις The Jewish teachers extended the Precept concerning the sanctifying of the Sabbath even that far. Whence the Blessed D. Bald. in Idea Dispositionum Bibl. p. 213, warns that Christ here argues from an abundance. This hypothesis being posited: If it were otherwise a sin in the highest degree to pluck ears of corn on the Sabbath, which the Pharisees opined, it is nevertheless no sin of the disciples of Christ, who knew that this deed was prohibited by no law of GOD.

TO CHAPTER XII. SUMMARY AND DISPOSITION.

Latin:

*(v. 2. Quod non licet facere in Sabbatho. Vulg. minùs rectè Sabbathis. Colligit verò ex his verbis Franc. Ribera Villacastinensis l. 5. de Templo c. 1. contigisse historiam praesentē non festo aliquo die, sed Sabbatho propriè dicto, utpote quo escae parari non poterant, cùm aliis festis diebus id licitum esset,Exod. 12, 16. Coeterùm minimè lege divinâ erat prohibitum, ne quis etiam Sabbatho propriè dicto spicas ad manducandum, quasi in transcursu, evellat, patet ex Deut. 23, 25. sed saltem per παραδόσεις suas eousque Praeceptum de sanctificando Sabbatho Iudaeorum Magistros extendebant. Unde B. D. Bald. in Idea Dispositionum Bibl. p. 213. monet, quòd Christus hîc argumentetur ex abundanti. Positâ hâc hypothesi. Si maximè aliàs peccatum esset, in Sabbatho evellere spicas, quod Pharisaei opinabantur, nullum tamen est peccatum discipulorum Christi, qui factum hoc nullâ lege DEI prohibitum esse sciebant.)*

AD CAP. XII. SUMMA AC DISPOSITIO.

## 12:3
v. 3. What David did &c. It is evident from the example of David, approved by the Lord, that ceremonial laws yield to moral ones even in the second table, when, namely, both cannot have a place. But how they also elsewhere prove by the example of David that it is lawful in a case of necessity to profane the Sabbath, namely to decline the danger of death, Lud. Cappellus shows from כרבר רבה Spicil. p. 22 & 35. But however in that example of David, to which Christ looks back, it is not a matter of the Sabbath, the Savior nevertheless rightly brings it forward, arguing namely from the genus to the species; and conversely from the species of this deed to the genus, and thus showing that those divine laws were so sanctioned that they yield to necessity, which causes those things to become lawful which otherwise were not lawful by the law. Thus B. D. Chemn. in H. E. Dn. D. Walth. H. B. p. 767.

Latin:

*(v. 3. Quid fecerit David &c. Patet ex Davidis exemplo, à Domino approbato, quòd ceremonialia cedant moralibus etiam in secundâ tabula, quando sc. utraque locum habere nequit. Quomodo verò alibi quoque Apellae Davidis exemplo probent, licere in casu necessitatis prophanare Sabbathum, ad mortis nempe declinandum periculum, ostendit ex כרבר רבה Lud. Cappellus Spicil. p. 22. & 35. Ut ut verò in illo Davidis exemplo, ad quod Christus respicit, non agatur de Sabbatho, rectè tamen illud Salvator adducit, argumentando nempe à genere ad speciem; & vicis sim à specie huius facti ad genus, & ita ostendendo, quòd leges istae divinae ita sancitae sint, ut cedant necessitati, quae facit, ut licita fiant illa, quae aliàs per legem non licebant. Ita B. D. Chemn. in H. E. Dn. D. Walth. H. B. p. 767.)*

## 12:4
v. 4. What Matthew says here εἰ μὴ τοῖς ἱερευα, that Mark c. 2 v. 26 explains ἱερευσι μονοις. The use of which observation is in the disputation concerning the exclusive particle. (Conf. B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 499.)

And ate the showbread &c. August. l. 12: against Faustus c. 33. When David ate the showbread, which it was not lawful to eat except for the Priests alone, he prefigured that both would be in one person, i.e., in one Lord J. C., Kingdom and Priesthood. (Conf. Id. August. l. 1. de Consens. Ev. c. 3.) Furthermore, the example of David brought forward by Christ seems to be contrary to 1. Sam. 21, 2.7. But one must distinguish between the receiving of the same, and the eating itself. David alone had come to Abimelech the Priest 1. Sam. 21, 1. because he had ordered his ministers to wait outside, but he did not eat alone from those showbreads, but he also shared them with his ministers. (This reconciliation also pleases Dn. D. Walth. in H. E. at this place.)

*( Showbread. This is treated in Lev. 24. It is said there, v. 5. that the individual loaves ought to have two tenths, namely of an Ephah. Now the tenth part of an Ephah was called otherwise a Gomer, likewise an Assaron. Whence Josephus in book 3 of the Antiquities of the Jews, chapter 3, writes: The loaves were unleavened, made from the flour of two assarons, which measure of the Hebrews contains seven Attic cotylae. But since an Ephah is the tenth part of a Cor, which kind of measure corresponds to our modius, which consists of about two hundred pounds, it is clear that the individual loaves weighed about four pounds. Whence also in the Ernestine Bibles in the Gloss Lev. 24, 5. it is noted that individual loaves of this kind sufficed for individual men for two days. It is added in the same place that they were like cakes. And if that is so, they err who have taken care to have them delineated or engraved in copper like common loaves, which is what the Jesuit Tirinus did, whom the Londoners also followed in the Apparatus to the Holy Bible in the Trissagion. More is treated concerning these loaves in Exod. 25, 30.c. 35, 13.c. 39, 36. Compare Josephus book 3 of the Antiquities, chapter 9. Ribera book 2 on the Temple, chapter 10. Villalpando on Ezekiel.)*

*( Have you not read in the law. Namely Exod. 29, 36.Num. 28, 9.)*

Latin:

v. 4. Quod Matthaeus h. l. dicit εἰ μὴ τοῖς ἱερευα, id Marcus c. 23 26. exponit ἱερευσι μονοις. Cuius observationis usus in disputatione de particulâ exclusivâ. *(Conf. B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 499.)*

Et panes propositionis edit &c. August. l. 12: contra Faustum c. 33. David cùm panes propositionis manducavit, quos non licebat manducare, nisi solis Sacerdotibus, in unâ personâ utrumq; futurum i. e. in uno Domino I. C. Regnum & Sacerdotium figuravit. *(Conf. Id. August. l. 1. de Consens. Ev. c. 3.) *Caeterùm exemplum Davidis à Christò adductum contrariari videtur 1. Sam. 21, 2.7. Distinguendum autem inter acceptionem eiusdem, & ipsam comestionem. David solus venerat ad Abimelech Sacerdotem 1. Sam. 21, 1. quia ministros iusserat foris expectare, sed non manducavit solus ex panibus illis propositionis, verùm communicavit etiam ministris. *(Placet haec conciliatio etiam Dn. D. Walth. in H. E. ad h. l.)*

*( Panes propositionis. De his agitur Lev. 24. Dicitur verò ibi, v. 5. quòd singuli panes duas decimas habere debeant, videl. Ephi. Vocabatur autem aliàs decima Ephi pars Gomer, item Assaron. Unde Iosephus lib. 3. Antiquit. Iud. c. 3. scribit: Erant panes azymi è farina duorum assarorum, quae mensura Ebraeorum septem Cotylas Atticas continet. Cùm verò Ephi sit decima pars Cori, quod mensurae genus nostro modio, qui ducentis circiter constat libris, respondet, patet, quòd singuli panes libras habuerint circiter quatuor. Unde etiam in Bibliis Ernestinis in Glossâ Lev. 24, 5. notatur, quòd singuli huiusmodi panes suffecerint singulis hominibus ad biduum. Additur ibidem, quòd instar placentarum fuerint. Quod si ita est, errant qui instar panum vulgarium delineari vel aeri incidi curârunt, id quod Iesuita Tirina fecit, quem secuti etiam sunt Londinenses in Appar. ad SS. Bibl. in Trissagio. Pluribus de istis panibus agitur Exod. 25, 30.c. 35, 13.c. 39, 36. Conf. Iosephus l. 3. Antiq. c. 9. Ribera l. 2. de Templ. c. 10. Villalp. ad Ezech.)*

*( Annon legistis in lege. Nempe Exod. 29, 36.Num. 28, 9.)*

## 12:5
v. 5. Βεβηλοῦσι, i.e., from the hypothesis of the Pharisees, who thought that the Sabbath is polluted by any action of the hands. *(There is therefore a Catachresis, as noted by B. D. Glassius in Philologia Sacra, p. 466. Others note that Christ speaks κατ᾽ ἔνδοξον, as elsewhere more often. See the notes on Matth. 8, 12.)* D. Kimchi in chapter 6 of Joshua: He who commanded the Sabbath, commanded also to violate the Sabbath. The Rabbis say: Danger to souls and the crisis of death drives away the Sabbath; just as if someone is sick with danger to life, or if a boy has fallen into the sea. See the Talmud volume on the Sabbath and Circumcision. R. Jonathan son of Joseph says concerning the Sabbath: It is delivered as a sign into your hand, and you are not delivered into its hand.

*( And to be without crime. The reason is because necessity was present, namely the divine precept, by which they were commanded to offer victims even on the Sabbath, which without the labor of hands s. could not be done by servile work. See Isidore of Pelusium book 1, epistle 72. Thus, because it is likewise commanded to us by God that we preserve our own life and that of our neighbor, it is clear that those works are done on the Sabbath without crime, without which our life or that of our neighbor could not otherwise be preserved.)*

Latin:

v. 5. Βεβηλοῦσι, sc. ex hypothesi Pharisaeorum, qui putabant, Sabbatum pollui quacunque manuum actione. *(Est igitur Catachresis, notante B. D. Glassio Rh. S. p. 466. Alii notant, quòd Christus loquatur κατ᾽ ἔνδοξον, ceu alibi saepiùs. Vid. notata ad Matth. 8, 12.)* D. Kimchi in c. 6. Iosuae: Is qui praecepit Sabbatum, praecepit etiam violare Sabbatum. Rabbini dicunt: Periculum animarum & mortis discrimen pellit Sabbatum; velut si quis cum periculo vitae aegrotet, aut si puer in mare ceciderit. Vid. Talmud volum. de Sabb. & Circumcis. R. Ionathan filius Iose de Sabbato dicit: Traditum est signum in manu vestrâ, & vos non estis traditi in manum eius.

*( Et sine crimine esse. Ratio est, quia aderat necessitas, praeceptum nempe divinum, quo iubebantur etiam Sabbatho victimas offerre, id quod abs-ue manuum labore s. operâ servili fieri haut poterat. Vid. Isid. Pelus. l. 1. ep. 72. Sic quia itidem divinitùs nobis praeceptum est, ut nostram & proximi vitam cōservemus. patet quòd sine crimine Sabbato illa opera fiant, sine quibus nostra vel proximi vita aliàs conservari non posset.)*

## 12:6
v. 6. Τοῦ ἱεροῦ μείζων ᾽δςιν ὧδε. Some codices read μεῖζον in the neuter gender, which Casaubon approves. There is something here greater than the temple. Which reading, besides ancient copies and Theophylact, is confirmed by similar passages, below v. 41. 42. *(The blessed D. Glassius, Gr. S. p. 76, prefers this latter reading to the former for the reasons just adduced. But the Orientals, the Syrian, the Ethiopian, and the Persian follow the former reading, just as B. Luther also does in the German version. The Greek MS Eclogae of the Nuremberg Library confirm the same.)* The sense is, that the manual labors which the priests employ on the Sabbath in the temple do not profane the Sabbath, therefore the plucking of ears of corn by the disciples following Christ on the Sabbath is to be considered much less a profanation of the Sabbath. *(Indeed, with Christ permitting it: since He is holiness itself. So it is held in the Gloss. Bibl. Ernest.)*

Latin:

v. 6. Τοῦ ἱεροῦ μείζων ᾽δςιν ὧδε. Quidam Codd. legunt μεῖζον in genere neutro, quod probat Casaubonus. Est hic aliquid maius templo. Quam lectionem etiam praeter vetera exemplaria & Theophylactum consirmant similes loci, infrà v. 41. 42. *(Praefert hanc posteriorem lectionem B. D. Glassius Gr. S. p. 76. ob adductas modò rationes priori. Sed priorem lectionem sequuntur Orientales, Syrus, Aethiops ac Persa, quemadmodum etiam B. Lutherus in vers. Germ. Confirmant eandem Eclogae MSS. Graecae Bibl. Norib.)* Sensus est, qui operae manuariae, quas Sacerdotes adhibent Sabbatho in templo, non profanant Sabbathum, ideo multò minùs Sabbathi profanatio censenda est, quòd discipusi Christum secuti Sabbato spicas evellunt. *(Imò Christo concedente: cùm hic sit sanctitas ipsa. Ita habetur in Gloss. Bibl. Ernest.)*

## 12:7
v. 7. καὶ οὐ is placed for rather than, as Prov. 12, 7. *(Compare what is noted at c. 9, 13.)*

Latin:

v. 7. καὶ οὐ ponitur pro potiùs quàm, ut Prov. 12, 7. *(Confer quae notata ad c. 9, 13.)*

## 12:8
*(v. 8. Κύριος γάρ ᾽δςι καὶ του σαββάτου &c. Beza notes that the particle καὶ was missing in ancient copies. But although the Orientals also omit it, it seems by no means to be omitted, since it is emphatic. Just as the Greek MS Eclogae also rightly acknowledge the same. The Vulgate and B. Luther have expressed the emphasis remarkably well.)*

Some establish that by son of man in a general sense is understood any man, who through a Hebrew periphrasis is everywhere in Scripture called son of man, because Luke, with the article omitted, says: ιἱὸς του ἀνθρώπου And Mark derives that sentiment from another, pronounced concerning man in general. The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. But it is more consistent with the text to understand by son of man Christ, who, since He first instituted the Sabbath, can therefore prescribe or change the manner of observing it . *(Indeed, this power of loosening the Sabbath belongs to Christ not only according to His divine, but also according to His human nature, namely through and on account of the grace of the personal union, which the Savior Himself indicates not obscurely, while) The Son of man, which name is attributed to Christ by reason or respect of his human nature, he says is Lord of the Sabbath. Whence it also appears that Ioh. Piscator of Herborn erred not lightly in several places, namely Vol. 3. Thes. Theol. L. 25. th. 18. p. 321. L. 26. th. 40. p. 333. &c. Annot. Bibl. ad c. 2. Lucae v. 51. f. 234. item Resp. Apol. ad Parasc. Vorstii part. 2. c. 8. p. 187. asserting that the active obedience of Christ is not the meritorious cause of our redemption, and he adds the reason, since Christ according to his humanity was bound to perform it for himself, both by the right of creation and by the right of the divine covenant, but if he was bound to perform it for himself, he could not for others. But the reasons of Piscator are frivolous, since he considers Christ as ψλάνσθρωπον, when nevertheless he was θεἀνθρωπος, that is, in the unity of the person he himself is Jehovah and that supreme legislator. We argue from this place against the Herborn theologian: If Christ as Son of man, i.e., according to the assumed human nature, is Lord of the Sabbath, it follows that he is not a servant of the same, and consequently not of the remaining precepts, and therefore he was not bound to perform obedience to the law for himself. But the former is true. Therefore the latter is also. The connection is proved, because it is contrary for one and the same person to be a servant and Lord in one and the same respect. Furthermore, the reason for all divine precepts is equal, and he who is Lord of one cannot be called a servant or debtor of others. And the observation of some here is beautiful, that Christ had respect to his human nature v. 5. and 6. when his body, as the antitype of the temple, Iohan. 2, 19. is that temple in which dwells the whole fullness of the Godhead, Col. 2, 9. And it is evident moreover from other sayings of Holy Scripture, namely Matth. 16, 27. c. 19, 28. c. 23, 31. c. 28, 18. Act. 2, 36. c. 10, 36. 38. &c. that this sublimity is by no means to be denied to Christ as man, namely that he is Lord of all. But that Christ, having received by circumcision, bound himself to the observance of the law, which Piscator also urges, from that indeed nothing else can be gathered than that he willed to be subjected to the law in our place. Gal. 4, 4. 5. and to perform perfect obedience for us and on our account, for unto us he is born, unto us he is given,Es. 9, 6.Ioh. 3, 16. We now omit very many most serious errors, which flow from that opinion of Piscator, as the blessed D. Fewrbornius has excellently shown in Synt. Theol. l. part. 3. diss. 2. p. 512. et seqq. Whence also long ago he was deserted by his own, refuted, and indeed even abandoned, as it is evident, because Georgius Carletanus the Englishman in Lib. de Consensu Eccl. Cathol. contra Concil. Trid. part. 3. c. 3. has expressly impugned that error. The same opinion is also rejected by Ioh. Camero in Myroth. Evang. ad h. l. p. 16. Beza, Polanus, and other Calvinists. But on the other hand, Matthias Martinius, Rudolphus Goclenius, Hermannus Ravenspergerus, and furthermore, if faith is to be had in Wendelinus, Ursinus, Paraeus, Petiscus, and Scultetus have embraced it. But Wendelinus in Exerc. 123. § 6. likewise urges the reasoning of Piscator, and distinguishes especially between for our good, and to act in our place. He asserts that the former embraces active and passive obedience, but the latter only passive. And under the shield of this distinction he thinks himself safe. But what is to be held concerning it will be advised more prolixly in Anal. ad Gal. 4, 5. Moreover, the following ought to be consulted here especially: B. D. Mentzerus Dispp. Giesens. Tom. 3. Disp. 15. B. D. Eckardus in a special disquisition on this matter, printed here at Jena in the year 1606. B. Par. L. de Iustif. §. 56. B. D. Bald. Comm. in ep. ad Gal. p. 817.

Latin:

*(v. 8. Κύριος γάρ ᾽δςι καὶ του σαββάτου &c. Notat Beza, particulam καὶ in veteribus exemplaribus defuisse. Verùm licet Orientales quoque omittant, minimè tamen omittenda videtur, cùm sit emphatica. Sicuti etiam Eclogae Gr. MSS. rectè eandem agnoscunt. Egregiè verò emphasin expresserunt Vulgatus ac B. Lutherus.)*

Quidam statuunt per filium hominis in genere intelligi quemvis hominem, qui per periphrasin Hebraicam passim in Scripturâ filius hominis appellatur, quia Lucas omissô articulô dicit: ιἱὸς του ἀνθρώπου Et Marcus sententiam illam deducitex aliâ, de homine in genere pronūciatâ. Sabbatum propter hominem factum est, non homo propter Sabbatum. Sed textui magis congruit, per filium hominis intelligere Christum, qui cùm primus instituerit Sabbatum, ideò modum illud servandi potest praescribere vel mutare. *(Competit verò haec potestas solvendi Sabbatum, Christo non solùm secundùm divinam, verùm etiam secundum humanam naturam, nempe per ac propter unionis personalis gratiam, id quod non obscurè indicat ipse Salvator, dum Filium hominis, quod nomen Christo ratione sive respectu humanae naturae tribuitur, Dominum Sabbati esse dicit. Unde etiam patet, quòd haut leviter errarit Ioh. Piscator Herbornensis, plusculis locis, videl. Vol. 3. Thes. Theol. L. 25. th. 18. p. 321. L. 26. th. 40. p. 333. &c. Annot. Bibl. ad c. 2. Lucae v. 51. f. 234. item Resp. Apol. ad Parasc. Vorstii part. 2. e. 8. p. 187. adserens, obedientiam Christi activam non esse causam meritoriam nostrae redemtionis, additque rationem, quoniam Christus iuxta humanitatem suam debuerit illam praestare pro se, tum iure creationis, tum iuro foederis divini, si verò pro se debuit eam praestare, non potuit pro allis Sed frivolae sunt Piscatoris rationes, quippe considerantis Christum ut ψλάνσθρωπον, cùm tamen fuerit θεἀνθρωπος, h. e. in unitate personae ipse Iohova ac summus ille legislator. Argumentamur ex h. l. contra Herbornensem: Si Christus Filius hominis s. secundùm adsumtam humanam naturam est Dominus Sabbati, sequitur quòd non sit servus eiusdem, & per consequens nec reliquorum praeceptorum, adeoque nec pro se ad obedientiam legi praestandam obstrictus fuerit. Atqui prius est verum. E. & posterius. Connexio probatur, quia contraria sunt, unum aliquem uno eodemque respectu esse servum & Dominum. Praetereà omnium praeceptorum divinorum par ratio, & qui unius Dominus est, non potest dici aliorum servus, sive debitor. Ac pulchra est quorundam hîc observatio, quòd Christus ad humanam naturam respectum habuerit v. 5. & 6. cùm ipsius corpus, utpote templi antitypon, Iohan. 2, 19. sit illud templum, in quo habitat tota Deitatis plenitudo, Col. 2, 9. Et constat insuper ex aliis Sc. S. dictis, videl. Matth. 16, 27.c. 19, 28.c. 23, 31.c. 28, 18.Act. 2, 36.c. 10, 36.38. &c. quòd ista sublimitas Christo, ut homini minimè sit deneganda, quòd nempe sit Dominus omnium. Quòd verò Christus circumcisione acceptâ ad legis observationem sese obstrinxerit, quod etiam Piscator urget, ex eo sanè nihil colligi aliud potest, quam quòd nostri loco legi voluerit subiici Gal. 4, 4. 5. eidemque pro nobis ac propter nos perfectam obedientiam praestare, nobis enim natus est, nobis datus,Es. 9, 6.Ioh. 3, 16. Omittimus iam plurimos gravissimos errores, qui ex illâ Piscatoris sententia profluunt, ceu egregiè monstravit B. D. Fewrbornius Synt. Theol. l. part. 3. diss. 2. p. 512. seqq. Unde etiam pridem à propriis desertus, refutatus imò etiam, sociennis ille fuit, quemadmodum constat, quòd Georgius Carletanus Anglus in Lib. de Consensu Eccl. Cathol. contra Concil. Trid. part. 3. c. 3. ex professo errorem illum impugnarit. Eandem sententiam reiicit quoque Ioh. Camero Myroth. Evang. ad h. l. p. 16. Beza, Polanus ac alii Calviniani. Amplexi verò econtrà illam sunt Matthias quoque Martinius, Rudolphus Goclenius, Hermannus Ravenspergerus, praetereà etiam, si fides habenda Wendelino est, Ursinus, Paraeus, Petiscus & Scultetus. Urget verô Wendelinus Exerc. 123. § 6. itidem rationem Piscatoris, & distingvit cumprimis inter nostro bono, ac nostro loco facere. Illud activam & passivam obedientiam complecti adserit, hoc verò passivam tantùm Atque sub huius distinctionis scuto salvum se putat. Verùm quid de eâ habendum sit, prolixiùs monebitur in Anal. ad Gal. 4, 5. Consuli autem cumprimis hic debent B. D. Mentzerus Dispp. Giesens. Tom. 3. Disp. 15. B. D. Eckardus in pec. disquis. de hâc materiâ, excusâ hîc Ienae An. 1606. B. Par. L. de Iustif. §. 56. B. D. Bald. Comm. in ep. ad Gal. p. 817.)*

## 12:9
*(v. 9. He came into the Synagogue. Concerning the Synagogues of the Jews, it will be treated in Analect. ad Marc. 1, 21.)*

Latin:

*(v. 9. Venit in Synagogam. De Synagogis Iudaeorum agetur in Analect. ad Marc. 1, 21.)*

## 12:10
v. 10. And behold there was a man. From the Gospel of the Nazarenes, which is called according to the Hebrews, it is understood that this man was a mason. Hieron. in Comm. in h. l. In the Gospel, which the Nazarenes and Ebionites use, which I recently translated into the Greek and Hebrew language, and which is called by many the authentic [Gospel] of Matthew, that man who had a withered hand is written as a mason, begging for help with these words: Mason—

I was, seeking a living with my hands, I pray Thee, Iesu, that Thou wouldst restore health to me, lest I beg shamefully. But that Gospel is not authentic.

Hand ξηρὰ. 1 Kings 13, 4.John 5, 3.

Matthew says that Jesus was questioned: but in Mark ch. 3, 4. and Luke ch. 6, 6. it is said that he questioned them. Theophylact reconciles this in such a way that the Pharisees, anticipating, questioned him, and Jesus questioned them anew. They can also be understood in such a way that Jesus questioned them, and they, by questioning in turn, questioned him back. The Pharisees first asked: Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, as it is in Matthew; Christ responded through ἀντερώτησιν: Is it lawful to do good or evil on the Sabbath, as it is in Mark and Luke. *(Mr. Dr. Walth. Harm. Bibl. p. 768 embraces this latter opinion.)*

*( εἰ ἔξεςι εἰ in this place is taken interrogatively, as elsewhere in many places; See below ch. 19, 3. Luke 22, 49.Acts 1, 6. etc. The same subject matter proposed. Luke 14, 13.ch. 13, 16.John 5, 9.ch. 7, 22.)*

Latin:

v. 10. Et ecce homo erat. Ex Evangelio Nazaraeorum, quod secundùm Hebraeos vocatur, intelligitur, hunc hominem fuisse caementarium. Hieron. in Comm. in h. l. In Evangelio, quo utuntur Nazareni & Ebionitae, quod nuper in Graecum ac Ebraeo sermone transtuli, & quod vocatur à plerisq; Matthaei authenticum, homo iste qui aridam habebat manum, caementarum scribitur istius modi vocibus auxilium precans: Caementar—

eram manibus victum quaeritans, precor Te, Iesu, ut mihi restituas sanitatem, ne turpiter mendicem. Sed Evangelium istud non est authenticum.

Manusξηρὰ.1. Reg. 13, 4.Ioh. 5, 3.

Matthaeus dicit, Iesum interrogatum fuisse: in Marco verò c. 3, 4. & Luca c. 6, 6. dicitur, hunc interrogasse. Theophylactus hoc ita conciliat, quoòd Pharisaei antevertentes interrogaverint, & Iesus interrogaverit denuò. Possunt etiam ea sic accipi, quòd interrogaverit eos Iesus, & ipsi alter cando rursum interrogaverint. Pharisaei primùm interrogârunt: Anfas sit sanare Sabbato, ut est apud Matthaeum; Christus per ἀντερώτησιν respondit: An fas est Sabbato bonum vel malum agere, ut est apud Marcum & Lucam. *(Postremam hanc sententiam amplectitur Dn. D. Walth. Harm. Bibl. p. 768.)*

*( εἰ ἔξεςι εἰ h. l. accipitur interrogativè, uti alibi passim; Vid. infrà c. 19, 3. Luc. 22, 49.Act. 1, 6. &c. Eadem materia proposita. Luc. 14, 13.c. 13, 16.Ioh. 5, 9.c. 7, 22.)*

## 12:11
*(v. 11. Who will there be among you etc. Since in the Talmud of the Jews, which is to them like canon law, it is prohibited that they should not pull a beast out of a pit on the Sabbath, R. Lipmann seizes from there in נעחוז an occasion for caviling, as if the Savior in this place had attributed something to the Jews, implying that they were accustomed to do such a thing lawfully on the Sabbath day. But it is by no means credible that, if Christ had falsely attributed this to the Jews, they would have passed over or concealed it with silence: but since this was done by them, it is clear that that prohibition, which is read today in the Talmud concerning not pulling a beast out of a pit on the Sabbath day, was inserted into the Talmud subsequently and some centuries later, a thing which also seems so to Buxtorf in Synag. Iudaicae ch. XI, where he simultaneously shows at length how many things, very ineptly and ridiculously, they require today for the celebration of their Sabbath. Let W. Schickard also be compared in de Iure Regio Ebr. tr. p. 145. seqq.)*

Latin:

*(v. 11. Quis erit ex vobis &c. Cùm in Iudaeorum Talmud, quod iuris instar canonici illis est, prohibitum sit, ne pecudem Sabbato è fovea extrahant, arripit inde R. Lipmannus in נעחוז occasionem cavillandi, ac si Salvator h. l. aliqua Iudaeis affinxerit, innuens quipp, etale quid eos die Sabbati licite facere solere. Verùm minimè credibile est, si falsò hoc Christus Iudaeis tribuisset, eostum silentio id praetermissuros vel dissimulaturos: hoc verò cum factum ab eis sit, patet, prohibitionem illam; quae de pecude die Sabbato nonextrahendâ è foveâ, hodie in Talmud legitur, postliminio ac aliquot seculis pòst Talmudo intrusam esse, id quod etiam Buxtorffio videtur Synag. Iudaicae c. XI. ubi simul prolixè ostendit, quàm multa perquàm ineptè & ridiculè ad Sabbati sui festivitatem Apellae hodie requirant. Conferatur quoque W. Schickardus in de Iure Regio Ebr. tr. p. 145. seqq.)*

## 12:12
*(v. 12. Καλῶς ποιεῖν. Pfochenius thinks that since among the Greeks καλῶς δρᾷν and καλῶς πράττειν occur for ευδρᾷν etc., καλῶς ποιεῖν also does not taste of Hebraism placed then namely for εὐποιεῖν. He presupposes indeed that τὸ ποιεῖν, πράττειν, καὶ διο, obtains the same signification. But Thomas Gataker sufficiently convicts him of error in his work on the style of the New Testament, chapter 27. And indeed, to all who have tasted even with the first lips the Ethical writings of the Philosopher, it is known that in the same author ποίζιν, and ποιεῖν καὶ πράττειν. differ greatly. See book 6 of the Ethics, chapter 4. But Franciscus Piccolomineus of Siena shows the difference between ποίησιν i. e. making, and πρίζιν i. e. acting at greater length in his Moral Philosophy, Grade 5, chapter 52, page 506 and following.

Latin:

*(v. 12. Καλῶς ποιεῖν. Existimat Pfochenius, quòd cùm apùd Graecos καλῶς δρᾷν & καλῶς πράττειν pro ευδρᾷν &c. occurrant, etiam καλῶς ποιεῖν non sapere Ebraismum positum tum sc. pro εὐποιεῖν. Praesupponit vero τὸ ποιεῖν, πράττειν, καὶ διο, eandem signficationem obtinere. Sed satis de errore covicit illum Thom. Gatakerus de styl. N. T. c. 27. Et sanè omnibus, qui vel primis saltem labris Philosophi degustarunt scripta Ethica, notum est, quòd apud eundem plurimum differant ποίζιν, adeo-ue ποιεῖν καὶ πράττειν. Vid. l. 6. Ethic. c. 4. Plusculis verò differentiam inter ποίησιν i. e. effectionem, & πρίζιν i. e. actionem ostendit Franc. Piccolomineus Senensis Philos. Moral. Grad. 5. c. 52. p. 506. seqq.)*

## 12:14
v. 14. Οἱ -φαρισαῖοι συμβούλιον ἔλαβενκατ αὐτου ἐξελθόντες. It is a transposition, for which Theophylact reads more clearly thus: λαβεν.

Latin:

v. 14. Οἱ -φαρισαῖοι συμβούλιον ἔλαβενκατ αὐτου ἐξελθόντες. Traiectio est, pro quâ Theophylactus ita legit planiùs: λαβεν.

## 12:15
v. 15. But Jesus, knowing this. Cf. below v. 25; likewise ch. 9, 4. Luke 9, 47. ch. 11, 17. Ps. 94, 11. 1 Cor. 3, 20. Col. 2, 3. 9. Caspar Barthius notes in book 48 of his Adversaria, chapter 9, that the translator into our language (by whom he means Luther) frequently falls into this error: that almost whenever our Lord Jesus is said to have known what was being done, or said, or known secretly among others, he makes it appear that the Son of God needed outside help or the passage of time to perceive it, thereby removing it from His present and spontaneous knowledge. Where accordingly Blessed Luther translates "Uber Iesus da Er muste," Barthius prefers to render it: "Iesus aber solches wissende." What is to be thought of this observation must be left to the judgment of others.) * (

Secessit illinc. | He withdrew from there. See what was noted above at verse 23 of ch. 10, p. 564, and add to the authors cited there the Blessed D. Hutter, Loci Theologici, page 963.)*

Latin:

*(v. 15. Iesus autem quum hoc nosset. Conf. infrà v. 25. it. c. 9, 4. Luc. 9, 47.c. 11, 17.Ps. 94, 11.1. Cor. 3, 20.Col. 2, 3.9. Notat Caspar Barthius l. 48. Advers. c. 9.
