Interpretem nostri Idiomatis (per quem Lutherum intelligit) saepè errorem hunc errare, ut quoties ferè de Domino nostro Iesu dicitur, eum cogua habuisse, quae clam apud alios vel fierent, vel dicerentur, vel cognorentur, ille quasi alienâ ope aut tempore adea percipienda DEI filius opus habuisset, ab intellectu eius praesente & spontaneo ea removeat. Ubi proinde B. Luth. vertit. Uber Iesus da Er muste/ Barthius mavult reddere: Iesus aber solches wissende. De quâ animadversione quid censendum sit, aliorum esto arbitrii.)*

*( Secessit illinc. Vid. quae not. suprà ad vers. 23. c. 10. p. 564. ac adde autoribus ibi adductis B. D. Hutterum LL. Theol. pag. 963.)*

## 12:16
v. 16. Interminabatur eis. | He strictly charged them. The Son of God did not wish to be preached by spirits, he who became flesh; by the impure, he who is pure; by liars, he who is truthful; by the condemned, he who is righteousness and salvation. *(Why the Savior did not wish to be manifested, and the miracles performed by him to be proclaimed by many, was indicated above at ch. 8, 4, also at ch. 9, 30; add what was noted at Marc. 7, 36. )* *(

Latin:

v. 16. Interminabatur eis. Filius DEI noluit praedicari à spiritibus, ipse caro factus; ab impuris, ipse purus; à mendacibus, ipse verax; à condemnatis ipse iustitia & salus. *(Cur Salvator noluerit se manifestari, ac miracula à se facta multis depraedicari, suprà indicatum ad c. 8, 4. it. ad c. 9, 30. add. quae notata ad Marc. 7, 36.)*

## 12:17
*(v. 17. That it might be fulfilled, which was spoken &c. It is known that although the Evangelists and Apostles, in citing testimonies from the Old Testament, for the most part follow the Greek version of the Seventy, as that which was at that time most received among the Jews, especially the Hellenists, they nevertheless embrace the Hebrew text itself rather than the Greek version where the Seventy deviate from it. Which observation can be confirmed in the present passage, for when the Seventy-two depart from the authentic text by inserting the name Of James, Matthew omitted that. Which thing is also noted by Jerome in his Commentary on Is. 42, 1. and likewise in his epistle to Algasia.)*

Latin:

*(v. 17. Ut impleretur, quod dictum erat &c. Notum est, quòd cum Evangelistae & Apostoli in allegandis testimoniis è T. V. ut plurimùm Graecam LXX. sequantur versionem, ut quae tum temporis inter Iudaeos, cumprimis Hellinistas, receptissima, eosdem tamen, ubi septuaginta à textu Ebraeo deviant, hunc potiùs amplecti, quàm versionem Graecam. Quae observatio praesenti loco confirmari potest, Cum enim LXXII. discedant à textu authentico, sinserendo nomen Iacobi, omisit illud Matthaeus. Id quod etiam notatum Hieronymo Comm. ad Es. 42, 1. itemque in ep. ad Algasiam.)*

## 12:18
v. 18. Behold my servant &c. This prophecy of Isaiah, cited according to the sense, not the words, and always understood by the ancient interpreters concerning the Messiah, can conveniently be said to refer to v. 15. Nor can we approve the corruption of Jerome admitted through the carelessness of scribes. *(The Targum, or the most ancient Chaldean version, which expressly has הא עברי משיחא., accepts this prophecy concerning the Messiah. Cf. Ezech. 34, 23.c. 37. 24.)*

*( Ὁ ἀγαπητόςμου. In Isaiah c. 42, 1. there is בחיר which properly denotes elect. add. c. 43, 10. But Christ is called the elect servant of God, both by reason of peculiar love, whence also Matthew rightly expressed it by ἀγαπητὸς, and in the same way the holy angels also 1. Tim. 5, 21. are called ἐκλεκτοὶ, and also by reason of the eternal decree & election, for the work of redemption to be perfected. See 1. Petr. 1, 20.)*

εἰ ὃν εὐδόκησα, for ἐ ᾧ εὐδόκησεν. Heb. In whom my soul is well pleased. Παῖς is taken for servant, namely, Christ established in μορφῇ δούλου. *(Cf. what is noted at Philipp. 2, 7. The Ethiopian translates my son.)*

He shall announce judgment to the Gentiles. By the name of judgment, the right manner of divine worship is understood, that he shall announce, Heb. עיא- he shall bring forth, he shall make go forth to the Gentiles. Tossanus explains judgment as that they ought to do penance and cease from all injustice, Matth. 4, 17. Some understand it concerning the preaching of the Gospel, made to the Gentiles by the Apostles. *(The blessed Par. also embraces the first exposition, L. de Extr. Iudic. § 5. The passages Matth. 28, 19.Marc. 16, 15. make for the latter acceptance.)*

Latin:

v. 18. Ecce servus meus &c. Commodè hoc vaticinium Esaiae, iuxta sensum, non verba allegatum, & à veteribus Interpp. semper de Messiâ intellectum, ad v. 15. respicere dici potest. Nec Hieronymi corruptelam ex incuriâ Scribatum admissam probare possumus. *(De Messia accipit vaticinū hoc Targhum s. versio Chaldaica antiquissima, quae expressè habet הא עברי משיחא. Conf. Ezech. 34, 23.c. 37. 24.)*

*( Ὁ ἀγαπητόςμου. Apud Esaiam c. 42, 1. est בחיר quod propriè electum notat. add. c. 43, 10. Dicitur verò Christus electus Dei servus, tùm ratione peculiaris dilectionis, unde etiam Matthaeus rectè expressit per ἀγαπητὸς, eodemque modo Angeli quoque sancti 1. Tim. 5, 21. dicuntur ἐκλεκτοὶ, tùm etiam ratione aeterni decreti & electionis, ad opus redemtionis perficiendum. Vid. 1. Petr. 1, 20.)*

εἰ ὃν εὐδόκησα, pro ἐ ᾧ εὐδόκησεν. Ebr. Cui benè vult anima mea.Παῖς pro servo accipitur, Christo sc. in μορφῇ δούλου constituto. *(Conf. quae notata ad Philipp. 2, 7. Aethiops vertit filius meus.)*

Iudicium gentibus annunciabit. Iudicii nomine intelligitur recta cultûs divini ratio, illud annunciabit, Hebr. עיא-proferet, exire faciet gentibus. Tossanus exponit iudicium, quòd debeant agere poenitentiam & cessare ab omni iniustitiâ, Matth. 4, 17. Quidam intelligunt de praedicatione Evangelii, per Apostolos gentibus factâ. *(Primam expositionem amplectitur quoque B. Par. L. de Extr. Iudic. § 5. Pro posteriori acceptione faciunt loca Matth. 28, 19.Marc. 16, 15.)*

## 12:19
v. 19. He shall not cry out. i. e. he shall not preach and commend his deeds. He will not make much noise about it.

Latin:

v. 19. Non clamabit. i. e. non praedicabit & commendabit sua facta. Er wird nichi viel Geschrenes davon niachen.

## 12:20
v. 20. Smoking flax. Syr. he will not extinguish the crackling lamp. He describes a dying lamp from the sign that it crackles. *( He will not break. It is a beautiful observation that the adverbs of negation applied to verbs often denote with emphasis the affirmed contrary of that which they express. According to which rule (of which many examples are given in the H. S. See Lev. 10, 1. Prov. 12, 2. below v. 32. 1. Cor. 10, 1. &c.) by τὸ he will not break &c. it would be indicated here that he will consolidate the bruised reed and kindle the smoking flax. The blessed D. Luther observed this emphasis in t. 4. Jena Lat. f. 330. b. By the bruised reed and smoking flax are understood contrite and faint-hearted sinners, whom the merciful Lord is not about to reject, but to console, and to confirm their faith.)*

Ἕως αὔ ἐκβάλλειν εἰς νίκος τὴνκρίσιν. It signifies to bring forth true judgment concerning enemies unto victory. Us-; until he shall have brought forth judgment unto victory, with a certain force, while the world and Satan struggle in vain, he will bear sentence and judgment. Until he pronounces the sentence by which he declares himself the victor over all his enemies, which was done when the Gospel was promulgated throughout the whole world. *(The interpretation of the blessed D. Glassius follows in Gr. S. p. 457.)* Until he shall have executed his office in these lands, and shall have ascended gloriously and victoriously into heaven, then he will also call the nations to his kingdom. In Isaiah it is said The isles. But the nations are understood, who dwell in the isles, i. e., in remote and far-distant places. *(Conf. c. 44, 1.)* In Isaiah it is also said, the nations shall hope in his law, in the Evangelist in his name: but the matter returns to the same thing, because by the law of Christ the Gospel is understood. *(From the fact that not all things which the Evangelist here alleges from Isaiah pertain directly to the present scope, the Photinians in the Racovian Catechism p. 98 attempt to prove that likewise not all things pertain to Christ which Heb. 1, 10. are alleged from the O. T. as regards the creation of the world, and therefore that an argument cannot be drawn from thence for the Deity of Christ from the creation attributed to him, although the prophecy of the Psalmist is accommodated to Christ insofar as the abolition of the world ought to be accomplished through him. But although it be granted as much as possible that sometimes certain testimonies are alleged from the O. T. which do not entirely make directly for the present scope, nor are they alleged for that end, it is nevertheless sufficient for us that they speak of the same person. Thus, although perhaps the whole prophecy of Isaiah is not alleged here for that end, that it makes directly for this in its entirety, it nevertheless speaks entirely of Christ. If the Photinians have granted that in the passage Heb. 1, 10., we have what we want.)*

Latin:

v. 20. Linum fumigans. Syr. lucernam crepitantem non extinguet. Describit moribundā lucernam ex notâ, quòd crepitet. *( Non confringet. Pulcra est observatio, quòd Adverbia negandi verbis apposita saepè eius, quod exprimunt, contrariū affirmatum cum emphasi denotent. Iuxta quam regulā (cuius plurima dantur in Sc. S. exempla. Vid. Lev. 10, 1.Prov. 12, 2. infrà v. 32.1. Cor. 10, 1. &c.) per τὸnon confringet &c. indicaretur hîc, arundinem quassatam consolidabit & linum fumigans accendet. Observavit hanc emphasin B. D. Lutherus t. 4. Ienens. Lat. f. 330. b. Intelliguntur verò per arundinem conquassatam & linum fumigans peccatores contriti & pusillanimes, quos misericors Dominus non reiecturus est, sed consolaturus, fidemque illorum confirmaturus.)*

Ἕως αὔ ἐκβάλλειν εἰς νίκος τὴνκρίσιν. Significat iudicium verum proferre de hostibus ad victoriam. Us-; dum pretulerit ad victoriam iudicium, cum vi quadam, frustrà obnitente mundo & Satana, feret sententiam & iudicium. Donec pronunciet sententiam, quâ se victorem declaret omnium inimicorum suorum, id quod factum est, cùm Evangelium promulgaretur per universum orbem. *(Sequitur interpret. B. D. Glassius Gr. S. p. 457.)* Donec officium suum in his terris fuerit executus, & gloriosè ac victoriosè in coelum adscenderit, tunc etiam gentes ad suum regnum vocabit Apud Esaiam dicitur Insulae. Intelliguntur verò gentes, quae in Insulis i. e. in remotis ac procul dissitis locis habitant. *(Conf. c. 44, 1.)* Apud Esaiam quoque dicitur, gentes sperabunt in lege eius, apud Evangelistam in nomen eius: sed res eodem redit, quia per legem Christi intelligitur Evangelium. *(Ex eo, quòd non omnia, quae Evangelista h. l. ex Esaia allegat, ad praesentem scopum directè pertineant, evincere conantur Photiniani in Catech. Racov. p. 98. quòd pariter non omnia ad Christum pertineant, quaeEbr. 1, 10.ex V. T. allegantur quod spectat nempe mundi creationem, adeoque nec argumentum inde pro Christi Deitate ex creatione ei tributâ depromi possit, licet eatenus vaticinium Psalmographi ad Christum accommodetur, quatenus mundi abolitio per eum peragi debet Verùm licet quàm maximè concedatur, aliquando ex V. T. testimonia quaedam allegari, quae non integra directè ad scopum praesentem faciunt, nec eo fine etiam allegentur, sufficit tamen nobis, quòd de eadem personâ loquantur. Ita quamvis fortè non totum vaticinium Esaiae eo fine hîc allegetur, quòd directè huc integrum faciat, loquitur tamen totum de Christo. Id si Photiniani in loco quoque Ebr. 1, 10. concesserint, habemus quod volumus.)*

## 12:21
(v. 21. Then was brought to him &c. A huge discrepancy of the Oriental Interpreters occurs in this verse, as we shall advise in its own place.)

Latin:

*(v. 21. Tunc oblatus est &c. Ingens in versiculo hoc occurrit Interpretum Orientalium discrepantia, uti suo loco monebimus.)*

## 12:22
(v. 22. And he healed him. From the fact that Christ by his own power healed the blind and mute demoniac, it is rightly asserted against the Photinians that he himself is the true eternal God. Yet he did not perform these miracles only as God, but also as man in the unity of an undivided person, and indeed by a truly divine power, personally communicated to the human nature. Against the Calvinists, Hieron. Zanchius t. 8. l. 2. de Incarn. p. 146. Zach. Ursinus defens. Admon. Neust. c. 1. &c.)

Latin:

*(v. 22. Et sanavit eum. Ex eo quod Christus propriâ virtute Daemoniacum coecum & mutum sanavit, rectè contra Photinianos adseritur, quòd ipse sit verus aeternus Deus. Neque tamen solùm ut Deus, sed etiam ut homo in unitate indivisae personae ista fecit miracula, & quidem virtute verè divinâ, humanae naturae personaliter communicatâ. Contra Calvinianos, Hieron. Zanchium t. 8. l. 2. de Incarn. p. 146. Zach. Ursinum defens. Admon. Neust. c. 1. &c.)*

## 12:24
v. 24. He does not cast out demons, except in Beelzebub. R. Acha (as R. Mose Hadarschan writes in exposit. Ps. 74, 9.) predicted that the generation of the wicked among the Jews would not believe in the signs which the Messiah was to perform, but would say that they were done by Magic art and names of uncleanness.

( Except by Beelzebub. Some read Beelzebul. Concerning which reading what should be determined will be shown in the Analects to Marc. 3, 22. Now at least concerning the meaning of the name Beelzebub. The common opinion is that it sounds God of flies, and was thus called the Deity of the Accaronites. But whether that name was imposed by the Accaronites themselves upon their idol, because when they were gravely vexed by flies, they hoped that they would be freed from that plague by that one appeased by victims, which opinion pleases the Gloss of the Ernestine Bibles) 2. Reg. 1, 2. And the passage of Pliny, book 10, chapter 28, favors the same, or because their divinity, that is to say, the devil, exhibited himself to them in such a form to be seen in this way. (Just as it has also been handed down to memory that he thrust himself upon men in the form of a fly, and so obsessed them. Martin Del Rio, in book 3 of his Disquisitiones Magicae, part 1, question 7, page 433, relates an example from the 5th book of Johannes Nider. A certain minister of our Church also published last year a history of an obsessed girl, in which something similar is read, and it is likewise reported concerning the spirits, which they call familiar, that they are kept in the likeness of a fly.) To this point it serves that it is believed by some that Beelzebub denotes not so much the god of the fly, as the god fly. Indeed, Flavius Josephus, the Jewish historian, explains it simply Μιῖαν.. Which the Greek interpreters of the Seventy also do, and those who follow their version, and Franciscus Junius notes from Nazianzen ςηλιτευτ. β against Julian, that Beelzebub had the figure of a fly. But whether by the Jews out of contempt, because when the Temple of Jerusalem counted this also among those singular privileges granted to it by God, that although so many victims were slaughtered in it daily, yet no fly was ever seen there, as it is in Pirke Abhoth, chapter 5, § 6, 7. On the contrary, however, the shrines of the Accaronites and other nations consecrated to Jupiter swarmed with flocks of flies. Since that Accaronitic Jupiter could not drive them away, they judge that for this reason he was contemptuously called Beelzebub by the Jews, when otherwise, as Philo and Augustine teach, he was called by them Beelsames (as by the Romans Jupiter Olympius, as Josephus Castalio notes in chapter 9 of his Variae Lectiones), that is to say, Lord of heaven. And this latter opinion especially pleases Hugo Grotius in his Annotations to chapter X, Matth. v. 25. But what is to be determined concerning the most ancient coin, which is believed to be of the Phoenicians, and therefore also of the Accaronites? It presents on one side half, for instance the front part of a stag, and on the other the image of a fly. Such a one I also keep in my antiquarian collection. Are we to conclude that such coins were minted by the Jews in contempt of the idol of the Phoenicians? Let the Jew Apella believe that, not I. But if such things were procured by the Phoenicians or Accaronites themselves, it is by no means credible that they would have done such a thing in contempt of their own Jupiter. Furthermore, since by the heathens themselves Jupiter ἀπόμιιος (Pasor in Etym. Nom. Propr. has ἐπομιῖος i. e. called the driver away of flies, both because Pausanias in the Arcadian books, and Pliny book 10, ch. 18, and book 29, H. N. ch. 6, record that when the Cyrenaeans had sacrificed to the God of flies, Acaron, and the Greeks to Jupiter, whom they named Myiodes, as if you would say Fly-catcher, all the flies flew away as if by one impulse and departed outside the territory. From this, Io. Bodinus of Angers in his De Magorum Daemonomaniâ, book 1, ch. 3, suspects that if the report about the Toletan and Venetian Palace is certain, that in the latter there is no fly, but in the former at least one, it must be concluded entirely that some idol had been buried under the threshold of the Palace. Especially, however, it seems to be contrary to the opinion of Grotius that the idolatrous King Ahaziah, about to seek help from that idol, is read to have distinguished it by that name himself. For when he fell down from his fall, he sent messengers, and said to them: Go, inquire of בבעל זבזב אלהי עקווז Baalzebub the God of Ekron, if I shall live from this infirmity.2. Reg. 1, 2. It is, however, by no means credible that Ahaziah, about to demand aid, would have distinguished the idol by a name imposed upon it out of contempt. Nor did Jonathan and the Arab Interpreter in the said place render it sufficiently to the mind of Ahaziah, of whom the former translates the Hebrew אלהי עקרוז as טעות עקרוז,, the latter i. e. the idol of Acron. Whence also Selden rightly determined in Synt. 2. de diis Syr. ch. 6, that the God of the Accaronites themselves was called Baalzebub. In which opinion our great Chemnitius also is in Harm. Evang. ch. 69; he thinks, however, perhaps in the language of the Accaronites, by whom that name was imposed upon the idol, it signified something else; but the Jews afterwards, according to the etymology of their own language, judged that this appellation did not ill befit the prince of Demons, so that he is Baal and Lord of the flies, i. e. of the demons, which are called flies, either because they have power in the air, they fly around like swarms of flies because of their multitude, seeking whom they may devour: or because the malice and power of the demons is thus described, זביב for it does not simply signify a fly, but a poisonous one, which with its infection destroys the most precious things. We omit other things brought forward by Selden on this matter, such as that the Arcadians were accustomed to render τὸν Μιἱαγρον propitious by a solemn sacrifice every year, likewise that Hercules was worshipped Κορνωπίων by the Trachinians, because he had driven away κόρνοπας i. e. locusts, (Casaubon also reads it thus, but in Strabo book 13, page 411, it is read κωνωπίων, and a reason is added, that he had driven away cononas i. e. gnats, or had freed them from them) similarly that the same was called ἰποκτόνος by the Erythraeans, because he killed the worms infesting the vines, and that, as Aelian testifies in book 9. de Animalibus, Annual sacrifices were accustomed to be made to flies in the temple of Apollo at Actium. Which things clearly persuade that that name was imposed upon their Deity by the Accaronites themselves. So that there is no need for the conjecture of the illustrious Scaliger, who thinks בעל זבוב was made out of contempt from בעל זבחים i. e. God or Lord of sacrifices or of victims. Gerardus Ioannes Vossius, however, embraces this conjecture in book 2, de Idolol. ch. 4, p. 323.)*

Prince of the Demons. As there are certain orders among the good Angels, so it can hardly be denied that there is also some order among the evil ones, such that one is indeed greater in power than another. And the Jews seem to have looked to this here, while they name one of the devils as prince of the rest. The blessed Pareus reviews the doctrine concerning that order of Devils in Coll. Isag. L. de Angel. c. 6. §. 21; but Alphonsus Tostatus discourses at length on the same subject in Comm. in h. l. q. 60.)*

Latin:

v. 24. Non eiicit daemoes, nisi in Beelzebub. R. Acha (ut scribit R. Mose Hadarschan in exposit. Ps. 74, 9.) praedixit, quod generatio scelestorum inter Iudaeos non creditura sit signis, quae Messias facturus, sed dictura, quòd facta sint arte Magica. & nominibus immunditiei.

*( Nisiper Beelzebub. Quidam legunt Beelzebul. De quâ lectione quid statuendum sit ostendetur in Analectis ad Marc. 3, 22. Iam nunc saltem de significatione nominis Beelzebub. Communis est sententia, quòd sonet mus-ae Deum, atque ita dictum Accaronitarum Numen. Num verò ab Accaronitis ipsis idolo suo id nomen impositum fuerit, eò quòd cùm à muscis graviter vexarentur, sperârint, sese per illud victimis placatum ab ista plaga liberatum iri, quae sen-entia placet Gloss. Bibliorum Ernestinorum 2. Reg. 1, 2. favetque eidem locus Plinii l. 10. c. 28. vel quòd Numen eorum h. e. diabolus sub hâc forma ita conspiciendum sese iis exhibuerit. (Sicuti etiam proditum memoriae est, quòd sub muscae formâ hominibus sese ingesserit, eosque ita obsederit. Exemplum ex Ioannis Nideri lib. 5. refert Mart. Del. Rio l. 3. Disq. Magic. part. 1. q. 7. p. 433. Edidit quoque superiori anno Minister quidam nostrae Ecclesiae Historiam puellae obsessae, in qua simile quid legitur, ac de spiritibus, quos vocant, familiaribus pariter refertur, quòd in muscae specie adserventur.) Huc facit, quòd Beelzebub nontam muscae Deum, quàm Deum Muscam notare quibusdam creditum. Sanè Flav. Iosephus, historicus Iudaicus exponit simpliciter Μιῖαν. Quod faciunt quoque LXX. Interp. Graeci, & qui eorum sequuntur versionem, ac notat Fr. Iunius ex Nazianz. ςηλιτευτ. β contr. Iulian. Beelzebub muscae figuram habuisse. An verò à Iudaeis per contemtum, quòd cùm Templum Hierosolymitanum inter singularia illa privilegia divinitùs ei concessa & hoc numeraret, quòd cum tot victimae cottidie in eo mactarentur, nulla tamen unquam ibi musca conspiceretur, ut est in Pirke Abhoth. c. 5. §. 6. 7. E contrario verò Accaronitarum aliarumque gentium delubra Iovi consecrata muscarum gregibus scaterent. Quos cùm Iupiter illa Accaroniticus depellere haut posset, censent, quòd ob hoc contemtim Beelzebub fuerit à Iudaeis dictus, cùm aliàs, uti Philo & Augustinus docent, Beelsames (ceu à Romanis Iupiter Olympius, ut notat Iosephus Castalio c. 9. Var. lect.) i. e. Dominus coeli ab iisdem appellaretur. Et haec postroma senrentia Hugoni cumprimis arridet Grotio Annot. ad cap. X. Matth. v. 25. Sed quid de moneta statuendum antiquissima est, quae Phoenicum, adeoque & Accaronitarum esse creditur? Ea in altero latere dimidiam, puta priorem cervi partem, altero muscae effigiem sistit. Cuiusmodi & in meo antiquario adservo. Num à Iudaeis in contemtum idoli Phoenicum talia numismata cusa statuamus? Id verò credat Iudaeus Apella, non ego. Si verò ab ipsis Phoenicibus sive Accaronitis talia procurata, minimè credibile est, quòd in Iovis sui contemtum tale quid fecerint. Accedit, tum quòd ab Ethnicis ipsis Iupiter ἀπόμιιος (Pasor in Etym. Nom. Propr. habet ἐπομιῖος i. e. muscarum abactor dictus, tum quod Pausanias in Arcadic is, ac Plinius lib. 10. c. 18. ac l. 29. H. N. c. 6. memorant, quòd cùm Cyrenaei Deo muscarum Acaroni sacrificassent, & Graeci Iovi, quem Myiodem quasi dicas Muscatium nominabant, muscae omnes unô quasi impetu evolarint & extra territorium abierint. Suspicatur hinc Io. Bodinus Andegavensis de Magorum Daemonomaniâ lib. l. c. 3. quòd si certa est relatio de Toletano Veneticoq; Palatio, quòd in hoc nulla, in illo verò unica saltē musca sit, omninò statuendum sit, idolum aliquod sub Palatii limine fuisse conditum. Cumprimis v. Grotii opinioni adversari videtur, quòd idololatricus Rex Achazias, auxilium ab idolo isto petiturus, ipse eô nomine insignivisse illud legitur. Quum enim à lapsu decumberet, misit nuncios, dixitque ad eos: Ite, inquiriteבבעל זבזב אלהי עקווזper Baalzebub Deum Ecron, si vivam de hâc infirmitate.2. Reg. 1, 2. Credibile autem minimè est, Achaziam opem efflagitaturum nomine per cōtemtum idolo imposito illud insignivisse. Nec satis etiam ad mentem Achaziae reddiderunt Ionathan & Interpres Arabs d. l. quorum ille Ebr. אלהי עקרוז vertit טעות עקרוז, hic i. c. idolum Acron. Unde etiam rectè statuit Seldenus Synt. 2. de diis Syr. c. 6. Accaronitis ipsis Deum eorum Baalzebub dictum fuisse. In quâ sententia etiam magnus noster Chemnitius est Harm. Evang. c. 69. existimat tamen, forsitan linguâ Accaronitarum, à quibus nomen illud idolo impositum fuit, aliud significasse; Iudaeos verò postea, iuxta et-mologiam suae lingvae iudicasse, hanc appellationem non malè convenire principi Daemoniorum, ut sit Baal & Dominus muscarum h. e. daemoniorum, quae muscae appellantur, vel quia in aëre, potestatem habent, tanquam muscarum examinae prae multitudine circumvolitant, quaerentes quos devorent: vel quia daemoniorum malitia & potentia & ita describitur,זביבenim non simpliciter muscam significat, sed venenatam, quae sua infectione vepretiosissima corrumpit. Omittimus alia, à Seldeno in rem hanc adducta, ut quòd Arcades solenni sacrificio τὸν Μιἱαγρον quotannis reddere consveverint propitium, item quod Hercules Κορνωπίων à Trachiniis cultus, quòd κόρνοπας i. e. locustas abegerat, (Ita etiam legit Casaubonus, sed apud Sti abonem l. 13. pag. 411. legitur κωνωπίων, ac additur ratio, quod cononas i. e. culices abegerit s. eos ab illis liberaverit) similiter quòd idem Erythraeis ἰποκτόνος appellatus, quia vermiculos vitibus infestos occidit, ac quòd teste Aeliano l. 9. de Animalibus, Muscis annua sacra fieri solita in Apollinis Actu fano. Quae planè persuadent, ab Accaronitis ipsis Numini eorum id nomen fuisse impositum. Ut adeò non opus sit -oniecturâ illustris Scaligeri, existimantis בעל זבוב factum esse per contemtum ex בעל זבחים i. e. Deus s. Dominus sacrificiorum vel victimarum. Amplectitur tamen coniecturam hanc Gerardus Ioannes Vossius lib. 2. de Idolol. c. 4. p. 323.)*

*( Principem Daemoniorum. Uti inter inter bonos Angelos certi quidam ordines sunt, ita inter malos quoque ordinem aliquem esse, ut nempe alter altero sit potestate maior, negari vix potest. Et huc quoque respexisse hîc Iudaei videntur, dum aliquem è diabolis reliquorum principem nominant. Scholast. de isto Diabolorum ordine doctrinam recenset B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. de Angel. c. 6. §. 21. cumprimis verò de eadem materiâ prolixè disserit Alphonsus Tostatus Comm. in h. l. q. 60.)*

## 12:25
v. 25. Every kingdom divided against itself shall be brought to desolation. Eusebius, book 2 of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 11, cites from Plato, book 2 of the Republic, the saying: κτόνος. If we wish to preserve the Republic, it is fitting that we consider it a most shameful thing if one person easily pursues another with hatred. Cicero, On Friendship: What house is so stable, what state so firm, that it cannot be utterly overturned by hatreds and dissensions? (Buxtorf recites in the Talmudic Rabbinical Lexicon from the Talmud, Derech Erez, chapter 5, a similar Hebrew sentiment: טעות

that is Every house in which there is dissension will eventually be destroyed.)* Furthermore, the Jews could have objected here: that the casting out was done by collusion with Satan. *(To this pertains what Eusebius, book 4 of the Praeparatio Evangelica, the last chapter, reports from Porphyry, that Serapis among the Egyptians is that god who is named Pluto among the Greeks, and that he is the prince of wicked demons. For that one, says Porphyry, gave symbols to men by which demons are expelled. From this, the Blessed D. Quistorpius concludes that it is manifest that the symbols by which the heathens cast out demons flowed from the discipline of the prince of demons, and that these Jews seem to have looked to this, who impiously slander our Savior for having cast out demons in Beelzebub, the prince of demons. For the Jews call him Beelzebub, who is the Egyptian Serapis.)* Resp. The thing itself testifies to the contrary, because the Devil was being driven out of his lodging unwilling and reluctant, Matth. 8, 29. 2. Christ not only freed the bodies of the possessed, but also expelled Satan from their hearts through the Holy Spirit. *(Alphonsus Tostatus argues in q. 61 that although one demon can cast out another, since one is inferior in strength to the other, yet he does not do it: not because they love one another, but because any demon pursues men with more hatred than other demons. But what is to be determined concerning magicians, who from time to time cast out demons, by diabolical art indeed? Cornelius à Lapide answers in this place, that this is done by a composed collusion so that they may draw men to magicians and magic, that is, to society with the demon. Compare Crespetius, book 1, on the hatred of Satan, discourse 15. Petrus Binsfeld, in the Confession of Malefactors, prelude 6. The same must be said concerning the exorcists among the Papists, about whom Martin Del Rio can be consulted in Disquisitiones Magicae, book 6, chapter 3, to whose exorcisms the devil yields, so that he may confirm them in that superstition and draw more into his nets from time to time. And it is certain that God also by a just judgment sometimes permits that those who do not wish to acquiesce to the revealed word, which ought to have been a light in their paths, be tempted in this way. There is no reason, therefore, why the Papists should boast so much about their exorcists. See Del Rio in the cited place. Petrus Cotonus, Institutiones Theologicae, book 3, chapter 61. Suarez on Thomas, part 3, q. 63, art. 4, disp. 15. Don Franciscus Torreblanca Villalpandus, Daemonologia, book 2, chapter 53, p. 401.)*

Latin:

v. 25. Omne regnum in se divisum desolabitur. Eusebius lib. 2. praepar. Evang. c. 11. ex Platone lib. 2. de Republ. adducit dictum: κτόνος.Si Remp. conservare volumus, decet, ut existimemus, rem turpissimam esse. si alter alterum facilè odio prosequatur. Cicero de amicitia: Quae domus tamstabilis, quaetam, firma civitas est, quae non od-s atque dissidiis funditus possit everti? *(Recitat Buxtorff. Lex. Talmud. Rabb. ex Talm. Derech erez c. 5. similem Ebraeorum sententiam: טעות

i. e. Omnis domus, in quâ est dissensio, tandem destruetur.)* Coeterùm poterant hic obvertere Iudaei: eiectionem fieri collusione cum Satanâ. *(Quo facit, quod Eusebius lib. 4. de Praepar. Ev. c. ult ex Porphyrio tradit, Serapin apud Aegyptios illum esse Deum, qui apud Graecos Pluto nominatur, ac pravorum daemonum esse principem. Nam iste, inquit Porphyrius, symbola dedit hominibus, quibus daemones expelluntur. Colligit hinc B. D. Quistorpius, manifestum esse, Symbola, quibus eiiciebant Eth-ici daemonia, ex principis daemoniorum manasse disciplinâ, ac videri haec Iudaeos hosce spectasse, qui impiè calummantur, Servatorem nostrum eiecisse daemonia in Beelzebub principe daemoniorum. Quippe Beelzebub Iudaei eum appellant, qui Aeg-ptus Serapis.)* Resp. res ipsa testatur contrarium, quia Diabolus invitus ac reluctans è suo hospitio pellebatur, Matth. 8, 29. 2. Christus non solùm corpora obsessorum liberabat, sed etiam ex cordibus per Sp. Sanctum expellebat Satanam. *(Disputat Alph. Tostatus q. 61. quòd licet unus daemon alterum possit eiicere, cùm alter altero viribus inferior sit, illud tamen non faciat: non quòd invicem diligant, sed quod quilibet daemon magis odio prosequatur homines, quàm alios daemones. Sed quid statuendum de Magis, qui subinde daemones eiiciunt, arte utique diabolicâ. Respondet Corn. à Lapide in h. l. fieri hoc ex compositâ collusione ut homines ad magos & magiam, id est societatem cum daemone pertrahant. Conf. Crespetius lib. 1. de odio Satanae disc. 15. Petrus Binsfeld. in Confess. malef. praelud. 6. Idem dicendum de Exorcistis apud Pontificios, de quibus consuli poterit Martinus Del Rio disquis. Magic. l. 6. c. 3. ad quorum exorcismos diabolus cedit, ut eos in superstitione istâ confirmet ac plures subinde in retia sua pertrahat. Ac certum est, quod Deus etiam iusto iudicio aliquando permittat, ut hac ratione tententur, qui verbo revelato, quod debebat illis esse lumen in viis suis, acquiescere nolunt. Non est igitur, cur tantopere de exorcistis suis Pontificii glorientur. Vid. DelRio l. c. Petrus Cotonus Instit. Theolog. lib. 3. c. 61. Svarez in Thomam p. 3. q. 63. art. 4. disp. 15. Don Franciscus Torreblanca Villalpandus Daemonologiae l. 2. c. 53. p. 401.)*

## 12:26
(v. 26. How then shall his kingdom stand i. e. it will by no means persist. For thus interrogations are sometimes used in the H. S. See below v. 34. Luke 14, 5. &c.)

Latin:

*(v. 26. Quomodo erga stabit regnum eius i. e. minimè persistet. Ita enim interrogationes aliquando in Sc. S. adhibentur. Vid. infrà v. 34. Luc. 14, 5. &c.)*

## 12:27
v. 27. By whom do your sons cast them out? Some take this concerning the Apostles & the LXX disciples, who performed miracles, and yet were not called into suspicion of collusion with Satan. August. b. 20. on the C. of G. ch. 5. refers it to the Apostles, who shall sit in the day of judgment upon twelve seats and shall judge Israel. Jerome takes the passage concerning the Exorcists, who were running about at that time, adjuring unclean spirits: he confesses, however, that it can also be understood of the Apostles, who were sons of the Hebrews according to the flesh. The Syr. renders it your countrymen. In the tract Senhedrin ch. 2. Everyone who teaches the son of his associate the law, the Scripture holds it for him as if he begat him. Basil: πςατολ Acts 19, 13. mention is made of certain Jews, namely the sons of Sceva ἀχριερέως, who were exorcists, and attempted to drive devils out of the possessed. (From the fact that there were Exorcists among the Jews, who cast out Devils by a certain formula of adjuration, and yet the H. S. does not express by whom they were instituted, Bailius in his Controversial Catechism tr. 1. q. 9. attempts to prove, among other things, that the H. Scripture is imperfect. Resp. 1. distinguish between perfection regarding the monuments of histories, and the dogmas of faith. Regarding these, we assert that H. S. is perfect, so that there is no dogma of faith necessary to be known for salvation which is not clearly proposed in H. S. But as for Historical narrations, we easily grant that, just as Christ did many things which are not annotated in detail, John 21, last, so also the institution of Exorcists among the Jews was not reduced to H. letters. 2. Note that it is a matter of controversy both among the ancients and the more recent interpreters, who are to be understood here by sons of the Jews. Hilary, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius, understand the Apostles, and judge that these things happened after the mission of the Apostles, made by Christ, as Corn. à Lapide notes in this place. The Jesuit Maldonatus follows them; Others, and indeed almost all the more recent ones at least from the Papists, such as Card.

Toletus, Fr. Lucas, Corn. Jansenius, Corn à Lapide, Conzen. &c. in this place, likewise Mart. Del Rio Disq. Mag. vol. 1. b. 2. q. 30. s. 2. accept the exorcists of the Jews, who by an art handed down from Solomon, as is in Joseph. b. 8. ch. 2. expelled demons. If you embrace the former opinion, which besides the Fathers cited by Cornelius, also has as approvers Athanasius on the common essence of the F. S. and H. S., Augustine b. 20. on the C. of G. ch. 5., from sermon 11. on the words of the Lord according to Matthew, Jerome in this place, the imperfection of H. S. will by no means be able to be proved from this place. For it is sufficiently evident from ch. 10. Matth. v. 8. and likewise from Luc. 9, 1. that the Apostles received from Christ the power of casting out demons. If you follow the latter, likewise nothing is taken away from the perfection of Holy Scripture. For what, I ask, will be taken away from the doctrine of saving faith, if we should even greatly ignore who taught the peddlers among the Jews the art of casting out demons, by means of a root applied to the nostrils of the possessed, just as Josephus describes in the cited place. That such indeed were those who are mentioned in Act. 19, 13., Corn. à Lapide hints at this place. And if it is true that Solomon taught that art, it must be asserted entirely with Aquinas and Victoria, whom DelRio cites, that Solomon professed it at the time when he was an idolater. And that such Exorcists, who indeed cast out demons by a pact and covenant which they entered into with Satan, are to be understood in this place by sons of the Pharisees, the Blessed D. Chemnitius also teaches. Although those very men, after Christ began to announce the kingdom of God in his ministry, sensing that their magical arts were empty, took up the name of Jesus, and used it in expelling demons, yet by this they did not cease to be disciples of the Pharisees, inasmuch as they otherwise embraced the doctrine of the Pharisees and Scribes in all things. And that these are treated in Matth. 7. 22.Marc. 9, 38.Luc. 9, 49.Act. 19, 13.. The same man asserts that these will be the judges of the Pharisees, and will condemn them, for the reason that when they themselves, the Pharisees, sensed that a power greater than diabolical or Magical was present here, (inasmuch as Christ cast out demons against their will and resisting, and thus in no way through collusion with the devil,) they nevertheless referred those miracles to the Devil, and thus not out of any ignorance or simplicity, but out of incurable malice and more than Satanic hatred they suppressed Christ's miracles with an iniquitous judgment. But the Pharisees approved and extolled with their votes the incantations of those Exorcists, inasmuch as they embraced their doctrine, as a thing excellently done. The Blessed D. Chemnitius urges against the former opinion: 1. that at that time the Apostles had not yet received from Christ the power of casting out demons. 2. that if he had spoken about the Apostles, he would not have said, your sons, since the Apostles were not the sons of the disciples of the Pharisees, but of Christ. The Blessed Doctor Quirstopius embraces the former opinion in this place, and opposes the latter opinion, because it is not probable that Christ wished to compare that power, which He exercised in casting out demons, with the collusions of charlatans . Likewise, the Blessed Doctor Calixtus in his Concordance of the Gospels, as well as Erasmus and Beza, understands this of the Apostles and disciples of Christ; just as, conversely, the Blessed Doctor Glasfius in his Exegesis of the Gospel for Oculi Sunday, p. 644, Lord Doctor Friedl. in his Observations on Church History, p. 84, and the Gloss of the Ernst Bible, compare it in this place Mark 9:38Luke 9:49Acts 19:13. But since neither exposition, both that which understands it of the Apostles and that which understands it of the charlatans who cast out demons by the collusion of Satan, is without difficulty, it might perhaps be conceded that there were among the Jews exorcists who cast out demons entirely by divine aid and by invoking the Supreme Deity with pious prayers. Nor, however, does anything depart from the perfection of the Holy Scriptures by this omission, as to who instituted such exorcists, since we defend the perfection of the Holy Scriptures at least in that it embraces all things which are necessary for all to know for obtaining eternal salvation. To which the institution of exorcists does not pertain. But since it cannot be proven firmly enough from the Holy Scriptures that the Jewish exorcists cast out demons in a legitimate manner, that is, by invoking the Supreme Deity (which Hugo Grotius indeed strives to evince in this place from Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Theophylact, and others, who therefore also maintains that Christ understands such exorcists in this place: yet Episcopius seems to dissent, Theological Institutions, book 4, page 429), it is better to maintain that the Savior, if the discourse is about the Jewish exorcists, speaks of charlatans. Nor is it inconsistent that He defends Himself by their example, since although they cast out demons by collusion with Satan, the Pharisees nevertheless persuaded themselves, however falsely, that it was done by a power granted to Him from God. So that Christ may argue in this way κατ᾽ ᾶσθρωπον, and it is evident from other places as well, that Holy Scripture sometimes speaks κατὰ τὸ ἔνδοξον. See, if you please, what was noted above at Matth. 8, 12 p. 477. Also at Matth. 9, 12. p. 516)*

Latin:

v. 27. Filii vestri in quo eiiciunt? Quidam accipiunt de Apostolis & LXX. discipulis, qui miracula ediderunt, nec tamen in suspicionem collusionis cum Satana vocati sunt. August. l. 20. de C. D. c. 5. refert ad Apostolos, sessuros in die iudicii super sedes duodecim & iudicaturos Israel. Hieronymus accipit locum de Exorcistis, qui tùm temporis discurrebant, spiritus immundos adiurando: fatetur autem, de Apostolis etiam intelligi posse, qui erant filii Hebraeorum secundùm carnem. Syr. reddit vestrates. In tract. Senhedrin c. 2. Omnis qui docet filium socii sui legem, id pro eo habet Scriptura, ac si g-gneret eum. Basilius: πςατολAct. 19, 13. mentio fit quorundam Iudaeorum, Scevae sc. ἀχριερέως filiorum, qui fuerint exorcistae, ac tentaverint, diabolos ex obsessis pellere. *(Ex eo, quòd inter Iudaeos fuerint Exorcistae, qui certâ adiurandi formulâ Diabolos eiiciebant, neque tamen exprimat Sc. S. à quibus illi instituti, evincere inter alia conatur Bailius in Catechesi Controv. tr. 1. q. 9. quòd Sc. Sacra sit imperfecta. Resp. 1. dist. inter perfectionem quoad historiarum monumenta, & fidei dogmata. Quoad haec Sc. S. perfectam esse adserimus, ita ut nullum fidei dogma ad salutem scitu necessarium sit, quod non clarè in Sc. S. propositum. Quod verò Historicas narrationes attinet, facilè largimur, quòd sicuti Christus multa fecit, quae non sunt sigillatim annotata, Ioh. 21, ult. ita etiam Exorcistarum apud Iudaeos institutio non fuerit in S. litteras redacta. 2. Not. quòd controversum tùm inter veteres tum recentiores interpp. sit, quinam per filios Iudaeorum intelligendi hîc sint. Hilarius, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Euthymius, intelligunt Apostolos, censentque, haec contigisse post missionem Apostolorum, factam à Christo, uti notat Corn. à Lapide in h. l. Sequitur illos Iesuita Maldonatus; Alii, & quidem ferè recentiores saltem è Pontificiis, uti Card.

Toletus, Fr. Lucas, Corn. Iansenius, Corn à Lapide, Conzen. &c. in h. l. item Mart. Del Rio Disq. Mag. tom. 1. l. 2. q. 30. s. 2. accipiunt exorcistas Iudaeorum, qui arte à Salomone traditâ, ut est apud Ioseph. l. 8. c. 2. expellebant daemones. Si priorem amplectaris sententiam, quae praeter allegatos à Cornelio Patres, approbatores quoque habet Athanasium de comm. essentia P. F. & Sp. S. Augustinum l. 20. de C. D. c. 5. de serm. 11. de verbis Domini secundùm Matthaeum, Hieronymū in h. l. minimè ex h. l. probari S. S. imperfectio poterit. Constat enim satis ex c. 10. Matth. v. 8. itemque ex Luc. 9, 1. quòd à Christo Apostoli acceperint potestatem daemones eiiciendi. Si posteriorem sequaris, itidem nihil decedit Sc. S. perfectioni. Quid enim, quaeso, decedet doctrinae fidei salvificae, si vel maximè ignoremus, quis circulatores apud Iudaeos artem eiiciendi daemones, per radicem naribus obsessi admotam, prout Iosephus l. c. describit, docuerit. Tales verò fuisse eos, quorum Act. 19, 13. fit mentio, Corn. à Lapide h. l innuit. Et si verum est, quòd Salomon istam artem docuerit, omninò cum Aquinate & Victoria, quos adducit DelRio, adserendum, quòd Salomon tunc professus illam fuerit, cùm esset idololatra. Atq; huiusmodi Exorcistas, qui nempe expacto & foedere, quod cum Satana inierunt, daemones eiiciebant, h. l. per filios Pharisaeorum intelligi, docet quoque B. D. Chemnitius. Licet verò illi ipsi, postquam Christus in ministerio suo regnum Dei annunciare coepit, sentientes, artes suas magicas inanes esse, nomen Iesu adsumserint, eoq; in expellendis daemoniis usi fuerint, per hoc tamen non desierunt Pharisaeorum esse discipuli, utpote cùm aliàs in omnibus doctrinam Pharisaeorum & Scribarum amplecterentur. Atque de his agi Matth. 7. 22.Marc. 9, 38.Luc. 9, 49.Act. 19, 13. Hos verò Pharisaeorum Iudices futuros esse, adserit idem, eosque condemnaturos, propterea quòd cùm ipsi, Pharisaei, senserint, virtutem hîc adesse diabolicâ aut Magicâ maiorem, (quippe cùm Christus invitos & repugnantes, adeoque minimè per collusionem cum diabolo, daemones eiiceret,) nihilo tamen minùs ad Diabolum ea miracula referrent, adeôque non exignorantiâ aliquâ vel simplicitate, sed ex incurabili malitiâ & odio plusquam Satanico Christimiracula iniquâ censurâ premerent. Illorum verò Exorcistarum, utpote qui doctrinam eorum amplectebantur, in cantationes tanquam rem praeclarè gestam, suffragiis suis Pharisaei comprobabant & extollebant. Urget B. D. Chemnitius contra ptiorem sententiam. 1. quòd tum temporis Apostoli nondum acceperint à Christo potestatem da mones eiiciendi. 2. quòd si de Apostolis fuisset loquutus, non dixisset, filii vestri, cùm Apostoli nofuerint filiis discipuli Pharisaeorum, sed Christi. Priorem sententiam amptectitur B. D. Quirstopius in h. l. ac posteriori sententiae opponit, quòd probabile haut sit, Christum vim illam, quam in eiiciendis daemonibus exercebat, cum c-rculatorum collusionibus comparare vol-isse. Pariter de Apostolis ac discipulis Christi accipit B. D. Calixtus in Concordiâ Evang. it. Erasmus, Beza. quemadmodum vice versa de Iudaeorum Exorcistis s. agyrtis B. D. Glasfius Exeg. Evang. Dom. Oculi p. 644. Dn. D. Friedl. Obs. in H. E. p. 84. it. Gloss. Bibliorum Ernst. conferentes in h. l. Marc. 9, 38.Luc. 9, 49.Actor. 19, 13. Cùm verò utra-; expositio, tum quae de Apostolis, tùm quae de circulatoribus, qui collusione Satanae daemones eiiciebant, accipit, non careat difficultate, concedi forte posset, fuisse apud Iudaeos Exorcistas, qui divino omninò auxilio ac invocato piis precibus Numine supremo daemones eiiciebant. Nec tamen per praeteritionem, quis tales Exorcistas instituerit, Sc. Sacrperfectioni quicquam decedit, cùm nos saltem Sc. S. persectionem defendamus, quòd videl. complectatur omnia, quae omnibus ad salutem aeternam consequendam scitu necessaria sunt. Ad quae Exorcistàrum institutio non pertinet. Ast cùm ex Sc. S. probari non satis firmiter queat, Exorcistas Iudaeorum legitimô modô h-e. invocatô Supremo Numine eiecisse daemones (quod quidem ex Iustino Martyre, Irenaeo, Tertulliano, Theophylacto aliisque evincere satagit Hugo Grotius in h. l. qui proindè etiam statuit, Christum huiusmodi Exorcistas h. l. intelligere: dissentire tamen videtur Episcopius Instit. Theol. l. 4. pag. 429.) satius est, statuere, quòSalvator, si de Iudaeorum Exorcistis sermo ei est, loquatur de Agyrtis. Nec absonum est, quòd eorum ipse defendat se exemplo, cùm licet illi collusione cum Satana daemones eiicerent, Pharisaei tamen sibi utut falsò persuaderent, virtute divinitùs ei concessâ id fieri. Ut ita Christus argumentetur κατ᾽ ᾶσθρωπον, ac constat ex aliis quoque locis, quòd Sc. S. aliquando κατὰ τὸ ἔνδοξον loquatur. Vide sis quae notata suprà ad Matth. 8, 12 p. 477. item ad Matth. 9, 12. p. 516)*

## 12:28
v. 28. Εφθασεν φθάνειν here is to arrive, at other times it signifies to anticipate, which likewise has a place here, because the kingdom of GOD so arrives to us, that it anticipates. That ejection of demons is a public testimony that the Messiah has come, and has initiated his kingdom of grace, 1. Ioh. 3, 8. The end of the advent of Christ is the crushing of the serpent's head.

*( By the Spirit of GOD. i. e. by the Holy Spirit. Compare Act. 10, 38. And thus the Blessed Fathers also explain it, Coll. Isag. p. 314, and other Interpreters in this place. But the Photinians foolishly gather from the fact that the Holy Spirit is called Spirit of God, that he himself is not God, since they ought to distinguish between the different acceptance of the word GOD. For it is taken sometimes οὐσιωδῶς, and thus the Holy Spirit is God, while sometimes ὑπςατολῶς, and thus it is the spirit of GOD, also the finger of GOD, Luc. 11, 20. Now indeed the finger of GOD is of the same substance with God.)*

Latin:

v. 28. Εφθασεν φθάνειν hîc est pervenire, aliàs significat praevenire, quod itidem hîc habet locum, qúia regnum DEI ita ad nos pervenit, ut praeveniat. Eiectio illa daemoniorum est publicum testimonium, quòd Messias venerit, & regnum suum gratiae inchoarit, 1. Ioh. 3, 8. Finis adventûs Christi est capitis serpentini contririo.

*( Per Spiritum. DEI. i. e. per Sp. Sanctum. Conf. Act. 10, 38. Atque ita exponunt etiam B. P. Coll. Isag. p. 314. aliiq; Interpp. in h. l. Ineptè verò ex eo, quòd Sp. Sanctus dicitur Spiritus Dei, colligunt Photiniani, quòd ipse nō sit Deus, cùm distinguere debeant inter diversam vocis DEI acceptionem Sumitur n. aliquando οὐσιωδῶς, & sic Sp. S. est Deus, cùm aliquando ὑπςατολῶς, & sic est spiritus DEI, item digitus DEI, Luc. 11, 20. Iam verò digitus DEI est eiusdem substantiae cum Deo.)*

## 12:29
v. 29. Strong man. That strong man is the Devil; his house is the world; the vessels are men. Christ seems to allude to Es. 49, 24. 25. Irenaeus l. 3. c. 8. p. 178. We were his vessels and house, when we were in Apostasy: for he used us as he wished, and the unclean Spirit dwelt in us. For he was not strong against him who was binding him and plundering his house, but against those who were men in his use. August. l. 20. de C. D. c. 7. By the strong man he understands the Devil, because he himself was able to hold the human race captive, but by his vessels, which he was about to snatch away, he understands his future faithful ones, whom he possessed in various sins and impieties. *(Of that struggle between Christ and Satan and the victory brought back, one can read everywhere in the sacred letters. See Gen. 3, 15.Es. 53, 12.Ioh. 12, 31.c. 14, 30.Rom 16, 20.

Ebr. 2, 16.Col. 2, 15.Eph. 4, 8.1. Ioh. 3. 8. And so Christ truly conquered Satan, that for all men the door is as it were opened, the bars everywhere broken, all prisons unlocked, so that they cannot be detained any longer by the Devil, unless they themselves by their own malice prefer to remain captives of Satan, rather than by the liberty procured by Christ and offered to them in the preaching of the Gospel. Wendelinus denies this. For in Exerc. 117. §. 25. he does not hesitate to write: The genuine interpretation of the passages 1. Ioh. 3, 8.Es. 49, 8. 9.25.Matth. 12, 29. does not need the false hypothesis of absolutely universal redemption and sufficient grace; the head of the serpent has been perfectly and fully crushed, with respect to the elect children of GOD. I answer: Nay rather, just as no enemy can be said to have occupied the palace or fortress of his enemy and to have thoroughly conquered the enemy, unless liberty to exit from captivity has been acquired for all those held in captivity by him: so it could not be affirmed of Christ that he bound that strong armed man, namely the devil, and plundered his house, unless liberty to exit from the prison had been acquired for all through that victory. Although the malice of very many men is such that they do not wish to enjoy such a benefit, but prefer to remain captives of the Devil rather than to renounce sins and adhere to Christ, it does not follow from that, however, that Christ, as far as in him lies, has not acquired liberty for all.)*

Latin:

v. 29. Fortis. Fortis ille est Diabolus; domus eius mundus; vasa sunt homines. Videtur Christus alludere ad Es. 49, 24. 25. Irenaeus l. 3. c. 8. p. 178. Vasa eius & domus nos eramus, cùm essemus in Apostasia: utebatur enim nobis, quemadmodum volebat, & Spiritus immundus habitabat in nobis. Non enim adversus eum, quise alligabat & domum eius diripiebat, fortis erat, sed adversus eos, qui inusu eius erant homines. August. l. 20. de C. D. c. 7. Per fortem intelligit Diabolum, quia ipse genus humanum potuit tenere captivum, vasa verò eius, quae fuerat erepturus, fideles suos futuros intelligit, quos ille in diversis peocatis utq; impietatibus possidebat. *(Depugna illâ inter Christum & Satanam ac reportatâ victoriâ passim legere est in sacris litteris. Vid. Gen. 3, 15.Es. 53, 12.Ioh. 12, 31.c. 14, 30.Rom 16, 20.

Ebr. 2, 16.Col. 2, 15.Eph. 4, 8.1. Ioh. 3. 8. Ita vero Christus Satanam devicit, ut omnibus hominibus ianua quasi aperta sit, vectes ubique confracti, omnes carceres reserati, udetineri ampliùs à Diabolo nequeant, nisi ipsi propriâ malitiâ Satanae permanere captivi malint, quàm libertate a Christo partâ & in Evangelii praedicatione iis oblatâ frNegat hoc Wendelinus. Exerc. enim 117. §. 25. scribere non dubitat: Locorum1. Ioh. 3, 8.Es. 49, 8. 9.25.Matth. 12, 29.genunia interpretatio non eget hypothesi falsâ de absolutè universali redemtione & sufficiente gratiâ, Perfectè & plenè contritum est caput serpentis, respectu electorum DEI filiorum. Resp. Imò verò sicuti nemo hostis sui palatium s. arcem occupasse hostemque penitùs devicisse dici potest, nisi omnibus in captivitate ab illo detentis libertas exeundi è captivitate si: acquisita: sic de Christo affirmari nō poslet, quòd validum lilum armatum, nempe diabolum, vinxerit ac domum illius diripuerit, nisi omnib per istam victoriam acquisita exeundi è carcere libertas fuisset. Licet v. ea hominum plurimorum malitia sit, ut tanto beneficio frui nolint, sed Diaboli captivi permanere malint, quàm peccatis renunciare ac Christo adhaerere, exinde tamen minimè peccatis renunciare ac Christus, quantum in se est, non omnibus libertatē acquisiverit.)*

## 12:30
v. 30. He who is not with me &c. Christ opposes this to the Pharisees, who were unwilling to betake themselves into the kingdom of Christ, and to propagate his doctrine, and yet did not wish to appear to belong to the kingdom of the devil: but Christ shows that there is no middle kingdom between his own and the kingdom of the devil. (In another way the Savior brings forth the same sentiment Mark 9, 40. Although indeed among the Latins these sentences are contrary, as is evident from the Orations of Cicero for Ligarius, here however in a different respect both are true, as will be advised more fully at the said place of Mark. Furthermore, the Jesuit Costerus rightly concludes from this place in Enchir. Controv. p. 93. that there is a single faith, namely, salvific, and he who does not have it, has no faith, again understand salvific, and therefore neither is saved, but descends into hell. Since however that single salvific faith consists in the fiducial apprehension of the merit of Christ, Conf. Acts 4, 12.

it is evident that, by the judgment of Costerus himself, all those Papists err gravely, (in whose number also is that huge Patron of the Jesuits, and the same grandiloquent interpreter of the Council of Trent, Iacobus Payva Andradius,) as many as attribute salvation to the Gentiles, outside the light of the revealed word and that which is comprised in the Holy Scriptures. Blessed P. recounts the trifles of these, Conf. Cath. l. 2. art. 2. c. 4. §. 4. Moreover, ineptly from that assertion, That there is no other than a single saving faith, that same Jesuit Costerus strives to prove, you know that by their own opinion all our ancestors are condemned: for the reason that we maintain that the Papal religion is heretical. But the Jesuit falsely presupposes here 1. That our ancestors had no other faith than the Papistic, that is, human traditions ἀντίγρφας, such as those concerning Purgatory, the invocation of saints, the adoration of relics, the religious worship of images, the primacy and absolute infallibility of the Roman Pontiff, and the merit of good works, etc., equating them with the divine word. But the Jesuit is egregiously deceived. The blessed D. Hopffnerus sufficiently demonstrated the contrary in the Preface to the Saxon Evangelicals. And although the Jesuits use many lies here (such as that one concerning the most pious and most constant Elector John, whom they trifle to have made a secession from the A. C. before the end of his life, as the blessed P. shows in the Catholic Confession, book 1, p. 918), they have not yet been able to show thus far that even a single Ecclesiastical Writer, who lived some centuries ago, embraced or professed all those and individual articles of faith for which the Papists fight as for their altars and hearths, and which today constitute the faith, that is, the Papistic religion. 2. That that is the true and saving faith which our ancestors embraced. Since rather one must judge concerning the true faith from the Holy Scriptures. Our Savior taught this, as often as, having rejected the traditions of the Fathers, to which the Jews attributed very much, He referred them to the writings of Moses and the Prophets alone. Which the Apostles also did. Truly, if our ancestors, to whom the Gospel was first preached, had possessed that true and saving faith which their fathers and grandfathers embraced, no one of them ought to have permitted himself to be imbued with the rites of the Christian religion, since their ancestors were Gentiles. For the Jesuit will not be so absurd as to maintain that those most remote ancestors of ours, the Germans, had a saving faith before the Gospel was preached to them, which Baronius teaches in his Ecclesiastical Annals at the year of Christ 731 was done only in the eighth century. And let him not exclude them from the kingdom of heaven, or clamor that their faith is the only and saving one.)

Spargit. The Syrian: Spargendo spargit i. e. he utterly disperges.

Latin:

v. 30. Qui non est meum &c. Hoc opponit Christus Pharisaeis, qui nolebantse in Christi regnum conferre, & doctrinam eius propagare, nec tamen videri volebant ad diaboli regnum pertinere: sed ostendit Christus, non esse medium aliquod regnum inter suum ac diaboli regnum. *(Raullo aliter eandem sententiam profert Salvator Marc. 9, 40. Ut ut verò apud Latinos sententiae hae contrariae sint, ceu patet ex Orat. Cic. pro Ligario, hîc tamen diverso respectu utraque vera, ceu pluribus monebitur ad d. l. Marci. Rectè porrò ex h. l. concludit Iesuita Costerus Enchir. Controv. p. 93. esse unicam fidem, scil. salvificam, & qui eam non habet, fidem habere nullam, iterum intellige salvificam, adeoque nec salvari, sed in infernum descendere. Cùm verò unica illa fides salvifica consistat in fiduciali apprehensione meriti Christi, Conf. Act. 4, 12.

patet, quòd ipsius Costeti iudicio, graviter errent omnes illi Pontificii, (in quorum etiam numero est ingens ille Iesuitarum Patronus, idemque magniloquus Concilii Tridentini interpres Iacobus Payva Andradius,) quotquot gentilibus, extra verbi revelati inque Sc. S. comprehensi lumen salutem tribuunt. horum verò non naucos recenset B. P. Conf. Cath. l. 2. art. 2. c. 4. §. 4. Coeterùm ineptè ex adsertione illâ, quod non nisiunica fides detur salvifica, idē ille Iesuita Costerus evincere satagit, nosti â ipsorum sentiâ omnes maiores nostros damnari: eò quòd statuimus, religionem Pontificiam esse haereticam. Verùm falsò hîc praesupponit Iesuita 1. Maiores nostros nullam habuisse fidem aliam, quàm Papisticam h. e. traditiones humanas ἀντίγρφας, quales sunt de Purgatorio, invocatione sanctorum, reliquiarum adoratione, religiosô imaginum cultu, P. R. primatu & absolutâ infalsibilitate, B. O. merito &c. verbo divino exaequantem. At egregiè decipitur Iesuita. Contrarium satis demonstravit B. D. Hopffnerus in Praefat. ad Sax. Evang. Et licet multis hîc utantur Iesuitae mendaciis (quale est illud de Electore pientissimo ac constantissimo Iohanne, quem ante finem vitae ab A. C. s-cessionem fecisse nugantur, uti ostendit B. P. Confess. Cath. l. 1. p. 918.) nondum tamen ostendere hactenus potuerunt, quòd vel unicus Scriptor Ecclesiasticus, qui aliquot abhinc secuiis vixit, omnes illos & singulos fidei articulos, pro quibus Papistae tanquam pro aris & socis pugnant, & quae fidē s. religionem Papisticam hodiè constituūt, amplexus vel professus fuerit. 2. eam esse fidem veram & salvificam, quàm maiores amplexi sunt. Cùm potiùs ex Sc. S. iudicandum de verâ fide sit. Docuit hoc Salvator noster, quoties reiectis Patrum traditionibus, quibus plurimum Iudaei tribuebant, ad sola Mosis & Prophetarum scripta eos remittebat. Quod ipsum Apostoli quoq; secerunt. Sanè si maiores nostri, quibus primitùs praedicatum Evangelium fuit, illam fidem veram ac salvificam habuissent, quam patres eorum atque avi amplexi fuerunt, nemo eorum, Christianae religionis sacris ut imbueretur, debuisset permittere, cùm maiores eorum fuerint gentiles. Neque enim adeò ab surdus futurus Iesuita, ut statuat, remotissimos illos maiores nostros Germanos fidem habuisse salvificam priùs, quàm praedicatum iis Evangelium fuit, quod octavo demum seculo factum esse, docet Baronius in Annal. Eccles. ad A. C. 731. E. nec illos regno coelorum excludat, vel illorum fidem unicam & salvificam esse clamitet.)*

Spargit. Syrus: Spargendo spargit i. e. prorsus dispergit.

## 12:31
*(v. 31. Every sin shall be remitted i. e. is accustomed to be remitted, if indeed a man performs serious repentance. Against the Novatians, Photinians etc. Conf. Luc. 24, 47.Matth. 10, 29.c. 18.Ioh. 20, 21. Marcar. serm. 4. God shows himself long-suffering toward each one of us, waiting for when he may repent, βλάπ. )*

The spirit of blasphemy shall not be remitted to men. This sin is said to be committed against the Holy Spirit and is contradistinguished from blasphemy against the Son, not by reason of the person, but of the benefit and office of the same considered relatively. Concerning the sin against the Holy Spirit see Isid. Pelus. l. 1. ep. 59. & LL. Th. t. 2. Against the Spirit i. e. against the testimony of the Spirit. *(Just as also the Arab rightly translates i. e. blasphemy in or against the Holy Spirit. Similarly the Persian and Syrian, except that the latter omits the name holy and not badly. The Ethiopian: Who has blasphemed the Holy Spirit.)*

βλασφημί is said as if βλάπτουσα τὴνν φήμην, injuring reputation: by others as if βλάπτουσα τῷ φάναι injuring by speaking. Camer. ἀπὸ του βάλλειν τῇ φὴμη to cast infamy upon someone.Phil. 2. βλὰξ, which is the voice of one despising i. e. foolish, stupid, and φημὶ I speak, because in such contumely God is affected with reproach, as if stupid or absolutely nothing.

Latin:

*(v. 31. Quodvis peccatum remittetur i. e. remitti solet, si nempe homo seriam agat poenitentiam. Contra Novatianos, Photinianos &c. Conf. Luc. 24, 47.Matth. 10, 29.c. 18.Ioh. 20, 21. Marcar. serm. 4. Deus longanimum se praestat erga unumquemq; nostrûm, expectans quando resipiscat,βλάπ.)*

Spiritus blasphemiae non remittetur hominibus. Peccatum hoc dicitur committi in Sp. S. & contradistingvitur blasphemiae in Filium, non ratione personae, sed beneficii & officii eiusdem relatè considerati. De peccato in Spiritum Sanctum vid. Isid. Pelus. l. 1. ep. 59. & LL. Th. t. 2. Contra Spiritum i. e. contra testimonium Spiritûs. *(Sicuti etiam Arabs rectè vertit i. e. blasphemia in vel contra Sp. Sanctum. Similiter Persa & Syrus, nisi quòd hic nomen sancti omittit nec malè. Aethiops: Qui Spiritum Sanctum blasphemavit.)*

βλασφημί dicitur quasi βλάπτουσα τὴνν φήμην,laedens famam: aliis quasi βλάπτουσα τῷ φάναιlaedens dicendo. Camer. ἀπὸ του βάλλειν τῇ φὴμηinfamiam in aliquem coniicere.Phil. 2.βλὰξ, quae est vox contemnentis i. e. fatuus, stupidus, & φημὶloquor, quia in tali contumelia Deus probro afficitur, quasi stupidus aut prorsus nihil.

## 12:32
*(v. 32. Whoever shall have spoken against the Son of man. B. D. Quistorpius notes examples of this sin to be had below c. 13, 55. c. 27, 63. Luc. 7, 33.Ioh. 6, 42.c. 8, 48. Conf. also B. D. Frantz. de Interpr. Sc. S. p. 165. B. D. Fewrb. diss. de pecc. in Sp. S. c. 36.)*

It shall not be forgiven. i. e. it shall be punished both in this and in the future age. Such are: he does not rejoice the father of a fool i. e. he grieves vehemently. Treasures of wickedness do not profit i. e. they harm very much. To accept a person in judgment is not good i. e. it is very bad. Mark 3, 29. it is explained thus: --κἔξει ἄφεσινεἰς τὸν αἰῶνα. August. serm. 11. on the words of the Lord: What is written: it has no forgiveness forever, but he shall be guilty of an eternal offense, what else is it, than that which is read according to Matthew: it shall not be forgiven him neither in this age, nor in the future? For by other words and another manner of speaking the very same sentence is expressed. It is called unforgivable both by reason of man, and with respect to GOD. By reason of man both adjunctively on account of final impenitence, and formally on account of the quiddity and requirements. By reason of GOD on account of vindictive and avenging justice. (Furthermore, what things are required for this, that some sin may be able to be called sin against the Holy Spirit, B. D. Fewrbornius shows in many ways in a special Dissertation on sin against the Holy Spirit printed at Giessen in the year 1619. B. D. Hutter. LL. Th. Mai. p. 367. B. D. Glassius Exeg. Evang. Dom. Oculi p. 626. sqq. B. D. Frantzius on the Interpreters of Holy Scripture p. 165. sqq. B. D. Martini Photin. p. 281. B. D. Bald. Cas. Cons. p. 230. 231. also Comm. on the Epistles of Paul p. 1263. & 1268. B. D. Hunnius in this place. B. Par. Coll. Isagog. Book on Actual Sin c. 5. § 9. sqq. The same Blessed Father also wrote a certain letter on sin against the Holy Spirit to B. D. Hoë, which has not yet seen the light, yet it will see it sometime, when the occasion has been given. In this place we warn at least this, that sin against the Holy Spirit is called unforgivable 1. not as if it is forgiven with difficulty, as Lyranus, Greg. de Valentia, Mald. and Cornelius à Lapide in this place, Pazmannus in the Hodegus, Bell. book 1 on the Word of God c. 17. book 2 on penance c. 16. and other Papists think. Nor 2. because it is not forgiven without repentance. 3. nor because those committing that sin are reprobates. 4. nor because that sin does not have an excuse before men. 5. nor because the sinner does not have that from which he might merit forgiveness. But it is called so, because it directly attacks the very means of salvation, namely the ministry of the Holy Spirit, and is joined with external hardening of the heart and final impenitence. It is called therefore unforgivable 1. not on account of a defect of divine grace 2. nor on account of a defect of the merit of Christ. Whence also the sayings are in no way contrary to this assertion of Christ Ezech. 18, 32.Matth. 11, 28.1. Ioh. 1, 7.c. 2, 2. &c. 3. But because of the stubborn contempt of the means, through which the Holy Spirit is accustomed to be effective for conversion and the forgiveness of sin. And from this it is also easily clear what must be answered to the question which the blessed D. Meisner treats more lengthily than others, Qq. Vexat. n. 3. Whether Christ also made satisfaction for final impenitence. More things pertinent to this will be brought forward at Luc. 12, 10. where the singular opinion of the Arminian Episcopius concerning the sin against the Holy Spirit, which he proposes in Resp. ad 64. Qq. q. 14, will also be examined.

Neither in the world to come. A triple world to come is established by the Rabbis, as Isaac Abarbanel noted in the book which is inscribed possession of the Fathers. The first is the world of the Messiah, the second after this life, the third after the resurrection of the dead. Now the ancient Jews believed that in the times of the Messiah all sins would be forgiven. Hence the old proverb: it will not be forgiven him, neither in this world, nor in the world to come. Compare Drusius. *(Corn. à Lapide, Tirinus, Conzenius on this passage, likewise Coturius Epit. Controv. Demonstr. 22. p. 444. just as also very many other Papists, whom the blessed D. Meisnerus alleges in his second opusculum, opposed to the Indulgences of the Roman Pontiff, p. 365. and 366. and the blessed Par. Confess. Cath. t. 4. p. 498. strive to kindle the fire of Purgatory from this passage. For it would be vain, writes Corn. à Lapide on this passage, and absurd to say: It will not be forgiven him, neither in this world, nor in the world to come, if no sin is forgiven in the world to come: just as one would vainly and ineptly say, I will not take a wife at all, neither in this world, nor in the world to come, since no wife can be taken in the world to come. In the same way also the Jesuits Maldonatus and Tirinus break in on this passage, likewise Julius Caes-r. Coturius in the cited place. But truly a miserable inference: The sin against the Holy Spirit is not forgiven neither in this, nor in the world to come. Therefore, certain sins are forgiven in the world to come, namely in Purgatory. It would be just as if someone wished to infer thus: Those Jesuits, whom the most powerful King of England in the year 1604 ordered to leave his kingdom as traitors, or whom the Sorbonne Resp.

Venetian in the year 1606, as disturbers of the public peace, judged by public decree should be expelled from his dominion, and indeed in such a way that they should not be received back into eternity, (as the words of the Response have it, given by the Procurators of St. Mark to the Legate of the King of France, interceding for the reception of the Jesuits,) neither in this nor in future years will they be received into the Kingdom of England or the dominions of the Republic of Venice. Therefore, other Jesuits will be received. Μὴ γένοιτο! Μὴ γένοιτο! The English and the Venetians will exclaim, nor will they ever concede this consequence. Although according to the rules of prudence (such, indeed, as Bellarmine, Maldonatus, Peltanus, and other Papists prattle that the consequence of that argument constructed for Purgatory from this passage is, or rather that this conclusion follows from Jesuitical fallacies), it by no means follows according to the rules of the dialecticians, which alone the learned and those who are rightly wise know to have the power of binding. And the reason, also, why such a consequence is null is manifest, because the negation of one is not immediately the position of another. Thus the Savior says to a certain fig tree Matth. 21, 19. May fruit never be born from you forever, yet it by no means follows from this: Therefore, some fig trees will bear fruit in the future age, namely in eternity. Alphonsus Tostatus, Bishop of Avila in Spain, also saw this well, of whom it is common among the Papists: This is the wonder of the world, who discusses all that can be known, and whose commentaries on the N.T. the Jesuit Possevinus calls admirable in his Appar. He, indeed, says thus concerning this passage, q. 74, in Matthew: It must be said that Christ does not imply from the letter that some sins are forgiven after death, but He said this for the sake of superabundance, lest anyone might think that, although sins were not forgiven him here, they could be forgiven after death: and again: Christ could say this, not supposing that any sin would be forgiven in the future after death: but to remove the error of some who might think that sins are forgiven after death which had not been forgiven to the living. So that Christ spoke κατ᾽ ἔνδοξον, that is, according to the sense of others, not according to the truth of the matter (which the Papists themselves teach was done by Him elsewhere also. See the Jesuits Corn. à Lapide on c. 24. Matth. v. 29. and on c. 3. Ioh. v. 13. & 16., Maldonatus on c. 26 Matth. v. 24. c. 2. of Luke v. 27., and others.) The Papists are therefore rash , who strive to establish from His own words that very error which Christ in this passage refuted and wished to remove. How much more rightly Fulgentius of Carthage, Bishop of Ruspe, a most holy and learned man, in the judgment of Bellarmine, and who flourished around the beginning of the century, book 1 de remiss. pecc. to Euthymius c. 24. With this word, he writes, our Lord and Savior did not insinuate that some sins are to be forgiven in the future age which were not forgiven in this age, but he showed to those understanding well, not other sins, but only those are to be forgiven in the future age which in this age were forgiven to each one in the one and true Catholic Church. And a little later: What therefore the holy Church has not loosed in this age, remains so insoluble, that it can in no way be loosed even in the future age. But so that the matter may become clearer, it must be noted further I. that the example, which the Jesuits are accustomed to bring forward in place of an instance, and from which they attempt to prove that the Savior would have spoken foolishly unless sins were remitted in the other age, is entirely irrelevant. So that even if it were granted in the highest degree that he speaks ineptly who would say that he does not wish to take a wife either in this or in the future age, it does not follow that Christ also spoke ineptly. The reason is because from Matth. 22, 29. it is sufficiently established that in the resurrection, or in the future age, all will be ἀγάμους.. But that all are to be scorched by the flames of eternal fire in the other age is most false: for it is established that very many will be immune from those, namely those to whom in this life all sins have been remitted on account of the merit of Christ alone apprehended by true faith, Ioh. 3, 15. 18. Nor indeed is it necessary that if anyone is to be immune from eternal torments, he should finally obtain the remission of sins in the other life, namely in the fictitious Purgatory of the Papists, since that remission which a faithful man has obtained in this life has that power, that he is not punished eternally. 2. It must be known that by not being remitted in this place nothing else is indicated than being punished, as Johannes Ferus, formerly preacher of the high church of Mainz, rightly observed, who explicitly on this place p. 264 says: By saying less he signifies more. For he means that such a sin is punished not only in the future, but also here. (And it is not unusual in Holy Scripture to use a less vehement word than one intends to signify. Many examples are presented by the blessed D. Glasius, Gr. S. p. 286. 287. especially it is evident from Matth. 24. 22. Compare also the Jesuit Tirinus, Idiot. L. E. page 85. Where it is well to be noted, that although the Papal Censors castrated the Commentaries on Matthew of the said Writer, although otherwise a Roman Catholic, in the edition which appeared at Lyon of the Gauls in the year 1609, in very many places, they nevertheless left the present passage intact, and thus approved that explanation with their own vote. And why not? For it is conformable to the exposition of the ancient Doctors of the Church, from whose number John Chrysostom is brought forward by Jansenius, Bishop of Ghent, in Conc. Evang. on this passage, p. 379, thus: Of all men, some will pay penalties both here and there, as the Sodomites, and these of whom it is treated here; others only in the present life, as the incestuous Corinthian; others only in the future, as the rich man at the feast; others neither in the future nor in the present, as the Prophets and Apostles. What if the Jesuit Suarez, vol. 4, in 3. p. Disp. 45. s. 1. n. 11, confesses that the present saying is expounded by Chrysostom, hom. 24. on Matthew and the Greek Fathers far otherwise than concerning Purgatory. The Jesuit Conzen also expressly says that Chrysostom says that these (namely, sinners against the Holy Spirit) are to be punished in the future and in this age. And a little later: he is entirely (Chrysostom) intent on dissuading from sins, he makes no mention of purgatory here. Although Conzen immediately adds: he asserts it elsewhere. and also brings forward as a place of confirmation a passage from hom. 69 to the people of Antioch, he nevertheless achieves nothing other than to betray his own malice or ignorance to the world. For the Jesuit ought to have known from his fellow member of the society, and the same E. R. Cardinal Bellarmine, l. de Script. Eccl. p. 120, that that homily 69 to the people of Antioch is of doubtful faith. For thus the Cardinal says in the said place: Those things which are contained in the fifth volume of Chrysostom, are almost all certain and undoubted, except (NB) the homilies to the people of Antioch, of which only twenty-one are said to be found in manuscript in ancient libraries. On the contrary, however, the homilies on Matthew are without doubt Chrysostom's, as the same Cardinal has in the said place. Having therefore suffered a rebuff from Chrysostom and other Greeks, the Jesuit Conzen appeals to the Latins. But of these also very few twist this passage to that fictitious Purgatory, indeed none. Hilary, Jerome, Fulgentius, and as many as have commented on this passage repel the Jesuit client. Whence he does not even dare to name them. He produces, however, Augustine, uri The older, he says, and of great authority, who in book 21 of The City of God, chapter 24, infers Purgatory from this place. But although Bellarmine also and Cornelius à Lapide equally seek the patronage of Augustine in this place, they are deceived and they deceive. For Ludovicus Vives, born in Valencia, and at whose death no one more learned remained in Spain, in the judgment of Paolo Giovio, testifies that those twelve verses, in which sins are said to be forgiven even in the future age, are not found in many ancient Bruges and Cologne codices, and it is likely that they were first written in the margin, and afterwards crept into the text. Where it again deserves observation that, convinced by the force of truth, both the Louvain Censors and other Papist Expurgators of books, or more correctly corruptors, although they have most shamefully castrated the Commentaries of Ludovicus in many places, especially in the newest edition which appeared at Cologne in the year 1616, nevertheless left the alleged passage intact. And yet they dare nonetheless to oppose us with that passage of Augustine even now. So that even from this their malice and fraud may be sufficiently evident. Augustine indeed has in another place, namely book 6 against Julian, chapter 15, something concerning remission in the other age, but at the final judgment. But what does such remission have to do with Purgatory? Furthermore, 3, it is to be noted that Mark chapter 3, 31, whom the Jesuit Maldonatus in this place and Greg. de Valentia in the book on the indissoluble bond of matrimony, chapter 4, § Thirdly, of Matthew, acknowledge to be and to be used as an interpreter, and concerning whom Cornelius à Lapide in the Argument of Mark, page 572, 2, a, writes, that he explains certain things more clearly than Matthew, as one who wrote the Gospel after Matthew, and indeed as he had heard Peter preaching, as Bellarmine says in book 2 of the Roman Pontiff, chapter 2, relates the words of Christ thus, he does not have forgiveness forever, but will be guilty of an eternal sin. From which words this alone is elicited by contrast, that some will not be guilty of an eternal sin, which we easily grant.
