## 13:36
v. 36. The parable of the tares Cyprian also explains this parable from the ancients in lib. 4. Epist. 2 and likewise August. tr. 61. in Iohan. de fide & oper. c. 5. *(Furthermore the Jesuit Becanus lib 1. Man. cap. 1. quaest 4. §. 1. from the fact that the Apostles sought the interpretation of the parable proposed by Christ, gathers that Scripture is obscure. But it must be known that we do not say that Scripture is so clear in all places whatsoever, that it can be immediately understood by anyone, but we assert this, that there is no article of faith, no precept of life, which is not clearly proposed somewhere in Holy Scripture. If therefore the Papists should even most strongly maintain that some Parables proposed by Christ were a little more obscure, they will nevertheless evince nothing against us from that, unless they simultaneously prove that certain articles of faith necessary for salvation were proposed in them, which are not proposed in clear words elsewhere. The contrary of which is manifest, and is evident from this very passage, since Christ has subjoined the genuine sense of the parable clearly enough. 2. that we say Holy Scripture is perspicuous in such a way that, on account of the darkness innate to the mind, we by no means deny that the interior illumination of the Holy Spirit must be sought from GOD with pious prayers. Therefore, just as here the Apostles seeking the explanation of the parable from Christ were made partakers of their wish, so even today GOD will give the Holy Spirit to all who ask, who will supply to them the true understanding of Holy Scripture, but through Holy Scripture, which without doubt Corn â -ap hints at, when he explains it thus at this place:) I am the sower of the good seed, that is, of the Gospel and the word of God, for I sow this, that is, I preach it not only through myself, but also through my Apostles, in such a way that what they preach outwardly from my doctrine, I preach inwardly in the minds of the hearers, and I cause them to understand, love, etc., the same things. And other Papists, such as Bellarmine, Costerus, etc., pondering this very thing with themselves, where they attempt to prove the obscurity of the Holy Scriptures, omit this example of the disciples .

Latin:

v. 36. Parabolam zizaniorum Explicat quoque hanc parabolam ex veteribus Cyprianus lib. 4. Epist. 2 it. August. tr. 61. in Iohan. de fide & oper. c. 5. *(Coeterùm Iesuita Becanus lib 1. Man. cap. 1. quaest 4. §. 1. ex eo, quòd Apostoli prabolae à Christo propositae interpretationem petierunt, colligit, Scripturam Sl esse obscuram. Verùm sciendum, quòd non dicamus, Scripturam in omnibus omninò locisita esse claram, ut â quolibet statim intelligi possit, sed hoc adserimus, quòd nullus sit fidei articulus, nullum vitae praeceptum, quod non alicubi in Sc. S. clare propositum sit. Si igitur vel maxime obtinerint Pontificii, qudd Parabolae aliquae à Christo propositae, fuerint paullò obscuriotes, nihil tamen contra nos inde evincent, nisi simul probaverint, propositos in iis quosdam fidei articulos, ad salutē scite necessarios, qui alibi non claris proponantur verbis. Cuius contrarium manifestum est, & ex hoc ipso loco constat, cùm Christus gennimum parabolae sensum satis calrè subiunxerit. 2. quòd Ita Sc. Sacram dicamus perspicuam, ut ob connatas menti tenebaras interiorem Sp Sancti illuminationem piis precibus à DEO efflagitandam esse hautqua quam eamus inficias. Quemadmodum igitur hîc Apostoli explicationem parabolae à Christo petentes sui voti facti fuerunt compotes, ita adhuc hodie quoque DEUS omnibus petentibus dabit Sp. Sanctum, qui verum Sc. S. intellectum illis suppeditabit, sed per Scripturam Sacram, quod dubio procul Corn â -ap de innuit, quando ita h. l. exponit: Ego sum seminator boni seminis put a Evangelii & verbi Dei, hoc enim semino i. e. praedico nō solùm per me, sed & per meos Apostolos sedita, ut quòd ills ex meâ doctrinâ praedicant exteriùs, praedicem interiùs in mentibus audientium, facioque ut eadem ipsi intelligant, ament &c. ## 13:37
v. 38. The good seed are the children of the Kingdom. The Calvinists gather from this. See Piscator on this place; likewise Bucanus, Book 48, question 46, that the word is sometimes sounds the same as signifies, and therefore is also accepted in that way in the words of the Holy Supper. But it must be known that Christ is speaking of seed that is not corruptible, but heavenly: wherefore the proper meaning of the substantive verb well has a place here. Whence also Wendelin, although in the Christian Theology, as he calls it, he has gathered examples from the Holy Scriptures everywhere to prove that τὸ is is used in the sacred writings for τᾡ signifies, and heaps up many things to establish that assertion, both in System. Theol. book 1, chapter 23, page 907, following, and Exerc. 96, § 9, following, nevertheless hesitated to call the present passage to his aid, not obscurely revealing and acknowledging that it had been impertinently adduced by his associates up to this point.

The field is the world. From this passage some Calvinists try to prove that the name "world" is sometimes taken for the elect alone, so that they may thereby overturn our orthodox view concerning the universal mercy of God, the merit of Christ &c., which is established from John 3, 16 and other sayings where the word "world" is used. But it is quite clear from the context that by no means only the elect are understood here by the name "world," but also the reprobate, since only some part of that field, which came to Christ under the name of "world," bore good fruit—quite apart from the fact that Chamier (t. 3, l. 6, cap. 3) urges that that field denotes not even the church alone, but the world. Hence that interpretation is deliberately omitted in this passage by Wendelin—in Exercise 64, and likewise in book 1 of his System of Theology, ch. 17, §10—whereas elsewhere he labors to prove that special acceptation of "world.")* 677

(v. 37. Good seed. Guil. Bucanus in Instit. Theol. L. 20. quaest. 13. rightly warns that the Evangelical word of GOD is called good seed, because it has the power of regenerating, or because its effect is to regenerate. But since that good seed is also sown among stony ground and among thorns v. 20. 22. that is, is preached ροσκαίροις, and is also received by them with joy, it is evident that not only the elect are regenerated. Which thing, however, elsewhere, namely L. 47. q. 54. the same Bucanus with other Calvinists less correctly affirms.)

Children of the kingdom. They are truly pious and believers, reborn through the spiritual seed of the word and called to the kingdom of heaven.

Children of iniquity, i. e. πονηρο΅ i. e. of the devil, are all the impious. (Since therefore in the militant Church there are good and evil, it appears that both the Audaeans and the Novatians erred formerly, making a secession from the Church. And the former indeed, because usurers and the impure are tolerated in it: the latter indeed (the Novatians) because some truly otherwise faithful had denied the truth in the time of persecution, even if they returned afterwards. The Anabaptists insist on the footsteps of those, denying that that assembly is the Church, to which some not holy are mixed in regard to external conversation. The Papists do not depart far from these, to whom it is always in the mouth, that our Church is not the true Church of Christ, for the reason that the Anabaptists have gone out from us. But it is so far from this detracting anything from our Church, that it rather offers us a firm argument that our Church is the true Church, since here Christ testifies that the enemy of GOD, the devil, especially sows tares in the field of the Lord. The sayings Acts 20, 30. 2 Thess. 2, 4. 2 Pet. 2, 1. 1 John 2, 19. also contribute to this. Therefore those heretics went out from us, because they were not of us. That indeed in the external society of the Church there are also not holy ones, is evident from Matt. 7, 21. chap. 18, 7. chap. 20, 16. chap. 22, 14. 1 Cor. 11, 19 Meanwhile it is by no means denied that the Church properly so called, i. e. in so far as those proclamations attributed to it in the Holy Scripture ought to belong to it, namely that it is the mystical body of Christ Rom. 12, 5. 1 Cor. 10, 17. the spouse and friend of Christ Cant. 4, 7. and in so far as it is called the daughter of the King of heaven Psalm 45, 14. etc. is the congregation of the saints. Therefore one must distinguish accurately 1. between the Church properly i. e. strictly, and broadly and improperly so called. 2. between the Church considered in respect of divine of calling, and of internal regeneration; or with respect to external society, and internal. Concerning which matter the blessed Pareus treats at length in Confes. Cath. vol. 2, page 1059 et seqq. item L. de Eccles. §. 48. Finally, the impious are called Sons of Satan, not by generation, but by imitation. Conf. noted at John 8, 44.

Latin:

v. 38. Bonum semen sunt filii Regni. Colligunt hinc Calviniani. Vid. Piscator. in h. l. it. Bucanus L. 48. quaest. 46. verbum est aliquando idē sonare ac significat, adeoque etiam eo modo accipi in verbis S. Coenae. Verùm sciendum, quòd Christus, loquatur de semine non corruptibili, sed coelesti: quare propria significatio verbi substantivi benè hîc locum habet. Unde etiam Wendelinus, ut ut in Christiana, quam vocat. Theologia undiqueè Sc. S. exempla conquisiverit, quò probaret, τὸest in sacris litteris pro τᾡsignificat adhiberi, & adsertioni isti stabiliendae multa congerat tum System. Theol lib. 1. cap. 23. pag. 907. seqq. tum Exerc. 96. §. 9. seqq. praesentem tamen locum in subsidium vocare dubitavit, non obscurè prodens & agnoseens, impertinenterà socis hactenus fuisse illum adductum.)*

*( Ager est mundus. Conantur ex h. l. nonnulli Calviniani evincere, quòd mundi nomen aliquando pro solis electis accipiatur, ut ita evertant orthodoxā nostram sententiam de universali DEI misericordia, Christi merito &c. quae ex Iohan. 3, 16. aliisque dictis, ubivocabulum mundi adhibetur, adstruitur. Verùm satis ex contextu patet, minimè solos electos hîc nomine mundi intelligi, sed etiam reprobos, cùm aliqua tantùm agri illius, qui Christo mundi nomine venit, pars bonum fructum protulerit, quid quod Chamier t. 3. l. 6. cap. 3. urgeat, agrum illum ne quidem solam Ecclesiam denotare, sed mundum. Unde e-am â Wendelino, Exercit 64. itemque lib. 1. Syst. Theol. cap. 17. §. 10. ubi aliàs specialem illam mundi acceptionē probare satagit, studiò h. l. omittitur.)*

*(v. 37. Bonum semen. Rectè monet Guil. Bucanus Instit. Theol. L. 20. quaest. 13. verbum DEI Evangelicum vocari bonum semen, quia habet vim regener andi, sive quia eius effectus est regenerare. Cùm verò semen illud bonum spargatur quoque in petrosa & in spinas v. 20. 22. h. e. praedicetur ροσκαίροις, & ab iis quoque suscipiatur cum gaudio, patet, quòd non soli electi regenerentur. id quod tamen alibi, nempe L. 47. q, 54. idem Bucanus cum aliis Calvinianis minùs rectè affirmat.)*

Filii regni. Sunt verè pii & credentes, per spirituale semen verbi renati & ad regnum coelorum vocati.

Filii iniquitatis, i. e. πονηρο΅ s. diaboli, sunt omner--pii. *(Cùm igitur in Ecclesia militante sint boni & mali, paut errasse quondam tum Audaeanos, tûm Novatianos, ab Ecclesia secessionem facientes. &illi quidem, quòd in eâ tolerentur foeneratores & impuri: hi verò (Novatiani) quòd nonnulli verè aliàfideles tempore persecutionis veritatem abnegassent, ut ut postea redirent. Illorum vestigiis insistunt Anabaptistae, negantes, coetum illum esse Ecclesiā, cui quoad externam conversationem admixti quidam non sancti. Haut procul ab his abeunt Pontificii, quibus semper in ore, qu-d Ecclesia nostra non sit vera Christi Ecclesia, eò, quòd exierint à nobis Anabaptistae. Verùm tantum abest, ut hoc detrahat quicquam nostrae Ecclesiae, ut potiùs sirmum argumentum nobis praebeat, quòd Ecclesia nostra sit vera Ecclesia, cùm hîc Christus testetur, quòd hostis DEI diabolus potissimùm in agro Domini zizania spargat. Faciunt quoque huc dicta Act. 20, 30.2. Thess. 2, 4.2. Pet. 2, 1.1. Iohan. 2, 19. Egressi igitur sunt haeretici illi ex nobis, quia non fuerunt ex nobis. Quod verò in externa Ecclesiae societate sint quoque non sancti, patet ex Matth. 7, 21.cap. 18, 7.cap. 20, 16.cap. 22, 14.1. Cor. 11, 19 Intereà minimè negatur, quòd Ecclesia propriè sic dicta, h. e. quat. Illi competere debent praeconia, in Sc. S. ei tributa, Videl. quòd sit Christi corpus mysticum Rom. 12, 5.1. Cor. 10, 17. Christi sponsa & amica Cant. 4, 7. ac quat. dicitur filia Regis coelest is Psalm. 45, 14. &c. sit congregatio sanctorum. Distinguendum igitur accuratè est 1. inter Ecclesiam propriè s. strictè, & latè atq; impropriè sic dictam. 2. inter Ecclesiam consideratam respectu divirae vocationis, & internae regenerationis; sive respectu societatis externae, & internae. quâ de re prolixè agit B. Par. Confes. Cath. t. 2. pag. 1059. seqq. it. L. de Eccles. §. 48. Denique impii dicuntur Filu Satanae, non generatione, sed imitatione. Conf. notata ad Iohan. 8, 44.)*

## 13:38 Addition
That which the Jesuits note on the present passage, namely, that Christ did not simply command that the tares be tolerated, but that one must as it were serve the time, and that they are to be pulled up only then, when no danger threatens the wheat through their pulling up. otherwise it is to say to the Church, that both are to be permitted to grow. The Most Serene Venetian Republic seems to me to have observed the same counsel. For although before this it cast out the Jesuits as rebels and traitors from its territory and thus pulled up those most harmful tares, and firmly established with itself by public decree never to permit, that tares of that kind should grow up again among them, yet now it has deemed that one must equally serve the time, and with the decreeing sentence changed, it thinks those tares are to be tolerated for so long, until they can be thoroughly pulled up and extirpated without detriment. Which I have therefore thought should be mentioned, lest anyone think, as if I labored under too gross an ignorance, when in the preceding Disputation on chapter 12, v. 32, I wrote, nor will it be in future years that the Jesuits are received into the territories of the Venetian Republic. I confess indeed that I had previously read in the news-sheets that the Jesuits not only vehemently urged their reception by the Most Serene Republic by offering a huge amount of gold, but also that they finally became masters of their wish in the year 1657, the aforementioned Republic, being at that time not a little pressed by the Turks, looking far beyond doubt to the fact that by those various arts for which this race is especially famous, it might obtain money or aid from Christian Princes, whose courts the Jesuits creep through, at this dangerous time. But since those news-sheets often lie, I did not wish to put faith in them, until at last Carolus Caffa, a Doctor of Pontifical Theology promoted at Rome, who, having recognized the heavenly truth, associated himself with us, and on this very day on which I write these things, is having his revocation speech, as a witness ἀυτόπτης confirmed to me the reception of the Jesuits. Furthermore, the Decree or response of the Procurator of St. Mark to the intercession of the Ambassador of the King of France for the reception of the Jesuits, given together with the Oration or Intercession, from which it appears sufficiently how completely the Most Serene Republic could not then be moved, although the French Ambassador brought forward no light persuasive arguments, stands as follows.

Most Serene Prince, most praiseworthy and most magnificent fathers of the fatherland, my embassy to the Most Christian King having been completed, I ask one thing of you: that you most clemently hear me as I pray for the restoration of the fathers of the Society of Jesus. All Catholics with me speak with one voice that this serves honesty most of all: for while that order stands, the authority of the Supreme Pontiff, the integrity of councils, the health of republics, and indeed the foundation of the whole Christian world will stand. For what order has defended the majesty of the Roman Pontiff against the Greek and German heretics more sharply, or protected it more spiritedly? That of the Jesuits. Who has subjected the authority of councils to the Chair of St. Peter? The Jesuits. Who has exalted this most serene Republic to the heavens, restored it even to the shedding of blood, repaired it, and illuminated it? The Jesuits. Who has extinguished growing heresies, calmed rebellions, and restored the Catholic Church to almost its pristine splendor? In a word, the Jesuits. Therefore, for the sake of your ancient prudence and wisdom, Most Serene Prince, Most Illustrious Senators, strive that you do not exterminate, but propagate this divine treasure, by which ancestral piety flourishes and the weights of arts and sciences revive; do not cast them out, but receive them; do not say a final farewell to them, but store them in your bosom, in your heart.

Certainly Henry IV, the Most Christian King of France, of blessed memory, seemed to be marked with greater ignominy than you, than your Republic; yet, the innocence of this order having been discovered, he remitted whatever perverse opinions had preceded, he forgave with a royal spirit, he pardoned, and indeed he willed that glory should follow ignominy, and life should follow death. Imitate, I beseech you, the most Christian example of the Most Christian King, overcome yourselves, receive a poor and begging order, and there will be joy in Rome with the Supreme Pontiff, with the Most Christian King of France, with the Catholic King of Spain, with the Grand Duke of Tuscany, with the other Kings of Europe, and especially with the Most Serene Austrian House, to whom this order is especially gracious. But if the order falls or is rejected, the authority of the Supreme Pontiff, which you are nevertheless bound to protect and defend whole and intact along with the head of the Church, will gradually be weakened; the Apostolic faith, which it defends even to the blood, will collapse; the Catholic Church (whose foundation is Peter alone, while heretics gnash their teeth) will cease to thrive, to live, to flourish; the profession of the clergy will be empty; and to embrace everything in a few words, all things will be turned upside down, and the door will be opened to the Antichrist. Therefore, lest these evils redound upon the Catholic Church, receive into your trust that sodality for which Christ has died in a singular way, which the Blessed Virgin has loved above other orders. For with this safe, the majesty of your Empire, the dignity of the Republic, and the utility of both internal and external peace will be revealed to the whole world along with the immortality of your name. I HAVE SPOKEN.

ORATION OF THE AMBASSADOR OF THE MOST CHRISTIAN KING OF THE GAULS TO THE MOST SERENE DUKE OF THE VENETIANS FOR THE RESTORATION OF THE JESUITS.

Although to decree among our Venetian nobles concerning the restoration of the Jesuits is a most certain sign of rebellion, Most Ample Lord Legate, yet because you intercede for the same in the name of the Most Christian King of the Gauls, the Most Serene Doge and the Most Ample Senators repeat the decree that they shall never be received, If you knew the causes of the refusal, you would not intercede, but would think otherwise. They are dangerous men, by the testimony of very many Catholics as well, holding religion before them, but in the very act seeking the region. Our ancestors studied piety and holiness before this order. These are companions of Jesus only according to being called, and not according to being. These new men have attended no ancient Council, yet whose court of an Emperor and Catholic King have they not crept through? Whose archives of a Catholic Elector have they not plundered? Whose Archduke’s counselors are they not? Since, therefore, the life of St. Mark is the death of St. Ignatius, and the life of St. Ignatius is in vain the death of St. Mark, the Most Ample Venetian Republic will rather follow the peaceful and blessed St. Mark than, having abandoned him, commit its life and fortune to these curious and wretched Jesuits. This the Most Illustrious Senators wished you to know, to whom in other matters they defer their zeal, and likewise offer honor and love to the Most Christian King of the Franks.

RESPONSE OF THE PROCURATOR OF ST. MARK OF VENICE.

I. The beheading of John the Baptist is proposed. v. 1.—12. II. The withdrawal of Christ and the miraculous feeding of five thousand men by five loaves and two fish. v. 13—21. III. The ascent of the same into a mountain to pray v. 23. IV. The tossing of the disciples on the sea, and their liberation. v. 24. 33. V. The healing of many sick Nazarenes. v. 34. to the end.

Latin:

Id quod Iesuitae ad praesentem locum notant, nempe, Christus non simpliciter mandasse, ut zizania tolerentur, sed temperi quasi inserviendum esse, ac tum demum evellenda esse, cùm nullum per evulsionem eorum tritico periculum imminet. aliàs di re Ecclesiae esse, ut permittantur utraque crescere. Idem mihi consilium observasse videtur Serenissima Resp. Veneta. Etenim licet antehac Iesuitas ut perduelles ac proditores è territorie suo eiecerit atque ita zizania illa nocentissima evulserit, publicoque decreto firmiter secum constituerit, nunquam permittere, ut istiusmodi zizania apud se iterum succrescerent, iam nunc tamen pariter tempori inserviendum duxit, ac mutatâ decretoriâ sententiâ tantisper zizania ista toleranda putat, dum absque detrimento penitus evelli atque extirpari queant. Id quod propterea monendum duxi, ne quis existimet, quasi nimis crassâ ignorantiâ laborarim, quando Disp. praeced. ad cap. 12. v. 32. scripsi, nec futuris annis fore, ut Iesuitae in Reip. Venetae ditiones recipiantur. Fateor sanè, me antehac in novellis legisse, quòd Iesuitae non solùm receptionem apud Sereniss. Remp. oblatâ ingenti auri vi vehementer urserint, verùm etiam quòd voti tandem sui Ann. 1657. facti fuerint compotes, procul ambiguo praedictâ Rep. à Turcis tùm non parùm pressâ, eò respiciente, quòd variis illis artibus, quibus gens haec cumprimis famosa est, pecuniam vel auxilia à Christianis Principibus, quorum aulas Iesuitae perrepunt, periculoso isthoc tempore impetrare possit. Sed cùm novellae illae saepè mentiantur, nolui illis habere fidem, donec tandem Carolus Caffa, Theologiae Pontificiae Doctor Romae promotus, qui agnità veritate coelesti nobis sese adsociavit, & hoc ipso quo haec scribo die, revocatoriam habet orationem, testis ἀυτόπτης Iesuitarum receptionem mihi confirmavit. Coeterùm Decretum sive responsio Procuratoris S. Marci ad Intercessionem Legati Regis Galliarum pro Iesuitarum receptione, data, iuxta cum Oratione sive Intercessione, è quibus satis apparet, quàm prorsus tum non potuerit Serenissima Resp. moveri, licet argumenta persuasoria non levia Legatus Gallicus attulerit, ita sese habet.

Sereniss. Princeps, patres patriae laudatiss. magnificentiss. Christianissimi Regis meis legatione expeditâ, unum à Vobis peto, utme pro patrum Societatis Iesu restitutione orantem clementissimè audiatis. Honestati autem illam maximè inservire, Catholicimecum omnes uno ore loquuntur: Stante enim illo ordine, stabit Pontificis Max. autoritas, conciliorum integritas, Rerump. sanitas, imò totius Christiani orbis fundamentum. Quis enim ordo maiestatem Pontificis Romani erga Haereticos Graecos & Germanos acriùs defendit, animosiùs tutatus est? Iesuitarum: Quis Conciliorum autoritatem D. Petri Cathediae subiecit? Iesuitarum. Quis Serenissimam hanc Remp. in coelum extulit, ad sanguinis usque profusionem restituit, reparavit, illustravit? Iesuitarum. Quis haereses gliscentes extinxit, rebelliones sedavit, & Ecclesiam Catholicam pristino penè nitori restituit? Uno verbo, Iesuitarum. Quare pro antiqua prudentia & sapientia, Serenis. Princeps, Illustriss. Senatores, innitimini ut hoc peculium divinum, quo pietas avita floret, artium & scientiarum pondera reviviscunt, non exterminetis, sed propagetis, non eiiciatis, sed recipiatis; non illi extremum vale dicatis, sed in sinum, in cor vestrum recondatis.

Certè Heinricus IV. Christianissimus Rex Galliae, b. m. maiori ignominiâ quàm vos, quàm vestra Resp. videbatur notatus, deprehensâ tamen huius ordinis innocentiâ, quicquid antecesserat opinionum perversarum, remisit, Rex regio animo condonavit, ignovit, imò voluit, ut ignominiam gloria, mortem vita sequeretur. Imitamini, quaesò, Christianissimi Regis christianissimum exemplum, vos ipsos vincite, pauperem & mendicantem ordinem recipite, & gaudium erit Romae apud summum Pontificem, apud Regem Galliae Christianissimum, apud Regem Hispaniarum Catholicum, apud magnum Ducem Hetruriae, apud Reges caeteros Europae, inprimis apud Serenissimam Domum Austriacam, cui ordo hic inprimis est gratiosus. Labente autem ordine vel repudiato, Summi Pontificis autoritas, quam tamen sartam tectam cum capite Ecclesiae tueri & defendere tenemini, paulatim labefactabitur, fides Apostolica, quam ad sanguinem usque defendit, concidet, Ecclesia Catholica, (cuius fundamentum est solus Petrus frendentibns Haereticis) vigere, vivere, florere desinet, Clericorum professio inanis erit, & ut paucis omnia complectar, omnia sursum & deorsum vertentur, & ianua Antichristo aperietur. Ne ergò mala haec in Ecclesiam Catholicam redundent, recipite in fidem vestram eam sodalitatem pro qua Christus singulariter est mortuus, quam Beata Virgo prae caeteris ordinibus dilexit. Hac enim salvâ Imperii vestri ma estas, Reip. dignitas; pacis cùm internae tùm externae utilitas toti mundo cum nominis vestri immortalitate patescet. DIXI.

ORATIO. CHRISTIANISSIMI GALLIARUM REGIS LEGATI AD SE-RENISSIMUM DUCEM VENETORUM PRO RESTITUTIO-NE IESUITARUM.

Quanquam inter Nobiles nostrates Venetos de Iesuitarum restitutione decernere, rebellionis signum est certissimum, Amplissime Dn. Legate, tamen quia pro iisdem nomine Christianissimi Regis Galliarum, intercedis, Serenissimus Dux, Amplissimiq; Senatores decretum repetunt, ne illi in aeternum recipiantur, Causas negationis si scires, non intercederes, sed aliter sentires. Periculosi sunt homines, plurimorum etiam Catholicorum testimonio, religionem prae se ferentes, sed facto ipso regionem petentes. Maiores nostri ante hunc ordinem pietati & sanctitati studuerunt. Hi sunt socii Iesu tantùm secundùm dici, & non secundùm esse. Homines isti novi nulli antiquo Concilio interfuerunt, at cuius Imperatoris & Regis Catholici aulam non perreptarunt? Cuius Electoris Catholici archiva non involarunt? Cuius Archiducis Consiliarii non sunt? Cum ergo S. Marci vita sit D. Ignatii mors, & D. Ignatii vita frustra sit S. Marci mors, potiùs S. Marcum pacificum, beatum Amplissima Resp. Veneta sequetur, quàm hoc relicto Iesuitis curiosis & miseris vitam & fortunā committet. Quod Te Illustrissimi Senatores scire voluerunt, cui in rebus aliis, studia, nec non Christianissimo Regi Francorum honorem & amorem deferunt.

RESPONSIO PROCURATORIS S. MARCI VENETI.

Proponitur I. Iohannis Baptistae decollatio. v. 1.—12. II. Christi secessio ac miraculosa quinque mille virorum per quinq; panes ac duos pisces cibatio. v. 13—21. III. Eiusdem in montem ad orandum adscensio v. 23. IV. Discipulorum in mari iactatio, eorumq; liberatio. v. 24. 33. V. Multorum aegrotorum Nazarenorum curatio. v. 34. ad sin.

## 13:41
(v. 41. Πάντα τὰ σκάνδαλα, καὶ τοὺ τοὺς &c. Note that the particle καὶ here has the meaning of declaring, and sounds the same as that is. Similar examples are had at John 10, 33.Col. 2, 8. so the blessed Pareus accepts it in Comm. in pr. Petr. p. 49.)

Latin:

*(v. 41. Πάντα τὰ σκάνδαλα, καὶ τοὺ τοὺς &c. Nota, quòd particula καὶ hîc declarandi significationem habeat, idemque sonet, ac idest. Similia exempla habentur Ioh. 10, 33.Col. 2, 8. ita accipit B. P. Comm. in pr. Petr. p. 49.)*

## 13:42
v. 42. Into the furnace of fire. He does not say into fire, but into a furnace of fire, so that he may express the inevitable and perpetual intensity of that heat. For just as those who are cast into a burning furnace cannot escape the punishment of the fire, but are enclosed on all sides as much by the fire as by the furnace: so for the impious there will never be an opening for exit or liberation from the torments of that eternal fire.

Latin:

v. 42. In fornacem ignis. Non dicit in ignem, sed in caminumignis, ut ardoris illius vehementiam inevitabilem & perpotuam exprimat. Ut enim illi, qui in fornacem ardentem iniecti sunt, non possunt ignis supplicium effugere, sed undique tàm igne, quàm formace conclusi sunt: sic impiis nunquam ex inferno patebit egressus aut liberatio ex cruciatibus ignis illius aeterni.

## 13:43
v. 43. Ἐκλάμψουσιν they shall shine forth, namely, with rays of light sent forth like the stars.

( As the sun. It is treated here, as Augustine also advised in the book de cognit. verae vitae chap. 46. vol. 9. Op. concerning the glory of the blessed ἁπλῶς, not συγκριτικῶς, that is, concerning glory itself, not concerning its degrees, concerning which see Dan. 12, 3.1. Cor. 15, 41. 42. After Chamier, vol. 3. Panstr. book 25. chap. 4. Bucanus acknowledges this in L. 37. quest. 14. &c. Wendelin also in System. Theol. page 1260. and 1261. where he also rightly not only departs from his associates Peter Martyr, Gregorius Schönfeld, and others, but also responds to the arguments of the same. That which was also done before him by the blessed Pareus L. de vit. aet, §. 131. seqq: Johannes Crocius in Anti Bec. part 2. page 924. hesitates, and asserts that there are probable reasons on both sides. Nevertheless, the Calvinists are stronger in inclining toward our opinion. Furthermore, he who desires to shine at some time in the triumphant Church, that is, in eternal life, as the sun, it behooves him to put on Christ the sun of righteousness in the militant Church Mal. 4, 2. namely through faith, Gal. 3, 14. and a holy conversation of life Rom. 13, 14. Thus the Church appeared clothed with the Sun Apoc. 12, 1. August. l. de Vanit. secul. c. 2. What kind of splendor of souls will there be then, when the light of bodies will have the brightness of the sun.)

In the kingdom of their Father. The Ethiopian adds who is in heaven. The same also emphatically expresses the following: i.e. he who has ears, let him hear by hearing. )* *(

Latin:

v. 43. Ἐκλάμψουσινeffulgebunt, emissis scil radiis lucis instar stellarum.

*( Sicut sol. agitur hîc, uti etiam monuit August. libr. de cognit. verae vitae cap. 46. t. 9. Op. de gloria beatorum ἁπλῶς, non συγκριτικῶς, h. e. de gloriâ ipsâ, non de eius gradibus, de quibus vid. Dan. 12, 3.1. Cor. 15, 41. 42. Agnoscit hoc post Chamierum t. 3. Panstr. lib. 25. cap. 4. Bucanum L. 37. quaest. 14. &c. Wendelinus quoque System. Theol pag. 1260. & 1261. ubi etiam rectè non solùm à sociennis suis Petro Martyre, Gregorio Schōnfeldio aliisque discedit, sed ad argumenta quoque eorundem respondet. Id quod ante eum quoque factum à B. Par. L. de vit. aet, §. 131. seqq: Iohan. Crocius in Anti Bec. part. 2. pag. 924. haeret, adseritque, in utramque partem esse rationes probabiles. potiores tamen Calviniani in nostram inclinant sententiam. Coeter-m qui desiderat, aliquando in Ecclesia triumphante s. in vitâ aeternâ fulgere ut sol, illum oportet in Ecclesia militante inducre Christum solem iustitiae Mal. 4, 2. nempe per fidem, Gal. 3, 14. ac sanctam vitae conversationem Rom. 13, 14. Ita Ecclesia apparuit amicta Sole Apoc. 12, 1. August. l. de Vanit. secul. c. 2. Qualis tune erit splendor animarum, quando solis claritatem habebit lux corporum.)*

* In regno Patris corum. Aethiops addit qui est in coelis. Idem quoque seqq. emphaticè exprimit: i. e. qui habet aures, andiendo audiat.)*

## 13:44
v. 44. He sells all things, and buys that field. Since heavenly benefits cannot be bought by our merits, but come to us freely, Is. 55, 1. it is to be noted thence that in parables not everything is to be examined accurately. See the notes on v. 3. Whence the Jesuit Maldonatus rightly writes on this passage: It does not, he writes, signify that the Gospel is to be bought: but it signifies that it is to be valued so highly that he who has found it ought to do everything to obtain it: even if all goods must be sold, and even if all must be lost, etc. )*

Latin:

*(v. 44. Vendit universa, & emit agrum illum. Cùm eoelestia beneficia non possint meritis nostris emi, sed gratis nobis obtingant, Es. 55, 1. inde notandum, quòd in Parabolis nonomnia accuratè examinanda sint. Vid. notata ad v. 3. Underectè Iesuita Maldonatus in h. l. Non, scribit, significat, emendum Evangelium: sed significat, tanti aestimandum, ut qui invenerit, nibil non, ut illud obtineat, facere debeat: etiamsiomnia bona vendenda, etiamsiperdenda &c.)*

## 13:46
v. 46. Finding a pearl of great price &c. Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, ep. 183, explains the parable of the pearl and applies it to Christ. Ambrose, sermon 6, vol. 3, p. 230, explains it in the same way. Ephrem the Syrian, on the precious pearl, f. 667. Cyprian, on Works and Alms, chapter 8, f. 352, understands it as eternal life. Nazianzen, oration 12, f. 193, and Luther in the margin, of the word of the Gospel. Augustine, in Matth. 9. 13. vol. 4, f. 367, (as well as tract 5 on John), Bede, vol. 5, f. 46, Anselm, f. 66, understand it of charity, which is the most excellent of all virtues *(Athanasius, Disputation in the Council of Nicaea against Arius, vol. 1, page 82, of piety.)* These interpretations are not contradictory but subordinate. The properties of pearls can be beautifully compared with Christ and the Gospel. 1. Pliny, book 9, chapter 35. They report that shells, when the generative hour has stimulated them, opening themselves with a certain gaping, are filled with dew, and that afterwards they bring forth the offspring of the shells, which are pearls, according to the quality of the dew received. Ephrem, in the same place: It is not the union of shells that forms the pearl, but the mixture of lightning and water. The same is proven by Elias of Crete on Nazianzen. 2. Pearls are bitter and are extracted from the shells with danger. 3. Pearls are rendered more beautiful the heavier the storms and waves are. Isidore of Charax in Athenaeus, book 3, f. 93. 4. Although it is small, it is powerful, says Ephrem, for it is useful against vertigo, palpitation of the heart, and dimness of the eyes. Concerning the price of pearls, see Pliny book 9.

chapter 35. *(The same, ibid. The entire dowry of pearls consists in whiteness, size, roundness, smoothness, and weight. Christ is the Pearl, small in humility, precious in value, easy to carry, healthy to eat. Let us acquire this pearl for ourselves, let us wear it. Let us wear it on the forehead, through the confession of faith; in the breast and heart, through the constant remembrance of divine benefits; in the ears, through the observation of the commandments; on the arms, through honest action; on the ring finger, through the discernment of spirits; in our garments, through a holy conversation of life and the imitation of the humility of Christ. Christ is compared with the Pearl, 1. by reason of generation. Cf. Is. 66, 2. 2. by reason of medical operation. It is useful in vertigo, John 16, 20. and following, in palpitation of the heart, ibid. v. 31. Rom. 5. 1. 1. John 3, 19. in poisonous infection, Hos. 13, 14. in dimness of the eyes, Eph. 1, 18. Apoc. 3, 18. Christ is the most white pearl, through the innocence of life; the most bright, through divine wisdom; the most precious, through the grace of spiritual gifts. Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 12, page 193, who can be consulted, applies this passage a little differently.) *

How we sell all things for that one pearl. Resp. In general, by expending every care. In particular, 1. by renouncing sins, which are properly our own. 2. by turning the heart away from earthly things, by deserting all things in spirit, and by renouncing all things in persecutions for the sake of Christ. 3. by dedicating ourselves wholly to God. August. 9, 13. on Matthew: The price of the pearl is we ourselves: who are not free to possess it, unless all things which are possessed temporally are despised for our liberation. For he who sells our things receives no greater price for them than ourselves, because we were not our own while entangled in such things: so that we may again give ourselves for that pearl, not because we are worth so much, but because we cannot give more. 4. by casting away confidence in our own merits. 5. by preferring Christ to mortal life.

Furthermore, the parables of the hidden treasure and the pearl look to the fact that the Gospel is such a great treasure, and such a precious jewel, that it is deservedly preferred to all the goods of the world, and we would rather lose all things than lack it. *(The saying Phil. 3, 7. is relevant to this. How indeed a man, having found this precious pearl, ought to trade, Anselm shows beautifully in his Morals.) cap. 75. item author of the Oper. Imperf. hom. 53. Add. B Par. H. E. cap. 164 pag. 855.) *

Latin:

v. 46. Inventâ magni pretii margarita &c. Parabolam de margaritâ exponit Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 1. ep. 183. & ad Christum accommodat. Eodem modo exponit Ambrosius serm. 6. tom. 3. s. 230. Ephrem Syrus de Marg. prec. f. 667. Cyprianus de Op. & Eleemos. cap. 8. f. 352. intelligit de vitâ aeternâ. Nazianz. orat. 12. f. 193. & Lutherus in marg. de verbo Evangelii. August. in Matth. 9. 13. t. 4. f. 367. (nec non tr. 5. in Ioh.) Beda tom. 5. f. 46. Anselmus f. 66. intelligunt de caritate, quae est virtutum omnia praestantissima *(Athan. Disp. in Con. Nic. contra Atium t. 1. page 82. de pietate.)* Hae interpretationes non sunt contrariae sed subordinatae. Possunt proprietates margaritarum cum Christo & Evangelio pulcrè comparari. 1. Plinius lib. 9. cap. 35.Conchai, ubigenialis annistimulaverit hora, pandentes sese quadam oscitatione impleri roscido conceptutradunt, gravidas posteà enits partumque concharum esse margaritas pro qualitate roris accepti Ephrem. l. d. Margaritam non concharum coniunctio format, sed fulguris & aquae commixtio. Idem probat Elias Cretensis ad Nazianz. 2. Margaritae sunt amarae & cum periculo è conchis eximuntur. 3. Margaritae eò redduntur pulchriores, quò graviores sunt tempestates & fluctus. Isidorus Characenus apud Athen. lib. 3. f. 93. 4. parva cùm sit, magnapotest, inquit Ephrem prodest enim contra vertiginem, palpitationem cordis & caliginem oculorum. De pretio margaritarum vid. Plinius lib-. 9.

cap. 35. *(Idem ibid. Margaritarum omnis dos consistit in candore, magnitudine, orbe, laevore, pondere. Christus est Margarita, humilitate parva, valore pretiosa, portatu facilis, esu salubris. Hanc margaritam nobis comparemus, hanc gestemus. Gestemus in fronte, per fidei confessionem; in pectore ac corde, per iugem beneficiorum divinorum recordationem; in auribus, per mandatorum observationem; in brachiis, per honestam actionem; in digito annulari per spirituum discretionem; in vestimentis, per sanctā vitae conversationem & humilitatis Christi imitationem. Confertur autem Christus cum Margarita, 1. ratione generationis Conf. Es. 66, 2. 2. ratione medicae operationis. Prodest in vertigine, Iohan. 16, 20. seqq in cordis palpitatione ibid. v. 31.Rom. 5. 1.1. Iohan. 3, 19. in venenata infectione, Hos. 13, 14. in oculorum caligine, Eph. 1, 18.Apoc. 3, 18. Christus est margarita candidissima, per vitae innocentiam; lucidissima, per divinam sapientiam; pretiosissima, per donorum spiritualium gratiam. Paulò aliter hunc locum accommodat Gregotius Nazianz. Orat. 12. pag. 193. qui potest evolvi.) *

Q Quomodo omnia vendamus propter unicam illam margaritam. Resp. in genere omnem curam impendendo. In specie 1. peccatis, quae propriè nostra sunt, renunciando. 2. corâ terrenis avertendo, spiritu omnia deserendo, & in persecutionibus propter Christum cunctis renunciando. 3. Deo nos totos addicendo. August. 9, 13. in Matth. Precium margaritae est nos ipsi: qui adeam possidendam non sumus liberi, nisiomnibus pro nostrâ liberatione contemtis, quae temporaliter possidentur. Vendit is enim rebus nostris nullum earum maius accipimus pretium, quàm nos ipsos, quia talibus impliciti nostri non eramus: ut rursus nos spsos pro illâ margarita demus, non quiatanti valeamus, sed quia plus darenon possumus. 4. fiduciam propriorum meritorum abiiciendo. 5. Christum mortali vitae praeferendo.

Spectant porrò parabolae de thesauro abscondito & margarita eò, quòd Evangelium tantus sit thesaurus, & tam pretiosum clinodium, ut meritò praeferatur omnibus mundi bonis, ac omnia malimus amittere potiùs, quàm eo carere. *(Facit huc dictum Phil. 3, 7. Quomodo verò homo inventâ pretiosa istâ margarita negotiari debeat, pulcrè ostendit Anselmus in Moral. cap. 75. item auctor Oper. Imperf. hom. 53. Add. B Par. H. E. cap. 164 pag. 855.) *

## 13:48
*(v. 48. They cast the bad ones out. Cornelius à Lapide notes here that Augustine rightly proves from this passage against the Donatists, that in the Church there are not only good, but also bad and reprobate men. Although we ourselves also readily grant this concerning the Church, when considered in terms of external society, the Jesuit Maldonatus nevertheless inveighs against us, and prattles, that Augustine did not compose as many books against the Donatists as he did against the Lutherans who would come long after. But in order for the Jesuit to persuade the reader that the Lutherans teach that only the good constitute the Church, he falsely attributes to us that we maintain that even all hypocrites, who outwardly feign faith, are truly faithful, and thus heirs of eternal life. We do not think so at all: But we teach that those alone will be participants in future blessedness who belong to the Church in respect of internal society. That internal society consists in regeneration and renewal, not in a naked and vain boasting of faith, as the blessed Par. shows at greater length in Confess. Cath. t. 2. p. 1059. Let there also be compared on this matter the notable passage of Justin Martyr Apol. 2. for the Christians p. 49. f.)*

Latin:

*(v. 48. Malos foràs eiecerunt. Notat hîc Corn. à Lapide, rectèex hoc loco Augustinum contra Donatistas probare, in Etclesiâ non tantùm esse bonos, sed etiam malos & reprobos. Quod ipsum ut ut nos quoque de Ecclesia, ratione externae societatis consideratâ ultrò largiamur, invehitur tamen in nos Iesuira Maldonatus, garritque, quòd Augustinus tot libros, quot adversus Donatistas composuit, nontam contra illos, quàm contra longè post futuros Lutheranos composuerit. Quò vero Iesuita lectori persuadeat, quòd doceant Lutherani, non nisi bonos Ecclesiam constituere, affingit nobis, quasi statuamus, omnes etiam hypocritas, qui exteriùs fidem simulant, verè fideles esse, adeòquevi tae aeternae haeredes. ita vero minimè sentimus: Sed eos demum futurae beatitudinis participes fore docemus, qui internae socie tatis respectu ad Ecclesiam pertinent. consistit verò societas illa interna in regeneratione & renovatione, non in nudâ ac vanô fidei iactantiâ, uti pluribus ostendit B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. 2. p. 1059. Conferatur quoque in hanc rem insignis locus Iustini Martyris Apol. 2. pro Christianis p. 49. f.)*

## 13:52
v. 52. Μαθητευθεὶς instructed in doctrine, which leads to the kingdom of heaven. Or instructed concerning the kingdom of heaven, as if to say, looking toward the kingdom of heaven. Or in the kingdom of heaven, as if εἰς were placed for ὐν. Irenaeus lib. 4. cap 21. pag. 246. Those things which they bring forth from the treasure, old and new, he calls the two Testaments without contradiction. The old indeed, because the giving of the law had been before, but the new, he shows, is the conversation which is according to the Gospel. Gallasius in the notes: The simpler interpretation of this passage is this. For a good steward and prudent dispenser of household affairs, that which he may supply to the family is always at hand, so that the necessary things are never lacking to them, for he has not only fresh fruits in hand, but also has old grain stored in the granary, and keeps in the pantry whatever use demands: so the upright Rectors of the Church gather and store up all things with study, diligence, and care, which they may bring forth in their own time to nourish and protect the family of GOD, which has been entrusted to them. They were instructed concerning the Mysteries of the heavenly kingdom and appointed as Teachers and Stewards of the Church, therefore Christ exhorts them, that by the example of a prudent Steward they should store all these things in the inner chambers of their heart and bring them forth at some time for the use of the Church. *(It is also indicated by this saying, that the ministers of the Church ought to treat different chapters of heavenly doctrine according to the diversity of the hearers; to the stubborn, the headstrong, and the impenitent they ought to propose the threats of the law, but to contrite and terrified consciences they ought to propose the Gospel. To which also pertain the passages Cant. 8, 13.Apoc 15, 3.1. Cor. 3, 2.2. Tim. 2, 15. Conf. B. Par. L. de Minist. §. 189. Hom. Acad. part. 2, p. 788.)*

*( Ἐκβάλλει. The blessed D. Quist. notes in this place that the word ὐκβάλλειν does not here denote a violent, but a valid and powerful impulse, just as it is also accepted above in chapter 7, 4. 5. chapter 9, 25. 38. Iohan. 10, 4.)*

Latin:

v. 52. Μαθητευθεὶςedectus in doctrina, quae ducit adregnum coelorum. Vel edoctus de regne coelorum, qs. d. respiciendo ad regnum coelorum. Vel in regno coelorum, ut εἰς positum sit pro ὐν. Irenaeus lib. 4. cap 21. pag. 246. Ea quae de thesauro proferunt, vetera & nova, sine contradictione dus Testamenta dicit. Vetus quidem, quòd ant è fuerat legis datio, no va autem, quae secundùm Evangelium est, conversatio estendit. Gallasius in notis: Simplicior huius loci interpretatio haec est. Probo Oeconomo & prudenti dispensatori rei familiaris semper in promtu est, quod suppeditet familiae, it a ut nunquam illi necessaria desint, nec enim tantùm recentes fruges in manu, sed annonam veterem in horreo recondit am habet, & in penu servat quicquidusu postulat: it a probi Ecclesiae Rectores studio, diligentiâ & curâ omnia congerunt & recondunt, quod suo tempore depromant ad alendam & tuendam familiam DEI, qui ipsis credita est. Instituti erant de Mysteriis regni coelestis & constituti Ecclesiae Doctores & Oeconomi, ideò Christus eos hortatur, ut exemplo prudentis Oeconomi haec omnia in penetralia cordis sui reponant & ad Ecclesiae usum aliquando depromant. *(Indicatur quoq; hoc dicto, quòd Ecclesiae ministri pro diversitate auditorum alia atque alia doctrinae coelestis capita tractare; pervicacibus, praefractis & impoenitētibus legis comminationes, contritis vero ac territis conscientiis Evangelium proponere debeant. quo faciunt etiam loca Cant. 8, 13.Apoc 15, 3.1. Cor. 3, 2.2. Tim. 2, 15. Conf. B. Par. L. de Minist. §. 189. Hom. Acad. part. 2, p. 788.)*

*( Ἐκβάλλει. Notat B. D. Quist. in h. l. verbum ὐκβάλλειν hîc non notare violentum, sed validum ac potentem impulsum quomodo etiam accipiatur suprà cap. 7, 4. 5. cap. 9, 25. 38. Iohan. 10, 4.)*

## 13:54
v. 54. Into his own country. Nazareth is called the country of Christ, because he was educated there. *( Matth. 2. 23.Luc. 4, 16. and conceived, Luc. 1, 26. following. And thus Chrysostom, Euthymius, Jerome, Theophylact, etc., accept it in this place; add Luc. 4, 16.Marc. 6, 1. Otherwise Capernaum is also called the country of Christ, because he was frequently occupied there. Similarly Bethlehem, because he was -ated there.)*

Latin:

v. 54. Inpatriam suam. Nazareth dicitur Christi patria, quia ibi fuit educatus. *( Matth. 2. 23.Luc. 4, 16. ac conceptus, Luc. 1, 26. seqq. Et ita accipiunt h. l. Chrysost. Euthymius, Hieronymus, Theophylactus &c. add. Luc. 4, 16.Marc. 6, 1. Aliàs Capernaum quoq; Christi patria dicitur, quia frequenter ibi fuit versatus. Similiter Bethlehem, quia ibi -atus.)*

## 13:55
*(v. 55. Is not this the carpenter's son &c. See Annotations to Marc. 6, 3.)*

*( And his sisters i. e. kinswomen. Born indeed from Cleophas, brother of Joseph, to whom Mary, the Mother of Christ, was betrothed. Moreover, Cleophas, who is also called Alphaeus, begat four sons, James the Less, Joses, Judas Thaddaeus, and Simon. Furthermore two sisters, namely Salome, the wife of Zebedee, and Mary, of whom these in this place and elsewhere are called sisters, and those brothers, of Christ, by a Hebrew phrase, namely, by which cousins are called brothers and sisters. See Gen. 20, 12.cap. 24, 60.cap. 26, 7.Tob. 8, 9. and add the Commentaries of the blessed Par. and the blessed D. Rungius on the said places, also Mr. D. Muller on Judaism p. 1005. following. There are also those who maintain that the wife of Cleophas was also the uterine sister of Mary ever virgin, so that in a double respect the sons and daughters of Cleophas were kinsmen of Christ. See Analysis to the Epistle of Jude page 11. following.)*

Latin:

*(v. 55. Nonne hic est fabri filius &c. Vid. Annot. ad Marc. 6, 3.)*

*( Et sorores eius i. e. agnatae. natae quippe ex Cleophâ, fratre Iosephi, cui desponsata Maria Christi Mater. Genuit autē Cleophas, qui eniam Alphaeus dictus, quatuor filios, Iacobū Minorem, Iosen, Iudam Thaddaeum, ac S-monem Praeterea duas sorores, Salomonem nempe, uxorem Zebedaei, ac Mariam, quarum hae hoc loco & alibi Christi sorores, illi fratres dicuntur, phrasi scil. Ebraeâ, qua consobiini fratres ac sorores dicuntur. Vid. Gen. 20, 12.cap. 24, 60.cap. 26, 7.Tob. 8, 9. ac add. Comm. B. Par. ac B. D. Rungii in dd. ll. item Dn. D. Mullerum Iudaismi p. 1005. seqq. Sunt etiam, qui Cleophae quoque uxorem, Mariae semper virginis sororem uterin am fuisse statuunt, ut ita duplici respectu Cleophae filii filiaeque Christi fuerint agnati. Vid. Anal. ad Epist. Iudae pag. 11. seqq.)*

## 13:57
v. 57. A prophet is not without honor &c. Conf. Marc. 6, 4.Luc. 4, 24.Ioh. 4, 44. Juvencus book 3, 30.

Miracles are always despised in their own lands, And Prophets remain without honor under their native seat. Jerome, book 2, on Matt. ch. 13. It is almost natural for citizens to envy citizens. For they do not consider the present works of the man, but they remember his fragile infancy, as if they themselves had not arrived at mature age through the same steps. Theophylact, in this place, f. 58. εἰώθαμεν Plutarch, on Exile, f. 426. τῶν φρονημωτάτων (who are exalted in their fatherland.) But especially D. Chemnitius in Harm. page 221 explains the causes which make a Prophet despised in his own fatherland. Proverbs are understood concerning those things which for the most part happen: thus also this must be accepted concerning prophets dishonored in their fatherland. The causes of contempt are various. 1. A kind of innate envy among fellow citizens, by which an equal bears with difficulty that an equal be honored before him, and there is greater emulation among acquaintances than among others. 2. Familiarity breeds contempt, especially when youthful pursuits and familiar conversations are agitated before the assumption of office. 3. Such is the human disposition, that we admire foreign things and those which come from afar more than domestic ones. 4. The Prophets of the Old Testament were nowhere in lower esteem than in Judea.

Latin:

v. 57. Non est Propheta inhonoratus &c. Conf. Marc. 6, 4.Luc. 4, 24.Ioh. 4, 44. Iuvencus l. 3, 30.

Temnuntur propriis miracula semper in oris, Et sine honore manent patria sub sede Prophetae. Hieronymus l. 2. in Matth. cap. 13.Propemodum naturale es--eives semper civibus invidere. Non enim consider ant praesentiaviri opera, sed fragilis recor dantur infantiae, quasinon & ipsiper -dem gradus ad maturam aetatem pervenerint. Theophyl. h. l. f. 58. εἰώθαμεν Plutarchus de Exitio, f. 426. τῶν φρονημωτάτων (qui in patriâ sint evecti.) Cumprimis vero causas, quae Prophetam in patriâ contemtum faciunt, exponit D. Chemnitius in Harm. pag 221. Intelliguntur proverbia de illis, quae utplurimum fiunt: ita quoque hoc de prophetis in patriâ inhonoratis accipiendum. Causae contemtûs sunt varie. 1. ingenita quasi invidia inter concives, quâ aequalis aequalem aegrè fertprae se honorari, & inter notos maior est aemulatio, quàm inter alios. 2. familiaritas parit contemtum, maximè quando agitantur studia iuvenilia & familiares conversationes ante susceptum officium. 3. tale est humanum ingenium, ut extranea & quae è longinquo veniunt, magis admiremur, quàm domestica 4. Prophetae Vet. Test. nullibi in minori pretio fuerunt, quàm in Iudaea.

## 13:58
*(v. 58. And he did not do many miracles there because of their unbelief. Arabic: because of the smallness (I do not know why the Londoners translate because of the scarcity of believers)*

Latin:

*(v. 58. Et non fecitibi virtutes multas propter incredulitatem eorum. Arabs: propter parvitatem (nescio cur Londinenses vertant propter penuriam) sideitorum)*

## 14:1
v. 1. Herod the tetrarch. This Herod was surnamed Antipas, the son of Herod the Great, who was not a King, like his parent, but a tetrarch. *(The Ethiopian renders the word τετράρχης by which otherwise signifies King. Either because he thought that a tetrarch is the same as a King, or because he otherwise lacked a convenient term to employ. (Whence he also uses the same word in Luke 9, 7. and also Acts 13, 1. elsewhere he even omits it entirely, as in Luke 3, 19.) or rather, because he knew that the same Herod was distinguished by the name of King by the Evangelist Mark himself, 6, 27. Furthermore, the Arab and the Persian rendered the word ποραρχου itself quite conveniently, of whom the latter translates: i. e. prefect of the fourth part of the kingdom: But the former i. e. prince of the fourth. The Syrian retained the Greek word in this place, in Luke 3, 1 he rendered it: i. e. prince of the fourth, viz. part. Moreover, this Herod was called Antipas, Tetrarch, because, as is evident from Josephus, book 27, A. I. ch. 10 & 13, his father Herod the Great had divided his whole Kingdom in his will into as it were four parts, of which two were to go to Archelaus, another of the remaining to Herod Antipas, and another to Philip. Whence there is no doubt that the word πτράχ-ς is more correctly expressed here by prince of the fourth part, than by prince of four prefectures or provinces, as if ᾶρχων τῶν τεσάρων viz. ἐπαρχῶν, as Georgius Pasor in his Lexicon wishes. Even less conveniently did the authors of the Greek-Latin Lexicon, looking toward the instruction of the sacred Apparatus prefixed to the Royal Bibles, render the same word as Quadruple.)* Herod indeed thought that the soul of John had migrated into Christ, Matth. 16, 14. or that the Spirit of John had been given to Christ, 2. Reg. 2, 9.

NOTES TO CHAPTER XIV. SUMMARY AND DISPOSITION.

*( Ακοὴν Ἰησοῦ, the fame of Jesus i. e. concerning Jesus. The Syrian, Arab, and Persian imitate this mode of speaking. The Ethiopian translates: i. e. the sound of the speech of the Lord Jesus. But how then at last did Herod hear something about the miracles of Christ? Resp. this happened either through his own negligence, or the malice of the courtiers, who often prevent Princes from learning those things which it is nevertheless of the greatest importance for them to know. There are, however, those who think that most of Christ's miracles occurred while Herod was distracted partly by a Roman journey, partly by an Arabian war. Grotius thinks so. But the former opinion is more pleasing to most Interpreters and also pleases Chrysostom.)*

Latin:

v. 1. Herodes tetrarcha. Herodes iste cognominatus fuit Antipas, Herodis Magni filius, qui non fuit Rex, sicut parens, sed tetrarcha. *(Aethiops vocem τετράρχης reddit per quod aliàs Regem significat. Vel quod existimaret, tetrarcham esse eundem cum Rege, vel quod aliàs vocabulum commodum ei deesset, quod adhiberet. (Unde eâdem quoque voce utitur Luc. 9, 7. it. Act. 13, 1. alibi etiam prorsus omittit, uti Luc. 3, 19.) vel potiùs, quòd ab ipso Evang. Marcoc. 6, 27. eundem Herodem Regis nomine insignitum sciret. Ipsam porrò ποραρχου vocem satis commodè reddiderunt Arabs ac Persa, quorū hic vertit: i. e. praefectus quartae partis regni: Ille verò h. e. princeps quantae. Syrus vocem Graecam h. l. retinuit, Lucae 3, 1. reddidit: i. e. princeps quartae, sc. partis. Dictus autem fuit Herodes hic Ant-pas, Tetrarcha, quòd, ceu ex Iosepho l. 27. A. I. c. 10. & 13. constat, Pater eius Herodes Magnus totum suum Regnum in testamento in quatuor quasi partes divisisset, quarum duae Archelao, reliquarum altera Herodi Antipae, altera Philippo cederet. Unde non est dubium, quin vox πτράχ-ς rectiùs hîc exprimatur per quartae partis principem, quàm per principem qua---r praefectur arum sive provinciarum, qs. ᾶρχων τῶν τεσάρων sc. ἐπαρχῶν, ceu Georgius Pasor in Lex. vult. Minùs etiam commodè eandem vocem autores Lexici Graeco-Latini, ad Apparatûs sacri, Bibliis Regiis praemissi instructionem spectantis, reddiderunt per Quadruplalem.)* Existimavit verò Herodes, quòd anima Iohannis immigraverit in Christum, Matth. 16, 14. vel quòd Spiritus Iohannis Christo fucrit datus, 2. Reg. 2, 9.

NOTAE AD CAP. XIV. SUMMA AC DISPOSITIO.

*( Ακοὴν Ἰησοῦ,famam Iesu i. e. de Iesu. Imitantur hunc loquendi modum Syrus, Arabs, Persa. Aethiops vertit: i. e. sonitum sermonis Domini Iesu. Sed quomodo tum demum Herodes aliquid de Christi miraculis inaudiit? Resp. factum hoc vel propriâ ipsius negligentiâ, vel aulicorum malitiâ, qui saepè impediunt, ne Principes ea resciscant, quae scire tamen plurimum corum inest. Sunt tamen qui existimant, pleraque Christi miracula contigisse Herode partim itinere Romano, partim bello Arabico distento. ita sentit Grotius. Sed prior sententia magis arridet plerisque Interpp. & placet quoque Chrysostomo.)*

## 14:2
v. 2. Hic est Iohannes. [This is John.] See the notes on v. 1, and compare the Analecta on Marc. 6, 16. Furthermore, Luc. 9, 7. it is said that Herod hesitated, i. e. doubted, concerning Christ, as to who he might be. Resp. [Response:] Some think that he doubted at first, but afterwards fully persuaded himself that the soul of John had migrated into Christ. Others, however, among whom is Grotius, maintain that Herod did not assert this here either, but, doubting, said to the servants of his court whether what certain people were saying, that John had come back to life, was true.)*

Latin:

* (v. 2. Hic est Iohannes. Vid. notata ad v. 1. ac conser Analecta ad Marc. 6, 16. Coeterùm Luc. 9, 7. dicitur, quòd haesitaverit s. dubita verit Herodes de Christo, quisnam esset. Resp. Existimant nonnulli, quòd primò dubitârit, posteà autem penitus sibi persvaserit, quòd anima Iohannis migrarit in Christum. Alii verò, inter quos & Grotius, statuunt, quòd nec hîc Herodes adseverârit, sed dubitans ad aulae mancipia dixerit, an quod quidam dicebant, Iohannem revixisse, verum esset.)*

## 14:3
v. 3. Nam Herodes ceperat Iohannem. [For Herod had seized John.] The world and reason think that John, whose birth was foretold by the Prophets and illustrated by so many miracles, ought to enjoy the best fortune in these lands, but the exact opposite happens. 1. So that an example of constancy may be given to all. 2. Of patience. 3. So that it may be taught that the contempt of the Gospel is avenged by the premature death of its Teachers. 4. So that it may be a testimony concerning the future judgment.

*( Εδησσεν ὰυτὸν. enall A-risti 1. for the pluperfect he had bound. Conf. a similar example Luc. 13, 16. Furthermore, Herod himself had not bound John with his own hands, but had ordered it to be done through his satellites. Whence it is to be noted, that in Holy Scripture those things are attributed to those commanding which are done by others at their own order. Ier. 36, 23.25.27. Thus God says things are done by Himself which are done by His order and command. See 2. Sam. 12, 7. To this also can be referred the passage 1. Reg. 18, 40.)*

Latin:

v. 3. Nam Herodes ceperat Iohannem. Mundus ac ratio cogitant, Iohannem, cuius nativitas praenunciata per Prophetas & tot miraculis illustrata, optimâ in his terris fortunâ debere perfrui, sed contrarium planè accidit. 1. ut omnibus detur exemplum constantiae. 2. Patientiae. 3. Ut contemtus Evangelii praematurâ morte Doctorum vindicari doceatur. 4. ut sit testimonium de futuro iudicio.

*( Εδησσεν ὰυτὸν. enall A-risti 1. pro plusquam perfacto vinxerat. Conf. simile exemplum Luc. 13, 16. Coeterùm non ipse Herodes propriis manibus Iohannem vinxerat, sed per suos satellites id fieri iusserat. Unde notandum, quòd mandantibus tribuantur in Sc. S. ea, quae iubentibus ipsis per alios facta. Ier. 36, 23.25.27. Sic Deus à se facta dicit, quae ipsius iussu & mandato facta. Vid. 2. Sam. 12, 7. Huc quoque referri potest locus 1. Reg. 18, 40.)*

## 14:4
v. 4. It is not lawful for you to have her. Chrysostom hom. 1. to the People of Antioch, vol. 5. col. 24. says that John said these things with confidence in the middle of the forum. The same, hom. 28. on 2. Cor. Col. 866. They are more the words of one teaching than of one rebuking: of one instructing than of one punishing; of one instituting than of one traducing; of one correcting than of one insulting. Jerome in this place records that Herod had married the wife of his brother still living. The same is recorded by Josephus book 18. Antiq. c. 7. Eusebius book 1. Hist. c. 12. Jerome calls the brother Philip, Josephus Herod. Nicephorus book 1. H. E. c. 19. Herod, his own wife having been rejected (this was the daughter of Aretas, King of the Arabs) having sent back a messenger regarding his loves, he preferred his vain and exhausted affection toward Herodias to all things. When he knew that she was the wife of his brother Philip, he had married her against the constitution of the law, for he had offspring from his brother, and indeed while he was still surviving, as it seems to Josephus. It was not lawful for Herod to have the wife of his brother, whether he were living or dead, because offspring had already been conceived from that marriage, namely that daughter of Herodias, whom Chrysostom teaches was conceived from a prior marriage, hom. 49. in Matth. & it is sufficiently evident from the fact that the death of John fell at the very beginning of the marriage of Herod with Herodias, as is clear from Josephus book 18. Antiq. c. 10. For if at that time the girl already knew how to dance, she had certainly been born many years, nor is it likely that John would have waited so many years before he rebuked Herod for that public crime. Bell. on Matrim. c. 27. *(B. Par. L. on Marriage § 299 deals with this incest of Herod at greater length, where he also warns that since Herod joined his sister-in-law to himself under a certain guise of honesty, ὅτι

ἐγάμησεν ἀυτὴν, as Mark has it, he was nevertheless gravely rebuked for this by John, from which it may be evident that those Laws concerning prohibited degrees, Levit. 18. proposed, were not merely forensic, looking only to the Jewish polity, but pertain to natural and moral law. Grotius also seems to agree in this place. Bellarm. book 1. on Matrim. c. 17, Conzen in this place, and other Papists except, That John rebuked the deed of Herod because Philip was still among the living. Resp. Although Eusebius, Nicephorus, and the author of the Hebrew History, praised by Drusius, and indeed Jerome himself, following Josephus, maintain that Philip was still among the living, they do not, however, establish this with a sufficiently firm foundation, nor is anything of this matter to be found even in sacred history. Furthermore, Grotius well notes that John accuses not only the beginning, i.e., that while Philip was still living Herod had snatched his wife and joined her to himself, but the very τὸ ἔξειν. So that not only the abduction and adultery, but the very marriage in such a degree of proximity was disapproved by John.)*

Latin:

v. 4. Non licet tibi habere eam. Chrysostomus hom. 1. ad Pop. Antioch. t. 5. col. 24. dicit, Iohannem cum fiducia in medio foro haec dixisse. Idem hom. 28. in 2. Cor. Col. 866. Sunt magis verba docentis, quàm reprehēdentis: erudientis, quàm punientis; instituentis, quàm traducentis; corrigentis quàm in saltantis, Hieronymus in h. l. memorat, Herodem fratris adhuc viventis uxorem duxisse. Idem memorat Iosephus lib. 18. Antiq. c. 7. Euseb. lib. 1. Hist. c. 12. Hieronymus fratrem vocat Philippum, Iosephus Herodem. Nicephorus l. 1. H. E. c. 19. Herodes propriâ reiectâ coniuge (filia haec erat Arabum Regis Aretae) amoribuseius nuncio remisso vanam & effaetam erga Herodiaden affectionem rebus omnibus anteponebat. Hanc ille cùm uxorem esse sciret fratris Philippi, contra legis constitutionem, semen enim habebat ex fratre, & quidem eo adhuc superstite, ut Iosepho videtur, duxerat. Non licebat Herodi, uxorem fratris sui habere, sive is viveret, sive mortuus esset, quia proles ex eo matrimonio iam erat suscepta, nimirum filia illa Herodiadis, quam ex priore matrimonio susceptam fuisse, docet Chrysostomus hom. 49. in Matth. & satis constat ex eo, quòd mors Iohannis incidit in ipsum initium coniugii Herodis cum Herodiade, ut patet ex Iosepho lib. 18. Antiq. c. 10. Si enim eo tempore iam tripudiare puella noverat, certè multis annis nata fuerat, nec verisimile est, Iohannem expectaturum tot annos, antequam Herodem publici illius criminis reprehenderet. Bell. de Matrim. c. 27. *(Pluribus de hoc Herodis incesto agit B. Par. L. de Coniug. § 299. ubi etiam monet, quòd cùm Herodes fratriam suam, sub specie quadam honestatis sibi coniunxerit, ὅτι

ἐγάμησεν ἀυτὴν, ut habet Marcus, nihilo tamen minùs graviter ob hoc reprehensus fuerit à Iohanne, exinde pateat, Leges illas de prohibitis gradibus, Levit. 18. propositas, non suisse merè forenses, ad Iudaicam tantùm politiam spectantes, sed pertinere ad ius naturale ac morale. Videtur consencire & Grotius in h. l. Excipiunt Bellarm. l. 1. de Matrim. c. 17. Conzen in h. l. aliique Pontificii, Proptereà Iohannem factum Herodis reprehendisse, quòd adhuc Philippus fuerit in vivis. Resp. Licet Eusebius, Nicephorus ac autor Hist. Ebraeae, à Drusio laudatus, quin ipse Hieronymus, Iosephum secuti statuant, quòd Philippus adhuc fuerit in vivis, id tamen fundamento satis firmo haut astruunt, nec quicquam huius rei etiam in historiâ sacrâ reperire est. Praetereà benè notat Grotius, quòd Iohannes non solùm initium accuset, h. e. quòd vivente adhuc Philippo Herodes eius uxorem rapuerat, sibique iunxerat, sed ipsum τὸ ἔξειν. Ut adeò non solùm raptus & adulterium, sed ipsum coniugium in tali propinquitatis gradu improbatum à Ioh. fuerit.)*

## 14:5
(v. 5. Ως προφήτην. partic. ὡς responds in this place to the Hebrew בבף האמתי, that is, the caph of truth. For John was held by the people to be a true Prophet. But why he himself denies that he is a Prophet, has been explained above. See the Annotations c. XI. v. 9. In the Annals of the Hebrew Kings of Israel, or the Chronicle of the second temple, fol. 58, and also in the Hebrew History, c. 63, John is saluted as High Priest, as Drusius reports in Praet. p. 34. But H. Grotius rightly observes that John is called בהז Priest, καταχρηςικῶς, so that he might be understood as an excellent minister of GOD, just as Moses is also called in the Psalm בהז. Which observation must be opposed to the apostate Nihusius, who, from the fact that Ps. 99, 6. Moses is said to have called upon the name of the Lord with the Priests, concludes that he himself was a Priest properly so called, and even a High Priest. But the weakness of the Nihusian conclusion was long ago shown by B. D. Glass. in App. Rhet. S. annexed p. 1491. et seqq. Furthermore, Josephus the Jewish historiographer, book 18 of the Antiquities of the Jews, c. 7, writes thus concerning the slaughter of John: Among the Jews there was an opinion that Herod's army was destroyed by a just vengeance of God, on account of John, who was surnamed the Baptist. For the Tetrarch killed this excellent man, who was inciting the Jews to the pursuit of virtues, and especially of piety and justice, etc. But Josephus is considered to err when he immediately adds that Herod therefore bound him and sent him to Machaerus, because he feared that when a great concourse of men was made to him (John), such authority of the man might cause some defection. The Evangelist designates another cause in this place v. 3. And it is well to be noted that the author of the Hebrew History, cited by Drusius in Praet., establishes as the cause of the killing of John not the fear of sedition, but that same rebuke. But these opinions can be reconciled if it is said that Herod indeed had in mind even before to kill the Baptist, fearing the defection of the Jews to him: yet afterwards he was more and more incited by that intrepid rebuke. The same Josephus calls Herod's brother Philip also Herod, in which matter Beza, Baronius, Montacutius, Petavius, and others think he lapsed in memory. But Grotius undertakes the defense of Josephus, establishing that Philip was binominal, following in this matter Card. Caietanus. B. D. Quistorpius reconciles Josephus with the Evangelist differently, noting that Herodias had been married three times, first having married Herod born of Mariamne, and to him having borne a daughter Salome, of whom vers. 6. mention is made, afterwards having married Philip, and finally Herod Antipas. But that Josephus does not mention Philip, because he had died ἄπαις without having received any offspring. The Jesuit Conzen, in order to defend the Vulgate Interpreter, who omitted the name Philip both here and Luc. 3, 19., boldly asserts that it is sufficiently certain that that name was added here from a gloss. Namely, so that the Vulgate Interpreter may not be thought to have omitted something which is nevertheless a genuine part of the text, rather the text itself must be established as corrupt, and indeed all the Oriental versions, namely the Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic, Persian, as in which the name Philip is read constantly both here, and in Luke 3, 19, and finally in Mark 6, 17. The same Jesuit Conzen attempts to undermine the opinion of Caietanus, who establishes that Philip was called by the compound name of his brother Herod Philip Herod, from the fact that it was not the custom among the Hebrews for names

to double. And yet the contrary is evident from very many places of Holy Scripture, and the associates of Conzenius grant it willingly. Many among the Hebrews were binominal, writes the Jesuit Tirinus explicitly commentary on 1 Chronicles 6, 34. Similarly Cornelius à Lapide commentary on Genesis chapter 36, 1. Note, he says, that men and women were formerly polyonymous. Compare the same, Prolegomena to the Pentateuch, canon 19.)*

Latin:

*(v. 5. Ως προφήτην. partic. ὡς respondet h. l. Ebrao בבף האמתי h. e. caph veritatis. Habebatur enim Ioha-es à populo pro verô Propheta. Cur verò ipse neget, se esse Prophetam, supra expositum. Vid. Annot. c. XI. v. 9. In Annalibus Ebr. Regum Israel s. Chron. templi sec. f. 58. it. in Hist. Ebr. c. 63. salutatur Iohannes Sacerdos magnus, prout refert Drusius in Praet. p. 34. Rectè autem observat H. Grotius, quòd Iohannes בהזSacerdos dicatur καταχρηςικῶς, ut intelligeretur excellens DEI minister, quomodo & Moses in Psalmo בהז vocatur. Quae observatio opponenda Apostatae Nihusio, qui ex eo, quòd Ps. 99, 6. Moses dicitur invocâsse nomen Domini cum Sacerdotibus, colligit, ipsum fuisse Sacerdotem propriè dictum, adeoetiam Pontificem summum. Sed infirmitatem collectionis Nihusianae pridem ostendit B. D. Glass. in App. Rhet. S. annexae p. 1491. seqq. Coeterùm Iosephus Historiographus Iudaeus lib. 18. Antiq. Iud. c. 7. ita de caede Iohannis: Apud Iudaeos fuit opinio, iustâ ultione naminis deletum Herodis exercitum, propter Iohannē, qui Baptista cognominatus est. Hunc enim Tetrarcha necavit virum optimum, Iudaeos excitantem ad virtutum studia, & imprimis pietatis ac iustitiae &c. Errare verò Iosephus censetur, quando statim subiicit, quòd Herodes proptereà vinxerit & Machaeruntem miserit, quoniam veritus fuerit, ne cùm magnus hominum concursus ad eum (Iohannem) fieret, tanta hominis autoritas defectionem aliquam pareret. Aliam causam designat Evangelista h. l. v. 3. Et probè notandum, quòd autor Historiae Ebraeae, à Drufio in Praet. adductus, causam interfectionis Iohannis non seditionis metum, sed istam reprehensionem itidem statuat. Possunt verò sententiae istae conciliari, si dicatur, quòd quidem Herodes iam ante habuerit in animo, Baptistam interficere, metuens Iudaeorū ad illum defectionem: Postmodum tamen magis ac magis fuerit incitatus per intrepidam istam reprehēsionem. Idem Iosephus Herodis fratrem Philippum, voeat itidem Hercdem, quâ in re memoriâ lapsum eum putant Beza, Baronius, Monta cutius, Petavius, alii. Sed patrociniam Iosephi suscipit Grotius, Philippum binominem fuisse statuens, sequutus hac in re Card. Caietanum. Aliter conciliat Iosephum cum Evangelista B. D. Quistorpius, monens, Herodiaden trigamam fuisse, primò nupsisse Herodi è Mariamne nato, & huic peperisse filiam Salomen, cuius vers. 6. mentio fit, posteà nupsisse Philippo, ac denique Herodi Antipae. Iosephum verò Philippi non meminisse, quòd nullâ susceptâ prole ἄπαις obierat. Iesuita Conzen, quò Vulgatum Int-rpretem, qui tum hîc, tum Luc. 3, 19. nomen Philippi omisit, defendat, audacter adferit, satis constare, nomen illud hic additum ex glossa. Scil. ne Vulg. Interpres existimetur aliquid omisisse, quod genuina tamen textûs pars est, potiùs ipse textus corruptus statuendus est, imò & omnes versiones O--entales, videl. Syriaca, Arabica, Aethiopica, Persica, ut in quibus nomen Philippi tum hîc, tum Lucae 3, 19. tum Marci denique 6, 17. constanter legitur. Idem Iesuita Conzen Caietani sententiam, statuentis, Philippum fratris Herodis nomine composito Philippum Herodem vocatum esse, labefactare conatur exinde, quòd mosnon fuerit apud Hebraeos, nomina

geminare. Atqui contrarium è plurimis Sc. S. locis patet, & ultrò largiuntur Conzenii socienni. Multi apud Ebraeos erant binomines, scribit disertè Iesuita Tirinus Co-. in 1. Paral. 6, 34. Similiter Corn. à Lap. Co-. in Gen. c. 36, 1. Nota, inquit, viros & feminas olim fuisse polyonymos. Conf. idem Proleg. in Pentat. can. 19.)*

## 14:6
(v. 6. γενεσέων Ο ἀγομθύων ). Erasm. When the birthday was being celebrated. Heinsius thinks that this should be understood not of the birthday of life, but of the reign. Grotius also understands it in the same way, bringing forward for this matter a passage from Herodotus. But however much it might perhaps be conceded that Kings also celebrated the birthday of their reign, yet no necessity urges why we should understand it in this place of the birthday of the reign rather than of life. Thus indeed the passage Gen. 40, 20., which Grotius compares with the present one, is to be understood entirely. And so also, namely of the birthday of life, Chrysostom long ago understood it, whom the Interpreters commonly follow. See B. D. Hunnius on this place. B. D. Chemn. H. E. page 810. It is known, however, from ancient Writers that formerly almost all peoples, especially the Romans, religiously celebrated their birthday. And Marcellus Donatus in his Dilucidations on Suetonius Tranquillus, Tiberius c. 5, Gruterus in his Animadversions on Seneca p. 753, Mr. Dilherrus in his Academic Disputations vol. 1, p. 421 ff., Rosinus in his Roman Antiquities passim, Polydorus Vergil on the Inventors of Things book 6, c. 7, and Petrus Faber book 1, Semestria c. 6, show this from many sacred as well as profane monuments. Furthermore, that speaking absolutely the custom by which Magnates celebrate their birthday is not to be disapproved, and how likewise a birthday ought to be rightly celebrated, namely 1. by thanksgiving, 2. by recollection of the life passed, 3. by devout prayer, etc., B. D. Chemn. H. E. chapter 74, page 811, shows at length.)

( Ὠρχήσατο. Some seize upon this as an occasion for simply reproving dances. But that dances in themselves are not illicit has long since been shown by our people. See Ana-. on Matthew XI, 17. In this place it is at least to be noted that the Adversaries grant that dances can be tolerated if the segregation of the sexes is observed. But here such a thing happened, and yet it is deservedly disapproved.

On the contrary, God never prohibited honest recreation to his people, to which dances can also be referred. See B. D. Chemn. H. E. p. 812. b.)

Latin:

*(v. 6. γενεσέων Ο ἀγομθύων). Erasm. Cùm celebraretur natalis. Existimat Heinsius, accipiendum hoc non de natali vitae, sed regni. Eodem modo accipit quoque Grotius, adducens in hanc rem locum ex Herodoto. Verùm ut ut fortè concedi possit, quòd regni quoque natalem Reges celebrarent, nulla tamen necessitas urget, cur de regni potiùs, quàm vitae natali h. l. accipere debeamus. Ita sanè omninò intelligendus locus Gen. 40, 20. quem cum praesenti Grotius confert. Et ita quoq;, nempe de natali vitae, iam olim accepit Chrysostomus, quem sequuntur Interpp. communiter. Vid. B. D. Hunnius in h. l. B. D. Chemn. H. E. pag. 810. Notum verò è Scriptoribus antiquis, quòd olim ferè omnes populi, cumprimis Romani, diem natalem religiosè celebrarint. Idque multis è sacris iuxta ac profanis monumentis ostendunt Marcellus Donatus Dilucid. in Sveton. Tranq. Tiberium c. 5. Gruterus Anim. ad Senec. p. 753. Dn. Dilherrus Disp. Acad. t. 1. p. 421. seqq. Rosinus Antiq. Rom. passim. Polydorus Vergil. de Rerum inventor. l. 6. c. 7. Petrus Faber l. 1. Semest. c. 6. Quod porrò absolutè loquendo non improbandus sit mos, quo Magnates diem suum natalem celebrant, quomodo item dies natalis ritè celebrari debeat, videl. 1. gratiarum actione. 2. vitae transactae recordatione. 3. devotâ oratione &c. prolixè ostendit B. D. Chemn. H. E. cap. 74. pag. 811.)*

*( Ὠρχήσατο. Arripiunt hinc nonnulli occasionem, simpliciter reprehendendi choreas. Ast quòd choreae per se non sint illicitae, pridem à nostratibus ostensum. Vid. Ana-. ad Matth. XI, 17. Hoc loco illud saltem notandum, quòd Adversarii largiantur, saltationes ferri posse, si segregatio sexûs observetur. At hîc tale factum, & tamen meritò improbatur.

Contrà Deus populo suo honestam recreationem, ad quam etiam choreae referri possunt, nunquam prohibuit. Vid. B. D. Chemn. H. E. p. 812. b.)*

## 14:7
v. 7. Ὡμολόγησεν ἀυτῇ he had confessed i. e. he had promised that he would perform that.

*( Ὃ ἐὰν αἰ τήσηται. Mark c. 6, 23. expresses it more specifically, adding: Ἔως ἡμίσους τῆς βασιλείας μου. Such a promise we also read was made to Esther Esth. 5, 3.)*

Latin:

v. 7. Ὡμολόγησεν ἀυτῇconfessus fuerat i. e. promisisset, se id praestiturum.

*( Ὃ ἐὰν αἰ τήσηται. Marcus c. 6, 23. exprimit specialiùs, addens: Ἔως ἡμίσους τῆς βασιλείας μου. Quale promissum etiam Estheri factum legimus Esth. 5, 3.)*

## 14:8
v. 8. Προβιβασθεῖσα, suborned, instructed, persuaded, prepared, previously instructed. Deut. 6. v. 7. Προβιβάσσεις ἀυτὰ τοῖς ιἱς σου. Someone translates brought forward from an observation of a Plinian passage. But because συμβιβάζειν otherwise in the N. T. signifies to build up by speaking, or to teach, traces of that meaning can also be retained here, so that ῶρροβιβασθεῖα may be previously taught.

*( Give me the head of John. From this shines forth the dire hatred of Herodias against John, who was taxing her unchaste morals. Thus, indeed, the hatred of the truth cannot be satisfied unless by human blood innocently shed. Conf. Gen. 4, 8.1. Reg. 19, 2.Esth. 5, 14.Ierem. 37, 15.Ioh. 19, 15.Apoc. 17, 6. See B. D. Chemn. H. E. p. 813.)*

Latin:
