v. 8. Προβιβασθεῖσα,subornata, instructa, persuasa, praem--tita, priùs instructa.Deut. 6. v. 7.Προβιβάσσεις ἀυτὰ τοῖς ιἱς σου. Quidam vertit producta ex observatione loci Pliniani. Quia verò συμβιβάζειν aliàs in N. T. significat adstruere dicendo, sive docere, possunt etiam eius significationis vestigia hîc retineri, ut ῶρροβιβασθεῖα sit priùs edocta.

*( Da mihi caput Iohannis. Elucescit hinc dirum odium Herodiadis adversus Iohannem, impudicos eius mores taxantem. Ita nempe odium veritatis satiari non potest, nisi sangvine humano innocenter effuso. Conf. Gen. 4, 8.1. Reg. 19, 2.Esth. 5, 14.Ierem. 37, 15.Ioh. 19, 15.Apoc. 17, 6. Vid. B. D. Chemn. H. E. p. 813.)*

## 14:9
v. 9. He was saddened. *(He was feigning sadness. B. D. Chemnitius H. E. notes that the custom of courtiers is depicted here, and he compares the present passage with the following 1. Sam. 18, 17.2. Sam. 3, 17.c. 20, 9.c. 13, 28.cap. 15, 6.1. Reg. 21, 9.Dan. 6, 6. The complaints Ps. 55, 22.Ps. 28, 3.Ps. 57, 5.Prov. 23, 7. and the warnings, Syr. 9, 20. Ezech. 2, 6.Ps. 146, 3. also look to this.)* Tossanus: He was saddened, not because he abhorred the slaughter of John, but because he was compelled to stain his birthday with blood. In the fragments of Varro concerning the custom of the ancient Romans, these things are held: Our ancestors held to this custom and institution, that when they paid the annual gift to their genius on their birthday, they would keep their hand from slaughter and blood, lest on the day on which they themselves had received the light, they should take it from others. *(B. D. Glassius Rhet. S. p. 63. observes that τὸ to be saddened in this place is taken for the fact that Herod appeared outwardly as if he had been saddened, and feigned grief, when v. 5. it is clearly said that he wanted to kill John, but feared the people. Nor does the passage Marc. 6, 19. 20. stand in the way.

For by this it is only indicated that at first indeed Herod held John in esteem, but afterwards, at the instigation of Herodias, he was otherwise disposed toward him. That the opinion of men is sometimes put for the thing itself in the Holy Scripture, the cited Glassius proves there with several examples. Conf. also Dn. D. Walth. Harm. Bibl. Prol. §. 69. Sanctius in the books of Kings p. 183. also in Zach. c. 7. n. 4. The description of Herod favors this exposition Luc. 13, 32.

διὰ τοὺς ὄοκους. It is either an enallage of number, or it is signified that Herod repeated those adjurations more often. (Nor, however, was the promise, even if confirmed by a more often repeated oath, to be kept, because it was base and illicit. See what B. Par. collected regarding this matter from Canon Law and other authors, L. de Lege DEI §. 121. item L. de Coniug. §. 149. add Analect. to Marc. 6, 26. and compare what was noted above to c. 5, 33. 44. p. 316. 317. The Jesuit Adam Conzen himself also approves those opinions of the ancients, that in evil promises faith must be rescinded, but he denies that they can be drawn to rescind the vow of perpetual celibacy. He urges that many men and many women have kept vows of this kind. 2. that if anyone, with a spouse absent or sick, however much he may be driven to crime by Satan, yet ought not to bind himself to a new marriage, but with divine grace invoked, ought to keep faith to the spouse and chastity to God: the same ought also to be done by him who has a vow of chastity. Resp. As far as the first pertains, the case is still under the judge, how so many men and so many women in the Papacy have kept that vow. As concerns those who, with a spouse sick or absent, feel the impulses of the flesh, certainly the reason for them is far different from that of those who rashly and without a calling vow continence, as B. Par. shows in many places, L. de Coni. § 527.)

Latin:

v. 9. Tristabatur. *(Fingebat tristitiam. Notat B. D. Chemuitius H. E. depingi hîc morem aulicorum, ac confert cum praesenti loco seqq. 1. Sam. 18, 17.2. Sam. 3, 17.c. 20, 9.c. 13, 28.cap. 15, 6.1. Reg. 21, 9.Dan. 6, 6. Spectant etiam huc querelae, Ps. 55, 22.Ps. 28, 3.Ps. 57, 5.Prov. 23, 7. ac monita, Syr. 9, 20. Ezech. 2, 6.Ps. 146, 3.)* Tossanus: Tristabatur, non quòd abhorreret à caede Iohannis, sed quòd cogeretur natalem suum sanguine commaculare. In fragmentis Varronis de more veterum Romanorum haec habentur: Id moris institutiq; matores nostri tenuerunt, ut cùm die natali munus annale genio solverent, manum à caede & sangvine abstinerent, ne die, quâ ipsi lucem accepissent, aliis demerent. *(B. D. Glassius Rhet. S. p. 63. observat, quòd τὸtristari h. l. accipiatur pro eo, quòd visus fuerit Herodes exteriùs ac si contristatus esset, doloremq; simulaverit, cùm v. 5. clarè dicatur, eum voluisse Iohannem occidere, sed metuisse populum. Nec obstat locus Marc. 6, 19. 20.

Quippe quo hoc solùm indicatur, quòd primùm quidem Herodes Iohannem in aestimio habuerit, posteà tamen instigante Herodiade aliter erga eum fuerit affectus. Quòd verò opinio hominum aliquādo pro reipsâ in Sc. S. ponatur, probat laudatus Glassius ibi aliquot exemplis. Conf. etiam Dn. D. Walth. Harm. Bibl. Prol. §. 69. Sanctius in libb. Regum p. 183. it. in Zach. c. 7. n. 4. Favet huic expositioni descriptio Herodis Luc. 13, 32.)*

διὰ τοὺς ὄοκους. Vel est enallage numeri, vel significatur, Herodem adiurationes illas saepiùs repetivisse. *(Neq; tamen promissum, licet saepiùs repetito iuramento confirmatum, servandum erat, quia turpe fuit & illicitum. Vid. quae hâc de re è Iure Canonico aliisque autoribus collegit B. Par. L. de Lege DEI §. 121. it. L. de Coniug. §. 149. adde Analect. ad Marc. 6, 26. ac confer quae suprà notata ad c. 5, 33. 44. p. 316. 317. Ipse quoque Iesuita Adamus Conzen seutentias illas veterum, quòd in malè promissis rescindenda sit fides, approbat, negat verò, trahi eas posse ad rescindendum perpetui coelibatûs votum. Urget quòd multi ac multae huiusmodi vota servarint. 2. quòd si quis absente vel aegrâ coniuge, utut vel maximè à Satanâ ad erimen impellatur, tamen novo matrimonio non debet se illigare, sed gratiâ divinâ invocatâ coniugi fidem, Deo castitatem servare: idem etiam fieri debeat ab eo, qui votum castitatis habet. Resp. quod primum attinet, adhuc sub iudice lis est, quomodo tam multi ac tam multae in Papatu illud votum servârint. Quod concernit eos, qui aegrâ vel absente coniuge sentiunt carnis impulsus, sanè longè dispar ratio est illorum itemque corum, qui temerè & absque vocatione continentiam vovent, uti multis ostendit B. Par. L. de Coni. § 527.)*

## 14:10
(v. 10. καὶ τέμψας ἀπεκεφάλισε etc. That something is missing here is manifest. But Mark supplies it c. 6, 27, adding σῶεκουλάτωρα. The Oriental interpreters indeed imitated the same ellipsis here. Erasmus supplies it here by translating: & with executioners sent. But why with no executioner sent in the singular, as Mark has it, and as the Oriental interpreters followed there, except for the Ethiopian, who likewise translates in the plural: And the King immediately sent executioners, and commanded that his head be brought.)*

*( In the prison. Namely, Herod wished to conceal the slaughter of John. Thus, indeed, the world flees the light, John 3:20. But in vain does he promise himself impunity and the concealment of crimes committed. See Gen. 4:102 Sam. 12:1)*

Latin:

*(v. 10. καὶ τέμψας ἀπεκεφάλισε &c. Deesse hîc aliquid, manifestum est. Supplet verò Marcus c. 6, 27. addens σῶεκουλάτωρα. Imitati verò eandem hîc ellipsin Interpp. Orientales. Erasmus hîc supplet vertendo: & missis carnisicibus. Cur verò non misso carnifice in singulari, uti Marcus habet, cumque secuti ibi Interpp. Orientales, praeter Aethiopem, qui itidem in plurali vertit: Et misit Rex statim speculatores, & praecepit, ut afferrent caput eius.)*

*( In carcere. Voluit nempe Herodes celare caedem Iohannis. Ita nempe mundus fugit lucem, Ioh. 3, 20. At frustrà sibi impunitatem ac scelerum commissiorum occultationem pollicetur. Vid. Gen. 4, 10.2. Sam. 12, 1.)*

## 14:11
v. 11. It was given to the girl &c. Salome, the daughter of Herodias, a little harlot, is said to have pricked the tongue of John with needles. But a most just punishment for her cruelty followed. Herod and his incestuous wife were driven into exile to Lugdunum in Gaul. Salome, walking incautiously upon the ice, was submerged, her head being severed by fragments of ice. Niceph. lib. 1. Hist. Eccl. c. 20. The same [happened] to her (the daughter of Herodias), since it was wintertime and a river had to be crossed, which, when it had been constricted and joined together by ice, she was crossing on foot. But the ice having broken, and that not without the divine power of GOD, she is immediately submerged up to her head, and while she was acting wantonly with the lower parts of her body and moving herself softly, she dances not on land, but in the waves: but her wicked head, frozen by the cold and ice, and then also wounded, and severed from the rest of her body not by iron, but by crusts of ice, exhibits a dance in the ice itself &c. v. 12. They took up the body &c. Concerning the beheading of John, see Niceph. l. 1. Hist. c. 19, where he adds these things concerning the burial. Herodias, fearing the rebuke of John even after the severing of his head, and fearing to join it entirely to the rest of the body, decided that it should be buried in a more secluded place of the palace, with witnesses removed; but she ordered the trunk itself to be cast away somewhere: when, however, his disciples secretly took it up and buried it with solemn veneration in a certain celebrated place.

Latin:

v. 11. Datumest puellae &c. Salome Herodiadis filia meretricula aciculis linguam Iohannis pupugisse dicitur. Sequuta autem est poena crudelitatis iustissima. Herodes & incestuosa ipsius coniux in exilium Lugdunum Galliae pulsi sunt. Salome incautiùs glaciei inambulans submersa est, capite per glaciei frusta amputato. Niceph. lib. 1. Hist. Eccl. c. 20. Eundem ei (filiae Herodiadis) quoniam brumali tempore erat & -luvius traiiciendus, qui cùm glacie constrictus coagmentatusque esset, pedes eum transibat. Glacie autem ruptâ, idq; non sine DEI numine, demergitur illa statim capitetenus, & inferioribus corporis partibus lasciviens, molliusque sese movens, saltat non in terrâ, sed undis: caput verò scelestum frigore & glacie concretum, deinde etiam convulneratum, & à reliquo corpore non, ferro, sed glaciei crustis resectum in glacie ipsa saltationem exhibet &c. v. 12. Sustulerunt corpus &c. De decollatione Iohannis vide Niceph. l. 1. Hist. c. 19. ubi de sepultura haec addit. Herodias Iohannis reprehensionem quodammodo etiam post capitis resectionē verita, coniungereid prorsus reliquo corpori timens apud se remotis arbitris in obstrusiore. Regiae loco sepeliendum duxit: truncum autem ipsum abiicere quopiam iussit: cum porrò solum discipuli eius furtim sublatum cum solenni veneratione in celebri quodam sepeliere loco.

## 14:13
v. 13. He withdrew ὐκεῖθεν. From where? Whether from his own country, into which he is said to have come earlier in ch. 13:54 and Mark 6:1, or rather ὐκεῖθεν i.e., from that place in which he was when the death of the Baptist was announced to him. Namely, alone, removed from the crowd: for it is gathered from Mark 6:31 that the disciples were with him. *(Concerning flight, see the note on Matt. 10:1423

it. c. 15, 21.Luc. 9, Ioh. Nicephorus, book 1, chapter 19, establishes the cause of the withdrawal to have been that he might relieve sadness. More correctly Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius, and others, that he might avoid the fury of Herod. For the hour of his passion and death had not yet come. But there is no doubt that Herod, stimulated especially by the fact that the people held Christ for the Messiah, applied every effort to remove him from the midst. Having imitated, of course, his father Herod the Ascalonite, of whom above c. 2, 16.

Latin:

v. 13. Secessitὐκεῖθεν. Ad unde? an è patria sua, in quam venisse dicitur superiùs c. 13, 54. & Marc. 6, 1. an potiùs ὐκεῖθεν i. e. ex illo loco, in quo erat, quando mors Baptistae ei fuit denunciata. Solus sc. à turba remotus: discipulos enim cum ipso fuisse, colligitur ex Marc. 6, 31. *(De fugâ vid. not. ad Matth. 10, 14.23.

it. c. 15, 21.Luc. 9, Ioh. Causam secestûs statuit Niceph. l. 1. c. 19. fuisse, ut levaret tristitiam. Rectiùs Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Euthymius, alii, ut Herodis furorem declinaret. Nondum enim venerat hora passionis ac mortis. Nullum verò dubium, quin Herodes, stimulatus cumprimis eo, quòd populus Christum pro Messia habebat, omne adhibuerit studium, quò illum è medio tolleret. Imitatus scilicet patrem Herodem Ascalonitam, de quo suprà c. 2, 16.)*

## 14:14
v. 14. Σπλαγχνίζεσθα. He notes a vehement affection of compassion, by which the very bowels are moved. Ebr. 2, 17.c. 4, 15.Luc. 1, 78.

Latin:

v. 14. Σπλαγχνίζεσθα. Notat vehementem commiserationis affectum, quo ipsa viscera commoventur. *(Cont. Ebr. 2, 17.c. 4, 15.Luc. 1, 78.)*

## 14:15
v. 15. When evening had come, his disciples approached him. But v. 23. it is said that when evening had come, Christ was alone. Resp. Mr. Dr. Walth. in H. B. p. 774. and B. Par. Co-. in Gen. p. 338. warn that there is a distinction between the evening of the sun, in which it sets, and of the light or of the day, which appears for some time in the clouds after the setting of the sun. That the former is treated in the present verse, the latter in v. 23. R. Aben Ezra provides that distinction in Exod. 12, 6., whose words the praised Mr. Dr. Walth. recites in the cited place p. 208. Conf. Grotius on this passage.

Latin:

*(v. 15. Vespere facto accesserunt eum discipuli eius. Atqui v. 23. dicitur, quòd vespere facto Christus fuerit solus. Resp. Dn. D. Walth. in H. B. p. 774. ac B. Par. Co-. in Gen. p. 338. monent, quòd dist. sit inter vesperam solis, quâ is occidit, & luminis seu diei, quae post solis occasum in nubibus aliquamdiu apparet. De illâ agi versu praesenti, de hâc v. 23. Suppeditat verò distinctionem illam R. Aben Ezra in Exod. 12, 6. cuius verba recitat laudatus Dn. D. Walth. l. c. p. 208. Conf. Grotius in h. l.)*

## 14:19
v. 19. Ἐπὶ τοὺς χόρτους to recline. From this DoLaur. Ramirez de Prato proves that Judea was grass-bearing. And he compares with the present passage the parallel Marc. 6, 39., likewise Ioseph. book 7, B. I. c. 5. & 7. The same refers the custom of carrying grass received among the Jews to the fact that it was a pledge to the Jewish nation, so that they might refresh the memory of the Edict of Pharaoh, by which it was provided that they themselves must collect straw, grass, and stubble to make bricks. Exod. 5, 7.

Ἀναβλέψας εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν. Christ asked as a man, and indeed in the state of emptying, God the heavenly Father so that he might be able to effect this miracle. See also Iohan. 11, 41.43. Furthermore, Damascenus treats of the Prayer of the Lord in a peculiar chapter, namely XXIV of book III of the Orthodox Faith, on which passage-let the commentary of Iodocus Clichtoveus be seen entirely Neopor--en--. add also B. D. Chemn. Harm. Ev. p. 324.

καὶ εὐλόλὸγησε. B. Par. L. de S. Coenâ §. 145 shows how many times the Savior εὐλογία is read to have used in Scripture. Why Christ indeed εὐλογίᾳ was the usage, the Same teaches §. 143. Concerning the blessing see 1. Sam. 9, 13.Matth. 26, 30. Tertullian concerning the Christians of his own age: They do not recline before prayer is tasted to God, and prayer likewise breaks up the banquet. Compare B. D. Franz. on the Interpretation of Holy Scripture Orac. 119. following, where he explains this whole History at length.)*

Latin:

*(v. 19. Ἐπὶ τοὺς χόρτουςdiscumbere. Probat hinc DoLaur. Ramirez de Prato, Iudaeam foeniferacem fuisse. Ac confert cum praesenti loco parall. Marc. 6, 39. item Ioseph. l. 7. B. I. c. 5. & 7. Idem consuetudinem gestandi foenum inter Iudaeos receptam eò refert, quòd pignus fuerit genti Iudaicae, ut memoriam refricarent Edicti Pharaonis, quo cautum fuit, ad conficiendos lateres ipsos debere paleas colligere, foenum ac stipulas. Exod. 5, 7.)*

*( Ἀναβλέψας εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν. Rogavit Christus ut homo, & quidem in statu exinanitionis, Deum Patrem coelestem quò miraculum hoc efficere posset. Vid. etiam Iohan. 11, 41.43. Caeterùm de Oratione Domini peculiari capite, videl. XXIV. libri III. de Orthod. Fide agit Damascenus, in quem locum-deatur omninò commentarius Iodoci Clichtovei Neopor--en--. add. quoq; B. D. Chemn. Harm. Ev. p. 324.)*

*( καὶ εὐλόλὸγησε. Quot vicibus Salvator εὐλογία in Sc. legatur usus, ostendit B. Par. L. de S. Coenâ §. 145. Cur Christus verò εὐλογίᾳ fuerit usus, docet Idem §. 143. De benedictionevid. 1. Sam. 9, 13.Matth. 26, 30. Tertullianus de sui seculi Christianis: Non priùs discumbitur, quàm oratio ad Deum praegustetur, & aequè oratio convivium dirimit. Conf. B. D. Franz. de Interp. S. S. Orac. 119. seqq. ubi totam hanc Historiam prolixè exponit.)*

## 14:20
*(v. 20. Τὸ περεσθεῦον τῶν κλασμάτων. The Blessed D. Franz. warns in on the Interpretation of Holy Scripture that κλάσματα, is one thing, concerning which here and below c. 15, 37, and ψιχία, is another, concerning which c. 15, 27. and Luc. 16, 21. he says these are little scrapings and little rubbings; those are fragments almost such as guests have on the tables upon the platters, or such as are accustomed to be distributed to beggars.)*

*( Twelve baskets full. A basket was a vessel woven from osiers, and especially in use among the Jews, as Ramirez shows from Juvenal Satyr. 3, 13. Satyr. 6, 542. and Martial l. 5. Epigr. 17. in Pentecont. c. 40. p. 304.)*

Latin:

*(v. 20. Τὸ περεσθεῦον τῶν κλασμάτων. Monet B. D. Franz. in de Interp. Sc. S. aliud esse κλάσματα, de quibus hîc & infrà c. 15, 37. aliud ψιχία, de quibus c. 15, 27. ac Luc. 16, 21. haec dicit esse abstersiunculas ac defri catiunculas; illa frusta propemodum talia, qualia in mensis convivae super orbes habent, vel qualia mendicis distribui solent.)*

*( Duodecim cophinus plenos. Cophinus vas erat viminibus contextum, maxime-ue in usu apud Iudaeos, uti ex Iuvenali Satyr. 3, 13. Satyr. 6, 542. ac Martiali l. 5. Epigr. 17. ostendit Ramirez in Pentecont. c. 40. p. 304.)*

## 14:22
v. 22. Καὶ εὐθέως etc. Matthew here signifies that Christ commanded his disciples to cross over, before he was in the boat. But Luke and Mark indicate that he commanded this to them when he was already in the boat. Response: These words let us cross over were spoken by the Lord twice and perhaps even three times. First, further from the boat, when he was still in the city, as Matthew has it. Secondly, when he had already approached the sea. Thirdly, when he had boarded the boat with his disciples, as Luke reports.

Ἠνάγκασεν. He compelled them, both because they were torn away from his side with difficulty, and because they hesitated to entrust themselves to the sea at night without his presence.

Ἐις τὸ πέραν. Mark expresses the place to which Christ ordered the disciples to go before him, namely the city of Bethsaida. From which it is understood how τὸ πέραν ought to be taken here. For it does not signify that which is above c. 8, 28; for there it is understood concerning the other bank of the lake of Gennesaret, but here indeed it is not to be taken concerning the other bank, but concerning the same, since the desert and Bethsaida and Capernaum are situated on the same side. Casaub. in the notes. Τὸ πέραν therefore here is τὸ πρόσιο. Thus the Hebrew עבר signifies sometimes on this side, sometimes across, nor can the meaning be established unless the place of the speaker or the hearer is considered. *(Compare also Glass. Gr. S. p. 542. where he also notes , similarly the word πέραν to be received Mark 10:1.John 1:28.)*

Latin:

v. 22. Καὶ εὐθέως &c. Matthaeus hîc significat, Christum praecepisse discipulis suis transfretare, antequam esset in navi. Sed Lucas & Marcus indicant, id eum praecepisse illis, cùm iam esset in navi. Resp. Bis & fortè etiam ter dicta sunt haec verba à Domino transfretemus. Primò longiùs à navi, cum adhuc in civitate esset, ut habet Matthaeus. Secundò cùm iam ad mare accessisset. Tertiò cùm navim cum suis discipulis conscendisset, referente Lucâ.

Ἠνάγκασεν.Compulit eos, tùm quia aegrè ab ipsius latere avellebantur, tum quia noctu sine ipsius praesentiâ mari sese credere dubitabant.

Ἐις τὸ πέραν. Marcus exprimit locum, quo Christus iussit discipulos sibi praeire, nempe Bethsaidam urbem. Ex quo intelligitur, quomodo τὸ πέραν hîc accipi debeat. Non enim id significat, quod suprà c. 8, 28. ibi enim de altera lacûs Genesare-ci ripâ intelligitur, hîc verò non de alterâ ripâ, sed de eadem est accipiendum, cùm eremus & Beth saida atq; Capornaum ad idem latus sint sitae. Casaub. in notis. Τὸ πέραν igitur hîc est τὸ πρόσιο. Sic Ebraeum עבר significat interdum cis, interdum trans, nec nisi considerato dicentis aut audiendis loco constitui significatio potest. *(Conf. quoque Glass. Gr. S. p. 542. ubi etiam notat, similiter vocem πέραν accipi Marc. 10, 1.Ioh. 1, 28.)*

## 14:23
*(v. 23. Κατ᾽ ἰδίαν. Laurentius Valla rightly corrects the Vulgate Interpreter here, in that he rendered these words alone, when they nevertheless mean apart, that is, into a secret place. Looking to which also, the Arab translates , which word the Latin Interpreter in the London edition renders alone, more correctly apart. Τὸ For the Arabs are accustomed to express alone by , just as in this very place a little later the Greek μόνος was rendered. The Syrian, however, and the Persian expressed both the phrase κατ᾽ ἰδίαν, and the word μόνος with the same expression.)*

Apart, that he might pray. Christ prayed apart on the mountain: Thus in prayers we ought to turn our mind away from all creatures and turn it to God alone. Conf. Ioh. 17, 1. Marc. 1, 35. The woman in the Apocalypse flees into the wilderness, when the red Dragon wished to devour her, c. 12, 7. Let us also flee in temptations into the silence and solitude of prayer. See B. Par. in Aphor. Pract. Theol. tit. Prayer.)* *(

*( He was there alone. See the notes at v. 15.)*

Latin:

*(v. 23. Κατ᾽ ἰδίαν. Rectè corrigit hîc Laur. Valla Vulgatum Interpretem, eò quòd verba haec reddiderit solus, cùm tamen sonent seorsum h. e. in secretum locum. Quo etiam respiciens Arabs vertit quam vocem Interpres Latinus in edit. Lond. reddit solus, rectiùs seorsum.Τὸsolus enim Arabes exprimere solent per quomodo hoc ipso loco paullo pòst Graecum μόνος redditum. Syrus tamen ac Persa eadē dictione tum phrasin κατ᾽ ἰδίαν, tum vocem μόνος expresserunt.)*

*( Seorsim ut oraret. Christus in monte seorsum orabat: Sic in precibus mentem ab omnibus creaturis avertere & ad solum Deum convertere debemus. Conf. Ioh. 17, 1.Marc. 1, 35. Mulier in Apocalypsi fugit in solitudinem, quando ruffus Draco voluit eam devorare, c. 12, 7. fugiamus & nos in tentaionibus in silentium & solitudinem orationis. Vid. B. Par. in Aphor. Pract. Theol. tit. Oratio.)*

*( Solus erat ibi. Vid. notata ad v. 15.)*

## 14:25
v. 25. The fourth watch of the night. The ancient Jews divided the night into three watches, the Romans into four; the former, having been subjugated, subsequently followed the custom of the latter. See Grot. in h. l.)* *(

Jesus went to them. For the Lord does not desert his own, but is present to them, seeing their calamities. Compare Exod. 3. 7. Ps. 34, 16. Ps. 56, 9. 94, 9. Ier. 32, 19. Es. 49, 15. Habac. 2, 3. *(

Walking upon the waters. The divine power of Christ is proven from this. For he restrained the natural gravity of the body, so that it would not sink. Hugo Grotius compares with this passage the saying Iob. 9, 8. and warns that Christ visibly fulfilled most of the things that were said about God in the books of the Prophets. Moreover, by the same virtue he also sustained Peter, so that he would not sink, v. 31. August. serm. 13. on the words of the Lord: He (Peter) was able to do what the Lord did (namely, to walk upon the waters) not in himself, but in the Lord. Compare also Exod. 14, 22. Ios. 3, 15. 2. Reg. 2, 8. Ps. 115, 3. Matth. 28, 18. )* *(

Latin:

*(v. 25. Quarta noctis vigilia. Iudaei Veteres noctem in ternas, Romani in quaternas vigilias dividebant, horum morem illi subiugati postmodum sequebantur. Vid. Grot. in h. l.)*

*( Abiit ad eos Iesus. non deserit quippe suos Dominus, sed praesto illis est, videns eorum calamitates. Confer Exod. 3. 7.Ps. 34, 16.Ps. 56, 9.94, 9.Ier. 32, 19.Es. 49, 15.Habac. 2, 3.

*( Ambulans super aquas. Sol-t hinc probari divina Christi potentia. Naturalē enim corporis gravitatem cohibuit, ne illud mergeretur. Hug. Grotius confert cum h. l. dictum Iob. 9, 8. monetq; quod pleraq; quae de Deo dicta in libb. Prophetarū, Christus visibiliter impleverit. Eadem autem virtute Petrum quoq; fustentavit, ne mergeretur, v. 31. August. serm. 13. de verbis Domini: Potuit (Petrus) quod Dominus (ambulare sc. super aquas) non inse, sed in Domino. Conf. etiam Exod. 14, 22.Ios. 3, 15.2. Reg. 2, 8.Ps. 115, 3.Matth. 28, 18.)*

## 14:28
(v. 28. Bid me come to you upon the waters. The Magdeburgenses prove from this that Peter was not immune from every sin, and therefore not the head of the Church. But that is evident from the fact that he attempted an arduous work, which he himself did not know whether he could perform. Bellarmine replies by denying that Peter was rash in that matter, since the miracles of GOD do not cooperate with our sins. Response: On the contrary, the opposite is evident from the deed of Moses, who, although he struck the rock twice out of diffidence, nevertheless water flowed forth from it miraculously.)

Latin:

*(v. 28. Iubeto me venire ab te super aquas. Probant hinc Magdaeburgenses, Petrum non fuisse ab omni peccato immunē, adeoque nec caput Ecclesiae. Constare verò illud inde, quòd tentarit opus arduum, quod num praestare posset, ipse nesciverit. Regerit Bell. negando, Petrum eâ in re fuisse temerarium, siquidem miracula DEI peccatis nostris non cooperentur. Resp. Imò verò contrarium patet ex facto Mosis, qui licet ex diffidentiâ petram iteratô percuteret, tamen aquâ miraculosè inde profluebat.)*

## 14:29
v. 29. Peter walked upon the waters. Christ confers upon Peter the power of walking upon the waters. 1. So that He might place his infirmity before his eyes, just as birds allow their chicks desiring to fly away to crawl a little from the nest, and soon draw them back. Chrysostom. 2. So that He might show that this miracle does not conflict with the truth of the body, for it is doubtful to no one that Peter had a true body. * Justin Martyr, Qq. & Resp. ad orth. page 363. The Lord did not walk upon the sea by a change of body into spirit, but by His divine power He rendered the sea, which could not be trodden by feet, suitable and passable for walking, not only for His own body, but also for Peter's. Similarly Jerome, Epistle to Pammachius: Peter walks upon the waters with a heavy and solid body. And not much differently Leontius in this place, and likewise Augustine, sermon 159 de tempore. It is evident, therefore, how little firmly the Marcionites, Valentinians, and Manichaeans strove to prove from the fact that Christ walked in a liquid and flowing element, that He did not have a true and solid body, but one only shadowed and feigned in appearance, namely, airy. Jerome refutes their error, among other things, from the fact that if this collection were firm, it would follow that Peter also had at least a feigned and empty body. Therefore, He who could sustain Peter's true body by His own divine power so that it would not be submerged, why could He not also have sustained His own body in that way? Nor is there need, however, that we should therefore establish that the waves were solidified or hardened, in the manner in which we see the sea constricted by northern frosts in the winter time. So that it must be established that the miracle did not happen in the body of Christ and Peter, the force of whose native weight the Lord restrained, but in the sea. Which seems so to Calvin, book 4, Inst. ch. 17, sect. 29: for it conflicts with v. 30, where it is said of Peter, that he began to sink. Rightly, therefore, the Jesuit Coton disapproves of that opinion of Calvin, though perhaps ignorant that the Scholastics themselves once embraced the same, from whose number John Major in this place establishes, that the miracle concerning Peter, walking upon the waters, was done in one of three ways, viz., that Christ by divine power held Peter so that he would not sink, or that He did not concur with the gravity of Peter's body so as to make him heavy, or that He did not concur with the water so that it would yield to his place. Which opinion of Major, Corn. à Lapide reports in such a way that he determines nothing. Just as also Tirinus, though the name of the creditor is suppressed. Furthermore, that seems of greater importance, that from that walking of Peter upon the waves of the sea, some Papists strive to prove his Primacy or Monarchy. See Bell. l. 1. d. P. R. c. 19. Coton l. 2. Instit. Cathol. p. 213. Conzen in this place p. 396. alleging for this matter the words of Bernard l. 2. de Consid. c. 8. But however much we may not unwillingly confess that Bernard in the said place writes less considerately by allegorizing, that very thing, that Peter did not arrive at Christ in one ship as the others did, (Bernard refers to the history John 21, 7. 8.) but walked upon the sea, was a sign of the singular Pontificality of Peter, through which he began to govern not one ship, as the others anyone, but the world itself. Yet this prejudices our opinion in nothing, since we know well that Bernard lived at a time when the feigned holiness of the Roman harlot had blinded many pious men. If, however, the Papists value those books of Bernard so highly, let them also lose other things which the religious Abbot excellently whispers there to the Roman Pontiff Eugenius, especially when in l. 2. Consid. p. 277. a. he writes: It is plain, lordship is forbidden to the Apostles. Therefore you, either dare to usurp for yourself both the apostolate if you are lording, or lordship if you are apostolic. You are clearly prohibited from either. If you wish to have both alike, you will lose both. (He deals especially with the pride of the R. P. in l. 4. p. 280. b.) likewise when in epistle 125 he writes concerning the Roman Pontiff Agapetus: That beast of the Apocalypse, to whom a mouth was given speaking blasphemies and to wage war with the saints, occupies the chair of Peter, like a lion prepared for prey. From which words, when B. Pareus in Confess. Cath. l. 2. spec. part. 1. p. 704. proved that the Roman Pope is the Antichrist to St. Bernard, the Jesuit Erbermannus exclaims in the Prooemium of the Bellarminian Compendium ( Nerves of bones inscribed with an ill-omened title. For what else are the nerves of Bellarmine of bones in the body, than Bellarmine flayed, i.e., scarcely clinging to nerves and bones any longer. Thus, indeed, is the Cardinal miserably torn apart by an ungrateful disciple, who nevertheless professes that after God he owes it to no one more than to him, that he is a Catholic-Roman, i.e., that he began προςέχειν Tit. 1, 14. This sycophancy is clear. The Jesuit proves it, because Bernard said these things about Peter son of Leo, whom the Romans had intruded for Innocent II. But did not B. Pareus himself already satisfy this exception in the cited place, which if the Jesuit had inspected, he would have discovered, I think, that B. Pareus is not a sycophant, but concluded rightly from Bernard. But on this matter another day, where, however, the Jesuit may have used that moderation of style in examining the arguments of B. P., which may be a source of admiration to not a few. With which he boasts that he has attacked the Titian Ostension. Which, however, the prooemium of the Vindications, hitherto scattered throughout the learned world, scarcely allows one to hope. But we must return to where we digressed. We grant that Bernard, as it happened to him to write in the midst of the darkness of the Papacy, around the year 1130 according to Bell. de script. Eccl. or 1140 according to Coster, attributes too much at times to the Roman see: but it is not yet proven from that, that the primacy of Peter can be established from this place. The true reason why Peter strove for Christ through the sea without a ship is indicated by Chrysostom hom. 57. in Matth. and Cyril, l. 12. in John c. 63. who attribute it to Peter's fervor. For it is abundantly clear from Holy Scripture that he was himself πανταχοῶ as Chrysostom speaks. Impatient of delay, therefore, he hastened to jump down, not waiting until he should come with the others. Which haste, however, did not always turn out well for him, just as Christ also permitted here, that he began to sink, so that he might recognize the of his own faith. which reason

Corn. à Lap. assigns here, who himself also observes from Theophylact in this place, That Peter in the passion of Christ, struck by the strong wind of the temptation of the Jews, fell, denied Christ, of which this temptation was a type, and as it were a preamble signification. But Cornelius does not dare to prove the primacy of Peter from the present walking upon the waves, just as neither do other Jesuits, such as Titinus, Maldonatus, etc. Indeed, Maldonatus, Comment. on ch. 21 of John (which passage Bellarmine and Coton join with the present one, and from both attempt to establish the primacy of Peter), p. 1015, after he had expounded the literal sense, adds: This is the sense, nor do I think there is anything mystical here besides. The Jesuit Alf. Salmero wisely says in this place, vol. 6, tr. 28, p. 184: He sought to walk upon the waters, not because he was prior in dignity, because to walk upon the sea is not an act of the Pontificate. Which very thing perhaps other Jesuits also weighing, such as Becanus in his Manual, page 69, where he recounts thirteen prerogatives of Peter, then in the Compendium of the Manual, p. 107, where he adds yet another, Costerus likewise in his Enchir. Controv., and others, otherwise seeking out the prerogatives of Peter with the greatest zeal, pass over this passage, not wishing to look for a knot in a bulrush. But let fair judges of things consider whether an equal, if not greater, power was given by Christ to the remaining Apostles, and here to Peter. See Luc. 10, 19.2. Cor. 12, 4.

Latin:

v. 29. Petrus ambulabat super aquas. Christus Petro confert potestatem ambulandi super aquas. 1. ut infirmitatem suam ipsi ob oculos ponat, quemadmodum volucres pullos suos avolare cupientes è nido paulùm prorepere sinunt, mox v. eosdem retrahunt. Chrysost. 2. ut ostendat, miraculum hoc non pugnare cum veritate corporis, neque enim ulli dubium, quin Petrus habuerit verum corpus. * Iustinus Martyr, Qq. & Resp. ad orth. pag. 363. Non mutatione corporis in spiritum Dominus super mari deambulavit, verùm divinâ potentiâ suâ mare, quod pedibus calcari nequiret, ad in ambulandum commodum & pervium reddidit, non suo ipsius tantùm corpori, sed & Petri. Similiter Hieronymus Epist ad Pammachium: Petrus super aquas ambulat, gravi & solido corpore. Nec multò aliter Leontius in h. l. itemque Augustinus serm. 159. de tempore. Constat igitur, quàm parùm firmiter Marcionitae, Valentiniani ac Manichaei ex eo, quòd Christus liquido in elemento & fluenti inambulavit, evincere sategerint, nō habuisse eum corpus verum ac solidum, sed in speciem tantùm adumbratum & fictum, sc. aëreum. Quorum errorem inter alia redarguit Hieronymus ex eo, quòd si collectio isthaec esset firma, sequatur, etiam Petrum habuisse saltem fictum & inane corpus. Qui igitur Petri verum corpus divinâ suâ potentia potuit sustentare ne submeregeretur, cur non & proprium suum corpus potuisset ita sustentare. Nec opus tamen, ut proptereà statuamus, undas fuisse solidatas vel induratas, ad eum modum? quo tempore hyberno frigoribus Aquilonaribus mare constringi videmus. Ut ita miraculum non in Christi ac Petri corpore, cuius nativi ponderis vim Dominus cohibuit, sed in mari contigisse statuendum sit. Quod Calvino l. 4. Inst. c. 17. sect. 29. videtur: repugnat enim v. 30. ubi dicitur de Petro, quod coeperit demergi. Rectè proinde Iesuita Cotonus sententiā istam Calvini improbat, ignorans tamē fortè, quod eandem amplexi quoque Scholastici quondam fuerint, è quorum numero Ioh. Maior in h. l. statuit, quòd miraculum circa Petrum, super aquas ambulantem, factum sit modo uno è tribus, sc. quòd Christus divinâ vi Petrum ne meregeretur, detineret, aut quòd non concurrerit cum gravitate corporis Petri, ut eum gravidaret, aut quòd non concurrerit cum aquâ ut loco cederet. Quam sententiam Maioiis Corn. à Lapide ita refert, ut nihil determinet. Quemadmodum & Tirinus, suppresso tamen creditoris nomine. Coeterùm id maioris videtur momenti, quòd ex illPetri super undas maris obambulatione, eiusdem Primatum s. Monarchiam evincere nonnulli Pontificii satagunt. Vid. Bell. l. 1. d. P. R. c. 19. Cotonus l. 2. Instit. Cathol. p. 213. Conzen in h. l. p. 396. allegantes in hanc rem verba Bernhardi l. 2. de Consid. c. 8. Verùm ut ut haut inviti fateamur, Bernhardum d. l. minùs consideratè allegorizando scribere, illud ipsum, quòd Petrus nō unâ navi ut coeteri ad Christum pervenerit, (respicit Bernh. ad historiam Ioh. 21, 7. 8.) sed ambularit super mari, fuisse signum singularis Pontificii Petri, per quod non navem unam, ut coeteri quisuam, sed seculum ipsum coeperit gubernandum. Nihil tamen praeiudicat hoc nostrae sententiae, probè quippe scientes, quòd Bernhardus eo vixerit tempore, quo Romanae meretricis ficta sanctitas multos pios viros excoecaverat. Si tamen tanti istos Bernhardi libros aestimant Pontificii, perperdant quoq; & alia, quae egregiè ibi Pontifici Romano Eugenio insusurrat religiosus Abbas, cumprimis quando l. 2. Consid. p. 277. a. scribit: Planum est, Apostolis interdicitur Dominatus. Iergo tu, & tibi usurpare aude aut dominans apostolatum, aut apostolicus dominatum. Planè ab altero prohiberis. Si utrumsimiliter habere voles, perdes utrum-. (De fastu cumprimis P. R. agit l. 4. p. 280. b.) item quando epist. 125. de Pontifice Romano Agapeto scribit: Be--ia illa de Apocalypsi, cui datum est os loquens blasphemias & bellum gerere cum sanctis, cathedram Petri occupat, tanquam leo paratus ad praedam. Equibus verbis cùm B. Par. Confess. Cath. l. 2. spec. part. 1. p. 704. probarit, Papam Rom. S. Bernhardo esse Anti Christum, exclamat Iesuita Erbermannus in Prooemio Compendii Bellarminiani ( Nervi absmole infausto omine inscripti. Quid enim nervi Bellarmini absmole corporeâ aliud, quàm Bellarminus excoriatus h. e. vix nervis & ossibus ampliùs haerens. Ita nempe miserè ab ingrato discipulo, qui tamen post Deum nemini magis ac illi debere se profitetur, quòd Catholico-Romanus sit, h. e. quod coeperit προςέχεινTit. 1, 14. dilaceratur Cardinalis.) Perspicua est haec Sycophantia. Probat Iesuita, quia haec Bernhardus dixerit de Petro Leonis filio, quem Romani pro Innocentio II. intruserant. Annon verò exceptioni huic iamtum satisfecit ipse B. Parens loco citato, quem si inspexisset Iesuita, deprehendisset, puto, non esse Sycophantam B. Parentem, sed rectè conclusisse ex Bernhardo. Ast hac de re alio die, ubi tamen eam styli moderationem Iesuita in examinandis B. P. arguementis adhibuerit, quae non paucis sit admirationi. Quali se Ostensionem Titianam aggressum esse gloriatur. Id quod tamen vix sperare sinit Vindiciarum prooemium, per orbem litteratum hactenus sparsum. Sed unde digressi sumus, redeamus oportet. Largimur, Bernhardum, utpote cui contigit, in mediis Papatûs tenebris, circa Annum scil. 1130. iuxta Bell. de script. Eccl. vel 1140. iuxta Costerum, scribere, nimium aliquando tribuere sedi Romanae: sed nondum inde evictum, quòd primatus Petri ex h. l. stabiliri possit. Veram rationem cur Petrus per mare absque navigio ad Christum contenderit indicant Chrysostomus hom. 57. in Matth. ac Cyrillus, l. 12. in Ioh. c. 63. qui Petri fervori id tribuunt. Constat quippe abunde è Script. S. quòd fuerit ipse πανταχοῶ ut loquitur Chrysostomus. Morae igitur impatiens occupavit desilire, non expectans, dum veniret cum aliis. Quae tamen festinatio non benè semper ei cessit, sicuti etiam Christus hîc permisit, ut coeperit demergere, quò suam suaefidei infirmitatem agnosceret. quam rationem

Corn. à Lap. hîc adsignat, qui ipse etiā ex Theophylacto h. l. observat, quòd Petrus in passione Christi valido pulsatus tentationis Iudaeorum vento ceciderit, negaveritChristum, cuius haec tentatio fuerit typus, & quasi praeambula significatio. Non audet verò Corneli-è praesenti Petri ambulatione super undis, eiusdem primatum probare, quemadmodum nec alii Iesuitae, uti Titinus, Maldonatus &c. Imò Maldonatus Comment. in cap. 21. Ioh. (quem locum Bellarminus ac Cotonus cum praesenti coniungunt, & ex utroque primatum Petri stabilire conantur.) p. 1015. postquam litteralem sensum exposuisset, subiungit: Hic sensus, nec quicquam praeterea mysticum hîc esse arbitror. Cordatè Iesuita Alf. Salmero in h. l. t. 6. tr. 28. p. 184. Petiit ambulare super aquas, non quòd prior esset dignitate, quia ambulare super mare non est actus Pontificatûs. Quod ipsum etiam fortè perpendentes alii Iesuitae, uti Becanus in Manuali pag. 69. ubi trecedim Petri praerogativas recenset, tum in Manualis Compendio p. 107. ubi adhuc aliam super addit, Costerus item in Enchir. Controv. ac alii, summo studio alioqui praerogativas Petri conquirentes, locum hunc praetern vigant, nolentes nodum in scirpo quaerere. Cogitent verò aequi rerum Iudices, annon aequalis, si non maior potestas reliquis Apostolis à Christo facta, ac hîc Petro. Vid. Luc. 10, 19.2. Cor. 12, 4.)*

## 14:30
(v. 30. But seeing the strong wind etc. The word seeing in this place has the meaning of perceiving, feeling thoroughly. Just as also sight, being the noblest of all the senses, is accustomed to be adapted to the objects of the remaining senses, as Isidore notes, Orig. l. 2. c. 1, and Thomas Gataker confirms with many examples in his De Stylo N. Test. c. 38.)

Latin:

*(v. 30. Videns autem ventum validum &c. Videndi verbum h. l. percipiendi, persentiscendi significationem habet. Sicuti etiam visus, utpote sensuum omnium nobilissimus, reliquorum sensuum obiectis adaptari solet, notante Isidoro Orig. l. 2. c. 1. multisque exemplis confirmat Thomas Gatekerus in destylo N. Test. c. 38.)*

## 14:31
v. 31. Διςάζειν is οἱονεὶ to have as it were two stations in the mind, to waver and limp with an uncertain mind.

Latin:

v. 31. Διςάζειν est οἱονεὶ duas quasi stationes habere in mente, incertá mente vacillare & claudicare.

## 14:32
v. 32. Ἐκόπασεν ἡ ἄνεμος. κοπάζειν properly signifies to rest from anger. By metaphor it is transferred to inanimate things. Num. 11, 2. it is said of the fire sent divinely into the camp ὐκόπασε τὸ πῦρ Gen. 8, 1. of the waters of the flood, καὶ ἐπήγαγον Esth. 2, 1. καὶ μετὰ

τού τους Corresponds to the Hebrew שבך.

Latin:

v. 32. Ἐκόπασεν ἡ ἄνεμος. κοπάζειν propriè significat conquiescere ab ira. per metaphoram transfertur ad res inanimatas. Num. 11, 2. de igne divinitus in castra immisso dicitur ὐκόπασε τὸ πῦρGen. 8, 1. de aquis diluvii, καὶ ἐπήγαγονEsth. 2, 1.καὶ μετὰ

τού τους Respondet Ebr. שבך.

## 14:33
(v. 33. Ἀληθῶς θεοῦς εἶ. See below c. 27, 43. & 54. The rule of the Photinians is convicted of falsity from these examples, that the name θεὸς placed in the position of a predicate and lacking an article does not denote God the creator of all things. What Crellius objects, the learned Dr. Calovius has solidly discussed in Theol. Nat & Revel. p. 475. seqq. It is evident furthermore from this confession of the disciples, that Bellarmine, in order to prove the primacy of Peter from Matth. 16, falsely writes in book I. de P. R. cap. 19. § Quarta praerog. that Peter, first of all the Apostles, was taught by God to know the highest mysteries of our faith, namely the distinction of persons in GOD, and the incarnation. He indeed responds to this passage, that the Apostles here called Christ the Son of GOD in that way in which all saints are called Sons of GOD. But the Doctors of the primitive Church teach the contrary more correctly, from whose number Jerome on this passage, To one, writes, a sign having been rendered by the tranquility of the sea, which after excessive storms sometimes happens even by chance, the sailors and passengers truly confess the Son of GOD: and does Arius preach a creature in the Church? Similarly Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria, book 14. in Ioh. c. 29. The same in book 2. Dial. de Trin. teaches that the divinity of Christ is truly proven from this passage. Chrysostom also in this passage warns that the Apostles, from the miracles which they had seen, namely walking upon the waters, and the calmed tempest, had been led into faith, and said, Thou art the Son of GOD. The footsteps of whom also Nicolaus de Lyra, having been made a Christian from a Jew, faithfully followed, who thus on this passage It is said truly not metaphorically, nor by adoption as the saints: but properly and of the same nature. Dionysius also from Rickel, called the Carthusian, expressly writes, that the doctors commonly affirm, that they adored (the disciples and nature on this passage) him (Christ) with the adoration of latria as the natural son of God, true God. The Carthusian indeed departs from this common opinion of the Doctors, moved by this, that if they had been established in this faith, they would not have doubted so easily afterwards, as is revealed in the following chapter, and especially at the time of the passion, when the words of the believers seemed to them like ravings. But if this doubt were a firm argument, that the disciples had not professed and adored Christ here as the natural Son of GOD, the same which must be said of Peter, as to whom no less than to the remaining Apostles the words of the women, testifying about the resurrection of Christ, seemed like ravings. Luke 24, 11. The Jesuit Maldonatus seems to refute the opinion of Cardinal Bellarmine ex professo; when he comments thus on the words: You are truly the Son of GOD, Not by adoption, but by nature they confess him not as a just man, but as the true God. Namely in the same way that the Pharisees denied that he was the Son of GOD, taking it for the same, of GOD that he is God, John. 10, 33. c. 19, 7. Matt. 27, 4. &c. and it is concluded Thus this passage is valid against the Arians. Nor do the remaining Jesuits dissent; Adam Conzen likewise writes explicitly in this place to the question How they worshipped. They worshipped, as the true & natural son of GOD: for the Jews perceived that he said such a thing, and that he was said to be such, John. 10, 33. c. 19, 7. Corn. à Lapide mentions that Cardinal Cajetan and the Bishop of Ghent establish the opinion that the rude crowd of sailors did not recognize the mystery of the Trinity, and therefore they called Jesus the Son of GOD, not but through the excellence of virtue and dignity. But he adds: But we see that the sailors understood it thus, certainly the Apostles, who were passengers in the ship who had lived with Christ for a long time, knew from so many of his sermons & that he was the natural & only-begotten Son of GOD, and confirmed in that faith by this new miracle of the calmed tempest they exclaimed: You are truly the Son of GOD, namely by nature he alleges the same Abulensis for this exposition. Since therefore the Apostles recognized and worshipped Christ as the true and natural Son of GOD, by the admission of the Jesuits themselves—Maldonatus, Conzen, Corn. à Lapide &c.—it is clear that the assertion of Bellarmine is false, that Peter, first of all the Apostles, taught by GOD, recognized the distinction of persons in GOD. But if this assertion is false, the foundation is also slippery, which the Cardinal places for the primacy of Peter and therefore of and the common people of the Papists rely upon it. But indeed Bellarmine urges in the said place that the Fathers Hilary, Athanasius, Chrysostom, Cyril, Augustine and Leo teach that Peter first recognized that mystery. Resp. Setting aside Hilary, who perhaps but without support, and to whom we therefore deservedly oppose the rest, it is denied whether it be Athanasius, or Chrysostom, or Cyril or Augustine, if they speak of the knowledge itself. But rather from an inspection of the places alleged by it is manifest that they are dealing with the act of that confession at that time, when Christ Matt. 16. asked whom the Apostles said he was, Peter anticipated the others by answering. From that however it follows that he was the first of all the Apostles to recognize that mystery

## 14:36
*(v. 36. They might touch the hem. See Anal. on c. 9, 20.)*

This chapter comprises: I. The rejection of human commandments . from v. 1 to 9. II. The instruction of the crowds and the disciples concerning the source of sins. v. 10--20. III. The deliverance of the daughter of the Canaanite woman from a demon v. 22--28. and the healing of many sick people v. 30--31. IV. The miraculous feeding of four thousand men. v. 32 to the end.

Filiae mulieris Cananaeae à Daemonio liberationem v. 22--28. multorumque aegrotorum sanationem v. 30--31. IV. Miraculosam quater mille virorum cibationem. v. 32. ad fin.

Thus the Ethiopian also supplied long ago, translating in this place And then came those who had come to him from Jerusalem scribes &c. ## 15:2
(v. 2. παράδοσιν τῶν πρεσβυτέρων. By πρεσβυτέρους in this place are understood the same ones whom the Savior elsewhere calls ἀρχαίους. Furthermore, the Pharisees δευτερώσεις i.e. παραδοσεις referred those to Moses himself and the Prophets, as Josephus mentions 1. 18. A. I. c. 18. Jerome on the holy faith Book 2. p. 96. Galat. 1. 1. on the Arcane Catholic truth c. 2. and especially at length Grotius in this place. But the name παραδόσεω is general and therefore is also used for Christian doctrine, as is evident from 1. Cor. 11, 2. 23. c. 15, 2. and in the same writing, 2. Thess. 2, 15. concerning which passage let the Blessed Pareus be consulted in Exeg. L. de Scr. S. §. 404. But that unwritten law of the Pharisees was also called ἀκοὴ Heb. שמעתה likewise διαδοχὴ Heb. קבלה. Worthy of note is the observation of Cameron in Myroth. on this place that these unwritten traditions of the Pharisees are never in the N. T. simply or absolutely traditions, let them be called, but let them always be noted with some epithet, as when they are called Traditions of the elders, human traditions, your traditions, as in this place Col. 2, 22. but never simply and absolutely Traditions; indeed, if ever the word Tradition is placed simply, let it be taken in a good sense without any addition. For the word of GOD itself is a tradition. Consult more things pertinent to this in Cameron, loc. cit., Pelargus, Questions and Answers on Matthew, p. 172.

CHAPTER XV. SUMMARY AND DISPOSITION.

Ὅταμ ἄρτονἐσθίωσι. Hence it appears that this tradition required washing not only before lunch and dinner, but also while eating. Compare Mark 7, 3. (how much that transgression of the elders concerning the washing of hands was esteemed is evident from that saying of the Rabbis: To eat bread with unwashed hands is the same as to lie with a harlot. But it is asked whether the Apostles were therefore rebuked by the Pharisees because they did not wash before food, or because they did not repeat the washing while eating. The former pleases Abulensis, Lyranus, Carthusianus, Conzenius. But the latter opinion seems more probable, which Caietanus, Iansenius, and others also embrace. For it is not to be thought that the Apostles of Christ did not wash their hands at all. But the Pharisees rebuked them because they did not observe so accurately the manner of washing hands handed down by the Elders of the Jews and superstitiously forced upon them by the Pharisees. See Analecta on Mark 7, 3 and Luke 11, 38. Otherwise it is known that the Gentiles also washed their hands before the table, and that both for cleanliness and for health. See Virgil, Aeneid 1 v. 705, Guid. Panciroll. Rerum Memor. t. 51 p. 501, which custom is still observed among Christians, and is not at all rebuked by the Savior. That also is evident from Clement, book 8, Constitutions 38, and Tertullian, On Prayer, ch. 11, that in the primitive Church those about to pray washed their hands first. Which custom, however, can in no way be proven from 1 Tim. 2, 8., as indeed Corn. à Lap. on v. 19. of the present chapter persuades himself, reading there: washing pure hands: for in the Greek text it is ἐπαίροντες lifting up, raising. as the Oriental Interpreters also have it, the Syrian, Arabic, Ethiopian. And thus Cornelius himself reads in his Commentary on the Epistles of Paul. But by pure hands the Apostle does not understand corporally cleansed ones, but ones alien from anger, disputation, avarice, slaughter, and other vices. Just as even Corn. notes. όσίους to note holy. And even paganism itself required such things, as Barnabas Brissonius teaches at length in De Formulis et Sollemnibus Populi Romani, book 1, page 4, and following.

## 15:3
v 3. Transgress ye &c. αὐτέγκλημα, with the same words repeated, having been instituted.

Because of your traditions. Epiphanius records that among the Jews four authors of traditions are celebrated: 1. Moses himself, 2. Rabbi Akiba, 3. Addam or Judah, 4. the Asmonean posterity. Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 26: He does not say that the law given through Moses is the precepts of men, but the traditions of the elders themselves, which they had invented, by which they frustrated the law of God, and on account of this they were not subject to His word. Benedict Arias Montanus notes in this place that shortly before the age of Christ, in the times of Herod, there were Scribes by whom traditions were concocted, with this intention, that the Law might be kept more religiously by their observance, especially in those kinds of things which concerned the ceremonial aspect. Those traditions were afterwards written into the form of a book, and contained the responses and opinions of the Scribes, consisting of an ingenious questioning of the sacred precepts in that category, yet human, that is, for the most part vain and superstitious. And that he had diligently read this book found at Venice. *(Compare Fagius on the Chapters of the Fathers, immediately following, Buxtorf's Rabbinical and Talmudic Lexicon, and Schindler's Pentaglot Lexicon under the word קבל.. Cornelius à Lapide, so that he may provide a cloak for Popish traditions, deceives the reader, saying that there were also among the Jews certain traditions far different from the traditions of the Pharisees, which the Savior here reproves, and which were therefore entirely to be observed. And he says that in their number are the books of Moses, Isaiah, &c., are canonical, that God is one in essence but three in persons, that infants contract original sin, &c. But it must be noted that all those things which Cornelius sells as unwritten traditions are by no means such, since they are proposed in Holy Scripture itself, such as that God is one in essence and three in persons, &c. Although these κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν are not read in Holy Scripture, it is sufficient for us, however, that they can be proven from it by firm and immovable consequence. And not from the New Testament alone, which the Papists do everywhere, but also from the Old Testament.

as Cardinal Bellarmine by no means denies in book 2 of De Christo, chapter 6. And Cornelius à Lapide himself everywhere constructs the mystery of the Trinity from the Old Testament. See his commentary on the same in Gen. 1, 1. where he writes explicitly; Elohim in the plural hints at the plurality of persons in God, just as the unity of essence in God is hinted at by the singular verb ברא, as Lyranus, Burgensis, Galatinus, Eugubinus, Catharinus, the Master, and the Scholastics teach against Caietanus & Abulensis l. 2. Sent. Dist. 1. Compare the same Comin c. 1, 26. c. 18, 2. Gen. and in c. 3, 6. acc. 6, 5. Exodus and elsewhere passim. But as for what concerns the traditions of the Papists, since they are partly frivolous, partly superstitious, they can by no means prove κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν, nor by a firm consequence from Holy Scripture, and thus there is a huge difference between those and what Cornelius wishes to be held as traditions in the O.T. Furthermore, as regards the question about the Canonical books, whence indeed it is established whether the books of Moses etc. are Canonical, it must be observed there that it is one thing to ask whether the books of Moses are Canonical books, another whether they were written by Moses. The latter pertains to historical knowledge, the former to saving faith. Which certainly does not depend at all, either solely or primarily, upon the tradition of the testimony of the Church, which holds the books of Moses and the Prophets as Canonical books, but rather primarily upon the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit. While the Church adds its own testimony to His testimony, it does not forge a new article of faith, but at least as a ministerial cause it testifies concerning that of which the Holy Spirit Himself, speaking in those canonical books, testifies. But the Papists will by no means be able to show such testimony of the Holy Spirit concerning their own traditions, which they foist upon the Church. The same Corn. à Lap. at v. 6. distinguishes that some traditions are divine, some Ecclesiastical, some civil. But concerning the Ecclesiastical ones he adds, that they are not so much human as divine, because the Church is governed by the Holy Spirit. But he ought to have added, if it has remained in the words of Christ and has heard the voice of Christ. For if the Church strives to foist superstitious, impious, and contrary-to-the-word-of-God traditions under the guise of divine worship, it is by no means governed in that by the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

v 3. Transgredimini &c. αὐτέγκλημα, repetitis iisdem vocibus institutam.

Propter traditiones vestras. Epiphanius memorat, quòd apud Iudaeos celebrentur quatuor autores traditionum. 1. ipse Moses 2. R. Akiba 3. Addam sive Iuda. 4. posteritas Asamonaea. Iren lib. 4 c. 26. Non per Mosen datam legem dicit praecepta hominum, sed traditiones Presbyterorum ipsorum, quas finxerant, qu. is vindicantes frustrabantur legem DEI, & propter hoc nec verbo eius subiecti sunt. Bened Arias Montanus h l. annotat, paullò ante Christi aetatem, Herodum temporibus suisse Scribas, à quibus conciunatae sint Traditiones, hoc consilio, ut ex earum observatione Lex religiosiùs custodiretur, maximè in iis, quae ceremonialem rationem spectabant, generibus. Traditiones illas in libri formam posteà fuisse conscriptas, continuisseq; Responsa & sententias Scribarum ingeniosa, sacrorum in eo genere praeceptorum interrogatione constantes, humanas tamen h. e. in plerisque vanas & superstitiosas. Atque hunc librum Venetiis repertum se diligenter legisse. *(Conf Fagium ad Cap. Patrum, statim mitio, Buxtorff. Lexic Rabb. Talmud. ac Schindl. Lex Pentagl. voce קבל. Cornelius à Lapide quò Papisticis traditionibus mantellū conciliet, lectori fucum facit, fuisse quoque apud Iudaeos traditiones quasdam longè diversas à traditionibus Pharisaeorum, quas Salvator hîc reprehendit, adcoque omninò observandas. Inque earum numero esse dicit, libros Mosis, Isaiae &c. esse canonicos, Deum esse unum in essentia, sed trinum in personis, parvulos contrahere peccatum originale &c. Verùm notandum, quòd omnia ea, quae Cornelius pro traditionibus non-scriptis vendicat, minimè tales sint, siquidem in Scripturâ Sacrâ ipsâ proponuntur, ut Deum esse unum in essentiâ & trinùm in personis &c. Licet verò ista κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν in Sc. S. non legantur, sufficit tamen nobis, quòd per firmam immotamque consequentiam inde probari posint. Nec ex N. solùm Tesamento, quod passim factitant Pontificii verùm etiam ex V. T.

ceu minimè inficias it Card. Bell. lib. 2. de Christo c. 6. Imipse Corn. à Lapide Trinitatis mysterium è V. T. passim adstruit. Vid. Comm eiusd. in Gen. 1, 1. ubi disertè scribit; Elohim plurale innuit in Deo pluralitatem personarum, sicut unitas essentiae in Deainnuitur per verbum singulareברא,uti contra Caietanum & Abulèsem doce-t Lyranus, Burgensis, Galatinus, Eugubinus, Catharinus. Magister & Scholastici l. 2. Sent. Dist. 1. Confer. idem Comin c. 1, 26. c. 18, 2. Gen. it. in c. 3, 6. acc. 6, 5. Exodi & alibi passim. Quod verò Pontificiorum concernit traditiones, cùm partim frivolae, partim superstitiosae sint, minimè nec κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν, nec perfirmam consequentiā ex Sc. S. probare possunt, adeoq; inter illas ac ea, quae Cornelius pro traditionibus in V. T. receptis haberi vult, ingens discrimen est. Quod porrò spectat quaestionē de libris Canonicis, unde nempe constet, an libri Mosis &c. sint Canonici, ibi observandum, quòd aliud sit quaerere, an libri Mosis sint libri Canonici, aliud, an sint à Mose scripti. Hoc spectat ad cognitionem Historicam, illud ad fidem salvificam. Quae sane minimè vel solitariè vel praecipuè dependet à traditione testificatione Ecclesiae, pro libb. Canonicis libros Mosis ac Prophetarum habentis, sed potiùs cumprimis ab interno Sp. S. testimonio. Cuius testimonio dùm suum addit Ecclesia, non novum fidei articulum cudit, sed saltem ut causa ministerialis testatur de eo, quo de ipse Sp. S. in libris illis canonicis loquens testatur. Tale verò Sp. S. testimonium hautquaquam de suis traditionibus, quas Ecclesiae obtrudunt, Pontificii ostendere poterunt. Idem Corn. à Lap. ad v. 6. distingvit, quod quaedam traditiones sint divinae, quaedam Ecclesiasticae, quaedam civiles. De Ecclesiasticis verò addit, quòd non tam humanae sint, quàm divinae, quiae Ecclesia regatur Sp. Sancto. Verùm debuisset addere, si permanserit in verbis Christi ac vocem Christi audiverit. Quod si enim Ecclesia traditiones superstitiosas, impias ac verbo DEI contratias sub specie cultûs livini obtrudere satagit, hautquaquam regitur in eo à Spiritu Sancto.)*

## 15:4
v. 4. Honor your father &c. Hieron. in ep. ad Gerontiam In the Gospel the Lord discusses the commandment of the law, in which it is said: Honor your father and your mother, not in the sound of words, by which one might frustrate the parents with empty flattery, but that it ought to be understood in the providing of the necessities of life. (Gernella has the same at this place Honor, he writes, in the Scriptures is felt not so much in the offering of greetings, as in alms and the offering of gifts. Conf. & Chrys. at this place and also Seldenus l. 7. de Iure nat. & gent. c. 2. These things are consistent with the dogmas of some of the Rabbis themselves. For thus R. Salomo Levit. 10, 3. What is the honor which a son ought to show to his father and mother? He gives them food and drink he shoes them, leads them in, and leads them out. Thus in the book Chaskuni or the Commentary of R. Chiskia on the Pentateuch these things are found: We read, honor God with your wealth, &, honor father and mother, God is to be honored if you have it; parents, whether you have it or not: for if you have nothing, you ought to beg door-to-door for them. I. Drusius brings forward both passages in lib. 1. Praeterit. p. 35. and notes that twins are also held in the book Musar c. 5. Moreover, the very word to honor is sometimes taken in Holy Scripture for to be relieved, to be affected by benefits. This is clearly evident from Num. 22, 7. coll. with v. 18. & 38. and that it is also taken by Paul 1. Tim 5, 8 & 17. is noted by Camero in Myroth at this place, Cosinas, Magalianus Oper. Hierarch. l. 1. p. 567. Grotius at this place, and others. Furthermore, Corn. à Lapide conveniently warns at this place that the honor owed to parents comprises three things: Reverence, obedience, and beneficence. He adds, that the right and bond of piety, by which children are obligated to feed poor parents, is of the law of nature, to which therefore every vow, every offering, all bonds, introduced by divine or human law, ought to yield and be postponed. But if every vow and all bonds ought to yield to the piety owed to parents, it follows that it is not lawful for children, against the will of their parents, to vow religion or a monastic life, or if such a vow has been made, that parents can pronounce it void. Contrary to what the Papists otherwise teach. See B. Par. Conf. Cath t 3. art 7. c. 4.)

Latin:

v. 4. Honora patrem &c. Hieron. in ep. ad Gerontiam In Evangelio Dominus disserit, man ditum legis, in quo dicitur: Honora Patrem tuum & matrem tuam, non in verborum sono, quimopiam parentum cassâ potest adulatione frustrare, sedin victûs necessuriis administrandis debere intelligi. *(Gernella habet idem ad h. l. Honor, scribit, in Scripturis non tam in salutationibus deferendis, quàm in elcemosynis ac munerum oblatione sentitur. Conf. & Chrys. in h. l. nec non Seldenus l. 7. de Iure nat. & gent. c. 2. Consentanea haec sunt ipsorum quoque nonnullorum Rabbrnorum dogmatibus. Ita enim R. Salomo Levit. 10, 3.Quis est honor, quem filius debet exhibere patri & matri? Dat eis eibum & potum calciat-, introducit & educit. Sic in libro Chaskuni sive Comment. R. Chiskiae in Pentat. haec reperiuntur: Legimus, honora Deum de opibus tuis, &, honora patrem & matrem, Deus honorandus, si habeas; parentes, sive habe as, sive non: nam sinihilihates, debes mendicare ostiatim pro eis. Adducie utrum que locum I. Drusius lib. 1. Praeterit. p. 35. notatque, gemella etiam haberi in libro Musar c. 5. Quin etiam ipsum verbum honorart aliquando in Sc. S. accipitur pro sublevari, beneficiis affici. clarè id patet ex Num. 22, 7. coll. cum v. 18. & 38. atq; ita à Paulo quoq; accipi 1. Tim 5, 8 & 17. notant Camero in Myroth ad h. l. Cosinas Magalianus Oper. Hierarch. l. 1. p. 567. Grotius in h. l. alii. Coeterùm commodè monet Corn. à Lapide in h. l. quòd honor parintibus debitus tria complictatur: Reverentiam, obedientiam & beneficentiam. Addit, quòd ius & vinculum pietatis, quo filii obligantur alere parentes pauperes, sit legis naturae, cui proinde omne votum, omnis oblatio, omniavincula, iure divino vel humano inducta, cedere & postponi debeant. Quod si omne votum, omniaq; vincula cedere debent, pietati parentibus debitae, sequitur quòd neclicitum sit filiis, invitis parentibus religionem s. vitam monasticam vovere, vel si tale votum factum, parentes illud irritum pronunciare possint. Contrà ac Ponttficii aliàs docenti Vid. B. Par. Conf. Cath t 3. art 7. c. 4.)*

## 15:5
v. 5. But you say. Whoever shall have said to father or mother, etc. Theoph. h. l. The Pharisees, persuading children that they should bestow nothing upon their parents, but rather consecrate their goods to the treasury of the temple, taught them to say, it is a gift, i.e., it is consecrated to God by me, that with which you ask to be helped by me; and thus the Pharisees shared the money with the children, but the wretched parents were deserted in their old age without any help.

Scaliger in the Elenchus of the Trihaeresium of Serarius. The most sorrowful half-sentences are accustomed to be cited by the Rabbis and Latin Doctors. Therefore, when someone offered Corban, he used to say: This Corban, which I offer to GOD, may it profit me and mine. By this pact he thought himself free from the debt of charity toward his parents, and finished with every duty of charity toward them, by that gift which he had offered to GOD, so that when provoked by his parents or admonished of his duty concerning the providing of food, or the performing of other duties, he would push them away with the exception of that offering. The gift, which I have offered for you, father, frees me from this entire exception. Bened. Arias Montanus explains in his notes concerning the oath of convenience, whom see Ioh. Alba in Manipulo Scripturae dictorum: This sentence is defective: If anyone shall say to father or mother Corban. For the other part of the sentence is suppressed, which it is necessary to understand with these words: If a man shall say to father or mother Corban, which is a gift, whatever from me (or by me, to wit, shall have been offered in the temple) shall have profited you (or shall also profit you, shall also be offered for you) he is free from the law, nor shall he be held to honor i. e. to nourish his parents. Conf. Tossanus. Andreas Masius in Iosuam: This was the solemn formula of swearing or rather vowing among the Hebrew doctors, Corban i. e. Let it be Anathema and a devoted thing, whatever that may be, by which I might profit you. By which vow when someone has used it with anyone, however much he is bound to him by necessity and even toward his own parent, the Rabbis decree it a sin to help him with any kind of benefit or duty, lest that which he has devoted to God should serve human conveniences. *Scaliger refutes the opinion of Masius and embraces the former; but Ioh. Camero undertakes the defense of Masius in Myroth. in h. l. S. August. lib. 1. QEvang. c. 16. explains it thus. The gift, whatever from me, shall profit you. i. e. the gift, which you offer for my sake, will already pertain to you, and adds: By which words the sons signify that there is no longer need for them of the parents' offering for them, because they had arrived at that age that they could now themselves offer for themselves. In this age therefore they were established, so that they could say this to their parents, when they had said this, the Pharisees denied that they were guilty, if they did not perform honor to their parents. Besides the commentators on Matthew, Drusius l. 2. de Sect. Iudaeorum c. 17, Dn. Dilherrus Disp. Acad. c. 2. p. 40. seqq., Eclog. Syr. p. 412. seqq., B. D. Ioh. Tob. Maior in pecul. disput. de Iuram. Orient. c. 1, Cappellus in Diatriba Spicilegio subiuncta p. 142. seqq., Sam. Petitus lib. 1. Var Lect. c. 4, Seldenus de Iure Nat. & Gent. lib. 7. c. 2, Raynoldus in Colloq. cum Hardo p. 507, H. Grotius in h. l. treat of this place at greater length.

Against that most wicked custom, by which not only the honor due to parents was withheld by their children, but also those things which were necessary for their sustenance, Ambrose discourses excellently in Luke c.

Latin:

v. 5. Vos autem dicitis. Quicundixeritpatri aut matri &c. Theoph. h. l. Pharisaeiper suadentes liberis, ut parentibus, nihil largirentur, sed templi the sauro potiùs sua bona consecrarent, docebant eco dicere, donume est, h. e. Deo, mi pater, consecratum est à me id, quô petis iuvari à me, at it a partiebantur Pharisaei pecunias cum liberis, miseri aurem parentes in senectute sine, ullô auxiliô deserebantur.

Scaliger in Elencho Trihaeresium Serarii. Tristissimae sententiae dimidiatae solent citari à Rabinis & Doctoribus Latinis. Cùm igitur quis offerebat Corban, dcebat: Hoc Corban, quodegDEO offero, prosit mihi & meis. Hoc pacto putabat se liberum à debitâ charitate in parentes, & defunctum omni caritatis officio erga illos, eo dono, quod DEO obtulisset, ita ut provocatus à parentibus aut admonitus officii de alimentis dandis, aut aliis officiis praestandis, eos ille summoveret exceptione illius oblationis. Munus, quod pro te, pater, obtuli, me hoc omni exceptione liberat. Bened. Arias Montanus in notis explicat de iuramento commoditatis, quem vid. Ioh. Alba in Manipulo Scripturae dictorum: Oratio haec est defectiva: Si quis dixerit patri aut matri Corban. Reticetur enim altera pars sententiae, quam eportet subintelligere his verbis: Si dixerit homo patri vel matri Corban, quod est donum, quodcunq; ex me (vel â me, scil. oblatum fuerit in templo) tibi profuerit (vel tibi etiam proderit, pro te etiā offeretur) liber est à lege, nec tenebitur honorare i. e. alereparentes. Conf. Tossanus. Andreas Masius in Iosuam: Doctorum Hebraeorum haec iurandi aut potiùs vovendi solennis fuit formula, Corban i. e. Anathema & res devota esto, quicquid illud sit, quo ego tibi prosim. Quô votô cùm quis apud aliquem usus est, quantavis ei necessitudine obligatum atq; adeò erga suum ipsius parentem nefas esse statuunt Rabini, illum ullo beneficii aut officii genere hūc iuvare, ne quod Deo devoverit, id humanis commodis serviat. *Masii sententiam refutat Scaliger ac priorem amplectitur; sed Masii patrocinium suscipit Ioh. Camero in Myroth. in h. l. S. August. lib. 1. QEvang. c. 16. ita exponit. Munus, quodcunex me, tibi proderit. i. e. munui, quod offers causâ mei, ad teiam pertinebit, & addit: Quibus verbis significant filii, iam non sibi opus esse parentum pro se oblatione, quòd ad eam aetatem pervenissent ut possent iam ipsi offerre pro se. In hâc ergò aetate cōstitutos, ut possent parentibus suis hoc dicere, cùm hoc dixissent, negabant Pharisaei, reos esse, si Parentibus suis non praestarent honorem. Pluribus de h. l. praeter Commentatores in Matthaeum agunt Drusius l. 2. de Sect. Iudaeorum c. 17. Dn. Dilherrus Disp. Acad. c. 2. p. 40. seqq. Eclog. Syr. p. 412. seqq. B. D. Ioh. Tob. Maior in pecul. disput. de Iuram. Orient. c. 1. Cappellus in Diatriba Spícilegio subiuncta p. 142. seqq. Sam. Petitus lib. 1. Var Lect. c. 4. Seldenus de Iure Nat. & Gent. lib. 7. c. 2. Raynoldus in Colloq. cum Hardo p. 507. H. Grotius in h. l.

Contra pessimum istum morem, quo Parentibus à liberis non solùm honor debitus, sed etiam ea, quae ad sustentationem illis necessaria erant, subtrahebantur, egregiè disserit Ambros. in Luc. c. 18.)*

## 15:6
v. 6. Ἠκυρώσατε you have made void. i. e. you have given an effective occasion, by which it is less observed. *(According to Cameron in Myrothec on this passage, by twisting the words of the law into a foreign sense, you have abrogated it. But the Jews erred in this, that they thought even the ceremonial precepts of the first table should be preferred to the moral ones of the second table of the Decalogue: but vows look toward ceremonial matters. These are void, if they fight with the charity of the neighbor. And the reason is, because they ought to be made concerning those things which are in our power. But it is not in our power to vow such a thing that fights with the second table of the Decalogue, i. e. with the piety owed to parents. Compare also on this matter Grotius on this passage.)*

*( Because of your traditions. Compare similar complaints Is. 29, 13.Ezek. 20, 18.Matt. 5, 21. seqq. Mark 7, 9.Col. 2, 8. and 22. Tit. 1, 14. add. B. Par. Comm. in pr. ep. Petri c. 1. p. 119)*

Latin:

v. 6. Ἠκυρώσατεirritum fecistis. i. e. occasionem efficacem dedistis, quo minùs observetur. *(Iuxta Cameronem in Myrothec ad h. l. verba legis in alienum sensum detorquendo eam abrogastis. Errarunt verò Iudaei in eo, quòd putarunt, etiam ceremonialia primae tabulae praecepta praeferenda esse moralibus secundae Decalogi tabulae: ad ceremonialia verò spectant vota. Irrita verò haec sunt, si pugnent cum charitate proximi. ac ratio est, quia fieri debent de iis, quae in nostra sunt potestate. Non autem est in nostrâ potestate, tale quid vovere, quod pugnat cum secundâ decalogi tabula h. e cum pietate parentibus debitâ Conf. etiam inhanc rem Grotius in h. l.)*

*( Propter traditiones vestras. Confer similes querelas Es. 29, 13.Ezech. 20, 18.Matth. 5, 21. seqq. Marc. 7, 9.Coloss. 2, 8. ac 22. Tit 1, 14. add. B. Par. Comm. in pr. ep. Petri c. 1. p. 119)*

## 15:7
*(v. 7. Isaiah prophesied about you. See B. D. Chemnitius Harm. Evang. c. 12.)*

Latin:

*(v. 7. De vobis prophetavit Esaias. Vid. B. D. Chemnitium Harm. Evang. c. 12.)*

## 15:8
*(v. 8. Ἐγγίζειμοι ὁ λαὸς οὗτος στόματι ἀυτττῶν. The Vulgate Interpreter does not acknowledge these words, just as neither the Syrian, nor the Ethiopian, nor the Persian have the same. Indeed, not even the ancient Greek Codex of Beza. They are nevertheless a genuine part of the Greek Codex, just as the Greek Codices in general, which the Parisians and Londoners have collated, with the exception only of that one just mentioned, those most ancient and most approved ones, present the same. And they are also read in the Arabic, even of the Roman edition.)*

*( Their heart is far from me, because their sins divide between me and them, Is. 59, 2. To this point makes the beautiful maxim of Prosper Sent. 123. One does not approach God by intervals of places, but likeness makes one near; unlikeness makes one far away.)*

Latin:

*(v. 8. Ἐγγίζειμοι ὁ λαὸς οὗτος στόματι ἀυτττῶν. Non agnoscit haec verba Interpres Vulgatus, quemadmodum eadem nec Syrus, nec Aethiops, nec Persa habent. Imò nec antiquus Codex Graecus Bezae. Sunt tamen genuina Codicis Graeci pars, quemadmodum Codd. Graeci in universum, quos Parisienses ac Londineses contulerunt, exceptô solô istô modò memoratô, antiquissimi illi ac probatissimi, eadem sistunt. Ac leguntur quoque apud Arabem, etiam editionis Romanae.)*

*( Cor eorum procul abest à me, quia peccata eorum dividunt inter me & eos, Es. 59, 2. Huc facit pulcra gnome Prosperi Sent. 123. Non locorum intervallis acceditur ad Deum, sed similitudo facit proximum; dissimilitudo longinquum.)*

## 15:9
v. 9. Μάτην. This little word is not found in Isaiah 29:13 in the Hebrew, but παραφραςικῶς was added by the LXX Interpreters. (Just as also in certain other places in this passage, regarding certain words, some discrepancy is perceived between the Hebrew text and the Greek in Isaiah, and in this passage. The most important reason for this is that in this passage Christ followed the LXX version. And Christ and the writers of the N.T. follow this LXX version everywhere, as being at that time most accepted among the Jews, unless perhaps it deviates from the Hebrew text regarding the sense, as Origen in ch. 15 of the epistle to the Romans, Jerome in Questions on Genesis ch. 46, Augustine book 15 of the City of God ch. 14, book 18 ch. 44, and our theologians show in many places, have long since observed. See D. Erantzius on the Interpretation of Holy Scripture p. 38, Dr. Walther, Biblical Office p. 283, B. Par. Coll. Isagog. p. 85, Harmony of the Gospels part 1 p. 580, Disputation on the Prophet Amos Disputation 9 th. 32, Commentary on Genesis p. 785, 809, Commentary on the first epistle of Peter ch. 1 v. 25, on the Epistle to the Hebrews p. 230 and 421, and elsewhere passim. Among the Calvinists, Sam. Peritus, Various Readings p. 29, Fried. Spanhem, Evangelical Doubts Part 1 p. 3 & 21, Pasor: Lexicon of the N.T. p. 83, 104, 200, 510, Ioh. Camero, Lectures on Matt. ch. 18, 15. page 4, 63, 90, etc., agree; indeed, the Jesuit Lorinus himself, Commentary on the Acts of the Apostles p. 94, so that he ineptly concludes from the fact that the passage from Isaiah is cited differently in this passage and among the LXX Interpreters than it is read in the Hebrew text today, that Morinus concludes its corruption, and the Jesuit Conzen does not seem to think differently. But Dr. Calovius, Critical Sacred Scriptures p. 527, 528, who must be read entirely, has solidly proven the integrity of the Hebrew text against Morinus in this passage. Furthermore, just as Justin Martyr long ago rightly opposed this passage to the traditions of the Jews and urged it against Trypho the Jew in the Dialogue held with him p. 289, so even now the Orthodox oppose the same to the ἐθελοθρησκεἰαις of the Papists. Following in this part the sounder Papists themselves, Ioh. Ferus on this passage, Georg. Cassander in Consultations art. 25, Clingius LL ch. 118. Cardinal Baronius, vol. 1 Annals to the year 53 n. 6, Bellarmine book 4 on the Word of God ch. 10, Paludanus in Vindications of this passage, Corn. à Lapide on this passage do indeed except that only those things are disapproved which are done against the law, and thus at least the more recent traditions invented by the Pharisees, but not the old unwritten Traditions, whose author is Moses and the Prophets.

Response.
