It is clear from the context that Christ condemns not only those traditions and forms of worship which are repugnant to the word of GOD (for this was already known to the Pharisees beforehand, and was conceded by them) but also all those which are not commanded by the word of GOD, of which kind were the washings of hands which the Pharisees urged, which nevertheless as such are nowhere prohibited in Holy Scripture. It is to be noted furthermore 1. that the Jews indeed had ancient traditions, see Schickard, Bechin. Happeruschim p. 35, but they were by no means derived from Moses or the Prophets: nor do the Fathers anywhere teach that Moses handed down any oral law, as Dan Chamier, vol. 1 Panstr. book 8 ch. 12, long ago proved against the Papists, nor can any dogma of faith or doctrine of worship given to the Jews through the oral tradition of Moses be brought forward. 2. That Christ reproves the most ancient traditions, used in the time of Isaiah himself. 3. That Christ expressly opposes the written word and traditions, and refers us to Scripture alone. John 5, 39. 40.Luke 16, 29.ch. 24, 27. Conf. Num. 15, 39. 40Deut. 12, 8.32. 4. Those traditions of the Pharisees were not all and in themselves impious, as is evident from the frequent washings: Meanwhile, because they were thrust forward as a necessary worship, they were reproved and consequently were impious. As the Jesuit Conzen himself grants. Conf. B. Par. Exeg. L. de Sc. S. §. 394. Dn D. Walth. Off. Bib. §. 218. But let any prudent person consider whether the matter does not stand thus with most traditions among the Papists, that even if they contain nothing evil in themselves, they are nevertheless thrust forward as a necessary worship of GOD. How the same Papists also dogmatically transgress the commandment of GOD through their traditions, the Saxon Theologians show at length in Fundam. Defens. Pupillae p. 101. 102.

Latin:

v. 9. Μάτην. Vocula haec non habetur Esaiae 29, 13. in Ebraeo, sed παραφραςικῶς à LXX. Interpp. est addita *(Sicuti etiam in aliis quibusdam h. l. quoad verba quaedam textum Ebraeum inter apud Esaiam, & h. l. Graecum discrepantia aliqua cernitur. Cuius potissima ratio, quòd h. l. Christus LXX. versione nsecutus. Atque hanc LXX versionem, ut pote tumtemporis inter Iudaeos receptissimam passim sequuntur Christus ac Scrip ores N. T. nisi fortè quoad sensum deviet illa à textu Ebraeô, uti pridem observârunt Origenes in c. 15. epist. ad Rom. Hieronymus in Qq. super Genesin c. 46. Augustinus l. 15. de C. D. c. 14. lib. 18. c. 44. ac pluribus ostendunt nostrates Theologi. Vid. B. D. Erantzius de Interp. Sc. S. p. 38. Dn D. Waltherus Offic. Bibl. p. 283. B. Par. Coll. Isagog. p. 85. Harm. Evangel. part. 1. p. 580. Disp. in Proph. Amos Disp. 9. th. 32. Comment. in Gen. p. 785. 809. Commin prior. ep. Petr. c. 1. v. 25. in Epist. ad Ebr. p. 230. ac 421, & alibi passim. Adstipulantur ex Calvinianis Sam. Peritus Var. Lect p. 29 Fried. Spanhem Dub Evang. Part. 1. p. 3. & 21. Paso: Lex. N. T. p 83. 104 200. 510. Ioh. Camero Praelect. ad Matt. c 18, 15. pag. 4 63. 90. &c. quin ipse Iesuita Lorinus Comm. in Act. Apost p. 94. ut ade ineptè exeô, quòd locus ex Esaiâ h. l. & apud LXX. Interpp aliter adducatur, quàm in textu Ebraeô hodiè legitur, colligat Morinus eiusdem corruptionem, nec diversum sentire videtur Iesuita Conzen. Sed solidè integritatem textûs Ebraici contra Morinum h. l. evicit Dn. D. Calovius Critici Sacri pag 527 528. qui omninò evolvendus. Caeterùm quem admodum iam olim Iustinus Martyr rectè hunc locum traditionibus Iudaeorum opposuii ac contra Tryphonem Iudaeorum ursit in Dialogô cum eô habitô p. 289 ita etiamnū Orthodoxi eundem Pontificiorum ἐθελοθρησκεἰαις opponunt Sequuti hac in parte ipsos saniores Pontificios Ioh. Ferum in h. l. Georg. Cassandrum in Consult. art 25. Clingium LL c. 118. Excipiunt quidem Card. Baroniust. 1 Annal. ad A 53. n. 6. Bellarm. l. 4. de V. D. c 10. Paludanus in Vindic h. l. Corn à Lapide in h. l. improbari solùm ea, quae fivat contra legem, adeóque recentiores saltem traditiones à Pharisaeis inventas, non verò veteres non-scriptas Traditiones, quarum autor Moses ac Prophetae.

Resp. Patet ex contextu, quòd Christus non solùm illas damnet traditiones ac cultus, qui verbo DEI repugnant, (hoc enim iam antè Pharisaeis notum erat, & ab iisdem concedebatur) sed etiā omnes eos qui non sunt verbô DEI mandati, cuiusmodi erant lotiones manuum, quas Pharisaei urgebant, quae tamen ut tales nullibi in Sc. S sunt prohibitae. Notandum praetereà 1. traditiones quidem Iudaeos habuisse antiquas, Vid Schickard. Bechin. Happeruschim p. 35. sed à Mose vel Prophetis minimè prosectas: neq; Patres etiam ullibi docent, quòd Moses legem tradiderit aliquam oralem, uti contra Pontificios pridem evicit Dan Chamier t. 1. Panstr. l 8. c. 12. nec potest quoque ullum proferri fidei dogma vel doctrina cultûs per traditionem Mosis oralem Iudaeis data. 2. Christum reprehendere antiquissimas traditiones, ipsius Esaiae tempore usitatas 3. Christum expressè opponere verbum scriptum, & traditiones, & ad unicam scripturam nos remittere, Ioh. 5, 39. 40.Luc 16, 29.cap. 24, 27. Conf. Num. 15, 39. 40Deut. 12, 8.32. 4. Traditiones illa Pharisaeorum non omnes ac per se fuisse impias, uti ex crebris lotionibus patet: Interim quia tanquam cultus necessarius obtrudebantur, fuisse reprehensas ac consequenter fuisse impias. Ut ipse Iesuita Conzen largitur. Conf B. Par. Exeg. L. de Sc. S. §. 394. Dn D. Walth. Off. Bib. §. 218. Cogitet verò quilibet prudens, annon cùm plerisq; traditionibus apud Pontisicios ita sese res habeat, quòd si vel maximè in se nihil mali contineant, tamen ut cultus DEI necessarius obtrudantur. Quomodo iidem Pontificii per traditiones suas dogmaticè etiam transgrediantur mandatum DEI, prolixè ostendunt Dnn. Theologi Saxonici in Fundam Defens. Pupillae p. 101. 102.)*

## 15:11
*(v. 11. What enters &c. The divine constitution seems to stand in the way of this assertion, by which in the O. T. certain animals were prohibited as unclean. Resp. 1. M. Ioh. Mettingerus, formerly Ecclesiastes of Augsburg, part 1. of his Harmony p. 740, attributes to Iustinus, that in quest. 35 he maintains, in the O. Test. certain animals were pronounced pure, certain ones impure, at least by reason of sacrifices, and on that account he also censures Iustinus, since the words of the Mosaic law indicate otherwise, namely, that there are certain unclean animals also by reason of eating,Deut. 14, 3.Lev. 11, 2.29.Acts 10, 14. But it must be known that Iustinus, or whoever is the author of the Qq. and Resp. attributed to Iustinus, by no means maintains that God in the O. T. pronounced certain animals impure at least by reason of sacrifices; for he writes expressly: God promised that the Israelites should slaughter clean animals in sacrifices, but not even eat others, as being unclean, τὰ δὲ μὴ ἐσθιει ὡς ἀκάθαρτα, & a little before: τινὰ δὲ ἀκόθαρτα ὠνόμασεν, ὧν τὴ βρῶσιν ἀυτοὺς ἀπειργε. 2 It must be known that, as Mettingerus rightly observes in the said place, Christ here does not treat of the eating of unclean animals, but of the impurity of hands, tables, cups &c. as is evident from the context, namely that by these a man is not rendered unclean, or contaminates himself with sins, if he does not observe the Jewish constitutions concerning those purifications. Meanwhile, it is also rightly gathered from this passage that Christ abolished the Levitical distinction between clean and unclean animals in the N. T., as Felicianus Capitonus, Bishop of Avignon, himself admits, Explic. Cathol. part. 2. p. 542. 3. Dist. between the time of the O. and N. T. For although in the O. T. certain animals were pronounced unclean by ceremonial law, so that those who ate such things then sinned, not because those animals infected the heart of man by themselves, but because of the transgression of the divine law, just as the eating from the forbidden tree in paradise rendered the protoplasts unclean. Thus when someone gorges himself with wine and sins, it is not to be imputed to the wine, but because he abuses wine against the divine interdict, Eph. 5, 17.. Because, however, the ceremonial laws were abolished through Christ, thence those animals which were unclean in the O. T. by ceremonial law are judged clean in the N. T. Conf. Acts 10, 15.Rom. 14, 20.Col. 2, 16.1. Tim. 4, 4.Tit. 1, 15 Add that there is also a distinction in the O. T. between Levitical and moral uncleanness. 4. If anyone urges that even today it is harmful to eat certain animals and herbs, then I respond that the eating of such is prohibited not by reason of transgression, i.e., that a man directly contaminates himself with sin if he eats such things; but by reason of health.)*

*( That which goes out of the mouth i. e. out of the heart, that is, the will. The Savior uses the word mouth by anatanaclasis, since He had used it in its proper meaning a little before. See August. book 25 on the Trinity, ch. 10; book on Lying to Consentius, ch. 16; book 16 against Faustus, ch. 31; Jerome in the Epistle to Salvia on the preservation of virginity. Nevertheless, the proper Grotius thinks that the mouth's acceptance also has a place in this passage, since many sins are accustomed to be committed by the mouth.)*

To make common is to make impure or unclean, Act. 10, 14. *(& so also most interpreters, both Eastern and Western, have rendered it in this passage, namely by τὸ to defile, to contaminate &c)* Luke adds for the sake of explanation: ἢ ἀκάθαοτον. Bell. lib. 2 de B. O. in part. c 8 thinks that the Lord wished by those words to rebuke the superstition of the Jews, who thought that foods taken with unwashed hands contract I know not what filth, by which the soul is infected. Resp. The occasion of Christ's words was special, which the superstition of the Jews concerning the washing of hands provided, meanwhile the sense of the words themselves is and remains general, as the very sound of them makes manifest. Just as elsewhere also ὑπόθεσις is accustomed to be reduced to θέσιν.

*(Just as also the Blessed Augustine, book against Adimantus the Manichaean, ch. 15, rightly observed, writing thus: The Jews had raised a question about unwashed hands, on the occasion of which the Lord gave a judgment generally concerning those things which enter into the mouth, and go into the belly, and are cast out into the draught, that is, concerning our foods. Just as, moreover, the same Augustine rightly gathers from this passage against the Manichaeans, who prohibit the eating of meat, that the distinction of foods, observed in the Old Testament, was abolished by the coming of Christ, since observations of this kind bore at least a shadow of things to come, and so the Manichaeans now have no place from which they may take away foods from the throats of men, and bind them with the snare of superstition: so also it is rightly gathered from this against the Papists, that they themselves are superstitious when they prohibit certain specific foods on certain days. Whence John Paludanus, Doctor and Professor of Theology in the Academy of Louvain, in Vindic. Theol. page 227, unjustly inveighs against Luther, whom he trifles to have embraced the Jovinian heresy in that he teaches that any foods whatsoever are lawful for any men whatsoever on any days whatsoever without distinction. But he himself excepts to this passage by conceding, that food, as it is food and as it enters into the mouth, does not defile a man: but the contempt of an Ecclesiastical precept, insofar as namely it is forbidden, defiles much, that this is evident he adds in the forbidden fruit in Paradise. Felicianus Capito in Expl. Cathol. on this passage, Alphonsus de Castro, Cornelius à Lapide, Conzen, Barradius, and others have similar things. Resp. Paludanus, Capito, and other Papists conclude ineptly from a divine interdict to a human or Ecclesiastical one, and indeed one that fights with Christian liberty. For since Christ has freed us from this distinction of foods also, just as from other Levitical ceremonies, 1. Cor. 10, 25.Col. 2, 16.Tit. 1, 15. (And to this also looks Justin in Qq. & Resp. ad Orth. page 319, writing: κατὰ τών) it is preposterous and contrary to Christian liberty to obtrude a distinction of foods in the New Testament under the opinion of necessity. Indeed, the Apostle 1. Tim. 4, 1. & 3. calls that very prohibition of foods, promulgated in the New Testament by some under the pretext of some singular holiness and under the guise of worship, a doctrine of demons. But in that way the Papists urge abstinence from a certain kind of food and on certain days. What the same people except to the Pauline dictum will be discussed in its own place. Meanwhile, let the authors who have written about fasting, alleged above in the Analecta to Matth. 9, 14., be compared. In this place it is at least to be noted that Cardinal Cajetan himself to the words Marc. 6. He commanded them that they should take nothing for the way &c. writes: It differs from the whole Evangelical doctrine to give commands concerning food, drink, clothes, beard, hair, and things of this sort, which are indifferent. Felicianus Capito cites the passage in the place cited and adds that Ambrosius Catharinus said those words of the Cardinal are false and consonant with the pernicious dogmas of heretics. But for us the ingenuous confession of so great a Cardinal suffices. Finally, this also is to be noted, that the Jews by no means pronounced certain foods unclean for that reason, or established that a man is defiled if he takes food with unwashed hands, as if the soul were infected by the foods themselves, as indeed Grotius in this passage p. 277 and p. 282 and before him Tostatus Abulensis attribute to them, just as also Conzen in this passage p. 312. Or that foods had a natural uncleanness, but that the tradition of the elders was violated in this way. Since, however, they were rebuked by Christ for this very reason, certainly neither are the Papists to be heard, prohibiting certain foods, an Ecclesiastical prohibition

They, pretending here the tradition of the elders, even if they should grant in the highest degree, that no foods are by nature unclean.) v. 12. That the Pharisees were offended. Bened Arias Montanus in this place. There was a distinction between the observations of the people of the land, and the observations of the Pharisees. The people of the land are bound to observe the precepts expressed in the Bibles or deduced from a manifest interpretation of the Bibles. The Pharisees observed not only these, as they themselves boasted, but those which either they themselves had added, or had accepted from others as added, even the most trivial, such as to fast twice in the Sabbath, to wash hands a hundred times in a day, etc. This so exact and minute observation they themselves greatly boasted of in the name of holiness. When therefore Christ, having called the crowds to himself, that is, the people of the land, was teaching the true reason of these things, he seemed to the Apostles to have affected the Pharisees with great offense, whose vain sanctimony he affirmed to be that which was placed in observing these indifferent things.

Latin:

*(v. 11. Quod ingreditur &c. Videtur huic adserto obstare constitutio divina, quâ in V T. quaedam animal aut immunda prohibebantur. Resp 1. M Ioh Mettingerus, Ecclesiastes quondam Augustanus part. 1. Harmoniae p 740. Iustino tribuit, quòd quaest. 35 statuat, in V. Test. animalia quaedam pura pronunciata fuisse, quaedam impura, saltem ratione sacrificiorum, eôque etiam nomine Iustinum perstringit, cùm verba: extûs Mosaici aliud indicent, esse scil, quaedam immunda animalia etiam ratione esû,Deut. 14, 3.Lev. 11, 2.29.Act. 10, 14. Verùm sciendum quòd Iustinus vel quicunque autor Qq. ac Resp Iustino tu butarum, minimè statuat, Deum in V T. animalia quaedam im pura pronunciasse saltem ratione sacrificiorum; etenim disertè scribit. Deum promisisse, ut Israelitae munda in sacrificiis macta, rent, aliis autem ne vesci quidem, tanquam immundis,τὰ δὲ μὴ ἐσθιει ὡς ἀκάθαρτα, & paullò antè: τινὰ δὲ ἀκόθαρτα ὠνόμασεν, ὧν τὴ βρῶσιν ἀυτοὺς ἀπειργε. 2 Sciendum, quòd, uti rectè observat Mettingerus d. l. Christus hîc non agat de esu animalium immundorum, sed de impuritate manuum, mensarum, poculorum &c ut ex contextu patet, quòd nempe per haec homo non reddatur immundus, vel peccatis se contaminet, si const tutiones Iudaicas circa istas purgationes non observârit. Intererectè ex hoc locô etiam colligitur, quòd Christus discrimen Leviticum inter animalia munda & immunda in N. T. sustulerit, ceu ipse fatetur Felicianus Capitonus, Avinionensis Episcopus, Explic. Cathol part. 2. p. 542. 3. Dist. inter tempus V. ac N. T. Etenim licet in V. T. quaedam animalia lege ceremoniali fuerint immunda pronunciata, ut adeò peccarint, qui talia tum ederunt, non quòd per se illa animalia cor hominis infecerint, sed ob transgressionem legis divinae, quomodo etiam esus de arb ore vetitâ in paradisô protoplastos immundos reddicit. Sic quando a-iquis vinô sese ingurg tans peccat, non vinoid imputandum, sed quia contra interd. ctum divinum, Eph. 5, 17. vinô abutitur. Quia tamen leges ceremoniales per Christem fuerunt sublatae, inde animalia illa, quae lege ceremoniali in V. T. erant immunda, in N. T munda iudicantur. Conf. Act. 10, 15.Rom 14, 20.Col. 2, 16.1. Tim 4, 4.Tit. 1, 15 Adde quòd dist. etiam in V T. interimm nditiem Leviticam, & moralem. 4. Si aliquis urgeat, quòd etiimnum hodie noxium sit, certis, vibusdam animalibus ac herbis vesci, tum resp. quòd talium esus sit prohibitus non ratione transgressionis, sc. quòd omo directe peccato se contaminet, sitalibus vescatur; sed r. t one valctadinis.)*

*( Quod egred tur ex ore i. e. ex corde s. voluntate Utitur autem Salvator voce oris per anatanaclasin, cùm illâ in proprià significatione paullò antè fuerit usus. Vid. August. l. 25. de Trin. c. 10. lib. de Mendac. ad Consent. c. 16. lib. 16. cont. Faustum. c. 31. Hier. in Ep. ad Salviam de Virg. serv. Propriam tamē oris acceptionem etiam h. l. habere locum, existimat Grotius, cùm multa peccata ore soleant peragi.)*

Communem reddere est impurum s. immundum reddere,Act. 10, 14. *(& ita quoque Interpp plerique tum Orientales tum Occidentales h. l. reddiderunt, nempe per τὸinquinare, contaminare &c)* Lucas explicandi gratiâ addit: ἢ ἀκάθαοτον. Bell. l. 2. de B. O. in part. c 8. existimat, voluisse Dominum illis verbis superstitionem Iudaeórum reprehendère, qui existimabant, cibos illotis manibus sumtos contrahere, nescio quas sordes, quibus anima insceretur. Resp. occasio verborum Christi fuit specialis, quam superstitio Iudaeorum de manuum ablutione praebuit, interim verborumipsorum sensus est & manet generalis, ut ipse sonus eorum manifestum facit. Sicut alibi quoq; ὑπόθεσις ad θέσιν reduci consvevit.

*(Quemadmodum etiam B. August. lib. contra Adimantum Manich. c. 15. rectè observavit, ita scribens: De non lotis manibus Iudaei moverant quaestionem, cuius occasione Dominus generaluter de iis, quae in osintrant, & in ventrem vadunt, & in secessum, emittuntur, hoc est, de alimentis nostris dixit sententiā. Sicuti v. rectè idem Augustinus ex h. l. contra Manichaeos, carnis esum prohibentes, colligit, sublatum esseper Christi adventum discrimē cihorum, in V. Test. observatum, cùm observationes istiusmodi umbram saltem geslerint futurorum, adeoque non habere iam Manichaeos, unde auferant cibos de faucibus hominum, & eos laqueo superstitionis adstringant: ita quoque rectè contra Pontificios hinc colligitur, quòd superstitiosi ipsi sint quando certos quosdam cibos certis diebus prohibent. Unde iniuriâ Ioh. Paludanus, Theologiae D. ac Prof. in Acad. Lovaniensi. Vindic. Theol. pag. 227 in Lutherum, quem Iovinianae amplexum esse haeresin nugatur in eo, quòd doceat, quoslibet cibos, quibuslibet diebus omnibus quibus cunq; hominibus sine discrimine licitos esse, in vehitur. Excipit verò ipse ad h. l. concedendo, cibum, quat. cibus est & quat. in os intrat, hominem non coinquinare: sed praecepti Ecclesiastici contemtum, quatenus videl. vetitus est, multum coinquinare, idpatere addit in sructu vetito in Paradiso. Gemella habet Felicianus Capito Expl. Cathol. in h. l. Alph. de Castro, Corn. à Lap. Conzen, Barradius & alii. Resp. ineptè concludunt Paludanus, Capito aliiq; Pontificii ab interdicto divino ad humanum sive Ecclesiasticum, & quidem cum libertate Christiana pugnans. Cùm enim Christus ut ab aliis Leviticis ceremoniis, ita ab hoc quoq; ciborum discrimine nos liberaverit, 1. Cor. 10, 25.Col. 2, 16.Tit. 1, 15. (Atque huc respicit quoq; Iustinus in Qq. & Resp. ad Orth. pag. 319. scribens. κατὰ τών) praeposterum est ac Christianae libertati adversum, discrimen ciborum in N. T. sub opinione necessitatis obtrudere. Imò stam cibi prohibitionem, in N T. à quibusdam sub praetextu singularis cuiusdam sanctitatis ac sub specie cultûs promulgaram, Apostolus 1. Tim. 4, 1. & 3.doctrinam Daemoniorum vocat. Isto verò modò Pontificii abstinentiam à certo ciborum genere ac certis diebus urgent. Quae iidem ad dictum Paulinum excipiunt, suo discutientur loco. Confer antur interea autores, qui de Ieiunio scripsêre, suprà in Analectis ad Matth. 9, 14. allegati. Hoc loco illud saltem notandum, quòd ipse Cardinalis Caietanus ad verba Marc. 6.Praecepit illis, ne quid tellerent in viâ &c. scribit: Ab universâ doctrinâ Evangelicâ discrepat, mandare de cibo, potu, vestibus, barbâ capillis, & huiusmods, quae indifferentia sunt. Locum adducit Felic. Capito l. c. additq. quòd Ambrosius Catharinus verba illa Cardinalis falsa esse & haereticorum perniciosis dogmatis consentanea dixerit. Nobis verò sufficit ingenua tanti Cardinalis confessio. Denique & hoc notandum, Iudaeos minimè proptere à cibos quosdam immundos pronunciasse, vel statuisse, hominem coinquinari, si illotis manibus sumat cibum. qs. ab ipsis cibis animae inficerentur, uti quidem Grotius h. l. p. 277. ac p. 282. & ante eam Tostatus Abulensis illis tribuit, quemadmodum etiam Conzen h. l. p. 312. Vel quòd cibi naturalem haberent immunditiam, sed quòd traditio maiorum hoc modo violaretur. Cùm verò ob hoc ipsum à Christo fuerint illi reprehensi, sanè nec Pontificii audiendi sunt, cibos quosdam prohibentes, Ecclesiasticam prohibitionē

h. e. maiorum traditionem hî praetendentes, si vel maximè largiantur, nullos cibos naturâ esse immundos.)* v. 12. Pharisaeos esse offensos. Bened Arias Montanus in h. l. Erat distinctio inter observationes populiterrae, & observatioves Pharisaeorum. Terrae populus tenetur observare praecepta expressaein Bibliis aut deducta ex Bibliorum manifesta interpretatione. Pharisaei observabant non solùm haec, ut ipsi iactabant, sed quae vel ipsiaddiderant, vel ab aliis addita etiam levissima acceperant, ut ieiunare bis in Sabbatho, manus in die centies lavare &c. Hanc adeò exactam & minutam observationem ipsi sanctitatis nomine maximopere iactabant. Cùm ergo Christus turbas ad se convocatas h. e. populum terrae veram harum rerum doceret rationem, visus est Apostolis Pharisaeos magnâ offensione affecisse, quorum vanam sanctimoniam eam esse affirmaret, quae in iis adiaphoris rebus observandis collocaretur.

## 15:13
v. 13. Every planting etc. Some expound this concerning human traditions, not instituted by God, Act. 5, 38. others concerning the impious and hypocrites, who are found in the external society of the Church, which is the garden of God, but are not rooted by faith in Christ. Col. 2. v. 7. Tossanus. The former exposition is to be preferred. Hilarius in this place signifies that the tradition of men is to be rooted out, by whose favor they have transgressed the precepts of the law. *(August. 1. contra Adimant. Manich c. 15. by the planting not planted by GOD, understands the infidelity of the Jews.)*

*( Let them alone. They are blind leaders of the blind. Compare below. c. 23, 16. This is a faithful admonition concerning avoiding the seductions of heretics. How necessary this flight of seduction is today, B. D. Glassius teaches in many ways in Exeg. Dom. 4. post Trin. p. 982. But Lud Cappellus shows in Spicil. on this place p. that the similitude which Christ uses here is twin to that which one may read also in the author of the book הובת הלבנות. )*

Latin:

v. 13. Omis plantatio &c. Quidam exponunt de humanis traditionibus, à Deo non institutis, Act. 5, 38. alii de impiis & hypocritis, qui in Ecclesiae, quae est hortus Dei, externâ societate inveniuntur, sed non sunt fide in Christo radicati. Col. 2. v. 7. Tossanus. Prior expositio praeferenda. Hilarius in h. l. significat, traditionem hominum eruendam esse, cuius favore transgressi sunt praecepta legis. *(August. 1. contra Adimant. Manich c. 15. per plantationem à DEO non plantatam, infidelitatem Iudaeorum intelligit.)*

*( Omitte illos. Duces sunt coeci coecorum. Conf. infrà. c. 23, 16. Fidelis est haec admonitio de cavendis haereticorum seductionibus. Quae seductionis fuga quàm hodie necessaria, sit, multis docet B. D. Glassius Exeg. Dom. 4. post Trin. p. 982. Similitudinem verò, illi, quâ Christus hîc utitùr, gemellam, legi quoque apud autorem libri. הובת הלבנות ostendit Lud Cappellus in Spicil. h. l. p. )*

## 15:15
v. 15. Explain to us this parable. The Hebrews call what is said wisely or somewhat obscurely a parable; especially that which is concerning the nature or duty of man.

Latin:

v. 15. Edissere nobis parabolam istam. Ebraei quod vis sapienter vel subobscurè dictum vocant parabolam; maximè, quod est de hominis naturâ vel officio.

## 15:16
*(v. 16. Are you also still etc. For not only Peter, but also the remaining disciples asked him concerning that similitude.)* Mark 7:17.)*

Ἀκμὴν. It is placed adverbially, as if κατ᾽ ἀκμὴν according to vigor, so that it may be signified that something still flourishes and endures. In the same way Justin uses it in the Dialogue with Trypho. Casaubon in the notes ἀκμὴν is worth ἔτι καὶ νῦν. Polybius a. ἐκ παραλλήλων. said ἀκμ-ν ἐτι καὶ νῦν book 15. Mark interprets οὕτω, chap. 7:18.

Latin:

*(v. 16. Aduc & vos &c. Etenim non solùm Petrus, sed & reliqui discipuli interrogarunt eum de istâ similitudine. Marc. 7, 17.)*

Ἀκμὴν. Adverbialiter ponitur, quasi κατ᾽ ἀκμὴνsecundum vigorem, ut significetur, adhuc aliquid vigere ac durare. Eodem modo usurpat Iustinus in Dialogo cum Tryph. Casaub. in not. ἀκμὴν valet ἔτι καὶ νῦν. Polyb. a. ἐκ παραλλήλων. dixit ἀκμ-ν ἐτι καὶ νῦν lib. 15. Marcus interpretatur οὕτω,cap. 7, 18.

## 15:17
v. 17. Whatever enters &c. Jerome: Although thin moisture and liquid food is poured into the body, yet when it has been concocted and digested in the veins and limbs through the hidden passages of the body, which the Greeks πόρους call, it slips down to the lower parts, into the privy, it goes. Maldonatus: Christ speaks not philosophically, but popularly. For because a minimum remains, he speaks thus, as if he signifies that nothing remains. And Thomas also feels thus, that Christ indeed speaks κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον, because the doctrine concerning concoction is not known to the common people. Others respond that there is no food so pure, from which something does not go into the belly and is cast out. More correctly others, that it is a synecdoche, every i.e., of everything that enters into the mouth, something is cast out through the privy. *(But the Savior speaks here of bodily and natural foods. Whence the Calvinists ineptly oppose this passage, see Chamier 4. Panstrat. l. 11. c. 16. Wendel. System. Maior. l. 1. c. 23. Exerc. 111. §. 2. Beza Vol. 3. in Apol. ad Acta Conventus Torgensis p. 34. Bucanus Instit. Theol. L. 48 q. 60. Eilshem in Cleinod. p. 845. to the oral eating of the body of Christ, as that concerning which such a thing is a sin to think. We concede that such a thing is a sin, nay blasphemous, to think concerning the body of Christ, but we deny that Christ speaks here of spiritual food and drink, such as the body and blood of Christ, but he speaks of eating, i.e., external, bodily, and natural foods. Conf. more things making for this among the Lords Theologians of Marburg in Fundam. Deduct. p. 802 seqq. B. Par. L. de S. Coenâ §. 187.)*

Latin:

v. 17. Quic quid ingreditur &c. Hieronymus: Quamvis tenuis humor & lique scens esca in corpus fundatu, tamen cùm in venis & artubus concocta fuerit & digesta per occultos meatus corporis, quos Graeciπόρουςvocant, ad inferiora delabitur, in secessum, vadit. Maldonatus: Loquitur Christus non philosophicè, sedpopulariter. Nam quia minimum remanet, loquitur ita, qs. nihil significet remanere. Et ita Thomas quoque sentit, quòd Christus nempe loquatur κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον, quia doctrina de concoctione non nota vulgo. Alii respondent, quòd nullus cibus tam purus, sit, ex quo non aliquid in ventrem vadat & eiiciatur. Rectiùs alii, esse synecdochen, omne i. e. de omni, quod in os intrat, aliquid per secessum, eiicitur. *(Loquitur autem hîc Salvator de cibis corporalibus ac natur alibus. Unde ineptè hunc locum Calviniani, vid. Chamiert. 4. Panstrat. l. 11. c. 16. Wendel. System. Maior. l. 1. c. 23. Exerc. 111. §. 2. Beza Vol. 3. in Apol. ad Acta Conventus Torgensis p. 34. Bucanus Instit. Theol. L. 48 q. 60. Eilshem in Cleinod. p. 845. opponunt manducationi orali corporis Christi, ut de quo tale quid cogitare nefas sit. Concedimus, quòd tale quid de corpore Christi cogitare nefas imò blasphemum sit, sed negamus, quòd hîc Christus loquatur de cibo ac potu spirituali, qualis corpus & sangvis Christi, sed loquitur de manducatione, s. cibis externis, corporalibus ac naturalibus. Conf. plura huc facientia apud Dnn. Theol Marp. in Fundam. Deduct. p. 802 seqq. B. Par. L. de S. Coenâ §. 187.)*

## 15:18
*(v. 18. Which proceed out of the mouth, go out from the heart. Concerning the mouth of the heart see August. l. 15. de Trin. c. 10. Furthermore, that Benjamin F. R. of the Jews uses a similar sentiment in the Introduction, shows Const. L'Empereur in Annot. ad ὁδοιπορ. Mose Kimchi p. 28. where he also rightly warns that the heart is occasionally accepted as the seat of the mind and will, And

thus it is commonly accepted by our Theologians. See B. D. Hutter. in F. C. p. 93.)*

Latin:

*(v. 18. Quae prodeunt ex ore, e-orde egrediuntur. De ore cordis vid August. l. 15. de Trin. c. 10. Simili porrò sententiâ Beniaminum F. R. Iudae in Introd. uti, ostendit Const. L'Empereur in Annot. ad ὁδοιπορ. Mose Kimchi p. 28. ubi etiam rectè monet, corpro mentis ac voluntatis sede subinde accipi, Atq;

sic communiter à nostris Theologis accipitur. Vid. B. D. Hutter. in F. C. p. 93.)*

## 15:19
(v. 19. From the heart come forth thoughts. The source of actual sins is indicated, namely the corruption of our nature through the fall, i.e., original sin. Conf. Matth. 12, 34.Rom. 7, 8.Gal. 5, 17.19. 20.Iac. 1, 14. 15. Isidore of Pelusium looks to this, when in book 1, ep. 194, he writes thus: Whence, he writes, is it, you ask, that evil thoughts come forth from the heart, and defile a man? Surely, because the farmers are sleeping, etc. εἰ γδ κόρῳ i.e., for unless (James Billius does not translate it sufficiently conveniently: For if) we had betrayed our guard through gluttony and lethargy, the sower of tares, by which he might creep upon us, would not have found the divine image defiled, i.e., the excellent seed adulterated, etc. But rightly against the Flacians, who were striving to gather from this passage that original sin is the very substance of man, it is to be noted that the heart is the source of actual sins, not as such, but as it is corrupt, and has inherent depravity. But φθορὰ is one thing, φθαρτὸν, is another, as is evident from 1. Cor. 15, 53. Conf. B. Par. Disp. Isag. p. 987. B. Hutt. in F. C. p. 117. who himself also in the l. c. p. 63. wishes it to be rightly noted that the Savior expressly asserts here that evil thoughts are in the heart: Therefore, he says, evil thoughts will be one thing, the heart another.)

( Evil thoughts, murders &c. Mark c. 7, 20 reports the words of Christ a little differently. But the Fathers derive from this a distinction of sins, that some are sins of the heart, as evil thoughts, some of the mouth, some of the deed. Let Lactantius be seen, book 6, Instit. div. c. 13. Gregory the Great on 1. Reg. c. 13. Bernh. in Parv. serm. 30. Col. 444. Beautifully Chrysostom, serm. 171. This new order of warring: nations go forth from man against man to wage war: we ourselves beget the enemies, we arm them, we bring them forth into battle.)

Βλασφημίαι. By βλασφημίας are understood curses, by which the reputation of a neighbor is harmed, for the etymology of the word shows that.

Latin:

*(v. 19. Ex corde exeunt cogitationes made. Indicatur fons peccatorum actualium, nempe naturae nostrae per lapsum cortuptio s. peccatum originale. Conf. Matth. 12, 34.Rom. 7, 8.Gal. 5, 17.19. 20.Iac. 1, 14. 15. Respicit huc Isidorus Pelusiota, quando lib. l. ep. 194. ita: Unde, scribit, est, inquis, quòd malae co-tationes ex corde exeunt, & coin quinant hominem? Nimirum, quia dormiunt agricolae &c.εἰ γδ κόρῳ h. e. nisi enim (Iacobus Billius non satis commodè reddit: Namsi) ingluvie & veterno custodiam nostram prodidissemus, divinâ videl. imagine centaminat à h. e. praeclaro semine adulterato, ziz aniorum sator, quâ ad nos irraperes, non invenisset &c. Probè verò contra Flacianos, qui ex hoc loco colligere satagebant, quòd pecc. originis sit ipsa hominis substantia, notandum, quòd cor sit fons peccatorum a & valium, non quat. tale, sed quat. corruptum est, & habet pravitatem inhaerentem. Aliud verò est φθορὰ aliud φθαρτὸν, ceu patet ex 1. Cor. 15, 53. Conf. B. Par. Disp. Isag. p. 987. B. Hutt. in F. C. p. 117. qui ipse etiam l. c. p. 63. probè notari vult, quòd Salvator expressè hîc adserat, pravas. cogitationes esse in corde: Ergò, inquit, aliud erunt cogitationes pravae, aliud cor.)*

*( Cogitationes malae, homicidia &C. Paullò aliter Christi verba refert Marcus. c. 7, 20 Desumunt verô hinc Patres distinctionem peccatorum, quòd quaedam sint peceata cordis, ut Cogitationes malae, quaedam oris, quaedam operis. Videatur hactantius lib. 6. Instit. div. c. 13. Gregorius M. in. 1. Reg. c. 13. Bernh. in Parv. serm. 30. Col. 444. Pulcrè Chrysostomus serm 171. Novus hic ordo bellandi: de homine contra hominem gentes exeunt bellaturae: ipsos hostes nos gignimus, armamus, in praelium producimus.)*

Βλασφημίαι. Per βλασφημίας intelliguntur maledicta, quibus laeditur fama proximi, id enim etymologia vocis osteneit.

## 15:21
(v. 21. And departing from there Jesus, withdrew into the parts of Tyre & Sidon. The following history concerning the Canaanite woman is accustomed to be treated more prolixly in the Homilies on the Sunday Gospels, in the explanation of the Gospel.

for the Sunday Reminiscere. Therefore, our learned Doctors Meisner, Glassius, Hunnius, Hoë, Bakius can be unfolded here, also B. Par. in Homil. Acad. and also Dn. D. Walther in Quadragena Miscell. Theolog. in the Explanation on the Gospel for Sunday Reminiscere, which itself is also inserted into the Elenchtic Disputations, held under the presidency of the Blessed Father, from p. 366 to 408. Whence many things can be sought, making for the illustration of the present History.)

*( He withdrew into the parts of Tyre &c. The Savior therefore turns aside here among the Gentiles. As the Interpreters also commonly feel. See Theophylact, Jansenius, Salmero, Granatensis. Nor does it stand in the way that Christ was a minister of the circumcision, Rom. 15, 8. distinguish between the ordinary office of Christ, and the extraordinary, if we may so speak, grace, which ἀλλοφύλοις he exhibited to certain ones. Compare Ioh. 4, 39. 40. Luc. 17, 16. The Gospel indeed had to be preached first to the Jews Matth. 10, 5. as those to whose fathers the promise had been made: but when the Jews rejected it, the Apostles turned themselves to the Gentiles Act. 13, 46. Theophylact judges that the same was done by Christ here, who himself however also responds in another way, that Christ went into Tyre and Sidon, cities of the Gentiles, not as one about to preach there, since as Mark says, he hid himself. H. Grotius explains τὸ εἰς here as towards, since it does not seem to him that Christ went out of the borders of the land of the Hebrews.)*

Latin:

*(v. 21. Et egressus illinc Iosus, recessit inpartes Tyri & Side-. Historia sequens de muliere Cananaea solet prolixiùs per-actari in Homiliis super Evang. Dominicalia, in expl. Evang.

Domin. Reminiscere. Evolvi igitur hîc è nostratibus BB DD. Meisnerus, Glassius, Hunnius, Hoë, Bakius possunt, it. B Par. in Homil. Acad. nec non Dn. D. Waltherus in Quadragena Miscell. Theolog. in Explicat. super Ev. Dom. Remin. queipsa inserta quoq; Disp. Elenchticis, sub praesidio B. P. habitis, à p. 366. ad 408. Unde plurima peti possunt, ad illustrationem praesentis Historiae facientia.)*

*( Recessit in partes Tyri &c. Divertit igitur Salvator hîc apud gentiles. Uti etiam communiter Interpp. Sentient. Vid. Theoph. Iansenius, Salmero, Granatensis. Nec obstrat, quòd Christus fuerit minister circumcisionis,Rom. 15, 8. dist. emm inter ordinarium Christi munus, & extraordinariam, ut ita loquamur, gratiam, quam ἀλλοφύλοις quibusdam exhibuit. Cons. Ioh. 4, 39. 40.Luc. 17, 16. Debuit quidem priùs Evangelium praedicari Iudaeis Matth. 10, 5. utpote quorum patribus facta crat promissio: repellentibus verò illud Iudaeis, ad gentes sese converterunt Apostoli Act. 13, 46. Idē à Christo hîc factum censet Theophy lactus, qui ipse tamen etiam alio modo respondet, quòd Christus iverit in Tyrum & Sidonem gentilium civitates, non ut ibi praedicaturus, cùm ut Marcus dicit, se occultaverit. H. Grotius τὸ εἰς exponit hîc per versus, cùm ipsi non videatur Christus exiisse terrae Ebraeorum fines.)*

## 15:22
v. 22. A Canaanite woman. That the Canaanites lived near Sidon is evident from Iudic. 1. v. 31. & 32. hence the Canaanite woman is said to have come out from the borders of Tyre and Sidon. By Mark she is called ἑλληνης, because she followed the religion and customs of the Greeks. Camer cana- she is called, either because she was sprung from the small town of Cana, situated on the borders of Phoenicia and Galilee, or because she was by birth from the Canaanite peoples. *(The former pleases Adrichomius in the Theater of the Holy Land in the description of the Tribe of Asher n. 31. Arias Montanus in Caleb p. 9. the latter Chrysostom hom. 53. in Matth. B. D. Glassius in Philological Grammar p. 812. and most Interpreters. And this opinion is favored by the writing both Greek in the text itself, and of the Oriental Interpreters, the Syrian, Arabic, Persian and Ethiopian, by whom the city of Cana Ioh, 2, 1. is written with a kaph, just as the Greek with κ. but this woman with a Caph, the Greek with κ. especially because the town of Cana was in the Tribe of Asher, so this woman would have been a Jew by blood, the contrary of which however is evident from the context. Just as also)* Mark c. 7, 26. calls Greek, i. e. Gentile.Gal. 3, 28. *( Rom. 1, 16.c. 2, 9. 10. Nor yet must it be thought that this woman was even then still a worshiper of idols, but rather it is established that even then there were ἐυσεβεῖς. among the Gentiles. See Act. 10, 2.c. 17, 4. The same also Mark calls a Syrophoenician by race. For indeed the Phoenicians also drew their origin from the Canaanites. Wherefore also where in the Hebrew text there is כנען Canaan, the LXX sometimes have φοινίκην. See Exod. 16, 35. also for כנעוים they use the name φοινίκων Iob. 40, 25. Add Ios. 5, 1. There are those who think that the Canaanites were ashamed of their name on account of the curse spoken to their parent, Genes. 9, 25. 26. and so preferred to be called Phoenicians, rather than Canaanites. Which we leave in the middle.)*

*( She cried out. A great voice, an indicator of great affection, of great sadness, of great desire. Yet there is also given a cry of the heart. See Exod. 14, 15.)*

*( Have mercy on me, for she loved her daughter as herself: recognize from this maternal affection.)*

*( Son of David. Compare above c. 1, 27. c. 12, 23. below chapter 20, 31. also Luc. 18, 43.Ioh. 7, 42.)*

Latin:

v. 22. Mulier Cananaea. Ad Sidonem habitasse Chananaeos, patet ex Iudic. 1. v. 31. & 32. hinc dicitur à finibus Tyri ac Sdonis egressa mulier Chananaea. A Marco vocatur ἑλληνης, quod Graecorum religionem & mores sequeretur. Camer cana- vocatur, vel quòd fuerit oriunda ex oppidulo Cana, in finibus Phoeniciae & Galilaeae sito, vel quòd fuerit ex Chananaeis populis ortu. *(Prius arridet Adrichomio in Theatro terrae sanctae in descript. Tribus Aser n. 31. Ariae Montano in Caleb p. 9. posterius Chrysostomo hom. 53. in Matth. B. D. Glassio Gr. S. p. 812. ac Interpp. plerisq;. Favetquehuic sententiae scriptio tum Graeca in ipso textu, tum Interpp. Orientalium Syri, Araois, Persae & Aethiopis, quibus civitas Cana Ioh, 2, 1. per kaph seribitur, quemadmodum Gr. per κ. haec verò mulier per Caph, Gr, per κ. cumprimis quòd Cana oppidum fuerit in Tribu Asser, ita mulier haec sangvine Iudaea fuisset, cuius tamen contrarium è contextu patet. Sicuti etiam)* Marcus c. 7, 26. vocat Graecum i. e. Ethnicam.Gal. 3, 28. *( Rom. 1, 16.c. 2, 9. 10. Neq; taman existimandum, quòd mulier haec tum adhuc idolorum fuerit cultrix, quin potiùs constat, quòd etiam iamtum inter Ethni-os fuerint ἐυσεβεῖς. Vid. Act. 10, 2.c. 17, 4. Idem etiam Marcus vocat Syrophoenissam genere. Etenim & Phoenices ex Cananaeis originem trahebant. Quapropter etiam ubi in textu Ebr. est כנעןCanaan, LXX. aliquando habent φοινίκην. Vid. Exod. 16, 35. it. pro כנעוים iidem utuntur nomine φοινίκωνIob. 40, 25. Add. Ios. 5, 1. Sunt qui putant, Cananaeos puduisse sui nominis propter anathema ipsorum parenti dictum, Genes. 9, 25. 26. adeoque maluisse audire Phoenices, quàm Cananaeos. Quod in medio relinquimus.)*

*( Clamavit. magna vox magni affectûs, magnae tristitiae, magni desiderii indicina. Datur tamen & clamor cordis. Vid. Exod. 14, 15.)*

*( Miserere mei, filiam enim amabat ut semetipsam: agnosce hinc affectum maternum.)*

*( Fili David. Conf. suprà c. 1, 27. c. 12, 23. infrà cap. 20, 31. it. Luc. 18, 43.Ioh. 7, 42.)*

## 15:23
v. 23. --κ ἀπεκρίθη αὐτῷ λόγον. Αόγος. is placed after the manner of the Hebrews, who take speech for a thing indeterminately, just as the Greeks also in that manner of speaking εἰπεῖ λόγον to speak. A wonderful thing! The Word of the Father does not speak. The Wisdom of GOD answers nothing. The Physician does not heal. The Fountain of mercy turns away from misery. He who calls those not seeking, rejects one calling upon Him. *(Compare Es. 30, 19.c. 65, 24.)* Basil. Orat. 20. on the Canaanite. ἡ του δεσῶότου σιωπὴ τῆς Ξανανίδος ἔπαινος. The Lord's silence was the Canaanite woman's praise. Chrysost. hom. 44. on Gen. The Lord knew the hidden pearl which He did not wish to be hidden from us, therefore He delayed, He did not deem her worthy of a response, so that the woman's diligence might be a great lesson for all posterity. *(The same hom. 24. on the ep. to the Eph. dealing with Anna; If He had given before the petition, the alacrity of the woman's mind would not have appeared, her virtue would not have been manifest, she would not have acquired so great a reward. Wherefore the delay was not of envy, but of care and providence. Compare

id. hom. 97. to the people & hom. 53. on Matth. and also hom. 38. on Genesis. Christ does not answer the woman, not so that he might deny mercy, but that he might kindle desire, prove her faith, explore her patience, manifest her constancy, and thus show to us an example of living solid faith. See Augustine, sermon 74 de Temp. also in Ps. 65. Moreover, from the fact that Christ towards the Canaanite woman showed himself outwardly harsh and severe, yet was of fatherly affection towards her, the Calvinists strive to prove that it is not repugnant to God to establish a twofold will in him, of sign and of good pleasure. And from there they further infer that God, by the will of sign, which he has revealed in the Scriptures, declares that he wills the salvation of all men, but inwardly in his secret counsel or will of good pleasure has decreed far otherwise. But one must distinguish between lawful simulation and unlawful. The former is profitable and teaches; the latter deceives and harms. The former, as it is not opposed to the law, so it also falls into a good man, and such also is that by which Christ here simulated himself to be harsh; the latter (unlawful) is opposed to the will of GOD and the salvation of one's neighbor, and such is that which the Calvinists, by that distinction between the will of sign and of good pleasure, attribute to God. Conf. B. D. Meisn Ἀνθρωπ. Sacrae Disp. 12. q. 1. §. 33.)

*( Send her away -mat after us. Corn à Lapide in this place explains: Free both her from the pain and labor of crying out, and us from the annoyance of hearing, lest she dull our ears. The Disciples seem indeed to have interceded for this woman not so much out of mercy and readiness to help, as out of impatience. Conf. Marc. 6, 35.Luc. 18, 5. nor is it read that the woman even begged for the intercession of the Apostles. Whence also the Jesuit Salmero asserts it doubtfully. Perhaps, he writes, the Apostles interceded having been asked by her. A slippery argument, therefore, is that which the Papists fabricate from this place for the intercession of the dead, and the invocation of the same on account of it. See Stapleton in Promt. Cathol. part. 3. fer. 5. hebd. prim. quadr. p. 41. And even if it were granted in the highest degree that the Apostles were solicited by the Canaanite woman for intercession, and also that the Apostles interceded out of commiseration, it does not follow, however, that the dead are therefore to be invoked. The calamity of the woman was known to the Apostles. But concerning the dead, that is by no means certain, but rather on the contrary the Sacred letters teach us. There is, moreover, a great difference between the naked calling upon the living, of which very many examples are given in the Holy Scriptures, and between the religious invocation of the dead, of which the Papists have hitherto shown no proven example, nor will they ever be able to. See the Analecta on c. 8. Matth. v. 5. and add the Lord D. Walth. l. c. p. 392. also the Blessed D. Mentzer Disp. 6: against Pistor. the Blessed D. Chem Part. 3. Exam. of the Council of Trent. the Blessed D. Giesen Papism. Disp. 23. & 24. the Blessed D. Lobech. Disp. 23. on the A. C. c. 3. Note Theophylact on this passage: Observe, that although the saints (that is, pious men still living with us) pray for us, just as the Apostles did for that (Canaanite woman), yet we are heard more when we pray for ourselves. Which observation is taken from Chrysostom on this passage, who also proves the same by the example of this woman, as he says she was repulsed when others asked, but heard when she herself prayed.)*

Latin:

v. 23. --κ ἀπεκρίθη αὐτῷ λόγον. Αόγος. ponitur more Ebraeorum, qui sermonem pro re indeterminatè accipiunt, sicut & Graeci in illo dicendi genere εἰπεῖ λόγον logui. Orem miram! Verbum Patris non loquitur. Sapientia DEI nihil respondet. Medicus non curat. Fons misericor diae aversatur miseriam. Qui non-quaerentes vocat, se invocantem respuit. *(Conf. Es. 30, 19.c. 65, 24.)* Basil. Orat. 20. in Chanan. ἡ του δεσῶότου σιωπὴ τῆς Ξανανίδος ἔπαινος.Domini silentium erat Chananaeae encomium. Chrysoft. hom. 44. in Gen. Sciebat Dominut reconditam margaritam quam latere nos nolebat, idcircò differebat, nresponso dignabatur, ut posteris omnibus mulieris sedulitas maegna foret doctrina. *(Idem hom. 24. in ep. Eph. de Anna agens; Si dedisset ante petitionem, non apparuisset mulieris animi alacritas, non fuisset manifesta eius virtus, non tant am acquisivisset mercedem. Quamobrem dilatio nō erat invidiae, sed curae ac providentiae. Conf.

id. hom. 97. ad popul. & hom. 53. in Matth. nec non hom. 38. in Genesin. Non respondet Christus mulieri, non ut misericordiam negaret, sed ut desiderium accenderet, fidem eius probater, patientiam exploraret, constantiam manifestaret, sicque vivae nobis solidaefidei exemplum monstraret. Vid. Augustin. serm. 74. de Temp. it. in Ps. 65. Coeterùm ex eo quòd Christus ergCananaeam forinsecus durum atque severum se ostenderit, eum tamē paterno affectu erga eam fuerit, probare Calvinianisatagunt, non repugnare Deo, duplicem in eostatuere voluntatem, figni ac beneplaciti. Atque inde porrò inferunt, quòd Deus voluntate signi, quam in Scripturis patefecerit, omnium hominum salutem se velle declaret, intus autem in arcano suo consilio sive voluntate beneplaciti longè aliud decreverit. Verùm disting, inter simulationem licitam, & illicitam. illa prodest & docet; hac fallit ac nocet. Illa uti non adversatur legi, ita etiam in bonum virum cadit, & talis quoque est ea quâ Christus hîc se durum simulavit; haec verò (illicita) adversatur DEI voluntati ac proximi saluti, & talis est, quam Calviniani distinctione illâ inter voluntatem signi & beneplaciti, Deo tribuunt. Conf. B. D. Meisn Ἀνθρωπ. Sacrae Disp. 12. q. 1. §. 33.)*

*( Dimitte eam -mat post nos. Corn à Lapide in h. l. explicat: Libera & illam à dolore, & labore clamandi, acte & noà molestia audiendi, ne nobis, aures obtundat. Videntur sanè Discipuli non tam ex misericordiâ & juvandi promtitudine, quam ex impatientiâ pro hâc muliere intercessisse. Conf. Marc. 6, 35.Luc. 18, 5. nec legitur etiam mulier Apostolorum intercessionem esslagitasse. Unde etiam Iesuita Salmero dubitanter id adserit. Fortè, scribit, ab eâ rogati intercesserunt Apostoli. Lubricum ergò essargumentū, quod ex h. l. pro defunctorum intercessione, eorundemq; ob eam invocatione Pontificii fabricant. Vid. Stapletonus in Promt. Cathol. part. 3. fer. 5. hebd. prim. quadr. p. 41. Et si vel maximè concedatur, Apostolos à Cananaea ad inter cessionem fuisse solicitatos, it. Apostolos ex commiseratione interpellasse, non tamen sequitur, quòd defuncti proptereà sint invocandi. Apostolis mulieris calamitas fuit nota. De defunctis verò minimè id constat, sed potiùs contraSacrae literae nos docena. Magnum praetereà discrimen est inter nudam viventium compellationem, cuius plurima in Sc S. dantur exempla, & inter religiosam defunctorum invocationem, cuius nullum hactenus Pontificii probatum ostenderunt exemplum, nec poterunt etiam unquam. Vid Analect. ad c. 8. Matth. v. 5. ac add. Dn. D. Walth. l. c. p. 392. it. B. D. Mentzerum Disp. 6: contra Pistor. B. D. Chem Part. 3. Exam. Concilii Trid. B. D. Giesen. Papism. Disp. 23. & 24. B. D. Lobech. Disp. 23. in A. C. c. 3. Notanter Theophy lactus in h. l. Observa, quòd licet sancti (f. nobiscum adhuc versantes pii homines) orent pronobis, sicut pro illâ (muliere Cananaea) Apostoli, attamen nos pro nobis ipsis petenies magis audimur. Quae observatio desumta ex Chrysostomo in h. l. qui eandem quoq; probat exemplo huius mulieris, ut quam repulsam dicit, cùm alii rogarent; auditam, cùm ipsa precaretur.)*

## 15:24
*(v. 24. I am not sent except &c. That these things and πειραςικῶς were uttered by Christ in a feigned manner, the Blessed D. Glassius Rh. S. p. 89 well observes, where he also elegantly says: He separates her outwardly from the sheep, and by that very act he secretly cherishes and comforts her as his own tender sheep. He compares her outwardly to dogs, and by that very act he places her at the royal table of sons and daughters. The same man also conveniently brings forward the words of Chrysostom hom. 44 in Gen. The Lord knew the hidden pearl, which he did not want to be hidden from us, therefore he delayed, and did not deign to respond, so that the diligence of the woman, being manifest to all, would be a great lesson. Christ was a minister of the circumcision, Rom. 15, 8. so that he might show his bodily presence only to those to whose fathers he was promised. August. tract. 31. in Ioh. Piscator in Annot. on this passage rightly writes: I am not sent, understand as a Prophet. See t. 2. Loc. de Eccl. Tossanus also rightly warns, this is to be understood only of that time, in which Christ was occupied on earth. One part of the office was διακονία, another ἀπολύτρωσις. *(Another office of redemption, according to which Christ was sent to all. see 1. Timoth. 2, 6. 2. Peter. 2, 1. also to the gentiles, Es. 49, 6. c. 60, 3. Ioh. 10, 16. c. 11, 52. another Ministry of preaching, according to which, to be performed in his own person, he was sent only to the Jews, See Rom. 15. 8. also Act. 13, 46. and Cons. Isidore of Pelusium l. 1. ep. 121. Cyril t. 5. l. 5. in Isaiah page 590. August. t. 9. tr. 47. in John also Qq. Evang. lib. 1. c. 18. Christ speaks here of this, not of that. Augustine teaches this excellently tr. 31. in Ioh. According to the appearance of the body, which the Jews saw and despised, Christ was not among us, because this also had been said of him, as the Apostle says, for I say that Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God to confirm the promises made to the fathers: he ought to have come to those from whose fathers and whose fathers he was promised, therefore he himself also says thus: I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel. But what does the Apostle say in the following? And that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy: What also the Lord himself? I have other sheep, which are not of this fold: he who had said, I am not sent, but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel: how does he have others, to whom he was not sent? unless because he signified that by his bodily presence he did not show himself sent except to the Jews alone, who saw and killed, and yet many from thence both before and after believed etc. Similar things from the same sermon 74 de Temp. which B. Par. L. de Reprob. §. 121 even cites from Calvin himself in this place. They also admit this explanation, that namely Christ speaks here of the Prophetic office, to be administered immediately, that is, in his own person, Abrah. Scultetus in Observ. ad Ev. c. 43. p. 59. Perkins t. 1. of his Works in Expl. Symb. p. 779. Tilenus part. 2. Syntagm. Disput. 2. pag. 477. Marloratus in this place. Grossius in Theatr. Bibl. in this place. Hilarius in Matth. Canon. XV. He answered that he was sent to the lost sheep of Israel etc. not that salvation was not also to be imparted to the Gentiles. But the Lord had come to his own and into his own, he unfolds the first fruits of faith to those from whom he had arisen, with the rest to be saved subsequently by the preaching of the Apostles. But that Christ, as regards his Priestly or Mediatorial office, was not only sent to the elect, but is the redeemer of all men entirely, is evident abundantly from the sacred scriptures. See Ioh. 1, 9.c. 3, 16.Rom. 5, 8.18. 19.c. 8, 32.c. 4. 16.1. Cor. 8, 11.2. Cor. 5, 14.Ebr. 6, 14.1. Ioh. 2, 2. Therefore they are inept who strive to impugn the general redemption of Christ from this present saying of the Savior, as Paraeus dared, in his additions to the Catechism of Ursinus, not considering that by this very thing he excludes himself and his associates from the benefit of the redemption provided by Christ. For if the benefit of redemption is to be restricted to the lost sheep of the house of Israel alone, it follows that Christ died for no one except him who could show his birth among the Jews. Since Paraeus will be able to prove this of himself with difficulty, it is certainly necessary that he deprive himself of the benefit of Christ's redemption. Nor is there any reason why he should object that he, through lost sheep to understand spiritual Israelites. For such a woman also was the Canaanite, inasmuch as Christ proclaims her faith great, and yet at the same time denies that He was sent to her. Compare more on this matter in B. P. L. de Elect. & Reprob. §. 121.)*

To the lost sheep The Syriac: to the sheep, which have wandered from the house of Israel. *(Compare what is noted at Matth. 10, 6. I. Malderus, Bishop of Antwerp, in Anti Synod. understands spiritual Israel by lost sheep of the house of Israel. But since Christ in this place excludes the Canaanite woman, who nevertheless belonged entirely to the spiritual Israel, from the lost sheep of the house of Israel, it is manifest that the discourse in this place is about the posterity of Israel, as Theophylact also rightly explains.)*

Latin:

*(v. 24. Non sum missus nisi &c. Simulanter haec & πειραςικῶς à Christo fuisse prolata, benè observat B. D. Glassius Rh. S. p. 89. ubi & eleganter: Ab ovibus eam exteriùs segregat, & eo ipso occultè ut tenellam ovem suam fovet & confortat. Catellis eam exteriùs aequiparat, & eo ipso in filiorum filiarumq; mensam regiam collocat. Commodè etiam idem adducit verba Chrysostomi hom. 44 in Gen. Sciebat Dominus reconditammar garitam, quam latere nos noleb at, idrircò differebat, nec response dignabatur, ut postoris omnibus mulieris sedulitas, magna foret doctrina.)* Christus fuit minister circumcisionis,Rom. 15, 8. ut ipsis solis. exhiberet praesentiam corporalem quorum patribus promissus est. August. tract. 31. in Ioh. Piscator in Annot. h. l. rectè scribit: Non sum missus, intellige ut Propheta. Vid. t. 2. Loc. de Eccl. Tossanuquoq; rectè monet, hoc intelligendum tantùm de illo tempore, quo Christus in terris fuit versatus Alia pars officii fuit διακονία, alia ἀπολύτρωσις. *(Aliud officium redemtionis, secundùm quod Christus ad omnes missus. vid. 1. Timoth. 2, 6.2. Peter. 2, 1. etiam ad gentes, Es. 49, 6.c. 60, 3.Ioh. 10, 16.c. 11, 52. aliud Ministerium, pradicationis, secundùm quod, in propriâ persona peragendum, solis missus Iudaeis, Vid. Rom. 15. 8. it. Act. 13, 46. ac Cons. Isid. Pelusiotam l. 1. ep. 121. Cyrillum t. 5. l. 5. in Esaiam pag. 590. August. t. 9. tr. 47. in Iohannem it. Qq. Evang. lib. 1. c. 18. De hoc, non de illo Christus h. l. loquitur. Egregiè hoc docet August. tr. 31. in Ioh. Secundùm speciem corporis, quam viderunt Iudaei & contemserunt, non apud nos fuit Christus, quia & hoc de illo dictum erat, sicut Apostolus dicit, dico enim, Christum fuisse ministrum circumcisionis propter veritatem DEI ad confirmandas promisiones Patribus factas: ad illos debuit venire, à quorum patribus & quorum Patribus est promissus, ideò & ipse sic ait: Non sum missus nisi ad oves, quae perierunt, domûs Israel. Sed quid dicit Apostolus in sequenti? Gentes autem super misericor diâ glorificare Deum: Quid & ipse Dominus? Habeo alias oves, quae non sunt ex hoc ovili: qui dixerat, non sum missus, nisi ad oves quae perierunt domus Israel: quomodo habet alias, ad quas non est missus? nisi quia significavit, per praesentiam corporalem non se missum exhibere nisi solis Iudaeis, qui viderunt & occiderunt, & multi tamen inde & antea & postea crediderunt &c. Similia ex eiusdem serm. 74. de Temp. quin ipso etiam Calvino in h. l. adducit B. Par. L. de Reprob. §. 121. Admittunt quoq; explicationem hanc, quòd videl. Christus loquatur hîc de officio Prophetico, immediatè s. in propriâ personâ administrando, Abrah. Scultetus in Observ. ad Ev. c. 43. p. 59. Perkin sus t. 1. Operum in Expl. Symb. p. 779. Tilenus part. 2. Syntagm. Disput. 2. pag. 477. Marloratus in h. l. Grossius in Theatr. Bibl. h. l. Hilarius in Matth. Canon. XV. Ovibus se perditis Israel missume esse respondit &c. non quòd non & gentibus impertienda salus esset. Sed suis Dominus atq; in sua venerat, primitias fidei his, à quibus erat ortus, explicat, coeteris deinceps Apostolorum praedicatione salvandis. Quòd verò Christus quoad officium Sacerdotale vel Mediatorium non solùm ad electos missus, sed omnium omninò hominū redemtor sit, patet è sacris scripturis abunde. Vid. Ioh. 1, 9.c. 3, 16.Rom. 5, 8.18. 19.c. 8, 32.c. 4. 16.1. Cor. 8, 11.2. Cor. 5, 14.Ebr. 6, 14.1. Ioh. 2, 2. Inepti igitur sunt, qui è praesenti Salvatoris dicto generalem Christi redemtionē impugnare satagunt, uti Paraeus ausus fuit, add. ad Catech. Ursini, non confiderans, quòd hoc ipso se suosq; sociennos à redemtionis per Christum praestitae beneficio excludat. Etenimsi beneficium redemtionis ad solas oves perditas de domo Israel restringendum sequitur, quòd Christus pro nemine mortuus sit nisi qui natales suos inter Iudaeos ostendere valuerit. Quod cùm difficulter Paraeus de se praestiturus sit, necesse sanè est, ut seipsum redemtionis Christi beneficio privet. Nec est, quòd excipiat, se per oves perditas intelligere spirituales Israelitas. Etenim talis quoque mulier Chananaea erat, utpote cuius fidem magnam depraedicat Christus, & tamen simul negat, se ad eam esse missum. Conf. plura in hanc rem apud B. P. L. de Elect. & Reprob. §. 121.)*

Ad oves perditas Syrus: ad oves, quae erraverunt è domo Israel. *(Confer quae notata ad Matth. 10, 6. I. Malderus, Episcopus Antverp. in Anti Synod. intelligit spiritualem Israel per oves perditas de domo Israel. Verùm cùm Christus h. l. Cananaeam mulierem, quae tamen omninò ad spiritualem Israel pertinebat, excludat ab ovibus perditis de domo Israel, manifestum est, quòd de posteritate Israelis h. l. sermo sit. uti etiam rectè exponit Theophylactus.)*

## 15:25
v. 25. And she worshipped him. From the fact that Christ in the days of his flesh was worshipped, as is evident both from this place and others, see above c. 2, 11. c. 8, 25: below c. 17, 15. c. 20, 3 &c., the orthodox rightly conclude both that he himself is the true eternal God, against the Photinians; and that truly divine and infinite gifts were communicated to his human nature. Against the Calvinists and Jesuits.)* *(

Latin:

*(v. 25. Et adoravit eum. Ex eo quòd Christus in diebus carnis fuit adoratus, ceu tum ex h. l. tum aliis, vid. suprà c. 2, 11. c. 8, 25: infrà c 17, 15. c. 20, 3 &c fuit adoratus, rectè colligunt orthodoxi, tum quòd ipse sit verus aeternus Deus, contra Photinianos; tum quòd humanae eius naturae dona verè divina & infinita fuerint communicata. Contra Calvinianos ac Iesuitas.)*

## 15:26
v. 26. To the children. The Israelites were children of the covenant. Likewise children of the kingdom, above c. 8, 12. The Israelites were children on account of adoption, Rom. 9, 4. the Gentiles on the contrary [were] dogs, both on account of filthiness, 2. Petr 2, 22. and vileness, 2 Sam 3, 8. 2. Reg. 18, 13. )*

Bread. By bread are understood those peculiar benefits, as being due to the Jews as children of GOD Exod 4, 22 on account of the covenant Gen. 17, 7. *(Theoph. bread in this place explains as virtue & a great sign. )*

Dogs. Thus the Gentiles are called, because on account of the foreskin they were detested and despised among the Jews. The Gentiles are compared to dogs on account of the filth of idolatry. The word dog otherwise figuratively in almost all languages denotes a most vile, impudent, and detested man. Flac in Clav. part. l p. 89 *(Compare Gatak. in Cinno p 362. Pelarg in this place and Comment. on 1. Sam. 17, 43c. 24, 15.

2. Sam. 9, 8. Moreover, since a diminutive is used here, it seems at least that Christ in this place wished to indicate the difference between -children and strangers.)*

Here it is pious to consider that great benefit of GOD, that He rejected His own children the Israelites on account of disobedience, and distributed to us miserable little dogs not crumbs, but the treasure of His heavenly benefits. Compare also Luc. 1, 79 with Es. 9, 2. and Eph. 2, 12. with v. 14. 15. Concerning which benefit the blessed Pareus, L. de Eccl. §. 43, treats at greater length. See also Luc. 14, 16. Rom. 11, 17. c. 15, 8. 9. Add by all means also Theodoret on Ps 9. and Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, ep. 143. Furthermore, even if by dogs in this place one were to understand not only specifically the Gentiles, which interpretation the scope of Christ nevertheless demands, but in general impious men, even those established in the very bosom of the Church, the Calvinists nevertheless infer less firmly from this (see Ursinus in Catech. p. 593) that in the Holy Eucharist the unworthy do not truly and in reality receive the body of Christ sacramentally. For although we may easily grant that they do not receive the body of Christ unto salvation, but unto judgment, 1. Cor. 11, 29, it is nevertheless not permitted to infer that they do not receive it at all. Notably Peter Damian in the booklet Gratissimus c. 6 writes: Was that morsel which the Lord handed to Judas not good? But that which was a cause of salvation became for him a matter of condemnation, because he who was not at peace received the instrument of peace. And a little later: Nor did it cease to be a Sacrament because the execrable one received it: but rather it must be asserted that because the thing was made an occasion of death to the unworthy, which was procured for the good as a remedy of salvation. Compare more things pertinent to this in the Anal. on 1. Cor. 11, 29. As far as the present passage is concerned, the contrary can rather be gathered from it. For just as dogs truly receive and eat the bread either undeservedly thrown to them or even snatched away from the children: so also the unworthy truly receive and eat the body of Christ in the Holy Eucharist, although they at least feign piety, and thus snatch it for themselves undeservedly. Meanwhile, we easily grant that just as it is not honorable that bread be snatched away from children, so also notorious impenitent sinners ought not to be admitted to the communion of the Holy Supper. Concerning which matter see the blessed Pareus, L. de S. Coenâ §. 223 and compare the Anal. on cap. 7. Matth. v. 6

Furthermore, the scope of the Savior here is not to treat of the Holy Eucharist, but of the grace of miracles. Nor, finally, does Beza, vol. 1, p. 343, correctly infer from the present passage, That since Christ distinguishes between children and dogs; God, from the time when Adam sinned, ceased to be the father of the human race, and began to be the father at least of those whom he chose in another Ad-mo to eternal life from eternity. But the Savior by no means in this distinction here has regard to the elect and the reprobate, but as is evident from the context, to the Jews and the Gentiles. For if by the name of children in this place were understood only the elect, and by the name of dogs only the reprobate, it follows that all the Jews were elected to eternal life, since the same are understood here by the name of children, who a little before were understood by the name of sheep. Now indeed, with Calvin himself as interpreter, by the name of the lost sheep of the house of Israel is understood here the entire posterity of Abraham. On the contrary, if by the name of dogs in this place were understood at least the reprobate, it would be a consequence that this woman was in the number of the reprobate, whose faith, however, is celebrated as great.

Latin:

*(v. 26. Filiis. Israelitae fuerunt filii foederis. Item filii regni, suprà c. 8, 12. erant Israelitae filii propter adoptionem, Rom. 9, 4. gentes contrà canes tum propter spurcitiem, 2. Petr 2, 22. tum vilitatem, 2 Sam 3, 8.2. Reg. 18, 13.)*

Panem. Per panem intelliguntur peculiaria illa beneficia, Iudaeis utpote DEI filiis Exod 4, 22 propter foedus Gen. 17, 7. debita. *(Theoph. panem h. l. exponit virtutem & signum magnum.)*

Canes. Ita dicuntur gentes, quia propter praeputium erant exosi & contemti apud Iudaeos. Comparantur gentes canibus ob idololatriae spurcitiem. Canis vocabulum aliàs figuratè in omnibus ferè lingvis vilissimum, impudentem & exo um hominem notat. Flac in Clav. part. l p. 89 *(Conf. Gatak. in Cinno p 362. Pelarg h. l. ac Comment. ad 1. Sam. 17, 43c. 24, 15.

2. Sam. 9, 8. Coeterùm cùm diminitivum hîc adhibeatur, videtur saltem Christus h. l. indicare voluisse differentiam inter -lios & extraneos.)*

*(Piè hîc considerandum ingens illud DEI beneficium quòd filios suos Israelitas propter inobedientiam repulit. & nobis miseris catellis non micas, sed thesaurum coelestium beneficiorum suorum distribuit. Conf. etiam Luc. 1, 79 cum Es. 9, 2. it Eph. 2, 12. cum v. 14. 15. De quo benesicio prolixiùs er Luc. 14, 16.Rom. 11, 17.c. 15, 8. 9. agit B. Par. L. de Eccl. §. 43. Add omninò quoque Theodoretus in Ps 9. & Isidor. Pelusiota lib. l. ep. 143. Caeterùm si vel maximè per canes intelligantur h. l. non solùm in specie gentiles, quam tamen acceptionem Christi scopus exigit, sed in genere homines impii, etiam in ipso Ecclesiae gremio constituti, minùs tamen firmiter exinde colligunt Calviniani, (vid. Ursinus in Catech. p. 593.) quòd in S. Eucharistia indigni non verè & reipsa accipiant sacramentaliter corpus Christi. Etenim licet facilè largiamur, quòd non accipiant corpus Christi ad salutē, sed ad iudicium, 1. Cor. 11, 29 non tamē inferre licet, quòd planè non accipiant. Notanter Petrus Damiani in libello Gratissimo c. 6. Nūquid, scribit, bucella illa, quā Iudae Dominus porrexit, bona non fuit? Sed quod erat causa salutis, illi factum est materia condemnationis, quia instrumētum pacis non pacatus accepit. Et paullò pòst: nec ideò Sacramentū esse desiit, quia execrandus accepit: sed potiùs adserendum est, quia indigno res facta est occasio mortis, quae bonis procurata est ad remedium salutis. Conf. plura huc facientia in Anal ad 1. Cor. 11, 29. Quod praesentem locum attinet, potiùs contratium inde colligi potest. Quemadmodum enim canes panevel immeritò eis obiectum, vel filiis etiam praereptum, verè accipiunt atque edunt: ita quoq; indigni corpus Christi in S. Eucharistiâ verè accipiuntac manducant, licet pietatem saltem simulent, adeoque immeritò sibi illud rapiant. Interea facilè largimur, quòd quemadmodum honestum non est, ut panis filiis praeripiatur, ita quoq; notorii impoenitentes peccatores ad S. Coenae communionem admittendi haut sint. Quâ de re vid B. Par. L. de S. Coenâ §. 223 ac Conf. Anal. ad cap. 7. Matth. v. 6

Praeterea scopus Salvatoris hîc non est agere de S. Eucharistiâ. sed de miraculorum gratia. Nec rectè deniq; Beza vol. 1. p. 343. ex praesenti loco colligit, quòd cùm Christus distingvat inter filies & canes; Deum, ex quo Adaemus peccavit, desiisse esse patrem humanigeneris, & eorum saltem patrem esse coepisse, quos in altero Ad-mo ad vitam aeternam ab aet. elegit. Verùm minimè distinctione eâ Salvator hîc respicit ad electos & reprobos, sed uti ex cōtextu patet, ad Iudaeos & gentiles. Quod si enim nomine filiorum h. l. intelligerentur soli electi, ac nomine canum soli reprobi, sequitur, omnes Iudaeos fuisse ad vitam aeternam electos, cùm iidem hîc nomine filiorum intelligantur, quipaullò antè nomine ovium. Iam verò, interprete ipso Calvino, nomine ovium perditarum de domo Israel intelligitur hîc universa Abrahami posteritas. Contrà si nomine canum h. l. intelligarentur saltem reprobi, consequens esset, hanc mulierem fuisse in numero reproborum, cuius tamen fides magna celebratur.)*

## 15:27
v. 27. But she answered. Ambrose in chapter 7 of Luke. This woman was persistent in prayers, wise in responses, faithful in words. She called back the one passing by, she asked the one who was silent, she adored the one who was making excuses, she inclined the one who was refusing. *(Let us indeed learn constancy in prayer from this woman, following the admonition of Chrysostom, homily 30 on Genesis: Whether we obtain what we ask, or do not obtain it, let us always persevere in prayer. And let us not only give thanks if we obtain it, but also if we have suffered a refusal. For when God denies us something, it is no less than if He had granted it: for we do not know what is profitable for us. He, however, knows.)*

They eat. Syriac: Even the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from the tables of their masters and live. The Paraphrast added this word to illustrate the text. It could be translated and are to be saved or are to be preserved. *(Chrysostom thus in this place: If I am a dog, I am not a stranger. You call me a dog, therefore feed me as a dog, I cannot leave the table of my Lord.)*

Latin:

v. 27. Haec autem respondit. Ambrosius in c. 7. Lucae. Mulier hac fuit pertinax in precibus, sapiens in responsis, fidelis in verbis. Praetereuntem revocavit, tacentem rogavit, excusantem adoravit, negantem inclinavit. *(Discamus verò ab hac muliere in oratione constantiam, secuti monitum Chrysostomi hom. 30. in Gen. Sive consequamur, quod petimus, sive non consequamur, perseveremus semper in oratione. Et non solùm gratias agamus, si consequamur, sed etiam si repulsam passi fuerimus. Nam cùm Deus aliquid nobis denegat, non minus est, quàm si concessisset: nescimus enim nos quae nobis, conducant. Ipse verò novit.)*

Edunt. Syr. Etiam canes comedunt de micis, quae caedunt è mensis dominorum suorum & vivunt Hoc verbum addidit Paraphrastes ad illustrandum textum. Posset verti & salvandi seu servandi sunt. *(Chrysost. ita in h. l. Si canis sum, non sum aliena. Canem me dicis, ergo nutrime ut canem, non possum relinquere mensam Domini mei.)*

## 15:28
v. 28. Great is your faith. This woman is deservedly called mother and crown of believers. Origen in this place: Nothing in the sight of GOD is wonderful, however precious and great it may be, except faith alone. Charity of the woman shone forth in the requested healing of her daughter, and in the preference of the Jews; Piety in the inquiry of the true GOD; humility in prostration and the confession of unworthiness; hope in prayer; prudence in responses, perseverance in repulses. Christ, however, praises faith alone, 1. because it alone is the medium through which divine benefits are received. 2. because it is the root of the remaining virtues. *(Although, therefore, faith alone justifies, it is nevertheless never alone. And St. Augustine also looks to this when, in the book On Faith and Works, ch. 16, he writes: I wonder, he writes, if he would praise in it faith without works, i.e., faith not such as can already work through love, a dead faith: and what James did not hesitate to say, the faith not of Christians, but of demons, etc. He repeats the same in the book On the Eight Questions of Dulcitius, q. 1. It is also evident from this that justifying faith is not completed by knowledge and assent, but that trust is also required for it, as that which, clinging to the word, ought to overcome temptations, as can be seen here in the Canaanite woman, who in the most grievous struggle of faith most bravely overcame temptations concerning unworthiness and particularity. How, furthermore, the faith of believers is called ἰσότιμος in 2 Pet. 1, 1, when one is small, another great, as here the faith of the Canaanite, the Blessed Pareus explains in his Commentary on that place; see the notes above on ch. 8, 10. But especially in this woman it is to be considered that she prayed wisely, ardently, faithfully, urgently, constantly, as Mr. Dr. Walther beautifully extracts from the bowels of the context in Quadrag. Miscel. Theol. them. 8, p. 377, who himself also in the same place, p. 384, warns that it is worthy of eternal observation that Christ admired the faith of no man except that of Gentiles, the Centurion, Matt. 8, 10, the Samaritan Leper, Luke 17, 19, and this Canaanite. Finally, Theophylact provides a spiritual exposition of the present history, which can be consulted.)*

*( Let it be done to you as you wish. Concerning the efficacy and dignity of faith, see by all means the Blessed D. R-nig Append Cas. Catech. case 1, p. 20, 21. Pelargus, Questions and Answers on Matthew, p. 176. Furthermore, from this imperial voice, Isidore of Pelusium gathers, l. IV, ep. 166, that Christ reigns with equal power with the Father, since these things are fitting not for a leader or a soldier arrogating to himself the dignity of a King, but for a King: I say to you, τὸ γδ he continues, τὸ γδ

Latin:

v. 28. Magna est fides tua. Mulier haec meritò vocatur mater & corona credentium. Origenes h. l. Nihil in conspectu DEI est mirabile, quävis pretiosum sit & magnum, nisi tantùm fides. Caritas mulieris enituit in filiae petitâ curatione, & Iudaeorum praelatione; pietas in veri DEI inquisitione; humilitas in prostratione & indignitatis confessione; spes in oratione; prudentia in responsis, perseverantia in repulsis. Christus tamen solam fidem laudat, 1. quia sola est medium, per quod beneficia divina recipiuntur. 2. quia est radix virtutum reliquarum. *(Licet igitur sola fides iustificet, nunquam tamen est sola. Atq; huc respicit etiam S. August. quando lib. de fide & operibus c. 16. Miror, scribit, si laudaret in ea fidem sine operibus, i. e. fidem non talem, quae per dilectionem iam possit operari, fidem mortuam: & quod Iacobus dicere minimè dubitavit, fidem non Christianorum, sed doemonum &c. Eadem repetit lib. de Octo Dulcitii Qq. q. 1. Patet etiam hinc, quòd fides iustificans non absolvatur notitia & adsensu, sed quòd eam quoque requiratur fiducia, uti quae verbo inhaerens tentationes vincere debet, ceu hîc in Cananaeâ videre licet, quae in gravissimâ fidei luctâ tentationes de indignitate & particularitate fortissimè superavit. Quomodo porrò credentium fides ἰσότιμος dicatur 2. Petr. 1, 2 cùm alia fit parva, alia magna, ut hîc fides Cananaeae, exponit B. Par. in Comm. eius loci vid. notata suprà ad c. 8, 10. Cumprimis verò in muliere hâc considerandum, quòd oraverit sapienter, ardenter, fideliter, urgenter, constanter, ceu pulcrè è contextûs visceribus eruit Dn. D. Waltherus in Quadrag. Miscel. Theol. them. 8. p. 377. qui ipse etiam l. c. p. 384. monet, dignum esse aeternâ observatione, Christum nullius hominis fidem admiratum esse, nisi gentilium, Centurionis, Matth. 8, 10. Leprosi Samaritani, Luc. 17, 19. & huius Cananaeae. Spiritualem tandem praesentis historiae expositionem suppeditat Theophylactus, qui potest evolvi.)*

*( Fiat tibi ut vis. De fidei efficaciâ & dignitate vid. omninò B. D. R-nig Append Cas. Catech. casu 1. p. 20. 21. Pelargus Qq. ac Resp. in Matth. p. 176. Porrò ex imperatoriâ hâc voce colligit Isidorus Pelusiota, l. IV. ep. 166. quòd Christus pari potestate cum Patre regnet, siquidem non duci, vel militi, dignitatem Regis sibi arroganti, sed Regi isthaec talia conveniant: Ego dico vobis,τὸ γδ pergit, τὸ γδ

## 15:29
v. 29. καὶ ἀναβὰς εἰς τὸ ὄρος. He ascended into the mountain, either that he might secure rest and a convenient place for prayer, conf. above c. 14. v. 23. or that he might be more conspicuous to all, because it is immediately subjoined that the crowds came to him, namely, while he was sitting on the mountain. *(Christ was delighted with mountains. See above c. 5, 1.c 14, 23. below c. 17, 1.c. 26, 16.Act. 1, 12. and Conf. B. Par. in Post. Epist. Petri p. 130. Chrysostom and Euthymius warn that Christ frequently ascended into a mountain, that he might teach that those who desire to approach God ought to be elevated from the soil. Jerome in this place He ascended into the mountain, that like a bird he might provoke his tender offspring to flight.)*

Latin:

v. 29. καὶ ἀναβὰς εἰς τὸ ὄρος. In montem ascendit, vel ut quietem & commodum orationis locum captaret, conf. suprà c. 14. v. 23. vel ut omnibus magis conspicuus esset, quia immediatè subnectitur, turbas ad eum, in monte sc. sedentem, venisse. *(Christus montibus fuit delectatus. Vid. suprà c. 5, 1.c 14, 23. infrà c. 17, 1.c. 26, 16.Act. 1, 12. ac Conf. B. Par. in Post. Epist. Petri p. 130. Chrysostomus atq; Euthymius monent, Christum frequenter adscendisse in montem, ut doceret, à solo elevari eos oportere, qui Deo appropinquare cupiunt. Hieronym in h. l. Ascendit in montem, ut tanquam avis teneros foetus provocaret ad volatum.)*

## 15:30
v. 30. And great crowds came to him, bringing the lame &c. Theoph. in this place. See their faith, how they even ascend into the mountain. And you, therefore, ascend into the mountain of the commandments, where Jesus sits; and if you are blind, not being able to see for yourself what is good, and if you are lame, seeing indeed what is good, but not being able to attain to it, &c. Go to the feet of Jesus, and touch the footprints of his life, you will have care. )*

Latin:
