*(v. 30. Et accesservnt ad eum turbae multae, adducentes claudos &c. Theoph. in h. l. Vide fidem illorum, quomodo & in montem adscendant. Et tu igitur adscende in montem mandatorum, ubi sedet Iesus; & si coecus fueris, non valens videre perteipsum quod bonum, & si claudus, videns quidem quod bonum, sed non valens ad hoc pervenire &c. Vadas ad pedes Iesu, & vestigia vitae illius attinge, curamhabebis.)*

## 15:31
v. 31. Κυλλοὺς. Arias Montanus translates weak, for it is a matter of those to whom members are not lacking, but they have become ἄχρηςα. They are not weak ἀσθενεῖς, but those who are hindered by some defect, so that they are less able to use all the members of their body. *(In the Vulgate version this member κυλλοὺς ὑγιεῖς is omitted against the faith of the Greek Codices. The Syriac Interpreter also acknowledges it, the Arab substitutes for it i. e. the deaf to hear, the Persian the lepers and elephantiasiacs to be cleansed. The Ethiopian indeed, and also the author of the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew edited by Munster, likewise omit it. It is also to be observed that Christ first healed the sick, afterwards offered food. Which the Gloss, expounding mystically, says thus in this place First the Lord takes away weaknesses and afterwards feeds, because first sins must be removed, and afterwards souls must be nourished with the words of GOD.)*

Latin:

v. 31. Κυλλοὺς. Arias Montanus vertit debiles, agitur enim de iis, quibus membra non desunt, sed facta sunt ἄχρηςα. ## 15:39
v. 39. εἰς τὰ ὅρια Μαγδαλὰ A place in the tribe of Judah, says Jerome. Which, however, Erasmus observed to read Μαγοδὰν here with the old Interpreter. Hugo Grotius gathers from this that it formerly had the Greek reading Μαγαδὰν.. He adds, that even now codices of the best quality have it so, and that this scripture seems to rely on many testimonies. But which those codices of the best quality are, Grotius keeps silent, perhaps because he only persuaded himself so. Certainly, out of sixteen codices which the Parisians compared with the greatest zeal and from which Franciscus Lucas Brugensis also exhibits variant readings, not one, namely the second, and that one adorned here and there according to the old Latin version, has Μαγαδὰν.. From those best and most ancient codices also, which the Londoners sought out with the greatest zeal, likewise not one presents that reading, whereas on the contrary, the received reading, which has Μαγδαλὰ,, is approved by Chrysostom and Theophylact, the Arab and the Ethiopian, of whom the latter has and the former . The Syriac by apocope has Magodu, similarly almost the Persian . Some suspect that the discrepancy arose from the permutation of the letters Nun and Lamed. See Lud. de Dieu Comm. on this place) Mark c. 8, 10. it is said that Christ came into the borders of Dalmanutha. Some therefore think that Dalmanuth- is the name of the region, Magdala of the city. Some also say that in Mark it should be read Magdala. מנרל tower. Magdala was a castle, not far distant from the lake of Gennesaret. (Compare B. Glass. Gr. S. p. 828. B. D. Quistorpius notes, that there were two -icinos villages Mageda or Magdala, and Dalmanutha. That the region lying between these was named now by this, now by that . Thus, he continues, Matthew here says that Christ came into the borders of Mageda, Mark 10. into the parts of Dalmanutha. In the same way the Evangelists are reconciled in this place in -. -liis Ernestinis, and a similar passage is added Mark 7, 24.)

This chapter presents I. The dispute of Christ with the Pharisees concerning a sign . v. 1-4. II. The faithful admonition of the Savior concerning avoiding the leaven of the Pharisees. v. 6-12. III. The question concerning the person of Christ, and the excellent confession of Peter v. 13-18. and the delivery of the keys of the kingdom of heaven. v. 19. IV. The prediction of the passion, death, and resurrection of Christ. v. 20-23. V. The instruction concerning self-denial, the patiently taking up of the cross, and future remuneration. v. 23 to the end.

Colligit inde Hugo Grotius; olim Graecam habuisse Lectionem Μαγαδὰν. Addit, etiam nunc optimae notae Codices ita habere, ac pluribus testimoniis scripturam istam niti videri. Sistit hoc caput I. Christi cum Pharisaeis de signo disputationem. v. 1-4. II. Fidelem Salvatoris de vitando Pharisaeorum fermento admonitionem. v. 6-12. III. De Christi personâ quaestionem, & egregiam Petri confessionem v. 13-18. claviumq; regni coelorum traditionem. v. 19. IV. Passionis, mortis & resurrectionis Christi praedictionem. v. 20. -23. V. De sui abnegatione, cruce patienter suscipiendâ ac futura remuneratione instructionem. v. 23. ad fin.

## 16:1
*(v. 1. Pharisees and Sadducees. Here sects otherwise very contrary conspire in a friendly manner against Christ. Compare Luke 23, 12. One ought to treat here of Syncretism, which the Calvinists vehemently affect. But the nature of the pages does not admit a lengthy treatise. But what ought to be observed concerning it, the Orthodox have long since warned. See Blessed D. Chemnitz, Harm. Ev. at this place. Blessed D. Sigwart against the Irenicum of Pareus. Mr. D. Hulsemann in Calv. Irreconc. Blessed D. Nic. Hunnius in the Disquisition on the fundamental disagreement of the doctrine of the Evangelical Lutheran and Calvinist. Blessed D. Hutter, Probl. Theol. Whether a syncretism of faith between the Lutheran and Calvinist can be entered into, printed at Wittenberg A. 1615. Blessed D. Garthius in the preface to vol. 1 of the Works of Hunnius. Blessed D. Polycarp Leyser in the Vindications, printed at Leipzig A. 1616, and others)*

Επηρώτησαν. Ερωτᾷν. and ἐπερωτᾷν properly signifies to interrogate, but here it is placed for to ask.

*( A sign from heaven. Such as was brought forth by Moses, Exod. 16, 14. John 6, 31. and Elijah 2 Kings 1, 10. If Christ were to refuse that, they had in mind to pretend from that, that he himself was not the true Messiah, since he was unwilling to perform such signs as those brought forth by Moses and Elijah. A similar demand is also read above chap. 12, 38. Rightly, however, Theophylact convicts those hypocrites of foolishness, namely, being ignorant that not all signs that are from heaven are from God; (since the fire which descended from heaven upon the cattle of Job was from demons) nor are all things that are on earth from demons.)*

NOTES ON CHAP. XVI. SUMMARY AND DISPOSITION.

*(v. 1. Pharisaei & Sadducaei. Hîc sectae perquam aliàs contrariae amicè contra Christum conspirant. Conf Luc. 23, 12. Agendum hîc esset de Syncretismo, quē Calviniani vehementer adfectant. Sed pagellarum ratio prolixam tract. non admittit. Quid verò cirea illum observandum sit, pridem monuerunt Orthodoxi. Vide B. D. Chemnn. Harm. Ev. h. l. B. D. Sigwartum contra Irenicum Paraei. Dn. D. Hulsem. in Calv. Irreconc. B. D. Nic. Hun. in Diascepsi de fundam dissensu doctrinae Evang. Luth. & Calvin. B. D. Hutterū Probl. Theol. Επηρώτησαν. Ερωτᾷν. & ἐπερωτᾷν propriè significat interrogare, hîc autem ponitur pro rogare.

*( Signum è coelo. Quale sc à Mose, Exod. 16, 14.Ioh. 6, 31. & Elia 2, Reg. 1, 10. editum. Id si Christus renueret, in animò habebant, inde praetendere, quòd ipse non esset verus Messias, quippe non volens ea signa perpetrare, cuiusmodi à Mose & Elia edita. Simile postulatum legitur quoque suprà cap. 12, 38. Rectè verò Theophylactus insipientiae arguit istos hypocritas, ignorantes nempe, quòd non omnia, quae è coelo signa, à Deo; (cùm ignis qui è coelo descendit super pecora Iobi, à daemonibus fuerit) neq; quae in terrâ, omnia à daemonibus sint.)*

NOTAE AD CAP. XVI. SUMMA AC DISPOSITIO.

## 16:2
v. 2. Ευδία. i.e. ἔσται There is a certain emphasis in that aposiopesis. Behold serenity, i.e. there will be. Ἐυδία signifies the goodness of the air, from the Adv. εὐ and the accus. διὰ, of the noun ζεὺς. by the name Jupiter is understood metonymically heaven or air.

*( πυῄῥάζει γδ. part. γδ here is not causal, but συλλογηςικὴ noting a sign of serenity. It occurs also in the same sense below c. 25, 35. Likewise τὸ ὅτι is sometimes used, as will be warned more fully in the Anal. Luke 7, 47.)*

Latin:

v. 2. Ευδία. sc. ἔσται Est in illa aposiopesi emphasis quaedam. Ecce sorenitas, sc. erit.Ἐυδία significat aëris bonitatem, ex Adv. εὐ & accus. διὰ, nominis ζεὺς.Iovis nomine metonymicè intelligitur coelum s. aër.

*( πυῄῥάζει γδ. part. γδ hîc non est causalis, sed συλλογηςικὴ notans signum serenitatis. Eodem quoque sensu occurrit infrà c. 25, 35. Pariter τὸ ὅτι aliquando adhibetur, uti pluribus monebitur in Anal. Luc. 7, 47.)*

## 16:3
v. 3. The sky is gloomy. The sky is said ςυγνάζειν to be gloomy, by an elegant metaphor. Aratus:

*( and they enlarge the borders of their garments.

Ἀμνηςεῖν ὑετοῖο. It is not, he says, to be forgotten about rains, if a thin cloud rises before the Sun, and he himself following this breaks forth in such a way that the rays are colored. And again: τὸ ἐλθ If the Sun touches the evening waves without clouds, but when they are not near these following red ones, not then, not the next day are rains to be feared. Morning redness for the most part denotes winds or rains, because the Sun draws a watery and red cloud toward us, which if it is dewy, rains fall: if it is less dewy, yet better cooked, it provides material for winds. Evening redness is an index of serenity, because the Sun draws the watery cloud into another horizon, and by the cold of the night that watery cloud is meanwhile condensed, so that it cannot be resolved into rain. Morning and evening light is seen through vapors collected around the horizon. Whence the light turns purple, but at midday it turns more yellowish, because it is seen through rarer vapors and those thinned by the excellence of the Sun. Just as also fire appears in different colors according to how it is seen through different media, when nevertheless by its own nature it is most luminous and imbued with no color. So also when many smokes and exhalations are gathered around the horizon, which the Sun cannot consume on account of an oblique ray, the light seen through them appears purple.

But why do purple clouds signify serenity in the evening, but in the morning rains? The cause is that the evening redness is more in a cloud dried by the daily heat of the Sun, into which the ray falling does not penetrate, but being reflected is doubled: or because these vapors are near the earth, and on account of a lack of heat cannot be raised to the middle region of the air, whence by the nocturnal cold they are converted into dew; or because the air for the most part follows the motion of the heaven being snatched. Whence perhaps at night there exist rains in the other hemisphere, but in the morning serenity follows, the air having been purged by the nocturnal rain, which however we did not sense in our hemisphere. The opposite happens in morning redness. But in the morning the cloud is red, because it is watery, which is raised by the heat of the Sun and easily dissolved into rain. *(Compare more on the prognostics of winds, rains, tempest, and serenity, and thus on this very pronouncement of the Savior in Gerardus Ioannes Vossius book 3 de Theol. Gentili p. 791. seqq.)*

Hypocrites &c. Jerome in this place: The meaning is manifest, that from the order of the elements and their constancy, both fair and rainy days can be known. But how does Christ's response fit the Pharisees' demand? Christ wishes to say this. You diligently observe the signs of rain and fair weather in the sky, why do you not much more consider the signs and testimonies proposed in the Prophets concerning my coming? If you were to do that, you would need no other sign. Tossan. *(In the same way in the gloss of the Ernestine Bible. But Lud de Dieu dissents, thinking that the Greek is better translated: You cannot [discern] the signs of the opportunities. So that the meaning is: You do not discern the opportune times of salvation which God bestows upon you.)*

*( Τὸ ρόσωπον τοὑ οὐρανοῦ. The Philosopher in book 3 of Rhetoric reproves Lycophron, because he said πολυρόσωπον οὐρανὸν, since indeed ρόσωπον belongs to man alone, as it also seemed to Pliny in book XI of Natural History, ch. 37. But it must be known that among the Hebrews the word פנים,, for which the LXX use the name ροσώπου, denotes any external appearance of a thing, also a surface. See Gen. 2, 6.c. 4, 14.c. 7, 4.23.Exod. 16, 14.c. 26, 9.c 30, 6.1 Sam. 20, 15.1. Reg 3, 15.c. 8, 22. &c. Luke also uses it in the same way in ch. 21, 35. Furthermore, just as a man looks at something, so Pliny also attributes to the Sun in book 2 of Natural History, ch. 6, that it sees and hears all things.)*

τὰ δὲ σημεῖα &c. By τὰ σημεῖα he understands either all things in the universe by which the Prophets signified the time of the Messiah, or specifically the miracles which he performed in the days of his flesh.

οὐ δύναεθε. Lyranus interprets it affirmatively, so that the sense may be: I assert that you are also unable to judge concerning the coming of Christ by such signs. But this is less correct, because he would have spoken inappropriately, that the coming could not be known by these natural signs, since the Pharisees had demanded a supernatural sign from heaven, which would be declarative of the Messiah's coming. Therefore, it is more correctly read and accepted interrogatively, so that Christ does not deny them the power of knowing, but rather reproves them for their blindness and perversity, because that which they ought deservedly to know and could easily have known, they were unwilling to acknowledge of their own accord. *(So that the sense may be: if you know the face of the sky, i.e., the signs of fair weather and rain, which is more difficult and uncertain, how is it that you do not know, i.e., are unwilling to know, the signs of the times of my coming, consigned by so many prophecies and confirmed by me with so many miracles? Thus, indeed interrogatively, Hilary, Jerome, Euthymius, and Bede accept it.)*

Latin:

v. 3. Coelum triste. Coelum dicitur ςυγνάζεινtriste esse, per metaphoram elegantem. Aratus:

Μήδ᾽ Τὴν δὲ μετ᾽

Ἀμνηςεῖν ὑετοῖο.Non esse, ait, imbrium obliviscendum, si tenuis nubes ante Solem oriatur, & ipse hanc sequens ita erumpat, ut radii colorentur. Et rursus: τὸ ἐλθSi tetigeru undas Sol vespertinas absnubibus, sed cum his sequentibus se proximè rutilis non sunt, netunc, nepostridie metuendi imbres. Rubedo matutina plerumque ventos aut pluvias notat, quia Sol attrahit nubem aquosam & rubram ad nos, quae si rorulenta est, pluviae decidunt: sin minùs rorida, meliùs tamen percocta, ventorum suppeditat materiam. Rubedo vespertina serenitatis index est, quia Sol aquosam nubem in alium horizontem detrahit, & frigiditate noctis aquea illa nubes interim condensatur, ne in pluviam resolvi possit. Mane & vesperi conspicitur lumen per vapores circa horizontem collectos. Unde lumen purpurascit, in meridie verò magis flavescit, quia per vapores rariores & praestantiâ Solis subtiliatos conspicitur. Quemadmodum etiam ignis comparet diverfis coloribus prout per diversa media conspicitur, cùm tamen suâ naturâ sit lucidissimus & nullo colore imbutus. Sic etiam quando circa horizontem congregantur multi fumi atq; exhalationes, quas Sol propter obliquum radium absumere nequit, lumē per illas conspectum apparet purpureum.

Cur autem nubes purpureae serenitatem vesperi significant, mane verò pluvias? Causa est, quòd vespertina rubedo magis est in nube siccata diurno aestu Solis, in quam radius incidens non penetrat, sed repercussus duplicatur: vel quia hi vapores sunt terrae vicini, & propter defectum caloris elevari non possunt ad mediam regionem aëris, unde frigore nocturno convertuntur in rorem; vel quia aër utplurimum motum coeli raptum sequitur. Unde fortasse noctu existunt pluviae in altero haemisphaerio, mane verò subsequitur serenitas, purgato aëre pluviâ nocturnâ, quam tamen nos in nostro hemisphaerio non sensimus. Contrarium in rubedine matutinâ accidit. Manè verò rubet nubes, quia est aquosa, quae calore Solis elevatur ac facilè in pluviam dissolvitur. *(Confer plura de ventorum, imbrium, tempestatis ac serenitatis prognosticis, adeoque de hoc ipso etiam Salvatoris pronunciato apud Gerardum Ioannem Vossium lib 3. de Theol. Gentili p. 791. seqq.)*

Hypocritae &c. Hieron. in h. l. Sensus manifestus est, quòd ex elementorum ordine atconstantiâ possint & sereni & pluviae dies cognosci. Quomodo verò Christi responsum convenit Pharisaeorum postulato? Christus hoc vult dicere. Diligenter observatis signa pluviarum & serenitatis in coelo, cur non multò magis consideratis signa ac testimonia in Prophetis de meo adventu proposita. Id si faceretis, nullo alio signo indigeretis. Tossan. *(Eod. modo in gloss. Bibl. Ernestinorum. Sed dissentit Lud de Dieu, existimans, meliùs Graeca verti. Signa opportunitatium non potestis. Ut sensus sit. Opportuna salutis tempora, quae vobis Deus largitur, non discernitis.)*

*( Τὸ ρόσωπον τοὑ οὐρανοῦ. Reprehendit Philos. l. 3. Rhet. Lycophronem, quod πολυρόσωπον οὐρανὸν dixerit, siquidem soli homini ρόσωπον competat, uti etiam Plinio visum l. XI. Hist. Nat. c. 37. Sciendum verò, quòd apud Ebr. vox פנים, pro quâ LXX. nomine ροσώπου utuntur, notet quamlibet externam rei speciem Item superficiem. Vid. Gen. 2, 6.c. 4, 14.c. 7, 4.23.Exod. 16, 14.c. 26, 9.c 30, 6.1 Sam. 20, 15.1. Reg 3, 15.c. 8, 22. &c. Eodem modo utitur quoq; Lucas c. 21, 35. Praeterea quemadmodum homo aliquid intuetur, ita Soli etiam Plinius lib. 2. H. N. c. 6. tribuit, quòd omnia videat audiatque.)*

τὰ δὲ σημεῖα &c. Per τὰ σημεῖα intelligit vel omnia in universum, quibus Prophetae tempus Messiae significarunt, vel specialiter miracula, quae in diebus carnis operabatur.

οὐ δύναεθε. Lyranus affirmativè interpretatur, ut sit sensus. Ego adsero, vos etiam non posse per signa eiusmodi de Christi adventu iudicare. Sed minùs rectè, quia inconvenienter dixisset, per signa haec naturalia non posse adventum cognosci, cùm Pharisaei signum supernaturale de coelo postulassent, quod esset Messiae adventûs declarativum. Rectiùs ergò legitur & accipitur interrogativè, ita ut Christus ipsis non deneneget potentiam cognoscendi, sed potiùs coecitatis ac perversitatis eos redarguat, quòd illud, quod meritò scire debebant & facilè poterant, ultrò cognoscere nollent. *(Ut ita sensus sit. si faciem coeli cognoscitis i. e signa serentiatis & pluviae, quod difficilius & incertius est, quomodo signa temporum adventûs mei tot Prophetiis consignata ac tot miraculis à me comprobata, cognoscere nescitis s. non vultis? Ita, nempe interrogativè, accipiunt Hilarius, Hieronymus, Euthymius, Beda.)*

*(v. 4. A wicked and adulterous generation. Wicked, as being tempting; adulterous as departing from GOD, and adhering to the Devil. Theoph.)*

Chemnitius in Harm. c. 84, where he also beautifully shows how Jonah was a sign both of the passion and resurrection of Christ, and to the Jews.)*

*( Nisi signum Ionae. q. d. tale signum vobis dabitur, quod nisi poenitentiam agatis, praesentissimum exitium vobis afferet. Ita B. D. Chemnitius in Harm. c. 84. ubi etiam pulcrè ostendit, quomodo Ionas tum passionis ac resurrectionis Christi, tum Iudaeis fuerit signum.)*

## 16:5
*(v. 5. And when his disciples had come &c. Jerome thinks that those things which now follow happened on the sea itself while sailing. The Jesuit Maldonatus denies that he can concede this, since Luke c. 12, 1. writes that, with many crowds surrounding him, so that they trampled upon one another, Christ began to say to his disciples, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees. But Grotius responds to this that the history which is in Luke is different from the present one. To which the observation of Corn. à Lapide contributes, noting that τὸ ἐλθόντες here denotes when they had gone, i.e., when they had boarded the ship. By Hebraism, since Hebrew words often signify an act not completed, but begun. Grotius, however, judges that the diversity of the history is evident from this, that in Luke it is a matter of the leaven of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees; there Christ addresses the whole multitude, here at least the disciples; there he deals with evil examples, here with dogmas.)*

Latin:

*(v. 5. Et cùm venissent eius discipuli &c. Hieronymus ea, quae iam sequuntur, in ipso mari inter navigandum accidisse putat. Negat Iesuita Maldonatus, se id concedere posse, siquidem Lucas c. 12, 1. scribat, multis circumstantibus turbis, ita ut se conculcaret, coepisse Christum discipulis dicere, attendite à fermento Pharisaeorum. Verùm respondet ad hoc Grotius, eam quae apud Lucam est historia, diversam esse à praesenti. Quo facit observatio Corn. à Lapide, notantis, τὸ ἐλθόντες hîc notare cùm ivissent. s. cùm navem conscendissent. Per Ebraismum, cùm Ebraea verba saepè actum non perfectum, sed inchoatum significent. Grotius verò diversitatem historiae exinde patere arbitratur, quòd apud Lucam agatur de sermento Pharisaeorum ac Sadducaeorum; ibi Christus alloquatur totam multitudinem, hic saltem discipulos; ibi agat de malis exemplis, hîc de dogmatibus.)*

## 16:6
v. 6. Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees. False doctrine is compared to leaven, because heretics are fervent with audacity, pride, rashness, etc. Conf. Rom. 1. 6,18. The Apostle 1. Cor. 5, 6.Gal. 5, 9. gives this reason. As a little leaven infects the whole mass, and makes it sour: so a little false doctrine corrupts the whole system. *(Theophyl otherwise: just as leaven is bitter and old, so also the doctrine of the Sadducees bites souls, being bitter, and introducing the traditions of the old and sounder ones. And just as leaven is a mixture of water and flour, so also the doctrine of the Pharisees is mixed from speech and a corrupted life.)*

*( And of the Sadducees. Mark substitutes the word Herod's for the name of the Sadducees. Some respond that certain of the Sadducees were Herodians. Thus Grotius. But the leaven of Herod was hypocrisy. Luc. 12, 1. Concerning the Herodians, however, it will be treated in the Analysis to c. 22, 16.)*

Latin:

v. 6. Cavere à fermento Pharisaeorum. Falsa doctrina comparatur fermento, quia haeretici fervent audaciâ, superbiâ, temeritate &c. Conf. Rom. 1. 6,18. Apostolus 1. Cor. 5, 6.Gal. 5, 9. reddit hanc rationem. Ut parum fermenti inficit totam massam, eamque acidam reddit: sic parum doctrinae falsae corrumpit totum systema. *(Theophyl aliter: quemadmodum fermentum amarum est & vetus, ita & Sadducaeorum doctrina mordet animas, amara existens, & veteres saniorum tradiriones introducens. Et sicut fermentum est temperatura aquae & farinae, sic & doctrina Pharisaeorum mixta est ex sermone & vita corrupata.)*

* ( Et Sadducaeorum. Marcus pro nomine Sadducaeorum substituit vocem Herodis. Respondent nonnulli, Sadducae orum quosdam fuisse Herodianos. Ita Grotius. Herodis verò fermentum fuit hypocrisis. Luc. 12, 1. De Herodianis autem agetur in Anal. ad c. 22, 16.)*

## 16:7
v. 7. We have taken no bread. The disciples thought that they were to go hungry, since they were prohibited from the eating of breads in which there was the leaven of the Pharisees; therefore Christ recalls to their memory the miracle of the five thousand satisfied with a few loaves. *(But the first member is missing in that proposition of the disciples, namely: thus Christ speaks. Glassius, Gr. S. p. 707. seqq., exhibits many examples of a similar ellipsis.)* *(

Latin:

v. 7. Panes non sumsimus. Putabant discipuli, sibi esuriendum esse, cùm prohibeantur ab esu panum in quibus fermentum Pharisaeorum, ideò Christus revocat illis in memoriam miraculum saturatorum quinque millium paucis panibus. *(Deest verò in illâ discipulorum propositione prius membrum, nempe: ita Christus loquitur. Similis ellips. exempla plura exhibet Glassius Gr. S. p. 707. seqq.)*

## 16:8
*(v. 8. Why do you think among yourselves. An argument for the omniscience of Christ. See B. Dn. Iac. Martini Photinian. and Conf. Ioh. 2, 25.c, 21, 17.Col. 2, 3.Apoc. 2, 23.)*

*( Ὀλιγόπιστοι. Conf. above c. 11, 25. c. 14, 31.)*

*( Ὀλιγόπιστοι. Conf. suprà c. 11, 25. c. 14, 31.)*

v. 9. Do ye not yet understand, namely, my divine omnipotence, that I can sustain you even without bread.)* *(

## 16:10
*(v. 10. Neither the seven loaves of the four thousand. There is no doubt that the word men is to be understood, just as Beza also supplied that ellipsis in this way. Erasmus likewise and Schmidius, who serves that other version of Erasmus, namely of Rotterdam, with these things:) When they were men q. m. Moreover, no one of the Oriental interpreters supplied the ellipsis, except the Persian alone, adding the word which denotes a man.)*

Latin:

*(v. 10. Neque seprem illos panes quater mille. Nullum dubiū, quin subintelligenda, vox hominum, quem admodum etiam ellipsin istam ita supplevit Beza.
