Coeterùm nullus Interpp. Orientalium Ellipsin supplevit, nisi solus Persa, addens vocem quae virum notat.)*

## 16:11
*(v. 11. How is it that you do not understand? τὸ πῶς in this place is not of one who is ignorant, but of one who is rebuking, as if to say How does it happen that you do not understand?)*

That you should beware of the leaven of the Pharisees. And yet Matth. 13, 23. Christ commands to hear the Pharisees sitting in the Chair of Moses, and to observe and do whatever they shall have said. Resp. Distinguish between the office of the Pharisees itself, and the vice adhering to them. The Pharisees were established in the public duty of teaching, so that they might publicly read the writings of Moses and the Prophets, and they were to be heard in that. But because those men were mixing the leaven of human traditions and superstitions into the pure mass of heavenly doctrine, comprised in the Mosaic and Prophetic writings, the pure had to be rightly discerned from the impure, i.e., the traditions having been rejected, the heavenly doctrine was to be retained. Conf. 1. Thess. 5, 21. 1. Cor. 12, 10. 1. Ioh. 4, 1. )*

Latin:

*(v. 11. Quomodo non intelligitis.τὸ πῶς h. l. non estignorantis, sed obiurgantis, q. d. Quîfit, ut non intelligatis.)*

*( Ut caveretis à fermento Pharisaeorum. Atqui Matth. 13, 23. iubet Christus Pharisaeos sedentes in Cathedrâ Mosis audire, & quaecundixerint, servare & facere. Resp. Disting. inter ipsum Pharisaeorum officium, & adhaerens illis vitium. Pharisaei constituti erant in publico docendi munere, ut scripta Mosis ac Prohetarum publicè praelegerent, & eat. audiendi erat. Sed quia purae isti massae doctrinae coelestis, in scriptis Mosaicis ac Propheticis comprehensae, humanarum traditionum & superstitionum fermentum admiscebant, purum ab impuro probè discernendum erat, h. e. reiectis traditionibus coelestis doctrina retinenda. Conf. 1. Thess. 5, 21.1. Cor. 12, 10.1. Ioh. 4, 1.)*

## 16:13
v. 13. Into the parts of Caesarea Philippi. It was so called because it had been founded by Philip the tetrarch, son of Herod the Great, brother of Herod Antipas, in honor of Caesar Tiberius. Formerly it was called Paneas. Ioseph. lib. 18. Antiq. c. 3. There was another Caesarea built by Herod the Great, mention of which is made in Actor. 8, 4. c. 9, 30. c. 10, 1. Afterwards that was called Neronia, a town of that part of Palestine which was called Phoenicia, at the roots of Mount Lebanon, not far from the springs of the Jordan. *(

*( Who do they say that I am &c. Well does Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, ep. 235. Ὀλιγόπ &c. Compare B. D. Glass. Rhet. Sacr. p. 122. Also the Analysis on John 11, 34.)*

*( The Son of man. See the notes on Mark 8, 27. Herman Ravensperger, D. and Prof. of Theol. in the Academy of Groningen, in the Theological Garden p. 464, on the occasion of this passage raises the question, whether the phrase Christ man is of Scripture, and the same as that man Christ. And having premised that something is said to be of the Scriptures either as to the words, or as to the sense, he concedes that although by the former reason that phrase cannot be said to be of Scripture, yet by the latter reason it is of Scripture, if indeed it is correctly expounded. He adds: for the phrase can be understood either by limitation, or by distribution, or by apposition. He continues: If it is taken limitatively, Christ as man, that is, insofar as he is man: the interpretation is sometimes correct, sometimes erroneous. Correct concerning the attributes of the human nature, as Christ as man suffered, was crucified and died, that is, insofar as he is man. Erroneous concerning the attributes of the divine nature, as Christ as man is omnipotent, omniscient and τοῦ λόγου. For that opinion, which affirms that Christ as man, that is, insofar as he is man, is , not only to the Apostolic Creed and sacred history Acts 1 but also to the truth and property of the human nature is repugnant. I respond 1. when our people teach that Christ as man or according to his human nature is omnipotent, omniscient, etc., they by no means understand it as if naturally or from natural properties or essentially the human nature of Christ were omnipresent or omnipotent: but personally. For just as they assert the power of vivifying, so also they assert that the remaining divine attributes, such as omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence, have been communicated to and are rightly attributed to the human nature, assumed into the infinite hypostasis. 2. If the power of vivifying could be communicated to the human nature of Christ, so that the flesh of Christ was vivifying, and yet the truth of the human nature was not overturned by this, it follows that the same was not overturned by the communication of omnipotence and omniscience. But the former is established from John 6, 50, 51, 53. 55 The consequence is proven, because the power of vivifying is established by the Calvinists in the Colloquy of Montbéliard p. 338 as equally proper to the Deity as other divine attributes. 3. Indeed, if the power of administering judgment universal was given to Christ as man, John 5, 27 it follows that omniscience and omnipotence were also communicated to the same. The reason for the connection is because that power embraces omniscience and omnipotence. This shines forth from the resuscitation of the dead, which universal judgment requires beforehand, likewise from the citation and congregation of all men to judgment, and also from the execution of the decisive sentence, that from the manifestation of the most hidden things. 4. As concerns the passage Acts 1, 9, 10, 11 and the Apostolic Creed, in which we profess that Christ ascended into the heavens and will return to judge the living and the dead, those certainly do not at all oppose our orthodox opinion concerning the omnipresence of Christ as man, since the return of Christ to judgment is by no means opposed and Absolutely and simply of the omnipresence of the whole person, otherwise our Savior would not even be present to us on this earth according to his divine nature, which not even the Adversaries themselves assert, but only in a certain manner of presence. Which the Angels themselves teach in the same place v. 11. This Jesus, saying, who has been taken up from you into heaven, οὕτως will come in such a way, ὃν τρόπον as you have seen him going into heaven. Therefore, one must distinguish accurately between visible presence, and invisible, and from the negation of the former, the latter is not to be immediately inferred as well. Whence also that same Savior of ours, who visibly ascended into heaven and from there is also to return visibly for judgment, promised also that he wishes to be with us, namely invisibly, until the consummation of the age, Matth. 28, 20. add. Matth. 18, 20. Eph. 1, 23. c. 4, 10. See more in B. Par. L on the Final Judgment § 42. & 34.)

Moreover, Jerome in his commentary on this passage denies that Christ, as if arrogantly inquiring about himself, said, Whom do [they] say that I am, but whom do they say that the Son of Man is. Indeed, even the Arab and Ethiopian interpreters do not acknowledge the pronoun me here, nor is it sufficiently clear from Origen and Chrysostom whether that was read in the Greek copies which they themselves used. But since the Greek codices consistently read it, which the Syriac and Persian also follow, as well as the ancient Latin alongside Theophylact, that pronoun is deservedly retained as a genuine part of this passage. Erasmus also rightly advises that the argument for modesty is to be understood not in the omitted pronoun, but in the added particle, the Son of Man.]* *(

Latin:

v. 13. In partes Caesareae Philippi. Dicebatur ita, quia condita fuerat à Philippo tetrarcha, Herodis Magni filio, Herodis Antipae fratre, in honorem Caesaris Tiberii. Olim dicta fuit Paneas. Ioseph. lib. 18. Antiq. c. 3. Alia fuit Caesarea ab Herode Magno extructa, cuius mentio fit Actor. 8, 4.c. 9, 30.c. 10, 1. Postea dicta illa fuit Neronia, oppidum Palaestinae eius partis, quae Phoenicia dicta est, ad radices montis Libani, non procul à fontibus Iordanis.

*( Quem me dicunt &c. Benè Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 1. ep 235. Ὀλιγόπ &c. Conf. B. D. Glass. Rhet. Sacr. p. 122. It. Anal. ad Ioh. 11, 34.)*

*( Filium hominis. Vid. notata ad Marc. 8, 27. Herman. Ravenspergerus D. & Prof. Theol. in Acad. Groning. in Horto Theologico p. 464. occasione huius loci quaestionem movet, an phrasis Christus homo sit Scripturae, & eadem cum illâ homo Christus. Praemissôque quòd Scripturae aliquid esse dicatur vel, quoad verba, vel quoad sensum, concedit, quòd licet priori ratione phrasis illa Scripturae dici non possit, posteriori tamen ratione sit Scripturae, si nempe rectè exponatur. addit: potest quippe phrasis intelligi vel per limitationem, vel per distributionem, vel per appositionem. Pergit: Limitativè si accipiatur, Christus homo, id est, quaetenus homo: interpretatio nunc recta, nunc erronea est. Recta de attributis naturae humanae, ut Christus homo passus, crucifixus & mortuus est, id est, quat. est homo. Erroneae de attributis naturae divinae, ut Christus homo est omnipotens, omniscius & ubi-. Opinio enim illa, quae affirmat, quòd Christus homo, id est, quatenus homo, sit ubi-, non modo Symbolo Apostolico & historiae sacraeActor. 1.sed etiam veritati & proprietati naturae humanae repugnat. Resp. 1. quando nostrates docent, Christum hominem sive secundùm humanam naturam esse omnipotentem, omniscium &c. id minimè ita intelligunt, qs. naturaliter sive ex proprietatibus naturalibus vel essentialiter humana Christi natura omnipraesens vel omnipotens sit: sed personaliter. Sicuti enim virtutem vivificandi, ita etiam reliqua attributa divina, uti omniscientiam, omnipotentiam, omnipraesentiam humanae naturae, in infinitam τοῦ λόγου hypostasin adsumtae, communicatam esse ac rectè tribui, adservnt. 2. si virtus vivificandi humanae Christi naturae potuit communicari, ita ut caro Christi fuerit vivifica, nec tamen per hoc veritas humanae naturae fuit eversa, sequitur, eandem nec eversam fuisse per omnipotentiae & omniscientiae communicationem. At prius constat ex Ioh. 6, 50 51,53.55 Conseq. probatur, quia vis vivificandi aequè Deitatis propria statuitur à Calvinianis in Colloq. Momp. p. 338. ac alia attributa divina. 3. quin si potestas iudicii universalis administrandi Christo homini fuit data, Ioh 5, 27. sequitur, quòd etiam omniscientia & omnipotentia eidem communicata fuerint. Ratio connexionis est, quia potestas illa complectitur omniscientiam & omnipotentiam. Haec elucescit ex mortuorum resuscitatione, quam iudicium universale praerequirit, item ex omnium hominum ad iudicium citatione & congregatione, nec non ex sententiae decisivae executione, illa ex occultissimorum manifestatione. 4. quod concernit locum Actor. 1, 9. 10. 11. ac Symbolum Apostolicum, in quo profitemur, Christum adscendisse in coelos ac rediturum ad iudicandum vivos ac mortuos, illa sanè minimè orthodoxae nostrae de omnipraesentia Christi hominis sententiae adversantur, quippe cùm reditus Christi ad iudicium hautquaquam opponatur & absolutè & simpliciter totius personae omnipraesentiae, aliàs ne quidem secundùm divinam naturam nobis in his terris Salvator noster praesens adesset, id quod ne ipsi quidem Adversarii adservnt, sed certo duntaxat praesentiae modo. quod ipsi Angeli docent d. l. v. 11.Hic Iesus, dicentes, qui à vobis adsumtus est in coelum,οὕτωςsic veniet,ὃν τρόπονquemadmodum vidistis eum euntem in coelum. Distingvendum igitur accuratè est inter praesentiam visibilem, & invisibilem, nec ex illius negatione huius quoq; statim inferenda. Unde etiam idem ille Salvator noster, qui visibiliter adscendit in coelum indeque etiam visibiliter rediturus ad iudicium est, promisit quoque, quòd nobiscum velit esse, nempe invisibiliter, usad consummationem seculi,Matth. 28, 20. add. Matth. 18, 20.Eph. 1, 23.c. 4, 10. Vide plura apud B. Par. L de Extr. Iudic. § 42. & 34.)*

*[Coeterùm Hieronymus in comment. h. l. negat, Christum, velut arroganter de se percontantem dixisse, Quem me dicunt esse, sed quem dicunt esse filium hominis. Sanè etiam Arabs & Aethiops Interpp. non agnoscunt hîc pronomen me, nec ex Origine atq; Chrysostomo satis patet, num in xemplaribus Graecis, quibus ipsi usi fuerunt, lectū illud fuerit. Verùm cùm Graeci Codd. constanter illud legant, quos sequuntur etiam Syrus ac Persa, tum quoque iuxta cum Theophylacto antiquus Latinus, meritò pronomen illud ut pars genuina h. l. retinetur. Rectè quoque Erasmus monet, modestiae argumentum non in omisso pronomine, sed in additâ particulâ, filium hominis, intelligi.]*

## 16:14
v. 14. Some indeed [say] John the Baptist &c. These sayings flowed from a false opinion concerning metempsychosis. Concerning which see some things in the Analecta on Marc. 6, 16. )* *(

*( But others Jeremiah. Theoph. in this place Those who called Christ Jeremiah, were saying this, that he was endowed with similar wisdom, which he had learned from no one: For Jeremiah, when he was a boy, was taken up as a Prophet. Grotius thinks, in the same place, that this can be referred to παλιγτενεσίαν, he adds: For the Hebrews were expecting the return of Jeremiah, as appears from Gorionides.)*

Latin:

*(v. 14. Alii quidem Iohannem Baptistam &c. Profluxere hi sermones ex falsâ opinione de metemphychosi. De quâ vid. nonnulla in Analect ad Marc. 6, 16.)*

*( Alii verò Ieremiam. Theoph. h. l. Qui Christum Ieremiam nominabant, hoc dicebant, quòd simili sapientiâ praeditus esset, quam à nullo didicerat: Etenim Hieremias, quum puer esset, in Prophetam adsumtus est. Grotius existimat, ibidem hoc ad παλιγτενεσίαν referri posse, addit: Nam Ebraei exspectabant reditum Ieremiae, ut ex Gorionide apparet.)*

## 16:15
(v. 15. But you, who do you say that I am? It is asked, why did Christ here demand of the Apostles that they bear witness to the truth, when John 5, 34. He denies that He receives testimony from men? Resp. 1. The Savior speaks in John not ἁπλῶς, but κατα τι, nor does He deny that He receives any testimony from men, but that He not only, nor principally relies on human testimony, since the works which He does also testify of Him, as does the Father Himself, who sent Him v. 36. 37. 2. In the Greek text there is λαμβάννω, which is rendered by some as having taken, so that Christ in that place at least removes from Himself the pursuit of empty glory, not all testimony. 3. The Savior in that place primarily intends that on account of Himself or for His own sake He does not desire or have need of the testimony of any man: meanwhile He by no means denies that we have need of divine testimonies concerning Him, so that, namely, by having faith in them we may be saved through Him. Thus in this place He elicits from Peter the testimony and confession concerning Himself, so that by approving that confession He may confirm the disciples more and more in this truth and faith once acknowledged.)

Latin:

*(v. 15. Vos autem, quem me dicitis esse. Quaeritur, cur hîc Christus ab Apostolis exegerit, ut veritati testimonium perhibeant, cùm Ioh. 5, 34. neget, se ab hominibus testimonium accipere? Resp. 1. Loquitur Salvator apud Ioh. nō ἁπλῶς, sed κατα τι n. nec negat, quòd ullum ab hominibus testimonium accipiat, sed quòd non solùm, nec principaliter humano nitatur testimonio, cùm opera quae facit, etiam testentur de ipso, quin ipse Pa ter, qui eum misit v. 36. 37. 2. in textu Graeco ibi est λαμβάννω, quod à nonnullis redditur capto, ut ita Christus d. l. saltem à se removeat inanis gloriolae studium, non omne testimonium. 3. Id. d. l. Salvator cumprimis intendit, quòd propter se vel sui causâ nō desideret s. opus habeat ullius hominis testimonio: intereà minimè negat, quòd testimoniis divinis de ipso nobis opus sit, quò videl. fidem illis habendo per ipsum salvemur. Ita h. l. elicit Petri de se testimonium ac confessionē, quò in veritate hâc fideque agnitâ discipulos magis ac magis, confessionem illam approbando, confirmet.)*

## 16:16
v. 16. Σὺ εἶ ὁχριςὸς, ὁ ιἱὸς του θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶτος. The articles are emphatically repeated. You are that true and living Son of that living and living GOD. (Conf. Ps. 2, 7.Matt. 27, 54.John 1, 14.c. 11, 27.c. 20. 31.Acts 8, 37.c. 9, 20.Rom. 8, 32.c. 9, 5.) 1. John 4, 15.c. 5, 5.) Hilarius l. 6. de Trinit. p. 102. In that which Peter says, You are, he explained the power and property of natural truth, and by saying Father, This is my Son, he revealed to Peter, so that he might say: You are the Son of God: because in that which is said, This is: it is the indication of the one revealing; but in that which is answered, You are, it is the acknowledgment of the one confessing. (Similarly Theophylactus: Truly Peter confesses him (Christ) to be the Son of GOD. For he did not say: You are Christ a son of the living GOD, without the article: but with the article, that Son i.e. that very one, who is sole and unique: not a son by grace, but who is begotten from the very substance of the Father. Because there were also many Christs, all Priests and Kings, but Christ with the article is one. So also Chrysost. hom. 55. in Matth. ἦ ὁ χρις etc. Which opinion of the Doctors of the primitive Church our own have deservedly followed. See B. D. Mart. in Th. Phot. p. 121. B. D. Tarn. de Trin. p. 353. who rightly refer this confession

of Peter among those testimonies, from which the true Deity of Christ is proved against the Photinians. But the said heretics object, that phrase Son of the living God, that regard should be had at least to the temporal birth of Christ, and the anointing to his kingly office, since Mark and Luke omit the word Son in the confession of Peter. But the blessed D. Meisner solidly discussed this frivolous exception in Consid. Theolog. Photin page 482. Compare also the Lord Theologians of Wittenberg, Refutation of the Racovian Catechism. Lord D. Calovius in A. C. vol. 2. § 382. c. 3. 9. add. Analects to John 3:16. But Simon Episcopius the Arminian presses the thumb upon the Photinians, when in book IV of his Instit. Theol. Sect. 2. c. 34, he teaches, although Holy Scripture everywhere testifies that Christ is the Son of God, and asserts that this is necessary to be believed; yet it does not assert that it is necessary to be believed that the Father produced him from his own substance. For this is only then necessary to be believed, if Holy Scripture asserted that Jesus is the Son of God in only this one way, or if Jesus could not be the Son of God unless in this one way. But since in four other ways also, which he himself recounts in the preceding chapter , it calls Jesus the Son of God, it is gathered from thence that it is possible for someone to believe that Jesus is the Son of God, even if he either does not know or does not believe that he is the Son of God also in this peculiar way, namely by reason of eternal generation. But what is to be determined concerning those four modes of sonship, and how vain the Photinians are here, whose footsteps Episcopius follows, Lord D. Calovius shows at length in Socinismi Proflig. art. 2. controv. 7. 8. 9. and 10. add also B. Par, Exeg. L. de. L. pers. & off. Christi §. 54. In this place we wish at least to note the passages Ps. 2:7 John 1:14 c. 3:16 c. 5:18 Rom. 8:32 Col. 1:15 by which the orthodox opinion is most beautifully established, and then also the testimony of Isidore of Pelusium, whose epistle 236, which is to Serenus, book 1, sounds thus: οὕτως Furthermore, among the prerogatives by which Bellarmine strives to establish the primacy of Peter, this also is recounted by him, that a peculiar revelation was made to him, and that he was the first confessor of Christ. I reply by denying, both that it follows from thence that he was constituted the supreme monarch of the Church, and that Peter was the first. For did not the remaining Apostles already before this acknowledge and adore Christ as the Son of God, as was noted at c. 14:33. Indeed, even before these, John the Baptist, by pointing out Christ with his finger, confessed him quite clearly as the Savior of the world and therefore also as the only-begotten Son of God. But if, therefore, he who first confessed Christ deserved by this that he should be constituted Monarch of the Church, certainly that honor seems to be deferred with greater right to the Baptist than to Peter. Indeed, even to Nathanael, who used almost the very same words, Ioh. 1, 50. where Peter is in this place. Nor is there any reason why anyone should think that Nathanael professed Christ to be the Son of GOD in that sense at least in which other holy men are considered sons of GOD: For the words which he added immediately stand in the way: You are that King of Israel. Namely, the promised Messiah. Whence also Aug. tr. 7. on John writes, that the same utterance and confession was issued by Nathanael, which Peter issued so much later.

Latin:

v. 16. Σὺ εἶ ὁχριςὸς, ὁ ιἱὸς του θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶτος. Articuli emphaticè repetuntur. Tues verus & vivus ille DEI illius viventis & vivi Filius. *(Conf. Ps. 2, 7.Matth. 27, 54.Ioh. 1, 14.c. 11, 27.c. 20. 31.Act. 8, 37.c. 9, 20.Rom. 8, 32.c. 9, 5.) 1. Ioh. 4, 15.c. 5, 5.)* Hilarius l. 6. de Trinit. p. 102. In eo, quod ait Petrus, Tu es, virtutem & proprietatem naturalis veritatis explicuit, & Pater dicendo, Hic est Filius meus, Petro revelavit, ut diceret: Tu es Filius Dei: quia in eo, quod dicitur, Hic est: revelantis est indicium; in eo verò, quod respondetur, Tu es, confitentis agnitio est. *(Similiter Theophylactus: Verè confitetur Petrus ipsum (Christum) esse Filium DEI. Non enim dixit: Tu es Christus filius DEI viventis, absarticulo: sed cum articulo, ille Filius h. e. ille ipse, qui solus & unicus: non gratiâ filius, sed qui ex ipsâ Patris substantiâ genitus. Quia & multi Christi erant, Sacerdotes & Reges omnes, sed Christus cum articulo unus est. Sic quoque Chrysost. hom. 55. in Matth. ἦ ὁ χρις &c. Quam primitivae Ecclesiae Doctorum sententiam meritò sequuti nostrates. Vide B. D. Mart. in Th. Phot. p. 121. B. D. Tarn. de Trin. p. 353. qui rectè confessionē

hanc Petri referunt inter illa testimonia, è quibus vera Christi Deitatis contra Photinianos probatur. Excipiunt verò dicti haeretici, phrasi illa filius Dei viventis respectum haberi saltem ad temporalem Christi nativitatem, & unctionem ad regium eius officium, siquidem Marcus & Lucas in confessione Petri omittant filii vocem. Sed frivolam istam exceptionem solidè discussit B. D. Meisnerus in Consid. Theolog. Photin pag. 482. Conf. etiam Dnn Theologi Witteb. Refut. Catech. Racov. Du. D. Calovius in A. C. t. 2. § 382. c. 3. 9. add. Analect. ad Ioh. 3, 16. Pollicem verò premit Photinianis Simon Episcopius Arminianus, quando lib. IV. Instit. Theol Sect. 2. c. 34. docet, licet Script. Sacrapassim testetur, Christum esse Filium DEI, & hoc creditunecessarium esse, etiam adserat; non tamen creditu necessarium esse, quòd Pater ipsum de substantiâ suâ produxerit. Hoc enim tum demum creditu necessarium esse, si Sc. S. Iesum Filium DEI esse adsereret unico tantùm isto modo, aut si Iesus non posset esse Filius. DEI, nis iunico isto modo. At cùm quatuor aliis etiam modis, quos ipse c. p-aeced. recenset, Iesum Filium DEI vocat, exinde colligi, fieri posse, ut quis Iesum credat esse Filium DEI, etsi aut nesciat aut non credat, eum esse isto etiam peculiari modo, nempe ratione aeternae generationis, Filium DEI. Sed quid de quatuor illis filiationis modis statuendum sit, & quàm vani hîc sint Photiniani, quorum vestigia premit Episcopius, prolixè ostendit Dn. D. Calovius Socinismi Proflig. art. 2. controv. 7. 8. 9. & 10. add. etiam B. Par, Exeg. L. de. L. pers. & off. Christi §. 54. Hoc loco notari saltem volumus loca Ps. 2, 7.Ioh. 1, 14.c 3, 16.c, 5. 18.Rom. 8. 32.Col. 1, 15. quibus sententia orthodoxa pulcerrimè stabilitur, tum verò & testimonium Isidori Pelusiotae, cuius epist. 236. quae ad Serenum est, lib. 1. ita sonat: οὕτως Coeterùm inter praerogativas, quibus Bellarminus Petri primatum stabilire satagit, haec quoq; ab ipso recensetur, quòd ei facta fuerit peculiaris revelatio, quòd que primus fuerit Christi confessor. Resp. negando, tum quòd inde sequatur, ipsum supremum Ecclesiae monarcham esse constitutum tùm quòd Petrus primus fuerit. Annon enim reliqui Apostoli iam antè Christum Filium DEI agnoverunt & adorarunt, uti ad c. 14, 33. monitum. Imò & ante hos Iohannes Baptista Christum digito monstrando, sat clarè eum mundi Salvatorem adeoque & unigenitum DEI Filium confessus est. Quòd si igitur is, qui primùm Christum confessus est, per hoc meruit, ut Ecclesiae Monarcha constitueretur, sanè maiori iure honor ille Baptistae, quàm Petro videtur deferendus. Imò & Nathanaëli, qui iisd. omninò propè verbis usus est, Ioh. 1, 50. quo Petrus h. l. Nec est, quòd aliquis putet, eo saltem sensu Nathanaëlem Christum professum esse DEI filium, quo alii sancti DEI filii censentur: Obstant enim verba quae statim addidit: Tu es ille Rex Israel. Promissus sc. Messias. Unde etiam Aug. tr. 7. in Iohannem scribit, eandem vocem ac confessionem à Nathanaele fuisse editam, quam tantò pòst Petrus edidit.)*

## 16:17
*(v. 17. Blessed are you &c. Bell. l. 1. on Justification c. 8. attempts to prove from the present passage and some other sayings, that the object of justifying faith is not the special mercy of GOD, because the faith of Peter is praised here, who nevertheless believed nothing except the Deity of Christ. Resp. I deny the consequence. For it does not follow: in this place the object of faith is referred to as the Deity of Christ. Therefore its object is not the special mercy of GOD. For although mention of special mercy is not made here, nevertheless elsewhere, where justifying faith is treated of expressly, the Holy Scripture teaches it throughout. See Rom. 3, 24. 25.c. 4, 24. 25.c. 10, 4.9.Act. 10, 43. Conf. in more detail B. P. Confess. Cath. t. 4 p. 613. But from the fact that Peter's confession was confirmed by that magnificent approval by Christ, Bell. strives to prove that such a revelation was made to him first, and from there he further attempts to infer the Monarchical primacy of Peter. Resp. by denying the consequence. It does not follow, Christ approved Peter's confession, therefore the revelation of the Deity of Christ was made to him first. The Jesuit Salmero himself acknowledged the weakness of the consequence, whence in t. 4. part. 3. tr. 1. he writes: It was said of Abraham that he believed, and that it was reckoned to him for righteousness, and yet many believed before him. And even if the Deity of Christ had been revealed to Peter first of all, and his confession approved with a magnificent response, it would not however be possible to infer his monarchical power from this. Also to be noted in this place is the error of the Jesuit Keller, who although he concedes that Peter, because of his faith Blessed is preached by Christ, yet he denies that this faith is trust, but rather insists that it was at least assent. But if this were so, the devils would also have been preached as blessed, inasmuch as they quite often confessed Christ to be the Son of GOD. See B. D. Zaeman in manifestat. Pap. Acath. vol. 2. page 98.)*

Είμω βὰς Ιωνᾶ. This is from the Syrian custom, among whom the letter Chet is frequently accustomed to be cast away. In ancient books Ioh 1 43. & in the ancient Interpreter it is read Βαο-Ἰννου Son of John, which however is thought by many to be corrupted, as Hievat notes, son of a dove. Others simply accept that Simon, i.e., Peter, is the son of John, according to the interrogation of another place; Simon son of John, do you love me &c. And they wish it to be depraved by the fault of the scribe, so that for Bar-Iohanna i.e. son of John Bar-Iona was written if-, with one syllable removed. Iohanna however is interpreted as the grace of the Lord. *(Whatever may be the case regarding the reading Βαο-Ἰννου, it is certain that that reading is also very ancient, which has Βαρ Ἰωνᾶ. Thus certainly the Syrian reads, the most ancient interpreter, who at this place has it, with both names also explained i.e. son of a dove, Similarly the remaining Oriental Interpreters read, the Arab see the Ethiopian & the Persian, who likewise explain the former name. For thus he translates here that one this one And thus also the same have Ioh. 1, 48. and ch. 21, 15. 16. with the exception only of the Ethiopian who reads i.e. son of John having inserted indeed the letter The same however Ioh. 21, 15. & 16. likewise as in this place has but in place of the name he employs the mark of the Genitive Theophylact likewise also reads thus, adding: As you are the son of Jonah, so I am of my Father, existing consubstantial with Him.)*

Flesh and blood has not revealed it to you. By flesh & blood in the Scriptures is understood 1. human reason, such as it is after the fall, not yet regenerated by the Spirit of GOD. 2. Man consisting of flesh &

blood, Gal. 1, 16.Eph. 6, 12. Both meanings fit this passage, yet the former more so. Indeed, revelation of flesh and blood is the manifestation of things acquired through any power of human reason, without the spiritual dictation of the divine word. Spirit is called the interior understanding of things, which surpasses the grasp of common reason. *(As this interpretation pleases most interpreters, so it is also to be preferred to the exposition of the Jesuit Ioh. Pineda, who in q. 1. Comm. Iobi. c. 10. v. 4. n. 3. says that by flesh in this place is signified something fat, obtuse, thick, not at all subtle and per- spicacious. The parallel passage is 1. Cor. 2, 14. add. Roman. 16, 25.2. Cor. 31, 5. Victorinus Strigelius in Hypomn. ad h. l pag. 61. rightly notes, that the Gospel is not wisdom invented by men. He adds: nor does the human mind assent to the Gospel, unless God ASSISTING. If by these words he only means that the human mind cannot of itself assent to the Gospel if it is destitute of divine illumination, he thinks rightly, and this same thing is evident from the cited passages. But if he hints that man in spiritual matters is not entirely dead to spiritual good, but only gravely wounded, and thus although the mind of an unregenerate man cannot of itself assent to the Gospel, it can do so if the Holy Spirit calls through the Gospel, and thus assist conversion, he errs. Just as our people have prolixly refuted this error of the Synergists. See D. Hutter in Expl. lib. Christ. Concord. p. 196. 197. Although God illuminates us through Holy Scripture, it must nevertheless be well observed against the Photinians that internal illumination is not therefore to be excluded, through which God illuminates us internally, so that we may be illuminated by Holy Scripture. Since otherwise, without that internal illumination, we cannot salutarily understand Holy Scripture with the aid of the intellect alone. On which matter the Blessed Father treats at greater length in Exeg. L. de Sc. S. §. 431. 432. Let Alphonsus Mendoza Controv Theolog. q. 3. n. 7. also be consulted, where he disputes at length against Scotus, who asserts that knowledge of the Most Holy Trinity can be obtained naturally by an Angel.)*

*( But my Father. The principal efficient cause of faith is indicated here, namely God. To which also pertain the sayings Ioh. 6, 29.Phil. 2, 13.Coloss. 2, 12.Eph. 6, 23,23. Indeed, the bestowing of faith is a work of GOD ad extra, and it is so far from the case that faith is not a gift of the Holy Spirit, as the Photinians prattle, see Ostorodus in Disp Germ. opposed to Tradelio p. 203. that it rather pertains to the Holy Spirit in a peculiar way, since illumination, regeneration, etc., are attributed to Him. See. 1. Cor. 12, 3.)*

Latin:

*(v. 17. Beatus es &c. Bell. l. 1. de Iustif. c. 8. è praesenti loco aliisque nonnullis dictis evincere conatur, quòd fidei iustificantis obiectum non sit misericordia DEI specialis, eò quod fides Petri hîc laudetur, qui tamen nihil crediderit, nisi Christi Deitatem. Resp. Neg. conseq. Non enim sequitur: h. l. fidei obiectum refertur Christi Deitas. E. eius obiectum non est specialis DEI misericordia. Etenim licet hîc non fiat specialis misericordiae mentio, alibi tamen, ubi ex professo de fide iustificante agitur, Sc. S. passim id docet. Vid. Rom. 3, 24. 25.c. 4, 24. 25.c. 10, 4.9.Act. 10, 43. Conf. pluribus B. P. Confess. Cath. t. 4 p. 613. Astn. ex eo, quòd Petri confessio magnificâ istâ approbatione à Christo fuerit confirmata, probare Bell. satagit, quòd primo ei talis facta fuerit revelatio, atque inde porrò Monarchicum Petri principatum evincere conatur. Resp. negando consequentiam. Non sequitur, Christus Petri confessionem approbavit, ergò primò ei facta fuit revelatio Deitatis Christi. Conseq. infirmitatem agnovit ipse Iesuita Salmero, unde t. 4. part. 3. tr. 1. scribit: De Abrahamo dictum est, quòd crediderit, & quòd reputatum id ei fuerit ad iustitiam, & tamen ante ipsum multi crediderunt. Et si vel maximè primò omnium Petro Deitas Christi fuisset revelata, eiusque confessio magnificô responsô approbata, non tamen hinc monarchicam eius potestatem statem inferre ficeret. Notandus quoque h. l. error Iesulta Kelleri, qui licet concedat, Petrum ob fidem suam beatum à Christo praedicari, negat tamen, fidem istam fiduciam esse, quin adsensum saltem fuisse dictitat. Quod si hoc, etiam Diaboli beati praedic adi essent, utpote qui sae pius culè Christum filium DEI eonfess sunt. Vid. B. D. Zaeman in manifestat. Pap. Acath. t. 2. pag 98.)*

Είμω βὰς Ιωνᾶ. Est hoc ex consuetudine Syra, apud quos littera Chet frequenter abiici soler. In antiquis libris Ioh 1 43. & apud veterem Interpretem legitur Βαο-ἸννουFilius Ie-annis, quod tamen à multis corruptum putatur, ut notat Hievat filius columbae. Alii simpliciter accipiunt, quòd simon i. e, Petrus sit filius Iohannis, iuxta alterim loci interregationem; Simon Iohannis diligis me &c. Et volunt Scripterum vitio depravetum, ut pro Bar-Iohanna i. e. filius Iohannis Bar-Iona scriptum si-, unâ detractâ syllabâ. Iohanna autem interpretatur Domini gratia. *(Quicquid sit de lectione Βαο-Ἰννου, certum est, quòd vetustissima etiam sit illa lectio, quae habet Βαρ Ἰωνᾶ. Ita certe legit Syrus, interpres antiquissimus, qui h. l. habet, exposito quoque nomine utroque i. e. fili columbae, Similiter legerunt reliqui Interpp. Orient, Arabs vid. Aethiops & Persa, qui itidem prius nomen exponunt. Ita enim hic vertit ille iste Et ita quoque iidem habent Ioh. 1, 48. ac c. 21, 15. 16. excepto solo Aethiope qui legit i. e. filius Iohannis insertanempe litera Idem tamen Ioh. 21, 15. & 16. pariter uti h. l. h-bet loco nominis verò adhibet notam Genitivi Theophy lactus pariter quoque ita legit, addens: Sicus tu Ionae filius, ita ego Patris mei, confubstantialis illi existens sum.)*

Caro & sangvis non revelavit tibi. Per carnem & sangvinem in Scripturis intelligitur 1. ratio humana, qualis est post lapsum, nondum Spiritu DEI regenerata. 2. Homo constans carne &

sangvine, Gal. 1, 16.Eph. 6, 12. Utraque significatio huic loco congruit, magis tamen prior. Est verò carnis & sangvinis revelatio, manifestatio rerum per quamlibet rationis humanae virtutem acquisita, absque spirituali verbi divini dictamine. Spiritus dicitur interior rerum intelligentia, quae rationis communis captum superat. *(Quae interpretatio uti Interpp. arridet plerisque, ita etiam praeferenda expositioni Iesuitae Ioh. Pinedae, quit. 1. Comm. Iobi. c. 10. v. 4. n. 3. per carnem significari h. l. dicit aliquod pingve, obtusum, crassum, minimèsubtile ac per. spicax. Locus parall. est. 1. Cor. 2, 14. add. Roman. 16, 25.2. Cor. 31, 5. Victorinus Strigelius in Hypomn. ad h. l pag. 61. rectè annotat, quòd Evangelium non sit sapientia ab hominibus inventa. Addit: nec mens humana adsentitur Evangelio, nisi Deo ADIUVANTE. Quibus verbis si hoc solùm vult, quòd ex semens humana non possit Evangelio adsentiri, si divinâ illuminatione destituatur, rectè sentit, & patet idem hoc ex locis allegatis. Si verò id innuit, quòd homo in rebus spiritualibus non prorsus ad bonū spirituale emortuus, sed tantùm graviter vulneratus sit, adeoque licet mens hominis irrigeniti non possit ex se Evangelio adsentiri, possit tamen hoc, si Sp. S. per Evangelium vocat, adeo-ue conversionem adiuvare, errat. Quemadmodum etiam istum Synergistarum errorem prolixè refutarunt nostrates. V. d. B. D. Hutter. in Expl. lib. Christ. Concord. p. 196. 197. Licet verò Deus per Scripturam S. nos illuminet, probè tamen contra Photinianos observandum, quòd proptereà non excludenda sit illuminatio interna, per quam Deus nos internè illuminat, ut Sc. S. illuminemur. Cùm aliàs absque illâ internâ illuminatione non possimus solius intellectus auxilio Scripturam S. salutariter intelligere. Quâ de re pluribus agit B. P. Exeg. L. de Sc. S. §. 431. 432. Consulatur quoque Alphonsus Mendoza Controv Theolog. q. 3. n. 7. ubi contra Scotum adserentem, naturaliter posse obtineri ab Angelo notitiam Sacro Sanctae Trinitatis, prolixè disputat.)*

*( Sed Pater meus. Indicatur hîc causa efficiens principalis fidei, nempe Deus. Quo faciunt etiam dicta Ioh. 6, 29.Phil. 2, 13.Coloss. 2, 12.Eph. 6, 23,23. Est verò fidei collatio opus DEI ad extra, tantum-ue abest, ut fides non sit Sp. Sancti donum, quod Photiniani garriunt, vid. Ostorodus in Disp Germ. Tradelio opposita p. 203. ut potiùs peculiari ratione Sp. S. competat cùm illi tribuatur illuminatio, regeneratio &c. Vid. 1. Corinth. 12, 3.)*

## 16:18
*[v. 18. You are Peter. The name παρωύμως, was imposed upon the Apostle Peter, and that both παθητικῶς because among the various temptations of Satan he was to cling with firm faith to Christ, the rock of true salvation, and upon that, as a living stone, he was to be built up Luke 22, 31. 32. and ἐεργητικῶ, because by his ministry and confession he was to build up very many upon Christ, the true rock, by His power, 1. Pet. 2, 5. Thus the Blessed D. Glass. Exeg. Dom. 5. after Trinity p. 1128. By no means, however, can the building of an Ecclesiastical or Papal Monarchy be constructed from this, as has long since been shown by many of our own, see especially the Saxon Theologians in the foundation of the Defense of the Pupil p. 733. seqq. D. Heilbrunnerus Papatus Acathol. art. 14. p. 287. seqq. the same, Apol. p. 291. seqq. Mr. D. Both sacc. contradict. Pontif. c. 29. B. P. Conf. Cath. t. 1. p. 271. & 290. t 2. p. 537. 671. Mr. D. Danhaverus in the Idea of a good Interpreter p. 283. seqq. Dispp. Gies. t. 8. Disp. 10. §. 28. seqq. Marcus Antonius de Dominis, formerly Archbishop of Split, excellently showed in book 1. de Rep. Eccles. c. 6. To whom can be added Daniel Chamier Panstratiae t. 1. lib. 3. c. 3 t. 2. l. 11 c. 2. 3 7. 16. Ioh. Camero t. 2. Praelect. p. 1. seqq. Grossius in the Biblical Theater in the Vindications of this place.]*

Upon this rock. Georgius Dousa, son of Ianus, includes in his journey to Constantinople a letter of Meletius, Pope and Patriarch of Alexandria, to his father Ianus Dousa, whose words are as follows: We acknowledge the Roman Pontiff as a Pontiff, we preach Christ as the one head of the universal Church with Paul. That he is the same cornerstone καὶ δπὶ ταύτη, on which He Himself said the Church must be built, we acknowledge him from His own words, καὶ δπὶ ταύτη, for He says, τῇ πέτρα, ἡ δὲ πέτρα, Paul says* [ 1. Cor. 10, 4. add. 1. Cor. 3, 11.]* ἦ ὁ χριστὸς. For not on you Peter, but on Me, as Augustine most diligently notes, I will build, He says, the Church means This is Meletius. See also the Gloss in c. Dominus dist. 19. And upon this. *[The passage brought forward from Augustine exists in sermon 13. on the words of the

Lord. Conf. The same Aug. tr. 124. in John. Absurdly, therefore, do the Papists [interpret] the voice πέτρα in this place refer to the person of Peter, and the version to which Bell. l. 1. de P. R. c. 10. Iansen. in Comm. c. 66 Lorinus in Acta p. 39. Baron. t. 1. Annal. A. 31. n. 24. and others appeal, the Syriac, does not help them at all, as has been shown long ago by our people. See B. D. Glass. Rh. S. p. 527. Mr. Dilherrus Eclog. Syr. p. 85. Let it be noted at this place at least, that although the Syrian uses the same word in both places, namely , nevertheless he indicates the distinction by placing the masculine before the former, and the feminine before the latter.

I will build my Church. Salmero t. 4. part. 3. tr. 3. interprets the words of Christ thus: Upon this rock i. e. upon you I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against that same rock. He proves it. 1. Christ, about to reward the confession of Peter, repeated the conjunction three times &, namely: And I say to you, and upon this rock, and the gates of hell etc. Where you see that the discourse is to be taken from the preceding and following words concerning Peter. 2. That it is a new thing, into the Universal Church, founded upon the rock, that hell the world cannot prevail. Resp. 1. That rock is neither Peter, nor the seat of Peter, but Christ. 2. When they interpret the rock in the words of Christ, they stubbornly shout that the pronoun must be referred to that which immediately preceded, where, however, there is not only a pronoun: but here, where there is only a pronoun, it, they investigate something more remote. 3. Chrysostom, Euthymius, Theophylact, Anselm in this place, Athanasius in the Oration in which he argues that Christ is one, the Syriac version also etc., expressly refer it to the Church. To the 1st argument of Salmero Resp. the particle and has nothing that is repugnant to the construction which we defend. The Syrian also expressed it, who nevertheless by the change of gender shows that the pronoun it must be referred to the Church. Nor does it follow, if the preceding and following parts are understood concerning Peter, that the middle part must also be understood concerning Peter. For that indeed happens not by the force of that particle, but of the pronoun YOU are, I will give to YOU. Afterwards, however, the phrase is changed into the third person, this rock, against it. But the thread of discourse is scarcely accustomed to be broken in such a way that, while the same person remains, we say now you, now him. To the 2nd, why would it not be a new statement concerning the firmness of the Church, and if not new, why not great? (Stapleton urges an example from Genesis, where God says to Abraham: You shall be called Abraham, with the reason added, because I have made you the father of many nations. Just as, therefore, in that place the reason for the naming added concerns Abraham himself, so in this place Stapleton thinks the added reason is founded in the person of Peter himself. But we respond that there is a difference, since there the pronoun You is added, which does not appear here. Furthermore, even if the reason for the naming were to be sought in Peter, it is not necessary, however, that it be founded in the person of Peter; it suffices that it be in the confession. Others urge that it is said that the Church is still to be built upon the rock. But indeed, it had already long ago been built upon Christ. We respond that the Church is said to be built upon Christ, that is, upon the confession concerning Christ, insofar as the heavenly doctrine is to be spread throughout the whole world in the New Testament and the Church is to be gathered. It is also said of Christ that he will save his people, Matth. 1, 21. and yet he had already long ago also saved his people from their sins. But someone might say: Here Christ says that he wishes to build the Church upon the rock. Now, however, no one builds upon himself. We respond that Christ builds upon himself, while he himself gives the increase from himself; Eph. 4, 16. And it is well to be noted that Peter says, believers are built as living stones upon the rock Christ, 1 ep. 2, 4; therefore he by no means believed that the Church was built upon himself. (Whence the Interpreters well note that the relative τὰυτῃ is to be referred not to the immediately preceding, or to Peter, whose mention had immediately preceded, but to Christ, whom Peter v. 16. had confessed, or to the confession of Christ issued by Peter. See B. D. Glass. Rhet. S. p 183. Nor is it unusual also for the pronouns οὗτος, etc. to be referred sometimes to a more remote thing. See Ioh 8, 10. where οὗτος is to be referred not to the immediately preceding v. 49. but to the more remote v. 48.. The passage Ioh 2, 15. also contributes to this. And thus, namely concerning Christ, or what amounts to the same thing, concerning true faith in Christ and his confession, not only the Fathers understood it, Isidorus Pelus. l. 1. Ep. 235. Jerome in this place, also l. 2. adv. Iovin. and Comm in c. 54. Es. Hilary l. 6. de Trin. p. 74. Augustine serm. 15. de verbis Dom, also tr. 124. in Ioh. Ambrose de incarn. c. 5. Cyril of Alexandria lib. 33. in Ex. c. 3. Bede and Theophylact on this passage. Gregory of Nyssa in the sermon as the rock of life Christ p. 255, edition of Sifanius. But even the first Roman Pontiffs themselves, as B. Par. shows at length in Conf. Cath. b. I. gen. p. 291. Most clearly Eutychianus 1st Ep. Rom. (who sat about A. 275, in Decretal Epist. 1 to John & all the Bishops of the Province of Baetica, vol. 1 of the Councils) writes: This one immovable foundation, this one happy rock of faith, confessed by the mouth of Peter, Thou art Christ, that Son of the living God. So also Gregory the Great in Pf. 7, cited by Cornelius à Lapide himself on this passage: Christ, he says, is the rock, from which Peter received his name, and upon which he said he would build (the Church). Felix, the younger called 3rd, Felix 3rd called 4th, Gregory the Great, Adrian 1st, Nicholas 1st and others have similar things, cited by B. P. in the same book. What of the fact that the Council of Trent itself in Decree 3, Session §. I believe, professes: The Symbol of faith is as that principle in which all who profess the faith of Christ necessarily agree as a firm and unique foundation, against which the gates of hell will never prevail. Alph. Mendoza, Controv. Theol. Quest. 4, p. 295, and other Papists indeed except: Christ is indeed the foundation and the rock: but Peter is also, and so also his successors in the Roman see. But in truth, since so many examples of Roman Pontiffs who have fallen into heresy (which B. Par. brings onto the stage in Confess. Cath. b. 1. Gen. p. 224, so that the boasting of the Jesuit Coster in Enchir. Controv. p. 137 is vain: That in such a great number of Pontiffs who succeeded Blessed Peter, not even one up to Paul V could be brought forward, who either taught heresy or fell into error.) sufficiently testify that the Roman Pontiffs, who boast that they are successors of Peter, have been caught deviating from the faith, as the Canon Law says, c. si Papa dist. 40, it is manifest that the foundation of the Church would be very slippery if it had to be sought in the person of those who boast themselves to be successors of Peter. Rather, Nicholas de Lyra (who lived about A. 1320, as Bellarmine notes in de script. Eccl. and also the Jesuit Ant. Possevino in Appar., by whom he is also greeted as a very learned man) wrote correctly on this passage: The Church does not consist in men by reason of power or ecclesiastical or secular dignity, because many Princes & SUPREME PONTIFFS

& others of lower rank have been found TO HAVE APOSTATIZED FROM THE FAITH, for which reason the Church consists in those persons in whom there is knowledge & true confession of faith & truth. Erasmus of Rotterdam should also be compared entirely in his Annotations on this passage. Especially it is also to be noted that we are also said to be built upon the foundation of the Apostles & Prophets i.e. upon their faith, preached & announced by them, as Vasquez explains in 2. 2. disp. 210. c. 7, Gagnaeus in Ep. ad Eph. the doctrine handed down to us by them, Eph. 2, 20. add Apoc. 21, 14. which if therefore it were permitted to conclude: The Church is built upon the Rock i.e. the Confession or doctrine of Peter concerning Christ, therefore Peter himself and his fictitious successors the PP. RR. are infallible, by the same reasoning we could also conclude from Eph 2.. Therefore the Apostles and their successors, namely all the faithful Ministers of the Church, are infallible. Cornelius à Lapide indeed excepts on this passage: that Peter is the foundation & rock of the whole Church, and even of the Apostles themselves. And he adds, For it was the duty of Peter, as primate and prince, to contain, direct, and, if they should err, to correct the Apostles in faith, religion & duty. I reply: the same power was given to the Apostles over Peter, as is sufficiently evident from Gal. 2, 11. where Paul quite sharply, as Bellarmine himself says in b. 1. de P. R. c. 27. §. Apostolus, rebuked Peter, or as Cornelius à Lapide has in the Prooemium on the Epistles of Paul, he refuted, recalled & corrected him deviating from the right path. There is no doubt, however, that the same right which Paul had over Peter, the rest of the Apostles also had over him, when he deviated from the right path. And finally, assuming that the Apostle Peter had the privilege of infallibility, it is nevertheless by no means permitted to subsume this to the Roman Supreme Pontiffs, since, as Melchior Cano warns in b. 6. LL. c. 8, it must be well noted that it is not revealed in the Holy Scriptures by itself that the Roman Pontiff succeeds Peter, but it is evident from elsewhere, namely from the fact that the most serious Histories have reported that Peter placed his Chair at Rome etc. But those historians who commemorated this were men. Now, however, every man is a liar. Whence it is clear that the infallibility of the Roman Pontiff rests upon a fallible and slippery foundation, even if Peter had received the privilege of infallibility here from Christ. And just as the infallibility of the Roman Pontiff can by no means be proved from the present saying, so the monarchical

The sycophants of the Roman grandmother strive in vain to establish his dominion from the present saying. Certainly, Christ did not grant such a thing to St. Peter or to the other Apostles, but rather seriously exhorted them against desiring it. Conf. Matt. 20, 25. 26. 27.c. 23, 8. 9. 10. and it does not at all agree even with the act of Peter himself. See Act. 8, 14.c. 15, 5.Gal. 2, 14.1. Petr. 5, 3. Compare more things making for this in B. D. Hutter. LL. Theol. p. 32. B. Par. Confess. Cathol. lib. 2. Spec. part. 1 art. 3. c. 1. & c. 2. also L. de Minist. Eccles. §. 217. Furthermore, the Photinians maintain that not even the universal Church itself has in this place the promise that it will endure until the end of the world, and thus they except to the present passage, that it is not promised that there will always be believers, but if they are to be, then Christ will be present with them. Response. What need would there be for a promise of gracious presence and protection, if the Church were not to exist? Therefore they except otherwise, namely, that by the gates of hell is not understood the power of the devil, but the necessity of remaining in death. But this exception will soon be satisfied.)*

*( My church. An argument for the deity of Christ can be sought from here, as was long ago observed by Theophylact, who says thus in this place, When he said, My church, he showed himself to be the Lord of the universe: for all things serve GOD.)*

Gates of hell The gates of the ancients were fortified towers, similar to our courts. Whence by them are signified metonymically Empires. The gate of the Osmanids is the royal seat of the Turkish Sultans. The gates of hell in this place are put for the councils of the ministers of Satan accustomed to meet often, and for the empires waging wars against the Church. We see here 1. The building of the Church. 2. The assault of the same. The gates signify civil and other contests, by which it is customary to fight most fiercely about great matters, for in the gates formerly judgments and consultations were exercised. He affirms, therefore, that the Church can be overturned neither by the impious fraud of heretics, nor by the manifest force of Tyrants. *(Isid. Pelusiota lib. 1. ep. 238. ροσκαίρ The same person explains it in the same way also in ep. 373. also l. 3. ep. 5. So also August. in Ps. against the party of Donatus, and other ancient Interpreters , as well as most recent ones. But beyond the cause, Hugo Grotius wonders here, that this passage about the Devil or even the machinations of the wicked is explained with such consensus. But he urges against the received exposition, that it is nowhere found ἅδου that the word is used either among the Hellenists, or among the writers of the New Testament in any other meaning than either death or the grave, or the state after death. Resp. The explanation of H. Grotius is not new, but Camero proposed the same long ago, from whom he drew it without a doubt, although he conceals the author. Unless one prefers to say that he learned that interpretation of his, which the man κενόφιλος καὶ καινόφιλος vainly prefers to the opinion received in the Orthodox Church, from the Photinians, see Ostorod. Instit. Germ. p. 413. Smalc. against Frantz. disp. 7. p. 409. Socin. tr. de Eccl. p. 69, whose opinion Sim. Episcopius also greedily embraces in his own way, lib. 4. Instit. s. 1. c. 13. item Respons. ad Epist. Wadingi t. 2. Op. p. 118. But how the poison of the Photinian heresy lies hidden under this exposition, the same B. Par. teaches in L. de Inferno §. 6. who himself also in the said §. 4. & 5. and likewise L. de Morte §. 173. shows in many ways that the name שאול and Gr. ἃδης is altogether used of hell, and indeed of the Devil also. Conf. Dn. D. Calov. Socin. Proflig p. 930. 9We grant that Christ promised the faithful immunity from the empire of death. Conf. Ioh. 6, 39. 40.44c. 11, 25. 26. But the question is not about these. But it is disputed whether he did not also promise his militant Church in this place that all the insults and machinations of Satan will not prevail against it. But it is well to be noted that the Savior speaks generally, and by no means grants such perpetual duration to any certain assembly. And experience also testifies that the gates of hell have more often prevailed against particular churches. Whence if the Papists have even most strongly proven that the visible Church (about which, however, B. Par. proves in many ways that Christ is not speaking in this place, L. de Eccles. §. 79. Whence also Cardinal Caietanus rightly explains it of the Church, which consists of the congregation of the faithful, in one faith, hope and charity. Similarly Ioh. Ferus in this place. But such is invisible, since faith cannot be infallibly known in anyone.) will not utterly fail, they have not yet obtained what they want, namely, that the Roman Church, or insofar as it adheres to the Roman Pontiff and acknowledges his dictatorial authority, will prevail against the gates of hell. For that this is a particular church, Alphonsus de Madrigal, Bishop of Avila, of the highest authority among the Papists, long ago warned, writing explicitly in Prologo 2. q. 4. super Matth. Venetian edition A. 1529. p. 26. a. The Church of the Latins is not the Universal Church, but a certain part of it: therefore even if it had entirely erred, the universal Church will not err. Nor does it follow, this promise was given to the universal Church. Therefore, the gates of hell will not prevail against the Roman Church, as being a part of it. For we respond that the Roman Church is a part of the universal, that is, the true and Catholic Church, only when it sincerely embraces the Catholic faith, that is, the faith comprehended in the writings of the Prophets and Apostles. Otherwise, if it has embraced a contrary doctrine, the promises given by Christ to the universal Church do not pertain to it. Nor does it follow: such a promise was made to the Catholic Church. Therefore, the Roman Church is not to be excluded. We respond that a Rule is to be noted here, which the Jesuits propose, Sanctius in Act. c. 10. n. 56. and Corn. à Lapide in the preface to the Gospels p. 21. A. In promises, a condition is understood, which is explained elsewhere. And likewise that other one, also founded in the Holy Scriptures, which Mr. Dr. Walther suggests in the Prolegomena to the Holy Bible §. 44. When the promises of God are not read as fulfilled, the fault was not in God, but in men, not receiving them worthily. Although therefore the promise of stability was made to the universal Church, and thus also to particular ones, it is nevertheless certain that as regards particular Churches it must be understood that this was done with a certain condition, namely if those Churches have remained in the word of Christ, Iohan. 8, 31. if they remain built upon the rock. Which condition not being fulfilled, it is necessary that the promise also not be fulfilled. And finally it is to be noted that this promise is fulfilled, even if at some time the true Church is greatly pressed by persecutions, so that it is not seen by all. However, the saying of the Savior Luc. 18, 8. seems to stand in the way of the promise concerning the stability of the Church. But how that is to be understood will be advised in the Analects to that place. More things pertaining to this are suggested by B. Par. Confess. Cathol. l. 2. spec. part. l. p. 17. Mr. Dr. Muller in Judaism p. 115. Furthermore, if that limitation is understood in this place, that is, that the gates of hell will not prevail against the pious only if they themselves do not depart from Christ, the rock of salvation, that is, if they adhere to him with firm faith, we easily grant that even any pious person may be able to lift himself up with this promise. But it is by no means permitted to infer from this that the faithful cannot absolutely lose faith and the Holy Spirit, as John Camero indeed persuades himself in Myroth. Evang. to this place. He urges against us, whom he calls Semi-Pelagian Innovators, That if the Church were at any time separated from Christ, that is, if the truly faithful were at any time to fall away from the faith, and fall into total apostasy, the gates of hell would certainly prevail against the Church. Resp. I distinguish between the Church considered by reason of divine election or by reason of persevering faith, and the same considered by reason of gracious calling or by reason of present faith. As regards the elect, we concede that they cannot finally lose the faith, and thus the gates of hell do not prevail against them. This notwithstanding, however, they can for a time by sins against conscience shake off the Holy Spirit, whence they also totally lose the faith. As concerns ροσκαίρους, the Church does not consist in them. Whence if they should even in the highest degree lose the faith both totally and finally, and thus the gates of hell prevail against them, yet nothing by this departs from the promise of Christ. Conf. Theoph. in this place and the notes at 1. Ioh. 3, 6.

ὀυ κατιχύσουσι shall not prevail. Satan is strong, but he does not prevail.

Super hanc petram. Georgius Dousa-Iani filius, itineri suo Constantinopolitano inservit Epistolam Meletii Papae ac Patriarchae Alexandrini ad patrem Ianum Dousam, cuius verba sic habent: Rom. Pontificem agnoscimus Pontificem, Christum unum universalis Ecclesiae caput cum Paulo praedicamus.
