## 17:1
v. 1. After six days &c. Matthew and Mark agree concerning the number of days. Luke, however, reports that about eight days had intervened. Chrysostom, hom. 57 in Matt., reconciles this in this way, by saying that Matthew and Mark had calculated only those days which had intervened between the sermon delivered and the approach to the mountain. Luke, however, had also counted the two extreme days, namely the one on which the prior sermon was delivered, and the one on which they climbed the mountain. * (And this reconciliation of Chrysostom is embraced by the Orthodox: B. D. Luther t. 4. Lat. Ienens. p. 368. b. Dn. D. Walth. H. B. p. 776. B. D. Hafenreff. in LL. Th. p. 167. B. D. Bald. in Ideâ Dispos. Bibl. pag. 159. B. D. Glassius Exeg. Ev. Dom. 27. post Trin. p. 1253. Dn. D. Friedlieb. and very many others. Just as also not a few of the ancients. D. Jerome on this passage The answer is easy, because here (in Matthew and likewise in Mark) the middle ones The days are placed, there (in Luke) the first is added and the last. Theophylact and Bede also establish the same in this place. Most Papist commentators also follow the same interpretation, as is evident from Tostatus Abulensis, Dionysius the Carthusian, Barradius, Jansenius, Maldonatus, Conzenius, Cornelius à Lapide, Tirinus, etc., in this place; likewise Didacus de Yanguas, Prompt. Concion. de fest. praecip. p. 212. But it must be well observed that Luke does not say absolutely, after eight days, but after these words about eight days. So that he might signify that the intermediate and full days were only six, just as Matthew and Mark have it. There is therefore a synecdoche in Luke, by which he took a part of the day, both that in which Christ predicted it would happen, and that in which he showed it fulfilled, for the whole day. Since therefore the reconciliation of that apparent contradiction is easy, in the judgment of Jerome cited above, there is no reason why the Jesuit Becanus, intending to prove the obscurity of ὐναντίοφαύειαν, should bring this forward also as a place of confirmation. Since, moreover, the question between us and the Papists is not about the perspicuity of Holy Scripture in general, but in particular, whether Holy Scripture is clear and perspicuous regarding the dogmas of faith to be believed and the precepts of morals. Now indeed it is certain that ὐναντιοφ this is chronological. Furthermore, similar examples of such a synecdoche occur elsewhere in Holy Scripture. See Analecta on Matt. 12, 40. likewise Tirinus on the Idioms of the Hebrew Language §. 28. (which treatise the Londoners inserted into their Apparatus, as Mr. Dr. Walther teaches in the preface) and Sanctius on Zech. ch. 1. n. 61. likewise on Acts ch. 2 n. 15. ch. 12. n. 11.) Others propose such a reconciliation, that Matthew understands six days elapsed from that time when he had preached to the disciples about his passion; but that Luke makes mention of eight days, having made the beginning of the computation from that sermon in which he had given the hope of seeing the kingdom of God to the three disciples. Conf. August. b. 3. de Doctrinâ Christ. cap. 35. b. 2. de Cons. Evang. c. 56. & Epiph. haeres. 69. The author of the Commentary on Mark under the name of Chrysostom, establishes that this diversity is to be attributed either to a lapse of memory in the Evangelists or to an error of the scribe. Andreas Osiander reconciles it thus: that Christ, after six days, i.e., on the seventh, as Luke says, had joined to himself Peter, James, and John, having been called away from the other disciples,

NOTES ON CHAPTER XVII.

so that they might accompany him the next day into the mountain, but that on the eighth he set out, and arrived at the mountain, and there spent the night in prayer, and on the ninth day, i.e., after eight days, as Matthew and Mark say, he was transfigured. (Just as the Savior, after fasting, temptation, and the struggle in the desert, was glorified on the mountain, so we too must finally be glorified through many tribulations and enter into the kingdom of God. Conf. Act. 14, 22 Just as the Hebrew slave served for six years and only afterwards went out free, Exod. 21. so it is incumbent upon us also, that we work for six days, before we arrive at rest. Conf. Exod. 20, 8.Ezech. 46, 1. A comparison can also be instituted between the ascent of Christ onto the mountain, and the ascent of Moses, concerning which Exod. 24, 16.

( He took Peter and James and John. He took three witnesses of his glorification, according to that Deut. 19, 19,15. But why he specifically employed these, the reason for it is not sufficiently clear. Anselm allegorizes here. He took, he writes, three, so that he might signify that only the faithful, who are imbued with the faith of the Holy Trinity, are to be taken up into the brightness of the future resurrection. The names also agree, one for who is the faithful one must be Peter, i.e., firm in faith, afterwards James, the supplanter of vices: furthermore John, ascribing all things to the grace of GOD, against the pride of life. It seems most simply to be able to be said that Christ took those three because they were friends of intimate admission, and because he wanted them to be witnesses especially as confessors of the truth and of the divinity of Christ. See Act 12, 2.Ioh. 1, 14.1 Ioh. 1 1 2. 3. 2. Petr. 1, 18. Just as he also for that reason took the same ones to witness the miracle of the raised daughter of Jairus. Marc 5, 37. Furthermore, the most wise Master wished to consult the weakness of his disciples. And it pleased him that his divine majesty should be made known to them on Mount Tabor, lest his admirable humility on another mountain, namely of olives, should scandalize them afterwards. Compare entirely B. D. Chemn. Harm. Ev. 87 p 962.)

( He leads them up into a high mountain. Christ leads the disciples up into a mountain, so that by this very thing he might teach that he who wishes to be held worthy of divine contemplation must be lifted up from earthly humility, according to Euthym. in this place, or also, according to Theophylact, so that he might show that those who expect the fruit of the resurrection and who long to see the king in his beauty, ought to dwell in thought in the heights. But onto which mountain did they ascend? Ephrem thinks it was Mount Sinai, so that just as GOD showed his glory on it to his servant Moses: so here Christ might likewise exhibit his divine majesty to be beheld by his disciples. Tertullian, book 4 against Marcion, inclines to the same, although he assigns another cause. It was fitting, he writes, that the New Testament be recorded on that mountain on which the Old had been written. But most interpreters understand this as Mount Tabor. Thus, among the ancients, Cyril of Jerusalem in Catech. 12, Jerome in ep. 27, in which the Epitaph of Paula is presented, likewise in ep. 17, Damascene in his sermon on the Transfiguration of the Lord, Euthymius on Ps. 88, Bede on the holy places c. 17, Philo Carpathius on Canticles, Nicephorus l. 8 c. 30, and among the more recent, our own theologians commonly. See B. D. Glass. in Exeg. Ev. Dom. 27 after Trinity, B. Brentius in the preface to his Commentary on Exodus, B. D. Calixtus in Conc., B. Par. in post. Pert. p. 12. 4; so also among the Papists, Alf. Tostatus, Maldonatus, Toletus, Iansenius, Barradius, Corn. à Lapide, and others on this passage. Adrichomius in his description of the Holy Land. To these add the geographers, Heidmann in Palestine c. 9 n. 37, Bunting part 2, Description of the Holy Land p. 33, Vadianus in the Epitome of the three parts of the world, p. 142. Iacobus Faber Stapulensis and Fr. Lucas Brugensis dissent, and understand it as Mount Lebanon, urging that Mark c. 9, 30 says that after the transfiguration Christ passed through Galilee with the Apostles. But the response is that in the Greek in Mark it is ραπορεύεσθαι, which does not mean to pass by or to pass over, but to pass through, not -mb- but to pass through. Furthermore, it is evident from the context that Christ immediately descended from the transfiguration to Capernaum, which city is near Mount Tabor, see Matt. 17, 92224 and compare Pelargus Qq. Evang. in Matth. p. 192, 193.

Latin:

v. 1. Post sex dies &c. De numero dierum consentiunt Matthaeus & Marcus. Lucas verò tradit, octo fermè dies interc--ssisse. Chrysostomus hom. 57. in Matth. id conciliat hoc modo, ut dicat. Matthaeum ac Marcum eos tantùm dies supputasse, qui medii intercesserant inter sermonem habitum & montis accessum. Lucam verò duos etiam extremos computasse, nempe eum, quo prior habitus est sermo, & eum, quo montem conscenderunt. * (Atque hanc Chrysost. conciliationem amplectuntur ex Orthodoxis B. D. Lutherus t. 4. Lat. Ienens. p. 368. b. Dn. D. Walth. H. B. p. 776. B. D. Hafenreff. in LL. Th. p. 167. B. D. Bald. in Ideâ Dispos. Bibl. pag. 159. B. D. Glassius Exeg. Ev. Dom. 27. post Trin. p. 1253. Dn. D. Friedlieb. aliique plurimi. Sicuti etiam veterum non pauci. D. Hieronymus in h. l. Facilis est responsio, quia hîc (in Matth. itemque apud Marcum) medii ponuntur dies, ibi (in Luca) primus additur & extremus. Idem quoque statuunt Theophylactus ac Beda in h. l. Sequuntur eandem interpretationem Pontificii etiam commentatores plerique, ceu patet ex Tostato Abulensi, Dionys. Carthusiano, Barradio, Iansenio, Maldonato, Conzenio, Cornelio à Lapide, Tirino &c. in h. l. it. Didaco de Yanguas Prompt. Concion. de fest. praecip. p. 212. Probè autem observandum est, quòd Lucas non absolutè dicat, post octo dies, sed post haec verba fere octdies. Ut significaret, dies intermedios ac plenos tantùm fuisse sex, quemadmodum Matthaeus & Marcus habent. Est igitur synecdoche apud Lucam, quâ partem diei, tum quo Christus praedixit futurum, tum in quo id ostendit impletum, accepit pro totâ die. Cùm igitur facilis sit apparentis illius contradictionis conciliatio, iudice Hieronymo suprà adducto, non est, cur Iesuita Becanus Sc. S. obscuritatem probaturus, hanc quoque ὐναντίοφαύειαν confirmationis loco adducat. Cùm praetereà quaestio inter nos ac Pontificios nōsit de Sc. S. perspicuitate in genere, sed in specie, an quoad credenda f. fidei dogmata ac morum praecepta Sc. S. clara & perspicua sit. Iam verò constat, quòd ὐναντιοφ haec sit chronologica. Coeterùm similia istiusmodi synecdoches exempla & alibi in Sc. S. occurrunt. Vid. Analecta ad Matth. 12, 40. item Tirinum de Idiot. Ling. Ebr. §. 28. (quem tractatum Apparatui suo Londinenses inservere, uti Dn. D. Walth. in praefat. docet) ac Sanctium in Zach. c. 1. n. 61. it. in Act c. 2 n. 15. c. 12. n. 11.)* Alii talem proponunt conciliationem, quòd Matthaeus intelligat sex dies elapsos ab eo tempore, quô de suâ passione discipulis fuerat concionatus; Lucam verò facere mentionem octo dierum facto computationis initio à sermone illo, quo spem videndi regni Dei fecerat tribus discipulis. Conf. August. l. 3. de Doctrinâ Christ. cap. 35. lib. 2. de Cons. Evang. c. 56. & Epiph. haeres. 69. Autor Comment. in Marcum sub nomine Chrysostomi, statuit, vellapsui memoriae in Evangelistis vel Scribae errori hanc diversitatem esse tribuendam. Andr. Osiander sic conciliat: Christum post sex dies i. e. septimâ, ut ait Lucas, Petrum, Iacobum & Iohannem ab aliis discipulis sevocatos sibi adiunxisse,

NOTAE AD CAP. XVII.

ut postridie ipsum comitarentur in montem, octavâ autem profectum esse, & in montem pervenisse, ibiq; in oratione pernoctasse & sub nonum diem i. e. post octo dies, ut Matthaeus & Marcus dicunt, transformatum esse. *(Quemadmodum verò Salvator post ieiuniū, tentationē & pugnam in deserto, in monte clarificatus est, ita nos quoq; per multa demum tribulationes oportet glorificari & ingredi in regnum Dei. Conf. Act. 14, 22 Sicuti servus Ebraeus sex annis serviebat ac postea demum liber egrediebatur, Exod. 21. ita nobis quoque incumbit, ut sex diebus operemur. prius quam perveniamus ad requiem. Conf. Exod. 20, 8.Ezech. 46, 1. Institui quoq; collatio potest inter adscensum Christi in montē, & adscensum Mosis, de qua Exod. 24, 16.)*

*( Adsumsit Petrum ac Iacobum & Iohannem. Tres adsumsit glorificationis suae testes, iuxta illud Deut. 19, 19,15. Cur verò hos cumprimis adhibuerit, eius causa non satis liquet. Anselmus hîc allegorizat. Tres, scribit, adsumsit, ut fideles tantum, qui fide SS. Trinitatis imbuti sunt, in claritate futurae resurrectionis adsumendos significaret. Nomina etiam cōveniunt, unus quisenim fidelis debet esse Petrus i. e. firneus in fide, poste à Iacobus, supplantator vitiorum: praetereà Iohannes, adscribens omnia gratiae DEI, contra vitae superbiam. Simplicissimè videtur dici posse proptereà Christum tres illos adsumsisse, quia erant intimae admissionis amici, & quia cumprimis veritatis confessores ac divinitatis Christi esse testes eos volebat. Vid. Act 12, 2.Ioh. 1, 14.1 Ioh. 1 1 2. 3. 2. Petr. 1, 18. Quemadmodum etiam propterea eosdem adscivit ad spectandum miraculum excitatae filiae Iairi. Marc 5, 37. Voluit praeterà sapientissimus Magister consulere imbecillitati suorum discipulorum. Placuitq; ei; ut nota ipsis in monte Thabor fieret divina eius maiestas, ne scandazaret illos postea in altero monte, puta oliveti, admiranda eiusdē humilitas. Conf. omninò B. D. Chemn. Harm. Ev. 87 p 962.)*

*( Subducit illos in montem excelsum. In montem Christus discipulos subducit, ut hoc ipso doceret, à terrenâ sublevari humilitate eum opportere, qui divinâ contemplatione dignus haberi vult, iuxta Euchym in h. l. vel. etiam, iuxta Theophylactum, ut ostenderet, eos qui fructum resurrectionis expectant, quique regem in decore suo videre gestiunt, cogitatione in excelsis habitare debere. Sed in quem adscenderunt montem? Ephrem putat fuisse montem Sinai, ut quemadmodum DEUS in eo gloriam suam Mosi servo suo ostendit: ita hîc Christus discipulis suis itidem divinam suam maiestatem conspiciendam exhiberet. Eodem inclinat Tertull. l. 4. adv. Marc. quamvis aliam adfignet causam. Oportebat scribit, in eo suggestu consignari Novum Testamentum, in quo conscriptum fuerat Vetus. Ast Interpp. plerique accipiunt de monte Tabor. Ita è veteribus sentiunt Cyrillus Hieros. in Catech. 12. Hieron. ep. 27. quâ exhibetur Epit. Paulae, it. epist. 17. Damasc. serm. de transf. Dom. Euthym. in Ps. 88. Beda de locis sanctis c. 17. Philo Carpathius in Cant. Niceph. l. 8. c. 30. è recentioribus nostrates Theologi communiter. Vid. B. D. Glass. in Exeg. Ev. Dom. 27. post Trin. B. Brentius in praef. Comm. super Exod. B. D. Calixtus in Conc. B. Par. in post. Pert. p. 12. 4. ita etiam ex Pontificiis statuunt Alf. Tostatus, Maldonatus, Toletus, Iansenius, Barradius, Corn. à Lapide, alii in h. l. Adrichomius in descript. terrae sanctae. His adde Geographos, Heidmannum in Palaestina c. 9. n. 37. Bunting. part. 2. Descript. terr. fanct. P. 33. Vadianum in Epit. trium part. orb. terr. pag. 142. Dissentiunt Iacobus Faber Stapulensis ac Fr. Lucas Brugensis, & de monte Libano intelligunt, urgentes, quòd Marcus c. 9, 30. dicat, post transfigurationem Christum cum Apostolis praetergressum esse Galilaeam. Verùm resp. in Gr. apud Marcum est ραπορεύεσθαι, quod non significat praetergredi s. praeterire, sed pertransire, nicht -mb-sondern durchziehen. Praeterea constat ex contextu, quòd Christus mox à transfiguratione descenderi: Capernaum, quae urbs vicina monti Tabor, vid. Matth. 17, 9.22.24. ac confer Pelargum Qq. Evang. in Matth. p 192. 193.)*

## 17:2
v. 2. He was transfigured before them. Proclus in his homily on the Transfiguration of the Lord, p. 91. Not rashly ( βὀκ ἁπλῶς ) was Christ transfigured, but so that He might represent to us the future transformation of nature * the future second heavenly advent with the Angels in the clouds and fire. Isidorus Pelus. l. 1 ep. 239. The transfiguration of Christ on the mountain prefigured our resurrection from death to life, which indeed even they were commanded to keep silent among themselves until His resurrection, as it would then find faith, as it would then be perceived in reality. *(Moreover, the Savior willed to be transfigured not only 1. for the prefiguration of the future resurrection, concerning which the cited sayings of the Fathers treat; but also 2. for the adumbration of the majesty of His return to the final judgment, as Chrysostom notes in hom. 57 on Matthew, and likewise Jerome on this passage, and especially 3. for the manifestation of His divine glory, which essentially belongs to Him according to His divine nature, and was communicated to the assumed human nature in the very first moment of conception, but was kept secret. Concerning which matter Basilius speaks at length in his Oration on the Transfiguration, and Ephrem Syrus, likewise in his Oration on the Transfiguration of Christ t. 3; finally 4. for the healing of the disciples, to whom the discourse about the future cross seemed very harsh. See Leo M. sermon on the Transfiguration p. 184)* Moreover μεταμορφ σθαι is to be transformed not by reason of substance, but by reason of qualities. *(Whence rightly Theophyl. on this passage: By transformation understand not a change of character and features, but that, while remaining as he was before, an increase of ineffable light took place. Bede the Venerable similarly in his homily: The transfigured Savior did not lose the substance of true flesh; but showed the glory of the future resurrection, whether His own or ours. In the same way Jerome and Euthymius. Furthermore, B. Par. institutes a lengthy comparison of this transfiguration of Christ with our future glory in his Book on Eternal Life § 22. 1. by reason of time. 2. by reason of witnesses and spectators. 3. by reason of place. 4. by reason of form. 5. by reason of those speaking. 6. by reason of the consequences. See also B. D. Glass. Exeg. Evang. Domin. 27 after Trinity, and also in Exeg. Ev. on the Feast of the Ascension p. 282, 283.)*

His face shone as the sun. By this splendor, the divine majesty of Christ was signified, Conf. c. 13, 43. Apoc. 1, 16. Mark chap. 9, 2. 3. has nothing concerning the splendor of the face, Luke chap. 9, 29. says the appearance of his countenance was made different. But the Blessed D. Bald. rightly advises in Ideâ dispos. Bibl. p. 159, that this discrepancy takes nothing away from historical truth, inasmuch as all agree on the matter.)*

His garments were made white as light, Mark, as snow. As its own darkness belongs to shadows, so its own whiteness belongs to light, and therefore it is the same, whether the comparison is taken from snow or from light. In Luke, whiteness and shining light are attributed to one and the same garment. (The Jesuit Ioh. de Pineda notes in Comm. in c. 9. Iob. v. 30. n. 6. when the garments of Christ are called white or shining, nothing else is indicated than that they were bright, resplendent. Compare also B. Par. Harm. Evang. c. 192. p. 1882. and besides the Comm. in h. l. Petrus Thyraeus de Appar. Christi lib. 1. n. 42. Furthermore, the Vulgate here also in this place has as snow. Which reading Don. Laur. Ramirez in Pentecont. c. 2. p. 40. judges should be marked with a white stone, and that both on account of the authority of the Latin Fathers, Hilary etc. and especially of the Vulgate Interpreter, and on account of reason, since that air enclosed in snow, until it exits, represents to us such a whiteness as we are able to conceive with our eyes looking at the light. But since almost all Greek copies have the word φῶς,, as Ramiresius himself admits, and furthermore the Greek Fathers, as well as the most ancient Syriac Interpreter, and also the Arab read it so, we think this is entirely to be preferred to the other, which has ὡς χιών in this place. The Ethiopian also embraces that other one, translating: as snow. The Persian has simply: his garment white and shining. But Corn. à Lapide reveals his ignorance in languages of this kind when he writes in his Comm. in h. l. that the Ethiopian interpreter translates as crystal, but the Persian as snow.

Latin:

v. 2. Transformatusest coram illis. Proclus in homil. in Transf. Dom. p. 91. Non temerè ( βὀκ ἁπλῶς) transformatus est, Christus, sed ut nobis repraesentaret futurā naturae transformationē * futurum alterum adventum coelestem cum Angelis in nubibus & igne. Isidorus Pelus. l. 1. ep. 239. Christiin monte transfiguratio nostram à morte ad vitam excitationem praesignabat, quam quidem etiam usad ipsius resurrectionem tacitam apud se tenere spectatores inbebantur, utpote tum fidem inventuram, ut quaeiam reipsa perspiceretur. *(Coeterùm transfigurari voluit Salvator non solùm 1. ad futurae resurrectionis praefigurationem, de quâ allegata Patrum dicta agunt: verùm etiam 2. ad reditû sui ad extremum iudicium maiestatici adumbrationem, notante Chrysostomo hom 57. in Matth. itemque Hieronymo in h. l. ac cumprimis 3. ad divinae suae gloriae, secundùm divinam quidem naturam essentialiter ipsi competentis, humanae verò naturae adsumtae in primo quidem conceptionis momento communicatae, sed secretò habitae, manifestationem. Quâ de re prolixè agunt Basilius Orat. de Transfig. ac Ephrem Syrus, itidem Orat. de Transf. Christi t 3. denique 4. ad discipulorum, quibus concio de cruce futura admodùm videbatur dura, curationem. Vid. Leonem M. serm. de Transf. p. 184)* Coeterùm μεταμορφ σθαι est transformari non ratione substantiae, sed ratione qualitatum. *(Unde rectè Theophyl. h l. Per transformationem intellige non characteris & lineamentorum immutationem, sed manente, qualis priùs erat, ineffabilis lucis factum esse augmentum. Beda Venerabilis similiter in homil. Transfiguratus Salvator non substantiam verae carnis aneisit; sed gloriam futurae vel suae vel nostrae resurrectionis ostendit. Eod. modo Hier. & Euthymius. Porrò prolixam transfigurationis huius Christi cum futura nostra gloriâ collationem instituit B. Par. L. de vitâ aeternâ § 22. 1. ratione temporis. 2. ratione testium & spectatorum. 3. ratione loci. 4. ratione formae. 5. ratione allocutorum. 6. ratione consequentium. Vid. etiam B. D. Glass. Exeg. Evang. Domin. 27. post Trinit. nec non in Exeg. Ev. in Festo Ascens. p. 282. 283.)*

*( Splenduit facies eius sicut sol. Significata fuit splendore ísto divina Christi maiestas, Conf. c. 13, 43. Apoc. 1, 16. Marcus cap. 9, 2. 3. de faciei splendore nihil habet, Lucas cap. 9, 29. speciem vultûs aliam factam dicit. Sed benè monet B. D. Bald. in Ideâ dispos. Bibl. p. 159. discrepantiam hanc veritati historicae nihil adimere, utpote in quo omnes consentiunt.)*

Vestimenta autem illius facta sunt candida sicut lumen, Marcus, sicut nix. Ut sua caligo est tenebris, ita luci suus candor, adeoque perinde est, sive à nive, sive à luce comparatio sumatur. Apud Lucam uni & eidem amictui albedo & fulgidum lumen tribuuntur. *(Notat Iesuita Ioh. de Pineda Comm. in c. 9. Iob. v. 30. n. 6. quando Christi vestimenta dicuntur alba vel candida, nil indicari aliud, quàm quòd fuerint fulgida, splendentia. Conf. etiam B. Par. Harm. Evang. c. 192. p. 1882. ac praeter Comm. in. h. l. Petrus Thyraeus de Appar. Christi lib. 1. n. 42. Porrò Vulgatus heîc quoque loci habet sicut nix. Quam lectionem albo calculo notandam censet Don. Laur. Ramirez in Pentecont. c. 2. p. 40. idque tùm ob autoritatem Patrum Latinerum, Hilarii &c. ac cumprimis Vulgati Interpretis, tùm ob rationem, siquidem aër ille inclusus in nive donec exeat, nobis talem alborem repraesentet, qualem oculis concipere valemus adspicientes licem. Verùm cum omnia ferè exemplaria Graeca habeant dictionem φῶς, ipso fatente Ramiresio, ac insuper Patres Graeci, tùm quoque antiquissimus Interpres Syrus, nec non Arabs ita legant, omninò hanc alteri, quae habet ὡς χιών h. l. praeferendam putamus. Amplectitur tamen alteram illam Aethiops quoque vertens: sicut nix. Persa nudè habet: amictus eius candidus & lucidus. Prodit verò ignorantiam suam in huiusmodi lingvis Corn. à Lapide, quando in Comm. h. l. scribit, Aethiopicum interpretem vertere, sicut crystallus, Persam autem sicut nix.)*

## 17:3
v. 3. And behold there were seen Moses & Elias. Moses sees in the transfiguration the heavenly brightness of Christ, which he had seen prefigured in the burning bush τυπικῶς. Moses & Elias appear, so that it may be understood that Christ is he of whom the Prophets and Moses spoke, Ioh. 1, 45. Hilary can. 17. in Matth. p. 297. That Moses & Elias from the whole number of the saints stand by, Christ is in the kingdom in the midst between the law & the Prophets. For with these he will judge Israel, by whose witnesses he was preached, at the same time so that it might be taught that the glory of the resurrection was decreed for human bodies, when Moses had stood by visible. Aug. de quinque haeres. c. 7. p. 50. Who are Moses & Elias, if not the law & the Prophets? They were speaking with him, because they had spoken about him. (Jerome has similar things t. o. in Matth. f. 25, also l. 2. adv. Iovin. c. 10. Ambrose l. 7. Comm. in Luc.

t. 5. p. 93. Theophylactus in h. l. He has three reasons 1 that it may be shown that He is the Lord of both the Law and the Prophets, of the living and the dead. 2. that it may appear that Christ is not an adversary to the Law. 3. that He may remove the suspicion of those who said that He was Elijah or one of the Prophets. Cyril of Alexandria, book 6 on Leviticus, notes, for this reason, when Christ had been transformed into glory, Moses and Elijah also appeared with Him in glory, so that we may know that the Law and the Prophets and the Gospel always come into one and remain in one glory. add Augustine, epistle 119. item tractate 17 on John. Origen Co-. 6 on Leviticus. Maldonatus on this passage, p. 352, judges the most true reason why Moses and Elijah appeared to be this, that Christ wished to represent an image of His future advent, since from Apoc. 11, 3. 4. 5. & 6. it is gathered not obscurely that before the second advent of Christ, Moses and Elijah are to come. But although we do not approve of that opinion, which very many Papists embrace, thinking that by those two men Apoc. 11. not Moses, but Enoch and Elijah are designated, as Ludov. ab Alcasar reports in his Commentary on the said passage, we nevertheless consider that hypothesis false, that Moses is to return before the second advent of Christ. And besides Blas. de Viegas on the said passage, who writes expressly: it is left manifest, that Moses will not come at the time of the Anti-Christ, and that the contrary opinion is altogether improbable. Alphonsus Mendoza especially, Theological Controversies p. 411, where he refutes that opinion concerning the return of Moses ex professo. To Conzenius the Jesuit also, that reason for the appearance of Moses and Elijah seems solid, that He might approve of the old law and its heralds . But Tertullian, On Monogamy c. 8, concluded ridiculously from this passage that since Christ in the revelation of His glory joined to Himself Moses and Elijah from so many saints, one a monogamist, the other a eunuch, we if we wish to see that glory, ought to be similar to one or the other. But besides the fact that parabolic theology is not argumentative, we oppose to Tertullian Josephus, book 2 of Jewish Antiquities chapter 10., revealing that Moses had two wives, Zipporah and Tharbis, the daughter of the King of the Ethiopians, who is called the Ethiopian woman, Num. 12, 1. And Isidore and Eusebius establish the same. Pelargus indeed denies this in his Commentary on the said passage, having brought forward some reasons, just as also Mr. Dr. Friedlieb, and the Blessed Dr. Quistorpius, establishing that Zipporah herself is called here An Ethiopian woman, since Midian, from where she drew her origin, produces somewhat darkened women. They add: Midian was also considered to have been Ethiopia. But D. Osiander in Bibl. Gloss. affirms and warns that it appears from the context of the speech that the cause of the expostulation was still recent, because the Ethiopian woman had been taken as a wife by Moses only very recently. Either because his former wife Zipporah had already died, or because supporting several wives at the same time was not foreign to the customs of the Israelites. But because she was not only a foreigner, but also an Ethiopian: they thought this pertained to the disgrace of the whole family, and to the contempt of his person and of his office itself.

Moses. That Moses and Elijah truly appeared here in their own bodies is rightly asserted by the author of the miracles of Scripture, who is believed to be Augustine, lib. 3. c. 10. and he warns that other ancient authors unanimously maintain this. Therefore, our people rightly gather from this that God resurrected the body of Moses from the dead, a little after he had died and been buried, and restored it reunited to his soul in the heavens, and thus notably foreshadowed the universal resurrection of the dead, which is to be in the end of the ages. Conf. Analect. in Epist. Iudae p. 31. 32. and add by all means B. D. Chemnitz in Harm. Ev. p. 965. item Pelargus and Corn. à Lapide both to this place and in Comm. ad c. ult. Deut. v. 5. as well as Metting. Conc. Loc. Sc. S. p. 889. and Ludov. Capellus Spicil. ad h. l. p. 24. But it is asked, from where did the Apostles know Moses and Elijah, never seen before. Capellus answers in the said place that this is to be understood in such a way that they were recognized not from their face and the features of their countenance, but from their conversation and speech. But just as Adam, from the light of the divine image, recognized Eve, whom he had never seen before, and the blessed also are to recognize one another in eternal life, so it is probable that πρόγευσιν some measure of future blessedness was given to the Apostles, and that they were irradiated by God with a certain singular light, so that they recognized Moses and Elijah, never seen before, not only from their speech, but even from their face and the features of their countenance. Conf. B. Par. L. de vitâ aet. § 147. and several authors alleged by the same there. But that seems of greater moment, that some Papists strive to prove the apparitions of the dead and consequently purgatory from this present apparition of Moses and Elijah. Alphonsus Mendoza, Augustinian Hermit, Doctor of Theology and prefect of the Scotist Chair in the Academy of Salamanca, Controv. Theol. q. 5. p. 405. among the more illustrious testimonies by which he tries to evince, That the souls of the deceased have many times appeared to the living, he places this apparition in the first place, and although he himself confesses that it has been doubted by many (Papists) whether they appeared in their own body, or in one assumed or foreign, he thinks nevertheless that whether this or that is asserted, the truth of the apparitions is not taken away: since the question is not about men in their own body, but about the souls of the deceased themselves. Resp. 1. The question between us and the Papists is about the apparition of the deceased, i.e., those who have truly died. Now, however, from 2. Reg. 2. it is sufficiently established concerning Elijah that he was translated alive into heaven. Whence Mendoza does not speak conveniently enough about him, that he, having already died many centuries before, appeared in the transfiguration of Christ. For if he uses that word in the customary meaning, by which it denotes the same as to die, he openly contradicts Holy Scripture; but if otherwise, namely as it signifies no longer to be involved in the affairs of mortals, he brings forward an example foreign to the question, nor does he prove what he ought to have proven. 2. As regards the example of Moses, we concede entirely that Moses was truly dead, nor do we deny it, but rather we assert constantly against Hugo Cardinalis (concerning which matter Pelargus also treats at length in Qq. Ev. in Matth. p. 194) that he truly appeared in his own body in the transfiguration of Christ. But granted that he appeared in a foreign body, this nevertheless helps the desperate cause of the Papists not at all. For what, I ask, does the soul of Moses have to do with souls sweating in purgatory? For the Papists themselves, if I am not mistaken, however erroneously and beyond his merit they exclude him from heaven, do not dare nevertheless to relegate him to purgatory, but assign to him a lodging in limbo. See Corn. à Lapide in h. l. 3. Nor do I think also that those blind patrons of Purgatory believe that Elijah was also carried into purgatory by fiery horses: unless perhaps they wish to understand devils by those fiery horses, and attribute a place for purgatory in heaven. Frivolous is the evasion of Alphonsus, warning that Elijah did not into heaven, but towards heaven he ascended, for neither does the sacred code place purgatory more towards heaven, than into heaven. And perhaps Alphonsus would do better if he had placed that same thing towards Utopia, rather than towards heaven. Certainly Cornelius à Lap. in this place does not dare to assert that Elijah was carried here from limbo or purgatory, but writes either from paradise, or from the place into which he was translated by God, he was suddenly translated here. 4. The corpse of the consequence is: Moses & Elijah appeared in the transfiguration of Christ. Therefore, souls also burning in Purgatory appear, so that they may solicit the living, that they may relieve them by their own prayers. The Holy Scripture explicitly affirms the former; concerning the latter, not even γρ- exists in either the Old or New Testament. 5. Blessed D. Chemn. well warned in part 3 of the Examination of the Council of Trent, p. 206, that God for this reason took Elijah away in a fiery chariot, and buried Moses himself, so that no one knew his sepulcher, so that he might signify that he would use their bodies & spirits for a peculiar dispensation at some time: furthermore, they brought nothing new outside of or beyond Holy Scripture (which those Satanic specters do, which the Papists trifle are souls feeling heat in Purgatory), but they spoke of the departure of Christ to be fulfilled in Jerusalem, as the same book in the same place holds. Compare Blessed D. Meisn. Op. 2. on Purgatory, p. 721. I will not now mention that the sounder Papists themselves hold the apparitions of souls, which those peddlers of trifles boast of, to be Satanic illusions, as Blessed Par. shows at greater length in L. on Death §. 285. likewise Confess. Cathol. l. 2. Spec. part. 2. art. 9. p. 466.)

* ( ΩΦτησαν. Wendelinus Exerc. 46. §. 16. from the fact that the glorified bodies of Moses & Elijah were seen by the χοικο-ς disciples, attempts to evince that, just as the blessed are not changed into angels, nor do they cease to be men, so they do not cease to have truly human, solid, visible & palpable bodies. And from there he further gathers that the body of Christ is nowhere, unless where it is actually felt and seen. I respond 1. by conceding that the blessed will by no means be -σαγγέλς, such that they are changed into angels or cease to be men: for we assert and also openly profess that they altogether retain truly human bodies. 2. by denying that those same bodies will be so visible & palpable that they are nowhere, unless where they are actually seen and felt. For it is evident then from the example of Christ, manifesting himself after his resurrection to whomever he wished and again denying the sight of himself, from Matth. 27, 5. That it is in the power of a glorified body to be seen, and not to be seen by men not yet glorified or by χοι--ς. eyes. 3. It does not follow, the glorified bodies of Moses and Elijah were seen by χοιηοις eyes. Therefore, they are always actually visible, or they are nowhere, where they are not seen. Indeed, rather, from their sudden disappearance it is easy to infer the contrary. 4. Nor is the consequence firm. Christ, about to prove the truth of his body after the resurrection, commands that it be touched and seen, therefore it is so visible that it is actually always seen, or it is nowhere, unless it is seen and touched. For it suffices for the blessed to prove the truth of their body, that they are endowed with the power divinely granted to them, so that they can offer their glorified bodies to be seen and touched. Christ therefore offered himself to be touched to the disciples after the resurrection, not because it is an essential property of a glorified body to be actually seen and touched, but he did that out of a free economy, so that he might render the disciples certain of his resurrection, as the Blessed Par. N. E. c. 212. p. 2171 advises. What therefore the ancients write concerning the eating of Christ after the resurrection, See Theoph. Beda in h. l. Damasc. l. 4 de O. F. c. 1. that it was done not out of necessity of nature, but out of free economy, dispensation and will, the same must also be determined concerning that state, that the Savior offered his body to be touched. Furthermore, Polanus in Synt. Theol. p. 148. and from him Grossius in Theatro Biblico p. 931. attribute to our people, as if they offer the omnipresence, or ubiquity, of the assumed human nature from the transfiguration of Christ. collecting in this manner: The body which was transfigured, is everywhere. The body of Christ was transfigured. Therefore. Resp. 1. With the word ubiquity dismissed, which was devised by the Zwinglians to reconcile the envy of our doctrine concerning the Majesty of the Son of man, it has long since been advised by our people, see D. Hutter. Explic. libri Concord. p. 823. it must be observed 2. that no one of our people collects so nakedly: for we know from Phil. 3, 21. that the Savior will also transform our bodies at some time, so that he may render them conformed to his glorious body, nor is any of our people so absurd as to think that our glorified bodies will be everywhere. We do indeed assert that glorified bodies will not be enclosed in a place, but from that it does not follow, Therefore they will be everywhere. 3. But the omnipresence of the human nature of Christ itself not from not from the transfiguration, but from the personal union, and indeed from Christ's infallible promise, his glorious ascension and sitting at the right hand of God, and his fulfilling and ruling of all things — all this our own [theologians] prove. 4. If any oppose this passage to the Calvinists, they gather from it at least this much, that it is not an essential property of a true body to be enclosed in a place, as indeed the Adversaries maintain, and from that false hypothesis they impugn the omnipresence of Christ the man, that is, of the human nature of Christ)*

Latin:

v. 3. Et ecce conspecti sunt Moses & Elias. Moses videt in transfiguratione coelestem claritatem Christi, quam in rubo ardente τυπικῶς praefiguratam viderat. Apparent Moses & Elias, ut intelligatur, Christum esse illum, de quo Prophetae loquuti sunt & Moses, Ioh. 1, 45. Hilarius can. 17. in Matth. p. 297. Quòd Moses & Elias ex omni sanctorum numero adsistunt, medius inter legem & Prophetas Christus in regno est. Cùm his enim Israelem, quibus testibus praedicatus est, iudicabit, simulut & humanis corporibus decreta esse resurrectionis gloria doceretur, cùm Moses conspicabilis adstitisset. Aug. de quinque haeres. c. 7. p. 50. Qui sunt Moses & Elias, nisi lex & Prophetae? Loquebantur cum illo, quia locutierant de illo. *(Similia habet Hieronymus t. o. in Matth. f. 25, it. l. 2. adv. Iovin. c. 10. Ambros. l. 7. Comm. in Luc.

t. 5. p. 93. Theophylactus in h. l. Habet tres causas 1 ut ostendatur, quòd & legis & Prophetarum sit Dominus, viventiumac mortuorum. 2. ut appareat, quòd Christus non sit legi adversarius. 3. ut suspicionem tollat eorum, qui ipsum Eliam vel unum ex Prophetis dicebant. Cyrillus Alexandrinus lib. 6. in Levit. notat, propterea, quum Christus in gloriam esset transformatus, etiam Mosen & simul cū ipso apparuisse in gloria, ut sciamus, quia lex & Prophetae & Evangelium in unum semper veniūt & in una gloria permanent. add. Aug. ep. 119. it. tr. 17. in Ioh. Origen. Co-. 6. in Levitic. Maldonatus in h. l. p. 352. verissimam causam, cur Moses & Elias apparuerint, esse arbitratur, quòd voluerit Christus futuri adventûs sui imaginem, repraesentare, siquidem exApoc. 11, 3. 4. 5. & 6.haut obscurè colligatur, ante secundum Christi adventum Moysen & Eliam venturos esse. Verùm licet non probemus sententiam illam, quam plerique Pontificii amplectuntur, per istos duos viros Apoc. 11. non Mosen, sed Enochum & Eliam designari existimantes, ceu refert Ludov. ab Alcasar Comm. ad d. l. falsam tamen existimamus & illam hypothesin, quòd Moyses sit ante secundum Christi adventum rediturus. Adstipulaturque nobis praeter Blas. de Viegas in d. l. qui dissertè: manifestum relinquitur, scribit, Mosen non venturum esse Anti Christi tempore, contrariamque opinionem esse omninò improbabilem. Alphonsus cumprimis Mendoza Controv. Theol p. 411. ubi exprofesso sententiam illam de reditu Mosis refellit. Conzenio quoque Iesuitae ea ratio apparitionis Mosis & Eliae solida videtur, ut veterem legem eiusque praecones appro-aret. Ridiculè verò ex hoc loco Tertull. de Monog. c. 8. conclusit, quòd cum Christus in revelatione gloriae suae de tot sanctis Mosen & Eliam sibi coniunxerit, unum monogamum, alterum eunuchum, nos quosi velimus videre ius gloriam oporteat alterutri esse similes. Verùm praeterquam quòd Theologia parabolica non sit argumentativa, opponimus Tertulliano Iosephum, l. 2. Antiq. Iudaic. cap. 10. prodentem, quòd Moses duas habuerit uxores, Zephoram & Tharbin, filiam Regis Aethiopum, quae dicatur Aethiopissa, Num. 12, 1. Idēq; statuunt Isidorus & Eusebius. Negat quidem hoc Pelargus in Comm. ad d. l. adductis aliquot rationibus, quemadmodum etiam Dn. D. Friedlieb, ac B. D. Quistorpius statuentes, ipsum Zipporam hîc vocari Aethiopissam, siquidem & Midian, unde illa originem duxerit, aliquat. in fuscatas generet mulieres. addunt: Midian etiam Aethiopiam fuisse aestimatam. Ast. D. Ofiander in Bibl. Gloss. affirmat monetque, apparere ex orationis contextu, fuisse adhuc recentem causam expostulationis, quòd nuper admodùm Aethiopissa fuisset à Mose ducta in uxorem. vel quia prior eius uxor Sephora iam obiisset, vel quia plures uxores simul alere, ab Israëlitarum moribus non erat alienum. Quia verò non alienigena modò, sed & Aethiopissa erat: existimabant, hoc pertinere ad familiae totius dedecus, & ad personae & ad muneris ipsius contemtum)*

*( Moses. Verè suis corporibus Mosen & Eliam hîc apparuisse, recte adserit auctor de mirabilibus Scripturae, qui Augustinus creditur, lib. 3. c. 10. monetque, quòd autores veteres alii -nanimiter ita statuant. Rectè proinde hinc colligunt nostrates, quòd Deus Mosis corpus, paullò post, quàm mortuus ac sepultus fuit, è mortuis resuscitaverit, & in coelis animae redunitum reposuerit, atque sic universali mortuorum resurrectione, in fine seculorum futurae, insigniter praeluserit. Conf. Analect. in Epist. Iudae p. 31. 32. ac adde omninò B. D. Chemnitium in Harm. Ev. p. 965. item Pelargum & Corn. à Lap tum ad h. l. tum Comm. ad c. ult. Deut. v. 5. nec non Metting. Conc. Loc. Sc. S. p. 889. ac Ludov. Capellum Spicil. ad h. l. p. 24. Sed quaetitur, unde cognoverint Apostoli Mosen & Eliam, nunquam --ea visos. Respondet Capellus d. l. intelligendum hoc ita, quòd agniti fuerint non ex facie & lineamentis vultûs, sed ex eorum colloquio & sermone. Verùm quemadmodum Adamus ex luce divinae imaginis, Evam nunquam priùs visam, agnoscebat, ac beati quoque in vitâ aeternâ invicem agnituri sunt, ita probabile est, Apostolis πρόγευσιν aliquam futurae beatitudinis suisse datam, adeoque singulari quadam luce divinitus fuisse eos irradiatos, ut non solùm ex sermone, verùm ex facie etiam ac lineamentis vultûs Mosen atque Eliam, nunquam antè visos, agnoverint. Conf. B. Par. L. de vitâ aet. § 147. ac plusculos autores ab eod. ibi allegatos. Id verò maioris videtur momenti, quòd Pontificii nonnulli, mortuorum apparitiones & per consequens purgatorium è praesenti Mosis & Eliae apparitione probare satagunt. Alphonsus Mendoza Eremita Augustinianus, Theol. D. & in Acad. Salmant. Cathed. Scoti praefectus, Controv. Theol. q. 5. p. 405. inter illustriora testimonia, quibus evincere conatur, animas defunctorum vivis multoties apparuisse, apparitionem hanc primo loco ponit, & licet ipse fateatur, à pleris- (Pontificiis) dubitatum esse, an in corpore proprio, vel adsumto vel alieno apparuerint, putat tamen, sive hoc, sive illud adseratur, non tolli apparitionum veritatem: cùm quaestio non sit de hominibus in proprio corpore, sed de animabus ipsis defunctorum. Resp. 1. Quaestio inter nos ac Pontificios est de apparitione defunctorum s. qui reverà mortui sunt. Iam verò ex 2. Reg. 2. satis constat de Eliâ, quòd vivus fuerit translatus in coelum. Unde non satis commodè de eo loquitur Mendoza, quòd antè mult as annorum centurias iam defunctus, apparuerit in transfiguratione Christi. Etenim si verbo illo in usitatâ utitur significatione, quâ idem notat ac mori, apertè Sc. Sacrae contradicit; sin aliter, nempe prout idem sanat, ac non ampliùs -ebus mortalium interesse, exemplum à quaestione alienum adducit, nec probat, quod probare debebat. 2. Quod spectat exemplum Mosis, concedimus omninò, quòd Moses re verâ fuerit mortuus, nec inficias imus, sed potiùs contra Hugonem Cardinalem constanter adserimus, (qua de re etiam prolixè agit Pelargus Qq. Ev. in Matth. p. 194.) quòd vero suo corpore apparuerit in Christi transfiguratione. Positô verò, quòd in alieno corpore apparuerit, nil tamen hoc iuvat desperatam Pontificiorum causam. Quid enim, quaeso, animae Mosis negotii cum animabus in purgatorio sudantibus. Ipsi enim, nî fall or, Pontificii, ut ut perquàm erroneè ac praeter eius meritum coelo eum excludant, non audent tamen in purgatorium relegare, sed in limbum hospitium ipsi adsignant. Vid. Corn. à Lapide in h. l. 3. Nec existimo etiam, quòd coeci isti Purgatorii patroni Eliam quoq; in purgatorium equis igneis vectum credant: nisi fortè per equos illos igneos diabolos intelligere velint, ac purgatorio in coelo tribuere locum. Frivola est tergiversatio Alphonsi, monentis quòd Elias non in coelum, sed versùs coelum adscenderit, neque enim purgatorium magis versùs coelum, quàm in coel. Codex sacer locat. Satiusque faceret fortè Alphonsus, siversus Utopiam, quàm versùs coelum idem illud locasset. Certè Cornelius à Lap. in h. l. Eliam ex limbo vel purgatorio vectum huc esse, adserere non audet, sed vel exparadiso, velloco, in quem à Deo translatus, subitò huc translatum scribit. 4. Cadaver consequentiae est: Moses & Elias apparuerunt in Christi transfiguratione. E. animae quoque in Purgatorio aestuantes apparent, ut vivos solicitent, quò suis ipsas precibus sublevent. Illud disertè affirmat Sc. Sacra, de hôc ne γρ- quidem neque in V. neque N. T. extat. 5. Benè monuit B. D. Chemn. part. 3. Exam Concilii Trid. p. 206. Deum ideò Eliam curru igneo abstulisse, ac Mosen sepelivisse ipsum, ita ut nemo sepulcrum eius cognoverit, quò significaret, se ipsorum corporibus & spiritibus ad peculiarem aliquando dispensationem usurum: praetere à nec novi ali quid extra vel praeter Sc. S. illi attulerunt, (quod faciunt illa spectra Sataniaca, quae animas in Purgatorio aestum sentientes esse, Pontificii nugantur,) sed de excessu Christi in Ierusalem complendo loquuti sunt, ut habet idem l. c. Conf. B. D. Meisn. Op. 2. de Purg. p. 721. Non iam commemorabo, quòd ipsi saniores Pontificii apparitiones animarum, quas iactitant isti nugivenduli, pro illusionibus Satanicis habent, uti pluribus ostendit B Par. L. de Morte §. 285. it. Confess. Cathol. l. 2. Spec. part. 2. art. 9. p. 466.)*

* ( ΩΦτησαν. Wendelinus Exerc. 46. §. 16. ex eo, quòd Mosis & Eliae corpora glorificata à χοικο-ς discipulis visa sunt, evincere conatur, quod uti beati non in angelos mutantur, nec nomines esse desinūt, ita nec corpora verè humana, solida, visibilia & palpabilia habere desinant. Atq; inde porrò colligit, quòd Christi corpus nullibi sit, nisi ubi actu palpetur ac videatur. Resp. 1. concedendo, beatos minimè ita fore -σαγγέλς, ut in Angelos mutentur vel homines esse desinant: adserimus enim ac palam quoq; profitemur, quòd omninò verè humana corpora retineant. 2. negando, quòd eadem illa corpora ita visibilia & palpabilia sint futura, ut nuspiam sint, nisi ubi actu videantur ac palpentur. Patet enim tum ex exemplo Christi, post resurrectionem suam quibuscunque voluit sese manifestantis ac rursus conspectum sui negantis, ex Matth. 27, 5. quòd in potestate corporis glorificati sit videri, & non videri ab hominibus nondum glorificatis sive oculis χοι--ς. 3. Non sequitur, Mosis & Eliae corpora glorificata oculis χοιηοις visa sunt. E. semper actu sunt visibilia, sive nuspiam sunt, ubi non videntur. Imò potius ex subitanea eorundem disparitione contrarium colligere pronum est. 4. Nec firma est sequela. Christus corporis sui veritatem probaturus post resurrectionem, palpari ac videri illud iubet, ergo ita visibile est, ut actu semper videatur, vel nullibi sit, nisi videatur ac palpetur. Sufficit enim beatis ad probandam corporis sui veritatem, quòd potestate divinitus eis concessâ praediti sint, ut corpora sua glorificata videnda ac palpanda praebere possint. Christus proinde palpandum sese post resurrectionem discipulis praebuit, non quòd essentialis corporis glorificati propriot as sit, actu videri & tangi, sed fecit illud ex liberâ Oeconomiâ, ut discipulos de resurrectione sua redderet certos, uti monet B. Par. N. E. c. 212. p. 2171. Quod proinde de manducatione Christi post resurrectionem scribunt veteres, Vid. Theoph. Beda in h. l. Damasc. l. 4 de O. F. c. 1. quòd facta ea sit non ex naturae necessitate, sed ex liberâ oeconomiâ, dispēsatione ac voluntate, idem quoque de eo statuendum, quòd palpandum suum corpus Salvator praebuit. Porrò Polanus in Synt. Theol. p. 148. & ex eo Grossius in Theatro Biblico p. 931. nostratibus attribuunt, ac si ex transfiguratione Christi humanae naturae adsumtae omnipraesentiam, sive ubiquitatem praebent. h. m. colligentes: Corpus quod fuit transfiguratum, est ubique. Corpus Christi fuit transfiguratum. E. Resp. 1. Misso voce ubiquitatis, quam à Zvinglianis ad conciliandam doctrinae nostrae de Maiestate Filii hominis invidiam excogitaram, pridem à nostratibus monitum, vid D. Hutter. Explic. libri Concord. p. 823. observandum 2. quòd nemo nostratium ita nudè colligat: novimus enim ex Phil. 3, 21. Salvatorem etiam nostra corpora aliquando transformaturum, ut conformia reddat corpori suo glorioso, neq; tamen quisquam nostratium stratium adeò absurdus est, ut sentiant, corpora nostra glorificata ubique futura. Id quidem adserimus, corpora glorificata non fore loco inclusa, sed ex eo non sequitur, E ubique erunt. 3 Ipsius verò humanae Christi naturae omnipraesentiam non ex transfiguratione, sed ex personali unione, tum verò ex infallibili Christi promissione, gloriosâ adscensione & ad dextram DEI sessione, omnium impletione ac dominatione nostrates probant. 4. Si qui hunc locum Calvinianis opponunt, hoc saltem ex eo colligunt, quòd non sit eslentialis veri corporiproprietas, loco includi, uti quidem Adversarii statuunt, & ex falsâ istâ hypothesi Christi hominis s. humanae Christi naturae omnipraesentiam impugnant)*

## 17:4
v. 4. "It is good for us to be here." It is better to remain here than to go up to Jerusalem to the Passion. *(Compare Gregory the Great, bk. 8, Moral., ch. 41, and bk. 2, exposition on 1 Kings, ch. 3. Beautifully, Augustine in the Soliloquies, ch. 22: "He tasted one drop of sweetness, and loathed every other sweetness besides: what do you suppose he would have said, had he tasted that great abundance of your sweetness, O God, which you have hidden away for those who fear you!" The ancients accuse Peter here of imprudence and inexperience, as one who did not know what he was saying. See Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria, bk. 6 on Leviticus, p. 681; Augustine, bk. 6 against Faustus, ch. 17; Chrysostom on this passage; Origen; and others. The Magdeburg writers follow these, Cent. 1, bk. 2, ch. 10, columns 558–559. The Papists take this ill, Bellarmine, bk. 1, de P. R., ch. 28, §. Resp. quod Petrus; Gretser, Defens. Bellarmini, t. 2, p. 650 — inasmuch as by that assertion the crime of lèse-majesté against the Pope is indirectly committed. But how very far the Magdeburg writers, as well as some of the ancients, are mistaken in attributing error here to Peter, William Whitaker shows at greater length in de P. R., p. 321. Compare also Franciscus Junius, t. 2, Opera, p. 699.)*

Latin:

v. 4. Bonum est nos hîc esse. Praestat hîc manere, quam Hierosolymas ad passionem proficisci. *(Conf. Gregor. M. l. 8. Moral. c. 41. ac l. 2. expos. in l. 1. Reg. c. 3. Pulcrè Aug in Soliloq. c. 22. Unam ille stillam dulcedinis gustavit, & omnem aliam fastidivit dulcedinem: quid put as, dixisset si magnam illam multitudinem dulcedinis tuae gustasset, quam abscondisti, ô Deus! timentibuste. Veteres imprudentiae ac imperitiae accusant hîc Petrum, tanquam qui ne sciret, quid diceret. Vide Cyrillum Alexandr. Episcopum lib. 6. in Lev. p. 681. Augustinum lib. 6. contra Faustum c. 17. Chrysost. in h. l. Origenem, alios. sequuntur hos Magdeburgenses Cent. 1. lib. 2. c. 10. column. 558. 559. Dolenter id ferunt Pontificii, Bell. lib. 1. de P. R. c. 28. §. Resp. quod Petrus. Grets. Defens. Bell. t. 2. p. 650. utpote cûm indirectè adsertione illâ crimen laesae maiestatis Papalis committatur. Verùm quàm minimè Magdebur genses, sicuti & veterum no-nulli errent, errorem hîc Petro tribuentes, prolixiùs ostendit Guil. Whitakerus de P. R. p. 321. Conf. & Franc. Iuniust. 2. oper. pag. 699.)*

## 17:5
v. 5. Behold a bright cloud. In the shining cloud, overshadowing the Apostles, the Holy Spirit manifested himself, the author of our inward illumination. *(But how, if the Holy Spirit manifested himself in the cloud, did the voice come forth from it: This is my beloved Son, etc., which must surely be attributed to the Father? Answer: The cloud indeed was the external symbol of the Holy Spirit, but the voice heard from the cloud was the external symbol of the Father. He who speaks from the cloud was the Father, not he whose symbol the cloud was. But)* If the voice sounded from a cloud, how is it said that the voice2. Petr. 1, 18.is from heaven έξ ούρανού ένηχθιού; Resp. The cloud was descending miraculously from heaven, and from it the voice of the Father was heard, therefore the voice is said to have been brought from heaven. Chrysostom and Ambrose observe that that voice sounded from the cloud, which was already raised higher from the earth, and indeed after the departure of Elijah and Moses, so that the Apostles might be certain that this voice was directed to Christ alone. But how the mystery of the Trinity can be proven from this manifestation will be shown in the Analysis to Mark 9, 7.

( Voice from a cloud. See Annotations to Matthew 3, 17. This is my beloved Son etc. from Psalm 2, 7. Isaiah 42, 1. Compare Annotations to chapter 3, 17.)

Hear him. See above chapter 3, near the end. (Especially also the annotation to Mark 9, 7. as well as the Commentary of the Blessed Pareus to Deuteronomy 18, 19. The Jesuit Costerus, Enchiridion Controversiarum, p. 106, from the fact that Christ commands the Apostles to hear the same clear and sensible voice, Luke 10, 16. who subsequently founded visible churches, just as here the heavenly Father presented Christ the Son to the Apostles, concludes that the Church is visible, and that an invisible one is not given. But I respond: 1. The position of one is not the exclusion of the other. The same Church, which by reason of external calling, preaching, and profession is visible, by reason of internal communication with Christ the head is invisible. 2. From whence it does not follow: the Church, that assembly where the word of God is preached and the Sacraments are administered, can be seen, and Christ commanded that we should hear the Apostles and their successors, which cannot be done unless they are seen. Therefore, the reborn with respect to faith and the internal gifts of the Holy Spirit can also be seen. Rightly therefore 3. the Blessed Doctor Graverus, Vol. 1, Disputations Against the Jesuits, p. 242, warns that we deny that the Church is visible as regards saving faith, but not as regards the external and public ministry. But this ministry of the word, and consequently also Councils and the decrees of Pontiffs, are to be heard only when they have Christ as their leader, but by no means when they obtrude their own opinions. For then we rightly urge this heavenly oracle: Hear him. What Felicianus Capitonus objects in the Explanatio Catholica will be discussed in the Analysis to Luke 10, 16., as it is from that passage in particular that he strives to establish his opinion. Compare John 10, 27. chapter 8, 31.)

Latin:

v. 5. Ecce nubes candida. In nube lucidâ, Apostolos inobumbrante, manifestavit se Spir. Sanctus, interioris nostrae illuminationis autor. *(Sed quomodo, si Sp. S. in nube sose manifestavit, vox ex eâ prodiit: Hic est Filius meus &c. quae utiq Patri tribuenda? Resp. Nubes quidem fuit Symbolum externum Sp. Sancti, sed vox ex nube audita, fuit Symb. ext. Patris. qui ex aube loquitur, fuit Pater, non autem is, cuius symb. fuit nubes, Ast si ex nube sonuit vox, quomodo2. Petr. 1, 18.vox diciturέξ ούρανού ένηχθιού; Resp. Nubes miraculosè descendebat de coelo, & ex illâ audiebatur vox Patris, E. è coelo dicitur vox allata. Chrysost. & Ambrosius observant, quòd vox illa è nube iamtum altiùs è terrâ elevatâ, & quidem post discessum Eliae & Mosisinsonuerit, quò Apostoli certi essent, hanc vocem ad solum Christū dirigi. Quomodo verò ex hâc manifestatione Trinitatis mysteriū probari queat, ostendetur in Anal. ad Marc. 9, 7.)*

*( Vox è nube. Vid. Annot. ad Matth. 3, 17.Hic est Filius meus dilectus &c. ex Ps. 2, 7.Esai. 42, 1. Conf. Annot, ad c. 3, 17.)*

Hunc audite. Vid. suprà c. 3. sub finem. *(Cumprimis etiam annot. ad Marc. 9, 7. nec non Com. B. Par. ad Deut. 18, 19. Iesuita Costerus Enchir. Controv. p 106. ex eo, quòd Christus eadem clarâ & sensibili voce Apostolos audire iubeat, Luc. 10, 16. qui deinceps visibiles Ecclesias fundarunt, ceu hîc Pater coelestis Christum Filium Apostolis exhibuit, colligit, Ecclesiam esse visibilem, nec dari invisibilem. Verùm Resp. 1. unius positio non est alterius exclusio. Eadem Ecclesia, quae ratione externae vocationis, praedicationis & professionis est visibilis, ratione internae cum Christo capite communicationis est invisibilis. 2. unde non sequitur, Ecclesia s. coetus ille, ubi verbum DEI praedicatur & Sacramenta administrantur, potest videri, ac Christus iussit, ut Apostolos horumq; successores audiamus, quod fieri non potest, nisi videantur. Ergò renati respectu fidei internorumq; Sp. S. donorum videri quoq; possunt. Rectè proinde 3. B. D. Graverus Tom. 1. Dispp. Anti Ies. p. 242. moner, quòd Ecclesiam saltem quoad fidem salvificam visibilem esse negemus, non verò quoad exiernum & publicum ministerium. Hoc verò verbi ministerium adeoq; etiam Concilia & Pontificum decreta tum demum audienda sunt, quando Christum habent ducem, minimè autem cùm sua obtrudunt placita. Tum enim rectè urgemus oraculum hoc coeleste: Hunc audite. Qua Felicianus Capitonus in Expl. Cathol. excipit, discutientur in Anal. ad Luc. 10, 16. utpote è quo cumprimis loco suam stabilire sententiam satagit. Conf. Ioh. 10, 27.c. 8, 31.)*

## 17:6
(v. 6. And they feared. Q. What was the cause of the fear? Corn. à Lapide answers, the disciples feared, first because this cloud seemed to them to bring forth something new, great, and divine. Secondly because, as the Syrian has it, they saw Moses and Elias departing to enter the cloud, and through it to vanish from their eyes. For they feared, continues Cornelius, lest Moses should hurl lightnings and thunders from the cloud, as he had once done, receiving the law from God and giving it to the people on Sinai Exod. 19, 16. and lest Elias should hurl fires from the cloud, as he had once done, 4. Reg. 1, 10. But the Syrian Interpreter does not even have that γρυ which the Jesuit attributes to him, so that there is no doubt that Cornelius, ignorant of the Syriac language, was deceived by someone. The true cause why the Apostles were terrified is that either they could not bear the voice having fallen strongly from heaven like thunder, as Ephrem determines from the ancients in his Orat. de Transfig. and among the more recent of our own B. D. Chemn. in H. E. B. D. Hunnius in Matth. p. 390, and from the Papists Alphonsus Tostatus; or that they were not able to sustain the sight of such great glory, which reason Jerome also assigns to that fear, with Cornelius not disagreeing. Compare also Exod. 20, 19. Deut. 5, 25. c. 18, 16. Iudic. 13, 22.)

Latin:

*(v. 6. Et timuerunt. Q. Quae fuerit timoris causa? Respondet Corn. à Lapide, timuisse discipulos, primò quia nubes haec videbatur eis novum quid magnum & divinum parturire. Secundò quia, ut habet Syrus, videbant Mosen & Eliam abeuntes intrare nubem, ac per eam ex oculis eorum evanescere. Timebant enim, pergit Cornelius, ne Moses è nube fulmina & tonitrua iacularetur, ut olim fecerat, accipiens à Deo & dans populo legem in SinaExod. 19, 16.ac ne Elias è nube iacularetur ignes, uti olim fecerat,4. Reg. 1, 10. Verùm ne γρυ quidem illius habet Interpres Syrus, quod Iesuita ei tribuit, ut adeò nullum sit dubium, quin Lingvae Syriacae ignarus ab aliquo fuerit Cornelius deceptus. Vera causa, cur Apostoli fuerint territi, est, quòd vel vocem è coelo forte instar tonitrui fortiter delapsam ferre non potuerunt, uti è veteribus statuit Ephrem Orat. de Transfig. & inter recentiores ex nostratibus B. D. Chemn. in H. E. B. D. Hunnius in Matth. p. 390. è Pontificiis Alphonsus Tostatus; vel quòd conspectum tantae gloriae sustinere non valuerunt, quam rationem Hieronymus isti timori etiam adsignat, non repugnante Cornelio. Conf. etiam Exod. 20, 19.Deut. 5, 25.c. 18, 16.Iudic. 13, 22.)*

## 17:7
(v. 7. Arise. Jerome in this place: Whom he had healed with his hand, he heals with a command. The Jesuit Corn. à Lapide also rightly warns, that the humanity of Christ raised up the Apostles, whom the voice and majesty of God thundering had prostrated, so that he might set them up again, having been raised, to God. For to this, he says, he himself had come, who is the Mediator of God and men. Our B. Chemnitius has more on the same matter. But since Christ, ascending into heaven, did not lay aside his human nature, but placed it at the right hand of God, the Papists certainly act ineptly when they present Christ to the simpler folk as an angry judge, who cannot be appeased except by the intervention of other Mediators. Our Savior certainly still stands at the right hand of the Father as an Advocate, and he succors our infirmity, and raises us up. Compare Rom. 8, 34. Ebr. 4, 15, 16.)

Latin:

*(v. 7. Surgite. Hieronymus in h. l. Quos manu sanaverat, sanat imperio. Rectè quoque monet Iesuita Corn. à Lapide, quòd Apostolos, quos D E I tonantis vox & maiestas prostraverta, Christi humanit as erexerit, ut erectos rursum sistat Deo. Ad hoc enim, inquit, venerat ipse, qui est Mediator DEI & hominum. In eandem rem plura habet B. noster Chemnitius. Cùm verò Christus humanam naturam in coelum adscendens non deposuerit, sed collocarit ad dextram DEI, sanè ineptè agunt Pontificii, quando simplicioribus Christum ut iratum iudicem sistunt, qui non nisi interventu aliorum Mediatorum placari possit. Stat certè Salvator noster etiamnum ad dextram Patris ut Advocatus, ac succurrit nostrae infirmitati, nosque erigit. Conf. Rom. 8, 34.Ebr. 4, 15, 16.)*

## 17:8
(v. 8. Lifting up their eyes they saw no one, except Jesus. Reasonably, writes Jerome in this place, after they arose, they saw no one except Jesus alone: lest if Moses and Elias had remained with the Lord, the voice of the Father might seem uncertain, to whom he was especially giving testimony. But To what end were Moses and Elijah translated so suddenly? Cornelius à Lapide answers without hesitation, that Moses was brought to the limbo, and Elijah to his own place, just as he was brought, so also he was brought back by an angel. But who would believe that Moses, glorified in body and soul, was sent back to the limbo, that dark place, as the Papists prattle about it, and as it were the vestibule of hell itself? But as for Elijah, since the Papists wish heaven to be closed to him for a time, while Christ ascends, nor yet do they dare to thrust him into the limbo, they assign to him some peculiar place, and if I am not mistaken, even a certain stable and fodder for the horses by which he is said to have been carried into heaven. Indeed, the Jesuit Becanus, intending to attack our opinion that Elijah was carried into heaven and made a partaker of eternal happiness, asks, whether that chariot with the horses, by which Elijah was carried into heaven, is still in heaven, and what the horses do there, and on what fodder they feed. If, therefore, according to Becanus, the reason why Elijah was not carried into heaven is this, that there no place can be assigned to that chariot and horses, nor fodder on which the horses may feed, it is certainly a consequence, according to the opinion of Becanus at least, and if there ought to be any strength in his objection, that Elijah was carried into some place where provision was made for the horses for fodder. Nor is this perhaps absurd according to the Jesuits, since Thomas Aquinas, in whose Master's words all are otherwise compelled to swear, as Gravina mentions, p. 3. q. 49. art. 5., maintains that Elijah was translated into the earthly paradise, from which Adam was expelled. If this is so, it will perhaps not be absurd to provide fodder for the horses there. But Cornelius, if I am not mistaken, abandons Thomas here; certainly he does not dare to express the place to which Elijah was translated. Similarly, the same Cornelius doubts in Comm. on 2 Chron. c. 21. v. 12. and likewise in 4 Kings c. 2. 11. Thus, indeed, the Jesuits are stuck in their minds when they close heaven to those who died believing in the O.T., and do not know what kind of refuge they ought to assign to them at last. But B. Par. treats of this matter at greater length in L. de Morte §. 172. 173. But as far as concerns the fiery chariot and the fiery horses by which Elijah was carried into heaven, Ambrose long ago warned in the Apostles' Creed towards the end, and rightly, that by that phrase nothing else is understood than the carrying by angels, as they are spirits and a flame of fire. And that same Ambrose also in lib. de Parad. c. 3., just as Dorotheus in the Synopsis in the chapter on the life of Elijah, Jerome likewise in chapter 9 of Amos, and Alcimus in book 4, judge that Elijah was truly caught up into heaven, and there lives as it were as a heavenly inhabitant. So that there is no need either to doubt with Cornelius about the place to which Elijah was translated, or to be tormented with Becanus as to where the fiery horses receive their fodder.)*

Latin:

*(v. 8. Levantes oculos suos neminem viderunt, nisi Iesum. Rationabiliter, scribit in h. l. Hieronymus, postquam surrexerunt, non viderunt, nisi solum Iesum: ne si Moses & Elias perseverassent cum Domino, Patris vox videretur incerta, cui potissimùm daret testimonium. Sed quorsum tàm subitò translati Moses ac Elias? Respondet sine tergiversatione Corn. à Lapide, Moysen ad limbum, Eliam ad locum suumper Angelum, uti adductus fuit, it a & reductum fuisse. Ast quis credat, Moysen corpore animâque glorificatum remissum ad limbum, tenebricosum illum, uti Pontificii de eo garriunt, locum, ipsiusque inferni vestibulum quasi. Eliae verò cùm coelum trantisper praeclusum velin Pontificii, dum Christus adscendit, nec in limbum tamen detrudere audent, peculiarem aliquem locum ei adsignat, ac ni fallor, equis etiam quibus evectus in coelum dicitur, certum stabulum ac pabulum. Sanè Iesuita Becanus impugnaturus nostram sententiam, quòd in coelum vectus Elias fuerit ac felicitatis aeternae particeps redditus, querit, an currus il-e cum equis, quo in coelum vectus est Elias, in coelo adhuc sit, & quid agant ibi equi, & quo pabulo vescantur. Quòd si igitur iuxta Becanum causa, cur Elias non in coelum vectus, haec est, quod ibi currui illo & equis non possit adsignari locus, nec pabulum, quo equi vescantur, consequens sanè est, è Beeani quidem sententia, & si robur aliquod instantiae eius inesse debet, vectum esse Eliam in locum aliquem, ubi equis de pabulo prospectum. Nec hoc fortè secundum Iesuitas absurdum, cùm Thomas de Aquino, in cuius Magistri verba aliàs iurare coguntur omnes, memorante Gravina, p. 3. q. 49. art. 5. statuat, Eliam in paradisum terrestrem, è quo Adam pulsus, translatum fuisse. Quod si hoc, non absurdum fortè erit, equis pabulum ibi tribuere. Sed deferit, nî fallor Thomam Cornelius hîc, certè non audet exprimere locum, ad quem translatus sir Elias. Similiter dubitat idem Cornelius Comm. in. 2. Paral. c. 21. v. 12. itemque in 4. lib. Reg. c 2, 11. Ita nempe animo haerent Iesuitae, quando credentibus in V. T. defunctis coelum praecludunt, nesciuntque, quale tandem adsignare illis sospitium debeant. Sed hâc de re pluribus agit B. Par. L. de Morte §. 172. 173. Quod verò currum igneum & equos igneos concernit, quibus Elias vectus in coelum, pridem Ambrosius monuit in symbolum Apostol. sub finem, & rectè, quod ista phrasi nihil intelligatur aliud, quàm Angelorum subvectio, ut qui sunt spiritus & flamma ignis. Atque is ipse quoque Ambrosius lib. de Parad. c. 3. sicuti & Dorotheus in Synopsi cap. de vitâ Eliae, Hieronymus item in cap. 9. Amos & Alcimus lib. 4. censent, Eliam verè fuisse raptum in coelum, ibique quasi coelitem degere. Utadeò non opus sit vel de loco, ad quem Elias translatus fuerit, cum Cornelio dubitare, vel cum Becano cruciari, ubi equi ignei pabulum accipiant.)*

## 17:9
v. 9. Tell no one. Isid. Pelus. l. 1. ep. 239. The transfiguration of our Lord and Savior on the mount prefigured our own resurrection from death to life: which indeed the spectators were commanded to keep silent among themselves until his own resurrection, inasmuch as it would then find faith, as something that would already be perceived in reality. Jerome furthermore thinks the manifestation was prohibited, lest after such great glory the following cross should cause scandal to unrefined minds. This is also the opinion of Chrysostom, Bede, and others. Cf. more things pertinent to this at Pelargus on this passage.) (

The vision. Vision here denotes not that the bodies of Moses and Elijah were seen as if they were present merely through a dream. But the truth is indicated here entirely, and it is to be well noted that the disciples, even when awakened, saw the majesty of Christ and those two men. Luke 9:32. ) (

Latin:

*(v. 9. Nemini dixeritis. Isid. Pelus. l. 1. ep. 239. Domini ac Salvatoris nostri in monte transfiguratio nostram à morte ad vitam excitationem praefigurabat: quam quidem etiamusq ad ipsius resurrectionem, tacit am apud se tenere spectatores iubebantur, utpete tum fidem inventuram, ut quae iam reipsâ perspiceretur. Hierony mus praetere à prohibitam manifestationem putat, ne post tantam gloriam apud rudes animos sequens crux scandalum faceret. Id quod etiam placet Chrysostomo, Bedae, aliis. Conf. plura huc facientia apud Pelargum in h. l.)*

*( Visionem. Notat hîc visio non, quòd Mosis & Eliae corpora saltem per somnium ita visa fuerint ac si essent praesentia. Sed indicatur omninò hîc veritas, ac probè notandum, quòd etiam expergefacti discipuli viderint Christi maiestatem ac duos illos viros. Luc. 9, 32.)*

## 17:10
(v. 10. And the disciples asked him: Why then do the scribes say that Elias must come first. i.e. before. How the word ωςωθαν is also accepted John 19, 39. 2 Thess. 2, 3. the sense is according to Erasmus: Why do the scribes, from the authority of Malachi ch. 4, 5, say that before the Messiah comes, Elias the Tishbite is to come. Since he did not precede your advent, but today at last has been seen on the mountain. Others explain it thus. The scribes say that Elias ought to come, not to depart, just as he has now disappeared again, but to amend all things, to teach the people, and to point out the Messiah, v. 11. The Apostles are indeed speaking about the first advent of Christ, that before this, namely, Elias according to the opinion of the scribes is to come, but by no means about the second advent of Christ, as the Papists strive to persuade the simpler folk. But with the context itself protesting, as Camero also shows in Myroth. page 47. item vol. 2. Praelect. page 213.)

Latin:

*(v. 10. Et interrogaverunt eum Discipuli: Cur igitur scribae dicunt, quòd Eliam oporteat venire primùm. 1. e. priùs. Quomodo vox ωςωθαν etiam accipitur Ioh. 19, 39.2. Thess. 2, 3. sensus est iuxta Erasmum: Cur Scribae ex autoritate Malach. c. 4, 5. dicunt, quòd priùs, quàm veniat Messias, venturus sit Elias Tisbites. Cùm is non praecesserit tuum adventum, sed hodiè demum visus sit in monte. Alii ita exponuut. Dicunt Scribae, quòd venire debet Elias, non abiturus, sicuti iam disparuit iterum, sed omnia emendaturus, docturus populum, ac monstraturus Messiam, v. 11. Loquuntur verò Apostoli de primo Christi adventu, quòd ante hunc sc. Elias iuxta Scribarum sententiam sit venturus, minimè verò de secundo Christi adventu, ceu Pontificii simplicioribus persuadere satagunt. Sed reclamante ipso contextu, uti etiam ostendit Camero in Myroth. pag. 47. it. t. 2. Praelect. pag. 213.)*

## 17:11
(v. 11. Veniet. in Gr. est έρχέραι, which is placed for έλευσετοι as is evident from the following αποηαθαςησει. It is said 1. this not with respect to the thing itself having been done, for thus he had already come, but with respect to the Prophecy of the O. Testament, just as it is also used as future Matth. 2, 4. as noted by B. D. Glass. Phil. h. l. 3 p 382. Compare also on c. 11, 14. item Dnn. Theol. Sax. in Defens. Pupillae p. 341. B. Par. L. de Extr. Iudic. §. 108. it. Confess. Cath. t. 2. p. 769. and compare the notes at Apoc. 11, 3.)
