*(v. 11. Veniet. in Gr. est έρχέραι, quod positum pro έλευσετοι ceu patet ex seq. αποηαθαςησει. Dicitur 1. hoc non respectu ipsius rei gestae, sic enim iamtum venerat, sed respectu Prophetiae V. Test. sicuti etiam futurum adhibetur Matth. 2, 4. notante B. D. Glass. Phil. h. l. 3 p 382. Conf. etiam super c. 11, 14. item Dnn. Theol. Sax. in Defens. Pupillae p. 341. B. Par. L. de Extr. Iudic. §. 108. it. Confess. Cath. t. 2. p. 769. ac conf. notata ad Apoc. 11, 3.)*

## 17:11
(v. 11. & 12.) to receive, i.e. John the Baptist. But let Cornelius know that not only the Calvinists understand the prediction of Malachi concerning John the Baptist alone: but that Roman Catholic writers do the same. For thus Bened. Arias Montanus, a Spanish theologian of great authority with the King of Spain, whom he placed in charge of the Royal Bible work, determines in ch. 4 of Malachi. Similarly Hentenius in the preface to the Commentary of Aretius on the Apocalypse, Ioh. Ferus in ch. 11 of Matthew, nay, by the admission of Cornelius himself, even Burgensis, Clarius, etc. Concerning Bishop Jansenius, Cardinal Bellarmine himself likewise testifies that he asserts, the prophecy of Malachi concerning Elijah was not to be fulfilled in his own person; but in him who was to come in the spirit and power of Elijah. And the same testimony is granted to us by tacit consent by the otherwise most impudent Jesuit Erbermannus. But John the Baptist is he who came in the spirit and power of Elijah, Luc. 1, 17. Therefore the prophecy of Malachi was fulfilled in John. Nor is there any reason for Cornelius, with Bellarmine, to urge, Elijah will come before the great and terrible day, which cannot be understood of the first coming of Christ. For this objection has long since been satisfied by our people. (See the authors cited a little earlier. And to those from the Calvinists add Chamier, vol. 2 Panstr. b. 17, ch. 5, § 9.) Sixtus Senensis, a Papal writer, also satisfied it in b. 7 of the Holy Library, heresy 3, where he proves at length, that even the first coming of Christ according to the flesh is called great and terrible; either because of the blinding and ruin of the Hebrews, which was terrible; or because of the day of the birth and passion of Christ according to Bede. For the earth then trembled, the rocks were split, etc. Compare also Acts 2, 9, and Matth. 3, 10. But one may wonder at the rashness of Corn. à Lapide, who, although convinced by the force of truth, concedes in this place, that Christ explained here that axiom of the Scribes, taken from Malachi: Elijah will come, and to show that it can mystically be applied to his first advent. nevertheless, in his Commentary on Mal. 4, 3. among other foundations by which he tries to prove that by Elijah in Malachi must be understood the true Elijah, namely the Tishbite, he urges that Christ explained it so Matth. 17, 10. Although Christ does not have even a word in this place by which he indicates that Elijah the Tishbite must still be expected. But let someone urge, that John the Baptist did not restore all things. Resp. Dionysius the Carthusian, following the common opinion of the Papists, explains the aforementioned words of Christ, that Elijah was to lead the whole race of the Jews back to God, by converting them to Christ. He will open for, he writes, the lies of the Antichrist, which being done, the Jews will receive the faith. Whence it is read in Malachi: He will turn the heart of the fathers to the children etc. Yet the same man rightly adds: Thus therefore says the Savior. Elijah will restore all things, just as he professes elsewhere about himself, if I be lifted up, I will draw all things to myself. Now, Christ did not draw all men whatsoever to himself, indeed not even all the Jews: Therefore, he is not speaking of such a restoration to be performed by Elijah, by which the conversion of all the Jews is to be expected. And so those words of Christ, he will restore all things, indicate nothing other than what the prediction of Malachi has, namely that the promised Elijah is to turn the heart of the fathers etc. And John the Baptist performed that, unless someone wishes to assert that the Angel spoke falsely Luc. 1, 16. 17. And it is well to be noted that our Evangelist immediately v. 13. adds, the Disciples understood that Christ had spoken to them of John the Baptist, namely whatever he had said both v. 12. and v. 11. Not undeservedly, therefore, the philologist of great name Caspar Barthius, b. 50 Advers. ch. 2, writes that he cannot wonder enough at the thoughtlessness of even the greatest writers, who for so many centuries after Christ have wished to hope for the coming of Elijah from paradise; when the truth itself testifies that John the Baptist was the Elijah who was to return, as had been predicted by the Prophet Malachi, Matth. 16. Furthermore, against the modern Jews, who fall into the same error as the Papists, that Elijah the Tishbite is to return before the last coming of Christ, Mr. D. Mull. argues at greater length in Judaism p. 1054 seqq., D. Hoornbeck in book 8 against the Jews p. 559. Finally, it is evident from this error, that Elijah is to precede the second coming of Christ, that the opinions of the Fathers are not always the rule of truth: for it is certain that very many Fathers, such as Tertull. b. on the soul ch. 50, Gregory hom. 12 on Ez., Damasc. b. 4 O. F. ch. 27, Hilary can. 29, and others, have embraced that error.)*

Latin:

(v. 11. & 12.) accipere, sc. Ioh. Baptistam. Verùm sciat Cornelius, quòd non Calviniani solùm praedictionem Malachiae de solo Ioh. Baptista intelligant: sed idem quoque faciant Scriptores Catholico-Romani. Ita enim statuit Bened. Arias Montanus, Theologus Hispanus magnaeque apud Regem Hispaniae autoritatis, ut quem operi Bibliorum Regio praefecit, in c. 4. Malach. Similiter Hentenius praef. ad Comm. Aretae in Apoc. Ioh. Ferus in c. 11. Matth. quin, ipso fatente Cornelio, etiam Burgensis, Clarius &c. De Episcopo Iansenio, pariter testatur ipse Card. Bellarminus, quòd adserat, vaticinium Malachiae de Elia non implendum fuisse in propriâ eius personâ; sed in eo, qui venturus erat in spiritu & virtute Heliae. Idemque testimonium ta citô consensu largitur nobis impudentissimus aliàs Iesuita Erbermannus. At Iohannes Bapt. is est, qui ven-t in spiritu & virtute Eliae,Luc. 1, 17. Ergò vaticinium Malachiae in Ioh. fuit impletum. Nec est, quòd Cornelius cum Bellarm. urgeat, Eliam venturum ante diem magnum & terribilem, quod non possit intelligi de primo Christi adventu. Pridem enim huic obiectioni satisfactum à nostratibus est. (Vide autores paulo antè adductos. lisque ex Calv inianis adde Chamier. t. 2 Panstr. l. 17. c. 5. §. 9.) satisfecit etiam Sixtus Senensis, Scriptor Pontificius l. 7 Bibl. sanctae haer. 3. ubi prolixè probat, etiam primum Christi adventum secundùm carnem, dici magnum & terribilem; vel propter ex-oecationem & ruinam Ebraeorum terribilem; vel propter diem nativitatis & passionis Christi iuxta Bedam. Terra enim tum contremuit, petrae scissae &c. Conf. etiam Actor. 2, 9. it. Matth. 3, 10. Mirari verò licet temeritatem Corn. à Lapide, qui ut ut veritatis vi convictus concedat in h. l. Christum explicasse hîc illud Scribarum axioma, ex Malach â desumtum: Elias viniet, & ostendere, quòd mysticè primo eius adventu appli-ari possit. nihilo tamen minùs in Com. ad Mal. 4, 3. inter alia fundamenta, quibus probare conatur, quòd per Eliam pud Malach. debeat intelligi verus Elias, nempe Thaesbites, urget, quòd ita explicarit Christus Matth. 17, 10. Cùm tamen ne verbum quidem h. l Ch-istus habeat, quo indicet, quòd adhuc debeat Hias expectari Tesbites. Sed urgeat quis, Iohanne-n Bapt. non restituisse omnia. Resp. Dionysius à Rickel praedicta verba Christi, sequutus communē Pontificiorum sent. exponit, quòd totum genus Iudaeorum Elias reducturus ad Deum, cōvertendo eos ad Christum. Aperiet nam-, scribit, AntiChristi mendacia, quo facto Iudaei fidem recipient. Unde in Malach. legitur: Conve-tei corpatrum ad filios &c. benè tamen idem subiicit: Sic ergò ait Salvator. Elias restituet omnia quomodo alibi de se profitetur, si exaltatus fuero omnia traham ad meipsum. Iam verò Christus non omnes omninò homines ad se traxit, imò ne omnes quidem Iudaeos: E. nec de tali loquitur restitutione, pei Eliam praestanda, quâ Omnium Iudaeorum conversio expectanda. Adeòque verba illa Christi, omnia restituet, nihil aliud indicant, quàm quod praedictio Malachiae habet, quòd nempe promissus Elias conversurus sit cor patrum &c. Id verò Iohannes Bapt. praestitit, nisi quis adserere velit, falsum dixisse Angelum Luc. 1, 16. 17. Et probè notandum, quòd Ev. noster statim v. 13. subiungat, intellexisse Discipulos, quòd Christus de Iohanne Baptista dixisset ipsis, nempe quicquid dixerat tùm v. 12. tùm v. 11. Haut immeritò igitur magni nominis Philologus Caspar Barthius l. 50. Advers. c. 2. non posse se satis mirari sci ibit, scriptorumetiam summorum incogitantiam, qui tot seculis post Christum sperare adhuc adventum ex paradiso El -ae voluerunt; cùm Eliam rediturum, ut à Prophetâ Malachiâ praedictum erat, Ioh. Baptistam fuisse, ipsamet veritas testetur,Matth. 16. Coeterùm contra Iudaeos hodiernos, eundem cum pontificiis errantes errorem, quòd Elias nempe Tesbites ante ultimum Christi adventum rediturus sit, prolixiùs disputant Dn. D. Mull. Iudaismi p. 1054. seqq. D. Hoornbeck lib 8. cent. Iudaeos p 559. Patet denique ex isto errore, quòd Elias secundum Christi adventum praecessurus sit, quòd Patrum sententiae non semper sint veritatis regula: constat enim, quòd plurimi Patres, uti Tertull. l. de anima c 50. Gregorius hom. 12. in Ez Damasc l. 4. O. F. c. 27. Hilarius can. 29. aliique illum amplexi errorem fuerint.)*

## 17:12
(v. 12. I say to you, that Elias has already come. It is evident from this explanation of the Prophetic prediction of Christ Mal. 4, 5., that the Papists foolishly expect the return of Elias the Tishbite before the last day: Indeed, they strive to prove that the Roman Pontiff is not the Anti-Christ, for the reason that Elias has not yet come. See Becanus in Man. l. 1. c. 6. §. 24. For the Prophet speaks of John the Baptist, as we have Christ as an infallible interpreter. Nor does the negative response of John himself c. 1, 12 contradict this. For Christ speaks of the office. Compare Luc. 1, 17. John however speaks of the person, and denies that he is Elias, namely in that sense in which the Jews understood it, that is, that the soul of Elias had transmigrated into him. See Dn. D. Müll. Iudaism. p. 1054. B. Par. Harm. Evang. p. 1879. Camero Myroth. Evang. p. 136. Compare also Hoornbeckius lib. 2. pro convinc. Iudaeis p 205. 206. Drus. Lect. in Mal. p. 1066. 1067. it. lib. 1. Praeter. p. 27. Ludovicus Alcasar in Apoc. c. 11, 3. not. 6. It is certain that the passage of Malachi concerning the spiritual coming of Elias in the person of John was explained by Christ the Lord, Matth. 11, 14. & 17, 10. where note, those words: Elias indeed is to come, can be explained thus, as if he were saying, it is certain from Scripture that Elias will be about to come, namely before the first coming of the Lord, indeed spiritually. Corn. à Lapide objects, that Christ concedes that some Elias will precede both comings of Christ, but in the first it will be typical, in the second a literal and true Elias. But Christ says nothing about Elias, that he is to return in his own person before his last coming. And it suffices that the Prophecy of Malachi was fulfilled in John. Corn. à Lapide indeed thinks, that all these things which Malachi predicted concerning Elias cannot be referred to the first coming of Christ, and therefore the Calvinists wrongly the same Elias in both-

Latin:

*(v. 12. Dico vobis, Eliam iamtum venisse. Patet ex hâc Christi vaticinii Prophet. Mal. 4, 5. explicatione, quòd ineptè Pontificii Eliae Tesbit. reditum ante diem extremum expectent: Quin, Pontificem Rom. non esse Anti Christum, evincere satagant, eò quòd Elias nondum venerit. Vid. Becanus in Man. l. 1. c. 6. §. 24. Loquitur enim Proph. de Iohanne Baptista, ceu infallibilem habemus interpretem Christum. Nec repugnat negativa responsio ipsius Iohannis c. 1, 12. Loquitur enim Christus de officio. Conf. Luc. 1, 17. Iohannes verò de personâ, negatq;, quòd sit Elias, nempe eo sensu, quo Iudaei intelligebant h. e. quòd anima Eliae in ipsum transmigraverit. Vid. Dn. D. Müll. Iudaism. p. 1054. B. Par. Harm. Evang. p. 1879. Camero Myroth. Evang. p. 136. Conf. etiam Hoornbeckius lib. 2. pro convinc. Iudaeis p 205. 206. Drus. Lect. in Mal. p. 1066. 1067. it. lib. 1. Praeter. p. 27. Ludovicus Alcasar in Apoc. c. 11, 3. not. 6. Certum est, Malachiae locum de spirituali Eliae adventis inpersonâ Iohannis fuisse à Christo Domino explicatum,Matth. 11, 14. & 17, 10.ubi nota, verba illa: Elias quidem venturus est, ita posse explicari, qs. dicat, certum ex Scr. esse, Eliam fore venturum, nempe ante primum Domini adventum, nimirum spiritualiter. Excipit Corn. à Lapide, Christum concedere, Eliam aliquem praecursurum utrumq Christi adventum, sed in primo fore typicum, in secundo literalem & verum Eliam. Sed Christus nihil de Eliâ, quòd in propriâ personâ ante ultimum eius adventum sit rediturus. Sufficitque, quòd Prophetia Malachiae in Iohanne fuerit impleta. Existimat quidem Corn. à Lapide, non posse omnia haec, quae de Eliâ Malachias praedixit, ad primum Christi adventum referri, adeoq perperam Calvinianos Eliam eundem utrobi-

## 17:14
* (v. 14. Γονυπετῶν ἀυτῷ. γονυπετεῖν is πίπτειν εἰς τὰ γόνα τα. *From the fact that Christ in the New Testament was adored by the faithful, compare with the preceding passage also Matth. 2, 11.Ioh. 9, 38. the Orthodox rightly conclude that divine glory was truly communicated to the human nature of Christ. add also Ps. 72, 11.Ps. 97. 8.Dan. 7, 14.Es. 45, 23.Ebr. 1, 6.Phil. 2 10. The blessed D. Hutt. LL. Th. p. 178 treats this argument at length, who can be consulted. Wendelin in Exerc. Theol. Exerc. 59. §. 31. et seqq. also Exerc. 133. et seqq. is prolix both in explaining and defending the opinion of his Socinians, and in convicting ours of absurdity. But since the nature of the present undertaking does not admit an examination of the prolix Wendelinian discourse, it must be observed at least in this place: 1. that we by no means establish that the cult of adoration is to be attributed to the human nature of Christ, existing separately or apart, but that that very nature is worshipped together with the divine nature in one and the same adoration. 2. that we likewise by no means assert that the cult of adoration belongs to the human nature of Christ essentially, through and of itself, nor that it has been substantially changed into the divine nature, but because it has been assumed into the hypostasis τοῦ λόλου. If, therefore, Wendelin, by that phrase, that the human nature of Christ is not an adequate object of adoration, understands this, that it alone and existing separately is not to be adored, or that religious adoration does not belong to it of and by itself, he has us in no way contradicting him, and if he attributes such an opinion to us, he does us an injury. 3. that it is so far from the case that by our assertion concerning the human nature of Christ being affected with one and the same adoration as the divine, the argument against the Photinians, taken from adoration for demonstrating the Deity of Christ, is weakened, as indeed Wendelin with the Jesuits persuades himself, that it is rather beautifully confirmed from this. For unless Christ in the unity of his person were true God, to whom according to his divine nature the cult of adoration essentially belonged, that glory could not have been personally communicated to the human nature assumed into the hypostasis του λόγου. See B. Par Dispp. Acad. p. 753. 754. Confess. Cathol. 1. 2. p. 393. Exeg. L. de pers. & off. Christi § 48. & 249.

Latin:

* (v. 14. Γονυπετῶν ἀυτῷ. γονυπετεῖν est πίπτειν εἰς τὰ γόνα τα. *(Ex eo, quòd Christus in N. Test. à fidelibus fuit adoratus, Conf. cum praes. loco etiam Matth. 2, 11.Ioh. 9, 38. rectè colligunt Orthodoxi, quòd humanae Christi naturae gloria divina verè fuerit communicata. add. quoque Ps. 72, 11.Ps. 97. 8.Dan. 7, 14.Es. 45, 23.Ebr. 1, 6.Phil. 2 10. Pluribus hoc argumentum pertractat B. D. Hutt. LL. Th. p. 178. qui potest evolvi. Wendelinus in Exerc. Theol. Exerc. 59. §. 31. seqq. it. Exerc. 133. seqq. prolixus est tum in sociennorum suorum sententia explicanda defendendâque, tùm in nostrâ absurditatis convincendâ. Sed cùm instituti praesentis ratio prolixius discursûs Wendeliniani examen non admittat, observandum saltem h. l. 1. nos hautquaquam statuere, quasi cultus adorationis humanae Christi naturae, seorsim vel separatim existenti, tribuendus sit, sed quòd ipsa illa unà cum divina natura unâ eademque adoratione colatur. 2. nos itidem minimè adserere, quòd humanae Christi naturae essentialiter, per & ex se cultus adorationis competat, nec quòd in divinam naturam substantialiter ea sit mutata, sed quia ipsa in hypostasin τοῦ λόλου est adsumta. Si igitur Wendphrasi illâ, quòd humana Christi natura non sit adaequatum adorationis obiectum, hoc intelligit, quòd ipsa sola & separatim existens non sit adoranda, vel quòd eidem ex & per se adoratio religiosa non competat, minimè nos sibi habet contradicentes, & si talem nobis sententiam tribuit, iniuriâ nos afficit. 3. quòd tantum absit, ut per adsertionem nostram de humanâ Christi naturâ, unâ eademque adotatione cum divinâ afficiendâ, argumentum contra Photinianos, ex adoratione pro demonstrandâ Christi Deitate petitum, enervetur, uti quidem Wendelinus cum Iesuitis sibi persuadet, ut potiùs hinc pulcrè confirmetur. Etenim nisi Christus in personae unitate esset verus Deus, cui secundùm divinam naturam cultus adorationis essentialiter competeret, non potuisset illa gloria humanae naturae, in hypostasin του λόγου adsumtae, personaliter communicari. Vid. B. Par Dispp. Acad. p. 753. 754. Confess. Cathol. 1. 2. p. 393. Exeg. L. de pers. & off. Christi § 48. & 249.)*

## 17:15
v. 15. Σεληνίαζεται, he suffers from the Moon, because certain diseases vary according to the motions of the Moon, and are sometimes more intense, sometimes more remiss. Juvenal expressed its force thus:

For the body of the Eunaenati is twisted for me by the art of a demon.

This disease is called Comitial, sacred, Herculean, Lunatic, either because those born during the interlunium are especially affected by this evil, or because the Comitial or epileptic paroxysms coincide with the quadratures, opposition, and conjunction of the Moon. * (Although this disease truly arises from natural causes, the fury of Satan has nevertheless been added. See v. 18 and compare v. 17 with Marc. 9, 17. Camero treats many things concerning this passage, and thus also in general concerning the efficacy of demons in the human body, in t. 2. praelect. p. 222. seqq. also Myroth. Ev. ad h. l. add. Del Rio Disquis. Magic. l. 3. part. 1. q. 3. sect. 5.)*

Latin:

v. 15. Σεληνίαζεται, à Luna patitur, quia quidam morbi iuxta motus Lunae variantur, ac modò sunt intensiores, modò remissiores. Vim eius sic expressit Iuvenalis:

Nam corpus Eunaenatum mihi daemonis arteTorquet

Dicitur hic morbus Comitalis, sacer, Herculeus, Lunaticus, vel quòd interlunio nati hoc malo porissimùm afficiantur, vel quod paroxysmi Comitiales seu epileptici congruant cum Lunae quadraturis, oppositione & coniunctione. * (ut ut verò morbus hic à causis naturalibus oriatur, accessit tamen furor Satanae. Vid. v. 18. ac conf v. 17. cum Marc. 9, 17. Multis verò de hoc loco, adeoq; etiam in genere de Daemonum efficaciâ in humano corpore agit Camero t. 2. praelect. p. 222. seqq. it. Myroth. Ev. ad h. l. add. Del Rio Disquis. Magic. l. 3. part. 1. q. 3. sect. 5.)*

## 17:17
* (v. 17. O faithless generation. It is asked here, what faith Christ desired then in the father of the Lunatic c. 9. of Mark v. 17. Luke 9. v. 40. 41. and then in the disciples v. 20.? for that what is called the faith of miracles cannot be understood here seems to be evident from the fact that it is a peculiar gift of God; nor does it seem to be a discourse about justifying faith, since those things are required here which are not contained in the object of justifying faith. Furthermore, Camero treats this question at length in t. 2 praelect. p. 226. seqq. of which a summary is also held in Myroth. p. 51. But it must be known briefly that although the proper object of justifying faith, insofar as it is trust, is the promises of the Gospel concerning Christ the Mediator, the object of the same faith, insofar as it also includes knowledge and assent, is the whole word of GOD. Therefore Christ rebukes the Disciples, because when he himself had given them the power of casting out demons, they did not apply faith to this promise. For if this had been done by them, they certainly could have healed the demoniac: but he rebukes the father of the lunatic and the Jews, because when he himself had often professed himself to be the Son of GOD, and thus was endowed with the power of casting out demons and of conferring this power upon others, they nevertheless doubted about that matter no less. But the Blessed D. Chemn. rightly observes in H. E. c. 89. 981. that Christ makes a threefold infidelity, since one is infidelity of contumacy, as in the Scribes; another of infirmity, as in the father of the lunatic; another of security and negligence, as in the Apostles.)*

Latin:

* (v. 17. O natio incredula. Quaeritur hîc, quam fidem Christus tum in patre Lunatici c. 9. Marci v. 17. Luc. 9. v. 40. 41.tum in discipulisv. 20.desiderarit? quò minùs enim ea, quae miraculorum dicitur, intelligi hîc possit, videtur inde patere, quòd illa sit peculiare Dei donum; nec de iustificante videtur sermo esse, cùm hîc requirantur ea, quae obiecto fidei iustificantis non continentur. Coeterùm multis quaestionem hanc pertractat Camero t. 2 praelect. p. 226. seqq quorum etiam summa habetur in Myroth. p. 51. Sciendum verò breviter, quòd licet fidei iustificantis, prout est fiducia, obiectum proprium sint promissiones Evangelii de Christo Mediatore, eiusdem tamen fidei, quat. etiam notitiam & adsensum includit, sit omne DEI verbum. Reprehendit igitur Christus Discipulos, quòd cùm ipse illis dedisset potestatem eiiciendi daemones, huic promissioni non adhibu-rint fidem. Hoc enim si factum ab eis esset, utique daemoniacum sanare potuissent: Patrem verò lunatici Iudaeosq; reprehendit, quòd cùm ipse saepiùs se Filium DEI professus esset, adeòque potestate daemones eiiciendi aliisque etiam potestatem hanc conferendi praeditus, nihilo tamen minùs adhuc ea de re dubitarent. Rectè autem observat B. D. Chemn. in H. E. c. 89. 981. quòd Christus triplicem faciat infidelitatē, cùm alia sit infidelit as contumaciae, ut in Scribis; alia infirmitatis, ut in in patre lunatici; alia securitatis & oscitantiae, ut in Apostolis.)*

## 17:18
* (v. 18. καὶ ἐέπετίμησε -πῷ, and he rebuked it, namely the demon. So that the relative pronoun refers to the consequent. Which pleases the Blessed Glassius in Phil. lib. 3, p. 193, and Lord Dr. Friedlieb on this passage, and is also evident from Luke 9, 42 and likewise from Mark 9, 25.) Others, however, prefer to refer it to the antecedent, namely to the lunatic possessed by a demon. Thus Erasmus.

Latin:

* (v. 18. καὶ ἐέπετίμησε -πῷ,& increpavit illud, nempe daemonium. Ita ut relativum ad consequens referatur. Quod B. Glassio in Phil. l. 3. p. 193. ac Dn. D. Friedlieb in h. l. placet ac patet etiam ex Luc. 9, 42. itemque ex Marc. 9, 25.)* Alii tamen malunt referre ad antecedens, nempe ad lunaticum daemonio obsessum. Ita Erasmus.

## 17:20
v. 20. ὡς κοκκο σιναπεως, i.e. καὶ ὡς κόκκον σινάπεως, or as much faith as is a grain of mustard seed. A hyperbolic comparison. The meaning is: If you have as much faith as is a grain of mustard, which is counted among the smallest things. Whence the Rabbis say: The whole world under the vault of the firmament is like a grain of mustard. The faith of miracles, in the place of an object, looks to the omnipotence of God: saving faith looks to the mercy of GOD, promised in Christ. *(That it is a matter here of the faith of miracles is taught excellently from the context by the Blessed Dr. Frantzius in his treatise on the Interpretation of Holy Scripture, Oracle 39; add the Blessed Par. Harm. Evang. c. 149 p. 275.)*

*( You shall say to this mountain. Procopius thinks that by mountain is to be understood the demon, who is so called either from strength, or from sublimity, or because idols, i.e., demons, were worshipped on mountains. Lord Dr. Friedlieb thinks that Christ alluded to the custom and saying of the Jews, who, extolling their Masters, used to say of them (especially of Sinai and Rabba): he uproots mountains. It seems to the same person, however, to have arisen from Job 9, 5. But the Blessed Par. also alludes to that acceptance of Procopius when he writes in his Academic Homilies, part 1, p. 589: The devil, because of his temptations, is compared to a great mountain, but by faith in Christ we can move this mountain. The Blessed Par. also has more on this matter in his Harm. Evan. c. 149, as does Gasp. Sanctius Centumputeolanus in his Comm. on Zach. p. 92. But there is no doubt that the words of the Savior are to be taken literally. However, although it is not read of the Apostles that they moved mountains from one place to another, it is not to be doubted that if the glory of GOD and the salvation of men had demanded such a thing, they could have done this very thing. Which Chrysostom also hints at when he writes in Homily 58 on Matthew: But if anyone says, when did they move mountains? We shall answer that they did much greater things: for they raised many dead; for it is not equal to move mountains, and to recall the soul of a man. Some say, however, that afterwards certain ones, much lesser than them in holiness, did that when the matter demanded it. (Gregory of Nyssa in his life commemorates such a thing concerning Gregory Neocaesariensis, the Bishop, and called Thaumaturgus from the magnitude of his miracles. Likewise Eusebius, book 7 H. E. c. 25, and Jerome reports a similar thing about St. Hilarion in his life. Indeed, even the Asiatic Letters and Marcus Paulus Venetus in Tartary, s. lib. 1, Hist. Orient. cap. 18, report that they moved a mountain in Tartary according to this promise of Christ, when a Tyrant demanded it of them. Consult also Gregory the Great, lib. 1, Dialog. c. 7, Ruffinus l. 1, c. 10, Sozomenus lib. 3, H. E. c. 6.) Whence it is evident that if there had been need, they would have moved mountains : Therefore he did not say, you will move mountains entirely, but you will be able to move; but if they did not do it, it is not an argument of impotence. For we are not ignorant that greater things were done by them, but since the matter had not demanded it, they did not want to: although it is possible that something such was done, and not written. For not all the miracles of the saints are written.

Καί ουδὲν ἀδυνατήσει ύμῖν. Not only this, but absolutely nothing will be impossible for you. Syriac: And nothing will be more powerful than you. *(Since faith looks to the word of GOD, it is clear how all things are possible to the believer, namely if the glory of GOD and the salvation of men demand that something be done. For then God wills to grant to believers even those things which are arduous and otherwise placed above human possibility. Conf. Gen. 18, 14. 2. Chron. 14, 11. but by no means if someone wishes to attempt or undertake such a thing merely out of curiosity. See B. D. Chemn. H. E. c 98. B Par Harm Evang. c. 149. p. 277.) *Chrysostom on this passage Since these things are not done in the Church today, shall we therefore say that Christians are destitute of faith? God forbid that we should think so ill of the people of GOD. Justifying faith is one thing, but that which is of miracles has now ceased. Conf. B D Hutt. in L. L. Maioribus p. 455.)*

Latin:

v. 20. ὡς κοκκο σιναπεως, h. e. καὶ ὡς κόκκον σινάπεως, vel tantam fidem, quantum est granum finapis. Comparatio hyperbolica. Seusus est: Si tantum fidei habueritis, quantum est granum sinapi, quod inter minima recensetur. Unde dicuat Rabini: Totus mundus sub fornice firmamenti est sicut granum sinapis. Fides miraculorum obiecti loco respicit Dei omnipotentiam: fides salvifica misericordiam DEI, in Christo promissam. *(Agi verò h. l. de fide miraculorum egregiè è contextu docet B. D. Frantzius in de Interpr. Sc. S. tract. Orac. 39. add. B. Par. Harm. Evang. c. 149. p. 275.)*

*( Dicetis monti huic. Procopius per montem putat intelligi daemonem, qui ita dicatur, aut à robore, aut à sublimitate, aut quòd in montibus idola i. e. daemones colerentur. Dn. D. Friedlieb existimat; Christum allusisse ad consuetudinem & dictum Iudaeorum, qui Magistros suos extollentes, de iis (praeprimis de Sinai & Rabba) dicebant: montes eruit. Videtur autem eidem ortum ex Iob. 9, 5. Ad illam verò Procopii acceptionem alludit quoque B. Par. quando Homil. Acad. part. 1. p. 589 scribit: Diabolus ob suas tentationes confertur magno monti, sed fide in Christum hunc montem transferre possumus. Plura quoq; in hanc rem habent B. Par. Harm. Evan. c. 149. it. Gasp. Sanctius Centumputeolanus Comm. in Zach. p. 92. Sed non est dubium, quin verba Salvator is propriè accipienda sint. Ut ut verò non legatur de Apostolis, quòd montes de uno loco in alium transtulerint: non tamen dubitandum, quin si gloria DEI ac hominum salus tale quid exegisset, illi hoc ipsum facere potuissent. Id quod etiam Chrysostomus sub innuit, quando homil. 58. in Matth. Si verò, scribit, quispiam dicet, ecquando montes transtulerunt? Respondebimus, quia multò maiora fecerunt: multos enim mortuos excitarunt: aequale quippe non est, montes transponere, & animam hominis revocare. Dicunt autem nonnulli, postea quosdam sanctitate illis multò minores, id re postulante fecisse. (Tale quid de Gregorio Neocaesariensi Episcopo, & à miraculorum magnitudine Thaumaturgo dicto, commemorant Greg. Nyssenus in eius vitâ. itemque Eusebius lib. 7 H. E. c. 25. ac simile de S. Hilarione refert Hieronymus in eius vita. Quin etiam de Christianis Epistolae Asiaticae & Marcus Paulus Venetus in Tartaria s. lib. 1. Hist. Orient. cap. 18. tradunt, quòd montem in Tartariâ ex hoc Christo promisso transtulerint, cùm Tyrannus id ab eis exigeret. Cons. quoque Gregorius M. lib. 1. Dialog. c. 7. Ruffinus l. 1. c. 10. Sozomenus lib. 3. H. E. c. 6.) Unde patet, quia si opus fuisset montes quotranstulissent: Ideò non, dixit, transponentes omninò montes, sed transponere poteritis: si autem non fecerunt, non est argumentum impotentiae. Maiora enim ab ipsis facta non ignoramus, sed quoniam res non postulaverat, noluerunt: quamvis possit etiam aliquid tale factum esse, & non scriptum. Non enim omnia miracula sanctorum scripta sunt.

Καί ουδὲν ἀδυνατήσει ύμῖν. Non hoc solum, sed omninò nihil erit vobis impossibile. Syrus: Et aliquid nō erit potentius vobis. *(Cùm fides verbum DEI respiciat, patet, quomodo credenti omnia possibilia sint, nempe si DEI gloria ac hominum salus aliquid fieri exigat. Tum enim Deus etiam ea, quae ardua sunt ac aliàs supra humanam possibilitatem sunt posita, credentibus largiri vult. Conf. Gen. 18, 14. 2. Paral. 14, 11. minimè verò, si quis ex curiositate saltem tale quid velit tentare vel suscipere. Vid. B. D. Chemn. H. E. c 98. B Par Harm Evang. c. 149. p. 277.) *Chrysostomus h. l. Cùm hodiè ista in Ecclesiâ non fiant, an proptereà dicemus, Christianos fide destitui? Avertat Deus, ut de populo DEI cam malè sentiamus. Aliud est fides iustificans, sed ea, quae miraculorum est, iam desiit. Conf. B D Hutt. in L. L. Maioribus p. 455.)*

## 17:21
v. 21. This kind &c. Some think that Christ is speaking of those demons which excite epilepsies or Comitial diseases. Basil in Ps. 15. But Chrysostom hom. 58. in Matth. thinks that not only the Lunatics, but αθόλου the entire kind of demons is understood by Christ *(The same is the opinion of Athanasius, and likewise of Thomas on this passage. But John Camero t. 2. Praelect. p. 247. thinks the opinion of those is better, who wish it to be understood here as a certain, and that the worst, kind of demons.)*

By prayer and fasting. Εν διαδύο, by prayer joined with fasting, that is, serious and ardent. Flacius understands it concerning repentance, of which fasting was formerly the exercise and external sign. Insofar as fasting serves for the mortification of the flesh and the preparation of the spirit for prayers. * (Therefore, the power of fasting in casting out demons is by no means the same as that of prayer. Nor does it stand against the present assertion of Christ, that demons are cast out by prayers and fasting, that faith is required for the casting out of demons, since the Savior ascribes it to the unbelief of the Jews and the disciples that they could not heal the lunatic afflicted by a demon. For it must be known that Christ speaks of faithful prayer. True faith compels to prayers, and those prayers at last are pleasing to GOD and are heard, which are made with faith, leaning upon the divine promise. Conf. Mark 11, 24.James 1, 6-7. it. c. 5, 15. it. B. D. Franz. de Interpr. Sc. S. p. 609. B. Par. Hom. Acad. part. 1. p. 589. and also B. D. R-nig Append. C C. p. 22. But however much Christ may require faith, prayer, and fasting for the casting out of demons, it is by no means to be thought as if fasting merits the putting to flight of demons, and of itself puts the demon to flight by tormenting it, as Corn. à Lapide maintains in this place. Certainly, fasting by itself accomplishes little, and is little esteemed by the Devil: yet it is required by Christ, because it renders a man more apt for prayers. Therefore, by itself it does nothing toward the expulsion of demons, nor does it merit it. As also the blessed D. Chemn. long ago observed in Harm. Ev. c. 89. Christ therefore hands down such a gradation, by which fasting excites prayer, prayer sharpens faith, but faith by the virtue of Christ expels demons. As the same d. l. has it according to 1 John 5, 4. If, however, faith expels demons not by its own, but by Christ's virtue or merit, how much less is such merit to be ascribed to fasting, as that which even falls to hypocrites, Is. 58, 3. Furthermore, concerning fasting, and insofar as it is not only approved by the Orthodox, but also commended, then also what is disapproved in the fasting of the Papists, has been treated above in the Anal. to c. 9. v. 14. Conf. also Camero t. 2. Praelect. p. 247. seqq.)*

Latin:

v. 21. Hoc genus &c. Quidam putant, Christum de illis daemoniis agere, quae epilepsias seu morbos Comitiales excitant. Basil. in Ps. 15. Sed Chrysostomus hom. 58. in Matth. non modò Lunaticorum, sed αθόλου universum genus daemoniorum a Christo intellectum existimat *(Eadem est sententia Athanafii, itemque Thomae in h. l. At Iohan. Camero t. 2. Praelect. p. 247. potiorem illorum putat sententiam, qui volunt, intelligi hîc certum, idque deterrimum daemonum genus.)*

Per precationem & ieiunium.Εν διαδύο, per precationem cum ieiunio coniunctam h. e. seriam & ardentem. Flacius intelligit de poenitentia, cuius exercitium & signum externum fuit olim ieiunium. Quatenus ieiunium inservit carnis mortificationi & spiritûs ad preces praeparationi. * (Minimè igitur eadem vis ieiunii in eiiciendis daemoniis, quae orationis. Nee obstat praesenti Christi adsertioni, per preces & ieiunium daemonia eiici, quòd fides requiratur ad daemonum eiectionem, siquidem Salvator incredulitati Iudaeorum ac discipulorum adscribit, quòd hi lunaticum à daemone afflictum sanare non potuerint. Sciendum enim, quòd Christus loquatur de Oratione fideli. Vera fides compellit noad preces, ac eae demumpreces DEO gratae sunt & exaudiuntur, quae fiunt fide, innitente promissioni divinae. Conf. Marc. 11, 24.Iac. 1, 67. it. c. 5, 15. it. B. D. Franz. de Interpr. Sc. S. p. 609. B. Par. Hom. Acad. part. 1. p. 589. nec non B. D. R-nig Append. C C. p. 22. Ut ut verò Christus ad daemonum eiectionem requirat fidem, orationem ac ieiunium, minimè tamen sentiendum est, quasi ieiunium mereatur daemonum fugationem, & ex se daemonem cruciando fuget. ceu Corn. à Lapide in h. l. statuit. Sanè ieiunium per se parùm praestat, ac parvi à Diabolo aestimatur: requiritur tamen à Christo, quia hominem reddit aptiorem ad preces. Per se igitur nihil facit ad daemonum expulsionem, nec eam meretur. Uti etiam pridem B. D. Chemn. in Harm. Ev. c. 89. observavit. Christus igitur talem gradationem tradit, quâ ieiunium excitat orationem, oratio acuit fidem, fides autem virtute Christi daemonia expellit. ut habet idem d. l. iuxta 1. Ioh. 5, 4. Si verò fides non suâ, sed Christi virtute vel meritô Daemones expellit, quantò minùs ieiunio tale meritum adscribendum est, ut quod etiam in hypocritas cadit, Es. 58, 3. Coeterùm de ieiunio, & quatenus non solùm ab Orthodoxis approbatur, sed etiam commendatur, tùm quoque quid in ieiunio Pontificiorum improbetur, suprà in Anal. ad c. 9. v. 14. actum. Conf. etiam Camero t. 2. Praelect. p. 247. seqq.)*

## 17:22
v. 22. Ἀναςςεφομ-ύων ἀυ τῶν ἐν Γαλιλαίᾳ. From the series of the history it seems to be understood that these things were done after the return of Christ from Caesarea Philippi into Galilee. And so in this place ἀναςρεφασθαι can also signify return: however, the other interpretation seems to be preferred, while they were staying in Galilee: which these words of Mark confirm: παρεπορεύοντο διὰ τῆς Ταλιλαίας. Casaub.

Latin:

v. 22. Ἀναςςεφομ-ύων ἀυ τῶν ἐν Γαλιλαίᾳ. Ex Historiae serie intelligi videtur, gesta esse haec post reditum Christi è Caesarea Philippi in Galilaeam. Itaque potest etiam hoc loco ἀναςρεφασθαιreditum significare: altera tamen interpretatio videtur praeferenda, versantibus ipsis in Galilaea: quam confirmant haec verba Marci: παρεπορεύοντο διὰ τῆς Ταλιλαίας. Casaub.

## 17:23
* (v. 23. Καί τᾗ τρέτῃ ἡμέρα ἐγερθήσεται. Excellently from the comparison of this place can be understood the place above chapter 12, 40. where see the Anal.)*

Latin:

* (v. 23. Καί τᾗ τρέτῃ ἡμέρα ἐγερθήσεται. Egregiè ex collatione huius loci intelligi potest locus suprà cap. 12, 40. ubi vid. Anal.)*

## 17:24
v. 24. Οἱ τὰ δίδραχμα λαμβάνοντες. Syr. two drachmas of silver of the poll tax. Whence some explain two drachmas i. e. the half of the shekel of the sanctuary. For a shekel was of four drachmas. Therefore a didrachma is half a shekel. Some call it a common shekel, but the other a shekel of the law and of the sanctuary. They say in the Talmud that a drachma is in different places the same coin, which by the proper name of the nation was called ῔ῢ῞, which is the sixth part of a denarius, and contains as much silver as is the weight of 16 grains of barley, so that two drachmas, which were to be paid by each, contained the weight of silver of 32 grains of barley. * (But the discourse here is about the tribute to be paid to the Romans, not about the shekel of the poll tax to be brought to the Temple. Which is evident 1. from the explanation of Christ himself: for immediately he adds v. 25. The kings of the earth from whom do they receive τέλη ἢ κῆνσον. in which words it is to be noted both that he speaks about Kings -. Political Magistrate, and about the tribute to be paid to them, and finally that he uses the word census, by which name that tribute came, which had been imposed by the Romans upon the Jewish people, as is clear from Matth. 22, 18.. 2. from the consideration of the place and persons, where namely and from whom δίδραχμα were being exacted here. For the sacred tax for the use of the temple was collected in the Jerusalem Temple, and indeed from all who had exceeded the twentieth year. But Διδραχμα, about which it is treated here, were collected at Capernaum, and indeed from Christ alone and Peter, as inhabitants and citizens. Which reason the Jesuit Salmero urges. Bellarmine indeed objects to this opinion, that the tribute imposed by the Romans was a Denarius,) Matth. 22, 19. But Barradius, lib. 10, Harm. cap. 32, p. 717, already responded to the companion, noting that that census is called a denarius, not as if it were one denarius, since it is established that two denarii were paid by individual citizens; or if even at most one denarius was paid to the Romans in place of tribute, Herod, however, who ruled Capernaum, exacted two, and thus δὶδραχμα. 3. Our opinion shines forth from the collation of the Oriental Interpreters. Indeed, the Arab τὸ οἱ τὰ δίδραχμα λαμβάνοντες translates by i.e., exactors, collectors of tributes, and a little later in the same verse for δίδραχμα he uses the word which he uses in the following verses 25 for the Greek κῆνσον.. And similarly in cap. 22, 17. But especially the Ethiopian favors our opinion, using for δίδραχμα at the beginning of this verse, i.e., the census of the denarius. Afterwards, noting simply census, as is evident both from verse 25 and from Matt. 22, 17. where, however, it is described more fully just as a little before, namely . The Persian translates by i.e., poll tax, which phrase he also uses in Matth. 22, 17. where there is undoubtedly talk of secular tribute.

Latin:

v. 24. Οἱ τὰ δίδραχμα λαμβάνοντες. Syr. duas drachmas argenti capitationis. Unde quidam exponunt binas drachmas i. e. sicli sanctuarii dimidium. Siclus enim erat quatuor drachmarum. Ergo didrachma est dimidium sicli. Quidam vocant siclum communem, alterum verò siclum legis & sanctuarii. Drachmam aiunt in Talmud diversis in locis idem esse numisma, quod propriâ gentis appellatione dicebatur ῔ῢ῞, quod sexta pars denarii est, & tantum argenti continet, quantum est pondus 16. granorum hordei, ita ut duae drachmae, quae cuique solvendae erant, continerent argenti pondus 32. granorum hordei. * (Sermo verò hîc est de tributo, Romanis persolvendo, non de capipitationis siclo, Templo inferendo. Id quod patet 1. ex ipsius Christi explicatione: statim enim subdit v. 25. Reges terrae â quibus accipiunt τέλη ἢ κῆνσον. in quibus verbis notandum tum quòd de Regibus -. Magistratu Politico loquatur, tum de tributo illis persolvendo, tum denique utatur voce census, quo nomine veniebat tributum illud, quod à Romanis populo Iudaico erat impositum, uti ex Matth. 22, 18. liquet. 2. ex loci ac personarum, ubi sc. & quibus δίδραχμα hîc exigebantur, consideratioae. Colligebatur enim sacrum ad templi usum vectigal in Hierosolymitano Templo, & quidē ab omnibus, qui annum excessetant vigesimum. Διδραχμα verò, de quibus hîc agitur, colligebantur Capernaumi, & quidem à Christo solùm ac Petro, tanquam incolis & civibus. Quam rationem urget Iesuita Salmero. Obiicit quidem sententiae huic Bellarminus, quòd Tributum à Romanis indictum, fuerit Denarius, Matth. 22, 19. Verùm iamtum respondit socienno Barradius l. 10. Harm. c. 32. p. 717. notans, censum illum denarium vocari, non quasi unus fuerit denarius, cùm constet, duos fuisse solutos à singulis civibus denarios; aut si vel maximè Romanis unus saltem denarius tributi loco fuit solutus, Herodem tamen, qui Capernanmi imperabat, exegisse duos, adeoque δὶδραχμα. 3. Elucescit nostra sententia ex Interpretum Orientalium collatione. Sanè Arabs τὸ οἱ τὰ δίδραχμα λαμβάνοντες vertit per i. e. exactores, tributorum collectores, & paulò pòst in eod. versu pro δίδραχμα utitur voce quam v. seqq. 25. usurpat pro Gr. κῆνσον. Similiterque c. 22, 17. Cumprimis verò sententior nostrae favet Aethiops, pro δίδραχμα initio huius versus adhibens i. e. censum denarii. Postea nudè cēnsum notans, ceu patet tum è v. 25. tum ex Matt. 22, 17. ubi tamē pariter ut paullò antè pleniùs describitur, videl. Persa vertit per i. e. census capitis, qua phrasi etiam utitur Matth, 22, 17. ubi indubiè de tributo profano sermo est.)*

## 17:25
v. 25. The kings of the earth, from whom do they receive tribute? etc. Chrysost. in h. l. Εἰ τοῦ οἱ τῆς γῆς βασιλείς ἀπὸ τῶν μων ὠυτῶν οὐ λαυβανουσν, ἀλλ ᾽ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀλλ οτρίων πόλλέ μάλλον ἐμὲ άππλλάχθανόει σης απαιτήσεως τάυτης --κ ἀπιγείου βασιλέως, άλλα τού τῷ -ύρο- ό-α -όν καὶ βασιλέα. For if the kings of the earth do not receive from their sons, but from strangers, much more ought I to be free from this exaction, as being the son not of a terrestrial King, but of a heavenly one, and he himself also King. Dion. Carthus. By this Christ intended to conclude that he was free from giving tribute, as the son of the King, subject to no human law of necessity. *(Bell. lib. de Cler. cap. 28. propos. 5. Maldonatus in h. l. and some other Papists attempt to prove from the present passage that clerics are absolutely exempt by divine law from the power of the civil Magistrate, and especially from tributes or real burdens. For thus Bellarmine subsumes: The sons are free, Christ saying. But it is certain that all Clerics properly belong to the family of Christ, who is the Son of the King of Kings. Resp. 1. Among the ancients Hilary, as the Jesuit Maldonatus reports in h. l., likewise among the more recent ones Cardinal Baronius, Franciscus Lucas Brugensis, and others, as Corn. à Lapide testifies in h. l., indeed Bellarmine himself in the same place, propos. 4, establish, The didrachma, which was exacted here, was the sacred didrachma, which had to be paid to the temple, according to the law laid down by GodExod. 30, 13. And this opinion is proven at length, with the others also refuted, by Ioh. Camero in his prelections, vol. 2, p. 260 ff., and Grotius embraces the same in this place. Sim. Episcopius also embraces it, vol. 1 of his Works, p. 95. With this exposition standing, nothing is proven against us from this place, since the question is about civil burdens, that is, about tributes which are paid to the civil Magistrate. 2. Most Scholastics, as can be seen in Leonh. Lessius, On Justice and Law, book 2, chap. 33, doubt 4, deny that the exemption of clerics rests on divine law. And the Jesuit Conzen seems to agree with this opinion in this place, question 4. But if this is true, those who strive to prove that exemption from the Holy Scriptures are foolish. Whence Corn. à Lapide gravely says in this place, From this reasoning of Christ, the Canonists do not rightly conclude that clerics are immune and free from every tribute by divine law. 3. Maldonatus distinguishes between domestics or members of Christ's household, to whom he refers the Apostles and their successors the clerics, and adopted sons, that is, Christians in general. He adds, Christ speaks in this place not of these, but only of those. But this distinction, as being less suitable to this business, was rejected by Maldonatus's fellow, Corn. à Lapide, and his copyist Tirinus. Whence, after he had mentioned that the collection of the Canonists is nothing, he adds: By the same reasoning it would be concluded that all Christians are immune from the same (tribute), as the Anabaptists wish. For Christians are adopted sons of God, reborn in Baptism through grace; yet that this is false, the Apostle teachesRom. 13, 7.& the whole Church: for this adoption is of a higher inheritance and order, namely, heavenly, not earthly. Since these things are so, Bellarmine openly confesses in the cited book chap. 3 §. To the first, that Christ speaks here only of himself. Similarly Corn. Iansenius, and likewise the Jesuits Salmero and Maldonatus, expressly warning that Christ speaks of natural sons, and although he speaks in the plural, that nevertheless holds place only in Christ, and would hold also in more, if there were more natural sons. However, even if Corn. à Lap. and Tirinus add, that kings and princes nevertheless rightly and aptly exempt ecclesiastics from tribute according to this saying of Christ, who are as it were of the house and family of Christ. Yet anyone sees that the consequence is not firm, since first the Jesuits themselves confess that ecclesiastics are at least as it were of the house and family of Christ, and subsequently grant that Christ speaks at least of natural sons. But there is a great difference between him who is a natural son, and him who is at least as it were of the family. Besides, who would doubt that adopted sons enjoy greater privileges than other domestics, and those who are at least as it were of the family. Compare at greater length B. Par. L. on Civil Magistrate § 463, and Confess. Cuth. vol. 2, p. 159 ff., also B. D. Roenig, Cases of Conscience, p. 735.

Latin:

v. 25. Reges terrae à quibus accipiunt tributa &c. Chrysost. in h. l. Εἰ τοῦ οἱ τῆς γῆς βασιλείς ἀπὸ τῶν μων ὠυτῶν οὐ λαυβανουσν, ἀλλ ᾽ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀλλ οτρίων πόλλέ μάλλον ἐμὲ άππλλάχθανόει σης απαιτήσεως τάυτης --κ ἀπιγείου βασιλέως, άλλα τού τῷ -ύρο- ό-α -όν καὶ βασιλέα.Nam si Reges terrae non à suis filis accipiunt, sed ab alienis, multò magis me l berum esse oportet huius exactionis, utpote non terreni Regis, sed coelestis filium, ipsumq etiam Regem. Dion. Carthus. Per hoc Christus intendebat concludere, se liberam esse à dando tributo, tanquam filium Regis, Regum nulli legi humana de necessitate subiectum. *(Bell. lib. de Cler c. 28. propos. 5. Maldonatus in h. l. aliique nonnulli Pontificii è praesenti loco evincere conantur, quòd clerici iure divino à potestate civilis Magistratûs, cumprimis verò à tributis s. oneribus realibus absolutè sint exemti. Ita enim subsumit Bellarminus: Libersunt filii, dicente Christo. Certum autem est, Clericos omnes proprie ad familiam Christi, qui est Filius Regis Regum, pertinere. Resp. 1. E veteribus Hilarius, referente Iesuita Maldonato h. l. item è recentioribus Cardinalis Baronius, Franciscus Lucas Brugensis, aliique, teste Corn. à Lapide in h. l. quin ipse Bell. l. c. propos. 4 statuunt, didrachmum, quòd hîc fuit exactum, fuisse didrachmum sacrum, quod pendendum erat templo, iuxta legem â Deo latamExod. 30, 13. Et hanc sententiam prolixè, refutatis etiam coeteris, probant Ioh. Camero praelect. t. 2. p. 260. seqq. ac Grotius in h l. amplectitur etiam eand. Sim. Episcopius t. 1. Op. p 95. Quâ stante expositione nihil ex h. l. contra nos evincitur. Cùm quaestio sit de oneribus civilibus s. de tributis, quae Magistratui civili persolvuntur. 2. Plerique Scholastici, ceu videre licet apud Leonh. Lessium de Iust. & iure l. 2. c. 33. dub. 4. negant, quòd clericorum exemtio nitatur iure divino. Cui sententiae & Iesuita Conzen h. l. q. 4. accedere videtur. Quod si verum, inepti sunt, qui è Sc. S. exemtionem illam probare nituntur. Unde graviter Corn. à Lapide in h. l. Ex hâc Christi ratiocinatione, non rectè colligunt Canonistae, iure divino clericos esse immunes & liberos ab omni tributo. 3. Maldonatus distingvit inter domesticos s. familiares Christi, ad quos Apostolos, eorumq; successores clericos refert, & inter filios adoptivos i. e. Christianos in genere. Addit, non de his, sed de illis solùm Christum h. l. loqui. Verùm distinctionem hanc, utpote minùs huic negotio convenientem, reiecit Maldonati sociennus Corn. à Lapide, eiusque exscriptor Tirinus. Unde postquam commemorassat, quòd collectio Canonistarum nulla sit, subiicit: Pari ratione colligeretur, ab eodem (tributo) immunes esse omnes Christianos, uti volunt Anabaptistae. Christiani enim sunt filii Dei adoptivi, renati in Baptismo per gratiam; quod tamen falsum esse, docet ApostolusRom. 13, 7.& tota Ecclesia: nam haec adoptio altioris est haereditatis & ordinis, sc. coelestis, non terreni. Quae cùm ita sint, apertè fatetur Bell. l. c. c. 3. §. Ad primum, Christum hîc de seipso tantùm loqui. Similiter Corn. Iansenius, itemque Iesuitae Salmero ac Maldonatus, expressè monentes, Christum loqui de filiis natur alibus, & licet in pl. loquatur, illud tamē tantùm locum habere in Christo, habiturum etiam in pluribus, si plures essent filii naturales. Ut ut verò Corn. à Lap. ac Tirinus addant, rectè tamen & appositè ad hoc Christi dictum, reges & principes à tributo eximere Ecclesiasticos, qui sunt quasi de domo & familiâ Christi. Quilibet tamen videt, quòd consequentia non sit firma, cùm primùm ipsi lesuitae fateantur, quòd Ecclesiastici sint saltem quasi de domo & familia Christi, de inceps largiantur, quòd Christus saltem de naturalibus filiis loquatur. Magnum verò discrimen est inter eum, qui est naturalis filius, & qui est saltem quasi de familiâ. Praetereà quis ambigat, maioribus gaudere privilegiis filios adoptivos. quàm domesticos alios, ac qui saltim quasi de familia sunt. Conf. pluribus B. Par. L. de Magist. Pol. § 463. ac Confess. Cuth. t. 2. p. 159. seqq. it. B. D. Roenig Cas. Cons. p. 735.

## 17:27
v. 27. You will find a stater. A stater is a whole shekel, which Peter paid for two, namely for himself and Christ. For it contained four drachmas. By the proper name of the nation it was called ῐ ῕ῙῪ῝ῐ. * (But a stater or two didrachmas, reduced to our currency, constitute half an Imperial. Furthermore, it is asked whether that stater was newly created by Christ in the mouth of the fish, or whether it was at least known to Christ that a stater existed in that fish, perhaps taken from elsewhere. The latter seems to be hinted at by Hugo Grotius in the words εὑρήσεις στατῆρα.. so that this passage might provide an argument at least for omniscience, but not for omnipotence. But the former pleases Isidore of Pelusium, who writes in book 1, epistle 206, that Christ by that very thing showed the power τῆς σθείκῆς δυνάμεως καὶ --εεγείας of divine power. The same Isidore of Pelusium, l. 1. -p. 206. p. 50. explains allegorically what is signified by this stater. That stater, he says, which Peter was ordered to take hidden in the fish, designated our form covered with vicious affections, by which the Lord recalls it in himself to the original exemplar &c.

* ( Give to them for me and you. Because Christ paid the tribute, and not for himself alone, but also for Peter, our countrymen conclude from this that the Roman Pontiff, as one who desires to be heard as the successor of Peter, ought not to withdraw himself and his clerics from the jurisdiction of the Civil Magistrate. Cardinals Baronius t. 1. Ann. 33. n. 31. and Bellarmine l. de Cler. c. 28. §. He objects, that that passage is to be understood not of the tribute which was paid to Caesar, but which God had imposed upon the sons of Israel for the temple. But although already among the ancients Chrysostom, Theophylact likewise and Hilary understood it of the sacred didrachma, although in a sense a little different, and among our own people B. D. Lyserus Harm. Evang. c. 91. likewise maintains it, then also men most versed in antiquity, see W. Schickard in de Iure Regio Ebr. p. 84. and Is. Casaubon Exerc. 15. ad Ann. Baronii s. 19. incline to the same: indeed among the Calvinists John Camero Praelect. Theol. p. 206. seqq. and also Myroth. p. 55. strives to defend that opinion at length, yet something else seemed so long ago to Isidore of Pelusium, who l. 1. ep. 206. The Lord, he writes, commanded that this (stater) be given for Himself, as having been made man, and subject to all our conditions: nor permitting resistance to the Emperor, when he commands those things which are in no way harmful and pernicious. Similarly, regarding the profane tax, or that which the Emperor Augustus imposed upon the Jews, Jerome and Bede also explain; what is more, the Jesuit himself, Corn. à Lapide, rejects that opinion concerning the sacred didrachma. For after he had recounted that Baronius, Fr. Lucas, and others accept it as concerning the sacred tribute, he adds: But that this didrachma was not sacred, and to be paid to the temple, but profane, and to be paid to the Romans or to Herod Antipas, because he had been appointed by the Romans as King of Galilee, is evident from the words of Christ to Peter in the following verse. From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute? Therefore this tax was royal, and was exacted for the King or Emperor. The same is evident from ch. 22. v. 21. &c. The same opinion (which also among our own is embraced and proven with many arguments by B. D. Chemn. H. E. ch. 91, and the same is followed by B. D. Hunnius on this passage, likewise Mr. D. Waltherus Cent. Miscell. Theol. ch. 2, p. 43, Ba-th. Mayerus Phil. S. book 1, p. 254, from Calvin, Sam. Petitus Var. lect. book 2, 84, Buxt. Lex. Talm. p. 2080, the former opinion of the Cardinals having been rejected) is embraced by other Papists, such as Corn. Iansenius, and especially also by the Jesuits. For thus Alf. Salmero thinks, thus Sebast. Barradius, thus Iacobus Tirinus, thus Ioan. Maldonatus, and others almost commonly. The doubts also which Bellarm. moves against this opinion are solved by his fellow Jesuit Barradius, who can be consulted. Indeed, Conzen himself does not seem averse to this opinion. Therefore he objects otherwise, namely that it is ridiculous to argue from the deed of Christ concerning the right of the Pontiff. We concede this, knowing well that there is an immense difference between Christ and the Roman Pontiff, since He was an example of humility, and had not where He might lay His head, whereas this Roman Pontiff swells with intolerable pride, and for whom the riches of the world scarcely suffice, by which the sacred hunger for gold, from which he himself suffers, is satisfied. But we add, it is also ridiculous that the Roman Pontiff boasts himself to be the vicar of Christ, and desires to be held as such by the universal Church. Conzen continues: Christ commands the stater to be paid, not as a debt, but lest they be scandalized through ignorance; therefore He did not detract from the Pontiff's right, but rather preserved it. Resp. We concede that Christ did not pay the tribute as a debt. And the reason is because He was the natural Son of God. But since the Roman Pontiff is not such, there is no reason why he should say that he himself ought not to be subject to the jurisdiction of the civil magistrate by debt. We now omit other reasons brought forward by Bellarmine in the aforementioned place, proposition 4, why Christ by no means had to pay tribute by debt. Which no one unless insane will assert to be seen in the Roman Pontiff. Bellarmine adds, that Christ paid the tribute because He willed to, that is, out of the choice of spontaneous subjection, for the reason which he himself explains, lest He give scandal, but rather that He might invite others by His example to render obedience to the magistrate. But since this reason is general, there is no reason why the Roman Pontiff with his clergy should be reluctant to imitate the promptness of Christ. Further, Conzen insists: The exactors do not demand boldly and by authority, nor do they approach Christ, but they ask modestly of Peter. Then they are content with the payment of the stater. Resp. The question is not about the quantity of the tribute, but about the universal exemption which the Roman Pontiff arrogates to himself and his clergy. Whether the publicans urged the tribute from Peter boldly or modestly, it matters little: it suffices for us that the Savior ordered the tribute to be paid for Himself and Peter, and thus the Papal clergy can by no means defend themselves by the example of Christ: but rather that the deed of Christ brings them to shame. Furthermore, the Blessed Father discusses the exemption of clerics at length, both in the Book on the Ministry of the Church, § 461 and following, and in the Catholic Confession, volume 3; add the Blessed Doctor Hōpfn. in the Catholic Saxon, p. 473; the Blessed Doctor Bald. in Cases of Conscience, book 4, chapter 12, Case 14; Lord Doctor Walth. in the Miscellaneous Centuries, chapter 2; especially Arnisaeus in his particular treatise on the exemption of clerics. Furthermore, the Papists also strive to establish the primacy of Peter, and consequently of the Roman Pontiff, as the fictitious successor of that man, from the fact that Christ ordered the tribute to be paid for Himself and Peter, not for the other Apostles. Thus Bellarmine, book 1 on the Roman Pontiff, chapter 19; Alphonsus de Castro against heresies, under the word The Pope. Costerus in Enchir. Controv. p. 121. Becanus lib. 1. Man. c. 4. §. 45. Cotonus in Inst. Cath. Cornelius also à Lapide writes in this place, that this was done for the sake of honor, so that the Savior might signify, namely, that he (Peter) was destined by him to be the vicar of his family and Church, and the head and prince of all the other Apostles. Maldonatus, Conzen, and other Jesuits in this place attempt to defend the same opinion, that by this the primacy of Peter was indicated. But I reply 1. Lyranus thinks that Christ did not pay for the other Apostles, either because only the heads of families were obligated to this tribute, or because the disciples of Christ were poor. Which latter opinion also pleases Franc. Lucas. 2. Some, following Chrysostom, establish that this was done to the praise of the faith of Peter. For since the faith of Peter was great, as one who did not doubt to go to the sea to catch the fish, they say that he deserved to become the consort of Christ in the making of the payment of the didrachma from that stater. 3. The true reason for the tribute being paid for Peter alone is that that tribute, which is treated here, was to be paid per head by individuals, not by those passing through, but by inhabitants and citizens, as Cornelius à Lapide well observes in this place. Now, however, it is uncertain whether the remaining Apostles had houses in Capernaum, such that they were inhabitants and citizens. But concerning Peter, it is sufficiently evident from chapter 8 of Matthew that he had a house and family in Capernaum, and therefore was obligated to the tax, as the Jesuit Salmero himself advises in vol. 6, tr. 37. Therefore, Christ ordered the tribute to be paid for him as a citizen and inhabitant. And Alphonsus Tostatus assigns this reason for the tribute being paid for Peter alone, and deservedly prefers it to the others, nor does Cornelius disagree. But if, for that reason, the tribute was paid for Peter and not for the other Apostles, certainly the prerogative of Peter can in no way be proven from it. For if the other Apostles had also been citizens of Capernaum, without ambiguity Christ would have paid the tribute for them as well. Maldonatus indeed objects that Peter no longer had a house in Capernaum, according to Matthew 19, 27. But our people have long since warned that that desertion concerned at least the care and administration, which the Apostles entrusted to others. And it is well to be noted that even the Catholic Roman writers accept it in this way, with Maldonatus himself advising at cap. 8. Matth. Conzen insists that Andrew also had a house in Capernaum, Marc. 1. but the aforementioned Abulensis has long since responded to this doubt, namely that Peter and Andrew constituted one family, since they had one house, so that there was at least one head of the household, namely Peter, while Andrew was as a minor under the power and governance of Peter. Finally, how, even if it were granted in the highest degree that this passage deals with the tribute which was paid to the Magistrate, and that Christ and his disciples were immune from paying it, it would have been proven, yet it does not follow that this privilege also applies to the successors of the Apostles, Camero shows in many places in t. 2. Praelect. p. 267. seqq. Nor is it improbable that, since Christ had lodging with Peter in the city of Capernaum, he wished to remunerate his host in such a way. Finally, even if we grant that Peter was affected here by a peculiar benefit from Christ, it is not immediately permissible to infer from that a Monarchical power or primacy over the rest, which is what the Papists intend.

I. The discourse of Christ with the Apostles concerning the question: who is the greatest in the Kingdom of heaven? v. 1. 5. II. An admonition concerning avoiding scandal v. 6. 11. III. The reception of penitent sinners v. 12. 14. IV. The correction of a sinning brother v. 15. 17. V. The delivery of the keys v. 18. 20. VI. Fraternal forgiveness v. 21. to the end.

Latin:

v. 27. Invenies staterem. Stater est siclus integer, quem Petrus pro duobus solvit, pro se scil. & Christo. Continebat enim quatuor drachmas. Proprio gentis nomine dicebatur ῐ ῕ῙῪ῝ῐ. * (Stater verò sive duo didrachma, ad nostram monetam redacta constituunt dimidium Imperialem. Caeterùm quaeritur, an de novo fuerit Stater ille in ore piscis à Christo creatus, an verò saltem Christo notum fuer it, in eo pisce extare staterem, fortè aliunde exceptum. Posterius Hugoni Grotio innu ere videntur verba εὑρήσεις στατῆρα.. Ut sic locus hic praebeat argu mentum saltem omniscientiae, non verò omnipotentiae. Verùm prius placet Isidoro Pelusiotae, qui lib. 1. epist. 206. scribit, Christum eo ipso divinae potentiaeτῆς σθείκῆς δυνάμεως καὶ --εεγείας vimc facultatem ostendisse. Idem Isidor. Pelus. l. 1. -p. 206. p. 50. quid per hunc staterem significetur, allegoricè exponit. Stater ille, in quit, quem Petrus in pisce abstrusum capere iussus est, formam nostram vitiosis affectionibus coopertam designabat, qua Deminus in seipso ad primigenium exemplar revocat &c.

* ( Da eis pro me & te. Quia Christus tributum solvit, nec pro se solùm, sed etiam pro Petro, colligūt inde nostrates, quòd P. R. ut qui Petri successor audire gestit, Magistratûs Civilis iur isdictioni se suosque clericos subtrahere haut debeat. Excipiunt Cardinales Baronius t. 1. Ann. 33. n. 31. ac Bellarm. l. de Cler. c. 28. §. Obiicit, locum illum intelligendum esse non de tributo, quod Caesari solvebatur, sed quod imposuerat Deus siliis Israel-eisum templi. At licet iamtam è veteribus Chrysostomus, Theophylactus item ac Hilarius de sacro acceperiut didrachmo, quamvis sensu paululum diverso, è notratibus quoque B. D. Lyserus Harm. Evang. c. 91. similiter statuat, tum quoque viri in antiquitate versatissimi, vid. W. Schickardus in de Iure Regio Ebr. p. 84. ac. Is. Casaubonus Exerc. 15. ad Ann. Baronii s. 19. eodem incilinet: imò è Calvinianis sententiam eam prolixè defendere satagat Ioh. Camero Praelect. Theol. p. 206. seqq. nec non Myroth. p. 55. aliud tamen iam olim visum Isidoro Pelusiotae est, quil. 1. ep. 206. Dominus, scribit, pro se hunc (staterem) daripraecepit, ut homo effectus, atque omnibus nostris conditionibus subiectus: nec Imperatori, cùm eâ imperat, quae minimè noxia & perniciosa sunt, obluctari permittens. Similiter de vectigali profano, sive quod Augustus Imperator Iudaeis imposuit, exponunt etiam Hieronymus ac Beda, quid quòd ipse Iesuita Corn. à Lapide, sententiam illam de sacro didrachmo reiiciat. Postquam enim recensuisset, quòd Baronius, Fr. Lucas aliique accipiant de tributo sacro, subiicit: Verùm hod didrachma non fuisse sacrum, & pendendum templo, sed profanum, & pendendum Romanis vel Herodi Antipae, quià Romanis constitutus erat Rex Galilaeae, patet ex verbis Christi ad Petrum vers. seq. Regesterrae à quibus accipiunt censum? Ergò hic census erat regius, & pro Rege vel Imperatore exigebatrr. Idem patet ex c. 22. v. 21. &c. Eandem sententiam (quam etiam ex nostratibus amplectitur, ac multis probat B. D. Chemn. H. E. c. 91. sequiturque eandem B. D. Hunnius in h. 1. it. Dn. D. Waltherus Cent. Miscell. Theol. c. 2. p. 43. Ba-th. Mayerus Phil. S. lib. 1. p. 254. ex Calvin. Sam. Petitus Ver. lect. l. 2. 84. Buxt Lex. Talm. p. 2080. reiectâ priori Cardinalium,) amplecruntur alii Pontificii, ui Corn. Iansenius, ac cumprimis etiam Iesuitae. Ita enim sentit Alf. Salmero, ita Sebast. Barradius, ita Iacobus Tirinus, ita Ioan. Maldonatus, aliiq; fere communiter. Dubia etiam, quae contra hanc sententiam movet Bellarm. solvit eias sociennus Iesuita Barradius, qui potest evolvi. Quin ipse Conzen non alien us ab hâc sententia videtur. Aliter igitur excipit, nempe ridiculum esse, ex Christi facto de iure Pontificis argumentari. Concedimus, probè scientes, quòd immensum sit Christum inter ac Pontificem Romanum discrimē, cùm ille fuerit humilitatis exemplum, & nō habuerit ubi caput suum reclinaret, hic verò P. R. intolerabili fastu turgeat, ac cui vix orbis opes sufficiant, quibus sacra auri fames, qua laborat ipse, sedatur. Sed addimus, ridiculum etiam esse, quòd P. R. sese Christi vicarium iactitet, talisq; ab universâ Ecclesiâ haberi concupiscat. Pergit Conzen: Solvere staterem Christus iubet, non tanquam debitum, sed ne ignorantes scandalizarentur, non ergò Pontifici ius detraxit, sed potiùs adservit. Resp. concedimus, quòd Christus non tan quam debitum solverit tributum. Ac ratio est, quia fuit Filius Dei naturalis. Talis verò cùm P. R. non sit, non est, quòd dicat, qs. nec ipse ex debito Magistratûs civilis iurisdictioni subesse debeat. Omittimus iam alias rationes, à Bell. d. l. propos. 4. adductas, quare Christus minimè ex debito tributum solvere debuerit. Quas nemo nisi insanus in Pontifice R. conspici adseret. Bellarminus addit, quòd Christus tributum solverit, quia voluit, h. e. ex arbitrio spontaneae subiectionis, ob causam, quam ipse exponit, ne scandalum daret, sed potiùs ut alios suo exemplo ad obedientiam Magistratui praestandam invitaret. Haec verò ratio cùm generalis sit, non est cur. P. R. cum suo clero Christi promtitudinem imitari repugnet. Ulteriùs instat Conzen: Exactores non audacter & pro imperio postulant, nec Christum adeunt, sed modestè à Petro quaerunt. Deinde solutione stateris sunt contenti. Resp. non quaestio est de tributi quantitate, sed de exemptione universali, quam P. R. sibi ac suo clero arrogat. An audacter porrò urserint Publicani à Petro tributum, an modestè, parùm interest: nobis sufficit, quòd Salvator pro se ac Petro tributum solvere iusserit, adeòque Christi exemplo clerici Papales tueri se minimè queant: sed quòd potiùs Christi factum in ruborem eos det. Coeterùm de Exemt. clericorum prolixè disserit B. P. tum in L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 461. seqq. tum Conf. Cath. t. 3. adde B. D. Hōpfn. in Sax. Cathol. p. 473. B. D. Bald. Cas. Consc. l. 4. c. 12. Cas. 14. Dn. D. Walth. Cent. Misc. c. 2. cumprimis Arnisaeum in pec. tr. de Exemt. clericorum. Coeterùm primatum quoq; Petri, ac consequenter Pontificis Romani, utpote fictitii illius successoris, Pontificii exinde stabilire satagunt, quòd Christus pro se ac Petro tributum solvere iuflerit, non pro aliis Apostolis. Ita Bell. l. 1. de P. R. c. 19. Alph. de Castro adv. haeres. verbo Papa. Costerus in Enchir. Controv. p. 121. Becanus lib. 1. Man. c. 4. §. 45. Cotonus in Inst. Cath. Corn. quoque à Lapide h. l. scribit, factum id honoris causâ, ut innueret nempe Salvator, ipsum (Petrum) suae familiae & Ecclesiae vicarium, ac coeterorum Apostolorum omnium caput & principem à se destinari. Eandem sententiam, quòd per hoc Petri primatus fuerit indicatus, defendere conantur Maldonatus, Conzen, aliique Iesuitae in h. l. Verùm resp. 1. Lyranus existimat, Christum pro coeteris Apostolis non solvisse, vel quia ad hoc tributum obligabantur solum capita familiarum, vel quia discipuli Christi pauperes erant. Quae posterior sententia etiam Franc. arridet Lucae. 2. Quidam, sequuti Chrysostomum statuunt, hoc factum ad laudem fidei Petri. Cùm enim magna fuerit Petri fides, ut qui non dubitavit ire ad mare ad tenendum piscem, dicunt, eum meruisse: ut consors Christi in solutione didrachmi facienda de illo statere fieret. 3. Vera ratio persoluti prosolo Petro tributi est, quòd tributum illud, de quo hîc agitur, capitatim solvendum erat à singulis, non transeuntibus, sed incoli& civibus. uti benè observat Corn. à Lapide h. l. Iam verò incertum, an reliqui Apostoli habuerint domos Capernaumi, ita ut fuerint incolae ac cives. De Petro verò ex cap. 8. Matth. satis paet, quòd domum & familiam habuerit Capernaumi, ideoobligatus fuerit ad censum, uti ipse Iesuita Salmero t. 6. tr. 37. monet. Christus igitur pro eo, tanquam cive & incolâ tributum solvere iussit. Atque hanc rationem persoluti pro solo Petro tributi adsignat, coeterisque meritò praefert Alph. Tostatus, nec adversatu Cornelius. Quod si verò propter eam rationem pro Petro, & non pro aliis Apostolis tributum persolutum, sanè minimè Petri praerogativa inde probari potest. Etenim si alii quoque Apostoli cives Capernaumi fuisset, procul ambiguo pro illis quoque Christus tributum persolvisset. Excipit quidem Maldonatus, quòd Petrus non ampliùs domum Capernaumi habuerit, iuxtaMatth. 19, 27. Verùm pridem monuerunt nostrates, quòd illa desertio respexerit saltem curam & administrationem, quam Apostoli aliis demandarunt. Ac probè notandum est, quòd etiam Catholico Romani Scriptores ita accipiant, ipso monente Maldonato ad cap. 8. Matth. Instat Conzen quòd etiam Andreas habuerit domum Capernaumi, Marc. 1. verùm ad hoc dubium pridem respondit allegatus modò Abulensis, videl. quòd Petrus & Andreas unam constituerint familiam, cùm unam domum habuerint, adeo unusaltem fuerit Paterfamilias, sc. Petrus, Andreas verò tanquam minor sub potestate & regimine Petri. Denique quomodo, si vel maximè concedatur, agi h. l. de tributo, quod Magistratui dependebatur, & ab hoc solvendo Christus eiusque discipulos immunes fuisse, probatum fuerit, tamen non sequatur, hoc privilegium etiam Apostolorum successoribus convenire, multis ostendit Camero t. 2. Praelect. p. 267. seqq. Nec improbabile est, quòd cùm Christus apud Petrum in urbe Capernaum diversorium habuerit, hospitem suum ita remunerari voluerit. Tandem ut ut largiamur, peculiari beneficio hîc à Christo Petrum fuisse affectum, non statim tamen inde Monarchicam potestatem vel primatum super reliquos inferre licet, id quod Pontificii intendunt.

## 18:1
v. 1. In that hour, namely, in which Christ had entered Capernaum; meanwhile they had already dealt among themselves on the way concerning this question, which they propose. Mark 9. v. 33.

* ( They approached. But Mark 9, 35. it is said that Christ had summoned the disciples. Dr. Walther H. B. page 776 έναντιοφ: reconciles this by noting that Christ first questioned some disciples, since their dispute on the journey was known to him Luke 9. 47., and afterwards the disciples approached Christ and set the question before him. From where that altercation arose, Pelargus discusses at length in this place.) *

Who is the greatest in the Kingdom of heaven * (in Greek it is μέιζων., therefore the comparative is placed for the superlative: as Mark 4. 31. 32. John 10. 29. 1. Corinthians 15. 19. &c.) *. They had heard that Christ, as the son of the highest King, was not bound to pay tribute; on this occasion they dispute who was greater in this Kingdom of Christ, which they imagined would be worldly. What they call the kingdom of heaven, that they had heard often from the mouth of Christ, therefore they retain that appellation, although not understood.

* ( ἐςὶ seems to be placed by Enallage of tense for ἔσται,; the Syrian inserts perhaps) *

* ( μείζων. there are those who think the comparative is placed here for the superlative, and the Blessed Luther accepts it so, whom Mr. Fesselius follows in book 4, ch. 2, §. 4, and proves that species of enallage with similar passages, as above ch. 11, ch. 13. 32, thus also Mark 4. 31. 32. 1. Cor. 13. 13. Others, however, think the comparative has a place here entirely, so it seemed to the Vulgate and Erasmus) *

NOTES ON CHAPTER XVIII OF MATTHEW. SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER.

* ( ἐν τῇβασιλείᾳ τῶν οὐρανῶν. Although elsewhere by this phrase in Holy Scripture is denoted for the most part the spiritual kingdom of Christ, which is twofold, of grace and of glory, and is called the Kingdom of Christ, the Kingdom of the heavens both by reason of the King, Ioh. 3, 13. and by reason of the subjects, whose πολίπυμα in the heavens Philip. 3, 20. and finally by reason of the government Ioh. 18, 39. See Cameron. vol. 2. Praelect. p. 280. (Cf. notes above on c. 3, 2. c. 4, 17. c. 5, 3. item Camer. in Myroth. Ev. p. 59.) yet in this place by the name of the Kingdom of the heavens is not understood the future age, as Chrysost. thinks, but an earthly and worldly kingdom, such as the Jews even today, and the Apostles at that time, were hoping would exist under the Messiah, and in this the Apostles were then eager to excel above others, as Justin Martyr well pointed out in quest. 112, and it is sufficiently evident from Luc. 22, 25. Act. 1, 6. being rebuked for this also by the Lord. But it is asked, how that gross ignorance and desire for vain glory in the disciples could stand with saving faith, which it cannot be doubted they were endowed with. Resp. by distinguishing between ignorance of simple negation, and of depraved disposition; to the former, not to the latter, is that ignorance of the disciples of Christ to be referred. Item between knowledge of the Kingdom of the Messiah confused, and distinct, and finally between the time which preceded the visible outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles, and that which followed it. See at greater length B. D. Chemnit. H. E. c. 84. pag. 921. it. c. 85. pag. 13900. B. Par. H. E. pag. 1168. & 1519. Camero vol. 2. Myroth. Ev p. 282. seqq. who himself also in the same place p. 312. & seqq. at length shows how that pride of the disciples, i.e., the desire for worldly glory, about which Pelargus in this place recounts the testimonies of some Fathers, could stand with true faith. The Jesuit Costerus is ridiculous, when in Enchir. Controv. pag. 121 he writes from that ambition of the Apostles it is understood, what was the mind of Christ in establishing ecclesiastical polity, namely that the supreme power in the Church should be in the hands of one visible head. But so far is that mind of Christ from being able to be gathered or understood from there, that rather the contrary is evident to the eye from the deed and grave warning of Christ, v. 2. 3. For how can the mind of Christ be understood from the ambitious, as Cornelius à Lap. himself indicates, and erroneous question of the disciples of Christ? Indeed if that had been the mind of Christ, which the Papists imagine, he would by no means have rebuked the disciples, certainly he would not have kept them in suspense in that difficult matter: but rather he would have indicated to them in clear words that Peter would be the greatest in the Kingdom of the heavens, especially when, as indeed Marcus Anton. de Domin. l. 1. de Rep. Eccles. c. 1. §. 96. and Bell. vol. 1. Controv l. 1. de P. R. c. 28. from the payment of the didrachma for Christ and Peter c. 17. at the end, although erroneously maintain, the disciples had already suspected then that Peter was to be preferred to all. And not him alone, but also all his successors in the Roman curia or see, and thus with easy effort every dispute would have been settled, both that which was being agitated among the disciples at that time, and that which is even now moved concerning the Roman Pope) *

Latin:

v. 1. In illa horâ, sc. quâ Christus Capernaum ingressus erat; interim iam ante in via de hâc quaestione, quam proponunt, inter se egerant. Marc. 9. v. 33.

* ( Adierunt. Sed Marc. 9, 35. dicitur, quod Christus discipulos accersiverit. Conciliat D. Waltherus H. B. pag. 776. έναντιοφ: hanc monendo, quòd Christus primùm nonnullos discipulos interrogaverit, cum nota ei fuerit eorum in itinere disputatio Luc. 9. 47. postea discipulos Christum accessisse, eidemque quaestionem exposuisse. Unde verò nata ista altercatio sit, prolixè disquirit Pelargus in h. l.) *.

Quis maximus est in Regno coelorum * (in Graeco est μέιζων. ponitur igitur Comparativus pro superlat: uti Marc. 4. 31. 32.Ioh. 10. 29.1. Corinth. 15 19. &c.) *. Audierant Christum ut filium summi Regis non teneri ad pendendum tributum, hac occasione disputant, quis in hoc Christi Regno, quod mundanum fore cogirabant, esset maior. Quod vocant regnum coelorum, id ex ore Christi soepins audierant, ideò appellationem illam, licet non intellectam, retinent.
