Fesselius lib. 4. c. 2. §. 4. probatque istam enallag. speciem similibus locis, uti supra c. 11. c. 13 32. sic quoque Marc. 4. 31. 32.1. Cor. 13. 13. Alii tamen omninò comparativum hîc locum habere putant, ita visum Vulgato ac Erasmo) *

NOTAE AD CAP. XIIX. MATTHAEI. SUMMA CAPITIS.

* ( ἐν τῇβασιλείᾳ τῶν οὐρανῶν. Licet aliàs phrasi hâc in Scripturâ S. denotetur plerumq; spirituale Christi regnum, quod duplex, gratiae & gloriae, diciturq; Christi Regnum, coelorum Regnum tum ratione Regis, Ioh. 3, 13. tum ratione subditorū, quorū πολίπυμαin coelisPhilip. 3, 20. tum deniq; ratione gubernationis Ioh. 18, 39. Vide Cameron. t. 2. Praelect. p. 280. (Conf. not suprà ad c. 3, 2. c. 4, 17. c. 5, 3. item Camer. in Myroth. Ev. p. 59.) hoc tamen loco nomine Regni coelorum non intelligitur futurum seculum, ce Chrysost. putat, sed terrenum ac mundanum regnum, quale ceu hodienum Iudaei, ita tum temporis Apostoli sub Messia fore sperabant, & in hoc eminere prae aliis Apostoli tum gestiebant, uti benè monuit Iustinus Martyr quaest. 112, ac satis patet ex Luc. 22, 25.Act. 1, 6. reprehensi ob hoc etiam à Dn. Sed quaeritur, quomodo crassa illa ignorantia ac inanis gloriolae studium in discipulis potuerit stare cum fide salvifica, quâ praeditos fuisse eos dubitari non potest. Resp. distinguendo inter ignorantiam simplicis negationis, ac pravae dispositionis; ad illam, non ad hanc referenda illa discipulorum Christi ignorantia est. Item inter notitiam Regni Messiae confusam, & distinctam, ac denique inter tempus, quod visibilem Spiritus Sancti super Apostolos effusionem praecessit, & quod hanc secutum est. Vid. pluribus B. D. Chemnit. H. E. c. 84. pag. 921. it. c. 85. pag. 13900. B. Par. H. E. pag. 1168. & 1519. Camero t 2. Myroth. Ev p. 282. seqq. qui ipse etiam d. l. p. 312. & seqq. prolixè ostendit, quomodo fastus ille discipulorum s. gloriolae mundanae cupiditas, de qua Pelargus in h l. aliquot Patrum testimonia recenset, cum verâ fide stare potuerit. Ridiculus est Iesuita Costerus, quando in Enchir. Controv. pag. 121 ex ista Apostolorum ambitione intelligi scribit, quae fuerit mens Christi in constituenda Ecclesiastica politia, nempe ut penes unū visibile caput esset summa in Ecclesia potestas. Verùm tantum abest, ut mens illa Christi in de colligi s. intelligi possit, ut potiùs contrarium ad oculum pateat ex Christi facto ac gravi monito, v. 2. 3. Ecquomodo enim ex ambitiosa, ceu ipse Cornelius à Lap. indigitat, & erronea discipulorum Christi quaestione, mens Christi intelligi potest? Sanè si ea fuisset Christi mens, quam Pontificii fingunt, hautquaquā discipulos reprehendisset, certè in ardua illa re minimè suspensos eos tenuisset: sed claris potiùs illis indicasset verbis, Petrum fore in Regno coelorum maximum, praeprimis cùm, ceu quidem Marcus Anton. de Domin. l. 1. de Rep. Eccles. c. 1. §. 96. ac Bell. t. 1. Controv l. 1. de P. R. c. 28. ex solutione didrachmae pro Christo & Petro c. 17. in fin. licet erroneè statuunt, discipuli suspicati iam tum fuerint, Petrum omnibus esse anteponendum. nec illum modò, verùm omnes quoque eius in curia vel sede Romana successores, & ita facili negotio omnis diremta lis fuisset, tum quae inter discipulos eo tempore agitabatur, tum quae etiamnum Papae movetur Romano) *

## 18:2
v. 2. Having called the little boy to himself. Concerning this little boy they determine * (thus Simon Metaphrastes feels) * that he was Ignatius, the disciple of the Apostles. Niceph. book 2. Eccles. Hist. ch. 35. *(which opinion is deservedly rejected by the more prudent. See Beza on this passage. Others, such as Anselm, Nicholas of Lyra, Thomas Aquinas, think he was Martial, Bishop of the Limousins: But this opinion is likewise not approved by Cornelius à Lapide himself. Still less probable is the opinion of Jerome, maintaining that it was the Holy Spirit whom he placed in the hearts of the disciples, so that he might change pride into humility. Likewise of Bernard, hom. 4 on 'missus est', and Bede on this passage, who think it was Christ himself, Matth. 11, 29. It is said, however, concerning this little boy, that Christ called him, προσκαλεσάμενος, from which, however, it is by no means to be inferred that that little boy had at that time the use of reason, as John Cameron, a not undistinguished Calvinist, well observes, both in his Myrothecium Evangelicum on this passage, and in vol. 1 of his lectures, page 318. And he proves this, both because a boy, approaching that age which is called adolescence, cannot be a suitable example of this humility and simplicity to which Christ exhorts his own, and from parallel passages Mark 9, 36 and Luke 9, 47. And he notes furthermore that the passage in the following chapter, v. 13, is similar to this, where for the word παιτα Luke ch. 18, 15. is used βξεΦη, which in Greek signifies nursing children, and that this is also evident from Luke 2, 12.16.1. Peter 2, 2.Acts 7, 19. nay, an infant still enclosed in the womb is so called Luke 1, 41.44. concerning the passage 2. Tim 3, 15. see B. Par. Book on Baptism §. 219.)*

Unless you are converted and become as little children etc. He does not demand that we become similar to little ones simply, but by reason of humility and lowliness . Therefore these words of Christ can be understood κασ ὑποκείμενον, because children think nothing and do not contend about the primacy and glory of this age, about which there was then contention among the disciples. Basil in ἀσκητ. Then the kingdom of God is received like a child, when we are like a learning child toward the doctrine of the Lord, μὴ ἀντιλέοντι, μητε ςικαιολογουμένῳ πρὸςτοὺδ διδασκαλους, πιςῶς δὲ καὶ ἐυπεισθῶς ὸεχομένῳ τδιδάλματα. 1. As infants desire the milk by which they are nourished: so let us desire the milk of the word 1. Petr. 2, 1. 2. 2. parents about to depart promise gifts to their children, whence they await the return of their parents with desire: so let us acquiesce in divine promises. 3. infants flee to their parents in dangers: so let us to the heavenly Father. 4. they allow themselves to be ruled. 5. they are ignorant of pride. 6. they are not tenacious of anger.

* (Isidorus Pelusiota l. 1. ep. 207. When the Lord demands this of us, that we approach the likeness of children, he does not require of us that we return to infancy etc. But that we deny wickedness, and so prepare ourselves, that childlike simplicity may be in us. And he shows this through those things which he said. οὐκ εἰπὼν ἐὰν μὴ γένησθε παιδέα, ἀλλ᾽ ὡςτα παιδία, τῇ τοῦ, ως, προσθηκῃ τὴν μίμησιν ἐμφαινων τον πράγματος. Conf. the same d. l. ep. 440. Cyprianus lib. de livore & Zelo c. 3. & 4 it l. 3. ad Quir. c. 5. and add. Camero t. 2. Praelect. pag 320. 321. item Conr. Rittershusius Ictus Sacr. Lect. l. 3. cap 23. circa finē. B. Par. Com. in pr. Ep. Petri p. 151.) *

Furthermore Christ wants us to be like children, St. Paul unlike. 1. Cor. 14, 20. Resp. we ought to be like children in true humility, having a holy infancy; but unlike, lest we be childishly foolish, and be carried about with every wind of doctrine, Eph. 4, 14. * (Briefly: we ought to become like children in pious simplicity, (which produces τὸ ἀνυπόκριτον, τὸ ἄδολον, τὸ ἤπιον and τὸ ἀπέρίερλον.) not foolish credulity. and not only as regards the absence of malice, but also as regards the possession of saving faith, as that from which true and God-pleasing humility flows. But if we ought to become like those little children as regards the possession of saving faith, it is certainly necessary to establish that there was faith in them, and that therefore baptized infants believe, which the Savior also expressly affirms concerning those little children, of whom the discourse is to Christ in this place v. 6. and the Father id-m 1. from the expressed assertion of Christ. l. c. and Mark 9, 42. 2. From the example of John the Baptist Luke 1, 44. and of circumcised infants Gen. 17, 18.Rom. 4, 11. 3. From the property of faith, Ps. 22, 10, 11.1 John 2, 12.14. and its effect Ps. 8, 3.Matt. 21, 16.John 1, 13.1 John 5, 4.Matt. 19, 13. etc. 4. From the testimony of David, Ps. 71, 5. 5. From Baptism received Luke 3, 3.Eph. 5, 26. etc. 6. From the consequent absurdity. For since it cannot be denied that certain infants die immediately after having received Baptism, who, if they are saved, it is necessary that they have had faith. Bellarmine, book 1 on Baptism, chapter 11, Adam Tanner in the Ratisbon Colloquy, page 269, Beza, part 2, response to the Acts of the Montbéliard Colloquy, pages 79, 98, Vorstius in Anti-Bellarmine, page 375, Herm. Ravensperger in Florilegium Theologicum, page 170, Wendelin, Exercise 119, § 12, following, object: that Christ is speaking about infants of this kind who are able to come on their own feet. Also who can be scandalized, a thing which cannot be said of infants recently born. Response: Although it is granted as much as possible (for there are not lacking, even from the Papists themselves, see Conzenius on verse 3, question 2, Haraeus in parallel passages on this place, who teach that the discourse here is about the same little children about whom Matt. 19, 14Luke 18, 15, 16. but of these it is said that they were brought in arms to the Savior) that by little ones in this place are understood little boys of two, three, or four years old, and thus who, having been called, could have come on their own feet, nevertheless nothing of this detracts from our opinion, since such are equal to infants, and equally as inept as nursing infants at perceiving and understanding the heads of religion. Wendelin indeed denies this, inasmuch as there are found in many two-year-olds and three-year-olds excellent progress in piety. Response: The question is not whether little boys of two or three years old can prayers and certain heads of piety, which we easily grant; but it is asked concerning this, whether they have the perfect use of reason, or such judgment that they can give an account of their faith, and thus judge concerning the articles of faith from the word heard and understood. This is what we deny. But W. urges especially that they are scandalized. Response: Distinguish between scandal committed regarding the intellect, and regarding the senses. Although infants do not have the use of the intellect, they nevertheless have the use of the senses, and thus they are most greatly offended, namely when they store up things seen and heard in their memory, and afterwards, when they have arrived at the years of discretion, they refresh and excite their species. W. hisses this away.

and denies, any of those things which he saw and heard before the use of reason, he remembers after the use of reason has been received. But experience testifies to the contrary. Furthermore, if even two-year-old infants cannot be scandalized by moral scandal, by bad example, they can nevertheless be scandalized by real scandal, by a bad deed, insofar as access to Christ is blocked for them, insofar as they are despised and afflicted with injuries, which makes it so that for Chrysostom and others to scandalize here is the same as to despise, to do evil. But especially to be noted is the rule that in Scripture that action is sometimes also called a scandal, which can offend others, even if it does not offend by the act itself, since God regards the will, intention, and operation of the agent more than the outcome of the action. A most clear example is had Matth. 16 23. From which passage we infer thus: If Peter is rightly said to have been a scandal to Christ, even though Christ was not scandalized by the act itself, it follows that infants can rightly be said to be scandalized, even if they are not scandalized in act. But the former is true, E and the latter. It suffices therefore for this, that little children be said to be scandalized, if any do something, from which others could be scandalized, i.e., that which in itself will be scandalous, B. D. Quistorpius in this place also refers here the passage 1. Cor. 8, 13. But that canon, that in Holy Scripture active words do not always designate the act, but sometimes only the power of acting, the editors of the London Polyglot Bible also approve in the edition of L. E. & G. §. 59. Finally, that also is to be observed, that both the Papists, see Bell. 1 de Bapt. c. 8. Costerus Enchir. Controv. p. 379. and the Calvinists, unfold Calvin. l. 4 iustit. c. 16. Wendel. Syst. Mai. p. 856 Polanus Synt. p. 495. prove paedobaptism, that is, the baptism of infants just brought into the light, from the parallel passage Matth. 19, 14. nay, from this very passage Canisius Inst Catechist. pag. 183. against the Anabaptists, which they would do altogether ineptly, unless they believed that infants could be supported from this place. Otherwise, for more on the present passage, one can consult B. D. Affelmannus in a special dissertation on the faith of infants q. 1 §. 3 following. The Lords Theologians of Marburg in Fundam deduct. p. 525. B. Par. L. de S. Bapt. §. 218 219 B. D. Winckelm. App. disp. Gies. d. 17. §. 22. following. B. D. Meisn. Theol. -hot. p. 616.) *

* ( He is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. i. e. he will enter it, as is evident from the preceding verse. add. Matth. 19, last c. 5, 19. see Glas. R. h. S. p. 533. Here Camero refutes the Papists, who draw an argument from this place, by which they prove that there are various and distinct degrees of glory in heaven. But however much we may grant that it is less firmly concluded from this place that degrees of glory are given in the life to come, it is nevertheless certain from other oracles of the Holy Scriptures, as was noted above at Matth. 13. 43., that those things which Ioh. Camero replies to the arguments of our people in 2. Praelect. p. 325. seqq., as well as those by which he attempts to establish the contrary opinion, will be discussed in their own place.

v. 2. Accersitum ad se puellum. De hoc puello statuunt * (ita sentit Simon Metaphrastes) * fuisse Ignatium Apostolorum discipulum. Niceph l. 2. Histor. Eccles. c 35. *(quae sententia meritò à prudentioribus reiicitur. Vid. Beza in h. l. Alii, uti Anselmus Nic. de Lyra, Thomas de Aquino putant fuisse Martialem Lemovicensium Episcopum: Sed haec opinio itidem ipsi Cornelio à Lap. non probatur. Minùs adhuc probabilis est sententia Hieronymi, statuentis, fuisse Spiritum S. quem posuerit in cordibus discipulorum, ut superbiam in humilitatem mutaret. Item Bernhardi hom. 4. super missus est, ac Bedae in h l existimantium, fuisse Christum ipsum, Matth. 11, 29. Dicitur verò de hoc puerulo, quod Christus eum advocarit, προσκαλεσάμενος, è quo tamen minimè inferēdum, quod puerulus ille habuerit tum usum rationis, uti benè observat Ioh. Camero, Calvinianus non in celebris, tum in Myroth Ev. ad h. l. tum t. 1. praelect pag. 318. idque probat tum, quod puer, accedens ad aetatem illam, quae adolescentia dicitur, non possit esse idoneum exemplum huius humilitatis & simplicitatis ad quā Christus suos hortatur, tum ex locis parallelis Marc. 9, 36 ac Luc 9, 47. ac notat insuper, similem huic esse locum c. seq. v. 13. ubi pro voce παιταLuc. c. 18, 15. usur pet βξεΦη, quod Graecè significet pueros lactentes, idque etiam patet ex Luc. 2. 12.16.1. Petr. 2. 2.Act. 7. 19. imò infans adhuc in utero conclusus ita vocatur Luc. 1. 41.44. de loco 2. Tim 3. 15. vid. B. Par. L. de Bapt §. 219.)*

Nisi conversi fueritis & efficiamini sicut puelli &c. Non simpliciter, sed ratione humilitatis ac demissionis parvulis -ofieri similes exigit. Possunt igitur haec verba Christi intelligi κασ ὑποκείμενον, quia pueri nihil cogitant nec contendunt de primatu & gloria huius seculi, de quo tunc erat inter discipulos contentio. Basil. in ἀσκητ.Tunc accipitur regnum Dei instar pueri, cùm erga doctrinam Domini similes sumus discenti puero,μὴ ἀντιλέοντι, μητε ςικαιολογουμένῳ πρὸςτοὺδ διδασκαλους, πιςῶς δὲ καὶ ἐυπεισθῶς ὸεχομένῳ τδιδάλματα. 1. Ut infantes appetunt lac, quo enutriuntur: sic nos appetamus lac verbi 1. Petr. 2, 1. 2. 2. parentes discessuri liberis promittunt dona, unde cum desiderio expectant reditum parentum: sic nos acquiescamus in divinis promissis. 3. infantes ad parentes confugiunt in periculis: sic nos ad patrem coelestem. 4. patiuntur se regi. 5. fastum ignorant. 6. non sunt tenaces irae.

* (Isidorus Pelusiota l. 1. ep. 207. Cùm Dn. id à nobis exposcit, ut ad puerorum similitudinem accedamus, non id à nobis exigit, ut ad infantiam redeamus &c. Verùm ut improbitatem abnegemus, sicque nos comparemus, ut puerilis in nobis simplicitas insit. Atque hoc per ea, qui dixit, ostendit.οὐκ εἰπὼν ἐὰν μὴ γένησθε παιδέα, ἀλλ᾽ ὡςτα παιδία, τῇ τοῦ, ως, προσθηκῃ τὴν μίμησιν ἐμφαινων τον πράγματος. Conf. idem d. l. ep. 440. Cyprianus lib. de livore & Zelo c. 3. & 4 it l. 3. ad Quir. c. 5. ac add. Camero t. 2. Praelect. pag 320. 321. item Conr. Rittershusius Ictus Sacr. Lect. l. 3. cap 23. circa finē. B. Par. Com. in pr. Ep. Petri p. 151.) *

Coeterùm Christus vult similes nos esse pueris, D. Paulus dissimiles.1. Cor. 14, 20. Resp. pueris similes esse debemus verâ humilitate, sanctam habentes infantiam; dissimiles autem, ne pueriliter desipiamus, & quovis doctrinae vento circumferamur, Eph. 4, 14. * (Breviter: similes fieri debemus pueris piâ simplicitate, (quae gignit τὸ ἀνυπόκριτον, τὸ ἄδολον, τὸ ἤπιον ac τὸ ἀπέρίερλον.) non stultâ credulitate. nec solùm quoad ab sentiam malitia, sed etiam quoad possessionem fidei salvificae, utpote ex qua vera Deoque grata humilitas profluit. Si verò similes fieri debemus istis puerulis quoad fidei salvificae possessionem, necesse fanè est statuere, quòd in illis fuerit fides, quodque adeò infantes baptizati credant, id quod etiam disertè de illis puerulis, de quibus Christo h. l. sermo est, Salvator affirmat v. 6. Paterque id-m 1. ex Christi expresso adserto. l. c. ac Marc. 9, 42. 2. Ex Iohannis Bapt. Luc. 1, 44. ac circumcisorum infantum Gen. 17, 18.Roman. 4, 11. exemplo 3. ex fidei proprio, Ps. 22, 10, 11.1. Ioh. 2, 12.14. eiusque effecto Ps. 8, 3.Matth. 21. 16.Ioh 1, 13.1. Ioh. 5, 4.Matth. 19, 13. &c. 4. Davidis testimonio, Ps. 71, 5. 5. Ex Baptismo suscepto Luc. 3, 3.Eph. 5, 26. &c. 6. ex consequente absurdo. Cùm enim negari haut possit, quosdam infantes statim post perceptum Baptismum mori, qui si salvantur, necesse est, ut habuerint fidem. Excipiunt Bellarminus l. 1. de Bapt. cap. 11. Adam Tannerus in Coll. Ratisbon. pag. 269. Beza part 2. resp. ad Act. Coll. Mompelg. p. 79 98. Vorstius in Anti-Bell. pag. 375. Herm. Ravensp. in Floril. Theol. p 170. Wendelinus Exerc. 119. §. 12. seqq. Christum loqui de huiusmodi infantibus, qui venire suis pedibus queant. item qui possint scandalizari, id quod de infantibus recens natis dici nequeat. Resp. Licet quàm maximè concedatur, (etenim non desunt, etiam ex ipsis Pontificiis, Vide Conzenium ad v 3. q. 2. Haraeum in locis parall. ad h. l. qui de iisdem puerulis hîc sermonem esse docent, de quibus Matth. 19, 14Luc. 18, 15. 16. at de his dicitur, quòd ad Salvatorē in ulnis fuerint allati) per parvulos h. l. intelligi puerulos bimulos, trimulos aut quadrimulos, adeoque qui vocati pedibus suis venire potuerint, nihil tamen per hoc nostrae decedit sententiae, cùm tales infantibus sint pares, & ad percipienda atque intelligenda religionis capita aequè ac infantes lactentes inepti. negat quidem hoc Wendelinus, siquidem reperiantur in multis trimulis & quadrimulis egregii in pretate progressus, Resp. quaestio non est, an pueruli bimuli, trimuli possint pr-ces ac capita quaedam pietatis recitare, quod facilè largimur; Sed de eo quaeritur, an habeant perfectum rationis usum, sive tale iudicium, ut possint fidei suae rationem reddere, adeoque ex verbo audito & intellecto de fidei articulis iudicare. id quod nos negamus. Sed cumprimis urget W. quòd scandalizentur. Resp. dist. inter scandalum commissum circa intellectum, & circa sensus. Licet infantes usum intellectûs non habeant, habent tamen usum sensuum, & sic maximè offenduntur, quando nempe visa & audita in memoria reponunt, eorumque species postea, ubi ad annos discretionis pervenerunt, refricant & excitant. Exsibilat hoc W.

negatque, ullum eorum, quae ante omnem rationis usum vidit audivitque, post acceptum rationis usum recordari. Sed experientia testatur contrarium. Praeterea si vel maximè infantes bimuli non possint scandalizari scandalo morali, malo exemplo, possunt tamen scandalizari scandalo reali, malo facto, quatenus illis aditus ad Christum intercluditur, quatenus contemnuntur & iniuriis afficiuntur, quo facit, quod Chrysostomo aliisque scandalizare hîc idem est, quod contemnere, malefacere. Cumprimis verò notanda regula, quod in Scriptura aliquando ea etiam actio dicatur scandalum, quae alios offendere potest, licet ipso actu non offendat, cùm Deus magis voluntatem, intentionem & operationem agentis respiciat, quam actionis eventum. Exemplum clarissimum habetur Matth. 16 23. Ex quo loco ita inferimus: Si Perrus rectè dicitur Christo fuisse scandalo, licet Christus ipso actu non fuerit scandalizatus, sequitur quòd infantes rectè possint dici scandalizari, licet actu non scandalizentur. Atqui prius est verum, E & posterius. Sufficit igitur ad hoc, ut pueruli dicantur scanda izari, si qui aliquid fa-iant, unde alii scandalizari poterant, s. quod in se scandalosum erit, B. D. Quistorpius h. l. refert quoq; huc locum 1. Cor. 8, 13. Canonem verô istum, quod in Sc. S. verba activa non semper actum, sed solam agendi virtutē quamdoque designent, approbant quoque editores Bibliorum Polygl. Londin in de Idit. L. E. & G. §. 59. Denique & illud observandum, quòd tum Pontificii, vid. Be l. 1 de Bapt. c. 8. Costerus Enchir. Controv. p. 379. tum Calviniani, evolv. Calvin. l. 4 iustit. c. 16. Wendel. Syst. Coeterùm pluribus de praesenti loco consuli possunt B. D. Affelmannus in pecul diss. de fide infantum q. 1 §. 3 seqq. Dnn. Theologi Marpurg. in Fundam deduct. p. 525. B. Par. L. de S. Bapt. §. 218 219 B. D. Winckelm. App. disp. Gies. d. 17. §. 22. seqq. B. D. Meisn. Theol. -hot. p. 616.) *

## 18:4
*(v. 4. Whoever shall humble himself etc. the quality of those to be saved is described, not the cause of salvation.)*

Latin:

*(v. 4. Quisquis se humiliaverit &c. describitur qualitas salvandorum, non causa salutis.]*

## 18:5
v. 5. Whoever receives such a child. Tossanus: whoever receives such a one from among my disciples, who is without pride and devoid of malice like a child. *[Some urge that Christ is not speaking about infants, but about older children. Thus Bell. l. 1. de Bapt. c. 11. and Beza respons. 2. ad Coll. Mompelg p. 97 98. accept it.]* Doubtless he wished by this reasoning to crush the argument which we draw from this place for the faith of infants: But the context shows the contrary. *(We by no means deny, however, that some of our own people also sometimes allege this saying in such a way that by μιχρές they understand those who are still tender or weak in faith, and not yet sufficiently informed in Christian doctrine. See B. D. Hutter. in Expos. F. C. page 1027. Especially it is also to be noted Mark 9, 36. it is reported that the Savior later took into his arms that child whom he had previously set in the midst.)* *( Receives i. e. amends, brings back to the way, educates well, as is evident from the opposite.)*

*( in my name. See Matth 7, 21.)*

Latin:

v. 5. Qui talem puerum suscipit. Tossanus: qui talem ex me is discipulis suscipit, qui absque fastu & malitiae expers est instar pueri. *[Nonnulli urgent, quòd Christus non loquatur de infantibus, sed de pueris grandioribus. ita accipiunt Bell l. 1. de Bapt. c. 11. ac Beza respons. 2. ad Coll. Mompelg p. 97 98.]* Nimirum voluit hâc ratione elidere argumentum, quod pro fide insantum ex hoc loco ducimus: Sed contextus ostendit contrarium. *(Minimè tamen negamus, quòd nonnulli ex nostratibus etiam hoc dictum ita allegent quandoque, ut per μιχρές intelligant adhuc tenellos s. imbecilles in fide, & in doctrinâ Christianâ nondum satis informatos. Vid. B. D. Hutter. in Expos. F. C. pag. 1027. Cumprimis etiam notandum Marci 9, 36. referri, quòd Salvator puerum illum, quem priùs in medio statuerat, postea in ulnas suas susceperit.)* *( Suscipit i. e. emendat, in viam reducit, benè educat, ceu patet ex opposito.)*

*( in nomine meo. Vid. Matth 7, 21.)*

## 18:6
*(v. 6. who believe in me. This seems absurd both to the Jesuits and to the Calvinists. Whence they invent that by little ones in this place are understood not infants, but simple men and devoid of malice like infants, or if the discourse is entirely about infants, then it is indeed granted that they believe, but by the faith of their parents. As concerns the former exception, it was dealt with a little before at v. 5; as for the latter, we oppose to it the sayings Hab 2, 4Rom 1, 17. Others except that Christ is speaking here about older children, but the parallel place Mark 10, 15. protests against this exception. Conf. also the notes at v. 2.)*

( συμΦέρει άυτω. For who would doubt that it is better, in order that scandal may be prevented, to be cast into the sea, that is, to suffer extreme bodily punishments, than for one who causes scandal to be cast into the abyss of hell,Apoc. 20, 10.Marc. 9, 43. 44.)

Μύλον ονιυόν some explain as a great stone, such as an ass turns around in a mill while grinding. Thus Hilary. Erasmus in Annot. page 60. It signifies a huge rock, for in millstones the rock which is placed underneath, so that it may support the other which is turned around, ίνος is called. (But such a stone is considered a millstone, because larger millstones were driven by asses, just as hand-mills, being smaller, were driven by hands. Catullus looked to that when he writes at to deliver to the mill, that is, to make someone a mill-ass. And the Philistines imposed such a servile and most abject work also upon the defeated hero Samson, as is evident from Iud 16, 21 just as Christian interpreters rightly explain τό to grind in that place, contrary to the Jews, whom Nic. de Lyra also follows, who take it concerning the venereal act, whom Alf. de Tostato refutes.) Christ indicates a certain punishment, familiar to the Palestinians, and he exaggerates it both by the size of the stone and by the depth of the sea. Hieron. in h l. But what he said, it is better for him &c. he speaks according to the custom of the province, by which that was the punishment for greater crimes among the Jews, that they should be submerged into the deep with a stone tied to them. (Compare also Tertull. l. 4. adv. Marcionem. But this kind of punishment was considered in the place of the greatest penalty, because for those submerged in such a way all hope of burial would be cut off, since the sea otherwise casts out the dead.) Drusius in Praet. N. T. writes that among the kinds of punishments which were customary in that nation, no mention is made of submersion. However, Casaubon shows from Diodorus Siculus l. 16 that this kind of punishment was not unusual even among the Greeks. (Therefore these words can and ought to be taken literally, contrary to what was done by Aug. l. 1. QEv. c. 24 and Greg. M. l. 6. Moral cap. 26, who understand by those things the occupations and labors of temporal affairs. But the Savior wished by this serious and severe admonition to recall to the memory of parents also, above all, that the blood of their children damned by their neglect is to be required no less from their hands than the blood of hearers damned by their neglect is to be required from the Ministers of the word, Ezech. 33, 8.

How gravely God is also offended, and how much He is moved to anger, if anyone scandalizes others, that is, makes them sin by bad example, is evident among other things also from the fact that as often as God almost wishes to denote some impious person in the review of the Kings of Israel, He compares him with Jeroboam, adding that he made Israel to sin. So that God could almost not cease to remember the scandal given by Jeroboam to the Israelite people. To this also pertains the fact that authors are punished more severely Ioh. 19, 12. Satan and our first parents can serve as an example. And hence but the Apostles exhort us to a conversation of holy life, so that we may not, to wit, provide a scandal to others. See Philip. 2, 5.1. Petr. 2, 12.2. Petr. 3, 11.

( όν τω πελάουει τηρυ θαλάης in the depth of the sea. The Chaldean Paraphrast also uses a similar phrase Ps. 46, 3 שב where in Hebrew it is שב in the heart of the sea. Rightly therefore B. Luther: Into the sea/where it is deepest.)

## 18:7
(v. 7. Woe &c. The Savior proposes five foundations, which being placed before our eyes we shall more diligently avoid scandals, and will be able to avoid them. 1. The memory of hellfire, v. 7. 2. The flight of occasion, v. 8. 9. 3. The reverence of the Angels, v. 10. 4. The grace of the advent or incarnation, v. 11. 5. The mercy of the heavenly Father toward repenting sinners, v. 12. seqq.)

( It is necessary that scandals come, and indeed in the very Church, of which there is speech in this place. Therefore it is evident that in this world, in the external assembly of the Church, there are also non-holy ones. Which opinion B. Par. proves at length in L. de Eccl. §. 48. Furthermore, it is manifest that Christ, by saying it is necessary that scandals come, does not speak of absolute necessity, or of the consequent, but hypothetical or of the consequence. Namely, the cunning of the Devil and the security and malice of men being posited. The Devil therefore is the efficient cause of scandals, while he moves and incites men to iniquity and scandals. See Matth. 3, 36. seqq. and compare B. D. Frantzium in de Interpret. Sc. S. Orac. 14. B. Par. Coll. Isagog. L. de Provid. c. 1. § 9. Beautifully Chrysostom homil. 59. in Matth. When he says necessity, he does not destroy the freedom of the will, nor does he subject it to the necessity of some things, but he predicts what will altogether come to pass. Ού τοίνον ή πέόρρησις ωτου ος σχάνδαλα άλε άπαλε. ουδέ έπειδή αροείπε, Να τούτο λινετα. άλλ)

πειδή πντων έμελλεν έσεσθείπεν. i. e. therefore his prediction is not to be thought to induce scandals. For not because he predicted that scandals were future, do they therefore come, but because they were altogether about to come , for that reason he predicted them. For they would not happen, if wicked and pestiferous men did not wish to devise them . But if they were not about to come, he himself would not have predicted them as future. Isidore of Pelusium lib. 1. epist. 56, Augustine lib. 5. de C. D. c. 9, and other Doctors of the primitive Church, cited by B. Par. Harm. Evang. c. 172. p. 1139, have similar things. If anyone observes these very things, he will not greatly care for those things which Camero disputes at length here concerning necessity and contingency in Myrothecio Evangel. p. 62. seqq. and likewise in Praelect. p. 345. seqq. For we do not, while we deny that God is the cause of scandals, introduce Him as an idle spectator of human actions; but we assert that He so governs and directs scandals or the evil actions of men by His divine providence, that they yield to the glory of His divine name and the advantage of the pious, although against the opinion and efforts of Satan and the pious. Benedictus Aretius, not otherwise an uncelebrated Calvinist, also agrees with the aforementioned Chrysostom, when he writes orthodoxly in Cap. 1. Actor.: How was it necessary for the Scripture to be fulfilled? did it bring necessity upon Judas? will he be excused here by necessity? By no means. The necessity was not simple or absolute, but of the consequent (more correctly of the consequence) For because he did not cease to obey the counsels of Satan, he finally arrived at that state of affairs. David Paraeus, likewise a sufficiently noble Calvinist, l. 3. de Gr. & Lib. Arb. c. 4. p. 398. and lib. 5. c. 14. p. 737 likewise teaches that it is a matter here of necessity by hypothesis, or what is inevitable on account of the corruption of nature. Furthermore, the observation of B. D. Calixtus is not to be omitted, who in Concord. Ev. ad d. l. warns that that of the Apostle 1. Cor. 11, 19. is similar to the present statement.)

*( Necesse est, ut ut veniant scandala, & quidem in ipsa Ecclesiâ, de qua h. l. sermo. E. patet, quòd in hoc mundo, in externo Ecclesiae coetu sint etiam non-sancti. Quam sententiam prolixè probat B. Par. L. de Eccl. §. 48. Manifestum porrò est, Christum. dicendo necesse est, scandala venire, non loqui de necessitate absotâ, sive consequentis, sed hypothetica sive consequentiae. Positâ nempe Diaboli astutiâ ac hominum securitate atque malitiâ. Diabolus igitur est causa efficiens scandalorum, dum movet & incitat homines ad iniquitatem & scandala. Vid. Matth. 3, 36. seqq. ac confer B. D. Frantzium in de Interpret. Sc. S. Orac. 14. B. Par. Coll. Isagog. L. de Provid. c. 1. § 9. Pulcrè Chrysostomus homil. 59. in Matth. Cùm necessitatem dicit, non destruit libertatem arbitrii, neq necessitati aliquarum rerum illam supponit, sed quod omninò venturum est, praedicit.Ού τοίνον ή πέόρρησις ωτου ος σχάνδαλα άλε άπαλε. ουδέ έπειδή αροείπε, Να τούτο λινετα. άλλ

πειδή πντων έμελλεν έσεσθείπεν. i. e. non ergò praedictio ipsius scandala inducere putanda est. Non enim quia futura scandala praedixit, idcircò veniunt, sed quoniam omninò ventura -rant, idcirco praedixit. Non n. fierent, si nollent ea excogitare nequahomines atq pestiferi. Quod si ventura non fuissent, nec ipse futura praedixisset. Similia habent Isidorus Pelufiota lib. 1. epist. 56. August. lib. 5. de C. D. c. 9. ac alii primitivae Ecclesiae Doctores, allegati à B. Par. Harm. Evang. c. 172. p. 1139. Quae ipsa si quis observaverit, non magno pere curabit ea, quae prolixè hîc de necessitate ac contingentiâ disputat Camero in Myrothecio Evangel. p. 62. seqq. itemque in Praelect. p. 345. seqq. Neque enim, dum negamus, Deum esse scandalorum causam, ipsum otiosum actionum humanarum spectatorem introducimus; sed adserimus, quòd divinâ suâ providentiâ scandala sive malas hominum actiones ita gubernet ac dirigat, quò ad nominis sui divinigloriam ac piorum commodum, licet contra Sat-nae ac piorum opinionem & conatus, cedant. Facit verò cum Chrysostomo modò adducto Benedictus etiam Aretius, non incelebris aliàs Calvinianus, quando in Cap. 1. Actor. orthodoxè scribit: Quomodo oportuit impleri Scripturam? anne attulit Iudae necessitatem? an hîc necessitate excusabitur? Minimè. Necessitas non erat simplex aut a-soluta, sed consequentis (rectiùs consequentiae) Quia enim non destitit obsequi Satanae consiliis, tandom eò rerum devenit. David quoque Paraeus, Calvinian pariter satis nobilis l. 3. de Gr. & Lib. Arb. c. 4. p. 398. ac lib. 5. c. 14. p. 737 itidem docet, agi hîc de neces-tate ex hypothesi, sive quod inevitabile est propter naturae corruptionem. Porrò non omittenda observatio B. D. Calixti, qui in Concord. Ev. ad d. l. simile praesenti effato esse monet illud Apostoli 1. Cor. 11, 19.)*

## 18:8
v. 8. If --nutua &c. is an obstacle to you &c. Hand is taken by some to mean spouse, who is to the husband as it were another hand. Gen. 2. Eye for friend, who can assist you with counsel. The sense therefore is that a friend or spouse is not to be valued more than God Himself. *(But it is by no means to be inferred from this that crime, i. e. if one of the spouses impels the other to sin, in such a way that the other cannot live with him without the danger of offending God, is a legitimate and sufficient cause for divorce, as some, according to Bellarmine de Matrim. c. 14. §. 5., strive to elicit from the present saying. For just as no bodily amputation of a hand is required or that someone should pluck out an eye, when those members scandalize us: but it suffices if we resist the evil lusts of the eyes, --a likewise if a wife solicits us to sin, it is not necessary that a bodily separation be made, or a divorce be undertaken: for spiritual amputation suffices, i. e. if we stoutly resist the wife soliciting us to sin, and do not prefer her love to the pursuit of piety. See entirely B. D. Mentzerus tr. de Coniugio p. 224 seqq.)* Irenaeus lib. 4. c. 46. p. 282. Just as there (in the O. T.) those who acted wickedly and exterminated the rest were condemned and cast out, similarly here also the eye that scandalizes is plucked out, and the foot and the hand, lest the rest of the body perish likewise. Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 1. epist. 83. p. 22. Christ called the eye and the right hand the nearness of necessary and most faithful friends, namely those who are of a benevolent mind toward us to bring help and assistance sincerely, calling by those names those by whose work we now execute those things which are to us. *(Chrysostomus hom. 60. in Matth. These things were not said about the members of the body, but about friends and necessary persons, whom we call joined to us like members: but nothing is so pernicious and pestiferous as the company of wicked men and conversation &c. therefore he commanded with a certain great vehemence that those who are harmful be from us near the very consequence of things signifies, who are the authors of scandal. Nothing, however, prevents this passage from being explained in the same way as above c. 5, 29. Conf. Rom. 6, 12.16. 17.19.cap. 5, 13.Gal. 5, 24Coloss. 3, 5. Some wish these things to be said by hyperbole and hypothetically, i. e. that the eye is rather to be plucked out than that we should suffer ourselves to be the authors of scandals. For which interpretation Camero brings forward some things in h. l. Let also the Analecta above to c. be compared. 5, 30. Otherwise, unless these words are taken by hyperbole their proper meaning cannot have a place here, since if taken in their proper acceptance they strike against the fifth commandment. Whence also Theologians almost commonly teach that it must be taken figuratively, namely concerning the amputating of the occasion of sin, which is commanded here concerning the amputation of the right hand, of the eye &c. See B. D. Bald. in Ideâ Dispos. Bibl. c. 2. p. 24. Dn. D. Danhawerus Ideâ Boni interpr. p 105. & 109. B. Par. Disp. Acad. p. 950. where he shows at length how ineptly the Weigelians understand this mandate according to the proper acceptance of the words.)*

*( Into eternal fire. Conf. c. 25, 42. Jude v. 7. Apoc. 14, 10. Elsewhere it is called πύρ άσΒεςον, Matth 3, 12.Mark 9, 43.Luke 3, 17. is a description of infernal fire. It is also proved from this, that infernal punishments will be eternal. This is what B. D. Winckelmannus in Dispp. Giesens. T. 3. p. 499, Mr. D. Calovius in Socinismi Profligati page 1120. seqq., likewise in Arminianismi Consider. p. 519. seqq., B. Par. L. de inferno §. 57, Hinckelmannus in Collegii Anabapt. Disp. 18. c. 2. err. 2, prove against many heretics, both ancient and modern (such as the Photinians, Arminians, Anabaptists). But that error is condemned also in the Augsburg Confession, art. 17, for which reason those who have commented on the A. C. can also be consulted.)*

Latin:

v. 8. Si --nutua &c. obstaculo tibi est &c. Manus à quibusdam accipitur de coniuge, quae est marito quasi altera manus. Gen. 2.Oculus pro amico, qui te consilio iuvare potest. Sensus ergo est, quòd non sit pluris faciendus amicus, vel coniux, quàm ipse Deus. *(Minimè verò hinc inferendum, quòd crimen, h. e. salter coniugum impellat alterum ad peccatum, ita ut non possit alter cum eo sine periculo Deum offendendi cohabitare, sit legitima & sufficiens divortii causa, ceu nonnulli, referente Beilarmino de Matrim. c. 14. §. 5. è praesenti dicto elicere satagunt. Etenim sicut non requiritur corporalis aliqua manûs abscissio rel ut aliquis oculum erunt, quando membra illa nos scandalizant: sed sufficit, si malae oculorum concupiscentiae resistamus, --a quo-ue si uxor ad peccatum nos sollicitat, non necesse est, corporalis fiat seiunctio, vel divortium suscipiatur: sufficit enim spiritualis abscissio, h. e. si uxori ad peccatum nos sollicitanti fortiter resistamus, nec amorem eius pietatis studio praeferamus. Vid. omninò B. D. Mentzerus tr. de Coniugio p. 224 seqq.)* Irenaeus lib. 4. c. 46. p. 282. Quemadmodum illic (in V. T.) condemnabantur & proiiciebantur hi, qui malè operabantur & reliquos exterminabant, similiter hîc oculus quoq effoditur scandalizans, & pes & manus, ne reliquum corpus pariter pareat. Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 1. epist. 83. p. 22. Oculune ac manum dextram op-umus Christus necessariorum ac fidelissimorū amicorum propinquitatem nuncupavit, eos nimirum, qui ad opem & auxilium sincerè nobis afferendum benevolo erga nos animo sunt, iis nominibus appellans, quorum opera nunc ea, quae nobis cor-i sunt, exequimur. *(Chrysostomus hom. 60. in Matth. Non haec de membris corporis dicta sunt, sed de amicis ac necessariis. quos quasi membra nobis coniunctos dicimus: nihil autem it a pernic-osum ac pestiferum est, ut consuetudo pravorum hominum & conversates &c. ideô magna quadam cum vehementiâ iussit nocentes à nobis propinquo consequentia ipsa rerum significat, qui scandali authores sunt. Nihil tamen impedit, quò minùs locus hic eodem modo explicetur, quo suprà c. 5, 29. Conf. Rom. 6, 12.16. 17.19.cap. 5, 13.Gal. 5, 24Coloss. 3, 5. Nonnulli per hyperbolem haec dicta volunt ac hypotheticè, h. e. quòd potiùs eruendus fit oculus, quàm ut patiamur, nos esse autores scandalorum. Pro quâ interpretatione nonnulla adducit Camero in h. l. Conferantur etiam Analecta suprà ad c. 5, 30. Aliàs nisi per hyperbolen d. mverba haec accipiantur, propria eorum significatio locum habere hîc nequit, cùm in propriâ acceptione sumta impingant in praeceptū quintum. Unde etiam Theologi ferè communiter docent, figuratè accipiendum esse, nempe de amputandâ peccandi occasione, quod hîc de abscissione dextrae, oculi &c. praecipitur. Vid. B. D. Bald. in Ideâ Dispos. Bibl. c. 2. p. 24. Dn. D. Danhawerus Ideâ Boni interpr. p 105. & 109. B. Par. Disp. Acad. p. 950. ubi prollxi-s ostendit, quàm ineptè Weigeliani mandatum hoc secundùm propriam verborum acceptionem intelligant.)*

*( In ignem aeternum. Conf. c. 25, 42. Iudae v. 7. Apoc. 14, 10. Alibi vocatur πύρ άσΒεςον,Matth 3, 12.Marc. 9, 43.Luc. 3, 17. est descriptio ignis infernalis. Probatur etiam hinc, poenas infernales fore aeternas. Id quod multis contra veteres pariter ac recentiores (uti Photinianos, Arminianos, Anabaptistas) haereticos probant B. D. Winckelmannus Dispp. Giesens. T. 3. p. 499. Dn. D. Calovius Socinismi Profligati pag. 1120. seqq. it. in Arminianismi Consider. p. 519. seqq. B. Par. L. de inferno §. 57. Hinckelmannus Collegii Anabapt. Disp. 18. c. 2. err. 2. Damnatus verò error ille in Augustanâ quoque Confessione est, art. 17. quare evolvi etiam possunt, qui in A. C. commentati sunt.)*

## 18:10
v. 10. Of these little ones. Toslanus by little ones understands the poor & despised Christians, who would serve GOD in true fear & piety. *(And so also Chrysostom explains it in hom. 60 in Matth. Camero also eagerly seizes upon this interpretation in Myroth. and strives to strengthen it by a collation of several places of Holy Scripture, where lit-- for despised are taken. But the question is not whether vile and despised men are sometimes called little ones in H. S., for we grant that willingly: but the question is about this, whether in this place by μιχρς such are understood, and not rather children or little ones in age)* for the context shows that, on the occasion of a child placed in the midst, Christ is speaking in general about believing little ones. *(See note on v. 5. and consult the excellent exegesis of this whole verse handed down by B. D. Winckelm., App. Dispp. Gies. Disp. 17.)*

*( Contemnatis, i. e. neglect. Conf. Prov. 14, 21. thus honorare for to care for, 1. Tim. 5, 3. add. Anal above to c. 15, 4.)*

*( Their angels. It is customary from this to prove that to each of the pious there is a certain angel assigned by GOD as a guardian. Since this opinion was accepted among the Jews, (just as very many in the primitive Church also felt this way. See Jerome in this place, and also in the last chapter of Isaiah, Basil the Great, book 3 against Eunomius, Theodoret, Oration 11, p. 715), Hugo Grotius thinks that it is very probable that this opinion is approved here by Christ. But what is to be held concerning this opinion, which Grotius in the aforementioned place, as well as the Scholastics in Commentaries on Book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 11, and other Papist writers, (see Hannibal Rosselus, Commentary on the Pymander of Mercurius Trismegistus, book 2, q. 7, c. 1, p. 319; Becanus, Scholastic Theology, part 1, tr. 3, c. 6; Ludovicus Molina on the first part of Thomas, q. 113; Altenstaig, Theological Lexicon, p. 49; Ignatius Derkennis, Treatise on the One God, and indeed on the Creator, Disp. 6, c. 3, §. 1) strive to construct from this place, the Blessed Pareus explains in a few words in the Collegium Isagogicum, Book on Angels, c. 8, §. 7, namely, that it can be said probably that ordinarily one angel is destined for the custody of a living pious person; but extraordinarily several angels are sent to individuals. And that is evident from Gen. 32, 2. 2. Kings 6, 17. Ps. 34. Ps. 91, 11. Heb. 1, 14. Otto Casmann discusses the same question in Angelographia, Part 2, c. 7, q. 1; Suarez, book 6 on Angels, c. 17, n. 8 et seqq. (where he also tries to prove against the Magdeburgians that to the unfaithful also and the impious there is given by GOD an angel as guardian. But although Theophylact also in this place seems to feel this way, it is nevertheless more correctly established that angels as guardians are given by God only to the faithful.) Our opinion, however, also pleases Origen and the author of the Opus Imperfectum. What is more, Molina himself in the aforementioned place admits, that that assertion, that every single man has his own peculiar angel, although it is the common opinion of the Saints (Fathers) and Doctors (Scholastics), is nevertheless not a matter of faith. Derkennis establishes the same in the aforementioned place, p. 519. Furthermore, this doctrine concerning the custody and presence of the Holy Angels is useful 1. for thanksgiving, namely for the immense goodness of GOD. 2. for consolation. Conf. 2. Reg. 6, 16.Ps. 103, 20. for the flight from and detestation of sins. Cf. 1. Cor. 11, 10.)*

*( Of them, i.e., of the little ones. But the holy Angels are called the Angels of the little ones, because they are sent by GOD on their behalf. Ebr. 1, 14. and indeed for the same reason that Paul calls himself Apostle of the gentiles Rom. 11, 13. because he was sent to the gentiles. Henricus LanceloMechlin, Doctor of Sacred Theology of the Order of Hermit Friars of St. Augustine, writes in his Anatomy of the deformed Christian, p. 329, from the fact that Christ directed this assertion: Their Angels etc. to all little ones whatsoever offered, good and faithful, or unfaithful; whether baptized or not baptized, the Scholastic Doctors in 2. dist. 7. & 11. and the Fathers gather that to all men whatsoever, faithful and unfaithful, are assigned proper and individual guardians, Which opinion the said Lanceroz strives to defend in many places there. But the hypothesis of Lancelozi is false, that the Savior directed those words to all infants whatsoever, whether faithful or unfaithful. The contrary is clearer than the midday sun from v. 6 preceding. But as for the controversy itself: Whether to every single man whatsoever, faithful and unfaithful, a certain Angel- guard-n is assigned, it was dealt with in the Analysis to the preceding chapter, and it will be dealt with at greater length in the Analecta to Actor. c. 12. 15. In this place we note at least that Felicianus Capito, Archbishop of Avignon, in his Catholic Explanation of the O. and N. T., p. 570, concedes that not only is Thomas de Vio Cardinal Cajetan ours, but he also grants that these words of Christ do not compel.)*

Their Angels in heaven. Lucas Brug. In heaven i.e., heavenly, whose proper dwelling is in heaven. By this epithet they are distinguished from -al Angels (although the Syrian does not read that) whose proper dwelling is in the infernal regions. Others read, in heaven they see. Gregor. lib. 2. moral. c. 2. How can they both always stand by, & always see the face of the Father, if they are sent to the ministry of the exterior for our salvation? which we shall nevertheless solve more quickly if we weigh of what great subtlety the Angelic nature is. For they do not go forth from the divine division in such a way that they are deprived of the joys of internal contemplation. And after: And therefore they are sent and stand by, to whom they go forth by that which they are circumscribed, and by that which they are also present in the one to whom they are sent, they never depart. And they always see the face of the Father, and yet they come to us, because they both go forth to us by spiritual presence, and yet they remain there, whence they had departed, through internal contemplation. Beda on Luke apud Lombard. l 1. dist. 37. segm. 13. When Angels come to us, they so fulfill the ministry exteriorly, that they nevertheless stand by before God interiorly through contemplation, because although an Angel is a circumscribed Spirit, the highest Spirit, which is God, is uncircumscribed, within whom the Angel runs, whithersoever he is sent. Corn. Iansenius c. 71. Concord. It is to be noted that Angels, even when they are not in heaven, but have been sent to us, do not lack the most blessed contemplation of GOD, but wherever they are, they enjoy the contemplation of GOD, who is everywhere present, and by reason of that contemplation they are said to be in heaven. Goclenius in Prodr. Lex. Philos. p. 707. Angels when they are on earth, see the face of the heavenly Father, not by presence, but by internal contemplation or intuition. It is more correctly said that heaven, when it is enunciated concerning Angels, then signifies the heavenly state, and not indeed any place or corporeal space, in which heavenly state the Angels are always, wherever they may also be and exist.

(Conf. B. P. Coll. Isag. L. de Ang. c. 4. §. 8. B. D. Winckelman. Append. Dispp. Gies. Disp. 17. §. 12. Thus indeed, namely for the blessed state, the term heaven is accepted also elsewhere in Holy Scripture. See Matth. 6, 20.Luc. 10, 18.Phil. 3, 20. Rightly therefore the Blessed Doctor Chemnitius H E. c. 92. p. 1004. gathers from this passage that heaven, earth, and hell are distinguished not by intervals of places, but by respect of blessedness and unhappiness. And he notes that Augustine on the Triple habitation, Bernard in the book on the soul c. 38, and other Doctors of the Church teach this. But because the holy Angels always enjoy the beatific vision of GOD, it is clear that Camero in Myrothec. Ev. p. 74. teaches less correctly that the same reason is in this place as that of the passage 1. Reg. 10, inasmuch as and that the ministers of Solomon altogether departed from his sight at times.)

*( They always see the face of the heavenly Father. From this, theologians prove that the good angels, who persisted in their concreated holiness, are so confirmed in good that they can never fall for eternity. To indicate this confirmation, the same theologians think that the good angels are called elect,1 Tim. 5:21 holy,Mark 8:38 angels of light.2 Cor. 11:14 Prosper in De vita contemplativa c. 3: By a divine and just judgment it was brought about that there should be a voluntary and happy necessity of remaining. I conclude that because he says here concerning the angels in heaven that Νά παντός they see the face of the heavenly Father, and indeed they are to be blessed -ἄγγελοι, c. 22:30, our people also rightly gather that the blessed enjoy the beatific vision of GOD, by which what is understood, the blessed Par. explains at length in L. de vita aet. §. 134, and in Harm. Evang. c. 180, p. 1710. 6. Furthermore, Hugo Grotius thinks in this place that those words: they always see the face of the heavenly Father, pertain to this, that not just anyone, but more distinguished angels are understood to be assigned as guardians of the pious. But since this description is of confirmation in good (See Ps. 16:11Ps. 15Job 19:27Matt. 5:81 Cor. 13:12 whatever the Remonstrants may also chatter to the contrary, having followed Arminius, Declar. sentent. p. 278 ff.), which confirmation in good is common to all holy angels, there is no reason why any distinction should be invented here. Otherwise, we readily grant that there is some order among the good angels no less than among the bad. Grotius perhaps drew that opinion from the Scholastics, whose leader Thomas Aquinas, 1. part. p. 113, art. 3, ad 1, interprets this place concerning the supreme angels yet not in the first but in the ninth and lowest order, so that in this, the first are guardians of men, the middle of animals, the lowest of plants)*

They see. Conrad Vorstius ineptly gathers from this that God is not infinite, because He is seen by the Angels. For a distinction must be made between the beatific vision and physical comprehension. Concerning which matter more will be said in the Analecta on 1. Cor. 13, 12. ) (

Latin:

v. 10. Ex his pufillis. Toslanus per parvulos intelligit pauperes & contemtos Christianos, qui DEO in vero timore & pietate servirent. *(Atque ita etiam Chrysostomus exponit hom. 60 in Matth. Avidè quoque interpretationem hanc arripit Camero in Myroth. eamque locorum aliquot Scripturae Sacrae, ubi par-- pro contemtis -umuntur, collatione firmare nititur. Verùm non quaeritur, an homines viles & contemti in Sc. S. aliquando parvi dicantur, id enim ultrò largimur: sed de eo est quaestio, an h. l. per μιχρς ta-es intelligantur, ac non potiùs aetate pueri sive parvuli)* contextus enim ostendit, occasione pueri, in medium collocati Christum in genere de parvulis credentibus loqui. *(Vid. not ad v. 5. ac consule egregiam totius huius versicull exegesin à B. D. Winckelm. traditā, App. Dispp. Gies. Disp. 17.)*

*( Contemnatis, i. e. negligatis. Conf. Prov. 14, 21. sic honorare pro curare,1. Tim. 5, 3. add. Anal suprà ad c. 15, 4.)*

*( Angeli eorum. Solet hinc probari, unicuiq piorum certum à DEO adsignatum à DEO Angelum esse custodem. Quae opinio cùm inter Iudaeos fuerit recepta, (quemadmodum etiam plurimi in primitivâ Ecclesiâ ita senserunt. Vid. Hieronymus in h l. nec non in c. ult. Esaiae, Basilius M. lib. 3. contra Eunomium, Theodoretus Orat. 11. p. 715) existimat Hugo Grotius, admodùm probabile esse, sententiam eam hîc à Christo approbatam. Quid verò de sententiâ hâc, quam multis Grotius d. l. sicuti & Scholastici Comment. in L. 2. sentent. dist. 11. aliique Pontificii Scriptores, (vid. Hannibal Rosselus Comment, in Pymad. Mercurii Trism. l. 2. q. 7. c. 1. p. 319. Becanus Theolog. Scholast. part. 1. tr. 3. c. 6. Ludovicus Molina in pr. Thomae q. 113. Altenstaig. Lexici Theo. log. p. 49. Ignatius Derkennis Tr. de Deo uno, & quidem de Creatore Disp. 6. c. 3. §. 1.) ex h. l. adstruere satagunt, habendum sit, paucis exponit B. Par. Colleg. Isag. L. de Angelis c. 8. §. 7. nempe, probabiliter dici posse, ordinariè unum Angelum evivis pio ad custodiam destinatum esse; extraordinariè verò plures Angelos ad singulos mitti. Idque constat ex Gen. 32, 2.2. Reg. 6, 17.Ps. 34.Ps 91, 11.Ebr. 1, 14. Ventilant eandem quaestinem Otto Casmannus in Angelograph. Part. alt. c. 7. q. 1. Suarez. l. 6. de Angel. c. 17. n. 8. seqq. (ubi etiam contra Magdeburg. evincere conatur, infidelibus quoq & impiis dari à DEO Ang-lum custodem. Ast licet Theophylactus etiam in h. l. sentire ita videatur, rectiùs tamen statuitur, solùm fidelibus dari à Deo Angelos custodes.) Arridet verò ententia nostra Origeni quoq; atque autori Op. Imperf. Quid quòd Molina ipse d. l. fateatur, quòd adsertio illa, unum quemque hominem suum peculiarem habere Angelum, licet communis sit sententia Sanctorum (Patrum) atq, Doctorum (Scholasticorum) non tamen de fide sit. Idem statuit Der-Kennis d. l. p. 519. Coeterùm prodest doctrina haec de custodiâ & praesentiâ S. Angelorum 1. ad gratiarum actionem, pro immensâ scil. DEI bonitate. 2. ad consolationem. Conf. 2. Reg. 6, 16.Ps. 103, 20. ad peccatorum fugam ac detestationem. Conf. 1. Cor. 11, 10.)*

*( Eorum, sc. pusillorum. Dicuntur verò S. Angeli puerulorum Angeli, quia mittuntur à DEO propter eos. Ebr. 1, 14. atque adeò eadem ratione, quâ Panlus se gentium Apostolune nominat Rom. 11, 13. quia ad gentes missus. Scribit Henricus LanceloMechlin. Ord. Frat. Erem. t. August. Th. D. D. in Anatome Christani deformati p. 329. ex eo, quòd Christus adsertionem hanc: Angeli eorum &c. ad omnes prorsus parvulos oblatos direxerit s. bono& fideles, sive infideles; sive baptizatos s. non baptivatos, Dd. Scholasticos in 2. dist. 7. & 11. ac Patres colligere, omnibus omninò hominibus fidelibus & infidelibus adsignatos esse proprios & singulos custodes, Quam etiam sententiam dictus Lanceroz multis ibi defendere satagit. Verùm falsa est hypothesis Lancelozi, quòd Salvator ad omnes omninò infantes s. fideles s. infideles illa verba direxerit. Contrarium Sole meridiano clarius est ex v. 6. praecedente. Quod verò ipsam controversiam: An singulis omninò hommibus, fidelibus & infidelibus certus adsignatus Angel- cust-s sit, concernit, de eâ in Anal. ad cap. praeced. actum, & pluribus de eâ agetur in Analect. ad Actor. c. 12. 15. Hoc loco illud saltem notamus, quòd Felicianus Capito, Avinion, Archi Ep. in Explic. Cathol. LL. V. & N. T. p. 570. concedat, non solùm nostrum esse Thomam de Vio Cardinalem Caietanum, verùm etiam largiatur, verba haec Christi non cogere.)*

Angeli eorum in coelis. Lucas Brug. In coelis i. e. coelestes, quorum propria habitatio in coelis est. Hoc epitheto disting vuntur à -alis Angelis (etsi Syrus illud non legat) quorum propria habitatiin infernis est. Alii legunt, in coelis vident. Gregor. lib. 2. moral. c. 2. Quomodo aut semper adsi--ere, & videre sem per faciem Patris possunt, si ad ministerium exteri-s pro nostrâ salute mittuntur? quid tamen citiùs solvemus, si quantae subtilitatis sit Angelica natura, pensamus. Neq enim sic à divinâ divisione foràs exeunt, ut internae contemplationis gaudiis priventur. Et post: Et mittuntur igitur & adfistunt quibus per hoc quod circumscripti sunt, exeunt, & per hoc, quod inius quoq praesentes sunt, nunquaem recedunt. Et faciem ergsemper Patris vident, & tamen adnos veniunt, quia & ad nos spirituali praesentiâ foràs exeunt, & tamen ibise, unde recesserant, per internam contemplationem servant. Beda super Lucam apud Lombard. l 1. dist. 37. segm. 13. Cùm ad nos Angeli veniunt, sic extetius implent ministerium, ut tamen ante Deum interius per contemplationem adsistant, quia etsi Angelus est Spiritus circumscriptus, summus tamen Spiritus, qui Deus est, incircumscriptus est, intra quem currit Angelus, quocunq mittatur. Corn. Iansenius c. 71. Concord. Notandum, Angelos etiam cùm non sunt in coelo, sed ad nos missi suni, non carere beatissimâ DEI contemplatione, sed ubicunque sunt, DEI, qui ubiq praesens est, perfrui contemplatione, atq ratione eius contemplationis dici esse in coelo. Goclenius in Prodr. Lex. Philos. p. 707. Angeli cùm in terris sunt, vident faciem Patris coelestis, non per praesentiam, sed per internam contemplationem seu intuitionem. Rectiùs dicitur, quòd coelum, quando de Angelis enunciatur, tunc statum coelestem significet, non verò locum aut spatium aliquod corporeum, in quo statu coelesti sunt Angeli semper, ubicunque etiam sint & existant.

*(Conf. B. P. Coll. Isag. L. de Ang. c. 4. §. 8. B. D. Winckelman. Append. Dispp. Gies. Disp. 17. §. 12. Ita verò, nempe pro statu beato, vocabulum coeli, accipitur etiam alibi in Sc. S. Vid. Matth. 6, 20.Luc. 10, 18.Phil. 3, 20. Rectè proinde B. D. Chemnitius H E. c. 92. p. 1004. ex hoc loco colligit, coelum, terram & infernum non locorum intercapedinibus, sed beatitudinis & infelicitatis respectu distingvi. Idque Augustinum de Triplici habit. Bernh. lib. de anima c. 38. alios Dd. Eccl. docere monet. Quia verò Angeli sancti semper fruuntur visione DEI beatificâ, patet, quòd minùs rectè eandem h. l. rationem esse Camero in Myrothec. Ev. p. 74. doceat, quae loci 1. Reg. 10 utpote cùm con--et, quòd Salomonis ministri omninò à conspectu eius quandoque discesserint.)*

*( Semper vident faciem Patris coelestis. Probant hinc Theologi, bonos Angelos, qui in concreatâ sanctitate perstiterunt, ita confirmatos esse in bono, ut in aeternum cadere nequeant. Ad quam confirmationem indicandam putant iidem, Angelos bonos dici electos,1. Tim. 5, 21.sanctos,Marc. 8, 38.Angelos lucis,2. Cor. 11, 14. Prosper in vitâ contempl. c. 3. Divino iustoque iudicifactum est, ut fieret permanendi voluntaria felixq necessitas. Exeo, quòd hîc de Angelis in coelo dicit, quòd Νά παντόςvideant faciem faciem Patris coelestis, & verò beati futuri sint -ἄγγελοι, c. 22, 30. rectè quoque colligunt nostrates, quòd beati fruantur visione DEI beatificâ, per quam quid intelligatur, prolixè exponit B. Par. L. de vita aet. §. 134. it. Harm. Evang. c. 180. p. 1710. 6. Existimat porrò Hugo Grotius in h. l. verba illa: semper vident faciem Patris coelestis, eo pertinere, ut non quivis, sed insigniores Angeli intelligantur piorum custodes adsignati. Verùm cùm descriptio haec sit confirmationis in bono. (Vid. Ps. 16, 11.Ps, 15.Iobi 19, 27.Matth. 5, 8.1. Cor. 13, 12. quicquid etiam contrà garriant Remonstrantes, secuti Arminium, Declar. sentent. p. 278. seqq.) quae confirmatio in bono omnibus sanctis Angelis communis. non est, cur hîc distinctio aliqua fingatur. Aliàs inter bonos non minùs, quàm malos Angelos ordinem aliquem esse, ultrò largimur. Hausit autem Grotius fortè opinionem illam ex Scholasticis, quorum Antesignanus Thomas de Aquino 1. part. p. 113. art. 3. ad 1. h. l. interpretatur de supremis Angelis non tamen in primosed nono ac infimo ordine, ita ut in hoc primi sint custodes hominum, medii animalium, infimi plantarum)*

*( Vident. Ineptè hinc colligit Conradus Vorstius. Deum non esse infinitum, eò quòd ab Angelis videatur. Disting vendum enim est inter beatificam visionem, & physicam comprehensionē. Quâ de re pluribus agetur in Analect. ad 1. Cor. 13, 12.)*

## 18:11
*(v. 11. The Son of man came to save άπολωλό what was lost, that is, lost man. A parallel passage is found in Luke 19:10. The neuter is put for the masculine. See D. Glass. Gr. S p. 76. The discourse here, however, is not about the second coming of Christ, but the first, as one which is not judicial, John 3:17 c. 12:47, but medicinal, as Augustine speaks in sermon 36 on John. But since Christ did not come so that he might free man contaminated by sin from the poison of sin, and save him, it is evident that sin is not the very substance of man, as the Flacians used to trifle. Johannes Piscator also errs when he writes in Obs. ad h. l.:) We must take care, lest we abuse those words to establish the opinion of those who say that Christ redeemed all men entirely. Nay rather, this is most correctly gathered from thence. Conf. Ioh. 3, 16.1. Ioh. 2, 2. Concerning the arguments of Piscator in this place, item in his book against Hemming, p. 21. 22. 139, and also Vol. 2. Thes. Theol. in the Appendix of the Disputation on Predestination, p. 282. Amandus Polanus, book 6. Syntagma Theologiae, ch. 18. p. 403. Grossius in Theatrum Biblicum in this place, and of other Calvinists, by which they attempt to prove that by το ατολωλος is understood here at least the elect, it is to be noted 1. that although the Savior does not say ηαθα το ρητον, whatever had perished, yet ηαθα την -άνοιαν: says that; for there would be no consequence in the argument of Christ, by which he proves that none of the little ones ought to be despised or scandalized, unless the Angels were sent for all, and unless the Son of man had come to save all. 2. that by sheep, v. 11, not only the elect are understood, but rather all men, as those who all were wandering sheep, Esa. 53, 6. nor does the Savior say in Ioh. 10, 15. that he laid down his life for his elect sheep alone. 3. that it does not follow: if not all men receive eternal salvation in actual fact, therefore Christ did not come to save all, or he himself is frustrated in the end of his coming. For it must be known that the end of Christ's coming was not that all, even those who maliciously persevere in their unbelief, should be made partakers of eternal salvation in actual fact. But rather this was the end of Christ's coming, that all might believe, and through faith be made possessors of eternal salvation, as is evident from Ioh. 3, 16. 4. that if Grossius understands by the efficacy of the death of Christ this, that indeed Christ died for all, and that his death was sufficient λύτρον, with this end also paid, that all might be saved; yet the greatest part of men fall away from salvation by their own fault, in that they are unwilling to apprehend by true faith the merit of Christ, which is nevertheless sufficient for expiating the sins of the whole world, then he does not have us as opponents. But without doubt that is not the mind of Grossius. For how the Calvinists pervert the distinction between sufficiency and efficiency of the merit of Christ ; B. Par. shows in Coll. Isag. Book on Reprobation, ch. 6. §. 8. Conf. also B. D. Fewrb. Syntag. 1 Disquis. Theol. page 320. following. Although indeed the redemption made through Christ extends to the whole human race, as far as the acquisition of salvation is concerned: yet it must by no means be extended to the devils and fallen angels, as is evident from Heb. 2, 162 Pet. 2, 4. But why God did not spare the sinning Angels, or provide a Redeemer for them, various causes of that are brought forward, some of which B Par Comment. on the said Petrine passage exhibits from the Fathers. Add Flaccus Albinus, Prooem. book 3 on the Trinity; also Haymo on ch. 2 of the epistle to the Hebrews. Finally, there are those who testify that this verse is omitted in some Greek Codices. But without a doubt such Codices are corrupt. For this verse is a genuine part of the text. Just as the most approved and most ancient Greek MSS Codices also present it, just as the Oriental Interpreters also do, the Syrian, Arab, Ethiopian, Persian. The Greek Interpreters also explain the same: Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius.

Latin:

*(v. 11. Venit Filius hominis salvareάπολωλόperditum, h. e. hominem perditum. Locus parallelus habetur Luc. 19, 10. Neutrum pro Mascul. ponitur. Vid. D. Glass. Gr. S p. 76. Sermo verò hîc non est de adventu Christi secundo, sed primo, ut qui non est iudicialis, Ioh. 3, 17 c. 12, 47. sed medicinalis, ceu loquitur Augustinus serm. 36. in Ioh. Cùm verò Christus non venerit, ut hominem peccato contaminatum à peccati veneno liberaret, eumque salvaret, patet, quòd peccatum non sit ipsa hominis substantia, ceu Flaciani nugabantur. Errat quoque Iohannes Piscator, quando in Obs. ad h. l. scribit: C-vendum, ne abutamur illis verbis ad stabiliendam opinionem eorum, qui dicunt, Christum redemisse omnes omninò homines. Imò potiùs, rectissimè hoc inde colligitur. Conf. Ioh. 3, 16.1. Ioh. 2, 2. Circa argumenta Piscatoris in h. l. item lib. contra Hemming. p. 21. 22. 139 nec non Vol. 2. Thes. Theol. in Append. Disp. de Praedest. p. 282. Amandi Polani l 6. Syntagm. Theolog. c. 18. p. 403Grossi in Theatro Bibl. h. l. aliorumque Calvinianorum, quibus evincere conantur, per το ατολωλος intelligi hîc saltem electos, notandum 1. quòd licet ηαθα το ρητον non dicat Salvator, quicquid perierat, id ramen dicere ηαθα την -άνοιαν: nulla enim esset consequentia in argumento Christi, quo probat, nullum è pusillis debere sperni s. scandalizari, nisi propter omnes mitterentur Angeli, ac nisi Flius hominis propter omnes salvandos venisset. 2. quòd per oves v. 11. non solùm intelligātur electi, sed potiùs omnes homines, ut qui omnes fuerūt oves errantes,Esa. 53, 6. nec Ioh. 10, 15. dicit Salvator, quòd pro solis suis ovibus electis animam suam posuerit. 3. quòd non sequatur: si nō omnes homines ipso actu salutem accipiunt aeternā. E. Christus propter omnes salvandos nō venit, aut ipse frustratur adventûs sui fine. Sciendum enim est, quòd finis adventûs Christi non fuerit, ut omnes, etiam qui malitiosè in suâ incredulitate perseverant, ipso actu salutis aeternae reddantur participes. Quin potiùs hic fuit adventûs Christi finis, ut omnes credant, & per fidem reddantur salutis aeternae compotes, ceu patet ex Ioh. 3, 16. 4. quòd si Grossius per efficaciam mortis Christi intelligat hoc, quòd quidem Christus mortuus fuerit pro omnibus, quòdque adeò mors eius sufficiens fuerit λύτρον, hoc fine etiam persolutū, ut omnes salventur; maximam tamen hominum partem propriâ suâ culpâ excidere salute, eò quòd meritum Christi, quod tamen sufficiens pro totius mundi peccatis expiandis, nolint verâ fide apprehendere, tunc nos non habeat repugnantes. Sed procul ambiguo mens ea Grossi haut est. Quomodo enim distinctionem inter sufficientiam & efficientiam meriti Christi Calviniani pervertant; ostendit B Par. Coll. Isag. L. de Reprob. cap. 6. §. 8. Conf quoque B. D. Fewrb. Syntag. 1 Disquis Theol. pag. 320. seqq. Licet verò ad totum genus humanum redemtio per Christum facta, quantum a. l salutis acquisitionem spectet: tamen ad Diabolos s Angelos lapsos minimè extendi ea debet, ceu patet ex Ebr. 2, 162. Petr. 2, 4. Cur verò Deus Angelis peccantibus non pepercerit, sive de Redemtore illis prospexerit, illius variae afferuntur causae, quarum nonnullas ex Patribus exhibet B Par Comment. in d. l Petrinum. Adde Flaccum Albinum Prooen. l. 3. de Trin. it. Haym. in c. 2. epist. ad Ebr. Sunt denique, qui versiculum hunc in Codd. nonnull is Graecis omissum testantur. Sed dubio procul corrupti tales Codd. sunt. Est enim versus hic genuina textûs pars. Sicuti etiam probatissimi & antiquitsimi Codd MSS. Graeci illum sistunt, que madmodum etiam Interpp. Orientales, Syrus, Arabs, Aethiops, Persa. Exponunt quoque eundem Interpp. Graeci Chrysost. Theophyl. Euthymius.)*

(v. 12. If a man has a hundred sheep. See a fuller declaration of this parable in the Analecta on Luke 15, 4. and following.)

## 18:13
(v. 13. He rejoices more over it etc. το επι in this passage is more correctly translated by because of than over, as he proves from a comparison of other passages. Corn. Bonavent. Bertramus, Lucubr. Franckth p. 107. Beda -n Comm. When he finds the sinner, he rejoices more over him, i.e., he makes his own rejoice. Compare with this exposition the Parable Luke 15, 32 But nothing stands in the way, which is less accepted concerning God himself. Thus a leader in pr-he pl-s loves that soldier more, who after flight has returned and bravely pr-mit the enemy, than him who never retreated, and never did anything bravely. Gregory, hom. 34 on the Gospels.)

More than over the ninety and nine, which went not astray. Hilary Can. 18 in Evang. The one sheep is to be understood as man: qut--n by the error of one Adam the whole human race went astray: Therefore both the one seeking man is Christ, and the ninety nine left behind, are the multitude of heavenly glory. But by the 99 sheep not erring, likewise in this place are understood men, but pious ones, i.e., those who have not fallen into more grievous s-el-ra. See Anal. on Luke 15, 7. )* *(

( God does not will that one of these little ones should perish. And he himself min-m by some absolute decree adjudged the greatest part of men to eternal destruction. For if he does not will that any should perish, it follows that he by no means wills, by some simple decree of reprobation, that the greatest part of men should perish: but rather that all should be saved. To which also the parallel sayings contribute.) 1. Timoth. 2, 4.2. Petr. 3. 9.Ioh. 3, 16. If, however, God does not will that any should perish, it follows that he does not will to give saving faith to the elect alone. This is what Piscator asserts in part 3 of the Fratern. on page 7 and following. The same man, however, objects to the present statement that Christ is speaking here about little ones who believe in him, v. 6. I reply: on the contrary, in the present verse he is speaking about the whole human race, which had perished. Compare v. 11. Furthermore, many of those who have truly believed are damned because they fall away, Luc. 8, 13. therefore, even if Christ were speaking most especially about believers alone, it does not follow that he is also speaking about the elect alone, since not all believers are elect.

Cùm invenit peccatorem, magis super eum, gaudet, i. c. suos gaudere facit. Conf. cùm hâc exposit. Parab. Luc. 15, 32 Sed nihil obstat, quae minus de ipso Deo accipiatur. Sic dux in pr-he pl-s eum militem diligit, qui post fugam conversus hostem fortiter pr-mit, quàm illū, qui nunquamt rgapr aebuit, & nunquam aliquid fonr ter fecit. Gregor hom. 34. in Evang.)*

Verùm per 99. oves non errantes itidemh l intelligunt-r homines, sed pii s. qui in graviora s-el-ra non pr--pii. Vid Anal. ad Luc. 15, 7.)*

*( non vult Deus, ut pereat unus ex parvul-s. E ipsi min-m exabsoluto quodam decreto maximam hominum partem aeterno exitio adiudicavit. Si enim non vult ut ullus pereat, sequitur, quòd haud quaquam ex simplici aliquo reprobationis decreto velit, ut maxima hominum pars pereat: sed potiùs ut omnes salvi fiant. Quo etiam faciunt dicta parall. 1. Timoth. 2, 4.2. Petr. 3. 9.Ioh. 3, 16. Si verò Deus non vult ut ullus pereat, sequitur, quòd non solis electis fidem salvificam dare velit. Id quod Piscator adserit part. 3. Fratern. pag. 7. seqq. Excipit verò idem ad dictum praesens, quòd Christus hîc loquatur de parvulis, qui in ipsum credunt v. 6.
