## 18:15
v. 15. If your brother has sinned against you. Syr. -- has acted foolishly. Up to this point Christ had spoken about those who scandalize others; now he proceeds to deal with those who are scandalized by others. In the book Musar 221: He who reproves his companion ought first to do this gently between himself and him alone with soft words, so that he does not put him to shame. If he repents, it is well; if not, he ought to reprove him sharply and put him to shame between himself and him. If he does not repent, he ought to employ companions and put him to shame before them: if not even in this way does he profit anything, he ought to put him to shame before many and publish his offense. Bernard, sermon 2 on Easter: He requires three members of the body in him who is about to correct a brother: the mind, the tongue, the hand. In the mind let there be compassion of affections, zeal of righteousness, and discretion of spirit. In the tongue let there be modesty in rebuking, abundance in exhorting, and efficacy in persuading. In the hand let there be continence in the flesh, mercy in the brother, patience in piety. Cyril, book 3 on Leviticus, col. 643, on this matter: He does not wish, (the Savior) if by chance you see the sin of your brother, to fly immediately to the public and to proclaim everywhere and divulge the sins of others: which would certainly be the act not of one correcting, but rather of one defaming. Alone, he says, between you and him, correct him. For where he who sins sees that the mystery is being kept for him, he himself will also keep the shame of amendment: but if he sees that he has been defamed, he will immediately turn to the impudence of denial: and you will not have -ded the sin, but will have doubled it. Add.

also Augustine, vol. 10, sermon 16 on the words of the Lord, col. 72. Ambrose, book 18 on Luke. Friendly correction profits more than turbulent accusation: the former strikes shame, the latter moves indignation. Concerning the degrees of admonition and ecclesiastical punishment, see B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 286. B. Dedek. in Consil. Theol. Pelagius in h. l. p. 206. Avianus Prax. Eccl. p. 74. seqq. B. D. Roenig Cas. Catech. p. 745. seqq. among the Calvinists, Camero t. 1. Praelect. p. 4. seqq. Zepperus de Polit. Eccl. l. 1. c. 16. 17. Furthermore, from the fact that the Savior says here that it is possible to sin against a man, the Photinians strive to prove that our people do not sufficiently solidly gather from the fact that Matth. 12, 31. mention is made of an irremissible sin committed against the Holy Spirit, that the Holy Spirit is true eternal God. But I respond by distinguishing between primary and secondary objects of sins; proper and improper. Properly and principally one sins only against God Ps. 51, 6. That it is indeed sinned in such a way against the Holy Spirit is evident both because that sin is called irremissible, and because that sin is graver than the sin against the Son of man. Moreover, from this passage compared with 1. Sam. 2, 25. Tit. 2, 12. it is clear that some sins are committed against God, some against a neighbor, some against ourselves. Meanwhile, by sinning against a neighbor and against oneself, one also sins against God, namely mediately and consequently.

Against thee. That is, if he has injured, offended thee, so that εις in this place is taken in the same signification as -- in the preface 1 Sam. 19, 4. Gen 42, 22. and -- 1. Sam. 19, 4. and 1. Reg. 8, 31. so thinks Lud. Capellus in Spicil. p. 27. The Savior speaks indeed of private injuries, which are inflicted upon individuals, and the remission of which is in our power, as B. D. Chemn. well observes in H. E. c 92. and is evident from the comparison Luc. 17, 3. The matter stands otherwise if someone has sinned publicly and with many conscious of it and has provided a grave scandal to others, Gal. 2, 11. likewise if someone has sinned against God, e.g., by blasphemy, or even against a neighbor and persists in sin, and there is no hope of amendment, for then the admonition of the Apostle must be observed 1. Tim 5, 20.)*

So that the Jesuit Becanus is in vain when he attempts to argue from this passage that Holy Scripture is obscure, l. 1 Man. c. 1. p 13. because the Apostle seems to contradict it 1. Tim. 5, 20. For neither does Christ prohibit that public, impenitent persons, and those persevering in their sins, of whom the Apostle's discourse is, be corrected publicly, i.e., before all. As Chrysost. rightly observes from v. 16. 17. hom. 61. in Matthew. Add August. serm. 16. de Verbis Domini: But what says the Apostle? Argue the sin before all. Sometimes therefore you should know that a brother is to be rebuked alone, but sometimes before all. If you alone know, then he sinned against you alone. But if he did you an injury with many hearing, he sinned against them also. Therefore those things which are sinned before all must be rebuked before all. But what is to be done, if someone has sinned against God, with you alone being aware? Camero answers in Myroth. p. 77. It is to fight both with prudence, and also with piety, to bring into the light those sins which lie hidden, in such a way that they cannot be brought into the light; but not, he adds, they will not be able to be brought into the light, if they were committed with you alone being aware. Thus judges are often even compelled to dismiss those whom they certainly know to be most guilty, because arguments are not available by which they may be convicted. But it does not at all fight with piety to bring into the light those sins of which I am certainly convinced, although no one else is aware of them. But how that same thing does not fight even with prudence is clear from the ventilation of the question. Whether a judge ought to judge according to acts and proofs, or indeed according to conscience. Concerning which let B. Par. L. de Magist. Polit. § 291. 292 be consulted.

You have gained your brother, both for GOD, and also for himself, so that both God may as it were recover his possession, and he himself the possession of the grace of GOD, 1. Cor. 9, 19. *(These words are to be understood not exclusively, i.e., as if the salvation of one's neighbor could not also be promoted by the other two modes of correction, but inclusively: we are said to gain a brother by private correction, because this is the first degree of love, as the second is of fear, the third of shame, as Hugo distinguishes.)*

Latin:

v. 15. Si frater tuus in te peccaverit. Syr. --stultè egerit. Hactenus dixerat Christus de illis, qui alios scandalizant, iam porrò agit de illis, qui ab aliis scandalizantur. In libro Musar 221. Qui arguit socium suum, debet primùm hoc facere placidè inter se & ipsum solum verbis mollibus, it a ut non pudefaciat eum. Si resipiscit, benè est; sin, debet eum acriter redarguere & pudefacere interse & ipsum. Si non resipiscit, debet adhibere socios, ipsumq coram illis pudore afficere: si nec hoc modo quicquam proficit, debet eum pudefacere coram multis, eiusq delictum publicare. Bernhardus serm. 2. Pasch. tria corporis membra requirit in eo, qui correpturus est fratrem: mentem, lingvam, manum. In mente sit compassio affectuum, zelus rectitudinis & discretio spiritûs. In lingvâ sit modestia in increpando, copia in exhortando, & efficacia in persuadendo. In manu sit continentia in carne, misericordia in fratre, patientia in pietate. Cyrillust. 1. l. 3 in Levit. col. 643. de h. d. Non vult (Salvator) si fortè videris peccatum fratris tui, continuò evolare ad publicum, & proclamare passim, ac divulgare aliena peccata: quod esset utiq non corrigentis, sed potiùs infamantis. Solus, inquit, inter te & ipsum corripe eum Ubi enim servari sibi mysterium viderit ille, qui peccat, servabit & ipse emendationis pudorem: si verò diffamarise viderit, illieò ad denegandi impudentiam convertetur: & non -daveris peccatum, sed & duplicaveris. Add.

quoque August. t. 10. serm. 16. de verbis Dom. col. 72. Ambros. l. 18. in Luc. Plus proficit amica correptio, quàm turbulenta accusatio: illa pudorem incutit, haec indignationem movet. De gradibus admonit. ac poenae Eccles. vid B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 286. B. Dedek. in Consil. Theol. Pelagius in h. l. p. 206. Avianus Prax. Eccl. p. 74. seqq. B. D. Roenig Cas. Catech. p. 745. seqq. ex Calvinianis Camero t. 1. Praelect. p. 4. seqq. Zepperus de Polit. Eccl. l. 1. c. 16. 17. Coeterùm ex eo, quòd hîc Salvator dicit, etiam in hominem posse peccari, evincere satagunt Photiniani, non satis solidè nostrates exinde quòd Matth. 12, 31. mentio fit peccati irremissibilis, in Sp. S. commissi, colligere, quòd Sp. S. sit verus aeternus Deus. Verùm resp disting. inter obiecta peccatorum primaria & secundaria; propria & impropria. Propriè & principaliter in solum Deum peccatur Ps. 51, 6. Quòd verò ita in Sp. S. peccetur, constat tum quia illud peccatum dicitur irremissibile, tum quia pecc. illud gravius peccato in Filium hominis. Porrò ex hoc loco collat. cum 1. Sam. 2, 25.Tit. 2, 12. patet, quòd quaedam peccata committantur contra Deum, quaedam contra proximum, quaedam contra nos ipsos. Interea peccando contra proximum ac contra seipsum etiam in Deum peccatur, nempe mediatè & consequenter.

In te. Id est, si te lae (erit, offenderit, ut ita εις h. l. eâdem accipiatur significatione, quâ -- praef. 1 Sam. 19, 4.Gen 42, 22. ac --1. Sam. 19, 4. ac 1. Reg. 8, 31. ita censet Lud. Capellus in Spicil. p. 27. Loquitur verò Salvator de privatis iniuriis, quae singulis inferuntur, & quarum remissio in nostrâ potestate est, uti benè observat B. D. Chemn. in H. E. c 92. & constat ex coll Luc. 17, 3. Secus sese res habet, si quis publicè multis que consciis peccarit ac grave aliis scandalum praebuerit, Gal. 2, 11. item si quis in Deum peccaverit, V. G. blasphemiâ, vel etiam in proximum aut in peccato perseveret, nec spes fuerit emendationis, tum enim observandū monitum Apostoli 1. Tim 5, 20.)*

Ut adeò frustra sit Iesuita Becanus, quando ex h. l. obscuritatis arguere Sc. Sacram conatur l. 1 Man. c. 1. p 13. eò quòd contrariari videatur Apostolus 1. Tim. 5, 20. Etenim nec Christus prohibet, publicos, impoenitentes & in peccatis suis perseverantes, de quibus Apostolo sermod. l. est, publicè s. coram omnibus corripi. Ut rectè ex v. 16. 17. Chrysost. hom. 61. in Matthaeum observat. Add. August. serm. 16. de Verbis Domini: Sed quid di--Apostolus? peccatum coram omnibus argue. Aliquando ergoscias corripiendum esse fratrem solum, aliquando autem coram omnibus. Si tu solus nosti, tunc in te solum peccavit. Sed si multis audientibus tibi fecit iniuriam, etiam in illos peccavit. Ergò ipsa corripienda sunt coram omnibus quae peccantur coram omnibus. Sed quid agendum, si aliquis peccaverit in Deum, te solo conscio? Respondet Camero in Myroth. p. 77. Pugnare tum cum prudentiâ, tum etiam cum pietate, ea peccata in lucem proferre, quae latent, ita ut in lucem proferri non possint; non autem, addit, non poterunt proferri in lucem, si te solo conscio admissa sunt. ItaIudices saepè etiam eos coguntur dimittere, quos certò sciunt esse nocentissimos, quia non suppetunt argumenta, quibus convincantur. Ast minimè pugnat cum pietate ea peccata in lucem proferre, de quibus certò mihi constat, licet nemo praeterea illorum conscius sit. Quomodo verò nec cum prudentia id ipsum pugnet, patet ex ventilatione quaestionis. An iudex se cundùm acta & probata, an verò secundùm conscientiam iudicare debeat. De quâ consulatur B. Par. L. de Magist. Polit. § 291. 292)*

Lucratus es fratrem tuum, tum DEO, tum etiam ipsi, ut & Deus possessionem eius quasi recuperet, & ipse possessionē gratiae DEI, 1. Cor. 9, 19. *[Intelligenda haec verba non exclusivè, h. e. quasi non etiam reliquis duobus correctionis modis, proximi salus possit promoveri, sed inclusivè: dicimur privatâ correctione lucrari fratrem, quia primus hic gradus est amoris, ficut alter timoris, tertius pudoris, uti Hugo distingvit.)*

## 18:17
v. 17. Tell the Church. By the Church are understood the Presbyters and Overseers, as appears from the following verse. *[And so also Chrysostom explains hom. 61. in Matt. and likewise Euthymius in this place.)*

*( If he will not hear the Church. It is evident from this, that the role of judge indeed belongs to the Church, but a ministerial one. For the highest and absolute judge of controversies is God alone, speaking to us through His word contained in the Holy Scriptures, as B. Par. proves at length in Coll. Isag. Book on Holy Scripture c. 15. § 2. and also in Exeg. Theol. Book on Holy Scripture § 453. Because, furthermore, the Savior was still speaking about the state of those times, some think that in this N. T. passage the word Ἐκκλησίας is used for the Jews (which opinion B. D. Ioh. Maior deduces at length in the Preface to the Judgment of Valerius Magnus on the rule of believing for non-Catholics) and indeed in one place, whereas elsewhere the Church of the O. T. always comes under the name συναγαγης.. But besides the O. T. passages Deut. 31, 30. Joshua 8, 35. Judg. 20, 2. there is also available another passage in the N. T., where the word εχηλησιας is used for the people of the O. T., namely Acts 7, 38. Furthermore, the warning of Christ is rightly observed even now. But by the name of the Church, the Roman Pontiff should by no means be understood, whose highest and authentic judge-ment in matters of faith the Papists strive in vain to prove from the present passage. Ies. Cotur--s in Epit. Controv p. 63. reasons thus: Those alone are to be heard in controversies of religion, whom Christ commanded to be heard. But such-only are the Princes of the Church, and especially the Vicar of Christ and Succes-sor of Peter. Therefore. Resp. 1. The present passage deals with any particular Church, not indeed the universal one, as Albertus Pighius book 5 of Hierarch. Eccles. c. 4 explicitly teaches, and it is sufficiently evident from the context also. If, therefore, the infallibility of the Church or of the Prelates of the Church could be proved from this place, it would follow that every particular Church, or the Prelates of any particular Church, would enjoy the gift of infallibility. Which, however, the Papists would not easily concede. See what B. Par. presents on this matter from their opinion in Confess Cathol. Book 1. Gener. p. 528. Nor is there any reason for them to say, that this belongs to the Roman Church alone, or-rather to the Roman Pontiff (for to this the final analysis of the Papists eventually aims). For whence, I ask, will the Papists prove this? Certainly not at all from this place. For the Roman, indeed the entire Latin Church, is also a particular one, according to the judgment of Alphonsus Tostatus, Pro-logue in Matt. Nor can one person be called the Church, according to the opinion of Bellarmine himself, book 3 de Eccles. c 17. near-the end. Whence neither does the Jesuit Coturius dare to arrogate that gift here to the Roman Pontiff alone. 2. It deals here with the office of the keys and ecclesiastical discipline, and thus with particular questions of fact, as is manifest from the context, and the Cardinal Bellarmine himself grants in l. 3. de V. D. c. 5. § 2. but in these matters the Papists readily concede that the Roman Pontiff is by no means immune from the danger of error. See c. à nobis exira de sent. excomm. Lombardus dist. 18. lit H. What of the fact that Bellarm. lib. 4 de P. R. c. 2. § 3. expressly writes that all Catholics agree that the Pontiff, even as Pontiff, can err with a General Council in particular controversies of fact. 3 If by Church one were to understand here Peter and his (to whom alone it is sown and measured here) fictitious successor the Roman Pontiff, then it would be the same as if Christ had said: Tell it to yourself which is utterly ridiculous. Compare more on this matter in B. Par. Confess. Cathol. T. 1. p 528. 4. We concede that to be gathered in the name of Christ can also be explained as to be gathered by the authority of Christ (see Matth. 21, 23 I-h. 5, 43. Actor 4, 7.) and therefore also that the Church gathered by his authority or the Prelates of the Church are to be heard, but only if they themselves have first heard the voice of the supreme Shepherd, sounding in the Scriptures. But if they have dared to equate, or even to prefer, their own opinions and h-man inventions to the revealed word, certainly no one except a fool would say that they are to be heard. Conf. M--h 2, 2 -um Matth. 16, 11 item Iohan. 10, 27.Matth. 28, 19. Ga-at. -, 8. and add B. Par. l. c. as well as Cameron in Myrothec. p 82. 83. it. Praelect. t. 1. p. 39. seqq. Since, however, as was warned above, by the name If by Churches in this place are understood the leaders of particular Churches, it is evident that the Papists (see Franc. Costerus in Enchir. Controv. p. 107, and Franc. Haraeus in the Scholia to this place) attempt in vain to impugn from the present statement our opinion, that the Church properly so called is a congregation of saints, and therefore invisible. For we are speaking of the Catholic Church, that is, the universal, whereas here the matter concerns particular Churches. And we distinguish furthermore between the Church by reason of calling and external profession, and the same considered by reason of internal union with Christ its head.)

*( Let him be to you as a Gentile and a Publican. Bellarmine is ridiculous when, in book 1 of De Laicis, chapter 21, he strives to prove by these words that heretics ought to be handed over to the Magistrate for the infliction of capital punishment. For if Bellarmine's consequence is legitimate, it follows also that Gentiles and Publicans ought to be handed over for capital punishment, which is nevertheless absurd. But it is well, Bellarmine himself acknowledged in the said place in the response to the 3rd argument that Christ neither commanded here, nor forbade, that heretics should be burned, and therefore nothing can be deduced from this place. Thus Franc. Haraeus, Theologian of Louvain, in the Scholia to the Vulgate Bible on this place, cites the statement of Cyprian, epistle 62: To be sure, he says, the proud and contumacious are killed by the spiritual sword, and are cast out of the Church . For they cannot live outside. Similarly, Corn. à Lapide explains it concerning excommunication in this place, warning that Chrysostom, Hilary, Augustine, the Glossa, and others explain it in this way also. Bellarmine indeed limits his opinion, that he is speaking of heretics who are disturbers of the public peace. But the houses of the holy inquisition testify to the contrary. But the passage Deut. 17, 12 seems to favor the Papists: And the man who will not obey the Priest, let him die the death. For if he who will not obey the Priest ought to die the death, how much more he who will not obey the Church, since the Church is greater than the Priest. I respond by distinguishing 1. between the time of the Old and New Testament. In the former there was greater rigor than in the New Testament. Likewise between the moral and the judicial or forensic in the Mosaic laws. Concerning which matter B. Par. discourses at length in Book on the Political Magistrate § 344345 and 346, 2. distinguishing between the causes for which obedience is denied to the Priest and .

Moses Deut. 17, 12. speaks not only of ecclesiastical and civil cases, but even of criminal ones: but the Savior deals with those things which are of common life, and in which one offends another, even by a slight injury. 3. It is to be noted that by the Priest is not understood only the Pontiff of the O.T., but the whole Sanhedrin, as being that in whose power was the absolute authority. Compare more things making for this in B. Par. Comm. in Deut. p 1031. M. Ioh Mettingerum Harmon. part. 1. p. 757. seqq. But how the primitive Church inflicted the punishment of excommunication upon the obstinate and all sinners despising public admonitions, and avoided their company, is evident in some way from Rom. 16, 17.1. Cor. 5, 11.2. Cor. 2, 6. 7.2. Thess. 2, 14.Tit. 2, 10.2. Ioh. 10. Furthermore, Bell. tries less solidly to construct from this place the opinion of the Papists, that the excommunicated, whether they have been justly or unjustly excommunicated, cease to be members of the Church. Although Christ speaks only of the justly excommunicated. That priests can sometimes err in such a case, and thus even unjustly excommunicate some, is shown by Aug. l. de vera relig c. 6. Jerome in c. 16. Matth. and others, B. Par. L. de Ec l. §. 61. nor do we deny that the unjustly excommunicated are separated from the communion of the visible and particular Church.

*( As a Gentile έθνιηαι among the LXX are those who in Heb. -- by which name in the O.T. come both peoples ignorant of God, and the Jews themselves. See Gen. 33. 13.Ios. 3, 17. Yet never in the whole Holy Scripture is one person marked with this name. Whence the Jews betray their malice as well as ignorance when they usurp this name in contempt of one Christian, just as of one Christian woman. -- while in their books -- they are accustomed to pray -- i.e. Blessed are you Jehovah God King of the world, that you have not made me a gentile, a slave, a woman. Nor does the passage Gen. 20. 4. support the error of the Jews, as is evident from the context.)*

*( And a publican. See Analecta to c. 5, 46. also c 9, 9. and add Mr. Fessel lib. 4. Advers. Sacr. c. 6. §. 20. also Cameron. Myroth. Ev in this place, and also in Praelect. T. 1. p. 32. 33.)*

Latin:

v. 17. Dic Ecclesiae. Per Ecclesiam intelliguntur Presbyteri & Praepositi, ut apparet ex vers. seq. *[Atque ita etiam Chrysostomus exponit hom. 61. in Matth. nec non Euthymius in h. l.)*

*( Si Ecclesiam non audierit. Patet hinc, quòd Ecclesiae utique iudicis partes competant, sed ministerialis. Summus enim & absolutus controversiarum iudex est solus Deus, per verbum suum in Sc. S. comprehensum ad nos loquens, ceu prolixè probat. B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. de Sc. S. c. 15. § 2. it. Exeg. L. Theol. de Sc. S. §. 453. Quia porrò de statu illorum temporum adhuc loquebatur Salvator, existimant nonnulli, quòd h. N T. loco de Iudaeis vox Ἐκκλησίας usurpetur (quam sententiam prolixè deducit B. D. Ioh. Maior in Praefat. ad Iudicium Valeriani Magni de Acathol. credendi regula) & quidem uno, alibi verò semper Ecclesia V. T. veniat nomine συναγαγης. Verùm praeter loca V. T. Deut. 31, 30. Iosuae 8, 35. Iudic. 20, 2. suppetit etiam alius adhuc in N. T. locus, ubi vox εχηλησιας de populo V. T. adhibetur, videl. Actor. 7, 38. Coeterùm rectè monitum Christi etiamnum observatur. Minimè verò nomine Ecclesiae intelligi Pontifex Romanus debet, cuius summum & authenticum in rebus fidei iudic-ū frustra è praesenti loco Papicolae probare satagunt. Ies. Cotur--s in Epit. Controv p. 63. ita ratiocinatur: Illi soli in controversiis religionis audiendi sunt, quos audire Christus iussit. Sed tal-soli sunt Principes Ecclesiae, ac potissimùm Christi Vicarius ac Succe-sor Petri. E. Resp. 1. Agitur in praesenti loco de qualibet Ecclesiâ particulari, nō verò universali, uti disertè docet Albertus Pighius lib. 5. Hierarch. Eccles. c. 4 & fatis ex contextu quoq; patet. Quod si igitur ex h. l. Ecclesiae sive Praesulum Ecclesiae infallibilitas probari posset, sequeretur, quamlibet particularem Ecclesiam, sive cuiuslibet particularis Ecclesiae Praesules infallibilitatis done gaudere. Quod tamen haut facilè Pontificii concusserint. Vide quae in hanc rem sistit ex illorum mente B. Par. Confess Cathol. L. 1. Gener. p. 528. Nec est, quòd di-ant, id soli Romanae competere Ecclesiae, vePontifici potiùs Romano (huc enim collimat tandem ultima Pontificiorum analysis.) Unde enim, qùaeso, probabunt hoc Papicolae? Sanè minimè ex h. l. Est enim Romana quoq;, imò tota Latina Ecclesia particularis, iudice Alphonso Tonstato, Pr--loq. in Matth. Nec una persona potest dici Ecclesia, iuxta ipsius Bellarmini sententiam lib. 3 de Eccles. c 17. c-rca finem. Unde nec Coturius Iesuita soli Pontifici Romano donum illud hîc arrogare audet. 2. Agitur hîc de officio clavium s. disciplina Ecclesiastica, adeoq; de quaestionibus facti particularibus, ceu ex contextmanifestum est, atq; ipse Cardinalis largitur Bellarm. l. 3. de V. D. c. 5. § 2. in iis verò Pontificem Romamanum ab erroris periculo hautquaquam immunem esse, ultrò concedunt Pontificii. Vid c. à nobis exira de sent. excomm. Lombardus dist. 18. lit H. Quid quòd Bellarm. lib. 4 de P. R. c. 2. § 3. expressè scribit convenire omnes Catholicos, posse Pontificē, etiam ut Pontificem cum Generali Concilio errare in controversiis facti particularibus. 3 Si per Ecclesiam intelligendus hîc esset Petrus eiusq (cui hîc soli seritur ac metitur) fictitius Successor P. Romanus, tunc perinde esset, ac si Christus dixisset: Dic tibi ipsi quod perquam ridiculum. Confer plura in hanc rem apud B. Par. Confess. Cathol. T. 1. p 528. 4. Concedimus, in nomine Christi congregari posse quoq exponi, autoritati Christi congregari (vid. Matth. 21, 23 I-h. 5, 43. Actor 4, 7.) adeoque etiam eius autoritate congregatam Ecclesiam sive Praesules Ecclesiae esse audiendos, sed si ipsi priùs audive-int vocem Pastoris summi, in Scriptur is sonantem. Qùod si verò propria sua placita & adinventiones h-manas verbo revelato aequare, imò & praeferre ausi fue-int, sanè nemo visi insip-enaudiendos eos esse dixerit. Conf. M--h 2, 2 -um Matth. 16, 11 item Iohan. 10, 27.Matth. 28, 19. Ga-at. -, 8. ac adde B. Par. l. c. nec non Cameronem in Myrothec. p 82. 83. it. Praelect. t. 1. p. 39. seqq. Cùm verò, ut suprà monitum, nomine Ecclesiae h. l. intelligantur particularium Ecclesiarum Praesules, patet, quòd Pontificii, (videatur Franc. Costerus in Enchir. Controv. p. 107. ac Franc. Haraeus in Scholiis ad h. l.) frustra è praesenti dicto sententiam nostram, quòd Ecclesia propriè dicta, congregatio sanctorum sit, adeoque invisibilis, impugnare conentur. Loquimur enim de Ecclesiâ Catholicâ s. universali, cùm hîc agatur de Ecclesiis particularibus. Et disting insuper inter Ecclesiam ratione vocationis & professionis externae, eandēq; ratione coniunctionis cum Christo suo capite internae consideratam.)*

*( Sit tibi velut Ethnicus & Publicanus. Ridiculus est Bellarminus, quando lib. 1. de Laic. c. 21. His verbis probare satagit, haereticos tradi Magistratui debere ad irrogandum, capitale supplicium. Etenim si Bellarmini consequentia legitima, sequitur etiam Ethnicos & Publicanos tradi ad supplicium capitale debere, quod tamen absurdum. Sed benè habet, agnovit Bell. ipse d. l. in resp. ad 3. arg. Christum nec praecipisse hîc, nec prohibuisse, ut comburerentur haeretici, ac proinde nihil ex h. l deduci posse. Sic Franc. Haraeus Theol. Lovan in Scholiis ad Bibl. Vulg. h. l. adducit dictum Cypriani ep. 62. Scilicet, inquit, spirituali gladio superbi & contumaces necantur, & de Ecclesiâ --iciuntur. Neq enim vivere foris possunt. Similiter de excommunicatione exponit Corn. à Lapide in h. l. monens, quòd Chrysostomus Hilarius, Augustinus, Glosta & alii ita quoque exponant. Limitat quidem Bell. sententiam suam, quôd loquatur de haereticis, qui sint pacis publicae turbatores. Sed sanctae inquisitiionis aedes contrarium testantur. Sed favere videtur Pontificiis locus Deut. 17, 12.Et vir, qui non obedierit Sacerdoti, morte moriatur. Etenim si is, qui non obedierit Sacerdoti, morte mori debet, quantò magis, qui Ecclesiae non obedierit, cùm Ecclesia sit maior Sacerdote. Resp dist. 1. inter tempus V. ac N. Test In illo maior rigor erat, quàm in N T. item inter morale, ac iudiciale s. forense in legibus Mosaicis. Quâ de re prolixè disserit B. Par. L. de Magist. Polit. § 344345 & 346, 2. dist. inter causas, ob quas obedientia Sacerdoti & denegatur.

Moses Deut. 17, 12. loquitur non solùm de causis Ecclesiasticis & civilibus, verùm etiam de criminalibus: at Salvator agit de iis, quae sunt vitae communis. & in quibus alter alterum offendit, eriam leviculâ iniuriâ. 3. notandum est, quòd per Sacerdotem non intelligatur solus Pontifex V. T. sed totum Synedrium, utpote penes quod fuit absolua potestas. Conf. plura huc facientia apud B. Par. Comm. in Deut. p 1031. M. Ioh Mettingerum Harmon. part. 1. p. 757. seqq Quomodo verò excommunicationis poenam pertinacibus omnesq; publicas admonitiones contemnentibus peccatoribus primitiva Ecclesia inflixerit illorumq; consortium vitarit, patet aliquo modo ex Rom. 16, 17.1. Cor. 5, 11.2. Cor. 2, 6. 7.2. Thess. 2, 14.Tit. 2, 10.2. Ioh. 10. Porrò Bell minùs solidè ex h. l. adstruere conatur sententiam Pontificiorum, quòd excommunicati, sive iustè s. iniustè fuerint excommunicati, desinant esse membra Ecclesiae. Cùm tamen Christus tantùm loquatur de iustè excommunicatis. Posse verò Sacerdotes aliquando in ta-i casuerrare, adeoque etiam iniustè aliquos excommunicare, ex August. l. de verâ relig c. 6. Hieronymo in c. 16. Matth. aliisque ostendit B. Par L. de Ec l. §. 61. nec inficias quoque imus, iniustè excommunicatos, à communione Ecclesiae visibilis & particularis separari)*

*( Velut Ethnicusέθνιηαι apud LXX sunt, qui Ebr. -- quo nomine in V. T. veniuntum populi Deum ignorantes, tum ipsi Iudaei. Vid. Gen. 33. 13.Ios. 3, 17. Nunquam tamen in tota Sc. S. una persona isthonomine insignitur. Unde suam Iudaei produnt malitiam iuxta & ignorantiam quando de uno Christiano percontemtum hoc nomen usurpant, sicuti de una foem. Christiana. -- dum in libb. suis -- orare solent -- i e. Benedictus tuiehova Deus Rex secuti, quòd non fecisti me gentilē, servum, foeminam. Nec patrocinatur Iudaeorum errori locus Gen. 20. 4. ceu ex contextu patet)*

*( Et publicanus. Vid. Analecta ad c. 5, 46. it. c 9, 9. atque adde Dn Fesselium lib. 4. Advers. Sacr. c. 6. §. 20. it. Cameron. Myroth. Ev in h. l. nec non in Praelect. T. 1. p. 32. 33.)*

## 18:18
v. 18. Whatever you shall bind upon earth &c. In previous centuries there was a double use of keys, not only in opening, but also in closing doors, just as we see here and there even now in certain temples, especially the older ones, such doors are found to be fortified with robust bolts or bars, which cannot be closed unless the key is inserted into the lock and gradually turned back. Thus Scripture attributes to Christ the key of heaven, i.e., the power of unlocking and locking it. Christ shared this power with the Apostles. *(And indeed in such a way that they not only signify to penitents that their sins are forgiven in heaven, but also actually forgive them, as the Lords Theologians of Marburg teach at length in the Fund. Deduct. p. 1045ff. Nor did Christ grant the power of forgiving sins to the Apostles alone, but also to any Christian whatsoever, with this difference, however, that the ministers of the Church forgive sins publicly and solemnly, and even to those by whom they themselves were not injured; whereas a brother's power of forgiving, i.e. of loosing, is only private, and scarcely extends beyond the person by whom he himself was offended. Cf. the Blessed Doctor Hülsemann on the Augsburg Confession, p. 332ff. Further, on the words "binding" and "loosing" see at greater length the Blessed Doctor Glassius, Rhet. S., p. 391, Cameron in the Myrothecium p. 8641, as well as vol. 1 of the Praelectiones, p. 38. As for the rest, against the Jesuit Bail, who in his Catechismus Controversiarum, tr. 3, q. 13, labors to prove papist Indulgences from this very passage, (just as also the Jesuits Cornelius à Lapide, on Matth. 16, and Pierre Coton, in his Institutiones Catholicae, l. 4, c. 7, are greatly perplexed as to how the Indulgences given by the Roman Pontiff to those who are said to be sweating in Purgatory can agree with that restriction added by Christ, Matth. 16:19, "upon earth," since those who are in Purgatory are under the earth, not upon it) — we here set against them the candid confession of Durandus of Saint-Pourçain alone, Bishop of Meaux, who flourished about the year 1320, in Bk. 4 of the Sentences, dist. 20, q. 3, where among other things he writes thus: "That which was said to Peter, Matth. 16, 'I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatsoever you shall bind,' etc., is understood of the power given to him in the forum of penance; but it does not pertain to the granting of Indulgences, as to how that is to be understood." But from the fact that the Savior here promises that whatever shall have been loosed on earth shall also be loosed in heaven, it is firmly concluded that those who are truly penitent, having received absolution from a minister of the Church, can and ought in no way to doubt the remission of their sins, and that accordingly they can be certain of their salvation. Bellarmine raises two objections. First, that no one can be certain that he has performed serious repentance. Secondly, that certainty of faith cannot be had concerning the intention of the Minister, without which the Sacrament is not perfected. Resp. As far as the former pertains, Bellarmine presupposes that there cannot be serious repentance unless there is present an enumeration of all mortal sins before the Priest, and likewise satisfaction, by which sins and the punishments of sins are compensated by certain works. But this hypothesis is false, and has no foundation anywhere in Holy Scripture: because true repentance consists rather in serious sorrow for committed sins and true faith in Christ, of which good works are the handmaids. As regards the latter, it is likewise most false that the Sacrament is not perfected, i.e., becomes void, without the intention of the minister. Although, therefore, God in Holy Scripture has not revealed to this or that person, by expressing his name, that his sins have been forgiven, it is not permitted, however, for the Papists to infer from this (see Becanus, book 1, Manual, chapter 16, page 284): therefore this cannot be believed by justifying faith, or, no one can be certain of the remission of his own sins, since there exists in this place a general promise given to the Ministers of the Church: Whatever you shall loose, etc. Add John 20:23. Thus, the divine law does not accuse this or that person specifically by expressing his name, yet the Apostle asserts Galatians 3:22 that Scripture has concluded all things under sin, so that from this, only a madman would deny that his sins are accused by the law, for the reason that his name is not specifically expressed in Holy Scripture. Just as, however, the defect of the intention of the Minister hinders nothing, so that a man who is seriously penitent is truly absolved, and thus can be certain of the remission of his sins: so it is not to be thought that the Savior, through the particle Whatever, conferred upon the Ministers of the Church an absolute and ἀυτοκρατορικὴν power: nay rather, it is ministerial, and restricted to the commands of the Lord, so that they ought and can remit sins only to the penitent, but retain the same for the impenitent. Whence Gregory the Great rightly says, Homily 26 on the Gospel: Then the absolution of the one present is true, when it follows the judgment of the eternal judge, etc., and Lombard, book 4, Sentences, distinction 18, section 4: Then the sentence of the Priest is approved by the judgment of GOD, when it proceeds so that the merits of those whom he absolves or excommunicates do not contradict it. Let Isidore of Pelusium also be consulted entirely, eruditely treating these very things also, book 3, epistle 260. The same also, book 2, epistle 5, in many teaches what great dignity it is that the Savior conferred upon his disciples, both by admitting them to familiar conversation and by conferring upon them the power of remitting sins. Finally, this also is to be noted, that less firmly from the collation Matth. 23, 24 with Matth. 16, 19. Bellarmine, book 4, on the Roman Pontiff, chapter 16, gathers that by the binding key Matth. c. 16, 19. is understood the power of making laws throughout the whole Church. For 1. if the word to bind c. 16, 19. has that force, it must be shown that it does not retain the same c. 18, 18. But not even the Papists themselves concede that any ministers of the Church have such power. 2. It does not follow, Matth. 23, 4. the word to bind signifies to make a law. Therefore, it also denotes the same Matth. 16, 19. 3. Nor is the question about any power of making laws, but about the power of making such laws to which the whole Church might be bound. 4. What kind of power is indicated by the word binding here and Matth. 16, 19. is sufficiently clear from parallel passages Luc. 24, 27. Ioh. 20, 23. 5. Some add that they are distinct words δεσμωρ, Matth. 23, 4. and ςέω c. 16, 19 and in this place, and therefore they do not always denote one and the same thing.

*( They shall be bound also in heaven. How ineptly some seek the foundation of the monarchical Papal power in the plural number οὐρανοῖς Matth 16, 19. is shown in the same place. Franciscus Haraeus, a Louvain theologian, acknowledges the weakness, writing thus on this place: Origen indeed in this place notes this also specially: He did not say, he says, in the heavens, as he said to Peter, but in one heaven, because they are not of such perfection as Peter. He adds: Thus indeed Origen. Hilary however and others seem to confound heaven and heavens, or to hold them for the same. But it is clear from this place the gravity of excommunication, about which D. Pelargus has gathered many things in this place p. 206, add D. Calixt. Concord. Ev. book 5, pages 238, 239.)*

Latin:

v. 18. Quaecunq alligaveritis super terram &c. Superioribus seculis erat duplex usus clavium, non solùm in aperiendis, verùm etiam in occludendis foribus, quemadmodum videmus passim etiamnum in templis quibusdam, praesertim vetustioribus, huiusmodi ianuas robustis obicibus aut repagulis communitas inveniri, quae nisi clave in seram immissa & sensim reductâ claudi nequeant. Sic Scriptura clavem coeli i e. eius reserandi & occludendi potestatem Christo tribuit. Es. 22, 22.Apoc. 3, 7. Christus eam Apostolis communicavit. *(Et quidem ita, ut non solùm poenitentibus significent, peccata eorum in coelis remissa esse, sed etiam, ut realiter remittant, ceu prolixè docent Dnn. Theologi Marpurg. in Fund. Deduct. p. 1045. seqq. Neque Apostolis solùm, sed etiam cuivis Christiano potestatē remittendi peccata Christus concedit, hâc tamen differentiâ, quòd ministri Ecclesiae publicè & solenniter peccata remittant, ac illis etiam. à quibus ipsi non fuerunt laesi: fratris verò potestas remittendi s. solvendi sit saltem privata, ac ferè non ultra illum, à quo fuit offensus, se extendat. Conf. B. D. Huelsem. in A. C. p. 332. seqq. Porrò de verbis ligandi & solvendi pluribus vid. B. D. Glass. Rhe-. S p 391. Camero in Myroth. p. 8641. nec non t. 1. l. Praelect. p. 38. Coeterùm Iesuitae Bailio, qui in Catech. Controv. tr. 3. q. 13. Indulgentias -apisticas è praesenti loco probare satagit, (quemadmodum etiam Iesuitis, Corn. à Lapide ad c. 16. Matth. ac Petro Cotono Instit. Cath l. 4. c. 7. valdè anxiis, quomodo Indulgentiae iis, qui in Purgatorio sudare dicuntur, à P. R datae conveniant cum restrictione illâ à Christo additâ Matth. 16, 19.super terram, eùm qui in Purgatorio sunt, sub terra sint, non super terram) opponimus hîc solius Durandi de S. Portiano, Episcopi Meldensis. qui floruit circa A. 1320. ingenuam confessionem in 4. Sent. dist 20. q. 3 ubi inter alia ita: Quod dictum est PetroMatth. 16. Tibi dabo claves regni coelorum, & quodcunque ligaveris &c. Intelligitur de potestate ei data in foro poenitentiae, de colla--one autem Indulgentiarum non est, quomodo debeat intelligi. Ex eo verò quòd Salvator promittit hîc, quòd quicquid in terris fuerit solutum etiam in coelo solutum esse debeat, firmiter colligitur, quòd verè poenitentes acceptâ à Ministro Ecclesiae absolutione, de peccatorum remissione nullatenus dubitare s. possint s. debeant. quòdque adeò de salute suâ possint esse certi. Dupliciter excipit Bellarminus. Primò, neminem posse esse certum, quòd seriam ege-poenitentiam. Secundò non posse haberi certitudinem fidei de intentione Ministri, sine quâ non perficiatur Sacramentum. Resp. quod prius attinet, prae supponit Bellarminus, non posse esse seriam poenitentiam, nisi adsit omnium peccatorum mortalium coram Sacer-ote enumeratio, itemq satisfactio, quâ certis operibus peccata & peccatorum poenae compensentur. Sed hypothesis haec falsa est, nec ullibi in Sc. S. habet fundamentum: quia consistit potiùs vera poenitentia in serio de admissis peccatis dolore ac vera in Christum side, cuius pedissequae sunt B. O. Quod spectat posterius, itidem falsissimum est, quòd Sacramentum non perficiatur h. e. irritum fit sine intentione ministri. Licet igitur Deus in Scriptura S. non revelaverit huic aut isti, nomen eius exprimendo, quòd peccatae ipsi sint remissa, non tamen inferre hinc Pontificiis, (vid. Becanus l. 1. Man. c. 16 p. 284) licet: ergò non potest hoc credi fide iustifica-te, sive E. nemo de peccatorum suorum remissione potest esse certus, cùm extet h. l. generalis promissio Ecclesiae Ministris data: Quodcunq solveritis &c. Adde Ioh. 20, 23. Sic lex divina non in specie hunc vel illum accusat, nomen eius exprimendo, tamen adserit Apostolus Gal. 3, 22. quòd Scriptura omnia concluserit sub peccatum, ut hinc non nisi insanus neget, peccata sua à lege accusari, eò quòd nomē eius in specie non exprimatur in Sc. Sacrâ. Quemadmodum verò defectus intentionis Ministri nil impedit, quò minùs homo seriò poenitens verè absolvatur, adeoque de peccatorum suorum remissione certus esse queat: ita nec existimandum est, quòd Salvator per particulam Quaecunque Ministris Ecclesiae absolutam & ἀυτοκρατορικὴνpotestatem contulerit: imò potiùs ministerialis illa est, & ad Domini mandata restricta, ita ut non nisi poenitentibus peccata remittere, impoenitentibus verò eadem retinere debeant possintque. Unde rectè Gregorius M. hom. 26 in Evang. Tunc vera est absolutio praesentis, cùm aeterni arbitrium sequitur iudicis &c. ac Lombardus l. 4. sent. dist. 18. sect. 4. Tunc sententia Sacerdotis approbatur DEI iudicio, cùm i-procedit, ut corum quos absolvit, vel excommunicat, merit a non contradicant. Videatur omninò quoque Isidorus Pelusiota, eruditè haec ipsa quoque pertractans lib. 3. ep. 260 Idem etiam lib. 2 ep. 5. multis docet, quanta dignitas sit, quam Salvator in discipulos suos, tum ad colloquium familiare eos admittendo, tum potestatem peccata remittendi illis conferendo, contulit. Deniq; & hoc notandum, quòd minùs firmiter ex collatione Matth. 23, 24 cum Matth. 16, 19. colligat Bell. l. 4. de P. R. c. 16. quòd per clavem ligantemMatth. c. 16, 19. intelligatur potestas ferendi leges per universam Ecclesiam. Etenim 1. si verbum ligarec. 16, 19. istam habet vim, ostendendum est, quòd non eandem retineat c. 18, 18. Ast nec ipsi Pontificii concedunt, quòd quilibet ministri Ecclesiae talem habeant potestatem. 2. non sequitur, Matth, 23, 4. verbum lig are significat legem ferre. E. etiam idem notat Matth. 16, 19. 3. Nec quaestio est de quacunque potestate ferendi leges, sed de potestate ferendi tales leges, ad quas tota Ecclesia sit adstricta. 4. Qualis potestas verbo ligandi hîc & Matth. 16, 19. indicetur, satis patet ex locis parall. Luc. 24, 27.Ioh. 20, 23. 5. nonnulli addunt, quòd sint distincta verba δεσμωρ,Matth. 23, 4. & ςέωc. 16, 19 ac h. l., adeoque non unum semper idemque notent.)*

*( Erunt ligata & in coelo. Quàm ineptè nonnulli monarchicae potestatis Papalis fundamentum quaerant in plurali numero οὐρανοῖςMatth 16, 19. ibid. ostensum. Agnoscit infirmitatem Franc. Haraeus Theologus Lovaniensis, ita in h. l. scribens: Origenes quidem h. l. istud etiam specialiter notat: Non dixit, inquit, in coelis, sicut dixit Petro, sed in coelo uno, quia non sunt tantae perfectionis, sicut Petrus. Addit: it a quidem Origenes. Hilarius tamen & alii videntur coelo & coelis confundere, seupro iisdem habere. Patet verò ex h. l. iustae excommunicationis gravitas, de quâ multa congessit D. Pelargus in h. l. p 206, add. D. Calixt. Concord. Ev. l. 5. pag. 238. 239.)*

## 18:19
*(v. 19. πάλιν. in this place denotes the same as furthermore. Compare concerning the various signification of this diction in Holy Scripture Mr. Dilherr, Vol. 1, Academic Disputations, likewise Cameron in Myrothecium, page 86, 87. Ineptly, however, from the fact that in certain Greek Codices, which the Arab also follows, for πάλιν, is read Ἀμὴν,, Morinus gathers a corruption of the authentic text. When he ought to distinguish between corruption of the text, and a variant reading.)*

*( Αέγω ὑμῖν i.e., certainly and as having divine authority, I promise to you. See the notes to Marc 2, 11.)*

If two etc. Rabbi Hanina son of Theradion in the book Aboth ch. 3. Where two sit conferring about the words of the law, there the divinity dwells among them. *(Moreover, one must be careful lest these words of Christ be accepted in such a way, as disjunctive prayers are otherwise accustomed to be accepted, so that one is posited and the other destroyed. Concerning which matter see Lord Dr. Danhaver in Idea boni Interpr. p. 119. But the Anabaptists and Ochino basely abuse this passage to break the force of our argument, which we draw from Matt. 19, 5. against polygamy. The Anabaptists therefore urge that if in this passage by the word two it is not prohibited that it be permitted for more to agree on the same thing, neither is it prohibited by the same word in Matt. 19, 5. that more be joined into one flesh, and thus one man can take more wives. Resp. The word two is accepted either inclusively or exclusively. In the former way it is accepted in this place, as is evident from the context, for it is expressly added, or three. But in the latter way it is taken in Matt. 19, 5 just as it is likewise manifest from the context there, and also from the parallel passages Matt. 5, 32.c. 19, 9.Rom. 7, 2. 3.1. Cor. 7, 4.39.1. Tim. 3, 2. Titus 1, 7. Conf. Blessed Dr. Tarnovius on Marriage p. 644. B. Par. L. on Marriage §. 207.)*

*( Concerning every thing, which they shall ask, it shall be done for them by the Father etc. See those things which were noted above at chapter 7, 7. 8. and especially Conf. 1. John 5, 14. & James 4, 3.)*

Latin:

*(v. 19. πάλιν. h. l. idem notat, quod praeterea. Conf. de variâ dictionis huius in Sc. S. significatione Dn. Dilherrum T. 1. Disp. Acad. it. Cameronem in Myroth. E. p. 86. 87. Ineptè verò ex eo, quòd in quibusdam Codd. Graecis, quos etiam Arabs sequitur, pro πάλιν, legitur Ἀμὴν, colligit Morinus corruptionem textûs authentici. Cùm distingvere deberet inter textûs corruptionem, & variantem lectionem.)*

*( Αέγω ὑμῖν i. e. certò ac tanquam divinam habens autoritatem vobis pollice or. Vid. notata ad Marc 2, 11.)*

Si duo &c. R. Hanina filius Theradionis in libro Aboth c. 3. Ubi duo sedent conferentes de verbis legis, ibi divinit as moratur inter eos. *(Coeterùm cavendum, ne haec verba Christi ita accipiantur, ceu disiunctivae aliàs orationes accipi solent, ita ut unum ponatur, alterum destruatur. Quâ de re vide Dn. D. Danhaverum in Ideâ boni Interpr. p. 119. Turpiter verò hôc loco abutuntur Anabaptistae & Ochinus ad infringendam vim nostri argumenti, quod depromimus ex Matth. 19, 5. contra polygamiam. Urgent proinde Anabaptistae, si hoc loco per vocem duo non prohibetur, quò minùs pluribus consentire in idem liceat, nec Matth. 19, 5. eadem voce prohiberi, quò minùs plures in unam carnem coniungantur, adeoque unus vir plures ducere uxores possit. Resp. Vocabulum duo accipitur vel inclusivè, vel exclusivè. Priori modo accipitur h. l. ceu ex contextu patet, expressè enim additur, veltres. Posteriori verò modo sumitur Matth. 19, 5 prout itidem ex contextu ibi manifestum est, tum quoque ex locis parallelis Matth. 5, 32.c. 19, 9.Rom. 7, 2. 3.1. Cor. 7, 4.39.1. Tim. 3, 2. Titum 1, 7. Conf. B. D. Tarnovium de Coniug. p. 644. B. Par. L. de Coniug. §. 207.)*

*( De omni re, quam petierint, fiet illis à Patre &c. Vid. quae notata suprà ad cap. 7, 7. 8. ac cumprimis Conf. 1. Ioh. 5 14. & Iacobi 4, 3.)*

## 18:20
v. 20. In my name. The connection is such. If two agreeing in prayers obtain what they ask, how much more will that which the Church does be ratified before GOD. To be gathered in the name of Christ, is to be gathered by his command and for his glory. To subject oneself to the word of Christ, to admit the governance of the Spirit of Christ. *(It is otherwise accustomed to be proved from this passage by the Orthodox, that the pure preaching of the word is a mark of the Church, since Christ in this passage promises that if two or three shall have been gathered in his name, i.e., according to his word (See John 10, 27.c. 14,24,23.) he wishes to be in their midst. Whoever therefore hear the word of Christ, they are gathered in his name and are the true Church; but those who do not hear the word of Christ, are not gathered in his name, and thus are not the true Church either.)*

*( In my name. See the notes above at c. 6, 9. and Cameron in Myroth. page 89. But where they do not agree in the name of Christ, but for perpetrating crimes or defending errors. then the Savior is very far from them by his gracious presence, Prov. 15, 29.)*.

*( I am there. The omnipresence of Christ according to his human nature is proved from this place. For Christ speaks here θεανθραπος, and promises his gracious presence, but if he were present to us only according to his divine nature, then he would be present to us according to that nature, according to which he is a consuming fire: Nay rather, he is present to us also according to that nature, by reason of which he is our brother. For he wishes to be in our midst, who is the Son of man and the good Shepherd, who came to save what had perished. Conf. Eph. 3. The Calvinists object, (see Barth. Keckermannus l. 1. Syst. Log. c. 20. 22. l. 3. Syst. Theol c 2. p. 318. Marcus Fried. Wendelinus Exerc. 55. §. 9.) by denying, that the consequence from the whole of Christ to the whole of Christ is necessary It does not follow, writes Keckermannus in the said place, the whole man understands. Therefore also the belly. Thus also it cannot be inferred: The whole Christ is omnipresent. Therefore also his human nature. But it must be known, that there is a distinction between actions, passions, and affections, and between presence. Regarding the former, it is conceded that the consequence from the whole to its individual parts is not valid, and such is the inference of Keckermannus concerning the man understanding. (And to this pertains the most useful admonition of the F. C. page 770. seqq. which the Lords Theologians of Saxony declare at length in the Apol. Tubing. page 782 seqq.) But he does not rightly infer from this a denial of presence, for I rightly say, the man is present. Therefore as to body and soul he is present. The reason is because the parts as such, always are and remain united with the whole. Since therefore the human nature after the union has been made is as it were a part ροῦ λόγου, it is a consequence, that wherever λο γος is ἔνσαρκος, there also is the assumed human nature. But it must be well noted, that our discourse is about λόγω ἐνσάρκω, not ασωρηῳ, for the human nature assumed is not a part of this, but as it were a part of that. Whence our opinion is in no way hindered by the passage Ioh. 8, 55 inasmuch as in it the subject is λόγῳ ασάοκῳ. But Wendelinus explains otherwise in the said place; and exclaims, that our own people that consequence from the whole Christ ἀνσάρκῳ regarding the whole, of Christ, they acknowledge there to be none, as long as they deny, indeed, that Christ in the state of Exinanition according to his human nature, was present without distance and by substantial proximity to all creatures in place and ποῦ, and yet they do not concede, λόγον that he was anywhere ἄςαρκον to avoid the heresy of Nestorius. They are stuck here, exclaims the vain victor, and Wendelin, a dreamer of some victory or other reported by the Orthodox, between the sacred and the stone: most unhappily this first and general attack indeed, has yielded. We respond. Even if Christ according to his human nature in the state of exinanition was not present to all creatures, nothing nevertheless can be concluded from this against our opinion, since we, when we say that Christ according to his human nature is omnipresent, speak of him, considered in the state of exaltation. For one must accurately distinguish between χρῆσιν and κτησιν of the divine idioms. Regarding which distinction, one must see above all the Saxon Theologians in the Apol. Decis. against the Tubingensians p. 677. and 680. who also in the same place p. 723. and following, rightly warn, that the personal union is indeed to be held as a foundation for the omnipresence of Christ according to the flesh among creatures, but not as the sole or unique one. They prove: For the real omnipresence of Christ is joined with the government of the whole universe: which real, continuous, and incessant government, has as its foundation not only ἔνωσιν, but also that which, after the completion of the state of κενώσεως followed, ὑπερύψωσιν, as shown in its place from Eph. ch. 1, and 4. It is not difficult to judge the rest of W.'s exceptions from what has been said, and an opportunity will be given to examine them more lengthily elsewhere. Meanwhile, let the Saxon Theologians in the aforementioned Apol. passim, B. D. Chemnitius in the book on the two natures in Christ ch. 30 p. 186, B. Ioh. Schroterus in the Royal Scepter of Christ book 5 ch. 1, B. Par. Exeg. L. on Christ §. 219, who discuss more copiously the present and parallel passage ch. 28, 20, be unrolled. Furthermore, with almost the same battering ram that Wendelin uses, Amandus Polanus in Synt. Theol. and from him Ioh. Georg. Grossius in Theatr. Bibl. on this passage have long since attempted to undermine our opinion; where he also maliciously writes that some of our people, while they teach the omnipresence of the man Christ, did not hesitate to write, that the body of Christ fills all places, all beer mugs, all the leaves of trees, even (may God forgive the one reporting these blasphemous words)

sewers. But who of our people has ever spoken in this way? This is a consequence of the Calvinists, which they strive quite ineptly to elicit from our doctrine. But this consequence is inept. The body of Christ is wherever λόγος is. Therefore, it is also in the sewers. The Lord rebuke you, Satan!

Do the Calvinists dare to think and speak so blasphemously about λόγω;? Our own opinion, however, is this: that after the exaltation λογος he is never outside the flesh, nor is the flesh outside λόγον,, and thus he is omnipresent, not locally, but illocally. The things which the Adversaries are accustomed to oppose to the omnipresence of Christ elsewhere, especially the ascension into the heavens, the return to judgment, etc., are discussed elsewhere. In this place, at least, it must be noted that from the negation of a certain mode of presence, the consequence does not hold for denying another mode of presence, or an omnipresence of every kind. Otherwise, the omnipresence of GOD himself would have to be denied, from 1 Kings 19:11 Exodus 33:3 John 14:23. But Polanus urges in his Syntagma, and with him Grossius in this place, p. 950, that the Fathers from this place prove that Christ is the true God. I reply: we do not oppose this. But what follows from that? It is certainly so far from hindering our opinion that it rather confirms it. For unless Christ in the unity of his person were at once God and man, and thus essentially omnipresent according to his divine nature, he could not have personally communicated the glory of omnipresence to the assumed human nature, since the foundation of the omnipresence communicated to the human nature is that it itself subsists in the infinite ὺποςάσει τοο λόγου and has been raised to the right hand of GOD. The Jesuit Conzen, at this place, q. 2, p. 356, opposes our opinion, which he calls an absurd error, this, that it is a matter here of a singular presence, by which he is so present to the pious and concordant that he is not present to the impious and dissenting. But indeed, he subsumes, if he is everywhere by the mass of his body, that is, omnipresent, and the words of Christ are to be understood concerning that presence, he is present even to the impious, the Gentiles, and the publicans. I reply: It is less correct that a gracious presence is opposed to a glorious or majestic one, that is, a presence, as they call it, of power. Since the former rather presupposes the latter. Therefore, just as from the fact that God promises to the pious that he wishes to be graciously present to them, but threatens the impious that he wishes to withdraw from them, it should by no means be inferred that he is not omnipresent, so neither from the fact that Christ wishes to be graciously present to the pious alone, should it be collected, nor can it be, that he will not be omnipresent to the rest: otherwise it would follow that he himself is not omnipresent even according to his divine nature, since he is not present to the impious by his grace. The same Jesuit opposes our opinion with the sayings of Augustine in his epistle to Dardanus and tractate 50, and likewise Cyril, book 6 on John, chapter 14, and book 9, chapter 21. But those things confirm our opinion rather than destroy it. For the Fathers speak of a carnal and visible presence, which they deny, which we also do. See entirely the Blessed Doctor Chemnitz, Harm. Evang. ch. 92, p. 1009, especially in his golden little book on the two natures in Christ, chapter 30. Add Dunning, Theol. Sax. in Def. Fundam. Pupill--p. 379, following, and p. 648, 649. The Blessed Doctor Kessler in Refut. Belli Ubiq. Foereri, book 2, section 2, chapters 6 and 7. Blessed Pareus, Confess. Cath. book 2, special part 1, p. 376, following. Lord Doctor Walther, Cent. Miscell. Theol. p. 457, following, and 451, following, in Quadrag. Miscell. Theol. p. 608, 609. Blessed Doctor Tarnov, de SS Trinit. p. 8, 6, 857, 858. But however easily we may argue that Christ is by no means visibly present to us, so that he can be consulted and met face to face: it by no means follows from this, That it was fitting that, departing into the heavens, He should appoint a Vicar, namely the Roman Pontiff, as the Jesuit Costerus reasons, whose absurdities B. D. Grawerust has quite clearly exposed. 1. Dispp. Anti Iesuit. page 504. It is sufficient for the Church that Christ first left the Holy Scripture, which is a lamp to our feet. Secondly, that He ordained the ministry of the word, and gave to the Church teachers and pastors. Thirdly, neither can the Roman Pontiff always be met by everyone, nor do the Roman Pontiffs themselves sufficiently agree among themselves.

Or three, -bi I am in the midst of them. Jerome in this place, Ambrose book 7 on Luke ch. 13 explain it thus: When these three, body, soul, and spirit are united through virtues to pray, I am in the middle between -lla. (Moreover το έηειεμιμινμέσω αυτων. there seems to be a pleonasm in these. But Camero notes in Myroth. Ev. p. 90, that although το έν μέσω often signifies at least the same as to be present, conf. Gen. 23, 6.Ezech. 1, 1.2. Cor. 6, 17. yet by the phrase of Scripture he is also said to be in the midst, who is over, or presides over the rest, as Ps. 82, 1 and so this place is also to be accepted. Furthermore, the Jesuit Tirinus in this place explains it thus: in the midst of them i.e. among them, working from within in them, a-sisting from without, cooperating, directing, so that they may infallibly obtain that for the sake of which they have gathered. He adds: Who therefore can henceforth doubt concerning the infallible authority of a full and legitimate Council? Corn. à Lapide, Maldonatus, and other Jesuits have similar things in this place, just as also Bellarmine book 2 de Concil. cap. 2, and likewise Alphonsus de Castro book adv. haeres. under the word Council. Resp. These words pertain to any believers and Christians whatsoever: since the Apostles here --strained their person, as the Jesuit Corn. à Lap. himself rightly observes. But the Savior is dealing with the hearing of prayers, not with the privilege of infallibility. For if this were being dealt with, it would follow that even two or three gathered in the name of Christ, whoever they might be, whether laymen or clerics, could fabricate an infallible decree concerning controversial articles of faith, which however the Papists do not concede, as they expressly profess that even particular or provincial Councils (where however not two or three, but twenty, thirty, and more Bishops are gathered) can err, as Alph. de Castro himself confesses in the same book, who also in book 1, ch. 8, expressly writes, provincial Councils can err in faith, just as it has been found that many such Councils have erred. But Maldonatus objects that particular Councils erred for the reason that they were not gathered in the name of Christ. Where however they were gathered in the name of Christ, he denies that they can err. What then is it for them to be gathered in the name of Christ? To gather by the authority of Christ. Well. He adds: then ei-they gather by authority, when they are convoked and confirmed by the authority of the Roman Pontiff, his vicar. Conzen has twin things in this place p. 354. But what if it has been shown that even then Councils have erred? That sans quite clearly teaches Cardinal Baronius A. 897, dealing with the Conventicle of Bishops, Presbyters, and Cardinals, collected by the Roman Pontiff Stephen. What if they almost unanimously concede that Councils, even those gathered by the Pontiff, can err in questions of fact, and Bellarmine deems that this is placed beyond the hazard of doubt, book 2 -Concil. c. 7. §. Resp. primò. it. c. 8. §. Respondeo quaedam. But if indeed Councils can err in questions of fact, e-even those gathered by the Roman Pontiff, it follows that the authority of the Pontiff gathering them does not render the Councils infallible. Or the reason for the diversity must be shown from the bowels of the text, i.e., that the Savior [intended] an infallible

judgment to a Council, gathered by the authority of the Roman Pontiff, he promised in questions of faith, but not equally so in questions of fact. It is truly a wonder that none of the ancient Doctors of the Church who explained this passage, that interpretation, that To gather in the name of Christ should be to gather by the authority of the Roman Pontiff, as it has supplied to miserable mortals. Truly, this happiness was reserved for the Jesuits, the defenders of the Papal see. It must be known, however, that this perversion of the text does not please all the Jesuits themselves: for the Jesuit Alphonsus Salmeron of Toledo, (whom his associate Ant. Possevinus in his Sacred Appendix commemorates as being adorned with great gifts from God, and as having performed the office of Theologian sent by Pius IV to the Council of Trent) expressly denies that this passage deals with Councils, and thus he by no means accepts τὸ to be gathered in the name of Christ as meaning that which is to be gathered by the authority of the Roman Pontiff. His words in vol. 4, Op. tr. 10, part 3, p. 462, are as follows: Christ prescribed nothing here concerning the celebration of Councils, but commends to us the pious consensus of Christian unity and the common efficacy of the prayer of the faithful. He cites the passage in good faith, B. Par. t. 1. C. C. p. 518, and compares similar things from Nic. de Clemangis and Stapleton. Perhaps the Jesuit Maldonatus was not ignorant of this, whence he writes thus on this passage: This testimony is accustomed to be brought forward to prove the authority of Councils, which not only heretics, but even some Catholics deny can be done, because it was a matter of prayer, not of the power of decreeing, etc. Although these may be ingenious men, yet they do not seem to perceive the force of the argument. Thus, forsooth, no one of the ancient Doctors, nor even his own associates, who nevertheless desire to be considered the most acute of mortals, could grasp the force of the Jesuitical argument. Let the prudent reader consider, however, how alien to the present text is the sense which the Jesuits Corn. à Lapide, Maldonatus, etc., attach to it, namely that to be gathered in the name of Christ is the same as to be gathered by the authority of the Roman Pontiff, and conversely, that those who are not gathered by the authority of the Roman Pontiff are not gathered in the name of Christ. Perhaps hereafter to those new interpreters of Holy Scripture, to ask for something in the name of Christ, Ioh. 16, 23. will sound the same as to ask by the authority of the Roman Pontiff, and to be baptized in the name of Christ, or of the Son of God, Matth. 28, 29. will infallibly have this sense, to be baptized by the authority of the Roman Pontiff, and it will thus be necessary that those who desire to become heirs of eternal life will soon be baptized only by the authority of the Roman Pontiff, nor will baptism administered by the ministers of our Church be considered valid any longer among the Papists, for the reason that it was not conferred by the authority of the Roman Pontiff. Furthermore, our theologians have shown the weakness of the Jesuitical argument in more detail. See Mr. Dr. Calovius p. 884 of the Critici Sacri, B. Par. Confess. Cathol. l. 1. General part 2, c. 10, p. 515.)*

Latin:

v. 20. In nomine meo. Connexio talis est. Si duo in precibus consentientes impetrant, quod petunt, quanto magis coram DEO ratum erit, quod Ecclesia agit. In nomine Christi congregari, est ipsius mandato & in gloriam ipsius congregari. Subiicere se verbo Christi, admittere gubernationem Spiritûs Christi. *(Solet aliàs ex h l. ab Orthodoxis probari, quòd pura verbi praedicatio sit nota Ecclesiae, cùm Christus h. l. promittat, quòd si duo vel tres fuerint congregati in ipsius nomine h. e. secundum verbum eius (Vid. Ioh. 10, 27.c. 14,24,23.) velit esse in medio eorum. Quicunque igitur Christi verbum audiunt, illi congregantur in nomine eius & sunt vera Ecclesia; qui verò non au-iunt verbum Christi, non congreg. in eius nomine, adeoque nec vera Ecclesia sunt.)*

*( In nomine meo. Vid. notata suprà ad c. 6, 9. it Cameronem in Myroth. pag. 89. Ubi verò non conveniunt in nomine Christi, sed ad flagitia perpetranda vel errores defendendos. tunc Salvator gratiosâ suâ praesentiâ longissimè ab iis abest, Prov. 15, 29.)*.

*( Ibi sum. Probatur ex h. l. omnipraesentia Christi secundùm humanam naturam. Loquitur enim hîc Christus θεανθραπος, promittit praesentiam suam gratiosam, iam verò si tantùm secundùm divinam naturam nobis praesens esset, tunc iuxta eam naturam nobis praesens esset, iuxta quam est ignis consumens: Imò potiùs iuxta eam etiam naturam nobis praesens est, ratione cuius est noster frater. Ille enim vult esse in medio nostri, qui est Filius hominis & Pastor bonus, qui venit servare quod perierat Conf. Eph. 3. Excipiunt Calviniani, (videantur Barth. Keckermannus l. 1. Syst. Log. c. 20. 22. l. 3. Syst. Theol c 2. p. 318. Marcus Fried. Wendelinus Exerc. 55. §. 9.) negando, à tote Christi ad totum Christi consequentiam esse necessariam Unon sequitur, scribit Keckermannus d. l. totus homo intelligit. E. & venter. Ita quoq inferri nequit: Totus Christus est omnipraesens. E. etiam natura ipsius humana. Verùm sciendum, quòd dist. sit inter actiones, passiones, atq affectiones, & inter praesentiam Quoad illas conceditur, quòd non valeat consequentia à toto ad singulas eius partes, & talis est illatio Keckermanni de homine intelligente. (Atque huc pertinet utilissima admonitio F. C pag; 770. seqq. quam prolixè declarant Dnn. Theol. Sax. in Apol. Tubing. pag. 782 seqq) Sed non rectè hinc infert negationem praesentiae rectè enim dico, homo est praesens. E. quoad corpus & animam prae-ens est. Ratio est quia partes ut tales, semper sunt ac manent cum toto unitae. Cùm igitur humana natura post factam unio-em sit quasi pars ροῦ λόγου, consequens est, quòd ubicunq; λο γος est ἔνσαρκος, ibi quoque sit humana natura adsumta. Probè verò notandum est, quòd sermo nobis sit de λόγω ἐνσάρκω, non ασωρηῳ, neque enim huius, sed illius pars quasi est humana natura ad-u--ta. Unde minimè nostrae s-ntentiae obstat locus Ioh. 8, 55 utpote in quo agitur de λόγῳ ασάοκῳ. Verùm aliter ex---it Wendelinus d. l; & exclamat, quòd ipsi nostrates consequentiam istam, à toto Christo ἀνσάρκῳ ad totum, Christi, nullam esse agnoscant, quamdiu nempe negant, Christum in statu Exinanitionis secundùm naturam humanam, indistanter & propinquitate substantiali omnibus creaturis adfuisse loco &ποῦ,& tamen non concedunt,λόγονalicubi fuisseἄςαρκονad evit andam Nestorii haeresin. H--rent hîc, exclamat vanus triumphator, & nescio cuius ab Orthodoxis reportatae victoriae somniator Wendelinus, inter sacrum & saxum: infelicissimè primus hic impetus & generalis quidem, cessit Respondemus. Etsi Christus secundùm humanam naturam in statu exinanitionis non fuit omnibus creaturis praesens, nihil tamen hinc concludi contra nostram sententiam potest, cùm nos, quando Christum secundùm H. N. omnipraesentē esse dicimus, loquamur de ipso, in statu exaltationis considerato. Etenim accuratè disting. inter χρῆσιν & κτησιν idiomatum divinorum. quâ de distinct. cumprimis videndi Dnn. Theologi Saxonici in Apol. Decis. adv. Tubingenses p. 677. & 680. qui etiam l. c. p. 723. & seqq. rectè monent, quòd omnipraesentiae Christi secundùm carnem apud creatur as unio personalis pro fundamento quidem so--do, sed non solitario vel unico habenda sit. Probant: Omnipraesentiae -nim Christi realis cum regimine totius universi est coniuncta: quod Regimen reale, continuū & incessans, fundamenti loco habet nō tantùmἔνωσιν,sed & eam, quae post finitionem statûsκενώσεωςsecuta est,ὑπερύψωσιν,uti ex Ephes; c. 1, & 4. suo ostensum loco. De reliquis W. exceptionibus iudicari haut difficulter ex dictis potest, alibique prolixiùs eas excutiendi occasio dabitur. Evolvantur interea de praesenti ac parall. dicto c. 28, 20. copiosiùs disserentes Dnn. Theologi Saxonici in all. Apol. passim, B. D. Chemnitius lib. de duabus naturis in Christo c. 30. p. 186. B. Ioh. Schroterus Sceptri Regalis Christi lib. 5. cap. 1. B. Par. Exeg. L. de Christo §. 219. Coeterùm simili ferè ariete, quo Wendelinus utitur, iampridem sententiam labefactare nostram conati sunt Amandus Polanus in Synt. Theol. & ex eo Ioh. Georg. Grossius in Theatr. Bibl. h. l; ubi etiam malitiosè scribit, nonnullos nostratium, dum Christi hominis omnipraesentiam docent, seribere non dubitasse, corpus Christi implere omnia loca, omnes cantharos cerevisiarios, omnia arborum folia, etiam (ignoscat Deus, verba blasphema referenti)

cloacas. Ast quis unquam nostratium loquutus ita est? Calvinianorum haec sequela est, quam admodùm ineptè ex nostrâ doctrinâ elicere satagunt. Sed inepta est haec consequentia. Corpus Christi est, ubicunque λόγος est. E. etiam in cloacis est. Increpet te Dominus, Satanas!

Aud-ntne Calviniani tam blasphemè sentire & loqui de λόγω; Nostra verò sententia haec est, quòd post exaltationem λογος nunquam sit extra carnem, nec caro extra λόγον, adeoque omnipraesens sit Non verò localiter, sed illocaliter. Quae aliàs omnipraesentiae Christi opponere Adversarii solent, cumprimis adscensionem in coelos, reditum ad iudicium &c. alibi discutiuntur. Hoc loco saltem illud notandum, quòd à negatione certi praesentiae modi non valeat consequentia ad negandum alium praesentiae modum, vel omnimodam praesentiam. Aliàs neganda & ipsius DEI omnipraesentia foret, ex 1. Reg. 19, 11.Exod. 33. 3.Ioh. 14, 23. Sed urget Polanus in Synt, & cum eo Grossius in h. l. p. 950. quòd Patres ex h. l. probent, Christum esse verum Deum. Resp. non repugnamus. Ast quid inde? tantum certè abest, ut id nostrae obsit sententiae, ut potiùs eandem confirmet. Etenim nisi Christus in unitate personae esset simul Deus & homo, adeoque secundùm divinam suam naturam essentialiter omnipraesens, non potuisset ipse gloriam omnipraesentiae humanae naturae adsumtae personaliter communicare, cùm fundamentum omnipraesentiae, humanae naturae communicatae, sit, quòd ipsa illa in infinitâ ὺποςάσει τοο λόγου subsistat & ad dextram DEI evecta. Iesuita Conzen ad h. l. q 2. p 356. opponit nostrae sententiae, quam absurdum vocat errorem, hoc, quòd agatur hîc de praesentiâ singulari, quâ ita adest piis & concordibus, ut non adsit impiis & dissentientibus. Ast verò, subsumit, si corporis mole ubique est s. omnipraesens, atq de illâ praesentiâ verba Christi accipienda sunt, etiam impiis, Ethnicis & publicanis est praesens. Resp. Minùs rectè praesentia gratiosa opponitur gloriosae vel maiestaticae, s. praesentiae, ut vocant, potentiae. Cùm potiùs illa hanc praesupponat. Quemadmodum igitur ex eo, quòd Deus piis promittit, quòd gratiosè illis adesse velit, impiis verò comminatur, quòd ab illis velit recedere, hautquaquam debet inferri, quòd non sit omnipraesens, ita nec ex eo, quòd solis piis Christus gratiosè praesens esse vult, colligi debet, nec potest, quòd reliquis non futurus sit omnipraesens: alioquisequetur, quòd nec secundùm divinam naturam omnipraesens ipse sit, cùm gratiâ suâ impiis non adsit. Opponit idem Iesuita nostrae sententiae dictâ Augustini epistolâ ad Dardanum & tr. 50 it. Cyrill. l. 6. super Ioh. c. 14 & l. 9. c. 21. Sed ea potiùs sententiam nostrā confirmant, quàm ut eam destruant. Loquuntur enim Patres de praesentiâ carnali & visibili, quam negant, quod & nos facimus. Vid omninò B. D. Chemn. Harm. Evang. c. 92. p. 1009 cumprimis in aureo libello de duabus naturis in Christo cap 30. Add. Dun. Theol. Sax. in Def. Fundam. Pupill--p 379. seqq. it. p 648. 649. B. D. K-sler. in Refut. Belli Ubiq. Foereri l. 2. s. 2. c. 6. & 7. B. Par. Confess. Cath. lib. 2. spec. part. 1. p. 376 seqq. Dn. D. Wa-therus, Cent. Miscell. Theol. p 457 seqq. it 451 seqq. in Quadrag. Miscell Theol. p. 608. 609. B. D. Tarnov. de SS Trinit. p. 8, 6. 857. 858. -oeterùm utut facilè argiamur Christum minimè visibiliter nobis adesse, ita ut coràm consuli possit ac conveniri: haut quaquam tamen hinc sequitur, quod decuerit, ut in coelos abiens Vicarium constitueret, nempe P. R. ceu ratiocinatur Iesuita Costerus, cuius ineptias satis luculenter detexit B. D Grawerust. 1. Dispp. Anti Iesuit. pag. 504 Sufficit Ecclesiae, quòd Christus primò reliquerit Sc. Sacram, quae est lucerna pedibus nostris. Deinde quòd ordinârit ministerium verbi. dederitque Ecclesiae Dd. & Pastores. Tertiò nec P. R ab omnibus semper potest conveniri, nec ipsi inter se Rom. Pontifices satis conveniunt.)*

Aut tres, -bi sum in medio eorum. Hieron. in h. l. Ambrosius lib 7. in Lucam c. 13 sic exponunt. Cùm haec tria, corpus, anima & spiritus uniuntur per virtutes ad orandum, ego sum medius inter -lla. *(Coeterùm το έηειεμιμινμέσω αυτων. Videtur in his esse pleonasmus. At notat Camero Myroth. Ev. p. 90. quòd licet το έν μέσω saepè idem saltem significet, quod adesse, conf. Gen. 23, 6.Ezech. 1, 1.2. Cor. 6, 17. phrasi tamen Scripturae etiam is dicatur esse in medio, qui prae est, sive praesidet reliquis, ut Ps. 82, 1 & ita h l. accipi quoque. Porrò Iesuita Tirinus h. l. ita exponit: in medio eorū i. e. inter eos, ab intus in eis operans, à foris illis a-sistens, cooperans, dirigens, ut id, cuius causâ convenerunt, infallibiliter consequantur. Addit: Quis ergo de infallibili autoritate pleni & legitimi Concilii possit exinceps dubitare? Similia habent Corn. à Lapide, Maldonatus & alii Iesuitae in h. l. quemadmodum etiam Bellarminus lib. 2. de Concil. cap. 2. itemque Alphonsus de Castro l. adv. haeres. verbo Concilium. Resp. Pertinent haec verba ad quosvis fideles & Christianos: cùm eorum personam hîc --stinuerint Apostoli, uti ipse Iesuita Corn. à Lap rectè observat. Agit verò Salvator de precum exauditione, non de infallibilitatis privilegio. Si enim de hoc ageretur, sequeretur, quòd etiam duo vel tres in Christi nomine congregati, quicunque etiam fuerint, sive laici sive clerici, infallibile decretum de controversis fidei articulis fabricari possint, quod tamen Pontificii nō concedunt, utpote disertè profitentes, ipsa quoque Concilia particularia s. provincialia (ubi tamen non duo vel tres, sed viginti, triginta & ampliùs Episcopi congregati sunt,) errare posse, uti ipse fatetur Alph. de Castro l. c. qui etiam l. 1. c. 8. disertè scribir, provincialia Concilia errare posse in fide, sicut de multis talibus Conciliis errasse compertum sit. Ast excipit Maldonatus, quòd Concilia particularia propterea errarint, quia non fuerint congregata in nomine Christi. Ubi tamen in nomine Christi fuerint congregata, negat, errare illa posse. Quid v. ipsi est, in nomine Christi congregari? Christi autoritate convenire. Benè. Addit: tunc ei-autoritate conveniunt, cùm Romani Pontificis, eius vicarii autoritate convocantur & confirmantur. Gemella habet Conzen in h. l. p. 354. Quid verò, si & tunc errasse Concilia, fuerit ostensum. Id sansatis clarè docet Cardinalis Baronius A. 897. agens de Conventiculo Episcoporum, Presbyterorum ac Cardinalium, à P. R. Stephano collecto. Quid quòd unanimiter ferè concedant, Concilia etiam à Pontifice congregata, posse errare in quaestionibu--cti, idque extra dubitationis aleam positum censet Bellar. l. 2. -Concil. c. 7. §. Resp. primò. it. c. 8. §. Respondeo quaedam. Quod si verò Concilia in quaestionibus facti errare possunt, e-iam à P. R. congregata, sequitur quòd autoritas Pontificis congregantis, Concilia non reddat infallibilia. Aut ostendenda ex textûs visceribus diversitatis ratio est, h. e. quòd Salvator infallibile

iudicium Concilio, autoritate P. R. congregato, promiserit in quaestionibus fidei, non aequè verò in quaest. facti. Mirum verò, quòd nullus Veterum Ecclesiae Dd. qui locum hunc exposuerunt, interpretionem illam, quòd in Christi nomine convenire sit autoritate P. R. convenire, miseris mortalibus suppeditaverit. Scilicet felicitas haec reservata fuit Iesuitis, sedis Papalis defensoribus. Sciendum verò, quòd nec ipsis Iesuitis omnibus ista textûs perversio placeat: etenim Iesuita Alphonsus Salmeron Toletanus, (quem sociennus eius Ant. Possevinus in App. Sacro magnis à Deo dotibus ornatum, & in Synodo Tridentinâ à Pio IV. missum Thelogi officio functum esse co-emorat) disertè negat, h. l de Conciliis agi, adeoque neutiquam τὸin nomine Christi congregari accipit pro eo, quod autoritate P. R. congregari. Verba eius t. 4. Op. tr. 10. part. 3. p. 462. sic habent: Nihil de Conciliis celebrandis Christus hîc praescripsit, sed pium Christianae unitatis consensum & communem fidelium orationis efficaciam nobis commendat. Allegat locum bonâ fide B. Par. t. 1. C. C. p. 518. similiaque confert ex Nic. de Clemangis ac Stapletono. Non ignoravit fortè id Iesuita Maldonatus, unde ita h. l. Solet hoc testimonium ad probandam Conciliorum autoritatem adduci, quod non haeretici modò, sed nonnulli etiam Catholici fieri posse negant, quia de oratione, non de decernen-i potestate &c. agebatur. Hi licet ingeniosi homines sint, sentire eamen vim argumenti non videntur. Ita videl. nemo veterum Dd., quin nec socienni proprii, qui tamen mortalium acutissimi haberi cupiunt, vim argumenti Iesuitici adsequi potuit. Cogitet verò prudens lector, quàm alienus à praesenti textu sit sensus, quem ei affingunt Iesuitae Corn. à Corn. à Lapide, Maldonatus, &c. quòd nempe in nomine Christi congregari sit idem, ac autoritate Pontificis Romani gregari, & vice versa, qui non congregati sint autoritate P. Romani, illi nec in nomine Christi sint congregati. Fortè deinceps novis illis Sc. Sacrae interpretibus, petere aliquid in nomine Christi,Ioh. 16, 23. idem sonabit, ac petere autoritate Pontificis Romani, & baptizari nomine Christi, s.
