Filii DEI,Matth. 28, 29. hunc habebit infallibiliter sensum, baptizari autoritate PontificiRomani, eritque adeo necesse, ut qui vitae aeternae haeredes fieri cupiunt, propediem non nisi autoritate Pontificis Romani baptizentur, nec ratus ampliùs erit apud Pontificios baptismus ab Ecclesiae nostrae ministris administratus, eo quòd non collatus fuit autoritate Pontificis Romani. Coeterùm pluribus infirmitatem argumenti Iesuitici ostenderunt nostrates Theologi. Vid. Dn. D. Calovius p. 884. Critici Sacri, B. Par. Confess. Cathol. l. 1. Gener. part. 2. c. 10 p. 515.)*

## 18:21
(v. 21. Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me &c. The conditional conjunction if is omitted, & the particle how often ought to be referred to the following member. The sense is: if my brother shall sin against me more often , how often ought I to forgive him?)

(I will forgive him i. e. I ought to forgive. The rule which the Jesuit Tirinus proposes, and the Londoners after him in the Apparatus §. 57, pertains here: By active verbs, not rarely, not the act, but the debt of acting or the duty is designated. The blessed D. Glassius provides examples in Philol. S. book 3. treatise 3. p. 247. Namely, Gen 20, 9.Neh. 5, 8Mal. 1, 6.c 2, 7.Matth. 26, 52.Luc. 3, 14.c 6, 42.Ebr. 5, 4. Tirinus illustrates with the example Ebr. 13, 17. Compare also Sanctius on Acts c. 23. n. 15)

Latin:

*(v. 21. Domine, quoties peccabit in me &c. Omissa est coniunctio conditionalis si, & part. quoties debet ad seq. mebrum referri. Sensus est: si saepiùs pec-averit in me frater meus, quoties debeo ei remittere?)*

*( Remittam ei i. e. remittere debeo. Spectat huc regula, quam proponit Iesuita Tirinus & ex eo Londinenses in Apparatu §. 57 Verbis activis haut rarò non actus, sed agendi debitum s. officium designatur. Exempla suppeditat B D. Glassius Philol. S. l. 3. tr. 3. p. 247. Videl. Gen 20, 9.Neh. 5, 8Mal. 1, 6.c 2, 7.Matth. 26, 52.Luc. 3, 14.c 6, 42.Ebr. 5, 4. Tirinus illustrat exemplo Ebr. 13, 17. Conf. etiam Sanctius in Act. c. 23. n. 15)*

## 18:22
(v. 22 Until seventy times seven. A certain number is put for an uncertain one. And the sense is: you ought to forgive as often as your neighbor sins against you. Chrysost. on this passage: When he says until seventy times seven, he does not set a determined number, but signifies that which is continuous & always. Let Nicetas on Orat. 44 of Nazianzen be compared, Ambrose book 2. on Jacob c. 5. 6. August; sermon 15. on the words of the Lord. But just as Peter is commanded to forgive his brother sinning against him seventy times seven, so God, for His immense mercy μυριοντάκις τὰπτὰ thousand times seven, grants pardon to those repenting, as Athanas. t. 2. q. 93. and Justin Martyr q. 97. excellently teach.)

Latin:

*(v. 22 Usque septuagies sep-ies. Ponitur numerus certus pro incerto. Ac sensus est: toties remittere debes, quoties peccat in te proximus tuus. Chrysost. in h. l. Cùm dicit usque septuagies septies, non numerum determinatum ponit, sed quod continuo & semper est, significat. Conferatur Nicetas ad Orat. 44. Nazianzeni, Ambrosius lib. 2. de Iacobo c. 5. 6. August; serm. 15. de verbis Domini. Quemadmodum verò Petrus septuagies septies fratri in se peccati remittere iubetur, ita Deus pro immensâ suâ misericordia μυριοντάκις τὰπτὰ mi-lies septies resipiscentibus veniam largitur, ceu egregiè docent Athanas. t. 2. q. 93. ac Iustinus Martyr q. 97.)*

## 18:23
(v. 23. Ὡμοιὰθη is likened, or is made similar. Since every likeness is also in some way unlike, it is to be well noted that it suffices here if at least with respect to the scope of Christ a likeness has been shown. But the scope of the Savior is to teach that, just as that King who out of mere mercy had forgiven a huge debt to a debtor, punished the unmerciful servant severely: so also God, when He likewise without any of our merits or works, and thus out of mere grace in Christ, forgives our sins to us, will severely punish us, when we have been unmerciful and implacable toward our neighbor. Furthermore, the blessed D. Bald. presents the application of this parable to the Ministry of the word in Idea Disp. Bibl. p. 283.)

Latin:

*(v. 23. Ὡμοιὰθηsimile est, vel adsimilatur. Cùm omne simile etiam aliquo modo dissimile, probè notandum est, quòd sufficiat hîc, si saltem quoad s-opum Christi similitudo fuerit ostensa. Est verò scopus Salyatoris, docere, quòd ceu Rex ille qui ex merâ misericordiâ debitori ingens debitum remiserat, immisericordem servum graviter punivit: ita & Deus, cùm itidem absque ullis nostris meritis vel operibus, adeoque ex merâ gratiâ in Christo nostra nobis peccata remittat, severè nos puniturus sit, ubi in proximum nostrum immisericordes & implacabiles fuerimus. Caeterùm applicationem huius parabolae ad Ministerium verbi sistit B. D. Bald. in Ideâ Disp. Bibl. p. 283.)*

## 18:24
* (v. 24. He was brought to him &c. The Jesuit Sanctius correctly observes in Comm. on c. 8. Acts p. 192. that the word brought here signifies a judicial action, and that the word נגש Is. 53, 7. is also accepted in this way. But if this is so, why do the Jesuits so strongly oppose our opinion, when we teach that in our justification the word justifies: has a judicial or forensic meaning, since Christ, according to the Jesuit Sanctius in this place, was seized by the creditor as our guarantor)*

v. 24. Ten thousand talents. The Hebrews call a talent כבר Cicar, but the Chaldeans and Syrians ככèא cacera, which, as R. D. Kimchi reports in the Book of Roots, contained 60 pounds of silver or gold, or of another metal. Tremel. Some estimate this sum at six million gold crowns, or seven million five hundred thousand thalers, i.e., sixty tons of gold. Alexander the Great is said to have buried Hephaestion for this much, as Plutarch writes in the life of Alexander. King Ahasuerus is said to have had such a sum, Esth. 3, and M. Crassus is written to have found such a sum in the temple of Jerusalem. See Joseph. l. 14 c. 8. Plutarch in Pomp. Furthermore, the Syriac and Persian also present this sum, namely ten thousand talents. The Arabic translates indefinitely i.e., a sum of talents, the Ethiopic i.e., a thousand talents, as Lud. de Dieu renders it. Or rather ten thousand talents, as Dudley Loftus interpreted it, in the version added to the London Polyglot Bibles. For the Ethiopic use the expression to express a myriad or ten times a thousand as can be seen from 1 Cor. 4, 15.c. 10, 8.c 14, 19. but they circumscribe the number of a thousand periphrastically by ten times a hundred, as is evident from Ps. 90, 2 Pet. 3, 8., and noted by Ludov. de Dieu in Animadv. on Acts 2, 41 p. 27. So that there is no need to posit a typographical error here in the Ethiopic version with the same . Indeed, by this almost immense sum, the huge burden of our sins is indicated. Which we must ponder repeatedly, and therefore not minimize our sins, but with serious contrition We must multiply, following Manasseh in the Prayer v. 5, 9, David Ps. 38, 4 and Ps. 40, 13, because when we have done this, and have fled with true faith to the throne of divine mercy, GOD will institute for us another far more delightful multiplication, Mic. 7, 18 Rom. 5, 20. Let there be added, however, also on our part a subtraction, which happens if we daily subdue and crucify our flesh. See Gal. 5, 24 2 Cor. 7, 1 Col. 3, 5, 6 Eph. 4, 22. It will contribute greatly to this subtraction if we outwardly subtract something from our body from time to time through temperance and fasting, Rom. 13, last. How, moreover, both addition and division ought to be instituted, the Blessed D. Glassius elegantly shows in Exeg. Dom. 9 after Trinity. Furthermore, for the application of the present parable to the Ministry of the word, see, if you please, the Blessed D. Bald. in Idea Disposit. Bibl. p. 283.

Latin:

* (v. 24. Oblatus est ei &c. Rectè observat Iesuita Sanctius Comm. in c. 8. Act. p. 192. quòd vox oblatus hîc iudicialem significet actionem, & ita quoque vocem נגשEs. 53, 7. accipi. Quod si hoc, cur tantopere Iesuitae nostrae adversantur sententiae, dum edocemus, in nostri iustificatione verbum iustificat: iudicialem s. forensem habere significationem, quippe cùm Christus, iuxta Iesuitam Sanctium h. l. ceu noster fideiussor fuerit raptus à creditore)*

v. 24. Decem mille talenta. Talentum Ebraei vocant כברCicar, Chaldaei verò & Syri ככèאcacera, quod, ut refert R. D. Kimchi in libro Radicum continebat libras 60 argenti vel auri, aut alterius metalli. Tremel. Quidam summam hanc aestimant sexagies entenis millibus aureorum coronatorum, vel septuagies quinquies centenis millibus talerorum i. e. sexaginta tonnis auri. Tanti Alexander M. Ephestionem funerasse dicitur, ut scribit Plutarchus in vitâ Alexandri. Tantam summam habuisse dicitur Rex Ahasverus, Esth. 3 & M. Crassius scribitur talem summam in templo Hierosol invenisse. Vid. Ioseph. l. 14 c. 8. Plutarch in Pomp. Coeterùm summam hanc, deciens nempe mille talentorum, exhibent quoque Syrus ac Persa. Arabs indefinitè verrit i. e. summam talentorum, Aethiops i. e. mille talenta, prout Lud. de Dieu reddit. Vel potiùs decem millia talenta, prout interpretatus est Dudleius Luftusius, in vers. B--liis Polyglottis Londinensibus adiecta. Etenim dictione utuntur Aethiopes ad exprimendam myriaden s. de-ies mille ceu videre est ex 1 Cor. 4, 15.c. 10, 8.c 14, 19. numer-m verò mill enariū periphrasticè iidem circumscribūt per decies centum, uti ex Ps. 90, Petr. 3, 8. patet, ac notatum Ludov. de Dieu in Animadv. ad Actor 2, 41 p. 27. Ut adeò non sit opus, in Aethiopicâ versione erratum cum eodem statue-hîc typographicum. Indicatur verò hâc immensâ quasi summâ ingens peccatorum nostrorum onus. Quod subindè perpendere, adeoq; peccata nostra non extenuare, sed seriâ contritritione multiplicare debemus, sequuti Manassem Orat. v. 5. 9. Davidem Psal. 38, 4. it. Psal. 40, 13. quòd ubi fecerimus, & verâ fide ad misericordiae divinae thronum confugerimus, DEUS aliam longè iucundissimam multiplicationem nobis cum instituet, Mich. 7, 18.Rom. 5, 20. Accedat tamen & ex nostra parte subtractio, quae fit, si indies carnem nostram domuerimus ac crucifixerimus. Vid. Gal. 5, 24.2. Cor. 7, 1.Col 3, 5. 6.Eph. 4, 22. Plurimùm huic subtractioni inserviet, si exteriùs corporinostro aliquid subinde subtraxerimus per temperantiam, ieiunium, Rom. 13. ult. Quomodo praeterea & additio & divisio institui debeat, eleganter ostendit B. D. Glassius Exeg. Dom. 9. post Trinit. Coeterùm applicationem praesentis parabolae ad Ministerium verbi vide sis apud B. D. Bald. in Idea Disposit. Bibl. p. 283. )*

## 18:25
(v. 25. To sell his wife and children etc. For formerly among the Jews a debtor, reduced to poverty, could be sold to the creditor along with his wife and children, as is evident from Exod. 21, 1 seqq., c. 22, 4 Lev. 25, 39 47 2 Kings 4, 1 seqq. The Talmudists, however, limit this in some way, as Dionysius Vossius warns in ch. 4, § 6 of the book on Idolatry by Maimonides; also Tostatus Abulensis on 1 Kings 4, 1. The same also obtained among the Greeks, as is evident from Plutarch in Solon, and also among the Romans, just as Livy reports from the laws of the XII Tables, Hist. Rom. decad. 1, c. 27. Compare also Dionys. Halicarn. l. 2; also Ammianus Marcell. l. 7, c. 16. That such a custom also once passed to the Christians can be gathered from the complaint of Ambrose in the book on Job, c. 8, and also from l. 2, on fathers who sold their children, lib. 4, Cod. tit. 43.)

Latin:

*(v. 25. Vendere uxorem & liberos &c. Poterat enim olim apud Iudaeos debitor, ad egestatem redactus, iuxta cum uxore ac liberis addici creditori, ceu patet ex Exod. 21, 1. seqq. c 22, 4.Lev. 25, 39.47.2. Reg. 4, 1. seqq. Limitant tamen hoc aliquo modo Talmudistae, monente Dionysio Vossio ad c. 4. §. 6. l. de Idolol. Maimonidis. it. Tonstato Abulensi ad 1. Reg. 4, 1. Idem & apud Graecos obtinebat, uti ex Plutarcho in Solone constat, nec non apud Romanos, quemadmodum ex legg. XII. Tabul Livius l. 2. Hist. Rom. decad. 1. c. 27. refert. Conf. etiam Dionys. Halicarn. l. 2. it. Ammianus Marcell. l. 7. c. 16. Ad Christianos quoque talem morem olim manasse, ex querelâ Ambrosii lib. de Iob. c. 8. colligere licet, nec non ex l. 2. de patrib. qui filios distraxerunt lib. 4. Cod. tit. 43.)*

## 18:27
(v. 27. He forgave him the debt. The Socinians infer from this: that just as a creditor here could forgive a debt to a debtor without an intervening satisfaction, so also God can forgive sins to men freely and without any intervening satisfaction, so that there was no need for Christ's satisfaction for our sins. Which these said heretics also impudently deny. I respond: 1. The scope of Christ in this place is not to treat of the redemption provided for us through Christ, which very many Holy Scripture passages establish, and teach was done through the blood of Christ, as a most precious άντιλύτρω. (see Matt. 20, 28 c. 26, 28 Luke 22, 19

Rom. 3, 24, 25 1 Cor. 6, 20 Eph. 4, 23 Col. 1, 14 1 Tim. 2, 6 1 Pet. 1, 18, 19) but of the remission of private offenses, which we ought to forgive our neighbor. I distinguish, therefore, 2. between debts, of which some are external and civil, which concern goods of fortune; some are internal, which injure the honor of the creditor. The former can be forgiven freely, the latter not equally so. What is more, we are not always bound to forgive even debts of the former kind freely. 3. between a private creditor and a pecuniary one; and between a public creditor and a judicial one, i.e., an exactor of justice. The former can, with justice preserved, grant a debt to a debtor, but the latter cannot. But our sins are debts in the latter way, and God is such a creditor. Such a creditor, however, cannot forgive those debts without satisfaction, since His injured justice does not admit such a thing. Compare Heb. 9, 22. 4. Nor do they conflict with each other, that sins are forgiven to us by grace, and by the intervention of the satisfaction of Christ. For Holy Scripture brings forward both. See Is. 53, 5, 6 11, 12 Eph. 2, 8. Grace, therefore, and freely in the article of justification are not opposed to the merit and satisfaction of Christ, but to our merits and our satisfaction. By grace God forgives our sins to us, but because His justice was injured, the satisfaction of Christ was required. See Gen. 2, 17 Ps. 45, 8 and add Giesens. Append. Dispp. p. 709, 710. Compare more things pertaining to this in the Blessed D. Grawerus, Polem. Sacr. p. 690 seqq., the Blessed D. Feurborn. in Anti-Oster. p. 516, 517, B. Par. L. de Iustif. L. 49, Camer. in Myroth. p. 91, also Praelect. p. 401. Furthermore, however easily we may grant that the parable proposed by Christ deals with a pecuniary debt, it cannot be denied that the application is made to a moral debt, or sin. Whence the exception of Wendelin is of no moment, when in Exerc. 116 § 11, to the argument of our people for the amissibility of faith taken from this place (namely such as: To whomever sins are forgiven, he had true and justifying faith. But to that servant, who later became unmerciful, sins are forgiven. Therefore he had faith.), he responds: the minor speaks not of a moral debt or sin, but a civil or pecuniary one, and the debt was moreover forgiven not by GOD, the inspector of hearts, but by the master, a man, whom that wicked and envious servant deceived by his hypocrisy.

But although the simile is taken from a human master, who could be deceived, and likewise from a pecuniary debt: the scope of Christ, however, is to show to whom God, the searcher of hearts, forgives sins, as Wendelin himself admits in the said place. But when that master, through whom God is prefigured, forgave the servant the debt, through which sins are prefigured, and that indeed could not have happened unless the servant had had true and saving faith, as without which the remission of sins cannot take place: it is certainly manifest that that same servant, who was afterwards handed over to the torturers on account of his unmercifulness, had previously, i.e., when his sins were forgiven him, possessed the faith which he cast off through unmercifulness. The most constant benevolence of GOD toward the saints, which Wendelin urges so much here, is by no means denied by us. But it must be known that that same benevolence is not absolute, but conditional, as this very parable teaches clearly enough.

Latin:

* (v. 27. Etaes alienum remisit ei. Inferunt hinc Sociniani. quòd ceu creditor hîc debitori potuit debitum remittere absq satisfactione interveniente, ita etiam Deus hominibus peccata remittere possit gratis ac nullâ interveniente satisfactione, ut adeò non opus fuerit Christi satisfactione pro nostris peccatis. Quam etiam protervè dicti haeretici negant. Resp. 1. Christi scopus h. l. non est. agere de nostri per Christum praestitâ redemtione, quam plurima Sc. S. dicta adstrnunt, & mediante Christi sangvine, ceu pretiosissimo άντιλύτρω factam docent. (vid. Matth. 20, 28.c. 26, 28.Luc. 22, 19.

Rom. 3, 24. 25.1. Cor. 6, 20.Ephes. 4, 23.Coloss. 1, 14.1. Tim. 2, 6.1 Petr. 1, 18, 19.) sed de privatarum offensarum, quas proximo condonare debemus, remissione. Dist. igitur 2. inter debita, quorum quaedam externa & civilia sunt, quae bona fortunae respiciunt; quaedam interna, quae laedunt honorem creditoris. Illa remitti gratis possunt, haec non aequè. Quid quòd nec prioris generis debita gratis semper remittere teneamur. 3. inter creditorem privatum ac pecuniarium; & inter creditorem publicum ac iudiciarium h. e. iustitiae exactorem. Ille salvâ iustitiâ potest debitori donare debitum, sed hic non. Peccata verò nostra ut posteriori modo debita sunt, ita & Deus creditor. Talis verò creditor absque satisfactione remittere debita illa non potest, cùm tale quid non admittat iustitia eius laesa. Conf. Ebr. 9, 22. 4. Nec pugnant inter se, ex gratiâ nobis peccata remitti, & interventu satisfactionis Christi. Utrumque enim adferit Sc. S. Vid. Es. 53, 56.11 12.Eph. 2, 8.Gratia igitur & gratis in art. iustificationis non opponuntur merito & satisfactioni Christi, sed nostris meritis ac nostrae satisfactioni. Ex gratiâ Deus nostra nobis peccata remittit, sed quia iustitia eius fuit laesa, Christi requirebatur satisfactio. Vid. Gen. 2, 17.Ps. 45. 8. ac add. Giesens. Append. Dispp. p. 709. 710. Confer plura huc facientia apud B D. Grawerum Polem. Sacr p. 690. seqq. B. D. Fewrborn. in Anti-Oster. p. 516. 517. B. Par. L. de Iustif. L. 49. Camer. in Myroth. p. 91. it. Praelect. p. 401. Coeterùm ut ut facilè largiamur, simile à Christo propositum, agere de debito pecuniario, negari tamen haut potest, quòd applicatio fiat ad debitum morale, sive peccatum. Unde nullius momentiest exceptio Wendelini, quando Exerc. 116 §. 11. ad argumentum Nostratium pro fidei amissibilitate ex h. l. desumtum, (tale nempe: Cuicunque remittuntur peccata, is veram ac iustificantem habuit fidem. Atqui servo illi, qui postea factus immisericors, remittuntur peccata. E. habuit fidem.) respondet, minorem loqui non de debito morali sive peccato, sed civili sive pecuniaro, & debitum insuper condonatum fuisse non à DEO cordium inspectore, sed ab hero, homine, quem hypocrisi suâ nequam ille & lividus servus deceperit.

Ast licet simile sit desumtum ab hero homine, qui potuit decipi, item à debito pecuniario: scopus tamen Christi est, ostendere, quibus Deus cordium scrutator peccata remittat, ut ipse Wendelinus d. l. fatetur. Cùm verò herus ille, per quem Deus praefiguratur, servo remiserit debitum, per quod peccata praefigurantur, id verô fieri haut potuisset, nisi servus veram & salvifica habuisset fidem, utpote quâ sine peccatorum remissio locum hahere nequit: manifestum sanè est, quòd idem ille servus, qui postea propter immisericordiam tortoribus fuit traditus, priùs h. e. quando peccata illi fuere remissa, habuerit fidem, quam per immisericordiā excussit. Constantissima DEI erga sanctos benevolentia, quam tantopere Wendelinus hîc urget, minimè à nobis negatur Id verò sciendum est, quòd eadem illa non sit absoluta, sed conditionata, ceu haec ipsa parabola satis clarè docet. *

## 18:28
v. 28. He found one of his fellow-servants su-. Syr. of his own surname, i.e., who was called by the name of the same master or condition. It is a periphrasis for fellow-servant. Some refer it to the Hebrew word , which the Chaldeans interpret as , minister, which meaning is more apt and close.

רנèÐ δηνάριον, was a coin, called by the Hebrews Zuz by its proper name, although also Denara by a barbaric term, which they had received from the Romans. It contained, however, a weight of silver of 96 barleycorns, i.e., it is equivalent to six drachmas. They estimate the sum of a hundred denarii at ten gold pieces. A denarius is worth as much as an Angelic or two batzen with us. These hundred denarii, therefore, would amount to thirteen florins or thereabouts.

* ( And holding him, he choked him. See what Mr. Fesselius collected on this matter in book 4, Adv. Sacr. c. 14.)*

Latin:

v. 28. Invenit unum de conservis su-. Syr. de cognominatione suâ, h. e. qui de nomine eiusdem heri vel conditionis vocabatur. Periphrasis est conservi. Quidam referunt ad vocem Ebraicam , quam Chaldaei interpretantur ,ministrum, quae significatio est magis apta & propinqua.

רנèÐδηνάριον, numisma erat, Hebraeis vocatum Zuz propriâ appellatione, licet etiam Denara barbaro vocabulo, quod à Romanis acceperant. Continebat autem argenti pondus 96. granorum hordei i. e. aequivalet sex drachmis. Summam centum denariorum aestimant decem aureis. Denarius valet tantum, quantum apud nos Angelicus vel duo baceni. Centum igitur hi Denarii efficerent tredecim florenos vel praeter propter.

* ( Et tenens suffocabat eum. Vid. quae in rem hanc collegit Dn. Fesselius l. 4. Adv. Sacr. c. 14.)*

## 18:34
v. 34. He delivered him βασανισταῖς to the tormentors. Syr. למנגרגא to those who torment or scourge. See below c. 20, 19. & they shall scourge him.

* ( Till he should pay all the debt. Chrysostom rightly advises hom. 62. in Matth. τὸ ἕέως οὗ is placed for the infinite. Until, he writes, is placed for the infinite, that is, he may always be paying, but he will never pay off, but will be punished eternally. And although the gifts of God are irrevocable, yet malice has prevailed so much, --t & has overcome this law. Haraeus himself, a Louvain Theologian, brings forward this exposition of Chrysostom in his scholia to this place. Compare above Anal. to c. 5, 26. where it is shown that the particle until does not always exclude the following time, but often includes it. In this place we add at least this, that Remigius understands by tormentors the demons, who in a thousand ways most grievously torment and torture the souls of sinners in hell, till they should pay, i. e. to be tormented eternally: for they will never be able to pay off such a debt of 120. millions. Thus S Chrys. Theoph. Euthymius, as noted and approved by Corn. à Lap. in this place. The Jesuit Conzen also brings forward this explanation of Chrysostom and opposes it to the Origenists in this place, warning that the Origenists taught from the end of this place that there would be a thousand years of punishments and then an end, when here the servant is delivered to eternal torments.)*

v. 34. Tradidit eumβασανισταῖςtortoribus. Syr. למנגרגאillis qui torquent vel flagellant. Sie infra c. 20, 19. & flagellabunt eum.

* ( Quoad usque redderet universum debitum. Rectè monet Chrysostomus hom. 62. in Matth. τὸ ἕέως οὗ poni pro infinito. Quousque, scribit, ponitur pro infinito, id. est, semper solvat, sed nunquam persolvet, sed aeternaliter punietur. Et quamvis irrevocabilisint charismata Dei, tamen tantum valuit malitia, --t & hanc legem super averit. Adducit hanc Chrysostomi expositionē ipse Haraeus, Theologus Lovaniensis in scholiis ad h. l. Conf. suprà Anal. ad c. 5, 26. ubi ostenditur, quòd part. donec non semper excludat tempus sequens, sed saepè illud includat. Hoc loco illud saltem addimus, quòd Remigius per tortores intelligat daemones, qui animas peccatorum mille modis gravissimè torqueant & crucient in gehenna, quoadusque redderent, i. e. in aeternum torquendum: nun quam enim tantum debitum 120. millionum exsolvere poterunt. Ita S Chrys. Theoph. Euthymius, ipso notante & approbante Corn. à Lap. in h. l. Chrysost. quoque explicationē adducit & Origenistis opponit Iesuita Conzen. in h. l. monens, Origenistas mille annos poenarum & deinde finē fore, ex h. l. fine ratione docuisse, cùm hic servus tradatur aeternis tormentis.)*

## 18:35
* (v. 35. So also my heavenly Father &c. See Prov. 21, 13.Matth, 5, 7.c. 6, 12.14. and compare B. D. Glas. Exeg. Ev. Dom. 4. post Trinit. From that v. that this King delivered the wicked and unmerciful servant to the tormentors, to whom however he had previously forgiven the whole debt, arises the dispute, whether the previous debt of sins which was forgiven and blotted out through true and serious repentance and faith returns on account of a new debt as it were contracted? Which question is treated by Mr. Dr. Iohan. Olearius Scholae patient. page 883. but more prolixly from the Papists Felicianus Capito Narniensis, Archbishop of Avignon, in Expl. Cath. part 2. p. 573. seq. and also Corn. à Lapide in this place and Thomas 3. p. q. 88. Artic. 1. & 3. It is evident however from this utterance of the Savior how great a punishment awaits the unmerciful, to which also the sayings Eccles. 28, 1. 2. Iac. 2, 13. look. Compare B. Par. Homil. Acad. part 2. p 448. Furthermore, by this command is not taken away 1. the office of the Political Magistrate in punishing the wicked, since it was divinely committed to him, Rom 13, 4. 2. nor the office of the Ecclesiastical Ministry, likewise divinely commanded, 1. Tim. 5, 20.2. Tim. 4, 2. 3 nor the office of a neighbor, prescribed above v. 15. 16. 17.. Compare 1. Corinth. 5, 3. 4.Prov. 27, 5. 6. 4. nor in particular that of Parents. See 1. Sam. 4, 18. 5. nor is it commanded that one should receive an adulteress.)*

* ( You have forgiven. But God alone forgives sins, Mic. 7, 18. Resp. God alone forgives sins properly and by His own authority. But man is said to forgive sins when he lays aside anger, hatred, etc., against a neighbor by whom he was offended. Furthermore, let someone say: If God does not wish to forgive our sins unless we also have forgiven, and on the contrary forgives if we have forgiven, it follows that man obtains or attains the forgiveness of sins from God by his own merits. Resp. by denying the consequence. See what has been brought forward above on this matter at c. 6, 12. Finally, the following ought to incite us to compassion and the condoning of guilt: 1. The sweetness of examples. For not only do Jacob, Joseph, David, and other pious men, who were very easy in this matter, shine forth: but above all we ought to weigh the example of GOD, who forgives us our sins, which are like the sand of the sea, and with which we offend Him daily, out of mere mercy. 2. The joy of the angels and the pious. For just as they are saddened when they see us cruel, Ps. 119, 158. so they rejoice at our mercy. 3. The emptiness of our prayers. For neither is the forgiveness of sin or the bestowal of any good to be hoped for from God if we have been unmerciful. 4. The gravity of the punishment, concerning which it is treated in this place, where above all its eternity is to be noted. Conf. Jas. 2, 13. 5. The pleasantness of the rewards. For if we have forgiven, God will forgive us our sins. But where there is the forgiveness of sins, there is the tranquility of conscience, eternal life, and the bestowal of all goods whatsoever.)*

## 19:1
v. 1. μετῆρεν i.e. ἐαυτόν, he transferred himself i.e. he went away or departed. The Syrian has the word שקל which signifies to lift up, to raise, so that it must be translated he raised or he took up, understand his feet, from Galilee. A similar locution is had Genes. 29, 1. Jacob raised his feet, and went into the land of the East. Christ is that heavenly Jacob, whose days were the days of pilgrimage.

Δπο, This particle refutes Hilary, who affirms that Christ did not migrate from Galilee, but into Galilee.

Latin:

v. 1. μετῆρεν sc. ἐαυτόν,transtulit seipsum i. e. abiit seu discessit. Syrus habet verbum שקל quod significat attollere, levare, ut vertendum sit levavit vel sustulit, subaudi pedes suos, à Galilaea. Similis locutio habetur Genes. 29, 1.Levavit Iacob pedes suos, & abat in terram Orientis. Christus est coelestis ille Iacobus, cuius dies fuerunt dies peregrinationis.

Δπο, Particula haec refutat Hilarium, Christum non à Galilaea, sed in Galilaeam migrasse affirmantem.

## 19:3
v 3. For any cause. Luth. umb irgend einer Ursache. The sense is, whether it is lawful to make a divorce for any cause whatsoever, even the lightest: for thus it was the custom among the Jews. *(He notes indeed elsewhere ἀιτία in Sc. S also crime or fault, as is evident from Marc. 15. 26. Ioh. 18, 38. c. 19, 4. However, since divorces among the Jews were for the most part made not on account of some crime or fault, but for that cause which deserves the name of calamity rather than fault, it is better, in this place, to retain the customary signification of the word ἀιτίας, which, namely, in general denotes some occasion. See B. Par. Comm. in Deut. p. 1439. Cameron. Myroth Evang. p 93 Compare also the note to v. 10.)* Bened. Arias Montanus in this place. There were two most famous families of Scribes in Jerusalem, and in all Judea. The followers of one were called Samai, those of the other v. the house of Hillel. These defended various opinions in various arguments and in explaining the reasons of doctrine; Among these one question was concerning the causes of divorces. The house of Samai asserted that there was only one cause for which a divorce might be tolerated, and that it was the suspicion of adultery, they prove this from those words of Moses: for some filthiness. For the House of Shammai said that only filthiness could be the cause of divorce, and they defined filthiness only as unchastity. But the House of Hillel admitted every cause, or even the slightest offense, to the right of divorce, with those words only being used: And he has not found favor in his eyes. There was a certain third opinion, which supported the House of Shammai in the genus of the cause, but that genus of filthiness expanded that genus into many species.

NOTES TO CHAPTER XIX. SUMMARY.

* ( ἀπολύσαι. the Pharisees use this word, either because they thought that the bond of matrimony was dissolved by divorce, or because they wished to express a harsh thing with a soft word. For it is evident that wives were for the most part dismissed against their will. Just as also the repudiated woman in Holy Scripture is called גרוישה expelled. Or because in Holy Scripture the word שלח, to which the word άπολύσαι corresponds, also denotes he cast out against his will. See Exod, 12, 33.Ps. 43, 3. where also the LXX use the word ἐκβάλλειν. Or finally because the Seventy Interpreters sometimes use the same word for גרש. See Ps. 33, 1.)*

Latin:

v 3. Quacunque de causa. Luth. umb irgend einer Ursache. Sensus est, an liceat propter quamvis etiam levissimam causam divortium facere: ita enim apud Iudaeos moris erat. *(Notat quidem aliàs ἀιτία in Sc. S etiam crimen vel culpam, ceu patet ex Marc. 15. 26.Ioh. 18, 38.c. 19, 4. Attamen cùm divortia apud Iudaeos plerumque fierent non ob crimen aliquod vel culpam, sed ca de causa, quae calamitatis potiùs quàm culpae nomen meretur, satius est, h. l. usitatam vocis ἀιτίας significationem retinere, quat. videl. in genere notat occasionem aliquam. Vid. B. Par. Comm. in Deut. p. 1439. Cameron. Myroth Evang. p 93 Conf. etiam not. ad v. 10.)* Bened. Arias Montanus h. l. Duae fuére celeberrimae familiae Scribarum Hierosolymis, & in omni Iudaea. Alterius sectatores dicebantur Samai, alterius v. domus Hillel. Hi variis in argumentis atque doctrinae rationibus explicandis varias sententias defendebant; In his una quaestio erat de divortiorum causis. Domus Samai unam tantùm causam esse adseverabat, quamobrē divortium toleraretur, eamq; esse adulterii suspicionem, probant hoc ex verbis illis Mosis: propter aliquam foeditatem. Domus enim Samai solam soeditatem aiebat esse posse causam repudii, & foeditatem tantùm impudicitiam definiebant. Domus v. Hilel omnem causam vel minimam quamque offensionem ad repudii ius admittebant, illis verbis tantùm usurpatis: Et non invenerit gratiam in oculis eius. Erat tertia quaedam opinio, quae suffragabatur domui Samai causae genere, sed in species multas genus illud foeditarem dilatabat.

NOTAE AD CAP. XIX. SUMMA.

* ( ἀπολύσαι. utuntur Pharisaei hâc voce, vel quòd existimabant, per repudium solvi vinculum matrimonii, vel quòd rem duram molli vocabulo exprimere cupiebant. Constat enim. uxores plerumque invitas fuisse dimissas. quemadmodum etiam repudiata in Sc. S. dicitur גרוישהexpulsa. Vel quia in Sc. S. verbum שלח, cui verbum άπολύσαι respondet, notat quoque invitum eiiceret. Vid. Exod, 12, 33.Ps. 43, 3. ubi etiam LXX. utuntur verbo ἐκβάλλειν. Vel denique quia Septuaginta Interpretes eodem verbo quandoque utuntur pro גרש. Vid. Ps. 33, 1.)*

## 19:4
v. 4. Who answering &c. Christ altogether rejects from himself the cause of dividing an inheritance Luc. 12. 14. but he does not simply reject the question concerning divorces: nay rather, from the word of GOD he shows what agrees with the norm of the institution, and what is repugnant to it. He signifies, therefore, that because in matrimonial causes many cases of conscience occur, therefore the ministers of the Church cannot simply reject matrimonial causes from themselves to the political Magistrate.

Have ye not read. Matthew & Mark (c. 10, 6.) do not disagree. The former respects the words rather than the will of Christ; the latter wished to express the will rather than the words of Christ. In the former, Christ directly interrogates the Jews; in the latter, indirectly.

He made man from the beginning. The beginning of time is twofold. For it either signifies the beginning of creation, or in general the beginning of production. The beginning of creation is accepted in two ways, either in the total sense, or in the partial sense. In the total sense, or according to breadth, it signifies the beginning of creation and of all creatures in general, created in the hexaemeron, and it insinuates their beginning of origin and order at the same time. In the partial sense, i.e., according to strict signification, it signifies the beginning of the creation of any thing in species. Or it signifies beginning of origin, by which any created thing began to be. This beginning of production is primarily threefold: 1. of ordination,Matth. 19, 8. 2. of order,Sirac. 25, 33. 3. of preaching or proclamation of the Gospel,Marc. 1, 1.

* ( ἐποίησεν ἀυτούς, understand ἀνθρωπουστ. Hebraism. For it is customary in the Hebrew language for a relative pronoun to be employed, looking back to something as an antecedent, which nevertheless does not appear. See Ps. 10, 5. To this also pertains Marc. 9, 46.)*

Latin:

v. 4. Qui respondens &c. Christus causam dividendae haereditatis prorsus à se reiicit Luc. 12. 14. sed quaestionem de divortiis non simpliciter reiicit: quinimò ex verbo DEI ostendit, quid cum normâ institutionis consentiat, quid v. pugnet. Significat ergò, quia in causis matrimonia libus multi accidunt casus conscientiarum, ideò Ecclesiae ministros non posse simpliciter causas matrimoniales à se ad Magistratum politicum reiicere.

Annon legistis. Matthaeus & Marcus (c. 10, 6.) non dissentiunt. Ille potiùs verba, quàm Christi voluntatem respicit; hic potiùs voluntatem, quàm Christi verba exprimere voluit. In illo Christus directè interrogat Iudaeos, in hoc indirectè.

Fecit hominem ab initio. Principium temporis duplex est. Vel enim significat initium creationis, vel in genere initium productionis. Principium creationis dupliciter accipitur vel in sensu totali, bel in sensu partiali. In sensu totali sive secundùm latitudinem significat initium creationis & omniū creaturam in genere, in hexaëmero creatarum, earumque initium originis & ordinis simul insinuat. In sensu partiali i. e. secundùm strictam signifi at onem significat initium creationis cuiuslibet rel in sp-cie. five significat initium originis, quo quaelibetres creata esse coepit. Hoc principium productionis potissimùm triplex est, 1. ordinationisMatth. 19, 8. 2. ordinis,Sirac. 25, 33. 3. concionis vel praedicationis Evangelii,Marc. 1, 1.

* ( ἐποίησεν ἀυτούς, subintellige ἀνθρωπουστ. Ebraismus. Solet n. in Ling. Ebr. pronomen relativum adhiberi, aliquid tanquam antecedens, quod tamen non apparet, respiciens. Vid. Ps. 10, 5. Huc facit etiam Marc. 9, 46.)*

## 19:5
* (v. 5. And he said &c. Here the words are attributed to God: A man shall leave &c. But in Gen. 2, 24. they seem to be attributed to Adam. Resp. Some, such as the Blessed Gesner and Rungius in Genesis on chapter 2, also Calixtus in the Harmony of the Gospels Hack-panius in the treatise on the Use of Rabbinical Scripture annexed to Lippomannus page 452, say that although these words are attributed to Adam instrumentally, since he spoke them from divine inspiration, they pertain to God principally. Others attribute these immediately to GOD himself, in such a way that v. 24. is joined with v. 22. and verse 23. is taken as inserted by parenthesis. Thus the Blessed Par. determines, both in the Commentary on Genesis page 63, and in the Annotations on the first epistle to Timothy p-91. & others.)*

* ( A man shall leave i.e. a male, just as the name ארם is also used in Gen 2, 15. But to leave in this place does not denote ceasing from reverence, love, and duties to be shown to parents according to the fourth commandment, but at least indicates a change of cohabitation. Hence also the reconciliation of this passage with Sirac. 3, 3. is easy)*

προσκολληθήσεται shall be glued. A metaphor taken from those things which are joined together by glue in such a way that you would think them to be one, Chrysost. hom. 63. in Matth. Cyprian also in the epistle to Florentius says with a similar metaphor that the Church is united by the glue of charity. *(Conf. 1. Cor. 6, 17.)*

* ( And the two shall be. Although the word two ῥητῶς is not had in Genes. 2, 24., it is nevertheless had διανοητικῶς, because at that time there were none except two: indeed in v. 25 it is expressly added, and they were both naked, Conf. Marc. 10, 8.1. Cor. 6, 16.Eph. 5, 31.)*

*( Είς σάοκα μίαν. the preposition είς in this place πλεονὰζει, just as also am a-there. See 1. Ioh 5, 8. the sense is, they shall be one man, no a m-not only, but also by the conjunction of bodies.

(See what D. Conr. Rittershussus collects on this matter in Sacred Readings book 3. c. 19.) because male and female are joined to each other by an indissoluble covenant. And from this it is also clear that the argumentation of Bernhard Ochino is very frivolous, who among other things strives to establish polygamy from it, That just as the law concerning loving one's neighbor is fulfilled, even if one loves very many neighbors; so also the commandment concerning loving one's wife, as one's own flesh, can be fulfilled, even if a polygamous husband loves very many wives. For one must distinguish between Christian love, which consists at least in the union of souls, and marital union, which embraces the union of bodies as well. In the former, a multitude can have a place; in the latter, it cannot. Cf. 1 Cor. 7:4. It is added that this union of spouses is far tighter than that of friends or Christians, indeed so much so that no tighter one is given in nature, since even the union that exists between children and parents yields to it. But let someone say, all the faithful are the bride of Christ. Therefore, many women can also be the wife of one man. I respond: not individual believers are the bride of Christ, speaking properly, but the whole Church, which embraces all the faithful, is the Bride of Christ. But in marriage, not all at once, but each one separately is a wife. Distinguish, furthermore, between spiritual marriages and bodily ones. But let someone oppose the example of the Patriarchs. Ambrose responds: When it was the custom, it was not a crime. Augustine in his Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians excuses the Patriarchs thus: that they themselves used women not to satisfy lust, but for the succession of offspring. Chrysostom, Homily 56 on Genesis chapter 6, inclines almost to the same: Then, he writes, because it was the beginning, it was permitted to be joined with two or three or more wives, so that the human race might be multiplied, and piety might receive increase. He adds: Christ arriving both planted virtue in men, and made men (so to speak) into Angels, and abolished that common old custom. etc. B. Dedekennus treats the polygamy of the Patriarchs at greater length in Consil. Theolog. Vol. 3, book 1, section 4; B. D. Finck, Qq. Illustr. p. 1014; B. D. Tarnov, book 2, on Marriage, chapter 25; B. Par. L. on Marriage, § 221 seqq., also Comm. on Deut. pages 340, 1057, 1264 seqq., and 1529; Comm. on Genesis p. 344, 345, and 573; B. D. Rungius on Genesis p. 151, 466; B. D. Gesner on Gen. p. 355 and 585; B. D. Balduinus, Comm. on the Epistle to the Galatians, c. 4, part 3, q. 2; B. D. Chemn. in Exam. Concil. Trid. part 2, in Exam. Canon 2, on Marriage. One may also compare the singular disputation which D. Andreas Libavius held concerning the Polygamy of the Patriarchs, printed at Coburg in the year 1612. The opinions of the Scholastics may be seen in Tanner, Vol. 4, Theol. Scholast. Disp. 8, q. 4, dub. 6, p. 2174 seqq.

Latin:

* (v. 5. Et dixit &c. Hîc Deo tribuuntur verba: Relinquet homo &c. At Gen. 2, 24. Adamo tribui videntur. Resp. Quidam, uti Bb. Dd. Gesnerus ac Rungius in Genes. ad cap. 2. it. Calixtus in Concord. Ev. Hack-panius tr. de Util. Script. Rabb. Lippomanno annexo pag. 452. dicunt, licet Adamo verba haec tribuantur instrumentaliter, cùm tamen ex inspiratione divinâ proloquutus ipse ea fuerit, pertinere illa ad Deum principaliter. Alii ipsi DEO immediatè haec tribuunt, ita quidem ut v. 24. coniungatur cum v. 22. ac versus 23. per parenthesin accipiatur insertus. Ita statuit B. Par. tum Comm. in Gen. pag. 63. tum in Annot ad pr. ep. ad Tim. p-91. & alii.)*

* ( Deseret homo i. e. vir, quomodo etiam nomen ארם adhibetur Gen 2, 15.Deserere autem h. l, non notat desistere à reverentiâ, amore & officiis, parentibus iuxta quartum praeceptum exhibendis, sed saltem cohabitationis mutationem indicat. Inde & facilis loci huius conciliatio est cum Sirac. 3, 3.)*

προσκολληθήσεται agglutinabitur. Metaphora sumpta ab his, quae glutine sic committuntur, ut putes esse unum, Chrysost. hom. 63. in Matth Cyprianus etiam in ep. ad Florentium simili Metaphorâ dicit, Ecclesiam esse glutine caritatis unitam. *(Conf. 1. Cor. 6, 17.)*

* ( Eterunt duo. Licet vocabulum duoῥητῶςGenes. 2, 24. non habeatur, habetur tamen διανοητικῶς, quia tunc non erant, nisi duo: quin v. 25. disertè subiungitur, & erant ambo nudi, Conf. Marc. 10, 8.1. Cor. 6, 16.Eph. 5, 31.)*

*( Είς σάοκα μίαν. praepositio είς h. l. πλεονὰζει, quemadmodum et am a-ibi. Vid. 1. Ioh 5, 8. sensus est, erunt unus home, no a m-rum solùm, sed etiam corporum coniunctione.

(Vide quae in hanc rem colligit D. Conr. Rittershussus Sacr. Lect. lib. 3. c. 19.) quia mas & foemina indissolubili foedere sibi invicem iuncti. Atque hinc etiam patet, quòd frivola admodùm sit argumentatio Bernhardi Ochini, ex eo inter alia polygamiam stabilire satagentis, quòd ceu lex de diligendo proximo impleatur, licet quis vel maximè plures proximos diligat: ita quoque praeceptum de diligenda uxore, tanquam propriâ carne impleri possit, si vel maximè plures uxores maritus polygamus diligat. Etenim disting. inter Christianam dilectionem, quae in animorum saltem coniunctione consistit, & inter maritalem coniunctionem, quae corporum quoque coniunctionem complectitur. Ibi multitudo potest habere locum, hîc non. Conf. 1. Cor. 7, 4. Accedit quòd haec coniugum coniunctio longè arctior sit, quàm illa amicorum s. Christianorum, ita nempe, ut nulla in naturâ detur actior, quippe cui etiam coniunctio, quae inter liberos ac parentes est, cedat. Sed dicat aliquis, omnes fideles sunt Christi sponsa. E. etiam multae foeminae possunt esse unius viri uxor. Resp. non sin guli fideles sunt Christi sponsa, propriè loquendo, sed tota Ecclesia, quae omnes fideles complectitur, Christi Sponsa est. At in matrimonio non omnes simul, sed unaquaeque seorsim uxor est. Dist. praeterea inter nuptias spirituales, ac corporales. Ast opponat aliquis exemplum Patriarcharum. Respondet Ambrosius: Quando mos erat, crimen non erat. Augustinus in Expos. ep. ad Gal. ita Patriarchas excusat, quòd ipsi usu fuerint foeminis non ad explendam libidinem, sed ad prolis successionem. Chrysostomus hom. 56. in Genes. cap. 6. eodem ferè inclinat: Tunc, scribit, quia principia erant, permissum fu-t, cum duabus aut tribus, aut pluribus uxoribus misceri, ut humanum genus multiplicaretur, & pietas incrementum caperet. addit: Adveniens Christus & virtutem in hominibus plantavit, & Angelos (ut ita dicam) ex hominibus fecit, communemque illam veterem consuetudinem abolevit. &c. Prolixiùs de Patriarcharum polygamia agunt B. Dedekennus Consil. Theolog. Volum. 3. lib. 1. sect. 4. B. D. Finck. Qq. Illustr. p. 1014 B. D. Tarnov. l. 2. de Coniug. cap. 25 B. Par. L. de Coniug. §. 221. seqq. it. Comm. in Deut. pag. 340. 1057. 1264 seqq. & 1529. Comm. in Genesin p. 344. 345. ac 573. B D. Rungius in Genesin p. 151. 466. B. D. Gesner. in Gen. p. 355. ac 585. B. D. Balduinus Comm. in Epistol. ad Gal. c. 4. part. 3. q. 2. B. D. Chemn in Exam. Concil. Trid. part. 2. in Exam. Canon. 2. de Matrimonio. Conferri quoque potest singularis disput. quam de Polyg. Patriarch. habuit D. Andreas Libavius, typis descriptam Coburgi Anno 1612. Scholasticorum opiniones videantur apud Tannerum Tom. 4. Theol. Scholast. Disp 8. q. 4. dub. 6. p. 2174. seqq.)*

## 19:6
v. 6. They are no longer two. Christ, inferring from the Mosaic statement that spouses are no longer two, shows by his own example that it is permitted to collect from Scripture what is not written.

But one flesh. There is between spouses unity 1. natural, on account of the participation of the same human nature. 2. moral, on account of familiar conversation. 3. Spiritual, on account of the spiritual coalition in the head of the Church. 4. bodily. (* Camero also discourses beautifully concerning this conjunction in Myroth. p. 96. add. B. D. Konig Cas. Consc. p. 533. Some think that the Apostle also looks to this Rom. 5, 12. and by through one man understands Adam and Eve there. See B. Par. Comm. in Genes. page 88.)*

*( What God has joined, let not man put asunder. Some use this axiom against the Papists, who tear apart the wine and blood of Christ in the Holy Eucharist. Becanus replies in Disp. de Com. sub utraque specie, that it clearly appears from thence that they are either insane or remarkably petulant. For what, he continues, connection is there, Man cannot separate husband from wife: Therefore he cannot communicate under one species. He adds: If they proceed in this way, they will without doubt persuade that no criminal, however wicked, no wild beast, cattle, etc., can be killed by man: Why? because what GOD has joined, let not man put asunder: but God has joined the soul with the body, etc. I reply 1. No one of our side argues in that way, as the Jesuit slanders. But as he himself was forced to admit at the beginning, the argument is this: Christ Matthew 19. said: What God has joined, let not man put asunder. But God has joined both species. Therefore the Pontiff cannot separate one from the other. If anyone compares this argumentation with the connection which Becanus agitates as if it were ours, he will discover that the Jesuit confuses the subsumption with the major proposition. We do not seek the argument from the subsumption of Christ, but from the major, which consists of that axiom: That is, whatever God has joined, let no man put asunder. 2. That the Jesuit denies that this axiom of Christ is universal, and therefore cannot be applied to all joined things without absurdity, concerns the axiom itself. We also confess the same, adding however that a distinction must be made between those things which are naturally united, and those which are by divine ordination joined. Of the former kind are those things which the Jesuit opposes to us, and are therefore foreign to the question, for it is not denied that things united in such a way can be torn apart; although it must not be denied that when God has joined soul and body in man, no one, unless a divine command intervenes, ought to tear those parts asunder and kill an innocent man. That, however, a guilty person is killed with impunity by the Magistrate, happens on account of a special command of GOD. Gen. 9, 6.Rom. 13, 4. As far as things of the latter kind are concerned, the axiom of Christ remains firm and universal for the time being, until the Jesuit brings forward an example to the contrary. Thus, because God has joined male and female, no one ought to separate spouses after marriage has been legitimately celebrated. Similarly, because in Baptism water and the word are divinely joined, no one can or ought to administer Baptism without water or without the word, or separate one from the other in the administration of Baptism. The reason for the symbols in the S. Eucharist is equal to that of the heavenly thing. 3. Finally, it is to be observed that hardly one or two of our people use this argument against communion under one kind. Philip Mornay certainly, to whom Becanus attributes this argument, brings forward the axiom of Christ in an entirely different way, as the blessed Doctor Balduinus taught long ago in his notes to the Disputation of Becanus, page 280. Compare also the blessed Pareus, Catholic Confession, volume 3, book 2, special part 1, article 15, chapter 7, examination of the exception to argument 7. Furthermore, it stands against this divine pronouncement that God himself is read to have ordained Exod. 21, 4. that a servant in the seventh year is commanded to go out alone, and to leave his wife, together with his children, to his master, if, namely, he had given him a wife before that time, namely a foreign maidservant. Response: This was a ceremonial law, promulgated to the end that no Jew would so easily descend into marriage with a foreigner, as the Lord Doctor Walther shows more prolixly (H. B. on chapter 2 of Genesis, verse 24)*

Latin:

v. 6. Itaiā non sunt duo. Christus ex dicto Mosaico inferens, coniuges non ampliùs esse duo, suo exemplo ostendit, licere ex scripto colligere, quod non est scriptum.

Seduna caro. Est inter coniuges unitas 1. naturalis, propter eiusdem humanae naturae participationem. 2. moralis, propter familiarem conversationem. 3. Spiritualis, propter spiritualem in Ecclesiae capite coalitionem. 4. corporalis. (* Pulcrè quoque de hac coniunctione disserit Camero in Myroth. p. 96. add. B. D. Konig Cas. Consc. p. 533. Putant nonnulli, quòd huc quoque respiciat Apostolus Rom. 5, 12. ac per unum hominem ibi intelligat Adamum & Evam. Vid. B. Par. Comm. in Genes. pag. 88.)*

*( Quod Deus coniunxit, homo non separet. Utuntur hoc axiomate aliqui adversus Pontificios, vinum & sanguinem Christi in S. Eucharistiâ divellentes. Respondet Becanus Disp. de Com. sub utraque specie, exinde plane apparere, aut insanos aut insigniter cos petulantes esse. Quae enim, pergit, connexio est, Homo non potest separare virum ab uxore: E. non potest communicare sub unâ specie. addit: Si sic pergant, sine dubio persuadebunt, nullum reum, quantumvis sceleratum, nullam feram, pecudem &c. necari ab homine posse: Quare? quia quod DEUS coniunxit, homo non separet: sed Deus coniunxit animam cum corpore &c. Resp. 1. Nemo nostratium ita argumentatur, ceu Iesuita calumniatur. Sed uti ipse initiò fateri co actus fuit, h. m. ChristusMatth. 19.dixit: Quod Deus coniunxit, homo non separet. At qui Deus coniunxit utramq speciem. E. Pontifex non potest unam ab alter â separare. Quam argumentationem si quis conferat cum connexione, quam Becanus quasinostram exagitat, deprehendet, quòd Iesuita confundat subsumtionem cum propositione maiore. Non petimus argumentum à subsumtione Christi, sed à maiore, quae constat axiomate isto: Quod s. quicquid Deus coniunxit, homo non separet. 2. Quod ipsum axioma Christi concernit, negat Iesuita, id universale esse, adeoque non posse sine absurditate ad omnia coniuncta applicari. Idem & nos fatemur, addentes tamen, quòd disting. sit inter ea, quae naturaliter sunt unita, & inter ea quae ex ordinatione divinâ sunt coniuncta. Prioris generis sunt ea, quae Iesuita nobis opponit, adeoque à quaestione aliena, neque enim negatur, quòd taliter unita divelli queant; quamvis nec id negandum sit, quòd cùm Deus animam & corpus in homine coniunxerit, nemo nisi ubi divinum mandatum accedat, partes illas divellere, hominemq; innocentem interficere debeat. quòd v. reus impunè interficitur à Magistratu, fit propter speciale DEI mandatum. Gen. 9, 6.Rom. 13, 4. Quod posterioris generis unita concernit, tantisper firmum ac universale manet Christi axioma, donec Iesuita exemplum in contrarium adducat. Sic quia Deus coniunxit marem & foeminam, nemo debet coniuges, post nuptias legitimè celebratas, seiungere. Similiter quia in Baptismo divinitus coniuncta sunt aqua & verbum, nemo absque aqua vel absque verbo potest aut debet Baptismum administrare, vel unum ab altero in Baptismi administratione separare. Par ratio symbolorum in S. Eucharistiâ est cum re coelesti. 3. Denique observandum, quòd vix unus aut alter ex nostratibus argumento isto contra communionem sub unâ utatur. Philippus certè Mornaeus, cui argumentum hoc Becanus tribuit, prorsus aliter axioma Christi adducit, uti pridem docuit B D. Balduinus in notis ad Disp. Becani pag. 280. Conf. etiam B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. 3. s. l. 2. Sp. part. 1. arc. 15. c. 7 exam. Exc. ad arg 7. Coeterùm obstat huic pronunciato divino, quòd Deus ipse sancivisse legitur Exod. 21, 4. quòd servus in anno septimo iubeatur egredi solus, suamque uxorē, una cum liberis relinquere domino, si sc. ei antehac uxorem, nempe ancillam alienigenam dederit. Resp. Fuit haec lex ceremonialis, promulgata eo fine, ne quispiam Iudaeus adeo facilè in coniugium cū alienigenâ descenderet, uti prolixiùs ostendit Dn. D. Walth. (H. B. ad c. 2. Gen. v. 24)*

## 19:7
*(v. 7. Ενετείλατο — "he commanded." But Moses had not commanded, but had only permitted; hence also the Savior in v. 8 appears to correct the Pharisees' statement — so that from this someone might persuade himself that the Pharisees had deliberately exaggerated the matter, unless one prefers to say that, just as the word צוה signifies not only to command but also to permit (as John Cameron observes in his Myrothecium Evangelicum, p. 98, proving this from 1 Kings 5:6), so too the word ἐνετείλατο, which the LXX sometimes use for צוה, is employed here in the same sense. The same Cameron notes in the same place that a precept is spoken of in two ways: either as pertaining to law, or as pertaining to a relaxation of the law. If it pertains to law, he writes, it is properly called a precept; if it pertains to a relaxation of the law, it is a moral permission. He illustrates this with the example of a magistrate who, though he takes no pleasure in any vice, nevertheless permits many things — that is, provided they are done in a certain regulated way, he does not punish them — not because he approves of them, even when done in that regulated way, but because otherwise he cannot prevent a greater evil. Nor is the magistrate's conscience thereby bound, provided he does whatever can be done in that regard to preserve the commonwealth, since, were it overthrown, the good, mixed in with the wicked, would also perish. This explanation coincides with the interpretation of those who say that Moses, in the precept concerning the giving of a bill of divorce, conducted himself after the manner of a political legislator, and so permitted the giving of a bill of divorce — not as though this were in accord with the eternal norm of divine justice, or with the institution of marriage, but only in the civil forum, lest something worse should occur. For the Jews were a stiff-necked people (Exod. 32:9), and they treated their wives, against whom they had conceived such hatred, with such inhumanity and cruelty that wife-murder was to be feared if they had been compelled always to keep them. Compare the Blessed D. Balduin, Commentary on Malachi, ch. 2, pp. 979–980. It is also worth observing that Moses permitted divorce as though reluctantly. For he commands that a bill of divorce be written, and moreover provides that it should not be lawful for a husband afterward to take back into his house the wife whom he had divorced. The former provision was meant to check the impulse of passion and to leave room for deliberation; the latter, so that they would not hold so cheaply a thing for the recovery of which no further hope would remain. Finally, it was not for just any cause, but on account of some impropriety — either newly arising, or discovered by the husband only after the marriage had been contracted — that it was permitted to the husband to give a bill of divorce. But this too must not be passed over here: that an equal power was not granted to wives over their husbands, such that it was also lawful for them to depart from unwilling husbands. The reason for this is not only that divorces would otherwise have been too frequent, but also that the husband is the head of the wife. Just as, then, a father sometimes deals harshly with his son without wrongdoing, though the same is by no means granted to the son against the father, so also the right which husbands had over wives was not the same as that which wives had over husbands. Compare the Blessed Par., Commentary on Deuteronomy.)*

Βίβλος ἀποστασίου. In Hebrew it is called in Syriac The writing of desertion. *(The form of the bill of divorce was as follows: On this day of the week, on this or that day of the month N. in this or that year of the creation of the world, according to the number by which we are accustomed to count here in the place N. That I N. son of N. from the place N. and every other name or surname which is mine or my ancestors', of my country, or the country of my parents, have willed with the free will of my mind, not compelled, and I have repudiated and dismissed and cast out. Thee, I say, N. daughter of N. who art from the city N. or if there is any other name or surname for thee or thy parents, or thy country, or the country of them, namely thy parents, who wast my wife heretofore, now truly I dismiss and cast thee out, I repudiate, that thou mayest be free and mistress of thyself to go away and to marry any man whom thou shalt wish, and let no one be rejected through thee on account of my name, from this day even unto eternity. And thus be thou lawful to every man, and this shall be for thee from me a bill of expulsions, and a bill of divorce, and a letter of dismissal, according to the law of Moses and Israel. The Hebrew words are reported from R. Moses ben Maimon, Hal. Gerusch. c. 4. fol. 59. and illustrated with annotations by Johannes Buxtorf around the end of the Chaldean Grammar p. 399. A more recent example of a bill of divorce is presented likewise in Hebrew and Latin by Wilhelm Schickard in On the Law of the Hebrew Kings p. 73. That is worthy of observation, that the bill of divorce could not be written by the husband himself, but by a certain public scribe, who would first attempt, as much as was in his power, to bring the estranged spouses back to their former concord. Johannes Drusius teaches this from Augustine, book 19 against Faustus the Manichaean, c. 26, in book 14 of Observations, c. 10. Let the same be added, book 1 of Preterita p. 13, likewise Samuel Petit, book 2 of Various Readings, c. 9, Paulus Fagius in Annotations to the Chaldean Paraphrase of Deut. 24. B. Par. collected more on divorce in Commentary on Deut. p. 1435. et seqq., likewise L. on Marriage § 595. et seqq.)*

Let not man put asunder. Theophylactus ἀνθρώπου interprets Moses. ρη --κ εἶπε *(When I, God, by the intervention of the death of one of the spouses, dissolve the bond of matrimony, then the surviving party can pass to second nuptials. Which is also taught elsewhere. See Rom. 7, 2.1. Corinth. 7, 39.1. Tim. 5, 14. The Savior is speaking, to be sure, of separation made by human will, which He teaches is repugnant to the primordial institution of marriage. Bell, however, deceives and is deceived when he asserts likewise that a separation is made by God, where a faithful spouse is separated from an unfaithful one, and that 1. Cor. 7, 12.15. the Apostle teaches this, concerning which [I speak] more prolixly at the said place. Furthermore, when the Magistrate institutes divorce, while he gives the innocent party the power of entering into a new marriage, when indeed the other party has separated himself or herself either through adultery or through malicious desertion, he does not oppose the divine ordinance, but administers the judgments of God.)*

Latin:

*(v. 7. Ενετείλατοmandavit. Atqui Moses non mandaverat, sed permiserat saltem: unde etiam Salvator v. 8. corrigere videtur Pharisaeorum sermonem. ut hinc persuadere sibi aliquis possit, Pharisaeos de industriâ rem in maius auxisse: nisi dicere malit, quòd uti verbum צוה non solùm praecipere, verùm etiam permittere notat, (observante Ioanne Camerone in Myroth. Evang. p. 98 idque probante ex 1 Reg. 5, 6.) ita quoque verbum ἐνετείλατο, quo LXX. pro צוה aliquando utuntur, hîc adhibeatur. Idem Camero d. l. notat, quòd praeceptum duobus modis dicatur, vel ut sit iuris, vel ut pertineat ad iuris relaxationem; si iuris est, scribit, praeceptum propriè dicitur; si pertinet ad iuris relaxationem, permissio moralis. Illustrat rem hanc exemplo Magistratùs, qui etsi nullo delectetur vitio, attamen multa permittat, hoc est, modò certâ ratione fiant, non puniat, non quòd ea probet, etiam facta certâ illâ ratione, sed quia aliter malo obviam ire non potest. Neque tamen propterea obstrictam teneri Magistratûs conscientiam, dummodo faciat, quicquid in eo genere fieri possit ad conservandam Rempublicam, quâ eversâ etiam boni malis mixti pereunt. Coincidit cum explicatione hâc eorum interpretatio qui dicunt, quòd Moses in praecepto de libello repudii dando sese gesserit instar legislatoris Politici, adeoque permiserit, dare libe lum repudii, non quasi hoc congrueret cum normâ iustitiae divinae aeternâ, aut cum coniugii institutione, sed in foro Politico saltem, ne quid peius accideret. Erant enim Iudaei populus durae cervicis,Exod 32, 9. uxoresque suas, quas contra conceperant odium tantâ, inhumanitate & truculentiâ tractabant, ut uxoricidium metuendum esset, si coacti fuissent, eas semper retinere. Conf. B. D. Balduin. Comm. in Malach. c. 2 p 979. 980. Observationem meretur quoque, quòd Moses quasi invitus divortium permiserit. Etenim iubet scribi libellum repudii, ac insuper cavet, ne marito liceret inposterum uxorem, quam repudiaverat, revocare domum. Illud quò animi impetus sufflaminaretur, spatiumque deliberandi eis relinqueretur; hoc, ne adeò parvi aestimarent, cuius recuperandi nulla spes ampliùs esset relicta. Denique non ob quamcunq; causam, sed propter foeditatem aliquam, vel de novo supervenientem, vel post matrimonium contractum demum à marito deprehensam, integrum marito erat, libellum repudii dare. Sed nec illud praetereundum hîc, quòd non par potestas uxoribus concessa in maritos fuerit, ita ut eis quoque licuerit, à maritis invitis discedere. Cuius rei ratio est non solùm, quòd nimis aliàs divortia fuissent frequentia, verùm etiam, quia vir uxoris caput est. Quemadmodum igitur Pater sine iniuriâ quandoque in filium saevit, quod tamen haut aequè filio concessum in Patrem est: ita etiam non idem ius, quod viris in uxores erat, his quoque in illos fuit. Conf. B. Par. Comm. in Deut.)*

Βίβλος ἀποστασίου. Ebraicè dicitur Syriacè Scriptura desertionis. *(Forma libelli repudii talis erat: Isto die septimanae, isto vel isto mensis N. anno isto vel isto creationis mundi, iuxta numerum, quo consvevimus numerare hîc in loco N. Quòd ego N. filius N. ex loco N. & omne nomen aliud vel cognominatio, quae est mihi vel maioribus meis, patriae meae, aut patriae parentum meorum, volui voluntate libera animi mei non coactè, & repudiavi & dimisi & expulite. Te, inquam, N. Filiam N. quae es ex urbe N. aut si quod nomen aliud aut cognomen est tibi aut parentibus tuis, aut patriae tuae, aut patriae ipsorum, scilicet parentum tuorum, quae fuisti uxor mea antehac, nunc verò dimitto & expello te, repudio, ut fias libera & Domina tui ipsius ad abeundum & nubendum omni viro, cui volueris, & nemo reiiciatur per te propter nomen meum, à die hoc usq in seculum It aq licita esto omni homini, & hicce erit tibi à me libellus expulsionum, & libellus repudii, & epistola dimissionis, iuxta legem Mosis & Israel. Verba Ebrae a ex R. Mose, ben Maymon Hal. Gerusch. c. 4. fol. 59. refert & annotationibus illustrat Ioh. Buxtorffius circa finem Gram. Chald p. 399. Recentius verò exemplar libelli repudii sistit itidem Ebraicè ac Lat. Wilhelm. Schickardus in de iure Reg. Ebr. p. 73. Illud observatione dignum est, quòd libellus repudii non potuerit ab ipso marito scribi, sed àscriba quodam publico, qui priùs conaret ur. quantum in se erat, distractos cō-uges in pristinam reducere concordiam Docet id ex August. l. 19. contra Faustum Manich. c. 26. Iohan. Drusius lib. 14. Observ. c. 10. Addatur idem lib. 1. Praeteritorum p. 13. it. Samuel Petitus lib. 2. Variar. lect. c. 9 Paulus Fagius in Annot ad Paraphr. Chald. Deut. 24. Plura de repudio collegit B. Par. Com. in Deut. p. 1435. seqq. it. L. de Coniug. § 595. seqq.)*

Homo non separet. Theophylactus ἀνθρώπου interpretatur Mosen. ρη --κ εἶπε *(Quando ego Deus interventu mortis alterius ex coniugibus matrimonii vinculum solvit, tunc pars superstes ad secundas transire nuptias potest. Quod etiam alibi docetur. Vid. Rom. 7, 2.1. Corinth. 7, 39.1. Tim. 5, 14. Loquitur nempe Salvator de separatione arbitrio humano factâ, quam primaevae coniugii institutioni repugnare docet. Fallit autem ac fallitur Bell, quando itidem à Deo separationem fieri adserit, ubi fidelis coniux ab infideli feparatur, idq1. Cor. 7, 12.15.Apostolum docere scribit, de quo ad d. l. prolixiùs. Quando porrò Magistratus divortium instituit, dum parti innocenti potestatem facit novum coniugium ineundi, quando nempe altera pars vel per adulterium vel per malitiosam desertionem sese separaverit, non adversatur ille ordinationi divinae, sed iudicia Dei administrat.)*

## 19:8
v. 8. Πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν, for the hardness of your heart, i.e., having regard to it. It was not a marriage-law but a defense-law. He taught that it is best to cleave to one's wife, but that a greater evil to be feared from the contumacious might be avoided, He granted it. *(The observation of our theologians pertains to this, that Moses sustained a double person, as it were, namely, first as Prophetic Doctor. Then as Political Legislator. In the former way, if he is considered, it was well known to him that divorces and Polygamy are repugnant to the primordial institution of marriage, but in the latter way viewed, he permitted divorces to the contumacious people to avert a greater evil, lest γυν αικομίσοι they should become γυναικοφὸνοι. The Pharisees did not observe that distinction, as they interpreted that law, promulgated by Moses as a political Legislator to prevent a greater evil, as if it were good in itself and before God to give a bill of divorce. They are gravely rebuked by Christ on that account, who [are] of their ἐνετείλατο changes here into ἐπέτρεψεν. See Lord Dr. Danhawerus in Idea boni Interpr. p. 278. B. Par. l. de Leg. Cerem §. 37. also Com. in ep. ad Rom. p. 94. B. D. Hùlsem. Brev. Extensi p. 424. Lord Dr. M-llerus Iudaismi p. 1068 seqq. B. D. Tarnov. de coniug. p. 624. Hack-pan. tr. de utilit lect Rabb. p. 413. Add. Camero in Myroth. Ev. p. 97 98)*

*(Q. here 1. Can the polygamy of the Fathers also be said to have been granted on account of σκληροκαρδίαν in the O. T.? Resp. The Savior indeed deals directly here with divorce, meanwhile the same answer κατ ἀναλογίαι can also be applied to polygamy. Furthermore, just as among the Jews polygamy was granted on account of σκληροκαρδίαν, so for the same reason and for the sake of avoiding a greater evil, legal experts teach that concubinage was formerly permitted by civil law, as is evident from the title ff. & C. de concubinatu. See Giphanius in Antinomiis Iuris. l. 1. disp. 3 p. 58 n. 10. 11. Concubinage was, however, later abolished even by civil law, as can be seen from Constitut. 91. of Emperor Leo. But whether concubinage has also been abolished by Canon Law , authors disagree, just as the blessed Par. L. de coniug. §. 557. 558. notes, also the blessed D. Roenig Cas. Catech pag. 535. & seqq where he also teaches that the same was severely prohibited by the Constitutions of the Roman Emperor, with the prior Sc. S., and therefore he also concludes and proves with many arguments that a manifest concubinary cannot be admitted with a good conscience to the use of the Lord's Supper.)*

Q. 2. Was the power of giving a bill of divorce also granted to wives? Resp. B. Par. in his Commentary on Deut. c. 24, p. 1442, warns that this indeed obtained in the polities of other nations, but not among the Jews. Certainly, Camero in Myrothecium Evangelicum, p. 182, notes that it is evident from Mark 10:12 that wives among them were also accustomed to perform a divorce: but the same author rightly teaches in the aforementioned place, p. 97, that this was by no means granted to them by divine law, nor was it done through the presentation of a bill of divorce. Although it can by no means be denied that, on account of the husband’s adultery, a Hebrew wife could formerly rightly seek from the Magistrate the dissolution of the marriage and the power to enter into a new one, just as the same obtains among Christians today.)* *( Επέτρεψεν |

*( Επέτρεψνελ permitted, did not command, as is well observed by Isidorus Pelusiota, who in book 3. op. 76. No, he writes, it was not that he ought to cast out those who violated the law of marriage less, but that he might repress a greater and more serious evil , he did not indeed sanction the lesser evil by law, but permitted it. See more on this matter in the same place in the same book.)*

Ἀπ ἀρχῆς. Beginning is understood as production through ordination* (or the primordial institution of marriage)* He teaches that the reason for all things which are observed by the Church must be traced back to the beginnings. Tertullian, book on prescription, ch. 13. Thus it is manifested from the order itself, that that is the Lord's and true, which was delivered first: but that is foreign and false, which was introduced later. *(It is evident, therefore, from this what true antiquity is, namely, not some inveterate custom, or an opinion of some prescription, but that which is drawn from the sacred and divine letters. Against the Papists, who clamor that antiquity, even if destitute of the protection of the divine word, is a genuine mark of the Church. How erroneous an opinion this is, B. Par. shows at length in Confess. Cath. book 2, spec. part 1, p. 1152, seqq. and L. on the Church §. 162)*

*( It was not so. Chrysostom on the bill of divorce: If this had been the case, he would not have made one man and one woman, but with one Adam created, he would have made two women, if indeed he had wished for one to be cast out and another to be brought in)*

Latin:

v. 8. Πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν,ad duritiem cordis, sc. respectum habens. Es ist nicht ein Eehr-sondern Wehr-Beser gewesen. Optimum esse docuit, uxori suae adhaerere, sed ut maius malum à contumacibus metuendum caveretur, concessit. *(Huc facit observatio nostratium Theologorum, quòd Moses duplicem quasi sustinuerit personam, videl. primò ut Doctoris Prophetici. Deinde ut Legislatoris Politici. Priori modô si consideretur, probè ipsi notum fuit, divortia & Polygamiam primaevae coniugii institutioni repugnare, posteriori verò modo spectatus permisit contumaci populo divortia ad maius malum avertendum, ne γυν αικομίσοι illi fierent γυναικοφὸνοι. Discrimen illud Pharisaei non observarunt, ut qui legem illam ad praecavendum maius malum à Mose ut politico Legislatore promu-gatam ita interpretabātur, ac si per se & coram Deo bonum esset, libellum repudii dare. graviter à Christo propterea reprehenduntur, qui ipsorum ἐνετείλατο commutat hîc in ἐπέτρεψεν. Vid. Dn. D. Danhawerus in Idea boni Interpr. p. 278. B. Par. l. de Leg. Cerem §. 37. it. Com. in ep. ad Rom. p. 94. B. D. Hùlsem. Brev. Extensi p. 424. Dn. D. M-llerus Iudaismi p. 1068 seqq. B. D. Tarnov. de coniug. p. 624. Hack-pan. tr. de utilit lect Rabb. p. 413. Add. Camero in Myroth. Ev. p. 97 98)*

*(Q. hîc 1. An etiam Polygamia Patrum propterσκληροκαρδίανin V. T. concessa dici queat? Resp. Agit quidem Salvator directè hîc de repudio, intereàeadem responsio κατ ἀναλογίαι ad polygamiam applicari quoque potest. Caeterùm sicuti apud Iudaeos polygamia propter σκληροκαρδίαν concessa erat, ita ob candem causam & maioris mali evitandi causa iure civili, ceu patet ex tit. ff. &C. de concubinatu, concubinatum olim permissum fuisse, Iure consulti docent. Vid. Giphanius in Antinomiis Iuris. l. 1. disp. 3 p. 58 n. 10. 11. Sublatus tamen postea concubinatus etiam iure civili est, uti videre licet ex Constitut. 91. Imper. Leonis. An verò etiam Iure Canonico co-cubinatus sublatus sit, dissentiunt autores, quemadmodum annotat B. Par. L. de coniug. §. 557. 558. it. B. D. Roenig Cas. Catech pag. 535. & seqq ubi etiam docet, quod idem per Constitutiones Imper. Romani, praevia Sc. S. severè prohibitus fit, adeoqque etiam concludit ac multis probat, quod concubinarius manifestus bonâ conscientia admitti, ad usum Coenae Dominicae non possit.)*

*(Q. 2. An etiam uxoribus uxoribus concessa fuerit facultas dan-s repudii? Resp. Monet B Par. Comm in Deut. c. 24. p. 1442. -aliarum quidem gentium politiis id obtinuisse, non verò apud Iudeos. Sanè & apud hos uxores solitas fuisse divortium facere, Camero in Myroth. Ev. p. 182 ex Marc. 10, 12. patere notat: Verùm minimè lege divinâ illis hoc ipsum concessum fuisse, vel per repudii libelli exhibitionem id factum esse, idem d. l. p. 97. rec-e docet. Quamvis minimè negari possit, quòd propter mariti adulterium uxor olim Ebraea rectè solutionem matrimonii, ac novi ineundi potestatem à Magistratu perere potuerit, ceu adhuc inter Christianos idem obtinet.)*

*( Επέτρεψνελpermisit, non praecepit, uti probè observat lsidorus Pelusiota, qui lib. 3. op. 76. Non, scribit, tanquam eas, quae matrimonii legem minùs violarunt, eiicere oporteret, sedut maius & gravius malum repr-meret, minus malum non quidem lege sanxit, sed permisit. Conf. plura in hanc rem apud eund. l. c.)*

Ἀπ ἀρχῆς.Initium intelligitur productionis per ordinationem* (sive primaeva coniugii institutio)* Docet, omnium quae observantur ab Ecclesia, rationem reducendam ad initia. Tertullianus lib. de praescript. c. 13. Ita ex ipso ordine manifestatur, id esse Dominicum & verum, quod sit priùs traditum: id autem extraneum & falsum, quod sit posteriùs immissum. *(Patet igitur hinc, quae sit vera antiquitas, scil. non inveterata quaedam consuet-do, vel praescriptionis cuiusdam opinio, sed quae ex sacris litteris divinisque depromitur. Contra Pontificios, qui antiquitatem, licet verbi divini praesidio destitutam, genuinam Ecclesiae notam esse clamitant. quae quàm erronea opinio sit, prolixè ostendit B. Par. Confess. Cath. l. 2. spec, part. 1. p. 1152. seqq. it L. de Eccles. §. 162)*

*( Non fuit sic. Chrysostomus de libello Repudii: Si hoc fuisset, non unum virum & unam mulierem, sed uno Adam condito duas fecisset mulieres, si quidem voluisset, unam quidem eiici, alteram induci)*

## 19:9
*(v. 9. Whoever shall divorce his wife, except for fornication &c. Isidore of Pelusium, book 3, p. 76. Christ himself commanded those who violate the law of marriage to be cast out: but unless this happens, he commanded that all other vices of a wife be borne, nay, he pronounced it to be necessary. Nor indeed is that in vain and rashly. For other vices do not at all look to each of those who are joined by the law of marriage: adultery tends to the marriage covenants themselves, καὶ τὴν τῶν παίδων καθυβρίζει ευγένειαν i. e. the nobility of children, or as Conr. Ritterhusius prefers, affects well-born character with insult, and tears apart relationships, and finally ruins and overturns all human life. Furthermore, if Christ commanded a wife to be cast out and divorced on account of adultery, it follows that the innocent party can separate themselves from the guilty party, not only as to the bed, but also as to the bond, and enter into another marriage. Not, however, by private daring, but by the prior decision of the Magistrate. Which opinion, flowing from the words of Christ, the Council of Trent, sess. 24, can. 7, strikes with anathema in vain, and the rest of the Papists commonly attack vehemently, but in vain. They have indeed supported the same both from other sayings of Holy Scripture, and from the present place B. D. Hi--sem. Breviar. Extenso p. 446. B. Par. Confess. Cathol. book 2 spec. part 3, p. 247. also L. on Marriage §. 564, seqq. Corn. à Lapide excepts to this place in his Commentary on this place.) First, Augustine, book 1, On Adulterous Marriages, ch. 9, τὸ unless, to take negatively, so that τὸ except for fornication is the same as outside the case of fornication. He adds: The Greek and the Syriac favor this, which have: not an adulteress: as if Christ only wishes to affirm that a faithful and chaste wife cannot be dismissed, but wishes to say nothing about an unfaithful one, i.e., an incestuous and adulterous one, to avoid the ill will of the Pharisees and the people, since at that time the repudiation of adulteresses and new marriages with others were lawful and customary. I reply: 1. Did Christ therefore dissemble the truth to decline the ill will of the Pharisees and the people? The sufficiently sharp sermons, with which He taxed the vices of the Pharisees, teach the contrary. See Matthew 23, v 13 and following. His own enemies also testify to the contrary, Matthew 22, 16. 2. It is false that the Greek text favors that opinion, which wishes these words to be taken negatively: for the particles εἰ μὴ unless are used no less exceptively than negatively, as is clear from an inspection of ch. 11, 27, ch. 12, 4, 39, ch. 19, 17, ch. 21, 19, ch. 24, 36, etc., in which places the Papists themselves acknowledge that the particles εἰ μὴ are exclusive or exceptive. See Corn. à Lapide on ch. 11, 27, ch. 12, 4, ch. 24, 36. Compare more things pertaining to this in B. Hackspan, Disp. 3, On Sacred Locutions, § 29 and following. That those particles ought to be explained exceptively rather than negatively in this place is clear from a collation of the parallel place, ch. 5, 32, where παρεκτός, is held and is expressly rendered by the Vulgate except for the cause of fornication. There is no doubt, therefore, that if in the parallel place τὸ παρεκτός is taken exceptively, as it is rightly explained by the Vulgate Matthew 5, it can and must be explained in this place τὸεἰ μὴ in the same way.
