It is strange, however, that Corn. à Lapide embraces the opinion, -ui, he implies that the Greek text favors it, having deserted that which the Vulgate version favors, when he ought to have been mindful of the decree of the Council of Trent, session 4, where it is said the Council established, that the old and Vulgate Latin edition be held as authentic in public readings, disputations, and expositions, and that no one dare or presume to reject it under any pretexts. Ioh. Paludanus, Doctor of Theology and Professor of Louvain, in Theological Vindications on Matthew 5, 32, and Felicianus Capito, Archbishop of Avignon, in Catholic Explanation of the Books of the Old and New Testament on Matthew 5, p. 406, urge against us 1. parallel sayings 1 Corinthians 7, 10, 11, Romans 7, 3, Ephesians 5, but about these in their own place. 2. that the words of the Lord are to be gathered from all the Evangelists together: since therefore both in Mark ch. 10 and in Luke ch. 16, 18 Christ is brought forward as absolutely denying that a wife is to be dismissed, the place Matthew 5 where the Savior seems to teach that a wife is not to be dismissed, unless for the cause of fornication, is to be explained according to the rest. I reply: Rather, because Christ adds a limitation at Matthew ch. 5, 32 and here, the remaining Evangelists are not to be understood absolutely, but with such a limitation. But Bellarmine insists, that indeed sometimes one Evangelist adds something that the others omitted, but never in such a way that the sentence is rendered false, because otherwise they would have deceived the men to whom they delivered their Gospels, with no mention made of the other Evangelists. I reply: 1. Why then, if deception is feigned to the Evangelists from an addition, do Bellarmine and other Papists add a restriction to the general or certainly indefinite words of the Evangelists, at least for a marriage contracted between the faithful? Which restriction or exception, however, was added neither by Christ nor by any of the Evangelists. 2. God willed that the entire volume of the New Testament should exist, among other ends also for this, that those things which were omitted by one or another Evangelist might be supplied from the rest. Although, therefore, that very Evangelist who omits some circumstance or restriction does not make mention of the other Evangelists, it suffices, however, that the writings of all the Evangelists have been entrusted to the Church. Paludanus objects, if marriage were dissolved through adultery, it would follow that the bill of divorce was not altogether abolished, which however was granted to the Jews at least because of the hardness of their heart. I reply: I distinguish between a divorce, undertaken for a light cause and outside the case of adultery by private judgment, such as was in use among the Jews, as Nicolaus de Lyra, who became a Christian from a Jew, testifies in his Postilla on ch. 24 of Deuteronomy, and a divorce, because of adultery, made by the public judgment of the Magistrate. Christ abrogated divorce considered in the former way, not in the latter. Just as, therefore, our Savior

Elsewhere he abrogated and condemned private, rash, etc. judgments, while nevertheless saving the right of public judgments, which are made by the Magistrate: thus here he disapproved of private, rash, and lightly undertaken divorces, yet in such a way that he at the same time approves of repudiation and divorce (on account of preceding adultery) made through the Magistrate, since he adds in express words a limitation to the prohibition, namely, except for fornication. The same Paludanus urges the authority of Innocent I, epistle 3 to Exup. c. 6. Likewise Alexander III, chapter Ex parte, and finally the African Council, c. 69, the Council of Forum Julii, canon 10, the Councils of Nantes, Florence, and Trent. But long ago Thomas de Vio, Cardinal Cajetan, whom they otherwise extol with great papal praises, responded to this objection. He, however, says explicitly on this passage: Understand from this law of the Lord Jesus Christ that it is lawful for a Christian to dismiss his wife on account of the carnal fornication of the wife herself, and to be able to marry another, always saving the definition of the Church, which does not yet appear. For the papal decretals on this matter are not definitive of faith, but judicial of fact. Moreover, the Pontiffs themselves profess, as is evident in c. 4 de divortiis, and in the chapter Licet de sponsa duorum, that the Roman Pontiffs have sometimes erred in these judgments of marriages. Nor am I the first who has understood the text of the Gospel in this way, since a thousand years ago Blessed Ambrose, understanding it thus, taught the same. Ambrose Catharinus, Bishop of Conza, agrees with Cajetan both in a specific booklet on this question and in his Commentary on 1 Corinthians 7. Felicianus Capitonus indeed retorts in the cited place that one must judge with the Master of the Sentences that the books of Ambrose were stained with the spots of errors by heretics, and that he did not hold that opinion. But since no foundation is brought forward for this conjecture, it is rejected with the same ease with which it is adduced. That, however, must be well held, that both Capitonus in the cited place and Sixtus of Siena admit Pope Zachary I, and the Councils of Elvira, Mainz, and Tribur granted divorce, even regarding the bond itself. Since their decrees are in agreement with the words of Christ, they are deservedly preferred to the decrees of those Pontiffs and Councils which Paludanus brings against us. How ineptly Erbermannus defended Bellarmine in the present controversy , while he touches upon barely the tenth thesis of those which Blessed Pareus disputed against Bellarmine in the Bellarminus Orthodoxus, it is worth the reader's effort to learn from his defenses in volume 3. Blessed D. Chemnitius in Part 2 of the Examination of the Council of Trent near the end, Blessed Pareus in the Confessio Catholica, book 2, Special part 3, article 19, chapter 2, and Tarnovius in book 3 de Coniug. chapter 13, who himself also in the said place, chapter 35, excellently notes, have more prolixly constructed our opinion and placed a barrier against all the evasions of the Papists. That although fornication or adultery is expressed by Christ as one legitimate cause of divorce, under it nevertheless are comprehended the rest, which equally tear apart the substance of marriage, such as are sodomy, bestiality, incest. Furthermore, the Blessed Doctor Bald. in his Commentary on Malachi, pp. 981, 982, recounts more causes of divorce. Add the Lord Doctor Carpzovius, Ecclesiastical Jurisprudence, book 2, title 11, definition 190, et seqq. B. Par. L. on Marriage, § 602. But it is certain that when Christ adds here, & he who marries her who is dismissed, he is by no means speaking of a wife dismissed on account of fornication. For the contrary is sufficiently evident from the context. Whence also Cardinal Caietanus annotates thus on this passage: Therefore he who marries a dismissed woman who is not a fornicator. But why our Lord does not say, that such a dismissed woman marrying another commits adultery, but that a man marrying such a woman commits adultery, Franciscus Lucas Brugensis teaches in this passage, who can be consulted. Bellarminus, however, urges against our opinion, that thus the condition of the innocent and chaste woman is worse than that of the adulteress, since the latter is established as free, and can marry another; but the former can neither have her former husband, nor marry another. We respond by denying that the condition of the guilty, that is, the adulteress, is better than that of the innocent, that is, the chaste woman. For a husband deserting an innocent woman can either be compelled by the Magistrate to cohabit again with the deserted one, and thus she can have her former husband. Or if the deserter persists in his malice, so that he is entirely unwilling to receive the innocent wife and cohabit with her, then that man is to be held as a malicious deserter, and then that passage of the Apostle 1 Cor. 7:15 pertains to the innocent wife, so that a free path to new nuptials is open to her. Since such a persistent deserter, as far as this is concerned, can and ought to be held as an infidel, 1 Tim. 5:8. Furthermore, an argument against polygamy can also be sought from this passage. For if he commits adultery who marries another after dismissing his former spouse, except for the cause of fornication, how much more will he commit adultery who, while retaining his former , marries another. Nor is there any reason for anyone to say, that someone can superinduce another wife upon a consenting first wife. For it must be known that this consent is null, since it is contrary to the first institution of marriage. It is also manifest that the Savior speaks in this place of bodily fornication, and not indeed of spiritual. For neither is heresy or infidelity a legitimate cause for dissolving a marriage, against the Papists. See B. Par. Confess. Cath. book 2, spec. part art. 19, ch. 4, §. 2. It is to be noted furthermore, that Christ speaks here of voluntary fornication, and likewise committed without the consent of the other party. For if a husband prostitutes his wife, it is so far from the case that the bond of marriage is dissolved through such fornication of the wife, that rather such a husband, as a most base pimp, ought to be gravely and deservedly punished for this crime. Compare B. P. L. on Marriage, §. 612, 621. But that also must be observed, that although the innocent party can by right dismiss the guilty party on account of fornication, that is, adultery, yet there is no command present that he must do this. For a husband can retain an adulterous wife, if she has acknowledged the sin, promised a serious amendment of life, and has begged for pardon, and can receive her back into favor. Compare Judg. 19, 2. 1 Sam. 25, 42. provided that a new marriage has not intervened. It is truly a wonder why, when our Savior grants that a dissolution or divorce, properly so called, can be instituted on account of adultery if indeed the innocent party seeks this from the Magistrate, the Papists impugn it so vehemently, who nevertheless do not doubt at all to dissolve a marriage in such a case where it is by no means granted in the Holy Scriptures. Thus they themselves teach that a marriage can be dissolved if such persons have contracted it between whom a spiritual kinship intervenes. Likewise if a wife during the marriage has been corrupted by such an infirmity that she is no longer able to render the debt to her husband, just as the blessed D. Calixtus shows in Concord. Ev. p. 271. How finally the Apostle 1 Cor. 7, 15., freeing the faithful from the bond if the infidel (to whom the malicious deserter is to be equated) has been the author of the breaking, or has been unwilling to cohabit, does not contradict Christ, the same learned man explains, just as also the blessed D. Mentzer and the blessed D. Tarnovius in the treatise on Marriage, likewise B. Par. L. on Marriage. The Savior speaks indeed of voluntary divorce, the Apostle of involuntary.

Latin:

*(v. 9. Quicunrepudiaverit uxorem suam, nisi ob stuprum &c. Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 3. -p. 76. Christus ipse eas, quae matrimonii legem violant, eiicere iussit: Hoc autem nisi contingat, omnia alia uxorem vitia ferre praecepit, immò necessarium esse pronunciavit. Neque id quidem frustra & temerè. Nam coetera quidam vitia unumquēq eorum, qui matrimonii lege copulantur, minimè intuentur: adulterium ad ipsa matrimonii pacta tendit,καὶ τὴν τῶν παίδων καθυβρίζει ευγένειαν i. e. filiorum nobilitatem, vel ut mavult Conr. Ritterhusius, benè natam indolem contumeliâ afficit, & cognationes lacerat, ac deniq humanam omnem vitam pessundat & evertit. Coeterùm si Christus uxorem ob adulterium eiicere ac repudiare iussit, sequitur, quòd pars innocens non solùm quoad thorum, sed etiam quoad vinculum à parte nocente sese separare ac aliud matrimonium inire possit. non privato tamen ausu, sed prae viâ Magistratûs decisione. quam sententiam, ex Christi verbis profluentem frustra Concil. Tridentinum sess. 24. can. 7. anathemate percutit, ac Pontificii reliqui communiter vehementer, sed frustra impugnant. Adstruxere verò eandem tum ex a-iis Sc. S. dictis, tum è praesenti loco B. D. Hi--sem. Breviar. Extenso p. 446. B. Par. Confess. Cathol. lib. 2 spec. part. 3. p. 247. item L. de Coni. §. 564. seqq. Excipitad h. l. Corn. à Lapide Comm. h. l. primò, Augustinum lib. 1. de adult Coni. c. 9. τὸnisi accipere negativè, ut τὸnisi ob fornicationem idem sit, quod extra causam fornicationis. addit: favent Graeca & Syrus, quae habent; non adulteram: quasi Christus tantum velit affirmare, uxorem fidam & castam non posse dimitti, de infida verò i. e. incesta & adulterâ nil velit dicere, ad vitandam invidiam Pharisaeorum & populi, cû illo tempore licitae & usitata erant adulterorum repudia, & novae cum aliis nuptiae. Resp. 1. Ergone Christus ad declinandam Pharisaeorum ac populi invidiam dissimulavit veritatem? contrarium docent satis acres conciones, quibus Pharisaeorum vitia taxavit. Vid. Matth. 23. v 13. seqq contrarium etiam testantur ipsi eius hostes, Matth. 22, 16. 2. Falsum est, favere isti sententiae, quae negativè verba haec accipi vult, textum Graecum: particulae enim εἰ μὴnisi non minùs exceptivè, quàm negativè adhibentur, ceu patet ex inspectione c. 11, 27.c. 12, 4.39.c. 19, 17.c. 21.19.c. 24, 36. &c in quibus locis ipsi Pontificii agnoscunt, particulas εἰ μὴexclusivas s. exceptivas esse. Vid Corn. à Lapide ad c. 11, 27.c. 12, 4.c. 24, 36. Confer plura huc facientia apud B. Hackspan. Disp. 3. de Locut. Sacris §. 29. seqq. Quòd verò hôc locô particulae illae potiùs exceptivè, quàm negativè exponi debeant, patet ex collatione loco parall. c. 5, 32. ubi habetur παρεκτός, & expressè redditur à Vulg. exceptâ fornicationis causâ. Non igitur dubium quin si in loco parallelo τὸ παρεκτόςexceptivè accipitur, uti rectè à Vulgato Matth. 5. exponitur, etiam hoc loco τὸεἰ μὴ ita exponi possit debeatque. Mirum verò, quòd Corn. à Lapide amplectatur sententiam, -ui Graecum textum favere innuit, desertâ eâ, cui versio vulgata favet, cùm memor esse debuisset decreti Concilii Trident ni sess 4. ubi dictum Con-ili-m statuit, ut vetus ac vulgata editio Latina, in publicis lect. disput. & exposition. pro authentica habeatur, & ut nemo illam reiicere quovis praetextis audeat vel praesumat. Ioh. Paludanus, Th. D. & Profess. Lovaniensis in Vindic. Theol. ad Matth. 5. 32. & Felicianus Capito, Avinion. ArchiEp. in Expl. Cathol. LL. V. ac Nov. Test. ad Matth. 5. p. 406. urgent contra nos 1. dicta parallela1. Cor. 7. 10. 11.Rom. 7, 3.Eph. 5. sed de ist is suo loco. 2. quòd verba Domini ex omnibus Evangelistis simul sint colligenda: cùm igitur tùm apud Marcumc. 10. tùm apudLucam c. 16, 18.Christus ut absolutè negans dimittendam esse uxorem adducatur, locumMatth. 5.ubi videatur docere Salvator, non esse dimittendam uxorem, nisi ob causam fornicationis, esse iuxta reliqua exponendum. Resp. Imò potiùs, quia Christus apud Matth. c. 5, 32. ac hîc limitationem addit, reliqui Evangelistae non absolutè sunt intelligendi, sed cum tali limitatione. Verùm instat Bellarminus, quòd quidem aliquando unus Evangelista aliquid addat quod coeteri omiserunt, sed nunquā ita, ut sententiae reddatur falsa, quia alioquin decepissent homines, quibus sua Evangeliatradidissent, nullâ mentione factâ aliorum Evangelistarum. Resp. 1. Eccur verò, si ex additione deceptio affingitur Evangelistis, Bellarminus ac alii Pontificii addunt restrictionem ad verba Evangelistarum generalia vel certè indefinita, ad matrimonium inter fideles saltem contractum. Quae tamen restrictio sive exceptio nec à Christo nec ab ullo Evangelistarum adiecta. 2. Voluit Deus, ut integrum N. T. volumen extaret, initer alia etiam fine isto, quô ea, quae ab uno vel altero Evangelista praetermissa sunt, è reliquis suppleri queant. Licet proinde ipse ille Evangelista, qui aliquam circumstantiam vel restrictionem omittit, non mentionem faciat aliorum Evangelistarum, sufficit tamen, quòd omnium Evangelistarum scripta Ecclesiae concredita sint. Excipit Paludanus, si per adulterium solveretur matrimonium, se qui, libellum repudii omninò sublatum non esse, qui tamen ob cordis duritiem Iudaeis saltem fuerit concessus. Resp. dist. inter repudiū, levi de causa & extra adulterii casum privatô arbitriô susceptum, quale, apud Iudaeos in usu erat, ceu inter alios testatur Nicolaus de Lyra, è Iudaeo factus Christianus in Postilla ad c. 24. Deut. & inter repudium, ob adulterium, publico Magistratus iudiciô factum. Christus repudium priori modo, non posteriori consideratum abrogavit. Quemadmodum igitur Salvator noster

alibiiudicia privata, temeraria &c. abrogavit ac damnavit, salvo tamen publicorum iudiciorum, à Magistratu quae fiunt, iure: sic hîc privata, temeraria ac levi de causa suscepta divortia improbavit, ita tamen ut simul repudium ac divortium, (ob antegressum adulterium) per Magistratum factum approbet, quippe expressis verbis addens prohibitioni limitationem, videlicet, nisi ob fornicationem. Urget idem Paludanus autoritatem Innocentii I. ep. 3 ad Exup. c. 6. Alexandri item III. cap. Ex parte, ac deniq Concilia Africanum, c. 69. Foroiuliense can. 10. Nammetense, Florentinum, Tridentinum. Verùm pridem ad hanc obiectionem respondit Thomas de Vio, Cardinalis Caietanus, quem magnis aliàs Pontificii laudibus evehunt. Hic verò disertè ad hunc locum: Intellige ex hac Dn. I. C. lege, licitum esse Christiano dimittere uxorem ob fornlcationem carnalem ipsius uxoris, & posse ducere aliam, salva semper Ecclesiae definitione, quae hactenus non apparet. Nam decretales Pontificiae de hac materia nō sunt definitivae fidei, sed iudiciales facti. Profitentur autem ipsimet Pontifices, ut patet in c. 4. de divortiis, & in cap. Licet de sponsa duorum, Romanos Pontifices aliquando in his iudiciis matrimoniorum errâsse. Nec ego sum primus, qui sic intellexi Evangelii textum. quoniam ante annos mille B. Ambrosius sic intelligens idem docuit. Cum Caietano quoque facit Ambrosius Catharinus Compsanus Episcopus tum in peculiari de hâc quaestione libello, tum in Comm. 1. ep. ad Cor. 7. Regerit quidem Felicianus Capitonus l. c. cum Magistro Sententiarum arbitrandum esse, Ambrosii libros ab haereticis fuisse errorum maculis conspersos, nec tenuisse eum illam sententiam. Sed cùem coniecturae huius nullum afteratur fundamentum, eâdem facilitate reiicitur, quâ adducitur. Illud verò tenendum probè est, quòd tum Capitonus l. c. tum Sixtus Senensis fateantur. Zachari-Papam I it. Concil. Elibertinum, Moguntiense, ac Triburense concessisse divortium, quoad ipsum quoq vinculum. Quorum decreta cum verbis Christi consentanea sint, meritò illorum Pontificum ac Conciliorum, quae Paludanus contra nos affert, decretis praeferuntur. Quàm ineptè verò Erbermannus Bellarminum in praesenti controversiâ vindi-arit, dum vix decimam thesin ex iis, quae B. Parens in Bell. Orthod. teste contra Bellarminus disputavit, tangit, operae pretium est, ut lector ex eius vindiciis t. 3. cognoscat. Prolixiù verò nostram sententiam adstruxerunt, omnibusque Pontificiorum effugiis obicem opposuerunt B. D. Chemnitius Part. 2. Exam. Concil. Trid. circa finem, B. Parens Confess. Cathol. l. 2. Spec. part. 3. art. 19. c. 2. Tarnovius l. 3. de Coniug. c. 13. qui ipse etiam d. l. c. 35. egregiè notat, quòd licet fornicatio sive adulterium unum legitima divort-causa à Christo exprimatur, sub eâ tamen quocomprehendantur reliqua, quae pariter matrimonii substantiam convellunt, uti sunt Sodomia, bestialit as, incestus. Plures praeterea divortii causas recenset B. D. Bald. Comm. in Mal. p. 981, 982. Adde Dn. D. Carpzovium Iurispr. Eccles. lib. 2. tit. 11. d. 190. seqq. B. Par. L. de Coni. §. 602. Certum autem est, quòd quando Christus subiungit hîc, & qui dimissam duxerit, hautquaquam de uxore propter fornicationem dimissâ loquatur. Contrarium enim satis ex contextu patet. Unde etiam Card. Caietanus ita ad h l. annotat: E. qui dimissam non fornicariam ducit. Cur verò Dominus noster non dicat, quòd talis mulier dimissa alteri nubens moechetur, sed quòd vir talem ducens moechetur, docet Franciscus Lucas Brugensis in h. l. qui potest evolvi. Bellarminus autem contra sententiam nostram urget, quòd sic innocentis & castae deterior sit conditio, quàm adulterae, cùm haec libera statuatur, alterinubere possit; illa verò nec priorem habere, nec alteri nubere possit. Respondemus, negando, meliorem esse conditionem nocentis h. e. adulterae, quàm innocentis s. castae. Etenim maritus deserens innocentem vel compelli potest à Magistratu, ut desertae iterum cohabitet, & sic illa priorem maritum habere potest. Vel si desertor in malitiâ suâ perseverarit, ita ut innocentem uxorem recipere illique cohabitare planè nolit, tunc habendus pro malitio so desertore ille est, & tum spectat ad uxorem innocentem illud Apostoli 1. Cor. 7, 15. ut adeò liber illi ad novas nuptias pateat aditus. Siquidem talis pertinax desertor, quantum ad hoc haberi pro infideli & possit & debeat, 1. Tim. 5, 8. Peti porrò ex h l. argumentum quoque contra polygamiam potest. Etenim si moechatur, qui priori coniuge, exceptâ causâ fornicationis, dimissâ aliam ducit, quantò magis adulterium committet, qui retentâ priori alteram ducit. Nec est, quòd aliquis dicat, posse aliquem priori uxori consentienti alteram superinducere. Sciendum enim, quòd is consensus nullus sit, cùm adversetur primae coniugii institutioni. Manifestum etiam est, loqui h. l. Salvatorem de fornicatione corporali, non verò spirituali. Neq; enim haeresis vel infidelitas matrimonii solvendi causa legitima est Contra Pontificios. Vid. B. Par. Confess. Cath. l. 2. spec. partart. 19. c. 4. §. 2. Notandum insuper, quòd Christus loquatrhîc de fornicatione voluntariâ, itemque absque alterius partis consensu factâ. Si enim maritus prostituer it uxorem, tantum abest, ut per talem uxoris fornicationem co~iugii vinculum -olvatur, ut potius talis maritus ceu leno turpissimus ob scelus hoc graviter ac meritò puniri debeat. Confer. B. P. L. de Coniug. §. 612, 621. Sed illud quoque observandum, quòd licetpars innocens iure possit partem nocentem ob fornicationem s. adulterium dimittere, non tamen ut hoc faciat praeceptum adfit. Potest enim maritus uxorem adulteram, si peccatum agnoverit, seriam vitae emendationem promiserit, ac deprecata fuerit, retinere, iterumque in gratiam recipere. Conf. Iudic. 19, 2. 1 Sam. 25, 42. modò novum non intercesserit matrimonium. Mirum verò est, cur cùm Salvator noster concedat, posse propter adulterium dissolutionem sive divortium, propriè sic dictum, institui si pars nempe innocens à Magistratu hoc petat: Pontificii adeò vehementer id impugnent: qui minimè tamen dubitant, matrimonium tali in casu solvere, ubi in sacris litter is hautquaquam conceditur. Sic docent ipsi, solvi matrimonium posse si tales personae co~traxerint, quos inter cognatio spiritualis intercedit. Item si uxor durante matrimonio tali infirmitate corrupta fuerit, ut non valeat ampliùs marito debitum reddere, quemadmodum ostendit B. D. Calixtus Concord. Ev. p. 271. Quomodo denique Apostolus 1. Cor. 7, 15. à vinculo liberans fidelem si infidelis (cui aequiparandus malitiosus desertor) rumpendi autor fuerit, vel cohabitare noluerit, non contradicat Christo, exponit idem d. l. quemadmodum etiam B. D. Mentzerus ac B. D. Tarnovius tr. de Coniug. it. B. Par. L. de Coniug. Loquitur nempe Salvator de divortio voluntario, Apostolus de involuntario)*

## 19:10
v. 10. Ἀιτία. It signifies in this place the same as condition, with the manner of speaking taken from the Roman forum. Thus the case of the publicans is said to be better l. 1. §. 4. D. de publ. & victigal.

Latin:

v. 10. Ἀιτία. Significat h. l. idem quod conditio, loquendi genere à foro Romano sumto. Sic publicanorum causa dicitur melior l. 1. §. 4. D. de publ. & victigal.

## 19:11
v. 11. Who said to them, Mark does not disagree here with Matthew. The former says that Christ repeated it privately before the disciples, meanwhile he does not exclude the public discourse: The latter understands the general and public discourse to the people. In the former, Christ proposed his words and explains them further; in the latter, certain circumstances are omitted.

Not all receive this word, that is, this matter, by a Hebrew phrase. Although the business of a man with a wife is so arranged, it is not therefore in general not expedient γαμῆ;σαι: But it is expedient only for those who are capable of this thing, namely, endowed with the gift of continence. Not all are fit to receive this word and live chastely outside of marriage. Which explanation the Apostle confirms 1. Cor. 7, 1. 2.7. Bellarmine in his disputation on the Celibacy of Priests contradicts Christ to his face. 1. Christ says, not all receive this word; Bellarmine *(just as also Maldonatus, Corn. à Lapide on this place, and other Papists)* there is no one who cannot contain, if he wishes. *(But this is frivolous; experience testifies to the contrary, concerning which see B. Par. L. de Coniug. §. 539. Nor is there any reason why the Papists should urge, see Ioannes Lensaeus de Libert. Christi. p. 551. seqq. Pistorius in B. D. Menzer. disp. 13. Anti Pist. §. 91. that this can be obtained by prayers: for it is known that God hears prayers only then if they are poured out according to his will, 1 Ioh. 5, 14. Now indeed this is the divine will, that those who are burning should use the remedy of marriage, 1. Cor. 7, 9. (and not rashly impose a snare upon themselves v. 35.) which remedy concerns clergy and laity equally, as will be shown in its place. Conf. Epist. Dionysii in Euseb. l. 4. H. E. c. 23. Let the remaining exceptions of Bellarmine be seen discussed in B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccles. §. 337. also L. de Coniug. §. 526. seqq. also §. 494.)* Christ says, that only those receive this word to whom it has been given, Bellarmine that there is no one who cannot contain, if he wishes. *(Furthermore, the same Bellarmine l. 2. de Monachis brings forward this saying for the confirmation of evangelical counsels. But it must be known that Christ by no means teaches that it is a work of supererogation or a merit of eternal life, if anyone abstains from marriage, (for the contrary is from) 1. Tim. 4, 1. it is permitted to gather.) But this at least teaches that, whereas in the O. T. sterility was held in the place of a reproach, in the N. T. it is not only free to live outside of matrimony, for those indeed to whom it is given, but also sometimes useful, if indeed it be done for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, by which phrase what is indicated here is clear from 1. Cor. 7, 32. Compare more things making for this in B. part. L. on the Gospel §. 96. Isidore of Pelusium also treats of this saying in book 4, ep. 165. Furthermore, B. D. Hulsem. notes in the manual of the A. C. p. 146 that it is gathered from history that by the power of receiving this word is not designated by Christ the faculty of powers for performing this thing, i. e. celibacy: but that it is on the contrary the denied faculty of the intellect, so that it is able εὐνούχισαν to reconcile with the perpetual obligation of spouses. He proves this, because the disciples did not understand this, for they are said to have asked Christ about this business separately in the house. As they were accustomed to inquire privately about those things of which they did not have a sufficiently informed understanding. He urges furthermore, that the phrase not to receive is not found for that, which is not to have the faculty of performing that which is signified by the word. Finally he adds, if even these words were to be taken most of all concerning the faculty of powers, nevertheless evangelical counsels could not be built from this, since they are mandatory words, like those, he who has ears to hear, let him hear; not concessive or consultatory

Latin:

v. 11. Qui dixit illis, Marcus hîc à Matthaeo non dissentit. Ille dicit, Christum repetiisse coram discipulis privatim, interim non excludit sermo-em publicum: Hic intelligit generalem & publicum ad populum sermonem. In illo Christus sua verba proponebat & ulterius explicat, in hoc circumstantiae quaedam omittitur.

Non omnes capiunt sermonem hunc, id est, rem hanc, phrasi Ebraeâ. Etsi negotium hominis cum uxore ita comparatum est, non tamen proptereà in universum non expedit γαμῆ;σαι: Sed illis tantùm expedit, qui huius rei sunt capaces, praediti scilicet continentiae dono. Non omnes sunt idonei, ut capiant hoc verbum & extra matrimonium castè vivant. Quam explicationem comprobat Apostolus 1. Cor. 7, 1. 2.7. Bellarm in disp. de Coelib. Sacerdotum, in faciem Christo contradicit. 1. Christus dicit, non omnes capiunt verbum hoc; Bellarm. *(quemadmodum & Maldonatus, Corn. à Lapide in h. l. & alii Pontificii.)* nemo est, qui continere non possit, si velit. *(Ast frivolum hoc est, contrarium testatur experientia, de qua B. Par. L. de Coniug. §. 539. Nec est quòd urgeant Pontificii, vid. Ioannes Lensaeus de Libert. Christi. p. 551. seqq. Pistorius apud B. D. Menzer. disp. 13. Anti Pist. §. 91. Precibus hoc obtineri posse: etenim notum est, quòd tum demum Deus preces exaudiat, si fundantur secundùm ipsius voluntatem,1 Ioh. 5, 14. Iam verò divina voluntas haec est, ut qui uruntur, remedio coniugii utantur, 1. Cor. 7, 9. (non verò temerè sibi laqueum imponant v. 35.) quod remedium aequè clericos ac laicos respicit, ut suo ostendetur loco. Conf. Epist. Dionysii apud Euseb. l. 4. H. E. c. 23. Reliquae Bellarmini exceptiones discussae vîdeantur apud B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccles. §. 337. it. L. de Coniug. §. 526. seqq. it. §. 494.)* Christus dicit, illos tantum capere verbum hoc, quibus datum est, Bellarm. nominem esse, qui continere non possit, si velit. *(Porrò idem Bellarm. l. 2. de Monachis dictum hoc pro confirmatione consiliorum Evangelicorum adducit. Verùm sciendum, quòd Christus minimè opus supererogationis vel vitae aeternae meritum esse doceat, fi quis à matrimonio abstinuerit, (contrarium enim ex 1. Tim. 4, 1. colligere licet.) Sed hoc saltem docet, quòd cùm in V. T. sterilitas loco opprobrii haberetur, in N. T. non solùm liberum esse, extra matrimonium vivere, illis nempè quibus datum est, sed etiam quandoque utile, si nimirum id fiat propter regnum coelorum, qua phrasi quid hîc indicetur, patet ex 1. Cor. 7, 32. Confer plura hûc facientia apud B. par. L. de Evangel. §. 96. Agit quoq; de dicto hoc Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 4. ep. 165. Coeterùm notat B. D. Hu-lsem. in manuali A. C. p. 146. ex historia colligi, per potentiam capiendi verbum hoc non designatam à Christo facultatem virium ad praestandam rem hanc i. e. caelibatum: sed contrà esse, negatam facultatem intellectus, ut possitεὐνούχισανcum perpetua coniugum obligatione componere. Probat hoc, quia discipuli hoc non intelligebant, dicuntur enim seorsim in domo de hoc negotio ex Christo quaesivisse. Ceu consueverant ea, de quibus intelligentiam non satis informatam habebat, privatim inquirere. Urget praetereà, quòd non reperiatur phrasis non capere pro eo, quod non habere facultatem id praestandi, quod verbo significatur. Addit deniq;, si vel maximè haec verba de virium facultate accipiātur, non tamen hinc exstrui posse consilia Evangelica, cùm sint verba mandatoria, ceu illa, qui habet aures ad audiendum, audiat; non concessiva sive consultatoria)*

## 19:12
v. 12. εὐνοῦΧοι. are said from that which is, τὴν εὐνὴν έΧειν, to keep the bed, because formerly they were employed for guarding the Gynaecea of Kings. The Syrian adds by ῐῠ῞Ῑ῔῞ noting the same thing as the Hebrews ῟῞ῐῠ faithful, because the faith of Eunuchs was chosen for guarding beds. Julius Caesar Scaliger thinks they are so called παρὰτὸ ἐυ νοῦν ἔΧειν, because they are well affected in mind.

*( There are Eunuchs, who were born so from their mother's womb. See concerning these Zaurus Lusitanus Medic. Princip. Histor. book 3 q 32. Ioh. Buxtorff. in Lex. Talmud Rabb in the word ῝ῙῨ῝. Concerning these our people rightly pronounce, that they ought not only to abstain from marriage, but also to be barred from it. See B. Par. on Marriage §. 235 Add. Carpz. εὐνούΧισαν ἑαυτοὺς. * ΕὐνουΧιζειν ἑαυτὸν in this place by no means denotes to castrate oneself and render oneself unfit for marriage. Just as Origen, from a perverse understanding of these words, is reported by Eusebius lib. 6. Hist. Eccles. c. 7. to have castrated himself. It is a wonder, writes Caspar Barthius lib. 5. Advers. c. 14. concerning this deed, how Origen divested himself of all mind, not being ignorant that there exists no example of any saint, when nevertheless the Lord speaks as if of a known thing. And yet there were found even after Origen those who followed his example, as Wierus lib. 3. de Praestig. Daemonum c. 18. records about a certain Monk, that he castrated himself. But that gross and detestable error was long ago noted by S. Chrysostom, writing thus hom. 63. in Matth.: He does not speak of the cutting off of members: far from it! but he understands the destruction of thought: for he who cuts off a member is subject to a curse. For he who attempts such a thing undertakes the work of a murderer, and provides an occasion for those who slander the workmanship of GOD. He opens the mouths of the Manichaeans, and commits the same iniquity with those who are mutilated among the gentiles. Theophylactus also inveighs against the same error in this place. Thus it is a wonder that the same had once prevailed so much that it had to be repressed by a public decree of Councils. As we read it sanctioned in the Nicene Council can. 1, that no one who, being sound, had cut himself off, should be ordained into the clergy, or if he were already established in the clergy, had dared to do this same thing, he should be suspended from office. But whether that error had already prevailed in the time of the Apostles, so that some out of a vain persuasion of piety cut themselves off, is not without reason doubted. And from this it can be judged what should be judged concerning the antiquity of the Canons which are ascribed to the Apostles. Thus indeed Canon XXII sounds: Ὁ ἀκρω τηςιάσαν ὲαυτὸν, μὴ γινὲοθω κληριαός. άντοΦονευτὴς γδ ἐ-ςὶν ἐαυτοῦ καὶ τὦς τοῦ θεοῦ

διμιουργί ας ἐφσθρός. Thus also canon XXIII is established as follows: εἴ τὶς κληρικὸς ων ἑαυτὸν ἐκρωτηριάσει, κασθαιείσθω. Φονευςγ--ἐστὶν ἑαυτοῦ. But concerning laymen it is decreed in the following canon as follows: Λαίκὸς ἑαυτὸν ἀκρωτηριάσας άφοριζέσθω ἔτη τςία. Ἐπίβουλος γῆ ἐ-ςι τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ζωῆς. Where it is to be noted, that τὸ ἀκρὼτηςιάζειν here does not denote to take away or cut off at least the extremity of the skin, by which the penis is covered, (for this is called πειτέμνειν in Holy Scripture, see Ioh. 7, 22. Acts 15, 5.c. 21, 21. &c.) but it is the same as ἐυνουχίζειν to cut off, i.e., to render a man unfit for procreating offspring, as also appears from the context. 2. that not only is he guilty of this crime, ὁ χερσὶν οἰκείαις ἀποκόψας τὸ μόςιον, but also ὁ ἄλλῶ ἑκὼν καὶ χωρὶς ἀνάγκης (by which word the danger of a more serious disease or even of death, otherwise to be avoided by no remedies, is understood here) ἑαυτὸν εἰς ἐκτομὴν ἐ-πιδοὴς, as Zonaras rightly comments on can. 1. of the Nicene Council. 3. that even by Civil laws and Canon Law such castration is severely prohibited, as is evident from tit. 42. l. 4. Cod. de Eunuchis, also from Iur. Can. dist. 3. Eunuchus si, likewise c. si quis abscid. Let Balsamon and Zonaras be added Comm. in can. 24. Apost. 4. that the reason for those who have been castrated by others through force is far different. Therefore, as far as the present passage concerns, it must be known that the Savior speaks either of spiritual castration, by which, with the motions of the flesh suppressed, the affections of evil work are cut off; or of a firm purpose of not entering into matrimony, so that one may better be able to care for the things that are of the Lord, 1. Corinthians 7, 34. And Isidorus Pelusiota also accepts this place in such a sense, l. 3. ep. 13. writing, that this saying pertains to either sex. And that this is evident from the fact that very many have both begun and performed this. Our Savior's words are also explained concerning spiritual castration by B. D. -o-nig Cas. Catech. p. 49. and likewise B. Frantzius in de Script. S. interpretatione p. 978. where he rightly warns that this locution is similar to Matth. 5. v. 28. Therefore εὐνουχίζειν ἑαυτὸν ) * metaphorically signifies having a firm purpose of not taking a wife, so that he appears to be a Eunuch. Theophylactus εὐνουχίζεοθαι interprets διδάσκεοθαι, and εὐνουχίζειν έαυτόν accepts concerning those who are άνἀυτοδίδακτοι and better than the rest. Tossanus, who have made a vow or have firmly proposed to themselves to remain outside of marriage, as if they were

Eunuchs, that is to say, for as long as they feel that they have the gift of chastity. Therefore Christ does not a vow, but approves a purpose of virginity in suitable persons. *(Erasmus of Rotterdam, whom the Roman Pontiff Leo X calls his beloved in the epistle prefixed to the version of the N.T., gravely says in this place: The Lord had distinguished three kinds of eunuchs: one of those who by nature cannot, or do not desire to, have intercourse with a woman. Another of those who are castrated by force. The third, who willingly for the kingdom of GOD keep themselves continent. In which class shall we place the kind of those who are thrust into celibacy either by art or by fear, so that it is permitted to fornicate, but not permitted to take a wife: to such an extent that if they profess a concubine, they are Catholic Priests; but if they prefer to be called a wife, they are thrown into the fire. In my opinion, parents would treat their children more mercifully if, when they had destined them for celibacy, they took care to have them castrated while still boys, than if they threw them, whole, unwilling or unaware, into this conflagration of lust. Bellarmine urges for the vow, that if the Lord in this place were speaking of those who live celibate without any vow, He would say, who castrate themselves daily, not who have castrated themselves. Since therefore, he continues, He said, who have castrated themselves, He signifies that they have by a single voluntary action amputated from themselves every faculty of contracting marriage. Similarly, they prove the vow of continence of the monastery from this place: Felicianus Capito, Expl. Cathol. part 2, p. 55; Petrus Cotonus, Instit. Cathol. lib. 3, c. 3, c. 16; Ioh. Lensaeus, Theol. Prof. Lovan., l. 10, de Libert. Christ., c. 6, and other Papist writers commonly. But we respond: 1. Distinguishing between a vow broadly and strictly so-called. In the former way, the word vow being taken, insofar as it denotes a firm purpose of living in celibacy, yet in such a way that if it cannot be kept rightly and without burning, marriage may be entered into, we easily grant that someone can vow celibacy, i.e., conceive such a purpose within himself. And in that meaning of the word vow, the Fathers use it when they commend the vow of celibacy. But in the latter way, that word being accepted, i.e., insofar as it denotes a perpetual abjuration of matrimony (and indeed with the interposition of an invocation of the divine name, and with the addition, whether explicitly or implicitly, of an execration if it is not kept, whatever case may occur, in which way Papists are accustomed to vow celibacy today), in such a way, I say, it is denied that a vow of celibacy is licit, or approved by Christ here. Whence also the ancients, just as B. D.

Chemnitius in the Examination of the Council of Trent, part 3, c. 8, rightly observes that they did not vow celibacy in such a way that they abjured marriage in perpetuity: but with this exception and limitation, insofar as human frailty permits, so that they reserved for themselves the liberty to use the remedy of marriage against burning and fornication, ordained by God for those who cannot contain. 2. It must be known that the Papists also err in this, while they [hold] celibacy with the opinion of some of merit or of justification can be undertaken, which opinion, since it detracts greatly from the most sufficient merit of Christ, which is the sole cause of our justification and salvation, and leads men away from Christ to a vain confidence in their own merits, is deservedly rejected. 3. The Jesuit Tirinus, a companion of the same Bellarmine, acknowledges the weakness of the consequence in the argument of Bellarmine, when he observes in this place, that this castration is done either by a vow, or at least by a firm purpose. But if the castration, of which Christ speaks here, can also be done by at least a firm purpose, it follows that from the past tense, they have castrated, a vow is less firmly and absolutely inferred. 4. It follows from the opinion of Bellarmine that many, even when Christ said this to the Apostles, had already, in the Papistic manner, vowed celibacy or abjured marriage. But in the Old Testament, the customs of the Israelites, as Augustine warns in the book on Holy Virginity, ch. 4, refused the vow of virginity, and according to Bede in ch. 1 of Luke, Mary was the first of women who decided to dedicate herself to such a virtue. What of the fact that Bellarmine himself, in the book on marriage, ch. 17, response to the 4th objection, admits that perpetual celibacy was not customary in the old law. Other absurd and false things, which flow from that hypothesis of Bellarmine, are shown by B. Par. L. on Marriage §. 509. Let the same be compared with the Confess. Cathol. l. 2. spec. part. 2. p. 333. seqq. also p. 287.)

*( For the sake of the kingdom of heaven i. e. ἕνεκεν τοῦ Πυαγτελίου, Mark 10, 29. or, so that they might undertake the duty of preaching the Gospel more expeditiously and conveniently, and indeed in the whole world, as our blessed D. Frantzius rightly explains in on the Interpretation of Holy Scripture p. 978. and Franciscus Lucas Brugensis himself acknowledges, noting in this place that Paul 1. Cor. 7, 32. 34. 35. explains these words of the Lord. Now indeed Paul, in the said place, shows that for this end celibacy is undertaken by some, so that they might serve God without impediment, and propagate His kingdom.

but not, as the Jesuit Corn. à Lapide explains in this place, impudently proclaiming our explanation as heretical, that through the virtue of continence they might merit the kingdom of heaven or eternal life. For the contrary is evident from Luc. 17, 10Rom. 6, 23.c. 8, 18c. 11, 6. and other oracles of Holy Scripture. Isidore of Pelusium notes in book 1, ep. 286. ει παρθενεύει τις, καὶ -πὶ τούτῳ ἐυχεῖ (this indeed the Monks do to the greatest degree) του μείζονος κασθορσθωματος τῆς ταπεινωσεως ἀςοχεῖ. ού γπαρθενεύων γέγραπται, ἐλλ ᾽ ὁαπεινῶν ἑαυτόν ύψωθἠσεται. i. e. If anyone practices virginity, and boasts on this account, that person surely from the greater virtue, that is, from humility departs. For it is not written, he who cultivates virginity, but he who humbles himself, shall be exalted. The same author has more on this matter in the same place. Let similar opinions of the Papist writers themselves also be compared, for instance, those of John Gerson and Cardinal Bellarmine in B. Pareus, Confess. Cath. art. 19. c. 5. p. 320. Our interpretation is indeed sufficiently clear from the context. For Christ was speaking then to the Apostles, who had been sent away into the whole world to preach the Gospel to every creature. While marriage did not indeed conflict with this vocation of the Apostles, celibacy was meanwhile more expedient for the office of the Apostolate. And for that reason, although Christ does not command celibacy to the Apostles, he nevertheless approves and commends it to them, and indeed at least to the extent that they were endowed with the gift of continence, or to the extent that they could remain celibate without injury to conscience, as B. Pareus rightly explains in L. de Coniugio §. 500. For that celibacy was not absolutely commanded and enjoined even upon the Apostles themselves, the Apostle sufficiently indicates 1. Cor. 9. 5. But much less is celibacy enjoined by divine command upon the other ministers of the Church, as it is not so necessary for them, as it was for the Apostles, in ecclesiastical function, since they, the Apostles, had to preach the Gospel in the whole world and therefore undertake journeys now here, now there; but these, the other ministers of the Church, to teach the word in a certain and fixed place. In what sense some of the ancients wrote that some choose celibacy on account of the kingdom of heaven, i. e. eternal life, B. Pareus long ago showed in the same place, demonstrating that they by no means spoke in the Papist sense, i. e. as if celibacy were the greatest satisfaction for sins and a merit of the kingdom of heaven, but that eternal life is given equally by grace on account of Christ to the faithful, both married and celibate: for indeed διὰ by no means denotes here a meritorious cause, but at least this, that celibacy is chosen for the more convenient performance of the ministry of the word and other offices of piety. Whence Marc. 10, 29. is applied ἕνεκεν. Meanwhile, however, just as one star differs from another in brightness, so those who rightly use celibacy, and in this state of life labor more in the preaching of the Gospel and other exercises of piety, are to have a certain prerogative in the glory of eternal life. Although the Savior does not indicate that very thing in this place, since by the name kingdom of heaven, taken for eternal life, there usually comes in Holy Scripture the blessedness common to all the elect. See above c. 5, 3. 10. c. 7, 21. c. 8, 11. Ioh. 3, 5. Notably St. Augustine, book on Virginity c. 51. The gift of virginity, the more great (greater) I see it, the more I fear for it, lest it perish, the future pride. I say confidently, humble married people follow the lamb more easily than proud virgins. Let the Monks think this is said to them, who by their forced and impure celibacy, which they boast is meritorious even of eternal life, are so proud that with a high brow they despise humble married people. To whose opinion, finally, it does not provide patronage that many of the ancients sometimes commend celibacy too immoderately. For to this admiration of celibacy, and then also to the hyperbolic disparagement of the same, the familiarity of pagan fornication, the atrocity of persecutions, and the inequality of marriages, especially the depravity of heretics, who despise celibacy and introduce impurity of life, seem to have provided an opportunity to the ancients. See B. Par. l. c.)

*( He that can receive it, let him receive it. Τὸ χωρείτω that it is not a precept by which Christ wished to impose a law of celibacy either in general on all the pious, or specifically on the Ministers of the Church, and not even on those who are instructed with the gift of continence, absolutely and simply, is evidently gathered from 1. Cor. 7, 25. For if Christ had brought any law here, certainly the Apostle would have received a commandment of the Lord concerning celibacy, as B. Par. well advises, L. de Coniug. §. 496. add. Confess. Cathol. t. 3. p. 333. Therefore the Savior does not command celibacy here, but leaves it free to those who are endowed with the gift of continence, that they may estimate the measure of the gifts divinely given to them, and choose that which they have perceived to be joined with less danger to their conscience. Which the Apostle also does in the said place, v. 2. 7. 8. 26.)*

εὐνούΧισαν ἑαυτοὺς. * ΕὐνουΧιζειν ἑαυτὸν h. l. minimè notat seipsum castrare ac ineptum reddere ad coniugium. Quemadmodum Origenes ex pravo horum verborum intellectu castrasse se ab Euseb. lib. 6. Hist. Eccles. c. 7. refertur. Mirum, scribit de hoc facto Caspar Barthius lib. 5. Advers. c. 14. quàm omnem mentem exuerit Origenes, nullum sancti alicuius exemplum extare non ignorans, cùm tamen tanquam de re not a loquatur Dominus. Et reperti tamen sunt etiam post Origenem, qui eiusdem sequuti exemplum sunt, ceu de Monacho quodam Wierus lib. 3. de Praestig. Daemonum c. 18. memorat, quòd seipsum castrarit. Atqui crassum illum errorem ac detestandum pridem notavit S. Chrysostomus, ita hom. 63. in Matth. scribens: Non de abscissione membrorum dicit: absit! sed cogitationis interemtionem intelligit: nam qui membrum incidit, maledictioni subiectus est. Homicidae enim opus, qui tale quid tentat, aggreditur, & DEI opificium criminantibus occasionem praebet. Manichaeorum ora recludit, & eandem iniquitatem cum illis committit, qui apud gentes mutilantur. In eundem errorem invehitur quoque Theophylactus in h. l. Ita v. invaluisse olim eundem mirum est, ut publico Conciliorū detreto reprimendus fuerit. Ceu in Concilio Nicaeno can. 1. sancitum legimus, ne quis, qui sanus seipsum excidisset, in clerum ordinaretur, aut si in clero iam constitutus, id ipsum ausus esset, ab officio suspenderetur. Num verò iamtum Apostolorum tempore error ille invaluerit, ut quidā vanâ pietatis persuasione seipsos exciderint, haut immeritò dubitatur. Atque hinc iudicari potest, quid de Canonum, Apostolis qui adscribuntur, iudicandum antiquitate sit. Ita verò Canon XXII. sonat: Ὁ ἀκρω τηςιάσαν ὲαυτὸν, μὴ γινὲοθω κληριαός. άντοΦονευτὴς γδ ἐ-ςὶν ἐαυτοῦ καὶ τὦς τοῦ θεοῦ

διμιουργί ας ἐφσθρός. Sic quoq; canon. XXIII. statuitur ita: εἴ τὶς κληρικὸς ων ἑαυτὸν ἐκρωτηριάσει, κασθαιείσθω. Φονευςγ--ἐστὶν ἑαυτοῦ. Concilii Nicaeni comētatur. 3. quòd etiam legibus Civil, ac Iure Canonico talis castratio severè prohibita sit, quemad. patet ex tit. 42. l. 4. Cod. de Eunuchis, it. ex Iur. Can. dist. 3. Eunuchus si, item c. si quis abscid. Addantur Balsamon ac Zonaras Comm. in can. 24. Apost. 4. quòd longè alia ratio eorum sit, qui per vim ab aliis castrati. Quod praesentem igitur concornit locum, sciendum est, quòd Salvator loquatur vel de spirituali castratione, quâ compressis carnis motibus affectus pravi operis abscinduntur; vel de firmo proposito non ineundi matrimonium, quò meliùs quis possit curare ea, quae sunt Domini, 1. Corinth. 7, 34. Atque de tali proposito accipit quoque h. l. Isidorus Pelusiota, l. 3. ep. 13. scribens, quòd dictum hoc ad utrumsexum pertineat. Idq hinc constare, quòd permultae hoc & coeperint & praestiterint. De spirituali castratirne exponunt quoque Salvatoris nostri verba B. D. -o-nig Cas. Catech. p. 49. itemque B. Frantzius in de Script. S. interpretatione p. 978. ubi rectè monet, similem esse hanc locutionem Matth. 5. v. 28. Proinde εὐνουχίζειν ἑαυτὸν) * metaphoricè significat firmum habere propositum, non ducendi uxorem, ita ut Eunuchus esse videatur. Eunuchi, tamdiu scilicet, quamdiu sentiunt, se castitatis donum habere. Christus igitur non votum, sed propositum virginitatis in personis idoneis approbat. *(Graviter Erasmus Roterodamus, quem Pontifex Rom. Leo X. in epist. verfioni N. T. praefixâ dilectum suum vocat, in h. l. Dominus tria Eunuchorum genera distinxerat, unum eorum, qui naturâ non possunt, aut non appetunt congredi cum muliere. Alterum eorum, qui vi execantur. Tertium, qui volentes ob regnum DEI sese continent. In quâ classe ponemq eorum genus, qui vel arte vel metu detruduntur in coelibatum, ut scortari liceat, uxorem ducere non liceat: adeò ut si profiteantur concubinam, sint Catholici Sacerdotes; sin uxorem dici malint, coniiciantur in ignem. Meâ sententiâ clementiùs tractarent suos liberos parentes, si quos coelibatui destinassent, pueros etiamnum curarent execandos, quàm si integros nolentes aut inscios coniicerent in hoc incendium libidinis. Bellarminus pro voto urget, quòd si Dominus h. l. loqueretur de his, qui sine ullo voto coelibes vivunt, diceret, qui se castrant quotidie, non qui se castraverunt. Cùm ergo, pergit, dixerit, qui se castraverunt, significat, eos unicâ actione voluntariâ amputasse sibi omnem facultatem contrahendi nuptias. Similiter votum continentiae monasticae ex hoc loco probant Felicianus Capito Expl. Cathol part. 2. p. 55. Petrus Cotonus Instit. Cathol. lib. 3. c. 3. c. 16. Ioh. Lensaeus, Theol. Prof. Lovan. l. 10. de Libert. Christ. c. 6. aliique Pontific ii scriptores communiter. Sed respond. 1. disting. inter votum latè & strictè sicdictum. Priori modo dictione voti sumtâ, quatenus nempe firmum denotat propositum, in coelibatu vivendi, ita tamen ut si rectè & absq; ustione servari non possit, coniugium ineatur, facilè largimur, posse aliquem coelibatum vovere, h. e. tale propositum secum concipere. Atque in eâ significatione voti dictione utuntur Patres, quando coelibatus votum commendant. Ast posteriori modo voce istâ acceptâ h. e. quat. notat perpetuam matrimonii abiurationem, (& quidem interpositâ obtestatione nominis divini, & additâ, sive explicitè sive implicitè execratione, si non servetur, (quicunque etiam incidat casus, quo modo Papistae hodiè vovere coelibatum solent.) tali inquam modo negatur, coelibatûs votum licitum esse, vel à Christo hîc approbari. Unde etiam veteres, sicuti B. D.

Chemnitius in Examine Concilii Tridentini part. 3. c. 8. rectè observat, non ita coelibatum vovebant, ut coniugium in perpetuum abiurarent: sed cum hâc exceptione & limitatione, in quantum humana fragilitas permittit, ut adeò libertatem sibi reservarent, remedio coniugii contra ustionem & scortationem divinitùs illis, qui continere non possunt, ordinato, uti. 2. Sciendum est, quòd Pontificii in eo quoque errent, dum coelibatum opinione alicuius meriti sive iustificationis suscipi posse docent, quae opinio cum sufficientissimo Christi merito, quod unica iustificationis ac salutis nostrae causa est, plurimum detrahat, hominesque ad inanem in propriis meritis fiduciam à Christo abducat, meritò reiicitur. 3. infirmitatem consequentiae in arg. Bellarmini agnoscit eiusdem sociennus Iesuita Tirinus, quando in h. l. observat, castrationem hanc fieri vel voto, vel saltem firmo proposito. Atqui si castratio, de quâ Christus hîc loquitur, firmo saltem proposito etiam fieri potest, sequitur, quòd ex praeterito, castraverunt minùs firmiter absolutè inferatur votum. 4. Sequitur ex sententiâ Bellarmini, multos iamtum, quando Christus hoc ad Apostolos dixit, more Papistico coelibatum vovisse sive matrimonium abiurasse. At in V. T. mores Israelitarum, monente Augustino lib. de S. Virginitate c. 4 Votum virginitatis recusabant, ac iuxta Bedam in c. 1. Lucae, Maria prima foeminarum fuit, quaetantae se virtuti mancipare decreverit. Quid quòd Bellarm. ipse lib. de matrimonio c. 17. respons. ad 4. obi. fateatur, perpetuum coelibatum non fuisse in veteri lege usitatum. Alia absurda ac falsa, quae ex hypothesi illa Bellarmini fluunt, ostendit B. Par. L. de Coniug. §. 509. Conferatur idem Confess. Cathol. l. 2. spec. part. 2. p. 333. seqq. it. p. 287.)*

D. Frantzius noster in de Interpr. Sc. S. p. 978. & agnoscit ipse Franciscus Lucas Brugensis, annotans in h. l. Paulum1. Cor. 7, 32.34. 35.haec verba Domini explicare. non verò, uti Iesuita Corn. à Lapide h. l. exponit, protervè nostram explicationē ceu haereticam proclamans, ut per virtutem continentiae regnum coelorum sive vitam aeternam mereantur. Contrarium enim ex Luc. 17, 10Rom. 6, 23.c. 8, 18c. 11, 6. aliisque Sc. S. oraculis patet. Si quis virginitatem praestat, athoc nomine gloriatus, nimirum ille à maiore vir-ute h. e. ab humilitate ab--rat. Neq enim scriptum est, qui virginitatem colit, sed qui seipsum humiliat, exaltabitur. Plura hanc in rem habet idem d. l. Conferantur quoque similes sententiae ipsorum scriptorum Pontificiorum, Ioh. puta Gersonis ac Cardinalis Bellarmini apud B. Par. Confess. Cath. art. 19. c. 5. p. 320. Patet verò interpretatio nostra satis è contextu. Loquebatur enim tum Christus ad Apostolos, qui in universum terrarum orbem ad Evangelium omni creaturae praedicandum ableg-n-i erant. Cùm hâc Apostolorum vocatione non pugnabat quidem coniugium, interim tamen ad officium Apostolatûs expeditior erat coelibatus. Atque eâ ratione licet non praecipiat Christus Apostolis coelibatum, probat tamen & commendat illis, & quidem eatenus saltem, quatenus continentiae dono instructi erant, sive quatenus absque cons-ientiae laesione coelibes manere poterant, uti rectè exponit B. Parens L. de Coniugio §. 500. Quòd enim nec ipsis etiam Apostelis coelibatus absolutè praeceptus ac mandatus sit, satis indicat Apostolus 1. Cor. 9. 5. Multò verò adhuc minùs mandato divino iniunctus coelibatus coeteris Ecclesiae ministris est, ut quibus non adeò, ceu Apostolis, in functione Ecclesiasticâ est necessarus, cùm illi, Apostoli, in universo terrarū orbe praedicare Evangelium debuerint adeoq; modò huc modò illuc iter suscipere; hi verò, alii Ecclesiae ministri, in certo & fixo loco verbum DEdocere. Quo -ensu verò veterum nonnulli scripserint, quòd quidam propter regum coelorum i. e. vitam aeternam coeliba-um eligant, pridem ostendit B. Par l. c. mon-ns, quòd minimè ita loquuti fuerint sensu Pontificio, h. e. quasi coelibatus sit satisfactio peccatorum maxima ac regni coelorum meritum, sed quòd vita aeterna ex gratiâ propter Christum aequè detur fidelibus tam coniugatis, quàm coelibibus: etenim διὰ minimè hîc notat causam meritoriam, sed saltem hoc, quòd ad ministerium verbi & alia pietatis officia commodiùs obeunda coelibatus eligatur. Unde Marc. 10, 29. adhibetur ἕνεκεν. Interim tamen sicut stella differt à stella in claritate, ita illi, qui rectè coelibatu utuntur, & in hoc vitae statu plus laborant in Evangelii praedicatione aliisque pietatis exercitiis, praerogativam quandam in vitae aet. gloriâ sunt habituri. Quamvis id ipsum Salvator haut indicet h. l., cùm nomine regni coelorum, pro vitâ aeternâ accepto, in Sc. S. usitatè veniat beatitudo, omnibus electis communis. Vid. suprà c. 5, 3. 10. c. 7, 21. c. 8, 11. Ioh. 3, 5. Notanter S. Augustinus l. de Virgin. c. 51. Virginitatis donum quantò magnum (maius) video, tantò ei, ne pereat, futuram superbiam pertimesco. Fidenter dico, faciliùs sequuntur agnum coniugati humiles, quàm superbientes virgines. Id sibi dictum putent Monachi, qui coelibatu suo coacto & impuro, quem vitae etiam aeternae meritorium gloriantur, ita superbiunt, ut alto supercilio cōtemnant humiles cōiugatos. Quorum denique opinioni non patrocinatur, quòd multi veterum nimis immodicè coelibatum aliquando commendent. Huic etenim coelibatûs admirationi, tum quoque hyperbolicae eiusdem depraedicationi ansam veteribus praebuisse videtur Ethnicae scortationis familiaritas, persecutionum atrocitas & coniugiorū imparitas, cumprimis haereticorum, coelibatum contemnentium ac vitae impuritatem introducentium pravitas. Vid. B. Par. l. c.)*

## 19:14
(v. 14. Suffer the little children to come unto me. Bellarmine ineptly gathers from this that it is lawful for younger persons to vow perpetual continence. For 1. younger persons are not hindered from coming to Christ, although they are hindered from making such a vow, which is not in their own power. Nor does Holy Scripture anywhere mention such a vow among the means of arriving at Christ. 2. The Savior is speaking, as is evident from the text, about infants to be offered to him through Baptism, pious prayers, and instruction. Whence also Bellarmine himself in book 1 on Baptism, chapter 8, proves infant baptism from this saying, and refutes the Anabaptists, who maintain that the Gospels speak of children who already have the use of reason. But the Papists do not demand a vow except from such. Much more rightly, therefore, is it proved from this benevolent invitation of Christ against the Papists, that one ought to hope well also concerning the salvation of infants born in the Christian Church, and for whom the prayers of the Church and of pious parents are poured out, even if they should not have been made participants of Baptism. Which opinion we have set forth a little more fully elsewhere in a peculiar Disputation. Compare also the blessed Doctor Huelsemann in Anti-Hager page 267, the blessed Doctor Bald. in Cases of Conscience page 140, the blessed Par. L. on Baptism §. 237. following, likewise the Catholic Confession book 2, special part 2, article 12, chapter 1. There is also held among the works of Gregory of Nyssa a Discourse on Infants prematurely snatched away, which can be read concerning this matter.)

For of such is the kingdom of heaven. Tossanus understands not only those who by reason of age are still children, but also those who are devoid of guile, hypocrisy, and pride like children, Matth. 18. 3. (This can be observed against the common opinion of the Calvinists, who deny that baptized infants believe, since faith comes from hearing. See Beza, response 2 to the Acts of the Colloquy of Montbéliard; Piscator, vol. 1, disputation on Faith § 32, and in this place. But if the kingdom of heaven and eternal life belong to infants, it follows that they are pleasing to GOD. Now, however, without faith it is impossible to please GOD, Ebr. 11, 6. Furthermore, D. Ioh. Georgius Grossius urges in the Theatrum Biblicum, p. 964: 1. that the discourse here is not about infants, but about children who are capable of instruction. But the contrary will be shown a little later. 2. that Christ called these children to himself, Luc. 18, 16. and that they came to him. Response: as if Christ could not have called them, and they could not have come to Christ, who were offered by parents, which Luke ch. 18, 5 expressly testifies. 3. that the word ἐναγκαλισαμ-ενος is referred also to an adult, when Marci 9, 36. it is said that Christ embraced that little child whom he had set in the midst. Response: I grant that these little children were two or three years old, for such can certainly be set in the midst, yet this in no way hinders our opinion, nor does it help the error of the Adversaries in any way, since such a two or three-year-old child, inasmuch as he has not yet reached the years of discretion at that age, can no more judge concerning the articles of faith than an infant still nursing. 4. that the name βρεφ- is applied to a child capable of doctrine, 2. Tim. 3, 15 Response: A two or three-year-old child can also be capable of doctrine insofar as he learns something, and yet such a one does not have the perfect use of reason. 5. that in Holy Scripture faith is nowhere required, except from adults, as those who are capable of hearing, through which faith is given, Rom. 10, 17. Ebr. 11, 6. Response: The passage Rom. 10, 17. deals with adults, or with the organs of the faith of adults, not of little ones, whence even Calvin himself, book 4 of the Institutes, ch. 16, § 19, denies that the Apostle in that place prescribes a perpetual rule for God, that he cannot use another method (namely, in the granting of faith and salvation). Nor does it follow: Faith is from hearing. Therefore, it is from hearing alone. Indeed, rather, just as the Sacrament of Baptism is the washing of regeneration, Tit. 3, 5. Ioh. 3, 5. so also is it a means of approaching faith. Then an argument for Infant Baptism can be sought from this place, in this manner: Those whom Christ wishes to be brought to Himself are not to be kept away from Baptism, as being the ordinary means of divine grace, and indeed, as far as infants are concerned, the only one. But tender infants &c. Therefore. To this pertains that of Bernard, ep. 140 to Count Hildolph: The way of Christ is blocked to the little ones of Christians, while the grace of baptism is denied: nor are they allowed to approach salvation, although the Savior piously cries out for them: Suffer &c. Compare more things pertaining to this in the Analysis on Ioh. 3, 5. The Anabaptists and Photinians object, 1. That Christ in the persons of the little ones blessed such by innocence and humility, but not by age. Resp. Although Christ commends humility and innocence to us in those little ones, yet at the same time He shows that infantile age is not alien to the kingdom of GOD. 2. That the little ones brought to Christ were somewhat older, since they were called by Christ, and set in the midst, Matth. 18, 2. and when they are commanded to permit them to come to Christ, Marc. 10, 14. Now truly none but the older ones come. Resp. Concerning the passage Matth. 18, 2. it was treated above in the Analysis on the said place. Here at least let it be observed that according to Marc. 10, 10. ἀναγκαλισάμενος He embraced them, or as the Syrian notably expresses and when He had taken them upon His arms. Similarly the Ethiopian: and placed them in His bosom and the Persian received them into His bosom. Whence it is evident that the word to come, in a broader signification Marc. 10, 14. is used, namely for to be brought, to be carried &c as is also sufficiently manifest from Luc. 18, 15. Compare more on this matter in B. D. Meisner, Photin Theol. p. 596. B. Par. L. de Bapt. §. 18 and §. 219.

*(v. 14. Sinite parvulos ad me venire. Ineptè hinc colligit Bellarminus, licitum esse iunioribus, perpetuam continentiam vovere. Sacra ullibi tale votum inter media ad Christum perveniendi commemorat. 2. loquitur Salvator, ceu è textu patet, de infantibus per Baptismum, pias preces ac informationem ad eum offerendis. Unde etiam Bell. ipse lib. 1. de Bapt. c. 8. ex hoc dicto probat paedobaptismum, ac refellit Anabaptistas, statuentes, quòd Evangelia loquantur de pueris, qui iamtum usum rationis habent. At non nisi à talibus Pontificii votum exigunt. Talium enim est regnum coelorum. Tossanus intelligit non solùm eos, qui ratione aetatis adhuc sunt pueri, sed eti-m qui doli, hypocriseos & fastûs sunt expertes instar puerorum,Matth. 18. 3. *(Observari hoc potest contra communem Calvinanorum sententiam, negantium, infantes baptizatos credere, cùm fides sit ex auditu. Vid. Beza resp. 2. ad Act. Coll. Mompelg. Piscator vol. 1. disp. de Fide §. 32. & in h. l. Ast si infantium est regnum coelorum s vita aeterna, sequitur quòd DEO placeant. Iam verò sine fide impossibile est DEO placere,Ebr. 11, 6. Coeterùm urget D. Ioh. Tim. 3, 15 Resp. Potest quoque bimu us vel trimulus puerulus doctrinae esse capax quatenus aliquid ediscit, nec tamen talis perfectum usum rationis habet. 5 quòd in Sc. S nus quam requiratur fides, nisi ab adultis, ut qui sunt capaces auditus, per quē datur fides,Rom. 10, 17.Ebr 11, 6. Resp. Locus Rom. 10, 17. agit de adultis, sive de organis fidei adultorum, non parvulorum, unde etiam Calvinus ipse l. 4. Instit. c. 16. § 19. negat, Apostolum d. l. perpetuam Deo praestituere regulam, ne aliâ uti ratione (in fidei & salutis puta donatione) possit, Nec sequitur: Fides est ex auditu. Deinde peti ex h. l. argumentum pro Paedobaptismo potest, h. m Quos Christus vult sibi adduci, illi à Baptismo, utpote gratiae divinae medio ordinario, & quidem quantum ad infantes unico, non sunt arcendi. Atqui infantes tenellos &c. Ergò. Quo facit illud Bernhardi ep. 140 ad Hildoph. ## 19:17
(v. 17. Why callest thou me good, there is no one &c. Christ does not answer according to his own mind, but to those who ask, (and therefore

he does not deny then that Good he may be, Ioh. 10, 11. then because he is God, 1. Ioh. 5, 20.) But he had not called Christ good in any other sense than he would have called any other Master. Whence Christ rebukes him for calling Him good, if he did not believe Him to be God, who is άυ-αγαθόν, άκρο-άτως καί ούσιωδως άγαθόν,. Thus B. Par. explains in Exeg. L. de Nat. Dei §. 99. where he alleges very many ancients to this effect, such as Nazianz. orat. 5. de Theol. Basil the Great lib. 4. contra Eunomium, Epiphanius haeresi 69. Ambros. l. 2. de Fide c. 1. Chrysost. in h. l. to whom can also be added Hilarius lib. 9. de Trinit. and Basilius ep. ad Amphilochium. Caesarius Dialog. 1. explicitly: Not that He denies goodness in Himself, nor exempting Himself from divinity, He says God alone is good. And from this it is also clear that the Arians of old, and the Jews even today (concerning whom Mr. Dr. M-llerus in Iudaismo), in vain impugn the true deity of Christ from the present statement.)

*( There is no one good, except one God. For God alone is from Himself and through Himself, immutably and always, singularly and perfectly, originally and independently good, because He is the cause of every good. Clearly Damascenus lib. 2. Orthod. Fid. c. 29. Μόνος ό θεός έςι φύση άγαθός καί σοφός. Thus also even before him Nazianzenus orat. 2. de Filio: τό άκρως άγαθόν μόνου του θεού. Creatures indeed are also good, Gen. 2, 13. But it is one thing for the essence of a thing to be good, another for a thing through its own essence to be good. Consult more things making for this in B. Par. Coll. Isag. Loc. 2. c. 6. §. 4. B. D. Walther. Harm. Bibl. h. l. Altenstaig. Lex. Theol. tit. good. With a vain attempt, however, the Jesuit Becanus lib. 1. Manual. controv. c. 7. n. 21. strives to evince from the collation of this passage with 3. Reg. 8, 39. that just as God is said here to be alone good, yet so that goodness also pertains to others, not indeed by essence, but by participation: so also God alone is said to search the hearts of men, because indeed He alone knows them from Himself. Notwithstanding which, it can also be said of the deceased saints that they know the hearts of men, not indeed from themselves, but by knowledge or revelation received from GOD. But the answer is easy. For 1. although God may have sometimes revealed the thoughts of another's heart to one or another, that very thing does not prove that this ordinarily happens to the saints in heaven. 2 if religious invocation could be gathered from such an extraordinary revelation, it would follow that the survivors also are to be religiously invoked, since such a revelation of that kind has sometimes been made to such persons, see. Exod. 7, 14.1. Sam. 23, 12.Matth 2, 13. 3 That God has communicated His own goodness to creatures in a certain way is read in the Holy Scriptures; but nowhere is it read that He ordinarily communicates the thoughts of hearts to creatures. Rather, that is recorded in Scripture as pertaining to God alone.)*

*( If you wish to enter into life etc. The Papists strive to establish many erroneous dogmas from this present utterance of the Savior. First, Bellarmine, book 5 on Grace and Free Will, ch. 19, argues for Free Will from this place with all his might as follows: Either it is in our power to perform the offered condition, or it is not: if the first is granted, Free Will will be demonstrated; if the second, that is not a true promise under condition, but a manifest mockery etc. Resp. 1. Distinguish between Evangelical promises, and Legal ones. These indeed require the perfect observation of the commandments in all respects, which man after the fall can by no means perform, and therefore it is by no means now in man's power to perform the offered condition. But one may not infer from this, therefore the promises are useless, or some mockery of God is to be thought of in them: rather it must be known that God wished by this very thing to indicate what He can rightfully demand of us, as from His creatures and whom He had instructed in Adam with sufficient powers to fulfill the divine law. But because we cannot now perform it, He wishes that we should thereby recognize our infirmity after the fall, lament it, and flee to Christ, who is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes, Rom. 10, 4. cf. c. 8, 3. Gal, 3, 24. See Blessed D. Hutter in F. C. p. 361. 362. who himself also on the said page 372 writes that to keep the commandments can also be expounded as to believe in Christ. To which the comparison of Matth. 7, 21. with Ioh. 6, 40. likewise Ioh. 8, 51. with Ioh 5, 24. contributes. 2. Distinguish between a regenerate man, and an unregenerate one. When we deny that man after the fall has free will in spiritual matters, then our discourse is about the unregenerate man, and what a regenerate man can perform from natural powers. 3. It must be known that a regenerate man cannot perform perfect obedience to the divine law from natural powers, yet he can perform begun obedience through new powers given by the Holy Spirit, which, although it may be imperfect, and not meritorious of eternal life, is nevertheless pleasing to God and accepted on account of Christ, whom the regenerate man apprehends by true faith, and upon whose most sufficient [merit] he relies λύτρω. 4. If every promise is either ironical, or presupposes that it is in our natural powers to perform what is promised under some condition, it follows that the very conversion of man to God is a work of Free Will. But the Papists themselves do not admit the consequent. See Bellarmine, book 6, on Grace and Free Will, chapter 5. The consequence is proved from Rom. 10, 9. Secondly, the same Bellarmine, book 4, on Justification, chapter 2, attempts to evince from the present passage that Evangelical promises are conditional, or require the condition of obedience or of fulfilling the law. And for the sake of this matter the Papists compare -um in this place the things said in Ioh. 15, 14. Iac. 2, 8. Compare Maderus, Bishop of Antwerp, in Anti-Synod, p. 198. But it must be noted that that young man, who addressed Christ here, had been instructed in the school of the Pharisees, and was therefore inflated with the opinion of his own righteousness, as is evident from verse 20, and especially from the question proposed by him: What good shall I do &c. and consequently he wished to be saved by the law, that is, by works . This is what not even the Papists themselves dare to deny. Certainly the Jesuit Alphonsus Salmeron, volume 7, Disputation, p. 51, calls him a Jew attending to works. Thomas Stapleton also, formerly royal Professor in the Academy of Louvain, in the Promptuarium for the 12th Sunday after Trinity, inclines to the same: He was seeking, he writes, by doing what, that is, by works he might possess eternal life. Therefore he desired to be saved by the works of the law. Christ therefore acts in this present matter to convince him that he loves neither God nor men perfectly, since, because of a special command of GOD, verse 21, he is unwilling to abandon everything and distribute his goods to the poor. (And from this it is also manifest that the merits of Good Works can in no way be proved from this passage, which nevertheless the Papists, such as Costerus in Enchiridion of Controversies, p. 274 & 291 & others, think. For although Christians are not free from the observation of divine commandments by the Evangelical law, see B. D. Franz, on the Interpretation of Holy Scripture, Oracle 65, p. 815, it does not follow from this that the observation of the commandments is therefore meritorious, since all our righteousness is imperfect, owed, and therefore can in no way subsist in the judgment of GOD, as has been shown elsewhere.) Compare more on this matter in B. D. Hülsemann, in Breviarium Extensum, p. 112, B. Pareus, L. on the Gospel, §. 23, and 97, where he confirms this very opinion with the suffrages of the ancient Doctors of the Church. Clearly St. Hilary on this passage. Christ sends this man, insolent from the law and anxious about salvation, back to the law: so that in that very thing, in which he boasted, he might understand that he had done nothing from it of a right work. For the Lord answered him with the words of the law: but the young man, like an insolent people and one boasting in the law, trusts in it, to which, however, he has not been obedient in any way. Thirdly, the same Bellarmine attempts to prove Evangelical counsels from this same passage, explaining it thus: If you are not content with eternal life, to which you can aspire through the keeping of the commandments, but desire a more excellent degree in eternal life, go, sell all things. To this inept interpretation, B. Par. rightly opposes in the same place that if Christ's words: Go, sell all things, prescribe a counsel of perfection, it would follow 1. that Christ approved this boasting of the youth, which was nevertheless most false, just as also Thomas Aquinas rightly writes in 2. 2 q 189. art. 1., from Jerome: The young man lies, for if he had fulfilled in deed this, which is proposed in the commandments: you shall love your neighbor as yourself, how did he afterwards, hearing, go, sell all things that you have, depart sad? The same is the opinion of Hilary, the author of the Opus Imperfectum, Ambrose, Augustine, Bede, and several Greeks, as the Jesuit Maldonatus testifies, whom Cornelius à Lapide, however, although he desires to be heard as a great admirer of the Fathers, rashly deserts here, and proclaims this young man to be a rare example of youth. Cornelius indeed urges, just as other Papists also do, that Christ loved this young man. But he would not have loved one lying, or presuming otherwise from arrogance than was right, as Stapleton has it in the Antidotum Evang. to c. 13. of Matthew. But the same Stapleton rightly adds, that it is even more probable that he had not truly kept the commandments, because he was still laboring under the disease of avarice, as his subsequent sadness, upon hearing Christ's response, makes manifest. He notes the same, that Basil judges him to have clearly labored notably under the disease of avarice. 2. That the young man did not sin by not obeying this precept. Since, according to Bell. l. 2. de Monach. c. 7. §. 2., a precept by its own force obliges, but a counsel is placed in the will of man. That this young man sinned most gravely by not obeying, is evident from v. 22. If even this command of Christ had been a counsel of perfection, he would not have said: How difficultly shall a rich man enter into the kingdom of heaven, but how difficultly shall a rich man obtain a little crown or greater glory. 3. To sell all things and give them to the poor is above charity, the contrary of which, however, the Apostle teaches 1 Cor. 13, 3. Compare more in the notes to the words: follow me. item to the words, sell all that you have. Fourthly, the Jesuit Costerus in Enchir. Controv. p. 184, gathers from this place, that no one can be certain of his own salvation, for the reason that the Evangelical promises also always have a condition attached, as in this place, if you wish, etc. Now, indeed, man is uncertain of his own constancy in virtues, that is, in the observation of the commandments. Resp. 1. A little before it was shown that this precept is not Evangelical, but legal. 2. Although a man cannot be certain that he will be constant in faith and good works until the end of life through his own powers; nevertheless, a believer can be certain of his constancy through the divine promises concerning the goodness, faithfulness, truth, and omnipotence of GOD, John 10, 28. Rom. 11, 29 1 Cor. 10, 13. Phil. 1, 6. 2 Tim. 1, 12. 3. distinguish between absolute certainty, and certainty ordered to certain means. item between certainty of grace of GOD present, and future salvation item between certainty of faith, and carnal security. Compare more things pertaining to this in B. Par. dispp. Acad. p. 793. Confess. Cath. lib. 2. spec. part. 3. art. 23. c. 5. Colleg. Isag. L. de Elect. & Reprob. c. 9. §. 10. seqq. B. D. Hutterus LL. Mai. Th. p. 811. 816. Finally, maliciously Jews from a collation of this place with Acts 5, 10 argue, that Christ and the Apostles contradict themselves. But that there is no contradiction between the present place and the other from the Acts of the Apostles is clear from the scope of Christ, concerning which it is sufficiently established from what has been said. Compare also Dn. D. M-llerus Iudaismi p. 1368. seqq.

Latin:
