*(v. 17. Cur me vocas bonum, nemo &c. Christus non secundùm suam mentem, sed interroga-tis respondet, (adeoq;

non negat tum quòd bonus sit, Ioh. 10, 11. tum quôd Deus sit, 1. Ioh. 5, 20.) Ille verò non alio sensu Christum appel-averat bonum, quàm appellasset quemvis alium Magistrum. Unde Christus eum redarguit, quòd se bonum appellaret, si Deum, qui est άυ-αγαθόν, άκρο-άτως καί ούσιωδως άγαθόν, non crederet. Ita exponit B. Par. Exeg. L. de Nat. Dei §. 99. ubi in hanc sententiam plurimos allegat veteres, uti Nazianz. orat. 5. de Theol. Basilium M. lib. 4. contra Eunomium, Epiphanium haeresi 69. Ambros. l. 2. de Fide c. 1. Chrysost. in h. l. quibus addi quoq; potest Hilarius lib. 9. de Trinit. it. Basilius ep. ad Amphilochium. Caesarius Dialog. 1. disertè: Non quòd neget in semetipso bonitatem, nede divinitate se eximens, solum inquit bonum esse Deum. Atque hinc etiam patet, quòd frustra olim Ariani, & adhuc hodiè Iudaei (de quibus Dn. D. M-llerus in Iudaismo) è praesenti dicto veram Christi deitatem impugnent.)*

*( Nullus est bonus, nisi unus Deus. Deus enim solus à seipso ac per seipsum, immutabiliter & semper, singulariter & perfectè, originaliter & independenter bonus est, quia omnis boni causa. Clarè Damascenus lib. 2. Orthod. Fid. c. 29. Μόνος ό θεός έςι φύση άγαθός καί σοφός. Sic quoque iam ante eum Nazianzenus orat. 2. de Filio: τό άκρως άγαθόν μόνου του θεού. Creaturae quidem etiam bonae sunt, Gen. 2, 13. Sed aliud est rei essentiam esse bonam, aliud rem per suam essentiam esse bonam. Cons. plura huc facientia apud B. Par. Coll. Isag. Loc. 2. c. 6. §. 4. B. D. Walther. Harm. Bibl. h. l. Altenstaig. Lex. Theol. tit. bonus. Irrito verò conatu Iesuita Becanus lib. 1. Manual. controv. c. 7. n. 21. ex collatione huius loci cum 3. Reg. 8, 39. evincere satagit, quòd quemadmodum Deus dicitur hîc solus bonus, ita tamen ut aliis quoque bonitas competat, non quidem per essentiam, sed per participationem: ita quoque solus Deus corda hominum scrutari dicatur, quia nempe solus ex se ea noverit. Quo tamen non obstante etiam de sanctis defunctis dici posse, quòd corda hominum noverint, non quidem ex se, sed acceptâ à DEO cognitione aut revelatione. Verùm facilis est responsio. Etenim 1. licet Deus aliquando alieni cordis cogitationes uni atque alteri revelarit, id ipsum tamen non probat, quòd ordinariè hoc sanctis in coelis fiat. 2 si ex tali extraord. revelatione religiosa invocatio colligi posset, sequeretur, quòd & superstites religiosè invocandi sint, cùm talibus etiam aliquando istiusmodi revelatio facta sit, vid. Exod. 7, 14.1. Sam. 23, 12.Matth 2, 13. 3 Deum creaturis suam bonitatem certo modo communicasse, in Sc. S. legitur; nullibi verò, quòd cordium cogitationes ordinariè creaturis communicet. Quin potiùs id tanquam soli DEO competens in Scr. memoratur.)*

*( Si vis ad vitam ingredi &c. Multa è praesenti Salvatoris effato dogmata erronea stabilire Pontificii satagunt. Primò Bellarminus lib. 5 de Grat. & Lib. Arbit. c. 19. ita pro viribus L. A. ex h. l. argumentatur: Aut est in potestate nostra praestare conditionem oblatam, aut non est: si detur primum, demonstrabitur Liberum Arbitrium; si secundum, illa non est vera sub conditione promissio, sed manifesta irrisio &c. Resp. 1. disting inter promissiones Evangelicas, & Legales. Hae requirunt quidem numeris omnibus perfectam mandatorum observationem. quam hautquaquam praestare homo post lapsum potest, adeoq; minimè in hominis protestate iam est, conditionem oblatam praestare. Non verò hinc inferre licet, ergo inutiles sunt promissiones, vel irrisio aliqua DEI cogitanda in illis est: quin potiùs sciendum, Deum voluisle hôc ipso indicare, quid iure à nobis, uti à creaturis suis & quas in Adamo sufficientibus viribus instruxerat legem divinam implendi, exigere possit. Quia verò iam praestare non possumus, vult ut inde infirmitatem nostram post lapsum agnoscamus, deploremus, & ad Christum, qui est finis legis ad iustitiam omni credenti, Rom. 10, 4. conf. c. 8, 3. confugiamus, Gal, 3, 24. Vid. B. D. Hutter. in F. C. p. 361. 362. qui ipse etiam d. l. p. 372. scribit, Tò servare mandata posse quoque exponi per credere in Christum. quo facit collatio Matth. 7, 21. cum Ioh. 6, 40. it. Ioh. 8, 51. cum Ioh 5, 24. 2. Dist. inter hominem regenitum, & irregenitum. Quando negamus, hominem post lapsum habere in rebus spiritualibus liberum arbitrium, tunc sermo nobis est de homine irrigenito, it quid homo regenitus ex naturalibus viribus praestare possit. 3. Sciendum, quòd homo regenitus non possit perfectam obedientiam ex viribus naturalibus legi divinae praestare, possit tamen per novas à Sp. S. donatas vires inchoatam obedientiam praestare, quae licet imperfecta sit, nec meritoria vitae aeternae, grata tamen DEO est & accepta propter Christum, quem homo regenitus vera fide apprehendit, & cuius sufficientissimo nititur λύτρω. 4. Si omnis promissio vel ironica est, vel praesupponit, in nostris naturalibus viribus esse, quod sub conditione aliqua promittitur, praestare, sequitur quòd ipsa hominis ad Deum conversio sit opus L. A. At consequens nec ipsi Pontificii admittont. Vid. Bell. l. 6. de G. & L. A. c. 5. Conseq. probatur ex Rom. 10, 9.Secundò idem Bellarminus lib. 4. de Iustif. c. 2. è praesenti loco evincere conatur, promissiones Evangelicas esse condition at as, sive exigere conditionem obedientiae vellegis implendae. Atque huius rei causa conferunt Pontificii -um hoc loco dicta Ioh. 15, 14.Iac. 2, 8. Conf. Ma-derus Episc. Antverp. in Anti Synod. p 198. Verùm notandum quòd adolescens ille, q 11 Christum hîc compellavit, fuerit in scholâ Pharisaeorum institutus, adeoq; opinione propriae iustitiae inflatus, ceu patet ex v. 20. cumprimis verò ex quaestione ab eo propositâ: Quid boni faoiam &c. ac proinde è lege s. ex operibus vo-uerit salvari. Id quod nec ipsi Pontificii negare audent. Certè Iesuita Alphonsus Salmeron t 7. Disp. p, 51. vocat Iudaeum ad opera attendentem. Thomas quoque Stapletonus, regius quondam in Acad. Lovaniensi Professor, in Promptuario Dom. 12. post Trinit, eod. inclinat: Quaerebat, scribit, quid faciendo, id est, per quopera vitam aeternam possideret. Per opera igitur legis salvari cupiebat. Christus proinde hoc in praesens agit, ut ipsum convin at, quòd nec Deum, nec homines perfectè diligat, cùm propter speciale DEI mandatum, v. 21. nolit omnia deferere & pauperibus bona sua erogare. (Atque hinc etiam manifestum est, quòd minimè B. O. merita ex h. l. probari possint. quod tamē Pontificii, uti Costerus Enchir. Controv p. 274 & 291 & alii, putant. Licet enim nec Christiani lege Evangelicâ ab observatione mandatorum divinorum liberi sint, vid. B. D. Franz. de Interp. Sc. S. Orac. 65. p. 815. non tamen hinc sequitur, quòd propterea mandatorum observatio sit meritoria, cùm omnis nostra iustitia sit imperfecta, debita, adeoque minimè in iudicio DEI subsistere queat, ut alibi ostensum.) Conf plura in hanc rem apud B. D. H-lsem. in Brev. Extenso p. 112. B Par. L de Evang. §. 23. ac 97. ubi hanc ipsam sententiam veterum Ecclesiae Doctorum suffragiis confirmat. Ciarè S. Hilarius in h. l. Hunc ex lege insolentem, solicitum de salute remitt it Christus ad legem: ut in eâ ipsâ, in quâ gloriaretur, intelligeret, nihil se exin de recti operis fecisse. Verbis enim legis ei Dominus respondit: sed adolescens tanquam populus insolens & glorians in lege confidit, cui tamen obsecutus iis nullo est. Tertiò idem Bellarminus ex eodem hoc loco consilia Evangelica probare conatur. ita eum explicans: Si non es contētus vitâ aeternâ, ad quam per mandatorum observationem adspirare potes, sed desider as excellentiorem gradum in vitâ aeternâ, vade, vende omnia. Cui ineptae interpretationi rectè opponit B. Par. l. c. quòd si Christi verba: Vade, vende omnia, praescribunt consilium perfectionis, sequatur 1. -hristum approbasse hanc iuvenis gloriat onem, quae tamen fa sissima erat, sicuti etiam rectè Thomas de Aquino 2. 2 q 189. art. 1. ex Hieronymo: Mentitur, scribit, adolescens, si enim hoc, quod propositum est in mandatis: diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum, opere comple visset, quomodo postea, audiens, vade, vende omnia, quae habes, tristis recessit? Eadem est sententia Hilarii, autoris it. Operis Imperf., Ambrosii, Augustini, Bedae ac nonnullorum Graecorum, teste Iesuita Maldonato, quos Cornelius tamen à Lapide, licet magnus Patrum admirator audire gestiat, temerè hîc deserit, ac rarum iuventutis exemplum adolescentem hunc esse clamitat. Urget quidem Cornelius, sicuti & alii Pontificii, quòd Christus iuvenem hunc dilexerit. Non dilexisset verò mentientem, vel ex arrogantiâ aliter praesumentem, quàm par erat, ut habet Stapletonus in Antidoto Evang. ad c. 13. Matth. Verùm rectè subiicit idem Stapletonus, quòd magis adhuc probabile s-, quòd verè mandata non servaverat, quia morbo avaritiae adhuc laborabat, sicuti subsequens eius tristitia, audito Christi responso manifestum facit. Idem annotat, quòd Basilius eum planè avaritiae morbo insigniter laborasse censeat. 2. Iuvenem non peccasse, huic praecepto non obtemperando. Siquidem, iuxta Bell. l. 2. de Monach. c. 7. §. 2. praeceptum vi suâ obligat, consilium verò in arbitrio hominis est positum. Agravissimè hunc Iuvenem non obtemperando peccasse, constat ex v. 22. Si etiam confilium perfectionis fuisset mandatum hoc Christi, non dixisset: quàm difficulter intrabit dives in regnum coelorum, sed quàm difficulter dives aureolam vel maiorem gloriam obtinebit. 3. Vendere omnia & pauperibus ea dare, esse supra caritatem, cuius tamen contrarium docet Apostolus 1. Cor. 13, 3. Conf. plura in not. ad verba: sequere me. it. ad verba, vende omnia, quae habes. Quartò Iesuita Costerus in Enchir. Controv. p. 184. ex h. l. colligit, neminem de suâ salute pesse esse certum, eò quòd promissiones quoque Evangelicae semper adiectam habeant conditionem, ceu h. l. si vis &c. Iam verò homo incertus sit de suâ in virtutibus h. e. in mandatorum observatione canstantiâ. Resp. 1. paullò antè ostensum, quòd praceptum hoc non sit Evangelicum, sed legale. 2. licet homo non possit esse certus, quòd per proprias suas vires constans in fide ac bonis operibufuturus usque ad vitae finem sit; potest tamen fidelis de constatiâ suâ esse certus per promissiones divinas de DEI bonitate, fidelitate, veritate aomnipotentiâ, Ioh. 10, 28.Rom. 11, 291. Cor. 10, 13.Phil. 1, 6.2 Tim. 1, 12. 3. dist. inter certitudinem absolutam, & ad certa media ordinatam. it. inter certitudinem gratiae DEI praesentis, ac salutifuturae it. inter fidei certitudinem, & carnalem securitatem. Conf. plura huc facientia apud B. Par. dispp. Acad. p. 793. Confess. Cath. lib. 2. spec. part. 3. art. 23. c. 5. Colleg. Isag. L. de Elect. & Reprob. c. 9. §. 10. seqq. B. D. Hut terus LL. Mai. Th. p. 811. 816. Denique malitiosè -udaei è collatione huius loci cum Act. 5, 10 argutantur, quòd Christus & Apostoli sibi contradicant. Sed quòd nulla inter praesentem locum & alterum ex Actis Apost. contradictio sit, patet ex Christi scopo, de quo ex dictis satis constat. Confer. quoque Dn. D. M-llerus Iudaismi p. 1368. seqq.)*

## 19:18
v. 18. You shall not commit murder etc. Christ enumerates only the precepts of the second table, 1. because the transgression of them falls more into the eyes. 2. because the Jews boasted greatly of divine worship, when meanwhile they oppressed their neighbor with avarice, frauds, and injustice. (Dn. D. Walth. in H. B p. 779. notes.

for that reason only the precepts of the second table are enumerated here, both because the second table presupposes the first as the foundation of the love of the neighbor, and because it is easier to love the neighbor than God, 1 Ioh. 4. so that in this way, as if by a more easy path, we may be led to the observance of the commandments through the second table. Furthermore, since Mark c. 10, 19. and Luke c. 18, 20. commemorate that Christ began with the commandment: you shall not commit adultery, it is accustomed to be asked what order Christ observed. Resp. B. D. Walth. l. c. p. 780. It is likely that Christ followed that order which Mark and Luke note, as one which Paul also observed.)*

Latin:

v. 18. Non facies homicidium &c. Christus enumerat tantùm praecepta secundae tabulae, 1. quia transgressio eorum magis in oculos incurrit. 2. quia Iudaei plurimùm gloriabantur de cultu divino, cùm interim proximum avaritiâ, fraudibus & iniustitiâ. opprimerent. *(Dn. D. Walth. in H. B p. 779. notat.

propterea tantùm secundae tab. praecepta hîc enumerari tum quia secunda tabula primam ceu fundamentum dilectionis proximi praesupponat, tum quòd faciliùs sit proximum diligere, quàm Deum, 1 Ioh. 4. ut ita tanquam per viam magis facilem ad observ. mandatorum per secundam tabulam deducamur. Porrò cùm Marcus c. 10, 19. & Lucas c. 18, 20. commemorent, Christum inchoasse à praecepto: non moechaberis, quaeri solet, quem ordinem Christus observarit. Resp. B. D. Walth. l. c. p. 780. Veresimile esse, Christum secutum esse eum ordinem, quem Marcus & Lucas annotant, ut quem Paulus quoque observarit.)*

## 19:19
*(v. 19. Honor your father &c. Since Christ does not observe that order of the commandments of the Decalogue which was observed by Moses, it is clear that the cardinal number of the commandments is indeed certain, (since they are expressly called ten words, Deut. 4, 13. c. 10, 4.) but not equally the ordinal. Whence it is not observed even by Paul Rom. 13, 9. & 10.. Christ indeed also omits in the recitation of the fourth commandment the clause added by Moses: that it may be well with you &c. because he had been asked by the young man about the of the commandments themselves, not about their promises, as B. D. Waltherus H. B. page 780 well observes.)*

*( And you shall love your neighbor &c. Mark and Luke omit this general commandment. Origen, tr. 8. in Mat., conjectures from this that it had been added by some other person in Matthew. But B. D. Waltherus H. B. p. 780 rightly notes that this is a bold conjecture, but rather it should be known that it is not unusual among the Evangelists not to recite all and individual sayings and deeds of the Savior in such a way that they all occur in one. What is more, Mark c. 10, 19 expresses the same sum of all the commandments with another negative locution, as the praised D. Walth. l. c. p 817 beautifully shows)*

Latin:

*(v. 19. Honora patrem &c. Cùm Christus non observet eum praeceptorum Decalogi ordinem, qui à Mose fuit observatus, patet, quòd numerus quidem praeceptorum cardinalis certus sit, (cùm disertè decem vocentur verba,Deut. 4, 13.c. 10, 4.) haut aequè ordinalis. Unde nec à Paulo Rom. 13, 9. & 10. observatur. Omittit verò etiam Christus in recitatione quarti praecepti clausulam à Mose adiectum: ut bene sit t-bi &c. quia à iuvene rogatus fuerat de praeceptiipsis, non de eorum promissionibus, uti benè observat B. D. Waltherus H. B. pag. 780.)*

*( Et proximum tuum diliges &c. Omittunt hoc generale mandatum Marcus & Lucas. Coniicit hinc Origenes tr. 8. in Mat. additum fuisse ab alio quodam apud Matthaeum. Verùm rectè notat B. D. Waltherus H. B. p. 780. audacem hanc esse coniecturam, quin potiùs sciendum, quòd non insolitum apud Evangelistas, non omnia ac singula Salvatoris dicta & facta ita recitare, ut apud unum occurrant universa. quid quod Marcus c. 10, 19 aliâ locutione negativâ eandem omnium praeceptorum summam exprimat, uti pulcrè ostendit laudatus D. Walth. l. c. p 817)*

## 19:20
*(v. 20. All these I have kept from my youth. Rightly Basil the Great, hom. 18. in Luke, Chrysostom, hom. 64. in Matt., Theophylact in h. l., likewise the Author of the Opus Imperfectum in Matt., hom. 33., call this young man frivolous, greedy, and a liar. Just as also the Jesuit Maldonatus in h. l. admits that Hilary, Jerome, Augustine, and others are also of this opinion. He does indeed add, That Basil and Chrysostom think differently, but inspection testifies to the contrary. The words of Thomas Aquinas, likewise brought forward from Jerome calling this young man a liar, were cited a little earlier.)*

Latin:

*(v. 20. Omnia haec servari â iuventute meâ. Rectè Basilius M. hom 18. in Lucam, Chrysostomus hom. 64. in Matth. Theophylactus in h. l. item Autor op. Imperf. in Matth. hom. 33. iuvenem hunc levem, avarum & mendacem vocant. quemadmodum etiam iesuita Maldonatus in h. l. fatetur, Hilarium, Hieronymum, Augustinum aliosque in hâc quoque esse sententiâ. addit quidem, Basilium & Chrysostomum diversum sentire, sed inspectio contrarium testatur. Thomae de Aquino verba, itidem ex Hieronymo mendacem iuvenem hunc vocantis adducta paullò antè sunt.)*

## 19:21
*(v. 21. If you wish to be perfect. In the parallel passage, namely Mark 10:21, there is έν σοι ύςερεί. There is still something that you lack, namely necessary for insisting on the journey of eternal life. As Grotius rightly explains in this place. For although Good Works are not the cause of salvation or the merit of eternal life, they are nevertheless required from those who are to be saved, insofar as they remove an obstacle, an impediment otherwise, by which we might be less able to arrive happily at eternal salvation through true faith in Christ. Thus, the selling of all goods is not per se necessary for salvation, since many rich people, provided they do not set their heart on riches, have become partakers of eternal life: insofar, however, as through that selling of assets and distribution among the poor an impediment had to be removed, which was hindering that young man from following Christ, to that extent that selling was necessary for the young man of whom there is talk here. Furthermore, in what sense some are called perfect in Holy Scripture has long been shown by our people, see D. B. Hafenreff. LL. Theol. p. 465. D. B. Lobech. in A. C. art. 9. p. 190. D. B. Balduinus Comm. in Ep. ad Rom. c. 3 part 2. quaest. 2. also in 2. ad Cor. c. 13. part. 2. quaest. 1. B. Par. Confess. Cathol. l. 2. spec. part. 3. p. 808, 809 LL. Theol. L. de Lege DEI. §. 194. also de Iustif. §. 258. namely, it is by no means to be accepted as if the reborn could perfectly fulfill the law of GOD, and thus be saved through the righteousness of the law. (For remnants of sins also adhere to the reborn while they are in this life Isa 64:6Ps 32:6Ps 15:131 Cor 13:9121 John 1:8, 9, 10) But the pious are sometimes called perfect in Holy Scripture, 1. by imputed perfection, Heb 5:9Col 1:28 2. by inchoate perfection. 3. by perfection removed from the vice of hypocrisy 4. by perfection compared with the injustice of others, that is, in comparison with other wicked, worldly men, etc., who do not even offer external obedience to divine laws.)*

*( Sell all that you have. This precept is specifically personal: For Christ wished to convince the young man, instructed in the School of the Pharisees and falsely boasting of the perfect fulfillment of the law, by this very thing, that he had by no means fulfilled the first commandment concerning loving God above all things. See the notes against 17. Although v. Absolutely speaking, the selling of all things is not necessary for salvation, nor commanded by Christ or by the Apostles, See 2 Cor. 8, 13. 14.Eph. 4. 28.1 Thess. 4, 11. nor even proposed as an Evangelical counsel, (which is what the Papists teach, and thus they strive to support the vow of Monastic poverty in this place. See Alphonsus Mendoza Controv. Theolog p. 676.) yet rightly against the Jesuit Conzen, who teaches that the abandonment of wealth was not necessary for this young man for salvation, Guilielmus Estius, Professor of Theology in the Academy of Douai, determines that it was necessary for this young man, as one who set his heart upon riches, for salvation (not indeed to merit it, but lest he fall from it). Therefore, by those words: one thing is lacking to you ( Mark 10, 21.) it is signified that it is lacking for salvation, not for perfection. And thus also falls the objection which the Jesuit Becanus draws from the passage, and by it attempts to prove that in the words of the Apostle 1 Cor. 11, 26. there is not contained a commandment concerning the taking of the cup, but only concerning the commemoration of the death and passion of Christ, and that not absolutely, but under the condition, if we wish to drink the cup, that we do this in memory of Christ. Just as if in this place it were not commanded absolutely that we sell all things and give to the poor, but if we wish to follow Evangelical perfection. But the reason for the cited passages is clearly different, since in this place a special commandment is proposed, but by Paul a general one. Furthermore, it is not commanded only to the young man that he sell all things, as if this were necessary for him at least for perfection, but because this was necessary for him for salvation itself, as Estius, cited a little earlier, rightly advises. Whence also, convinced by the force of truth, Becanus's associates Gregorius de Valentia, Suarez, and Vasquez acknowledge that concerning the drinking itself there is contained a commandment in those words of Christ: Do this. To which the Apostle in the said place refers, as will be shown more prolixly in its own place.)

*( And give to the poor. The Papists strive to prove from this the vow of poverty, which the Monks boast of. But the selling of all things, and their distribution among the poor, suits no class of men less than the Monks. For so far is it from the case, that those who enter Monasteries distribute their goods to the poor, that they rather assign a great part of their goods to the Monastery, which abounds in lands and fields. What of the fact that very many retain proprietary possession confirmed by Papal Bulls, as the Blessed P. shows in Confess. Cath. book 3 p. 289. also p. 313. Concerning the feigned poverty of the Monks, see the same in his commentary on the latter epistle of Peter page 268.)*

And follow me. From this, the Papists attempt to prove the counsel of religious obedience, since one kind of following of Christ is common to all Christians, while another is counseled only to those who wish to be perfect, as Bellarmine has it, *De Monachis*, bk. 1, ch. 7, § *sexto*. Response: Bellarmine himself, in the aforementioned place, admits that the following of Christ in this passage is to be understood as the imitation of Christ. But this is not a matter of counsel, but of precept, and therefore necessary for all the truly pious, 1 Cor. 11:1, Eph. 5:1, 1 Pet. 2:21, whence the same Bellarmine in the said place concedes that this concerns obedience which is necessarily owed to God. Furthermore, the Papists describe a counsel as that to which a greater reward in heaven is promised. But here Christ does not promise a greater reward, but eternal life itself, as is evident from a comparison with Matt. 6:10. Compare more in the blessed Pareus, *Confessio Catholica*, bk. 2, especially through the whole of art. 7, p. 288, et seqq. (

Latin:

*(v. 21. Si vis perfectus esse. In loco parallelo, puta Marc. 10, 21. est έν σοι ύςερεί.Est adhuc quod tibi desit, nempe ad insistendum vitae aeternae iter necessarium. Uti rectè exponit exponit Grotius h. l. Licet enim B. O. non sint salutis causa vel meritum vitae aeternae, requiruntur tamen à salvandis, quatenus nempe removent obicem, impedimentum aliàs, quò minùs feliciter verâ in Christum fide pervenire ad salutem aeternam possimus. Sic venditio bonorum omnium non est perse ad salutem necessaria, cùm multi divites, modò non cor apponant divitiis, salutis aeternae facti participes sint: quatenus tamen per illam facultatum venditionem & inter pauperes distributionem removeri debuit impedimentum, quod iuvenem illum sufflaminabat, quò minùs Christum sequeretur, eatenus venditio illa iuveni, de quo hîc sermo est, fuit necessaria. Porrò quo sensu nonnulli in Sc. S. dicantur perfecti, pridem ostensum à nostratibus, vid. B. D. Hafenreff. LL. Theol. p. 465. B. D. Lobech. in A. C. art. 9. p. 190. B. D. Balduinus Comm. in Ep. ad Rom. c. 3 part 2. quaest. 2. it. in 2. ad Cor. c. 13. part. 2. quaest. 1. B. Par. Confess. Cathol. l. 2. spec. part. 3. p. 808, 809 LL. Theol. L. de Lege DEI. §. 194. it. de Iustif. §. 258. videl id minimè ita accipiendum, quasi renati perfectè legem DEI possint implere, adeoque per legis iustitiam salvi fieri. (adhaerent enim renatis quoque, dum in hac vitâ sunt, peccatorum reliquiae Es 64, 6.Ps. 32, 6.Ps. 15, 13.1. Cor. 13, 9,12.1. Ioh. 1, 8 9. 10.) Sed dicuntur pii aliquando in Sc. S. perfecti, 1. perfectione imputatâ,Ebr. 5, 9.Col. 1, 28 2. perfectione inchoatâ. 3. perfectione ab hypocriseos vitiremota 4. Perfectione cum aliorum iniustitiâ collatâ, h. e. in collatione cum aliis hominibus improbis, mundanis &c. qui ne quidem externam obedientiam legibus divinis praestant.)*

*( Vende omnia quae habes. Est praeceptum hoc specia-e sve personale: Voluit enim Christus iuvenem in Scholâ Pharisaeorum institutum, & de perfectâ legis impletione falsò gloriantem hoc ipso cōvincere, quòd primum praeceptum de Deo super omnia diligendo nequaquum impleverit. Vid. notata adv. 17. Licet v. absolutè loquendo, omnium venditio non sit necessaria ad salutem, necâ Christo vel ab Apostolis mandata, Vid. 2. Cor. 8, 13. 14.Eph. 4. 28.1. Thess. 4, 11. nec etiam ut consilium Evangelicum proposita, (id quod Pontificii docent, adeoque votum paupertatis Monasticae fulcire hoc loco satagunt. Vid. Alphonsus Mendoza Controv. Theolog p. 676.) rectè tamen contra Iesuitam Conzen, docentem, relictionem opum non fuisse iuveni huic ad salutem necessariam, statuit Guilielmus Estius, Theologiae in Acad. Duacensi Professor, fuisse eam huic iuveni, ut qui cor divitiis apponebat, ad salutem (non quidē promerendam, sed ne illâ excideret) necessariam. Proinde verbis illis: unum tibi deest ( Marc. 10, 21.) significari, deesse ad salutem, non ad perfectionem. Atque ita etiam cadit instantia, quam ex loco petit Iesuita Becanus, eâdemque evincere conatur, quòd in veris Apostoli 1. Cor 11, 26. non contineatur praeceptum de sumtione calicis, sed tantùm de commemoratione moris & passionis Christi, idnon absolutè, sed sub conditione, si velimus bibere calicem, ut faciamus hoc in memoriam Christi. planè ceu h. l. non praecipiatur absolutè ut vendamus omnia & demus pauperibus, sed si velimus sequi perfectionem Evangelicam. Verùm diversa planè locorum allegatorum ratio est, cùm h. l. proponatur praeceptum speciale, sed à Paulo generale. Praeterea non praecipitur solùm uveni, ut vendat omnia, quasi hoc ad perfectionem saltem necessarium ei sit, sed quia ad ipsam salutem necessarium hoc illi erat, ut rectè monet Estius, paullò antè adductus. Unde etiam vi veritatis convicti, Becani socienni Gregorius de Valentiâ, Suarez & Vas quez agnoscunt, de ipsâ bibitione contineri praecep-um in verbis illis Christi: Hoc facite. ad quae Apostolusd. l. respicit, uti suo loco ostendetur prolixiùs.)*

*( Et da pauperibus. Pontificii votum paupertatis, quam Monachi iactitant, probare hinc satagunt. Sed omnium venditio, eorumque inter pauperes distributio, nulli hominum generi minùs quàm Monachis competit. Tantum enim abest, ut qui Monasteria ingrediuntur, bona sua pauperibus distribuant, ut potiùs magnam bonorum partem Monasterio addicant, fundis & agris abundanti. Quid quòd plurimi proprietariam possessionem retineant P. R. Bullis confirmatam, uti ostendit B. P. Confess. Cath. l. 3 p. 289. it. p. 313. De fictâ Monachorum paupertate videatur Idem comm. in post. ep. Pet-i pag. 268.)*

*( Et sequere me. Conantur hinc probare Pontificii consilium religiosae obedientiae, cùm alia fit sequela Christi omnib-Christianis communis, alia quae solis illis consulitur, qui volu-esse perfecti, ut habet Bell. 1. de Monach. c. 7. §. sext. Argm. Resp. Ipse Bell. l. c. fatetur, per sequelam Christi in h. l. accipiendam esse Christi imitationem. At haec non est consilii, sed praecepti, adeoque omnibus verò piis necessaria, 1. Cor. 11, 1.Eph. 5, 1.1. Petr. 2, 21. unde etiam idem Bellarm. d. l. concedit, agi hîc de -be dientia, quae necessariò debetur Deo. Porrò Pontificii consilium describunt, quòd ei promittatur maius in coelo praemium. Sed hîc Christus non promittit maius praemium, sed ipsam vitam aeternam, ceu patet ex collt. cum Matth. 6, 10. Conf. plura apud B. Par. Confess. Cath. l, 2. spec. per t. art. 7. p. 288. seqq.)*

## 19:22
(v. 22. For he had many goods. Riches indeed are a gift of God, Prov. 3, 6.c. 14, 1. add. Gen. 31, 9.c. 33, 11. 3 Kings 3. 13. and so they can be possessed with a safe conscience. Provided that work is applied, lest we ourselves be possessed by riches, and become slaves of Mammon, as an example is set before us in this young man. If therefore riches are added to us, we must beware, lest we set our heart upon them, Ps. 62, 11. which happens, if we either abuse riches for pride or for avarice, or trust in them, or ascribe them to our own labors and industry . Since this can easily happen, let us keep before our eyes the divine exhortations of Sirach 31, 1. seqq. 1. Tim. 6, 17. praying with David, Ps. 119, 36. and let us be as having not, 1. Cor. 7, 29 seqq. But if earthly goods are not added to us, let us consider that a mind content with its own lot is the greatest wealth. Moreover, let us render thanks to God, because He has thus freed us from immense cares and dangers. See

the excellent opinions of the Fathers pertinent to this, in B. Par. Aphor. Pract. tit. Avarice & poverty.)*

Latin:

*(v. 22. Habebat enim bona multa. Divitiae quidem sunt donum Dei, Prov. 3, 6.c. 14, 1. add. Gen. 31, 9.c. 33, 11. 3 Reg. 3. 13. adeoque salvâ conscientiâ possideri possunt. Modò operadhibeatur, ne ipsi à divitiis possideamur, ac Mammonae ser-i efficiamur, ceu exemplum in hoc iuvene nobis sistitur. Si proinde divitiae nobis adiiciuntur, cavendum, ne cor illis apponamus, Ps. 62, 11. quod fit, si vel ad fastum vel ad avaritiam divitiis abutamur, vel illis confidamus, aut nostris laboribus industriae que eas adsribamns. Id quod cùm facisè contingere possit, ob oculos habeamus deh orrationes divinas Sirac. 31, 1. seqq. 1. Tim. 6, 17. precantes cum Davide, Ps. 119, 36. simusq; habentes tanquam non habentes, 1. Cor. 7, 29 seqq. Si verò non ad-iciuntur nobis bona terrena, cogitemus, animum suâ sorte contentum esse maximas divitias. quin & gratias persolvam-s Deo, quod immensis curis & periculis nos ita liberârit. Conf.

egregias Patrum sententias huc facientes, apud B. Par. Aphor. Pract. tit. avaritia & paupertas.)*

## 19:23
*(v. 23. A rich man shall hardly enter into the kingdom of heaven. Salvian treats this argument at length in his book on avarice, Lactantius in book 6 of the Divine Institutes, ch. 11, 12, and following, likewise book 7, ch. 1 and following. Jerome, Augustine, & other Fathers throughout.)*

Latin:

*(v. 23. Dives difficilè in trabit inregnum coelorum. Argumentum hoc prolixè tractant Salvianus lib. de avaritia, Lactantius P. 6. instit. Divin. c. 11, 12, seqq. it. lib. 7. c. 1. seqq. Hieronymus, Augustinus & alii Patres passim.)*

## 19:24
v. 24. It is easier. Jerome, book 1 against the Pelagians: In this it is not said what can be done, but an impossible thing is compared to an impossible thing. For just as a camel cannot enter the eye of a needle, so also a rich man does not enter into the kingdom of heaven. Franciscus Lucas on this passage: Because he uses the comparative easier, he does not mean that one impossible thing is more impossible than another, but it is a hyperbole used in such kinds of speaking, such as that one about those between whom there is an incurable disagreement, that a wolf would sooner take a sheep as a wife. Jansenius in chapter 100 of the Concordance: Nor yet was it necessary to say that the Lord signified an impossibility by this sentence, but it would be most simple that it is a hyperbole in this locution, by which the Lord, speaking in a common manner, only wished to signify that it is very difficult for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God. *(Nay, it is equally impossible for a rich man, who sets his heart upon riches, and does not lay aside the hump of the soul clinging to riches, to enter into the kingdom of heaven, as for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle. God, however, can bring it about that a rich man be saved, not insofar as he clings to riches, but by changing the mind of the rich man, so that he may lay aside that burden with his depraved desire, just as He can bring it about by His omnipotence that a camel may pass through the eye of a needle. Although we can by no means attain to this very thing by our human reason. What is more, it is easier for God that a camel should pass through the eye of a needle than that a rich man, trusting in riches, should be saved. Since the former can be done by the absolute power of God, but the latter is not permitted by the justice and truth of God, as the blessed D. Tarnovius rightly warns in Exercise p. 15. And also from this our people firmly prove against the Calvinists from the present passage, that God can perform more than we understand, and that from this we ought to captivate our reason in articles of faith clearly proposed in Holy Scripture. Eph. 3, 20. Compare the note below on verse 26.)*

A camel to pass through the eye of a needle. Jerome takes camel for living being, having followed Origen. Theophylact, from the opinion of others, notes that camel signifies a nautical rope, because this fits better with the eye of a needle. τινές ηάμηνοι φασι ένθάςε ού ζωον, αλλα παχύ χοινιονωρας τα ς αγηύωας επιτηςειον. Erasmus follows Jerome. Some invent. *(Nicholas of Lyra mentions this opinion, and Maximus the Bishop also seems to look to it in his homily on Matthew ch. 18, where he says: He who has been puffed up by honors and expanded by treasures, as a burdened animal and hindered, will not be able to pass through the narrow path of the kingdom, etc.)* That there was a gate in Jerusalem, the name of which was needle. *(But because there is deep silence regarding that gate, which had the name needle, both in Holy Scripture and in other historical records: therefore that opinion is despised with the same ease with which it is proven, as Lyra rightly judges in this place.)* Others wish impossible to be put for difficult. Angelus Caninius in Disquis. Loc. Nov. N. T. ch. 9. No good Greek or ηαμιλον or κάμηλον uses it for a rope or any cable. (He should have excepted Suidas.) It is therefore more correctly said that Christ wished to signify a αςύναθαν παροιμιαηως thing, and used a proverb familiar to the ancient Jews. For in the Talmud, Perec Haroch, it is read: i. e. Nor an elephant entering through the eye of a needle, to wit, has anyone seen. Christ, instead of elephant, which few had seen, said camel, a beast most well-known in Syria. Compare Drusius, book 1, Obser. ch. 11, p. 12 & 1. *(B. D. Meisner approves of Drusius's opinion, that ηάμηλος in this place denotes animal, in Theol. Phot. Consid. p. 324.)* Clement, book 2, Strom., the Author of the Opus Imperfectum on Matthew, homily 33, Theophylact on Matthew, Augustine Q-. Evang. book 2, q. 47, Jerome on ch. 60 of Isaiah, Ambrose on ch. 18 of Luke, Hilary, Canon 19 on Matthew, Juvencus, book 3, Hist. Evang. 525, Sedulius, book 3, Oper. Pasch. v. 348, take the name camel for beast of burden. *(The Arab likewise takes it for an animal, for he has the word , so also the Syrian, the Ethiopian, and the Persian. For they use the same word here, the former indeed , but here , the latter , which they use above in ch. 3, 4, and Mark 1, 6, likewise below ch. 23, 24, where there is no doubt that the discourse is about) animal.)* Tarnovius in Exerc. p. 122. proves at length that the discourse is about a true quadruped animal, not about a nautical rope. *(Let there also be added B. D. Frantzius de Interp. Sc. S. Orac. 138. Buxtorfius Lex. Rabb. Talm. voc. p. 1722. Cosmas Magalianus lib. I. de Eccles. Princip. p. 746.)* Some wish for a nautical rope to be understood. But neither the Hebrew nor the Syriac nor the Greek κάμηλος (for η,, for ηάμιλον per 1. Suidas in the letter η. is παχύ χοινιον) or Latin is used in this signification. Suidas: ηάμηλος το αχθοΦόραν ζφον, ηαμιλος ςέ τό παχύ χοινιον. Bellarmine lib. 3. de Sacr. Eucharistiae c. 6. & l. 2. de Poenit. c. 16. takes it as animal, but l. 2. de Monach. c. 13. and l. 3. de Gr. & L. A. c. 16. as a nautical rope. *(And thus among others it is also taken by Ioh. Calvinus Harm. Evang. p. 294.)* Compare also Wittak. de Sacram. p. 547. *(Moreover, although B. D. Hunnius in Comm. h. l. takes the word κάμηλος for a nautical rope, the opinion of those who understand the saying as an animal is more pleasing. And this interpretation is favored by 1. the writing. For it does not denote κάμηλος but κάμιλος a nautical rope. (What of the fact that learned men affirm that κάμιλος is not found in an ancient writer for a nautical rope? For as to what some urge is found thus in Aristophanes, Drusius replies to this that the passage is suspected of a mistake, for in antiquity the character of the letter μ. was the same as the letter β., so that in Aristophanes it should have been written κάβιλος. But the inspection of the Greek Eclogues, which are observed in the Nuremberg Library, beautifully confirms Drusius's opinion concerning the remarkable agreement of the letters μ. & β. in ancient manuscripts.) Now, indeed, the Greek codices, both those which the Parisians and those which the Londoners collated, those most ancient and most approved ones, constantly have κάμηλον. in the said passage. And thus also the said MS. Greek Eclogues have in places parallel to this one of ours, Marc. 10, 25.Luc. 18, 25. in which, however, without ambiguity, by a fault of the writer, κάμιλος. is read here. 2. Christ's intention. For Christ wished to institute a comparison between those things which among men are impossible, but to God alone are possible, v. 26. Now, indeed, for a nautical rope to pass through the eye of a needle is not impossible among men, although it is by far most difficult, and joined with immense labor, if indeed it is done by the pulling of one thread after another. 3. A comparison of a similar proverbial expression, about which a little before. 4. The attestation of the Syrian and Arabic Interpreter, about which above, which the Blessed D. Frantzius especially commends here in the place cited. 5. The exposition of the Doctors of the Primitive Church. For thus the Fathers almost unanimously expound. Drusius class. 1. lib. 3. Prov. 9. alleges for this opinion Ambrose and Jerome, the Blessed D. Tarnovius Exerc. Bibl. p. 151. Juvencus lib. 3. on the History of the Gospel. Bellarmine lib. 3. on the Sacrament of the Eucharist, Origen, Hilary, Chrysostom. Lactantius also looks to this lib. 6. Divin. Institut. c. 12. item lib. 7. c. 1. Jerome ep. to Hedibia q. 1. The camel is tortuous and curved, and is burdened with a heavy load. And we therefore, when we enter upon crooked paths, and are burdened with the riches of the world or the weight of sins, are not able to enter the kingdom of GOD &c.

How hard it is for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of GOD. The rich are judged either by possession, or by affection. The former can be saved, even if they remain rich; the latter by no means. Anselm in this place Possessing riches with love. Augustine lib. 2. Qq. Evang. c. 47. Covetous of temporal things and proud of such things. Salvian lib. 1. against Avarice p. 32. He will not say to the rich man: you are to be tortured, because you are a murderer: you are to be tortured, because you are a fornicator; but only, because you are rich, that is, because you use riches badly, because you do not understand the riches given to you for a holy work. For riches themselves are not harmful by themselves, but the minds of those using them badly are criminal: nor are wealth itself causes of punishment to a man, but the rich make punishments for themselves out of wealth: because while they do not wish to use riches well, they convert the riches themselves into torments for themselves &c. Ambrose in Luke serm. 29. Let the rich learn, that the crime is not held in the faculties, but in those who do not know how to use them: for as riches are impediments to the wicked, so they are aids of virtues to the good. Jerome in Psalm 52. it is said of the rich man: Fool, this night &c. Not that it is an evil to have riches, only that they be held from a just source; let thanks be rendered to GOD, who gave them. Not so, but it is an evil to place hope in riches &c. It is permitted to have riches for necessity, but it is not permitted to have them out of love. For both Abraham and the remaining good men had riches: but they did not place their hope in riches. The same epist. to Salvina: Neither does wealth hinder the rich man, if he uses them well, nor does poverty make the poor man more commendable. Augustine in the books Q-.

N. T. q. 27. and in Ps. 131.God does not attend to ability, but to desire: and He judges even the beggar and the poor man according to the desire with which he gapes after temporal things, not according to the ability which he did not even happen to attain. See also Ritterhusius, Commentary on the aforementioned passage of Salvian, p. 447. It should be known, moreover, that the primitive Church condemned Pelagius and other heretics who taught their disciples that the rich could not be saved unless, after Baptism, they bestowed their riches upon the poor. As Cosmas Magalianus reports, book 1 of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, page 746.)*

Εξεπλησθονθο σφόδρα. They were astonished beyond measure, and marveled. They marvel either by reason of themselves, because they hoped for a worldly Kingdom of the Messiah; or by reason of others, because they saw that most people pursued riches with such great impetus. *(A certain admiration is placed in praise, a certain one is not without fault. See Blessed Parent, Elenctic Disputations on the Sunday Gospels, p. 127; also Blessed Doctor Tarnovius on Zechariah, p. 114.)*

Latin:

v. 24. Facilius est. Hieronymus l. 1. contr. Pelag In hoc non quod fieri potest dictum, sed impossibile impossibili comparatum. Quomodo enimcamelus, non potest intrare foramen acus, ita & dives non ingreditur in regna coelorum. Franciscus Lucas in h. l. Quod comparativo facilius utitur, non intelligit impossibili magis impossibile esse, s-d hyperbole est in huiusmodi loquendi generibus usurpata, quale est illud de iis, inter quos insanabile dissidium est, priùs ovem lupus ducat uxorem. Iansenius in c. 100. Conc. Nec tamen necesse fuit dicere, hâc sententiâ Dominum significasse impossibilitatem, sed simplicissimum fuerit, hyperbolen esse in hac locutione, quâ Dominus vulgari modo locutus, tantùm significare voluit, valdè difficile esse, divitem ingredi in regnum Dei. *(Imò aequè impossibile est, divitem, qui cor divitiis apponit, nec gibbum animi divitiis adhaerescentis deponit, ingredi in regnum coelorum, quàm camelum transire per foramen acûs. Deus tamen efficere potest, ut dives salvus fiat, non quatenus divitiis adhaeret, sed mutando animum divitis, ut deponat sarcinam illam cum prava cupiditate, sicuti efficere potest per suam omnipotentiam, ut camelus per foramen acûs transeat. Licet hoc ipsum ratione nostrâ humanâ adsequi haud possimus. Quid quòd facilius Deo, ut Camelus transeat per foramen acûs, quàm ut dives, in divitiis confidens, salvus fiat. Cùm illud per potentiam Dei absolutam fieri possit, hoc verò non patiatur Dei iustitia ac veriras, uti rectè monet B. D. Tarnovius in Exerc. p 15. Atque eriam hinc firmiter è praesenti loco nostrates contra Calvinianos probant, quòd Deus plus possit praestare, quàm nos intelligimus, quòd que exinde rationem nostram in fidei articulis, clarè in Scriptura. S. propositis, captivare debeamus. Eph. 3, 20. Conf. not. infrà ad vers. 26.)*

Camelum per foramen acûs transire. Hieronymus camelum accipit pro animante, sequutus Origenē. Theophylactus ex aliorum sententiâ notat, Camelum significare rudentem nauticum, quòd hoc magis quadret ad foramen acûs. τινές ηάμηνοι φασι ένθάςε ού ζωον, αλλα παχύ χοινιονωρας τα ς αγηύωας επιτηςειον. Erasmus sequitur Hieroymū Quidam comminiscuntur. *(sententiae huius meminit Nic. de Lyra, eò quoque respicere nonnullis videtur Maximus Episcopus hom. super Matth c. 18 ubi: Qui honoribus inflatus fuerit & aurithesauris dilatatus, tanquamonustū animal & impeditum per angustū regni iter transire nō poterit, &c.)* Hierosolymis fuisse portam, cui nomen fuerit acus. *(Sed quia de illâ portâ, cui acus nomen fuerit, altum tùm in Script. S. tùm in aliis historicis silentium est: ideò eâdem facilitate sententia illa contemnitur, quâ probatur, ut rectè iudicat Lyranns in h. l.)* Alii impossibile positum esse volunt pro difficili. Angelus Caninius in Disquis. Loc. Nov. N. T. c. 9. Nullus bonus Graecus autηαμιλονvelκάμηλονpro rudente aut quovis fune usurpat. (Suidam excipere debuisset.) Rectiùs igitur dicitur, Christum rem αςύναθαν παροιμιαηως significare voluisse, & usum esse proverbio priscis Iudaeis familiari. Nam in Talmud Perec Haroch legitur: i. e. Neelephantem intrantem per foramen acûs, scil. vidit quis. Christus pro elephanto, quem pauci viderant, camelum, bestiam Syriae notis simam, dixit. Conf. Drusium l. 1. Obser. c. 11. p 12. & 1 *(Drusii sententiam, quòd ηάμηλος h. l. animal notet, approbat B. D. Meisnerus in Theol. Phot. Consid. p. 324.)* De iumento nomē Cameli accipiunt Clemens l. 2. Strom., Autor Oper. Imperf. in Matth. hom 33. Theophyl. in Matth. Augustinus Q-. Evang. l. 2. q. 47. Hieron in c. 60. Esaiae, Ambrosius in c. 18. Lucae, Hilarius Canon. 19. in Matth. Iuvencus l. 3. Hist. Evang. 525. Sedulius l. 3. Oper. Pasch. v. 348. *(Arabs itidem pro animali accipit, habet enim vocem sic Syrus quoq;, Aethiops & Persa. Eandem quippe vocem hîc adhibentes, ille quidem hic verò iste qua utuntur suprà c. 3, 4. ac Marc. 1, 6. item infrà c. 23, 24. ubi nullum dubium est, sermonem esse de animali.)* Tarnovius in Exerc. p. 122. prolixè probat, sermonem esse de vero animali quadrupede, non de fune nautico. *(Addantur quoque B. D. Frantzius de Interp. Sc. S. Orac. 138. Buxtorfius Lex. Rabb. Talm. voc. p. 1722. Cosmas Magalianus lib. I. de Eccles. Princip. p. 746.)* Quidam volunt intelligi funem nauticum. Atqui nec Ebraeum nec Syriacum nec Graecum κάμηλος (per η, nam ηάμιλον per 1. Suidae in litt. η. est παχύ χοινιον) vel Latinum in hâc significatione usurpatur. Suidas: ηάμηλος το αχθοΦόραν ζφον, ηαμιλος ςέ τό παχύ χοινιον. Bellarminus lib. 3. de Sacr. Eucharistiae c. 6. & l. 2. de Poenit. c. 16. de animali accipit, sed l. 2. de Monach. c. 13. ac l. 3. de Gr. & L. A. c. 16. de fune nautico. *(Atque ita inter alios accipit quoq; Ioh. Calvinus Harm. Evang. p. 294.)* Conf. etiam Wittak. de Sacram. p. 547. *(Coeterùm licet etiam B. D. Hunnius in Comm. h. l. pro fune nautico vocem κάμηλος accipiat, magis tamen arridet eorum sententia, qui de animali intelligunt dictum. Favetque huic interpretationi 1. scriptio. neque enim κάμηλος sed κάμιλοςfunena nauticum notat. (Quid quòd nec κάμιλος apud antiquum Scriptorē pro fune nautico reperiri, viri docti affirment. quod enim apud Aristophanem ita inveniri, nonnulli urgent, ad hoc reponit Drusius, locum suspectum esse de mendo, nam antiquitus characterem litt. μ. eundem fuisse cum litt. β. ut adeò apud Aristophanem scribendum fuerit κάβιλος Drusii verò sententiam de insigni convenientiâ litt. μ. & β. in antiqui, MSS., pulcrè confirmat inspectio Eclogarum Graecarum, quae in Bibliothecâ Norib. observantur.) Iam verò Codd. Graeci tum quos Parisienses, tum quos Londinenses contulerunt, anti quissimos illos probatissimosque, constanter d. l. habent κάμηλον. Et ita quoque habent dictae Eclogae Graecae MS. in locis huic nostro parallelis, Marc. 10, 25.Luc. 18, 25. in quibus tamen, procul ambiguo, scriptoris vitio, hîc legitur κάμιλος. 2. Christi intentio. Voluit enim Christus comparationem instituere inter ea, quae apud homines impossibi-ia sunt, Deo verò soli possibilia, v. 26. Iam verò funem nauticum per foramen acûs transire, non est apud homines impossibile, licet longè difficillimum sit, & cum immenso labore coniunctum, si nempe fiat per unius fili postalterum traiectionem. 3. similis proverbialis locutionis, de quâ paullò antè, collatio. 4. Syri & Arabis Interpretis de quibus suprà, attestatio, quam cumprimis hîc commendat B. D. Frantzius l. c. 5. Primitivae Ecclesiae Doctorum expositio. Ita enim Patres ferè unanimiter exponunt. Drusius class. 1. lib. 3. Prov. 9. pro hâc sententiâ allegat Ambrosium & Hieronymum, B. D. Tarnovius Exerc. Bibl. p. 151. Iuvencum lib. 3. de Histor. Evang. Bellarminus lib. 3. de Sacramento Eucharistiae, Origenem, Hilarium, Chrysostomum. Respicit quoque huc Lactantius lib. 6. Divin. Institut. c. 12. it. lib. 7. c. 1. Hieronymus ep. ad Hedibiam q. 1. Camelus tortuosus & curvus est, & gravi sarcinâ praegravatur. Et nos ergo, quando pravas ingredimur semitas, & oneramur mundi divitiis sive pondere delictorum, regnum DEI ingredi non valemus &c.)*

Quàm divitem in regnum DEI ingredi. Divites censentur vel ex possessione, vel ex affectu. Illi possunt salvi fieri, etsi maneant divites; hi minimè. Anselmus h. l. Possidens divitias cum amore. Augustinus l. 2. Qq. Evang. c. 47. Cupidus rerum temporalium & de talibus superbiens. *(Salvianus lib. 1. contra Avaritiam p. 32. Non dicet diviti: torquendus es, quia homicida es: torquendus es, quia fornicator; sed tantummodo, quia dives h. e. quia divitis malè uteris, quia datas tibi ad opus sanctum divitias non intelligis. Non enim ipsae divitiae per se noxiae, sed mentes malè utentium criminosae: nec ipsae opes homini poenae causae sunt, sed opibus sibi poenus divites faciunt: quia dum uti divitiis benè nolunt, ipsas sibi divitias in tormenta convertunt &c. Ambrosius in Lucam serm. 29. Discant divites, non in facultatibus crimen haberi, sed in iis, qui uti nesciant: nam divitiae ut impedimenta sunt improbis, ita bonis sunt adiumenta virtutum. Hieron. in Psal. 52. de divite dicitur: Stulte hac nocte &c. Non quòd malum sit, divitias habere, tantùm ut de iusto habeantur; DEO gratiae referantur, qui eas dedit. Non, sed malum est, spem in divitiis ponere &c. Divitias licet habere ad necessitatem, sed non licet habere ex amore. Nam & Abraham & reliqui boni divitias habuerunt: sed spem in divitias non miserunt. Idem epist. ad Salvinam: Nec opes obsunt diviti, si illis benè utatur, nec egestas facit pauperem commendabiliorem. Augustinus in libb. Q-.

N. T. q. 27. & in Ps. 131.Non attendit Deus facultatem, sed cupiditatem: & iudicat etiam mendicum & pauperem secundum cupiditatem, quâ inhiat rebus temporalibus, non secundum facultatem, quam non contigit etiam adipisci. Conf. quoque Ritterhus. Comment ad all. locum Salviani p. 447. Sciendum praeterea, primitivam Ecclesiā damnâsse Pelagium aliosq; haereticos, qui docuerunt discipulos suos, divites non posse salvari, nisi post Baptismum divitias pauperibus elargirentur. Ceu refert Cosmas Magalianus l. 1 de Hierarch. Eccles. pag. 746.)*

Εξεπλησθονθο σφόδρα. Supra modum reddebantur attoniti, & mirabantur. Mirantur vel ratione sui, quia sperabant Regnum Messiae mundanum; vel ratione aliorum, quòd viderent, plerosque tanto impetu sectari divitias. *( Admiratio quaedam in laude ponitur, quaedam vitio non caret. Vide B. Parentem Dispp. Elencht. sup. Evang. Domin p. 127. it. B. D. Tarnovium in Zach. p 114.)*

## 19:26
v. 26. With God all things are possible. Bardesanes the Syrian in Eusebius, book 6 of the Preparation for the Gospel, ch. 10, f. 165. θεού ευπινευσαντος πανθα ςύναθα καὶ ανεμποςιςα. τηλς έηεινού βούλησει ούςέν αντιςηναι δύναται. With God assenting, all things are possible, nor can anything be hindered. For nothing can resist His power. *(H. Grotius, who can be consulted, brings forward twin sentiments from Homer, Epicharmus, Linus, Callimachus, and other profane writers on this passage.)*

The sense, however, of this passage is: If we look at the corrupt nature of men, it is impossible for those who trust in riches to be saved, but God can change the hearts of men so that they recognize the vanity of riches and prefer heavenly things to earthly ones. Thus Tossanus. Man left to himself cannot resist concupiscences, but [he can] through the grace of GOD. *(Parallel sayings to the present dictum are Gen. 18, 14.Iob. 42, 2.Ier. 32, 17.26.Zach. 8, 6.Luc. 1, 38.Eph. 3, 20. And from this it is also evident that the articles of faith are not only above reason, but also against reason, if indeed this [reason] itself is considered as left to itself, or insofar as it does not contain itself within its own sphere. Concerning which matter Blessed P. L. treats at greater length in De Eccles. §. 252, Academic Disputation, p. 1477 et seqq. Add Blessed Doctor Meisner, Photinian Theology.

p. 310 et seqq. Blessed Doctor Maior in the Disputation on sin concerning the Question: Whether the Mysteries of faith are only above, and not against reason, Blessed Doctor Balduinus, Commentary on Zechariah, p. 492. 492. Blessed Doctor Hunnius on this passage, and especially the Lords of Theology Marpin, Fundamental deductions, p. 80 et seqq. But when Christ says, That all things are possible to GOD, then it speaks of those things which are not repugnant to the perfection of GOD, such as justice, goodness, etc. Thus He cannot lie, Num. 23, 23. die, 1. Tim 1, 17. etc. Yet from this it can by no means be inferred that He Himself is not omnipotent. For although such things as these may seem to attribute some non-power to GOD according to the sound of the words, yet according to the thing signified by the truth, they attribute supreme power to GOD. St. Augustine, Sermon 119 de Temp. Omnipotent is God to do all things which He wills to do. The same, book 5 de C. D. ch. 10. God is called omnipotent by doing what He wills, not by suffering what He does not will: for if that were to happen to Him, He would by no means be omnipotent. And therefore He cannot do certain things, because He is omnipotent. Furthermore, the Savior speaks of impossibilities of nature, i.e., that God can also do those things which are impossible with respect to human power and knowledge, but not of impossibilities by nature. For those things which truly imply a contradiction, even God cannot do. See the notes on Luc. 18, 27. and compare B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. de Nat. DEI ch. 6. §. 2.)*

Latin:

v. 26. Apud Deum omnia possibilia sunt. Badisana Syrus apud Eusebium l. 6. de praepar. Evang. c. 10. f. 165. θεού ευπινευσαντος πανθα ςύναθα καὶ ανεμποςιςα. τηλς έηεινού βούλησει ούςέν αντιςηναι δύναται. Deo annuente omnia possibilia sunt, nec quicquam impediri potest. Illius enim potestati nihil potest resistere. *(Gemellas sententias ex Homero, Epicharmo, Lino, Callimacho aliisque profanis Scriptoribus adducit H. Grotius in h. l. qui potest evolvi.)*

Sensus verò huius loci est. Si corruptam hominum naturam respiciamus, impossibile est eos, qui in divitiis confidant, salvari, sed Deus potest hominum corda immutare, ut vanitatem divitiarum agnoscant, & coelestia terrenis praeferant. Ita Tossanus. Homo sibi relictus non potest concupiscentiis resistere, sed per DEI gratiam. *(Dicta praesentis dicti parall. sunt Gen. 18, 14.Iob. 42, 2.Ier. 32, 17.26.Zach. 8, 6.Luc. 1, 38.Eph. 3, 20. Atque hinc etiam patet, quòd articuli fidei non solùm sint supra rationem, sed etiam contra rationem, si nempe haec ipsa consideretur ut sibi relicta, vel quat. sese intra suam sphaeram non continet. qua de re prolixiùs agit B. P. L. deEccles. §. 252. Disp. Acad. p. 1477. seqq. Add. B. D. Meisn. Theol. Photin.

p. 310. seqq. B. D. Maior in Disp. pec. de Quaest. An Myesteria fidei solùm sint suprà, non verò contra rationem, B. D. Balduinus Comm. in Zachar. p. 492. 492. B. D. Hunnius in h. l. cumprimis verò Dnn. Theol. Marpin Fundam. deduct. p. 80. seqq. Quando verò Christus dicit, quòd DEO omnia sint possibilia, tunc loqu tur de iis, quae non repugnant DEI perfectioni. uti iustitiae, bonitati &c. sic non potest mentiri,Num. 23, 23.mori,1. Tim 1, 17. &c, Equo tamen minimè inferri potest, quòd ipse non sit omnipotens. Etenim licet ista talia quoad sonum verborum aliquam non potentiam D E O tribuere videantur, quoad rem tamen, veris significatam, summam potentiam DEO tribuunt. S. August. serm. 119. de Temp. Omnipotens eDeus ad facienda omnia, quae facere voluerit. Idem l. 5. de C. D. c. 10. Dicitur Deus omnipotens faciendo, quod vult, non patiendo quod non vult: quod si ei accideret, nequaquam esset omnipotens. Undpropt rea quaedam non potest, quia est omnipotens. Loquitur praeterea Salvator de impossibilibus naturae h. e. quòd Deus etiam ea possit facere, quae respectu humanae potentiae ac scientiae impossibilia sunt, non verò de impossibilibus naturâ. Quae enim reverà contradictionem implicant, ea nec Deus facere potes-, Vid. notata ad Luc. 18, 27. ac conf. B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. de Nat. DEI c. 6. §. 2.)*

## 19:27
v. 27. We have left all things etc. How do they boast that they have left much, who were poor fishermen? Chrysostom answers: they left and dismissed much, who renounced with the re-possessed and with desires, and studied to serve the calling. But it is answered more correctly that Peter speaks from affection. *(Thus Jerome writes in ep to Pammachius on the death of Paulina, that the Apostles as far as riches left nothing, as far as the will they left the whole world. Obs. that this following of which the Apostles speak here; is not prescribed to all as is evident from Luc. 9, 58. and Marc 5, 18. There is indeed another following of Christ, which is necessary for all true Christians, by which we follow Christ by believing, living piously, and patiently bearing the cross. And this following is not only counseled, but commanded. See 1. Cor. 11, 1. Eph. 5, 1. 1. Pet. 2, 21. Nor is that following of Christ and desertion of faculties, of which Peter speaks here, to be taken as if the Apostles had utterly cast away all their things, and had entirely renounced their ownership and possession: but that desertion is to be understood in such a way that they had turned their mind away from secular business and faculties to the extent that they could be an impediment in their calling: but finally when by the special command of Christ they had to go out into all the earth, they brought all things into common, as B. Par. explains that desertion L. de Minist. Eccles. §. 333. add. B. D. Quist. in h. l. which explanation is also confirmed by the collation of the loc. Matth. 9, 10.Marc. 1, 29. and Ioh. 21, 3. But as concerns the wives of the Apostles (of whom Matth. 8, 14.Marc. 1, 30.Luc. 4, 38. and what kind all the Apostles, except John and Paul, had, Ambrose testifies in 2. Cor. 11, indeed not even Paul excepted, according to Ignatius in his epistle to the Philadelphians. Compare also Clement of Alexandria, book 3 of the Stromata, p. 210, Basil on the renunciation of the world, Eusebius, book 3 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 27), they were not in the number of those things which were left for the sake of the name of Christ, and therefore they were not separated from them by the Apostles themselves: but rather they offered themselves as companions of the journey to the Apostles, as is gathered from 1. Cor. 9, 5. And such a spontaneous desertion of wives would also conflict with the primordial law of marriage, a man shall leave etc., and with the Apostolic rule 1. Cor. 7, 10. 11. Nor do the words of Christ in verse 29 and following, everyone who has left his wife etc., imply such a desertion of a wife. For Christ passes from the hypothesis to the thesis, and proposes consolation to those who, through the violent persecution of tyrants, are separated not only from goods, but also from wife and children, from whom they ought not otherwise to separate themselves by a voluntary act. Compare at greater length B. Par. Confess. Cathol. book 2, spec. part 2, article 6, chapter 4, p. 123, also B. D. Tarnov. on marriage. Furthermore, a comparison of the parallel passage Luc. 14. shows that the sentence of Christ is not to be understood concerning spontaneous desertion, but concerning violent seizure, and that such a thing must be borne patiently on account of the confession of the truth. Thus he also joins soul to those whose loss must be borne patiently for the sake of Christ. He does not, however, in the least wish that we should kill ourselves for the sake of the Gospel. Let Hilary be consulted entirely in his Enarrations on Psalm 119. But if from this desertion of goods, the celibacy of the clergy could be inferred as absolutely necessary, it would follow that a total desertion of all manner of faculties would be required much more from the clergy, and therefore also from Bishops, and would be likewise absolutely necessary. But the writings of the Papists testify to the contrary, and daily practice speaks much more. For who is unaware of the riches and the sacred hunger for gold of the Cardinals, and likewise the arts of the Roman Pontiffs for growing rich, as it is customary for them to enrich their nephews and nieces and to raise them to the highest dignities, a thing which no one but a fool will persuade himself is done with a casting aside of the care for temporal things.)*

Latin:

v. 27. Nos reliquimus omnia &c. Quomodo multum se reliquisse gloriantur, qui erant pauperculi piscatores? Chrysostomus respondet: multum reliquerunt & dimiserunt, qui cum re-possessâ & concupiscentiis renunciarunt, & vocationi inservir-studuerunt. Sed rectiùs respondetur, ex affectu Petrum loqui. *(Sic Hieronymus in epad Pammachium super obitum Pau linae scribit, quòd Apostoli quantum ad divitias nihil, quantum avoluntatem totum mundum reliquerint. Obs. quòd haec seque ade quâ Apostoli hîc loquuntur; non sit omnibus praescripta --u constat ex Luc. 9, 58. ac Marc 5, 18. Est verò sequela Christi alia, quae omnibus verè Christianis necessaria est, qua Christum sequimur credendo, piè vivendo & crucem patienter ferendo. Atque haec sequela non consulitur tantùm, sed praecipitur. Vid. 1. Cor. 11, 1.Eph. 5, 1. 1. Pett. 2, 21. Nec illa quoque Christi seque-a ac facultatum desertio, de quâ Petrus hîc loquitur, ita accipienda, quasi Apostoli omnia sua penitus abiecerint, eorumqu proprietate & possessione omninò se abdicarint: sed ita d-fertio illa intelligenda est, quòd animum eatenus à negotiis scularibus ac facultatibus averterint, quat. in vocatione imp-dimento esse poterant: tandem verò cùm peculiari mandat. Christi in omnem terram illis exeundum erat, omnia in commune contulerint, uti desertionem illam explicat B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccles. §. 333. add. B. D. Quist. in h. l. quae etiam explicatio confirmatur collatione loc. Matth. 9, 10.Marc. 1, 29. ac Ioh. 21, 3. Quod verò Apostolorum uxores (de quibus Matth. 8, 14.Marc. 1, 30.Luc. 4, 38. qualesque omnes Apostolos, excepto Iohanne ac Paulo, habuisse, testatur Ambrosius in 2. Cor. 11, quin nec. Paulo excepto, iuxta Ignatium ep. ad Philadeph. Conf. quoque Clem. Alexandrinus l. 3. Strom. p. 210. Basil. de abdic. feculi, Eusebius l. 3. H. E. c. 27.) concernit, illae non fuerunt in numero eorum, quae nominis Christi causâ fuerunt relicta, adeoque nec fuerunt ab ipsis separatae: quin potiùs itineris comites sese Apostolis illae praebuerunt, ceu ex 1. Cor. 9, 5. colligitur. & pugnaret etiam talis spontanea uxorū desertio cum lege coniugii primaevâ, relinquet homo &c. ac cum regulâ Apostolicâ 1. Cor. 7, 10. 11. Nec inferunt quoque istiusmodi uxorem desertionem verba Christi v. 29. seq. omnis qui reliquerit uxorem &c. Transit enim Christus ab hypothesi ad thesin, & consolationem proponit illis, qui per violentam Tyrannorum persecutionem non à bonis solùm, sed etiam ab uxore & liberis separantur, à quibus voluntario ausu se aliàs non deberent separare. Conf. pluribus B. Par. Confess. Cathol. l. 2. spec. part. 2 art. 6. c. 4. p. 123. it. B. D. Tarnov. de coniug. Praeterea collatio loci paralleli Luc. 14. ostendit, quòd Christi sententia non de spontanea desertione intelligenda sit, sed de violenta ereptione, quòd que talis propter veritatis confessionem patienter ferenda sit. Sic animam quoque coniungit iis, quorum iactura propter Christum patienter ferenda. Minimè tamen vult, ut nos ipsos propter Evangelium interficiamus. Videatur omninò Hilarius in Enarr. Psalmi 119. Quòd si verò ex hâbonorum desertione, clericorum coelibatus tanquam absolutè necessarius inferri posset, consequens foret, multò magis facultatum omnimodam desertionem à clericis, adeoque & Episcopis requiri, pariterq; absolutè necessariam esse. At contrarium testantur scriptPontificiorum, ac multò magis loquitur praxis. cottidiana. Quem enim latent divitiae ac sacra auri fames Cardinalium, artes item ditescendi Pontificum Romanorum, ut quibus solenne est, nepotes suos neptesque locupletare & ad summas evehere dignitates, id quod abiectâ rerum temporalium curâ fieri, nemo nisi insipiens sibi persuadebit.)*

## 19:28
v. 28. έν τη παλιγγενεσίᾳ, in regeneration and renovation or rather after the renovation of the world in the other age. *(Just as the Syrian also translates: in the new age, the Arab: in the coming generation. The Persian, however, seems to have understood it concerning regeneration, which happens in this age. Similarly also the Ethiopian. And thus also the author of the Imperfect Work hom. 33 long ago understood it, likewise Macarius hom. 7, and also Bede on this passage. Of the more recent ones, Camero in Myroth. Coquaeus in Aug. book 20 de C. D. ch. 5)* Just as Peter calls that day the day of ἀποηαθαςασεως παντων, Acts 3:21. Augustine book 20 de C. D. ch. 5. What he says in the regeneration, he undoubtedly wished the resurrection of the dead to be understood by the name of regeneration. For thus our flesh will be regenerated through incorruption, just as our soul is regenerated through faith. *(The same has similar things in book 3 against the two Epistles of the Pelagians ch. 3, likewise book 4 against the same ch. 11, book 2 against Julian. In the same way also Gregory the Great book 4 Moral. ch. 23 and Bernard in Declam. understand it, whose words B. Par. L. de Resurr. §. 4 cites. Similarly Euthymius and Theophylactus explain it on this passage, and Leonh. Coquaeus Comm. ad Aug. de C. D. p. 355 also refers here the passage Psalm 2:7, which Paul Acts 13:33, 34 interprets concerning the resurrection of Christ. Scripture therefore makes mention of a double regeneration, of which one happens in this life, and indeed both through Baptism, John 3:5, Titus 3:5, and through the word, 1 Peter 1:23, James 1:18, the other after this life, i.e., on the day of Judgment, of which Christ speaks in this passage. Add Ambrose serm. 48 on the sepulcher of Christ. That regeneration happens spiritually, this one miraculously. Compare also B. P. H. E. p. 464.)*

It does not pertain to the description of the subject, but to the determination of time, which is added to the predicate, as is evident from the following ἐζηγήσει, by the very construction in this text and the comparison of the remaining Evangelists, Mark 10. Luke 18. In the Syriac there exists another word in this place than Tit. 3, 5. where Baptism is called not παλιγγενεσίᾳ, itself but λοῦτςον παλιγγενεσίας.. Some refer the word ἐν τχ παλιγγενεσίᾳ with Hilary to that which precedes, understanding either the restoration made through Christ, or explaining the preposition ἐν ἀντὶ τοῦ διὰ and thus it is said, you who have followed me in the regeneration. But the more unblemished codices and more accurate interpreters teach that it must be accepted concerning the regeneration which will be in the resurrection. The Syriac has in the new age or to come. Regeneration here signifies the restoration of our whole nature, with sin and death abolished, which will happen then, when the Son of God will raise all the dead, and will introduce the pious into eternal tabernacles.

Upon twelve seats etc. Augustine, book 20 of the City of God, chapter 5. We ought not to think that because he says they will sit upon twelve seats, twelve men alone are to judge with him. For by the number twelve a certain totality of those judging is signified, on account of the two parts of the number seven, by which universality is often signified, which two parts, that is, three and four, multiplied one by the other make twelve. For both four times three and three times four are twelve, and if any other reason for this number twelve is found which is valid for this. Otherwise, since we read that the Apostle Matthias was ordained in the place of Judas the traitor, the Apostle Paul, who labored more than all of them, will not have where he may sit to judge. Concerning those to be judged themselves, there is a similar cause in this number twelve. For it is not because it is said, judging the 12 tribes of Israel, the tribe of Levi, which is the thirteenth, will not be judged by them, or that he will judge only that people and not also the other nations. *(The same author has similar things in the enarrations of Psalm 49. Also Bede in chapter 19 of Matthew. But it is said more conveniently to the text that Christ in this place promises to the Apostles a certain peculiar and excellent honor above all the remaining faithful on the day of judgment, just as they will also obtain greater glory in eternal life. Compare B. P. Harm. Ev. c. 173. p. 1180. Meanwhile, it is by no means denied that all the pious also will judge in their own way on the final day. See Wis. 3, 8. 1. Cor. 6, 2 namely 1 in Christ the head. 2. by standing by or sitting by. 3. by approving. 4. by testifying. 5. by the example of faith and repentance. add. B. Par. in the cited book. As far as the Apostle Paul is concerned, he is as little excluded from the College of the Apostles as he is from the communion of Apostolic rewards. It is the common opinion that by that session, promised here by Christ, not some bodily session is signified, but a mystical one. Which the Fathers interpret as a certain extraordinary glory, which the Apostles are to have in the final judgment above the rest of the saints. See Chrysostom and Theophylact on this passage. item. Augustine in the enarrations on Ps. 121. and Bernard in the Declamations. By a similar locution, John the Theologian indicates the glory of all the faithful of the Church of God, according to Augustine and Primasius, in Apoc. c. 2, 26. c. 4, 4. and c. 11, 16. Compare also the twin visions Dan. 7, 9.Apoc. 20, 4. add Analysis on Matth 12, 26. item. 1. Cor. 6, 2 It is indeed well to be noted that between that glory, promised to the Apostles and other blessed ones by this metaphorical locution, and that which was communicated to the human nature of Christ by virtue of the personal union, Ioh. 5, 27. there is an infinite difference. For the Apostles are not to be judges so much, ἀυτοκρατορικὴν by exercising the power of judging, as they are to be assessors and witnesses in the judgment to be instituted by Christ, and approvers of the sentence most justly passed by Him. In which way Leonh. Coquaeus himself also explains it in his Commentary on c. 5. book XX. of Augustine De C. D. Whence it can also be noted that Apoc. 3, 21. a distinction is made between the throne of the Father, (to which Christ alone was raised by the Father, and nothing else is indicated by it than His divine and infinite majesty) and the throne of Christ. (to which the saints are also raised by Christ, and by it is signified a certain singular glory, which Christ will one day confer upon the saints.) The throne of the Father is one, Apoc. 3, 21. but the thrones, onto which the saints are to be raised, are many, here and in Apoc. c. 4, 4. c. 20, 4. Compare S. Ambrose book 5. de fide c. 2, 6. So that thus the argument of the orthodox may remain firm, which for the communication of the majesty truly divine and infinite from Ioh. 5, 27. they draw forth. See more things making for this in B. Par. L de Extr. Iudic. §. 41. 42. also Harm Ev. c. 173. p. 1181. Also worthy of note is the passage Ebr. 1, 13. But if the saints are to be future judges themselves, how will they be judged by Christ? Resp. In the beginning all men, and among them even the saints, will be set before the tribunal of Christ, and thus will be judged by him, but soon these will be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ 1. Thes. 4, 7 and then together with Christ they will judge the world, that is, worldly men and evil angels. See B. Par. l c §. 43 Who himself also in the same place §. 126. defends the opinion of our countrymen, when from this place he proves degrees of glory in eternal life.)*

*( Judging the twelve tribes of Israel. But 1. Cor. 6, 2. it is said that the saints are to judge the world. Which seems a greater prerogative. Resp. Some by tribes of Israel understand all true believers, and compare with this passage the sayings Rom. 4, 12. Gal. 3, 9. c 6, 16. Rom. 9, 8. But since on the last day the faithful are not to be judged, but the impenitent and unbelievers, Ioh. 3, 18. c. 5. 24. that explanation cannot have a place. It must be said therefore, that the positing of one is not the exclusion of the other. Thus indeed the Apostles are to judge the faithless and unbelievers from the Jews, so that nevertheless the faithless from the Gentiles are not excluded. In particular, however, mention is made of the tribes of Israel, because Christ in the office of teaching had been sent only to the twelve tribes of Israel, and the Apostles had thus far preached the Gospel only to the twelve tribes of Israel. It is added that the Jews had created the greatest troubles for the Apostles, Matth. 10, 14. following. Christ therefore consoles them, that they are one day to judge those before whom they had stood to be judged. Compare more things making for this in B. Par. in Harm. Ev. c. 173. p. 1182. 1183. The apostles, however, will judge, not only by approving the most just judgment of Christ, but also in regard to their Gospel, comprised in the Biblical books, Rom. 2, 16. Apoc. 20, 12. Furthermore, although because of the double portion of Joseph's children there were thirteen tribes, nevertheless usually at least twelve are named. See Act. 7, 8. ac. 1, 1. Apoc. 21, 12 and that is for the reason that the tribe of Levi did not have its own seats separately, nor its own μεριδάρχην, as Grotius well notes on this passage. Otherwise, by that name in Holy Scripture are expressed not only the Jews, but rather all the elect. See B. Par. Comm. ad Apoc. 21, 12.)*

Latin:

v. 28. έν τη παλιγγενεσίᾳ,in regeneratione ac renovatione vel potiùs post mundi renovationem in altero seculo. *(Quomodo & Syrus vertit: in seculo novo, Arabs: in generatione venturâ. Persa tamen de regeneratione, quae in hoc seculo fit, accepisse videtur. Similiter & Aethiops. Et ita quoque iam olim accepit auct. operis Imperf. hom. 33. it. Macarius hom. 7. nec non Beda in h. l. Ex recentioribus Camero in Myroth. Coquaeus in Aug. lib. 20. de C. D. c. 5)* Sicut Petrus diem illum vocat diem ἀποηαθαςασεως παντων,Actor. 3, 21. Augustinus l. 20. de C. D. c. 5. Quod ait in regeneratione, procul dubio mortuorum resurrectionem nomine voluit regenerationis intelligi. Sic enim caro nostra regenerabitur per incorruptionem, quemadmodum est anima nostra regenerata per fidem. *(Similia habet idem l. 3. cont. duas Epist. Pelagii c. 3. it. l. 4. cont. easd. c. 11. l. 2. cont. Iulianum. Eodem quoque modo accipiunt Gregorius M. l. 4. Moral. c. 23. ac Bernh. in Declam. quorum verba adducit B. Par. L. de Resurr. §. 4. Similiter exponunt Euthymius ac Theophylactus in h. l. refertque etiam huc Leonh. Coquaeus Comm. ad Aug. de C. D. p. 355. locum Psalm. 2, 7. quem Paulus Actor. 13, 33. 34. de resurrectione Christi interpretatur. Scriptura igitur duplicis regenerationis mentionem facit, quarum altera fit in hâc vitâ, & quidē tum per Baptismum, Ioh. 3, 5.Tit. 3, 5. tum per verbum, 1 Petr. 1, 23.Iac. 1, 18. altera post hanc vitam s. in die Iudicii, de quâ Christus h. l. Add. Ambros. serm. 48 de sepulcro Christi. Illa regeneratio fit spiritualiter, haec mirabiliter. Conf. etiam B. P. H. E. p. 464.)*

Non pertinet ad descriptionem subiecti, sed ad determinationem temporis, quae est adiecta praedicato, ut constat ex sequente ἐζηγήσει, ipsâ constructione in hoc textu & collatione reliquorum Evangelistarum, Marc. 10.Luc. 18. Apud Syrum extat aliud vocabulum hoc loco, quàm Tit. 3, 5. ubi Baptismus vocatur non ipsa παλιγγενεσίᾳ, sed λοῦτςον παλιγγενεσίας. Quidam vocem ἐν τχ παλιγγενεσίᾳ cum Hilario ad id, quod praecedit, referunt, intelligentes vel restaurationem, per Christū factum, vel exponentes praepositionem ἐν ἀντὶ τοῦ διὰ ac sic dictum, qui secuti estis me per regenerationem. Sed Codd. emaculatiores ac Interpp. accuratiores docent, de regeneratione quae futura est in resurrectione, id accipiendum esse. Syrus habet in seculo novo seu venturo. Regeneratio hîc significat totius naturae nostrae instaurationem, abolito peccato & morte, quae fiet tunc, cùm Filius DEI omnes mortuos suscitabit, & pios in aeterna tabernacula introducet.

Super sedes duodecim &c. August. l. 20. de C. D. c. 5. Non quoniam super sedes duodecim sessuros ait, duodecim solos homines cum ipso iudicaturo sputare debemus. Duodenario quippe numero universa quaedam significata est iudicantium multitudo, propter duas partes numeri septenarii, quo significatur plerumq universitas, quae duae partes i. e. tria & quatuor, alter â per alteram multiplicatâ duodecim faciunt. Nam & quatuor ter & tria quatuor duodecim sunt, & si qua alia huius duodenarii numeri, quae ad hoc valet, ratio reperitur. Alioquin quoniam in locum Iudae proditoris Apostolum Matthiam logimus ordinatum, Apostolus Paulus, qui plus omnibus illis laboravit, ubi ad iudicandum sedeat, non habebit. De ipsis quoque iudicandis in hoc numero duodenario similis causa est. Non enim quia dictum est, iudicantes 12 tribus Israel, tribus Levi, quae tertia decima est, ab eis, iudicanda non erit, aut solum illum populumnon etiam coet eras gentes iudicabit. *(Similia habet idem in enarr. Psalmi 49. item Beda in cap 19 Matth. Sed textui convenientiùs dicitur, Christum h. l. Apostolis peculiarem & eximium quendam honorem prae reliquis fidelibus omnibus in die iudicii promittere, perinde ut in vita aet. maiorem quoq, obtinebunt gloriam. Conf. B. P. Harm Ev. c. 173. p. 1180. Interea minimè negatur, quòd omnes quoque pii suo modo in die extremo iudicaturi sint. Vid. Sap. 3, 8. 1. Cor. 6, 2 nempe 1 in Christo capite. 2. adsistendo s. adsidendo. 3. approbando. 4. testificando. 5. fidei & poenitentiae exemplo. add. B. Par. l. cit. Quod Apostolum Paulum concernit, ille uti minimè à Collegio Apostolorum, ita nec à communione praemiorum Apostolicorum excluditur. Communis sententia est, per illam sessionem, à Christo hîc promissam, non corpoream aliquam sessionem significari, sed mysticam. Quam de eximiâ quadam gloriâ Patres interpretantur, quam prae reliquis sanctis in extremo iudicio Apostoli sint habituri. Vid. Chrysostomus & Theophyl. in h. l. it. August. in enarr. Ps. 121. ac Bernhardus in Declam. Simili locutione gloriam omnium fidelium Ecclesiae Dd. iuxta Augustinum ac Primasium indicat Iohannes Theologus in Apoc. c. 2, 26. c. 4, 4. ac c. 11, 16. Conf. quoque visiones gemellae Dan. 7, 9.Apoc. 20, 4. add Anal. ad Matth 12, 26. it. 1. Cor. 6, 2 Probè verò notandum, quòd inter gloriam illam, Apostolis aliisque beatis metaphoricâ istâ locutione promissam, ac eam, quae Christi humanae naturae vi unionis personalis communicata est, Ioh. 5, 27. infinitum sit discrimen. Etenim Apostoli non tam iudices futuri sunt, ἀυτοκρατορικὴν iudicandi potestatē exercendo, quàm adsessores ac testes in iudicio à Christo instituendo, atque approbatores sententiae iustissimè ab ipso latae. Quo modo ipse quoque Leonh. exponit Coquaeus Comm. ad c. 5. lib. XX. Aug. de C. D.
