Unde etiam notari potest, quòd Apoc. 3, 21. distinguatur inter thronum Patris, (ad quem solus Christus à Patre evectus fuit, nihilq: indicatnr per illum aliud, quàm divina atque infinita eius maiestas) & inter thronum Christi. (ad quem etiam sancti à Christo evehuntur, significaturque eo singularis quaedam gloria, quam Christus sanctis aliquando conferet.) Thronus Patris unus est, Apoc. 3, 21. sed throni, in quos sancti evehendi, plures, hîc & Apoc. c. 4, 4. c. 20, 4. Conf. S. Ambros. l. 5. de fide c. 2, 6. Ut ita firmum maneat orthodoxorum argumentum, quod pro communicatione maiestatis verè divinae ac infinitae ex Ioh. 5, 27. depromunt. Conf plura huc facientia apud B. Par. L de Extr. Iudic. §. 41. 42. it. Harm Ev. c. 173. p. 1181. Notari quoque -umprimis meretur locus Ebr. 1, 13.Si verò Apostolialiisancti futuri ipsi iudices, quomodo à Christo iudicabuntur? Resp. Initiò omnes homines, interque eos etiam sancti coram Christi tribunali statuentur, & sic ab ipso iudicabuntur, mox verò hi in occursū Christi in aëra rapiētur, 1. Thes. 4, 7 atque tum unà cum Christo mundum h. e. homines mundanos malosque Angelos iudicabunt. Vid. B. Par. l c §. 43 Qui ipse etiam d l. §. 126. vindicat nostratium sententiam, quando ex h. l. gradûs gloriae in vitâ aeternâ probant.)*

*( Iudicantes duodecim tribus Israel. At 1. Cor. 6, 2. dicitur, quòd sancti mundum iudicaturi sunt. Quae maior videtur praerogativa. Resp. Quidam per tribus Israël intelligunt omnes verè credentes, ac conferunt cum hoc loco dicta Rom. 4, 12.Gal. 3, 9.c 6, 16.Rom. 9, 8. Ast cùm in die extremo non sint iudicandi fideles, sed impoenitentes & increduli, Ioh. 3, 18.c. 5. 24. exp-icatio illa locum habere non potest. Dicendum igitur, quòd unius positio non sit alterius exclusio. Ita nempe iudicaturi sunt Apostoli infideles & incredulos ex Iudaeis, ut tamen non excludantur infideles ex gentilibus. In specie verò tribuum Israel fit mentio, quia Christus in docendi officio solis duodecim tribubus Israel missus fuerat, & Apostoli hactenus solis duodecim tribubus Israel Evangelium praedicarant. accedit, quòd Apostolis Iudaei maximas creaverant molestias, Matth. 10, 14. seqq. Christus ergo solatur eos, quòd iudicaturi aliquando sint, coram quibus steterant iudicandi. Conf. plura huc facientia apud B. Par. in Harm. Ev. c. 173. p. 1182. 1183. Iudicabunt autem apostoli, non solùm iudicium Christi iustissimum approbando, sed etiam quoad suum Evangelium, in libb. Bib icis comprehensum, Rom. 2, 16.Apoc. 20, 12. Coeterùm utut propter duplam Iosephi liberorum portionem tredecim factae tribus fuerint, plerumq; tamē saltē duodecim nominantur. Vid. Act. 7, 8. ac. 1, 1. Apoc. 21, 12 idque ideò, quia tribus Levi non habebat seorsim suas sedes, nec proprium μεριδάρχην, uti benè notat Grotius ad h. l. Exprimuntur aliàs isto nomine in Sc. S. non solùm Iudaei, sed potiùs omnes electi. Vid. B. Par. Comm. ad Apoc. 21, 12.)*

## 19:29
v. 29. And everyone who has left &c. August. b. 20. on the City of God ch. 7. The whole world is the wealth of a faithful man. Justin in Questions and Answers to the Orthodox q. 110. p. 360. If the Lord promised to repay a hundredfold to those who leave father and mother &c., are they also going to receive a hundred wives? Answer. Just as he calls those fathers and mothers, brothers and sisters, who have received Christ with the affection of familiar intimacy, and have left father and mother, brothers and sisters: so also he calls her a wife, who at the time of the abandonment for the sake of Christ takes care of the one abandoning, by nature a wife. Theophyl. on this passage instead of carnal relatives, they will have familiarity and brotherhood with God; instead of fields, paradise, and instead of stone houses, the heavenly Jerusalem. *(The observation of some contributes to this, that τὸ -τοκα-νταπλάσιον does not denote a hundredfold things or a hundredfold, but a hundred times as much, -as is worth a hundred times as much as what they left. Thus the Blessed D. Calixtus explains in Harmony of the Gospels p. 277. Capellus in Spicilegium p. 28 brings forward a twin sentiment from the Targum. But the Savior speaks in this passage not of the spontaneous dismissal or abandonment of father, mother, wife, and children, (inasmuch as that conflicts with divine ordination, of the wife indeed with the primordial institution of marriage, commended by Christ v. 6. but of father, mother, and children with that of the Apostle 1. Tim. 5, 8.) but of the violent separation from a spouse, parents, &c., which persecutors inflict on account of the confession of the Gospel. As the Blessed D. Walth. correctly advises in Biblical Office p. 389. and it is clear from the context, and the Blessed P. L. shows in more detail in On Marriage §. 680. likewise Catholic Confession b. 2. special part 2. art. 6. p. 123. Notably August. ep. 89. Sometimes a point of necessity occurs, where either a wife must be dismissed, or Christ &c. So also Chrysostom: He does not command marriages to be dissolved, but that I should prefer the piety of religion to all other things -s. The passage Matth. 16, 25. and ch. 10, 37 serves to illustrate this same matter. Compare also the Blessed D. Calixtus Harmony of the Gospels p. 278. As regards the example of the Apostles, that is singular. They could have had a special command, so that they might leave their goods for a time, so that indeed they might the better perform the assigned duty, namely of preaching the Gospel in the whole world. So that the Papists ineptly from this passage strive to prove now the vow of Monastic poverty, now of perpetual continence, now even the celibacy of Priests. Cornelius Jansenius, Bishop of Ghent, acknowledged this in some way, whence he writes in his Commentary on the Harmony of the Gospels on this passage: Evang. ad h. l. scribit: A man happens to leave his own things or his own people in two ways. Either on account of the fruit of a better life and the desire for perfection, and thus it is not permitted to dismiss a wife, unless she consents, indeed not even parents or children, if they are in need of our care. Or on account of preserving the spiritual life itself, that is, so that we do not fall away from the grace of Christ already possessed, and thus just as houses and fields are to be left behind when a persecutor of the faith snatches them away, and parents and children are to be left behind when they offer an impediment to the faith and -tae of the Christian life, so also a wife. In the same way also do Caietanus, Salmeron, Barradius, and Fr. Lucas Brugensis explain this passage, as noted by B. Par. Confess. Cath. vol. 3, p. 123. Leonh. Coquaeus also writes in his Comm. on book 20 of Aug. de C. D. ch. 5, that Jerome in ep. 28, Augustine in Ps. 49. and others, not improbably teach that all those who have acquired for themselves great perfection of virtue in this life, although they have not professed a state of perfection, will sit with Christ in judgment. Whence there is no reason why the Papists should so greatly commend the Monastic state from this. And it is well to be noted that Christ says that this remuneration is obtained in the heavens not on account of persecutions, but he means this, that these persecutions can in no way deprive us of these promised heavenly goods. And from this it can also be judged what is to be held concerning the opinion of Bell. who in book 5 de Iustif. ch. 3, B. O. strives to construct merit from the present passage. Whom B. P. Confess. Cath. art. 23, ch. 8, p. 881 refutes.

*( οἰκ-ας. Houses. Thus also, namely in the plural, the Syriac reads, and B. Luth., yet the Arab and the Vulgate, just as also the author of the Gospel of Matthew, read in the singular. And Beza testifies that in two codices he read οίκ-αν. The Persian translates i.e. members of the household, and in the last place ἀγροὺς he renders the same possessions and estates.)*

*( καὶ ζωὴν αἰώνιον κληρονομήσαι. Bell. book 5 de Iustif. ch. 3, argues thus from this. Eternal life is promised to Good works. But a promise made with the condition of a work not only makes the promised thing due, but also causes that he who has fulfilled the work may seem to have earned the promised thing, and to be able to demand it as a reward by his own right. The major premise, as we have said, the Cardinal takes both from this passage and from v. 17, and also from 1. Tim. 4, 8.Iac. 1, 12. Response: concerning the other passages, it will be dealt with in its own place. Regarding the present passage, it is to be noted 1. that Bellarmine himself does not obscurely betray that there is little strength in his argument formed from this, when he uses the word to seem, which no one who knows the pride of the man will easily believe was employed by the Cardinal for the sake of modesty. 2. that Cornelius à Lapide, in his commentary on this passage, notes that the Syriac has, he shall possess by inheritance, and the Arabic, he shall become heir of eternal life. By this very fact, the Jesuit tacitly acknowledges that these interpreters have better attained the emphasis of the authentic Greek text than the Vulgate interpreter, who translates: and shall possess eternal life. Cornelius adds, He who for the sake of Christ has left his inheritance just as his equals &c., shall receive a hundredfold for them in this age, and the inheritance of life in the future &c. Now, it is certain that an inheritance is not a wage owed on account of merits, but that one becomes a participant in it by the right of sonship. This is something that not even Bellarmine himself can deny, lib. 5 de Iustif. c. 20, denying that eternal life is a wage, insofar as it is an inheritance. But here eternal life is promised as an inheritance. Therefore, it is not as a wage, and thus no merit can be elicited from this present promise of Christ . Compare more in the Annotations on Matth. 25, 34. But let us be comforted by this inheritance laid up for us in the heavens, if it happens that we are deprived of an earthly inheritance.)*

Latin:

v. 29. Et omnis qui reliquerit &c. August. l. 20. de C. D. c. 7. fidelis hominis totus mundus divitiarum. Iustinus in Qq. & Resp. ad Orthodoxos q. 110. p. 360. Si Dominus patrem aumatrem &c. relinquentibus centuplum retribuere pollicitus est, num & uxores centum illi recepturisunt? Resp. Quemmad. patres & matres, fratres & sorores eos dicit, qui affectione familiaris consuetudinis Christum receperunt, & patrem atque matrem, fratres ac sorores reliquerunt: sic & uxorem eam vocat, quae tempore derelictionis propter Christum curam gerit derelinquentis naturâ uxorem. Theophyl. h. l. Prcarnalibus cognatis, familiaritatem & fraternitatem cum Deobabebunt; pro agris paradisum, & pro lapideis aedibus coelestem Hierosolymam. *(Huc facit observatio non nullorum, quòd τὸ -τοκα-νταπλάσιον non notet centuplicata vel centuplicia, sed centies tanti, -as hundertmahl so viel werth ist / als ex verlassen. Ita exponit B. D. Calixtus Concord. Ev. p. 277. Gemellam praesenti sententiam è Targum adducit Capellus in Spicil. p. 28. Loquitur verò Salvator h. l. non de spontaneâ patris, matris, uxoris & liberorum dimissione vel derelictione, (utpote quae pugnat cum divinâ ordinatione, uxoris quidem cum primaevâ coniugii institutione, à Christo commendatâ v. 6. patris verò, matris & liberorum cum illo Apostoli 1. Tim. 5, 8.) sed de violentâ, quam persecutores propter Evangelii confessionem inferunt, à coniuge, parentibus &c. separationem. uti rectè monet B. D. Walth. Offic. Bibl. p. 389. & è contextu liquet, ac pluribus ostendit B. P. L. de Coniug. §. 680. item Confess. Cathol. l. 2. spec. part. 2. art. 6. p. 123. Notanter August. ep. 89. Occurrit aliquando necessitatis articulus, ubi aut uxor dimittatur, aut Christus &c. Sic quoque Chrysostomus: Non praecipit dirimenda matrimonia, sed ut religionis pietatem reliquis omnibus anteferam--s. Eidem huic rei illustrandae servit locus Matth. 16, 25. it. c. 10, 37. Conf. quoque B. D. Calixcus Concord Ev. p. 278. Quod attinet exemplum Apostolorum, illud singulare est. Potuerunt e-habere praeceptum speciale, ut bona sua ad tempus relinquerent, quò nempe eò melius damandato officio, praedicandi nempe Evang, in universo terrarum orbe fungi possent. Ut adeò ineptè ex h. l. Pontificii modò paupertatis Monasticae, modò perpetuae continentiae votum, modò etiā Sacerdotum coelibatum probare satagant. Agnovit hoc aliquo modo Cornelius Iansenius, Gandavensis Episcopus, unde in Comm. ad Harm. Evang. ad h. l. scribit: Dupliciter contingit, hominem relinquere sua vel suos. Aut propter melioris vitae frugem & perfectionis desiderium, & sic non licet dimittere uxorem, nisi consentientem, imò nec parentes aut filios, si nostrâ indigent curâ. Aut propter ipsam vitam spiritualem conservandam, h. e. ut à gratiâ Christi habitâ non excidamus, & sic quemadmodum domus & agri sunt relinquendi, dum persecutor fidei ea eripit, & parentes & filii suntre linquendi, dum impedimentum praebent fidei & -tae Christianae, ita & uxor. Eodem modo exponunt quoq; h. l. Caietanus, Salmeron, Barradius, Fr. Lucas Brugensis, notante B. Par. Confess. Cath. t. 3. p. 123. Scribit quoq; Leonh. Coquaeus Comm. ad lib. 20. Aug. de C. D. c. 5. Hieronymum ep. 28. August. in Ps. 49. aliosq;, non improbabiliter docere, omnes eos, qui in hac vita magnam virtutis perfectionem sibi compararint, licet perfectionis statum non sint professi, cum Christo in iudicio consessuros Unde non est, cur tantopere Pontificii hinc Monasticum statum commendent. Et probè notandum, quòd Christus istam remunerationem in coelis obtingere dicat non propter persecutiones, sed hoc velit, quòd istae persecutiones minimè nos queant privare istis promissis bonis coelestibus. Atq; hinc iudicari quoq; potest, quid habendum sit de sententiâ Bell. qui lib. 5. de Iustif. c. 3. B. O. meritum exstruere è praesenti loco satagit. Quem refutat B. P. Confess. Cath. art. 23. c. 8. p. 881.)*

*( οἰκ-ας.Domos. Ita quoq;, nempe in pl. legit Syrus, ac B. Luth., Arabs tamen ac Vulg. quemadmodum & autor Ev. Matt. Ebraei legerunt in sing. Ac testatur Beza, in duobus Codd. se legisse οίκ-αν. Persa vertit i. e. domesticos, ac ultimo loco ἀγροὺς reddit idem possessiones ac praedia.)*

*( καὶ ζωὴν αἰώνιον κληρονομήσαι. Bell. lib. 5. de Iustif. c. 3. ita hinc argumentatur. Vita aeterna est promissa Bonis operibus. At promissio facta cum conditione operis non solùm debitam facit renpromissam, sed etiam facit, ut qui opus impleverit, meruisse rem promissam, eamut mercedem -ure suo exigere posse videatur. Maiorem, uti diximus, desumit Cardinalis tum ex. h. l. tum ex v. 17. nec non ex 1. Tim. 4, 8.Iac. 1, 12. Resp. de locis coeteris suo agetur loco. Circa praesentem locum notandum 1. quòd Bellarm. ipse parum roboris argumento suo, hinc formato, inesse nō obscurè prodat, quando utitur verbo videri, quod modestiae causâ à Cardinali adhibitū fuisse, nemo facilè credet, cui fastus hominis cognitus. 2. quòd Corn. à Lapide Com. in h. l. annotet, Syrū habere, haereditate possidebit, Arabicum, haeres fiet vitae aeterne. Quo ipso Iesuita tacitè agnoscit, interpretes hosce meliùs adse cutos esse emphasin textûs Graeci authentici, quàm InterpretVulgatum, qui vertit: & vitam aeternam possidebit. Subiicit Corn. Qui suam haereditatem aequè ac suos par-es &c. Christi causâ rehquerit, pro eis recipiet centuplum in seculo, & haereditatem vitae -t in futurô &c. Iam verò constat, quòd haereditas non sit merces, propter merita debita, sed quòd iure filiationis illius quis fiat particeps. id quod nec ipse Bell. diffiteri potest. lib. 5. de lustif. c. 20. negans, vitam aeternam esse mercedem, quat. est haereditas Ast hîc vita aeterna promittitur, ut haereditas. E. non ut merces, adeoque nullum B. O. meritum elici è praesenti Christi promissione potesConf. plura in Annot. ad Matth. 25 34. Solemur autem nos haereditate hâc in coelis nobirepositâ, si contingat privari nos haereditate terrenâ.)*

## 19:30
v. 30. But many that are first &c. Tossanus understands this concerning the time of the calling. Do not trust in the fact that I called you before others as first, and that you followed me first. For it is not enough to begin well, unless constancy is present: and it can happen that he who was called in the last place may outstrip him who was called first.

*( The last i. e. shall fall away from eternal life. Compare more in chapter 5, 19.)*

*( Who are last i. e. who here seem cast off and humble, such as the Apostles were, and indeed other grave sinners, but penitent ones. See below c. 21, 31. also Luc. 13, 30)*

There is proposed in the present Chapter 1. The hiring of laborers into the vineyard, v. 1-7. The remuneration of the same or the payment of the promised denarius v. 8. 9. The murmuring of certain ones v. 10. 1-. and their just rebuke, v. 13 15. Christ's epiphonema and conclusion, v. 16. II. The prediction of Christ's passion and resurrection, v. 17, 19. III. The preposterous petition of the mother of the sons of Zebedee v. 20. 21. likewise Christ's response, consisting of a refutation, a mutual question v. 22 and a tacit admonition concerning the pursuit of humility, v. 23. The indignation of the disciples v. 25. and the more abundant instruction of the Savior v. 25. 28. IV. The healing of two blind men, v. 29. to the end.

v. 1. For. B. Luther omitted this particle in the German version, perhaps following the Vulgate, which was also done by the Arab and the Persian. But the Syriac and the Ethiopian rightly retained it. For it indicates the coherence of this chapter with the preceding discourse of Christ, from which this parable must also be understood, as Jerome advises in this place. Peter was boasting near the end of the preceding chapter that he had left all things, persuaded that he had greatly merited much in the kingdom of God by that desertion. Christ, intending to remove that vain glory from the mind of Peter and the remaining disciples, teaches in the present parable that neither Peter nor anyone else can merit eternal life by his own works, but that all good things come to us from the naked and mere grace of God.)* *(

*( The kingdom of heaven. Lyra understands by the kingdom of heaven Christ and evangelical grace. Aretius, the evangelical profession. Maldonatus and Jansenius, the Church not only militant, but also triumphant. But it is a question here of such a kingdom in which murmuring has a place. *(Therefore, by the kingdom of heaven is understood only the militant Church of Christ, so called because in it we taste the powers of the world to come, Ebr. 6. and although we still live in it, πλίτευυα yet our citizenship is in heaven Phil. 3, 10.)*

To a man, a householder. GOD is called householder because he sustains three families: the triumphant in heaven because of glory, the trembling in hell because of wrath, the militant on earth through grace. Iacobus de Voragine, sermon 1. Sept. Hilarius, can. 20. in Matth. Author of the Opus Imperfectum, hom. 34. *(But especially regard is had to the militant Church, which is the mystical house of GOD. 2. Tim. 2, 20.c. 3, 15.Ebr. 3, 56.)* Theophylact in this place specifically understands Christ.

Latin:

v. 30. Multi autem primi &c. Tossanus de tempore vocationis accipit. Nolite in eo confidere, quòd vos ante a ios primos vocaverim, quòdque primi me secuti sitis. Non enim sufficit, benè incipere, nisi adsit constantia: ac fieri potest, ut qui ultimo loco vocatus est, antevertat eum, qui primô vocatuest.

*( Ultimi i. e. vitâ aeternâ excident. Confer. plura cap. 5, 19.)*

*( Qui ultimi i. e. qui hîc videntur abiecti & humiles, quales erant Apostoli, quin & alii peccatores graves, sed poenitentes. Vid. infrà c. 21, 31. it. Luc. 13, 30)*

Proponitur in praesenti Capite 1. Operariorum in vineam conductio, v. 1-7. eorundem remuneratio sive promissi denarii per-olutio. v. 8. 9. quorundam obmurmuratio v. 10. 1-. ac iusta eorum obiurgatio, v. 13 15. Christi epiphonema ac conclusio, v. 16. II. Passionis & resurrectionis Christo praedictio, v. 17, 19. III. Praepostera matris fillorum Zebedaei petitio v. 20. 21. item Christi responsio, constans redargutione, mutua quaestione v. 22 ac tacitâ de humilitatis studio admonitione, v. 23. Discipulorum indignatio v. 25. & uberior Salvatoris informatio v. 25. 28. IV. Duorum Coecorum sanatio, v. 29. ad finem.

*(v, 1, Nam. Omisit B. Lutherus in vers. Germanicâ, Vulgatum fortè sequutus, hanc particulam. quod etiam factum ab Arabe & Persa, Sed rectè eandem retinuerunt Syrus atque Aethiops. Indicat enim ea cohaerentiam capitis huius cum praecedente Christi sermone, unde etiam parabola haec intelligenda est, monente Hieronymo h. l. Gloriabatur Petrus circa Cap. praeced. finem, quòd omnia reliquerit, persuasus, se multum eâ desertione in regno DEI esse promeritum. Christus v. inanem istam gloriam animo Pet-i ac reliquorum discipulorum exemturus docet in praesenti parabola, quòd nec Petrus, nec alius quisquam vitam aeternam operibus suis possit promereri, sed quòd omnia bona ex nudâ & merâ DEI gratiâ nobis obtingant.)*

*( Regnum coelorum. Lyra per regnum coelorum intelligit Christum & gratiam Evangelicam. Aretius professionem Evangelicam. Maldonatus & Iansenius Ecclesiam non solùm militantem, sed & triumphantem. Atqui de tali regno hîc agitur, in quo murmur habet locum. *(Intelligitur proinde per regnum coelorum tantùm militaus Christi Ecclesia, sic dicta, quod in eâ gustemus virtutes futuri seculi, Ebr. 6. ac licet in eâ adhuc v-vamus, πλίτευυα tamen nostrum in coelis sit Phil pp. 3, 10.)*

Homini patri familias. Dicitur DEUS paterfamiliâs quia litres sustētat familias, triumphantem in coelis propter gloriam, trepidantem in gehenna propter iram, militantem in terra per gratiam. Iacobus de Voragine serm. 1. Sept. Hilarius can. 20. in Matth. Autor Operis Imperf. hom. 34. *(Cumprimis verò respectus habetur ad Ecclesiam militantem, quae mystica DEI domus est. 2. Tim. 2, 20.c. 3, 15.Ebr. 3, 56.)* Theophylactus in h. l. speciatim intelligit Christum.

## 20:1
CHAP. XX. SUMMARY AND DISPOSITION.

He went out. Augustine, sermon 59 on the words of the Lord: For the householder to go out is to become known, since he who is in the house is in secret, he is not seen by those who are outside. When Christ is not understood and acknowledged, he is in secret; but when he is acknowledged, he has gone out to hire. *(But since God does not always call men immediately into the vineyard of his Church, but uses the Ecclesiastical Ministry for this work, 2. Cor. 5, 20. let us therefore acknowledge the dignity of the Ecclesiastical Minister, and let us comply with the divine calling made through the Ministers, Luke 10, 16. This is an outgoing of grace, Luke 1, 78. 79. which, unless we worthily receive Christ coming to us, an outgoing of judgment and wrath will follow. Cf. Is. 26, 21. Let us therefore receive him with devout listening to the divine word and serious amendment of life, etc., so that he may come to us and make his dwelling with us, John 14, 23.)*

To hire etc. A similar parable exists in the book Musar ch. 10 and in Ilmedenu or Ielammedenu f. 38. col. 2. concerning a certain king who had hired laborers for his work, and had hired one of them to walk until evening, who nevertheless received equal wages with the others. *(Thus Drusius reports in book I. Praeterit. page 42. By Ludovicus Capellus in Spicil. this parable is attributed to R. Jonah. See below Anal. on v. 12.)* Furthermore, God calls into the vineyard of the Church through the preaching of the saints, through the bestowing of benefits, through internal inspiration, and through the correction of scourges.

Laborers. The laborers called into the vineyard are not only Ministers of the Church, to whom Hilary can. 20 in Matt., Irenaeus book 4 ch. 70 p. 305, Jerome book 2 against Jovinian p. 42, Chrysostom hom. 34 in the Imperfect Work, and Gregory homily 19 in the Gospels adapt this parable. *(And in this respect, rightly also from the present place, in that the Ministers of the Church are called laborers, Marcus Antonius de Dominis, Archbishop of Spalato, book 1 of the Ecclesiastical Republic p. 16, gathers,) that the faithful servants of Christ ought to exercise a ministerial work, not a Dominion over the family of Christ. The same person compares with the present passage the sayings Luc 12, 37,43.1. Cor. 4, 1. & many other good things, which can deservedly be urged against the Dominion of the Roman Prelate.)* but in general all Christians. And thus Origen hom. 10. in Matth. August. serm. 59. de verbis Dom. Nazianz. Orat. 40. which is on the Holy Bapt. p. 650. Chrysost. hom. 65 in Matth. understand it. *(The ancients therefore explained this parable in various ways, just as B. Par. L de B. O. §. 114. also brings forward some interpretations. Conf. the same L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 53. also B. D. Glassius in Exeg. Conf. 1. Cor. 3 6Act. 9. 31.Col. 3, 16.1. Thess. 5, 11. Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 1. ep. 49. writing to the Coenobiarch, also rightly urges this Parable against idle Monks and those having slothful hands. That which, he writes, is found to have been neither done by Christ, nor observed by Paul the wise Doctor &c. But this passage by no means supports L. A. powers in spiritual matters. For we do not work by our natural [power], but by the power of GOD,Phil. 2, 13. Nor can merit also B. O. be elicited from this, since eternal life is the gift of GODRom. 6, v. last, not the merit of our works. Nor are B. O. the cause of justification, as is evident from Rom. 3. 28.c. 4, 2. seqq. But in what sense it may be said that wages are given to workers, will be explained below.)*

Into the vineyard. By the vineyard Irenaeus l. 4. c. 70. Euthymius, & Chrysost. in this place understand the commandments of GOD. Theophylactus each one's soul. Athanasius q. 52. the whole world. Nauseus Cent. 4. hom. p. 813. Origen & Gregory hom. 19. in Evang. the Church. It is to be noted, however, that not only that Church is compared to a vineyard which began in Abraham, as Salmer. tr. 33. sect. 16. wishes, but also that which was in the cradles of the world: For Christ speaks in the present time. *(Our people also commonly understand it concerning the Church See B. D. Glass. part. 2. Exeg. Ev. Dom. Dom. Septuag. B. P. in Hom. Acad. part. 1. p. 460. And it is customary in Holy Scripture for the Church to be compared with a vineyard. See Deut. 32, 32.Ps. 80, 9.Es. 3, 14c. 5, 1,8c. 60, 21.Ier. 2, 21.c. 12, 10.Ezech. 17, 6. Cantic. Canticor, c. 2, 12.cap. 6, 10.cap. 7, 12.cap 8, 11. Below chapter 21, -2.

Luc. 20, 9. The members of the comparison are treated at length by B. Par. L. de Eccles. §. 22. also part. 1. Hom. Acad. p. 460. 461. B. D. Tarnov. in Mich. p. 158. B. D. Glassius Exeg. Domin. Septuag. pag. 184. Dn. Binchius in Mellif. part. 4. p. 242. Briefly: A correspondence is given between the Church and the vineyard 1 in preciousness. Conf. Ps. 104, 15.Es. 54, 11. 12.Act. 20, 23. 2. in the necessity of planting. 3. in the necessity of undertaking labor around both. Conf. Ioh. 15, 1. seqq. 4 in the quality of the shoots. 5. in external vileness. Conf. Ezech. 15, 2.6. in the sweetness of the fruits. See Judg. 9, 18. Eccles. 9, 7.Es. 62, 5.Ierem. 2, 2.Gal. 5, 22.Phil. 1, 11.c. 4, 18. This vineyard is invigorated by the most penetrating heat of the Sun of righteousness Mal. 4, 2.Luc. 1, 78., it is irrigated by the most fruitful dew and heavenly rain, Es. 27, 3.c. 44, 3.Psal. 68, 10., it is fortified by God with a most strong wall, Esa, 5, 2Zach. 2, 9. To this also pertains the comparison of the Church with a vine, which Dn. D. Botsacus shows in Prompt. Alleg. p. 720. also that of Christ himself with the vine, as one who produced the most precious and sweetest grapes of our redemption, with God of propitiation, of deliverance from death and sin . Conf. 1. Ioh. 4, 10. The soul of each can also be compared with a vineyard, as one that is planted in the earth of this body, whose faculties are ordered as vines; faith and works of charity as wine. The vines are to be tied to the stake of the cross, for whose foot we dig a pit, always thinking of the burial. This vineyard is to be kept and diligently guarded, Cant 1, 6. from the boar (Ps 80, 14.) of obscene pleasure, from the wild beast of pride, from the fox of craftiness, from the wolf of voracity and avarice &c. This vineyard produces the tears of compunction (to this pertains that of Bernard serm 30. in Cant, the tears of the penitent are the wine of the Angels.) it emits the odor of consolation, it brings forth the grapes of commiseration and love. Here the highest φιλανθςωπία, of GOD is to be acknowledged and proclaimed, while from the human race, which because of sin was like dry wood, and useful for nothing else except to be cast into the fire Matt 3, 10.Ezech. 15, 4., He does not disdain to plant a vineyard. Let us therefore apply ourselves diligently, so that we may bring forth much fruit, Iohan. 15, 5. which God eagerly expects, Es. 5, 3. Woe to him who frustrates the expectation of GOD. Conf. Deut. 32, 32. &c.)*

Latin:

CAP. XX. SUMMA AC DISPOSITIO.

Exiit. Augustinus serm. 59. de verbis Domini: Exire patrem familias est innotescere, q-niam qui in domo est, in abdite est, non videtur ab iis, qui foris sunt. Christus quando non intelligitur & agnoscitur, in secreto est, quando autem agnoscitur, exiit conducere. *(Cùm verò Deus non immediatè semper homines in vineam Ecclesiae suae vocet, sed utatur ad hoc opus Ministerio Ecclesiastico, 2. Cor. 5, 20. quare agnoscamus Minist. Ecclesiastici dignitatem, ac vocationi divinae per Ministros factae morem geramus, Luc. 10, 16. Est hic egressus gratiae, Luc. 1, 78. 79. quem, nisi Christum ad nos adventantem dignè exceperimus, sequetur egressus iudicii & irae. Conf. Es. 26, 21. Excipiamus igitur ipsum devotâ verbi divini auscultatione seriâ vitae emendatione &c. quò ad nos veniat, & habitationē apud nos faciat, Ioh. 14, 23.)*

Ad conducendum &c. Similis parabola extat in libro Musar c. 10. & in Ilmedenu sive Ielammedenu f. 38. col. 2. de quodam rege, qui cōduxerat operariosad opus suum, & ex iis unum conduxerat prodeambulatum usque ad vesperam, qui tamen parem mercedem cum aliis accipiebat. *(Ita refert Drusius lib. I. Praeterit. pag. 42. à Ludovico Capello in Spicil. tribuitur parabola haec R. Ionae. Vid. infrà Anal. ad v. 12.)* Coeterùm vocat Deus in vineam Ecclesiae per sanctorum praedicationem, per beneficiorum largitionem, per internam inspirationem, per flagellorum correctionem.

Operarios. Operarii in vineam vocati non solùm sunt Ministri Ecclesiae, ad quos parabolam hac accommodant Hilarius can. 20. in Matth. Irenaeus lib. 4. c. 70. p. 305. Hieronymus lib. 2. contra Iovin. p. 42. Chrysost. hom. 34. Oper. Imperf. Gregorius homil. 19. in Evang. *(Atque hoc respectu rectè etiam è praesenti locos. eò quòd Ministri Ecclesiae operarii vocantur, Marcus Anton. de Dominis Archi Episcopus Spalat. lib. 1. de Rep. Eccles. p. 16. colligit, fideles Christi servos ministeriale opus, non Dominium in Christi familiam exercere debere. Confert idem cum praesenti loco dicta Luc 12, 37,43.1. Cor. 4, 1. & alia benè multa, quae meritò contra Praesulis Romani Dominatum urgeri possunt.)* sed in genere omnes Christiani. Atque ita accipiunt Origenes hom. 10. in Matth. August. serm. 59. de verbis Dom. Nazianz. Orat. 40. quae est de Sancto Bapt. p. 650. Chrysost. hom. 65 in Matth. *(Diversimodè igitur parabolam hanc exposuere veteres, ceu nonnullas etiam interpretationes adducit B. Par. L de B. O. §. 114. Conf. idem L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 53. it. B. D. Glassius in Exeg. Conf. 1. Cor. 3 6Act. 9. 31.Col. 3, 16.1. Thess. 5, 11. Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 1. ep. 49. scribens ad Coenobiarcham, rectè quoq; Parabolam hanc urget adversùs Monachos inertes ac desides manus habentes. Id quod, scribit, nec à Christo factum, nec à Paulo sapiente Doctore observatum reperitur &c. Hautquaquam verò locus hic L. A. viribus in rebus spiritualibus patrocinatur. Operamur enim non -ostrâ naturali, sed DEI virtuti,Phil. 2, 13. Nec meritum quoque B. O. elici hinc potest, cùm vita aeterna sit DEI donumRom. 6, v. ult. non operum nostrorum meritum. Nec B. O. iustificationis causa sunt, ceu patet ex Rom. 3. 28.c. 4, 2. seqq. Quo sensu verò operariis merces da-i dicatur, infrà exponetur.)*

In vineam. Per vineam Irenaens l. 4. c. 70. Euthymius, & Chrysost. h. l. intelligunt mandata DEI. Theophylactus cuiusq animam. Athanasius q. 52. totum mundum. Nauseus Cent. 4. hom. p. 813. Origenes & Gregorius hom. 19. in Evang. Ecclesiam. Notandum autem, non tantùm illam Ecclesiam vineae comparari, quae in Abrahamo coepit, ut vult Salmer. tr. 33. sect. 16. sed etiam eam, quae in cunabulis mundi fuit: Loquitur enim Christus in tempore praesenti. *(De Ecclesia etiam nostrates communiter intellig Vid. B. D. Glass. part. 2. Exeg. Ev. Dom. Dom. Septuag. B. P. in Hom. Acad. part. 1. p. 460. Usitatumq; est in Sc. S. Ecclesiam cum vineâ conferri. Vid. Deut. 32, 32.Ps. 80, 9.Es. 3, 14c. 5, 1,8c. 60, 21.Ier. 2, 21.c. 12, 10.Ezech. 17, 6. Cantic. Canticor, c. 2, 12.cap. 6, 10.cap. 7, 12.cap 8, 11. Infràcap. 21, -2.

Luc. 20, 9. Membra comparationis prolixè pertractant B. Par. L. de Eccles. §. 22. it. part. 1. Hom. Acad. p. 460. 461. B. D. Tarnov. in Mich. p. 158. B. D. Glassius Exeg. Domin. Septuag. pag. 184. Dn. Binchius in Mellif. part. 4. p. 242. Breviter: Convenientia Ecclesiam inter & vineam datur 1 in pretiositate. Conf. Ps. 104, 15.Es. 54, 11. 12.Act. 20, 23. 2. in plantationis necessitate. 3. in laboris circa utramq; suscipiendi necessitate. Conf. Ioh. 15, 1. seqq. 4 in palmitum qualitate. 5. in externâ vilitate. Conf. Ezech. 15, 2.6. in fructuum suavitate. Vid ludic. 9, 18. Eccles. 9, 7.Es. 62, 5.Ierem. 2, 2.Gal. 5, 22.Phil. 1, 11.c. 4, 18. Vegetatur haec vinea calore So-is iustitiae Mal. 4, 2.Luc. 1, 78. penetrantissimo, irrigatur rore ac pluviâ coelesti, Es. 27, 3.c. 44, 3.Psal. 68, 10. foecundissimo, munitur à Deo muro fortissimo, Esa, 5, 2Zach. 2, 9. Huc facit quoque comparatio Ecclesiae cum vite, quam ostendit Dn. D. Botsacus in Prompt. Alleg. p. 720. it. ipsius Christi cum vite, utpote qui produxit uvas pretiosissimas ac dulcissimas nostrae redemtionis, cum Deo propitiationis, de morte & peccato lib-rationis. Conf. 1. Ioh. 4, 10. Potest quoque anima cuiusque -de-is conferri cum vinea, ut quae plantata in terrâ huius corporis, cuius facultates ordinatae sunt vites; vinum fides & opera charitatis. Vites alligandae palo crucis, cuius pedi foveam fodimus, semper de sepulturâ cogitantes. Servanda haec vinea & diligenter custodienda, Cant 1, 6. ab apro ( Ps 80, 14.) voluptatis obscoenae, â ferâ superbiae, à vulpe astutiae, à lupo voracitatis & avaritiae &c. Producit haec vinea lacrymas compuctionis (huc facit illud Bernhardi serm 30. in Cant, lacryma poenitentium sunt vinum Angelorum.) emittit odorem consolationis, profert uvas commiserationis & dilectionis. Agnoscenda ac depraedicanda hîc summa DEI φιλανθςωπία, dum ex genere humano, quod propter peccatum instarligni aridi, nec ad aliud quicquam utile erat, nisi ut in igne miniiceretur Matt 3, 10.Ezech. 15, 4. non dedignatur plantare -neam. Demus igitur operam sedulò, quò fructum proferamus multum, Iohan. 15, 5. quem Deus avidè expectat, Es. 5, 3. Vae illi, qui DEI expectationem frustratur. Conf. Deut. 32, 32. &c.)*

## 20:2
v. 2. συμφωνήσας. Metaphor is from the voice of musicians proper. For just as sweet harmony is excited from diverse voices, so there is harmony between the one hiring and the one hired, when they agree concerning the quantity of the wage. (Since, as was indicated above, some understand by laborers in this place specifically the ministers of the Church, it is accustomed to be asked, Is it lawful for the Ministers of the word to seek or receive a stipend? Our people affirm it, and prove it solidly 1. by clear oracles of Holy Scripture, Num. 18, 31.Deut. 18, 1.Matt. 10, 10.Luke 10, 7.Rom. 15, 27.1 Cor. 9, 7.14.Gal. 6, 6. 2. By the weight of reasons, which the Apostle urges 1 Cor. 9, 7. 3. By examples, of the Levites & Priests of the O. T. Num. 5, 9.c. 18, 18.21.c. 24, 8. of the Apostles, 1 Cor. 9, 4.2 Cor. 11, 8.Phil. 4, 10. The Anabaptists strive to defend the negative, concerning whom see D. Wigandus on the Anab. p. 8. Danaeus Comm. on 1 Tim. 5. p. 307. Hinckelmannus Coll. Anabapt. Disp. 8. err. 4. and others. also the Weigelians. See Weigelius part. 1. Postill. p. 218. and also in the Dialogue on Christian. page 101. But our people have solidly discussed their sophistries everywhere. Conf. B. D. Tarnov. Comm. on Mich. p. 74. also a special Theol. dissertation on the abdication of the Ministers of the word &c. c. 12. §. 24. seqq. B. Dedekennus -onsil. Theol. Volum. part. 3. memb. 4. sect. 2. B. D. Balduinus Instit. Minist. of the word p. 295. seqq. B. Par. L. on the Ministers of the Church §. 325. also Acad. Dispp. p. 880. Furthermore, the Papists attempt to construct merits of good works from this passage, when the Householder, by whom God is understood, having made an agreement with the laborers for a denarius a day, sent the laborers into his vineyard. Franciscus Costerus, a famous Jesuit, in Enchir. Controv. p. 274, adorns this error of the Papists with this discourse: Thus, he writes, the most patient God deals with us in His mercy, just as we are accustomed to deal with laborers. For first we agree upon the price, and with the wage established, so that the matter may be more secure, we give an earnest. Afterwards we inspect and examine the work now completed. Finally, if the work is finished according to the terms of the agreement, we bestow the wage. In the same manner, God first indeed makes an agreement with the human race and especially with Christians. Just as it is explained in the parable of the Householder. Who, having made an agreement with the laborers for a daily denarius, sent them into his vineyard. For God said to Abraham: I am thy reward exceeding great. And Christ: If thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments &c. And again p. 290. God indeed, without any agreement, but by His own singular goodness, promised the forgiveness of sins freely to those who approach Him as suppliants etc. But He promised eternal life in place of a reward for works, an agreement having been made with the workers for a daily denarius. Resp. 1. Parabolic theology is not argumentative, nor in parables should all members be compared too solicitously, since otherwise many false and absurd things would follow, but the principal scope of the parable speaking, which is sufficiently evident from the antecedents and consequents, must be attended to. Which canon we have elsewhere proven at greater length, both from the Fathers and from the Doctors of the Papists themselves. Now it pleases to add at least the consent of Corn. à Lapide, who writes explicitly in this place, that whatever in this parable pertains to the scope of Christ, (who, according to the same Cornelius, is here to teach that it will be by the grace of GOD and without any injustice or injury to anyone, that those who seemed to hold the first places here, will hold the last on the last day, and those who held the last here, like the Apostles and the abject faithful followers of Christ, will be preferred in the kingdom of heaven to the Scribes and Pharisees, as those who, having been set over the law and (NB.) works, falsely arrogated to themselves the kingdom of GOD from them, and therefore rejected Christ the faith of Christ. Whence they deservedly fell from this kingdom. &c.) must be noted and explained; but those things which do not pertain to it must be omitted in the explanation of the parable Since they are added only as emblems of the parable itself. Since, therefore, the scope of Christ is to show that those who trust in works falsely arrogate to themselves the kingdom of GOD, i.e., eternal life; and indeed the Papists, teaching that Good Works are meritorious of eternal life, trust in their own works, it is manifest that this parable rather destroys their opinion. It is so far from confirming it, that some emblems, such as that the householder made an agreement with the workers concerning the reward, and that they labored, etc., might perhaps seem to support their error. 2. There is added the interpretation of Gregory Nazianzen, calling the first workers, who became the last, those who did not believe nor enter into the vineyard before a reward had been established for them by an agreement. Since the Papists are such, as those who openly teach that it is permitted to do good works with a view to the reward of eternal life. (Concerning which Papist error see B. Par. L. de B. O. §. 126.) it is manifest that these very ones are such workers, who desire to enter into the vineyard only after an agreement has been made, and thus are the first who are to be the last. 3. Nor does the saying of Christ help them Matth. 19, 17. inasmuch as it is legal. Now indeed no flesh is justified by the law. Rom. 3, 20. if anyone wishes to accept that as an Evangelical commandment, it can be said that in it is described the quality of the subject to be saved, but not the cause of salvation or merit. 4. that the reason is not the same, when God promises a reward to men, and when men promise a certain reward to laborers, is sufficiently evident from Luc. 7, 10 and from Rom. 6, last. 5. If by the denarius, which is promised here to the laborers as a reward, eternal life is understood, it follows that in eternal life there is murmuring among the blessed. That a harsh rebuke of GOD has a place in beatitude v. 15. Is your eye evil. Both of which Cornelius à Lapide deservedly removes from the blessed in this place p. 379. Compare more in the Analysis to v. 8.)*

*( A denarius for each day. By the denarius in this place is not understood precisely eternal life, (since it was given also to those murmuring, and now indeed in heaven among the blessed there is no murmuring, as the Jesuit Corn. à Lapide himself confesses at v. 1.) but by this name are understood either in general any gifts of GOD, whether of this life or of the future life; (See the notes at v. 9. & thus Corn. à Lapide accepts it, who not ineptly explains that: take what is yours, in this way: take, not Pharisee, your riches and honors, which I gave to you in this life, and which you coveted over eternal life. Be content with these etc.) or this ought to be referred at least to the ornamentation of the parable, not to the essential parts or the goal of Christ. For indeed, with the day now ending, it is mentioned as given. Now indeed temporal blessing does not easily have a place then. Compare more at v. 9. Furthermore, the denarius was otherwise among the Romans the daily wage of a laborer, and also of a common soldier. See Corn. Tacitus book 1 of the Annals and Lipsius at the said place.)*

Latin:

v. 2. συμφωνήσας. Metaphora est à voce Musicorum propria. Ut enim ex diversis vocibus suavis excitatur harmonia, sic harmonia est inter conducentem & conductum, cùm de mercedis quantitate consentiunt. *(Cùm, ut suprà indicatum, nonnulli per operarios h. l. in specie intelligant ministros Ecclesiae, quaeri solet, an lice at Ministris verbi petere vel accipere stipendium? Nostrates affirmant, ac sol-dè probant 1. claris Sc. Sacrae oraculis, Numer. 18, 31.Deuter. 18, 1.Matth. 10, 10.Luc. 10, 7.Rom. 15, 27.1. Cor. 9, 7.14.Gal. 6, 6. 2. Rationum momentis, quae urget Apostolus 1. Cor. 9, 7. 3. Exemplis, Levitarum & Sacerdotum V. T. Num. 5. 9.c. 18, 18.21.c 24, 8. Apostolorum, 1. Cor. 9, 4.2. Cor. 11, 8.Phil. 4, 10. Negativam defendere satagunt Anabaptistae, de quibus vid. D. Wigandus de Anab. p. 8. Danaeus Comm. in 1. Tim. 5. p. 307. Hinckelmannus Coll. Anabapt. Disp. 8. err. 4. alii. it. Weigeliani. Vid. Weigelius part. 1. Postill. p. 218. nec non in Dialogo de Christian. pag. 101. Argutias verò eorum solidè discusserūt nostrates passim. Conf. B D Tarnov. Comm. in Mich. p. 74. it. pecul. dissert. Theol. de Ministr. verbi abdicatione &c. c. 12. §. 24. seqq. B. Dedekennus -onsil. Theol. Volum. part. 3. memb. 4. sect. 2. B. D. Balduinus Instit. Minist. verbi p. 295. seqq. B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccles. §. 325. it. Dispp. Acad. p. 880. Coeterùm conantur ex h. l. Pontificii B. O. merita exstruere, cùm Paterfamiliâs, per quem Deus intelligitur, conventione factâ cum operariis, in sing. dies de-ario, miserit operarios in vineam. Franciscus Costerus, Iesuita famosus in Enchir. Controv. p. 274. errorem Pontificiorum hoc exornat discursu: Ita, scribit, agit misericordiâ suâ nobiscum patientissimus Deus, quomodo nos cum operariis solemus. Primùm enim de pretio convenimus, mercedeq constitutâ, qú res sit cautior, ar-ham damus. Postea opus iam effectum inspicimu & exploramus. Deniq si ex ratione conventionis perfectum opus est, mercedem tribuimus. Ad eundem modum Deus primò quidem cum humano genere ac praesertim cum Christianis, convenit. Sicut in parabola Patris familiâs explicatur. Qui conventione factâ cum operariis de denario diurno, misit illos in vineam suam. Deus enim Abrahae dicebat: Egero merces tua magna nimis. Et Christus: Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata &c. Et iterum p. 290. Deus quidem sine conventione ullâ, sed singulari suâ bonitate promisit gratis peccatorum condonationem his, qui illum supplices adierint &c. Vitam aeternam autem promisit mercedis loco operibus factâ cum operariis conventione ex denario diurno. Resp. 1. Theologia parabolica non est argumentativa, nec in parabolis omnia membra nimis solicitè conferenda, cum aliàs multa falsa & absurda sequantur sed principalis parabolae dicentis scopus, qui ex antecedentibus & consequentibus satis patescit, attendendus. Quem canonem alibi tum ex Patribus, tum ex ipsis Dd. Pontificiiprolixiùs probavimus. Iam n-nc placet addere saltem conse-sum Corn. à Lapide, in h. l. disertè scribentis, quòd quaecunin parabolâ hâc ad scopum Christi, (qui, iuxta eundem -ornelium, hîc est, docere, ex DEI gratiâ & sine ullâ iniustitiâ vel cuiuspiam iniuriâ fore, ut qui hîc primas tenere visi sunt, in di novissimo postremas teneant, & qui hîc postremas, ut Apostoli & abiecti fideles sequaces Christi, in regno coelorum Scribus & Pharisaeis praeferantur, ut qui legi & (NB.) operibus praefisi, falsò ex illis DEI regnum sibi arrogabant, ideoChristum Christifidem repelle-ant. Unde meritò â regno hoc exciderunt. &c.) pertinent, annotanda & explicanda sint; quae verò ad eum non pertinent in explicatione parabolae omittenda Cùm addantur duntaxat ut emblemat a ipsius parabolae. Cùm igitur scopus Christi sit, ostendere, quòd qui operibus confidunt, falsò sibi regnum DEI s. vitam aeternam arrogent; & verò Pontificii, docentes, B O. esse vitae aeternae meritoria, in operibus suis confidant, manifestum est, quòd hec parabola potiùs illorum sententiā destruat. Tantum abest, ut cōfirmet, utut nonnulla emblemata, uti sunt ea, quòd paterfamil às cum operariis de mercede convenerit, it. quòd laborarint &c. errori eorum patrocinari videri fortè possint. 2 Accedit interpretatio Gregorii Nazianzeni, primos operarios, qui postremi facti sunt, vocans eos, qui nō priùs orediderunt nec ingressi in vineam sunt, quàm ipsis ex conventu merces constituta fuisset. Tales cùm Pontificii sint, ut qui palàm docent, quòd liceat intuitu merced-s vitae aeternae bona operari. (De quo Pontif. errore vid. B. Par. L. de B. O. §. 126.) palàm est, quòd hi ipsi sint tales operarii, qui non nisi priùs conventione factâ ingredi in vineam cupiunt, adeoque primi, qui postremi futuri. 3. Nec iuvat eos dictum Christi Matth. 19, 17. quippe quod est legale. Iam verò ex lege non iustificatur ulla caro.Rom. 3, 20. si quis tanquam Evangelicum mandatum accipere illud velit, dici potest, quòd in eô describatur qualitas subiecti salvandi, non verò salutis causa vel meritum. 4. quòd non sit eadem ratio, quando Deus hominibus mercedem promittit, ac quando homines operariis certam mercedem promittunt, satis patet ex Luc. 7, 10 it. ex Rom. 6, ult. 5. Si per denarium, qui hîc operariis tanquam merces promittitur, intelligitur vita aeterna, sequitur quòd in vita aeterna inter beatos sit murmur. Quòd in beatitudine locum habeat dura DEI increpatio v. 15. An oculus tuus nequam. Quod utrumque meritò à beatis removet Cornelius à Lapide in h. l. p. 379. Conf. plura in Anal. ad v. 8.)*

*( Denario in singulos dies. Per denarium hoc loco non intelligitur praecisè vita aeterna, (cùm murmurantibus quoque datus fuerit, iam verò in coelis inter beatos nullum est murmur, uti ipse fatetur Iesuita Corn. à Lap. ad v. 1.) sed intelliguntur hoc nomine vel in genere quaelibet DEI dona sive huius, sive futurae vitae; (Vid. notata ad v. 9. & ita Corn. accipit à Lapide, qui non ineptè illud: tolle quod tuum est, exponit h. m. tolle, non Pharisaee, tuas opes & honores, quos tibi in hâc vitâ dedi, & quos prae vitâ aeternâ ambivisti. Iis contentus esto &c.) vel ad ornatum saltem parabolae referri hoc debet, non ad partes essentiales sive Christi scopum. Etenim finiente iam die memoratur datus. Iam verò benedictio temporalis tum non facilè locum habet. Conf. plura ad v. 9. Caeterùm denarius aliàs apud Romanos erat merces diurna mercenarii, it. militis gregarii. Vid. Corn. Tacitum l. 1. Annalium & Lipsium ad d. l.)*

## 20:3
v. 3. About the third hour. The diversity of the hours is referred to -ity μακροκόσμου by Irenaeus book 4, ch. 70, Bede in this place, Origen hom. 10 on Matthew *(in the same way Nazianzen explains it in Orat. 40 on Baptism p. 651, Hilary, and others from the ancients, whom from the more recent ones B. D. Hunnius, Corn. à Lapide, Iacobus Tirinus, and others follow)* It is referred to μικροκὸσμον by Jerome, Isidore of Pelusium, Basil the Great, Fulgentius, Ambrose, Hilary can. 10. *(Theophylact makes mention of both expositions, likewise St. Jerome Comm. in this place, and this one indeed after he had commemorated that it seemed to him that the laborers of the first day were Samuel, Jeremiah, and John the Baptist, as those who can say with the Psalmist:) From my mother's womb you are my God. But he adds regarding the workers of the third hour, who began to serve GOD from puberty, etc.: There are those who explain this parable differently. At the first hour they wish Adam and the other Patriarchs to have been sent into the vineyard up to Noah, at the third hour Noah himself and up to Abraham. At the sixth from Abraham, etc. But the Savior does not seem to have wished to signify anything peculiar in individual circumstances. For how much less can the faithful in the O.T. be understood by the workers who labored at the first hour is evident, because they themselves are said to have murmured against the householder. That which cannot at all be said of the faithful of the O.T. Most commonly these are referred to among the ornaments of the parable.

In the marketplace idle. Men established in a state of sin expose their souls as if for sale in a marketplace, where the devil conducts trade. *(It can also be gathered from this how null the powers of Free Will are after the fall in spiritual matters. add. John 15, 5.Rom. 9, 16.Eph. 2, 1.2. Cor. 3, 5.Phil. 2, 13. The Devil is also accustomed to expose wares for sale in this marketplace of the world, concerning which 1. John 2, 16. In acquiring these we are by nature most busy, just as we are entirely idle in good works, Ps. 14, 2. 3. We sleep in the bosom of Delilah, Judg. 16, 19. from which, unless we repent, we are by no means transferred into the bosom of Abraham, Luke 16, 22. Let us therefore rise from the sleep of sin. Rom. 13, 11, 12.Eph. 5, 4. But after we have been awakened, let us not be idle, but let us prove ourselves to God 1. by laboring diligently. 2. by bearing the cross patiently, and not murmuring. 3. by desiring solely the denarius of eternal life. 4. by committing all other things to God.)*

Tertiae verò horae operarios, qui à pubertate DEO servire coeperunt &c. subiungit: Sunt, qui hanc parabolam aliter disserant Primâ horâ volunt missum esse in vineam Adam & alios Patriarchas us adNoë, tertiâ ipsum Noë atque ad Abrahamum. Sextâ ab Abrahamo &c. Sed non videtur Salvator in singulis circumstantiis peculiare quid significare voluisse. Quò minûs enim per operarios, qui primâ horâ laborarunt, accipi possi-fideles in V. T. patet, quia murmurasse ipsi dicuntur adversùs patremfamiliâs. Id quod de fidelibus V. T. dici haut potest. Communissimè haec inter parabolae ornamenta referuntur.)*

In foro otiosos. Homines in statu peccati constituti animas quasi in foro exponunt venales, ubi diabolus mercaturam facit. *(Colligi etiam hinc potest, quàm nullae sint vires L. A. post lapsum in rebus spiritualibus. add. Iohan 15, 5.Rom. 9, 16.Eph. 2, 1.2. Cor. 3, 5.Philipp. 2, 13. Solet etiam Diabolus in hoc mundi foro venales exponere merces, de quibus 1. Ioh. 2, 16. In his comparandis naturâ sumus negotiosissimi, sicuti in operibus bonis prorsus otiosi, Ps. 14, 2. 3. Dormimus in Delilae sinu, Iud. 16, 19. è quo, nisi resipiscamus, minimè in sinu Abrahae transfecimur, Luc. 16, 22. Surgamus igitur à somno peccati. Rom. 13, 11, 12.Eph. 5, 4. Sed postquam excitati fuerimus, non simus otiosi, sed Deo nos probemus 1. diligenter laborando. 2. crucem patienter ferendo, nec obmurmurando. 3. aeternae vitae denarium unicè desiderando. 4. coetera omnia Deo committendo.)*

## 20:7
* (v. 7. καὶ ὃ ἐὰν ἦ δίκαιον λήφεσθε. Franciscus Lucas Brugensis thinks in his various readings that these words are superfluous in the Greek and Syriac copies. If you ask for the reason for this opinion, you will hear no other than that the Latin Vulgate Interpreter does not have them. Also that Hilary and Jerome do not seem to have acknowledged them. Resp. 1. The Vulgate can prejudice the Greek text in no way, (it is known that quite often the said interpreter omitted not only individual expressions, but entire periods here and there) especially if the most ancient Greek codices agree, as in this place according to Beza. The most ancient manuscript Eclogues of the Nuremberg Library also agree excellently. Nor do we disguise, however, that the same are missing in a certain Greek codex of Cambridge and another of the Marquis of Valois, as noted by Walton in the Polyglot English Bible. 2. Not only the Syriac, but also the Arabic and Ethiopic interpreters agree with the Greek codices in this place, though the Persian dissents. 3. The parallel text v. 4 approves the received reading, as do the Greek expositors, Chrysostom, Theophylact, etc. 4. to that, That Hilary and Jerome do not seem to have acknowledged it, we respond that they seem altogether to have acknowledged it, as is evident from inspection. Furthermore, Cornelius à Lapide, from the fact that here the Householder promises the laborers that he will give them what is just, gathers the merit of good works, as that which merits a reward as if from justice. But since all our good works are imperfect, and already owed to GOD beforehand, they cannot be meritorious of eternal life. See the note to v. 8. Besides, the word δικαιον, denotes here fair rather than just, just as the Hebrew שוה does. In which meaning, according to H. Grotius, it is accepted in Philipp. 1, 8.Col. 4, 1.2. Petr. 1, 13.

Latin:

* (v. 7. καὶ ὃ ἐὰν ἦ δίκαιον λήφεσθε. Putat Franci cus Lucas Brugensis in variis lectionibus, verba haec in Graecis Syricisque exemplaribus superfluere. Si quaeras opinionis huius rationem, nullam audies aliam, quàm quòd Interpres LatinuVulgatus non habet. item quòd Hilarius & Hieronymus non videantur ea agnovisse. Resp. 1. Vulgatus nihil praeiudicare textui Graeco potest, (notum, quòd saepiusculè non solùm singulares dictiones, sed integras periodos dictus interpres hinc inde omiserit) cumprimis si Codd. Gr. antiquissimi consentiant, uti h. l. teste Beza. Adstipulantur quoque egregiè Eclogae antiquissimae MSS. Bibl. Noribergensis. Neque tamen dissimulamus, quòd eadem desiderentur in Codice quodam Graeco Cantabrigiensi ac alio March. Valesii, momente Walthono in V. L. Bibl. Angl. 2. Consentiunt cum Codd. Graecis h. l. non solùm Syrus, verùm etiam Arabs & Aethiops Interpp, dissentiente tamen Persâ. 3. Approbant receptam lectionem textus parallelus v. 4. nec non Expositores Graeci, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus &c. 4. ad illud, quòd Hilarius ac Hieronymus non videantur agnovisse, respondemus, quòd omninò videantur agnovisse, ceu ex inspectione patet. Porrò Cornelius à Lapide ex eo, quòd hîc Paterfamiliâs promittit operariis, se illis daturum, quod iustum est, colligit meritum bonorum operum, ut quod quasi ex iustitia meretur mercedem. Verùm cùm omnia nostra B. O. sint imperfecta, iam antè DEO debita, non possunt esse vitae aeternae meritoria. Vid. not. ad v. 8. Praeterea vocabulum δικαιον, perinde ut Ebr. שוהaequum potiùs hîc notat, quàm iustum. In quo significatu, iuxta H. Grotium accipitur Philipp. 1, 8.Col. 4, 1.2. Petr. 1, 13.)*

## 20:8
(v. 8. Όψίαστ δὲ γενομεὺλης. By evening is understood not only the time of the universal judgment, but also the particular judgment of each person, which happens at death. Whence it is evident that the Jesuit Becanus, tr. 1 de Beat. c. 1. q. 12. n. 13. proves less firmly from this place that the Fathers of the O.T. did not enter into the kingdom of heaven before the death of Christ, since the denarius was not given to the morning laborers, by whom he wishes believers in the O.T. to be understood, before the evening ones. But to pass over for now that in parables not all circumstances are to be anxiously examined, but the scope ought to be looked at, noting besides many others, about whom elsewhere, Becanus himself, tr. de visione DEI q. 9. n. 3. (mention is made of evening, because among men, only when labor has been exhausted, i.e., around evening, is the wage usually paid to the laborers), let us suppose that Christ by morning laborers understands believers in the O.T. through Evening believers in the N. T., yet Becanus will effect nothing from that. For since by the evening the day of the final judgment or the end of the world ought to be understood here, which pleases Cornelius à Lapide and other Papist Commentators, it will be a consequence that neither the evening ones, i.e., those who after Christ's incarnation and ascension, that is, his entry into the kingdom of heaven, have labored in the vineyard of the Church, i.e., have believed in Christ, have entered into the kingdom of heaven thus far, but have the necessity to wait for the denarius of eternal life until the very last day. Which thing, I think, not even the Papists themselves will concede.)*

*( τῷ ἐ-πιτρόπῳ By this is understood Christ himself. See B. D. Glass. Exeg. Domin. part. 2. p. 705. See Ioh. 5. 23. & 24.Act. 17, 31.*

*( Call the laborers. Well does Dn. D. Olearius in the School of patience p. 1257 gather from this place that God is such a householder that without his will it is not permitted for anyone to cease from the assigned labors.)*

*( Pay them the wages. Compare c. 16, 27. Rom. 2, 6.2. Cor. 5, 10.Apoc. 22, 12. From these and similar places, where mention is made of wages, the Papists strive especially to build up the B. O. merits. See Bell. l. 5. de Iustif. c. 3. Alphonsus Mendoza Controv. Theol. p. 110. Becanus lib. 1. Manual. Controv. c. 18. q. 2. But in vain! For it must be known, as far as the present place is concerned, 1. that parabolic Theology is not argumentative. Compare Irenaeus l. 2. adv. haeres. c. 46. Chrysost. hom. 65. in Matth. Nor is it necessary in parables to explore individual parts more subtly (as the more prudent Papists themselves well warn. See Ruitzius reg. 25. Jesuit Suarez in Thom. t. 4. q. 88. art. 4. sect. 1. Disp. 13. Padulanus in this place, Corn. à Lapide in the Canons, Comment. ad Evang. prefixed p. 24. also to c. 15. Ioh. v. 1. p. 475. Maldonatus in c. 2. Lucae v. 6. c. 11. Matth. v 6. and elsewhere passim.) but the principal scope of the parable must be regarded, which in this place, as appears from the epiphonema v. 16. 30, is to teach that those who think themselves first, i.e., who trust that they have fulfilled the law perfectly, and have merited eternal life by their own works, are last before the judgment of GOD. So far, therefore, is this parable from establishing B. O. merits, that it is rather directly opposed to that opinion and boasting. Which thing Prosper also taught long ago in his book de vocatione gentium c. 5, warning that for this reason in the parable concerning those who labor in the vineyard, the same reward and the same wages are given to all the laborers, whether they have labored much or little, so that those who have sweated in much labor, and have received no more than the latest, may understand that they have received the gift of grace, not the reward of works. Ludov. Granatensis acknowledges the same in Epit. Concion. p. 124, saying: The whole parable looks especially to this, to demonstrate the liberality and freedom of the Lord in the distribution of his gifts. And what, I ask, do the words of the householder: Is it not lawful for me etc. is your eye evil, because I am good? indicate other than that God does not look to the dignity of the one working or laboring, but only to his own goodness. 3. It must be known that the name reward is accepted not only for the reward of debt, but also for the reward of grace. And eternal life is called reward in this way, not in that. See the notes at c. 5. v. 12. and compare more on the present passage in B. Par. L. de B. O. S. 114. item. Confess. Cathol t. 4 pag. 872. seqq. Although in this place, by reward, eternal life cannot even be understood, speaking absolutely. For it would otherwise follow that eternal life is also given to those murmuring against GOD, and as it were accusing him of iniquity. Which, however, everyone will confess to be absurd to assert. Augustine well says in l. de Gr. & L. A. c. 9. Eternal life is the grace of GOD, so that we might understand that God leads us to eternal life not for our merits, but for his own mercy. And no less beautifully Anselm in the book de mensur crucis: If a man were to serve God for a thousand years, even most fervently, he would not deserve by condignity to be in the kingdom of heaven for half a day.

Latin:

*(v. 8. Όψίαστ δὲ γενομεὺλης. Per vesperam intelligitur non solùm tempus iudicii universalis, sed etiam particulare cuiusque iudicium, quod in morte contingit. Unde patet, quòd Iesuita Becanutr. 1. de Beat. c. 1. q. 12. n. 13. minùs firmiter ex h. l. probet, Patres V. T. non priùs introivisse in regnum coelorum, nisi post mortem Christi, siquidem denarius non priùs datus fuerit matutinis operariis, per quos credentes in V. T. intellectos vult, quàm vespertinis. Verùm ut iam nunc taceamus, quòd in parabolis non omnes circumstantiae anxiè examinandae sint, sed scopus spectari debeat, mon-nte praeter alios plures, de quibus alibi, ipso Becano tr. de visione DEI q. 9. n. 3. (fit autem vesperae mentio, quia apud homines exantlato demum labore h e. circa vesperam merces operariis p-rsolvi solet.) ponamus, Christum per matutinos operarios intelligere credentes in V. T. per vespertinos credentes in N. T., nihil tamen inde Becanus efficiet. Cùm enim per vesperam extremi iudicii dies sive finis mundi intelligi hîc debeat, quod Cornelio à Lapide aliisque Commentatoribus Pontificiis arridet, consequens erit, nec vespertinos, h. e. qui post Christi incarnationem atq; ascensionem s. ingressum in regnum coelorum, in vineâ Ecclesiae laborarunt h. e. in Christum crediderunt, ingressos hactenus in regnum coelorum esse, sed ad extremum usque diem vitae aeternae denarium expectare necesse habere. Id quod nec ipsi, puto, Pontificii concedent.)*

*( τῷ ἐ-πιτρόπῳ Per hunc intelligitur ipse Christus. Vid. B. D. Glass. Exeg. Domin. part. 2. p. 705. Vid. Ioh. 5. 23. & 24.Act. 17, 31.*

*( Voca operarios. Benè ex h. l. colligit Dn. D. Olearins in Scholâ patientiae p. 1257. Deum talem esse patremfamiliâs, ut absque eius voluntate n-mini integrum sit, cessare à demandatis laboribus.)*

*( Redde illis mercedem. Conf. c. 16, 27. Rom. 2, 6.2. Cor. 5, 10.Apoc. 22, 12. Ex his similibus que locis, ubi mercedis mentio fit, Pontificii B. O. merita adstruere cumprimis nituntur. Vid. Bell. l. 5. de Iustif. c. 3. Alphonsus Mendoza Controv. Theol. p. 110. Becanus lib. 1. Manual. Controv. c. 18. q. 2. Sed frustrà! Etenim sciendum, quantum ad praesentem quidem locum, 1. quòd Theologia parabolica non sit argumentativa. Conf. Irenaeus l. 2. adv. haeres. c. 46. Chrysost. hom. 65. in Matth. Nec in parabolis oportet singulas partes subtiliùs explorare (uti benè monent ipsi prudentiores Pontificii. Vid. Ruitzius reg. 25. Iesuita Suarez in Thom. t. 4. q. 88. art. 4. sect. 1. Disp. 13. Padulanus in h. l. Corn. à Lapide in Canonibus, Comment. ad Evang. praemissis p. 24. it. ad c. 15. Ioh. v. 1. p. 475. Maldonatus in c. 2. Lucae v. 6. c. 11. Matth. v 6. alibique passim.) sed respiciendus est parabolae scopus principalis, qui h. l. est, ceu ex epiphon. v. 16. 30. apparet, docere, illos, qui se existimant primos, h. e. qui confidunt, se legem implevisse perfectè, suisque operibus aeternam promeritos esse vitam, coram DEI iudicio esse novissimos. Tantum igitur abest, ut parabola haec B. O. merita stabiliat, ut potiùs directè opinioni illi ac gloriationi opposita sit. Id quod iampridem etiam docuit Prosper lib. de vocatione gentium c. 5. monens, ideò in parabola de his, qui -aborant in vinea, dari idem praemium, eandemque mercedem omnibus operariis, sive multum, sive parum laborarint, ut ii, qui in multo labore sudârunt, nec ampliùs, quàm novissimi acceperunt, int elligant, donumse gratiae, non operum accepisse mercedem. Idem etiam agnoscit Ludov. Granatensis in Epit. Concion. p. 124. Tota, inquiens, parabola huc potissimùm spectat, ut liberalitatem & libertatem Domini in donorum suorum distributione demonstret. Et quid quaeso aliud verba patrisfamiliâs: Annon licet mihi &c. an oculus tuus malus est, quòd ego bonus sum? Indicant aliud, quàm quòd Deus non ad operantis vel laborantis dignitatem, sed tantùm ad suam bonitatem respiciat, 3. Sciendum est, mercedis nomen accipi non solùm pro mercede debiti, sed etiam pro mercede gratiae. Atque hoc, non illo modo vita aeterna merces dicitur. Vid notata ad c. 5. v. 12. ac confer pluribus de praesenti loco B. Par. L. de B. O. S. 114. it. Confess. Cathol t. 4 pag. 872. seqq. Quamvis h. l. per mercedem ne quidem, absolutè loquendo intelligi vita aeterna possit. Consequens enim aliàs foret, vitam aeternam dari quoque murmurantibus contra DEUM, eumque iniquitatis quasi insimulantibus. Quod tamen ineptum esse adserere, nemo non fatebitur. Be-è Augustinus l. de Gr. & L. A. c. 9. Gratia DEI vita aeterna, ut intelligeremus, non pro meritis nostris Deum nos ad vitam aeternam, sed pro suâ misericordiâ perducere. Nec minùs pulcrè Anselmus lib. de mensur crucis: Si homo mille annis Deo serviret, etiam ferventissimè, nō mereretur ex condigno, dimidium diem esse in regno coelorum.)*

## 20:9
v. 9. They received each a denarius. Irenaeus determines that the denarius signifies the image of GOD in man and the knowledge of J. C. through which we are rendered immortal. Hieron. lib. 2. contra Iovin. f. 42. One denarius is not one reward, but one life and one liberation from hell. August. serm. 59. de verb. Dom. Col. 220. tract. 67. in Ioh. That denarius is eternal life. lib. de s. Virgin. c. 26. The denarius signifies something which all will have in common, just as eternal life itself, the kingdom of heaven itself, where all will be whom God predestined, called, justified, glorified. Ambrosius 1. de vocatione gentium cap. 5. pag. 13. Under the agreement of the denarius, the equality of eternal life is signified. Iansenius c. 101. harm. p. 614. that one must be entirely silent about the denarius, says Iacob. de Vorag. pag. 72. Maldonatus, Hugo Cardinalis, Stapletonus Prompt. moral. pag. 301. Granat. Epit. conc. pag. 126. understand eternal life, which is so called because it is given for the observance of the decalogue. Likewise the Fathers, but in another sense, namely, not that it is owed to the merits of works, but is granted from the most benign promise of GOD. It seems safest and most analogous to faith if by denarius we understand all the promises of GOD concerning the corporal and earthly or eternal retribution of good works, 1. Tim. 4, 9. for indeed 1. a denarius is given to those murmuring. But eternal life does not happen except to the pious and humble. 2. A denarius is given as a reward and prize of labors. But between our works and eternal life there is no proportion. Gregory rightly teaches, that no one murmuring has received eternal life, for no one who receives it can murmur. Meanwhile, let it remain certain that eternal life is a gratuitous gift of GOD, Rom. 6, last. For in reward, as Luther notes de servo arbitr. t. 3. Lat. pag. 199. either dignity or consequence is regarded. *(Jovinian urged this passage against the diversity of rewards to be conferred upon the blessed in eternal life. But 1. It is denied that by denarius in this place eternal life can be directly and precisely understood, since a denarius also fell to those murmuring, and likewise to those who are not elect, as is gathered from the epiphonema. So that therefore the rewards promised to those laboring in the vineyard of the Lord are more rightly understood to be either temporal or eternal. 2. If even at most by denarius in this place eternal life is signified, one must nevertheless distinguish between the essential beatitude itself, or eternal life, which will be common to all the blessed, and between the degrees of beatitude, between accidental rewards, the foundation of which, although it is not to be sought with the Pontificals in the dignity of our merits, but in the gratuitous remuneration of GOD and divine benignity, nothing nevertheless prevents them from varying according to the liberal remuneration of GOD, as is evident from the sayings Dan. 12, 3. 1. Cor. 15, 42. Ioh. 14, 3. to which also is referred

it is accustomed, 1 Cor. 9:6. This was long ago observed by Augustine, who writes in his book *On Virginity*, ch. 26: Eternal life itself will be equal for all the saints. For an equal denarius has been given to all, and yet in this denarius one will not live more fully than another in an unequal way. But because in that very eternal life the lights of merits (i.e., of works) will shine distinctly, there are many mansions with the Father, in which one is honored more brightly than another. Compare B. P. L. *On Eternal Life* §§.128 and 131. 3. Christ's purpose is, in this parable, to show that eternal life is a free gift of God. And B. P. L. in *On Good Works* §.114 rightly observes that two kinds of laborers are set before us in this parable. Some, in their works, look to the reward, and reckon that their labors are worthy of recompense; therefore for greater labor they demand greater pay, they count up their merits before God, they envy their neighbor God's grace, they exalt themselves above others, they murmur against the master of the house, they accuse him of injustice, and in their own opinion and judgment they are first; these receive the denarius, that is, they are forced to be content with the rewards of this life. For God is so generous that he leaves no good deed whatsoever without its reward; but those who wish to trust in their works, to boast of the same, etc., are dismissed with a small portion of the rewards of this life, for they are compelled to depart, having no grounds to complain of having been wronged. Others, however, do not look to reward in their works, but are content with that free promise of the master of the house: "What is just, I will give you." They submit to their calling, they labor diligently, they serve God in the simplicity of their heart, and in their own eyes they are the last, judging themselves and their works to be unworthy of any reward, and committing themselves wholly to divine grace, etc.; these become first, that is, God embraces them by his grace, and rewards their piety, out of grace, with the recompenses of this life and of the life to come. 4. And this exposition is consistent with the analogy of faith. For that good works are not meritorious of eternal life is sufficiently clear from the sole assertion of Christ in Luke 17:10 and of the Apostle in Romans 6, at the end. See by all means Dr. Wellerus's Commentaries, both on the aforementioned chapter 6 of the Epistle to the Romans and on ch. 4:5, p. 258; and Dr. Friedlieb, *Observations on H. E.*, p. 160, who, following Drs. Lyserus, Balduinus, Meisnerus, Bakius, and Erythrophilus, takes the denarius to refer to Christ himself, who had already once answered that he would be Abraham's reward, Gen. 15, 2. This, he says, all receive who are introduced through Baptism into the vineyard of the Church, Gal. 3, 27 The master of the house pays this about the eleventh hour, i.e., Christ came in the old age of the world in the flesh. And the same man observes that it does not stand against this opinion that even those who murmured are said to have received the denarius. Since they received it as to the offering, not as to the application. So that to them Christ was made a denarius of judgment, because they did not rightly use that which they received. Furthermore, Ioh. Paludanus, Doctor and Professor of Louvain, in Vindic. Theol. p. 233, writes: It must be known that Luther asserts the same thing with many sectarians of this time, which Jovinian once taught, as it pertains to the Blessed, whom he made all equal even to the B. Virgin in holiness and merits before GOD, just as Jovinian made all virtues equal among themselves. The foundation of the sectarians is this, because they think that men are just through the righteousness of Christ: but not their own. Furthermore, that the righteousness of Christ is equally imputed to all who have faith: likewise they say that all receive the reward not through their own merits, but through the merits of Christ, which are equally applied to all who have faith. These things being posited, he concludes, what wonder if they agree with Jovinian. Resp. 1. Distinguish between the imputed holiness of Christ, by which alone we are justified and saved, as that which alone can subsist before the rigorous judgment of GOD, and inherent holiness begun, by which, although we are neither justified, since it is imperfect and contaminated by many adhering infirmities and sins, nor do we merit eternal life, as it is the gift of GOD in Christ Jesus, Rom. 6. last, add. chap. 11, 6, yet it is not denied by us that in one it is greater than in another, and so in this latter respect there was greater holiness in the B. Virgin than in the converted thief, or even other believers. 2. Nor does B. Luther speak of this, but of the former holiness. For he writes explicitly: it was as necessary for B. Mary to aspire to grace (justifying) through the blood of Christ, as it was for us. 3. Nor does it follow that we obtain eternal life solely by the merit of Christ apprehended by faith, and cannot merit it by any of our works: therefore no degrees of glory are given in eternal life. For, as we have already pointed out above, one must accurately distinguish between eternal life or blessedness itself, and the degree of blessedness. For although all the pious dying in Christ will be equally blessed with essential blessedness; yet the degrees of glory will be distinct. 4. Nor does it follow that no one can merit either eternal life itself or a degree of glory in eternal life by his own works or inherent righteousness. Therefore, there are no degrees of glory. For, although neither eternal life itself nor a degree of glory is obtained from the merit of our works, conf. Rom. 8, 18., nevertheless, accidental blessedness or a degree of glory can vary from the liberal promise of GOD, as He who is about to give to each according to, not on account of works, Matth 16, 27. Rom. 2, 6. 2. Cor. 5, 10. Apoc. 22, 12. 1. Cor. 3, 8. The foundation of the diversity of glory is not to be sought in the meritorious dignity of our works, but in the gratuitous liberality of GOD. 5. And that this is the very mind and opinion of our B. Luther, clearly appears from his explanation of chap. 15 of the first to the Corinthians, vol. 6 of the Jena edition, p. 256, 261. Augustine says beautifully in the book on Grace and Free Will, chap. 9: The grace of GOD is eternal life, so that we might understand that God does not lead us to eternal life for our merits, but for His own mercy. Conf. the same in Ps. 32. Prosper of Aquitaine, book 1 on the calling of the Gentiles, chap. 5: He does not pay a price for labor, but pours out the riches of His goodness upon those whom He chooses without works, so that even those who have sweated with much labor, and received no more than the last, might understand that they have received the gift of grace, not the wage of works.

Latin:

v. 9. Acceperunt singuli denarium. Irenaeus statuit, denarium significare imaginem DEI in homine & cognitionem I. C. per quam reddimur immortales. Hieron. lib. 2. contra Iovin. f. 42. Unus denarius non unum est praemium, sed una vita & una de gehenna liberatio. August. serm. 59. de verb. Dom. Col. 220. tract. 67. in Ioh. Denarius ille vita aeterna est. lib. de s. Virgin. c. 26. Denarius significat aliq-id, quod omnes commuviter habebunt, sicut & ipsa vita aeterna, ipsum regnum coelorum, ubi erunt omnes, quos Deus praedestinavit, vocavit, iustificavit, glorificavit. Ambrosius 1. de vocatione gentium cap. 5. pag. 13. Sub pactione denarii vitae aeternae significatur aequalitas. Iansenius c. 101. harm. p. 614. de denario prorsus tacendum esse, inquit iacob. de Vorag. pag. 72. Maldonatus, Hugo Cardinalis, Stapletonus Prompt. moral. pag. 301. Granat. Epit. conc. pag. 126. intelligunt vitam aternam, quae sic dicatur, quòd detur pro observatione decalogi. Patreitidem, sed alio sensu, videl. non quòd operum meritis debeatur, sed ex benignissimâ DEI promissione concedatur. Tutissimum & fidei maximè analogum videtur, si per denarium intelligamus omnes DEI promissiones de corporali & terrena vel aeternâ bonorum operum retributione, 1. Tim. 4, 9. etenim 1. denarius datur murmurantibus. Atqui vita aeterna non contingit, nisi piis & humilibus. 2. Denarius datur ut merces ac praemium laborum. Atqui inter opera nostra & vitam aeternam nulla est proportio. Gregorius rectè docet, nullum murmur antem vitam aeternam accepisse, nullum enim, qui accipit, murmurare posse. Interim certum maneat, vitam aeternam esse donum DEI gratuitum, Rom. 6, ult. In mercede enim, ut notat Lutherus de servo arbitr. t. 3. Lat. pag. 199. spectatur vel dignitas vel sequela. *(Ursit hunc locum Iovinianus contra praemiorum in vitâ aeternâ beatis conferendorum diversitatem. Ast 1. Negatur, quòd per denarium h. l. directè ac praecisè intelligi vita aeterna possit, cùm etiam murmurantibus denarius obtiger it, item que illis, qui non sunt electi, ceu ex epiphonemate colligitur. Ut proinde rectiùs praemia in vineâ Domini laborantibus promissa, s. ea temporalia sint, sive aeterna, intelligantur. 2. si vel maximè per denarium h. l. significetur vita aeterna, distinguendum tamē inter ipsam beatitudinē essentialem s. vitam aeternam, quae omnibus beatis futura communis, ac inter beatitudinis gradus, inter praemia accidentalia, quorum fundamentum licet non quaerendum cum Pontificiis in meritorum nostrorū dignitate sit, sed in gratuitâ DE remun-ratione, ac divinâ benignitate, nil tamen impedit, quò minùs pro liberali DEI remuneratione eadem varient, ceu constat ex dictis Dan. 12, 3.1. Cor. 15, 42.Ioh. 14, 3. quo etiam referri

solet, 1. Cor. 9, 6. Pridem hoc observatum Augustino, qui lib de Virg. c. 26. Ipsa, scribit, vita aeterna pariter erit omnibus sanctis. Aequalis enim denarius omnibus est attributus, ac per hoc in denario quidem non impare vivet alius alio prolixiùs.
