In hac num Christi vicarius Pontifex Romanus sit, & annon potiùs apertè ei contrarius, facilè iudica bit, qui plusquàm regiam Praesulis Romani pompam & superbissima edicta consideraverit. Egregiè proinde P. R. convenit gravis invectio Chrysostomi, quam ex Chrysostomo hom. 40. in 1. Cor. ipse refert Corn. à Lapide h. l.)*

## 20:28
*(v. 28. Ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ αν᾽θρο που --κ ἦλθε διακονηθῆναι. The Vulgate does not translate sufficiently in Latin: The Son of man did not come to be ministered unto. Yet Philip of Caroli undertakes its defense: but with unhappy success, as Mr. Dilherrus beautifully shows in his Academic disputation vol. 1. p. 49. Compare also concerning the vices of the V. V. B. D. Walth. in Off. Bibl. page 319. Mr. D. Calovius Crit. Sacr. p. 567. seqq. Observe furthermore the twofold advent of Christ, of which the first into the flesh, made in humility, was medicinal, the other to judgment in glory, will be judicial. Since, however, Christ still comes to us through the word, let us receive Him by faith, so that we may be able to escape those things which are to be in the last advent, and to stand before the Son of man, Luc. 21, 36.)*

*( To minister. And thus to make satisfaction for the robbery of divine Majesty, committed by the first-formed, Gen. 3, 5. seqq. Christ therefore, as man in the state of humiliation, divested Himself of plenary dominion, having assumed the form of a servant, Phil. 2, 7. Isaiah 43, 22. 23. 24. Since therefore our Savior ministered not according to the divine, but according to the human at least nature assumed in time, and indeed in the state of humiliation, it is clear that R. Isaac Ben Abraham (alleged by Mr. D. Mueller in Judaism p. 974.) ineptly impugns the true Deity of Christ from the present saying, and likewise tries to prove from this that He was not the true Messiah, in that God does not minister, and all peoples ought to serve the true Messiah. For it must be known that Christ did not minister according to His divine nature, nor even in the state of exaltation. To which also the greatest regard is had in those sayings where it is treated of the dominion of the Messiah. As Ps. 72, 11.Dan. 7, 27.Ps. 11, 2.Eph. 1, 21, 22.Philipp. 2, 8.10. Let us indeed learn humility from Christ, Compare Matth. 11, 29.Ioh. 13, 14. seqq. Phil. 2. 3. seqq.)*

*( And he might give his soul. Conf. below c. 26, 38. Luc. 23, 46.Ioh. 10, 15.18.c. 12, 27. which passages are to be noted against the ancient heretics, the Arians, Manichaeans, Marcionites, Apollinarians, and among the more recent, Felgenhauer. Against whom orthodox theologians dispute throughout. See B. D. Mylius in A. C. p. 46. B. Par. Coll. Isag. p. 356. B. D. Hutt. in LL. Mai. p. 123.)*

*( Redemption. In Greek λύτρθον or the price of redemption. Conf. B. D. Glass. in Exeg. Ev. Dom pert. 1284. H. Grotius in this place (who rightly observes that this word was added εηξηιχως, so that incidentally the principal cause of the death of Christ might be explained. add. Gen. 3, 15.1. Ioh. 3, 8.1. Tim. 2, 6.1. Ioh. 2, 20) Therefore the dogma of the Photinians is false, that Christ is not our redeemer properly so called, or one who by satisfying and taking our punishments upon himself has liberated us. But someone may say: If the death of Christ is satisfactory and the price of redemption for us, it follows that we are not justified and saved freely, Rom. 3, 24, 25. c. 6, last. Resp. We are said in Holy Scripture to be justified and saved freely, not in respect to Christ, who redeemed us dearly, 1. Cor. 6, 20.1. Petr. 1, 19. but in respect to us. Because no merit of ours intervenes, on account of which we might be justified. Conf. Es. 52, 3.Rom. 11, 6. But the Photinians urge that the death of Christ cannot be called satisfactory, in that in satisfaction an equivalent price is required: now indeed in the passion and death of Christ no such thing is found, since they were only temporal passions; but we have deserved eternal punishments for our sins. Resp. Although the passions of Christ by reason of time they were finite, yet by reason of the value and dignity of the person suffering, as ρεανρωτου, they are infinite, that is, of infinite price. See B. Par. L. on Justif. §. 50. B. D. Graw. dissert. on the satisf. of Christ p. 40. 95. 95 120.)*

*( For many. From this the Calvinists attempt to prove that Christ did not shed his blood for all men, but only for those who believe in him. They do indeed add that he shed his blood for all as to sufficiency, but not as to efficiency. Thus David Paraeus distinguishes in Irenico p. 142. But 1. it is to be noted that that phrase as to sufficiency is ambiguous. For either by sufficiency is understood potential sufficiency, i.e., that Christ could indeed have shed his blood for all, and thus satisfy for the sins of all men, but by the absolute decree of GOD he did not will to; or actual sufficiency is understood, i.e., that Christ according to the counsel of GOD the Father actually shed his blood for the sins of all men. But that the reprobate are not made partakers of the saving fruit, stands by them. In the latter sense the Orthodox teach that Christ shed his blood for the sins of all men as to sufficiency, (as is evident from B. D. Chemnitius in H. E. l. 2. pag. 83. And in the same sense that distinction is also used by Lyranus in 1. John 1.) but in the former sense the Calvinists. As can be seen from Beza in Thes. Genev. fol. 123. Paraeus in Apol. Bibl. Neostad, fol. 97. likewise in Irenico l. c. Yet Beza himself l. c. acknowledges, ἀκυρολογίαν that there is in that phrase, as indeed it is used by the Calvinists, Christ died for all men sufficiently, since whether one looks at the counsel of GOD, or the effect of the passion, or in no way did he die for the impious. Whence also Piscator L. 9. vol. 1. th. 13. openly writes, that that distinction (in the Calvinist sense, that is) implies a contradiction, since Christ in no way died for the reprobate, whether sufficiently or efficiently. Disp. against Schassm. §. 110. Therefore it would be better for them and

the remaining Calvinists, if they would completely abandon that distinction, and not strive to cast a cataract over the eyes of the simpler ones with it. 2. So also in the phrase, As to efficiency, there is ambiguity. That the merit of Christ is not applied to all men, we teach is brought about by the own fault of men, who stubbornly reject the means of salvation, or by their unbelief; the Calvinists, and those among the Papists who follow in their footsteps, maintain that this happens from the absolute decree of GOD. 3. It is known that the word many is often used in Holy Scripture for all, because all are in reality many, as Euthymius rightly notes, and is evident from Dan. 12, 2. compared with Ioh. 5. 28. also Rom. 5, 15. collated with v. 19. also above v. 16. with Matth. 28, 19. That the word many is also to be taken in this way in this place and in similar places, such as Marc. 10, 45. below c. 26, 28. Marc. 14, 24. is evident from the collation of Es. 53, 6. and 12. Rom. 5, 18. c. 8, 32. 2. Cor. 5, 14. 15. 1. Tim. 2, 6. 1. Ioh. 2. 2. Let the Calvinists therefore give a reason why the universal proposition, that Christ suffered and died for all men, which is founded upon the passages just mentioned, should rather be restricted by the particular, than the particular be extended by the universal. 4. It must be known that because of the twofold respect of the merit of Christ, Holy Scripture speaks distinctly about it. For if it is considered in itself and without respect to application, it is universal; but if it is considered by reason of application, it is rendered particular, namely by the fault or vice of men, who reject it, as the Blessed Par. shows at greater length in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews p. 246. 247. And thus, namely as it is joined with saving application, St. Jerome receives the redemption of Christ in this place, writing in his Commentary on this place: He did not say, that he gave his soul as a redemption for all, but for many, i.e., for those who have willed to believe. Where note, that the Holy Father does not seek the cause of the particularity in an absolute and hidden decree of GOD or an absolute εύδοκίᾳ, of GOD, but in the own will of man, and thus teaches clearly enough that Christ did not give his soul as a redemption at least for those who have not willed to believe, that is, who have stubbornly and maliciously rejected the offered means of salvation. In the same way also Origen receives it in Homily 12 on Matthew. H. Grotius follows Jerome on this place, thinking that the word δοῦναι and the preposition ἀ-τὶ that it must be understood with effect, and thus it is a matter of those who are about to believe in Christ, who for that reason are called many in this place &Dan. 9, 27.so that it may be understood that not only Jews, but also foreigners pertain to that number. But there is no urgent cause present why τὸ πολλοὸ cannot and should not be taken universally. In which way it is also taken in this place by the Blessed Doctor Walther in Quadr. Misc. Theol. p. 93. the Blessed Doctor Sigwart in Adm. Christ. to -ren. Paraeus p. 312. and others.)*

Latin:

*(v. 28. Ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ αν᾽θρο που --κ ἦλθε διακονηθῆναι. Vulg. non satis Latinè vertit: Filius hominis non venit ministrari. Patrocinium tamen eius suscipit Philippus Caroli: sed infelici successu, uti pulcrè ostendit Dn. Dilherrus disp. Acad. t. 1. p. 49. Conf. etiam de vitiis V. V. B. D. Walth. in Off. Bibl. pag. 319. Dn. D. Calovius Crit. Sacr. p. 567. seqq. Obs. praeterea duplex Christi adventus, quorum primus in carnem, factus inhumilitate, fuit medicinalis, alter ad iudicium in gloriâ, erit iudicialis. Cùm verò adhuc veniat ad nos Christus per verbum, fide ipsum excipiamus, quò effugere possimus ea, quae futura sunt in novissimo adventu, & stare ante Filium hominis, Luc. 21, 36.)*

*( Ut ministraret. Atque ita satisfaceret pro raptu Maiestatis divinae, à protoplastis commisso, Gen. 3, 5. seqq. Exuit igitur se Christus homo in statu exinanitionis plenario dominio, servi formâ adsumtâ, Phil. 2, 7. Esaiae 43, 22. 23. 24. Cùm proinde Salvator noster non secundùm divinam, sed secundùm humanam saltem in tempore adsumtam naturam, & quidem in statu exinanitionis ministrarit, patet, quòd ineptè R. Isaac Ben Abraham (allegatus à Dn. D. Muellero Iudaismi p. 974.) è praesenti dicto veram Christi Deitatem impugnet, itemque evincere hinc conetur, quòd nō fuerit verus Messias, eò quòd Deus non ministret, ac vero Messiae omnes populi servire debeant. Etenim sciendum, quòd Christus secundùm divinam suam naturā non ministrarit, nec etiam in statu exaltationis. Ad quem etiam potissimùm respectus habetur in illis dictis, ubi de Messiae dominio agitur. Ceu Ps. 72, 11.Dan. 7, 27.Ps. 11, 2.Eph. 1, 21, 22.Philipp. 2, 8.10. Discamus verò à Christo humilitatem, Conf. Matth. 11, 29.Ioh. 13, 14. seqq. Phil. 2. 3. seqq.)*

*( Ac daret animam suam. Conf. infr. c. 26, 38. Luc. 23, 46.Ioh. 10, 15.18.c. 12, 27. quae loca notanda contra veteres haereticos Arianos, Manichaeos, Mareionitas, Apollinaristas, & ex recentioribus Felgenhawerum. Quos contra passim disputant Theologi orthodoxi. Vid. B. D. Mylium in A. C. p. 46. B. Par. Coll. Isag. p. 356. B. D. Hutt. in LL. Mai. p. 123.)*

*( Redemtionem. Graecè λύτρθον s. pretium redemtionis. Conf. B. D. Glass. in Exeg. Ev. Dom pert. 1284. H. Grotium h. l. (qui rectè observat, vocem hanc additam fuisse εηξηιχως, ut obiter explicaretur causapraecipua mortis Christi. add. Gen. 3, 15.1. Ioh. 3, 8.1. Tim. 2, 6.1. Ioh. 2, 20) Ergò falsum est dogma Photinianorum, quòd Christus non sit redemtor noster propriè sic dictus, seu qui satisfaciendo ac poenas nostras in se suscipiendo nos liberarit. Sed dicat aliquis: Si Christi mors est satisfactoria ac pretium redemtionis pro nobis, sequitur, quòd non gratis iustificemur & salvemur, Rom. 3, 24, 25. c. 6, ult. Resp. Dicimur in Sc. S. gratis iustificari & salvari, non respectu Christi, qui carè nos redemit, 1. Cor. 6, 20.1. Petr. 1, 19. sed respectunostri. Quia non intercedit ullum nostrum meritum, propter quod iustificemur. Conf. Es. 52, 3.Rom. 11, 6. Ast urgent Photiniani, Christi mortem non posse dici satisfactoriam, eò quòd in satisfactione requiratur pretium aequivalens: iam verò in Christi passione ac morte tale quid non inveniri, cùm tantùm fuerint passiones temporales; nos verò peccatis nostris aeternas poenas promeriti fuerimus. Resp. Etsi passiones Christi ratione temporis fuerint finitae, tamen ratione valoris & dignitatis personae patientis, utpote ρεανρωτου, sunt infinitae s. pretii infiniti. Vid. B. Par. L. de Iustif. §. 50. B. D. Graw. dissert. de satisf. Christi p. 40. 95. 95 120.)*

*( Pro multis. Conantur hinc Calviniani evincere, quòd Christus non pro omnibus hominibus sungvinem suum effuderit, sed tantùm pro iis, qui in ipsum credunt. Addunt quidem, quòd pro omnibus sanguinem suum effuderit quantum ad sufficientiam, non verò quantum ad efficientiam. Ita distingvit David Paraeus in-renico p. 142. Verùm 1. notandum, quòd phrasis illa quantum ad sufficientiam sit ambigua. Vel enim per sufficientiam intelligitur sufficient-potentialis h. e. quòd Christus potuerit quidem sanguinem suum effundere pro omnibus, adeoque satisfacere pro omnium hominū pe-catis, sed absoluto DEI decreto noluerit; vel intelligitur sufficientia actualis, h. e. quòd Christus iuxta consilium DEI Patris actu pro omnium hominum peccatis sanguinem suum effuderit. Quò minùs verò reprobi salutaris fructûs reddantur participes, per ipsos stare. Posteriorisensu Orthodoxi, Christum pro omnium hominum peccatis quantum ad sufficientiam effudisse sanguinem suum, docent, (ceu patetex B. D. Chemnitio in H. E. l. 2. pag. 83. Eodemque sensu adhibetur quoque distinctio illa à Lyrano in 1. Ioh. 1.) priori verò sensu Calviniani. Uti videre est ex Beza in Thes. Genev. fol. 123. Paraeo in Apol. Bibl. Neostad, fol. 97. item in Irenico l. c. Ipse tamen Beza l. c. agnoscit, ἀκυρολογίανesse in illa phrasi, prout nempe à Calvinianis adhibetur, Christus mortuus est pro omnibus hominibus sufficienter, cùm sive DEI consilium, sive passionis effectum, sive utrumspectris, nullo modo pro impiis sit mortuus. Unde etiam Piscator L. 9. vol. 1. th. 13. apertè scribit, quòd distinctio illa (in sensu puta Calviniano) sufficienter & efficienter contradictionem implicet, cùm Christus nullo modo pro reprobis sit mortuus, sive sufficienter sive efficienter. Disp. contra Schassm. §. 110. Satius proinde agerent &

reliqui Calviniani, fi distinctionem illam prorsus missam facerent, nec simplicioribus eâ ipsâ glaucoma obiicere satagerent. 2. Sic etiam in phrasi, quantum ad efficientiam, est ambiguitas. Quò minùs meritum Christi omnibus hominibus applicetur, nos propriâ hominum, salutis media protervè reiicientium culpâ sive incredulitate fieri docemus; Calviniani, & qui ex Pontificiis eorum vestigiis insistunt, ex absoluto DEI decreto id fieri statuunt 3. Notum est, quòd vox multorum saepè in Sc. S. ponatur pro omnibus, quia omnes reverà sunt multi, uti rectè notat Euthymius, & patet ex Dan. 12, 2. collato cum Ioh. 5. 28. it. Rom. 5, 15. coll. cum v. 19. it suprà v. 16. cum Matth. 28, 19. Quòd v. etiam h. l. ac locis similibus, uti Marc. 10, 45. infrà c. 26, 28.Marc. 14, 24. nomen multorum ita accipiatur, patet ex collatione Es. 53, 6. ac 12. Rom. 5, 18.c. 8, 32.2. Cor. 5, 14. 15.1. Tim. 2, 6.1. Ioh. 2. 2. Dent igitur Calviniani rationem, quare potiùs universalis propositio, quòd Christus pro omnibus hominibus sit passus ac mortuus, quae in allegatis modò dictis fundatur, per particularem sit restringenda, quàm particularis per universalem extendenda. 4. Sciendum, quòd propter duplicem meriti Christi respectum Scriptura S. distinctè de eo loquatur. Si enim in se ac citra applicationis respectum consideretur, universale illud est; si verò ratione applicationis, particulare illud redditur, culpâ nempe sive vitiohominum, illud reiicientium uti pluribus ostendit B. Par. Com. in Epist. ad Ebraeos p. 246. 247. Atq; ita, nempe prout cum salutari applicatione coniuncta est, Christi redemtionem h. l. accipit S. Hieronymus, Comment. h. l. Non dixit, scribens, animam suam redemtionem dare pro omnibus, sed pro multis i. e. pro his, qui credere voluerint. Ubi nota, quòd S. Pater causam particularitatis non quaerat in absoluto & abscondito quodam DEI decreto s. absolutâ DEI εύδοκίᾳ, sed in propriâ hominis voluntate, atque adeò satis clarè doceat, quòd Christus pro illis saltem animam suam non dederit redemtionem, qui credere noluerunt, h. e. qui oblata salutis media protervè & malitiosè reiecerunt. Eodem quoque modo accipit Origenes Hom. 12. in Matth. Hieronymum sequitur H. Grotius in h. l. putans, verbum δοῦναι & praepositio nem ἀ-τὶcum effectu intelligendam esse, adeoque agi de credituris in Christum, qui ideò vocentur multi h. l. &Dan. 9, 27.ut intelligatur, adeum numerum non Iudaeos tantùm, sed & alienigenas pertinere. Verùm nulla adest causa urgens, quare τὸ πολλοὸ non universaliter accipi possit ac debeat. Quo modo h. l. etiam accipitur à B D. Walthero in Quadr. Misc. Theol. p. 93. B. D. Sig warto Adm. Christ. ad -ren. Paraei p. 312. aliis.)*

## 20:29
*(v. 29. And as they were going out from Jericho. Jericho is a type of the world (as Binchius shows in many ways in Mellif. part. 2. page 269.) Therefore, just as the crowd, spiritually enlightened by Christ, went out from Jericho, so also let us, after we have received the light of the saving knowledge of GOD, go out from this world, abandoning the world with its pleasures; but on the contrary, let us adhere to Christ, and follow him uniquely and constantly. Jericho is otherwise explained as moon. The moon borrows light from the Sun. The blind men near Jericho were illuminated by Christ. We also, if we have approached Christ, will receive from him the true light of faith, and only then will we ascend with him to the heavenly Jerusalem.)*

Latin:

*(v. 29. Egredientibus autem illis à Iericho. Iericho est typus mundi (ceu multis ostendit Binchius Mellif. part. 2. pag. 269.) Quemadmodum igitur turba, à Christo spiritualiter illustrata exiit è Iericho, ita & nos, postquam lucem salutaris DEI cognitionis accepimus, exeamus ex hoc mundo, deserentes mundum cum voluptatibus suis; contrà verò Christo adhaereamus, eumque unicè ac constanter sequamur. Iericho aliàs luna exponitur. Luna à Sole foeneratur lucem. Coeci prope Iericho à Christo illuminati sunt. Nos quoque, si Christum accesserimus, veram fidei lucem ab eo accipiemus, ac tum demum cum ipso coelestem Hierosolymam adscendemus.)*

## 20:30
v. 30. Two blind men. But Luke says that Jesus healed one blind man before he came to Jericho. Mark says that he healed one while leaving Jericho. Theophylactus: γοῦν ματθαὶος παιλοσύντομος ὢν περιέλαβον ἐν ταῦτα τοὺς δύο. Others explain that these things were said by the figure συνεκδοχῆς. Matthew & Mark c. 10., 46. describe one and the same history, but Luke c. 18, 35. a different one, because those circumstances cannot be reconciled, because Luke says the blind man was healed before entering the city of Jericho, Matthew & Mark after leaving. *(The same is maintained by Saint Augustine, l. 2 de Consensu Evang. c. 65. & lib. 2. Q-. Evang. c. 48. Bb. Dd. Hunnius in this place, Lyserus in H. E. c. 136. Winckelmannus on Luke, Bakius part. 2. Enarr. Ev. page 25. Glass. in Ex. Ev. Dom. p. 386 Lord Doctor Friedlieb. Obs. in H. E. p. 126. Corn. also Iansenius & some others. Hugo Grotius however in this place judges that this healing happened entirely while Jesus was leaving the town. And he thinks it does not stand in the way that Luke says, ἐν τῷ ἐγγίζειν ἀυτὸν εἰς Ιερικφὼ, when έγγιζειν since it does not always signify movement to a place, but often only distance. The meaning therefore is, when he was not far from the town. Attale which is that of Luke c. 19, 29. *(But why does Matthew mention two, Mark only one? Resp. either because one, Bartimaeus, was better known than the other, just as Matthew has two demoniacs, whom Christ healed in the region of the Gerasenes, but Mark Chap. 5, 2. & Luke c. 8, 27. report only about one; or because, as Euthymius & others judge, those two blind men were different from that Bartimaeus, of whom Mark treats, for Christ also uses a different way of healing, in Matthew he touches their eyes, in Mark he heals with a word.)* Andreas Osiander in Harm. If we have diligently observed the propriety of the words, we will discover that not only Luke, but also Matthew describes a different History from Mark. For Bartimaeus was healed in the city of Jericho or at least at the gate of the city: but those other two were cured in the middle of the journey, sitting between Jericho & Bethany. He gathers this from the word ἐκπορευομεύου, that he heard the noise of one leaving the city, but Matthew has the word προάγειν. Zacharias Chrysopolitanus confuses all these blind men into one. Tossanus also thinks that one and the same history is described by the three Evangelists, he reconciles it therefore in this way, that Christ encountered these blind men, & that they began to cry out to him, when he was approaching Jericho: but that he did not immediately hear them, nor give place to their prayers, but wanted to test their faith & constancy, until they followed him & cried out again while he was leaving Jericho, where at last they were heard by him. *(Chrysostomus & Theophylactus, as recorded by Lord Doctor Walth. H. B. page 782 likewise acknowledge one and the same history, & feel that φιλοσ-ύτομον Matthew has encompassed both, both that one whom Luke describes; & that one whom Mark calls Bartimaeus as the more famous one, nor is there a dissonance in π-ρ-ςάσεσι. For the one had acclaimed Christ as he was approaching; the other, when he was leaving Jericho, had run up, & with a huge cry, with faith not feigned, both had requested & obtained help. And this opinion Lord Doctor Walther prefers to the opinion of Augustine, l. 2. de Consensu Evang. c. 65. & l. 2. Q-. Ev. c. 48. maintaining, that they are different histories, because otherwise the circumstances cannot be reconciled. Ambrose in c. 18. of Luke, & following him Dion. Carthusianus,

Franc. Lucas, Maldonatus, and Corn. à Lapide likewise maintain that it was one and the same blind man, who first at the entrance of the city asked to be enlightened by Christ, but when he was not heard by the crowd, and Christ pretended not to hear him, so that He might sharpen his faith and hope, he presented himself the next day at the gate of the city, and there again asked for and obtained sight from Christ as He was leaving. Let B. D. Glassius be consulted entirely regarding this whole history in the Disp. held under the presidency of B. Par., Disp. Elencht. p. 49. seqq.)*

(The blind.Mark 10:46. Concerning Bartimaeus, one of these blind men, it is reported that he begged. Therefore, both poverty and bodily blindness had made him unhappy. But he was made far most happy by faith in Christ, as through it he beheld the true light, which had come into the world, and obtained true riches.)

Latin:

v. 30. Duo coeci. At Lucas dicit, quòd Iesus unum coecum sanaverit, prius quam Hierichuntum veniret. Marcus ait, quòd unum sanaverit Hierichunte exiens. Theophylactus: γοῦν ματθαὶος παιλοσύντομος ὢν περιέλαβον ἐν ταῦτα τοὺς δύο. Alii explicant, haec esse dicta per figuram συνεκδοχῆς. Matthaeus & Marcus c. 10., 46. unam eandemque historiam describunt, sed Lucas c. 18, 35. diversam, quia circumstantiae illae non possunt conciliari, quòd Lucas dicit, ante ingressum in urbem Iericho coecum sanatum, Matthaeus & Marcus post egressum. *(Idem statuunt S. Augustinus, l. 2 de Consensu Evang. c. 65. & lib. 2. Q-. Evang. c. 48. Bb. Dd. Hunnius in h. l. Lyserus in H. E. c. 136. Winckelmannus in Lucam, Bakius part. 2. Enarr. Ev. pag. 25. Glass. in Ex. Ev. Dom. p. 386 Dn. D. Friedlieb. Obs. in H. E. p. 126. Corn. it. Iansenius & alii nonnulli. Hugo tamen Grotius in h. l. censet, omninò contigisse sanationem hanc Iesu exeunte ex oppido. Nec obstare putat, quòd Lucas dicit, ἐν τῷ ἐγγίζειν ἀυτὸν εἰς Ιερικφὼ,cùmέγγιζεινnon semper motum ad locum, sed saepè distantiam tantùm significet. Sensum igitur esse, cùm non procul ab oppido esset. Attale quoesse illud Lucae c. 19, 29. *(Cur autem Matthaeus duorum, Marcus unius tantùm meminit? Resp. vel quia unus Bartimaeus notior fuit alterô, sicut Matthaeus. habeduos daemoniacos, quos Christus in regione Gergesenorum sanarit, Marcus autem Cap. 5, 2. & Luc. c. 8, 27. tantùm de uno referunt; vel quia, ut Euthymius & alii censent, duo illi coeci diversi fuerunt ab illo Bartimaeo, de quo Marcus agit, nam & diverso sanādi modo Christus utitur, in Matthaeo tangit eorum oculos, in Marco sanat verbo.)* Andreas Osiander in Harm. Si verborum proprietatem diligenter observaverimus, deprehendemus, non Lucam solùm, sed etiam Matthaeum diversam à Marco describere Historiam. Nam Bartimaeus in urbe Iericho aut certè ad portam urbis sanatus fuit: illi autem duo alii in medio itinere, inter Iericho & Bethaniam considentes, curati fuere. Colligit hoc ex voce ἐκπορευομεύου, quòd audierit strepitum egredientis ex urbe, Matthaeus verò habet verbum προάγειν. Zacharias Chrysopolitanus hos coecos omnes in unum confundit. Tossanus quoque à tribus Evangelistis unam eandemque historiam describi existimat, conciliat igitur hoc modo, quòd Christus hos coecos offenderit, & quòd coeperint ad ipsum clamare, cùm ierichunti appropinquaret: sed quòd non statim illos exaudiverit, nec precibus ipsorum locum dederit, sed fidem & constantiam ipsorum probare voluerit, donec ipsum sequerentur & Ierichunte exeuntem denuò inclamarent, ubitandem ab ipso exauditi. *(Chrysostomus ac Theophylactus, memorante Dn. D. Walth. H. B. pag. 782 itidem unam eandemque agnoscunt historiam, ac φιλοσ-ύτομον Matthaeum utrumque complexum sentiunt, tum illum, quem Lucas describit; tum quem Marcus velut celebriorem Bartimaeum vocat, nec esse dissonan tiam in π-ρ-ςάσεσι. Alterum enim Christo appropinquanti acclamâsse; alterum, ubi exiret de Iericho, accurrisse, ingentiq; clamore, fide non fictâ, opem utrumque postulâsse & impetrâsse. Atque hanc sententiam Dn. D. Waltherus praefert opinioni Augustini, l. 2. de Consensu Evang. c. 65. & l. 2. Q-. Ev. c. 48. statuentis, diversas esse historias, quia aliàs circumstantiae conciliari nequeant. Ambrosius in c. 18. Lucae, & eum sequuti Dion. Carthusianus,

Franc. Lucas, Maldonatus, Corn. à Lapide itidem statuunt, unum eundemque fuisse coecum, qui priùs in ingressu urbis petierit à Christo illuminari, verùm cùm à turbâ non audiretur, & Christus audire se dissimularet, ut eius fidem & spem acueret, postridie se stiterit ad portam urbis, ibique à Christo egrediente rursus visum postularit & impetrarit. Conferatur omninò de totâ hâc historiâ B. D. Glassius in Disp. sub B. Par. praesidio habitâ, Disp. Elencht. p. 49. seqq.)*

*( Coeci.Marc. 10, 46. de Bartimaeo, altero horum coecorum, refertur, quòd mendicarit. Infelicem igitur eum fecerat tum paupertas, tum corporalis coecitas. Sed longè felicissimus factus fide in Christum, ut per quam veram lucem, quae in mundum venerat, adspexit, verasque divitias consecutus est.)*

## 20:31
(v. 31. But the crowd rebuked them etc. Perhaps the companions of Christ thought that they were begging for alms so importunately. Gregory the Great, homily 2 on the Gospels, mystically explains this thus: that the crowds of carnal desires and the tumults of vices, before Jesus comes to our heart, dissipate our thought with their temptations and disturb the voices of the heart in prayer. These crowds are to be overcome by the clamor of fervent prayer. Saint Augustine also beautifully advises on the same matter in sermon 18 on the words of the Lord, that bad Christians hinder the good, whose mockeries and taunts are to be overcome by contempt. For we must always think that the first virtue of a Christian is to despise and to be despised, as Saint Augustine holds. The crowds that hinder can also be mystically explained as doubt and diffidence, worldly cares, etc.)

Latin:

*(v. 31. Turba autem increpabat eos &c. Existimabant fortè Christi comites, quòd stipem illi adeo importunè peterent. Gregorius M. hom. 2. Evang. mysticè hoc ita exponit, quòd turbae desideriorum carnalium ac tumultus vitiorum priùs, quàm Iesus ad cor nostrum veniat, tentationibus suis cogitationem nostram dissipent, & voces cordis in oratione perturbent. Quae turbae fervidae orationis clamore superandae sint. Pulcrè quoque in eandem rem S. Augustinus de verbis Domini serm. 18. monet, quòd mali Christiani bonos prohibeant, quorum irrisiones & dicteria contemtu vincenda sint. Etenim semper nobis cogitandum, quòd prima Christiani virtus sit contemnere & contemni, ut habet S. Augustinus. Possunt quoque mysticè turbae impedientes, exponi de dubitatione ac diffidentiâ, curis mundanis &c.)*

## 20:32
(v. 32. What do you want etc. Jerome on this passage: He asks as if ignorant of what they want, so that from the answer of the blind men their manifest weakness may be revealed, and his power may be known from the remedy. Interlinear Gloss: He is not ignorant, but he wishes to hear the confession of him who knew their intention. Indeed, he even asked so that he might provide an opportunity for the blind men to profess their religious faith in Christ before the people, as the blessed D. Hunnius rightly advises on this passage. Conf. note to v. 21. Let us learn from the example of Christ to bring aid to the poor and miserable, since Christ values them so much that he wishes to consider what is done to them as done to himself. Conf. below c. 25 35. 36. 40.)

(v. 32. Lord, that our eyes may be opened. For what is blindness, if not constant sorrow and death. Conf. Tob. c. 5, 12. Indeed, what the sky is without the sun, that is man without sight, especially spiritual sight. Therefore, for the sake of restoring this in us, what is not undertaken in the Church? That we may also receive this, we ought to desire it alone, to pant for it alone, Ps. 27, 4.)

Latin:

*(v. 32. Quid vultis &c. Hieronymus in h. l. Interrogat quasi ignorans, quid velint, ut ex responsione coecorum manifesta debilitas pateat, & virtus ex remedio cognoscatur. Glossa Interlin. Non ignorat, sed vult audire confessionem, qui noverat intentione. Imò etiam quaesivit, ut ansam praeberet coecis, suam in Christum religiosam fidem coram populo profitendi, ut rectè monet B. D. Hunnius h. l. Conf. not. ad v. 21. Discamus Christi exemplo, pauperibus, ac miseris opem ferre, cùm Christus tanti eos faciat, ut quod eis factum, sibi factum reputare velit Conf. infrà c. 25 35. 36. 40.)*

*(v. 32. Domine, ut aperiantur oculi nostri. Quid enim coecitas, nisi adsiduus moeror ac mors. Conf. Tob. c. 5, 12. Imò quod Coelum sine Sole, id homo sine visu, maximè spirituali. Ad hunc proinde in nobis reparandum, quid non in Ecclesia suscipitur? Hunc etiam ut recipiamus, unicè desiderare, ad hunc unicè anhelare debemus, Ps. 27, 4.)*

## 20:34
(v. 34. And immediately they saw. To this place must also be referred others, to whom Christ restored sight. Concerning whom our c. 9 27. c. 12, 22. c. 21, 14. Marc. 8, 24.Ioh. 9, 7.)

( They followed him. Not so much with their feet, as with virtues, as St. Jerome wishes in this place. Nor could they have offered a more pleasing gift to Christ than themselves. Let us imitate the example of these men. Conf. Ps. 150, 15 it. Ps. 103. 107. &c.)

I. The solemn entry of Christ, carried on an ass into the city of Jerusalem, v. 1. -2. II. The casting out of those selling from the Temple, v. 12. -15. The healing of the blind and the lame in the same place, v. 14. The indignation of the priests at the children crying out, and the defense of that deed undertaken by Christ, v. 15. 16. III. The withering of the cursed fig tree, v. 19. And the instruction of the disciples concerning the efficacy of faith, v. 20. 21. 22. IV. The Savior's disputation with the Pharisees concerning his calling, v. 23-27. and the just rebuke of the stubbornness of the Jewish people, v. 28. to the end.

Latin:

*(v. 34. Et confestim viderunt. Huc referri debent & alii, quibus Christus visum restituit. De quibus noster c. 9 27. c. 12, 22. c. 21, 14. Marc. 8, 24.Ioh. 9, 7.)*

*( Siquuti sunt eum. Non tam pedibus, quàm virtutibus, ut vult S. Hieron. in h. l. Nec potuerunt etiam gratius Christo munus offerre, quàm seipsos. Imitemur horum exemplum. Conf. Ps. 150, 15 it. Ps. 103. 107. &c.)*

I. Christi asinâ vecti in urbem Hierosol. solennis ingressio v. 1. -2. II. Vendentium è Templo eiectio v. 12. -15. Coecorum ac claudorum ibid. sanatio v. 14. Sacerdotum in pueros acclamantes indignatio, susceptaque à Christo facti illius defensio, v. 15. 16. III. Ficûs maledictae arefactio, v. 19. Discipulorumque de fidei efficacia instructio v. 20. 21. 22. IV. Salvatoris cum Pharisaeis de vocatione suâ disputatio, v. 23-27. ac iusta contumaciae populi Iudaici reprehenfio, v. 28. ad finem.

## 21:1
*(v. 1. Ἦλθον i. e. ἐπορεύοντο, as Grotius rightly observes) For they had not yet arrived there, but according to Mark and Luke, they were very near. The Evangelist proposes for consideration in that solemn entry 1. the preparation of the disciples. 2. the mount of Christ. 3. the retinue of the people.)*

*( εἱς. Near. How it is also understood Mark 10, 46.Luke 18, 35. The Syrian uses in its place the prefix which can be explained by in, through and at, just as also which the Arab uses here. The Ethiopian uses the word which is used variously, indeed denoting near, to, towards, at, beside. It must be known, however, that Bethphage, Bethany, and Jerusalem were sufficiently near. A lengthy delineation of those places can be seen in Adrichomius in the Theater of the Holy Land, Bünting in the Itinerary, Heitmann in Palestine, and other Geographers.)*

Βηθφαγῇ. Tremellius explains it as the place of the fountain, so that the Syrian name derives from the Greek πηγῇ, and the place has its name from the fountain, which was there. For as a fountain is called πηγῇ by the Greeks, so the Syrians, Chaldeans, and Talmudists call it פיגי or פאגא. And hence Tremellius thinks the name Bethphage was compounded, as if to say. house or place of the spring.

CHAP. XXI. SUMMARY.

(The opinion of Tremellius seems best to Mr. D. Friedlieb. Observ. on this passage p. 165. for he himself thinks that there is an allusion to Judg. 15, 19. But John Buxtorf raises a scruple in Lex. Rabb. Talmud. p. 1691. noting that the Talmudists call a spring by the Greek word גיפי pigi, and not פאגי pagi.) The Talmudists make mention of this place, as the author of the book Aruch records. ( -is returned indeed to the same Talmudists, that place. חוץ לחומות outside the walls, that is, of the city of Jerusalem. See Pesach f. 63. 2. 91. 1. for as the Gloss to So af. 45. 1. has it, everything that is within the outer circuit of the city of Jerusalem is called Bethphage. Bartenora also notes, with Buxtorf citing him, that Maimonides writes that Bethphage was a place adjacent to the mount of the Temple on the outside, where they were accustomed to cook the evening food offerings. Santes Pagninus and Schindler in their Lexicons explain it as place of unripe figs. But Buxtorf objects to this explanation, because nothing is read among the Hebrews concerning unripe figs. John Drusius interprets it as house of slaughtering or immolation, because in some ancient Codices it had been read Βεθσφαγὴ. Pagninus in his booklet on the Interpretation of Proper Names, likewise Georg Pasor and several others consider it a decomposed word, so that it is from בית house, פה mouth, and גי valley and it may denote house of the mouth of the valley. The Londoners in their Explanation of proper names determine nothing certain, but bring forward various interpretations) Some explain it as house of the jaws. (Thus St. Jerome, Origen, Bede on this passage translate it. Chrysostom homily 11. on Mark. Bernard also seems to look to the same in his sermon to the knights of the temple v. 12. rendering it house of the cheek. But different reasons for this appellation are usually brought forward. John Buxtorf in the place cited, following Origen hom. 14. on Matthew, thinks this place was so called because it was that of the Priests, whose proper portion by law was the jaw. Origen also notes in the place cited that there was a spring around those places, which was called spring of the jaw, from which Samson had drunk, when he had thirsted. He alludes to Judg. 15, 19.) Others add, that Christ wished to prepare himself in that place for his royal entry, in which Samson had struck the Philistines with the jawbone of an ass. So that the place itself might admonish us of the spiritual battle and victory of this King, which he brought back from the infernal Philistines. (The fact that the people also points to the same) He carried palm branches, Ioh. 12, 13. it is certain, however, that the palm was a sign of victory among the ancients. See 1. Macc. 13. b. 2. ch. 10. Apocal. 7, 9. add B. Par Postill. Salom. Sunday 14. after Trinity. item Demsterus à Muresk in Paral. ad Rosin. b. 10. A. R. ch. 29. p. 1690. Cornelius à Lapide adds, that Christ for that reason wished to pass through the valley of Iosaphat in triumph, so that he might signify that in the same valley he would perform the tremendous judgment of all men on the day of judgment etc. But, although the Jews had already long ago -osaphat embraced this same opinion, namely, about celebrating the final judgment in the valley of -osaphat, there are nevertheless many reasons which persuade one to think otherwise. Those can be seen in B. D. Calixtus, in his separate treatise on the supreme Judgment p. 101. seqq. B. Par. L. on the Final Judgment §. 75.)

To the Mount of Olives. This mount is famous for the procession of Christ to the cross, Matth. 26, 30. & to the light, Actor. 1, 9. 12. that is, of His passion & ascension, Marc. 16, 19. According to Origen in this place, the Mount of Olives is the Church, in which the faithful who bear fruit can say: But I, as a fruitful olive tree in the house of GOD. Ps. 51, 10. Ambrose has similar things in lib. 9. in Lucam.)* *(

*( He sent two disciples. The author of the Imperfect Work, homily 73, says that these two disciples were Peter and Philip, who later were the first to evangelize to the Gentiles, Acts 8. and 10. Origen, homily 14 on Matthew, says that these disciples denoted Peter and Paul, because the Gospel of the uncircumcision was entrusted to Paul, just as that of the circumcision was to Peter, Gal. 2, 7. *(Chrysostom, Theophylact, Hilary, Ambrose, and Bede follow Origen. Cornelius Iansenius and another Cornelius, namely à Lapide, judge it more likely in this place that -os these two were Peter and John, inasmuch as Christ also sent them ahead to prepare the Paschal lamb. This same thing pleases our countryman Mr. D. Friedlieb in this place. Furthermore, it is asked here how our Evangelist is to be reconciled with John, when the latter writes, That Christ found a donkey, but ours, that Christ, having sent two disciples, that they might lead it? Resp. The word εὑρίσκειν, which John uses, does not only signify to find, but also to obtain something by one's own labor. Therefore, the Evangelist John wishes nothing else, than that Christ had obtained the donkey. Conf. Beza in Annot. Mai. ad Matth. 16, 25.

Latin:

*(v. 1. Ἦλθον i. e. ἐπορεύοντο, ut rectè observat Grotius) Neque enim iam pervenerant illuc, sed iuxta Marcum & Lucam, proximè aberant. Consideranda verò in solenni illo ingressu Evangelista proponit 1. discipulorum apparatum. 2. Christi equitatum. 3. populi comitatum.)*

*( εἱς.Propè. Quomodo etiam accipitur Marc. 10, 46.Lucae 18, 35. Syrus eius loco utitur praefixo quod per in, per & ad exponi potest, quemadmodum & quo Arabs hîc utitur. Aethiops utitur voce quae variè adhibetur, notans quippe propè, ad, versùs, apud, iuxta. Sciendum verò, quòd Bethphage, Betania & Ierusalem satis fuerint propinqua. Locorum verò istorum prolixa delineatio videri potest apud Adrichomium in Theatro terrae sanctae, Büntingum in Itinerario, Heitmannum in Pelaest. aliosque Geographos.)*

Βηθφαγῇ. Tremellus exponit locum fontis, ita ut nomen Syriacum ortum ducat ex Graeco πηγῇ, ac locus nomen habeat à fonte, qui ibi erat. Ut enim Graecis fons πηγῇ dicitur, ita Syri, Chaldaei & Talmudistae eum vocant פיגי vel פאגא. Atq; hinc Tremellius conflatum censet nomen Bethphage, q. d. domus vel locus fontis.

CAP. XXI. SUMMA.

*(Tremelli sententia optima videtur Dn. D. Friedlieb. Observ. in h. l. p. 165. existimat enim ipse, alludi ad Iudic. 15, 19. Sed scrupulum movet Ioh. Buxtorfius in Lex. Rabb. Talmud. p. 1691. annotans, quòd Talmudistae fontem voce Graecorum גיפיpigi, non verò פאגיpagi appellent.)* Talmudistae huius loci meminerunt, ut commmemorat autor libri Aruch. *( -reditur verò ii-dem Talmudistis, locus ille. חוץ לחומותextra muros, puta urbis Ierusalem. Vid. Pesach f. 63. 2. 91. 1. ut enim Glossa ad So af. 45. 1. habet, omne, quod est intra circuitum exteriorem urbis Ierusalem vocatur Bethphage. Notat quoque Bartenora, allegante Buxtorfio, Maimonidem scribere, Bethphage fuisse locum vicinum monti Templi extrinsecus, ubi soliti fuerint coquere oblationes vespertinas cibarias. Santes Pagninus ac Schindlerus in Lex. exponunt locum grossorum. Sed obiicit expositioni huic Buxtorfius, quòd de grossis nihil legatur apud Ebraeos. Iohannes Drusius interpretatur domum mactationis vel immolationis, eò quòd in antiquis nonnullis Codd. lectum fuerit Βεθσφαγὴ. Pagninus in libello Interp. Nom. propriorum, item Georg. Pasor & alii nonnulli pro voce decomposita habent, ut sit ex ביתdomus,פהos, &גיvallis notetque domum oris vallis. Londinenses in Expl. nominum propriorum nihil certi determinant, sed varias interpretationes adducunt)* Quidam exponunt domum maxillarum. *(Ita vertunt S. Hieronymus, Origenes, Beda in h. l. Chrysostomus homil. 11. in Marcum. Eodem quoque respicere Bernhardus serm. ad milites templi v. 12. Videtur, r-ddens domum buccae. Rationes verò appellationis huius afferri diversae solent. Ioannes Buxtorsius l. c. secutus Originem hom. 14. in Matth. locum hunc ideò sic dictum censet, quoniam illa fuerit Sacerdotum, quorum pars propria ex lege erat maxilla. Notat quoque Origenes l. c. fuisse circa illa loca fontem, qui dictus fuerit fons maxillae, de quo biberat Samson, cùm sitîsset. Alludit ad Iudic. 15, 19.)* Addunt alii, quòd Christus eo in loco sese praeparare ad ingressum regium voluerit, in quo Samson maxillâ asini percusserat Philistaeos. Ut ita locus ipse admoneat nos de spirituali pugna & victoriâ huius Regis, quam ex infernalibus Philistaeis retulit. *(Eodem quoque spectat. quòd populus ramos palmarum praetulit, Ioh. 12, 13. constat verò, quòd palma victoriae signum apud veteres fuerit. Vid. 1. Macc. 13. l. 2. cap. 10. Apocal. 7, 9. add. B. Par Postill. Salom. Domin. 14. post Trinit. item Demsterus à Muresk in Paral. ad Rosin. l. 10. A. R. c. 29. p. 1690. Cornelius à Lapide addit, Christum propterea triumphantem voluisse transire vallem Iosaphat, ut innueret, in eadem valle se in die iudicu peracturum tremendum omnium hominum iudicium &c. Verùm, licet iam olim eandem hanc sententiam, de celebrando nempe iudicio extremo in valle -osaphat, Iudaei fuerint amp-exi, multae tamen adsunt rationes, quae diversum suadent sentire. Videri illae possunt apud B. D. Calixtum tract. singul. de supremo Iudicio p. 101. seqq. B. Par. L. de Extr. Iudicio §. 75.)

*( Ad montem Oliveti. Celebris hic mons processione Christi ad crucem,Matth. 26, 30. & ad lucem,Actor. 1, 9.12. h. e. eiusdem passione & adscensio-e,Marc. 16, 19. Iuxta Origenem in h. l. mons Olivarum Ecclesia est, in quo fructificantes fideles dicere possunt: Ego autem sicut oliva fructificavi in domo DEI.Ps. 51, 10. Similia habet Ambros. lib. 9. in Lucam.)*

*( Misit duos discipulos. Autor Operis Imperf. homil. 73. dicit, hos duos discipulos fuisse Petrum & Philippum, qui postea primi gentibus evangelizarunt, Actor. 8. & 10. Origenes homil 14. in Matth. dicit, hos discipulos denotasse Petrum & Paulum, quia Paulo concreditum! Evangelium praeputii, sicut Petro circumcisionis, Gal. 2, 7. *(Origenem sequunitur Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Hilarius, Ambrosius, Beda. Cornelius Iansenius ac alter Cornelius puta à Lapide, in h. l. verisimilius esse censent. d-os hos fuisse Petrum & Iohannem, utpote quos etiam Christus praemisit ad parandum agnum Paschalem. Idem hoc arridet è nostratibus Dn. D. Friedlieb in h. l. Coeterùm quaeritur hîc, quomodo Evangelista noster conciliandus cum Iohanne sit, cùm hic scribat, Christum invenisse asellum, noster verò, quòd Christus, duos miseris discipulos, ut adducerent? Resp. verbum εὑρίσκειν, quo Iohannes utitur, non solùm significat invenire, sed etiam labore suo aliquid consequi. Nil igitur Evang. Iohannes vult aliud, quàm quòd Christus asinam consecutus fuerit. Conf. Beza in Annot. Mai. ad Matth. 16, 25.)*

## 21:2
(v. 2. εἰς τὴν κώμην into the village, for instance Bethany. Nicolaus de Lyra, Tostatus Bishop of Avila, Hugo the Cardinal, and certain others think it was a citadel, perhaps deceived by the Vulgate, which translates it castle. However, it is evident from 1. Sam. 6, 18. and 2. Chron. 13, 19. that there is a distinction between πόλιν and κώμην.)

You will find an ass. Cyril, book 8 on John, chapter 10: That he enters Jerusalem carried by an ass, it was done so that through this the learned might recognize him to be the very Christ, whom prophecy sent forth long ago had signified would come in such a way. Chrysostom, homily 67 on Matthew: Let the Jew be asked, which of the Kings entered Jerusalem carried by an ass? They will certainly be able to name no one except Christ. Nicephorus, book 1 of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 27: Sitting upon the foal of a beast of burden, he who is carried by the thrones of the Cherubim enters Jerusalem through the open gates. Just as an ass carries burdens and garments, so Christ carried the sins of the whole world upon his shoulders. *(At the letter S Jerome allegorizes in his Commentary on this place, as will be noted below at verse 5.)*

*( Alligatam. By this binding, the ancients, especially Origen in homily 14 on Matthew, Ambrose in book 9 on Luke, and Jerome in this place, think it is indicated that men are bound by the ropes of sins, which Christ came to loosen. Compare Matth. 11. 28.c. 16, 19.c. 28, 19.)*

*( πῶλον. Such a foal is understood, which might conveniently carry a rider. How also is employed by the LXX. Judg. 10, 4.ch. 12, 14.)*

Latin:

*(v. 2. εἰς τὴν κώμηνin vicum, puta Betaniam. Nicolaus de Lyra, Tostatus Episcopus Abulensis, Hugo Cardinalis & alii quidam arcem fuisse existimant, decepti fortè â Vulgato, qui castellum vertit. Constat autem ex 1. Sam. 6, 18. ac 2. Paral. 13, 19. quòd discrimen sit inter πόλιν & κώμην.)*

Invenietis asinam. Cyrillus l. 8. in Ioh. c. 10. Quòd asinâ vectus Hiero solymam ingreditur, factum est, ut per hoc eruditus quiscognosceret, ipsum esse Christum, quem sic venturum prophetia olim praemissa signarat. Chrysostomus homil. 67. in Matth. Interrogetur Iudaeus, quinam Regum asinâ vectus Hierosolymam intrarit? Neminem profectò praeter Christum dicere poterunt. Nicephorus lib. 1. Hist. Eccl. c. 27. Pullo subiugalis iumenti, qui thronis Cherubim vehitur, infidens patentibus portis Hierosolymam ingreditur. Quemadmodum asinus fert onera & vestes, sic Christus delicta totius mundi in humeris suis portavit. *(A liter S Hieronymus allegorizat Comm. in h. l. uti infrà ad vers. 5. monebitur.)*

*( Alligatam. Ligaturâ hâc veteres, cumprimis Origenes hom. 14. in Matth. Ambrosius l. 9. in Lucam, & Hieron. in h. l. indicari putant, quòd homines peccatorum funibus vincti sint, quos Christus venerit solvere. Conf. Matth. 11. 28.c. 16, 19.c. 28, 19.)*

*( πῶλον. Intelligitur talis pullus, qui sessorem commodè ferret. Quomodo etiam adhib-tur à LXX. Iud. 10, 4.c. 12, 14.)*

## 21:3
(v. 3. And if anyone &c. From the fact that Christ foreknew what the master of the donkey was going to say, and that he was going to release it immediately, it is evident that he himself sometimes exerted some rays of his divine majesty, communicated to the assumed flesh, in the state of humiliation. Conf. Matth. 26, 18.Marc. 14, 13.Ioh. 1, 48.c. 3, 13. See B. Par. Disp. Elencht. on the Lord's Gospels p. 672. following.)*

εὐθέως ἀποστελεῖ ἀυτοὸς. Others have translated this passage in different ways. The Vulgate rendered it: And if anyone shall say anything to you, say that the Lord has need of them, and immediately he will let them go. Luther in the same way. *(Similarly the Syrian and the Arab. But the Ethiopian most clearly: And if there shall be any who say to you, what is he doing? Say the Lord has need of them:& immediately they will send, namely the owners, them. The Persian: & immediately bring them hither.) *Erasmus: And immediately he sends them forth, namely Christ his disciples. For he reads with Theophylact ἀποστέλλει. Beza: The Lord has need of these: but immediately he will send them back, the colt and the ass. So that both may be referred to Christ, both that he has need, and that he is about to send back the beasts of burden. For a messenger was not only carrying the thing and the commands of another to others, but usually also the very words and speech of the one commanding. Therefore he enjoins two heads of excuse upon the disciples. 1. that the Lord has need of these. 2. that he is about to send back the beasts of burden immediately. *(This opinion is also embraced by Aretius in his Commentary and, of our own, B. D. Bakius in his Enarrations on the Gospels p. 17. But Dn. D. Friedlieb follows the reading of B. Luther , likewise B. D. Glassius in his Annotations on the Gospels on this place, 1st Sunday of Advent, page 65, and Mark c. 11. 6 favors it. Piscator yet otherwise: The Lord has need of them, but immediately he will send them, sc. the Lord of them. The Jesuit Conzen also follows this interpretation in this place p. 391.)*

*( Lord. ὁ κὺριοστ. Jehovah. Compare Luc 2, 11.Iohan. 13, 13.Act. 7,1. Cor. 2, 8.c. 8, 5 6.c 15, 47.1 to Timothy 6, 15.)*

Latin:

*(v. 3. Et siquis &c. Ex eo, quòd Christus praescivit, quid dominus asinae esset dicturus, quòdq; eam statim esset dimissurus, patet, quòd ipse radios aliquos divinae suae maiestatis, adsumtae carni communicata, in statu exinanitionis aliquando exeruerit. Conf. Matth. 26, 18.Marc. 14, 13.Ioh. 1, 48.c. 3, 13. Vid. B. Par. Disp. Elencht. super Evang. Dom. p. 672. seqq.)*

εὐθέως ἀποστελεῖ ἀυτοὸς. Locum hanc alii aliter verterunt. Vulgatus reddidit: Et si quis vobis aliquid dixerit, dicite, quòd Dominus his opus habet, & confestim dimittet eos. Eodem modo Lutherus. *(Similiter Syrus ac Arabs. Clarissimè verò Aethiops: Et si qui erunt, qui dixerint vobis, quid facit is? DiciteDominus e-rū opus habet iis:& statim mittent, nempe possessores, eos. Persa: & statim huc adducite.) *Erasmus: Et confestim emittit eos, discipulos nempe suos Christus. Legit enim cum Theophylacto ἀποστέλλει. Beza: Domino his opus est: statim autem remittet eos, pullum atq; asinam. Ut utrumque referatur ad Christum, tum quòd opus habeat, tum quòd remissurus sit iumenta. Nuncius enim non tantùm rem & mandata alterius ad alios perferebat, sed ferè etiam ipsa mandantis verba & orationem. Duo igitur excusationis capita discipulis iniungit. 1. quòd Domino his opus sit. 2. quod statim iumenta sit remissurus. *(Sententiam hanc amplectuntur quoque Aretius in Comm. & ex nostratibus B. D. Bakius in enarr. Evang. p. 17. Sed B. Lutheri -ectionem sequitur Dn. D. Friedlieb, item B. D. Glassius in Annot. Annot. Evang. ad h l. Domin. 1. Adv. pag. 65. ac favet Marcus c. 11. 6. Piscator adhuc aliter: Dominus eis opus habet, statim autem mittet eos, sc. Dominus illorum. Sequitur hanc interpretationem Iesuita quoque Conzen. in h. l. p. 391.)*

*( Dominus.ὁ κὺριοστ. Iehova. Confer. Luc 2, 11.Iohan. 13, 13.Act. 7,1. Cor. 2, 8.c. 8, 5 6.c 15, 47.1 ad Timoth 6, 15.)*

## 21:4
*(v. 4. Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled etc. Hence, Father, how ineptly the Jews twist the passage of Zechariah now to Ezra, now to Nehemiah, now to Mordecai, now to Zerubbabel, when it is certain that that prophecy ought to be accepted concerning Christ alone. Which is evident 1. from the expressly added denomination of King. Now indeed none of them was King. 2. from the description of the pomp. But none of them entered the city of Jerusalem in such a way. 3. from the mention made of poverty. But it is not recorded of any of them in Holy Scripture that he was reduced to poverty. 4. from the infallible interpretation of Matthew, the writer. θεοπνεὺςου, Here, however, it is to be well noted that the Evangelist, according to the custom received among the writers of the New Testament, did not look so much to the words of the Prophet as to the sense.)*

( διὰ τοῦ προφήτου. But not from one, but from two Prophets, namely from Isa. ch. 62, 11. andZech. 9, 9.the words which follow immediately are brought forward by the Evangelist. Resp. Although the former words, say to the daughter of Zion, are not of Zechariah, but of Isaiah: because however they are brought forward here at least for the sake of emphasis, it pleased the Evangelist to make mention of at least one Prophet, whose principal sentence it is, namely Zechariah. Thus in the Syriac and Persian version, Mark 1, 2. when the testimonies of two Prophets, namely Isa. 40, 3. and Mal. ch. 3, 1. are brought forward by the Evangelist, even in the Greek text it is said ἐν τοῖς προφήταις, it is restricted to Isaiah alone, inasmuch as the Evangelist seems to have looked there principally to the prophecy of Isaiah.)

Latin:

*(v. 4. Hoc autem totum factum est, ut impleretur &c. Pater hinc, quàm ineptè Iudaei locum Zachariae modò ad Esdram modò ad Nehemiam, modò ad Mardochaeū, modò ad Zerobabel torqueant, cùm certum sit, de solo Christo Prophetiam illamaccipi debere. Id quod patet 1. ex disertè adiecta Regis denominatione. Iam verò nullus illorum fuit Rex. 2. ex pompae descriptione. Aft nullus eorum ita urbem Hieros. ingressus est. 3. ex paupertatis factâ mentione. At de nullo illorum commemoratur in Sc. S. quòd ad paupertatem fuerit redactus. 4. ex infallibili Matthaei, scriptorisθεοπνεὺςου,interpretatione. Hîc verò probè notandum, quòd Evangelista more apud N. T. Scriptores recepto, non tàm ad verba Prophetae respexerit, quàm ad sensum.)*

*( διὰ τοῦ προφήτου.At non ex uno, sed ex duobus Prophetis, nempè ex Esa. c. 62, 11. acZach. 9, 9.verba quae mox sequuntur, ab Evangelista adducuntur. Resp. Licet priora verba, dicite filiae Sionis, non Zachariae, sed Esaiae sint: quia tamen saltem emphaseos causâ hîc addueuntur, unius saltem Prophetae, cuius praecipua sententia est, puta Zachariae, mentionem facere, Evangelistae placuit. Ita in versione Syriaca & Persica, Marc. 1, 2. cùm duorum Prophetarum, puta Esai. 40, 3. & Malach. c 3, 1. adducantur ab Evangelista testimonia, etiam in textu Graeco dicatur ἐν τοῖς προφήταις, ad solum Esaiam hoc restringitur utpotè cùm praecipuè ad Esaiae prophetiam Evangelista ibi respexisse videatur.)*

## 21:5
v. 5. Daughter of Zion is called by a Hebrew phrase the city of Jerusalem built upon Mount Zion. *(

Behold. Compare especially Zech. 9, 9; Isa. 7, 14; John 1, 29; Rev. 5, 5. )* *(

King. See Isa. 2, 6; Matt. 2, 2; John 11, 49; ch. 12, 15. Moreover, since our Savior is not only called *King*, but it is also added concerning him in Zechariah: *and his dominion shall be from sea even to sea*, Rabbi Solomon rightly infers from thence that this prophecy treats of the Messiah; and since he is furthermore named *poor*, his Kingdom must be understood spiritually, inasmuch as a temporal kingdom and poverty cannot exist together. )*

He comes to you etc. Chrysost. hom. 37. oper. imperf. If you have understood, he comes to you, i. e. that he may save you; if you have not understood, he will come against you, that he may destroy you. Calvin writes, that the words of the Prophet are Metaphorical, when he says, the King will come, riding upon an ass; and a figurative speech, by which the Prophet intimates, that Christ would be an obscure man, & -unc is the genuine sense.

And yet 1. by this reasoning Matthew would not have brought forward the genuine sense. 2. the remaining allegations also will be suspect, because we are uncertain, whether they brought forward the prophecies according to a proper or figurative sense. 3 the force of the demonstration against the Jews vanishes from this Prophetic text, 4. What need would there have been for the distinct mention of the foal and the ass. 5. a single epithet עני, could have satisfied the figurative sense. But for עני, which Zechariah ch. 9, 9 has, noting the poor, the afflicted, Matthew seems to have read in some places עני meek. But there is no need for us to correct the text of the prophet, for he who is poor and afflicted learns meekness from calamities, just as Dido says in the Poet: Not ignorant of evil, I learn to succor the wretched. The rich are for the most part haughty, the poor are meek. Christ was both poor and meek, therefore both are rightly predicated of him. Conf. Matt. 11, 29. What if עני and עני are often interchanged among the Hebrews, and thus עני also denotes meek, as the Chaldean interpreter Jonathan, whom Kimchi follows, also accepted in Zechariah. *(But it is asked, how can that poverty of Christ consist with his royal majesty ? Resp. One must distinguish 1. between a worldly kingdom, and a spiritual one. 2. between the κτ-ῖσιν- of all things and Χρῆσιν, i.e. between possession, and use; and thus the state of humiliation, and exaltation. See by all means B. D. Feurborn. syntagm. Theol. second Diss. 14. §. 37. seqq. where he also shows what riches Christ acquired for us by his poverty. Alphonsus Mendoza in controvers. Theolog. p. 677. from Jacob Almain, l. de potest. Eccl. c. 8 warns, that it is one thing to ask whether Christ was King, another whether he was Lord. But Christ is called not only King, but also Lord in this very place, see v. 3. But the poverty of Christ by no means supports the poverty of the Papists, as they call it. For although the action of Christ is our instruction, we read nowhere that he either commanded or even persuaded that one should have nothing of one's own. Whence also Bell. l. 4. de P. R. c. 14. §. thirty-fifth etc. writes: Nicholas defined that Christ taught meritorious poverty, consisting in the abdication of all things, with all dominion cast off, both in common and in particular. Pope John XXII judged this opinion to be openly heretical. Platina records concerning the same that he burned many of the order of the minors who had been condemned because they wished to imitate that religious poverty of Christ. Corn. also Jansenius in Comm. Ev. c. 29. There was, he writes, the error of Vadianus, who taught that ecclesiastics cannot possess any riches, because such was the life of Christ. Nor is there any reason for the Jesuits to object, that Christ was poor to the extent that he had the virtue of poverty, which one can have in the midst of riches, as Abraham, David etc. had. For Alphonsus Mendoza denies this l. c. and urges, that Christ is called poor absolutely, but that Abraham, David and others, who had poverty, cannot be truly called poor. But B. Par. discusses this controversy at greater length Confess. Cath. l. 2. Spec. part. 2. art. 7. In Zechariah just is added. But the Savior is just not only οὐιωδῶς, but also ἐνεργητικῶς, insofar as he imputes his own righteousness to us through faith, so that his poverty is pregnant with eternal riches, as B. D. Hunnius speaks. In the same prophet ch. 9, 9 is also added נושע i. e. saved. The Jews infer from this, that the Messiah is not true God. Resp. this epithet is attributed to Christ not according to his divine, but according to his assumed human nature. According to which he was saved from all miseries, and thus from death itself. Conf. Ps. 69, 2.Acts 2, 32.Rom. 4, 24.Heb. 5, 7. From which, however, it does not follow that he was not true God, since as the essence of all three persons of the H. Trinity is the same, so also is the power, whence he also saved himself, resurrected etc. Conf. Isa. 63, 5.John 2, 19.c. 10, 18. Christ the Savior came, that he might free us from the yoke of sins and infernal enemies, as King that he might defend, as meek that he might raise up, as poor that he might enrich, as despised that the mystery of redemption might be hidden from the Devil. Let us learn from him humility and meekness,Matt. 11, 29.*

Sitting upon an ass and a colt. That is, as some wish, upon a colt carrying an ass, ἑνδιαδύο. For that He was carried by the colt alone, some gather from the narrative of the remaining Evangelists Marc. c. 11, 7.Luc. c. 19, 35.Iohan. c. 12, 14. who make mention of the colt alone, likewise from that which Mark says, that no one had yet sat upon that colt. (This opinion pleases from the Fathers Jerome, Euthymius and others, from the Lutherans, Blessed Luther himself in Postill. Eccl. Blessed D. Calixtus H E. p. 28. and p. 354. Blessed D. Glassius in Not. Exeg. §. 1. p. 73. Lord D. Calovius in Crit. S. p. 595. Blessed D. Paul Tarnov. in Ioh. p. 870. & p. 871. Blessed D. John Tarnov. in Zach. p. 242. From the Papists Abulensis, Maldonatus in h. l. Franc. Lucas in Annot. p. 338. Iansenius in Concord. Ev. c. 110. Salmeron t. 6. l. 74. From the Calvinists Franc. Iunius, Beza, Bucer, Piscator, Tossanus, Hugo Grotius in h. l. Ludovicus de Dieu, others. And it relies on these reasons 1. because three Evangelists make no mention of the ass. 2. because it seems shameful for the Lord to sit upon an ass. 3. because it seems that it could scarcely have happened that in so short a space He sat upon different animals. 4. Because among the Hebrews there is not an infrequent repetition, by which the latter is exegetical of the former. Hugo Grotius to this, which in v. 7 is said ἐπάνω ἀυτῶν to have sat, he answers, ought to be explained as upon him, i. e. upon one of the beasts of burden, as the Syrian translates and the Latin interpreter how he received it. There are similar examples of this kind of expression: he was buried in the cities of Gilead, he went down into the sides of the ship. See Gen. 8, 4. Jud. 12, 7 Matt. 26, 1. c. 27, 44. But when Zechariah has explicitly prophesied concerning this entry of Christ thus c. 9. 9. Thy King comes, riding upon an ass and upon a colt, and the Apostles also received an express command to bring both, and they themselves also both- brought them, and our Evangelist uses plural pronouns three times notably, and with them embraces both animals more than manifestly, clearly saying indeed: that Christ himself testified that he had need of them, namely for riding, likewise: that the Apostles placed garments upon them, and furthermore: that the same made him ἐπάνω ἀυ--ν, sit upon them, namely the ass and the colt, the explanation of the Blessed D. Walther H. B. p. 783 pleases more, that Christ was carried upon both beasts of burden in that solemn entry, successively indeed, first indeed upon the ass, but afterwards upon the colt. Which opinion is embraced from the ancients by Augustine l. 2. de Consensu Evangel. c. 66. Chrysostom hom. 65. in Matth. likewise Theophyl. in h. l. Remigius, Bede, Strabus, Rabanus & others. From the Lutherans Bb. Dd. Osiander ad Zach. Hunnius in h. l. Franzius tract. de interpr. Sc. S. p. 1009 B. P. in Harm. Evang. p. 104.

Kirstenius in h. l. Meelfurerus in Vindic. Evang. super Dom. 1. Advent. From the Papists Albertus, Hugo, Lyra, Thomas Aquinas, Caietanus, Toletus, Cornel. à Lapide, Franc. Lucas in h. l. but especially the Jesuit Adamus Conzen in h. l. p. 389. seqq. likewise Sanctius in Zachariam p. 191. 192. That the Lord did this, however, the Blessed D. Walth. teaches l. c. 1. to fulfill the prophecy of the Prophet. 2. to inculcate both the humble mystery of his abjection, and the dominion of his infinite Majesty. 3. To designate his most ample empire. The same answers the reasons brought forward for the former opinion in the said place at length. Just as also B. Par. in H. E. l. c. we oppose the Arab to the Syrian interpreter, who explicitly And they placed their garments upon them, and he sat upon them. Although the Ethiopian translates the latter words absolutely The Lord Jesus was carried. yet he correctly explains the former words likewise: And they placed their garments upon them. Finally, the Persian most clearly expresses only the colt, and furthermore considers that not the garments of the Apostles, but his own were placed upon it. Thus rendering, And they brought the ass with the colt: i. e. but Jesus placed his garment upon the colt and sat. Furthermore, mystically by the ass, according to St. Jerome in this place, is understood the Jewish people, accustomed to carrying the burdens of Mosaic ceremonies; but by the colt, the multitude of the Gentiles, which would hereafter show itself obedient to Christ . B. D. Hunnius in this place, B. D. Calixtus in Conc. Ev. p. 290, and others treat these things at greater length. Furthermore from the fact that Christ, whom we venerate as our Savior, entered Jerusalem carried upon an ass, the Gentiles seized the opportunity to traduce Christians. See Tertullian in Apol. c. 16. But Claudius of Spain, against Jonas of Orleans, Bishop, from the fact that when Christ riding upon an ass touched this very thing, and yet is not on that account worshipped as an ass, concludes, that neither the cross of Christ nor any other wood, made in the shape of a cross, is to be worshipped. Finally, to the question, why Christ wished to be carried by an ass and a colt,

wished, he answers that this was done 1. for the fulfillment of Scripture, 2. for our instruction, so that we may learn humility from him.)* Some explain the name ὄνον as ass, and take the conjunction καὶ as ἐπεξηγητικῶς.. But because in v. 2 and 7 mention is made of the ass and the colt together, therefore also in this place mention is made of both.

υἱὸν ὑποζυγίου. Hebraism. See Exod. 29, 1.Gen. 49, 10.Zach. 9, 9.Levit. 14, 30.2. Chron 35, 7. v. 114, 14. *(In approximately the same way, profane Greek authors employ the word τέκνα, as Thomas Gataker shows at length in his work on the style of the New Testament, p. 166.)*

Latin:

v. 5. Filia Sion phrasi Hebraica dicitur civitas Hierosolymae super montem Sionem exstructa.

*( Ecce. Conf. cumprimis Zach. 9, 9.Esa. 7, 14Ioh. 1, 29.Apoc. 5, 5.)*

*( Rex. Vid. Es. 2, 6.Matth. 2, 2.Ioh. 11, 49,c. 12, 15. Caeterùm cùm Salvator noster non modò Rex appelletur, verùm etiam apud Zachariam de eo subiiciatur: & dominium eius à mari usq ad mare esse, rectè infert inde R. Salomon, de Messiâ vaticinium hoc agere, cumque ipse insuper pauper nominetur, Regnum eius spiritualiter intelligendum esse, siquidem regnum temporale & paupertas simul esse non possint.)*

Venit tibi &c. Chrysost. hom. 37. oper. imperf. Si intellexeris, venit tibi, i. e. ut salvet te; si nō intellexeris, veniet cōtrate, ut perdat te. Calvinus scribit, verba Prophetae esse Metaphorica, quando dicit, veniet Rex, equitās super asina; & sermonē figuratū, quo Propheta innuat, Christū fore hominem obscurū, & -unc esse genuinū sensum.

Atqui 1. hâc ratione Matthaeus non adduxisset genuinum sensum. 2. reliquae etiam allegationes erunt suspectae, quia incerti sumus, an secundùm proprium vel figuratum sensum vaticinia adduxerint. 3 evanescit vis demonstrationis contra Iudaeos exhoc textu Prophetico, 4. Quid opus fuisset muli & asinae distinctâ mentione. 5. unicum epitheton עני, figurato sensui potuisset satisfacere. Caeterum pro עני, quod Zacharias c. 9, 9. habet, notans pauperem, afflictum, Matthaeus quibusdam legisse videtur עניmansuetus. Sed non opus est, ut textum propheti-um corrigamus, qui enim pauper & afflictus est, ille ex calamitatibus mansuetudinem discit, sicut Dido apud Poëtā inquit: Non ignara mali miseris succurrere disco. Divites plerumque fastuosi, pauperes mansueti. Christus & pauper & mansuetus fuit, utrumq; igitur de ipso rectè praedicatur. Conf. Matth. 11, 29. Quid quòd עני & עני apud Ebraeos saepè permutentur, adeo-ue עניmansuetum etiam notet, quomodo etiam apud Zachariam accepit interpres Chaldaeus Ionathan, quem Kimchi sequitur. *(Quaeritur verò, quomodo paupertas illa Christi cumregiâ eius maiestate consisterpossit? Resp. Distingvendum 1. inter regnum mundanum, & spirituale. 2. inter rerum omnium κτ-ῖσιν- & Χρῆσιν, s. inter possessionem, & usum; adeoq; statum exinanitionis, & exaltationis. Vid. omninò B. D. Feurborn. syntagm. Theol. secundi Diss. 14. §. 37. seqq. ubi etiam ostendit, quas divitias Christus paupertate suâ nobis acquisiverit. Alphonsus Mendoza in controvers. Theolog. p. 677. ex Iacobo Almaino, l. de potest. Eccl. c. 8 monet, quòd aliud sit quaerere, an Christus fuerit Rex, aliud an fuerit Dominus. Verùm Christus non solùm Rex, sed etiam Dominus hoc ipso loco, vide v. 3. appellatur. Minimè verò Christi paupertas Pontificiorum paupertatis, quod vocant, voto patrocinatur. Licet enim Christi actio sit nostra institutio, nullibi tamen legimus, quòd vel praeceperit vel etiam suaserit, nihil proprii habere. Unde etiam Bell. l. 4. de P. R. c. 14. §. tricesimus quintus &c. scribit: Nicolaus definivit, Christum docuisse, meritoriam paupertatem, abiectô omni dominiô tàm in communi, quàm in particulari, in rerum omnium abdicatione consistere. Papa Iohannes XXII. hanc sententiam apertè haereticam esse iudicabat. Platina de eodem memorat, quòd multos de ordine minorum damnatos exurerit, quòd illam Christi religiosam paupertatem imitari voluerint. Corn. quoq; Iansenius in Comm. Ev. c. 29. Erat, scribit, Vadiani error, qui docuit, Ecclesiasticos non posse possidere ullas divitias, quia talis fuit vita Christi. Nec est, quod excipiant Iesuitae, Christum eatenus fuisse pauperem, quatenus virtutem paupertatis habebat, quam in mediis divitiis habere quis potest, ceu habuerunt Abraham, David &c Negat enim hoc Alphonsus Mendoza l. c. urgetque, quòd absolutè Christus pauper vocetur, at verò Abraham, David & alii, qui paupertatem habuerunt, verè pauperes dici nequeant. Sed de hâc controversiâ prolixiùs disputat B. Par. Confess. Cath. l. 2. Spec. part. 2. art. 7. Apud Zachariam additur iustus. Est verò Salva-or iustus non solùm οὐιωδῶς, sed etiam ἐνεργητικῶς, quatenus suam nobi iustiam per fidem imputat, ut ita eius paupertas sit aeterndivitiis gravida, ut loquitur B. D. Hunnius. Apud eundem rophetam c. 9, 9. additur quoque נושע i. e. salvatus. Inferunt hinc. Iudaei, quòd Messias non sit verus Deus. Resp. tribuitur hoc epitheton Christo non secundùm divinam, sed secundùm assumtam humanam naturam. Iuxta quam ex omnibus miseris, adeoq; ex ipsâ morte fuit salvatus. Conf. Psal. 69, 2.Act. 2, 32.Rom. 4, 24.Ebr. 5, 7. Ex quo tamen non sequitur, quòd non fuerit verus Deus, cùm ut eadem omnium trium S. S. Trinit. personarum essentia, ita & potentia sit, unde etiam se ipsum servavit, resuscitavit &c. Conf. Esa. 63, 5.Ioh. 2, 19.c. 10, 18. Venit Christus Salvator, ut à peccatorum iugo & infernalibus hostibus nos liberaret, Rex ut defenderet, mitis ut erigeret, pauper ut ditaret, contemtus ut redemtionis mysterium Diabolum lateret. Discamus ab ipso humilitatem & mansu-tudinem,Matth. 11, 29.)*

Insidens asinae & pullo. Id est, ut quidam volunt, pullo asinam portanti,ἑνδιαδύο. Quòd enim solo pullo vectus sit, colligunt nonnulli, ex narratione reliquorum Evangelistarum Marc. c. 11, 7.Luc. c. 19, 35.Iohan. c. 12, 14. qui solius pulli meminerunt, item ex eô, quod Marcus dicit, neminem adhuc superillum pullum sedisse. *(Arridet haec sententia ex Patribus Hieronymo, Euthymio aliisque, ex Lutheranis, B. Luthero ipsi in Postill. Eccl. B. D. Calixto H E. p. 28. ac p. 354. B. D. Glassio in Not. Exeg. §. 1. p. 73. Dn. D. Calovio in Crit. S. p. 595. B. D. Paulo Tarnov. in Ioh. p. 870. &p. 871. B. D. Ioh. Tarnov. in Zach. p. 242. Ex Pontificiis Abulensi, Maldonato in h. l. Franc. Lucae in Annot. p. 338. lansenio in Concord. Ev. c. 110. Salmeroni t. 6. l. 74. Ex Calvinianis Franc. Iunio, Bezae, Bucero, Piscatori, Tossano, Hugoni Grotio in h. l. Ludovico de Dieu, aliis. Nititurque his ration bus 1. quia tres Evangelista asinae nullam faciunt mentionem. 2. quia turpe videtur, Dominum insidere asinae. 3. quia vix fierpotuisse videtur ut in tàm brevi spatio diversis insiderit animalibus. 4. Quia apud Ebraeos non infrequentalis repetitio, quâ posterius exegeticum prioris. Hugo Grotius ad hoc, quod v. 7. dicitur ἐπάνω ἀυτῶνsedisse, respondet, exponi debere super eum, i. e super alterum ex iumentis, guomodo Syrus vertat ac Latinus interpres quoacceperit. Essesimilia huius modi locutionis exempla: sepultus est in urbibus Galaad, descendit in latera navis. Vid.Gen. 8, 4.Iud. 12, 7Matth. 26, 1.c. 27, 44. Ast cùm disertè Zacharias de hoc Christi ingressu ita vaticinatu fuerit c. 9. 9. Venit Rextuus, equitans super asina & super pullo, Apostoli quoque expressum mandatum acceperint, utrumque adducendi, ipsi quoque utrum- adduxerint, ac noster Evangelista numeri pluralis pronominibus ter notanter utatur, iisque utrumque animal plus quàm manifestè complectatur, clarè quippe dicens: Christum ipsum testatum, eis sibiopus esse, nimirùm ad equitandum, item: Apostolos super ea posuisse vestimenta, quin etiam: eosdem fecisse illumἐπάνω ἀυ--ν,super ea, nempè asinam & pullum, sedere, magis B. D. Walthero H. B. p. 783. placet explicatio, quòd Christus super utroque iumento in solenni illo ingressu vectus sit, successivè nempè, priùs quidem super asinâ, posteà verò super pullo. Quam sententiam amplectuntur è veteribus Augustinus l. 2. de Consensu Evangel. c. 66. Chrysostomus hom. 65. in Matth. item Theophyl. in h. l. Remigius, Beda, Strabus, Rabanus & alii. E Lutheranis Bb. Dd. Osiander ad Zach. Hunnius in h. l. Franzius tract. de interpr. Sc. S. p. 1009 B. P. in Harm. Evang. p. 104.

Kirstenius in h. l. Meelfurerus in Vindic. Evang. super Dom. 1. Advent. E P ontificiis Albertus, Hugo, Lyra, Thomas Aquinas, Caietanus, Toletus, Cornel. à Lapide, Franc. Lucas in h l. cumprimis verò Iesuita Adamus Conzen in h. l. p. 389. seqq. item Sanctius in Zachariam p. 191. 192. Fecisse autem hoc Dominum, docet B. D. Walth. l. c. 1. ad implendum Prophetae vaticinium. 2. ad inculcandum tum humile abiectionis suae mysterium, tum infinitae Maiestatis dominium. 3. Ad designandum amplissimum suum imperium. Ad rationes pro priori sententia allatas responder idem dicto loco prolixè. Quemadmodum etiam B. Par. in H. E. l. c. Syro interpreti opponimus Arabem, qui disertè & posuerunt vestimenta sua super eos, & sedit super eos. Aethiops licet posteriora verba absolutè vertat Vectus est Dominus Iesus. priora tn. verba itidē rectè exponit: & imposuerunt vestimenta sua super eis. Persa denique clarissimè solum pullum exprimit, & insuper non Apostolorum, sed ipsius vestimenta illi imposita censet. Ita reddens, & asinam cum pullo adduxerunt: i. e. vestimentum autem suum Iesus pullo imposuit & insedit. Coeterùm mysticè per asinam, iuxta S. Hieronymum in h. l. intelligitur populus Iudaicus, oneribus Mosaicarum ceremoniarum portandis adsuerus; per pullum verò gentium multitudo, quae se posthac Christo obsequen-em praebitura sit. Prolixiùs haec pertractant B. D. Hunnius in h. l. B. D. Calixtus Conc. Ev. p. 290. alii. Porrò ex--, quòd Christus, quem ut Salvatorem nostrum veneramur, as no vectus Hierosolymam ingressus fuit Gentiles occasionem arripuerunt, Christianos traducendi. Vid. Tertul-ianus in Apol. c. 16. Claudius verò Hispan. adv. Ionam Aurelianens. Epic. ex eo, quòd cùm Christus equitans super afinâ hanc ipsam attigerit, nec tamen proptere à asina adoretur, colligit, nec crucem Christi vel aliud lignum, schemate crucis factum, adorandum esse. Denique ad quaestionem, cur Christus asinâ ac pullo vol-

voluerit, resp. factum hoc esse 1. ad Sc. impletionem, 2. ad nostri informationem, ut diseamus nempe ab eo humilitatem.)* Quidam nomen ὄνον exponunt asinum, & coniunctionem καὶ accipiunt ἐπεξηγητικῶς. Sed quia v. 2. ac 7. asinae & pulli simul mentio fit, ideò etiam h. l utriusque mentionem fieri.

υἱὸν ὑποζυγίου. Ebraismus. Vid. Exod. 29, 1.Gen. 49, 10.Zach. 9, 9.Levit. 14, 30.2. Chron 35, 7. v. 114, 14. *(Eodem circiter modo adhibent vocem τέκνα Graeci autores profani, uti multis ostendit Thom Gatakerus de stylo N. T p 166.)*

## 21:6
(v. 6. Going, disciples. The disciples of Christ provide an example for us, that we ought not to examine the commands, ordinances, etc., of God by the standard of our own reason , but rather to take captive our reason under the obedience of faith. Compare John 2, 5.7. Furthermore, from the fact that the Lord immediately released the beasts of the ass and the colt, Chrysostom gathers the divine power of Christ. For it is evident from this, that the Lord had the mind of the owner of those beasts in his hand, and directed it to where he wished. Compare Prov. 21, 1.)

Latin:

*(v. 6. Euntes discipuli. Exemplum nobis praebent discipuli Christi, quòd mandata, ordinationes &c. Dei non examinare ad rationis nostrae amussim debeamu-, sed captivare potiùs rationem nostram sub obsequium fidei. Confer Ioh. 2, 5.7. Porro ex eo, quòd Dominus asinae ac pulli statim dimiserit iumenta, divinam Christi potentiam Chrysostomus colligit. Patet enim hinc, quòd Dominus animum possessoris iumentorum illorum in manu sua habuerit, eoque quò voluit, direxerit. Conf. Prov. 21, 1.)*

## 21:7
v. 7. They brought the she-ass and the colt. *(Let the promptness of the disciples be observed here. They bring the she-ass with the colt, they adorn the brought animal with garments, they place the Lord upon the adorned one.)* The colt of an ass is called υἱὸς ὑποζυγίου, i.e. the offspring of a yoked she-ass, in the Hebrew phrase. In Zechariah it is read the son of she-asses, by Synecdoche, from the fact that two she-asses are accustomed to be coupled under one yoke. Ὄνον most interpret as a she-ass. Vatablus and others interpret ἀρσενικῶς as an ass, and understand the remaining words exegetically, not copulatively. For the Hebrew חמור, which Zechariah uses, perhaps once signifies a she-ass in the sacred code, otherwise always an ass. Athon is a she-ass. They add that when ὄνος signifies a she-ass, either an article or some adjective of the feminine gender is always added; since that is not done in this place, the very absence of the article proves that by ὄνον an ass is signified. Aben Ezra on the passage Exod. 4, 20. notes: The Septuagint in the place of an ass substituted ὑποζύγιον a yoked beast of burden, because it was contemptible and indecorous for the wife of the Prophet to be carried on an ass with two sons. But others show by examples that among the Israelite people that was not contemptible.

Num. 22, 22. When Balaam was about to set out, his donkey was saddled, and for Abraham, Gen. 22, 3. his donkey. Abigail, a wealthy woman, is carried on a donkey, 2 Sam. 25, 20. and the family of the King, 2 Sam. 16, 2. and the man of God, 1 Kings 13, 13.. The sons of Jair also rode upon donkey colts. Judg. 10, 4. where R. David Kimchi is to be consulted. Since, therefore, it was in use among the Jews that even nobles and the wealthy were carried on donkeys, see besides the passages just cited Gen. 27, 3. Judg. ch. 12, 14. how is it brought forward as a peculiar sign of the Messiah, that he would enter the city of Jerusalem riding on a donkey? Answer: From the time of Solomon, through trade with Egypt and other foreign peoples, the supply of horses increased among the Jews, and the use of donkeys became cheap. Furthermore, it must be observed that the Prophet speaks notably of a donkey under the yoke, that is, one that was not kept for making a journey, but whose use was for carrying burdens.
