Just as the poor are accustomed to be carried on the same beast of burden with which they plow their fields. Added to this, moreover, is the consideration of the retinue and the devout acclamation. It is also well to note that the Author of Bereshith Rabba and Midrash Koheleth interpret the passage of Zechariah concerning the Messiah. Since, therefore, Christ entered the city in that manner, just as Zechariah predicted, the Jews of today wait in vain for another Messiah. Compare entirely B. D. Hutter in LL. Mai. p. 844. seqq. B. Par. Dispp. Elencht. p. 687. B. D. Helvicus in Vindiciis locorum v. 7. Mr. B. Mueller in Judaism, Mr. Havemann in Hodego Jud. from the Calvinists D. Hornbeck, in תשובח יהוךה and others. Furthermore, to the objection that Christ entered the city of Jerusalem as a poor man, but the Roman Pontiff, who nevertheless desires to be called the vicar of Christ, uses more than royal pomp when he makes a journey, the Jesuit Adam Conzen replies, that this is done so that the status befitting the Roman Pontiff may be observed. He adds candidly, however, that there is no doubt for him that if Pontiffs and Bishops spend the treasures of the Church on unnecessary and useless expenses beyond their status, they are guilty of a most grave crime. For some examples, he continues, have taught us that many of the ecclesiastics, while they attempt to fill their relatives with sacred wealth, have oppressed them, so that families have either been reduced to poverty or extinguished by miserable events. Let the current Pontiff Alexander VII hear this warning and recall it to his mind, and perhaps less

he will hear the complaints from the Roman people, who do not hesitate to attribute the five years of Nero to him. Furthermore, how great a discrepancy, or rather, repugnance, there is between Christ and the Roman Pope, the blessed Pareus teaches at length in his Expos. Elencht. Ev. Dom. p. 681. 682.

Ἐπάνω ἀυτῶν, to the other of those animals, namely, the foal of an ass, as some wish, whom Mark also seems to favor. The Old Interpreter reads ἐπεκάθισαν ἐπάνω ἐυτὸν, and they made them sit upon them. Which reading Casaubon approves, because it is also said in Luke: καὶ ἐ-πιῤῥί ψαντες ἑαυτῶν τὰ ἱματια ἐ-πὶ τὸν πῦλον ἐπεββιβασαν τὸν Ινσοῶν. See Meelfuer. Vindic. Domin. I. Advent. th. 32. Theophylact explains it thus, ἐπ άνω ἀυτῶν, namely των ἱίυατίων. Or first he sat upon the ass, and then also upon the foal. ἐ-πὶ καὶ πρῶτον ἐπ--νεπάυσατο τῆ τῶν Ιουδαίοφν συναγωγῇ, εἶτα τῷ ἐξ ἐθνῶν λαῷ. *(Jerome and Nic. de Lyra also embrace this mystical exposition in this place; likewise Chrysost. hom. 36. and ie-uita Conz-n declares it at length in this place. But that it should be taken literally concerning the ass and the foal, or that the Savior sat upon both—which the same Jerome (whom very many also follow, so as to maintain that Christ sat upon at least one beast of burden, namely the foal, as among our own B. Luther himself, likewise the learned doctors Glassius, Calixtus, etc., and among the Papists -ansenius, Salmeron, and others, think, as was indicated above) or that it involves an impossibility or indecency. But others deny this in turn, and maintain that our Savior sat upon both animals, namely the ass and the foal, though successively. In this opinion are the learned doctors Bakius in Enarr. Evang. p. 24. 25. Dan. Cramerus in Schola Prophetica class. 4. Vatic. 3. Wolffg. Frantzius de Interpr. Sc. S. p. 1007. B. Par. Harm. Evang. p. 105. Among the Papists, the Jesuit Adamus Conzen embraces the same opinion in his Comm. in this place. Bernard explains this mystically in serm. 7. in Psalm. Qui habitat f. 69., writing: Glorify, most beloved, and carry Christ in the internal body, a delightful burden: a sweet weight, a saving load: even if it happens to seem to press at times.)*

Latin:

v. 7. Adduxerunt as-nam & pullum. *(Observetur hîc discipulorum promtitudo. Asinam cum pullo adducunt, adductam vestibus ornant, ornatae Dominum imponunt.)* Pullus asini dicitur υἱὸς ὑποζυγίου, i. e. proles asinae subiugis, phrasi Hebraicâ. Apud Zachariam legitur filius asinarum, per Synecdochen, ex eo, quod duae asinae sub uno iugo copulari solent. Ὄνον plerique interpretantur asinam. Vatablus & alii ἀρσενικῶς interpretantur asinum, & reliqua verba exegeticè, non copulativè intelligunt. Nam Hebraeum חמור, quô Zacharias utitur, semel fortassis asinam significat in sacro codice, aliàs semper asinum. Athon est asina. Addunt, quòd cùm ὄνοςasinam significat, semper vel articulus vel adie ctivum aliquod foeminini generis adiiciatur, id cùm h. l. non fiat, ipsa articuli absentia evincat, per ὄνονasinum significari. Aben Ezra ad locum Exod. 4, 20. annotat. Septuaginta in locū asini reposuisseὑποζύγιονiumentum subiuge, quod contemtibile & indecorum erat, uxorem Prophetae cum duobus filiis asinâ vehi. Sed exemplis ostendunt alii, in populo israëlitico illud non fuisse contemtibile.

Num. 22, 22. Balaamo profecturo sternitur asina, & Abrahamo, Genes. 22, 3. asinus. Abigail opulenta mulier, asino vehitur, 2. Sam 25, 20. & familia Regis, 2. Sam. 16, 2. & vir Dei, 1. Reg. 13, 13. Filii quoque Iair equitârunt super asellos. Iud. 10, 4. ubi videndus R. David Kimchi. *(Cùm igitur apud Iudaeos in usu fuerit, ut proceres quoque & divites asinis veherentur, vid praeter loca modò adducta Genes. 27, 3.Iudic. cap. 12, 14.quomodo tanquam peculiare Messiae signum adducitur, quod asinvectus urbem Hierosolymam ingressurus sit? Resp. Ex quo Salomonis tempore per commercia cum Aegytiialiisque exteris pupulis equorum copia apud Iudaeos crevit, asinorum usus eviluit. Praeterea observandum, quòd Propheta notanter loquatur de asina subiugali, h. e. quae non alebatur ad-iter faciendum, sed cuius usus erat ad onera gestanda. Ceu pauperes eôdem iumentô, quô agros suos arant, vehi solent. Accedit praetereà comitatûs consideratio & devota acclamatio. Probè quoque notandum est, quòd Autor Bereschith Rabba ac Midras Koheleth locum Zachariae de Messia accipiant. Cùm igitur Christus eo modo, ceu Za harias praedixit, urbem ingressus sit, frustrà alium Messiam hodierni Iudaei expectant. Conf. omninò B. D Hutter. in LL. Mai. p. 844. seqq. B. Par. Dispp. Elencht. p. 687. B. D. Helvicus in Vindiciis locorum v. 7. Dn. B. Muellerus in Iudaismo, Dn. Havemannus in Hodego Iud. ex Calvinianis D. Hornbeck, in תשובח יהוךה alii. Porrò ad obiectionem, quòd Christus pauper ingressus urbem Hierosol. fuerit, Pontifex verò Romanus, qui Christi tamen vicarius audire gestit, plusquàm regiâ pompâ utatur, cùm iter facit, respondet Iesuita Adamus Conzen, id fieri, ut status Pontifici Romano conveniens observetur. Candidè tamen addit, sibi dubium non esse, Pontifices & Episcopos, si praeter statum in sumtus non necessarios atq inutiles, Ecclesiae thesauros impendant, gravissimi sceleris esse reos. Quaedam enim, pergit, exempla nos docuerunt, multos Ecclesiasticorum, cognatos suos, dum opibus sacris implere conantur, oppressisse, ut familiae aut ad paupertatem redactae fuerint, aut miseris eventibus extinctae. Audiat hoc monitum hodiernus Pontifex Alexander VII. illudque in animum revocet, ac fortè minus

audiet querelarum à popu-o Romano, qui quinquennium Neronis tribuere illi non dubitant. Quanta porrò inter Christum & Papam Rom. discrepantia imò & repugnantia sit, prolixè docet B. Par. Expos. Elencht. Ev. Dom. p. 681. 682.)*

Ἐπάνω ἀυτῶν, alteri nempe eorum animalium, scil. pullo asinae, ut quidam volunt, quibus & Marcus favere videtur. Vetus Interpres legit ἐπεκάθισαν ἐπάνω ἐυτὸν, & cum desuper sedere fecerunt. Quam lectionem probat Casaubon., quia etiam apud Lucam dicitur: καὶ ἐ-πιῤῥί ψαντες ἑαυτῶν τὰ ἱματια ἐ-πὶ τὸν πῦλον ἐπεββιβασαν τὸν Ινσοῶν. Vid. Meelfuer. Vindic. Domin. I. Advent. th. 32. Theophylactus sic explicat, ἐπ άνω ἀυτῶν, nempe των ἱίυατίων. Vel primùm asinae insedit, de inde etiam pullo. ἐ-πὶ καὶ πρῶτον ἐπ--νεπάυσατο τῆ τῶν Ιουδαίοφν συναγωγῇ, εἶτα τῷ ἐξ ἐθνῶν λαῷ. *(Mysticam hanc expositionem amplectuntur quoque Hieronymus & Nic. de Lyra h. l. it. Chrysost. hom. 36. & prolixè declarat ie-uita Conz-n in h. l Ut verò secundùm litteram accipiatur de asinâ & pullo, sive quòd utriquè Salvator insedericyidem Hieronymus, (quem plurimi etiam eat. sequuntur, ut statuant, quòd uno saltem iumento, sc. pullo Christus insed-rit, ceu ex nostratibus B. Lutherus ipse, item BB. DD. Glassius, Calixtus &c. ex Pontificiis -ansenius, Salmeron, alii. ita sentiunt, prout suprà indicatum.) vel impossibilitatem, vel turpitudinem habere existimant. Sed negant vicissim alii, & utrique animali, asinae nempe & pullo, successivè tamen, Salvatorem nostrum omninò insedisse, statuunt. In quâ sententiâ sunt Bb. Dd. Bakius in Enarr. Evang. p. 24. 25. Dan. Cramerus in Schola Proplietica class. 4. Vatic. 3. Wolffg. Frantzius de Interpr. Sc. S. p. 1007. B. Par. Harm. Evang. p. 105. Ex Pontificiis eandem amplectitur sententiam Iesuita Adamus Conzen Comm. h l. Mysticè hoc exponit Bernhardus serm. 7. in Psalm. Qui habitat f. 69. scribens: Glorificate, dilectissimi, & portate Christum in corpore interno, onus delectabile: suave pondus, sarcinam salutarem: et amsi premere aliquando fortè videtur.)*

## 21:8
*(v. 8. -ςρωσαν ἀυτῶν τὰ ἱμάτια. Hugo Grotius confirms in this place that this custom was accepted among the ancients with the testimonies of Aeschylus in Agamemnon and Plutarch in Cato. Especially also the history of Jehu seems to pertain to this, 2. Kings 9, 13. Furthermore, we can still spread garments before our Savior today, when we promote his spiritual entry, taking pains that the Ministry of the word is honestly sustained, the poor are relieved, etc. Cf. Matt. 25, 35. 36. Beda writes a little differently concerning Palm Sunday: Who, he writes, spreads his garments on the road, who humbles the members of his body in the present, so that God may exalt them in the future, mindful of that Davidic saying: Because the humbled bones shall exult, Ps. 51, 10. Greg. hom. 24. What are all earthly things, if not certain garments of the body? Distribute earthly goods to the poor: to cut branches from trees is to receive the examples of the saints. To cry Hosanna is to ask for heavenly salvation from Christ. By that reason, indeed, we spread garments before Christ better than if we were almost solely occupied with the excessive ornamentation of temples and altars. No one who has associated with them will easily deny that this is done among the Papists, whose entire religion is almost situated in the superstitious decoration of altars, images, and relics. Learned men have long since noted that abuse of the primitive Church. Of whose number S. Jerome writes in his 8th epistle to Demetrias, ch. 7, vol. 1: Let others build churches, clothe walls with slabs of marble, bring in masses of columns, decorate their heads, not feeling the precious ornament, etc. I do not reprehend, I do not deny, let everyone abound in his own sense, it is better than to brood over stored-up wealth; but for you another purpose is proposed, to clothe Christ in the poor, to visit him in the languishing, etc. Isidore of Pelusium has similar things in book 2, ep. 246. But especially S. Bernard speaks gravely in his Apology to Abbot William, col. 1134: The Church shines splendidly, he says, in its walls; it clothes its stones in gold, and leaves its children naked; it serves the eyes of the rich at the expense of the needy. While we whisper these things to the Papists, there is no reason why the Jesuits should take it so painfully and annoyingly, and accuse us from that, as if we either had no care for temples, or were visiting the holy dead with ignominy. We entirely praise the external worship of God, and we maintain that a portion of ecclesiastical goods should be attributed to the repair and ornamentation of sacred buildings.

And we teach that the bodies of the pious, that is, of those who have died in true faith in Christ, are to be buried honorably. See B. Par. loc. de Magistr. Pol. §. 191. B. D. Bald. contr. Patm. p. 334. But the Papists do not rest in this, but they proceed further, even to the point that they exhibit religious worship to images and relics, that is, to bones and garments (by prostrating themselves before them, by lighting candles to them, by overturning altars in which no relics of martyrs are preserved) and they establish that the decoration of temples is a certain meritorious work. This, this is what we censure in the Papists. Whence nothing is effected against us from this passage, unless they wish to establish that the disciples and companions applauding Christ also exhibited religious worship to the donkey and to the garments which Christ had sanctified by his touch.

*( ἔκοπτον κλάδους ἀπὸ τῶν δένδρων. Conf. Ioh. 12, 13. The rite of carrying τὰ Βά-α or θήρσους, and of acclaiming Hosanna certainly pertained to the τὰ ὀοχοφόρια, which fell in the month of September Lev. 23 39. 40. Meanwhile, since the Jews constantly believe that feast days not only contain the memory of the Egyptian exodus, but are also a presage of the times of the Messiah, in which they are as if about to celebrate a triumph (it was, however, a custom among the Greeks as well as the Romans that in triumphs soldiers should carry branches of palms, as can be seen from Livy Decad. 10. at the end, and Plutarch 8. Sympos. 9. 8.) with all their enemies conquered. Hence it is credible that this people, having been taught by so many miracles of Christ that he was the Messiah, used the rite and the word τῇς ὀοχοφορόας as if the presage were fulfilled, as Hugo Grotius conjectures in this place. He himself also not inconveniently observes that these signs of public joy were used elsewhere also, and that this is evident from 2. Macc. 10, 7.c. 13, 51. add. Apoc. 7, 9. But since the entry of Christ was made from the Mount of Olives, where there are many olive trees, it is possible to conjecture that branches of olive trees were also cut and carried before Christ. This also fits him beautifully, since he is our peace, Ioh. 14, 27.Eph. 2, 14. the prince of peace, Es. 9, 6. and it is known that branches of olive trees were a symbol of peace. See Livy Decad. 3. l. 9. & 10. Virgil book 8. Aeneid. Yet he is the same also as victor and triumpher, 1. Cor. 15, 57.Apoc. 5, 5. to whom palms are deservedly carried before him. Conf. August. tr. 51.

in Iohannem. Let us also carry palms before Christ, let us cut branches of trees, and let us adorn the way through which he is to go. Let us adorn our hearts, so that we may provide a pleasing entry for our Savior, Ioh. 14, 23. Let us be fruitful and fertile in the B. O. Let us walk worthily of the Gospel. Let our Light shine before men, Matth. 5, 16.Philipp. 1, 11.Col. 1, 10.Gal. 5, 22. let us always be mindful that sterile trees are to be cast into eternal fire, Matth. 3, 10. Conf. Anal. ad v. 5. & 19.)

Latin:

*(v. 8. -ςρωσαν ἀυτῶν τὰ ἱμάτια.Morem hunc apud Veteres receptum fuisse, confirmat Hugo Grotius in h. l. testimoniis Aeschylis in Agamemnone ac Plutarchi in Catone. Cumprimis quoque huc facere videtur historia Iehu,2. Reg. 9, 13.Coeterùm Salvatori nostro adhuc hodiè vestimenta substernere possumus, quando spiritualem eius ingressumpromovemus, operam dantes, ut Ministerium verbi honestè sustentetur, pauperes subleventur &c. Conf.Matth. 25, 35. 36.Paullò aliter Beda de Domin. Palmarum: Quis-, scribit, sternit vestimenta sua in viâ, qui membra sui corporis humiliat in praesenti, ut exaltet ea Deus in futuro, memor illius Davidici: Quia exultabunt ossa humiliata, Ps. 51, 10. Greg. hom. 24. Quid sunt terrena omnia, nisi quaedam corporis indumenta? Bona terrena pauperib-erogate: ramos de arboribus caedere, est sanctorum exempla accipere. Osanna clamare, est salutem supernam à Christo postulare. Istâ sanè ratione meliùs Christo vestes substernimus, quàm si circa templorum & altarium nimium ornatum unicè ferè occupati fuerimus. Id quod apud Pontificios fieri, ut quorum tota propè religio in superstitiosâ altarium, imaginum & reliquiarum exornatione sita est, nemo facilè, qui inter eos versatus est, inficias iverit. Iampridem abusum illum primitivae Ecclesiae Dd. notarunt. E quorum numero S. Hieronymus ad Demetriadem epist. 8. c. 7. t. 1. Alii, scribit, aedificent Ecclesias, vestiant parietes marmorum crustis, columnarum moles advehant, earumdecorent capita, pretiosum ornatum non sentientia &c. Non reprehendo, non abnuo, unus quisin suo sensu abundet, meliusest, quàm repositis opibus incubare; sed tibi aliud propositum est, Christum vestire in pauperibus, visitare in languentibus &c. Similia habet Isidorus Pelusiota l. 2. ep. 246. Cumprimis verò graviter S. Bernhardus in Apolog. ad Guilielm. Abbatem col. 1134. Splendidè, inquit, fulget Ecclesia in parietibus; lapides suos auro induit, & filios suos nudos deserit; de sumtibus egenorum servitur oculis divitum. Haec dum Pontificiis insusurramus, non est, cur adeò dolenter molesteque ferant Iesuitae, nosque exinde accusent, quasi vel nullam templorum curam habeamus, vel sanctos defunctos ignominiâ afficiamus. Laudamus omninò cultum Dei externum, partem bonorum Ecclesiasticorum aedium sacrarum reparationi & ornatui tribuendum statuimus.

ac piorū h. e. qui verâ in Christum fide obierunt, corpora honestè sepeliēda esse docemus. Vid. B Par. loc. de Magistr. Pol. §. 191. B. D. Bald. contr. Patm. p. 334. Sed in hoc nō acquiescunt Papicolae, verùm longiùs progrediuntur, eousque nempe, ut imaginibus ac reliquiis h. e. ossibus ac vestibus cultum exhibeant religiosū (coram illis sese prosternēdo, candelas illis accēdendo, altaria, in quibus nullae martyrum reliquae adservantur, evertendo) ac templorum ornatum opus quoddam meritorium esse statuant. Hoc, hoc est, quod in Pontificiis reprehendimus. Unde nihil ex hoc loco contra nos efficitur, nisi statuere velint, discipulos ac comites Christo applaudentes, asinae quoq; ac vestimentis quae Christus contactu sanctificaverit, cultum religiosum exhibuisse.)*

*( ἔκοπτον κλάδους ἀπὸ τῶν δένδρων. Conf. Ioh. 12, 13. Pertinebat quidem ritus ferendi τὰ Βά-α sive θήρσους, & acclamandi Hosana ad τὰ ὀοχοφόρια, quae incidebant in mensem septembrē Lev. 23 39. 40. Interea cùm Iudaei constanter credant, festos dies non tantùm continere memoriam Aegyptiaci exitûs, sed & praesagium esse temporum Messiae, quibus triumphum quasi celebraturi sint (fuit autem apud Graecos iuxta ac Romanos in more positum, ut in triumphis milites ramos palmarum ferrent, ceu ex Livio Decad. 10. in fin. ac Plutarcho 8. Sympos. 9. 8. videre est.) cunctis suis hostibus devictis. Inde credibile est. populum hunc, tot quippe Christi miraculis edoctum, Mesfiam eum esse, velut impleto praesagio ritùs & verbā τῇς ὀοχοφορόας usurpare, ceu coniicit Hugo Grotius in h. l. Qui ipse etiam nō incommodè observat, alibi etiā isthaec publicae laetitiae signa fuisse adhibita, idq; patere ex 2. Macc. 10, 7.c. 13, 51. add. Apoc. 7, 9. Cùm verò Christi ingressus factus fuerit de monte Oliveti, ubi frequentes Olivae, coniicere licet, olearum quoq; ramos fuisse caesos ac Christo praelatos. Id quod pulerè quoque ipsi competit, cùm sit pax nostra, Ioh. 14, 27.Eph. 2, 14. princeps pacis, Es. 9, 6. notum verò est, quòd rami olearum pacis symbolum fuerint. Vid. Livius Decad. 3. l. 9. & 10. Virgilius lib. 8. Aeneid. Idem tamen etiam victor ac triumphator, 1. Cor. 15, 57.Apoc. 5, 5. cui meritò palmae praeferantur. Conf. August. tr. 51.

in Iohannem. Praeferamus autem & nos Christo palmas, caedamus ramos arborum, viamque per quam illi eundum, exornemus. Ornemus corda nostra, quò gratum Salvatori nostro praebeamus ingressum, Ioh. 14, 23. Simus foecundi ac fertiles in B. O. Ambulemus dignè Evangelio. Luceat Lux nostra coram hominibus, Matth. 5, 16.Philipp. 1, 11.Col. 1, 10.Gal. 5, 22. semper simus memores, quòd arbores steriles in ignem aeternum mittendae, Matth. 3, 10. Conf. Anal. ad v. 5. & 19.)*

## 21:9
v. 9. ωσαννά. ךושע נא in the prayers of the Hebrews signifies save now. But this does not seem to suit this Evangelical passage, Hosanna to the son of David. For what will it be: save now to the son of David? It is found, however, Hoschia with the Dative Ezech. 34, 22.Ps. 44, 4.Ps. 98, 1. *(So also Deut. 22, 27.Iudic. 7, 2.1. Sam. 25, 26.)* But there is no absurdity if it be said that this word is of those congratulating and invoking for the salvation of the Messiah, i.e., grant salvation to the son of David. *(For this formula was according to some in use among the Jews, by which they would congratulate a new King and pray well for him, as today among the French: Vive le Roy. As for what τὸ נא concerns, it can be translated by now, also I beseech, I pray. But the former meaning pleases Rivetus more here in his Comm. on Ps. 118. Nor is there any doubt that this acclamation was taken from Psalm. 118, 25. 26. And thus from the ancients also Jerome and others establish it, from the more recent, and indeed from our own Blessed Doctors Selneccerus and Glassius in Expl. Domin. Palm. Tarnovius in Ioh. p. 866. from the Calvinists Casaubonus Exerc. 16. ad Ann. Baronii n. 5. Rivetus l. c. from the Papists Genebrardus in Ps. 118. Cantipratensis, Maldonatus, Hentenius, Tirinus in h. l. Caninius in disquis. ad LL. diff. But it is asked, how the people could acclaim Christ and pray that God might save him, when he himself intercedes for all, but for him no one, because he is salvation itself? Resp. Christ in the H. S. is not only called ישוע Savior, in an active sense, but also נושע saved--, in a passive sense, Zach. 9, 9. because indeed when he was about to redeem us by his passion and death and to descend into the depth of our misery, it was necessary that he himself be saved i.e. preserved, (according to the assumed human nature) so that being saved he might also save us,* Esai. 65, 5. By what reasoning it was altogether rightly acclaimed to Him, that God might save Him. Others, however, prefer to take this vow concerning the mystical body of Christ, that is, concerning the Church, rather than concerning Christ Himself, so that the sense may be: Save, I beseech Thee, O God, the kingdom of Christ our King, and cherish, rule, and amplify it, just as we pray in the Lord's Prayer: Thy kingdom come. Some (such as Irenaeus l. 4. adv. haer. c. 26., Origen tr. 15. in Matth., Hilary can. 1-, Ambrose in c. 19. Lucae, Bede, Thomas Aquinas, Nic. de Lyra, Tostatus Abulensis, Dionysius the Carthusian, Toletus, Barradius in h. l., whose opinion the Jesuit Conzen embraces and defends at length) maintain that they were praying for salvation from Christ Himself. But although we may easily grant that help and salvation can be sought from Christ, as the true τεανθρωπω, and we may also concede that the people received Christ as the Messiah, we nevertheless deny that they invoked Christ in this place, since that exposition is opposed to -rsetur, because it is expressly added γω Δαυΐδ. (See B. D. Tarnovius in Ioh. p. 868 & 869.)* Furthermore, since the Jews at the feast of tabernacles frequently sang ---, whence for the sake of brevity it became Hosanna, they also called the bundles of river willows, because of the frequent shoutings of the Jews who repeatedly responded Hosanna, Hosannas: Thus it is taken in the Talmud Perek Iubal Haggazul, where it is read: When you bind the Hosannas, make a handle for them. But because willows are found everywhere, while cedars, palms, and myrtles are not, the custom prevailed that the branches of all trees, which the Hebrews carried at the feast of tabernacles, repeatedly shouting Hosanna, obtained that name. *(See Elias Levita in Tisbi at the word --- and by all means add B. D. Glassius in Annot. Exeg. h. l. p. 77. seqq.)* The same name is also used in the second Targum of Esther c. 3, 8. The crowds therefore confess that they are carrying Hosanna, i. e., branches of willows, palms, or other trees, to the son of David, and that they acknowledge Him as the Messiah . *(Hugo Grotius in h. l. thinks that ωσανν α is used here for the hymn itself, and the sense is: we sing this auspicious hymn to King Messiah. The former exposition, however, pleases Angelo Caninio l. c. c. 4. and Schindler Lex. Pentag. pag. 819 more.)*

Hilary in h. l. they interpret Osanna, because it is redemption of the House of David, which Jerome therefore criticizes in his book to Damasus, because he did this out of ignorance of the Hebrew language. *(Ambrose also agrees with Hilary in ch. 19 of Luke. But Drusius in his Commentaries on the words of the N.T. and the Jesuit Maldonatus in this place have undertaken the defense of both. Justin Martyr, or whoever is the author of the Questions and Answers to the Orthodox, Q. 51, p. 328, explains μεγαλωσονην -ωερηειμλύην; Clement of Alexandria παιςαγ. p. 38. αινο;ν, Suidas in his Lexicon ςόξαν. That the people acclaimed Christ with more things besides Hosanna, and those things which are related here, is evident from Mark 11. 9. 10.Luke 19, 38. Although therefore the remaining Evangelists relate the acclamation of the people a little differently, yet that detracts nothing from the divine authority of the Holy Scripture. Since it is by no means credible that all those acclaiming used exactly the same words in that solemn congratulation. Whence, however, the people had those words, King of Israel, when it is not read in Psalm 118. 25., the Blessed D. Tarnovius discusses in John, p. 869.)* Augustine, book 2 of Christian Doctrine and tractate 51 on John, thinks that Hosanna is a word of one rejoicing, which cannot be rendered into Latin. But the contrary is evident from what has been said. *(The Jesuit Corn. à Lapide, in order to display his own, namely, αναρολοηοπολυγλωττοπνωσει wisdom, or ignorance, notes in this place that the Egyptian and Arabic interpreters have here Hosanna, the Ethiopic Hosanna, the Persian Hissianna. But if anyone examines the cited interpreters, he will discover, not without great care, that the Jesuit could scarcely read them, let alone interpret them. For the Arab has --- Huschana, the Ethiopian --- Hosana, and finally the Persian --- Uschana. But these ω έν παραςρομη, and that at least so that readers may know what is to be attributed to Cornelius, who everywhere rattles on about the Arab and the other Oriental interpreters.)*

*( Blessed. Conf. Rom. 1, 25.ch. 9, 5.2 Cor. 11, 21.)*

In the name of the Lord. Christ is said to come in the name of the Lord 1. because He comes, sent by GOD; 2. because He was instructed by divine power. *(Conf. John 5, 43. where ΚῸ to come in the name of the Lord or of GOD, and in his own name are opposed. Add Daniel 9, 26.Matthew 11, 3. Augustine warns in tractate 51 on John, that this, in the name of the Lord, can also be understood as in his own name, because also

Christ himself is the Lord. The people therefore acknowledge that Christ, sent by God, is King and Savior. But let us learn from the example of this acclaiming people to acknowledge 1. human infirmity, and thus to work out salvation with fear and trembling, Philippians 2, 12. The people indeed began well in this way, but many of them fell shamefully, for a little later they were crying out crucify,Mark 15, 13. 14. He therefore who stands, let him see that he does not fall,1 Corinthians 10, 12. let us ask God that He may deign to perfect the good work which He began in us, Philippians 1, 6. 2. the inconstancy and vanity of the world, Behold indeed, how suddenly the inconstant people changed olives and palms into thorns; Hosanna into reproaches; blessed and well done, into take away, crucify. Let us therefore by no means trust in the world, but let us flee from it, lest we perish with the perishing world. But on the contrary, let us seek only those things which are above, Colossians 3, 1. Let us go forth daily by the contempt of worldly things to meet the Lord. Let us strew in the way branches of virtues and accommodate the works of mercy to the feet of Christ. Let us take palm fronds, triumphing over the princes of darkness, over the allurements of worldly pleasures. Let nothing remain in us that does not go forth to meet Jesus: because not even one hoof is to be left for Pharaoh in Egypt. Let the hand and the heart harmonize with the tongue, and always sound: Hosanna in the highest. See Drogon, Bishop of Ostia, book on the Sacrament of the Lord's Passion.)*

*( ην ὑψίστοις. Conf. Luc. 2, 14.Eph. 1, 3. from the O. T. Psal. 148, 1.Iobi 31, 2. Add. Tertull. adversus Praxeam c. 17.)*

*( The whole city was moved. Conf. above c. 2, 3. B. D. Hunnius in this place maintains that this happened because they feared for themselves from a sedition, because Christ was arriving with such a retinue, and because such solemn acclamations were being made to him as are accustomed to be paid to Kings, and he notably adds: carnal men always suppose that heaven is about to fall if hospitality is given to Christ and his kingdom. Unaware that where Christ is received, there is a safe refuge.)*
