## 21:12
v. 12. Jesus entered into the temple. Chrysost. in this place: Our Savior, about to cure the city of Jerusalem, entered the temple first, that he might first chastise the sins of the Priests, like a good Physician, who cures a disease from the root. *(But since the business was not carried on in the temple itself (in the interior one, suppose, which is called by some the third, and was open only to Priests and Levites, from whose number since Christ was not, some think , see Ribera lib. 1. de Templ. c. 32. that almost all things which we read in the Gospels that the Lord did in the temple, were done in the exterior temple, i.e., the court of the laity, which was as it were an intermediate place between the court of the Gentiles, i.e., Solomon's Porch, and the interior temple, as is evident from the delineation prefixed to the English Polyglot Bible p. 38), but at least in its porches, Conf. John 12, 20, it is to be noted that either the word temple is taken here in a wider signification, or the preposition έν is put for at, near. In which way it is also accepted Luke 9, 31 coll. with c. 13, 33 it. John 10, 23 Heb. 9, 4. Furthermore, St. Jerome in this place judges this miracle to be especially wonderful among almost all that Jesus did, such as that he raised Lazarus, restored sight to the man born blind, etc. Namely for this reason, that one man, and at that time contemptible and so vile that he would afterwards be crucified, with the Scribes and Pharisees raging against him, etc., could at the lashes of a single whip cast out such a multitude, and even do those things which an infinite army would scarcely have done. Nevertheless, Mr. Dr. Friedlieb thinks in this place p. 166 that the Jews permitted capital punishment to be inflicted on a man έπαυροθόρω caught by the Zealots, i.e., private individuals led by zeal, as often as any Jew violated the holiness of either God or the temple or the nation, so that he seemed openly to either despise or deny it: and that from that custom this ejection of those buying and selling seems to have arisen, since otherwise the Scribes and Pharisees would scarcely have restrained themselves from acting against the Lord concerning public violence. But although it can scarcely be denied that the Scribes and Pharisees, convicted by conscience, could not disapprove of that zeal, whence also among the various calumnies with which they labored excessively to burden the innocent Christ before Pilate, they by no means urged or mentioned this ejection: yet this deed by no means seems to lack a miracle.)*

*( He cast out those who sold and bought. For although it was divinely granted, see Deut. 14, 24. ff., that those who traveled to Jerusalem from more remote places might buy victims there for money: nevertheless, it ought by no means to be done in the temple, nor even in its porticoes, as they were to be destined for the Gentiles who were about to convert to the true religion, not to be let out to sellers)*

The tables of the money-changers. It was the custom while the temple still stood, according to the most ancient tradition of the Fathers, as is read in the Talmud, tractate on shekels, ch. 1, on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month, to place tables in the temple and to set money-changers over the tables, so that those by whom the half-shekel was to be offered according to the law of the Lord, Exod. 30., might find money ready there with the money-changers, either by the exchange of other currency, or by giving a pledge, and thus there would be no delay in the payment of the tax, when all Israel would pay the imposed tax from the aforementioned day until the Passover. *(St. Jerome relates that the money-changers were placed in the temple for another reason, namely, that those who came to the temple and did not have money to purchase sacrifices, the money-changers would lend it to them under security. But when it was commanded by law that no one should take interest, and therefore money lent at interest could not be profitable, they devised, as the same Jerome warns, another trick, that they should make money-changers into small-change dealers, who would accept cheap little gifts, such as roasted chickpeas, raisins, and fruits of various kinds. Moreover, the blessed D. Hunnius not inappropriately warns in this place that that trading carried on by the people in the Jerusalem temple with the permission of the priests is a figure and type of the trafficking of the Antichrist. For it is certain that under the dominion of the Roman Pontiff, spiritual benefits, obtained through Christ, which He Himself nevertheless commanded to be applied freely to the penitent, were prostituted for sale. Monks sold their works, temples were for sale, priests, etc. Compare concerning the trafficking of the Roman Pontiffs, B. D. Hoë, Commentary on the Apocalypse, ch. 18, page 488 ff., and B. D. Hunnius in this place at greater length.)*

*( Of those who sold doves. See Levit. 1, 14.c. 5.c. 12, 6.8.c. 14, 22.c. 15, 14.29.Numer. 6, 10.Luc. 2, 24.)*

Latin:

v. 12. Intravit Iesus in templum. Chrysoft. h. l. Salvator noster curaturus civitatem Hierosolymam ingressus est priùs templum, ut peccata Sacerdotum primò castigaret, instar boni Medici, qui morbum à radice curat. *(Caeterùm cùm negotiatio non in ipso templo (interiori puta, quod à nonnullis tertium vocatur, solisque patebat Sacerdotibus ac Levitis, è quorum numero cùm Christus non esset, existimant nonnul-i, vide Riberam lib. 1. de Templ. c. 32. omnia ferè, quae in Evangeliis Dominum in templo fecisse legimus, in templo exteriori s. atrio laicorum, quod intermedius quasi erat locus inter atrium gentium s. Porticum Salomonis & templum interius, ceu patet ex delineatione, Bibliis Polygl. Angl. praemissâ p. 38. facta esse,) exercita fuerit, sed in eius porticibus saltem, Conf. Ioh. 12, 20. notandum est, vel templi vocem in latiori significatione hîc sumi, vel praepositionem έν poni pro apud, iuxta. Quomodo etiam accipitur Luc. 9, 31. coll. cum c. 13, 33. it. Iohan. 10, 23.Ebr. 9, 4. Porrò S. Hieronymus in h. l. miraculum hoc inter omnia propè, quae Iesus fecit, ut quod Lazarum resuscitârit, coeco nato visum restituerit &c. cumprimis mirabile esse censet. Ideò nempè, quod unus homo & illo tempore contemtibilis & in tantum vilis, ut posteà crucifigeretur, Scribis & Pharisaeis contra se saevientibus &c. potuerit ad unius flagelli verbera tantam eiicere multitudinem, atque adeò ea facere, quod infinitus vix fecisset exercitus. Putat tamen Dn. D. Friedlieb in h. l. p. 166. quòd Iudaei capitale supplicium in homineέπαυροθόρωdeprehenso à Zelotis i. e. privatis Zelo ductis infligi permiserint, quoties sanctitatem sive Dei sive templi sive gentis Iudaeus aliquis violaret, ut palàm sive spernere eam sive negare videretur: atex illo more ortam videri hanc ementium & vendentium eiectionem, cùm aliàs vix sibi temperassent Scribae & Pharisaei, quin egerint adversùs Dominum de vi publicâ. Verùm licet negari vix possit, Scribas & Pharisaeos, conscientiâ convictos Zelum illum improbare non potuisse, unde etiam varias inter calumnias, quibus Christum innocentem coram Pilato gravare nimiopere laborabant, eiectionem hanc minimè urgebant vel commemorabant: hautquaquam tamen factum hoc miraculo carere videtur.)*

*( Eiiciebat vendentes & ementes. Licet enim divinitùs fuerit concessum, vid. Deut. 14, 24. seqq. ut illi, qui à remotioribus locis Hierosolymas migrabant, pro pecunia ibi victimas emerent: in templo tamen id fieri minimè debebat, quin nec in porticibus eius, ut quae gentibus ad veram religionem se conversuris erant destinandae, non vendentibus elocandae)*

Mensas nummulariorum. Consveverunt durante adhuc templo, ex antiquissima Patrum traditione, sicut legitur in Talmud tr. de siclis c. 1. vigesima quinta die mensis duodecimi mensas collocare in templo & nummularios mensis praeficere, ut, quibus dimidius siclus esset ex lege Domini offerendus, Exod. 30. in promtu ibi invenirent pecuniam apud nummularios, sive permutatione alterius monetae, sive dato pignore, & ita nulla esset in censûs pensione mora, quando totus Israēl à commemorato die usque ad Pascha impositum censum penderet. *(Alia de causa nummularios in templo positos fuisse, tradit S. Hieronymus, videlicet, ut qui venirent ad templum. nec haberent pecuniam ad sacrificia comparanda, nummularii mutuò eam darent sub cautione, Cùm verò lege fuerit praeceptum, ut nemo usuras acciperet, adeoq; prodeste non posset pecunia foenerata, excogitârunt, eodem Hieronymo monente, aliam technam, ut pro nummulariis collybistas facerent, qui vilia munuscula, puta frixi ciceris, uvarumque passarum, & poma diversi generis acciperent. Caeterùm non incommodè monet B. D. Hunnius in h l. nundinationem illam in Hierosolymitano tempio permissu Sacerdotum à populo agitatam, figuram esse ac typum negotiationis Anti Christi. Constat quippe quòd sub dominatu Romani Pontificis venalia fuerint prostituta beneficia spiritualia, per Christum parta, quae ipse tamen poenitentibus gratis applicari praecepit. Monachi vendebant sua opera, venalia erant templa, sacerdotes &c. Conf. de nundinatione PP. RR. B. D. Hoë Comm. in Apoc. c. 18. pag. 488. seqq. ac B. D. Hunnius h. l. pluribus.)*

*( Vendentium columbas. Vid. Levit. 1, 14.c. 5.c. 12, 6.8.c. 14, 22.c. 15, 14.29.Numer. 6, 10.Luc. 2, 24.)*

## 21:13
v. 13. My house, a house of prayer etc. That accusatory complaint exists in Jer. 7, 11. it. Isa. 57, 7. Irenaeus b. 4. ch. 5. p. 235. He did not accuse the house, nor did he blame the law, which he had come to fulfill, but he argued against those who were not using the house well, and those who were transgressing the law. Temples are called houses of prayer or oratories, whence also the name proseuchae. Juvencus: In which I seek you, proseucha. (Cf. Mal. 3, 1. Moreover, Bell. b. 3. on the worship of the Sacraments, ch. 4. §. Third proposition. Stapleton in Prompt. Cathol. Sunday after Pentecost. §. 1. and other Papists try to prove from this passage that prayers in temples are more sacred, and more easily heard. But it must be noted 1. that we readily grant that temples were erected among other ends also for this reason, that with joined hands, as it were, we might knock at divine kindness, since this force is pleasing to God. Whence it is also so far from the case that we esteem prayers poured out in a temple lightly, that rather we seriously admonish the hearers in our Churches not to neglect public Ecclesiastical assemblies, according to that of the Apostle Heb. 10, 25. Indeed, our own people are also accustomed to commend that of Chrysostom hom. 3. on the incomprehensible nature of God: Common prayer excels private prayer much, because in it there is something more, namely concord, conspiracy, a bond of love and charity. See B. Par. Hom. Acad. part. 1. p. 366. seqq. So that it is false what Bell. in the said place §. 1. writes, that the Lutherans, from the ends enumerated by him, among which is also that sacred buildings were erected for praying, acknowledge only the fourth, namely that they were erected to feed the people with the word of God and the Sacraments. 2. that the worship of the N. T. is no longer, as in the O. T., tied to a certain place, and therefore neither are prayers. Mal. 1, 11.Matt. 6, 6.John 4, 21.1 Tim. 2, 8. and that consequently 3 one can pray just as ardently at home, and be equally certain of being heard if one has prayed at home, as if in a temple, when, for instance, one is prevented by ill health or other more serious impediments from being able to frequent public assemblies. Bellarmine urges against the cited passages, Matt. 6, 6. and John 4, 21. that the Lord said what is held here after all those things. But it must be noted that the precept of the Apostle 1 Tim. 2, 8. is even later. The question therefore is not whether God hears prayers in a temple, or whether prayers ought to be poured out in a temple, for this we readily grant, but it is asked only about this, whether the prayers which one pours out even solitarily in a temple, are more sacred and more easily heard, and that for the reason that they are made in a temple. Which the Papists affirm, but we deny. But the scope of Christ must be considered, which is certainly not here to show that prayers poured out in a temple are more easily heard than those at home, but that a temple consecrated to prayer and the preaching of the word ought not to be profaned by business, as was being done by the Jews at that time. Which we concede with both hands. Furthermore, it must be known that the Papists teach that prayers poured out in a temple are more easily heard, That Christ in the Eucharist, namely when reserved and even outside the use divinely instituted, is present there, which hypothesis is false and erroneous. But Bellarmine insists, certainly God is more present in the Temple. Resp. By denying it concerning the time of the N. T. Furthermore, although we vehemently commend public prayers which are made in Temples, that is nevertheless by no means to be extended so far as if one ought to pray alongside the Papists and Calvinists in their temples. For this very thing, since it can scarcely be done without grave scandal to the simpler folk, is deservedly disapproved of by our people. Let the blessed D. Hutter be seen discussing this matter at length in I. L. Maior. p. 976. and 977. where he also solidly responds to the passage 2. Reg. 5, 18. & 19. which might seem to favor communion of this kind. St. Jerome in this place adapts this history to the Church, in which Bishops and Presbyters sell the dove, if they sell the grace of the Holy Spirit (as one who appeared in the symbol of a dove) sell: likewise to every individual Christian man, as one who ought to be a temple of the Holy Spirit, 1. Cor. 3, 16. 2. Cor. 6, 16. Let there not be in the house of our breast negotiation, not the greed of worldly things, lest Jesus enter angry and rigid, and not otherwise cleanse his temple, unless a scourge be applied. &c.)

A den of thieves. The temple is called so, because oppressions and injustices of every kind against the poor were practiced in it. Ps. 14, 4 Mich: 3, 2. 3. The blessed D. Hunnius in this place establishes that the temple is said to have been made a den of thieves, because the Doctors and Priests, by permitting that profanation of the Temple to the people, converted the Temple into a robbery of souls, likewise, because by false doctrine they eternally slaughtered the souls of men. But R. Lusitanus quite ineptly gathers from this that the prophecy of Haggai c. 2, 8. seqq. cannot be adapted to our Savior, for the reason that Haggai says, the glory of the second Temple (or of that, to which the Messiah was to come) would be greater than the glory of the first Temple. Now indeed, Apella subsumes, the glory of that temple, to which our Christ came, could by no means be called greater than that of the former, since Christ himself asserts of it in this place, that those buying and selling in that temple had made it a den of thieves. I respond by conceding that those buying and selling in the Temple had made it a den of thieves: but Christ cleansed it again, and taught in it the words of life, so that consequently, on account of the singular presence of the Messiah, the glory of this temple was made greater than that of the former was.)*

Latin:

v. 13. Domus mea, domus orationis &c. Querela illa accusatoria extat Ierm. 7, 11. it. Es. 57, 7. Irenaeus l. 4. c. 5. p. 235. Net domum incusabat, nec legem reprehendebat, quam venerat adimplere, sed eos, qui non benè utebantur domo, & eos qui legem transgrediebantur, arguebat. Templa vocantur domus orationis s. oratoria, unde & nomen proseuchae. Iuvencus: In quâ te quaero proseucha. *(Conf. Mal. 3, 1. Coeterùm Bell. l. 3. de cult. Sacr. c. 4. §. Tertia propos. Stapletonus in Pomt. Cathol. Dom. post Pentecost. §. 1. & alii Pontificii ex hoc loco probare conantur. preces in templis sacratiores esse, faciliusexaudiri. Verùm notandum 1. quòd facilè largiamur, templa, inter alios fines etiam propterea erecta esse, ut iunctis quasi manibus divinam pulsemus benignitatem, cùm haec vis Deo grata sit. Unde etiam tantum abest, ut preces in templo fusas parvi aestimemus, ut potius seriò auditores in nostris Ecclesiis admoneantur, ne publicos conventus Ecclesiasticos negligant, iuxta illud Apostoli Ebr. 10, 25. Imò commendare & ipsi nostrates solent illud Chrysostomi hom. 3. de incompreh. Dei natura: Cōmunis oratio multùm praestat privatae, quia in illa est plus aliquid, videlicet concordia, conspiratio, copula amoris & caritatis. Vid. B. Par. Hom. Acad. part. 1. p. 366. seqq. Ut adeò falsum sit, quod Bell. d. l. §. 1. scribit, Lutheranos ex enumeratis ab ipso finibus, inter quos etiam ille, quòd aedes sacrae erectae sint ad or andum, quartum solùm agnoscere, nempè quòd erectae sint ad populum verbo Dei & Sacramentis pascendum. 2. quòd cultus N. T. non ampliùs ut in V. T. ad certum locum sit alligatus, adeoque nec preces. Mal. 1, 11.Matth. 6, 6.Ioh. 4, 21.1. Tim. 2, 8. quòdque proinde 3 aequè ardenter domi quis precari possit, pariterq; certus de exauditione esse, si domi orarit, quàm si in templo, cùm videl. vel adversâ valetudine vel aliis gravioribus impedimentis, quô minùs publicos conventus frequentare possit, prohibeatur. Urget Bellarm. contra dicta, Matth. 6, 6. ac Iohan. 4, 21.quòd Dominus hoc, quod hîc habetur, post omnia illa dixerit. Verùm notandum, quòd praeceptum Apostoli 1. ad Tim. 2, 8. adhuc posterius sit. Quaestio igitur non est, an Deus preces in templo exaudiat, vel an preces in templo effundi debeant, hoc enim facilè largimur, sed de eo saltem quaeritur, an precesquas quis etiam solitariè in templo effundit, sint sacratiores & faciliùs exaudiantur, idque propterea, quòd in templo fiunt. Id quod Pontificii affirmant, nos verò negamus. Considerandus verò Christi scopus, qui sanè hîc non est, ostendere, quòd faciliùs exaudiantur preces in templo, quàm domi effusae, sed quòd templum orationi ac praedicationi verbi consecratum negotiatione profanari, ceu à Iudaeis tunc fiebat, non debeat. Id quod ambabus manibus concedimus. Praetereà sciendum. Pontificios proptereà preces in templo fusas faciliùs exaudiri docere, quòd Christus in Eucharistiâ, nempe repositâ & etiam extra usum divinitùs institutum, ibi praesens sit, quae hypothesis falsa & erronea est. Sed instat Bellarminus, certè Deum magis praesentem esse in Templo. Resp. Negando de tempore N. T. Porrò licet publicas preces, in Templis quae fiunt, vehementer commendemus, id tamen minimè eò usque extendendum est, ac si iuxta cum Pontificiis & Calvinianis in ipsorum templis orandum sit, Hoc ipsum enim cum absque gravi simpliciorum scandalo fieri vix possit, meritò à nostratibus improbatnr. Videatur prolixè hâc de re differens B. D. Hutterus in I. L. Maior. p. 976. & 977. ubi etiam ad locum 2. Reg. 5, 18. & 19. qui huiusmodi communioni videri possit favere, solidè respondet. S. Hieronymus in h. l. accommodat hanc historiam ad Ecclesiam, in quâ Episcopi & Presbyteri columbam vendant, sigratiam Sp. Sancti (ut qui in columbae symbolo apparuit) vendant: item ad unumquemque hominem Christianum, uti qui templum Sp. S. esse debeat, 1. Cor. 3, 16.2, Cor. 6, 16. Non sit in domo pectoris nostri negotiatio, non mundanorum cupiditas, ne ingrediatur Iesus iratus & rigidus, & non aliter mundet templum suum, nisi flagello adhibito. &c.)*

Spelunca latronum. Dicitur ita templum, quia omnis generis oppressiones & iniustitiae adversùs pauperem in eo exercebantur. Ps. 14, 4Mich: 3, 2. 3. B. D. Hunnius in h. l. statuit, propterà templum speluncam latronum factum dici, quòd Dd. & Sacerdotes profanationem istam Templi populo permittentes in latrocinium animarum Templum converterint, item, quòd falsâ doctrinâ animas hominum aeternum iugulârint. Satis rerò ineptè hinc colligft R. Lusitanus, quòd vaticinium Haggai c. 2, 8. seqq. non possit accommodari ad nostrum Salvatorem, eò quòd Haggai dicat, gloriam secundi Templi (sive illius, ad quod venturus Messias sit) maiorem fore gloriâ primi Templi. Iam vero, subsumit Apella, gloria templi illius, ad quod Christus noster venit, haut quaquam maior dici potuit, quàm prioris, cùm de eo ipse a-serat h. l. Christus, quòd ementes ac vendentes in templo eo fecerint lud speluncam latronum. Resp. concedendo, quòd ementes ac vendentes in Templo fecerint illud speluncam latronum: Christus verò iterum purgavit illud, ac in eo docuit verba vitae, ut proinde ob singularem Messiae praesentiam gloria huius templi maior facta fuerit, quàm prioris fuit.)*

## 21:15
*(v. 15. they were indignant. Envying Christ, namely, that honor, because he was celebrated as the Messiah. It is to be observed here, that the Evangelist Luke alone, c. 19, 45, commemorates that Christ wept when he approached Jerusalem, foreseeing, namely, the destruction imminent upon the Jews on account of their impenitence.)*

Latin:

*(v. 15. indignati sunt. Invidentes nempe Christo honorem illum, quòd pro Messiâ celebraretur. Observandum hîc, quòd Evangelista Lucas solus c. 19, 45. comemoret, Christum illacrymâsse, cùm Hierosolymas adpropinquaret, praevidens nempè imminentem Iudaeis propter eorum impoenitentiam interitum.)*

## 21:16
v. 16. Out of the mouth of infants &c. Piscator thinks, infants are said to sing praises to God for this reason, because they show divine providence in procuring for them nourishment from the breasts of their mothers. But more is contained in that Davidic oracle. Tessanus follows Piscator, annotating thus: Just as it is a peculiar testimony of divine providence that it miraculously preserves and nourishes infants and sucklings: so it is a manifest testimony that I am the true Messiah, predicted by David, because God publicly declares that through the praise of these boys and refutes your incredulity. The Church in this life is an infant, because it cannot narrate the mysteries of God. And at the same time it is a suckling, i.e., it always draws some doctrine and consolation from the word, as if from a maternal breast.

*(This testimony is taken from the eighth Psalm which is also expounded elsewhere concerning Christ. See 1. Cor. 15, 27.Heb. 2, 7. seqq. Moreover, this passage makes 1. for the faith of baptized infants, which has been proven more prolixly elsewhere. See Analecta to Matt. 18. v. 3. & 6. and to c. 19, 14. As far as the present passage is concerned, D. Rivetus in his Comm. on Ps. 8, 3. opposes to our opinion two passages of the Fathers from which he tries to prove that infants, according to the opinion of those Fathers, do not have understanding, i.e., the perfect use of reason, nor can they themselves believe in Christ, or be participants of justifying faith. But it is to be noted that Tertullian himself in the loc. cit. expressly writes, It is a wonder that infancy is naturally spirited, not having a soul, and naturally affectionate, not having an intellect. But if infancy is naturally spirited and affectionate, although it does not have a soul and intellect, that is, the perfect use of reason, how much more true will it be that God supernaturally works justifying faith in infants, regenerated through baptism and inserted into Christ, although they are not yet endowed with the perfect use of reason. Justin also teaches the same thing, when in the passage alleged by D. Rivetus he writes, that infants sang a hymn to Christ not by their own counsel, but by divine grace. Certainly, we do not say that baptized infants believe in Christ by their own counsel or from their own natural powers, or that they apprehend the Savior by justifying faith, but we ascribe all this to divine grace, which is efficacious in infants through baptism. Therefore, it is so far from the case that those Fathers patronize the opinion of the Calvinists, that they rather excellently confirm our own. Here the Jesuits press their thumb against the Calvinists, as those who likewise deny that infants have a motion of faith or actual faith. See Salmeron Disp. 1. on c. 6. to the Rom. c. 3. p. 487. Bellarm. lib. 1. de Bapt. c. 10. §. last. To whom for the present I oppose at least the exposition and words of their own fellow, the Jesuit Maldonatus. For this very man, after he had mentioned in his Commentary on this passage that it is doubtful whether those who were crying out were infants at all, or boys already somewhat older, adds: Chrysostom, Euthymius, and Theophylactus think they were infants. Which I approve of much more, both because it increases the glory of Christ more, and because the words signify that etc. Let the parallel passages also be noted Apoc. 11, 18.c. 19. 5. Furthermore, this 2nd passage makes for the Deity of Christ . For in the eighth Psalm, from which our Savior proves that he was rightly acclaimed by the boys, the subject is the divine praise to be established forever. Finally, Jerome rightly wonders here at the wisdom of the Lord in the dexterity of his response, because by neither saying, the boys are well, he gave the Pharisees a handle for calumny; nor again by saying : they err, you ought to forgive their age, he may have injured the truth: but rather by opening the mouths of the simple, he may have closed the mouth of the wise, and confounded the wisdom of the enemies.)*

Latin:

v. 16. Ex ore infantum &c. Piscator existimat, infantes proptereà dici laudes Deo canere, quia ostendunt divinam providentiam in procurando ipsis alimento ex uberibus matrum. Sed plus continetur in oraculo illo Davidico. Piscatorem sequitur Tessanus, sic annotans: Quemadmodum est peculiare testimonium divinae providentiae, quòd infantes & lactentes mirabiliter conservat ac nutrit: sic manifestum est testimonium, quòd sim verus Messias, à Davide praedictus, quia Deus per laudem horum puerorum illud publicè declarat & incredulitatem vestram arguit. Ecclesia in hac vita est infans, quia non potest enarrare mysteria Dei. Et simul est lactens, i. e. semper aliquid doctrinae & consolationis ex verbo haurit, tanquam ex ubere materno.

*(Desumtum testimonium hoc è Psalmo octavo estqui alibi quoque de Christo exponitur. Vid. 1. Cor. 15, 27.Ebr. 2, 7. seqq. Facit autem locus hic 1. pro fide infantum baptizatorum, quae alibi prolixiùs probata. Vid. Analecta ad Matth. 18. v. 3. & 6. it ad c. 19, 14. Quod praesentem attinet locum, D. Rivetus Comm. in Ps. 8, 3. sententiae nostrae duo oppon-t P--rum loca, alterum ex Tertulliano lib. de animâ cap. 19. in fine, alterum ex Iustino Martyre, è quibus probare conatur, quò infantes è Patrum illorum sententiâ non habeant intellectum, h. e. perfectum rationis usum, nec credere quoque ipsi in Christum possint, sive fidei iustificantis esse participes. Verùm notandum, quòd Tertuilianus ipse l. c. disertè scribat, mirum esse, quòd infantia naturaliter animosa sit, non habens animum, & naturaliter affectuosa, non habens intellectum. Si verò insantia naturaliter animosa & affectuosa est, licet non hab-at animum & intellectum, h. e. perfectum rationis usum, quantò magis verum erit, quòd Deus supernaturaliter in infantibus, perbaptismum regenitis ac Christo insertis fidem iustificantem operetur, licet nondum perfectô rationis usu praediti sint. Idem etiam docet Iustinus, quando loco à D. Riveto allegato scribit, infantes non suopte consilio, sed gratiâ divinâ hymnum Christo decantâsse. Sanè nec nos dicimus, quòd infantes baptizati suopte consilio, vel ex propriis naturalibus viribus in Christum credant, sive fide iustificante Salvatorem apprehendant, sed omne hoc gratiae divinae, per baptismum in infantibus efficaci adscribimus. Tantum igitur abest, ut Patres illi Calvinianorum sententiae patrocinentur, ut nostram potiùs egregiè confirment. Calvinianis pollicem hîc premunt Iesuitae, ut qui pariter negant, infantes habere fidei motum sive fidem actualem. Vid. Salmeron Disp. 1. in c. 6. ad Rom. c. 3. p. 487. Bellarm. lib. 1. de Bapt. c. 10. §. ult. Quibus inpraesentiarum oppono saltem expositionem ac verba socienni ipsorum, Iesuitae Maldonati. Hic ipse enim, postquam in Comm. h. l. commemorasset, dubium esse, an qui clamabant, infantes omninò fuerint, an pueri iam grandiusculi, subiungit: Chrysostomus, Euthymius & Theophylactus infantes fuisse putant. Quod ego multò magis probo, & quia Christi gloriam magis auget, & quia verbaid significant &c. Notentur quoque loca parallela Apoc. 11, 18.c. 19. 5. Facit porrò 2. locus hic pro Christi De-tate. Agitur enim in Psalmo octavo, è quo Salvator noster probat. rectè sibi à pueris fuisse acclamatum, de laude divinâ in aeternum stabi iendâ. Meritò denique miratur hîc Hieronymus Domini sapientiam in responsi dexteritate, quòd neque dicendo, benè sat--nt pueri, Pharisaeis ansam calumniae praebuerit; neq; rursus dicendo: errant, debetis aetati ignoscere, veritatem laeserit: sed potiùs aperiendo ora simplicium, os occluserit sapientum, ac sapientiam confuderit hostium.)*

## 21:17
*(v. 17. He went out. Both that he might remove from himself every suspicion of an affected earthly kingdom. Conf. John 6, 15. and that he might be the more tranquil in devoting himself to prayers.)*

Latin:

*(v. 17. Egressus est. Tùm ut omnem affectati regni terreni suspicionem à se amoveret. Conf. Ioh. 6, 15. tùm ut precibus eò tranquilliùs vacaret.)*

## 21:18
*(v. 18. He hungered. He hungered, writes Jerome in this place, either showing the truth of human flesh, or hungering for the salvation of believers. (Indeed, all men who consequently do not satisfy this hunger and desire of Christ, but repel the offered grace from themselves, are deservedly dried up and cursed.) Chrysostom in this place & Alphonsus Tostatus q. 103, whom Corn à Lapide follows, think that Christ did not hunger with a natural hunger, since it was morning, and he had dined the previous evening at Martha's, so that he could not be hungry so soon. They therefore maintain that Christ stirred up this hunger in himself, so that through it he might have an occasion of cursing the unfruitful fig tree. But although there was not such a great hunger, as that in Matt 4, 2. because he nevertheless voluntarily subjected himself to our infirmities and it can entirely happen, and happens not rarely, that someone who has used a moderate dinner in the evening, hungers the next morning, that is, is held by a desire to take food again, there is no reason why without urgent necessity some miracle or singular thing should be established here. The Jesuit Conzen himself agrees in this place. Moreover, firmly from this, and similar places, as above c. 4, 2. c. 8, 24 Luke 9, 41. etc. the true humanity of Christ is proved against the Valentinians, Eutychians, Anabaptists etc. item the state of emptying. Conf. Phil 2, 7.Heb 2, 17.cap. 4, 15.)*

Latin:

*(v. 18. Esuriit. Esuriit, scribit Hieronymus in h. l. vel veritatem humanae carnis ostendens, vel esuriens salutem credenitum. (Imò omnium hominum, qui proinde fami huie ac desiderio Christi non satisfaciunt, sed oblatam gratiam à se repellunt, meritò siceantur ac maledicuntur.) Chrysostomus in h. l. & Alphonsus Tostatus q. 103. quos sequitur Corn à Lapide, existimant. Christum non esurie naturali esuriisse, cùm fuerit manè, & pridie vesperi apud Martham coenârit, ut tam citò esurire non posset. Statuunt igitur, Christum excitâsse hanc in se esuriem, ut per eam haberet occasionem maledicendi fievi infrugiferae. Verùm licet non tanta fuerit esuries, ceu illa Matth 4, 2. quia tamen nostris ipse infirmitatibus spontè sese subie-it, & omninò fi-ri possit, fiatque haut rarò, ut aliquis, qui vesperimoderata coenâ usus est, altero mane esuriat h. e. desiderio teneatur, cib-m iterum capiendi, non est, ut ab-que urgente necessitate miraculum aliquod sive singulare quid hîc statuatur. Adstipulatur ipse Iesuita Conzen in h. l. Firmiter autem ex hoc, similibus que locis, uti suprà c, 4, 2. c. 8, 24 Luc. 9, 41. &c. vera Christi humanitas contra Valentinianos, Eutychianos, Anabaptistas &c. probatur. item status exinanitionis. Conf. Philipp 2, 7.Ebr. 2, 17.cap. 4, 15.)*

## 21:19
*(v. 19. When he had seen a fig tree by the way, or in the way. But Mark says c. 11, 13. that the Lord saw it from afar. Resp. It was entirely a fig tree in the way, which nevertheless notwithstanding was seen by the Lord from afar, that is, before he arrived at that place of the way where the fig tree was.)*

*( He came, and found nothing. Q. Why did Christ approach the fig tree, when he nevertheless knew that he would find no fruits there, since it was not the time of figs, according to the witness of Mark c. 10, 13? Resp. 1. Some maintain that fig trees produce double fruits. First green figs, which come forth immediately in early spring together with the leaves, and also ripen quickly; Then figs, which they bring forth only then, when other trees bring forth their fruits. Of these, therefore, they say, the discourse is in Mark at the end of v. 13, but of those in the same verse in the middle, and here. Although, therefore, it was not yet the time of figs, it could nevertheless have been, indeed it was, the time of green figs, that is, when the fig tree could produce green figs. Thus Mr. Dr. Mueller removes the scruple in Judaism p. 979, 980. But since Mark expressly gives this reason for why Christ did not find fruit on the fig tree, that it was not yet the time of figs, it seems indeed that he speaks of nothing but figs both at the end of the verse and in the middle of it, just as our Evangelist also does. 2. Other interpreters, therefore, as the blessed Dr. Hunnius in his Commentary on this passage, respond that Christ approached the fig tree, not because He was ignorant that He would find nothing there (for it is not likely that Christ was ignorant of those things which even boys would have known, namely that a fig tree in the month of March, when trees are only just putting forth leaves and buds, does not yet produce figs, as the blessed Dr. Hunnius well notes from Augustine, sermon 44 de tempore, in the cited place), but so that He might have an occasion for performing a miracle. They think, therefore, that this passage is similar to Gen. 18:21. Cf. John 6:5-6. That Christ otherwise, according to the assumed human nature in the state of humiliation, was truly ignorant of certain things, is shown elsewhere. See the Analysis on Mark 13:32 and cf. the blessed Dr. Feuerborn, Synt. 2, p. 429. But the Jews err gravely when, from that ignorance by which Christ as man, and indeed in the state of humiliation, was truly ignorant of certain things (not from any imperfection, but by free will, and not from an ignorance of depraved disposition, but of simple negation), they attack the true Deity of Christ, which nevertheless our Savior proved sufficiently even in this very place, when by a single true and sole command He caused the fig tree to wither. This is something that could not have been done except by divine power. To say nothing now of the other very many great miracles of Christ, such as that He raised the dead, changed water into wine, cast devils out of the possessed, etc. All of which clearly confirm the true Deity of Christ. Although Christ in the state of humiliation was truly ignorant of certain things, it is nevertheless certain that divine omniscience was truly and really communicated to the assumed human nature of Christ at the very first moment of the incarnation. Yet it does not follow from this that it was also communicated essentially. Nor is it permitted to infer thus with Danaeus (whom the remaining Calvinists, just as the Jesuits for the most part, follow): The omniscience of Christ or Essentially it was communicated to the assumed human nature, or accidentally. If the former, the soul of Christ is constituted God, and indeed a new and recent one; if the latter, accidentally, then it was communicated by effusion! We answer, indeed, that there is a third way, namely personal communication. If the Jesuit Conzen had correctly weighed this very thing, he could have more easily extricated himself from the objections of Danaeus. But as for the fact that the same man, with his Gretser, maintains that the soul of Christ was endowed with -created (at least) but not uncreated knowledge, in that he errs not lightly. See what the blessed Pareus disputes regarding this matter in book 2, Conf. Cath. part 1, art. 2, c. 1 & 2.)

*( Unless leaves. Hypocrites are like a tree in this respect. See 2 Tim. 3:5, Jude ep. v. 12)*

May no fruit grow from you hereafter. Nicephorus, book 1, Ecclesiastical History, c. 27. Since there was no fruit in the fig tree, he immediately invokes the final end upon it through execration, inasmuch as it was the first author of transgression. (He alludes to the fact that our first parents are considered to have tasted of the fruit of the fig tree.) And afterwards, Perhaps, however, the fig-tree-like one, withering, expressed by a certain covering the sterility of the Synagogue of the Jews and the lack of bearing fruit. And indeed every rational soul subject to incredulity and diffidence toward Christ, even if it is thought to flourish greatly by the laws of the letter as if by leaves: although it falls away from the law of faith in Christ, by which it is most greatly nourished and cherished, it withers, far removed from the blessing of GOD. That curse, of which we speak here, did not proceed from some untimely effervescence of bile or desire for vengeance, but Christ wished to denote 1. the destruction of the Israelite people, inasmuch as it allows itself to be corrected by no admonitions, not even those proceeding from the mouth of children. *(Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, epistles 358 & 359, thinks that Christ, when he had betaken himself to the fig tree for the third time and had not found fruit on it, cursed it, and by this very act indicated that men had rejected God three times: 1. by the transgression of the primal commandment concerning not eating the fruit of the tree of truth. 2. by the adoration of the golden calf. 3. by the rejection of Christ, saying: We have no King &c.)* 2. the virtue of faith, which Christ himself explains the reason for in v. 21. See Tossanus in this place. The leaves of the fig tree signify hypocrisy Gen. 3. *(But how the Prophets and other holy men sometimes cursed and prayed for evil upon both men and other things as well, will be discussed in its own place. See B. D. Balduinus in Cases of Conscience. But especially the Scholastics treat this matter at length. Let them be unrolled, if it pleases, Thomas Aquinas in Summa 2. 2. q. 76. art. 1. following. Gregorius de Valentia, Theological Commentaries vol. 3. Disp. 5. q. 19. on Cursing, point 1. & 2. Franciscus Fevardentius on v. 9. Epistle of Jude. Other commentators may also be consulted both on this place and on Gen. 3, 17.Deut. 28, 16.2. Kings 1, 21. But it is asked here 1. Why Christ cursed the fig tree, when nevertheless, as Mark ch. 11, 13. reveals, the time of figs had not yet arrived for them to bear fruit? Mr. Dr. Waltherus answers that Christ did this parabolically. He sought fruit on the fig tree on purpose, which he knew did not have fruit, because he also seeks fruit from man, whom he likewise knows to lack fruit. In the same way Mr. Dr. Friedlieb answers on page 211, who nevertheless, just as Mr. Dr. Muellerus also, in Judaism p. 982, with Nicephorus, Augustine in Gospel Questions ch. 68, Bede on ch. 11 of Mark, Emissenus in the homily for Tuesday after the first Sunday, Gregory book 8, chapter 42, takes it specifically concerning the Jewish people, namely that the Savior sought with desire the conversion of the Jews and the fruits of repentance in them, but found nothing among them except the fruitless leaves of vain boasting &c. Mr. Dr. Mullerus however also distinguishes between the different fruits of the fig tree, concerning which matter it was treated above at the words: he found nothing. Q. 2. Why Christ cursed the fig tree, when nevertheless it did not sin? Athanasius answers in volume 2 in the sayings and parables of the Gospel, Interpretation q. 22, that Christ did this to declare his omnipotence to his disciples, and that he could easily strike his enemies, who were already about to crucify him, with dryness, had he not come rather to save the human race, than to destroy it. Let us learn indeed from this, that the sterility of good works is punished by dryness, that is, by the removal of the fructifying divine grace. Conf. Heb. 6, 8.

Nor indeed can the present act of Christ, cursing the fig tree, be censured for any reason, since He Himself as true God and creator of all things has the power of reducing all things to nothing. Nor, however, did He do this without cause: for by that very act He manifested His glory, namely that He is the Lord of all things, and that all things stand at His nod. Matth. 8, 26.c. 28, 18. Let us therefore revere Him, fear Him, & flee for refuge to Him.)*

Latin:

*(v. 19. Cùm vidisset fici arborem iuxta, sive in viâ. At Marcus dicit c. 11, 13. quòd à longè Dominus eam prospexerit. Resp. Fuit omninò ficus in viâ, quo tamen non obstante conspectus fuit à Domino à longè h. e. priusquam ad illum viae locum, ubi ficus erat, pervenit.)*

*( Venit, & nihil invenit. Q. Cur Christus accesserit ficum, cùm tamē sciret, se nihil fructuum ibi inventurum, quippe cùm non esset tempus ficuum, teste Marco c. 10, 13? Resp. 1. Quidam statuunt, quòd ficus duplices proferant fructus. Primùm grossos, qui primo statim vere unà cum foliis prodeant, ac citò etiam maturescant; Deinde caricas, quas tùm demum proferant, cùm aliae arbores fructus suos proferunt. De his igitur, aiunt, sermonem esse apud Marcum in fine v. 13. de illis verò apud eundem vers. eod. in medio, & hîc. Licet proinde nondum fuerit tempus caricarum, potuit tamen esse, imò fuit tempus grossorum, h. e. quo ficus grossos producere poterat. Ita scrupulum eximit Dn. D. Muellerus in Iudaismo p. 979. 980. Verùm cùm Marcus expressè rationem eius, quòd Christus non invenit fructus in fico reddat hanc, quòd nondum tempus fuerit ficorum, videtur sanè non nisi de caricis tum in fine versiculi, tum in medio eius loqui, quemadmodum etiam noster Evangelista. 2. Alii igitur interpretes, uti B. D. Hunnius Comm. h. l. respondent, Christum ficum accessisse, non quòd ignoraret, se nihil ibi inventurum (neque enim verisimile est, Christum ea ignorâsle, quae vel pueri scivissent, nempe ficum mense Martio, quo arbores folia demum & gemmas protrudunt, nondum proferre possficos, ut benè ex Augustino serm. 44. de tempore monet B. D. Hunnius l. c. sed ut occasionem patrandi miraculi haberet. Similem proinde hunc locum esse putant illi Genes. 18, 21. Conf. Ioh. 6. v. 5. 6. Quòd verò aliàs Christus secundùm adsumtam humanam naturam in statu exinanitionis quaedam reverà ignorarit, alibi ostenditur. Vid. Anal. ad Marc. 13, 32. ac Conf. B. D. Fewrborn. Synt. 2. p. 429. Graviter a. hallucinantur Iudaei, quando ex ignorantiâ illâ, quâ Christus homo & quidem in statu exinanitionis, quaedam reverà ignoravit, (non ex imperfectione aliquâ, sed liberâ voluntate, neque ex ignorantiâ pravae dispositionis, sed simplicis negationis) veram Christi Deitatem impugnant, quam tamen satis vel hoc ipso loco Salvator noster probavit, quando unico vero ac solo mandato effecit, ut ficus exaruerit. Id quod non nisi divinâ virtute fieri potuit. Ut iam nunc taceamus ingentia Christi miracula alia plurima, ut quòd mortuos resuscitârit, aquā in vinum mutârit, Diabolos ex obsessis eiecerit &c. Quae omnia veram Christi Deitatem luculenter confirmant. Licet verò Christus in statu exinanitionis quaedam reverà ignorarit, certum tamen est, quòd adsumtae humanae Christi naturae in primo statim incarnationis momento omniscientia divina verè ac realiter fuerit communicata. Neque tamen hinc sequitur, quòd etiam essentialiter. Nec ita licet inferre cum Danaeo, (quem reliqui Calviniani, ficuti & Iesuitae plerumque sequuntur:) Omniscientia Christi aut essentialiter humanae naturae adsumtae communicata fuit, aut accidentaliter. Si illud, anima Christi Deus constituitur, & quidem novus ac recens; si hoc, accidentaliter, tum communicata fuit per effusionem! Respondemus enim, dari terrium, communicationem nempe personalem. Quod ipsum si rectè perpendisset Iesuita Conzen, faciliùs se è Danaei obiectionibus extricare potuisset. Quod verò idem cum Gretsero suo statuit, animam Christi -reatâ (saltem) non verò increatâ scientiâ donatam esse, in eo haut levitet errat. Vid. quae hanc in rem disputat B. Par. lib. 2. Conf. Cath. part. 1. art, 2. c. 1. & 2.)*

*( Nisi folia. Arbori hinc similes sunt hypocritae. Vid. 2. Tim. 3, 5. Iudae ep. v. 12.)*

Ne posthac ex te fructus nascatur. Nicephorus lib. 1. Histor. Ecclesiast. c. 27. Cùm ficui nullus inesset fructus, ultima statim ei per execrationem imprecatur, utpote quae autor primùm & transgressionis fuerit. (Alludit eò, quòd primi parentes de fructu ficûs gustasse censentur.) Et postea Fortasse autem ficuista arescens involucro quodam Synagogae Iudaeorum sterilitatem ferendorumfructuum inopiam expressit. Et profectò omnis anima rationalis incredulitati & diffidentiae in Christum obnoxia, etiamsi legibus litterae tanquam foliis admodùm florere existimetur: tametsi lege fidei in Christum, quâ illa maximè nutritur, & fovetur, excidat, longè à benedictione DEI dissita exarescit. Maledictio illa, de quâ hîc, non est profecta ex intempestivâ quadam bilis effervescentiâ vel vindictae cupiditate, sed voluit Christus denotare 1. populi Israëlitici exitium, utpote quae nullis, ne quidem ex puerorum ore profectis admonitionibus se patiatur emendari. *(Existimat Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 1. epist. 358. & 359. Christum cùm tertiò ad ficulneam se contulisset, nec fructum in eâ invenisset, illi male dixisse, atque hoc ipso indicasse, quòd hommes ter Deum reiecerint, 1. primaevi mandati de non comedendo fructu arboris veritae transgressione. 2. vituli aurei adoratione. 3. Christi reiectione, dicentes: Non habemus Regem &c.)* 2. fidei virtutem, quam rationem ipse Christus v. 21. exponit. Vid. Tossanus in h. l. Folia ficûs significant hypocrysin Genes. 3. *(Coeterùm quomodo Prophetae aliique sancti viri aliquando tum hominibus, tum aliis quoque rebus maledixerint, & imprecati fuerint, suo discutietur loco. Vid. B. D. Balduinus in Casibus Conscient. Cumprimis verò prolixè hac de re agunt Scholastici. Evolvantur, si lubet, Thomas de Aquino in Summa 2. 2. 9. 76. att. 1. seqq. Gregorius de Valentiâ, Comment. Theolog. t. 3. Disp. 5. 9. 19. de Maledict. puncto 1. & 2. Franciscus Fevardentius ad v. 9. Epist. Iudae. Consuli quoque possunt Commentatores alii tum ad h. l. tum ad Gen. 3, 17.Deuter. 28, 16.2. Reg. 1, 21. Sed quaeritur hîc 1. Cur Christus ficui maledixerit, cùm tamen, uti Marcus c. 11, 13. prodit, ficorum tempus h. c. ut fructum ferrent, nondum advenisset? Respondet Dn. D. Waltherus, fecisse hoc Christum parabolicè. Quaesivisse de industriâ fructum in ficu, quam fructum non habere sciverit, quia etiam quaerit fructum ab homine, quem itidem fructu carere scit. Eodem modo respondet Dn. D. Friedlieb pag. 211. qui tamen, sicuti etiam Dn. D. Muellerus, in Iudaismo p. 982. cum Nicephoro, Augustino Qq. Evang. c. 68. Beda in c. 11. Marci, Emisseno homil Fur. 3. post pr. Domin. Gregorio l. 8. cap. 42. in specie de populo Iudaico accipit, quòd nempe Salvator cum desiderio Iudaeorum conversionem ac fructus poenitentiae in illis quaesiverit, sed nil nisi folia infructuosa vanae gloriationis apud eos invenerit &c. Distingvit tamen etiam Dn. D. Mullerus inter diversos ficûs fructus, quâ de re actum suprà ad verba: nihil invenit. Q. 2. Cur Christus ficui male dixerit, cum tamen non peccarit? Respondet Athanasius tom. 2. in dict. & parab. Ev. Interpret. q. 22 fecisse hoc Christum ad declarandam discipulis suis suam omnipotētiam, quòdq; hostes suos, qui iam ipsum erant crucifixuri, facilè posset ariditate percutere, nisi potiùs venisset adservandum genus human--, quàm ad perdendum. Discamus verò hinc, honorum operum sterilitatem ariditate h. e. gratiae divinae foecundantis ablatione puniti. Conf. Ebr. 6, 8.

Neque verò reprehendi praesens Christi, ficui maledicentis, factum ullâ ratione potest, cùm ipse ut verus Deus ac rerum omnium creator potestatem habeat, omnia in nihilum redigendi. Neque tamen absque causa hoc fecit: eo ipso enim manifestavit suam gloriam, quòd nempe sit rerum omnium Dominus, quòdque omnia stent ad eius nutum. Conf. Matth. 8, 26.c. 28, 18. Ipsum igitur revereamur, timeamus, & ad ipsum confugiamus.)*

## 21:20
v. 20. Πρς έξηρανθη Παραχρημα η συκῆ. Casaubon advises that, for the sake of avoiding ambiguity, it should rather be translated: how did the fig tree wither at once? than with others: in what manner &c. since τόπως here is not of one asking, but of one admiring. *(Evang. Mark c. 13, 20. hints that the Apostles discovered this only on the following day, how therefore is it said here that it Παραχρημα withered at once? Augustine answers in lib. 3. de Consens. Evang. c. 68. although the disciples observed only on the following day that the fig tree had been dried up from the roots, as Mark has it in the said place, yet they noticed at once that the leaves of the fig tree had withered.)*

Latin:

v. 20. Πρς έξηρανθη Παραχρημα η συκῆ. Casaubonus monet, vitandae ambiguitatis causâ vertendum potiùs esse: ut statim exaruit ficus? quàm cum aliis: quomodo &c. cùm τόπως hîc non sit quaerentis, sed admirantis. *(Evang. Marcus c. 13, 20. innuit, postero demum die Apostolos hoc deprehendisse, quomodo igitur hîc dicitur, quòd statim Παραχρημα exaruerit? Respondet Augustinus lib. 3. de Consens. Evang. c. 68. licet discipuli postero demum die observarint, quòd ficus radicitùs fuerit arefacta, ceu habet Marcus d. l. statim tamen eos animadvertisse, quòd folia ficûs aruerint.)*

## 21:21
*(v. 21. And you shall not hesitate. Parallel places are 1. Tim. 2, 8.Ebr. 11, 4. following Iacob. 1, 6. This promise must indeed be understood concerning prayers which are made according to the will of GOD, that is, which lean upon the word of GOD. Conf. B. D. Fewrborn. Synt. 2. p. 590. 591. also Annot. above on c. 7, 7. We also learn from this place that faith is not correctly defined by hesitation. Against Bell,)*

*( If you shall say to this mountain. Jerome on this place The dogs of the Gentiles bark against us in their volumes, asserting that the Apostles did not have faith, because they could not move mountains. What shall we answer? That many signs were done by the Lord according to the testimony of John ( c. 20.) which if they were written, the world could not contain, that is, that they could not bear the magnitude of the signs in the face of miracles and incredulity. Therefore we also believe that the Apostles did these things, but that they were not written for this reason, lest a greater occasion for contradicting be given to the unfaithful. Otherwise let us ask them whether they believe these signs which the writings narrate, or not? And when we have seen them to be incredulous, we shall consequently prove that they would not have believed greater things, who did not believe lesser ones. Furthermore, let us understand the mountain to be the proud devil, which is called a corrupt mountain by the Prophet (Jerem. c. 51.) And when he has possessed the soul of a man, and has been rooted in it, he can be moved by the Apostles, and by those who are like the Apostles, into the sea, that is, into places that are salty and fluctuating and bitter, which have no sweetness of GOD, and among the mind of the incredulous, like the two thousand swine, to be suffocated. Conf. more in Anal. on c. 17, 20. To which add that the martyrologies report that by the prayers of Nonnosus a rock of huge mass was moved to Soracte. Conf. Euseb. l. 7. c. 5 Gregory Dialog. 1. c. 7. Nyssen in the life of Gregory Thaumaturgus. Thus Hugo Grotius testifies that writers not to be despised testify that something similar was performed by an Armenian Bishop, at the instance of the Babylonian Caliph in the year 1225. Grotius himself, however, thinks that Christ speaks here at least proverbially, and that the sense is, you will perform the most difficult things, and nothing will be so high that it will not vanish at your prayers. And B. D. Hunnius accepts it in this way, adding that it can also be accepted so that the species of miracle is put for the genus: but as far as concerns us, not unless spiritually can that promise of Christ be accommodated to us, so that we are said to move mountains when we overcome the height of diabolical temptations by faith, so that the gates of hell cannot harm us. Matth. 16. It is asked, however, how does Christ attribute to little faith the moving of mountains, but the Apostle1. Cor. 13, 2.seems to refer this very thing to the greatest faith? Ans. The Savior speaks of faith necessary for performing miracles; but the Apostle speaks of the faith of miracles in comparison to saving faith.)*

Latin:

*(v. 21. Et non haesitaveritis. Loca parall. sunt 1. Tim. 2, 8.Ebr. 11, 4. seqq. Iacob. 1, 6. Intelligenda verò promissio haec de precibus, quae iuxta DEI voluntatem fiunt h. e. verbo DEI innituntur. Conf. B. D. Fewrborn. Synt. 2. p. 590. 591. it. Annot. suprà ad c. 7, 7. Discimus quoque ex h. l. quòd fides non rectè per dubitationem definiatur. Contra Bell,)*

*( Si monti huic dixeritis. Hieronymus in h. l. Latrant contra nos gentilium canes in suis voluminibus, adserentes, Apostolos non habuisse fidem, quia montes transferre non potuerint. Quid respondebimus? multa facta esse signa à Domino iuxta Iohannis testimonium ( c. 20.) quae si scripta essent, mundus capere non posset, h. e. quòd magnitudinem signorum prae miraculis & incredulitate ferre non possent. Igitur & haec credimus fecisse Apostolos, sed ideò scripta non esse, ne infidelibus contradicendi maior daretur occasio. Alioquin interrogemus eos, utrum credant his signis, quae scripta narrant, annon? Et cùm incredulos viderimus, consequenter probabimus, nec maioribus eos credituros fuisse, qui minoribus non crediderint. Coeterùm nos montem diabolum intelligamus superbientem, qui à Propheta (Ierem. c. 51.) mons corruptus appellatur. Et cùm animam hominis possiderit, & in eâ fuerit radicatus, ab Apostolis, & his, qui similes Apostolorum sunt, transferri potest in mare h. e. in loca salsa & fluctuantia & amara, quae nullam habent dulcedinem DEI, & apud incredulorum mentem, ut porcorum duo millia, suffocari. Conf. plura in Anal. ad c. 17, 20. Quibus adde, quòd martyrologia prodant, Nonnosi precibus ingentis molis saxum ad Soracte translatum. Conf. Euseb. l. 7. c. 5 Gregorium Dialog. 1. c. 7. Nyssenum in vitâ Gregorii Thaumaturgi. Ita Hugo Grotius testatur, Scriptores haut spernendos testari, simile quid ab Episcopo Armenio praestitum, instante Calipha Babylonio A. 1225. Ipse tamen Grotius existimat, quòd Christus saltem proverbialiter hîc loquatur, ac sensum esse, res difficillimas praestabitis, nihilq adeò erit excelsum, quod non adpreces vestras evanescat. Atque h. m. B. D. Hunnius accipit, addens, posse quoque ita accipi, ut species miraculi ponatur pro genere: quod verò ad nos attinet, non nisi spiritualiter promissionem illam Christi accommodari ad nos posse, ut tum transferre dicamur montes, quando altitudinem tentationum diabolicarum fide superamus, ut portae inferorum nocere nobis nequeant. Matth. 16. Quaeritur autem, quomodo Christus exiguae fidei tribuat, montes transferre, Apostolus verò1. Cor. 13, 2.ad maximam fidem hoc ipsum referre videatur? Resp. Loquitur Salvator de fide ad miracula efficienda necessariâ; Apostolus autem de fide miraculorum in comparatione ad fidem salvificam.)*

## 21:22
(v. 22. καὶ πάνβα οσα &c. See John 14, 12. and compare the notes at v. 21. also above c. 7, 7. Especially relevant here is the passage 1 John 5, 14. where it is to be noted that we ask those things according to God's will which He Himself has defined in His word that He wishes to give to us. Hugo Grotius therefore well notes that the universal voice from the nature of the thing is to be restricted here, in this manner: if good men ask for good things, well, for a good purpose. The first restriction is taught John 9, 31. & 1 ep. 3, 21. 22. the second in this place v. 21. the third Luke 18, 1.James 1, 56.7. the fourth of James 4, 3. Although Christ here properly treats of miraculous faith, it is nevertheless well gathered from this that we ought to flee to God with prayers, and in no way doubt concerning the hearing. Conf. Psalm. 34, 7.Psalm. 50, 15.Matth. 7, 7.Ioh. 16, 24. Let us therefore persist in prayer Luc. 18, 1. and following 1. Thess. 5, 17.Coloss. 4, 2. &c.)*

Latin:

*(v. 22. καὶ πάνβα οσα &c. Vid. Ioh. 14, 12. ac confer notata ad v. 21. it. suprà c. 7, 7. Cumprimis etiam huc facit locus 1. Ioh. 5, 14. ubi notandum, quòd ea iuxta Dei voluntatem petamus, quae ipse in suo verbo definivit, quòd dare nobis velit. Hugo proinde Grotius benè notat, quòd universalis vox ex rei naturâ hîc restringēda sit, h. m. si boni petant bona, benè, ad bonum. Prima restrictio docetur Ioh. 9, 31. & 1. ep. 3, 21. 22. secunda h. l. v. 21. tertia Luc. 18, 1.Iacob. 1, 56.7. quarta Iacobi 4, 3. Licet verò Christus hîc propriè agat de fide miraculosâ, benè tamen hinc colligitur, quòd precibus ad Deum confugere debeamus, nec de exauditione ullatenus dubitare. Conf. Psalm. 34, 7.Psalm. 50, 15.Matth. 7, 7.Ioh. 16, 24. Instemus igitur oratione Luc. 18, 1. seqq. 1. Thess. 5, 17.Coloss. 4, 2. &c.)*

## 21:23
*(v. 23. πρεσβύτεροι τού λαού. Thus are called the elders of the tribes, who were admitted into the great Sanhedrin. Compare more concerning the Presbyters in Analect. on Tit. 1, 5.)*

By what authority do you do this, namely, that you teach in the temple. Some interpret this concerning the royal entry into the city and the cleansing of the temple. *(Moreover, just as the Pharisees anxiously asked Christ by what authority he cleansed the temple, and likewise from John the Baptist, Ioh. 1, 25. why he baptized: so the Pontiffs still today ask by what authority B. Luther undertook the work of reformation. To whom it is most safely answered that, just as Christ cleansed the temple because the Jews had profaned it, so those horrible abuses which had crept into the temple of the Church of God provided the handle for B. Luther for this work. Compare B. D. Hoepffn. Saxon. Evangel. p. 20. and following. Dnn. Theol. Saxon. in Fundamentali Defens. Pupillae p. 1. and following. B. Par. Confess. Cathol. lib. 1. Gener. part. 1. c. 7.)*

Latin:

*(v. 23. πρεσβύτεροι τού λαού. Ita dicuntur proceres tribuum, qui adsciscebantur in Synedrium magnum. Conf. plura de Presbyteris in Analect. ad Tit. 1, 5.)*

Ex quâ autoritate illud facis, quòd scil. in templo doces. Quidam de regio in urbem ingressu & repurgatione templi accipiunt. *(Coeterùm quemadmodum Pharisaei ex Christo solicitè quaesiverunt, ex quâ autoritate templum repurgaret, item ex Iohanne Baptista, Ioh. 1, 25. cur baptizaret: ita Pontificu adhuc hodiè quaerunt, ex quâ autoritate B. Lutherus opus reformationis susceperit. Quibus tutissimè respondetur, quod quemadmodum Christus templum purgavit, quia Iudaei illud prophanaverant, ita ansam B. Luthero ad hoc opus praebuerint horrendi illi abusus, qui in Ecclesiam Dei templū irrepserant. Conf. B. D. Hoepffn. Saxon. Evangel. p. 20. seqq. Dnn. Theol. Saxon. in Fundamentali Defens. Pupillae p. 1. seqq. B. Par. Confess. Cathol. lib. 1. Gener. part. 1. c. 7.)*

## 21:24
*(v. 24. I will ask you &c. Q. here, why did Christ not answer the proposed question before he proposed his own? Ans. Jerome in c. 14. Ezech. He does not deserve to hear the truth who asks fraudulently, but he must be caught by his own heart. Compare Proverb. 23, 9. c. 26. 4. 5. Others warn that Christ did indeed answer the proposed question, although not directly, yet indirectly. For since the Jews had impiously rejected the authority of the heavenly Father, to which he himself had hitherto appealed in his teaching (namely, that he is the promised Messiah sent by Him, that he has testimony from Him, and that therefore he deservedly cleanses the house of his Father, and rightly admits the applause of the people, who receive him as the Messiah), see Ioh. 5. and 8. he proves his divine mission here by another testimony, namely that of John, whom the Jews themselves held in high regard. But he had testified clearly enough concerning the divine office of Christ, and that he was the promised Messiah. See above c. 3. 11. 12. Ioh. 1, 26. and following. In order that this very thing may be better understood, it should be noted that a dilemma underlies the question of Christ proposed in this place. So that the Priests had to answer either that the ministry of John was at least from men, which they dared not say at all because of the crowd, because everyone held John to be a Prophet; or that it was from heaven, i.e., that he himself was a Prophet sent by God, whose testimony must be admitted entirely. If so, then Christ could firmly infer, Therefore you ought also to admit this testimony of John, because he publicly testified that I am the Messiah, to whom both the congratulation of the people and the cleansing of the temple belong by right and merit.)*

*( The Baptism of John. It is so called, not as if John baptized by private daring and without divine mission and command, but because John administered the baptism, yet by divine order and command. Thus the Gospel, which Paul preached, he calls his Gospel Rom. 2, 16.2. Tim. 2, 8. because indeed he preached it having been taught by Christ, as Corn. à Lapide explains. Therefore, the Papists, see Bell. l. 1. de Bapt. cap. 20, absurdly attempt to prove from this that the Baptism of John was not a Sacrament divinely instituted, effective for the remission of sins. For it is called the Baptism of John, because he himself, having been taught and sent by God, administered the Baptism.)*

Latin:

*(v. 24. Interrogabo vos &c. Q. hîc, cur Christus non priùs ad quaestionem propositam responderit, quàm suam proposuerit? Resp. Hieronymus in c. 14. Ezech. Non meretur veritatem audire, qui fraudulenter interrogat, sed suo corde capiendus est. Conf. Proverb. 23, 9. c. 26. 4. 5. Alii monent, quòd omninò Christus ad quaestionem propositam responderit, licet non directè, tamen indirectè. Cùm enim Iudaei Patris coelestis autoritatem, ad quam ipse in doctrinâ suâ hactenus provocaverat, (quòd nempe promissus Messias ab eo missus sit, testimonium ab illo habeat, quòdque adeò domum Patris sui meritò purget, & applausum populi, pro Messia ipsum recipientis, iure admittat,) impiè reiecissent, vid. Ioh. 5. & 8. alio testimonio divinam suam missionem hîc probat, nempe Iohannis, quem Iudaei ipsi magni faciebant. Is verò satis clarè de divino Christi officio, quòdque is promissus Messias esset, testatus fuerat. Vid. suprà c. 3. 11. 12. Ioh. 1, 26. seqq. Hoc ipsum ut rectiùs intelligatur, notandum, quòd quaestioni Christi h. l. propositae dilemma subsit. Ut adeò Sacerdotes necesse habuerint respondere, vel quòd Iohannis ministerium ab hominibus saltem fuerit, id quod minimè audebant dicere propter turbam, quia omnes Iohannnem habebant pro Prophetam; vel quòd fuerit è coelo h. e. quòd ipse à Deo missus sit Propheta, cuius testimonium omninò admittēdum sit. Si ita, firmiter tunc inferre poterat Christus, Ergo & in hoc testimoniū admittere Iohannis debetis, quia publicè testatus ille est, quòd sim Messias, cui & populi gratulatio & templi repurgatio iure merito competit.)*

*( Baptismus Iohannis. Dicitur ita, non quasi Iohannes privato ausu & absque divinâ missione ac mandato baptizarit, sed quia Iohannes baptismum administravit, iussu tamen ac mandato divino. Sic Evangelium, quod Paulus praedicavit, vocat suum Evangelium Rom. 2, 16.2. Tim. 2, 8. quia nempe praecicavit illud edoctus à Christo, uti Corn. à Lapide exponit. Ineptè proinde Pontificii, vid. Bell. l. 1. de Bapt. cap. 20. evincere hinc conantur, Baptismum Iohannis non fuisse Sacramentum divinitùs institutum, ad remissionem peccatorum efficax. Dicitur enim Baptismus Iohannis, quia ipse à Deo edoctus ac missus Baptismum administravit.)*

## 21:25
v. 25. εξ ούρανων i. e. from God, because heaven is the seat of GOD. *(R. Elias Levita in Tisbi explicitly: --- i. e. they call God, that holy blessed one, --- heaven, for the reason that they (the heavens) are his seat. Not as if God were included in heaven, or by reason of his substance were only in heaven, but because he manifests his glory primarily to the blessed. Against Vorstius. Against whom the blessed D. Martini disputes at length in Photinianismo p. 44. seqq. That indeed the word heaven is used for God, was also shown above in Analect. ad c. 3, 2. c. 5, 34. c. 6, 9. Add Angel. Caninius de Nomin. Ebr. c. 2. Dn. Dilherrus Dispp. Acad. t. 1. p. 314. 315. Buxtorff. Lex. Rabb. Talm. under the word --- Dn. D. Danhawerus in Idea Boni Interpret. p. 8Bartol. Meyerus Prodr. Philol. Sacrae part. 2. p. 169. Ioh. Drusius l. 3. Praeter. p. 102. also l. 5. Observ. c. 11. Rivetus in Ps. 2, 4. p. 12. a. But especially the following sayings are relevant here Psal. 73, 9.Daniel. 4, 23.Luc. 15, 18.21.c. 20, 4.1. Macc. 3, 18. 19.c. 4, 10.c. 12, 15.

Conf. Matth. 11, 11. with Luc. 7, 28. Iohannes Camero Myroth. Evangel. p. 230. and 355. also draws to this place 1. Cor. 15, 4. item Apoc. 18, 4. But these places are accustomed to be explained differently by others.)* Furthermore, Christ by this άντερωτησει shows that power given to him divinely according to the testimony of John, which they did not dare to repudiate, Ioh. 1, 19.26.29.c. 5, 33.35. *(Com. à Lapide in h. l. rightly warns that Christ intends this; You ask from whom I have power, from God, or from men? I in turn ask you, from whom did John the Baptist have the power of preaching and baptizing; from God, or from men? If he had that from God, as all confess &c. Add. Luc. 3, 2.Ioh. 1, 6.32. This must be opposed to the common opinion of the Papists, by which they establish that the Baptism of John was not from God, but was instituted at least by John, and therefore was not a Sacrament, effective for the remission of sins. Which error B. Par. Confess. Cathol. art. 12. c. 4. §. unâ refutes at length)*

Latin:

v. 25. εξ ούρανων i. e. â Deo, quia coelum est DEI sedes. *(R. Elias Levita in Tisbi disertè: --- i. e. vocant Deum, sanctum benedictum illum,---coelum, eô quòd ipsi (coeli) sunt sedes eius. Non quasi Deus coelo includatur. vel ratione substantiae suae tantùm in coelo sit, sed quia cumprimis beatis gloriam suam manifestat. Contra Vorstium. Quem contra latè disputat B. D. Martini in Photinianismo p. 44. seqq. Quòd vero coeli vox pro Deo adhibeatur, ostensum quoque suprà fuit in Analect. ad c. 3, 2. c. 5, 34. c. 6, 9. Adde Angel. Caninium de Nomin. Ebr. c. 2. Dn. Dilherrum Dispp. Acad. t. 1. p. 314. 315. Buxtorff. Lex. Rabb. Talm. roce --- Dn. D. Danhawerum Ideâ Boni Interpret. p. 8Bartol. Meyerum Prodr. Philol. Sacrae part. 2. p. 169. Ioh. Drusium l. 3. Praeter. p. 102. it. l. 5. Observ. c. 11. Rivetum in Ps. 2, 4. p. 12. a. Cumprimis verò huc faciunt dicta seqq. Psal. 73, 9.Daniel. 4, 23.Luc. 15, 18.21.c. 20, 4.1. Macc. 3, 18. 19.c. 4, 10.c. 12, 15.

Conf. Matth. 11, 11. cum Luc. 7, 28. Iohannes Camero Myroth. Evangel. p. 230. ac 355. trahit quoque huc locum 1. Cor. 15, 4. item Apoc. 18, 4. Verùm loca haec ab aliis aliter exponi solent.)* Coeterùm Christus hâc άντερωτησει ostendit, potestatem illam sibi divinitùs datam iuxta testimonium Iohannis, quod ipsi repudiare non audebant, Ioh. 1, 19.26.29.c. 5, 33.35. *(Com. à Lapide in h. l. rectè monet, Christum hoc velle; Vos quaeritis à quo potestatem habeam, à Deo, an ab hominibus? ego vicissim quaero à vobis, à quo praedicandi & baptizandi potestatem habuit Iohannes Baptista; à Deo, an ab hominibus? Si ille istam à Deo habuit, utomnes confitentur &c. Add. Luc. 3, 2.Ioh. 1, 6.32. Opponendum hoc communi Pontificiorum sentetiae, quâ statuunt, Iohannis Baptisma non fuisse à Deo, sed saltem à Iohanne fuisse institutum, adeoque nec fuisse Sacramentum, ad remissionem peccatorum efficax. Quem errorem prolixè refellit B. Par. Confess. Cathol. art. 12. c. 4. §. unâ)*

## 21:26
*(v. 26. Πάντες έχούσι Laur. Valla rightly warns that the Vulgate Interpreter less correctly translates τό έχούσι by they had. For the Evangelist does not speak from his own opinion, but indicates what the Chief Priests thought among themselves. Whence Arias Montanus & Erasmus more correctly translate they have.)*

Latin:

*(v. 26. Πάντες έχούσι Rectè Laur. Valla monet, Vulgatum Interpr. minùs rectè τό έχούσι vertere per habebant. Etenim Evangelista non ex suâ loquitur sententiâ, sed indicat, quid Pontifices secum cogitarint. Unde rectiùs Arias Montanus & Erasmus vertunt habent.)*

## 21:27
*(v. 27. We do not know. They are lukewarm men, concerning whom Ioh. 12, 42.Apoc. 3, 15 16.)*
