## 22:11
(v. 11. Having entered. This inspection will be instituted finally at the last judgment. Conf. above c. 19, 39. 40. 49.) Not having a wedding garment The wedding garment is true faith in Christ, which is effective through charity, Isa. 61, 10.Gal. 3, 27. Rev. 19, 7. Osiander: That wedding garment is Christ, whom we put on when we apprehend his most absolute merit by true faith, and when we strive to imitate his innocence in our whole conversation. (Similarly, from our own people, Mr. Dr. Friedlieb explains this in this place, and also from the Calvinists, Gomarus. Nor does it stand in the way that Christ is himself the Bridegroom and the food. Since he is so called in a different respect. Just as elsewhere he is called the victim, priest, altar &c.) Basil in c. 9. Isaiah t. 3. p. 448. Truly the garment of Christians, covering the baseness of our sin, is faith, by which we believe in Christ. For whoever of you have been baptized into Christ, have put on Christ. Ambrose l. 4. on faith c. 1. calls it the wedding garment of faith. Chrysost. hom. 41. Imperfect Work t. 2. col. 1043. the wedding garment is true faith. Conf. Augustine l. 1. Qq. Evang. q. 13. also lib. 15. on the Trinity c. 8. Hilary c. 24. in Matt. Gregory homil. 38. on the Gospel also Isa. 61, 10.Col. 3, 10.2 Cor. 5, 3.Eph. 4, 24. (This garment of the righteousness of Christ covers all sins, Ps. 32, 1. Becanus, in book 1 of his Manual of Controversies, chapter 16, does not try to prove inherent righteousness from this passage firmly enough, understanding by the wedding garment the gift of charity, which the Holy Spirit pours into our hearts. Although, as has been shown thus far, faith ought to be understood by that garment. Indeed, those things through which we are regenerated, renewed, and thus please God, are accustomed to be compared to garments in the Holy Scriptures, as is evident from Isa. 61, 10. Rom. 13, 14. 2 Cor. 5, 24. Gal. 3, 27. Eph. 4, 24. Col. 3, 12. Rev. 16, 15. Furthermore, Cornelius à Lapide, in his Commentary on this passage, opposes our exposition, which is that of the most ancient Doctors of the Church, by which indeed the wedding garment is understood as true faith in Christ, that is, the fiducial apprehension of the merit of Christ, arguing that all in this banquet of the Church have faith, indeed they could not have entered into it except through faith. Therefore, he continues, this garment is charity, and the probity and holiness of morals: for a pure and holy life is like a clean garment. And thus he advises that Hilary, Chrysostom, Tertullian, and others explain it. Felicianus Capitonus of Narni, Archbishop of Avignon, in his Catholic Explication, p. 596, urges for the same opinion the authority of Gregory the Great in his Homily on this passage. He adds, moreover, that the parable in Matt. 25 concerning the ten virgins favors this opinion, of whom five are wise, because they hold faith and the works of charity; the rest, however, are foolish, because they have faith, but do not hold charity. For, he writes, if they did not have faith, they would not say, Lord, Lord, open to us etc. He adds that the sayings in Matt. 7, 21 and James 2, 19 favor the same opinion. But it must be known that when we say that faith is to be understood by the wedding garment, we are by no means speaking either of historical faith, for it is evident from Jas. 2, 19 that even the devils have such, or of hypocritical faith, but of true faith. 2. Nor of faith separated from good works or charity, of which Matt. 7 and 25 speak, but of that which is efficacious through charity. (Explicitly, the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, p. 73: Love and works follow faith. Wherefore they are not excluded in such a way that they do not follow, but the confidence of the merit of love or works is excluded in justification. Let the Epitome of Controversial Articles, page 586, and likewise the Solid Repetition, page 692, be compared entirely.)

For we do not exclude good works, even in the very article of Justification, from by the act of presence, but by the communication of efficiency, nor that they are denied to be present to faith and the justified, but that they are denied to cooperate with faith in the act of justification, as B. Par. Conf. Cath. art. 23. c. 3. §. 1, and L. de Iustif. §. 191, teach at length. But we deny that all who live in the external assembly of the Church, and enter into the Church through calling, have such a faith, which is efficacious through charity. They have it indeed by reason of knowledge, but not by reason of trust. We readily grant that he had the former and was this unworthy guest: but we deny that he had a true and living faith, which consists in the trustful apprehension of the merit of Christ . For if he had had this, he would also have had charity , since a true and living faith is always fruitful and efficacious through charity, Gal. 5, 6. nay, that also convinces, that this guest was cast into outer darkness, i.e., eternally damned. Now, however, he who believes in Christ, that is, has true faith, is not condemned, Ioh. 2, 18. and Marc. 16, 16. And St. Gregory the Great also looked to this when he explains not having a wedding garment, as having faith, i.e., an external profession of faith or hypocritical faith, not works of charity. Similarly, the other Fathers to whom Cornelius appeals are also to be understood. It is, however, well to be noted that it is one thing to ask whether good works are required of the guests of the heavenly wedding by reason of presence, and another whether they are required by the same reason of efficiency, and by reason of merit. But if Hugo Grotius understands it in the former way, who wishes the wedding garment here to be a walk worthy of the vocation, Ephes 4, 1 likewise works, which make the calling sure, 2. Petr. 1, 10. he does not have us as opponents. For we do not deny that the pious and those who believe in Christ, by whose righteousness alone we are saved, also put him on through a holy conversation of life, Rom. 13, 14. But it is by no means necessary that with the same Grotius we should understand by σιχαιόμαεεοα τόν άγιω Apoc. 19, 8. absolutely works testifying to our obedience: nay rather, by the same is primarily understood the righteousness of Christ, which alone justifies us, and is imputed to us through faith. Es. 6, 10. Gal. 3, 27. But why is mention made here of only one, when nevertheless very many called ones live in the external assembly of the Church who lack the wedding garment? The answer is made to this 1. because the same judgment is for similar ones, and this one was a mirror of the others. 2. so that it may be signified that not even one impious person and hypocrite can escape the sight of the omniscient judge. Furthermore, from the fact that the Church militant is compared with a banquet, at which are present not only those clothed with a wedding garment, but also those lacking and destitute of it, our people gather, that there are some not holy in the external assembly of the Church. Whence according to August. Post. Collat. against the Donatists ch. 20. in this one, who lacks the wedding garment, the great body of all the evil is figured, mixed into the Lord's banquet before the judgment of the Lord. Conf. a little later the note to v. 12. And other parables also look to this, above ch. 13, 24. 37. 47. below chapter 25, 22. likewise the similitudes Matth 3, 10.1. Tim. 15. and especially the clear testimonies of Scripture, above c. 7, 21.c. 18, 7.c. 20, 16.Ioh. 8, 39. etc. But it by no means follows: In the Church, i.e., in the external assembly of the Church, there are given good and evil, i.e., those conspicuous by the wedding garment and those lacking the same, therefore there is not given an invisible Church, consisting of only the good, as the Jesuit Costerus in Enchirid. Controv. p 106 infers. For it is to be noted that the Church is considered in two ways, by reason of internal union with Christ, and in this way it is said to be invisible, and to consist of only the good; and again by reason of external conversation, in which way it is indeed visible, and consists of the evil as well as the good. The same Jesuit concludes with a very weak consequence, since the faithful are distinguished from the unfaithful; that if sinners lack faith, it follows that they are unfaithful, separated from the Church after the manner of the Heathens, when nevertheless Holy Scripture testifies in many places that sinners belong to the Church. Which very thing the Jesuit also strives to prove among other things from the present passage. But we repeat the distinction between the Church, considered by reason of internal union with Christ its head, and external profession. Now if it is asked whether sinners, i.e., those sinning against knowledge and conscience, belong to the Church, then it is granted concerning the Church considered in the latter way, but by no means concerning the Church considered in the former way. Next, distinguish between sinners considered by reason of present state, and by reason of divine election. Someone can in the latter way be a member of the invisible Catholic Church, who nevertheless in the former way can by no means be held as a member of it. And finally distinguish between faith taken for mere knowledge or naked cognition (or even assent) of divine things, and faith taken for trust or the fiducial apprehension of the merit of Christ. We teach that by sins committed against knowledge and conscience, faith is not shaken off in the former, but in the latter sense taken. It is evident therefore that it does not follow that such sinners, inasmuch as they have been regenerated through Baptism and received into the bosom of the Church, and who dwell in the external assembly of the Church, and furthermore have the form of a pious and Christian life, do not cease to be members of the visible Church, or the reason for these and the Heathens is not the same, therefore they have true faith, and thus are and remain members of the invisible Church, namely by reason of their present state. But especially it is to be noted that on account of a lack of trust someone is not immediately called unfaithful, in that sense namely in which Pagans and Heathens are called unfaithful, because these are destitute of the Christian faith, even by reason of knowledge, they have never been members of the visible Church, nor do they enjoy the same Sacraments as the truly faithful; on the contrary, however, those who are called unfaithful on account of the sole lack of the fiducial apprehension of the merit of Christ or of saving faith, yet live in the external assembly of the Church, and use the same Sacraments as the truly faithful, as hypocrites are wont to do, are and remain entirely members of the visible Church.)*

Latin:

*(v. 11. Ingressus. Haec lustratio instituetur demum in extremo iudicio. Conf. suprà c. 19, 39. 40. 49.)* Non vestitum veste nuptiali Vestis nuptialis est vera in Christum fides, quae per charitatem efficax eft, Es. 61, 10.Gal. 3, 27. Apocal. 19, 7. Osiander: Vestis illa nuptialis Christus est, quem induimus, quando verâ fide absolutissimum eius meritum apprehendimus, & quando in totâ nostrâ conversatione ipsius innocentiam imitari studemus. *(Similiter ex nostratibns exponit Dn. D. Friedlieb in h. l. nec non ex Calvinianis Gomarus. Nec obstat, quòd Christus sit ipse Sponsus & cibus. Cùm diverso respectu ita vocetur. Sicut alibi victima, sacerdos, altare &c. dicitur.)* Basilius in c. 9. Esai. t. 3. p. 448. Sanè Christianorum vestimentum, obnubens peccati nostri turpitudinem, fides est, quâ in Christum credimus. Quicunenim in Christum baptizati estis, Christum induistis. Ambrosius l. 4. de fide c. 1. vocat nuptiale fidei vestimentum. Chrysost. hom. 41. Oper. Imperf. t. 2. col. 1043. nuptiale vestimentum est fides vera. Conf. August. l. 1. Qq. Evang. q. 13. it. lib. 15. de Trinit. c. 8. Hilarius c. 24. in Matth. Gregorius homil. 38. in Evangel. it. Es. 61, 10.Coloss. 3, 10.2. Cor. 5, 3.Eph. 4, 24. *(Haec vestis iustitiae Christi tegit omnia peccata, Ps. 32, 1. Haut satis proinde firmiter Becanus lib. 1. Manual. Controv. c. 16. iustitiam in haerentem ex hoc probare loco conatur, intelligens per vestem nuptialem donum charitatis, quod Sp. Sanctus diffundat in cordibus nostris. Cum tamen, ut hactenus ostensum est, per vestem illam intelligi fides debeat. Solent verò ea, per quae regeneramur, renovamur, adeoque placemus, cum vestimentis in Sc. S. conferri, ceu patet ex Esa. 61, 10.Rom 13, 14.2. Cor. 5, 24.Gal. 3, 27.Ephes. 4, 24.Coloss. 3, 12.Apoc. 16, 15. Coeterùm Corn. à Lapide Comment. in h. l. expositioni nostrae, quae antiquissimorum Ecclesiae Doctorum est, quâ nempe per vestem nuptialem intelligitur vera in Christum fides h. e. fiducialis meriti Christi apprehensio, opponit, quòd omnes in hoc Ecclesiae convivio habeant fidem, imò non nisi per fidem in illud ingredi potuerint. Ergo, pergit, vestis haec est charitas, morumque probitas & sanctitas: Vita enim pura & sancta est instar vestis mundae. Atque ita Hilarium, Chrysostomum, Tertullianum & alios exponere monet. Felicianus Capitonus Narniensis, Archi Episcopus Avinionensis, Explic. Cathol. p. 596. pro eadem sententiâ urget autoritatem Gregorii M. in Homil. super h. l. Addit praeterea, quòd sententiae huic faveat parabola Matth. 25. de decem virginibus, quarum quinque sint prudentes, quia fidem & charitatis opera teneant; reliquae autem fatisae, quia fidem habeant, charitatem autem non teneant. Senim, scribit, fidem non haberent, non utidicerent, Domine, Domire, aperi nobis &c. Eidem sententiae favere subdit, dicta Matth. 7, 21. ac Iacobi 2, 19. Verùm sciendum, quòd quando per vestem nuptialem fidem intelligendum esse dicimus, tunc minimè loquamur sive de fide historicâ, talem enim & diabolos habere, ex Iac. 2, 19. constat, sive de fide hypocritica, sed de vera. 2. nec de fide, à bonis operibus sive charitate separata, de quâ Matth. 7. & 25, sed quae per charitatem est efficax. (Disertè Apologia Augustanae Confessionis p. 73. Dilectio & opera s-qui fidem debent. Quare non sic excluduntur, ne sequantur, sed fiducia meriti dilectionis aut operum in iustificatione excluditur. Conferatur omninò Epitome Articul. Controv. pag. 586, item Solida Repetitio pag. 692.)

Neque enim excludimus, etiam in ipso Iustificationis articulo, bona opera ab actu praesentiae, sed à communicatione efficientiae, Nec ut adesse fidei & iustificatis, sed ut fidei in actu iustificationis cooperari negentur, ceu prolixè docet B. Par. Conf. Cath. art. 23. c. 3. §. 1 add. L. de Iustif. §. 191. Talem verò fidem, quae per charitatem efficax est, omnes, qui in externo Ecclesiae coetu vivūt, & per vocationem in Ecclesiam ingrediuntur, habere negamus. Habent quidem ratione notitiae, non verò ratione fiduciae. Illam & ho spitem hunc indignum habuisse, facilè largimur: sed quòd veram & vivam fidem, quae in fiduciali meriti Christi apprehēsione con---tit, habuerit, negamus. Hanc n. si habuisset, caritatem quoq; h--uisset, cùm vera & viva sides semper sit frugifera & efficax per charitatem, Gal. 5, 6. quin illud quoq; convincit, quòd cōiectus fuerit hospes ille in tenebras exteriores, h. e. aeternùm damnatus. Iam verò qui in Christum credit, hoc est, veram habet fidem, nō condemnatur, Ioh. 2, 18. add. Marc. 16, 16. Et huc quoq; respexit S. Gregorius M. quando TÒ non habentem vestem nuptialī explicat, fidem habentem, h. e. externam fidei professionem seu fidem hypocriticam, non opera charitatis. Similiter coeteri quoque intelligendi Patres sunt, ad quos Cornelius provocat. Probè autem notandum, quòd aliud sit, quaerere, an B. O. requirantur à convivis coelestium nuptiarum ratione praesentiae, aliud verò an requirantur eadem ratione efficientiae, ac ratione meriti. Quod si priori modo intelligit Hugo Grotius, qui vult vestem nuptialem hîc esse ambulationem dignam vocatione,Ephes 4, 1 item opera, quae ratam faciunt vocationem,2. Petr. 1, 10. non habet nos repugnantes. Neque enim negamus, quòd pii & credentes in Christum, cuius iustitiâ unicè salvamur, induant etiam eum per sanctam vitae cōversationem, Rom. 13, 14. Hautquaquam verò necesse est, ut cum eodem Grotio per σιχαιόμαεεοα τόν άγιωApoc. 19, 8. intelligamus absolutè opera obedientiam nostram testantia: imò potiùs per eadem cumprimis intelligitur iustitia Christi, quae sola nos iustificat, & per fidem nobis imputatur. Es. 6, 10.Gal. 3, 27.Sed cur unius saltem hîc fit mentio, cùm tamen plurimi vocati in externo Ecclesiae coetu vivant, qui veste nuptiali carent? Resp. fit hoc proptereà 1. quia idem iudicium de similibus est, & hic speculum fuit coeterorum. 2. ut significetur, ne unum quidem impium & hypocritam iudicis omniscii conspectum effugere posse. Porrò ex eo. quòd Ecclesia militans confertur cum convivio, cui intersunt non solùm veste nuptiali induti, sed eâ etiam carentes ac destituti, colligunt nostrates, esse in externo Ecclesiae coetu quosdam non sanctos. Unde iuxta August. Post. Collat. contra Donatistas c. 20. in hoc uno. qui veste nuptiali caret, grande corpus figuratur omnium malorum, ante Domini iudicium convivio Dominico permixtorum. Conf. paullò post not. ad v. 12. Et huc spectant quoque parabolae aliae, suprà c. 13, 24. 37. 47. infrà cap. 25, 22. item similitudines Matth 3, 10.1. Tim. 15. ac cumprimis clara Scripturae testimonia, suprà c. 7, 21.c. 18, 7.c. 20, 16.Ioh. 8, 39. &c. Hautquaquam verò sequitur: In Ecclesia h. e. in externo Ecclesiae coetu dantur boni & mali h. e. veste nuptiali conspicui & eâdem carentes, ergo non datur Ecclesia invisibilis, solis bonis constans, prout Iesuita Costerus in Enchirid. Controv. p 106. infert. Etenim notandum, quòd Ecclesia dupliciter consideretur, ratione coniunctionis cum Christo internae, atque hoc modo dicitur invisibilis, ac solis bonis constare; & iterum ratione conversationis externae, quomodo utique visibilis est, ac malis iuxta bonisque constat. Idem Iesuita infirmâ admodùm sequelâ colligit, cùm fideles ab infidelibus distinguantur; quòd sifide careant peccatores, sequi, fore eos infideles, adt-more Ethnicorum ab Ecclesiâ separatos, cùm tamen Scriptura S. multis in locis testetur, peccatores ad Ecclesiam pertinere. Quod ipsum etiam inter alia è praesenti loco Iesuita probare saragit. Verùm repetimus distinctionem inter Ecclesiam, consideratam ratione coniunctionis cum Christo capite suo internae, & professionis externae. Iam si quaeritur, an peccatores h. e. contra scientiam & conscientiam peccantes ad Ecclesiam pertineant, tum de Ecclesia posteriori modo consideratâ conceditur, nequaquam verò modo consideratâ priori. Deinde disting. inter peccatores consideratos ratione statûs praesentis, & ratione divinae electionis. Potest aliquis posteriori modo membrum esse Ecclesiae Catholicae invisibilis, qui tamen priori modo minimè pro membro eius haberi potest. Ac tandem disting. inter fidem acceptam pro solâ notitiâ sive nudâ rerum divinarum cognitione (vel etiam adsensu,) & inter fidem sumtam pro fiduciâ sive fiduciali meriti Christi apprehēsione. Per peccata contra scientiam ac conscientiam commissa, fidem non priori, sed posteriori sensu acceptam excuti docemus. Patet igitur, quòd non sequatur, tales peccatores, utpote qui per Baptismum regeniti sunt & in Ecclesiae gremium recepti, quique in externo Ecclesiae coetu versantur, ac formam praeterea habent piae & Christianae vitae, non desinunt esse membra Ecclesiae visibilis, vel non eadem horum ac Ethnicorum ratio est, ergo habent fidem veram, adeoque sunt ac manent membra Ecclesiae invisibilis, puta ratione statûs praesentis. Cumprimis verò notandum, quòd propter carentiam fiduciae non statim aliquis dicatur infidelis, eo nempe sensu, quô Pagani & Ethnici infideles dicuntur, quia hi Christianâ fide, etiam ratione notitiae destituuntur, nunquam Ecclesiae visibilis membra fuerunt, nec iisdem gaudent cum verè fidelibus Sacramentis; è contra verò qui ob solam fiducialis meriti Christi apprehensionis sive fidei salvificae carentiam infideles dicuntur. in externo tamen Ecclesiae coetu vivunt, iisdemq; Sacramentis cum verè fidelibus utuntur, ceu hypocritae solent, omninò Ecclesiae visibilis membra sint ac maneant.)*

## 22:12
v. 12. Εταίρε. It is not a word of love, but of status. He names him friend by άντίθρασιν. Matth. 26, 50. the Savior says to Judas έταίρε έθ όν πάρει. *(Jerome thinks that by this very name He convicts that guest of impudence, in that he, having been invited in a friendly manner, came in a rustic manner, namely without a wedding garment.)*

How did you enter here i. e. how do you dare to profess yourself a believer, why do you seek a place in Ecclesiastical congregations &c.

έθιμόθη. As if a halter had been thrown on him, he was forced to be silent. For θημός is a halter for horses. Gregory hom. 28. Then every argument of excuse ceases, when He rebukes from without, who as a witness of the conscience accuses the soul from within. Origen: What he says here to one, he wishes to be understood as said against all others: for he spoke singularly of one only, because all are of one kind, who keep malice after the faith, which they had before the faith. *(The passage Rom. 1, 20. also applies here. For if the Gentiles, who were at least called by the light of nature, are inexcusable, because they held the truth in unrighteousness, how much more will those, who have been called by the voice of the Gospel, and yet have held the truth in unrighteousness, be inexcusable one day, and thus will be silent in that severe judgment.)*

Latin:

v. 12. Εταίρε. Non est verbum amoris, sed statûs. Nominat amicum per άντίθρασιν.Matth. 26, 50. dicit Salvator ad Iudam έταίρε έθ όν πάρει. *(Hieronymus existimat, quòd hoc ipso nomine impudentiae arguat illum hospitem, eò quod amicè invitatus rusticè venerit, absque veste nempe nuptiali.)*

Quomodo huc intrasti i. e. quomodo audes, te profiteri fidelem, cur in congregationibus Ecclesiasticis locum quaeris &c.

έθιμόθη. Quasi iniecto capistro obmutescere coactus fuit. θημός enim est capistrum equorum. Gregorius hom. 28. Tunc cessat omne argumentum excusationis, quando ille foris increpat, qui testis conscientiae intus animum accusat. Origenes: Quod hîc dicit ad unum, id contra omnes alios dictum vult: ideò enim singulariter dixit de uno tantùm, quia unius generis sunt omnes, qui servant malitiam post fidem, quam habuerant ante fidem. *(Facit etiam huc locus Rom. 1, 20. Quod si verò Gentiles, qui saltem per lumen naturae vocati, inexcusabiles sunt, quòd veritatem in iniustitiâ detinuerunt, quantò magis illi, qui per vocem Evangelii vocati sunt, & tamen veritatē in iniustitiâ, detinuerunt, inexcusabiles olim erūt, adeoq; in severo illo iudicio obmutescēt.)*

## 22:13
v. 13. Bind his hands and feet &c. By this emblem it is signified that from the damned every faculty and every power is taken away, both to resist divine vengeance and to do anything good thereafter.) ( Ἄρατε αὐτόν.

*( Αεατε αὐτὸν. Take him away. This is read in all the Greek Codices which Beza consulted. Just as also in Theophylact. But the Vulgate Latin Interpreter omitted it, and indeed also the most ancient Syriac Interpreter, just as also the Arabic and Ethiopic. The Persian, however, seems to have read it, translating the present verse thus: The King commanded his ministers that they should carry him out bound hand and foot, and cast him into darkness.)*

Cast him into the outer darkness. Gregory, book 25 of the Morals, ch. 11. Then those who are now blinded by their own perverse interior desires will be forced and cast into the outer darkness. *(To some, the darkness in this parable seems to be contrasted with the abundant light of torches and lamps by which dining rooms are illuminated. Others judge that by it is denoted a prison, which is for the most part a dark place. Thus below in ch. 25, he who had buried the entrusted talent is ordered to be thrust out into the outer darkness, where, however, no mention of a banquet preceded.)*

εχότος τό έξότεεον. Camer. takes εις τόν σχοσινόν τόπον, τι ίξω as into a dark place further out. *(Compare the Analysis on ch. 25, 30. Gregory the Great, homily 38. Interior darkness is the blindness of the heart; exterior is the night of eternal damnation. Darkness is called that is outer, i.e., outermost, because it is most remote from the region of light. St. Peter mentions that the same punishment is reserved for false teachers in his second epistle, ch. 2, v. 17, just as also St. Jude, v. 13. The same Apostle delineates the future punishments of the devils in a nearly similar way in his 1st epistle, ch. 2, 4, and Jude, v. 6. Compare also above ch. 8, 12, below ch. 25, 50. Those shadows encompass and denote: 1. natural darkness, Job 38, 19. 2. spiritual darkness, i.e., blindness of the mind, ignorance, for instance, of the true God Is. 42, 2. Luke 1, 79. Eph. 5, 8 perversity of the will, and all-encompassing calamity. Note Dionysius the Carthusian, Commentary on the latter epistle of Peter, ch. 2. Wicked men in this life walk in the darkness of sins. Thence they are precipitated from the darkness of vices into the darkness of torments. Ο βρυγμός [The gnashing].

Ο βρυγμὸς. Hesychius: βρυγμὸς άπό τού βρέχειν, όέςι τούς έσόνεοας πιέζονεοα -όφονλποτε ός όν ριγει σομφαινει, ετρισμός ισόντων. To make a noise by pressing the teeth together, which happens in intense cold, or the gnashing of teeth. *( Of teeth, notes the interlinear gloss from Gregory, who rejoiced in gluttony. Furthermore, from that gnashing of teeth, some Papists infer that there will be true cold in hell. Yet they do not assign the same cause for this assertion. For some, following Jerome, Bede, and others, cited by B. Par. L. de Inferno §. 71., think that this cold proceeds from a very wide receptacle of most frigid waters in hell, into which the damned pass from the fire, snatched by demons, from which the gnashing of teeth arises. Abulensis in Matth. writes that this cold proceeds from the earth, which surrounds the damned. Because that earth is very cold, since it has nothing there from which it could be changed from its natural frigidity. But how that cold acts upon the damned the Scholastics dispute at length. Certainly hardly otherwise than if they had spent some space of time in those places. Let those things be seen which Alphonsus Mendoza exhibits on this matter from the mind of the Scholastics, Controv. Theol. q. 6. pag 499. seqq. B. Par. L. de Inferno l. c. writes that that gnashing of teeth is more correctly explained by certain ancients as concerning the envy and fury of the damned, and thus also that cold is taken improperly.)*

Latin:

*(v. 13. Ligate illi manus & pedes &c. Significatur hoc emblemate, quòd damnatis omnis facultas omnisque adempta facultas sit, tum ad resistendum divinae ultioni, tum ad faciendum deinceps quicquam boni.)

*( Αεατε αὐτὸν.Tollite eum. Legitur hoc in omnibus Codd. Graecis, quos consuluit Beza. Quemadmodum etiam in Theophylacto. Omisit verò Interpres Vulgatus Latinus, imò & intiquissimus Interpres Syrus, quemadmodum etiam Arabs ac Aethiops. Persa tamen videtur legisse, sic vertens praesentem versiculum: Rex ministris suis mandavit, ut manibus ac pedibus ligatum efferrent, & in tenebras coniicerent.)*

Mittite eum in tenebras exteriores. Gregorius lib. 25. Moral. c. 11. Tunc coacti in tenebras exteriores mittentur, qui nunc interioribus volunt ariè excoecantur. *(Videntur quibusdam tenebrae in hâc parabolâ opponi copioso taedarum ac lampadum lumini, quo coenacula illustrantur. Alii censent, quòd per illas denotetur carcer, qui plerumque locus tenebricosus. Sic infrà c. 25. ille, qui talentum concreditum defoderat, iubetur extrudi in tenebras exteriores, ubi tamen convivii nulla praecessit mentio.)*

εχότος τό έξότεεον. Camer. accipit εις τόν σχοσινόν τόπον, τι ίξω in tenebrosum exteriùs locum. *(Conf. Anal. ad c. 25, 30 Gregor. M. hom. 38. Interiores tenebrae sunt coecitas cordis; exteriores aeternae damnationis nox. Dicuntur verò tenebrae ill-exteriores h. e. extimae. quia à regione lucis remotissimae. Idem supplicium falsis Doctribus reservatū memorat D. Petrus poster. epist. c. 2. v. 17. quemadmodum etiam D. Iudas v. 13. Similiter ferè etiam Diabolorum futuras poenas delineat idem Apostolus 1. ep. c. 2, 4. ac Iudas v. 6. Conf. quoque suprà c. 8, 12. infrà c. 25, 50. Complectuntur tenebrae illae denotantq; 1. tenebras naturales,Iob. 38, 19. 2. tenebras spirituales, h. e. mentis coecitatem, ignorantiam puta veri Dei Es. 42, 2.Luc. 1, 79.Eph. 5, 8voluntatis perversitatom, omnigenamque calamitatem. Notanter Dionysius à Rickel Comm. in Post. e. Petri c. 2. Homines flagtiosi in hac vita ambulant in tenebris peccatorum. Inde de tenebrvitiorum praecipitantur in tenebras tormentorum.)*

Ο βρυγμὸς. Hesychius: βρυγμὸς άπό τού βρέχειν, όέςι τούς έσόνεοας πιέζονεοα -όφονλποτε ός όν ριγει σομφαινει, ετρισμός ισόντων. Dentes premendo strepitum efficere, quod fit in vehementi frigore, aut stridor dentium. *( Dentium, notat glossa interlin. ex Gregorio, qui de edacitate gavisi sunt. Porrò ex stridore illo dentium colligunt nonnulli Pontificii, verum frigus fore in inferno. Cuius tamen adsertionis causam non eandem adsignant. Nonnulli enim Hieronymum, Bedam aliosque, à B. Par. L. de Inferno §. 71. allegatos, sequuti existimant, frigus illud provenire à latissimo frigidissimarum aquarum receptaculo in inferno, in quod ex igne transeant damnati, à daemonibus rapti, ex quo stridor dentium oriatur. Abulensis in Matth. frigus hoc à terrâ, quae damnatos circumstet, provenire scribit. Eò quod terra illa valdè sit frigida, cùm non habeat ibi, unde à frigiditate suâ naturali immutari possit. Quo modo verò frigus illud in damnatos agat prolixè disputant Scho-astici. Certè vix aliter, ac si per aliquod temporis spatium in locis illis fuissent versati. Videantur quae in rem hanc ex Scholasticorum mente exhibet Alphonsus Mendoza Controv. Theol. q. 6. pag 499. seqq. B. Par. L. de Inferno l. c. stridorem illum dentium à veteribus quibusdam rectiùs de livore & furore damnatorum exponi scribit, adeoque & frigus impropriè accipi.)*

## 22:14
*(v. 14. For many are called. See the notes above at c. 20, 16. and add by all means B. D. Frantzium de Interpret. Sc. S. p. 589.)*

*( Called. Thus are commonly called all those who live in the external assembly of the Church, of whom some are hypocrites, but some truly believe, but do not persevere. Finally, even in the strictest signification, the elect are so called. See Rom. 8, 28. Concerning the distinction of the Calvinists.) see after others Grossius in Theatr. Bibl. h. l.) between efficacious calling and inefficacious, by which they strive to overturn the grace of universal calling, the Lords Theologians of Marburg treat at length in Fundam. Deduct. p. 308. seqq. and others of our countrymen.)*

Latin:

*(v. 14. Multi enim vocati. Vide notata suprà ad c. 20, 16. & adde omninò B. D. Frantzium de Interpret. Sc. S. p. 589.)*

*( Vocati. Dicuntur it a communiter omnes illi, qui in externo Ecclesiae coetu vivunt, quorum quidam sunt hypocritae, quidam autem verè credunt, sed non perseverant. Denique etiam in significatione strictissimâ electi ita vocantur. Vid. Rom. 8, 28. De distinctione Calvinianorum.) vide post alios Grossium in Theatr. Bibl. h. l.) inter vocationem efficacem & inefficacem, quâ universalis vocationis gratiam evertere satagunt, prolixè agunt Dnn. Theologi Marpurg. in Fundam. Deduct. p. 308. seqq. aliique nostratium.)*

## 22:15
v. 15. παγισό-ίειν is to ensnare, παγισες are snares, which are fixed for catching in hunting. Lyranus: A man is more easily caught in words than in deeds. *(Indeed, the Pharisees were acting in such a way as to elicit from the Savior that by the pretext of which they might be able to accuse Him before the Roman Governor, as if He were plotting new things. Since otherwise no hope remained of removing Him from the midst.)*

Latin:

v. 15. παγισό-ίειν est irretire,παγισες sunt laquei, qui ad capiendum in venationibus affiguntur. Lyranus: Faciliùs homo capitur in verbis, quàm in factis. *(Id verò Pharisaei agebant, ut ex Salvatore elicerent, cuius praetextu accusare eum apud Praesidem Romanum possent, ac si res novas moliretur. Cùm aliàs nulla spes superesset, ipsum è medio tollendi.)*

## 22:16
v. 16. His disciples. Chrysostom hom. 25. Op. Imperf. These disciples were younger in age than their masters, but equal in malice.

With the Herodians. *(Through these, the Blessed Doctor Hunnius simply understands the ministers of Herod the Tetrarch. Others explain it either as admirers of Herod, or evil worshippers, that is, those who held him to be the Messiah; or as his tax-collectors, that is, those who applied their effort to him in collecting tributes. The former opinion is embraced by Tertullian de Praescript. near the end, Epiphanius advers. haeres. heresy 20, Damascene de haeres., Theophylact on Matthew & Mark on this passage, Hegesippus book 6 de Excidio Hierosol, Victor of Antioch on Mark c. 12, Euthymius on heresies, and others. Jerome adv. Lucif c. 8 likewise writes that the Herodians received King Herod as Christ. On this passage, however, perhaps forgetting himself, he notes that some of the Latins ridiculously think the Herodians were those who believed Herod to be Christ, because we read this nowhere at all, he adds. He himself, however, on this passage establishes that the Herodians were Herod's soldiers, so called in jest by the Pharisees, because they paid the tribute, over which Herod had been placed in charge, to the Romans, that is, in collecting and extorting tribute for the Romans, they applied their effort to Herod. And this latter opinion was also held long ago by Origen hom. 21 on Matthew, just as by Eusebius of Emesa, and also Anselm. The same are followed among the Papists by Dionysius the Carthusian, the Jesuit Sebast. Barradius and others on this passage, Pomerius Pelbardus de Themeswar, and also Thomas Stapleton in Promt Morali Dom. 22 after Pentecost. Similarly among the Lutherans, Mr. Dr. Friedlieb in Obs. ad h. l. p. 211, and the Blessed Doctor Bakus in Expl. Ev. Dom.; among the Calvinists, Beza, Aretius, and some others. But that this opinion cannot be admitted, the Blessed Par. shows by several reasons in Disp. Elencht. super Evang. Domin. p. 1239 and 1240. Therefore, not unlearned authors prefer the former opinion to this latter one. For to Tertullian subscribe Scaliger in Eusebium, Emanuel Sa in Scholiis h. l., Casaubonus Exerc. advers. Baron. 1. c. 5, Hugo Grotius ad Matth. 16, 6. and --ostratibus Mr. Dilherrus Acad. Disp. vol. 2. p. 317. But Baronius explains the cause or occasion by which those Herodians descended into that heresy, in the Appendix to the Annals, no. 5, writing: When the Herodians saw that the kingdom had failed in the tribe of Judah, impelled by the outcome of the divine oracle, they believed Herod to be the Messiah. But Samuel Petitus attempted to refute this opinion again in book 2 of his Var. Lect. c. 1, which can be consulted.)* The Hebrew Gospel, which Mercerus published, translates: With the servants of Herod, that is, the courtiers. Beustius: The Herodians were opposed to the Romans and maintained that King Herod the Great ought to be held rather than that one should obey a foreign and Gentile magistrate. These are named Zealots by Josephus, because with serious zeal under the pretext of religion and the temple, they defended the liberty of this people. The author of the Lexicon, who is Baal Aruch to the Hebrews: King Herod brought Greeks from the desert and raised them in the habitable land, who instituted a certain rite. What is that rite? They celebrated the birthday of Herod, who had nourished them, on which day they also placed lighted lamps and violet-crowned ones in the windows: This first, then they believed him to be the Messiah. Drusius book 1 Praeterit. p. 45. also on the three sects book 1 c. 3. *(Isaac Casaubon repeats the same in Exerc. 1 against Baronius, Beza in his Greater Annotations and others, having followed Drusius. But as far as the former words concern the Greeks brought from the desert, Buxtorf rightly warns in his Rabb. Talm. Lex. p. 631 and 632 that Drusius had hallucinated, since the author of the Lexicon called Baal Aruch is not dealing with men, but with doves brought from the desert. And the slip was easy, since the word ---- can be explained as Greeks, and doves, depending on the punctuation. Otherwise it is known from Persius that there were certain flatterers who religiously celebrated Herod's birthday.)* Tossanus from a comparison of Matth. 16, 6. and Marc. 8, 15. gathers that this sect was the same as the sect of the Sadducees *(or rather a part of that sect, which pleases Grotius: Whence they are also distinguished from the Sadducees in v. 23 and Luc. 20, 27..)* But Tossanus thinks it was so named from Herod, who corrupted and mixed the doctrine of religion so that it might serve lust and tyranny. Nicolaus Serarius in his Herod reports ten discrepant opinions as to why they were so called.

*(The Syrian translates ---- who are of the house of Herod, that is, the domestics or courtiers of Herod. The same opinion pleases also our own Bb. Dd. Luther, Chemnitz, Hunnius, in this place. B. Par. in the place cited, among the Calvinists Beza, Piscator, Gualther, among the Papists Franc. Lucas, Salmeron, Barradius. The Arab rendered ---- Herodians. The Ethiopian: ---- Men of Herod. The Persian ---- followers of Herod. The Hebrew Gospel of Matthew has ---- servants of Herod. Furthermore, Ludov. de Dieu not vainly suspects that an error lies hidden in the Leyden Erpenian Arabic edition of the N. T., since in it is seen ---- i. e. & they sent to him (I do not know why Lud. de Dieu translates to them, when anyone can see that τό is a suffix of the singular number, nor yet is this same thing seen to be changed in the typographical errata) his disciples the Herodians. Better, therefore, the Roman edition has ---- and no less well the London one ---- his disciples with the Herodians. But however much the Pharisees may not have agreed well with the Herodians at other times, here, however, when the action is against Christ, they easily conspire. For this is the custom of the enemies of the Gospel. See Luc. 23, 12.Act. 4, 27.c. 6, 9.c. 23, 6. For they are like the foxes of Samson, which, although they disagree in their heads, yet being tied by their tails, they lay waste the harvest of the Lord, as B. D. Hunnius well notes in this place.)

Latin:

v. 16. Discipulos suos. Chrysostomus hom. 25. Op. Imperf. Discipuli hi erant Magistris suis aetate minores, malitiâ autempares.

Cum Herodianis. *(Per hos B. D. Hunnius simpliciter intelligit ministros Herodis Tetrarchae. Alii exponunt vel de Herodis admiratoribus, sive malis adoratoribus h. e. qui ipsum pro Messia habebant; vel de eiusdem exactoribus h. e. qui in colligendis tributis operam illi navabant. Priorem sententiam amplect-ntur Tertullianus de Praescript. circa finem, Epiphanius advers. haeres. haeresi 20. Damascenus de haeres. Theophylactus in Matth. & Marcum super h. l. Egesippus lib 6. de Excidio Hierosol Victor Antiochenus in Marci c. 12. Euthymius in de haeresibus, alii. Hieronymus adv. Lucif c. 8. itidem scribit, quòd Herodiani Regem Herodem pro Christo susceperint. in hunc tamen locum, sui fortè oblitus, notat, quosdam Latinorum ridiculè Haerodi anos putare, qui Herodem Christum esse credebant, quòd nusquam omninò, addit, legimus. Ipse verò in h. l. statuit, Herodianos fuisse Herodis milites, per lusum à Pharisaeis ita dictos, quòd tributum, cui Herodes fuerat praefectus, Romanis solverent, h. e in colligendo & extorquendo tributo pro Romanis, Herodi operam navarent. Atque hanc posteriorem sententiam iam olim tenuit quo que Origenes hom 21. in Matthaeum, sicuti & Eusebius Emissenus, nec non Anselmus. Sequuntur eandem ex Pontificiis Dionysius Carthusianus, Iesuita Sebast. Barradius aliiq; super h. l. Pomerius Pelbardus de Themes war, nec non Thomas Stapletonus in Promt Morali Dom. 22. post Pentecost. Similiter è Lutheranis Dn. D. Friedlieb in Obs. ad h. l. p. 211. ac B. D. Bak us in Expl. Ev. Dom. è Calvinianis Beza, Aretius ac alii nonnulli. Quò minùs verò sententia haec admitti possit aliquor rationibus ostendit B. Par. Disp. Elencht. super Evang. Domin. p. 1239. ac 1240. Priorem igitur sententiam posteriori huic praeferunt autores non indocti. Tertulliano enim subscribunt Scaliger in Eusebium, Emanuel Sa in Scholiis h. l. Casaubonus Exerc. advers. Baron. 1. c. 5. Hugo Grotius ad Matth. 16, 6. è --ostratibus Dn. Dilherrus Disp. Acad. t. 2. p. 317. Causam verò vel occasionem, quâ Herodiani illi in eam descenderint haeresin, exponit Baronius, in Append. Annal. n. 5. scribens: Herodiani cùm viderent, defecisse regnum in tribu Iuda, eventu divini oraculi impulsi crediderunt, Herodem Messiam esse. Sed iterum sententiam hanc refutare conatus est Samuel Petitus lib. 2. Var. Lect. c. 1. qui potest evolvi.)* Evangelium Ebraicum, quod Mercerus edidit, vertit: Cum servis Herodis i. e. aulicis. Beustius: Herodiani adversabantur Romanis & statuebant, potiùs habendum esse Regem Herodem Magnum, quàm peregrino & Ethnico Magistratui parendum. Hi à Iosepho nominantur Zelotae, quod serio Zelo sub praetextu religionis & templi, libertatem huius populi defendebant. Autor Lexici, qui Baal Aruch Ebraeis: Herodes Rex adduxit Graecos è deserto & educavit eos in terrâ habitabili, qui instituerunt certum ritum. Quis ille ritus? Herodis, qui eos aluerat, natalem celebrabant, quo die etiam lucernas accensas & violis coronat as in fenestris ponebant: Hoc primum, deinde credebant, eum Messiam esse. Drusius lib. 1. Praeterit. p. 45. it. de tribus sectis lib. 1. c. 3. *(Eadem repetunt Isaacus Casaubonus Exerc. 1. contra Baronium, Beza in Annot. Maioribus & alii, Drusium sequuti. Verùm quod priora attinet verba de Graecis è delerto adductis, rectè monet Buxtorfius in Lex. Rabb. Talm. p 631. & 632. hallucinatum fuisse Drusium, cùm Auctor Lexici Baal Aruch dicti, non agat de hominibus, sed de columbis è deserto adductis. ac lapsus facilis fuit, cùm vox ---- pro ratione punctationis & Graeci, & columbae exponi possit. Aliàs è Persio cōstat fuisse quosdem adulatores, qui Herodis natalem religiosè celebrabant.)* Tossanus ex collatione Matth. 16, 6. ac Marc. 8, 15. colligit, hanc sectam fuisse eandem cum sectâ Sadducaeorum *(vel potiùs partem eius sectae, quod Grotio arridet: Unde etiam à Sadducaeis v. 23. ac Luc. 20, 27. distingvuntur.)* Putat verò Tossanus, ita dictam ab Herode, qui doctrinam religionis corrupit & commiscuit, ut libidini & tyrannidi inserviret. Nicolaus Serarius in suo Herode decem discrepantes opiniones refert, cur ita dicti.

*(Syrus vertit ----qui è domo Herodis, h. e. domesticos vel aulicos Herodis. Eadem sententia arridet, quoque è nostratibus Bb. Dd. Luthero, Chemnitio, Hunnio, in h. l. B. Par. l. c. ex Calvinianis Bezae, Piscatori, Gualtero, è Pontificiis Franc. Lucae, Salmeroni, Barradio. Arabs reddidit. ----Herodianos. Aethiops: ----Homines Herodis. Persa ----adseclas Herodis. Evangelium Matth. Ebr. habet ----servos Herodis. Coeterùm haut vanè suspicatur Ludov. de Dieu, mendum latere in edit. N. T. Arabicâ Leydensi Erpenianâ, cùm in eâ conspi ciatur ---- i. e. & miserunt ad eum (nescio, cur Lud. de Dieu vertat ad eos, cùm quilibet videat, τό & esse suffixum singularis numeri, nec tamen in erratis typographicis hoc ipsum mutatum cernitur) discipulos suos Herodianos. Meliùs igitur Romana editio habet ---- nec minùs benè Londinensis ----discipulos suos cum Herodianis. Ut ut verò aliàs Pharisaeis cum Herodianis non benè convenerit, hîc tamen cùm contra Christum agitur, facilè conspirant. Est nempe hic mos hostium Evangelii. Vid. Luc. 23, 12.Act. 4, 27.c. 6, 9.c. 23, 6. Sunt nâmq; instar vulpium Samsonis, quae licet capitibus dissideant caudis tamen colligatae messem Domini vastant, ut benè notat B. D. Hunnius in h. l.)*

## 22:17
v. 17. To give tribute. By tribute is understood the denarius commonly of the sanctuary, equivalent to two common ones, i. e., a didrachma. For the publicans counted by common denarii, but the priests by double ones, i. e., a didrachma. *(Thus this tribute is usually understood by most, namely as the half-shekel, which was to be paid annually by each one for the preservation of the temple by divine constitution, Exod. 30, 15. 16.. For they think that this very thing was assigned in later times by the Asiatic and Roman Kings to the imperial treasury. Others, however, and perhaps more correctly, think that the denarius was paid as tribute to the Romans, and the didrachma likewise to the temple head by head. Thus Beza, Casaubon in Exerc. ad Baronium, Salmeron determine. And B. Par. himself also prefers this opinion in Harm. Ev. c. 154. p. 425 to the other.)*

Latin:

v. 17. Censum dare. Intelligitur per Censum denatius communiter sanctuarii, duobus vulgaribus aequivalens i. e. didrachmum. Nam publicani per vulgares denarios numerabant, sacerdotes verò per duplares i. e. didrachmum. *(Ita à plerisq; census hic ac cipi solet, nempe de dimidio siclo, qui quotannis ad templi conservationem ex constitutione divinâ, Exod. 30, 15. 16. ab unoquoque persolvendus erat. Hunc ipsum enim sequioribus temporibus à Regibus Asiaticis & Romanis fisco imperiali adsignatum putant. Alii tamen, & fortè rectiùs, existimant, quòd & Romanis in tributum fuerit solutus denarius, & didrachma pariter templo viritim. Ita statuunt Beza, Casaubonus in Exerc. ad Baronium, S-lmeron. Atque hanc sententiā ipse quoq; B. Par. Harm. Ev. c. 154. p. 425 alteri praefert.)*

## 22:18
v. 18. Having known their malice. Jerome well says: The first virtue of one who answers is to know the mind of the one who asks. But since it is the property of the divine majesty to search the hearts, 1. Reg. 8, 39. Ierem. 17, 10. and yet here it is attributed to Christ, that He perceived the malice of the Pharisees lying hidden within, Conf. Ioh. 2, 24. our people gather from this that divine majesty was communicated to Christ as man, or according to His human nature. Now the mind of the Pharisees here was to entangle Him in inextricable bonds by an insidious dilemma: for they thought that if He had answered affirmatively, they would traduce Him before the people as a traitor to the liberty of the fatherland; if negatively, they would cast Him into danger before Herod and the Roman Governor as a seditious person.) (

Why do you tempt me, you hypocrites. Author of the *Opus Imperfectum*. They flatter in order to destroy, but Christ rebukes in order to save: for God angry is more useful than man propitious. ) (

Latin:

*(v. 18. Cognitâ eorum malitiâ. Benè Hieronymus: Prima virtus respondentis est, cognoscere interrogantis mentem. Coeterùm cùm divinae maiestatis sit, corda scrutari, 1. Reg. 8, 39.Ierem. 17, 10. hîc verò Christo tribuatur, quòd malitiam Pharisaeorum intus latentem perspexerit, Conf. Ioh. 2, 24. colligunt inde nostrates, quòd Christo homini sive secundûm humanam naturam divina maiestas fuerit communicata. Mens autem Pharisaeorum hîc erat, insidioso dilemate inextricabilibus nexibus eum involvere: etenim si affirmativè respondisset, cogitabant, apud populum ceu patriae libertatis proditorem traducere; si negativè, in discrimen praecipitare apud Herodem ac Praesidem Romanum tanquam seditiosum.)*

*( Quid me tentatis hypocritae. Autor Op. Imperf. Blandiuntur ut perdant, Christus verò increpat, ut salvet: utilior enim est Deus iratus, quàm homo propitius.)*

## 22:19
v. 19. Show me. Since Christ, beyond any ambiguity, handled with His hands the denarius shown or exhibited to Him, it is clear how ridiculous certain monks are, who, out of an opinion of some singular holiness, dread to handle money. To whom not only this present example of Christ should be opposed, but also that of the Virgin Mary, Luc. 2, 11 likewise of Barnabas, of Saul, Actor 11, 30 and of very many others. Superstitious men ought, indeed, to distinguish between the use and the abuse of a thing. Since the Savior also does not disapprove or reject the denarius marked with the image of Caesar, it is manifest that images are not to be simply disapproved or rejected by Christians today, but only their superstitious abuse is to be disapproved. Nor do I think the Calvinists themselves cast away Hungarian gold coins, or Bavarian Imperials, or likewise Salzburg coins, upon which the image of the Virgin Mother of God is impressed, upon these indeed with the inscription: We fly to thy protection; upon those: A shield to all who hope in thee, upon the others: Patroness of Hungary. ) Νόμισμα. |

Νόμισμα. The saying άπό τουόμου. of Aristotle in the 5th book of the Ethics, chapter 8: οίον -ωάλλαγμα τες χρειας τό νόλισμα γέγονε χαεοα σννφεχην χαί -μενα εοοανομα έχει νόμισμα, ότι ού φασμεν, άλλά νόμω όςι χαί έφ εμίν, μεεοαβάλλειν χαί ποιεσαι άχρηςον. In place of need, money has succeeded by a kind of compact and agreement of men, called so by law, because it is valid not by nature, but by law, and it is in our power to change it and render it useless. (The Evangelist Mark writes in chapter 12, 15, that Christ asked denarius, Matthew therefore expresses a paraphrase of the words of Christ, not the very words themselves.)*

Κενσου. Κενσος is accepted among the Syrians for poll-tax s-u money imposed upon individual heads, which had been enumerated by the command of Caesar and included in the registration. And this poll-tax, as Dio testifies, was instituted by Augustus in two ways: namely, upon heads of households or individual homes, and upon persons or each individual head. *(The Arab translates ---- treasury, Similarly also the Persian, for it has ----, which why the Interpreter in the London Bibles translates census of the head, does not sufficiently appear, since it is a general term, denoting treasury, wealth. For thence the word Gaza flowed to the Latins, as Isidore of Seville teaches in book 20, chapter 9, and from him Matthaeus Martinius in the Etymological Lexicon under the word Gaza. And hence the Jerusalem Treasury, about which the blessed D. Chemnitius, Hugo Grotius on Mark 12:41 and other authors everywhere. The Ethiopian renders ---- i.e. tribute of the denarius. Hugo Grotius also thinks that χενσο is accepted here for poll-tax.)*

*( They offered a denarius. Since, as is clear above from chapter 17:24, the Jews paid a didrachma for the census; but the denarius was of only one drachma, it is asked, how did they exhibit a denarius here? Resp. 1. Iansenius, Maldonatus and some others think, that the didrachma for the sake of convenience had been divided into two denarii, and they paid two denarii for the census, i.e. a didrachma. 2. Hug. Grotius maintains, that σίσεαχμον, about which Exodus 30:15 and above chapter 17:24, is far different from this Roman tribute. about which besides others compare especially Lipsius on Roman Magnitude, book 2, chapter 3, Casaubon in Exercises 6, Salmasius on Lampridius p. 216, Selden on Hebrew Law, book 6, chapter 17. 3. Arias Montanus distinguishes between greater denarii, and lesser. 4. Corn. à Lapide thinks, that this denarius, which the Herodians showed to Christ, was double: inasmuch as Tiberius, as also the other Emperors, ordered a denarius of that value to be minted which they wanted to be given to them by the Jews for the census, because, as Baronius might teach from Lampridius, the Romans were accustomed to mint coins at that value and weight, at which they wanted them to be paid to themselves as tribute . The same thing also, that namely the denarius was not a certain or perpetual, although most common, mode of tribute among the Romans, Grotius also notes in this place. Some Papists also embrace the same opinion, such as Alphonsus Salmeron vol. 8, tract 59, Franciscus Lucas Brug. in this place, and others. But the Jesuit Barradius rejects it in turn, for this reason especially, that Lampridius, upon whose authority the approvers of that opinion chiefly rely, speaks of the peculiar act of Alexander Severus, who lived long after Tiberius. He himself, however, thinks that any money is understood here, through which the census was paid to the Romans. This pleases the blessed Parent in Disputations Elencht. p. 12 48, where he furthermore warns, that it is evident from Pliny, book 33, Natural History, chapter 3, That the Romans were accustomed to demand silver as tribute from the nations, not gold. And from this it is to be understood in this place to be a silver denarius. But as for the fact that above in c. 17, 25, mention is made of a didrachma, which Christ paid, he himself thinks in Harm. Evang. p. 430, that it is perhaps because Herod, tetrarch of Galilee, exacted a double tax in Capernaum, and therefore a didrachma, through his prefects, namely, one denarius for himself, the other for Caesar, whose tributes Herod himself was indeed collecting.)*

Latin:

*(v. 19. Ostendite mihi. Cùm Christus procul ambiguo ostensum sive exhibitum sibi denarium manibus contrectarit, patet, quàm ridiculi sint monachi quidam, qui singularis cuiusdam sanctitatis opinione pecuniam contrectare reformidant. Quibus non solùm praesens exemplum Christi opponendum, sed & Mariae Virginis, Luc. 2, 11 item Barnabae, Sauli, Actor 11, 30 ac plurimorum aliorum. Distinguere nempe debebant superstitiosi homines inter rei usum & abusum. Cùm quoque Salvator denarium Caesaris imagine signatum non improbet vel reiiciat, manifestum est, quòd nec hodie à Christianis imagines simpliciter improbandae vel reiiciendae sint, sed superstiosus saltē eorum improbandus abusus. Nec ipsos Calvinianos abiicere puto aureos Hungaricos, ac Imperiales Bavaricos itemque Salisburgenses, quibus Virginis Deiparae impresla imago, his quidē cum inscriptione: sub tuum praesidium confugimus; illis: Clypeus omnibus in te sperantibus, istis: Patrona Ungariae.)*

Indigentiae loco ex hominum quasi compacto & convento quod ammodo successit nummus à lege dictus, quia non naturâ, sed lege valeat, sitque in nobis situm, eum immutare inutilemque reddere. *(Evangelista Marcus c. 12, 15. scribit, Christum petiisse denarium, Matthaeus igitur paraphrasin verborum Christi, non ipsa verba exprimit.)*

Κενσου. Κενσος accipitur apud Syrum pro capitatione s-u pecuniâ indictâ in singula capita, quae mandato Caesaris fuerant recensita & descriptione comprehensa. Atque haec capitatio, Dione teste, ab Augusto duobus modis fuit instituta: nempe in patresfamilias vel domos singulas, & in personas vel capita singularia quaeque. *(Arabs vertit ----gazam, Similiter & Persa, habet enim ----, quam cur Interpres in Bibliis Londinensibus vertat censum capitis, non satis apparet, cùm sit dictio generalis, notans gazam, opes. Inde enim ad Latinos vocabulum Gaza manavit, ceu docet Isidorus Hispalensis l. 20. c. 9. & ex eo Matth. Martinius in Lex. Etymol. voce Gaza. Atque hinc Gazophylacium Hierosolymitanum, de quo B. D. Chemnitius, Hugo Grotius ad Marc. 12, 41. aliique autores passim. Aethiops reddit ---- i. e. tributum Denarii. Pro capitationeχενσο hîc accipi, Hugo quoque existimat Grotius.)*

*( Obtulerunt denarium. Cùm, ceu suprà ex c. 17, 24. liquet. Iudaei pro censu solverint didrachmum; denarius verò unius tantùm fuerit drachmae, quaeritur, quomodo denarium hîc exhibuerint? Resp. 1. Iansenius, Maldonatus & alii nonnulli censent, didrachmum commoditatis causâ fuisse divisum in duos denarios, ac singulos pro censu solvisse duos denarios h. e. didrachmum. 2. Hug. Grotius statuit, σίσεαχμον, de quo Exod. 30, 15. ac suprà c. 17, 24. longè aliud esse ab hoc Romano tributo. de quo praeter alios conf. cumprimis Lipsius de Magnit. Rom. l. 2. c. 3. Casaubonus Exerc. 6. Salmasius ad Lampridium p. 216. Seldenus de Iure Ebr. l. 6. c. 17. 3. Arias Montanus distinguit inter denarios maiores, & minores. 4. Corn. à Lapide existimat, denarium hunc, quem Herodiani Christo monstrarunt, fuisse duplicem: siquidem Tiberius, uti & coeteri Imperatores, eius pretii denarium cudi iusserint quem vellent sibi à Iudaeis in censum dari, quia, ceu ex Lampridio doceat Baronius, Romani soliti fuerint numismata eo cudere pretio & pondere, quo illa sibi volebant in tributum pendi. Idem quoque hoc, quòd nempe denarius non certus sive perpetuus, quamvis usitatissimus, tributi modus apud Romanos fuerit, Grotius quoque notat in h. l. Eandem sententiam amplectuntur etiam Pontificii nonnulli, uti Alphonsus Salmeron t. 8. tr. 59. Franciscus Lucas Brug. in h. l. alii. Sed reiicit vicissim illam Iesuita Barradius, eòcumprimis, quòd Lampridius, cuius potissimùm nituntur sentētiae illius approbatores autoritate, loquatur de Alexandri Severi, qui longè post Tiberiū vixit, peculiari facto. Existimat verò ipse, intelligi hîc quamvis pecuniam, per quam census Romanis fuit solutus. Placet hoc B. Parenti Dispp. Elencht. p. 12 48. ubi insuper monet, è Plinio l. 33. H. N. c. 3. patere, Romanos solitos fuisse gentibus in tributum argentum imperare, non aurum. Atque hinc intelligendum h. l. esse denarium argenteum. Quòd verò suprà c. 17, 25. didrachmi mentio fiat, quod Christus persolverit, putat ipse in Harm. Evang. p. 430. fortè inde esse, quòd Herodes Galilaeae tetrarcha Caparnaumi duplicatum censum, ac proinde didrachmum per praefectos suos exegerit, videl. unum denarium pro se, alterum pro Caesare, cuius quippe tributa & ipse Herodes colligebat.)*

## 22:20
v. 20. Whose is this image &c. Cujacius lib. 19. Observ. c. 25. The Roman Caesars used to imprint their image on money both gold and silver. But the Kings of the Persians only on silver. See also 1. Maccab 15, 6. also Marquardus Freherus Orat apud Scultetum in Annot. c. 60. Guntherus lib. 3.

He thinks the coin figured by the King is the King's, and the image of Caesar shines under Caesar and the Lord.

*( The image of Caesar. August. in libb. Qq. V. ac N. Test. q 35. The King bears the image of GOD, therefore he is to be honored and loved, if not for his own sake, at least for the sake of his calling and function.)*

*( ἀπόδοτε. In the same way the Apostle Rom. 13, 7. speaks. So that we may learn from this that the payment of tribute is owed, since it is incumbent upon the Magistrate to preserve public peace, and money to be collected from tributes is the sinew of things to be done. But it is asked, how Christ could firmly prove against the Jews from the fact that they used a denarius, marked with the image of the Caesars, that tribute was rightly paid to the Romans by them, since we use the coins of many Kings and Princes, marked with their image, to whom, however, tribute is by no means to be paid by us. Resp. Some think that since the Princes or Roman Emperors named themselves from the subjugated provinces, as Asiatic, Parthian, Germanic, and among other things also Syrian, and thus they took care that their own coins also be marked; but that the Jews used denarii of this kind, the Savior wished to be gathered from that, that they themselves by this very fact voluntarily confessed that on account of their sins they had come under the power of the Romans 2. Others maintain that while the liberty of the Jewish Republic stood, it was by no means accepted among the Jews to use the currency of foreign Princes. But as far as concerns contracts and commerce, they used a crude mass of gold and silver, which, contracting with foreigners, they weighed out in turn. But although it is easily conceded that before coins were struck, the ancients used crude gold and silver: it is nevertheless denied that the same was done after coins were struck in huge abundance, as it is established was done by the Romans. Certainly that opinion cannot be supported by the authority of any approved Writer. Furthermore, since it is established how very close the treaty was between the Romans and the Jews, in the time of the Maccabees, so that by them also the right of minting money was granted as a sign of liberty, it is hardly probable that the Jews were so ungrateful, that they rejected Roman coins, at least after that time. 3. Others distinguish between the free and the necessary use of foreign money. Although therefore they think that the dominion of him, whose money one is compelled to use at a prescribed value, shines forth not from the former, but from the latter. But since even by the statute of one's own Magistrate a certain price of foreign money can be established, nor can it be proven that the value of Roman money was established for the Jews by the prescription of the Romans, nor does it seem that the proposed doubt can be solved in that way. Others therefore 4. think that not so much from the denarius itself, as from the census, i.e., from the certain kind of money by which the Jews were bound to pay the census to the Romans, and that indeed was the denarius, Christ proved that they acknowledged the empire of the Romans, and therefore were bound by right to pay the census to them. Which opinion it seems especially to confirm that Christ He had asked for the coin of the census, which the Pharisees also produced. So that this is the sense of Christ's words here: Since you do pay the census to Caesar, as the Denarius, marked with the image of Caesar Tiberius, which you yourselves have shown me, testifies, you ought to recognize from this that you have deserved by your sins that your liberty should have been taken away from you, and that you should have been reduced under the power of the Romans, to whom accordingly, as to rightful lords, you are bound in justice to pay tribute. Which last opinion, simple as it is, likewise commends itself to *(the Blessed Father, in H. E. c. 154, p. 432)*.

Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, etc. Prosper, in his summary of Augustine, ch. 15: Let the image of Caesar be rendered to Caesar, let the image of God be rendered to God. The coin of Caesar is gold, the coin of God is man. Augustine on Psalm 4: Just as Caesar requires from you the stamped impression of his image, so too does God, so that just as the coin is rendered to him, so the soul, illumined and sealed with the light of his countenance, is rendered to God. Tertullian, On the Soldier's Crown, ch. 12: You are a soldier and a servant of another, and if of two, of God and of Caesar, certainly then not of Caesar, when you owe yourself to God. Even in common matters, I believe, the stronger claim prevails. The same author, On Idolatry, ch. 15: The things that are Caesar's are to be rendered to Caesar. It is well that he added, and the things that are God's, to God, that is, the image of Caesar, to Caesar, which is on the coin, and the image of God, to God, which is in man, so that indeed you render money to Caesar, but yourself to God. *(Theophylact on this passage: In bodily and external matters one must obey the king; but in internal and spiritual matters, God alone. Similar things are found in Justin Martyr, Apology 2, Hilary, Origen, Augustine, Book 1 against the Epistle of Parmenian, ch. 7, Bernard, in the book on the Lord's Passion, cited by Cornelius à Lapide on this passage. These are consonant with the apostolic saying, Acts 5:29: One must obey God rather than men. Add Exodus 1:15, 17. For the obedience owed to the magistrate by subjects is not absolute, but determined, and has fixed limits. If therefore the magistrate commands something that is against piety, the truth of religion, the freedom of conscience, or the honesty of morals, subjects are not bound to obey the magistrate. Compare the divine command, Numbers 22:12, the approved examples, Exodus 1:17, ch. 2:2, compared with Hebrews 11:23, 1 Samuel 22:1, Daniel 3:18, ch. 6:10, Acts 4:18, and the sure rewards, Exodus 1:21.)*

Tob. 2:9. Hence Polycarp, in Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. l. 4, c. 15, says to the Proconsul: "We have been so instructed that to principalities and powers ordained by God we should render the honor that is fitting, provided it does not harm us." The same Polycarp, in his Epistle to the Smyrnaeans: "All honor is to be rendered to the magistrate, insofar as this can be done with a safe conscience." So too his contemporary *(σύγχρονος)* Ignatius, in the Epistle to the Antiochians: "Be subject to Caesar, in those things in which subjection involves no danger to the soul." Likewise Chrysostom: "When you hear that the things that are Caesar's are to be rendered to Caesar, do not doubt that only those things are meant which do nothing to hinder piety and religion: for whatever is harmful to faith and virtue is not Caesar's tribute and due, but the devil's." Since, therefore, the payment of tribute contains nothing contrary to piety or to freedom of conscience, the Savior gravely admonishes that tribute be paid to Caesar, inasmuch as the Jews were then under his power and protection. Compare the Saxon Theologians in the Fundamental Defense of the Pupilla, p. 87 ff.; also p. 671. B. D. Hutterus, Loci Theol. Mai., p. 1041, and p. 500. B. Par. L. de Ministr. Polit. §. 474. * Isidore of Pelusium, l. 1, ep. 209: "Whatever is peculiar to matter, whatever is an instrument of error, whatever is a semblance of deceit that inward sloth has cast upon us—this the Lord wills to be thrown back by us to the maker and fashioner of glass. On the contrary, whatever is a token of virtue, whatever is a mark of honesty, whatever gain of vigilance and caution—this we ought to be persuaded has come to us by the kindness of God, and we ought to render to Him the praise that is due." Tossanus explains the passage thus: "Because from the use of Roman coin it appears that you have been brought under the power and jurisdiction of the Roman Emperor, therefore render the tribute owed to the Emperor; but this ought not to prevent you from giving the half-shekel required in the Law, Exod. 30:12, to God, and from serving Him according to the prescription of His word, since the Romans have granted you freedom of religion." *(Since, moreover, among the things that are to be given to Caesar tribute also belongs, which we are commanded to give to this end: that he may be able to afford protection to his subjects and to exercise vengeance against disturbers of the public peace—it is manifest that this is in accord with divine law and the divine will, that by the magistrate... [text corrupt] ...and so, if several should join together, war against... Against the Photinians.)*

Against whom B. D. Meisner argues at length in Theolog. Photin. Consid. page 223. B. Par. L. on Ecclesiastical Ministry § 3-7. Furthermore, Bernard gathers from this assertion of the Savior that even clerics are not exempt from the payment of tribute. For thus he writes in epistle 42, which is to the Archbishop of Sens: What he spoke here with his mouth, he soon took care to fulfill with his work. The Creator of Caesar did not hesitate to pay the tax to Caesar. For he gave an example to you (the clergy) that you also should do likewise etc. Cf. Rom. 13, 1.2. Peter 2, 13.Rom. 13, 1. following. Cornelius à Lapide himself alleges the statement of Bernard. Let Chrysostom also be added on ch. 13 of the epistle to the Romans. But the exposition of this command which -acobus de Terano, chamberlain of Urban VI, brings forward is ridiculous, establishing that they did not have the force of a command until his (Christ's) ascension, but after the ascension all Empires were to be transferred from Caesar and Kings to the vicar of Christ (he understands the Roman Pontiff). And he tries to prove this from John 12, 32. But the contrary is evident from the command of Peter (whom, however, the Papists dream was the first vicar of Christ to sit at Rome), 1. ep. 2, 13. Likewise of Paul Rom. 13, 1. following, Tit. 3, 1. The first teachers of the Church taught otherwise. The warning of Bernard was brought forward a little earlier. The same, l. c., writes, Let every soul be subject to the higher powers: if every, then yours also. Who excepted you from the whole? If anyone tries to except, he tries to deceive. Let the same be compared, ep. 170. Likewise Chrysostom, hom. 23, on the epistle to the Romans. Nor, however, do we mean this as if a Christian Magistrate could not or ought not to adorn the clergy with certain privileges and immunities by the example of Joseph, Gen. 47, 22. of Artaxerxes, l. 1, Ezra ch. 7, 24, and others. But the question is at least about this, whether the clergy are exempt by Divine Law from public burdens and the authority of the Political Magistrate. This is what is denied by us. Similarly, this statement can be urged against the Libertines, who deny that the subjection owed to the Magistrate in the N. T. has been abolished by Christian liberty. But more will be treated about them in the Analects on John 8, 36. Finally, it is evident from this place that one must obey even an impious Magistrate, such as Caesar was, namely a parricide, adulterer, fornicator, etc., in matters which are not opposed to piety. And this is evident 1. from the general sayings of Holy Scripture, Rom. 13. 2. from approved examples. Cf. John 19, 11. 3. from a like case, namely harsh Masters 1. Peter 2, 18. 19. 20. and severe Parents. 4. from prayers, to be poured out even for Heathen Princes. See Jer. 29, 7.1. Tim. 2, 2. The matter stands otherwise if a Prince commands something that is opposed to piety. For then one must supplicate, or flee. Cf. more things looking to this in B. D. Winckelm. Dispp. Marpurg. t. 5. Disp. 14. B. D. Lobechius in A. C. p. 407. B. D. Roenig Casuum Catechet. p. 43. B. Par. L. de Magistr. Polit. § 80. item Dispp. El-ncht. p. 1253. The force of truth compelled the Jesuit Costerus, so that in Enchir. Controv. p. 113. he wrote: Christ did not change the political method of administration by his coming, but left it to the princes. Render, he says, etc. For even those who wander entirely from the right path of faith can care for external or civil peace, from whom he did not wish the Right of Empire to be taken away, etc. The Jesuit indeed limits this proposition by adding the particle then. If by this very thing he implies that Christ indeed then, when he lived in the flesh, did not wish to take away authority from impious or heathen Magistrates, but today his fictitious successors, the Roman Pontiffs, can do so by right, he is vehemently deceived and deceives. Conf. Dnn. Theolog. Sax. in Fundam. Defens. p. 668. & 685. it. B. Par. Confess. Cath. l. 2. art. 3. c. 9.)*

Latin:

v. 20. Cuius est imago haec &c. Cuiacius lib. 19. Observ. c. 25. Romani Caesares imaginem suam imprimebant monetae tam aureae quùm argenteae. Persarum verò Reges argenteae tantùm. Vid. etiam 1. Maccab 15, 6. it. Marquardus Freherus Orat apud Scultetum in Annot. c. 60. Guntherus lib. 3.

Rege figuratam Regis putat esse monetamCaesaris, & Domino sub Caesare fulget imago.

*( Imago Caesaris. August. in libb. Qq. V. ac N. Test. q 35. Imaginem DEI Rex gestat, idcirco colendus & amandus est, si non propter se, saltem vocationis & functionis suae causâ.)*

*( ἀπόδοτε. Eodem modo Apostolus Rom. 13, 7. loquitur. Ut hinc discamus, tributi solutionem esse debitam, cùm Magistratui incumbat, publicam quietem conservare, pecunia vero ex tributis colligenda, rerum gerendarum nervus sit. Quaeritur verò, quomodo Christus ex eo, quòd Iudaei denario, Caesarum imagine signato uterentur, firmiter evincere cōtra eosdem potuerit rectè tributum Romanis ab iis persolvi, cùm multorum Regum ac Principum nummis, imagine eorum signatis utamur, quibus tamen hautquaquā tributum solvendum à nobis. Resp. Quidam existimant, quòd cùm Principes s. Imperatores Romani à subiugatis provinciis se denominarint, ut Asiaticos, Parthicos, Germanicos, & inter alia quoq; Syriacos, atque ita numismata quoque sua insigniri curarint; Iudaei verò huiusmodi denariis uterentur, Salvator colligi inde voluerit, illos hòc ipso ultrò fateri, quòd propter peccata sua in Romanorum potestatem pervenerint 2. Alii statuunt, quòd apud Iudaeos stante Reipubl. Iudaicae liberrate minimè receptum fuerit, exterorum Principum monetâ uti. quod verò contractus & mercaturam concernit, usos illos fuisse rudi auri & argenti massâ, quam cum exteris contrahentes, invicem appenderint. Verùm licet facilè concedatur priùs quàm numismata percussa fuere, veteres rudi auro & argento esse usos: negatur tamen, quòd idem factum fuerit, postquam nummi ingenti copiâ, ceu à Romanis factitatum constat, percussi fuerunt. Certè nullius probati Scriptoris autoritate sententia illa ful-iri potest. Praeterea cùm constet, quàm arctum admodùm fuerit foedus Romanos inter ac Iudaeos, tempore Maccabaeorum, ita ut ab illis quoque in signum libertatis concessum fuerit ius cudendae monetae, vix probabile est, Iudae os adeò fuisse ingra-os, ut mumismata Romana, saltem post illud tempus, reiecint. 3. Alii distingvunt inter usum exterae monetae liberum, & necessarium. Quamvis igitur non ex illo, tamen ex hoc imperium illius, cuius monetâ ex praescripto valore uti quis cogitur, elucescere putant. Verùm cùm etiam ex proprii Magistratûs statuto certum constitui exterae monetae pretium possit, nec evinci queat, quòd ex Romanorum praescripto valor monetae Romanae Iudaeis fuerit constitutus, nec isto modo propositum dubium solvi posse videtur. Alii proinde 4. existimant, quòd non tàm ex denario ipso, quàm ex censu h. e. ex certo monetae genere, quo censum Romanis persolvere Iudaei teneb antur, is verò denarius erat, Christus evicerit, eos Romanorum imperium agnoscere, adeoque iure censum illis persolvere. Quam sententiam id firmare cumprimis videtur quòd Christus numisma censüs petierit, quod Pharisaei quoque exhiberunt. Ut adeò verborum Christi hic sensus sit. Quandoquidem Caesari censum persolvatis, ceu Denarius Caesaris Tiberii imagine insignitus, quem ipsimet mihi exhibuistis, testatur, cognoscere inde debitis, quòd peccatis vestris promeriti sitis, ut libertas vobis fuerit ademta, vosque in Romanorum protestatem sitis redacti, quibus proinde tanquam iustis Dominis iure tributum solvere tenemini. Quae postrema sententia sicuti simplicissima est, ita etiam B. Parenti in H. E. c. 154. p. 432. arride-.)*

Reddite Caesari, quae sunt Caesaris &c. Prosper in sentent. Augustini c. 15. Imago Caesaris reddatur Caesari, imago DEI reddatur Deo. Moneta Caesaris aurum, moneta DEI nomo. Augustinus in Psalm. 4.Quemadmodum Caesar à vobis exigit imp-essionem imaginis suae, fic & Deus: ut quemadmodum illi redditur nummus, sic Deo anima, lumine vultûs eius illustrata atq signata. Tertullianus de Coronâ milit. c. 12. Tu miles ac servus alterius es& si duorum, DEI & Caesaris, certè tunc non Caesaris, cùm te Deo debes. Etiam in communibus credo potiori. Idem de Idolol. c. 15 Reddenda sunt Caesari, quae sunt Caesaris. Benè, quòd apposuit, & quae sunt Dei, Deo, i. e. imaginem Caesaris, Caesari, quae in numme est, & imaginem Dei, Deo, quae in homine est, ut Caesari quidem pecuniam reddas, Deo temetipsum. *(Theophyl. in h. l. In corporalibus & externis obediendum est Regi; in -nternis autem & spiritualibus soli Deo. Similia habent Iustinus Martyr Apol. 2. Hilarius, Origenes, Augustinus lib. 1. contra epist. Parmen. c. 7. Bernhardus lib. de Passione Dom. adducti à Corn. à Lapide ad h. l. Quae consona sunt effato Apostolico Actor. 5, 29.Oportet Deo plus obedire, quàm hominibus. Adde Exod. 1, 15.17. Est enim obedientia Magistratui à subditis debita, non absoluta, sed determinata, certosque habet limites. Si igitur Magistratus aliquid imperat, quod est contra pietatem, religionis veritatem, conscientiae libertatem, morum honestatem, non tenentur subditi obedire Magistratui. Conf. divinum mandatum Num. 22, 12. probata exempla, Exod. 1, 17.c. 2, 2. collata cum Ebr. 11, 23 1. Sam. 22, 1-, Daniel. 3. 18.c, 6, 10.Actor. 4, 18. certa praemia, Exod. 1, 21.

Tob. 2, 9. Unde Polycarpus apud Eusebium l. 4. Hist. Eccles. c. 15. ad Proconsulem: Sic instituti sumus, ut principatibus & potestatibus à Deo ordinatis, honorem qui competat, nec nobis obsit, exhibeamus. Idem Polycarpus ep. ad Smyrnenses: Omnis honor Magistratui est praestandus, quatenus salvâ conscientiâ fieri potest. Sic quoque illi σύγχρονος Ignatius Epist. ad Antiochenos: Caesari subiecti estote, in iis, quibus subdi, nulium animae periculum est. Similiter Chrysostomus: Tu cùm audis, reddenda esse Caesari, quae sua sunt, illa solùm dici, non dubita, quae pietati & religioni nihil officiunt: nam quod fidei & virtuti obest, non Caesaris, sed diaboli tributum & vectigal est. Cùm proinde tributi solutio nihil contineat, quod pietati vel conscientiae libertati adversetur, graviter monet Salvator, ut Caesari, utpote sub cuius potestate & protectione Iudaei tum erant, tributum persolvant. Conf. Dnn. Theolog. Saxon. in Fundam. defens. Pupillae p. 87. seqq. it. p. 671. B. D. Hutterus LL. Theol. Mai. p. 1041. ac pag. 500. B. Par. L. de Ministr. Polit. §. 474., * Isidorus Pelusiota lib 1. ep. 209. Si quid materiae proprium, si quod erroris instrumentum, si quod imposturae simulacrum intestina nobis socordia iniecit, hoc Dominus ad vitri architectum & effectorem à nobis proiici vult. Contrà si quod virtutis symbolum, si quod honestatis insigne, si quod vigilantiae atq cautionis lucrum, hoc DEI beneficio nobis contigisse, persuasum nobis habere, debitamq laudem illi offerre. Tossanus ita h. l. exponit: Quia ex usu monetae Romanae apparet, vos esse sub potestatem & iurisdictionem Romani Imperatoris redactos, ideò tributum debitum Imperatori praestate: id verò non debet impedire, quò minùs dimidium ficli in lege requisitum detis Deo, Exod. 30, 12. & iuxta praescriptum verbi ipsi serviatis, cùm Romani libertatem religionis vobis concesserint. *(Cùm verò inter ea, quae danda Caesari sunt, tributum etiam pertineat, quod hoc fine dare iubemur. quò subditis defensionem praestare ac vindictam adversùs pacis publicae turbatores exercere possit, manifestum est, quòd iuri eivino & voluntati divinae congruum sit, à Magistrati. pu-i-imalos, adeoque si plures sese coniunx-rint, bel-um adversùs e- ge-i. Contra -hotinianos.

quos contra pluribus agunt B. D. Meisner in Theolog. Photin. Consid. pag. 223. B. Par. L. de Minist. Ecclesiastico § 3-7. Colligit porrò ex hoc Salvatoris adserto Bernhardus, etiam clericos non esse exemtos à persolutione tributi. Ita enim in ep. 42. quae ad Archi Episco pum Senonensem est, scribit: Quod hîc ore locutus est, mox opere implere curavit. Conditor Casaris, Caesari non cunctatus est censum reddere. Exemplum enim dedit vobis (clericis) ut & vos ita faciatis &c. Conf. Rom. 13, 1.2. Petri 2, 13.Rom. 13, 1. seqq. Dictum Bernhardi ipse allegat Corn. à Lapide. Addatur quoque Chrysostomus in c. 13. ep. ad Rom. Ridicula verò est expositio huius mandati, quam affert -acobus de Terano, Urbani VI. Cubicularius, statuens, quod non nisi usq ad adscensionem eius (Christi) praecepti vim habuer-nt sed post ascensionem omnia Imperia à Caesare & Regibus ad Christi vicarium (Pontificem intelligit Romanum) fuerint transferenda. Idq; probare conatur ex Ioh. 12, 32. Verùm contrarium patet ex mandato Petri, (quem tamen primum Christi vicarium Romae sedisse Pontificii somniant.) 1. ep. 2, 13. Pauli item Rom. 13, 1. seqq. Tit. 3, 1. Aliud etiam docuerunt primitiae Ecclesiae Doctores. Bernhardi monitum paullò ante allatum fuit. Idem l. c. Omnis, scribit, anima potestatibus sublimioribus sit subdita: si omnis, & vestra. Quis vos excepit ab universitate? si quis tentat excipere, conatur decipere. Conferatur idem ep. 170. item Chrysostomus hom. 23. in epist. ad Rom. Neque tamen hoc volumus, quasi non possit debeatve Magistratus Christianus exemplo Iosephi, Gen. 47, 22. Artaxerxis l. 1. Esdrae c. 7, 24. aliorumque, privilegiis atque immunitatibus quibusdam clericos ornare. Sed de eo saltem quaestio est, an clerici de Iure Divino ab oneribus pubicis & Magistratûs Politici imperio sint exemti. Id quod à nobis negatur. Similiter contra Libertinos, qui in N.
