T. subiectionem Magistratui debitam per Christianam libertatem sublatam esse negant, urgeri dictum hoc potest. Sed de illis pluribus agetur in Analect. ad Ioh. 8, 36. Patet denique ex h. l. quòd impio etiam Magistratui, qualis erat Caesar, parricida nempe, adulter, scortator &c. in rebus, quae pietati non adversantur, parendum sit. Idque patet 1. ex generalibus Script. S. dictis, Rom. 13. 2. probatis exemplis. Conf. Ioh. 19, 11. 3. à pari, duris scil. Dominis 1. Petr 2, 18. 19. 20. ac Parentibus severis. 4. ab orationibus, fundendis etiam pro Principibus Ethnicis. Vid. Ierem. 29, 7.1. Tim. 2, 2. Secus sese res habet, si Princeps aliquid, quod pietati fuerit adversum, praecipiat. Tunc enim supplicandum, vel fug-endum. Conf. plura huc spectantia apud B. D. Winckelm. Dispp. Marpurg. t. 5. Disp. 14. B. D. Lobechium in A. C. p. 407. B. D. Roenig Casuum Catechet. p. 43. B. Par. L. de Magistr. Polit. § 80. item Dispp. El-ncht. p. 1253. Vis veritatis coë git Iesuitam Costerum, ut in Enchir. Controv. p. 113. scriberet: Christus politicam administrandi rationem adventu suo non immutavit, sed principibus reliquit. Reddite inquit &c. Quietem enim externam aut civilem cur are possunt etiam qui à rectâ fidei viâ prorsus aberrant, quibus Ius Imperii auferri noluit &c. Limitat quidem Iesuita propositionem hanc, addendo particulam tunc. Quâ ipsâ si hoc innuit, quòd Christus quidem tunc, cùm in carne vixit, impiis vel ethnicis Magistratibus imperium adimere noluerit, hodie verò fictitii eius successores, Pontifices Romani, iure id possint, vehementer fallit ac fallitur. Conf. Dnn. Theolog. Sax. in Fundam. Defens. p. 668. & 685. it. B. Par. Confess. Cath. l. 2. art. 3. c. 9.)*

## 22:21
v. 23. The Sadducees approached. The Syriac: The Sadducees approached & said to him. There is no resurrection of the dead, & they questioned him. Therefore, the proposition and the scope of the disputation are contained in these words. Furthermore, concerning the Sadducees, see Schidl. in Lex. under the word -- *(Conf. Anal. ad c. 3, 7. Matth.)*

Latin:

v. 23. Accesserunt Sadducaei. Syrus: Accesserunt Sadukai & dixerunt ei. Non est resurrectio mortu-rum, & interrogarunt cum. Continetur ergo in his verbis propositio & scopus disputationis. Coeterùm de Sadducaeis vid. Schidl. in Lex. in verbo -- *(Conf. Anal. ad c. 3, 7. Matth.)*

## 22:22
*(v. 22. And hearing. Conf. Ps. 9, 16.Prov. 21, 30.)*

*( Μη έίναι άνάςαοιν. Conf. Actor. 23, 8. For they supposed that the souls of men, just like those of beasts, are reduced to nothing when released from bodies. Let Josephus be compared, lib. 18. A. I. c. 2. also lib. 2. de B. I. c. 7. Jerome explicitly concerning the same: They thought the soul perishes with the bodies. Whence they also taught that no rewards of this life were established by God for those keeping the law.)*

Latin:

*(v. 22. Et audientes. Conf. Ps. 9, 16.Prov. 21, 30.)*

*( Μη έίναι άνάςαοιν. Conf. Actor. 23, 8. Existimarunt enim, animas hominum perinde ut brutorum, in nihilum redigi, à corporibus solutas. Conferatur Iosephus, lib. 18. A. I. c. 2. it. lib. 2. de B. I. c. 7. Hieronymus disertè de iisdem: Animam putabant interire cum corporibus. Unde etiam non nisi huius vitae praemia legem servantibus à Deo constitui, docebant.)*

## 22:24
v. 24. The Sadducees propose an absurd case of a wife of seven husbands. For they attempted to prove by three arguments that there is no resurrection. The first is what Christ refutes in this place.

The second is from the unwritten, which is refuted below v. 32. For they received the law in such a way that they entirely rejected the exposition of the wise. The third is mentioned by the author of the Talmudic Lexicon: For if, they said, our Fathers had believed that the dead would rise again, and that rewards remain after this life, they would not have rebelled so often.

ρπι γαμβςευσει. γαμβρός is properly that which is called in Latin son-in-law, and ρπι γαμβρεία is the joining to a son-in-law. That is said to be in the law of Moses, that when someone has died without children, his brother should become a son-in-law in his place, namely of him whose brother had died, i.e., that he should take the wife of this man, and raise up children in the name of his brother. Which is called in the Hebrew phrase to raise up seed for a brother.* (That Mosaic law concerning marrying a brother's wife was ceremonial, regarding only the Jews, to whom God therefore gave such a law, so that estates would not be alienated from their tribe. see Num. 36. Ruth ch. 3 & 4, and so that the tribes would not be confounded, and thus it might be more correctly established concerning the birth of the Messiah, born from the seed of David. That that custom existed even before the Mosaic law, however, is clear from Gen. 38. Hugo Grotius notes in this place that the law of marrying a brother's wife had a place only when not even a daughter was present, since by Hebrew law a grandson from a daughter could be inserted into the grandfather's family. This becomes clear from Num 27, 3. Polygamy, however, can by no means be proven from that divine constitution concerning marrying a brother's wife, since the surviving brother of the childless deceased should have taken the widow as a wife only if he were not yet bound to another spouse, as B. Par. correctly proves from the context of Deut. 25, 5. in his Commentary on the said law, as well as B. D. Tarn. book 2, on Marriage ch. 25, who also treat this custom at greater length. Let there be compared also, if you please, Simon Episcopius the Arminian, book 3 of Theological Institutions, ch. 10, p 115, 116, who nevertheless exempts the brother from the levirate in that case at least, if he already had the sister or daughter of the brother's wife joined to him in marriage. But the context seems to require that in general everyone already married be excepted from the Levirate.)*

Latin:

v. 24. Proponunt Sadducaei casum absurdum septemvirae uxoris. Tribus enim argumentis probare conabantur, non esse resurrectionem. Primum est, quod Christus hoc loco refellit.

Secundum est à non scripto, quod refellitur infrà v. 32. Nam legem ita recipiebant, ut expositionem sapientum omninò reiicerent. Tertium memorat autor Lexici Talmudici: Si enim, inquiebant, Patres nostri credidissent, mortuos resurrecturos, & praemia manere post hanc vitam, non tam saepè rebellassent.

ρπι γαμβςευσει. γαμβρός propriè is est affinis, qui Latinè dicitur gener, atque ρπι γαμβρεία est generi adiunctio. Id dicitur esse in lege Mosis, ut mortuo aliquo sine liberis ipsius loco frater eius fiat gener, illius scilicet, cuius fuerat frater mortuus, i. e. ut ducat uxorem huius, & suscipiat liberos nomine fratris sui. Quod phrasi Ebraicâ dicitur suscitare semen fratri.* (Fuit autem lex illa Mosaica de fratriâ ducendâ ceremonialis, solos Iudaeos respiciens, quibus propterea Deus talem dedit legem, ne feuda à suâ tribu abalienarentur. vid. Numer. 36. Ruth. c 3. & 4. nec tribus confunderentur, atque ita de Messiae, è semine Davidis prognati ortu rectiùs constaret. Fuisse tamen consuetudinem illam etiam iam ante legem Mosaicam, patet ex Gen. 38. Notat Hugo Grotius in h. l. quod lex deducenda fratriâ tum demum habuerit locum, quando ne quidem filia aderat, cùm iure Ebraeo nepos ex filiâ in avi familiam inseri potuerit. Clarum hoc evadit ex Num 27, 3. Minimè autem polygamia ex constitutione illa divinâ de ducenda fratriâ probari potest, cùm tum demum frater superstes defuncti illiberis viduam ducere uxorem debuerit, si nondum alteri coniugi alligatus esset, uti rectè è contextu Deut. 25, 5. probat B. Par. Comm, ad d. l. nec non B. D. Tarn. l. 2. de Coniug. c. 25, qui etiam pluribus de consuetudine istâ agunt. Conferatur etiam si placet, Simon Episcopius Arminianous l. 3. Instit. Theol. c. 10. p 115. 116. qui tamen in eo saltem casu fratrem à levitatu eximit, si fratriae sororem vel filiam habuerit iam tum matrimonio sibi iunctam. Sed contextus requirere videtur, ut in genere omnis iam ante uxoratus à Leviratu excipiatur.)*

## 22:29
v. 29. You err, not knowing the Scriptures etc. Two principles of all errors. Ignorance of the Scriptures, and disputes concerning the power of GOD. *(The Sadducees are deservedly referred to Holy Scripture, since in it the will of God, which for reasons even the most firm should suffice for all the pious, has been revealed to us, as well as to the power of God, which, since it is infinite, can neither be nor ought to be examined by the standard of human reason, circumscribed by such small limits. Whence it is by no means to be asserted that God cannot perform those things which we cannot comprehend by our reason. Especially when a divine promise exists, as in this place. To which pertain the sayings Luc. 1, 37.Eph. 3, 20. & the example of Abraham Gen. 17.Rom. 4, 17. -oeterùm the sayings of Holy Scripture asserting the resurrection of the dead, in the O. T. besides the oracle brought here by the Savior, occur not a few. Among which stand out Iob. 19, 25.Esai. 26, 19.c. 66, 14.Ezech. 37, 1. and 9. Daniel 12, 13. So that the Photinian opinion is false, that eternal life was not promised to the faithful in the O. T., or that there does not exist an open promise of eternal life in the O. T. as Smalcius has it in De Divinit. I. C. c. 7. nay, not even of the resurrection, according to Ioh. Crellius. Respons. ad librum Hug. Grotii de Satisfact. p. 30. Whose error is sufficiently refuted even from this passage at least. For if the covenant, which God struck with Abraham &c., endured even after their death, it follows that they themselves also live after their death, and indeed with eternal life, since no other is given after death. If furthermore God remained the God of Abraham even after death, it follows that Abraham believed in the resurrection or another life from the divine promise. Otherwise it would follow that God remained the God of Abraham even after his death, an unfaithful one. Nor can it be said that this promise was not open, since the promise of eternal life can be elicited from that divine promise made to Abraham only through consequences. For it suffices for us that the consequence, which our Savior formed from that promise, was so firm that the Sadducees were so constrained that they had nothing to reply. Nor is it to be passed over that Sim. Episcopius also, otherwise excellently favoring the Photinians, l. 5. Instit. Theol. c. 5. c. 4. pag. 409. constrained by the force of truth confesses that God wished to include the promise of a better life, to be given even after death, in His promises Gen. 15, 1. and c. 17, 7.. Conf. the same p. 33. We learn indeed from the present disputation, which Christ had with the Sadducees, that those also exist in Holy Scripture, and ought to be held as articles of faith, which are elicited from it through a firm and immovable consequence. Concerning which B. D. Fewrborn treats at greater length in Anti Osterodo Disp. 4. §. 6. seqq. B. D. Roenig. Vindic. Sacr. L. 23. §. 4i. and L. 53. §. 6. The Lords Theologians of Saxony in Prolix. Pupillae Deduct. pag. 143 also in Necess. Defens. A. C. p. 115. 116. B. D. Balduinus contra Patzm p. 649. B. Par. Confess. Cathol. l. 2. Spec. art. 1. c. 3. §. 5. also Dispp. Acad. p. 1069. Dn. D. Calovius Socin. Proflig. p. 70. seqq. also in Armin. Consid. p. 54. From the ancients, S. Athanasius can be consulted above all t. 1. p. 415. 439. 703. Excellently Greg. Nazianzenus l. 5. de Theologiâ: What is gathered from the Scriptures is to be held just as if it were written in them. The Blessed Par. Confess. Cath. l. c. p. 252. seqq. produces Papist writers teaching the same thing, whatever the fabricators of a new art may decree to the contrary. Let there also be compared above all Mr. D. Chemnitius, colleague and relative, and likewise brother in Christ most to be honored, in Disp. 4 on the Sense of Holy Scripture § 13. Rivetus may also be added in Isag. ad Sc. S. c. 17. Explicitly Felicianus Capitonus, Archbishop of Avignon, in Explic. Cathol. p. 548. It is to be noted that something is founded in the Scriptures in two ways: formally, or virtually. Formally indeed, that which is held in express words, as that the world was created by God. Virtually however, that which is gathered from them by necessary deduction, as the consubstantiality of the persons, from Matthew the last. &c.)*

*( ηδέ τήν δύναμιν τού θεού. H. Grotius disputes in this place that the Sadducees denied the resurrection, not so much because they believed that the dissolved parts of the body could not be put back together, as because they thought that souls could not be sustained without a body.)*

Latin:

v. 29. Erratis, nescientes Scripturas &c. Duo principia omnium errorum. Ignorantia Scripturarum, & disputationes de potentiâ DEI. *(Meritò verò ad Scripturam Sacram remittuntur Sadducaei, quippe cùm in illa volun as Dei, quae pro rationibus etiam firmissimis piis omnibus sufficere debet, revelata nobis sit, tum quoque ad Dei potentiam, quae cùm infinita sit, ad rationis humanae, exiguis adeò terminis circumscriptae, amussim examinari nec potest, nec debet. Unde haut quaquam adserendum, quòd Deus ea, quae ratione nostrâ comprehendere non possumus, praestare nequeat. Maximè quando divina extat promissio, ut h l. Quo faciunt dicta Luc. 1, 37.Eph. 3, 20. & exemplum Abrahami Gen. 17.Rom. 4, 17. -oeterùm dicta Sc. Sacrae resurrectionem mortuorum adstruentia, in V. T. praeter oraculum à Salvatore hîc allatum, occurrunt non pauca. Inter quae eminent Iob. 19, 25.Esai. 26, 19.c. 66, 14.Ezech. 37, 1. ac 9. Danielis 12, 13. Ut adeò falsa sit Photinianorú opinio, quòd fidelibus in V. T. vita aeterna non fuerit promissa, sive quòd non extet apertum vitae aeternae in V. T. promissum. ut habet Smalcius de Divinit. I. C. c. 7. quin nec resurrectionis, iuxta Ioh. Crellium. Respons. ad librum Hug. Grotii de Satisfact. p. 30. Quorum error vel ex hoc saltem loco satis refellitur. Si enim foedus, quod Deus cum Abrahamo &c. pepigit, etiam post mortem eorum duravit, sequitur, quòd ipsi etiam post mortem suā vivant, & quidem vitā aeternā, cùm alia post mortem non detur. Si praeterea Deus etiam post mortem mansit Deus Abrahami, sequitur, quòd Abrahamus resurrectionem vel vitam alteram crediderit ex promissione divinâ. Alioquin sequeretur, quòd Deus etiam Abrahami infidelis manserit Deus post mortem eius. Nec dici potest, promissionem hanc non fuisse apertam, quippe cùm non nisi per consequentias ex promissione illâ divinâ Abrahamo factâ possit elici vitae aeternae promissio. Etenim sufficit nobis, quòd consequentia, quam Salvator noster ex illâ promissione formavit, adeò fuerit firma, ut Sadducaei ita fuerint constricti, ut quod regererēt, nil haberent. Nec praetermittendum, quòd Sim. quoque Episcopius, egregiè aliàs Photinianis favens, l. 5. Instit. Theol. c. 5. c. 4. pag. 409. vi veritatis constrictus fareatur, Deum promissionem vitae melioris, etiam post mortem dandae, promissis suis Gen. 15, 1. ac c. 17, 7. compre hendere voluisse. Conf. idem p. 33. Discimus verò è praesenti disputatione, quam Christus cum Sadducaeis habuit, quòd illa quoque in Sc. Sacrâ extent, ac pro fidei haberi articulis debeant, quae per firmam & immoram consequentiam inde eliciuntur. Quâ de prolixiùs agunt B. D. Fewrborn. in Anti Osterodo Disp. 4. §. 6. seqq. B. D. Roenig. Vindic. Sacr. L. 23. §. 4i. ac L. 53. §. 6. Dnn. Theologi Saxon. in Prolix. Pupillae Deduct. pag. 143 it. in Necess. Defens. A. C. p. 115. 116. B. D. Balduinus contra Patzm p. 649. B. Par. Confess. Cathol. l. 2. Spec. art. 1. c. 3. §. 5. item Dispp. Acad. p. 1069. Dn. D. Calovius Socin. Proflig. p. 70. seqq. it. in Armin. Consid. p. 54. E veteribus consuli cumprimis potest S. Athanasius t. 1. p. 415. 439. 703. Egregiè Greg. Nazianzenus l. 5. de Theologiâ: Quae colliguntur ex Scripturis, perinde sunt habenda, ac si in illis scripta essent. Pontificios Scriptores idem docentes, quic quid etiam novae artis fabricatores statuant contrà, producit B. Par. Confess. Cath l. c. p. 252. seqq. Conferatur quoque cumprimis Dn. D Chemnitius, Collega atque Affinis, itemque in Christo Frater pl. honorandus in Disp. 4 de Sensu Sc. S. § 13. Addi etiam potest Rivetus in Isag. ad Sc. S. c. 17. Disertè Felicianus Capitonus, Archi Episcopus Avinionensis in Explic. Cathol. p. 548. Notandum, fundari quippiam iScripturis dupliciter: formaliter, vel virtualiter. Formaliter quidem, quod expressis verbis habetur, ut mundum à Deo creatum. Virtualiter autem, quod ex illis necessaria deductione colligitur, ut personarum consubstantialitas, ex Matth. ult. &c.)*

*( ηδέ τήν δύναμιν τού θεού. Disputat H. Grotius in h. l. Sadducaeos negasse resurrectionem, non tam quòd crederent, dissolutas corporis partes non posse re componi, quàm quòd putarent, non posse sustentari animas fine corpore.)*

## 22:30
v. 30. In the resurrection they shall neither contract marriage &c. Iosephus Albo Soriensis in the book of the articles of faith, sermon 4, c. 30. The future age is the age after death, when the soul is separated from the body, in which they do not eat, nor drink, nor engage in Venus. *(The Vulgate rendered Το γαμιζονται as they shall marry, not sufficiently in Latin. Whatever Philippus Caroli may clamor to the contrary. See Mr. Dilherr. disp. Acad. t. 1. p. 47.)*

They shall be ιςάγγελοι, Not by reason of essence, but as regards the mode of living, the most happy condition and immortality. Not through of human substance into angelic mutation, as Hincmar's error has it, which the Magdeburg Centuriators rebuke, Cent. 9. c. 4. p. 205. but accidental perfection in qualities. *(Compare 1. Cor. 15, 42. seqq. Philipp. 3, 21. Tertullian lib. de Resurr. Carnis c. 62. He did not say, they will be angels, lest he deny they were men, but as angels, that he might preserve them as men. They will not be blessed similar to the angels by reason of ούςίας or by the essence of nature, but they will be as the angels, or they will be similar to them by reason of ποιό τητος or by the agreement of qualities and glory. So that just as the angels have no need of food, drink, clothing, marriage, because they are spirits. (Now indeed a spirit does not beget, as Thomas Aquinas shows at length p. 1. q. 51. art. 3. Thus the same neither eat nor drink, as the Gentiles themselves teach.) so neither will the blessed have need of these. Because they will have bodies πνευμαΤιΚά. Well Augustine in Qq. Evangel. at Luc. 20, 35. Marriages are for the sake of children, children for the sake of succession, succession for the sake of death. There, therefore, death is not, nor marriages. Furthermore, just as the angels, inasmuch as they were created by God in that number which seemed sufficient to Him, have no need of multiplication through generation: So also when the number of the blessed in eternal life has been filled, there will be no need for it to be increased through generation. But the sophistries of the Sadducees, by which they attempted to overturn or at least to weaken the resurrection of the dead, philosophy itself also refutes. Since indeed those three souls, considered according to that part which is called φυσιΚη faculties, namely the nutritive, the augmentative, and the generative, are excluded by the Philosopher himself from the communion of the highest moral Good, how much more will they be excluded from the communion of the ultimate end of the Christian man. Conf. Apocal. 7, 16. Moreover, this also must be well noted, that that perfection of qualities ought not to be extended too much: but that one must look to the scope of Christ. As the Jesuit Barradius also well observed, when in t. 3. Comm. in Evang. lib. 8. c. 15. p. 502. he writes: They will be similar and equal to the angels, as far as pertains to marriage, and the same is noted by the Jesuit Cornelius à Lapide, teaching in this place that that ισαγγελότης consists 1. in purity. 2. in life spiritual. 3. in incorruption and immortality, 4. in happiness and glory. The Jesuit therefore errs, and the same R. E. Cardinal Patmannus, when in l. 13. Hodegi c. 3. following Lindanus, Richeomus, Costerus, and others Papists, attempts to prove the omniscience, if I may so speak, of the deceased saints from this also among other things, that they themselves will be ισαγγελοι. For not to touch upon the fact that even if the angels knew some human things in the highest degree, such knowledge would nevertheless by no means suffice for religious invocation, it is denied that it consists in that ισαγγελότης, indicated here by Christ. Namely, that just as the angels are present to pious men on account of the office divinely committed to them and thus know some human things, as much as is necessary for them for the administration of their office, from divine revelation, so also the blessed dead know human things. Holy Scripture says that angels are ministering spirits. But it records nothing of the sort concerning the deceased saints. Furthermore, against the Photinians and Weigelians, denying that the same bodies as to essence will one day receive the extreme day, when the blessed are said to be ισαγγελοι it must be noted that ισότης -αι όμοιότης, is one thing, ταυτότης. is another; similar is not the same. Conf. on this matter Tertullian cited above, likewise Methodius in Epiphanius l. 2. t. 1. against heresies p. 18-. alleged by B. P. L. de Resurr. Mort. §. 74. Furthermore, from the fact that the blessed are said to be ισαγγελοι, it is gathered 1. their confirmation in good. To which also Apoc. 3, 12. looks. see B. Par. L. de vita aeternâ §. 39. 2. that there will be degrees of glory in eternal life. Conf. likewise B. Par. d. l. §. 128.)* Finally, while Christ makes mention of the angels, he tacitly strikes at the Sadducees, who denied that there were angels. * (But the question, how Christ argues against the Sadducees from the example of the angels, whom they nevertheless denied. Hugo Grotius answers, Christ is solving an argument, not arguing. Now indeed, he who answers, can use suppositions denied by the adversary.)*

Latin:

v. 30. In resurrectione neq matrimonium contrahent &c. Iosephus Albo Soriensis in lib. artic. fidei serm. 4. c. 30. Seculum futurum est seculum post mortem, cùm anima separata est à corpore, in quo non comedunt, neq bibunt, neque Veneri operantur. *(Vulgatus Το γαμιζονται reddidit nubentur, non satis Latinè Quic quid etiam clamitet contrà Philippus Caroli. Vid. Dn. Dilherr. disp. Acad. t. 1. p. 47.)*

Eruntιςάγγελοι, Non ratione essentiae, sed quoad modum vivendi, felicissimam conditionem & immortalitatem. Non per humanae substantiae in Angelicam mutationem, ut Hincmari habet error, quem reprehendunt Centur. Magdeburg. Cent. 9. c. 4. pag. 205. sed accidentalem in qualitatibus perfectionem. *(Confer 1. Cor. 15, 42. seqq. Philipp. 3, 21. Tertullianus lib. de Resurr. Carnis c. 62. Non dixit, erunt Angeli, ne homines negaret, sed tanquam Angeli, ut homines conservaret. Non erunt beati Angelis similes ratione ούςίας sive per naturae essentiam, sed sicut Angeli erunt, sive similes illis erunt ratione ποιό τητος sive per qualitatum ac gloriae convenientiam. Ut quemad modum Angeli non opus habent cibo, potu, vestitu, coniugio, quia sunt spiritus. (Iam verò Spiritus non generat, ceu latè ostendit Thomas Aquinas p. 1. q. 51. art. 3. Sic iidem nec edunt nec bibunt, ipsis docentibus gentilibus.) ita nec beati his opus habituri sint. Quia corpora habituri sunt πνευμαΤιΚά. Benè Augustinus in Qq. Evangel. ad Luc. 20, 35.Connubia sunt propter filios, filii propter successionem, successio propter mortem. Ibi ergo mors non est, neq connubia. Praeterea sicut Angeli, utpote cùm eo numero creati à Deo sint, qui ipsi fufficiens visus, non opus habent multiplicatione per generationem: Ita quoque cùm numerus beatorum in vitâ aeternâ fuerit impletus, non opus erit, ut per generationem ille augeatur. Argutias verò Sadducaeorum, quibus mortuorum resurrectionem evertere. vel labefactare saltem conabantur, ipsa quoq; -hilosophia redarguit. Cùm n. tres illae animae, secundùm eam partem, quae φυσιΚη dicitur, consideratae facultates, puta altrix, auctrix & procreatrix, secundùm ipsum Philosophum à comunione summi Boni moralis excludantur, quanto magis à communione ultimi hominis Christiani finis eae excludentur. Conf. Apocal. 7, 16. Caeterùm & hoc notandum probè est, quod illa qualitatum perfectio non extendi nimium debeat: sed quòd ad Christi scopum respiciendum sit. Ceu benè etiam observavit Iesuita Barradius, quando t. 3. Comm. in Evang. lib. 8. c. 15. p. 502. scribit: Erunt similes & aquales Angelis, quod attinet ad nuptias, idemque notatum Iesuitae Cornelio à Lapide, docenti h. l. quòd illaισαγγελότηςconsistat 1. in puritate. 2. in vitâ spirituali. 3. in incorruptione & immortalitate, 4. in felicitate. & gloria. Errat igitur Iesuita, idemque R. E. Cardinalis Pat-mannus, quando l. 13. Hodegi c. 3. Lindanum, Richeomum, Costerum, aliosq; Pontificios sequutus, omniscientiam, ut ita loquar, sanctorum defunctorum ex eo quoque inter alia probate conatur, quòd ipsi futuri ισαγγελοι. E-enim utiam non tangam, quòd si vel maximè Angeli sciant aliquas res humanas, talis tamen scientia ad invocationem religiosam hautquaquam sufficiat, negatur, quòd in eo ισαγγελότης, à Christo hîc indicata, consistat. Nempè quòd ceu Angeli propter officium divinitùs illis commissum piis hominibus adsunt adeoque res aliquas humanas, quantum eis ad officii administrationem necessarium est, ex revelatione divinâ sciunt, ita etiam beati defuncti res humanas sciant. Angelos administratorios spiritus esse, sacra Sc. dicit. at de sanctis defunctis nil tale commemorat. Porrò contra Photinianos ac Weigelianos, negantes, eadem corpora quoad essentiam aliquando in die extremnos recepturos esse, cùm beati dicanturισαγγελοι notandum, quòd aliud sit ισότης -αι όμοιότης, aliud ταυτότης.simile non est idem. Conf. hanc in rem Tertullianus suprà adductus, item Methodius apud Epiphanium l. 2. t. 1. adversùs haeres. p. 18-. alleg. à B. P. L. de Resurr. Mort. §. 74. Porro ex eo, quòd beati futuri dicuntur ισαγγελοι, colligitur 1. eorundem confirmatio in bono. quo etiam spectat Apoc. 3, 12. vid. B. Par. L. de vitaeternâ §. 39. 2. gradus gloriae fore in virâ aeternâ. Conf. itidem B. Par. d. l. §. 128.)* Denique dum Christus mentionem facit Angelorum, tacitè perstringit Sadducaeos, qui Angelos esse inficiabantur. * (Q. verò, quomodo Christus contra Sadducaeos ab exemplo Angelorum argumentetur, quos tamen ilii negabant. Respondet Hugo Grotius, Christum solvere argumentum, non argumentari. Iam verò, qui respondet, uti posse suppositionibus, ab adversario negatis.)*

## 22:31
v. 31. That which was said to you by God. He answers from Moses 1. because the Sadducees received no Scriptures besides the law. (Thus think Origen, Jerome, Bede, and others. And Josephus, , explicitly reveals this about the Sadducees, namely that they received only the books of Moses, in book 18, chapter 2. But Scaliger denies this in Elench. motus, especially for this reason, That he was addicted to the sect of the Sadducees, and was elected and constituted High Priest, Acts, 5, 17. a thing which would by no means have happened, if he had rejected the Prophets. Resp. I distinguish between the state of the Republic and the rectitude of the Jewish Church, and the corrupt state. Certainly, while sincere religion was flourishing, such a man would by no means have been constituted High Priest. But at that time all things were in confusion. And what wonder is it that a High Priest was tolerated who called the authority of the Prophetic books into doubt, if he was tolerated who denied the resurrection of the dead and the immortality of the soul. Which indeed a Sadducean High Priest did. Furthermore, it cannot even be certainly gathered from the alleged passage Acts 5, 17. that the High Priest himself was addicted to the heresy of the Sadducees. They did indeed read the Prophets and the Psalms, but just as we read the books of the Maccabees, 2. because they had set Moses against them.

Latin:

v. 31. Quod vobis dictum est à Deo. Ex Mose respondet 1. quia Sadducaei praeter legem nullas recipiebant Scripturas. *(Ita sentiunt Origenes, Hieronymus, Beda, alii. Ac disertè de Sadducaeis id, quòd nempe solos libros Mosis receperint, prodit Iosephus lib. 18. c. 2. Ast negat hoc Scaliger in Elench. motus eâ cumprimis ratione, quòd Sadducaeae sectae addictus, electus & constitutus fuerit Pontifex,Actor, 5, 17.id quod minimè factum, si Prophetas respuisset. Resp. disting. inter statum Reip. & Ecclesiae Iudaicae rectum, & corruptum. Sanè florente religione sincerâ, utique talis non fuisser Pontifex constitutus. Sed tum omnia erant confusa. Et quid mirum, toleratum fuisse Pontificem, qui autoritatem librorum Propheticorum in dubium vocavit, si toleratus fuit, qui resurrectionem mortuorum & animae immortalitatem negavit. Quod utique Sadducaeus Pontifex fecit. Praeterea nec certò ex loco allegato Act. 5, 17. colligi potest, quòd ipse Pontifex haeresi Sadducaeorum fuerit addictus.)* Legebant quidem Prophetas & Psalmos, sed ficut nos legimus libros Maccabaeorum, 2. quia Mosen ipsi obiecerant.

## 22:32
v. 32. I am the God of Abraham &c. Aben Ezra in Lev. 18, 3. Idedicit, I will be the Lord your God, to show that they themselves will live in both ages. To whom God promised that He wishes to be their God and Father forever, they are not dead, but live, otherwise they could not have enjoyed the promised grace. But God promised this to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, namely in the peculiar covenant which He entered into with them. And they live. Just as they now live according to the soul, so in the resurrection they are also to live according to the body, because God did not enter into that covenant with the soul alone: nay, the sign of the covenant received in the body shows that the body also will be a participant in eternal glory. But how is God not the God of the dead, when Christ is said to have risen for this reason, that He might have dominion over the dead and the living, Rom. 14, 9. Resp. These things are said ηατ -ωοληψιν accommodated, namely, to the opinion of the Sadducees concerning the dead, whom they maintained to perish utterly. Paul calls dead those who have departed from this life, even if they still live by their better part. *(Thus also explain B D. --nig Vind. Sacr. L. 66. B. D. Calixt. Concord. Evang. p. 301. it. tr. de Immort. Animae p. 35. B. D. Fewrborn. in Anti Ostorod. Disp. 4. §. 7. others.)* Others accept the saying of Christ thus. God is not the true God whom the dead worship, i. e., those who have perished utterly and are nothing.

(1. The Sadducees thought that men perish completely through death, establishing indeed that souls are extinguished together with the body. See Josephus, book 18, Antiquities of the Jews, chapter 2. How the ancient Jews constructed the resurrection of the dead against the Sadducees, W. Schikardus shows from the Talmud in Bechin Happeruschim, p. 160 et seqq. Compare also Petrus Galatinus in Arcan. Cathol. verit. Furthermore, by this statement of the Savior, the error of the Psychopannychians is destroyed, that the souls of the pious before the final day, as if lulled to sleep, do not perceive the joys of eternal life. For life consists in action. See B. Par. L. de Morte §. 299. Regarding the exceptions of the Photinians, who establish that to the pious in the Old Testament no promise of eternal life was made, it is to be noted 1. that the Savior speaks in the present Luke 20, 38 They live. 2. That the fathers are therefore said to live, because their souls live. For it is a customary synecdoche in Holy Scripture, by which that which belongs to the part is attributed to the whole. See Luke 23, 43 Phil. 1, 23. 3. That God does not say I was, as if He had once done good, but I am, as Christ alleges. 4. That the Apostle, when he calls Christ Lord of the dead and of the living, understands by the dead those who no longer live in these lands, yet meanwhile live a blessed life in heaven as to the soul. Compare the same B. Par. l. c. §. 144 (where he also alleges excellent testimonies of the ancient Doctors of the Church, confirming our opinion:) as well as B. D. Martini Consid. Photin. c. 8. 115. seqq. B. Hackspan. Orat. Inaug. Moreover, the argument of Christ, which He used here against the Sadducees, is explained at greater length by B. D. Calixtus in his one book on the Immortality of the Soul, c. 5. D. Rivetus in Exodus, and likewise in Isag. ad Sc. S. Hugo Grotius in this place, who can be consulted. Especially also let the Epistle to the Hebrews c. 11, 16 and 1 Cor. 15, 18 be compared. But why the Lord did not refute the Sadducees from other, perhaps clearer, sayings of the Old Testament, but from such a saying, from which the resurrection of the dead was to be elicited only by consequence, is usually debated in various ways. See D. Calixtus l. c. p. 36. 37. and compare the notes to v. 31.)

Latin:

v. 32. Ego sum Deus Abraham &c. Aben Ezra in Lev. 18, 3.Idedicit, ego ero Dominus Deus vester, ut ostendat, ipsos victuros in utroq seculo. Quibus Deus promisit, quòd in aeternum velit esse ipsorum Deus ac pater, illi non sunt mortui, sed vivūt, alias nō potuissēt promissâ gratiâ frui. Atqui Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo Deus hoc promisit, in peculiari scil. foedere, quod cū ipsis iniit E. vivunt. Sicut iam vivunt secūdùm animam, ita in resurrectione etiam secundùm corpus victuri sunt, quia Deus non cum solâ animâ illud foedus iniit: quinimò signum foederis in corpore susceptum ostendit, etiam corpus gloriae aeternae particeps futurum. Sed quomodo Deus non est Deus mortuorum, cùm Christus ideò dicatur resurrexisse, ut mortuis ac viventibus dominetur,Rom. 14, 9. Resp. Haec dicuntur ηατ -ωοληψιν accommodata sc. ad Sadducaeoru opinionem de mortuis, quos ipsi statuebant funditus interire. Paulus vocat mortuos eos, qui ex hâc vitâ decesserunt, etiamsi adhuc parte sui meliore vivant. *(Ita etiam explicant B D. --nig Vind. Sacr. L. 66. B. D. Calixt. Concord. Evang. p. 301. it. tr. de Immort. Animae p. 35. B. D. Fewrborn. in Anti Ostorod. Disp. 4. §. 7. alii.)* Dictum Christi alii sic accipiunt. Deus verus non est Deus, quem mortui colunt, h. e. illi, qui penitus interierunt ac nihil sunt.

*(Iam 1. Sadducaei existimabant, homines poenitus per mortem interire, statuentes quippe, animas unà cum corpore extingui. Vid. Ioseph. l. 18. A. I. c. 2. Quomodo v. veteres Iudaei contra Sadducaeos mortuorum resurrectionem adstruxerint, ostendit ex Talmud W. Schikardus in Bechin. Happeruschim p. 160. seqq. Conf. quoque Petrus Galatinus in Arcan. Cathol. verit. Fortiter porrò effato hoc Salvatoris, error Psychopannychitarum destruitur, quòd animae piorum ante diem extremum somno quasi sopitae non persentiscant gaudia vitae aeternae. etenim vita in actione consistit. Vid. B. Par. L. de Morte §. 299. Circa exceptiones Photinianorum, statuentium, quòd piis in V. T. non facta fuerit vitae aeternae promissio, notandum 1. quòd Salvator in praesenti loquatur Luc. 20, 38.Vivunt 2. quòd patres ideò dicantur Vivere, quia animae eorum vivunt. Usitata enim in Sc. S. synecdoche est, quâ toti tribuitur, quod est partis. Vid. Luc. 23, 43.Phil. 1, 23. 3. quòd Deus non dicat fui, quasi olim benefecerit, sed ego sum, allegante Christo. 4. quòd Apostolus, quando Christum vocat Dominum mortuorum & viventium, per mortuos intelligat eos, qui non ampliùs in his terris vivunt, interim tamen in coelo quoad animam beatam vivunt vitam. Conf. idem B. Par. l. c. §. 144 (ubi etiam egregia veterum Ecclesiae Dd testimonia, sententiam nostram confirmantia, allegat:) nec non B. D. Martini Consid. Photin. c. 8. 115. seqq. B. Hackspan. Orat. Inaug. Coeterùm argumentum Christi, quo contra Sadducaeos hîc usus est, prolixiùs exponunt B. D. Calixt. lib. uno de Immort. animae c. 5. D. Rivetus in Exod. itemq; in Isag. ad Sc. S. Hugo Grotius in h. l. qui possunt evolvi. Cumprimis quoq; conferantur epist. ad Ebr. c. 11, 16. ac 1. Cor. 15, 18. Cur autem Dominus non ex aliis, clarioribus fortè, V. T. dictis Sadducaeos refutarit, sed tali dicto, è quo per consequentiam demum mortuorum elicienda resurrectio erat, disputari variè solet. Vid. D. Calixtum l. c. p. 36. 37. ac confer notata ad v. 31.)*

## 22:34
(v. 34. οτο ηφιμωσε. That He had imposed silence, properly having cast a halter, He had closed their mouths. Ministers of the Church ought to imitate this deed of Christ. Tit. 1, 11. Compare Eph. 6, 17. Irenaeus book 1 against heresies, c. 35. adduced by B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccles. §. 172.)

Latin:

*(v. 34. οτο ηφιμωσε. Quòd silentium imposuisset, propriè capistro iniecto os ipsis occlusisset. Hoc Christi factum imitari & Ecclesiae Ministrae debent. Tit. 1, 11, Conf. Eph. 6, 17. Irenaeus l. 1. adv. haeres. c. 35. addduct. à B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccles. §. 172.)*

## 22:35
v. 35. Theophylact notes that νομιηοι first indeed approached Christ with a malicious mind so that he might παμιςολισι, but by the prayer of Christ he so progressed that, departing from Christ, he carried away an honorable eulogy, as witnessed by Mark, who reports οτι έμβλέσας αυτω ο Ιησούς, ηγαπησεν αυτόν. *(B. D. Calovius in Concord. Evang. p. 302, Cornelius à Lapide in this place, and several other interpreters embrace the opinion of Theophylact)* But this is μνημόνιηον αμαρ τημα of Theophylact: for that passage Mark 10, 21. pertains nothing to him who is treated here and Mark 12, 28. (Moreover, it is usually asked here, whether γραμματεις and Νομιηοι were the same? It is certain that these names were not an appellation of a sect, as the names of the Pharisees, Sadducees, and Essenes, but of an office. Furthermore, it cannot be denied that both the Scribes and the Lawyers were occupied about the interpretation of Holy Scripture. Meanwhile, that they were not the same, Scribes and Lawyers, which Grotius thinks in this place, Camero gathers in Myroth. Evang. p. 103, from Luke 11, 45. 46. and warns that it seems to him that Scribes were interpreters of the law who publicly interpreted the law in the synagogues and performed an ecclesiastical duty; but Lawyers were those whom the Hebrews call ---- i.e., wise men, and who indeed likewise interpreted the Law, but privately. And he thinks that is gathered from Luke 11, 12.)

(* πειραζων. H. Grotius thinks that the word πειραζει. is not to be taken here in the sense of calumny, but in the way the Queen of Sheba is said to have come πειρασαι Solomon, 1 Kings 10, 1. But B. D. Hunnius more correctly establishes in this place that ομιηός did not approach our Savior out of a love of learning, but out of a desire to test, having been suborned by the rest, namely the Pharisees, the most bitter enemies of Christ.)

Latin:

v. 35. Notat Theophylactus, νομιηοι primùm quidem animo maligno ad Christum acce-sisse, ut eum παμιςολισι, sed oratione Christi ita profecisse, ut discedens à Christo honestum tulerit elogium, teste Marco, qui referat, οτι έμβλέσας αυτω ο Ιησούς, ηγαπησεν αυτόν. *(Theophylacti sententiam amplectuntur B. D. Cali-tus in Concord. Evang. p. 302. Corn. à Lapide in h. l. aliique nonnulli Interpretes)* Sed est μνημόνιηον αμαρ τημα Theophylacti: nam ille locus Marci 10, 21. nihil ad eum pertinet, de quo hîc agitur & Marc. 12, 28. (Caeterùm quaeri hîc solet, numγραμματειςacΝομιηοιiidem fuerint? Certum est, nomina haec non sectae fuisse appellationem, ceu Pharisaeorum Sadducaeorum & Essaeorum nomina, sed officii. Deinde negari non potest, quòd tum Scribae tum Legisperiti cir-a Scripturae Sacrae interpretationem fuerint occupati. Interea non fuisse eosdem, Scribas ac Legisperitos, quod Grotius h. l. existimat, colligit Camero in Myroth. Evang. p. 103. ex Lucae 11, 45. 46. monetque, videri sibi, Scribas fuisse legis interpretes, qui publicè in Synagogis legem interpretabantur, ac munere fungebantur Ecclesiastico; Legisperitos verò fuisse eos, quos Ebr. ---- i. e. sapientes vocant, quique itidem quidem Legem interpretabantur, sed privatim. ldque colligi putat ex Luc. 11, 12.)*

(* πειραζων. Existimat H Grotius, non sumendum hîc verbum πειραζει. in calumniae significatione, sed quomodo Regina Sabae venisse dicitur πειρασαι Salomonem, 1. Reg. 10, 1. Ast rectiùs B. D. H-nnius in h. l. statuit, quòd ομιηός non amore discendi, sed studio tentandi à reliquis quippe Pharisaeis, in fendissimis Christi hostibus subornatus, Salvatorem nostrum accesserit.)*

## 22:36
v. 36. The connection is as follows. Because there is to be a resurrection of the dead, and another life remains after this one, as you rightly answered the Sadducees, therefore the question is how we may arrive at it and merit the same. In the Talmud, five hundred and thirteen traditions are enumerated.

*( μεγάλη i. e. μεγιςη, by Enallage of the Comparative for the Superlative. See v. 38.)

Latin:

v. 36. Connexio talis est. Quia futura est mortuorum resurrrectio, & alia post hanc restat vita, uti rectè respondisti Sadducaeis, ideò quaeritur, quom do ad eam pervenire, eandemque promereri possimus. In Talmud recensentur quingentae & tredecim traditiones.

*( μεγάλη i. e. μεγιςη, per Enallagen Compar. pro Superlativo. Vid. v. 38.)

## 22:37
v. 37. Thou shalt love the Lord thy God &c. God is to be loved ardently, constantly, wisely, strongly. *(in regard to which the Syriac, after Τό with all thy soul, inserts ---- with all thy strength. Similarly the Ethiopic. ---- with all thy strength. The same Ethiopic has: & with all ---- i. e. thy thought or intention, but by no means, as Cornelius à Lapide alleges the Ethiopic, & with all the power that is thine. Thus neither does the same Cornelius correctly allege the Persian, as if it rendered, with all the excess of thy mind, when rather the words which the Persian has, viz. ---- ought to be translated, & with thy strength.)*

*( With all thy heart &c. A fourfold ολον is inculcated 1. of the object to be loved 2. of the subject loving. 3. of the actions 4. of the time. as the blessed D. Meisner elegantly shows in Theol. Photin. p. 730. Since no one can provide this most exact love, it is evident that the divine law after the fall can be perfectly fulfilled and observed by no one. Cornelius à Lapide also errs, when he wishes to note here that this commandment is possible to be kept by any man, since there is not commanded here the whole or highest love of GOD extensively or intensively, but only comparatively, finally and appreciatively. The Photinians also incline to the same, when they establish that this at least is required in the commandment concerning loving God, that whatever is alive in us, that whole we should convert to the obedience and glory of GOD. But the emphasis of the words shows the contrary sufficiently, and the blessed Pareus shows it with more in Confes. Cathol. b. 2. spec. part. 3. art. 23. c. 7. But that some are called in Holy Scripture perfect, which the Jesuit urges, that is not to be accepted concerning absolute perfection or of degrees, but respective, or of parts, as the blessed Pareus likewise teaches in the same place p. 809. Hugo Grotius on this passage opposes to the opinion of Augustine and other Orthodox Interpreters, that namely that perfection is signified by those words with all thy heart &c., which in this life no one has had, or could have had, certain passages, as 1. Reg. 14, 8.1. Sam. 7, 3.2. Reg. 10, 31. c. 23, 3. 2. Par. 152. where it is affirmed concerning the pious Kings, that they so loved God. He adds, that the law wills that this love be rendered according to one's strength, that is, as much as a man can, that is, with an entire and sincere heart. But as regards those examples, a distinction must be repeated between perfection of degrees and of parts. Also between the Evangelical fulfillment of the law, and the Legal, concerning which distinction the Blessed Father treats in the same place, l. c. But especially against that common insistence of the Pelagians, Scholastics, and Papists, that if it were not in our power to fulfill the commands of GOD, they would have been promulgated in vain, it is to be noted 1. that from a precept the consequence does not hold to the performance of something from one's own powers. See Ioh. 11, 43. 2. that there is a distinction between the legal and Evangelical fulfillment of the commandments. 3. that they are not in vain: just as neither are promises, although a man cannot fulfill them from his own powers or perfectly. As the Blessed D. Hutter shows at length in Eplic. F. C. p. 212 seqq.)*

Latin:

v. 37. Diliges Dominum Deum tuum &c. Diligendus Deus ardenter, constanter, sapienter, fortiter. *(quo respiciens Syrus, post Τόex totâ animâ tuâ, inservit ----ex totâ virtute tua. Similiter Aethiops. ---- ex totâ virtute tua. Idem Aethiops habet: & in tota---- i. e. cogitatione s. intentione tuâ, hautquaquam verò, ceu Cornelius à Lapide Aethiopem allegat, & ex totâ potentiâ, quae tibi. Sic nec Persam idem Cornelius rectè allegat, quasi reddat, ex totâ nimietate mentis tuae, cùm potiùs verba, quae Persa habet, sc. ---- verti debeant, & viribus tuis.)*

*( Ex toto corde &c. Quadruplex ολον inculcatur 1. obiecti diligendi 2. Subiecti diligentis. 3. actionum 4. temporis. uti eleganter ostendit B. D. Meisn. Theol. Photin. p. 730 Quam exactissimam dilectionem cùm nemo praestare possit, patet quòd lex divina post lapsum à nemine perfectè impleri & observari possit. Errat quoque Cornelius à Lapide, quando notari hîc vult, praeceptum hoc cuivis homini servatu esse possibile, cùm non praecipiatur hîc totus vel summus amor DEI extensivè aut intensivè, sed tantùm comparativè, finaliter & appretiativè. Eod. inclinant & Photiniani, quando id saltem in praecepto de Deo diligendo requiri statuunt, ut quicquid in nobis vivium est, id totum ad DEI obsequium ac gloriam convertamus. Verùm contrarium verborum emphasis satis ostendit, pluribusque ostendit B. Par. Confes. Cathol. l. 2. spec. part. 3. art. 23. c. 7. Quòd verò nonnulli dicuntur in Scriptura Sacra perfecti, quod Iesuita urget, id non accipiendum de perfectione absolutâ seu graduum, sed respectiva, seu partium, uti itidem docet B. P. l. c. p. 809. Hugo Grotius in h. l. sententiae Augustini aliorumque Orthodoxorum Interpretum, quòd nempe ea perfectio verbis illis ex toto corde &c. significetur, quam in hâc vita nemo habuerit, aut habere potuerit, opponit loca quaedam, uti 1. Reg. 14, 8.1. Sam. 7, 3.2. Reg. 10, 31. c. 23, 3. 2. Par. 152. ubi de piis Regibus affirmatur, quòd ita Deum dilexerint. addit, legem velle, amorem istum praestari pro viribus h. e. quantum homo potest i. e. corde integro & sincero. Verùm quod attinet illa exempla, repetenda dist. inter perfectionem graduum & partium. it. inter impletionem legis Evangelicam, & Legalem, de qua dist. ibidem agit B. P. l. c. Cumprimis verò contra communem illam Pelagianorum, Scholasticorum ac Pontificiorum instantiam, quòd si non esset in nostris viribus mandata DEI implere, frustra promulgata fuissent, notandum 1. quòd à praecepto non valeat consequentia ad praestationem alicuius rei ex propriis viribus. Vid. Ioh. 11, 43. 2. quòd dist. inter impletionem mandatorum legalem, & Evangelicam. 3. quòd non frustranea ea sint: sicuti nec promisfines, licet homo nō possit ea ex propriis viribus vel perfectè implere. Uti multis ostendit B. D Hutter. in Eplic. F. C. p. 212 seqq.)*

## 22:38
v. 38. This is the greatest. The commandment concerning the love of GOD is greatest, both by reason of the object, because it is directed to God, who is greater than heaven and earth, and by reason of the end, because all the remaining precepts are referred to it. *(The Blessed Par. L. de Magist. Pol. §. 213. likewise warns, that it is greatest as the first concerning love of GOD both by reason of the subject, because it is immediately directed to God, best in goodness, greatest in power, and by reason of dignity and order, because from the love of GOD the love of the neighbor arises)*

And the first commandment. It is first in dignity and order of nature, because from the love of GOD the love of the neighbor flows. *(Capellus in Spic. p. 46. warns, that the particle καὶ here does not distinguish different things, but is rather έξηγητιηόν, so that πςρτη η μεγαλη is the same, which πρρτη τού τέςι μεγαλη. )*

Latin:

v. 38. Hoc est maximum. Mandatum de dilectione DEI est maximum, tum ratione obiecti, quia dirigitur ad Deum, qui coelo ac terrâ maior est, tum ratione finis, quia omnia praecepta reliqua ad illud referuntur. *(B. Par. L. de Magist. Pol. §. 213. itidem monet, quòd maximum sit primum de dil-ctione DEI tum ratione subiecti, quia immediatè dirigitur ad Deum, bonitate optimum, potentiâ maximum, tum ratione dignitatis & ordinis, quia ex dilectione DEI proximi dilectio oritur)*

Et primum mandatum. Primum est dignitate & ordine naturae, quia ex dilectione DEI promanat dilectio proximi. *(Capellus in Spic. p. 46. monet, particulam καὶ hîc non distinguere diver sa, sed esse potiùs έξηγητιηόν, ita ut πςρτη η μεγαλη s-t-dem, quod πρρτη τού τέςι μεγαλη.)*

## 22:39
v. 39. And the second is like unto it. How is the commandment concerning the love of the neighbor like the commandment concerning the love of GOD? He answers η ςοτ τέρα έιβολη ἐστιν ομοιως μένιηη καὶ ηεΦαληωςης καὶ μεγάλη καὶ ομοιως ευπιβαχΘεισα, according to the Greek Scholia. It is therefore first like 1. in the genus of moral worship. For each requires interior and spiritual obedience. 2. in the genus of eternal punishment, because the transgression of either is joined with the guilt of eternal curse. 3. in coherence, because if anyone loves God, it is necessary that he also love his neighbor. *(Compare 1. Ioh. 4, 20. Some add, that the second precept is like the first 4. by reason of the efficient cause. 5. and by reason of the reward, promised to those who obey. For those offices of humanity which we render to the neighbor, God will reward most bountifully, not otherwise than if they had been rendered to Himself. Compare B. D. Martini in Pho-in. c. 10. §. 9.)* The Rabbis call the commandment concerning the love of the neighbor a great universal in the law. See Drus. l. 1. praeterit. p. 47. Manahemus Ricinensis fol. 147. col. 4. He who loves his companion, who was made in the image of GOD, loves God and honors Him. Theophylactus in this place: The law concerning the love of the neighbor is to be performed with no less supreme zeal than that concerning the love of GOD. And he says the second is like the first, in that they are connected together. For he who loves God, he loves also His creature. *(But the second commandment is not like the first in this sense, as if God is not to be loved more than the neighbor. Whence the rule was born: Obedience to the first table derogates from the second. When, namely, both cannot have place at the same time. Compare Luc. 14, 26. And some observe, that the second precept is said to be ομοιον like, not ισον equal to the first.)*

*( As yourself. that is, just as you desire to be loved by him. Compare above c. 7, 12. Tobiae 4, 16. For Christ does not mean this, that we ought to embrace our neighbor with the exact same love with which we pursue ourselves. For charity begins with oneself, and degrees of love are given. But Augustine well observes, that we shall finally fulfill that precept concerning the love of GOD and neighbor in the other life. book on the Spirit and the letter. To which Bernard also concurs, serm. 50. on the Song of Songs, writing: Charity, which is commanded in the law, can in no way be fulfilled, nor could it be, by any man in this life. For who would dare to arrogate to himself that which Paul himself confesses he has not apprehended.)*

Latin:

v. 39. Secundum autem simile est huic. Quomodo mandatum de dilectione proximi est simile mandato de dilectione DEI? Resp. η ςοτ τέρα έιβολη ἐστιν ομοιως μένιηη καὶ ηεΦαληωςης καὶ μεγάλη καὶ ομοιως ευπιβαχΘεισα, iuxta Scholia Graeca. -st ergo primo simile 1. in genere cultûs moralis. Utrumque enim requirit interiorem & spiritualem obedientiam. 2. in genere poenae aeternae, quia utriusque transgressio cum reatu aeternae maledictionis coniuncta est. 3. in cohaerentia, quia si quis Deū diligit, is proximum etiam diligat, necesse est. *(Conf. 1. Ioh. 4, 20. addunt aliqui, quòd secundum praeceptum primo simile sit. 4. ratione causae efficientis. 5. ac ratione praemii, obsequentibus promissi. Quae enim proximo praestamus -umanitatis officia, ea Deus largissimè remunerabitur, haut aliter, ac si ipsi praestita essent. Conf. B. D. Martini in Pho-in. c. 10. §. 9.)* Rabbini mandatum de dilectione proximi vocant universale magnum in lege. Vid. Drus. l. 1. praeterit. p. 47. Manahemus Ricinenfis fol. 147. col. 4. Qui amat socium suum, qui factus est ad imaginem DEI, amat Deum & honor at eum. Theophylactus h. l. Lex de dilectione proximi non minùs summo studio praestanda est, quàm illa de dilectione DEI. Et secundum primo simile dicit, eo quòd simul inter se connexa sunt. Qui enim Deum diligit, is diligit etiam facturam eius. *(Non verò mandatum secundum simile est primo hoc sensu, quasi Deus non magis sit diligendus, quàm proximus. Unde nata regula: Obedientia primae tabulae der-gat secundae. Quando sc. utraq; simul locum habere nequit. Conf. Luc. 14, 26. Et observant nonnulli, quòd secundum praeceptum primo dicatur ομοιονsimile, non ισον aequale.)*

*( Sicut teipsum. h. e. sicuti tu ab eo diligi cupis. Conf. suprà c. 7, 12. Tobiae 4, 16. Neque enim Christus hoc vult, quòd eodem omninò amore, quo nos ipsos prosequimur, & proximum complecti debeamus. Charitas enim incipit à seipso, ac dantur amoris gradus. Benè autem observat Augustinus, quòd praeceptum illud de dilectione DEI & proximi demum in alterâ vit â perfectè simus impleturi. l. de Spir. & litt. Cui etiam suffragatur Bernhardus, serm. 50. in Cantic. scribens: Charitas, quae in lege iubetur, minimè in vitâ -stâ ab aliquo hominum potest vel potuit impleri. Quis enim arrogare sibi audeat, quòd se Paulus ipse fatetur, non apprehendisse.)*

## 22:40
v. 40. On these two etc. That Christ wished to conclude all his sermons and miracles with this conversation about the Law and the Gospel, by that very fact he signified that all sermons and therefore all things which are contained in the sacred writings ought to be recalled to these two heads, namely to the law and to the testimony. Is. 8, 19. where by the name of testimony is understood the doctrine of the Gospel John 1, 17. The Law through Moses &c. Rom. 11, 32. God hath concluded all &c. See Luth. vol. 3. Jena. Germ. f. 31. 32. item vol. 6. f. 393. vol. 8 fol. 339.

The Prophets. By the Prophets Christ does not understand all and singular things contained in their writings, but speaking χατα τι he understands only the legal precepts, or explanations, repetitions, inculcations of the law, and admonitions deduced therefrom.

Q. What is signified by the word κρέμανται? Paul Rom. 13, 9. has most aptly expressed it by the word ανοεχεφαλαιούσΘαι. Gal. 5, 14. he has the word πληρούσΘαι. Casaubon maintains that in the word κρέμανται there is a mere Latinism, without any allusion to τά Φυλαητηριαι. To hang is the same as to be contained and as it were special and particular things to be referred to their genus and whole. *(Hugo Grotius also embraces Casaubon's opinion. The Rabbis use a similar expression, writing likewise concerning the first precept ---- i. e. that all things hang from it, as it is in Maimonides.)*

But if the law hangs from two commandments, why does Paul, Rom. 13, 9. in this commandment at least, you shall love your neighbor as yourself, assert that the whole law is contained? Resp. This happens because of the very tight connection of both tables. For he who loves his neighbor as himself, it is necessary that he also love God, and he who does not love his neighbor, he does not love God either. This was noted long ago by Augustine, who, in book 8 of De Trinitate, ch. 7, writes: Since there are two commandments, on which the law and the Prophets hang, the love of GOD and of neighbor, not undeservedly does Scripture for the most part put one for both: either only of GOD, as is that: we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, and again: but whoever has loved God, this one is known by Him, etc. or only of the neighbor, as is that: The whole law is fulfilled in one word, you shall love your neighbor as yourself, etc. And we find many other things in the holy letters, in which only the love of the neighbor seems to be commanded for perfection, and there is silence concerning the love of GOD, when the law and the Prophets hang on both. But this is because, since he who loves the neighbor, it follows that he loves love itself especially. Moreover, God is love etc.)* *(

Latin:

v. 40. In his duobus &c. Quòd Christus omnes conciones & miraculasua hoc colloquio de Lege & Evangelio concludere voluit, eo ipso significavit, quòd omnes conciones adeoque omnia, quae in sacris litteris continentur, ad haec duo capita revocari debeant, ad legem scil. & ad testimonium. Es. 8, 19. ubi testimonii nomine intelligitur doctrina Evangelii Ioh. 1, 17.Lex per Mosen &c. Rom. 11, 32.Conclusit Deus omnia &c. Vid. Luth. t. 3. Ienens. Germ. f. 31. 32. item t. 6. f. 393. t. 8 fol. 339.

Prophetae. per Prophetas non intelligit Christus omnia & singula, ipsorum scriptis contenta, sed χατα τι loquens tantùm legalia praecepta, seu explicationes, repetitiones, inculcationes legis & commonefactiones inde deductas intelligit.

Q. Quid verboκρέμανταιsignificetur? Paulus Rom. 13, 9. Verbo ανοεχεφαλαιούσΘαι aptissimè expressit. Gal. 5, 14. habet verbum πληρούσΘαι. Casaubonus statuit, in voce κρέμανται merum Latinismum inesse, sine ullâ allusione ad τά Φυλαητηριαι.Pendere est idem, quod contineri & tanquam specialia & particularia ad suum genus & totum referri. *(Casauboni sententiam amplectitur quoque Hugo Grotius. Rabbini simili utuntur locutione, itid. de primo praecepto scribentes ---- i. e. quòd pendeani ab eo omnia, ut est apud Maimonidem.)*

*( Sed si à duobus pendet lex mandatis, cur PaulusRom. 13, 9.in hoc saltem praecepto, diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum, legem totam contineri adserit? Resp. Fit hoc propter arctissimum utriusque tabulae nexum. Qui enim proximum diligit ut seipsum, is, Deum quoque diligat, necesse est, & qui proximum non diligit, is nec Deum diligit. Pridem hoc notatum Augustino. qui lib. 8. de Trin. c. 7. Cùm duo, scribit, sint praecepta, in quibus pendet lex & Prophetae, dilectio DEI & proximi, non immeritò Scriptura plerumque pro utroque unum ponit: sive tantùm DEI, sicuti est illud: scimus, quoniam diligentibus Deum omnia cooperātur in bonum, & iterum: quis quis autem dilexit Deum, hic cognitus est ab illo &c. sive tantùm proximi, sicut est illud: Omnis lex in uno sermone impletur, diliges proximum sicut teipsum &c. Et pleraq alia reperimus in litteris sanctis, in quibus sola dilectio proximi ad perfectionem praecipi videtur, & taceri de dilectione DEI, cùm in utroq lex pendeat & Prophetae. Sed hoc ideò, quia qui proximum diligit, consequens est, ut ipsam praecipuè dilectionem diligat. Deus autem dilectio est &c.)*

## 22:43
v. 43. How then does David &c. in Ps. 110. of course. Modern Jews say that Psalm 110 does not treat of the Messiah, but of David. And yet from this dialogue it is manifest that their ancestors conceded this hypothesis to Christ. (Just as also Jonathan in the Targum, likewise R. Barachias, R. Levi, Isaac Benarama on Gen. 47. and others of the true Rabbis, as testified by R. Moses and Genebrard on the said Psalm, explain the same concerning Christ. R. Kimchi objects, that no battles were fought by Jesus. I answer, distinguish between corporal battles and spiritual ones. R. Isaac Ben Abraham no. 1. on Matthew and R. Lusitanus in Colloq. Mittelb. f. 168. ineptly infer from this, that Christ himself here confesses that he is not the son of David, and therefore not the promised Messiah. For Christ by no means denies that he is the son of David (for if he had done so, the Evangelists and Apostles would by no means have preserved it. But they do this everywhere, see Matt. 1, 1.6.16. 1-. Luke 3, 3.Rom. 1, 3.2. Tim. 2. 8. And this was so well known to the common people that our Savior was commonly called the Son of David . See above c. 9, 27.c. 12, 23.c. 15, 22.c. 21, 9.15. Christ by no means contradicts this common opinion, nor does he argue it of error. See especially c. 21, 16. What of the fact that the Angel sent by GOD also clearly testifies to it Luke 1, 32.) but by this instance he wished to convince the Pharisees that he himself, the promised Messiah, is not a mere man, namely the Son of David, which was by no means called into doubt by the people, but at the same time true GOD, and therefore true θεάνθρωπος. The Pharisees ought therefore to have solved that instance, and answered the proposed doubt, that Christ according to his human nature is the son of David, but according to his divine nature is the Lord and God of the same. But R. Lusitanus insists in the same place, why, when the Pharisees did not understand this mystery, did Christ not explain it to them. I answer, this was done by our Savior for this reason, because they were unworthy of such a benefit, inasmuch as, even if he had taught it in the clearest words, they would nevertheless have had no faith in him. See

below c. 26, 65. Ioh. 5, 18.c. 8, 58. 59.c. 10, 33. He was unwilling, therefore, to cast pearls before swine, Matth 7, 6. Finally, that modern Jews have no just cause at all for doubting that Psalm 110 treats of the Messiah, nay, that there are grave reasons why they ought to concede it, Simon Episcopius the Arminian shows at length in lib. 3. Instit. Theol. sect. 4. cap. 17. pag. 194.)*

*( In the spirit. See 2. Sam. 23, 2.Act. 1. 16,c. 2, 30.2. Petr. 1, 21. & add Barthol. Meyerum de Sept. Hebdom. Danielis p. 148.)*

He calls Him Lord. Someone might say that the major premise in Christ's argument is not universal. For he concludes thus: A father never calls his son Lord. But David calls the Messiah his son Lord Ps. 110. Therefore, the Messiah is not David's son. Here someone could object that if a son is raised to be King, and the father remains a citizen, in that case the father could call the son Lord. I respond: David was a most powerful King, who acknowledged no superior except God alone. Thus, therefore, the argument must be fully and completely formed. A father, who is King, and acknowledges no one as superior except God alone, cannot call his son Lord. Such a King was David. Therefore. *(Furthermore, from the fact that The Lord said to my Lord is commemorated as having been said by David, that He should sit at the right hand of GOD, and since Christ is indeed Lord according to His divine nature, the Calvinists gather that Christ sits at the right hand of GOD not according to His assumed human nature, but according to His divine nature, since He is Lord according to His Deity. I respond: 1. By denying that Christ is Lord only according to His divine nature: for just as according to His divine nature He is the begotten Lord, God from God: so according to human nature He was made Lord,Act. 2, 36.1. Cor. 15, 47. namely personally, or because of the personal union. Conf. Matth. 28, 18.Phil. 2, 9. seqq. Luc. 1, 32. seqq. 2. By denying the consequence. For it does not follow: The Lord said to my Lord, that He should sit etc. Therefore He sat down according to His divine nature. Nay, rather, Christ sat down at the right hand of GOD according to that nature according to which He could receive glory in time , and thus according to His human nature. Whence also the Fathers explicitly explain the sitting at the right hand of GOD concerning this nature. Most clearly Ambrose l. 2. de fide c. 2. Because of the reason of the body, he says, sit at my right hand. Similarly Theophylact in c. 1 of the epistle to the Hebrews: The Father does not say as to God: sit at my right hand: For his throne is eternal. Therefore, as man, he is a participant in this honor. Compare more things pertinent to this in the Analecta to c. 26, 64.

ο κύριος. H. Grotius rightly notes that not only the LXX, but also the other Hellenists, and among them the writers of the New Testament, use this word where in the Hebrew there is τό τητραγραμμαβαν.. The same man also truly affirms that the Jews once pronounced the name Jehovah, and not only they themselves, but also foreigners, as often as they spoke about the GOD of the Hebrews; but that the later Jews ceased to pronounce it, happened because other names declared a certain general knowledge of GOD, or of a thing which was held for God: but that name was οιαηριτιηον, by which the God of the Hebrews was distinguished from the others. Namely, a name in which there is no participation between the creator and anything else, as Maimonides speaks. Let B. D. Waltherus Spicil. Controv. part. one Controv. 6. seqq. be compared entirely.

Sit at my right hand. That by the right hand of GOD is not understood any corporeal right hand or any created place, but the infinite majesty and power of GOD, has long since been proven by our people. See B. D. Hunnius in this place p. 565. seqq. B. D. Hutterus in Expl. F. C. p. 628 & 871. seqq. also in LL Mai. p. 195. 196. B. D. Lobech. in A. C. p. 140. B. Par. Exeg. L. de Pers. & Off. Christi p. 291. 491. 496 seqq. B. D. Chemn. tr. de Duab. nat. in Christo p 127. seqq. also p. 144. 153. Compare also below the Analecta to c. 26, 64. The rest, which could be noted concerning the present passage, and also to verses 45 & 46, will be brought forward in the Analecta to Mark XII, 35. seqq.

Three things are proposed in this chapter. I. The faithful instruction of our Savior, how the Pharisees are to be heard, v. 1 3. 11. the delineation of their hypocritical holiness, v. 4. 8 a grave threatening, v. 13. 36. III. The just reproach of the ingratitude of the Jewish people, v. 3. 7 to the end.

Latin:

v. 43. Quomodo ergò David &c. in Ps. 110. scilicet. Iudaei hodierni dicunt, Psaimum 110. non agere de Messiâ, sed de Davide. Atqui ex hoc dialogismo manifestum est, maiores ipsorum hanc hypothesin Christo concessisse. *(Quemadmodum etiam ionathan in Targhum, it. R. Barachias, R Levi, Isaac Benarama ad Gen. 47. aliique ve-erum Rabbinorum, teste R. Mose ac Genebrardo in dictum Ps. eundem de Christo exponunt. Opponit R. Kimchi, nulla praelia à Iesu esse pugnata. Resp. dist. inter praelia corporalia, & spiritualia. R. Isaac Ben Abraham n. 1. in Matthaeum ac R. Lusitanus in Colloq. Mittelb. f. 168. ineptè hinc inferunt, quòd Christus ipse hîc confiteatur, se non esse Davidis filium, adeoq nec promissum Messiam. Etenim Christus minimè negat, se esse filium Davidis, (id enim si fecisset, Evangelistae & Apostoli minimè id adservissent. At hoc passim faciunt, vid. Matth. 1, 1.6.16. 1-. Luc. 3, 3.Rom. 1, 3.2. Tim. 2. 8. Eratque hoc adeò in vulgus notum, ut communiter Salvator noster Filius Davidis adpel-aretur. Vid. suprà c. 9, 27.c. 12, 23.c. 15, 22.c. 21, 9.15. Cui etiam communi sententiae minimè Christus contradicit, vel erroris eam arguit. Vidcumprimis c 21, 16. Quid quod Angelus à DEO missus id clarè quoque testetur Luc. 1, 32.) sed instantiâ hâc convincere Pharisaeos voluit, quòd ipse, promissus Messias, non sit nudus homo, Filius nempe Davidis, quod à populo minimè in dubium vocabatur, sed simul verus DEO, adeoque verus θεάνθρωπος Debuissent proinde Pharisaei solvere istam instantiam, ac respondere ad propositum dubium, quòd Christus secundùm humanam vaturam sit filius Davidis, sed secundùm divinam eiusdem Dominus ac Deus. Sed instat R. Lusitanus d l. cur cùm Pharisaei mysterium hoc non intelligerent, Christus illud iis non exposuerit. Resp. Ideò hoc à Salvatore nostro factum, quia ipsi tanto beneficio indigni erant, utpote qui, si vel maximè claris id ipse docuisset verbis, minimè tamen fidem ei habuissent. Vid.

infra c. 26, 65. Ioh. 5, 18.c. 8, 58. 59.c. 10, 33. Noluit igitur margaritas proiicere potcis, Matth 7, 6. Denique quòd Iudaei hodierni nullam omninò iustam dubitandi causam habeant, quòd Psalmus 110 de Messia agat, imò graves adesse causas, cur id concedere debeant, prolixè ostendit Simon Episcopius Arminianus lib. 3. Instit. Theol. sect. 4. cap. 17. pag. 194.)*

*( In spiritu. Vid. 2. Sam. 23, 2.Act. 1. 16,c. 2, 30.2. Petr. 1, 21. & adde Barthol. Meyerum de Sept. Hebdom. Danielis p. 148.)*

Vocat Dominum. Dixerit aliquis, maiorem in argumento Christi non esse universalem. Sic enim concludit. Pater nunquam appellat filium suum Dominum. At David Messiam appellat filium suum Dominum Ps. 110. E. Messias non est Davidis filius. Hîc posset aliquis obvertere, quòd si filius evehatur in Regem, ac pater maneat civis, eo in casu pater filium appellare possit Dominum. Resp. David erat Rex potentissimus, qui nullum agnoscebat superiorem nisi solum Deum. Sic ergò plenè & integrè formandum est argumentum. Pater, qui Rex est, & neminem nisi solum Deum superiorem agnoscit, non po-est filium suum vocare Dominum. Talis Rex erat David. E. *(Coeterùm ex eo, quòd Dominus ad Dominum dixisse commemoratur à Davide, ut sedeat ad dextram DEI, iam verò Christus iuxta divinam naturam Dominus sit, colligunt Calviniani, Christum non iuxta adsumtam humanam, sed iuxta divinam naturam sedere ad Dextram DEI, quippe cùm iuxta Deitatem Dominus sit. Resp. 1 Negando, quòd Christus saltem secundùm divinam naturam Dominus sit: etenim quem-dmodum secundùm divinam naturam est genitus Dominus, Deus de D-o: ita secundum huma-am naturam factus est Dominus,Act. 2, 36.1. Cor. 15, 47. nempe personaliter, sive propter unionem personalem. Conf. Matth. 28, 18.Phil. 2, 9. seqq. Luc. 1, 32. seqq. 2. Negando consequentiam. Non enim sequitur, Dominus dixit Domino, ut sedeat &c. Ergò secundùm divinam naturam consedit. Imò potiùs Christus secundùm illam naturam consedit ad dextram DEI, secundùm quam in tempore gloriam potuit accipere, adeoque secundùm humanam naturam. Unde etiam Patres disertè de isthac natura sessionem ad dextram DEI exponunt. Clarissimè Ambrosius l. 2. de fide c. 2. Propter rationem corporis dicit, sede à dextris meis. Similiter Theophylactus in c. 1. ep. ad Ebr. Pater non tanquam Deo dicit: sede à dextris meis: Thronus enim eius aeternus est. Ut homo ergo huius honoris particeps est. Conf. plura huc facieutia in Anal. ad c. 26, 64.)*

Verè etiam affirmat idem, nomen Iehova Iudaeos olim pronunciasse, nec ipsos tantùm, sed & alienigenas, quoties de Hebraeorum DEO loquebantur; quòd verò posteriores Iudaei pronunciare illud desierint, factum inde, quòd alia nomina generalem quandam DEI, aut rei quae pro Deo haberetur, notitiam declararent: illud verò nomen esset οιαηριτιηον, quo Deus Ebraeorum à coeteris disernebatur.
