## 23:4
(v. 4. They bind heavy burdens &c. By those heavy burdens are understood those almost innumerable precepts, (of which the Jews even today count as many as a man has limbs and bones,) devised outside of and beyond the word of GOD. Furthermore, that Τό to bind in this place denotes to impose laws, we readily concede. Cf. Acts 15, 10. & 28. yet it cannot be immediately gathered from this, as Bellarmine in book 4 de P. R. persuades himself, that Matt. 16, 19. and c. 18, 18. the word of binding is to be taken in the same way. For how it ought to be taken in these places is evident both from the circumstances of the text and from the parallel passages John 20, 23Luke 24, 47. For to bind in that place (Matt. 16, 19.) is the same as to retain the sins of the impenitent by having denounced the sentence of eternal curse.)

They do not wish to move them with their finger. They are so far from wishing to take them upon their shoulders that they do not even wish to touch them. *(They do not touch them with a finger, because if they ever perform even the greatest external obedience to the divine law, they do this not for the glory of GOD, but for their own glory, and so that they may be seen before men)*

Latin:

*(v. 4. Alligant onera gravia &c. Per onera illa gravia intelliguntur innumera ferè illa praecepta, (quorum quippe tot Iudaei adhuc hodie numerant, quot homo membra & ossa habet,) extra & praeter verbum DEI excogitata. Coeterùm Τόalligare h. l. notare leges ferre, facilè quidem concedimus. Conf. Actor. 15, 10. & 28. neque tamen exinde statim colligere licet, uti Bellarminus lib. 4. de P. R. sibi persvadet, quòd etiam Matth. 16, 19. ac c. 18, 18. verbum ligandi ita accipiatur. Quomodo enim in his locis accipi debeat, tum ex circumstantiis textûs patet, tum ex locis parallelis Ioh. 20, 23Luc. 24, 47. Etenim ligare d. l. ( Matth. 16, 19.) idem est, quod impoenitentibus denunciatâ aeternae maledictionis sententiâ peccata retinere.)*

Digito suo nolunt ea movere. Tantum abest, ut ea in humeros velint suscipere, ut ne quidem velint attingere. *(Digito non attingunt, quia si vel maximè externam obedientiam legi divinae aliquando praestant, faciunt tamen hoc non ad DEI, sed ad propriam suam gloriam, & ut videantur coram hominibus)*

## 23:5
v. 5. Πλατύνουσι τά Φυλακτήρια. Φυλακτήρια as if you were to say preservatives, because in these the memory of the law is preserved. This superstition had its occasion partly from Deut. 6, 8.c. 11, 18. These words, which I command you today, shall be in your heart, and you shall tell them to your children, and you shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be and shall be moved between your eyes. Partly from Num. 15, 38. Speak to the children of Israel and say to them, that they make for themselves fringes &c. Hence the Pharisees, catching the popular breeze and seeking gains from silly women, used to make large fringes, and they bound very sharp thorns in them, so that, clearly, while walking or sitting, they might sometimes be pricked, and not be allowed to forget the law. See by all means Paulus Fagius on Num. 15.c. 38. and Exod. 13. *(Jerome in this place: Not understanding that these things are to be carried in the heart, not in the body, otherwise even cupboards and chests have books, and do not have the knowledge of GOD. The same person also shows more lengthily that God did not command phylacteries in the given places, Camero t. 3. Prael. page 35. 36)* Jerome writes concerning the -harisees, that so that they might appear very observant of the law, they wrote the Decalogue on membranes or two volumes, one of which they placed around their forehead in place of a crown, the other on their arm, so that whether they reached out their hand, they would be in sight, or if they moved their eyes, they would be before their eyes. Jerome testifies that this custom lasted until his own age among the Jews, Persians, and Babylonians, and that those who do this are held to be religious among them. The Syrian has ---- from the root ----, which among other things signifies he joined, he connected, whence ---- is called prayer, because it joins us to God through meditation and affection, hence ---- frontlets, appendages Exod. 13, 16. Deut. 6, 8. c. 11, 18. *(Camero in Myrothec. and likewise t. 3. Praelect. from there he thinks those phylacteries are called ----, because their principal use was in prayer, indeed in that manner in which the French Papists are accustomed to call their chaplets or rosaries Patenostres.)* Jerome calls those phylacteries little patches, (for which is wrongly read little painted things. πιττάκων is properly a morsel of bread, hence also small parchment slips are called little patches) They were called preservatives. *(Paulus Fagius in chapter 13 of Exodus, Nicolaus Fuellerus in book 5 of Miscellanies, chapter 7, Buxtorff both in the Chaldean and Talmudic Lexicon p. 870, and in the Jewish Synagogue p. 134 seqq., B. Par. Comm. on Deut. p. 431 seqq., Rivetus Comm. on Exod. 13., Scaliger in Elench. chapter 8, Drusius book 2 on sects chapter 14, Mart. Del Rio Disquis. Magic. last book p. 922, treat at length concerning these Tephillin. Nor yet do the authors sufficiently agree as to how many verses such Tephillin consisted of. For Nicolaus de Lyra, having been made a Christian from a Jew, reveals that the Jews are accustomed to inscribe twelve verses on them, namely Deut. 6. v. 1. 6. and likewise c. 11. v. 1. 11. Jerome, however, Bede, and Theophylact judge that the Decalogue was accustomed to be inserted in them; others, at least the commandment concerning the love of one's neighbor. More correctly Fagius in the cited place, whom B. Par. also follows in the cited place, likewise Schind. in the Pentaglot Lexicon and others, establishes that the departure from Egypt was described in them, comprised in four ---- sections or readings. Of which the first consists of v. 5-9 of chapter 6 of Deut. The second of v. 1 10 of chapter 13 of Exodus. The third of v. 11-16 of chapter 13 of Exodus. The fourth of v. 13-21 of Deut. so that the whole structure might thus consist of thirty verses as it were.)

A little differently Camero recounts in t. 3. Praelect. page 35, who can be consulted. Indeed the Jews are accustomed to write those readings sometimes in such a way that they assign individual particles of leather or parchment to individual sections, as he himself [has] two of this kind ----, namely the second and the fourth, I possess in my antiquarian collection, given to me as a gift from the library of the renowned Daniel Schwenter; sometimes, however, they are accustomed to join two, just as likewise such a small parchment is in my possession. And thus Fagius and Schindler seem to be able to be reconciled in some way, of whom the latter writes in Lex. Pentagl. p. 699, that two plates or small parchments enclosed in leather are spoken of, of which one is bound to the forehead, the other to the left hand. And he adds, that in these the exodus from Egypt is described in four sections. Fagius, however, testifies that the receptacles or little houses, in which the four ---- or readings written on small parchments are contained enclosed, ought to be four according to the Jews. Fagius adds: If there were more or fewer receptacles, the Jews maintain that a most grave sin is committed. Which, however, perhaps not all seem to think. Theophylact rightly makes mention of at least two small parchments, for thus he notes on this passage: They used to write (the Jews) on two small papers the decalogue of the law, and they placed one upon the forehead and suspended the other upon the right hand. Epiphanius, in heresy 15, denies that anything was inscribed on the phylacteries, nor that they were small parchments: but he writes that they were certain broad marks of purple, bordered on conspicuous places of their cloaks. But he seems to confuse the Tephillin with the fringes. Furthermore, however much from the ancients Justin Martyr in his Dialogue with Trypho the Jew, Isidore of Pelusium in book 2, ep. 150, likewise Chrysostom, and following him Euthymius and Theophylact, then also the illustrious Scaliger maintain that the words Deut. 6, 8., in which the Jews seek the foundation of that custom, κατά τό ρητόν ought to be taken literally, nevertheless Jerome, Lyranus, and Alphonsus Tostatus, in whose footsteps most Papist commentators, such as Leonh. Marius, Corn. à Lapide, etc., as well as H. Grotius, insist, think more correctly, teaching that those words are to be taken metaphorically. For God does not command there concerning words, but concerning things, that is, He warns that they should often remember His benefits and precepts. Thus in the Proverbs of Solomon ch. 3, 3, ch. 6, 21, wisdom commands, ---- to bind his precepts to your neck. Compare Isaiah 49, 16. Against Samuel Petitus, book 2 of Various Readings, who thinks that these ---- or phylacteries were entirely commanded by GOD to the Jews, and for this reason, that when the Israelites, while they were sojourners in Egypt, were protecting their foreheads with the superstitious and obscene amulets of the Egyptians, God commanded that, those things of the nations being cast away, they should wear the Decalogue written on small membranes upon their foreheads. The Jews even today attribute very much to the wearing of these Tephillin. Just as R. David Kimchi also writes, that Scripture attributes as much to him who observes the precept concerning applying the Tephillin, as if he were learning the law of GOD day and night. Furthermore, those skilled in Jewish matters note that the Tephillin are held by the Apelles to be like an amulet. Whence they are also believed by some to be called φυλακτήρια, since φυλακτηςιον in Greek is ωείαμμα an amulet, which is applied to the body against fascinations. To which opinion the Jesuit Corn. à Lapide also gives credence, writing, that Chrysostom understands by phylacteries amulets of health. Cornelius adds: for the scribes judged such things to be the membranes of the law already mentioned. (suppose Deut. 6, 1. following) Just as some Christians hang the Gospel of John to their neck as an amulet and a preservative of health. But just as long ago St. Jerome in his Commentary on this place, and likewise the author of the Imperfect Work on Matthew, homily 43, rightly reproved such ineptitudes in certain superstitious little women, so likewise that custom and κακοζηλία of certain religious, or as I might more correctly say, overly superstitious people, is to be censured and mocked. Just as it was also long ago condemned by the Synod of Antioch, as Schindler witnesses in the place cited. Add Canon 36 of the Synod of Laodicea. And yet there are among the Papists those who, if they do not defend that superstition, at least strive to palliate it. See Salmeron, vol. 4, p. 614. Moreover, those Tephillin are called by our Evangelist Φυλακτήρια or preservatives, for the reason that they comprehend the sum of the law. Just as the Savior also says concerning the law: You shall love the Lord your God etc. Matth. 22, 40., that on it hang or are comprehended the whole Law and the Prophets. Let there also be compared concerning these phylacteries, Isidore of Pelusium, book 2, ep. 150; Barthol. Meyer, Sacred Philology, book 1, p. 124 following.) Φυλακτηείοις,

Augustinus Steuchus Eugubinus, the Apostolic Librarian, and several others think that καί μεγαλωό ουσι τά κεά ωηδα των ίματίων άυτων. the φυλακτηρια of the Pharisees was nothing other than fringes, and consequently that έξηγησεως was added to the former member at least for the sake of later explanation. But the contrary is manifest. For they differ Φυλακτηρια καί κεάωεδα 1. by reason of the material. For those were fashioned from leather. They were, in fact, small membranes marked with certain sayings of Holy Scripture: but these were made from the material of the garment or cloak thrown over the shoulders, which consisted of cloth, though usually of cotton or silk. For they hung from the individual corners of the cloak, and were attached by threads of a hyacinth or violet color, eight or twelve fingers wide. 2. by reason of the subject place. Those were placed between the eyes or applied to the forehead and to the left hand; these hung from the corners of the cloak or, as some think, of any garment, both inner and outer, and encircled the extremities of the garments. And that our Savior also wore such κεάωεδα, according to the divine command Num. 15, 37. 38., is gathered from Matt. 9, 20. and chap. 14, 36. Mark 6, 50.. How much the Jews value that precept concerning fringes, and what else they hand down concerning such fringes, Buxtorf shows at length in Synag. Iud. c. 4. p. 128. et seqq. Since, therefore, God commanded that fringes be worn, and for this purpose, that the Jews, as often as they looked upon them, might be reminded of the obedience owed to the law, it is well to note that Christ censures not the use of the fringes itself, but the abuse, i.e., that the Pharisees wore them at least for the purpose that they might be seen before men, and thus falsely persuaded themselves that the wearing of fringes was sufficient, even if they did not touch the law of GOD itself even with a finger. But as to the question, why did God command that those scarlet fringes be worn? Theophylact answers, that God declared by this very thing that it is necessary for us to be marked by the blood of the Lord. But this matter must be dealt with at greater length in the Notes on Num. 15, 37. 38. Camero in Myroth. p. 106 teaches that they also sewed to the fringes a membrane or parchment, inscribed with the words of the law, taken from the places mentioned above , and that this parchment ---- they called them. The same author notes that the Jews called this little scroll or membrane, marked with certain words of the law, when it was fitted to the head or arm, ----:, when to the door ----;, when to the garment ----,, according to that saying of the Jews ----. Furthermore, the Monks, and especially the Jesuits, are similar to the Pharisees, who likewise desire to display a feigned holiness by the habit of their body, and thus are accustomed to deceive the simpler folk remarkably, when they pretend to be Catos, but live like Bacchanalians. Let the works on the hypocrisy, lasciviousness, luxury, opulence, etc., of the Monks, to whom the Jesuits also ought to be reckoned, be unrolled. B. D. Hulsem. in AntiHagero p. 551. 552. B. D. Hopffn. in Evangelica Saxon. page 650. B. Par. Comment. in post. Epist. Petri page 268. Hospinianus de Monachis, and many others. But especially the feigned poverty of the Jesuits is betrayed by those things which the nobleman à Mandeslo in his Indian Itinerary has most famously recorded concerning the more than royal apparatus in food as well as in dress of those of them living in the most remote shores, namely in Goa.

Latin:

v. 5. Πλατύνουσι τά Φυλακτήρια. Φυλακτήρια quasi dicas conservatoria, quòd in his conservetur memoria legis. Superstitio haec occasionem habuit partim ex Deut. 6, 8.c. 11, 18.Erunt verba haec, quae ego praecipio tibi hodie, in corde tuo, & narrabis ea filiis, & ligabis ea quasi signum in manu tua, eruntq & movebūtur inter oculos tuos. Partim ex Numer. 15, 38.Loquere filiis Israel & dic ad eos, ut faciant sibi fimbrias &c. Hinc Pharisaei captantes auram popularem & sectantes lucra ex mulierculis, faciebant grandes fimbrias, & acutissimas in eis spinas ligabant, quò videlicet ambulantes aut sedentes aliquando pungerentur, nec sinerentur legis oblivisci. Vide omninò Paulum Fagium ad Num. 15.c. 38. & Exod. 13. *(Hieronymus in h. l. Non intelligentes, quòd haec in corde portanda sint, non in corpore, alioquin & armaria & arcae habent libros, & notitiam DEI non habent. Idem etiam hoc, quòd Deus dd. ll. phylacteria non mandaverit, prolixiùs ostendit Camero t. 3. Prael. pag. 35. 36)* Hieronymus de -harisaeis scribit, quòd ut viderentur admodùm observantes legis, Decalogum scripserint in membranis seu duobus voluminibus, quorum alterum fronti coronae vice circumponebant, alterum brachio, ut sive quò manum porrigerent, essent in conspectu, sive oculos movissent, ob oculos essent. Hunc morem testatur Hieronymus ad suam usque aetatem durasse apud Iudaeos, Persas atque Babylonios, a-que eos, qui id faciunt, apud eos haberi religiosos. Syrus habet ---- à rad. ----, quod inter alia significat coniunxit, connexuit, unde ----oratio dicitur, quòd nos Deo coniungat per meditationem & affectum, hinc ----frontalia, appendicesExod. 13, 16.Deut. 6, 8.c. 11, 18. *(Camero in Myrothec. itemque t. 3. Praelect. exinde phylacteria illa ---- vocari putat, quòd eorum praecipuus usus esset in oratione, ad eum nempe modum, quo Pontificii Galli suas corollas seu rosaria vocare solent Patenostres.)* Hieronymus phylacteria illa vocat pittaciola, (pro quo perperam legitur pictaciola.πιττάκων est propriè frustum panis, hinc & indicula membranacea vocantur pittaciola) Dicta sunt conservaoria. *(Prolixè de his Tephillin agunt Paulus Fagius in cap. 13. Exodi, Nicolaus Fuellerus l. 5. Miscell. c. 7. Buxtorffius tum in Lex Chald. Talmud. p. 870. tum in Synag. Iudaica p. 134. seqq. B. Par. Comm. in Deut. p. 431. seqq. Rivetus Comm. ad Exod. 13. Scaliger in Elench. c. 8. Drusius l. 2. de sectis c. 14. Mart. Del Rio Disquis. Magic. lib. ult. p. 922. Neque tamen satis conveniunt autores, quot versiculis constiterint huiusmodi Tephillin. Etenim Nicolaus de Lyra, è Iudaeo factus Christianus, prodit, quòd duodecim versus inscribere illis iudaei soleant, nempe Deut. 6. v. 1. 6. itemque c. 11. v. 1. 11. Hieronymus autem, Beda ac Theophylactus censent, Decalogum illis inseri consvevisse; alii, mandatum saltem de dilectione proximi. Rectiùs Fagius l. c. quem sequitur etiam B. Par. l. c. it. Schind. in Lex. Pentagl. ac alii, statuit, descriptam in illis fuisse egressionem ex Aegypto, quatuor ---- sectionibus seu lectionibus comprehensam. Quarum prima constet v. 5-9. c. 6. Deut. Altera v. 1. 10. c. 13. Exodi. Tertia v. 11. -16. c. 13. Exodi. Quarta v. 13. -21 Deut. ut ita ipsis quasi tringinta versibus tota constet compages.

Paullò aliter recenset Camero t. 3. Praelect. pag. 35. qui potest consuli. Solent verò istas lectiones aliquando ita scribere Iudaei, ut singulis sectionibus singulas corii seu membranulae particulas tribuant, ceu ipse duas huiusmodi ----, secundā nempe & quartam, in antiquario meo possideo, è CL. Danielis Sch wenteri Bibliotheca dono mihi quodā datas; aliquādo tamen & coniungere duas solent, sicuti pariter talis membranula penes me est. Et ita conciliari aliquo posse modo videntur Fagius ac Schindlerus, quorum hic in Lex. Pentagl. p. 699. scribit, ----dici duas laminas seu membranulas corio inclusas, quarum una alligetur fronti, alter a manui sinistrae. Additque, quòd in his describatur egressio ex Aegypto quatuor sectionibus. Fagius autem testatur, receptaculorum seu domunculorum, in quibus quatuor----seu lectiones in membranulis scriptae, continentur inclusae, quatuor iuxta Iudaeos esse oportere. Subiicit Fagius: Si vel plura vel pauciora essent receptacula, gravissimum committi peccatum, Iudaeos statuere. Id quod tamen non omnes fortè sentire videntur. Rectè Theophylactus duarum saltem membranularum facit mentionem, ita enim ad h. l. notat: Scribebant (Iudaei) in duabus chartulis de calogum legis, & ponebant unam super frontem & alteram super dextram suspendebant. Epiphanius haer. 15. negat, quicquam phylacteriis fuisse inscriptum, nec membranulas ea fuisse: sed latas quasdam fuisse purpurae notas scribit, conspicuis palliorum locis praetextas. At videtur confundere Tephillin cum fimbriis. Ut ut porrò è veteribus Iustinus Martyr in Dialogo cum Tryphone Iudaeo, Isid. Pelusiota l. 2. ep. 150. Chrysostomus item, eumque sequuti Euthymius ac Theophylactus, tum quoque illustris Scaliger statuant, verba Deut. 6, 8. in quibus consuetudinis istius fundamentum Iudaei quaerunt, κατά τό ρητόν accipi debere, rectiùs tamen Hieronymus, Lyranus, Alphonsus Tostatus, quorum vestigiis plerique commentatores Pontificii, uti Leonh. Marius, Corn. à Lapide &c. item H. Grotius, insistunt, sentiunt, docentes, verba illa metaphoricè accipienda esse. Etenim non de verbis, sed de rebus praecipit ibi Deus, h. e. monet, ut beneficiorum ac praeceptorum saepè recordentur. Sic in Proverbiis Salomonis c. 3, 3. cap. 6, 21. iubet sapientia, alligari collo praecepta sua. Conf. Esaiae 49, 16. Contrà Samuel Petitus lib. 2. Var. lect. omninò à DEO dd. ll. huiusmodi ---- sive phylactiria Iudaeis mandata putat, idque ideò, quòd cùm Israelitae, dum inquilini in Aegypto servirent, & Aegyptiorum superstitiosis & obscoenis amuletis frontem munirent, Deus praeceperit, ut abiectis illis gentium Φυλακτηείοις, Decalogum in membranulis descriptum in frontibus gestent. Gestationi verò horum Tephillin Iudaei adhuc hodie plurimum tribuunt. Quemadmodum etiam R. David Kimchi scribit, Scripturam illi, qui observat praeceptum de applicandis Tephillin, tantum tribuere, acsi disceret legem DEI dies ac noctes. Notant porrò rerum Iudaicarum periti, Tephillin amuleti instar ab Apellis haberi. Unde etiam φυλακτήρια quibusdam dicta ea creduntur, cùm φυλακτηςιον Graecis sit ωείαμμαamuletum, quod corpori applicatur adversùs fascinationes. Cui etiam sententiae fidem adhibet Iesuita Corn. à Lapide, scribens, Chrysostomum per phylacteria accipere amuleta sanitatis. Subiicit Cornelius: talia enim censobant scribae esse membranas legis iam dictas. (puta Deut. 6, 1. seqq.) Sicuti Christiani nonnnulli Evangelium Iohannis collo appendunt quast amuletum & conservatorium salutis. Quemadmodum verò iam olim S. Hieronymus Comm. ad h. l. item que autor Op. Imperf. in Matth. hom. 43. ineptias huiusmodi in superstitiosis quibusdam mulierculis meritò reprehenderunt, ita pariter mos ille ac κακοζηλία Iudaica religiosorum quorundum, vel ut rectiùs dicam, nimis superstitio sorum vituperandus, iuxta ac deridendus est. Quemadmodum etiam iampridem à Synodo damnatus Antiochenâ est, teste Schindlero l. c. Adde Canon. 36. Synod. Laodicenae. Et sunt tamen inter Pontificios, qui superstitionem illam si non defendere, palliare tamen satagunt. Vid. Salmeron t. 4. p. 614. Vocantur autem Tephillin illae ab Evangelistâ nostro Φυλακτήρια seu asservatoria, eò quod summam legis comprehendant. Quemadmodum Salvator quoque de lege: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum &c. Matth. 22, 40. dicit, quòd ex illâ pendeant seu comprehendantur universa Lex & Prophetae. Conferatur quoque de istis phylact. Isid. Pelusiota lib. 2. ep. 150. Barthol. Meyerus Philol. Sacrae lib. 1. p. 124. seqq.)*

*( καί μεγαλωό ουσι τά κεά ωηδα των ίματίων άυτων. Augustinus Steuchus Eugubinus, Bibliothecarius Apostolicus, ac alii nonnulli existimant, φυλακτηρια Pharisaeorum nihil aliud fuisse, quàm fimbrias, ac proinde έξηγησεως saltem causâ posterius hoc membrum priori addi. Verùm contrarium manifestum est. Etenim differunt Φυλακτηρια καί κεάωεδα 1. ratione materiae. Illa enim ex corio conficiebantur. Erant enim membranulae, certis Sc. S. dictis insignitae: haec verò ex vestis seu pallioli, humeris iniecti, quod è pannis constabat, plerumque tamen bombycis vel sericis, materiâ. Dependebant enim â singulis pallioli angulis, erantque affixa hyacinthini seu violacei coloris filis, octo vel duodecim digitos lata. 2. ratione subiecti loci. Illa inter oculos collocabantur seu fronti applicabantur ac manui sinistrae; haec de pallioli vel, uti nōnulli existimant, cuiusq; vestis, tum interioris, tum exterioris angulis dependebant, vestiumque extremitates cingebant. Atque talia κεάωεδα Salvatorem quoque nostrum, iuxta mandatum divinum Numer. 15, 37. 38. gestasse, ex Matth 9, 20. ac cap. 14, 36.Marc. 6, 50. colligitur. Quanti verò Iudaei praeceptum illud de fimbriis aestiment, & quae aliàs de huiusmodi fimbriis tradant, multis ostendit Buxtorff. in Synag. Iud. c. 4. p 128. seqq. Cùm igitur Deus fimbrias gestare praeceperit, idque eo fine ut Iudaei, quoties illas intuerentur, obedientiae legi debitae recordarentur, probè notandum est, quòd Christus non ipsum fimbriarum usum, sed abusum taxet, h. e. quòd Pharisaei eas eo saltem fine gestarint, quò coram hominibus viderentur, adeoque falsò sibi persvaserint, gestationem fimbriarum sufficere, si vel maximè legem DEI ipsam ne digito quidem tangerent. Q. autem, cur Deus praeceperit, coccineas illas fimbrias gestare? Respondet Theophylactus, Deum hoc ipso declarasse, quòd oporteat nos sanguine Domini signari. Sed hâc de re pluribus agendum in Notis ad Num. 15, 37. 38 Camero in Myroth. p. 106. docet, quòd etiam fimbriis adsuerint membranam aut schedam, inscriptam verbis legis, ex locis suprà memoratis desumtis, atque istam schedam ---- appellarint. Notat idem, Iudaeos schedulam vel membranulam hanc certis verbis legis insignitam, cum capiti aut brachio aptaretur, vocasse ----: cùm ianuae ----; cùm vesti ----, iuxta illam Iudaeorū gnomen ---- Porrò Pharisaeis similes sunt Monachi, ac cumprimis Iesuitae, qui pariter fictam sanctitatem habitu corporis prae se ferre gestiunt, atque ita egregiè simpliciores decipere solent, cùm Catones simulent, ac Bacchanalia vivant. Evolvantur de Monachorum, quibus & Iesuitae accenseri debent, hypocrisi, lasciviâ, luxuriâ, opulentiâ &c. B. D. Hulsem. in AntiHagero p. 551. 552. B D. Hopffn. in Evangelica Saxon. pag. 650. B. Par. Comment. in post. Epist. Petri pag. 268. Hospinianus de Monachis, alii plures. Cumprimis verò ementitam Iesuitarum paupertatem produnt ea, quae de eorundem, in remotissimis oris, Goae nempe, degentium plusquam regio apparatu in victu pariter ac cultu notissimè commemoravit nobilis à Mandeslo in Itinerario Indico.)*

## 23:6
(v. 6. They love the first places at feasts etc. Cf. Luc. 14, 8.Rom. 12, 10.16. The Pharisees were indeed used more often by the Magnates at the table, inasmuch as hardly anything of any moment was undertaken without their counsel. See Ioseph. l. 13. A. I. c. 18.

Latin:

*(v. 6. Amant primos accubitus &c. Conf. Luc. 14, 8.Rom. 12, 10.16. Adhibebantur verò Pharisaei saepiùs à Magnatibus ad mensam, utpote cùm absque eorum consilio vix quicquam alicuius momenti susciperetur. Vid. Ioseph. l. 13. A. I. c. 18.

## 23:7
v. 7. Salutations in the marketplace. Macarius in Epist. Synod. ad Imperat. Act. 7. It is certain that άωασμόν, i. e. a salutation, is called by the Lord in this place ωεάσκύνσιν, i. e. adoration. For the Pharisees, endowed with a glorious spirit, and considering themselves righteous, strove to be adored by all. For they did not wish to be kissed with the mouth, for this would have been a sign of humility and by no means of Pharisaical arrogance.)

To be called Rabbi. Rabbi is said from ---- he multiplied, he magnified, either from an abundance of knowledge or from authority. Elias in Tisbi: The Rabbis say, every Rab and Mar is from Babylonia, i. e. those upon whom hands were laid in Babylonia. But every Rabbi is of the land of Israel. *(Camero in Myroth. Evang p. 07 otherwise distinguishes these titles, and thinks that Rabbi is the title of all teachers, but Rab κατ έζοΧην of such, as Rabban of those at least who flourished in the age that preceded the age of Christ. See also Ioh. Buxtorff. in Lex. Rabb. Talmud. dict. ---- Grotius in h. l. Camero also discourses at greater length on the distinction of those titles, t. 1, Praelect. p. 32. seqq.)

Latin:

v. 7. Salutationem in foro. Macarius in Epist. Synod. ad Imperat. Act. 7. Certum est, άωασμόν i. e. salutationem hoc loco à Domino appellari ωεάσκύνσιν i. e. adorationem. Pharisaei enim glorioso animo praediti, & seipsos existimantes iustos, abomnibus adorari studebant. Non enim ore osculari volebant, fuisset enim hoc humilitatis signum & haut quaquā Pharisaici supercilii.)*

Vocari Rabbi. Rabbi dicitur à ----multiplicavit, magnifi. cavit, vel à copiâ scientiae vel ab autoritate. Elias in Tisbi: Dicunt Rabini, omnis Rab & Mar est ex Babylo-ia i. e. quibus manus erant in Babylonia impositae. Omniverò Rabbiest d-t-rrâ Israel. *(Camero in Myroth. Evang p. 07 alit-r d-stingit istos titulos, putatque Rabbi esse titulum omnium doctorum, Rab verò κατ έζοΧην talium, ceu Rabban eorum saltem, qui seculo, quod Christi seculum praecessit, floruerunt. Vid. quoq; Ioh. Buxtorff. in Lex. Rabb. Talmud. dict. ---- Grotius in h. l. Pluribus quoque de discrimine illorum titulorum disserit Camero t. 1, Praelect. p. 32. seqq.)

## 23:8
(v. 8. Do not be called Rabbi. Andreas Bodenstein Carolstadius was ridiculous, (whom you might not inappropriately call an evil ---- Abc.) who, after the secession made from the Wittenberg Church, did not wish to be called Doctor any longer, but brother Andreas. Indeed, even a little before, when in the act of promotion he was conferring the titles of Doctors upon Iohannes Westermann and Godoschalcus Grapius, he publicly testified that he would confer the degree upon no one thereafter, because by promoting others to be Doctors, he would knowingly and prudently act against the saying of Christ Matth. 23, 8. But the prohibition of Christ ought not to be taken so nakedly and crudely: for it would otherwise follow that the appellation of Fathers ought not to be attributed to parents by children, v. 9, nor indeed the appellation of Masters to lords by servants, because of 1. Cor. 8, 6. The Apostle would also have acted less correctly by naming himself Teacher of the Gentiles, 1. Tim 2, 7. and 2. Tim. 1, 11. Conf. 1. Cor. 4, 15. Iohannes the Baptist would also have erred by permitting himself to be called Rabbi by his disciples, Ioh. 3, 26. Furthermore, among the orders established in the Church, Teachers are also numbered, Eph. 4, 11. Therefore, our Savior wishes at least this, as is evident from the circumstances of the text in this place, that authentic authority and the highest magisterium in articles of faith must be left to God alone, see Gal. 1, 8. likewise that in matters of faith we ought not to depend in the least upon the mouth or judgment of any man. (While therefore the Papists attribute infallibility to their Roman Idol, it is manifest that they are little mindful of the present command.) And that no one ought to arrogate to himself the title of Doctor or Master out of ambition. Conf. more things pertaining to this in Dn. D. Weller, Comm. in ep. ad Rom. d. 481. B. Par. L. de Min. Eccl. §. 137. it. B. D. Frantz. de Interpret. Sc. S. Orac. 85. B. D. Walth. Misc. Theol. Cent. p. 255.)

( For one is your Master. Christ, namely, who alone is to be heard, Deut. 18, 18. Iohan. 10, 27. Matth. 17, 5.

c. 28, 20. Conf. Eph. 2, 10. Gal. 1, 8. For He Himself brought forth and revealed to us the hidden wisdom of GOD from the bosom of the Father, Ioh. 1, 18. And hence in the Evangelical History He is called διδάσκαλοσ here and there. See above c. 8, 19. c. 9, 11. Ioh. 13, 13. namely κατ έζοΧην. See B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 31. Otherwise, this name is also attributed to others. See Act 13, 1. 1. Cor. 12, 28. 29. Eph 4, 11.)

Latin:

*(v. 8. Nolite vocari Rabbi. Ridiculus fuit Andreas Bodenstein Carolstadius, (quem per ---- haut praeter rem malum Abc. dixeris) qui post secessionem ab Ecclesiâ Wittebergensi factam, nolebat ampliùs vocari Doctor, sed frater Andreas. Quin etiam paulò ante, cùm in actu promotionis Iohanni Westermanno ac God oschalco Grapio Doctorum titulos conferret, publicè testatus est, se posthac nemini gradum esse collaturum, eò quòd promovendo alios in Doctores, sciens ac prudens faciat contra dictum Christi Matth. 23, 8. Verùm Christi prohibitio non ita nudè ac crudè accipi debet: sequeretur enim aliàs, quòd nec Patrum appellatio Genitoribus tribui à liberis deberet, v. 9. imò nec Dominorum appellatio heris à servis, ob 1. Cor. 8, 6. Minùs rectè fecisset quoque Apostolus, gentium se Doctorem nominando, 1. Tim 2, 7. ac 2. Tim. 1, 11. Conf. 1. Cor. 4, 15. Errasset quoque Ioh. Baptista, permittendo, à suis se discipulis vocari Rabbi,Ioh. 3, 26. Praeterea inter ordines in Ecclesiâ constitutos numerantur quoque Doctores,Eph. 4, 11. Hoc igitur saltem Salvator noster, ceu ex circumstantiis textûs patet, h. l. vult, quòd authentica autoritas & summum in fidei articulis magisterium soli Deo sit relinquendum, vid. Gal. 1, 8. item quòd in rebus fidei minimè ab ullius hominis pendere ore vel arbitrio debeamus. (Dum igitur Pontificirtalem infallibilitatem Idolo suo Romano tribuunt, manifestum est, quòd mandati praesentis parum memores sint.) Quòdque nemo etiam ex ambitione Doctoris vel Magistri titulum arrogare sibi debeat. Conf. plura huc facientia apud Dn. D. Wellerum Comm. in ep. ad Rom. d. 481. B. Par. L. de Min. Eccl. §. 137. it. B. D. Frantz. de Interpret. Sc. S. Orac. 85. B. D. Walth. Misc. Theol. Cent. p. 255.)*

*( Unus enim est Magister vester. Christus nempe, qui solus audiendus est, Deut. 18, 18.Iohan. 10, 27.Matth. 17, 5.

c. 28, 20. Conf. Eph. 2, 10.Gal. 1, 8. Ipse enim ex sinu Patris absconditam DEI sapientiam nobis protulit atque revelavit, Ioh. 1, 18. Atque hinc in Histor. Evangelica passim vocatur διδάσκαλοσ Vid. suprà c. 8, 19.c. 9, 11.Ioh. 13, 13. nempe κατ έζοΧην. Vid. B. Par. L. de Minist. Eccl. §. 31. Coeteroquin & aliis hoc nomen tribuitur. Vid. Act 13, 1.1. Cor. 12, 28. 29.Eph 4, 11.)*

## 23:9
v. 9. And call no man your father &c. We are prohibited from calling anyone father on earth, not absolutely, but comparatively to God, and to the ambitious usage of the Pharisees. In comparison to GOD, no one ought to be a father or teacher to us. (Conf. John 6, 45.1. Thess. 4, 9. The observation makes for this, that among the Jews, those who were learned, with the name of Doctor also claimed for themselves the authority, as it seemed, of teaching, and they wanted to be believed. Whence some followed these, others those masters, and hung entirely upon their mouth and authority, See H. Grotius on this place. And when some attempted to introduce this custom into the Christian Church, we read that it was reproved by the Apostle, 1. Cor. 1, 12. The Apostle James also seems to look to the same thing in his epistle c. 3, 1. indeed long ago God had dissuaded the Israelite people, lest in matters pertaining to the worship of GOD, they should observe the traditions of the Fathers, Exod. 20, 18. 19.) But with respect to the usage of the Pharisees, the same appellation is prohibited, lest, namely, we be called Fathers or Teachers ambitiously and gloriously, or call others so. Augustine in Psalm 77. This was not said so that the term of human honor should be taken away from the custom of speaking, but lest the grace of GOD, by which we are regenerated into eternal life, should be attributed to the nature or power, or even the holiness of any man. (Understand as the principal cause. For since God does not regenerate us immediately: but uses the Ecclesiastical Ministry for this work, it is not a sin from that, if we call the Ministers of the Church our spiritual fathers, (to which pertains that the Apostle himself names himself father of the Corinthians, 1. Corinth. 4, 15. Conf. 1. Tim. 1, 2.Tit. 1, 4. Philem. v. 10.) provided the power of begetting children of GOD is attributed to them in no other sense, than that God wills to be effective through their ministry. Let B. D. Bald. Comm. on the Ep. of Paul p. 336. & 1533 be compared entirely. Thus neither in the Economic state is it prohibited, that parents Let us call them Fathers: for Christ neither abrogated nor abolished the fourth commandment. It is evident, however, from Maimonides, that Father was formerly among the Jews a name of honor, shown to certain ones by reason of their learning. For thus were those surnamed who, established in the third rank among the Doctors, were otherwise called Rabbi. Buxtorf presents the passage of Maimonides in Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 10. Compare the same in Abbr. Ebr. p. 72. et seqq. Although the Savior indeed seriously dissuaded the Jews from attributing infallibility to any Doctor at all (unless those who are known to have written by divine inspiration, such as the Prophets, Apostles, and other holy men, ωό πνεοματοσ άγίου φεπο μσυοι, 2. Pet. 1, 20.), likewise, from attending as oracles to doctrines recently invented by their Doctors (for B. D. Frantzius, de Interpr. Sc. S. 876, judges that they were called Fathers, Doctors and Masters by them primarily for this reason, and he thinks that in this sense also it is finally prohibited by Christ, that anyone should desire to be called Master or Father, namely by devising or foisting upon hearers new dogmas of faith and new explanations of Holy Scripture): it is evident, however, that he profited little among most of them. For how much they value the pronouncements of their Doctors, especially those which are inserted into the Talmudic work, learned men have long since shown. See Buxtorf, Synag. Iudaic. c. 1. §. 59. et seqq. But Sebastian Barradius is ridiculous, when in his commentary on the Harm. Evang. tr. 3. l. 8. c. 24 he writes, that Christ gives counsel to those who affect perfection, and who have sent word to their affections, their honors, and their parents. And yet if Christ gave counsel to those who live in Monasticism, that they should not desire to be called Rabbi and Fathers, why do the Jesuits take such great delight in those titles? But it is a figment that the Savior here prescribes a counsel of perfection. Nay, the Savior prohibited in this place that we should attribute mastership or infallibility in articles of faith to any man, unless those who are known to have written from the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit. So that the admirers of the Pope, who so greatly defend the authentic judgment of the Roman Pontiff pronouncing from the chair, contradict Christ. But how egregiously they are deceived has long since been shown by our people. See B. Par. Confess. Cathol. l. 1. Gen. pert. post. c. 2. and Dispp. Acad. p. 1241. et seqq. it. p 1469. seq.)* *( One is your Father. Compare Psalm 103, 13.Is. 49, 15. 16.Malach. 1, 6. above c. 6, 8.c. 7, 11.John 20, 17.

Latin:

v. 9. Et patrem vestrum neminem &c. Prohibemur aliquem in terrâ patrem vocare, non absolutè, sed comparatè ad Deum, & ad Pharisaeorum usum ambitiosum. DEI comparatione nemo nobis debet esse pater vel praeceptor. *(Conf. Ioh. 6, 45.1. Thess. 4, 9. Huc facit observatio, quòd inter Iudaeos, qui eruditi erant, cum nomine Doctoris etiam autoritatem sibi vendicarent, quod visum esset, docendi, & credi sibi volebant. Unde alii hos, alii istos sectabantur magistros, totique ab ipsorum ore pendebant atque autoritate, Vid. H. Grotius in h. l. Atque hunc morem quum quidam in Ecclesiam Christianam introducere conarentur, ab Apostolo reprehensum legimus, 1. Cor. 1, 12. Eodem & respicere Apostolus Iacobus videtur in epist. suâ c. 3, 1. imô iampridem Deus populum Israeliticum dehortatus fuerat, ne in rebus ad cultum DEI pertinentibus, traditiones Patrū observarent, Exod. 20, 18. 19.)* Pharisaeorum autem usûs respectu prohibetur eadem appellatio, ne scil. ambitiosè glorioseque Patres aut Praeceptores appellemur ipsi vel alios appellemus. Augustinus in Psalm. 77.Hoc non ideo dictum est, ut vocabulum honoris humani de loquendi consuetudine tolleretur, sed ne gratia DEI, quà in aternam vitam regeneramur, naturae vel potestati, vel etiam sanctitati cuiusque hominis tribueretur. *(Intellige ut causa principali. Cùm enim Deus non immediatè nos regeneret: sed utatur ad hoc opus Ministerio Ecclesiastico, inde non peccatur, si Ministros Ecclesiae spirituales nostros patres vocemus, (quò pertinet, quòd Apostolus ipse Corinthorum se patrem nominat, 1. Corinth. 4, 15. Conf. 1. Tim. 1, 2.Tit. 1, 4. Philem. v. 10.) modò rictus generandi filios DEI, non alio illis tribuatur sensu, quàm quòd Deus per eorum ministerium velit esse efficax. Conferatur omninò B. D. Bald. Comm. in Ep. Pauli p. 336. & 1533. Sic nec in statu Oeconomico prohibitum est, ut genitores Patres appellemus: neque enim Christus quartum praeceptum abrogavit aut sustulit. Constat autem ex Maimonide, quòd Pater fuerit olim apud Iudaeos nomen honoris, ratione eruditionis quibusdam exhibiti. Ita enim cognominabantur illi, qui in tertio inter Doctores gradu constituti, aliàs Rabbi vocabantur. Locum Maimonid is exhibet Buxtorffius Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 10. Conf. idem in Abbr. Ebr. p. 72. seqq. Licet verô Salvator seriò dehortatus Iudaeos fuerit, ne ulli omnino Doctori (nisi quos ex divinâ inspiratione scripsisse constat, quales Prophetae, Apostoli aliique sancti viri, ωό πνεοματοσ άγίου φεπο μσυοι,2. Petr. 1, 20.) infallibilitatem tribuerent, item, ne doctrinis, recens â Doctoribus eorum adinventis, (ab his enim cumprimis Patres, Doctores ac Magistros eos appellatos censet B. D. Frantzius de Interpr. Sc. S. 876. & hoc quoque demum sensu à Christo prohiberi putat, ne quis Magister vel Pater audire gestiat, excogitando nempe vel obtrudendo auditoribus nova fidei dogmata, novasque Sc. S. explicationes.) tanquam oraculis attenderent: constat tamen, quòd parum apud plerosq; profecerit. Quanti enim Doctorum suorum effata Apellae aestiment, ea cumprimis, quae Talmudico operi inserta sunt, pridem ostenderunt viri eruditi. Vid. Buxtorff. Synag. Iudaic. c. 1. §. 59. seqq. Ridiculus verò est Sebast. Barradius, quancomm. in Harm. Evang. tr. 3. l. 8. c. 24 scribit, Christum consilium dare iis, qui perfectionem affectant, quiq tum affectibus, tum honoribus, tum parentibus nuncium miserunt. Atqui si Christus illis, qui in Monachatu vivunt, consilium dedit, ne Rabbi & Patres appellari gestiant, cur Iesuitae tantopere istis titulis delectantur? Ast figmentum est, quòd Salvator hîc praescribat perfectionis consilium. Imò prohibuit Salvator h. l., ne ulli homini, nisi quos constat, ex immediat â Spl. S. inspiratione scripsisse, magisterium aut in fallibilitatem in fidei articulis tribuamus. Ut ita Christo repugnent Papae admiratores, qui authenti cum Pontificis Romani, de cathedra pronunciantis iudicium tantopere propugnant. Sed quàm egregiè decipiantur, pridem à nostratibus ostensum est. Vid. B. Par. Confess. Cathol. l. 1. Gen. pert. post. c. 2. ac. Dispp. Acad. p. 1241. seqq. it. p 1469. seq.)* *( Unus est pater vester. Conf. Psalm. 103, 13.Es. 49, 15. 16.Malach. 1, 6. suprà c. 6, 8.c. 7, 11.Ioh. 20, 17.)*

## 23:10
v. 10. καθηγητὴς leader. But he is understood who leads others by his teaching. Syrian: neither be called Teachers leaders, from he led.

v. 10. καθηγητὴςductor. Intelligitur autem qui alios ducit suâ doctrinâ. Syrus: nec vocemini Doctoresduces, à duxit.

## 23:12
v. 12. Moreover, he who exalts himself shall be humbled, etc. Christ used this proverbial speech quite often. Tractatus Inubin c. 1. Everyone who humbles or lowers himself, the blessed God exalts him: and everyone who exalts himself, the blessed God humbles him. Aesop, when asked by Chilon what God was doing, replied: τὰ μην ύψηλα βαπεινούν, τα βαπειναύψούν. that He humbles the high things, and exalts the humble. Diogenes Laertius reports this in book 1, p. 25. (To this also look the sayings of Holy Scripture Prov. 16, 18.c. 29, 23. and examples, for instance the King of Assyria, Is. 10. and 37. Nebuchadnezzar, Dan. 4. Haman in the book of Esther, the Pharisee Luke 18. especially the Devil.)

( He who humbles himself shall be exalted. Compare Psalm 113, 8.6Ezech. 21, 26.Luke 14, 11.1. Peter 5, 5. 6. Let Isidore of Pelusium also be seen, book 1, epistle 286. Bernard, sermon 2 on the Ascension: Christ, when by the nature of divinity He did not have where He might grow, found how He might grow by descent. Compare many things on this matter in B. Par. in Aph. Pract. title Humility. also Schol. Pietat. l. 3 c. 15.)

Latin:

v. 12. Porrò qui se extollit, deprimetur &c. Christus hoc proverbiali sermone saepiùs usus est. Tractatus Inubin c. 1. Omnis, qui humiliat aut deprimit seipsum, Deus benedictus extollit eum: & omnis, qui extollit seipsum, Deus benedictus humiliat eum. Aesopus à Chilone interrogatus, quidnam Deus faceret, respondit: τὰ μην ύψηλα βαπεινούν, τα βαπειναύψούν.ipsum excelsa humiliare, & humilia extollere. Refert Diogenes Laertius lib. 1. p. 25. *(Huc spectaut quoque Scripturae S. dicta Prov. 16, 18.c. 29, 23. & exempla, Regis puta Affyrii, Es. 10. & 37. Nabuchodonosoris, Dan. 4. Hamanis in lib. Ester, Pharisaei Luc. 18. cumprimis Diaboli.)*

*( Qui se humiliarit, extolletur. Conf. Psalm. 113, 8.6Ezech. 21, 26.Luc. 14, 11.1. Petr. 5, 5. 6. Videatur etiam Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 1. epist. 286. Bernhardus serm. 2. de ascens. Christus cùm per naturam divinitatis non haberet, quo cresceret, per descensum quomodo cresceret, invenit. Conf. plurima in hanc rem apud B. Par. in Aph. Pract. tit. Humilitas. item Schol. Pietat. l. 3 c. 15.)*

## 23:13
(v. 13. Woe to you. Just as the Savior Matt. 5. enumerates eight beatitudes, as if so many blessings of the pious: so here He brings forth eight curses of the impious. Compare Deut. 27, 12. It is to be noted, however, that Τό woe of Christ is not only of one threatening and predicting grave punishment, but also of one condoling and of one pitying, if indeed men have done penance. It is also evident from this place that condemnations of false dogmas are lawful. Concerning which matter B. D. Balduinus deals at greater length in his Theological Discourse on Anathematisms, printed at Wittenberg in the year 1620, also in his Commentary on c. 3, ep. to the Galatians, p. 837, and also in 1 ep. to the Corinthians, c. 16, part 2, q 3. B. D. Hunnius on this place. B. Par. L. on the Ministry of the Church, § 270.)

( You shut. The heavenly doctrine, which is as a key , opening the entrance into the kingdom of heaven, by depraving it with various corruptions.)

Latin:

*(v. 13. Vae vobis. Sicuti Salvator Matth. 5. octo enumerat beatitudines, quasi tot piorum benedictiones: ita hîc octo profert impiorum maledictiones. Conf. Deut. 27, 12. Notandum verò, quòd Τόvae Christi non solùm sit comminantis ac grave supplicium praedicentis. sed etiam condolentis ac commiserantis, si nempe homines egerint poenitentiam. Patet quoq; ex h. l. quòd falsorum dogmatum condemnationes sint licitae. Quâ de re pluribus agunt B. D. Balduinus in Discursu Theologico de Anathematismis, excuso Witteb. A. 1620. it. Comment. in c. 3, ep. ad. Gal. p. 837. nec non in 1. ep. ad Corinth. c. 16. part. 2. q 3. B. D. Hunnius in h. l. B. Par. L. de Minist. Ecel. §. 270.)*

*( Clauditis. Doctrinam coelestem, quae tanquam clavis est, ingressum in regnum coelorum aperiens, variis corruptelis depravando.)*

## 23:14
v. 14. κατεσθίετε τας οἰκίας των χηρων κατὰ increases the meaning of the word. Cicero: not having consumed, but having devoured the patrimony. οιηια also signifies domestic property and patrimony. ὀδ. α. έςοντεςοιεον έμον. (Cornelius à Lapide not inconveniently explains this passage in such a way that the Scribes are said to devour the houses of widows, while they milk money from them, namely by selling to them with the pretense of holiness long public prayers. That very thing can certainly not inconveniently be affirmed of the Mass-priests, since it is established that they are accustomed to scrape together very many of the widows' monies by the frequent celebration of masses. See D. Zeaemannus, Disputation on the Sacrifice of the Mass §. 47. B. Par. Catholic Confession, vol. 4, p. 1269. The Theologians of Saxony in the Fundamental Deduction, p. 211.)

You shall be punished more severely. For there are given degrees of infernal torments. See the notes to c. 10, 15. Parallel passages are c. 11, 22. 24. Luc. 12, 47. 48. Rom 2, 9. There is also added the equality itself, and the reason of divine justice, so that, namely, those who lived more wickedly in the flesh may be tormented more severely in hell. Just as therefore in heavenly beatitude one will be more glorious than another: so in hell one will be more miserable than another, according to Augustine in Enchir. c. 3. Whence also seducers will be punished more severely than the seduced. Compare concerning the degrees of glory in eternal life, and of ignominy and torments in hell, which were noted in the analects above at c. 10, 15. c. 11, 21. and below at c. 25, 21. and add Macarius the Egyptian Hermit, homil. 40. page 460. A wicked teacher brings upon himself as many hells as he corrupts souls, because when he ought to be a promoter of salvation, he becomes its betrayer; he converts prayers and vows, which are holy things, into snares for money.)* *(

## 23:15
v. 15. That you may make a proselyte. The Savior denounces woe to the Pharisees in this place, not because they made a proselyte, but because when they had made such a one, they imbued him with their own errors and with the pride and arrogance of their own sanctity. A similar locution is had in Rom. 6, 17. where the Apostle gives thanks to GOD, that although the Romans had been servants of sin, they obey &c. where he certainly does not give thanks to GOD that the Romans had been servants of sin, but that they had been made obedient.

Proselytes were first called by the Jews those who, from among the Gentile inhabitants of the land of promise, which God bestowed upon His people, embraced the Jewish religion, so called because they were . ωρασηλθέντες approaching to the Jewish religion. Then those also were proselytes d-cted, who although they had no domicile in the land of Israel, nevertheless professed the Jewish religion, and set out to Jerusalem for the more solemn Feasts to worship. These were called גר item גר i. e. proselytes of righteousness and proselytes of the covenant; but those גר i. e. proselytes of the gate, Deut 14. 29. item במי i. e. proselytes of the sojourners. Now formerly proselytes of righteousness were made, and men indeed, גר i. e. by circumcision, baptism and oblation; but women at least by baptism and oblation: and such proselytes were held to observe the whole law or all the precepts, of which more than 600 are accustomed to be numbered; but for proselytes of the gate it sufficed if they observed at least the seven precepts of the sons of Noah, concerning which, as concerning the Proselytes themselves, let W. Schickard be consulted in de Iure Regio Ebr. cap. 5. pag. 125. seqq. Schindler Lex. Pentag. under the word גר & ור Buxtorf. Lex. Rabb. Talmud. likewise under the word גר (it is to be noted here in passing, that Buxtorf rightly observes, in the Lex. Pentagl. of Schindler under the word גר it is said less correctly concerning proselytes of the gate, that they were bound to the observation of the precepts of the sons of Noah, in that they wished to be circumcised and to observe the remaining precepts, and that the contrary is rather true. It must be known, however, that this error is by no means to be ascribed to Schindler himself, for the contrary is evident both from the context, especially those things which are immediately subjoined there, and from the discourse of the same Schindler under the word גר but it is at least a typographical error, since for wished, wished not ought to be read, a slip very easy for printers, which nevertheless was not removed even in the repeated edition.) B. Parens Comment. ad c. 14. Deuter. pag 883. but especially B. Slevogtius and Mr. Frischmuthius, my colleague and singular Friend, the former indeed in Disputat. Acad. Dissert. 14. the latter however in a twin Disputation concerning the seven precepts of Noah.)

ξηραν. Thucyd. lib. 8. το ξηραν for γαια he placed. The land is called Arid or dry, Gen. 7, 22. Jonah 1, 9. κατ έξοχην from the predominant quality of that thing: for it is a dry element. Thus a cup of ψυχρος i. e. water, Matth. 10.

You make him a child of hell ςιπχλοτεραν ύμων, twice as much as you are, as if both were by a double name children of hell. But here the convert is more so than they. So that we may understand that they are evil by only one name, because they did not keep the law in which they were born; the convert by a double name, first, because he is a Gentile and an idolater, and soon not an upright Jew, while he relapses into his former life, and from an evil Gentile becomes a worse Jew. Thus Erasmus in Annot. page 72. Thomas p. 2. 2. q. 189. art. 9. According to Hilary that word of the Lord was a prediction of the perverse zeal of the Jews, by which after the preaching of Christ, by drawing Gentiles or even Christians to the Jewish rite they make them twice the children of hell, because, namely, both the former sins which they committed in Judaism are not forgiven them, and nevertheless they incur the guilt of Jewish perfidy. According to Jerome it is referred to the Jews, also for that state in which he, who was converted by them to Judaism, while he was a Gentile, was simply erring, but seeing the vices of the Masters, he returns to his vomit, and having become a Gentile as it were a prevaricator he is worthy of a greater punishment. *(B Par. I. de Eccles. §. 118. explains this thus, that proselytes through Pharisaic corruptions, traditions and superstitions more greedily accepted and more pertinaciously defended, were rendered children of hell. For more easily from Ethnicism, than from Judaism, where to the former vices is added most shameful hypocrisy and the vain persuasion of feigned holiness, could such have been converted to Christianity.)*

Child of hell is he, who Matth. 5, 22. is said to be liable to the fire of hell. Thus children of the kingdom Matth. 8, 2. who are in the kingdom. children of wisdom Matth 11, 19. who are held for children of wisdom child of perdition Ioh. 17, 12. a most lost child.

*(Thus 1. Sam. 20, 31. 2. Sam. 12, 5. child of death i. e. owed to death.)*

*( Διπλότερον ύμων. Grotius confirms the truth of this assertion from Josephus in this place.)*

Denunciat Salvator Pharisaeis h. l. vae, non quòd facerent proselytum, sed quòd cùm talem feciffent, erroribus suis ac propriae sanctitatis opinione ac fastu imbuerent. Similis locutio habetur Rom. 6, 17. ubi Apostolus gratias agit DEO, quòd cùm Romani fuerint servi peccati, obediant &c. ubi sanè non agit DEO grates, quòd Romani fuerint servi peccati, sed quòd facti fuerint obediētes.

Proselyti Iudaeis primùm dicebantur, qui ex gentilibus inquilinis terrae promissionis, quam Deus populo suo largitus est, Iudaicā amplectebantur religionem, dicti ita, quòd fuerint qs. ωρασηλθέντεςaccedentes ad religionem Iudaicam. Deinde illi quoque proselyti fuerunt d-cti, qui licet nullum haberent in terrâ Israel domicilium, profitebantur tamen Iudaicam religionem, ac solennioribus Festis Hierosolymas proficisce bantur ad adorandum. Hi dicebantur גר item גר i. e. proselyti iustitiae ac proselyti foederis; illi verò גר i. e. proselyti portae,Deut 14. 29. item במי i. e. proselyti incolae. Fiebant autem olim iustitiae proselyti, & viri quidem, גר i. e. circumcisione, baptismo & oblatione; foeminae autem saltem baptismo & oblatione: atque tales proselyti totam legem sive omnia praecepta, quorum ultra 600. numerari solent, observare tenebantur; portae verò proselytis sufficiebat, si observarent saltem septem praecepta filiotum Noachi, de quibus, sicuti de Proselytis ipsis, consulantur W. Schickardus in de Iure Regio Ebr. cap. 5. pag. 125. seqq. Schindlerus Lex. Pentag. voce גר & ור Buxtorff. Lex. Rabb. Talmud. itidem voce גר (obiter hîc notandum, quòd Buxtorfius rectè observet, in Lex. Pentagl. Schindleri in voce גר minùs rectè de proselytis portae dici, quòd ad observationem praeceptorum filiorum Noachi fuerint obstricti, eò quòd circumcidi ac reliqua praecepta observare volebant, ac contrarium potiùs verum esse. Sciendum autem, quòd minimè error hic ipsi Schindlero adscribendus sit, contrarium enim tum ex contextu patet, illis cumprimis quae immediatè ibi subiiciuntur, tum ex discursu eiusdem Schindleri ad vocem גר sed erratum saltem typographicum sit, cùm pro volebant, legi debeat nolebant, lapsu apud typographos admodùm facili, qui tamen neo in iteratâ editione sublatus.) B. Parens Comment. ad c. 14. Deuter. pag 883. cumprimis verò B. Slevogtius ac Dn. Frischmuthius, collega atque Amicus meus singularis, ille quidem Disputat. Acad. Dissert. 14. hic verò in Disputatione geminâ deseptem praeceptis Noachi.)*

Facitis eum filium gehennaeςιπχλοτεραν ύμων,duplicius, quàm vos estis, quasi utrique sint duplici nomine filii gehennae. Verùm hic advena magis, quàm illi. Ut intelligamus, illos duntaxat uno nomine malos esse, quòd non servarent legem, in quâ nati essent; advenam gemino nomine, primùm, quòd Ethnicus & idololatra, mox nec Iudaeus probus, dum relabitur in vitam pristinam, & ex malo Ethnico fit peior Iudaeus. Ita Erasmus in Annot. pag. 72. Thomas p. 2. 2. q. 189. art. 9. Secundùm Hilarium verbum illud Domini fuit praenum ciativum perversi studii Iudaeorum, quo post Christi praedicationem, gentiles vel etiam Christianos ad Iudaicum ritum trahendo faciunt dupliciter gehennae filios, quia scil. & peccata pristina, quae commiserunt in Iudaismo, eis non dimittuntur, & nihilominus incurrunt Iudaicae perfidiae reatum. Secundùm Hieronymum refertur ad Iudaeos, etiam pro eo statu, quo ille, qui ab eis ad Iudaismum convertebatut, dum esset gentilis, simpliciter errabat, videns autem Magistrorum vitia, revertitur ad vomitum suum, & gentilis factus quasi praevaricator maiori poenâ dignus sit. *(B Par. I. de Eccles. §. 118. hoc ita exponit, quòd proselyti per Pharisaicas corruptelas, traditiones & superstitiones avidiùs acceptas & pertinaciùs, defensas, redditi fuerint filii gehennae. Faciliùs namque ex Ethnicismo, quàm ex Iudaismo, ubi ad priora vitia accedit turpissima hypocrisis ac fictae sancti-atis vana persuasio, ad Christianismum converti tales potuissent.)*

## 23:16
*(v. 16. He who swears by the temple. It is also evident from the Talmud, Kidduschin f. 71. 1. that the Jews swore by the temple. Whence the gloss on the said place בש i. e. it is an oath, By the temple of GOD. See the notes above on c. 5, 34.)*

He who swears by the gold of the temple. i. e. what is brought into the temple and sacrificed. The Pharisees spoke thus for this reason, that those things which were dedicated to the temple by a vow might be rendered, and thus their avarice might be satisfied. There was a singular oath of the Jews, the name of which was Corban, which was in use by no men except themselves. But Corban signifies δῶρον understand θεού, a gift dedicated to GOD, according to the interpretation of Josephus l. 1. against Appian.

*( Blind guides &c. See the notes above on c. 15, 14. and Compare the Analysis on Luke 6, 39. also Rom. 2, 19. 20.)*

## 23:20
*(v. 20. He therefore who swears by the altar &c. It seems in this place the Savior approves of oaths by creatures, when nevertheless Scripture H. See. Deut. 6, 13.c. 10, 20.Exod. 23, 13.Ier. 5, 7.Zeph. 1, 5. above c 5, 35. 36. it is fitting that one should swear in the name of the only true God, and by no means by creatures. Ioh. Piscator of Herborn in his Commentary on this place, and following him Ioh. Georg. Grossius in Theatro Bibl. p. 1027, respond that it was permitted, other things being equal, to swear by the temple, the altar, heaven; therefore, at least rash and false oaths are prohibited. But it is permitted to swear by God alone simply and absolutely, as by καρςιογνωςην and the avenger of perjury. But it must be known that it is one thing to approve of oaths by creatures; another thing to command that such things, even if they have been done, must be kept. Christ commands the latter here; he prohibits the former in c. 5, 35. The foundation of this latter is because creatures also are God's, who is present in all things and alone has power over all. Whence he who swears by creatures also swears by God. As the blessed D. Chemnitius well warns in Harm. Evang. c. 51. It is added that sometimes mention is made of creatures in the formulas of an oath, as if by obtestation, or as if by pledging, as when we deposit some precious thing dear to us as if it were a pledge with God, so that if we have deceived, God may punish our perfidy in that thing dear and precious to us, as who by his head, soul, and glory. But Christ denounces that not even the smallest creature should be rashly pledged to God in this way by an oath, so that it may be permitted to break faith with impunity. For those things which seem the least among creatures and most in our power, such as the hairs of the head, are the work of God, as the same Chemnitius warns in the same place. The foundation of the former assertion is because an oath is a worship owed to GOD alone and an invocation of GOD, by which we ask that he, by whom we swear, may be a witness of our mind, that we do not wish to deceive; and an avenger, if we have deceived. But God claims this invocation and obtestation for himself alone. See Deut. 6, 13.Ier. 5, 7.Zephan. 1, 5. Whence it also sufficiently appears what is to be determined concerning oaths made by deceased saints. As regards the example of Joseph Gen. 42, 15. and 1. Sam. 1, 26. But the blessed D. Walth. Harm. Bibl. p. 745. et seqq., the blessed D. Hunnius on this place p. 516. 516., the blessed D. Calixtus Conc. Ev. p. 204., the Lord D. Danhaverus Gen. c. 42. p. 1206. treat of this matter at greater length. But the blessed D. D. Walth. Harm. Bibl. p. 745. et seqq., the blessed D. Hunnius on this place p. 516. 516., the blessed D. Calixtus Conc. Ev. p. 204., the Lord D. Danhaverus Idea Boni Interp. p. 279. et seqq., and others treat of this matter at greater length. Compare also, if you please, the Annotations on c. 5, 35. But it must be considered here that if it is not permitted to rashly devote something dear to GOD by an oath, how gravely those sin who, with detestable rashness or a most wicked habit, devote themselves to the devil, with horrible execrations added.)*

Latin:

*(v. 20. Qui ergoiurat per altare &c. Videtur h. l. Salvator approbare iuramenta per creaturas, cùm tamen Scriptura S. Vid. Deut. 6, 13.c. 10, 20.Exod. 23, 13.Ier. 5, 7.Zeph. 1, 5. suprà c 5, 35. 36. deceat, in solius veri Dei nomine esse iurandum, miniminimè verò per creaturas. Ioh. Piscator Herborn. in Com. h. l. eumque sequutus Ioh. Georg. Grossius in Theatro Bibl. p. 1027. respondēt, licuisse caeteris paribus iurare per templum, altare, coelum; Prohiberi igitur saltem iuramenta temeraria ac falsa. per solum Deum verò licere iurare simpliciter & absolutè, tanquam per καρςιογνωςην & vindicem periurii. Verùm sciendum, quòd aliud sit iuramenta per creaturas approbare; aliud, quòd talia etiā, si facta fuerint, sint servanda, mandare. Hoc Christus hîc iubet; illud c. 5, 35. prohibet. Huius, posterioris, fundamentum est, quia creaturae quoque Dei sunt, qui in omnibus praesens est ac solus in omnes habet potestatem. Unde qui per creaturas iurat, etiam per Deum iurat. Uti benè monet B. D. Chemnitius Harm. Evang. c. 51. Accedit, quòd aliquando mentio fiat cteaturarum in formulis iuramenti, tanquam per obtestationem, vel quasi oppignorationem, ut cùm rem aliquam pretiosam & nobis caram, quasi pignus apud Deum deponimus, ut si fefellerimus, Deuperfidiam nostram puniat in re illa nobis chara & pretiosa, ut quiper caput, animam, & gloriationem suam. Christus verò denun-iat, ne minutissimam quidem creaturam hoc modo per iuramentum Deo temerè quasi oppignorandam esse, ut impunè liceat fidem fallere. Quae enim in creaturis videntur minima & maximè esse in nostrâ potestate, sicut sunt capilli capitis, sunt opus Dei, monente eodem Chemnitio l. c. Prioris adsertionis fundamentum est, quia iuramentum est cultus soli DEO debitus ac invocario DEI, quâ petimus, ut is, per quem iuramus, sit testis de animo nostro, quòd non velimus fallere; & vindex, si fefellerimus. Hanc verò invocationem & obtestationem Deus sibi soli vendicat. Vid. Deut. 6, 13.Ier. 5, 7.Zephan. 1, 5. Unde etiam satis patet, quid staruendam sit de iuramentis, per sanctos defunctos factis. Quodattinet exemplum Iosephi Gen. 42, 15. it. 1. Sam. 1, 26. Sed de hâc materiâ pluribus agunt. B. D. Walth. Harm. Bibl. p. 745. seqq. B. D. Hunnius in h. l. pag. 516. 516. B. D. Calixtus Conc. Ev. p. 204. Dn. D. Danhaverus Gen. c. 42. p. 1206. Sed de hâc materiâ pluribus agunt B. D. D. Walth. Harm. Bibl. p. 745. seqq. B. D. Hunnius in h. l. pag. 516. 516. B. D. Calixtus Conc. Ev. p. 204. Dn. D. Danhaverus Idea Boni Interp. p. 279. seqq. alii. Conf. etiam si placet, Annot. ad c. 5, 35. Cogitandum verò hîc, quod si non licet aliquid carum temerè per iuramentum DEO devovere, quàm graviter illi peccent, qui s. temeritate detestandâ, sive consuetudine pessimâ seipsos diabolo devovent, additis horrendis execrationibus.)*

## 23:21
(v. 21. He who dwells in it, i.e., the temple. But how God is said to dwell in the temple, when nevertheless the heavens of heavens cannot contain Him, 1 Kings 8, 27. add Acts 7, 48. is clear from those things which were noted above at ch. 6, 9. For God dwells in the temple and in heaven not comprehensively, that is, so that He is contained by the temple or heaven, since He is an infinite and immense being, but majestically, graciously, and gloriously.)

Latin:

*(v. 21. Qui habitat in eo, sc. templo. Quomodo verò Deus dicatur in templo habitare, cùm tamen coeli coelorum ipsum comprehendere nequeant, 1. Reg. 6, 27. add. Act. 7, 48. patet ex iis, quae notata suprà ad c. 6, 9. Habitat nempe Deus in templo ac coelo non comprehensivè, h. e. ut templo vel coelo comprehendatur, cum sit ens infinitum & immensum, sed maiestaticè, gratiosè ac gloriosè.)*

## 23:23
v. 23. Mint, cumin, etc. they used to tithe by the tradition or discipline of the elders, not by the law: for in the law it is commanded to give tithes of the produce. But herbs are not called produce, nor are they included under that name. Which is noted in the book of precepts 145. 4. But the contrary is proven in the Harm. Evang. (See the most recent edition of the H. E. ch. 158. p. 584. seqq. Furthermore, examples of this kind of Pharisaical hypocrisy occur Matt. 9, 11. ch. 12, 2. ch. 27, 6. John 18, 28. But Papists, especially Jesuits and monks, show themselves similar to the Pharisees, who establish it as a huge sin if anyone transgresses their traditions: but on the contrary, they often do not value highly other more serious sins, condemned in the H. Sc. Examples are, if any layman reads the H. Scripture, uses communion under both kinds, eats meat on Friday, or a Minister of the Church desires to live in honest marriage, etc. Furthermore, concerning the tithing of mint and similar things, and thus concerning the reason for the tithes themselves, W. Schickard discourses skillfully in On the Royal Law of the Hebrews ch. 4. p. 106. etc. Compare also the Analects to Luke 18, 12.)

Judgment. By judgment He understands the vindication of those, who are unjustly oppressed, by Mercy is every kind of beneficence toward one's neighbor, through faith, constancy in keeping promises. גר properly faith, גר truth. The root of both is the same. *(But how did the Pharisees neglect judgment? The Blessed D. Hunnius answers in this place that their negligence in duty is censured, namely, that when they ought as teachers of the people to have been authors and persuaders to the Magistrates to administer justice, which comes under the name of judgment, they themselves neglected this command, most frequently required in the law, as light and frivolous. The same D. Hunnius and several others -nterpret by faith in this place trust in Christ, whom the Pharisees rejected and blasphemed. H. Grotius also determines this, who thinks these words of Christ are clearly taken from Mich. 6, 7. Mr. D. Friedlieb understands by judgment the virtue that guards itself against inflicting injury on a neighbor; by mercy, the virtue of assisting a neighbor and the needy. By faith, sincerity in words, so that we do not deceive anyone by perjury.)*

Latin:

v. 23. Mentham, cyminum &c. decimabant ex traditione sive disciplina maiorum, non ex lege: nam in lege praecipitur dare decimas proventûs. Olera autem non vocantur proventus, nec sub eo nomine comprehenduntur. Quod notatur in libro praeceptorum 145. 4. Ast contrarium probatur in Harm. Evang *(Vid. H. E. edit, no vissimae cap. 158. p. 584. seqq. Coeterùm exempla huiusmodi hypocrisis Pharisaicae occurrunt Matth. 9, 11.c. 12, 2.c. 27, 6.Ioh. 18, 28. Similes verò Pharisaeis sese praestant Papistae, Iesuitae cumprimis ac Mona-hi, qui ingēs statuunt peccatum, si quis traditiones eorum transgrediatur: contrà verò peccata alia graviora, in Sc. S. condemnata, saepè haut magni aestimant. Exempla sunt, si quis laicus Scripturam S. legat, utatur communione sub utraque, edat carnem die Veneris, it. Minister Ecclesiae cupiat vivere in matrimonio honesto &c. Coeterùm de decimatione menthae ac similium, adeoque de ipsarum decimarum ratione scitè disserit W. Schickardus in de Iure Reg. Ebr. c 4. p. 106. &c. Conf. quoque Analect. ad Luc. 18, 12.)*

Iudicium. Per iudicium intelligit vindicationem eorum, qui iniustè opprimuntur, per misericordiam omne genus beneficentiae erga proximum, per fidem, constantiam in servandis promissis. גר propriè fides,גרveritas. Utriusque eadem radix. *(Sed quomodo Pharisaei iudicium negligebant? Respondet B. D. Hunnius in h. l. taxari eorum negligentiam in officio, quòd nempe cùm deberent tanquam Doctores populi esse Magistratibus autores & suasores ad iustitiam administrandam, quae iudicii nomine venit, ipsi hoc mandatum, in lege frequentissimè requisitum, tanquam leve & frivolum neglexerint. Idem D. Hunnius ac alii nonnulli -nterpr. per fidem h. l. intelligunt fiduciam in Christum, quem Pharisaei reiiciebant ac blasphemabant. Ita statuit quoque H. Grotius, qui haec Christi verba planè desumta arbitratur ex Mich. 6, 7. Dn. D. Friedlieb per iudicium intelligit virtutem, quae sibi cavet ab iniuriâ proximo inferenda; per misericordiam, virtutem subveniendi proximo & egenti. Per fidem sinceritatem in verbis, ne quem fallamus periurio.)*

## 23:24
v. 24. Blind guides, who strain out a gnat &c. It is a proverbial sentence about those who are περιέργοι, in the smallest matters, secure in great danger. The metaphor is taken from liquids, which, once a gnat has fallen in, are strained again so that they can be drunk. *(R. Moses Maimonides reports from Cholin such a proverb: He who strains wine or vinegar or strong drink, and eats the gnats, or flies and worms, which he has strained out, is beaten.)* Jerome explains, they neglect the great commandments of God, but demonstrate an opinion of religion in the diligent observation of ceremonies. *(Isid. Pelus. l. 4. ep. 92. Μη σχιαμάχει μηδὲ περι των τυχοντων φιλονιηων, έν τοις μεγιςοις καὶ ηαιριοις σαυτόν ηατάΒλαπτε. μηδὲ ζηλού τούς την κάμηλον ηαταπινονταςδ, καὶ τόν κώνωπα ςιύλιζοντας. But the Papists in vain from this place, see Bell. l. 1. de Amiss. gratiae & statu peccati cap. 9. §. Alia duo, strive to prove that certain sins are by their nature venial, since there is such a difference between a gnat and a camel by the nature of the thing, that there seems to be almost no proportion between them. For 1. it is known that parabolic theology is not argumentative, even by the admission of the Papists themselves. 2. it is to be observed that Christ does not institute a comparison between sins, but between moral and ceremonial commandments, and rebukes the Pharisees because they place all the worship of God in lesser ceremonial matters, while meanwhile securely neglecting the weightier moral ones. 3. that if anyone should wish to say that Christ is instituting a comparison of sins here, it would follow that he commands them to commit mortal sins, and not to omit the lesser, i.e., venial ones. To establish that is absurd.)*

Latin:

v. 24. Daces coeci, qui excolatis culicem &c. Proverbialis sententia est de illis, qui in rebus minimis sunt περιέργοι, in periculo magno securi. Metaphora desumta àliquidis, qui culice illapso denuò percolantur, ut bibi possint. *(Refert R. Mose Maimonides ex Cholin tale perverbium: Qui percolat vinum aut acetum aut sicerā, & comedit culices, aut muscas & vermes, quos percolavit, vapulat.)* Hieronymus exponit, magna Dei praecepta negligunt, opinionem autem religionis in diligenti observatione ceremoniarum demonstrant. *(Isid. Pelus. l. 4. ep. 92. Μη σχιαμάχει μηδὲ περι των τυχοντων φιλονιηων, έν τοις μεγιςοις καὶ ηαιριοις σαυτόν ηατάΒλαπτε. μηδὲ ζηλού τούς την κάμηλον ηαταπινονταςδ, καὶ τόν κώνωπα ςιύλιζοντας. Frustra autem ex hoc loco Pontificii, vid. Bell. l. 1. de Amiss. gratiae & statu peccati cap. 9. §. Alia duo, evincere satagunt, quaedam peccata naturâ suâ esse venialia, cùm inter culicem & camelum tantum ex natura rei discrimen sit, ut nulla ferè inter ea proportio esse videatur. Etenim 1. notum est, quòd Theologia parabolica non sit argumentativa, ipsis Pontificiis concedentibus. 2. observandum, quòd Christus non instituat comparationem inter peccata, sed inter praecepta moralia ac ceremonialia, reprehendatq; Pharisaeos, quòd in ceremonialibus minoribus omnem Dei cultū ponant, moralia interim graviora securè negligant. 3. quòd si quis dicere velit, Christum peccatorum comparationem hîc instituere, sequeretur, quòd mortalia peccata facere iubeat, minora s. venialia non intermittere. Id quòd statuere, absurdum est.)*

## 23:25
*(v. 25. Having been cleansed, etc. On this superstitious custom of the Jews, see Buxtorf, Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 644.)*

The inward parts are full of rapine and uncleanness, i.e. of foods obtained by rapine and devoted to intemperance. *(Cf. Isa. 1, 23. 24. Ezek. 28, 15. In much the same way R. Salomon the son of Gabirol also describes the hypocrite, whose words Cappellus gives in the Spicilegium p. 30. By the name "rapine" are understood the frauds and impostures by which, under the specious pretext of piety and of rather lengthy prayers, the Pharisees drew to themselves the substance of simpler folk—just as today the Jesuits and Monks, through masses, works of supererogation, etc., and especially by claiming to instruct the young more faithfully than others, heap up immense wealth and enrich their Colleges. But what is to be said of the R. P. [Roman Pontiff] who through the trafficking of indulgences has scraped together the riches of the whole world? Cf. B. D. Höpffner, in Saxon. Evang. p. 126 and 650. B. Par., Confess. Cathol. l. 2. Spec. part. 3. art. 16. c. 7. Here others too are at the same time admonished not to seek riches by evil arts. To which point belong Isa. 5, 8. Amos 8, 5. 1 Thess. 4, 6.)*

Latin:

*(v. 25. Purgatis &c. De superstitiosâ hâc Iudaeorum consuetudine consulatur Buxtorff. Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 644.)*

Interioraplena sunt rapina & immundicie, i. e. cibis, per rapinam comparatis, & intemperantiae destinatis. *(Conf. Ies. 1, 23. 24.Ezech. 28, 15. Eodem circiter modo hypocritam describit quoque R. Salomon Fil. Gabirol, cuius verba exhibet Cappellus in Spic. p. 30. Rapinae nomine intelliguntur fraudes ac imposturae, quibus sub specioso pietatis ac precum prolixiorum praetextu Pharisaei simpliciorum facultates ad se trahebant, planè ut hodiè Iesuitae ac Monachi per missas, opera supererogationis &c. ac cumprimis quòd iuventutem prae coeteris fideliter informent, ingentes opes coacervant ac Collegia sua ditant. Quid virò dicendum de R. P. qui per indulgentiarum nundinationes totius orbis divitias corrasit? Conf. B. D. Höpffn. in Saxon. Evang. p. 126. & 650. B. Par. Confess. Cathol. l. 2. Spec. part. 3. art. 16. c. 7. Monentur quoque simul hîc alii, ne malis artibus divitias conquirant. Quo spectant Es. 5, 8.Amos 8, 5.1. Thess. 4, 6.)*

## 23:26
*(v. 26. First cleanse what is inside the cup, etc. Take care that food and drink have not been acquired by evil means. Christ means by this that regard for conscience must be had before all else, so that it may be kept pure and undefiled. For conscience is like a chaste virgin, who does not endure the embraces of many. From conscience flows the goodness or wickedness of all actions, and this alone accuses and condemns us before God. Grotius observes, moreover, that the other clause is omitted in these words of Christ, as being one that could easily be understood. Examples of this sort of thing occur also in Rom. 9, 33; 1 Pet. 2, 6; Heb. 6, 7. 8; ch. 11, 26; ch. 12, 25. For the rest, our faith purifies our hearts, Acts 15, 9, namely insofar as it apprehends the merit of Christ. Compare Acts 10, 43; 1 Cor. 1, 2; 1 John 1, 7; Rev. 1, 5, etc.)*

Latin:

*(v. 26. Purga priùs, quod est intra pocu-um &c. Cura, ne cibus & potus malis artibus sit acquisitus. Christus hoc vult, quòd conscientiae ante omnia habenda ratio sit, quò pura & illibata conservetur. Est enim ea pudicae instar virginis, quae non patitur multorum amplexus. à conscientia profluit omnium actionum s. bonitas s. malitia, & haec sola apud DEum nos accusat ac damnat. Observat autem Grotius, alterum membrum in his Christi verbis omissum esse, utpote quodfacilè possit intelligi. Cuius rei exempla occurrant quoqueRom. 9, 33.1. Petr. 2, 6.Ebr. 6, 7. 8.c. 11, 26.c. 12, 25.Coeterùm fides nostra corda purificat,Actor. 15, 9.quat. nempe Christi meritum apprehendit. Conf.Act. 10, 43.1. Cor. 1, 2.1. Ioh. 1, 7.Apoc. 1, 5.&c.)*

## 23:27
(v. 27. You are like whitewashed sepulchers. This is, as it were, a property of heretics, to simulate holiness. Lord Dr. Weller, Comm. on Ep. to Rom. p. 756, confirms this very thing with the examples of the Manichaeans, Arians, and others. Whence also our people rightly teach that the holiness of life, with the sincerity of doctrine having been set aside, is not a genuine mark of the Church. See B. Par. Place on the Church §. 259. Confess. Cathol. art. 5. c. 4. §. 10. In this place I add at least this, that Corn. à Lapide, Comm. on Matth. p. 161, himself confesses that heretics often live better than Catholics. To which also the sayings Matth. 7, 15. 2. Corint. 11, 14. 15. contribute. Let us therefore test the spirits, whether they are from that God, 1. Ioh. 4, 1. We are warned, however, by this grave rebuke of the Pharisees, and by the comparison with whitewashed sepulchers, that we should flee hypocrisy, weighing that God is καρςιογνωςης. Conf. 1. Sam. 16, 7.Esa. 11, 34.1. Cor. 4, 5.)

Latin:

*(v. 27. Similes estis sepulcris dealbatis. Est hoc proprium quasi haereticorum, sanctitatem simulare. Exemplis Manichaeorum, Arianorum aliorumque hoc ipsum confirmat Dn. D. Wellerus Comm. in Ep. ad Rom. p. 756. Unde etiam rectè docent nostrates, quòd vitae sanctitas, sequestratâ nempe doctrinae sinceritate, non sit genuina Ecclesiae nota. Vid. B. Par. Loco de Eccl. §. 259. Confess. Cathol. art. 5. c. 4. §. 10. Hoc loco illud saltem addo, quòd Corn. à Lapide Comm. in Matth. p. 161. ipse confiteatur, haereticos saepè meliùs vivere quàm Catholicos. Admonemur autem gravi istâ Pharisaeorum reprehensione, & cum dealbatis sepulcris comparatione, ut fugiamus hypocrisin, perpendentes, quòd Deus sit καρςιογνωςης. Conf. 1. Sam. 16, 7.Esa. 11, 34.1. Cor. 4, 5.)*

## 23:29
v. 29. Woe to you, because you build the sepulchers of the Prophets, Conf. Luc. 11, 48. Origen asks, Why does Christ curse the Pharisees with this name? For they are not to be execrated by this name, because they were building monuments of the Prophets, nor in this, that they were born from the murderers of the Prophets, since in the one case it is a duty, the other is not in our hand. But it must be known that they are rebuked for this reason, that they were building monuments of the saints to simulate holiness, and were falsely denying that they would have consented to their slaughter if they had lived in the same times, when in reality they were declaring that they would have raged even more cruelly against the Prophets, since they were preparing to kill Christ himself. Christ does not threaten them with woe because of the buildings erected in honor of the prophets, but because as soon as they saw any Prophet arise, they immediately designated a burial and death for him, not being able to bear him.
