Ambrose in this place: by the building of the tombs of the Prophets they were arguing against the wickedness of those who had killed them, and by the emulation of similar deeds they were also declaring themselves heirs of their fathers' iniquity: therefore not the building, but the emulation is estimated as the place of the crime. Chrysostom hom. 75. in Matth. Not because they build, nor because they accuse their fathers , did he say woe to them, but because doing so and saying so, they dared to condemn their fathers, when they themselves were committing worse things. ib. he adds: The Jews were accustomed to build the sepulchers of the Prophets, not that they might honor the Prophets, but that they might show the strength and power of their ancestors, because they were able to kill the Prophets. The same ibid. warns that they by no means built their monuments out of zeal toward the Prophets, but so that a trophy and trace of the noble crime committed by their ancestors might not be missing, and thus others might be deterred from the freedom of rebuking. Jerome in this place says that the ancient Jews killed the Prophets out of pride, but the more recent ones out of pride and ambition built the sepulchers of the same, and therefore by that deed consented to their works. Cajetan notes that he who buries one who has been killed can do it either to honor the dead or to complete the act of the murderer. Even if the Jews said that they were building the sepulchers of the Prophets to honor them, yet they seemed to do it to complete the works of their fathers, because the ancestors killed the Prophets, but they themselves killed Christ and the Apostles. (Although they had not yet killed Christ and the Apostles at that time, they had nevertheless fully conceived of doing it shortly.) There are those who think that the Pharisees are rebuked by Christ for the built or repaired and adorned sepulchers of the Prophets, because, namely, they exacted money for this work from the poor. Now, however, it is certain that martyrs do not rejoice to be honored from those monies in which the poor weep. It can also be said that Christ rebuked the Pharisees for this reason, that they constituted the chief part of divine worship in external ceremonies, thinking themselves to have fully performed their duty if they widened their phylacteries and built the sepulchers of the Prophets, while in the meantime they were completely destitute of the interior fear of GOD, true humility, etc. In which part our people rightly observe that the Papist doctors have them as imitators, in γειΨανογατρεία i.e. χαί σχεγεευγατρεία,. See B. Par. L. on Death §. 95. seqq. Thus the same Papists adorn the sepulchers of the martyrs, i.e., they build magnificent temples in their memory, undertake pilgrimages to the places which they call of the saints, etc., when yet we, who profess that doctrine and faith which the Apostles and others once

the martyrs left to us in their writings, and sealed with their own blood, are persecuted with the same cruelty which tyrants once exercised against the martyrs, . On which matter the Blessed D. Hunnius discourses elegantly in this place.)*

Latin:

v. 29. Vae vobis, quoniam aedificatis Prophetarum sepulcra, Conf. Luc. 11, 48. Origenes quaerit, Cur Christus hoc nomine Pharisaeis vae imprecetur. Neq enim hoc nomine execrandi sunt, quòd extruerent monumenta Prophetarum, neq in hoc, quòd ab homicidis Prophetarum essent progeniti, cùm in altero sit officium, alterum non sit in manu nostra. Verùm sciendum est, ideò eos reprehendi, quòd ad simulandam sanctimoniam extruerent monumenta sanctorum, & falsò negarent, se consensuros fuisse in illorum caedem, si iisdem temporibus vixissent, cùm reipsâ declararent, se crudeliùs etiam saevituros fuisse in Prophetas, cùm ipsum Christum pararent occidere. Non comminatur illis, Christus vae propter aedificia, in prophetarum honorem extructa, sed quòd cùm primùm viderent aliquem Prophetam surgere, statim illi designarent sepulturam & necem, ferre eum non valentes. Ambrosius in h. l. Propheti-orum aedificatione tumulorum sceleris eos, qui occiderant, arguebant, & similium aemulatione factorum se quoq declarabant paternae iniquitatis haeredes: non igitur aedificatio, sed aemulatio loco criminis aestimatur. Chrysostomus hom. 75. in Matth. Non quia aedificant, nec quia patres tres suos accusant, vae illis dixit, sed quoniam it a facientes & ita dicentes, Patres suos condemnare audebant, cùm ipsi peiora committerent. ib. addit: Iudaeos aedificare solitos sepulcra Prophetarum, non ut honorarent Prophetas, sed ut ostenderent vires & potentiam maiorum suorum, quia Prophetas occidere potuerunt. Idem ibid. monet, illos hautquaquam studio erga Prophetas extruxisse monumenta illorum, sed ne nō extaret trophaeum ac vestigium egregii facinoris, à maioribus patrati, atque ita deterrerentur coeteri à libertate reprehendendi. Hieronymus in h. l. dicit, antiquos Iudaeos ex superbia occidisse Prophetas, recentiores autem ex superbia & ambitione aedificasse eorūdem sepul-ra, & proinde eo facto operibus ipsorum consensisse. Caietanus notat, eum, qui sepelit occisum, posse id facere, vel ut honoret mortuum, vel ut compleat actum homicidae. Iudaei etiamsi dicerent, se aedificare sepulcra Prophetarum, ut eos honorarent: tamen id facere videbantur, ut complerent opera patrum suorum, quia maiores Prophetas, ipsi verò Christum & Apostolos occiderunt. *(Licet verò tùm nondum Christum & Apostolos occidissent, omninò tamen conceperant, id propediem facere. Sunt, qui propterea Pharisaeos à Christo reprehendi ob aedificata vel refecta atque exornata sepul-ra Prophetarum censent, quia nempe pecuniam ad hoc opus exigerint à pauperibus. Iam verò constat, quòd Martyres non gaudeant ex iis pecuniis honorari, in quibus pauperes plorant. Potest etiam dici, Christum eo nomine Pharisaeos reprehendisse, quòd praecipuam cultûs divini partem in externis ceremoniis constituerent, abunde se perfunctos officio suo rati, si phylacteria dilatarent, ac Prophetarum sepulcra aedificarent, interiori DEI timore, verâ humilitate &c. interim penitus destituti. Quâ in parte Pontificios Dd. imitatores eos habere, in γειΨανογατρεία sc. χαί σχεγεευγατρεία, rectè observant nostrates. Vid. B. Par. L. de Morte §. 95. seqq. Sic iidem Pontificii martyrum sepulcra exornant h. e. magnifica templa in eorum memoriam exstruunt, peregrinationes ad loca, quae vocant, sanctorum suscipiunt &c. cùm tamen nos, qui eam profitemur doctrinam ac fidem, quam olim Apostoli & alii

martyres in scriptis suis nobis reliquerunt, suoque sangvine obsignarunt, eadem crudelitate, quam olim tyranni in martyres exercebant, persequant-r. Quâ de re eleganter disserit B. D. Hunnius in h l.)*

## 23:31
v. 31. μαρτυρεΐτε έαυτοΐς i. e. χαΤ' έαυτων or άφ έαυτούς. A similar phrase exists Mark 6, 11.Luke 9, 5.

That you are the sons of them who killed the Prophets, namely, insisting upon their footsteps, as is gathered from the following verse.

Latin:

v. 31. μαρτυρεΐτε έαυτοΐς i. e. χαΤ' έαυτων sive άφ έαυτούς. Similis phrasis extat Marc. 6, 11.Luc. 9, 5.

Quòd sit is filii eorum, qui Prophetas occiderunt, scil. vestigiis eorum insistentes. ut colligitur ex vers. seq.

## 23:32
*(v. 32. χαί ύμεΐς πληρώσατε. You also fill up. Luther: Bohlan/erfuellet auch ihr &c. as if he were saying, since you leave no room for the most faithful dissuasions, it is permitted by just divine judgment that you fill up the measure of your fathers. For that the word πληρώσατε. is not in this place a word of command or of precept, but at least denotes permission and prediction, is evident from the added threatening of the most grave punishments, in the following verse. But God is not the author of that of which He is the avenger, as Fulgentius holds. Therefore the Calvinists err not lightly, when they do not blush to assert that the impious sin by the secret impulse of God. The contrary is evident from Psalm 5, 5. Cf. Eccles. 15, 12. Whence Damascenus rightly, book 4 de O. F. c. 20. All these things (which seem to be ascribed to GOD, as if He makes the wicked or commands them to sin) are not to be accepted as God acting, but permitting. And a little later: Therefore to call His permission His action is customary for Holy Scripture. This rule applies to understanding the sayings 1 Kings 22, 22.John 2, 19. c 13, 27. 2 Thess. 2, 11.2 Cor. 4, 4. It is therefore insinuated at least in this and similar places divine patience in tolerating sinners, concerning which matter Hugo Grotius discourses at length in this place. The sayings Gen. 15, 16.Job 22, 22.Isa. 27, 8.1 Thess. 2, 16. also look to this. Known is that saying of the Rabbis -- i. e. God, Blessed be He, does not take vengeance from a man, until his measure has been filled. It is read in Sota f. 9. 1. and is proved from Job 20, 22. where the Chaldaic Paraphrase is to be seen. Cf. also the notes below at v. 38. item Pineda Comm. in Job c. 33, 30. n. 5.)*

Latin:

*(v. 32. χαί ύμεΐς πληρώσατε.Vos quoq implete. Lutherus: Bohlan/erfuellet auch ihr &c. quasi dicat, quandoquidem fidelissimis dehortationibus nullum relinquatis locum, permittur iusto iudicio divino, ut vos impleatis mensuram patrum vestrorum. Quod enim verbum πληρώσατε. non sit hoc loco verbum mandati sive praecepti, sed saltem permissionem ac praedictionem notet, patet ex adiectâ comminatione poenarum gravissimarum, v. seq. Deus verò non est autor, cuius est ultor, ut habet Fulgentius. Errant proinde haut leviter Calviniani, quando adserere non erubescunt, quòd impii arcano Dei impulsu peccent. Contrarium patet ex Psal. 5, 5. Conf. Eccles. 15, 12. Unde rectè Damascenus l 4. de O. F. c. 20. Haec omnia (quae DEO adscribere videntur, ac si malos faciat vel iubeat peccare) non ut Deo agente accipienda sunt, sed permittente. Et pauliò pòst: permissionem igitur eius ut actionem eius dicere, consuetum est S. Scripturae. Facit haec regula ad intelligenda dicta 1. Reg 22, 22.Ioh. 2, 19. c 13, 27. 2. Thess. 2, 11.2. Cor. 4, 4. Insinuatur igitur saltem in hoc similibusque locis divina patientia in tolerandis peccatoribus, quâ de re prolixè disserit Hugo Grotius in h. l. Spectant etiam huc dicta Gen. 15, 16.Iob. 22, 22.Esa. 27, 8.1. Thess. 2, 16. Notum est illud Rabbinorum -- i. e. Non sumit Deus S. B. I. ultionem ab homine, donec impleta fuerit mensura eius. Legitur in Sota f. 9. 1. probaturque ex Iob. 20, 22. ubi videnda Paraphrasis Chaldaica. Conf. quoque notata infra ad v. 38. it. Pineda Comm. in Iob. c. 33, 30. n. 5.)*

## 23:33
*(v. 33. Serpents, generation of vipers. The Savior calls the Pharisees thus by a metaphor customary in Holy Scripture, because they were from their father the devil, Ioh. 8, 44. who under the appearance of a serpent had seduced Eve 2. Cor. 11, 3. and for that reason he is also sometimes called serpent in the H. S. See Luc. 10. 19. coll. with v. 17. Apoc. 12, 9. c. 20, 2. and compare the note to v. 7. c. 3. Add also the Anal. to v. 13.)*

Latin:

*(v. 33. Serpentes, genimata viperarum. Appellat ita Salvator Pharisaeos consuetâ in Sc. Sacrâ metaphorâ, quia ex patre diabolo erant, Ioh. 8, 44. qui sub specie serpentis seduxerat Evam 2. Cor. 11, 3. proptereaque etiam in Sc. S. aliquando serpens vocatur. Vid. Luc. 10. 19. coll. cum v. 17. Apoc. 12, 9. c. 20, 2. ac confer not. ad v. 7. c. 3. Add. etiam Anal ad v. 13.)*

## 23:34
(v. 34. Behold I send to you. We learn from this 1. that the true Doctors of the Church ought not to intrude themselves, but to await a divine mission or calling. To which pertain the sayings Jer. 23, 21. c. 27, 9. 14. Matt. 7, 15. c. 24, 24. John 5, 43. c. 10, 8. Rom. 10, 15. Against the Photinians, Anabaptists, Weigelians. 2. that because the faithful heralds of the divine word are sent by GOD, and are therefore His ambassadors, 2 Cor. 5, 20. we ought to receive and honor them with reverence, Gal. 4, 14. Phil. 2, 29. and to obey the word preached by them, not to resist them, much less to do them injury.)

*( Prophets &c. Hilary: The Apostles, by the revelation of future things, are Prophets; by the knowledge of Christ, wise men; by the understanding of the law, Scribes. Prophets are otherwise called in Holy Scripture other Teachers also, who are endowed with the faculty of explaining Holy Scripture, or are heralds of the divine word. In which sense the name of Prophets is accepted Jer. 26, 11.Matt. 10, 41.1. Cor. 14, 29.32. Compare also v. 1. 3 31.)*

(The Wise. So called, because they profess heavenly wisdom, or mysteries revealed by God.)

*( Scribes. These were so called, because they were occupied with the explaining of Holy Scripture. Conf. Matth. 13, 52. it. above v 2.)*

*( From these you shall kill &c. See Acts 4, 3.7.12. 13. 14.2 Cor. 11. item Eusebius book 2. Ecclesiastical History ch. 23. Origen homily 23. on Numbers: And I today if I do not hear the words of the Prophet, if I despise his warnings, I stone the Prophet, and as much as is in me, I kill him, whose words as if dead I do not hear. We learn indeed from this, that cruelty is joined to false doctrine. For heretics are driven by the spirit of the devil, who is a murderer from the beginning, John 8, 44.)*

You shall be scourged in your synagogues. By the name of synagogues in this place are not understood houses of prayer but civil and judicial assemblies, as H. Grotius shows at length at Matth. 10, 17.

Latin:

*(v. 34. Ecce ego mitto ad vos. Discimus hinc 1. quòd veri Doctores Ecclesiae non debeant sese intrudere, sed missionem seu vocationem expectare divinam. Quò faciunt dicta Ier. 23, 21. c. 27, 9. 14. Matth. 7, 15. c. 24, 24. Ioh. 5, 43. c. 10, 8. Rom. 10, 15. Contra Photinianos, Anabaptistas, Weigelianos. 2. quòd quia fideles verbi divini praecones à DEO mittuntur, adeoque eius legati sunt, 2. Cor. 5, 20. cum reverentia excipere eos ac honorare debeamus, Gal. 4, 14.Philipp. 2, 29. ac verbo ab ipsis praedicato morem gerere, non repugnare eis, multo minùs iniuriâ illos afficere.)*

*( Prophetas &c. Hilarius: Apostoli revelatione futurorum, Prophetae; Christi agnitione, sapientes; legis intelligentiâ, Scribae. Prophetae aliàs in Sc. S. dicuntur alii quoque Doctores, qui facultate Scripturam S. explicandi praediti, vel divini verbi praecones sunt. Quo sensu accipitur nomen ProphetarumIerem. 26, 11.Matth. 10, 41.1. Cor. 14, 29.32. Conf. etiam v. 1. 3 31.)*

*( Sapientes. Dicti ita, quòd sapientiam profiteantur coelestem, sive divinitus revelata mysteria.)*

*( Scribas. Ita dicti hi, quòd circa Scripturam S. exponendam occupati fuerint. Conf. Matth. 13, 52. it. suprà v 2.)*

*( Ex his occidetis &c. Vid. Actor. 4, 3.7.12. 13. 14.2. Cor. 11. item Eusebius lib. 2. Hist. Eccl. c. 23. Origenes hom. 23. in Numeros: Et ego hodie si Prophetae non audiam verba, si monita eius spernam, lapido Prophetam, & quantum in me est, occido, cuius tanquam mortui verba non audio. Discimus verò hinc, quòd falsae doctrinae adiunctum sit crudelitas. Aguntur enim haeretici spiritu diaboli, qui homicida est ab initio, Ioh. 8, 44.]*

*( Flagellabitis in synagogis vestris. Nomine Synagogarum h. l. non intelliguntur Proseuchae sed civiles & iuridici conventus, ceu prolixè ostendit H. Grotius ad Matth. 10, 17.]*

## 23:35
(v. 35. That upon you may come &c. But the son ought not to bear the iniquity of the father, Ezech. 18, 20. nor does God wish to visit the sins of the parents upon the children beyond the third and fourth generation, Exod. 20, 5. Resp. The sayings Ezech. 18, 20. and Exod. 20, 5. are to be understood with ωροσθήχη, if they themselves repent, and do not persist in the footsteps of their parents. But the matter stands otherwise when these imitate the same cruelty of their parents, and fill up the measure of their sins. This is what the Jews, of whom Christ is speaking here, did. Whence Theoph. in h. l. Upon the Jews, he writes, who were then, he says, will come all the blood unjustly shed: for they will be punished more than their fathers. For neither were they amended after so many examples. For just as also Lamech after Cain was punished more, although he had not killed his brother, for the reason that he had not been amended by the example of Cain. Conf. Gen. 15, 16. 1. Reg. 15, 16. Deut. 5, 9.)

All blood i.e., the vengeance of righteous blood. See Matth. 27, 25. id. Lev. 20, 9. 13. 1. Reg. 2, 32. Ps. 9. 12. Therefore the world does not persecute the ministers of Christ with impunity. See 2. Par. 24, 22. following. Ps. 9, 14. Apoc. 6, 10. Compare also Apoc. 17, 6. with Apoc 18, 5. 6. )* *(

From the blood of Abel (Q How is the slaughter of Abel imputed to the Jews, when they do not descend from Cain? Ans. Although they are not the sons of Cain (who is proposed in Holy Scripture as the parent of all murderers, see 1. Ioh. 3, 12. Jude v. 11) by generation, they are nevertheless by imitation. Cain was the parent of the Jews, if not by blood and race, yet by malice and mind; if not naturally, yet morally, that is, by evil example, namely by killing the righteous Abel. Thus, similarly, it shall be imputed by GOD to the Babylonian harlot, who is drunk with the blood of the saints, Apoc. 17, 6. all the righteous blood of the martyrs, or of the confessors of the Evangelical truth, shed by heathen tyrants from the very times of the Apostles.)* *( έως.

( έως. It is asked, why Christ says that it will come to pass that all the blood shed innocently shall come upon the Jews, from the blood of Abel even to the blood of Zacharias, son of Barachias, when nevertheless this Zacharias was not the last who was killed innocently by the Jews? Resp. It is to be noted that the particle έως defines a certain time in such a way that it does not exclude what is later than it, as has been shown at length elsewhere. See above in the Analysis to chapter 5, 26. p. 303. 304.)

From the blood of Zacharias &c. Who is that Zacharias, son of Barachias? Some bring forward a fable from apocryphal books, that there was a certain place designated in the temple where virgins would stand while sacred rites were being performed; that while the mother of Jesus stood in it, who was known to have already given birth, and the common people did not understand that she had conceived by divine power, and the people took this indignantly, and yet she was defended by Zacharias, the father of John the Baptist, he was killed during a tumult between the inner temple and the altar. Thus Origen, tract. 26 on Matthew. Basil, homily on the Nativity of Christ, Theophylact and Euthymius on this passage. *(Epiphanius on the lives of the Prophets, p. 134.)* But without doubt that apocryphal tradition seduced them, as St. Jerome hints clearly enough, mentioning that some refer it to Zacharias, the father of John the Baptist, and approve it from apocryphal dreams, that he was killed for this reason, because he preached the coming of the Savior. But he notably adds: Because this has no authority from the Scriptures, it is rejected with the same ease with which it is approved. Others bring forward other causes, although they themselves hesitate greatly. *(Nevertheless, the Papists commonly embrace this opinion. See Baronius, vol. 1, Annals, n. 53; Toletus on chapter 11 of Luke, Annot. 10; Christoph. à Castro on Zacharias; Franciscus Lucas Brugensis on this passage; Marchantius, Hort. Past., tr. 4, p. 538; with whom also agree Matth. Flacius, Clav. Sc. Sacrae, title Temple; Georg. Maior, vol. 3, p. 669; Hadrianus Iunius on Matthew, p. 193; Cocceius on Zacharias, p. 468, who testifies that it pleased Constantine L'Empereur as well. However, Lud. de Dieu, Commentary on this passage, attributes a different opinion to the aforementioned L'Empereur. The Jesuit Maldonatus also gives little faith to that tradition upon which this opinion rests: but he expressly confesses that that tradition is not proven from good books, and that Epiphanius reports such a thing about the Gnostics in their heresy, and that it is read today in I know not what (as it is called) Protevangelium. Sebastianus Barradius, a man of the same society, likewise refutes that tradition, vol. 3, Harm. Evang., book 1, ch. 28.)* Theophylact mentions that some refer it to that Zacharias, who is held among the twelve Prophets, son of Barachias, Zach. 1, 1. But it is nowhere read concerning the Prophet Zacharias, that he was killed between the temple and the altar. Therefore it is more correctly understood of Zacharias the son of Jehoiada, whom King Joash killed between the altar and the temple, 2 Chron. 24, 21. But as for the fact that the father's name objects to this, they solve it in this manner, that Jerome testifies, In the Gospel of the Nazarenes, Zechariah is said to be the son not of Barachiah, but of Jehoiada, hinting that in our Codices, through the error of the scribes, Barachiah was written instead of Jehoiada. *(Ludwig Cappellus embraces this same thing in Spic. p. 30, although all the Oriental Interpreters, as those who consistently make mention of Barachiah here, dissent, and perhaps no Greek Codex favors this suspicion; indeed, which can be borne least of all, he thinks that the Evangelist himself by a slip μνημονιχω did not distinguish Zechariah the Son of Barachiah, (whose Prophecy exists in the book of the XII Minor Prophets) from Zechariah the Son of Jehoiada, who was killed between the temple and the altar. How, (continues Cappellus, heaping error upon error) by a similar slip μνημονιχω Stephen seems not to have distinguished, but to have confounded into one, two histories. Acts 7, 16. But this is a violent reconciliation, if I may say anything more serious. The opinion of Chrysostom is safer, concerning which see further in B. Par.)* Chrysostom answers, that Barachiah was binominal, and the same man was also called Jehoiada. Those who think that the Lord is speaking here of Zechariah, the father of John, their chief reason is that they think Christ embraced all the Prophets killed by the Jews, naming Abel as the first of all, and Zechariah as the last of all, which the word εως, suggests, which Baronius urges in Ann. 1. n. 53. But the word εως defines time -ertum in such a way that it does not exclude the later, Matt. 1, 25. if we accept it in this way in this place, there will be no need for the help of the apocrypha. *(Josephus also, book 5 of the Jewish War, ch. 1, makes mention of a certain Zechariah, son of Baruch, killed by the Jews in the middle of the temple, -ed he was killed finally 40 years after the Lord's resurrection, but Christ speaks of such a Zechariah, not who was yet to be killed by the Jews, but whom the Jews had killed long ago. Isaiah also, ch. 8, 2, likewise brings forward a certain Zechariah, son of Barachiah. But concerning this one, the Scripture of the O. Test. nu-libi reveals that he was killed. Theophylact and Jerome report that some take this to be about Zechariah, the penultimate of the Prophets.)*

Thus indeed among the ancients, Tertullian in Scorpiacus ch. 8, Chrysostom in the homily on the nativity of John the Baptist, and the author of the Ordinary Gloss thought so, whom among our own people the Blessed Doctors follow: Brentius in the book on the office of a Prince, vol. 8 of Works, f. 184; Balduinus on Zechariah, p. 124, 125; Aegydius Hunnius on this passage; from the Papists, Ribera, Sanctius on Zechariah ch. 1, and also in ch. 12 of the 4th book of Kings, p. 1492, where for the same he alleges Vatablus, Arias Montanus, Stunica, and the Gloss; to whom may be added Contzen and Sanchez on this passage; from the Calvinists, Rudolph Gualterus on this passage. But especially Dn. Christianus Wasewitz deduces this opinion at length in Turture Iohannaeo ch. 19, p. 231 seqq. But this opinion is not only destitute of the testimony of Holy Scripture and Ecclesiastical Writers, but Epiphanius on the lives of the Prophets also contradicts it in a certain way. It remains, therefore, that it be accepted concerning that Zechariah of whom we read in 2 Chron. 24, 20, 22, 21. And this opinion was embraced among the ancients by Jerome on this passage, Augustine in book 2 against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets, ch. 5; among the more recent, the Blessed Luther in the Marginal Schol., Zehnerus in notes to Epiphanius, p. 114 seqq., D. Quistorp on this passage, Glassius in Sacred Philology book 1, p. 153, D. Waltherus H. B. p. 790, 791, B. Par. in the Harmony of the Gospels ch. 158, p. 613, D. Friedl. Observations on the H. E. p. 70 and 212, D. Muellerus in Judaism p. 1339, D. Tarnovius on Zechariah p. 3, Calixtus in the Harmony of the Gospels p. 205, Lossius on this passage, Osiander on the 4th book of Kings ch. 12, Dietr. in the Analysis of the Festival Gospels p. 205. Just as also among the Papists, Alph. Salmeron vol. 4, p. 525, Cornel. Iansenius in the Harmony p. 477, Sebast. Barrad. vol. 3, book 8, ch. 28, p. 546, Ioh. Maldonatus and Corn. à Lapide on this passage, Lorinus on ch. 7 of Acts, p. 333, Adrichomius in the Theater of the Holy Land; among the Calvinists, I. Calvin himself in the Harmony of the Gospels p. 350, Ravanellus part 2 of the Sacred Bible p. 894, Lud. de Dieu in the Commentary on this passage. Compare also Hugo Grotius on this passage. Who also render this very thing excellently proven, and at the same time respond quite at length to those things which seem to stand against it. The Savior makes mention of this Zechariah for this reason, because he was the last one whom the Scripture of the O. T. records as having been killed. It is added that he himself demanded the vengeance of his blood, 2. Par. 24, 22. just as it is recorded concerning the blood of Abel, that it cried out to God, Gen. 4, 10.

Whom you killed. And yet the Jews, with whom Christ speaks here, had not killed Zechariah the son of Berechiah, concerning whom 2 Chron. 24, 22. Resp. Interpreters note that that slaughter is attributed to the Jews then present, because it was the same people throughout many centuries. And they advise that a similar manner of speaking occurs in Matt. 10, 3. John 6, 32. c. 7, 19. 22. Acts 7, 38. )*

Latin:

*(v. 35. Ut veniat super vos &c. Atqui filius non debet portare iniquitatem patris,Ezech. 18, 20.nec ultratertiam ac quartam generationem Deus visit are vult parentum peccata in filiis,Exod. 20, 5. Resp. Dicta Ezech. 18, 20. ac Exod. 20, 5. intelligenda sunt cum ωροσθήχη, si ipsi resipiscant, nec parentum vestigiis insistant. Aliter verò sese res habet, quando hi eandam parentum crudelitatem imitantur, ac peccatorum mensuram implent. Id quod Iudaei, de quibus Christo hîc sermo est, fecerunt. Unde Theoph. in h. l. Super Iudaeos, scribit, qui tunc erant, dicit, veniet omnis sanguis iniustè effusus: plus enim punientur, quàm patres sui. Nam neq post tanta exempla emendati fuerunt. Sicut enim & Lamech post Cain plus punitus fuit, quamvis non intermisset fratrem, eo quòd non fuisset ad exemplum Cain emendatus. Conf. Gen. 15 16.1. Reg. 15, 16.Deut 5, 9.)*

*( Omnis sanguis i. e. vindicta sanguinis iusti. Vid. Matth. 27, 25. it. Lev. 20, 9.13.1. Reg. 2, 32.Ps. 9. 12. Non igitur impunè mundus Christi ministros persequitur. Vid. 2. Par. 24, 22. seqq. Ps. 9, 14.Apoc. 6, 10. Conf. etiam Apoc. 17, 6. cum Apoc 18, 5. 6.)*

*( A sangvine Abelis (Q Quomodo Abelis caedes Iudaeis imputetur, cùm tamen non descendant à Caino? Resp. Licet non sint Caini, (qui tanquam omnium homicidarum parens in Sc. S. vid. 1. Ioh. 3, 12. Iudae v. 11 proponitur) fi-ii generatione, sunt tamen imitatione. Fuit Cain Iudaeorum parens si non sanguine & gente, tamen malitia & mente; si non naturaliter, tamen moraliter, h. e malo exemplo, interficiendo nempe iustum Abelem. Ita similiter imputabitur à DEO meretrici Babylonicae, quae ebria de sanguine sanctorum, Apoc. 17, 6. omnis sangvis iustus martyrum, sive veritatis Evangelicae Confessorum, effusus per tyrannos Ethnicos ab ipsis usq; Apostolorum temporibus.)*

*( έως. Quaeritur, cur Christus dicat, futurum esse, ut veniat super Iudaeos omnis sangvis innocenter effusus, à sang. Abelis usque ad sanguinem Zachariae, Barachiae F., cùm tamen hic Zacharias non fuerit ultimus, qui innocens à Iudaeis interfectus? Resp. Notandum quòd part. έως ita tempus certum definiat, ut non excludat posterius illo, uti alibi prolixè ostensum Vid. suprà Anal. ad c. 5, 26. p. 303. 304.)*

Usq ad sangvinem Zachariae &c. Quis ille Zacharias, Barachiae filius? Quidam Fabulam adducunt ex apocryphis libris, fuisse in templo certum locum designatum, ubi inter sacra peragenda consisterent virgines, in eo dum staret mater Iesu, quam constabat iam peperisse, nec vulgus intelligeret, divinitus eam concepisse, idque populus indignè ferret, & tamen à Zacharia, patre Iohannis Baptistae defenderetur, per tumultum interfectum fuisse, inter aedem posteriorem & altare. Ita Origenes tract. 26. in Matth. Basilius homil. Nativ. Christi, Theophylactus & Euthymius in h. l. *(Epiphanius de vit. Prophet. p. 134.)* Procul verò ambiguo seduxit eos traditio illa apocrypha, prout satis clarè innuit S. Hieronymus, commemorans, quosdam referre ad Zachariam, Ioh. Bapt. patrem, idque ex apocryphis somniis approbare, quòd propterea occisus sit, quia Salvatoris praedicaverit adventum. Sed notanter addit: Hoc quia de Scripturis non habet autoritatem, eadem facilitate cōtemnitur, quâ probatur. Alii alias afferunt causas, quanquam ipsi perquam haesitent. *(Nihilo tamen minùs amplectuntur sententiam hanc Pontificii communiter. Videantur Baronius t. 1. Annal. n. 53. Toletus in c. 11. Lucae, Annot. 10. Christoph. à Castro in Zachar. Franciscus Lucas Brugensis in h. l. Marchantius Hort. Past. tr. 4. p. 538. cum quibus etiam faciunt Matth. Flacius Clav. Sc. Sacrae tit. Templum, Georg. Maior t. 3. p. 669. Hadrianus Iunius in Matth. p. 193. Cocceius in Zachar. p. 468. qui eandem & Constantino L Empereur placuisse testatur. Aliam tamen sententiam laudato L Emper. tribuit Lud. de Dieu, Comment. in h. l. Iesuita quoq; Maldonatus traditioni illi, cui sententia haec innititur, parum fidei tribuit: sed expressè fatetur, traditionem eam ex bonis libris non probari, & tale quid de Gnosticis proferre Epiphanium in eorum haeresi, hodieque legi in nescio quo (ut vocetur) Protevangelio. Sebastianus Barradius, eiusdem societatis homo, itidem traditionem illam refutat t. 3. Harm. Evang. l. 1. c. 28.)* Theophylactus memorat, quosdam referre ad illum Zachariam, qui inter duodecim Prophetas habetur, filius Barachiae, Zach. 1, 1. At de Propheta Zacharia nuspiam legitur, quòd occisus sit inter templum & altare. Ideò rectiùs de Zacharia Ioiadae filio accipitur, quem occidit Rex Ioas inter aram & templum, Paral. 24, 21. Quod autem patris nomen reclamat, id solvunt h. m. quòd Hieronymus testetur, in Evangelio Nazaraeorum Zachariam non Barachiae dici filium, sed Ioiadae, innuens, in Codd. nostris errore librariorum, pro Ioiada scriptum Barachiam. *(Idem hoc, licet omnes Interpp. Orientales, ut qui constanter hîc Barachiae mentionem faciunt, dissentiant, nec ullus fortè Codex Graecus suspicioni huic faveat, amplectitur Ludov. Cappellus in Spic. p. 30. imò, quod tamen ferri minimè potest, existimat, ipsum Evangelistam sphalmateμνημονιχωnon distinxisse Zachariam Filium Barachiae, (cuius Prophetia extat in libro XII. Proph. Minorum) à Zacharia Filio Ioiadae, qui interfectus fuit inter templum & altare. Quomodo, (pergit Cappellus, errorem errore cumulans,) simili sphalmateμνημονιχωvidetur StephanusAct. 7, 16.non distinxisse, sed confudisse in unum, duas historias. Ast violenta, ne quid gravius dicam, conciliatio haec est. Tutior Chrysostomi sententia est, de qua porrò B. Par.)* Chrysostomus respondet, Barachiam fuisse binominem, eundemq dictum etiam Ioiadam. Qui putant, Dominum de Zachariâ, patre Iohannis hîc loqui, eorum praecipua ratio est, quòd existimant, Christum omnes à Iudaeis occisos Prophetas fuisse complexum, nominatis omnium primo Abele, & omnium ultimo Zachariâ, quod suadet vox εως, quam urget Baronius Ann. 1. n. 53. At vox εως ita tempus -ertum definit, ut posterius non excludat, Matt. 1, 25. si hoc loco sic accipiamus, subsidio apocryphorum non erit opus. *(Iosephus quoque lib. 5. de B. I. c. 1. cuiusdam Zachariae Baruchi F. à Iudaeis in medio templo interfecti, mentionem facit, -ed hic 40. demum annis post Domini resurrectionem occifus fuit, Christus verò loquitur de tali Zachariâ, non qui adhuc à Iudaeis occidendus erat, sed quem pridem Iudaei occiderant. Esaias quoque c. 8, 2. itidem Zachariam quendam producit Barachiae filium. Sed de hoc pariter V. Test. Scriptura nu-libi prodit, quòd occisus fuerit. De Zachariâ, penultimo Prophe-arum quosdam accipere Theophylactus ac Hieronymus produnt.

Ita verò è veteribus senserunt Tertullianus in Scorpiaco c. 8. Chrysost. hom. de nativ. Ioh. Bapt. autor Glossae Ordinariae, quos è nostratibus sequuntur BB. Dd. Brentius lib. de off. Principis. t. 8. Op. f. 184. Balduinus in Zach. p. 124. 125. Aegydius Hunnius in h. l. ex Pontificiis Ribera, Sanctius in Zach. c. 1. nec non in c. 12. lib. 4. Reg. p. 1492. ubi pro eadem allegat Vatablum, Ariam Montanum, Stunicam & Glossam. quibus addantur Contzen ac Sanchez in h. l. ex Calvinianis Rudolph. Gualterus in h. l. Cumprimis verò prolixè sententiam hanc deducit Dn. Christianus Wasewitz in Turture Iohannaeo c. 19. p. 231. seqq. Ast haesententia non solùm destituitur testimonio Sc. S. ac Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum, sed eidem quodammodo etiam contradicit Epiphanius de vit. Proph. Restat proinde, ut de illo Zacharia accipiatur, quo de 2. Paral. 24, 20. 22. 21. legimus. Atque hanc sententiam amplexi è veteribus sunt Hier. in h. l. August. l. 2. cont. Advers. Leg. & Proph. c. 5 è recentioribus Bb. Lutherus in Schol. Marg. Zehnerus in not. ad Epiph. p. 114. seqq. D. Quistorp. in h. l. Glassius Philol. S. l. 1. p. 153. D. Waltherus H. B. p. 790. 791. B. Par. Harm. Evang. c. 158. p. 613. D. Friedl. Obs. in H. E p. 70. & 212. D. Muellerus in Iudaismo p. 1339. D. Tarnovius in Zach. pag. 3. Calixtus Concord. Ev. p. 205. Lossius in h. l. Osiander in 4. lib. Reg. c. 12. Dietr. Analysi Evang. Fest. p. 205. Quemadmodum etiam è Pontificiis ita statuunt Alph. Salmeron t. 4. p. 525. Cornel. Iansenius Concord. p. 477. Sebast. Barrad. t 3. l. 8. c. 28. p. 546. Ioh. Maldonatus ac Corn. à Lapide in h. l. Lorinus in c. 7. Actor. p. 333. Adrichomius Theatr. terr. Sanctae. è Calvinianis I. Calvinus ipse Harm. Evang. p. 350. Ravanellus part. 2. Bibl. Sacrae p. 894. Lud. de Dieu Comm. in h. l. Conf. etiam Hugo Grotius in h. l. Qui hanc ipsam etiam egregiè probatam reddunt, simulque ad ea, quae illi obstare videntur, satis prolixè respondent. Facit autem propterea Zachariae huius Salvator mentionem, quia ultimus is fuit, quem Sc. S. V. T. interfectum memorat. Accedit, quòd idem ille vindictam sangvinis sui requisiverit, 2. Par. 24, 22. ceu de Abelis sangvine memoratur, quòd ad Deum clamarit, Gen. 4, 10.)*

*( Quem occidistis. Atqui Iudaei, cum quibus Christus hîc loquitur, non occiderant Zachariam Barachiae filium, de quo 2. Par. 24, 22. Resp. Notant Interpp. propterea Iudaeis praesentibus caedem illam tribui, quia idem populus fuerit per multa secula. Simileque loquendi genus occurere monent Matth. 10, 3.Ioh. 6, 32.c. 7, 19.22.Act. 7, 38.)*

## 23:36
v. 36. Jerusalem, Jerusalem. He repeats the name Jerusalem 1. by reason of love. For the Lord loves the gates of Zion. 2. by reason of a double persecution, because they persecuted His doctrine both corporally and spiritually. 3. on account of unworthiness. Jerusalem is called "peaceful." But they killed the Prince of peace. *(4. on account of the severity of divine righteous judgment, and the gravity of the punishments that followed, )* *(

You stone. 2 Chron. 24, 21. Acts 7, 59. * *( αὐτὴν

*( άυτΤιύ Theodoret thinks Τό αυΤήν is placed here for σεαυΤήν. But Lud. de Dieu abandons this opinion in his Appendix to Matthew, p. 546, and notes that it is a pure and simple Hebraism, which the Syrian and also the Arab, retaining άυτήν translated by the third person, following the idiom of their own languages. Indeed, Camerarius also noted that in his old codex it is read άυτήν, and that it is a harsh enallage of person: But Lud. de Dieu denies this in the place cited, if regard is had to the Oriental languages. The same man adds: nor did the Ethiopic translator hesitate to render it: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the Prophets, and stones the Apostles, who are sent to her. Where it is to be noted that the Ethiopic Interpreter has -- and -- which are composed from a suffix, which, since it changes the last vowel of the verb on account of the rejected -- into the vowel o or that of the seventh class, it happens that it cannot easily be known whether the verb is of the second or indeed of the third person. Whence also the Interpreter who adorned the Latin version in the English Bibles, Hiobus Loftusius, rendered it in the second person you kill, and you stone. Against this, Lud. de Dieu is in the third person. And if I am not mistaken, more correctly, since the affixes of the third person after a letter of the first or sixth order, such as the third person has, but not the second, -- reject, with their vowel transferred to the preceding one, as Mr. D. Ludolf correctly noted in his Ethiopic Grammar, p. 58, so that thus it ought to be rendered word for word from the verb : And he said: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the Prophets, and which will stone the Apostles, who are sent to it. The Persian, however, seems to have read σεαυτήν, or σε, (just as that most ancient Cambridge codex and the second of Stephanus also have, as well as our blessed Luther), for he translates, who are sent to you.

*( σθπισυναγαγεΐν Conf. Heb. 10, 25.Jas. 2, 2. It is evident from this how ineptly Bellarmine writes in book 3, On the Church Militant, chapter 1, that the people of the New Testament are never called a synagogue, but always a church. He adds: For to be gathered is common to man with the beasts, etc. Furthermore, it is to be noted that the Fathers of the Council of Trent themselves call their assembly a congregation, Session 9 and 10.)*

As a hen etc. The duties of a hen are 1. to incubate eggs, and to hatch the chicks. 2. to warm the hatched ones with vital heat. 3. to feed and rule the same. 4. to call those wandering about kindly to herself. 5. to defend the unfledged against tyrannical birds. The Son of GOD performs all these duties for us. Beautifully Jerome: He who had named Herod, who was lying in wait for his life, a fox, compares himself to a hen. A hen warms and hatches foreign eggs placed under her: this can be applied to the calling of the Gentiles. A hen confers life upon the chicks: thus from Christ we have corporal, spiritual, and eternal life. A hen feeds the chicks, thus Christ brought to us from the granary of the heavenly Father the seed of the heavenly word, by which he nourishes us to eternal life. A hen gathers the chicks, thus we were dispersed by the infernal kite, but Christ gathers us by his word. A hen warms the chicks, covers them with her wings, fights for them: thus Christ defends us, fights for us, etc. A hen does not suffer herself to be separated from the chicks: thus Christ is with us even to the consummation of the age. A hen goes before the chicks, sweetly refreshes them: thus Christ precedes us by word and life, he provides a sweet shade, Isa. 4. Conf. c. 31, 5. 4 Esdr. c. 1, 30. Augustine in Ps. 90. No bird is so weakened with its chicks as a hen. For we recognize the hen in the weakness of her voice and in the relaxation of her feathers, she is totally changed by the affection for her chicks. Because they are weak, she makes herself weak etc. Because therefore we also were weak, the wisdom of the Lord made itself weak, because the word was made flesh, and

dwelt in us, that we may hope under his wings. *(Mr. Binchius in his Mellificium and Corn. à Lapide in this place bring forward several more members of the comparison between Christ and the Hen, who can be consulted.)*

*( And you would not. Conf. Heb. 10, 26. Christ therefore willed to gather even those who do not wish to come. And so it is not His will that any should be deprived of the salutary means of obtaining eternal salvation by some absolute decree of GOD, but the primary cause of perdition is in man himself. To this also pertain the sayings Is. 65, 2. and 12. Prov. 1, 24.Jer. 7, 13.Ezek. 18, 23.32.c. 33, 11.c. 24, 13. Hosea 13, 19. Matt. 11, 28.c. 28, 19.Luke 7, 30.c. 14, 24.John 3, 19.36.Acts 7, 51.c. 13, 44.46.Rom. 11, 20.Col. 1, 28.2 Pet. 3, 9. The Emdani at the Synod of Dordrecht, part 1, q. 838, object that Christ speaks at least of the will of sign, not of good pleasure. But since that will of sign, which is posited as contrary to the will of good pleasure, makes God a hypocrite, that distinction is deservedly rejected. Others, in whose number is Steinius, part 3, fratern. page 116, also Wendel, Exerc. 74, § 8, think they can sufficiently refute the force of our argument if they say that Christ here speaks at least of external calling, but by no means of internal. But the contrary is evident from this, because Christ speaks of such a gathering and calling through which they could have been saved, if they had wished. Conf. John 5, 40. Furthermore, He denounces grave punishments because they did not wish to come. See more in the Deduct. Dnn. Theol. Marpp. p. 266. What of the fact that He shows the example of the hen herself, who by no means feignedly calls together her chicks, that the will of Christ was serious? But let someone say with Wendel, Exerc. 75, § 2: If Christ willed seriously, and indeed by internal calling, it follows that they were converted, or that Christ is not omnipotent, so that He could have converted them. Resp. Distinguish between the absolute will of Christ, of which there is speech in Isaiah 46, 10.Rom. 9, 19.Ps. 115, 3. and the conditional. But John Pisator in notes to the treatise of Vorstius on God, note 4, to p. 58, and Macovius, Disp. 3, object that the conditional will of GOD is nothing, since it makes God mutable. Resp. by denying the consequence; for change does not occur in God, but in men. That a conditional will of GOD is given is evident not only from this place, but also from Jer. 18, 7. seqq. Nor is inferred also through that conditional will of GOD any change or impotence in Him. For then change or impotence would be posited in God if God had absolutely willed the salvation of all men: because therefore He did not will that except under certain conditions and means, His will is by no means changed, nor can He Himself be argued of any impotence, however it may be posited that not all are actually saved; likewise, that He wills the eternal damnation of those who reject and despise the means of salvation, namely by a just judgment that contempt Luc. 7, 30. and resistance, Act. 7, 51. by vindicating. Compare more things making for this in B. Par. Exeg. t. 1. LL tr. de nat. DEI §. 271. also Comm. in Post. Ep. Petri p. 392. Ioh. Camero in Myroth. Ev. p. 110. excepts, that Christ speaks here not insofar as He is God and omnipotent Mediator, but insofar as He was man, Minister, Pastor, Doctor of the Church, teaching externally by the word, and that He said these things with such an affection as was in Him when He wept for Lazarus, namely with a human affection. But just as this is an old song of the Calvinists, as is evident from Beza part. 2. Resp. ad Colloq. Mompelg. p. 171. Ioh. Piscator on this place and in Notes to the Amica Collat. of Vorstius sect. 116. p. 200. and sect. 126. p. 219. also in Resp. ad amicam eiusdem Duplicationem part. 1. p. 67. 257. and elsewhere, also Ioh. Georg. Grossius in Theatr. Bibl. p. 1031. 1032. so long ago the Blessed D. Fewrbornius solidly showed its vanity in Syntag. 1. Sacr. Disquis. Dissert. 4. p. 118. seqq. For that Christ speaks here as true God, i.e., insofar as He is omnipotent God, is proved 1. from the consideration of the antecedents. We argue thus: In the same way Christ speaks here, as He spoke a little before, v. 34. But there He spoke of Himself insofar as He is true God. For the mission of the Prophets is an action of GOD Himself. Therefore. 2. from the collation of parallel places. Luc. 11, 49. The mission of the Prophets is attributed to the WISDOM of GOD, which name is attributed to the Savior according to the divine nature and already in the O. T., Prov. 8, 22. 23. 24. 3. from the usurpation of the past tense. I have willed, says Christ. 4. from the addition of the particle how often. For it is insinuated by that, that not once but more often and as if through continuous degrees of succession by sending other and other Prophets He Himself willed to gather the Jews. Compare 2. Par. 36, 14. 15. 16. Prov 1, 24.

Es. c. 50, 2. c. 65, 16. c. 66, 4. Ierem. 13. 27. c. 11, 8. c. 35, 15. c. 44, 4. 5. 5. from the conformation of the analogy of faith. For that God wills the salvation of all men, and therefore also of those who perish, the oracles of H. S. clearly testify. Compare Ezech. 18, 32. 33. c. 33, 11. Iohan. 3, 16. Rom. 11, 32. 6. from the reason of the Prophetic office. For the prophetic office no less belongs to Christ according to both natures than the Sacerdotal and mediatorial. For it is likewise ἀποτέλεσμα θεανδρικὸν to manifest to us the divine will concerning our salvation. Compare Ioh. 1, 17. 18. Whence also Wendelinus System. Mai. p. 652. rightly teaches, that Christ in the N. T. performed the Prophetic office according to both natures, by teaching the Jews with an external voice and internal illumination. Now if Christ taught the Jews according to both natures, it follows that He also called the Jews according to both natures, and therefore spoke not as a mere man, but also as God and Mediator omnipotent. Those things of Wendelinus agree with Piscator vol. 1. Disp. 11. thes. 2. 3. 13. 14. 15. and likewise with Sohnius t. 2. art. p. 224. 7. from the removal of the contrariety between the divine and human will in Christ. For although it is easily granted, nay even against the Monothelites it is asserted, that there is a diversity of the divine and human will, which is evident from Matth. 26, 39. Yet it is denied that there is contrariety. Such, however, must be posited, if it is said that Christ as man seriously willed to gather even those who did not want to come, but as God did not seriously will that same thing. But that the human will of Christ was not contrary to the divine, is evident both from the l. c. and from Ioh. 7, 16. 17. 28. c. 8, 28. c. 12, 49. & seqq 8. from the consequence of absurdity. For if it is posited that Christ as man absolutely willed certain things, namely the gathering and salvation of those who nevertheless do not want to be gathered, which nevertheless as God He does not will, it follows that Christ as man willed something deformed to the divine will, and therefore sinned. Which is absurd, and contrary to H. Sc. See Ioh. 8, 46. Nor is there reason for Piscator to retort, that the human will of Christ was contrary to the divine will, not ethically or morally, (because He never willed with a human will what He knew with a human mind that God did not will) but Logically. For to Christ even according to the human nature

divine omniscience was communicated, so that in no way can ignorance of the divine will be attributed to him. And even if he had sinned most of all out of ignorance of the divine will, he would still have sinned. Which is absurdly posited. Furthermore, if Christ at least as man willed the Jews to be gathered, which will of his was contrary to the divine secret will of his good pleasure, it follows that the Jews, not willing to be gathered, did not sin, nor maliciously to have been unwilling, as Paraeus speaks of these things in L. A. p. 132. and so that they had not even deserved punishments. The reason is, because sin is an aberration from the divine law, the rule of the divine will, as also of the secret will and of good pleasure. But if it was not the divine will that they should be gathered, they did not sin by being unwilling to be gathered. And yet by this very thing they sinned, and also deserved temporal and eternal punishment for those sins, here and Luke 19:41c. 21:20. Therefore. As regards the example brought forward by Cameron, that he wept for Lazarus, nothing else is proven from it than that there was a human affection of compassion in Christ: But that human affections contrary to the divine will were in him, such as that would have been, if he had willed the gathering of the Jews, which however God had not willed, can in no way be proven from it. Finally, our opinion is proven by the confession of the Adversaries themselves. Calvin himself in book 3 of the Institutes, ch. 24, § 17, explicitly writes: I confess that Christ is not only speaking in the person of a man, but is upbraiding them, because in all ages they had rejected his grace. William Whitaker, an English theologian, in vol. 2, p. 379, explicitly writes, that Jerusalem was unwilling to be gathered under the wings of Christ: just as also they (the Jews) did not believe the oracles of the Prophets, and perpetually rejected the grace and mercy offered to them. Compare entirely B. D. Fewrb. in the cited place. B. D. Meisner Ἀνθρωπολ.. S. Disp. 20. John Malderus, Bishop of Antwerp, formerly Professor of Theology at Louvain, also excellently agrees with the Orthodox in Anti Synod. p. 135 and 136. Where he furthermore rightly notes, that Scripture is full of testimonies that there is a certain will of GOD which is not always fulfilled, not because God cannot fulfill it, but because he wills that men also should will that same thing which he himself wills. When therefore men are unwilling, that is, when they perversely reject the means of salvation, then the will of GOD concerning their salvation is not fulfilled either, because indeed they themselves do not will what God wills. But just as this divine oracle is rightly opposed to the Calvinists, the assertors of particular grace: so the Papists (See Bell. book 5 de G. & L. A. ch. 20, Costerus Enchir. Controv. p. 192), Synergists, and other heretics ineptly [use it] from this, The powers of free will in unregenerate man they attempt to prove. For it does not follow: Man can resist the Holy Spirit, and hinder conversion, not come to Christ. Therefore also of himself he can assent to GOD, cooperate with divine grace, and salutarily come to Christ. This is indeed a corpse of a consequence, and the most serious Theologian B. D. Mylius judges rightly in A. C. part. 1. p. 228, that there is hardly an infant who does not understand how invalid this consequence is. For the sacred letters teach the contrary explicitly. See Rom. 8, 7.Act. 26, 18.Eph. 4, 18.c. 5, 8.1. Cor. 2, 14.2. Cor. 3. 5. And the reason for the diversity is manifest, because the nilling is from the corrupt flesh, but the willing is excited by GOD alone. The opinions of the Fathers also testify to the contrary. Known is that saying of the most august Bishop of Hippo in Soliloq. c. 15. That I fell, was from me, that I rose, was from thee. Beautifully also Ambrose l. 2. de vocat. gent. c. 9. Although it is in man to nill the good, yet unless it is given he does not have to will the good. Nature contracted the former after the fault, nature receives the latter through grace. Furthermore it does not follow, man has liberty or external willing, and can conduct himself rightly in pedagogical actions. Therefore he also has internal liberty, or spiritual willing, of salutarily converting himself to God. For this is ascribed entirely to GOD. See Phil. 2, 13. Then distinguish between natural repugnance, & affected or morose. Concerning which matter they treat at greater length in Disp. 22. q. 4. §. 35. also Disp. 23. §. 18. 19. B. D. Lobechius Disp. 20. in A. C. §. 37. 39. B. Par. Disp. Isag. L. de L. A. c. 3. §. 3. Confess. Cathol. art 22. c. 4. p. 568. 566. B. D. Hutter. in Expl. F. C. p. 211. 215. also in LL. Mai. p. 285. seqq. B. D. H-lsem. in A. C. p. 131. B. D. Hunnius in h. l.

Behold your house. By house he understands the temple & the polity of the Jews. *(Compare similar threats Es. 1, 7.c. 42, 15.24.Ier. 8, 13. 14. add. Isid. Pelusiota lib. 4 ep. 74. also Const.

L'Emper. ad Itin. Beniam. p. 171. We learn from this threat of Christ, that God is accustomed to predict future calamities, so that the impious may be inexcusable, but the pious may be able to escape them. Conf. Amos 3, 7.Gen. 18, 19. Jonah 1, 2. &c.)*

It shall be left desolate. i. e. it shall be deserted by me, and delivered to your Roman enemies, who shall lay it waste and devastate it. *(Cf. Jer. 12, 7.c. 22, 5. Our people rightly establish that this threat of the Savior ought to be extended so far that the meaning is, behold your polity and temple shall remain overturned and desolate, until the end of the world. So that by this oracle the opinion of those is overturned, both those who establish that the Jews are to be led back into the land of Canaan before the final Judgment, and those who think that the Antichrist will sit in the Jerusalem temple, and that Christians will dwell securely in the holy land. Blessed Pareus deals with this error in his Book on the Final Judgment, §. 109. God indeed deferred for 40 years the punishment which he had threatened to the Jews, so that he might grant them a time of repentance. And this is by the customary manner, concerning which Isa. 5, 2.Job 24, 23.Luke 13, 7.Rev. 2, 21. Origen in Matthew, tract. 26, c. 23, writes: Not immediately, he writes, as soon as a sin has been committed, is the generation of sinners punished, but when the subsequent generation, being bound to amend in itself the sin of its fathers, has still added worse things to the sins of its fathers; and thus many generations have sinned in some nation or in a city, the nation is punished or the city is destroyed. To which also pertains that saying of a pagan man, (Valerius Maximus, book 1, Memorable Deeds, c. 1, for instance) uttered with an almost Christian mouth: divine wrath proceeds with a slow step to its vengeance, it compensates for the slowness of the punishment with its severity. Let the very beautiful epistle of Isidore of Pelusium be compared, which is 380, book 1. To this also looks the saying of the Apostle Rom. 2, 4. 5. 6. We learn furthermore from the example of the Jews, that the sins of a people, and especially the contempt of the divine word and the persecution of the sincere heralds of heavenly truth, bring devastation and destruction to kingdoms and cities. Cf. Gen. 19, 13.24.2 Kings 17, v. 24. & 25.Isa. 45.Jer. 50. 51. The world indeed, with Caiaphas and the Pharisees, John 11, 47. ff., persuades itself otherwise: but it is vehemently deceived.)*

Latin:

v. 36. Ierusalem, Ierusalem. Ingeminat nomen Ierusalem 1. ratione dilectionis. Dominus enim diligit portas Sion. 2. ratione duplicis persecutionis, quia corporaliter & spiritaliter ipsius doctrinam persecuti sunt. 3. propter indignitatem. Ierusalem dicitur pacifica. At ipsi occiderunt Principem pacis. *(4. propter iusti iudicii divini severitatem, ac poenarum insecutarum gravitatem,)*

*( Lapidas. 2. Paral. 24, 21. Actor. 7, 59.*

*( άυτΤιύ Theodor. censet, Τό αυΤήν positum hîc esse pro σεαυΤήν. Verùm deserit opinionem hanc Lud. de Dieu Append. ad Matth. p 546. notatque, esse purum putum Ebraismum, quem Syrus quoq atq Arabs retinentesάυτήνverter-nt per tertiam personam, sequentes linguarum suarum idiotismum. Sanè & Camerarius notavit. in veteri fuo codice legi άυτήν,eamq duram esse personae enallagen: At negat hoc Lud. de Dieu l. c. si respectus habeatur ad Orientales Linguas. Addit idem: nec dubitavit Aethi-picus vertere: O Ierusalem, Ierusalem, quae occidit Prophetas, & lapidat Apostolos, qui missi sunt ad eam. Ubi notandum, quòd Aethiops Interpres habeat -- & -- quae composita sunt ex suffixo, quod cùm ultimam verbi vocal-m propter abiectum -- in vocal-m o sive classis septimae mutet, fit ut non facilè cognosei possit, num verbum sit secundae, an verò tertiae personae. Unde etiam Interpres, qui in Bibliis Anglicanis Latinam versionem adornavit Hiobus Loftusius, reddidit in secunda persona occidis, & lapidas. Contrà Lud. de Dieu in tertia personâ. & ni fallor, rectiùs, siquidem affixa tertiae personae post litteram primi vel sexti ordinis, qualem habet persona tertia, non verò secunda, -- abiiciant, vocali sua in praecedentem translatâ, uti rectè notavit Dn, D. Ludolfus Gramm. Aethiop. p. 58. ut ita de verbo ad verbum reddi debeat: & dixit: Ierusalem, Ierusalem quae occidet eos Prophetas, & quae lapidabit eos Apostolos, qui mis-su-t ad eam. Persa tamen legisse videtur σεαυτήν, vel σε, (sicut etiam habet vetustissimus ille codex Cantabrigiensis ac secun dus Stephani, tum quoque B. noster Lutherus) vertit enim, qui ad te mittuntur.)*

*( σθπισυναγαγεΐν Conf. Ebr. 10, 25.Iac. 2, 2. Patet hinc, quàm ineptè scribat Bell. l. 3. de Eccl. milit. c. 1. Populum N. Test. nusquam dici, synagogam, sed semper Ecclesiam. Addit: Congregari enim commune est homini cum bestiis &c. Praeterea notandum, quòd Patres Concilii Tridentini ipsimet conventum suum vo-ent congregationem Sess. 9. & 10.)*

Sicut gallina &c. Gallinae officia sunt 1. incubare ovis, & exclud-re pullos. 2. exclusos fovere vitali calore. 3. pascere & regere eosdem. 4 palantes comiter ad se vocare. 5. defendere implumes adversùs tyrannicas aves. Haec officia omnia praestat nobis DEI Filius. Pulcrè Hieronymus: Qui Herodem vitae suae insidiantem nominaverat vulpem, se ipsum gallinae comparat. Gallina fovet & exludit ova aliena sibi supposita: hoc applicari potest ad vocationem gentium. Gallina confert pullis vitam: sic à Christo habemus vitam corporalem, spiritualem & aeternam. Gallina cibat pullos, sic Christus ex granario Patris coelestis attulit nobis semen verbi coelestis, quo nos alit ad vitam aeternam. Gallina congregat pullos, sic ab infernali milvio dispersi eramus, sed Christus nos congregat suo verbo. Gallina fovet pullos, alis suis eos tegit, pro illis pugnat: sic Christus nos defendit, pro nobis pugnat &c. Gallina non patitur se à pullis seiungi: sic Christus nobiscum est usq; ad consummationem seculi. Gallina praecedit pullos, suaviter eos recreat: sic Christus verbo & vita nos antecedit, praestat suave umbraculum, Es. 4. Conf. c. 31, 5. 4. Esdr. c. 1, 30. August. in Ps. 90.Nulla sic avis infirmatur cum pullis suis, quomodo gallina. Gallinam enim cognoscimus in infirmitate vocis & in relaxatione plumarum, tota mutatur affectu pullorum. Quia illi infirmi sunt, infirmam se facit &c. Quia ergo & nos infirmi eramus, infirmam se fecit sapientia Domini, quia verbum caro factum est, &

habitavit in nobis, ut sub alis eius speremus. *(Pluscula comparationis inter Christum & Gallinam membra affert Dn. Binchius in Mellificio, Corn. à Lapide in h. l. qui possunt consuli.)*

*( Et noluisti. Conf. Ebr. 10, 26. Voluit ergo Christus etiam illos congregare, qui venire nolunt. Adeoq; non est eius voluntas, ut ullus ex absoluto aliquo DEI decreto salutaribus consequendae salutis aeternae mediis privetur, sed in ipso homine est prima perditionis causa. Quo etiam faciunt dicta Es. 65. 2. ac 12. Prov. 1, 24.Ierem. 7, 13.Ezech. 18, 23.32.c. 33, 11.c. 24, 13. Hoseae 13, 19. Matth. 11, 28.c. 28, 19.Luc. 7, 30.c. 14, 24.Ioh. 3, 19.36.Act. 7, 51.c. 13, 44.46.Rom. 11, 20.Col. 1, 28.2. Petr. 3, 9. Emdani in Synodo Dordrecht. part. 1. q. 838. excipiunt, quòd Christus loquatur saltem de voluntate signi, non beneplaciti. Verùm cùm voluntas illa signi, quae beneplaciti voluntati contraria statuitur, Deum hypocritam faciat, meritò distinctio illa reiicitur. Alii, in quorum numero Steinius est part. 3. fratern. pag. 116. it. Wendel. Exerc. 74. §. 8. satis vim nostri argumenti elidere se posse censent, si dicant, Christum hîc saltem loqui de vocatione externâ, hautquaquam verò internâ. Verùm contrarium exinde patet, quia Christus loquitur de tali congregatione & vocatione, per quam potuissent salvari, si voluissent. Conf. Ioh. 5, 40. Praeterea graves denunciat poenas, quòd venire noluerint. Vid. plura iu Deduct. Dnn. Theol. Marpp. p. 266. Quid quòd ipsius gallinae, minimè simulanter pullos suos convocantis, exemplum ostendat, quòd seria Christi voluntas fuerit. Sed dicat aliquis cum Wendel. Exerc. 75. §. 2. Si Christus seriò voluit, & quidem vocatione internâ, sequitur, ipsos fuisse conversos, vel Christū non esse omnipotentem, ut ipsos convetere potuerit. Resp. Dist. inter voluntatem Christi absolutam, de quâ sermo est Esai. 46, 10.Rom. 9, 19.Ps. 115, 3. & conditionatam. Instant verò Ioh. Pisator in not. ad tr. Vorstii de Deo not. 4. ad p. 58. ac Macovius Disp. 3. conditionatam DEI voluntatem esse nullam, cùm faciat Deum mutabilem. Resp. negando conseq. neque enim in Deo fit mutatio, sed in hominibus. Quod verò detur conditionata DEI voluntas, non solùm ex h. l. patet, verùm etiam ex Ierem. 18, 7. seqq. Nec infertur quoque per conditionatam illam DEI voluntatem aliqua in ipso mutatiovel impotentia. Tum enim mutatio vel impotentia statueretur in Deo, si Deus absolutè omnium hominum salutem voluisset: quia igitur non nisi sub certis conditionibus ac mediis illud voluit, minimè ipsius volūtas mutatur, vel impotentiae alicuius argui ipse potest, utut statuatur, quòd non omnes actu salventur; item, quòd illorum, qui media salutis reiiciunt ac contemnunt, aeternum velit damnationem, iusto nempe iudicio contemtum istum Luc. 7, 30. ac repugnantiam, Act. 7, 51. vindicando. Conf plura huc facientia apud B. Par. Exeg. t. 1. LL tr. de nat. DEI §. 271. it. Comm. in Post. Ep. Petri p. 392. Ioh. Camero in Myroth. Ev. p. 110. excipit, Christum hîc loqui non quatenus Deus & Mediator omnipotens, sed quatenus erat homo, Minister, Pastor, Doctor Ecclesiae, docens extrinsecus verbo, & eo affectu haec dixisse, qualis in eo fuit, cùm fleret Lazarum, humano nempe affectu. Verùm sicuti vetus est haec Calvinianorum cantilena, ceu patet ex Beza part. 2. Resp. ad Colloq. Mompelg. p. 171. Ioh. Piscatore super h. l. & in Notis ad Amicam Collat. Vorstii sect. 116. p. 200. ac sect. 126. p. 219. it. in Resp. ad amicam eiusdem Duplicationem part. 1. p. 67. 257. & alibi, Ioh. item Georg. Grossio in Theatr. Bibl. p. 1031. 1032. ita pridem illius vanitatem solidè ostendit B. D. Fewrbornius Syntag. 1. Sacr. Disquis. Dissert. 4. p. 118. seqq. Quòd enim ut verus Deus s. quat. Deus omnipotens est, Christus hîc loquatur, probatur 1. ex antecedentium consideratione. Argumentamur ita: Eodem modo hîc Christus loquitur, quomodo loquutus fuit paulò antè, v. 34. At ibi loquutus fuit de se quat. est verus Deus. Missio enim Prophetarum est actio ipsius DEI. E. 2. ex locorum parall. collatione.Luc. 11, 49. Missio Prophetarum tribuitur Sapientiae DEI, quod nomen Salvatori secundùm divinam naturam & in V. iamtum T. tribuitur, Prov. 8, 22. 23. 24. 3. ex praeteriti temporis usurpatione. Volui, inquit Christus. 4. ex particulae quoties adiectione. Infinuatur enim illâ, quòd non semel sed saepiùs ac quasi per continuos successionis gradus alios atq; alios Prophetas mittendo congregare Iudaeos ipse voluerit. Conf. 2. Par. 36, 14. 15. 16.Prov 1, 24.

Es. c. 50, 2.c. 65, 16.c. 66, 4.Ierem. 13. 27.c. 11, 8.c. 35, 15.c. 44, 4.5. 5.ab analogiae fidei conformatione. Quod enim Deus omnium hominum, adeoque & pereuntium salatem velit, clara testantur S-. S. oracula Conf. Ezech. 18, 32. 33.c. 33, 11.Iohan. 3, 16.Rom. 11, 32. 6. ab officii Propheticiratione. Etenim non propheticum minùs officium Christo secūdùm utramq; naturam competit, quàm Sacerdotale ac mediatorium. Itidem enim ἀποτέλεσμα θεανδρικὸν est, divinam de salute nostrâ voluntatem nobis manifestare. Conf. Ioh. 1, 17. 18. Unde etiam rectè Wendelinus System. Mai. p. 652. docet, quòd Christus in N. T. functus fuerit officio Prophetico secundùm utramnaturam, externâ voce & internâ illuminatione Iudaeos docendo. I am si secundùm utramq; naturam Christus Iudaeos docuit, sequitur quòd etiam secundùm utramque naturam Iudaeos ipse vocarit, adeoque loquutus fuerit non ut nudus homo, sed etiam ut Deus & Me-iator omnipotens. Consentiunt verò illa Wendelini cum -iscat. vol. 1. Disp. 11. thes. 2. 3. 13. 14. 15. itemque Sohnio t. 2. art. p. 224. 7. à contrarietatis inter divinam ac humanam volun-atem in Christo remotione. Licet enim facilè concedatur, imò -tiam contra Monotheletas adseratur divinae ac humanae vo-untatis diversitas, quae patet ex Matth. 26, 39. Negatur tamen -dversitas. Talis verò staruenda, si dicatur, Christum ut ho-ninem seriò voluisse etiam illos congregare, qui venire no-erunt, ut Deum verò id ipsum non voluisse seriò. Quòd verò -oluntas Christi humana divinae non fuerit contraria, patet -m exl. c. tum ex Ioh. 7, 16. 17.28.c. 8, 28.c. 12, 49. & seqq 8. ab -bsurdi conseq vutione. Quod si statuatur, Christum ut homi-em absolutè quaedam voluisse, eorum nempe congregationē salutem, qui tamen congregari nolunt, quae tamen ut Deus non velit, sequitur, Christum ut hominem aliquid voluisse voluntati divinae difforme, adeoque peccasse. Quod est absurdum, ac Sc. Sacrae contrarium. Vid. Ioh. 8, 46. Nec est, quòd regerat Piscator, voluntatem Christi humanam voluntati divinae fuisse contrariam, non ethicè seu moraliter, (quia nunquam voluerit voluntate humanâ, quod mente humanâ sciret, Deum non velle) sed Logicè. Etenim Christo etiam secundùm humanam naturam

omniscientia divina fuit communicata, ut adeò minimè ignorantia voluntatis divinae tribui ipsi possit. Et si vel maximè ex ignorantiâ voluntatis divinae ipse peccasset, tamen peccasset. Quod absurdè statuitur. Porrò si Christus saltem ut homo voluit, Iudaeos congregari, quae eius voluntas divinae arcanae voluntati s. bene placiti contraria fuerit, sequitur, Iudaeos congregari nolentes non peccasse, nec malitiosè noluisse, ut loquitur de iis Paraeus de L. A. p. 132. adeo que nec poenas fuisse promeritos. Ratio est, quia peccatum est aberratio à lege divinâ, voluntatis divinae, uti que & arcanae ac beneplaciti, regulâ. Si verò non fuit divina voluntas, ut ipsi congregaretur, non peccarunt, congregari nolentes. Atqui hoc ipso peccarunt, & poenam quoque temporalem & aeternam peccatis illis promeriti sunt, hîc & Luc. 19, 41.c. 21, 20. E. Quod attinet exemplum, à Camerone allatum, quòd Lazarum fleverit, nihil aliud inde evincitur, quàm in Christo commiserationis fuisse affectum humanum: Sed quòd affectus humani, voluntati divinae contrarii in eo fuerint, qualis fuisset ille, si Iudaeorum congregationem voluisset, quam tamen Deus noluisset, minimè inde evinci poterit. Probatur denique 9. sententia nostra ipsorum Adversariorum confessione. Calvinus ipse l. 3. Instit. c. 24. §. 17. disertè scribit: Fateor, Christum non tantùm in personâ hominis loqui, sed exprobrare, quòd seculis omnibus repudiaverint suam gratiam. Guil. Whitakerus, Theologus Anglus t. 2. p. 379. disertè scribit, Hierusalem noluisse sub Christi alas congregari: quemadmodum & Prophetarum oraculis (Iudaei) non crediderint, & oblatam gratiam ac misericordiam perpetuò respuerint, Conf. omninò B. D. Fewrb. l. c. B. D. Meisnerus Ἀνθρωπολ.. S. Disp. 20. Orthodoxis quoq; egregiè adstipulatur Ioh. Malderus Episcopus Antverpiensis, Theologiae quondam Lovanii Profess. in Anti Synod. p. 135. & 136. Ubi insuper rectè notat, Scripturam plenam esse testimoniis, quòd quaedam sit voluntas DEI, quae non semper impletur, non, quòd Deus eam implere non possit, sed quia idem illud quod ipse vult, etiam velit homines velle. Quando igitur homines nolunt, h. e. quando salutis media protervè reiiciunt, tunc nec DEI voluntas de eorum salute impletur, quia nempe ipsi. quod Deus vult, nolunt. Quemadmodum verò oraculum hoc divinum rectè opponitur Calvinianis, particularis gratiae adsertoribus: ita ineptè hinc Pontisicii, (Vid. Bell. l. 5. de G. & L. A. c. 20. Costerus Enchir. Controv. p. 192.) Synergistae, aliique haeretici, vires L. A. in homine irregenito probare conantur. Etenim non sequitur: Homo potest Spiritui Sancto resistere, ac conversionem impedire, non venire ad Christum. E. etiam ex se DEO adsentire, gratiae divinae cooperari, ac salutariter ad Christum venire potest. Est sanè cadaver hoc conse quentiae, rectèque iudicat gravissimus Theologus B. D. Mylius in A. C. part. 1. p. 228, quòd vix infans sit, quin intelligat, quàm in valida haec sit consequentia. Etenim contrarium disertè docent sacrae litterae. Vide Rom. 8, 7.Act. 26, 18.Eph. 4, 18.c. 5, 8.1. Cor. 2, 14.2. Cor. 3. 5. Et ratio diversitatis est manifesta, quia nolitio est à corruptâ carne, volitio autem à solo DEO excitatur. Contrarium etiam testantur Patrum sententiae. Notum est illud augustissimi Hipponensium Episcopi in Soliloq. c. 15. Quòd cecidi, fuit ex me, quòd surrexi, fuit ex te. Pulcrè quoq; Ambrosius l. 2. de vocat. gent. c. 9. Licet insit homini nolle bonum tamen nisi donatum non habet velle bonum. Illud contraxit natura post culpam, hoc recipit naturaper gratiam. Praeterea non sequitur, homo habet libertatem sive velle externum, potestque in actionibus paedagogicis rectè se gerere. E. etiam habet libertatem internam, sive velle spirituale, salutariter ad Deum sese convertendi. Hoc enim insolidum DEO adscribitur. Vid. Phil. 2, 13. Deinde disting. inter repugnantiam naturalem, & affectatam sive morosam. Quâ de re pluribus agunt Disp. 22. q. 4. §. 35. it. Disp. 23. §. 18. 19. B. D. Lobechius Disp. 20. in A. C. §. 37. 39. B. Par. Disp. Isag. L. de L. A. c. 3. §. 3. Confess. Cathol. art 22. c. 4. p. 568. 566. B. D. Hutter. in Expl. F. C. p. 211. 215. it. in LL. Mai. p. 285. seqq. B. D. H-lsem. in A. C. p. 131. B. D. Hunnius in h. l.)*

Ecce domus vestra. Per domum intelligit templum & politiam Iudaeorum. *(Conf. similes comminationes Es. 1, 7.c. 42, 15.24.Ier. 8, 13. 14. add. Isid. Pelusiota lib. 4 ep. 74. it. Const.

L'Emper. ad Itin. Beniam. p. 171. Discimus ex hâc Christi comminatione, quòd Deus calamitates futuras praedicere soleat, quò impii sint inexcusabiles, pii verò istas effugere possint. Conf. Amos 3, 7.Gen. 18, 19. Ionae 1, 2. &c.)*

Relinquetur deserta. i. e. à me deseretur, & hostibus vestris Romanis tradetur, qui eam desolabunt ac devastabunt. *(Conf. Ier. 12, 7.c. 22, 5. Rectè verò statuunt nostrates, comminationem hanc Salvatoris eo usque extendi debere, ut sensus sit, ecce politia ac templum vestrum manebunt eversa ac desolata, usque ad finem mundi. Ut ita oraculo hoc evertatur sententia eorum, tum qui statuunt, Iudaeos ante extremum Iudicium reducendos in terram Canaan, tum qui existimant, Anti Christum in templo Hierosolymitano sessurum, & Christianos in terrâ sanctâ securè habitaturos. Quo de errore agit B. Par. L. de Extr. Iudic. §. 109. Distulit verò Deus per 40. annos poenam, quam comminatus Iudaeis fuit, quò nempe tempus poenitentiae illis concederet. Et hoc more consueto, de quo Esai. 5, 2.Iob. 24, 23.Luc, 13, 7.Apoc. 2, 21. Origenes in Matth. tract. 26. c. 23 Non statim, scribit, ut factum fuerit peccatum, punitur peccantium generatio sed quum subsequens generatio, debens emendare in se peccatum patrum suorum, adhuc adiecerit peccatis patrum suorum peiora; & sic multae generationes peccaverint in gente aliquâ vel in civitate, punitur gens vel destruitur civitas. Quo facit etiam illud hominis gentilis, (Valerii puta Maximi lib. 1. Fact. Memor. c. 1.) ore propè Christiano prolatum: lento gradu ad vindictam sui divina procedit ira, tarditatemsupplicii gravitate compensat. Conferatur pulcerrima Isidori Pelusiotae epistola, quae est 380. lib. 1. Huc spectat quoque dictum Apostoli Rom. 2, 4. 5. 6. Discimus porrò è Iudaeorum exemplo, populi peccata, cumprimis verò verbi divini contemtum ac sincerorum coelestis veritatis praeconū persecutionem regnis & civitatibus vastitatem interitumq; affere. Conf. Gen. 19, 13.24.2. Reg. 17. v. 24. & 25.Es. 45.Ierem. 50. 51. Mundus quidem cum Caipha ac Pharisaeis, Ioh. 11, 47. seqq. aliud sibi persuadet: sed vehementer fallitur.)*

## 23:39
v. 39. Until you say &c. that is, until the end of the world, when I am about to come to judgment. Which some of you, that is, the converted, will congratulate me upon. The meaning is, that as far as my bodily presence is concerned (for he had spoken before of a gracious presence), I shall depart from you, nor will you see me, until I come to judgment in heavenly glory. Then even against your will you will be forced to acknowledge that I am he to whom the honor is due, which the children attributed to me in their hymn, and which you envied me, c. 21, 15. Cf. below c. 26, 64, thus Tossanus. *(Who took this explanation from Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius, and St. Augustine, book 2, On the Consensus of the Evangelists, c. 75. And thus it will be, that they may confess Him even against their will, and those who despised Him in His humility, may acknowledge Him in His power, as the author of the Opus Imperfectum speaks. Grotius also follows this interpretation in this place and thinks that the passage Phil. 2, 10 pertains to this. Our own interpreters also embrace the same exposition. See B. D. Hutter, and others. B. D. Calixtus in Conc. Evang. p. 205 thinks that this passage can also be explained thus, you will not see me by the light of intellect and faith, until you yield to the truth and acknowledge me as blessed of the Lord, and he compares Rom. 11, 25 Hos. 3, 4 5. Cornelius à Lapide adds yet another explanation, noting, that this passage can also be taken concerning the Jews, who at the end of the world are to be converted to Christ through Elijah, so as to acknowledge Christ, who is about to come shortly after to judgment, as the Messiah blessed by the Lord etc.: But that hypothesis concerning the return of Elijah is false, and the opinion concerning a certain universal conversion of the Jews shortly before the last day is uncertain, as has been shown elsewhere. Whence we rightly consider the former exposition to be preferred to this latter one.

The following are contained in the present chapter: I. The prediction of the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, and what signs are to precede it, v. 1-14. II. Instruction on how the inhabitants ought to conduct themselves then, v. 15-27. III. A prophecy concerning the final times, v. 29-31. IV. Information from our faithful Savior on how we ought to prepare ourselves for the final day, v. 32 to the end.

Latin:

v. 39. Usdum dicatis &c. id est usque ad finem mundi, quo adventurus sum ad iudicium. Quem nonnulli ex vobis, conversi sc., mihi gratulabuntur. Sensus est, quòd etiam corporalem meam praesentiam attinet (priùs enim de gratiosa praesentiâ dixerat,) à vobis discedam, nec videbitis me, donec veniam ad iudicium in gloriâ coelesti. tunc etiam contra voluntatem vestram agnoscere cogemini, me esse illum, cui debetur honor, quem pueri in suo hymno mihi tribuerunt, quemque mihi invidistis, c. 21, 15. Conf infrà c. 26, 64 ita Tossanus. *(Qui hanc explicationem desumsit ex Chrysostomo, Theophylacto, Euthymio & S. Augustino l. 2. de Consensu Evang. c. 75. Atque ita futurum, ut ipsum confiteantur inviti, & & qui contemserunt in humilitate, agnoscant in potestate, ceu autor Operis Imperf. loquitur. Sequitur etiam interpretationem hanc Grotius in h. l. ac huc pertinere putat locum Philipp 2, 10. Eandem expositionem amplectuntur quoque nostrates Interpp. Vid B. D. Hutterū, alios. Existimat B. D. Calixtus Conc. Evang. p 205. posse quoque hunc locum ita exponi, non videbitis me lumine intellectûs & fidei, usdum veritati manus detis & me benedictum Domini confireamini, ac confert Rom. 11, 25.Hos. 3, 4 5. Cornelius à Lapide addit adhuc explicationem aliam, notans, posse hunc locum etiam accipi de Iudaeis, qui in fine mundi per Eliam ad Christum cōvertendi sint, adeoChristum paullò pòst adiudicium venturum agnituri, ut Messiam à Domino benedictum &c: Verùm hypothesis illa de reditu Eliae falsa est, sententia verò de universali quadam Iudaeorum paullò ante diem extremum conversione, incerta, uti alibi ostensum. Unde expositionem priorem meritò huic posteriori praeserendam ducimus.)*

Continentur in praesenti cap. seqq. I. Eversionis urbis Ierusalem, & quae signa praecessura eam sint, praedictio, v. 1. 14. II. quomodo incolae sese tum gerere debeant, instructio, v. 15, 27. III. De extremis temporibus vaticinatio, v. 29. 31. IV. Fidelis Salvatoris nostri, quomodo ad extremum diem praeparare nos debeamus, informatio, v. 32. ad finem.)*

## 24:1
v. 1. He went out of the temple &c. Christ goes out of the temple, as if never to return to it.

His disciples came to him. Mark 13:1 it is said that one of the disciples came to him and showed the structures of the temple to Christ; here, however, many are said to have come. Resp. Perhaps one was doing it, with the others present, or others were showing him the buildings of the temple, and one was saying: See, what manner of stones. (B. D. Glass. Philol. S. b. 3. tr. 1. c. 27. thinks that this passage can be conveniently explained in this way, if it is said that first one of the disciples came to Christ, just as he was leaving the Temple, and said to him: Teacher &c. as it is in Mark, but that afterwards the rest also came and commended the magnificence of the Temple to Christ.)

Buildings of the temple. That temple had been constructed most magnificently by Herod, as Josephus shows in many places, book 15 of the Antiquities of the Jews, last chapter. (add Villalpandus on the Temple of Jerusalem, Heitman in Palestine c. 2. B. Par. Harm. Ev. c. 160. Bunting Itinerary of the Holy Land, also Hugo Grotius on this passage, who also brings forward the testimonies of Tacitus, Josephus, and Philo, and rightly observes, (just as the same was also noted by D. Hoornbeek l. 2. against the Jews c. 1. p. 164. also Const. L' Empereur ab Oppik Preface to Middoth, and others.) that although Herod, in order to enlarge the temple, renewed it from the foundations; yet since he both used the old material, and did not tear down the whole temple at once, but only in parts, as much as had to be renewed at any given time, it is rightly said that this temple was the same as that which had been constructed by Zerubbabel. While this temple was standing, the Messiah was to be expected. See. Hagg 2. 9.Malach. 3, 1.)*

CHAPTER XXIV. SUMMARY AND DISPOSITION.

But it is asked, Why did they show Christ the building of the temple? Resp. Christ had predicted that the house would be left desolate and abandoned. Therefore, they marvel at the structure of the temple that was to be destroyed, and they think it ἀδύνατον. *(Hilary thinks that by this very thing they wished to move Christ to pity or to revoke the sentence of destruction. However, God willed that the Jerusalem temple should be so magnificent that by its fame the nations might be invited to the Israelite religion and the worship of the true God. Whence it also appears that the Gentiles were by no means excluded from grace by some absolute decree of GOD even in the O. Testament. Conf. Ioh. 12, 20.Act. 2, 5.c. 8, 27.)*

Latin:

v. 1. Egressus è templo &c. Christus è templo exit, tanquam nunquam ad illud reversurus.

Accesserunt discipuli.Marci 13, 1. dicitur unus ex discipulis accessisse, & structuras templi Christo ostendisse: hîc verò plures dicuntur accessisse. Resp. Fortè unus id faciebat, reliquis praesentibus, aut alii ostendebant illi aedificia templi, & unus dicebat: Vide, quales lapides. *(B. D. Glass. Philol. S. l. 3. tr. 1. c. 27. existimat, ita hunc locum commodè explicari posse, si dicatur, quòd primùm unus ex discipulis ad Christum, sub ipsum Templi egressum, accesserit, eique dixerit: Praeceptor &c. ut est apud Marcum, postremum verò etiam reliqui accesserint, ac Christo magnificentiam Templi commendarint.)*

Aedificia templi. Templum illud admodùm magnificè ab Herode erat extructum, ceu multis ostendit Iosephus lib. 15. Antiquit. Iud. c. ult. *(adde Villalpandum de Templo Hieros., Heitman num in Palaestinâ c. 2. B. Par. Harm. Ev. c. 160. Būntingum Itiner. Terrae sanctae, it.
