Hugonem Grotium h. l qui adducit quoque testimonia Taciti, Iosephi ac Philonis, probeque observat, (quemadmodum etiam idem notatum D. Hoornbekil. 2. contra Iudaeos c. 1. p. 164. it. Const. L' Empereur ab Oppik Praef. ad Middoth, ac aliis.) quòd licet Herodes, ut templum augeret, à fundamentis illud innovarit; tamē cùm & materiâ usus sit veteri, & non totum simul templum diruerit, sed per partes saltem, quantū quoque tempore innovandum erat, rectè dicatur, templum hocidem fuisse cum eo, quod exstructum erat à Zorobabele. Hoc templo stante expectandus Messias erat. Vid. Hagg 2. 9.Malach. 3, 1.)*

CAPUT XXIV. SUMMA AC DISPOSITIO.

Quaeritur verò, Cur Christo templi aedificium ostenderint? Resp. Christus praedixerat, domum desertum & relictū iri. Mirantur proinde templi structuram destruendam, ac illud ἀδύνατον existimant. *(Hilarius putat, quòd hôc ipsô Christum voluerint ad commiserationem sive ad revocandam excidii sententiam commovere. Voluit autem Deus, templum Hierosolymitanum adeò esse magnificum, ut eius celebritate gentes ad religionem Israeliticam ac cultum veri Dei invitarentur. Unde etiam apparet, quòd minimè gentiles etiam in V. Test. absoluto quodam DEI decreto à gratiâ fuerint exclusi. Conf. Ioh. 12, 20.Act. 2, 5.c. 8, 27.)*

## 24:2
v. 2. Do you not see &c. Some Codices read: οὐ βλέπετε ταῦτα πάν τα; but it is read more correctly as βλέπετε ταῦτα πάντα, with the negation removed, as appears from the ancient Interpreter and Theophylact. *(And the Arab also read it thus. The remaining Oriental Interpreters, however, read do you not.)*

Not one stone shall be left upon another. See Josephus, Wars, book 7, ch. 18, and Scaliger, Canon. Isagog. p. 304, from whom you will learn that a plow was even drawn over it. *(Jerome also testifies to the same in ch. 8 of Zechariah.)* Indeed, and over the temple itself by a certain Turnus Rufus, whom he himself calls Turranus. Some *(among whom is Cornelius à Lapide, from whom, however, his fellow member Maldonatus feels differently in this place)* think it is a hyperbole, concerning the greatest and most disastrous subversion of the city. For it does not seem likely to them that the Romans were so curious or rather so idle that they had the time or the desire to tear out individual stones: *(Nicephorus Callistus, however, testifies in book 3, H. E. ch. 24, that Hadrian (the Emperor) had completely demolished whatever had still remained from the ancient buildings and had leveled them to the ground in such a way that not even a stone remained upon a stone. Conf. more on this matter in Const. L' Empereur, Notes on Beniam. Tudel. Itiner. p. 171, seqq. Nicephorus adds, however, in the loc. cit. that then the oracle of the Savior was brought to its fulfillment. But Don Laur. Ramirez in Pentecont. ch. 43 thinks it was finally done in the time of Julian, concerning which later. Because Josephus reports in book 7, ch. 18, that some towers were left by Titus. Some note that just as in the construction of the temple) A stone placed upon a stone is said Hag. 2, 16., so in its destruction not a stone is left upon a stone. We learn, v. 3, from the overthrow of Jerusalem, a city both most powerful and most fortified, and once held as if in delight by God, 1. that no city is so powerful that it cannot be occupied and subverted by plague, famine, sedition, etc. Whence confidence is by no means to be placed in human defenses, but one must trust in God alone. Conf. Psalm. 46, 1. seqq. Psal. 118, 6. seq. Prov. 18, 10.Es. 26, 1.3.Nahum. 1, 7. Tyre the most fortified, Babylon the most spacious, Jerusalem the most holy, Carthage the most strong, Rome the most august, etc., have been overturned, nor can any be shown which could escape the fatal, if I may so speak, term divinely established. 2. that the Messiah has come, and therefore is still expected in vain by the Jews. Conf. Dan. 9, 26. Nor should that be passed over here, that although Julian the Apostate granted the Jews permission to rebuild the temple, yet by an earthquake the mass of the building collapsed, and it was burned by fire bursting forth from the earth, and when they were unwilling to desist from the work, fire falling from heaven consumed the workmen themselves. Witnesses are Nicephorus lib. 10. H. E. c. 32. & 33. Sozomen lib. 5. H. E. c. 22. Theodoret lib. 3. H. E. c. 20. Socrates l. 3. H. E. c. 20. Chrysost. homil. 4. in Matth. Ammianus Marcell. lib. 23. S. Ambrose ep. 29. to the Emperor Theodosius.

Latin:

v. 2. Nonne videtis &c. Quidam Codd. legunt: οὐ βλέπετε ταῦτα πάν τα; sed rectiùs legitur βλέπετε ταῦτα πάντα, sublatâ negatione, ut apparet ex vetere Interprete ac Theophylacto. *(Et ita quoque legit Arabs. reliqui tamen Orientales Interpp. legerunt nonne.)*

Non relinquetur lapis super lapidem. Vide Iosephum Halos. lib. 7. c. 18. Scaligerum Canon. Isagog. p. 304. à quo disces, etiam aratrum inductum fuisse. *(idem testatur quoque Hieronymus in c. 8. Zachariae.)* Imò & templo ipsi à quodam Turno Rufo, quem ipse Turranum vocat. Quidam *(quos inter & Cornelius à Lapide est, à quo tamen diversum sentit eiusdem sociennus Maldonatus in h. l.) putant, esse hyperbolen, de maximâ & funestissimâ urbis subversione. Neq; enim verisimile illis videtur, tam fuisse curiosos aut potiùs otio sos Romanos, ut eis vacarit vel libuerit, singulos lapides evellere: *(Testatur tamen Nicephorus Callistus l. 3. H. E. c. 24. Hadrianum (Imperatorem) quaecunex vetustis aedificiis reliqua adhuc fuerant, diruisse prorsus & solo ita aequasse, ut ne lapis quidem super lapidem maneret. Conf. plura in hanc rem apud Const. L' Empereur Notis in Beniam. Tudel. Itiner. p. 171. seqq. Addit verò Nicephorus l. c. quòd tum oraculum Salvatoris ad exitum fuerit perductum. Ast Don Laur. Ramirez in Pentecont. c. 43. demum tempore Iuliani id putat factum, de quo posteà. Quia aliquot turres à Tito relictas tradit Iosephus lib. 7. c. 18. Notant quidam, quòd sicuti in exstructione templi lapis super lapidem positus dicitur Hag. 2, 16. ita in eiusdem destructione non relinqui lapis super lapidem. Discimus v. ex Hierosolymae, urbis & potentissimae & munitissimae, & Deo in deliciis quasi olim habitae eversione, 1. quòd nulla urbs adeò potēs sit, quae non peste, fame, seditione &c. occupari & subverti queat. Unde haut quaquam fiducia in praesidiis humanis ponenda, sed soli Deo fidendum. Conf. Psalm. 46, 1. seqq. Psal. 118, 6. seq. Prov. 18, 10.Es. 26, 1.3.Nahum. 1, 7. Eversa Tyrus munitissima, Babylon amplissima, Hierosolyma sanctissima, Carthago fortissima, Roma augustissima &c. nec ostendi potest, quae fatalem, ut ita loquar, terminum, divinitùs constitutum, effugere potuerit. 2. quòd Messias venerit, adeoque frustrà à Iudaeis adhuc expectetur. Conf. Dan. 9, 26. Nec illud hîc praetereundum, quòd licet Iulianus Apostata concederet Iudaeis, ut templum reaedificarent, per terrae tamen motum moles aedificii corruerit, quin igne è terrâ erumpente fuerit exusta, cùmque ab opere desistere nollent, ignis de coelo delapsus opifices ipsos absumserit. Testes sunt Nicephorus lib. 10. H. E. c. 32. & 33. Sozomenus lib. 5. H. E. c. 22. Theodoritus lib. 3. H. E. c. 20. Socrates l. 3. H. E. c. 20. Chrysost. homil. 4. in Matth. Ammianus Marcell. lib. 23. S. Ambrosius ep. 29. ad Theodos. Imperatorem.)*

## 24:3
v. 3. And the disciples came to him. Who these disciples were is explained Marc. 13, 3. Namely Peter, James, John, and Andrew. The disciples ask Christ jointly about the time of the Jerusalem destruction and the coming to the final judgment, because they thought these would be immediately connected to one another, on the occasion that Christ in the preceding chapter had spoken about both v. 38 & 39. (Conf. B D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 727. B. D. Calixtus lib. de Supremo Iudic. p. 3. 4. H. Grot. adds that the disciples also asked in this place about the worldly kingdom of Christ, and that therefore παρουσία must be distinguished here from his coming to the final judgment. But if the Apostles thought so, this must be ascribed to their infirmity and vain persuasion about the worldly kingdom of Christ. But they sent a message to those thoughts after the Holy Spirit was poured out upon them. Therefore, the Chiliasts of today, who even from those words try to construct a golden, if I may so speak, age, err not lightly. Concerning whom let B. D. Walther. Miscell. Theol. p. 217. seqq. be consulted.)

*(v, 4. See to it that no one leads you astray. Conf. Mark 13, 5.)*

Latin:

v. 3. Et adierunt eum discipuli. Quinam fuerint hi discipuli, exponitur Marc. 13, 3. Videlicet Petrus, Iacobus, Iohannes & Andreas. Quaerunt autem Christum dicipuli coniunctim de tempore excidii Hierosolymitani & adventûs ad iudicium extremum, quia existimabant, haec invicem fore immediatè connexa, occasione eâ, quòd Christus in cap. praeced, de utroq; dixerat v. 38 & 39. *(Conf. B D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 727. B. D. Calixtus lib. de Supremo Iudic. p. 3. 4. Addit H. Grot., quòd etiā de mundano Christi regno h. l. Discipuli quaesiverint, quòdq; proinde παρουσία distinguēda hîc sit ab eiusdē advētu ad extremū iudiciū. Quod si ita senserunt Apostoli, infirmitati eorum vanaeq; persuasioni de mūdano Christi regno hoc adscribendū est Sed cogitationibus illis nuncium ipsi miserunt, postquam Sp. S super illos fuit effusus. Errant proinde non leviter hodie Chiliastae, qui etiam ex illis verbis aureum, ut ita loquar, seculum exstruere conantur. De quibus consulatur B. D. Walther. Miscell. Theol. p. 217. seqq.)*

*(v, 4. Videte, ne quis vos seducat. Conf. Marc. 13, 5.)*

## 24:5
*(v. 5. Many will come in my name &c. However these words properly and principally pertain to the times preceding the destruction of Jerusalem, (for there were of the number of deceivers Theudas and Judas the Galilean, Acts 5, 36. 37. likewise a certain Egyptian, Acts 21, 38. Conf. Josephus lib. 18. A. I. c. 1. l. 20. c. 2. and lib. 2. de B. I. c. 12. it. Histor. Tripart. l 2 c. 11. But especially into the number of those deceivers is accustomed to be referred a certain Ben or Bar Cocab, who nevertheless stirred up new things long after the destruction, as one who sold himself for the Messiah, with Justin Martyr as witness in Apolog. ad Anton. Pium, Eusebius l. 4. H. E. c. 6. and others. Let there be seen concerning the same from the more recent ones the illustrious Scaliger in Chron. Euseb. ad A. 548. Dn. D. Muellerus Iudaism. p. 506. seqq. D. Hoornbek lib. 3. advers. Iudaeos c. 1. p. 209. Ioh. Buxtorfius Synag. Iud. c. 26. Dionys. Petavius part. 1. Ration. Temp. l. 5. 7. p. 283. Boxhornius Hist. Univers. p. 195. just as among the same deceivers is also mentioned the Pseudo Moses of Crete, truly a Cretan i. e. a liar, Tit. 1, 12. concerning whom must be seen Josephus lib. 7. H. E. c. 37. Some refer here Simon Magus, as one who, with Jerome as witness, said: I am the word of GOD, I am the beautiful, I am the paraclete, I am the almighty, I am all things. Conf. concerning the same Irenaeus lib. 1. contra haeres. c. 20. Origen l. 2. adv. Celsum and tr. 27. in Matth. Others mention still others, concerning whom Dn. D. Muellerus and D. Hoornbek in the places cited a little before.) Secondarily, however, and consequently they can also be referred to the state of the times which precede the final judgment, as is evident 1. from the collation of parallel places. Dan. 11, 38. 2. Thess. 2, 4. Luke 18, 7. 2. from the consideration of the consequences. For immediately it is subjoined: for just as the lightning goes forth &c. so also will be the coming of the son of man. 3. from the exposition of the Fathers. Among them Jerome explicitly: Then according to some of the devastation of Jerusalem: for many princes stood forth in the time of the Jewish captivity, who said they were Christs. But it is better understood concerning the consummation of the age. From the more recent ones, B. D. Hunnius in h. l. B. Par. L. de Extr. Iudic. § 85. proves this more prolixly; Corn. à Lapide in h. l. also decides that this prediction is to be accepted concerning the AntiChrist, and proves it from Ioh. 5, 45. But if the prophecy concerning the Pseudo-Christs, who are to boast that they are Christ, is to be accepted concerning the times which will precede the final judgment, it is asked, who were such? Resp. The Savior speaks principally of the Great AntiChrist, the Roman Pontiff, whom the Papists babble to be Peter in power, Christ in anointing, and Spouse of the Church. Secondarily also, according to the opinion of some, there can be referred here Francis, who is commonly heard among the Papists as a typical Jesus, likewise Ignatius Loyola with his retinue, who, not content with the company of other Christians, erected a peculiar sect, which feigns the society of Jesus. To those deceivers can also be referred those who sold themselves for Christ, such as a certain Pole, Jacob Melstinckius, concerning whom Zwingerus in Theatro f. 1326. David Georgius, concerning whom Megisserus in Nucleo Histor. part 1. p. 87. Ezechiel Meth or Esaias Stieffel, concerning whom let different treatises be read, published by B. D. Weber against his heresy and blasphemies; James Naylor, the Prince of the modern Anabaptists in England, who are called Quakers.)*

*( In my name. Falsely protecting my name, or because they will be the future liberators of the people See Luke 24, 21)*

Latin:

*(v. 5. Multi venient in nomine meo &c. Utut verba haec propriè ac principaliter ad tempora, excidium Hierosolymitanum praecedentia pertineant, (fuerunt etenim è numero seductorum Theudas ac Iudas Galilaeus,Actor. 5, 36. 37. item Aegyptius quidam, Actor. 21, 38. Conf. Iosephus lib. 18. A. I. c. 1. l. 20. c. 2. ac lib. 2. de B. I. c. 12. it. Histor. Tripart. l 2 c. 11. Cumprimis verò in seductorum istorum numerum referri Ben-sive Bar Cocab quidam, qui tamen longè post excidium res novas molitus est, solet, ut qui pro Messia se venditavit, testibus lustino Martyre in Apolog, ad Anton. Pium, Eusebio l. 4. H. E. c. 6. aliis. Videantur de eodem ex recentioribus illustris Scaliger in Chron. Euseb. ad A. 548. Dn. D. Muellerus Iudaism. p. 506. seqq. D. Hoornbek lib. 3. advers. Iudaeos c. 1. p. 209. Ioh. Buxtorfius Synag. Iud. c. 26. Dionys. Petavius part. 1. Ration. Temp. l. 5. 7. p. 283. Boxhornius Hist. Univers. p. 195. quemadmodum inter eosdem seductores memoratur quoque Pseudo Moses Cretensis, verè Cretensis i. e. mendax,Tit. 1, 12. de quo videndus Iosephus lib. 7. H. E. c. 37. Nonnulli referunt huc Simonem Magum, ut qui teste Hieronymo, dixit: Ego sum sermo DEI, ego speciosus, ego paracletus, ego omnipotens, ego omnium. Conf. de eodem Irenaeus lib. 1. contra haeres. c. 20. Origenes l. 2. adv. Celsum ac tr. 27. in Matth. Alii adhuc alios memorant, de quibus Dn. D. Muellerus ac D. Hoornbek locis paullò antè allegatis.) Secundariò tamen ac consequenter ad statum temporum, quae iudiciumextremum praecedent, referri quoque possunt, ceu patet 1. ex locorum parallelorum,Dan. 11, 38.2. Thess. 2, 4.Luc. 18, 7.collatione. 2. ex consequentium consideratione. Statim enim subiungitur: sicut enim exit fulgur &c. ita & adventus filii hominis. 3. ex Patrum expositione. Inter eos Hieronymus disertè: Tunc secundùm quosdam devastationis Hierosolymae: nam multi tempore captivitatis Iudaicae principes extitere, qui Christos se esse dicerent. Sed mel-ùs de consummatione seculi intelligitur. Erecentioribus prolixiùs hoc probant B. D. Hunnius in h. l. B. Par. L. de Extr. Iudic. § 85. de AntiChristo praedictionem hanc accipiendam esse, statuit quoque Corn. à Lapide h. l. probatq; ex Ioh. 5, 45. At si de temporibus, quae extremum iudicium praecedent, vaticinium de Pseudo Christis, qui se Christum esse, gloriaturi sint, accipiendum, quaeritur, quinam tales fuerint? Resp. Principaliter loquitur Salvator de AntiChristo Magno, Pontifice Romano, quem potestate Petrum, unctione Christum esse ac Sponsum Ecclesiae, Papicolae garriunt. Secundariò quoque ex sententiâ nonnullorum referri huc possunt Franciscus, qui communiter apud Pontificios Iesus typicus audit, item Ignatius Loiola cum satellitio suo, quo non contentus coeterorum Christianorum consortio, peculiarem sectam, quae Iesu societatem mentitur, erexit. Ad deceptores illos referri quoque illi possunt, qui se pro Christo venditarunt, uti Polonus quidam, Iacobus Melstinckius, quo de Zwingerus in Theatro f. 1326. David Georgius, de quo Megisserus in Nucleo Histor. part 1. p. 87. Ezechiel Meth s. Esaias Stieffel, quo de legantur tractatus diversi, à B. D. Webero cōtra eius haeresin ac blasphemias in lucem editi; Iames Naylor, hodiernorum in Angliâ Anabaptistarum, qui Quater dicti, Princeps.)*

*( In nomine meo. Falsò protexentes meum nomen, sive quòd futuri sint populi liberatores Vid. Luc. 24, 21)*

## 24:6
v. 6. That you may hear of wars. By wars can be understood both the seditions stirred up in Judea before the final destruction, and the wars and persecutions that arose in the world on account of the preaching of the Gospel. *(Likewise here Christ properly, principally, and ηαβα τό ρητόν treats of the times before the Jerusalem destruction, the fulfillment of which prophecy Josephus in book 2 of the Jewish War, ch. 11 et seqq., book 20 of the Antiquities of the Jews, ch. 6, Eusebius in book 3 of the Ecclesiastical History, ch. 18, and Hegesippus in book 2 describe at length: meanwhile this prediction can likewise be most conveniently referred to the state of the last times, just as Hilary, Gregory the Great in homily 1 on the Gospel, and Irenaeus in book 5 against heresies, ch. 25 teach, and Blessed Par. L. on the Last Judgment § 86 also shows this with many points. So that thus the remote antecedents of the final judgment may be established according to the prediction of our Savior and of Daniel, and likewise of the Apostles, 1. the multiplication of heresies, v. 5. 2. the disturbance of the whole world, v. 6. 7. 8. 3. horrible persecution, v. 9. 10. 4. the inundation of supine security, v. 12. 5. universal preaching of the Gospel throughout the world, v. 14. as B. Par. deduces this at length in the place cited §. 58. But the proximate signs are 1. the notable tottering of the fourth monarchy , Dan. 2, 31. et seqq. 2. the revelation of the Anti-Christ, 2. Thess. 2, 3. 8, 25. 3. the observation of various signs, here v. 29, 30. Concerning which B. Par. likewise treats in the place cited §. 91. et seqq.)*

Latin:

v. 6. Ut audiatis bella. Per bella intelligi possunt tum leditiones, in Iudaeâ excitatae ante ultimum excidium, tum bella & persecutiones, propter praedicationem Evangelii in orbe exortae. *(Itidem hîc Christus propriè, principaliter ac ηαβα τό ρητόν agit de temporibus ante excidium Hierosolymitanum, cuius prophetiae etiam complementum Iosephus lib. 2. de B. I. c. 11. seqq. l. 20. A. I. c. 6. Euseb. l. 3. H. E. c. 18. Egesippus l. 2. latè describunt: interim pariter ad statum novissimorum temporum praedictio haec referri commodissimè poteest quemadmodum docent Hilarius, Gregorius M. hom. 1. in Evang. Irenaeus l. 5. contra haer. c. 25. idque multis quoque ostendit B. Par. L. de Extremo Iudicio §. 86. Ut ita antecedentia remota extremi iudicii statuantur iuxta Salvatoris nostri ac Danielis, itemque Apostolorum praedictionem, 1. haeresium multiplicatio, v 5. 2. totius orbis conturbatio, v. 6. 7. 8. 3. horribilis persecutio, v. 9 10. 4 supinae securitatis inundatio, v. 12. 5. universalis per orbem Evangelii praedicatio, v. 14. ceu prolixè hoc deducit B. Par. l. c. §. 58. Proxima verò signa 1. insignis quartae monarchiae lab-factatio,Dan. 2, 31. seqq. 2. Anti Christi revelatio,2. Thess. 2, 3.8, 25. 3. Variorum signorum observatio, hîc v. 29, 30. De quibus itidem agit B. Par. l. c. §. 91. seqq.)*

## 24:7
*(v. 7. έμερΘησετογ έΘνος οιπι έΘνος &c. How this prophecy was fulfilled before the devastation of the city of Jerusalem, H. Grotius shows in this place, who may be consulted.)*

Εσονταγ λιμοι καὶ λοιμοι, there shall be pestilences and famines. The paronomasia teaches that pestilence is accustomed to follow from famine and the dearness of grain. *(See here Act. 11, 28. Josephus, book 20, B. J. ch. 2. But that historians did not annotate so accurately that pestilences and earthquakes occurred around those times when Jerusalem was overturned, B. D. Calixtus thinks happened because they were the least among the remaining calamities. Therefore it can also be believed that no mention of pestilence and earthquakes is made by Josephus, because it is otherwise known that both are accustomed to accompany war and famine as if they were their companions. Although Josephus may have passed over those earthquakes in silence, they were nevertheless observed by other historians, whom you may see, if you wish, in Grotius in this place.)*

Latin:

*(v. 7. έμερΘησετογ έΘνος οιπι έΘνος &c. Quomodo hoc vaticinium ante urbis Hieros. devastationem fuerit impletum, ostendit H. Grotius in h. l. qui potest consuli.)*

Εσονταγ λιμοι καὶ λοιμοι,erunt pestilentiae & fames. Paronomasia docet, ex fame & annonae charitate pestem solere consequi. *(Vid. hîc Act. 11, 28. Iosephum l, 20. B. I. c. 2. Quòd verò pestes ac terrae motus circa ea tempora, quando Ierusalē fuit eversa, factos Historici non ita accuratè annotarint, factum B. D. Calixtus putat inde, quòd inter reliquas calamitates minimae illae fuerint. Ideò quoque pestis ac terrae motuum nullam à Iosepho fieri mentionem credi potest, quòd notum aliàs sit, utrumque bellum & famem perfe quasi comitari solere. Licet velmaximè Iosephus istos terrae motus silentio praeterierit, observati tamen iidem Historicis aliis, quos vide sis apud Grotium h. l.)*

## 24:8
v. 8. παντα ταύτα αρχη ὠδίνων of vehement and severe torments, such as those who are in labor suffer. *(Thus, indeed, in Holy Scripture the most severe pains are accustomed to be expressed. See Ps. 48, 7. Es. 13, 8. c. 66, 7. Ierem. 30, 6. 7. Ambrose well says in chapter 21, 9 of Luke: Because we are at the sunset of the age, certain sicknesses of the world precede. But the Savior especially looks to the calamities which will accompany the overturning of Jerusalem. It is indeed worth the effort to note that the teachers of the Jews, from observations of the ancients, hand down that in the time of the Messiah there will be huge calamities and

persecutions, as Ioh. Buxtorff excellently shows in Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 700. 701.)*

Latin:

v. 8. παντα ταύτα αρχη ὠδίνων vehementium & gravium -ruciatuum, quales perpetiuntur parturientes. *(Ita nempe in Sc. S. gravissimi dolores solent exprimi. Vide Ps. 48, 7.Es. 13, 8.c. 66, 7.Ierem. 30, 6. 7. Benè Ambrosius in cap. 21, 9. Lucae: Quia in occasu seculi sumus, praecedent quaedam aegritudines mundi. Cumprimis verò respicit Salvator ad calamitates, quae eversionem Hierosolymarum comitabuntur. Operae verò pretium est notare, quòd Iudaeorum Magistri è v-terum observationibus tradant, tempore Messiae ingentes fore calamitates &

persecutiones, uti egregiè ostendit Ioh. Buxtorff. Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 700. 701.)*

## 24:9
v. 9. Then they shall deliver you up &c. See Rom. 16, 17. 2. Cor. 11, 13. 26. Gal. 4, 17. Phil. 3, 2. 18. 2. Tim. 1, 15. ) (

For my name’s sake that is, on account of the bare profession of Christianity. See 1. Petr. 4, 16. Add Tertullian’s Apology against the Gentiles, the Epistles of Trajan and Pliny the Younger, and Eusebius, Book 4 of the Ecclesiastical History, ch. 15, concerning Polycarp. Meanwhile, it must by no means be concealed that they generally raged against Christians by attributing horrendous crimes to them, as Ludovicus Vives shows in his Commentary on Book 18, ch. 52 of Augustine’s *City of God*. Let Leonhard Coquaeus also be added on the said passage. Indeed, Satan incited the nations to that cruelty against Christians through his idols, not unaware that the Christian religion, being the only saving one, would bring the greatest detriment to his kingdom.) (

Latin:

*(v. 9. Tunc tradent vos &c. Vid. Rom. 16, 17.2. Cor. 11, 13.26.Gal. 4, 17.Phil. 3, 2.18.2. Tim. 1, 15.)*

*( Propter nomen meum h. e. ob nudam Christianismi professionem. Vid. 1. Petr. 4, 16. Adde Tertulliani Apolog. adv. Gentes, Traiani & Plinii Sec. Epistolas, Eusebiuml. 4 H. E. c. 15. de Polycarpo. Interea minimè dissimulandum, quòd plerumque adfictis horrendis sceleribus in Christianos saevierint, ceu ex Svetonio ac Tacito oftendit Ludov. Vives Comm. in l. XIIX. c. 52. Augustini de C. D. Addatur quoque Leonh. Coquaeus ad d. l. Instigavit verò Satanas per sua idola gentes ad istam crudelitatem in Christianos, non nescius, quòd religio Christiana utpote sola salvifica, maximum regno suo allatura esset detrimentum.)*

## 24:11
v. 11. And many false prophets. The same was predicted by the Apostle Act. 20, 29. 30. Cornelius à Lapide ridiculously includes Luther among them. To this unjust and malevolent judgment of the Jesuit concerning Luther, we deservedly oppose the honorable judgments of other Papists, which B. Par. recounts in *Confess. Cathol.*, Book 1, General, ch. 5, et seqq. Indeed, the same Jesuit rightly includes the Antichrist as the head of all among these false prophets. But since all the requirements of the great Antichrist, handed down in the Holy Scriptures, apply to the Roman Pontiff, it follows that he himself is the head of all heresiarchs.) ( Πλανήσουσι. [

*( Πλαιησούοι. That this was done especially through Syncretism, H. Grotius shows at length and elegantly in this place.)*

Latin:

*(v. 11. Et multi Pseudoprophetae. Idem praedictum ab Apostolo Act. 20, 29. 30. Ridiculè Corn. à Lapide inter illos Lutherum quoque refert. Cui iniquo ac malevolo Iesuitae de Luthero iudicio meritò opponimus aliorum Pontificiorum honorifica iudicia, quae recenset B. Par. Confess. Cathol. lib. 1. Gener. c. 5. seqq. Rectè verò idem Iesuita inter istos Pseudoprophetas AntiChristum tanquam omnium caput recenset. Cùm verò Pontifici Romano omnia AntiChristi magni requisita, in Sc. S. tradita, competant, consequens est, quòd omnium ipse haeresiarcharum caput sit. *)

*( Πλαιησούοι. Hoc potissimùm factum esse per Syncretismum, prolixè & eleganter ostendit H. Grotius in h. l.)*

## 24:12
*(v. 12. Charity shall grow cold. Therefore it was present before with true faith, otherwise it could not be extinguished. But if charity and faith can be extinguished, it follows that faith can be lost, indeed by the reborn both totally and finally; but by the elect not indeed finally, yet totally. Conf. B. D. Meisn. ΑνΘραπ. S. Disp. 19. § 6. Dnn. Theol. Marp. Deduct. Fundam p. 269. seqq. In vain does D. I. Georg. Grossius retort in Theatro Bibl. p. 1034 that the discourse here is not about charity, infused by the Holy Spirit, but about the natural love of kindred blood. For the contrary is evident from the following v. 13. from which it is evident that such charity can be lost, in which if anyone has persevered, he can be saved.)*

Latin:

*(v. 12. Refrigescet charitas. Ergò antea adfuit cum fide verâ, aliàs non posset extingvi. Si verò charitas & fides extingvi possunt, sequitur, fidem posse amitti, à renatis quidem & totaliter & finaliter; ab electis verò non quidem finaliter, tamen totaliter. Conf. B. D. Meisn. ΑνΘραπ. S. Disp. 19. § 6. Dnn. Theol. Marp. Deduct. Fundam p. 269. seqq. Frustra regerit D. I. Georg. Grossius in Theatro Bibl. p. 1034 Sermonenhîc esse non de charitate, à Sp. S. infusâ, sed de amore naturali cognati sanguinis. Etenim contrarium patet ex v. subs. 13. è quo patet, talem charitatem amitti, in quâ si quis perseverarit, possit salvari.)*

## 24:13
(v. 13. He who shall have persevered &c. To this point look the sayings of Holy Scripture Ezech. 18, 24. above c. 10, 22.Marc. 13, 13.Luc. 21, 19.2. Tim. 2.c. 4, 7. 8.Ebr. 3, 6.14.Apoc. 2, 10. and the testimonies of the Fathers. Jerome, epistle to Furia: Beginnings are not sought in Christians, but the end. Tertullian: No one is a Christian, except he who perseveres even to the end. Cyprian: And faith itself, like birth, does not give life unless it is received and guarded. Gregory, book 1 of Morals: Good is done in vain, if it is abandoned before the end of life. Compare more things making for this in B. Par. in Practical Aphorisms. Furthermore, since according to this present oracle of our Savior, those alone are to be participants of eternal salvation who shall have persevered in faith even to the end of life; and since now no one can be certain that he will so persevere, according to 1. Cor 10, 12Rom. 11, 20.Philipp. 2, 12. the Papists collect from thence, see Bell. book 3 on Justification, ch. 12 & 13, that no one can be certain of the grace of GOD and salvation, unless a peculiar revelation intervenes. But we distinguish between the certainty of the spirit, and the security of the flesh; also between limited certainty, manifested in the word, and absolute certainty, that is, founded in some absolute decree of GOD. The former we assert, the latter we deny. See B. D. Hunnius, Loci Communes, p. 812. following. B. Par. Academic Disputations, p. 793. also Isagoge of Theological Places, Book on Predestination, ch. 9. § 10. following. Compare also the Analysis above to c. 14, 17.)

Latin:

*(v. 13. Qui perseverarit &c. Huc spectant dicta Sacrae Scripturae Ezech. 18, 24. suprà c. 10, 22.Marc. 13, 13.Luc. 21, 19.2. Tim. 2.c. 4, 7. 8.Ebr. 3, 6.14.Apoc. 2, 10. ac testimonia Patrum. Hieronymus ep. ad Furiam: Non quaeruntur in Christianis initia, sed finis. Tertullianus: Nemo Christianus, nisi qui ad finem usq perseverat. Cyprianus: Et fides ipsa ut nativitas, non accepta, sed custodita vivificat. Gregorius lib. 1. Moral. In cassum bonum agitur, si ante vitae terminum deseratur Conf. plura huc facientia apud B. Par. in Aphor. Practicis. Coeterùm cùm iuxta praesens Salvatoris nostri oraculum illi demum aeternae salutis participes futuri, qui in fide usque ad finem vitae perseverarint; iam verò nemo possit esse certus, se ita perseveraturum esse, iuxta 1. Cor 10, 12Rom. 11, 20.Philipp. 2, 12. colligunt inde Pontificii, vid Bell. l. 3. de Iustif. c. 12. & 13. neminem posse esse certum de gratiâ DEI & salute, nisi peculiaris interveniat revelatio. Ast dist. inter certitudinem spiritûs, & securitatem carnis; it. inter certiiudinem limitatam, in verbo manifestatam, & certitudinem absolutam, s. in absoluto quodam DEI decreto fundatam. Priorem nos adserimus, posteriorem negamus. Vid. B. D. Hunnium LL. Mai. p. 812. seqq. B. Par. Dispp. Acad. p. 793. item Isagoge LL. Theol. L. de Praedest. c. 9. § 10. seqq. Conf. etiam Anal. suprà ad c. 14, 17.]*

## 24:14
v. 14. The Gospel of the kingdom. It is so called, because men are called by it and gathered into the heavenly kingdom, and because it preaches chiefly concerning the kingdom of GOD.

έν ολη ιη οιηούμεν. That by οιηούμένην in the Scriptures and Profane Writers is understood not absolutely the whole globe of the earth, but that part of the world which at that time was known and inhabited, Chamier proves, vol. 2, book 16, ch. 3, § 14. Strabo book 1, ηαλούμεν λού οιηούμένην, ην οιηούμεν καὶ γνωριζομεν. We call οιηούμρνην that which we inhabit and have known. Jerome in this place: The sign of the Lord's coming is the preaching of the Gospel through the whole world, so that no one may be excusable, which we see is either already completed, or will be completed shortly. For I do not think that any nation has remained, which is ignorant of the name of Christ: and although it may not have had a preacher, yet from neighboring nations it cannot be ignorant of the opinion of the faith. But the Savior proposes 1. the calamity of the times, immediately preceding the day of judgment. 2. the swiftness of his coming to judgment. Although Christ properly treats of the Jerusalem destruction, as is evident 1. from the occasion of the sayings. 2. from the denomination of the place: yet it can be referred to the final judgment, 1. because of the coupled question. 2. because of the condition of the type. The particular judgment of the Jews is a type of the universal. 3. because of the connection of the text. Both the antecedents and the consequents treat of the final judgment. (Compare more on this matter in B. Par. Book on the Final Judgment § 89. Dn. D. Mueller, Judaism p. 1109. following. B. D. Calixtus, book on the Supreme Judgment, p. 26. following. That indeed by the phrase ολης, and πασης της οιχούμένης, not absolutely the whole world of the earth, with no part of it excepted, is signified in Holy Scripture, is evident from Luc. 2, 1. and is granted by Corn. à Lapide and Conzen in their Commentaries on that place. It is evident therefore, how not sufficiently firm is the collection of the Papists, (See Bell. book 3 on the Roman Pontiff, ch. 4. Adam Conzen on this place q. 1. Corn. à Lapide on this place) while from the fact that the Gospel has not yet been preached in the whole world of the earth, with no part of it at all excepted, they attempt to prove that the Anti-Christ has not yet come. For, to say nothing now of the fact that although even now the Gospel is not preached in act, yet in the time of the Apostles and a little later it was preached in the whole world, see Matth 28, 19.Luc. 24, 47.Marc. 16, 20.Col. 1, 6.23.Rom. 1, 8.c. 10, 18.c. 15, 19.2. Cor. 2, 14. and compare entirely B. D. Balduinus in c. 1. Epistle to the Colossians q. 2. yet it has not been proven by the Papists that the phrase έν ολη τη οἰκουμένῃ implies more than έν παντι τω ηοσμω, Col. 1, 6. The Jesuit Conzen insists on this place: if this prophecy ought to be accepted concerning at least a part of the world, then already in the time of the Apostles it had been fulfilled. Answer: What then? For we ourselves assert that Christ properly and principally treats here of the signs that were to precede the Jerusalem destruction (and this is also taught here and there by Interpreters, even Papists, see Lyranus, Maldonatus, Ioh. Ferus on this place, Dionysius the Carthusian and Pererius on the Epistle to the Romans c. 10.

Salmeron vol. 4, p. 655, and others, whom Mr. D. Botsaccus cites in Contradict. Pontif. ch. 29, no. 85 and 86, and B. Par. Confess. Cath. bk. 2, spec. art. 3, ch. 6, p. 756, following, yet in such a way that the same signs can also be accommodated to the consummation of the age. Regarding which matter, more may be seen in B. Par. Book on the Final Judgment, § 89. In this place, let this at least be noted, that Conzenius himself admits. Alfonso Tostado, Bishop of Avila, whom the Papists deservedly esteem highly elsewhere, to support that opinion, that Christ is speaking of the signs of the desolation of Jerusalem, and that in the same way they seem to understand this place: Chrysostom, hom. 76 on Matthew, Euthymius, Theophylact, and Jerome on this place, Ambrose, book 10 on Luke, Hilary, can. 25 &c. (not only do the cited Fathers seem to understand it so, but others also, such as Anselm, Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, likewise Victor of Antioch, on chapter 13 of Mark. Similarly the author of the Questions to Antiochus, ascribed to Athanasius, q. 136.) What of the fact that Cornelius à Lapide himself notes, that since we see the Gospel being propagated everywhere in America after the discovery of the New World, and that is clearly half of the whole world, we can gather from this that we are gradually approaching the end of the world. He adds: For from the rest of the world nothing remains which has not at some time received the faith of Christ, unless perhaps China, where nevertheless our Nicolaus Trigaultius shows by certain testimonies that there were once Christians and churches of Christ. So also Jacobus Tirinus, a man of the same society, although he maintains, that the Gospel is not to be promulgated in the whole world secretly, as happened in the time of the Apostles, but publicly and solemnly, with all the kings and kingdoms of the earth permitting, nay even embracing it. he adds however, that this will not be all at once, unless perhaps towards the end of the world, but successively and in turn. In which words it is to be noted that the Jesuit himself hesitates whether towards the end of the world the Gospel must be preached again in some illustrious way. They err certainly without ambiguity, who persuade themselves that it can be evidently proven from this place, that just as in the time of the Apostles and before the destruction of Jerusalem the Gospel was preached in the whole world: so similarly before the end of the world it must be preached again to all peoples, even those who maliciously rejected the grace of the evangelical preaching offered to them, and that

furthermore no one will be going to resist the preached Gospel. Against which error Mr. Ursinus argues in Introduction to the Apocalypse, p. 114, seqq., likewise p. 192, seqq., also B. Par. Disputations Elenchtic on the Gospel for Misericordia Sunday, p. 773. Finally against Calvinists it is to be observed, that if the Gospel, and indeed according to the command of Christ, Matth. 28 19.Marc. 16, 15. has been preached in the whole world, (a thing which Daniel Chamier, deservedly quite famous among Reformed Theologians, shows also at length and excellently in tom. 2. Panstrat. lib. 16. c. 3.), the grace of the calling is universal, and no one has been excluded from eternal salvation by some absolute decree of GOD . The exceptions of the Calvinists will be satisfied in the Analecta to Marc. 16, 15. add also Anal. to Matth. 28, 29.

*( In testimony &c. Conf. Rom. 1, 20.Ioh. 12, 48.)*

*( Then the consummation shall come. Of both the city and the whole world. For the Savior speaks of the destruction of the city in such a way that he looks at the same time to the destruction of the whole world, or to the consummation of the age.)*

Latin:

v. 14. Evangelium regni. Dicitur ita, quia homines eo vocantur & colliguntur in regnum coeleste, & quia praecipuè de regno DEI concionatur.

έν ολη ιη οιηούμεν. Per totam οιηούμένην in Scripturis & Prophanis Scriptoribus intelligi non absolutè universum orbem terrarum, sed eam partem orbis, quae tum temporis erat cognita & habitata, probat Chamierus t. 2. l. 16. c 3. §. 14. Strabo l. 1. ηαλούμεν λού οιηούμένην, ην οιηούμεν καὶ γνωριζομεν.Vocamusοιηούμρνηνeam, quam habitamus & cognitam habemus. Hieron. in h. l. Signum Dominici adventûs est Evangelii per totum orbem praedicatio, ut nullus sit excusabilis, quod aut iam completum, aut brevi cernimus esse complendum. Non enim puto, aliquam remansisse gentem, quae Christi nomen ignoret: & quanquam non habuerit praedicatorem, tamen ex vicinis nationibus opinionem fidei non potest ignorare. Proponit autem Salvavor 1. temporum, diem iudicii proximè antecedentium calamitatem. 2. adventûs sui ad iudicium celeritatem. Quamvis propriè Christus agat de Hierosolymitano excidio, ut patet 1. ex dictorum occasione. 2. ex loci denominatione: tamen referri potest ad extremum iudicium, 1. propter copulatam quaestionem. 2. propter typi conditionem. Particulare Iudaeorum iudicium est typus universalis. 3. propter textûs connexionem. Et antecedentia & consequentia agunt de extremo iudicio. *(Conf. plura in hanc rem apud B. Par. L. de Extr. Iud § 89. Dn. D. Mueller. Iudaismi p. 1109. seqq B. D. Calixtum lib. de Supr. Iudic. p. 26. seqq. Quòd verò phrasi ολης, it πασης της οιχούμένης, non absolutè totus terrarum orbis, nulla eius parte exceptâ, in Sc. S. significetur, patet ex Luc. 2, 1. ac largiuntur Corn. à Lapide ac Conzen Comment. ad d. l. Patet igitur, quàm non satis firma sit collectio Pontificiorum, (Vid. Bell. l. 3. de P. R. c. 4. Adamus Conzen in h. l. q. 1. Corn. à Lapide in h. l.) dum ex eo, quòd Evangelium nondum in universo terrarum orbe, nullâ omninò eius parte exceptâ, praedicatum sit, evincere conantur, Anti Christum nondum venisse. Etenim, ut iam taceamus, quòd licet iam nunc non amp-iùs actu Evangelium praedicetur, tamen tempore Apostolorum ac paullò pòst in universo orbe fuerit praedicatum, vid. Matth 28, 19.Luc. 24, 47.Marc. 16, 20.Col. 1, 6.23.Rom. 1, 8.c. 10, 18.c. 15, 19.2. Cor. 2, 14. ac confer omninò B. D. Balduinum in c. 1. Epist. ad Coloss q. 2. nondum tamen evictum à Pontificiis, quòd phrasis, έν ολη τη οἰκουμένῃ plus inferat quàm, έν παντι τω ηοσμω,Col. 1, 6. Instat Iesuita Conzen h. l. si de parte saltem orbis hoc vaticinium accipi debeat, tunc iamtum Apostolorum tempore illud fuisse impletum. Resp. Quid tum? Ipsi enim nos adserimus, quòd Christus propriè ac principaliter hîc agat de signis, excidium Hierosolymitanum praecessuris (idque etiam passim docent Interpretes, etiam Pontificii, vid. Lyranus, Maldonatus, Ioh. Ferus in h. l. Dionysius Carthusianus ac Pererius in ep. ad Rom. c. 10.

Salmeron t. 4. p. 655. & alii, quos adducunt Dn D. Botsaccus in Contradict. Pontif. c. 29 n. 85. & 86. & B. Par. Confess. Cath. l. 2. spec. art. 3. c. 6. p. 756. seqq.) ita tamen ut eadem signa ad consummationem seculi accommodari etiam possint. Quam in rem plura videantur apud B. Par. L. de Extr. Iudicio §. 89. Hoc loco illud saltem notetur, quòd ipse Conzenius fateatur. Alphonsum Tostatum, Abulensem Episcopum, quem meritò aliàs Pontificii magni faciunt, sententiam illam, quòd Christus agat de signis vastationis Hierosolymitanae, adstruere, quòdq eodem modo h. l. intelligere videantur Chrysostomus hom. 76. in Matth. Euthymius, Theophylactus ac Hieronymus in h. l. Ambrosius lib 10. in Lucam. Hilarius can. 25. &c. (non verò solùm laudati Patres ita intelligere videntur, verùm etiam alii, uti Anselmus, Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, item Victor Antiochenus, in cap. 13. Marci. Similiter autor Qq. ad Antiochum, Athanasio adscriptarum q. 136.) Quid quòd ipse Cornelus à Lapide notet, quòd cùm post inventum novum orbem passim propagari in America Evangelium videamus, illa verò planè dimidia orbis totius pars sit, colligere hinc possimus, nos sensim appropinquare ad finem mundi. Addit: Ex reliquo enim orbe nihil superest, quod aliquando fidem Christi non receperit, nisi fortè China, ubi tamen aliquando fuisse Christianos, Christiq Ecclesias, certis testimoniis ostendit noster Nicolaus Trigaultius. Sic quoque Iacobus Tirinus, eiusdem societatis homo, licet statuat, Evangelium non clam, ut tempore Apostolorum contigit, toto orbe promulgandum esse, sed publicè & solenniter, permittentibus, imò & amplexantibus il-ud omnibus regibus & regnis terrae. addit tamen, id non simul fore, nisi fortè sub finem mundi, sed successivè & vicissim. In quibus verbis notandum, quòd ipse Iesuita haereat, an sub finem mundi Evangelium iterum illustri quodam modo praedicari debeat. Errant certè procul ambiguo, qui sibi persuadent, evidenter ex h. l. posse evinci, quòd sicuti Apostolorum tempore atque ante Hierosolymae eversionem Evangelium in toto orbe praedicatum fuit: ita similiter ante mundi finem omnibus populis, etiam illis, qui gratiam praedicationis Evangelicae oblatam malitiosè reiecerūt, iterum praedicari debeat, quòdq;

ampliùs nemo praedicato Evangelio repugnaturus sit. Quem contra errorem disputat Dn. Ursinus in Introduct. ad Apoc. p. 114. seqq. it. p. 192. seqq. item B. Par. Dispp. Elencht. super Evang. Dom. Miseriocord. p. 773. Denique contra Calvinianos observandum, quòd si Evangelium, & quidem iuxta Christi mandatum, Matth. 28 19.Marc. 16, 15. in universo praedicatum orbe fuit, (id quod etiam prolixè & egregiè ostendit, merito suo satis celebris inter Reformatos Theologos Daniel Chamier tom. 2. Panstrat. lib. 16. c. 3.) vocationis gratia universalis sit, ac nemo ex absoluto quodam DEI decreto à salute aeter-â sit exclusus. Calvinianorum exceptionibus fiet satis in Analectis ad Marc. 16, 15. add. quoq; Anal. ad Matth. 28, 29.)*

*( In testimonium &c. Conf. Rom. 1, 20.Ioh. 12, 48.)*

*( Tunc veniet consummatio. Tum urbis, tum orbis terrarum. Ita enim loquitur Salvator de interitu urbis, ut simul respiciat ad interitum totius orbis, seu ad consummationem seculi.)*

## 24:15
v. 15. Abomination &c. Abomination of desolation by Hebrew is abominable desolation. *(See similar examples of the Hebrew idiom Matth. 5, 22.Rom. 9, 31.1. Cor. 1, 21.Gal. 3, 14. &c.)* But the Savior understands the beginning of that desolation, when, namely, the Romans rushed into Judea and besieged Jerusalem, Luc. 21, 20. Suidas. βδέλυγμα έρημωσεως τον Αςριανού τού βασιλέως ανςριανβα. The same elsewhere: βδέλυγμα έρημωσεως, οημειον της έρημωσεως. ησαν ειηονες τινές απηγορορμέναι τω νομω εις ρούβα ειοηομιζομεναι. ο ςη πιλατος πεποιηηαι νύητωρ εις τόν ναόν τού βσιλέως ειηόνα εισαγαγαν. Βδέλυγμα in Holy Scripture it signifies an idol everywhere: sometimes by metonymy it denotes the men themselves contaminated by idolatry, and on that account to be abominated. Therefore the Roman forces are called abomination, because they were abominable through idolatry and profane rites. Abomination of desolation, because they brought desolation and extreme devastation to the temple and the city. *(This opinion is of Augustine ep. 80. to Hesych of Origen tr. 26. of the Author of the Work -mperf. &c. Not only does he embrace the same, but also from parallel passages of the other Evangelists, and likewise

Daniel c. 9, 27. B. D. Frantzius confirms in de Interpr. Sc. S. page 1148. The same pleases B. D. Glassius in Gr. Sacrae p. 39. Mr. D. Danhawerus in Id. Boni Interpr. p. 166 B. D. Calixtus in Concord. Evang. p. 309. from the Papists Franciscus Lucas in h. l. from the Calvinists Hugo Grotius in h. l. Who himself however not so much He understands military forces, rather than standards, by τό βδέλυγμα, and this is because the standards not only had the figure of a cross, to which shields were affixed one above the other, and on them were engraved the images of the Caesars who had been deified; but also because the standards were worshipped on account of those images. And that same Jesuit Maldonatus at the cited place shows at length that Titus placed those standards in his camp, as if it were a temple contrary to the Jerusalem temple. Others oppose this opinion, as it was also the opinion of others before Grotius, that the Roman forces cannot be understood, since the desolation is said to stand in the holy place, that is, in the temple, in which, however, the Roman army, just as perhaps the standards, stood only after it was devastated. But it must be noted that not only the temple, but also the whole district around the city was considered holy by the Jews, as Grotius shows in the same place. Theodore Beza in his greater Annotations on this passage thinks that Christ is looking back to Daniel 12, 11, where the Septuagint use the same phrase as the Savior: but his fellow Socinian Ludovicus Cappellus rightly denies this in his Spicilegium, p. 31, conveniently warning that Daniel, both in chapter 11, 31 and in chapter 12, deals with the persecution which the Jews suffered from Antiochus Epiphanes. Between that and the one which the same people suffered from the Romans, although there is some similarity, it is nevertheless certain that the Prophet Daniel in the cited places looked directly only to the former. Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius, and some others explain it as the statue of Titus placed in the temple. But this opinion is not undeservedly opposed, both because Josephus, the most diligent historiographer of Jewish affairs, makes no mention of this matter, and because it would have been too late a sign for flight. Alphonsus Tostatus on this passage, question 89, Cardinal Baronius in volume 1 of his Annals, and Cornelius Jansenius in his Harmony of the Gospels explain it as the crimes of the Zealots, who had occupied the temple and were committing many unspeakable things in it, as is found in Josephus, book 6 of the Jewish War, chapter 1. And Seb. Barradius and Corn. à Lapide judge this opinion to be better than the rest on this passage. The Jesuit Tirinus and Franc. Lucas on this passage accept it as referring both to the Zealots and to the profane Roman eagles and phalanxes. B. D. Hunnius on this passage understands the idolatrous statue of Caesar Caligula, which by the order of Caesar was brought into the Jerusalem temple by Petronius, the governor of Syria, in the name of Jupiter. But because this happened under Caligula, and the destruction of the city followed only under Vespasian, with an interval of about thirty years, the same man thinks that both Petronius and his successors, the governors of Syria and Judea, acted at the request of the Caesars so that that abominable statue might be left in the holy of holies against the will of the Jews, and that it would not be lawful to remove it and cast it out from there. So that, standing in the holy place for the entire time that lies between that act of Caligula and the overthrow of the city, it might be a continuous sign of the profanation and calamity soon to follow, foretold by both Daniel and Christ. To this opinion, which the Blessed Doctor Osiander in his Gloss. Bibl. and several others also embrace, the Blessed Doctor Frantzius objects many things in de Interpret. Sc. S. Orac. 124. p. 1138. et seqq. Furthermore, Felicianus Capito, Archbishop of Avignon, in his Expl. Cathol. part. 2. pag. 604. et seqq., comments on this passage as follows: It is a blasphemy which heretics fabricate in this place, teaching: that the Roman Pontiff is that abomination, concerning which Daniel prophesied as the final sign of the devastation of the city of Jerusalem and of the end of the whole world: and which Christ confirms: because, they say, sitting in the house of GOD, he orders himself to be adored as GOD. It is (I say) a blasphemy: since no one has ever seen the Roman Pontiff sitting in the temple of GOD, so that he might exhibit himself to be adored as God, etc. Resp. 1. Whether by abomination, both in Daniel ch. 9 (which passage is parallel to the present one) and in this passage, the Western AntiChrist, that is, the Roman Pontiff, is understood, there is not one single opinion of all the Doctors of our Church. For there are those who affirm it, and there are others who deny it. The Blessed Doctor Frantzius, in the place cited a little before, when he had recounted that St. Jerome had asserted in this passage, that which is said here concerning the Abomination of desolation can be taken either simply concerning the AntiChrist, or concerning the image of Caesar etc., adds this: concerning the first (namely, whether it can be taken concerning the AntiChrist) There is nothing that we should care about, since it is certain to everyone today that those words cannot be understood concerning the Antichrist. See also the blessed D. Gesner, Disputation on chapter 9 of Daniel, § 193 & 194. On the contrary, others judge that the Roman Pontiff is described by Christ in Daniel chapter 8 and also in this place as clearly as if a historian had described him. Thus the Lord Theologians of Saxony determine in Fundam. Defens. Pupillae p. 713. Add also Flacius, part 1, Clav. Script. col. 6. B. Par., although he easily grants in his Academic Homilies on the explanation of the Gospel for the 25th Sunday after Trinity, that the Savior is speaking about the destruction of Jerusalem, and that therefore in that way and respect the abomination of desolation is not understood as the Antichrist, because however the destruction of Jerusalem was a type of the destruction of the world, from which he further infers that the Antichrist, who is the Roman Pontiff, is the revelation that will precede the end of the world. Capito himself also confesses that it is the common opinion of interpreters that the abomination, of which there is speech here, will be a sign of the consummation of the whole world. He adds that all who have written understand it then concerning the Antichrist. Now indeed the R. P. is the Antichrist, since all and singular the marks of the Antichrist belong to him. Therefore. 2. It is false that it is blasphemy to say that the R. P. is that -bomination, which will precede the consummation of the whole world. Nay rather, it is the truth itself, since it is revealed to us in the H. S. 3. Nor do those things move us which Felicianus opposes with little success, namely that the R. P. does not sit in the temple of GOD, in such a way that he presents himself to be adored as God. For who does not know that the Church is called in the H. S. the temple of GOD, 1. Cor. 3, 16 17. 2. Cor: 6, 16. Since therefore the Roman Pontiff sits in the Church, that is, in that assembly in which even now very many spiritual sons and daughters are begotten to God through the word and Sacraments, although the ministry is corrupted, it certainly cannot be denied that he himself sits in the house of GOD. It does not escape us indeed that most of the Fathers understand by the temple of GOD in this place the Jerusalem temple: but Jerome judges the truer opinion to be that the Antichrist will sit in the Church, just as also Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, and Oecumenius prefer to understand by the name of temple the temples of Christians, as the Jesuit Barradius himself notes in book 9, chapter 6, Commentary on the Gospel, p. 571.

But that must be proven, that the Roman Pontiff presents himself to be adored as God. But it is to be noted here that common saying, there is no need for words where the testimonies of things are present. Although therefore the Roman Pontiff proclaims himself the servant of servants, it is known that these are mere frauds and verbal deceptions, since it escapes no one that intolerable pride by which the Roman Pontiff exalts himself above everything that is called God, that is, above Emperors, Kings, and Princes, striving to cast them down from their thrones whenever it seems good to him. Nor do we say that the Roman Pontiff presents himself to be adored, but with the Apostle discussing the Antichrist 2 Thess. 2, 4. we profess that he exalts himself above everything that is God. Nor can it be denied that the Roman Pontiff also exalts himself above the true God, by preferring his own mandates to divine precepts, as has already been shown by our people. But Felicianus urges, that no one of the Catholics, explaining either the passage of Daniel or this of the Evangelists, has written that the Roman Pontiff is the predicted abomination. He adds: For Jerome says: this can be accepted either of the image of Caesar, which Pilate placed in the Temple, or of the equestrian statue of Hadrian, which remained in the very holy of holies up to that time. Resp. Although the Doctors of the primitive Church perhaps do not explain the abomination of desolation in clear words concerning the Roman Pontiff, they nevertheless hint not obscurely that it is to be so accepted, since they teach that it can be accepted most simply concerning the Antichrist. Thus S. Jerome has it explicitly, which Felicianus, poorly conscious of himself, conceals: nay, the Jesuit himself Sebast. Barradius, Professor of Sacred Letters in the Academy of York, book 9, Commentary on the Concordance of the Gospels, chapter 3, notes that not only Jerome is of this opinion, but also Irenaeus book 5, chapter 25, Hilary in Canon 25, Ambrose, and the interlinear Gloss. Nay, Barradius himself in the cited place demonstrates at length that by the abomination of desolation, the Antichrist is understood here. That this is the Roman Pontiff, all and singular the marks attributed by Daniel, Paul, and John to that great Antichrist, who was predicted by them to come, which singular marks fit no one better than the Roman Pontiff, sufficiently teach. Compare B. Par. Disputations Elencht. page 1302, and very many other authors who have written about the Antichrist, alleged by us elsewhere. What that even in the midst of the Papacy there have not been lacking witnesses of heavenly truth, who do not hesitate to profess publicly that the Roman Pontiff is the Antichrist, namely that Great one, predicted by Christ, Daniel, Paul, and John. Let their testimonies be seen in B. Par. Catholic Confession, book 2, Spec. part 1, article 3, chapter 6. Ioannes Paludanus, Doctor and Professor of Theology at Louvain, in Theological Vindications, page 230, urges against the explanation of this passage concerning the Roman Antichrist, that Daniel predicted not of the Roman, but of the Jerusalem desolation. Concerning this, he adds, the ancients, Irenaeus, Jerome, Chrysostom, &c., understand it everywhere. But we respond: The position of one is not the negation of another. Nor does it follow that, because the prophecy of Christ deals literally with the sign preceding the destruction of Jerusalem, therefore it cannot be accepted even by mystical and typical accommodation concerning the sign of the last day, that is, the tyranny of the Anti-Christ. For Christ so prophesies here concerning the signs of the destruction of Jerusalem, that He simultaneously deals with the consummation of the age, of which, just as the destruction of Jerusalem was a type, so some signs of the destruction of Jerusalem were immediate types of the sign that would precede the last day. And among them, that concerning the abomination of desolation is also accustomed to be referred. Whence also Felicianus Capito grants that interpreters commonly accept it concerning the Anti-Christ, supposing those who determine that the Savior is dealing here with the consummation of the age or the signs that would precede the consummation of the age . That Jerome among others accepts it thus, was shown above. And similarly, even before Jerome, Irenaeus explained it in book 5 against heresies, chapter 21. Furthermore, no one of our side, as far as I know, explains this passage concerning the devastation or Roman desolation, that is, that Rome is to be overturned, but that the Roman Pontiff, through his Anti-Christian dogmas, is to bring about a horrendous and abominable desolation or corruption of orthodoxy or of the Church. Let the pious consider whether those horrendous Papal dogmas are not an abomination concerning the adoring of saints, whom they call deceased, likewise the blessed host, images of the saints, celibacy, likewise forced, or rather concerning the whoredoms of Monks and Priests, in which it is considered a lighter offense if they keep a concubine than if they contract marriage. Conf. B. Par. Dispp. Elencht. p. 1300. & 1301. Finally, some Jesuits, as Pererius book 10. Comm. in c. 9. Dan. & others, [explain] this abomination concerning They take it as the idol of Antiochus. But Christ, just as the Angel also does in Daniel, does not speak of more remote signs, but of those closest to the overthrow of Jerusalem. Yet the idol of Antiochus was placed in the temple of Jerusalem 160 years before the coming of Christ, as Pererius himself is forced to concede: whence this prophecy, or the abomination of which there is speech here, cannot be taken directly concerning it.)*

*( εη τόπω άγίω. Grotius rightly determines that this is to be taken not concerning the temple itself (inasmuch as it was not a sign of a future disaster, but the disaster itself most present), but in the sight of the temple, in the ground around the city; and that this ground is called holy because it ought to have been sacred to the one GOD, not to the gods of the nations. And he proves that the region around Jerusalem was also held in this way, from book 1 of Mark, chapter 10, 31, and from Josephus.)*

Qui legit, intelligat. [Let him who reads, understand.] i.e., let him read with attention: And thus not only the prophetic writings, but the whole Holy Scripture is to be read.See John 5:39, Acts 17:11, 2 Peter 1:19.)*

Latin:

v. 15. Abominationem &c. Abominatio desolationis per Ebr. est abominabilis desolatio. *(Vid. similia dicti Ebr. exempla Matth. 5, 22.Rom. 9, 31.1. Cor. 1, 21.Gal. 3, 14. &c.)* Intelligit verò Salvator initium istius desolationis, quando scil. Romani in. Iudaeam irruerunt & Hierosolymam obsedeunt, Luc. 21, 20. Suidas. βδέλυγμα έρημωσεως τον Αςριανού τού βασιλέως ανςριανβα. Idem alibi: βδέλυγμα έρημωσεως, οημειον της έρημωσεως. ησαν ειηονες τινές απηγορορμέναι τω νομω εις ρούβα ειοηομιζομεναι. ο ςη πιλατος πεποιηηαι νύητωρ εις τόν ναόν τού βσιλέως ειηόνα εισαγαγαν. Βδέλυγμα in Sc. Sacrâ passim significat idolum: interdum per metonymian notat homines ipsos idololatriâ contaminatos, & eo nomine abominandos. Dicuntur ergo abominatio Romanorum copiae, quia erant idololatriâ & profanis ritibus abominabiles. Abominatio desolationis, quia templo & urbi desolationis & extremam vastitatem attulerunt. *(Sententia haec est Augustini ep. 80. ad Hesych Orig-nis tr. 26. Autoris Operis -mperf. &c. Eandem amplectitur non solùm, sed etiam ex locis parall. reliquorum Evangelistarum, itemq;

Daniele c. 9, 27. confirmat B. D. Frantzius de Interpr. Sc. S. pag. 1148. Eadem arridet B. D. Glassio Gr. Sacrae p. 39. Dn. D. Danhawero Id. Boni Interpr. p. 166 B. D. Calixto Concord. Evang. p. 309. ex Pontificiis Francisco Lucae in h. l. ex Calvivinianis Hugoni Grotio in h. l. Qui ipse tamen non tam copias militares, quàm signa per τό βδέλυγμα intelligit, idque ideò quia signa non solùm crucis habebant figuram, quibus clypei alter super alterum affixi, iis que Caesarum eorum, qui in divos relati, imagines insculptae; verùm etiam quia propter eas imagines signa adorabantur. Atque ista signa Titum in castris suis posuisse, quasi templum Hierosolymitano contrarium, idem ille prolixè ostendit l. c. Iesuita Maldonatus. aliiq; opponunt huic sententiae, ut quae & aliorum fuit ante Grotium, quòd non possint intelligi Romanorum copiae, cùm desolatio dicatur stare in loco sancto h. e. in templo, in quo tamen devastato demum exercitus Romanorum, sicuti & signa foriè, steterint, Verùm notandum, quòd non solùm templum, sed & totus districtus circa urbem sanctus fuerit à sudaeis reputatus, prout ibid. ostendit Grotius. Theodorus Beza in Annot. mai. h. l. existimat, Christum respicere ad Daniel 12, 11. ubi LXX. eâdem, quâ Salvator, utuntur phrasi: Verùm rectè id negat eiusdem sociennus Ludovicus Cappellus in Spicil. p. 31. commodè monens, quòd Daniel tum c. 11, 31. tum. c. 12. agat de persecutione, quam Iudaei perpessi sunt ab Antiocho Epiphane. Inter quam ac eam, quam perpessi fuerunt iidem à Romanis, licet similitudo aliqua sit, certum tamen est, quòd Propheta Daniel ll. cc. ad illam solùm directè respexerit. Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Euthymius & alii nonnulli de statua Titi in templo collocatâ exponunt. Ast sententiae huic non immeritò opponitur, tum quòd Iosephus, historiographus rerum ludaicarum diligentissimus, nullam rei huius mentionem faciat, tum quòd nimis serum fugae signum id fuisset. Alphonsus Tostatus in h. l. q. 89. Cardinalis Baronius tom. 1. Annal. Cornelius Iansenius in Conc. exponunt de sceleribus Zelotarum, qui templum occupaverant, & in eo multa nefanda committebant, ut est apud Iosephum lib. 6. de B. I. c. 1. Atque hanc sententiam reliquis meliorem iudicant Seb. Barradius ac Corn. à Lapide in h. l. Iesuita Tirinus ac Franc. Lucas h. l. accipiunt tùm de Zelotis, tùm de profanis Romanorū aquilis ac phalangibus. B. D. Hunnius in h. l. intelligit statuam Caesaris Caligulae idololatricam, quae nomine lovis iussu Caesaris à Petronio Syriae praeside templo Hierosolymitano illata fuerit. Quia verò hoc accidit sub Caligula, & excidium urbis demum sub Vespasiano sequutum est, interiecto triginta circiter annorū spacio, existimat idem, & Petronium & successores eius, Syriae ac Iudaeae praesides Caesarum postulatu hoc egisse, ut abominabilis illa statua contra voluntarem Iudaeorum in sancto sanctorum relinqueretur, & ne fas esset, illam removere, & inde eiicere. Ut ita stans in loco sancto per integrum id tempus, quod ab illo Caligulae facto usque ad eversionem urbis interiacet, continuum fuerit signum mox secuturae profanationis & calamitatis, à Daniele simul & Christo praenunciatae. Huic sententiae, quam etiam B. D. Ofiander in Gloss. Bibl. aliique nonnulli amplectuntur, multa opponit B. D. Frantzius in de Interpret. Sc. S. Orac. 124. p. 1138. seqq. Coeterùm Felicianus Capito, Avinionensis Archi Episcopus Expl. Cathol. part. 2. pag. 604. seqq. ita in h. l. commentatur: Blasphemia est, quam hoc loco confingunt haeretici, docentes: Romanum Pontificem esse abominationem illam, de quâ veluti extremo signo devastationis urbis Ierusalem & totius orbis finis vaticinatus est Daniel: & quem confirmat Christus: quia inquiunt, in domo DEI sedens, iubet se tanquam DEUM adorari. Blasphemia (inquam) est: quoniam Romanum Pontificem, nunquam in templo DEI sedentem, ut se tanquam Deum exhiberet adorandum, vidit quispiam &c. Resp. 1. Num per abominationem cùm apud Danielem c. 9. (qui locus praesenti parallelus est) tum h. l. AntiChristus Occidentalis s. Romanus Pontifex intelligatur, non una omnium nostrae Ecclesiae Dd. sententia est. Sunt enim, qui affirmant, sunt rursus, qui negant. B. D. Frantzius loco paullò ante alleg. cùm recensuisset, quòd S. Hieronymus in h. l. adservisset, posse id, quod de Abominatione desolationis hîc dicitur, accipi aut simpliciter de AntiChristo, aut de imagine Caesaris &c. huc subiicit: de primo (nempe num de AntiChristo accipi possit) nihil est, quod curemus, siquidem omnibus hodie certum est, de AntiChristo ea verba non posse intelligi. Conf. quoque B. D. Gesnerus Disp. in c. 9. Danielis §. 193. & 194. Contrà alii Pontificem Romanum apud Danielem c. 8. tùm etiam h. l. à Christo ita clarè descriptum censent, ac si Historicus illum descripsisset. Ita statuunt Dnn. Theologi Saxonici in Fundam. Defenf. Pupillae p. 713. Add. quoque Flacius part. 1. Clav. Script. col. 6. B. Par. licet facilè largiatur in Homiliis Acad. in expl. Ev. Dom. 25. post Trinitatis, quòd Salvator loquatur de excidio Hierosolymitano, quòdq; adeo eo modo & respectu per abominationem desolationis non intelligatur AntiChristi, quia tamen excidium Hieros. typus fuit interitûs mundi, unde porrò infert, quòd praecessura fit mundi finem AntiChristi, qui Pontifex Romanus, revelatio. Ipse etiā Capito fatetur, quòd communis Interpp sententia sit, abominationem, de qua hîc sermo, futurū signum consummationis totius orbis. Addit, quòd tunc de Anti Christo intelligant, quotquot scripserunt. Iam verò P. R. est AntiChristus, cùm omnes & singulae AntiChristi notae illi competant. Ergò. 2. Falsum est, blasphemiam esse dicere, quòd P. R. sit illa -bominatio, quae totius orbis consummationem praecessura sit. Imò potiùs est ipsa veritas, quippe in Sc. S. nobis revelata. 3. nec quicquam movent, quae Felicianus parum feliciter opponit, nempe quòd P. R. non fedeat intemplo DEI, ita quidem, ut setanquam Deum adorandum exhibeat. Etenim quem fugit, quòd Ecclesia in Sc. S. dicatur templum DEI,1. Cor. 3, 16 17.2. Cor: 6, 16. Cùm igitur Pontifex Romanus in Ecclesiâ h. e. in illo coetu, in quo adhuc plurimi spirituales filii & filiae Deo per verbum & Sacramenta generantur, licèt ministerium sit corruptum, sedeat, sanè negari nō potest, quòd ipse in domo DEI sedeat. Non fugit equidem nos, Patrum plerosque per Templum DEI h. l. intelligere templum Hierosolymitanum: ast Hieronymus veriorem censet sententiam, quòd AntiChristus in Ecclesia sessurus sit, quemadmodum etiam Chrysostomus, Theodoretus, Theophylactus & Oecumenius nomine templi, Christianorum templa intelligi malunt, ceu ipse Iesuita Barradius l. 9. c. 6. Comm in Conc.

Ev. p. 571. notat. Ast illud videtur probandum, quòd P. R. se ut Deum adorandum exhibeat. Verùm notandum hîc tritum illud, non opus est verbis, ubi rerum testimonia adsunt. Licet proinde P. R. se servum servorum proclamet, notum est, quòd merae sint fraudes ac verborum praestigiae, cùm neminem fugiat intolerabilis illa superbia, quâ P. R. sese supra omne, quod Deus nominatur h. e. supra Imperatores, Reges ac Principes, ex-ollat, illos ipsos, quando ei visum fuerit, è thronis suis deiicere satagens. Nec dicimus, quòd P. R. sese adorandum exhibeat, sed cum Apostolo de Anti Christo disserente 2 Thess. 2, 4. profitemur, quòd supra omne, quod Deus est, sese extollat. Nec id quoque negari potest, quòd P. R etiam supra verum Deum sese efferat, mandata sua praeceptis divinis praeferendo, uti iampridem à nostratibus ostensum. Sed urget Felicianus, quòd nemo unquam Catholicorum vel Danielis locum, vel hunc Evangelistarum exponens, scripserit. Pontificem Romanum esse abominationem praedictam. Addit: Hieronymus enim ait: hoc posse accipi vel de imagine Caesaris, quam Pilatus posuit in Templo, vel de Adriani equestri statua, quae in ipso sancto sanctorum usq ad illius tempor a permansit. Resp. Licèt primitivae Ecclesiae Dd. desolationis abominationem de Pontifice Romano fortè non claris exponant verbis, haut obscurè tamen innuunt, quòd ita accipiāt, quippe de Anii Christo simplissimè accipi posse docentes. Sic ita disertè habet S. Hieronymus, quod malè sibi cōscius dissimulat Felicianus: imò ipse Iesuita Sebast. Barradius, Sacr. litt. in Ebor. Acad. Professor l. 9. Comm. in Conc. Ev. c. 3. sententiae huius esse notat non Hieronymum saltem, verùm etiam -renaeum l. 5. c 25. Hilarium Canone 25. Ambrosium ac Glossam interlinearem. Imò Barradius ipse l. c. prolixè demonstrat, quòd per abominationem desolationis Anti Christus hîc intelligatur.) Hunc verò Pontificem Romanum esse omnes ac singulae notae à Daniele, Paulo ac Iohanne Anti Christi illi magno, qui venturus ab ipsis praedictus fuit, attributae, quae singulae aulli me-iùs, quàm Pontifici Romano competunt, satis docent. Conf. B. Par. Dispp. E-encht. p. 1302. item auctores alii plurimi, qui de Anti Christo scripserunt, alibi à nobis allegati. Quid quòd nec in medio Papatu defuerint veritatis coelestis testes, qui publicè profiteri non dubitant, Pont. Romanum esse AntiChristum, puta illum Magnum, à Christo, Daniele, Paulo ac Iohanne praedictum. Videantur illorum testimonia apud B. Par. Confess. Cath. lib. 2. Spec. part. 1 art. 3. c. 6. Ioannes Paludanus, Theol. D. & Profess. Lovan. in Vindiciis Theol. pag. 230. urget contra explicationem huius loci de Anti Christo Romano, quòd Daniel praedixerit non de Romana, sed de Hierosolymitanâ desolatione. De hâc, addit, passim intelligunt veteres, Irenaeus, Hieronymus, Chrysostomus &c. Verùm respondemus: Unius positio non est alterius negatio. Nec sequitur, vaticinium Christi litteraliter de signo eversionem Hieros. praecessuro agit, ergo ne quidem per accommodationem mysticam & typicam de signo extr. diei h. e. Anti Christi tyrannide accipi potest. Etenim ita Christus de signis eversionis Hierosolymorum hîc vaticinatur, ut simul agat de seculi consummatione, cuius uti typus fuit eversio Hierosolymitana, ita signa eversionis Hieros. nonnulla, typi fuerunt proximi signi diem novissimum antecessuri. Et inter ea referri quoque solet illud de abominatione desolationis. Unde etiam Felicianus Capito largitur, quòd Interpp. communiter de Anti Christo accipiant, puta qui de consummatione seculi seu signis seculi consummationem praecessuriSalvatorem hîc agere statuunt. Hieronymum inter alios ita accipere, suprà ostensum fuit. Similiterque iam ante Hieronymum exposuit Irenaeus lib. 5. advers. haeres. c. 21. Praeterea nemo nostratium, quantum mihi constat, h. l. exponit de vastatione sive desolatione Romanâ h. e. quòd Roma sit evertenda, sed quòd P. R. per Anti Christiana sua dogmata horrendam & abominandam desolationem seu corruptelam orthodoxiae seu Ecclesiae sit all aturus. Cogitent pii, annon abominatio sint horrenda illa dogmata Papalia de adorandis sanctis, quos vocant, defunct-s, item hostiâ benedictâ, imaginibus sanctorum, coelibatu item coacto vel potiùs de scortationibus Monachorum & Sacerdotum, in quibus levius censetur delictum, si concubinam alant, quàm si matrimonium contrahant. Conf. B. Par. Dispp. Elencht. p. 1300. & 1301. Tandem Iesuitae nonnulli, uti Pererius lib. 10. Comm. in c. 9. Dan. & alii abomin. hanc de Antiochi accipiunt idolo. Verùm Christus, quemadmodum etiam Angelus apud Danielem, non loquitur de signis remotioribus, sed proximis eversionis Hierosol. Ast Antiochi idolum positum fuit in templo Hierosol. 160. annis ante Christi adventum, ceu ipse Pererius concedere cogitur: unde de eo vaticinium hoc seu abominatio, quâ de hîc sermo est, directè accipi non potest.)*

*( εη τόπω άγίω. Non de ipso templo (utpote quod nota venturae cladis non erat, sed ipsa clades praesentissima) verùm in templi conspectu, in solo circa urbem, accipiendum hoc esse, rectè statuit Grotius; dici verò solum hoc sanctum, quòd DEO uni, non gentium Diis sacrum esse oportuerit. Atq; ita etiam regionem illam circa Ierusalem fuisse habitam, idem è l. 1. Marc. c. 10, 31. ac Iosepho probat.)*

*( Qui legit, intelligat. h. e. cum attentione legat: Atque ita non prophetica solùm scripta, sed tota Sc. S. legenda est. Vid. Ioh. 5, 39.Act 17, 11.2. Petr. 1, 19.)*

## 24:16
v. 16. Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, epistle 210, explains it mystically. Let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains: i. e., those who are fixed and strengthened in piety (for that is what Judea signifies) let them cast their eyes to the sublime refuge, namely, fenced and fortified by the protection of their own confession. But he who is on the housetop, let him not descend to take anything from his house. i. e., he who has despised the present house and counted it for nothing, and has trampled underfoot the whole scene of this life, and has become high and sublime in life, and has banished the internal motions of the soul, let him draw nothing from them, not fear, not sloth, not vain glory, not the desire for wealth, for that is what a descent from signifies. But Christ speaks literally in this place. Whence also the Christians, mindful of this warning, when the Roman army approached, withdrew into the town of Pella, as witnessed by Eusebius, book 3 of Church History, chapter 5. Josephus also testifies that at the beginning the exit was free. The Jews, on the contrary, were shut in as if in prisons, for on account of the feast they had flowed into Jerusalem in a huge number from outside regions as well, and were being reserved for divine vengeance. See Josephus in Eusebius, book 3 of Church History.

chapter 5. But that Christ exhorts the pious, when the siege of Jerusalem is impending, to flee into the mountains, Franc. Lucas thinks this was said from the common custom of those fleeing, by which those fleeing are accustomed to betake themselves to the mountains and to pathless and inaccessible places. Since the Romans also conquered the mountains of Judea, and the Christians, observing the warning of the Savior, did not flee into the mountains, but into the city of Pella, under the dominion of Agrippa. Add also Epiphanius, book on weights and measures, and Nicephorus, book 3 of Church History, chapter 3.)*

To the mountains. There were three principal mountains. 1. Sinai, to which we may flee through true contrition. 2. Sion, to which we may flee through the confident apprehension of Christ. 3. Thabor, to which we may flee through renewal. *(There are those who think that an allusion is made here to the history of Lot, Gen. 19 1-. Although furthermore the best remedy in calamities is, in the stated manner, to flee to God through true and serious repentance: yet it ought by no means to be considered simply prohibited that we might also sometimes use bodily remedies. If indeed it is done in such a way that the honor of God and conscience is not harmed, the Church is not exposed to the snares of enemies, and scandal is not offered to others. This is what a Minister of the Church ought to observe above all. But to that which Tertullian, book on flight in persecution, ch. 4, opposes, namely that persecution comes from God, we respond by giving an instance concerning diseases, which are likewise sent by God, and yet it is not prohibited to use medicine. But especially relevant here is Christ's 1. precept, Matth. 10, 23. 2. example, Matth. 12. 15c. 14, 13. proposed to us, and therefore also to the ministers of the Church as an example, in personal persecutions. This is what St. Augustine long ago warned, tract. 15 on John. He could indeed, he writes concerning Christ, not be held by them while present, if He did not wish it: not be killed, if He did not wish it; because He could also not be born, if He did not wish it: but because in everything which He performed as a man, He was providing an example for men who were to believe in Him: because every servant of God does not sin if he has withdrawn into another place, seeing the fury perhaps of those persecuting him, or seeking his soul for evil. But the servant of God would seem to sin if he did so, unless the Lord had gone before in doing it; that good Master did this, to teach, not because He was afraid. Conf. The same, ep. 180 to Honoratus. it.

Socrates book 3. H. E. ch. 6. Nicephorus Callistus book 10. H. E. ch. 16. and you may see the Analecta above on ch. 10, 23. it. B. Par. Dispp. Elencht. on the Sunday Gospels p. 1305.)*

Latin:

v. 16. Tunc qui in Iudaea sunt, fugiant in montes. I sidorus Pelusiota l. 1. epist. 210. mysticè exponit. Qui in Iudaeâ sunt, fugiant ad montes: i. e. qui in pietate fixi ac firmati sunt (nam id Iudaea sonat) ad sublime perfugium oculos con-iciant, suae videlicet confession is praesidio septi ac communiti. Qui autem in tecto est, non descendat, aliquid tollere de domo suâ. i. e. qui praesentem domum contemsit ac pro nihilo duxit, atq omnem huiusce vitae scenam pedibus protrivit, vitâq altus & sublimis effectus est, & intestinos animorum motus ablegavit, nihil ex ipsis attrahat, non metum; non ignaviam, non inanem gloriam, non opum cupiditatem, id enim ex al-o descensus significat. Sed Christus h. l. litteraliter loquitur. Unde etiam Christiani, moniti huius memores, cùm Romanus exercitus adventaret, secesserunt in oppidum Pellam, teste Eusebio l. 3 Hist. Eccl. c. 5. Iosephus quoque testatur, initiò liberum fuisse exitum. Iudaei contrà tanquam carceribus conclusi, nam propter festum è regionibus quoque exteris ingenti numero Hierosolymam confluxerant, divinae ultioni adservabantur. Vid. Iosephus apud Eusebium lib. 3. Histor.

Eccles. c. 5. Quòd verò Christus hortatur pios, ingruente Hierosol, obsessione, in montes confugere, id Franc. Lucas ex vulgari fugientium consvetudine, quâ fugientes ad montes & loca invia atque inaccessa se recipere solent, dictum putat. Siquidem Romani etiam montes Iudaeae expugnârint, & Christiani, monitum Salvatoris observantes, non in montes, sed in urbem Pellam, sub Agrippae ditione, confugerint Add quoque Epiphan. lib. de mens. ac Nicephorus l. 3. H. E. c. 3.)*

Admontes. Montes tres erant potiores. 1. Sinai, ad quem confugiamus per veram contritionem. 2. Sion, ad quem confugiamus per fiducialem Christi apprehensionem. 3. Thabor, ad quem confugiamus per renovationem. *(Sunt qui alludi hîc censent ad historiam Lothi, Genes. 19 1-. Licèt porrò optimum in calamitatibus remedium sit, dicto modo per veram ac seriam poenitentiam ad Deum conf-gere: hautquaquam tamen simpliciter prohibitum censeri debet, quò minùs etiam corporalibus remediis quandoque utamur. Si nempe id ita fiat, ne honor DEI ac conscientia laedatur, Ecclesia hostium insidiis exponatur, aliis scandalum praebeatur. Id quod cumprimis observare Minister Ecclesiae debet. Ad illud verò, quod Tertullianus l. de fuga in persecut. c. 4. opponit, videl. quòd persecutio à DEO eveniat, respondemus, dando instātiam de morbis, qui itidem à DEO immittuntur, neq; tamen prohibitum est, medicinâ uti. Cumprimis verò huc facit Christi 1. praeceptum, Matth. 10, 23. 2. exemplum. Matth. 12. 15c. 14, 13. nobis, adeoq; etiam Ecclesiae ministris ad exemplum, in personalibus persecutionibus, propositum. Id quod pridem monuit S. August. tr. 15. in Iohannem.
