Sicuti iris potuit ordinari à Deo post diluvium, ut esset signum divinae gratiae, licèt iam ante diluvium fuerit, ita quoque eclipses, cumprimis si cumulentur, possunt esse signum extremi diei, licet aliàs sint naturales. Huc inclinat B. D. Hunnius h. l. qui tamen addit, fieri posse, ut Sol & Luna etiam supernaturali aliquâ ratione obscurentur, ut luce multò debiliore fulgeant, & promtum hinc sit statuere, finem mundi ante fores esse. Idē sentit B. D. Quistorpius in h. l. Quidā, ut Hilarius, Hieronymus, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus exponunt, mysticè & allegoricè, de luce doctrinae in Ecclesia per corruptelas obscuratâ. Christus n. cùm sit Sol iustitiae, laetitiae & vitae, à quâ Ecclesia, quae est Luna, omnem splendorem ac lucem accipit: obscuratâ igitur coelestis Doctrinae luce per traditionum humanarum tenebras, spirituales in Ecclesiâ sequi tenebras, necesse est. Vid. B. Par. l. c.) *

Stellae de coelo cadent. i. e. Christo cedent, & suo loco movebuntur. * (suxta Chrysostomum homil. ad Neoph. t. 5. Alii tamen, ut Hieronymus ac Beda, quos sequuntur Scholastici, item Corn. à Lapide in h. l. exponunt per TÒ ita obscurari, ut hominibus videantur coelo excidisse, cùm Scriptura saepè loquatur de rebus, non ut in se sunt, sed uti hominibus apparent. Qui allegorias sectantur, accipiunt cum autore Op. Imperf. metaphoricè de magnorum Ecclesiae Dd. apostasiâ. Quò faciunt dicta Ps. 14. 12.Apoc. 8, 10,12.c. 12, 4.Dan. 8, 10. Augustinus lib. 20. de C D. c. 24. accipit de exhalationibus in aëre accensis, & post conflagrationem decidentibus. Alii ex Ioelis 3, 15. exponunt h. m. cadent non ratione substantiae, sed lucis, quia lumen suum retrahent, ut quasi è coelo cecidisse, nec ampliùs in eo esse videantur. Ita accipit B. D. Hunnius, nempe de inclinatâ stellarum virtute & imminente earum lumine. Alii denique figuratè & comparatè accipiunt hoc sensu: Tanta erit totius machinae coelestis concussio, ut stellae ipsae è coelo cadere putentur. Sententias has ordine recenset B. Par. L. de Extr. Iudic. §. 99. ac concludit, eventum ac diem Domini omnium optimè illa expositurum. B. D. Calixtus lib. de Suprem. Iudic. p. 7. omnia haec de ingentibus saltem calamitatibus accipit, siquidem qui his obruuntur, iis coelum mole suâ incūbere terra tremere, lux in tenebras, dies candidus in atrum verti dicatur. Atque ita habitum animi, in maximo metu & dolore constituti, describi solere. Confert in hanc rem loca Amos. 8, 9. Ioel. 2, 30.Es. 13, 10.c. 34, 5.Ezech. 32, 7.) *

Virtutes coelorum i. e. firmamentum coel. ste & Angeli sese movebunt. Ita Tossanus, vel etiam exercitus, quia δυνὰμεις etiam exercitum significant, sicut LXX. Dominus Sebaoth reddide. runt κύριος δυνάμεων. Vide Theodor. in Epit. Divin. Dogm. Drusium l. 10. Observ. c. 14. Quidam * (ut Augustinus, Hieronymus, Gregorius) * intelligunt de Angelis, qui Ebraeis dicuntur צבאת השמים Quidam exponunt h. m. virtutes coelorum i. e. coeli quantumvis robustissimi, per hypallagen Ebraeam. Virtutes coelorum i. e. coeli virium h. e. viribus pollentes seu firmissimi. * (Conformis est huic sententiae eorum opinio, qui de virium coelestium decremento haec accipiunt. item qui exponunt de insigni aliquâ in coelo aethereo & aêreo mutatione ac mirabili eius facie, ita ut denotentur inusitata chasmata, cometae, turbines ventorum, grandines, novae stellae &c. quam interprationem coeteris praefert B. Parens L de Extr. Iudic. §. 100. Cornelius à Lapide in h. l. existimat, planissimè per virtutes coelorum accipi polos & cardines, q. d. Coeli oinnes in fine mundi concutientur & à suis polis & cardinibus convelletur, ut deorsum ruere videantur. Putatque, alludere Christum ad Iob. 26, 11. ac Esaiae 34, 4. Hugo Grotius nomine οὐρανοῦ existimat indicari Ecclesiam Christianam, ut ita indicetur magna rerum mutatio in Ecclesia. Sed non opus est, ut absq; urgente necessitate à littera discedamus.) *

## 24:30
v. 30. The sign of the Son of man. Some understand by the Son of man the Son of man himself, as the most certain sign of his coming to judgment, just as Abraham is said to have received the sign of circumcision, that is, circumcision itself, Rom. 4, 11. to which opinion it seems to favor that Matthew ἐξηγητικῶς seems to subjoin: And then they shall see the Son of man etc., and that the remaining Evangelists omit that sign, and simply say, then they shall see the Son of man, finally that it is not new or unusual in the Scriptures for Christ himself to be called a sign, Es. 7, 14.Luc. 2, 34. (This opinion seems to please Origen among the ancients in tr. 30 in Matth., and among the more recent ones B. D. Luther t. 2. epist. f. 155. b., B. D. Glassius Gramm. S. p. 15., B. D. Calixtus Concord. Evang. p. 312.) Some understand by the sign of the Son of man likewise the Son of man himself, but they explain this phrase, They shall see the Son of man marked, i.e., the body of the man marked with wounds, namely with scars, etc., which interpretation, as it has probability both from that which is subjoined, then all the tribes of the earth shall wail, and from Zach. 12, 10. and Apoc. 1, 7. it seems it can be reconciled, so the Author of the Opus Imperfectum in Matthew, homily 49, declares the same at length. (But this, just as the preceding opinion, seems to be opposed by the fact that Matthew distinctly says, the sign of the Son of man shall appear in heaven, and then they shall see the Son of man etc.) Tossanus thinks it can be taken concerning a certain special brightness and lightning, which shall precede Christ, and in a moment shall extend itself through the world (but this opinion rests on mere conjecture). Some take it concerning the image of the cross to be seen in the air. Closest to this opinion approaches that which is expounded concerning the sign of the cross, which most of the ancients embrace. See Blasius de Viegas in Apoc. p. 42. Compare B. Par. L. de Extr. Iud. §. 101. and in Harm. Ev. c. 161. where he brings forward to this opinion Hippolytus the Martyr in his Oration on the Consummation of the World, Methodius in his Oration on the Consummation of the World, Hilary canon 25 in Matthew, Cyril of Jerusalem Catechesis 15, Chrysostom homily 77 in Matthew, Jerome, Theophylact, Euthymius, and Bede on chapter 24 of Matthew; likewise Ephrem, who wrote a special oration on the appearance of the cross at the time of judgment. To establish this opinion, it is usually brought forward: 1. that Christ speaks of the sign of the Son of man as of some certain and known sign. Now, it is known that Christ suffered and was crucified. 2. that Constantine the Great, about to fight against Maxentius, saw the figure of a cross in the sky with this inscription: in this sign you shall conquer, as witnessed by Eusebius, book 1, on the life of Constantine the Great. 3. that the Church has sung from ancient times concerning the sign of the cross: This sign shall be in heaven, when the Lord shall come to judgment. 4. that it seems most fitting to establish that the sign of the cross will then appear publicly with great splendor, both for the glory of the cross and of the pious, and for the confusion and ignominy of the infidels, etc., as B. Par. deduces these things at greater length in H. E. in the said place, p. 743 and 744, where he also subjoins that he does not disapprove of this opinion of the pious ancients; meanwhile, however, since that very cannot be established with apodictic certainty, for that reason all things must be committed to the future event. Cornelius à Lapide, both in this place and in Post. Epist. Petr. c. 3, 12, [cites] the common [opinion] of the Papists, (see Gregorius de Valentia vol. 4, Comm. col. 3313, Bessaeus Conc. 4, de Extr. Iudic. part 5, Osorius vol. 2, Concion. p. 915, Tiraeus de glorios. Filii appar. c. 12. &c.) having followed the opinion, he accepts concerning of the very wood of the cross, to which indeed Christ was affixed, (and which now divided into the smallest particles, is proposed among relics to be viewed in many places, nay even to be adored,) which cross, just as also other instruments and monuments of the passion of Christ, are to be then divinely reformed, carried by Angels, and demonstrated to the world. The same thing Gretser also defends at length in book 1 of the Cross, chapter 92. But Suarez, part 3, volume 2, Disputation 57, section 2, having followed Anselm in the Elucidarium, Antoninus, part 4, title 24, chapter 11, section 4, Tostatus, Jansenius, and others commenting on this place, and also Thomas Aquinas in 4, distinction 48, question 1, article 2, to the second, and also opusculum 2, chapter 43, judges that opinion to be more conformable to the ancient Fathers and more probable, which holds that that sign of the cross will be formed only from the air. Which opinion is favored both because miracles should not be multiplied without sufficient foundation (would that the Papists observed this elsewhere too). But truly and especially, because for this matter there seems to be need of a sign of the cross far greater than the true cross is. And in this very opinion rests also the most famous Jesuit Adam Tanner, Scholastic Theology, volume 4, Disputation 2, question 4, doubt 3, number 99. So that those Papists are inept, who attempt to cloak the religious worship of the particles of the cross, which they are accustomed to display everywhere, with that opinion. Against which error, or more truly idolatry, besides our own men, Daniel Chamier disputes at length, volume 2, Panstratia, book 22, chapters 4 and 5. Jerome in this place asserts that there will be some standard of the triumphant victory, to which is akin the opinion of Chrysostom in the homily on the cross and the thief, which is attributed to Augustine, and is sermon 130 on the season. This opinion is favored among the more recent by Mr. Ursinus, Theologian of Regensburg, in the Introduction to the Apocalypse, page 333. B. Mr. Aegidius Hunnius in this place accepts it as a new and a certain unusual star, the announcer of the Lord's advent. Hugo Grotius [takes] that sign properly, or the evident argument of the divine power of Christ , for the Church (which heaven is said) to be brought forth for good, it is thought to be noted here, because it is described Apoc. 19, 11. where John says that he saw heaven opened, and in it a white horse. The white horse, however, he continues, as is gathered from a comparison of the history of Jewish affairs, which is in the same Apocalypse c. 6. is the pure preaching of Evangelical doctrine. This, therefore, Christ says is to be restored after so many corruptions of morals, doctrine, and government in not a few places, with a certain wonderful efficacy, through the ministry of those witnesses who are to come in the spirit of Moses and Elijah. That the restoration of sound doctrine will be especially among the Jews, he himself contends. What is to be thought of this opinion has been explained elsewhere. In this place we note at least this, that the Savior distinguishes the sign of the Son of Man from the preaching of the Gospel, since he had dealt with that in v. 14. Daniel Heinsius understands by sign a vocal sign, which will strike terror into all, namely a trumpet, which is itself also called a sign, and to give a sign. But Christ speaks here not of an audible sign, but of a visible one. For he says expressly: καὶ τότε φανήσεται. Mr. D. Friedlieb in this place determines, that the simplest meaning is that the clouds are indicated, in which Christ is to return visibly to judgment, just as he once ascended visibly in them to the heavens.Acts. 1.Apoc. 1.) *

* (And then all the tribes of the earth shall mourn. Ambrose lib. 10. in Luc. p. 151. whom some Calvinists follow, thinks that this interior grief and exterior lamentation will have a place only in the impious alone: but Blessed Luther determines, that not even the pious will be entirely immune from this anxiety and fear of mind. The causes of which, Blessed Par. L. de Extr. Iudic. §. 102. notes will be 1. the severity of divine wrath. Conf. Sap. 5, 18. Rom. 1, 18. 2. The tyranny and cruelty of the devil. See Apoc. 12, 12. 3. The extreme impiety of men Matt. 24, 12.Hos. 4, 2.2. Petr. 3, 4. 4. The heap of punishments and manifold calamity. We do not, however, deny in the least that this mourning should be taken more principally of the impious. For they will mourn for this reason, because they crucified him, whom it was fitting to be adored, according to Chrysostom. (Conf. also the author of the Imperfect work homil. 49. likewise Bernard serm. 16. in Cantic. add. Apoc. 6, 15. seqq.) or, as Blessed D. Hunnius has it, because they will so tremble and be terrified at the sight of the supreme judge that they will no longer be able to collect themselves from those ineffable terrors, but will be absorbed from there into despair and damnation. Therefore we must be vigilant, lest the last day find us unprepared. See. Luc. 21, 36. see below v. 42. Let us acknowledge our sins, and let us lament the same here, lest we be compelled to weep then, but too late. Matth. 26. last. Luc. 7, 38.)

(And they shall see the son of man &c. Conf. Dan. 7, 13.Matth. 26, 64. Grotius rightly explains these things concerning the last coming of Christ, inasmuch as it is described in a similar manner Act. 1, 9.11. and 1. Thess. 4, 16., who nevertheless, moved by I know not what reasons, draws the preceding things elsewhere.)

(Coming in the clouds. Therefore the return of Christ will be local. Conf. 1. Thess. 4, 17. and our people write this in express words. See B. D. Luth. Confess. on the Supper, Brentius in the book on the union of the two natures p. 81. B. Par. L. on the Last Judgment §. 35. Therefore the pronouncement of Marcus Frid. Wendelin is false, when in the Greater System page 1247 he does not fear to write, that the Lutherans, through the absurd hypothesis of ubiquity, deny that the return of Christ to judgment will be local. This assertion of the same man is also false, that, our hypothesis standing, a negative follows. The contrary has long since been shown by our people. Let there be seen, besides authors just now alleged, B. D. Hutt. LL. Th. p. 182. B. Schr--derus in Scept. Reg. Chr. p. 663. Furthermore, our people probably gather from this place that the extreme judgment will precede the total conflagration of the world. Conf. c. 26, 64. Apoc. 14, 14.Marc. 13, 26.Luc. 21, 27. and B. Par. L. on the Last Things in general §. 11. 1)

(With power and great glory. Conf. above c. 19, 27. 28. below c. 25, 31. also Luc. 227, 69.Ebr. 1, 3.c. 8, 1.c. 12, 2. See B. D. Chemn. book on the two natures in Christ c. 24. p. 129. Power will appear in the resuscitation of the dead, the administration of judgment and the execution of the sentence, that is, the glorification of the pious, but the casting of the impious into hell . Majesty in the splendor of the body, the beauty of the company of Angels, the brightness of the thunders &c.)

Latin:

v. 30. Signum Filii hominis. Quidam per Filium hominis intelligunt ipsum Filium hominis, tanquam signum certissimum adventûs eius ad iudicium, sicut Abraham dicitur accepisse signum circumcisionis h. e. ipsam circumcisionem, Rom. 4, 11. cui sententiae favere videtur, quòd Matthaeus ἐξηγητικῶς subiicere videatur: Et tunc videbunt Filium hominis &c quòdq; reliqui Evangelistae illud signum praetermittunt, ac simpliciter dicunt, tunc videbunt Filium hominis, deniq; quòd in Scripturis novum non sit aut insolitum, Christum ipsum vocari signum, Es. 7, 14.Luc. 2, 34. * (Arridere sententia haec videtur ex veteribus Origeni tr. 30. in Matth. ex recentioribus B. D. Luthero t. 2. epist. f. 155. b. B. D. Glassio Gramm. S. p. 15. B. D. Calixto Concord. Evang. p. 312.) * Quidam per signum Filii hominis itidem intelligunt ipsum Filium hominis, sed phrasin h. m. exponunt, videbunt Filium hominis signatum, i. e. corpus hominis signatum vulneribus, nempe cicatricibus &c. cui interpretationi uti probabilitas tum ex eo, quod subiicitur, tunc plangent omnes tribus terrae, tum ex Zach. 12, 10. ac Apoc. 1, 7. conciliari posse videtur, ita eandem prolixè declarat Autor Oper. Imperf. in Matth. hom. 49. * (Sed huic sicuti & praecedenti sententiae obstare videtur, quod Matthaeus distinctè dicit, apparebit signum Filii hominis in coelo, & tunc videbunt Filium hominis &c.) * Tossanus putat, accipi posse de speciali quadam claritate & sulgure, quod Christum praecedet, & in momento per mundum se extendet * (sed haec sententia merâ nititur coniectura) * Quidam accipiunt de imagine crucis in aēre cōspiciendâ. Huic sententiae proximè accedit ea, qua de signo crucis exponitur, quam amplectuntur pleriq; veterum. Vid. Blasius de Viegas in Apoc. p. 42. * Conf. (B. Par. L. de Extr. Iud. §. 101. & in Harm. Ev. c. 161. ubi in hanc sententiam adducit Hippolytum Martyrem in Orat. de Consumm. seculi, Methodium in Orat. de mundi consummatione, Hilarium can. 25. in Matth. Cyrillum Hierosol. Catech. 15. Chrysostom. hom. 77. in Matth. Hieronymum, Theophylactum, Euthymium, & Bedam in c. 24. Matth. it. Ephremum, qui peculiarem orationem de apparitione crucis tempore iudicii, scripserit. Pro hâc sententia stabiliendâ afferri solet, 1. quòd Christus de signo filii hominis tanquam de certo aliquo & noto signo loquatur. Iam verò notum est, Christum passum fuisse ac crucifixum. 2. quòd Constantinus M. contra Maxentium pugnaturus viderit crucis figuram in coelo, cum hâc inscriptione: in hoc signo vinces, teste Euseb. l. 1. de vit. Constant. M. 3. quòd Ecclesia iam indo ab antiquis temporibus de signo crucis canat: Hoc signum erit in coelo, cùm Dominus ad iudiciū venerit. 4 quòd convenientissimū videtur statuere, signum crucis tum publicè magno cum splendore appariturum, tum ad crucis & piorum gloriam, tum ad infidelium confusionem & ignominiam &c. ceu pluribus haec deducit B. Par. in H. E. d. l. p. 743. & 744. ubi etiam subiicit, quòd hanc piorum veterum sententiam non improbet; interim tamen cùm ea ipsa apodicticâ certitudine stabili non possit, propterea futuro eventui omnia committenda sint. Cornelius à Lapide tum in h. l. tum in Post. Epist. Petr. c. 3, 12. communem Pontificiorum, (vid. Gregorius de Valentia t. 4. Comm. col. 3313. Bessaeus Conc. 4. de Extr. Iudic. part. 5. Osorius t. 2. Concion. p. 915. Tiraeus de glorios. Filii appar. c. 12. &c.) opinionem sequutus, accipit de ipso ligno crucis, cui nempe Christus affixus fuerit, (& quae nunc minimas in particulas divisa, inter reliquias pluribus in iocis spectanda, imò adoranda proponitur,) quae crux, sicut & alia passionis Christi instrumenta ac monumenta divinitus sint tunc reformanda, ab Angelis portanda, ac mundo demonstranda. Idem hoc prolixè quoque defendit Gretserus l. 1. de Cruce c. 92. Ast Suarez part. 3. t. 2. Disp. 57. sect. 2. sequutus Anselmum in Elucid., Antoninum 4. part. tit. 24. c. 11. §. 4. Tostatum, Iansenium aliosque Comm. in h. l. it. Thomam de Aquino in 4. dist. 48. q. 1. art. 2. ad 2. nec non opusc. 2. c. 43. antiquis Patribus conformiorem ac probabiliorem censet eam sententiam, quae tenet, signum illud crucis solùm ex aëre formatum iri. Cui sententiae faveat tum quòd miracula abssufficienti fundamento non sint multiplicanda (quod utinam & alibi Pontificii observarent.) tum verò & praesertim, quia ad hanc rem opus esse videatur signo crucis longè maiori, quàm sit verae crucis. Atque in hâc ipsâ sententia acquiescit etiam Iesuita famosissimus Adamus Tannerus Theol. Scholast. t. 4. Disp. 2. q. 4. dub. 3. n. 99. Ut adeò inepti sint Pontificii illi, qui religiosum particularum crucis, quas ostentare passim solent, cultum palliare opinione illâ conantur. Quem contra errorem, vel idololatriam veriùs, praeter nostrates, prolixè disputat Daniel Chamier. t. 2. Panstr. lib. 22. c. 4. & 5. Hieronymus in h. l. adserit, fore aliquod vexillum victoriae triumphantis, cui affinis est sententia Chrysostomi homil. de cruce & latrone, quae Augustino tribuitur, & est sermo 130. de tempore. Favet huic sententiae è recentioribus Dn. Ursinus, Theologus Ratisbonensis in Introduct. ad Apocal. p. 333. B. D. Aegid. Hunnius in h. l. accipit de novâ & insolitâ quadam stellâ, adventûs Dominici praenuncia. Hugo Grotius propriè illud signum, sive divinae Christi potentiae evidens argumentum, Ecclesiae (quae coelum dicatur) bono editum, notari hîc arbitratur, quod describatur Apoc. 19, 11. ubi Iohannes dicit, vidisse se coelum apertum, & in eo equum cādidum. Equus autem candidus, pergit, ut ex collatione historiae rerum. Iudaicarum, quae in eadem Apocalypsi est, colligitur c. 6. est pura Evangelicae doctrinae praedicatio. Hanc igitur dicit Christus post tot non paucis in locis, morum, doctrinae & regiminis corruptelas mirâ quadam efficaciâ restituēdam esse, per ministerium illorum testium, qui venturi sunt in spiritu Mosis & Eliae. Eam verò restaurationem sanae doctrinae cumprimis apud Iudaeos fore, ipse contendit. Quâ de opinione quid habēdum sit, alibi expositum. Hoc loco illud saltem notamus, quòd Salvator signum filii hominis distinguat ab Evangelii praedicatione, quippe de quâ v. 14. egerat. Daniel Heinsius per signum intelligit signum vocale, quod terrorem omnibus sit incussurum, tubam scilicet, quae & ipsa signum dicatur, & signum dare. Verùm Christus loquitur hîc non de audibili signo, sed de visibili. Expressè enim dicit: καὶ τότε φανήσεται. Dn. D. Friedlieb in h. l. statuit, simplicissimam esse sententiam, indicari nubes, in quibus Christus visibiliter ad iudicium rediturus, prout in eis ad coelos olim visibiliter adscendit.Actor. 1.Apocal. 1.) *

* (Et tunc plangent omnes tribus terrae. Ambrosius lib. 10. in Luc. p. 151. quem Calviniani nonnulli sequuntur, interiorem hunc dolorem & planctum exteriorem in solis impiis duntaxat locum habiturum existimat: ast B. Lutherus statuit, ne pios quidem ab hac animi anxietate & metu prorsus futuros immunes. Cuius causas fore notat B. Par. L. de Extr. Iudic. §. 102. 1. irae divinae severitatem. Conf. Sap. 5, 18. Rom. 1, 18. 2. Diaboli tyrannidem & crudelitatem. Vid. Apoc. 12, 12. 3. extremam hominum impietatem Matt. 24, 12.Hos. 4, 2.2. Petr. 3, 4. 4. Poenarum congeriem & multiplicem calamitatem. Minimè tamen negamus, quòd principaliùs ploratus hic de impiis accipi debeat. Ideò verò hi plorabunt, quia crucifixerunt eum, quem adorari oportebat, iuxta Chrysostomum. (Conf. & autor operis Imperf. homil. 49. item Bernhardus serum. 16. in Cantic. add. Apoc. 6, 15. seqq.) vel, uti habet B. D. Hunnius, quia ita ad supremi iudicis conspectum trepidabunt & expavescent, ut ex inenarrabilibus illis terroribus sese recolligere ampliùs haut queant, sed inde in desperationem & damnationem absor. beantur. Vigilandum igitur, ne imparatos nos dies extremus deprehendat. Vid. Luc. 21, 36. seqq. infrà v. 42. Agnoscamus nostra peccata, eademque hîc deploremus, ne tunc, sed nimis serò, plorare cogamur. Matth. 26. ult. Luc. 7, 38.) *

* (Et videbunt filium hominis &c. Conf. Dan. 7, 13.Matth. 26, 64. Rectè haec de ultimo Christi adventu, utpote qui Act. 1, 9.11. ac 1. Thess. 4, 16. simili modo describatur, exponit Grotius, qui tamen praecedentia, nescio quibus motus rationibus, aliorsum trahit.) *

* (Venientem in nubibus. Localis ergo erit Christus reditus. Conf. 1. Thess. 4, 17. idque disertis verbis scribunt nostrates. Vide B. D. Luth. Confess. de Coena, Brentium lib. de unione duarum natur. p. 81. B. Par. L. de Extr. Iudic. §. 35. Falsum prionde est Marci Frid. Wendelini pronunciatum, quando in Syst. Maiori pag. 1247. scribere non veretur, Lutheranos per absurdam hypothesin ubiquitatis negare, Christi reditum adiudicium fore localem. Falsum & hoc est eiusd. adsertum, quòd stante nostrâ hypothesi, negativa sequatur. Contrarium pridem ostensum à nostratibus est. Videantur praeter a-tores modò allegatos, B. D. Hutt. LL. Th. p. 182. B. Schr--derus in Scept. Reg. Chr. p. 663. Porrò probabiliter ex h. l. nostrates colligunt, iudiciū extremum antecessurum esse totalem mundi conflagrationē. Conf. c. 26, 64. Apoc. 14, 14.Marc. 13, 26.Luc. 21, 27. ac prolixè hâc de re disserentem B. Par. L. de Noviss. in genere §. 11. 1) *

## 24:31
(v. 31. And he shall send his angels with a trumpet. The mission of Angels is a work belonging to GOD alone. Because therefore to Christ both here, and elsewhere, see Apoc. 1, 1.c. 22, 6. is attributed, from which it is proved, among other things, that he himself is the true God. Thus Grotius also considers it an argument for divine power, that a trumpet or an omnipotent voice is attributed to Christ, which is otherwise attributed to GOD himself Exod. 20, 18.Ps. 47, 6. But a trumpet is also attributed to the Angels, because they themselves will be the attendants and heralds of Christ. However, it seems that this phrase refers to the custom of the Jews, who used a trumpet in calling together the people, see Numer. 10, 12.Ps. 81, 4. Some understand by this trumpet the voice of the son of GOD himself,Ioh. 5, 28.1. Cor. 15, 52.1. Thess. 4. 16.Apoc. 12, 7. others a blast, formed by the Angels. The reasons which can be brought forward for either side are presented by the Blessed Par. L. on the Resurrection of the Dead §. 66, who leaves the whole matter in the middle. But he deservedly criticizes the idle disputation of Suarez, whether that trumpet is to be of silver or of bronze. The Blessed D. Hunnius understands by the voice of the trumpet the voice and thunder of the omnipotent GOD. And he adds: That voice and trumpet of GOD is indeed heard every year in the storms and clouds of heaven: but it was heard most of all formerly in the promulgation of the Decalogue. But this storm was merely particular, nor was it heard in the whole world, like that final one, which with its tremendous crash will move the vast globe of the earth from its foundations and convert it into nothingness. The same man notes that this blast is attributed to the Angels, because the Lord will stir up that storm by their ministry.) *

* (They shall gather his elect from the four winds. i. e. from the four corners of the world, from where the winds blow. Compare Es. 43, 5. 6.Marc. 13, 27.Apoc. 7, 1. Furthermore, concerning the process of the final judgment, especially whether it is to be celebrated in the valley of Jehoshaphat, which Corn. à Lapide in this place and the Papists commonly desire, the Blessed D. Calixtus in his separate book on the Final Judgment, and the Blessed Par. L. on the Final Judgment §. 5, treat at length. Let the Blessed D. Tarnovius and other Commentators on Joel c. 3, v. 2. 12 also be compared. We learn also from this, what among other things is the office of the Angels. For they delight in the salvation of the pious. Compare Luc. c. 15, 10.c. 16, 22. above 13, 30. 39. Apoc. 14, 15. following. Let us therefore show ourselves worthy of the fellowship of the Angels by a holy life &c.) *

* (from the ends of the heavens i. e. from the regions of the lands, subject to the diverse quarters of the sky. Compare similar expressions Deut. 4, 32.c. 28, 94.Ps. 19, 7.) *

Latin:

* (v. 31. Et mittet angelos suos cum tubâ. Missio Angelo-um est opus soli DEO competens. Quia igitur Christo tum hîc, tum alibi, vid. Apoc. 1, 1.c. 22, 6. tribuitur, inde ipsum verum Deum esse, inter alia probatur. Sic divinae quoque potentiae argumentum censet Grotius, quòd tuba sive omnipotens vox Christo tribuatur, quae aliàs ipsi DEO tribuitur Exod. 20, 18.Ps. 47, 6. Angelis verò etiam tribuitur tuba, quia ipsi illi erunt Christi accensores ac praecones. Videtur autem respici hac phrasi ad consuetudinem Iudaeorum, qui in convocando populo tubâ utebantur, vid. Numer. 10, 12.Ps. 81, 4. Quidam per hanc tubam intelligunt vocem ipsius filius DEI,Ioh. 5, 28.1. Cor. 15, 52.1. Thess. 4. 16.Apoc. 12, 7. alii clangorem, ab Angelis formatum. Sed haec tempestas erat duntaxat particularis, nec toto audiebatur mundo, ceu illa novissima, quae tremendo suo fragore vastissimum terrarum orbem eximis sedibus commovebit & in nihilum convertet. Angelis verò tribui istum clangorem, monet idem, quòd ipsorum ministerio illam tempestatem Dominus sit excitaturus.) *

## 24:32
v. 32. παραβολὴν. A parable here in general signifies a likeness or a comparison. In that way it is accepted Mark 3, 23.c. 4, 30.

now learn the parable from the fig tree. When the branch is ἁπαλὸς tender, moist i.e. and succulent, τὰ φύλλα ἐκφύῃ the leaves sprout again, so that the word ἐκφύειν is placed intransitively. * (Symbolically this is accustomed to be explained by some in this way: Just as with the leafing fig tree a most joyful summer is imminent, which produces the sweetest fruits: so when you shall have seen the elect leafing with such patience, in the winter of such great tribulations, know that the summer of resurrection and happiness is at hand) *

* ( τὸ θέρας. summer, It is accepted here in a broader signification, by which it also embraces spring, and that in the Hebrew manner, since in the H. S. the year is divided into at least two parts, summer and winter. They are accustomed, however, also the same to distinguish the year into four parts in our manner, just as Schindler in the Pentaglot Lexicon p. 778 recounts the names of all the parts.) *

Latin:

v. 32. παραβολὴν. Parabola hîc in genere significat similitudinem sive comparationem. Eo modo accipitur Marc. 3, 23.c. 4, 30.

à ficu autem discite parabolam. Cùm ramus est ἁπαλὸςtener, humidus sc. ac succulentus, τὰ φύλλα ἐκφύῃfolia repullulant, ut verbum ἐκφύειν ponatur intransitivè. * (Symbolicè hoc ita exponi à nonnullis solet: Sicut frondente ficu imminet aestas laetissima, quae suavissimos fructus producit: sic cùm videritis electos frondere tantâ patientiâ, in hieme tantarum tribulationum, scitote quòd instet aestas resurrectionis & felicitatis) *

* ( τὸ θέρας.aestas, Accipitur hîc in latiori significatione, quâ etiam ver complectitur, idque more Ebraeo, cùm in Sc. S. annus in duas saltem dividatur partes, aestatem & hyemem. Solent tamen etiam iidem annum in quatuor partes distingvermore nostro, quemadmodum nomina omnium partium recenset Schindl. Lexico Pentagl. p. 778.) *

## 24:34
v. 34. This generation shall not pass away &c. Theophylact explains it in two ways. The generation, i.e. of the Apostles, shall not depart, and thus these things will be understood concerning the captured Judea: or the generation of those faithful to Christ and believing the Gospel shall not depart, so that it may be accepted concerning the end of the world. * (thus together with Origen, Hilary, Chrysostom, the Blessed D. Calixtus accepts it in Concord. E. p. 312.) * It is understood most simply, that many of those who were living then, are to live so long, until those disasters happen. For the destruction happened in the fortieth year after this prediction. According to Tossanus the sense is, those things which I have already predicted to you, which are to happen before my coming to judgment, will begin to be fulfilled shortly, es wird noch ben Mannes -eben anfangen crf-llet zu werden/ because the destruction of the temple, the dissipation of the people, the seductions of the False Prophets, the rumors of wars &c. followed within a few years. * (And in this way also Grotius understands it. But the Blessed D. Hunnius accepts it concerning the whole present world, the end of which is not to be expected before these things happen, all which Christ predicted concerning the signs preceding the consummation of the age. Mr. D. Friedlieb writes in this place that the best opinion is that of Luther, Winckelmann, Bakius,) That Christ wished to teach that the Jews, in the destruction of Jerusalem, were not to be utterly destroyed, but were to endure among men like a sign even to the consummation of the age; and he judges that this is relevant here, Rom. 11, 25 *

Latin:

v. 34. Aetas haec non praeteribit &c. Theophylactus bifariam explicat. Non abibit aetas, sc. Apostolorum, atque ita intelligentur haec de captâ Iudaeâ: vel non abibit aetas Christo fidelium & credentium Evangelio, ut de mundi fine accipiatur. * (ita iuxta cum Origine, Hilario, Chrysostomo accipit B. D. Calixtus Concord. E. p. 312.) * Simplicissimè intelligitur, quòd multi ex illis, qui tunc vivebant, tamdiu victuri sint, donec clades illae eveniant. contigit enim excidiū anno quadragesimo post hanc praedictionem. Iuxta Tossanum sensus est, quae vobis iam praedixi, ante adventum meum ad iudicium eventura, incipient brevi impleri, es wird noch ben Mannes -eben anfangen crf-llet zu werden/ quia destructio templi, dissipatio populi, Pseudoprophetarum seductiones, bellorum rumores &c. intra paucos annus sunt secuta. * (Atque h. m. etiam intelligit Grotius. Verùm B. D. Hunnius accipit de toto mundo praesente, cuius non priùs sit expectandus finis, quàm haec fiant omnia, quae de signis antecessuris seculi consummationem Christus praedixit. Dn. D. Friedlieb in h. l. optimam sententiam esse Lutheri, Winckelmanni, Bakii, scribit, quòd Christus docere voluerit, Iudaeos in vastatione Ierosolymorum non esse totaliter delendos, sed ad consummationem seculi velut signum inter homines perduraturos, ac facere huc censet Rom. 11, 25) *

## 24:35
v. 35. Heaven and earth, etc. Some think that this is a comparison of unequal things, with an impossibility being adduced, as being the easier case. But in reality there is an opposition, affirming that heaven will pass away. *(and indeed according to substance. Namely, the force of the opposition. For in whatever sense and respect the word of GOD is said to remain, in that same sense heaven and earth are said to pass away. Now the word of GOD is said to remain by reason of its οὐσία, or material being: for according to its πάθη or accidents — namely its being read, being written, etc. — it will not remain. So heaven and earth are said to pass away in this sense, because their οὐσία will pass away. Cf. B. Par. L. de Consumm. seculi; also Comm. in Post. Epist. Petri p. 413 ff.; likewise B. D. Hunnius on this passage. Cornelius à Lapide, on this passage, in order to uphold the opinion of the Papists — namely that the world will perish not according to substance, but only according to qualities — adds that this saying could be taken not assertively, but comparatively; as if to say: the heavens will sooner pass away than my words. Just as, therefore, the heavens will never perish, so much more shall my words — that is, my oracles and decrees — not fail, but shall actually be fulfilled. But the opposition is manifest. From this we learn further that, although heaven is judged to be naturally incorruptible, yet it will perish at GOD's command (which was also foretold by David, Ps. 102:26–27; add also Ps. 72:7; Job 14:12; 2 Pet. 3:7; Rev. 20:11), that GOD is not bound to secondary causes and the course of nature. Cf. Joshua 10:13–14; 2 Kings 20:21 (?); 3:17; 4:4, 6; the Prayer of Azariah v. 20, etc.)*

But my words &c. — namely, those things which the Lord had just now spoken concerning the end of the age, he himself asserts that these can by no means pass away, without the smallest point of them being fulfilled by a glorious event. So the blessed D. Hunnius in this passage. It can, however, also be applied in general to the divine promises. Compare Deut. 32, 4. John 3, 33. ch. 14, 6. Rom. 3, 4. ch. 4, 20. ch. 11, 29. Apoc. 6, 10.

Latin:

v. 35. Coelum & terra &c. Quidam putant, esse collationem imparium, adhibito impossibili, tanquam faciliori. Sed revera est oppositio, affirmans coelum transiturum. * (& quidem secundùm substantiam. Vinempe oppositionis. Etenim quo sensu ac respectu verbum DEI dicitur manere, eo sensu coelum ac terra dicuntur transire. Iam verò verbum DEI dicitur manere, ratione οὐσίας, seu materialis: etenim secundùm. πάθη seu accidentia, nempe lectionem, scriptionem &c. non manebit. E. coelum & terra eo sensu dicuntur transir-, quia οὐσία eorum transibit. Conf. B. Par. L. de Consumm. seculi it. Comm. in Post. Epist petri p. 413. seqq. nec non B. D. Hunnium h. l. Cornelius à Lapide ad h. l. quò Pontificiorum sententiam, quòd nempe mundus non secundùm substantiā, sed saltem secundùm qualitates sit interiturus, tueatur, addit, quòd gnome haec accipi posset non adsertivè, sed comparativè. q. d. citiùs coeli transibunt, quàm mea verba. Sicut ergò coeli nun quam peribunt, sic multò magis verbameai. e. oracula & decreta mea non excident, sed reipsa complebuntur, Verùm oppositio est manifesta. Discimus verò etiam hinc, cùm coelum iudicetur naturaliter incorruptibile, & tamen DEI iussu interiturum sit, (quod etiam à Davide praedictum Ps. 102, 26. 27. add. etiam Psal. 72, 7.Iob 14, 12.2. Petr. 3, 7.Apoc. 20, 11.) Deum non esse alligatum ad causas secundas ac naturae cursum. Conf. Iosuae 10, 13. 14. Reg. 2, 21. c. 3, 17. c. 4, 4. 6. Orat. Asariae v. 20. &c.) *

* (Verba autem mea &c. Quae nempe modò fecerat Dominus de fine seculi, haec nullo pacto praeterire posse ipse adserit, quin minutissimus illorum apex illustri eventu compleatur. Ita B. D. Hunnius in h. l. Potest tamen etiam in genere accommodari ad promissa divina. Conf. Deut. 32, 4.Ioh. 3, 33.c. 14, 6,Rom. 3, 4.c. 4, 20.c. 11, 29.Apoc. 6, 10.) *

## 24:36
Concerning that day no one knows. By "that day" is understood the day of the last judgment. Compare 2 Peter 3:10, as it is called so κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν (par excellence). See above ch. 7:22, below ch. 26:29, Luke 21:34, 1 Thess. 1:10, 2 Tim. 1:18. Elsewhere it is called the great and very terrible day, Joel 2:11. Compare Jude v. 6, Rev. 16:14; the day of Jesus Christ, 1 Cor. 1:5, 5:5, 2 Cor. 1:14, Phil. 1:6, 10, 2:16. But this present utterance of our Savior, the Best and Greatest, is to be understood not only of the present time—as though no one indeed knows the last day now, but afterward will come to know it, either by revelation, or by calculation, or by diligent comparison of Holy Scripture—but absolutely. This is what the teachers of the primitive Church long ago pointed out. St. Augustine elegantly, in book 18 of *De Civitate Dei*, ch. 53: He has loosed the fingers of all who calculate about this matter, and bidden them be still, who says: It is not for you to know the times. The same author, in his Enarration on Psalm 6: What the Lord has not willed us to know, let us willingly not know. Likewise Theophylact on this passage, writing that in saying this he also forbids them to strive to learn it afterward. So too St. Athanasius, Sermon 4 against Arius: He has restrained our curiosities, lest we attempt to know or investigate that which is unknown to the angels, and cannot be known. Irenaeus has similar statements, book 2, Against Heresies, ch. 48; so does Prosper, book 1, On the Calling of the Gentiles, ch. 8: Let us not desire to have known what God has willed to be secret. But above all the Lord willed us to be ignorant of that last day, lest we fall asleep on the pillow of false security. This is the common opinion of the Fathers. See Hilary, book 9 On the Trinity, p. 194, also canon 26 on Matthew; Ambrose, book 5 On the Faith, ch. 8; Augustine, Epistle 80 to Hesychius; Gregory the Great, Homily 13 on the Gospels; whose sayings are cited by B. Par. in his book On the Last Judgment, §76.

*(And "hour." See 1 John 2, 38. Apoc. 3, 10. c. 14, 7. 15.)*

Not even the angels of heaven. Since, therefore, the holy angels, who nevertheless rejoice in the beatific vision of God, do not know the hour of the last day, it is clear how weak is the hypothesis of certain Pontiffs, who, from the beatific vision of GOD, which is attributed to the saints (as they call them) who have died, attempt to prove that they know our calamities, our prayers, and therefore also that they may rightly be invoked. Concerning this error see the Analecta on Luke 16, 23.

"Nor the Son," etc. Erasmus holds that these words, οὐδὲ ὁ υἱὸς, are to be restored to Mark's text, since they were found in almost all the ancient manuscripts, and thus Chrysostom, Theophylact, and very many others read them. *(Hugo Grotius rightly holds the contrary, and B. D. Hutter also confirms this from Augustine and Ambrose, LL. Theol. Mai. p. 174. This is supported by the fact that all the Oriental translators omit these same words here, except only the Ethiopic, which inserts here from Mark 13:32: "nor the Son." But the question arises, how could the Son of God be ignorant of the day of the last judgment, since he himself is true God, since in him are hidden all the treasures of knowledge and wisdom, Col. 2:3, and since he knows all things, John 21:17. Answer: Here one must distinguish, 1. between the human and the divine nature of Christ. For that he himself, as God, or according to his divine nature, is not ignorant of the last day, is clear, because he is of the same essence as God the Father. Hence here that rule must be repeated which was explained elsewhere—see the Analecta on Matth. 11:27—namely, that the particle "alone," when applied to God, does not exclude the other persons of the Deity, but only creatures. 2. One must distinguish between the human nature considered in its own natural and essential principles, and the same nature as assumed into the hypostasis of the Logos. 3. Between the state of emptying (in which Christ truly was ignorant of certain things—compare Luke 2:52, Phil. 2:7) and the state of exaltation. 4. Between the use (χρῆσις) and the possession (κτῆσις) of the communicated properties. In the former sense Christ was ignorant of the day of the last judgment, but not in the latter. For how could he be ignorant of the day of the last judgment, who himself is the judge to come of the living and the dead? See John 5:22, 27; Acts 17:30. Cyril speaks plainly of this, book 9, Thesaurus, ch. 4: "He is ignorant as man." (Compare the same author's book against the Anthropomorphites, ch. 4.) Likewise Nazianzen, Orat. 36: "He knows as God, but is said to be ignorant as man." In the same way it is explained by Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, ep. 117; Ambrose, book 5, On the Faith, ch. 8; Athanasius, Orat. 4 against the Arians; Basil, ep. 1 to Amphilochius. Euthymius too, in this passage, makes mention of this explanation, though he notes that it is more fitly explained thus: "the Son does not know, except the Father"—that is, he knows inasmuch as the Father knows; for since the Father knows, the Son also knows. But B. D. Fewrbach rightly observes, in the Κενωσιγραφία, sect. VI, ch. 9, that this interpretation of Euthymius cannot stand with Christ's purpose; nor yet is he simply ignorant according to the assumed human nature as such, but rather, as we have said, insofar as that nature is considered in its own natural, essential principles. As Gregory the Great clearly teaches, book 8, ep. 42. The incarnate only-begotten in the nature of humanity indeed knew the day and hour of judgment, but yet he did not know this from the nature of humanity. Therefore, what he knew in it, he did not know from it. John of Damascus asserts the same in book 3 of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 21. Most of the ancients, as B. Par. shows at length in his book on the Final Judgment, § 76, teach that Christ denied that he knew the day of the final judgment at least in so far as he was sent as an ambassador of GOD to preach, not to reveal the day of judgment to us. B. D. Calixtus follows this opinion from among our own in Conc. Ev. p. 312, and from the Papists, Corn. à Lapide, Suarez 3. part. 9. 10. art. 2, and Bellarmine, who also cites for this opinion Gregory the Great, book 8, ep. 42, Ambrose, book 5, on the Faith, chapter 8, Jerome, Chrysostom, Theophylact on this passage, Basil, book 4, against Eunomius, and Augustine, book 1, on Genesis against the Manichaeans, chapter 22. But rightly, with B. Luther in his Sermon on the Nativity of Christ, B. Parl. in the cited book warns that there is no need for this gloss. For although it is true that Christ did not know that day for us; yet this does not at all satisfy the emphasis of the text. For the same knowledge of the final day that is taken away from men and angels is also taken away from the Son of Man. Now, indeed, men and angels are ignorant of that day not only to others, but also to themselves. Therefore, the Son of Man also was ignorant of that day for himself (namely, on account of the interrupted plenary use of the divine majesty communicated to the assumed human nature), and he did not fail to know it merely for the sake of revealing it to others. B. D. Feuerborn embraces this exposition in Κενωσιγρ. sect. 6, p. 185 ff., B. D. Hutter in LL. Mai. p. 174, Mr. D. Müller in Judaism p. 984, B. D. Quistorp on this passage, and others. Furthermore, to the Arians, who from this attempted to undermine the true deity of Christ because he is ignorant of the final day, St. Jerome opposes in his Commentary on chapter 21 of Matthew that which is read there in verse 37: They will perhaps reverence (NB. in the Greek text the particle of doubting is not found in this passage, but only in the parallel passage Luke 20, 13) my son. This, he writes, does not come from ignorance. For what would the householder not know, who in this passage is understood as God the Father? But God is said to be always in doubt, so that free will may be reserved for man. Let us question Arius and Eunomius:

Behold, the Father is said to be ignorant, and he tempers the judgment, and as far as it is in you, he is proven to have lied. Whatever they might answer on behalf of the Father, let them understand this of the Son, who says that he is ignorant of the day of the consummation. But there is no need to flee to that, since the answer is easy, if at least the distinctions brought forward at the beginning are noted. With these also observed, it will also be easy to answer those things which the Calvinists (see Chamier vol. 2, book 4, ch. 1) are accustomed to bring forward from the present passage against the communication of attributes, or against the omniscience communicated to Christ as man.

But the Father alone The name Father is accepted here essentially. For it is opposed not to the Son, nor to the Holy Spirit, who, since they are one God with the Father, also have one and the same knowledge: but to Angels and men. * (The rule of antiquity is noted: When in those things which pertain properly to the deity considered absolutely , anything is either affirmed or denied in the Scriptures concerning one person, whether of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Holy Spirit, and an exclusive particle is found added: then that exclusive is not opposed to the remaining persons: but is accommodated to excluding only those things which are outside the Trinity. Hence Cyril lib. IX. of the Thesaurus c. 4. If the Holy Spirit does not ignore the last day, as one who searches the depths of GOD,1. Cor. 2.how, I ask, will the Son ignore the same, who nevertheless is the giver and bestower of the all-knowing Spirit? Furthermore, it is clear from this place compared with Mark 13, 32. that τὸ except is not inconveniently explained by the added exclusive particle alone or only. For what Mark expresses by τὸ except, Matthew insinuates by τὸ except alone. Therefore, the Blessed Luther ought by no means to be reproved, because when the Apostle writes Gal. 2, 16. that a man is not justified, except through the faith of Jesus Christ, he himself Rom. 3, 28. expressed the same sentiment by τὸ justified by faith alone. *)

Latin:

* (v. 36. De die illa nemo scit. Per diem illum intelligitur dies extremi iudicii. Conf. 2. Petr. 3, 10. ut qui κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν ita vocatur. Vid. suprà c. 7, 22. infrà c. 26, 29. Luc. 21, 34,2. Thess. 1, 10.2. Tim. 1, 18. Dicitur aliàs dies magna ac terribilvaldè, Ioelis 2, 11. Conf. Iudae v. 6. Apoc. 16, 14.dies Iesu Christi,1. Cor. 1, 5.c. 5, 5.2. Corinth. 1, 14.Philipp. 1, 6.10c. 2, 16. Intelligitur verò praesens Salvatoris nostri Opt. Maximi effatum non solùm de praesenti tempore, quasi iam nunc quidem nemo diem extremum sciat, postea tamen vel per revelationem, vel per calculationem, vel per diligentem Scripturae Sacrae collationem id sciturus sit: sed absolutè. Id quod pridem monuerunt primitivae Ecclesiae Doctores. S. Augustinus eleganter lib. 18. de. D. c. 53. Omnium hâc de re calculantium digitos resolvit & quiescere iussit ille, qui dicit: Non est vestrum scire tempora. Idem in Enarr. Ps. 6.Quod Dominus nos scire noluit, libenter nesciamus. Similiter Theophylactus in h. l. Hoc, scribens, dum dicit, etiam prohibet, eos anniti, ut discant postea. Sic quoque S. Athanasius serm. 4. contra Arium: Refrenavit curiositates nostr as, ne, scire aut investigare tentemus id, quod Angelis est ignotum, scirinon potest. Gemella habet & Irenaeus l. 2. adv. haeres. c. 48. Prosper lib. 1. de vocatione Gentium c. 8. Non appetamus habere cognitum, quod DE us voluit esse secretum. Cumprimis verò diem illum extremum Dominus ignorare nos voluit, ne securitatis pulvinari indormiamus. Quae communis Patrum sententia est. Vid. Hilarius l. 9. de Trin p. 194. it. can. 26. in Matth. Ambrosius lib. 5. de Fide. c. 8. Augustinus ep. 80. ad Hesychium, Gregorius M. hom. 13. in Evang. quorum gnomas adducit B. Par. L. de Extr. Iudic. §. 76.) *

* (Et horâ. Vid. 1. Ioh. 2, 38.Apoc. 3, 10.c. 14, 7.15.) *

* (Ne Angeli quidem coelorum. Cùm igitur sancti Angeli, qui beatific â tamen Dei visione gaudent, ignorent diei extremi horam, patet, quàm infirma sit hypothesis quorundam Pontificiorum, dum ex visione DEI beatifica, quae sanctis, quos ita vocant, tribuitur defunctis, probare conantur, scire illos nostras calamitates, preces nostras, adeoque etiam rectè invocari. De quo errore vid. Analecta ad Luc. 16, 23.) *

Nefilius &c. Erasmus statuit, verba haecοὐδὲ ὁ -ὸςex Marco esse restituenda, cùm fuerint in libris antiquis ferè omnibus, atsic legant Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, aliiplurimi. * (Contrarium rectè tenet Hugo Grotius, idque ex Augustino atq; Ambrosio confirmat quoque B. D. Hutterus LL. Theol. Mai. p. 174. Facit huc, quòd eadem verba omnes Interpretes Orientales hîc omittant, excepto solo Aethiope, qui ex Marc. 13, 32. hîc inserit: neFilius. Coeterùm quaeritur, quomodo Filius DEI ignoret diem extremi iudicii, cùm ipse sit, verus Deus, sintin eo absconditi omnes thesauri scientiae ac sapientiae,Col. 2, 3. sciat omnia, Ioh 21, 17. Resp. Disting. hîc 1. inter humanam, ac divinam Christi naturam. Quòd enim ipse ut Deus, sive secundùm divinam suam naturam extremum diem non ignoret, patet, quia est eiusdem essentiae cum Deo Patre. Unde hîc repetēda regula illa, alibi exposita, vid. Analecta ad Matth. 11, 27. quòd particula solus de DEO adhibita, non excludat reliquas Deitatis personas, sed saltem creaturas. 2. inter naturam humanam consideratam in principiis suis naturalibus ac essentialibus, & quat. eadem adsumta in hypostasinτοὺλὸλου. 3. inter statum exinanitionis (in quo Christus verè quaedam ignoravit, Conf. Luc. 2, 52.Philipp, 2. 7.) & exaltationis. 4. inter communicatorumχρῆσιν, & κτῆσιν. Priori modo Christus diem extremi iudicii ignoravit, non verò posteriori. Quomodo enim ignoret extremi iudicii diem, qui ipse futurus iudex vivorum & mortuorum? Vid. Ioh. 5, 22.27.Actor. 17, 30. Disertè Cyrillus l. 9. Thess. c. 4. Ignorat ut homo. (Conf. idem libro contra Anthropomorphitas c. 4.) Similiter Nazianz. Orat. 36. γινώσκειὡς ὁ θεὸς, ἀγνοειν δὲ φήσινὡς ἄνσθρωπος Eodemque modo exponunt Isid. Pelus. l. 1. ep. 117. Ambros. l. 5. de fide c. 8. Athanasius Orat. 4. contr. Arian. Basilius ep. 1. ad Amphil. Mentionem quoque expositionis huius facit Euthymius in h. l. qui tamen monet, aptiùs exponi him. NeFilius scit, nisi Pater, videl. sciat: quia verò Pater scit, scit uti& filius. Sed rectè monet B. D. Fewrb. in Κενωσιγρ. sect. VI. c. 9. hanc Euthymii interpretationem cum Christi scopo consistere non posse neq; tamen simpliciter secundùm humanam naturam adsumtam ignorat, sed quat. uti diximus, in principiis suis naturalibus essentialibus consideratur. Ceu clarè docet Gregorius M. l. 8. ep. 42. Incarnatus unigenitus in naturâ quidem humanitatis novit diem & horam iudicii, sed tamen hunc non ex naturâ humanitatis novit. Quod ergo in ipsâ novit, non ex ipsâ novit. Idem quoque adserit Ioh. Damascenus lib. 3. Orthod. Fid. c. 21. Pleriq; veterum, uti prolixè ostendit B. Par. L. de Extr. Iud. §. 76. docent, Christum eatenus saltem, se diem extremi iudicii scire, negare, quatenus nempe ut DEI legatus missus erat ad praedicandum, non ut diem iudicii nobis revelaret. Sequitur hanc sententiam è nostris B. D. Calixtus Conc. Ev. p. 312. è Pontific. Corn. à Lapide, Suarez 3. part. 9. 10. art. 2. Bellarminus, qui etiam pro hâc sententia allegat Gregor. M. l. 8. ep. 42. Ambros. l. 5. de Fid. c. 8. Hieron. Chrysost. Theophylactum in h. l. Basilium l. 4. in Eunomium, August. l. 1. de Genesi contra Manich. c. 22. Verùm rectè cum B. Luthero Concion. de Natali Christi, B. Parl. l. c. monet, non opus esse hâc glossâ. Licet enim verum sit, Christum diem illum nobis nescivisse; minimè tamen hoc emphasi textûs satisfacit. Quae enim diei extremi scientia hominibus & Angelis detrahitur, eadem quoque Filio hominis detrahitur. Iam verò homines & Angeli ignorant diem illum non solùm aliis, sed etiam sibi ipsis. E. & Filiis hominis sibi quoq; diem illum (sc. ob intermissum plenarium maiestatis divinae, humanae naturae adsumtae communicatae usum) ignoravit, nec ad revelandum duntaxat aliis nescivit. Amplectuntur expositionem hanc B. D. Fewrb. in Κενωσιγρ. sect. 6. p. 185. seqq. B. D. Hutt. in LL. Mai. p. 174. Dn. D. M-llerus in Iudaismo p. 984. B. D. Quistorpius in h. l. alii. Coeterùm Arianis, qui inde veram Christi deitatem labefactare conabantur, eò quòd ignoret diem extremum, opponit S. Hieronymus Comm. ad c. 21. Matth. illud, quòd ibi v. 37. legitur. Verebuntur fortè (NB. in Graecotextu particula dubitandi h. l. non habetur, sed saltem in loco parall. Luc. 20, 13.) filium meum. Non, scribit, hoc de ignorantia venit. Quid enim nesciat paterfamilias, qui h. l. Deus pater intelligitur? Sed semper ambigere dicitur Deus, ut libera voluutas homini reservetur. Interrogemus Arium & Eunomium:

Ecce Pater dicitur ignorare, & sententiam temperat, & quantum in vobis est, probatur mentitus. Quicquid pro Patre responderint, hoc intelligant profilio, qui se dicit ignorare consummationis diem. Ast non opus est, eo confugere, cùm facilis sit responsio, si notentur saltem distinctiones initiò adductae. Quibus etiam observatis, facilè quoque erit, respondere ad ea, quae contra communicationem id omatum, seu contra omniscientiam Christo homini communicatam Calviniani (vid. Chamier t. 2. lib. 4. c. 1.) è praesenti loco afferre solent.) *

Sed solus Pater Nomen Patris accipitur hîc essentialiter. Opponitur enim non Filio, nec Spiritui Sancto, qui cùm sint unus cum Patre Deus, unam etiam eandemque habent notitiam: sed Angelis & hominibus. * (Nota est regula antiquitatis: Quando in iis, quae deitati absolutè consideratae prop-iè competunt, quippiam de unâ persona sive Patris, sive Filii, sive Spiritûs Sancti in Scripturis vel affirmatur, vel negatur, & exclusiva particula adiecta reperitur: tum ea exclusiva non personis reliquis opponitur: sed iis duntaxat, quae extra Trinitatem sunt, excludendis accommodatur. Inde Cyrillus lib. IX. Thesauri c. 4. Si Spiritus Sanctus diem novissimum non ignorat, ut qui scrutatur profunditates DEI,1. Cor. 2.quomodo quaeso, Filius ignorabit eundem, qui tamen est dator & largitor, omnia scientis Spiritûs? Coeterùm patet ex h. l. collato cum Marc. 13, 32. quòd τὸnisi non incommodè exponatur per additam particulam exclusam solus vel solùm. Quòd enim Marcus exprimit per τὸnisi, Matthaeus insinuat per τὸnisi solus. Minimè proinde reprehendi B. Lutherus debet, quòd cùm Gal. 2, 16. scribat Apostolus, hominem non iustificari, nisi per fidem Iesu Christi, ipse Rom. 3, 28. eandem sententiam expresserit per τὸiustificari solâ fide.) *

## 24:37
* (v. 37. As in the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of man. Some Papists gather from this that just as in the days of Noah the waters of the flood could not bring any harm to the starry heaven, so also the fire, by which the world will one day burn, will not ignite the celestial orbs. Resp. The comparison is not to be extended beyond the third point, for which is employed. Christ institutes a comparison between the life and morals of men who lived immediately before the flood, with the state of the last times, as is clear from the verse immediately following, but he by no means asserts that the manner of destruction will be equal in both cases. Whence also Corn. à Lapide not inconveniently explains this verse thus: As the flood was unexpected and sudden, which overwhelmed all: so my coming will be unexpected and sudden, which will encompass all. Tertullian also once erred in ad Uxor. c. 5. likewise in Exhortat. Castitatis c. 9. and Jerome in his epistle to Gerontia, while they were attacking second marriages from this place, namely because the Sodomites and the ante-diluvian men were punished by GOD, because they repeated marriages. But the Holy Scripture indicates far other causes of that divine punishment, as is clear from Gen. 6, 1. and following, and ch. 18. also Ezech. 16, 49. but by no means second marriages. Finally, how Noah was in many things a type of Christ, the blessed Pareus teaches in his Exegesis, Book on the Person and Office of Christ, § 31.) *

Latin:

* (v. 37. Sicut in diebus Noë, ita erit adventus Filii hominis. Colligunt hinc nonnulli Pontificii, quòd ceu in diebus Noê aquae diluvii non potuerunt coelo stellato ullum afferre nocumentum, ite etiam nec ignis, quo mundus aliquando conflagrabit, orbes coelestes accensurus sit. Resp. Comparatio non est extendenda ultra tertium, propter quod adhibetur. Christus instituit comparationem inter vitam ac mores hominum, qui immediatè ante diluvium vixerunt, cum statu novissimorum temporum, ceu patet ex vers. statim subsequente, nequaquam verò modum excidii utrobique parem fore adserit. Unde etiam Corn. à Lapide non incommodo versiculum hunc ita explicat: Sicut inopinatum & subitum fuit diluvium, quod omnes obruit: sic inopinatus & subitus erit adventus meus, qui omnes comprehendet. Errarunt quoq; olim Tertullianus ad Uxor. c. 5. it. in Exhortat. Castitatis c. 9. ac Hieronymus ep. ad Gerontiam, dum ex h. l. nuptias secundas impugnabant, propterea sc. Sodomitas ac homines ante diluvianos fuisse à DEO punitos, quòd nuptias iterarint. Verùm Sc. Sacra longè alias poenae illius divinae indicat causas, ceu patet ex Gen. 6, 1. seqq. ac c. 18. it Ezech. 16, 49. minimè verò nuptias secundas. Deniq; quomodo Noachus in multis Christi typus fuerit, docet B. Parens Exeg. L. de Pers. &. Off. Christi § 31.) *

## 24:38
* (v. 38. Eating and drinking, i. e. feasting and carousing, without care and acting wantonly as if no evil were to come, as Chrysostom explains. Thus to drink wine Prov. 31, 4. signifies to be inebriated with wine. Compare the blessed D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 264.) *

* (Contracting marriage &c. i. e. burning with the desire of propagating the race and the name, and thus even defiling themselves with the marriages of the impious. This, therefore, is what displeased GOD in the marriage of the Sodomites, but not that they had entered into second marriages, i. e., having taken another wife after the former spouse had died. As indeed they falsely persuaded themselves, and from that slippery reasoning attacked, nay condemned, second marriages, Tertullian to his Wife, ch. 5, and in his exhortation ch. 9. Jerome, epistle to Gerontia, Vol. 1, p. 43. (Leonhardus Coquaeus attempts to excuse Jerome in his Commentary on Augustine, On the City of God, p. 384. But we oppose to him the Jesuit Salmeron, who in his Commentary on 1. Cor. 7. Disp. 14, § on the doubt, explicitly writes that Jerome, where he occurs to be dissuading from marriage, is sharper and more fervent. Certainly, if this had been the cause of divine indignation against the Sodomites, Abraham, the father of believers, would never have celebrated second marriages, for instance with Keturah, Gen. 25. Whence notably Augustine, Book 16, On the City of God, ch. 43. What if this also was provided against future heretics, adversaries of second marriages, so that in the very father of many nations, after the death of his spouse, it might be demonstrated that to marry again is not a sin.) *

Latin:

* (v. 38. Comedentes & bibentes, i. e. epulantes & convivantes, sine cura & tanquam nullo venturo malo lascivientes, ut exponit Chrysostomus. Sic bibere vinumProv. 31, 4. significat vino inebriari. Conf. B. D. Glass. Gr. S. p. 264.) *

* (Contrahentes matrimonium &c. i. e. uni-è generis nominisque propagandi desiderio flagrantes, adeoque etiam impiorum connubiis se inquinantes. Hoc igitur est, quod DEO in Sodomitarum coniugio dispicuit, non verò quòd nuptias iterarinth. e. defuncta priore coniuge aliam duxerint uxorem. Uti quidem sibi falsò persuaserūt, & ex lubrica ista ratione secundas nuptias impugnarunt, imo condemnarunt Tertullianus ad Vuxorum c. 5. & in exhort. c-stit. c. 9. Hieronymus ep. ad Gerotiam T. 1. p. 43. (Hieronymum excusare conatut Leonhardus Coquaeus Com. in Aug. de C. D. p. 384. Sed opponimus ei Iesuitam Salmeronem, qui Comm. in 1. Cor. 7. Disp. 14. §. ad dubiam, disertè scribit, Hieronymum ubi occurrit dehortando à matrimonio, acriorem esse atferventiorem. Sanè si haec indignationis divinae adversus Sodomitas causa fuisset, nunquam Abraham pater credentium secundas nuptias celebrasset, puta cum Cethura, Gen. 25. Unde notanter August. l. 16. de C. D. c. 43. Quid si & hoc provisum est contra haereticos, futuros secundarum adversarios nuptiarum, ut in ipso patre multarum gentium post obitum coniugis, iterum coniugari, demonstraretur non esse peccatum.) *

## 24:39
* (v. 39. They have not known. i. e. they have not attended. For γινώσκειν is used for προσέχειν, Conf. Ps. 90, 11. Ecclesiastes 4, 17. Isaiah 1, 3. Luke 19, 44. add. B. D. Glass. Rhet. Sacrae p. 12.) *

* (So also will be the coming of the Son of man. Therefore we must by no means expect a golden age, in which all the impious are to be destroyed, before the coming of Christ. Conf. Luke 18, 8. Apocal. 12, 12. 15. seqq. against the Chiliasts.) *

Latin:

* (v. 39. Non cognoverunt. i. e. non attenderunt. Adhibetur enim γινώσκειν pro προσέχειν, Conf. Ps. 90, 11. Ecclesiastae 4, 17. Esaiae 1, 3. Luc. 19, 44. add. B. D. Glass. Rhet. Sacrae p. 12.) *

* (Ita etiam erit adventus Filii hominis. Minimè igitur aureum seculum, in quo omnes impii delendi sint, ante adventum Christi expectare debemus. Conf. Luc. 18, 8. Apocal. 12, 12. 15. seqq. contra Chiliastas.) *

## 24:40
*(v. 40. One is taken &c. not from some absolute good pleasure of GOD, but on account of the different disposition of the men themselves. For when others strive for the contention of the mind and vigils, others languish in inertia & negligence, hence it happens that when the Lord will come in glory, those are to be taken, these are to be left, as Isidore of Pelusium has it, book 1, ep. 283. But beyond necessity and the common opinion of Interpreters, Hugo Grotius explains this prophecy not concerning reception into glory, but into grace, through the preaching of the Gospel which is to be.) *

Latin:

*(v. 40. Unus adsumitur &c. non ex absoluto quodam DEI beneplacito, sed ob diversum ipsorum hominum institutum. Cùm enim alii animi contentioni ac vigiliis studeant, alii inertiâ & negligentiâ langueant, hinc fit, ut cùm Dominus in gloriâ veniet, illi adsumendi sint, isti reliquendi, ut habet Isidorus Pelusiota l. 1. ep. 283. Praeter necessitatem verò ac communem Interpretum sententiam Hugo Grotius vaticinium hoc non de receptione in gloriam, sed in gratiam, per Evangelii praedicationem quae futura, exponit.) *

## 24:41
v. 41. Two grinding. See Isidore of Pelusium book 1, ep. 285. * (add. Exod. 11, 5.Isai. 47, 2.) *

Latin:

v. 41. Duae molentes. Vid. Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 1. ep. 285. * (add. Exod. 11, 5.Esai. 47, 2.) *

## 24:42
v. 42. Watch. Vigilance comprises 1 temperance. 2. diligence in the labors of one's vocation. 3 providence, through which the deceits of Satan & the world are avoided. 4. assiduity of prayers. * (Conf. more in Anal. on Luke 21, 36.) *

* (You do not know at what hour &c. One day is hidden, so that all days may be observed. Basil the Great, book 4 against Eunomius: Since it is not expedient for men to know the time of judgment, therefore the Savior kept silent. For expectation makes us apply ourselves more fervently to piety. We know that there will be some final hour, but we cannot define it with certainty. See Irenaeus book 2, c. 48 August. serm. 21. on Matth. Chrysost. Euthymius. Conf. Acts 1, 7. When, however, we know that most of the signs which were to precede the final day have been fulfilled, let us believe that without doubt, it is very near. Therefore, one must accurately distinguish here between distinct knowledge or discrete, & confused. The Savior denies not this, but that. See more things pertaining to this, at B. Par. in Dispp. Elencht. on the Lord's Gospels p. 1417.

But God did not wish to reveal the hour of the final day to us in his word, so that 1. he might repress the vain curiosity of some. 2. he might excite us to vigilance & constant piety. 3. we might shake off supine security.) *

Latin:

v. 42. Vigilate. Complectitur vigilantia 1 temperantiam. 2. diligentiam in laboribus vocationis. 3 providentiam, per quam Satanae & mundi fraudes caventur. 4. precum adsiduitatem. * (Conf. plura in Anal. ad Luc, 21, 36.) *

* (Nescitis quâ horâ &c. Latet unus dies, ut observentur omnes dies. Basilius M. lib. 4. contra Eunomium: Quoniam hominibus non expedit, tempus iudicii nosse, iccircò reticuit Salvator. Siquidem expectatio facit, ut fervidius pietati incumbamus. Scimus fore horam aliquam novissimam, sed certò eam definire non possumus. Vid. Irenaeus lib. 2. c. 48 August. serm. 21. in Matth. Chrysost. Euthymius. Conf. Act 1, 7. Cùm v. signa pleraque quae diem extremum praecessura erant, impleta sciamus, illud indubitatò credamus, illum proximè abesse. Accuratè igitur distingvendum hîc inter notitiam distinctam sive discretam, & confusam. Non hanc, sed illam negat Salvator Vid. plura huc facientia, apud B. Par. in Dispp. Elencht. super Ev. Dom. p. 1417.

Noluit verò Deus diei extremi horam nobis in verbo suo revelare, ut 1. reprimeret vanam quorundam curiositatem. 2. excitaret nos ad vigilantiam & iugem pietatem. 3. excuteremus supinam securitatem.) *

* (v. 43. At what hour the thief is to come. Conf. Apoc. 16, 151, Thess. 5, 4) *

Latin:

* (v. 43. Quâ horâ fur venturus. Conf. Apoc. 16, 151, Thess. 5, 4) *

## 24:44
* (v. 44. Who is it. Titus of Bostra on Luke 12:43. He said it not out of ignorance, who, do you think, is: But that he might demonstrate what is rare and worthy of much honor.) *

Latin:

* (v. 44. Quisnam est. Titus Bostremus in Luc. 12, 43.Non ignorans dixit, quis putas, est: Sed ut quod rarum est & multo honore dignum demonstraret.) *

## 24:45
* (v. 45. Faithful servant. The ministers of the Church are δοῦλοι or servants. Compare above c. 20, 25, Mark 10, 24.Luke 22, 25.1 Cor. 4, 1.2 Cor. 4, 5.c. 1, 24.c. 6, 4.c. 11, 23.Eph. 3, 7.Coloss. 1, 23.25.1 Thess. 3, 2.1 Tim. 4, 6.1 Peter 5, 3. Not lords, or having a political government committed to them. Compare B. P. L. on the Ministers of the Church § 7. Furthermore, from the fact that the Savior used a doubtful manner of speaking here, by saying: who, do you think, is the faithful servant. Isidore of Pelusium gathers the difficulty of the ecclesiastical office. See book 4, ep. 145.) *

Latin:

* (v. 45. Fidelis servus. Ministri Ecclesiae sunt δοῦλοι seu servi. Conf. suprà c. 20, 25, Marc. 10, 24.Luc. 22, 25.1. Cor. 4, 1.2. Cor. 4, 5.c. 1, 24.c. 6, 4.c. 11, 23.Eph. 3, 7.Coloss. 1, 23.25.1. Thess. 3, 2.1. Tim. 4, 6.1. Petr. 5, 3. Non domini, seu regimen Politicum sibi commissum habentes. Conf. B. P. L. de Minist. Eccles. § 7. Porrò ex eo, quòd Salvator dubitabundâ oratione hîc usus, dicendo: quis, putas, est fidelis servus. colligit Isid. Pelusiota difficultatem muneris Ecclesiastici. Vid. l. 4. ep. 145.) *

## 24:46
(v. 46. Amen I say to you, he shall appoint him over all his goods (the faithful servant.) Conf. Apoc. 4, 10. and add the likeness of Joseph Gen. 41, 40. Bellarmine, in book 1 of On the Blessedness of the Saints, chapter 18, section 'the same', ineptly strives to prove from this passage that the dead saints preside over the whole world, so that they may rule and govern the Church. For 1. this is a parable, from which apodictic arguments can by no means be drawn, unless Scripture itself shows the application, as Bellarmine himself teaches in book 3 of On the Word of God, chapter 3. 2. If anyone wishes to accommodate all the members of the parable too curiously to the dead saints, it would follow that Christ in heaven girds himself and ministers to the saints. To say which is absurd. It is evident, therefore, 3. that by those words nothing else is indicated than that the glory and honor of the blessed will be great. And thus, namely in general concerning the excellence of the reward and blessedness, both the Fathers and the Pontificians themselves explain it, brought forward by B. Par. L. on Death, section 357, as well as the Catholic Confession, book 2, part 2, p. 615. Toletus, Cardinal and Jesuit, on chapter 12 of Luke, p. 798, writes: By these words, Christ signifies the excellence of the reward and blessedness, which consists in the perfect vision of GOD, therefore it is said 'over all'. But all the blessed enjoy the perfect vision of GOD. Cornelius Jansenius on this passage writes: that the faithful servants are to be set over all goods by Christ, when he himself shall have returned for judgment. But then the Church will no longer exist.

militant, which the saints dwelling in the triumphant Church govern. And it can also be observed here, that the Jesuit Adamus Conzen in his Comment. on the Four Gospels (in which he acts chiefly to establish the errors of the Papists,) passes over this passage in silence. Corn. à Lapide also seeks no knot in this bulrush, but expressly adds: What I said about the Bishop, (namely that God is going to make him Lord of heaven and earth, and of the whole world, that is, is going to endow him with greater glory than private believers) apply to any head of a household; for this man is to his house as it were a Bishop, as Augustine says, just as a believer of his own self. But if the saying of Christ ought to be applied equally to every head of a household, it follows that also every head of a household who has died in Christ rules the whole world. This is something the Papists will scarcely grant. The same observation of Cornelius, (that in this place not only Ministers of the Church are understood specifically, or those who are rich in speech, now indeed giving drink to those who are fed with milk, now however speaking wisely, as Paul did, but also in general, those who are rich in possessions and money, as Euthymius also explains in this place,) is also to be noted against Bellarmine, who in his book on the Clergy, chapter 14, tries to prove from this place that Bishops, by the power of jurisdiction granted by divine law, are greater than Presbyters. But especially it is to be observed that Gregory the Great, formerly Roman Pontiff, in part 3 of his Pastoral Care, takes this oracle not only concerning Bishops, but concerning all Ministers of the Church, from whom it is right for the Jesuit to depart in his religion. Just as also Fulgentius in sermon 1, whom Cornelius à Lapide also follows in this place. That interrogation, he writes, who do you think, implies that there are few such servants, suppose Bishops and Pastors, who are faithful to Christ in all things in the care of the flock. Although Hilary and other Fathers collect from this place that a special solicitude has been entrusted to the princes of the people, i.e., the Bishops, they do not do this exclusively, but teach that the Savior exhorts us in common to an indefatigable care of vigilance, as the express words of Hilary have it. Whence there is no reason why Bellarmine should oppose the authority of the aforementioned Hilary to us here.) *

Latin:

*(v. 46. Amen dico vobis, super omnia bona sua constituet eum (servum fidelem.) Conf. Apoc. 4, 10. ac add. simile Iosephi Gen. 41, 40. Ineptè ex h. l. evincere satagit Bell. l. 1. de beat. sanct. c. 18. §. idem sancto defunctos praesidere toti mundo, ut Ecclesiam regant & gubernent. Etenim 1. parabola haec est, è quâ minimè apodictica duci possunt argumenta, nisi Scriptura ipsa monstret adplicationem. Bell ipso l. 3. de V D. c. 3. docente. 2. si nimis curiosè omnia parabolae membra accommodare ad sanctos defunctos quis velit, sequeretur, quòd Christus in coelis praecingat se, sanctisq; ministret. Id quod dicere absurdum est. Patet igitur 3. quòd verbis illis nil indicetur aliud, quàm quòd magna futura sit gloria ac honor beatorum. Et ita, nempe in genere de excellentiâ praemii & beatitudinis, exponunt tum Patres, tum ipsi Pontificii, adducti à B. Par. L. de Morte §. 357. nec non Confess. Cathol. lib. 2. spec part. 2. p. 615. Toletus Cardinalis ac Iesuita in c. 12. Lucae p. 798. His verbis, scribit, Christus significat excellentiam praemii & beatitudinis, quae in perfectâ DEI visione consistit, ideò dicitur super omnia. At perfectâ DEI visione omnes beati fruuntur. Corn. Iansenius in h. l. tum à Christo servos fideles omnibus bonis praeficiendos scribit, cùm ipse ad iudicium redierit. At tunc non ampliùs futura Ecclesia.

militans, quam sancti in Ecclesia triumphante versantes gubernent. Et observari quoq; hîc potest, quòd Iesuita Adamus Conzen in Comment. ad Quatuor Ev. (in quibus praecipuè id agit, ut errores Pontificiorum stabiliat,) hunc locum silentio praetermittat. Corn. etiam à Lapide nullum in scirpo hoc quaerit nodum, sed disertè addit: Quod de Episcopo dixi, (nempe quòd Deus illum facturus sit coeli ac terrae, totiusq; mundi Dominum, hoc est maiore gloriâ donaturus sit, quàm fideles privatos) applica cuilibet patrifamilias; hic enim domui suae est quasi Episcopus, ut ait Augustinus, aequè ac fidelis quissui ipsius. Si verò dictum Christi aeque ad unumquemq; patremfamiliàs applicari debet, se quitur, quòd etiam quilibet paterfamilias in Christo defunctus totum mundum regat. Id quod vix largientur Pontificii. Eadem Cornelii observatio, (quòd h. l. non solùm in specie intelligantur Ministri Ecclesiae, sive qui divites sunt in sermone, nunc lacte quidem potantes, nunc autem sapienter loquentes, uti Paulus fecit, verùm etiam in genere, qui divites sunt possessionibus ac pecuniis, quemad. Euthymius etiam h. l. exponit,) notanda quoque contra Bellarminum est, qui lib. de Cleric. c. 14. ex h. l. evincere conatur, Episcopos potestate iurisdictionis, iure divino concessa, esse maiores Presbyteris. Cumprimis verò observandum, quòd Gregorius M. Pontifex quondam Romanus part. 3. Curae Pastoralis non de solis Episcopis, sed de omnibus Ministris Ecclesiae oraculum hoc accipiat, à quo meritò religio sit Iesuitae discedere. Quemadmodum etiam Fulgentius serm. 1. quos etiam Corn. à Lapide in h. l. sequitur. Interrogatio ista, scribit, quis putas, innuit, paucos esse tales servos, puta Episcopos & Pastores, qui per omnia in curâ gregis Christo sint fideles. Licet verò Hilarius aliique Patres ex h. l. colligant specialem populi principibus i. e. Episcopis sollicitudinem esse demandatam, non tamen exclusivè hoc faciunt, sed in communi nos ad indefessam vigilātiae curam Salvatorem adhortari, docent, uti expressa habent Hilarii verba. Unde non est, quòd Bell. praedicti Hilarii autoritatem hîc nobis opponat.) *
