## 26:15
v. 15. ἔςηκαν they appointed Theophylact: συνεφώνησαν they agreed together that they would give, or even they presented i.e. they weighed out, for this is what ἱςὰναι & ςῆσαι. signifies * (so that in this way the present act is used for a promise, a destination. to which similar examples contribute below v. 25. John 10, 32.) * Those who weigh or append things, they set the tongue of the balance i.e. they cause it to stand erect, and thus the weights placed in the scales correspond to one another: now indeed it is established that the ancients were accustomed to weigh out money * (see Gen. 23, 16.) * The LXX Interpreters Zech. 11, 12. in the prediction of this matter used the word ἔστησαν they weighed out. Furthermore, from a comparison of Mark 14, 11. & Luke 22, 5. it appears that a pact and promise of that reward preceded. Therefore some appoint, money had been deposited by agreement with a certain man, so that they might the more incite him to betrayal. (For it seems hardly likely to Lud. de Dieu, Heinsius, and several others, that the Jewish priests had such trust that they would count out in advance the coins, the price of an abominable crime, but one not yet performed. They prove this exposition from Mark 14, 11. Luke 22, 5. The Fathers profusely execrate this detestable avarice of Judas, as Chrysostom especially in hom. 81 on Matthew, on this occasion gravely and at length dissuades his hearers from avarice, who must be read here entirely.)

(And I will deliver him unto you. see the notes above on v. 2.)

They appointed thirty pieces of silver. Anselm in dial. de pass. Those denarii were Ishmaelite, by which Joseph also was sold many years before, and they had devolved to the Jews by hereditary succession. The Syriac has from the root to covet, to desire, because silver is desirable. The Hebrews observe that wherever in the Scriptures mention is made of pieces of silver, without the species of the silver coin being expressed, the shekel of the sanctuary is understood, equivalent to four denarii. See Annot. Syr. Matthaeus Hostus in book 4 of his work on coinage, ch. 5, shows that the sacred shekels are tetradrachms, which make up the sum of fifteen Imperial thalers, each silver piece being worth a stater, i.e., half a thaler or a Joachim thaler of the valley. Dilherrus approves this calculation along with the Gloss. Norib. and excellently confirms it in Dispp. Acad. vol. 1, p. 409. But those recede entirely further from the truth who, with Baronius A.D. 34, p. 175, explain a silver piece as a pound of silver, by which reasoning 30 silver pieces would make 900 Brabantine florins, as calculated by Corn. à Lapide, (who for that reason also rejects the opinion of Baronius,) just as B. D. Meisnerus also refutes the same in Com. on Hosea p. 295. The Cardinal followed Joachim Camerarius, who in his book on Greek and Latin coinage established that Christ was sold for about three hundred crowns; as well as those who with St. Ambrose, book 3 de Sp. S. ch. 18, estimate those thirty pieces of silver at thirty denarii, so that the whole sum would scarcely rise to four Imperials at which price a field could certainly by no means be bought: as well as those who extend their price too much, among whom Beza comes closer to the mark, estimating those thirty pieces of silver at more or less twenty-one French livres. The Jesuits, Maldonatus, Pererius, Salmeron, and others, who by They understand silver pieces as shekels, for instance sacred ones: thus Christ would have been sold for about thirty Brabantine florins, according to the calculation of Cornelius à Lapide. But Cornelius abandons this opinion of his associates, both because in Jer. 32, 9 a stater or shekel is distinguished from silver pieces, and indeed and especially because at Paris, as witnessed by Budaeus in book 5 of De Asse, and likewise at Rome in the church of the Holy Cross, a coin, which is believed to be one of those silver pieces for which Christ was sold, is found, weighing at least two Attic drachmas or two Julii or two Spanish Royals; therefore Cornelius à Lapide himself determines that Christ was sold for at least fifteen Brabantine florins or six crowns or Rhenish gold coins. But this opinion likewise rests upon a hypothesis that is, if not false, at least highly uncertain, as if, namely, those coins which are preserved at Rome and Paris and are shown as the genuine silver pieces for which the Savior was sold, were in truth of that number; a thing which, however, rests upon mere conjecture or rather a pious deception. Indeed, such a coin was also once shown to me in Brabant near Louvain, in the monastery of the Celestines, by whom it was preserved quite religiously in a certain gilded casket, with the monks likewise holily affirming, and all but swearing, that it was of the number of silver pieces for which Christ was sold by the traitor Judas. But to me inquiring whence they were so certain about this matter, the monks replied that the Roman Pontiff had given that coin as a gift to the Duchess of Arscot (the said monastery indeed belonged to the Dukes of Arscot, not a few of whom were also committed to the earth there) as a badge κειμήλιον, and she had entrusted this sacred deposit to their faith. That coin, however, was marked on one side with the image of a lily or rose with the inscription PODION, while on the other it displayed a sun or the radiant face of a youth. I myself also possess a coin minted in this form in my antiquarian collection, of exactly equal weight with those common denarii of the Roman Emperors which are seen everywhere, eight of which scarcely equal an Imperial or Joachim thaler. But since it is not credible that a field, even if most sterile, near so populous a city could have been purchased for so cheap a price, the opinion of those who affirm that Christ was sold for fifteen sacred or sanctuary shekels, each of which corresponds to half an Imperial, is altogether to be preferred. Although indeed shekels of this kind of two types are in circulation (just as I myself once possessed both forms), some of which are found marked with a Samaritan character, and others and indeed the majority with a Hebrew one, on the other side with the words שקל ישראל i. e. shekel of Israel with an impressed censer, and on the other side ירושלים קרשה i. e. Jerusalem the holy with the rod of Aaron, conspicuous with extended almond branches: yet the weight and value of all is the same; namely, that which was just indicated, so that whoever among these may be accepted as genuine (for the dispute about this matter is still sub iudice.) it is nevertheless certain that these are rather the shekels of the Jews, (which are commonly called ἀργύεια in the H. S., but by no means those Roman coins, such as those coins appear to be entirely, conspicuous with the image of a rose or lily.) than those coins which certain Papists show, marked with the image of a rose, that they are of that number, at least as far as the appearance is concerned, for which Christ was sold. Furthermore, concerning the reason, form, weight, difference, etc., of these shekels, one may consult Arias Montanus in Appar., Beza on c. 17 of Matthew, Waserus on Hebrew Coins, Matthias Flacius in the Key to Scripture, Villalpandus on the Temple of Ezekiel, the Londoners in the Appendix to the Polyglot Bible, and others.) But whatever the case may be, whether they were Jewish shekels or coins marked with the image of a Rose, it is nevertheless certain that it was an altogether small sum for which the Lord of the world was valued and sold. Whence St. Ambrose, book 3 on the Holy Spirit, c. 18: O Judas, he exclaims, traitor, you value the ointment of his passion at three hundred denarii, and his passion you sell for thirty denarii : rich in estimation, vile in crime. Jerome on this passage: Unhappy Judas, the loss which he believed he had made from the pouring out of the ointment, he wished to compensate for with the price of the Master. But it is asked here 1. how could a field be bought for so small a price? Resp. either the field was unfit for plowing and other uses, and thus served only for the burial of strangers; or something was added to this price from the corban or treasury. Q. 2. How was the sale of Joseph, made by his brothers, a type of the sale of Christ, when Christ was sold for 30 pieces of silver, but Joseph for 20. Resp. Jerome: it was not fitting that a servant should be sold for as much as the Lord. And yet servants were also accustomed to be sold for this price in former times, but free men for sixty shekels, if faith is to be had in R. Moses Maimonides in More Nevochim, book 3, c. 40, on Exod. c. 21, 32. Nor is it inconvenient that our Savior, the Best and Greatest, was sold for the price of a servant, since he himself did not disdain to assume the form of a servant for our redemption, Phil. 2, 7.)

Latin:

v. 15. ἔςηκανstatuerunt Theophylactus: συνεφώνησανconvenerunt se daturos esse, vel etiam repraesentarunt i. e. appenderunt, hoc enim significat ἱςὰναι & ςῆσαι. * (ut ita actus praesens adhibeatur pro promissione, destinatione. quò faciunt exempla similia infrà v. 25. Ioh. 10, 32.) * Qui res ponderant sive appendunt, illi sistunt lingulam bilancis i. e. efficiunt, ut illa stet erecta, atq; ita pondera lancibus imposita inter se respondeant: iam verò constat, solitos esse veteres pecuniam appenre * (vid. Gen. 23, 16.) * LXX. Interpp. Zach. 11, 12. in praedictione huius rei usi sunt verbo ἔστησανappenderunt. Coeterùm ex collatione Marc. 14, 11. & Luc. 22, 5. apparet, praecessisse pactum & pollicitationem istius mercedis. Quidam igitur statuunt, pecuniam ex pacto apud certum hominem suisse depositam, ut eò magis ad proditionem eum instigarent. * (vix enim verisimile videtur Lud. de Dieu, Heinsio, ac aliis nonnullis, eam fidem habuisse Sacerdotes Iudae, ut in antecessum nummos, pretium abominandi sceleris, sed non exhibiti numerarent. Probant expositionem hanc ex Marc. 14, 11.Luc. 22, 5. Detestandam hanc Iudae avaritiam prolixè execrantur Patres, ceu Chrysostomus cumprimis hom. 81. in Matth. occasione hâc graviter multisque auditores suos ab avaritiâ dehortatur, qui omninò hîc evolvendus.) *

(* Et ego vobis tradam. vid. notata suprâ ad v. 2.) *

Statuerunt triginta argenteos. Anselmus in dial. de pass. Denarii illi fuerunt Ismaëlitici, quibus & Ioseph venditus fuit ante multos annos, & haereditariâ successione fuerunt ad Iudaeos devoluti. Syrus habet à rad. concupiscere, desiderare, quia argentum est desiderabile. Observant Hebraei, ubieunque in Scripturis argenteorum fit mentio, non expressâ numismatis argentei specie, intelligi siclum sanctuarii, aequivalentem quatuor denariis. Vid. Annot. Syr. Matthaeus Hostus lib. 4. rei num. c. 5. ostendit, sielos sacros tetradrachmos, qui conficiunt summam thalerorum Imperialium quindecim, singulis sc. argenteis valentibus staterem i. e. semissem thaleri seu Ioachimici Vallensis. Approbat hanc supputationem iuxta cum Gloss. Norib. & egregiè firmat Dilherrus Dispp. Acad. t. 1. p. 409. Longiùs verò omninò à veritate recedunt tùm qui cum Baronio A C. 34. p. 175. argenteum de argenti libra exponunt, quâ ratione 30. argentei efficerent 900. florenos Brabanticos, supputante Corn. à Lapide, (qui proptereà etiam sententiam Baronii reiicit,) quemadmodum etiam eandem refutat B. D. Meisnerus Com. in Hoseam p. 295. Sequutus autem Cardinalis Ioachimum Camerarium est, qui lib. de Numism. Gr. & Lat. statuit, Christū venisse coronatis circiter trecentis; tùm qui cum S. Ambrosio l. 3. de Sp. S. C. 18. triginta illos argenteos triginta denariis aestimant, ut ita tota summa vix ad quatuor adsurgat Imperiales quo pretio sanè minimè ager emi potuit: tùm, qui nimium illorum pretium extendunt, quorum in numero propiùs scopum attingit Beza, triginta iftos argenteos Francicis libris plus minus viginti & una aestimans. Ab hac sententia proximè abeunt Iesuitae, Maldonatus, Pererius, Salmeron & alii, qui per argenteos intelligunt siclos, puta sacros: ita Christus venditus fuerit triginta circiter florenis Brabanticis, iuxta supputationem Cornelii à Lapide. Verùm deserit hanc sociorum suorum sententiam Cornelius, tum quod Ierem. 32, 9. stater five sielus distinguatur ab argenteis, tùm verò & quidem cumprimis quòd Parisiis, teste Budaeo l. 5. de Asse, itemque Romae in templo S. Crucis, numus, qui unus creditur ex illis argenteis, quibus venditus fuit Christus, reperiatur, duas saltem drachmas Atticas sive duos Iulios aut duos Regales Hispanicos appendens, ipse igitur Cornelius à Lapide statuit, quòd Christus venditus fuei it quindecim saltem florenis Brabanticis sive sex scutis sive aureis Rhenanis. Ast nititur sententia itidem, si non falsa, maximè tamen incertâ hypothesi, quasi videlicet numi illi, qui Romae & Parisiis adservantur & tanquàm genuini argentei, pro quibus Salvator venditus fuerit, ostenduntur, revera ex eorum numero sint; id quod tamen merâ nititur coniecturâ vel piâ potiùs fallaciâ. Sanè & mihi aliquando huiusmodi numus ostensus in Brabantia propè Lovanium fuit, in coenobio Monachorum Coelestinorum, à quibus religiosè admodùm in capsulâ quadam inauratâ adservabatur, itidem Monachis sanctè affirmantibus, ac tantùm non iurantibus, quòd è numero argenteorum esset, pro quibus Christus suerit à proditore Iuda venditus. Sciscitanti verò, unde adeò certi de hâc re essent, respondebant Monachi, Pontificem Romanum numum illum Ducissae de Arscot (spectabat verò dictum Monasterium ad Duces de Arscot, quorum haut pauci etiam ibi terrae mandati sunt) ut insigne κειμήλιον dono dedisse, quae sacrum hoc depositum fidei eorum commiserit. Insignitus verò numus ille ab alterâ parte lilii seu rosae imagine erat cum inscriprione PODION, ab alterâ verò exhibebat solem sive faciem iuvenis radiantem. Ipse quoque numum hâc formâ cusum in antiquario meo possideo, aequali omninò pondere cum vulgaribus illis Romanorum Impp. denariis, qui passim conspiciuntur, quorum ipsi octo vix aequant Imperialem seu Ioachimicum. Sed cùm haut credibile sit, agrum etsi vel maximè sterilem propè urbem tam populosam pretio adeò vili comparari potuisse, praeserenda omninò sententia illorum est, qui Christum quindecim siclis sacris sive sanctuarii, quorum singuli dimidio Imperiali respondent, venditum fuisse affirmant. Licet vero duplicis generis sicli huiusmodi circumferantur, (quemadmodum ipse mèt utriusque formae olim possedi) quorum aliqui charactere Samaritano, aliqui & quidem plerique Ebraeo insigniti deprehenduntur, ab altero quidem latere voeibus שקל ישראל i. e. siclus Israel cum impresso thuribulo, ab alterô verò ירושלים קרשה i. e. Ierusalem sancta cum virga Aronis, extensis ramis amygdaliferis conspicua: idem tamen omnium pondus ac pretium est; videl. quod modò indicatum, ut adeò quicunque tandem ex his ut genuini admittantur (nam adhuc de istâ re sub iudice lis est.) certum tamen sit, hos potiùs Iudaeorum siclos, (qui comuniter ἀργύεια in Sc. S. vocantur, neutiquam verò illa numismata Romana, qualia omninò videntur numi illi, rosae vel lilii imagine conspicui.) quàm numos illos, quos Pontificii quidam ostendunt, rosae imagine infignitos, ex illorum esse numero, saltem quantum ad speciem, pro quibus Christus fuit venditus. Coeterùm de siclis horum que ratione, formâ, pondere, differentia &c. consuli possunt Arias Montanus in Appar. Beza ad c. 17. Matth. Waserus de Numism. Ebr. Matthias Flacius in clavi Scripturae, Villalpandus de Templo Ezech. Londinenses in App. Bibl. Polygl. alii.) Quicquid verò tandem sit, sive sicli Iudaici suerint, sive numi Rosae imagine signati, certum tamen est, fuisse omninò exiguam summam, quâ orbis Dominus fuit aestimatus ac venditus. Unde S. Ambrosius l. 3. de Sp. S. c. 18. O Iuda, exclamat, proditor, unguentum passioms eius trecentis denariis aestimas, & passionem eius triginta denariis vendis: dives in aestimatione, vilis in scelere. Hieronymus in h. l. Infelix Iudas damnum, quod ex effusione unguenti se fecisse credebat, magistri pretio volebat compensare. Sed quaeritur hîc 1. quomodo pro pretio adeò exiguo potuerit emi ager? Resp. vel fuit ager ad arandum aliosque usus ineptus, quique adeò tantum servivit ad sepulturam peregrinorum; vel aliquid superadditum pretio huic fuit ex corban sive gazophylacio. Q. 2. Quomodo venditio Iosephi, à fratribus facta, typus fuerit venditionis Christi, cum Christus venditus fuerit 30 argenteis, Iosephus verò 20. Resp. Hieronymus: non par erat, tanti servum, quanti Dominum venire. Atqui servi etiam pretio hoe vendi olim solebant, liberi verò sexaginta siclis, si fides habenda R. Mosi Maiemonidi est in More Nevochim l. 3. c. 40. super Exod. c. 21, 32. Nec inconveniens, Salvatorem nostrum Opt. Max. servi praetio fuisse venditum, cùm ipse haut dedignatus est, servi formam ob nostri redemtionem adsumere, Phil. 2, 7.) *

## 26:17
v. 17. On the first day of the unleavened bread. Matthew observes the method of counting customary among the Romans. Therefore, the deeds narrated here on the first day of the unleavened bread must be understood to have been done on the day immediately preceding, as the Jews indeed distinguished days: for it is plain that these deeds were done before the evening on which Jesus ate the Passover with his disciples: but from that evening the first day of the unleavened bread, which was the day of the Passover, began according to the Jews. Matthew calls it the first day of the unleavened bread, because among the Romans the natural day νυχσθήμερον begins from midnight.

* (Ludovicus de Dieu embraces this opinion and deduces it at greater length in Comm. on the Evangelists p. 121 and 234. Furthermore, the interpreters observe that Christ did not celebrate the last Passover on the same day as the Jews, since the Jews, on account of the impending Sabbath day, postponed the feast of the Passover to the Sabbath, following the traditions of their fathers, but Christ ate the Paschal lamb according to the divine institution, as is evident from John 19, 14 coll. with ch. 18, 28. Whence also the head of the household could not greatly wonder at it, as it did not escape him that Christ, having rejected the traditions of the elders, diligently observed the law of GOD; nor did the priests, who were accusing Christ, dare to object that deed to him as a crime. See more on this matter in B. D. Calixtus, Concord. Ev. p. 319. Sam. Petitus in Eclog. Chronolog. lib. 1. c. 8. seqq. Sigonius lib. 3. de Rep. Ebr. c. 9. Ludovicus de Dieu comm. in Matth. p. 122. B. Par. Harm. Ev. latest edition p. 934, where he brings forward very many authors on that subject. Also Corn. à Lapide in this place notes that Rupert, Ioannes Lucidus, Gagneius, Iansenius, Maldonatus, and especially Salmeron subscribe to this opinion. But he himself, having followed Bellarmine, book on the Eucharist ch. 8, Toletus, Suarez, Thomas, Abulensis, Ribera book 5 on the Temple ch. 3, p. 325, Salianus in the preface to vol. 6 of the Ecclesiastical Annals, and others, warning that that custom of the Jews is more recent, established, That Christ and the Jews celebrated the Passover on the same day prescribed by the law, namely, on the 14th of the month Nisan in the evening. Beza and Grotius also hold the same, who however distinguish between πάοχα σθὐσιμον, and μνημονευτικὸν., warning that this at least, but not that (inasmuch as, being prevented by death, he could not celebrate it, but rather he himself was to be sacrificed as the true Passover on the true day of the Passover), was celebrated by Christ. Various reasons are accustomed to be brought forward on either side, which the narrowness of the paper does not allow to be adduced here. Those can be seen in the cited authors, especially in Corn. à Lap. in h. l. Let Lud. de Dieu in h. l., Ioan. Cocceius in tr. Sanhedrin. c. 1. p. 11. 12., and Ioh. Cloppenburg in epist. sing. also be seen.

Latin:

v. 17. Primâ autem azymorum. Matthaeus observat rationem numerandi Romanis usitatam. Quae ergo hîc narrantur gesta primo die azymorum, ea oportet intelligi gesta esse die proximè praecedente, prout Iudaei quidem dies distinguebant: etenim planum est, haec gesta esse ante vesperam, quâ Iesus cum discipulis pascha edit: at ab illa vespera primus dies azymorum, qui erat dies Paschatis, secundùm Iudaeos incipiebat. Matthaeus vocat diem primum azymorum, quia apud Romanos dies naturalis νυχσθήμερον incipit à mediâ nocte.

* (Amplectitur hanc sententiam & prolixiùs deducit Ludovicus de Dieu Comm. in Evangelistas p. 121. & 234. Observant porrò Interpp. quòd Christus non eodem cum Iudaeis die ultimum Pascha celebraverit, cùm Iudaei propter imminentem diem Sabbathi Paschatis festum in Sabbathum reiecerint, sequuti Patrum suorum traditiones, Christus verò iuxta institutionem divinam agnum Paschalem comederit, ceu pateat ex Ioh. 19, 14. coll. cum c. 18, 28. unde etiam nec Pater familias id mirari magnopere potuit, ut quem non fugiebat, Christum reiectis maiorum traditionibus diligenter legem DEI observare; nec Sacerdotes, qui Christum accusabant, ausi fuerunt criminis loco factum illud ei obiicere. Vid. pluribus hâc de re B. D. Calixtus Concord. Ev. p. 319. Sam. Petitus in Eclog. Chronolog. lib. 1. c. 8. seqq. Sigonius lib. 3. de Rep. Ebr. c. 9. Ludovicus de Dieu comm. in Matth. p. 122. B. Par. Harm. Ev. edit. noviss. p. 934. ubi plurimos autores eam in rem adducit. Etiam Corn. à Lapide in h. l. annotat, sententiae huic subscribere Rupertum, Ioannem Lucidum, Gagneium, Iansenium, Maldonatum ac cumprimis Salmeronem. Ipse vero sequutus Bellarminum l. de Euchar. c. 8. Toletum, Suarez, Thomam, Abulensem, Riberam lib. 5. de Templ. c. 3. p. 325. Salianum praefat. in t. 6. Annal. Eccles. aliosque, monentes, quòd consuetudo illa Iudaeorum recentior sit, statuit, Christum & Iudaeos eadem die è lege praescriptà Pascha celebrasse, scil. 14. mensis Nisan ad vesperam. Idem etiam tenent Beza ac Grotius, qui tamen distinguit inter πάοχα σθὐσιμον, & μνημονευτικὸν. Hoc saltem, non autem illud (utpote quod morte praeventus celebrare non potuerit, sed ipse potiùs verum Pasclia vero Paschatis die sacrificandus) à Christo fuisse celebratum monens. Rationes in utramque patrem variae afferri solent, quas hîc adducere chartae angustia non patitur. Videri illae apud allegatos autores possunt, cumprimis apud Corn. à Lap. in h. l. Videantur quoque Lud. de Dieu in h. l. Ioan. Cocceius in tr. Sanhedrin. c. 1. p. 11. 12. Ioh. Cloppenburg in epist. sing.) *

## 26:18
v. 18. εἰς τὴν πόλιν into that city namely, Jerusalem.

* πρὸς δεῖνα, whom, namely, having followed the man carrying a pitcher of water, Luc. 22, 10. you shall find in the house of the master of the house. Furthermore, the word δεῖνα seems to Cameron to be from the Chald. הרק through the Heb. הῖה ) *

My time is near. This can be referred to the eating of the Paschal lamb, and to the passion,

* ( πρὸς σέ with you it is also used in this way Ioh. 1, 1.) *

* ( ποιῶ τὸ πάχα i. e. I have decreed to make, or I will make the Passover through an enallage of tense most customary to the Hebrews. see. Exod. 12, 48.Num. 9, 2.6.14.) *

Latin:

v. 18. εἰς τὴν πόλινin illam urbem sc. Hierosolymam.

* πρὸς δεῖνα, quem scil. sequuti hominem hydriam aquae gestantem, Luc. 22, 10. in aedibus patrem samilias deprehenderitis. Porrò vox δεῖνα Cameroni esse videtur à Chald. הרק per Ebr. הῖה) *

Tempus meum propè est. potest hoc ad manducationem agni Paschatis, & ad passionem referri,

* ( πρὸς σέapud te ita etiam adhibetur Ioh. 1, 1.) *

* ( ποιῶ τὸ πάχα i. e. decrevi facere, sive faciam Pascha per enallagen temporis Ebraeis usitatissimam. vid. Exod. 12, 48.Num. 9, 2.6.14.) *

## 26:20
v. 20. He was reclining. That Christ is said to have reclined could seem to conflict with the divine institution: for it is commanded Exod. 12, 3. that eating the Passover, they should have their loins girded, their feet shod, and hold a staff in their hand, and that they should eat quickly, which cannot be done by those reclining. Resp. It is commanded there in what manner they ought to eat the Passover on that first occasion when they were about to go out of Egypt, before they left Egypt and began their journey, because the necessity of that time so required. * (see Philo in the booklet on the Sacrifice of Abel and Cain, about the middle) * but in the law thereafter, where it is commanded that that ceremony of the paschal lamb be renewed annually, those things are not added. Wherefore all Hebrew doctors, both ancient and recent, testify with the highest consensus that that command concerning the sprinkling of the doorposts with blood, the putting on of shoes, the girding of loins, the taking of staffs, and the eating of the lamb with haste did not extend to future generations, but belonged only to that night in which they were about to go out of Egypt.

* (Among the Papists, Menochius and Pererius embrace this opinion. Others, however, such as Maldonatus and Emanuel Sáa, attempt to reconcile the present passage with the divine institution Exod. 12. by advising that the word reclining καταχρησκῶς, is to be accepted here and that nothing else is denoted by it than a posture composed for taking food, whether one were standing, or sitting, or reclining. The Jesuit Franciscus Ribera, book 5 on the Temple, chapter 4, clearly denies that the Jews ate the lamb standing, even in the first celebration of the Passover.) * Indeed, there was a most ancient tradition among them (which is mentioned in the Talmud, treatise on the Passover) that those about to eat the Passover should recline as a sign of attained liberty. Tremellius in the notes. * (Johannes Buxtorf also mentions the same tradition in Synag. Iud. c. 13., but Hugo Grotius doubts it, inasmuch as the custom of sitting seems either no less ancient than the custom of reclining, or close to the first custom, from Gen. 43, 33. and also from 1. Sam. 20, 25. He adds that the Jews today in that commemorative supper use a sitting posture, but one softer and more honorable than usual, and with a reclining of the body. Furthermore, concerning the custom of reclining, see Stuckius in Antiquities of Banquets, Rosinus in Roman Antiquities, book 5, chapter 28, and Dempster of Muresk in the said book, Paralipomena, Lambinus to Horace, ode 27, book 2, p. 66, also to book 2, Satires, p. 151, Guido Pancirollus, Memorable Things, title 51, p. 495 ff., and Henricus Salmuth in his notes on that, p. 513, 514, Petrus Ciacconius on the Triclinium, Aldus Manutius on Questions by Letter, book 1, question 4, Friederich Taubmann on Plautus. B. Socer, G. Henricus Plathnerus, Jurisconsult and formerly Saxon Councilor, also treats of the same custom.) ἀνεκδόοτ- in Juvenal Sat. 2. There also exists a small dissertation by the blessed brother German, Johann Gerhard, concerning the custom of feasting among the ancients, published at Wittenberg.) * It could also be answered that Christ first reclined with the disciples, but afterwards rose from the table for the sake of eating the paschal lamb. * (This especially pleases Mr. Dr. Friedlieb in this place, p. 174, b. from the Papists, the Jesuit Tirinus, and others) *

* (With the twelve disciples. Q. here, Whether Judas the traitor also took part in the celebration of the Passover and the Eucharist, and partook of it? St. Hilary, Theophylact in this place, Clement of Rome book 5 Constit. c. 16, Innocent III book 4 on the Mysteries of the Eucharist c. 13, Rupert book 10 on Matthew at the end, Tatian, Ammonius, and others deny it, led by the reason that Judas was unworthy of such great mysteries and deservedly to be kept away from the Holy Supper. More correctly, Origen, Cyril, Chrysostom, Augustine, Rabanus, Bede, Thomas, Suarez, and others commonly affirm it, whom Cornelius à Lapide also follows in this place. The opinion of our own people is also the same. See Blessed Dr. Chemnitz, Loci Theologici part 3, p. 153; Blessed Dr. Grawer on the A.C. second part, p. 275, 276; Blessed Dr. Harbart in the chapters of pure doctrine, p. 523; Blessed Dr. Hutter, Loci Theologici Mai. p. 724; Blessed Dr. Mylius on the A.C. p. 169; Blessed Pareus both in the Harmony of the Gospels c. 171, and in Loci Theologici on the Holy Supper § 223 and 235, where he also alleges Cyprian, Jerome, Theodoret, and others for this opinion. And he proves this opinion at length and responds to the exceptions of the adversaries from Lutherans B. D. Fōsterus Dispp. Catech. Dec. 3. §. 84. seqq. B. Par. L. de S. Coenâ §. 235. B. D. Keslerus in a special Dissertation on Judas the Traitor as a guest at the Holy Supper, but from the Papists Cornelius à Lapide on this passage. What is more, not only does Calvin himself in book 4 of the Institutes, ch. 17, §. 34, acknowledge that Judas was present when Christ distributed the Holy Eucharist, but also William Whitaker, the English theologian, in his treatise on Scripture, q. 6, ch. 12, explicitly writes that that opinion, that Judas was absent, contradicts not only the Scriptures, but also the Fathers, Dionysius, Augustine, Chrysostom. The same is also admitted by those from the Calvinists Martyr, Beza, and others. Most, however, such as Danaeus, W. Musculus, I. Piscator, etc., think that the whole matter should be left in the middle. This is also the opinion of certain Papists, such as Turrianus, Barradius, Salmeron, and others.) *

Latin:

v. 20. Discumbebat. Quod Christus discubuisse dicitur, videri poterat cum divino instituto pugnare: praecipitur enim Exod. 12, 3.ut edentes Pascha, lumbos accinctos, pedes calceatos habeant & baculum teneant manu, & ut citò comedant, quae fieri nequeunt à discumbentibus. Resp. Ibi praecipi, quâ ratione exituri ex Aegypto primâ illâ vice comedere debeant pascha pavilò antequam Aegypto exeant & iter ingrediantur, quia ita exigebat temporis illius necessitas. * (vid. Philo libello de Sacrificio Habelis & Caini, in medio circiter) * sed in lege deinde, ubi praecipitur, ut ceremonia illa agni paschatis quotannis renovetur, ea non adduntur. Quapropter omnes Hebraei Dd. tum antiqui, tum recentes summo consensu testantur, mandatum illud de aspergendis sanguine postibus, de induendis calceis, cingendis lumbis, sumendis baculis & cum festinatione comedendo agno non se extendisse ad generationes secuturas, sed tantùm fuisse illius noctis quâ egressuri erant ex Aegypto.

* (Amplectuntur hanc senteutiam ex Pontificiis Menochius, Pererius. Alii vero, uti Maldonatus, Emanuel Sáa ita praesentem locum cum institutione divinâ Exod. 12. conciliare conantur, ut moneant accipiendum hîc esse verbum discumbendiκαταχρησκῶς, ac nihil aliud eo notari, quàm gestum compositum ad capiendum cibum, sive staretur, sive sederetur, sive accumberetur. Iesuita Franciscus Ribera l. 5. de Templo c. 4. planè negat Iudaeos vel in prima etiam Paschatis celebratione, stantes agnum comedisse) * Imò antiquissima fuit apud eos rraditio. (quae in Talmud. tr. de Paschare memoratur) ut manducaturi Pascha in signum adeptae libertatis discumberent. Tremell. in notis. * (Eiusdem traditionis meminit quoque Ioh Buxtorff. in Synag. Iud. c. 13. subdubitat verò Hugo Grotius, utpote evi sedendi mos aut non minus antiquus, ac mos accumbendi, aut primo mori proximus videtur ex Gen. 43, 33. itemque ex 1. Sam. 20, 25. Addit, Iudaeos hodie in coenâ illâ commemorativâ sessionem usurpare, sed solito molliorem & honoratiorem, & cum reclinatione corporis. Porro de more accumbendi vid. Stuckius in Antiquit. Conviv. Rosinus in Antiquit. Romanis l. 5. c. 28. & Dempsteri à Muresk in d. l. Paralipomena, Lambinus ad Horat. od. 27. l. 2. p. 66. it. ad lib. 2. Satyr. p. 151. Guido Pancirollus Rerum Memorab. tit. 51. p. 495. seqq. & Henr. Salmuth. in illum notae P. 513. 514. Petrus Ciacconius de Triclinio, Aldus Manutius de Quaes. per epist. l. 1. q. 4. Fried. Taubmannus in Plautum. Agit quoque de ead. consuet. B. Socer. G. Henr. Plathnerus, Ictus as Consil. quondam Saxon. Comm. ἀνεκδόοτ- in Iuven. Sat. 2. Extat etiam Dissertatiuncula B. Fratris Germani, Iohannis Gerhardi, de more Convivandi veterum, Wittebergae luci exposita.) * Posset etiam responderi, Christum primò quidem discubuisse cum discipulis, postea verò agni paschalis manducandi ergo à mensâ surrexisse. * (Arridet hoc cumprimis Dn. D. Friedlieb. in h. l. p. 174, b. ex Pontificiis Iesuitae Tirino, aliis) *

* (Cum doudecim discipulis. Q. hîc, An Iudas proditor interfuerit quoque celebrationi Paschae & Eucharistiae, illamque sumserit? Negant S. Hilarius, Theophylactus in h. l. Clemens Romanus l. 5. Constit. c. 16. Innocentius III. l. 4. de Myst. Euchar. c. 13. Rupertus l. 10. in Matth. in fine, Tatianus, Ammonius & alii, adducti eâ ratione, quòd Iudas fuerit indignus tantis mysteriis & à S. Coenâ meritò arcendus Rectiùs affirmant Origenes, Cyrillus, Chrysostomus, Augustinus, Rabbanus, Beda, Thomas, Suarez, aliique communiter, quos sequitur etiam Corn. à Lapide in h. l. Eadem quoque nostratium sententia est. vid. B. D. chemnitius LL. Theol. part. 3. p. 153. B. D. Grawerus in A. C. part. post. p. 275. 276. B. D. Harbart in capp. purae doctrinae p. 523. B. D. Hutterus LL. Theol. Mai. p. 724. B. D. Mylius in A. C. p. 169. B. Parens tum in Harm. Evang. c. 171. tum in LL. Theol de S. Coenâ §. 223. & 235. ubi etiam pro hâc sententia allegat Cyprianum, Hieronymum, Theodoretum, & alios. Atque hanc sententiam prolixè probat & ad Adversariorum exceptiones respondent ex Lutheranii B. D. Fōsterus Dispp. Catech. Dec. 3. §. 84. seqq. B. Par. L. de S. Coenâ §. 235. B. D. Keslerus in pecul. Dissert. de Iuda Prodit. S. Coenae hospite, ex Pontificius verò Cornelius à Lapide in h. l. Quid quòd non solùm Calvinus ipse l. 4. Instit. c. 17. §. 34. agnoscat, Iudam fuisse praesentem, cùm Christus S. Eucharistiam distribueret, verùm etiam Guil. Whitakerus Theologus Anglus tr. de Scr. q. 6. c. 12. disertè scribat, sententiae illi, quòd Iudas absuerit, contradicere non solum Scripturas, sed & Patres, Dionysium, Augustinum, Chrysostomum. Idem etiam admittunt ex Calvinianis Martyr, Beza ac alii. plerique tamen, uti Danaeus, W. Musculus, I. Piscator &c. rem totam in medio reliquendam esse existimant. quae etiam sententia est quorundam Pontificiorum, uti Turriani, Barradii, Salmeronis, aliorumque.) *

## 26:21
* (v. 21. One of you is about to betray me. The prediction is by no means an impulsive or necessitating cause for Judas to betray. See the notes on ch. 13, 13, and 14, and also Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, ep. 56. Certainly, Judas did not betray Christ because Christ foresaw and predicted this; but because Judas was going to sin with the Devil suggesting it and his own avarice impelling him, from which Christ, as true GOD, could not but foresee this. Unless Judas had been going to betray Christ, Christ would neither have foreseen nor predicted the betrayal. In the same way, the Doctors of the primitive Church are accustomed to respond, as Mr. D. Well. brings forward the express words of Chrysostom in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, p. 624. Furthermore, it is asked, why did Christ not name Judas? Resp. 1. This was done in order to consult his reputation. 2. In order to provoke Judas to repentance by this gentleness. Looking to this, St. Jerome writes: He sends, he writes, the crime into the number, so that the one who is conscious may do penance.) *

Latin:

* (v. 21. Unus vestrûm me proditurus est. Praedictio minimè est causa impulsiva vel necessitans Iudam, ut proderet. Vide notata ad c. 13, 13. ac 14. it. Isidotum Pelusiotam lib. 1. ep. 56. Certè non propterea Iudas Christum prodidit, quia Christus hoc praevidit & praedixit: verùm quia Diabolo suggerente & propriâ avaritiâ impellente peccaturus erat Iudas, unde non potuit non Christus uti verus DEUS, hoc praevidere. Nisi Iudas proditurus Christum fuisset, nec Christus proditionem praevidisset, nec praedixisset. Eodem modo & primitivae Ecclesiae Dd. respondere solent, ceu expressa Chrysostomi verba adducit Dn. D. Well. Comm. in ep. ad Rom. p. 624. Coeterùm quaetitur, cur Christus Iudam non nominarit? Resp. 1. Factum hoc ideò, ut eius famae consuleret. 2. ut Iudam lenitate hac ad poenitentiam provocaret. Huc respiciens S. Hieronymus: Mittit, scribit, crimen in numero, ut conscius agat poenitentiam.) *

## 26:22
* (v. 22. ἤρξαντο λέγειν they began to say i. e. they said. It occurs in the same way Lev. 21, 9.) *

Latin:

* (v. 22. ἤρξαντο λέγεινcoeperunt dicere i. e. dixerunt. itaetiam occurrit Lev. 21, 9.) *

## 26:23
v. 23. He who dips with me &c. Most establish that the traitor is designated by these words. Piscator objects that it could have happened that more than Judas, or at least someone other than Judas, dipped with him in that manner, and that individuals would have been careful not to dip with him in that way, likewise, that after these words were already spoken, Judas finally asks; Am I the one? Finally, because it appears from the narrative of John that the disciples perceived no certain sign of the betrayer from the words of the Lord. He therefore maintains that in these words there is contained not a designation of the betrayer, but a complaint about the magnitude of his ingratitude, as one who is about to betray his master, who daily deserved well of him, and lived familiarly with him. Tossanus follows the same view, He who dips i.e., one of those who takes food with me Ps. 41. 10.Marc. 14. 18. * (and already before these, Erasmus and Beza explained it in the same way.) * But the reasons of Piscator are not of such moment and weight that one should depart from the received opinion on account of them. * (Whence also Lud. de Dieu, having deserted that opinion, insists on the beaten path, and rightly urges against that exposition that Christ, if He described the betrayer only by mutual association, and not indeed by a certain action, would have answered nothing (since all were equal in the association), when nevertheless the disciples had anxiously asked who it was who was about to betray Him. It is added that the Savior seems to point His finger to that very dish in which was ἔμβαυυα that which the Jews call חרוסת, as Camero rightly notes in Myroth. p. 113. Who also reveals from the rituals of the Jews that that sauce was a certain thick condiment, made from various sweet and acid things, like mud, in memory, namely, of the Egyptian calamity, because their ancestors were forced to make bricks from mud. See also Ribera de Templo p. 333. But to that which seems to have moved Erasmus above all, namely that if those words of the Savior: he who dips with me, were to be taken properly or strictly, they would have been a manifest and undoubted sign of the betrayer, and thus there would have been no need at all then to inquire further among themselves about the author of the betrayal. To this, I say, Hugo Grotius responds by noting, that Judas reclined near Christ, so that when there were several dishes at the Supper, he ate from the same dish from which Christ was eating: for thus, he continues, it could more easily happen that Christ, to him asking whether he was the one of whom He was speaking, answered submissively and with most not hearing, σὺ εῖπας, and that with him not heard, John, prompted by Peter, asking who it was who would dare such a crime, might receive a certain sign from Christ, that he was the one to whom Christ Himself would give a morsel dipped from the dish. *

Latin:

v. 23. Qui intingit mecum &c. Plerique statuunt, his verbis designari proditorem. Piscator opponit, quòd fieri potuerit, ut plures quàm Iudas aut saltim alius quàm Iudas ad eum modū unà cum ipso intingeret, quòdq; singuli fuissent cauturi, ne sic cum eo intingerent, item, quòd post haec verba iam dicta Iudas demū interrogat; Num ego is sum? Deniq; quòd ex narratione Iohannis appareat, discipulos ex verbis Domini nullū certum proditoris signum percepisse. Statuit igitur, his verbis non designationem proditoris contineri, sed querelam de summâ illius ingratitudine, ut qui proditurus sit herum suum, qui quotidie benè de ipso merebatur, & familiariter cum ipso vivebat. Idem sequitur Tossanus Qui intingit i. e. unus ex illis, qui mecum cibum capit Ps. 41. 10.Marc. 14. 18. * (& iam ante hos Erasmus ac Beza eodem modo exposurunt.) * Sed rationes Piscatoris non sunt eius momenti ac ponderis, ut propter eas à receptâ sententiâ sit discedendū. * (Unde etiam Lud. de Dieu, desertâ illâ sententiâ tritae insistit viae, ac rectè contra expositionem illam urget, quòd Christus, si proditorem tantùm à mutuo convictu, non verò à certâ actione descripsit, nihil responderit (quippe cùm omnes in convictu pares fuerint.) cùm tamen discipuli anxiè quaesivissent, quis esset, qui eum proditurus esset. Accedit, quòd Salvator digitum intendere videatur ad eam ipsam paropsidem, in qua erat ἔμβαυυα illud, quod Iudaei vocant חרוסת, uti rectè notat Camero in Myroth. p. 113. Qui etiam è Iudaeorum ritualibus prodit, quòd embamma illud fuerit spissum quoddam condimentum, ex variis rebus dulcibus & acidis confectum, luti adinstar, in memoriam scil. calamitatis Aegyptiacae, quòd maiores ipsorum ex luto lateres conficre coacti fuerint. Vid. etiā Ribera de Templo p. 333. Ad illud verò, quod cumprimis Erasmum movisse videtur, nempè quòd si verba illa Salvatoris: qui intingit mecum, propriè s. strictè accipienda essent, manifestum atque indubitatum proditoris signum fuissent, adeòque minimè tum opus fuisset, porrò inter se de proditionis autore inquirere. Ad hoc, inquam, Hugo Grotius respondet monendo, Iudam prope Christum accubuisse, ita ut cùm plures essent in Coenâ catini, ille ex eodem catino ederet, ex quo edebat Christus: ita enim, pergit, facilius fieri potuit, ut Christus illi interroganti, an ipse esset, de quo loqueretur, submissè & plerisque non audientibus responderet,σὺ εῖπας,utque eo non audito Iohannes à Petro monitus, quaerens quis ille esset, qui tantum scelus esset ausurus, certum à Christo signum acciperet, eum hanc esse, cat ipse Christus datarus esset de catino tinctam iure offulam.) *

## 26:24
(v. 24. ὑπάγει. Camero in Myroth. Ev. p. 113. thinks that this word is used here with the same meaning with which the Hebrew הלך Ps. 58, 9. & אזל 1. Sam. 9, 7.Iob. 14, 11. is used, so that it denotes not simply departure, but destruction: But if he understands death, it can easily be granted, since it is certain that the word חלך is also used in this way Gen. 15, 2.)

It were good for that man if he had not been born. See concerning the genuine sense of these words B. Par. L. de Inf. §. 78. Damascenus l. 4. O. F. c. 22. rightly observes, this was said by the Lord not because He disapproved of His own creature, but that He might the more blame the malice which, to the creature of GOD good in itself, was added from its own will, and might express the gravity of the punishment that would follow. B. P. L. de pecc. §. 24. brings forward this opinion and illustrates this very thing with a beautiful simile. Theophyl. ἡ ἀνυπαρξία κρείττων τῆς ἐν ἁμαρτίαις ὑπ άρξεως. is good: For the positive is placed here for the comparative: and it is called good or better, not positively, as if it were a greater good, since it is not a good at all: but negatively, because it is less evil, that is, the misery of one never born is less than that of one born, but who has fallen into such misery by his own fault. A similar expression is had 2. Petr. 2, 21. Among the Talmudists there are also twin expressions, as Buxtorf notes in Lex. Talm. p. 1316. & 2294. Hackspan tr. de util. lect. Rabb. p. 442. and Ludov. Cappellus in Spicil. p. 36. The Jesuit Maldonatus thinks that that phrase: it were good &c. seems to be taken from, or that there is an allusion in it to Iobi. 3, 3.11.c. 18, 10.19.Ierem. 20. v. 14. which Cappellus also approves l. c.)

Latin:

* (v. 24. ὑπάγει. Existimat Camero in Myroth. Ev. p. 113. verbum hoc eâ significatione hîc adhiberi, quâ Ebr. הלךPs. 58, 9. & אזל1. Sam. 9, 7.Iob. 14, 11. ita ut notet non simpliciter abitum, sed interitum: Quod si mortem intelligit, facilè concedi potest, cùm conster, quòd ita etiam verbum חלך adhibeatur Gen. 15, 2.) *

* (Bonum erat ei, si non natus fuisset homo ille. Vid. de genuino horum verborum sensu B. Par. L. de Inf. §. 78. Damascenus l. 4. O. F. c. 22. rectè observat, hoc à Domino dictum esse non quòd propriam suam creaturam improbarit, sed ut malitiam, quae creaturae DEI per se bonae, ex propria ipsius volunt ate accessit, eòmagis vituperaret, & poenae secuturae gravitatem exprimeret. Sententiam hanc adducit, ac pulero simili hoc ipsum etiam illustrat B. P. L. de pecc. §. 24. Benè Theophyl. ἡ ἀνυπαρξία κρείττων τῆς ἐν ἁμαρτίαις ὑπ άρξεως. Ponitur enim hîc positivus pro comparativo: dicitur que bonum seu melius non positivè quasi maius sit bonum, cùm nec sit bonum: sed negativò, quia minùs malum h. e. minor est nunquam nati, quàm nati, sed in tantum seculus propriâ culpâ prolapsi miseria Similis locutio habetur 2. Petr. 2, 21. Apud Talmudicos gemellae etiam habentur loquelae, ceu notant Buxtorffius in Lex. Talm. p. 1316. & 2294. Hackspanius tr. de util. lect. Rabb. p. 442. ac Ludov. Cappellus in Spicil. p. 36. Iesuita Maldonatus existimat, phrasin illam: bonum er at &c. videri desumtam, aut in eâ alludi ad Iobi. 3, 3.11.c. 18, 10.19.Ierem. 20. v. 14. quod approbat etiam Cappellus l. c.) *

## 26:25
v. 25. Who was betraying him i. e. who was soon about to betray. Ion. 1, 2. he found a ship going i. e. soon about to go. Whither therefore I go, i. e. I am about to go shortly. Others render, who was betraying i. e. was preparing or thinking to betray.

Rabbi. The other disciples were saying κύριε, which was attributed even to commoners, but Judas said, Rabbi Master, which is more honorable. His hypocrisy is therefore noted. * (Judas indeed asks; not as if he were ignorant of what he himself is about to do, but so that he might feign a good conscience with audacity, as St. Jerome speaks.) *

* ( σὺ εῖπαι Cons. v. 64. & c. 27. 11. & Luc. 22. 70. the sense is: your own conscience holds you bound, and convicts you, that you are the traitor, although by a feigned interrogation you outwardly pretend not to know.) *

Latin:

v. 25. Qui prodebat eum i. e. qui mox proditurus erat. Ion. 1, 2.invenit navem euntem i. e. mox ituram. Quò ergò vado, i. e. iturus sum propediem. Alii reddunt, qui prodebat i. e. prodere parabat vel cogitabat.

Rabbi. Reliqui discipuli dicebant κύριε, quod tribuebatur etiam plebeiis, sed Iudas dixit, Rabbi Magister, quod magis honorificū. notatur igitur ipsius hypocrisis. * (Interrogat verò Iudas; non quasi nescius, quid sacturus ipse sit, sed ut audaciâ bonam conscientiā mentiretur ut loquitur S. Hieronymus.) *

* ( σὺ εῖπαι Cons. v. 64. & c. 27. 11. & Luc. 22. 70. sensus est: tua ipsius conscientia te tenet obstrictum, teque convincit, quòd tu sis proditor, licet fictà interrogatione te nescire, exteriùs prodas.) *

## 26:26
v. 26. And as they were eating. Concerning the words of the Lord's Supper see Macarius homil. 27. p. 382. Nicephorus lib. 1, H. E. c. 28. when he had confirmed that it was truly his body and his blood, as if by interposing faith. * (It is well to be observed here, that a triple supper was celebrated on that night or evening. 1. The supper of the Paschal lamb, according to the divine institution, Exod. 12. 2. 2. The common supper, which the Jews were accustomed to institute after the Paschal feast was finished, Ioh. 13, 2. seqq. and the words Matth. 26, 19. are to be taken concerning this. 3. The Lord's Supper. whence the Apostle 1 Cor. 11, 25. and Lucas c. 22, 20. say μετὰ τὸ δειπνῆσαι. Nor does that custom of the Jews stand in the way, by which, according to the witnesses Scaliger de Emend. Temp. f. 537. and Buxtorf Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 616. it is said to have been forbidden to eat anything after the cup of the Hymn or the Paschal cup. For it must be known, that this custom is more recent and was introduced only after the second temple was destroyed. Furthermore, the Jesuit Cornelius à Lapide inveighs here against the Orthodox without merit, in that they call the Eucharist the Supper, when he himself is forced to concede, not only that Christ instituted it at the second hour of the night, but also that the first Christians for some time celebrated the Eucharist at supper by the example of Christ, as is gathered from 1. Cor. 11, 25.. add that even John c. 21, 20. himself names it so. But since no reason is brought forward by the Jesuit why the S. Eucharist cannot be distinguished by the appellation of S. Supper or Lord's Supper, I do not wish to be more prolix. One may see concerning this controversy B. Par. Confesl. Cathol. l. 2. Spec. part. 2. art. 14. c. 1. In the same place the Jesuit writes erroneously, that the bread after the consecration did not remain bread, but during the giving by the power of the words and of the consecration of CHRIST it had been converted into the body of CHRIST. But concerning this error and the figment of transubstantiation it will be treated a little later.) *

* ( εὐλογήσας. By the power of this ἐυλογίας,, although once uttered by Christ, yet even today, as often as the words of Institution are recited in the administration of the Holy Supper, it happens that by means of the Eucharistic bread the body of Christ, and by means of the Eucharistic wine the blood of Christ is distributed, as the blessed Par. L. on the Holy Supper §. 143 notes from Ambrose lib. 4. de Sacr. C. 4. t. 4. p. 439. and Chrysostom homil. 30. de Prodit. Iudaet. 5. p. 85. Although H. Grotius in this place shows to many that it was a custom received among the Jews that they would take no food or wine unless they had first given thanks to GOD the giver, with a prayer added, yet it is sufficiently clear from the context here that this blessing of Christ and institution of the Holy Eucharist was far different from that common blessing or prayer received among the Jews.) *

* ( ἒκλασε. Although Christ broke the Eucharistic bread, it is not immediately permissible to infer from this that wherever the Holy Supper is administered, the Eucharistic bread must be broken. Since there is a distinction between δόσιν the thing itself, and δόσεως τρόπον.. Why, however, we do not admit the Calvinian breaking of bread (which the Photinians also urge, see Ostorodus Instit. Germ. de Coenà Dom.) in our Churches, the blessed D. Fewerborn, Synt. 2. disquis Theol. diss. 17. §. 8. and the Lords Theologians of Marburg in Fund. deduct. c. 8. p. 663 teach at length. It is added that it was a custom among the Jews that the father of the family would break and distribute the bread, as Camero notes in this place. Hence the phrase was born to break bread, that is, to make others partakers of it. See Is. 58, 7. Lam. 4, 4. Mark 8, 19. Whence it also appears that it is by no means necessary that where mention is made in the N. T. that they gathered to break bread, it must necessarily be conceded that the use of the Holy Eucharist is being discussed there. Against the Papists, who strive to prove communion under one kind from the sayings Luke 24, 30. Acts 2, 46. c. 20, 7. and 11. c. 27, 35., falsely presupposing that the Holy Supper is being discussed in those places because mention of the breaking of bread is made in them.) *

* (To the disciples. Since Judas was also in the number of these, it follows that he too was a guest at the Holy Supper. And that clearly appears from Luke 22, 13. 14. 15.21. compare what was noted a little earlier at verse 20. Nor does John 13, 30. stand in the way, for εὐθέως can be taken in some breadth of time, or even a figure of anticipation can be established among the other Evangelists, since Luke, more than the other Evangelists, observed the order of histories most accurately. see C. 1, 3.) *

* (that is, E. bread is changed or transubstantiated into the body of Christ. Thus the Papists conclude from this place. see Bellarm. b. 3. on the Eucharist, c. 19. Gregorius de Valentia vol. 4. Disp. 1. q. 2. point 3. Felicianus Capito, Catholic Explanation on this place, p. 617. when he had recited the words of institution, he adds: You see how the Evangelist, before the consecration, calling it bread and the cup, afterwards says it is the body and blood &c. because therefore Christ says: This is my body, and does not say: This bread is my body, so that together with the bread there is also the body of Christ. he does not say: Receive in this bread, or under this bread my body, but simply and clearly he says with that article, This, signifying the substance: This is my body. Therefore Christ, who is the truth &c., is to be believed more than the subversive heretics, who deny transubstantiation. But it must be known 1. that we in no way contradict Christ, for Christ did not use this proposition: Bread is my body, but that one: This is my body. 2. the pronoun this does indeed denote the bread, but not only that, but rather the whole συμπεπλεγυένον or complex: for otherwise it would have to be said, not τοῦτο, but οὗτος, since ἄρτος is of the masculine gender. Furthermore, even the consecrated bread, or after the consecration, is still called bread, lest anyone think that after the consecration has been performed, it ceases to be bread and is transubstantiated into the body of Christ. That is evident from Matthew 26, 16.Mark 14, 22.Luke 22, 19.1. Cor. 11, 17.c. 11, 26. and following. In vain do the Papists object and except, see the Jesuit Hager in the Collation of the Augsburg Confession with the Council of Trent, p. 121. wine, which nevertheless had been water, is called water even after transubstantiation John 2, 9. For it must be known that that wine is not absolutely called water, but ὕδωρ ὖινον γεγεννημένον water turned into wine, or wine, which had been water. But Hager makes another exception in the same place, p. 118.

namely that among the Hebrews any food is called bread, and thus also the body of Christ, or bread transubstantiated into the body of Christ bread may be called. But we reply, although it is by no means denied that the name לחם is sometimes used in this way among the Hebrews: it does not follow, therefore, that it is always, or even in this place, accepted in that breadth. For one must not depart from the received signification (which is that it denotes natural bread, as it is distinguished from spiritual), unless necessity urges, which here is none. Nay, it is rather certain that the customary signification ought to be retained here, since the Apostle speaks of such bread as Christ took into his hands, broke, distributed to the Apostles, and which was distributed and broken in the Holy Eucharist among the Corinthians, and which is κοινωνία or the communion of the body of Christ. Suppose that by bread nothing is signified here except spiritual bread, the sense of the words of Christ will be, the body of Christ is the body of Christ. It remains, therefore, that by τὸ this, in the words of Christ: this is my body, bread alone cannot be understood: (for grammatical construction stands in the way, since there is in the authentic text τοῦτο, not οὗτος) nor only spiritual bread or only the body, because it would be an identical proposition. It is therefore 3. a demonstrative and exhibitive proposition, in which the subject denotes the whole complex, but the predicate expresses the more worthy and less obvious to the sense, the foundation of which propositions is the union, conjunction, and simultaneous exhibition of two things. Just as therefore in common speech, a cask being shown, we say, this is wine: and purses being exhibited, this is money, where however there is no transubstantiation of the cask into wine, and the purses into money, but the conjunction and conjoined exhibition of both: so in this sacramental proposition: this is my body, transubstantiation of bread into the body of Christ is not to be thought of: but rather it is indicated that together with and under this blessed bread the body of Christ is given, etc. Nevertheless 4. it is well to be noted, that the comparison between this sacramental and other exhibitive propositions is instituted not on account of the specific identity of the union, as if the body were in the bread just as wine is in a cask, by no means: but on account of the mode of predication flowing from the generic union. For we well know that this union is mystical, sacramental, and thus hidden from every human intellect. Let it be seen at greater length in B. Par. L. de S. Euchar. §. 81. 93. and 134. B. D. Höpfn. pec. tr. de S. Coenâ. Dn D. Wellerus Comm. in Ep. ad Rom. p. 288. 289. Dn. D. Danhaw. Idea Boni Interpret. p. 130. seqq. B. D. Huls A. C. Manuali. p. 301. B. D. Fewrb. Synt. 2. S. Disq. Dissert. 18. it. p. 484. seqq. Furthermore the places of Holy Scripture, from which the Calvinists attempt to prove that τὸ is sometimes used for signifies, will be discussed in their proper places. In this place we observe at least two things, 1. that Buxtorf himself writes that this is the sense of the words of Christ: Behold, you have just slaughtered and eaten the body of the paschal lamb, as a memorial of the Egyptian liberation, and a type of my body, but now I wish the body of that lamb to be abrogated, and I exhibit to you plainly by means of bread my body, which is even now about to be delivered into death for you. he cites Mr. Dr. Friedlieb. 2. that Constant. L'Empereur in Annot. to Gr. Mosis Kimchi p. 52 seeks in vain to find patronage for the error of the Calvinists among the Orientals, as those who are destitute of a word which signifies denotes, and therefore use in its place the word is. For even if it were granted in the highest degree concerning the Hebrews, it is nevertheless denied concerning the Syrians, as those who for signifies use the word it. concerning the Arabs, to whom is in use in this signification. Now indeed the Oriental interpreters ὁμοσθυματὸν in this place translate τοὲςι by is. For the Syrian has this is my body. The Arab this is my body. The Ethiopian indeed inserts the name of bread, meanwhile τοῦ he makes no mention of signifies. for he translates this bread is my body. The Persian: this is my body. But what must be observed above all, it is certain that GOD left the new covenant to us not originally in Hebrew or Syriac, but in Greek. Since therefore the Greeks are by no means destitute of a word which signifies denotes, namely σημαίνει, and yet the Evangelists, ours in this place Mark Ch. 14, 22. Luke Ch. 22, 19. constantly have ἐςι, it is truly rash to expound that very thing by τὸ signifies.

Furthermore, that τὸ ῥητὸν in the words of the Holy Supper is to be constantly retained, has long since been solidly demonstrated by our own people. Let the Blessed D. Chemnitius be consulted in the Foundations of Sacred doctrine concerning the true & substantial presence of the body & blood of Christ in the Holy Supper, the Blessed D. Bald. in the ordinary Disputations concerning the words of the Testament, the Blessed D. Iac. Martini in Photinianism p. 432. following, the Lords Theologians of Marburg in the Fundamental Deduction, the Blessed D. Feuerborn in Synthesis 2. Sacred Disquisitions Dissertation 18., the Blessed D. Grawerus in the Anti-Paraean Bulwark, the Blessed Par. L. concerning the Holy Supper §. 69. following, the Lord D. Christ. Chemnitius Disputation 8. on the F. C., the Blessed D. Gerlachius Volume 1. Theological Disputations Disputation 9. 10. 11. 12. & 13. likewise Volume 2. Disputation 20. 21.) *

* (Body.Luke Ch. 22, 19. adds, which is given for you, & furthermore: do this in remembrance of me, which latter addition indeed pertains not to the substance, but to the fruit, since the former is understood from the context: Paul. 1. Cor. 11, 24.which shall be delivered for you.) *

Latin:

v. 26. Coenantibus autem eis. De verbis Coenae Dominicae vide Macarium homil. 27. p. 382. Nicephorus lib. 1, H. E. c. 28. cùm verè corpus suum & sanguinem suum esse, quasi fide interpositâ confirmasset. * (Probè hîc observandum, quòd triplex coena eâ nocte vel vesperâ fuerit celebrata. 1. Coena agni Paschalis, iuxta institutionem divinam, Exod. 12. 2.Communis Caena, quam absoluto Paschali convivio Iudaei instituere solebant, Ioh. 13, 2. seqq. & de hac accipienda verba Matth. 26, 19. 3. Coena Dominicae. unde Apostolus 1 Cor. 11, 25. & Lucas c. 22, 20. dicunt μετὰ τὸ δειπνῆσαι. Nec obstat consuetudo illa Iudaeorum, quâ testibus Scaligero de Emend. Temp. f. 537. ac Buxtorffio Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 616. prohibitum fuisse dicitur, quicquam comedere post poculum Hymni sive Paschale. Etenim sciendum, quòd consuetudo haec sit recentior ac post eversum templum secundum demum introducta. Coeterùm praeter meritum invehitur hîc in Orthodoxos Iesuita Cornelius à Lapide, eò quòd Eucharistiam vocent Coenam, cùm tamen ipsement concedere cogatur, non solùm Christum horâ noctis secundâ illam instituisse, sed primos quoque Christianos aliquamdiu in Coena exemplo Christi Eucharistiam celebrasse, ceu ex 1. Cor. 11, 25. colligatur. adde. quòd ipse etiam Iohannes c. 21, 20. ita nominet. Verùm cùm nulla à Iesuita ratio afferatur, quare S. Eucharistia S. Coenae vel Coenae Dominicae appellatione insigniri nequeat, nolo esse prolixior. Videri autem de controversiâ hâc poterit B. Par. Confesl. Cathol. l. 2. Spec. part. 2. art. 14. c. 1. Ibid. erroneè scribit Iesuita, panem fact â consecratione non mansisse panem, sed inter dandum vi verborum & consecrationis CHRISTI conversum fuisse in corpus CHRISTI. Sed de errore hoc & transubstantiationis figmento paullò post agetur.) *.

* ( εὐλογήσας. Vi huius ἐυλογίας, semel quidem à Christo prolatae, sed adhuc hodie, quoties verba Institutionis in S. Coenae administratione recitantur, fit, ut mediante pane Eucharistico corpus Christi, & mediante vino Eucharistico sanguis Christi distribuatur, ceu ex Ambrosio lib. 4. de Sacr. C. 4. t. 4. p. 439. ac Chrysostomo homil. 30. de Prodit. Iudaet. 5. p. 85. monet B. Par. L. de S. Coenâ §. 143. Licet verò multis H. Grotius in h. l. ostendat, more apud Iudaeos receptum suisse, ut cibum nullum aut vinum sumerent, nisi priùs DEO datori gratias egissent, additâ precatione, satis tamen è contextu hî patet, quòd haec Christi benedictio ac S. Eucharistiae instituio longè diversa fuerit ab illâ communi apud Iudaeos recept â benedictione s. precatione.) *

* ( ἒκλασε. Licet Christus panem Eucharisticum fregerit, non tamen statim hinc inferre licet, quòd ubique, ubi S. Coena administratur, panis Euch. frangi debeat. cùm dist. sit inter δόσιν ipsam, & δόσεως τρόπον. Cur vero in nostris Ecclesiis fractionem panis Calvinianam (quam & Photiniani urgent, vid. Ostorodus Instit. Germ. de Coenà Dom.) non admittamus, prolixè docent B. D. Fewerborn. Synt. 2. disquis Theol. diss. 17. §. 8. Dnn. Theol. Marpurg. in Fund. deduct. c. 8. p. 663. Accedit, quòd in more apud Iudaeos positum fuerit, ut pater familias panem frangeret ac distribueret, ceu Camero h. l. monet. Nata hinc phrasis frangere panem, id est participes eius alios reddere. Vid. Es. 63, 7.Thren. 4, 4.Marc. 8, 19. Unde etiam patet, hautquaquam necessarium esse, ut ubi in N. T. fit mentio, quòd convenerint frangere panem, ibi necessariò de usu S. Eucharistiae agi concedatur. Contra Pontificios, qui ex dictis Luc. 24, 30.Actor. 2. 46.c. 20, 7. & 11.c. 27. 35. communionem sub una probare satagunt, falsò praesupponentes, in iis locis de S. Coena agi, eò quòd fractionis panis in illis fiat mentio.) *

* (Discipulis. in horum numero cùm & Iudas fuerit, consequens est, quòd & ipse S. Coenae fuerit hospes. idque clarè patet ex Luc. 22, 13. 14. 15.21. conf. paulò antè notata ad vers. 20. Nec obstat Ioh. 13, 30. potest enim εὐθέως in latitudine aliqua temporis accipi, vel etiam figura anticipationis apud reliquos Evang. statui. cùm Lucas prae coeteris Evangelistis ordinem historiarum accuratissimè observarit. vid. C. 1, 3.) *

* (est. E. panis mutatur vel transsubstantiatur in corpus Christi. Ita colligunt ex h. l. Pontificii. vid. Bellarm. l. 3. de Euchar. c. 19. Gregorius de Valentia t. 4. Disp. 1. 9. 2. punct. 3. Felicianus Capito Explic. Cathol. ad h. l. p. 617. cùm verba institutionis recitâsset, subiungit: Vides, quomodo Evangelista ante consecratinem panem & calicem appellans, pòst corpus & sanguinem dicit &c. quia igitur Christus inquit: Hoc est corpus meum, & non dicit: Hic panis est corpus meum, ut simul cum pane sit etiam corpus Christi. nedicit: Accipite in hoc pane, vel sub hoc pane corpus meum, sed simpliciter & clarè inquit cum illo articulo, Hoc, substantiam significante: Hoc est corpus meum. Ergò Christo quiest veritas &c. magis credendum est, quàm subversis haereticis, qui transsubstantiationem negant. Astsciendum 1. quòd minimè Christo contradicamus, neque. enim Christus usus est hâc propositione: Panis-est corpus meum, sed illâ: Hoc est corpus meum. 2. pronomen hoc denotare quidem panem, sed non solum, verùm totum συμπεπλεγυένον sive complexum: dicendum enim aliàs foret, non τοῦτο, sed οὗτος, cùm ἄρτος sit generis Masculini. Praetereà etiam panis consecratus, sive post consecrationem, adhuc panis dicitur, ne quis existimet, quòd post factam consecrationem, panis esse definat, & in corpus Christi transsubstantietur. Illud patet ex Matth. 26, 16.Marc. 14, 22.Luc. 22, 19.1. Cor. 11, 17.c. 11, 26. seqq. Frustra obiiciunt & excipiunt Pontificii, vid. Iesuita Hagerus in Collat. A. C. cum Concil. Trident. p. 121. vinum, quod tamen aqua suerat, etiam post transsubstantiationem vocari aquamIob. 2, 9. Etenim sciendum, quòd vinum illud non absolutè aqua vocetur, sed ὕδωρ ὖινον γεγεννημένονaqua in vinum versa, sue vinum, quod aqua suerat. Aliter verò adhuc excipit Hagerus d. l. p. 118.

nempe quòd apud Ebraeos quilibet cibus dicatur panis, adeoque & Christi corpus, vel panis in Christi corpus transsubstantiatus panis vocetur. Verùm resp. licet minimè negetur, ita apud Ebraeos nomen לחם adhiberi quandoque: non tamen sequitur, ergò semper, vel etiam hoc etiam loco in ista latitudine accipi. neque enim discedendum à receptâ significatione, (quae est, ut notet panem naturalem, prout distinguitur à spirituali,) nisi necessitas urgeat, quae hîc nulla est. Quim certum potiùs est, quòd usitata significatio retineri hîc debeat, cùm Apostolus de tali loqùatur pane, quem Christus in manus sumsit, fregit, Apostolis distribuit, & qui in S. Eucharistiâ apud Corinthios distribuebatur ac frangebatur, & qui est κοινωνία sive communicatio corporis Christi. Pone, per panem nil significari hîc, nisi panem spiritualem, verborum Christi sensus erit, corpuc Christi est corpus Christi. Manet igitur, quòd per τὸhoc, in verbis Christi: hoc est corpus meum, non possit solus panis in telligi: (obstat enim constructio Grammatica, cùm habeatur in textu authentico τοῦτο, non οὗτος) nec solus panis spiritualis sive solum corpus, quia foret propositio identica. Est igitur 3. propositio demonstrativa & exhibitiva, in qua subiectum totum notat complexum, praedicatum verò exprimit dignius & sensui minùs obvium quarum propositionum fundamentum est rerum duarum unio, coniunctio, & simultanea exhibitio. Sicuti igitur in communi sermone, monstrato dolio, dicimus, hoc est vinum: & exhibitis loculis, hoc est pecunia, ubi tamen nulla est transsubstantiatio dolii in vinum, & loculi in pecuniam, sed utriusq; coniunctio & coniuncta exhibitio: ita in hâc propositione sacramentali: hoc est corpus meum. non cogitanda transsubstantiatio panis in corpus Christi: sed id potiùs indicatur, quòd un à cum & sub pane lioc benedicto detur corpus Christi &c. Attamen 4. probè notandum, quòd collatio inter hanc sacramentalem & alias exhibitivas propositiones in stituatur non propter specificam unionis identitatem, quasi ita corpus sit in pane, sicut vinum in dolio, minimè: sed propter modum praedicationis ex generica unione profluentem. probè enim scimus, quòd unio haec sit mystica, sacramentalis, adeòque omni humano intellectui abscondita. Videatur pluribus B. Par. L. de S. Euchar. §. 81. 93. ac 134. B. D. Höpfn. pec. tr. de S. Coenâ. Dn D. Wellerus Comm. in Ep. ad Rom. p. 288. 289. Dn. D. Danhaw. Idea Boni Interpret. p. 130. seqq. B. D. Huls A. C. Manuali. p. 301. B. D. Fewrb. Synt. 2. S. Disq. Dissert. 18. it. p. 484. seqq. Loca porrò Sc. Sacrae, è quibus probare conantur Calviniani, quòd τὸest aliquando adhibeatur pro significat, propriis discutientur sedibus. Hoc loco duo saltem observamus, 1. quòd ipse Buxtorffius hunc verborum Christi sensum esse scribat: Ecce modò mactastis & comedistis corpus agni pa schalis, ut memoriale liberationis Aegyptiacae, & typum corporis mei, sed nunc corpus agni illius abrogatum volo, & planè pane mediante exhibeo vobis corpus meum, quod iamiam pro vobis in mortem tradi debet. allegat Dn. D. F-iedlieb. 2. quòd frustrà Constant. L'Empereur Annot. ad Gr. Mosis Kimchi p. 52. errori Calvinianorum patrocinium quaerat apud Orientales, ut qui destituantur verbo, quod significat denotet, atinde eius loco ut antur voce est. Etenim si vel maximè concedatur de Ebraeis, negatur tamen de Syris, ut qui pro significat ut untur verbo it. de Arabibus, quibus in hac significatione in usu est. Iam verò Orientales Interpp. ὁμοσθυματὸν h. l. vertunt τοὲςιper est. Etenim Syrus habet hoc est corpus meum. Arabs hoc est corpus meum. Aethiops quidem inserit nomen panis, interea τοῦ significat non meminit. vertit enim hic panis corpus meum. Persa: hoc est corpus meum. Sed quod praeprimis observandum venit, constat, quòd DEUS novum foedus non Ebraicè vel Syriacè, sed Graecè originaliter nobis reliquerit. Cùm igitur Graeci minimè destituantur verbo, quod significat notat, nempè σημαίνει, & tamen Evangelistae, noster h. l. Marcus C. 14, 22.Lucas C. 22, 19. constanter habeant ἐςι, temerarium sanè est, illud ipsum per τὸsignificat exponere.
