## 26:27
* (v. 27. Having taken the cup. The external symbol is indicated: For that there was wine in the cup, is evident both from v. 29. following, & from 1. Cor. 11, 23. 24. 25. & indeed, as was the custom in those warmer regions, tempered with water. compare on this matter, what Hugo Grotius brings forward in this place, see Proverbs 9, 2. 5. Revelation 18, 6.)*

* (Drink ye all of this. The evasions of the Papists are inept, when, about to defend communion under one kind, they except to this place 1. that Christ did not command the taking of the cup to all, but at least to those twelve, & whom they represented, namely the clergy, not the laity. Bell. book 4. on the Eucharist Ch. 24. resp. to 2. Corn. à Lapide in this place, Becanus book 1. Manual ch. 9. 110. For it is false, that the Apostles in that first institution & administration of the Holy Supper, represented the person of at least the clergy. And this is acknowledged by Georg. Cassander, a most learned Papist writer, and once highly esteemed both by Maximilian II. & Ferdinand I., in Consultation art. 22. & the thing itself speaks. Nor has it been shown by the Papists by any probable reason thus far. But rather the contrary, that is, that the Apostles represented not the office & duty of Priests, as such, but of those approaching the Holy Supper, is evident from thence, because, according to the hypothesis of the Papists themselves, it is of Priests, as such, to To perform & to sacrifice. It is added that, according to the opinion of the Cardinals, Toletus in John 20 year 17, and Bellarmine book 1 on the P. R. ch. 23, prerogative -2. The priestly dignity finally reached the Apostles after the resurrection of Christ. Furthermore, unless all the Apostles in general had represented those communicating at that time, the institution of the Holy Eucharist would not exist for the laity, but at least for the clergy, which not even the Papists themselves would concede. 2. That Christ in the dispensation of the Holy Eucharist therefore said to the Apostles: Drink from this ALL, so that the first might understand that not the whole was to be drained by him, but only so much was to be left as would suffice for all, as the Jesuit Maldonatus warns, who also boasts that he was the first to notice this. Bellarmine in the cited book and Becanus in the cited book also agree with this. But who, I ask, would believe the Apostles were so fond of wine that it had to be guarded against by a special mandate, lest one person drain the Eucharistic cup, which could suffice for twelve persons? Conf. B Par. vol. 3. Confess. Cathol. p. 1095 and 1287. also Book on the Holy Supper §. 32. Indeed, the causal particle immediately subjoined clearly teaches that just as that reason why all ought to drink—namely, because the blood of Christ is offered, which, having been shed for all, pertains to all—regards the laity no less than the clergy, so also the mandate about drinking from the cup obliges all, as the blessed Hackspan shows more learnedly and at greater length in Disp. 2 on Sacred Places §. 43 et seqq. Nor does the passage Luke 22, 27 favor this Jesuit evasion, since Luke is dealing with the paschal cup. But that is worthy of note, that Cornelius à Lapide in this place willingly acknowledges the error of Bellarmine, who states in book 4 on the Eucharist, ch. 27, to 2, that Christ did not immediately after the consecrated bread consecrate the cup. whence he further tries to prove, if we wish to speak properly and according to the Gospel, the Supper of the Lord does not consist of anything but one species, since Luke ch. 22 records that while they were eating, Christ took bread. And afterwards, with many things interspersed: likewise also the cup. But as we have said, the Jesuit Cornelius willingly grants that Bellarmine erred here, and says, that it is far truer that Christ immediately after the consecration of the bread subjected the consecration of the cup, both because so narrate Matthew, Mark, and Luke: and because the reason of the Sacrament and Sacrifice of the Eucharist demanded it etc. Now if Christ immediately subjected the consecration of the cup to the consecration of the bread; and indeed the mandate eat, was not terminated to that time alone, but to future times as well; nor to the disciples alone, but to all Christians who might wish to use the Holy Eucharist; it follows that neither the mandate, drink, ought to be restricted either to that time alone or to the Apostles alone, since Christ considered the Apostles in exactly the same respect both when he said to them eat, and when he said to the same ones drink. The opinion of other Papists and Jesuits is the same, such as Barradius, Suarez, Maldonatus, etc., whose words B. Par. cites in Confess. Cath. book 2 spec. part 2. art. 14. ch. 7. Felicianus Capito excepts, that nothing is lost to the laity, nor are they harmed, nor do they suffer any inconvenience from it, when they take one species of bread, since Christ is contained whole under both species. For even if, he writes, by the signification of the words, the body is contained under the species of bread, and the blood under the species of wine: yet because Christ now lives, no longer to die, neither is his body without blood, nor is his blood without body. It follows therefore necessarily that nothing is lost to those receiving, because the whole is received under any part. Therefore, it is only on account of the body of Christ whether you take one or if you take two species. Nor is it to be feared that they have fewer or less of the graces of the sacrament in one than in two species of it. For the Divinity, which has been united to both soul and flesh from the beginning of the incarnation of Christ, is never separated from them. It is therefore joined to both flesh and blood, and where it works the effects of graces. Whether therefore anyone takes the blood in the cup, or the flesh in the bread, in both cases he has received Christ the whole man joined with the divinity and the fullness of graces. Resp. 1. This whole discourse rests upon that erroneous dogma of concomitance, so often overthrown by our people, to which the Orthodox rightly oppose the institution of Christ, which Christ is nowhere read to have either changed or retracted. By no means, therefore, is one to judge from the natural union of body and blood, but from the institution of the Holy Eucharist concerning this mystery, how it ought to be celebrated.

and it must be established. 2. Thus neither from the personal union, since the sacramental union is far different than the personal; in the latter the divine nature is united with the human in the one person of Christ, in the former the blessed bread and the body of Christ are united sacramentally, likewise the blessed wine and the blood of Christ. 3. It was by no means unknown to Christ that wherever he himself is, he is present in his entirety, nevertheless he none the less instituted the Holy Eucharist and willed it to be celebrated by us in such a way that his body is received only under the blessed bread, and his blood only under the blessed wine. 4. and therefore he did not say Eat my blood, namely under the species of bread, but drink, understand under the species of wine. 5. If the whole Christ is received sacramentally under one species of bread, why does the mass-priest communicate under both? The arguments which the same Capito brings forward for communion under one from John 6 and Luke 24 will be discussed in their own places. The same man urges, that the ordinance of the Church rests on this reason, that greater reverence and religion might be shown to this sacrament. But what reverence can there be, which is opposed to the institution of Christ? Truly, if by this the blessed cup is treated irreverently when it is shown to the laity, the same must be said of the blessed bread. More things against communion under one, and for communion under both, may be read in B. D. Chemn. in Exam. Concil. Trid. part 2, page 185 et seqq. B. D. Bald. in Not. ad Ep. Becani de Comm. sub utraque. B. D. Menzer. Disp XI. Antipistor. B. D. Mylium in Explic. A. C. part 2, p. 8 et seqq. B. D. Fewrborn. Synt. 2. Sacr. disquis. dissertatione 13. B. Par. Confess. Cathol. l. 2. Spec. part 2, art. 14, c. 7. Dn. Musaeum in pec. tr. de comm. sub utraque. B. D. Calixtum both in pec. dissert. de C. sub utr. and in Notis ad Cassandri tr. dec. sub utr. Furthermore, our Savior, according to Buxtorf, Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 616, in these words: Drink from this all, seems to have looked to the custom of the Jews, among whom it was the law that all present at the paschal supper should drink from the paschal cup, whether they were men or women, etc. But Christ did not pronounce these words immediately after the celebration of the paschal lamb, but after the institution of the Holy Eucharist. This is what must be diligently observed against the Papists.

Latin:

* (v. 27. Accepto calice. Indicatur externum symbolum: Etenim in calice fuisse vinum, patet tùm ex v. 29. seqq. tùm ex 1. Cor. 11, 23. 24. 25. & quidem, uti mos erat in calidioribus illis regionibus, aqua temperatum. conf. in hanc rem, quae adducit Hugo Grotius h. l. vid. Proverb. 9, 2. 5. Apocal. 18, 6.)*

* (Bibite ex hoc omnes. Ineptae sunt tergiversationes Pontificiorum, quando communionem sub una specie defensuri, excipiunt ad h. l. 1. Christum non omnibus sumtionem poculi praecepisse, sed saltem duodecim illis, & quos ipsi repraesentabant, videl. clericis, non laicis. Bell. l. 4. de Euch. C. 24. resp. ad 2. Corn. à Lapide in h. l. Becanus l. 1. Man. c. 9. 110. Etenim falsum est, Apostolos in primâ illâ S. Coenae institutione & administratione, clericorum saltem repraesentâffe personam. idque agnoscit Georg. Cassander, Scriptor Pontificius doctissimus, magnique olim tùm Maximiliano II. tùm Ferdinando I. aestimatus, in Consult. art. 22. & res loquitur ipsa. Nec ulla quoq; probabili ratione hactenus à Pontificiisid ostensum. quin potiùs contrarium, h. e. quòd Apostoli non Sacerdotum, quatenus talium, sed accedentium ad S. Coenam officium ac munus repraesentarint, exinde patet, quia, ex Pontificiorum quidem hypothesi, Sacerdotum quatenus talium, est conficere & sacrificare. Accedit, quòd ex sententia Cardinalium, Toleti in Ioh. 20. ann. 17. ac Bellarmini l. 1. de P. R. c. 23. praerog. -2. Apostolis demum post Christi resurrectionem sacerdotalis dignitas obtigit. Praetereà, nisi Apostoli omnes in universum communicantes tùm repraesentâssent, non exstaret S. Eucharistiae institutio pro laicis, sed saltem pro clericis. quod ne ipsi quidem Pontificii concesserint. 2. Christum in dispensatione S. Eucharistiae ideò ad Apostolos dixisse: Bibite ex hoc OMNES, ut intelligeret primus, non totum sibi exhauriendum, sed tantum relinquendum, quod omnibus sufficeret, monente Iesuita Maldonato, qui & primum se hoc animadvertisse gloriatur. Arridet hoc etiam Bell. l. c. ac Becano l. c. At quis quaeso adeò vinosos credat fuisse Apostolos, ut iterum peculiari mandato cavendum fuerit, ne unus calicem Eucharisticum exhauriret, qui duodecim personis sufficere poterat. Conf. B Par. t. 3. Confess. Cathol. p. 1095. ac 1287. it. L. de S. Coenâ §. 32. Imò verò causalis particula proximè subiuncta clarè docet, quòd sicuti ratio illa, cur omnes bibere debeant, quia nempe sanguis Christi praebeatur, qui pro omnibus effusus, ad omnes spectat, laicos non minùs, quàm clericos, ita quoque mandatum de calice bibendo obliget omnes, prout eruditè ac prolixiùs ostendit B. Hackspan. Disp. 2. de Loc. Sacris §. 43. seqq. Nec favet effugio huic Iesuitico locus Luc. 22, 27. cùm Lucas agat de poculo paschali. Illud verò notatu dignum est, quòd Cornelius à Lapide in h. l. ultrò agnoscat errorem Bellarmini, statuentis lib. 4. de Euchar. c. 27. ad 2. Christum non statim post consecratum panem consecrásse calicem. undè porrò evincere conatur, si propriè & secundùm Evangelium loqui velimus, Coenam Domini non constare nisi ex unâ specie, siquidemLucas C. 22.commemor at, quòd Coenantibus illis Christus acceperit panem. & postmodùm multis interiectis: similiter & calicem. Verùm uti diximus, ultrò largitur Iesuita Cornelius, Bellarminum hîc errâsse, dicitque, longè verius esse, Christum immediatè consecrationi panis subiecisse consecrationem calicis, tum quia it a narrant. MatthaMarcus & Lucas: tum quia id exigebat ratio Sacramenti & Sacrificii Eucharistiae &c. Iam si immediatè consecrationi panis subiecit Christus consecrationem calicis; & verò mandatum edite, non fuit terminatum ad illud solûm tempus, sed ad futura quoque tempora; nec ad solos discipulos, sed ad omnes Christianos, qui S. Eucharistia uti vellent; sequitur, quod nec mandatum, bibite, restringi vel ad illud solùm tempus vel ad solos Apostolos debeat, cùm eodem omninò respectu Apostol-s confideraverit Christus, tum quando ad illos dixit edite, tum quando ad eosdem dixit bibite. Eadem est sententia aliorum Pontificiorum, & Iesuitarum, uti Barradii, Suarez, Maldonati &c. quorum verba adducit B. Par. Confess. Cath. l. 2 spec. part. 2. art. 14. c. 7. Felicianus Capito excipit, nihil deperire laicis, nec laedi, vel quic quam inde pati eos incommodi, cùm unam panis speciem sumunt, siquidem sub utraque specie Christus totus contineatur. Nam et si, scribit, ex verborum significatione, sub specie panis corpus, & sub specie vini sanguis contineatur: tamen quia Christus iam vivit, ampliùs non moriturus, neque corpus eius sine sanguine, neque sanguis sine corpore est. sequitur ergò necessariò, nihil deperire sumentibus, quia totum sub qualibet parte accipiatur. Igitur ex parte corporis Christi tantum est, si unam, atsi duas sumseris species. Neque enim verendum est, minores vel pauciores habere sacramenti gratias in una, quàm illius duabus speciebus. Divinitas namque, quae tam animae quam carni à principio incarnationis Christi unita est, nunquam ab illis separatur. Est ergò tàm carni quàm sanguini eoniuncta, & eosdem ubioperatur gratiarum effectus. Sive igitur quispiam sumat sanguinem in calice, vel carnem in pane utrobique suscepit Christum totum virum cum divinitate coniuncta gratiarumque plenitudine. Resp. 1. Totus hic discursus nititur erroneo illo ac toties à nostratibus prostrato concomitantiae dogmate, cui meritò Orthodoxi opponunt Christi institutionem, quam Christus nullibi legitur vel mutâsse vel retractâsse. Hautquaquam igitur ex unione naturali corporis & sanguinis, sed ex S. Eucharistiae institutione de hoc mysterio, quomodo celebrari debeat, iudicandum est

ac statuendum. 2. Sic nec ex unione personali, cùm unio sacramentalis longè alia sit, quàm personalis in hac unitur divina cum humana natura in una Christi persona, in illâ uniuntur sacramentaliter panis benedictus ac corpus Christi, it. vinum benedictum & sanguis Christi. 3. Christo minimè ignotum fuit, quòd ubicunque ipse est, totus adsit, nihilo tamen minùs ita S. Eucharistiam instituit ac celebrari à nobis voluit, ut non nisi sub pane bened. corpus, ac non nisi sub vino benedicto sanguis eius accipiatur. 4. adeoque non dixit edite sanguinem meum, nempe sub specie panis, sed bibite, intellige sub specie vini. 5. si totus Christus sacramentaliter accipitur sub una specie panis, cur sacrificuli sub utraque communicat? Quae idem Capito pro comm. sub unâ ex Ioh. 6. ac Luc. 24. affert, suis discutientur locis. Urget idem, Ecclesiae ordinationem niti hac ratione, quò maior reverentia & religio sacramento huic exhibeatur. Sed quae possit esse reverentia, quae Christi institutioni adversatur. Sanè si per hoc calix benedictus irreverenter tractatur, quando laicis exhibetur, idem de pane benedicto dicendum. Plura contra communem sub una, & pro communione sub utraque legantur apud B. D. Chemn. in Exam. Concil. Trid. part. 2. pag. 185. seqq. B. D. Bald. in Not. ad Ep. Becani de Comm. sub utraque. B. D. Menzer. Disp XI. Antipistor. B. D. Mylium in Explic. A. C. part. 2. p. 8. seqq. B. D. Fewrborn. Synt. 2. Sacr. disquis. dissertatione 13. B. Par. Confess. Cathol. l. 2. Spec. part. 2. art. 14. c. 7. Dn. Musaeum in pec. tr. de comm. sub utraque. B. D. Calixtum tum in pec. dissert. de C. sub utr. tum in Notis ad Cassandri tr. dec. sub utr. Coeterùm videtur Salvator noster Buxtorffio Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 616. verbis his: Bibite ex hoc omnes, respexisse ad consuetudinem Iudaeorum, apud quos lex fuerit, ut ex poculo Paschali omnes praesentes in coenâ paschali biberent, sive viri essent, sive foeminae &c. Ast Christus verba haec non immediatè post celebrationem agni paschalis, verùm post institutionem S. Eucharistiae pronunciavit. id quod contra Pontificios observandum diligenter est.) *

## 26:28
* (v. 28. Blood of the New Testament. Compare regarding the phrase of the New Testament B. D. Hutterus LL. Maiorum p. 490. seqq. B. Par. L. de Evangel. §. 120. seqq. The sayings Jer. 31, 32. Heb. 8, 8. c. 9, 20. contribute to this. And it is to be noted, that almost no covenants were formerly struck without the shedding of blood or a slaughtered victim. As is evident from Gen. 15. & Jer. 34. Let H. Grotius be compared in Matt. 24. p. 454. and if it pleases, the disputation concerning the Covenants of the Hebrew Nation, previously ventilated in the Academy of Wittenberg under my presidency.) *

* (Which is shed &c. The shedding for the remission of sins is the effect of the blood of Christ. It is therefore attributed to the cup not ἁπλῶς, but ἑνωτικῶς, namely on account of the sacramental union of the wine & the blood of Christ in the blessed cup; Since, however, it is not the work of a mere creature to free from sins, it is also evident from this that Christ is σθεανσθρωπος. Let B. D. Chemnitius be seen in his book on the two natures in Christ c. 24 p. 133. Nor yet is it to be inferred from this, because τὸ the shedding for the remission of sins is not absolutely attributed to the cup, but ἑνωτικᾶς or on account of the union of the wine with the blood of Christ, therefore a Mass-sacrifice or unbloody sacrifice is given, since Christ thus immolated himself. For it suffices that Christ was even then about to shed his blood for our sins. Nor are there lacking even among the Papists themselves those who understand the shedding of the chalice at least as being into the mouths of the disciples, just as B. D. Hulsemanus in Man. A. C. p. 1291 alleges for this matter Guil. Estius in Annot. aur. in Luke 22, 20. The same B. D. Hulsemannus l. c. shows that Augustine, Chrysostom, Bede, Anselm, Thomas, Card. Caietanus, Dionysius the Carthusian, and the Jesuits, Emanuel Saa and also Barradius, explain it concerning the tradition and shedding to be in the future on the altar of the cross. The Vulgate version, pronounced authentic in the Council of Trent, favors this opinion, which has shall be shed, and not is being shed. If it is accepted in this way, no patronage will remain from this place for a Mass-sacrifice. Compare also B. D. Hutterus tr. de Missa, B. Par. Confess. Cath. l. 2. Spec. part. 2. art. 15. c. 1. p. 1193. seqq. B. D. Gerlach. Tom. 2. Dispp. Theol. Disp. 24. B. D. Zeaeman. de Missa, and others.) *

* For many. Therefore, the Calvinists infer from this, Christ did not shed his blood for all, and thus he died for the elect alone. see Wendelinus Exerc. 63. §. 1. p. 995. seqq. & other Calvinists passim. Resp. 1. the word many in Holy Scripture is very often used for all, as is evident from the comparison of Daniel 12, 2. with John c. 5, 28. Isaiah 53, 12. compared with v. 6. & 1. Cor. 5, 15. Matth. 20, 28. compared with 1. Tim. 2, 6. 2. that it must also be taken in this sense in this place, namely for all, is likewise clear from the comparison of the present place with Rom. 5, 12. seqq. also from 2. Cor. 5, 14. 15. 1. Cor. 8, 11. 2. Petr. 2, 1. Ebr. 2, 9. 1. Ioh. 2, 2. Add the comparison of Gen. 17, 4. with Gen. 22, 18. and see Augustine l. 20. de C. D. c. 23. & Coquaeus in the said place. Conf. also B. Par. L. de Elect. as Reprob. §. 118. also Analect. ad Matth. 20, 28. In vain does Wend. urge the places Ioh. 10, 15. Eph. 5, 25. Act. 20, 28. for particularity. For it is well to be noted, that the name sheep in Holy Scripture is taken either generally, by reason of redemption, and thus all men are Christ's sheep; or specially, by reason of regeneration and sanctification, and thus only believers are Christ's sheep. The force of truth compelled John Cameron, so that in Myroth. Ev. on this place he himself compared with the present place Daniel 12, 1. where, by his own admission, the word רגים is not taken comparatively, but absolutely, for an immense multitude (indeed for all, as John Piscator, and other Calvinist Interpreters expressly explain it in the said place, also Petrus Martyr in LL. CC. p. 705. 706.) The same man indeed adds, that it is nevertheless most certain, that by the blood of Christ life is obtained for no one, who is not also a member of Christ. But he confuses the acquisition of life and salvation, which is universal, with the application of Christ's merit, which by the proper fault of men is particular. The same is also to be observed concerning Grotius's annotation on this place, who by the word πολλοὺς understands those here both from the Jews and from the Gentiles, who embrace the conditions of the covenant. But although the greatest part of men by their own fault do not embrace the covenant, but reject it, despise it, and thus deprive themselves of the benefits acquired by Christ: it remains nevertheless firm; that Christ died for all, acquired salvation for all, offered the covenant to all, into which all could and ought to be received, provided they did not maliciously despise the means of salvation, but embraced Christ with true faith. Finally, a notable [point] from this place for The satisfaction of Christ argument can be drawn against the Photinians, as the blessed D. Meisner clearly teaches in Theol. Photin. consid. p. 833. seqq. and the blessed D. Iac. Martini in Photin. pag. 555. seqq.) *

* (For the remission of sins. Concerning the fruit of the Holy Eucharist, and also concerning the end for which our Savior instituted the Holy Eucharist, the blessed Par. discourses at length in a separate treatise on the S. Euchar. c. 23. Among the Papists, Corn. à Lapide can be consulted on this passage, who nevertheless mixes in many false things. By this oracle, the blasphemy of the Photinians, that the blood of Christ is of no more benefit to our salvation than that of any animal, can also be repelled, which horrendous blasphemy the blessed Par. also refutes in L. de Iustif. §. 85., the blessed D. Meisn. in Consid. Theolog. Photin p. 833. seqq., and the blessed D. Stegmannus in Photinianismo p. 819. seqq. And the places of Holy Scripture contribute especially to this. Eph. 1, 7.c. 5, 2.Ebr. 7, 27.c. 9, 14. 15.c. 10, 15.19.2. Cor. 5, 151. Ioh. 1, 7.Gal 1, 4.Tit. 2, 141. Petr. 1, 18. Furthermore, the calumny of the Papists, Bell l. 4. de Not. Eccl. c. 8. §. From which, Fōreri in Man. Luther. p, 588 59., Kelleri t. 2. Cathol. Papatûs art. 12. t. 3. p. 637., that among the Lutherans there is no true Holy Eucharist, in that the ministers of our Church are not legitimately called and ordained, the blessed D. Fewerb. wipes away at length and solidly refutes in Synt. 2. disquis. Sacr. p. 523. seqq.) *

Latin:

* (v. 28. Sangus novi Testamenti. Confer. de phrasi N. Testamenti B. D. Hutterus LL. Maiorum p. 490. seqq. B. Par. L. de Evangel. §. 120. seqq. Faciunt huc dicta Ier. 31, 32.Ebr. 8, 8.c. 9, 20. Et notandum, quòd nulla ferè olim foedera absque sanguinis effusione sive hostiâ caesa fuerint percussa. ceu patet ex Genes. 15. & Ierem. 34. Conferatur H. Grotius in Matth. 24. p. 454. ac si placuerit, disputatio de Foederibus Gentis Ebraeae, antehac in Acad. Witteb. sub praesidio meo ventilata.) *

* (Qui effunditur &c. Effusio pro peccatorum remissione est effectus sanguinis christi. tribuitur igitur poculo non ἁπλῶς, sed ἑνωτικῶς, nempe propter unionem sacramentalem vini & sanguinis Christi in poculo benedicto; Cùm verò merae creaturae opus non sit, à peccatis liberare, constat quoque hinc, quòd Christus sit σθεανσθρωπος. Videatur B. D. Chemnitius lib. de duabus naturis in Christo c. 24 p. 133. Neque tamen hinc inferendum, quia τὸeffusio pro peccatorum remissione, poculo non absolutè tributur, sedἑνωτικᾶςsive propter unionem vini cum sanguine Christi, ergò datur Sacrificum missaticum s. incruentum, eùm ita Christus seipsum immolarit. Sufficit enim, quòd Christus iam iam erat sanguinem suum pro nostris peccatis effusurus. Nec desunt etiam inter ipsos Pontificios, qui de effusione calicis in ora discipulorum saltem accipiunt, quemadmodum hanc in rem B. D. Hulsemanus Man. A. C. p. 1291. allegat Guil. Estium in Annot. aur. in Luc. 22, 20. Idem B. D. Hulsemannus l. c. ostendit, quòd Augustinus, Chrysostomus, Beda, Anselmus, Thomas, Card. Caietanus, Dionysius Carthusianus, ac Iesuitae, Emanuel Saa itemq; Barradius, de traditione & effusione in ara crucis futurâ exponant. Cui sententiae favet vulgata versio, in Concilio Tridentino authentica pronunciata, quae habet effundetur, non verò effunditur. quod si ita acceptetur, nihil patrocinii ex h. l. reliquum erit pro sacrificio missarico. Conf. quoque B. D. Hutterus tr. de Missa, B. Par. Confess. Cath. l. 2. Spec. part. 2. art. 15. c. 1. p. 1193. seqq. B. D. Gerlach. Tom. 2. Dispp. Theol. Disp. 24. B. D. Zeaeman. de Missa, alii.) *

* (Pro multis. Ergò, inferunt hinc Calviniani, Christus non pro omnibus effudit sanguinem, adeoque pro solis electis mortuus est. vid. Wendelinus Exerc. 63. §. 1. p. 995. seqq. & alii Calviniani passim. Resp. 1. vox multorum in Sc. S. saepiusculè adhibetur pro omnibus, ceu patet ex collat. Daniel. 12, 2. cum Iohann-s c. 5, 28. Esaiae 53, 12. coll. cum v. 6. & 1. Cor. 5, 15.Matth. 20, 28. collato cum 1, Tim. 2, 6. 2. quòd verò & h. l. hoc sensu, nempe pro omnibus, accipi debeat, itidem liquet ex collat. praesentis loci cum Rom. 5, 12. seqq. it. ex 2. Cor. 5, 14. 15.1. Cor. 8, 11.2. Petr. 2, 1.Ebr. 2, 9.1. Ioh. 2, 2. Adde collat. Gen. 17, 4. cum Gen. 22, 18. ac vide Augustinum l. 20. de C. D. c. 23. & Coquaeum in d. l. Conf. etiam B. Par. L. de Elect. as Reprob. §. 118. it. Analect. ad Matth. 20, 28. Frustra pro particularitate urget Wend. loca Ioh. 10, 15.Eph. 5, 25.Act. 20, 28. Etenim probè notandum, quòd ovium nomen in Sc. S. sumatur vel generaliter, ratione redemitionis, & sic omnes homines sunt Christi oves; vel specialiter, ratione regenerationis & sanctificationis, & sic soli credentes Christi oves sunt. Vis veritatis coegit Ioh. Cameronem, ut in Myroth. Ev. ad h. l. ipse cum praesenti loco contulerit Daniel. 12, 1. ubi, eodem monente, voxרגיםnon comparatè, sed absolutè sumitur, pro immensâmultitudine (imo pro omnibus, ceu disertè ita exponunt Ioh. Piscator, & alii Interpretes Calviniani in d. l. it. Petrus Martyr in LL. CC. p. 705. 706.) Addit quidem idem, certissimum tamen esse, sanguine Christi nemini vitam esse partam, qui idem non sit membrum Christi. Sed confundit vitae ac salutis acquisitionem, quae universalus est, cum meriti Christi applicatione, quae propriâ hominum culpâ particularis. Idem etiam observandum circa Grotii annotationem h. l. qui voce πολλοὺς eos hîc tum ex Iudaeis tum ex gentilibus intelligit, qui foederis conditiones amplectuntur. Ast licet maxima hominum pars propriâ suâ culpa foedus non amplectatur, sed reiiciat, contemnat, adeoque beneficiis à Christo acquisitis se privet: manet tamen firmum; quòd Christus pro omnibus mortuus fuerit, omnibus salutem acquisiverit, omnibus foedus obtulerit, in quod etiam omnes recipi possent ac deberent, modò media salutis malitiosè non contemnerent, sed verâ fide Christum amplecterentur. Insigne tandem ex h. l. pro satisfactione Christi argumentum contra Photinianos depromi potest, ceu luculenter docet B. D. Meisnerus Theol. Photin. consid. p. 833. seqq. B. D. Iac. Martini in Photin. pag. 555. seqq.) *

* (In remissionem peccatorum. De fructu S. Eucharistiae, tum quoque de fine, cur Salvator noster S. Eucharistiam instituerit, prolixè disserit B. Par. Tract. singulari de S. Euchar. c. 23. E Pontificiis consuli potest Corn. à Lapide in h. l. qui tamen multa admiscet falsa. Retundi quoque oraculo hoc Photinianorum blasphemia potest, quòd sanguis Christi non plus prosit ad nostram salutem, quàm cuius vis animalis. quam horrendam blasphemiam refellit quoque B. Par. L. de Iustif. §. 85. B. D. Meisn. in Consid. Theolog. Photin p. 833. seqq. B. D. Stegmannus in Photinianismo p. 819. seqq. Faciuntque huc cum primis loca Sc. Sacrae. Fewerb. Synt. 2. disquis. Sacr. p. 523. seqq.) *

## 26:29
v. 29, I will not drink from this time &c. Matthew places these words after the distribution of the Sacramental cup. Luke narrates that these words were pronounced by the Lord concerning the cup of the Paschal Supper c. 22, 18. Some therefore maintain that the same words were spoken by Christ twice, once indeed concerning the Paschal cup, then again concerning the Eucharistic cup * (And the blessed Par. confirms and approves this opinion with several reasons in Harm. Ev. c. 171. p. 118.) * Piscator understands it concerning the metaphorical drinking of wine in the kingdom of heaven. To drink wine is taken for to feast and to be joyful: to feast for to enjoy heavenly joys.

1148 He opposes this to the interpretation concerning drinking after the resurrection. 1. ( that no mention is made of drink. (the contrary explicitly exists Act. 10, 41.) * (nevertheless it is rightly brought forward, that Christ denies that he will drink wine anymore in this age, for those things which were done after the resurrection were not of necessity, but of free οἰκονομίας. cf. Anal. on the Passage Act. 10, 41. 2.) * that it was not the custom among the Jews to drink wine at daily lunches and dinners, but only at more solemn banquets. (The contrary is gathered from the fact that they call Christ οἰνοπίτην. ) 3. that by the kingdom of God are understood, according to the custom of Scripture, the joys to be perceived in heaven. Tossanus follows Piscator, explaining it thus: until I make you partakers of eternal joy and salvation in my kingdom. because that joy is compared to a banquet, Matth. 8, 11.c. 22, 4.Luc. 14, 15.Apoc. 3, 20. * (add. Ps. 16, 11.Psal. 17, 15.Luc. 22, 30.Apoc. 19, 9. B. Par. also embraces this interpretation in Harm. Evang. c. 171. p. 1120. and notes that it is confirmed by 1. Christ's purpose, because it was proposed to Christ to admonish his disciples that he would not henceforth be visibly conversing with them in these lands. 2. The phrase of Scripture, because it is customary in the sacred writings for heavenly joy to be described through a banquet and weddings, not because the joys of eternal life consist in external food and drink or bodily delights, but because Scripture through a certain συγκατάφασιν describes spiritual and eternal things to us by means of bodily and temporal things. And hence it is also clear that the Chiliasts ineptly attempt to establish their error from this oracle. as B. Par. also shows in L. de consum. seculi §. 91. 3. the Apostolic passage Eph. 5, 5. 4. the interpretation handed down by Christ himself in Luke c. 22, 29. Nor, however, does it follow from that that Christ himself partook of his own body and blood in the Holy Supper. which indeed some formerly established from the Fathers: St. Augustine lib. 2. de C. D. c. 9. Jerome ep. 150. to Hedibia q. 2. Chrysostom homil. 83. on Matthew, Euthymius and Theophylact on this passage (Origen also, according to the Jesuit Maldonatus on this passage tr. 30. on Matthew, Cyprian epist. to Caecilius 68. Epiphanius heresy 47. against the Encratites, Augustine Qq. Evangel. c. 42. understand by fruit of the vine in this passage the blood of Christ, and thus the Eucharistic wine) whom the Papists commonly follow. See Jansenius in Concord. Evang. c. 131. Gregorius de Valentia and Franc. Suarez in part. 3. of Thomas q. 81. art. 1. Dominicus de Soto in 4. Sentent. dist. 12. q. 2. art. 1. Ioh. de Turrecremata in c. Not Moses dist. 2. de Consecr. Thomas Aquinas himself part. 3. q. 81. art. 1. Corn. à Lapide on v. 27. of this chapter, and Bonaventure in 4. sentent. dist. 9. q. 4. art. 1. pronounces this to be the common opinion of the Doctors, nay, Vasquez in the said place of Thomas affirms that all Catholics, whom he himself has read, clearly agree in this. Bellarmine, however, in the said place, and likewise Maldonatus, Corn. à Lapide, Franciscus Lucas, and others, in this place, lest they be forced to concede that the wine which was handed by Christ to the Apostles in the chalice remained wine even after consecration, deny that the saying, namely the fruit of the vine, was spoken by Christ after consecration: but that it pertains rather to the chalice of wine which the Lord gave to the Apostles after the eating of the Paschal lamb, before the consecration of the mysteries. Corn. à Lapide adds on v. 26. that even if these words are taken after consecration, the blood of Christ can nevertheless be called wine, just as the body of Christ is called bread by Paul, namely by reason of the substance of the bread and wine, which was there before consecration. But just as the wine, into which water was transubstantiated at the wedding in Cana, is not called water absolutely after it was turned into wine: so neither could the wine and bread be designated by these names any longer after consecration, if through it they were transubstantiated or converted into the body and blood of Christ. Furthermore, what Cornelius excepts, that the very species or accidents of the wine, because they were born and produced from the vine, are rightly called the fruit of the vine, hardly deserves a response. Moreover, both these and the remaining exceptions of the Jesuits, being sufficiently worn out, our people have long since refuted, see B. Par. Confess. Cathol. l. 2. Spec. part. 2. art. 14. c. 2. p. 1005. et seqq. But not only the Papists affirm that Christ in the Holy Supper partook of his own body and blood, but also not a few Calvinists are of the same opinion, (and they establish this for this purpose, that they may obtain, The Eucharistic wine is only figuratively blood, since Christ could not have drunk his own blood, and eaten his own body. For thus teach Bergius in Disp. de Coenâ Domin. q. 2. Paraeus lib. 3. de lit. & sent. verborum S. Coenae c. 8. p. 129. Petrus Martyr class. 4. LL. Commun. c. 10. §. 17. 38. Guil. Bucanus Instit. Theolog. L. 48. q. 59. Wendelinus Exerc. 97. §. 25. p. 1551. Piscator in h. l. Vorstius in Anti Bell. contracto p. 390. Daniel Chamier. t. 4. Panstratiae lib. 11. c. 16. Buxtorffius in dissert. pec. and they attempt to prove this from this passage. But in vain. For although we may easily grant that Christ pronounced these words after the consecration, since they are immediately joined by our Evangelist to the words of the Institution of the Holy Supper, and are joined by the particle δὲ with the command concerning drinking from the Sacramental cup, yet it cannot be inferred from this that Christ, indeed, drank from the Eucharistic cup. Since, as the blessed Pareus long ago warned in Harm. Evang. c. 171. p. 1119, likewise the blessed D. Feuerborn, Synt. 2. Sacr. Disq. p. 477, and the blessed D. Hutterus in LL. Theol. Mai. p. 725, Christ by the pronoun τοῦτο understands not that particle of wine in species which was in the Eucharistic cup, but in genus that wine which had been prepared for this last supper, from which the sacramental chalice had been filled by his command; nay, he denies that he will drink any fruit of the vine whatsoever, from which he will drink hereafter (namely, in the human manner to refresh his strength), since he had already drunk from it with them, the Apostles, several times, and a little before even in the distribution of the Paschal cup. Conf. B. Par. L. de S. Coenâ §. 230. Camero himself also in Myroth. Ev. p. 117 rejects that opinion, that Christ drank his own blood, and rightly warns that by the pronoun ἀυτὸ is signified here the same not in species or in number, but by analogy. And he compares with this passage the saying Apoc. 3, 20. Thus Grotius also warns at this passage, that it appears from Luke that these things were said in the supper itself, and therefore before the consecration of the bread and wine: but because the mention of wine had preceded here, therefore it seemed good to Matthew to append that saying here. Mr. D. Friedlib embraces this observation at this passage. To Johannes Buxtorff in Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 616, the Savior seems to have looked to that custom of the Jews, by which it was forbidden, once the cup of the hymn was exhausted, to taste more wine that night. Which is from Orach Chaiim n. 48. 1. Buxtorff proves this, so that Christ seems to wish to say that he will do nothing in this against the tradition of the Jews; but in such a way that not only will he taste no more wine that night, but for all that time in which he is still to be in the world.) *

* (Of this fruit of the vine. In the same way the Syriac. The Ethiopic: of this fruit of the vine. The Arabic: of the juice of this vine. The Savior speaks of true wine: he by no means calls the species of the consecrated wine still remaining, as indeed the Jesuit Tirinus teaches in this place, so that he may establish the fiction of transubstantiation. Nor is it even necessary that that wine which was presented to the Apostles in the eucharistic cup be understood here specifically and precisely, as was shown a little before. And it is known from the ritual books of the Jews that wine in general is indicated by the phrase פרי הגפז fruit or offspring of the vine, especially in ἐυλογία that which they used in the Paschal supper.) *

* ( ἔως τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκείνης. see the notes at c. 24, 36.) *

* (New: Thus indeed τὰ αλληγοροὺμενα. are accustomed to be indicated and restricted by some addition. See 1. Cor. 10, 4.Gal. 4, 26.1. Petr. 2, 5. Somewhat differently Mr. Dr. Friedlieb, who notes that this is the sense of the words of Christ: hitherto I have conversed in assumed weaknesses etc. hereafter that custom will cease. I will not eat or drink compelled by the use of daily life, ἕως τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκείνης, until that day, when I shall drink in the kingdom of my father, not because there are delights and food of earthly infirmity there, but because the particle ἕως so excludes the past, that it nevertheless does not posit the future. Examples of which idiom are had in Matth. 1, 25. & elsewhere. Therefore Christ by no means wishes this, as if he were about to drink the same wine either in number or species in the kingdom of the Father, but by analogy at least, concerning which some things were warned at the beginning of this verse.) *

Latin:

v. 29, Non bibam ab hoc tempore &c. Matthaeus haec verba postponit distributioni calicis Sacramentalis. Lucas haec verba narrat esse pronunciata à Domino de poculo Coenae Paschalis c. 22, 18. Statuunt ergo quidam, eadem verba à Christo bis esse dicta, semel quidem de poculo Paschali, deinde iterum de poculo Eucharistico * (Atque sententiam hanc aliquot rationibus confirmat approbatque B. Par. Harm. Ev. c. 171. p. 118.) * Piscator intelligit de Metaphoricâ bibitione vini in regno coelesti. Bibere vinum accipitur pro convivari & bilarem esse: convivari pro frui coelestibus gaudiis.

Interpretationi de bibitione post resurrectionem opponit hoc. 1. quòd nulla potûs fiat mentio. (contrarium disertè extat Act. 10, 41.) * (rectè tamen nihilominus adferitur, quòd Christus neget, se bibiturum ampliùs in hoc seculo vinum, quae enim post resurrectionem facta sunt, non fuerunt necessitatis, sed liberaeοἰκονομίας. conf. Anal. ad Locum Act. 10, 41. 2.) * quòd non fuerit moris apud Iudaeos, bibere vinum in prandiis ac coenis quotidianis, sed tantùm in solennioribus conviviis. (Contrarium colligitur ex eo, quòd Christum vocant οἰνοπίτην.) 3. quòd per regnum Dei intelligantur ex more Scripturae gaudia in coelo percipienda. Piscatorem sequitur Tossanus, ita exponens: donec vos aeterni gaudii & salutis in regno meo participes faciam. quia gaudium illud comparatur convivio, Matth. 8, 11.c. 22, 4.Luc. 14, 15.Apoc. 3, 20. * (add. Ps. 16, 11.Psal. 17, 15.Luc. 22, 30.Apoc. 19, 9. Interpretationem hanc amplectitur quoq: B. Par. Harm. Evang. c. 171. p. 1120. notatq; confirmare illam 1. Christi scopum, quia Christo fuerit propositum, discipulos suos admonere, quòd imposterum non sit visibiliter cum ipsis in his terris conversaturus. 2. Phrasin Scripturae, quia usitatum in sacris literis, gaudium coeleste per convivium & nuptias describi, non quod in externo cibo ac potu vel corporalibus delitiis gaudia vitae aet. consistant, sed quia Scriptura per συγκατάφασιν quandam spiritualia & aeterna per corporalia & temporalia nobis describit. Atq; hinc etiam patet, quòd ineptè Chiliastae ex hoc oraculo errorem suum stabilire conentur. uti etiam ostendit B. Par. L. de consum. seculi §. 91. 3. locum Apostolicum Eph. 5, 5. 4. interpretationem à Christo ipso apud Lucam traditam c. 22, 29. Neq; tamen inde sequitur, quòd Christus ipse in S. Coenâ corpus & sanguinem suum sumserit. quod quidem ex Patribus statuerunt quondam S. Augustinus lib. 2. de C. D. C. 9. Hieronymus ep. 150. ad Hedibiam q. 2. Chrysostomus homil. 83. in Matthaeum, Euthymius ac Theophy lactus in h. l. (Origenes quoque, teste Iesuita Maldonato in h. l. tr. 30. in Matthaeum, Cyprianus epist. ad Coecilium 68. Epiphanius haeres. 47. contra Encratitas, Augustinus Qq. Evangel. c. 42. per genimen vitis h. l. sanguinem Christi, adeoque vinum Eucharisticum intelligunt) quos Pontificii communiter sequuntur. Vid. Iansenius in Concord. Evang. c. 131. Gregorius de Valentiâ ac Franc. Suarez in part. 3. Thomae. q. 81. art. 1. Dominicus de Soto in 4. Sentent. dist. 12. q. 2. art. 1. Ioh. de Turrecremata in c. Non Moses dist. 2. de Consecr. Thomas de Aquino ipse part. 3. q. 81. art. 1. Corn. à Lapide ad v. 27. huius capitis, & hanc communem esse Dd. sententiam, pronunciat Bonaventura in 4. sentent. dist. 9. q. 4. art. 1. imò omnes Catholicos, quos quidem ipse legerit, planè in hoc convenire, affirmat Vasquetz in d. l. Thomae. Bellarminus tamen l. c. itemque Maldonatus, Corn. à Lapide, Franciscus Lucas alii, in h. l. ne concedere cogantur, illud vinum, quod in calice à Christo Apostolis suit traditum, etiam post consecrationem mansisse vinum, dictum videl genimen vitis, negant, Christum haec verba pronunciasse post consecrationem: sed pertinere potiùs ad calicem vini, quem Dominus Apostolis dederit, post esum agni Paschalis, ante consecrationem mysteriorum. Corn. à Lapide ad v. 26. addit, quòd si vel maximè accipiantur haec dicta post consecrationem, posse tamen sanguinem Christi vocari vinum, sicut corpus Christi à Paulo vocatur panis, nimirum ratione substantiae panis & vini, quae priùs ante consecrationem fuit. Verùm sicuti vinum, in quod aqua in nuptris Cananaeis fuit transsubstantiata, non vocatur absolutè aqua, posteaquam versa fuit in vinum: ita nec vinum ac panis possent amplius his nominibus post consecrationem insigniri, si per eam transsubstantiarentur vel converterentur in corpus & sanguinem Christi. Quod porrò excipit Cornelius, etiam ipsas species sive accidentia vini, quia nata & orata sunt ex vite, recte genimen vitis nuncupari, vix meretur responsionem. Coeterùm tum has tum reliquas Iesuitae exceptiones, utpote satis tritas, iam pridem refutarunt nostrates vid. B. Par. Confess. Cathol. l. 2. Spec. part. 2. art. 14. c. 2. p. 1005. seqq. Sed non Pontificii solùm affirmant, Christum in S. Coenâ suum corpus & sanguinem sumsisse, verùm Calviniani quoque non pauci in eadem sunt sententiâ, (idque hoc fine statuunt, ut obtineant, vinum Eucharisticum non nisi figuratè, esse sanguinem, cum Christus non potuerit proprium sanguinem bibere, ac proprium corpus edere.) Ita enim docent Bergius in Disp. de Coenâ Domin. q. 2. Paraeus lib. 3. de lit. & sent. verborum S. Coenae c. 8. p. 129. Petrus Matryr class. 4. LL. Commun. e. 10. §. 17. 38. Guil. Bucanus Instit. Theolog. L. 48. q. 59. Wendelinus Exerc. 97. §. 25. p. 1551. Piscator in h. l. Vorstius in Anti Bell. contracto p. 390. Daniel Chamier. t. 4. Panstratiae lib. 11. c. 16. Buxtorffius in dissert. pec. idque ex h. l. evincere conantur. sed frustra. Etenim licet facilè largiamur, Christum haec verba post consecrationem pronunciasse, siquidem immediatè ab Evangelista nostro verbis Institutionis S. Coenae subiunguntur, ac per particulam δὲ cum praecepto de bibendo ex poculo Sacramentali coniunguntur, non tamen illud, quòd Christus nempe de poculo Eucharistico biberit, inferri hinc potest. cùm, uti pridem monuit B. Par. Harm. Evang. c. 171. p. 1119. it. B. D. Fewrborn, Synt. 2. Sacr. Disq. p. 477. ac B. D. Hutterus in LL. Theol. Mai. p. 725. Christus per pronomen τοῦτο intelligat non in specie illam particulam vini, quae erat in poculo Eucharistico, sed in genere vinum illud, quod in hanc ultimam coenam paratum erat, ex quo calix sacramentalis ipsius iussu impletus fuerat; imò quodcunque genimen vitis, ex quo imposterum sese bibiturum, (nempe more humano ad vires reficiendas) negat, cùm priùs aliquoties, & paulò ante etiam in distributione poculi Paschalis, ex eo cum ipsis, Apostolis, biberat. Conf. B. Par. L. de S. Coenâ §. 230. Ipse quoque Camero in Myroth. Ev. p. 117. reiicit illam sententiam, quòd Christus proprium suum sanguinem biberit, ac rectè monet, pronomine ἀυτὸ significari hîc idem non specie aut numero, sed analogiâ. ac confert cum h. l. dictum Apoc. 3, 20. Sic Grotius quoque ad h. l. monet, ex Lucâ apparere, dicta haec in ipsa coenâ, & proinde ante panis & vini consecrationem: quia vero vini mentio hic praecesserit, ideò visum esse Matthaeo, id dictum hîc subtexere. Amplectitur observationem hanc Dn. D. Friedlib in h. l. Iohanni Buxtorffio in Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 616. Salvator respexisse videtur ad consuetudinem illam Iudaeorum, quâ vetitum erat, exhausto poculo hymni plus vini eâ nocte gustare. quam ex Orach Chaiim n. 48. 1. probat Buxtorff. ut adeò Christus hoc dicere velle videatur se in hoc nihil contra Iudaeorum traditionem facturum; sed ita ut non solùm eâ nocte nullum ampliùs vinum sit gustaturus, sed toto eo tempore, quo adhuc in mundo sit futurus.) *

* (De hoc genimine vitis. Eod. modo Syrus. Aethiops: de hoc fructu vitis. Arabs: de succo huius vitis. Loquitur Salvator de vero vino: minimè verò ita vocat species vini consecrati adhuc reliquas, uti quidem Iesuita Tirinus, quò transsubstantiationis figmentum stabiliat, h. l. docet. Neque etiam necesse est, ut in specie ac praecisè intelligatur hîc illud vinum, quod impoculo eucharistico Apostolis fuit exhibitum, uti paullò antè ostensum. ac notum est ex libris ritualibus Iudaeorum, quòd vinum in genere phrasi פרי הגפזfructus sive genimen vitis indigitetur, cum primis in ἐυλογία illâ, quâ in coenâ Paschali utebantur.) *

* ( ἔως τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκείνης. vid. notata ad c. 24, 36.) *

* (Novum: Ita nempe τὰ αλληγοροὺμενα. ad ditamento aliquo solent indicari ac restringi. Vid. 1. Cor. 10, 4.Gal. 4, 26.1. Petr. 2, 5. Paulo aliter Dn. D. Friedlieb, qui hunc verborum Christi esse sensum notat: hactenus conversatus fui in adsumtis imbecillitatibus &c. imposterum desinet illa consuetudo. non edam vel bibam vitae quotidianae usu coactus, ἕως τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκείνης,usque ad illum diem, quo bibam in regno patris, non quòd ibi delitiae & infirmitatis terrenae pabulum habeantur, sed quia particula ἕως ita excludit praeteritum, ut tamen non ponat futurum. cuius idiotismi exempla habentur Matth. 1, 25. & alibi. Proinde minimè Christus hoc vult, quasi idem vel numero vel specie vinum bibiturus sit in regno Patris, sed analogiâ saltem, de quâ initiò huius vers. quaedam monita.) *

## 26:30
* (v. 30. And when a hymn was said. In Greek καὶ ὑμνήσαντες, when they had sung.

Gasp. Sanctius gathers from this in his Commentary on Isaiah chapter 5, page 71, that Christ sang, not merely recited the hymn in the customary way of speaking. Indeed according to the custom of the Jews, who used music also in banquets. Which he thinks is also clear from Ecclesiasticus 32, 6. c. 49, 2. Amos 6, 6. Luc. 15, 25. Q. v. what kind of hymn it was? Bede answers, that it was those prayers which John noted down c. 17. H. Grotius also thinks that, just as Christ added a new thanksgiving to the old one, consistent with his own institution, so it is also credible that he did the same regarding the hymn, and perhaps said those very things which are read in John c. 17 in the manner of a hymn. For, he adds, the Hebrews were accustomed to pour forth hymns extemporaneously according to the occasion, bound by no meters, such as the songs of Deborah, Anna, Zacharias, Mary, etc. David excelled especially in this art, whom Philo for that reason also calls ὁμνόγροφον in his work On the World. But this opinion is opposed by the fact that the Apostles are also said to have sung along: for the plural number is used όμνήσα-τες. but how could the Apostles have sung along to a new and unknown song? Therefore Paulus Burgensis, Ioh. Buxtorff in Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 614, Franc. Lucas Burgensis, Baronius, and others more correctly establish that it was seven Psalms composed from the Hallelujah, which begin from Psalm 113, Praise the Lord, O ye children, and end at Ps. 118. confess to the Lord. There is no doubt that Christians took the custom of singing from there, of whom Acts 16, 25. likewise the Apostles Eph. 5, 19. Col. 3, 16. add Tertullian in Apol. c. 39, Cyprian in his letter to Donatus, the 4th Council of Toledo, canon 12. Compare also what Conr. Rittersh. IC. collected on this matter in Book 3 of his Sacred Readings, c. 21. Chrysostom well advises in homily 83 on Matthew that our table also ought to be begun with prayers and ended in thanksgiving.

Latin:

* (v. 30. Et hymno dicto. Graecè καὶ ὑμνήσαντες,cùm cecinissent.

Colligit hinc Gasp. Sanctius Comm. in Es. cap. 5. pag. 71. Christum cecinisse, non modo loquendi consueto recitasse hymnum. ad morem nempe Iudaeorum, quiin conviviis quoque Musicam adhibuerint. quod liquere etiam censet ex Ecclesiastici 32. 6. c. 49, 2. Amos 6, 6. Luc. 15, 25. Q. v. qualis hymnus fuerit? Respondet Beda, fuisse preces illas, quas Iohannes annotavit c. 17. H. quoq; Grotius existimat, quòd sicuti Christus ad veterem gratiarū actionem novam addidit, suo instituto congruentem, ita credibile quoque sit, & de hymno fecisse, ac fortè ea ipsa hymni in modum dixisse, quae apud Iohannem c. 17. leguntur. Nam, addit, solebant pro re natâ ex tempore hymnos effundere Ebraei, nullis numeris adstrictos, qualia carmina Deborae, Annae, Zachariae, Mariae &c. Cumprimis in arte hâc excelluit David, quem propterea quoque Philo in de mundo ὁμνόγροφον vocat. Ast obstat sententiae huic, quòd Apostoli quoque accinisse dicantur: habetur enim pluralis num. όμνήσα-τες. quomodo verò accinere Apostoli novam & ignotam cantilenam potuissent? Proinde Paulus Burgensis, Ioh. Buxtorff. in Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 614. Franc. Lucas Burgensis, Baronius ac alii rectiùs statuunt, fuisse septem Psalmos ex Halleluia conflatos, qui incipiunt à Psalmo 113. Laudate pueri Dominum, & finiunt in Ps. 118.confitemini Domino. Non dubium quin morem canendi inde acceperint Christiani, de quibus Actor. 16, 25. it. Apostolous Eph. 5, 19.Col. 3, 16. adde Tertull. in Apol. c. 39. Cyprianum ep. ad Donatum, Synodum Toletanam 4. canone 12. Conf. etiam quae hanc in rem collegit Conr. Rittersh. IC. Lib. 3. Sacr. Lect. c. 21. Benè monet Chrysost. hom. 83. in Matth. quòd & nostra mensa à precibus inchoari, & in gratiarum actione terminari debeat.) *

## 26:31
(v. 31. You will all suffer a stumbling block. But Luc. 22, 28. he attributes to the Apostles the praise that they remained with him in his temptations. The Jesuit Becanus therefore relies on this to prove the obscurity of Scripture. Resp. It is one thing to speak of the past, another of the future. The present passage is to be understood of the latter, that which is said in Luc. 22. of the former. That this distinction of time is to be observed here, the Savior himself teaches, when. Ioh. 6, 31. & 32. He says to the Apostles: Now you believe: Behold the hour comes, and is now come, that you shall be scattered every man to his own, and shall leave me alone. And it is well to be noted, that the Apostles then, when Christ was apprehended, did not only leave his flesh with their own flesh, but also left the faith with their mind, as Augustine has it, tract 103 on John. Hilary: You shall suffer scandal, i.e., you shall be disturbed by fear and infidelity. So also Euthymius: The faith which you have in me shall be shaken from you. Specifically concerning Peter, Theophylact in this place: Because of much confidence of mind, Peter alone promised that he would not be scandalized, and therefore Christ permitted him to fall: that he might teach that no one should confide in himself, but in God: and the words of Christ are to be esteemed more worthy of faith than our own conscience. add. Aug. tr. 10. in Iohann.) *

* (It is to be noted from this 1. against the Calvinists, that even the regenerate can shake off faith and the regenerate indeed sometimes totally, sometimes finally; but the elect indeed not finally, yet totally. This is what the example of the Apostle Peter confirms sufficiently clearly above all. Wendelinus denies this to the contrary, and writes that it seems to them that they are denying that the sun shines at midday, Exerc 121. §. -1. who affirm that faith was totally shaken off by Peter, which Holy Scripture Luke 22, 31. 32. teaches was preserved by the intercession of Christ, and which Tertullian, Augustine, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and others deny had fallen away entirely. But he pronounces that the words of Theophylact are memorable: I have prayed for you etc. that you may not either fall away from me entirely, and become an enemy from a disciple, or fall into despair on account of the lapse which you will commit. But, Wendelinus adds, he would have been made an enemy from a disciple, if he had fallen away totally. Resp. by denying the consequence. For one must distinguish between total loss and final. Not the former, but the latter is joined with despair, and makes one a sworn enemy of Christ, or such an Apostate, who tramples the blood of Christ underfoot, see Heb. 6. and 10. Just as also Christ Luke 22, 32. speaks at least of the final loss of saving faith. For that the Apostle Peter fell away totally from the grace of GOD through the denial of Christ, is sufficiently evident, if that of Christ be compared. Matt. 10, 33. Whoever shall deny me, etc. Far therefore from ambiguity Peter would have perished eternally, on account of that denial of Christ, had he not deplored his most grave sin, worthy of eternal death, with thick tears, and raised himself up again by true faith in Christ. But Wendelinus urges, that Peter was not led to the denial by a predetermined malice and full will, but by the magnitude of the pressing danger, and that therefore that denial proceeded from infirmity. Resp. Again, a distinction must be made between simple infirmity or human weakness, in which way all, even the most holy, fall daily out of infirmity; and infirmity joined with atrocity and a horrendous violation of conscience or exacerbated, such as it was in Peter, devoting himself to eternal destruction if he knew Christ, v. 72, 74. We assert that saving faith is shaken not by the former, but by the latter. But that Peter's horrendous fall would have brought upon him eternal death, if like Judas he had despaired of the grace of GOD, and had not converted himself to Christ through serious repentance, Calvin himself seems to concede, expressly writing, that Christ healed Peter from so lethal a ruin. The remaining things which Wendelinus objects in the said place are rejected with the same ease with which they are brought forward. Compare more below in the Analecta to v. 74.

2. Against the Papists, that from a grave fall and great sin (as Capito has it, Expos. Cathol. p. 639.) this Peter is by no means to be excepted. For although Jerome wishes that he denied out of ardent affection toward the Lord, which Christ predicted, which also Cyril lib. 11. in John c. 41. seems to think, and indeed Origen hom. 35. on Matthew teaches, that it was not possible then for Peter to confess Jesus, (which error Felicianus Capito rightly and deservedly refutes, Expos. Cath. p. 636. seqq.) yet Chrysostom and Euthymius more correctly attribute confidence to him here. For, as Theophylact has it in this place, it was full of pride to say: if all etc. for he is shown to be arrogant and ignorant of his own infirmity. Whence also Ambrose serm. 48. and Turrecremata lib. 1. de Eccles. c. 30. and c. 61. (witness Corn. à Lapide in this place) establish that Peter lost his faith. Felicianus Capito in the said place, that Peter perjured himself. The Papists, seeing that this conflicts with the absolute infallibility of the Roman Pontiff, distinguish between the loss of faith itself, and the loss of the profession of faith. that Peter did not lose his faith, (and yet having suffered a scandal, which is a mortal sin, as Capito speaks clearly in the loc. cit. p. 640.) but they wish that he had sinned against the profession of faith, by denying that he was a disciple of Christ. Thus Iohannes Paludanus in Vindiciis Theol. p. 240. item the Jesuits. Maldonatus, Corn. à Lapide, and others in this place. So also Suarez tr. de fid. Disp. 9. sect. 3. Bell. l 3. de Eccl. c. 17. Similarly from the Calvinists Amandus Polanus in Synt. Theol. That this opinion has been received by all (Papists) is written, writes Card. Toletus in C. 18. Ioh. annot. 11. They take the primary foundation of this opinion from Luc. 22, 32. But how clearly the aforementioned passage does not prove what the Papists and Calvinists wish, will be shown more prolixly in the Annotations to that saying. In this place at least let it be noted, that where there is faith of the heart, there also is confession of the mouth, Rom. 10, 9. Let B. Par. Confess. Cathol. t. 1. p. 286. seq. 333. and 1. 2. pag. 572. 570. be consulted. Furthermore, this also must be observed, that Corn. à Lapide himself in this place warns that in the Greek there is ἀπαρνήσ- i. e. you will deny, nay you will abjure, as if to say, You will do worse, Peter, than the others. Furthermore, concerning the denial of Christ see Matth. 10, 33. Let us learn indeed from this, to work out our salvation with trembling and fear, Phil. 2, 12. and he who thinks he stands, let him see that he does not fall, 1. Cor. 10, 12. For what are we to expect, unless GOD sustains us, if they fall, if they lose their faith, who had seen so many miracles of the Master, who had heard the words of life from the mouth of the Master, who had cast out demons through his name, and had performed many other miracles.?

* (For it is written. namely Zach. 13. the particle γὰρ here is not causal, but ratiocinative. For a prediction is not the cause of apostasy. see the note to C. 13. Matth. v. 14.) *

* (the shepherd. The discourse is about Christ alone, as is clear from the collation with Ioh. 1, 1. C. 10, 30. C. 14, 10. 11. For Christ is that shepherd and Bishop, 1. Petr. 2, 25. Nor does Grotius move me either, who writes that it is so far from being the case that he thinks Christ is looked to in the words of Zacharias, that he believes much more that it is a matter there of some not good shepherd, and indeed of the same one, about whom it was treated without the head 11. But not less in the eleventh than in the thirteenth chapter by Shepherd in Zach.

Christ is understood, as B. D. Bald. taught prolixly in Comm. in Zach. where he also most beautifully deduces how Christ shows himself to us as a Shepherd.) *

Latin:

* (v. 31. Omnes vos offendiculum patiemini. At Luc. 22, 28. tribuit Apostolis elogium, quod permanserint cum eo in tentationibus eius. Nititur igitur hinc probare Iesuita Becanus Scripturae obscuritatem. Resp. Aliud est loqui de praeterito, aliud de futuro. de hoc intelligendus est locus praesens, de illo dictum Luc. 22. Quod temporis discrimen observandum hîc esse, docet ipse Salvator, qn. Ioh. 6, 31. & 32. ad Apostolos ait: Modò creditis: Ecce venit hora, & iam venit, ut dispergamini unusquisque in propria, & me solum relinquatis. Et probè notandum, quod Apostoli tùm, quando Christus comprehensuc fuit, non carne tantummodò suâ eius carnem, sed etiam mente reliquerint fidem, ut habet August. tr. 103. in Iohannem. Hilarius: Scandalum patiemini i. e. metu & infidelitate turbabimini. Sic quoque Euthymius: Excutietur à vobis fides, quam in me habetis. In specie de Petro Theophylactus in h. l. Ob multam mentis confidentiam, Petrus solus pollicebatur, se non scandalizatum iri, & idcircò permisit illum Christus cadere: ut doceat, ne quis in seipso confidat, sed in Deo: & fide digniora sunt aestimanda verba Christi, quàm nostra conscientia. add. Aug. tr. 10. in Iohann.) *

* (Notandum hinc 1. contra Calyinianos, quòd etiam renati possint excutere fidem & renati quidem tùm totaliter, tùm finaliter; electi verò non quidem finaliter, tamen totaliter. Id quod cumprimis exemplum Apostoli Petri satis clarè confirmat. Negat hoc contrà Wendelinus, ac solem in meridie lucere, illos sibi videri negare scribit Exerc 121. §. -1. qui fidem totaliter à Petro excussam affirmant quam Christi intercessione conservatam Scriptura S.Luc. 22, 31. 32.doceat, & quam omninò excidisse, negent Tertullianus, Augustinus, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, alii. Memorabilia verò esse pronunciat Theophylacti verba: rogavi pro te &c. ne aut prorsus à me deficias. & ex discipulo hostis fias, aut propter lapsum, quem committes, in desperationem ruas. Atqui, subiungit Wendelinus, ex discipulo hostis fuisset factus, si totaliter defecisset. Resp. negando consequentiam. distinguendum enim inter amissionem totalem, ac finalem. non illa, sed haec cum desperatione coniuncta est, ac iuratum Christi hostem facit, sive talem Apostatam, qui sanguinem Christi pedibus conculcat, vid. Ebr. 6. & 10. Quemadmodum etiam Christus Luc. 22, 32. de finali saltem loquitur fidei salvificae amissione. Quod enim totaliter gratiâ DEI Apostolus Petrus per abnegationem Christi exciderit, satis patet, si conferatur illud Christi. Matth. 10, 33.Quicunme negaverit, &c. Procul igitur ambiguo aeternùm periisset Petrus, propter illam Christi abnegationem, nisi peccatum suum gravissimum aeternâque morte dignum, spissis lacrymis deplorasset, ac verâ in Christum fide iterum se erexisset. Sed urget Wendelinus, non destinatam malitiam & plenam voluntatem induxisse Petrum ad abnegationem, sed instantis periculi magnitudinem, adeòque ex infirmaitate abnegationem illam fuisse profectam. Resp. iterum distinguendum est inter infirmitatem simplicem seu imbecillitatem humanam, quomodo omnes etiam sanctissimi quotidiè ex infirmitate labountur; & inter infirmitatem cum atrocitate & conscientiae violatione horrenda coniunctam sive exasperatam, qualis erat in Petro, aeterno exitio sese devovente, si Christum nosset, v. 72. 74. Non per illam, sed per hanc fidem salvificam excuti adserimus. Quòd verò Petri lapsus horrendus aeternam illi mortem attraxisset, si instar Iudae de gratiâ DEI desperasset, nec per seriam poenitentiam ad Christum se convertisset, ipse concedere Calvinus videtur, expressè scribens, quòd Christus Petrum à ruinâ tàm lethali fanarit. Reliqua quae Wendelinus d. l. excipit, eadem facilitate reiiciuntur, quâ afferuntur. Conf. plura infrà in Analectis ad v. 74.

2. Contra Pontificios, quòd à gravi lapsu & grandi peccato (ut habet Capito Expos. Cathol. p. 639.) minimé excipiendus hic Petrus sit. Licet enim Hieronymus velit, quòd ex ardenti erga Dominum affectu negarit, quod Christus praedixit, quod & Cyrillus lib. 11. in Ioh. c. 41. sentire videtur, quin & Origenes hom. 35. Matth. doceat, non possibile fuisse tùm Petro, confiteri Iesum, (quem errorem iure merito refellit Felicianus Capito Expos. Cath. p. 636. seqq.) rectiùs tamen Chrysostomus atq; Euthymius confidentiam illi hîc tribunt. etenim, ut habet Theophylactus in h. l. superbiâ plenum erat dicere: si omnes &c. ostenditur enim esse arrogans & ignorans suam infirmitatem. Unde etiam Ambrosius serm. 48. ac Turrecremata lib. 1. de Eccles. c. 30. ac c. 61. (teste Corn. à Lapide in h. l.) statuunt, Petrum sidem perdidisse. Felicianus Capito l. c. Petrum peierasse. Videntes Pontificii, puguare hoc cum absoluta P. R. infallibilitate, distingvunt inter ipsius sidei, & professionis fidei amosionem. non fidem amisisse Petrum, (& tamen scandalum, quod mortale peccatum, passus, ceu disertè loquitur Capito l. c. p. 640.) sed contra professionem fidei peccasse, negando, se esse Christi discipulum, volunt. ita Iohannes Paludanus in Vindiciis Theol. p. 240. item Iesuitae. Maldonatus, Corn. à Lapide, alii in h. l. Sic quoque Suarez tr. de fid. Disp. 9. sect. 3. Bell. l 3. de Eccl. c. 17. Similiter ex Calvinianis Amandus Polanus in Synt. Theol. Quin sententiam hanc ab omnibus (Pontificiis) esse receptam, scribit Card. Toletus in C. 18. Ioh. annot. 11. Praecipuum huius sententiae fundamentum desumunt ex Luc. 22, 32. Sed quàm planè non dictus locus probet, quod Pontificii & Calv. volunt, prolixiùs in Annot. ad illud dictum ostendetur. Hoc loco saltem notetur, quòd ubi est fides cordis, ibi quoque sit confessio oris, Rom. 10, 9. Consulatur B. Par. Confess. Cathol. t. 1. p. 286. seq. 333. ac. 1. 2. pag. 572. 570. Praeterea & hoc observandum, quòd Corn. à Lapide ipse h. l. moneat, in Graeco esse ἀπαρνήσ- i. e. abnegabis, imò adiurabis, q. d. Peius facies Petre, quàm coeteri. Porrò de abnegatione Christi vid Matth. 10, 33. Discamus verò hinc, cum tremore & timore operari salutem nostram,Phil. 2, 12.& qui se existimat stare, videat ne cadat,1. Cor. 10, 12. Quid nobis enim expectandum, nisi DEUS nos sustentaverit, si illi cadunt, si illi fidem amittunt, qui tot Magistri miracula viderant, qui verba vitae ex Magistri ore audiverant, qui per nomen eius Daemonia eiecerant, ac multa alia miracula patraverant.?) *

* (Scriptum est enim. puta Zach. 13. part. γὰρ hîc non est causalis, sed ratiocinativa. Praedictio enim non est causa apostasiae. vid. not. ad C. 13. Matth. v. 14.) *

* (pastorem. Sermo est de Christo solo, ceu patet ex coll. cum Ioh. 1, 1.C. 10, 30.C. 14, 10. 11. Christus enim est pastor ille & Episcopus, 1. Petr. 2, 25. Nec movet etiam Grotius, qui tantùm abesse scribit, ut Zachariae verbis Christum respici putet, ut multò magis credat, agi inibi de aliquo non bono pastore, & quidem de eodem, de quo actum sine capitis 11. Ast non minùs undecimo, quàm decimo tertio capite per Pastorem apud Zach.

Christus intelligitur, uti prolixè docuit B. D. Bald. Comm. in Zach. ubi etiam pulcerrimè deducit, quomodo Christus ut Pastorem erga nos se exhibeat.) *

## 26:32
* (v. 32. προὰξω ὑμᾶς. conf. inf. C. 28, 7.) *

c. 33. Est omnes scandalizati fuerint [If all shall be offended] &c. Cornelius à Lapide rightly warns that Peter sinned here in a threefold manner: 1. by contradicting Christ too boldly. 2. by preferring himself too arrogantly to the others. 3. by trusting too much in his own strength. Let us, however, learn to acknowledge the weakness of our own powers, and to trust solely in divine virtue.) (

Latin:

* (v. 32. προὰξω ὑμᾶς. conf. inf. C. 28, 7.) *

* (c. 33. Est omnes scandalizati fuerint &c. Rectè monet Corn à Lapide, quòd Petrus tripliciter hîc peccaverit 1. audaciùs Christo obstrependo. 2. arrogantiùs se coeteris praeferendo. 3. nimiùm viribus suis confidendo. Discamus verò virium nostrarum imbecillitatem agnoscere, ac divinae virtuti unicè confidere.) *

## 26:34
v. 34. gallus cantet [the cock shall crow], understand twice, from Mark 14, 30. see here D. Calixt. Concord. p. 3. 24. The true Deity of Christ can be proven from this, as He is one who predicts future events. Hence Bede on Luke ch. 22, v. 34: As GOD, He predicts the manner, time, hour, and number of the denial. The objection of the Portuguese Rabbi in Colloq. Mittelb. f. 7 is frivolous: that Christ did not predict this from foreknowledge, but that it was at least a conjecture. But the express naming of almost all the circumstances testifies to the contrary, and Mr. Dr. Muller shows this in many ways in *Iudaismo* p. 1126. Furthermore, the interpreters rightly warn here: that the prediction of Christ in no way took away the freedom of the Apostles, but rather presupposed it and its abuse. For Christ predicted that they would fall away from Him for this reason: because they were truly and freely going to fall away from Him. For if this were not truly going to happen, Christ would neither have foreseen it nor predicted it. Who, indeed, would wish to be so absurd as to persuade himself that Christ internally incited the Apostles to this denial and abjuration.) (

Latin:

* (v. 34. gallus cantet, intellige bis, ex Marc. 14, 30. vid. hîc D. Calixt. Concord. p. 3. 24. Probari hinc potest vera Christi Deitas, ut pote praedicentis futura. Inde Beda in C. 22. Lucae v. 34. Ut DEUS modum, tempus, horam ac numerum negationis praedicit. Frivola est exceptio R. Lusitani in Colloq. Mittelb. f. 7. quòd Christus non ex conscientia id praedixerit, sed quòd saltem fuerit coniectura. Verùm omnium propè circumstantiarum expressa denominatio contrarium testatur, idque multis ostendit Dn. D. Muller. in Iudaismo p. 1126. Porrò rectè monent hîc Interpp., praedictionem Christi minimè Apostolis ademisse libertatem, sed eampotiùs eiusque abusum praesupponere. Ideo enim Christus praedixit, eos à se defecturos, quia ipsi verè & liberè à se defecturi erant. quod nisi reverà futurum fuisset, Christus nec praevidisset, nec praedixisset. Quis verò adeò velit esse absurdus, ut sibi persuadeat, Christum ad hanc abnegationem & abiurationem Apostolos internè incitasse.) *

## 26:36
* (v. 36. Gethsemane. Mr. Dilherrus reviews the various opinions of authors as to what Gethsemane denotes, t. 2. Dispp. Acad. p. 15. The common opinion is that it signifies the valley of oil, because oil was pressed there. Therefore, just as oil was pressed there from olives, so Christ's blood had to be pressed there in his agony. This is the spiritual oil by which we are refreshed, anointed, healed, and fed. Compare Cant. 1, 3.Luc. 10, 34.Es. 63, 3. There was indeed a garden in that same place, where Christ suffered, so that he might expiate the sin of the first-formed man committed in the garden of Paradise. Compare Cant.

c. 8, 5. and so that we ourselves might become a garden, adorned with various little flowers of virtues, Cant. 4, 12.

( καθίσατε ἀυτοῦ. Conf. Gen. 22, 5.)

Latin:

* (v. 36. Gethsemane. Varias autorum sententias, quid Gethsemane notet, recenset Dn. Dilherrus t. 2. Dispp. Acad. p. 15. Communis sententia est, quòd significet vallem olei, quia ibi oleum expressum fuit. Proinde sicuti ibi oleum exprimebatur ex olivis, ita Christi sanguis in agone exprimi ibi debuit. hoc est spirituale oleum, quo reficimur, ungimur, sanamur, pascimur. Confer Cant. 1, 3.Luc. 10, 34.Es. 63, 3. Erat verò ibidem hortus, ubi Christus passus est, ut expiaret peccatū protoplast. in horto Paradisi commissum. Conf cant.

c. 8, 5. utque fiamus & ipsi hortus, variis virtutum flosculis exornatus, Cant. 4, 12.) *

* ( καθίσατε ἀυτοῦ. Conf. Gen. 22, 5.) *

## 26:37
(v. 37. And taking Peter &c. He takes three witnesses see Deut. 17, 6.c. 19, 16. and conf. noted at c. 17, 1.)

(He began to be affected with sadness. See Es. 53, 4. following. Cyril errs in book 10 of the Thesaurus, c. 3, when he removes every sense of true pain from Christ. In which error he was, as was also the Emperor Justinian, if faith is to be given to Evagrius, book 4, Hist. c. 39. But Ambrose rightly taught the contrary in book 10 on Luke; likewise Athanasius on the Incarnation of Christ against Apollinaris, whence also the Blessed D. Chemn. in the book on the two natures in Christ, c. 3, p. 15, 16, and in II. Theol. part. l. p. 68, writes that the pains which Christ sustained for us were by no means simulated or putative, but true, and indeed greater than any human mind can attain to by thinking. And he concludes, that the dispute concerning simulated pains of Christ denies true ἀννλυτροντί and true satisfaction, and therefore redemption itself. Furthermore, the Blessed Fathers in H. E. p. 1743, Mr. D. Olearius in Schol. Patient. p. 900, and Mr. D. Friedl. on this passage p. 275, weigh the emphasis of the words λυπ εῖσθαι and ἀδημονεῖν. The etymologist explains by ἀλ-ειν, δποςεῖν, ἀμηχανεῖν. )

Latin:

* (v. 37. Et adsumto Petro &c. Tres adsumit testes vid. Deut. 17, 6.c. 19, 16. ac conf. notata ad c. 17, 1.) *

* (Coepit tristitiâ affici. Vid. Es. 53, 4. seqq. Errat Cyrillus l. 10. Thes. c. 3. quando à Christo omnem veri doloris sensum removet. in quo errore fuit, quoque Iustinianus Imperator, si fides habenda Evagrio est lib. 4. Hist. c. 39. At contrarium rectè docuit Ambrosius lib. 10. in Lucam. it. Athanasius de Incarn Christi contra Apollin. unde etiam B. D. Chemn. lib. de duabus nat in Christo c. 3. p. 15. 16. it. II. Theol. part. l. p. 68. scribit, quòd minimè simulati vel putativi fuerint dolores, quos Christus pro nobis sustinuit, sed veri, & quidem maiores, quàm ulla humana mens cogitatu adsequi potest. Et concludit, quòd disputatio de simulatis Christi doloribus neget verumἀννλυτροντί& veram satisfactione, adeoque ipsam redemtionem. Coeterùm emphasin verb. λυπ εῖσθαι & ἀδημονεῖν expendunt B. P. in H. E. p. 1743. Dn. D. Olearius Schol. Patient. p. 900. Dn. D. Friedl. in h. l. p. 275. Etymologus exponit per ἀλ-ειν, δποςεῖν, ἀμηχανεῖν.)*

## 26:38
(v. 38. περίλυπος. besieged and surrounded on all sides by sorrow, like a city besieged by most hostile enemies, so that there is no exit anywhere. Concerning this sadness of Christ it is to be noted that it was 1. true, against Cyril; 2. freely and voluntarily assumed, or voluntary. Conf. Ps. 40. add. Damasc. book 3 de E. O. c. 23; 3. long since predicted, Ps. 116, 3. 4. for us most salutary and profitable. see Es. 53, 4. Leo sermon 3 on the passion: He took care to participate in the affections of our infirmity, and by undergoing the fear of penal experience, he drove it away. Therefore, in us the Lord trembled with our dread, so that he might put on the assumption of our infirmity, and clothe our inconstancy with the solidity of his virtue.)

(My soul. Conf. note to C. 20, 28. Against the Pontificians it is to be noted from this place that Christ suffered in soul and body. Which thing Dan. Chamier proves at length in t. 2, panstr. l. 5, c. 12, 13.)

Latin:

* (v. 38. περίλυπος. undique moerore obsessa & circumvallata, instar civitatis, ab infensissimis hostibus obsessae, ita ut nullibi pateat exitus. De hâc Christi tristitia notandum, quòd fuerit 1. vera, contra Cyrillum 2. liberè ac sponte adsumta sive voluntaria. Conf. Ps. 40. add. Damasc. lib. 3. de E. O. c. 23. 3. dudum praedicta,Ps. 116, 3. 4. nobis maximè salutaris ac proficua. vid. Es. 53, 4. Leo serm. 3. de passione: Nostrae infirmitatis affectus participandocurabat, & poenalis experientiae metum subeundo pellebat. In nobis ergo Dominus nostro pavore trepidabat, ut susceptionem nostrae infirmitatis indueret, & nostram inconstantiam suae virtutis soliditate vestiret) *

* (Anima mea. Conf. not. ad C. 20, 28. Contra Pontificios notandum ex hoc loco, quòd Christus animâ & corpore fuerit passus. Id quod prolixè probat Dan. Chamier t. 2. panstr. l. 5. c. 12. 13.) *

## 26:39
* (v. 39 He fell on his face. This was done to declare 1. the gravity of the sorrow. 2. the admirable humility, conf. Gen. 17, 17. 1. Eccles. 5, 19.1. Macc. 4, 40. 3. the immensity of our sins. 4. the truth of the surety. (See more on the gestures of those praying in Rittershus. Ictum lib. 5. Sacr. Lect. c. 10. also in Anal. ad Actor. 7, 60.Ephes. 3, 14.) *

* ( προσευχόμενος. Conf. Ebr. 5, 7.) *

* (If it is possible. Absolutely indeed this was not impossible, see Marc. 14, 36.Luc. 1, 37. above c. 19, 26. but hypothetically, i. e. if the human race had to be reconciled and redeemed to GOD (which could not be done while preserving justice, except by the intervention of death,) it was impossible. Since therefore the present petition of Christ was hypothetical, it is no wonder that he himself was not heard. For in those things which he asked absolutely, he was always heard. see Ioh. 11, 22.42. But on this matter D. Rivetus discourses at greater length in com. in Ps. 20, p. 21. where he also explains the question Whether Christ had need of prayer. Others warn that something is possible either in reality, or by right. In reality, when it does not exceed the power of acting; By right, when it consents to it. In the former way it was possible for the cup of passion to be taken away from Christ; but not in the latter: for the constant will of GOD and the infallibility of the predictions stood in the way. But the question, why did Christ undergo martyrdom with trembling as it were and fear, when many of the martyrs approached torments with a joyful spirit? Resp. Christ suffering felt the wrath of GOD the just judge, since he had taken upon himself as a sponsor the punishments of our sins, conf. Es. 53, 6. seqq. Ioh. 1, 29.Ebr. 2, 9. but the pious when they experience calamities, know that they themselves proceed from the hand of the Father, reconciled to us through Christ.) *

Let the cup pass from me. He says in Luke: if you are willing, take it away. not that he was ignorant that the Father was unwilling, but to show that the natural affection of his will to flee death was joined with all subjection to the paternal will, and it is the same as if he said, I will that what I will not should not happen, i. e. I will with a deliberate will, which regards the object with all circumstances, that what I will with a will which refers to the object considered only in itself, should not happen. * (Christ also wished to show and teach us by this prayer that we ought to resign our will to the divine and prefer this to our own.) * Athanasius Orat. 4. contra Arianos: ἈμΦότερο παρὰ τοῦ αὐτοῦ ἐλέγοντο, ἵ-α δείξη, ὅπ, θεὸς ἦν θέλων μ-ὸ αὐτὸς, λεγόμενος δὲ ἄνθρωπος εἶχε δειλιῶσν σάρκα, δἰ -ν συνεκέ-σε τὸ ἑαυτοῦ θέλημα τἀσθενεία. ἵνα καὶ τοῦτο πὰλιν ἀφανίσας θαῤάλεον -ν ἀνθρωπορ πὰλιν πρὸς -ν θάνατον κατασκευάση. Both were said by the same one, to show that he was GOD, and that he himself indeed willed it, but having been made man he had a timid flesh, having regard for which he tempered his own will with human infirmity, so that by this very thing he might delete the other time and establish man as confident, as far as death is concerned. * (Excellently Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 1. ep. 289. Ἄνθρωπος κατ᾽ ἀλήθειαι τοῦ θεοῦ λόλος γενόειος, πὰν-α σὺν ἀληθεία -ὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐπλήρωσεν. ὅυτω καὶ ἐν τῶ τοῦ πάθουκαιρπαραιτεῖται ποτήριον. δεικ-υς ὅτι οὐ χρὴ ὁμόσε τοῖς κινδυὺοις χωρεῖν, εἰσελθόντας δὲ δέχεκαρτερῶς. μελτώμενον τὸν ςαυρὸν παρ-τεῖτο -ποφανθέντα δὲ, ἐπ᾽ ὤμων ὡς νικηφόρος λαβὼν ἠυ-μόλει Conf. also Ioh. Damasc. l. 3. de O. F. c. 18. Origenes tr. 35. in Matth. Cyrillus Alexandr. l. 4. in Ioh. c. 1. Hieronymus in h. l. Augustinus t. 2. ep. 121. c. 14.) * Theoph. in h. l. γἀνθρωπίνης φύσεως τὸ δειλιᾶν θάνα-ν, διόκαὶ φύσιν εἰσῆλθεν, ὁ θάνατος, καὶ διὰ τοτο ἡ Φύσις Φεύγει τοῦτον. For it is of human nature to shudder at death, because death arrived contrary to nature, and therefore nature flees from it. Basilius Seleuciensis in h. l. But, someone will say, the disciples are armed to undergo dangers for Christ, rejoicing, delighted by scourges. But Christ receives the cross with anxiety, and fear precedes his passion. How is this? For indeed Christ compares himself against death still living, and joins battle with tyranny not yet dissolved. For until now hell was showing its empire over man from Adam onwards.
