But Christ set forth death as killed, as if some dead thing, to those who were to be afterwards, for the struggle. Therefore he himself, as one who against

he might stand living in the battle line, he is most truly affected. Conf. B. D. Chemn. L. Theol. part. 1. p. 69. Moreover, just as in Christ, so also in the saints such a subjection is discovered, by which they submit themselves against their natural will to the divine will. Conf. Ioh. 21, 18. with Apoc. 12, 11.Act. 21, 13) *

* (transfer. Q. here, did Christ pray for himself? Damascenus answers in book 3 of De Fide Orthodoxa, chapter 24, that in prayer he expressed our person in himself. see Analysis on Heb. 5, 7. Furthermore, from the fact that Christ asks for the cup of the passion to be transferred from himself, it is not to be gathered with the Socinians, as if Christ died either unwillingly or only occasionally, and therefore his death is not satisfactory. Which horrible error the blessed D. Hutter refutes in Loci Communes, p. 423.) *

* (this cup. Just as here the passion and death of Christ is called a cup, so Paul in the epistle to Heb. Ch. 2, 9. uses the same metaphor, saying that Christ tasted death. Some observe that it almost happens in usage that when we exaggerate things that are troublesome and hard, we signify them as it were by εἰρωνικῶς the words of those things which are sweet and pleasant in life, and that the same notion is also used for a bath. see the notes above in Ch. 20, 22. But the word cup can also be used here by a simple metaphor, since both bitter and pleasant drinks are offered from a cup, so that that word denotes both lots. The blessed D. Glassius brings forward several examples of both significations in Rhetorica Sacra, p. 399. Compare Mr. Dilherr, Disputationes Academicae, vol. 1, p. 422. et seqq. There are those who do not want the passion of Christ to be understood by the cup, which Christ asks to be transferred from himself, but the destruction of the Jews, etc. But erroneously, as the blessed D. Chemnitius shows in his book on the two natures in Christ, p. 16, and also in Loci Theologici, part 1, p. 69.) *

* (not as I will, sc. let it be done. It is to be noted here against the Monothelites, that just as there are two natures in Christ, divine and human, so also there was a double will in him, yet not contrary, but distinct; not adverse, but diverse, as D. Ioh. Georg. Grossius the Calvinist notes from Iohannes Piscator himself, in Theatrum Biblicum p. 1090, and Amandus Polanus à Polansdorss also admits in Syntagma Theologiae. Therefore, this passage in no way favors the opinion of the Calvinists, (as indeed is evident in Piscator, part 3, Responsio ad Duplicem, p. 20, 28, 142) That fromMatt. 23, 37.the serious will of GOD to call and save all men cannot be proven, since the will of Christ at least is indicated there, which was only human. But that this exception is inept, the Blessed D. Fewrb. Synt. 1. Sacr. Disquis. Diss. 4. §. 22. seqq., the B. D. Menzerus in Anti-Crocio p. 109., the B. D. Chemnitius de duabus naturis in Christo C. 3. p. 15., the B. D. Lobechius in A. C. p. 97. 98., the B. D. Hutterus in LL. Theol. Mai. p. 122. seqq. show solidly. Furthermore, Ioh. Crellius the Photinian ineptly strove to destroy the true Deity of Christ from this passage, since, as he himself indeed reasons, the supreme GOD permits to no other person the power of deciding concerning Himself, and indeed of deciding contrary to what He Himself might desire. For thus he acknowledges a superior. But Christ does this. Therefore. He further insists, if Christ had been of the same essence with the Father, there would also have been one will for Him with the Father. But this is denied here, Therefore, and that must be denied. But we respond: in the same way that Christ said: The Father is greater than I,John 14, 28. in the same way He permitted to the Father the power of deciding concerning Himself. But He speaks according to at least the human nature, and that considered in the state of humiliation, while He calls the Father greater than Himself, which S. Athanasius and Nazianzenus, cited elsewhere, long ago noted, Therefore, and according to this nature of Christ at least, and that considered in the lowest degree of humiliation, it is to be understood when Christ permitted to the Father the power of deciding concerning Himself. Let the two natures in Christ therefore be distinguished, and the Scriptures will agree. But Crellius insists, that it is impossible and absurd, that there were contrary wills in Christ at the same time concerning the same matter etc. We respond by denying that this will of Christ was contrary to the will of the Father, although it was different. But that different wills in Christ according to two really distinct natures, namely the divine, according to which He is one with God the Father, and the human (according to which in the state of humiliation He turned away from death, since Christ assumed the same human weaknesses as us, sin however excepted,) could have a place, is evident from the example of Paul Rom. 7, 19. For if the Apostle could say , that he does not will the evil which he does, namely according to the flesh, but wills, suppose according to the spirit, although there were not two really distinct natures in the Apostle, how much more can such a thing be affirmed of Christ, since in the one person of Christ there are two really distinct natures. Nor yet do we concede that Christ absolutely did not will death, but rather he says this, not as I would, etc., suppose according to the weakness of the assumed flesh. Otherwise, as regards the divine nature of Christ, he certainly willed the same thing as the Father, as is evident from Ps. 40, 9.Ioh. 10, 18. Let Mr. Dr. Calovius be compared entirely in Exam. libb. Crellii §. 182. 183. 184. And from these very things the objection of Crellius against the Deity of Christ, taken from the fact that he prayed and implored the aid of GOD the Father, etc., can also be refuted. Since all this must be understood at least according to the human nature, considered in the state of humiliation, as likewise warned by Mr. Dr. Calovius l. c. §. 206. seqq.) *

* (but as you. Whether this resignation of the natural will into the will of GOD the Father can be called a correction, Daniel Chamierus disputes at length against Bell. & Gretserus, Tom. 2. Panstr. lib. 4. C. 12. §. 18. seqq. But let us learn from this prayer of Christ, how we ought to seek corporal things from GOD, namely if the divine will so carries it, i. e. if this yields to promoting the glory of GOD, our salvation and that of our neighbor. On which matter the Blessed D. Hutterus discourses in LL. Mai. p. 974. Conf. Actor. 21, 44. it. Anal. ad C. 6, 0.) *

Latin:

* (v. 39 Procidit in faciem. Factum hoc ad declarandam 1. doloris gravitatem. 2. admirandam humilitatem, conf. Gen. 17, 17. 1. Eccles. 5, 19.1. Macc. 4, 40. 3. peccatorum nostrorum immensitatem. 4. vadimonii veritatem. (Vide de gestibus orantium pluscula apud Rittershus. Ictum lib. 5. Sacr. Lect. c. 10. it. in Anal. ad Actor. 7, 60.Ephes. 3, 14.) *

* ( προσευχόμενος. Conf. Ebr. 5, 7.) *

* (Si possibile est. Absolutè quidem hoc non erat impossibile, vid. Marc. 14, 36.Luc. 1, 37. suprà c. 19, 26. sed hypotheticè, h. e. si genus humanum debuit DEO reconciliari ac redimi (quodsalvâ iustitiâ fieri non poterat, nisi mortis interventu,) fuit impossibile. Cùm igitur praesens Christi petitio fuerit hypothetica, non mirum est, quòd non fuerit ipse exauditus. in iis enim quae absolutè petiit, semper fuit auditus. vid. Ioh. 11, 22.42. Sed hâc de re prolixiùs disserit D. Rivetus com. in Ps. 20, p. 21. ubi etiam explicat quaestionemAn Christus opus habuerit oratione. Alii monent, quòd possibile aliquid sit vel re, vel iure. Re, cùm illa operandi potentiam non excedit; Iure, cùm ei consentit. Priori modo fuisse possibile, passionis poculum à Christo auferri; non verò posteriori: obstabat enim constans DEI voluntas, & praedictionum infallibilitas. Q. verò, cur Christus cum tremore quasi & timore subierit martyrium, cùm multi martyrum laeto animo tormenta aggressi fuerint? Resp. Christus patiens sensit iram DEI iusti iudicis, quoniam nostrorum peccatorum poenas tanquam sponsor in se susceperat, conf. Es. 53, 6. seqq. Ioh. 1, 29.Ebr. 2, 9. pii verò quando calamitates experiuntur, sciunt, quòdillae ipsae proficiscantur à manu reconciliati nobis per Christum, Patris.) *

Transeat à me calix. Dicit apud Lucam: si vis, transfer. non quòd ignoraret, Patrem nolle, sed ut octenderet, affectum naturalem suae voluntatis ad fugiendam mortem, coniunctum esse cum omni subiectione ad paternam voluntatem, & idem est, ac si diceret, volo, ut non fiat quod volo, i. e. volo voluntate deliberatâ, quae respicit obiectum cum omnibus circumstantiis, ut non fiat, quod ego volo voluntate, quae refertur in obiectum secundùm se tantùm consideratum. * (Ostendere quoque Christus ac docere nos voluit oratione hâc, quòd nostram voluntatem divinae resignare debeamus & hanc nostrae praeferre.) * Athanasius Orat. 4. contra Arianos: ἈμΦότερο παρὰ τοῦ αὐτοῦ ἐλέγοντο, ἵ-α δείξη, ὅπ, θεὸς ἦν θέλων μ-ὸ αὐτὸς, λεγόμενος δὲ ἄνθρωπος εἶχε δειλιῶσν σάρκα, δἰ -ν συνεκέ-σε τὸ ἑαυτοῦ θέλημα τἀσθενεία. ἵνα καὶ τοῦτο πὰλιν ἀφανίσας θαῤάλεον -ν ἀνθρωπορ πὰλιν πρὸς -ν θάνατον κατασκευάση.Utrumque ab eodem dictum, ut ostenderet, se DEUM esse, & ipsum quidem velle, at factum hominem habere quidem timidam carnem, cuius habità ratione & temper asse suam voluntatem humanâ infirmitate, ut hoc ipso altera vice deleto considentem hominem constitueret, quod ad mortem attinet. * (Egregiè Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 1. ep. 289. Ἄνθρωπος κατ᾽ ἀλήθειαι τοῦ θεοῦ λόλος γενόειος, πὰν-α σὺν ἀληθεία -ὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐπλήρωσεν. ὅυτω καὶ ἐν τῶ τοῦ πάθουκαιρπαραιτεῖται ποτήριον. δεικ-υς ὅτι οὐ χρὴ ὁμόσε τοῖς κινδυὺοις χωρεῖν, εἰσελθόντας δὲ δέχεκαρτερῶς. μελτώμενον τὸν ςαυρὸν παρ-τεῖτο -ποφανθέντα δὲ, ἐπ᾽ ὤμων ὡς νικηφόρος λαβὼν ἠυ-μόλει Conf. quoque Ioh. Damasc. l. 3. de O. F. c. 18. Origenes tr. 35. in Matth. Cyrillus Alexandr. l. 4. in Ioh. c. 1. Hieronymus in h. l. Augustinus t. 2. ep. 121. c. 14.) * Theoph. in h. l. γἀνθρωπίνης φύσεως τὸ δειλιᾶν θάνα-ν, διόκαὶ φύσιν εἰσῆλθεν, ὁ θάνατος, καὶ διὰ τοτο ἡ Φύσις Φεύγει τοῦτον.Est enim humanae naturae, horrere mortem, propterea quòd praeter naturam mors advenit, ideoque eam natura refugit. Basilius Seleuciensis in h. l. At, inquiet aliquis, discipuli ad subeunda pro Christo pericula armantur, gaudentes, flagris delectati. Christus vero cum anxietate crucem excipit, eiusque passionem timor praecedit. qui fit? enim verò Christus contra viventem adhuc mortem comparat se, atque cum tyrannide nondum solutâ manus confert. Hactenus enim infernus suum iam inde ab Adamo in hominem imperium ostentabat. At Christus mortem interfectam, tanquam mortuum aliquem iis, qui post futuri erant, obiecit ad luctam. propterea ipse quidem, ut qui contra

viventem in acie consisteret, verissimè afficitur. Conf. B. D. Chemn. L. Theol. part. 1. p. 69. Caeterùm sicuti in Christo, ita quoque in sanctis talis subiectio deprehenditur, qua contra naturalem voluntatem divinae se voluntati submittunt. Conf. Ioh. 21, 18. cum Apoc. 12, 11.Act. 21, 13) *

* (transfer. Q. hîc, num Christus pro se orarit? Respondet Damascenus l. 3. de O. F. c. 24. quòd in oratione nostram in se expresserit personam. vid. Anal. ad Ebr. 5, 7. Coeterùm exeo, quòd Christus transferri à se petit calicem passionis, non colligendum cum Socinianis, quasi Christus vel invitus vel tantùm occasionaliter mortum fuerit, adeòque mors eius non sit satisfactoria. Quem horrendum èrrorem refutat B. D. Hutter. LL. Mai. p. 423.) *

* (poculum hoc. Quemadmodum hîc passio ac mors Christi peculum vocatur, ita Paulus in ep. ad Ebr. C. 2, 9. eadem metaphorâ dicit, Christum gustâsse mortem. Observant nonnulli, quòd ferè usu veniat, ut quae sunt molesta ac dura, ea dum exaggeramus, significemus veluti εἰρωνικῶς earum rerum vocabulis, quae in vitâ suavia sunt & iucunda, eademque notione etiam lavacrum usurpari. vid. notata suprà C. 20, 22. Sed potestetiam simplici metaphorâ vocabulum calicis hic adhiberi, cùm ex poculo tàm amari, quàm iucundi potus exhibeantur, ut ita utramque sortem vox illa notet. Exempla utriusque significationis pluscula adducit B. D. Glass. Rhet. s. p. 399. Conf. Dn. Dilherr. Disp. Acad. t. 1. p. 422. seqq. Sunt qui nolunt, per calicem seu poculum, quod Christus à se transferri petit, intelligi Christi passionem, sed Iudaeorum perditionem &c. Ast erroneè, uti ostendit B. D. Chemn. lib. de duab. nat. in Chr. p. 16. it. LL. Theol. part. 1. p. 69.) *

* (non sicuti ego volo, sc. fiat. Notandùm hîc contra Monotheletas, quòd sicuti duae in Christo naturae sunt, divina & humana, ita quoque duplex in ipso fuerit voluntas, non tamen contraria, sed distincta; non adversa, sed diversa, ceu ex Ioh. Piscatore ipso annotat D. Ioh. Georg. Grossius Calvinianus, in Theatro Biblico p. 1090. ac fatetur quoque Amandus Polanus à Polansdorss in Synt. Theol. Minimè igitur hic locus favet sententiae Calvinianorū, (uti quidem Piscator part. 3. Resp. ad Duplic. p. 20. 28. 142. patet) quòd exMatth. 23, 37.non possit seria DEI voluntas, omnes homines vocandi & salvandi probari, cùm voluntas saltem Christi ibi indicetur, quae tantùm humana fuerit. Sed ineptam esse hanc exceptionem, solidè ostendunt B. D. Fewrb. Synt. 1. Sacr. Disquis. Diss. 4. §. 22. seqq. B D. Menzerus in Anti-Crocio p. 109. B. D. Chemnitius de duabus naturis in Christo C. 3. p. 15. B. D. Lobechius in A. C. p. 97. 98. B. D. Hutterus in LL. Theol. Mai. p. 122. seqq. Ineptè porrò ex hoc loco Ioh. Crellius Photinianus veram Christi Deitatem destruere sategit, siquidem, uti ipse quidem ratiocinatur, DEUS summus nulli alii personae de se statuendi, & contra quidem quàm ipse cuperet, decernendi arbitrium permittit. Sic enim superiorem agnoscit. At Christus hoc facit. E. Instat porrò, si Christus eiusdem fuisset cum Patre essentiae, unae etiam illi cum Patre voluntas fuisset. At hoc negatur hîc, E. & illud negandum. Verùm resp. quomodo Christus dixit: Pater maior me est,Ioh. 14, 28. eodem modo de se statuendi arbitrium Patri permisit. At secundùm humanam saltem naturam, eandemque in statu exinanitionis consideratam loquitur, dum Patrem se maiorem vocat, quod pridem notarunt S. Athanasius ac Nazianzenus, alibi adducti, E. & secundùm hanc saltem Christi naturam, eandemque in infimo exinanitionis gradu consideratam intelligendum, quando Christus Patri de se statuendi arbitrium permisit. Distinguantur igitur duae in Christo naturae, & concordabunt Scripturae. Ast instat Crellius, impossibile esse atabsurdum, in Christo eodem tempore contrarias de eadem re fuisse voluntates &c. Resp. Negando, fuisse voluntatem hanc Christi voluntati Patris contrariam, licet fuerit diversa. Quòd verò diversae in Christo voluntates secundùm duas realiter distinctas naturas, divinam nempe, secundùm quam unum est cum Deo Patre, ac humanam (secundùm quam in statu exinanitionis mortem aversatus est, quippe cùm easdem nobiscum imbecillitates humanas, excepto tamen peccato, Christus adsumserit,) locum habere potuerint, patet ex exemplo Pauli Rom. 7, 19. Si enim Apostolus dicere potuit, se malum, quod facit, nempe secundùm carnem, nolle, puta secundùm spiritum, cum tamen non duae in Apostolo naturae realiter distinctae fuerint, quanto magis de Christo tale quid affirmari potest, cùm in unâ Christi persona duae realiter distinctae naturae sint. Neque tamen concedimus, quòd Christus absolutè noluerit mortem, sed potiùs hoc dicit, non sicuti ego vellem &c. puta secundùm carnis adsumtae imbecillitatē. Aliàs quod divinam Christi naturam spectat, utiq; idem voluit, quod Pater, ceu patet ex Ps. 40, 9.Ioh. 10, 18. Conferatur omninò Dn. D. Calovius in Exam. libb. Crellii §. 182. 183. 184. Atqque ex his ipsis refelli quoq; potest obiectio Crellii contra Christi Deitatem, ex eo desumtam, quòd oraverit ac opem imploraverit DEI Patris &c. Cùm omne hoc saltem secundùm humanam naturam, in statu exinanitionis consideratam, intelligendum sit, ceu itidem monitum à Dn. D. Calovio l. c. §. 206. seqq.) *

* (sed sicut tu. An haec voluntatis naturalis resignatio in voluntatem DEI Patris, correctio vocari possit, prolixè contra Bell. & Gretserum disputat Daniel chamierus Tom. 2. Panstr. lib. 4. C. 12. §. 18. seqq. Discamus verò ex h-c Christi oratione, quomodo corporalia petere à DEO debeamus, nempe si sic ferat divina voluntas, h. e. si cedat hoc ad promovendam DEI gloriam, nostram & proximi salutem. quâ de re disserit B. D. Hutterus LL. Mai. p. 974. Conf. Actor. 21, 44. it. Anal. ad C. 6, 0.) *

## 26:40
* (v. 40. watch. conf. Actor. 20, 31.1. Cor. 16, 13.Apoc. 3, 2.) *

* (that you may not enter into temptation. i. e. that you may not be overcome. And so also D. Hieronymus and Theophylactus explain it, of whom the former writes: That you may not enter, into temptation, that is, that temptation may not overcome you, and conquer you, and hold you entangled in sin within its snares; the latter, however, although from the mind of others: that you may not enter into temptation, that is, that you may not be overcome by temptation. For he does not command us to be without temptation: but that we may not be absorbed by temptation, and enter into its belly, as if of some beast. He commands us to pray for this. For he who is conquered by temptation, enters into it, that is, is absorbed by it. So that ἐισέρχεσθαι is the same in this place as ἐπιπίπτειν, 1. Tim. 6, 9. conf. Anal. above to C. 6, 12.) *

* The spirit indeed is willing. There are those, among whom is Robertus Stephanus, who understand this passage in such a way that the readiness, swiftness, cunning, and zeal for harming of the hostile spirit or the devil approaches the infirmity of our flesh, or that the flesh is weak for resisting, but the devil is ready for tempting, and thus a huge danger threatens miserable mortals from both. As even Ioh. de Pineda makes mention of this exposition in Comm. on Iob. C. 5, 7. n. 10. But besides the fact that the word spirit, placed absolutely and with an article and opposed to the flesh, is hardly found anywhere in Holy Scripture for an evil spirit, (a thing which S. Hieronymus in C. 2. Mich. t. 6. Op. and August. ad Simplic. q. 1. and lib. de inearn. verbic. 17. have long since observed) but on the contrary, when it is opposed to the flesh, it is always in a good sense, see Ioh. 3. 6.Rom. 8, 13.15.Gal. 5, 16. 17. it is sufficiently clear from the context that Christ is speaking about the spirit of man or about the inner man. And the discourse in this place is indeed about the spirit of the Apostles and of the faithful, but not in general about the spirit of all men. This is what Origenes noted, writing: All flesh is weak, but not also the spirit of all men is willing, but only that of the Saints, who mortify the works of the flesh with a willing spirit. To this point also contributes the observation of some, that among the Hebrews that faculty of the soul which is vital and sensitive, is called נפש but that which uses reason, רוח or πνεῦμα. and thus the Apostle uses this word Rom. 8, 16.1. Cor. 2, 11.c. 6, 20.Ebr. 4, 12. Nor is this, however, perpetual. see Actor. 19, 21. Therefore, Hilarius in the Catena Aurea, Theophylactus, Lyranus, and Beda in this place expound this passage concerning the Disciples of Christ or the faithful, likewise Prosper l. 2. de vocatione gentium C. 28. whom among our own follow B. D. Hunnius, Gesnerus, Osiander, Avenarius, and most others, among the Papists Iansenius, Ferus, Maldonatus, Iacobus Tirinus, Corn. à Lapide etc., among the Calvinists Calvin himself, Bucerus, Bullingerus, Gualterus, Piscator etc. Others concerning the very They interpret Christ, but not in one way; for some understand by spirit the Deity of Christ, and by flesh His humanity. And from there, furthermore, against the Monothelites and Apollinarians, they prove a twofold will in CHRIST, as is evident from Act. 4. 10. and 18. of the VI Constantinopolitan Synod. Likewise Gregory of Nyssa in his book against Apollinarius, and Cyril in book 4 of his Commentary on John. And among the Papists, Thomas Aquinas follows these in part 3, q. 18, art. 6, and Lombard in book 3 of his Sentences, dist. 17, who also cites Jerome on this passage in support of this opinion. Others, again, interpret it likewise concerning CHRIST, but at least according to human nature, that is, with respect to the different parts within it, namely, so that readiness of spirit is understood as the faculty of the soul λογιςικ,, but weakness of flesh as the faculty of the soul φυσικῇ καὶ ἀισθητικ-,. And this opinion seems to have pleased John of Damascus above all, as is evident from book 2 de O. F. c. 22, and book 3, c. 15, 18, 23, and following. And in the same way, the blessed Luther himself also interpreted it, Comm. Gen. C. 15. f. 174. All these expositions, except for that which understands spirit as the devil, although they are such that none contains anything absurd, meanwhile, as the first approaches the context most closely, so it seems to be preferred over the others. Especially since the word spirit is also understood in this way elsewhere, when it is opposed to flesh. And the blessed Pareus also embraces this very opinion in H. E. C. 182, p. 1762; but that which interprets it concerning Christ seems to be favored especially by the Petrine statement 1 ep. c. 3, 18, and the Pauline assertion, 2. Cor. 13, 14.)

* (flesh is weak. Indeed, in spiritual matters, it is destitute of all strength. conf. Ioh. 3, 6.Rom. 8, 7.13.)

Latin:

* (v. 40. vigilate. conf. Actor. 20, 31.1. Cor. 16, 13.Apoc. 3, 2.) *

* (ne intretis intentationem. i. e. ne vincamini. Atq; ita etiam exponit D Hieronymus ac Theophylactus, quorum ille: Ut non intretis, scribit, in tentationem, hoc est, ne tentatio vos superet, & vincat, & peccato irretitos intra casses suos teneat; hic verò, quamvis ex aliorum mente: ne intretis in tentationem, id est, ne vincamini à tentatione meâ. Non enim iubet nos sine tentatione esse: sed ne à tentatione absorbeamur, & intremus in ventrem eius, quasi bestiae cuiusdam. Hoc iubet orare. Nam victus à tentatione, ingreditur in eam, hoc est, absorbetur ab ea. Ut ita ἐισέρχεσθαι idem sit h. l. ac ἐπιπίπτειν,1. Tim. 6, 9. conf. Anal. suprà ad C. 6, 12.) *

* (spiritus quidem promtus est. Sunt, quos inter & Robertus Stephanus, qui hunc locum ita intelligunt, quòd a carnis nostrae infirmitatem accedat spiritûs inimici seu diaboli promtitudo, celeritas, astutia ac studium nocendi, sive, quòd caro sit infirma ad resistendum, diabolus verò promtus ad tentandum, adeòque ex utroque ingens periculum miseris mortalibus immineat. ceu expositionis etiam huius mentionem facit Ioh. de Pineda Comm. in Iob. C. 5, 7. n. 10. Ast praeterquam, quòd vox spiritus, absolutè & cum articulo posita ac carni opposita, vix reperiatur ullibi in Sc. S. pro spiritu malo, (id quod dudum etiam observarunt S. Hieronymus in C. 2. Mich. t. 6. Op. & August. ad Simplic. q. 1. ac lib. de inearn. verbic. 17.) contrà verò quando carni opponitur, semper in bonam partem, vid Ioh. 3. 6.Rom. 8, 13.15.Gal. 5, 16. 17. satis ex contextu patet, quòd Christus loquatur de spiritu hominus sive de interiori homine. Et sermo quidem h. l. est de spiritu Apostolorum ac fidelium, non verò in genere de spiritu omnium hominum. Id quod Origenes notavit, scribens: Omnium caro infirma est, non autem & omnium hominum spiritus promtus, sed tantùm Sanctorum, qui spiritu promto opera carnis mortificant. Huc facit & observatio nonnullorum, quòd apud Ebraeos ea animae facultas, quae vitalis & sensitiva, dicatur נפש ea verò quae ratione utitur, רוח sive πνεῦμα. atque ita hac voce utitur Apostolus Rom. 8, 16.1. Cor. 2, 11.c. 6, 20.Ebr. 4, 12. Neque tamen hoc perpetuum est. vid. Actor. 19, 21. De Discipulis igitur Christi seu de fidelibus locum hunc exponunt Hilarius apud Aquinatem in Catenâ Aureâ, Theophylactus, Lyranus ac Beda in h. l. item Prosper l. 2. de vocatione gentium C. 28. quos ex nostratibus sequuntur B. D. Hunnius, Gesnerus, Osiander, Avenarius & alii plerique, ex Pontificiis Iansenius, Ferus, Maldonatus, Iacobus Tirinus, Corn. à Lapide &c. ex Calvinianis Calvinus ipse, Bucerus, Bullingerus, Gualterus, Piscator &c. Alii de ipso Christo accipiunt, sed non unô modô, quidam enim per spiritum intelligunt Christi Deitatem, per carnem eiusdem humanitatem. atque inde porrò contra Monotheletas & Apollinaristas duplicem in CHRISTO voluntatem probant, ceu patet ex Act. 4. 10. & 18. Synodi Constantinopolitanae VI. item Gregorio Nysseno l. contra Apollin. Cyrillo l. 4. Comm. in Ioh. Atque hos ex Pontificiis sequuntur Thomas Aquinas part. 3. q. 18. art. 6. Lombardus l. 3. Sent. dist. 17. qui etiam in hanc sentententiam allegat Hieronymum ad h. l. Alii rursus itidem quidem de CHRISTO accipiunt, sed saltem secundùm humanam naturam, puta respectu diversarum in ea partium, nempe ut promtitudo spiritûs accipiatur de facultate animae λογιςικ,carnis autem infirmitas de facultate animae φυσικῇ καὶ ἀισθητικ-, Atque haec sententia cumprimis arrisisse Iohanni Damasceno videtur, ceu patet ex l. 2. de O. F. c. 22. l. 3. C. 15. 18. 23. seqq. Eodemque modo ipse quoque B. Lutherus interpretatus est, Comm. Gen. C. 15. f. 174. Omnes hae expositiones, exceptâ, illâ, quae spiritum de diabolo accipit, licet ita sese habeant, ut nulla aliquid absurdi contineat, intereà prima uti contextui proximè accedit, ita reliquis praeferenda videtur. Cumprimis quoniam alibi quoque vox spiritus ita accipitur, quando carni opponitur. Et hanc ipsam sententiam amplectitur quoque B. Par. in H. E. C. 182. p. 1762. illi verò, quae de Christo accipit, cumprimis favere videtur dictum Petrinum 1. ep. c. 3, 18. it. adsertum Paulinum, 2. Cor. 13, 14.) *

* (caro imbecillis. Imò in spiritualibus, omnibus viribus destituta. conf. Ioh. 3, 6.Rom. 8, 7.13.) *

## 26:42
* (v. 42. εἰ if i. e. since.)

Latin:

* (v. 42. εἰsi i. e. quandoquidem.) *

## 26:43
* (v. 43. & prayed the third time. Why the Lord prayed three times, there are various opinions of the ancients. Theophylact thinks that Christ wished to confirm by this very thing that He is man; but Augustine thinks it was done on account of the threefold temptation of the passion. Rabanus writes that CHRIST prayed three times, , so that we might pray for pardon for past sins, protection from present evils, and caution against future dangers, and direct all prayer to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, and that our whole spirit, and soul, and body may be preserved. It is said most simply that Christ prayed three times, and thus rather frequently, 1. to declare the magnitude of His sorrow. To which the bloody sweat also contributes Luc. 22, 41. 2. that he might salutarily inform us, that we ought to persevere in prayer, and not only to seek and to ask, but also to knock. See above c. 7, 7. & 8. add. 2. Cor. 12, 8.

( ἁμα τωλ-ν. thus the Gentiles were called by the Jews. see Gal. 2, 15. otherwise also ἄνομοι, Act. 2, 23.1. Cor. 9, 21. Interpreters therefore think that Roman soldiers of the garrison are understood here, whom Pilate had granted to the Jews for the custody of the temple at this time. Over these, as well as the daily watchmen, one of the Priests presided, next in dignity to the high Priest himself. Concerning which Magistracy there is discourse in Act. 4, 1.c. 5, 24.29. likewise in Josephus l. 8. A. I. c. 5. & 8.)

Latin:

* (v. 43. & oravit tertiò. Cur ter Dominus orarit, diversae sunt veterum sententiae. Theophylactus censet, Christum hoc ipso confirmare voluisse, se esse hominem; Augustinus verò id factum putat propter trinam tentationem passionis. Rabanus ideò CHRISTUM ter orasse, scribit, ut nos à praeteritis peccatis veniam, à praesentibus malis tutelam, & à futuris periculis cautelam oremus, & omnem orationem ad Patrem, & ad Filium & ad Spiritum Sanctum dirigamus, & ut integer spiritus noster, & anima & corpus servetur. Simplicissimè dicitur, Christum ter, adeoque saepiusculè orasse, 1. ut tristitiae magnitudinem declararet. quò facit etiam sudor sanguineus Luc. 22, 41. 2. ut nos salutariter informaret, quòd in oratione perseverare, nec solùm quaerere ac petere, sed etiam pulsare debeamus. Vid. suprà c. 7, 7. & 8. add. 2. Cor. 12, 8.) *

* ( ἁμα τωλ-ν. ita gentiles vocabantur Iudaeis. vid. Gal. 2, 15. aliàs etiam ἄνομοι,Act. 2, 23.1. Cor. 9, 21. Existimant igitur Interpretes, intelligi hîc milites Romanos praesidiarios. quos hoc tempore templi custodiae Pilatus Iudaeis concesserat. his, uti & quotidianis vigilibus unus è Sacerdotibus praecrat, ipsi summo Pontifici dignitate proximus. De quo Magistratu sermo sit Act. 4, 1.c. 5, 24.29. item apud Iosephum l. 8. A. I. c. 5. & 8.) *

## 26:45
(v. 45. Sleep on now and take your rest. A rule is to be noted here, that Imperatives are sometimes to be explained permissively, since they do not always signify a precept, but sometimes συγχάρηιν. see 1. Reg. 22, 22.2. Reg. 2, 17.Matth. 8, 32. What is more, in the H. S. sometimes that seems to be commanded, which nevertheless those who use that mode of speaking do not wish to be done, as Iudic. 10, 14.Es 21, 5.Ezech. 20, 39.Ioh. 13, 27.Apoc. 22, 11. and not undeservedly does B Par. Comm. in post. Epist. Petri p. 287 also refer the present passage here. In almost this same way Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius also accept it. On the contrary Augustine lib. 3. de Consensu Evang. c. 4. Bede and others, (whose opinion Corn. à Lapide embraces,) maintain, that Christ, as if sympathizing with the infirmity of the Apostles, indulged them a little sleep, until, Judas approaching, he said, it is enough. and to this Cornelius especially refers that which is read here in Greek, καθεύδετε τὸ οιπὸν, which he explains, sleep, which is the rest, that is, sleep for a little time, which remains, until the arrival of Judas.)

Latin:

* (v. 45. Dormite iam & quiescite. Notanda hîc regula, quòd Imperativi quandoque exponendi sint permissivè, eùm non semper praeceptum, sed interdum συγχάρηιν significent. vid. 1. Reg. 22, 22.2. Reg. 2, 17.Matth. 8, 32. Quid quòd in Sc. S. aliquando id videatur iuberi, quod tamen fieri non debere volunt, qui eo loquendi modo utuntur, uti Iudic. 10, 14.Es 21, 5.Ezech. 20, 39.Ioh. 13, 27.Apoc. 22, 11. atque huc non immeritò etiam praesentem locum refert B Par. Comm. in post. Epist. Petri p. 287. Hoc ferè modo eundem accipiunt quoq; Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Euthymius. Contrà Augustinus lib. 3. de Consensu Evang. c. 4. Beda ac alii, (quorum sententiam amplectitur Corn. à Lapide,) statuunt, quòd Christus quasi compatiens in firmitati Apostolorum aliquantulum somni eis indulserit, donec appropinquante Iuda dixerit, sufficit. hucque cumprimis refert Cornelius illud, quòd in Graeco hîc legatur, καθεύδετε τὸ οιπὸν, quod explicat, dormite, quod reliquum est, id est, dormite modico tempore, quod restat, usque ad adventum Iudae.) *

## 26:47
* (v. 47. πρεσβυτέρων τοῶ λάου. This is a description of the Great Sanhedrin, concerning which it was treated above.) *

Latin:

* (v. 47. πρεσβυτέρων τοῶ λάου. Est descriptio Synedrii Magni, de quô suprà actum.) *

## 26:48
* (v. 48. σημεῖον. For CHRIST was not so well known to the Roman soldiers.) *

Latin:

* (v. 48. σημεῖον. Erat enim CHRISTUS militibus Romanis non usque adeò notus.) *

## 26:49
* (v. 49. He kissed him. Concerning this deceitful kiss, full of poison, Victor of Antioch speaks well in C. 14, 45 of Mark: To him for whom he was laying lethal snares, the unhappy man offered a greeting with a kiss. Similarly Augustine, sermon 1 on the Passion: You kiss, and you lay snares; you feign a friend, when you are a traitor. Judas surely follows Joab, who, as Judas was goaded by avarice, so he was goaded by envy, and kissed Amasa under the guise of friendship, and at the same time secretly struck him with a sword, 2. Sam. 20, 9. Christ, however, on the contrary, although he well knew the mind and deceit of Judas, nevertheless admitted the kiss, so that he might surely affect the traitor more, to whom he did not deny the offices of love, as Ambrose speaks on C. 21 of Luke; then also, so that he might teach us that all enemies, even those whom we know are going to rage against us, must be loved, as Hilary warns. Furthermore, concerning the custom of the ancients of honoring, greeting, and bidding farewell with a kiss etc., and the various kinds of kisses, Tertullian treats from the ancients in his book on Prayer p. 793, Justin Martyr in his 2nd Apology for the Christians page 76, and from the more recent ones H. Grotius on this passage, B. Par. in the preface to the epistle of Peter p. 856, 870, 871, 882, Conradus Rittershusius in his Commentary on Salvian p. 379, 380, Barthol. Meyerus on the 70 Weeks of Daniel p. 125 ff., Mr. Dilherrus in vol. 1 of his Academic Disputations p. 491, and commentators everywhere on Gen. 29, 11.13.C. 31, 2855.C. 33, 4.C. 45, 15.Exod. 4, 27.c. 18, 7.Ruth 1, 14.1. Sam. 10, 1.2 Sam. 14, 35.1. Reg. 19, 18.20. Job 31, 27. Psalm. 2, 12.Luc. 7, 45.Act. 20, 37.Rom. 16, 16.1. Cor. 16, 20.2. Cor. 13, 12.1. Thess. 5, 26.1. Petr. 5, 14. Indeed, even now that custom prevails among some peoples, especially the French and the Belgians, which Aretius also notes in Matthew p. 214.) *

Latin:

* (v. 49. Osculatus est eum. Benè de osculo hoc doloso ac veneni pleno, Victor Antiochenus in C. 14, 45. Marci: Cui lethales insidias struebat, illi infelix salutem cum osculo offerebat. Similiter Augustinus serm. 1. de Passione: Oscularis, & insidiaris; amicum fingis, cum proditor sis. Sequitur nempe Iudas Ioabum. qui ceu Iudas avaritiâ, ita ille invidiâ stimulatus Amasam sub amicitiae specie osculatus est, simulque latenter gladio percussit, 2. Sam. 20, 9. Christus verò contrà licet probè animum ac dolum Iudae cognoseeret, osculum tamen admisit, ut plus nempe proditorem afficeret, cui amoris officia non negaret, ut loquitur Ambrosius ad C. 21. Lucae tum quoque, ut doceret nos, inimicos omnes, eosetiam, quos scimus in nos desaevituros esse, diligendos esse, monente Hilario. Porrò de consuetudine veterum osculo honorandi, salutandi, valedicendi &c. variisque osculorum generibus aguntex veteribus Tertullianus lib. de Orat. p. 793. Iustinus Martyr Apol. 2. pro Christianis pag. 76. è recensioribus H. Grotius in h. l. B. Par. in pr. ep. Petri p. 856. 870. 871. 882. Conradus Rittershusius Comm. ad Salvianum p. 379. 380. Barthol. Meyerus de 70. Hebd. Danielis p. 125. seqq. Dn. Dilherrus t. 1. Dispp. Acad. p. 491. & Commentatores passim ad Gen. 29, 11.13.C. 31, 2855.C. 33, 4.C. 45, 15.Exod. 4, 27.c. 18, 7.Ruth 1, 14.1. Sam. 10, 1.2 Sam. 14, 35.1. Reg. 19, 18.20. Iobi 31, 27. Psalm. 2, 12.Luc. 7, 45.Act. 20, 37.Rom. 16, 16.1. Cor. 16, 20.2. Cor. 13, 12.1. Thess. 5, 26.1. Petr. 5, 14. Quin etiamnum mos ille apud populos nonnullos, Gallos cumprimis ac Belgas obtinet, quod notat quoque Aretius in Matth p. 214.) *

## 26:51
* (v. 51. τὴν μάχαιρον. Nic, de Lyra, Menochius & others, whom Mr. Dr. Friedlieb also follows in this place, judge that it was a larger knife, which Peter had for the use of fishing and boating business, but was kept by him for cutting the meat of the Paschal lamb, since a just sword is called μεγάλη μάχαιρο, Apoc. 6, 4. but a knife by the LXX absolutely μάχαιρο, Gen. 22, 6.Iudic. 19, 29. Proverb. 30, 14. Others however determine otherwise. conf. Anal. Luc. 22, 36.) *

* (he cut off his ear. Mystically Isidore of Pelusium lib. 1. ep 291. Peter, because the Jews were suffering from the disease of stubbornness, cut off the ear of the servant who belonged to the Priest. Showing by this, clearly, that the Priest was a slave to the disobedience of the law, and that he needed the sword for the cutting off of his own reluctance.) *

Latin:

* (v. 51. τὴν μάχαιρον. Nic, de Lyra, Menochius & alii, quos sequitur etiam Dn. D. Friedlieb. in h. l. censent, fuisse cultrum maiorem, quem in piscatorīae & naviculatoriae rei usum Petrus habuerit, retentus verò ab ipso fuerit ad scindendas carnes agni Paschalis, cùm gladius iustus vocetur μεγάλη μάχαιρο,Apoc. 6, 4. culter verò à LXX absolutè μάχαιρο,Gen. 22, 6.Iudic. 19, 29. Proverb. 30, 14. Alii tamen aliter statuunt. conf. Anal. Luc. 22, 36.) *

* (amputavit auriculam eius. Mysticè Isiodorus Pelusiota lib. 1. ep 291. Petrus, quoniam contumaciae morbo laborabant Iudaei, famuli qui ad Sacerdotem attinebat, auriculam amputavit. hinc videlicet Sacerdotem in. obedientiae legis servum esse ostendens, atque ad reluctationis suae praecisionem gladio indigere.) *

## 26:52
* (v. 52. Put up the sword &c. Ambrose in C. 22. of Luke: He did not wish to be defended by the wound of his persecutors, who wished to heal all by his own wound.) *

* (into its place It is a description of a sheath. The Rabbis use the word בית in this way, adding however the name of the content. see B. D. Glass. Gramm. S. p. 144. Buxt. Lex. Rabb. Talmud. under the word בῙת. ) *

* (all who take the sword &c. understand by the desire and rashness of private vengeance, or by complying with their own desire, (as Peter was doing here) but not by public authority, or by exercising the judgment of GOD. Therefore, the right of the sword, granted to the Magistrate by GOD, is by no means destroyed here, Rom. 13, 4. Whence also the Fathers observe that Christ did not say, who carries the sword, namely that which is given and committed by GOD, Rom. 13, 4. but who has taken, that is, has claimed for himself by private authority. Furthermore, to Peter, as one called to the Ecclesiastical Ministry, the sword of the word had been committed, Eph. 6, 17. add. 2. Cor. 10, 4. and conf. against the political affectation of the Pope's jurisdiction B D. Hutt. LL. Th. p. 570. & 1003. B. P. C. C. t. 2. p. 840. et seqq. Therefore this passage by no means supports the Weigelians, Photinians and Anabaptists, who are busy trying to wrench the sword from the hands of the Political Magistrate. As for the rest, how this prohibition is to be reconciled with the command Luc. 22, 36., in the analysis of Luke, will be noted. Nor are all Wars simply prohibited by this oracle in the New Testament. For the Magistrate does not take the sword for himself, but receives it handed down from GOD, who in a just war acts for the cause of GOD, that is: with the glory of GOD and the salvation of subjects proposed to him, he seizes arms against an enemy disturbing the public peace, and advances into the battle line against the same. Provided this is done without pride, avarice, etc., and confidence is not placed in the number of soldiers, but in divine aid. Conf. Not. to Rom. 13, 4.

* (He will perish by the sword. The word sword is taken here generally; for any punishments whatsoever, inflicted by the Magistrate; to whom the sword has been girded by GOD. So it is also taken in Rom. 13, 6.. It is evident indeed from this place that it pertains to the Magistrate to inflict capital punishments upon murderers (and other criminals; such as adulterers, poisoners, etc.). The Photinians except; Valentinus Smalcius against the 7th Disputation of D. Franzius on the B. O. page 14, also Disputation 6: on civil matters page 290. Ostorodus in the German Institution page 190. that these words of CHRIST contain a prediction, by which He indicates what ordinarily happens, but does not teach what can or ought to be done by right. Resp. 1. We easily concede indeed that it happens sometimes, as if some murderers escape the deserved punishment to be inflicted by the Magistrate; or perish again in a duel or by the bites of serpents, or the invasion of wild beasts (see Plutarch, book on the slow vengeance of the Divinity, also Act. 28, 4.). Nevertheless 2. since not all the blood of a murderer is actually shed by man, as experience testifies; it follows, if these words of CHRIST, and those of Gen. 9, 6. (where the discourse is clearly similar to here, as Ostorodus himself warns in the cited place) contained at least a prediction, that a divine prediction would sometimes contain a falsehood. To say which is absurd and impious. But 3. that it will be is read both here and in Moses, it is to be noted that it is placed in the Hebrew manner for an Imperative.

which kind of Hebraism also occurs not rarely in divine precepts. see. Exod. 20. or it can also be said that the future by Τὸ ought to be explained with its own infinitive, as examples of such a locution occur Ps. 32, 8.Ezech. 34. 2.Malach. 1, 6.Luc. 3. 14. and elsewhere. Furthermore 4 how these words of CHRIST are to be understood is sufficiently clear both from the divine decree Gen. 9, 6. from where they are taken and which CHRIST here confirms, (for there is no doubt that the Savior looked to that.) and from Rom. 13, 4. 5. it is also evident from the circumstances of the text that Peter had seized the sword by private authority against those who had been sent by the Magistrate. Although it may be lawful otherwise to repel force with force: yet the matter stands otherwise when subjects are afflicted with injury by the Magistrate. Compare more things pertaining to this in B. D. Kōnig Cas. catech. page 44, 45. B. Par. L. de Magistr. Polit. §. 298.) *

Latin:

* (v. 52. Converte gladium &c. Ambrosius in C. 22. Lucae: Noluit persecutorum vulnere defendi, qui voluit suo vulnere omnes sanare.) *

* (in locum suum Est descriptio vaginae. Rabbini utuntur ita voce בית adiiciendo tamen nomen contenti. vid. B. D. Glass. Gramm. S. p. 144. Buxt. Lex. Rabb. Talmud. dictione בῙת.) *

* (omnis qui acceperit gladium &c. intellige privatae vindictae cupiditate ac temeritate, sive cupiditati suae obsequendo, (quomodo Petrus hîc faciebat) non verò publicâ autoritate, sive DEI iudicium exercendo. Minimè proinde hîc destruitur ius gladii, Magistratui à DEO concessum, Rom. 13, 4. Unde etiam observant Inter pp. quòd Christus non dixerit, qui gestarit gladium, à DEO scilicet datum ac commissum, Rom. 13, 4. sed qui acceperit, hoc est, privatâ sibi autoritate vendicarit. praetereà Petro, ut potè ad Ministerium Ecclesiasticum vocato, commissus erat gladius verbi,Eph. 6, 17. add. 2. Cor. 10, 4. ac conf. contra affect. iurisdict. Papae Polit. B D. Hutt. LL. Th. p. 570. & 1003. B. P. C. C. t. 2. p. 840. feqq. Minimè igitur locus hic patroci-atur Weigelianis, Photinianis & Anabaptistis, gladium è manibus Magistratûs Politici extorquere satagentibus. Coeterùm quomodo prohibitio haec concilianda sit cum mandato Luc. 22, 36., in anal. ad Luc. monebitur. Nec prohibentur hoc oraculo omnia simpliciter Bella in Nov. Test. Etenim non sumit sibi, sed à DEO traditum accipit gladium Magistratus, qui iusto bello DEI causam agit, hoc est; propositâ sibi DEI gloriâ ac subditorum salute adversùs hostem, pacem publicam turbantem, arma arripit, ac contra eundem in aciem progreditur. modò hoc fiat citra superbiam, avaritiam &c. neque fiducia in militum numero; sed divino auxilio collocetur. Conf. Not. ad Rom. 13, 4.) *

* (Gladio peribit. Gladii vox hîc generaliter accipitur; pro quibusvis suppliciis, à Magistratu; cui gladius à DEO accinctus est, irrogatis. ita etiam sumitur Rom. 13, 6. Patet vero exh. l. ad Magistratum pertinere; supplicia capitalia homicidis (aliisque sceleratis; uti adulteris; veneficis &c.) irrogare: Excipiunt Photiniani; Valent. Smalcius contra 7. Disp. D. Franzii de B. O. pag. 14. it. Disp. 6: de rebus civilibus pag. 290. Ostorodus in Inst. Germ. pag. 190. continere haec verba CHRISTI, praedictionem, qua indicet, quid ordinariè fiat, non verò doceat; quid fieri iure possit vel debeat. Resp. 1. Facilè equidem concedimus, fieri quandoque, ut si qui homicidae promeritam poenam, à Magistatu infligendam effugiant; vel in duello vel serpentum ictibus, aut ferarum invasione (vid. Plutach. lib. de serâ Numinis vindictâ, it. Act. 28, 4.) iterum pereant. Attamen 2. cùm non omnis homicidae sanguis per hominem actu effundatur, ceu experientia testatur; sequitur, si haec verba CHRISTI, & illa Gen. 9, 6. (ubi similis planè ut hîc sermo est, ipso Ostorodo monente l. c.) saltem praedictionem continerent, praedictionem divinam aliquando falsum continere. id quod dicere; absurdum & impium est. quod verò 3. tum hîc, tùm apud Mosen futurum legitur, notandum, quòd illud ponatur more Ebraeo pro Imperativo.

qualis Ebraismus in praeceptis quoque divinis haut rarò occurrit. vid. Exod. 20. vel dici quoque potest, quòd futurum perΤὸdebet cum proprio infinitivo exponendum sit, ceu huiusmodi locutionis exempla occurrunt Ps. 32, 8.Ezech. 34. 2.Malach. 1, 6.Luc. 3. 14. alibi. Coeterum 4 quomodo haec verba CHRISTI accipienda sint satis patet tum ex decreto divino Gen. 9, 6. unde ea desumta & quod CHRISTUS hîc confirmat, (nullum enim dubium est, quin eò Salvator respexerit.) tum ex Rom. 13, 4. 5. constat etiam ex circumstantiis textûs, quòd Petrus privatâ autoritate arripuerit gladium contra illos, qui à Magistratu erant missi. Licet verò aliàs licitum sit, vim vi repellere: tamen aliter sese res habet, quando subditi à Magistratu iniuriâ afficiuntur. Confer plura huc facientia, apud B. D. Kōnig Cas. catech. pag. 44, 45. B. Par. L. de Magistr. Polit. §. 298.) *

## 26:54
* (v. 54. Do you think &c. twelve legions of Angels. It is permitted to gather from this in some way how great the multitude of good Angels is. Since according to Vegetius lib. 2. de re militari c. 6. 12 Legions comprise 73200 infantry and 8760 cavalry, twelve legions therefore would be 81960. The sayings 2. Reg. 6, 17.Dan. 7, 11.Ebr. 12, 22. also pertain to this. Moreover, CHRIST making mention of twelve legions, looks to the Roman military, among whom 12 legions constituted a full army. Nor is it unusual even in Holy Scripture for Angels to be compared with a military army. see Gen. 32, 2. Furthermore, concerning the Roman army see Lips. in de militia Rom. especially concerning the legions lib. 2. dial. 6. Add Dn. Dilherri disp. Acad. t. 1. page 492. Concerning the power of Angels, however, one can judge from 2. Reg. 19, 35. Although GOD sends His Angels as guardians to the pious, and likewise CHRIST wished here to raise up the prostrate Disciples by making mention of them, it does not follow from this, therefore they are to be religiously invoked, since the honor of religious invocation is to be shown to GOD alone, Matth. 4, 10. Whence Corn. à Lapide in h. l. is inept. CHRIST teaches us here, in every danger, temptation, and affliction to invoke the holy angels, especially our guardians: for these are most wise, most powerful, and most loving toward us, because they know that this is pleasing to GOD, nay, commanded to them, according to thatPsalm 90andPsalm 33. But concerning this error, it has been treated more prolixly elsewhere. See Analecta on Apoc. c. 19, 10.

v. 54. How then shall the Scriptures be fulfilled. See altogether the notes at ch. 13, 14. To this point also pertains that of Leo, sermon 1 on the Passion. We owe you nothing of grace, O Jews, nothing to you, Judas. Your impiety indeed served our salvation, though you did not intend this, and through you was done whatever the hand of GOD and His counsel decreed should be done; therefore death frees us, but accuses you: deservedly you alone do not possess that which you wished to perish for all. ) * * (

(55. ἐκαθεζόμην etc. See the notes above on c. 23, 2. also on Luc. 4, 20.)

Latin:

* (v. 54. An putas &c. duodecim legiones Angelorum. Colligere hinc aliquo modo licet, quanta sit bonorum Angelorum multitudo. Cùm iuxta Vegetium lib. 2. de re militaric. 6. Legiones 12. comprehendant pedites 73200. equites 8760. duodecim igitur legiones effent 81960. Huc faciunt quoque dicta 2. Reg. 6, 17.Dan. 7, 11.Ebr. 12, 22. Mentionem autem faciens CHRISTUS duodecim legionum, respicit ad militiam Romanorum, apud quos 12. legiones iustum constituebant exercitum. nec insolens etiam in Sc. S., Angelos cum militari exercitu conferri. vid. Gen. 32, 2. De exercitu porrò Rom. vid. Lips. in de militia Rom. cumprimis de legion. lib. 2. dial. 6. Add. Dn. Dilherri disp. Acad. t. 1. pag. 492. De potentiâ verò Angelorum iudicari potest ex 2. Reg. 19, 35. Licet verò DEUS mittat Angelos suos piis custodes, pariterque CHRISTUS prostratos Discipulos mentione illorum factâ erigere hîc voluerit, non tamen hinc sequitur, ergò religiosè invocandi illi sunt, cùm honor religiosae invocationis soli DEO exhibendus sit, Matth. 4, 10. Unde ineptè Corn. à Lapide in h. l. Docer nos hîc CHRISTUS, in omni periculo, tentatione & afflictione invocare sanctos angelos, praesertim custodes nostros: hi enim sapientissimi sunt, potentissimi & nostri amantissimi, quia sciunt, hoc DEO gratum esse, imò sibi imperatum, iuxta illudPsalm. 90acPsalm. 33. At de errore hoc alibi actum prolixiùs. Vid. Analecta ad Apoc. c. 19, 10.) *

* (v. 54. Quomodo ergo Scripturae implebuntur. Vid. omninò notata ad cap. 13, 14. Huc facit quoque illud Leonis serm. 1. de Pass. Nihil vobis gratiae, ô Iudaei, nihil tibi, Iuda, debemus. Salvationi quidem nostrae, non hoc vobis volentibus, impictas vestra servivit, & per vos factum est, quicquid manus DEI & consilium decreverunt fieri; mors igitur nos liberat, vos accusat: meritò soli non habetis, quod omnibus perire voluistis.) *

* (55. ἐκαθεζόμην &c. Vid. notata suprà ad c. 23, 2. it. ad Luc. 4, 20.) *

## 26:56
v. 56. Then the Disciples fled &c. Q. Whether this flight was lawful? Cornelius à Lapide brings forward arguments on both sides in this place, who may be consulted. Furthermore, in what case a minister of the Church may and ought to flee, it was advised above at ch. 10, 23.) * * (

Latin:

* (v. 56. Tunc Discipuli sugerunt &c. Q. An fuga haec fuèrit licita? Rationes in utramque partem adducit Corn. à Lapide in h. l. qui potest evolvi. Porrò quo in casu Ecclesiae minister fugere possit ac debeat, suprà ad c. 10, 23. monitum fuit.) *

## 26:57
v. 57. to Caiphas. John ch. 18, 13. records that they led CHRIST first to Annas, perhaps because as they were going to Caiphas, the house of Annas occurred to them; or so that He might be detained there for a while, until the Sanhedrin gathered in the house of Caiphas. They preferred, however, to stay with Annas rather than another, because he was the father-in-law of Caiphas, Ioh. 18, 13. ) * * (

Latin:

* (v. 57. ad Caipham. Iohannes c. 18, 13. memorat, quòd priùs ad Annam CHRISTUM duxerint, fortè quia euntibus ad Caipham, Annae aedes illis occurrerunt; vel ut tantisper ibi detaneretur, dum Synedrium in domo Caiphae conveniret. Maluerunt autem apud Annam potiùs, quàm alium commorari, quia ipse socer erat Caiphae, Ioh. 18, 13.) *

## 26:58
v. 58. and Peter having entered within. Cornelius à Lapide rightly advises in this place that Peter sinned by imprudence and rashness, in that he inserted himself among the ministers and exposed himself to danger. conf. Eccles. 3, 27. ) * * (

Latin:

* (v. 58. & ingressus Petrus intro. Rectè monet Corn. à Lapide h. l. peccasse Petrum imprudentiâ & temeritate, quòd se ministris inserverit, & exposuerit periculo. conf. Eccles. 3, 27.) *

## 26:60
v. 60. two false witnesses. Mention is also made of these by the Jews themselves in the Jerusalem Talmud, and indeed where the Son of Stada is treated, through whom they themselves understand Christ, as J. Buxtorf advises in Lex. Rabb. Talm. page 1461.) * 1171

Latin:

* (v. 60. duo falsi restes. Mentio quoque horum fit ab ipsis Iudaeis in Talmud Hieros. & quidem ubi de Filio Stadae agitur, per quem ipsos Christum intelligere, I. Buxtorffius in Lex. Rabb. Talm. pag. 1461. monet.) *

## 26:61
* (v. 61. I can destroy. Chrysostom well observes in this place that CHRIST did not say I can loose, but loose, and that He did not speak of that Temple, but of His own body. Nor had CHRIST said δύναμαι οἰκοδομῆσαι, but ἐγερῶ, as is evident from Ioh. 2, 19., indeed alluding to the resuscitation of His own body. They, however, feigned as if CHRIST had spoken of the Jerusalem temple, as is evident from Marc. 14, 58., when nevertheless He had spoken of the temple of His body, Coloss. 2, 9.; furthermore, among the Jews it was considered a capital crime to utter savage prophecies against the Temple. See Actor. 6, 13.) *

* ( διὰ τριῶν ἡμέρων. in Ioh. c. 2, 19. is ἡμέραις. said for διαγενομένων τριῶν. Conf. Deut. 15, 1. Walthon. de Idiot. §. 28. Simon Episcopius lib. 3. Instit. p. 192. see also above cap. 20, 19. Marc. 9, 31.cap. 10. 34.Luc, 9, 22.c. 13, 32.c. 24, 7.46. & add. Analecta above to cap. 12, 40.) *

Latin:

* (v. 61. Possum destruere. Benè observat Chrysost. in h. l. CHRISTUM non dixisse solvo: vel possum solvere, sed solvite, nec de illo Templo, sed corpore suo dixisse. Nec dixerat CHRISTUS, δύναμαι οἰκοδομῆσαι, sed ἐγερῶ, ceu patet ex Ioh. 2, 19. alludens quippe ad resuscitationem sui corporis. Illi verò singebant, quasi CHRISTUS loquutus fuisset de templo Hierosolymitano, ceu patet ex Marc. 14, 58. cùm tamen dixisset de templo sui corporis,Coloss. 2, 9. coeterùm apud Iudaeos capitale censebatur, saeva vaticinia contra Templum proferre. Vid. Actor. 6, 13.) *

In stit. p. 192. vid. etiam suprà cap. 20, 19. Marc. 9, 31.cap. 10. 34.Luc, 9, 22.c. 13, 32.c. 24, 7.46. & add. Analecta supra ad cap. 12, 40.) *

## 26:63
* (v. 63. But JESUS was silent. He was silent, says Chrysostom in this place, because He saw no place for an excuse: for it was the appearance of a trial there, but in reality the assault of robbers. Jerome similarly: He was silent, because He knew that whatever He might have answered, it would be twisted into a calumny. In which case even the wise Gentiles themselves advised silence. Plinius lib. 7. ep. 6. It is sometimes no less oratorical to be silent than to speak. Euripides: σιωπὴ σοΦοῖς -πὸκρισις. Conf. also Grotius in this place. Otherwise it is by no means denied that everyone ought to render an account of their faith before a magistrate. Concerning which matter it will be treated more lengthily in Analect. to 1. Tim. 6, 13. see also above note to cap. 10, 32. Mystically the Author of the commentary on Mark, ascribed to Jerome, The silence of CHRIST absolves the apology of Adam.) *

* (I adjure you. see Num. 5, 19.Levit. 5, 1.Ios. 7, 19.26.1. Sam. 14, 27. 28.1. Reg. 2, 43.cap. 22, 16. 2. Par. 18, 15. Ioh. 9, 24.) *

* (Son of GOD. Socinus ineptly gathers from the fact that in the parallel place Luc. 22, 67. only the name CHRIST is used, Christ) The Son of GOD is said, at least on account of the temporal anointing and royal office, since Christ and the Son of GOD signify the same thing, and the one is interchanged with the other. But how vain the collection of Socinus is, the blessed D. Meisner teaches beautifully in Consid. Theol. Phot. p. 481. seqq. In this place we deem it at least to be noted, 1. that Luke also does not omit the name Son of GOD, as is to be seen from v. 70. 2. that when Christ said that he was the Son of God, the Jews concluded from this that he blasphemed, which they certainly would not have done, unless they had understood him by the phrase Son of God, who is begotten from the substance of God. Furthermore, Grotius notes that among the Jews also, that expected Messiah was accustomed to be called Son of God. Namely from the second Psalm, which the ancient Hebrews κατὰ τὸ μυςικώτερον interpreted concerning the Messiah. Indeed, from this very thing it is sufficiently clear that the ancient Jews expected such a Messiah, who would be σθὰνσθρωπος. concerning which matter the blessed D. Hutter treats more prolixly LL. Mai. p. 861. D. Hoornbeck lib. 5. against the Jews c. 1.) *

Latin:

## 26:64
v. 64. You have said it. Christ answers here to the question, whether he is the Son of GOD, clearly and openly enough, so that he might take away namely every excuse of the Jews, as Chrysostom advises in this place, and so that in the day of judgment no excuse might remain for them as to why they had not believed in Christ. Compare also Rom. 1, 20. C. 2, 1. likewise above at v. 25.) * * (

* (à mollô. The custom of Holy Scripture is to be noted in this place, inasmuch as it does not always speak according to our reckoning, but more often according to the divine reckoning, in which a thousand days are as one day. see the notes to chapter 24, 29. Grotius, however, thinks that regard is had to the mission of the Holy Spirit, Act. 2, 33. Others to the resurrection, others otherwise. Daniel Heinsius thinks that the accent has imposed upon the learned, and from the distinction of the place as well, for it must be read πλὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ἀπαρ-, ὄ-εσθε &c. and that λέγω -παρ- is the same as in these books ἀμὴν λέγω, so that it is certainly and truly, plainly and expressly I say to you. But this conjecture is opposed by the fact that the Greek codices, both the Parisian ones according to Fr. Lucas, and those which the Londoners compared in the Appar. Bibliol. Polygl., which the ancient Greek manuscript Eclogae of the Nuremberg Library also support, constantly approve the received reading. The Syrian and Persian interpreters also support clearly Τὸ ἀπἄρπ referring to the following member. It is therefore better to retain the first exposition here, especially since this conjecture of Heinsius excellently favors the corruption of the Papists of the passage Apoc. 14, 13. concerning which see B. Par. L. de Morte §. 192. B. D. Bald. against Patzm. p. 1237. B. D. Meisn. Opusc. second on Purgatory.) *

* (You shall see. in effect indeed, because then they will experience the virtue and omnipotence of Christ in the glorification of the pious, but in the condemnation of the impious.) *

At the right hand of power. i. e. powerful or glorious and omnipotent. Some think the abstract noun τῆς δυνάμεως is an epithet of GOD, which is called האל i. e. power, and by more recent Jews הגכורה ἡ δύναμις, * (see Kimchi in chapter 7 of Joshua.) * so that the sense may be, at the right hand of that power i. e. of that supremely powerful or most powerful one; but that Luke, in order to illustrate a Hebraism unaccustomed to Greek ears, added τοῦ σθεοῦ c. 22, 69. namely ἐκ δεξιῶτῆς δυνάμως τοῦ σθεοῶ i. e. at the right hand of that most powerful one, namely, of God himself. * (Interpreters think, however, that the plural number δεξιῶν was used to denote the excellence of the thing, and they compare the passage Apoc. 1, 4. It is to be noted here that Cornelius à Lapide in this place admits that Christ sits at the right hand of GOD, not only as God, but also as man, and since to sit at the right hand of GOD the Father, is the same as to be of equal dignity, majesty, and glory with him, as the same author holds, it is evident that to Christ as man or according to his human nature, a truly divine and infinite power has been given. Which, however, the Jesuits otherwise deny along with the Calvinists, against whom B. Par. argues in Confess. Cath. art. 2. c. 1. sect. post. §. 1. Compare also the Analect. above on c. 22, 44.) *

* (coming in the clouds. see Dan. 7, 13.Marc. 13, 26.Luc. 21, 27.Act. 1, 11.1. Thess. 4, 17.) *

Quod tamen aliàs Iesuitae cum Calvinianis negant. quos contra disputat B. Par. Confess. Cath. art. 2. c. 1. sect. post. §. 1. Conf. etiam Analect. suprà ad c. 22, 44.) *

## 26:65
* (v. 65. He tore his garments. This was the custom among the Jews both in mourning, see Gen 37, 29.34.c. 44, 13.Num. 14, 6.Ios. 7, 6.Iudic. 11, 35.1. Reg. 4, 12.2. Reg. 1, 11.c. 13, 19.Iudith. c. 14, 15. and when blasphemy was heard, see 2. Reg. 19, 1. Isaiah 37, 1. and out of indignation, see Act. 14, 14. To this also refers the Supreme Deity in Joel c. 2, 13. compare W. Schickard in de Iure Regio Heb. ch. 4. theor. 19. Buxt. Lexic. Talm. under the word קרע, see Faber, book 2, Semestt. ch. 10, p. 108, following. The same custom of rending garments, in heavy mourning or out of indignation, also prevailed among other peoples. Concerning the Lacedaemonians, it is established from Herodotus, book 6; concerning the Sabines, from Livy, Decad. 1, book 1. Add Virgil, book 12, Aeneid. Compare also Kirchman, on Roman Funerals, p. 241; Mr. Dilherr, Vol. 1, Academic Disputations, p. 131, 132, 497.) *

* (The high priest rent his garments. Jerome on this passage brings forward a mystical exposition of this matter: He rends, he writes, his garments, so that he may show that the Jews have lost the glory of the Priesthood, and that the high priests have an empty seat. Eugerius of Lyon has nearly similar things on the Sunday of Palm Branches; likewise Leo, sermon 6 on the Passion, and Origen. But it is asked, whether the high priest acted here against the divine law, Lev. 10, 6. and ch. 21, 10. 11. Resp. Corn. à Lapide on this passage judges, that Caiaphas rent his garment illicitly here, since he did this against the prohibition Lev. 21, 10. The same was also asserted even before Cornelius by Cardinal Baronius, who writes that Caiaphas did this first among all the high priests, as if driven by fury, so that he might more more incite the minds of the other bystanders to the destruction of Christ. But it must be known that this prohibition regards at least the case on account of the dead or in private mourning, as is clear from the context: otherwise, that the High Priest also rent his garments on account of a public disaster or in public mourning is gathered from 1 Macc. 11, 71. Selden, from the Talmud, distinguishes between priestly garments, that is, those of which there was use in sacred ministries, and common clothing. He denies that it was permitted to tear the former, since it was not lawful for anyone to enter the atrium of the temple with torn garments; but he concedes it regarding common clothing. He warns, moreover, that the high priest tore the garment from the bottom part toward the top, laymen on the contrary. We learn furthermore from this act of the high priest that even in the best and most honest things the wicked can be scandalized. Which scandal is taken, not given, concerning which distinction of scandal, and other things pertaining to that matter, it was treated in the Analysis above at ch. 5, 30; acc. 18, 7.) *

* ( ἐβλασφήμησεν. But Christ had hitherto demonstrated by very many, and those truly divine miracles, that he was the promised Messiah and true God. From which orthodoxy nothing is detracted by the fact that he was born a man, Ioh 1. 46.c. 7, 27.52. and that he brought with him no external splendor, Marc. 6, 3. For it was fitting that the Messiah should be σθεάνθρωπον, and that he should for a time assume the form of a servant. Phil. 2, 7.) *

Virgil. l. 12. Aeneid. Conf. quoq; Kirchman. de Fun. Rom. p. 241. Dn. Dilherr. T. 1. Dispp. Acad. p. 131. 132. 497.) *

* (Pontifex disrupit vestimenta sua. Hieronymus in h. l. mysticam affert rei huius expositionem: Scindit, scribit, vestimenta sua, ut ostendat, Iudaeos Sacerdotii gloriam perdidisse, & vacuam sedem habere Pontifices. Ferè similia habet Eugerius Lugdunensis Domin. in Ramis palmarum. item Leo serm. 6. de Pass atque Origenes. Sed quaeritur, annon egerit hîc Pontifex contra legem divinam,Levit. 10, 6. ac c. 21, 10. 11. Resp. Corn. à Lapide in h l. censet, illicitè hîc Caipham vestem scidisse, cùm fecerit hoc contra prohibitionemLev. 21, 10. Idem etiam iam ante Corneliū adservit Card Baronius, qui primum inter omnes Pontifices fecisse hoc Caipham scribit, quasi furore percitum, ut coeterorum adstantium animos in Christi perditionem magis magisconcitaret. Ast sciendum, quòd prohibitio haec respiciat saltem casum propter mortuos sive in luctu privato, ceu ex contextu liquet: alioqui propter publicam cladem seu in publico luctu Pontificem quoque Maximum discidisse vestimenta sua, è. 1. Macc. 11, 71. colligitur. Seldenus ex Talmud distinguit inter vestes Sacerdotales h. e. quarum in ministeriis sacris usus erat, & amictum vulgarem. Illas lacerare concessum fuisse negat, quippe cùm nulli fas fuerit dilaceratis vestibus atrium templi ingredi; de amictu verò vulgari concedit. Monet praetereà, quòd Pontifex ab im â parte dilacerarit vestem versùs summam, laici contrà. Discimus porrò ex hoc Pontificis facto, quòd etiam in rebus optimis honestisque mali possint scandalizari. quod scandalum acceptum est, non datum, de qua scandali distinctione, aliisque ad materiam illam spectantibus actum in Anal. suprà ad c. 5, 30. acc. 18, 7.) *

## 26:67
v. 67. They spat in his face. see Num. 12, 14 Gaspar Sanctius, in his commentary on Isaiah, p. 647, thinks this was done because it was the custom among the Jews that anyone might heap mockery and injuries upon a man who was held and declared to be condemned, as Christ was here, though innocent. Furthermore, the prophecy of Isaiah 50, 6 was fulfilled here. But how great this injury was, can scarcely be expressed in words. Whence Euthymius: Shudder, he exclaims, O heaven and earth, O all creation! At what a face, what an injury they have inflicted! Similarly Titus of Bostra on Luc. 22. Upon that face which the waves of the sea revered, which the sun, seeing it on the cross, hid its rays &c. He is struck with fists, he who measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and weighed the heavens with a span. Es. 40. He is dishonored with slaps, the brightness of the Father's glory and the express image of his substance, Ebr. 1, 3. ) (

## 26:74
* (v. 74. And he began to curse and to swear, i. e., to devote himself. The Evangelist alludes to that custom by which the Jews were accustomed to strike the guilty with an anathema. On which custom see Mr. Dilherrus, Academic Disputations, vol. 2, p. 320, and Buxtorff, Rabbinical and Talmudic Lexicon, p. 828. Regarding anathemas, one may also consult Conrad Rittershus, Sacred Readings, book 6, ch. 12. Furthermore, it is evident from that perjury of Peter that he himself lost faith and cast off the Holy Spirit, although not finally (for so Christ's promise Luke 22:32. is to be understood), yet totally. That faith and the grace of God are totally lost through such a denial is evident, because Christ wishes to deny such deniers, i. e., to judge them unworthy of His grace, Matthew 10:33. Observe this against the Calvinists, who deny that the elect can totally cast off faith. See Richard Thomson the Englishman, Diatribe on the Intercision of Grace, ch. 18. Cornelius à Lapide in this place maintains that Peter, by denying Christ, sinned mortally, and indeed lost the grace and charity of GOD; nevertheless, that it is doubtful whether he lost faith. How these things can be consistent, if he speaks of salvific faith, it hardly appears. Compare also the notes at v. 31.) *

Latin:

* (v. 74. Et coepit detestari & iurare, i. e. seipsum devovere. Alludit Evangelista ad consuetudinem illam, quâ Iudaei solebant reos anathemate percutere. de quô more videantur Dn. Dilherrus Dispp Acad. t. 2. p. 320. & Buxtorff. Lex. Rabb. Talmud. p. 828. De Anathematismis consuli quoque potest Cont. Rittershus. Lectionum Sacr. l. 6. c. 12. Constat porrò ex illo periurio Petri, quòd ipse fidem amiserit, & Sp. S. excusserit. licet non finaliter (ita enim intelligenda Christi promissio Luc. 22, 23.) tamen totaliter. Quòd verò per talē abnegationem fides & gratia Dei totaliter amittantur, patet, quia tales abnegatores Christus vult abnegare, h. e. gratiâ suâ indignos censere, Matth. 10, 33. Obs. hoc contra Calvinianos, negantes, electos totaliter posse excutere fidem. vid. Richardus Thomson Anglus, Diatr. de intercis. gratiae c. 18. Cornelius à Lapide in h. l. statuit, Petrum abnegando Christum, peccasse mortaliter, quin & DEI gratiam & charitatem perdidisse; nihil ominus tamen dubium esse, an fidem perdiderit. quae, quomodo consistere possint, si de fide loquitur salvificâ, vix sanè apparet. conf. etiam notata ad v. 31.) *

## 26:75
* (v. 75. And Peter remembered, etc. after, of course, Christ looked upon him, as Luke expressly indicates in chapter 22, 61. Whence Jerome beautifully says: It could not be that he should remain in the darkness of denial, whom the light of truth had drawn back. Concerning the same look, St. Augustine in his book on the grace of Christ against Pelagius and Coelestius, ch. 45, argues thus: The Lord looked upon him; it was done within, it was done in the mind, in the will, the Lord secretly helped by mercy, touched the heart, recalled the memory, visited Peter with interior grace, moved the interior man even to exterior tears, and brought forth the affection. One must not omit that well-known saying of Leo, sermon 3 on the Passion of the Lord, ch. 5, and sermon 9, ch. 4: He looked with the eyes of the mind, not of the body; mercifully, not corporally; because Peter was outside and below, but Christ was within and above. Perhaps, however, the Lord was there at that time, where He could see Peter even with the eyes of the body: He looked, by giving the knowledge and displeasure of sin. For the grace of GOD is necessary, not only that he who repents may obtain the remission of sins, but also that he who is evil may be converted to repentance. Furthermore, in that Leo thinks that that look of Christ was not corporal, but spiritual, he seems in that to have followed Augustine, as one who likewise in the place cited above establishes, that it cannot be said that the Lord looked upon Peter with corporal eyes. Others, however, more correctly establish that our Lord looked upon Peter altogether also externally with the eyes of the body. And that is evident 1. from the fact that spiritually Christ was never turned away from Peter. 2. because the word ςροφεὶς clearly implies it, namely that Christ, with His face turned away from those sitting in the council, and the same turned toward Peter, looked upon him. 3. because in other places, see above ch. 16, 28. Luke 7, 9. John 20, 14. the same word ςρέφειν is similarly used. Nor does it stand in the way that in v. 69 Peter is said to have been ἔζω τῆἀυλῆς, while Christ was in the atrium itself. For it can be said, either that Christ after Peter's third denial was led from the upper hall into the lower atrium; or that He looked from the upper hall even to the lower atrium with His face turned back, since it cannot be proven that a wall was interposed. Compare B. Par. H. E. ch. 188. Sebastianus Barradius thinks that CHRIST drew Peter to Himself into the higher place, in which He Himself was, and thus looked upon him with corporal eyes. Nor does he reject the former reconciliation either. Let us truly learn from the present fact 1. the weakness of human nature. 2. the necessity of help and divine grace in our conversion. 3. the sweetness and utility of the look of Christ. Even today Christ looks upon us, although not with corporal eyes, yet with spiritual ones, when in His word, comprised in the sacred letters, He places before our eyes the gravity of our sins, the severity of divine wrath, the eternity of infernal punishment, and the opportunity of time for doing penance. Let us therefore strive diligently, lest we let the time of grace pass by, etc.) *

before the cock crows, etc. Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, ep. 357, explains this mystically. Victor of Antioch on chapter 14 of Mark: Admonished by the cock’s crow, as if awakened from a heavy sleep, having returned to himself, etc.) * * (

you will deny me three times. See Isidore of Pelusium, b. 1, ep. 356, 358, and 359. Those who extenuate Peter’s fall do not sufficiently weigh Christ’s prediction, nor the tears of Peter, who wept so bitterly on account of that fall. Christ’s threatening also pertains to this, Matth. 10, 43. of which Peter had been little mindful, nor indeed of his own protestation, above v. 33. But what wonder, if God predicted true things, but man presumed false things, writes Augustine on chapter 18 of John.) * * (

* (He went out and wept bitterly. Beautifully St. Jerome: He goes out from the council of the wicked, so that he may wash away the filth of his fearful denial with bitter weeping. A most ample field for speaking here would be opened up regarding the utility of a penitent's tears, if we were doing that now. For what Sedulius sang beautifully concerning the tears of Peter:

—and with the following groan, the fault flees, sins yield to the shed tears, and bitter weeping has generated sweet forgiveness.

The same can be most rightly affirmed concerning the tears of all who are truly and seriously penitent. In such people, he who shall sow in tears, shall reap in joy, Psalm. 126, 5. 6. Whence most beautifully Chrysostom, hom. 6 on Matthew: Just as after vehement rains the air becomes clean and pure, so also the serenity of the mind follows the rains of tears and tranquility, and all that darkness poured out from the shadows of sins is dissolved. And just as we are purified from water and spirit, so again we are purified from tears and confession: provided that we do not do it for ostentation and praise. I seek those tears which do not proceed for ostentation, but for compunction; which are poured out secretly, and which flow from that pain which is hidden within the treasury of the conscience and the secrets of the breast; which roll down the afflicted cheeks with no human witness; which fall in the highest silence and quiet; which bubble up from the innermost part of the heart; which are offered to the eyes of God alone. Thus far Chrysostom. Skillfully also St. Jerome in his epistle: O humble tear, you do not fear the tribunal, you impose silence on the accusations of your friends: there is no one who forbids you to approach, if you have entered alone; you will not return empty. You torment the devil more than infernal punishment. What more? You conquer the invincible: you bind the omnipotent: you incline the son of the Virgin. The same on Isaiah: Prayer softens God, but tears compel; the former anoints, the latter stings. Women in the Old Testament for their purification did not offer goldfinches, nor nightingales, or other birds of this kind, which delight the ears of men with their song, but moaning turtledoves or pigeons. Thus, a sinner can offer no sacrifice to God more pleasing, none more acceptable, than if he, moaning, acknowledges his sins, deplores them, and with true faith apprehends Christ; by this sacrifice at last he will be purified and freed from spiritual impurity. By this laver the filth of sins will be washed away and wiped off. Ambrose, book 9 on Luke: I do not find what he said (Peter,) but that he wept. Lest, however, anyone should think that while the Doctors of the primitive Church commend tears, they at the same time construct the merit of good works, or establish satisfaction, it must be well noted that the same Ambrose, in the said book, writes of the tears of Peter: I read: but what cannot be defended, can be washed away.

Briefly but elegantly Nilus, decad. 20, paraen. 4: The tears of prayer are the bath of the soul. They are the same and the wine of the Angels, as Bernard somewhere designated them, and a great relief in the burden of sins. For Ambrose most truly said concerning the death of Valentinian, that grief often evaporates with tears. Why therefore are we so sluggish? Why do we not follow Peter, if we have fallen with Peter? Why not also David? The sinful woman, Luc. 7. why not other illustrious examples?

I. The despair of Judas v. 1-10. II. The condemnation of Christ v. 11-26. III. The mockery of the same and his leading away to the punishment of the cross v. 27-32. IV. The crucifixion v. 33-50. V. The following of the miracles v. 51-54. VI. The procurement of the burial of Christ v. 57-61 and the sealing of the sepulchral stone v. 62 to the end.

* (v. 75. Et recordatus est Petrus &c. postquam nimirum christus ipsum respexit, ceu expressè Lucas indicat cap. 22. 61. Unde pulerè Hieronymus: Fieri non poterat, ut in negationis tenebris permaneret, quem lux retraxerat veritatis De eodem adspectu S. Augustinus lib. de gratia Christ. contra Pelagium & Coelest. c. 45. ita dislerit Respexit eum Dominus; intus actum est, in mente, in voluntate actum est, misericordia Dominus latenter subvenit, cor tetigit, memoriam revocavit, interiore-ua gratia visitavit Petrum, interioris hominis usq; ad exteriores lacrymas movit, & produxit affectū. Non omittendum scitum illud Leonis serm. 3. de Pass. Domini c. 5. & serm. 9. c. 4. Respexit oculis mentis, non corporis; misericorditer, non corporaliter; quia Petrus foris erat & inferius, Christus verò intus & superius. Forte tamen ibi tunc erat Dominus, ubi Petrum oculis etiam corporis videre posset: respexit, dando peccati cognitionem & displicentiam. Gratia enim DEI est necessaria, non solùm, ut qui poenitet, remissionem peccatorum consequatur, sedetiam, ut qui malus est, ad poenitentiam convertatur. Coeterùm quod Leo existimat, illum Christi respectum non fuisse corporalem, sed spiritualem, in eo sequutus Augustinum videtur, ut qui pariter loco suprà allegato statuit, non posse dici, quòd corpor alibus oculis Petrum Dominus respexerit. Alii tamen rectiùs statuunt, quòd omninò etiam externès. oculis corporis Dominus noster Petrum adspexerit. idque constat 1. inde, quia spiritualiter Christus nunquam fuit à Petro aversus. 2. quia verbum ςροφεὶς clarè id innuit, nempe quòd Christus aversâ à concilii adsessoribus facie, eademque ad Petrum conversâ ipsum respexerit. 3. quia in aliis locis, vid. suprà c. 16, 28. Luc. 7, 9.Ioh. 20, 14. idem verbum ςρέφειν similiter adhibetur. Nec obstat, quòd v. 69. Petrus dicitur fuisse ἔζω τῆἀυλῆς, Christus verò in ipso atrio. potest enim dici, vel quod Christus post tertiam Petri abnegationem fuerit ex aula superiori in inferius atrium ductus; vel quod ex aulâ etiam superiori ad inferius atrium facie retroversa respexerit, quippe cùm non possit probari, interiectum fuisse parietem. Conf. B. Par. H. E. c. 188. Sebastianus Barradius existimat. CHRISTUM ad se in locum superiorem, in quo ipse erat, Petrum traxisse, & sic corporalibus oculis respexisse. neque tamen reiicit etiam conciliationem priorem. Discamus vero è praesenti facto 1. humanae naturae imbecillitatem. 2. auxilii ac gratiae divinae in nostri conversione necessitatem. 3. adspectus Christi suavitatem atque utilitatem. Adhuc hodie Christus nos respicit, licet non oculis corporalibus, tamen spiritualibus, quando in verbo suo, sacris litteris comprehenso, ob oculos ponit peccato. rum nostrorum gravitatem, irae divinae severitatem, supplicii infernalis aeternitatem, ac temporis poenitentiam agendi opportunitatem, Demus proinde operam sedulo, ne tempus gratiae praetermittamus &c.) *

* (priusquam Gallus cantet &c. Mysticè hoc exponit Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 1. ep. 357. Victor Antiochenus in c. 14. Marci: Galli cantu admonitus, quasi à gravi somno excitatus, ad se reversus &c.) *

* (ter me negabis. Vid. Isidorus Pelus. l. 1. ep. 356. 358. & 359. Qui Petri lapsum extenuant, non satis perpendunt Christi praedictionem, nec Petri, ob lapsum istum tam amarè flentis, lacrymas.
