* (egressus foràs flevit amarè. Pulcrè S. Hieronymus: Egreditur foràs de impiorum concilio, ut pavidae negationis sordes amaris fletibus lavet. De Lacrymarum poenitentis utilitate amplissimus hîc dicendi ape-iretur campus, si hoc nunc ageremus. Quod enim de Petri lacrymis pulerè cecinit Sedulius:

—gemituque sequenteCulpa fugit, cedunt lacrymis delicta profusis,& dulcem veniam fletus generastis amari.

Idem de omnium verè ac seriò poenitentium lacrymis rectissimè affirmari potest. In talibus qui seminaverit lacrymis, in exultatione metet,Psalm. 126, 5. 6. Unde pulcerrimè Chrysostomus hom. 6. in Matth. Sicut post vehementes imbres mundus aër ac purus efficitur, ita etiam lacrymarum pluvias serenitas mentis sequitur atque tranquillitas, omnisq; illa de peccatorum tenebris offusa caligo dissolvitur. Et sicut ex aquà & spiritu, sic rursus ex lacrimis & confessione purgamur: modò ne ad ostentationem & laudem faciamus. Illas ego requiro lacrymas, qui non ostentationi proficiunt, sed compunctioni; quae funduntur occultè, quaeq; ex illo dolore pro--uunt, qui intra conscientiae thesaurū & pectoris arcana celatur quae per afflictas genas nullo hominum teste volvuntur: quae summo in silentio & quiete desiliunt: quae ex intitimo cordis ebulliunt. quae solius Dei oculis offeruntur. Hactenus Chrysostomus. Scitè quoq; S. Hieronymus in ep. O lacryma humilis, tribunal non vereris, amicorum tuorum ac cusationibus silentium imponis: non est, qui te accedere vetet, si sola intraveris; vacua non redibis. magis crucias diabolum, quàm poena infernalis. Quid plura? Vincis invincibilem: ligas omnipotentem: inclinas filium Virginis. Idem super Esaiam: Oratio Deum lenit, sed lacrymae cogit; haec ungit, illa pungit. Foeminae in V. T. pro purgatione sua non cardueles, non philomelas, aut alias huiusmodi volucres, quae cantu suo hominum aures oblectant, sed gemebundos turtures aut columbas offerebant. Sic peccator nullum offerre Deo sacrificium gratius potest, nullum acceptius, quàm si gemebundus peccata sua agnoscat, deploret, verâq; fide christum apprehendat hoc sacrificio demum à spirituali impuritate purgabitur ac liberabitur. Hoc lavacro peccatorum sordes abluentur & abster gentur. Ambrosiusl. 9. super Lucam: Non invenio, quid dixerit (Petus,) sed quòd flevit. Ne tamen quis existimet quasi dum primitivae Ecclesiae Doctores lacrymas commendant, simul bonorum operum meritum adstruant, vel satisfactionem stabiliant, probè notandum quòd idem Ambrosius d. l. Lacrymas Petri, scribat, lego: sed quod defendi non potest, ablui potest.

Breviter sed eleganter Nilus decad. 20. paraen 4. Precum lacrymae sunt balneum animae. Sunt eaedem & vinum Angelorum, prout Bernhardus alicubieas insignivit, magnumq; levamen in onere peccatorum. verissimè enim dixit Ambrosius de obitu Valentiniani, quòd plerumq; gravis lacrymis evaporet dolor. Cur igitur adeo segnes sumus? cur non sequimut Petrum, si cum Petro fuimus lapsi? cur non etiam Davidem? mulierem peccatricem, Luc. 7. cur non alia exempla illustria?) *

## 27:1
* (v. 1. But when morning was come. Leo serm. 3. on the Passion This morning for you (O Jews) it destroyed the temple and altars, it took away the law and the Prophets, it removed the kingdom and the Priesthood, it turned all feasts into eternal mourning.) *

* (All the chief priests &c. There is no doubt that the discourse is at least about the majority, or that some contradicted the decree, yet they were oppressed by the clamor of the others, for it is not permitted to doubt that some dissented. See Luke 23, 51. Meanwhile it is certain that when they conclude by a majority of votes, this whole Council erred, not only in fact, but also in faith, because indeed it passed the sentence that Jesus was not the Christ, nor the Son of GOD: but that he falsely arrogated both titles to himself, and therefore was guilty of death. All of which things are erroneous and heretical, as Corn. à Lapide rightly warns. But lest the opinion of the Papists, by which they establish that Oecumenical councils cannot err in faith, should receive any detriment from this, Cornelius himself excepts, that this Council was particular and small, to wit, consisting only of Jews, nay, only of the inhabitants of Jerusalem: but it is otherwise concerning the Oecumenical Councils of Christians, to which are summoned the Bishops of all provinces, who represent the whole Church, and therefore from the promise of Christ have the Holy Spirit assisting them, so that they may not err in faith. But we answer. 1. Other Papists, as Melchior Canus l. 5. LL. c. last, resp. to arg 2. Harding in resp. to the Anglican Apology p. 6. c. 6. s. 3. concede that this Council was legitimate, but they deny that it erred. But if, as Canus and Harding defend, this Council was legitimate and universal, indeed In which, after a long and varied deliberation, Caiaphas, who as High Priest presided over the Council, spoke that sentence to which almost all agreed, etc., as the words of Canus have it, and yet, as Corn. à Lapide admits in this place (following Bellarmine in this opinion, who writes explicitly in l. 2 de Concil. c. 8. resp. ad 2, that Caiaphas erred most perniciously in faith with the universal Council,) he erred in faith, it follows that even legitimate Councils, and those in which the Pope presides and speaks the sentence, can err in faith. 2. We deny that this Council was particular, and for this reason, because the Jewish Church at that time had no Council besides that which passed that decisive and bloody sentence against Christ. Even if it were granted that that Council was particular, nevertheless this example greatly hinders the doctrine of the Papists, who assert indeed that a Council (N. B. indefinitely, whether it be that particular one or a universal one) gathered by the authority and consent of the Pope cannot err in faith. See Bell. lib. 1. adv. haer. c. 4. 3. It is false that for those Councils which the Papists thrust upon us as Ecumenical, such as the Florentine, the Tridentine, etc., bishops of all provinces were summoned or had been summoned; the contrary is indeed entirely manifest. The remaining exceptions of the Papists were discussed by the blessed Pareus, lib. 1. Confess. Cath. part. 2. c. 10. p. 493. seqq.

CHAPTER XXVII. SUMMARY AND DISPOSITION. 1.

Latin:

* (v. 1. Mane autem. Leo serm. 3. de Pass. Hoc mane vobis (ô Iudaei) templum & altaria diruit, legem & Prophetas ademit, regnum & Sacerdotium sustulit, in luctum aeternum omnia festa convertit.) *

* (Omnes Principes Sacerdotum &c. Non dubium, quin vel saltem de plerisque sermo, vel aliqui contradixerint decreto, coeterorum tamen clamore fuerint oppressi, neque enim dubitare licet, quin aliqui dissenserint. Vid. Luc. 23, 51. Interea certum, quòd cùm plura vota concludant, totum Concilium hoc errarit, non tantùm in facto, sed etiam in fide, quia nempe sententiam tulit, Iesum non esse Christum, nec DEI Filium: sed utrumque titulum falsò sibi arrogare, ideoq; reum esse mortis. Quae omnia sunt erronea & haeretica, ceu rectè monet Corn. à Lapide. Ne verò aliquid Pontificiorum sententia, quâ statuunt, Concilia oecumenica non posse errare in fide. detrimenti hinc capiat, excipit ipse, Cornelius, fuisse hoc Concilium particulare & exiguum, scil, ex solis Iudaeis, imò ex solis Hierosolymae incolis constans: secus verò esse de Conciliis Oecumenicis Christianorum, ad quae convocentur Episcopi omnium provincia. rum, qui totam Ecclesiam repraesentent, ideoex promissione Christi adsistentem habeant Sp. Sanctum, ut in fide non errent. Verùm respondemus. 1. Alii Pontificii, uti Melchior Canus l. 5. LL. c. ult. resp. ad arg 2. Hardingus in resp. ad Apolog. Anglicanam p. 6. c. 6. s. 3. concedunt, Concilium hoc fuisse legitimum, sed negant, illud errasse. Si verò, quod Canus ac Hardignus defendunt, legitimum ac universale Concilium hoc fuit, quippe in quo post longam variamdeliberationem Caiphas, qui ut summus Pontifex Concilio praesidebat, sententiam illam, cui omnes ferè consenserunt, dixit &c. ut habent verba Cani, & tamen, quod Corn. à Lapide hoc loco fatetur, (sequutus hâc in sententia Bellarminum, disertè l. 2. de Concil. c. 8. resp. ad 2. scribentem, errasse Caipham cum universo Concilio in fide perniciosissime) in fide erravit, sequitur quòd etiam legitima Concili a & in quibus Pontifex praesidet sententiamque dicit, in fide errare possint. 2. Negamus, Concilium hoc fuisse particulare, idque ideo, quia Iudaica Ecclesia tum temporis non habuit Concilium praeter illud, quod decretoriam & sangvineam illam contra Christum tulit sententiam. Posito etiam, Concilium illud fuisse particulare, nihilominus multum officit exemplum hoc doctrinae Pontificiorum, adserentium quippe, Concilium (N. B. indefinitè, seu particulare illud sit, seu universale) Papae autoritate & consensu congregatum non posse in fide errare. vid. Bell. lib. 1. adv. haer. c. 4. 3. Falsum est, ad Concilii illa, quae Pontificii nobis ut Oecumenica obtrudunt, ut Florentinum, Tridentinum &c. convocari vel convocatos fuisse Episcopos omnium Provinciarum; contrarium sanè oppidò manifestum est. Reliquas exceptiones Pontificiorum discussit B. Par. lib. 1. Confess. Cath. part. 2. c. 10. p. 493. seqq) *

## 27:2
(v. 2. They delivered him bound to Pilate. For capital punishments had been taken away from the Jews by the Romans, nor did anything remain for them except the cognizance of a case, if any pertained to their law. Conf. Ioh. 18, 31. Actor 25, 19. Add. Ioseph. l. 20. A. I. c. 8. Hieron. This is Samson bound by Delilah, Christ by the Synagogue.)

( τῷ ἡρεμόνι. Grotius at this place shows at length that Pilate was at least a procurator, not a president, strictly or properly so called, and what the office of the procurators was. Conf. also Casaubon p. 403. But the president of Syria at that time was Cumanus, if faith is to be given to Josephus. Regarding Pontius Pilate, who he was and what his origin was, the blessed D. Frantzius presents some things in de Interpret. Sc. S. Orac. 139 p. 1314. 1315.)

Ioh. 18, 31.Actor 25, 19. Add. Ioseph. l. 20. A. I. c. 8. Hieron. Hic est Samson vinctus à Delila, Christus à Synagoga.) *

## 27:3
(v. 3. Led by repentance, he brought back the silver pieces etc. Since all the parts of repentance which the Papists enumerate are found in Judas, and yet he himself despaired, it is evident that they enumerate the parts of true and saving repentance less than sufficiently, by omitting, namely, the fiducial apprehension of the mercy of GOD, founded in the merit of Christ. See B. Pareus Confess. Cathol. lib. 2. spec. part. 2. art. 16. c. 2. p. 20. 22. Corn. à Lapide objects at this place.) that the repentance was forced, tormenting, and desperate, not true and genuine, since the latter includes the hope of pardon, which Judas lacked. John Ferus has similar things in this place, John de la Haye in Triumpho verit. c. 182, Francis Lucas Brugensis in this place, and others. But this very thing is what we mean, namely that it is not true repentance which lacks the hope of pardon or faith. And from this we also establish that faith is an essential part of repentance.

(To the Chief Priests. Rightly Ambrose, l. 1 de Poenit. c. 5. I believe, he writes, that Judas could also have not been excluded from pardon by such great mercy, if he had performed his repentance not among the Jews, but before Christ.)

(He returned the thirty pieces of silver. Beautifully Ambrose: Even if the repentance of the traitor is useless, there is still some shame in crime, to acknowledge the fault: and although he is not absolved, yet the impudence of the Jews is refuted, whom, although the profession of the seller convicts, they nevertheless wickedly claim for themselves the rights of the contract.)

Latin:

* (v. 3. Poenitentiâ ductus retulit argenteos &c. Cùm omnes partes poenitentiae, quas Pontificii enumerant, apud Iudā deprehendantur, & tamen ipse desperarit, patet, quòd minùs sufficienter illi verae ac salutaris poenitentiae partes enumerent, omittendo fcil. fiducialem misericordiae DEI, in Christi merito fundatae apprehensionem. Vid. B. Parens Confess. Cathol. lib. 2. spec. part. 2. art. 16. c. 2. p. 20. 22. Excipit Corn. à Lapide in h. l. fuisse poenitentiam coactam, cruciantem & desperabundam, non veram & genuinā, cùm haec spem veniae quâ iudas caruerit, includat. Similia habent Ioh. Ferus in h. l. Ioh. de la Haye in Triumpho verit. c. 182. Franc. Lucas Brugensis in h. l. alii. Ast hoc ipsum est, quòd volumus, nempe quòd illa non sit vera poenitentia, cui spes veniae seu fides deest. Atque hinc etiam statuimus, quòd fides sit essentialis poenitentiae pars.) *

* (Principibus Sacerdotum. Rectè Ambros. l. 1 de Poenit. c. 5. Arbitror, scribit, quòd Iudas etiam potuisset tantâ miseratione non excludi à veniâ, si poenitentiam non apud Iudaeos, sed apud Christum egisset.) *

* (Retulit triginta argenteos. Pulcrè Ambrosius: Etsi eassa est poenitentia proditoris, est tamen ullus in scelere pudor, culpam agnoscere: & quanquam ille non absolvitur, Iudaeorum tamen impudentia confutatur, quos cum professio redarguat venditoris, sceleratè tamen sibi vendicant iura contractus.) *

## 27:5
(v. 5. He hanged himself with a noose. Peter Acts 1, 18. commemorates the end of the deed, as ours here commemorates the beginning. There is no doubt that Judas ἀυ τόξειρ fell from eternal salvation, since he brought violent hands upon himself out of despair. Yet it is by no means to be asserted absolutely of all who in any way or by any accident kill themselves. See B. Par. L. de Lege DEI §. 155. Concil. Theol. Dedekenni vol. 1. m. 3. sect. 4. n. 13. 14. 15. vol. 2. sect. 7. n. 7. 8. sect. 17. n. 7. also Append. ad vol. 1. lib. 1. m. 2. sect. 4. n. 3. B. D. König Cas. Catech. p. 45. B. D. Bald. C. C. p. 693. seqq. But how Judas died is explained more lengthily in the Annotations to Acts 1, 18. Conf. Buxtorff. Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 1480.) Concerning this hanging of Judas, Leo serm. 3. You have been more wicked and more unhappy than all, Judas, whom not repentance recalled to the Lord, but despair drew to the noose. Augustine l. homil. 50. homil. 27.

What he did in his body, (Judas), this was done in his soul. Just as those who tie a rope around their necks kill themselves thereby, because the spirit of this air does not enter them: so those who despair of the indulgence of GOD, by that very despair suffocate themselves within, so that the Holy Spirit cannot visit them. And this is the almost common opinion of both the ancients and the more recent Doctors, namely that Judas, by tightening his neck with a noose, made a long letter out of himself, as Staphyla speaks in the Aulularia of the Prince of Comedians. Thus they establish, besides Leo and Augustine, just cited, among the ancients, Oecumenius Comm. in Acts c. 1., Rupert of Deutz lib. XI. in Matth., Bernard serm. 8. and in Ps. 91., and much older than these, Ignatius ep. ad Philipp. and Irenaeus in Eusebius l. 5. H. E. c. 15., whom Chrysostom seems to have followed in serm. 3. de Iuda, and likewise in Ps. 7., Nazianzen, de Christo patiente, Prudentius in Psychom., Beda in Loc. sanct. c. 4. And among the more recent, and indeed from the Lutherans, Luther himself establishes it thus in the German Bible version, B. D. Osiander, and B. D. Cramer in this place, B. D. Arcularius in C. 1. Act., B. D. Calixtus in Conc. Evang., B. Par. Harm. Ev. c. 90., and others. From the Papists, Adam Contzen, Alf. Salmeron, John Maldonatus, Corn. à Lapide, James Tirinus the Jesuits in this place, Corn. Jansenius in Conc. Ev. p. 1011., Francis de Mendoza in lib. 1. Kings c. 2. n. 36. p. 555., also in C. 3. n. 18. p. 107., Dionys. Carthusianus of Rickel can be referred here. From the Calvinists, Calvin himself in Harm. p. 410., Junius, Gvalterus, Piscator, and others in this place, Isaac Casaubon Exerc. 16. ad Annal. Baronii, and most recently that monster of a man, the illustrious Salmasius. Nor do the Oriental Interpreters seem to have been of a different opinion, since they use such a word which is commonly used for strangulation or for such a constriction by which a noose is as it were cast upon the neck, as in Matth. 18. 28., just as also from the same root is the noun חנק, by which strangulation, a certain kind of punishment among the Jews in former times, is denoted. But especially the Syriac notably translates he strangled himself (for the noun is accustomed to have such a meaning in Syriac). The Arabic similarly and he suspended himself (as they have rightly translated

The Londoners in the Polyglot Bibles.) The Ethiopian adds & obiit. Thus indeed he translates: i. e. & was strangled, or as Mr. Ludolf translates in his Ethiopic Lexicon p. 220, he strangled himself, & died. The Persian: i. e. & going away he strangled himself. So that even for the sake of novelty alone the opinion of some is suspect, who think that since ἀπάγχεσθζ is general, denoting any suffocation whatsoever, not only that which is done by a noose, but which also has an internal cause, such as in quinsy, Judas put an end to his life by a different kind of death rather than hanging, namely by the disease of quinsy, which he contracted from grief on account of the most shameful crime committed. It must be known, however, that the word ἀπάγχεσθζ hardly occurs anywhere in this meaning, to signify, namely, to be suffocated by quinsy. On the contrary, it very often denotes ending life by a noose intercepting the breath. Thus it occurs several times in Diogenes Laertius. Among other things, a pleasant story is commemorated in the life of Diogenes the Cynic p. 401; Diogenes was once picking fruit from a fig tree, and when the guard warned: ἀυτόσθεν πρώτην ἄνσθωποςἀπήγξατο i. e. here a man was recently hanged, he replied: But I will cleanse it. In the same place, concerning the same, it is read: ἰδών ποτε γυναικας ἀπ᾽ ἐπηγχονσμένας. We also read in Thucydides: ἐκ τῶν δένδων ἀπήγχοντο. I omit now adding more on this matter. But a scruple still remains: Whether Judas cast the noose upon himself, or was truly snatched into the air by the Devil, and strangled by the same ? To which latter opinion it seems to favor, both because the verb of middle meaning, which is had here, among the Greeks signifies both actively and absolutely, and indeed, although rarely, purely passively. In which meaning it is also accustomed to be explained in Laertius, and because it is not unusual for the Devil to transport his instruments through the air, why not also, GOD permitting, kill and strangle there? see the Analecta above at C. 4, 5. Nor are there perhaps lacking in Historians examples of those who were thus removed from the midst. But truly, although novelty may entice this opinion, just as it did the former, (whence also it strongly pleased the Dutch Philologists), yet because, if such a thing had happened with Judas, without ambiguity it would have been noted and more clearly expressed by the Evangelists as a singular example of just divine vengeance, I consider it better to adhere here to the received opinion, than to depart from the beaten path without necessity.

Latin:

* (v. 5. Laqueo se suspendit. Petrus Actor. 1, 18. facti finem commemorat, ceu noster hîc initium. Non est dubium, quin Iudas ἀυ τόξειρ salute aeternâ exciderit, cùm ex desperatione violentas sibi intulerit manus. Minimè tamen de omnibus absolutè, qui quocunque modo vel casu seipsos interficiunt, id adserendum est. Vid. B. Par. L. de Lege DEI §. 155. Concil. Theol. Dedekenni vol. 1. m. 3. sect. 4. n. 13. 14. 15. vol. 2. sect. 7. n. 7. 8. sect. 17. n. 7. it. Append. ad vol. 1. lib. 1. m. 2. sect. 4. n. 3. B. D. König Cas. Catech. p. 45. B. D. Bald. C. C. p. 693. seqq. Quomodo verò interierit Iudas, prolixiùs expositum in Annot ad Actor. 1, 18. Conf. Buxtorff. Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 1480.) * De hoc Iudae suspendio Leo serm. 3. Scelestior omnibus Iuda & infelicior extitisti, quaem non poenitentia revocavit ad Dominum, sed desperatio traxit ad laequeum. Augustinus l. homil. 50. homil. 27.

Quod in corpore suo fecit (Iudas), hoc factum est in anima ipsius. Quomodo qui sibi collum ligant, inde se occidunt, quia non ad eos intrat spiritus aëris huius: sic illi, qui desperant de indulgentia DEI, ipsa desperatione intus se suffocant, ut eos Sp. S. visitare non possit. Estque haec communis ferè tum veterum, tum recentiorum Dd. sententia, quòd videlicet Iudas laqueo collum obstringendo litteram ex se longam, ut Staphyla apud Comicorum Principem in Aulularia loquitur, fecerit. Ita statuunt, praeter Leonem & Augustinum, modò adductos, ex veteribus Occumenius Comm. in Act. c. 1. Rupertus Tuitiensis lib. XI. in Matth. Bernhardus serm. 8. & in Ps. 91. & his multò antiquiores, Ignatius ep. ad Philipp. ac Irenaeus apud Euseb. l. 5. H. E. c. 15. quos secuti videntur Chrysostomus serm. 3. de Iuda, itemq; in Ps. 7. Nazianzenus, de Christo patiente, Prudentius in Psychom. Beda in Loc. sanct. c. 4. Erecentioribus verò & quidem è Lutheranis, statuunt ita Lutherus ipse in vers. Bibl. Germ. B. D. Osiander, & B. D. Cramerus in h. l. B. D. Arcularius in C. 1. Act. B. D. Calixtus in Conc. Evang. B. Par. Harm. Ev. c. 90. alii. è Pontificiis referri huc possunt Adamus Contzē, Alf. Salmeron, Ioh. Maldonatus, Corn. â Lapide, Iacobus Tirinus Iesuitae in h. l. Corn. sansenius in Conc. Ev. p. 1011. Franciscus de Mendoza in lib. 1. Reg. c. 2. n. 36. p. 555. it. in C. 3. n. 18. p. 107. Dionys. Carthusianus à Rickel. ex Calvinianis Calvinus ipse in Harm. p. 410. Iunius, Gvalterus, Piscator, alii in h. l. Isaacus Casaubonus Exerc 16. ad Annal. Baronii, ac novisimè monstrum illud hominis CL. Salmasius. Nec Interpretes qu que Orientales in aliâ fuisse sententiâ videntur, tale quippe adhibentes verbum, quod communiter de strangulatione adhibetur vel de tali coarctatione, qua collo quasi laqueus iniicitur, uti Matth. 18. 28. quemadmodum etiam ab ead. radice est nomen חנק, quo strangulatio, certum olim supplicii genus apud Iudaeos, denotatur. Cumprimis vero Syrus notanter vertit strangulavit seipsum (talem enim significatum nomen apud Syrum habere solet.) Arabs similiter & suspendit se (prout rectè transtulerunt

Londinenses in Bibliis Polyglottis.) Aethiops addit & obiit. Ita quippe transfert: i. e. & strangulatus fuit, vel prout Dn. Ludolfus in Lex. Aethiopico p. 220. vertit, seipsum strangulavit, & mortuus est. Persa: i. e. & abiens seipsum strangulavit. Ut adeo vel solius novitatis nomine suspecta sit quorundam opinio, existimantium, quòd cum ἀπάγχεσθζ generale sit, quamvis suffocationem notans, non eam solùm, quae laqueo fit, sed quae internam quoque habet causam, qualis in angina. Iudam alio potiùs mortis genere, quàm suspendio, vitae pausam fecisse, puta anginaemorbo, quem ex moerore ob turpissimum scelus commissum contraxerit. Sciendum autem, quòd vix ullibi in hac significatione verbum ἀπάγχεσθζ occurrat, ut significet, nempe, ex anginâ suffocari. Contrà vero saepissimè laqueo spiritum intercipiente vitam finire notat. Ita apud Diogenem Laêrtium aliquoties occurrit. Inter alia in vitâ Diogenis Cynici p. 401. iucunda commemoratur historia; Ex ficu poma legebat aliquando Diogenes, monente autem custode: ἀυτόσθεν πρώτην ἄνσθωποςἀπήγξατο i. e. hîc novissimè homo suspensus est, respondit ille: Ego verò illam purgabo. ibid. de eod. legitur: ἰδών ποτε γυναικας ἀπ᾽ ἐπηγχονσμένας. Apud Thucydidem quoque legimus: ἐκ τῶν δένδων ἀπήγχοντο. Omitto nunc adiicere in hanc rem plura. Sed adhuc restat scrupulus: Num Iudas sibimet ipsi laqueum iniecerit, an vero â Diabolo in aërem raptus fuerit, ab eodemstrangulatus? Cui quidem posteriori sententiae favere videtur, tum quòd verbum mediae significationis, quod hîc habetur, apud Graecos tum act vè tum absolutè significet, quin etiam, quamvis rarò, purè passivè. In qua significatione apud Laêrtium exponi etiam solet, tum quòd non insolens sit, Diabolum organa sua per a-ra transportare, quidni &, DEO permittente, ibidem interficere ac strangulare? vid. Analecta suprà ad C. 4, 5. Nec desunt etiam fortè in Historicis exempla eorum, qui ita è medio sublati. Verùm enim verò etsi novitas opinioni huic, sicuti & superiori lenocinetur, (unde etiam Belgis Philologis vehementer illa) arrisit, quia tamen, si tale quid cum Iudâ contigisset, procul ambiguo id ab Evangelistis tanquam singulare iustae vindictae divinae exemplum fuisset annotatum ac clariùs expressum, satius duco, receptae sententiae hîc inhaerere, quàm praeter necessitatem à trita via recedere.) *

## 27:6
* (v. 6. κορβονᾶν. Place, where σθσαυρὸ ἱερὸς was kept, Sacred treasury.) *

Latin:

* (v. 6. κορβονᾶν. Locus, ubi σθσαυρὸ ἱερὸς adservabatur, Gazophylacium sacrum.) *

## 27:7
* (v. 7. In the potter's field. We are all pilgrims in these lands, 1 Pet. 2, 11. let us therefore seek rest in the Church, acquired and bought by the blood of Christ. Let us die to sin, so that we may live to God. cf. Col. 3, 3. Furthermore, that sepulchers were located outside the city in the fields, both among the Romans and among the Jews, is shown by Laurentius Ramirez in Pentecont. c. 17. p. 159. I. Kirchmannus de Funeribus Roman. l. 2. c. 22. and others. The question, however, whether it is better for sepulchers to be inside or outside the city, is ventilated by B. Par. L. de Morte §. 88. *)

Latin:

* (v. 7. In sepulcrum peregrinorum. Nos omnes peregrini sumus in his terris, 1. Petr. 2, 11. quaeramus igitur requiem in Ecclesiâ, sanguine Christi acquisitâ & emtâ. Moriamur peccato, quò vivere possimus Deo. conf. Colos. 3, 3. Coetetùm quòd sepulcra tum apud Romanos, tum apud Iudaeos extra urbem in agris fuerint, ostendunt Laurentius Ramirez in Pentecont. c. 17. p. 159. I. Kirchmannus de Funeribus Roman. l. 2. c. 22. alii. Quaestionem vero, an satiùs sit, ut sepulcra sint intra vel extra urbem, ventilat B. Par. L. de Morte §. 88. *.

## 27:8
* (v. 8. It was called Aceldama &c. Chrysostom in h. l. The name given to the place proclaims their wicked slaughter more clearly than any trumpet. That is notable, if true, which Adrichomius in Descript. Ierusalem n. 216. p. 73. reports about this field, namely that its earth has such a power that it reduces the bodies of deceased Christians to dust in the space of twenty-four hours, which power it does not lose at all when carried to other regions. And that this is still observed at Rome near the Campo Santo, to which place the Empress Helena took care to have as much of this earth transported as several ships could hold. He adds that it rejects the bodies of Romans, and admits only the bodies of pilgrims, of which it also completely consumes the entire substance of the flesh within 24 hours. This very thing Corn. â Lapide confirms with his own calculation. Authors report something similar about the cemetery of the Holy Innocents, which is in Paris. We therefore leave it to Cornelius to consider whether perhaps something of this earth had been transported there as well) *

Latin:

* (v. 8. Vocatus est haceldama &c. Chrysostomus in h. l. Nomen loco inditum omni clariùs tubâ sceleratam eorum praedicat caedem. illud notabile, si verum, quod Adrichomius in Descript. Ierusalem n. 216. p. 73. de agro isthoc refert, quòd nempe eam habeat terra eius virtutem, ut defunctorum Christianorum corpora viginti quatuor horarum spatio in pulverem redigat, quam virtutem etiam in alias regiones divecta minimè perdar. Idque Romae iuxta Campum Sanctum etiamnum observari, in quem locum Imperatrix Helena tantum huius terrae, quantum plures naves capere poterant, advehi curarit. Addit, quòd Romanorum corpora respuat, solaq; peregrinorum corpora admittat, quorum etiam omnem carnis substantiam intra 24. horas prorsus absumat. Quod ipsum suo quoque calculo Corn. â Lapide confirmat. Simile quid de coemeterio S. Innocentii, quod Lutetiis Parisiorum est, autores produnt. Cogitandum igitur Cornelio relin quimus, an fortè & illuc terrae huius advectum quid fuerit) *

## 27:9
* (v. 9. Which was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet. But it is not read that it was pronounced concerning the thirty pieces of silver, for which Christ was sold, in Jeremiah, but in Zechariah.

Resp. 1. St. Jerome mentions that a certain apocryphal book of Jeremiah was offered to him by a Jew of the Nazarene sect, in which these things were read word for word. 2. Some think that this prophecy was once read also in the Prophet Jeremiah, namely in that prophecy which is still held among the Canonical books, but was erased and removed by the Jews. Origen and Euthymius seem to think so in h. l. also Eusebius l. 10. Demonstr. Evang. c. 5. But all the weights of reasons can be opposed to this opinion, which are accustomed to be urged by the Orthodox for the integrity of the authentic text, which B. Par. Confess. Cath. lib. 2. Spec. part. 1. art. 1. c. 2. presents to be seen as if in one glance. cf. also B. D. Bald. in Zach. p. 731. 3. Some think that an error underlies it, but these in turn are split into different parties. For others The Evangelists themselves do not fear to attribute a lapse of memory, and Erasmus of Rotterdam seems to be involved in this error in his Annotations on this place. Matthias Flacius in his Glosses on this place attributes this same error also to Augustine and Eusebius: but against the truth, as is clear from an inspection of Eusebius just alleged, and will soon appear concerning Augustine. Bellarmine rightly notes said error in Erasmus, lib. 3 de V. D. c. 6. He ought also to have added Melchior Canus, Bishop of the Canaries and Albert Pighius, Provost of Utrecht, as being involved in the same error, as B. Par. shows in Conf. Cath. l. 2. Spec. p. 1. pages 313 and 314. How grave that error is, D. Rivetus well warned in Isag. ad Sc. S. c. 2. §. 12. seqq., which if his fellow-sectarian Lud. Capellus, Professor at Saumur, had observed in Spicil. p. 30, 71, 74, he would have done well. St. Augustine also expressly disapproved of the same, both in l. 2 de consensu Ev. c. 12, and in ep. 8 and 19 to Jerome. For this opinion is, if not blasphemous, certainly highly dangerous. Which therefore Jerome also removed very far from himself. For when he had written in his Commentary on this place, that this testimony is not found in Jeremiah, but that a certain similarity is referred to in Zechariah, lest anyone should gather from these things as if he himself attributes σφάλμα μ ημονικὸν to the Evangelist, elsewhere, namely in his treatise on the Best Kind of Interpreting, before the middle, he explains his mind more clearly, writing:

But far be it from the follower of Christ that he could be argued to be in error, as one to whom it was a care not to hunt for words, but to set forth the meanings of doctrines. And indeed it is plain that the Evangelist looked to the matter itself or the type, rather than that he counted the words of the Prophets. Others attribute the error to amanuenses, indeed in such a way that they substituted the name Jeremiah for Zechariah. (So think, from the Papists, Card. Baronius A. C. 34, Corn. Jansenius in Conc. Ev., the Jesuit Maldonatus on this place, Suarez 3. part. tom. 2. Disp. 34. sect. 1; from the Calvinists, Calvin himself in Harm. and Beza on this place. From our own, B. D. Lucas Osiander in Explic. h. l. and B. D. Hunnius in Comm. ad h. l. seem to think the same.) Or that it was inserted into the text by some unlearned scribe from the margin, where it had been abbreviated Ζοῦ, for which he read Ιοῦ,, when before it had been read indefinitely in it: then was fulfilled that which was spoken by the Prophet. So think Nic. de Lyra, Matth. Flacius in the Gloss, Joh. Piscator on this place, and others. But the former assertion is not sufficiently probable, since between the name Zechariah and Jeremiah, as far as the writing is concerned, there is no slight difference. Even assuming that those names of the Prophets had been permuted by one or two copyists, this error could not, however, have crept into all the Greek Codices so easily at once. Now, however, it is certain, and those who have compared the most ancient and most approved Codices collected from everywhere testify, that in the Greek MSS. Codices the name Jeremiah is constantly read. So that the Jesuit Sanctius rightly judges in Comm. in Zachar., that it is very harsh, and from which piety recoils, that the name of others should have been inveterate in the sacred letters for so long, and that that stain, as it were, should have adhered to a most pure thing. As concerns the latter opinion, it seems to favor it that both the most ancient Syriac Interpreter and certain Latin Codices (of which witnesses are Augustine lib. 3 de Consensu Evangel. c. 6, Lyranus on this place, the Glossa Ordinaria, Lucas Brugensis, as also Corn. à Lapide in c. 11 of Zechariah p. 202 testifies that he saw at Rome ancient MS. Bibles in the Angelica Library of the Hermit Fathers of St. Augustine, in which the name Jeremiah is missing) omit the name of Jeremiah, and finally that our Evangelist is accustomed to allege the Scriptures of the O. T. in such a way that he does not express the name of the Prophet specifically, as is clear above from c. 1, 12; c. 2, 5, 15; c. 13, 35; c. 21, 4; and in the present chapter v. 35. Hence this opinion is attractive.

B. D. Calixtus in Conc. Ev. p. 391. But since the reasons brought forward do not seem of such moment that they can shake the authority of the consenting Greek Codices, to which the Oriental Interpreters, the Arab, the Ethiopian, and the Persian here excellently agree, that opinion is deservedly abandoned. Especially since it is likewise the custom of our Evangelist that he sometimes expresses the name of a Prophet specifically, as can be seen above from c. 3, 3. c. 4, 14. c. 8, 17. etc. Whence also St. Augustine l. c. judges thus concerning this opinion. Let him use this defense, whoever pleases, but for me, the reason why it does not please is because both more codices have the name of Jeremiah: and those who have considered the Gospel more diligently in Greek copies, thus claim to have found it in the older Greek ones: and there was no reason why he should add this name, so that an error might be made. But why it might be removed from some codices, there was a reason, that bold ignorance might do this, when it was troubled by the question that this testimony was not found in Jeremiah. Therefore 4 other authentic codices recognize the name of Jeremiah here as a genuine part. But they bring forward diverse methods of reconciling: for some think 1. that this prophecy was drawn by the Evangelist from an Apocryphal book, of which thing examples are not entirely lacking in Holy Scripture, just as some were also brought forward in the Prolegomena to the Epistle of Jude, so this opinion pleases B. D. Kesler above others in his inaugural Disputation on the allegation of Old Testament sayings in the New, §. 14. and the same pleased Origen among the ancients in tract 32 on Matthew, Tertullian in book 4 Against Marcion, ch. 39, Jerome in this place, and it especially pleases the Jesuit Salmeron. 2. Others judge that this prophecy was sought from oral tradition. Hugo Grotius is of this opinion, who nevertheless thinks that traditions of this kind, received from the Fathers, were afterwards privately annotated. Dionysius the Carthusian seems to be of the same mind. But B. D. Thummius in his Disputation on the Word of God, page 106, thinks that to be most false, and this most vain. 3. Again others from the Prophecy of the Prophet Zechariah, who was also called Jeremiah. For that it was not unusual among the Jews for several names to be imposed or attributed to one person and place has long been noted by others. It is added that names are not rarely interchanged which are joined together in sense, such as Jeremiah and Zechariah. Thus we know the Apostle Peter was called and Cephas. Since these things are so, B. D. Tarnovius in his Commentary on Zechariah, page 311, judges it safest to remove the difficulty in that way, just as B. D. Thummius also judges this opinion to be preferred to all others, in his Disquisition on the Word of God, p. 107. The same pleased Francis Gomarus among the Calvinists, especially, Professor in the Academy of Leiden, and John Ferus among the Papists. But since it cannot be proven by any testimony of Scripture that Zechariah had two names, it is rejected by Salmeron. Meanwhile, B. D. Balduinus in his Commentary on Zechariah, p. 733, seems not at all to reject it, who nevertheless concludes that B. following the counsel of Luther, we ought not to be too anxious about the mention of the author, since it is enough that the prophecy itself, whole and incorrupt, just as it is found in Zechariah, is alleged by the Evangelist. Others 4. From Jeremiah himself they think this prophecy is taken, yet that Zechariah is cited studiously by the Evangelist, and that the names of the Prophets are so interchanged, that it may be shown that all the Prophets were impelled by one and the same spirit, and hence in prophetic prophecies one must look not so much to the instrumental cause as to the principal, i.e., the Holy Spirit, by whom they were published. Which very thing Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, Luc. 1, 70. in his Canticle seems to intimate, saying, God spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets, who have been from of old. He does not say through mouths, but through mouth, so that he may declare that they, even though they prophesied in different places and times, nevertheless with one mouth, as it were, prefigured the same Christ. And to this also St. Chrysostom looked, who in ch. 1 of the epistle to the Galatians writes: κᾂν μύριοι γράφωσιν ἐυαγέλια, τὰ δὲ άυτὰ γράφωσιν, ἓν ἐςτὰ πολλά. This opinion is especially pleasing to St. Augustine, who in the said place determines that this, that our Evangelist wrote Jeremiah instead of Zechariah, was done by a more secret counsel of the providence of GOD, by which the minds of the Evangelists were governed. For it could, he says, have happened that in the mind of Matthew, writing the Gospel, Jeremiah occurred instead of Zechariah, as is wont to happen: which, however, he would have corrected without any hesitation, at least being admonished by others, who could have read this while he was still living in the flesh, unless he thought that it had not occurred in vain to his memory, which was ruled by the Holy Spirit one name of a Prophet for another, except because the Lord thus determined this to be written. But why the Lord so determined, that first cause most useful ought to be most easily thought of: that it was even thus insinuated, that all the Prophets spoke by one spirit, and that they stand together in wonderful agreement among themselves, so that this is much more than if all things of the Prophets were said by the one mouth of one: and therefore it ought to be accepted without doubt, whatever the Holy Spirit said through them, both individual things are of all, and all things are of individuals. The same most praised father adds more to this matter, who nevertheless does not reject the opinion about which we are now about to treat. There are, therefore, 5 who, likewise following Augustine in the said place, think that the Evangelist joins the prophecies of two Prophets, namely Jeremiah and Zechariah, since in the former it is a matter of the purchase of a field, and in the latter of the price of the purchase. This opinion is excellently favored by the fact that elsewhere also similar examples are found in the N. T., i.e., where from two testimonies of the O. T., and sometimes even of different authors, one is exhibited fused together. Such occurs Actor. 1, 20. from Psalm. 69. 27. & 109, 8. 1. Petr. 2. 7. from Ps. 118, 22. & Es. 3, 14. Rom. 3. 10. seqq. from Es. 59, 7. & Prov. 1, 16. Rom. c. 10, 15. from Es. 52, 7. & Nahum 1, 15. above c. 21, 5. from Es. 62, 11. & Zach. 9, 9. in the same chapter v. 13. from Es. 56, 7. & Ierem. 7, 11. Marc. 1, 1. 1. from Es. 40, 3. & Mat. 3, 1. What of the fact that places are found where, when testimonies of two are brought forward, with one omitted, the name of only one is expressed, or at least the whole testimony is alleged as if it were of only one. see Matth. 21, 5. But that the Evangelist wished to make mention of Jeremiah rather than Zechariah, although he looked to the prophecy of both, can seem to have happened because he wished to give an account not so much of the price by which Christ was bought, as of the field bought for that price. The Evangelist therefore seems to look to Jer. 32, and a beautiful analogy can be shown between the type and the antitype. As both these latter opinions take nothing away from the authentic text or the divine authority of Holy Scripture, but rather excellently confirm the same, so it is to be preferred entirely to the rest, just as also those of our own have embraced the same, B. D. Walther Harm. Bibl. p. 802. B. D. Glassius Philol. S. lib. 1. p. 161. B. D. Tarnovius on Zechariah p. 312. B. Par. H. E. in this place Dn. D.

Friedlieb in H. E. p. 206. who also wishes to be noted, those words, which Matthew ascribes to Jeremiah, were indeed spoken by Jeremiah (since the Evangelist does not say, this was written by Jeremiah, but ῥηθὲν was spoken,) but were committed to writing by Zechariah. Compare on this matter Simon also Episcopius Instit. Theol. p. 200. To this may also be referred the observation of Hugo Grotius in this place, warning that later prophets were accustomed to use the words of the ancient prophets, just as Ezekiel has many things word for word, taken from Jeremiah, as is evident from a comparison of Jer. 31, 29. 30. with Ezek. 18, 12.3. 4. Especially, writes the said Grotius, Zechariah loves to imitate the expressions of Jeremiah. For who does not see, that what is in the same c. 1, 4. is taken from Jer. 18, 1. & c. 35, 15. that which is in him c. 1, 6. from Jer. Lam. c. 23, 5. Whence also the Jews are accustomed to say, that the spirit of Jeremiah was in Zechariah. Among the Papists, the opinion that the Evangelist brought the testimony from the prophecies of Jeremiah & Zechariah combined is embraced especially by Sanctius, on Zechariah, among the Calvinists by Heinsius, and others.) *

Latin:

* (v. 9. Quod dictum est per Ieremiam prophetam. Ast pronunciatum de triginta argenteis, quibus Christus fuit venditus, non legitur apud Ieremiam, sed apud Zachariam.

Resp. 1. S. Hîeronymus memorat, â Iudaeo Nazaraenae sectae librum quendam Ieremiae Apocryphum sibi fuisse oblatum, in quo haec ad verbum legerentur. 2. Nonnulli existimant, vaticinium hoc apud Prophetam quoque Ieremiam, in eâ nempe prophetia, quae etiamnum inter libros Canonicos habetur, lectum olim fuisse, sed â Iudaeis erasum sublatumq;. Ita sentire videntur Origenes & Euthymius in h. l. it. Eusebius l. 10. Demonstr. Evang. c. 5. Sed sententiae huic omnia opponi rationum pondera possunt, quae pro textûs authentici integritate urgeri ab Orthodoxis solent, quae uno quasi intuitu conspicienda sistit B. Par. Confess. Cath. lib. 2. Spec. part. 1. art. 1. c. 2. conf. etiam B. D. Bald. in Zach. p. 731. 3. Quidam errorem subesse putant, sed hi rursus in partes scinduntur diversas. Alii enim ipsi Evangelistae memoriae lapsum tribuere non verentur, & in hoc errore versari Erasmus videtur Roterodamus Annot. in h. l. Matthias Flacius in Glossis ad h. l. eundem hunc errorem tribuit quoque Augustino & Eusebio: sed invitâ veritate, prout ex inspectione Eusebii modo allegati patet, & de Augustino mox apparebit. Meritò vero dictum errorem in Erasmo notat Bell. lib. 3. de V. D. C. 6. Debuisset quoque adiungere Melchiorem Canum, Episcopum Canariensem & Alb. Pighium Praepositum Ultraiectinum, in eodem versantes errore, ceu ostendit B. Par. Conf. Cath. l. 2. Spec. p. 1. pag. 313. & 314. Quàm gravis verò error ille sit, benè monuit D. Rivetus Isag. ad Sc. S. c. 2. §. 12. seqq. quae si observasset eiusd. sociennus Lud. Capellus Professor Salmuriensis, in Spicil. p. 30. 71. 74. benè fecisset. Improbavit quoque eundem S. Augustinus disertè tum l. 2. de confensu Ev. c. 12. tum ep. 8. & 19. ad Hieronymum. Est enim sententia haec si non blasphema, certè summè periculosa. Quam -roinde longissimè â se removit etiam Hieronymus. Etenim cùm Comm. in h. l. scripsisset, testimonium hoc in Ier-miâ non inveniri, sed in Zachariâ quandam similitudinem referri, ne quis ex his colligat, ac si ipse σφάλμα μ ημονικὸν Evangelistae tribuat, alibi puta tride Optimo interpretandi genere, ante medium, clariùs mentem suam explicat, s-ribens:

Sed absit de pedissequo Christi, quòd possit argui def-lso, utpote cui cura fuit, non verba aucupari, sed sententias dogmatum ponere. Et sanè palam est, quòd ad rem ipsam potiùs s. typum respexerit Evangelista, quàm quòd Prophetarum verba numerarit. Alii amanuensibus errorem tribuunt, ita quidem, ut vel pro Zacharia substituerint Ieremiae nomen. (ita sentiunt ex Pontificiis Card. Baronius A. C. 34. Corn. Iansenius in Conc. Ev. Iesuita Maldonatus in h. l. Suarez 3. part. tom. 2. Disp. 34. sect. 1. è Cal. vinianis Calvinus ipse in Harm. ac Beza in h. l. Ex nostratibus idem sentire videntur B. D. Lucas Osiender in Explic. h. l. B. D. Hunnius in Comm. ad h. l.) vel ab indocto quodam scriba è margine, ubi abbrev. fuerit Ζοῦ, pro quo legerit Ιοῦ, textui insertum sit, cùm antè indefinitè in eo fuerit lectum: tunc impletum est, quod dictum per Prophetam. Ita sentiunt Nic. de Lyra, Matth. Flacius in Glossâ Ioh. Piscaror in h. l. alii. Sed prior adsertio non satis probabilis est, cùm inter nomen Zachariae ac Ieremiae, quantum ad scrip tionem, non leve discrimen sit. posito etiam, ab uno vel altero librario nomina illa Prophetarum fuisse permutata, minimè tamē error hic in omnes statim Codd. Graecos adeô facilè irrepere potuisset. Iam verò constat, ac testantur illi, qui Codd. antiquissimos probatissimosq; undique conquisitos contulerunt, quòd in Codd. Graecis MSS. constanter nomen Ieremiae legatur. Ut adeò rectè Iesuita Sanctius Comm. in Zachar. iudicet, quòd valde durum sit, & â quo pietas abhorret, tamdiu in sacris litteris aliorum inveterasse nomen, & in re purissima illam quasi labem adhaesisse. Quod posteriorem concernie sententiam, favere quidem illi videtur quòd tum antiquissimus Interpres Syrus, tum Latini quidam Codd. (de quibus testes sunt Augustinus lib. 3. de Consensu Evangel. c. 6. Lyranus, in h. l. Glossa Ordinaria, Lucas Brugensis, quemadmodum etiam Corn. â Lapide in c. 11. Zachariae p. 202 testatur, vidisse se Romae Biblia MSS. vetusta in Bibliotheca Angelica Patrum Eremit. S. Augustini, in quibus desit nomen Ieremiae,) nomen Ieremiae omittunt, tum deniq; quòd Evangelista noster ita V. T. Scripturas allegare soleat, ut nomē Prophetae in specie non exprimat ceu suprà ex c. 1, 12. c. 2, 5. 15. c. 13, 35. c. 21, 4. praesenti c. v. 35. patet. Arridet hinc sententia isthaec

B. D. Calixto in Conc. Ev. p. 391. At cùm tanti non videantur rationes adductae momēti, ut consentientium Codd. Graecorum, quibus hîc egregie Interpretes Orientales, Arabs, Aethiops, Persa adstipulantur, labefact are autoritatem possint, meritò & illa sentētia deseritur. Praeprimis cùm pariter in more positū Evangelistae nostro sit, ut aliqn. Prophetae nomen in specie exprimat, ceu suprà ex c. 3, 3. c. 4, 14. c. 8, 17. &c. videre est. Unde etiam S. Augustinus l. c. ita de sententia hac iudicat. Utatur ista defensione, cui placet, mihi autem cur non placeat, haec causa est, quia & plures Codd. habent Hieremiae nomen: & qui diligentiùs in Graecis exemplaribus Evangelium consideraverunt, in antiquioribus Graecis itase perhibent invenisse: & nulla causa fuit, cur adderet hoc nomen, ut mendositas fieret. Cur autem de nonnullis Codd. tolleretur, fuit uticausa, ut hoc audax imperitia faceret, cùm turbaretur quaestione, quòd hoc testimonium apud Hieremiannon inveniretur. Proinde 4. alii ceu genuinam codd. authentici partem nomen Ieremia hìe agnoscunt. Sed diversas conciliandi rationes afferunt: quidam enim 1. ex libro Apocrypho vaticinium hoc ab Evangelista haustum putāt, cuius uti rei exempla in Sc. S. non omninò dantur nulla, prout etiam quaedam in Proleg. ad ep. Iudae adducta sunt, ita sententia haec prae coeteris arridet B. D. Keslero in Disp. inaugurali de dict. V. T. in Novo allegatione §. 14. placuitq; eadem è veteribus Origeni tr. 32. in Matth. Tertulliano lib. 4. Contra Marc. c. 39. Hieronymo in h. l. & cumprimis placet Iesuitae Salmeroni. 2. alii ex traditione orali vaticinium hoc petitum censent. In hâc sententia Hugo Grotius est, qui tamen existimat, traditiones huiusmodi â Patribus acceptas, postea privatim fuisse annotatas. Idem sentire videtur Dionys. Carthusianus. Ast B. D. Thummius in Disp. de V. D. pag. 106. illud falsissimum esse putat, hoc vanissimum. 3. Rursus aliiè Prophetae Zachariae, qui & Ieremias dictus fuerit, Prophetia. Quòd enim non insolens fuerit inter Iudaeos, uni personae & loco plura fuisse imposita vel attributa nomina, pridem ab aliis notatum. Accedit, quòd nomina haut rarò permutentur, quae sensu inter se sunt coniuncta, qualia Ieremias & Zacharias. Ita Apostolum Petrum & Kepham dictum novimus. Quae cùm ita sint, tutissimum censet B. D. Tarnovius Comm. in Zach. pag. 311. difficultatem eo modo tollere, quemadmodum etiam sententiam hanc reliquis omnibus praeferendam censet B. D. Thummius, in Disquis. de V. D. p. 107. Eadem ex Calvinianis Francisco cumprimis placuit Gomaro, Professori in Acad. Leydensi, è Pontificiis Ioh. Fero. Sed cùm nullo Scripturae testimonio probari possit, quòd Zacharias fuerit binominis, reiicitur eadem â Salmerone. Interea minimè respuere illam videtur B. D. Balduinus Comm. in Zach. p. 733. qui tamen concludit, quòd B. Lutheri consilium secuti non debeamus de autoris mentione nimium esse solliciti, cùm satis sit, vaticinium ipsum integrum & incorruptum, quemadmodum apud Zachariam reperitur, ab Evangelista allegari. Alii 4. ex ipso Ieremiâ vaticinium hoc desumtum putant, citari tamen studiò ab Evangelista Zachariam, adeoq; Prophetarum nomina permutari, ut ostendatur, uno eodemq; spiritu omnes Prophetas fuisse impulsos, atque hinc in propheticis vaticiniis non tam ad causam instrumentalem, quàm principalem, h. e. Spiritum sanctum, â quo sunt edita, respiciendum esse. Quod ipsum & Zacharias Iohannis Baptistae pater, Luc. 1, 70. in Canti-o suo innuere videtur, dicens, Deum loquutum esse per os sanctorum, qui â seculo fuerunt, prophetarum suorum. Non dicit per ora, sed per os, ut declaret, illos, tametsi diversis & locis & temporibus prophetarint, uno tamen quasi ore eundem Christum praesignificasse. Et huc respexit quoq; S. Chrysostomus, qu. in c. 1. ep. ad Gal. scribit: κᾂν μύριοι γράφωσιν ἐυαγέλια, τὰ δὲ άυτὰ γράφωσιν, ἓν ἐςτὰ πολλά. Placet haec sententia cumprimis S. Augustino, qui d. l. statuit, omninò hoc, quòd pro Zacharia Evangelista noster Ieremias scripserit, secretiori consilio providentiae DEI actum effe, qua mentes Evangelistarum sunt gubernatae. Potuit enim, ait, fieri, ut animo. Matthaei, Evangelium conscribentis pro Zacharia Ieremias occurrerit, ut fieri solet: quod tamen sine ullâ dubitatione emendaret, saltem ab aliis admonitus, qui ipso adhuc in carne vivente hoc legere potuerunt, nisi cogitaret, recordationi suae, quae Sancto Spiritu. regebatur, non frustra occurrisse aliud pro alio nomen Prophetae, nisi quia ita Dominus hoc scribi constituit. Cur autem ita constituerit Dominus, prima illa causa util-ssima debet facillimè cogitari: etiam sic esse insinuatum, ita omnes Prophetas uno spiritu locutos, mirabili inter se consensione constare, ut hoc multo amplius sit, quàm si omnia Prophetarum uno unius ore dicerentur: & ideo indubitanter accipi debere, quaecunper eos Sp. Sanctus dixit, & singula esse omnium, & omnia singulorū. Plura in hanc rem subiungit idem laudatissimus pater, qui tamen nec eam, de quâ iam acturi sumus, sententiam reiicit. Sunt igitur 5. qui itidem Augustinum dicto loco sequuti, Evangelistam duorum vaticinia Prophetarum, Ieremiae nempe & Zachariae, coniungere existimant, cùm apud illum agatur de agri emptione, apud hunc de emtionis pretio. Cui sententiae egregiè favet, quòd alibi quoque similia in N. T. exempla deprehenduntur, h. e. ubi ex duobus V. T., ac diversorum etiam quandoq; autorum, testimoniis unum conflatum exhibetur. Tale occurrit Actor. 1, 20. ex Psalm. 69. 27. & 109, 8.1. Petr. 2. 7. ex Ps. 118, 22. & Es. 3, 14.Rom. 3. 10. seqq. ex Es. 59, 7. & Prov. 1, 16.Rom. c. 10, 15. ex Es. 52, 7. & Nahum 1, 15. suprà c. 21, 5. ex Es. 62, 11. & Zach. 9, 9. eod. cap v. 13. ex Es. 56, 7. & Ierem. 7, 11.Marc. 1, 1. 1. ex Es. 40, 3. & Mat. 3, 1. Quid quòd reperiantur loca, ubi cùm testimonia adducuntur duorum, omisso altero, alterius tantùm nomen exprimitur, vel certè totum testimonium ita allegatur, ac se unius tantùm esset. vid. Matth. 21, 5. Quòd vero Evangelista Ieremiae potius, quàm Zachariae, licet utriusq; prophetiam respexerit, facere voluerit mentionem, inde factum videri potest, quòd ipse non tam pretii, quo Christus fuit emtus, quàm agri eo pretio emti reddere rationem voluerit. Videtur igitur Evangelista respicere ad Ierm. 32. ostendiq; pulcra analogia inter typum & antitypum potest. Utraque haec postrema sententia uti nihil textui authentico vel divinae Sc. S. auteritati detrahit, sed eandem egregiè potiùs confirmat, ita reliquis omninò praeferenda est, ceu etiam eandem amplexi sunt ex nostratibus B. D. Waltherus Harm. Bibl. p. 802. B. D. Glassius Philol. S. lib. 1. p. 161. B. D. Tarnovius in Zachariam p. 312. B. Par. H. E. in h. l. Dn. D.

Friedlieb in H. E. p. 206. qui etiam notari vult, verba illa, quae Matthaeus adscribit Ieremiae, â Ieremiâ quidem dicta esse (cùm non dicat Evangelista, hoc â Ieremia scriptum, sedῥηθὲν dictum est,) verùm â Zacharia in litteras relata. Conf. in hanc rem Simon quoqEpiscopius Instit. Theol. p. 200. Huc referri quoq; potest observatio Hugonis Grotii h. l. monentis, veterum Prophetarum verbis uti solitos Prophetas posteriores, ceu Ezechiel multa verbotenus habeat, ex Ieremiâ desumta, prout pateat ex collatione Ier. 31, 29. 30. cum Ezech. 18, 12.3. 4.Cumprimis, scribit dictus Grotius, Zacharias amat imitari locutiones Ieremiae. Quis enim non videt, quod apud eundem est c. 1, 4. desumtum esse exIerem. 18, 1.&c. 35, 15.quod apud eum est c. 1, 6. ex Ierem.Thren. c. 23, 5.Unde etiam dicere solent Iudaei, spiritum Ieremiae fuisse in Zacharia. Ex Pontificiis sententiam quòd ex Ieremiae & Zach. vaticiniis coniunctis Evangelista testimonium attulerit, amplectitur cumprimis Sanctius, in Zachariam, ex Calvinianis Heinsius, alii.) *

## 27:12
* (v. 12. He answered nothing. Isid. Pelus. l. 4. p. 128. Christ did not use his power, nor defense, nor appeal, so that he might clearly show, that he had come here for this reason, ὅτι τὸν θάνατον θανατώσων δευῤ ἀφῖκτο, that he might put death to death. August. serm. 118. de Tempore: The Lord does not strengthen his accusation by remaining silent but despises it by not repelling it: better is the cause, which is not defended, & is proven: fuller is the justice, which is not built up by words, but is supported by truth. The Savior, who is wisdom, knew how he might conquer by being silent, how he might overcome by not answering. Ambros. in c. 12. Luke: He does well to be silent, who does not need a defense. Let those seek to be defended, who fear to be conquered. What would he fear, who did not seek safety? He alone of all gives up his own, so that he may acquire that of all. The same serm. 17. in Ps. 118. Christ, attacked by slanders, maintained a triumphal silence.) *

Latin:

* (v. 12. Nihil respondit. Isid. Pelus. l. 4. p. 128. Christus nepotentiâ suâ, nedefensione, neappellatione usus est, ut liquido ostenderet, se huc propterea venisse,ὅτι τὸν θάνατον θανατώσων δευῤ ἀφῖκτο,ut mortem morte afficeret. August. serm. 118. de Tem. pore: Accusationem suam Dominus tacendo non firmat sed despicit non repellendo: melior est causa, quae non defenditur, & probatur: plenior iustitia, quae non verbis adstruitur, sed veritatfulcitur. Scivit Salvator, qui est sapientia, quomodo tacendo vinceret, quomodo non respondendo superaret. Ambros. in c. 12. Lucae: Benè tacet, qui defensione non indiget. Ambiant defendi, quitiment vinci. Quid timeret, qui non ambiret salutem? Solus omnium suam prodit, ut acquirat omnium. Idem serm. 17. in Ps. 118.Christus calumniis appetitus silentium retulittriumphale.) *

## 27:15
* (v. 15. Κατὰ ἑορτὴν, τὸ πάοχα i.e., which was thus called κατΊ ἐξοχὴν. See above c. 26, 25. John 4, 45. Oriental interpreters seem to take it concerning all the more solemn feasts, for thus the Syrian translates in every feast. So also the Arab similarly the Ethiopian: i. e. & at any feast. Unless one wishes to limit it in this way, namely according to the subject matter, at any feast of the Passover, recurring every year. This is what the Persian seems to insinuate, translating: it was the custom for the governor, that every year, on the day of the feast, viz. of the Passover.) *

* (He was accustomed to release a prisoner &c. Concerning this custom, namely when it was introduced, and whether it should be approved &c. the blessed Doctor Georg. K-nig in his Catechetical Cases page 564. seqq. Hugo Grotius in this place, B. Par. Harm. Ev. c. 193. p. 1889. the blessed Doctor Winckelm. in Mark p. 504. who can be consulted, treat more at length. Corn. à Lapide in this place writes, this custom was formerly introduced among the Jews in memory of Israel being freed from Egyptian captivity through Moses, Exod. 14. But Grotius holds the contrary in this place, since the law of Moses was χωρὶς οἰκτιρμῶν, Heb. 10, 28. Therefore the Lord Doctor Friedlieb in this place p. 178. thinks it likely that this was from the Romans, and that this favor was granted to the Jews by Augustus, that a prisoner should be released at the Feast of the Passover. and something similar was done afterwards by Christian Emperors. It is probable that this custom was introduced by the Jews themselves, yet beyond, nay against divine approval, and therefore deservedly to be disapproved, (see Prov. 17, 15.) as the blessed Father clearly shows in the place cited.) *

Latin:

* (v. 15. Κατὰ ἑορτὴν, τὸ πάοχα sc., quod ita dicebatur κατΊ ἐξοχὴν. Vid suprà c. 26, 25. Ioh. 4, 45. Interpretes Orientales de omnibus festis solennioribus accipere videntur, ita enim Syrus vertit in omni festo. Sic quoque Arabs similiter Aethiops: i. e. & quolibet festo. Nisi ita limitare quis velit, nempe secundùm subiectam materiam, quolibet festo Paschatis, singulis annis recurrente. Id quod insinuare Persa videtur, vertens: praefecto mos fuit, ut quolibet anno, die festi, sc. Paschatos.) *

* (Consueverat dimittere vinctum &c. De consvetudine hâc, quando nempe introducta fuerit, & num approbanda sit &c. prolixiùs agunt B. D. Georg. K-nig Cas. Catechet. pag. 564. seqq. Hugo Grotius in h. l. B. Par. Harm. Ev. c. 193. p. 1889. B. D. Winckelm. in Marc. p. 504. qui possunt evolvi. Corn. à Lapide in h. l. scribit, morem hunc olim apud Iudaeos inductum fuisse in memoriam liberati ex Aegyptia captivitate Israelis per Mosen,Exod. 14. Sed contrarium tenet Grotius in h. l. cùm lex Mosis fuerit χωρὶς οἰκτιρμῶν,Ebr. 10, 28. Verisimile proinde putat Dn. D. Friedlieb in h. l. p. 178. à Romanis hoc esse, & ab Augusto hanc gratiam concessam Iudaeis, ut Paschatos Festo dimitteretur captivus. ac simile quid à Christianis Imperatoribus postea factum. Probabile est, omninò ab ipsis Iudaeis consuetudinem hanc fuisse introductam, praeter tamen, imò contra approbationem divinam, adeoque meritò improbandam, (vid. Prov. 17, 15.) ceu luculenter ostendit B. P. l. c.) *
