## 27:19
* (v. 19. I have suffered many things in a dream. Q. Whence and by whom were these dreams sent to the wife of Pilate? Ignatius ep. 8. to the Philippians, Saint Cyprian, or whoever the author of that sermon ascribed to Cyprian may be, sermon on the Passion, Bernard sermon 1. on the Passover, Bede, Lyranus, Rabanus, Dionysius the Carthusian, Cardinal Cajetan and some others maintain, that these dreams were sent by an evil demon, inasmuch as he already recognized that Jesus was the Christ, and therefore wished to prevent his death, lest through it men should be saved. But if the devil had wished to prevent the death of Christ, or if he had known that the human race was to be liberated through the death of Jesus, he would have moved the Jews and the Princes to pity for Jesus, rather than the woman. They oppose, also besides this opinion some others that, That he attributes that dream to Christ the praise of justice. That the Devil would not do. Others therefore, such as Origen, Hilary, Jerome, Theodoret, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius, in this place; likewise Augustine, sermon 121 de Tempore, St. Ambrose book 10 in Luke c. 23, whom our own men follow, Dn. D. Friedsieb in this place p. 216, B. D. Calixtus in Concord. l. 6. c. 11, B. Par. H. E. c. 193, likewise in Dispp. Elench. p. 212, and others. Among the Papists, Corn. à Lapide and Jansenius, likewise the Jesuit Maldonatus, among the Calvinists H. Grotius, Ioh. Piscator in Obs. ad h. l. think that these dreams were sent to the wife of Pilate by God through a holy Angel. And this 1. so that Christ might receive a testimony of innocence from both sexes. 2. so that he might publicly manifest the innocence of Christ to all. 3. so that Pilate might be warned not to condemn an innocent man. Grotius adds in this place that it could have happened that Pilate's wife was a woman θεοσεβὴς. But this opinion hardly deserves applause among others. Nor does it even favor the opinion of Grotius, that the dream was sent to her by God. For it is established that dreams are sometimes sent by God even to Gentiles, not yet converted to the true Church, and to the impious in the Church μαντικὰ, especially terrible ones, as B. P. in H. E. l. c. shows from Gen. 20, 3.c. 31, 24.c. 41, 1.Dan. 2, 1.c. 4, 2.. The distinction of dreams must not be passed over in this place, that some are δεὺπεμπτα or θεὁπνευςα i.e. sent by God or divine, of which kind are commemorated here and there in Holy Scripture, see Genes. c. 20, 6.28, 12.c. 31, 24.c. 37, 5. seqq. c. 40, 12.c. 41, 1. seqq. Dan. 2, 27.c. 4, 16. in the N. T. Matth. 1, 21.c. 2, 12. 13.19.Act. 16, 9. and the divine promise Numer. 12, 6. is also to be understood concerning these. (That dream of Anthony is usually referred here, about which Sozomenus book 6 c. 5, likewise what is related by the same book 6 c. 2 in these words: On the same day Didymus the Ecclesiastical Philosopher, living at Alexandria and saddened because of the Emperor's (Julian's) obstinacy against the Churches, both because he had been seduced and because the Churches were being despised, fasted and prayed to God for this reason: and since he was pressed by that care, he took no food, not even when night was falling, but sitting in his chair he fell into a sleep: and as if caught up into an ecstasy. It seemed to him that he saw white horses running, and those who were sitting on them, as if with a herald's voice crying out, announce to Didymus, on this day about this hour Julian has been killed, and let him signify this to Bishop Athanasius. Sozomenus adds: And these things, indeed, as they were seen both by a friend and intimate of Julian, and by a Philosopher, I perceived to have been done thus, and neither of them in those things which he saw (for concerning that intimate of Julian, the same person had likewise narrated a dream about the death of the Emperor Julian a little before) strayed from the truth, as it appeared afterwards. (Compare the twin account in Theodoret, book 5, Ecclesiastical History, chapter 24.) Concerning divine dreams, or those which have been sent divinely, it is generally agreed that they fix a certain singular sting in the minds of men, from which they can also be distinguished in a certain way even from natural ones. Although God does indeed still deal sometimes with pious men through dreams, by warning them of future dangers or certain other events: nevertheless, He is by no means accustomed to warn men any longer through dreams in doctrine or articles of faith, since we have the word of GOD sufficiently clearly revealed. Furthermore, other Dreams are διαβολικὰ, sent by the devil by the permission of GOD or diabolical, and therefore superstitious, concerning which the sayings Deut. 13. 1.Ierem. 23, 16.25.c. 27, 9.c. 29, 8.Zach. 10, 2. are to be understood. Hither are also accustomed to be referred those dreams by which God is recorded to have terrified Job, Job 7, 14, namely through Satan. Finally, other dreams are φυσικὰ natural, or, if we may so speak, human, which namely arise from the constitution of the body and soul. Of the body indeed, from the diverse disposition of the humors; of the soul, however, from an internal commotion, forming for itself certain figures, or recalling to its memory things done a little before, or moved by some affection of the body, or stirred by unusual fear or joy, etc. And concerning these, Solomon is to be understood, Ecclesiastes 5, 2. 6. likewise Siracides c. 34, 1. 2. 3. 7. In general, however, it is to be judged concerning dreams from the word of GOD and the outcome, the Orthodox well advise. To which pertains Ier. 28. 9. From those things brought forward thus far, it is evident both that one should not, with Xenophanes and the Epicureans, of whom La-ritus, simply deny faith to all dreams, and that one should not, with Protagoras and the Stoics, attribute faith to all or believe them. Compare more things pertaining to this in B. D. Rungius, Comment. in Gen. p. 576. 856. 1076. and 1159. B. D. Gesnerus in Gen. p. 562. seqq. B. D. Dietricus both in libr. Sap. c. 14. p. 699 seqq. and in a peculiar treatise or Philosophical-Theological discourse on Dreams. B. Par. H. E. and in Dispp. Elencht. dd. II. it. Comm. in Gen. p. 591. 706. 709. 716. B. B. D. Bald. Cas. Consc. p. 804. 810. seqq. Schickardus, Bechinath Happer. p. 9. Franc. Torreblanca in Daemonol p. 142. seqq. item p. 259. 260. Pelargus, Comm. in Matth. p. 31, 32.

Latin:

* (v. 19. Multa passa sum per visum. Q. Unde & à quo somnia haec uxori Pilati fuerint immissa? Ignatius ep. 8. ad-hilipp. S. Cyprianus, vel quisquis sermonis illius, Cypriano adscripti autor, serm. de Passione, Bernhardus serm. 1. de Paschate, Beda, Lyranus, Rabanus, Dion. Cathusianus, Cardinalis Caietanus ac alii nonnulli statuunt, somnia haec à daemone malo immissa fuisse, utpote iam agnoscente, Iesum esse Christum, ideoeius necem impedire volente, ne per eam homines salvarentur. At si diabolus Christi mortem impedire voluisset, vel si scivisset, per mortem Iesu liberandum esse genus humanum, potiùs Iudaeos ac Principes ad commiserationem Iesu flexisset, quàm mulierem. Opponunt, etiam praeterea huic sententiae nonnulli illud, quòd Christo somnium illud tribuat laudem iustitiae. Quod Diabolus non faciat. Alii igitur, uti Origenes, Hilarius, Hieronymus, Theodoretus, Chrysostomus. Theophylactus. Euthymius, in h. l. item August. serm. 121. de Tempore, S. Ambrosius lib. 10. in Lucam c. 23. quos sequuntur è nostratibus Dn. D. Friedsieb in h. l. p. 216. B. D. Calixtus in Concord. l. 6. c. 11. B. Par. H. E. c. 193. it. in Dispp. Elench. p. 212. alii. è Pontificiis Corn. à Lapide ac Iansenius, it. Iesuita Maldonatus, è Calvinianis H. Grotius. Ioh. Piscator in Obs. ad h. l. existimant, à Deo per Angelum sanctum somnia haec uxori Pilati fuisse immissa, Idque 1. ut Christus ab utroque sexu innocentiae testimonium reportaret. 2. ut innocentiam Christi omnibus publicè manifestaret. 3. ut Pilatus admoneretur, ne innocentem damnaret. Addit Grotius h. l. fieri potuisse, ut Pilati uxor fuerit mulierθεοσεβὴς. Sed haec sententia vix apud alios meretur applausum. Nec favet etiam sententiae Grotii, quòd à Deo illi somnium fuerit immissum. Constat enim, quòd aliàs etiam Ethnicis, nondum ad veram Ecclesiam conversis, atq; impiis in Ecclesiâ à Deo immittātur somnia quaedam μαντικὰ, praesertim terribilia, ceu ex Gen. 20, 3.c. 31, 24.c. 41, 1.Dan. 2, 1.c. 4, 2. ostendit B. P. in H. E. l. c. Non praetereunda hoc loco somniorum distinctio, quòd alia nempe sint δεὺπεμπτα seu θεὁπνευςα h. e. à Deo immissa vel divina, cuiusmodi in Sc. S. passim commemorantur, vid. Genes. c. 20, 6.281. 32.c. 31, 24.c. 37, 5. seqq. c. 40, 12.c. 41 1. seqq. Dan. 2, 27.c. 4, 16. in N. T. Matth. 1, 21.c. 2, 12. 13.19.Act. 16, 9. ac de his intelligenda quoque promissio divina Numer. 12, 6. (Referri hue solet somnium illud Antonii, quo de Sozomenus lib. 6. c. 5. item quod refertur ab eodem lib. 6. c. 2. his verbis: Eodem die Didymus Philosophus Ecclesiasticus, Alexandriae degens ac propter Imperatoris (Iuliani) adversùs Ecclesias obstinationem contristatus, cùm quòd ille seductus esset, tum quòd Ecclesiae contemnerentur, ieiunavit & Deo hâc de causa supplicavit: & quoniam eâ curâ premebatur, nihil cibi, ne nocte quidem ingruente, accepit, sed sic in sede constitutus in somnum incidit: ac velut in ecstasin raptus. Visum est ipsi, videre se equos albosin cursantes, & eos, qui illis insidebant, quasi praeconis voce clamantes, annunciate Didymo, hoc die circa hanc horum occisum esse Iulianum, & is hoc Athanasio Episcopo significet. Subiungit Sozomenus: Et haec quidē cum ab amico & familiari Iuliani, tum à Philosopho visa, sic gesta esse percepi, & neuter ex illis in his quae vidit (nam de familiari illo Iuliani pariter somnium de Imperatoris Iuliani morte pullò ante narraverat idem) à veritate aberravit, sicut postea patuit. Conf. gemella apud Theodor. lib. 5. H. E. c. 24.) De divinis insomniis seu quae divinitus immissa sunt, constat ferè, quòd singularem quendam aculeum hominum animis infigant, unde etiam à naturalibus dignosci etiam quodammodo possunt. Licet verò adhuc agat Deus quandoq; cum piis hominibus per somnia, admonendo illos de futuris periculis vel aliis quibusdam eventibus: minimè tamen in doctrinâ vel fidei articulis per somnia ampliùs monere homines solet, cùm habeamus verbum DEI sat clarè revelatum. Porrò alia somnia sunt διαβολικὰ, à diabolo DEI permissione immissa sive diabolica, adeoque superstitiosa, de quibus intelligenda sunt dicta Deut. 13. 1.Ierem. 23, 16.25.c. 27, 9.c. 29, 8.Zach. 10, 2. Huc referri quoq; solent illa somnia, quibus Deus terruisse Iobum memoratur Iobi 7, 14 nempe per Satanam. Alia denique somnia sunt φυσικὰnaturalia, sive, ut ita loquamur, humana, quat. nempe ex corporis animiq; constitutione oriuntur. corporis quidem, ab humorum diversa dispositione animi autem ex interna commotione, figuras aliquas sibi formantis, vel res paulò ante gestas, in memoriam sibi revocantis, vel ab aliqua corporis affectione commoti, vel metu aut gaudio insolito concitati &c. ac de his intelligendus Salomon est, Ecclesiastae 5, 2. 6. item Siracides c. 34, 1. 2. 3. 7. In genere autem de somniis iudicandum ex verbo DEI & eventu esse, benè monent Orthodoxi. Quo facit Ier. 28. 9. Equibus hactenus allatis patet tum quòd neq; cum Xenophane & Epicuraeis, de quibus La-ritus, omnibus insomniis simpli iter deroganda fides sit, tum quòd nec cum Protagora & Stoicis omnibus tribuenda sit fides vel iis credendū. Confer plura huc facientia apud B. D. Rungium Comment. in Gen. p. 576. 856. 1076. ac 1159. B. D. Gesnerus in Gen. p. 562. seqq. B. D. Dietricus tum in libr. Sap. c. 14. p. 699 seqq. tum in peculiari tractatu seu discursu Philosophico Theologico de Insomniis. B. Par. H. E. & in Dispp. Elencht. dd. II. it. Comm. in Gen. p. 591. 706. 709. 716. B. B. D. Bald. Cas. Consc. p. 804. 810. seqq. Schickardus Bechinath Happer. p. 9. Franc. Torreblanca in Daemonol p. 142. seqq. item p. 259. 260. Pelargus Comm. in Matth. p. 31, 32.) *

## 27:21
* (v. 21. Whom do you wish that I release? Q. here, whether Pilate truly wished to release Christ? Rupert denies it, and thinks that Pilate feigned it like a fox: but Augustine affirms it more correctly, and applies to this Luke ch. 23, 20. & Acts 13, 28. Nor yet is Pilate to be judged innocent on that account of the death of Christ, since he himself ought by no means to have consented to the most iniquitous demands of the Jews concerning releasing the robber Barabbas, and crucifying the most innocent Christ, but rather to have resisted them by force. Whence he also paid the just penalties of his injustice, as among others B. D. Frantzius shows at length in De Sc. S. Interpret. Orac. 139. p. 1315. et seqq. Conf. & B. Par. in H. E.) *

* (They said, Barabbas, Beautifully Isidore of Pelusium lib. 1. ep 292. It is no wonder, that the city of blood, sons of murderers, freed from the danger of death Barabbas, the companion of their crimes and a murderer, and let him go as if innocent. For since they cared little for slaughters, as those who had been accustomed to slaughters, they now granted pardon to the authors of slaughters, now on the contrary against the storehouse of life τῷ τῆς ζωῆς καὶ ἀφθαρσίας ταμείῳ and immortality, they brought in the cross and burial.) *

Latin:

* (v. 21. Quem vultis dimittam. Q. hîc, an verè Pilatus Christum voluerit dimittere? Negat Rupertus, putatque, Pilatum instar vulpis simulasse: sed rectiùs affirmat Augustinus, facitq; huc Luc. c. 23, 20. & Act. 13, 28. Neque tamen innocens propterea censendus Pilatus â morte Christi est, quippe cùm ipse minimè iniquissimis Iudaeorum postulatis de latrone Bar. rabbâ dimittēdo, ac Christo innocentissimo crucifigendo annuere debuisset, sed potiùs vi illis resistere. Unde etiam iustas iniustitiae poenas luit, ceu inter alios prolixè ostendit B. D. Frantzius de Sc. S. Interpret. Orac. 139. p. 1315. seqq. Conf. & B. Par. in H. E.) *

* (Dixerunt, Barrabbam, Pulchrè isid. Pelusiota lib. 1. ep 292. Nil mirum, quòd urbs sanguinum, athomicidarum filii, facinorum suorum socium & homicidam Barrabbam mortu periculo liberarunt, ac velut insontem missum fecerunt. Nam cùm parum de caedibus laborarent, ut qui caedibus assuevissent, nunc caedium autoribus veniam impertiebant, nunc contrà vitae atimmortalitatis promtuario, ( τῷ τῆς ζωῆς καὶ ἀφθαρσίας ταμείῳcrucem ac sepulturam inducebant.) *

## 27:22
* (v. 22. What then shall I do with Jesus? Is this indeed the way of a just judge, to act with the accused according to the whim of the accusers?) *

Latin:

* (v. 22. Quid igitur faciam Iesu? Hoccine verò iusti iudicis est, pro lubitu accusatorum agere cum accusato?) *

## 27:23
* (v. 23. But the governor said: What evil has he done. Sweetly Anselm: What have you done, sweetest boy, that you should be judged thus? what have you committed, O most loving youth, that you should be treated so vilely? What is your crime? what is your guilt? what is the cause of death? what is the occasion of condemnation? I am the cause of your pain, the guilt of your slaughter. I am the bruise of your passion, the labor of your torment, the merit of your way, the shame of your vengeance. Conf. entirely Is 53.1. Pet. 2, 24.2. Cor. 5. 21.

Bernard: O good Jesus, what is it to you? We ought to have died, and do you pay the penalty? We have sinned, and do you suffer? A work without example, grace without merit, charity without measure.) * σταυρωθήτω. [Let him be crucified.] Conf. [Compare] Actor.

* σταυρωθήτω. Conf. Acts 21:36c. 22:22 Crucifixion was indeed a most ignominious punishment. See Cicero in the last Oration against Verres. Lipsius on the Cross, where he treats of this matter ex professo, so to speak; to which may also be added Cardinal Baronius in the Annals, vol. 1, 2, 3. Bisciola in the Epitome of the Annals. Against these, however, Isaac Casaubon rightly asserts that crucifixion was not an ordinary punishment of the Jews, such as were otherwise stoning, burning, beheading, strangulation: but was transferred from the Romans to the Jews, as the most learned M. I. E. Bornitius, a friend most dear to me while he lived for his singular candor of mind, piety, and erudition, proved learnedly against Philippus Caroli, who strives to bring aid to Baronius, in a special dissertation on the cross of the Hebrews.) *

Latin:

* (v. 23. Praeses autem dixit: Quid mali fecit. Suaviter Anselmus: Quid fecisti, dulcissime puer, ut sic iudicareris? quid commisisti, ô amantissime iuvenis, ut tam viliter tractareis? Quod scelus tuum? quae noxtua? quae est causa mortis? quae occasio damnationis? Ego sum tui causa doloris, tua culpa occisionis. Ego tuae passionis livor, tui cruciatûs labor, tuae viae meritum, tuae vindictae flagitium. Conf. omninò Es 53.1. Petr. 2, 24.2. Corinth. 5. 21.

Bernhardus: ô bone Iesu, quid tibi est? Mori nos debuimus, & tu solvis? nos peccavimus, & tu luis? opus sine exemplo, gratia sine merito, charitas sine modo.) *

* σταυρωθήτω. Conf. Actor. 21, 36.c. 22, 22. Erat verò crucisixio ignominiossimum supplicium. Vid. Cicero in Verrem Orat. ultimâ. Lipsius de Cruce, ubi de hâc materia ex professo, ut ita loquar, agit; quibus adiūgi quoq; possunt Card. Baronius in Anal. t. 1. 2. 3. Bisciola in Epit. Annal. Contra eosdem verò rectè adservit Isaacus Casaubonus, quòd crucifixio non fuerit supplicium Iudaeorū ordinarium, qualia aliàs erant lapidatio, ustio, decollatio, strangulatio: sed à Romanis ad Iudaeos translatum, prout eruditè contra Philippum Caroli, qui Baronio opem ferre satagit, evicit Doctissimus M. I. E. Bornitius, Amicus, ob singularem animi candorem, pietatem ac eruditionem, dum viveret, mihi carissimus, in pecul. dissert. de cruce. Ebraeorum.) *

## 27:24
* (v. 24. Having taken water, he washed his hands. Origen on this deed says thus: He used a Jewish custom, wishing to appease them regarding the innocence of Christ, not only by words but also by the deed itself. That custom was indeed accepted among the Jews, see Deut. 21:6Ps. 26:6 Josephus, book 12, Antiquities of the Jews, ch. 11. (Regard is also had to this in Gittin, fol. 56, 1, where it is read: ובעי לכפורῙ ייה: קודשא בוך חוא ῑעי לחרוי ῑיתיה i.e., The Holy One, blessed be He (that is, God) desires to lay waste His house and desires to wash His hands. that is, to declare that He is innocent, since His people have drawn that punishment upon themselves by their sins.) Meanwhile, among other peoples also, they designated purity by the element of water. On which matter Grotius brings forward some things from Demosthenes, Sophocles, and others on this passage. Conf. vol. 1, Academic Disputations of Mr. Dilherr, p. 202 and 503. Casaubon, notes on this passage. Taubmann on Virgil, likewise Caspar Barth in Adversaria, p. 1096.) *

* I am innocent &c. Titus of Bostra, or whoever the author of the Commentary under his name is, on ch. 23:22 of Luke: Although he washed his hands and said he was innocent, nevertheless that permission was of a little-manly spirit, he conducted that matter most cowardly: for he ought not to have delivered him to them at all, but rather to have snatched him away, just as the tribune later did Paul, Acts 21:33 Similar things are held by Augustine, sermon 118.

on the Time, and Leo, sermon 8 on the Passion. Furthermore, that it was of ancient custom that judges, about to condemn someone according to the laws, would testify with hands raised to the Sun, ἀθῶοιὑπάρχειν τού αἷματος τοῦ α-σθρώπου, is from book 2 of the Apostolic Constitutions of Clement, ch. 52, as Grotius proves in this place.)

(Of the blood of this just man. Compare entirely Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, ep. 128, Leo the Great, sermon 7, The shedding of the blood of the just for the unjust was so powerful for a privilege, so rich for a price, that if the whole body of captives believed in their redeemer, no tyrannical chains would hold them. Compare entirely the sayings of Holy Scripture Is. 52, 11.Jer. 23, 5.c. 33, 15. above v. 19. Acts 3, 14.c. 7, 52.1 Pet. 2, 18. Christ is therefore Just not only οὀσιωδῶς, but also ἐνεργητικῶς. Compare Rom. 10, 4.Gal. 2, 17.2 Tim. 4, 8.)

Latin:

* (v. 24. Acceptâ aquâ lavit manus. Origenes de hoc facto ita: Iudaico usus est more, volens eos de Christi innocentiâ non solùm verbis, sed etiam ipso facto placare. Fuit quidem mos ille apud Iudaeos receptus, vid. Deut. 21, 6.Ps. 26, 6. Ioseph. l. 12. A. I. c. 11. (Huc quoque respectus habetur in Gittin fol. 56. 1. ubi legitur: ובעי לכפורῙ ייה: קודשא בוך חוא ῑעי לחרוי ῑיתיה i. e. Sanctus benedictus ille (h. e. Deus) cupit vastare domum suam & cupit lavare manus suas. h. e. declarare quòd innocens sit, cùm populus eius peccatis suis istam poenam sibi attraxerit.) Interea apud alios quoq; populos puritatem elemento aquae designabant. Quam in rem nonnulla è Demosthene, Sophocle, aliis adfert Grotius in h. l. Conf. t. 1. Dispp. Acad. Dn. Dilherri p. 202. & 503. Casaubon. not. ad h. l. Taubmannus in Virgil. it. Casp. Barthius in Advers. p. 1096.) *

* (Innocens ego sum &c. Titus Bostrensis, vel quicunqe autor Comment. sub eius nomine. in c. 23, 22. Lucae: Tametsi lavit manus seinnocentem esse dicebat, nollu tamen parùmvirilis animi fuit illa permissio, ignavissimèid admodùm gessit: oportebat enim nullatemis illum eis tradere, quin potiùs eripere, sicuti posteatribunus Paulum,Act. 21. 33. Similia habēt Angust. serm. 118.

de Tempore, ac Leo serm. 8. de Passione. Coeterùm moris antiqui fuisse, ut iudices ex legibus aliquem damnaturi, manibus ad Solem elevatis testarentur, ἀθῶοιὑπάρχειν τού αἷματος τοῦ α-σθρώπου, è lib. 2. Constit. Apostol. Clem. c. 52. probat Grotius in h. l.) *

* (A sanguine huius iusti. Conf. omninò Isid. Pelus. l. 1. ep. 128. Leo M. serm. 7. Effusio sangvinis iusti pro iniustis tam potens fuit ad privilegium, tam dives ad pretium, ut si universitas captivorum in redemtorem suum crederet, nullum tyrannica vin ula retinerent. Confer omninò dicta Sc. S. Es. 52, 11.Ierem 23. 5.c. 33, 15. suprà v. 19. Actor. 3, 14.c. 7, 52.1. Petr. 2, 18. Est igitur Christus Iustus non solùm οὀσιωδῶς, verùm etiam ἐνεργητικῶς. Conf. Rom. 10, 4.Gal. 2, 17.2. Tim. 4, 8.) *

## 27:25
(v. 25. His blood be upon us. We have dealt elsewhere with this imprecation. See the Philosophical Disputation held under the presidency of Mr. Dilherr, Position 3. Among the Disputations of Mr. Dilherr, vol. 2, p. 121, following. Compare the same Disputations, p. 27. H. Grotius treats in this place of the ancient custom of devoting not only oneself but also one's children. This imprecation was fulfilled: for it is evident that the Jews expiated so horrible a crime not only with eternal but also with temporal punishments. To have Christ scourged and crucified, they moved Pilate; many of them were in turn scourged and tortured and affixed to a cross in the siege of Jerusalem, as Josephus testifies, book 6, on the Jewish War, ch. 12. Indeed, as Jerome writes, this imprecation persists to the present day upon the Jews, and the blood of the Lord is not taken away from them. Compare the same, treating this very argument at greater length, epistle to Dardanus, which is 129.)

Latin:

* (v. 25. Sangvis eius super nos. De imprecatione hâc alibi egimus. Vid. Disp. Philos. sub praesid. Dn. Dilherri habitam, Posit. 3. Inter Dispp. verò Dn. Dilh. t. 2. p. 121. seqq. Conf. eaed. Dispp. p. 27. De more veteri non se modò sed & liberos devovendi, agit H. Grotius in h. l. Impleta haec fuit imprecatio: neq; enim solùm aeternis, verùm etiam temporalibus suppliciis tam horrendum scelus Iudaeos expiasse constat. Christum ut flagellaretur & crucifigeretur, Pilatum moverunt, plurimi eorum rursus flagellati & praecruciati cruci affixi in obsidione Hierosol. teste Iosepho l. 6. de B. I. c. 12. Quin, ut scribit Hieronymus, perseverat usin praesentem diem haec imprecatio super Iudaeos, & sangvis Domini non aufertur ab eis. Conf. idem, prolixiùs hoc ipsum pertractans argumentum, epist. ad Dardan. quae est 129.) *

## 27:26
(v. 26. He delivered him, when he had scourged him, to be crucified, not because scourging according to Roman laws ought to precede crucifixion, Pilate ordered Christ to be scourged, as indeed Erasmus thinks, following Jerome in this place, but because he desired Christ to be set free, he hoped it would happen that in this way the cruelty of the Jews would be satisfied to some extent, and thus they themselves would seek the release of Christ. See entirely John 18, 39.c. 19, 43. Otherwise, however, it is by no means denied that those to be crucified were previously scourged. See Lipsius, book 2, on the cross, ch. 2. Muretus, Animadversions on Seneca, p. 775. Let Jerome in this place be added. Furthermore, it was Flagellation among the Romans was a vile punishment for slaves, as is evident from the ff. de poenis l. servorum, and l. Portia & Sempronia. Whence Paul, having been scourged Acts 16, 37. 38., expostulated gravely. If, however, any who were already condemned to death were scourged, even though they were otherwise free men, some report that they were. See also concerning flagellation among the Romans Grotius on v. 19 of this chapter, Barthius Advers. p. 22. 42. Rosinus Antiquit. Rom. lib. 6. c. 31. Barnabas Brissonius, President of the Paris Senate and Assessor of the Royal Consistory, in his most noble work de Formulis & Solemnibus pop. Rom. Verbis lib. V. pag. 481. 482. Furthermore, the sayings Gen. 49, 11. Job 16, 15. Ps. 72, 14. Ps. 129, 3. Matt. 20, 19. are accustomed to be taken concerning the scourging of Christ. Would that through those wounds, which Christ received in his scourging for our sake, we might behold his heart, and the bowels of his love, according to that: You see how love is carved into the whole body. *

Latin:

* (v. 26. Flagellatum tradidit, ut crucifigeretur, non quia flagellatio iuxta leges Romanas praecedere debebat crucifixionem, Pilatus Christum flagellari iussit, uti quidem Erasmus putat, sequutus Hieronymum in h. l. sed quia Christum liberatum cupiebat, sperabat fore, ut Iudaeorum crudelitati hoc modo ali quatenus satisfieret, sicque ipsi dimissionem Christi peterent. Vid. omninò Ioh. 18, 39.c. 19, 43. Aliàs tamen minimegrave; negatur, quòd crucifigendi priùs fuerint flagellati. Vid. Lipsius l. 2. de cruce c. 2. Muretus Animadv. in Senecam p. 775. Addatur Hieronymus in h. l. Erat porrò flagellatio apud Romanos vile supplicium servorum, ceu patet ex ff. de poenis l. servorum, ac l. Portia & Sempronia. Unde Paulus flagellatus Act. 16, 37. 38. graviter expostulabat. Si qui tamen damnati iam ad mortem erant, eos, licet homines alioquin liberos, flagellatos fuisse, nonnulli produnt. Vid. quoque de flagellatione apud Rom. Grotius ad v. 19. h. cap. Barthius Advers. p. 22. 42. Rosinus Antiquit, Rom. lib. 6. c. 31. Barnabas Brissonius, Senatûs Paris. praeses ac Regii Consistorii Adsessor in nobilissimo opere de Formulis & Solemnibus pop. Rom. Verbis lib. V. pag. 481. 482. Porrò de flagellatione Christi accipi solent dicta Genes. 49, 11.Iob. 16, 15.Ps. 72, 14.Ps. 129, 3.Matth. 20, 19. Utinam verò per illa vulnera, quae Christus in flagellatione nostri causâ suscepit, intueremur cor eius, & amoris viscera, iuxta illud: Cernis ut in toto corpore sculptus amor.) *

## 27:28
* (v. 28. They clothed him with a scarlet cloak. See Isidor. Pelus. lib. 1. ep. 251. Christ suffered himself to be clothed in a scarlet garment, that he might signify that he had taken upon himself our sins, which were red as scarlet. Is. 1, 18. Moreover, Mark and John call this tunic purple. From this, Ambrose in c. 23 of Luke suspects that these were different garments, and that Christ was clothed in both. But Athan. serm. de cruce & pass., Euthymius, and others more correctly establish that it was the same, because the scarlet color is similar to the purple. See L. Si cui lana D. de Legatis 3. §. versicoloribus. The chlamys was otherwise a purple royal garment. See Plut. in the life of Eumenes, also Claudin. l. 2. de Rapt. Proserp., Cassiod. l. 2. Varr. Ep. 2., Valer. Maximus l. 1. Mem. 6., Trebellius Pollio in Saturn. 21. Tyr. Although these things were done by the soldiers as an insult for a feigned kingdom: yet Christ willed to be clothed in purple, because he was about to receive the kingdom of the whole world. Ps. 2, 6. 7. also, because he acquired it for himself by fighting and shedding blood. For formerly in war they wore red garments. See Alex. ab Alexandro l. 1. c. 10. Ridiculously Corn. à Lapide in this place: Purple is given hence to Cardinals by the Pontiff, that it may remind them to shed their blood for Christ and the Church, when there is need. How much more correctly a certain distinguished and most celebrated Jurisconsult, and the same a Councilor of the King of the Spains in Brabant, Therefore Cardinals wear a purple tunic, a man at Louvain affirmed to me, because they breathe blood, that is, they are intent upon this, that they might disturb all things with wars. He confirmed this very thing with several examples, which I willingly omit here.

Latin:

* (v. 28. Circumdederunt ei chlamydem coccinam. Vid. Isidor. Pelus. lib. 1. ep. 251. Christus passus est, se coccinâ veste circumdari, ut significaret, se suscepisse in se peccata nostra, quae rubra erant, ut coccus,Es. 1, 18. Coeterùm Marcus & Iohannes vocant tunicam hanc purpuream. Suspicatur hinc Ambrosius in c. 23. Lucae, fuisse has vestes diversas, ac utrâvestitum fuisse Christum. Sed Athan. serm. de cruce & pass. Euthymius & alii rectiùs statuunt, fuisse eandem, quia color coccineus similis est purpureo. Vid. L. Si cui lana D. de Legatis 3. §. versicoloribus. Chlamys aliàs purpurea fuit regius vestitus. Vid. Plut. in vita Eumenis. it. Claudin. l. 2. de Rapt. Proserp. Cassiod. l. 2. Varr. Ep. 2. Valer. Maximus l. 1. Mem. 6. Trebellius Pollio in Saturn. 21. Tyr. Licet verò haec ad exprobrationem velut affectati regni à militibus fierent: voluit tamen Christus purpurâ vestiri, quia regnum totius mundi accepturus erat. Ps. 2, 6. 7. it. quia illud pugnando & sangvinem fundendo sibi acquisivit. Olim enim in bello russas gerebant vestes. Vid. Alex. ab Alexandro l. 1. c. 10. Ridiculè Corn. à Lapide in h. l. Data hinc Cardinalibus à Pontifice purpura, ut illos moneat, pro Christo & Ecclesia sangvinem fundere, cùm opus est. Quanto rectiùs insignis quidam ac celeberrimus Iure Consultus, idemque Regis Hispaniarum in Brabantia Consiliarius, ideò Cardinalespurpuream gestare tunicam, mihi Lovanii affirmabat, quòd sangvinem spirent, hoc est in id intenti sint, quò bellis omnia turbent. Confirmabat hoc ipsum exemplis aliquot, quae lubens hîc omitto.) *

## 27:29
(v. 29. They placed a crown of thorns upon his head. Isid. Pelusiota l. 1. ep. 95. -πειδὴ κατάρας ἦν ἡ ἄκανθα γεώργιον, ἣν ἡ γῆ κατεδικάσθη με-ὰ τὴν ἡμετέραν παρὰβασιν, πᾶσαν θεραπεὺσαι ἐν ἑαυτὁ Κύριος παρε--ε-α. τούτουχάριν ἐκάν πᾶς ὡς νικηφόρος ἐςεφανωσατο Jerome, Cyril, and Tertullian in his book on the Soldier's Crown have similar things, cited by B. P. Harm. Ev. c. 194. p. 1910. But let us remember here, that it is by no means fitting for the members to be delicate under a head crowned with thorns, as Bernard speaks. A thing which lascivious monks also observe less, vainly persuading themselves that by their tonsure, by which they think the crown of thorns of Christ is represented, See Beda l. 5. Hist. Angl. c. 22.) they sufficiently conform themselves to Christ. Christ is Him among the thorns, Cant. 2, 2. Cons. B. Par. Postill. Salom. Dom. 6. post Trinit.

Latin:

* (v. 29. Coronam de spinis imposuerunt capitieius. Isid. Pelusiota l. 1. ep. 95. -πειδὴ κατάρας ἦν ἡ ἄκανθα γεώργιον, ἣν ἡ γῆ κατεδικάσθη με-ὰ τὴν ἡμετέραν παρὰβασιν, πᾶσαν θεραπεὺσαι ἐν ἑαυτὁ Κύριος παρε--ε-α. τούτουχάριν ἐκάν πᾶς ὡς νικηφόρος ἐςεφανωσατο Similia habēt Hieronymus, Cyrillus ac Tertullianus lib. de Cor. militis, adducti à B. Angl. c. 22.) * satis se Christo conforment Est Christus Illum inter spinas, Cant. 2, 2. Cons. B. Par. Postill. Salom. Dom. 6. post Trinit.) *

## 27:31
(v. 31. They clothed him in his own garments, so that he might be more easily recognized by all on the way, yet so that no ignominy might be lost, they do not remove the crown of thorns.)

Latin:

* (v. 31. Induerunt eum vestimentis suis, quò ab omnibus nempe in viâ faciliùs cognosceretur ne tamen quid ignominiae decederet, coronam spineam non tollunt.) *

## 27:32
(v. 32. ἐξερχόμενοι. Going out: for Christ was crucified outside the city, see Ebr. 13, 12. That this was done according to the custom of both the Hebrews and the Romans, Grotius shows at length in this place.)

(They found a man Simon &c. Tertullian mentions in his book on Prescription c. 46. and l. 5. against Marcion, also Aug. 1. on Heresies, and also Euseb. l. 4. H. E. c. 8. that Basilides and Marcion dreamed that Christ had so blinded the eyes of the Jews that, while they were crucifying Simon, they thought they were crucifying Christ, who nevertheless had withdrawn himself.)

(A Cyrenian. see Act. 2, 10.c. 6, 9. Ioseph. l. 7. de B. I. C. 31)

( ἠγγὰρευσαν. Concerning the origin of the word ἀγγαρεύειν it was treated above at c. 41. Conf. Buxtorf. Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 13. & 2371. Don Laur Ramirez Pentecont. p. 146. seqq. Meurs. Glossar. Graeco-Bararum, Matth. Martin. in Lex. Etym. Here I add at least this, that the Persian interpreter in this place does not use the word derived from the Angari of the Persians, who himself nevertheless elsewhere μίλιον translates by a parasang, which according to Festus, is a space of thirty stadia among the Persians.) *

* (That he might take up his cross. At first indeed the Jews had imposed the cross upon Christ himself, afterwards, not at all touched by mercy, but as Lyranus rightly determines in this place, seeing that he was failing in strength and proceeding slowly, or perhaps would succumb entirely to the burden, impatient of delay they compelled Simon, so that he might carry the cross either entirely (which Laurentius Ramirez in Pentecont. p. 143. thinks is openly proven from this place, and in this matter also alleges St. Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine) alone as far as Mount Calvary, or at least by carrying it in part, might help the Lord, (to which some think St. Luke c. 23. v. 26 refers) which Christ had previously carried alone through the city, John 19, 17. In the fact, however, that Christ himself carried the wood of the cross, not only is the custom of the Greeks and Romans to be observed, among whom it was the custom that those being crucified should carry their own cross, (and this Chrysostom clearly indicates, hom. 84, also referring to the same thing Plutarch writes in On the Delay of Divine Vengeance: each of the evildoers carries his own cross, but malice produces and fabricates for itself the of tortures within itself. See also Artemidorus l. 2. c. 41. and compare entirely Lipsius on the Cross, Gretser on the Cross, and others passim.) But the Lord also wished by this very thing to fulfill what was prefigured in Isaac, Gen. 22. as Tertullian noted in his book against the Jews c. 10. Nor yet was Isaac the type of Christ in this alone, but also in many other things, as in the most gentle address of the Father, in the separation of companions, the leading out, the binding, the exhibition of patience, etc. as B. Par. Com. shows in many places in Gen. p. 443. 444. where he also teaches how we ought to devoutly contemplate those mysteries proposed to us in the immolation of Isaac. Furthermore, Origen elegantly: It was fitting not only for him to take up his cross, but it was also fitting for us to carry it, fulfilling for ourselves a salutary forced service, for thus he himself decreed: He who does not take up his cross, etc. Matthew 10, 38. Athanasius observes on the Passion of the Lord, that our Savior carried the cross himself at the beginning for this reason, because he was tending toward death of his own accord; but again he had Simon carry it, so that it might be made known to all, that the Lord was undergoing death not for his own sake, but for the sake of men.) *

* Golgotha, which is the place of a skull. It is Hebrew גלגלת Gulgoleth, thence for the sake of euphony, with the letter ל, elided, it becomes Golgotha. That mountain is indeed seen to be designated by that name, because the skulls of the slain were left there, as indeed Jerome, Bede, Jansenius, Franciscus Lucas, Schindler, and others maintain, whom the Londoners also follow in the Appendix to the Polyglot Bible. Cardinal Baronius and the Jesuits Lorinus and Gretser indeed oppose this opinion, that among the Jews there was no use of the sword and beheading, but only of stoning, crucifixion, and burning. But Cornelius à Lapide answers by denying that, and proving the contrary from Sanhedrin and Petrus Gregorius, book 31, Synt. chapter 16, to which can be added Hugo Grotius on this passage, though denying that the bare bones of heads remained there long after death. Cornelius thinks this is clear above all from the fact that Herod Antipas beheaded John the Baptist; and his nephew James, the brother of John the Apostle, Acts 12. Besides, even if not of the beheaded, yet the skulls of the stoned, the burned, and the crucified could have lain there. There are those who think it is called from Adam's skull, so it seemed to Athanasius and Epiphanius; because, namely, it was once found there. Indeed, Cornelius à Lapide on this passage testifies that it is the common opinion of the Fathers, Origen, Tertullian, Augustine, Cyril, and others, that it was so called because Adam was buried there, whom Christ redeemed there with his blood, dripping from the cross, and recalled to the life of grace, according to that Ephes. 5, 14. Others believe this mountain obtained that name because it was round like a skull. Let B. Par. Harm. Evang. Pass., Matthias Martinius in Lex. Etym., Pasor in Etym. Nominum propriorum, and others passim be compared. Furthermore, it is to be noted, 1. that Mount Moriah was very close to Mount Calvary, or rather one and the same mountain divided into two hills, on which Abraham was commanded by GOD to sacrifice his son, concerning which type Tertullian advers. Iudaeos, August. de Temp. fer. 6. post prim Dom. serm. 1., Leonh. Marius, Hugo de S. Charo, and others on chapter 2 of Genesis, and Lauretus in Sylva Allegoriarum can be seen. 2. That Christ willed to be crucified outside Jerusalem, h. l. and Heb. 13, 11. and following, to indicate that the virtue of his passion and death was to be transferred to all nations, so that thus, as Leo speaks in sermon 9 on the passion, the cross of Christ might not be the altar of a temple, but of the world. 3. That it is evident from the circumstances of the text and the manner of the crucifixion (concerning which see among our own people B. D. Calixtus, Mr. Dilherrus on the cross, B. D. Quistorpius Annot. Bibl. on ch. 19, 15 of John, B. Par. Harm. Pass.; from the Papists Lipsius, Gretserus and others on the Cross, Corn. â Lapide on the Gospels; from the philologists and jurists Petrus Faber book 2 semestr., Füllerus Miscell. book 4 ch. 12. -an. Gruterus in Senec. 789.) that Christ felt most intense pains in the crucifixion. 4. That Christ willed to be crucified, first that he might become a curse for us, Deut. 2, 15.Gal. 3, 13. Then that just as the first-formed sinned by extending their hands to the forbidden tree, so Christ might pay for this sin by extending his hands to the wood of the cross. see Augustin. in Append. de divers. serm. 4. Some add this mystical cause, that hanging in the air, between heaven and earth, he willed to reconcile the heavenly to the earthly. Likewise, that he might show that from the rising of the sun even to its setting a great people gathered from all languages and tribes would come under his wings, as Tertullian speaks in book 4 de Incarn. Christi, ch. 26. Conf. also Athan. de Incarn. verbi. Corn. â Lapide reviews more causes from the Fathers in this place.) *

Latin:

* (v. 32. ἐξερχόμενοι.Exeuntes: nam Christus extra urbem crucifixus est, vid. Ebr. 13, 12. Factum vero id esse tum more Ebraeorum, tum Romanorum, prolixè ostendit Grotius h. l.) *

* (Invenerunt hominem Simonem &c. Memorant Tertull. lib. de Praescript. c. 46. ac. l. 5. contra Marcionem, it. Aug. 1. de Haeres. nec non Euseb. l. 4. H. E. c. 8. Basilidem & Marcionem somniasse, quòd Christus ita perstrinxerit Iudaeorum oculos, ut Simonem crucifigentes putarint, se Christum crucifigere, qui tamen sese subduxerit.) *

* (Cyrenaeum. vid. Act. 2, 10.c. 6, 9. Ioseph. l. 7. de B. I. C. 31) *

* ( ἠγγὰρευσαν. De origine verbi ἀγγαρεύειν actum suprà ad c. 41. Conf. Buxtorf. Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 13. & 2371. Don Laur Ramirez Pentecont. p. 146. seqq. Meurs. Glossar. Graeco-Bararum, Matth. Martin. in Lex. Etym. Hîc illud saltem addo, quòd interpres Persicus h. l. non utatur verbo ab Angaris Persarum deducto, qui ipse tamen aliàs μίλιον vertit per parasangam, quod iuxta Festum, apud Persas triginta stadiorum spatium est.) *

* (Ut tolleret crucem eius. Priùs quidem Iudaei ipsi Christo crucem imposuerant, postea, minimè misericordiâ tacti, sed ut rectè quostatuit Lyramus in h. l. videntes, quòd viribus defectus lentè progrederetur, vel fortè prorsus oneri succumberet, morae impatientes adegerunt Simonem, ut crucem vel totam (quod Laurentius Ramirez in Pentecont. p. 143. apertè ex h. l. convinci putat, & in hâc rem etiam S. Ambrosium, Hieronymum atque Augustinum allegat) ad montem usq; Calvariae solus portaret, vel saltem ex parte eam portando, Dominum iuvaret, (quo respicere quibusdam D. Lucas c. 23. videtur v. 26.) quam priùs per urbem Christus solus portaverat, Ioh. 19, 17. In eo verò, quòd Christus crucis lignum ipse portavit, non solum observanda consvetudo Graecorum Romanorumque est, uti apud quos moris erat, ut crucifigendi crucem portarent ipsi, (idque indicat clarè Chrysost. hom. 84. eodem respiciens quoq; Plutarch. in de tardâ Dei vindicta, scribit: corpore quidem quismaleficorum suam effert crucem, malitia autem cruciatuum quemin se, ex se gignit & fabricatur. Vid. etiā Artemidorus l. 2. c. 41. ac conf. omninò Lipsius de Cruce, Gretserus de Cruce, alii passim.) Verùm voluit etiam hoc ipso implere Dominus, quod in Isaaco praefiguratum fuit, Gen. 22. ceu Tertull. notavit lib. adversùs Iudaeos c. 10. Neque tamen in hoc solo Isaacus Christi typus fuit, sed etiam in aliis plurimis, uti in blandissimâ Patris compellatione, in comitum separatione, eductione, ligatione, patientiae exhibitione &c. uti multis ostendit B. Par. Com. in Gen. p. 443. 444. ubi etiam docet, quomodo ista in Isaaci immolatione proposita nobis mysteria devotè contemplari debeamus. Coeterùm Origenes eleganter: Non solùm eum conveniebat accipere crucem suam, sed & nos conveniebat portare eam, salutarem nobis angariam adimplentes, sic enim ipse sanxit: Qui non accipit crucem suam &c.Matth. 10, 38. Observat Athanasius de Pass. Domini, Salvatorem nostrum crucem ideò initiò gestasse ipsum, quòd ultrò ad mortem tenderet; rursus autem gestasse Simonem, quò omnibus innotesceret, Dominum non sui, sed hominum causâ mortem obire.) *

* (Golgotha, quod est calvariae locus. Ebr. est גלגלתGulgoleth, inde euphoniae causâ, elisâ litt. ל, sit Golgotha. Designitus verò mons ille videtur eo nomine, quòd interemtorum calvariae ibi relictae, uti quidem Hieronymus, Beda, Iansenius, Franciscus Lucas, Schindlerus aliiq; volunt, quos sequuntur etiam Londinenses in Appendice ad Biblia Polyglotta. Opponunt quidem sententiae huic Cardinalis Baronius it. Iesuitae Lorinus & Gretserus, quòd apud Iudaeos gladii & decollationis non fuerit usus, sed tantùm lapidationis, crucifixionis, & combustionis. Respondet autem Corn. â Lapide, id negando, ac contrarium probando ex Sanhedrin ac Petro Gregorio l. 31. Synt. c. 16. quibus addi quopotest Hugo Grotius in h. l. negans tamen, mansisse ibi diu post mortem nuda capitum ossa. Cumprimis id liquere existimat Cornelius inde, quòd Herodes Antipas decollarit Ioh. Baptistam; & eius Nepos Iacobum, fratrem Io. hannis Apostoli,Act. 12.Praeterea si vel maximè non decollatorum, attamen lapidatorum, combustorum & crucifixorum crania iacere ibi potuisse. Sunt qui dictum putant ab Adami calvaria, ita Athanasio atq; Epiphanio visum; quòd nempe ibi aliquando inventa fuerit. Quin Corn. â Lapide in h. l. testatur, communē Patrum, Origenis, Tertulliani, Augustini, Cyrilli ac aliorum sententiam esse, ita dictum esse, quòd Adam ibi fuerit sepultus, quem Christus ibi sanguine suo, à cruce destillante, redemerit, & ad vitam revocarit gratiae, iuxta illud Ephes. 5, 14. Alii montem hunc id nominis sortitum esse credunt, quòd rotundus fuerit instar Calvariae. Conferantur B. Par. Harm. Evang. Pass. Matthias Martinius in Lex. Etym. Pasor. in Etym. Nominum propriorum, alii passim. Porrò notandum, 1. quòd monti Calvariae maximè vicinus fuerit, vel potiùs unus idemque mons in duos colles dissectus, mons Moria, in quo Abraham â DEO iussus fuit mactare filium suum, de quo typo videri possunt Tertllianus advers. Iudaeos August. de Temp. fer. 6. post prim Dom. serm. 1. Leonh. Marius, Hugo deS. Charo, aliiq; in c. 2. Gen. Lauretus in Sylva Allegoriarum. 2. Quòd Christus extra Ierusalem crucifigi voluerit, h. l. & Ebr. 13, 11. seqq. ut indicaret, virtutem suae passionis & mortis transferendam ad omnes gentes, ut ita, ceu loquitur Leo serm. 9. de passione, crux Christi non templi esset ara, sed mundi. 3. Quòd ex circumstantiis textûs ac more crucifixionis (quo de videndi è nostratibus B. D. Calixtus, Dn. Dilherrus de cruce, B. D. Quistorpius Annot. Bibl. ad c. 19, 15. Ioh. B. Par. Harm. Pass. è Pontificiis Lipsius, Gretserus & alii de Cruce, Corn. â Lapide in Evang. è Philologis & Ictis Petrus Faber l. 2. semestr. Füllerus Miscell. l. 4. c. 12. -an. Gruterus in Senec. 789.) pateat, Christum intensissimos sensisse in crucifixione dolores. 4. Quòd Christus crucifigi voluerit, primò ut fieret maledictum pro nobis, Deut. 2, 15.Gal. 3, 13. Deinde ut sicuti Protoplasti peccarunt, extendendo manus ad lignum vetitum, ita Christus pro hoc peccato lueret extendendo manus ad lignum crucis. vid. Augustin. in Append. de divers. serm. 4. Addunt nonnulli causam hanc mysticam, quòd pendens in aere, intercoelum & terram, coelites terrenis reconciliare voluerit. Item, ut ostenderet, ab ortu Solis usq; ad occasum magnum populum ex omnibus linguis & tribubus congregatum sub alas eius venturum, ut loquitur Tertullianus lib. 4. de Incarn. Christi, c. 26. Conf. & Athan. de Incarn. verbi. Plures causas è Patribus recenset Corn. â Lapide in h. l.) *

## 27:34
* (v. 34. Vinegar mixed with gall. But Mark ch. 15. 23. names myrrhed wine. Resp. 1. Some think that a fault of the writer lies here, and that for ὄξος one ought to read οἶνος, as it is in Mark. Thus decides Corn. â Lapide, who does not hesitate to write in this place, that both the Greek copies, and the Syriac (and the Persian, and the Arabic) and the Greek interpreters, Chrysostom, Titus of Bostra, Euthymius, Theophylact, read corruptly here -ξος for ὄιος, as the Vulgate version has. Theodore Beza also thinks this reading, which has οἶνο-,, is most true, inasmuch as Mark ch. 15, 23. itself confirms it. But although the Ethiopian also, and likewise both Hebrew Gospels of Matthew, nay even one or another Greek Codex, which the Londoners show in the various languages, favor the Vulgate: I think it is nevertheless rash to reject , witnesses from the whole East and West, (to whom Erasmus also adds Origen and Jerome; Alfonsus Salmeron vol. 10 tr. 35. p. 292 adds Hilary and the Greek interpreters commonly) without a most grave cause. 2. Others They judge that a fault of the scribe underlies it in Mark, and that οἶνος ought to be read in him instead of ὄξος.. But although the Persian version may have it so, it can by no means prejudice the reading of the original Greek text or of the other Oriental interpreters, the Syrian, the Arab, the Ethiopian, who consistently have wine in Mark. 3. Beza, although he judges that οἶνον: ought to be read here entirely, adds nevertheless that if even the Evangelist had written in Greek ὄξος, or in Syriac חלא, or in Hebrew חומק, he would not have signified vinegar, but spiced wine. On the contrary, Erasmus maintains that vinegar is rather to be understood, since there is not much difference between vinegar and acid wine, and that this agrees more with the Prophet, saying: they gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. ps. 69, 22. The same is the opinion of Ludovicus de Dieu, who therefore also judges that vinegar or acid wine is to be understood in Mark by οἶνον. 4. The same Erasmus rightly maintains that the same drink was not given to Christ here, which was given to him hanging on the cross. He adds: it appears that it was given twice, once before he was lifted onto the cross, by custom if I am not mistaken, which is also observed today: Again, when he was asking for it on the cross. Euthymius thinks that one drink is described by Matthew, another by Mark. And Salmeron, t. 10, tract 35, p. 293, maintains that this opinion is superior to the others, and therefore deservedly to be preferred. But it is clear from the context that one and the same drink is proposed by both Evangelists, by Matthew indeed here v. 34, but by Mark c. 15, 23. Meanwhile, we easily grant that Mark in the cited place speaks of another drink, and our Evangelist in v. 48, since Mark speaks of the drink which was given to Christ before the crucifixion, of which drink there is also talk here, but our author in v. 48 speaks of the drink which was offered to Christ when he was already driven onto the cross, and indeed in a sponge. 6. Cardinal Baronius, t. 1 Annal. A. 34, num. 95, thinks that wine was entirely offered to Christ, that it was called myrrhed because, having been poured into myrrh-cups, it provided a pleasant odor and taste. But he is refuted not only by Is. Casaubon in the Exercitations, Exerc. 16, c. 80. But he is also deserted by his own associates Conzenius, Corn. à Lapide, and others. Especially in this, while he maintains, that the soldiers gave that to Christ out of a feeling of compassion. The same opinion also pleases Maldonado in this place, Francisco Suarez, volume 1 on the 3rd part of Thomas, Disputation 36, section 3, and several other Papists. 6. The simplest opinion seems to be that certain pious women brought myrrhed wine, and that according to the custom of the nation, (Compare Proverbs 31, 6. Amos 2, 8. 9. Zechariah 12, 3. and add Drusius in Praet. Ramirez in Pentec. chapter 9, and likewise Lyranus in this place. Pliny, book 14, Natural History, chapter 13, and book 12, chapter 16, teaches that wines seasoned with the scent of myrrh were indeed most sumptuous.) but when they were prevented from approaching the Lord by the ferocious crowd, they gave it to the soldiers, who corrupted it with gall and other bitter matter, such as wormwood, according to Grotius in this place, and they even mixed in vinegar, so that they might fulfill their lust in mocking the Lord. And thus the Evangelist Mark wished to indicate the custom of that time, or the piety of the women; but ours [wished to indicate] the tyranny and cruelty of the soldiers. This method of reconciling the Evangelists pleases, among our own, Blessed D. Walther in Harm. Bibl. p. 803, Lord D. Friedlieb in this place, Blessed D. Calixtus in Conc. Ev. p. 397, compare also Blessed Par. H. E. p. 1951, among the Calvinists Casaubon in the cited place, and others)

He would not drink. Some think that Christ did not wish to drink that wine mingled with myrrh and gall because such a drink accelerates death; but He Himself wished to lay down His life of His own accord, Ioh. 10, 18. H. Grotius maintains that our Savior did not wish to drink it because such a drink was used to derange the mind, and, as it were, to induce drunkenness. Cf. also B. P. in Harm. Ev. l. c. Hackspan. Tract. de util. Lect. Rabb. p. 443.) * * (

Latin:

* (v. 34. Acetum cum felle mixtum. Ast Marcus c. 15. 23. nominat vinum myrrhatum. Resp. 1. quidam censent, scriptoris vitium hîc subesse, & pro ὄξος legi debere οἶνος, quomodo est apud Marcum. Itastatuit Corn. â Lapide, qui scribere h. l. non dubitat, tum Graeca exemplaria, tum Syrum (tum Persicum, tum Arabicum) tum Interpp. Graecos, Chrysostomum, Titum Bosterensem, Euthymium, Th-ophylactum corruptè hîc-ξοςlegere proὄιος,quomodo hab-t versio vulgata. Theodorus quoque Beza lectionem hanc, quae habet οἶνο-, verissimam putat, utpote quam confirmet ipse Marcus c. 15, 23. Astlicet Aethiops quoque, nec non utrumq; Evangelium Matthaei Ebraeum, quin unus quoque atq; alter Codex Grae us, quem monstrant Londinenses in LL, variis, Vulgato faveant: temerarium tamen puto, totex Oriente atque Occidente testes, (quibus Origenem atque Hieronymum quoque accenset Erasmus; Hilarium & Graecos Interpp. communiter Alfonsus Salmeron t. 10 tr. 35. p. 292.) absque gravissima causâ reiicere. 2. Alii apud Marcum vitium scriptoris subesse censent, ac pro οἶνος legi apud illum debere ὄξος. Astlicet Persa ita habeat, minimè tamen praeiudicare ille potest lectioni tum Graeci textûs originalis tum coeterorum Interpp. Orientalium, Syri, Arabis, AEthiopis, qui constanter apud Marcum habent vinum. 3. Beza, licet h. l. omninò legendum censet οἶνον: addit tamen, quòd si vel maximè Evangelista Graecè scripsissetὄξος,aut Syriacèחלא,aut Ebraicèחומק,non significarit tamen acetum, sed vinum conditum. Contrà Erasmus statuit, potiùs intelligendum acetum, cùm non multum intersit inter acetum & acidum vinum, idque magis congruere cum Propheta, dicente: dederunt in escam meam fel, & in siti mea potarunt me aceto. ps. 69, 22. Eadem est sententia Ludovici de Dieu, qui proinde etiam apud Marcum per οἶνον intelligendum censet acetum sive vinum acidum. 4. Idem Erasmus rectè statuit, non eundem potum hîc datum Christo, qui datus in cruce pendenti. Subdit: apparet, bis datum, semel ante, quam tolleretur in crucem, ex more nì fallor, quod & hodie servatur: Rursus in cruce poscenti. Euthymius existimat, alium potum describi â Matthaeo, alium â Marco. Atq; hanc sententiam coeteris praestantiorem esse, adeoq; meritò praeferendam statuit Salmeron t. 10. tract 35. p. 293 Sed ex contextu patet, unum eundemq; potum proponi ab utroq; Evangelistâ, â Matthaeo quidem hîc v. 34 â Marco autem c. 15, 23. Interea facilè largimur, quòd de alio potu loquatur Mar us l. c. & noster Evangelista v. 48. cùm Marcus loquatur de potu, qui Christo datus ante crucifixionem, de quo potu & hîc sermo est, noster verò v. 48. de potu, qui Christo in crucem iamtum acto porrectus, & quidem in spongiâ. 6. Cardinalis Baronius t. 1 Annal. A. 34. num. 95. existimat, omninò vinum Christo fuisse oblatum, myrrheumillud inde dictum, quòd inpocula Myrrhea infusum iucundum praebuerit odorem ac saporem. Sed refutatur non solùm ab Is. Casaubono in Exercitationibus, Exerc. 16. c. 80. Verùm etiam â propriis deseritur sociennis Conzenio, Corn. â Lapide, aliis. Maximè in eo, dum statuit, ex commiserationis affectu milites illud Christo dedisse. Eadem tamen sententia arridet quoq; Maldonato in h. l. Franc. Suarez t. 1. in 3. part. Thomae, Disp. 36. sect. 3. aliisq; non nullis Pontificiis. 6. Simplicissima videtur esse sententia, quòd mulieres quaedam piae attulerint vinum myrrhatum, idque more gentis, (Conf. Proverb. 31, 6. Amos. 2, 8. 9. Zach. 12, 3. ac adde Drusium in Praet. Ramirez in Pentec. c. 9. itemq; Lyratium in h. l. Lautissima vero fuisse vina Myrrhae odore condita, docet Plinius lib. 14. H. N. C. 13. ac lib. 12. c. 16.) cùm verò accedere Dominum, â ferociente turbâ impedirentur, dederint illud militibus, qui felle aliâq; materiâ amarâ, uti absynthio, iuxta Grotium h. l. corruperunt, quin acetum quoque admiscuerunt, ut suam in illudendo Domino implerent libidinem, Atque ita Evangelista Marcus indicare voluit illius temporis consvetudinem, vel muliercularum quotiùs pietatem; noster vero militum tyrannidem atque crudelitatem. Placet isthaec Evangelistas conciliandi ratio è nostratibus B. D. Walthero in Harm. Bibl. p. 803. Dn. D. Friedlieb in h. l. B. D. Calixto in Conc. Ev. p. 397. conf. etiam B. Par. H. E. p. 1951. è Calvinianis Casaubono l. c. aliis) *

* (Noluit bibere. Existimant nonnulli, Christum propterea vinum illud myrrhatum ac felle mixtū bibere noluisse, quòd talis potus mortem accelerat; ipse verò sponte animam deponere voluerit, Ioh. 10, 18. H. Grotius statuit, ideò Salvatorem nostrum bibere noluisse, quòd menti externandae talis potus adhiberetur, ac ebrietatem quasi conciliaret. Conf. etiam B. P. in Harm. Ev. l. c. Hackspan. Tract. de util. Lect. Rabb. p. 443.) *

## 27:35
v. 35. They crucified. Cf. the notes on v. 23. Furthermore, Hugo Grotius rightly advises in this place that Christ, as an author of sedition—though most falsely accused as such—was affixed to the cross by the dictatorial sentence of Pilate. Contrary to what Lactantius in lib. 4. Instit. Divin. c. 8. & Chrysostom in Orat. 2. de Eleem. supposed.) * * (

(They divided his garments etc., in such a way that from the outer cloak or toga they made four parts, by dissolving the seams, and so that a part fell to each soldier, (although indeed both here and in David Ps. 22, 19. Let the number be considered plural, yet it is certain that by an enallage of number it is placed for the singular; but concerning the inner tunic, because it was seamless, and so if it were divided, it would profit no one, they cast lots. Conf. more in Analect. to Ioh. 19, 23. 24.

(That it might be fulfilled. See Anal. above to c. 13, 14. The particle ἵνα in these and similar places, as Marc. 14, 49.Luc 2, 22.Ioh. 13, 18. is not causal, but demonstrative. For future sins are not predicted in Scripture so that they may happen, but because God, according to His omniscience, foresaw them as certainly future from the malice of those acting freely, therefore He predicted them in Holy Scripture. See B. D. Hafenreff. LL. Theol. p. 122. Furthermore, the place of Holy Scripture to which the Evangelist refers here is Psal. 22, 19. Although, therefore, the soldiers, according to the Roman custom (by which the spoils of the guilty fell to the executioners of the punishment, as Hug. Grotius in this place, and likewise Ramirez in Pentecont. c. 7. p. 81, show from Ulpian in L. Divus Adrianus 6. π. de bonis damnat.), divided Christ's garments among themselves, there is no doubt, however, that divine direction intervened here. Finally, that also is to be observed, that this whole member of this verse, ἵνα πληρωσθῇ etc., is missing in the most ancient and best-quality Greek Codices, just as the Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopian, and Persian also omitted it. Not undeservedly, therefore, does Grotius suspect that it was added here from Ioh. 19, 24.

Latin:

* (v. 35. Crucifixerunt. Conf. notata ad v. 23. Coeterùm rectè monet Hugo Grotius in h. l. Christum ceu seditionis autorem, falsissimè licet ita accusatum, dictatoriâ Pilati sententiâ cruci affixum fuisse. Contrà ac Lactantius lib. 4. Instit. Divin. c. 8. & Chrysostomus Orat. 2. de Eleem. existimarunt.) *

* (Diviserunt vestimenta eius &c. ita ut è pallio exteriori seu togâ quatuor fecerint partes, suturas dissolvendo, utq; ita unicuique militi pars cesserit, (licet verò tum hîc, tum apud Davidem Ps. 22, 19. Pluralis habeatur numerus, certum tamen est, quòd per enallagen numeri positus ille pro singulari sit) super interiorem verò tunicam, eò quòd inconsutilis esset, adeoque si divideretur, nulli profutura, sortem miserint. Conf. plura in Analect. ad Ioh. 19, 23. 24.) *

* (Ut impleretur. Vid. Anal. suprà ad c. 13, 14. Particula ἵνα in his similibusque locis, uti Marc. 14, 49.Luc 2, 22.Ioh. 13, 18. non est causalis, sed demonstrativae. Neque enim ideo in Scripturâ futura peccata praedicuntur, ut fiant, sed quia ex liberè agentium malitiâ Deus iuxta omniscientiam suam certò futura ea praevidit, ideò in Sc. S. praedixit. Vid. B. D. Hafenreff. LL. Theol. p. 122. Locus porrò Scripturae S., ad quem Evangelista hîc respicit, est Psal. 22, 19. Quamvis proinde milites ex more Romano, (quo supplicii exactoribus sontium spolia cedebant, ceu ex Ulpiano in L. Divus Adrianus 6. π. de bonis damnat. ostendunt Hug. Grotius in h. l. itemque Ramirez in in Pentecont. c. 7. p. 81.) Christi vestimenta inter se diviserint, nullum tamen dubium, quin divina directio hî intervenerit. Denique & illud observandam, quòd totum hoc versiculi huius membrum, ἵνα πληρωσθῇ &c. desideretur in vetustissimis optimaeque notae Codd. Graecis, quemadmodum etiam Syrus, Arabs, Aethiops & Persa illud omiserunt. Non immeritò igitur suspicatur Grotius, quòd ex Ioh. 19, 24. hîc adiectum sit.) *

## 27:37
(v. 37. The cause of him. i.e., of his death, as the Syriac and Augustine epist. 8 have it. The Arabic: and they placed over his head a written tablet. The sense is: they placed or affixed to the cross over Christ's head a tablet, on which was inscribed the cause of his death. According to the custom of the Romans, of which B. D. Calixtus in Concord. Ev. p. -99, H. Grotius in this place, and Barnabas Brissonius de Form. & solennibus P. R. verbis lib. 5. at the end, present some examples. By ἀιτίαν, however, is understood crime, ἔγκλημα. For although there was clearly no wickedness present, Pilate nevertheless wanted his death also to have a pretext. Whence the Persian notably: & the pretext of his death they inscribed on a paper. The Ethiopian expressed his own piety more than the mind and will of Pilate or the Priests, thus coming to this place: And they placed over his head an inscription, which was of those saying: i. e. This is the King of the Jews, the Lord Jesus. The Evangelist Mark c. 15, 26 records a very concise inscription. But it seems that the inscription was entirely adorned, as the Evangelist Iohannes c. 19. 19. reports, namely: Ιησοῶς ὁ Ναζωραῖος ὁβασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων. With which inscription Pilate indeed made it difficult for the Pontiffs and Priests; for us, however, who believe in Christ, all these things are a great consolation; for Christ is our Savior, Matth. 1, 21. He is the true Nazarene, see Numer. 6.Es. 11, 1.Ierem. 23. 5.Zach. 6, 12. He is King, Luc. 1, 33.Daniel. 7. 14.18 nay, King of Kings, Apoc. 17, 14.C. 16, 16.)

This is the King &c. That these things were written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, St. John expressly records c. 19, 20. In Hebrew, indeed, on account of the holiness of that language; in Greek, on account of the familiarity of that speech; in Latin, on account of the majesty of the Roman Empire. By this very thing it was also prefigured that the antiquity of the Jewish religion, the sublimity of Greek wisdom, and the celebrity of Roman power ought to be subjected to the cross of Christ. And thus the cross of Christ displayed, as it were, the names of the peoples to be converted to Christ.) * * (

Latin:

* (v. 37. Causam ipsius. sc. mortis, ut habet Syrus & Augustinus epist. 8. Arabs: & posuerunt super caput eius tabellam scriptam. Sensus est: posuerunt sive affixerunt cruci super Christi caput tabellam, cui inscripta erat mortis causam. Iuxta mo-rem nempe Romanorum, cuius aliquot etiam exempla sistunt B. D. Calixtus in Concord. Ev. p. -99. H. Grotius in h. l. Barnabas Brissonius de Form. & solennibus P. R. verbis lib. 5. in fine. Per ἀιτίαν verò intelligitur crimen,ἔγκλημα. Quamvis enim scelus planè nullum adfuerit, noluit tamen Pilatus. decesse quoque eius praetextum. Unde Persa notanter: & praetextum mortis eius chartae inscripserunt. Aethiops suam magis pietatem, quàm Pilati vel Sacerdotum mentem, ac voluntatem expressit, ita h. l. ventens: Ex posuerunt super caput eius inscriptionem, quae fuit dicentium: i. e. Hic est Rex Iudaeorum, Dominus Iesus. Evangelista Marcus c. 15, 26. admodùm concisam memorat inscriptionem. Videtur autem omninò fuisse inseriptionem adornatam, prout Evangelista Iohannes c. 19. 19. refert, nempe: Ιησοῶς ὁ Ναζωραῖος ὁβασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων. Quâ quidem inscriptione aegrè Pontificibus ac Sacerdotibus fecit Pilatus; nobis tamen in Christum credentibus magno omninò haec omnia solatio sunt; Est enim Christus Salvator noster, Matth. 1, 21. est verus Nazaraeus, vid. Numer. 6.Es. 11, 1.Ierem. 23. 5.Zach. 6, 12. est Rex, Luc. 1, 33.Daniel. 7. 14.18 imò Rex Regum, Apoc. 17, 14.C. 16, 16.) *

* (Hic est Rex &c. Scripta haec fuisse Ebraicè, Graecè ac Latinè, disertè commemorat D. Iohannes c. 19, 20. Ebraicè quidem, ob linguae huius sanctitatem, Graecè ob sermonis illius familiaritatem, Latinè ob Imperii Romani maiestatem. Praesiguratum quoque hôc ipso fuit, cruci Christi subiici debere religionis Iudaici antiquitatem, Graecae sapientiae sublimitatem, Romanae potentiae celebritatem. Atque ita Christi crux praetulit quasi nomina populorum ad Christum convertendorum.) *

v. 38. Two thieves &c. Isidore of Pelusium, lib. 1, epist. 255 & 256, which may be consulted, explains this mystically concerning the two peoples.) * * (

v. 39. Wagging their heads. A sign of insult. see 2. Kings 19, 21, Ps. 22. 8, Es. 37, 22, Lam. 2, 15.) * *

## 27:42
* v. 42. Let him come down. But Christ did not wish to do this, for grave reasons, which St. Augustine recounts in tractate 37 on John, where among other things he says: Because he was teaching patience, he was therefore deferring his power: for if, moved by their words, he were to come down, he would be thought to have been overcome by the pain of their insults. Compare also Theophylact on chapter 15 of Mark, and Gregory the Great, homily 21 on the Gospels. Briefly, Christ did not wish to come down, 1. so that he might fulfill the work of redemption. 2. So that he might show his patience, and stir us up to a similar one.) *

v. 42. Let him come down.The words of Satan, above c. 4, 6, repeated here through his instruments.) (

* (And we will believe. Saint Jerome well says on this passage: A fraudulent promise, what is more, to descend from the cross while still living, and to rise from the sepulcher while dead? He rose, and you did not believe: therefore if He had even descended from the cross, you would likewise not believe. Cornelius à Lapide cites this saying of Jerome, and adds: Thus today heretics say: We would believe the saints, if they performed miracles: but when the miracles of them are brought forward, they slander them as feigned, or magical, or phantastical. But there is a very great difference between the miracles of Christ and those which the Papists boast of regarding their saints. Since 1. concerning those, the miracles of Christ, the writers θεόπνευςοι, testify, namely the Evangelists and Apostles; but concerning these, the feigned miracles of the saints, there exist traditions that are at least uncertain. 2. The miracles of Christ were divine, directed toward the manifestation of divine glory and the eternal salvation of men; but the miracles of the saints, as they call them, are feigned, ridiculous, and devised for the confirmation of dogmas contrary to the word of GOD, as was long ago shown at length by the Blessed D. Zeaemann in his Sermon on the Pilgrimage to Betha, likewise in his Apology against Elias Graffius and Laur. Forerus for the Mirror of Miracles, by M. Georgius Ewaldus in the Manifestation of certain Papist abominations concerning miracles, opposed to Simon Schreiner. By the Blessed D. Kesler in part 1 of the Method of converting heretics. likewise Papism. c. 3. q. 5. in the Giessen Appendix p. 482. By the Blessed D. Höpfner in the Evangelical Saxony c. 62. & 230. By the Blessed Par. Catholic Confession lib. 2. Special part 1. p. 1228. 1242, following. likewise L. on the Church §. 175. and others.) *

Latin:

* v. 42. Descendat. Noluit vero Christus hoc facere, graves ob causas, quas recenset S. Augustinus tr. 37. in Iohan-nem, ubi inter alia: Quia patientiam docebat, ideò potentiam differebat: si enim commotus ad eorum verba descenderet, victus convitiorum dolore putaretur. Conf. & Theophylactus in C. 15, Marci, it. Gregorius M. homil. 21. in Evang. Breviter, descendere Christus noluit, 1. ut opus redemtionis impleret. 2. Ut patientiam suam ostenderet, nosq; ad similem excitaret.) *

* (v. 42. Descendat. Verba Satanae, suprà c. 4, 6. per organa sua hîc repetita.) *

* (Et credemus. Benè S. Hieronymus ad h. l. Fraudulenta promissio, quid est plus, de cruce adhuc descendere viventem, and de sepulcro mortuum resurgere? Resurrexit, & non credidistis: ergo si etiam de cruce descenderet, similiter non crederetis. Allegat hoc Hieronymi dictum Cornelius â Lapide, additque: Sic hodie haeretici dicunt: Crederemus sanctis, si facerent miracula: at cùm eorū miracula afferuntur, illa calumniantur ut ficta, vel magica, vel Phantastica. At maximum inter Christi, & ea, quae Pontificii iactitant de suis sanctis, miracula discrimen est. Cùm 1. de ilis, Christi miraculis, testentur Scriptores θεόπνευςοι, Evangelistae nempe & Apostoli; de his verò, fictis sanctorum miraculis, in certae saltem extent traditiones. 2. Christi Miracula fuerint divina, ad gloriae divinae manifestationem hominūq; aeternam salutem directa; sanctorum verò, quos ita vocant, miracula, ficta sint, ridicula, & ad confirmationem dogmatum, verbo DEI contrariorum excogitata, ceu pridem prolixè ostensum â B. D. Zeaemanno in Concion. de Peregrin. ad Betham, item in Apologiâ contra Eliam Graffium & Laur. Forerum pro speculo Miraculorum, M. Georgio Ewaldo in Manifestatione quarundam abominationum Pontificiarum de miraculis, oppos. Simoni Schreinero. B. D. Keslero part. 1. Methodi haereticos convertendi. it. Papism. c. 3. q. 5. Giesensibus Append. p. 482. B. D. Höpfnero in Saxonia Evangelicap. 62. & 230. B. Par. Conf. Cathol. lib. 2. Specialis part. 1. p. 1228. 1242, seqq. it L. de Ecclesia §. 175. aliis.) *

## 27:43
* (v. 43. I am the Son of GOD. understand Only-begotten, own. not adoptive, for otherwise, the Jews would not have held Christ to be a blasphemer. See Annotations on Ioh. 10, 33. Therefore we cannot approve the opinion of H. Grotius, writing that this does not pertain to birth (just as neither does that v. 40.) inasmuch as the people heard nothing about which, but to a special love of GOD, such as that with which fathers pursue their children . Furthermore, an example of a similar insult is had in the book of Wisdom c. 2. 15) *

Latin:

* (v. 43. Filius DEI sum. subintell. Unigenitus, proprius. non adoptivus, aliàs enim, Iudaei non habuissent Christum pro blasphemo. Vid. Annot. ad Ioh. 10, 33. Approbare ergo non possumus H. Grotii opinionem, scribentis, non ad nativitatem hoc pertinere (ceu nec illud v. 40.) utpotè de quâplebs nihil audiverit, sed ad specialem DEI amorem, qualis est, quo patres liberos suos prosequuntur. Porrò similis insultationis exemplum habetur in lib. Sapientiae c. 2. 15) *

## 27:44
* (v. 44. And the thieves. What is seen here to be attributed to both thieves, the Evangelist Luke c. 23, 39. 40. reports concerning only one. Therefore Jerome, both in this place and in his epistle to Marcellus, as well as Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius, Origen, and some others, establish that at the beginning both had reviled him, yet soon after, the one having seen the miracle, repented. Among the more recent authors, Menochius, Montacutius, and some others embrace this opinion. Augustine, book 3 de Consensu Evangelist. c. 16, Ambrose, book 10 in Luke, Leo, sermon de Passione, Cyprian, sermon de Passione Christi, Gregory the Great, book 27 Moral. c. 16 (whom among the more recent authors Mr. Dr. Muller in Iudaismo p. 1381. B. Dr. Walther in Harm. Bibl. p. 803. Mr. Dr. Friedlieb and Hugo Grotius in this place, Bellarminus, book 3 de Ecclesia c. 7. §. 10, Maldonatus, Corn. à Lapide, Franc. Lucas in this place, Thomas Gataker in Cinno p. 334, Ludov. de Dieu in this place, and others follow) judge that there is here an enallage of number, since with Matthew the discourse is not about individual persons, but only about the genus itself, and that thus our Evangelist wished to teach that Christ was assailed by the revilings of all, so that not even the thieves refrained. Augustine confirms that manner of speaking from Heb. 11, 33. A similar locution also occurs Luke 23, 36.) *

Latin:

* (v. 44. Et latrones. Quod utrique latroni tribui hîc videtur, Evangelista Lucas c. 23, 39. 40. de uno tantùm refert. Proinde Hieronymus, tum in h. l. tum in epist. ad Marcell. it. Chrysostomus, Theophy lactus, Euthymius, Origenes aliiq nonnulli statuunt, quòd initiò uterque convitiatus fuerit, mox tamen alter viso miraculo, resipuerit. Amplectuntur hanc sententiam è recentioribus Menochius, Montacutius, & alii nonnulli. Augustinus lib. 3. de Consensu Evangelist. c. 16. Ambrosius lib. 10. in Lucam, Leo serm. de Passione, Cyprianus serm. de Passione Christi, Gregorius M. l. 27. Moral. c. 16 (quos è recentioribus Dn. D. Mullerus in Iudaismo p. 1381. B. D. Waltherus Harm. Bibl. p. 803. Dn. D. Friedlieb ac Hugo Grotius in h. l. Bellarminus lib. 3 de Ecclesiâ c. 7. §. 10. Maldonatus, Corn. à Lapide, Franc. Lucas in h. l. Thomas Gatakerus in Cinno p. 334. Ludov. de Dieu in hl. aliique sequuntur) existimant, esse hîc enallagen numeri, cùm apud Matthaeum sermo sit non de singulis personis, sed duntaxat de ipso genere, utque ita Evangelista noster docere voluerit, omnium convitiis Christum fuisse impetitum, adeò ut ne latrones quidem abstinuerint, Confirmat Augustinus istam loquendi rationem ex Ebr. 11, 33. Similis quoque locutio occurrit Luc 23, 36.) *

## 27:45
* (v. 45. Now from the sixth hour &c. It is asked how Matthew (with whom also Mark c. 15, 33. and Luke c. 23, 44. agree) says that darkness was made from the sixth hour, Christ indeed hanging on the cross, is to be reconciled with John, c. 19, 14, writing that it was about the sixth hour, when Pilate said to the Jews: Behold your King? and it is also established from Mark c. 15, 25, that Christ was crucified at the third hour: how therefore could he finally be condemned by Pilate, sitting for judgment, at the sixth hour, if he was already crucified at the third hour? Resp. distinguish between simple hours, of which the Jews counted twelve, the beginning of the counting being made from the rising of the Sun, and compound hours, of which each comprised three simple ones, and obtained their naming from the beginning of the of each. The Evangelists do not speak here of the former, but of the latter. John therefore means this, that Pilate condemned Christ about the sixth hour, by no means having passed it, but when the third had begun, the end of which fell into the sixth. The remaining Evangelists likewise are not to be taken as if Christ was crucified precisely at the beginning of the third quadrant: it suffices that this was done within that quadrant of the day, which took its beginning from the third hour and was finished at the sixth. So that thus the judicial sentence altogether preceded the crucifixion, having been made indeed at the beginning of the second quadrant, but the crucifixion about the end of the same quadrant. Conf. more things pertaining to this in B. Dr. Walth. in H. B. p. 39. 40. 823. B. Par. H. E. c. 195. p. 1928. B. Dr. Thum. de Festis p. 3. 4. Add. Ramirez in Pentecont. c. 38. and also Anal. ad Mark 15, 25 *

* Darkness over the whole earth. It is evident from this that this eclipse was miraculous and supernatural, both because it was universal, and also because it happened at the full moon. (Now, in truth, an eclipse cannot otherwise happen at the full moon, because then the moon is at the greatest distance from the sun, and thus the sun cannot be interposed between it and our sight) for the 14th day of the first month, on which the Passover was celebrated among the Jews, falls on the full moon. See August. vol. 5, book 3, City of God, ch. 15. Chrysost. hom. 89 on Matthew. Euthym. & Theoph. on this passage. Athanas. on the Passion & cross of the Lord. Dionysius the Areopagite, ep. 7 to Polycarp against Apollophanes, reports that he saw that failure of the Sun at Heliopolis in Egypt, together with Apollophanes himself. Which he also repeats in ep. 10 to the same Apollophanes. Although some doubt the antiquity, and whether those writings which bear his name are genuine. On which matter B. Par. treats at length in Patrol. p. 18 seqq. add B. D. Calixt. Conc. Ev. p. 401. Robert. Cocum Censur. Script. p. 48 seqq. Tertullian also mentions in Apolog. ch. 21 that that eclipse was noted at Rome and recorded in the public commentaries. Of the Greek Historians, Phlegon, book 13 of the Olympiads, mentions this same eclipse, as witnessed by Origen tr. 35 on Matthew & Eusebius in the Chronicle under Tiberius. Lactantius, book 4 of the Institutes, ch. 19, reports that this eclipse had been predicted by the Sibyls. Dionysius and Thomas Aquinas indeed think that this eclipse happened from the interposition of the Moon between the Sun and the earth, yet not without a miracle, in that the Moon, when a little before it had been in its own position, being at the greatest distance from the Sun, was suddenly drawn back and placed before the Sun. Others think that it arose from the interposition of dense clouds between the Sun and the earth. Others finally hand down that it was done in such a way that God suspended His concurrence, so that the Sun could not emit rays, in that manner, just as the Babylonian fire could not burn, God withdrawing His concurrence. Leonh. Coquaeus is of this opinion in his Commentary on the said passage, and those things which Orosius once mentioned in book 1, ch. 4, also favor this opinion. Cyprian in his sermon on the Good of patience judges thus concerning this eclipse, that The sun, so that it might not be forced to look upon the crime of the Jews, withdrew both its rays and its eyes. Chrysostom has similar things in the Catena from a sermon on the Passion of the Lord. Compare very many things making for this in Grotius on Matthew, p. 491, where he also strives to prove that similar, if not equal, signs of divine wrath against more serious crimes have existed at other times as well. But the question, whether by the whole earth is understood only the land of Judea, or indeed the whole globe of the earth? Almost all interpreters hold the latter. Speaking, that is, of the upper hemisphere. For as concerns the lower hemisphere, there was not day there at that time, nor could there be, as Grotius well notes, who also brings forward many things on this matter. Origen, however, wished for the former, whom the Jesuit Maldonatus follows, who restricts this eclipse to Judea alone, whom for that reason his own fellow member Cornelius à Lapide refutes in this place. Calvin also established the same in his Harmony, p. 427, and urges 1. that if such a thing had happened, it ought not to have been omitted by so many who accurately handed down the history of those times. 2. that if the eclipse had been common to the whole world, it could have been seen as natural, but on the contrary, it was a more notable prodigy for Judea to be overwhelmed by darkness while the sun was shining elsewhere. But especially Isaac Peyrerius eagerly embraced the former opinion in his System of Theology, book IV, chapter 3, p. 199. But since the said author himself abjured his error concerning the Pre-Adamites, for whose sake he snatched up that hypothesis, and besides has been refuted by many most learned men, we do not wish to do what has already been done with this . Nor are the reasons of Calvin of such importance that they ought to move anyone from the received opinion, especially because it is entirely unusual in Holy Scripture, the phrase of all the earth to indicate only Judea.) *

* (Eli, Eli. The reconciliation of the Evangelists Matthew, who has -λὶ,, and Mark, with whom is ἐλωὶ,, was instituted by the Blessed D. Walth. Miscell. Theol. p. 370, which can be unrolled. add.
