The corruption of the guards, and the dissemination of a false rumor, v. 11-15. IV. The instruction and sending forth of the Apostles to preach the Gospel, v. 16 to the end.

Latin:

* (v. 66. Muniverunt sepulcrum obsignato lapide &c. Benè Theoph. in h. l. Ipsi quidem (Pharisaei) suâ malitiâ instigantur, ut vadant ad sepulcrum & muniant illud. DEI autem dispensatione hoc factum, ut resurrectio inimicis testibus comprobetur, dum sepulcrum munitur & custoditur. Ita nempe, ut pulcrè Hieronymus loquitur, diligentia hostium Christi fidei nostrae profecit. Quanto enim magis sepulcrum reservatur, tanto magis resurrectionis virtus ostenditur. Quemadmodum etiam ex eo, quòd cùm lacus, cui Daniel includebatur, sigillis munitus fuisset, Daniel. 6, 17. constare Deus voluit, divino auxilio eum fuisse servatum: ita & Christi sepulcrum sigillo muniri, divinae sapientiae placuit, quò itidem nempe omnibus manifestum fieret, corpus Christi divinitùs in sepulcro suisse custoditum, nec ab hominibus inde exemtum. Coeterùm curemus, ut nos quoque Christum corde receptum fideliter custodiamus, simus vigiles, nec patiamur, ut peccatorum somnus obrepat, ne quis nobis Iesum eripiat. Obsignemus cor nostrum adamantino quasi sigillo. Quin Deum rogitemus, ut Sp. suo Sancto, sigillo illo firmissimo, Eph. 1, 13.c. 4, 30. corda nostra obsignet. Denique de consuetudine veterum, sponsiones atque alia causâ maioris fidei annulo signatorio confirmandi, vid. Ioh. Kirchm. lib. sing. de Annul. c. 10. Con. radus Rittershus. l. 7. Sacr. Lect. cap. 19. pag. 556. alii.) *

Complectitur praesens caput I. Angeliiuxta Christi sepulcrum apparitionem, v. 1. 8. II. Ipsius Christi, mulieribus sese sistentis praesentationem, v. 9. -11. III. Custodum corruptionem, ac falsi rumoris disseminationem, v. 11-15. IV. Apostolorum ad praedicandum Evangelium instructionem & ablegationem, v. 16. ad finem.) *

## 28:1
(v. 1. In the end of the Sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week, &c. It is gathered from these words that Christ rose again when the Sabbath had passed. But Mark c. 16, 9. says that Christ rose early the first day of the week. Resp. Matthew by Sabbath understands the Great Sabbath, the day called Saturday among us; but Mark calls the first day of the Jewish week, which is called Sunday among us, one or the first of the Sabbath. For it must be known that among the Jews, in honor of the Sabbath day, all the days of the whole week are called Sabbaths: so that the first day, which follows the Sabbath that falls on Saturday, strictly so called, namely the day of the Sun, is called the first of the Sabbath, the one immediately after that, namely the day called Monday among us, the second of the Sabbath, and so on. That indeed τὸ μία in this place is the same as first, not only do authors prove from the Hebrew manner of speaking, see Gen. 1, 5.c. 8, 5. 2. Paral. 29, 57. Hagg. 1, 1.Ezech. 10, 16. 17.Nehem. 8, 2. passim, see B. D. Glassius Gr. S. p. 52. Thomas Gatakerus in Cinno p. 167. and others, but also that it can be proven from the nature of the Greek idiom, think Mr. Ostermanus Posit. Phil. concerning the context of the Greek N. T. 1. and Erasmus Schmidius in N. T. It is known otherwise that the whole week is called Sabbath among the Hebrews, and by their custom in the N. T., see Luke 18, 12., namely in honor of the Sabbath day. Conf. D. Quistorpius Annot. in N. T. p. 137. Ribera lib. de Templo c. 1. Buxtorf. Lex. Rabb. Talm. dict. שבת. Furthermore, since our Savior on the first of the Sabbath, i.e., on that day which immediately follows the Jewish Sabbath, and among us It was customary to call it the day of the Sun, he rose from the dead, the Apostles ordained that the same should be held solemn among Christians, and that still deservedly prevails. Compare Augustine, sermon 251 and 254 de Tempore. Theodore Balsamon, Patriarch of Antioch, Commentary on Canon LXVI of the Apostles, p. 267. τὴν κυριακὴν πανηγυρίζομευ, διὰ τὴν τοὺ Κρίου καὶ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῶ Ξριςοῶ παγκόσμιον χαρὰν καὶ ἀνάςασιν. Compare also the blessed D. Thummius on the Feasts of the Jews and Christians, p. 74 ff. item Analects on Acts 20, 7. Isidore of Pelusium, book 3, ep. 110, thinks that this day, on which Christ rose, is the same as the second-first Sabbath, concerning which Luke 6, 1., what is to be thought of this opinion will be advised in its own place. Finally, it is to be noted that by evening in this place is not understood the end of the past day, but the beginning of the dawning day. As is evident from Mark 16, 2. Luke 24, 1., and as the blessed D. Calixtus shows more fully in Harmony of the Gospels, p. 407. Mr. Danhaw. Id. Good Interpreter, p. 84. Mr. Dilherrus, vol. 1, Academic Disputations, p. 511. Compare also Corn. à Lapide, Hugo Grotius, and other Commentators on this place. item Drusius in Past Things.) *

CHAPTER XXVIII. SUMMARY AND DISPOSITION.

* (And the other Mary. See the Dissertation of Faber Stapulensis on the three Marys, also Cappellus in Spicil. p. 39. Gregory of Nyssa, Orat. 2 on Easter, Nicephorus book 1, H. E. ch. 33, Sedulius book 5, Carm., and several others understand this Mary to be the mother of the Lord. But Ludolphus the Carthusian, part 2, on the life of Christ ch. 70, rightly thinks the discourse is rather about another Mary. Tirinus takes it to be about the mother of James, according to Mark 16, 1. Furthermore, Matthew omitted Salome here, mentioned by Mark, and also Joanna the wife of Chuza, mentioned by Luke.) *

(That they might see the sepulchre. i. e. that they might anoint Christ. For they had prepared spices, that they might anoint him, as Mark ch. 16, 1. teaches. Gregory hom. 21 elegantly: Those women see the Angels, who came with spices, because, namely, those minds behold the heavenly citizens, which set out toward the Lord with the odors of virtues through holy desires. But the Papists (see Grodicius Conc. 2. on Easter Sunday) ineptly gather from this, that these women wished to anoint Christ, that elective acts of worship are not only lawful, but also approved by God. For one must distinguish between The duty of charity, such as was the desire of these women, wishing to anoint the body of Christ, (and that according to the custom received among the Orientals, concerning which see in the Analecta to the preceding chapter, v. 12, also to Mark 16, 1) and religious worship, such a kind of veneration as the Papists urge must be shown to God and the saints by their own invention. The same is also to be observed against Stapleton, part 1, p. 125, and other Papists, who strive to prove from this the religious worship of relics. We ourselves indeed assert that the bodies of the saints, or of those who have died blessedly in Christ, are to be honored or treated honestly (which is done if they are buried decently and in an honest place), but we deny that those very things, as is done among the Papists, are to be exhibited or offered to the people for the purpose of performing religious worship to them. But concerning this matter, more can be consulted in the Blessed Doctor Chemnitius, Exam. Concil. Trid., part 4, p. 1 et seqq.; the Blessed Doctor Meelfurerus, Vindic. Evang., Decad. 3, page 112 et seqq.; the Blessed Par., Confess. Cathol., lib. 2, Spec. part. 2, p. 658 et seqq., also L. de Morte §. 95 et seqq.; the Blessed Doctor K-nig, Vind. Theol., L. 39, §. 39; the Blessed Doctor Balduinus, Disp. 7, ad Artic. Smalk., Marpurg., T. 1, Dispp., p. 496; the Blessed Doctor Eckardus, in Pand. Controv. Pontif., p. 584 et seqq.; the Blessed Doctor Giesenius, Papismi Disp. 24, §. 27 et seqq., and others.) *

Latin:

* (v. 1. Vesperâ autem Sabbathi, quae illucescit in primâ Sabbathi. &c. Colligitur ex his verbis, quòd Christus resurrexerit, cùm transiisset Sabbathum. At Marcus c. 16, 9. dicit, resurrexisse Christum unâ sive primâ Sabbathi. Resp. Matthaeus per Sabbathum intelligit Sabbathum Magnum, Saturni apud nos dictum diem; Sed Marcus primum hebdomadae Iudaicae diem, qui apud nos dies Solis dicitur, vocat unam sive primam Sabbathi. Sciendum enim, quòd apud Iudaeos in honorem diei Sabbathi, omnes totius septimanae dies Sabbatha appellentur: ita ut primus dies, qui Sabbathum, quod in diem Saturni incidit, strictè dictum, sequitur, dies nempe Solis, vocetur prima Sabbathi, qui proximè post illum, dies nempe apud nos Lunae dictus, secunda Sabbathi, & sic porrò. Quòd verò τὸ μία h. l. idem sit, quod prima, nō solùm ex more loquendi Ebraeo, vid. Gen. 1, 5.c. 8, 5. 2. Paral. 29, 57. Hagg. 1, 1.Ezech. 10, 16. 17.Nehem. 8, 2. passim probant autores, vid. B. D. Glassius Gr. S. p. 52. Thomas Gatakerus in Cinno p. 167. alii, verùm etiam ex Graeci idiomatis indole evinci posse existimant Dn. Ostermanus Posit. Phil. Graerum N. T. contextum concern. 1. & Erasmus Schmidius in N. T. Notum aliàs, quòd tota septimana Sabbathum apud Ebraeos, horūq; consvetudine in N. T. dicatur, vid. Luc. 18, 12. in honorē videlicet diei Sabbathi. Conf. D. Quistorpius Annot. in N. T. p. 137. Ribera lib. de Templo c. 1. Buxtorf. Lex. Rabb. Talm. dict. שבת. Coeterùm cùm Salvator noster primâ Sabbathi, h. e. illa die, quae Sabbathum Iudaicum proximè sequitur, & apud nos dies Solis dici consuevit, à mortuis resurrexerit, sanxerunt Apostoli, ut eadem solennis inter Christianos haberetur, idque etiamnum meritò obtinet. Conf. Augustinum serm 251. ac 254. de Tempore. Theodor. Balsamon Antiochenus Patriarcha Comment. ad Canon. LXVI. Apost. p. 267. τὴν κυριακὴν πανηγυρίζομευ, διὰ τὴν τοὺ Κρίου καὶ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῶ Ξριςοῶ παγκόσμιον χαρὰν καὶ ἀνάςασιν. Conf. etiam B. D. Thummium de Festis Iud. & Christ. p. 74. seqq. item Analect. ad Actor. 20, 7. Existimat Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 3. ep. 110. diem hunc. quo Christus resurrexit, eundem esse cum Sabbatho deuteroproto, de quo Luc. 6, 1. quâ de opinione quid habendum sit, suo monebitur loco. Denique notandum, quòd per vesperam h. l. non intelligatur finis diei praeteritae, sed diei illucescentis initium. Ceu ex Marc. 16, 2.Luc. 24, 1. patet, & uberiùs ostendunt B. D. Calixtus Concord. Evang. p. 407. Dn. Danhaw. Id. Boni Interpr. p. 84. Dn. Dilherrus t. 1. Dispp. Acad. p. 511. Conf. etiam Corn. à Lapide, Hugo Grotius, aliique Comm. in h. l. it. Drusiu sin Praeteritis.) *

CAPUT XXIIX. SUMMA AC DISPOSITIO.

* (Et altera Maria. Vid. Dissert. Fabri Stapul. de tribus Mariis, it. Cappell. in Spicil. p. 39. Per Mariam hanc Gregorius Nyssenus Orat. 2. in Pascha, Nicephorus lib. 1. H. E. c. 33. Sedulius lib. 5. Carm. aliique nonnulli intelligunt matrem Domini. Ast Ludolphus Carthus. part. 2. de vitâ Christi c. 70. rectis de alia potiùs Maria sermonem esse putat. Tirinus accipit de matre Iacobi, iuxta Marc. 16, 1. Coeterùm omisit hîc Matthaeus Salomen, à Marco, item Iohannam uxorem Chusae, à Lucâ memoratas.) *

* (Ut viderent sepulcrum. i. e. ut Christum urgerent. Comparaverant enim aromata, ut illum urgerent, ceu Marcus c. 16, 1. docet. Gregorius hom. 21. eleganter: Illae mulieres Angelos vident, quae cum aromatibus venerunt, quia videl. illae mentes supernos cives adspiciunt, quae cum virtutum odoribus ad Dominum per sancta desideria proficiscuntur. Ineptè verò exeo, quòd mulieres istae Christum ungere voluerunt, Pontificii (vid Grodicius Conc. 2. in Domin. Pasch.) colligunt, cultus electitios esse non solùm licitos, sed etiam Deo probari. Etenim distingvendum inter charitatis officium, quale fuit desiderium harum mulierum, Christi corpus ungere cupientium, (idque more apud Orientales recepto, quo de in Analect. ad cap. praeced. 26. v. 12. it. ad Marc. 16, 1.) & inter religiosum cultum, cuiusmodi venerationem Pontificii ex propriâ adinventione Deo ac sanctis exhibendum esse urgent. Idem etiam observandum adversùs Stapletonum part. 1. p. 125. aliosque Pontificios, qui religiosureliquiarum cultum probare hinc satagunt. Sanè ipsi nos adserimus, sanctorum seu beatè in Christo defunctorum corpora esse honoranda sive honestè tractanda, (id quod fit, si decenrer & in loco honesto sepeliantur) negamus verò, illa ipsa, ceu apud Pontificios fit, populo ad religiosum iis praestandum cultum, esse exhibenda vel offerenda. Sed hac de re pluribus consuli possunt B. D. Chemnitius Exam. Concil. Trid. part. 4. p. 1. seqq. B. D. Meelfurerus Vindic. Evang. Decad. 3. pag. 112. seqq. B. Par. Confess. Cathol. lib. 2. Spec. part. 2. p. 658. seqq. it. L. de Morte §. 95. seqq. B. D. K-nig Vind. Theol. L. 39. §. 39. B. D. Balduinus Disp. 7. ad Artic. Smalk. Marpurg. T. 1. Dispp. p. 496. B. D. Eckardus in Pand. Controv. Pontif. p. 584. seqq. B. D. Giesenius Papismi Disp 24. §. 27. seqq. alii.) *

## 28:2
* (v. 2. He rolled back the stone: for it was the custom among the Jews to cover sepulchers with a lid, whether of wood or of stone or even of another material, as Ioh. Buxtorfius shows from Maimonides, Lex. Rabb. Talm., p. 437; add Schickard in de Iure Regio Ebr., p. 163, also the Commentators on the preceding chapter, v. 60, and John 11, 38. Gregorius Nyssenus, Orat. 2, de Resurr. Domin., p. 151: When the Angel had rolled back this (stone), he found that the Lord had risen, with the sepulcher, which had been fortified with seals and was guarded by the protection of soldiers, left closed, as befitted God, just as he approached the disciples while the penetrating into the dwelling, etc. Iustinus Martyr has similar things, q. 117, ad Orthodoxos, p. 363; Gregorius Nazianzenus in the Drama: Christus patiens, Ambrosius, lib. 10, in c. 24, Lucae, Chrysostomus, homil. 90, in Matth. & in c. 20, Iohannis, Hieronymus ad Pammach. & in Epitaph. Paulae, Augustinus de cognit. verae vitae, c. 45, serm. 138, 136, 158, 159, & 160, also de Tempore serm. 12, de verbis Apost. de agone Christi c. 24, Chrysologus serm. 75, Theophyl. & Euthymius in h. l., Isidorus Pelusiota l. 1, Epist. 404, Bernhardus serm. 1, de Paschate. Col. 129. And indeed if Christ could enter to the disciples through closed doors, Ioh. 20, 19.26. certainly He could also rise again with the sepulcher closed. It is added that Christ by the resurrection was declared the Son of God, Rom. 1, 4. Whence even Calvin himself in Harm. Evang. acknowledges, that Christ rose again before the sepulcher was opened by the Angel. The same is maintained by the Calvinists Wolff, Musculus, and Augustinus Marloratus, cited by B. Bar. in Harm. Evang. c. 207. p. 2090. where he also refutes the error of Sadeel, Zwingli, and other Calvinists, who deny this very thing. See also against the same B. D. Chemnitius, book on the two natures in Christ, c. 25. p. 146. 147. 148. also c. 30. p. 181. c. 132. p. 198. 199. Christ could easily effect this, not only because His human nature subsists in the infinite τοῦ hypostasis, but also because He already had a glorified body. Against the Photinians who maintain that He received such a thing only after the ascension. But that after the resurrection He still ate, retained the marks of the nails, etc., was done not out of necessity, but out of free will; it was πὐυδοκίας καὶ ὀικονουίας. not ἐνδείας. Hugo Grotius thinks, that the Angel rolled away the stone from the sepulcher, so that he might perform the office of a doorkeeper, not indeed necessarily, but honorably: That this could seem to be prefigured in Jacob's Gen. 29, 10. But if he means by this that Christ could indeed rise with the sepulcher closed, yet that He used the ministry of an angel in removing the stone for the sake of the women, so that they might indeed be able to enter it, this opinion can be left in the middle. Provided that it is not denied. Since for glorified bodies, and much less for the body of Christ, being hypostatically τῷ λόγῳ united, the penetration of dimensions is by no means impossible. Compare B. Par. Disp. Acad. p. 1431. seqq. Justin Martyr: The Angel rolled back the stone, not to open the door for the Lord who was about to go out, but to provide evidence to men of His departure which had already taken place. *

* ( He was sitting upon it, namely the stone, rolled back from the entrance, not of the monument or sepulcher, that is, of the cave hewn in the rock, but of the tomb. For neither the crypt nor the chamber had its own stone, which Augustine lib. 3. de consensu Evang. c. 24. Bede and Maldonatus in h. l. and also Brochardus in descript. terrae sanctae think. Compare B. D. Calixtus Conc. Ev. p. 410. Cornelius a Lapide in h. l. Thomas Aquinas offers the symbolic reasons for this sitting: He was sitting, he writes, in whom there was no weariness, as a doctor of the faith, as a master of the resurrection. He was sitting upon the rock, so that the solidity of the one sitting might give firmness to the believers. &c. Q. 5. here 1. How is it to be reconciled, that Matthew & Mark say that the Angel sat; but Luke indeed c. 24, 4. that he stood? Resp. Some note that τὸ by Hebraism is appropriate to any position, since it signifies being present, in whatever way it may happen. To this point belong Luc. 2, 9.c. 7, 38.Actor. 12, 7. Hugo Grotius brings forward other examples from profane Greek writers on this passage. Others wish that the narrative of Matthew and Mark is different from the narrative of Luke. And this opinion is embraced by our own B. Par. Harm. Ev. c. 207. from the Papists Corn. â Lapide, and others. Q. 2. HowMatth. v. 1.&4.does he say, that the Angel sat upon the rolled-away stone, i. e. outside the sepulcher, seen there by the guards, but Mark, that the women not outside, but inside the sepulcher (since they had already entered it,) saw the Angel? Resp. Some say that the Angel first sat outside the sepulcher, and was thus seen by the guards, and afterwards had entered the sepulcher, and was seen there by the women. Others more correctly say that τὸ entering in in this passage at least denotes an inchoate act i. e. that when they were beginning or desiring to enter the monument. The explanation of Grotius agrees in some way with this opinion, warning that Mark calls μνημεῖον the part of the garden which was separated from the rest of the garden by some fence or breastwork. And that into this, not into the cave, the women entering saw the Angel sitting, and indeed upon the stone, at the right part of the cave, towards which the head of the dead man had been placed, the same man believes, so that what John says πρὸς τῇ κεφαλῇ, is the same as that which Mark has, ἐν δεξιοῖς ) *

Latin:

* (v. 2. Revolvit lapidem: moris enim erat apud Iudaeos, sepulcra operculo, sive ex ligno sive ex lapide vel aliâ etiā materiâ tegere, ceu ex Maimonide ostendit Ioh. Buxtorfius Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 437. adde Schickardum in de Iure Regio Ebr. p. 163. item Commentatores ad cap. praeced. v. 60. ac Ioh. 11, 38. Gregorius Nyssenus Orat. 2. de Resurr. Domin. p. 151. Hunc (lapidem) cùm Angelus revolvisset, reperit resurrexisse Dominum, sepulcro, quod sigillis munitum fuerat, ac praesidio militum custodiebatur, sicut Deum decebat, clauso relicto, quemadmodum clausis quoianuis penetrans in domicilium, ad discipulos accessit &c. Similia habent Iustinus Martyr q. 117. ad Orthodoxos p. 363. Gregorius Nazianzenus in Dramate: Christus patiens, Ambrosius lib. 10. in c. 24. Lucae, Chrysostomus homil. 90. in Matth. & in c. 20. Iohannis, Hieronymus ad Pammach. & in Epitaph. Paulae, Augustinus de cognit. verae vitae, c. 45. serm. 138. 136. 158. 159. & 160. it. de Tempore serm. 12. de verbis Apost. de agone Christi c. 24. Chrysologus serm. 75. Theophyl. & Euthymius in h. l. Isidorus Pelusiota l. 1. Epist. 404. Bernhardus serm. 1. de Paschate. Col. 129. Et sanè si per clausas ianuas potuit Christus ad discipulos intrare, Ioh. 20, 19.26. utiq; etiam clauso sepulcro potuit resurgere. Accedit, quòd Christus per resurrectionem declaratus fuerit Filius DEI,Rom. 1, 4. Unde etiam Calvinus ipse in Harm. Evang. agnoscit, quòd Christus antè resurrexerit, quàm ab Angelo sepulcrum aperiretur. Idem statuunt ex Calvinianis Wolff. Musculus & Augustinus Marloratus, adducti â B. Bar. in Harm. Evang. c. 207. p. 2090. ubi etiam refellit Sadeelis, Cinglii & aliorum Calvinianorum errorem, hoc ipsum negantium. Vid. etiam contra eosdem B. D. Chemnitius lib. de duabus nat. in Christo c. 25. p. 146. 147. 148. it. c. 30. p. 181. c. 132. p. 198. 199. Facilè autem efficere hoc Christus potuit, non solùm quia humana ipsius natura subsistit in infinita τοῦ hypostasi, verùm etiam quia iamtum corpus habuit glorificatum. contra Photinianos statuentes, quòd post adscensionem demum tale acceprit. Quòd vero post resurrect. ipse adhuc comedit, vestigia clavorum retinuit &c. factum non ex necessitate, sed ex libera voluntate; fuit πὐυδοκίας καὶ ὀικονουίας.nonἐνδείας. Hugo Grotius existimat, Angelum devolvisse lapidem â sepulcro, ut ianitoris officio, non necessario quidem, sed honorifico fungeretur: Idpraefiguratum videri posse in IacobiGen. 29, 10. Quod si hoc vult, Christum sepulcro clauso resurgere quidem potuisse, angeli tamen ministerio usum fuisse in removendo lapide propter mulieres, quò ingredi nempe illud possent, in medio relinqui opinio haec potest. Modò illud non negetur. Siquidem corporibus glorificatis, multoq; adhuc minùs corpori Christi, quippe hypostaticè τῷ λόγῳ unito, dimensionum penetratio hautquaquam impossibilis est. confer. B. Par. Disp. Acad. p. 1431. seqq. Iustinus Martyr: Revolvit Angelus lapidem, non ut egressuro Domino ianuam pandat, sed ut egressûs eius iam facti hominibus praestet indicium,) *

* ( Sedebatsuper eum, sc. lapidem, devolutum nempe ab ostio, non monumenti vel sepulcri, h. e. antri in rupe excisi, sed conditorii. Neque enim tum crypta, tum camera suum habebat lapidem, quod Augustinus lib. 3. de consensu Evang. c. 24. Beda ac Maldonatus in h. l. itemq; Brochardus in descript. terrae sanctae existimant. Confer B. D. Calixtum Conc. Ev. p. 410. Cornelium â Lapide in h. l. Thomas de Aquino symbolicas huius sessionis profert causas: sedebat, scribit, cui nulla inerat lassitudo, ut fidei doctor, ut resurrectionis magister. Sedebat super petram, ut soliditas sedentis daret credentibus firmitatem. &c. Q. v. hîc 1. Quomodo conciliandum sit, quòd Matthaeus & Marcus dicunt, Angelum sedisse; Lucas verò c. 24, 4. eum stetisse? Resp. Quidam notant, τὸ per Ebraismum competere situi cuilibet, cùm significet praesentem, quocunque fiat modo. huc faciunt Luc. 2, 9.c. 7, 38.Actor. 12, 7. Alia exempla è profanis scriptoribus Graecis affert Hugo Grotius in h. l. Alii volunt, quòd alia sit narratio Matthaei ac Marci â narratione Lucae. Atq; sententiam hanc è nostratibus amplectitur B. Par. Harm. Ev. c. 207. è Pontific. Corn. â Lapide, alii. Q. 2. QuomodoMatth. v. 1.&4.dicat, Augelum sedisse super lapidem revolutum, h. e. extra sepulcrum, ibivisum â custodibus, Marcus verò, quòd mulieres non extra, sed intra sepulcrum (quippe cùm illud iamtum ingressae essent,) Angelum viderint? Resp. Nonnulli dicunt, primùm Angelum extra sepulcrum sedisse, & ita conspectum fuisse à custodibus, postmodum ingressum fuisse sepulcrum, ibidemq; à milieribus fuisse conspectum. Rectiùs alii dicunt, quòd τὸintroëuntes h. l. saltem notet actum inchoatum i. e. quôd cùm inciperent vel cuperent ingredi monumentum. Convenit cum hâc sententiâ quodammodo Grotii explicatio, monentis, Marcum vocare μνημεῖον partem horti, quae ab horto reliquo, sepimento aliquo sive lorica separabatur. Atq; in hanc, non in specum mulieres introëuntes vidisse Angelum sedentem, & quidem super lapidē, ad dextram speluncae partem, quam versùs caput mortui positum fuisse, idem credit, ut ita, quod Iohannes dicit πρὸς τῇ κεφαλῇ, idem sit cum eo, quod Marcus habet, ἐν δεξιοῖς) *

## 28:3
* (v. 3. And his appearance was like lightning. Conf. Ezech. 1, 14.Daniel 10, 5.Actor. 1, 10. Angels appear indeed like lightning on account of beauty, horror, splendor. But let the ministers of the Church also, as those who are likewise sometimes called Angels in the H. S., be in their sermons like lightning and thunderbolts Βοανεργὲς, ὅ ἐςσιν, --οὶ βροντῆς, Marc. 3, 17. thundering against vices & impiety. Conf. Apoc. 4, 5.)

(And his garment like snow. An angel appears in a white garment, which is a sign 1. of Sanctity or purity, see Dan. 7, 9.Apoc. 3, 4. 5.18.c. 6, 1.c. 7, 9.13. 2. of Mirth. Gregory homily 21 on the Gospels. Who appeared covered with a white star, because he announced the joys of the festival. etc. Herod foolishly imitated such an angelic garment, Act. 12. 22. conf. Josephus book 19, A. I. C. 7. But let us imitate it mystically, by striving for sanctity. Let us rise from dead works, to serve the living God,Ebr. 9, 14.)

Latin:

* (v. 3. Et erat adspectus eius sicut fulgur. Conf. Ezech. 1, 14.Daniel 10, 5.Actor. 1, 10. Apparent vero Angeli instar fulguris ob decorem, horrorem, splendorem. Sint vero & ministri Ecclesiae, ut qui itidem in Sc. S. quandoque Angeli appellantur, in concionibus suis fulguris instar ac fulminum, sint Βοανεργὲς, ὅ ἐςσιν, --οὶ βροντῆς,Marc. 3, 17. tonantes contra vitia & impietatem. Conf. Apoc. 4, 5.) *

* (Et vestimentum eius sicut nix. Angelus apparet in veste candida, quae signum 1. Sanctitatis s. puritatis, vid. Dan. 7, 9.Apoc. 3, 4. 5.18.c. 6, 1.c. 7, 9.13. 2. Hilaritatis. Gregorius homil. 21. in Evang. Qui stellâ candidâ coopertus apparuit, quia festivitatis gaudia nunciavit. &c. Vestem talem angelicam stultè imitari Herodes, Act. 12. 22. conf. Ioseph. lib. 19, A. I. C. 7. Imitemur verò nos illam mysticè, studentes sanctitati. Resurgamus ab operibus mortuis, ad inserviendum Deo viventi,Ebr. 9, 14.) *

## 28:4
(v. 4. They were terrified, conf. Es. 37, 36. Moreover, there was one cause of terror and fear in the soldiers who were guards, and another in the devout women. In the latter, it was the weakness of human nature, and indeed of their sex; in the former, the depravity of their conscience. add. Iudic. 13, 21.Daniel. 10, 8.Luc. 2. 9.)

Latin:

* (v. 4. Exterriti sunt, conf. Es. 37, 36. Coeterùm alia terrotis ac timoris causa in militibus custodibus fuit, alia in devotis mulieribus. In his naturae humanae, quin & sexûs imbecillitas; in illis conscientiae pravitas. add. Iudic. 13, 21.Daniel. 10, 8.Luc. 2. 9.) *

## 28:5
(v. 5. The Angel said. But Luc. 24, 4. mention is made of two Angels. Resp. Some think that one here spoke to the women in the name of both. And that this is customary among the Hebrews, H. Grotius notes in this place, who writes that the same is also evident from Gen. 18, 1.3. But by that Angel, whom Abraham addresses in the same place v. 3, one must not understand a created Angel, but the uncreated one, as has been shown elsewhere. Others maintain that this apparition is different from that which Luke commemorates, as was noted a little earlier at v. 2.)

(Do not be afraid. Thus, indeed, holy Angels are accustomed to raise up those who are dismayed. See Iudic. 6, 23.Daniel. 10, 12.Luc. 1, 13.30. Corn. à Lapide in this place notes thus: Witches and sorceresses imitate Eve, who, conversing with the Devil, draw in death: but Magdalene (to whom, just as to the other women, the Angel speaks here) imitates the penitent, who, invoking the Angels, obtain life. Resp. 1. We readily grant that Eve was seduced and shamefully deceived by the devil. 2. Nor do we deny that witches and sorceresses are even now being cast by the Devil into the abyss of eternal death. 3. But that is what the Jesuit ought to have proven, that Angels can either be invoked, or that those who invoke them obtain life. 4. Nor do we read concerning Mary Magdalene or these other women that they invoked the Angel appearing to them and announcing the resurrection of the Lord: indeed, our Evangelist here does not even record that they spoke with him. 5. Nor is any command, or proven example, or promise of being heard given in the Scriptures for the religious invocation of Angels. But the contrary can rather be clearly proven from that. See Analect. on the Epistle to the Colossians chap. 2, 18.)

Latin:

* (v. 5. Dixit Angelus. Ast Luc. 24, 4. Mentio fit duorum Angelorum. Resp. Quidam existimant, quòd unus hîc utriusq: nomine mulieres alloquutus fuerit. Idque apud Ebraeos solenne esse, monet H. Grotius in h. l. qui id ipsum patere quoq; scribit ex Gen. 18, 1.3. Verùm per Angelum illum, quem Abraham d. l. v. 3. alloquitur, non intelligendus Angelus creatus, sed increatns, ceu alibi ostensum, Alii statuunt, quòd haec apparitio diversa sit ab ea, quam Lucas commemorat, uti paullò antè ad v. 2. monitum.) *

* (Nolite timere. Ita nempe sancti Angeli consternatos erigere solent. Vid. Iudic. 6, 23.Daniel. 10, 12.Luc. 1, 13.30. Corn. à Lapide in h. l. ita annotat: Evam imitantur magae & sagae, quae cum Diabolo colloquentes hauriunt mortem: Magdalenam verò (ad quam sicuti & reliquas mulieres hîc Angelus loquitur) imitātur poenitentes, quae Angelos invocantes vitam nanciscuntur. Resp. 1. Evam à diabolo seductam turpiterque deceptam fuisse, facilè largimur. 2. nec negamus, sagas & magas etiamnum à Diabolo in baratrum aeternae mortis prae cipitari. 3. illud verò est, quod probare Iesuita debebat, Angelos vel invocari posse, vel qui eos invocant, vitam nancisci. 4. nec legimus de Maria Magdalena coeterisve mulieribus his, quòd Angelum ipsis apparentem & resurrectionem Domini annunciantem, invocarint: imò ne loquutas quidem cum ipso, Evangelista hîc noster commemorat. 5. nec ullum invocationis Angelorum religiosae in sacris vel praeceptum, vel probatum exemplum, vel exauditionis promissum datur. Sed contrarium potiùs liquidò exinde probari potest. Vid. Analect. in Epist. ad Coloss. cap. 2, 18.) *

## 28:6
* (v. 6. He is not here. Understand it in the way in which they were seeking him, namely among the dead, the dead one, Luc. 24, 5. and who would have need to be anointed: for he was no longer lying dead in the sepulcher, but was living glorious in his kingdom. Less firmly, therefore, do the Calvinists from this and similar passages, as above c. 26, 10. Marc. 14, 4. Ioh. 16, 28. Luc. 24, 44. impugn the omnipresence of the man Christ, and then also the substantial presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Holy Eucharist. For modes of presence must be distinguished. Nor from the negation of presence according to a certain mode should presence be denied absolutely. Otherwise it would follow that GOD is not omnipresent either, since according to gracious presence he is said to depart from the impious, Hos. 9, 12. To this also pertain the sayings Deut. 1. 42. 1. Reg. 19, 11. Prov. 15, 19. coll. with Act. 17, 27. It is therefore well to be noted that this and similar sayings remove local, natural, and visible presence of the body of Christ, but by no means personal, or gracious, or sacramental. As the blessed D. Chemnicius shows and confirms at greater length in Fundam. Coenae c 12. B. Par. L. de S. Coenâ §. 111 B. D. Fewrbornius in a peculiar dissertation on the universal and particular presence of Christ, B. D. Mentzerus against Crotium, B. Parens Exeg. L. de Pers. & Off. Christi, and others. Conf. & Analecta on Marc. 14, 24. Although indeed Christ was then no longer in the state of humiliation, he did not yet wish to exercise his divine majesty fully and universally.) *

* (He has risen. Gr. ἠγέρθη he has awakened. Conf. 1. Cor. 15, 51. for the death of Christ was like sleep, and it was as easy for him to rise from the dead as it is for us from sleep. Indeed, he himself brought it about through his resurrection that for us also death is sleep, Conf. Ioh. 11, 11.13.1. Cor. 15, 18.20.1. Thess. 2, 13. and following; and the resurrection of Christ is the pledge of our resurrection. Leo M. serm. 1. de Ascens. Whither the glory of the head has gone, thither is the hope of the body called. August. serm. 3. de Ascens. The death of Christ has brought us to life, his resurrection has raised us up, his ascension has consecrated us. Add entirely. 1. Cor. 15, 13. and following. Philipp. 3, 21. It is indeed well to be noted that Christ rose again by his own power, as is evident from Ioh 2, 19.c. 10, 8.. But why the Apostles, preaching the Gospel, said that Christ was raised by the Father,Act. 2, 24.32.c. 4, 10.c. 5, 30.Rom. 8, 11. etc., Gregorius Nyssenus teaches at length in Orat. 2. de Resurr. Domini, p. 151. add entirely B. Par. dispp. Acad. p. 1414. and following. Compare also the Analysis on Act. 2, 24. Briefly, the resurrection is attributed to the Father, not because of any weakness of the Son, but because of the equality of essence and power, since the essence and power of both are the same in number, equality,Ioh. 5, 19.c. 19, 30.1. Ioh. 5, 7. and thus not exclusively, but inclusively. Furthermore, at what time Christ rose again, is disputed among the Doctors. S. Cyrillus, Ambrosius, Hieronymus, Athanasius in his book de Virg., Gregorius Naziant. Orat. 2. de Resurr., whom among the more recent authors Eman. Saa and certain others follow, maintain that Christ rose again around midnight. But more correctly S. Hieronymus Ep. 150, Augustinus in Ps. 56, 9., Prosper sent. 203 (whom among the Lutherans B. Par. in Harm. Resurr. C. 207. p. 2094, Dn. D. Friedlib in h. l. p. 217, and among the Papists the Jesuits Maldonatus and Tirinus on this passage follow) maintain that he rose either a little before the rising of the Sun, or with the Sun itself rising. And it is proved from Marc. 16, 9. Nor does v. 1 of this chapter stand in the way, as was noted there. The question is also often raised, Whether Christ appeared naked, or indeed clothed? concerning which B. Par. Harm. Evang. p. 2111. a. and Dn. D. Friedlieb p. 219 can be consulted.

Latin:

* (v. 6. Non est hîc. Intellige eo modo, quo eum quaerebant, nemper inter mortuos mortuum,Luc. 24, 5. & qui ungi necesse haberet: non enim iacebat ampliùs mortuus in sepulero, sed vivebat gloriosus in suo regno. Minùs igitur firmiter ex hoc similibusque locis, uti suprà c. 26, 10. Marc. 14, 4.Ioh. 16, 28.Luc. 24, 44. omnipraesentiam Christi hominis, tum quoque substantialem corporis & sanguinis Christi in S. Eucharistiâ praesentiam Calviniani impugnant. Distinguendi namque praesentiae modi sunt. Nec ex negatione praesentiae secundùm certum modum, absolutè praesentia neganda. Aliàs fequeretur, quòd nec DEUS omnipraesens sit, cùm secundùm praesentiam gratiosam ab impiis recedere dicatur, Hos. 9, 12. Huc quoque faciunt dicta Deut. 1. 42.1. Reg. 19, 11.Prov. 15, 19. coll. cum. Act. 17, 27. probè igitur notandum quòd hoc & similia dicta localem, naturalem, & visibilem corporis Christi praesentiam tollant, nequaquam verò vel personalem, vel gratiosam, vel sacramentalem. Uti pluribus ostendunt, confirmantque B. D. Chemnicius in Fundam. Coenae c 12. B. Par. L. de S. Coenâ §. 111 B. D. Fewrbornius dissert. peculiari de praesentiâ Christi univ. & particulari, B. D. Mentzerus contra Crotium, B. Parens Exeg. L. de Pers. & Off. Christi, alii. Conf. & Analecta ad Marc. 14, 24. Licet verò Christus tum non ampliùs fuerit in statu exinanitionis, nondum tamen plenariè & universaliter divinam suam maiestatem exerere voluit.) *

* (Surrexit. Gr. ἠγέρθηevigilavit. Conf. 1. Cor. 15, 51. fuit enim Christi mors instar somni, ac tam facile ipsi fuit, ex mortuis resurgere, quàm nobis, à somno. Effecit verò ipse per suam resurrectionem, ut nobis quoque mors somnus sit, Conf. Ioh. 11, 11.13.1. Cor. 15, 18.20.1. Thess. 2, 13. seqq; estq; Christi resurrectio nostrae resurrectionis pignus. Leo M. serm. 1. de Ascens. Quo processit gloria capitis, eò spes vocatur & corporis. August. serm. 3. de Ascens. Nos mors Christi viuficavit, nos resurrectio erexit, nos adscensio consecravit. Add. omninò. 1. Cor. 15, 13. seqq. Philipp. 3, 21. Probè verò notandum, quòd Christus surrexerit propriâ virtute, ceu ex Ioh 2, 19.c. 10, 8. patet. Cur verò Apostoli, Evangelium praedicantes dixerint, Christum à Patre resuscitatum esse,Act. 2, 24.32.c. 4, 10.c. 5, 30.Rom. 8, 11. &c. prolixè docet Gregorius Nyssenus Orat. 2. de Resurr. Domini, p. 151. add. omninò B. Par. dispp. Acad. p. 1414. seqq. Conf. etiam Anal. ad. Act. 2, 24. Breviter, tribuitur Patri resuscitatio non propter aliquam Filii imbecillitatum, sed propter essentiae & potentiae, utpote cum utriusque eadem numero essentia ac potentia sit, aequalitatem,Ioh. 5, 19.c. 19, 30.1. Ioh. 5, 7. adeoque non exclusivè, sed inclusivè. Coeterùm quo tempore Christus resurrexerit, inter Dd. controvertitur. S. Cyrillus, Ambrosius, Hieronymus, Athanasius lib. de Virg. Gregorius Naziant. Orat. 2. de Resurr., quos è recentioribus sequuntur Eman. Saa, & alii quidam, statuunt, Christum resurrexisse circa mediam noctem. Rectiùs verò S. Hieronymus. Ep. 150. Augustinus in Ps. 56, 9. Prosper sent. 203. (quos è Lutheranis sequuntur B. Par. in Harm. Resurr. C. 207. p. 2094. Dn. D. Friedlib in h. l. p. 217. ex Pontificiis Iesuitae Maldonatus ac Tirinus ad h. l.) statuunt, quòd vel paullò ante Solis ortum, vel cum ipso Sole oriente resurrexerit. Probaturque ex Marc. 16, 9. Nec obstat v. 1. huius cap. ceu ibi monitum. Quaestio etiam moveri solet, Num Christus nudus, an verò vestitus apparuerit? de quâ consuli possunt B. Par. Harm. Evang. p. 2111. a. Dn. D. Friedlieb p. 219.) *

## 28:7
* (v. 7. Tell, etc. Gregor. Hom. 25. Because in paradise the woman offered death to the man, from the sepulcher the woman announces life to the men: and she narrates the words of her vivifier, which she had narrated the words of the deadly serpent, etc. Euthymius: because the woman was made for the man the cause of sorrow, now women become ministers of joy to men.) *

* (To the disciples, Mark adds: & to Peter. Where Gregory, Homily 21 on the Gospels, says beautifully: Because if he had not expressed by name him who had denied the Master, he would not have dared to come among the disciples: he is therefore called by name, lest he should despair because of his denial. *

* (He goes before you into Galilee. And yet he appeared to the disciples first in Jerusalem. Response: Since the disciples were reluctant to go into Galilee, Christ appeared to them in Jerusalem, indeed granting more than he had promised. But how many times and in what order Christ manifested himself after his resurrection, the blessed Pareus shows at length in his Harmony of the Gospels on the Resurrection of Christ.) *

Latin:

* (v. 7. Dicite &c. Gregor. Hom. 25. Quia in paradiso mulier viro propinavit mortem, à sepulcro mulier viris annunciat vitam: & dicta sui vivificatoris narrat, quae mortiferi serpentis verba narraverat &c. Euthymius: quia mulier viro facta est causa moeroris, nunc mulieres fiunt viris ministrae gaudii.) *

* (Discipulis, Marcus addit: & Petro. ubi pulcrè Gregor. hom. 21. in Evang. Quia si hunc nominatim non exprimeret, qui Magistrum negaverat, venire inter discipulos non auderet: vocatur ergo ex nomine, ne desperaret ex negatione.) *

* (Praecedit vos in Galilaeam. Atqui priùs in Hierusalem discipulis apparuit. Resp. cùm discipuli tergiversarentur ire in Galilaeam, Christus Hierosolymis eis apparuit, plus nempe praestando, quàm promiserat. Quoties verò & quo ordine Christus post resurrectionem suam sese manifestarit, prolixè ostendit B. Par. in Harm. Ev. Resurr. Christi.) *

## 28:8
* (v. 8. And with great joy. Grotius thinks that the women rejoiced not so much because they believed in Christ's resurrection (as they could not even sufficiently comprehend it in their minds) as because they had been deemed worthy of a heavenly vision. Luke 24, 22. But even if those disciples, to whom the women announce that vision and the resurrection of the Lord, are read to be at least astonished, there is nevertheless no doubt that these pious women, to whom nothing could be equally pleasant as the resurrection of the sweetest Savior, as that in which the hinge of our salvation turns, rejoiced vehemently, having received that joyful message about the resurrection of Christ.) *

Latin:

* (v. 8. Et gaudio magno. Existimat Grotius, quòd gavisae fuerint mulieres non tam quòd Christi resurrectionem crederent (ut quam ne animo quidem comprehendere satis potuerint) quàm quòd dignatae essent viso coelesti. Luc. 24, 22. Ast si vel maximè discipuli illi, quibus mulieres istam visionem ac resurrectionem Domini nunciant, saltim attoniti legantur, dubium tamen nullum est, quin piae hae mulieres ac quibus nihil aequè iucundum esse poterat, quàm dulcissimi Salvatoris resurrectio, utpote in qua cardo nostrae salutis versatur, vehementer gavisae fuerint, percepto laeto isto nuncio de Christi resurrectione.) *

## 28:9
* [v. 6. He meets them. Grotius establishes at this place a synecdoche or an enallage of number, since this vision was made only to Mary Magdalene: he believes, however, that this is the same appearance as that which is described in Mark 16, 9. and John 20, 17.. But the circumstances testify to the contrary. Whence there is no need to establish an enallage here.) *

* (v. 9. They held his feet. Christ permitted this so that the women might clearly perceive that he had truly risen: but he did not want to be touched by Mary, John 20, 17., because she had already been sufficiently taught about the truth of the resurrection. Thus, therefore, she wanted to touch or rather to retain him, so that he would be perpetually with her in these lands as an earthly King, which was a false persuasion. This opinion pleases H. Grotius, and also Mr. D. Friedlieb, p. 218. Others explain the passage in John 20. in such a way that Christ wanted Mary to carry the joyful message about his resurrection to the dismayed disciples more quickly, with no delay interposed, and not to weave delays by touching and embracing him, since there would be no lack of time to deal with him at greater length. Which opinion appeals to our own blessed D. Calixtus, Harmony of the Gospels, p. 413, and among the Papists to Suarez, Bagnasius, and others.) * The women held the feet of Jesus, moreover, out of reverence and love. Conf. 2 Kings 4:27John 20:17. From this, Corn. à Lapide seeks patronage in this place for that ridiculous custom by which at Rome they are ordered to kiss the feet of the Roman Pontiff. For after he had mentioned how the Magdalene had kissed the feet of Christ, and likewise how the Shunammite had grasped the feet of Elisha, he adds: Thus the faithful embrace and kiss the feet of the Pontiff, just as they do those of men illustrious for holiness. But it is a mere pretext of the Jesuit that the feet or shoes of the Pontiff are kissed at least in the same way as those of some other man illustrious for holiness. Nay, rather, other Papists candidly profess that kisses are fixed to the feet of the Roman Pontiff because he holds the place of Christ on earth; since they teach that this honor belongs to no one except the Roman Pontiff alone, it is clear that they by no means kiss the feet of the Roman Pontiff in the same way as those of some other holy man. Joseph Stephanus Valentinus expressly states in De Oscul. pedum R. P. c. 9: The Pontiff sustains the person of Christ, therefore he receives the kisses of the feet in his stead. But if the honor that belongs to Christ must also be shown to his feigned vicar, that is, the Roman Pontiff, why do they not also expressly admit that he ought to be adored, just as the women are read to have adored Christ here, namely with latria, as Corn. à Lapide rightly explains? Furthermore, the Saxon Theologians discuss that pride of the Roman Pontiff at greater length in Fundam. Defens. Pupillae, likewise B. Par. Conf. Cathol. book 2, Spec. part 1, art. 3, App. p. 955 seqq.) *

* (They adored. Christ is to be adored not only according to his divine nature, but also according to his human nature, see John 1:14Jer. 23 and 33; yet 1. the human nature of Christ, or his flesh, is not adored φύσει, but by reason of the hypostatic ἑνώσει. 2. observe that the divine and human nature of Christ are adored with one adoration. Conf. many things pertaining to this in B. D. Chemnit. book on the two natures in Christ c. 24, p. 135, 146, c. 25, p. 140, 141, c. 39.

p. 170, 171, 172, likewise LL. Theol. part 1, p. 78, B. Par. Confess. Cath. book 2, Spec. part 1, art. 2, c. 1, §. 5.) *

Latin:

* [v. 6. Occurrit illis. Statuit h. l. Grotius synecdochen sive numeri enallagen, cùm soli Mariae Magdalenae visio haec facta sit: censet verò eandem hanc esse apparitionem cum eâ, quae Marc. 16, 9. ac Ioh. 20, 17. describitur. Verùm circumstantiae contrarium testantur. Unde nec opus, enallagen hîc statuere) *

* (v. 9. Tenuerunt pedes eius. Permisit hoc Christus, ut mulieres evidenter perspicerent, ipsum verè resurrexisse: â Maria verò tangi noluit, Ioh. 20. 17. quia iamtum de veritate resurrectionis satis illa erat edocta. Ita igitur tangere vel potiùs retinere volebat, ut perpetuò cum ipsa in his terris tanquam Rex terrenus esset, quae falsa erat persvasio. Placet haec sententia H. Grotio, it. Dn. D. Friedlieb p. 218. Alii ita locum Ioh. 20. exponunt, quòd Christus voluerit, ut Maria ocyus, nullâ interpofitâ morâ laetum de resurrectione suâ nuncium ad consternatos discipulos perferat, nec ipsum tangendo & amplectendo moras nectat, cùm tempus cum eo pluribus agendi non sit defuturum. Quae sententia arridet è nostratibus B. D. Calixto Concord. Ev. p. 413. è Pontificiis Svarezio, Bagnasio, aliis. Tenuerunt autē mulieres pedes Iesu ex reverentiâ & amore. Conf. 2. Reg. 4, 27.Ioh. 20, 17. Patrocinium hinc, quaerit Corn. à Lapide h. l. ridiculae illi consvetudini, quâ Romi petae Pontificis Romani pedes osculari iubentur. Postquam enim memorasset, quomodo Magdalena Christi pedes fuerit osculata, it. quomodo Sunamitis apprehenderit pedes Elisaei, subiungit: Sic fideles amplectuntur & osculantur pedes Pontificis, aequè ac Virorum sanctitate illustrium. At merus praetextus Iesuitae est, quòd eo saltem modo Pontificis pedes sive calceos osculentur, quo alterius cuiusdam viri, sanctitate illustris. Imò potiùs ideò Pontificis Romani pediba oscula figi, alii Pontificii candidè profitentur, quòd Christi in terris viees gerat, quem honorem cùm nulli praeterquam soli P. R. competere doceant, patet, quòd minimè ita Pontificis Romani pedes osculentur, uti alterius cuiusdam sancti viri. Disertè Iosephus Stephanus Valentinus de Oscul. pedum R. P. c. 9. Pontifex Christi personam sustinet, ideo eius vice oscula pedum excipit. At si honor, qui Christo competit, etiam ficto eius vicario h. e. P. R. exhibendus, cur non etiam expressè fatentur, quòd adorari debeat, sicut Christum hîc mulieres adorasse, puta latriâ, uti rectè explicat Corn. à Lapide, leguntur. Coeterùm de fastu illo P. R. prolixiùs disserunt Dnn. Theologi Saxonici in Fundam. Defens. Pupillae, item B. Par. Conf. Cathol. l. 2. Spec. part. 1. art. 3. App. p. 955. seqq.) *

* (Adorarunt. Non solùm secundùm divinam, verùm etiam secundùm humanam naturam Christus adorandus est, vid. Ioh 1, 14.Ier. 23. ac 33. neque tamen 1. humana Christi natura s. caro adoratur φύσει, fed ex hypostat. ἑνώσει. 2. observ. quòd unâ adoratione div. ac humana Christi natura adorētur. Conf. plurima huc facientia apud B. D. Chemnit. lib. de duaus naturis in Christo c. 24. p. 135. 146. c. 25. p. 140. 141. c. 39.

p. 170. 171. 172. it. LL. Theol. part. 1. p. 78. B. Par. Confess. Cath. lib. 2. Spec. part. 1. art. 2. c. 1. §. 5.) *

## 28:10
* (v. 10. Go tell. The Jesuit Corn. à Lapide notes on this place, that Luther wrongly gathers from this saying of Christ, that it is permitted for women to preach: he adds: it is one thing to tell, another to preach. Resp. 1. We ourselves know well that there is a great difference between these. 2. Nor does that same thing escape Luther. But it is false 3. that the Blessed Luther either gathered from this saying, or ever even taught, that it is permitted for women to preach. Nay, rather he urged with the Apostle, that women should keep silence in the Church, as is evident from his book on the abuses of the Mass & his Commentary on the Epistle of Peter. But as to what he writes in t. 2. Ienens. Germ. fol. 14. 6. & page 316. a., it is better that in the lack of men even women should teach the word of GOD, than that it should be altogether silent, there he distinguishes between the public and ordinary proclamation of the word, which pertains to the Ecclesiastical Ministry, and the private instruction of a family or youth, the consolation of the sick etc. as the Blessed Pareus shows at greater length in his Confess. Cathol. lib. 2. spec. part. 2. art. 6. p. 201.) *

* (To my brethren. See Ps. 22, 22.Job 20, 17.Heb. 2, 11.Rom. 8, 29.) *

Latin:

* (v. 10. Nunciate. Annotat ad h. l. Iesuita Corn. â Lapide, perperam exhoc dicto Christi colligere Lutherum, foeminis quolicere concionari: addit: aliud est nunciare, aliud concionari. Resp. 1. Ipsimet probè novimus, quòd magnum inter haec discrimen sit. 2. nec fugit id ipsum Lutherum. Falsum autem est 3. quòd B. Lutherus vel ex hoc dicto collegerit, vel unquam etiam docuerint, foeminis licere concionari. Imò potiùs ursit cum Apostolo, ut mulieres in Ecclesiâ taceant, ceu patet ex lib. de abus. Miss. & Comment in Post. Petri. Quod vero t. 2. Ienens. Germ. fol. 14. 6. & pag. 316. a. scribit, praestare, ut in defectu virorum etiam foeminae doceant verbum DEI, quam ut illud prorsus taceatur, ibi dist. inter publicum & ordinarium verbi praeconium, quod ad Ministerium Ecclesiasticum spectat, & inter privatam familiae vel iuventutis informationem, aegrotorum consolationem &c. uti pluribus ostendit B. Parens Confess. Cathol. lib. 2. spec. part. 2. art. 6. p. 201.) *

* (Fratribus meis. Vid. Ps. 22, 22.Iob. 20, 17.Ebr. 2, 11.Rom. 8, 29.) *

## 28:11
* (v. 11. πορευοωμεύν αὐτῶν &c. Since it is hardly credible that the guards waited at the sepulcher while the women approached, but rather that as soon as the earthquake happened, they were struck with terror and fled into the city, thence ἐλθόντες & ἀπήγγειλαν seems to be rendered more correctly in the pluperfect, they had come, and had reported, than in the perfect.) *

Latin:

* (v. 11. πορευοωμεύν αὐτῶν &c. Cùm vix credibile sit, expectasse apud sepulcrum custodes, dum mulieres accesserunt, quinstatim ac terrae contigit motus, terrore perculsos in civitatem perfugisse, inde ἐλθόντες & ἀπήγγειλαν rectiù in plus quam perfecto, vener ant, & renunciaver ant, reddi videtur, quàm in perfecto.) *

## 28:12
* (v. 12. They gave money to the soldiers. Well Chrysost. on this place, They who had bought the blood of the living one, him who was of the resurrection of the crucified and revived one, again stifle the report through money. For they corrupt with money the guards, who were witnesses of the truth, so that they might become the architects of a lie and of falsehood.) *

Latin:

* (v. 12. Pecuniam dederunt militibus. Benè Chrysost. in h. l. Qui viventis sanguinem emerant, eum qui de resurrectione erat crucifixi & redivivi, rursus per pecunias sermonem suffocant. Corumpunt quippe pecuniâ custodes, qui testes erant veritatis, ut fiant architecti mendacii ac falsitatis.) *

## 28:13
* (v. 13. They came by night and stole him, while we were sleeping. Behold the blindness of the Priests! for, as Remigius rightly says, if the guards were sleeping, how did they see the deed? and no less gravely Augustine in Ps. 63. you produce sleeping witnesses. Truly then you yourself were asleep, you who did such things by searching. See also the bloody counsels. For not content with having killed the master, they also strive to destroy the disciples, as Severianus has in the Catena. intending indeed this, that Pilate might decree capital punishment for them, as for thieves. But happy were the disciples in that theft, unhappy on the contrary were the guards and Priests in their lie. For the soldiers clearly lost [Christ], the Jews destroyed him: but the Disciples took up their Master not by theft, but by faith; by virtue, not by fraud; by holiness, not by crime; living, not dead, Severianus writes skillfully in the said place.) *

Latin:

* (v. 13. Noctu venerunt & furati sunt eum, nobis dormientibus. En coecitatem Sacerdotum! nam, ut rectè Remigius, si custodes dormierunt, quomodo factum viderunt? nec minùs graviter Augustinus in Ps. 63.dormientes testes adhibes. Verè tum ipse obdormisti, qui scrutando talia fecisti. Vide quoque sanguinolenta consilia. Etenim non contenti interfeeisse magistrum, discipulos etiam perdere moliuntur, ut habet Severianus in Catenâ. hoc quippe intendentes, ut Pilatus iis, ceu furibus capitale supplicium constituat. Felices verò discipulos isto furto, infelices contra vigiles ac Sacerdotes suo mendacio. Etenim planè amiserunt [Christum] milites, perdiderunt Iudaei: sed Discipuli Magistrum suum non furto, sed fide; virtute, non fraude; sanctitate, non crimine; vivum, non mortuum sustulerunt, scitè scribit Severianus d. l.

## 28:15
* (v. 15. Among the Jews. But the Great Sanhedrin tried to persuade others of this fabrication to such an extent that, as Justin testifies, it sent an embassy to the Jews of the whole world, which would report concerning this theft of the disciples. H. Grotius deduces this at greater length in this place, who nevertheless adds that those words of the Evangelist, καὶ διεφημίσθη ὁλόγος &c., can also be understood concerning that wicked trafficking of a lie between the priests and the soldiers, which could by no means be so concealed that the truth would not find some crack through which it might emanate into the public. And that this very thing was a certain beginning of the conversion of many to Christ. He himself, however, prefers the former opinion to the latter. But this is noted, τὸ among the Jews, is added. For what, as Severianus speaks skillfully, a Jew obscured in Judea with gold; it shone forth in the whole world by faith. Indeed, very many of the Jews themselves, converted namely through the sermons of the Apostles, agreed with that lie of the guards, and derogated all faith from it. What of the fact that Josephus the Jewish historiographer, such also by race and religion, himself confirms the resurrection of Christ with his own calculation, as is evident from book 18, Antiquities of the Jews, chapter 4.) *

Latin:

* (v. 15. Apud Iudaeos. In tantum verò Synedrium Magnum figmentum hoc aliis persvadere conabatur, ut, teste Iustino, ad totius orbis Iudaeos legationem miserit, quae de furto isto discipulorum referret. Pluribus hoc deducit H. Grotius in h. locum qui tamen addit, posse etiam verba illa Evangelistae, καὶ διεφημίσθη ὁλόγος &c. accipi de sceleratâ istâ inter Sacerdotes & milites mendacii nundinatione, quae minimè ita celari potuerit, ut non rimam aliquam inveniret veritas, per quam in publicum emanaret. Atq; hoc ipsum initium quoddam fuisse multorum ad Christum conversionis. Ipse tamen priorem sententiam posteriori praefert. Notanter autem hoc, τὸapud Iudaeos, additur. Quod enim, ut scitè loquitur Severianus, in Iudaea Iudaeus obscurabat auro; fide toto claruit in mundo. Quin ex ipsis Iudaeis plurimi, conversi nempe per Apostolorum conciones, mendacio isti custodum condixerunt, omnemq; fidem illi derogarunt. Quid quòd Iosephus Historiographus Iudaeus, gente quoq; ac religione talis, ipsemet Christi resurrectionem calculo suo confirmet, ceu patet ex. l. 18. A. I. C. 4.) *

## 28:16
* (v. 16. ἕνδεκαι Grotius adds, that mention is made of eleven at least, because Judas had withdrawn himself from the sacred fellowship because of a wicked conscience. And yet Judas by that time, when he saw that Christ was condemned to death, had hanged himself with a noose, above chapter 27, 5. The things which the same Grotius brought forward to the contrary part at the said place have an easy explanation, as has been shown elsewhere.) *

Into the mountain, where Jesus had appointed for them. Euthymius thinks, that Christ had assigned the mountain before his death, or had signified it to the Apostles through the women. * (conf. above c. 29. 32. item this chapter v. 10. Marc. 14, 28.c. 16. 17) * This apparition was most famous, and common to all, therefore it was necessary for the place to be known, where they were to assemble. It is most famous, because without a doubt it was that, of which 1. Cor. 15, 6. He was seen by more than five hundred brethren at once. Soarius, Bishop of Coimbra, who explored the holy places of Jerusalem, Marc. 16. It is not to be understood that he would proceed into the province of Galilee but into the mountain, which is near the Mount of Olives. For when one comes into the valley of Josaphat, there are three preeminent mountains, the Mount of Olives, in the middle, preeminent over the others, the mountain of Galilee, and another mountain to the right of the Mount of Olives. On the mountain of Galilee the Galileans made a large house for staying, when they had come to Jerusalem for the sake of business: Whence the Mountain is called of Galilee, to this present day. To this Mountain the Lord predicted that he would go before the Apostles. But this opinion is repugnant to the words of the Evangelist: The disciples went into Galilee, into the mountain, where Jesus had appointed for them &c. They went into the province of Galilee, and into the mountain of the same province. * (Cornelius à Lapide agrees, who notably adds: For to that Galilee by the command of Christ were all the disciples called together, whom he had very many in Galilee, because there they were safer from the hatreds and persecution of the Jews, than in Judea. he brings forward for this opinion Chrysostom and Euthymius.) * Most establish that it was Mount Tabor. He had shown the likeness of his resurrection on it while still mortal: now already immortal he reveals the resurrection itself and immortality. * (Lyranus, Dionysius the Carthusian, Bonaventure, Jansenius accept it as being about Mount Tabor. Cornelius à Lapide, who nevertheless thinks that Maldonatus and others probably establish that those things which are mentioned in v. 16 and 17 were done and said on Mount Tabor; but those things which are appended in v. 18, 19, 20 pertain to the last apparition, which was made on the Mount of Olives, when he ascended glorious from it into heaven. The same is established from the Calvinists by Danaeus against D. Chemnitius p. 199.) *

Latin:

* (v. 16. ἕνδεκαι Addit Grotius, propterea undecim saltim fieri mentionem, quòd Iudas se abstituerit â sacro consortio obsceleris conscientiam. Atqui Iudas iamtum, quum vidit, Christum ad mortem condemnatum, laqueo se suspenderat, suprà c. 27, 5. quae in contrariam partem idem Grotius ad d. l. attulit, facilem habent explicationem, ut alibi ostensum.) *

In montem, ubi constituer at illis Iesus. Euthymius putat, Christum ante mortem montem assignasse, vel per mulieres Apostolis significasse. * (conf. suprà c. 29. 32. it. hoc cap. v. 10. Marc. 14, 28.c. 16. 17) * Haec apparitio fuit celeberrima, & omnibus communis, oportebat ergò locum sciri, quo erant conventuri. Celeberrima est, quia procul dubio fuit ea, de quâ 1. Cor. 15, 6.Visus est plusquam quingentis fratribus simul. Soarius, Episcopus conimbricensis, qui loca sancta Ierusalem exploravit, Marc. 16.Non est accipiendum, in Galilaeam provinciam processurum sed in montem, qui vicinus est monti Oliveti. Cùm enim venitur in vallem Iosaphat, sunt tres praeeminentes montes, mons sc Oliveti, in medio, coeteris praeminens, mons Galilaeae, & alter mons à dextris montis Oliveti. In monte Galiaeae fecerunt Galiaei domum amplam ad permanendum, quando Ierusalem negotiorum causâ venissent: Unde Mons dicitur Galilaeae, usin hodiernum diem. Ad hunc Montem Dominus praedixit se praeventurum Apostolos. Sed repugnat haec opinio verbis Evangelistae: Discipuli abierunt in Galilaeam, in montem, ubi constituerat illis Iesus &c. Abierunt in Galilaeam provinciam, & in montem eiusdem provinciae. * (Consentit Corn. à Lapide, qui notanter adiicit: Nam ad eam Galilaeam ex Christi praecepto convocati sunt omnes discipuli. quos plurimos habebat in Galilaea, quia ibi tutiores erant ab odiis & persecutione Iudaeorum, quàm in Iudaeà. adducit pro hâc sententiâ Chrysost. & Euthymium.) * Plerique statuunt, suisse Montem Thabor. Resurrectionis suae similitudinem in eo ostenderat adhuc mortalis: nunc iam immortalis resurrectionem ipsam & immortalitatem patefacit. * (De Monte Thabor accipiunt Lyranus, Dionysius Carthusianus, Bonavent. Iansenius. Corn. à Lapide, qui tamen existimat, probabiliter statuere Maldonatum & alios, quòd ea quae v. 16. & 17. memoratur, facta & dicta sint in monte Thabor; quae verò v. 18. 19. 20. subnectuntur, pertineant ad ultimam apparitionem, quae facta sit in monte Oliveti, cùm ex eo gloriosus in coelum adscendit. Idem statuit ex Calvinianis Danaeus contra D. Chemnitium p. 199.) *

## 28:17
* (v. 17. They worshipped him. The discourse is about worship properly so called, and thus an argument for the true Deity of Christ is rightly sought from here. Conf. Psal. 72, 11. and Psalm. 97, 7. collated with Ebr. 1, 6., adding above c. 2, 11. c. 8, 25. c. 14, 13. c. 15, 22., and B. Par. deduces this very thing in many places, Coll. Isag. L. de Pers. & Off. Christi c. 12. §. 72. Dn. D. Calovius in Theol. Nat. & Rev. p. 71. seqq.)

v. 17. For some doubted. (This reading seems suspicious to Beza, since it is not probable that the Apostles, who saw Christ alive, could have doubted his resurrection. He conjectures, therefore, that it ought to be read: οὐδὲ ἐδέςασαν. Nor did they doubt. But since not only all Greek Codices, but also the Oriental Interpreters, the Syrian, Arab, Ethiopian, and Persian, oppose this conjecture, it is better to retain the received reading.) Furthermore, it is not necessary to establish that these were from the number of the Apostles, since it can be understood of others who were present at the apparition and then first saw Christ. (for it seemed absurd to their reason that he, who a little before had been atrociously crucified and died, had risen from the dead.) It can also be understood of the doubt of the Apostles themselves before this apparition. They doubted, not on the mountain, but previously in Jerusalem. He speaks especially of Thomas, who doubted greatly. (Thus Theophylact understands it in this place, whom Barradius, Franc. Lucas Brugensis, and Grotius follow, who nevertheless not inconveniently advises that, since an indefinite time admits various meanings according to the circumstance of place, τὸ ἐδίστασαν can be translated: but some had doubted. Although only Thomas is read to have doubted concerning Christ's resurrection, this nevertheless detracts nothing from the Evangelist's discourse, since his words can be understood through an enallage of number, most customary in the H. S. Concerning which above at c. 26. 8. Otherwise, there is no doubt that the demonstrative article in this place ought to be explained by the distributive τιὲς but some. Just as the Syrian also sufficiently indicates, translating and of them, namely some. The Arab also explicitly and a part of them, or even some of them doubted. Similarly the Persian: and a part of them, or some of them doubted. Nor otherwise the author of the Hebrew version of Matthew, edited by Munster. וקצת הפתסקו & some or some have doubted. The Ethiopian, however, pays less attention to this. For he renders this little verse thus: & they saw, & they worshipped, & they doubted. *

Latin:

* (v. 17. Adorarunt eum. Sermo est de adoratione propriè sic dicta, adeoque rectè hinc argumentum pro vera Christi Deitate petitur. Conf. Psal. 72, 11. ac Psalm. 97, 7. coll. cum Ebr. 1, 6. add. suprà c. 2, 11. c. 8, 25. c. 14, 13. c. 15, 22. pluribusque hoc ipsum deducit B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. de Pers. & Off. Christi c. 12. §. 72. Dn. D. Calovius in Theol. Nat. & Rev. p. 71. seqq.) *

v. 17. Quidam enim dubitaverunt. * (Suspecta videtur Bezae haec lectio, cùm non sit probabile, Apostolos, qui Christum vivum viderunt, de eius resurrectione dubitare potuisse. Coniicit igitur, legi deberi: οὐδὲ ἐδέςασαν. Neque dubitarunt. Verùm cùm coniecturae huic repugnent non solùm omnes Codd. Graeci, verùm etiam Interpp. Orientales, Syrus, Arabs, Aethiops ac Persa, satiùs est, receptam lectionem retinere) * Praeterea nec necesse est, statuere, quòd hi fuerint ex numero Apostolorum, cùm possit accipi de aliis, qui apparitioni interfuerunt, & tunc primùm Christum viderunt. * (videbatur enim rationi eorum absurdum, eum, qui paullò ante atrociter crucifixus ac mortuus erat, è mortuis resurrexisse.) * Potest etiam accipi de dubitatione ipsorum Apostolorum ante hanc apparitionem. Dubitaverunt, non in monre, sed antea in Ierusalem. Loquitur cumprimis de Thoma, qui valde dubitavit. * (Ita accipit Theophylactus in h. l. quem sequuntur Barradius, Franc. Lucas Brugensis, Grotius, qui tameo non incommodè monet, quòd cùm indefinitum tempus pro circumstantiâ loci varias significationes admittat, τὸ ἐδίστασαν verti posse: quidam verò addubitaverant. Licet verò solus Thomus de Christi resurrectione dubitasse legatur, nihil tamen hoc derogat Evangelistae sermoni, cùm verba eius possint accipi per enallagen numeri, in Sc. S. usitatissimam. De quâ suprà ad c. 26. 8. Coeterùm non est dubium, quin articulus demonstrativus h. l. exponi debeat per distributivum τιὲςquidam verò. Quemadmodum etiam Syrus satis indicat, v-rtens & ex iis. sc. quidam. Arabs quoque disertè & pars eorum, vel etiam aliquis eorum dubitavit. Similiter Persa: & pars eorum, sive quidam ex illis dubitarunt. Nec aliter autor versionis Matthaei Ebraicae, à Munstero editae וקצת הפתסקו& pars seu quidam dubitarunt. Aethiops tamen minùs hoc attendit. Ita enim versiculum hunc reddit: & viderunt, & adorarunt, & dubitaverunt.) *

## 28:18
* (v. 18. All power is given unto me &c. It is customary for this passage to be proven by the Orthodox, that power was given to Christ as man both through the grace of personal union and through exaltation to omnipotence. The Calvinists object, that a distinction must be made between ἐξουσίαν, & δύναυιν. See Wendelinus Exerc. 56. §. 1. et seqq. But it must be observed that ἐξουσία that Luc. 22, 69. is called δύναμις θεοῦ. Now indeed ἐξουσία and δύναμις in God differ not at all. See Gen. 27, 7. Matth. 11, 24. and let there be noted besides the places Ps. 8, 5. et seqq. Dan. 7, 13. 14. Ioh. 5, 27. c. 17, 2. Actor. 10, 36. 1. Cor. 15, 26. 27. Ephes. 1, 20. 21. 22. Philipp. 2, 10. et seqq. Ebr. 2, 8. Apoc. 5, 12. c. 17, 14. It is added that δύναμις divine power is also attributed to Christ Luc. 4, 36. c. 6, 19. c. 9, 1. c. 12. 69. and that the words are added: in heaven & in earth, which is a description of divine power, as is evident from 1. Paral. 29, 11. Ps. 103, 19. above c. 11, 25. The sayings of the Fathers, and indeed of their very Adversaries, confirming this same thing are brought forward by the Saxon Theologians in Fundam. Pupillae Defensione p. 421. 422. B. D. Chemnitius lib. de duabus naturis in Christo c. 25. B. Par. L. de Pers. Christi §. 105. Exeg. L. de Pers. & Off. Chr. §. 214. Confess. Cath. l. 2. spec. art. 2. s. 1. §. 3. Add. B. D. Mentzer. contra Matth. Martinium, B. D. Mylius part. 1. in A. C. p. 64. 77. and others. Since therefore according to the divine nature Christ could have received no glory or power in time, conf. Ioh. 5, 26. it is manifest that those things which Christ received in time, and therefore of which He speaks here, must be understood as given to Christ according to the human nature. See Dan. 7, 14. Ioh. 17, 1. et seqq. For to God in time nothing can be given by which He might be perfected. Nor do we deny, however, that some of the ancients, such as Athanasius Orat. 40. contra Arianos, Nazianzen. Orat. de Filio, Cyrillus lib. 1. Thesauri c. 1. accommodate this passage to the eternal generation. But this we say, that it is more fitting to the text to understand it of things given in time, which giving is done according to the human nature. Some of the Calvinists, such as Camero Myroth. Evang. p. 227. &c. object, that this was given to the person of the Mediator. But the primitive Doctors of the Church have rightly taught the contrary, expressly warning that Christ received all things according to the human nature, that is, personally. Note Theophylactus in c. 3. Ioh. He gave all things into the hands of the Son, according to his humanity. Cyril, book 2, on John ch. 140. Insofar as he is God, he has this power naturally, but insofar as he was made man, he openly professed that he had received this power. Confer also Basil the Great, book 4, against Eunomius. St. Athanasius, discoursing on the saving advent of Christ: But if, he writes, you hear Peter speaking, 'God made this same Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ': of what do you understand this word 'made'? If of the divinity of the Word, why then do you rebuke the Arians? Since you hold the same opinion as they do. But if of the form of a servant, which was in the Word, why do you strive to fight with us? And from this it is also clear that the Jews, see R. Isaac, no. 27, foolishly strive to undermine the deity of Christ from this passage, in that he finally received certain things in time, when they ought entirely to distinguish between the divine and the human nature of Christ. Although that divine power was not indeed given to Christ the man only after the resurrection, but fell to him at the very moment of the incarnation or hypostatic union: yet it is rightly said to be given after the resurrection, namely with respect to the plenary usurpation, by which he had emptied himself in the state of humiliation, so that he could suffer and die. Conf. B. Par. Dispp. Elencht. on the Sunday Gospels, pages 1092, 1093. Homil. Acad. part 2, p. 402. B. D. Fewrborn. in Κενωσιγρ. sect. 4, p. 220. item in AntiOstorodo Disp. 3, §. 24, 25, 26, p. 210, and others.) *

* (In heaven. Conf. Acts 2, 23. Eph. 1, 10. Col. 1, 16. Phil. 1, 10. Heb. 1, 4. Add entirely B. D. Feurb. in Κενωσιγρ. Sect. 7, p. 151.) *

Latin:

* (v. 18. Data est mihi omnis potestas &c. Solet ex h. l. ab Orthodoxis probari, datam esse Christo homini tum per gratiam unionis personalis, tum per exaltationem omnipotentiam. Excipiunt Calviniani, distinguendum esse interἐξουσίαν,&δύναυιν. Vid. Wendelinus Exerc. 56. §. 1. seqq. Sed observandum, quòd ἐξουσία ista Luc. 22, 69. appelletur δύναμις θεοῦ. Iam verò ἐξουσία & δύναμις in Deo minimè differunt. Vid. Gen. 27, 7.Matth. 11, 24. ac notentur praeterea loca Ps. 8, 5. seqq. Dan. 7, 13. 14.Ioh. 5, 27.c. 17, 2.Actor. 10, 36.1. Cor. 15, 26. 27.Ephes. 1, 20. 21. 22.Philipp. 2, 10. seqq. Ebr. 2, 8.Apoc. 5, 12.c. 17, 14. Accedit, quòd δύναμις quoque divina Christo tribuitur Luc. 4, 36.c. 6, 19.c. 9, 1.c. 12. 69. quòdque addantur verba: in coelo & in terra, quae divinae potentiae descriptio est, ceu ex 1. Paral. 29, 11. Ps. 103, 19. suprà c. 11, 25. patet. Dicta Patrum, quin ipsorum etiam Adversariorum, idem hoc confirmantia adducūt, Dnn. Theologi Saxonici in Fundam. Pupillae Defensione p. 421. 422. B. D. Chemnitius lib. de duabus naturis in Christo c. 25. B. Par. L. de Pers. Christi §. 105. Exeg. L. de Pers. & Off. Chr. §. 214. Confess. Cath. l. 2. spec. art. 2. s. 1. §. 3. Add. B. D. Mentzer. contra Matth. Martinium, B. D. Mylius part. 1. in A. C. p. 64. 77. alii. Cùm igitur secundùm divin. naturam nihil gloriae vel potestatis potuerit Christus in tempore accipere, conf. Ioh. 5, 26. manifestum est, quòd ea, quae Christus in tempre accepit, adeoq; de quibus hâc loquitur, secundùm humanam naturam Christo data intelligi debeat. Vid. Dan. 7, 14.Ioh. 17, 1. seqq. Deo n. in tempore nihil potest dari, quo perficiatur. Neque tamen imus inficias, quòd veterum nonnulli, uti Athanasius Orat. 40. contra Arianos, Nazianzen. Orat. de Filio, Cyrillus lib. 1. Thesauri c. 1. ad aeternam generationem h. l. accommodent. Hoc verò dicimus, quòd textui magis conveniat, de datis in tempore accipere, quae secundùm human. naturam datio factio. Nonnulli è Calvinianis, uti Camero Myroth. Evang. p. 227. &c. excipiunt, quòd personae Mediatoris haec data sit. Verùm contrarium recte docuerunt primitivae Dd. Ecclesiae, disertè monentes, quòd secundùm humanam naturam Christus omnia acceperit, puta personaliter. Notanter Theophylactus in c. 3. Ioh. Omnia dedit in manus Filii, iuxta humanitatem. Cyrillus l. 2. in Ioh. c. 140.In quantum Deus, hanc potestatem naturaliter habet, in quantum autem homo factus est, accepisse se hanc potestatem, a pertè professus est. Confer quoque Basilium M. l. 4. contra Eunomium. S. Athanasius disserens de salutari Christi adventu: Quod si, scribit, audieritis Petrum loquentem, Christum & Dominum fecit hunc ipsum Iesum, quem vos crucifixistis: de quo hoc vocabulum fecit, intelligitis? Si de Verbi divinitate, cur Arianos igitur reprehenditis? Cùm idem cum illis sentiatis. Sin de forma servi, quae fuit in Verbo, cur nobiscum pugnare contenditis? Atque hinc patet quoque, quòd iudaei, vid. R. Isaac. n. 27. ineptè ex h. l. Christi deitatem, eò quòd in tempore demum quaedam acceperit, labefactare satagant, cùm omninò distinguere deberentinter divinam, ac humanam Christi naturam. Licet verò non demum post resurrectionem potestas illa divina Christo homini data sit, sed in ipso incarnationis sive unitionis hypostaticae momento ei obtigerit: data tamen post resurrectionem rectè illa dicitur, puta respectu plenariae usurpationis, quâ sese in statu exinanitionis evacuaverat, ut pati ac mori posset. Conf. B. Par. Dispp. Elencht. super Evang. Domin. pag. 1092. 1093. Homil. Acad. part. 2. p. 402. B. D. Fewrborn. in Κενωσιγρ. sect. 4. p. 220. it. in AntiOstorodo Disp. 3. §. 24. 25. 26. p. 210. alii.) *

* (In coelo. Conf. Actor. 2, 23.Ephes. 1, 10.Col. 1, 16.Philipp. 1. 10.Ebr. 1, 4. Adde omninò B. D. Feurb. in Κενωσιγρ. Sect. 7. p. 151.) *

## 28:19
* (v. 10. Teach etc. Because this is accomplished not only by preaching, but also by writing, for the Apostles had to teach the nations not only of the present, but also of the future time, it is clear that they themselves also received the command to write. This the Papists impudently deny. See Bellarmine, book 4.

on the Word of God, ch. 4. W. Lindanus, book 1 of the Panoplia, ch. 23, Franc. Costerus in Enchir. Controv. page 43, against whom B. Par. argues at length, Exeg. Loc. 1, §. 23, following, item Confess. Cathol. book 2, Spec. part 1, art. 1, ch. 4, §. 2. Laur. Laelius on the Word of God, in the preface. Add also Rivetus in Isagog. to the Holy Scriptures, ch. 24. Notably Augustine, book 1, on the Harmony of the Gospels, last chapter. Whatever (Christ) willed us to know concerning his deeds and words, he commanded to be written by the Apostles as if by his own hands. Which words Ederus himself, otherwise a most sharp defender of Papal errors, cites in book 3 of Oecon. Bibl. page 326. Let there also be added by all means Irenaeus book 3 against Heresies ch. 1. Nicephorus book 2 ch. 34. To this also pertains the observation of the author of the Manual of Curates, in which it is taught that preaching is done in one way in writing, as Paul wrote epistles to the Romans, Corinthians, etc.; in another way in deed, as every action of Christ is our instruction; in another way in word. Compare also Gabr. Biel in the Canon of the Mass lecture 71.) *

* (All nations. Compare Ps. 19, 5Marc. 16, 15.Luc. 24, 47.Actor. 17, 30.Rom. 10, 18.Col. 1, 6.28.2. Petr. 3, 9. Ambrose book 2 on the calling of the nations ch. 1. Was there by this command ( Matth. 28, 19.) any desertion of any nations or of any men? He deservedly excepted no one, separated no one by race, distinguished no one by condition. The Gospel of the cross was sent to absolutely all men, etc. Let the same be compared in the same place ch. 2, 5, 6. But let someone say, 1. If the Gospel ought to have been preached by all the Apostles to the nations, it seems less correctly done by Peter, that he himself, an agreement having been made, left the duty of preaching to the nations to Paul, while he himself preached at least among the Jews. I answer by distinguishing between the ordinary and extraordinary duty of preaching. Although Peter preached ordinarily and principally to the Jews, he did not however cease to preach to the nations at times, which thing was also done by Paul, as far as the Jews were concerned. 2. If the Apostles ought to have preached to all nations, and thus the calling and grace of GOD is universal, it follows that the Gospel ought also to have been preached to infants, indeed even to brutes, since Christ says: preach the Gospel to every creature. With this weapon Ioh. Piscator of Herborn strikes against our opinion on page 23 against Hemming. I answer: Although the audible word of the Gospel could not be preached to infants, that is, in such a way that through the hearing of the word they were converted to Christ and made partakers of eternal salvation: yet the Gospel was preached to them through the visible word, that is, they were baptized in the name of the F. S. and H. S. and thus regenerated, Compare Ioh. 3, 5.Tit. 3, 5. As far as the instance concerning brutes pertains, it is worthy of laughter and pity rather than refutation. For who does not see that Christ speaks explicitly, and that the Orthodox receive his words, only concerning rational creatures, that is, those who are capable of the benefits to be conferred through the preaching of the Gospel, of which kind are only men, not brute animals. Nor indeed without cause do the Calvinists strive to cast shadows upon this most clear oracle, since the universality of the divine calling is excellently proven from here, and that GOD has excluded no one from salvation by some absolute decree of reprobation. They do indeed object against the present passage in various ways. But those evasions have long since been abundantly satisfied by our people. see B. D. Menzerus in the Disputations against Steinius and Crocius, B. D. Meisnerus in Anthropology, B. D. Hutterus in L. L. Mai. B. Par. Coll. Isag. L. on Reprobation, and others passim. Wendelin's various exceptions Exerc. 71. §. 6. Exerc. 73. §. 2. following, Exerc. 117. §. 11. 12. which it is not permitted to examine right now due to the shortness of time, will be discussed in order in the Analecta on Marc. 16, 15.) *

* ( μαθητεύσατε, teach. Beza, make disciples. so that in this way regard may be had for the Hebrew word תמלר noting, to make a disciple: since it was the office of the Apostles to lay the foundation of the Church, but of their successors to increase the Church by teaching, 1. Cor. 3, 10.Ephes. 2, 21. And hence from the beginning all believers were called μαθηταὶ disciples, that is of Christ, not of this or that Apostle, 1. Corinth. 3, 4. which disciples were afterwards first called Christians at Antioch, Acts 11, 26. Furthermore, Ignatius Loyola, having become a monk from a Spanish soldier, affecting a certain prerogative above other Christians, preferred with his followers to be called of the Society of JESUS, rather than either a disciple of Christ or a Christian. Truly not without an omen! for the men of that sect or society are not more companions and friends of Christ than Judas Iscariot and others, who in Holy Scripture. ἑταῖροι i. e. associates are called. see Matth. 20. v. 13.cap. 22, 12.cap. 26. 50. How much more rightly did Benedictus Arias Montanus, a Spanish Theologian, and one well-deserving of literary matters, having turned away from that ominous name, prefer to call himself (see the subscription in the Antwerp Interlinear Bibles,) i. e. disciple, rather than associate of that order, which even among the Papists themselves is everywhere ill-spoken of.) *

* (All nations How the Apostles executed this command of the Savior, B. D. Hutterus LL. Mai. page 871, B. D. Balduinus in his Commentary on the ep. to the Coloss. chap. 1. part. 1 q. 2, teach at length. Add the Dispp. Anti Wend. held under B. Par. as presiding officer, and others.)

* (baptize them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Basil the Great ep. 78. We ought to be baptized as we have received, to believe as we are baptized, and to glorify as we believe, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The principal argument for establishing the mystery of the H. Trinity is drawn from this.
